questions.question: A patient with severe combined presentation of chronic asthma poorly responsive to standard biologics undergoes bronchoalveolar lavage revealing predominantly neutrophilic rather than eosinophilic inflammation. Which treatment approach is most appropriate for this asthma phenotype?
questions.explanation: Neutrophilic asthma is generally less responsive to corticosteroids and eosinophil-targeted biologics, which are most effective in type 2, eosinophil-high inflammation. Macrolide antibiotics such as azithromycin have demonstrated anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory properties independent of their antimicrobial action, providing modest benefit in reducing exacerbations in this neutrophil-predominant phenotype.

Omalizumab is a monoclonal antibody that binds circulating free IgE, preventing it from attaching to FceRI receptors on mast cells and basophils. This reduces mast cell sensitization and subsequent degranulation upon allergen exposure. It is used in refractory allergic asthma and chronic idiopathic urticaria.
options: Blocking histamine H1 receptors on skin vessels
Binding free IgE to prevent mast cell activation
questions.question: A patient with chronic urticaria has poor symptom control despite maximal antihistamine dosing. Omalizumab is added to therapy. What is its mechanism?

questions.explanation: Midostaurin is a multi-kinase inhibitor that targets the mutated KIT D816V receptor found in the majority of systemic mastocytosis cases, which drives uncontrolled mast cell proliferation. By inhibiting this constitutively active kinase, the drug reduces mast cell burden and associated symptoms, offering targeted therapy beyond symptomatic mediator-blocking treatments.
options: Direct mast cell membrane stabilization only
Blockade of histamine H1 and H2 receptors
Inhibition of tryptase enzymatic activity directly
Complement pathway inhibition within mast cell tissue
Inhibition of the mutated KIT tyrosine kinase receptor
questions.question: A patient with confirmed systemic mastocytosis is prescribed midostaurin. What is the mechanism of this targeted therapy?

questions.explanation: Omalizumab binds free IgE, but clinical improvement in chronic urticaria typically develops over weeks because mast cell surface FceRI receptor density gradually decreases as free IgE levels fall. This progressive downregulation reduces the mast cell's capacity for degranulation over time, explaining the delayed but sustained therapeutic benefit compared to its rapid pharmacokinetic action.
questions.question: A patient with chronic spontaneous urticaria is started on omalizumab but requires several weeks before noticeable improvement. What explains this delayed onset of action?
options: Slow hepatic conversion to an active metabolite
Gradual downregulation of FceRI receptors on mast cells
Delayed renal excretion prolonging drug half-life
Progressive depletion of circulating complement proteins
Gradual desensitization of central histamine receptors

questions.explanation: Latex-fruit syndrome occurs because natural rubber latex shares structurally similar proteins, such as class I chitinases, with certain fruits including banana, avocado, kiwi, and chestnut. IgE antibodies formed against latex proteins can cross-react with these homologous food proteins, explaining why patients with latex allergy often also react to these specific fruits.
questions.question: A patient with an anaphylactic reaction to latex during surgery is later found to have prior allergic reactions to banana and avocado. What explains this cross-reactivity pattern?
options: Coincidental unrelated IgE sensitization to each allergen separately
Cross-reactive complement proteins shared across species
Common bacterial contamination present in all three sources
Shared histamine content naturally present in each substance
Shared structurally similar plant proteins between latex and these foods

questions.explanation: Aspirin acetylates serine-530 in the active site of cyclooxygenase, irreversibly inactivating the enzyme. This is unique among NSAIDs; others are competitive, reversible inhibitors. Since platelets lack nuclei and cannot synthesize new COX-1, aspirin's antiplatelet effect lasts the platelet's lifespan (7-10 days). This property makes low-dose aspirin useful for cardiovascular protection.
questions.question: Aspirin irreversibly inhibits cyclooxygenase by:

questions.explanation: Somatic hypermutation occurs in germinal centers of secondary lymphoid organs during B cell activation and proliferation. This process introduces point mutations in the variable regions of immunoglobulin genes, creating variants with different affinities for antigen. B cells producing higher-affinity antibodies are preferentially selected, leading to affinity maturation of the immune response.
questions.question: Somatic hypermutation of immunoglobulin genes occurs in which lymphoid structure?

options: Gut-selective blockade of alpha-4 beta-7 integrin
Systemic depletion of circulating T lymphocytes broadly
Nonselective blockade of tumor necrosis factor everywhere
Broad calcineurin inhibition affecting all tissues
Systemic interleukin-6 receptor blockade throughout the body
questions.explanation: Vedolizumab selectively blocks the alpha-4 beta-7 integrin, which mediates lymphocyte homing specifically to gut-associated lymphoid tissue, without significantly affecting immune surveillance elsewhere in the body. This gut-selective mechanism reduces intestinal inflammation in inflammatory bowel disease while minimizing the systemic immunosuppression seen with broader-acting biologic agents.
questions.question: A patient with severe combined chronic inflammatory bowel disease flares despite mesalamine therapy is started on vedolizumab. What distinguishes this biologic's mechanism from systemic immunosuppressants?
The major dose-limiting toxicity of cyclosporine is:
questions.explanation: Nephrotoxicity is the major dose-limiting toxicity of cyclosporine, manifesting as acute reversible renal dysfunction or chronic irreversible damage with prolonged use. The mechanism involves renal vasoconstriction and direct tubular toxicity. Regular monitoring of renal function and cyclosporine blood levels is essential. Other significant toxicities include hypertension, diabetes, neurotoxicity, and gum hyperplasia.

options: Histamine H1 receptor on bronchial smooth muscle
Beta-2 adrenergic receptor on airway smooth muscle
questions.question: A patient with asthma poorly controlled on inhaled corticosteroids is started on montelukast. What is the therapeutic target of this drug?
questions.explanation: Montelukast is a selective antagonist of the cysteinyl leukotriene receptor 1 (CysLT1), blocking the bronchoconstrictive and pro-inflammatory effects of LTC4, LTD4, and LTE4. It is used as add-on therapy in asthma, particularly for exercise-induced and aspirin-sensitive asthma. Unlike zileuton, it does not inhibit leukotriene synthesis itself.

options: Direct vasoconstriction mediated by NSAID binding to alpha receptors
Increased renin release from reduced angiotensin feedback
Direct cardiac inotropic stimulation by NSAID compounds
Sodium and fluid retention from reduced renal prostaglandin synthesis
questions.question: A patient with severe combined chronic inflammatory arthritis on long-term NSAID therapy develops new-onset hypertension. Which mechanism explains this NSAID-associated blood pressure elevation?
questions.explanation: NSAIDs inhibit renal prostaglandin synthesis, which normally promotes natriuresis and counteracts vasoconstrictive stimuli. Reduced prostaglandin activity leads to sodium and water retention and unopposed vasoconstriction, contributing to elevated blood pressure. This effect can also blunt the efficacy of antihypertensive medications, particularly diuretics and ACE inhibitors, in patients on chronic NSAID therapy.

Certain HLA alleles, such as HLA-B*58:01, are strongly associated with increased risk of severe cutaneous adverse reactions including Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis in patients taking allopurinol. Pre-treatment genetic screening in high-risk populations can identify susceptible individuals and guide safer alternative urate-lowering therapy selection.
options: It predicts increased risk of severe cutaneous adverse reactions
It predicts reduced drug efficacy in gout treatment
It confirms resistance to xanthine oxidase inhibition
It indicates need for higher starting drug doses
It predicts increased renal clearance of the drug
questions.question: A patient develops Stevens-Johnson syndrome after starting allopurinol. Genetic testing later reveals a specific HLA allele. What is the clinical relevance of identifying this allele before starting the drug?
Secondary immunodeficiency is most commonly caused by:
questions.explanation: Globally, malnutrition is the most common cause of secondary immunodeficiency, affecting both innate and adaptive immunity. Protein-energy malnutrition impairs cell-mediated immunity more than humoral immunity. Micronutrient deficiencies (zinc, vitamin A, iron) also compromise immune function. In developed countries, HIV infection, chemotherapy, and immunosuppressive therapy are more common causes.

questions.question: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis develops neutropenia and recurrent infections after starting tocilizumab. Which receptor does this drug block?
questions.explanation: Tocilizumab is a monoclonal antibody that blocks both membrane-bound and soluble interleukin-6 receptors, preventing IL-6 mediated signaling that drives synovial inflammation and acute-phase protein production in rheumatoid arthritis. Because IL-6 also supports normal hematopoiesis and neutrophil function, blockade can predispose patients to neutropenia and increased infection risk.

Adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency causes accumulation of toxic metabolites that kill developing lymphocytes, resulting in SCID with absent T and B cell function. Affected infants have severe opportunistic infections and failure to thrive. ADA-SCID was the first disease treated with gene therapy and can also be managed with enzyme replacement or bone marrow transplantation.
questions.question: Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) most commonly results from deficiency in which enzyme?

questions.explanation: Patients who lose response to TNF-alpha inhibitors, particularly due to anti-drug antibody formation or TNF-independent disease drivers, may benefit from switching to a biologic targeting a distinct inflammatory pathway. Ustekinumab blocks the shared p40 subunit of interleukin-12 and interleukin-23, addressing Th1 and Th17-driven inflammation that persists despite TNF-alpha blockade, offering an alternative mechanism of disease control.
options: Ustekinumab provides identical mechanism with better absorption
IL-12/23 blockade directly restores TNF-alpha receptor sensitivity
Blocking IL-12/23 addresses inflammation independent of TNF-alpha resistance
Ustekinumab eliminates all immunogenicity concerns entirely
IL-12/23 blockade works only through calcineurin inhibition
questions.question: A patient with severe combined chronic inflammatory bowel disease is switched from infliximab to ustekinumab after loss of response. What is the mechanistic rationale for targeting a different pathway?

options: Complement consumption by immune complex deposition
Reduced complement half-life from renal loss alone
questions.explanation: In active lupus, circulating immune complexes activate the classical complement pathway extensively, consuming C3 and C4 faster than the liver can replenish them. Low complement levels therefore correlate with disease activity and are used clinically as markers of flares, particularly lupus nephritis, alongside anti-dsDNA antibody titers.
questions.question: A patient with systemic lupus erythematosus has low complement levels (C3 and C4) during a disease flare. What best explains this laboratory finding?
A patient with multiple sclerosis is started on natalizumab and develops progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy. Which mechanism links this drug to the opportunistic infection?
options: Direct depletion of circulating B lymphocytes
Blockade of leukocyte migration across the blood-brain barrier
Inhibition of complement mediated viral clearance
Induction of JC virus latency reactivation genes directly
questions.explanation: Natalizumab blocks alpha-4 integrin, preventing leukocyte adhesion and migration across the blood-brain barrier, which reduces central nervous system inflammation in multiple sclerosis. However, this same mechanism impairs immune surveillance within the brain, allowing reactivation of latent JC virus and development of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy in susceptible patients.

options: Direct depletion of donor T lymphocytes
Blockade of intracellular cytokine receptor signaling
Inhibition of complement mediated tissue injury
Blockade of antigen presentation by dendritic cells
questions.question: A patient with graft-versus-host disease after bone marrow transplantation is treated with a Janus kinase inhibitor. What is the pharmacologic basis for this therapy?
questions.explanation: Janus kinase inhibitors such as ruxolitinib block intracellular signaling downstream of multiple cytokine receptors, including those for interferon-gamma and interleukins involved in T-cell activation and proliferation. This broad cytokine signaling blockade reduces the inflammatory cascade driving graft-versus-host disease, offering an alternative for patients refractory to corticosteroid therapy.

Type I interferons (IFN-α and IFN-β) are produced by virus-infected cells and plasmacytoid dendritic cells in response to viral nucleic acids recognized by pattern recognition receptors. They induce an antiviral state in neighboring cells by upregulating interferon-stimulated genes that inhibit viral replication. Type I IFNs also enhance adaptive immune responses and are used therapeutically in hepatitis C and multiple sclerosis.
questions.question: Type I interferons (IFN-α/β) are produced primarily in response to:

questions.explanation: Prostaglandin E2 infusion into the posterior hypothalamus causes wakefulness, while PGD2 induces natural sleep when infused into cerebral ventricles. This differential effect demonstrates the opposing roles of different prostaglandins in sleep-wake regulation. PGE2's role in maintaining wakefulness is part of its broader functions in the central nervous system.
questions.question: Which prostaglandin is primarily responsible for maintaining wakefulness in the central nervous system?

questions.explanation: The Arthus reaction is a localized Type III hypersensitivity caused by immune complex deposition in tissues, leading to complement activation, neutrophil recruitment, and tissue damage. It typically occurs 3-8 hours after antigen exposure in a previously sensitized individual. Systemic immune complex disease is termed serum sickness.
questions.question: The Arthus reaction represents a localized form of which hypersensitivity type?
Goodpasture syndrome exemplifies which type of hypersensitivity reaction?
questions.explanation: Goodpasture syndrome is a Type II hypersensitivity where antibodies target basement membrane antigens in the kidney and lung, activating complement and causing tissue damage. These anti-GBM (glomerular basement membrane) antibodies lead to rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and pulmonary hemorrhage. Direct antibody-mediated cytotoxicity characterizes Type II reactions.

questions.question: Which eicosanoid mediator is most potent in causing bronchoconstriction in asthmatic patients?
questions.explanation: Cysteinyl leukotrienes (LTC4, LTD4, LTE4) are extremely potent bronchoconstrictors, stimulate bronchial mucus secretion, and cause mucosal edema. They are significantly more potent than histamine in causing bronchoconstriction, particularly in asthmatic individuals. These leukotrienes were previously known as slow-reacting substance of anaphylaxis (SRS-A) and are key mediators in asthma pathophysiology.

questions.question: Which mechanism allows lymphocytes to generate millions of unique antigen receptors from limited genetic information?
questions.explanation: Somatic recombination (V(D)J recombination) allows the immune system to generate tremendous diversity from a limited number of gene segments. Random joining of variable (V), diversity (D), and joining (J) gene segments, combined with junctional diversity, creates millions of unique B cell and T cell receptors. This mechanism enables recognition of virtually any pathogen without requiring separate genes for each possible antigen.

questions.question: Interleukin-10 functions primarily as:
questions.explanation: IL-10 is a key anti-inflammatory cytokine that inhibits production of pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6, IL-12) by macrophages and dendritic cells. It promotes resolution of inflammation and limits tissue damage from excessive inflammatory responses. IL-10 is produced by regulatory T cells, Th2 cells, and alternatively activated macrophages.

questions.question: Drug-induced hemolytic anemia most commonly results from:
questions.explanation: Drugs like penicillin can act as haptens, binding to red blood cell membranes and eliciting antibody formation. These antibodies recognize the drug-RBC complex, leading to complement activation or antibody-dependent phagocytosis and hemolysis. This represents Type II hypersensitivity. Discontinuing the offending drug usually resolves the condition.

questions.question: A patient on long-term methotrexate for psoriatic arthritis is advised to avoid alcohol consumption. What complication is this precaution primarily intended to prevent?
questions.explanation: Methotrexate carries a risk of hepatotoxicity with cumulative dosing, which can progress to fibrosis and cirrhosis over time. Alcohol consumption independently causes hepatic injury and significantly increases this risk when combined with methotrexate. Regular liver function monitoring and alcohol avoidance are standard precautions during long-term methotrexate therapy.

options: Direct nephrotoxic tubular necrosis by NSAIDs
Loss of prostaglandin-mediated afferent arteriolar vasodilation
Excess bradykinin causing efferent arteriolar dilation
questions.explanation: Renal prostaglandins, particularly PGE2 and PGI2, maintain afferent arteriolar vasodilation to preserve glomerular perfusion when renal blood flow is compromised. NSAIDs inhibit this compensatory prostaglandin synthesis, causing unopposed vasoconstriction and reduced glomerular filtration. This risk is heightened in patients with pre-existing renal impairment, heart failure, or volume depletion.
questions.question: A patient with chronic kidney disease is prescribed a nonselective NSAID for pain and develops worsening renal function. Which mechanism explains this?
A patient develops angioedema after starting an ACE inhibitor. Which autacoid accumulation is responsible?
questions.explanation: ACE inhibitors block the enzyme that normally degrades bradykinin, allowing it to accumulate in tissues. Bradykinin increases vascular permeability and causes vasodilation, leading to angioedema of the face, lips, and airway. This reaction is not IgE-mediated, so antihistamines and adrenaline are often less effective than icatibant, a bradykinin receptor antagonist.

Cross-presentation enables dendritic cells to present exogenous antigens on MHC Class I molecules to CD8+ T cells, bypassing the normal restriction of MHC Class I to endogenous antigens. This mechanism is crucial for initiating CD8+ T cell responses against viruses that do not directly infect dendritic cells and against tumor antigens. The molecular mechanisms of cross-presentation remain incompletely understood but are essential for anti-tumor immunity.
questions.question: Cross-presentation allows dendritic cells to present exogenous antigens via which MHC pathway?

questions.explanation: Dendritic cell maturation involves a phenotypic shift from capturing antigens in peripheral tissues to presenting them in lymphoid organs. Mature dendritic cells upregulate MHC molecules and costimulatory molecules (CD80, CD86) while downregulating phagocytic capacity. This maturation is triggered by pathogen recognition through pattern recognition receptors and inflammatory signals.
questions.question: The process by which immature dendritic cells shift from antigen capture to antigen presentation is called:

questions.explanation: All three agents neutralize TNF-α but differ structurally. Infliximab and adalimumab are monoclonal antibodies (chimeric and fully human, respectively) that bind soluble and membrane-bound TNF-α. Etanercept is a fusion protein combining TNF receptor with IgG1 Fc that binds TNF-α and TNF-β. All three are highly effective in RA, often combined with methotrexate to prevent anti-drug antibodies and enhance efficacy.
questions.question: The mechanism of action shared by infliximab, adalimumab, and etanercept is:
Celiac disease pathogenesis primarily involves which immune mechanism?
questions.explanation: Celiac disease is a T cell-mediated autoimmune disorder triggered by gluten peptides in genetically susceptible individuals (HLA-DQ2/DQ8). CD4+ T cells recognize deamidated gluten presented by antigen-presenting cells, leading to inflammatory damage of intestinal villi. Autoantibodies against tissue transglutaminase develop secondarily and serve as diagnostic markers.

Cyclosporine is extensively metabolized by CYP3A4, making its blood levels highly susceptible to alteration by enzyme inhibitors (which increase toxicity risk) or inducers (which risk therapeutic failure). Given the narrow therapeutic index of cyclosporine, monitoring drug levels is essential whenever interacting medications are added or removed from a patient's regimen.
questions.question: A patient with chronic idiopathic urticaria on cyclosporine develops hypertrichosis and hypertension. Which additional monitoring parameter is essential given known drug interactions?
options: Serum uric acid levels exclusively during therapy
Serum drug levels when co-administering CYP3A4 inhibitors or inducers
Thyroid function tests on a monthly basis
Serum ceruloplasmin levels periodically during treatment
Vitamin B12 levels every three months routinely

questions.explanation: Eosinophils are specialized for defense against large parasites like helminths through ADCC. They bind to IgE-coated parasites via their Fc receptors and release granule contents containing major basic protein and other toxic substances that damage parasite membranes. Eosinophils are attracted to sites of parasitic infection by chemokines and can also contribute to allergic inflammation.
questions.question: The principal cell type involved in antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC) against helminth parasites is:
The major mechanism of glucocorticoid-induced immunosuppression involves:
questions.explanation: Glucocorticoids profoundly inhibit cytokine production (IL-1, IL-2, IL-3, IL-6, TNF-α, IFN-γ) by T cells and macrophages through multiple mechanisms including NF-κB inhibition. This reduces T cell activation and proliferation, impairs delayed hypersensitivity, and inhibits inflammatory responses. Glucocorticoids also induce T cell apoptosis, inhibit antigen presentation, and reduce lymphocyte trafficking to inflammatory sites.

Deficiencies in terminal complement components (C5, C6, C7, C8, C9) that form the membrane attack complex increase susceptibility to Neisseria meningitidis and N. gonorrhoeae infections. These bacteria are particularly sensitive to complement-mediated lysis. Patients may experience recurrent or disseminated neisserial infections despite intact opsonization and phagocytosis.
questions.question: Terminal complement component deficiencies (C5-C9) specifically increase susceptibility to:

questions.explanation: TNF-α is produced primarily by activated macrophages in response to LPS and other inflammatory stimuli, though T cells, NK cells, and mast cells also produce it. TNF-α has numerous effects including endothelial activation, fever induction, acute phase response, and cachexia. In septic shock, excessive TNF-α contributes to hypotension, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and multiorgan failure.
questions.question: Tumor necrosis factor-α is primarily produced by which cells?

questions.explanation: IL-17 is the signature cytokine of Th17 cells, a distinct helper T cell subset involved in defense against extracellular bacteria and fungi. IL-17 recruits neutrophils and induces antimicrobial peptide production. Excessive Th17 responses contribute to autoimmune diseases including rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, and inflammatory bowel disease. IL-17 inhibitors are effective therapies for these conditions.
questions.question: Interleukin-17 is primarily produced by which T helper subset?

options: Direct inhibition of cyclooxygenase enzyme activity
Direct neutralization of circulating tumor necrosis factor
Selective blockade of interleukin-1 receptor signaling
Interference with toll-like receptor signaling in endosomes
questions.explanation: Hydroxychloroquine accumulates in acidic intracellular compartments and interferes with toll-like receptor 7 and 9 signaling within endosomes, reducing recognition of self-nucleic acids that drive autoimmune activation in lupus. This mechanism, distinct from classic anti-inflammatory pathways, underlies its disease-modifying effect and reduces flare frequency with long-term use.
questions.question: A patient with severe combined presentation of joint pain, malar rash, and photosensitivity is diagnosed with systemic lupus erythematosus and started on hydroxychloroquine. What is the proposed immunomodulatory mechanism of this drug?

A patient with severe combined presentation of recurrent pericarditis attacks despite colchicine and NSAID therapy is started on rilonacept. What is the mechanism of this biologic in recurrent pericarditis?
options: Selective tumor necrosis factor neutralization only
Direct calcineurin inhibition within pericardial tissue
Broad T lymphocyte depletion within pericardial fluid
Interleukin-1 alpha and beta trap reducing inflammatory signaling
questions.explanation: Rilonacept is a fusion protein that acts as a soluble decoy receptor, binding and neutralizing both interleukin-1 alpha and interleukin-1 beta, thereby reducing IL-1 driven inflammatory signaling implicated in recurrent pericarditis. This targeted approach offers an option for patients with disease refractory to colchicine and NSAID therapy, addressing the underlying autoinflammatory component.

questions.question: Sulfasalazine is metabolized to which two active components?
questions.explanation: Sulfasalazine is cleaved by colonic bacteria into sulfapyridine (absorbed systemically, responsible for immunomodulatory effects and side effects) and 5-aminosalicylic acid (5-ASA, acts locally in gut, responsible for inflammatory bowel disease effects). The mechanism in RA is unclear but may involve reduced IL-8, decreased neutrophil chemotaxis, and antioxidant effects. Efficacy is modest; it's often used in combination with other DMARDs.

questions.question: Systemic corticosteroids are indicated in acute severe asthma exacerbations because they:
questions.explanation: Systemic corticosteroids (oral prednisone or IV methylprednisolone) reduce airway inflammation and prevent late-phase asthmatic responses. Effects develop over 4-6 hours, so they don't provide immediate relief but are crucial for preventing progression and reducing recovery time. Short courses (3-10 days) for exacerbations don't require tapering. Long-term systemic corticosteroid use for asthma is avoided due to adverse effects; high-dose inhaled corticosteroids are preferred.

IL-1 and TNF-α are key pro-inflammatory cytokines in RA pathogenesis, produced by activated macrophages in the synovium. They promote synovial inflammation, cartilage degradation, bone erosion, and systemic effects. Both cytokines induce production of matrix metalloproteinases that destroy cartilage and bone. Blockade of these cytokines with biologic agents (TNF inhibitors, anakinra) is highly effective in treating RA.
questions.question: The primary cytokines involved in rheumatoid arthritis pathogenesis are:

A patient with severe combined chronic asthma exacerbation triggered by viral upper respiratory infection shows minimal response to bronchodilators alone. What additional pathophysiological mechanism explains this poor response?
questions.explanation: Respiratory viral infections damage airway epithelium, exposing sensory nerve endings and triggering release of additional inflammatory mediators and cytokines, which amplifies airway hyperresponsiveness and inflammation beyond simple bronchoconstriction. This combined inflammatory and structural insult explains why bronchodilators alone often provide incomplete relief during virus-triggered asthma exacerbations, necessitating concurrent anti-inflammatory therapy.
options: Virus-induced airway epithelial damage amplifying inflammatory mediator release
Complete resistance of viral particles to bronchodilator therapy
Direct viral inactivation of the beta-2 adrenergic receptor
Viral induced permanent airway smooth muscle paralysis
Viral suppression of endogenous corticosteroid production

questions.explanation: Penicillin can act as a hapten, binding to red blood cell membrane proteins and forming a neoantigen. IgG antibodies then target these modified erythrocytes, activating complement and Fc-receptor-mediated phagocytosis. This antibody-mediated destruction of host cells defines type II cytotoxic hypersensitivity.
questions.question: A patient with a history of penicillin-induced hemolytic anemia is asked to avoid the drug permanently. Which hypersensitivity type explains this reaction?
Graves' disease is caused by antibodies that:
questions.explanation: Graves' disease involves stimulating autoantibodies that bind to and activate thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) receptors, causing unregulated thyroid hormone production and hyperthyroidism. This represents an unusual form of Type II hypersensitivity where antibodies stimulate rather than destroy target cells. The antibodies mimic TSH's normal action but cannot be regulated by negative feedback.

Erythropoietin (EPO) is a glycoprotein hormone primarily produced by the kidney that stimulates red blood cell production in response to hypoxia. It promotes survival, proliferation, and differentiation of erythroid precursors in bone marrow. Recombinant EPO is used to treat anemia in chronic kidney disease, chemotherapy, and other conditions.
questions.question: Erythropoietin primarily stimulates production of:

questions.explanation: Omalizumab dosing is calculated using a combination of the patient's body weight and baseline total serum IgE level, since both factors influence the amount of free IgE that needs to be neutralized for adequate receptor downregulation. This dual consideration ensures appropriate dosing across a wide range of patient sizes and baseline IgE levels within the approved treatment range.
questions.question: A patient with severe combined chronic asthma is noted to have a strong response to omalizumab despite a relatively low baseline serum IgE level near the lower threshold for eligibility. What factor, beyond total IgE, is also considered when determining appropriate dosing?
options: Peripheral eosinophil count exclusively without other factors
Serum tryptase level measured at baseline only
Forced expiratory volume percentage predicted alone
Total serum complement C3 and C4 levels combined
Patient body weight in combination with baseline IgE level

questions.question: A patient receiving heparin therapy develops thrombocytopenia with paradoxical thrombosis. Which immune mechanism underlies heparin-induced thrombocytopenia?
questions.explanation: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia occurs when antibodies form against complexes of platelet factor 4 and heparin. These immune complexes bind Fc receptors on platelets, causing widespread platelet activation, aggregation, and consumption, paradoxically leading to thrombosis despite low platelet counts. Heparin must be stopped immediately and replaced with a non-heparin anticoagulant.

questions.question: Reye's syndrome is associated with aspirin use during which type of infection?
questions.explanation: Reye's syndrome, characterized by acute encephalopathy and fatty liver, is associated with aspirin use during viral illnesses, particularly influenza and varicella, in children. The mechanism is unclear but may involve mitochondrial dysfunction. Due to this risk, aspirin is contraindicated in children with viral infections. Acetaminophen is the preferred antipyretic in children.

questions.question: A patient with chronic asthma poorly controlled despite adherence to inhaled therapy is found to have significant nasal polyposis and elevated blood eosinophils. Which biologic targeting the alarmin pathway may be considered?
options: Benralizumab targeting the IL-5 receptor exclusively
questions.explanation: Tezepelumab is a monoclonal antibody that blocks thymic stromal lymphopoietin, an epithelial-derived alarmin cytokine that sits upstream of multiple inflammatory pathways, including both eosinophilic and non-eosinophilic asthma phenotypes. This broader mechanism allows efficacy across a wider range of severe asthma patients compared to biologics targeting a single downstream cytokine.

While candidiasis can occur in AIDS, uncomplicated Candida vaginitis is common in healthy women and is not AIDS-defining. AIDS-defining conditions include opportunistic infections (P. jirovecii pneumonia, CMV disease, toxoplasmosis, disseminated MAC, etc.) and malignancies (Kaposi's sarcoma, certain lymphomas) that occur with severe immunodeficiency (CD4 <200 cells/μL).
questions.question: AIDS-defining illnesses include all of the following opportunistic infections EXCEPT:

questions.explanation: Betahistine, a selective histamine analogue used for Meniere's disease, is contraindicated in asthma patients due to potential bronchospasm and in ulcer patients due to increased gastric acid secretion. Its vasodilating effects in the inner ear help control vertigo but these same properties can exacerbate these underlying conditions. The drug works as a weak H1 agonist and H3 antagonist.
questions.question: Betahistine is contraindicated in patients with which two conditions?
Muromonab-CD3 (OKT3) functions by binding to which molecule on T cells?
questions.explanation: Muromonab-CD3 is a murine monoclonal antibody against the CD3 component of the T cell receptor complex. Binding to CD3 blocks T cell function and causes T cell depletion from circulation. Its use is limited by development of human anti-mouse antibodies and cytokine release syndrome. Newer humanized antibodies have largely replaced OKT3 in clinical practice.

SLE involves formation of autoantibodies (particularly anti-nuclear and anti-DNA antibodies) that form immune complexes depositing in tissues, particularly kidneys, joints, and blood vessels. These complexes activate complement and recruit inflammatory cells, causing vasculitis and organ damage. SLE represents a Type III hypersensitivity reaction with features of Type II in some manifestations.
questions.question: Systemic lupus erythematosus primarily involves which pathogenic mechanism?

questions.explanation: First-generation antihistamines are lipophilic and readily cross the blood-brain barrier, causing CNS depression and sedation. Second-generation antihistamines are lipophobic with low capacity to cross this barrier, resulting in minimal CNS effects. The sedative effects occur because these drugs block H1 receptors in the brain that normally mediate wakefulness.
questions.question: Which mechanism explains how first-generation antihistamines cause sedation?

A patient with severe combined chronic asthma on high-dose inhaled corticosteroids is noted to have adrenal suppression on cosyntropin stimulation testing. What management step is most appropriate before any planned dose reduction?
questions.explanation: Chronic corticosteroid use, even inhaled formulations at high doses, can suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, and abrupt discontinuation risks precipitating adrenal insufficiency. A gradual, carefully monitored tapering approach allows the adrenal axis to recover function progressively, minimizing the risk of an adrenal crisis while still working toward the lowest effective maintenance dose.
options: Immediate abrupt discontinuation of all corticosteroid therapy
Doubling the current inhaled corticosteroid dose further
Gradual, monitored corticosteroid tapering rather than abrupt cessation
Switching directly to a short-acting beta agonist alone
Adding a leukotriene receptor antagonist without steroid tapering

questions.question: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome is characterized by deficiency primarily affecting which component?
questions.explanation: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome is an X-linked immunodeficiency featuring IgM deficiency, thrombocytopenia with small platelets, and eczema. The defective WAS protein affects cytoskeletal organization in hematopoietic cells. Patients have increased susceptibility to encapsulated bacteria due to poor antibody responses and increased risk of autoimmunity and malignancy.

Intranasal antihistamines such as azelastine act directly on nasal H1 receptors, providing relief within fifteen to thirty minutes, considerably faster than intranasal corticosteroids, which require days of regular use for maximal anti-inflammatory effect. This makes intranasal antihistamines useful for rapid breakthrough symptom control alongside baseline corticosteroid therapy.
questions.question: A patient with severe allergic rhinitis notes symptom relief with intranasal corticosteroids but seeks a faster-acting option for breakthrough symptoms. Which class provides the most rapid additional relief?
options: Mast cell stabilizer nasal spray alone

questions.explanation: Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies bind proteins such as proteinase-3 or myeloperoxidase on the surface of primed neutrophils, triggering premature activation and degranulation near the vascular endothelium. This releases reactive oxygen species and proteolytic enzymes that damage vessel walls, producing the necrotizing vasculitis characteristic of conditions such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
options: Blockade of neutrophil migration into tissue
Enhanced clearance of neutrophils by macrophages
Premature neutrophil activation causing endothelial injury
questions.question: A patient with severe combined vasculitis is found to have circulating anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies. Which mechanism links these antibodies to blood vessel damage?

options: Direct neutralization of circulating interleukin-5 protein
Competitive blockade of eotaxin chemokine receptors
Inhibition of eosinophil bone marrow precursor genes
questions.explanation: Benralizumab targets the interleukin-5 receptor alpha subunit on eosinophils and basophils, and its afucosylated Fc region enhances binding to natural killer cells, triggering antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity that directly destroys eosinophils. This mechanism produces more profound and rapid eosinophil depletion compared to antibodies that simply neutralize circulating IL-5.
questions.question: A patient with severe chronic asthma on benralizumab notices a marked reduction in blood eosinophil counts. What mechanism explains this near-complete eosinophil depletion, distinct from anti-IL-5 antibodies?

questions.explanation: Etanercept is a fusion protein combining the TNF receptor with the Fc portion of human IgG1, acting as a soluble decoy receptor that binds and neutralizes circulating TNF-alpha before it can activate cell surface receptors. This reduces the inflammatory cascade driving joint destruction in rheumatoid arthritis, distinguishing it from monoclonal antibodies that target the cytokine directly.
options: Monoclonal antibody depleting CD20 positive B cells
Soluble receptor fusion protein that neutralizes TNF-alpha
Janus kinase enzyme inhibitor blocking cytokine signaling
T-cell costimulation blocker preventing CD28 binding
questions.question: A patient with severe rheumatoid arthritis is switched from methotrexate monotherapy to combination therapy with a biologic after inadequate response. Etanercept is chosen. What is its mechanism of action?

questions.explanation: Topical calcineurin inhibitors such as tacrolimus and pimecrolimus carry a boxed warning regarding a theoretical increased risk of skin cancer and lymphoma based on findings in animal studies and case reports, despite limited definitive evidence in humans at approved topical doses. Patients are advised to minimize sun exposure and use sun protection while using these agents for eczema management.
questions.question: A patient with severe combined chronic dermatologic condition on a topical calcineurin inhibitor is counseled regarding a boxed warning associated with this drug class. What malignancy risk does this warning primarily address?

questions.explanation: HIV envelope protein gp120 binds to CD4 molecules on helper T cells (and macrophages), along with coreceptors CCR5 or CXCR4, enabling viral entry. Progressive destruction of CD4+ T cells leads to immunodeficiency with opportunistic infections and malignancies. CD4 count below 200 cells/μL defines AIDS, regardless of symptoms.
questions.question: HIV primarily targets which cells through CD4 molecule interaction?
T cell anergy develops when T cells receive signals through the TCR without:
questions.explanation: T cell anergy occurs when T cells engage with peptide-MHC complexes in the absence of costimulatory signals (particularly CD28-B7 interaction). This results in non-responsive T cells that cannot proliferate or produce IL-2 even when subsequently exposed to optimal activation conditions. Anergy serves as a peripheral tolerance mechanism to prevent autoimmune responses.

questions.question: Anti-venoms are typically prepared in which animals?
questions.explanation: Anti-venoms are primarily produced in horses, sheep, and goats by immunizing them with snake, scorpion, or spider venoms. These large animals can provide substantial quantities of antivenom. The heterologous antibodies provide effective treatment for envenomation but carry risk of serum sickness or anaphylaxis, particularly with repeated administration.

options: Complete loss of interleukin-1 receptor expression
Excessive inflammasome activation and interleukin-1 beta release
Loss of neutrophil chemotaxis and migration ability
Deficient complement activation through the classical pathway
questions.question: A patient with cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome is found to have a gain-of-function mutation in the NLRP3 gene. What is the direct consequence of this mutation?
questions.explanation: NLRP3 is a component of the inflammasome, a multiprotein complex that activates caspase-1 to cleave pro-interleukin-1 beta into its active form. Gain-of-function mutations cause constitutive inflammasome activation, leading to excessive, unregulated IL-1 beta release and the recurrent fever, rash, and systemic inflammation characteristic of cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes.

questions.question: Belatacept blocks T cell costimulation by binding to:
questions.explanation: Belatacept is a fusion protein (CTLA-4-Ig) that binds to B7 molecules (CD80/CD86) on antigen-presenting cells with high affinity, preventing their interaction with CD28 on T cells. This blocks the costimulatory signal required for T cell activation, inducing T cell anergy or tolerance. It represents a novel non-nephrotoxic immunosuppressive approach for transplantation.

questions.question: Which cells undergo positive and negative selection in the thymic cortex and medulla?
questions.explanation: T lymphocytes undergo positive selection in the thymic cortex where they interact with cortical thymic epithelial cells expressing MHC molecules. Negative selection occurs in the medullary region where medullary thymic epithelial cells present self-antigens to eliminate autoreactive T cells. This rigorous selection process ensures T cells are self-MHC restricted and self-tolerant, with over 98% of thymocytes dying during development.

IFN-? (Type II interferon) is produced primarily by Th1 cells and NK cells in response to IL-12 and other stimuli. It's the key macrophage-activating cytokine, enhancing microbicidal activity against intracellular pathogens. IFN-? also promotes Th1 differentiation, B cell class switching to opsonizing antibodies (IgG1, IgG3 in humans), and MHC expression.
questions.question: Interferon-gamma is produced primarily by which cell types?

questions.explanation: Selective IgA deficiency results in recurrent sinopulmonary and gastrointestinal infections due to impaired mucosal immunity. Many affected individuals are asymptomatic, but some develop allergies, autoimmune diseases, or recurrent infections. Patients may develop anti-IgA antibodies that can cause severe transfusion reactions if IgA-containing blood products are administered.
questions.question: Selective IgA deficiency is the most common primary immunodeficiency and predisposes to:

questions.explanation: Sirolimus binds to FKBP12 like tacrolimus but inhibits mTOR (mammalian target of rapamycin) rather than calcineurin, blocking IL-2 receptor signaling and preventing T cell proliferation. This complements calcineurin inhibitors, which block IL-2 production. Sirolimus is not nephrotoxic but causes hyperlipidemia, bone marrow suppression, and impaired wound healing.
questions.question: Sirolimus (rapamycin) differs from calcineurin inhibitors in that it:

questions.explanation: Tremor, particularly of hands, is the most common dose-limiting adverse effect of β2 agonists, resulting from stimulation of β2 receptors in skeletal muscle. It's usually mild and diminishes with continued use. Other adverse effects include tachycardia, palpitations (α1 stimulation at high doses), hypokalemia (β2-mediated intracellular potassium shift), and hyperglycemia. Effects are generally less severe with inhaled versus oral administration.
questions.question: The primary adverse effect limiting high-dose beta-2 agonist use is:

questions.explanation: Anakinra is a recombinant IL-1 receptor antagonist that competitively inhibits IL-1α and IL-1β binding to the IL-1 receptor, blocking their pro-inflammatory effects. It's used in rheumatoid arthritis (though less effective than TNF inhibitors) and rare autoinflammatory syndromes caused by excessive IL-1 production. Daily subcutaneous injection is required due to short half-life.
questions.question: Anakinra blocks the activity of which cytokine?

questions.explanation: Leukotrienes are synthesized from arachidonic acid through the lipoxygenase pathway, specifically by 5-lipoxygenase enzyme which adds hydroperoxy groups at specific positions. This pathway is distinct from the cyclooxygenase pathway that produces prostaglandins. The 5-lipoxygenase converts arachidonic acid to 5-HPETE, which is then converted to various leukotrienes including LTA4, LTB4, and cysteinyl leukotrienes.
questions.question: The conversion of arachidonic acid to leukotrienes occurs through which enzymatic pathway?

questions.explanation: Azathioprine is metabolized to 6-mercaptopurine and then inactivated partly by xanthine oxidase. Allopurinol inhibits this enzyme, leading to accumulation of active thiopurine metabolites and profound bone marrow suppression. When co-administration is necessary, azathioprine doses must be reduced substantially, typically by 65 to 75 percent, to avoid toxicity.
options: Xanthine oxidase inhibition reducing azathioprine metabolism
Competitive displacement of azathioprine from plasma proteins
Enhanced renal clearance of active azathioprine metabolites
Direct additive bone marrow toxicity unrelated to metabolism
questions.question: A patient on long-term azathioprine develops severe bone marrow suppression after starting allopurinol for gout. What is the mechanism of this interaction?

questions.explanation: Methotrexate exhibits immunosuppressive and anti-inflammatory effects at doses (7.5-25 mg weekly) much lower than those used in cancer chemotherapy (grams). At low doses, MTX primarily affects rapidly dividing lymphocytes and may work through mechanisms beyond folate antagonism, including adenosine release and decreased inflammatory cytokine production. This makes it useful in rheumatoid arthritis and other autoimmune diseases.
questions.question: Methotrexate exerts immunosuppressive effects at doses that are:
A patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is prescribed roflumilast alongside bronchodilators. Which enzyme does this drug inhibit to reduce inflammation?
questions.explanation: Roflumilast selectively inhibits phosphodiesterase-4, an enzyme that breaks down cyclic AMP within inflammatory and structural airway cells. By preserving cyclic AMP levels, the drug reduces release of inflammatory mediators from neutrophils and macrophages, decreasing exacerbation frequency in patients with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease associated with chronic bronchitis.

Dexamethasone is approximately 25-30 times more potent than hydrocortisone in anti-inflammatory activity with negligible mineralocorticoid effects. This high potency allows use of lower doses, but equivalent doses cause similar adverse effects. Dexamethasone's long half-life (36-54 hours) makes it suitable for alternate-day therapy but increases HPA suppression risk. It's used when high glucocorticoid activity with minimal fluid retention is desired.
questions.question: Dexamethasone has what approximate anti-inflammatory potency relative to hydrocortisone?
Which cells are the primary mediators of allergic asthma pathophysiology?
questions.explanation: Allergic asthma involves IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation releasing histamine, leukotrienes, and other bronchoconstrictors. Eosinophils recruited to airways release major basic protein and other mediators that damage epithelium and perpetuate inflammation. Both cell types contribute to bronchial hyperreactivity, mucus production, and airway remodeling in chronic asthma.

questions.question: Tofacitinib, unlike biologic DMARDs, is administered:
questions.explanation: Tofacitinib is an oral small molecule Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitor that blocks intracellular signaling from multiple cytokine receptors. It inhibits JAK1 and JAK3 (with some JAK2 activity), interfering with signaling from cytokines important in RA pathogenesis (IL-6, IL-12, IL-23, IFN-γ). Oral administration is more convenient than injectable biologics. Adverse effects include infections, particularly herpes zoster, and laboratory abnormalities (anemia, neutropenia, elevated lipids).

questions.question: The process of antibody-mediated enhancement of phagocytosis is specifically termed:
questions.explanation: Opsonization is the coating of pathogens with antibodies or complement components that enhance phagocytosis. Phagocytes possess Fc receptors that bind to the Fc region of antibodies and complement receptors that bind C3b, facilitating pathogen recognition and engulfment. This process dramatically increases the efficiency of phagocytic clearance of pathogens.

Endogenous cortisol secretion follows a circadian rhythm with peak levels in early morning and nadir at night. Morning glucocorticoid administration mimics this pattern and causes less HPA axis suppression than evening dosing. For severe diseases requiring multiple daily doses or evening dosing, alternate-day regimens using intermediate-acting glucocorticoids may reduce adverse effects while maintaining efficacy.
questions.question: Glucocorticoids should be administered in the morning to:

questions.explanation: Mepolizumab is a monoclonal antibody that binds interleukin-5, the primary cytokine responsible for eosinophil growth, differentiation, and survival. By neutralizing IL-5, the drug reduces circulating and tissue eosinophil counts, decreasing asthma exacerbations in patients with an eosinophilic phenotype. It is administered as an add-on biologic for severe eosinophilic asthma.
questions.question: A patient with severe persistent asthma is started on mepolizumab. Which cytokine does this drug target to reduce eosinophilic inflammation?
The most common adverse effect of NSAIDs is:
questions.explanation: Gastrointestinal adverse effects (dyspepsia, nausea, ulceration, bleeding) are the most common NSAID toxicities, resulting from COX-1 inhibition in gastric mucosa. Risk factors include high doses, prolonged use, age >60, concurrent corticosteroids or anticoagulants, and H. pylori infection. Proton pump inhibitors, H2 blockers, or misoprostol can reduce but not eliminate GI risk.

options: Maternal IgG against fetal RBC antigens
questions.question: Hemolytic disease of the newborn (erythroblastosis fetalis) results from which mechanism?
questions.explanation: Hemolytic disease occurs when maternal IgG antibodies against fetal red blood cell antigens (typically Rh D) cross the placenta and destroy fetal RBCs. This Type II hypersensitivity usually develops after maternal sensitization during a previous pregnancy or mismatched transfusion. Anti-D immunoglobulin (RhoGAM) administered to Rh-negative mothers prevents sensitization.

questions.question: A patient with recurrent gout attacks despite xanthine oxidase inhibitor therapy is switched to pegloticase. What distinguishes this drug's mechanism from standard urate-lowering therapy?
questions.explanation: Pegloticase is a recombinant uricase enzyme that directly converts uric acid into allantoin, a more water-soluble compound readily excreted by the kidneys, bypassing the need to reduce uric acid production. This mechanism allows for rapid and substantial reduction in serum uric acid, useful in patients with refractory tophaceous gout unresponsive to conventional therapy.
options: Inhibition of renal urate reabsorption transporters
Inhibition of purine synthesis in the liver
Direct enzymatic conversion of uric acid to a soluble metabolite
Blockade of xanthine oxidase enzyme activity
Chelation of excess uric acid in serum directly

questions.explanation: Cromolyn stabilizes mast cell membranes, preventing degranulation and release of histamine, leukotrienes, and other mediators following antigen-IgE interaction. It's used prophylactically for allergic asthma and exercise-induced bronchospasm but is ineffective for acute symptoms. Must be administered by inhalation as it's poorly absorbed orally. Nedocromil has a similar mechanism. Both are safe but less effective than inhaled corticosteroids.
questions.question: Cromolyn prevents asthma symptoms primarily by:
The mechanism underlying hyperacute transplant rejection involves:
questions.explanation: Hyperacute rejection occurs within minutes to hours when a recipient has preexisting antibodies against donor antigens (typically ABO blood group or HLA antigens). These antibodies bind to vascular endothelium, activating complement and causing thrombosis and graft necrosis. Cross-matching before transplantation prevents this devastating complication.

questions.question: A patient with severe combined presentation of urticaria, bronchospasm, and hypotension after peanut ingestion is treated in the emergency department. After adrenaline, which additional agents are given as adjuncts, not first-line therapy?
questions.explanation: While intramuscular adrenaline remains the definitive first-line treatment for anaphylaxis, antihistamines help relieve cutaneous symptoms such as urticaria and itching, and corticosteroids may reduce the risk of biphasic or protracted reactions. Neither should delay or substitute for adrenaline administration, as they act too slowly to reverse acute airway or cardiovascular compromise.

Central tolerance involves deletion (negative selection) of autoreactive lymphocytes during development in primary lymphoid organs. Peripheral tolerance mechanisms include anergy (functional inactivation), regulatory T cell suppression, and activation-induced cell death for autoreactive cells that escape central tolerance. These combined mechanisms prevent autoimmune responses while maintaining the ability to respond to foreign antigens.
questions.question: Immunological tolerance to self-antigens is primarily established through which two processes?

A patient with severe combined chronic granulomatous inflammation is found to have persistently elevated macrophage activity forming multinucleated giant cells around an indigestible antigen. What best describes the underlying stimulus for granuloma formation?
options: Rapidly cleared self-limiting bacterial antigen exposure
Transient IgE-mediated allergic reaction to inhaled particles
Persistent, poorly degradable antigen resisting phagocytic clearance
Acute complement activation resolving within hours
questions.explanation: Granulomas form when macrophages are unable to fully degrade or eliminate a persistent antigen, such as certain mycobacteria or foreign material, leading to chronic activation, cytokine release (particularly interferon-gamma and TNF-alpha), and fusion of macrophages into multinucleated giant cells in an attempt to wall off and contain the indigestible stimulus.

questions.question: Chediak-Higashi syndrome is characterized by defective function of which cellular process?
questions.explanation: Chediak-Higashi syndrome involves defective lysosomal trafficking and fusion, resulting in giant lysosomal granules in phagocytes and other cells. This impairs microbial killing despite normal phagocytosis and oxidative burst. Patients have recurrent bacterial infections, partial albinism, progressive neurologic dysfunction, and increased risk of hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis.

questions.question: A patient with hereditary angioedema experiences recurrent episodes of facial and laryngeal swelling without urticaria. Which deficiency underlies this condition?
questions.explanation: Hereditary angioedema results from deficiency or dysfunction of C1 esterase inhibitor, which normally regulates the complement, kinin, and coagulation cascades. Without adequate inhibition, excessive bradykinin is generated, causing recurrent non-pruritic swelling episodes. Because mast cells are not involved, antihistamines and adrenaline are typically ineffective, and specific C1 inhibitor concentrate or bradykinin antagonists are used instead.

questions.question: A patient with severe combined presentation of joint swelling and gout flare is treated acutely with colchicine. What is the mechanism by which this drug reduces the inflammatory response to urate crystals?
options: Inhibition of microtubule polymerization in neutrophils
Direct dissolution of monosodium urate crystals
Inhibition of xanthine oxidase enzyme activity
Blockade of interleukin-1 receptor signaling directly
Enhancement of renal uric acid excretion
questions.explanation: Colchicine binds tubulin and inhibits its polymerization into microtubules, disrupting neutrophil chemotaxis, phagocytosis, and degranulation in response to urate crystal deposition in joints. This anti-inflammatory action, rather than any effect on uric acid metabolism itself, underlies its rapid effectiveness in relieving acute gout flare symptoms.

IL-2 is the primary T cell growth factor, promoting proliferation of activated T cells in both autocrine and paracrine fashion. It's produced by activated CD4+ T cells following antigen recognition and costimulation. IL-2 also enhances cytotoxic T cell and NK cell activity. Therapeutic recombinant IL-2 (aldesleukin) is used to treat metastatic renal cell carcinoma and melanoma.
questions.question: Interleukin-2 primarily functions to promote:

questions.explanation: Abatacept is a fusion protein that binds CD80/CD86 on antigen-presenting cells, blocking their interaction with CD28 on T lymphocytes and preventing the second costimulatory signal required for full T-cell activation. Without this costimulation, T cells become anergic rather than fully activated, reducing the autoimmune inflammatory response in rheumatoid arthritis.
options: Direct depletion of circulating B lymphocytes
Neutralization of circulating tumor necrosis factor
Inhibition of Janus kinase enzyme activity
questions.question: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis on abatacept develops recurrent infections. What is the mechanism of immunosuppression with this biologic?
A patient with rheumatoid arthritis on a Janus kinase inhibitor develops deep vein thrombosis. Which class-related risk explains this monitoring requirement?
questions.explanation: Janus kinase inhibitors such as tofacitinib carry a recognized class warning for increased risk of venous thromboembolism, including deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, particularly in patients with pre-existing cardiovascular risk factors. This risk necessitates careful patient selection and monitoring, especially in older patients or those with additional thrombotic risk factors.
options: Direct platelet activation by the drug itself
Reduced hepatic synthesis of clotting factors
Increased fibrinolysis leading to compensatory clotting
Increased venous thromboembolism risk associated with JAK inhibition
Complete absence of any cyclooxygenase inhibitory activity
Selective blockade of leukotriene receptors directly
Weak peripheral cyclooxygenase inhibition minimizing leukotriene shunting
Direct antihistamine activity blocking H1 receptors
Inhibition of mast cell degranulation pathways specifically
questions.question: A patient with a history of NSAID-induced urticaria is prescribed acetaminophen for pain relief instead. What is the pharmacologic basis for this substitution being generally safer?
questions.explanation: Acetaminophen has weak and largely central cyclooxygenase inhibitory activity with minimal effect on peripheral prostaglandin synthesis, so it causes much less shunting of arachidonic acid toward the leukotriene pathway compared to classic NSAIDs. This makes it a generally safer alternative in patients with NSAID-exacerbated respiratory or cutaneous reactions, though rare reactions can still occur.

Bare lymphocyte syndrome involves defective MHC Class II expression (Type II) or MHC Class I expression (Type I) due to mutations in transcription factors or transport proteins. Type II BLS causes severe combined immunodeficiency because CD4+ T cells cannot be positively selected in the thymus without MHC Class II. Type I BLS is generally less severe.
questions.question: Bare lymphocyte syndrome results from defective expression of which molecules?

questions.explanation: Infusion reactions to monoclonal antibodies commonly result from cytokine release syndrome, where antibody binding to target cells activates immune cells to release large amounts of cytokines such as TNF-alpha, IL-6, and interferon-gamma. This produces fever, chills, and hemodynamic instability, distinct from classic IgE-mediated anaphylaxis, though severe cases can mimic it clinically.
questions.question: A patient receiving a first infusion of a chimeric monoclonal antibody develops fever, chills, and hypotension during the infusion. What is the most likely mechanism?
options: Cytokine release triggered by immune cell activation
Immune complex deposition in vessel walls

questions.explanation: Patch testing evaluates delayed, T-cell mediated (type IV) hypersensitivity, making it appropriate for contact dermatitis rather than immediate IgE-mediated food allergies. Skin prick testing or serum-specific IgE assays directly assess immediate hypersensitivity by measuring allergen-specific IgE, making them the appropriate diagnostic tools for suspected food-triggered type I reactions.
options: Repeat patch testing at a different body site
Intradermal testing with high allergen concentration
Skin prick testing or specific IgE serum testing
Delayed-reading patch testing over one week
Oral mucosal biopsy for eosinophil quantification
questions.question: A patient with severe combined eczema and food allergy undergoes epicutaneous patch testing that remains negative despite clinical suspicion of a specific food trigger. What type of testing is more appropriate for suspected IgE-mediated food allergy?

options: Immediately at the very first onset of symptoms only
Two hours before exercise for maximal effect
Only after exercise has already been completed
Fifteen to thirty minutes before beginning exercise
Continuously throughout the entire exercise session
questions.question: A patient with a history of exercise-induced bronchospasm is advised to use a short-acting beta agonist before exercise. What is the appropriate timing for optimal protective effect?
questions.explanation: Short-acting beta agonists such as salbutamol provide bronchoprotection when administered approximately fifteen to thirty minutes before exercise, allowing peak bronchodilator effect to coincide with the period of greatest bronchoconstrictive risk. This timing maximizes prevention of exercise-induced symptoms rather than simply treating them after they occur.

questions.question: The phenomenon where repeated exposure to the same antigen produces a faster, stronger immune response is called:
questions.explanation: The memory response (secondary immune response) occurs upon re-exposure to an antigen and is characterized by faster kinetics, higher antibody titers, and production of higher-affinity antibodies compared to the primary response. Memory B and T cells generated during the primary response persist for years and rapidly proliferate upon antigen re-encounter. This immunological memory forms the basis for vaccination effectiveness.

questions.question: A patient with severe combined chronic gout is started on febuxostat instead of allopurinol due to a prior hypersensitivity reaction. What is the mechanism of action shared by both drugs despite their different chemical structures?
options: Direct urate crystal dissolution in joints
questions.explanation: Both allopurinol and febuxostat inhibit xanthine oxidase, the enzyme responsible for converting hypoxanthine and xanthine to uric acid, thereby reducing uric acid production. Despite sharing this mechanism, their distinct chemical structures mean that patients who develop hypersensitivity to allopurinol, including HLA-associated severe cutaneous reactions, can often safely tolerate febuxostat instead.

options: Immediately initiating a biologic agent regardless of adherence
Doubling the current inhaled corticosteroid dose further
Addressing adherence barriers and confirming proper inhaler technique
Discontinuing all current therapy and restarting from baseline
Referring directly for bronchial thermoplasty without further assessment
questions.question: A patient with severe combined chronic asthma poorly controlled despite high-dose combination inhaler therapy is found to have significant treatment nonadherence on review of pharmacy refill records. What is the most appropriate next pharmacist intervention before escalating to biologic therapy?
questions.explanation: Before escalating to costly and invasive therapies such as biologics, it is essential to confirm that poor asthma control is not simply due to nonadherence or incorrect inhaler technique, both common and reversible causes of apparent treatment failure. Addressing these modifiable factors first ensures that any subsequent escalation in therapy is truly warranted by refractory disease rather than correctable behavioral issues.

questions.question: Live attenuated vaccines may revert to virulent forms through which process?
questions.explanation: Live attenuated vaccines contain organisms treated to reduce virulence while maintaining immunogenicity, but genetic mutations can potentially restore virulence. This risk is greatest with oral polio vaccine (Sabin), which can cause vaccine-associated paralytic poliomyelitis in rare cases. Despite this risk, live vaccines generally provide stronger, longer-lasting immunity than killed vaccines.

questions.question: Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis specifically involves defective immunity against:
questions.explanation: Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis involves selective T cell dysfunction against Candida, with normal immunity to other pathogens. Patients develop persistent Candida infections of skin, nails, and mucous membranes but rarely systemic candidiasis. Various genetic defects affecting Th17 responses or IL-17 signaling have been identified in different forms of the disease.

Intravenous immunoglobulin provides pooled donor antibodies that offer passive humoral immunity against a broad range of pathogens in patients unable to produce sufficient antibodies themselves. This replacement therapy does not correct the underlying immune defect but substantially reduces the frequency and severity of infections in antibody deficiency syndromes.
options: Stimulating endogenous B lymphocyte antibody production
Directly killing intracellular pathogens through opsonization
Replacing deficient complement components in circulation
Restoring normal T lymphocyte maturation in the thymus
Providing passive antibody protection against infections
questions.question: A patient with severe combined immunodeficiency is treated with intravenous immunoglobulin replacement therapy. What is the primary therapeutic goal of this treatment?
A patient with contact dermatitis from nickel-containing jewelry is evaluated. Which immune cells primarily mediate this delayed reaction?
questions.explanation: Nickel contact dermatitis is a classic type IV delayed hypersensitivity reaction mediated by sensitized CD4+ T lymphocytes. Upon re-exposure, these memory T cells release cytokines that recruit macrophages and cause local tissue inflammation over 24 to 72 hours. This delayed onset distinguishes it from immediate IgE-mediated reactions.

TLR4 specifically recognizes lipopolysaccharide (LPS), a component of Gram-negative bacterial cell walls. LPS recognition by TLR4, along with accessory proteins CD14 and MD-2, triggers signaling cascades leading to NF-κB activation and production of pro-inflammatory cytokines. Excessive TLR4 activation by LPS can lead to septic shock.
questions.question: Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) primarily recognizes which pathogen-associated molecular pattern?

A patient with severe combined presentation of recurrent anaphylaxis without identifiable trigger is diagnosed with idiopathic anaphylaxis after thorough allergy workup. What is the general approach to prophylactic management in this condition?
options: Complete avoidance of all foods and environmental allergens permanently
Long-term antihistamine and corticosteroid prophylaxis with an emergency plan
Immediate splenectomy to reduce mast cell mediator release
Lifelong daily epinephrine injections regardless of symptoms
Avoidance of exercise and all forms of physical activity
questions.explanation: Idiopathic anaphylaxis, where no specific trigger can be identified despite thorough evaluation, is managed with prophylactic antihistamines and, in frequent or severe cases, a tapering course of corticosteroids to reduce recurrence frequency. Patients are also equipped with an emergency action plan and adrenaline auto-injector for prompt treatment of breakthrough episodes.

Toxoid vaccines contain inactivated bacterial toxins and are effective against diseases where toxins cause pathology (diphtheria, tetanus, botulism). The toxoids maintain immunogenicity while losing toxicity, inducing antibodies that neutralize toxins during subsequent exposure. These vaccines do not prevent infection or colonization but prevent toxin-mediated disease.
questions.question: Toxoid vaccines are effective against diseases where pathology is primarily caused by:

questions.explanation: Vascular spasm or vasoconstriction is the immediate response to tissue injury, beginning within seconds and lasting a few minutes. This initial constriction is mediated by neurogenic reflexes and helps limit blood loss. It is followed by active vasodilation and increased vascular permeability that characterize the subsequent inflammatory response.
questions.question: The initial momentary vascular response to tissue injury involves:

questions.explanation: Myasthenia gravis involves autoantibodies against acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction, blocking neurotransmission and causing muscle weakness. This Type II hypersensitivity also leads to receptor internalization and complement-mediated destruction of the postsynaptic membrane. Treatment includes cholinesterase inhibitors and immunosuppression.
questions.question: Myasthenia gravis results from autoantibodies that:

questions.explanation: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis is characterized by marked tissue and blood eosinophilia driving vasculitic damage. Interleukin-5 is the principal cytokine sustaining eosinophil survival and activation, and its blockade with mepolizumab reduces eosinophil counts and disease activity, allowing corticosteroid dose reduction in affected patients.
options: Reducing eosinophil-driven vascular and tissue inflammation
Blocking B lymphocyte antibody production entirely
Suppressing complement mediated vessel injury directly
questions.question: A patient with severe combined chronic eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis is treated with mepolizumab as an adjunct to corticosteroids. What is the rationale for targeting interleukin-5 in this vasculitis?

options: Preventing rebound flare from premature discontinuation
Achieving faster resolution than topical corticosteroids alone
Avoiding systemic absorption seen with topical therapy
Preventing bacterial superinfection of the affected skin
Reducing the total cumulative corticosteroid dose needed
questions.question: A patient with severe allergic contact dermatitis to poison ivy over a large body surface area is treated with a tapering course of oral corticosteroids rather than topical therapy alone. What is the rationale for the longer taper duration used in this condition?
questions.explanation: Poison ivy contact dermatitis often has a prolonged course due to continued antigen exposure to urushiol retained in the skin, and short corticosteroid courses can lead to rebound flares once the drug is stopped prematurely. A gradually tapering course over two to three weeks allows the inflammatory response to subside fully while minimizing the risk of symptom recurrence.

Interferon-gamma receptor defects impair macrophage activation and cell-mediated immunity to intracellular pathogens, particularly mycobacteria. Patients develop severe, disseminated infections with weakly pathogenic mycobacteria (BCG, environmental mycobacteria) and Salmonella. This demonstrates IFN-γ's critical role in antimycobacterial immunity through macrophage activation.
questions.question: Interferon-gamma receptor deficiency specifically increases susceptibility to infections with:
X-linked agammaglobulinemia (Bruton's disease) is characterized by absence of which cells?
questions.explanation: X-linked agammaglobulinemia results from mutations in Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK) essential for B cell development. Affected males have absent or very low B cells and immunoglobulins, with normal T cell function. Patients develop recurrent bacterial infections, particularly with encapsulated organisms, starting after maternal IgG wanes around 6 months of age.

questions.question: Anaphylactic shock is most effectively treated with which immediate intervention?
questions.explanation: Epinephrine is the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis, acting as a physiologic antagonist to counter massive mediator release. It causes bronchodilation through ?2 receptors, vasoconstriction through ?1 receptors to restore blood pressure, and reduces mediator release from mast cells. Antihistamines and corticosteroids are adjunctive but do not address life-threatening cardiovascular and respiratory compromise.

questions.question: A patient develops a delayed maculopapular rash and eosinophilia several weeks after starting an anticonvulsant, along with fever and organ involvement. Which severe drug reaction is most consistent with this presentation?
options: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS)
Fixed drug eruption limited to skin
questions.explanation: DRESS syndrome is a severe, delayed T-cell mediated hypersensitivity reaction characterized by fever, extensive skin rash, eosinophilia, and multi-organ involvement, typically appearing two to eight weeks after starting the culprit drug. Aromatic anticonvulsants are common triggers. Early recognition and drug withdrawal are critical, as mortality can result from hepatic or other organ failure.

Chronic inflammation is characterized by predominance of macrophages, lymphocytes, and plasma cells rather than neutrophils. Macrophages release various mediators including reactive oxygen species that can cause tissue damage during prolonged inflammation. This persistent inflammation can lead to fibrosis and organ dysfunction when not properly resolved.
questions.question: Chronic inflammation is characterized by the predominance of which cell type?
Chemokines function primarily to:
questions.explanation: Chemokines are small cytokines specialized for directing cell migration (chemotaxis) through interaction with G-protein coupled receptors. They create concentration gradients that guide leukocytes to sites of infection or inflammation. Different chemokines attract different cell types: CXCL8 (IL-8) attracts neutrophils, CCL5 (RANTES) attracts T cells and monocytes, CCL11 (eotaxin) attracts eosinophils.

Mast cells are strategically located in tissues that interface with the external environment, particularly the skin and mucosal surfaces of the respiratory, gastrointestinal, and genitourinary tracts. This positioning allows rapid responses to pathogens and allergens that breach epithelial barriers. Mast cells also reside near blood vessels and nerves throughout the body.
questions.question: Mast cells are most abundant at which anatomical sites?

questions.explanation: Interleukin-8 (IL-8, also known as CXCL8) is a potent chemokine that specifically attracts neutrophils to sites of infection and inflammation. It is produced by macrophages, endothelial cells, and other cells in response to inflammatory stimuli. IL-8 binds to CXCR1 and CXCR2 receptors on neutrophils, triggering their migration and activation.
questions.question: The chemotactic factor most important for recruiting neutrophils to sites of bacterial infection is:
Mast cell stabilizers prevent allergic reactions by inhibiting which primary cellular process?
questions.explanation: Cromolyn and nedocromil function as mast cell stabilizers by preventing the degranulation of mast cells that occurs following antigen-IgE interaction. These drugs reduce the release of inflammatory mediators including histamine, leukotrienes, and prostaglandins from mast cells. By stabilizing mast cell membranes, they prevent the cascade of allergic and inflammatory responses without possessing antihistamine or anti-inflammatory properties themselves.

questions.question: Cyclosporine exerts its immunosuppressive effect by binding to which intracellular protein?
