questions.question:
A(i) Describe the biochemical definition of metabolic acidosis, state its cardinal blood gas findings, and explain how it is classified.
A(ii) List the causes of normal anion gap metabolic acidosis under (a) renal acidification defects and (b) gastrointestinal bicarbonate loss; and the causes of increased anion gap metabolic acidosis under (c) endogenous acid loads and (d) exogenous toxins.
B(i) Explain the urine anion gap and state how it distinguishes renal from gastrointestinal causes. State the targets and agents for alkali therapy.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Metabolic acidosis:
- Definition: addition of acid or loss of HCO₃⁻.
- Blood gas findings: high H⁺; pH <7.35; low HCO₃⁻; low pCO₂ (compensatory hyperventilation).
- Classification: high anion gap (HAG) and normal anion gap (NAG) metabolic acidosis.
- Anion gap formula: [Na] – [HCO₃⁻ – Cl⁻]; normal 4–12 (owing to serum albumin and unmeasured anions).
A(ii) Causes:
(a) Normal AG — renal acidification defects: proximal renal tubular acidosis; classic distal tubular acidosis; hyperkalaemic distal tubular acidosis; early renal failure.
(b) Normal AG — GI bicarbonate loss: diarrhoea; small bowel losses; ureteral diversions; anion exchange resins; ingestion of CaCl₂; acid infusion (HCl, arginine HCl, lysine HCl).
(c) Increased AG — endogenous acid loads: ketoacidosis (diabetes mellitus, alcoholism, starvation); uraemia; lactic acidosis.
(d) Increased AG — exogenous toxins with osmolar gap: methanol, ethylene glycol. Without osmolar gap: salicylates, paraldehyde.
B(i) Urine anion gap (UAG): UAG = [Na⁺ + K⁺] – [Cl⁻].
- UAG <0 (negative): GI cause (diarrhoea) — adequate urinary NH₄⁺ excretion.
- UAG >0 (positive): renal cause (type 1 RTA) — impaired renal NH₃ secretion.
Corrected HCO₃⁻ = measured HCO₃⁻ + (anion gap – 12); normal 22–26. If reduced → additional metabolic acidosis; if elevated → additional metabolic alkalosis.
Alkali therapy: indicated when serum HCO₃⁻ <12 mEq/L (newer recommendations: maintain level 20–25); dose 0.5–1 mEq/kg/day; formula: 0.3 × weight × BE; agent: NaHCO₃; K citrate in type 1 RTA. Other treatment: address underlying disorder; dialysis if indicated.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the embryological period during which all fetal heart structures are formed (organogenesis), the overall prevalence of congenital heart disease (CHD) in live births, and the three broad aetiological categories responsible.
A(ii) For each of the following chromosomal abnormalities state the cardiac defects most commonly associated: Trisomy 21, Trisomy 18, Trisomy 13, and Turner syndrome (XO).
B(i) Explain the anatomical and physiological basis of why most congenital defects are well tolerated in the fetus but cause problems after birth, and describe the pathological sequence by which a large ventricular septal defect eventually leads to reversal of shunt direction (Eisenmenger syndrome).
questions.answerText:
A(i) Embryological period: between 3–8 weeks gestation all fetal heart structures are formed (organogenesis). Prevalence of CHD: occurs in 0.5–0.8% of live births; higher among stillborns (3–4%), abortuses (10–25%), and premature infants (about 2%, excluding PDA); about 2–3 in 1,000 newborn infants will be symptomatic with heart disease in the first year of life; diagnosis is established by 1 week of age in 40–50% and by 1 month in 50–60%.
Three aetiological categories:
• Genetic/chromosomal (about 8% of cases): heart defect is usually part of a chromosomal disorder; no specific gene locus for CHD identified; a child born to a parent with CHD has a substantially increased likelihood (risk may be as high as 15%) of having a similar lesion; greater risk of transmission from mother than from father for certain lesions.
• Environmental (about 2% of cases): rubella infection, ingestion of lithium, fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS); CHD is a prominent component of FAS; anticonvulsant medications and exogenous female sex hormones have an uncertain role.
• Multifactorial inheritance: the majority of cases.
A(ii) Chromosomal abnormalities and associated cardiac defects:
• Trisomy 21 (50%): AV canal, VSD, ASD, and others.
• Trisomy 18 (80%): VSD, ASD, and others.
• Trisomy 13 (40%): VSD, ASD, PDA, and others.
• Turner syndrome (XO): bicuspid aortic valve.
B(i) Fetal tolerance: most congenital defects are well tolerated in the fetus because of the parallel nature of the fetal circulation — the right and left circulations run in parallel (not in series), so a septal defect does not cause significant haemodynamic derangement. After birth, the circulations separate and shunts become haemodynamically significant. Pathological sequence to Eisenmenger syndrome (using ASD as an example): a large left-to-right shunt causes chronic volume overload of the right heart and pulmonary circulation; elevated pulmonary blood flow raises pulmonary vascular resistance; this develops into pulmonary arterial hypertension; the high pulmonary pressure first reduces the left-to-right shunt, then makes it bidirectional, and finally reverses it (right-to-left); right ventricular pressure overload develops; pulmonary blood flow is reduced and the patient becomes cyanotic. In the most severe cases, an irreversible plexiform arteriopathy similar to that in primary pulmonary hypertension is present. Surgery is contraindicated when pulmonary hypertension approaches systemic levels because operative mortality is high and elevated pulmonary vascular resistance does not fall after surgery.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe Helicobacter pylori under the following headings: (a) morphological characteristics that facilitate colonisation, (b) virulence factors encoded by the pathogenicity island, (c) other bacterial enzymes and surface factors.
A(ii) Explain the sequence of H. pylori-mediated pathogenesis in duodenal ulcer (DU) formation, from antral infection to mucosal injury.
B(i) State the standard eradication regimens for H. pylori, specifying drug names, doses, and duration for both triple and quadruple therapy.
questions.answerText:
A(i) H. pylori characteristics:
(a) Morphological: spiral shape; flagella for motility; Gram-negative bacillus; found in the stomachs of humans in all parts of the world; transmission by faecal–oral and oral–oral routes; infection thought to occur in childhood and persist; capable of transforming into a coccoid form representing a latent state.
(b) Virulence factors encoded by the pathogenicity island: cytotoxin-associated gene protein (CagA) — stimulates local inflammation; vacuolating cytotoxin (VacA); pic B.
(c) Other bacterial factors: potent urease production (increases pH); catalase; lipase; adhesins; platelet-activating factor; surface factors chemotactic for neutrophils and monocytes.
A(ii) Pathogenesis of H. pylori-mediated DU:
Antral infection leads to increased gastric acid (HCl) production and increased duodenal acid → mucosal injury (leaking roof concept); basal and stimulated gastrin release are increased and somatostatin-secreting D cells may be decreased; increased acid secretion through direct and indirect actions of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-8, TNF, IL-1) on G, D, and parietal cells; decreased duodenal mucosal bicarbonate production; gastric metaplasia in the duodenum permits H. pylori to bind and produce local injury secondary to the host response.
B(i) Eradication regimens:
Triple therapy × 14 days: Proton pump inhibitor + clarithromycin 500 mg + (metronidazole 500 mg or amoxicillin 1 g), all twice daily. Tetracycline 500 mg can substitute for amoxicillin or metronidazole.
Quadruple therapy × 14 days (option 1): Proton pump inhibitor twice daily + metronidazole 500 mg three times daily + bismuth subsalicylate 525 mg + tetracycline 500 mg four times daily.
Quadruple therapy × 14 days (option 2): H₂-receptor antagonist twice daily + (bismuth subsalicylate 525 mg + metronidazole 250 mg + tetracycline 500 mg) four times daily.
PPI doses: omeprazole 20 mg, lansoprazole 30 mg, rabeprazole 20 mg, pantoprazole 40 mg, esomeprazole 40 mg. H₂RA doses: cimetidine 400 mg, famotidine 20 mg, nizatidine 150 mg, ranitidine 150 mg.

A(i) Alopecia — definition and classification:
Alopecia: hair loss reflecting loss of hair follicles, alteration in hair cycling, loss of hair shafts, or combinations of these. More often acquired. Scalp alopecia can be diffuse, patterned, or circumscribed/focal.
Scarring alopecia: stem cells (in the bulge region) are lost by the process with resultant permanent destruction of the hair follicle.
Non-scarring alopecia: stem cells are not affected, therefore destruction of the hair follicle is reversible.

Causes of non-scarring hair loss: early traction alopecia; tinea capitis (except inflammatory forms e.g. kerion); alopecia areata; male and female pattern hair loss (androgenetic alopecia); telogen effluvium including secondary syphilis; anagen effluvium; trichotillomania.

Causes of scarring hair loss: discoid lupus erythematosus; lichen planopilaris; frontal fibrosing alopecia; central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia (CCCA); folliculitis decalvans; acne keloidalis nuchae; dissecting cellulitis of the scalp; late traction alopecia.

A(ii) Key non-scarring alopecias:
Alopecia areata: autoimmune disorder presenting as round or oval patches of non-scarring hair loss; can affect body hairs, axilla, beard, pubic hairs, eyebrows, eyelashes; associated with other autoimmune diseases; ophiasis pattern (band-like along peripheral temporal and occipital scalp); sisaipho spares that periphery; nail changes (pitting) can be seen.

Androgenetic alopecia: androgen-dependent, hereditary physical trait resulting from conversion of terminal scalp hairs into miniaturised vellus hairs in a characteristic pattern; can affect both males and females.

Telogen effluvium: premature termination of anagen precipitating the follicle into catagen then transformation into a resting stage; presents with excessive shedding of normal telogen club hairs; most commonly occurs 3-5 months after premature conversion. Causes: postpartum (physiologic); postfebrile (high fevers e.g. malaria); severe infection; severe chronic illness (HIV, SLE); severe prolonged psychological stress; postsurgical; hypothyroidism and other endocrinopathies; crash/starvation diets; drugs (retinoids, anticoagulants especially heparin, antithyroid agents, anticonvulsants, beta-blockers, discontinuation of oral contraceptives).

Anagen effluvium: usually results from hair shaft fracture; frequently seen following cancer chemotherapeutic agents (antimetabolites, alkylating agents, mitotic inhibitors) causing temporary shutdown of the hair matrix; reversal usually occurs after offending drug is discontinued; cooling caps prior to chemotherapy are protective.

B(i) Hirsutism vs hypertrichosis:
Hypertrichosis: growth of excessive hair anywhere on the body; classified by distribution (generalised vs localised), age of onset (congenital/acquired), and type of hair (lanugo/vellus vs terminal).
Hirsutism: applied to women with excessive growth of terminal hairs in androgen-dependent sites (male pattern) due to hyperandrogenemia or increased end-organ sensitivity to androgens.
Investigations: hormonal assays; search for underlying malignancies.
Treatment: treat underlying cause; anti-androgens; oral contraceptives; physical methods: depilatories, laser.

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Lower urinary tract infection (cystitis). The anatomical reason for higher female susceptibility: the shorter urethra in females predisposes to a higher risk of UTI.
(ii) Risk factors: diabetes; advanced age and conditions that affect personal care habits (such as cerebral degenerative diseases and delirium); problems emptying the bladder completely; indwelling urinary catheter; bowel incontinence; enlarged prostate, urethral stricture, or anything that blocks the flow of urine; kidney stones; immobility for a long period of time (e.g., while recovering from a hip fracture); pregnancy; surgery or other procedure involving the urinary tract.
(iii) Lower UTI (cystitis) features: cloudy or bloody urine which may have a foul or strong odour; low-grade fever in some people; dysuria — pain or burning with urination; strangury — pressure or cramping in the lower abdomen or back; frequency — strong need to urinate often, even right after the bladder has been emptied. Upper UTI (pyelonephritis) features: chills and rigors or night sweats; fatigue and a general ill feeling; fever above 101 degrees Fahrenheit; pain in the side, back, or groin; flushed, warm, or reddened skin; mental changes or confusion (in the elderly, these symptoms often are the only signs of UTI); nausea and vomiting; abdominal pain.
(iv) Management: antibiotics to prevent the infection from spreading to the kidneys — usually a course of 3–5 days in straightforward infections; in complicated infections, antibiotics are for 7–14 days. Commonly used antibiotics include trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, amoxicillin, Augmentin, doxycycline, and fluoroquinolones (tell the patient if she might be pregnant before taking these drugs). Take plenty of water.
(v) Possible outcomes/complications: sepsis — risk is greater among the young, very old adults, and the immunocompromised (e.g., due to HIV or cancer chemotherapy); kidney damage or scarring; chronic kidney infection (chronic pyelonephritis). Bladder infection symptoms usually go away within 24–48 hours after treatment begins; kidney infection may take 1 week or longer for symptoms to go away.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Definition and epidemiology:
Dyspepsia is a medical term that refers to a vague constellation of upper abdominal symptoms. Dyspepsia is a symptom and not a disease. Patients often refer to these symptoms as 'indigestion', which is used synonymously.
Epidemiology: dyspepsia is prevalent in more than one-fourth of the general adult population and is a frequent cause for medical consultation. Based on population surveys, each year approximately 25% of adults have dyspepsia lasting several days. It accounts for up to 7% of office visits and over half of gastrointestinal complaints in general medical practice. The majority of patients have recurrent or intermittent life-long symptoms. It has a significant impact upon patient quality of life and results in enormous direct and indirect societal costs.
A(ii) Rome criteria definition and associated symptoms:
A consensus group (Rome criteria) has formally defined dyspepsia as pain or discomfort in the upper abdomen.
Associated symptoms: upper abdominal fullness, early satiety, bloating, nausea, or heartburn.
Distinction from GORD: the consensus group has attempted to distinguish patients with probable gastro-oesophageal reflux disease from other patients with dyspepsia. In Nigeria, the prevalence of dyspepsia varies from 26% in the North East to 45% in Jos, Plateau State.
B(i) Mucosal defence system (three levels):
1. Pre-epithelial level: mucus-bicarbonate layer — physicochemical barrier against acid, pepsin, and bile.
2. Epithelial level: surface epithelial cells that produce mucus and bicarbonate; maintain intracellular pH; restitution modulated by epidermal growth factor (EGF), transforming growth factor (TGF), and basic fibroblast growth factor (FGF); prostaglandins.
3. Sub-epithelial level: microvascular circulatory system that provides HCO₃⁻, micronutrients, and oxygen, and removes toxic metabolic by-products.
Acid-peptic disease concept: APDs (including gastro-oesophageal reflux, peptic ulcer, and stress-related mucosal injury) arise when the caustic effects of aggressive factors overwhelm the defensive factors of the GI mucosa.
Protective factors: mucous and bicarbonate secretion, prostaglandins, blood flow, natural process of healing and regeneration.
Aggressive factors: gastric acid, pepsin, bile, infection (H. pylori), drugs (NSAIDs, systemic steroids — long-term).

questions.answerText:
A(i) Distribution of calcium:
- Bones and teeth: 99%.
- Soft tissues: 0.9%.
- ECF: 0.1%; of this, protein-bound fraction = 0.05%, free Ca²⁺ = 0.05%.
- Only the 0.05% free Ca²⁺ in the ECF is closely regulated.
Calcium is the most abundant mineral in the body; 1% of the body contains serum calcium needed to support metabolic functions; 99% is stored in bones and teeth.
A(ii) Three regulating hormones: Parathyroid hormone (PTH), Calcitonin, and Vitamin D.
Response to chronic Ca²⁺ fall:
- PTH secretion increases → stimulates osteoclasts (bone dissolution, releasing Ca²⁺ and phosphate into plasma) → stimulates renal reabsorption of Ca²⁺ and renal secretion of phosphate → stimulates activation of vitamin D, promoting intestinal absorption of Ca²⁺.
- Net effect: plasma levels maintained at the expense of bone density.
B(i) Hypocalcaemia: serum calcium <9 mg/100 ml.
Primary cause: PTH or Vitamin D deficiency. Additional causes: hypoparathyroidism, hyperphosphataemia, chronic renal failure, sepsis, pancreatitis, liver disease (decreased albumin production), osteomalacia, malabsorption, vitamin D or magnesium deficiency.
Signs and symptoms: numbness and tingling, muscle cramps and pain, irritability, impaired mentation, seizures, cardiac problems, laryngospasm, bronchospasm, tetany.
Mechanism: low serum calcium makes nerves and muscle hyper-excitable → spastic contractions, even death from respiratory arrest.
B(ii) Hypercalcaemia: serum calcium >10.5 mg/100 ml.
Causes: overactive parathyroid glands (primary cause: parathyroid adenoma), cancer (lung cancer, breast cancer, bone metastasis), sarcoidosis and tuberculosis, hereditary factors, immobility, severe dehydration, medications, supplements.
Signs and symptoms: kidney stones, bone pain and fractures, anorexia, constipation, fatigue, weakness, joint pain, depression, memory loss, confusion, lethargy.
Mechanism: high serum calcium makes nerves and muscle hypo-excitable → cardiac arrhythmias, depressed activity of nerves and muscles.

Describe seborrhoeic dermatitis and its distinction from related conditions under the following headings:
A(i) Definition, sites of predilection, and characteristic clinical features.
A(ii) Compare seborrhoeic dermatitis with psoriasis — similarities and how they are distinguished.
B(i) Describe dyshidrotic (pompholyx) eczema: its clinical features and the full course of the condition.
B(ii) Describe the systemic allergic contact dermatitis variant: definition, mechanism, and examples.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Seborrhoeic dermatitis:
- A common chronic dermatosis characterised by redness and scaling occurring in regions where the sebaceous glands are most active: the face (including scalp), presternal area, and body folds
- Mild scalp seborrhoeic dermatitis causes flaking (dandruff)
- Lesions: hypopigmented macules/patches, papules of varying size; on the scalp, scaling is marked (dandruff)
- Pruritus is variable, mostly increased by perspiration
- It is an endogenous eczema — mediated by processes originating in the body

A(ii) Seborrhoeic dermatitis versus psoriasis:
Both: can produce scalp scaling and can affect similar seborrhoeic sites; dry appearance throughout their course.
Psoriasis distinguishing features: well-demarcated erythematous plaques with thick silvery-white scales; Auspitz's sign (bleeding points on scale removal); Koebner's phenomenon; favours extensor surfaces (elbows, knees); nail pitting and oil spot lesion characteristic.
Seborrhoeic dermatitis distinguishing features: scaling in sebaceous regions; dandruff; hypopigmented macules/patches; pruritus increased by perspiration; does not typically show Auspitz's sign.

B(i) Dyshidrotic eczema (pompholyx):
- Vesicular type of hand and foot dermatitis
- Can be acute or chronic; involvement of the fingers, palms, and soles
- Lesions are deep-seated, pruritic vesicles
- Bullae can occur; it can be infected
- Prone to recurrence
- Later course: scaling, fissure, and lichenification develop

B(ii) Systemic allergic contact dermatitis:
- Occurs when a patient who has had prior allergic contact dermatitis (ACD) to an allergen now has systemic exposure to that allergen or a closely related compound
- Mechanism: T cell-mediated reaction
- Examples: prior ACD to ethylenediamine with subsequent reaction to aminophylline; prior poison ivy dermatitis with subsequent reaction to ingestion of cashew nut

A(i) Fungal meningitis organisms: Cryptococcus, Histoplasma, Candida. Predilections and routes: cranial and pericranial infections (sinusitis, otitis, osteomyelitis, head trauma); neurosurgical sites; shunts; spina bifida; encephalocoele; haematogenous spread; septic emboli from valvular vegetations or lungs.
A(ii) Classification of meningitis by time course: acute, subacute, or chronic. By organism: viral, pyogenic, TB/fungal, aseptic/lymphomatous/carcinomatous. By anatomical layer: leptomeningitis (lepto) involves the arachnoid and pia mater; pachymeningitis involves the dura mater.
B(i) Clinical features of pyogenic meningitis: Systemic — fever, malaise, vomiting. Headache, photophobia, delirium. Kernig's sign, Brudzinski's sign. Neck stiffness. Seizures. Impairment of consciousness. Focal neurological deficits. Papilloedema. Specific meningococcal features: maculopapular rash; hypotension (Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome); chest/respiratory tract infection.
B(ii) Meningococcal vaccines: two meningococcal vaccines each containing antigens to serogroups A, C, Y, and W-135 are licensed. Major limitation: neither provides immunity against serogroup B, which is responsible for approximately one-third of cases. Both vaccines elicit protective levels of bactericidal antibody to all four serogroups in more than 97% of recipients (as measured at 28 days). Side effects: mild-to-moderate local reactions at the injection site and minor systemic symptoms (headache, fatigue, malaise, and low-grade fever) may occur after receipt of either vaccine.

questions.answerText:
A(i) KDIGO AKI definition: AKI is functional criterion — increase in serum creatinine by 50% within 7 days OR increase in serum creatinine by 0.3 mg/dL (26.5 µmol/L) within 2 days OR oliguria = AKI. Staging: Stage 1 — serum creatinine 1.5–1.9 times baseline or ≥26.5 µmol/L increase; urine output <0.5 mL/kg/hr for 6–12 hours. Stage 2 — serum creatinine 2–2.9 times baseline; urine output <0.5 mL/kg/hr for >12 hours. Stage 3 — serum creatinine 3.0 times baseline OR increase to ≥353.6 µmol/L OR initiation of dialysis; urine output <0.3 mL/kg/hr for >24 hours or anuria for >12 hours. AKI has replaced ARF; this terminology enables healthcare professionals to see the disease as a spectrum of injury which extends from less severe injury to more advanced injury when RRT is required.
A(ii) Pre-renal: hypovolaemia; excessive sweating (hot climate); excessive vomiting/diarrhoea; vasodilation from sepsis; cirrhosis (3rd space loss); cardiogenic shock; CCF, MI, pericardial tamponade; haemorrhage, APH, PPH, RTA; bilateral renal artery stenosis. Renal (intrinsic): AGN; AIN (infections); herbs; drugs (NSAIDs, gentamycin, radio-contrast); malaria; haemolytic crisis; snake bite; G6PD deficiency; illegal abortions; unsafe deliveries; crush injury. Post-renal: obstruction to flow of urine (extrinsic or intrinsic) causing damping back pressure, decreased GFR, and increased accumulation of uraemic toxins. STOOP mnemonic: Sepsis and hypoperfusion; Toxicity — drugs and contrast; Obstetric; Obstruction; Parenchymal kidney disease (glomerulonephritis, malignancy).
B(i) Clinical presentation: younger age group predominantly. History of risk factors (CCF, CLD, DM, APH, PPH, gastroenteritis); use of nephrotoxic agents (mercury soap, creams, exposure to Pb in paints); skin rash; use of herbs; reduction in urine output; coke-coloured urine; uraemic syndrome (nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, hiccups, asterixis). Urinalysis: proteinuria (3+, 4+ → intrinsic); haematuria (intrinsic glomerular disease); pyuria (AIN, pyelonephritis, AGN); crystalluria → poisoning (oxalate crystals in ethylene glycol, tumour lysis syndrome, ARVs, acyclovir, sulfonamides); urine osmolality, urine/plasma Cr and urea ratios, urinary Na, FENa, FEurea, Cr clearance. Lab: urine, blood (FBC, ESR, SEUC), ECG, radiology (USS, CXR, CT, MRI).
B(ii) Treatment: adequate volume replacement (use crystalloids instead of colloids); treat sepsis/haemorrhage; avoid/stop nephrotoxic agents; convert oliguria to non-oliguria; watch for polyuric phase (increased Na+, decreased K+); pharmacological Rx not helpful (loop diuretic, dopamine), but fenoldopam — a selective dopamine A-1 receptor agonist — is mentioned. Indications for RRT (clinical and biochemical): uraemic syndrome; uraemic encephalopathy; uraemic pericarditis; recalcitrant oedema/hypertension; severe azotaemia; hyperkalaemia.
questions.question:
Describe acute kidney injury (AKI) under the following headings:
A(i) Define AKI using the KDIGO definition and staging criteria including both serum creatinine and urine output thresholds.
A(ii) Classify the causes of AKI using the pre-renal, renal, and post-renal framework; list causes under each heading, and list the STOOP mnemonic.
B(i) Describe the clinical presentation of AKI including the history, symptoms, and the role of urinalysis in differentiating the cause.
B(ii) State the treatment of AKI including renal replacement therapy (RRT), and list the indications for RRT.

Describe seizures disorders under the following headings:
A(i) Definition of an epileptic seizure and epilepsy.
A(ii) The ILAE five-axis classification system (Axes 1 to 5): describe what each axis covers.
B(i) Describe the clinical features of complex partial seizures including the psychomotor triad, aura, automatisms, and interictal personality changes.
B(ii) Describe the clinical features of absence seizures, distinguishing typical from atypical absence, including EEG findings for each.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Definitions: Epileptic seizure — a paroxysmal event due to abnormal excessive hypersynchronous discharges from an aggregate of cerebral neurons. Epilepsy — a condition in which a person has spontaneous unprovoked recurrent seizures due to a chronic underlying process.
A(ii) ILAE five-axis classification:
Axis 1 — description of ictal semiology using standardised Glossary of Descriptive Terminology (motor or non-motor, positive or negative, simple or complex, autonomic, laterality or centricity, duration, timing, severity, prodrome, postictal).
Axis 2 — epileptic seizure type or types (from 1981 classification), including localisation within the brain and stimulus in reflex seizures; divided into self-limited vs continuous, and generalised vs focal seizures.
Axis 3 — syndromic diagnosis (from 1989 classification); includes epileptic syndromes, related conditions e.g. West and Lennox-Gastaut.
Axis 4 — aetiology: idiopathic, symptomatic, probably symptomatic, reflex, or reactive; 2010 paradigm: genetic, structural/metabolic, or unknown.
Axis 5 — impairment (optional): degree of impairment caused by the epileptic condition, covering body function, mental, and social domains.
B(i) Complex partial seizures: Psychomotor triad — motor changes, automatism, psychic changes. Aura (focal symptoms as in simple partial seizures). Absence (altered consciousness). Automatisms: mimicry (gelastic, lacrimic), ambulatory, verbal, oro-alimentary, responsive. Sudden onset and gradual recovery. Arise from temporal lobe (60%) or frontal lobe (30%). Interictal personality disorder: humourlessness, religiosity, obsessionalism, hypersexuality, violent behaviour, memory loss, psychosis (paranoid schizophrenia), psychic phenomena, hallucinations.
B(ii) Typical absence: sudden onset and cessation; blank stares; consciousness lost with total amnesia; minor signs — tone changes, blinking, eye rolling; duration less than 10 seconds in more than 80%; precipitated by drowsiness, relaxation, hyperventilation, photic stimulation; EEG shows typical 3-Hz spike. Atypical absence: onset and cessation often gradual; prolonged seizures; consciousness only partially impaired; focal signs more prominent — tone changes, motor spasm, clonic jerking, automatism; occurs in patients with diffuse brain damage, mental retardation, other seizure types; EEG usually less than 3-Hz spike.

A(i) HCM:
Definition: A clinically heterogeneous disease defined by a hypertrophied, non-dilated LV in the absence of another systemic or cardiac disease capable of producing the magnitude of wall thickening evident (e.g. systemic hypertension, aortic stenosis). Hypertrophy is usually asymmetric with a thickness ratio >1.3 between the interventricular septum and posterior wall (AHA Scientific Statement 2006).
Genetic basis: autosomal dominant; relatively common (1:500 of the general population for the disease phenotype recognised by echo); about 11 mutant genes encoding contractile proteins of the cardiac sarcomere identified, including: beta myosin heavy chain (chromosome 14q11-12), myosin-binding protein C (chromosome 11P11), cardiac troponin I (chromosome 19p13), cardiac troponin T (chromosome 1g3), regulatory and essential myosin light chains (chromosomes 12q23, 3P21), titin, alpha-tropomyosin (chromosome 15q2), alpha-actin (chromosome 15q11-14), alpha myosin heavy chain, and muscle LIM protein.
Echocardiographic features: asymmetric septal hypertrophy (ASH), concentric or apical hypertrophy; small ventricular cavity; systolic anterior motion (SAM) of the mitral valve; mid-systolic closure of aortic valves; Doppler shows turbulence flow and dynamic gradient in LV outflow tract; mitral regurgitation; diastolic filling pattern in 80% of patients; septum is 1.3–1.5 times the thickness of the posterior wall; septal motion is often reduced.
A(ii) Clinical basis of sudden cardiac death in athletes: HCM is the most common cause of sudden cardiac death in young competitive athletes. The first presentation may be sudden cardiac death — frequent in children and young adults during or after physical exertion. Factors conferring poor prognosis include younger age, male sex, family history of sudden death, history of syncope, genetic markers (mutations of arginine gene), and exercise-induced hypotension (worst predictor). Physical exertion triggers ventricular tachyarrhythmias (non-sustained VT is associated with 6–8% annual mortality) in a heart with structural LV outflow obstruction and diastolic dysfunction.
B(i) Distinguishing HCM from DCM:
• Ventricular dimensions: in HCM the ventricular cavity is small (non-dilated hypertrophied LV); in DCM the LV is dilated (both ventricles may be dilated).
• Systolic function: in HCM systolic function is normal or enhanced (hypercontractile); in DCM global systolic dysfunction is present with ejection fraction <50%.
• Diastolic function: in HCM diastolic dysfunction is the primary abnormality — increased LV end diastolic pressure leads to dyspnoea; in DCM diastolic dysfunction may also occur but systolic failure dominates.
• Characteristic echocardiographic finding: HCM — asymmetric septal hypertrophy with SAM; DCM — dilated left ventricle, global systolic dysfunction, possible spontaneous echo contrast or intracardiac clot, functional mitral and/or tricuspid regurgitation.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) under the following headings: definition, genetic basis (pattern of inheritance and specific proteins encoded by mutant genes), and the echocardiographic features that establish the diagnosis.
A(ii) Explain the clinical basis of why HCM is the most common cause of sudden cardiac death in young competitive athletes.
B(i) Distinguish between hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) and dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) under the headings: ventricular dimensions, systolic function, diastolic function, and the characteristic finding on echocardiography.

A(i) Describe the compartments of body fluid under the following headings: (a) total body water distribution between intracellular and extracellular fluid, (b) sub-divisions of extracellular fluid with their percentages, (c) what constitutes the transcellular ("third space") fluid.
A(ii) State the characteristics of sodium as the principal ECF electrolyte, and describe those of potassium as the principal ICF electrolyte.
B(i) Distinguish between depletional hyponatraemia and dilutional hyponatraemia in terms of causes, and compare their clinical manifestations.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Body fluid compartments:
(a) 2/3 (65%) of total body water (TBW) is intracellular (ICF); 1/3 is extracellular water.
(b) Extracellular water sub-divisions: 25% is interstitial fluid (ISF); 5–8% is in plasma (IVF, intravascular fluid); 1–2% is transcellular fluid.
(c) Transcellular (third space) fluid includes: CSF, intraocular fluids, serous membranes, and fluid in GI, respiratory, and urinary tracts. The ECF constitutes 20% of body mass (intravascular 25%; interstitial 75%; transcellular).
A(ii) Sodium (Na⁺): 90% of total ECF cations; normal plasma 136–145 mEq/L; pairs with Cl⁻ and HCO₃⁻ to neutralise charge; low in ICF; most important ion in regulating water balance; important in nerve and muscle function.
Potassium (K⁺): major intracellular cation; ICF concentration 150–160 mEq/L; determines resting membrane potential; regulates fluid and ion balance inside the cell; involved in pH balance. Regulated through the kidney, aldosterone, and insulin.
B(i) Depletional hyponatraemia: overall decrease in Na⁺ in ECF due to Na⁺ loss — from diuretics, chronic vomiting, chronic diarrhoea, decreased aldosterone, decreased Na⁺ intake.
Dilutional hyponatraemia: plasma Na⁺ diluted by water excess — causes include renal dysfunction with increased intake of hypotonic fluids, excessive sweating → increased thirst → intake of excessive pure water, SIADH, oliguric renal failure, severe congestive heart failure, cirrhosis (all leading to impaired renal excretion of water), and hyperglycaemia (which attracts water).
Clinical manifestations (both types): neurological — lethargy, headache, confusion, apprehension, depressed reflexes, seizures, coma; muscle — cramps, weakness, fatigue; gastrointestinal — nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, diarrhoea.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old man is admitted with generalised weakness, progressive abdominal distension, and yellow discoloration of the eyes. Laboratory results show: Hb 9.2 g/dL, MCV 105 fl, WBC 3,200/μL (neutropenia), platelets 85,000/μL; ALT markedly elevated, AST elevated with AST/ALT ratio >2, ALP elevated, serum albumin low, bilirubin elevated; BUN elevated, creatinine 1.8 mg/dL, urine albumin elevated.
(i) Identify the organ systems affected based on the laboratory clues and state what each abnormality indicates.
(ii) What is the most likely underlying condition linking the haematological, hepatic, and renal findings, and what is the clinical reasoning?
(iii) Describe what the macrocytic anaemia indicates in terms of aetiology, and what the MCV, haematocrit, and peripheral blood film would show.
(iv) What tumour markers and biopsy techniques are relevant if malignancy is suspected?
questions.answerText:
(i) Organ systems and laboratory interpretation:
Haematological: Hb 9.2 g/dL — anaemia; MCV 105 fl — macrocytosis (deficiency of vitamin B12 or folic acid, or hypothyroidism, or alcoholism); WBC 3,200/μL with neutropenia — leukopenia; platelets 85,000/μL — thrombocytopenia.
Hepatic: markedly elevated ALT — ALT is released into blood when liver is damaged, indicating hepatocellular damage (high result is a sign of liver damage); elevated AST with AST/ALT ratio >2 (De Ritis ratio >2) — suggests alcoholic liver disease; elevated ALP — may indicate liver damage, blockage of bile ducts, or bone disease; low serum albumin — albumin is the main protein made by the liver; a low result indicates abnormal liver function; elevated bilirubin — damaged liver cannot properly process bilirubin, leading to high serum bilirubin.
Renal: elevated BUN — BUN measures nitrogen in urea; high BUN may indicate kidney dysfunction (also affected by protein intake and liver function); elevated creatinine 1.8 mg/dL (normal women: 0.6–1.1, men: 0.7–1.3 mg/dL) — elevated creatinine is a more sensitive indicator of impaired kidney function than BUN; elevated urine albumin — damaged nephron filters may leak protein into urine; albumin levels can also be elevated with high blood sugar, bladder infections, or heavy exercise.
(ii) Most likely underlying condition: Alcoholic liver disease with associated hepatic encephalopathy/cirrhosis, causing secondary renal dysfunction (hepatorenal syndrome or direct toxic effect) and bone marrow suppression. Clinical reasoning: AST/ALT ratio >2 is characteristic of alcoholic hepatitis; macrocytic anaemia with thrombocytopenia and neutropenia suggests hypersplenism (from portal hypertension) and nutritional deficiencies (B12, folate) from alcohol; low albumin and elevated bilirubin confirm hepatic synthetic failure; raised creatinine and urine albumin indicate renal involvement.
(iii) Macrocytic anaemia: MCV >100 fl indicates macrocytosis; aetiology — deficiency of vitamin B12 or folic acid; also hypothyroidism; alcoholism.
Haematocrit: a low haematocrit level might mean anaemia; abnormal haematocrit levels may be a sign of blood or bone marrow disorder.
Peripheral blood film in macrocytic anaemia: macrocytosis (increased RBC size); polychromasia; normoblasts (in severe haemolysis). In haemolysis: fragmented red cells (schistocytes — suggests TTP, HUS, or mechanical damage); spherocytes (hereditary spherocytosis or AIHA).
(iv) Tumour markers and biopsy:
- AFP (alpha-fetoprotein): used for monitoring treatment for liver cancer.
- CA-125: used to monitor progress in ovarian cancer.
- PSA: monitored in prostate cancer.
Biopsy techniques: Fine needle aspiration (FNA) — fine needle on syringe inserted into a lesion with negative pressure to suck up cells for microscopy; checks for tumour cells. Excision biopsy — entire lesion removed and sliced into thin sections for microscopy. Core biopsy — small part of a lesion removed for microscopy to make a diagnosis. Cytology — obtaining normal tissue fluid and examining for early signs of cancer cells. Tissue histology: confirms malignant diagnosis.

(i) Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (AIHA) — the most common form of acquired haemolytic anaemia next to malaria.
Mechanism: an autoantibody is directed against a red cell antigen, triggering immune-mediated haemolysis. Clinical suspicion must be high in any patient with anaemia, jaundice, and splenomegaly; confirmed by the Coombs antiglobulin test.
(ii) Classification subtypes:
- Warm antibody AIHA.
- Cold antibody AIHA.
- Drug-induced (nitrates, chlorates, methylene blue, dapsone, cisplatin; arsine, stibine, copper, lead).
(iii) Treatment approach:
- First-line: glucocorticoids (1 mg/kg).
- Rituximab (anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody) — remissions in up to 80%.
- Transfusion of red cells (supportive).
- Second-line: long-term immunosuppression with low-dose prednisone, azathioprine, or cyclosporine.
- Splenectomy (for refractory cases).
(iv) Role of splenectomy in AIHA: used in refractory cases where first- and second-line immunosuppression fails.
Other haemolytic anaemia where splenectomy is indicated — Hereditary Spherocytosis (HS): splenectomy should be postponed until 4 years of age; indications — severe haemolysis, family history of death from similar disease, evidence of cholecystitis and cholelithiasis. H. influenzae vaccine must be given 2 weeks before splenectomy.
questions.question:
A 40-year-old woman presents with progressive fatigue, jaundice, and splenomegaly. Investigations reveal anaemia, elevated unconjugated bilirubin, and a positive direct Coombs (antiglobulin) test.
(i) What is the diagnosis, and what is the mechanism by which red cell destruction occurs?
(ii) What are the classification subtypes of this condition?
(iii) Describe the treatment approach from first-line to second-line therapy, naming drugs and their targets.
(iv) What is the role of splenectomy in this condition, and name one other haemolytic anaemia where splenectomy is also indicated with its specific timing restriction.

Describe sarcoidosis under the following headings:
A(i) Definition, introduction, and who is most affected by sarcoidosis.
A(ii) Describe the multi-organ involvement of sarcoidosis including the proportion affected, and describe Heerfordt-Waldenström syndrome.
B(i) Describe the differential diagnosis of granulomatous lung disease.
B(ii) Describe the summary of diagnosis and treatment criteria.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Definition: Sarcoidosis is a systemic, multi-organ, granulomatous disease of unknown aetiology, characterised by the presence of granuloma in various organs. It can affect almost any organ, but the lungs are the most affected. Usually associated with chest symptoms but also multiple extra-pulmonary manifestations such as erythema nodosum and lymphadenopathy. Symptoms can vary from asymptomatic (in up to 50%) to severe and life-threatening. Two spikes in incidence: in young adulthood and again around age 60. Women are affected more often; occurs more frequently in black people compared with other groups.
A(ii) Multi-organ involvement: Lungs (over 90%) — mediastinal lymphadenopathy, pulmonary fibrosis, pulmonary nodules. Liver (20%) — liver nodules, cirrhosis, cholestasis. Eyes (20%) — conjunctivitis, uveitis, optic neuritis. Skin (15%) — erythema nodosum (tender red nodules on shins from subcutaneous fat inflammation); lupus pernio (raised purple skin lesions on cheeks and nose); granulomas in scar tissue. Heart (5%) — bundle branch block, heart block, myocardial muscle involvement. Kidneys (5%) — kidney stones (due to hypercalcaemia), nephrocalcinosis, interstitial nephritis. CNS (5%) — nodules, pituitary involvement (diabetes insipidus), encephalopathy, facial nerve palsy. Peripheral nervous system (5%) — mononeuritis multiplex (painful, asymmetrical, asynchronous sensory and motor peripheral neuropathy involving isolated damage to at least 2 separate nerve areas). Musculoskeletal (2%) — arthralgia, arthritis, myopathy. Heerfordt-Waldenström syndrome: a rare subacute variant characterised by enlargement of the parotid or salivary glands, facial nerve paralysis, and anterior uveitis; granulomas with a peripheral lymphocyte deficit are found in affected organs.
B(i) Differential diagnosis of granulomatous lung disease: 1. Infectious conditions — tuberculosis; atypical mycobacterial infections; invasive fungal infections (histoplasmosis, aspergillosis, blastomycosis, Pneumocystis jirovecii). 2. Hypersensitivity pneumonitis; pneumoconiosis; drug-induced hypersensitivity pneumonitis. 3. Foreign body granulomatosis. 4. Vasculitides — granulomatosis with polyangiitis; eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Churg-Strauss syndrome); pulmonary lymphomatoid granulomatosis.
B(ii) Summary: Sarcoidosis is a systemic disease that can affect any organ, with the lungs and intrathoracic lymph nodes being the most frequently affected sites. Diagnosis relies on the presence of noncaseating granuloma on histopathological examination, compatible clinical presentation, and exclusion of other causes of granulomatous inflammation. Treatment is reserved for patients with disabling symptoms or progressive organ damage/dysfunction because spontaneous remission is frequent. Glucocorticoids are first-line therapy, whereas glucocorticoid-sparing agents and biologic agents are used in refractory/recurrent cases. Most common sign of sarcoidosis is lymphadenopathy.

(i) Atopic dermatitis (atopic eczema).
(ii) Risk factors and associations:
- Personal or family history of atopic dermatitis, allergic rhinitis, and asthma
- Skin barrier dysfunction
- IgE reactivity
- Genetic basis
- Disease usually begins in infancy and is characterized by dry skin and pruritus
(iii) Complications:
- Secondary bacterial infection (requiring MCS swabs to rule out)
- Scratching leads to increased inflammation and lichenification, which encourages further itching and scratching (itch-scratch circle)
- Excoriation, fissures
- Pigmentary changes (post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation/hypopigmentation)
- Chronic lichenification from the itch-scratch cycle
(iv) Management:
- Remove or reverse the underlying cause
- Anti-inflammatory agents: steroids (hydrocortisone for face and flexures); calcineurin inhibitors (role: provide anti-inflammatory effect at sensitive sites such as face and flexures where prolonged steroid use risks atrophy, making calcineurin inhibitors a steroid-sparing option)
- Treat secondary infection with topical or systemic antibiotics
- Antihistamines to reduce pruritus
- Keep fingernails short and filed to reduce excoriation
- Rest and elevation of affected limb where applicable (e.g. stasis eczema)
questions.question:
A 35-year-old woman presents with a 6-month history of intensely itchy skin lesions. She reports a history of childhood asthma, allergic rhinitis, and several family members with similar skin problems. Examination reveals erythema, scaling, papules, and lichenification predominantly in the flexures.
(i) What is the most likely diagnosis?
(ii) Identify the risk factors and personal or family associations.
(iii) Describe the complications that may develop if the itch-scratch cycle continues unchecked.
(iv) State the management options, justifying the role of topical calcineurin inhibitors.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Epidemiology and genetic basis:
- Occurs in 1-3% of the population
- Polygenic mode of inheritance: one parent = 8%, two parents = 41%
- HLA associations: HLA-B13, -B17, -Bw57, HLA-Cw6
- Age of onset: early peak at 20-30 years (early disease predicts more severe, long-lasting disease; positive family history usually present); late onset around 55 years
- Equal incidence in females and males
- Low incidence in West Africans, Japanese, and Inuits
- Disease is lifelong with chronic, recurrent exacerbations and remissions
- Trigger factors: physical trauma, infections, stress, drugs (lithium, beta-blockers, antimalarial agents, systemic steroids, interferon), alcohol ingestion

A(ii) Pathogenesis:
- Alteration of cell kinetics of keratinocytes: cell cycle shortened from 311 to 36 hours — 28 times normal production of epidermal cells
- Migration of keratinocyte from basal layer to stratum corneum shortened from 28 days to 3-5 days
- Increased proliferation driven by a cascade of inflammatory processes
- Psoriasis is a T cell-driven disease: Th1 and Th17 cells play a major role

B(i) Clinical features:
- Begin as red scaling papules that coalesce/enlarge to form round-oval erythematous plaques, easily distinguished from normal skin
- Scale is adherent, silvery white, and reveals bleeding points when removed — Auspitz's sign
- Psoriasis can develop at sites of trauma — Koebner's phenomenon
- Affects extensor surfaces more than flexors
- Common sites: elbows, knees, scalp, gluteal cleft, fingernails and toenails
Nail changes: pitting (most frequent), oil spot lesion (most characteristic), onycholysis, subungual hyperkeratosis, nail deformity (fragmentation and crumbling), splinter haemorrhages, leukonychia.

B(ii) Treatment:
Topical: steroids, calcineurin inhibitors, calcipotriene, tazarotene, tar (crude/anthralin derivative such as dithranol); intralesional steroids for small plaques; use with/without UV exposure; inflammation must be suppressed before initiating other treatment. Scalp: remove scale first with tar + salicylic acid shampoos; steroid gels with keratolytic base.
Systemic: methotrexate, PUVA, UVB, acitretin, cyclosporin, apremilast; rotational therapy/combination.
Biologics: etanercept, infliximab, adalimumab, ustekinumab, guselkumab, tildrakizumab, secukinumab, ixekizumab, bimekizumab.
Criterion for effective treatment: plaque is effectively treated when induration has disappeared — if the plaque cannot be felt when the finger is drawn over it, treatment can be stopped.
questions.question:
Describe psoriasis under the following headings:
A(i) Epidemiology and genetic basis — including HLA associations, age of onset, sex, and trigger factors.
A(ii) Pathogenesis, including cell kinetics of keratinocytes and the role of T cells.
B(i) Clinical features: describe the primary lesion, special signs, common sites, and nail changes.
B(ii) Treatment: list all topical agents and all systemic/biologic agents, and state the criterion for when a plaque can be considered effectively treated.

A 10-year-old boy is brought in with recurrent mild anaemia, intermittent jaundice, and splenomegaly. His mother had her gallbladder removed for pigment stones at age 35. Blood film shows microcytosis and numerous spherocytes. The direct Coombs test is negative.
(i) What is the most likely diagnosis?
(ii) What are the predisposing (genetic and structural) factors that underlie this condition?
(iii) Describe the pathophysiology that leads to the characteristic blood film findings and the clinical triad.
(iv) Outline the full management of this patient.
questions.answerText:
(i) Hereditary spherocytosis (HS).
(ii) Predisposing factors:
- Inherited as an autosomal dominant condition.
- Caused by a defect in proteins (spectrin, ankyrin) that anchor the lipid bilayer to the underlying cytoskeleton.
- Abnormality of any component of the membrane cytoskeletal complex leads to structural failure and haemolysis.
- Confirmed by molecular studies demonstrating a mutation in one of the genes underlying HS.
(iii) Pathophysiology:
- Defective cytoskeletal anchoring destabilises the red cell membrane, producing spherocytes — cells with reduced surface-to-volume ratio and increased osmotic fragility.
- Spherocytes are trapped and destroyed in the spleen → extravascular haemolysis → reduced RBC lifespan.
- Blood film: microcytosis, spherocytes; MCV ↓, MCHC ↑; osmotic fragility ↑ (pink test positive); autohemolysis test ↑ (10–15%; normal <4%); ↑ reticulocyte count.
- Clinical triad: anaemia (from haemolysis), unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and jaundice (↑ bilirubin production), splenomegaly (from sequestration), and pigment gallstones (↑ bile pigment production), and chronic leg ulcers.
(iv) Management:
- Blood transfusion in cases of severe haemolytic crises.
- Folic acid supplementation 5 mg/day.
- Splenectomy: should be postponed until age 4 years; indications — severe haemolysis, family history of death from similar disease, evidence of cholecystitis and cholelithiasis.
- H. influenzae vaccine must be given 2 weeks before splenectomy.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old man presents to the dermatology clinic with a 3-month history of skin lesions and numbness over one area of skin. On examination there is a single, erythematous plaque with raised and clear-cut edges, sloping towards a flattened hypopigmented centre. The surface of the lesion is anaesthetic, dry, and hairless. A thickened peripheral nerve is palpable at the edge of the lesion.
(i) State the most likely diagnosis and classify this patient within the Ridley-Jopling spectrum.
(ii) List the predisposing and epidemiological risk factors for this disease.
(iii) Describe the full spectrum of complications.
(iv) Outline the WHO-recommended treatment protocol for this patient's category, including drug names, doses, and duration.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Tuberculoid leprosy (TT) within the Ridley-Jopling spectrum.
Justification: single erythematous/purple plaque with raised and clear-cut edges sloping towards a flattened hypopigmented centre; surface is anaesthetised, dry, and hairless; thickened cutaneous nerve palpable at edge; no M. leprae found in skin smears; localised and asymmetrical. WHO classification: paucibacillary (TT, BT).

(ii) Predisposing/epidemiological risk factors:
- Endemic in developing countries: Asia, Africa, Latin America, Pacific
- Overcrowding, poor sanitation, poor nutrition
- Race: Africans tend toward tuberculoid form; light skin associated with lepromatous leprosy
- LL more common in males than females (2:1)
- In children, tuberculoid form predominates
- HIV is NOT a risk factor
- Transmission: contact with leprosy cases; more recently by respiratory route; handling/eating armadillos; insect transmission cannot be completely ruled out
- Incubation period: 6 months to 50 years

(iii) Complications:
Extremities: anaesthesia and myopathy; plantar ulceration; loss of distal digits (insensitivity, trauma, secondary infections, profound osteolytic process); nerve palsies.
Nose: chronic nasal congestion; epistaxis; anosmia; destruction of nasal cartilage (saddle nose).
Ocular: blindness; in tuberculoid leprosy — 7th and 5th nerve damage causing lagophthalmos, corneal erosion, keratitis; in lepromatous leprosy — massive bacillary infiltration causing keratitis, iritis, iridocyclitis.
Systemic: nephrotic syndrome/CKD; testicular dysfunction; impotence/infertility; leprae reactions/Lucio phenomenon; stigmatization; amyloidosis (seen in LL and ENL); nerve abscess/sepsis.

(iv) WHO MDT for Paucibacillary (TT/BT):
- Daily dapsone 100 mg for 6 months
- Monthly supervised rifampicin 600 mg
- Duration: 6 months
Five main principles of treatment: (1) Stop infection with chemotherapy; (2) Treat reactions; (3) Educate the patient; (4) Prevent disability; (5) Support the patient socially and psychologically.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old man presents with a 6-month history of progressive exertional dyspnoea, orthopnoea, and palpitations. He has no history of rheumatic fever. On examination his pulse is bounding with a wide pulse pressure; his apex beat is hyperdynamic and displaced; auscultation reveals a diastolic blowing murmur at the left sternal border.
(i) What is the most likely diagnosis? List the causes of chronic aortic regurgitation.
(ii) Explain the combined pressure and volume overload in this condition and the compensatory mechanisms that develop.
(iii) At what ejection fraction and clinical threshold do indications for surgery arise in asymptomatic chronic aortic regurgitation?
(iv) What is the treatment of acute aortic regurgitation and why must beta-blockers be avoided?
(v) State the echocardiographic role in monitoring and decision-making for this patient.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Chronic Aortic Regurgitation. Causes of chronic AR: rheumatic disease, infective endocarditis, bicuspid aortic valve.
(ii) Combined pressure and volume overload: aortic regurgitation causes leakage of blood into the LV during diastole due to ineffective coaptation of the aortic cusps (definition); this creates combined pressure AND volume overload — the LV receives its normal filling from the left atrium plus the regurgitant volume from the aorta during diastole. Compensatory mechanisms: LV dilation and LVH develop to accommodate the increased volume load; progressive dilation eventually leads to heart failure. Symptoms are typically absent until the 4th or 5th decade. Progressive symptoms include dyspnoea (exertional, orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea), nocturnal angina (due to slowing of heart rate and reduction of diastolic blood pressure), and palpitations (due to increased force of contraction).
(iii) Surgery threshold in asymptomatic chronic AR: any symptoms at rest or exercise; asymptomatic if EF drops below 50% OR LV becomes dilated.
(iv) Treatment of acute AR — true surgical emergency. Medications: positive inotrope (e.g. dopamine, dobutamine); vasodilators (e.g. nitroprusside). Beta-blockers must be avoided because mild-to-moderate tachycardia is beneficial in acute AR — it allows less time for the heart to have backfill, which lowers regurgitant volume; slowing the heart with beta-blockers would increase the diastolic filling time and worsen regurgitation. A balloon pump is also contraindicated in acute AR.
(v) Echocardiographic role: cornerstone for decision-making and follow-up. It allows evaluation of the aortic valve and aortic root with measurements of LV dimensions and function; serial echocardiograms monitor progression. Imaging schedule: general valve-disease follow-up guidance applies (mild disease reviewed every 2–3 years); serial echocardiography is used to monitor progression and to assess when EF falls below 50% or the LV becomes dilated, both of which act as triggers for surgery. Aortography is used to confirm severity of disease.

A(i) Epidemiology: Prevalence 43–84 per million population. Annual incidence rate 1 per 300,000. Under 40, F:M = 2–3:1. In later life, F:M = 2:3. Of patients with thymomas, majority are older (50–60 years) and males predominate. Modality: ocular (39.3%); generalized (28.5%); bulbar (31.3%); respiratory (0.8%).
A(ii) Associated diseases: thymic tumours in 10–15%; nonneoplastic lymphofollicular hyperplasia of thymic medulla in 65% or more; thyroid disorders (thyroiditis, Graves'); connective tissue diseases (Rheumatoid, SLE); other autoimmune diseases (vitiligo, Addison's); disorders interfering with treatment (diabetes, peptic ulcer, GI bleeding, renal disease, hypertension, asthma, osteoporosis, TB); exacerbating conditions — hypo/hyperthyroidism, occult infection, aminoglycosides, muscle relaxants, anti-arrhythmic drugs, quinine, penicillamine. Drugs and mechanisms: Penicillamine — may be directly antigenic after binding to AChR receptors; Aminoglycosides — impair AChR binding at postsynaptic receptor; Ciprofloxacin — both worsening and induction; Beta-adrenergic blockers — reported to induce myasthenic symptoms; Lithium carbonate — drug-induced reduction in ACh receptors; Procainamide — may worsen or induce MG; Corticosteroids — clinical worsening (myopathy, dose-dependent).
B(i) Management of myasthenic crisis: Timely and careful intubation followed by mechanical ventilation in a critical care unit. Respiratory failure in some may be managed with BiPAP. Anticholinergic drugs (exaggerate secretions) are best withdrawn at time of intubation. Plasma exchange hastens improvement and weaning from ventilator. IV gamma globulin is a useful alternative. Response to plasma exchange or immunoglobulin may occur in 1–2 days but often a week or more is required. Generally best to wait 2–3 weeks before committing to tracheostomy. Anticholinesterases are given.
B(ii) Anaesthesia: Any surgical procedure can cause decompensation. If unable to take medications orally, anticholinesterase IM (one-thirtieth of oral dose of pyridostigmine, one-tenth of neostigmine). Continue corticosteroids at same dose. Non-competitive neuromuscular blocking agents may have prolonged effect and should be avoided; if necessary, anticipate mechanical ventilation. Succinylcholine (not recommended) may require larger dose. Pregnancy: usually uncomplicated; IV cholinesterase inhibitors contraindicated (may induce uterine contractions); cytotoxic drugs generally avoided (fetal abnormalities); magnesium not recommended for eclampsia (neuromuscular blocking effects); breast-feeding not thought problematic for AChR antibody transmission.
questions.question:
Describe Myasthenia Gravis under the following headings:
A(i) Epidemiology including prevalence, annual incidence, sex and age of onset, and modality of presentation.
A(ii) Diseases associated with myasthenia gravis and drugs that worsen or induce it (with their mechanisms).
B(i) Describe the management of myasthenic crisis, from recognition through to definitive treatment.
B(ii) Describe the management of anaesthesia in a patient with MG, and the management of MG in pregnancy.

A 28-year-old woman known with atopy presents to the emergency department with a 6-hour history of severe breathlessness. She is unable to complete sentences, is visibly sweating, and has a respiratory rate of 28 cycles/min and a pulse rate of 115/min. Peak expiratory flow is measured at 40% of predicted. She uses a dust-mite-sensitized environment at home and recently started aspirin for joint pains.
(i) What is the diagnosis and what specific features in this presentation confirm acute severe rather than life-threatening asthma?
(ii) List all the risk and predisposing factors applicable to this patient, including phenotype classification.
(iii) Describe the airway pathology that underlies her current attack.
(iv) What is the immediate emergency management, including drug doses and routes, and what investigations must be performed?
(v) State the criteria that must be met before she is safely discharged from hospital.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Acute severe asthma. Features confirming acute severe (not life-threatening): diaphoresis, dyspnoea at rest, audible wheeze, talking in monosyllables/unable to complete sentences in one breath, agitation, tachypnoea with respiratory rate >25 cycles/min, tachycardia >110/min, and peak expiratory flow 33–50% of predicted or patient's best, hyperinflated chest, widespread polyphonic wheezes. Life-threatening features would include confusion, exhaustion, feeble respiratory efforts, cyanosis, bradycardia, silent chest, PEF ≤33% of predicted — none of which are present here.
(ii) Risk and predisposing factors: Parental history of asthma or atopy; atopic patients have a high prevalence of asthma, allergic rhinitis, urticaria, and eczema. Sensitization to allergies (dust mite) — directly applicable. Drug triggers: aspirin/NSAIDs — applicable; NSAID-sensitive (aspirin-sensitive) is a recognized phenotype (late onset/aspirin-sensitive asthma). Phenotype: This patient fits Allergic/Early Onset Disease (higher serum IgE, history of eczema possible) or Aspirin-Sensitive Asthma (may or may not have history of exacerbation in response to NSAID). Triggers include exercise, cold air, viral respiratory infection, allergen exposure (feather pillows and cat dander), seasonal factors (e.g., grass pollen), and drugs (beta-blocker, aspirin). Genes: ADAM33, FCER1B, TNF, ACE, B2-AR, IL-4R, IL-13 are susceptible genes.
(iii) Airway pathology: Asthma is a 2-component disease — smooth muscle dysfunction and airway inflammation/remodelling. Pathology includes: bronchial epithelial infiltration by eosinophils, mononuclear cells, and T-lymphocytes; endobronchial mucus plugging; mucosal oedema/microvascular leak; disrupted epithelium/shedding; hypertrophied smooth muscle; fibrosis under basement membrane, subepithelial fibrosis (deposition of type III and V collagen). Trigger factor irritates the airway releasing chemical mediators from mast cells. Bronchial tubes over-react on allergen exposure leading to constriction and spasm (airway hyper-responsiveness). Excess mucus and fluid accumulate (airway congestion). Long-term inflammation leads to formation of mucus plugs with airflow limitation (airway oedema). Normal airway tissues may be replaced by scar tissues (airway remodelling).
(iv) Immediate treatment: Oxygen 40–60%; Salbutamol 5mg via oxygen-driven nebuliser; Prednisolone tablets 40–50mg or IV hydrocortisone 100mg or both if very ill; No sedatives of any kind; Chest radiograph. Investigations: Lung function tests — PEF, spirometer, reversibility (200 µg of inhaled salbutamol, repeat PEF or FEV1 after 15–20 minutes, increased by 15–20%); Increased Total Lung Capacity; Arterial blood gases (ABG) — PaO2, PaCO2; Pulse oximeter — arterial O2 saturation (PaO2).
(v) Discharge criteria: Patient should have been on discharge medication for 24 hours and had inhaler technique checked and recorded; PEF >75% of best or predicted and PEF diurnal variability <25% unless discharge is agreed with respiratory physician; Treatment with oral and inhaled steroids in addition to bronchodilators; Own PEF meter and written asthma action plan; Determine reason(s) for exacerbation and admission.

A(i) Colorectal carcinoma epidemiology: relatively uncommon in Africans/Asians; second to lung cancer as cause of cancer death in USA; commonly affects those aged 50 and above. Risk factors: high socioeconomic class; decreased fibre diet; increased animal fat; IBD/Crohn's disease; polyposis coli; alcohol consumption; Streptococcus bovis bacteraemia; genetic/hereditary (mutations of K-ras gene, allelic losses in chromosomes 5q, 18q, and 17p, FAP, Torres's syndrome, Turcot's syndrome, familial juvenile polyposis syndrome, Peutz-Jeghers syndrome). Probable protective factors: high fibre diet, yellow-green vegetables, calcium, carotene-rich foods, vitamins E and C. Types: ulcerative, annular/tubular, cauliflower/polypoid, proliferative/fungating. Duke's classification: A — limited to mucosa; B — muscularis propria plus serosa; C — metastasis to nodes/serosa; D — distant metastasis.
A(ii) Symptoms: bloody/mucoid stools; change in bowel habit (constipation/diarrhoea); tenesmus; passage of pencil or pellet-like stools; crampy abdominal pains; weight loss; symptoms from anaemia (fatigue, weakness); DRE positive in about 50% of cases. Investigations: fibreoptic colonoscopy or proctosigmoidoscopy with multiple biopsies; barium studies; high-resolution ultrasonography (7.5 MHz probe); virtual colonoscopy with CT; MRI colonography; CEA (not good for early diagnosis); FOBT; detection of shed cancer cells by cytometry; biochemical and immunologic detection of fecal cancer-associated antigens; detection of mutated protooncogenes such as K-ras in stool. Treatment: staging is important; treatment mainly surgical; resectional surgery combined with chemotherapy may be curative; newer drugs: irinotecan (Campto), capecitabine (Xeloda — oral prodrug of 5-FU), oxaliplatin (Eloxatin); 5-FU plus folinic acid (leucovorin); combinations of immunomodulators (levamisole) with 5-FU better than 5-FU alone; radiotherapy as adjunctive therapy in selected cases; alpha interferon useful in carcinoid tumours.
B(i) Gallbladder carcinoma: most common biliary tract neoplasm and fifth most common GI malignancy in the USA; estimated annual incidence about 1.2 cases per 100,000; highest incidences in Chile, Israel, NE Europe, American Indian and Mexican-American populations; most commonly in seventh decade; women two to six times more commonly affected. Late presentation; paucity of effective treatments; 5-year survival about 5%. Aetiology: chronic epithelial irritation and inflammation from gallstones; bacterial contamination of biliary tree with gallstones and chronic cholecystitis; other chemical carcinogens (isoniazid, methyldopa, OCP — unproven); calcification of gallbladder wall. Histology: mostly adenocarcinomas; squamous, adenosquamous, or oat cell carcinomas are rare. Clinical features: constant upper abdominal pain; anorexia; weight loss; jaundice; pruritus; acholic stools. Investigations: serum tumour markers (CEA >4 ng/mL is 93% specific and 50% sensitive; CA 19-9 >20 U/mL has 79.4% sensitivity and 79.5% specificity); elevations of serum bilirubin and alkaline phosphatase; USS/CT/PTC/ERCP.
B(ii) Investigations for upper GIT diseases: Radiological — plain X-rays; contrast X-rays (barium meal); USS; CT scans; MRI. Endoscopic — oesophagogastroscopy; capsule endoscopy; laparoscopy. Plain abdominal X-rays: intestinal obstruction (multiple air/fluid levels); perforated DU or GU (air under the diaphragm); gastric outlet obstruction (pelvic J-shaped stomach). Barium meal: gastric outlet obstruction; stomach ulcers; carcinoma of the stomach. Abdominal USS: gallstones; PLCC; amoebic liver abscess. Upper GI endoscopy: diagnostic and therapeutic in bleeding ulcers; bleeding controlled by diathermy, clipping, and injection of vasoconstrictors; photographs and biopsies taken; also useful for endoscopic intra-luminal ultrasound scans of the pancreas. Abdominal examination findings: Inspection — upper abdominal peristalsis left to right suggests early gastric outlet obstruction; periumbilical ecchymosis (Cullen's sign) or flank ecchymosis (Grey Turner's sign) suggests haemorrhagic pancreatitis; distended veins around umbilicus (caput medusae) suggests portal hypertension. Percussion — tympanitic abdomen suggests intestinal obstruction; stony dull suggests fluid (ascites, blood, or urine); shifting dullness or fluid thrill confirms ascites. Auscultation — hyperactive bowel sounds in early obstruction; hypoactive in later phase; absent in peritonitis or severe paralytic ileus; arterial bruits over vascular liver tumours.
questions.question:
Describe colorectal carcinoma under the following headings:
A(i) Epidemiology, aetiology and risk factors, types, and Duke's classification.
A(ii) Symptoms, investigations, and treatment of colorectal carcinoma.
B(i) Describe gallbladder carcinoma: epidemiology, aetiology, histology, clinical features, and investigations.
B(ii) Describe the investigations and common clinical associations for upper gastrointestinal diseases on upper GIT symptoms, including the abdominal examination findings.

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Lichen planus — a chronic inflammatory dermatosis characterised by flat-topped, violaceous, shiny, pruritic polygonal papules with Wickham's striae (fine whitish reticulate network).

(ii) Predisposing factors, associated conditions, and inducing drugs:
Risk/predisposing: ages 30-60; familial predisposition; HLA associations (HLA-B7, -Aw19, -B18, -Cw8 familial; HLA-A3, -A5, -A28, -B8, -B16, -Bw35 non-familial); seasonal variation.
Associated conditions: autoimmune chronic active hepatitis, primary biliary cirrhosis, HCV (16-29%), syphilis, HSV, HBV, amoebiasis, chronic bladder infection, dyslipidaemia, metabolic syndrome.
Drugs commonly inducing LP: beta-blockers, gold salts, antimalarials, thiazide, frusemide, spironolactone, penicillamine.
Uncommonly: ACEI, CCB, sulphonamides, NSAIDs, tetracyclines, phenothiazines.
Rarely: methyldopa, anti-TB drugs, lithium, iodides.
Contact chemicals: colour developers, dental materials, gold, nickel, musk ambrette.

(iii) Pathophysiology:
- Immunologic — cell-mediated immunity (T cells)
- Three stages: (1) Antigen recognition → (2) Lymphocyte activation → (3) Keratinocyte apoptosis (basal cells)
Histologically: hyperkeratosis; wedge-shaped areas of hypergranulosis; elongated rete ridges (saw-tooth appearance); vacuolation/liquefaction of the basal layer; Civatte bodies at dermo-epidermal junction; band-like dense lympho-histiocytic infiltrate at papillary dermis abutting epidermis; IgM (less frequently IgA, C3) in colloid bodies on immunofluorescence; heavy deposition of fibrin at dermo-epidermal junction.

(iv) Treatment:
- Potent topical steroids (0.05% clobetasone propionate); occlusion enhances effectiveness
- Intralesional steroids (triamcinolone acetonide); repeated every 3-4 weeks
- Systemic steroids: 20-40 mg/day for 2-4 weeks; gradually reduced over 3 weeks
- Antihistamines
- Acitretin
- Azathioprine
- Cyclosporine: for severe, chronic LP
- PUVA: for generalised, symptomatic LP; maintenance may not be required once complete clearance attained
- Dapsone
- Hydroxychloroquine
- Low-dose enoxaparin

A 28-year-old woman presents with a 1-month history of itchy, purplish, shiny flat-topped papules on her wrists and lower extremities. She also reports white lacy lines visible on some lesions. Nail examination reveals longitudinal ridging and thinning of several nails.
(i) What is the diagnosis?

questions.answerText:
(i) Two major forms: Pyogenic liver abscess — acute presentation; high-grade swinging pyrexia; right upper quadrant pain; may present with shock; hepatomegaly; right upper quadrant tenderness. Amoebic liver abscess — subacute presentation; right upper quadrant pain; fever; malaise, myalgias, arthralgias; jaundice.
(ii) Sources of infection for pyogenic liver abscess: appendicitis; cholangitis; cholecystitis; diverticulitis; perforated peptic ulcer; peritonitis; may complicate HCC. Cryptogenic origin. Most are polymicrobial; most frequently isolated organisms are Escherichia coli, Klebsiella, Proteus, Pseudomonas, Streptococcus.
(iii) Investigations for both: abdominal ultrasound scan; culture of aspirated abscess material; computed tomography; blood culture; full blood count (anaemia, leucocytosis); liver function tests (elevated alkaline phosphatase). Additional for amoebic: aspiration typically yields reddish-brown pasty aspirate (anchovy paste or chocolate sauce); serologic testing (ELISA) to detect serum antibody levels.
(iv) Pathogenesis of amoebic abscess: ingestion of cysts from contaminated food/water → gastrointestinal tract → trophozoites in the colon → mucosal invasion → flask-shaped ulcers → portal circulation → liver → abscess. Abscesses can also form in the lungs, brain, pleural, pericardial, and peritoneal spaces.
(v) Treatment: Pyogenic — broad-spectrum antibiotics before culture result; antibiotics changed later based on culture result. Amoebic — metronidazole is the antibiotic of choice plus aspiration of the abscess.
questions.question:
A 55-year-old man with known chronic alcohol use presents with right upper quadrant pain of 2 weeks' duration associated with high-grade swinging pyrexia, hepatomegaly, and right upper quadrant tenderness. He is shocked on arrival.
(i) What are the two major forms of hepatic abscess and their differentiating features in terms of clinical presentation?
(ii) Outline the sources of infection for pyogenic liver abscess.
(iii) State the investigations required for each form of abscess, including the characteristic appearance of aspirated material in amoebic abscess.

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia (CCCA).
Absence of regrowth in the centre indicates scarring (cicatricial) alopecia: stem cells in the bulge region have been permanently lost, resulting in irreversible destruction of the hair follicle. Prognosis is grave for scarring alopecias.

(ii) Risk factors, predisposing factors, and pathological mechanism:
- Commonest in females
- Linked to caustic hair care products and/or hair styles causing traction (braids, weaves) — may aggravate the disease or hasten progression in genetically predisposed individuals
- Current hypothesis: patients are predisposed to follicular damage because of an anatomical abnormality (premature desquamation of the inner root sheath (IRS))

(iii) Treatment and prognosis:
Treatment:
- Potent topical steroids
- Intralesional steroids
- Doxycycline
- Antifungal shampoos
- Minoxidil
Prognosis: chronic and progressive disease with eventual spontaneous burn-out after years or decades. Grave for scarring alopecias as destruction is irreversible.

(iv) Full differential diagnoses of scarring alopecias:
- Discoid lupus erythematosus
- Lichen planopilaris
- Frontal fibrosing alopecia (a variant of LPP; progressive hair loss along anterior hairline and eyebrows)
- Central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia (CCCA)
- Folliculitis decalvans
- Acne keloidalis nuchae
- Dissecting cellulitis of the scalp
- Late traction alopecia
Investigations for this case: scalp biopsy (to confirm scarring and identify histology); trichoscopy; hormone assays; hair pull test; trichogram; scalp scraping for fungal studies.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Classification of haemolytic anaemia:
1. Intravascular vs extravascular haemolysis.
2. Acquired vs hereditary.
3. Intracorpuscular vs extracorpuscular.
4. Immune vs non-immune.
Hereditary (intracorpuscular) examples: haemoglobinopathies (HbS, thalassaemias); enzymopathies (G6PD deficiency, pyruvate kinase deficiency); membrane–cytoskeletal defects (hereditary spherocytosis, elliptocytosis, ovalocytosis, stomatocytosis); acquired red cell membrane abnormality (PNH).
Acquired (extracorpuscular) examples: AIHA (warm antibody, cold antibody); drug-induced; mechanical trauma (microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia); infection/direct toxic effect (malaria, Shiga toxin–producing E. coli O157:H7); splenomegaly; hereditary — familial HUS.
A(ii) Tests of increased red cell breakdown:
- Serum bilirubin — indirect/unconjugated: ↑.
- Urine urobilinogen: ↑.
- Faecal stercobilinogen: ↑.
- Serum haptoglobin: ↓ or absent.
- Plasma LDH: ↑.
- Evidence of intravascular haemolysis: haemoglobinaemia, haemoglobinuria, methaemoglobinaemia, haemosiderinuria.
B(i) Tests of increased red cell production:
- Reticulocyte count (RC): ↑.
- PBF: macrocytosis, polychromasia, normoblasts.
- Bone marrow: erythroid hyperplasia, raised iron stores.
- X-ray of bone: evidence of expansion of marrow space (tubular bones and skull).
PBF findings in specific haemolytic anaemias:
- Spherocytes: hereditary spherocytosis or AIHA.
- Fragmented red cells (schistocytes): TTP, HUS, or mechanical damage.
- Sickle cells: sickle cell disease.
- Heinz bodies (supravital stain): G6PD deficiency, unstable Hb.
- Target cells (leptocytes), acanthocytes (spur cells): various causes.
Positive direct Coombs antiglobulin test → immune-mediated haemolysis; negative → non-immune.

A(i) Classify haemolytic anaemia under four distinct classification schemes, providing examples under each category.
A(ii) Describe the laboratory tests used to demonstrate increased red cell breakdown, specifying the direction of change for each parameter.
B(i) Describe the tests that demonstrate increased red cell production, and explain how peripheral blood film (PBF) and bone marrow findings together confirm a haemolytic process.

questions.answerText:
(i) Oesophageal cancer.
Predisposing factors: excess alcohol consumption; cigarette smoking; other ingested carcinogens — nitrates (converted to nitrites); mucosal damage from physical agents — hot tea, radiation-induced strictures, chronic achalasia; chronic gastric reflux (Barrett's oesophagus).
(ii) Clinical features and metastatic complications:
- Dysphagia — the most common symptom; progressive (initially to solid, later to semisolids and liquids).
- Odynophagia (50%).
- Anorexia and weight loss (75%).
- Regurgitation or vomiting.
- Chest pain or pain radiating to the back.
- Haematemesis due to tumour ulceration.
- No specific physical findings; may appear chronically ill with weight loss; hepatomegaly, palpable lymph nodes, anaemia.
- Metastasis: pulmonary, hepatic, bone, and brain.
(iii) Initial management: investigations to stage the disease.
- Upper GI endoscopy; contrast oesophagography using barium; PA and lateral chest radiography; CT scanning of chest and upper abdomen.
(iv) Definitive treatment options depend on stage:
- Surgery alone — especially for early tumours.
- Chemotherapy with radiation therapy.
- Endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR) — for patients with superficial carcinoma.
Palliative therapy for advanced disease:
- Dilation using polyvinyl dilators or balloons.
- Stenting using self-expandable metallic oesophageal stents.
- Ablation using thermal therapy or laser.

He has also experienced significant weight loss (15 kg) and intermittent chest pain radiating to the back. Endoscopy reveals a mid-oesophageal lesion, and CT confirms involvement of the chest and upper abdomen.
