Describe the aetiology and pathophysiology of lung cancer under the following headings and state the anatomical basis of the clinical features:
A(i) Describe the aetiological factors for lung cancer, including quantitative risk figures.
A(ii) Describe the pathophysiology of lung cancer using the multiple-hit theory, including the role of genes and cell types.
B(i) Describe the mechanisms by which a bronchial carcinoma in the lung apex causes Horner's syndrome and Pancoast syndrome, naming the structures compressed and the resulting features.
B(ii) Distinguish between NSCLC and SCLC in terms of cell type distribution, management approach, and prognosis.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Aetiological factors with quantitative risk figures: active smoking is responsible for 90% of lung cancer cases (78% in men, 90% in women). Tobacco smoke contains more than 300 harmful substances with at least 40 known potent carcinogens. Cause-and-effect relationship established — relates to duration of smoking, number of cigarettes per day, depth of inhalation (intensity), tar and nicotine content (composition), and age of initiation. Secondhand smoke (passive/secondhand smoking): as many as 25% of lung cancers in non-smokers are believed to be caused by secondhand smoke; urinary levels of carcinogens are 1–5% of those in active smokers. Occupational agents account for 9–15%: asbestos increases risk by as much as 5 times; risk for persons who smoke and have asbestos exposure approaches 80–90 times that of control populations. Other occupational carcinogens: acrylonitrile, arsenic, beryllium, cadmium, mustard gas, ionising radiation — all have synergistic or multiplicative effects with cigarette smoking. Carcinogens from industrial pollution account for 5% of cases. Cigarette smoking rising incidence mirrors rise in 1940s–1980s with decline from 1985 to date; females' decline lags behind. Not all persons who smoke develop lung cancer — genetic susceptibility plays a causative role. Air pollution — diesel exhaust emission — may be an important risk factor.
A(ii) Pathophysiology using the multiple-hit theory: both environmental exposure to particular agents and an individual's susceptibility to these agents contribute to risk. The current multiple-hit theory suggests that a series of toxic cellular insults disrupts orderly genetic reproduction. Amplification of oncogenes and inactivation of tumour suppressor genes. Genes produce proteins involved in cell growth, differentiation, cell cycle processes, apoptosis, angiogenesis, tumour progression, and immune regulation. Disease generally takes a long time to develop. Epithelial cells under heavy and continuous exposure undergo the multiple-hit sequence. Symptoms ultimately develop from uncontrolled disorganised growth that interferes with local or distant anatomy or physiologic processes. Cell types: NSCLC accounts for 80% — large cell 15%, small cell 20% (small cell carcinoma, 20%, is classified separately from NSCLC), adenocarcinoma 30%, squamous 35%.
B(i) Horner's syndrome: stellate ganglion is squeezed in a pulmonary apical bronchial tumour. Resulting features: pin-point pupil (miosis), anhidrotic hemi-face (anhydrosis), partial ptosis. Pancoast syndrome: brachial plexus invasion with associated neuralgic pains; superior vena cava compression and direct invasion — resulting in non-pulsatile neck veins, swollen face with bluish discoloration (cyanosis), and later reduced flow into right atrium. Lymph node compression: over-grown lymph nodes compressing small hilar bronchus; or lymph node compression of small bronchi leads to bronchiectasis formation.
B(ii) NSCLC vs SCLC: NSCLC accounts for 80% of all bronchial carcinoma and requires detailed staging (TNM) before treatment. Cell types within NSCLC: large cell 15%, adenocarcinoma 30%, squamous 35%. TNM staging is essential for NSCLC. Following staging, definitive surgery, chemotherapy, radiation combined and/or singly may be undertaken. SCLC: small cell 20% of all bronchial carcinoma. SCLC is generally treated with chemotherapy with or without radiotherapy given its tendency for early systemic spread, in contrast to NSCLC where surgery is central to early-stage management. Prognosis is poor for all cell types; response to chemo and/or radiation depends on cell type. Immunotherapy is described as novel. Metastatic disease from or into the lungs may all have poor outcome.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old Nigerian man presents with a 4-week history of fever, anorexia, weight loss, constipation, headache, and malaise. In the second week he has a high plateau fever of 40°C with bradycardia. He was seen at a primary health centre and treated for malaria with no response. He now has hepatosplenomegaly, rose spots on his abdomen, and relative bradycardia.
(i) What is the most likely diagnosis and what organism causes it? Describe its transmission.
(ii) Describe the four stages of untreated disease including the complications that occur in the third week.
(iii) State the investigations used to confirm the diagnosis specifying which are most useful in each week.
(iv) Outline the drug treatment and management of complications.
(v) How is this condition prevented?
questions.answerText:
(i) Typhoid fever (Enteric fever). Caused by Salmonella typhi — a Gram-negative, short, motile bacillus (peritrichous flagella). Milder disease caused by Paratyphoid type A and B. Transmission: Salmonella typhi lives only in humans; persons carry bacteria in bloodstream and intestinal tract; shed in faeces by ill persons and carriers; spread through contaminated food or water, poor hygiene, flying insects feeding on faeces; spreads through the ileal patches into the bloodstream.
(ii) Four stages: Week 1 — temperature rises slowly; fever fluctuations with relative bradycardia (Faget sign); malaise, headache, cough; epistaxis and abdominal pain; leucopenia with eosinopenia and relative lymphocytosis; blood cultures positive; Widal test negative. Week 2 — high plateau fever around 40°C; bradycardia (Faget sign); delirium (calm or agitated — nervous fever); rose spots on lower chest and abdomen; hepatosplenomegaly; liver enzymes elevated; Widal test strongly positive with antiO and antiH antibodies; blood cultures sometimes still positive. Week 3 — complications: intestinal haemorrhage from bleeding Peyer's patches; intestinal perforation in distal ileum (septicaemia/diffuse peritonitis — abdominal distension, rigidity, guarding, rebound tenderness, absent bowel sounds, ascites); encephalitis; neurological/psychiatric symptoms (muttering delirium, coma vigil); metastatic abscesses (cholecystitis, endocarditis, osteitis); high oscillating fever; dehydration; delirium; platelet count falls. Week 4 — fever starts subsiding (defervescence).
(iii) Investigations by week: 1st week — blood culture; 2nd week — stool culture, bone marrow culture; 3rd week — urine microscopy, culture, and sensitivity; Widal test (serology for 4-fold rise in titre of O antibodies from 2nd week). Other tests: urinalysis; FBC; ascitic tap; abdominal/chest X-rays (air under diaphragm when ileal perforation occurs).
(iv) Treatment: hospital care with vital signs monitoring; oral rehydration; IV fluids if vomiting or peritonitis; blood transfusion for ileal bleeding. Drugs: ciprofloxacin, amoxicillin, chloramphenicol, Septrin (trimethoprim 160 mg plus sulphamethoxazole 800 mg). Complications: surgery for abscess drainage, bowel perforation, haemorrhage.
(v) Prevention: sanitation and hygiene; careful food preparation; hand washing. Vaccination — live oral Ty21a vaccine (sold as Vivotif) and injectable typhoid polysaccharide vaccine (sold as Typhim Vi or Typherix); both 50–80% protective; recommended for travellers to endemic areas; boosters every 5 years for oral vaccine and every 2 years for injectable form.

questions.question:
A(i) Compare hepatitis A virus (HAV) and hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection under the following headings: (a) incubation period, (b) route of transmission, (c) risk of fulminant hepatic failure (FHF), (d) risk of chronic infection, (e) severity comparison by age group.
A(ii) Describe the four clinical phases of acute viral hepatitis, naming the symptoms characteristic of each phase.
B(i) Distinguish the clinical course and chronicity risk of hepatitis C (HCV) from both HAV and HBV, and describe the significance of HBV serological markers.
questions.answerText:
A(i) HAV vs HBV comparison:
(a) Incubation period: HAV — 15–45 days (average 4 weeks); HBV — 40–160 days (average ~12 weeks).
(b) Route of transmission: HAV — faeco-oral route; HBV — percutaneous and permucosal (sharing of sharps, blood transfusion, haemodialysis, sexual transmission, vertical/mother-to-child transmission).
(c) Risk of FHF: HAV — less than 1% of cases; HBV — <1% of patients.
(d) Risk of chronic infection: HAV — does not persist and does not lead to chronic hepatitis. HBV — after acute hepatitis resolves, 95% of adults fully recover; about 5% of adults, 90% of infected infants, and 30–50% of children infected at age 1–5 years develop chronic infection.
(e) Severity by age: HAV — young children usually remain asymptomatic; acute hepatitis A is more severe and has higher mortality in adults than in children. HBV — clinical illness may range from mild to fulminant.
A(ii) Four clinical phases of acute viral hepatitis:
1. Incubation/viral replication phase — no symptoms.
2. Prodromal/pre-icteric phase (may or may not be symptomatic): fever, nausea, vomiting, chills, headache, anorexia, aversion to smoking, upper abdominal discomfort. Serum sickness occurs in 5–15% of HBV patients.
3. Icteric phase — most children do not become icteric; when present, lasts 2–6 weeks. Cholestatic pattern: dark urine, pale stool, generalised pruritus, greenish tinge of jaundice; also hepatocellular pattern. Patients may develop right upper abdominal pain and hepatomegaly.
4. Recovery/convalescent phase — resolution of acute infection; clinical and biochemical recovery within 6 months.
B(i) HCV course: viral incubation ~8 weeks; most cases of acute HCV infection are asymptomatic; even when symptomatic, tends to follow a mild course; aminotransferase levels rarely higher than 1000 U/L; does not usually cause FHF. Approximately 15–45% of patients resolve spontaneously; 55–85% remain viraemic and may develop chronic hepatitis.
HBV serological markers:
- HBsAg: acute or chronic infection.
- HBeAg: acute infection; if >6 months, implies high infectivity.
- HBV DNA: viral replication.
- Anti-HBs: immunity from previous exposure or vaccination.
- Anti-HBeAg: seroconversion.
- Anti-HBc IgM: acute hepatitis B; Anti-HBc IgG: chronic hepatitis B.
- Anti-HCV: usually positive 8 weeks from infection; HCV RNA detectable 1–8 weeks from infection.

questions.question:
Describe the nail disorders related to onycholysis, Beau's lines, and compulsive nail behaviours, and explain their systemic correlates under the following headings:
A(i) Describe onycholysis: definition, clinical appearance, and all causes.
A(ii) Describe Beau's lines and onychomadesis: clinical appearance, mechanism, and associations.
B(i) Describe onychophagia and onychotillomania: definitions, clinical consequences, and treatment.
B(ii) Describe trachyonychia, Muehrcke's lines, and pincer nails: clinical appearance, associations, and systemic correlates.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Onycholysis:
- Definition: spontaneous separation of the nail plate, usually beginning at the free margin and progressing proximally
- Discolouration usually occurs underneath the nail
- Causes: psoriasis, hand eczema, LP, atopic dermatitis, hyper/hypothyroidism, porphyria, pellagra, syphilis; manicuring; drugs (photo-onycholysis e.g. tetracyclines, psoralens, fluoroquinolones)

A(ii) Beau's lines:
- Transverse furrows that begin in the matrix and progress distally
- Due to temporary arrest of function of the nail matrix
- Associations: childbirth, measles, paronychia, acute febrile illnesses, high altitude exposure, drug reaction; trauma can induce a localised form; when process is intermittent the nail plate can resemble a corduroy

Onychomadesis:
- Periodic idiopathic shedding of the nail beginning at the proximal end (due to temporary arrest of function of nail matrix)
- Can appear as a periodic finding in runners
- Seen in: neurological disease, Kawasaki disease, pemphigus vulgaris, peritoneal dialysis, hand foot and mouth disease, SJS/TENS

B(i) Onychophagia and onychotillomania:
- Both are compulsive behaviours
- Onychophagia: nail biting; may markedly shorten the nail bed, damage the matrix, and at times lead to pterygium formation
- Onychotillomania: compulsive picking at the nails or trying to tear them off
- Both treated by cognitive-behavioural methods, hypnosis, or psychopharmacological agents

B(ii) Trachyonychia:
- Opalescent, thin, dull, fragile, and finely ridged (longitudinally) nail; referred to as twenty nail dystrophy when all finger and toe nails are involved (seen more in children)
- Seen in: alopecia areata, psoriasis, LP, atopy, ichthyosis vulgaris; can be familial or idiopathic
- Rx: spontaneous resolution, tazarotene +/- topical steroid

Muehrcke's lines:
- Narrow white transverse bands occurring in pairs
- Usually a sign of chronic hypoalbuminaemia
- May also be seen with chemotherapy

Pincer nails (trumpet nails / omega nails):
- Lateral edges of nail slowly approach one another, compressing the nailbed and underlying dermis
- Causes: inherited (AD), trauma, Kawasaki disease, renal disease, lupus erythematosus, use of beta-blockers

(i) Diagnosis: Typhoid fever (enteric fever).

(ii) Causative organism and transmission:
- Salmonella typhi: a Gram-negative short bacillus, motile due to its peritrichous flagella
- Transmitted by ingestion of food or water contaminated with the faeces of an infected person

(iii) Week-by-week clinical progression:
Incubation period: 7-14 days.
1st week: fever with relative bradycardia (temperature-pulse dissociation); diffuse abdominal pain and tenderness; constipation; dry cough; dull frontal headache; delirium; increasingly stuporous malaise.
2nd week: offensive diarrhoea 6-8 stools a day like pea soup (greenish); enlarged tender spleen and liver.
3rd week: complications can occur.
4th-5th week: reducing temperature (defervescence); death may occur if left untreated. Following recovery, patient may become an asymptomatic carrier of typhoid fever.

(iv) Diagnosis by week:
- 1st week: blood culture
- 2nd week: stool, bone marrow
- 3rd week: urine
Method: microscopy, culture, and sensitivity; Widal test. Exclude malaria, dysentery, or pneumonia.
Treatment: chloramphenicol, ciprofloxacin.
Prevention: sanitation and hygiene are the critical measures; careful food preparation and washing of hands; vaccination.
questions.question:
A 40-year-old man presents with a 2-week history of fever, diffuse abdominal pain, constipation, and a dry cough. On examination in the second week he develops offensive green diarrhoea with an enlarged tender spleen and liver.
(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) Identify the causative organism and mode of transmission.
(iii) Describe the week-by-week clinical progression and the complications.
(iv) State the diagnostic methods and treatment.

Describe obstructive uropathy under the following headings:
A(i) Definition and classification of obstructive uropathy, including both congenital and acquired (intrinsic and extrinsic) causes.
A(ii) Describe the pathophysiology of obstructive uropathy during the acute and chronic phases.
B(i) State the symptoms, signs, and investigations used in the diagnosis of obstructive uropathy.
B(ii) Explain the treatment options and prognostic factors that determine whether renal function can be recovered.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Obstructive uropathy is a structural or functional hindrance of normal urine flow which, if not relieved on time, will lead to loss of renal function (obstructive nephropathy). Obstruction to the flow of urine with its attendant stasis and elevation in urinary tract pressure impairs urinary conduit and renal functions. Classification: Congenital — uretero-pelvic narrowing/obstruction, uretero-vesical junction obstruction, ureterocele, retrocaval urethra. Acquired Intrinsic — ureteral: calculi, inflammation, trauma, tumour, blood clots, uric acid crystals, sloughed papillae; bladder: BPH, Ca prostate, Ca bladder, calculi, spinal cord disease; urethra: stricture, calculi, trauma. Acquired Extrinsic — ureteric: pregnant uterus, Ca cervix, retroperitoneal fibrosis, Ca colon, aortic aneurysm; bladder outlet/urethral: trauma, lymphoma, Ca uterus, prostate, surgical ligature. Causes differ by age: children — anatomic abnormalities (including posterior urethral valves or strictures/stenosis at ureterovesical or ureteropelvic junction); young adults — calculi; older adults — BPH, Ca prostate, retroperitoneal or pelvic tumours (including metastatic carcinomas), and calculi. Obstruction is much more common in males (BPH).
A(ii) Acute phase haemodynamic effects: increase in RBF; reduced GFR; reduced medullary blood flow; increase in vasodilatory prostaglandins and nitric oxide. Acute tubule effects: increase in tubular and ureteral pressures; increase in reabsorption of Na+, urea, and H2O. Chronic phase haemodynamic: reduction in RBF; further reduction in GFR; increased vasoconstriction prostaglandins; increase in renin-angiotensin production. Chronic tubule: reduced medullary osmolarity; reduced concentrating ability (structural damage, parenchymal atrophy); reduced transport functions for Na+, K+, H+.
B(i) Symptoms: pain is common when obstruction acutely dilates the bladder, collecting system (ureter and renal calyces), and renal capsule; flank pain and tenderness, suprapubic pain radiating to ipsilateral testis or labia; distribution of kidney and ureteral pain is T10–T11; pain may be accompanied by nausea and vomiting; difficulty in voiding or change in urinary volume; evidence of dilatation by abdominal bulging; hypertension; frequency; poor stream; dribbling; feeling of incomplete emptying of bladder; nocturia; oliguria; haematuria; fever; body swelling. Investigations: urinalysis (haematuria, pyuria, bacteriuria); SEUC; bladder catheterization; PR for BPH, rectal mass, or pelvic mass; abdominal plain X-ray for radiopaque stone; USS — renal size, bladder size, dilated calyces; cystourethroscopy and voiding cystourethrography (shows bladder neck and urethral obstruction); IVU, CT, MRI, radionuclide scans, renography.
B(ii) Treatment: immediate relief of obstruction — catheterization (urethral or suprapubic, nephrostomy, ureterostomy); prolonged antibiotic therapy is necessary; in prolonged obstruction, intermittent relief is advocated, then later elective surgery; treat BPH with alpha-adrenergic blockers and 5-alpha reductase inhibitors. With early relief of obstruction, the defect in function disappears completely. If obstruction persists, it may produce permanent loss of renal function, loss of renal mass, susceptibility to infection, and stone formation. Prognosis depends on: whether irreversible damage has been done (>8 weeks); whether complete or incomplete; unilateral or bilateral; whether UTI is involved. Acute renal failure due to calculus is reversible with adequate return of renal function. With chronic obstructive uropathy, renal dysfunction may be partially or completely irreversible, requiring RRT.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the three main pathways of lipid metabolism in the body: (a) the exogenous pathway, (b) the endogenous pathway, and (c) reverse cholesterol transport.
A(ii) Explain the role of LDL receptor activity in regulating plasma LDL concentration and intracellular cholesterol homeostasis.
B(i) Distinguish between high anion gap (HAG) and normal anion gap (NAG) acid-base disorders, specifying when renal failure produces each pattern and what happens to bicarbonate in each stage.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Three main pathways of lipid metabolism:
(a) Exogenous pathway: following digestion and absorption of dietary fat, TG and cholesterol are packaged to form chylomicrons in epithelial cells of the intestines. Chylomicrons circulate through the intestinal lymphatic system. In blood, circulating chylomicrons interact at the capillaries of adipose tissue and muscle cells releasing TG for storage and energy. Some apolipoproteins are transferred to HDL; the remaining chylomicron remnant particles are removed by chylomicron remnant receptors on the liver. Enzyme LPL hydrolyses the TG and free fatty acids are released.
(b) Endogenous pathway: the liver synthesises lipoproteins; TG and cholesterol ester are packaged into VLDL particles and released into the circulation. VLDL is processed by lipoprotein lipase (LPL) to release fatty acids and glycerol. Once processed, VLDL becomes a VLDL remnant. The majority of VLDL remnants are taken up by the liver via the LDL receptor; remaining remnant particles become IDL, then are hydrolysed by hepatic-triglyceride lipase to form LDL (smaller, denser particle).
(c) Reverse cholesterol transport: process by which cholesterol is removed from tissues and returned to the liver. HDL is the key lipoprotein. Nascent HDL is secreted by the liver and intestine; it proceeds through the 'HDL cycle' to attract cholesterol from cell membranes into the core of the HDL particle.
A(ii) LDL receptor regulation:
- LDL is the main carrier of circulating cholesterol; taken up by LDL receptors in the liver and extra-hepatic cells.
- As LDL is taken up, free cholesterol accumulates within cells.
- LDL receptor activity regulates plasma LDL by: (1) decreasing synthesis of HMG-CoA reductase (controls rate of cholesterol synthesis); (2) suppressing synthesis of new LDL receptors; (3) activating ACAT (acyl-coenzyme A cholesterol acyltransferase), which esterifies free cholesterol into cholesterol ester for storage.
B(i) Renal failure and acid-base:
- Early renal failure: impaired secretion of NH₃ → normal anion gap (NAG) metabolic acidosis at this stage.
- Later renal failure: retention of PO₄²⁻ and SO₄²⁻ and bicarbonate wastage → high anion gap (HAG) metabolic acidosis at this stage.
HAG metabolic acidosis: unmeasured anions deplete bicarbonate; corrected HCO₃⁻ = measured HCO₃⁻ + (anion gap – 12); if corrected level is reduced → additional metabolic acidosis; if elevated → additional metabolic alkalosis.
NAG metabolic acidosis: 2 large groups — renal or GI; distinguished by urine anion gap: positive UAG → renal cause; negative UAG → GI cause.

questions.question:
Describe the gross anatomy of the skin under the headings of layers of the epidermis, cell types in each layer, the dermis and its components, and adnexal structures. Then explain how each epidermal layer relates to the transit of the keratinocyte, and distinguish between the eccrine and apocrine sweat glands.
A(i) Layers of the epidermis and keratinocyte transit.
A(ii) Dermis and its components.
B(i) Adnexal structures.
B(ii) Eccrine versus apocrine sweat glands — distinguish across all features.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Layers of the epidermis (deep to superficial):
- Stratum basalis: contains basal immature keratinocytes (nucleated)
- Stratum spinosum
- Stratum granulosum
- Stratum lucidum: found on palms and soles only
- Stratum corneum
Transit: time from basal keratinocyte to stratum corneum is approximately 28 days. As cells mature upwards they lose their nuclei; nucleated cells in the stratum corneum represent parakeratosis.

A(ii) Dermis and components:
- Papillary dermis
- Reticular dermis
- Connective tissue; blood vessels; nerves; fibrous tissues
- SALT (Skin-Associated Lymphoid Tissue): immune surveillance, Langerhans cells, lymphocytes, lymphoid tissue

B(i) Adnexal structures:
- Hair follicles (largest number on the scalp; types: lanugo, vellus, terminal)
- Sweat glands: eccrine and apocrine
- Sebaceous glands (found on seborrhoeic areas: midline of back, forehead, face, external auditory meatus, anogenital surfaces; produce sebum; effective moisturizer; prevents water loss from epidermis; fungi and bacteriostatic properties)
- Nerves; blood cells; skin-associated lymphoid tissues

B(ii) Eccrine versus apocrine sweat glands:
Eccrine: found everywhere excluding mucous membranes; high concentration on soles and palms; nerve supply is sympathetic cholinergic; sweat is hypotonic, contains Na, Cl, K, urea, and lactate (levels of lactate higher in sweat; glucose present in small quantities); secretion is odourless but may contain drugs, garlic, or arsenic.
Apocrine: develops as part of the pilo-sebaceous unit; found in axilla, perianal region, and around the areola; activity is androgen-dependent; secretion is odourless but may give rise to body odour when acted on by bacteria.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old obese woman with a 5-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus presents with an HbA1c of 9.5%, fasting plasma glucose of 185 mg/dL, and symptoms of polyuria, polydipsia, and progressive weight loss. She has been on maximum doses of two oral glucose-lowering agents.
(i) What are the goals of glycaemic care for persons with diabetes, and what optimal targets should be set for this patient?
(ii) What are the risk factors and mechanisms behind her progression toward complications?
(iii) What are the management options available, and which is most appropriate at this stage? Justify your choice.
(iv) What are the complications of insulin therapy?
questions.answerText:
(i) Goals of glycaemic care and optimal targets:
Goals: early diagnosis; prevention of acute and chronic complications; prevention of premature mortality; promotion of self-management practices and empowerment; reduction of personal, family, and societal burden of diabetes.
Optimal targets: HbA1c <7%; fasting plasma glucose <110 mg/dL (6.1 mmol/L); postprandial plasma glucose <144 mg/dL (~8.0 mmol/L); blood pressure <130/80 mmHg; LDL-C <100 mg/dL; HDL-C >40 mg/dL (men) and >50 mg/dL (women); TG <150 mg/dL. Targets are individualised.
(ii) Risk factors and mechanisms for complications:
Hyperglycaemia is the key culprit in vascular complications. Lower glycaemia = lower risk of complications (UKPDS 35). Improvements in glucose, BP, and lipid control are central to preventing onset and progression of chronic complications.
Macrovascular disease: narrowing/occlusion of large blood vessels → cardiovascular disease (CAD, CVD, PVD).
Microvascular disease: narrowing of lumen of small blood vessels at capillary and arteriolar level → diabetic retinopathy, neuropathy, nephropathy.
(iii) Management options: non-pharmacologic (education, nutrition therapy, physical activity, weight loss); oral glucose-lowering agents; insulin therapy; GLP-1 receptor agonists; DPP-4 inhibitors; anti-obesity agents (orlistat, sibutramine); bariatric surgery.
Justified choice: Insulin therapy is the treatment of choice in this patient because: HbA1c >9%; symptoms of polyuria, polydipsia, and weight loss indicate severely uncontrolled diabetes with catabolism; she has failed maximum doses of two oral agents. Per current diabetes management guidelines: initiate combination therapy or insulin immediately for all patients with HbA1c at diagnosis >8.5%; A1c >9% → insulin therapy is the treatment of choice; insulin is the most effective drug at lowering glycaemia and has no maximum dose ceiling.
(iv) Complications of insulin therapy (common): hypoglycaemia; lipohypertrophy; weight gain; insulin allergy; localised and systemic reactions to insulin; insulin oedema.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old immunocompromised patient on long-term steroids presents with a 3-week history of haemoptysis. Chest X-ray shows a round radio-dense mass surrounded by a radiolucent halo in the right upper lobe, in a region of previous TB scar tissue. Bronchoscopy reveals fungal hyphal filaments in sputum.
(i) What is the 'spot diagnosis' and how does the radiological appearance confirm it?
(ii) State all the predisposing factors for this condition and the immune status required for each form of the causative organism's disease.
(iii) Describe the full pathophysiology and all clinical forms of disease caused by this organism.
(iv) State the diagnostic approach and all treatment options for this condition.
(v) Describe how other pulmonary fungal diseases present differently from this condition.
questions.answerText:
(i) Spot diagnosis: Aspergilloma. The radiological appearance — a round radio-dense (fungal ball) tumour-like mass with a radiolucent halo surrounding it — is the classical 'fungal ball' appearance. It occurs when fungal spores of Aspergillus fumigatus settle in a previous tuberculous cavity and grow into a fungal ball.
(ii) Predisposing factors: Aspergillus fumigatus is commonly associated with decaying fodder, hay, and trees and is quite ubiquitous. For aspergilloma — prior TB cavity is the predisposing lesion (not immune suppression per se). For allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis — associated with asthma; blood eosinophilia and IgE elevation suggest atopic/allergic background. For invasive aspergillosis — occurs in highly immunocompromised patients (widespread organ involvement including granulomatous liver lesion, brain abscess, meningitis, lytic bone lesions, and pneumonic lung lesion). General principle: fungal infectivity is low and fungi are often commensals, but when the host immune system deteriorates they become disease — immune depression from malnutrition, excessive antibiotic treatment, DM, reticuloendothelial diseases, cancers, chemotherapy, anti-graft rejection treatment, radiation, and HIV infection.
(iii) Clinical forms of aspergillosis: (1) Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) — fungus growth in bronchial tree; fleeting bronchial shadows; sputum has fungal hyphal filaments; causes bronchiectasis and even segmental lobe collapse; pulmonary interstitial fibrosis; clinical features include extrinsic asthma, bronchiectasis, and fibrosing lung disease; blood eosinophilia and IgE elevation. (2) Aspergilloma — fungal spores settle in previous TB cavity; grow into fungal ball with radiolucent halo; causes streaks of haemoptysis or even massive haemoptysis; requires surgical excision. (3) Invasive aspergillosis — occurs in highly immunocompromised; widespread organ involvement: granulomatous liver lesion, brain abscess, meningitis, lytic bone lesions, pneumonic lung lesion.
(iv) Diagnosis: antigen skin test — positive in allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis but negative in invasive and in aspergilloma; precipitin positive; chest X-ray; FBC; fungal hyphae in sputum and culture. Guided by presentation and history. Treatment: supportive (e.g., bronchodilators, corticosteroids); anti-fungal agents oral — itraconazole, fluconazole; parenteral amphotericin B; surgical excision of aspergillomata.
(v) Comparison with other pulmonary fungal diseases: Candida — oral thrush or occasional pneumonia; treated with topical nystatin, miconazole, or fluconazole. Histoplasmosis — fever, cough, chills, myalgia like primary TB (not like a fungal ball); cavity can house fungal mesh like aspergilloma; treated with ketoconazole or itraconazole then amphotericin B. Cryptococcosis — spores from pigeon droppings; subacute with hilar lymph nodes; commonly causes meningitis — not a cavity ball. Coccidioidomycosis — non-budding soil saprophyte; fever within 10 days, erythema nodosum, allergic conjunctivitis — inflammatory/exudative rather than a fungal ball. PCP — insidious breathlessness, fever, cough; CXR minimal but CT shows bilateral peri-hilar ground-glass infiltrates — not a localized ball lesion.

(i) Diagnosis: Malignant bronchial carcinoma (lung cancer). Epidemiology: lung cancer was a rare entity in the early 1900s but became the leading cause of preventable death. Globally, it is the most frequent malignancy in males and the fifth most common cancer in females. WHO statistics — slightly more than 1 million cases diagnosed annually worldwide. Highly lethal — highest recorded 5-year patient survival rates are 14%, 8% in Europe and the developing world. Global lung cancer trends follow trends in smoking with a lag time of several decades. The probability of developing lung cancer remains very low until age 39 years in both sexes; it slowly starts to rise and peaks among those older than 70 years. Lung cancer occurs predominantly in persons aged 50–70 years. Women have a higher incidence of localised disease at presentation and of adenocarcinoma; women are typically younger when they present with symptoms.
(ii) Aetiology: Active smoking is responsible for 90% of lung cancer cases (78% in men, 90% in women). Tobacco smoke contains more than 300 harmful substances with at least 40 known potent carcinogens. Cause and effect relationship established — relates to duration of smoking, number of cigarettes smoked per day, depth of inhalation (intensity), tar and nicotine contents (composition), and age of initiation. Secondhand smoke — as many as 25% of lung cancers in non-smokers are believed to be caused by secondhand smoke; urinary levels of carcinogens are 1–5% of those in active smokers. Occupational agents account for 9–15% — asbestos (increases risk by as much as 5 times; risk for persons who smoke and have asbestos exposure approaches 80–90 times that of control populations), acrylonitrile, arsenic, beryllium, cadmium, mustard gas, ionising radiation — all have synergistic or multiplicative effects with cigarette smoking. Air pollution — diesel exhaust emission; carcinogens from industrial pollution account for 5% of cases. Genetic susceptibility also plays a causative role.
(iii) Pathophysiology: Both environmental exposure and individual susceptibility are thought to contribute to risk. The current multiple-hit theory suggests a series of toxic cellular insults disrupts orderly genetic reproduction. Amplification of oncogenes and inactivation of tumour suppressor genes. Genes produce proteins involved in cell growth, differentiation, cell cycle processes, apoptosis, angiogenesis, tumour progression, and immune regulation. Disease generally takes a long time to develop. Epithelial cells under heavy and continuous exposure undergo the multiple hit sequence. Uncontrolled disorganised growth then interferes with local or distant anatomy or physiologic processes. Cell types (NSCLC accounts for 80%): large cell 15%, small cell 20%, adenocarcinoma 30%, squamous 35%.
(iv) Clinical features and compressive effects: Diagnosis — history of tobacco abuse directly or passively; clinical features of chronic cough with haemoptysis; sign of digital clubbing; local compression features; dyspnoea; features of bronchial collapse/consolidation. Space occupation effects — compression of stellate ganglion (in pulmonary apical tumour) resulting in Horner's syndrome: pin-point pupil, anhidrotic hemi-face, partial ptosis. Pancoast syndrome — brachial plexus invasion with neuralgic pains, superior vena cava compression and invasion resulting in non-pulsatile neck veins, swollen face with bluish discoloration (cyanosis), and later reduced flow into right atrium. Lymph node compression of small bronchi leads to bronchiectasis formation. Intramural obstruction — causes partial/complete blockage; blockage of main bronchus can cause total lung collapse; a branch can cause lobar or segmental collapse. Hormonal/non-metastatic features: ADH suppression causing pan-dilution syndrome; parathyroid-like hyperactivity (hypercalcaemia syndrome of polyuria, nocturia, constipation, lassitude, and even coma); ACTH excess. Haemoptysis from overgrown vessels necrosis.
(v) Diagnosis and treatment: Sputum cytology electron microscopy; pleural aspirate exam; bronchoscopy with tissue biopsy and histology; chest X-ray; CAT scan/MRI — CT with PET is most effective. Management: relief of symptoms — cough suppression, relief of intractable cough via radiotherapy; pain relief may require pain experts. Following staging using TNM, definitive surgery, chemotherapy, radiation combined and/or singly may be undertaken — TNM essential for NSCLC. Prognosis is poor; response to chemo and/or radiation depends on cell type. Immunotherapy is novel. Metastatic disease from or into the lungs may all have poor outcome. Tobacco abuse and radiation exposure should be avoided.
questions.question:
A 45-year-old man presents to the chest clinic with a 3-month history of progressive haemoptysis, digital clubbing, and significant weight loss. He has a 30-pack-year smoking history and works in an asbestos factory. Chest CT with PET scan is being arranged.
(i) What is the most likely diagnosis, and state the epidemiology of this condition.
(ii) State all the aetiological factors for this condition, including quantitative risk figures where given.
(iii) Describe the pathophysiology using the multiple-hit theory, and state the cellular types involved.
(iv) Describe the full range of clinical features including local compressive effects, hormonal effects, and non-metastatic manifestations.
(v) Outline the diagnostic approach and all treatment modalities, including the role of staging.

questions.answerText:
(i) Acute haemolytic episode due to G6PD deficiency, precipitated by sulfonamide exposure.
(ii) Three categories of triggers for acute haemolytic attack:
1. Fava beans (favism).
2. Infections (viral, bacterial infection, metabolic acidosis).
3. Drugs — including antimalarials (primaquine, pamaquine, dapsone), sulfonamides (sulfamethoxazole), antibacterials (cotrimoxazole, nalidixic acid, nitrofurantoin), antipyretics/analgesics (acetanilide, phenazopyridine), and miscellaneous agents (vitamin K, doxorubicin, methylene blue, furazolidone).
(iii) Enzymatic defect and genetics:
- G6PD plays a critical role in the red cell as the only source of NADPH, which directly and via glutathione defends cells against oxidative stress.
- Most common congenital shunt defect; X-linked trait — affects males, females are carriers.
- Normal G6PD is designated type B (found in 11% of African-American males).
- Most common significant clinical variant is A-negative, which confers partial protection against malaria.
- Population: X-linked trait; high incidence among Sephardic Jews, males of African and Mediterranean descent.
(iv) Mechanism and investigations:
- Oxidant stress depletes NADPH and glutathione → haemoglobin oxidation → Heinz body formation → red cell membrane damage → intravascular haemolysis of old RBCs (self-limited, affects old RBCs only).
- Acute episode: rapid fall in haematocrit (25–30%); intravascular haemolysis test positive.
- Blood film: Heinz bodies on supravital stain (crystal violet) — bite cells (fragmented red cells).
- Screening: methaemoglobin reduction test, fluorescent screening test, ascorbate cyanide screening test; enzyme assay on red cells.
(v) Management of acute episode:
- Avoid/correct precipitating (oxidant stress) factors; favism is entirely preventable by not eating fava beans; substitute alternative drugs.
- Hydration; blood transfusion for significant anaemia.
- If acute renal failure develops — haemodialysis.
questions.question:
A 22-year-old male of African descent presents with sudden onset of malaise, weakness, lumbar pain, dark urine, and jaundice 48 hours after starting treatment with sulfamethoxazole for a urinary tract infection.
(i) What is the most likely diagnosis?
(ii) What are the three main categories of triggers that precipitate an acute haemolytic attack in this condition?
(iii) Describe the enzymatic defect, its genetics, and its population distribution.
(iv) What is the mechanism of haemolysis, and what would a blood film and specific investigation show during an acute episode?
(v) Outline the full management of an acute episode, including when renal replacement therapy is indicated.

A(i) Describe the zones of the adrenal cortex under the headings: zone, main hormone produced, and principal function of each zone.
A(ii) Explain the clinical basis of the hyperpigmentation seen in primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease) but NOT in secondary adrenal insufficiency.
B(i) Distinguish between the adrenal cortex and the adrenal medulla under the headings: embryological origin, hormones produced, and physiological role.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Zones of the adrenal cortex:
• Zona glomerulosa — produces mineralocorticoids, mainly aldosterone; responsible for long-term regulation of blood pressure and electrolyte homeostasis through sodium reabsorption and potassium excretion; secretion is mainly controlled by the renin-angiotensin system.
• Zona fasciculata — produces glucocorticoids, mainly cortisol in humans; affects metabolism of carbohydrates, proteins and lipids; stimulates gluconeogenesis; suppresses immune response; secretion is controlled by ACTH from the anterior pituitary.
• Zona reticularis — produces androgens, mainly DHEA and DHEA-S; exerts actions after conversion to testosterone; responsible for male sexual characteristics in males and female sex drive in females.
A(ii) In primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease), the adrenal gland itself is destroyed (by autoimmune destruction, tuberculosis, fungal or viral infections, surgical removal, etc.), so cortisol output falls. The pituitary responds by secreting excess ACTH. ACTH and the related hormone MSH share a common precursor (POMC) and both stimulate melanocytes, producing hyperpigmentation of mucous membranes and skin. In secondary adrenal insufficiency (pituitary or hypothalamic disease), ACTH levels are low or inappropriately normal, so there is no melanocyte stimulation and hyperpigmentation does not occur.
B(i) Distinguishing the adrenal cortex from the adrenal medulla:
• Embryological origin: the cortex is derived from mesoderm; the medulla is an extension of the sympathetic nervous system (neural crest origin).
• Hormones produced: cortex produces steroid hormones (mineralocorticoids, glucocorticoids, androgens); medulla produces catecholamines — epinephrine (80%) and norepinephrine (20%).
• Physiological role: the cortex maintains metabolic processes, electrolyte balance, and sexual maturation; the medulla works in conjunction with the sympathetic nervous system and mediates the 'fight or flight' stress response. Epinephrine is ten times more potent in direct metabolic effects, while norepinephrine is more potent as a neurotransmitter.

(i) Diagnosis: Acute kidney injury (AKI) secondary to crush injury/rhabdomyolysis. This represents intrinsic (renal) AKI. The reddish-brown urine indicates myoglobinuria/haemoglobinuria due to the crush injury. Renal (intrinsic) AKI causes listed include crush injury/trauma.
(ii) Pre-renal causes: hypovolaemia; excessive sweating (hot climate); excessive vomiting/diarrhoea; vasodilation from sepsis; cirrhosis (3rd space loss); cardiogenic shock; CCF, MI, pericardial tamponade; haemorrhage, APH, PPH, RTA; bilateral renal artery stenosis. Renal (intrinsic) causes — applicable to this patient: crush injury. Other renal causes: AGN; AIN (infections); herbs; drugs (NSAIDs, gentamycin, radio-contrast); malaria; haemolytic crisis; snake bite; G6PD deficiency; illegal abortions; unsafe deliveries. Post-renal: obstruction to flow of urine (extrinsic or intrinsic) causing damped-back pressure, decreased GFR, and increased accumulation of uraemic toxins. STOOP: Sepsis and hypoperfusion; Toxicity; Obstetric; Obstruction; Parenchymal kidney disease.
(iii) Pathophysiology: AKI is abrupt cessation of renal function presenting often as unexplained acute uraemic emergencies. Reduction in urine output leads to oliguria. Accumulation of nitrogenous waste products contributes to uraemia — contamination of blood with uremic toxins. The uraemic syndrome is the constellation of findings in advanced renal failure; earliest manifestations include anorexia, pruritus, fatigue, difficulty with memory and concentration; advanced stages involve multiple organ systems. KDIGO functional criteria: increase in serum creatinine by 50% within 7 days OR increase by 0.3 mg/dL (26.5 µmol/L) within 2 days OR oliguria = AKI.
(iv) Treatment: adequate volume replacement (use crystalloids instead of colloids); treat sepsis/haemorrhage; avoid/stop nephrotoxic agents; convert oliguria to non-oliguria; watch for polyuric phase (increased Na+, decreased K+); pharmacological Rx not helpful (loop diuretic, dopamine), but fenoldopam — a selective dopamine A-1 receptor agonist — is mentioned. Indications for renal replacement therapy (clinical and biochemical): uraemic syndrome; uraemic encephalopathy; uraemic pericarditis; recalcitrant oedema/hypertension; severe azotaemia; hyperkalaemia.
(v) Warning signs to monitor: during the polyuric phase, monitor for hypernatraemia (increased Na+) and hypokalaemia (decreased K+) — these are important electrolyte disturbances that occur as the kidneys recover and produce excess urine. The team should monitor for development of uraemic pericarditis, uraemic encephalopathy, hyperkalaemia, recalcitrant oedema, hypertension, and severe azotaemia as these are all indications for RRT.

A(i) Classification: By time course — acute, subacute, or chronic. By organism — viral, pyogenic, TB/fungal, aseptic/lymphomatous/carcinomatous. By anatomical layer — leptomeningitis or pachymeningitis.
A(ii) Routes and predilections: cranial and pericranial infections (sinusitis, otitis, osteomyelitis, head trauma); neurosurgical sites, shunts, spina bifida, encephalocoele; haematogenous spread; septic emboli from valvular vegetations or lungs.
B(i) Clinical features of TB meningitis: Systemic — fever, weight loss, nocturnal diaphoresis, chronic cough or contact history, HIV. Neurological — headache, vomiting, papilloedema, meningeal signs, delirium, loss of consciousness, behavioural changes, lower cranial nerve palsies, seizures, motor/cortical deficits, choroidal tubercles, phlyctenular conjunctivitis.
B(ii) CSF in TBM: usually increased pressure; xanthochromic fluid that may form spider web on standing; protein 100–200 mg/dL (Froin syndrome); cells 50–600, usually lymphocytes predominate; glucose less than half; Ziehl-Neelsen stain; BACTEC culture for AAFB; PCR/RFLP; TB Quantiferon. Drug regimen: Intensive phase — four drugs (Isoniazid, Rifampicin, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol or streptomycin) for 2 months. Continuation phase — two drugs (Isoniazid and Rifampicin). Total treatment 9–12 months. Steroids, supportive care, rehabilitation, and treatment of complications (hydrocephalus, tuberculoma) are added.

A(i) Describe the H2-receptor antagonists under the following headings: (a) examples, (b) route of administration and bioavailability, (c) half-life and duration of action, (d) mechanism of action at the parietal cell, (e) acid secretion pattern most affected.
A(ii) Describe the adverse effects of H2 blockers, with particular attention to the differences between cimetidine and the other agents in terms of endocrine effects and cytochrome P450 interactions.
B(i) Explain the drug–drug interactions of cimetidine, naming the enzyme pathways inhibited and the drugs whose half-lives are prolonged. State which H2 blocker has the least interaction.
questions.answerText:
A(i) H2-receptor antagonists:
(a) Examples: cimetidine, ranitidine, famotidine (also nizatidine — not listed separately but referenced).
(b) Route: given orally usually; parenteral formulation exists. Well absorbed but subject to first-pass effect. Bioavailability ~50% (nizatidine has little first-pass metabolism and bioavailability of almost 100%).
(c) Half-life: T½ 1.5–4 hours, but duration of action much longer. Hepatic metabolism and renal excretion (glomerular filtration and tubular secretion); dose reduction required in renal impairment and the elderly.
(d) Mechanism: acts by competitive inhibition of H2 receptor at the parietal cell. Suppresses basal and meal-stimulated gastric acid secretion; also reduces acid secretion stimulated by histamine, gastrin, and cholinomimetic agents. Potency varies but all inhibit 60–70% of total 24-hour acid secretion.
(e) Acid secretion most affected: marked effect on nocturnal acid secretion; minimal effect on meal-stimulated acid secretion.
A(ii) Adverse effects:
- Extremely safe drugs with adverse effects in <3% of patients.
- Mental changes (confusion, hallucination, agitation) may occur with IV use.
- Cimetidine-specific endocrine effects: gynaecomastia and impotence in men (binds to dihydrotestosterone and androgen receptors); galactorrhoea in women.
- Compete with creatinine and procainamide for renal tubular secretion.
- Famotidine inhibits gastric first-pass metabolism of ethanol → may increase blood ethanol level.
B(i) Cimetidine drug–drug interactions:
Interferes with several hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes: CYP1A2, CYP2C9, CYP2D6, CYP3A4. Half-lives of drugs using these pathways are prolonged: warfarin, theophylline, phenytoin, lidocaine, quinidine, propranolol, labetalol, metoprolol, tricyclic antidepressants, several benzodiazepines, calcium channel blockers, sulfonylureas, metronidazole, and ethanol.
Best to avoid cimetidine in patients using these drugs.
Least interaction: ranitidine binds 4–10 times less avidly than cimetidine to cytochrome P450; negligible interaction occurs with nizatidine and famotidine.

A(i) Aetiology:
- Caused by Mycobacterium leprae: rod-shaped, AFB; first bacterium disease in humans; doubling time 12 days; cannot be cultured but grown in footpad of armadillo. Does not produce toxins. Penetrates and resides within macrophages. Preference for cool tissues: skin, peripheral nerves, anterior chamber of eye, upper respiratory tract, testes.
- Humans are only primary reservoir. Animal reservoirs: 9-banded armadillo, chimpanzee, mangabey monkeys.
- In 2009, M. lepromatosis announced as new cause: genetically similar to M. leprae; causes diffuse form lepromatous leprosy found in Mexico and the Caribbean.

A(ii) Classification:
Ridley-Jopling spectrum: TT (Tuberculoid) to BT (Borderline Tuberculoid) to BB (Borderline) to BL (Borderline Lepromatous) to LL (Lepromatous).
WHO classification: Paucibacillary = TT, BT. Multibacillary = LL, BL, BB, BT. Also: Pure neural leprosy; Indeterminate leprosy (single/few hypopigmented macules, 70% heal spontaneously, 30% progress to any determinate spectrum).

B(i) Nerve involvement:
Tuberculoid: asymmetrical; localised close to skin lesion; occurs early; damage due to inflammation.
Lepromatous: symmetrical; not localised close to skin lesion; occurs late; massive bacillary infiltration causes damage. In LL: progressive glove and stocking anaesthesia (light touch, pain, temperature) beginning at hands and feet, extending to whole body except axillas, groins, and scalp; position sense preserved; sweating lost; infiltration of corneal nerves causes anaesthesia predisposing to blindness.

B(ii) Leprae reactions:
Triggers: anti-leprosy therapy, intercurrent infection, vaccination, pregnancy.

Type 1 (Reversal/Downgrading reaction):
- Cell-mediated (Type IV hypersensitivity); occurs in borderline patients (BT, BB, BL)
- Delayed hypersensitivity caused by increasing recognition of M. leprae in skin and nerve
- Features: inflammation of existing lesions, possible new lesions, swelling of hands and feet, neuritis (ulnar nerve usually affected)
- Histology: perivascular and perineural oedema and large number of lymphocytes; reaction most severe in BL
- Treatment: prednisolone starting at 40-60 mg daily, reducing to 40 mg, then by 5 mg every 2-4 weeks; BT needs 2-4 months, BL may need 6 months; gabapentin 300 mg QID and amitriptyline 50-150 mg QID for neuropathic pain; splinting

Type 2 (ENL - Erythema Nodosum Leprosum):
- Immune complex mediated (Type III); occurs exclusively near lepromatous end (BL, LL), affecting nearly 50% of this group
- Features: crops of painful erythematous papules/nodules resolving spontaneously in days to a week but recurring; malaise and fever; may cause neuritis, lymphadenitis, uveitis, orchitis, glomerulonephritis; anaemia, leukocytosis, abnormal LFTs; rarely fatal
- Treatment: high-dose steroids (80 mg daily, tapered rapidly) or thalidomide (400 mg daily — drug of choice for young men with severe ENL; teratogenic — phocomelia in first trimester); clofazimine 300 mg/day has useful anti-inflammatory effect; chronic ENL with iritis or neuritis requires long-term suppression with thalidomide or clofazimine

questions.answerText:
(i) Two target organ complications evident:
• Brain: stroke (sudden onset left-sided weakness and difficulty speaking represent cerebrovascular accident — hypertension causes stroke and dementia).
• Heart: hypertensive heart disease (S4 gallop — fourth heart sound indicates decreased LV compliance from LVH, an ischaemic heart disease finding; hypertension causes ischaemic heart disease, hypertensive heart disease, and heart failure).
(ii) Investigations assessing cardiac involvement:
• ECG: may show rhythm abnormality, left axis deviation, chamber enlargement or hypertrophy, and evidence of ischaemic heart disease.
• Chest X-ray: aortic unfolding, cardiomegaly, redistribution of pulmonary blood flow (upper lobe diversion), and evidence of pleural effusion.
• Echocardiography: would show rhythm abnormality, cavity sizes, muscle thickness, contraction and relaxation of the heart, and valvular peculiarities — in hypertension would show LVH, possibly impaired diastolic function.
• Cardiac MRI: provides refined delineation of heart chambers, walls and cavity.
(iii) Other target organs at risk:
• Eyes — retinopathy/blindness.
• Kidney — chronic renal failure.
• Lower extremity blood vessels — intermittent claudication and various degrees of paraesthesia.
(iv) JNC 7 classification: BP ≥180/≥120 mmHg is classified as Severe hypertension (Stage 2 is ≥160/≥100 mmHg). Pharmacological management: the overall goal is to lower BP below 140/90 mmHg; drug therapy is recommended when BP is persistently high despite non-pharmacological therapy or is already high at this severe level; choice of drug class depends on race, age, sex and other compelling conditions. Drug classes include: diuretics (e.g. frusemide, thiazides — acting at nephrons of the kidneys); beta-blockers (e.g. atenolol, metoprolol — acting on the heart); ACE inhibitors (e.g. lisinopril, ramipril — acting on lungs and blood vessels); ARBs (e.g. losartan, valsartan — acting on blood vessels); calcium channel blockers (e.g. nifedipine, amlodipine, verapamil — acting on AV node and blood vessels); central acting alpha agonists (e.g. alpha methyldopa); direct vasodilators (e.g. hydralazine).
(v) Non-pharmacological measures: low sodium diet (no added salt); low dairy intake; increased dietary intake of potassium and fibres; moderate alcohol intake; stopping smoking; increased physical activity/aerobic exercise; reducing psychosocial stress; managing obesity especially truncal obesity; DASH diet (emphasises fruits, vegetables, low-fat dairy products, whole grains, poultry, fish and nuts with very low red meat, sweets, and sugar-containing beverages).

questions.answerText:
(i) Spot diagnosis: Atrial Septal Defect (ASD). Category: acyanotic congenital heart disease (left-to-right shunt) — CHD with little or no cyanosis.
(ii) Fixed splitting of S2: S2 is produced by closure of the aortic valve (A2) and pulmonic valve (P2) in that order. In normal individuals the A2-P2 interval widens with inspiration and narrows with expiration (physiological splitting). In ASD there is a large left-to-right shunt that causes chronic volume overload of the right heart and pulmonary circulation; the right ventricle takes longer to eject (delayed P2 regardless of respiratory phase); because the ASD equalises right and left atrial pressures, the normal respiratory variation in right heart filling that causes the A2-P2 interval to vary is abolished — both P2 delay and its respiratory variation are lost. The splitting therefore remains wide and FIXED in both inspiration and expiration. A chest X-ray reveals enlargement of the heart and signs of pulmonary over-circulation (large pulmonary trunk and increased pulmonary vascular markings); the severity reflects the size of the left-to-right shunt.
(iii) Two major complications:
• Pulmonary arterial hypertension: caused by elevated pulmonary vascular resistance; develops after adolescence in about 15% of cases; in the most severe cases an irreversible plexiform arteriopathy (similar to Eisenmenger syndrome or primary pulmonary hypertension) is present. As pulmonary hypertension progresses, the left-to-right shunt first decreases, then becomes bidirectional, and finally reverses (right-to-left), reducing pulmonary blood flow and causing cyanosis.
• Right ventricular failure: results from long-standing volume overload; usually affects patients older than 40 years; associated with atrial flutter or fibrillation and often linked to tricuspid regurgitation; eventually a syndrome of right- and left-sided congestive heart failure develops, making it difficult to differentiate from cardiomyopathy and mitral valve disease.
(iv) Surgical indication: prophylactic surgery is indicated in any patient in whom the ratio of pulmonary blood flow to systemic blood flow is 2:1 or greater; nearly all patients in whom ASD can be clinically diagnosed exhibit at least this degree of left-to-right shunt. Surgical contraindication: surgery is contraindicated when pulmonary hypertension approaches the level of the systemic circulation because operative mortality is high and elevated pulmonary vascular resistance does not fall after surgery.
(v) Non-surgical closure: using cardiac catheterisation with an umbrella-like device; applicable in patients with defects less than 2 cm in diameter, most of whom have been infants or small children.

questions.answerText:
(i) Pyogenic (bacterial) meningitis. In adults from the community, the most common organisms are Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae; Neisseria meningitidis (pathogenic serogroups A, B, C, Y, and W-135) is also a major cause.
(ii) Pathogenesis of complications: entrance, invasion, and spread of organisms leads to inflammation, organisation, and fibrosis; vasculitis with or without infarction; ventriculitis; hydrocephalus; cranial nerve palsies; three types of oedema; raised intracranial pressure; and septic thrombosis.
(iii) CSF findings: increased pressure, turbid fluid; pleocytosis predominantly neutrophils; red cells may be present; increased protein; low glucose with CSF/plasma glucose ratio less than half; Gram stain, Indian ink stain, culture, and PCR are performed.
(iv) Resuscitation and antibiotics: i.v. Cefotaxime 2 g 4-hourly, or i.v. Ceftriaxone 2 g 12-hourly, or i.v. Ceftazidime 2 g 12-hourly; steroids are given in the absence of HIV with the first dose of antibiotics; supportive care, anticonvulsants when indicated, rehabilitation, and vaccination.
(v) Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome: meningococcal infection causing sepsis with hypotension, associated with the maculopapular rash and chest or respiratory tract infection seen in meningococcal meningitis.

(i) Lipid abnormalities :
- Elevated total cholesterol: 6.0 mmol/L (threshold >5.17 mmol/L/>200 mg/dL).
- Elevated LDL-C: 4.0 mmol/L (threshold >3.36 mmol/L/>130 mg/dL).
- Low HDL-C: 0.9 mmol/L for a male (threshold <1.03 mmol/L/<40 mg/dL for males).
- Elevated triglycerides: 2.1 mmol/L (threshold >1.7 mmol/L/>150 mg/dL).
(ii) Secondary causes relevant to this patient:
Elevated total cholesterol/LDL-C: nephrosis; dysgammaglobulinaemia (SLE, multiple myeloma); progestin or anabolic steroid treatment; cholestatic liver diseases; protease inhibitors for HIV.
Elevated triglycerides/VLDL-C: chronic renal failure; type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM); obesity; excessive alcohol intake; hypothyroidism; antihypertensive medications (thiazide diuretics, beta-adrenergic blocking agents); corticosteroid therapy; orally administered oestrogens; protease inhibitors.
(iii) Differential pathologies producing this pattern: hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, diabetes mellitus, chronic renal failure, primary hyperlipidaemia.
Clinico-anatomical relationship: for every 1% increase in cholesterol level there is a 1–2% increase in the incidence of CHD; dyslipidaemia was estimated by WHO in 2002 to account for 18% of ischaemic heart disease, 56% of stroke, and more than 4 million deaths per year globally; elevated CRP (a marker of inflammation and atherosclerosis) correlates with increased risk for heart attack, stroke, and vascular disease.
(iv) Drug of first choice for raised LDL-C: Statin (statins are the most effective treatment for high LDL levels per clinical trials and guidelines).
Key considerations: liver function test prior to therapy and as clinically indicated thereafter; myalgias and muscle weakness in some individuals; potential for drug–drug interaction between some statins and CYP450 3A4 inhibitors, cyclosporine, warfarin, and protease inhibitors; myopathy/rhabdomyolysis in rare cases; simvastatin dosages should not exceed 40 mg in most individuals; statins usually administered in the evening (most hepatic cholesterol production occurs at night); atorvastatin may be given any time of day due to its longer half-life.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Cough is an intermittent, spasmodic forceful expiration of air following short inspiration. It could be at very sharp speed up to 500 miles/hour. It is physiologic (a protective mechanism) in response to clear irritation to the bronchial tree (pharynx, bronchi), interstitial pulmonary (fibrosing lung disease, pulmonary oedema), and external stimulation of the bronchial tree — like occurs in GERD. Sensory nerve stimulates the cough. Non-physiological cough is often voluntary — like clearing the throat before speech. In some people it can become a tic (habit). There is a cough centre in the Medulla Oblongata which seems to have higher controls also. The whole respiratory nervous network controlling breathing is functionally connected to the cough centre.
A(ii) Classification: (a) Duration — acute; chronic (greater than 6 weeks); acute on chronic. (b) Productive or non-productive — sputum expectoration (how much, what colour, consistency) vs nil or scanty sputum. (c) Sound produced — whoop/stridor: reflects partial obstruction (Bordetella pertussis); bovine: prolonged, low-pitched, associated with hoarseness of voice (e.g., single vocal cord paralysis).
B(i) Causes of cough: (a) Infections — post-viral pneumonitis: mild, short-lived, acute non-productive cough; infections (bacterial) in pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi — bacterial productive cough (colour depends on bacterium: yellow, green, blue); pharynx could be secondary to post-nasal drip of chronic sinusitis; pneumonia; tuberculosis. (b) Allergy — bronchospasm cough is asthma; ACE-inhibitor cough in 10–15% of females. (c) Irritation by neighbouring structure — stimulation by acids of oesophagus in gastro-oesophageal reflux (GERD) disease — causes persistent non-productive cough when no epigastric pains, can pass for cough of unknown origin. (d) Carcinomatous growth — bronchial or any part of bronchial tree growth; primary or secondaries. (e) Pulmonary (interstitial) changes — COPD; pneumonia (lobar, segmental); bronchopneumonia; fibrosing pulmonary disease; pulmonary oedema — lymphatics, pulmonary venous congestion. (f) Foreign body in airways.
B(ii) Management of cough: mild cough is self-limiting; remaining well hydrated is essential in all cough management; measures to aid expectoration with mucolytic agents, humidification, nebulisers; use of cough suppressants (e.g., dihydrocodeine, dextrophan) not encouraged; definitive treatment of the primary cause (e.g., cigarette smoking, allergen control, infections treatment, pulmonary oedema/left ventricular dysfunction, GERD, chronic sinusitis, otitis, neuronal); bronchoscopy for foreign body removal, lavage; tumour shrinkage — radiotherapy. Hiccup: spasmodic involuntary contraction of the diaphragm as the glottis closes in inspiration, called Synchronous Diaphragmatic Flutter (SDF). Causes — 'normal' short-lived (gas in tummy due to aerophagy, alcohol); intractable hiccups >48 hours (GERD, renal failure, hypo/hyperglycaemia, irritation of vagus/phrenic nerve). Treatment: grandmother's method (culturally varied); correcting the inherent metabolic/surgical disorder; drugs — chlorpromazine, metoclopramide, cinnarizine, haloperidol. Complications of cough: conjunctival haemorrhage; chest pains/costochondritis; hernia; headaches; abdominal pains.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Gross anatomy of adrenal glands:
Location: the adrenal glands (also known as suprarenal glands) are endocrine glands located on top of the kidneys.
Two distinct structures: (1) the adrenal medulla — the core of the adrenal gland; (2) the adrenal cortex — surrounds the medulla. The cortex is divided into 3 zones in the adult gland: zona glomerulosa (outer), zona fasciculata (middle), and zona reticularis (inner).
Five main functions of adrenal hormones: (1) maintaining metabolic processes such as managing blood sugar levels and regulating inflammation; (2) regulating the balance of salt and water; (3) controlling the 'fight or flight' response to stress; (4) maintaining pregnancy; (5) initiating and controlling sexual maturation during childhood and puberty.
A(ii) Cushing's syndrome — MOODIAH:
• M — Moon face: facial puffiness and rounding; face often looks redder than usual.
• O — Obesity and oedema from salt and water retention.
• O — Osteoporosis.
• D — Diabetes: hyperglycaemia from excess cortisol.
• I — Infections: immune suppression by excess glucocorticoids.
• A — Atherosclerosis.
• H — Hypertension.
Most common aetiology of Cushing's disease: pituitary adenoma (ACTH-dependent Cushing's disease); other causes include adrenal adenoma, ectopic paraneoplastic ACTH production (often small cell cancer of the lung), and iatrogenic (glucocorticoid administration — the only cause that produces adrenal atrophy and resultant poor response to stress).
B(i) The adrenal medulla is an extension of the sympathetic nervous system (neural crest origin) — neurons from the hypothalamus stimulate secretion of catecholamines. Because of this origin it produces catecholamines — epinephrine (80%) and norepinephrine (20%) — rather than steroids. It works in conjunction with the sympathetic nervous system and mediates the stress response. Epinephrine is 10 times more potent in producing direct metabolic effects; norepinephrine is more potent as a neurotransmitter. Phaeochromocytoma is a benign tumour of the adrenal medulla (90% arise in the adrenal; 10% occur elsewhere in the sympathetic chain); the cells (pheochromocytes) secrete epinephrine and/or norepinephrine autonomously in episodic bursts; large tumours and extra-adrenal tumours produce almost entirely norepinephrine. This autonomous catecholamine release causes episodes of hypertension (intermittent or constant), tachycardia, arrhythmias, sweating, headache, palpitations, anxiety, and weight loss — the classic symptoms. Diagnosis relies on measurement of urinary catecholamines and metabolites (preferably metanephrines) with three 24-hour urine collections; plasma chromogranin A (a storage vesicle protein) is raised; CT scan and MRI localise the tumour; [¹³¹I]mIBG scanning produces specific uptake in sites of sympathetic activity with about 90% success.

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: severe mitral stenosis (mitral valve area 1.2 cm², well below the 2 cm² threshold at which symptoms and transmitral gradients begin; normal MV area 4–6 cm²) with rheumatic aetiology and atrial fibrillation as a complication. Echocardiographic grading and management intervals: mild MS — echo every 3–5 years; moderate MS — echo every 1–2 years; severe MS — echo yearly.
(ii) Definitive interventional procedure: percutaneous mitral balloon valvotomy — identify patients early who might benefit from this procedure; also identify patients who can benefit from surgery. Medical therapy does not prevent progression because MS is a mechanical problem — medications (beta-blockers, CCBs, digoxin) only control heart rate and prolong diastole for improved diastolic filling, and diuretics manage fluid overload, but none reverses the structural valve lesion.
(iii) Medications appropriate for this patient with AF and MS:
• Rate control: beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers (CCBs), or digoxin — these control heart rate, prolonging diastole for improved diastolic filling and reducing transmitral gradient.
• Diuretics: for fluid overload/pulmonary congestion.
• Anticoagulation: rate control for atrial fibrillation with beta-blockers, CCBs, or digoxin; anticoagulation is indicated in atrial fibrillation to prevent thromboembolism (mentioned in MR section as applicable to AF; same principle applies in MS with AF).
(iv) Indications for surgery: identify patients who can benefit from surgery — guided by serial echocardiography and early identification of candidates for valvotomy or surgery. IE prophylaxis: patients with prosthetic valves or a history of infective endocarditis for dental procedures.
(v) Relationship between MS severity and S2-opening snap interval: a shorter S2-to-opening snap interval indicates more severe disease. In MS, the mitral valve opens early in diastole but is halted abruptly because of fusion at the leaflet tips (when leaflets are still mobile) — this abrupt halt produces the opening snap. The more severe the stenosis, the higher the left atrial pressure; a higher LA pressure causes the mitral valve to open earlier after aortic valve closure (earlier in diastole), shortening the S2-to-opening snap interval. Therefore, a short S2-OS interval = more severe MS.

A(i) Epidemiology, genetics, and associations:
- Prevalence 0.14-0.8% worldwide; no racial predilection
- Two-thirds of cases occur between ages 30-60; rare in the young and elderly
- Overall no sex variation; males present at younger age; females in 50s and 60s
- Seasonal variation has been reported; familial predisposition
- HLA associations: familial — HLA-B7, -Aw19, -B18, -Cw8. Non-familial — HLA-A3, -A5, -A28, -B8, -B16, -Bw35. Oral LP — B8; cutaneous LP — Bw35
- Associated conditions: autoimmune chronic active hepatitis, primary biliary cirrhosis, HCV (16-29%), syphilis, HSV, HBV, amoebiasis, chronic bladder infection, dyslipidaemia, metabolic syndrome

A(ii) Pathogenesis:
- Immunologic — cell-mediated immunity (T cells)
- Three stages: (1) Antigen recognition → (2) Lymphocyte activation → (3) Keratinocyte apoptosis (basal cells)

B(i) Clinical features:
4 P's: Purple (grey in blacks), Polygonal, Pruritic, Papule.
Primary lesion: extremely pruritic, purplish, planar, shiny papules and plaques (usually grey in blacks); thin adherent and transparent scales on each lesion.
Wickham's striae: fine whitish reticulate network easily observed with application of mineral oil, water, xylene; seen with dermatoscope or hand lens.
Koebner's phenomenon present.
Can cause scarring alopecia.
Nail features: longitudinal ridging, nail thinning, melanonychia, erythronychia, pterygium ungium.
Sites: bilateral symmetrical, flexural areas of extremities, thighs, lower back, trunk, neck. Face is often spared.

B(ii) Histology:
Epidermis: hyperkeratosis; wedge-shaped areas of hypergranulosis; elongated rete ridges (saw-tooth appearance); vacuolation/liquefaction of the basal layer.
Dermo-epidermal junction: colloid bodies (Civatte bodies).
Dermis: band-like, dense, lympho-histiocytic infiltrate at papillary dermis abutting the epidermis.
Immunofluorescence: heavy deposition of fibrin at the dermo-epidermal junction; IgM, less frequently IgA, C3 in the colloid bodies.

B(iii) Treatment:
- Potent topical steroids (0.05% clobetasone propionate); occlusion enhances effectiveness
- Intralesional steroids (triamcinolone acetonide) — reduces hypertrophic lesions; repeated every 3-4 weeks
- Systemic steroids: 20-40 mg/day for 2-4 weeks for generalised, severely pruritic LP; gradually reduced over 3 weeks to prevent recurrence
- Antihistamines
- Acitretin
- Azathioprine
- Cyclosporine: for severe, chronic LP
- PUVA: for generalised, symptomatic LP; maintenance may not be required once complete clearance attained
- Dapsone
- Hydroxychloroquine
- Low-dose enoxaparin

Describe hepatocellular carcinoma and its mimickers under the following headings:
A(i) Epidemiology of HCC including sex ratio, ranking among cancers, age of onset in black Africans, and prognosis especially in Nigeria.
A(ii) Describe the clinical features of HCC including features of underlying cirrhosis.
B(i) State the conditions that mimic HCC and explain the prevention strategies for HCC targeting HBV and HCV.
B(ii) Describe the approach to upper gastrointestinal symptoms covering the key features of the history of abdominal pain, vomiting character, and the significance of abdominal signs on palpation and auscultation.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Epidemiology of HCC: Most common primary malignant tumour of the liver. Men more susceptible than women at mean ratio of 2.4–3.7:1. Fifth most common cancer in men; eighth in women. Incidence increases with age. In black Africans, mean age is younger (under 30 years). Also known as primary liver cell carcinoma (PLCC). 5th common cause of cancer-related death worldwide; leading cause of cancer death in sub-Saharan Africa. In Nigeria: 6 months from diagnosis to death; 3 weeks from admission to death; 14 weeks from onset of illness; most die within 1 year of diagnosis.
A(ii) Clinical features of HCC: Features of cirrhosis — weakness, fatigue, anorexia, weight loss, abdominal swelling, mousy odour, haematemesis, melaena, jaundice, clubbing, white nails, asterixis, Dupuytren's contracture, gynaecomastia, female pubic hair pattern in males, ascites plus hydrocele, liver may be enlarged/normal/shrunken, splenomegaly, haemorrhoids, infertility, loss of sexual drive, testicular atrophy, amenorrhoea, beard and speech changes in females. HCC specific: hard nodular tender hepatomegaly; abdominal pain (RUQ); abdominal swelling; weight loss; jaundice; wasting; fever; ascites; hepatic bruit.
B(i) Mimickers of HCC: secondaries; hepatic amoebiasis; macronodular cirrhosis; hepar lobatum; polycystic liver disease; peliosis hepatis; FNH. Prevention of HCC via HBV/HCV control: immunisation; health education about transmission/prevention; antenatal screening; follow-up of carriers; treatment of chronic hepatitis; screening of blood/products (NBTS); control of HIV infection; vaccination against HBV at 0, 2, 6, and 12 months with booster every 5 years; treat all patients with chronic hepatitis B and C; regular follow-up of patients with chronic hepatitis and cirrhosis for early detection.
B(ii) Upper GIT symptoms history: Abdominal pain — onset (sudden or gradual; sudden severe pain waking patient suggests perforated viscus); location (upper abdomen favours PU, cholecystitis, pancreatitis; lower abdomen favours ruptured ovarian cyst, diverticulitis, PID); character (colicky pain suggests obstruction of tubular viscus; colicky becoming constant suggests strangulation); radiation (acute cholecystitis frequently radiates to right scapula and shoulder). Vomiting — character: projectile vomiting in infant is pathognomonic of IHPS; clear vomitus suggests pyloric obstruction; bile-stained (green) vomitus indicates obstruction distal to CBD entry; fresh blood or coffee-grounds suggests bleeding DU, GU, or stomach cancer. Palpation: Murphy's sign positive in cholecystitis; board-like rigidity suggests generalised peritonitis from perforated ulcer; doughy abdomen suggests abdominal TB; positive succussion splash suggests gastric outlet obstruction. Auscultation: hyperactive bowel sounds in early obstruction; hypoactive in later phase; absent in peritonitis or severe paralytic ileus; arterial bruits over vascular liver tumours.

A(i) Cardiac conduction system:
• SA node: generates action potential at an intrinsic rate of 60–100 beats/minute; it is the dominant pacemaker; delivers impulses to the atria and the AV node.
• AV node: back-up pacemaker with an intrinsic rate of 40–60 beats/minute; receives impulse from the SA node and delivers it to the bundle of His and Purkinje fibres.
• Bundle of His, bundle branches, Purkinje fibres: conduct the impulse to the ventricles; ventricular cells have an intrinsic back-up pacemaker rate of 20–45 bpm.
A(ii) Normal sinus rhythm parameters:
• Rate: 60–100 bpm.
• Regularity: regular.
• P waves: normal (representing atrial depolarisation).
• PR interval: 0.12–0.20 seconds.
• QRS duration: 0.04–0.12 seconds (representing ventricular depolarisation).
• T wave: represents ventricular repolarisation.
Any deviation from the above constitutes sinus tachycardia, sinus bradycardia, or an arrhythmia.
B(i) In acute rheumatic fever, pancarditis involves the myocardium; inflammation of the AV node region slows or blocks conduction through it, prolonging the PR interval (first-degree AV block is a minor Jones criterion; second-degree AV block rarely). PR interval prolongation cannot be counted as a minor criterion if carditis is already present as a major criterion. In complete heart block, the AV node fails to transmit any atrial impulse to the ventricles; the atria and ventricles beat independently at their own intrinsic rates (atria at 60–100 bpm, ventricles at 20–45 bpm). The resulting slow, dissociated ventricular rate dramatically reduces cardiac output, causing haemodynamic compromise, dizziness, syncope, and cardiac failure. The reduced synchrony between atrial and ventricular contraction also eliminates the contribution of atrial systole to ventricular filling.
