questions.answerText:
A(i) Mitral stenosis:
Definition: obstruction of LV inflow that prevents proper filling during diastole.
Normal mitral valve area: 4–6 cm².
Symptom/gradient threshold: transmitral gradients and symptoms begin at areas less than 2 cm².
Predominant aetiology: rheumatic carditis — rheumatic heart disease accounts for 77–99% of all cases; infective endocarditis accounts for 3.3%, mitral annular calcification for 2.7%.
Natural history — disease of plateaus: mild MS develops approximately 10 years after the initial RHD insult; moderate MS develops approximately 10 years after mild MS; severe MS develops approximately 10 years after moderate MS. Mortality results from progressive pulmonary congestion, infection, and thromboembolism.
A(ii) Haemoptysis: results from rupture of bronchial vessels due to elevated pulmonary venous pressure — the increased transmitral pressures lead to left atrial enlargement and pulmonary venous hypertension; this chronically elevated pressure causes bronchial vessel engorgement and eventual rupture with blood-stained sputum. Right heart failure: elevated pulmonary venous pressure → pulmonary arterial hypertension → right heart pressure overload → right-sided heart failure symptoms develop including elevated JVP, hepatomegaly, and peripheral oedema.
B(i) Distinguishing MS from MR:
Physical examination:
• MS: prominent 'a' wave in jugular venous pulsations (due to pulmonary hypertension and RVH); signs of right-sided heart failure in advanced disease; mitral facies (pinkish-purple patches on cheeks when cardiac output is diminished).
• MR: soft S1 on auscultation; S3 gallop (CHF/LA overload); exertional dyspnoea and exercise intolerance.
Auscultatory signs:
• MS: low-pitched diastolic rumble most prominent at the apex, heard best with patient on the left side in held expiration (bell); intensity of diastolic murmur does NOT correlate with severity; loud opening snap at apex when leaflets are still mobile; a shorter S2-to-opening snap interval indicates more severe disease.
• MR: soft S1; pan(holo)systolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla; in chronic MR the intensity of the murmur DOES correlate with severity.
ECG changes:
• MS: may show atrial fibrillation and LA enlargement.
• MR: may show LA enlargement, atrial fibrillation, and LV hypertrophy with severe MR.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe mitral stenosis under the following headings: definition and normal mitral valve area, the threshold valve area at which symptoms and transmitral gradients begin, the predominant aetiology, and the natural history described as 'disease of plateaus.'

Describe typhoid fever and hepatic abscess under the following headings:
A(i) Describe the history of typhoid fever, its causative organism, risk groups (carriers, special groups), and why the infection mimics many diseases.
A(ii) Describe pyogenic liver abscess and amoebic liver abscess side by side, comparing their source/aetiology, clinical presentation, investigations, and treatment.
B(i) describe the significance of the character of abdominal pain in three common upper GIT conditions (cholecystitis, duodenal ulcer, and pancreatic carcinoma) and how they are managed surgically.
B(ii) Describe the common associations and clinical features of gallstones, chronic duodenal ulcer, and gastric ulcer.
questions.answerText:
A(i) History of typhoid fever: Around 430–424 BC, a devastating plague believed to be typhoid fever killed one-third of the population of Athens. In 1880, Karl Joseph Eberth described the causative bacillus. Almroth Edward Wright developed the first effective typhoid vaccine in 1896. In 1909, Frederick F. Russell adopted it for the US Army. In 1908, chlorination of drinking water was a significant control step. Also called gastric fever, enteric fever, abdominal typhus, slow fever, nervous fever, and pythogenic fever. Caused by Salmonella typhi; transmitted by ingestion of food or water contaminated with faeces of infected persons. Carriers — particularly those with gallbladder disease or stones, urinary or rectal schistosomiasis. Special susceptible groups: cooks shedding organisms with poor hygiene; sickle cell patients; patients with achlorhydria (lack of gastric acid to kill organisms).
A(ii) Pyogenic vs amoebic liver abscess: Source/aetiology — Pyogenic: appendicitis, cholangitis, cholecystitis, diverticulitis, perforated PU, peritonitis, may complicate HCC; cryptogenic; polymicrobial (E. coli, Klebsiella, Proteus, Pseudomonas, Streptococcus). Amoebic: caused by Entamoeba histolytica; ingestion of cysts → trophozoites in colon → mucosal invasion → portal circulation → liver. Clinical presentation — Pyogenic: acute; high-grade swinging pyrexia; RUQ pain; may present with shock; hepatomegaly; RUQ tenderness. Amoebic: subacute; RUQ pain; fever; malaise, myalgias, arthralgias; jaundice. Investigations — Both: abdominal USS, CT, blood culture, FBC (anaemia, leucocytosis), LFTs (elevated ALP); aspirated material: amoebic yields reddish-brown anchovy paste; additionally ELISA serology for amoebic. Treatment — Pyogenic: broad-spectrum antibiotics (changed based on culture). Amoebic: metronidazole plus aspiration.
B(i) Upper GIT conditions and surgical management: Cholecystitis — right hypochondrial pain radiates around right costal margin to right scapula and shoulder; Murphy's sign positive on palpation; management: cholecystectomy (open or laparoscopic). Chronic duodenal ulcer — pain aggravated by hunger, NSAIDs, aspirin, spicy food; relieved by eating and antacids; wakes patient at night; complications (perforation, bleeding, pyloric stenosis) prompt surgical referral. Pancreatic carcinoma of head — obstructive jaundice, distended gallbladder (Courvoisier's law); DM may be present; management: Whipple's operation if early; biliary bypass when late.
B(ii) Gallstones: right hypochondrial pain aggravated by ingestion of fatty/oily meals; fat, fair, fertile, flatulent female of fifty; post-partum primipara who popped pills pre-pregnancy; Charcot's biliary triad (RHC pain, fever with chills, jaundice) suggests cholangitis from stone entering CBD. Chronic duodenal ulcer: pain aggravated by hunger, NSAIDs, aspirin, spicy food; relieved by eating and antacids; pain wakes patient at night around 1–2 am; exhibits periodicity activated by work, worry, or weather; complications: perforation, bleeding, pyloric stenosis. Chronic gastric ulcer: aggravated by eating food; associated with blood group A; may have malignant transformation potential; associated with hypochlorhydric states.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old man presents to clinic with a 3-month history of progressive dysphagia first to solids, then liquids, associated with odynophagia, significant weight loss, hoarseness, and haemoptysis. He smokes and drinks alcohol heavily. On examination he has cervical lymphadenopathy.
(i) What is the most likely diagnosis and which histological type is most common?
(ii) List the aetiological and associated factors for this condition.
(iii) Describe the complications of this condition.
(iv) Outline the investigations and treatment (palliative and definitive).
(v) What are the differential diagnoses of this presentation?
questions.answerText:
(i) Carcinoma of the oesophagus. Most common histological type: squamous cell carcinoma (more than 85% of cases). Adenocarcinoma accounts for 10–20%.
(ii) Aetiological/associated factors: sequence of dysplasia – carcinoma in situ – carcinoma; genetic factors (chromosomes 5q11, 6p21, 10q23, 12q24, 21q22); mucosal exposure to noxious substances — spirits (90% attributable to alcohol), smoking, chewing of noxious substances (betel nut, tobacco), nitrites, fungal toxins, hot tea; radiation-induced strictures; chronic achalasia; Plummer-Vinson/Patterson-Kelly syndrome; tylosis palmaris et plantaris; chronic gastric reflux (Barrett's/adenocarcinoma); deficiency of zinc and Vitamin A; HPV; low socioeconomic group.
(iii) Complications: tracheo-oesophageal fistula; oesophago-aortic fistula; electrolyte derangement; pneumonia; lung abscess.
(iv) Investigations: barium swallow; oesophagoscopy/biopsy; brush cytology; endosonography; chest CT; chromoendoscopy with iodine (confirmation by histology). Treatment — Palliative: tube/stent insertion; PEG/PEJ procedure for feeding; fluid and electrolyte correction; nutritional support; oncolytic therapy (laser beams or ethanol injection); EMR. Definitive: surgery; chemotherapy (FLEP regime = 5-FU, Leucovorin, Etoposide and Platinum); radiotherapy.
(v) Differential diagnoses: stricture; achalasia of the cardia; gastric carcinoma.

(i) JNC 7 classification: Stage 1 Hypertension (SBP 140–159 / DBP 90–99 mmHg).
(ii) Risk factors and their contribution:
• Cigarette smoking — a modifiable environmental factor that contributes to raised BP and increases cardiovascular risk.
• Excessive alcohol intake — a modifiable environmental risk factor that directly raises BP.
• Obesity (truncal) — increases body weight and truncal adiposity, which raises BP; manage obesity especially truncal obesity as part of hypertension control.
• Family history — genetic factors; hypertension runs in families and may be due to genetic makeup or a defect in the kidney nephrons shared in that family.
(iii) Target organ complications:
• Brain — stroke and dementia.
• Eyes — retinopathy and blindness.
• Heart — ischaemic heart disease, hypertensive heart disease, and heart failure.
• Kidney — chronic renal failure.
• Lower extremity vessels — intermittent claudication and various degrees of paraesthesia.
(iv) Non-pharmacological management: low sodium diet (no added salt); low dairy intake; increased dietary intake of potassium and fibres; moderate alcohol intake; stopping smoking; increased physical activity/aerobic exercise; reducing psychosocial stress; managing obesity especially truncal obesity; DASH diet (emphasises fruits, vegetables, and low-fat dairy products including whole grains, poultry, fish and nuts with very low red meat, sweets, and sugar-containing beverages).
(v) Pharmacological therapy should be started when BP is persistently high despite strict application of non-pharmacological therapy. The overall goal is to lower BP below 140/90 mmHg to reduce cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. The choice of drug class depends on race, age, sex and other compelling conditions; diuretics are noted to be useful in blacks, while ACE inhibitors/ARBs are preferred in Caucasians.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Pneumonia implies inflammation of the lung parenchyma. It is a syndrome caused by acute infection, usually bacterial, characterized by clinical and/or radiographic signs of consolidation of a part or parts of one or both lungs. Classification: community-acquired pneumonia; hospital-acquired pneumonia; aspiration pneumonia; pneumonia in immunocompromised. Below the larynx is normally sterile. Infections reach the lungs by inhalation, aspiration, direct inoculation (e.g., stab wound to chest), or blood borne (e.g., from intravenous drug misuse). Pathological stages: most pathogens responsible for CAP reach the lung by first colonizing the oropharynx; a phase of active hyperaemia occurs lasting approximately 24 hours, characterised by engorgement of arterial blood vessels; next stage is red hepatization — neutrophils and fibrin fill the alveoli, and massive extravasation of red blood cells produces homogenous opacity; next phase is grey hepatization — fibrin and exudative cells accumulate; then resolution.
A(ii) Clinical features — symptoms: abrupt onset of fever; chills and rigour; pleuritic chest pain; cough; sputum production (purulent/blood-stained); breathlessness; muscle aches; headaches and anorexia. Signs: most common sign is crackles; occasionally classical features of consolidation — dullness to percussion; bronchial breathing; enhanced vocal resonance; additionally raised temperature, raised heart and respiratory rates, low BP, and mental confusion. Investigations: chest radiograph — demonstrates consolidation, detects complications such as lung abscess or empyema; sputum gram stain/culture; blood culture; pleural fluid analysis; antigen detection (pneumococcal antigen in sputum, urine, pleural fluid, or blood — prior antibiotic use may limit sensitivity); serological tests (viruses, Mycoplasma pneumoniae/Chlamydia pneumoniae); haematology and biochemistry.
B(i) Differential diagnosis: acute bronchitis; COPD exacerbation; left ventricular failure; pulmonary embolism. Severity assessment: the CURB-65 score (Confusion, Urea >7 mmol/L, Respiratory rate ≥30/min, Blood pressure <90/60 mmHg, Age ≥65 years) — each criterion scores 1 point, and a higher score indicates greater severity and guides the decision for hospital admission.
B(ii) Treatment of pneumonia is guided by the likely causative organism. For pharyngitis and URTI-associated organisms: streptococcal infection — penicillin V or amoxicillin; Mycoplasma pneumoniae or Chlamydia pneumoniae — a tetracycline or macrolide antibiotic (erythromycin or clarithromycin). For influenza with secondary bacterial pneumonia: pneumonia associated with influenza may be severe, requiring broad-spectrum antibiotics — flucloxacillin because of Staphylococcus aureus infection. For sinusitis: amoxicillin, trimethoprim, nasal decongestants (ephedrine), and analgesia (paracetamol); surgical drainage may be required for chronic sinusitis.
questions.question:
Describe community-acquired pneumonia under the following headings:
A(i) Define pneumonia, state its classification, and describe the pathological stages of consolidation.
A(ii) Describe the full clinical features (symptoms and signs) and investigations required for pneumonia.
B(i) State the differential diagnosis of pneumonia and the severity assessment tool used in clinical practice.

A 62-year-old man presents with a 6-month history of progressive resting tremor of the right hand, slow shuffling gait, and difficulty initiating movements. His wife says his face has become expressionless. On examination he has a 4–6 Hz coarse rest tremor, cogwheel rigidity, bradykinesia, hypomimia, hypophonia, festinant gait, and a positive Myerson sign. He has no dementia.
(i) State the most likely diagnosis and identify the diagnostic criteria that distinguish this condition from Parkinson-plus syndromes.
(ii) State the risk factors for this condition.
(iii) Describe the neuropathology and pathophysiology, including the role of dopamine and the effect of reduced striatal dopamine on the thalamocortical pathway.
(iv) Outline the medical management strategy from early to advanced disease.
(v) State the indications, contraindications, and available surgical options.
questions.answerText:
(i) Parkinson's disease. Distinguishing features from Parkinson-plus syndromes: motor features are usually asymmetrical at onset and respond to L-dopa; there is no rapid disease progression, no early dementia, no early postural instability, no early hallucinations with low doses of levodopa, no ocular signs (supranuclear gaze palsy, nystagmus), no pyramidal or cerebellar signs, and no early autonomic failure.
(ii) Risk factors: age; male gender; use of pesticides and herbicides; proximity to industrial plants or quarries; occupational exposure (blacksmiths); head injury; well water; rural living; farming; genetic factors. Caffeine and smoking are protective.
(iii) Neuropathology: loss of pigmented dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta (60–80% are lost before onset of clinical symptoms); reduced dopamine in the striatum to 50–70% of normal; presence of Lewy bodies (characteristic but not pathognomonic). Pathophysiology: reduced striatal dopamine results in increased inhibitory output from the globus pallidus interna/substantia nigra pars reticulata, leading to increased inhibition of the thalamocortical pathway and bradykinesia.
(iv) Medical management: Early PD — MAO-B inhibitor (selegiline/rasagiline), dopamine agonist, anticholinergic, amantadine, or L-dopa preparation (avoid anticholinergics in elderly). Moderate disease — L-dopa preparations. End-of-dose deterioration — increase LD/CD dose, use sustained-release preparation, add DA or COMT inhibitor. Peak-dose dyskinesia — smaller doses of LD more frequently, add amantadine. Advanced disease — manage fluctuations, dyskinesias; consider apomorphine or surgical options.
(v) Surgical indications: (1) diagnosis of idiopathic PD; (2) clear response to levodopa; (3) significant intractable symptoms; (4) drug-induced dyskinesias and wearing-off. Contraindications: atypical PD, cognitive impairment, major psychiatric illness, substantial medical comorbidities, advanced age. Options: Deep Brain Stimulation (DBS) of subthalamic nucleus or globus pallidus interna; ablation procedures (thalamotomy, pallidotomy); transplantation of fetal nigral cells, adrenal medulla cells, or stem cells (currently NOT recommended).

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the WHO classification of cardiomyopathies (1995), naming each type and its defining anatomical and physiological characteristic.
A(ii) State how the anatomical characteristics of dilated cardiomyopathy relate to its clinical presentation and echocardiographic findings.
B(i) Explain why a patient with dilated cardiomyopathy may develop both left-sided and right-sided heart failure, and describe how thromboembolic complications arise and lead to a functional deficit in a distant organ.
questions.answerText:
A(i) WHO classification of cardiomyopathies (1995) — 4 broad types:
• Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM): enlarged ventricles (both ventricles); systolic dysfunction.
• Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM): thickened ventricle (non-dilated LV); diastolic dysfunction; obstruction to outflow.
• Restrictive cardiomyopathy: restrictive filling and decreased diastolic volume of either or both ventricles with normal or near-normal systolic function and wall thickness.
• Arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia/cardiomyopathy (ARVC): fibro-fatty replacement of RV myocardium and RV dilation, often confined to a triangle of dysplasia (RV inflow, outflow and apex).
Unclassified cardiomyopathies: include LV non-compaction, Takotsubo cardiomyopathy (broken heart syndrome), channelopathies.
A(ii) In DCM: the most common type of cardiomyopathy; most cases are idiopathic; LV dilatation and systolic dysfunction (EF <50%) are essential for diagnosis. Clinical presentation: heart failure symptoms — breathlessness, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, orthopnoea, leg swelling, hepatomegaly, ascites, third heart sound, murmurs, rales. Echocardiographic findings: dilated left ventricle (and other chambers may also be dilated); global systolic dysfunction; ejection fraction low (<50%); possible spontaneous echo contrast or intracardiac clot; functional mitral and/or tricuspid regurgitation.
B(i) In DCM, the dilated, poorly contracting LV fails to maintain adequate cardiac output, causing backward congestion in the pulmonary vasculature (left-sided failure: breathlessness, PND, orthopnoea, fine crepitations). As pulmonary hypertension develops, the right ventricle also dilates and fails, producing right-sided heart failure (elevated JVP, hepatomegaly, ascites, pedal oedema). The dilated hypokinetic ventricle promotes blood stasis, particularly at the apex, predisposing to intracardiac thrombus formation (demonstrated on echo as spontaneous echo contrast or visible clot). Thrombus can detach and embolise to distant organs — thromboembolism to the cerebral circulation causes ischaemic stroke with resulting neurological deficit (hemiplegia, aphasia etc.); embolism to the limb vessels causes acute limb ischaemia; pulmonary embolism may occur if a right-heart thrombus dislodges.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) under the following headings: (a) examples and structural class, (b) formulation and routes of administration, (c) mechanism by which the prodrug is converted to active form, (d) pharmacokinetics including bioavailability, half-life, and duration of acid inhibition.
A(ii) Describe the clinical uses of PPIs, specifying the conditions for which they are indicated.
B(i) State the adverse effects of PPIs and explain the nutritional consequence of prolonged PPI use on vitamin B12.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Proton pump inhibitors:
(a) Examples: omeprazole, esomeprazole, lansoprazole, dexlansoprazole, rabeprazole, pantoprazole. All are substituted benzimidazoles — structurally similar to H₂-receptor antagonists.
(b) Formulation: all available in oral formulation (delayed-release, acid-resistant, enteric-coated capsules or tablets; some available as powder and regular tablet). Esomeprazole and pantoprazole also available in IV formulation.
(c) Mechanism of prodrug activation: PPIs are administered as inactive prodrugs to protect the acid-labile drug from rapid destruction in the gastric lumen. After passing through the stomach into the alkaline intestinal lumen, the enteric coatings dissolve and the prodrug is absorbed. The prodrug is a lipophilic weak base (pKa 4–5) and diffuses readily across lipid membranes into acidified compartments (e.g. parietal cell canaliculus). Within the acidified compartment the prodrug is rapidly protonated and undergoes molecular conversion to the active thiophilic sulfonamide cation. The sulfonamide reacts with the H⁺/K⁺ ATPase, forms a covalent disulfide linkage, and irreversibly inactivates the enzyme. PPIs inactivate only active proton pumps; inhibit both fasting and meal-stimulated acid secretion.
(d) Pharmacokinetics: subject to first-pass effect; bioavailability 50%; hepatic metabolism, negligible renal clearance; short T½ ~1.5 hours but acid inhibition lasts ~24 hours (18 hours required to synthesise new H⁺/K⁺ ATPase); 3–4 days required for maximal effect; 3–4 days for full acid secretion to return after stopping.
A(ii) Clinical uses: peptic ulcer disease; gastro-oesophageal reflux disease; Zollinger–Ellison syndrome; multiple endocrine neoplasia; systemic mastocytosis; NSAID-associated ulcers; prevention of re-bleeding from peptic ulcers; prevention of stress-related mucosal bleeding; gastrinoma and other hypersecretory states.
B(i) Adverse effects: generally safe; diarrhoea, headache, abdominal pain in 1–5% of patients; increased cases of interstitial nephritis.
Nutritional consequence of prolonged use: vitamin B12 absorption requires acid (acid promotes food-bound B12 release); a minor reduction in vitamin B12 absorption may occur during proton pump inhibition.

questions.question:
Describe gastrointestinal malignancies under the following headings:
A(i) Describe gastric carcinoma: epidemiology, risk factors, histological types, location, and clinical features.
A(ii) Describe the investigations and treatment of gastric carcinoma, and the management of gastric lymphoma.
B(i) Describe carcinoma of the pancreas: epidemiology, histological types, location, aetiology, and clinical features.
B(ii) Describe the investigations and treatment modalities available for carcinoma of the pancreas.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Gastric carcinoma: second leading cause of cancer death; causes about 800,000 deaths worldwide annually; commoner in Japan, Chile, and Ireland, especially in low socioeconomic group; highest incidence in sixth decade of life. Risk factors: H. pylori (maltomas/adenocarcinomas), nitrites (nitrosamines) in dried/smoked/salted foods, alcohol, tobacco, atrophic gastritis, pernicious anaemia, gastric ulcer, blood group A, partial gastrectomy, gastroenterostomy, gastric dysplasia, celiac disease, low socioeconomic class. Histological types: 90–95% adenocarcinoma; 10% NHL/MALTOMAS; linitis plastica (diffuse/scirrhous infiltration — leather bottle appearance, worse prognosis); intestinal type. Location: 60% antral/pyloric; 20–30% body/greater curvature; 5–20% cardia. Clinical features: often non-specific; anorexia, asthenia, anaemia (3 As); nausea; early satiety; dyspepsia; upper abdominal discomfort/swelling; haematemesis; melaena; epigastric mass; malnutrition; acanthosis nigricans; Sister Mary Joseph's nodule; Blumer shelf; Virchow's node/Troisier's sign; Krukenberg tumour; metastases.
A(ii) Investigations: barium meal; endoscopy/biopsy; exfoliative cytology; FOBT; diagnostic laparotomy; CEA; CT/MRI; CXR. Treatment: Supportive — TPN, enterostomy tube, blood transfusion. Definitive — surgery; chemotherapy (cisplatinum, 5-FU, doxorubicin); methotrexate instillation for ascites; radiation. Gastric lymphoma: radiosensitive; MOPP regimen (methotrexate, cyclophosphamide, oncovin, procarbazine, prednisolone) often curative; anti-H. pylori therapy with combination antibiotics is useful in MALT lymphoma and may be curative.
B(i) Pancreatic carcinoma: 3% of cancers in Africa; 4th most common cause of cancer death in men in USA; 90% adenocarcinoma; other types — cystadenoma, cystadenocarcinoma, adenoacanthoma, MEN, insulinoma, glucagonoma, ZES, somatostatinoma; M:F 2:1; rare before 25 (usually 60+ years). Location: head 60%, body 20%, tail 10%, shared 10%. Aetiology: smoking, DM, chronic pancreatitis, some dietary/environmental agents. Clinical features: few signs early; presentation usually late; pale bulky oily stool; dull mid-epigastric pain radiating to back; anorexia; insidious weight loss with aversion for meat; jaundice in 50% (head); distended gallbladder (Courvoisier's sign); backache; migratory thrombophlebitis; intense pruritus; acute pancreatitis; psychiatric disturbance; haematemesis; melaena; DM features.
B(ii) Investigations: abdominal USS/CT/ERCP/MRI/PET; cytology/FNA; LFTs (bilirubin >15 mg/dl, alkaline phosphatase); rarely increased serum amylase; ESR; Ba meal plus follow through; tumour markers (CA 19-9, alpha-fetoprotein, CEA, RNase, galactosyltransferase II, oncofetal antigen); blood sugar; diagnostic laparoscopy; calcitonin; hCG; angiography; isoamylase variant (s-type isoamylase); urinalysis; serum trypsin and trypsin-creatinine clearance (increased). Treatment: surgery; chemotherapy (5-FU, gemcitabine, angiogenic inhibitor, mitomycin, streptozotocin, ifosfamide, doxorubicin); radiation; palliative (narcotics, celiac plexus block, percutaneous splanchnic nerve blocks, thoracoscopic splanchnicectomy).

questions.question:
A 42-year-old man presents with a 2-month history of insidious weight loss, anorexia, and progressive dyspepsia. On upper GI endoscopy an ulcerating mass is found in the antral region. Biopsy confirms adenocarcinoma.
(i) Identify the most likely diagnosis and state the histological types of gastric malignancy.
(ii) List the risk factors for this condition.
(iii) Describe the clinical features including specific eponymous signs and metastatic patterns.
(iv) Outline the investigations and surgical treatment, including the specific operation performed for linitis plastica.
(v) Outline the differential diagnoses of this presentation.
questions.answerText:
(i) Gastric carcinoma (adenocarcinoma). Histological types: 90–95% adenocarcinoma; 10% NHL/MALTOMAS; linitis plastica (diffuse/scirrhous — infiltration and thickening of stomach, leather bottle appearance, worse prognosis); intestinal type (cohesive neoplastic type).
(ii) Risk factors: H. pylori (maltomas/adenocarcinomas); nitrites (nitrosamines) in dried, smoked, and salted foods or food additives; alcohol; tobacco; atrophic gastritis; pernicious anaemia; gastric ulcer; blood group A; partial gastrectomy; gastroenterostomy; gastric dysplasia; celiac disease; low socioeconomic class.
(iii) Clinical features: anorexia, asthenia, anaemia (3 As); nausea; early satiety; dyspepsia; upper abdominal discomfort/swelling; haematemesis; melaena; epigastric mass; malnutrition; acanthosis nigricans; Sister Mary Joseph's nodule (umbilical nodule); Blumer shelf; Virchow's node/Troisier's sign (left supraclavicular lymph node); Krukenberg tumour (ovarian metastasis); ascites; metastases to liver and other organs.
(iv) Investigations: barium meal; endoscopy/biopsy; exfoliative cytology; FOBT; diagnostic laparotomy; CEA; CT/MRI; CXR. Surgical treatment: supportive (TPN, enterostomy tube, blood transfusion); definitive surgery; for linitis plastica — total gastrectomy; otherwise partial gastrectomy with Billroth I or II anastomosis; chemotherapy (cisplatinum, 5-FU, doxorubicin); radiation.
(v) Differential diagnoses: differential of an antral mass includes peptic ulcer disease; gastric lymphoma (MALTOMA — radiosensitive, MOPP regimen often curative, anti-H. pylori therapy useful in MALT lymphoma); benign gastric polyp; stricture.

(i) Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Characteristic triad: right upper abdominal pain and swelling plus jaundice.
(ii) Risk factors (from HCC PPT): chronic HBV infection; chronic HCV infection; alcohol; liver cirrhosis; repeated dietary exposure to aflatoxin B1; cigarette smoking; haemochromatosis; Wilson's disease; oral contraceptive steroids.
(iii) Paraneoplastic syndromes in HCC: polycythaemia; hypoglycaemia; hypercalcaemia; systemic arterial hypertension; neuropathy; osteoporosis.
(iv) Investigations: abdominal USS; abdominal CT; MRI; serum tumour markers (AFP, fucosylated AFP, des-γ-carboxy prothrombin, α-L-Fucosidase); liver biopsy; hepatic angiography; laparoscopy; liver function tests; PT/PTTK; FBC; CXR; electrolytes, urea, and creatinine.
(v) Treatment: Surgical resection (for early, small tumour with partial hepatectomy). Liver transplant (for selected patients meeting certain criteria). Intralesional techniques: ethanol injection; radiofrequency ablation. Chemoembolization; arterial embolization. Chemotherapy (after liver biopsy for histological confirmation) when late. Systemic chemotherapy: sorafenib; hepatic artery infusion chemotherapy. Palliative (Nigeria setting): pain control; dietary support; emotional and spiritual support; control of infections; ascitic fluid control; treatment of encephalopathy.

A(i) Common symptoms: alteration in level of consciousness; headaches; convulsions; limb weakness; difficulty with walking; difficulty with speaking; difficulty with swallowing/hoarseness; unsteadiness/ataxia/incoordination; confusion/forgetfulness/disorientation; difficulty with control of sphincters; spasms; neck pain/neck stiffness plus fever; involuntary movements; numbness in extremities or painless burns; abnormal pain sensation; visual impairment/blindness. Common signs: impaired consciousness; mono/hemi/quadriplegia/paresis; dysphasia; dysarthria/dysphonia; tremors/dyskinesia/hypokinesia; sensory deficit (dermatomal/glove and stocking/radicular); visual field defects; memory impairment; nystagmus; spasms; meningeal irritation (neck stiffness, Kernig's, Brudzinski's); gait abnormalities; gaze palsies; reflexes (blink, gag, corneal, jaw jerk, oculo-vestibular).
A(ii) Clinical approach: LOOK — level of alertness, gait, abnormal movements, deformities, body posturing, neglect of one side, seizures, gaze. LISTEN — coherence, neologisms, comprehension, detailed history in chronological order, risk/precipitating factors. EXAMINE — logical sequence from head to toe. THINK — differential diagnoses. INVESTIGATE. Tasks: Where is the lesion (localisation)? What is the lesion? What is the extent of involvement? What are the co-morbidities? What are the predisposing/precipitating factors?
B(i) Cortical lesions: depend on lobe involved; motor paralysis (hemi/paraparesis); aphasia (dominant or non-dominant hemisphere); hemi/anaesthesia/paraesthesia; amnesia; seizures; cortical blindness/visual illusions/hallucinations/scotoma; alteration in level of consciousness; apraxia. Subcortical/basal ganglia: caudate nucleus — chorea; putamen — dystonia; nigro-striatum — akinetic rigid syndrome; thalamus — dysaesthesia, sensory impairment; subthalamic nucleus — ballism; internal capsule — motor/sensory/visual field defects. Brain stem: dysarthria, dysphonia, dysphagia, dysequilibrium, diplopia, deafness, dizziness, dysaesthesia, cranial nerve palsy, nystagmus, quadriparesis, altered consciousness, pupillary changes, tongue atrophy/gag. Cerebellar: incoordination; intention tremor; horizontal nystagmus; dysarthria; adysdiadochokinesia; past-pointing; ataxic gait; pendular knee jerk; macrographia; rebound phenomenon.
B(ii) Signs in coma: bilateral dilated fixed pupils — mass lesion, anoxia, hydrocephalus, drug overdose (anticholinergics/sympathomimetics); pinpoint pupils — pontine haemorrhage or opiates; asymmetric limb response — CVD, tumour, trauma, encephalitis; symmetrical limb response — metabolic encephalopathy. UMN vs LMN: UMN — pyramidal pattern of weakness, slowing of dextrous movements, spasticity, no wasting (disuse), brisk tendon jerks, extensor plantars, diminished superficial reflexes. LMN — weakness, reduced tone (may be normal), wasting, absent or decreased reflexes, flexor plantars, fasciculations.

Describe the clinical presentation and pathophysiology of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) under the following headings:
A(i) Define COPD, chronic bronchitis, and emphysema.
A(ii) Describe the full range of symptoms and physical signs in COPD.
B(i) Describe the haemodynamic and tubular effects during both the acute and chronic phases of any obstructive process in the urinary tract, as applied by analogy to obstructive disease in the body — and relate this to why COPD ultimately causes cor pulmonale.
B(ii) Distinguish between the 'pink puffer' and 'blue bloater' clinical types.
questions.answerText:
A(i) COPD is defined as a common and preventable disease characterised by persistent airflow limitation that is usually progressive and associated with an enhanced chronic inflammatory response in the airway and the lungs to noxious particles or gases (GOLD 2013). Chronic Bronchitis is defined clinically as the presence of a chronic productive cough for 3 months during each of 2 consecutive years (other causes of cough being excluded). Emphysema is defined pathologically as an abnormal, permanent enlargement of the air spaces distal to the terminal bronchioles, accompanied by destruction of their walls without obvious fibrosis.
A(ii) Symptoms: productive cough; breathlessness (most significant symptom, usually does not occur until the sixth decade); wheezing. FEV1 is the most common variable used to grade severity of COPD. Signs: tachypnoea and respiratory distress with simple activities; use of accessory respiratory muscles and paradoxical indrawing of lower intercostal spaces (Hoover sign); cyanosis; elevated jugular venous pulse (JVP); peripheral oedema; warm peripheries and dilated superficial veins. Chest: pursed-lip breathing; hyperinflation (barrel chest); wheezing frequently heard on expiration; diffusely decreased breath sounds; hyper-resonance on percussion; loss of cardiac dullness and lowering of hepatic dullness; prolonged expiration; coarse crackles beginning with inspiration in some cases.
B(i) Regarding obstructive uropathy: acute phase haemodynamic effects — increase in renal blood flow, reduced GFR, reduced medullary blood flow, increased vasodilatory prostaglandins and nitric oxide; tubule effects — increase in tubular and ureteral pressures, increase in reabsorption of Na+, urea and H2O. Chronic phase — reduction in RBF, further reduction in GFR, increased vasoconstriction prostaglandins, increase in renin-angiotensin production; tubule — reduced medullary osmolarity, reduced concentrating ability (structural damage, parenchymal atrophy), reduced transport functions for Na+, K+, H+. By analogy, COPD causes cor pulmonale through a similar chronic-obstruction pathway: chronic airflow limitation causes alveolar hypoxia and hypercapnia, which drive sustained pulmonary vasoconstriction; over time this remodels the pulmonary vasculature and raises pulmonary vascular resistance, producing pulmonary hypertension; the right ventricle, facing this chronically elevated afterload, hypertrophies and eventually dilates and fails — the cor pulmonale of chronic COPD.
B(ii) 'Blue bloater' (chronic bronchitis-predominant): patients may be obese and cyanosed; frequent cough and expectoration are typical; use of accessory muscles of respiration is common; coarse rhonchi and wheezing on auscultation; patients often have signs of right heart failure (cor pulmonale). 'Pink puffer' (emphysema-predominant): thin, breathless but well-oxygenated (pink); barrel chest; pursed-lip breathing; hyper-resonance; prolonged expiration; diffusely decreased breath sounds.

(i) Diagnosis: Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN). RPGN is a form of glomerular inflammation with the same symptoms as AGN, but renal failure develops more rapidly (over days, weeks, or months). Typically, histology of most glomeruli shows crescent formation (crescentic glomerulonephritis). Crescents are half-moon shaped lesions in Bowman's space formed by parietal epithelium and monocytes. In contrast, acute GN develops over days to weeks with renal failure from obstruction of glomerular capillary lumens by inflammatory cells. Rapidly progressive GN differs in the formation of crescents, its faster progression to renal failure, and the weeks-to-months timeline.
(ii) Aetiology (primary renal): MPGN due to expansion and proliferation of mesangial cells as a result of deposition of complement and sub-endothelial and intramembranous deposits, with tram-line appearance; Berger's disease (IgA nephropathy) — diffuse mesangial deposition of IgG-IgA; mesangioproliferative GN; idiopathic RPGN characterised by glomerular crescents. Systemic causes: vasculitis — Wegener's granulomatosis; collagen-vascular disease — SLE; hypersensitivity vasculitis; cryoglobulinaemias; polyarteritis nodosa; Henoch-Schönlein purpura; Goodpasture's syndrome. Infectious causes: most common infectious cause is Streptococcus species; other bacteria — diplococci, other streptococci, staphylococci, mycobacteria, Salmonella, Brucella suis, Treponema pallidum, Corynebacterium bovis, Actinobacilli; viruses — CMV, coxsackievirus, EBV, hepatitis BV, rubella, rickettsiae, mumps. Miscellaneous: Guillain-Barré syndrome, irradiation of Wilm's tumour, DPT vaccine, epidermal growth factor activation.
(iii) Three immunofluorescence patterns: (1) Granular deposits of immunoglobulins — immune complex disease; C3 levels usually low; anti-GBM antibody negative; ANCA negative. Causes include post-streptococcal GN, bacterial endocarditis, shunt nephritis, lupus nephritis. (2) Linear deposits of Ig on GBM — anti-basement membrane GN; C3 level normal; anti-GBM antibody positive; ANCA negative. Caused by anti-GBM disease and Goodpasture's syndrome. (3) Pauci-immune GN — C3 levels normal; anti-GBM antibody negative; ANCA positive (suggesting dysregulation of immunity). Causes include Wegener's granulomatosis and microscopic polyarteritis nodosa.
(iv) Treatment in anti-GBM disease should be started early with glucocorticoids, cyclophosphamide, and plasmapheresis. Plasmapheresis is continued daily until anti-GBM antibodies are not detectable. In pauci-immune GN, most cases are treated aggressively with glucocorticoids with or without cyclophosphamide, azathioprine, or cyclosporine. Treatment with steroids and cytotoxic drugs has not been shown to be beneficial even in the crescentic type of post-streptococcal GN — treatment is therefore supportive. Prompt diagnosis and treatment are needed to avoid irreversible renal damage.
(v) Long-term outcome: in post-streptococcal GN, recovery is usually complete but some will eventually develop hypertension. In ESRD, dialysis and transplantation are needed. Chronic glomerulonephritis — characterised by persistent proteinuria with or without haematuria, and progressive renal insufficiency — is a common cause of CKD worldwide. Sometimes diagnosis of chronic GN is accidental following routine urinalysis, blood tests showing azotaemia or anaemia, ultrasound showing bilateral shrunken kidneys, evaluation for hypertension, or clinical exacerbation triggered by sore throat. Treatment is as in other cases of CKD.

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Chronic pancreatitis — characterised by irreversible damage to the pancreas and eventual destruction of exocrine and endocrine tissues.

(ii) Causes:
- Alcohol
- Genetic: hereditary pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis
- Metabolic: hypercalcaemia, hypertriglyceridaemia
- Obstructive
- Autoimmune
- Idiopathic
- Asymptomatic pancreatic fibrosis
- Radiotherapy
- Also: infection/autoimmune; blockage of common bile/pancreatic duct; medications (estrogens, corticosteroids, thiazide diuretics, azathioprine); hyperparathyroidism
- More common in men; often in ages 30-40

(iii) Physical findings: abdominal tenderness; weight loss; palpable abdominal mass (pseudocyst); jaundice; palpable spleen.
Investigations: raised alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin, serum amylase/lipase during acute exacerbations; direct hormonal stimulation with secretin (most sensitive); trypsinogen in serum; chymotrypsin/elastase in stool; faecal fat; IgG4; plain abdominal radiography; abdominal USS; CT scan; MRI/MRCP; ERCP; endoscopic ultrasound (EUS); exploratory laparotomy.
Complications: ascites; intestinal obstruction; portal vein thrombosis; pancreatic cyst; diabetes mellitus; malabsorption of nutrients and fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, K.

(iv) Management:
- Pain: analgesics; stop alcohol; antioxidants; surgical nerve block
- Maldigestion and steatorrhoea: enzyme supplements (pancrease); low-fat diet; small frequent meals; vitamins and calcium; limit caffeine
- Diabetes: insulin, oral antidiabetic drugs
- NG tube insertion; nil by mouth; IV fluids when needed
- Nutritionist input for diet management

A 55-year-old male smoker of 30 pack-years presents with progressive breathlessness, productive cough, and bilateral ankle swelling. He reports the cough has been present for the past 3 years, lasting all year round. On examination, there is barrel chest, pursed-lip breathing, hyper-resonance on percussion, prolonged expiration, and bilateral pitting ankle oedema. His jugular venous pressure is elevated.
(i) What is the diagnosis and how does the clinical pattern distinguish between the two subtypes of this condition?
(ii) Identify all aetiological factors for this condition.
(iii) Describe the full range of clinical features present in this condition across all stages.
(iv) What complications are evident in this patient and what additional complication must be considered?
(v) Outline the management of an acute exacerbation.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) with probable cor pulmonale. COPD is defined as a common and preventable disease characterised by persistent airflow limitation that is usually progressive and associated with an enhanced chronic inflammatory response in the airway and the lungs to noxious particles or gases. Chronic Bronchitis subtype: defined clinically as the presence of a chronic productive cough for 3 months during each of 2 consecutive years (other causes of cough being excluded) — fits this patient's 3-year history. Emphysema subtype: defined pathologically as abnormal, permanent enlargement of the air spaces distal to the terminal bronchioles, accompanied by destruction of their walls without obvious fibrosis — barrel chest and hyper-resonance suggest this component. Chronic bronchitis patients may be obese, have frequent cough and expectoration, use accessory muscles of respiration, have coarse rhonchi and wheezing, and may have signs of right heart failure (cor pulmonale).
(ii) Aetiology: (1) Tobacco smoking — total dose depends on age of starting smoking, depth of inhalation, and total number of cigarettes smoked (one 'pack year' is defined as the equivalent of 20 cigarettes per day for 1 year); (2) Dusty occupation — paint sprayer, cotton and grain dust workers, coal miners, cadmium workers; (3) Environmental pollution — linked with particulate pollution (urban) and household pollution due to cooking within a small space; air pollution appears to have a small (weak) role compared to cigarette smoking; socioeconomic state, occupation, perinatal events, childhood illnesses, recurrent bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, and diet are also factors; (4) Genetic factor — less than 1% of cases; early onset emphysema; inherited deficiency of alpha-1 anti-trypsin.
(iii) Clinical features: Symptoms — productive cough, breathlessness, wheezing; breathlessness is the most significant symptom but usually does not occur until the sixth decade of life; FEV1 is the most common variable used to grade severity, though not the best predictor of mortality. Signs — tachypnoea and respiratory distress with simple activities; use of accessory respiratory muscles and paradoxical indrawing of lower intercostal spaces (Hoover sign); cyanosis; elevated JVP; peripheral oedema; warm peripheries and dilated superficial veins. Chest: pursed-lip breathing; hyperinflation (barrel chest); wheezing frequently heard on expiration; diffusely decreased breath sounds; hyper-resonance on percussion; loss of cardiac dullness and lowering of hepatic dullness; prolonged expiration; coarse crackles beginning with inspiration in some cases.
(iv) Complications evident: cor pulmonale (elevated JVP, bilateral ankle oedema, signs of right heart failure). Additional complication to consider: acute exacerbation of COPD itself constitutes a respiratory emergency.
(v) Management of acute exacerbation: COPD exacerbation is one of the major respiratory emergencies, alongside acute severe asthma, pulmonary embolism, and respiratory failure. The underlying principle for all respiratory emergencies is that air must move in and out of the lung (ventilation) and blood must circulate through it (perfusion); anything that interferes with either process causes deterioration. General management: controlled oxygen therapy, nebulised bronchodilators, systemic corticosteroids, antibiotics if an infective trigger is suspected, and escalation to non-invasive or invasive ventilatory support if respiratory failure develops.

A(i) Gross anatomy: the thyroid gland has two lobes connected in the middle by an isthmus. Normally it cannot be seen and is barely felt. It produces thyroxine (T4) and tri-iodothyronine (T3). Thyroid hormones play a critical role in cell differentiation during development, maintaining thermogenesis, and metabolic homeostasis.
A(ii) Thyroid dysfunction and clinical syndromes:
• Thyrotoxicosis (hyperfunction): symptoms include tremors, heat intolerance, irritability, nervousness, increased sweating, increased appetite, palpitations, staring gaze, increased eye protrusion, diarrhoea/hyperdefaecation, weight loss despite good appetite, easy fatiguability, muscle weakness/wasting, oligomenorrhoea/amenorrhoea, reduced libido/erectile dysfunction. Signs include goitre, fine tremor, warm sweaty palms, tachycardia, bounding pulses, systolic hypertension, arrhythmias, eye signs (lid lag, lid retraction, exophthalmos), pretibial myxoedema, proximal muscle weakness, hyperreflexia, mental state changes. Cause includes Graves' disease, toxic multinodular goitre, thyroiditis, thyroid adenoma. Treatment depends on aetiology: thionamides, beta-blockers, radioactive iodine ablation, thyroidectomy.
• Hypothyroidism (hypofunction): in adults produces myxoedema; in children produces cretinism. Symptoms include fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, myalgia, slow movement and speech, muscle weakness/cramps/paraesthesia, menstrual irregularities. Signs: rough dry skin, puffy face and hands, coarse hair, enlarged tongue, hoarse voice, bradycardia, cardiomegaly. Primary causes include autoimmune disease (Hashimoto's thyroiditis), post-ablative, iodine deficiency, and drugs (antithyroid drugs, lithium, amiodarone). Treatment: replacement therapy with L-thyroxine with serial TFT monitoring.
B(i) In primary hypothyroidism the thyroid gland itself fails to produce adequate T4; the pituitary detects low circulating T4 and responds by secreting excess TSH in an attempt to stimulate the failing gland, so serum TSH is elevated. In secondary hypothyroidism, disease of the pituitary or hypothalamus means insufficient TSH (or TRH) is produced; the thyroid gland is not being stimulated, so T4 is low but TSH is also low or inappropriately normal rather than elevated. This distinction guides management: both require L-thyroxine replacement, but secondary hypothyroidism requires investigation and treatment of the pituitary or hypothalamic lesion as well as imaging studies of the sellar/suprasellar region.

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Acute exacerbation of COPD. COPD is defined as a common and preventable disease characterised by persistent airflow limitation that is usually progressive and associated with an enhanced chronic inflammatory response in the airway and the lungs to noxious particles or gases (GOLD 2013). Chronic Bronchitis is defined clinically as presence of chronic productive cough for 3 months during each of 2 consecutive years (other causes of cough being excluded). Emphysema is defined pathologically as abnormal, permanent enlargement of the air spaces distal to the terminal bronchioles, accompanied by destruction of their walls without obvious fibrosis.
(ii) Aetiology: (1) Tobacco smoking — total dose depends on age of starting smoking, depth of inhalation, total number of cigarettes smoked (one 'pack year' = equivalent of 20 cigarettes per day for 1 year); (2) Dusty occupation — paint sprayer, cotton and grain dust workers, coal miners, cadmium workers; (3) Environmental pollution — linked with particulate pollution (urban) and household pollution due to cooking within a small space; role of air pollution appears small (weak) compared to cigarette smoking; socioeconomic state, occupation, perinatal events, childhood illnesses, recurrent bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, and diet; (4) Genetic factor — <1% of cases; early-onset emphysema; inherited deficiency of alpha-1 anti-trypsin.
(iii) Clinical features: symptoms — productive cough; breathlessness (most significant, usually not until sixth decade); wheezing. FEV1 is the most common variable to grade severity. Signs — tachypnoea and respiratory distress with simple activities; use of accessory respiratory muscles and paradoxical indrawing of lower intercostal spaces (Hoover sign); cyanosis; elevated JVP; peripheral oedema; warm peripheries and dilated superficial veins. Chest: pursed-lip breathing; hyperinflation (barrel chest); wheezing frequently heard on expiration; diffusely decreased breath sounds; hyper-resonance on percussion; loss of cardiac dullness and lowering of hepatic dullness; prolonged expiration; coarse crackles beginning with inspiration in some cases. Chronic bronchitis pattern: patients may be obese; frequent cough and expectoration; use of accessory muscles common; coarse rhonchi and wheezing; signs of right heart failure (cor pulmonale).
(iv) COPD exacerbation is one of the major respiratory emergencies, alongside acute severe asthma, pulmonary embolism, and respiratory failure. The underlying principle for all respiratory emergencies is that air must move in and out of the lung (ventilation) and blood must circulate through it (perfusion); anything that interferes with either process causes deterioration. General management: controlled oxygen therapy, nebulised bronchodilators, systemic corticosteroids, antibiotics if an infective exacerbation is suspected, and escalation to ventilatory support if respiratory failure develops.
(v) Discharge criteria and follow-up: the patient should be stable on their discharge medication regimen for at least 24 hours, with inhaler technique checked and recorded; oxygenation should be satisfactory off supplemental oxygen (or at the patient's usual home-oxygen requirement); bronchodilator and corticosteroid therapy should be optimised; the patient should be given a written action plan and their own inhaler device; the reason for the exacerbation and admission should be identified and addressed (e.g., smoking cessation, vaccination, pulmonary rehabilitation referral); and follow-up should be arranged within 4–6 weeks.
questions.question:
A 65-year-old man with a 40-pack-year smoking history presents with progressive breathlessness, barrel chest, hyper-resonant percussion, and a FEV1/FVC ratio below 70%. He is brought in with acute worsening of breathlessness and increased purulent sputum over the past 24 hours.
(i) What is the diagnosis and what is the definition of this condition?
(ii) State all aetiological factors for this condition.
(iii) Describe the full range of clinical features — symptoms and physical signs — across all clinical subtypes.
(iv) Describe what an acute exacerbation of this condition is and list the treatment approach for acute severe cases.
(v) What discharge criteria and follow-up are important after managing an acute episode?

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Dilated Cardiomyopathy (DCM) with atrial fibrillation. Risk factors in this patient: chronic alcohol intake (toxic cause of DCM — alcohol is a predisposing risk factor/cause; alcoholic cardiomyopathy is reversible with abstinence; mechanism involves myocyte cell death and fibrosis, direct inhibition of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and fatty acid oxidation).
(ii) Investigations and expected findings:
• Chest X-ray: globular heart in severe cases (cardiomegaly).
• ECG: low limb voltages, arrhythmias (atrial fibrillation as found in this patient).
• Echocardiography: dilated left ventricle (other chambers may also be dilated), global systolic dysfunction, ejection fraction low <50%, spontaneous echo contrast or intracardiac clot, functional mitral and/or tricuspid regurgitation.
• BNP and NT-proBNP: markers of heart failure — elevated.
• Urea, creatinine, electrolytes: to assess renal function and electrolytes.
• Blood count: may show concomitant anaemia or evidence of infection (leucocytosis).
(iii) Thromboembolic complication: stroke/systemic embolism. The dilated hypokinetic LV promotes blood stasis; spontaneous echo contrast (seen on echo) is a marker of intracardiac thrombus formation. Atrial fibrillation further increases thrombus formation in the left atrial appendage. Dislodgement of thrombus causes arterial thromboembolism — most critically ischaemic stroke.
(iv) Pharmacological management of heart failure:
• Loop diuretics (e.g. frusemide) for fluid overload.
• Aldosterone antagonist.
• ACE inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers.
• Inotropic drugs (e.g. digoxin, dobutamine).
• Beta-blockers (e.g. bisoprolol, carvedilol, metoprolol).
• Anticoagulation/antiplatelets (e.g. heparin, low dose aspirin) — especially important given AF and intracardiac thrombus risk.
• Abstinence from alcohol is essential as alcoholic cardiomyopathy is reversible with abstinence.
(v) Surgical options for refractory heart failure: left ventricular assist devices; cardiac transplantation for refractory heart failure.
questions.question:
A 38-year-old man with a 10-year history of heavy alcohol consumption presents with progressive breathlessness and palpitations. ECG shows atrial fibrillation with low limb voltages. CXR shows a globular heart. Echocardiography reveals a dilated left ventricle with global systolic dysfunction and EF of 30%, with spontaneous echo contrast.
(i) What is the most likely diagnosis? State the risk factors identifiable in this patient.
(ii) List the investigations that support the diagnosis and give the expected finding in each.
(iii) What serious thromboembolic complication is this patient at immediate risk of, and why?
(iv) Outline the pharmacological management of this patient's heart failure.
(v) What surgical options exist for patients with refractory heart failure from DCM?

A 55-year-old hypertensive man is referred for cardiac evaluation after complaint of exertional breathlessness and palpitations. His clinic BP is 168/104 mmHg. An ECG is performed.
(i) State the 6-step approach to analysing a 12-lead ECG.
(ii) What specific ECG features would indicate left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) in this patient?
(iii) What additional cardiac investigations should be ordered, and state the expected abnormality from each in a hypertensive patient with heart failure?
(iv) What is the ECG standard paper speed and voltage calibration, and why is this important in ECG interpretation?
(v) Name two ECG findings that indicate cardiac involvement by hypertension and one finding that would indicate ischaemic heart disease as a complication.
questions.answerText:
(i) 6-step approach to analysing a 12-lead ECG:
1. Calculate RATE.
2. Determine RHYTHM.
3. Determine QRS AXIS.
4. Calculate INTERVALS.
5. Assess for HYPERTROPHY.
6. Look for evidence of INFARCTION.
(ii) ECG features of LVH in hypertension: tall R waves in precordial leads; left axis deviation; chamber enlargement or hypertrophy pattern; evidence of ischaemic heart disease.
(iii) Additional cardiac investigations and expected findings:
• Chest X-ray: aortic unfolding, cardiomegaly, redistribution of pulmonary blood flow (e.g. upper lobe diversion), evidence of pleural effusion.
• Echocardiography: rhythm abnormality, cavity sizes, muscle thickness, contraction and relaxation of the heart, valvular peculiarities — in hypertension with heart failure would show LVH, impaired diastolic/systolic function, and possibly reduced ejection fraction.
• Cardiac MRI: refined delineation of heart chambers, walls and cavity.
• FBS or RBS, fasting lipid profile, serum electrolyte, urea and creatinine, serum uric acid, urinalysis — to assess co-morbidities and target organ damage.
(iv) ECG paper standard: paper speed is 25 mm/second; voltage calibration is 10 mm = 1 mV. This is important because: horizontally — one small box = 0.04 seconds, one large box = 0.20 seconds; vertically — one large box = 0.5 mV. These standards allow accurate measurement of intervals, durations, and amplitudes — interpretation requires knowing these fixed parameters to correctly calculate rate, intervals, and hypertrophy criteria.
(v) ECG findings indicating cardiac involvement by hypertension: (1) rhythm abnormality (e.g. atrial fibrillation); (2) left ventricular hypertrophy pattern (tall R waves, left axis deviation). ECG finding indicating ischaemic heart disease as a complication: ST-segment and T-wave changes / evidence of infarction (pathological Q waves, ST elevation or depression).

questions.question:
A 28-year-old woman presents with a 3-month history of bilateral ptosis that is worse in the evening, diplopia, nasal speech, difficulty swallowing, and generalised weakness that is worse after repeated use of a muscle. Examination reveals fatigable ptosis, external ophthalmoplegia, proximal muscle weakness, and peek sign. She has a thymoma on CT chest.
(i) What is the diagnosis and what is the pathophysiology at the neuromuscular junction?
(ii) State the antibodies present in this condition and the consequences of antibody binding to receptors.
(iii) Describe the investigations used to establish this diagnosis.
(iv) Outline the treatment options including anticholinesterase drugs, immunosuppression, immunotherapy, and thymectomy (include indications, timing, and expected outcomes).
(v) How would you distinguish a myasthenic crisis from a cholinergic crisis?
questions.answerText:
(i) Myasthenia gravis (MG). Pathophysiology: autoimmune disease caused by antibody-mediated attack directed at acetylcholine receptors at neuromuscular junctions. Antibody binding causes blockage of receptor active sites, accelerated degradation of receptors through cross-linking, complement-mediated damage of receptors, and impaired neuromuscular transmission. Associated with HLA-B8, DRw3, and possibly DQw2.
(ii) Antibodies: 85% of MG patients are seropositive. Types present: acetylcholine receptor antibody; titin antibodies plus AchR antibodies; muscle-specific kinase antibodies; ryanodine receptor (RyR) antibody (associated with thymoma and poor prognosis). Consequences of binding: blockage of receptor active sites; accelerated receptor degradation through cross-linking; complement-mediated damage; impaired neuromuscular transmission.
(iii) Investigations: Tensilon test (IV Edrophonium 10 mg or Neostigmine 0.5 mg plus Atropine); ice pack test, rest test, sleep test, peek sign, curtain sign, lid twitch sign; neostigmine test; electromyography (decremental response); single-fibre EMG (SFEMG); chest X-ray; X-ray of thoracic inlet; CT chest; serology (AchR antibody); thyroid function tests; ESR.
(iv) Treatment: Anticholinesterase drugs. Immunosuppression — steroids 15–20 mg/day up to 60 mg; azathioprine 2–3 mg/kg/d; cyclosporin 5 mg/kg/d; methotrexate. Immunotherapy — plasma exchange (5 sessions of 3–4 L over 2 weeks); IV immunoglobulin 400 mg/kg/d for 5 days. Thymectomy — appropriate in all patients with uncomplicated MG between puberty and 55 years; remission rate approximately 35% if done in first 1–2 years after onset; another 50% improve; if restricted to ocular muscles for one year or more thymectomy is unnecessary; response is maximal by 3 years.
(v) Myasthenic crisis: rapid increase in weakness leading to respiratory failure and quadriparesis; precipitated by infection (RTI, malaria), sedative medications, or drugs blocking neuromuscular transmission; incipient failure marked by reduced vital capacity, restlessness, anxiety, diaphoresis, tremor; paradoxical chest/abdominal movement when diaphragm fails. Cholinergic crisis: adverse muscarinic effects of anticholinesterase drug — nausea, vomiting, pallor, sweating, salivation, bronchorrhoea, colic, diarrhoea, miosis, bradycardia; betrayed by miosis; IV atropine sulfate 0.6 mg if BP falls from bradycardia.

(i) Advanced gastric cancer.
Risk factors: gastric adenoma, dysplasia, H. pylori infection, chronic atrophic gastritis, intestinal metaplasia, postgastrectomy state, family history of gastric cancer, cigarette smoking, high salt intake, low intake of fresh fruits and vegetables.
(ii) Complications and metastatic signs:
- Migratory thrombophlebitis (Trousseau's sign); neuropathies; hyperpigmented patches in the axilla (acanthosis nigricans).
- Signs of bowel obstruction; hepatomegaly, ascites, lower extremity oedema.
- Infiltration of the umbilicus (Sister Mary Joseph's nodule).
- Ovarian metastases (Krukenberg's tumour).
- Mass in the pouch of Douglas (Blumer's shelf) palpable on rectal or vaginal examination.
(iii) Management options: surgery; endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR) of lesions confined to the mucosa; chemotherapy (5-FU, Mitomycin, Cisplatin, Doxorubicin, Methotrexate); radiation therapy (though the stomach is relatively resistant to radiation).
Justified choice: Surgery is the most appropriate option as the first-line treatment for most gastric cancers. However, given the evidence of distant spread (Blumer's shelf mass), the treatment intent shifts to palliation. Chemotherapy agents may be used to control disease, and radiation therapy may supplement this despite relative gastric resistance.
questions.question:
A 58-year-old man presents with a 3-month history of epigastric pain, progressive weight loss, early satiety, nausea, and intermittent melaena. On examination there is cachexia and an epigastric mass. Rectal examination reveals a mass in the pouch of Douglas (Blumer's shelf).
(i) What is the most likely diagnosis, and what are the recognised risk factors for this condition?
(ii) What complications and metastatic patterns does this diagnosis carry, and what are the named metastatic signs?
(iii) What are the management options, and which one is most appropriate at this stage? Justify your choice.

Describe the etiology of Mycobacterium tuberculosis under the following headings and explain the clinical and epidemiological significance of each component:
A(i) Taxonomic classification and morphological characteristics of M. tuberculosis.
A(ii) Other species within the M. tuberculosis complex and their distinguishing features.
B(i) Explain why acid fastness is both diagnostically important and a limitation when other organisms share this property.
B(ii) Distinguish between M. tuberculosis and M. bovis in terms of drug susceptibility, transmission route, and clinical significance.
questions.answerText:
A(i) M. tuberculosis belongs to the Kingdom Bacteria, Phylum Actinobacteria, Order Actinomycetales, Suborder Corynebacterineae, Family Mycobacteriaceae, Genus Mycobacterium. Robert Koch announced discovery of the tubercle bacillus in 1882 (March 24th is World TB Day annually). M. tuberculosis is a rod-shaped, non-spore-forming, thin aerobic bacterium measuring 0.5 µm by 3 µm. It is neutral on Gram's staining (or positive). Once stained, it cannot be decolorized by acid alcohol — hence 'acid-fast bacilli.' Acid fastness is due mainly to the organisms' high content of mycolic acids, long-chain cross-linked fatty acids, and other cell-wall lipids.
A(ii) Other members of the M. tuberculosis complex include: M. bovis (bovine tubercle bacillus — characteristically resistant to pyrazinamide, once an important cause of TB transmitted by unpasteurized milk, currently the cause of a small percentage of cases worldwide); M. caprae (related to M. bovis); M. africanum (isolated from cases in West, Central, and East Africa); M. microti (the 'vole' bacillus, a less virulent and rarely encountered organism); M. pinnipedii (infects seals and sea lions in the Southern Hemisphere, recently isolated from humans); M. canetti (a rare isolate from East African cases producing unusual smooth colonies on solid media).
B(i) Acid fastness is diagnostically valuable because it allows rapid identification of mycobacteria in smear microscopy — easy and quick — confirming presence of AFB. However, acid-fast microscopy does not confirm TB diagnosis because other mycobacteria besides M. tuberculosis are also AFB in smear microscopic examination. Other organisms showing some acid fastness include Nocardia spp., Rhodococcus, Legionella micdadei, Isospora, and Cryptosporidium. A positive culture for M. tuberculosis is required to confirm active disease.
B(ii) M. bovis is characteristically resistant to pyrazinamide, which is a significant drug susceptibility difference from M. tuberculosis. M. bovis was transmitted by unpasteurized milk whereas M. tuberculosis is transmitted by droplet inhalation. M. bovis is the bovine tubercle bacillus and was once an important cause of TB; it is currently the cause of a small percentage of cases worldwide. A culture of the AFB can distinguish the various forms of mycobacteria, making culture necessary when species-level differentiation matters for treatment.

questions.question:
Describe the approach to a patient with kidney disease under the following headings:
A(i) State the normal functions of the kidney and list all the symptoms of renal disease, including precise definitions where given.
A(ii) Describe all disturbances in the act of micturition, including precise definitions and their clinical causes.
B(i) Describe the causes of alteration in the amount and appearance of urine.
B(ii) Describe pain as a manifestation of renal disease, and state the general signs and symptoms of renal disease.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Normal kidney functions: excretion of waste products; regulation of fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance; production of erythropoietin, renin, and prostaglandins; metabolism of vitamin D. Symptoms of renal disease include: disturbance in the act of micturition; alteration in the amount and appearance of urine; pain (renal, ureteric, vesical, and urethral); general symptoms of renal disease. Defined terms: anuria — absence of urine production (<100 mL/day); oliguria — decreased urine production (<400 mL/day); polyuria — increased urine production (>3 L/day); gross haematuria — patient able to visualise blood; microscopic haematuria — blood determined by lab; proteinuria — >150 mg protein/day; pyuria — WBC in urine; dysuria — pain or discomfort with urination; frequency — need to urinate more frequently than usual; hesitancy — difficulty in initiating urination; renal colic — intermittent pain radiating from flank to groin (in excess of child bearing).
A(ii) Frequency: passing urine more often than usual without increase in amount; results from irritation of the bladder, reduction in capacity of the bladder, or pressure from a pelvic tumour. Dysuria: pain in passing urine; usually results from disease of the bladder, prostate, or urethra; pain experienced prior to, during, or following micturition usually in the urethra or suprapubic region; commonly due to infection of lower urethral tract. Nocturia: passing urine in the night (commonly associated with polyuria); other causes — prostatism, cystitis, bladder tumours. Strangury: severe suprapubic pain associated with inability to pass urine; seen in cystitis and bladder tumour. Hesitancy: delay in initiating urine flow; seen in males with prostatism. Pneumaturia: passing of air bubbles in the urine; most often caused by a fistula between the bladder and colon as a result of diverticular abscess or malignant tumour.
B(i) Oliguria: seen in acute renal failure, pre-renal failure (shock, haemorrhage, dehydration, cardiac failure). Anuria: must be differentiated from retention of urine; causes include infarction of a kidney or both kidneys, bilateral cortical necrosis, complete obstruction of both ureters. Haematuria — painless causes: urinary tract obstruction, tuberculosis, urogenital tumours, glomerulonephritis, renal cystic disease. Haematuria — urine becomes red or smoky brown; urine becomes blackish or coca-cola in colour; haemoglobinuria; myoglobinuria. Frothy urine: commonly due to proteinuria. Urine colour darkens on standing: porphyria, alkaptonuria.
B(ii) Pain in renal disease: burning sensation or discomfort over suprapubic region — cystitis; perineal pain or rectal pain — prostatitis; pain felt in flank, hypochondrium, or iliac fossa — renal pain; acute obstruction of ureters due to stone or blood clot — colicky pain radiates from loin to groin and to the testicle in the male; chronic obstruction — less severe pain, sometimes no pain; enlarged kidneys — dull, nagging, or flank pain; acute glomerulonephritis — typically painless. Fever may be associated with urinary tract infection with renal abnormality. General symptoms and signs: dyspnoea from fluid overload in renal impairment, metabolic acidosis in renal impairment, or pleural effusion in nephrotic syndrome; oedema (facial and dependent) in chronic kidney disease and nephrotic syndrome; pruritus in CKD; distal brown discolouration of nails in CKD; pallor in CKD; hyperpigmentation in CKD.

(i) Diagnosis: Acute pancreatitis — an acute inflammation of the pancreas with variable involvement of the regional tissues or remote organ systems.
Two most common causes in adults: gallstones and alcohol.
Clinical signs:
- Ecchymosis in both flanks: Grey Turner's sign — indicates retroperitoneal haemorrhage spreading to the flanks
- Ecchymosis in the periumbilicus: Cullen's sign — indicates retroperitoneal blood tracking to the umbilicus

(ii) All causes:
- Gallstones
- Causes of mechanical ampullary obstruction
- Alcohol
- Hypertriglyceridaemia
- Drugs
- Infections and toxins
- Trauma
- Pregnancy
- Post-ERCP
- Postoperative
- Structural abnormalities

(iii) Pathogenesis:
- Conversion of trypsinogen to trypsin within the acinar cells
- Trypsin catalyses the conversion of proenzymes (trypsinogen, precursors of elastase, phospholipase A2, and carboxypeptidase) to active enzymes
- Trypsin also may activate the complement and kinin systems
- Active enzymes autodigest the pancreas and initiate a cycle of releasing more active enzymes

(iv) Investigations: serum and urine amylase, serum lipase, plain abdominal film, abdominal USS, CT scan, MRI.
Management (mostly supportive):
- Analgesics for pain
- Intravenous fluids

He drinks alcohol regularly and has a history of gallstones. On examination he has abdominal tenderness, guarding, reduced bowel sounds, and ecchymosis in both flanks.
(i) What is the diagnosis? Name the two clinical signs present and what each indicates.

questions.answerText:
(i) Paget's disease of bone (osteitis deformans).
(ii) Predisposing factors and pathological cellular changes:
- Affects men and women equally; usually after 50 years of age.
- Most commonly affects: pelvis and tibia; next commonest: femur, skull, and spine.
- Usually asymptomatic and discovered because of pain, deformity, or complication.
- Pathological changes: characterised by enlargement and thickening of bone with abnormal internal architecture and brittle bone.
- It affects one or more sites; starts at one end of the bone and extends towards the diaphysis.
- Characteristic cellular change: marked increase in osteoblastic AND osteoclastic activity in an alternating pattern at both endosteal and periosteal surfaces → increased thickness of bone, but structure is weak and easily deformed.
(iii) Pathophysiology and X-ray progression:
- Excessive and alternating osteoclastic resorption and osteoblastic deposition result in structurally disorganised bone that is enlarged but mechanically weak.
- X-ray progression: during the resorptive phase — localised areas of osteolysis; later — bone becomes thick and sclerotic with coarse trabeculae, with or without fine cracks (stress fractures) on the convex sides of the shaft of long bones.
(iv) Complications: pathological fracture; osteoarthritis (OA); nerve compression; spinal stenosis; high-output cardiac failure; hypercalcaemia; sarcomatous transformation.
Indications for specific treatment: persistent bone pain; repeated fracture; neurological complications; high-output cardiac failure; hypercalcaemia.
Drugs: those that suppress bone turnover — calcitonin and bisphosphonates.
Note: most patients have no symptoms and require no treatment.
questions.question:
A 65-year-old man presents with progressive dull, constant pain in his right tibia and pelvis. On examination the affected tibia is bowed and thickened. X-ray shows areas of osteolysis with thick, sclerotic bone and coarse trabeculae. Serum calcium and phosphate are normal, but alkaline phosphatase is markedly elevated with increased urinary hydroxylproline excretion.
(i) What is the spot diagnosis?

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Pityriasis rosea — a papulosquamous disorder characterised by oval-shaped scaly plaques mostly on the trunk, neck, arm, and thighs, preceded by a herald (mother) patch.

(ii) Risk factors and predisposing factors:
- International spread
- Seasonal (commoner in warmer temperatures)
- Commoner in the young (10-30 years)
- Slightly commoner in females
- More florid in blacks
- Aetiology most likely viral: human herpes virus 6 and 7; drug-induced cases have also been reported

(iii) Pathophysiology and natural history:
- Associated URTI symptoms frequently precede the rash
- Herald (mother) patch appears first — oval patch with fine collarette of scales on trunk, enlarging over hours or days
- Multiple daughter (smaller but similar) lesions develop within hours or weeks
- Pruritus is variable
- Lesions usually follow lines of skin cleavage (oval in shape with crinkled surface); Christmas tree distribution on trunk
- Inverse distribution has also been reported (limbs, below elbow and knee)
- Atypical forms: urticated, vesicular, papular, purpuric, multiple herald patches, absent herald patch, inverse distribution
- Self-limiting: usually lasts 2-3 months; one attack usually protective, but multiple attacks have been reported

(iv) Must exclude: secondary syphilis in a sexually active person, especially in the presence of atypical features.
Management:
- Mild steroids
- Antihistamines
- Erythromycin
- High-dose acyclovir
- Watchful waiting
- Emollients
questions.question:
A 25-year-old man presents with a 2-week history of oval, scaly skin plaques on the trunk, preceded 2 weeks earlier by a single larger oval patch with a collarette of scales on the chest.
(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) State all risk factors and predisposing factors.
