questions.answerText:
(i) Acute hepatitis B (HBV). He has passed through the incubation phase, the prodromal/pre-icteric phase (malaise, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, headache, upper abdominal discomfort), and is now in the icteric phase (dark urine, pale stool, pruritus, jaundice of 2–6 weeks).
(ii) HBV may be directly cytopathic to hepatocytes; however, immune-mediated cytotoxicity plays the predominant role. The immune assault is driven by HLA class I-restricted CD8 cytotoxic T lymphocytes that recognise hepatitis B core antigen (HBcAg) and hepatitis B e antigen (HBeAg) on the membranes of infected hepatocytes.
(iii) Management goals: ensure adequate nutrition and hydration; prevent further liver damage; avoid transmission.
- Non-specific symptomatic care; balanced high-calorie diet; stop alcohol; limit hepatotoxic drugs.
- Prokinetic drugs (metoclopramide) for nausea and vomiting.
- Admit if significantly dehydrated or at high risk (IV fluids, multivitamins, bed rest, monitor for hepatic failure signs).
(iv) There are no specific medications to treat acute hepatitis. Most cases are mild and may not require hospitalisation. The very rare cases that lead to fulminant hepatic failure require hospitalisation and liver transplantation.
questions.question:
A 28-year-old man presents with a 3-week history of malaise, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, and upper abdominal discomfort. He now notes dark urine, pale stool, and generalised pruritus. On examination he has a low-grade fever, icteric sclerae, and a diffusely enlarged, tender liver with a firm, smooth edge.
(i) What is the most likely diagnosis, and what clinical phases of this illness has he already passed through?
(ii) What is the underlying pathological basis of this infection and what drives the liver injury?
(iii) What initial management should be instituted for this patient?
(iv) What is the definitive approach and under what clinical circumstance would liver transplantation be required?

questions.answerText:
A(i) UTI is said to exist when pathogenic organisms are detected in urine, urethra, kidney, or prostate, and is diagnosed when a colony count of 10^5 organisms is made from the culture of 1 mL of clean-catch urine with or without symptoms. In symptomatic individuals, a lower count may be significant — e.g., 10^2–10^4 organisms. For practical purposes, a urine microscopy revealing pus cells >5/HPF is suggestive of UTI, especially if there are symptoms.
A(ii) Anatomical sites: bladder (cystitis), kidneys (pyelonephritis), ureters (rarely the site of infection), urethra (urethritis). Lower UTI clinical features: cloudy or bloody urine which may have a foul or strong odour; low-grade fever in some people; dysuria (pain or burning with urination); strangury (pressure or cramping in the lower abdomen or back); frequency (strong need to urinate often, even right after the bladder has been emptied). Upper UTI clinical features: chills and rigors or night sweats; fatigue and a general ill feeling; fever above 101 degrees Fahrenheit; pain in the side, back, or groin; flushed, warm, or reddened skin; mental changes or confusion (in the elderly, these symptoms often are the only signs of a UTI); nausea and vomiting; abdominal pain.
B(i) Risk factors: diabetes; advanced age and conditions affecting personal care habits (e.g., cerebral degenerative diseases, delirium); problems emptying the bladder completely; indwelling urinary catheter; bowel incontinence; enlarged prostate, urethral stricture, or anything that blocks urine flow; kidney stones; immobility for a long period of time (e.g., while recovering from a hip fracture); pregnancy; surgery or other procedure involving the urinary tract. The shorter urethra in females predisposes to a higher risk of UTI.
B(ii) Investigations: urinalysis — to look for white blood cells, red blood cells, bacteria, and to test chemicals such as nitrites; 'clean catch' urine for microscopy, culture, and sensitivity; FBC and blood culture; CT scan of abdomen; intravenous pyelogram (IVP); kidney scan and ultrasound; micturating cystourethrogram. Treatment: antibiotics to prevent the infection spreading to the kidneys — 3–5 days in straightforward infections; 7–14 days in complicated infections. Commonly used antibiotics include trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, amoxicillin, Augmentin, doxycycline, and fluoroquinolones. Take plenty of water. Prognosis: most UTIs can be treated successfully; bladder infection symptoms usually go away within 24–48 hours; kidney infection may take 1 week or longer. Possible outcomes: sepsis (risk greater among the young, very old adults, and immunocompromised); kidney damage or scarring; chronic kidney infection (chronic pyelonephritis).
questions.question:
Describe urinary tract infection under the following headings:
A(i) Definition, including the diagnostic colony count thresholds.
A(ii) Anatomical sites affected and clinical features of lower versus upper urinary tract infection.
B(i) Risk factors for UTI and explain anatomically why females have a higher susceptibility.
B(ii) State the investigations required, the treatment regimens, and the possible outcomes of UTI if untreated or in a vulnerable host.

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Acne vulgaris — chronic inflammatory disease of the pilosebaceous follicles.
Basic underlying problem: sebum production, defective hair follicular structure, or both.

(ii) The comedo:
- A comedo is a clogged hair follicle (pore) in the skin; keratin (skin debris) combines with sebum to block the follicle. Can be open (blackhead) or closed by skin (whitehead).
- It is the basic lesion of acne.
- Produced by hyperkeratosis of the lining of the follicles; retention of keratin and sebum causes obstruction.
- At puberty, androgens increase sebum production from enlarged sebaceous glands, which become blocked and infected with Propionibacterium acnes, causing an inflammatory reaction.
- Plugging by the comedo dilates the mouth of the follicle; papules form by inflammation around comedones; rupture leads to nodules, cysts, and abscesses.

(iii) Aggravating factors:
- Steroids: oral/topical
- Anticonvulsants; phenytoin; barbiturates
- Iodides/bromides
- High humidity
- Emotional stress
- Occlusion from head bands
- Oral contraceptive pills
- Chlorinated hydrocarbons, petroleum oil, coal tar (contact acnegens)
- Polycystic ovarian syndrome; benign or malignant ovarian/adrenal/pituitary tumours
- Obesity and metabolic syndrome
- Disease of adrenal gland: partial deficiency of adrenal enzyme 21-hydroxylase
- Adenoma of the adrenal gland especially prolactinoma

(iv) Management including physical therapy:
Supportive: face washing; ultraviolet light helps; avoid irritant oils or comedogenic cosmetics; abrasive skin treatments can aggravate acne; do not scratch or pick.
Topicals: retinoid preparations (first-line for comedonal acne), azelaic acid, benzoyl peroxide, salicylic acid, tea tree oil products; topical clindamycin 1%, erythromycin 2%/4% with zinc acetate 1.2%.
Systemic: tetracycline (first-line), erythromycin, doxycycline, minocycline, trimethoprim; hormonal agents; isotretinoin for severe acne.
Physical therapy: sunlight (anti-inflammatory, brief); cryotherapy; intralesional steroid injections; comedone expression by cautery or diathermy; microdermabrasion for mild acne; lasers and blue light; X-ray treatment no longer recommended as it may cause skin cancer.
questions.question:

(i) What is the diagnosis and what is the basic underlying problem?
(ii) Describe the comedo: its formation and the role of bacteria.
(iii) List all aggravating factors.

A 14-year-old girl presents with high fever, rigors, right loin pain, nausea, and vomiting for 3 days. She had a UTI treated 2 months ago. On examination, she is febrile at 39°C, has right costovertebral angle tenderness, and appears toxic. Urine microscopy shows pyuria and bacteriuria. Urine culture grows E. coli in significant quantities.
(i) What is the diagnosis, and what features distinguish this from lower UTI?
(ii) State all the risk factors for UTI and comment on her specific predisposing factors.
(iii) Describe the full clinical features of both lower and upper urinary tract infection.
(iv) Outline the complete management including type of antibiotic, duration, and monitoring of response.
(v) State the possible complications of untreated or recurrent UTI, especially in the young.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Pyelonephritis (upper UTI). Features distinguishing upper from lower UTI: upper UTI features include chills and rigors or night sweats; fatigue and a general ill feeling; fever above 101 degrees Fahrenheit; pain in the side, back, or groin; flushed, warm, or reddened skin; mental changes or confusion (in the elderly, these symptoms often are the only signs of a UTI); nausea and vomiting; abdominal pain — all present here. Lower UTI features are limited to cloudy/bloody urine, low-grade fever, dysuria, strangury, and frequency without systemic toxicity.
(ii) Risk factors: diabetes; advanced age and conditions affecting personal care habits (cerebral degenerative diseases, delirium); problems emptying the bladder completely; indwelling urinary catheter; bowel incontinence; enlarged prostate, urethral stricture, or anything that blocks the flow of urine; kidney stones; immobility for a long period of time; pregnancy; surgery or other procedure involving the urinary tract. The shorter urethra in females predisposes to higher risk of UTI — applicable to this female patient. A history of prior UTI (2 months ago) suggests recurrence risk.
(iii) Lower UTI clinical features: cloudy or bloody urine, which may have a foul or strong odour; low-grade fever in some people; dysuria (pain or burning with urination); strangury (pressure or cramping in the lower abdomen or back); frequency (strong need to urinate often, even right after the bladder has been emptied). Upper UTI clinical features: chills and rigors or night sweats; fatigue and a general ill feeling; fever above 101 degrees Fahrenheit; pain in the side, back, or groin; flushed, warm, or reddened skin; mental changes or confusion (in the elderly, these are often the only signs of UTI); nausea and vomiting; abdominal pain.
(iv) Management: antibiotics to prevent infection from spreading to the kidneys; in complicated infections (upper UTI/pyelonephritis), antibiotics are for 7–14 days. Commonly used antibiotics include trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, amoxicillin, Augmentin, doxycycline, and fluoroquinolones. Take plenty of water. Investigations: urinalysis to look for WBCs, RBCs, bacteria, and to test chemicals such as nitrites; 'clean catch' urine for microscopy, culture, and sensitivity (to identify the infecting bacteria and determine the best antibiotic); FBC and blood culture; CT scan of abdomen; intravenous pyelogram (IVP); kidney scan and ultrasound; micturating cystourethrogram. Kidney infection (pyelonephritis) may take 1 week or longer for symptoms to go away.
(v) Complications: sepsis — risk is greater among the young, very old adults, and the immunocompromised (e.g., due to HIV or cancer chemotherapy) — particularly applicable to this young patient; kidney damage or scarring; chronic kidney infection (chronic pyelonephritis). With appropriate treatment, the outlook is usually good.

questions.question:
Describe Parkinson's disease and the classification of movement disorders under the following headings:
A(i) Classification of Parkinsonism into its four main categories with examples of each.
A(ii) Clinical clues suggestive of Parkinson-plus syndromes (list at least eight features).
B(i) Describe the motor and non-motor features of Parkinson's disease.
B(ii) Describe the hyperkinetic movement disorders and explain the basal ganglia motor circuit abnormality underlying bradykinesia in PD.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Classification of Parkinsonism:
1. Idiopathic/Primary — PD (sporadic and familial).
2. Secondary Parkinsonism — drug-induced, vascular, infectious, toxic (Mn, CO, MPTP, cyanide), trauma, tumour, hypoxia, NPH.
3. Parkinson-plus syndromes — MSA, PSP, CBGD, AD, DLB, FTD.
4. Heredodegenerative diseases with parkinsonian manifestations — HD, Wilson's disease, neuroacanthocytosis, SCA 2 and 3.
A(ii) Clues for Parkinson-plus syndromes: rapid disease progression; lack of response to levodopa/carbidopa or dopamine agonists in early stages; early onset of dementia; early onset of postural instability; early onset of hallucinations or psychosis with low doses of levodopa; ocular signs (supranuclear gaze palsy, blinking on saccade, square-wave jerks, nystagmus, blepharospasm, apraxia of eyelid opening or closure); pyramidal signs; cerebellar signs; early autonomic failure; prominent motor apraxia; marked symmetry of signs in early stages; truncal symptoms more prominent than appendicular; absence of structural etiology such as NPH.
B(i) Motor features: pill-rolling 4–6 Hz coarse rest tremors; akinesia/bradykinesia; hypokinesia; loss of arm swing; rigidity (cogwheel, lead pipe); festinant gait; simian posture; hypomimia; hypophonia; aprosody; dysarthria; tachyphemia; propulsion; retropulsion; short shuffling steps (marche à petit pas); micrographia; palilalia; freezing; sitting en bloc; Myerson sign (unhabituating glabellar tap reflex); snout reflex; palmomental reflex; striatal hand; striatal toe. Non-motor features: depression; cognitive impairment (bradyphrenia); sleep disturbances; sensory abnormalities; pain and paraesthesia; anosmia; seborrhoea; autonomic dysfunction; hypometric saccades; dysphagia; drooling of saliva; anxiety.
B(ii) Hyperkinetic disorders listed: tremors, chorea, athetosis, dystonias, myoclonus, tic disorders, stereotypy, ballismus. Basal ganglia motor circuit: in PD, reduced striatal dopamine results in increased inhibitory output from the globus pallidus interna/substantia nigra pars reticulata and eventual increased inhibition of the thalamocortical pathway, leading to bradykinesia.

questions.question:
A 20-year-old female undergraduate presents with a 1-year history of worsening headaches, a 6-month history of bilateral milky breast discharge (galactorrhoea), and a 3-month history of worsening visual difficulty — she can no longer see the lecture board peripherally.
(i) What pituitary disorder does this presentation suggest, and what is the likely responsible lesion?
(ii) Explain the anatomical basis for the visual field defect described.
(iii) What other symptoms would you expect if there is pituitary hormone excess from this lesion?
(iv) What investigations should be requested, and what would each be expected to show?
(v) What are the causes of primary adrenal insufficiency, and how does its clinical presentation differ from secondary adrenal insufficiency with regard to pigmentation?
questions.answerText:
(i) This presentation suggests a pituitary disorder — specifically a prolactin-secreting pituitary adenoma (prolactinoma). The likely responsible lesion is a pituitary tumour. The combination of galactorrhoea, visual field loss, and headaches in a young woman points to a sellar mass with suprasellar extension.
(ii) Anatomical basis for visual field defect: the optic chiasm lies directly above the pituitary fossa; a pituitary tumour expanding superiorly compresses the crossing fibres at the chiasm (which carry fibres from the nasal/medial retina of each eye, representing temporal visual fields); compression of the chiasm produces bitemporal hemianopia — loss of the temporal (lateral/peripheral) visual fields bilaterally, explaining why the patient cannot see the lecture board peripherally.
(iii) Other expected symptoms from pituitary hormone excess: growth hormone excess from pituitary tumour causes gigantism in children or acromegaly in adults; excess ACTH from a pituitary tumour causes Cushing's disease. Depending on the cell type secreting hormone, the patient may also develop amenorrhoea, oligomenorrhoea, reduced libido, and infertility from elevated prolactin suppressing gonadotrophins.
(iv) Investigations:
• Thyroid function tests: TSH (may be low or inappropriately normal in secondary thyroid disease from pituitary involvement), free T4.
• Adrenal function test: 8am cortisol with cosyntropin stimulation test — baseline 8am cortisol (normal 275–550 nmol/L); baseline plasma ACTH (normal 9–56 pg/ml).
• Imaging studies of sellar/suprasellar region: MRI is indicated and usually shows the lesion clearly.
• Serum prolactin level — key investigation to confirm prolactinoma and assess the degree of elevation.
(v) Causes of primary adrenal insufficiency: autoimmune destruction, tuberculosis, fungal infections, viral infections (HIV), surgical removal, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, infiltrative disease (sarcoidosis, amyloidosis), infiltration by malignant tumour, and drugs (medical adrenalectomy). Pigmentation distinction: in primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison's disease), there is hyperpigmentation of mucous membranes — because low cortisol stimulates excess ACTH (and co-secreted MSH) from the pituitary, stimulating melanocytes. In secondary adrenal insufficiency (from pituitary/hypothalamic disease), ACTH levels are low or inappropriately normal, so there is no stimulation of melanocytes and hyperpigmentation does not occur.

A(i) Definition and terminology:
- Eczema is an inflammatory skin reaction characterised clinically by itching, scaling, papulovesicles in acute stages, and histologically by spongiosis with varying degrees of acanthosis and a superficial perivascular lymphohistiocytic infiltrate.
- The word 'eczema' in Greek means 'to boil over' (or 'oozing'): refers to the tiny vesicles seen in early acute stages.
- Eczema and dermatitis are used interchangeably; in strict sense eczema is dermatitis but not all dermatitis is eczema. 'Dermatitis' is broader — inflammation of the skin from immunologic, infective, chemical, or physical factors.
- The skin has the capacity to react to insults; the most common pattern is eczema. It is not a single diagnosis but a set of symptoms and physical signs, and it usually has a secondary cause.

A(ii) Three morphological stages:
1. Acute: erythema and swelling; oozing and/or vesiculation. Histologically: spongiosis (intra- and intercellular oedema), erythematous papules/vesicles/bullae.
2. Subacute: crusting and scaling. Histologically: spongiosis subsides, acanthosis increases, parakeratotic stratum corneum evolves and contains serum and pyknotic inflammatory cells.
3. Chronic: lichenification/thickening; excoriations; fissures; post-inflammatory hypo/hyperpigmentation. Histologically: predominantly acanthosis and hyperkeratosis; dermis shows perivascular infiltration and capillary proliferation.

B(i) Classification:
Endogenous (mediated by processes originating in the body): atopic dermatitis, seborrhoeic dermatitis, discoid (nummular) eczema, pompholyx (dyshidrotic eczema), asteatotic eczema, lichen simplex, lichen striatus, juvenile plantar dermatosis, pityriasis alba, hand dermatitis, gravitational dermatitis, eczematous drug eruptions, lichenoid dermatitis.
Exogenous: irritant contact dermatitis, allergic contact dermatitis, systemic allergic contact dermatitis, photodermatitis, perioral dermatitis, photoallergic contact dermatitis, eczematous polymorphic light eruption, infective dermatitis, dermatophytids, post-traumatic eczema.

B(ii) Irritant vs allergic contact dermatitis:
Irritant contact dermatitis:
- Caused by irritant chemicals or physical agents (e.g. phenol, organic solvents, kerosene, potassium hydroxide)
- Occurs in everyone subject to penetrability of stratum corneum; toxic phenomenon; no prior sensitization required
- Threshold concentration above which they cause acute dermatitis; below which they do not
- Always sharply marginated — limited to area of exposure, does not spread
- May lead to necrosis in severe cases
Allergic contact dermatitis:
- T cell-mediated (delayed type hypersensitivity/Type IV) response
- Occurs only in sensitized individuals; minute amounts of allergen may elicit reaction depending on degree of sensitization
- Immunological reaction — involves surrounding skin (spreading phenomenon); may generalize
- Example: prior ACD to ethylenediamine with subsequent reaction to aminophylline; prior poison ivy dermatitis with subsequent reaction to cashew nut ingestion

questions.answerText:
(i) Congestive Cardiac Failure (CCF) / Acute decompensated heart failure with hypertensive heart disease as the likely underlying cause.
(ii) Pathophysiology: Heart failure results from any condition that decreases the efficiency of the cardiac muscle either through damage or overloading. Long-term neuro-hormonal activation (e.g. renin-angiotensin system, arginine vasopressin and sympathetic nervous system) leads to increased workload, fibrosis, dilation, and structural changes in the shape of the left ventricle (from elliptical to spherical). Long-term cardiac overload leads to reduced cardiac output from reduced contractility due to over-stretching with reduced cross-linking of actin and myosin filaments (failure of Frank Starling's law of the heart). Elevated filling pressures cause pulmonary congestion, producing breathlessness and frothy sputum.
(iii) Immediate resuscitation: Bed rest; oxygen therapy; salt and water restriction; daily weight monitoring; input-output chart; diuretics (loop diuretics such as frusemide) to relieve congestion; and close monitoring of vital signs.
(iv) Definitive treatment: Address the reversible cause (uncontrolled hypertension); pharmacological modalities include ACE inhibitors, diuretics, inotropics and anti-arrhythmics, vasodilators, and anticoagulants as appropriate; cardiac transplantation is reserved for refractory end-stage disease.
(v) Chest X-ray — would show cardiomegaly and pulmonary congestion (upper lobe diversion of blood flow, pleural effusion). Echocardiography — would show dilated left ventricle, reduced ejection fraction, and assess valve and muscle function.

A 30-year-old sexually active woman presents with a 1-week history of widespread scaly papules and plaques on the trunk following an upper respiratory tract illness 2 weeks prior. There is a single larger oval patch with a fine collarette of scales on the chest.
(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) Identify the predisposing factors and risk factors.
(iii) Describe the pathophysiology and progression of this disorder.
(iv) State the differential diagnosis that must always be excluded and the reasoning; then outline treatment.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Pityriasis rosea — papulosquamous disorder characterised by oval-shaped scaly plaques mostly on the trunk with a preceding herald (mother) patch.

(ii) Predisposing and risk factors:
- Commoner in the young (10-30 years)
- Seasonal (commoner in warmer temperatures)
- Slightly commoner in females
- More florid in blacks
- Aetiology most likely viral: human herpes virus 6 and 7; drug-induced forms have also been reported

(iii) Pathophysiology and progression:
- Associated URTI symptoms frequently precede the rash
- Herald (mother) patch appears first: oval patch with fine collarette of scales, usually on trunk, enlarging over hours or days
- Multiple daughter (smaller but similar) lesions develop within hours or weeks
- Pruritus is variable
- Lesions follow lines of skin cleavage (oval in shape with crinkled surface); Christmas tree distribution on trunk
- Inverse distribution has also been reported (limbs, below elbow and knee)
- Atypical forms: urticated, vesicular, papular, purpuric, multiple herald patches, absent herald patch, inverse distribution
- Self-limiting: usually lasts 2-3 months; one attack usually protective, multiple attacks have been reported

(iv) Differential to exclude and reasoning:
Must be differentiated from secondary syphilis in a sexually active person, especially in the presence of atypical features.
Treatment:
- Mild steroids
- Antihistamines
- Erythromycin
- High-dose acyclovir
- Watchful waiting
- Emollients

questions.question:
A(i) Describe diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) under the following headings: definition, the type of diabetes it is typically associated with, and the basic underlying pathophysiological defects.
A(ii) Using the pathophysiological cascade provided, trace the sequence from insulin deficiency to the development of ketonaemia, metabolic acidosis, and dehydration, naming each intermediate step.
B(i) Distinguish between DKA and hyperglycaemic hyperosmolar state (HHS) under the headings: ketosis, acidosis, plasma osmolarity, sensorium change, and common diabetes type association.
questions.answerText:
A(i) DKA:
Definition: an acute metabolic complication of diabetes mellitus.
Type of diabetes: typically associated with Type 1 DM, but can occur in Type 2 DM.
Basic underlying defects: (1) reduction in net effective action of insulin (insulin deficiency); (2) elevated levels of counter-regulatory hormones.
A(ii) Pathophysiological cascade from insulin deficiency to DKA:
• Insulin deficiency → reduced glucose uptake in peripheral tissues → hyperglycaemia.
• Insulin deficiency → increased lipolysis → release of free fatty acids and glycerol.
• Free fatty acids → ketogenesis in the liver → ketonaemia and ketonuria.
• Glycerol → gluconeogenesis → further worsens hyperglycaemia.
• Hyperglycaemia → glycosuria → osmotic diuresis → urinary water losses → electrolyte depletion → dehydration.
• Ketonaemia → metabolic acidosis (ketonuria; arterial blood pH falls).
• Dehydration and acidosis → electrolyte derangement (low bicarbonate; low or high potassium depending on severity).
• DKA is characterised by hyperglycaemia, significantly elevated levels of ketones in blood and urine, with metabolic acidosis; varying degrees of dehydration and serum electrolyte derangement.
B(i) Distinguishing DKA from HHS:
• Ketosis: DKA — significantly elevated ketones in blood and urine (ketonaemia, ketonuria); HHS — minimal or no ketosis.
• Acidosis: DKA — metabolic acidosis (low bicarbonate, low arterial pH); HHS — no significant acidosis.
• Plasma osmolarity: DKA — elevated but less extreme; HHS — marked increase in plasma osmolarity (hyperosmolar).
• Sensorium change: DKA — altered consciousness possible; HHS — altered sensorium (varying degrees), seizures may occur — more prominent neurological features.
• Common diabetes type: DKA — typically Type 1 DM (can occur in Type 2); HHS — typically Type 2 DM in older patients.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the gross pathology of endomyocardial fibrosis (EMF) under the following headings: definition, which ventricle is most commonly affected, the specific anatomical region involved, and the effect on atrioventricular valves.
A(ii) State how the anatomical location of fibrosis in right ventricular EMF relates to the clinical features observed on examination.
B(i) Explain the haemodynamic consequences of restrictive ventricular filling in EMF and describe how they account for the development of ascites and peripheral oedema in right ventricular disease.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Gross pathology of EMF:
Definition: endomyocardial fibrosis (EMF) is an idiopathic disorder of the tropical and subtropical regions characterised by the development of restrictive cardiomyopathy; it is characterised by fibrosis of the apical endocardium of the right ventricle, left ventricle, or both.
Most commonly affected ventricle: the right ventricle is most commonly affected, followed by biventricular involvement, with least isolated LV affectation.
Specific anatomical region: the apex of the ventricle is commonly affected by fibrosis; thrombus may also be present there, causing obliteration of the ventricular apex.
Effect on AV valves: normal valve leaflets but fibrosis binds down the posterior cusp of the AV valves, causing AV valve incompetence — resulting in tricuspid regurgitation (TR) and mitral regurgitation (MR).
A(ii) Right ventricular EMF: fibrosis restricts the RV apex and binds the tricuspid valve leaflets, causing TR. This produces: raised JVP (positive Kussmaul's sign); pulsatile hepatomegaly; gross ascites (egg on stick appearance) with concomitant protein-losing enteropathy; facial puffiness; impalpable apex; central cyanosis; low blood pressure; small volume pulse; and signs of tricuspid incompetence. Distant heart sounds may result from pericardial effusion. Exercise intolerance occurs because the restricted RV cannot increase cardiac output on demand. Retarded growth and sexual infantilism also occur.
B(i) Haemodynamic consequences: fibrosis reduces the ventricular cavity and restricts filling (restrictive physiology); this simulates constrictive pericarditis. The combination of AV valve regurgitation and reduced ventricular cavity leads to reduced stroke volume and cardiac output. Restriction of RV filling raises right atrial and systemic venous pressure — elevated systemic venous pressure drives transudation of fluid into body cavities: gross ascites accumulates as hepatic venous congestion and portal hypertension develop (pulsatile hepatomegaly); peripheral oedema (pedal oedema) develops from elevated venous hydrostatic pressure. Right-sided failure is further evidenced by elevated JVP, positive Kussmaul's sign (paradoxical rise in JVP with inspiration due to inability of the restricted RV to accommodate increased venous return). Prognosis is generally poor.

questions.question:
A 7-year-old boy is brought to the paediatric clinic 3 weeks after an episode of sore throat. He now has fever, migratory joint pains affecting his knees and ankles, and his parents notice he moves his hands and feet in a purposeless, involuntary manner. On auscultation a soft systolic murmur is heard at the apex.
(i) What is the most likely diagnosis? State the specific diagnostic criteria used.
(ii) List the predisposing factors and the pathogen responsible.
(iii) Explain the pathophysiology of cardiac involvement in this condition.
(iv) What investigations would confirm the diagnosis?
(v) Outline the management of this patient including secondary prophylaxis.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Acute Rheumatic Fever. Diagnostic criteria: Jones Criteria — diagnosis requires two major criteria OR one major criterion plus two minor criteria, plus evidence of preceding streptococcal infection.
Major criteria: polyarthritis, carditis (inflammation manifesting as CHF, pericarditis with rub, or new murmur), subcutaneous nodules (painless firm collagen nodules over bones/tendons), erythema marginatum (long-lasting reddish rash starting on trunk/arms as macules spreading outward, clearing in the middle to form rings, sparing the face), Sydenham's chorea (rapid purposeless movements of face and arms, late feature, occurs at least 3 months from infection onset).
Minor criteria: fever 38.2–38.9°C, arthralgia (joint pain without swelling — cannot be included if polyarthritis is present), raised ESR or CRP, leukocytosis, prolonged PR interval on ECG.
(ii) Predisposing factors: acute rheumatic fever is common in developing countries, disease of poverty, overcrowding and poor housing; rare in high-income countries; peak incidence ages 5–15. Pathogen: Group A beta-haemolytic streptococcus (pharyngeal infection).
(iii) Pathophysiology: infection with Group A beta-haemolytic streptococcus triggers an immune-mediated response; the organism has antigens that cross-react with cardiac myosin and sarcolemma membrane protein; antibodies produced against the bacteria also attack host endocardium, myocardium and pericardium (pancarditis) causing Aschoff nodules (pathognomonic — multi-nucleated giant cells surrounded by macrophages and T-lymphocytes seen in subacute/chronic stage).
(iv) Investigations: evidence of systemic illness (leucocytosis, raised ESR and CRP); evidence of preceding streptococcal infection (throat swab culture for Group A beta-haemolytic streptococcus; anti-streptolysin O antibody titres — rising titre or level >200 U in adults or 300 U in children); evidence of carditis (CXR — cardiomegaly, pulmonary congestion; ECG — first- and rarely second-degree AV block, pericarditis features, T-wave inversion; echocardiography — cardiac dilatation, valve abnormalities).
(v) Management: strict bed rest to lessen joint pain and reduce cardiac workload (temperature, ESR, and WCC used as guide); aspirin 60 mg/kg in 6 divided doses — relieves joint pains dramatically within 24 hours (helps confirm diagnosis), titrated to patient tolerance; penicillin — single dose benzyl penicillin 1.2 MU IM or phenoxymethyl penicillin 250 mg qid for 10 days (erythromycin or cephalosporin if allergic); corticosteroids (prednisolone 1–2 mg/kg/day) for severe arthritis/carditis given until ESR normalises then tapered; treatment of heart failure. Secondary prophylaxis: 1.2 MU IM benzyl penicillin monthly or oral phenoxymethylpenicillin 250 mg bd; continued for 10 years after the last episode or until age 40, whichever is longer; especially if residual heart disease or living in endemic area (e.g. Africa) or in occupations with exposure to infection.

A(i) Vasopressin:
(a) Produced in the hypothalamus.
(b) Stored in the posterior pituitary.
(c) Released in response to changes in osmolality (primary stimulus: water; normal plasma osmolality 280–295 mosm/kg).
(d) V1 receptors — cause vasoconstriction; V2 receptors — increase permeability of the collecting tubule.
(e) V2 receptor activation induces insertion of Aquaporin-2 water channels into the collecting tubule, increasing water reabsorption.
A(ii) Plasma osmolality formula: 2Na + glucose/18 + urea/6 (with allowance for alcohols). Normal range: 280–295 mosm/kg.
B(i) Dilutional hyponatraemia (SIADH):
Pathological basis — SIADH, oliguric renal failure, severe congestive heart failure, and cirrhosis all lead to impaired renal excretion of water; hyperglycaemia attracts water into the ECF; renal dysfunction with increased intake of hypotonic fluids; excessive sweating → increased thirst → intake of excessive amounts of pure water.
Clinical manifestations:
- Neurological: lethargy, headache, confusion, apprehension, depressed reflexes, seizures, coma.
- Muscle: cramps, weakness, fatigue.
- Gastrointestinal: nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, diarrhoea.
Treatment: limit water intake or discontinue causative medications.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Definition: Leprosy reactions are immunologically mediated episodes of acute or subacute inflammation affecting the skin, nerves, mucous membranes, and/or other sites which interrupt the chronic course of leprosy. Unless promptly and adequately treated, can result in deformity and disability. Five main principles of treatment of leprosy: (1) Stop the infection with chemotherapy; (2) Treat reactions; (3) Educate the patient about leprosy; (4) Prevent disability; (5) Support the patient socially and psychologically.
A(ii) Prevention of disability: monitoring sensation and muscle power in patient's hands, feet, and eyes; identify for each patient potentially dangerous situations (cooking, car repairs, smoking); an anaesthetised foot needs the protection of an appropriate shoe; for anaesthesia alone, a well-fitting trainer with firm soles and shock-absorbing inners provides adequate protection; once there is deformity (clawing), shoes must be made specially to ensure protection of pressure points and even weight distribution; ulcers in leprosy heal if protected from weight-bearing; physiotherapy exercises to maximise function of weak muscles and prevent contracture; contractures of hands and feet, foot drop, lagophthalmos, entropion, and ectropion are amenable to surgery. Rehabilitation: social and cultural background determines the nature of problems encountered; patient may have difficulty coming to terms with leprosy; community may reject the patient; education, gainful employment, confidence from family, friends, and doctor, and plastic surgery to correct stigmatising deformity all have a role.
B(i) Relapse: defined as new skin lesions and increase in bacteria index (BI) >2+ (>100 times). Early relapse causes: (1) original misclassification; (2) inadequate chemotherapy; (3) insufficient duration. Late relapse causes: (4) drug resistance particularly with past history of monotherapy or drugs given sequentially, especially to patients with resistance (effectively as monotherapy); (5) M. leprae persisters. Monitoring response: slit skin smears done annually; a score of 1+ indicates 1–10 bacilli in 100 fields, 6+ over 1000 per field.
B(ii) Prevention of leprosy: detection and prompt treatment of all leprosy cases; contact examination; case finding; development of vaccine; BCG. Substitution regimens: For Clofazimine or Rifampicin substitution — Minocycline 100 mg daily or Ofloxacin 400 mg daily. For multibacillary patients who cannot take Rifampicin: Clofazimine 50 mg daily, Minocycline 100 mg daily, Ofloxacin 400 mg daily for 6 months; then Clofazimine 50 mg daily plus either Minocycline 100 mg or Ofloxacin 400 mg daily for further 18 months.

questions.answerText:
(i) Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria (PNH).
(ii) Underlying defect:
- Rare acquired disorder of red cell membrane defect arising at stem cell level.
- A mutation affects myeloid progenitor cells, resulting in partial or complete deficiency of the anchor protein (GPI anchor).
- This makes RBCs sensitive to the lytic effect of complement.
- Anchor proteins affected: Decay Accelerating Factor (DAF) CD55 and Membrane Inhibitor of Reactive Lysis (MIRL) CD59 — both normally protect RBCs from complement.
(iii) Complications — thromboembolic:
- Venous and arterial thromboses account for approximately 40–67% of PNH-related deaths.
- Pulmonary embolism (PE) or deep vein thrombosis (DVT) is the most common clinical presentation.
- PNH thrombotic events (TE) occur in typical and atypical sites: DVT, mesenteric, and PE most common; Budd–Chiari, renal, and dermal less common.
- 64% of patients with PNH have chronic kidney disease (CKD).
- Other complications: haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, neutropenia; PNH may evolve into aplastic anaemia (AA) or rarely (estimated 1–2%) into acute myeloid leukaemia.
(iv) Treatment:
- Supportive: transfusion of filtered red cells; folic acid supplements (at least 3 mg/day — mandatory).
- Humanised monoclonal antibody eculizumab, directed against complement protein C5 (IV every 14 days).
- Allogeneic BMT: when an HLA-identical sibling is available, BMT should be offered to any young patient with severe PNH (definitive treatment).
- Acute thrombotic events (Budd–Chiari, cerebral thrombosis): thrombolytic agents — tPA/heparin/LMWH and warfarin.
- PNH–AA syndrome: immunosuppressive treatment with antilymphocyte globulin (ALG or ATG) and cyclosporine.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Rickets and osteomalacia:
They are different expressions of the same disease — defective mineralisation of bone; the bone tissue throughout the skeleton is incompletely calcified and softened.
- In children: effects on physical growth and ossification resulting in deformity of endochondral ossification (rickets).
- In adults: manifests as osteomalacia.
Causes: calcium deficiency; defects anywhere in the metabolic pathway for vitamin D — decreased intake, lack of exposure to sunlight, intestinal malabsorption, defective hydroxylation in the liver and kidney.
Metabolic pathway link: vitamin D is necessary for absorption of calcium; active vitamin D (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D) promotes intestinal calcium absorption; deficiency leads to low serum calcium and phosphate, impairing mineralisation.
A(ii) Clinical features of rickets in children:
(a) Early neuromuscular manifestations: tetany, convulsions, failure to thrive, muscle flaccidity.
(b) Skeletal deformities:
- Skull: craniotabes.
- Chest: enlargement of costochondral junction (rickety rosary); lateral indentation of the chest (Harrison's sulcus); thickening of the knees, ankle, and wrist from physeal overgrowth.
(c) Features after walking: knock knees, bow legs, swollen joints, disturbed gait.
B(i) Biochemical changes common to all types:
- Decreased serum calcium and phosphate.
- Increased serum alkaline phosphatase.
- Decreased urinary excretion of calcium.
X-ray findings in active rickets: thickening and widening of growth plate; cupping of metaphysis; bowing of the diaphysis (which may remain after healing).
Clinical features of osteomalacia in adults: backache, bone pain, muscle weakness, vertebral collapse, loss of weight; unexplained pain in the hip or one of the long bones preceding stress fractures.
Treatment principles: depends on the cause — correct the vitamin D, calcium, and phosphate deficiency; replace specific deficiencies based on aetiology.
questions.question:

A(ii) Describe the clinical features of rickets in children under the following headings: (a) early neuromuscular manifestations, (b) skeletal deformities of the skull, chest, and long bones, and (c) features after the child begins to walk.
B(i) Describe the biochemical changes common to all types of rickets and osteomalacia, and the X-ray findings. State the clinical features of osteomalacia in adults and the treatment principles.

Describe the nail signs of systemic diseases under the following headings:
A(i) Describe nail clubbing: definition, appearance, grading, and systemic associations.
A(ii) Describe koilonychia, half-and-half nails, and Terry nails: appearance and systemic associations for each.
B(i) Describe melanonychia and leukonychia: appearance, systemic and drug causes, and when biopsy is indicated.
B(ii) Describe yellow nail syndrome and nail-patella syndrome: clinical features, associations, and mode of inheritance where stated.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Nail clubbing:
- Can be idiopathic or acquired
- Appearance: increased longitudinal and transverse curvature; assessed by Lovibond's angle versus Schamroth's sign
- Systemic associations: pulmonary diseases, cardiac diseases, thyroid diseases, hepatic diseases, GIT diseases, HIV
- Note the grading
- Whenever encountered, an underlying systemic disease should be sought for

A(ii) Koilonychia (spoon nails):
- Nails are thin and concave with edges everted (can contain a drop of water)
- Systemic associations: iron deficiency anaemia, haemochromatosis, coronary artery disease, syphilis, polycythaemia, acanthosis nigricans; can be idiopathic or familial
- Manual trauma and exposure to cold can cause seasonal disease

Half-and-half nails (Lindsay's nails):
- Proximal portion of nail white; distal half red, pink, or brown with sharp line of demarcation
- Seen mostly in renal failure patients undergoing haemodialysis (up to 20%); also in HIV, hydroquinone abuse, chronic liver disease

Terry nails:
- Distal 1-2 mm shows normal pink colour; entire nail plate or proximal end has white appearance due to telangiectases in the nail bed
- Seen in cirrhosis, chronic CCF, adult-onset DM, very elderly people, hospitalised patients

B(i) Melanonychia:
- Black or brown pigmentation on a normal nail
- Seen in: blacks (normal feature), acanthosis nigricans, Addison's disease, vitamin B deficiency, Peutz-Jeghers syndrome
- Drug causes: chemotherapy, anti-malarials, minocycline, zidovudine, lamivudine, gold, arsenic, mercury
- Solitary nail longitudinal melanonychia raises concern of a nail matrix tumour (especially melanoma); biopsy should be considered in the presence of atypical features

Leukonychia:
- White nails; four forms: leukonychia punctata, leukonychia striata, leukonychia partialis, leukonychia totalis
- Causes: seen in normal people (especially punctata); trauma; Kawasaki disease; HIV; drugs (chemotherapy); TB; nephritis; complex regional pain; Hansen's disease; ulcerative colitis; typhoid fever; chronic liver disease; can be idiopathic or familial

B(ii) Yellow nail syndrome:
- Marked thickening and yellow to yellowish-green discolouration often associated with lymphoedema and compromised respiration
- Nails are overcurved, grow very slowly (<0.2 mm/week), often subject to onycholysis, loss of lunula and cuticle
- Preceded (mostly) by: lymphoedema, pleural effusion, chronic pulmonary infection, chronic sinusitis
- Associated with autoimmune disease, immunodeficiency, use of gold and D-penicillamine, malignancy
- Treatment: zinc, vitamin E, and fluconazole have been reported to improve nail findings

Nail-patella syndrome (Hereditary osteo-onychodysplasia / Fong syndrome):
- Characterised by: absence or hypoplasia of patella; congenital nail dystrophy (triangular lunulae are characteristic)
- Other bone features: thickened scapulae, hyperextensible joints, radial head abnormalities, posterior iliac horns
- Skin changes: webbing of elbows
- Eye changes: cataract, glaucoma, heterochromia of the iris; hyperpigmentation of pupillary margin of iris (Lester iris) is characteristic
- Renal: glomerulonephritis with albuminuria, haematuria, casts; 60% have renal abnormalities; 20% develop CRF
- Inheritance: autosomal dominant; mutation in LMX1B gene

A(i) Classification systems:
NYHA Functional Classification:
• Class I: No limitation of physical activity.
• Class II: Slight limitation of physical activity.
• Class III: Marked limitation of physical activity.
• Class IV: Symptoms occur even at rest; discomfort with any physical activity.
ACC/AHA Stages:
• Stage A: High risk of heart failure but no structural heart disease or symptoms of heart failure (pre-heart failure).
• Stage B: Structural heart disease but no symptoms of heart failure (pre-heart failure).
• Stage C: Structural heart disease and symptoms of heart failure.
• Stage D: Refractory heart failure requiring specialised interventions.
A(ii) Research has demonstrated that classifying heart failure using degree of exertion during exercise predicts prognosis. Cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPX testing) measures exhaled oxygen and carbon dioxide during exercise; it is usually required prior to heart transplantation as an indicator of prognosis. Peak oxygen consumption (VO2 max) is used as an indicator of prognosis: VO2 max less than 12–14 cc/kg/min indicates poor survival and suggests need for heart transplantation; VO2 max less than 10 cc/kg/min carries a clearly poorer prognosis. The heart failure survival score is calculated from a combination of clinical predictors and VO2 max. The criterion of VE/VCO2 slope >35 is also used.
B(i) Distinguishing HFrEF from HFpEF:
• Ejection fraction: HFrEF (previously 'systolic heart failure') — EF <40%; HFpEF (previously 'diastolic heart failure' or 'heart failure with normal ejection fraction') — EF is preserved (normal systolic contraction).
• Ventricular physiology: in HFrEF, systolic function is reduced — the LV cannot contract adequately; in HFpEF, LV contraction (systole) is normal but the LV is stiff with impaired relaxation (diastole) and hence impaired filling.
• Which is commoner in women: women with heart failure tend to be more likely to have diastolic dysfunction (HFpEF); women tend to be older at time of diagnosis (after menopause) and generally have lower overall quality of life after diagnosis.

questions.answerText:
(i) Colorectal cancer (cancer of the left colon, based on obstructive symptoms and haematochezia).
Risk factors: high fat, low bulk diet; age over 40 years; personal or family history of colorectal adenomas or colorectal carcinoma; colonic polyposis; inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis, Crohn's disease).
(ii) Site-dependent symptom pattern:
- Cancers of the proximal (right) colon: constitutional symptoms (fatigue, shortness of breath, angina) due to microcytic hypochromic anaemia; passage of 'mahogany faeces' (blood admixed with faeces); vague abdominal discomfort or palpable abdominal mass.
- Cancers of the left colon: obstructive symptoms (colicky abdominal pain, particularly after meals, change in bowel habits); haematochezia; tenesmus, especially with rectal cancers.
Complications of untreated disease: complete bowel obstruction; perforation; distant metastasis.
(iii) Management options: surgery (treatment of choice for most colorectal cancers); chemotherapy (useful to eradicate microscopic tumour foci after surgical resection — agents: 5-FU + levamisole; 5-FU + leucovorin); radiation therapy; palliation for advanced disease with metallic stents.
Justified choice: Surgery is the treatment of choice for most colorectal cancers. Given the sigmoid mass, surgical resection is the most appropriate primary intervention. Chemotherapy post-resection is appropriate to eradicate microscopic foci.
(iv) Investigations: colonoscopy (performed, confirms diagnosis); double-contrast barium enema; abdominal ultrasound scan; abdominal CT scan; faecal occult blood testing (FOBT); carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA); laboratory studies showing anaemia and positive test for faecal occult blood.

questions.answerText:
(i) Tuberculoid leprosy (TT). WHO classification: Paucibacillary leprosy. Lepromin test result in tuberculoid leprosy: positive — indicates cell-mediated immunity and host resistance to M. leprae; positive Mitsuda reaction at 3–4 weeks indicates the immune system is capable of mounting cell-mediated immunity. A negative result indicates lack of resistance and is seen in lepromatous leprosy (worse prognosis).
(ii) Epidemiology and transmission: endemic in many developing countries — Asia, Africa, Latin America, Pacific; risk factors include overcrowding, poor sanitation, poor nutrition; HIV is not a risk factor; race — Africans tend to get tuberculoid form; LL more common in males than females (2:1); children — tuberculoid form predominates. Etiology: Mycobacterium leprae — rod-shaped AFB; first bacterial disease in humans; humans are the only primary reservoir; animal reservoirs include 9-banded armadillo, chimpanzees, and mangabey monkeys; incubation period 6 months to 50 years. Transmission: exact mechanism not known; most widely accepted — contact between cases; recently transmission by the respiratory route is recognised; handling/eating armadillos; possibly through insects (cannot be completely ruled out); transmission in solid organ transplant recipients has been reported.
(iii) Tuberculoid leprosy: localised and asymmetrical; single macule or plaque, erythematous or purple with raised clear-cut edges sloping towards a flattened hypopigmented centre; surface is anaesthetised, dry, and hairless; thickened cutaneous nerve may be found at edge; peripheral nerve trunk involvement possible; no M. leprae on skin smears; good prognosis; many resolve without treatment; peripheral nerve trunk damage is limited. Nerve involvement in TT: asymmetrical; localised close to skin lesion; occurs early; damage due to inflammation. Lepromatous leprosy (LL): onset insidious; earliest lesions ill-defined, shiny, hypopigmented or erythematous macules; skin becomes infiltrated and thickened; nodules develop; leonine facies; madarosis (loss of lateral third of eyebrows); glove and stocking anaesthesia beginning at hands and feet extending gradually; sweating is lost; nerve damage symmetrical and occurs late; corneal nerve infiltration causes anaesthesia, predisposing to injury, infection, and blindness. Nerve involvement in LL: symmetrical; not localised close to skin lesion; occurs late; massive bacillary infiltration.
(iv) WHO MDT regimen: Paucibacillary — daily 100 mg Dapsone for 6 months; monthly supervised Rifampicin 600 mg. Multibacillary — monthly supervised Rifampicin 600 mg; monthly supervised Clofazimine 300 mg; daily Dapsone 100 mg and Clofazimine 50 mg; duration 24 months. Relapse rate 2–6%. Substitution for Clofazimine or Rifampicin: minocycline 100 mg daily or ofloxacin 400 mg daily.
(v) Complications of leprosy: blindness; nephrotic syndrome/CKD; testicular dysfunction (mild to severe); impotence/infertility; leprae reactions/Lucio's phenomenon; stigmatisation; amyloidosis (seen in LL and ENL); nerve abscess/sepsis; epistaxis; anosmia; destruction of nasal cartilage (saddle nose).
questions.question:

A 25-year-old HIV-positive man presents with a 3-month history of a painless, firm, erythematous neck mass involving the cervical and supraclavicular lymph nodes. He has no respiratory symptoms. Chest radiograph is normal. Fine needle aspiration reveals caseous granulomatous inflammation on histology with acid-fast organisms.
(i) What is the spot diagnosis?
(ii) What predisposing factors and conditions increase the risk of this presentation?
(iii) What is the pathophysiology of extrapulmonary spread, and which organ systems are most commonly involved?
(iv) Outline the full management including drug regimen, duration, and any adjunctive therapies.
questions.answerText:
(i) Tuberculous lymphadenitis (Scrofula) — the most common form of extrapulmonary tuberculosis.
(ii) Predisposing factors and conditions:
- HIV infection: incidence of EPTB has increased due to HIV; approximately 17% of HIV-seropositive patients are known to have EPTB.
- Close contact with an infectious TB case; abnormal-appearing chest radiograph; immunosuppressed patients (receiving equivalent of ≥15 mg/day of prednisone for at least 1 month); diabetes mellitus; chronic kidney disease (CKD); immunosuppressants.
- Diagnosis is usually delayed, especially when the lungs are not involved, due to the non-specific nature of symptoms.
(iii) Pathophysiology:
- EPTB results from haematogenous spread of bacilli to other organs.
- The two most commonly involved extrapulmonary sites are peripheral lymph nodes and the pleura, but any site or organ can be involved.
- Other common sites: well-vascularised areas — kidney, meninges, spine, and the growing ends of long bones.
- Lymphadenitis accounts for approximately 25% of extrapulmonary disease.
- Lymphadenitis usually manifests as a painless, erythematous, firm mass most commonly involving cervical and supraclavicular lymph nodes.
(iv) Management:
Drug regimen: EPTB is treated with standard anti-tuberculous agents for 6 months — 2-month intensive course using isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide; followed by 4-month continuation phase with isoniazid and rifampicin.
Adjunctive therapy: steroids are used in TB meningitis and pericarditis to reduce the risk of constrictive pericarditis and neurological deficit.
Diagnosis confirmed by: fine needle aspiration or excisional biopsy with histopathological examination, examination for acid-fast organisms, and culture for mycobacteria.
Prevention: BCG vaccination (live attenuated vaccine from M. bovis — protective in children but not adults); treatment of latent tuberculosis in immunosuppressed patients.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old HIV-positive man with CD4 count of 110 cells/µL presents with a 2-week history of insidious onset breathlessness, dry cough, and low-grade fever. Chest X-ray shows minimal changes but CT scan reveals bilateral peri-hilar ground-glass infiltrates.
(i) What is the most likely opportunistic pulmonary infection, and what is its biological classification?
(ii) Describe all the common pulmonary fungal infections presented, including their causative organisms and predisposing conditions.
(iii) For each major fungal infection, state the diagnostic approach.
(iv) State the full treatment for each fungal condition presented.
(v) Describe the role of the immune system in determining whether a fungal organism remains a commensal or causes disease.
questions.answerText:
(i) Most likely diagnosis: Pneumocystis carinii pneumonia (PCP). Biological classification: it is a contagion like a fungus genetically but it is intracellular. It is amoeboid-like trophozoite that multiplies into a sack of merozoites then ruptures into trophozoites again. CXR may not show changes but CT scan shows peri-hilar infiltrates becoming generalised ground glass, associated with very low CD4 count less than 200. It is consequent to failure of prophylaxis in an HIV patient whose immunity is severely compromised.
(ii) Fungal infections: (1) Candida albicans — natural commensal in pharynx, vulva, GIT; causes oro-pharyngeal candidosis (oral thrush) — cheesy white specks on tongue and buccal/pharyngeal mucosa, scrapping shows hyperaemic surfaces; can occasionally become pneumonic. (2) Histoplasmosis (Histoplasma capsulatum) — via inhalation of spores during moist soil/hay work, rich in bird droppings and bats; acute phase of fever, cough, chills, myalgia like primary TB; chronic form like pulmonary TB with infiltrates, fibrotic streaks, cavities. (3) Aspergillosis (Aspergillus fumigatus) — commonly associated with decaying fodder, hay, trees; forms: allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (fungus in bronchial tree; sputum has fungal hyphal filaments; causes bronchiectasis, lobar collapse, interstitial fibrosis; blood eosinophilia, IgE elevation); aspergilloma (fungal spores settle in previous TB cavity, grows into fungal ball with radiolucent halo); invasive aspergillosis (in highly immunocompromised — widespread organ involvement: granulomatous liver lesion, brain abscess, meningitis, lytic bone lesions, pneumonic lung lesion). (4) Cryptococcosis — spores inhaled; yeast-like fungi from pigeon droppings; subacutely with hilar lymph nodes, cough, pleural effusion, cavitation, fibrosis; commonly meningitis. (5) Coccidioidomycosis — non-budding soil saprophyte Coccidioides immitis; windstorms; fever within 10 days, malaise, erythema nodosum, allergic conjunctivitis, cough, pleural effusion; pulmonary cavitation. (6) PCP — described above.
(iii) Diagnosis: Candida — fungi seen in scrapings, sputum. Histoplasmosis — histoplasmin intradermal test like PPD for TB; serology (antibodies: complement fixation test, counter-current immunoelectrophoresis); culture; histology of tissue. Aspergillosis — antigen skin test positive in allergic bronchopulmonary but negative in invasive and aspergilloma; precipitin positive; chest X-ray; FBC; fungal hyphae in sputum and culture. Cryptococcosis and Coccidioidomycosis — history of exposure; skin tests with specific antigen; serology (precipitin tests and complement fixation tests). All fungal pulmonary diseases: guided by presentation and history.
(iv) Treatment: Candida — topical nystatin, miconazole, fluconazole (oral for more severe); parenteral amphotericin B in bronchopneumonia. Histoplasmosis — symptomatic treatment then oral ketoconazole or itraconazole, then systemic amphotericin B; surgical excision of histoplasmomas. Aspergillosis — supportive including bronchodilators and corticosteroids; anti-fungal agents oral itraconazole, fluconazole, and parenteral amphotericin B; surgical excision of aspergillomata. PCP — supportive; IV co-trimoxazole 100 mg/kg/day; or pentamidine; or atovaquone; or clindamycin/primaquine combination.
(v) Fungal infectivity is low and therefore fungi are often in nature as commensals, but when the host immune system deteriorates, they can become disease. Conditions causing immune depression include malnutrition in children, excessive antibiotic treatment, diabetes mellitus, reticuloendothelial system diseases (Hodgkin's, leukaemias), cancers, anti-cancer chemotherapy, anti-graft rejection treatment, radiation treatment, and HIV infection. In HIV patients, PCP is consequent to failure of prophylaxis when immunity is severely compromised (CD4 <200).

(i) Acne vulgaris — a chronic inflammatory disease of the pilosebaceous follicles.
(ii) Four core pathogenic mechanisms:
- Follicular hyperkeratosis
- Increased sebum production
- Propionibacterium acnes (P. acne) proliferation
- Inflammation
(iii) Complications of acne:
- Scarring: ice pick scars, rolling scars, boxcar scars
- Keloids
- Sepsis
- Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation
- Depression/psychological problems
(iv) Management:
Supportive: face washing; ultraviolet light helps; avoid irritant oils or comedogenic cosmetics; abrasive skin treatments can aggravate acne; do not scratch or pick; no proven relationship between particular foods and acne.
Topicals: Retinoid preparations (tretinoin 0.1-0.25%, isotretinoin 0.05%, adapalene 0.1%) — treatment of choice for comedonal acne, anti-inflammatory, prevents comedone formation, applied at bedtime. Azelaic acid (alternative anticomedonal). Benzoyl peroxide 2.5-10%. Salicylic acid. Tea tree oil products. Topical clindamycin 1%; erythromycin 2% and 4% with zinc acetate 1.2% — most useful when inflammatory lesions predominate; combine with retinoids to prevent resistance.
Systemic antibiotics: first-line tetracycline; second-line erythromycin, doxycycline, minocycline (causes SLE); trimethoprim increasingly used.
Hormonal agents: cyproterone acetate 2 mg with ethinyl estradiol 35 mg daily; spironolactone 25-300 mg/day (antiandrogenic); steroids for severe inflammatory acne.
Isotretinoin 0.5-1 mg/kg/day for 15-20 weeks — reserved for severe acne; reduces sebum production, comedogenesis, P. acne, keratinization; leads to remission lasting months to years; teratogenic.
Physical therapy: cryotherapy; intralesional steroid injections; comedone expression by cautery or diathermy; microdermabrasion for mild acne; lasers and blue light; X-ray treatment no longer recommended as it may cause skin cancer.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Four primary acid-base disorders :
1. Respiratory acidosis (RAc): CO₂ retention; pH <7.4; pCO₂ >40; HCO₃⁻ >24. Secondary response: increased renal acid excretion (increased HCO₃⁻, rarely >32 mEq/L).
2. Respiratory alkalosis (R Alk): loss of CO₂; pH >7.4; pCO₂ <40; HCO₃⁻ <24. Secondary response: decreased renal acid excretion (decreased HCO₃⁻, rarely <16 mEq/L).
3. Metabolic acidosis (MAc): addition of acid or loss of HCO₃⁻; pH <7.4 (specifically pH <7.35); pCO₂ <40; HCO₃⁻ <24. Secondary response: hyperventilation (compensatory respiratory alkalosis). NB: in respiratory acidosis and metabolic alkalosis, plasma pCO₂ and HCO₃⁻ are increased; in respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis, plasma pCO₂ and HCO₃⁻ are decreased.
4. Metabolic alkalosis (M Alk): addition of base or loss of acid; pH >7.4; pCO₂ >40; HCO₃⁻ >24. Secondary response: hypoventilation (pCO₂ usually <55 mmHg).
A(ii) Buffer systems:
1. Haemoglobin; 2. Plasma proteins; 3. Blood carbonic acid–bicarbonate system; 4. Urinary buffers (phosphate, sulphate); 5. Cerebrospinal fluid buffers.
Normal plasma pH: 7.40 ± 0.05.
Sources of acid: amino acids, metabolism, CO₂. Sources of alkali: fruits, drugs. Role of kidneys and lungs in maintaining pH.
B(i) Generation and fate of H⁺ in the proximal tubular cells:
Generation: proximal tubular cells; enzyme: carbonic anhydrase; reactions: H₂O + CO₂ → H₂CO₃; H₂CO₃ → HCO₃⁻ + H⁺.
Fate of H⁺:
- Ammonia secretion.
- Bicarbonate buffering.
- Combination with dibasic phosphate.
- Combination with sulphate.

questions.answerText:
(i) CNS tuberculosis — specifically tuberculous meningitis.
Clinical features prompting consideration: patients usually present with some combination of headache, abnormal behaviour, confusion, fever, cranial nerve abnormalities, and occasionally seizures. TB must be first suspected in: HIV-infected persons; close contacts with an infectious TB case; patients with abnormal-appearing chest radiograph; immunosuppressed patients (equivalent of ≥15 mg/day prednisone for at least 1 month); patients with diabetes mellitus; CKD; patients on immunosuppressants.
(ii) Diagnostic procedures and findings:
- CT and MRI: may provide evidence of basilar meningitis; may show hydrocephalus or tuberculous abscesses.
- To confirm diagnosis: cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) must be sampled for examination and culture — CSF protein is usually elevated.
- Demonstration/culture of Mycobacterium tuberculosis remains key to diagnosis.
- Tissue histology showing caseous granulomatous inflammation.
- Tuberculin skin testing and interferon-gamma release assay (note: not used in active tuberculosis).
(iii) Anatomical basis of cranial nerve abnormalities:
Basilar meningitis involves the meninges at the base of the brain where multiple cranial nerves exit. Inflammation and exudate at the basilar cisterns encases and compresses cranial nerves as they course from the brainstem through the subarachnoid space. Hydrocephalus (obstruction of CSF pathways) further increases intracranial pressure, adding to cranial nerve dysfunction. Tuberculomas may also compress adjacent cranial nerve structures directly.
(iv) Full treatment regimen:
Standard anti-TB: 6 months total — 2-month intensive phase with isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide; followed by 4-month continuation phase with isoniazid and rifampicin.
Adjunctive therapy specifically for CNS TB: steroids are used in TB meningitis to reduce the risk of neurological deficit.
questions.question:
