questions.answerText:
A(i) Phases of the cardiac action potential:
• Phase 0: rapid depolarisation — dominant inward Na⁺ current (fast sodium channels open); sharp upstroke of the action potential; represents atrial and ventricular depolarisation.
• Phase 1: early rapid repolarisation — inactivation of Na⁺ channels and transient outward K⁺ current.
• Phase 2: plateau phase — inward Ca²⁺ current balances outward K⁺ current; maintains depolarisation; represents the absolute refractory period (effective refractory period — ERP); the cell cannot be excited. Takes place between phase 0 and phase 3.
• Phase 3: rapid repolarisation — dominant outward K⁺ current; repolarisation towards resting membrane potential.
• Phase 4: resting membrane potential (pacemaker cells have spontaneous slow depolarisation in phase 4 — this allows automatic impulse generation in the SA node, AV node, and Purkinje system).
A(ii) ERP (also called absolute refractory period ARP): the period during which the cell cannot be excited (takes place between phase 0 and phase 3). During this period no stimulus, however strong, can produce another action potential. The relative refractory period (late phase 3) is when the cell can be excited by a stronger-than-normal stimulus. Class III drugs (K⁺ channel blockers) prolong repolarisation — they prolong both the duration of the action potential and the ERP, delaying repolarisation. A re-entry circuit requires a vulnerable window during which one limb is excitable while another is still refractory; by prolonging the ERP, Class III drugs eliminate this window so the re-entry circuit cannot be sustained, terminating re-entry tachycardia.
B(i) ECG characteristics:
• RBBB: both RBBB and LBBB show wide deformed QRS complex. RBBB shows rSR' pattern (RSR') in lead V1 — a 'rabbit ear' or 'M-shaped' pattern; wide QRS.
• LBBB: broad monophasic (or notched) R wave in leads V5 and V6; wide QRS.
Association with heart disease: unlike RBBB, LBBB is always associated with an underlying heart disease. RBBB may occur in normal individuals.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the phases of the cardiac action potential (phases 0 to 4) and for each phase state the dominant ion movement and the period it represents.
A(ii) Explain the difference between the effective refractory period (ERP) and the relative refractory period, and state why prolongation of the ERP by Class III antiarrhythmic drugs prevents re-entry tachycardia.
B(i) Describe the ECG characteristics of right bundle branch block (RBBB) and left bundle branch block (LBBB) and state which is always associated with underlying heart disease.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Hepatitis B virus: Common disease; about 5% of world's population are carriers; in Africa, prevalence 8–15%. Spread through: infected blood and blood products; infected surgical instruments; scarification; tattooing; sharing of sharps; circumcision with infected object; indiscriminate injections; sexual means; mother to child; intravenous injection use. People at risk: individuals living in endemic areas; injection drug users; homosexuals; household contacts of infected individuals; sexual partners; individuals with multiple sexual contacts; health-care workers; patients on haemodialysis. Incubation period: 30–180 days (4–12 weeks). Spectrum: acute viral hepatitis; chronic HBV infection; liver cirrhosis; hepatocellular carcinoma.
A(ii) HDV: defective RNA virus; requires helper function of HBV for replication and expression; worldwide about 15 million individuals with HDV infection; causes either coinfection or superinfection. HEV: transmission person to person via fecal-oral route; most common route is ingestion of faecally contaminated water; outbreaks commonly occur during rainy season and after floods; incubation period 14–60 days (5–6 weeks); spectrum — acute viral hepatitis and fulminant hepatitis; pregnant women are at increased risk of fulminant course.
B(i) Causes of hepatitis: bacteria, viruses, fungi, drugs, toxins (alcohol, toxin of poisonous mushroom), autoimmune, ischaemia from heart failure/hypotension/shock; viral aetiology is the most common. Common hepatotropic viruses: HAV, HBV, HCV, HDV, HEV. Other viruses affecting the liver: herpes simplex virus, cytomegalovirus, coxsackie virus, Epstein-Barr virus, yellow fever virus.
B(ii) Prevention of HAV and HEV: attention to public and personal health; virus inactivated by boiling for 20 minutes or chlorination; avoid drinking water or beverages from doubtful sources, eating uncooked shellfish, eating unwashed fruits and vegetables; vaccines and immunoglobulin for travellers to endemic areas and household contacts. Prevention of HBV and HDV: behavioural change; pre-exposure recombinant HB vaccine; post-exposure HB immunoglobulin. Prevention of HCV: no vaccine available; behavioural change; limit exposure to infected persons.
questions.question:
Describe the hepatotropic viruses under the following headings:
A(i) Describe Hepatitis B virus infection: modes of spread, people at risk, incubation period, and clinical spectrum.
A(ii) Describe Hepatitis D virus infection and Hepatitis E virus infection: their peculiarities, including mode of transmission, incubation period, spectrum of disease, and any special risk groups.
B(i) Describe the causes of hepatitis other than viruses, the common hepatotropic viruses, and the other viruses that can affect the liver.
B(ii) Describe the prevention of hepatitis A and E, hepatitis B and D, and hepatitis C.

Describe the approach to neurological localisation under the following headings:
A(i) Describe the changing pattern of CNS diseases in Ibadan between 1957–69 and 1987–89, and explain the clinical tasks required when approaching a patient with a CNS disorder.
A(ii) Describe the features of spinal cord lesions including sensory level, motor features, sphincteric dysfunction, and cutaneous markers of disease.
B(i) Describe the gait abnormalities listed and explain which neurological structures, when damaged together, produce lesions involving motor, sensory, and visual pathways; predominantly motor; predominantly sensory; 3rd/4th/6th/V1/V2 cranial nerves; and 6th/7th/8th cranial nerves.
B(ii) Describe what is examined under each component of the limb examination (tone, power, reflexes, co-ordination) and how muscle inspection contributes to localisation.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Changing pattern: In 1957–69 (N=8637), CNS infections were most common at 46.9%, followed by myelopathy (14.3%), peripheral neuropathy (10.6%), epilepsy (8.1%), stroke (6.9%), and others. In 1987–89 (N=1318), stroke increased to 21.1%, epilepsy to 20.8%, peripheral neuropathy to 11.8%, myelopathy to 11.5%, while CNS infections fell to 11.9%. Clinical tasks: Where is the lesion (localisation)? What is the lesion? What is the extent of involvement? What are the co-morbidities? What are the predisposing/precipitating factors?
A(ii) Spinal cord features: presence of sensory level; distal symmetrical weakness which may be spastic or flaccid (spinal shock) — paraparesis/quadriparesis; sphincteric dysfunction; back pain; presence and timing of pain onset useful in determining location and aetiology; lesions may be extra or intradural. Additional signs: paraplegia in flexion; paraplegia in extension; flexor spasms; spinal shock; cutaneous markers of diseases (café au lait spots, naevi, spinal dysraphism, herpetic rashes).
B(i) Gait abnormalities: ataxic, hemiparetic, high steppage, waddling, spastic/scissors, festinant, hysterical, senile. Localisation of closely related structures: Lesions involving motor, sensory, and visual pathways — internal capsule. Predominantly motor — frontal lobe. Predominantly sensory — parietal lobe/thalamus. Sensorimotor — fronto-parietal/internal capsule. 3rd, 4th, 6th, V1, V2 cranial nerves — cavernous sinus. 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 6th cranial nerves — superior orbital fissure. 6th, 7th, and 8th cranial nerves — cerebello-pontine angle. 9th and 10th cranial nerves — jugular foramen; bulbar syndrome.
B(ii) Limb examination: Tone — spastic, flaccid, plastic, cogwheeling. Power — bedside (MRC scale 1 to 5), truncal weakness, functional tests (stand on toes, heels, rise from squat), fatiguability. Reflexes — deep tendon; superficial (e.g. abdominal); plantars; others (e.g. Hoffman's). Co-ordination — finger-nose and heel-shin ataxia (worse on eye closure?); dysdiadochokinesia. Inspection of muscles: wasting; fasciculation; dexterity; bradykinesia; drift; tremor.

questions.question:
Describe lepromatous leprosy and the diagnosis and prevention of leprosy under the following headings:
A(i) Clinical features of lepromatous leprosy: skin, nerve, eye, and other organ involvement.
A(ii) Describe the diagnosis of leprosy: all methods, including slit skin smear scoring and lepromin testing.
B(i) Prevention of disability and social rehabilitation of leprosy patients.
B(ii) Causes of relapse in leprosy and prevention.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Clinical features of lepromatous leprosy (LL):
Onset: frequently insidious.
Skin: earliest lesions are ill-defined, shiny, hypopigmented or erythematous macules; skin gradually becomes infiltrated and thickened; nodules develop; facial skin thickening causes characteristic leonine facies; hair is lost, especially the lateral third of the eyebrows (madarosis).
Nerve: dermal nerves destroyed leading to progressive glove and stocking anaesthesia and sensory loss (light touch, pain, temperature) beginning at hands and feet and extending to the whole body except axillas, groins, and scalp; position sense preserved; sweating lost; damage symmetrical, occurring late; infiltration of corneal nerves causes anaesthesia predisposing to blindness.
Eye: in LL — massive bacillary infiltration causing keratitis, iritis, iridocyclitis.
Systemic: nephrotic syndrome/CKD; testicular dysfunction (mild to severe); impotence/infertility; amyloidosis (seen in LL and ENL); Lucio's phenomenon (variant of LL — recurrent crops of large, sharply marginated ulcerative/haemorrhagic lesions on lower extremities; immune complex-mediated; frequently fatal due to secondary infection and sepsis).

A(ii) Diagnosis:
- Characteristic skin lesions and neurological damage
Slit skin smear: small incision through epidermis; scraping of dermal material; smeared on glass slide; >6 sites sampled (earlobes, eyebrows, edges of active lesions); stained for AFB; logarithmic scoring: 1+ = 1-10 bacilli per 100 fields; 6+ = over 1000 per field; done annually to monitor response.
- Skin biopsy: useful for determining morphological index (number of viable bacilli per 100 bacilli)
- Growing bacilli in the footpad of mice
Lepromin test: injection of bacillary suspension (lepromin) into forearm; Fernandez reaction read at 48 hours (delayed HS to antigens of MB); Mitsuda reaction read at 3-4 weeks (positive = CMI capable, seen only in tuberculoid leprosy); negative result in LL indicates lack of resistance and worsened prognosis.
Other tests: histamine test (loss of normal flare response); methacholine sweat test; FLA-ABS test (non-specific); antibody to PGL-1 (false negative in paucibacillary); PCR.

B(i) Prevention of disability and social rehabilitation:
Prevention of disability: monitoring sensation and muscle power in hands, feet, and eyes; identify dangerous situations; anaesthetised foot needs appropriate shoe (well-fitting trainer with firm soles and shock-absorbing inners); once deformity develops, custom-made shoes; ulcers heal if protected from weight-bearing; physiotherapy to maximise function of weak muscles and prevent contracture; contractures, foot drop, lagophthalmos, entropion, and ectropion are amenable to surgery.
Social/psychological rehabilitation: education, gainful employment, confidence from family, friends, and doctor; plastic surgery to correct stigmatising deformity; patients reassured that once treatment started they are not infectious; the importance of compliance with antibiotic therapy needs to be emphasised.

B(ii) Causes of relapse and prevention:
Relapse defined as: new skin lesions and an increase in bacteria index (BI) >2+ (>100x).
Early relapse: (1) original misclassification; (2) inadequate chemotherapy; (3) insufficient duration.
Late relapse: (4) drug resistance — particularly with past history of monotherapy or drugs given sequentially; (5) M. leprae persisters.
Prevention: detection and prompt treatment of all leprosy cases; contact examination; case finding; development of vaccine; BCG.

A(i) Anatomical parts of the nail unit:
- Lunula: visible part of the nail matrix; best seen in the thumb, poorly in the little finger
- Cuticle: fold of skin tissue at base of the nail that overlaps lunula; protects nail folds and matrix from organisms and allergens
- Nail matrix: contains nerves, lymphatics, and blood vessels; responsible for production of the nail plate; proliferating cells of germinative matrix mostly contribute to nail plate growth; nail bed contributes to the ventral surface
- Nail bed: skin beneath the nail plate
- Nail plate: hard part of nail, made of translucent keratin protein (dead cells)
- Distal edge: anterior free margin of nail plate
- Proximal nail fold: epithelium with a granular layer; contains sweat glands (no pilosebaceous unit)
- Lateral nail folds: folds on both sides of the nail plate
- Hyponychium: epithelium located beneath nail plate between distal edge and skin of fingertip
- Eponychium: small band of epithelium from posterior nail wall onto base of nail; protects nail from invasion by micro-organisms
Clinical distinction: thinning of nail plate = sign of nail matrix disease; nail thickening = sign of nail bed disease. Complete replacement: fingernails 6 months, toenails 18 months.

A(ii) Functions of the nail: protection; sensory perception (augments sensation of touch); manual dexterity; scratching; picking up small objects; cosmetic.
Growth rate: fingernail 0.1 mm/day (3 mm/month); toenail 0.033 mm/day (1 mm/month).

A(iii) Physiological/environmental factors:
Faster: daytime, pregnancy, youth (increasing age), fingers, male, summer, right (dominant) hand, trauma/nail biting.
Slower: night, first day of life, old age, toes and thumb, female, winter, left (non-dominant) hand.
Pathological factors:
Faster: psoriasis, pityriasis rubra pilaris, hyperthyroidism, levodopa, arteriovenous shunts, bullous ichthyosiform erythroderma.
Slower: finger/toe immobilisation, fever, hypothyroidism, yellow nail syndrome, relapsing polychondritis, poor nutrition.

B(i) Nail psoriasis (occurs in 10-78% of cases; commoner in older patients, active exacerbation, psoriatic arthritis):
- Nail pitting, Beau's lines, leukonychia, trachyonychia
- Splinter haemorrhages
- Subungual hyperkeratosis, onycholysis (nail turns yellow, resembles fungal infection)
- Oil spot lesion (most characteristic): localised separation of nail plate, salmon colour appearance
- Onycholysis with lakes of pus in pustular psoriasis
- Nail deformity: extensive matrix involvement causes fragmentation and crumbling

Nail lichen planus (occurs in about 1-10% of LP; commoner in 5th or 6th decades):
- Nail plate thinning
- Longitudinal ridging and grooving
- Pterygium formation (most characteristic)
- Longitudinal erythronychia
- Subungual keratosis
- Trachyonychia, anonychia, subungual hyperpigmentation
questions.question:
Describe the structure of the nail fully under the listed headings, explain how nail matrix disease differs from nail bed disease in terms of clinical output, and distinguish between the principal nail signs of psoriasis and lichen planus:
A(i) Name and describe each anatomical part of the nail unit.
A(ii) Functions of the nail and nail growth rates (physiological/environmental and pathological factors).
A(iii) Physiological and pathological factors that increase versus decrease the rate of nail growth.
B(i) Nail signs of psoriasis versus nail signs of lichen planus — list all features given for each.

Describe leprosy under the following headings:
A(i) Define leprosy, describe its causative organism (characteristics, preference for tissues, ability to culture), and the classification of leprosy from indeterminate to polar forms using both Ridley-Jopling and WHO systems.
A(ii) Describe borderline tuberculoid, borderline (BB), and borderline lepromatous leprosy with their distinguishing skin and nerve features.
B(i) Describe leprosy reactions (Type 1 and Type 2/ENL) including management of each reaction type.
B(ii) Describe the investigations available for diagnosing leprosy including slit skin smear, lepromin testing, and other diagnostic tests listed.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Definition: chronic granulomatous disease caused by Mycobacterium leprae affecting peripheral nerves and skin; discovered by Gerhard Hansen in 1874 (hence Hansen's disease). M. leprae: rod-shaped AFB; first bacterial disease in humans; humans are only primary reservoir; animal reservoirs include 9-banded armadillo, chimpanzee, mangabey monkeys; very slowly growing (doubling time 12 days); cannot be cultured but can be grown in the footpad of armadillo; does not produce toxins; adapted to penetrate and reside within macrophages; preference for cool tissues (skin, peripheral nerves, anterior chamber of eye, upper respiratory tract, testes); incubation period 6 months to 50 years. In 2009, M. lepromatosis was discovered (similar to M. leprae, causes diffuse lepromatous leprosy in Mexico and Caribbean). Classification: Ridley-Jopling — Indeterminate; polar forms: Tuberculoid (TT) and Lepromatous (LL); Borderline: BT, BB, BL. WHO — Paucibacillary (TT, BT); Multibacillary (LL, BL, BB, BT). Pure Neural Leprosy also recognised. Indeterminate leprosy: single/few hypopigmented or faintly erythematous macules with ill-defined margin, slight sensory loss; 70% heal spontaneously, 30% progress.
A(ii) Borderline tuberculoid (BT): similar skin lesions to TT but may have few or many; margins less well-defined; satellite lesions; damage to peripheral nerves widespread and severe with several thickened nerve trunks; at risk of reversal reactions leading to rapid nerve function deterioration and deformities. Borderline (BB): most unstable part of spectrum; patients usually downgrade towards LL if untreated or upgrade towards TT during reversal reaction; numerous skin lesions — macules, papules, or plaques varying in size, shape, and distribution; annular lesions with broad irregular edge and sharply defined punched-out centre characteristic; nerve damage is variable. Borderline lepromatous (BL): widespread variable asymmetrical skin lesions; may be erythematous or hyperpigmented papules, succulent nodules or plaques; sensation in lesions may be normal; peripheral nerve involvement widespread.
B(i) Leprosy reactions: immunologically mediated episodes of acute or subacute inflammation affecting skin, nerves, mucous membranes, and/or other sites interrupting the chronic course; unless promptly and adequately treated can result in deformity and disability. Type 1 reaction: simple anti-inflammatory drugs rarely sufficient; any evidence of neuritis (nerve tenderness, new anaesthesia, motor loss) — start corticosteroids; Prednisolone starting at 40–60 mg daily, reducing to 40 mg after a few days, then by 5 mg every 2–4 weeks; BT reactions need 2–4 months; BL reactions may need 6 months; Gabapentin 300 mg QID and Amitriptyline 50–150 mg QID for neuropathic pain; splinting affected limb in functional position during acute period. Type 2 (ENL): difficult to treat; high-dose steroids (80 mg daily, tapered rapidly) or thalidomide; Thalidomide 400 mg daily is superior to steroids and is drug of choice for young men with severe ENL (risk of phocomelia in pregnancy); Clofazimine 300 mg per day for several months has anti-inflammatory effect; low-grade chronic ENL with iritis or neuritis requires long-term suppression with thalidomide or clofazimine.
B(ii) Diagnosis: Characteristic skin lesions and neurological damage. Bacteriological exam: Slit skin smear — small incision through epidermis, scraping dermal material, smeared on glass slide; more than 6 sites sampled (earlobes, eyebrows, edges of active lesions); stained; AFB counted on logarithmic scale (1+ = 1–10 bacilli/100 fields; 6+ = over 1000/field); done annually to monitor response. Skin biopsy — morphological index (viable bacilli/100 bacilli). Growing bacilli in footpad of mice. Lepromin test: bacillary suspension (lepromin) injected into forearm; Fernandez reaction at 48 hours (positive = delayed HS to antigens of MB); Mitsuda reaction at 3–4 weeks (positive = capable of mounting CMI, seen only in tuberculoid leprosy). Other tests: histamine test (loss of normal flare response); methacholine sweat test; fluorescent lepromin antibody absorbed test (FLA-ABS, non-specific); antibody to phenolic glycolipid 1 (PGL-1, false negative in paucibacillary); PCR.

A(i) Kidneys: paired organs; each weighs 120–200 g; dimensions: 10–12 cm vertically, 5–7 cm transversely, and 3 cm anteroposteriorly. The outer surface is divided into anterior side, dorsal side, upper pole, and lower pole. The lateral surface is convex. The medial surface is concave, deeply grooved (renal sinus), and forms the renal hilum. The ureter/renal pelvis, renal artery, renal vein, lymphatic vessels, and nerves enter or exit through the renal hilum. Cross-section shows cortex and medulla. Each kidney consists of millions of functional units — nephrons.
A(ii) Renal system pathway: Nephrons → Collecting Ducts → Minor calyces → Major calyces → Pelvis → Ureter → Urinary Bladder (which originates from the trigone of the bladder and continues through the external urethral orifice) → Prostatic urethra → Penile urethra → External urethral meatus. The kidneys have extensive blood supply: artery → afferent arteriole → efferent arteriole → veins. Following filtration → urine → urinary bladder (storage) → urethra (outside). 1–2 litres of urine produced daily depending on fluid intake, insensible loss, and kidney function. Both male and female urinary systems are essentially similar, the difference being only in the length of the urethra.
B(i) Normal kidney functions and clinical manifestations when each fails: (1) Excretion of waste products — failure leads to accumulation of nitrogenous waste (azotaemia) and uraemic syndrome (anorexia, pruritus, fatigue, difficulty with memory and concentration; advanced stages involve multiple organ systems); (2) Regulation of fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance — failure leads to dyspnoea (from fluid overload), oedema (facial and dependent in CKD and nephrotic syndrome), and metabolic acidosis; (3) Production of erythropoietin, renin, and prostaglandins — failure of erythropoietin leads to pallor (anaemia in CKD); failure of renin regulation contributes to hypertension; (4) Metabolism of vitamin D — the kidney performs the final hydroxylation of vitamin D to its active form; failure leads to reduced active vitamin D and contributes to metabolic bone disease (renal osteodystrophy).
B(ii) Painless haematuria causes: urinary tract obstruction; tuberculosis; urogenital tumours; glomerulonephritis; renal cystic disease. Haematuria presentation by colour change: urine becomes red or smoky brown (haematuria); urine becomes blackish or coca-cola in colour (characteristic of glomerulonephritis); haemoglobinuria (from haemolysis); myoglobinuria (from crush injury). Frothy urine is commonly due to proteinuria. Urine colour darkens on standing in porphyria and alkaptonuria. Acute glomerulonephritis — typically painless despite haematuria. Renal/ureteral colic — colicky pain that radiates from loin to groin and to the testicle in the male, associated with obstruction by stone or blood clot.
questions.question:
Describe the kidney as an organ under the following headings and explain the clinical significance of each component:
A(i) Gross anatomy of the kidneys including dimensions, surfaces, and the renal hilum contents.
A(ii) Describe the nephron structure and the renal system pathway from nephron to external urethral meatus.
B(i) Describe the normal functions of the kidney and explain how each function relates to a specific clinical manifestation when it fails.
B(ii) Distinguish between the renal causes of haematuria (painless) and the presentation of haematuria in terms of urine colour change and associated conditions.

A(i) Describe metabolic bone disease, and classify the three main types with a brief definition of each.
A(ii) Classify osteoporosis into primary and secondary types, further sub-classify primary osteoporosis into its two subtypes, and state the pathological mechanism underlying each subtype.
B(i) Describe the clinical features, X-ray findings, and drugs used in the treatment of post-menopausal osteoporosis. State the rate of bone loss at menopause versus the preceding decade, and the risk factors for the condition.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Metabolic bone disease: a diverse group of disorders of bone metabolism, most commonly caused by abnormalities of minerals (calcium or phosphorus) or vitamin D; any systemic condition that results in reduced bone strength, altered bone mineralisation or composition.
Three main types:
1. Osteoporosis: the quantity of bone mass is abnormally low.
2. Osteomalacia: osteoid tissue is present but poorly mineralised.
3. Osteitis fibrosa: PTH overproduction leads to bone resorption and replacement by fibrous tissue.
Bone structure: complex tissue including inorganic, organic, and cellular components. Major inorganic component: hydroxyapatite (complex calcium salt including phosphate, carbonate, magnesium, and other ions). Cellular components: osteoblasts (deposit bone mineral on surface); osteocytes (bone builders in interior); osteoclasts (large multinucleate cells, probably modified macrophages, that break down and remodel bone).
A(ii) Osteoporosis classification:
Primary osteoporosis: no cause found; usually due to ageing and decreased gonadal activity.
Secondary osteoporosis: due to a variety of metabolic, endocrine, neoplastic disorders.
Two subtypes of primary osteoporosis:
1. Early post-menopausal (Type I / high turnover): due to rapid increase in osteoclastic resorption.
2. Senile osteoporosis (Type II / low turnover): due to decreased osteoblastic activity and dietary insufficiency combined with chronic ill health.
B(i) Post-menopausal osteoporosis:
Rate of bone loss: women at menopause and 10 years after lose bone at 3% per year, compared to 0.3% during the preceding decade, due to increased bone resorption.
Risk factors: white race, positive family history, amenorrhoea, early hysterectomy, alcoholism, cigarette smoking, lack of exercise.
Clinical features: bone pain, backache, increased thoracic kyphosis.
X-ray findings: wedging or compression of one or more vertebral bodies.
Treatment (prevention and pharmacological):
- Women approaching menopause should maintain adequate dietary calcium, phosphate, and vitamin D; keep high level of physical activity; no smoking; no alcohol.
- Drugs: oestrogen medication (hormone replacement therapy), bisphosphonates, calcitonin, fluoride.

questions.question:
Describe acute kidney injury (AKI) under the following headings:
A(i) Provide the history of the terminology change from ARF to AKI and explain why the new terminology is preferred.
A(ii) Describe the clinical presentation of AKI, including all symptoms, signs, and the uraemic syndrome.
B(i) Describe the role of urinalysis in differentiating the cause of AKI, giving specific findings for each pattern.
B(ii) Distinguish between the three KDIGO staging levels of AKI using both serum creatinine and urine output criteria, and state the laboratory investigations required.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Before the advancement of modern medicine, AKI was referred to as 'uraemic poisoning.' Uraemia was described as contamination of blood with urine. In 1847, uraemia came to be used for decreased urine output (oliguria); it was thought to be urine mixing with blood instead of passing through the ureter/urethra. ARF (Acute Renal Failure) has now been replaced by AKI (Acute Kidney Injury). A universal definition/staging system was proposed. The new terminology AKI enables healthcare professionals to see the disease as a spectrum of injury which extends from less severe injury to more advanced injury when RRT is required (ARF). The purpose was to allow earlier detection and management of kidney injury.
A(ii) Clinical presentation: younger age group predominantly. History of risk factors (CCF, CLD, DM, APH, PPH, gastroenteritis); use of nephrotoxic agents (mercury soap, creams, exposure to lead in paints); skin rash; use of herbs; reduction in urine output; coke-coloured urine; uraemic syndrome (nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, hiccups, asterixis). The uraemic syndrome is described in the approach to kidney disease as: the constellation of findings observed in advanced renal failure; earliest manifestations include anorexia, pruritus, fatigue, difficulty with memory and concentration; advanced stages associated with involvement of multiple organ systems. Dyspnoea from fluid overload in renal impairment, metabolic acidosis, or pleural effusion in nephrotic syndrome. Oedema (facial and dependent) in chronic kidney disease and nephrotic syndrome. Pruritus, distal brown discolouration of nails, pallor, and hyperpigmentation in chronic kidney disease.
B(i) Urinalysis in AKI — KDIGO guidance: proteinuria (3+, 4+ → intrinsic renal disease); haematuria (intrinsic glomerular disease); pyuria (AIN, pyelonephritis, AGN); crystalluria → poisoning (oxalate crystals in ethylene glycol, tumour lysis syndrome, ARVs, acyclovir, sulfonamides). Additional parameters: urine osmolality; urine/plasma creatinine and urea ratios; urinary sodium; fractional excretion of Na (FENa); fractional excretion of urea (FEurea); creatinine clearance.
B(ii) KDIGO staging: Stage 1 — serum creatinine 1.5–1.9 times baseline OR ≥26.5 µmol/L increase; urine output <0.5 mL/kg/hr for 6–12 hours. Stage 2 — serum creatinine 2–2.9 times baseline; urine output <0.5 mL/kg/hr for >12 hours. Stage 3 — serum creatinine 3.0 times baseline OR increase to ≥353.6 µmol/L OR initiation of dialysis; urine output <0.3 mL/kg/hr for >24 hours or anuria for >12 hours. Laboratory investigations: urine; blood — FBC, ESR, SEUC (serum electrolytes, urea and creatinine); ECG; radiology (USS, CXR, CT, MRI).

A(i) Glomerular diseases are a spectrum of renal diseases, varied in aetiology and clinical presentation, all having clinical and pathologic evidence of glomerular damage; inflammation may not necessarily be a feature. Gross anatomy of kidneys: paired organs; each weighs 120–200g; dimensions 10–12 cm vertically, 5–7 cm transversely, and 3 cm anteroposteriorly. The outer surface can be divided into anterior side, dorsal side, upper pole, and lower pole. The lateral surface is convex. The medial surface is concave, deeply grooved (renal sinus), forming the renal hilum. The ureter/renal pelvis, renal artery, renal vein, lymphatic vessels, and nerves enter or exit through the renal hilum.
A(ii) Pathogenesis involves a complex interplay between cellular immunity, humoral immunity, complement system/cascade, coagulation cascade, and soluble factors. Immune mechanisms: antibody-mediated injury (in-situ immune complex deposition; circulating immune complex deposition with endogenous or exogenous antigens); cytotoxic antibodies; cell-mediated immune injury; activation of alternate complement pathway. The type of glomerular injury depends on: the initial immune response; the extent to which the immune response is perpetuated and provokes injury; the extent to which inflammation resolves without scarring or proceeds to destruction by rapid inflammation/necrosis or slowly progressive glomerulosclerosis and tubulointerstitial fibrosis. The four factors determining effect of immune deposit: site of deposit (mesangium, subendothelial, subepithelial); biological properties of immunoglobulins (complement-fixing IgG causes more damage); mechanism by which deposits are formed (deposits formed in glomerulus damage more than those passively trapped); amount of immune deposit. HLA-DR2 identifies a powerful relative risk of Goodpasture's syndrome.
B(i) Epidemiology: GN is recognised as the second commonest cause of ESRD worldwide (third place in Europe and USA). GN is the second commonest cause of chronic kidney failure in Nigeria from available reports. For every patient with clinically apparent GN receiving medical care, an estimated additional 5–10 patients have undiagnosed sub-clinical disease. GN is more common in males than females. There may be hereditary predisposition (e.g., Alport's syndrome). Acute glomerulonephritis usually has a self-limited course with a good prognosis.
B(ii) Investigations: CBC — normochromic normocytic anaemia; hyperlipidaemia/hypoalbuminaemia in nephrotic syndrome; viral screens, ANA, ANCA, cryoglobulins, urine and serum protein electrophoresis, ACR; blood glucose, urea and creatinine increased, GFR reduced; complement profile — reduced C3 and C4; urinalysis/urine sediment microscopy — nephritic/active or nephrotic; renal ultrasound scan; renal biopsy/histology. Renal biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosis. Candidates for biopsy: patients with individual or family history of renal disease, atypical presentation including massive proteinuria, nephrotic syndrome, or rapid rise in creatinine without resolution. Three immunofluorescence patterns: (1) granular deposits of immunoglobulins — immune complex disease (C3 low, anti-GBM negative, ANCA negative — causes include post-streptococcal GN, bacterial endocarditis, shunt nephritis, lupus nephritis); (2) linear deposits of Ig on GBM — anti-GBM GN (C3 normal, anti-GBM positive, ANCA negative — caused by anti-GBM disease and Goodpasture's syndrome); (3) pauci-immune GN (C3 normal, anti-GBM negative, ANCA positive — causes include Wegener's granulomatosis, microscopic polyarteritis nodosa).
questions.question:
Describe glomerular disease under the following headings:
A(i) Define glomerular diseases and describe the gross anatomy of the kidneys.
A(ii) Describe the pathogenesis of glomerular injury, listing all components, immune mechanisms, and the factors that determine the type of injury.
B(i) State the epidemiology of glomerulonephritis.
B(ii) Describe the investigations required including the role of renal biopsy, and distinguish the three immunofluorescence patterns and their associated serological markers.

questions.answerText:
(i) The most likely diagnosis is pulmonary tuberculosis. The causative organism is Mycobacterium tuberculosis, a rod-shaped, non-spore-forming, thin aerobic bacterium measuring 0.5 µm by 3 µm, belonging to the family Mycobacteriaceae and order Actinomycetales. It is also called 'acid-fast bacilli' because once stained, the bacilli cannot be decolorized by acid alcohol, due mainly to the organisms' high content of mycolic acids, long-chain cross-linked fatty acids, and other cell-wall lipids.
(ii) Epidemiological risk factors: The WHO estimated 9.4 million new cases of TB worldwide in 2009, 95% in developing countries. Africa carries 29% of the global burden of TB cases and 34% of related deaths. Nigeria is one of the 5 countries with the highest burden of TB. TB is one of the 3 largest single-agent infectious causes of morbidity and mortality worldwide. HIV pandemic, weak healthcare systems, inadequate laboratories and poor living conditions worsen the situation. TB reemerged in the 1980s following the AIDS pandemic and remains a leading cause of illness and death among people with HIV/AIDS. The average incidence in African countries more than doubled between 1990 and 2005 from 149 to 343 per 100,000 population. Causes of drug resistance include failure of re-treatment regimens, exposure to a known DR-TB case, failure of Category 1 treatment, and history of TB treatment outside the national programme.
(iii) Pathophysiology: Of those infected with M. tuberculosis, about 5% will develop active TB disease within five years of primary infection. The other 95% will develop a latent infection that may later progress to cause disease, depending on the status of the immune system. Overall, about 10% of infected individuals will eventually develop active TB. Before chemotherapy, one infectious source would transmit infection to 20 others during an average of two years. Without anti-TB treatment, about 65% of smear-positive cases will die, most within 2 years. Only 10–15% of smear-negative cases are expected to die.
(iv) Investigations: Sputum AFB microscopy — collect 3 sputum specimens if cough lasts 2 weeks or more. Culture techniques detect as many as 10–1,000 viable mycobacteria per mL; results may take six to eight weeks, but the BACTEC TB-460 system detects growth in 7–13 days in smear-positive specimens. Tuberculin Skin Test (TST): standard dose is 5 tuberculin units given intradermally in 0.1 mL, read at 48–72 hours; 5 mm or more is positive in HIV-positive persons or recent contacts; 10 mm or more is positive in recent arrivals from high-prevalence countries or persons with DM, steroid therapy, leukaemia, or renal disease; 15 mm or more is positive in persons with no known risk factors. IGRA (QuantiFERON-TB Gold or T-SPOT.TB) measures IFN-γ release after T-cell stimulation by ESAT6 and CFP10 antigens — high specificity unaffected by BCG vaccination. Adenosine Deaminase is useful for diagnosis of TB in body fluids. Nucleic Acid Amplification Tests permit diagnosis in as little as several hours. Gene Xpert and genetic sequencing are also available. Chest radiograph may show upper-lobe disease with infiltrates and cavities, but virtually any radiographic pattern may be seen.
(v) Treatment: Broad spectrum antibiotics (except fluoroquinolones) for 7 days then review after 2 weeks if AFB results are equivocal. First-line drugs have established dosages and adverse effect profiles. MDR-TB is TB caused by strains resistant to at least isoniazid and rifampicin. XDR-TB is resistance to isoniazid and rifampicin plus any fluoroquinolone and at least one of three injectable drugs: capreomycin, kanamycin, and amikacin. Totally drug-resistant TDR-TB is resistance to all anti-TB drugs. Standardized treatment in Nigeria for MDR-TB includes cycloserine, levofloxacin, prothionamide, kanamycin/capreomycin, and pyrazinamide for 18–24 months with an intensive phase of 8 months; injectables are stopped after the intensive phase.

A 35-year-old man presents with a 3-week history of productive cough, evening fever, drenching night sweats, anorexia, and significant weight loss. He reports a past history of frequent antibiotic use and close contact with a neighbour undergoing treatment for a chronic lung infection. Chest examination reveals dullness and bronchial breathing at the right upper zone.
(i) What is the most likely diagnosis, and what organism is responsible?
(ii) State all the risk factors and epidemiological factors that predispose this patient and his community to this condition.
(iii) Describe the pathophysiology of disease progression, including what determines whether primary infection leads to active disease.
