questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA). It is an acute metabolic complication of diabetes mellitus. The two metabolic abnormalities are: metabolic acidosis (pH 7.15, bicarbonate 12 mmol/L) and hyperglycaemia with ketonaemia/ketonuria (RBG 300 mg/dl, 4+ ketonuria).
(ii) Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus is most likely. Justification: the patient is a 19-year-old lean female; Type 1A DM has a peak incidence in childhood and adolescence, usually presents before 30 years of age with abrupt onset of characteristic symptoms over days to a few weeks, and patients are characteristically normal weight or lean. DKA is typically associated with Type 1 DM, though it can occur in Type 2 DM.
(iii) Pathophysiological sequence: insulin deficiency leads to reduced glucose uptake in tissues; increased lipolysis releases free fatty acids; the liver converts free fatty acids to ketone bodies (ketonesis) causing ketonaemia and ketonuria; hyperglycaemia results from unregulated gluconeogenesis and reduced peripheral glucose uptake; hyperglycaemia causes osmotic diuresis leading to urinary water losses and electrolyte depletion; glycerol from lipolysis also contributes to gluconeogenesis; the combination of ketonaemia and metabolic acidosis produces the deep rapid breathing (Kussmaul respiration) and impaired consciousness.
(iv) Low potassium in DKA: despite total body potassium depletion (from osmotic diuresis), serum potassium can be low, normal, or high at presentation. Low potassium at presentation indicates severe total body depletion. During treatment, insulin administration drives potassium into cells, further lowering serum levels, which can cause life-threatening hypokalaemia. Resuscitation must therefore include careful potassium replacement alongside insulin therapy and fluid resuscitation, with monitoring of serum electrolytes.
(v) Differential diagnoses:
• Hyperglycaemic Hyperosmolar State (HHS): characterised by marked increase in plasma osmolarity, altered sensorium, minimal or no ketosis — distinguished from DKA by absence of significant ketonuria and acidosis.
• Hypoglycaemic coma: RBG would be very low (not 300 mg/dl), no ketonuria, responds rapidly to intravenous glucose — distinguished by a low blood glucose measurement.
questions.question:
A 19-year-old lean female student is brought to the emergency room unconscious. Her parents report she had been excessively thirsty and urinating frequently for 10 days before becoming unresponsive. On examination she has a GCS of 7/15, RR of 30 breaths/min, appears dehydrated, and her breathing is deep and rapid. Urgent investigations show: RBG 300 mg/dl, urinalysis 4+ ketonuria, serum bicarbonate 12 mmol/L, pH 7.15, low potassium.
(i) What is the diagnosis? State the two metabolic abnormalities this case illustrates.
(ii) State the type of diabetes most likely and justify your answer using patient features.
(iii) Explain the pathophysiological sequence from insulin deficiency to the metabolic state present.
(iv) What is the significance of the low potassium, and how does this guide resuscitation?
(v) State two differential diagnoses of unconsciousness in a young diabetic patient and how you would distinguish each from the diagnosis in this case.

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Acute Aortic Regurgitation (in the context of infective endocarditis in an IV drug user). The two classic causes of acute AR are infective endocarditis and aortic dissection.
(ii) Comparison of acute vs. chronic AR:
Left ventricular response: in chronic AR, compensatory mechanisms (LV dilation and LVH) develop over years to accommodate the regurgitant volume; in acute AR, the LV has no time for compensation — the sudden volume load overwhelms the unprepared normal-sized LV.
Haemodynamic presentation: chronic AR — symptoms are absent until 4th or 5th decade; exertional dyspnoea and palpitations progress slowly; acute AR — florid pulmonary oedema develops rapidly; the patient presents with hypotension and severe breathlessness. Wide pulse pressure is present in both but most sensitive in chronic AR; physical findings in acute AR are also wide pulse pressure, diastolic murmur, and florid pulmonary oedema.
Pulse character: in chronic AR — wide pulse pressure is most sensitive; hyperdynamic and displaced apical impulse; palpitations due to increased force of contraction. In acute AR — wide pulse pressure and diastolic murmur with florid pulmonary oedema.
(iii) Acute AR is a true surgical emergency because the normal-sized LV cannot compensate for the sudden severe volume load — rapid deterioration occurs. Immediate medical stabilisation: positive inotrope (e.g. dopamine, dobutamine) to support cardiac output; vasodilators (e.g. nitroprusside) even in the setting of hypotension; avoid beta-blockers (they are contraindicated in acute AR as mild-to-moderate tachycardia is beneficial); do not use a balloon pump (also contraindicated).
(iv) Imaging for confirmation: echocardiography is the cornerstone for decision-making and follow-up — evaluation of the aortic valve and aortic root with measurements of LV dimensions and function. Aortography: used to confirm the severity of disease.
(v) Austin Flint murmur: heard at the apex in chronic aortic regurgitation. Mechanism: the regurgitant jet from the incompetent aortic valve impinges on the anterior mitral valve leaflet, causing it to vibrate; this vibration mimics the opening of a narrowed mitral valve and produces a low-pitched mid-diastolic rumble at the apex, resembling the murmur of mitral stenosis but without an opening snap or a loud S1.
questions.question:
A 28-year-old intravenous drug user presents to the emergency room acutely breathless and hypotensive. On examination his blood pressure is 80/40 mmHg (wide pulse pressure noted), he has florid pulmonary oedema, and a short diastolic murmur is heard at the left sternal border.
(i) What is the most likely diagnosis and what two causes of acute aortic regurgitation are identified?
(ii) Compare the clinical differences between acute and chronic aortic regurgitation under the headings: left ventricular response, haemodynamic presentation, and pulse character.
(iii) Why is acute AR described as a true surgical emergency and what immediate medical measures stabilise the patient?
(iv) State the imaging modality used to confirm the severity of AR and what it shows.
(v) What is an Austin Flint murmur and what is its mechanism?

A 19-year-old student presents during a college outbreak with a 2-day history of fever, jaundice, right upper quadrant pain, and dark urine. He reports eating food from a campus canteen. Multiple students are affected. His AST is 8 times the upper limit of normal.
(i) What is the most likely hepatitis virus causing this outbreak? State its mode of transmission and spread.
(ii) Describe the epidemiology of this virus, including the level of endemicity in Africa and who is most commonly infected.
(iii) What is the clinical spectrum of disease caused by this virus, including the definition of fulminant hepatitis?
(iv) What investigations would you order to confirm the diagnosis and assess severity?
(v) How is this infection prevented?
questions.answerText:
(i) Hepatitis A virus (HAV). Mode of transmission: person to person via the fecal-oral route; shed into stool in high concentration. Spread encouraged by close contact and poor hygiene through faecally contaminated food or water; consumption of contaminated uncooked or undercooked shellfish; food contaminated during preparation; food contaminated by an infected food handler.
(ii) Epidemiology: Africa is highly endemic for HAV infection; most people become infected within the first few years of life; by age 10 years, majority in the community are immune. Incubation period is 15–49 days (25 days).
(iii) Clinical spectrum: silent asymptomatic infection; fulminant hepatitis (severe, rapidly progressive loss of hepatic function due to viral infection or other cause of inflammatory destruction of liver tissue). It causes acute infection only (no chronic infection).
(iv) Investigations: liver function tests (AST and ALT up to 10 times upper limit of normal and greater; elevated bilirubin; alkaline phosphatase may be normal or elevated; total protein and albumin usually normal; prothrombin time may be prolonged); abdominal USS; blood glucose; FBC (transient neutropenia and lymphopenia, later relative lymphocytosis); urinalysis (microscopic haematuria, minimal proteinuria); elevated gamma globulin; serologic tests including anti-HAV.
(v) Prevention of HAV: attention to public and personal health; virus inactivated by boiling for 20 minutes or chlorination; avoid drinking water or beverages from doubtful sources, eating uncooked shellfish, eating unwashed fruits and vegetables; vaccines and immunoglobulin for travellers to endemic areas and household contacts of index cases.

questions.question:
Describe chronic pancreatitis under the following headings, and explain why disease may spread to cause distant functional deficits:
A(i) Definition, causes, and groups at risk.
A(ii) Clinical presentation and physical findings.
B(i) How the zones/parts of the pancreas relate to the common complications of this disease — explain why destruction of each zone causes its specific complication.
B(ii) All investigations and all treatment options.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Definition, causes, and groups at risk:
Chronic pancreatitis: irreversible damage to the pancreas and eventual destruction of exocrine and endocrine tissues.
Causes: alcohol; genetic (hereditary pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis); metabolic (hypercalcaemia, hypertriglyceridaemia); obstructive; autoimmune; idiopathic; asymptomatic pancreatic fibrosis; radiotherapy; also infection/autoimmune; blockage of common bile/pancreatic duct; medications (estrogens, corticosteroids, thiazide diuretics, azathioprine); hyperparathyroidism.
Groups at risk: more common in men than women; often affects ages 30-40.

A(ii) Clinical presentation and physical findings:
Presentation: abdominal pain (upper abdomen, lasting hours to days or continuous; worse with eating or drinking alcohol; radiates to the back; relieved by leaning forward); steatorrhoea and weight loss; diabetes mellitus; diarrhoea, nausea, and vomiting; fatty/oily pale or clay-coloured stools; chronic weight loss.
Physical findings: abdominal tenderness; weight loss; palpable abdominal mass (pseudocyst); jaundice; palpable spleen.

B(i) Pancreatic zones and complications:
- Destruction of exocrine tissue (acinar cells and ductal system) → malabsorption of nutrients and fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, K; steatorrhoea (fatty stools). Exocrine failure means digestive enzymes are absent: fat is not digested, causing fatty steatorrhoea and vitamin deficiency.
- Destruction of endocrine tissue (islets of Langerhans) → diabetes mellitus. Without insulin-secreting beta cells, glucose regulation fails.
- Ductal obstruction/inflammation → ascites; pancreatic cyst; portal vein thrombosis causing intestinal obstruction.
- Distant spread: exocrine deficiency causes systemic nutritional malabsorption; endocrine deficiency causes diabetes; ascites and intestinal obstruction arise from local complications.

B(ii) Investigations:
Raised alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin; raised serum amylase/lipase during acute exacerbations; direct hormonal stimulation with secretin (most sensitive); trypsinogen in serum; chymotrypsin/elastase in stool; faecal fat (quantitative and qualitative); IgG4; plain abdominal radiography; abdominal USS; CT scan; MRI/MRCP; ERCP; endoscopic ultrasound (EUS); exploratory laparotomy.
Treatment:
- Pain: analgesics; stop alcohol; antioxidants; surgical nerve block
- Maldigestion/steatorrhoea: enzyme supplements (pancrease); low-fat diet; small frequent meals; vitamins and calcium; limit caffeine
- Diabetes: insulin, oral antidiabetic drugs
- NG tube insertion; nil by mouth; IV fluids when needed

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the characteristics, normal values, and regulatory mechanisms of sodium in the extracellular fluid under the following headings: (a) proportion of ECF cations, (b) normal plasma concentration, (c) paired ions, (d) intracellular level, (e) physiological roles.
A(ii) Describe the tubular handling of sodium from filtration through to collecting tubule, naming the hormonal and neural systems involved.
B(i) Explain the clinical consequences of isotonic fluid loss versus isotonic fluid excess, distinguishing between hypovolaemia and hypervolaemia and naming the conditions that lead to each.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Sodium in the extracellular fluid:
(a) Na⁺ constitutes 90% of total ECF cations.
(b) Normal plasma concentration: 136–145 mEq/L.
(c) Pairs with Cl⁻ and HCO₃⁻ to neutralise charge.
(d) Low in ICF.
(e) Most important ion in regulating water balance; important in nerve and muscle function. Intake is 50–150 mmol/day.
A(ii) Tubular handling of sodium:
- Filtration at glomerulus; reabsorption in proximal tubule (PT), ascending limb of Henle (ALH), distal tubule (DT), and collecting tubule (CT); coupled to other substances via the Na pump.
- Tubuloglomerular balance maintains proportionality.
- Hormonal/neural control: renin–angiotensin system, sympathetic nervous system (SNS), natriuretic peptides (ANP, BNP), and aldosterone.
B(i) Isotonic fluid loss: TBW changes accompanied by equal changes in electrolytes; loss of plasma or ECF. Produces ↓ ECF volume, weight loss, dry skin and mucous membranes, ↓ urine output, and hypovolaemia (rapid heart rate, flattened neck veins, normal or ↓ BP — shock).
Isotonic fluid excess: caused by excess IV fluids, hypersecretion of aldosterone, or drugs such as cortisone. Produces hypervolaemia — weight gain, decreased haematocrit, diluted plasma proteins, distended neck veins, ↑ BP; can lead to oedema (↑ capillary hydrostatic pressure), pulmonary oedema, and heart failure.

(i) Diagnosis: Aortic Stenosis. Classic triad of symptoms: syncope (exertional), angina (increased myocardial oxygen demand — demand/supply mismatch), and dyspnoea (on exertion due to heart failure — systolic and diastolic). Sudden death may also occur.
(ii) Pathophysiology: A pressure gradient develops between the left ventricle and the aorta (increased afterload). LV function is initially maintained by compensatory pressure hypertrophy. When compensatory mechanisms are exhausted, LV function declines and LV dilatation sets in. Syncope results from failure to increase cardiac output during exertion (inadequate cerebral perfusion). Angina results from increased myocardial oxygen demand by the hypertrophied LV with a demand/supply mismatch. Dyspnoea results from diastolic and systolic heart failure as the LV dilates and fails. Sudden death results from severe outflow obstruction and arrhythmias.
(iii) Most valuable investigation: echocardiography — the most valuable test for diagnosis, quantification, and follow-up. Two measurements: (1) left ventricular size and function — LVH, dilation, and ejection fraction; (2) Doppler-derived gradient and valve area (aortic valve area, AVA).
(iv) Definitive treatment: surgical aortic valve replacement. Simplified indications for surgery: any symptomatic patient with severe AS (including symptoms with exercise); any patient with decreasing EF; any patient undergoing CABG with moderate or severe AS. Echo surveillance: mild every 5 years, moderate every 2 years, severe every 6 months to 1 year.
(v) Vasodilators: relatively contraindicated in severe AS as they can cause hypotension without relieving obstruction. Aortic balloon valvotomy: shows little benefit. Medical therapy has a limited role since AS is a mechanical problem. IE prophylaxis is indicated in dental procedures with prosthetic AV or history of endocarditis.
questions.question:
A 68-year-old man presents with exertional syncope, angina on moderate activity, and progressive breathlessness on exertion over the past year. On examination his carotid pulse is slow-rising and of small amplitude. Auscultation reveals a crescendo-decrescendo systolic ejection murmur best heard at the right second intercostal space, with a soft and split second heart sound and a fourth heart sound (S4).
(i) What is the most likely diagnosis? Name the classic triad of symptoms.
(ii) What is the pathophysiologic basis of the LV changes and the development of each symptom in this condition?
(iii) What investigation is the most valuable for diagnosis and quantification, and what two measurements does it provide?
(iv) State the definitive treatment and the simplified indications for surgical intervention.
(v) What is the role of vasodilators and aortic balloon valvotomy in this condition?

A 30-year-old man presents with a 4-week history of jaundice, dark urine, clay-coloured stools, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, and right upper quadrant pain. He had a blood transfusion 3 months ago. He is febrile and has hepatomegaly with right upper quadrant tenderness. His AST and ALT are 12 times the upper limit of normal.
(i) Name the most likely hepatitis virus given the history, and state its two best risk factors.
(ii) Describe the three phases of acute viral hepatitis.
(iii) State the expected laboratory findings including LFTs, FBC, and urinalysis.
(iv) Outline the treatment of acute viral hepatitis.
(v) What is the full clinical spectrum of disease that this virus can cause, and what preventive measures are available for it?
questions.answerText:
(i) Hepatitis C virus (HCV). The two best risk factors for HCV are injection drug use and transfusion of infected blood and blood products.
(ii) Three phases of acute viral hepatitis:
1. Prodromal phase: anorexia, nausea, vomiting, fatigue, malaise, arthralgias, myalgias, headache, pharyngitis, dark urine, clay-coloured stool, cough, fever.
2. Icteric phase: onset of yellowness of eyes, diminution of prodromal symptoms, pain in upper right abdomen, tender hepatomegaly (a variety of anicteric hepatitis also exists).
3. Recovery phase: constitutional symptoms disappear; hepatomegaly and abnormalities of LFTs still evident.
(iii) Laboratory findings: LFTs — AST and ALT up to 10 times upper limit of normal and greater; elevated bilirubin; alkaline phosphatase may be normal or elevated; total protein and albumin usually normal; prothrombin time may be prolonged. Abdominal USS. Blood glucose. FBC — transient neutropenia and lymphopenia, later relative lymphocytosis. Urinalysis — microscopic haematuria, minimal proteinuria. Elevated gamma globulin. Serologic tests — HBsAg, anti-HBc, anti-HCV, anti-HAV, anti-HEV.
(iv) Treatment of acute viral hepatitis: no specific therapy; bed rest; supportive treatment; normal diet if not in encephalopathy; vitamin supplements; avoid hepatotoxic drugs.
(v) Spectrum of HCV disease: acute viral hepatitis; chronic hepatitis C virus infection; liver cirrhosis; hepatocellular carcinoma. Prevention: no vaccine is available for HCV; behavioural change; limit exposure to infected persons.

(i) Diagnosis: Pulmonary embolism. Wells Prediction Rule scoring applicable to this patient: previous surgery or immobilization within last 30 days (postpartum, +1.5); heart rate >100 beats per minute (+1.5); clinical signs of deep vein thrombosis (if present, +3); alternative diagnosis less likely than PE (+3); haemoptysis (+1); total likely >7 = High clinical probability. Clinical probability: Low 0–1; Intermediate 2–6; High >7.
(ii) Acquired risk factors (general): age >40 years; recent surgery (high risk: orthopaedic, head and neck, thoracic); prolonged immobility; cancer; female sex (applicable); pregnancy — hypercoagulable state (applicable — 6 weeks postpartum); polycythaemia; obesity; trauma; previous DVT; nephrotic syndrome; lupus anticoagulant; antiphospholipid syndrome; connective tissue disease; idiopathic. Note: this patient's risk relates to the postpartum hypercoagulable state and female sex rather than OCP use. Genetic risk factors: protein C deficiency; protein S deficiency; factor V Leiden; hyperhomocysteinaemia; antithrombin deficiency.
(iii) Haemodynamic pathophysiology: Venous thromboembolism is a dynamic process from Virchow's triad of stasis, injury to the intima, and hypercoagulability. Sequence: RV pressure increase; RV dilatation and hypokinesia; RV dysfunction; tricuspid regurgitation and RV failure; RV overload bowing of septum with impaired filling, systemic hypotension, and cardiac arrest. Elevation of both pro-BNP and BNP occurs with RV overload. Massive PE: defined as thrombus occluding more than 50% of the pulmonary vasculature. Systolic blood pressure <90 mmHg or a drop in systolic blood pressure of 40 mmHg from baseline for >15 minutes not otherwise explained by hypovolemia, sepsis, or new arrhythmia. In 20% of cases the initial presentation is sudden death.
(iv) Investigations and expected findings: D-dimer assay; Chest X-ray — atelectasis, infiltrates, pleural effusion, focal oligaemia (Westermark's sign), pleural-based area of opacity (Hampton's hump); ECG — sinus tachycardia, S1Q3T3 pattern, right ventricular strain (present in this patient); Venous Compression USS; Ventilation perfusion scanning; Chest CT Angiogram.
(v) Initial management: basic life support — airway management (patent and clear), high-dose oxygen, IV fluid (circulation). Medical treatment: anticoagulation (e.g., heparin, enoxaparin — LMWH is safe and is the choice); thrombolytic therapy (e.g., streptokinase, alteplase). Surgical: inferior vena caval filters; embolectomy. PE could be fatal if not detected — majority are diagnosed at autopsy. Attention should be paid to risk stratification of each patient (risk factors/clinical probability). Prompt initial management may make the difference. Urgency is determined by haemodynamic instability (systolic BP <90 mmHg for >15 minutes in massive PE).
questions.question:
A 24-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset right-sided chest pain, breathlessness, and haemoptysis. She has been taking the combined oral contraceptive pill and is 6 weeks postpartum. Her BP is 90/60 mmHg and respiratory rate is 26/min. ECG shows sinus tachycardia and S1Q3T3 pattern.
(i) What is the diagnosis and what is the clinical probability based on the Wells Prediction Rule score?
(ii) Identify all acquired and genetic risk factors applicable to this patient and in the general population.
(iii) Describe the haemodynamic pathophysiology that explains her hypotension, and define massive PE.
(iv) State all the investigations required and their expected findings.
(v) State the initial management and all available treatment options, and what determines urgency.

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF). Four anatomical components:
1. Ventricular septal defect (VSD).
2. Pulmonary stenosis.
3. Overriding aorta.
4. Right ventricular hypertrophy.
(ii) The two essential anatomical components are VSD and pulmonary stenosis. The degree of pulmonary stenosis is critical: the stenosis is usually severe enough to cause a predominantly right-to-left shunt, cyanosis, and diminished pulmonary blood flow. The pulmonary stenosis may be either valvular or infundibular; the infundibular form usually predominates in adults.
(iii) Haemodynamic consequence: severe pulmonary stenosis creates high right ventricular pressure that exceeds left ventricular pressure through the VSD, producing a right-to-left shunt; deoxygenated blood passes directly into the systemic circulation via the overriding aorta; pulmonary blood flow is diminished (decreased pulmonary vascular markings on CXR); systemic arterial oxygen saturation falls, causing cyanosis and finger clubbing.
(iv) Complications without repair: infective endocarditis, cerebral thromboembolism, brain abscess; patients who survive to adulthood without surgery or with only palliative shunt operations (anastomosis of systemic artery to pulmonary artery) may become increasingly disabled as a result of gradual shunt closure and progression of infundibular pulmonary stenosis.
(v) Definitive surgical treatment: total correction of TOF — the technique has been well established since the 1960s and the defect is usually repaired in infancy or childhood. Operative mortality risk: less than five percent. Late complications: pulmonary valvular regurgitation and impaired contraction of the right ventricle occur in many patients despite correction. Corrective surgery should be considered in any patient with TOF regardless of whether a previous shunt operation has been performed.
questions.question:
A 4-year-old child with a known heart condition since birth is brought in with increasing cyanosis, finger clubbing, and an episode of squatting after exercise. The child is noted to be breathless at rest. CXR shows decreased pulmonary vascular markings and a boot-shaped heart. Echo confirms the diagnosis.
(i) State the diagnosis and list its four anatomical components.
(ii) State the two essential anatomical components and explain why the degree of pulmonary stenosis is critical to the clinical presentation.
(iii) Describe the haemodynamic consequence of these defects on pulmonary blood flow and arterial oxygen saturation.
(iv) What complications may arise if the defect is not surgically repaired?
(v) Describe the definitive surgical treatment, the operative mortality risk stated, and the late complications that may occur despite correction.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Vaughan Williams classification:
• Class I — sodium channel blockers; change the slope of phase 0 of the cardiac action potential; can abolish tachyarrhythmia caused by re-entry circuits. Subclasses: IA (quinidine, procainamide, disopyramide) — moderate phase 0 depression, slow conduction, prolong repolarisation; IB (lidocaine) — minimal phase 0 depression, shorten repolarisation; IC (flecainide) — marked phase 0 depression and slow conduction, little effect on repolarisation.
• Class II — beta-adrenergic blockers (propranolol, esmolol); decrease heart rate and conduction velocity; can indirectly alter K and Ca conductance.
• Class III — K⁺ channel blockers (amiodarone, sotalol, ibutilide); increase action potential duration and effective refractory period; delay repolarisation; inhibit re-entry tachycardia.
• Class IV — calcium channel blockers (verapamil, diltiazem); decrease inward Ca²⁺ currents; slow conduction in Ca²⁺ current-dependent tissues like the AV node; act on the heart only (unlike dihydropyridines).
A(ii) Drug choice:
(a) VF post-MI: first choice is Class II (beta-blockers) IV followed by oral, early after MI; amiodarone (Class III) is the second choice. Class IC must be avoided after MI as it increases mortality.
(b) Atrial flutter rate control: first reduce ventricular rate using Class II, Class IV, or digoxin; then convert to sinus rhythm using ibutilide or sotalol, or Class IA or IC.
(c) AVNRT: Class IV (verapamil or diltiazem) slows conduction in the AV node by blocking Ca²⁺ currents in Ca²⁺ current-dependent tissues; Class II also effective.
B(i) Class IA and IC prolong repolarisation (Class IA) or markedly slow conduction (Class IC); prolonged repolarisation increases the QT interval and creates conditions for an early after-depolarisation triggering torsades de pointes. Classes II and IV slow the heart rate: Class II blocks beta-adrenergic receptors reducing heart rate and conduction velocity; Class IV slows phase 4 spontaneous depolarisation in the SA node and slows AV node conduction; combining both classes produces additive bradycardia and they should not be combined.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the Vaughan Williams classification of antiarrhythmic drugs: for each class state the mechanism, the ion channel or receptor targeted, and the main cardiac action.
A(ii) State the safe choice of drug class for each of the following scenarios and give the anatomical/electrophysiological basis for your choice: (a) ventricular fibrillation after myocardial infarction; (b) atrial flutter requiring rate control; (c) AV nodal re-entry tachycardia.
B(i) Explain the anatomical basis of why Class IA and IC drugs may cause torsades de pointes, while Classes II and IV may cause bradycardia.

A 35-year-old woman presents with chronic diarrhoea with foul-smelling, fatty stools (steatorrhoea), significant weight loss, pallor, and generalised oedema. She also complains of bone pain and easy bruising. Laboratory results show: low haemoglobin, elevated INR, low serum albumin, low serum calcium, and the presence of fat globules in stool with reduced pancreatic elastase.
(i) What syndrome does this patient have, and what do the laboratory findings indicate about the severity and nutritional impact?
(ii) What investigations should be done to identify the site of the pathology, and what are the specific tests for each compartment?
(iii) List the differential pathologies that can produce this syndrome under each aetiological category.
(iv) What is the management principle, and what specific deficiencies must be replaced?
questions.answerText:
(i) Malabsorption syndrome — impaired absorption of one or more nutrients from the GIT.
Laboratory findings and their significance:
- Low haemoglobin → anaemia (may be due to iron, folic acid, or B12 deficiency).
- Elevated INR → vitamin K deficiency (impaired absorption causing bleeding tendency).
- Low serum albumin → impaired protein absorption/low plasma proteins causing oedema.
- Low serum calcium → vitamin D deficiency causing bone pain (rickets/osteomalacia spectrum) and risk of tetany.
- Fat globules in stool and reduced pancreatic elastase → evidence of steatorrhoea and defective luminal digestion (pancreatic insufficiency).
(ii) Investigations to identify the site:
- Document malabsorption: diarrhoea, weight loss, abnormal FBC, INR, presence of fat globules and pancreatic elastase in stool using ELISA; fat measurement from 5-day stool collection; D-xylose absorption test (excretion <2g in urine over 5 hours = abnormal) for carbohydrate; faecal nitrogen content for protein; vitamin B12 absorption.
- Identify mucosal site: jejunal biopsy (distal duodenal biopsy) for mucosal lesions.
- Identify structural causes: small bowel radiology (small bowel enema better than follow-through).
- Detect infection: aspiration of jejunal juice for G. lamblia and bacterial overgrowth; lactose breath test or mucosal enzyme assay for defective luminal digestion.
- Pancreatic lesion: imaging (USS, CT); EUS is the gold standard.
- Serum assays: calcium, albumin, iron, vitamin A, magnesium, vitamin B12, beta-carotene, cobalamin, folate.
(iii) Differential pathologies by aetiological category:
- Chronic pancreatic damage: alcohol excess, tropical pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis, obstructing carcinoma, gallstones, autoimmune, hypertriglyceridaemia.
- Chronic hepatobiliary disorders.
- Intestinal mucosal causes: coeliac disease, tropical sprue, Whipple's disease, parasites (giardiasis), drugs (cholestyramine), lactase deficiency, dermatitis herpetiformis.
- Intestinal structural causes: Crohn's disease, intestinal resection, bypass, stricture, diverticula, fistula, blind loop, post-irradiation, intestinal TB, amyloidosis, lymphoma, mesenteric arterial insufficiency.
- Motility disorders: systemic sclerosis, DM, thyrotoxicosis, carcinoid syndrome.
(iv) Management: treat the underlying condition; replace vitamins, iron, calcium, and trace elements; assess BMI and nutritional status.

questions.question:
A 24-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after a witnessed episode during which she suddenly lost consciousness, fell, cried out briefly, had stiffening of her whole body for about 20 seconds, then rhythmic jerking of all limbs for 40 seconds with cyanosis, tongue biting, and urinary incontinence. She was confused for 10 minutes afterwards and complained of headache and muscle pain.
(i) Name the seizure type and classify it according to the 1981 ILAE classification.
(ii) State the prodromal symptoms and describe the tonic phase, clonic phase, and post-ictal phase.
(iii) What is the significance of an aura preceding this type of seizure?
(iv) Describe the epileptogenesis: what neurotransmitters and ion channels are involved in seizure initiation and propagation?
(v) What is status epilepticus and what surgical treatments are available for refractory epilepsy?
questions.answerText:
(i) Generalised tonic-clonic seizure (GTCS). Under the 1981 ILAE classification it falls under: 2. Generalised seizures (convulsive or non-convulsive), subtype E — Tonic-clonic seizures.
(ii) Features: Prodromal period of vague ill-defined feeling and sometimes increasing myoclonic jerking. Tonic phase lasts 10–30 seconds. Clonic phase lasts 30–50 seconds with jerking, amplitude increasing and frequency slowing, cyanosis, apnoea, foaming, tongue biting, urinary incontinence, and autonomic features. Post-ictal phase of 1–10 minutes with confusion, drowsiness, sleep, headache, and muscle pain. Sudden onset and gradual recovery.
(iii) An aura preceding the seizure indicates partial onset; it means the GTCS is secondarily generalised from a focal onset, not primary generalised.
(iv) Epileptogenesis: Seizure initiation — high-frequency burst of action potentials from long-lasting depolarisation due to Ca⁺ influx and subsequent Na⁺ influx; hypersynchronisation of bursts from neurons. Excitatory neurotransmitter glutamate activates N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor; inhibitory transmitter GABA acts on GABA receptor. Absence seizure is due to T-type Ca²⁺ channel and K⁺ channel activation in thalamus. Propagation — increased extracellular K⁺, accumulation of Ca²⁺ in presynaptic terminals, activation of NMDA receptor, and structural changes in neuronal networks.
(v) Status epilepticus: prolonged seizures over 30 minutes or continuous repeated seizures without recovery of consciousness; only 5% of patients with epilepsy; usually occurs de novo in patients without epilepsy. Surgical options: temporal lobectomy, frontal lobectomy, lesionectomy, corpus callosotomy, hemispherectomy. Other treatments: vagal nerve stimulation, direct brain stimulation of the anterior thalamic nucleus, ketogenic diet.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old woman presents with a 2-month history of bilateral ptosis worse in the evenings, double vision, difficulty swallowing, and nasal regurgitation. She is referred for surgical thymectomy.
(i) What is the diagnosis and how does the Osserman classification help in management?
(ii) Compare myasthenia gravis with Lambert-Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome (LEMS) under the headings of pathogenesis, gender predilection, pattern of weakness, effect of activity, associated antibodies, DTRs, and therapy.
(iii) What are the indications and contraindications for thymectomy in MG and what outcomes are expected?
(iv) Describe the management of MG in pregnancy including the contraindication to specific drugs and the issue of neonatal MG.
(v) Describe the emerging therapies for MG.
questions.answerText:
(i) Myasthenia gravis. The Osserman classification helps categorise the severity and extent of disease — helping guide management decisions about the level of treatment intensity required including timing of thymectomy.
(ii) MG vs LEMS comparison: Pathogenesis — MG: reduced post-synaptic sensitivity (antibody-mediated AChR destruction); LEMS: reduced ACh vesicles (voltage-gated calcium channel antibodies). Gender — MG: females (2:1); LEMS: males (5:1). Pattern of weakness — MG: extraocular, facial, bulbar, skeletal; LEMS: proximal muscles. Effect of activity — MG: deterioration; LEMS: improvement. Other symptoms — MG: nil except autoimmune; LEMS: pain, muscle cramps, mouth dryness, autonomic symptoms. DTR — MG: preserved; LEMS: reduced/absent. Association — MG: thymic pathology; LEMS: malignancy (70%, carcinoma of lung). Therapy — MG: anticholinesterase; LEMS: 3,4-diaminopyridine. EMG — MG: decremental response; LEMS: incremental response. Antibody — MG: AChR; LEMS: VGCC.
(iii) Thymectomy indications and outcome: Appropriate in all patients with uncomplicated MG between puberty and 55 years. Elective surgery — not during acute deterioration. Remission rate approximately 35% if done in first 1–2 years after onset; another 50% improve to some extent. If restricted to ocular muscles for a year or longer, prognosis so good that thymectomy is unnecessary. Response is usually not evident for several months and is maximal by 3 years. In favourably responding cases, levels of circulating receptor antibody are reduced or disappear entirely. If possible, postpone until puberty (importance of gland in immune system development). Results not as predictable in patients with thymoma. A course of plasma exchange or immune globulin may be tried preceding the procedure.
(iv) Pregnancy in MG: usually uncomplicated. Some women may have difficulty with vaginal delivery. IV cholinesterase inhibitors are contraindicated because of the possibility of inducing uterine contractions. Cytotoxic drugs generally avoided because of potential for fetal abnormalities. Magnesium is not recommended for treatment of eclampsia because of its neuromuscular blocking effects. Breast-feeding is not thought to be a problem regarding transmission of AChR antibodies. Neonatal MG — mentioned as an associated condition.
(v) Emerging therapies: Mycophenolate mofetil 1 g twice daily for 6 months holds promise in refractory cases. Rituximab (200 mg/m² IV weekly for 4 weeks) — a chimeric mouse-human monoclonal antibody directed against CD20 protein. Potent immunoadsorbents for selective elimination of antibodies. Double filtration plasmapheresis (DFP) with KM 8800 membrane plasmapheresis monitor. Blockade of CD44-associated circulation mechanisms. Infliximab.

(i) This patient has Pancoast syndrome with Superior Vena Cava obstruction. Structures compressed/invaded: brachial plexus invasion results in associated neuralgic pains and right arm/shoulder pain; superior vena cava compression and direct invasion results in non-pulsatile neck veins, swollen face with bluish discoloration (cyanosis), and later reduced flow into right atrium. The mass is in the right upper lobe (pulmonary apex) — consistent with a Pancoast tumour. The stellate ganglion in a pulmonary apical tumour would cause Horner's syndrome (pin-point pupil, anhidrotic hemi-face, partial ptosis) — also possible here.
(ii) Local compressive and obstructive effects: (a) Over-grown lymph nodes compressing small hilar bronchus; or stellate ganglion squeezed in pulmonary apical tumour → Horner's syndrome (pin-point pupil, anhidrotic hemi-face, partial ptosis). (b) Pancoast syndrome — brachial plexus invasion with neuralgic pains, SVC compression and invasion → non-pulsatile neck veins, swollen face with bluish discoloration (cyanosis), reduced flow into right atrium. (c) Lymph node compression of small bronchi → bronchiectasis formation. (d) Intramural obstruction — intramural growth causes partial/complete blockage; blockage of main bronchus → total lung collapse; branch blockage → lobar or segmental collapse. (e) Over-grown vessels could necrose with release of air into consolidated tissue. (f) Space occupation by invasion — direct into tissues; via lymphatics → adenopathy; blood vessels → distant places.
(iii) Hormonal and non-metastatic (paraneoplastic) effects: ADH — anti-diuretic hormone → pan-dilution syndrome (hyponatraemia). ACTH (adeno-cortico-trophic hormone) excess. Parathyroid-like hormone → hypercalcaemia syndrome of polyuria, nocturia, constipation, lassitude, and even coma. Non-metastatic hormonal features are detectable in blood analysis. The malignant carcinoma also releases pyrogenic chemicals → poor appetite → weight loss.
(iv) Diagnostic approach: history of tobacco abuse directly or passively; clinical features of chronic cough with haemoptysis; sign of digital clubbing; local compression features; dyspnoea; features of bronchial collapse/consolidation; non-metastatic/hormonal features in blood analysis; sputum cytology electron microscopy; pleural aspirate examination; bronchoscopy with tissue biopsy and histology; chest X-ray; CAT scan/MRI — CT with PET is the most effective imaging modality.
(v) Treatment: relief of symptoms may involve cough suppression and relief of intractable cough via radiotherapy; pain relief may require pain experts. Following staging using TNM — TNM is essential for NSCLC — definitive surgery, chemotherapy, radiation combined and/or singly may be undertaken. Prognosis is poor; response to chemo and/or radiation depends on cell type. Immunotherapy is novel. Metastatic disease from or into the lungs may all have poor outcome. Tobacco abuse and radiation exposure should be avoided.
questions.question:
A 60-year-old woman is referred with a 2-month history of facial swelling, non-pulsatile dilated neck veins, and bluish discoloration of the face. She also reports right arm and shoulder pain. Chest CT shows a large right upper lobe mass with mediastinal involvement.
(i) Identify the syndrome and the specific structures being compressed or invaded.
(ii) Describe the full range of local compressive and obstructive effects that a bronchial carcinoma can produce, including effects on bronchi, blood vessels, and nerves.
(iii) State what hormonal and non-metastatic (paraneoplastic) effects can occur and what the clinical syndromes are.

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Borderline leprosy (BB — borderline).
Justification: numerous skin lesions (macules, papules, or plaques) varying in size, shape, and distribution; edges with streaming, irregular borders; annular lesions with broad, irregular edge and sharply defined punched-out centre are characteristic of BB; nerve damage is variable; it is the most unstable part of the spectrum. Patients may downgrade toward lepromatous or upgrade toward tuberculoid.

(ii) Risk factors and epidemiology:
- Endemic in developing countries: Asia, Africa, Latin America, Pacific
- Overcrowding, poor sanitation, poor nutrition
- Transmission: contact, respiratory route, handling/eating armadillos
- Incubation period: 6 months to 50 years
- HIV is NOT a risk factor
- Race: Africans tend toward tuberculoid form; LL more common in males (2:1)
- Children: tuberculoid form predominates

(iii) Complications:
Extremities: anaesthesia and myopathy; plantar ulceration; loss of distal digits; nerve palsies.
Nose: chronic nasal congestion; epistaxis; anosmia; destruction of nasal cartilage (saddle nose).
Ocular: blindness; lagophthalmos; corneal erosion; keratitis; iritis; iridocyclitis.
Systemic: nephrotic syndrome/CKD; testicular dysfunction; impotence/infertility; leprae reactions/Lucio phenomenon; stigmatization; amyloidosis; nerve abscess/sepsis.
Differential diagnoses: granuloma annulare, Kaposi sarcoma, nodulocystic acne, cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, neurofibromatosis, psoriasis (plaque), sarcoidosis, vitiligo, syphilis, tinea versicolor, xanthomas.

(iv) WHO MDT for Multibacillary (BB, BL, LL):
- Monthly rifampicin 600 mg: supervised
- Monthly clofazimine 300 mg: supervised
- Daily dapsone 100 mg + clofazimine 50 mg
- Duration: 24 months
Substitutions: minocycline 100 mg daily or ofloxacin 400 mg daily for clofazimine or rifampicin.
Management of Type 1 reaction: prednisolone starting 40-60 mg daily reducing to 40 mg after a few days then by 5 mg every 2-4 weeks; BT leprosy commonly needs 2-4 months, BL reactions may need 6 months; gabapentin 300 mg QID and amitriptyline 50-150 mg QID for neuropathic pain; splinting.
Management of Type 2 (ENL): high-dose steroids (80 mg daily, tapered rapidly) or thalidomide (400 mg daily; drug of choice for young men; teratogenic — phocomelia in first trimester); clofazimine 300 mg/day; chronic ENL with iritis or neuritis requires long-term suppression with thalidomide or clofazimine.
questions.question:
A 55-year-old male farmer presents with a 6-month history of scattered plaques and nodules on the trunk, limbs, and face. Examination reveals multiple skin lesions of varying size, shape, and distribution with irregular borders; some have annular punched-out centres. Sensation in the lesions is variable. Nerve function testing shows widespread nerve involvement.
(i) What is the diagnosis and where on the Ridley-Jopling spectrum does it fall?
(ii) State the risk factors and epidemiological factors.
(iii) Describe the complications and differential diagnoses.
(iv) Outline the WHO-recommended multidrug therapy and management of leprosy reactions.

Describe tumours of the respiratory tract under the following headings:
A(i) Classify benign tumours of the respiratory tract, including their percentage distribution.
A(ii) Describe the features specific to malignant bronchial carcinoma, including the mechanisms by which it causes symptoms and spreads.
B(i) Describe the epidemiology of malignant bronchial carcinoma including cell type distribution and aetiological factors.
B(ii) Explain the diagnostic approach and state all management options, including the role of staging.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Benign tumours (BT): can compress and push nearby tissues but there is no invasion, no tissue destruction, nor replacement, nor spread via lymphatics or haematology. Excessive growth of 'normal' tissue: <3 cm diameter is a nodule; >3 cm is a mass. Picked by CXRs and scans. More calcium, smoothly shaped with even colour. (1) Hamartomas — 55% of all BT; 80% in peripheral connective tissue; 8% of all lung tumours. Granulomas (sarcoid, TB, fungi) are classified with them. (2) Papilloma — tends to be pedunculated; squamous type in bronchial tree caused by Human Papilloma Virus (HPV), can transmute to cancer; glandular type more in main bronchus, left and right branches, trachea, and larynx in adults.
A(ii) Malignant bronchial carcinoma causes morbidity by space occupation, enhanced vascularity, and over-grown vascularity resulting in auto-necrosis bleeding (e.g., haemoptysis). Invasion — direct into tissues; via lymphatics to adenopathy and blood vessels to distant places. Release of pyrogenic chemicals causing poor appetite and weight loss. Hormones — ADH (pan-dilution syndrome); ACTH; parathyroid-like hormone (hypercalcaemia syndrome of polyuria, nocturia, constipation, lassitude, and even coma). Space occupation effects: over-grown lymph nodes compressing small hilar bronchus; or stellate ganglion squeezed in pulmonary apical tumour resulting in Horner's syndrome (pin-point pupil, anhidrotic hemi-face, partial ptosis); Pancoast syndrome (brachial plexus invasion with neuralgic pains, SVC compression and invasion — non-pulsatile neck veins, swollen face with bluish discoloration, reduced flow into right atrium); lymph node compression of small bronchi leads to bronchiectasis. Intramural obstruction — intramural growth causes partial/complete blockage; blockage of main bronchus can cause total lung collapse; branch blockage causes lobar or segmental collapse.
B(i) Epidemiology: rising incidence mirrors rising incidence of tobacco (cigarette smoking) — rise in 1940s–1980s with decline in 1985 to date; females' decline lags behind just as its rise; developing countries follow a similar pattern. Cell type distribution — NSCLC accounts for 80%: large cell 15%, small cell 20%, adenocarcinoma 30%, squamous 35%. Aetiology: cigarette smoking accounts for 90% of cases and correlates with quality and tar content; carcinogens from industrial pollution account for 5% of cases and reflect urban increase over rural; asbestos, beryllium, cadmium, and chromium are associated; metastasis from other cancers (e.g., renal — 'common balls', colonic) can also occur.
B(ii) Diagnosis: history of tobacco abuse directly or passively; clinical features of chronic cough with haemoptysis; sign of digital clubbing; local compression features; dyspnoea; features of bronchial collapse/consolidation; non-metastatic/hormonal features in blood analysis (ADH suppression causing pan-dilution syndrome; parathyroid-like hyperactivity; ACTH excess); sputum cytology electron microscopy; pleural aspirate exam; bronchoscopy with tissue biopsy and histology; chest X-ray; CAT scan/MRI — CT with PET is most effective. Management: relief of symptoms — cough suppression and relief of intractable cough via radiotherapy; pain relief may require pain experts. Following staging with TNM, definitive surgery, chemotherapy, radiation combined and/or singly may be undertaken — TNM is essential for NSCLC. Prognosis is poor; response to chemo and/or radiation depends on cell type. Immunotherapy is novel. Tobacco abuse and radiation exposure should be avoided.

A(i) History taking in dermatology:
- Symptoms
- Duration
- Evolution
- Associated factors: heat, cold, light, chemicals, pets, stress
- Recurrence
- Drug history/intervention
- Travel
- Past medical history
- Family history (infection, hereditary)
- Social history
- Occupation
- Review of systems
Additional history elements: when rash started and how long; course (episodic, previous rashes, continuous); site (where it started, whether it has spread locally or elsewhere); nature/description of rash.
Clinical principle: approximately 80% of dermatological diagnosis comes from history, 16% from examination, and 4% from investigations; the combined 96% from history and examination remains achievable in dermatology.

A(ii) Examination of the skin:
- Use natural light, preferable
- Good exposure of the patient
- Examine the presenting problem
- Examine other relevant areas, especially the mouth
- Relevant systemic examination
- Remember: systemic diseases have cutaneous manifestations

B(i) Primary and secondary skin lesions:
- Macule: area of discoloration
- Papule: raised solid lesion
- Nodule: solid raised lesion larger than 0.5 cm
- Plaque: solid, raised flat lesion
- Vesicle: raised, contains fluid less than 0.5 cm
- Bullae/blister: fluid-filled, larger than 0.5 cm
- Pustule: raised lesion containing pus
- Erythema: redness due to vasodilation
- Cyst: feels solid but contains fluid
- Crust: scabs from dried serum
- Scales: exfoliation of stratum corneum
- Fissure: crack or split in the epidermis
- Erosion: scratch marks
- Ulcer: total loss of epidermis
- Atrophy: loss of thickness of epidermis or dermis
- Lichenification: thickening of the epidermis
- Telangiectasia: dilated blood vessels

B(ii) Investigations:
- Skin scraping: for dermatophytes/fungi (microscopy, culture)
- Skin slit and smear: for organisms in leprosy; M/C/S to rule out secondary bacterial infection
- Skin swabs: M/C/S for secondary bacterial infection
- Skin snips: for organisms
- Skin biopsy: helpful in confirming diagnosis
- Skin tests: patch testing (for chronic eczemas and allergic contact dermatitis); prick test
- Scalp scraping for fungal studies
- Trichoscopy and trichogram: for hair disorders
- Hair pull test
- Hormone assays
- Distribution of lesions noted: seborrhoeic areas, flexure/extensor, photosensitive, exposed, symmetric, linear/annular/dermatomal

questions.answerText:
A(i) Traction alopecia:
- Caused by prolonged tension on the hair
- Common among African females due to peculiar hair-styling practices
- Implicated hair styles/practices: corn rows, tight braids, hair extensions, ponytails, dreadlocks, tight head gears, wigs, curlers (rollers)
- Pathognomonic sign: fringe sign
- Early traction alopecia is non-scarring (reversible); late traction alopecia is scarring (irreversible)

A(ii) Tinea capitis:
- Invasion of hair shafts by a dermatophyte fungus
- Common in school-age children; can occur in immunocompromised adults
- Causative organisms: Microsporum and Trichophyton spp: M. audouinii, T. schoenleinii, T. violaceum, M. canis, T. tonsurans, T. rubrum; can also affect the beard (tinea barbae)
- Clinical features: itching and presence of scales; inflammatory forms (e.g. kerion) can cause scarring alopecia

B(i) CCCA:
- A chronic and progressive disease with eventual spontaneous burn-out after years or decades
- Hair loss predominantly centred on crown/vertex, expanding in a roughly symmetric fashion; commonest in females
- Linked to caustic hair care products and/or hair styles causing traction (braids, weaves); current hypothesis: anatomical abnormality — premature desquamation of the inner root sheath (IRS) in genetically predisposed individuals
- Treatment: potent topical steroids; intralesional steroids; doxycycline; antifungal shampoos; minoxidil

Folliculitis decalvans:
- Presents with successive crops of pustules, crusts, or erosions leading to expansion of scarring alopecic patches
- Chronic staphylococcal infection thought to be contributory; Staphylococcus aureus can often be grown from pustular or crusted lesions
- Treatment: antibiotics (e.g. doxycycline); steroids

B(ii) Treatment of all scarring alopecias:
- DLE: potent topical steroids; antimalarials (hydroxychloroquine)
- Lichen planopilaris: potent topical steroids; antimalarials; retinoids (acitretin); minoxidil
- CCCA: potent topical steroids; intralesional steroids; doxycycline; antifungal shampoos; minoxidil
- Dissecting cellulitis of the scalp: antibiotics (doxycycline); steroids
- Acne keloidalis nuchae: antibiotics (doxycycline); steroids
Anatomical basis for poor prognosis: in scarring alopecia, the stem cells in the bulge region are permanently lost, resulting in irreversible destruction of the hair follicle. In non-scarring alopecia, stem cells are not affected so destruction is reversible. Hence prognosis is good for non-scarring alopecias and grave for scarring alopecias.
questions.question:
Describe traction alopecia and tinea capitis under the following headings, and explain the basis for the poor prognosis of scarring alopecias:
A(i) Define traction alopecia: cause, population at risk, implicated hair styles, and the pathognomonic sign.
A(ii) Describe tinea capitis: causative organisms, population at risk, and clinical features.
B(i) Describe CCCA and folliculitis decalvans: definition, clinical features, hypothesised cause, and treatment of each.
B(ii) Treatment principles for all scarring alopecias, and the anatomical basis for the poor prognosis of scarring compared to non-scarring alopecia.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Pathophysiology of heart failure:
Initial triggering mechanism: heart failure results from any condition that decreases the efficiency of the cardiac muscle either through damage or overloading.
Neuro-hormonal activation: long-term neuro-hormonal activation involves three systems: (1) the renin-angiotensin system (RAS); (2) arginine vasopressin (AVP); and (3) the sympathetic nervous system (SNS). These lead to increased workload.
Long-term structural consequence on the LV: fibrosis, dilation, and structural changes in the shape of the left ventricle from elliptical to spherical.
Failure of Frank-Starling law: long-term cardiac overload leads to reduced cardiac output from reduced contractility due to over-stretching with reduced cross-linking of actin and myosin filaments — failure of the Frank-Starling law of the heart.
A(ii) Framingham Criteria (100% sensitive, 78% specific): the simultaneous presence of at least two major criteria, OR one major criterion with two minor criteria.
Major criteria: cardiomegaly on chest X-ray; S3 gallop (third heart sound); acute pulmonary oedema; paroxysmal dyspnoea; rhonchi; central venous pressure >16 cmH2O at the right atrium; JV distension; positive abdominojugular reflux; weight loss.
Minor criteria (acceptable only if no other medical condition is responsible): tachycardia >120 beats per minute; nocturnal cough; breathlessness on exertion; pleural effusion; reduced vital capacity by one-third of maximum; hepatomegaly; bilateral ankle oedema.
B(i) High-output heart failure: occurs when the heart cannot maintain sufficient cardiac output to meet abnormally high peripheral demand, even though contractility may be initially normal. It occurs due to increased LV diastolic pressure with resultant pulmonary congestion in situations with abnormally high cardiac output. Three clinical conditions producing it: chronic severe anaemia (high output needed to compensate for reduced oxygen-carrying capacity), beriberi (vitamin B1/thiamine deficiency causing peripheral vasodilation), and hyperthyroidism (increased metabolic demand and heart rate). Other causes mentioned include cirrhosis, Paget's disease, multiple myeloma, and arteriovenous fistulae or malformations.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the pathophysiology of heart failure under the following headings: the initial triggering mechanism, the role of neuro-hormonal activation (naming the three systems involved), the long-term structural consequence on the LV, and the mechanism by which the Frank-Starling law ultimately fails.
A(ii) State the Framingham Criteria for the diagnosis of heart failure: list all major criteria and all minor criteria, and state the number of criteria required for diagnosis.
B(i) Explain the anatomical and physiological basis of why high-output heart failure occurs, naming three clinical conditions that produce it.

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Alopecia areata.
Specific pattern: Ophiasis pattern — band-like pattern of hair loss along the periphery of the temporal and occipital scalp. (Sisaipho, by contrast, spares the periphery of the temporal and occipital scalp.)

(ii) Risk factors and associations:
- Autoimmune disorder; associated with other autoimmune diseases
- Organ-specific autoimmune disease associations: rheumatoid arthritis, Type 1 DM, vitiligo
- Positive family history may point to alopecia areata
- The reticular variant is characterised by recurrent patchy disease

(iii) Complications:
- Can affect body hairs, axilla, beard, pubic hairs, eyebrows, and eyelashes
- Nail changes (in about 10% of cases; more in longstanding and extensive disease): uniform shallow pits (transverse/longitudinal), trachyonychia, onychomadesis, red or spotted lunula

(iv) Management:
- Spontaneous regression can occur, especially in young children with minimal area of affectation
- Potent topical steroids
- Intralesional steroids (triamcinolone)
- Short-term systemic steroids for rapidly evolving lesions
- Immunosuppressants: cyclosporine, azathioprine, MMF
- Prostaglandin analogs: latanoprost for eyelash areas
- Topical immunotherapy: diphencyprone (DPCP), squaric acid dibutyl ester (SADBE)
- Topical or oral photochemotherapy
- Janus kinase inhibitors: tofacitinib
questions.question:
A 16-year-old girl presents with patchy hair loss for 4 months. Examination reveals several round to oval patches of non-scarring hair loss on the scalp, with a band-like pattern of loss along the peripheral temporal and occipital scalp.
(i) What is the diagnosis and what specific pattern variant is described?
(ii) State the risk factors, associated conditions, and predisposing factors.
(iii) List all complications for this condition, including nail changes.
(iv) Outline the full management.

questions.answerText:
(i) Sarcoidosis. Classic syndrome: Löfgren's syndrome — characterised by a triad of erythema nodosum, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, and polyarthralgia (joint pain in multiple joints).
(ii) Pathophysiology: normally, immune cells are ready to spot and destroy foreign pathogens; in sarcoidosis, this process occurs over and over throughout the body without the presence of a specific pathogen — the immune system appears to be going haywire in the absence of a pathogen. Pathological changes: increased blood calcium level caused by excess Vitamin D produced by macrophages; increased level of angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) produced by T cells; elevated levels of T cells in the lungs on bronchoalveolar lavage. Characteristic pathological feature: non-caseating granuloma (confirmed by histology).
(iii) Staging based on chest radiograph: Stage 0 — no lung involvement; Stage I — bilateral lymphadenopathy (LAD); Stage II — LAD plus infiltrates; Stage III — parenchymal disease but no LAD; Stage IV — pulmonary fibrosis.
(iv) Investigations: Blood tests — raised serum ACE (used as screening test); hypercalcaemia (key finding); raised serum soluble interleukin-2 receptor; raised CRP; raised immunoglobulins. Imaging — chest radiograph; high-resolution CT (hilar lymphadenopathy). Histology — noncaseating granuloma; Langhans giant cells. Tests for other organ involvement: U&E for kidney; urine dipstick or urine albumin-creatinine ratio for nephritis; LFTs for liver; ECG and echocardiogram for heart; ultrasound abdomen for liver and kidney; ophthalmology review for eyes.
(v) Treatment: No treatment is first line in patients with no or mild symptoms as the condition often resolves spontaneously. Oral steroids are usually first line where treatment is required, given for 6–24 months; give bisphosphonates to protect against osteoporosis during long-term steroid use. Second-line options: methotrexate, azathioprine, or leflunomide. Newer biologic agents: rituximab, infliximab, golimumab, adalimumab. Lung transplant is rarely required in severe pulmonary disease.
questions.question:
A 35-year-old man presents with erythema nodosum on his shins, bilateral ankle joint pain, and is found on chest X-ray to have bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. He has no fever. His serum ACE level is elevated and serum calcium is high.
(i) What is the most likely diagnosis? State the triad that characterises the classic syndrome associated with these features.
(ii) Describe the pathophysiology of this condition including the role of immune cells, the pathological changes, and the reason for elevated ACE and hypercalcaemia.
(iii) Describe the staging system used for this condition based on chest radiograph findings.
(iv) What investigations are required for this condition, including blood tests, imaging, and tests for other organ involvement?

A(i) Define cardiac arrest and sudden cardiac death (SCD). Describe the four cardiac arrest rhythms under the headings: rhythm name, ECG characteristics, and whether each is shockable.
A(ii) Explain the clinical basis of why ventricular fibrillation (VF) is the commonest initial rhythm in adult cardiac arrest and why the interval from collapse to defibrillation is the most important determinant of survival.
B(i) Distinguish between basic life support (BLS) and advanced cardiac life support under the headings: definition, key interventions, and personnel/setting.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Definitions:
Cardiac arrest: an abrupt cessation of cardiac pump function, which may be reversible but will lead to death in the absence of prompt intervention; it is very rare for it to reverse spontaneously.
Sudden cardiac death (SCD): natural death from cardiac causes, heralded by abrupt loss of consciousness within 1 hour of the onset of acute symptoms.
Four cardiac arrest rhythms:
• Ventricular fibrillation (VF): bizarre irregular waveform; no recognisable QRS complexes; random frequency and amplitude; uncoordinated electrical activity; may be coarse or fine. Shockable.
• Pulseless ventricular tachycardia (pulseless VT): monomorphic VT — broad complex rhythm, rapid rate, constant QRS morphology; polymorphic VT (torsade de pointes). Shockable.
• Asystole: no electrical activity (flat line). Not shockable.
• Pulseless Electrical Activity (PEA): organised electrical activity without a palpable pulse. Not shockable.
A(ii) VF is the commonest initial rhythm in adult cardiac arrest because most cardiac arrests in adults result from acute coronary syndrome/CAD, which creates an electrically unstable myocardium prone to re-entry ventricular arrhythmias. VF consumes energy rapidly and converts to asystole within a few minutes. Electrical defibrillation is the most important treatment for VF. The probability of survival decreases with time — for every minute of delay the survival rate drops 7–10%; neurological survival is possible only within 6–10 minutes of defibrillation. BLS + defibrillation together achieve a survival rate of 49%.
B(i) Distinguishing BLS from advanced cardiac life support:
• Definition: BLS is defined by the first 3 links in the chain of survival (early access, early CPR, early defibrillation) with emphasis on resuscitation at the scene. Advanced life support involves use of medications, advanced airway management, and specialised monitoring.
• Key interventions in BLS: prompt recognition of cardiac arrest; high-quality chest compressions at 100–120/min; rescue breathing (30 compressions: 2 breaths in 1-rescuer CPR); early defibrillation with AED; airway opening (head-tilt chin-lift or jaw thrust). In advanced life support: IV drug therapy, endotracheal intubation, cardiac monitoring, post-resuscitation care.
• Personnel/setting: BLS is performed by lay rescuers and healthcare providers, both in-hospital and out-of-hospital; advanced life support is performed by professionally trained EMS providers or hospital resuscitation teams.

(i) Diagnosis: Pulmonary embolism. The Wells score of 7.5 indicates High clinical probability (>7). Wells Prediction Rule: Low 0–1; Intermediate 2–6; High >7. This patient scores: previous surgery or immobilization within last 30 days (+1.5) and alternative diagnosis less likely than PE (+3), tachycardia (heart rate >100 bpm, +1.5), plus clinical signs summing to >7.
(ii) Acquired risk factors: Age >40 years; recent surgery (high risk: orthopaedic, head and neck, thoracic — applicable to this patient post-hip replacement); prolonged immobility (applicable); cancer; female sex; pregnancy (hypercoagulable state); polycythaemia; obesity; trauma; previous deep venous thrombosis; nephrotic syndrome; lupus anticoagulant; antiphospholipid syndrome; connective tissue disease; idiopathic. Genetic risk factors: protein C deficiency; protein S deficiency; factor V Leiden; hyperhomocysteinaemia; antithrombin deficiency. Applicable to this patient: recent hip surgery (high-risk orthopaedic surgery) and prolonged immobility.
(iii) Haemodynamic pathophysiology of massive PE: Massive pulmonary embolism is defined as thrombus occluding more than 50% of the pulmonary vasculature. A systolic blood pressure <90 mmHg or a drop in systolic blood pressure of 40 mmHg from baseline for >15 minutes (not explained by hypovolemia, sepsis, or new arrhythmia). Sequence: RV pressure increase; RV dilatation and hypokinesia; RV dysfunction; tricuspid regurgitation and RV failure; RV overload causing bowing of the septum with impaired filling, systemic hypotension, and cardiac arrest. RV overload causes elevations of both pro-B-type natriuretic peptide and B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP). In 20% of cases the initial presentation is sudden death.
(iv) Investigations: D-dimer assay; Chest X-ray — atelectasis, infiltrates, pleural effusion, focal oligaemia (Westermark's sign), pleural-based area of opacity (Hampton's hump); ECG — sinus tachycardia, S1Q3T3 pattern, right ventricular strain; Venous Compression USS; Ventilation perfusion scanning; Chest CT Angiogram. Venous thromboembolism is a dynamic process resulting from interaction between acquired and genetic risks per Virchow's triad of stasis, injury to the intima, and hypercoagulability.
(v) Treatment: Initial management — basic life support: airway management (patent and clear), oxygen (high dose), IV fluid (circulation). Medical: anticoagulation (e.g., heparin, enoxaparin); thrombolytic therapy (e.g., streptokinase, alteplase). Surgical: inferior vena caval filters; embolectomy. Low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) is safe and is the choice. Attention should be paid to risk stratification. PE could be fatal if not detected — majority are diagnosed at autopsy. Prompt initial management may make the difference.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Asthma is derived from the Greek word 'aazein' meaning 'to labor in breathing.' Asthma is a chronic inflammatory disorder of the airways in which many cells and cellular elements play a role, in particular mast cells, eosinophils, T lymphocytes, neutrophils, and epithelial cells. In susceptible individuals, this inflammation causes recurrent episodes of wheezing, breathlessness, chest tightness, and cough, particularly at night and in the early morning. These episodes are usually associated with widespread but variable airflow obstruction that is often reversible either spontaneously or with treatment. Asthma is also characterized by airway inflammation and airway hyperresponsiveness. Cardinal symptoms: Wheeze — a harsh, rasping lung sound associated with infection, generally high-pitched, sometimes described as 'musical' sounds; Cough; Breathlessness; Chest tightness.
A(ii) Intermittent: Symptoms disappear for long periods; when they return, they may occur less than once a week; periods of attacks last only a few hours or a few days; when there are nocturnal symptoms, they occur less than twice a month. Mild Persistent: Symptoms occur less than once a day; nocturnal symptoms occur more than twice a month. Moderate Persistent: Symptoms occur daily; attacks affect activity and sleep patterns more than once a week. Severe Persistent: Symptoms are continuous with frequent attacks, limiting physical activity, and often occurring at night. Persistent: Symptoms never disappear for more than one week.
B(i) The basis for diagnosing asthma per GINA includes: a history of characteristic symptom patterns; evidence of variable airflow limitation from bronchodilator reversibility testing or other tests; asthma is usually characterized by airway inflammation and airway hyperresponsiveness, but these are not necessary or sufficient to make the diagnosis.
B(ii) Susceptible genes (ADAM33, FCER1B, TNF, ACE, B2-AR, IL-4R, IL-13) plus early life environment promote a TH2 subtype of CD4 response. The early life environment and susceptible genes drive the immune response toward TH2 rather than TH1. Atopic patients have a high prevalence of asthma, allergic rhinitis, urticaria, and eczema because of this TH2 skew. Factors that decrease prevalence and promote TH1 include farm environment in first year of life, presence of older siblings, early attendance of day-care during first 6 months of life, tuberculosis, and viral infections. Factors that increase prevalence include parental history of asthma or atopy, maternal smoking in pregnancy, sensitization to allergens (dust mite), widespread use of antibiotics, and western diet.

questions.answerText:
(i) Sarcoidosis. Characteristic pathological feature on histology: non-caseating granuloma (also Langhans giant cells identified on histology). Diagnosis relies on presence of noncaseating granuloma on histopathological examination, compatible clinical presentation, and exclusion of other causes of granulomatous inflammation.
(ii) Pulmonary manifestations (affecting over 90%): mediastinal lymphadenopathy; pulmonary fibrosis; pulmonary nodules; ground glass opacification; increased reticulation. Cardiac manifestations (affecting 5%): bundle branch block; heart block; myocardial muscle involvement.
(iii) Pathophysiology: sarcoidosis is an immunological disorder resulting in lots of small nodules forming throughout the body; immune system goes haywire in the absence of a specific pathogen; process occurs over and over without a specific pathogen. Elevated ACE: T cells produce angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE); hence raised serum ACE is a key finding and often used as a screening test. Elevated calcium (hypercalcaemia): macrophages produce excess Vitamin D, which leads to increased blood calcium level.
(iv) Investigations: blood tests — raised serum ACE; hypercalcaemia; raised serum soluble interleukin-2 receptor; raised CRP; raised immunoglobulins; HRCT chest; chest radiograph (staging). Histology — noncaseating granuloma; Langhans giant cells; caseating vs non-caseating granuloma distinction. Tests for cardiac involvement: ECG (confirms heart block); echocardiogram. Bronchoalveolar lavage — elevated levels of T cells in lungs.
(v) Differential diagnosis of granulomatous lung disease: Infectious conditions — tuberculosis; atypical mycobacterial infections; invasive fungal infections (histoplasmosis, aspergillosis, blastomycosis, Pneumocystis jirovecii). Hypersensitivity pneumonitis; pneumoconiosis; drug-induced hypersensitivity pneumonitis. Foreign body granulomatosis. Vasculitides — granulomatosis with polyangiitis; eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Churg-Strauss syndrome); pulmonary lymphomatoid granulomatosis.

A(i) Hair biology:
Types of hair: terminal hair; intermediate hair; vellus hair; lanugo.
About 90% of scalp hair are in anagen; 10% in telogen. Duration: anagen 3-5 years; telogen 3 months; catagen 10 days.
The hair follicle cycle is influenced by: genetics, hormones, drugs, inflammation, micronutrients.

A(ii) Functions of the hair:
- Social and sexual communication
- Protection against chemical and physical damage
- Protection against insects
- Provide sensory 'antennae'
- Insulation against heat loss, overheating, and desiccation
- Removal from the skin surface of parasites, dirt, debris, and squames by the outward-moving hair shaft
- Facilitation of sebum, apocrine sweat, and pheromone secretion
- Organ of scavenging and excretion via the melanised hair shaft, which serves to deposit and extradite unwanted molecules

B(i) Evaluation of patient with hair loss:
- Direct clinical history toward establishing the diagnosis and detecting precipitating factors
Key questions:
- Is there increased hair shedding (telogen effluvium) or reduction in hair density with visible balding or both?
- Is hair coming out by the roots (telogen effluvium), breaking near the scalp (alopecia areata, anagen effluvium), or breaking near the ends (hair shaft abnormalities)?
- Duration: <3 months = acute TE; >6 months = chronic TE
- In acute TE: search for triggers 2-3 months prior to onset
- In chronic TE: consider hypo/hyperthyroidism, drugs, chronic illnesses, exposures
Pattern assessment: patchy (alopecia areata, tinea capitis, lichen planus) vs diffuse (acute/postpartum TE, anagen effluvium, diffuse alopecia areata) vs patterned (androgenetic alopecia, frontal fibrosing alopecia, CCCA).
Associated symptoms: pain (pustules); diffuse pain and pruritus (cicatricial alopecia); dandruff (seborrhoeic dermatitis, psoriasis, tinea capitis); altered or crawling sensations (trichotillomania).
Identify associated comorbidities: autoimmune diseases in alopecia areata; hyperandrogenism (hirsutism, acne, irregular menses).
Summary evaluation axes: hair breakage vs shedding; congenital vs acquired; diffuse vs patchy; scarring vs non-scarring; family history; possible triggers; associated symptoms.
Investigations: hair pull test; trichoscopy; trichogram; scalp scraping for fungal studies; scalp biopsy; hormone assays; other specific investigations.
