A 19-year-old male presents with progressively worsening nodular, cystic, suppurating lesions on the face, chest, and back, with extensive scarring. He has been tried on topical treatments with no improvement.
(i) What is the severity grade of this acne and what clinical term is used to describe this presentation?
(ii) List the acneiform variants and special types of acne.
(iii) State the histological features of acne.
(iv) Outline the full systemic treatment for this severity of acne, including isotretinoin dosing, mechanism, and important side effects.
questions.answerText:
(i) Severity: the most severe form — Acne conglobata/nodulocystic acne: suppurating cystic lesions predominate and severe scarring results.

(ii) Acneiform variants and special types:
- Acne cosmetica: closed comedones and papulopustules on chin and cheeks due to comedogenic cosmetics; may take months to clear after stopping cosmetic product
- Acne venenata: contact with acnegenic chemicals (chlorinated hydrocarbons, petroleum oil, coal tar, radiation therapy)
- Acne detergicans: closed comedones from comedogenic soaps
- Acne aestivalis (Mallorca acne): rare, females 25-40 years, small papules on cheeks/neck/upper body; starts in spring, resolves by fall; comedones and pustules sparse or absent
- Excoriated acne (picker's acne): girls; minute or trivial primary lesions made worse by squeezing; crusts, scarring, and atrophy
- Acneiform eruptions: from industrial chemicals (chlorinated hydrocarbons, oils, coal tar) or drugs (iodides, bromides, lithium, steroids); not confined to usual sites of acne vulgaris
- SAPHO syndrome: synovitis, acne, pustulosis, hyperostosis, and osteomyelitis; chest wall is the most common site of musculoskeletal complaints
- Neonatal acne: first four weeks of life; facial papules or pustules
- Infantile acne: cases that persist beyond 4 weeks or have onset after
- Premenstrual acne: papulopustular lesions one week prior; estrogen-dominant contraceptive pills will diminish
- Steroid acne; drug-induced acne (iodides, bromides, lithium, steroids — oral medications)

(iii) Histological features:
- Perifollicular inflammation around comedones
- Exudate of lymphocytes and PMNs (polymorphonuclear leucocytes)
- Plasma cells, giant cells, and proliferation of fibroblasts
- Large cysts and epithelium-lined sinus tracts

(iv) Systemic treatment for severe acne:
Systemic antibiotics: first-line tetracycline; second-line erythromycin, doxycycline, minocycline (can cause SLE); trimethoprim increasingly used.
Hormonal: cyproterone acetate 2 mg with ethinyl estradiol 35 mg daily; spironolactone 25-300 mg/day (antiandrogenic); steroids for severe inflammatory acne.
Isotretinoin:
- Dose: 0.5-1 mg/kg/day once or twice daily for 15-20 weeks
- Mechanism: reduces sebum production, comedogenesis, P. acnes, keratinization
- Outcome: leads to remission lasting months to years
- Important side effect: teratogenic

(i) This patient most likely has nephrotic syndrome. Confirming features: frothy urine (commonly due to proteinuria); 4+ proteinuria; very low serum albumin (hypoalbuminaemia); elevated cholesterol (hyperlipidaemia); bilateral leg swelling and facial puffiness (oedema — facial and dependent). Oedema in nephrotic syndrome and chronic kidney disease is listed. Massive lipiduria can also be seen in nephrotic syndrome.
(ii) Primary renal causes (idiopathic, immune complex mediated): minimal change disease; focal segmental glomerulosclerosis; membranous nephropathy; mesangial proliferative glomerulonephritis; crescentic glomerulonephritis. Secondary — systemic causes: auto-immune (SLE, scleroderma, Sjögren syndrome, celiac disease); infections/infestations — bacteria (Strep., Staph., Pneum., Meningo., Syphilis, Leptospirosis, mycoplasma, leprosy, endocarditis), viral (HBv, HCv, HIV, Influenza A&B, EBV, CMV, mumps, measles, adenovirus, cryoglobulinaemia type II), protozoa (malaria, toxoplasma), helminths (schistosomiasis, filariasis); multisystemic diseases (hypertension, diabetes mellitus, thrombotic microangiopathies, SLE, Henoch-Schönlein, Goodpasture, Wegener's, sickle cell disease/polycythaemia, radiation nephritis, paraprotein deposition diseases); malignancies (lymphomas, leukaemias, carcinomas); drugs (penicillamine, hydralazine, allopurinol, rifampicin); inherited disorders (Alport's syndrome).
(iii) Pathogenesis involves complex interplay between cellular immunity, humoral immunity, complement system/cascade, coagulation cascade, and soluble factors. Immune mechanisms: antibody-mediated injury (in-situ immune complex deposition; circulating immune complex deposition with endogenous or exogenous antigens); cytotoxic antibodies; cell-mediated immune injury; activation of alternate complement pathway. The type of glomerular injury depends on the initial immune response, extent to which it is perpetuated, and extent to which inflammation resolves without scarring or proceeds by rapid necrosis or progressive glomerulosclerosis and tubulointerstitial fibrosis. Circulating immune complexes persist due to persistent antigenaemia or defective immune complex binding; they deposit via Fc receptors on mesangial cells or passive deposition in mesangium or sub-endothelial space. Local immune complex formation (in situ). Soluble factors — cytokines, chemokines, growth factors, vasoactive mediators, reactive oxygen species, proteases, proteins in the coagulation cascade — promote recruitment and activation of inflammatory cells, activate resident glomerular cells, directly cause tissue injury, and stimulate production of matrix proteins (basis of scarring).
(iv) Investigations: General — CBC (normochromic normocytic anaemia); hyperlipidaemia/hypoalbuminaemia in nephrotic syndrome; rule out secondary causes (viral screens, ANA, ANCA, cryoglobulins, urine and serum protein electrophoresis, ACR). Blood — blood glucose; urea and creatinine (increased); GFR (reduced); complement profile (reduced C3 and C4). Urinalysis — urine sediment microscopy (nephritic/active or nephrotic); massive lipiduria in nephrotic syndrome. Renal ultrasound scan. Renal biopsy/histology — the gold standard for diagnosis; candidates for biopsy include patients with individual or family history of renal disease and atypical presentation including massive proteinuria, nephrotic syndrome, or rapid rise in creatinine without resolution.
(v) The five major glomerular syndromes: (1) Asymptomatic haematuria and proteinuria; (2) Acute nephritic syndrome — onset over days or weeks, acute renal failure, haematuria, proteinuria <3.5 g/24 hrs, oedema, hypertension; (3) Nephrotic syndrome — massive proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, hyperlipidaemia, oedema; (4) Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis — renal failure over days, weeks, or months, crescentic GN histologically; (5) Chronic renal failure / chronic glomerulonephritis — persistent proteinuria with or without haematuria, progressive renal insufficiency; a common cause of CKD worldwide. Who presents with what is not specific — syndromes can overlap and progress from one to another.

(i) Most likely underlying diagnosis: Rheumatic Heart Disease following Acute Rheumatic Fever. The mitral valve is the most commonly affected, involved in 90% of cases of RHD; mitral regurgitation is the most commonly found in children and adolescents, while mitral stenosis represents longer-term chronic disease commonly in adults.
(ii) Pathognomonic lesion: Aschoff nodules. Histological composition: multi-nucleated giant cell surrounded by macrophages and T-lymphocytes; seen in the subacute or chronic stage of the disease; fibrin degeneration in the collagen of connective tissues also occurs.
(iii) Natural history of mitral regurgitation: compensatory phase lasts 10–15 years; patients with asymptomatic severe MR have a 5%/year mortality rate; once the patient's EF drops below 60% and/or the patient becomes symptomatic, mortality rises sharply; mortality results from progressive dyspnoea and heart failure.
(iv) Indications for surgery in chronic MR: any symptoms at rest or exercise (repair if feasible); asymptomatic patients if EF drops below 60%, or if new onset atrial fibrillation develops.
(v) Myxomatous degeneration (mitral valve prolapse) is a congenital/degenerative cause of chronic MR. It differs from rheumatic MR in that it is not preceded by streptococcal pharyngitis or acute rheumatic fever; it does not produce Aschoff nodules; and it results from myxomatous changes in the valve leaflets rather than immune-mediated carditis, fusion of commissures, or shortening of chordae tendinae as seen in rheumatic disease.

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Post-streptococcal acute glomerulonephritis. The common prototype of AGN is post-streptococcal GN, caused by nephritogenic strains of Group A, beta-haemolytic Streptococcus. These organisms cause several clinical problems including pharyngitis, impetigo, erysipelas, and scarlet fever. The incubation period is 10–14 days. Confirming features: onset 12 days after sore throat (fits incubation period of 10–14 days); tea-coloured urine (overt haematuria giving red or smoky urine); headache, nausea, anorexia; hypervolaemia, oedema, and hypertension; elevated serum creatinine; low C3 levels (C3 levels and CH50 are decreased in 90% of cases).
(ii) Pathophysiology: AGN is characterised by onset (over days or weeks) of acute renal failure due to obstruction of the glomerular capillary lumen by infiltrating inflammatory cells and proliferating resident glomerular cells. There is also intrarenal vasoconstriction and mesangial cell contraction due to local cytokines. Extracellular fluid volume expansion, oedema, and hypertension develop because of impaired GFR and enhanced tubular reabsorption of salt and water. Urinalysis typically shows RBCs and RBC casts, dysmorphic RBCs, WBCs, and proteinuria less than nephrotic range (<3.5 g/24 hrs). Histologically, there is proliferation of endothelium or mesangium. Most severe form — acute diffuse proliferative GN — involves >50% of glomerular cells. When <50% of cells involved, it is acute focal proliferative GN. Milder forms with mesangial cell proliferation are called acute mesangio-proliferative GN. Most forms of GN result from immunologic injury — autoimmune damage due to loss of tolerance of shared antigen or molecular mimicry with both humoral and cellular components, triggering release of cytokines and inflammatory mediators.
(iii) Investigations: Serum creatinine is elevated; C3 levels and CH50 are decreased in 90% of cases; most patients have a high anti-streptolysin O titre, anti-deoxyribonuclease B (anti-DNase B), anti-streptokinase, and antibodies against other streptococcal exoenzymes. Diagnosis is usually on clinical and serological grounds and biopsy is usually not needed. Renal biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosis when needed; specimen is subjected to light microscopy, electron microscopy, and immunofluorescence microscopy. Immunofluorescence shows three patterns: granular deposits of immunoglobulins (immune complex disease — C3 low, anti-GBM negative, ANCA negative); linear deposits of Ig on GBM (anti-GBM GN — C3 normal, anti-GBM positive, ANCA negative); few or no Ig (pauci-immune GN — C3 normal, anti-GBM negative, ANCA positive).
(iv) The five major clinical presentations of glomerular injury: (1) Acute glomerulonephritis (acute nephritic syndrome); (2) Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN) — renal failure develops more rapidly over days, weeks, or months; histology shows crescent formation (crescentic GN); (3) Nephrotic syndrome; (4) Asymptomatic urinary abnormalities; (5) Chronic glomerulonephritis — characterised by persistent proteinuria with or without haematuria, and progressive renal insufficiency; a common cause of CKD worldwide.
(v) Treatment and prognosis: It is an acute illness with spontaneous recovery in most cases. Irreversible renal damage occurs in less than 1% of children and a slightly higher percentage of adults. Treatment with steroids and cytotoxic drugs has not been shown to be beneficial even in the crescentic type — treatment is therefore supportive. Recovery is usually complete but some will eventually develop hypertension. In anti-GBM disease, treatment should be started early with glucocorticoids, cyclophosphamide, and plasmapheresis — plasmapheresis is continued daily until anti-GBM antibodies are not detectable. In ESRD, dialysis and transplantation are needed. In pauci-immune GN, most cases are treated aggressively with glucocorticoids with or without cyclophosphamide, azathioprine, or cyclosporine.

questions.question: The MOST important nursing instruction for a patient prescribed topical antibiotic eye drops for bacterial conjunctivitis is to:
questions.explanation: Patients must be instructed to complete the full prescribed course of antibiotic eye drops, typically five to seven days for bacterial conjunctivitis, even if symptoms resolve earlier. Stopping antibiotics prematurely promotes the development of antibiotic resistance and risks recurrence of the infection. Sharing medications between individuals is contraindicated due to the risk of cross-contamination and inappropriate treatment of potentially different conditions.

options: It is a reversible sign that resolves spontaneously with rest
It represents a benign sequelae of well-controlled chronic hypertension

questions.explanation: Optic disc edema (papilledema) in the context of severely elevated blood pressure can be indicative of impending stroke and possible death from malignant hypertension, representing a true medical emergency. The nurse explains to a glaucoma patient that their drops may cause eyelash growth. This side effect is MOST associated with which drug class?
options: Alpha-2 agonist drops such as brimonidine reducing aqueous secretion
Cholinergic miotic drops such as pilocarpine improving trabecular outflow
Prostaglandin analogue eye drops such as latanoprost or bimatoprost
Carbonic anhydrase inhibitor drops such as dorzolamide or brinzolamide
Beta-blocker eye drops such as timolol reducing aqueous production
questions.explanation: Eyelash growth (hypertrichosis) and changes in eyelash color and length are characteristic side effects of prostaglandin analogue eye drops such as latanoprost (Xalatan), bimatoprost (Lumigan), and travoprost. These drugs also cause darkening of the iris and periocular skin in some patients, which is important to discuss with patients before starting treatment. Prostaglandin analogues are among the most effective and commonly used first-line glaucoma medications due to their once-daily dosing and excellent IOP-lowering efficacy.

This philosophy underpins holistic ophthalmic nursing care that extends beyond simply carrying out tasks for the patient. It distinguishes nursing's supportive, educative role from a purely task- or order-based approach.

Focus exclusively on administering prescribed medications
Perform every procedure the patient physically requires
Assist the patient toward independence in daily activities
Replace the physician's diagnostic decision-making entirely
questions.question: An ophthalmic nurse is planning care for a newly admitted patient. According to Virginia Henderson's nursing philosophy, the nurse's primary role is to:

questions.explanation: An atrophic pterygium is characterized by being thin and attenuated with poor vascularity and a stationary, non-progressing nature. In contrast, a progressive pterygium is thick, fleshy, vascular, and actively advancing toward the center of the cornea. This distinction is clinically important because progressive pterygium often requires surgical intervention while atrophic forms may be managed conservatively with observation.
options: Primary pterygium affecting the temporal corneal quadrant
Progressive pterygium with active vascular invasion
questions.question: Which classification describes a pterygium that is thin, attenuated, with poor vascularity and is non-progressing?

options: Examine the retina and optic nerve for HIV-related opportunistic changes
Measure aqueous humor viral load using dilated pupil techniques
Assess the anterior segment for Kaposi Sarcoma lesion distribution
Measure the intraocular pressure in patients on antiretroviral therapy
Evaluate corneal clarity and endothelial cell density in AIDS
questions.question: The dilated fundus examination in HIV/AIDS patients is PRIMARILY performed to:
questions.explanation: The dilated fundus examination involves widening the pupils with eye drops to allow the ophthalmologist to examine the retina, optic nerve, and blood vessels at the back of the eye for HIV-related opportunistic infections such as CMV retinitis, toxoplasma retinochoroiditis, and VZV retinitis. This examination is a critical component of the regular ophthalmological monitoring recommended for HIV/AIDS patients, allowing early detection and treatment of retinal disease before irreversible vision loss occurs.

Following pterygium surgery, post-operative eye drops are prescribed at approximately four times daily for a period of four to eight weeks after surgery. A patch is placed on the eye overnight, and painkillers are recommended for the first one to two days as the eye may be quite uncomfortable. The eye may appear red for up to a month and there may be mild swelling during the healing period.
options: One to two years with gradual tapering
One to three days after the procedure
Four to eight weeks after surgery
questions.question: Following pterygium surgery, post-operative eye drops are typically prescribed for a duration of:

questions.explanation: Monitoring for signs of infection such as increased redness, swelling, or discharge is the priority post-operative nursing action following conjunctival cyst excision. Post-operative infection is a potential complication that requires prompt identification and treatment with antibiotic eye drops or ointments. Other key nursing actions include instructing the patient on proper wound care, administering prescribed medications, and educating on signs of complications such as excessive pain or vision changes.
options: Monitoring for signs of infection such as increased redness or discharge
Administering topical mydriatics to maintain pupil dilation
Encouraging vigorous eye rubbing to promote healing
Applying hot compresses every hour for the first 48 hours
Restricting all light exposure to prevent photophobia permanently
questions.question: Post-operative nursing care for a patient who underwent conjunctival cyst excision includes which PRIORITY action?

options: Spontaneous correction of myopia from immune-related refractive change
Bilateral presbyopia from accelerated lens aging in HIV patients
Optic neuropathy and neuro-ophthalmic complications from CNS involvement
Development of bilateral corneal ectasia from HIV-related collagen loss
Bilateral refractive error progression from retinal stretching
questions.explanation: HIV/AIDS can cause neuro-ophthalmic manifestations through direct CNS involvement, including optic neuropathy (from cryptococcal meningitis, CMV, or direct HIV optic nerve infection), cranial nerve palsies causing diplopia, and other visual pathway disorders. These neuro-ophthalmic complications reflect the CNS tropism of HIV and opportunistic organisms that affect the brain and visual pathways. Recognition of these manifestations requires careful ophthalmic assessment integrated with neurological evaluation.
questions.question: Neuro-ophthalmic manifestations of HIV/AIDS can include which of the following?

questions.explanation: Smoking raises the risk of developing Thyroid Eye Disease by seven to eight times and makes the active inflammatory phase of TED longer and more severe. Additionally, smoking decreases the effectiveness of treatment for thyroid eye disease. Smoking cessation is therefore the most important lifestyle modification that an ophthalmic nurse can recommend to patients with TED, as it significantly reduces disease severity, duration, and treatment resistance.
options: Causing direct toxic damage to the thyroid gland causing hypothyroidism
Reducing thyroid antibody titers and worsening autoimmune activity
Raising the risk of TED by seven to eight times and worsening the course
Stimulating orbital fibroblast regeneration causing faster disease resolution
Causing direct retinal vascular toxicity independent of TED activity
questions.question: Smoking affects Thyroid Eye Disease MOST significantly by:

options: Noninfectious conjunctivitis associated with systemic conditions
Bacterial conjunctivitis with purulent gonococcal discharge
Chemical conjunctivitis from industrial solvent exposure
Viral conjunctivitis caused by adenoviral respiratory infection
Allergic conjunctivitis caused by airborne allergen exposure
questions.explanation: Conjunctivitis can be associated with several systemic conditions, including Stevens-Johnson syndrome, keratoconjunctivitis sicca, nutritional deprivation, congenital metabolic syndromes, and immune-related disorders such as Reiter syndrome. These represent noninfectious causes of conjunctivitis arising from systemic pathology rather than a direct microbial infection. Recognizing these associations guides the nurse to consider a systemic workup in patients with atypical or recurrent conjunctivitis.
questions.question: Stevens-Johnson syndrome is associated with which type of conjunctivitis?

options: Allergic conjunctivitis triggered by seasonal environmental allergens
Autoimmune-related noninfectious conjunctivitis associated with systemic disease
Bacterial conjunctivitis from Staphylococcus aureus colonization
Chemical conjunctivitis from environmental irritant exposure
Viral conjunctivitis caused by adenovirus type 8 serotype
questions.explanation: Reiter syndrome is an autoimmune or immune-related disorder that can cause conjunctivitis as part of its systemic manifestation, making it a noninfectious cause of conjunctivitis associated with systemic disease. Other systemic conditions that cause conjunctivitis include Stevens-Johnson syndrome, keratoconjunctivitis sicca, vitamin A deficiency, and porphyria. Recognizing these associations is important for appropriate referral and holistic patient management.
questions.question: A nurse suspects that a patient's conjunctivitis may be due to Reiter syndrome. This condition belongs to which category of conjunctivitis etiology?
The Electronic Medical Record (EMR) system used in ophthalmic clinics is MOST important for:
questions.explanation: The Electronic Medical Record (EMR) system is used to document nursing assessments, diagnostic findings, and care plans, ensuring continuity and accuracy of care across the healthcare team. Proper documentation facilitates communication between the nurse, ophthalmologist, and other team members. It also provides a legal record of care rendered and enables monitoring of patient progress over successive clinic visits.
options: Documenting assessments to ensure continuity of care
Calculating the cost of patient investigations
Generating automated prescriptions for eye medications
Replacing the need for direct nurse-patient interaction
Notifying other hospitals of patient diagnoses

questions.question: Conjunctival Kaposi Sarcoma in HIV patients appears clinically as:
options: White fluffy cotton-wool spots on the conjunctival surface
Reddish-purple hemorrhagic lesions on the conjunctiva
Clear fluid-filled cysts on the palpebral conjunctiva
Pale yellow elevated deposits on the bulbar conjunctiva
Multiple white papillae on the upper tarsal conjunctiva
questions.explanation: Kaposi Sarcoma of the conjunctiva in HIV/AIDS presents as reddish-purple hemorrhagic lesions on the conjunctival surface, caused by proliferation of abnormal blood vessel-forming cells driven by Human Herpesvirus-8 (HHV-8) in the context of HIV-related immunosuppression. These lesions can be confused with subconjunctival hemorrhage but are distinguished by their firm, elevated texture and association with other systemic Kaposi lesions. Management includes ART optimization and local treatments.

questions.question: The MOST appropriate nursing action when a patient with scleritis reports worsening pain and sudden visual changes is to:
options: Report immediately to the healthcare provider for urgent reassessment
Reassure the patient that pain fluctuations are normal in scleritis
Document the finding in the medical record for the next clinic visit
Administer an additional dose of prescribed NSAID medication
Apply a warm compress to the eye to reduce periorbital discomfort
questions.explanation: Worsening pain and sudden visual changes in a scleritis patient may indicate dangerous complications such as scleral perforation, posterior extension, or associated choroidal or retinal involvement. The nurse must promptly report these findings to the healthcare provider for urgent reassessment and intervention. This escalation prevents delay in treatment that could otherwise result in irreversible vision loss. Documentation is also important but should not delay urgent clinical action.

Dendritic ulcers characterized by linear lesions with branches (dendrites) on fluorescein staining are the hallmark of Herpes Simplex epithelial keratitis. If untreated, these lesions widen and grow into geographic lesions resembling maps. The longer treatment is delayed, the more corneal scarring results, particularly if the center of the cornea is involved. This morphology on fluorescein staining is pathognomonic for HSV epithelial corneal infection.
options: Herpes Simplex epithelial keratitis with linear branching lesions
Bacterial keratitis caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Autoimmune peripheral ulcerative keratitis from rheumatoid arthritis
Acanthamoeba keratitis in contact lens users
Fungal keratitis following trauma with plant material
questions.question: A dendritic ulcer on fluorescein examination is MOST characteristic of which corneal condition?

options: Detects retinal vascular changes associated with systemic hypertension
Identifies the causative organism by direct microbial visualization
Provides a magnified view of the cyst and intraocular structures
Measures intraocular pressure by corneal applanation technique
Assesses the depth of corneal epithelial erosion by dye uptake
questions.question: Slit-lamp biomicroscopy of a conjunctival cyst provides which SPECIFIC diagnostic benefit?
questions.explanation: Slit-lamp biomicroscopy provides a magnified, detailed view of the conjunctival cyst and surrounding intraocular structures for microscopic examination. This allows the clinician to assess the size, location, transparency, and associated features of the cyst while examining the integrity of adjacent conjunctival and corneal tissues. It complements physical examination and helps determine the most appropriate management strategy for the cyst.

questions.question: A patient in the ophthalmic clinic has a nursing diagnosis of 'Impaired visual perception.' The BEST intervention to promote independence is to:
questions.explanation: Providing large-print objects and visual aids assists patients with impaired visual perception to see more clearly and promotes a sense of independence. Large-print materials improve access to information and educational resources during patient education, which is critical to treatment adherence and recovery. Restricting activities or removing objects creates dependency and fails to optimize the patient's remaining visual function.
options: Permanently restrict the patient from moving without staff assistance
Administer sedatives to prevent unnecessary eye movements
Discourage the patient from performing activities of daily living
Provide the patient with large-print objects and visual aids for reading
Remove all objects from the environment to prevent obstruction

questions.question: Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (PDR) is distinguished from Non-Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (NPDR) by:
questions.explanation: Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (PDR) is characterized by the growth of new, fragile blood vessels (neovascularization) on the retinal surface and vitreous, driven by ischemia-induced VEGF release. These new vessels bleed easily into the vitreous, causing floaters, severe vision loss, and retinal detachment from scar tissue formation. Non-Proliferative DR involves leaky and closed blood vessels without neovascularization. PDR is the more advanced and vision-threatening stage of diabetic eye disease.
options: The presence of macular edema causing central vision loss
The severity of intraretinal hemorrhages and cotton-wool spots
The degree of retinal arteriolar narrowing and AV nicking
The extent of hard exudate deposition within the macular region
The growth of new, fragile blood vessels (neovascularization) on the retina

questions.explanation: Signs of scleral perforation or progressive vision loss are critical findings in scleritis patients that require immediate ophthalmologist referral. Scleritis can lead to scleral thinning, necrosis, choroidal exposure, and ultimately globe perforation, particularly in necrotizing forms. The nurse plays a vital role in monitoring for these complications and escalating care promptly. Mild conjunctival changes or transient blurring do not carry the same urgency.
options: Watery discharge with minimal discomfort between episodes
Transient blurring of vision that resolves after blinking
Mild conjunctival injection without scleral involvement
Signs of scleral perforation or progressive vision loss
Mild periorbital edema resolving within twenty-four hours
questions.question: A nurse monitoring a patient for scleritis complications should be MOST alert to which clinical sign requiring immediate ophthalmologist referral?

options: Determine whether intraocular anti-VEGF injections are required
Confirm the grade of arteriovenous nicking on fundoscopy
Collaborate with the team to establish and maintain target BP goals
Calculate the patient's retinal arteriolar narrowing ratio
Adjust the patient's topical hypotensive glaucoma eye drops
questions.explanation: Regular blood pressure monitoring by the nurse is used to collaborate with the healthcare team in establishing and maintaining individualized target blood pressure goals based on current guidelines for hypertensive retinopathy management. Consistent blood pressure control is the cornerstone of preventing progression of retinal vascular damage. The nurse ensures that blood pressure readings are accurately documented, shares findings with the medical team, and educates the patient on the importance of consistent antihypertensive therapy.
questions.question: The nurse performing blood pressure monitoring in hypertensive retinopathy should MOST use findings to:

options: Risk of drug toxicity from long-term topical glaucoma medications
Risk of corneal decompensation from chronic topical preservative toxicity
Risk of systemic hypertension from optic nerve vascular compromise
Risk of cataract formation from chronic elevated intraocular pressure
Risk of falls and injury from progressive peripheral vision loss
questions.explanation: The most important patient safety concern in glaucoma nursing care is the risk of falls and injury arising directly from progressive peripheral vision loss. As glaucoma advances, the narrowing visual field (tunnel vision) severely impairs spatial awareness and detection of obstacles in the peripheral environment, significantly increasing fall risk. The nurse conducts environmental safety assessments, educates patients and caregivers on fall prevention strategies, and coordinates referral to low vision services and occupational therapy.
questions.question: Patient safety in glaucoma nursing care MOST importantly addresses which risk arising directly from the disease?

options: Always appear bright red without the characteristic violet-blue hue
Are distinctly separate from the overlying conjunctival vessels
Can be moved freely with a cotton-tipped applicator
Are adherent to the sclera and cannot be moved with a cotton-tipped applicator
questions.explanation: Inflamed scleral vessels in scleritis are adherent to the sclera and cannot be moved with a cotton-tipped applicator, which differentiates them from more superficial episcleral vessels that can be displaced. Additionally, deep scleral vessels do not blanch with 2.5-10% phenylephrine, while superficial episcleral and conjunctival vessels may blanch. This physical sign is an important bedside test used during slit-lamp examination to confirm scleritis.
questions.question: A key clinical sign in the physical examination of scleritis is that inflamed scleral vessels:

questions.explanation: The active or inflammatory phase of Thyroid Eye Disease can last for months up to three years, during which orbital inflammation, fibroblast activation, and tissue expansion are ongoing. Following this phase, the disease enters the stable phase when inflammation subsides. This prolonged active phase determines the window for immunosuppressive treatment, as interventions are most effective during the inflammatory phase and may have limited benefit once the condition has reached the stable fibrotic stage.
options: Months up to three years of active orbital inflammation
Forty-eight hours before entering the stable phase
Seven to ten days with appropriate steroid treatment
One to two weeks before spontaneous regression occurs
Twenty-four hours of maximal inflammation at disease peak
questions.question: The active (inflammatory) phase of Thyroid Eye Disease can last for approximately:

options: Chronic papilledema causing optic nerve head avascular necrosis
Toxic effects of elevated blood pressure on the optic nerve axons
Inadequate blood supply to the optic nerve head from vascular compromise
Inflammatory infiltration of the optic nerve sheath from choroiditis
Elevated cerebrospinal fluid pressure from malignant hypertension
questions.question: Ischemic optic neuropathy as a complication of hypertensive retinopathy results from:
questions.explanation: Ischemic optic neuropathy in hypertensive retinopathy results from inadequate blood supply to the optic nerve head due to vascular compromise caused by the hypertensive arteriosclerotic changes in the posterior ciliary arteries that supply the optic nerve. This ischemia causes infarction of the optic nerve head, presenting as sudden painless visual loss with an altitudinal visual field defect. It is a serious complication that can cause permanent visual loss if not managed through urgent blood pressure control.

options: Permanent lightening of the iris colour immediately
Immediate and complete loss of eyebrow hair
Complete and permanent loss of eyelashes
Widespread hair loss over the entire scalp
Darkening and thickening of the eyelashes
questions.question: The nurse explains to a glaucoma patient that their prostaglandin analogue eye drops may cause which recognised side effect?
questions.explanation: Prostaglandin analogue eye drops, a common first-line glaucoma treatment, are well known to cause increased eyelash length, thickness, and darkening, along with periorbital skin pigmentation changes and gradual, permanent darkening rather than lightening of the iris in some patients. They do not cause eyelash or eyebrow loss or generalised scalp hair loss. Informing patients of these recognised cosmetic side effects supports informed consent and treatment adherence.

questions.question: The ophthalmic nurse's MOST important responsibility when a thyroid eye disease patient reports sudden loss of vision is to:
questions.explanation: Sudden vision loss in a TED patient is a critical warning sign of compressive optic neuropathy, where expanded orbital tissues are compressing the optic nerve and threatening permanent vision loss. This is an ophthalmological emergency requiring immediate medical team notification and urgent surgical or medical intervention to decompress the orbit. Delay in reporting this sign can result in irreversible optic nerve damage and blindness, making prompt nurse escalation essential.
options: Apply cool compresses and reassure the patient as a common symptom
Report immediately to the medical team as it may indicate optic nerve compression
Reassess vision after 24 hours as transient blurring is common in TED
Document the finding and schedule an ophthalmology review at the next appointment
Administer lubricating eye drops to improve corneal surface clarity

questions.question: Nuclear cataract initially causes near vision to appear temporarily improved because:
options: The pupil dilates to avoid the nuclear opacity improving peripheral vision
Increased aqueous humor production enhances lens optical clarity briefly
The vitreous gel liquefaction reduces the effective axial length transiently
The nuclear opacity increases corneal curvature improving refraction
Index myopia from increased nuclear density improves near focus temporarily
questions.explanation: Nuclear cataract initially causes a temporary improvement in near vision (second sight) through index myopia, where the increasing density of the hardening lens nucleus changes its refractive index, effectively increasing its power and creating a myopic shift. This temporarily brings near objects into focus without reading glasses. However, as the cataract progresses, the lens becomes increasingly yellow-brown and opaque, gradually worsening both near and distance vision and eventually requiring surgical removal.

Conjunctivitis caused by Herpes Simplex Virus requires antiviral therapy, including antiviral eye drops such as trifluridine or ganciclovir, and in severe cases, systemic antiviral medication such as oral acyclovir. This specific antiviral approach targets the virus directly and prevents corneal involvement (herpetic keratitis), which can lead to scarring and vision loss. Antibiotics are ineffective against viral conjunctivitis and should not be used as primary treatment.
questions.question: A patient with conjunctivitis secondary to Herpes Simplex Virus requires which SPECIFIC treatment?
options: Topical antifungal medication applied twice daily
Antiviral eye drops and potentially systemic antiviral medication
Oral antihistamine combined with topical mast cell stabilizer
Intralesional corticosteroid injection under the conjunctiva
Broad-spectrum topical antibiotic ointment for fourteen days

questions.explanation: Inadequately treated Herpes Simplex Keratitis can lead to corneal scarring, particularly when the infection involves the central cornea or progresses to deeper stromal layers. These scars reduce corneal transparency and cause permanent visual impairment or blindness. Complications of HSK include glaucoma, cataract, and severe decreased vision. Corneal transplantation may ultimately be required in cases where medical treatment fails and scarring significantly impairs vision.
questions.question: Which complication of Herpes Simplex Keratitis can result from inadequate treatment?
options: Conversion to benign corneal pinguecula on the ocular surface
Development of corneal dermoid from proliferating stromal fibroblasts
Spontaneous resolution leaving no residual corneal abnormality
Development of bilateral glaucoma from immune-mediated trabecular damage
Corneal scarring leading to permanent visual impairment or blindness
Increasing protein intake to boost CMV antibody production
Daily self-examination of the fundus for early retinal changes
Avoidance of all social interactions to prevent secondary infection
Adherence to antiretroviral therapy and regular eye examinations
questions.question: Health promotion for an HIV patient with ocular complications MOST importantly includes encouraging:
questions.explanation: Health promotion for HIV patients with ocular complications centers on encouraging strict adherence to antiretroviral therapy, which controls the underlying HIV infection and preserves immune function, and regular ophthalmological examinations for early detection of ocular complications. The nurse also promotes a healthy diet, regular exercise, smoking cessation, and adherence to all prescribed medications. Regular eye exams are particularly critical because many serious retinal conditions develop without early symptoms.

options: Macular corneal dystrophy causing diffuse stromal opacity bilaterally
Congenital stromal dystrophy causing bilateral corneal opacity at birth
Posterior polymorphous dystrophy affecting Descemet's membrane
Fuchs endothelial dystrophy causing bilateral endothelial cell loss
Epithelial Basement Membrane Dystrophy affecting the anterior cornea
questions.question: Which corneal dystrophy affects the anterior surface and causes painful recurrent corneal erosions?
questions.explanation: Epithelial Basement Membrane Dystrophy (EBMD) is an anterior corneal dystrophy that affects the epithelium and its basement membrane, causing characteristic slit-lamp findings and resulting in decreased vision and recurrent corneal erosions. The recurrent erosions cause acute episodes of eye pain, usually on waking, when the eyelid tears the loosely adherent epithelium from the abnormal basement membrane. Management may include lubricants, bandage contact lenses, and phototherapeutic keratectomy.

options: Chemical conjunctivitis resolving spontaneously within a few days
Bacterial conjunctivitis caused by Staphylococcus aureus colonization
Gonococcal conjunctivitis presenting two to five days after birth
Chlamydial conjunctivitis presenting five to fourteen days after birth
Herpetic conjunctivitis with watery discharge and lid edema
questions.explanation: Chemical conjunctivitis occurs within 24 hours of instillation of silver nitrate solution, which was historically used for ocular prophylaxis in neonates. It is characterized by eyelid swelling, eye redness, and tearing, and typically resolves spontaneously within a few days without specific treatment. It is distinguished from gonococcal (2-5 days), chlamydial (5-14 days), and herpetic conjunctivitis (within 2 weeks) by its very early onset.
questions.question: Which form of conjunctivitis is characterized by symptoms arising within 24 hours of silver nitrate instillation that resolve spontaneously?
The primary nursing instruction for prevention of pterygium recurrence after surgical removal is to:
questions.explanation: The primary preventive instruction for pterygium recurrence is to wear UV-protective sunglasses and avoid prolonged exposure to sunlight, wind, and dust. UV radiation is the most significant trigger for pterygium development and recurrence. Additionally, patients are advised to use eye protection during dusty activities, use artificial tears, and attend regular eye examinations to detect early recurrence.
options: Avoid blinking to reduce mechanical stress on the autograft
Wear UV-protective sunglasses and avoid prolonged sun exposure
Use antibiotic eye drops indefinitely to prevent infection
Apply topical corticosteroids permanently following surgery
Apply ice packs to the eye for six hours post-operatively
Pupil reaction asymmetry suggesting posterior segment pathology
Exacerbation of diabetic macular edema causing central vision decline
Iris neovascularization from worsened proliferative diabetic retinopathy
Corneal epithelial healing progress and surface staining pattern
Intraocular lens decentration visible on slit-lamp examination
questions.explanation: One month after cataract surgery in a diabetic patient, the most important assessment is for exacerbation of diabetic macular edema (DME), which is a well-recognized complication that can occur or worsen after cataract surgery due to post-operative intraocular inflammation. This DME can cause significant central vision decline despite an otherwise technically successful cataract procedure. OCT assessment of macular thickness should be performed, and prompt anti-VEGF or steroid treatment initiated if DME is identified to prevent permanent central vision loss.
questions.question: The nurse providing follow-up care for a patient one month after cataract surgery in the presence of diabetes should MOST importantly assess for:

questions.explanation: Dietary management for hypertensive retinopathy focuses on controlling the underlying hypertension through a diet high in fruits and vegetables (rich in potassium and antioxidants), reducing sodium (salt) intake to lower blood pressure, limiting saturated fats to reduce cardiovascular risk, and restricting caffeine and alcohol. This dietary approach aligns with evidence-based guidelines for hypertension management and directly helps lower blood pressure to prevent further retinal vascular damage.
questions.question: The nurse instructing a patient with hypertensive retinopathy on diet should MOST specifically recommend:
options: A high-protein diet to repair damaged retinal blood vessels
A diet high in fruits, vegetables, and low in salt and saturated fats
A high-calorie diet to maintain weight during antihypertensive therapy
Unlimited caffeine and alcohol to maintain cardiovascular relaxation
A diet rich in refined carbohydrates to reduce dietary fat intake

questions.explanation: Keratomalacia results from severe Vitamin A deficiency, and dietary management centers on increasing intake of Vitamin A-rich foods such as carrots, liver, egg yolks, fish liver oils, dark green leafy vegetables (spinach, kale), yellow and orange fruits, and yellow vegetables (squash, pumpkin). Foods fortified with Vitamin A are also recommended. Oral or injectable Vitamin A supplementation is the primary medical treatment, complemented by these dietary modifications.
questions.question: Which food should a nurse MOST recommend to a patient with keratomalacia to address the underlying nutritional deficiency?
options: Carrots, liver, egg yolks, and dark green leafy vegetables
Whole grains and legumes rich in B-complex vitamins
Rice and white bread fortified with iron and folate
Lean protein sources such as fish and chicken breast
Citrus fruits and tomatoes rich in ascorbic acid

questions.question: The MOST significant risk factor for developing open-angle glaucoma after age 40 is:
questions.explanation: Elevated intraocular pressure is the most significant modifiable risk factor for developing open-angle glaucoma. Other risk factors include being over age 40, having a family history of glaucoma, being of African, Hispanic, or Asian heritage, being very nearsighted or farsighted, having thin central corneas, and having certain systemic conditions. However, elevated IOP is the primary therapeutic target because reducing IOP has been definitively proven to slow or halt glaucoma progression in clinical trials.
options: High myopia causing elongation of the axial length of the globe
Elevated intraocular pressure as the primary modifiable risk factor
Thin corneas causing underestimation of the true intraocular pressure
Advanced age beyond 40 years as the exclusive risk factor
Family history of glaucoma as the only independent risk factor

questions.question: Thyroid Eye Disease (TED) is BEST classified as:
options: An infectious disease caused by Graves thyroid viral reactivation
A degenerative condition caused by progressive thyroid hormone deficiency
A hereditary condition caused by genetic mutation of thyroid receptor genes
A nutritional disorder caused by iodine deficiency affecting the orbit
An autoimmune disease caused by orbital fibroblast activation by thyroid autoantibodies
questions.explanation: Thyroid Eye Disease (TED) is an autoimmune condition caused by the activation of orbital fibroblasts by autoantibodies directed against thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) receptors. This activation leads to inflammation, fibrosis around the extraocular muscles, and accumulation of excess extracellular matrix and fat in the periorbital space. The resulting tissue expansion causes protrusion of the eye (exophthalmos) and other characteristic orbital changes that define the clinical presentation of TED.

Low levels of selenium in the blood are a recognized risk factor for Thyroid Eye Disease. Selenium is an essential trace element that plays a role in thyroid autoimmune regulation and antioxidant defense, particularly through selenoprotein enzymes like glutathione peroxidase. Studies have shown that selenium supplementation in patients with mild active TED can reduce orbital inflammation and slow disease progression. The nurse should include selenium status in the assessment of patients with TED.
questions.question: Low selenium levels are a recognized risk factor for Thyroid Eye Disease PRIMARILY because:
options: Selenium supplementation directly inhibits TSH receptor autoantibody production
Selenium deficiency causes orbital fibroblast hypertrophy and inflammation
Selenium is important in thyroid autoimmune regulation and antioxidant defense
Selenium deficiency impairs thyroid hormone synthesis and causes hypothyroidism
Selenium deficiency promotes corneal vascularization in orbital disease

questions.explanation: Distraction techniques such as playing games or watching movies are non-pharmacological pain management strategies that work by diverting the patient's attention away from the pain experience, thereby reducing its perceived intensity. This approach is particularly useful in ophthalmic nursing where sedating medications may affect visual assessment, and where pain can be a significant cause of patient distress post-operatively or during inflammatory episodes.
questions.question: A distraction technique such as playing games or watching a movie is recommended in ophthalmic nursing care PRIMARILY to:
options: Prevent post-operative infection by limiting patient movement
Assist the patient in performing activities of daily living
Improve the patient's visual acuity during recovery
Reduce the patient's awareness and focus on pain
Avoids the need for donor corneal tissue in the procedure
Replaces the full-thickness cornea with donor tissue
Uses laser energy rather than a surgical blade for excision
Replaces only the anterior epithelial and Bowman's layers
Replaces only the posterior corneal endothelial layers
questions.explanation: Penetrating Keratoplasty (PK) involves replacement of the full-thickness cornea with donor tissue, making it suitable for conditions affecting multiple corneal layers or causing deep stromal scarring. Descemet's Stripping Endothelial Keratoplasty (DSEK), in contrast, selectively replaces only the posterior endothelial layers and is specifically indicated for endothelial dystrophies such as Fuchs dystrophy. The targeted nature of DSEK offers faster visual recovery and fewer complications than PK.
questions.question: Penetrating Keratoplasty (PK) differs from Descemet's Stripping Endothelial Keratoplasty (DSEK) in that PK:
Arteriovenous nicking in hypertensive retinopathy MOST accurately describes:
options: Dilation of a retinal venule distal to an occluded arteriole
Rupture of a retinal arteriole causing localized hemorrhagic infarction
Narrowing of a retinal arteriole throughout its entire visible length
New blood vessel formation crossing the arteriovenous junction
Compression of a venule where it is crossed by a sclerotic arteriole
questions.explanation: Arteriovenous (AV) nicking in hypertensive retinopathy describes the phenomenon where a small arteriole crosses a venule, compressing the vein at the crossing point due to the rigid, sclerotic arteriolar wall. This results in bulging of the vein on either side of the crossing and is a characteristic finding in hypertensive retinopathy. AV nicking reflects the degree of arteriosclerosis and chronic hypertensive vessel wall changes and is a known predictor of cardiovascular mortality in adults.

options: Open-angle glaucoma with elevated IOP unresponsive to medications
Angle-closure glaucoma where the iris blocks the drainage angle
Normal-tension glaucoma with optic nerve damage at normal IOP
Secondary glaucoma from corticosteroid-induced IOP elevation
Congenital glaucoma from developmental trabecular meshwork dysgenesis
questions.explanation: Laser iridotomy is the specific treatment for angle-closure glaucoma, where the iris blocks or is very close to the drainage angle. The procedure creates a tiny hole in the peripheral iris using a laser, which allows aqueous humor to flow more freely to the drainage angle and prevents the iris from blocking it. This relieves the angle closure, equalizes pressure between the anterior and posterior chambers, and prevents future acute attacks. It is also used prophylactically in the fellow eye of patients with angle-closure glaucoma.
questions.question: Laser iridotomy is the SPECIFIC treatment for which type of glaucoma?

options: Prevent corneal drying from increased respiratory rate
Eliminate the Chlamydia organisms from the respiratory tract
Correct dyspnea and improve oxygenation in the neonate
Stimulate surfactant production in the premature neonate
Reduce the intraocular pressure elevated by crying and distress
questions.explanation: Oxygen is administered to a neonate with an ineffective breathing pattern to correct dyspnea and improve oxygenation. In neonates with ophthalmia neonatorum complicated by respiratory involvement (especially from Chlamydia, which can cause pneumonia), inadequate gas exchange leads to hypoxemia that must be addressed urgently. Respiratory assessment, positioning, suctioning of secretions, and oxygen administration are key nursing interventions to maintain adequate respiratory function.
questions.question: A neonate with ophthalmia neonatorum develops an ineffective breathing pattern. The nurse administers oxygen PRIMARILY to:

questions.explanation: The priority nursing intervention for the diagnosis 'Risk for Infection related to compromised corneal integrity' is to assess for the presence and history of common causes of infection and monitor for local infectious signs such as redness, swelling, pain, and discharge. Early identification of infection allows prompt treatment, while education on avoiding contamination of the eye and proper medication administration reduces the infection risk. Regular white blood cell count monitoring and nutritional assessment support immune defense.
questions.question: The nursing diagnosis 'Risk for Infection related to compromised corneal integrity' requires which PRIORITY preventive intervention?
options: Administering prophylactic oral broad-spectrum antibiotics for one month
Applying pressure bandages to the cornea to prevent bacterial entry
Irrigating the eye with concentrated antiseptic solution twice daily
Fitting the patient with hard contact lenses to protect the corneal surface
Assessing for the presence of local infectious processes and monitoring for infection signs

questions.explanation: Normal-tension glaucoma, where optic nerve damage and visual field loss occur despite IOP within the normal range, is more common among people of Asian descent or Asian Americans. In these patients, the optic nerve appears particularly sensitive to IOP within the normal range, or other factors such as vascular dysregulation contribute to optic nerve vulnerability. This type of glaucoma highlights that IOP is not the only factor in glaucomatous optic nerve damage.
options: People of Asian descent or Asian Americans with normal IOP
Elderly Caucasian women with bilateral pseudo-exfoliation syndrome
Young adults of African descent with elevated intraocular pressure
Children of South Asian origin with anterior segment dysgenesis
Middle-aged men of European descent with steroid-induced glaucoma
questions.question: Normal-tension glaucoma is MOST commonly seen in which demographic group?
Which systemic side effect can result from glaucoma eye drops, particularly topical beta-blockers?
questions.explanation: Topical beta-blocker eye drops used in glaucoma treatment can be systemically absorbed and cause bradycardia, hypotension, and bronchospasm, particularly in patients with underlying cardiac conduction problems or asthma, making careful patient screening for contraindications essential before prescribing. Weight gain, hearing loss, joint pain, and skin pigmentation changes are not recognised systemic effects of this drug class. Nurses should educate patients on nasolacrimal duct occlusion technique to help minimise systemic absorption.
options: Sudden onset of severe joint pain
Permanent hearing loss in both ears
Significant weight gain over a short period
Bradycardia and bronchospasm in susceptible patients

questions.explanation: Patients on oral corticosteroids such as prednisolone for scleritis must be monitored for elevated intraocular pressure, decreased resistance to infection, gastric irritation, osteoporosis, and weight gain. Elevated intraocular pressure can worsen scleritis-related ocular damage, and decreased immune resistance increases vulnerability to opportunistic infections. The nurse plays a critical role in monitoring and educating patients about these side effects to ensure safe steroid use.
options: Irreversible corneal opacification from steroid crystallization
Elevated intraocular pressure and decreased infection resistance
Nephrotic syndrome and urinary protein loss
Cardiac arrhythmias and sodium depletion electrolyte imbalance
questions.question: A nurse caring for a patient on oral prednisolone for scleritis should monitor MOST closely for:
An HIV patient with 'Impaired social interaction related to visual impairment' would MOST benefit from which nursing intervention?
options: Administering anti-anxiety medications to reduce social avoidance
Restricting social visits to reduce infectious transmission risk
Facilitating referral to counseling, support groups, and low vision services
Advising the patient to use sunglasses indoors to hide visual impairment
Encouraging the patient to remain in isolation until vision improves
questions.explanation: The nursing intervention for 'Impaired social interaction related to visual impairment' includes facilitating referral to counseling, support groups, and low vision rehabilitation services. These resources help the patient adapt to visual impairment, maintain social connections, and develop coping strategies. Low vision aids, orientation and mobility training, and peer support groups can restore functional independence and social participation, significantly improving quality of life for HIV patients with visual impairment.

questions.question: Intraocular pressure (IOP) assessment in the ophthalmic clinic is MOST accurately measured using:
options: Snellen chart with standard occlusion technique
Slit-lamp biomicroscopy and anterior segment grading
Tonometry with a standard pressure-measuring device
Ophthalmoscopy with a dilated fundal examination
questions.explanation: Tonometry is the standard method for measuring intraocular pressure (IOP) in the eye and is a routine part of the ophthalmic nursing assessment. Elevated IOP is a significant risk factor for glaucoma and can indicate other ocular pathologies. Snellen charts measure visual acuity, while ophthalmoscopy and slit-lamp biomicroscopy assess structural features of the eye without quantifying pressure.

Rheumatoid arthritis is the most common autoimmune comorbidity associated with scleritis, although other autoimmune conditions such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis, systemic lupus erythematosus, relapsing polychondritis, and Sjögren's syndrome are also significantly associated. Scleritis may be the first presentation of an undiagnosed autoimmune condition in up to 30-40% of cases, making comprehensive systemic evaluation essential in all scleritis patients.
questions.question: The MOST common autoimmune disease associated with scleritis is:
options: Systemic lupus erythematosus causing bilateral diffuse scleritis
Inflammatory bowel disease causing recurrent diffuse anterior scleritis
Rheumatoid arthritis presenting as the most common autoimmune comorbidity
Sjögren's syndrome presenting with necrotizing posterior scleritis
Ankylosing spondylitis causing bilateral nodular anterior scleritis

questions.explanation: Fluorescein staining highlights areas of disrupted corneal epithelium, which appear as bright green under cobalt blue light illumination. This staining characteristic is essential for diagnosing corneal ulcers, abrasions, and epithelial defects. The extent and pattern of fluorescein uptake help determine the size and depth of the epithelial disruption and guide therapeutic decisions including antibiotic selection, patching, and referral for specialist care.
questions.question: Which finding on fluorescein staining of a corneal ulcer indicates epithelial disruption?
options: Blue-white fluorescence indicating deep stromal inflammation
Orange fluorescence indicating subepithelial fibrovascular growth
Bright green uptake of the dye in areas of epithelial defect
Yellow fluorescence showing mucous accumulation on the surface
Red fluorescence suggesting vascular ingrowth into the cornea

questions.explanation: Ophthalmic nurses are vital members of the multidisciplinary team who assess patients with eye complaints, provide initial and comprehensive nursing care, educate patients and families, and collaborate with ophthalmologists and other healthcare professionals. Their role is broad and encompasses clinical, educational, managerial, and research functions. They do not replace the ophthalmologist but complement and enhance the team's effectiveness.
options: Managing the clinic's administrative records exclusively
Performing all diagnostic tests independently without physician input
Replacing the ophthalmologist in routine eye consultations
Solely administering eye drops and wound dressings
Assessing patients, providing nursing care, educating, and collaborating with team
questions.question: Which of the following BEST describes the role of the ophthalmic nurse in the multidisciplinary team?

questions.explanation: When a pterygium becomes particularly inflamed, non-steroidal or steroid anti-inflammatory eye drops are prescribed for a short period under the supervision of an eye specialist. These reduce the inflammatory component of the pterygium and relieve symptoms such as redness and irritation. Long-term or unsupervised use of steroid drops risks complications including elevated intraocular pressure and cataract formation, which is why supervision is emphasized.
options: Long-term oral immunosuppressants for three months
Topical antibiotics combined with mydriatic eye drops
Topical antifungal agents combined with systemic steroids
Non-steroidal or steroid anti-inflammatory eye drops under supervision
Intravenous corticosteroids at one milligram per kilogram per day

Papillary reaction on the tarsal conjunctiva
Rapid response to topical antibiotic therapy
questions.explanation: Viral conjunctivitis, most commonly caused by adenovirus, classically presents with watery discharge and tender preauricular lymphadenopathy, reflecting the systemic viral immune response, a feature not typically seen with bacterial infection. Thick purulent discharge instead favours a bacterial cause, while prominent itching and papillary reaction favour an allergic aetiology. This clinical distinction helps avoid unnecessary antibiotic use in viral cases, which are self-limiting.
questions.question: Which finding on examination would most strongly suggest viral rather than bacterial conjunctivitis?

options: Sudden painless vision loss from posterior capsule rapture
Gradual monocular diplopia from early lens nucleus distortion
Reduced vision in bright light and halos around lights at night
Progressive hyperopia from lens nucleus thinning and flattening
Colour desaturation causing difficulty distinguishing red from green
questions.explanation: A posterior subcapsular cataract, which forms at the back of the lens in the path of light, most characteristically reduces vision in bright light (because the pupil constricts in bright conditions, directing more light through the affected posterior area) and causes halos or glare around lights at night. It particularly affects reading vision. This type of cataract tends to progress faster than nuclear or cortical cataracts and is often seen in younger diabetic patients and those on long-term steroid therapy.
questions.question: A posterior subcapsular cataract is MOST likely to cause which SPECIFIC visual complaint?

options: Epithelium forming the outermost protective oxygen-absorbing layer
Endothelium pumping excess fluid to maintain corneal clarity
Descemet's membrane separating the stroma from the endothelium
Stroma consisting of collagen fibers giving transparency and strength
Bowman's layer providing acellular anterior structural support
questions.question: Which layer of the cornea is described as the thickest and provides transparency and structural strength?
questions.explanation: The stroma is the thickest layer of the cornea, composed of collagen fibers arranged in a precisely regular pattern that gives the cornea its transparency and structural strength. It constitutes approximately 90% of the corneal thickness. Disruption of this regular collagen arrangement by disease, injury, or scarring results in corneal opacity and reduced visual acuity. The stroma's integrity is central to maintaining both visual function and corneal structural stability.

Prevention of diabetic cataract most effectively involves managing blood sugar levels (reducing sorbitol pathway activation), controlling blood pressure and cholesterol (reducing vascular risk factors that accelerate lens changes), quitting smoking, maintaining a balanced antioxidant-rich diet, and having regular dilated eye examinations as recommended by a doctor. These measures collectively address the metabolic and vascular factors that accelerate diabetic lens opacification, delaying cataract formation and reducing the need for early surgical intervention.
questions.question: Prevention of cataract in diabetic patients MOST effectively involves which combination of measures?
options: Annual lens examination and prophylactic removal before opacity develops
Routine topical antioxidant eye drop application to delay lens clouding
Managing blood sugar, blood pressure, and cholesterol with regular eye examinations
Wearing blue-light filtering spectacles to reduce phototoxic lens damage
Dietary supplementation with high-dose vitamin C to slow lens opacification

questions.question: Corneal topography in keratoconus is MOST useful for:
options: Diagnosing early keratoconus and monitoring its progression
Measuring the thickness of the central and peripheral cornea
Detecting endothelial cell density changes in corneal dystrophy
Assessing the need for corneal transplant by measuring opacity
Evaluating intraocular pressure change in response to treatment
questions.explanation: Corneal topography is described as the most accurate method for diagnosing early keratoconus and monitoring its progression. It uses computerized imaging to create a detailed map of the corneal curvature, revealing the characteristic inferior steepening and irregular astigmatism patterns of keratoconus before they are detectable by slit-lamp examination. Regular topographic monitoring allows clinicians to determine the rate of progression and the appropriate timing for interventions such as CXL.

A bacterial infection of the corneal stroma causing ulceration

questions.question: Pterygium is MOST accurately defined as:
questions.explanation: Pterygium is a degenerative condition characterized by fibrovascular outgrowth of conjunctival tissue over the cornea. It typically presents as a triangular or wing-shaped fold of tissue growing from the nasal corner of the eye. The condition is multifactorial, with ultraviolet radiation considered the most important trigger, and it differs from conjunctival cysts, cataracts, and keratoconus, which affect different structures.

options: Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria
National Association of Nigeria Nurses and Midwives
questions.explanation: The Nigerian Ophthalmic Nurses Association is an affiliate Specialist Organization of the National Association of Nigeria Nurses and Midwives (NANNM), which is responsible for protecting and advocating for ophthalmic nurses across Nigeria. This affiliation ensures that ophthalmic nurses have representation within the broader nursing professional framework and that their interests are integrated into national nursing policy and practice.

questions.explanation: Inclusion cysts are the most common type of conjunctival cyst, accounting for more than 80% of all conjunctival cysts. They form when a layer of the conjunctiva folds over onto itself, and a cyst fills with fluid in response to the irritation. Retention cysts, by contrast, form when tiny conjunctival ducts are blocked by allergens, dust, or debris. Understanding this distinction guides appropriate management decisions.
options: Mucous membrane cysts from goblet cell hyperplasia
Inclusion cysts from folded conjunctival epithelium
Retention cysts from blocked lymphatic ducts
Sebaceous cysts from Meibomian gland obstruction
Dermoid cysts from embryological tissue remnants

Treatment initiation should not be delayed while awaiting definitive diagnosis or ophthalmology follow-up, as early treatment is essential for optimal outcomes.

Seventy-two hours of disease onset to reduce complications
Twenty-four hours of the rash appearing in the ophthalmic distribution
Forty-eight hours of confirmed laboratory diagnosis only
One week from the time the rash first appears

questions.explanation: When breastfeeding is interrupted due to the neonate's illness and hospitalization, the nurse should support the mother to express and store breast milk to maintain lactation and provide breast milk for tube feeding during the separation period. Premature cessation of breastfeeding deprives the neonate of immune protection and nutritional benefits. Expressed breast milk can be administered via tube if necessary, and breastfeeding should be resumed as soon as the neonate's condition permits.
options: Supporting the mother to express and store breast milk during mother-infant separation
Introducing complementary feeds to supplement breastfeeding interrupted by illness
Administering formula feeding for six weeks while the infection is treated
Arranging for the nurse to bottle-feed the neonate exclusively during treatment
Advising the mother to permanently cease breastfeeding to prevent reinfection
