Visual field testing (perimetry) in glaucoma assessment is MOST important for:
questions.explanation: Visual field testing (perimetry) is the most important functional test for detecting changes in peripheral vision that indicate optic nerve damage from glaucoma. The optic nerve fibers that are most vulnerable in glaucoma serve the peripheral visual field, and defects in this area are the earliest detectable functional changes. Serial visual field tests allow monitoring of disease progression and assessment of treatment effectiveness over time. Structural imaging (OCT) complements but does not replace functional visual field assessment.
options: Measuring the thickness of the cornea and retinal nerve fiber layer
Detecting changes in peripheral vision that indicate optic nerve damage
Imaging the optic nerve head to detect disc cupping and pallor
Assessing aqueous humor drainage capacity through the trabecular meshwork
Measuring intraocular pressure at multiple time points during the day
Adenovirus type 8 causing epidemic keratoconjunctivitis globally
Varicella-Zoster Virus type 2 reactivating in the trigeminal ganglion
Herpes Simplex Virus primarily type 1 entering through corneal abrasions
Cytomegalovirus causing endotheliitis in immunocompromised patients
Epstein-Barr Virus causing corneal stromal infiltrates and keratitis
questions.question: Herpes Simplex Keratitis (HSK) involves the replication of which virus within corneal structures?
questions.explanation: Herpes Simplex Keratitis (HSK) is caused by the Herpes Simplex Virus, primarily type 1 (HSV-1). The pathophysiology involves viral entry into corneal epithelial cells through micro-abrasions, followed by establishment of latency in trigeminal ganglion neurons. Upon reactivation, the virus travels along sensory nerves to reach the cornea, leading to recurrent inflammation, dendritic lesions, and progressive corneal damage that can result in scarring and blindness.

questions.question: Giant Papillary Conjunctivitis (GPC) is MOST commonly caused by:
questions.explanation: Giant Papillary Conjunctivitis (GPC) is most commonly caused by mechanical irritation from contact lens wear, leading to inflammatory changes on the inner surface of the upper eyelid. Management involves addressing the underlying cause by discontinuing lens wear, switching to daily disposable lenses, or ensuring proper lens hygiene. Mast cell stabilizers or antihistamine eye drops may also reduce inflammation and discomfort associated with GPC.
options: Mechanical irritation of the conjunctiva by contact lenses
Vitamin A deficiency leading to conjunctival keratinization
Chronic topical steroid use causing papillary hypertrophy
Prolonged exposure to outdoor environmental allergens
Bacterial colonization of the conjunctival goblet cells

questions.explanation: Ophthalmic nurses play a significant role in achieving Universal Eye Health, as emphasized in descriptions of their professional responsibilities. They collaborate with ophthalmologists, educate communities, provide screening services, and assist in rehabilitation of visually impaired individuals. These activities collectively contribute to reducing preventable blindness and visual impairment, which are core objectives of the Universal Eye Health framework.
questions.question: Ophthalmic nurses are MOST involved in achieving which global eye health initiative?
options: Universal Eye Health as promoted by WHO

questions.explanation: Small, asymptomatic conjunctival cysts are best managed conservatively through watchful observation, as they often remain stable or may spontaneously regress over time. Surgical intervention is reserved for larger or symptomatic cysts that cause discomfort, visual disturbances, or difficulty closing the eyelid. This approach minimizes unnecessary procedural risk while ensuring that patients who develop complications are identified and treated appropriately.
options: Sclerotherapy injection to collapse the cyst immediately
Drainage under local anesthesia in the outpatient clinic
Watchful observation, as many cysts remain stable or regress
Administration of topical corticosteroids for three months
Immediate surgical excision to prevent rupture and infection
questions.question: A patient presents with a small asymptomatic conjunctival cyst. The MOST appropriate initial management is:

options: Image the optic nerve head using high-resolution fundus photography
Examine the iridocorneal angle where the iris and cornea meet
Measure the intraocular pressure using corneal applanation technique
Assess the visual field loss pattern in established glaucoma cases
Measure the thickness of the central cornea in millimeters
questions.explanation: Gonioscopy is a diagnostic procedure specifically used to examine the iridocorneal angle, the junction where the iris and cornea meet that contains the trabecular meshwork drainage system. This examination determines whether the drainage angle is open (as in open-angle glaucoma) or closed (as in angle-closure glaucoma), which is critical for classifying the type of glaucoma and selecting the appropriate treatment. Without gonioscopy, the drainage angle cannot be visualized by any other standard examination method.
questions.question: Gonioscopy in the diagnosis of glaucoma is used SPECIFICALLY to:

questions.explanation: OCT in glaucoma is used primarily to detect structural changes in the optic nerve head and retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL), which can show glaucomatous damage before visual field defects become detectable by perimetry. OCT measures the thickness of the RNFL around the optic nerve with high precision, providing objective, reproducible data for diagnosing early glaucoma and monitoring progression over time. Serial OCT measurements are increasingly used alongside visual field testing to guide treatment decisions.
questions.question: Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) is used in glaucoma diagnosis PRIMARILY to:
options: Identify aqueous humor flow patterns through the trabecular meshwork
Measure intraocular pressure continuously over twenty-four hours
Assess the blood flow in the optic nerve head vasculature
Look for structural changes in the optic nerve and retinal nerve fiber layer
Map corneal topography to detect thinning from elevated pressure

questions.explanation: The most effective preventive education for athletes at risk of corneal abrasions is to wear sport-specific protective eyewear designed to shield the eyes from impact, flying objects, and environmental debris. Protective goggles, face shields, or helmets with visors are recommended based on the sport. General eye hygiene, prompt medical attention for any eye injury, and avoidance of wearing contact lenses during high-impact activities further reduce the risk of corneal abrasion.
questions.question: The MOST effective patient education for preventing recurrent corneal abrasions in athletes includes:
options: Avoiding all sporting activity until corneal healing is fully confirmed
Wearing protective eyewear designed for specific sports activities
Applying antibiotic ointment before every sporting practice session
Inserting daily disposable contact lenses before contact sports
Performing warm-up eye exercises before engaging in physical sport
Correct high myopia by ablating the central stroma to flatten the cornea
Replace the diseased corneal tissue with donor tissue
Strengthen the corneal stroma by inducing collagen cross-linking
Restore endothelial cell function by laser stimulation of cell regeneration
Remove superficial corneal tissue to modify its shape and treat erosions
questions.question: Phototherapeutic Keratectomy (PTK) is used in the treatment of corneal dystrophies PRIMARILY to:
questions.explanation: Phototherapeutic Keratectomy (PTK) is a laser procedure used in corneal dystrophies to remove diseased superficial corneal tissue, treating recurrent corneal erosions and modifying the corneal surface shape. It is particularly useful for epithelial and anterior stromal dystrophies where surface irregularity and recurrent erosions compromise vision and cause pain. PTK can improve visual acuity and reduce the frequency of painful erosion episodes, providing significant quality-of-life benefit to affected patients.

questions.question: Surgery-induced necrotizing scleritis (SINS) is MOST commonly associated with which organism?
options: Staphylococcus aureus causing post-cataract surgical infection
Pseudomonas aeruginosa following pterygiectomy or scleral buckling
Aspergillus fumigatus following vitreoretinal surgical procedures
Herpes simplex virus type 1 following corneal debridement
questions.explanation: Surgery-induced necrotizing scleritis (SINS) is a rare complication of ocular surgery, most strongly associated with Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection following procedures such as pterygiectomy, cataract surgery, and scleral buckling. SINS typically presents weeks to months after surgery with a necrotizing wound-related inflammation. Prompt recognition and aggressive antibiotic treatment are essential to prevent progressive scleral destruction and vision loss.

questions.question: The MOST common form of ocular Kaposi Sarcoma location in HIV patients is:
questions.explanation: Kaposi Sarcoma most commonly affects the conjunctiva and eyelids in the ocular setting of HIV/AIDS, presenting as reddish-purple vascular lesions that are part of the systemic manifestation of Kaposi Sarcoma. Conjunctival KS can cause irritation, discharge, and cosmetic concern. Management includes optimization of antiretroviral therapy, local radiation therapy, chemotherapy, or surgical excision depending on the size and symptomatology of the lesions. It is categorized as a neoplastic ocular manifestation of HIV.
options: On the corneal surface causing recurrent epithelial erosions
Within the retinal nerve fiber layer causing cotton-wool spots
Within the vitreous cavity causing floaters and visual disturbance
On the conjunctiva and eyelids as part of systemic KS

The pain it causes is too severe for conventional analgesics to control
It always leads to anterior chamber hemorrhage requiring urgent drainage
questions.explanation: An acute angle-closure glaucoma attack is a true ocular emergency because the sudden, extreme elevation of intraocular pressure can cause irreversible optic nerve damage and blindness if not treated immediately. The iris blocks the drainage angle completely, causing IOP to rise rapidly to dangerous levels. Symptoms include sudden blurred vision, severe eye pain, headache, nausea, vomiting, and halos around lights. Immediate medical treatment to lower IOP and emergency laser iridotomy are required to prevent permanent blindness.

questions.explanation: Scleritis is described as a frightening and potentially debilitating condition that causes severe pain, visual disturbance, and significant psychosocial distress. Nurses provide emotional support to help patients and their families cope with the severity and implications of the condition, including the associated systemic autoimmune disease. Emotional support complements pharmacological treatment and improves the patient's ability to adhere to treatment and follow-up care.
questions.question: Emotional support is emphasized in scleritis nursing management PRIMARILY because:
options: Emotional distress directly causes recurrence of scleritis episodes
Emotional support directly reduces scleral inflammatory markers

questions.explanation: The conjunctival autograft technique involves harvesting healthy conjunctival tissue, often from beneath the upper eyelid, and suturing or gluing it over the exposed scleral bed after pterygium excision, significantly reducing recurrence rates compared with leaving the sclera bare. Amniotic membrane grafting is an alternative but uses donor tissue rather than the patient's own conjunctiva. This technique has become a preferred approach because of its favourable recurrence profile.
options: Cryotherapy applied directly to the pterygium
Simple excision without any tissue coverage
Bare sclera technique without any graft
questions.question: Which surgical technique for pterygium removal uses the patient's own conjunctival tissue to cover the exposed scleral bed?

options: Farmer's lung due to dust inhalation
Miner's elbow due to repetitive trauma
Hunter's thumb due to tool handling
Swimmer's ear due to water immersion
Surfer's eye due to UV and wind exposure
questions.question: Pterygium is also colloquially known as:
questions.explanation: Pterygium is colloquially known as 'Surfer's Eye' because it commonly affects individuals who spend prolonged periods outdoors and are exposed to ultraviolet radiation, wind, and dust-conditions typical of surfing environments. The UV radiation damages limbal stem cells and triggers fibrovascular proliferation across the cornea. This nickname reflects the dominant environmental etiology rather than an infectious or hereditary cause.

questions.question: A TED patient prescribed prisms in their glasses would MOST likely have which symptom?
options: Double vision (diplopia) caused by restricted extraocular muscle movement
Reduced colour vision caused by optic nerve compression
Unilateral proptosis causing periorbital asymmetry and cosmetic concern
Severe photophobia caused by corneal lagophthalmos and desiccation
Corneal exposure causing dryness and surface irregularity
questions.explanation: Prisms in glasses are prescribed specifically to correct double vision (diplopia) caused by restricted extraocular muscle movement in Thyroid Eye Disease. Inflammation and fibrosis of the extraocular muscles (most commonly the inferior and medial rectus muscles) impairs their ability to coordinate eye movements, resulting in misalignment and diplopia. Prisms help align the visual fields of both eyes to eliminate the double image, providing significant functional improvement while more definitive treatment is planned.

options: Advise the patient to blink rapidly every few minutes
Restrict the patient's fluid intake to reduce periorbital edema
Tape the eyelids open to ensure adequate ocular ventilation
Administer topical mydriatic drops to dilate the pupil
Apply lubricating eye drops to prevent corneal drying
questions.explanation: When a patient cannot close their eyelids completely following eye surgery or due to conditions such as thyroid eye disease, the cornea is at risk of dryness and ulceration. Applying lubricating eye drops or ointments prevents corneal exposure keratopathy by maintaining ocular surface moisture. Taping the eyelids open would worsen exposure, while mydriatic drops address pupil dilation rather than lid closure problems.
questions.question: Which nursing intervention is MOST appropriate when a post-operative ophthalmic patient reports inability to close their eyelids completely?

questions.explanation: A conjunctival cyst causes difficulty in eye closure when it grows large enough to mechanically interfere with the apposition of the upper and lower eyelids. This inability to close the eye may result in corneal exposure, causing dryness, tearing, itchiness, and burning sensation. The patient may also notice problems related to inadequate corneal protection during sleep, emphasizing the need for surgical intervention in large or symptomatic cysts.
questions.question: A conjunctival cyst MOST likely causes difficulty in eye closure when:
options: It is associated with mild conjunctival inflammation and redness
It is a retention cyst with minimal lymphatic involvement
It is a small asymptomatic inclusion cyst on the bulbar conjunctiva
It is located on the superior palpebral conjunctiva under the upper lid
It grows large enough to interfere mechanically with lid apposition

questions.question: Stage 4 hypertensive retinopathy is MOST specifically characterized by:
questions.explanation: Stage 4 hypertensive retinopathy is the most severe stage and is characterized by all changes seen in Stage 3 covering the entire fundus, plus bilateral papilledema (swelling of the optic disc), retinal edema, and exudative retinal detachment. This stage indicates a hypertensive emergency (malignant hypertension) with critically elevated blood pressure causing widespread retinal and optic nerve damage. It is associated with severe systemic end-organ damage and requires urgent blood pressure reduction.

A tube connecting the anterior chamber to the subconjunctival space
questions.question: Trabeculectomy in glaucoma surgery creates which structure to drain aqueous humor?
questions.explanation: Trabeculectomy creates a tiny surgical flap in the sclera through which aqueous humor drains from the anterior chamber, and a filtering bleb (a bubble-like space) beneath the conjunctiva where the fluid collects and is absorbed by surrounding tissue. The bleb is usually hidden under the upper eyelid. This surgical drainage pathway bypasses the obstructed trabecular meshwork and reduces intraocular pressure. Mitomycin C or 5-fluorouracil may be used to reduce scarring and maintain bleb function.

options: Fungal colonization of the conjunctival surface in immunosuppressed patients

questions.question: Bitot's spots, which are white foamy patches on the conjunctiva, are MOST associated with:
questions.explanation: Bitot's spots are white, foamy or cheesy-appearing patches on the bulbar conjunctiva that are a hallmark sign of Vitamin A deficiency. They represent keratinization and squamous metaplasia of the conjunctival epithelium. Bitot's spots are commonly found in malnourished children in developing countries and serve as a clinical indicator for xerophthalmia. Vitamin A supplementation is the primary treatment and can reverse early stages of deficiency before corneal involvement occurs.

questions.question: The MOST common cause of conjunctivitis that produces a watery discharge and is highly contagious, often spreading via respiratory secretions, is:
questions.explanation: Viral conjunctivitis is most typically caused by adenovirus, which is highly contagious and often associated with watery discharge, eye redness, and discomfort. It frequently spreads through contact with infected respiratory secretions and can occur in outbreaks. The condition is self-limiting, usually resolving within one to two weeks, and treatment focuses on symptom relief with artificial tears and cold compresses rather than antivirals, unless caused by herpes simplex virus.

questions.question: Microaneurysms in diabetic retinopathy are MOST directly caused by:
questions.explanation: Microaneurysms in diabetic retinopathy result directly from the loss of intramural pericytes of retinal capillaries due to hyperglycemia-induced sorbitol accumulation through the aldose reductase pathway. Pericytes normally provide structural support and autoregulate capillary tone; their loss results in weakness and eventual saccular outpouching of capillary walls, forming microaneurysms. These are the earliest detectable signs of diabetic retinopathy and reflect the underlying microvascular pathology.

The characteristic pain of scleritis is described as severe, dull, and boring in nature, and is exacerbated by eye movements due to the extraocular muscle insertions into the sclera. The pain may worsen at night and awaken the patient from sleep. It often radiates to involve the ear, scalp, face, and jaw. This distinctive pain pattern helps differentiate scleritis from episcleritis, which is much less painful.

Diabetic retinopathy is the MOST common cause of vision loss in which specific population?
questions.explanation: Diabetic retinopathy is the most common cause of vision loss in people with diabetes across all age groups. It affects blood vessels in the retina, causing them to leak, close, or grow abnormally. About one in three people with diabetes over age 40 already have some signs of diabetic retinopathy. The longer a person has diabetes and the poorer the metabolic control, the more likely they are to develop significant retinopathy leading to vision impairment or blindness.
options: Patients with secondary glaucoma from steroid-induced pressure elevation
Elderly patients over 80 years with age-related macular degeneration
Children under 12 years with poorly controlled Type 1 diabetes
Pregnant women with gestational diabetes mellitus
People with diabetes across all age groups globally

questions.explanation: Glaucoma drainage implants are most commonly indicated in patients who have failed previous trabeculectomy, have conjunctival scarring that compromises standard filtering surgery, or have complex forms of glaucoma (such as neovascular, inflammatory, or post-traumatic glaucoma) with a high risk of surgical failure from fibrosis. They provide an alternative drainage pathway that is less susceptible to scarring than trabeculectomy blebs and are increasingly used as a primary surgical option in certain high-risk cases.
options: Primary open-angle glaucoma as first-line surgical management
Failed trabeculectomy or have complex glaucoma with high recurrence risk
Early open-angle glaucoma responsive to single prostaglandin analogue
Normal-tension glaucoma with stable visual fields on two medications
Acute angle-closure glaucoma responding to laser iridotomy
questions.question: Glaucoma drainage implants are MOST indicated in patients who have:

questions.explanation: Anti-VEGF (vascular endothelial growth factor inhibitor) medications such as ranibizumab (Lucentis) and aflibercept (Eylea) are used in diabetic macular edema to prevent new blood vessel formation and reduce macular fluid leakage by blocking VEGF, the key growth factor driving neovascularization and vascular permeability. These injections not only stop the progression of macular disease but may also lead to improvement in vision by reducing macular swelling that impairs central vision.
options: Destroy abnormal retinal tissue by photochemical laser activation
Replace the antioxidant function of the damaged retinal pigment epithelium
Reduce the metabolic demand on the ischemic retinal tissue directly
Prevent new blood vessel formation and reduce macular fluid leakage
Improve the permeability of the blood-retinal barrier to antibiotic delivery
questions.question: Anti-VEGF injections in diabetic macular edema are used PRIMARILY to:
Systemic Acyclovir is used in herpetic ophthalmia neonatorum PRIMARILY to:
questions.explanation: Systemic Acyclovir is used in herpetic ophthalmia neonatorum caused by Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) to reduce the risk of systemic HSV infection, including neonatal herpes encephalitis and disseminated disease. Herpetic neonatal conjunctivitis occurs in the context of systemic and CNS infection, making systemic antiviral therapy critical. Topical antiviral treatment alone would be insufficient to address the systemic infectious burden of HSV in neonates.
options: Eliminate the silver nitrate chemical irritation in chemical conjunctivitis
Prevent chlamydial co-infection in immunocompromised neonates
Replace topical antiviral agents that are ineffective in neonates
Reduce the risk of systemic herpes simplex virus infection spreading
Accelerate healing of gonococcal corneal ulcers through antiviral action

questions.explanation: Fluorescein staining is applied to the surface of the eye to detect corneal abrasions or ulcers that may mimic conjunctivitis symptoms such as redness, discharge, and discomfort. Under blue-light illumination, areas of corneal epithelial damage take up the dye and appear bright green, allowing the examiner to differentiate conjunctival inflammation from more serious corneal pathology. This is important because corneal ulcers require different and more urgent management.
questions.question: Fluorescein staining is used in the diagnostic workup of conjunctivitis PRIMARILY to:
options: Identify the causative bacteria in the conjunctival discharge
Assess blood vessel dilation pattern in the sclera and episclera
Visualize the tarsal conjunctival papillae under slit-lamp
Detect corneal abrasions or ulcers that mimic conjunctivitis
Confirm the presence of giant papillae in contact lens wearers

questions.question: A pseudo-pterygium differs from a true pterygium in that it is caused by:
options: Injury or inflammation rather than benign degenerative growth
Recurrence of pterygium following inadequate surgical removal
UV radiation causing fibrovascular proliferation across the cornea
Familial hereditary factors causing bilateral nasal involvement
Primary degenerative overgrowth of limbal stem cells
questions.explanation: A pseudo-pterygium is a fold of conjunctiva caused by injury or inflammation, rather than the benign degenerative fibrovascular growth that characterizes a true pterygium. The distinction is clinically important because pseudo-pterygia can be attached to the cornea at any point along their length (not just at the tip as with true pterygia), and they arise from a different underlying mechanism, requiring a different clinical approach and management strategy.

questions.question: Which clinical feature MOST reliably distinguishes scleritis from episcleritis?
options: Scleritis exclusively affects the posterior segment of the globe
Both respond equally well to topical non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drops
Episcleritis causes deeper inflammation affecting the choroid and retina
Scleritis is more painful and may lead to vision loss; episcleritis is milder
Both conditions affect vision equally and cause similar discharge
questions.explanation: Scleritis is much more painful than episcleritis and can lead to vision loss through progressive ocular tissue inflammation or complications from an underlying collagen vascular disease. Episcleritis is a more superficial inflammation that typically does not threaten vision and responds to topical non-steroidal eye drops. The depth of inflammation, intensity of pain, and potential for systemic disease association are the key distinguishing features.

options: It provides antibiotic sensitivity data faster than culture methods
It has improved diagnostic sensitivity over clinical examination alone
It is less expensive than Gram staining in resource-limited settings
It directly visualizes the organism under electron microscopy
It can identify multiple organisms simultaneously in one reaction
questions.explanation: PCR of conjunctival scrapings has been shown to improve diagnostic sensitivity over clinical examination alone for organisms such as Chlamydia trachomatis and Herpes Simplex Virus in ophthalmia neonatorum. It identifies microbial DNA even when organisms are present in very low quantities and when culture may be negative. For HSV specifically, PCR is more sensitive than viral culture, making it the preferred method in modern ophthalmic neonatal diagnostics.
questions.question: Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is MOST useful in the diagnosis of ophthalmia neonatorum because:

questions.explanation: Necrotizing anterior scleritis is the most severe form of anterior scleritis, characterized by severe pain, extreme scleral tenderness, and severe vasculitis with infarction and necrosis, potentially exposing the choroid. It carries the highest risk of vision impairment, with 75% of cases eventually developing visual impairment. Scleromalacia perforans is a rare variant of necrotizing anterior scleritis that occurs without pain.
questions.question: The MOST severe form of anterior scleritis is:
options: Posterior scleritis with exudative retinal detachment
Necrotizing anterior scleritis with severe vasculitis and necrosis
Nodular non-necrotizing scleritis with discrete tender nodules
Diffuse non-necrotizing scleritis with uniform scleral edema
Scleromalacia perforans with painless avascular scleral thinning

questions.question: A nurse educating a patient with keratoconus should PARTICULARLY emphasize avoiding:
questions.explanation: Patients with keratoconus should be particularly educated to avoid vigorous eye rubbing, as this mechanical trauma can accelerate the thinning and progressive distortion of the cornea. Eye rubbing can also hasten the progression of keratoconus in patients who already have the condition. Additionally, treatment of underlying allergies and asthma that cause the urge to rub is important, as inflammation from these conditions has been linked to corneal tissue breakdown.
options: All forms of spectacle correction in favor of contact lens wear
Swimming or water sports without protective goggles
Bright sunlight exposure without polarized lenses while outdoors
Vitamin A-rich foods that may worsen the corneal thinning
Vigorous eye rubbing which can accelerate corneal thinning

questions.question: The nurse educates a glaucoma patient on the MOST important adherence behavior to prevent vision loss, which is:
questions.explanation: The most important adherence behavior for glaucoma management is using prescribed eye drops every day as directed, without interruption, even when the patient has no symptoms. Glaucoma eye drops control intraocular pressure to protect the optic nerve from further damage, but they only work when taken consistently. Non-adherence to topical glaucoma medication is the leading cause of progressive optic nerve damage and vision loss in glaucoma patients who have already been diagnosed and are receiving treatment.
options: Wearing UV-protective sunglasses to prevent glaucoma progression
Consuming a diet high in antioxidants to protect the optic nerve
Attending annual ophthalmology reviews without fail each year
Using prescribed eye drops every day as directed without interruption
Avoiding all strenuous exercise to prevent IOP fluctuations

questions.explanation: Patients with scleritis should be advised to wear sunglasses to protect their eyes from UV radiation and bright light that can exacerbate photosensitivity. They should also avoid contact sports or activities that may cause eye trauma, which can worsen scleral inflammation or lead to perforation in a weakened sclera. This protective advice is part of a comprehensive nursing education plan that complements pharmacological management.
options: Apply topical lubricants every hour to prevent corneal ulceration
Use cold compresses continuously to reduce scleral vascularity
Remove contact lenses permanently to prevent scleral trauma
Wear sunglasses and avoid activities that may cause eye injury
Perform gentle periorbital massage to improve scleral blood flow
questions.question: A nurse educating a patient with scleritis about eye protection should include which SPECIFIC advice?

options: Traumatic scleritis from penetrating eye injury
Autoimmune scleritis associated with rheumatoid arthritis
Infectious scleritis caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Drug-induced scleritis as a rare medication side effect
Surgically induced scleritis following scleral buckling
questions.explanation: Drug-induced scleritis is rare but most strongly linked to bisphosphonate medications, which are commonly used in the management of osteoporosis and bone metastases. The nurse should be aware of this association when taking medication histories from patients presenting with scleritis, as withdrawal of the offending drug may be part of the treatment. Bisphosphonate-induced scleritis can mimic autoimmune scleritis in its presentation.
questions.question: Bisphosphonate medications are MOST strongly linked to which cause of scleritis?

options: One in ten post-operative cataract surgery patients
One in approximately one thousand cataract surgery cases
One in every five thousand cataract surgery procedures
One in every three patients with pre-existing diabetic retinopathy
One in every hundred outpatient cataract procedures
questions.explanation: Acute bacterial endophthalmitis, described as a devastating complication of cataract surgery, occurs in approximately one in 1,000 cases. It typically presents within the first few days after surgery with severe pain, reduced vision, hypopyon, and marked vitritis. It requires immediate ophthalmic emergency treatment with intravitreal antibiotics and in some cases vitrectomy. Despite treatment, visual outcomes can be poor, making prevention through sterile surgical technique and post-operative antibiotic prophylaxis critically important.
questions.question: Acute bacterial endophthalmitis following cataract surgery occurs in approximately:

options: A community health worker interested in eye screening
A first-year student in secondary school with good WAEC results
A registered nurse with two years of clinical experience
A medical student specializing in ophthalmology
A doctor completing a fellowship in vitreoretinal surgery
questions.explanation: A registered nurse with one to two years of post-qualification clinical experience and the required academic qualifications (five credits in relevant subjects) is the appropriate candidate for a post-basic ophthalmic nursing program in Nigeria. The program is designed for practicing nurses who wish to specialize in ophthalmic care. Community health workers and medical students are in different training tracks and are ineligible for this specific program.
questions.question: Which of the following patients is MOST likely to benefit from referral to a post-basic ophthalmic nursing program in Nigeria?
A patient with allergic conjunctivitis should be instructed to AVOID which of the following activities during an acute episode?
questions.explanation: Sharing eye drops with household members is contraindicated as it can transfer infectious agents and alter the treatment intended for a specific condition. Each patient's medication is prescribed for their individual ocular condition, and sharing creates risk of cross-contamination and inappropriate treatment. Patients should be educated that eye medications are strictly personal and should never be shared, even among family members with apparently similar symptoms.
options: Applying cold compresses to reduce periorbital swelling
Wearing eye protection when outdoors in high pollen season
Using daily disposable contact lenses that are properly cleaned
Sharing eye drops with a household member to save costs
Taking prescribed antihistamine drops as directed by the physician

questions.explanation: In cataract surgery, the cloudy natural lens is surgically removed (most commonly by phacoemulsification) and replaced with an artificial intraocular lens (IOL) that is implanted inside the remaining lens capsular bag. The IOL restores the focusing power of the removed natural lens and provides clear vision. After surgery, patients often have significantly improved vision but may require a new glasses prescription for fine-tuning of distance or near vision, particularly if a standard monofocal IOL was implanted.
questions.question: Cataract lens surgery replaces the cloudy natural lens with which device?
options: A gas bubble supporting the posterior capsule after phacoemulsification
A polymethylmethacrylate contact lens fitted on the corneal surface
A silicone oil tamponade filling the vitreous cavity after lens removal
A collagen shield positioned on the corneal surface temporarily
An artificial intraocular lens implanted in the lens capsule

questions.explanation: The first nursing action for acute pain in an HIV patient with uveitis is to assess the severity, location, and characteristics of the pain using a validated pain rating scale. This assessment provides the baseline data necessary for planning appropriate pharmacological and non-pharmacological pain management interventions and for monitoring treatment effectiveness. Only after pain is accurately assessed can the appropriate analgesic or anti-inflammatory treatment be selected in consultation with the medical team.
questions.question: A nursing diagnosis of 'Acute pain related to ocular inflammation' in an HIV patient with uveitis requires which FIRST action?
options: Administering topical corticosteroids without ophthalmologist review
Applying bilateral warm compresses hourly to the periorbital area
Referring the patient for immediate retinal detachment surgery
Administering oral analgesics without prior pain assessment
Assessing the severity and characteristics of pain using a rating scale

questions.explanation: Giemsa staining of conjunctival scrapings is used to identify basophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions that are characteristic of Chlamydia trachomatis, which is an obligate intracellular organism. This staining technique helps differentiate chlamydial conjunctivitis from gonococcal infection, which is identified by Gram stain showing Gram-negative intracellular diplococci. PCR is more sensitive but Giemsa staining provides a rapid, accessible morphological identification.
questions.question: The Giemsa stain in the laboratory workup for ophthalmia neonatorum is used SPECIFICALLY to identify:
options: Gram-negative intracellular diplococci in gonococcal infection
Polymerase chain reaction amplification of chlamydial DNA
Herpes simplex viral particles on epithelial cell scraping
Basophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions in chlamydial infection
Direct fluorescent antibody staining for viral antigen detection

questions.explanation: For individuals aged 55-64 years, glaucoma testing should occur every one to two years, and for those over 65 every six months to twelve months. For a 60-year-old, a one-to-two-year screening interval reflects the increasing risk of glaucoma with age. Early detection through regular comprehensive eye examinations, including optic nerve assessment, visual field testing, and IOP measurement, is the only way to identify glaucoma before irreversible vision loss occurs, as the disease is asymptomatic in its early stages.
options: Once every decade sufficient for low-risk individuals over 60
Only when symptomatic as early screening is not cost-effective
Every one to two years based on age-stratified screening guidelines
Every six months only if family history of glaucoma is confirmed
Every five to ten years as symptoms are unlikely at this age
questions.question: The MOST appropriate glaucoma screening frequency for an individual aged 60 years is:
The nurse caring for a patient with cataract and concurrent diabetes must MOST carefully monitor which parameter after cataract surgery?
questions.explanation: After cataract surgery in a diabetic patient, blood glucose levels must be carefully monitored because hyperglycemia impairs wound healing, increases infection risk, and can exacerbate diabetic macular edema post-operatively. The stress of surgery can also cause significant glucose fluctuations in diabetic patients. The nursing role includes pre-operative glycemic optimization, intraoperative glucose monitoring, and post-operative blood sugar management in collaboration with the endocrinology team to minimize surgical complications.
options: Aqueous humor protein content to detect early blood-aqueous barrier breakdown
Blood glucose levels to prevent complications of glycemic dysregulation
Corneal endothelial cell density to detect post-operative decompensation
Vitreous hemorrhage in the posterior segment from proliferative retinopathy
Intraocular lens centration and position to ensure optimal optical alignment

questions.question: The CORRECT positioning for a neonate with ophthalmia neonatorum and respiratory difficulty is:
questions.explanation: Positioning a neonate with ineffective breathing pattern related to increased airway secretions in a semi-Fowler's (upright or head-elevated) position facilitates lung expansion and improves respiratory effort. This position reduces the work of breathing by allowing gravity to assist diaphragmatic descent. Suctioning and oxygen administration may also be necessary. Prone or Trendelenburg positions would worsen respiratory distress in the neonate.
options: Supine flat position with neck extension for airway opening
Trendelenburg position to promote venous return to the heart
Semi-Fowler's (upright) position to facilitate lung expansion
Left lateral decubitus position to prevent aspiration
Prone position to allow postural drainage of nasal secretions

questions.question: Open-angle glaucoma earns the name 'silent thief of sight' PRIMARILY because:
questions.explanation: Open-angle glaucoma is called the 'silent thief of sight' because it progresses without pain or noticeable symptoms in the early stages. The initial peripheral vision loss goes undetected by patients, and by the time significant visual impairment is noticed, the majority of optic nerve fibers may already have been destroyed. This asymptomatic progression makes regular eye examinations with optic nerve assessment and visual field testing essential for early detection and prevention of blindness.
options: It is invisible on standard fundoscopy until the optic nerve is fully destroyed
It exclusively causes blindness in patients over 80 years of age
It occurs painlessly only in the sleeping hours when patients cannot notice
It only causes vision loss when treated with excessive eye drop doses
It causes no warning signs and peripheral vision loss goes unnoticed until late

questions.explanation: Immune stromal keratitis appears following a previous episode of epithelial keratitis when the virus has become dormant. It is caused by inflammation from non-replicating viral particles trapped within the stromal layer rather than active viral infection. The corneal epithelium remains intact but the stroma becomes edematous, causing vision loss. This distinction is clinically important because treatment requires immunosuppression rather than antivirals that target active viral replication.
questions.question: Which type of HSK is caused by viral particles within the corneal stroma WITHOUT active viral replication?
options: Endotheliitis from direct viral infection of the endothelial layer
Stromal necrotic keratitis from active viral invasion of stroma
Epithelial keratitis with surface dendritic ulcer formation
Immune stromal keratitis without active viral presence
Recurrent epithelial erosion syndrome from dormant viral activity

questions.explanation: Tonometry is the standard, first-line test to confirm or rule out elevated intraocular pressure (IOP). The ophthalmic nurse performs this as part of the routine assessment in the clinic, and abnormal findings would prompt referral to the ophthalmologist for further evaluation. Fluorescein angiography, topography, Schirmer's test, and electroretinogram assess other specific aspects of eye function unrelated to measuring IOP directly.
questions.question: An ophthalmic nurse suspects a patient may have elevated intraocular pressure. Which test should be performed NEXT?

options: Sudden changes in vision or new floaters suggesting retinal involvement
Mild periorbital puffiness without proptosis or visual change
Mild bilateral conjunctival hyperemia without discharge
Transient photophobia resolving spontaneously within hours
Mild bilateral ptosis without restriction of eye movement
questions.explanation: Sudden changes in vision or the appearance of new floaters in an HIV-positive patient suggest serious retinal involvement such as CMV retinitis, toxoplasma retinochoroiditis, or retinal detachment, which are ophthalmic emergencies requiring urgent ophthalmological evaluation. Early detection and treatment of retinal opportunistic infections are critical to preventing irreversible vision loss. The nurse plays a vital role in monitoring for these symptoms and escalating care promptly to prevent blindness.
questions.question: A nurse monitoring an HIV-positive patient for ocular complications should MOST urgently report which finding?

questions.explanation: Visual acuity testing measures the clarity or sharpness of a patient's vision at various distances using an eye chart and a series of progressively smaller letters. This common test provides baseline data for monitoring changes and planning nursing care. It is distinct from tonometry, which measures intraocular pressure, or fundoscopy, which examines the posterior segment of the eye.
options: Assess intraocular pressure of the eye
Examine the posterior segment of the globe
Measure the clarity of the patient's vision
questions.question: Visual acuity testing in the ophthalmic clinic is primarily performed to:

options: Slow loss of side (peripheral) vision creating tunnel vision effect
Mild intermittent blurring of near vision with prolonged reading
Monocular diplopia from lens refractive index changes with IOP
Photophobia in bright light from pupil constriction dysfunction
Bilateral sharp central vision loss with intact peripheral vision
questions.question: The nurse assessing a glaucoma patient's visual function should be MOST alert to which symptom indicating significant optic nerve damage?
questions.explanation: Slow loss of side (peripheral) vision, creating an increasingly narrow visual field known as tunnel vision, is the hallmark symptom of significant optic nerve damage in open-angle glaucoma. Most patients do not notice this loss until it is severe because the brain compensates for peripheral field defects, and central vision is preserved until late stages. The nurse should ask specifically about difficulty navigating in unfamiliar environments, bumping into objects, or reduced driving confidence, which may indicate undetected or underestimated peripheral field loss.

options: Vigorous irrigation of the operative eye with normal saline hourly
Application of firm pressure bandage to prevent hyphema formation
Bilateral eye patching for 48 hours to ensure rest and healing
Instillation of prescribed antibiotic eye drops to prevent infection
Application of topical mydriatics to prevent posterior synechiae
questions.question: Which nursing intervention would be MOST appropriate as a postoperative comfort measure following conjunctival cyst excision?
questions.explanation: Instillation of prescribed antibiotic eye drops or ointments post-operatively is the most appropriate comfort and therapeutic measure after conjunctival cyst excision. This prevents post-operative infection, which is the most common and concerning complication. The nurse also monitors for signs of infection, educates the patient on proper wound care and eye cleaning, and schedules follow-up with the ophthalmologist for suture removal and wound assessment.

questions.question: A patient with conjunctivitis asks about complications of untreated disease. The nurse should explain that a MAJOR potential complication is:
options: Permanent discoloration of the conjunctival tissue permanently
Spontaneous resolution without any risk of recurrence
Corneal ulceration, particularly with severe or prolonged infection
Increased production of tears causing epiphora permanently
Development of benign conjunctival cysts as a sequela
questions.explanation: A major potential complication of untreated or inadequately managed conjunctivitis, particularly severe or prolonged cases, is corneal ulceration. This is especially dangerous in gonococcal conjunctivitis, where corneal perforation can occur rapidly if treatment is delayed. Other complications include conjunctival scarring, recurrent infections, and in neonates with gonococcal or chlamydial conjunctivitis, blindness. Early treatment is essential to prevent these outcomes.

questions.question: A nurse teaches a patient with diabetic retinopathy to use a home blood glucose monitoring device PRIMARILY to:
options: Monitor for hypoglycemia caused by intravitreal anti-VEGF injections
Ensure glucose levels stay within an optimal range to prevent PDR progression
Document glucose levels for monthly ophthalmology clinic reporting
Detect early signs of diabetic nephropathy through glucose spill
Replace the need for HbA1c laboratory testing every three months
questions.explanation: Teaching patients with diabetic retinopathy to use a home glucose monitoring device ensures that their blood glucose levels remain within an optimal target range, which is the most important modifiable factor in preventing and slowing the progression of diabetic retinopathy. Poor glycemic control is the primary driver of microvascular damage in the retina. Accurate home monitoring guides dietary choices, physical activity, and medication adjustments that collectively maintain metabolic control and protect retinal health.

questions.question: A pterygium patient due for surgery asks about the recurrence rate after conjunctival autograft surgery. The nurse should inform them that recurrence occurs in approximately:
options: One in every twenty patients using amniotic membrane graft
One in every ten patients who undergo bare sclera technique
One in every three patients regardless of surgical technique
One in five patients within the first year of surgery
One in fifty patients with conjunctival autograft technique
questions.explanation: With the Free Conjunctival Autograft technique, the risk of pterygium recurrence is approximately one in fifty, representing a significant improvement over the bare sclera technique, which has a much higher recurrence rate. The autograft uses healthy conjunctival tissue from under the upper eyelid as a transplant to the excised area, promoting better healing and reducing the inflammatory stimulus for regrowth. Fibrin glue is preferred over sutures to minimize post-operative irritation.

options: Producing an acute allergic hypersensitivity reaction
Inducing chronic oxidative damage to limbal stem cells
Directly causing bacterial colonisation of the conjunctiva
Causing sudden mechanical rupture of the sclera
Triggering immediate viral replication within the cornea
questions.question: Ultraviolet radiation is believed to contribute to pterygium formation primarily through which mechanism?
questions.explanation: Chronic ultraviolet exposure is thought to cause cumulative oxidative stress and damage to limbal stem cells and conjunctival tissue, triggering abnormal fibrovascular proliferation that manifests as pterygium over time, particularly in individuals with significant outdoor sun exposure. This mechanism is distinct from infectious, allergic, or acute traumatic processes. Understanding this pathophysiology underlies advice to use protective eyewear as a preventive measure.

options: Within two to five days due to gonococcal transmission
Within five to fourteen days from chlamydial infection
Within six weeks after discharge from the neonatal unit
Within two weeks after birth following systemic HSV infection
Within 24 hours of birth due to silver nitrate exposure
questions.question: Herpetic conjunctivitis in neonates is MOST likely to occur:
questions.explanation: Herpetic conjunctivitis (caused by Herpes Simplex Virus) in neonates typically occurs within two weeks after birth and is usually associated with systemic and CNS infection with the herpes simplex virus. It presents with watery discharge, skin lesions on the lid margins, eye redness, and eyelid edema. This timing helps differentiate herpetic from chemical (within 24 hours), gonococcal (2-5 days), and chlamydial (5-14 days) conjunctivitis.

options: Topical antifungal ointment applied twice daily to the affected eye
Intravenous NSAIDs for more potent anti-inflammatory corneal effect
Oral antihistamines reducing light sensitivity through central sedation
Topical corticosteroids reducing corneal epithelial inflammatory response
Cycloplegic agents that reduce ciliary muscle spasm and photosensitivity
questions.question: Corneal abrasion patients presenting with photophobia benefit MOST from which pharmacological intervention?
questions.explanation: Cycloplegic agents such as atropine or cyclopentolate are used in corneal abrasion management to reduce the painful ciliary muscle spasm that causes photophobia and contributes to the severe eye pain associated with corneal abrasions. By temporarily paralyzing the ciliary muscles, cycloplegics provide significant pain relief and reduce the photophobia that limits daily functioning. They are used alongside topical antibiotics and lubricating drops in the comprehensive management of corneal abrasions.

questions.question: Collagen Cross-Linking (CXL) is used in keratoconus management PRIMARILY to:
questions.explanation: Collagen Cross-Linking (CXL) is a minimally invasive procedure approved by the FDA in 2016 for the treatment of keratoconus. It works by using riboflavin (vitamin B2) eye drops combined with ultraviolet A light to create new bonds between collagen fibers in the corneal stroma, thereby strengthening the cornea and halting the progressive thinning and bulging. CXL addresses the underlying structural weakness of keratoconus and is particularly beneficial in younger patients with progressive disease.
options: Correct irregular astigmatism using excimer laser photoablation
Strengthen corneal collagen fibers to halt progressive corneal thinning
Replace the endothelial cells damaged by progressive corneal disease
Improve visual acuity by reshaping the corneal surface with riboflavin
Remove the scarred central corneal tissue and replace it with donor cornea

questions.question: The nursing diagnosis 'Disturbed Body Image related to Exophthalmos' in a TED patient MOST appropriately requires which intervention?
questions.explanation: The nursing diagnosis of Disturbed Body Image related to exophthalmos requires the nurse to acknowledge the patient's feelings about the visible change in their appearance and provide psychosocial support. The nurse should create a safe, supportive environment for the patient to express concerns, explore coping strategies, and access counseling or support groups if needed. Addressing body image disturbance is as important as managing the physical symptoms to ensure holistic patient-centered care in TED.
options: Performing bilateral tarsal taping to mechanically reduce globe prominence
Acknowledging the patient's feelings and providing psychosocial support
Administering systemic corticosteroids to rapidly reduce proptosis
Administering topical mydriatic drops to reduce periorbital puffiness
Restricting the patient's social activities until proptosis fully resolves

questions.question: Keratomalacia is MOST directly caused by a deficiency of:
questions.explanation: Keratomalacia is an ocular condition resulting from severe deficiency of Vitamin A (retinol), which is essential for maintaining normal vision and the health of mucosal epithelial surfaces including the conjunctiva and cornea. Vitamin A deficiency leads to drying and wrinkling of the conjunctiva, Bitot's spots, night blindness, corneal softening (keratomalacia), and ultimately ulceration and blindness if untreated. It is more common in malnourished populations and children with malabsorption disorders.
options: Vitamin D causing calcium deposition in the corneal stroma
Vitamin C causing impaired collagen synthesis in the cornea
Vitamin B12 resulting in optic nerve degeneration
Zinc deficiency impairing wound healing of corneal epithelium
Vitamin A leading to corneal softening and desiccation

questions.question: The optic nerve, which is examined during a dilated fundus examination, consists of approximately how many tiny nerve fibers?
questions.explanation: The optic nerve is made of more than one million tiny nerve fibers, often compared to an electric cable made of many small wires. As these nerve fibers die progressively due to conditions like glaucoma, blind spots develop in the patient's vision. Most blind spots go unnoticed until a majority of fibers are destroyed, which explains why glaucoma is called the 'silent thief of sight.'
options: Approximately two hundred fifty thousand fibers
Approximately seven hundred fifty thousand fibers
More than five hundred thousand fibers
More than one million tiny nerve fibers
Approximately one hundred thousand nerve fibers

questions.question: Ocular coherence tomography (OCT) in HIV-related ocular disease is MOST useful for:
options: Confirming the diagnosis of conjunctival Kaposi Sarcoma by imaging
Measuring the viral load of CMV directly within retinal tissue
Providing detailed cross-sectional retinal images detecting subtle changes
Measuring the CD4+ T-cell infiltration density in the retinal layers
Identifying the specific causative organism in retinal infections
questions.explanation: Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) is a non-invasive imaging technique that provides detailed cross-sectional images of the retina, allowing detection of subtle changes such as macular edema, retinal thinning, and structural abnormalities associated with HIV-related ocular disease. It enables clinicians to detect early retinal changes that may not yet be visible on clinical examination and to monitor disease progression and treatment response over time in patients with CMV retinitis and other retinal complications.

options: Secreting mucin to lubricate the corneal epithelial surface
Absorbing oxygen and nutrients from the tear film directly
Producing collagen fibers arranged in regular lamellar patterns
Pumping excess fluid out of the stroma to maintain clarity
Synthesizing glycosaminoglycans to maintain corneal hydration
questions.question: The endothelial layer of the cornea maintains corneal clarity PRIMARILY by:
questions.explanation: The corneal endothelium, the innermost single layer of cells, maintains corneal clarity by actively pumping excess fluid out of the corneal stroma. This prevents stromal edema and maintains the regular collagen fiber arrangement necessary for transparency. Loss of endothelial cells from dystrophies, surgery, or trauma reduces this pumping capacity, leading to stromal edema, corneal clouding, and reduced vision. Endothelial cell density can be measured by specular microscopy to monitor corneal health.

questions.question: A nursing care plan for a patient with conjunctivitis should include which measure PRIMARILY to prevent spread to others?
options: Prescribing corticosteroid eye drops for anti-inflammatory effect
Fitting the patient with opaque contact lenses during recovery
Performing a corneal biopsy to confirm the causative organism
Administering intravenous antibiotics for seven days
Educating patient on hand hygiene and avoiding eye contact with others
questions.explanation: Educating the patient on frequent handwashing and avoiding close contact with others is the primary nursing measure to prevent the spread of conjunctivitis, which is highly contagious especially when viral or bacterial in origin. Patients should also be instructed not to share towels, eye drops, or makeup. Good hygiene is more broadly impactful than antibiotic administration, which only targets bacterial forms of the condition.

options: Sudden onset of double vision from diabetic third nerve palsy
Bilateral gradual blurring of vision from symmetrical macular edema
Gradual painless narrowing of the peripheral visual field
Painful red eye with photophobia and corneal surface irregularity
Dark spots or floaters with possible sudden severe vision blockage
questions.explanation: Vitreous hemorrhage in diabetic retinopathy presents as dark spots or floaters in the field of vision when weak neovascular vessels bleed into the vitreous. If the bleeding is extensive, it can block all vision. Minor bleeding may resolve within weeks, but significant hemorrhage may require vitrectomy surgery. The nurse must educate diabetic retinopathy patients to report new floaters or sudden vision changes immediately, as these may indicate vitreous hemorrhage or retinal detachment requiring urgent intervention.
questions.question: A nurse monitoring a patient with diabetic retinopathy for the complication of vitreous hemorrhage should watch for:

questions.explanation: BMI assessment is performed as part of the comprehensive nursing assessment to provide baseline data about the patient's overall health status. Many systemic conditions associated with obesity, such as hypertension and diabetes, are significant risk factors for ocular complications including hypertensive retinopathy and diabetic retinopathy. Comprehensive baseline data guides holistic, evidence-based ophthalmic nursing care.
questions.question: During a patient encounter in the ophthalmic clinic, the nurse performs Body Mass Index (BMI) assessment PRIMARILY because:
options: BMI is required to calculate intraocular pressure
BMI is necessary before every slit-lamp examination
BMI directly measures visual acuity in overweight patients
BMI determines the dose of topical ophthalmic medications
BMI provides baseline data for comprehensive nursing assessment

questions.explanation: Retinal macroaneurysms are acquired focal dilations (outpouchings) of major retinal arterioles, distinct from diabetic microaneurysms in their size and location. They are associated with systemic hypertension and other vascular risk factors. Macroaneurysms may leak fluid causing macular edema or may rupture causing vitreous, preretinal, or intraretinal hemorrhages. Treatment may include laser photocoagulation or anti-VEGF therapy depending on the presence of macular involvement.
questions.question: Retinal Macroaneurysms in hypertensive retinopathy are BEST described as:
options: Acquired focal dilations of retinal arterioles prone to leakage and hemorrhage
Multiple tiny capillary outpouchings detected only on fluorescein angiography
Arteriovenous communications bypassing the retinal capillary bed
New blood vessel formations driven by ischemia-induced VEGF production
Calcified arteriolar plaques causing focal retinal infarction sites

questions.explanation: Cortical cataracts typically begin as wedge-shaped or spoke-like opacities radiating from the lens periphery toward the centre, in contrast to nuclear cataracts which begin centrally, or posterior subcapsular cataracts which are located just beneath the posterior capsule. This distinct pattern helps classify the type of cataract on slit-lamp examination and can have different implications for visual symptoms and rate of progression. Recognising the pattern assists in patient counselling about expected visual changes.
questions.question: Cortical cataract characteristically begins with which pattern of lens opacification?
options: A dense, uniform, central opacity affecting the nucleus only
Wedge-shaped or spoke-like opacities in the lens periphery
Complete opacification of the entire lens simultaneously
An opacity confined strictly to the posterior capsule only
A ring-shaped opacity confined to the lens equator only

questions.question: Corneal dystrophies are BEST classified according to which primary criterion?
questions.explanation: Corneal dystrophies are clinically classified according to the anatomical location within the cornea where the abnormality predominantly occurs: anterior dystrophies (epithelium, Bowman's layer), stromal dystrophies (corneal stroma), and posterior dystrophies (Descemet's membrane and endothelium). This anatomical classification guides diagnosis, symptom prediction, and treatment selection. Most corneal dystrophies are bilateral, hereditary, and progressive, though the rate of progression varies by type.
options: Age of onset and severity of corneal opacity at presentation
Causative genetic mutation and chromosomal locus identified
Degree of visual impairment and need for surgical intervention
Response to topical corticosteroid treatment and remission rate
Anatomical location within the layers of the cornea affected
Seal leaking microaneurysms and reduce retinal thickening
Replace the crystalline lens with an artificial implant
Directly lower elevated intraocular pressure readings
Completely remove the vitreous gel from the eye
Permanently cure the underlying diabetes mellitus
questions.question: Focal or grid laser treatment for diabetic macular oedema is primarily used to:
questions.explanation: Focal or grid laser photocoagulation targets specific leaking microaneurysms or areas of diffuse leakage identified on fluorescein angiography, sealing these vessels and reducing macular thickening in diabetic macular oedema, particularly in cases not primarily managed with anti-VEGF injections. It does not remove the vitreous, cure diabetes, replace the lens, or treat intraocular pressure directly. This targeted laser approach remains a useful treatment option in selected cases of diabetic macular oedema.

Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the most common cause of bacterial corneal ulcers in contact lens wearers, particularly associated with overnight lens wear, improper cleaning, or contaminated lens solutions. Pseudomonas produces proteolytic enzymes that rapidly destroy corneal tissue, causing ulcers that can progress to perforation within 24-48 hours. Contact lens wearers presenting with a painful red eye and corneal infiltrate should be urgently referred and empirically treated with fluoroquinolone antibiotics.
questions.question: A corneal ulcer in a contact lens wearer is MOST commonly caused by which organism?
options: Staphylococcus aureus causing marginal keratitis in blepharitis
Acanthamoeba species in domestic water contamination
Herpes Simplex Virus causing recurrent dendritic corneal ulceration
Fusarium species causing fungal ulcer after plant trauma
Pseudomonas aeruginosa causing bacterial keratitis from lens contamination

questions.question: Tonometry is defined as the standard test for:
options: Measuring the thickness of the central cornea in micrometers
Measuring the curvature of the corneal anterior surface topography
Measuring the length of the axial eye for intraocular lens calculation
Measuring the pressure (IOP) inside the eye to detect glaucoma
Measuring the diameter of the optic nerve cup to disc ratio
questions.explanation: Tonometry is the standard diagnostic test for measuring intraocular pressure (IOP) inside the eye. Elevated IOP is the most important modifiable risk factor for glaucoma and a key diagnostic criterion. Various methods of tonometry exist, including Goldmann applanation tonometry (gold standard), non-contact tonometry (air puff), and iCare rebound tonometry. The ophthalmic nurse performs tonometry as a routine part of the ophthalmic assessment and monitors IOP response to glaucoma treatment.

questions.question: Hypertensive retinopathy is MORE common among which population groups?
questions.explanation: Hypertensive retinopathy affects people of all ethnicities but is more common among Black people and people of Chinese descent, reflecting the higher prevalence and greater severity of hypertension in these populations. It generally affects adults over age 40. Higher blood pressure levels, longer duration of hypertension, and potentially genetic differences in vascular response to hypertension contribute to the increased prevalence of retinopathy in these demographic groups.
options: Young South Asian women with gestational hypertension
Children with secondary hypertension from renal artery stenosis
Black people and people of Chinese descent as more prevalent groups
Caucasian males over 40 years with isolated systolic hypertension
Postmenopausal women with new-onset essential hypertension

questions.question: A patient asks the nurse why glaucoma cannot be cured once damage has occurred. The nurse's MOST accurate explanation is:
questions.explanation: Glaucoma damage is permanent because the optic nerve fibers, once destroyed by elevated intraocular pressure or other glaucomatous mechanisms, cannot regenerate in the human central nervous system. The optic nerve is an extension of the central nervous system, which lacks the regenerative capacity of peripheral nerves. Treatment can only halt further progression by controlling intraocular pressure and other risk factors; it cannot restore the vision already lost. This is why early detection and prevention of damage are paramount.
options: Glaucoma damage cannot be reversed because the sclera has no blood supply
The aqueous humor pathway cannot be surgically reopened after angle closure
Retinal ganglion cells can regenerate but too slowly to restore lost vision
Optic nerve fibers, once destroyed, cannot regenerate in the human nervous system
Glaucoma damage is reversible with early and aggressive treatment intervention
It is the only organ that can completely regenerate after injury
It contains the highest concentration of sensory receptors
It is the only organ with a direct connection to the lymphatic system
Its interior can be examined without harming or entering the body
Its blood supply is entirely independent of the systemic circulation
questions.question: Which of the following BEST describes the unique characteristic of the eye that makes it valuable in systemic disease assessment?
questions.explanation: The eye is uniquely valuable in systemic disease assessment because its interior, including functioning blood vessels and nerve tissue, can be directly examined without harming or surgically entering the body. This allows clinicians to observe vascular changes that reflect systemic conditions such as hypertension, diabetes, and neurological disorders. No other organ provides this non-invasive window into the body's vascular and nervous system.

options: Directly removing corneal epithelial deposits causing optical distortion
Reducing intraocular pressure by improving aqueous outflow
Preventing herpes simplex virus reactivation in the trigeminal ganglion
Reducing eyelid margin inflammation that contributes to corneal irritation
Lubricating the corneal surface to replace deficient aqueous tear production
questions.question: Lid hygiene with warm compresses and lid scrubs in the management of corneal pain is MOST beneficial for:
questions.explanation: Lid hygiene with warm compresses and lid scrubs reduces eyelid margin inflammation (blepharitis), which contributes to corneal surface irritation and discomfort by altering the composition of the tear film and causing toxic changes to the corneal epithelium. Topical or oral antibiotics may be added to address bacterial colonization of the lid margins. This is part of a multimodal approach to managing corneal pain and surface disease, alongside lubrication and treatment of the primary corneal condition.

Cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis, one of the most common causes of blindness in HIV patients, occurs primarily with significantly reduced CD4+ T cell counts (typically below 50 cells/mm³) in advanced AIDS. At this level of immune compromise, CMV, which is usually a latent infection in immunocompetent individuals, reactivates and invades retinal tissue. Unlike other diseases, ocular infection in immunosuppressed HIV patients is associated with minimal inflammatory signs, making it challenging to detect early.
options: Concurrent co-infection with Herpes Simplex Virus type 1
Significantly reduced CD4+ T lymphocyte count in advanced AIDS
Use of antiretroviral therapy causing immune reconstitution inflammation
Elevated viral load without significant immune compromise
Malnutrition causing corneal exposure and secondary retinal infection
questions.question: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis in HIV patients is MOST commonly triggered by:

options: Degeneration of the vitreous gel causing increased floaters with age
Scarring of the corneal stroma causing permanent opacity and blindness
Clouding of the crystalline lens of the eye impairing vision
Deposition of calcium in the lens capsule from hypercalcemia
Atrophy of the iris dilator muscle causing fixed pupil constriction
questions.question: Cataract is BEST defined as:
questions.explanation: A cataract is defined as a clouding or opacification of the crystalline lens of the eye. The lens is normally transparent and focuses light onto the retina, but when it becomes cloudy due to protein aggregation, it scatters and blocks light, reducing visual clarity. Cataracts are common in the aging population but can also occur in individuals with diabetes, following eye injury or surgery, with steroid use, or congenitally. Surgery to remove the cloudy lens and replace it with an artificial lens is the definitive treatment.

options: Permanent darkening of the iris from intraocular lens UV-blocking coating
Permanent loss of all remaining vision without any further treatment
Mandatory bilateral surgery regardless of the monocular nature of the cataract
Requirement for lifetime daily antibiotic eye drop therapy after surgery
Retrobulbar hemorrhage, endophthalmitis, TASS, and posterior capsule rupture
questions.question: For a patient with cataracts requiring surgery, informed consent should MOST specifically cover which potential complication?
questions.explanation: Informed consent for cataract surgery must specifically cover potential surgical complications including retrobulbar hemorrhage (from local anesthetic injection), acute bacterial endophthalmitis (occurring in approximately 1 in 1,000 cases), Toxic Anterior Segment Syndrome (TASS, a sterile non-infectious inflammation), and posterior capsule rupture (which may complicate the surgery and delay visual recovery). Patients must understand both the risks and benefits, and alternative management options, to provide truly informed and voluntary consent.

options: Has no measurable effect on visual acuity at all
Occurs exclusively in patients without any diabetic retinopathy
Is confined strictly to the optic nerve head alone
Directly affects the fovea, the area of sharpest central vision
Affects only the peripheral visual field, sparing the centre
questions.explanation: Because the fovea within the macula is responsible for the sharpest central vision, fluid accumulation and swelling in this specific region from macular oedema has a disproportionately large impact on visual acuity and reading ability compared with changes elsewhere in the retina. It does not spare central vision or occur only in the absence of retinopathy, and it directly affects the macula rather than being confined to the optic nerve head. This central location explains why macular oedema is such a significant cause of vision-related disability in diabetes.
questions.question: Macular oedema is the most common reason people with diabetes experience central vision loss because it:
Glaucoma is MOST accurately defined as:
questions.explanation: Glaucoma is defined as a group of eye diseases that can cause vision loss and blindness by damaging the optic nerve at the back of the eye. The optic nerve damage in glaucoma results in characteristic visual field loss, typically beginning in the peripheral (side) vision. While elevated intraocular pressure is the most common risk factor, glaucoma can occur with normal eye pressure (normal-tension glaucoma). Crucially, glaucoma damage is permanent and cannot be reversed, making early detection essential.
options: A hereditary condition causing bilateral optic nerve hypoplasia from birth
An inflammatory condition of the anterior segment causing corneal edema
A group of eye diseases damaging the optic nerve causing vision loss and blindness
A single condition causing painless bilateral vision loss from retinal ischemia
A reversible loss of vision from elevated intraocular pressure only

questions.explanation: Posterior scleritis involves the sclera posterior to the insertion of the rectus muscles and may present with an apparently white eye with no obvious external signs. Ultrasonography or CT scan is necessary to confirm the diagnosis because the area of inflammation is not directly visible on external examination. Ophthalmoscopy may reveal exudative retinal detachment, macular edema, or optic disc edema, but imaging provides definitive confirmation.
options: Corneal topography mapping to exclude anterior segment involvement
Optical coherence tomography measuring retinal layer thickness
Ultrasonography or CT scan to confirm posterior scleral involvement
Fundus fluorescein angiography identifying retinal vascular leakage
Magnetic resonance imaging for optic nerve sheath assessment
questions.question: For posterior scleritis, which imaging modality is MOST often used to confirm the diagnosis?

options: Diverting aqueous humor to a subconjunctival reservoir for absorption
Reducing aqueous humor production in the ciliary body permanently
Stimulating trabecular meshwork regeneration at the drainage angle
Preventing vitreous prolapse into the anterior chamber after angle surgery
Restoring optic nerve axon function through neuroprotective mechanisms
questions.explanation: Glaucoma drainage implants (e.g., Ahmed or Baerveldt valves) treat glaucoma by diverting aqueous humor from the anterior chamber through a tube into a reservoir (bleb) created beneath the conjunctiva, where it is absorbed into surrounding blood vessels. This creates an alternative drainage pathway that bypasses the dysfunctional trabecular meshwork, effectively reducing intraocular pressure. Drainage devices are particularly useful in patients with failed trabeculectomy, scarred conjunctiva, or complex glaucoma.
questions.question: Glaucoma drainage devices (implants) MOST effectively treat glaucoma by:

questions.explanation: Entry into post-basic ophthalmic nursing programmes in Nigeria requires the candidate to already hold a registered general nursing or midwifery qualification, reflecting the specialty's foundation as an advanced, specialised area built upon basic nursing training. A medical degree or unrelated allied health qualifications do not meet the specific entry requirement for this nursing specialty programme. This requirement ensures that ophthalmic nurses bring core nursing competencies into their specialised training.
options: A first degree in medicine and surgery
Registered general nursing or midwifery qualification
A certificate in community health extension only
A diploma in laboratory science only
A diploma in environmental health only
questions.question: A candidate applying for a post-basic ophthalmic nursing programme in Nigeria is required to have completed which prior qualification?

questions.explanation: Seeing rings or halos around lights in a patient with diabetic retinopathy most likely indicates cataract formation, which is a recognized ocular complication of diabetes. The lens opacification in diabetic cataracts diffracts light as it passes through the lens, creating halo effects. Diabetic cataracts may occur earlier and progress faster than age-related cataracts, particularly in poorly controlled diabetes. Cataract extraction with intraocular lens implant is the treatment and often dramatically improves vision.
questions.question: A patient with diabetic retinopathy reports 'seeing rings around lights.' This symptom MOST likely indicates:
options: Cataract formation causing light diffraction and halos
Retinal detachment from neovascular scar tissue contraction
Corneal edema from overnight contact lens wear causing halos
Macular pucker from epiretinal membrane formation above the macula
Optic nerve head swelling from malignant hypertension

questions.question: In the general management of corneal pain, lubrication is SPECIFICALLY recommended for:
questions.explanation: Lubricating eye drops or ointments are specifically recommended in the management of corneal pain associated with conditions like dry eye syndrome (keratitis sicca), where dryness is a primary cause of corneal surface irritation. Lubrication maintains the tear film integrity, prevents desiccation, and reduces the discomfort caused by corneal surface irregularity. It is a supportive therapy rather than a curative one and is often combined with treatment of the underlying pathology.
options: Corneal dystrophies to dissolve the abnormal deposits in the stroma
Infectious keratitis to replace antibiotics in mild cases
Dry eye syndrome to maintain corneal moisture and reduce discomfort
