Open fractures still contain bone marrow, so the difference is not due to its absence. The difference in FES incidence is not explained by healing speed, transfusion requirements, or pain levels alone.
options: Open fractures having no bone marrow present
Closed fractures healing more slowly always
Closed fractures being more painful always
Open fractures requiring more blood transfusions
Lower intramedullary pressure in open fractures

questions.question: A client sustains a strain with limited fiber tearing, mild tenderness, and full but painful range of motion, with symptoms often delayed until the next day. This represents which degree of strain?
questions.explanation: A first degree, or mildest, strain involves a limited number of torn muscle fibers, mild tenderness, and a fully active and passive range of motion, with pain often delayed to the following day. Second degree strains involve nearly half the fibers torn with more pronounced pain and swelling, while third degree strains represent complete rupture. Fourth degree is not a recognized strain classification.

questions.question: A newborn presents with a complex congenital foot deformity involving malalignment of the hindfoot, midfoot, and forefoot, which if untreated can make walking difficult and painful. This deformity is best identified as:
questions.explanation: Talipes equinovarus, also known as clubfoot, is a complex congenital deformity of the foot involving malalignment of soft and bony structures in the hindfoot, midfoot, and forefoot, which if untreated can limit mobility and cause pain when walking. Polydactyly refers to extra fingers or toes, a different congenital anomaly. Genu valgum, scaphocephaly, and Dupuytren contracture affect the knee, skull, and palm respectively, not the foot in this manner.

Non-trauma related causes of fat embolism include pancreatitis, diabetes mellitus, osteomyelitis and panniculitis, bone tumor lysis, steroid therapy, sickle cell hemoglobinopathy, alcoholic liver disease, and fat infusion. Long bone fracture, soft tissue chest compression, bone marrow harvesting, and burn injury are all classified as trauma-related causes instead. Recognizing osteomyelitis as a non-traumatic cause broadens the nurse's differential when a fracture history is absent.
questions.question: A client with a history of intravenous drug use and chronic infection develops fat embolism syndrome without any recent fracture. Which non-trauma related cause listed is MOST consistent with this presentation?

questions.explanation: Fibrous dysplasia is a gene mutation that causes bone tissue to become fibrous and weakened, making it vulnerable to fracture, classified as a benign bone tumor. Osteochondroma and giant cell tumor are structural overgrowths rather than gene-mutation-driven fibrous changes. Osteosarcoma and chondrosarcoma are malignant lesions with different underlying mechanisms.
questions.question: A gene mutation causing bones to become fibrous and vulnerable to fracture is best described as which benign bone condition?

questions.explanation: After a hip dislocation, adduction, internal rotation, and hip flexion beyond 90 degrees place stress on the healing capsule and can force the femoral head out again. Crossing the legs combines adduction with rotation, making it the highest-risk movement. Nurses teach clients to keep the hip abducted and avoid low chairs.
options: Sleeping with a pillow between the knees
Sitting upright with feet flat on the floor
questions.question: A client is recovering after closed reduction of a posterior hip dislocation. Which position should the nurse instruct the client to avoid to prevent redislocation?

questions.explanation: Early identification of psychosocial risk factors involves assessing a patient's pre-existing mental health conditions and implementing targeted interventions before complications arise during rehabilitation. Proactive communication, social support, patient education, and occupational therapy referral are additional but distinct preventive strategies. Early identification specifically focuses on screening for risk factors at the outset of care.
options: Provision of robust social support systems
Early identification of psychosocial risk factors
questions.question: A nurse identifies that early assessment of a client's pre-existing mental health conditions before starting orthopedic rehabilitation is an example of which preventive measure?
A patient presents with a joint injury in which the articular surfaces of the bones forming the joint are no longer in anatomic contact at all. This injury is best classified as a:
questions.explanation: A complete dislocation, or luxation, occurs when the bones of a joint are totally separated and pushed out of their normal anatomic position. Subluxation refers to a partial dislocation where the bones remain partly in contact. Sprains, strains, and fractures involve ligament, muscle, or bone continuity defects rather than complete loss of joint congruity.

questions.question: A client who has been bedridden for an extended period due to illness, with no nerve damage, is most likely experiencing which type of muscle atrophy?
questions.explanation: Physiologic atrophy is caused by not using the muscles enough, commonly affecting people who are bedridden, have seated jobs, or experience decreased activity levels, and it can often be reversed with exercise and better nutrition. Neurogenic atrophy results from nerve injury or disease, such as poliomyelitis or spinal cord injury, and tends to occur more suddenly. Pathologic atrophy from Cushing disease relates to excess corticosteroid use rather than simple disuse.

questions.question: A client with an acute muscle strain reports pain at rest, bruising, and weakness of the muscle. Which additional finding would the nurse expect as part of the typical signs and symptoms of strain?
questions.explanation: Signs and symptoms of strain include swelling, bruising or redness, pain at rest, and pain when using the affected muscle or related joint, alongside muscle weakness. Loss of sensation, cyanosis, and absent pulses suggest neurovascular compromise rather than a simple strain. High grade continuous fever is not a typical local manifestation of muscle strain.

Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic inflammatory disease affecting the hand joints, with the most common clinical presentation being polyarthritis of the proximal interphalangeal, metacarpophalangeal joints, and wrist, leading to deformities in approximately 90% of patients. Dupuytren contracture involves the palmar fascia rather than joint inflammation. Talipes equinovarus, osteochondroma, and scaphocephaly affect the foot, bone, and skull respectively, not the hand joints in this inflammatory pattern.
questions.question: A client with a chronic inflammatory disease affecting the hand joints develops polyarthritis of the proximal interphalangeal, metacarpophalangeal joints, and wrist, with deformities occurring in approximately 90% of affected patients. This is best identified as:
A 70-year-old client is diagnosed with weakened bones and reduced bone mineral density, making fractures more likely. This condition, which often develops gradually, is best described as:
questions.explanation: Osteoporosis is a medical condition characterized by weakened bones with reduced bone mineral density, making them more susceptible to fractures, and it often develops gradually and is more common in older adults. Osteomyelitis is a bone infection, while osteosarcoma and osteochondroma are bone tumors. Osteoarthritis is a degenerative joint disease, not primarily a condition of reduced bone density.

questions.question: A client with a chronic history of recurrent ankle sprains is being counselled on surgical referral criteria. Which finding would most strongly support the need for surgical evaluation?
options: A single mild sprain with quick recovery
Full return of strength after physiotherapy
Resolution of swelling within one week
questions.explanation: Surgical repair is generally considered when conservative management and rehabilitation fail to restore mechanical stability, leaving the client prone to repeated giving-way episodes. A single uncomplicated sprain that heals well does not warrant surgery. Chronic instability increases the long-term risk of degenerative joint changes if left uncorrected.

questions.question: A client asks the nurse to explain the difference between a sprain and a strain in simple terms. Which response by the nurse is MOST accurate?
questions.explanation: A sprain is an injury to a ligament that connects bones at a joint, while a strain is an injury to a muscle or its tendon caused by overstretching or overuse. The two terms are not interchangeable despite having similar mechanisms and management. Neither injury primarily involves bones, skin, nerves, organs, or blood vessels as the main affected structure.
options: Sprain and strain are identical injuries
Sprain affects bones, strain affects nerves
Sprain affects organs, strain affects blood
Sprain affects skin, strain affects joints
Sprain affects ligaments, strain affects muscles

questions.question: A nurse is teaching an obese client with knee osteoarthritis about weight reduction. What is the PRIMARY benefit of weight loss for this client's joint health?
questions.explanation: Weight reduction relieves stress on the affected knees or hips, helping to slow further cartilage damage and reduce pain associated with osteoarthritis. It does not rapidly increase bone mineral density, cure the condition completely, or guarantee elimination of the need for walking aids or future fractures. Weight management remains an important adjunct alongside other conservative and pharmacologic measures.

options: Eliminate the need for oxygen therapy
Prevent any further sickling of cells
questions.question: A client in sickle cell crisis develops Fat Embolism Syndrome without any history of trauma. The nurse understands this can occur because bone marrow necrosis resulting from hypoxia may:
questions.explanation: Fat Embolism Syndrome can occur in sickle cell crisis because bone marrow necrosis as a result of hypoxia may release fat into the circulation, representing a non-traumatic cause of FES. This process does not increase bone mineral density, prevent further sickling, eliminate the need for oxygen therapy, or cause bone healing. Recognizing this non-traumatic pathway is important for clients with sickle cell disease presenting with respiratory or neurological symptoms during a crisis.

questions.question: A nurse is assessing a client with a suspected congenital deformity. According to medical management investigations, which test is specifically used to evaluate congenital causes?
questions.explanation: Genetic testing is specifically used for congenital deformities as part of the investigations alongside imaging studies and blood tests to identify metabolic or inflammatory conditions. Electrocardiogram, pulmonary function tests, audiometry, and visual acuity tests assess cardiac, respiratory, auditory, and visual function respectively, not congenital skeletal causes. This targeted testing helps differentiate congenital from acquired deformities.

questions.question: A client with acute pancreatitis and high levels of plasma C-reactive protein (CRP) develops non-traumatic fat embolism. According to the mechanism described, this may be caused by agglutination of which substances?
options: Red and white blood cells only
questions.explanation: Non-traumatic fat embolism may be caused by agglutination of chylomicrons and very low-density lipoproteins (VLDL) by high levels of plasma C-reactive protein, as occurs in conditions such as acute pancreatitis with certain types of hyperlipidaemia. Red and white blood cells, platelets and fibrin, electrolytes, and hemoglobin or myoglobin are not the substances described in this specific agglutination mechanism. Understanding this pathway helps explain fat embolism in clients without traumatic injury.

Positron emission tomography combined with computed tomography, abbreviated PET-CT, is listed among the medical investigations used to evaluate bone tumors. Plain X-ray shows bone abnormalities but cannot determine if a tumor is cancerous on its own. Ultrasound, electromyography, and bone mineral density scans are used for different clinical purposes unrelated to tumor staging.
questions.question: Which imaging investigation combines functional and anatomical information and is specifically noted among the medical investigations for bone tumors as PET-CT?

questions.explanation: A third-degree (Grade III) sprain involves complete rupture of the ligament, often with significant swelling, bruising, and pronounced joint instability. First-degree sprains show only minor stretching with mild swelling and no instability, while second-degree involves a partial tear with moderate instability. Strain grading describes muscle injuries and does not apply to ligament rupture.
questions.question: A client sustains an ankle injury described as a complete rupture of the ligament with significant swelling and obvious joint instability. According to sprain classification, this represents:

questions.explanation: A strain is an injury to the muscle-tendon unit typically caused by sudden, forceful, or excessive stretching, common in sprinting movements that rely heavily on eccentric hamstring contraction. The sensation of a 'pop' with immediate weakness reflects fibre disruption within the muscle belly or musculotendinous junction. Sprains, by contrast, involve ligaments at a joint rather than the muscle itself.
questions.question: A client describes sudden pain in the back of the thigh while sprinting, with a feeling of a 'pop' and immediate weakness. This mechanism is most consistent with which type of injury?
A bone lesion in a child's leg is identified as the only true cyst of bone, occurring as a simple solitary lesion. This description matches:
questions.explanation: The nonossifying fibroma, also called a unicameral bone cyst, is described as the only true cyst of bone and is usually found in the leg of children and adolescents. Osteochondroma involves bone and cartilage overgrowth near growth plates rather than a true cyst. Giant cell tumor, osteosarcoma, and Ewing sarcoma are distinct lesions occurring in different populations and locations.

Magnetic resonance imaging provides detailed visualization of soft tissues, including ligaments, tendons, and blood supply to the joint, which plain X-rays cannot show. X-rays primarily reveal bone position and associated fractures, while CT is reserved for inconclusive bone findings. Electromyography and nerve conduction studies assess nerve and muscle electrical activity rather than soft tissue integrity.
questions.question: Which diagnostic investigation is most useful for evaluating soft tissue structures such as ligaments and tendons after a suspected dislocation?

questions.explanation: A true contracture is characterized by fixed shortening of soft tissue that resists passive stretching and results in a joint held in an abnormal position even without active movement. Simple stiffness, by contrast, still allows a full or near-full passive range once gentle movement begins. Recognising this distinction is important because established contractures require more intensive intervention than routine mobility exercises.
questions.question: A nurse identifies that a bedridden client has decreased ability to actively move a limb through its full range. Which finding would most strongly suggest this has progressed to a true contracture rather than simple stiffness?
options: Mild discomfort only during active movement
Full passive range with slight residual stiffness
Temporary stiffness that resolves after a few movements
Normal muscle tone throughout the limb
Resistance to passive stretching with fixed joint positioning

questions.explanation: Maintaining neutral positioning of the affected limb prevents additional stress at the site of strain and supports healing during the early phase of recovery. Forceful stretching, immediate heat, and immediate weight bearing can aggravate the injury before the acute inflammatory phase has resolved. Removing all support increases the risk of further injury rather than promoting recovery.
questions.question: A nurse is positioning a client with an acute lower limb strain. Which positioning principle is appropriate during the early phase of nursing management?
A client recovering from orthopedic surgery shows changes in self-perception related to altered physical appearance and a perceived loss of independence. This is best described as:
questions.explanation: Changes in physical appearance or perceived loss of independence during rehabilitation may lead to self-esteem issues, emphasizing the importance of addressing psychological wellbeing alongside physical recovery. Adherence challenges relate to following prescribed routines, while employment issues relate to work adjustments. Coping with uncertainty and limited leisure participation are separate, though related, psychosocial concerns.

questions.question: A client presents with acute osteomyelitis that has developed rapidly. According to the typical timeframe, acute osteomyelitis develops over approximately how many days?
questions.explanation: Acute osteomyelitis develops rapidly over a period of approximately seven to ten days, presenting with symptoms such as fever, irritability, fatigue, and nausea. A timeframe of one to two hours is far too brief for this infectious process to develop. Six to twelve months and two to three years instead describe chronic disease progression, not the acute presentation described.

options: A normal response to everyday stress
A purely physical injury without emotion
An emotional response to a terrible event
A condition limited to bone fractures only
A chronic disease of slow progression
questions.explanation: The American Psychological Association defines trauma as an emotional response to a terrible event such as an accident, rape, or natural disaster, and it could also be a response to any physically or emotionally threatening or harmful event. Trauma is not purely physical or limited to bone fractures, since the definition emphasizes the emotional response component. It also differs from a chronic disease process and from a normal response to ordinary, non-threatening stress.
questions.question: According to the American Psychological Association, trauma is best defined as:

questions.explanation: Polydactyly refers to extra fingers or toes present at birth, which may include skin, soft tissue, and bone with joint, ligament, and tendon involvement, and is typically treated as outpatient surgery. Talipes equinovarus is a congenital foot deformity involving malalignment rather than extra digits. Trigonocephaly, genu varum, and Dupuytren contracture affect the skull, knee, and palm respectively, unrelated to extra digit formation.
questions.question: A newborn is found to have extra fingers present at birth, involving skin, soft tissue, and possibly bone with joint, ligament, and tendon structures, typically treated through outpatient surgery. This congenital deformity is best identified as:

A client undergoing prolonged orthopedic rehabilitation reports feeling lonely and withdrawn due to reduced mobility and changes in daily activities. This is best identified as which psychosocial issue?
questions.explanation: Social isolation may arise due to reduced mobility or changes in daily activities during orthopedic rehabilitation, contributing to feelings of loneliness and potentially hindering overall wellbeing. Dependency on medications, sleep disturbance, loss of productivity, and grief are distinct psychosocial issues with different presentations. Recognizing social isolation allows nurses to encourage social support and connection during recovery.

options: Determines blood glucose control over time
Assesses lung capacity and oxygen exchange
Evaluates cardiac function and rhythm pattern
Confirms diagnosis and identifies causative organism
Measures overall bone mineral density level
questions.explanation: A bone biopsy is necessary to confirm a diagnosis of osteomyelitis and also helps determine the type of organism, typically bacteria, causing the infection so that appropriate antibiotic medication can be prescribed. It does not measure bone mineral density, which would require a different type of scan. Cardiac function, lung capacity, and long-term blood glucose control are unrelated to this diagnostic purpose.
questions.question: A bone biopsy is performed on a client with suspected osteomyelitis. What is the PRIMARY purpose of this investigation?

questions.explanation: Sprains occur when a joint is forced to move into an unnatural position beyond its normal range, overstretching or tearing the ligament fibers. A direct blow to bone more typically causes fractures or contusions rather than ligament sprains. Prolonged immobility, steroid use, and vitamin D deficiency are linked to muscle atrophy and bone density loss, not acute sprain mechanisms.
questions.question: Which of the following is identified as the most common cause of sprains across various activities?

On arrival of a trauma patient, the nursing team begins the primary survey, which includes assessment of airway, breathing, circulation, disability, and exposure. This sequence is commonly remembered using which abbreviation?
questions.explanation: On patient arrival, the trauma team begins with triage and the primary survey, which includes an assessment of the patient's airway, breathing, circulation, disability, and exposure, commonly remembered as the ABCDE sequence. RICE refers to rest, ice, compression, and elevation used in soft tissue injury management, not primary trauma assessment. SOAP, SBAR, and PQRST are documentation, communication, and pain assessment frameworks unrelated to the primary survey sequence.

questions.question: A client taking long-term corticosteroid medication for an unrelated condition develops muscle wasting associated with aging and starvation-like states. This is best classified as:
questions.explanation: Pathologic atrophy is seen with aging, starvation, and diseases such as Cushing disease, which results from taking excessive corticosteroid medications. Physiologic atrophy results from simple disuse rather than medication or disease-driven processes. Neurogenic atrophy involves nerve injury or disease, while compartment syndrome and dislocation are acute mechanical injuries unrelated to this presentation.

Phase one, the destruction phase, is characterized by rupture and subsequent necrosis of myofibrils, hematoma formation in the space between ruptured muscle fibers, and proliferation of inflammatory cells. Phase two involves phagocytosis of necrotic tissue and regeneration with scar tissue formation, while phase three involves maturation and reorganization of scar tissue. Phase four and phase zero are not part of the recognized three-phase model.
questions.question: Following a stretch-induced muscular injury, which phase of strain pathophysiology is characterized by rupture and necrosis of myofibrils with hematoma formation and inflammatory cell proliferation?

questions.explanation: Literature indicates that ligament healing after a sprain typically takes about six weeks, which guides expectations for immobilization and rehabilitation timelines. A period of only two days or twelve hours is far too short for collagen tissue repair to occur. Ten months and three years grossly overestimate the typical recovery timeframe for most sprains.
questions.question: According to literature, how long does it typically take for an injured ligament to heal following a sprain?

A client with vertebral osteomyelitis reports back pain that is worse at night and unrelieved by rest. Which additional finding would most strongly support this diagnosis over simple mechanical back pain?
options: Associated fever and elevated inflammatory markers
Pain that improves significantly with gentle stretching
Pain confined only to movement, absent at rest
A history of chronic postural strain at work
questions.explanation: Vertebral osteomyelitis classically presents with persistent back pain that is worse at night and not relieved by rest, distinguishing it from typical mechanical back pain, and it is often accompanied by systemic signs of infection such as fever and elevated inflammatory markers. Mechanical back pain usually improves with rest and worsens with activity, the opposite pattern. Recognising these red-flag features prompts further investigation rather than routine conservative management.

questions.question: A nurse explains to a client that contracture prophylaxis is important for maintaining which combination of outcomes?
options: Blood pressure, heart rate, and temperature
Function, range of motion, and skin integrity
questions.explanation: Contracture prophylaxis is important to maintain function, range of motion, and skin integrity, particularly in clients at risk of prolonged immobility. Vital signs such as blood pressure, heart rate, and temperature are not the focus of contracture prevention measures. Digestion, sensory functions, and cognitive outcomes are addressed through other nursing interventions unrelated to contracture prophylaxis.

options: Complex trauma from multiple sources only
Acute trauma from a single event
questions.explanation: Chronic trauma results from repeated and prolonged exposure to highly stressful events, such as child abuse, bullying, or domestic violence, distinguishing it from acute trauma which results from a single stressful or dangerous event. Complex trauma specifically results from exposure to multiple different traumatic events rather than prolonged exposure to one type. Man-made and natural disaster trauma describe causes rather than the duration-based classification asked about here.
questions.question: A client has experienced repeated and prolonged exposure to highly stressful events, such as ongoing domestic violence over several years. This type of trauma is best classified as:

questions.explanation: Trauma can be categorized into three main mechanisms of injury: penetrating, blunt and sharp, and deceleration trauma. Infectious, congenital, degenerative, and neoplastic processes describe disease categories rather than traumatic mechanisms of injury. Recognizing which mechanism applies helps guide the focus of the primary and secondary survey during trauma assessment.
questions.question: Trauma can be categorized into three main types of mechanism of injury. Which of the following is one of these three categories?

questions.explanation: Eccentric contractions, which occur frequently during the deceleration phase of activity, can change muscle tension and induce myofibre overload injury, predisposing the muscle to strain. Concentric contractions involve muscle shortening under tension and are not specifically linked to this overload mechanism. Isometric, synergistic, and reflexive contractions are not identified as the predisposing factor in this context.
questions.question: A nurse explains predisposing factors for muscle strain to a student. Which muscle action, frequent during deceleration of activity, is described as predisposing the muscle to overload injury?
A client with early signs of contracture is started on passive range of motion exercises and splinting. According to core concepts of contracture management, this approach is MOST effective when:
questions.explanation: Prevention of contractures requires early diagnosis and initiation of physical medicine approaches such as passive range of motion and splinting before contractures are present or while they remain mild. Advanced, fixed contractures show little response to conservative interventions and may require surgical intervention instead. Splinting and ROM exercises are applied to at-risk limbs, not only unaffected ones, and are most effective proactively rather than reactively.
options: Reserved for clients without any risk
Applied only to the unaffected limb
Delayed until contractures are fully fixed
Blood vessels avoid the femur area
The femur contains no bone marrow
Bone tissue lacks any blood supply
questions.question: A client with a femoral fracture develops hypovolemic shock. The nurse understands that large quantities of blood may be lost in this situation primarily because:
questions.explanation: Because bone is very vascular, large quantities of blood may be lost as a result of trauma, especially in fractures of the femur and pelvis, contributing to hypovolemic shock. Bone tissue is not devoid of blood supply, and the femur does contain bone marrow with rich vascularity. Fractures do not always clot immediately, which is why significant blood loss can occur rapidly after such injuries.

questions.question: A client develops osteomyelitis after bacteria from a urinary tract infection travel through the blood and settle in a bone. This route of infection is best described as:
questions.explanation: Osteomyelitis can occur when bacteria travel through the bloodstream, known as bacteremia, and spread to the bone, often from an infection elsewhere in the body such as a urinary tract infection, pneumonia, or abscessed tooth. Direct inoculation through surgery and open fracture represent different mechanisms involving direct exposure of bone to pathogens. Contiguous spread from a skin ulcer and hematoma formation describe other distinct pathways not specifically matching this bloodstream-mediated route.

questions.question: A client with carpal tunnel syndrome experiences burning, tingling pain following damage to a nerve outside the central nervous system. This is best classified as:
questions.explanation: Peripheral neuropathic pain, such as in carpal tunnel syndrome, phantom limb pain, or postherpetic neuralgia, follows damage or sensitization of peripheral nerves outside the central nervous system. Central neuropathic pain instead results from malfunctioning nerves within the central nervous system, such as spinal cord injury or poststroke pain. Visceral and somatic nociceptive pain, as well as acute nociceptive pain generally, arise from intact nervous systems signaling tissue damage rather than nerve malfunction itself.

questions.question: The RICE protocol is commonly applied in the initial management of dislocations and sprains. What does the 'C' in RICE represent?
questions.explanation: RICE stands for Rest, Ice, Compression, and Elevation, all aimed at minimizing pain, swelling, and further tissue damage. Compression involves applying an elastic bandage to control edema formation around the injured joint. Closed reduction, casting, and prolonged immersion are separate medical interventions and not components of the RICE acronym itself.

Ewing sarcoma family tumors typically begin in the medullary cavities where bone marrow is produced and commonly affect the legs, pelvis, backbone, ribs, upper arms, and skull in adolescents and young adults, occasionally in children as young as five. Chondrosarcoma usually develops in middle-aged or older adults. Osteochondroma, giant cell tumor, and fibrous dysplasia are benign lesions with different age distributions.
questions.question: A bone cancer that begins within the medullary cavities of long bones, the pelvis, ribs, or skull, and typically affects adolescents and young adults but can occur in children as young as five years, is best identified as:

questions.explanation: Post-traumatic deformities are due to injury, accidents, infection, or tumors, and common limb presentations include fractures that heal at an odd angle, bone loss, asymmetry, limb length discrepancy, and malrotation. Congenital deformities are present from birth rather than resulting from injury. Skull suture deformities, rheumatoid arthritis-related hand deformity, and vitamin D deficiency-related deformities have distinct underlying causes unrelated to fracture malunion.
questions.question: A client sustains a fracture that heals at an odd angle, resulting in one limb appearing shorter than the other. This presentation is best classified as a:
A teenager presents with a bony and cartilaginous growth near the growing end of the femur. This presentation is most consistent with which benign bone tumor?
questions.explanation: Osteochondromas develop in adolescents and teenagers, are made of bone and cartilage, and form near the actively growing ends of long bones such as the femur. Osteosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma, and chondrosarcoma are malignant tumors with different age distributions and behaviors. Giant cell tumors occur in adults at the rounded ends of bones, not at the growth plate.

Osteoarthritis on X-ray is characterized by a progressive loss of joint cartilage, which appears as a narrowing of the joint space between the articulating bones. Widening of the joint space, complete absence of bone, multiple fracture lines, and isolated soft tissue calcification are not the classic radiographic findings of osteoarthritis. However, it is noted that only about 30% of patients with these X-ray changes report symptoms.
questions.question: On X-ray, osteoarthritis is characterized by progressive loss of joint cartilage, which appears as which specific radiographic finding?

questions.explanation: A footboard is useful in maintaining the functional position of the extremities and preventing complications such as foot drop during prolonged immobilization. It does not directly reduce swelling, control bleeding, or prevent neurovascular compression, which require elevation and monitoring instead. Promoting wound healing is unrelated since dislocation typically does not involve an open wound.
questions.question: A client with a hip dislocation is placed on bed rest with a footboard applied to the bed. What is the primary rationale for this nursing intervention?
A nurse explains that early detection of osteoporosis is crucial for effective intervention. Which investigation is used for this early detection?
questions.explanation: Early detection through bone density testing is crucial for effective intervention in osteoporosis, allowing timely initiation of preventive measures. Complete blood count, liver function tests, electrocardiograms, and urinalysis do not assess bone mineral density and are not used for osteoporosis screening. Bone density results guide decisions about dietary, exercise, and medication interventions.

questions.question: A client twists their ankle while running and reports pain over the lateral ankle ligaments with no joint instability on examination. This injury is best described as a:
questions.explanation: A sprain is an injury to a ligament, the collagen tissue connecting bones at a joint, caused by sudden forcing of the joint beyond its normal range. A strain involves muscle or tendon overstretching rather than ligament damage. Dislocation, bone tumor, and osteoarthritis involve different structures and presentations entirely.

questions.question: A client has elastic muscle tissue gradually replaced by nonstretchy, fiber-like tissue, resulting in continuous involuntary muscle tension that limits normal movement. This condition is best described as:
questions.explanation: A contracture develops when normally elastic tissue is replaced by inelastic, fiber-like tissue, causing continuous involuntary muscle tension that prevents normal movement without pain. A strain involves acute overstretching of muscle fibers rather than chronic fibrous replacement. Dislocation, bone tumors, and osteoporotic fractures involve entirely different structural changes.

questions.question: According to pathophysiology, muscle atrophy occurs when protein degradation exceeds protein synthesis, resulting in which direct consequence for myofibers?
options: Complete replacement by adipose tissue only
Conversion of muscle into bone tissue
questions.explanation: When protein degradation exceeds protein synthesis, this leads to a reduction of the cross-sectional area of myofibers and decreased muscle strength, the hallmark of muscle atrophy. It does not increase cross-sectional area or strength, which would represent hypertrophy instead. Complete conversion to fat or bone tissue is not the described mechanism of atrophy.

Plagiocephaly involves skull and facial asymmetry, with frontal asymmetry caused by premature fusion of the coronal suture on one side, and occipital asymmetry caused by a prematurely fused lambdoid suture. Trigonocephaly produces a wedge-shaped head from metopic suture fusion, while scaphocephaly produces a boat-shaped head from sagittal suture fusion. Brachycephaly results from bilateral coronal suture fusion, and talipes equinovarus is a foot deformity unrelated to the skull.
questions.question: An infant presents with skull and facial asymmetry caused by premature fusion of the coronal suture on one side at the front of the skull. This skull deformity is best identified as:

options: Have spread but are undetectable on scans
Are confined entirely within the bone
Are visible only on plain X-ray imaging
Cause only mild localized pain symptoms
Have already been surgically removed completely
questions.explanation: Systemic chemotherapy is often used to kill tumor cells that have spread into the bloodstream but cannot yet be detected on tests and scans, especially when cancerous tumors have a high likelihood of spreading. It is not limited to tumors confined entirely within the bone or already removed surgically. Chemotherapy use is determined by metastatic potential rather than the visibility of the tumor on plain X-ray.
questions.question: A client with a malignant bone tumor is told that systemic chemotherapy is typically used to address tumor cells that:

questions.explanation: Limb salvage surgery involves removing the cancerous section of bone while keeping nearby muscles, tendons, nerves, and blood vessels intact, with the excised bone replaced by a metallic implant or bone transplant. Amputation involves removal of all or part of the limb, considered when the tumor is large or vessels are heavily involved. Arthroplasty and osteotomy are surgical procedures used for degenerative joint conditions rather than malignant tumor removal.
questions.question: A client with malignant bone cancer undergoes surgery to remove the cancerous bone section while preserving nearby muscles, tendons, nerves, and vessels, with the bone replaced by a prosthesis. This procedure is known as:

questions.explanation: Benign bone tumors are noncancerous, grow with a symmetric and controlled pattern, and may compress adjacent healthy bone tissue without invading it. Malignant tumors instead invade and destroy adjacent bone tissue as they grow. Osteomyelitis and osteoporotic fractures involve infection and bone density loss respectively, not tumor growth patterns.
questions.question: A bone lesion is described as growing slowly, having a symmetric and controlled growth pattern, and placing pressure on adjacent bone tissue without invading it. This best describes a:
A client with osteoarthritis is started on acetaminophen as initial pharmacologic therapy. If this proves insufficient, which other class of medication may be considered?
questions.explanation: Initial analgesic therapy for osteoarthritis is acetaminophen, while some clients are responsive to NSAIDs, COX-2 enzyme blockers, opioids, and intra-articular corticosteroids if pain persists. Antifungal creams, antiviral medications, antihistamines, and antitussives are not part of the pharmacologic management of osteoarthritis pain. Pharmacologic therapy is one component of a broader conservative management approach.

Increased fluid intake within cardiac tolerance keeps the body well hydrated, decreasing the risk of urinary tract infection, stone formation, and constipation during periods of reduced mobility. It does not directly increase joint flexibility, speed fracture healing, or reduce the need for pain relief. Ligament rupture recurrence is unrelated to hydration status.
questions.question: A client with a hip dislocation reports increasing fluid intake to between 2000 and 3000 mL per day as advised by the nurse. What is the MAIN reason for this instruction?

questions.explanation: A compression bandage that is too tight can restrict blood flow, producing coolness, pallor, tingling, or numbness in the toes distal to the wrap. Correctly applied compression should feel firm but still allow a finger to slip beneath it and the toes to remain warm and pink. Any sign of impaired circulation requires the bandage to be loosened immediately.
questions.question: A client with a moderate ankle sprain is fitted with a compression bandage. Which finding would indicate the bandage has been applied too tightly?
options: Mild warmth felt over the bandaged area
Slight residual swelling above the ankle
Comfortable snug pressure with visible toes pink
Ability to slide one finger under the wrap
Coolness and tingling of the toes distal to the wrap

questions.explanation: After reduction, the stretched joint capsule and ligaments need a period of immobilization to heal and regain stability. A splint holds the joint in correct alignment and prevents movements that could cause redislocation. Range of motion exercises are introduced gradually only once healing has progressed.
questions.question: Following closed reduction of a dislocated elbow, the nurse applies a splint. What is the PRIMARY purpose of this splint?
options: To increase range of motion immediately
To prevent muscle atrophy from disuse
To replace the need for pain medication
To immobilize the joint and allow capsule healing

questions.explanation: During the acute inflammatory phase, the priority is to protect the injured muscle from further damage through rest, ice, compression, and elevation. Vigorous stretching, heat, or massage at this stage can increase bleeding and worsen the injury. Active rehabilitation is introduced only once the acute inflammation has subsided.
questions.question: A client is in the acute inflammatory phase following a grade 2 muscle strain. Which nursing intervention is MOST appropriate at this stage?
options: Vigorous stretching of the injured muscle
Rest and protection of the limb with elevation
Deep heat application to the area
Aggressive massage of the injured belly

questions.explanation: Fat embolism is the process by which fat emboli pass into the bloodstream and lodge within a blood vessel, while Fat Embolism Syndrome (FES) is a serious manifestation of fat embolism that occasionally causes multisystem dysfunction, with the lungs always involved and the brain affected next. FES is not simply the presence of fat droplets in circulation, since fat embolization itself is common and often asymptomatic. FES is a clinical diagnosis without a specific laboratory test, and it is strongly associated with fractures rather than unrelated to them.
questions.question: A nurse is taught that fat emboli passing into the bloodstream and lodging within a blood vessel represent a process called fat embolism, which is distinct from Fat Embolism Syndrome (FES). The KEY distinction is that FES specifically refers to:
options: Any presence of fat droplets in circulation
A diagnosis made only by laboratory testing
A serious manifestation causing multisystem dysfunction
A condition that never affects the lungs
A condition unrelated to fractures entirely

questions.question: A bone tumor causes the adjacent normal bone to respond by altering its remodeling pattern and forming new bone tissue. This response is described as:
questions.explanation: A tumor in the bone causes the normal bone tissue to react by either an osteolytic response, which is bone destruction, or an osteoblastic response, which is new bone formation. The osteoblastic response specifically describes the bone-forming reaction to the presence of a tumor. Osteoclastic destruction alone, synovial inflammation, and cartilage degeneration describe different processes not specific to this tumor response.

Warming up properly before exercise helps prepare the muscles and joints for the demands of activity, reducing the likelihood of sprains, strains, and dislocations. It does not permanently strengthen ligaments instantly, eliminate all injury risk, or replace the need for protective gear during sports. Increasing joint laxity is undesirable, as excessive laxity is itself a risk factor for dislocation.*
options: Eliminates all risk of any injury
Replaces the need for protective gear
Prepares muscles and joints for activity
questions.question: A client asks why warming up properly before exercise is recommended as a preventive measure for joint injuries. The nurse's BEST explanation is that warming up:

questions.explanation: Secondary osteoarthritis results from a previous joint injury or inflammatory disease, such as a prior sports-related injury that predisposes the joint to later degeneration. Primary or idiopathic osteoarthritis, by contrast, has no identifiable preceding cause. Septic, reactive, and psoriatic arthritis are inflammatory or infectious conditions unrelated to this mechanical, injury-related degeneration.
questions.question: A client developed osteoarthritis of the knee following a previous sports-related joint injury years earlier. This presentation is best classified as:
A client with a single long bone fracture is informed about the risk of developing Fat Embolism Syndrome (FES). According to the data presented, this risk increases under which circumstance?
questions.explanation: A single long bone fracture carries a 1 to 3% chance of developing Fat Embolism Syndrome, and this risk increases with the number of fractures sustained by the patient. The risk relationship described relates specifically to long bone and pelvic fractures rather than skull fractures. Age under five, analgesic administration, and timing of surgical treatment are not the factors identified as increasing FES risk in this context.
options: Only if the client is under five years old
With an increasing number of fractures
Only if the fracture is in the skull
Only if no analgesics are given
Only if the fracture is treated surgically immediately

questions.question: Degenerative musculoskeletal diseases such as osteoarthritis are associated with which combination of clinical effects on patients?
questions.explanation: Patients with degenerative musculoskeletal diseases such as osteoarthritis experience increased pain, decreased range of motion, and functional deficits that reduce quality of life. Increased height, improved vision, decreased pain, improved balance, and increased appetite are not characteristic effects of these conditions. These functional deficits also increase the risk of falling and reduce participation in society.

questions.question: A client with activity intolerance following a leg strain is being discharged. Which nursing instruction best promotes a measurable, progressive increase in activity tolerance?
questions.explanation: Scheduling activities around rest periods improves circulation and promotes quicker recovery while gradually building the client's tolerance for activity. Avoiding all movement can lead to stiffness, while performing maximum exercise immediately risks re-injury before adequate healing has occurred. Discontinuing analgesics and restricting fluids are unrelated to improving activity tolerance and may hinder comfort and recovery.
options: Limit fluid intake to reduce swelling
Avoid all movement until fully healed

questions.question: A client undergoing orthopedic rehabilitation expresses worry about re-injuring the affected limb during therapy exercises. According to identified psychosocial issues, this concern is best described as:
questions.explanation: Fear of re-injury is a common psychosocial issue in orthopedic rehabilitation that can significantly impact a patient's motivation and engagement in the rehabilitation process. Disturbed body image, financial strain, sleep disturbance, and communication challenges are separate psychosocial issues with different underlying causes. Addressing fear of re-injury often requires reassurance and patient education about safe progression of activity.
options: Disturbed body image from surgery scar
To rapidly identify and treat immediately life-threatening conditions
To obtain a complete social and family history
To document every minor bruise and abrasion
To complete detailed radiological imaging first
questions.explanation: The primary survey follows a systematic approach, commonly the ABCDE framework, specifically designed to rapidly identify and address immediately life-threatening problems with airway, breathing, circulation, disability, and exposure. Detailed history-taking and comprehensive documentation are appropriately deferred to the secondary survey once the client is stabilized. This prioritization saves lives by addressing the most urgent threats first.
questions.question: On arrival of a trauma client, the nursing team begins the primary survey. What is the PRIMARY purpose of this initial assessment?

questions.explanation: Primary, or idiopathic, osteoarthritis has no prior event or disease related to its development, distinguishing it from secondary osteoarthritis which results from previous joint injury or inflammatory disease. Rheumatoid, septic, and gouty arthritis are inflammatory or infectious joint conditions with different etiologies entirely. This classification helps guide assessment of contributing history during evaluation.
questions.question: A client is diagnosed with osteoarthritis that has no prior event or disease associated with its onset. This is classified as:
A client recovering from a lower limb sprain is advised to use crutches. What is the PRIMARY reason for this recommendation?
questions.explanation: Crutches are used for lower extremity injuries to provide added support, remove weight from the affected part, and ease pain during ambulation. They do not increase ligament flexibility, prevent bruising, or stimulate bone growth, which are unrelated to mechanical offloading. Ice therapy remains a separate and necessary component of management alongside crutch use.

questions.question: A client with a history of childhood radiotherapy for a different cancer is now being evaluated for bone cancer. Which class of chemotherapy drugs is also specifically linked with increased osteosarcoma risk?
questions.explanation: Treatment with chemotherapy drugs called alkylating agents is linked with increased osteosarcoma risk, particularly when combined with prior radiotherapy received during childhood. Antibiotic ointments, antacids, antihistamines, and laxatives are not associated with this increased malignancy risk. Awareness of this link supports long-term surveillance in cancer survivors.

questions.question: A client receiving intravenous lipid infusion at a rate greater than the body's normal clearance capacity develops fat embolism syndrome. This is classified as which type of cause?
questions.explanation: Drug-related causes of Fat Embolism Syndrome include infusion of lipids at rates greater than the normal clearance capacity, agglutination of lipid emulsion particles with fibrin, and agglutination of endogenous or infused exogenous fat such as Intralipid. This is distinct from trauma-related causes involving fractures or soft tissue injury. Congenital, infectious, and neoplastic causes describe entirely different categories not related to lipid infusion.

Chondrosarcoma usually develops in the hips, shoulders, and pelvis, and middle-aged and older adults are more likely than other age groups to develop this tumor type. Infants, newborns, toddlers, and very young children are far more associated with congenital or developmental conditions rather than chondrosarcoma. This age distribution helps differentiate it from osteosarcoma and Ewing sarcoma, which favor younger populations.
questions.question: A middle-aged adult is diagnosed with a malignant bone tumor developing in the hip and pelvis. Compared to other age groups, which population is MORE likely to develop this particular tumor type?

courses.title: Hematology II

questions.question:
(a) Define chronic myeloid leukaemia and state its epidemiology and risk factor.
(b) Describe the Philadelphia chromosome and the BCR-ABL fusion gene.
(c) Describe the three phases of the disease.
(d) Explain the clinical basis of splenomegaly, bone tenderness, gout, priapism and leukostatic symptoms.
(e) Explain how the targeted drug of choice acts, its side effects and the alternatives.
(f) Distinguish chronic myeloid leukaemia from a leukaemoid reaction and state how the diagnosis is confirmed.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• CML is a myeloproliferative neoplasm: a clonal stem cell disorder with predominant granulocytic proliferation involving all haematopoietic lines; Ph chromosome and/or BCR-ABL is present in all neoplastic cells; it is the commonest MPN.
• It accounts for 15% of leukaemias (1.5/100,000/year, M:F 1.6:1), typically affects older adults (only about 3% are under 20 years); ionizing radiation raises the risk dose-dependently (Hiroshima/Nagasaki survivors, radiotherapy patients).

(b)
The Ph chromosome is an acquired balanced reciprocal translocation t(9;22)(q34;q11.2) in all proliferating stem cells (never marrow fibroblasts), giving a lengthened chromosome 9 and a shortened chromosome 22; ABL from chromosome 9 joins BCR on 22 to form the chimeric BCR-ABL gene, the hallmark of CML (also seen in a minority of ALL).

(c)
• Chronic phase (3 to 5 years): cells keep the capacity to differentiate and mature, disease is responsive to chemotherapy and stable.
• Accelerated phase (70% of patients): increasing loss of differentiation, more proliferation and resistance to chemotherapy; most progress to blast crisis within months. Blast crisis = transformation to acute leukaemia, extremely resistant, median survival 2 to 6 months; about 30% skip the accelerated phase.

(d)
• Splenomegaly is due to leukaemic infiltration and extramedullary haematopoiesis (abdominal fullness); sternal tenderness and bone pain are due to marrow hypercellularity and periosteal irritation; gouty arthritis is due to raised uric acid from high leukaemic cell turnover.
• Leukostasis (sludging in pulmonary/cerebral vessels) causes dyspnoea, drowsiness, incoordination, confusion and priapism, mainly in accelerated or blastic phases; thrombocytosis/leukocytosis can cause venous thrombosis; basophil histamine can cause upper GI ulceration.

(e)
• Imatinib blocks the ATP-binding site of the BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase and inactivates it; side effects are nausea, periorbital swelling, oedema, rash and myalgia; for suboptimal response use dose escalation or dasatinib/nilotinib.
• Second-line drugs are hydroxyurea and α-interferon; hydroxyurea is also used for cytoreduction before TKIs; TKIs cut annual mortality from 10-20% to 2%.

(f)
• CML blood: Hb below 11 g/dL, leukocytosis (12-600×10⁹/L) with left shift through all granulocyte stages, blasts usually <10%, basophilia and eosinophilia, NAP/LAP score usually below 20 (normal 40-100).
• Leukaemoid reaction (infection, inflammation, malignancy or haemolysis): modest leucocytosis, left shift only to metamyelocyte/myelocyte with an occasional blast, NAP/LAP normal or increased.
• CML is confirmed by cytogenetics in about 95%; Ph-negative cases show BCR/ABL rearrangement by Southern blot, FISH or PCR and behave like Ph-positive CML; Sokal score (age, blasts, spleen size, platelets) gives prognosis.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the gross anatomy of the spleen, including its location, dimensions, capsule, and pulp.
(b) State how the white pulp and red pulp relate to the common pathologies affecting the spleen.
(c) Explain why disease of the spleen may cause a functional deficit in a distant part of the body.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The spleen is a lymphoid organ located in the left hypochondrial region, between the fundus of the stomach and the diaphragm; it consists of a meshwork of reticular fibres that filter circulating blood.
• It weighs 150-250g and has a length of 5 to 13cm; it is normally not palpable except when enlarged to over 14cm.
• It has a capsule, red pulp, white pulp, and trabeculae which consist of blood vessels and lymphatics; the medial groove (hilum) is where arteries and nerves enter and veins and lymph vessels leave.
• The red pulp is composed of splenic sinuses and splenic cords (of Billroth), occupies more than half the splenic volume, and is where senescent red cells are identified, destroyed, and their inclusions removed (pitting).
• The white pulp comprises the periarterial lymphatic sheath (T cells), lymphoid follicles (B cells), and the marginal zone (plasma cells, T and B lymphocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells).

(b)
• Red pulp pathology: haemolytic anaemias (haemoglobinopathies like sickle cell anaemia, thalassaemia; membranopathies like hereditary spherocytosis) cause abnormal red cells to be trapped and destroyed in the red pulp, producing splenomegaly.
• White pulp pathology: lymphoproliferative disorders (chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, hairy cell leukaemia, lymphomas) involve proliferation of the lymphoid elements of the white pulp.
• Other causes of splenomegaly include myeloproliferative disorders, infections (bacterial, viral, parasitic), storage disorders, congestive causes (portal hypertension), and systemic diseases.

(c)
• Splenomegaly may lead to hypersplenism, defined as increased/exaggerated activity of an enlarged spleen causing cytopenia of one or more cell lines despite compensatory bone marrow activity, through hypersequestration, increased splenic workload, and exaggerated splenic function.
• This causes a functional deficit at a distance from the spleen: bleeding from thrombocytopenia, symptoms of anaemia, and infections from leucopenia, all reflect peripheral consumption of blood cells by the diseased spleen.
• Conversely, splenectomy or hyposplenism causes overwhelming infection because the spleen's protection against encapsulated bacteria is lost, and other reticuloendothelial tissue cannot compensate for this specific function.
• The spleen also serves as a site of extramedullary haemopoiesis in chronic haemolysis, megaloblastic anaemia, thalassaemia major and myelofibrosis, so splenic disease can be linked to compensatory changes occurring at distant marrow and hepatic sites.

(a)
Acute promyelocytic leukaemia: AML-M3 (FAB) or AML with t(15;17)(q22;q12) PML/RARalpha (WHO); hypergranular form and microgranular (hypogranular, bilobed) M3 variant, which carries a poor prognosis.

(b)
APL is more frequent in persons of Spanish descent; AML in general is linked to radiation, benzene and petroleum products, tobacco, alkylating and cytotoxic drugs, MDS/MPD and inherited conditions such as Down syndrome and Bloom syndrome.

(c)
The translocation forms a fusion gene (PML-RARalpha) disrupting growth, survival and differentiation of progenitors; procoagulants released from the abnormal primary granules activate the coagulation cascade, causing DIC with consumption coagulopathy; hypofibrinogenaemia and haemorrhage are common.

(d)
• The leukaemic cells mature in response to ATRA; monitor PT, aPTT, fibrinogen and D-dimers; management of acute DIC needs frequent monitoring of haemostatic parameters, control of the haemorrhagic state and elimination of the precipitating cause.
• Conventional AML treatment is daunorubicin plus cytosine arabinoside with supportive care for infection, cytopenias and hyperuricaemia.
questions.question:
A patient with acute leukaemia has marked bruising and bleeding. The bone marrow shows cells with large atypical primary granules, kidney-shaped nuclei and bundles of Auer rods (some branched or adherent); the cells are positive for CD11, 13, 15 and 33, Sudan black B and peroxidase, and cytogenetics shows t(15;17).
(a) State the diagnosis, its classification and variants.
(b) List the predisposing factors.
(c) Explain the pathophysiology of the bleeding.
(d) Outline the management.

(a) Describe the structure of the red cell membrane under the following headings: lipid bilayer composition; integral (transmembrane) proteins; peripheral (skeletal) proteins; and the vertical and horizontal membrane interactions.
(b) Explain the clinical basis for why defects in these membrane components lead to premature destruction of red cells in the spleen.
(c) Distinguish between hereditary spherocytosis and hereditary elliptocytosis.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Lipid bilayer: comprises about 40-50% of membrane mass, containing unesterified cholesterol and phospholipids in about equal amounts, with small amounts of glycolipids; choline phospholipids (phosphatidylcholine, sphingomyelin) lie in the outer leaflet, while aminophospholipids (phosphatidylserine, phosphatidylethanolamine) and phosphatidylinositol lie in the inner leaflet; glycolipids carry red cell antigens A, B, H and P.
• Integral (transmembrane) proteins: embedded in the lipid bilayer by hydrophobic interactions, requiring detergents for extraction; include band 3 (the anion exchange channel for Cl-/HCO3- exchange) and glycophorins A, B and C; they function as transport proteins, receptors, signalling molecules and carriers of red cell antigens.
• Peripheral (skeletal) proteins: loosely attached to the cytoplasmic face of the bilayer, extractable by high/low salt or high pH; include spectrin (α and β chains, bands 1 and 2), ankyrin (band 2.1), protein 4.1, protein 4.2, and actin (band 5); they form the membrane skeleton, organised as a hexagonal lattice with spectrin forming the arms and actin/protein 4.1/adducin the corners.
• Vertical interactions: band 3-ankyrin-spectrin and glycophorin C-protein 4.1 anchor the skeleton to the bilayer; horizontal interactions: spectrin self-association into tetramers/oligomers and spectrin-actin-protein 4.1 interactions provide membrane flexibility.

(b)
• Loss of the band 3-ankyrin-spectrin complex causes loss of membrane surface area relative to volume, producing spherocytes; defects in horizontal spectrin/protein 4.1 interactions cause loss of structural stability, producing elliptocytes.
• Both spherocytes and elliptocytes are less deformable than normal red cells.
• Less deformable red cells cannot negotiate the splenic microcirculation and are trapped in the splenic cords, where they are conditioned or destroyed by macrophages, leading to their premature destruction (haemolysis) in the spleen.

(c)
• Hereditary spherocytosis: due to deficiency of ankyrin (most common), spectrin, band 3, or protein 4.2 (a vertical linkage defect); red cells are spherocytic, osmotically fragile, with a reduced surface area to volume ratio.
• Hereditary elliptocytosis: due to defective horizontal interactions, most commonly in spectrin, also protein 4.1 or glycophorin C; red cells are cigar-shaped elliptocytes.
• Hereditary spherocytosis is most commonly autosomal dominant (with autosomal recessive transmission in some cases) and is common in individuals of northern European ancestry, Japan, and southern Africa.
• Hereditary elliptocytosis is typically inherited as autosomal dominant, and is more prevalent in individuals of West African descent, possibly conferring resistance to malaria.
• Both conditions may be complicated by aplastic crisis (from parvovirus infection), megaloblastic crisis (from folate deficiency), and gallstones, and both may be treated by splenectomy in severe/symptomatic disease.

(a)
Sickle cell anaemia (homozygous HbSS).

(b)
Precipitating factors for painful episodes include infection, exposure to cold, dehydration, menses, and physical and emotional stress, though most episodes have no identifiable cause; genetic modifiers of severity include co-inheritance of α-thalassaemia trait, β-globin haplotype, modifiers of HbF production, UGT1A1 promoter polymorphisms, and genes protective against stroke.

(c)
Complications include vaso-occlusive and haematologic (aplastic, megaloblastic, haemolytic, sequestration) crises, acute chest syndrome, stroke, priapism, leg ulcers, proliferative retinopathy, avascular necrosis, renal papillary necrosis, growth and pubertal delay, and increased susceptibility to infection from functional splenectomy.

(d)
Management options include hydroxyurea (increases HbF, reduces crisis frequency and severity, has anti-inflammatory effects, reduces sickling and adhesiveness, and releases nitric oxide), chronic or partial exchange transfusion, and haematopoietic stem cell transplantation; stem cell transplantation is justified as the only therapy that can cure the disease, reserved for severely affected patients with an HLA-matched sibling donor because of its associated morbidity and mortality.
questions.question:
A child with sickle cell anaemia has recurrent painful vaso-occlusive episodes and is being considered for long-term therapy to reduce future crises and organ damage.
(a) What is the diagnosis?
(b) What factors precipitate painful vaso-occlusive crises, and what genetic factors modify disease severity?
(c) What complications can arise from this condition?
(d) What management options exist to reduce crises, and which would you justify as the only curative option?

questions.answerText:
(a)
Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (AIHA), a form of extracorpuscular, acquired, immune haemolytic anaemia in which the body produces antibodies directed against its own red cell antigens, characterised by a positive antiglobulin (Coombs) test.

(b)
Warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia may be idiopathic (for example, Evan's syndrome, which is idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura combined with autoimmune haemolytic anaemia) or secondary to chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, Hodgkin's lymphoma or non-Hodgkin's lymphoma; cold autoimmune haemolytic anaemia may be secondary to lymphoma, paroxysmal cold haemoglobinuria, or infections such as mycoplasma pneumonia and infectious mononucleosis.

(c)
Complications include anaemia, jaundice, splenomegaly and pigment gallstones (cholelithiasis); laboratory findings show unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, increased urinary urobilinogen, decreased or absent serum haptoglobin, increased faecal stercobilinogen, reticulocytosis, and reversal of the normal myeloid to erythroid marrow ratio.

(d)
In warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, treatment options are steroids (prednisolone), immunosuppressives such as cyclosporine or cyclophosphamide, daily folic acid, and blood transfusion in severe anaemia; steroids are justified as first-line since warm IgG antibodies coat the red cells for destruction by splenic macrophages bearing Fc receptors, a process that corticosteroids suppress, whereas cold autoimmune haemolytic anaemia is instead managed by keeping the patient warm since its IgM antibodies react optimally at 4 °C.
questions.question:
A woman presents with pallor, jaundice, and splenomegaly; investigations reveal a positive antiglobulin (Coombs) test.
(a) What is the diagnosis?
(b) What are the risk factors and associations of this condition?
(c) What complications are associated with this condition?
(d) What management options exist, and justify one for a patient with warm-reactive antibodies.

A middle-aged man who previously had a total gastrectomy presents with progressive weakness, breathlessness, a beefy red sore tongue, and numbness and tingling in his feet.
(a) What is the diagnosis?
(b) What is the pathologic basis of this condition?
(c) How should the patient be managed acutely, including any specific caution?
(d) What is the definitive treatment?
questions.answerText:
(a)
Megaloblastic anaemia due to vitamin B12 deficiency, the commonest cause of which is malabsorption, here following total gastrectomy, which removes the source of intrinsic factor needed for B12 absorption.

(b)
Megaloblastic anaemias are caused by impaired DNA synthesis; nuclear maturation depends on DNA synthesis and cell division depends on nuclear maturation, so lack of nuclear maturation prevents cell division while the cell continues to grow, producing abnormally large cells with nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony; methylation of dUMP to dTMP is the rate-limiting reaction, requiring the folate co-enzyme N5,10-methylene tetrahydrofolate.

(c)
Management includes treatment of heart failure if present, treatment of any infection, and avoidance of blood transfusion if possible except where anaemia is symptomatic or there is sepsis or heart failure; large doses of folic acid should not be given alone unless B12 deficiency has been excluded, as folic acid alone can cause a haematological response but may aggravate the neuropathy.

(d)
Definitive treatment is intramuscular hydroxocobalamin 1000 micrograms (1mg) on alternate days over two weeks, then weekly until the haemogram is normal, thereafter 1000 micrograms every three months for life; prophylactic hydroxocobalamin should be given in patients with total gastrectomy and ileal resection.

(a)
Bone marrow failure syndromes such as aplastic anaemia, in which the marrow is examined to confirm hypocellularity and exclude other causes of pancytopenia such as leukaemia or myelodysplastic syndrome.

(b)
Bone marrow aspiration and bone marrow biopsy (trephine biopsy), which usually happen together, using either two needles or repositioning the same needle.

(c)
A long hollow needle is inserted into a bone, typically the hip bone; the surrounding skin, subcutaneous tissue and the periosteum are infiltrated with a local anaesthetic agent before the procedure, as the periosteum must be punctured or penetrated to reach the medullary cavity.

(d)
Bone marrow cellularity decreases with age, as red marrow is replaced with fatty (yellow) marrow; marrow biopsy cellularity of less than 30% in patients below 60 years, or less than 20% in patients older than 60 years, is considered hypocellular, so age must be considered when interpreting cellularity.
questions.question:
A patient with unexplained cytopenias requires direct examination of the bone marrow to confirm the diagnosis.
(a) What condition might this examination be used to diagnose in this context?
(b) Name the procedure(s) performed.
(c) State the anatomical site/landmark used for this procedure.
(d) Is there a developmental/age-related variant relevant to interpreting the result of this procedure?

(a) Define thrombosis and distinguish it from a clot.
(b) State Virchow's triad and the components that matter for venous and arterial thrombosis.
(c) Describe the components of the haemostatic system and the natural anticoagulant and fibrinolytic mechanisms that limit thrombosis.
(d) Explain the clinical basis of the common acquired and inherited causes of venous thrombosis.
(e) Distinguish provoked, unprovoked and recurrent venous thrombosis in terms of duration of anticoagulation.
(f) Distinguish the risk factors for arterial thrombosis.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Thrombosis is the formation, from blood constituents, of a mass within the venous or arterial vasculature of a living animal; a clot or coagulated blood forms outside the vascular tree (e.g. haematomas).

(b)
Virchow (1854): decreased blood flow (stasis), inflammation of or near vessels (endothelial injury) and intrinsic alteration of the blood (hypercoagulability); increased coagulability and stasis matter most for venous thrombosis and endothelial injury for arterial.

(c)
• Six components: platelets, vascular endothelium, procoagulant factors, natural anticoagulants, fibrinolytic proteins and antifibrinolytic proteins; primary haemostasis makes the platelet plug and secondary haemostasis cross-linked fibrin.
• Antithrombin (enhanced by heparan sulfate and heparins) and activated protein C (cofactor protein S) confine thrombus; t-PA converts plasminogen to plasmin, regulated by antiplasmin and PAI-1; the net balance matters.

(d)
• Postoperative: elderly, obese, past or family history, major abdominal or hip operations; stasis and immobility (heart failure, MI, varicose veins, long journeys, muscle relaxants); atrial fibrillation.
• Malignancy: tumours produce tissue factor and a procoagulant activating factor X; inflammation up-regulates procoagulants and down-regulates protein C; oestrogen raises factors II, VII, VIII, IX, X and lowers antithrombin and t-PA.
• Inherited: factor V Leiden (APC resistance; venous only; 5-8 fold heterozygous, 30-140 fold homozygous), prothrombin G20210A (five-fold), protein C, protein S and antithrombin deficiency, hyperhomocysteinaemia, non-O blood group.
• Hospital-acquired thrombosis causes up to 50% of DVT/PE (within 90 days of hospitalization); also pregnancy, antiphospholipid syndrome, PV, ET, PNH.

(e)
• Provoked: treat or remove the inciting factor and give anticoagulation for 3-6 months after that.
• Unprovoked: handle the stimulating factor if present; anticoagulation possibly for life. Recurrent: anticoagulation for life.

(f)
• Arterial (atherosclerosis) risk factors: family history, male sex, hyperlipidaemia, hypertension, diabetes, gout, polycythaemia, hyperhomocysteinaemia, smoking, raised CRP, IL6 and fibrinogen, lupus anticoagulant, collagen vascular disease, Behcet's disease.
• Arterial thrombosis is usually managed by the cardiologist; venous thromboembolism comprises DVT and PE.

(a)
Monoclonal proliferation and accumulation of mature, functionally incompetent, long-lived B lymphocytes in the marrow with spillage into blood and accumulation in nodes, spleen and liver; the commonest adult leukaemia, more in males, peak 65-75 years.

(b)
Aetiology unknown; radiation, chemicals and previous chemotherapy are not associated; close relatives have increased risk (genetic predisposition); BCL2 overexpression with defective apoptosis delays death of CLL lymphocytes.

(c)
• Features: lymphadenopathy, tonsillar enlargement, splenomegaly, pallor, petechiae, fever, drenching night sweats, weight loss; FBC: normocytic normochromic anaemia, lymphocytosis, thrombocytopenia; marrow hypercellular (nodular, diffuse, interstitial).
• Immunophenotype CD19+, CD5+, CD23+, weak sIg, CD22-, FMC7-, CD79b-; cytogenetics: del 13q14, 11q23, trisomy 12, 17p abnormality; Coombs positive if autoimmune haemolytic anaemia.

(d)
• Rai: 0 lymphocytosis >15×10⁹/L; I plus enlarged nodes; II plus liver/spleen; III anaemia; IV thrombocytopenia.
• Binet: A 0-2 areas involved; B 3-5 areas, Hb >=10 g/dL, platelets >=100×10⁹; C Hb <10 g/dL and platelets <100×10⁹.
• Good prognosis: female, slow lymphocyte doubling time, nodular marrow, del 13q14, hypermutated immunoglobulin gene; prognosis also informed by stage.

(e)
• The disease may stay indolent, transform into a localized high-grade lymphoma (Richter's disease) or show increasing prolymphocytes resistant to treatment.
• Binet A: wait and watch; B and C: intervene. Supportive: central venous catheter, blood products (platelets if <10×10⁹/L, FFP, CMV-negative blood), avoid aspirin/clopidogrel, antiemetics, tumour lysis prevention (hydration, allopurinol, alkalinization), infection prophylaxis (ciprofloxacin/cotrimoxazole, reverse-barrier nursing).
• Specific: chlorambucil, COP, CHOP; fludarabine, FC and FCR (increased response and duration); rituximab (anti-CD20, CD20 low on CLL cells) and alemtuzumab (anti-CD52).
• Also autologous or allogeneic stem cell transplantation, ciclosporin, corticosteroids, splenectomy and immunoglobulin replacement.
• Baseline tests before treatment: liver function, urea, electrolytes and creatinine, serum uric acid.
questions.question:
(a) Define chronic lymphocytic leukaemia and state its epidemiology.
(b) Describe its aetiology and pathogenesis.
(c) Describe its clinical features, blood and marrow findings, immunophenotype and cytogenetics.
(d) Relate the Rai and Binet stages and the prognostic factors to disease behaviour.
(e) Explain how the disease may progress or transform, and outline its supportive and specific management by stage.

(a) Describe the structure of the haemoglobin molecule under the following headings: primary structure; secondary structure; tertiary structure; and quaternary structure.
(b) Explain the clinical basis for why an abnormality at the level of primary or quaternary structure can cause disease.
(c) Distinguish between HbA, HbA2 and HbF.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Primary structure: the amino acid sequence of the globin chains, numbered from the N-terminal end; the identity and position of amino acids cannot be changed without gross impairment of molecular function.
• Secondary structure: comprises nine non-helical sections joined by eight helical sections (identified by letters A-H), with non-helical sections labelled by the pair of adjacent helices (e.g. NA, AB).
• Tertiary structure: folding of each globin chain into an approximate sphere; intramolecular bonds impart rigidity to helical parts, causing folding to occur at non-helical parts; polar/charged side chains face outward (hydrophilic surface) while non-polar structures face inward (hydrophobic interior), and an open-topped haem pocket protects the ferrous ion from oxidation.
• Quaternary structure: four subunits arranged tetrahedrally, with contact areas α₁β₁/α₂β₂ (stability), α₁β₂/α₂β₁ (solubility), and α₁α₂/β₁β₂ (weak bonds permitting oxygenation/deoxygenation).
• Haem consists of a protoporphyrin ring with an iron atom at its centre, and each haemoglobin molecule has four haem groups, one per polypeptide chain.

(b)
• A change in primary structure, such as amino acid substitution in the β-globin chain (glutamic acid replaced by valine at the sixth position), produces an abnormal haemoglobin variant, as seen in sickle cell anaemia.
• Because the tertiary/quaternary contacts depend on correct amino acid positioning, primary structure abnormalities can disrupt stability (α₁β₁ contacts), solubility (α₁β₂ contacts), or the ability to bind/release oxygen (α₁α₂/β₁β₂ contacts), producing clinical disease.
• Absence or deletion of globin subunit production causes α thalassaemias, while mutations affecting the globin gene can lead to β thalassaemias.

(c)
• HbA (α₂β₂) is the normal adult haemoglobin, constituting 96-98% of normal adult blood.
• HbA2 (α₂δ₂) contains δ chains instead of β chains, and constitutes 1.5-3.2% of normal adult blood.
• HbF (α₂γ₂) is fetal haemoglobin, containing γ chains instead of β chains, and constitutes 0.5-0.8% of normal adult blood; the major switch from fetal to adult haemoglobin occurs 3-6 months after birth.
• Embryonic haemoglobins (Gower I, ζ₂ε₂; Portland, ζ₂γ₂; Gower II, α₂ε₂) precede HbF and HbA in development.

questions.question:
An elderly patient presents with bone pain, anaemia, recurrent infections, polydipsia, polyuria, anorexia, vomiting, constipation and mental disturbance. A skeletal survey shows punched-out lytic lesions in the skull, the blood film shows marked rouleaux, and the bone marrow shows clusters of abnormal plasma cells that are CD45 negative and CD38 and CD138 positive.
(a) State the diagnosis and how the disease is classified and staged.
(b) Explain the pathologic basis of the disease and of its clinical features.
(c) Outline the management of the complications.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Multiple myeloma, a malignant monoclonal expansion of plasma cells (spectrum MGUS, smouldering MM, MM, plasma cell leukaemia); classified by M protein: IgG 53%, IgA 25%, IgD 1%, light chain only 20%, or non-secretory; staged by Salmon-Durie or the International Staging System (β₂-microglobulin and albumin).

(b)
