• c-MYC and H-ras are overexpressed in more than 80%, bcl-2 is overexpressed, N-ras is mutated, and Rb and p53 are mutated in many; IL-6 is elevated and acts as a growth factor for the plasma cells.
• Features (BAHRAIN UV): bone pain, anaemia, hypercalcaemia, renal failure, amyloidosis, infection (deficient antibody production), hyperuricaemia, viscosity; light chains cause myeloma cast nephropathy; paraprotein may interfere with platelet function and coagulation factors.

(c)
• Uraemia: rehydrate, treat hypercalcaemia and hyperuricaemia, haemodialysis and allopurinol may be considered; hypercalcaemia: rehydrate with isotonic saline plus zoledronic acid or pamidronate; compression paraplegia: decompression laminectomy.
• Severe anaemia: packed red cell transfusion; severe recurrent infections: prophylactic broad-spectrum antibiotics and antifungals; bleeding from hyperviscosity/paraproteinaemia: repeated plasmapheresis.

(a)
Myelodysplastic syndrome, a clonal stem cell disorder with ineffective, disordered haemopoiesis, a hypercellular marrow and peripheral pancytopenia; WHO subtypes by blast percentage (RA, RARS, RCMD, RAEB-1 5-9%, RAEB-2 10-19%, MDS-U, del 5q); differentials include megaloblastic anaemia, aplastic anaemia and myelofibrosis.

(b)
Mostly idiopathic; median age 65 or more with male predominance; heritable (Down syndrome, congenital neutropenias, Fanconi anaemia, ataxia telangiectasia, NF-1); acquired (alkylators, topoisomerase II inhibitors, radiation, transplants, environmental exposures, aplastic anaemia, PNH, polycythaemia vera).

(c)
• Complications: anaemia (dyspnoea, angina, CHF), neutropenia with impaired chemotaxis and infections, thrombocytopenia with impaired haemostasis, Sweet's syndrome, myeloid sarcoma, autoimmune manifestations, and risk of transformation to acute leukaemia.
• Transfusion causes iron overload (about 200 mg per unit; haemosiderosis of liver, spleen, heart, pancreas) and alloimmunization.
• Poor prognosis: anaemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, trilineage dysplasia, blasts >10%, raised LDH, monosomy 7, complex karyotype, N-RAS or p53 mutation.

(d)
• Options: observation, RBC transfusion (Hb <90 g/L in the elderly), erythropoietin/G-CSF (may accelerate leukaemic transformation), iron chelation when ferritin reaches 1,000, azacytidine, decitabine, lenalidomide, anti-thymocyte globulin (hypoplastic MDS), intensive chemotherapy, allogeneic or autologous transplant.
• Justification: lenalidomide, an anti-angiogenic agent related to thalidomide, is very effective in the 5q- syndrome.
questions.question:
An elderly patient presents with fatigue, dyspnoea and palpitations. The blood shows pancytopenia with macrocytic anaemia, aniso-poikilocytosis and hypogranular neutrophils, and B12 and folate are normal. The bone marrow is hypercellular with dysplasia, ringed sideroblasts and a 5q deletion, and the blasts are below 5%.
(a) State the diagnosis and its classification.
(b) List the risk factors.
(c) Describe the complications and adverse prognostic features.
(d) List the management options and justify one.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Fanconi anaemia.

(b)
Inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern (may also be X-linked recessive from a mutant FANCB gene); thirteen Fanconi anaemia genes have been identified (A,B,C,D1,D2,E,F,G,H,I,J,L,M,N); it is a cause of bone marrow failure/aplastic anaemia.

(c)
Patients present with features of bone marrow failure plus physical anomalies: short stature, skin hyperpigmentation, upper limb anomalies (radii, ulna, hands, thumb), hypogonadal/genitalia changes, renal anomalies (ectopic or horseshoe kidney), and Fanconi facies (microcephaly, small eyes, epicanthal folds, abnormal ears); blood counts are often normal until 5-10 years of age when pancytopenia develops gradually, with thrombocytopenia preceding granulocytopenia and anaemia; bone marrow aspiration shows normal cellularity with erythroid hyperplasia and dyserythropoiesis early, becoming hypocellular later; chromosomal breakage is observed using diepoxybutane, which helps differentiate Fanconi anaemia from idiopathic aplastic anaemia.

(d)
Treatment is supportive and specific: support with blood component transfusions, give androgens such as oxymetholone and danazol; stem cell transplantation may be curative.
questions.question:
A child aged between 5 and 10 years presents with short stature, skin hyperpigmentation, an upper limb anomaly involving the radius and thumb, and gradually developing pancytopenia, with thrombocytopenia preceding the other cytopenias.
(a) What is the most likely diagnosis?
(b) What are the predisposing factors?
(c) Explain the pathophysiology/laboratory features.
(d) Outline the management.

(a) Define Hodgkin lymphoma and state its epidemiology and aetiology.
(b) Describe the Reed-Sternberg cell, its variants and immunophenotype.
(c) Describe the four classical subtypes under the headings frequency, age, EBV association, site and microscopy.
(d) Explain the clinical basis of the prognostic differences between histological types and between patients.
(e) Distinguish classical Hodgkin lymphoma from nodular lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin lymphoma.
questions.answerText:
(a)
A lymphoma characterized by Reed-Sternberg cells, of B-cell origin; M:F 1.5-2:1, peak age 15-40 years; cause unknown, EBV may be a cofactor; described by Thomas Hodgkin (1832), RS cell by Dorothy Reed and Carl Sternberg.

(b)
RS cells are outnumbered by a reactive infiltrate (eosinophils, plasma cells, lymphocytes, histiocytes); variants: mononuclear, lacunar, mummified, anaplastic; classical HL arises from a germinal or post-germinal centre B cell and is CD15+ and CD30+.

(c)
• Nodular sclerosis: commonest (40-70%), age 20-30, M=F, rarely EBV, mediastinal nodes; collagen bands dividing nodules, lacunar cells.
• Mixed cellularity: 20-25%, more in males, about 70% EBV+, older age with systemic symptoms and advanced stage, peripheral nodes; many RS cells with eosinophils, neutrophils, plasma cells, histiocytes.
• Lymphocyte-rich: about 5%, elderly, EBV in 40%, peripheral nodes; few RS cells in abundant small lymphocytes (nodular or diffuse).
• Lymphocyte-depleted: <5%, older HIV-positive patients, EBV >90%, retroperitoneal nodes, abdominal organs and marrow; many RS or pleomorphic cells with few lymphocytes (reticular or diffuse fibrosis).

(d)
• Lymphocyte-rich HL has a favourable prognosis and lymphocyte-depleted a less favourable one; >90% of stage I and II are cured versus 50-70% of stage IV.
• Male sex, older age, Hb <105 g/L, WBC >15×10⁹/L, stage IV, low albumin and lymphopenia (<0.6×10⁹/L) worsen outcome; each of the seven factors reduces 5-year survival by 8%.
• Presentation reflects the disease: painless cervical nodes fluctuating in size, alcohol-induced pain, systemic symptoms in 25% (fever, weight loss, pruritus, night sweats) and infections from defective cell-mediated immunity.

(e)
• NLPHL: about 5% of HL, not EBV-associated, mostly males aged 30-50, cervical or axillary nodes; nodular or diffuse small lymphocytes and histiocytes with LP (popcorn) cells; classical Hodgkin and RS cells are absent.
• LP cells are CD20+, CD45+, BCL6+ and CD15-, CD30-, EBV-, in contrast to classical RS cells (CD15+, CD30+).
• NLPHL arises from a germinal centre B cell at the centroblastic stage.

(a)
von Willebrand disease, the most common inherited bleeding disorder, from quantitative or qualitative defects of vWF (usually autosomal dominant), with platelet-type bleeding (mucosal, skin cuts); undiagnosed VWD likely accounts for many women with menorrhagia.

(b)
• Screening: PT, APTT, bleeding time, FVIII:C, PFA-100. Confirmatory: vWF antigen, vWF:RCo, vWF:CB, vWF:FVIII binding, RIPA, multimer analysis, DNA analysis.
• Use standardized assays with concordant results on at least two occasions: stress, exercise, illness and pregnancy raise vWF; blood group O has levels about 30% lower; liver disease, infection, oestrogen and specimen handling modify results.

(c)
vWF bridges platelets to the injured vessel wall by binding GPIb and GPIIb/IIIa.

(d)
Factor VIII: vWF is its plasma carrier and the non-covalent vWF-FVIII interaction is required for FVIII stability, so deficiency reduces FVIII as well as impairing primary haemostasis.

(e)
• Type 1 (65-80%) partial quantitative deficiency; type 2 (20-35%) qualitative: 2A, 2B, 2M, 2N; type 3 (1%) complete deficiency.
• Type 2N (autosomal recessive, reduced FVIII binding, FVIII 5-35%) is easily mistaken for mild haemophilia; platelet-type pseudo-VWD (GPIb mutation) must be excluded by mixing test or genetic analysis.
• Haemarthroses do not occur in typical mild dominant VWD, but type 3 resembles severe haemophilia A; treatment: desmopressin, vWF replacement, antifibrinolytics, oestrogen.
questions.question:
A woman presents with menorrhagia, recurrent epistaxis and prolonged bleeding after dental extraction. Platelet count and PT are normal, the bleeding time is prolonged and factor VIII is reduced. There are no haemarthroses and the family history suggests autosomal dominant transmission.
(a) State the diagnosis.
(b) Name the screening and confirmatory tests and the precautions in interpreting them.
(c) Name the platelet receptors through which the deficient protein acts.
(d) Identify the coagulation factor placed at risk by the deficient protein and explain why.
(e) Describe the subtypes and the variant that mimics mild haemophilia.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML); the WHO threshold is 20% blasts in blood or bone marrow (FAB used 30%).

(b)
• AML is a clonal malignant disease: mutations in haemopoietic stem cells cause increased proliferation, decreased apoptosis and failure to differentiate, so blasts accumulate in the marrow with impaired production of normal blood cells.
• Most cases carry a chromosomal translocation forming a fusion gene that disrupts control of growth, survival and differentiation (e.g. t(8;21); t(15;17) in APL); FLT3-ITD (about 1/3 to 1/4 of adults) confers a poor prognosis; deletions of chromosomes 5, 7 or 9 and trisomy 4, 8, 13 also occur.

(c)
• Infection (bacterial or fungal) is the major cause of morbidity and mortality: neutropenic fever (>38 °C) needs privacy nursing, hand washing, septic work-up, appropriate antibiotics and antifungals, and a central venous catheter (e.g. Hickman).
• Hyperleucocytosis (blasts >100×10⁹/L) needs urgent chemotherapy or leukocyte cytoreduction; hyperuricaemia is treated with allopurinol or rasburicase; cytopenias with G-CSF/GM-CSF and transfusion; a neutropenic diet (properly cooked food, no fresh fruit or vegetables) is advised.

(d)
• Remission induction: daunorubicin (3 days, 45-50 mg/m²) plus cytosine arabinoside (Ara-C, 7-10 days, 100-200 mg/m²/day) for one to two cycles; 60-70% achieve complete remission.
• Complete remission = ANC >1,500/cmm, platelets >100,000/cmm, marrow blasts <5% and no extramedullary disease, lasting at least 28 days.
• Consolidation (to prevent relapse in the first 2 years): further high-dose chemotherapy (e.g. HDAC up to 3 g/m²), chemotherapy with autologous stem cell transplant, or allogeneic stem cell transplant with or without prior chemotherapy.
questions.question:
A 60-year-old patient presents with fatigue, easy bruising, gum bleeding, fever and recurrent minor infections. The blood shows anaemia, thrombocytopenia and circulating blast cells. The bone marrow shows more than 20% blasts, some with Auer rods, that are positive for Sudan black B and myeloperoxidase.
(a) State the most likely diagnosis and the blast threshold that supports it.
(b) Explain the molecular and pathologic basis of the disease.
(c) Outline the special considerations and supportive measures needed during induction therapy.
(d) Describe the definitive treatment, including the definition of complete remission and the consolidation options.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Leukaemias are acute or chronic, myeloid or lymphoid; acute leukaemias are aggressive accumulations of early progenitor blasts, usually fatal untreated yet paradoxically easier to cure than chronic leukaemias; ALL, an accumulation of lymphoblasts, is the most common childhood malignancy.
• FAB: L1 uniform small blasts with scanty cytoplasm and high nuclear:cytoplasmic ratio; L2 larger, heterogeneous blasts with lower ratio; L3 vacuolated, deeply basophilic cytoplasm (usually B-ALL).

(b)
• Precursor B-ALL: CD19+, cytoplasmic CD22+, TdT+ (early pre-B CD10- = pro-B, often infants; early pre-B CD10+ = common ALL; pre-B with cytoplasmic mu); T-ALL: CD7 and cytoplasmic CD3; B-ALL: surface immunoglobulin, TdT-.
• WHO: B lymphoblastic leukaemia/lymphoma NOS or with t(9;22) BCR-ABL1, t(v;11q23) MLL, t(12;21) TEL-AML1, hyperdiploidy, hypodiploidy, t(5;14) IL3-IGH or t(1;19) TCF3-PBX1; and T lymphoblastic leukaemia/lymphoma.

(c)
• Marrow failure: anaemia (pallor, lethargy, dyspnoea), neutropenia (fever, malaise, infections of mouth, throat, skin, respiratory tract, perianal region), thrombocytopenia (bruises, purpura, bleeding gums, menorrhagia); organ infiltration of liver, spleen, nodes, meninges, brain, skin, testis.
• Favourable: low WBC, girls, child, c-ALL (CD10+), normal karyotype or hyperdiploidy (>50) or TEL rearrangement, blasts cleared from blood <1 week, remission <4 weeks, no CNS disease, MRD negative at 1-3 months.
• Adverse: WBC >50×10⁹/L, boys, adult or infant <2 years, B-ALL, Ph+ or 11q23 rearrangements, blast clearance >1 week, remission >4 weeks, CNS disease, MRD still positive at 3-6 months.

(d)
• Cytochemistry: MPO and Sudan black are positive in AML (including Auer rods); non-specific esterase in M4 and M5; PAS shows coarse block positivity in ALL versus fine blocks in M6; acid phosphatase shows Golgi staining in T-ALL and is diffuse in M6.
• Gene rearrangement: precursor B-ALL shows clonal immunoglobulin rearrangement and T-ALL clonal TCR rearrangement, whereas AML retains germline configuration.
• Epidemiology: ALL is predominantly a disease of children (75% under 6 years); AML accounts for 70% of acute leukaemias and mostly affects adults (median age about 60).
• Both need marrow aspirate and biopsy (morphology, cytogenetics, flow cytometry, molecular studies) for diagnosis.
• Both accumulate more than 20% blasts in the marrow, with clinical features from marrow failure and tissue infiltration.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the general classification of leukaemias and the FAB subtypes of acute lymphoblastic leukaemia.
(b) Describe the immunological markers and the WHO classification.
(c) Explain the clinical basis of the presentation and of the prognostic factors.
(d) Distinguish acute lymphoblastic leukaemia from acute myeloid leukaemia.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Acute chest syndrome in sickle cell disease.

(b)
The pathogenesis involves vaso-occlusion, infection, or embolisation of bone marrow fat; fat-laden pulmonary macrophages from bone marrow fat embolisation are present in about half of cases; the resulting hypoxia can cause widespread sickling and vaso-occlusion with risk of multiorgan failure.

(c)
Supplemental oxygen; antibiotic therapy with cefuroxime and erythromycin; close monitoring for persistent hypoxia; partial exchange blood transfusion, mechanical ventilation, nitric oxide and steroids are used in life-threatening cases.

(d)
Hydroxyurea reduces the incidence of acute chest syndrome; haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is the only therapy that can cure the underlying sickle cell disease, but is reserved for severely affected patients with an HLA-matched sibling donor because of its associated morbidity and mortality.
questions.question:
A child with known sickle cell disease develops fever, chest pain, tachypnoea and hypoxia, with a new pulmonary infiltrate on chest radiograph, following a painful vaso-occlusive episode.
(a) What is the diagnosis?
(b) What is the pathologic basis of this condition?
(c) How should this patient be resuscitated and managed acutely?
(d) What definitive treatment reduces recurrence of this condition and its underlying disorder?

A neonate of West African descent presents in the neonatal period with severe haemolytic anaemia, marked poikilocytosis and jaundice; the blood film shows cigar-shaped elliptocytes, microspherocytes and fragmented cells.
(a) What is the most likely diagnosis (including the severe variant)?
(b) What are the predisposing factors?
(c) Explain the pathophysiology.
(d) Outline the management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Hereditary elliptocytosis (HE), with the severe neonatal presentation suggesting hereditary pyropoikilocytosis (HPP), a subtype of common HE.

(b)
HE is typically inherited as an autosomal dominant disorder; HE is more prevalent in individuals of West African descent, possibly because elliptocytes may confer some resistance to malaria; HPP patients are homozygous or doubly heterozygous for an elliptocytogenic spectrin mutation and are also partially deficient in spectrin, while HE relatives are heterozygous for the same mutation.

(c)
The primary abnormality is defective horizontal interactions between components of the membrane skeleton (most commonly in spectrin, also protein 4.1 and glycophorin C), which impairs the ability of spectrin dimers to self-associate into tetramers, weakening the skeletal lattice and reducing the capacity of red cells to recover their normal biconcave shape after repeated distortion in the microcirculation; HPP additionally has a vertical defect (spectrin deficiency) causing microspherocytes and worsening the haemolytic anaemia.

(d)
Severe forms of HE presenting in the neonatal period may require red cell transfusion, phototherapy, or exchange transfusion; hemolysis usually abates between 9 and 12 months of age; in cases of severe HE and HPP, splenectomy has been palliative since the spleen is the site of erythrocyte sequestration and destruction, using the same indications as for hereditary spherocytosis; daily folate supplementation is given for significant haemolysis, and interval ultrasonography is performed to detect gallstones.

(a)
β thalassaemia major, characterised by severe microcytic hypochromic anaemia with hepatosplenomegaly from extramedullary haematopoiesis and marked erythroid hyperplasia.

(b)
Splenectomy may be considered to reduce hypersplenism and transfusion requirements.

(c)
Most of the haemoglobin present in β thalassaemia major is HbF (fetal haemoglobin), with only a slight increase in HbA2; this reflects failure of the normal postnatal switch from γ- to β-chain production because of the underlying β globin chain synthesis defect.
questions.question:
A child with β thalassaemia major on regular transfusions develops worsening hypersplenism with increasing transfusion requirements.
(a) What is the diagnosis contributing to the hypersplenism?
(b) What procedure may be considered to reduce transfusion requirements?
(c) What embryologic haemoglobin finding is characteristic of this underlying disorder?

questions.answerText:
(a)
The bone marrow, which shows malignant proliferation of plasma cells (multiple myeloma) with plasmacytosis on bone marrow aspiration (>10%) and suppression of normal immunoglobulin production.

(b)
The kidneys, since renal failure may be present in about 50% of patients; bone pain, especially back pain, is common and pathological fractures may be the initial presenting symptom.

(c)
Solitary plasmacytoma of bone, extramedullary plasmacytoma, Waldenström macroglobulinaemia, primary amyloidosis, heavy chain disease, monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS), and osteosclerotic myeloma/POEMS syndrome.

(d)
Malignant plasma cells migrate to the bone marrow under the influence of cytokines (stromal-derived growth factor, insulin-like growth factor) produced by bone marrow stromal cells; other stromal elements (endothelial cells, osteoclasts, osteoblasts) produce cytokines including IL-6, IL-1, TNF-α, TGF-β and OAF that classically stimulate osteoclasts and inhibit osteoblasts, producing the osteolytic lesions and bone pain, with pathological fractures as a consequence.
questions.question:
An elderly patient, more commonly black and slightly more often male, presents with back pain and is found on skeletal survey to have osteolytic lesions of the skull. He also has anaemia and deranged renal function tests.
(a) What organ system is primarily affected, and what is the underlying process there?
(b) What other structures may be compressed or affected as a result of this disease, and what complication may back pain herald?
(c) What are the differential diagnoses to consider among the plasma cell disorders?
(d) Explain the clinico-anatomical reasoning behind the bone pain and osteolytic lesions.

(a) Describe vitamin K: its nature, sources, absorption and storage.
(b) Describe its biochemical role and the proteins that depend on it.
(c) State the treatment and prophylaxis of deficiency bleeding in infants, with doses and routes.
(d) Explain the basis of the coagulopathy and its laboratory and diagnostic findings.
(e) Explain why infants are particularly prone to deficiency and state other causes.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• A group of lipophilic, hydrophobic vitamins needed for post-translational modification of proteins; fat-soluble, absorbed in the proximal small intestine with bile salts.
• Sources: green leafy vegetables and synthesis by large-intestine bacterial flora; small amounts are stored in the liver.

(b)
• It is a cofactor for vitamin-K-dependent carboxylase, which carboxylates glutamic acid residues (γ-carboxylation), yielding vitamin K 2,3-epoxide that is recycled by VKOR, the enzyme inhibited by coumarins.
• It is required by factors II, VII, IX, X and proteins C and S; their Gla domains allow calcium-dependent binding to negatively charged phospholipids.

(c)
• Non-life-threatening bleed: vitamin K1 (phytomenadione) slowly IV, 1-2 mg being enough up to 6 months; anaphylaxis is rare; PT should improve within 48 hours; oral replacement if no active bleeding and normal absorption.
• Severe bleeding: fresh frozen plasma or prothrombin complex concentrate; prophylaxis: a single IM injection of 1 mg, especially for exclusively breast-fed babies.

(d)
• Without vitamin K, γ-carboxylation fails and non-functional PIVKAs circulate; FVII falls quickly (short half-life) prolonging PT, then IX and X fall prolonging APTT.
• Platelet count and fibrinogen are normal and fibrin degradation products are absent; criteria: PT >4 x control plus a normal platelet count/fibrinogen/absent FDPs, correction after parenteral vitamin K, or PIVKA in plasma.
• PIVKA without a coagulation deficit marks subclinical deficiency.

(e)
• Infants: vitamin K does not cross the placenta, breast milk levels are low and colonic synthesis is low; factors are about half adult values at term, reaching adult levels by about 6 months (protein C not until adolescence).
• In adults deficiency is uncommon (recycling, gut flora) but occurs with poor intake plus antibiotics, malabsorption and cholestatic liver disease.
• The condition, once called haemorrhagic disease of the newborn, is now vitamin K deficiency bleeding, classed as early, classical and late types, presenting with bleeding.

(a)
Splenic sequestration crisis in sickle cell anaemia.

(b)
Removal of the spleen (splenectomy) can prevent recurrence.

(c)
Before birth, three embryonic haemoglobins (Gower 1, Gower 2 and Portland) are present, and there is an orderly switch from ε- to α-chain and ε- to γ-chain (fetal, HbF) production, followed by β- and δ-chain production after birth; because HbF does not participate in HbS polymerisation, infants do not develop sickling manifestations, including sequestration crises, until HbF declines toward adult values, which occurs around 3 to 4 months of age.
questions.question:
An infant with sickle cell anaemia and known splenomegaly develops sudden abdominal fullness, a rapidly enlarging spleen, pallor and circulatory collapse.
(a) What is the diagnosis?
(b) What procedure can be used to prevent recurrence of this event?
(c) What embryologic haemoglobin finding explains why this crisis typically occurs in infancy rather than at birth?

questions.answerText:
(a)
• NHL is a heterogeneous group of clonal malignant proliferations of lymphoid cells in lymphoreticular sites (nodes, marrow, spleen, liver, GIT); 80-90% are B-cell, the rest T or NK cell; it arises by clonal transformation at specific stages of B/T cell differentiation.
• About 80% show recurrent clonal chromosome abnormalities; a leukaemia-like picture can occur in up to 50% of children and about 20% of adults with some types.

(b)
Causes unknown in most; t(14;18) bcl-2 (follicular, diffuse large cell), t(11;14) mantle cell, t(8;14) c-myc (Burkitt); EBV (Burkitt), HTLV-1 (adult T-cell), HHV-8, hepatitis C, H. pylori (gastric MALT), HIV, congenital or iatrogenic immunodeficiency, pesticides and solvents.

(c)
The WHO classification uses morphology, immunophenotype, cytogenetics and molecular studies, allowing targeted therapy; earlier systems were Rappaport, Lukes and Collins, Kiel, Working Formulation and REAL (1994).

(d)
• Nodular growth (structure fairly preserved) is less aggressive; diffuse unstructured growth is very aggressive; small-lymphocyte lymphomas are indolent but relentless; large-cell lymphomas are aggressive.
• Low grade: watchful waiting; stage I radiotherapy; chlorambucil, fludarabine, monoclonal antibodies. High grade: intensive chemotherapy plus intrathecal therapy, high-dose chemotherapy with stem cell support, or monoclonal antibody plus chemotherapy.
• Localized stage I-II: radiotherapy; stage III-IV with good prognostic histology: continuous low-dose chlorambucil, COP, COPP, BACOPP; poor prognosis stage III-IV: COP, CHOP.

(e)
• Unlike Hodgkin lymphoma, NHL often arises in small lymphoid sites off the main lymphoid stream (GIT, oral cavity, nasopharynx, tonsils, skin, CNS, bone) and is often deep and widespread at presentation, with greater dissemination; marrow involvement (about 20%) is often early.
• Presentation: painless nodes in neck, axillae and groin (2/3), B symptoms (fever, night sweats, 10% weight loss), pruritus and extranodal symptoms.
• Work-up: adequate biopsy reviewed by a haematopathologist, CBC and ESR, LDH and β₂-microglobulin, renal function, chest radiograph, abdominopelvic CT, bilateral marrow biopsies, lumbar puncture in high grade or CNS involvement, PET and MRI.

(f)
• Ann Arbor: I single nodal region or single extranodal site; II two or more regions on the same side of the diaphragm; III both sides; IV liver, marrow or extensive extra-lymphatic involvement.
• Suffix B = unexplained fever, night sweats or 10% weight loss; A = absent; E = extranodal involvement.
questions.question:
(a) Define non-Hodgkin lymphoma and state its cell of origin and pathogenesis.
(b) State its causes and the cytogenetic abnormalities.
(c) State the modern classification system.
(d) Relate histological growth pattern and cell size to indolent or aggressive behaviour and to treatment.
(e) Explain why the disease is often widespread at presentation and arises at extranodal sites, and how it differs from Hodgkin lymphoma, including its investigation.
(f) State the staging system.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Anaemia of chronic disease, a mild to moderate, usually normocytic normochromic anaemia developing in response to systemic illness or inflammation.

(b)
It is associated with infections (AIDS/HIV, tuberculosis, malaria, hepatitis C, osteomyelitis, chronic abscesses, SLE, sepsis), inflammatory disease (rheumatoid arthritis, Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis), malignancy (carcinomas, myeloma, lymphomas), and other conditions such as diabetes mellitus and congestive heart failure; it is the second most common cause of anaemia after iron deficiency anaemia.

(c)
Studies have shown adverse consequences of red blood cell transfusion or erythropoiesis-stimulating agents in managing this condition, especially in critically ill patients, patients with renal failure, and cancer patients; among transfused patients, predicted probability of death was higher in those with a pretransfusion haematocrit above 0.25 to 0.30 than in those with a lower haematocrit, and erythropoietin increases haemoglobin without reducing transfusion frequency or mortality.

(d)
Management options are treating the underlying chronic disease (the ideal treatment), transfusion in more severe cases, erythropoietin, and iron replacement therapy; treating the underlying chronic disease is justified as ideal, since restraint is advocated regarding treatment of mild to moderate anaemia of chronic disease, as it may represent an adaptive response, and risks of treatment should be weighed carefully against potential benefits.
questions.question:
An elderly man with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis is found to have a mild, normocytic, normochromic anaemia on routine blood testing.
(a) What is the diagnosis?
(b) What are the risk factors and underlying conditions associated with this type of anaemia?
(c) What complications or consequences are associated with this condition and its treatment?
(d) What management options exist, and which would you justify given this patient's presentation?

questions.answerText:
(a)
Burkitt lymphoma, a high-grade B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma, occurring in tropical Africa and common in adolescents; EBV is the associated virus; t(8;14)(q24;q32) (also t(2;8), t(8;22)) with c-myc expression.

(b)
Adequate surgical biopsy reviewed by an experienced haematopathologist, detailed history and examination, CBC and ESR, alkaline phosphatase, renal function, LDH and β₂-microglobulin, chest radiograph, abdominopelvic CT, bilateral marrow needle biopsies, PET and MRI.

(c)
Ann Arbor: I single nodal region or one extranodal site; II two or more regions on the same side of the diaphragm; III both sides; IV liver, marrow or extensive extra-lymphatic involvement; B = unexplained fever, night sweats, 10% weight loss.

(d)
Marrow involvement (about 20% of NHL) is often early, and a prominent leukaemic phase, uncommon in aggressive lymphomas, occurs in Burkitt and lymphoblastic lymphomas; lumbar puncture is done in high-grade lymphoma and CNS involvement.

(e)
• Variants: small non-cleaved non-Burkitt type, lymphoblastic lymphoma; regional types include adult T-cell leukaemia-lymphoma (Japan, Caribbean) and IPSID (Middle East).
• High-grade treatment: intensive chemotherapy plus intrathecal therapy, high-dose chemotherapy with stem cell support, or monoclonal antibody plus chemotherapy; HIV-related lymphomas are aggressive and high grade.
questions.question:
An adolescent from tropical Africa presents with painless swelling of neck lymph nodes, unexplained fever, drenching night sweats and loss of 10% of body weight over six months. A lymph node biopsy shows a high-grade diffuse small non-cleaved cell lymphoma.
(a) State the diagnosis, the associated virus and the cytogenetic abnormality.
(b) Name the investigations required.
(c) State the staging system and its stages.
(d) Identify the sites at risk of spread and the precautions needed.
(e) List related variants and the treatment approach.

(a) Describe the structure of the lymph node under the following headings: capsule and hilum; afferent and efferent lymphatics; and the cortex, paracortex and medulla.
(b) Explain the clinical basis of lymphadenopathy in terms of this structure.
(c) Distinguish between the lymph node and the spleen as lymphoid organs.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Capsule and hilum: the lymph node is a bean-shaped lymphoid organ with a hilum where arteries and veins enter and leave.
• Afferent and efferent lymphatics: lymph enters via afferent lymphatic vessels on the convex surface, and leaves via a single efferent lymphatic vessel on the concave surface; there is only one efferent vessel per node.
• Cortex: located immediately after the capsule and subcapsular sinus, contains primary and secondary follicles, and houses B cells.
• Paracortex: houses T cells and dendritic cells.
• Medulla: the innermost zone, containing B cells, T cells, plasma cells and macrophages.

(b)
• Lymphadenopathy is abnormality of a lymph node in size, number or consistency, usually applied to enlargement, and can be localised/generalised or peripheral/non-peripheral; normal lymph node size is around 1cm.
• Mechanism of lymphadenopathy involves increased proliferation of lymphocytes in the follicles/cortex from infection or inflammation (hyperplasia), or infiltration of the node by malignant cells or lipid/glycoprotein-laden macrophages.
• This clinically explains why infective causes (tuberculosis, syphilis, brucellosis, HIV, infectious mononucleosis, rubella) and malignant causes (leukaemias, lymphomas, secondary cancers) both present as lymphadenopathy but via different structural mechanisms.

(c)
• The lymph node is located in various parts of the body (most prevalent in the neck, axilla and inguinal region) and is primarily a site for filtration of lymph, B lymphocyte maturation and immune function.
• The spleen, in contrast, is located in the left hypochondrial region between the fundus of the stomach and the diaphragm, and filters blood (not lymph), via red pulp (filtration/phagocytosis, storage) and white pulp (immune function).
• The lymph node has afferent and efferent lymphatic vessels; the spleen has no afferent lymphatics, its hilum instead carrying the splenic artery and nerve fibres in, and veins and lymph vessels out.
• Both are lymphoid organs and can enlarge (lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly) in similar disease categories (infection, malignancy), but the spleen additionally has haemopoietic, red-cell filtration, and blood-storage/reservoir functions not shared by the lymph node.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the structure of the platelet and of the blood vessel wall.
(b) State the functions of the platelet.
(c) Explain the clinical basis of the platelet-vessel wall interaction and of the bleeding pattern when either fails.
(d) Distinguish quantitative from qualitative platelet abnormalities.
(e) Distinguish inherited from acquired qualitative defects and state the diagnosis and treatment.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Platelets are small discoid cytoplasmic fragments of megakaryocytes (about 3.0 x 0.5 um), quiescent or rapidly activated after vessel damage; the cytoskeleton is spectrin and actin (actin gives rigidity); three granule types: dense, α and lysosomal.
• A vessel has adventitia (collagen and fibroblasts), media (smooth muscle and collagen) and intima (endothelial cells on a basement membrane of collagen and elastin).

(b)
Platelet functions are adhesion, aggregation and secretion, all aimed at haemostasis.

(c)
• The discoid shape and small size push platelets to the vessel edge, next to endothelial cells, so they are placed to respond to damage.
• Endothelium releases PGI2 and nitric oxide (EDRF), which inhibit aggregation of platelets and leucocytes by raising cAMP and cGMP.
• PGI2 binds a G-protein coupled receptor, activating adenyl cyclase; the rise in cAMP promotes Ca2+ uptake into the dense tubular system, inhibiting aggregation and granule release.
• Vascular or platelet bleeding is of mucous membranes and skin (petechiae, ecchymoses, persistent bleeding from cuts) with no gender difference.

(d)
• Quantitative abnormality (thrombocytopenia): failure of production, increased destruction or consumption, abnormal distribution, or dilutional loss.
• Qualitative abnormality: skin and mucosal bleeding with a prolonged bleeding time despite a normal platelet count.

(e)
• Inherited: Glanzmann thrombasthenia (GPIIb), Bernard-Soulier syndrome (GPIb, large platelets), storage pool disease and grey platelet syndrome.
• Acquired: aspirin, dipyridamole, clopidogrel, GPIIb/IIIa inhibitors (eptifibatide, abciximab, tirofiban), myeloma, Waldenström disease, myeloproliferative disorders, MDS and uraemia.
• Investigations: FBC, marrow aspiration, platelet function analysis, bleeding time, aggregation studies; treatment: platelet transfusion and treatment of the underlying problem.

questions.question:
A young woman presents with easy bruising, petechiae, gum bleeding and menorrhagia; full blood count shows an isolated low platelet count with normal white cell and red cell counts.
(a) What is the diagnosis?
(b) What are the predisposing factors for this condition?
(c) What is the pathophysiology?
(d) How is this condition managed?
questions.answerText:
(a)
Chronic idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP).

(b)
It is more prevalent in women aged 15 to 50 years; aetiology is not known but it may be seen in association with diseases such as systemic lupus erythematosus, human immunodeficiency virus infection, chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, and autoimmune haemolytic anaemia.

(c)
The body raises autoantibodies, usually IgG, directed against antigen sites on platelet glycoprotein Ib or IIb-IIIa; this leads to premature removal of platelets by the reticuloendothelial system, reducing the normal platelet lifespan of 7 to 10 days to a few hours; bone marrow aspiration may show normal or increased megakaryocytes.

(d)
Treatment includes corticosteroids; intravenous immunoglobulin, which increases platelets by blocking Fc receptors on macrophages or modifying autoantibody production; immunosuppressive drugs such as vincristine and cyclophosphamide; rituximab; thrombopoietin-receptor agonists (oral eltrombopag or subcutaneous romiplostim); platelet transfusion; and stem cell transplantation.

questions.question:
A patient presents with petechiae, ecchymoses, mucosal bleeding and persistent bleeding from skin cuts. The platelet count is normal, the bleeding time is prolonged and platelet aggregation studies show failure of aggregation.
(a) Identify the condition and its inheritance.
(b) Identify the structure affected and its role.
(c) List the differential diagnoses.
(d) Explain the clinical reasoning and the investigations and treatment.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Glanzmann thrombasthenia, a hereditary qualitative platelet disorder from deficiency of membrane glycoprotein IIb (chromosome 17), autosomal recessive, with failure of platelet aggregation.

(b)
The GPIIb/IIIa receptor, one of the two platelet receptors (with GPIb) through which vWF bridges platelets in adhesion and aggregation.

(c)
• Bernard-Soulier syndrome (GPIb deficiency, unusually large platelets, defective adherence to subendothelium, defective aggregation and vWF binding); storage pool disease/grey platelet syndrome (absent α granules, deficient dense granules, large platelets); von Willebrand disease.
• Acquired qualitative defects: aspirin, dipyridamole, clopidogrel, GPIIb/IIIa inhibitors (eptifibatide, abciximab, tirofiban), myeloma, Waldenström disease, myeloproliferative disorders, MDS and uraemia.

(d)
• Platelet or vessel bleeding is of skin and mucous membranes (petechiae, ecchymoses, persistent cut bleeding) with no gender difference; a qualitative defect shows a prolonged bleeding time despite a normal platelet count.
• Investigations: full blood count, marrow aspiration, platelet function analysis, bleeding time, platelet aggregation studies; treatment: platelet transfusion and treatment of the underlying problem.

(a)
Aplastic anaemia bone marrow is hypocellular, with replacement of haemopoietic marrow by fat cells.

(b)
Lymphocytes and plasma cells are increased, remaining haematopoietic precursors are normal in appearance, and no abnormal cells are seen; hypocellularity may be patchy.

(c)
• The pathogenesis is unknown, but genetic factors such as HLA-DR2 may play a role.
• Both stem cell and environmental factors are implicated, with subpopulations of T-cells and inappropriate release of cytokines such as interferon-γ contributing to marrow suppression.
• The marrow trephine shows fat replacement, and ferrokinetic studies show prolonged iron clearance with decreased iron utilisation matching disease severity.

(d)
• In aplastic anaemia, the marrow is hypocellular with fat replacement and no characteristic abnormal cells.
• In megaloblastic anaemia, the marrow is hypercellular.
• Megaloblastic anaemia shows megaloblastic red cell precursors with nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony and an open, immature nuclear chromatin pattern.
• Megaloblastic anaemia also shows giant bands and metamyelocytes, and megaloblastic megakaryocytes.
• The marrow becomes normoblastic within 48 hours of appropriate therapy in megaloblastic anaemia, although giant metamyelocytes may persist for up to 12 days.
questions.question:
Describe the bone marrow in aplastic anaemia under the following headings:
(a) cellularity
(b) its contents
(c) Explain the clinical basis for why the marrow becomes hypocellular in this condition.
(d) Distinguish the bone marrow appearance of aplastic anaemia from that of megaloblastic anaemia.

An older adult presents with fatigue, weight loss, anorexia and abdominal fullness. Examination shows pallor, sternal tenderness and splenomegaly. The blood shows Hb below 11 g/dL, marked leukocytosis with granulocytes at all stages of maturation, basophilia and a low NAP score, and cytogenetics shows t(9;22).
(a) State the diagnosis.
(b) List the risk factors.
(c) Describe the complications and natural course.
(d) List the treatment options and justify the one of choice.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Chronic myeloid leukaemia: Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22)(q34;q11.2) with BCR-ABL, confirmed by cytogenetics in about 95%; the NAP/LAP score (usually below 20) separates it from a leukaemoid reaction.

(b)
Ionizing radiation (dose-dependent; Hiroshima/Nagasaki survivors and radiotherapy patients), older age, male sex (1.6:1); the aetiology is unknown in most cases.

(c)
• Chronic phase (3-5 years) to accelerated phase (70%; loss of differentiation, chemotherapy resistance) to blast crisis (median survival 2-6 months); lymphadenopathy indicates progression and thrombocytopenia an impending accelerated or blast phase.
• Other complications: bleeding, retinal haemorrhage, venous thrombosis, leukostasis (dyspnoea, drowsiness, priapism), upper GI ulceration from basophil histamine, gouty arthritis.

(d)
• Options: imatinib (BCR-ABL inhibitor blocking the ATP-binding site); dose escalation or dasatinib/nilotinib if suboptimal response; hydroxyurea and α-interferon second-line; hydroxyurea for cytoreduction before TKIs.
• Justification: imatinib is the treatment of choice as the first targeted molecular therapy for a malignancy, and TKIs reduced annual mortality from 10-20% to 2%.

questions.question:
A Rh-negative mother, previously sensitised by a prior pregnancy, carries a Rh-positive fetus. Ultrasound and delivery findings show hydrops with hepatosplenomegaly, ascites and anasarca, with severe anaemia at birth.
(a) What structures/organs are primarily identified as involved, and what process occurs there?
(b) What other structure may be affected as a complication, and what is the resulting functional deficit?
(c) What are the differential features that distinguish this from ABO haemolytic disease of the newborn?
(d) Explain the clinico-anatomical reasoning for the findings described.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The spleen and liver, which show extramedullary haematopoiesis and compensatory erythroid hyperplasia (erythroblastosis in peripheral blood); the spleen shows splenomegaly from increased red cell phagocytosis, causing fetal anaemia through extravascular haemolysis by macrophages.

(b)
The basal ganglia may be affected by excessive unconjugated bilirubin, causing kernicterus, which may be fatal or cause neurological deficit.

(c)
Rh HDN occurs in utero and can cause hydrops fetalis, and there is correlation between maternal antibody levels (titres) and disease severity; ABO HDN is more common but milder, does not occur in utero, does not result in hydrops fetalis, shows no correlation between maternal antibody levels and disease progression, and usually occurs in a group O mother with a group A or B baby with maternal anti-A or anti-B titre usually greater than 1:64.

(d)
Maternal IgG antibodies (unlike IgM, which cannot cross the placenta) cross the placenta into the fetal circulation and coat fetal red cells expressing the corresponding antigen (RhD, Rh c, Kell, A or B); this leads to extravascular destruction of fetal red cells by macrophages in the spleen, producing fetal anaemia, compensatory erythroid hyperplasia with extramedullary haematopoiesis in the liver and spleen (hepatosplenomegaly), and release of unconjugated bilirubin which, in excess, deposits in the basal ganglia to cause kernicterus; in its most severe form this manifests as hydrops fetalis with hepatosplenomegaly, ascites and anasarca.

questions.question:
With reference to the pulmonary vasculature in sickle cell disease:
(a) Describe the origin of pulmonary hypertension in this condition.
(b) Describe the course by which chronic haemolysis contributes to this complication.
(c) Describe how this complication is detected.
(d) Describe the distribution of risk associated with this complication.
(e) Explain the anatomical basis of the functional deficit (cor pulmonale) that may follow chronic pulmonary vascular injury in this condition.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The significance of chronic intravascular haemolysis in sickle cell disease extends beyond anaemia, since release of free haemoglobin causes depletion of nitric oxide in the plasma.

(b)
This is linked to endothelial dysfunction and the development of several complications, including pulmonary hypertension.

(c)
Pulmonary hypertension is detected by echocardiography (ECHO), which shows elevated pulmonary artery systolic pressure greater than 35mmHg.

(d)
It is associated with a 10-fold increase in relative risk of death; hydroxyurea therapy, repeated transfusion, vasodilators, anticoagulants and oxygen therapy are used in severely affected patients.

(e)
• Chronic pulmonary problems seen in sickle cell disease are obstructive and restrictive lung disease, pulmonary hypertension, and hypoxia.
• Asthma, a form of obstructive lung disease, has a multifactorial pathophysiology in sickle cell disease, influenced by genetic factors, environmental factors, chronic underlying inflammation, and haemolysis-induced arginine-nitric-oxide dysregulation.
• Pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale can occur as a functional deficit resulting from this chronic pulmonary vascular injury.
• Hypoxia due to acute chest syndrome can result in widespread sickling and vaso-occlusion, with risk of multiorgan failure, illustrating how pulmonary vascular injury can produce a functional deficit that extends beyond the lungs themselves.
• Acute and chronic pulmonary complications are the leading cause of death in older patients with sickle cell disease.
• Fat-laden pulmonary macrophages in the airways, from fat embolisation from the bone marrow, are present in half of the cases of acute chest syndrome, a further mechanism of pulmonary vascular and airway injury.

questions.question:
An adult with chronic idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura remains severely thrombocytopenic and symptomatic despite corticosteroids and intravenous immunoglobulin.
(a) What is the diagnosis?
(b) What further procedure or management may be offered?
questions.answerText:
(a)
Chronic idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura refractory to first-line treatment.

(b)
Further management options for chronic ITP include stem cell transplantation, in addition to thrombopoietin-receptor agonists, rituximab and platelet transfusion; the disease mechanism of immune-mediated destruction of platelets by the reticuloendothelial system is described.

(a)
• Splenomegaly is present in infants and young children with sickle cell anaemia and is caused by reticuloendothelial hyperplasia.
• In later life, the spleen becomes small and fibrotic due to repeated splenic infarctions and is not palpable.
• The spleen, however, remains palpable in adults with sickle-cell β thalassaemia.

(b)
• In β thalassaemia major, ineffective erythropoiesis and haemolysis result in marked erythroid hyperplasia, bone marrow expansion, extramedullary haematopoiesis, and hepatosplenomegaly.
• In essential thrombocythaemia, approximately 40 to 50% of patients present with splenomegaly, and some have splenic atrophy due to infarction; about 20% present with hepatomegaly.
• Bone marrow examination in essential thrombocythaemia shows megakaryocytic hyperplasia with giant megakaryocytes and clusters of megakaryocytes.

(c)
• In sickle cell anaemia, children with splenomegaly can develop splenic sequestration crisis, a sudden massive accumulation of blood in the spleen causing rapid splenic enlargement, abdominal fullness, decreased circulatory volume, progressive anaemia, and circulatory failure.
• This is a common cause of death in young children, illustrating how splenic pathology produces a distant, systemic (circulatory) functional deficit.
• Increased risk of infections in sickle cell anaemia is due to impairment of splenic phagocytic function, described as functional splenectomy.
• This represents spread of splenic pathology to a systemic immune functional deficit, with susceptibility to fulminant infection by organisms such as S. pneumoniae, Salmonella, E. coli, H. influenzae and Shigella.
• Massive splenomegaly, as in tropical splenomegaly syndrome and chronic myeloid leukaemia, causes hypersplenism, a further example of splenic pathology producing a distant haematologic functional deficit through excessive trapping and destruction of blood cells.
• Recurrence of splenic sequestration in sickle cell anaemia can be avoided by removal of the spleen.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the changes in the spleen in sickle cell anaemia as the patient ages from infancy to adulthood.
(b) Explain how the zones/parts of splenic pathology relate to the disorders of thalassaemia and essential thrombocythaemia.
(c) Explain why splenic pathology may spread to cause a distant, systemic functional deficit.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Aplastic anaemia; full blood count shows pancytopenia – low packed cell volume, leucopenia with relative lymphocytosis, and thrombocytopenia; bone marrow aspiration/biopsy shows a hypocellular marrow with fat replacement.

(b)
Damage to the haemopoietic microenvironment affecting the stem cells, the progenitor cell compartment, and factors that stimulate haemopoiesis; immune mechanisms also play a role, with cytokines such as interferon and tumour necrosis factor produced by activated T lymphocytes suppressing haemopoietic stem cell growth; cytotoxic drugs, radiation, chemicals and viruses may directly or indirectly (via immune stimulation) damage the stem cell/progenitor compartment.

(c)
Supportive treatment: transfusional support with red blood cells and platelets (prophylactic platelet support when platelet count is <10×10⁹/L or <20×10⁹/L), broad-spectrum antibiotics and antifungals for infections, and iron chelating agents when serum ferritin is greater than 1000mg/L to avoid iron overload from repeated transfusion; transfusion from family members should be avoided in patients who may receive bone marrow transplantation.

(d)
Definitive/specific treatment depends on the age of the patient, disease severity, and availability of an HLA-identical donor; allogeneic stem cell transplantation is the treatment of choice in younger patients with severe aplastic anaemia who have an HLA-matched sibling donor, while immunosuppressives (antithymocyte globulin and cyclosporin) with or without androgens are options in older patients who cannot withstand transplantation.
questions.question:
A patient presents with body weakness, easy fatiguability, dyspnoea on exertion, mucosal and gingival bleeding, and recurrent infections. On examination there is no lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly or splenomegaly.
(a) What is the most likely diagnosis, and what does full blood count typically show?
(b) Explain the pathologic basis (mechanism) of this condition.
(c) How would you initially manage this patient (resuscitative/supportive measures)?
(d) What is the definitive treatment, and on what factors does the choice of specific treatment depend?

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Humans normally carry 8 functional globin genes arranged in two duplicate gene clusters.
• The β-like globin gene cluster is on the short arm of chromosome 11.
• The α-like globin gene cluster is on the short arm of chromosome 16.
• These genes code for 6 different globin chain types: α, β, γ, δ, ε and ζ.
• Ontogeny: embryonic haemoglobins (Gower I, Portland, Gower II) are produced first, followed by fetal haemoglobin (HbF, α₂γ₂), with the major switch from fetal to adult haemoglobin (HbA, α₂β₂) occurring 3-6 months after birth.

(b)
• Fetal DNA diagnosis and prenatal diagnosis are among the applications of genetics in disease diagnosis, using maternal serum screening, ultrasound, amniocentesis, chorionic villus sampling (CVS), and percutaneous umbilical blood sampling (PUBS).
• In the context of haemolytic disease of the newborn work-up, amniocentesis is used (usually at 28-34 weeks gestation) to determine amniotic fluid bilirubin, and cordocentesis is used to obtain fetal blood for blood group, bilirubin, haemoglobin levels and direct Coombs testing.
• Genetic testing for haematologic disorders is typically performed on a whole blood sample, and molecular/DNA testing can be performed on any tissue sample and requires only small amounts.

(c)
• In sickle cell disease, the abnormality is a change in the amino acid composition of the β-globin chain: replacement of glutamic acid by valine at residue 6.
• This corresponds to a base pair change in codon 6 of the β-globin gene, GAG to GTG (a missense mutation).
• This single amino acid substitution alters the surface property of the β-globin chain, producing an abnormal haemoglobin (HbS) that polymerises under deoxygenated conditions.
• This causes deformity of the red cell into the characteristic sickle shape, which is the molecular/anatomical basis of the vaso-occlusive and haemolytic complications of sickle cell disease.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the origin (chromosomal location) and course of expression (ontogeny) of the human globin genes.
(b) State the procedures used to safely obtain fetal material for prenatal genetic diagnosis of a globin gene disorder.
(c) Explain the anatomical/molecular basis of the deformity that follows a specific mutation of the β-globin gene.

(a) Describe the gross structure of the red blood cell, including its shape, dimensions, and life span.
(b) State how the structural components of the red cell (membrane, haemoglobin, enzymes) relate to the common inherited haemolytic anaemias.
(c) Explain why destruction of abnormal red cells in the spleen may cause disease at a distant structure such as the biliary system.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• At rest, the normal human erythrocyte is a flattened, bilaterally indented sphere, a shape referred to as a biconcave disc; on fixed, stained blood films it appears circular, about 7–8 µm in diameter, with an area of central pallor.
• Average mean cellular volume ranges from 80 to 100 fL; the red cell must repeatedly pass through microcirculation of about 3.5 µm diameter, a single circuit taking about 20 seconds, over a total lifespan journey of about 480km (300 miles).
• The red cell lacks a nucleus, mitochondria or ribosomes, and circulates for approximately 120 (±30) days; more than 95% of its cytoplasmic protein is haemoglobin.

(b)
• The membrane (40-50% lipid, 10% carbohydrate, and the remainder protein) accounts for the red cell's antigenic characteristics, discoid shape, stability, selective permeability and deformability; its skeletal proteins are spectrin, ankyrin, band 3, protein 4.1, protein 4.2 and actin.
• Membrane protein defects (spectrin, ankyrin, band 3, protein 4.2) cause hereditary spherocytosis and hereditary elliptocytosis, both hereditary haemolytic anaemias with abnormal red cell shape.
• Haemoglobin structural defects (e.g. β-globin chain amino acid substitution) cause haemoglobinopathies such as sickle cell anaemia, while absent/deleted globin genes cause the thalassaemias.
• Enzyme defects in metabolic pathways (e.g. G6PD deficiency in the hexose monophosphate shunt, pyruvate kinase deficiency in glycolysis) impair the red cell's ability to generate ATP or reducing power, causing haemolysis, particularly under oxidative stress.

(c)
• In all these conditions, the abnormal red cells (spherocytes, elliptocytes, sickle cells, or oxidatively damaged cells) are less deformable or more fragile and are trapped and destroyed in the spleen.
• This destruction is a form of extravascular haemolysis, releasing haemoglobin breakdown products, chiefly unconjugated bilirubin, into the circulation.
• Chronic increased bilirubin turnover from ongoing haemolysis leads to increased bilirubin excretion via the biliary system.
• This predisposes to the formation of gallstones (pigment gallstones), a recognised complication of chronic haemolytic anaemias such as hereditary spherocytosis and hereditary elliptocytosis; interval ultrasonography is used to detect them.
• Thus, disease that begins at the level of red cell structure, and is enacted at the spleen, produces a functional/structural consequence at a distant site, the gallbladder/biliary system, illustrating how splenic destruction of abnormal red cells has downstream anatomical effects.

questions.question:
(a) Compare the FAB and WHO classifications of acute myeloid leukaemia.
(b) List the WHO categories and the FAB subtypes.
(c) Relate the FAB subtypes to their characteristic pathologies.
(d) Explain why the disease can cause leukostasis, tumour lysis syndrome, coagulopathy and organ infiltration with functional deficit.
(e) Distinguish AML from myelodysplastic syndrome and list the differential diagnoses.
questions.answerText:
(a)
FAB is mainly morphologic; WHO also incorporates immunophenotypic, genetic and clinical features and lowers the blast threshold to 20% (FAB 30%), recognizing lower counts when AML-specific cytogenetic or molecular abnormalities are present.

(b)
• WHO: AML with recurrent genetic abnormalities (t(8;21) AML1/ETO, inv(16), APL t(15;17), 11q23 MLL), AML with multilineage dysplasia, therapy-related AML/MDS (alkylating agent or topoisomerase II inhibitor) and AML not otherwise classified.
• FAB: M0 undifferentiated, M1 myeloblastic without maturation, M2 with maturation, M3 promyelocytic (and M3 variant), M4 myelomonocytic, M5 monoblastic (M5a/M5b), M6 erythroleukaemia, M7 megakaryoblastic.

(c)
• M0 (about 5%): marrow failure, negative Sudan black B and MPO, CD13 and CD33 positive, poor prognosis; M3: hypofibrinogenaemia, haemorrhage and DIC, t(15;17), ATRA response.
• M4 (15-25%) and M5 (5-8%): bleeding common; M5 gum and cutaneous infiltration, extramedullary masses and CNS involvement; monoblast lysozyme is associated with DIC and renal tubular acidosis.
• M6: more than 50% erythroblasts; M7 (3-5%): pancytopenia, raised LDH, dry tap from myelofibrosis, common in Down syndrome, poor prognosis especially infants with t(1;22).

(d)
• Features arise from marrow suppression (anaemia, bleeding, neutropenia), organ infiltration (gum hypertrophy, leukaemia cutis, Sweet syndrome, granulocytic sarcoma, meningeal disease with headache, cranial nerve palsy, mental dysfunction) and hyperleukocytosis.
• Hyperleukocytosis (WBC >100,000/cmm, about 10%, poor prognostic factor) forms leukocyte thrombi in the vasculature, affecting the lungs and brain (mental status change, headache, dyspnoea) and needs urgent cytoreduction, or whole-brain radiotherapy if CNS symptoms are significant.
• TLS (spontaneous or treatment-related): hyperuricaemia, acidosis, hypocalcaemia, hyperphosphataemia, renal failure, life-threatening hyperkalaemia; DIC (commonest in M3, also M4 and M5) results from procoagulants released from abnormal primary granules.

(e)
• FAB uses 30% blasts and WHO 20% as the minimum for AML; patients below these cut-offs with excess blasts (>5%) have MDS; the decision rests on the clinical and morphologic picture.
• Differentials: ALL, myeloid metaplasia with myelofibrosis, agranulocytosis, aplastic anaemia, leukaemoid reaction, CML, B-cell lymphoma, MDS, myelophthisic anaemia.
• Untreated AML has a median survival of about 6 months.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the gross (quaternary) structure of the haemoglobin molecule and its contact areas.
(b) State how a structural abnormality at these contact areas relates to a common haemoglobinopathy.
(c) Explain why this haemoglobinopathy can lead to a functional deficit at a structure distant from the red cell itself, such as the spleen.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The quaternary structure of haemoglobin comprises four subunits (two α and two β chains in HbA) arranged tetrahedrally.
• The α₁β₁ and α₂β₂ contact areas confer stability of the molecule.
• The α₁β₂ and α₂β₁ contact areas confer solubility of the molecule.
• The α₁α₂ and β₁β₂ contact areas form weak bonds that permit oxygenation and deoxygenation.
• Each subunit contains a haem group, consisting of a protoporphyrin ring with a central iron atom, held within a hydrophobic haem pocket created by the tertiary folding of the globin chain, which protects the ferrous ion from oxidation.

(b)
• Amino acid substitution in the β-globin chain (glutamic acid replaced by valine at position 6, from a GAG to GTG codon change) produces the abnormal haemoglobin variant HbS, as seen in sickle cell anaemia.
• This substitution alters the surface properties of the β chain, promoting polymerisation of deoxygenated HbS and distortion of the normally flexible, biconcave red cell into a rigid sickle shape.

(c)
• Sickled red cells are less deformable and occlude small vessels (vaso-occlusion) and are also more prone to premature destruction (haemolysis).
• Splenomegaly may occur in sickle cell anaemia before autosplenectomy from repeated splenic infarction; sickle cell anaemia is also a cause of hyposplenism.
• Repeated splenic infarction from vaso-occlusion by sickled cells progressively destroys splenic tissue, eventually producing functional hyposplenism (autosplenectomy).
• Hyposplenism from this process causes decreased splenic function and hence overwhelming infection risk, since the spleen's protection against encapsulated bacteria (Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae type b, Neisseria meningitidis) is lost.
• This illustrates how a molecular-level structural abnormality in haemoglobin (at the level of the quaternary contact regions and the β-chain primary structure) produces, via red cell deformity and splenic infarction, a distant functional deficit – loss of splenic immune function and increased susceptibility to infection.

(a)
• The renal medulla is hypoxic and acidotic, and this favours vaso-occlusion, leading to destruction of the vasa recta.
• Impairment of renal concentrating function is a common and the earliest sign of kidney damage.
• Ischaemia of the renal medulla with papillary necrosis can develop, which manifests with sudden onset of haematuria.

(b)
• Hyposthenuria (impaired concentrating ability) results, leading to enuresis or nocturia, and dehydration in hot weather.
• Papillary necrosis from medullary ischaemia manifests as sudden haematuria.
• Proteinuria and nephrotic syndrome may also occur.

(c)
• The proteinuria and nephrotic syndrome represent spread of the renal medullary vascular pathology into a distant, systemic functional deficit, namely loss of protein from the circulation.
• Sickle cell trait, though usually asymptomatic, is also associated with deficient urine concentrating ability, infarction of the spleen, and haematuria from renal papillary necrosis, showing that even the heterozygous state can produce this distant functional deficit.
• Instances of sudden death have been reported in sickle cell trait following strenuous exercise, illustrating how vascular pathology beginning in the kidney and elsewhere can have systemic consequences.
• Vaso-occlusive crises at high altitude in sickle cell trait further illustrate this systemic vulnerability arising from renal and other regional hypoxia.
• Few target cells may be present on the blood films of persons with sickle cell trait, a laboratory reflection of this same underlying red cell pathology.
• In sickle cell anaemia, the more severe homozygous state, the same medullary vaso-occlusive process is more pronounced and is a recognised cause of the renal functional deficits described above.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the gross condition of the renal medulla in sickle cell disease.
(b) Explain how the affected zones/parts of the kidney relate to the specific renal pathologies of this condition.
(c) Explain why renal pathology in this condition may spread to cause a distant, systemic functional deficit.

An elderly patient with insidious onset presents with abdominal discomfort, easy satiety, weight loss, fever and night sweats. There is massive hepatosplenomegaly. The blood film shows a leucoerythroblastic picture with tear-drop poikilocytes, bone marrow aspiration gives a dry tap, and the trephine shows increased reticulin fibrosis with increased megakaryocytes. Serum urate and LDH are high.
(a) Identify the condition and its disease group.
(b) Identify the organs affected and explain the mechanism.
(c) Name the related conditions to be considered and the associated genetic mutations.
(d) Explain the clinical and laboratory findings.
(e) State the treatment options.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Primary myelofibrosis, a myeloproliferative neoplasm (with polycythaemia vera and essential thrombocythaemia) arising from marrow stem cells; secondary MF follows PRV, ET, certain drugs, chemicals, irradiation or transplant.

(b)
Progressive generalized reactive fibrosis of the marrow, secondary to hyperplasia of abnormal megakaryocytes; haemopoiesis develops in the spleen and liver (myeloid metaplasia/extramedullary haemopoiesis), giving massive hepatosplenomegaly.

(c)
Other MPNs: polycythaemia vera and essential thrombocythaemia; mutations: JAK2 V617F (about 55% in MF), CALR (25%), MPL (10%).

(d)
Marrow failure gives anaemia, thrombocytopenia and infection; hypermetabolic symptoms (weight loss, anorexia, fever, night sweats); fibrosis gives the dry tap; tear-drops and leucoerythroblastic film; high urate and LDH; 10% show increased bone density on X-ray.

(e)
Transfusions and folic acid, ruxolitinib (JAK2 inhibitor), hydroxycarbamide, splenectomy, allopurinol; allogeneic stem cell transplantation may be curative in the young; erythropoietin may enlarge the spleen.

questions.question:
An asymptomatic 60-year-old man is found on routine blood count to have a persistently elevated platelet count above 450×10⁹/L, with no evidence of iron deficiency, inflammation, or malignancy.
(a) What is the diagnosis?
(b) What are the predisposing/risk factors for this condition?
(c) What is the pathophysiology?
(d) How is this condition managed?
questions.answerText:
(a)
Essential thrombocythaemia (ET), a nonreactive, chronic myeloproliferative disorder with sustained megakaryocyte proliferation.

(b)
ET is more frequent in older patients, with a median age at diagnosis of 60 years, although up to 20% of patients are younger than 40; it is rare in children.

(c)
There is acquired mutation of genes coding for tyrosine kinase proteins, namely JAK2, MPL (thrombopoietin receptor), and CALR (calreticulin); 50-60% of patients show the JAK2(V617F) mutation, which causes a prothrombotic state by affecting platelet function; the most common mutation in JAK2-negative patients is CALR, and MPL mutation is seen in 4% of patients.

(d)
Treatment principles are to reduce risk of thrombosis and haemorrhage, with control of cardiovascular risk factors; low dose aspirin (75mg daily) is given to all patients, with aspirin alone sufficient for the low-risk group; high-risk patients are treated with hydroxyurea or anagrelide to reduce platelet count, and interferon alfa is used in younger patients and in pregnancy; plateletpheresis may be used in emergencies to rapidly reduce platelet count.

questions.question:
A young adult with sickle cell anaemia presents with a chronic non-healing ulcer over the medial malleolus of the leg.
(a) What structure is affected, and what process underlies the finding?
(b) What other structures may be affected by the same underlying process in this condition?
(c) What differential pathologies (organisms) should be considered in this ulcer?
(d) What clinico-anatomical reasoning links the site of the ulcer to the underlying disease?
questions.answerText:
(a)
The skin microvasculature over the medial or lateral malleolus is affected; the ulcer is caused by occlusion of skin microvasculature from sickled red cells.

(b)
The same vaso-occlusive process affects other structures, including bone (avascular necrosis of femoral or humeral heads, dactylitis in small children), the retina (proliferative retinopathy), the corpora cavernosa (priapism), and the renal medulla (papillary necrosis, hyposthenuria).

(c)
Organisms implicated in these leg ulcers include Pseudomonas, Staphylococcus aureus, and Streptococcus species.

(d)
Leg ulcers are common in HbSS patients, especially males, usually affecting the medial or lateral malleolus because this is a site of skin microvasculature vulnerable to occlusion by sickled cells; management includes debridement, wound dressing and probable skin grafting.

questions.question:
(a) Describe von Willebrand factor: its nature, gene and site of synthesis and storage.
(b) Describe its biosynthesis, multimers and release.
(c) State its functions.
(d) State the drug that raises von Willebrand factor and factor VIII, its mechanism and the disease types in which it is or is not effective.
(e) State its side effects and contraindication.
(f) Explain the basis of the dual haemostatic defect that follows deficiency of the factor.
(g) Explain why one subtype may be mistaken for mild haemophilia.
questions.answerText:
(a)
vWF is a large plasma glycoprotein (600,000 to 20 million daltons) encoded on chromosome 12p, synthesized exclusively in endothelial cells and megakaryocytes and stored in Weibel-Palade bodies and α granules.

(b)
Pre-pro-vWF undergoes dimerization and gives pro-vWF and mature multimers; ultra-large multimers are cleaved to smaller forms by ADAMTS-13; release agonists include thrombin, adrenaline, histamine, fibrin, C5-9 complex and vasopressin; plasma levels rise in the acute-phase response.

(c)
Functions: platelet attachment to subendothelial surfaces, platelet aggregation at sites of injury (bridging via GPIb and GPIIb/IIIa) and stabilization of factor VIII in the circulation as its carrier.

(d)
• Desmopressin (DDAVP), an analogue of ADH acting on type 2 vasopressin receptors, induces secretion of FVIII and vWF from endothelial Weibel-Palade bodies.
• It raises FVIII activity, vWF:Ag and vWF:RCo two- to five-fold for about 4 hours and often corrects the bleeding time in type 1.
• Response: usually effective in type 1; usually ineffective in 2A; may be contraindicated in 2B; predicted ineffective in 2M; rarely effective in 2N; ineffective in type 3.

(e)
Side effects: flushing, tachycardia, headache, dilutional hyponatraemia (seizures in elderly and very young), rarely acute arterial thrombosis; contraindicated in unstable coronary artery disease. Other options: vWF replacement, antifibrinolytics, oestrogen, topical agents, recombinant vWF.

(f)
• Deficiency of vWF gives a dual defect: reduced plasma FVIII (loss of carrier stabilization) and a defect in primary haemostasis (impaired platelet adhesion and aggregation).
• Type 1 (65-80%) is partial quantitative deficiency, type 2 (20-35%) qualitative and type 3 (1%) complete deficiency (vWF <5%, FVIII usually <10%) with severe bleeding resembling severe haemophilia A.

(g)
• Type 2N is autosomal recessive with reduced affinity for FVIII, so only FVIII is low (5-35%), disproportionately low relative to vWF, easily mistaken for mild haemophilia.
• Other subtypes: 2A loses high-molecular-weight multimers, 2B has increased GPIb affinity with thrombocytopenia, 2M is a loss-of-function mutation with normal multimers.
• Platelet-type (pseudo) vWD, from GPIb mutations, mimics vWD and must be excluded by a mixing test or genetic analysis before diagnosing type 2N.

questions.question:
A patient after major hip surgery has sudden swelling of one limb with pain and tenderness, warm skin, fullness of the veins beneath the skin and a change in colour.
(a) State the diagnosis and how it is confirmed.
(b) List the predisposing factors.
(c) Explain the pathophysiology.
(d) Outline the management, its duration and the complications.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Deep vein thrombosis; pretest probability by the Wells score, then D-dimer (sensitivity up to 100%, specificity only 35-60%) and venous ultrasonography (non-compressibility of the common femoral or popliteal vein; sensitivity 95% and specificity 96% for proximal DVT, 60-70% for isolated calf thrombosis); venography is invasive.

(b)
Surgery (especially abdominal, hip, knee), age, obesity, previous or family history, immobility, malignancy, oestrogen therapy, pregnancy and puerperium, hospital admission (up to 50% of DVT/PE), and hereditary factors (factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A, protein C, protein S and antithrombin deficiency).

(c)
Virchow's triad: stasis, endothelial injury and hypercoagulability, reflecting disruption of the balance between procoagulant and anticoagulant mechanisms; stasis and hypercoagulability are most important in venous thrombosis; 90% or more of PE originates from deep leg veins.

(d)
• Goals: prevent progression, PE, death from PE, recurrence and post-phlebitic syndrome; anticoagulate with UFH/LMWH then a vitamin K antagonist or DOAC; graduated compression stockings and limb elevation; IVC filter if anticoagulation is contraindicated; thrombolytics, antiplatelets and venous embolectomy are also used.
• Duration: provoked 3-6 months after removing the inciting factor; unprovoked possibly lifelong; recurrent lifelong.
• Complications: heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, osteoporosis, warfarin overdose bleeding, embolisation (PE), limb occlusion with wet gangrene and post-thrombotic syndrome (up to 60% of DVT).

questions.question:
Describe the α globin gene cluster under the following headings:
(a) its chromosomal location
(b) the genes it contains
(c) Explain the clinical basis for why loss of α globin genes produces a spectrum of clinical severity in α thalassaemia.
(d) Distinguish haemoglobin H disease from Bart's hydrops fetalis syndrome.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The α globin gene cluster is located on chromosome 16.

(b)
It contains the ζ, α 2, and α 1 genes.

(c)
• There are normally four α genes; loss of one gene produces the silent carrier state with a nearly normal α/β chain ratio and no haematologic abnormalities.
• Loss of two genes produces α thalassaemia trait with mild microcytic hypochromic anaemia; loss of three genes (only one functioning α gene) produces haemoglobin H disease; and loss of all four genes, with no functioning α chain genes, produces Bart's hydrops fetalis syndrome, so clinical severity increases with the number of α genes lost.

(d)
• Haemoglobin H disease is the second most severe form of α thalassaemia, usually caused by only one gene producing α chains, resulting in accumulation of excess unpaired γ or β chains; affected individuals are born with 10-40% Bart's haemoglobin, gradually replaced with haemoglobin H (β₄), reaching about 30-50% in adulthood.
• Bart's hydrops fetalis syndrome is the most severe form, incompatible with life, with no functioning α chain genes; the baby is born with hydrops fetalis, with oedema and ascites from severe anaemia.
• In Bart's hydrops fetalis, the predominant haemoglobin is haemoglobin Bart's, along with haemoglobin Portland and traces of haemoglobin H; haemoglobin Bart's has high oxygen affinity so cannot carry oxygen to tissues, and the fetus dies in utero or shortly after birth, whereas haemoglobin H disease is compatible with survival into adulthood.
• α thalassaemia trait (α thalassaemia minor), caused by two missing α genes, exhibits mild microcytic hypochromic anaemia with MCV between 70-75 fL and may be confused with iron deficiency anaemia, distinguishing it from both haemoglobin H disease and Bart's hydrops fetalis, which are more severe.
• Pregnancies with a Bart's hydrops fetalis fetus are dangerous to the mother, with increased risk of toxaemia and severe postpartum haemorrhage, a maternal complication not described for haemoglobin H disease.
• The silent carrier state, with deletion of only one α gene, shows no reliable way to diagnose by haematologic methods and must be diagnosed by genetic mapping, unlike haemoglobin H disease and Bart's hydrops fetalis, which have characteristic haematologic and haemoglobin electrophoresis findings.

(a)
The normal platelet lifespan of 7 to 10 days is reduced to a few hours in chronic idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura.

(b)
The antibodies raised in chronic idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura are directed against antigen sites on glycoprotein Ib or IIb-IIIa.

(c)
• The body raises autoantibodies, usually IgG, against the platelets.
• These antibodies are directed against antigen sites on glycoprotein Ib or IIb-IIIa, leading to premature removal of platelets by the reticuloendothelial system.

(d)
• In idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura, IgG autoantibodies coat platelets and these are prematurely removed by the reticuloendothelial system.
• In thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, thrombocytopenia is consumptive, resulting from deficiency of the metalloprotease ADAMTS-13.
• This deficiency prevents cleavage of ultralarge von Willebrand factor multimers, which bind platelet glycoproteins Ib and IIb/IIIa and aggregate platelets in the terminal circulation, forming intravascular thrombi.
• Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura is therefore a disorder of immune-mediated platelet destruction, while thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura is a disorder of pathological platelet consumption through aggregation.
• The Coombs test can help distinguish autoimmune haemolytic processes, but in thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura the Coombs test is characteristically negative, supporting a non-immune consumptive mechanism.
• Full blood count in thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura also shows low haematocrit and fragmented red blood cells, features not part of the immune platelet destruction seen in idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura.
questions.question:
Describe the platelet under the following headings:
(a) its normal lifespan
(b) the surface glycoproteins targeted in immune destruction
(c) Explain the clinical basis for why platelets are prematurely destroyed in chronic idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura.
(d) Distinguish the mechanism of thrombocytopenia in idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura from that in thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Chronic haemolytic anaemia with hypersplenism (e.g. from a red cell membrane disorder such as hereditary spherocytosis); hypersplenism is an increased or exaggerated activity of an enlarged spleen with cytopenia of one or more cell lines despite compensatory bone marrow activity.

(b)
Splenectomy.

(c)
