The spleen is located in the left hypochondrial region, between the fundus of the stomach and the diaphragm; it has a medial groove (the hilum) where the arteries and nerve fibres enter, and the veins and lymph vessels leave the spleen; the spleen becomes palpable only when enlarged to over 14cm.
questions.question:
A patient with chronic haemolytic anaemia due to a red cell membrane disorder has developed symptomatic splenomegaly with hypersplenism, and splenectomy is planned.
(a) What is the diagnosis being treated by splenectomy?
(b) Name the procedure.
(c) State the anatomical landmarks relevant to this procedure.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Allogeneic stem cell transplantation (SCT); it is the treatment of choice in younger patients with severe aplastic anaemia who have an HLA-matched sibling donor.

(b)
Bone marrow stem cell harvest.

(c)
Marrow is aspirated from both posterior iliac crests; about 500-1000ml of marrow content is required for allogeneic transplant, containing approximately 3×10⁸ nucleated cells/kg recipient body weight.

(d)
Sources of stem cells for transplantation include bone marrow, peripheral blood, and placental (cord) blood; cord blood stem cells have the advantage of a lower risk of graft-versus-host disease due to the immunological naivety of cord stem cells.
questions.question:
A young patient with severe aplastic anaemia has an HLA-matched sibling donor and is being prepared for allogeneic stem cell transplantation. The donor's stem cells will be harvested from the bone marrow under general anaesthesia.
(a) What is the treatment being offered, and why is it the treatment of choice in this patient?
(b) Name the procedure used to obtain stem cells from the donor's bone marrow.
(c) State the anatomical site(s) from which the marrow is aspirated.
(d) What embryologic or developmental variant exists in the source of stem cells used for transplantation?

(a) Describe the course of the antibody-antigen reaction and complement activation that occurs in an acute haemolytic transfusion reaction.
(b) State the safe practice/procedure that should be performed before transfusion to prevent this reaction.
(c) Explain the anatomical basis of the renal deficit that can occur as a complication.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• An acute haemolytic transfusion reaction is premature destruction of transfused red cells reacting with antibodies in the recipient (or, less commonly, destruction of recipient red cells by transfused antibodies, as with dangerous universal donors).
• It is usually due to ABO incompatibility, most commonly from clerical errors.
• Rapid red cell destruction results from binding of preformed antibodies, usually IgM, mainly anti-A or anti-B, to red cell antigens.
• This binding results in complement fixation/activation.
• Complement activation leads to intravascular haemolysis via the membrane attack complex (MAC), a major product of complement activation.
• Intravascular haemolysis results in disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), as thromboplastin-like materials released from haemolysed red cells activate the coagulation pathway.
• The anaphylatoxins C3a and C5a, liberated during complement activation, cause release of vasoactive amines and hydrolases from mast cells, basophils and granulocytes.

(b)
The safe practice to prevent this reaction is compatibility testing (crossmatch): the ABO and RhD groups of all recipients should be determined before transfusion, and donor red cells are routinely tested against recipient serum/plasma to detect potential incompatibilities, manually or electronically.

(c)
• Anaphylatoxins typically mediate/cause hypotension and acute renal failure.
• The severity of the reaction, and hence the degree of any renal effect, depends on whether destruction is intravascular or extravascular, the strength/class/subclass of the antibody, the number of incompatible red cells transfused, and the clinical state of the patient.
• Clinically, lumbar pain reflects involvement of the kidneys, and the patient may pass dark-coloured urine (haemoglobinuria) when asked to void.
• This shows that the vasoactive amines and anaphylatoxins released by complement activation act on the renal vasculature, producing hypotension and renal ischaemic injury that culminate in acute renal failure, an anatomical consequence distant from the site of the antibody-antigen reaction itself.

(a)
• Acute chest syndrome is characterised by hypoxia, tachypnoea, fever, chest pain and pulmonary infiltrate on chest radiography.
• It often follows a painful event, particularly in adults.
• Infections due to Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Legionella, pneumococcus, H. influenzae and viruses are more likely in children.

(b)
• The pathogenesis of acute chest syndrome involves vaso-occlusion, infection, or embolisation of bone marrow fat.
• Fat-laden pulmonary macrophages in the airways, from fat embolisation from the bone marrow, are present in half of the cases.
• Patients with low oxygen saturation can benefit from exchange transfusion, and are given adequate analgesia, incentive spirometry to prevent further infiltrates, and broad-spectrum antibiotics.

(c)
• Hypoxia due to acute chest syndrome can result in widespread sickling and vaso-occlusion, with risk of multiorgan failure.
• This illustrates how pulmonary vascular and airway pathology spreads systemically, since hypoxia arising in the lungs promotes further sickling and vaso-occlusion throughout the body's vasculature, not confined to the lungs.
• Chronic pulmonary problems seen in sickle cell disease include obstructive and restrictive lung disease, pulmonary hypertension, and hypoxia.
• Pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale can occur, representing a distant cardiac functional deficit arising from chronic pulmonary vascular pathology.
• Acute and chronic pulmonary complications are the leading cause of death in older patients with sickle cell disease, underscoring the systemic significance of this organ-based pathology.
• Supplemental oxygen, antibiotic therapy, close monitoring, and in life-threatening cases partial exchange transfusion, mechanical ventilation, nitric oxide and steroids are used to limit this systemic spread.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the gross clinical picture of the lung in acute chest syndrome in sickle cell disease.
(b) Explain how the affected zones/parts of the lung relate to the pathologies described in this condition.
(c) Explain why this pulmonary pathology may spread to cause a distant, systemic functional deficit.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Vascular damage results from elevated cerebral blood flow velocities and interaction of rigid or adherent sickle cells with the vessel wall.

(b)
Transient ischaemic attacks or stroke due to cerebral infarction or haemorrhage occur in 25% of patients with sickle cell disease, and the risk of stroke is increased with lower baseline haemoglobin, low HbF level, high leucocyte count, or high systolic blood pressure.

(c)
The site of bleeding in haemorrhagic stroke is frequently subarachnoid, and these patients present with severe headache, vomiting and coma.

(d)
Cerebral infarction is more common than haemorrhage; strokes are associated with significant morbidity and mortality, and recurrence of stroke is common.

(e)
• Cerebrovascular accidents are managed with prompt exchange transfusion during the acute episode to reduce HbS to less than 30%, which limits neurologic damage.
• Following this, regular blood transfusion therapy is started to prevent recurrence of strokes by maintaining this HbS level.
• The neurological deficit arises because rigid, adherent sickle cells interacting with the cerebral vessel wall cause ischaemic or haemorrhagic injury to brain tissue, and it is this vascular injury that regular transfusion therapy aims to prevent from recurring.
• Recurrence of stroke is common, underscoring that the underlying vascular injury, if not addressed by ongoing transfusion, persists as an anatomical basis for repeated neurological deficit.
• The genitourinary, ocular and skeletal systems in sickle cell disease show analogous vaso-occlusive vascular injury producing organ-specific deficits, illustrating the same underlying mechanism affecting different vascular beds.
questions.question:
With reference to the cerebral vasculature in sickle cell disease-related stroke:
(a) Describe the origin of the vascular damage.
(b) Describe the course of blood flow changes that precede the stroke.
(c) Describe the relations of the common site of bleeding in haemorrhagic stroke.
(d) Describe the distribution of stroke types (ischaemic versus haemorrhagic) in this condition.
(e) Explain the anatomical basis of the neurological deficit that follows vascular injury in this condition.

(a) Describe the origin and course of the coagulation activation pathway in disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), including the initiation, amplification and propagation phases.
(b) State the safe therapeutic (replacement) interventions used to correct the resulting deficiencies.
(c) Explain the anatomical basis of a specific organ deficit that can occur when a vessel is thrombosed as a consequence of DIC.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• DIC is an acquired syndrome of intravascular activation of coagulation with loss of localisation, in which activation is dispersed and uncontrollable, leading to intravascular fibrin formation and inefficiency of natural coagulation inhibitors.
• Initiation phase: occurs on the tissue-factor (TF)-bearing cell, initiated when injury exposes this cell to flowing blood, generating a small amount of activated factor IX and thrombin that diffuse to the platelet.
• Amplification phase: the small amount of thrombin generated activates platelets, releases von Willebrand factor, and generates activated forms of factor V, factor VIII and factor XI.
• Propagation phase: on the procoagulant membrane of the activated platelet, intrinsic tenase forms (binding of activated factor IX to activated factor VIII), generating activated factor X on the platelet surface; the prothrombinase complex then forms, producing a burst of thrombin directly on the platelet.
• Exposure of procoagulant tissue extracts (tissue factor) to blood is a major contributory factor in most forms of DIC, interacting with factor VIIa to activate the extrinsic pathway.
• Impaired physiological anticoagulant pathways (reduced antithrombin, depressed protein C system, insufficient tissue factor pathway inhibitor) and impaired fibrinolysis (release of plasminogen activator inhibitor type 1) further drive the coagulopathy.

(b)
• Replacement therapy corrects the deficiencies: platelet concentrates for platelets <50×10⁹/L with bleeding or <20×10⁹/L without bleeding; fresh frozen plasma (15-20ml/kg) if fibrinogen <100mg/dl or significant bleeding; cryoprecipitate for fibrinogen; and fresh whole blood if other products are unavailable.
• Restoration of deficient natural coagulation inhibitors (antithrombin, protein C/APC concentrates, tissue factor pathway inhibitor) is also a form of replacement therapy.
• Bleeding, ranging from oozing at venepuncture sites to major gastrointestinal or intracranial haemorrhage, is the archetypal manifestation, but organ failure from microvascular thrombosis is more common and often unrecognised.

(c)
• In meningococcal septicaemia (and rarely pneumococcal infection), thrombosis of the adrenal vessels can occur.
• This thrombosis of the adrenal vessels leads to adrenal insufficiency, known as Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome.
• This illustrates how microvascular thrombosis at a specific anatomical site (the adrenal gland vasculature) in DIC produces a distant organ (endocrine) deficit, rather than only causing generalised bleeding.

(a)
• Priapism occurs in two-thirds of males with sickle cell disease, with peak incidence in the second and third decades.
• It is caused by vaso-occlusion.

(b)
The vaso-occlusion leads to obstruction of venous drainage from the penis.

(c)
It typically affects the corpora cavernosa alone, resulting in a hard penis with a soft glans.

(d)
• Episodes can be brief (stuttering) or prolonged, lasting longer than three hours.
• In essential thrombocythaemia, priapism is also described, though as a rare complication.

(e)
• Recurrent priapism leads to fibrosis of the corpora cavernosa.
• This fibrosis results in eventual impotence.
• The deformity/dysfunction arises because repeated vaso-occlusive episodes cause structural damage confined to the corpora cavernosa rather than the rest of the penile anatomy.
• The soft glans, spared in acute episodes because it is not part of the corpora cavernosa, illustrates that the pathology is anatomically localised to the affected erectile tissue.
questions.question:
With reference to the vascular supply of the penis in sickle cell disease:
(a) Describe the origin of priapism in this condition.
(b) Describe the course of the pathological process leading to priapism.
(c) Describe the structure primarily affected.
(d) Describe the distribution/frequency of the resulting clinical effect.
(e) Explain the anatomical basis of the deformity or dysfunction that follows repeated episodes of this condition.

(a) Describe the gene location and inheritance of haemophilia.
(b) Relate the types of mutation to severity and state the transmission risks.
(c) Relate the severity classes to the clinical bleeding pattern and the laboratory findings, and compare haemophilia B.
(d) Explain why carrier females may bleed.
(e) Explain how repeated bleeding and treatment lead to distant structural damage and functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Sex-linked recessive; the FVIII gene lies near the tip of the long arm of the X chromosome (Xq28) near G6PD; deletion or mutation reduces or distorts FVIII synthesis; FIX is also X-linked, whereas vWF and FXI are autosomal dominant.
• A positive family history is found in the maternal grandfather, uncles and male cousins; 30% have no family history (spontaneous mutation), so a negative history does not exclude haemophilia.
• Incidence is about 1 in 10,000 (1:40,000 reported in Nigeria).

(b)
• Mild and moderate disease is mostly due to missense or frameshift mutations or deletions; severe disease mostly to inversions (intron 22 or 1); the intron 22 inversion causes 40-50% of severe cases.
• Carrier mother x normal father: 50% of sons affected, 50% of daughters carriers; affected father: all daughters carriers and no sons affected.

(c)
• Severe FVIII <2 u/dl, moderate 2-10, mild 10-30; severity correlates inversely with the level; bleeding from the umbilical stump, circumcision, gums, bruising in infancy; haemarthrosis of weight-bearing joints, muscle bleeds and haematuria in adults.
• Laboratory: prolonged PTTK, normal PT, thrombin time, bleeding time and platelet count, abnormal thromboplastin generation test, FVIII activity <35 u/dl; haemophilia B (FIX deficiency, Christmas disease) is identical clinically, 1/5 as common, distinguished only by factor assay.

(d)
Carrier females rarely bleed but may if lyonisation favours the normal X chromosome, if homozygous (carrier mother and affected father), or with Turner syndrome (XO); vWD is a more common cause of FVIII deficiency in females.

(e)
• Recurrent haemarthroses and muscle haematomas cause progressive joint deformity and disability; pressure causes entrapment neuropathy or ischaemic necrosis.
• Pseudotumours are encapsulated haematomas with cystic swelling in fascial and muscle planes, long bones, pelvis and cranium, with subperiosteal haemorrhage causing bone destruction and new bone formation (best seen on MRI).
• Spontaneous intracerebral haemorrhage is an important cause of death; haematuria, GI haemorrhage with obstruction from intramucosal bleeding, and prolonged bleeding after dental extraction also occur.
• Treatment complications: HIV (over 50% of treated haemophiliacs in the USA/Western Europe in the 1980s), hepatitis C with chronic hepatitis, cirrhosis and hepatoma, hepatitis B; FVIII inhibitors in 5-10%.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the structure of the bone marrow under the following headings: medullary cavity and periosteum; cellular components; vascular versus non-vascular regions; and the hematopoietic microenvironment.
(b) Explain the clinical basis for why the bone marrow must be sampled by needle aspiration/biopsy rather than by simple blood testing alone.
(c) Distinguish between red bone marrow and yellow bone marrow.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Medullary cavity and periosteum: bone marrow is a spongy, jelly-like material found in the medullary cavity at the centre of bones; the cavity is surrounded and protected by the periosteum, which must be punctured during aspiration or biopsy.
• Cellular components: hematopoietic tissue includes blood cells and their precursors, adventitial/barrier cells, adipocytes and macrophages, arranged in a particular, non-random organisation.
• Vascular versus non-vascular regions: the non-vascular region contains haemopoietic cells packed between fat cells, trabeculae, collagen fibres, fibroblasts and dendritic cells, where haematopoiesis occurs; the vascular region contains blood vessels supplying nutrients and carrying cells into circulation; there is no lymphatic drainage.
• Haematopoietic microenvironment: consists of adventitial reticular (barrier) cells, endothelial cells, macrophages, adipocytes, bone-lining cells (osteoblasts) and extracellular matrix, which support proliferation, differentiation and maturation of stem cells.

(b)
• A complete blood count (CBC), including reticulocyte count, gives only a general picture of marrow function by measuring the output of mature cells and the release of new red cells.
• Direct testing of the marrow is required to evaluate morphology and cytology, the myeloid:erythroid (M:E) ratio, iron stores, tissue inflammation, abnormal pigmentation, necrosis, presence of abnormal (e.g. neoplastic) cells, and infectious or parasitic organisms.
• Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy also allow fluorescence in situ hybridisation (FISH), flow cytometry, immunophenotyping, karyotyping, and PCR, none of which can be done on a peripheral blood count alone.
• Because these detailed cellular, cytogenetic and molecular assessments require actual marrow tissue, direct sampling by needle aspiration/trephine biopsy (typically from the hip bone, after local anaesthesia of skin, subcutaneous tissue and periosteum) is necessary.

(c)
• Red bone marrow (myeloid tissue) is fibrous tissue containing haematopoietic stem cells; in adults it produces all red cells and platelets and 60-70% of white cells.
• Yellow bone marrow is fattier, containing mesenchymal/marrow stromal cells that form connective tissue (fat, cartilage, muscle, bone).
• Yellow bone marrow stores fat and nutrients for red bone marrow and can convert to red bone marrow when the body is stressed (e.g. infection, severe blood loss).
• Marrow cellularity, and hence the proportion of red to yellow marrow, decreases with age, which is accounted for in interpreting cellularity on a bone marrow biopsy.

(a)
Pyruvate kinase deficiency.

(b)
Reduced red cell ATP leads to loss of membrane stability and haemolysis; there is increased 2,3-DPG causing increased oxygen off-loading; reticulocytes, which have the highest ATP needs and rely on mitochondria for ATP, undergo significant haemolysis because they cannot generate ATP in the hypoxic spleen; inheritance is autosomal recessive, with PKLR compound heterozygosity or homozygosity confirmed by enzyme activity assay and molecular sequencing.

(c)
Patients may need regular transfusions to manage the classic features and complications of haemolytic anaemia until splenectomy is performed.

(d)
Splenectomy is the definitive treatment; reticulocytosis becomes markedly pronounced after splenectomy (reticulocytes may increase from 10-15% to 30-70%) with only partial amelioration of the anaemia; the risk of gallstones and aplastic crisis persists after splenectomy, and the post-splenectomy blood film shows echinocytes whereas the pre-splenectomy smear is often bland.
questions.question:
A patient with a chronic haemolytic anaemia is found to have an autosomal recessive enzyme defect; splenectomy is later performed for management.
(a) What is the most likely diagnosis?
(b) Explain the pathologic basis of the haemolysis in this condition.
(c) How would this patient be managed before splenectomy (resuscitative/supportive measures)?
(d) What happens after splenectomy (definitive treatment), and what risks persist?

(a) Describe the role of the liver in iron storage and its involvement in hepatic pathology in sickle cell disease and thalassaemia.
(b) Explain how the affected parts/zones of the liver relate to specific pathologies in these disorders.
(c) Explain why hepatic iron pathology may spread to a distant structure and cause a functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The liver is a major site of iron storage; a direct relationship exists between the amount of circulating ferritin and body iron stores.
• In sickle cell disease, hepatic damage results from hepatic infarctions and transfusion-transmitted hepatitis; gallstones occur due to persistent elevation of serum bilirubin.
• Hepcidin, a key regulator of iron absorption and recycling, is produced by the liver.

(b)
• In sickle cell disease, hepatic infarction is a described complication affecting liver tissue directly.
• In β thalassaemia major, extramedullary haematopoiesis and hepatosplenomegaly occur as part of the marrow expansion response to ineffective erythropoiesis.
• Regular blood transfusions, usually begun around one year of age, are required for life in thalassaemia major, and this predisposes the liver to iron loading.

(c)
• Excessive transfusion without iron chelation results in transfusional haemosiderosis.
• Without iron chelation, the patient develops cardiac disease, showing that hepatic (and systemic) iron overload spreads to a distant structure, the heart, producing a functional deficit.
• Other dangers of continuous transfusion therapy include alloimmunisation (development of antibodies to transfused red blood cells) and risk of transfusion-transmitted diseases.
• Increased rates of infection have also been noted among patients with β thalassaemia major with iron overload, since iron is an essential nutrient for the growth of many microorganisms and iron loading promotes infection.
• This further illustrates how iron pathology, originating from hepatic storage overload, spreads systemically to affect immune (infective) function as a distant functional deficit.
• Free iron is toxic and its concentration must be tightly regulated to prevent this spread of pathology to distant organs.

(a)
Acute haemolytic transfusion reaction, usually due to ABO incompatibility.

(b)
Most commonly due to clerical errors; rapid red cell destruction results from binding of preformed antibodies (usually IgM, mainly anti-A or anti-B) to red cell antigens; severity depends on the amount of incompatible blood transfused, whether destruction is intravascular or extravascular, and the strength, class and subclass of the antibody.

(c)
Complement fixation/activation leads to intravascular haemolysis from the membrane attack complex; anaphylatoxins C3a and C5a cause release of vasoactive amines, leading to hypotension and acute renal failure; thromboplastin-like substances released from haemolysed red cells activate coagulation pathways, leading to disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), evidenced by oozing in the surgical field.

(d)
Management: stop the transfusion immediately but leave the IV line in-situ, begin infusion of normal saline, collect blood and urine samples for investigation, and check for clerical errors; the transfusion should be stopped permanently, since acute haemolytic transfusion reaction accounts for over 50% of deaths related to blood transfusion, and supportive management (airway, urine output, pulse, BP monitoring) is then instituted; when haemolysis is severe, urgent re-grouping, cross-matching and transfusion, FFP and platelet transfusion may be necessary.
questions.question:
Within less than an hour of starting a blood transfusion, a patient develops heat and pain at the cannulated vein, throbbing headache, facial flushing, chest tightness, nausea, lumbar pain, tachycardia, hypotension, and later passes dark-coloured urine.
(a) What is the most likely diagnosis?
(b) What are the risk factors/causes for this reaction?
(c) What complications may occur?
(d) What are the management options, and justify the first step taken.

A young adult presents with painless cervical lymphadenopathy that fluctuates in size, nodal pain after alcohol ingestion, fever, drenching night sweats, weight loss and pruritus. A lymph node biopsy shows large Reed-Sternberg cells among eosinophils, plasma cells, lymphocytes and histiocytes, and the large cells are CD15 and CD30 positive.
(a) Identify the condition.
(b) Identify the structures that may be affected.
(c) Describe the staging and the work-up.
(d) Explain the associated clinical and laboratory findings and state the treatment and prognosis.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Classical Hodgkin lymphoma, a B-cell lymphoma characterized by Reed-Sternberg cells (CD15+, CD30+); peak incidence 15-40 years, M:F 1.5-2:1, EBV a possible cofactor.

(b)
Lymph nodes (typically cervical); the liver and spleen may enlarge; extranodal disease is uncommon but lung, CNS, skin and bone may be involved; marrow is assessed by aspirate and trephine.

(c)
Cotswold-modified Ann Arbor staging after examination and cervical, thoracic, abdominal and pelvic PET/CT: I single node region; II two or more regions same side of diaphragm; III both sides; IV other organs (liver, marrow, CNS); A no symptoms, B fever, night sweats, weight loss >10% in 6 months, X bulky disease (>1/3 mediastinal widening or 10 cm mass), E extranodal.

(d)
• Systemic symptoms occur in 25%; defective cell-mediated immunity causes infections; laboratory: normocytic normochromic anaemia (autoimmune haemolysis may occur), leucocytosis, occasional eosinophilia, raised ESR and LDH, abnormal LFTs.
• Stage IA/IIA with favourable histology: radiotherapy alone; advanced disease (IB, IIB, III, IV): six cycles of ABVD; local radiotherapy for bulky or resistant sites; >90% of stage I and II are cured versus 50-70% of stage IV.

questions.question:
Describe the haemoglobin molecule under the following headings:
(a) composition
(b) the chromosomal location of the genes for its chain types
(c) Explain the clinical basis of why deoxygenated sickle haemoglobin is less soluble than deoxygenated haemoglobin A.
(d) Distinguish between haemoglobin A and haemoglobin F.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Haemoglobin is an oxygen-carrying pigment consisting of haem and globin.
• Haem is synthesised from ALA and succinylCoA; globin is an amino acid sequence arranged in chains.

(b)
• Genes for the α and α-like chains are located on chromosome 16.
• Genes for the β and β-like chains are located on chromosome 11.

(c)
• Point mutation (GAG to GTG) in the sixth codon of the β globin gene substitutes valine for glutamic acid.
• Deoxygenated HbS is less soluble than deoxygenated HbA and tends to crystallise out of solution inside erythrocytes when oxygen concentration is low, as in the tissues.

(d)
• Haemoglobin A has the molecular structure α₂β₂ and is the major haemoglobin of normal adult blood.
• Haemoglobin F (fetal haemoglobin) contains γ chains instead of β chains (α₂γ₂).
• An orderly switch from ε- to α-chain and from ε- to γ-chain production occurs during fetal development, followed by β- and δ-chain production after birth.
• HbF does not participate in HbS polymerisation, so infants with sickle cell anaemia do not develop manifestations until HbF declines to adult values.

(a)
• The blood supply to the spleen arises from the systemic circulation and the coeliac trunk.
• The coeliac trunk supplies blood to the spleen via the hilum, and on entering the spleen it forms the splenic artery.
• The splenic artery forms the trabecular artery as it progresses into the spleen.
• The trabecular artery enters the splenic pulp and divides longitudinally to form the central artery.
• The trabecular artery, dividing longitudinally on both sides, is immediately surrounded by a meshwork of lymphatics called the periarterial lymphatic sheath (PALS), which houses T cells.

(b)
• The spleen is located in the left hypochondrial region, between the fundus of the stomach and the diaphragm, and has a medial groove (hilum) where arteries and nerve fibres enter, and veins and lymph vessels leave.
• The spleen weighs 150-250g, with a length of 5 to 13cm.
• The spleen is normally not palpable, except when its size increases to over 14cm; this increase in size and weight above normal is termed splenomegaly.
• Age, sex, height and body build affect spleen size: the spleen shrinks with age (to as small as 50-70g in the elderly) and is larger in males and in taller, larger-built individuals.

(c)
• Splenic arterial thrombosis is a cause of hyposplenism, which is defined as decreased splenic function.
• Hyposplenism causes overwhelming infection, because the spleen's filtration, phagocytic and immunologic functions (particularly against encapsulated bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae type b and Neisseria meningitidis) are lost when its blood supply and hence its function are compromised.
• Blood film findings in hyposplenism (from disrupted splenic function) include target cells, acanthocytes, spur cells, Howell-Jolly bodies and Pappenheimer bodies, reflecting loss of the spleen's pitting and culling functions.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the origin and course of the blood supply to the spleen, including how it forms the periarterial lymphatic sheath (PALS).
(b) State how enlargement of the spleen is clinically detected, given the normal relations of the spleen.
(c) Explain the anatomical basis of the clinical consequence when the splenic blood supply is disrupted (e.g. by thrombosis).

questions.answerText:
(a)
Haemophilia A (classical haemophilia, factor VIII deficiency), confirmed by a specific factor VIII assay (activity <35 u/dl); severe <2 u/dl, moderate 2-10, mild 10-30.

(b)
• X-linked recessive; the FVIII gene lies near the tip of the long arm of the X chromosome (Xq28) near the G6PD gene; deletion, point mutation or inversion (intron 22 inversion in 40-50% of severe cases); 30% have no family history (spontaneous mutation).
• Carrier female x normal male: 50% of sons affected, 50% of daughters carriers; affected male x normal female: all sons normal, all daughters carriers.

(c)
FVIII is cofactor to FIX in converting FX to FXa in the intrinsic pathway; its lack slows FXa generation, tissue factor pathway inhibitor blocks the extrinsic route, and more thrombin is needed to activate TAFI, so clot formation is insufficient and clot removal rapid.

(d)
• Replace FVIII (concentrate, cryoprecipitate, FFP); 1 unit/kg raises the level 2 units/dl; targets: mild bleed 30%, major bleed 50%, major surgery 80-100%; half-life 8-12 hours; units = required rise x weight in kg / 2.
• Prophylaxis every 2-3 days (FVIII >1%) reduces joint disease but is limited by cost; desmopressin for mild to moderate disease; antifibrinolytics (ε-aminocaproic acid, tranexamic acid); rest of the joint, physiotherapy, orthopaedic care; liver transplantation can cure; gene therapy.
• Complications of therapy: inhibitors in 5-10% (managed with rVIIa, FEIBA, porcine FVIII, high-dose FVIII, immune tolerance) and transmission of HBV, HCV and HIV.
questions.question:
A male infant has excessive bleeding after circumcision and large bruises from minor knocks. Coagulation screening shows a prolonged PTTK with normal PT, thrombin time, bleeding time and platelet count. There are affected male relatives on the mother's side.
(a) State the diagnosis and the confirmatory test.
(b) Describe the predisposing genetic factors and the pattern of inheritance.
(c) Explain the pathophysiology of the bleeding.
(d) Outline the management and its complications.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Capsule and trabeculae: the spleen has a capsule, and trabeculae which consist of blood vessels and lymphatics extending into the pulp.
• Red pulp: composed of splenic sinuses and splenic cords (of Billroth), resembling a sponge, and occupies more than half the splenic volume.
• White pulp: composed of the periarterial lymphatic sheath (PALS, housing T cells), lymphoid follicles (housing B cells), and the marginal zone (plasma cells, T and B lymphocytes, macrophages, interdigitating dendritic cells).
• Blood supply/hilum: the medial groove (hilum) is where arteries and nerve fibres enter and veins and lymph vessels leave; blood is supplied via the coeliac trunk, which forms the splenic artery, then trabecular artery, then central artery, surrounded by the PALS.

(b)
• Splenic action on red cells involves three mechanisms: phagocytosis (irreversible removal of red cell inclusions, damaged or antibody-coated cells by macrophages), sequestration (reversible temporary trapping), and pooling (increased blood volume in continuous exchange with the circulation).
• Red cells with an abnormal membrane, or with inclusions that render them relatively inflexible, remain in the splenic cord where they are either conditioned for later transit or destroyed by macrophages.
• Siderotic granules, Howell-Jolly bodies, nuclear remnants and Heinz bodies are removed during temporary sequestration (pitting), after which the red cells are returned to circulation.
• Phagocytosis of antibody-coated cells occurs in the splenic cord, as seen in autoimmune haemolytic anaemia and autoimmune (idiopathic) thrombocytopenic purpura.
• This selective destructive/conditioning capacity resides in the red pulp, which is the site where senescent red cells are identified and destroyed.

(c)
• The white pulp, in contrast, is involved in humoral and cellular immune responses (B cells, T cells, plasma cells in the marginal zone), protecting against encapsulated bacteria, viruses and intra-erythrocyte parasites (Plasmodium, Babesia).
• The red pulp therefore functions in filtration/phagocytosis and blood storage/reservoir (about one-third of platelets are stored in the spleen), while the white pulp functions immunologically.
• This distinction explains why red pulp disease manifests as haemolytic disorders (destruction of abnormal cells) while white pulp disease manifests as immune/lymphoproliferative disorders.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the structure of the spleen under the following headings: capsule and trabeculae; red pulp; white pulp; and blood supply/hilum.
(b) Explain the clinical basis for why the spleen selectively destroys abnormal red cells.
(c) Distinguish between the red pulp and the white pulp of the spleen.

A child presents in childhood with mild to moderate anaemia, intermittent jaundice, and an enlarged spleen; a sibling or parent is similarly affected. During an intercurrent infection the child's anaemia suddenly worsens.
(a) What is the most likely diagnosis, and what does the peripheral blood film show that supports it?
(b) Explain the pathologic basis of this condition at the level of the red cell membrane.
(c) What is the cause of the sudden worsening of anaemia described above, and how would you manage this acute event?
(d) What is the definitive treatment for this condition in its severe form, and what precautions are taken before undertaking it?
questions.answerText:
(a)
Hereditary spherocytosis; the blood film shows spherocytosis – red cells that are smaller, lack central pallor and appear densely haemoglobinised (hyperchromic); MCHC is increased due to cell dehydration and the reticulocyte count is increased.

(b)
Normally the lipid bilayer is anchored to the underlying skeleton by two linkages: ankyrin-spectrin-band 3, and glycophorin C-protein 4.1; deficiency of spectrin, ankyrin, band 3 or protein 4.2 (ankyrin deficiency being most common) weakens these linkages, so unsupported bilayer is lost as lipid vesicles, decreasing surface area relative to volume and producing spherocytes; spherocytes are less deformable and are trapped and destroyed in the spleen.

(c)
This is a haemolytic crisis, an exacerbation of haemolysis during intercurrent infection due to hyperplasia of the monocyte-macrophage system; manage with transfusion support as needed and treatment of the underlying infection; folate should be given to prevent a megaloblastic crisis from increased erythroid turnover.

(d)
Definitive treatment of severe hereditary spherocytosis is splenectomy, which corrects the haemolytic anaemia (though the underlying skeletal defect and spherocytosis persist) and prevents complications such as gallstones; because of the life-long risk of sepsis from pneumococci and other encapsulated bacteria, splenectomy is deferred until the child is 6 years old, and children are immunised with polyvalent pneumococcal, H. influenzae and meningococcal vaccines and given penicillin prophylaxis.

questions.question:
A patient found to have sustained thrombocytosis on a routine blood count is examined and found to have an enlarged spleen, with imaging confirming splenomegaly.
(a) What is the enlarged organ, and what underlying disorder is suggested by this finding together with the thrombocytosis?
(b) What other structures may be affected by this disorder?
(c) What differential pathologies must be excluded before confirming the diagnosis?
(d) What clinico-anatomical reasoning links the splenic finding to the underlying disease process?
questions.answerText:
(a)
The enlarged organ is the spleen; approximately 40 to 50% of patients with essential thrombocythaemia present with splenomegaly, some with splenic atrophy due to infarction.

(b)
About 20% of patients present with hepatomegaly; patients with the JAK2 mutation can present with Budd-Chiari syndrome even when the platelet count is normal, due to splenomegaly.

(c)
Other causes of thrombocytosis must be ruled out, such as iron deficiency, inflammatory or malignant disorders, and myelodysplasia; other myeloid malignancies, namely polycythaemia vera, myelofibrosis, chronic myeloid leukaemia and myelodysplastic syndrome, must also be excluded, and BCR/ABL1 mutation seen in chronic myeloid leukaemia must be excluded.

(d)
A persisting platelet count above 450×10⁹/L is the major diagnostic feature; the disorder is a nonreactive, chronic myeloproliferative disorder associated with sustained megakaryocyte proliferation from acquired mutation of JAK2, MPL or CALR genes, and a red blood cell mass study is conducted to exclude polycythaemia vera, since in essential thrombocythaemia the red blood cell mass is normal.

questions.question:
An elderly patient presents with lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly, together with symptoms of blood hyperviscosity including visual and auditory impairment.
(a) What is the underlying disease process and where does it occur?
(b) What structures are affected, giving rise to the presenting symptoms?
(c) What are the differential diagnoses among the plasma cell/monoclonal gammopathy disorders?
(d) Explain the clinico-anatomical reasoning behind the hyperviscosity symptoms.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Waldenström macroglobulinaemia, characterised by neoplastic proliferation of small lymphocytes, lymphoplasmacytoid cells and plasma cells, with production of monoclonal IgM immunoglobulin (macroglobulin); it occurs mainly in elderly patients.

(b)
Lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly may be present on examination; the visual and auditory systems and general level of consciousness are affected due to blood hyperviscosity from the macroglobulins.

(c)
Multiple myeloma, monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS), solitary plasmacytoma of bone, extramedullary plasmacytoma, primary amyloidosis, heavy chain disease, and osteosclerotic myeloma/POEMS syndrome.

(d)
Neoplastic lymphoplasmacytoid cells and plasma cells produce excess monoclonal IgM (macroglobulin); because IgM is a large pentameric molecule, its accumulation in blood raises viscosity, impairing flow through small vessels supplying the eye, ear and brain, producing visual/auditory impairment and altered consciousness; treatment includes plasmapheresis (to physically remove the excess macroglobulin from the circulation) and chemotherapy (chlorambucil with or without prednisolone, fludarabine).

questions.question:
With reference to the vascular event occurring within the spleen during splenic sequestration crisis:
(a) Describe the origin of the crisis.
(b) Describe the course of blood flow that produces the crisis.
(c) Describe the group of patients (relations) in whom this occurs.
(d) Describe the distribution of clinical effects that result.
(e) Explain the anatomical/structural basis of why removal of the spleen prevents recurrence of this crisis.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Splenic sequestration crisis begins with sudden and massive accumulation of blood in the spleen.

(b)
This causes a rapid increase in the size of the spleen over a period of several hours.

(c)
It occurs in patients with sickle cell anaemia who have splenomegaly, namely infants or children, especially those aged 6 months to 3 years, or adults with sickle cell β thalassaemia.

(d)
The distribution of clinical effects includes abdominal fullness, decrease in circulatory volume, progressive anaemia, and circulatory failure.

(e)
• The crisis is a common cause of death in young children.
• Recurrence can be avoided by removal of the spleen.
• The underlying structural basis is that the spleen, once enlarged by sequestered blood, remains the organ capable of repeatedly pooling large volumes of blood in susceptible patients.
• Removing this organ therefore removes the structural site at which the pathological accumulation of blood occurs, preventing further episodes of circulatory compromise.
• Packed red cell transfusion is indicated in splenic sequestration crisis to improve oxygen-carrying capacity as an acute measure, separate from the definitive removal of the spleen.
• Splenomegaly and splenic pathology are also described in β thalassaemia and essential thrombocythaemia.

(a)
Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC).

(b)
Obstetric complications (abruptio placentae, amniotic fluid embolism, placenta previa, retained dead fetus syndrome), sepsis/severe infections, trauma, malignancy, vascular disorders, organ destruction (severe pancreatitis, hepatic failure), toxic reactions (snake bites) and immunologic reactions (haemolytic transfusion reaction); in abruptio placentae, decidual fragments and activated coagulation factors enter the maternal venous circulation following rupture of the basal decidual plate, exposing tissue factor.

(c)
Multi-organ failure from fibrin deposition and microvascular thrombosis; haemorrhage ranging from oozing at venepuncture sites to major gastrointestinal or intracranial bleeding; in meningococcal septicaemia, thrombosis of adrenal vessels can cause adrenal insufficiency (Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome).

(d)
Management includes treating/removing the causative factor, supportive therapy (antibiotics, ICU care, oxygen, dialysis), replacement therapy, and control of coagulation mechanisms; replacement therapy with fresh frozen plasma (15-20ml/kg) is justified here because it replaces multiple coagulation factor deficiencies and is indicated specifically in DIC with significant bleeding, along with platelet concentrates if platelets are <50×10⁹/L with bleeding and cryoprecipitate if fibrinogen is <100mg/dl.
questions.question:
A woman with abruptio placentae develops oozing from venepuncture sites and the surgical field, together with laboratory evidence of a consumptive coagulopathy.
(a) What is the most likely diagnosis?
(b) What are the risk factors/causes for this condition?
(c) What complications may occur?
(d) What are the management options, and justify the use of one of them in this patient.

Describe the β globin gene cluster under the following headings:
(a) its chromosomal location
(b) the genes it contains
(c) Explain the clinical basis for why mutations of this gene cluster commonly cause β thalassaemia rather than α thalassaemia.
(d) Distinguish β thalassaemia minor from β thalassaemia major.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The β globin gene cluster is located on chromosome 11.

(b)
It contains the ε, γ (G and A), δ and β genes.

(c)
• β thalassaemias are caused by mutations that nearly all affect the β globin locus and are extremely heterogeneous, leading to variable reduction in β globin chain output.
• In contrast, α thalassaemia is predominantly caused by large numbers of gene deletions in the α globin gene cluster, located on chromosome 16, so the mechanism and gene cluster affected differ between the two conditions.

(d)
• β thalassaemia minor is a heterozygous disorder with one normal and one mutated β gene, presenting as mild, usually asymptomatic hypochromic microcytic anaemia with haemoglobin in the 10 to 13 g/dL range and rarely hepatomegaly or splenomegaly.
• β thalassaemia major is a homozygous disorder resulting in severe transfusion-dependent haemolytic anaemia, detected early in childhood with failure to thrive, pallor, jaundice and hepatosplenomegaly.
• β thalassaemia minor has high HbA2 levels (3.5 to 8.0%) and normal to slightly elevated HbF, while β thalassaemia major shows predominantly HbF with only a slight increase in HbA2.
• β thalassaemia minor normally requires no treatment, while β thalassaemia major requires regular transfusions beginning around one year of age, continued throughout life.
• β thalassaemia intermedia lies in severity between minor and major, with patients able to maintain a minimum haemoglobin of 7g/dL or greater without transfusions.
• The silent carrier state is the mildest form, with nearly normal β/α chain ratio, no haematologic abnormalities, and normal levels of HbA2.

questions.question:
A 58-year-old patient presents with headache, dizziness, drowsiness, facial plethora with engorged conjunctival vessels, itching after a warm bath and splenomegaly. The full blood count shows a haematocrit above 0.50, an absolute neutrophil count above 10×10⁹/L and platelets above 450×10⁹/L, and serum erythropoietin is low.
(a) State the diagnosis and its molecular basis.
(b) List the risk factors and epidemiologic features of the condition.
(c) Describe the complications and the natural course.
(d) List the management options and justify the one you would use first.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Polycythaemia rubra vera: a clonal myeloproliferative disorder of a pluripotent stem cell with expansion of erythroid, granulocytic and megakaryocytic lines, an absolute rise in red cell mass independent of erythropoietin.
• A mutation in the V617 region of JAK2 removes the feedback that switches off the erythropoietic drive, so red cell production is uncontrolled.

(b)
Risk features: JAK2 V617 mutation; median onset 55-60 years; slight male excess (M:F 1.2:1); 2-3 per 100,000; rare in children.

(c)
• Thrombosis is the commonest presentation, arterial (MI, stroke, TIA) and venous (mesenteric, splenic, portal, DVT, PE), from hyperviscosity; also neurological ischaemia, hypertension, hyperuricaemia/gout and pruritus (basophilia and histamine).
• Untreated, 50% die within 2 years; the disease may transform to acute leukaemia or progress to myelofibrosis, both with worse prognosis.

(d)
• Options: regular venesection (haematocrit <0.45), allopurinol and fluids, antihistamines, LMWH (e.g. enoxaparin), antihypertensives, anti-gout drugs; cytoreduction with hydroxycarbamide, busulfan or interferon alfa; anagrelide for platelets; JAK2 inhibitor ruxolitinib.
• Justification: regular venesection to a haematocrit below 0.45 targets the hyperviscosity to which the thrombosis, neurological features, plethora and hypertension are attributed; with adequate treatment survival can reach 11 years.

questions.question:
A young woman presents with fatigue, pallor, brittle spoon-shaped nails, a sore tongue, and an intense craving to eat clay.
(a) What is the diagnosis?
(b) What are the predisposing factors for this condition?
(c) What is the pathophysiology, including the stages of its development?
(d) How is this condition managed?
questions.answerText:
(a)
Iron deficiency anaemia.

(b)
Predisposing factors include inadequate dietary intake of iron (especially vegetarian diet), defective absorption (gluten-induced enteropathy, gastrectomy, atrophic gastritis, inflammatory bowel disease, antacids, proton pump inhibitors), blood loss (gastrointestinal, renal, pulmonary, frequent blood donation), and increased demands (prematurity, growth, pregnancy, erythropoietin therapy).

(c)
There are three stages: depletion of iron stores (falling serum ferritin, absent stainable marrow iron); reduction in circulating iron with iron-deficient erythropoiesis (decreased serum iron and transferrin saturation, increased total iron binding capacity, increased free erythrocyte protoporphyrin); and development of iron deficiency anaemia, initially normocytic normochromic, progressing to microcytic hypochromic anaemia with MCV less than 80 fL and MCHC less than 30g/dL.

(d)
Treatment is with oral ferrous sulphate (one tablet thrice daily, providing 60mg elemental iron per 200mg tablet) continued for six months to replenish stores, alongside correction of the underlying cause of blood loss; parenteral iron (iron dextran or the safer iron sucrose) is indicated for gastrointestinal intolerance, advanced pregnancy with moderate to severe anaemia, malabsorption, non-cooperative patients, or when surgery is imminent.

questions.question:
(a) Define the plasma cell dyscrasias and state their spectrum.
(b) Describe non-secretory myeloma, light-chain myeloma and plasma cell leukaemia.
(c) Describe plasmacytoma and Waldenström macroglobulinaemia.
(d) State the investigations used in myeloma and the features they show.
(e) Explain the basis of the clinical features and complications of myeloma.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Benign or malignant monoclonal expansions of plasma cells; spectrum from MGUS to smouldering MM to multiple myeloma to plasma cell leukaemia; MGUS and SMM are asymptomatic without end-organ damage.

(b)
• Non-secretory MM: 10% or more clonal plasma cells or plasmacytoma, CD38 and CD138 positive, end-organ damage, no M band because heavy or light chain secretion is defective.
• Light-chain MM: 15%, poorer prognosis than IgG or IgA MM, light chains cause myeloma cast nephropathy; plasma cell leukaemia: more than 2×10⁹/L circulating plasma cells, rare, aggressive, dismal prognosis (median age 61 versus 51 in MM).

(c)
Plasmacytoma: solitary bone (70% progress to MM) or extramedullary (lungs, sinuses, liver, heart); no abnormal plasma cells elsewhere and no CRAB features. Waldenström: high IgM, raised serum viscosity, marrow infiltration by lymphoplasmacytic cells; hyperviscosity is common, lytic bone and renal disease uncommon.

(d)
• Serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation; blood film with rouleaux; marrow aspirate showing plasma cell clusters with Dutcher and Russell bodies (Mott cell has multiple Russell bodies) and trephine infiltration.
• Immunophenotype: CD45-, CD38+, CD138+, CD56 positive in 55-78% (CD56-negative in more aggressive disease); skeletal survey shows punched-out lytic lesions in about 75% (vertebrae, skull, ribs, sternum, proximal humeri, femur); also CT, PET-CT, MRI, bone scan.
• Staging: Salmon-Durie and International Staging System (β₂-microglobulin and albumin); 25% show renal failure and/or hypercalcaemia.

(e)
• Bone pain and lytic lesions, anaemia, hypercalcaemia (polydipsia, polyuria, anorexia, vomiting, constipation, mental disturbance) and renal failure.
• Infections from deficient antibody production (and neutropenia in advanced disease); bleeding tendency because myeloma protein may interfere with platelet function and coagulation factors.
• Hyperviscosity (2%, usually IgM): purpura, haemorrhages, visual failure, CNS symptoms; neuropathies from regional tumour compressing the spinal cord or cranial nerves; POEMS syndrome.
• Occasional macroglossia, carpal tunnel syndrome and diarrhoea.
• Pathogenesis: c-MYC and H-ras overexpressed in over 80%, bcl-2 overexpressed, N-ras mutated, Rb and p53 mutated, IL-6 as growth factor.

(a)
• Bone marrow is found in all bone cavities at birth, but by the teen years it is primarily found in axial bones – chest bones, ribs, spinal bones, collarbone, shoulder blades, skull, pelvic bones, and parts of the femur and humerus.
• There are two bone structures, cortical (about 80% of bones, strong and dense, little role in metabolism/haemopoiesis) and trabecular bones (20% of bones, performing metabolic functions); bone marrow is found within trabecular bones.
• Bone marrow is the fourth largest organ in the body by weight, accounting for 4-5% of total body weight, and lies within the medullary cavity, surrounded by the periosteum.
• There are two main types: red bone marrow (myeloid tissue), which is fibrous and contains haematopoietic stem cells – all red cells and platelets, and 60-70% of white cells, are formed here in adults; and yellow bone marrow, which is fattier and contains mesenchymal/marrow stromal cells that produce connective tissue.
• Yellow bone marrow stores fat and nutrients, and can transform back into red bone marrow under stress such as infection or severe blood loss.

(b)
• A hypocellular marrow with fat replacement and peripheral pancytopenia characterises aplastic anaemia, a bone marrow failure syndrome.
• A hypercellular marrow, or one infiltrated by abnormal cells, characterises pancytopenia from decreased production causes such as acute leukaemia, myelodysplastic syndrome, myeloma, or infiltration by lymphomas/solid tumours.
• Marrow cellularity criteria differ with age (decreasing physiologically as red marrow is replaced by fatty marrow), so cellularity of less than 30% below age 60, or less than 20% above age 60, is considered hypocellular.

(c)
• Bone marrow failure (whether monolineage, e.g. congenital dyserythropoietic anaemia, or multilineage, e.g. aplastic anaemia) causes decreased production of one or more haemopoietic cell lineages.
• This produces a functional deficit distant from the marrow: anaemia causes body weakness, easy fatiguability and dyspnoea on exertion; thrombocytopenia causes mucosal/gingival bleeding and petechiae; and neutropenia causes infections.
• Pancytopenia can also result from peripheral destruction distant from the marrow, such as splenomegaly (an example of peripheral blood cell destruction), even when marrow production is not primarily impaired.
• Bone marrow examination (aspiration/biopsy, morphology, cytogenetics, flow cytometry, immunophenotyping) is therefore central to diagnosing the cause of these distant, peripheral functional deficits.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the gross anatomy of the bone marrow, including its distribution in the skeleton and its two main types.
(b) State how the cellularity/type of bone marrow relates to common haematological pathologies.
(c) Explain why bone marrow disease may cause a functional deficit distant from the marrow itself.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), presenting with features of the classic pentad of anaemia, thrombocytopenia, fever, neurological abnormality and haematuria.

(b)
TTP is due to deficiency of the metalloprotease ADAMTS-13, either from mutation of the gene coding for it or from autoantibodies raised against it; this deficiency prevents cleavage of ultralarge von Willebrand factor multimers secreted from endothelial cells, so these multimers bind strongly to platelet glycoproteins Ib and IIb/IIIa and aggregate platelets in the terminal circulation, causing intravascular thrombi formation and consumptive thrombocytopenia with haemolysis.

(c)
Treatment includes red blood cell transfusion for anaemia, plasma infusions and plasma exchanges until platelets are above 150×10⁹/L, prednisolone administration, and fresh frozen plasma infusion where plasma exchange is not available.

(d)
Plasma exchange until platelet recovery is the definitive acute treatment; rituximab, cyclophosphamide and other immunosuppressives have also been used, and prophylactic plasma infusion is used in chronic recurrent TTP.
questions.question:
A previously healthy young woman presents with fever, confusion, easy bruising, and dark urine, and is found to have anaemia and thrombocytopenia.
(a) What is the diagnosis?
(b) What is the pathologic basis of this condition?
(c) How should this patient be managed acutely?
(d) What is the definitive treatment?

questions.answerText:
(a)
Hereditary haemochromatosis.

(b)
Autosomal recessive inheritance; mutations in the HFE gene, most commonly the C282Y mutation (cysteine to tyrosine substitution) or H63D mutation (histidine to aspartic acid), or C282Y/H63D compound heterozygosity; a first-degree relative with the condition; alcohol abuse and hepatitis C accelerate the disease; the disorder is more common and presents earlier in men because women have physiological iron loss through menstruation and pregnancy.

(c)
There is increased absorption of dietary iron from the upper intestine due to decreased expression of the iron-regulatory hormone hepcidin and altered function of the HFE protein; total body iron may reach 20-60g compared with a normal 3-4g, with net absorption of 3-4mg/day and accumulation of 500-1000mg iron per year; excess iron is deposited in the liver, pancreas, heart, joints and pituitary, and highly toxic non-transferrin-bound iron induces tissue injury and fibrogenesis, eventually causing cirrhosis, cardiomyopathy, diabetes and hypogonadism.

(d)
Diagnosis is confirmed by elevated transferrin saturation (>45%) and elevated serum ferritin, with liver biopsy as the gold standard; treatment is venesection (weekly removal of 450-500ml of blood, about 200-250mg iron) until serum ferritin is 20-30µg/L and transferrin saturation is <50%, followed by maintenance venesection; iron chelation therapy (e.g. deferoxamine, deferasirox) is used in patients who cannot tolerate venesection, such as those with anaemia and iron overload together; dietary restriction of iron-rich foods and avoidance of alcohol are also advised.
questions.question:
A man aged between 40 and 60 years presents with weakness and lethargy, skin that has a bronze or slate-grey discolouration, hepatomegaly, joint pain, and diabetes mellitus.
(a) What is the most likely diagnosis?
(b) What are the predisposing factors for this condition?
(c) Explain the pathophysiology.
(d) Outline the management.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Severe anaemia causes marked bone changes due to expansion of the marrow space for increased erythropoiesis.
• Patients have severe microcytic hypochromic anaemia, detected early in childhood, with infants failing to thrive.
• There is marked erythroid hyperplasia in the bone marrow, resulting in bone marrow expansion.

(b)
• The expanded marrow space produces characteristic changes in the skull, long bones, and hand bones.
• Affected children have protrusion of the upper teeth and Mongoloid facial features, with delayed physical growth and development.
• Peripheral blood shows markedly hypochromic, microcytic erythrocytes with extreme poikilocytosis, including target cells, teardrop cells and elliptocytes, with marked basophilic stippling and numerous nucleated red blood cells.

(c)
• The two phenomena of ineffective erythropoiesis and haemolysis result in severe anaemia and marked erythroid hyperplasia in the bone marrow.
• This causes bone marrow expansion, extramedullary haematopoiesis, and hepatosplenomegaly.
• Extramedullary haematopoiesis represents spread of the marrow's erythropoietic activity to distant organs, namely the liver and spleen, causing their enlargement.
• Regular transfusions, usually begun around one year of age, are required for life to manage the resulting severe anaemia.
• Excessive transfusions without iron chelation cause transfusional haemosiderosis and, without chelation, the patient develops cardiac disease.
• This represents a further functional deficit, as iron deposited from chronic transfusion spreads systemically to the heart.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the marrow space and its response to increased erythropoietic demand in β thalassaemia major.
(b) Explain how the affected zones of the marrow relate to the skeletal changes seen in this condition.
(c) Explain why this bone marrow pathology may spread to distant structures and cause a functional deficit.

A male newborn develops neonatal jaundice, and a few days after exposure to an oxidant drug he develops acute haemolytic anaemia with dark urine.
(a) What is the most likely diagnosis?
(b) What are the risk factors for this condition?
(c) What are the possible complications, especially in this age group?
(d) What are the treatment options, and why would methylene blue not be used to treat this patient?
questions.answerText:
(a)
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency.

(b)
Sex-linked (X-linked) inheritance affecting males and carried by females; belonging to West Africa, the Mediterranean, the Middle East or South East Asia; exposure to oxidant drugs (e.g. primaquine, sulphonamides, dapsone, nitrofurantoin, nalidixic acid), chemicals (naphthalene, phenylhydrazine) or fava beans; infections.

(c)
Neonatal jaundice; acute haemolytic anaemia in response to oxidant stress, with features of intravascular haemolysis; the blood film during crisis shows contracted and fragmented cells, bite and blister cells and Heinz bodies.

(d)
Treatment is to avoid the oxidative trigger and provide transfusion support if needed; methylene blue, which is used to increase reduction of methaemoglobin, cannot be used in G6PD deficiency because the reaction depends on NADPH, which is deficient in this condition.

(a)
• The bone marrow is composed of vascular and non-vascular regions; the non-vascular section contains haemopoietic cells of various lineages and maturity, packed between fat cells, trabeculae, collagen fibres, fibroblasts and dendritic cells – this is where haematopoiesis occurs.
• The vascular section contains blood vessels that supply nutrients to the bone and transport blood stem cells and mature blood cells into the circulation; the bone marrow has no lymphatic drainage.
• Ultrastructural studies show haemopoietic cells cluster around the vascular sinuses where they mature before being discharged into the blood.
• Lymphocytes are found surrounding the small radial arteries, whereas most immature myeloid precursors lie deep in the parenchyma.
• The bone marrow lies within the medullary cavity, surrounded by the periosteum, and its hematopoietic microenvironment includes adventitial reticular (barrier) cells, endothelial cells, macrophages, adipocytes, bone-lining cells (osteoblasts) and elements of the extracellular matrix.

(b)
• Bone marrow aspiration/biopsy is performed by inserting a long hollow needle into a bone, typically the hip bone.
• The surrounding skin, subcutaneous tissue, and the periosteum are infiltrated with local anaesthetic before the procedure, as the periosteum must be punctured to reach the marrow.
• Aspiration and biopsy usually happen together, using either two needles or repositioning of the same needle, and the sample can be used for morphology/cytology, M:E ratio, iron store evaluation, cytogenetics, flow cytometry, immunophenotyping and PCR.

(c)
• Damage to the haemopoietic microenvironment (affecting stem cells, the progenitor cell compartment, and factors that stimulate haemopoiesis) is a mechanism of bone marrow failure.
• This damage can be direct (cytotoxic drugs, radiation, chemicals, viruses acting on stem cells/progenitor cells) or indirect (these agents stimulating an immune response that then damages the stem cells/progenitor cells).
• Immunologic mechanisms are supported by the response to immunosuppressive therapy in aplastic anaemia, and by the finding that cytokines (interferon, tumour necrosis factor) from activated T lymphocytes suppress haemopoietic stem cell growth.
• Failure of haemopoiesis therefore results either from a defect/reduction in haemopoietic stem cells impairing self-renewal, proliferation and differentiation, or from a defect in the haemopoietic microenvironment and deficient haemopoietic stimulating factors.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the vascular architecture of the bone marrow, including the vascular and non-vascular regions and how haemopoietic cells relate to the vascular sinuses.
(b) State the safe site and technique for performing a bone marrow aspiration/biopsy.
(c) Explain the anatomical/pathological basis of bone marrow failure when the haemopoietic microenvironment is damaged.

questions.answerText:
(a)
PT tests the extrinsic and common pathways; prolonged in liver disease, vitamin K antagonism or deficiency (warfarin), DIC and defects of factors VII, X, V, II and fibrinogen.

(b)
APTT tests the intrinsic and common pathways; prolonged in liver disease, DIC, heparin therapy, vitamin K antagonism or deficiency, and defects of factors XII, XI, IX, VIII, X, V, II and fibrinogen.

(c)
Thrombin time evaluates fibrinogen and inhibition of thrombin action; prolonged in hypofibrinogenaemia, dysfibrinogenaemia, heparin therapy and DIC; the fibrinogen level is also measured.

(d)
• Platelet count, platelet aggregation test (aggregometry) and skin bleeding time.
• Low count: marrow examination, platelet antibodies, DIC screening; normal count: bleeding time, aggregation studies, special function tests (e.g. nucleotide pool assay) and a von Willebrand disease study.

(e)
• Haemophilia is insufficient activity of the tenase complex (FVIII or FIX deficiency); the screening test is an isolated prolonged APTT and the diagnostic test is a factor assay.
• Haemophilia A and B: normal platelet count, bleeding time and PT; low FVIII (A) or low FIX (B); sex-linked; bleeding into muscle and joints, post-trauma or postoperative.
• von Willebrand disease: autosomal dominant (incomplete); normal platelet count and PT; prolonged bleeding time; APTT prolonged or normal; FVIII moderately reduced; low vWF; impaired ristocetin-induced platelet aggregation; bleeding of mucous membranes and skin cuts.
• Diagnostic vWD tests: vWF antigen, vWF:RCo, vWF:CB, RIPA and multimer analysis.

(f)
• Thrombotic states: a shortened APTT suggests activated clotting factors; a prolonged APTT not corrected by normal plasma suggests a lupus anticoagulant or acquired factor inhibitor.
• A prolonged thrombin (and reptilase) time suggests an abnormal fibrinogen.
• In newborn vitamin K deficiency bleeding both PT and APTT are abnormal with normal platelets and fibrinogen.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the prothrombin time: the pathways it tests and the causes of prolongation.
(b) Describe the activated partial thromboplastin time in the same way.
(c) Describe the thrombin time and fibrinogen level.
(d) State the tests used for platelet disorders.
(e) Explain the basis of an isolated prolongation of the APTT in haemophilia and how the pattern of results distinguishes haemophilia from von Willebrand disease.
(f) State the pattern seen in thrombotic states.

With reference to the renal medullary vasculature and the vascular supply to the femoral and humeral heads in sickle cell disease:
(a) Describe the vascular environment of the renal medulla and how it favours vaso-occlusion.
(b) Describe the effect of this vaso-occlusion on the vasa recta and the distribution of its clinical effects.
(c) Explain the anatomical basis of the bony deformity that follows vascular injury to the femoral or humeral heads in this condition.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The renal medulla is hypoxic and acidotic, and this favours vaso-occlusion.

(b)
• This leads to destruction of the vasa recta.
• The distribution of clinical effects includes hyposthenuria, leading to enuresis or nocturia and dehydration in hot weather, as well as haematuria and proteinuria.
• Proteinuria and nephrotic syndrome may also occur as a further renal medullary consequence of this vaso-occlusion.

(c)
• Vaso-occlusive crises in bone cause avascular necrosis of the femoral or humeral heads.
• This occurs apart from the widening of the medullary cavity due to marrow hyperplasia seen in the skeletal system in this condition.
• Dactylitis (hand-foot syndrome), with painful, tender and swollen digits, occurs in small children as a related vaso-occlusive bony manifestation.
• Salmonella osteomyelitis is another skeletal complication described alongside this vaso-occlusive bone damage.
• The resulting bony deformity follows ischaemic vascular injury to the femoral or humeral heads from vaso-occlusion.

(a)
The findings identify impaired bone marrow DNA synthesis affecting red cell precursors; the finding of macrocytosis and neutrophil hypersegmentation strongly suggests megaloblastic anaemia.

(b)
Total white blood cell count and platelet count may be moderately reduced; the bone marrow shows a hypercellular marrow with megaloblastic red cell precursors showing nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony, giant bands and metamyelocytes, and megaloblastic megakaryocytes.

(c)
Other (non-megaloblastic) causes of macrocytosis that must be considered include pregnancy, neonatal age, alcohol, liver disease, myxoedema, myelodysplastic syndromes, antimetabolite drugs such as hydroxycarbamide, aplastic anaemia, smoking, reticulocytosis, and myeloma and paraproteinaemia.

(d)
Megaloblastic anaemia is distinguished by a low reticulocyte count (reticulocytopenia) despite the macrocytosis, red cell inclusions (basophilic stippling, Howell-Jolly bodies), and hypersegmented neutrophils, defined as at least 3% of neutrophils having five or more lobes, or even one neutrophil with six or more nuclear lobes, together with increased indirect bilirubin and lactate dehydrogenase from ineffective erythropoiesis, low serum cobalamin or reduced serum/red cell folate, and increased methylmalonic acid and homocysteine levels.
questions.question:
A patient is found to have anaemia with a raised mean corpuscular volume greater than 98 fL, and a blood film shows oval macrocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils.
(a) What process/structure do these findings identify, and what is the most likely diagnosis?
(b) What other cell lines/structures may be affected in this condition?
(c) What differential pathologies must be considered for macrocytosis?

questions.answerText:
(a)
• MPNs arise from marrow stem cells with clonal proliferation of one or more haemopoietic components (also liver and spleen): polycythaemia vera, essential thrombocythaemia and primary myelofibrosis.
• Polycythaemia is absolute (primary PV, or secondary from hypoxia or raised erythropoietin) or relative (reduced plasma volume); PV expands granulocytic, erythroid and megakaryocytic lines, erythroid most, independent of erythropoietin.

(b)
• Normally erythropoietin binds its receptor, second messengers JAK2 and STAT transmit the signal, and the V617 region of JAK2 intermittently switches off the erythropoietic drive.
• In PV a mutation in the V617 region of JAK2 in a pluripotent stem cell abolishes this feedback, giving uncontrolled erythropoiesis and a raised haemoglobin/haematocrit.

(c)
JAK2 V617F in 100% of PV and 60% of ET and MF, or exon 12 mutation; MPL (thrombopoietin receptor) and calreticulin (CALR) mutations; in MF, JAK2 about 55%, CALR 25%, MPL 10%.

(d)
• Thrombosis (commonest, arterial and venous) is due to hyperviscosity with displacement of platelets to the vessel wall; hyperviscosity ischaemia causes headache, dizziness, drowsiness, visual and hearing deficits; plethora and conjunctival engorgement; hypertension from increased vascular resistance.
• Pruritus after a warm bath is from basophilia and hyperhistaminaemia; hyperuricaemia and gout from increased cell turnover; splenomegaly.

(e)
Haematocrit >0.50, absolute neutrophils >10×10⁹/L, platelets >450×10⁹/L, low serum EPO, raised uric acid, splenomegaly on ultrasound, JAK2 mutation.

(f)
• Venesection (haematocrit <0.45), allopurinol and fluids, antihistamines, LMWH, antihypertensives; hydroxycarbamide, busulfan, interferon alfa, anagrelide, ruxolitinib.
• Differential: other MPNs (ET, CML, idiopathic myelofibrosis), secondary polycythaemia (chronic hypoxia, lung disease, high oxygen affinity haemoglobins, abnormal EPO secretion), idiopathic erythrocytosis.
• Myelofibrosis features fibrosis of the marrow secondary to hyperplasia of abnormal megakaryocytes, with extramedullary haemopoiesis in spleen and liver.
• Untreated, 50% die within 2 years; treated survival up to 11 years; PV may transform to acute leukaemia or progress to myelofibrosis, both with worse prognosis.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Antithrombin III (formerly heparin cofactor I), a serpin synthesized in the liver, chromosome 1q23-25, normal range 70-150 u/dl.
• Substrates: thrombin (IIa) and Xa, also IXa, XIa, XIIa and kallikrein.

(b)
Heparin cofactor II is a single-chain glycoprotein of 66 kd whose substrate is thrombin and whose activity is increased by heparin.

(c)
• TFPI is a proteinase inhibitor similar in structure to aprotinin, circulating bound to lipoproteins; platelets hold 8% of plasma TFPI, released on thrombin stimulation; a heparin-releasable pool sits on the endothelium.
• TFPI directly inhibits FXa; at high concentration it inhibits the FVIIa-tissue factor complex and at lower concentration the FXa-FVIIa/TF complex; unlike serpins its inhibition is reversible.

(d)
Heparin increases antithrombin activity more than 2000-fold, increases heparin cofactor II activity, raises TFPI 2-4 fold and enhances its anti-FXa activity; endothelial heparan sulfate also enhances antithrombin.

(e)
• Protein C is a vitamin K-dependent serine protease made in the liver (plasma 4 ug/mL), activated by thrombin, acting on factors VIIIa and Va; protein S is its cofactor, forming a complex on activated platelet phospholipid; a fall in free protein S gives a hypercoagulable state.
• Deficiency of protein C, protein S or antithrombin is associated with venous thromboembolism; antithrombin deficiency (autosomal dominant) gives recurrent venous, sometimes arterial, thrombosis from early adult life.
• Protein C deficiency (autosomal dominant, heterozygotes about 50%) causes warfarin skin necrosis; homozygous infants present with severe DIC or purpura fulminans; protein S deficiency is similar.

(f)
• α₂-antiplasmin, a single-chain glycoprotein of 70 kDa with plasmin as its major substrate, limits fibrinolysis; PAI-1 regulates plasminogen activator.
• Other controls: non-thrombogenic endothelium, blood flow and vasoconstriction, clearance of activated factor-inhibitor complexes by the liver and reticuloendothelial system.
• It is the net balance between opposing groups of proteins, not any single factor level, that is most critical to haemostatic regulation.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Vitamin K deficiency bleeding (VKDB, formerly haemorrhagic disease of the newborn), classified as early, classical and late types, presenting essentially with bleeding.

(b)
PT more than 4 x control with at least one of: normal platelet count, normal fibrinogen and absent FDPs; normalization of coagulation tests after parenteral vitamin K; or PIVKA in plasma. PIVKA without a coagulation deficit marks subclinical deficiency.

(c)
Factors II, VII, IX, X and proteins C and S are not γ-carboxylated, so non-functional PIVKAs circulate that cannot bind phospholipid via their Gla domains with calcium; FVII falls first (PT prolonged), then IX and X (APTT prolonged).

(d)
Non-life-threatening bleed: vitamin K1 (phytomenadione) 1-2 mg slowly IV (higher doses give no advantage; anaphylaxis rare); PT should improve within 48 hours; oral if no active bleeding and normal absorption; severe bleeding: FFP or prothrombin complex concentrate.

(e)
• Vitamin K does not cross the placenta, breast milk levels are low and colonic bacterial synthesis is low; a single IM injection of 1 mg prevents VKDB, especially needed in exclusively breast-fed babies.
• Adult deficiency arises from poor intake with antibiotics, malabsorption or cholestatic liver disease.
questions.question:
A young exclusively breast-fed infant who received no vitamin K presents with bleeding. The platelet count and fibrinogen are normal, fibrin degradation products are absent, the PT is more than four times the control and the APTT is prolonged.
