(c) Identify the coagulation proteins affected and the structural reason they fail.
(d) State the treatment.
(e) Explain the predisposition and state the prophylaxis.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, precursor B (common ALL, CD10+), the most common malignancy of childhood (75% under 6 years); FAB subtypes L1-L3. Differentials: aplastic anaemia, marrow infiltration by other malignancies (rhabdomyosarcoma, neuroblastoma, Ewing's sarcoma), infectious mononucleosis, pertussis, juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, ITP.

(b)
Malignant transformation causes accumulation of lymphoblasts (>20% in marrow); marrow failure gives anaemia, neutropenia and thrombocytopenia, and infiltration affects liver, spleen, nodes, meninges, brain, skin and testis; WHO genetic groups include t(9;22) BCR-ABL1, t(v;11q23) MLL, t(12;21) TEL-AML1, hyperdiploidy and hypodiploidy.

(c)
Central venous catheter; antiemetics (metoclopramide, phenothiazines, ondansetron, steroids, lorazepam, nabilone); allopurinol, intravenous fluids and urine alkalinization with sodium bicarbonate; prophylaxis and treatment of infection.

(d)
• Investigations: CBC, chemistry, clotting studies, viral serologies, HLA typing, marrow aspirate and biopsy (morphology, cytogenetics, flow cytometry, molecular), echocardiogram, chest radiograph, lumbar puncture if CNS symptoms.
• Chemotherapy (sometimes radiotherapy) in four components: remission induction (<5% blasts, normal counts), consolidation/intensification (high-dose multidrug), CNS-directed therapy (intrathecal methotrexate, cytarabine, hydrocortisone, with or without cranial irradiation) and maintenance.
• Good prognosis: low WBC, girls, child, c-ALL, normal or hyperdiploid (>50) or TEL rearrangement, blast clearance <1 week, remission <4 weeks, no CNS disease, MRD negative; poor: WBC >50×10⁹/L, boys, adult or infant <2 years, B-ALL, Ph+ or 11q23, CNS disease, MRD positive.
questions.question:
A child presents with pallor, lethargy, fever with a mouth and throat infection, spontaneous bruises and bleeding gums. The blood count shows anaemia, neutropenia and thrombocytopenia, and the bone marrow shows more than 20% lymphoblasts that are CD19, CD10 and TdT positive.
(a) State the diagnosis, its subtype and the differential diagnosis.
(b) Explain the pathologic basis of the disease and of its features.
(c) Outline the supportive management.
(d) Describe the investigations, definitive treatment and prognostic factors.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• A lymph node is a bean-shaped lymphoid organ, most prevalent in the neck, axilla and inguinal region.
• It has a hilum where arteries and veins enter and leave the node.
• Lymph enters via afferent lymphatic vessels on the convex surface of the node, and leaves via a single efferent lymphatic vessel on the concave surface.
• Lymph is interstitial fluid that has entered the lymphatic vessels; it is returned to the circulation at the lymphovenous junctions.
• The lymph node has three areas: the cortex (immediately deep to the capsule and subcapsular sinus, containing primary and secondary follicles and housing B cells), the paracortex (housing T cells and dendritic cells), and the medulla (the innermost zone, containing B cells, T cells, plasma cells and macrophages).
• When lymph enters the node, antigens are trapped and presented to B cells by antigen-presenting cells in the follicles, stimulating formation of secondary follicles whose germinal centres produce memory B cells and plasma cells.

(b)
• Normal lymph node size is around 1cm in diameter; lymphadenopathy is abnormality of a node in size, number or consistency, and may be localised or generalised, peripheral or non-peripheral.
• Cortical/follicular pathology relates to infective or inflammatory causes producing hyperplasia of B-cell follicles (e.g. tuberculosis, syphilis, brucellosis, HIV, infectious mononucleosis, rubella), while diffuse nodal pathology relates to infiltration by malignant cells (leukaemias, lymphomas, secondary cancers) or by lipid/glycoprotein-laden macrophages.
• Mechanism of lymphadenopathy therefore involves either increased lymphocyte proliferation from infection/inflammation, or infiltration of the node by malignant or storage material.

(c)
• Because the lymph node functions in filtration, B lymphocyte maturation and immune function, disease within it can allow antigens, infective organisms or malignant cells to pass onward via the single efferent lymphatic vessel to the next node or into the general circulation.
• This causes disease to spread to distant sites, for example malignant infiltration progressing to involve other nodal groups, or systemic spread of infection/malignancy producing constitutional symptoms.
• Investigation of lymphadenopathy (FBC, ESR, bone marrow aspiration, lymph node biopsy, imaging, HIV screening) is aimed at identifying such a distant or systemic cause of the local nodal finding.
questions.question:

(b) State how the zones of the lymph node relate to the common pathologies of lymphadenopathy.
(c) Explain why disease of the lymph node may spread to cause a functional deficit at a distant site.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the three named regions of the male urethra, giving the length and relations of each.
A(ii) Describe the two urethral sphincters — their type of muscle, location, and the mechanism by which each controls urinary continence.
B(i) Describe the female urethra, including its length, relations, and the location of its external orifice.
B(ii) State the layers visible in the structure of the urinary bladder wall.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Three regions of the male urethra:
• Prostatic urethra (2.5 cm): located within the prostate.
• Intermediate part of the urethra (membranous urethra) (2 cm): passes through the urogenital diaphragm from the prostate to the beginning of the penis.
• Spongy urethra (15 cm): passes through the penis and opens via the external urethral orifice.
• The male urethra carries both semen and urine.
A(ii)
Two sphincters:
• Internal urethral sphincter: involuntary (smooth muscle) at the bladder-urethra junction; contracts to open (its contraction, paradoxically, opens the sphincter as described — 'contracts to open').
• External urethral sphincter: voluntary (skeletal muscle) surrounding the urethra as it passes through the pelvic floor.
B(i)
Female urethra:
• Length: 3–4 cm.
• Relations: tightly bound to the anterior vaginal wall.
• External urethral orifice: anterior to the vaginal opening and posterior to the clitoris.
B(ii)
Layers of the urinary bladder wall:
• Peritoneum, rugae, detrusor (muscle), adventitia, ureteric orifices, trigone of bladder, bladder neck, internal urethral sphincter.

A(i)
Definition: Cartilage is a connective tissue in which the cells are relatively sparse and embedded in a large amount of firm characteristic matrix. It is a specialized form of connective tissue in which the firm consistency of the extracellular matrix allows the tissue to bear mechanical stresses without permanent distortion. Histogenesis: Cartilage is derived from the mesenchyme. The first modification observed is the rounding up of mesenchymal cells, which retract their extensions, multiply rapidly, and form mesenchymal condensations of chondroblasts (cells with ribosome-rich basophilic cytoplasm). Synthesis and deposition of matrix then begin to separate chondroblasts from one another. Differentiation takes place from center outward: central cells have characteristics of chondrocytes, peripheral cells are typical chondroblasts. The superficial mesenchyme develops into the perichondrium. Growth mechanisms: interstitial growth (from mitotic division of preexisting chondrocytes, expanding from within) and appositional growth (from differentiation of perichondrial cells, expanding from the outside). Nutrient supply: Cartilage is avascular; nourished by diffusion of nutrients from capillaries in adjacent connective tissue (perichondrium) or by synovial fluid. It has no lymphatic vessels or nerves. Chondrocytes exhibit low metabolic activity.
A(ii)
Hyaline cartilage: most common form; collagen type II is the principal collagen; found in nose, trachea, bronchi, rib-sternal joints, and synovial joints; resilient and shock absorbing. Elastic cartilage: contains abundant elastic fibers in addition to collagen type II; found in auricle of ear, external auditory canals, eustachian tubes, epiglottis, and cuneiform cartilage in larynx; elastic fibers allow flexibility. Fibrocartilage: rich in collagen type I (acidophilic matrix); found in intervertebral disks, attachments of certain ligaments to cartilaginous surfaces, and symphysis pubis; dense collagen provides strength for high-load sites.
B(i)
Articular cartilage is devoid of perichondrium and is sustained by diffusion of oxygen and nutrients from synovial fluid; this limited supply combined with low metabolic activity of chondrocytes means repair is slow. Hyaline cartilage is more susceptible to degenerative aging processes; calcification of the matrix, preceded by an increase in size and volume of chondrocytes followed by their death, leads to osteoarthritis. Role of exercise: participation in sports involving torsional loading, fast acceleration/deceleration, repetitive high impact increases risk of osteoarthritis. However, some levels of loading and exercise are beneficial: exercise enhances production of matrix molecules, which can have a positive effect on joint health. Exercise has both beneficial and detrimental effects on cartilage.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the gross anatomy of cartilage under the following headings: definition, histogenesis (development from mesenchyme), growth mechanisms, and nutrient supply.
A(ii) Relate the three types of cartilage to their specific locations and collagen types, explaining why each is suited to its location.
B(i) Explain why articular cartilage degenerates with age and state the role of exercise in cartilage health.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
An omentum is a double-layered extension or fold passing from the stomach and proximal duodenum to adjacent organs or to the abdominal wall; there are two types, lesser and greater.
A(ii)
The lesser omentum is a two-layered fold connecting the lesser curvature of the stomach and proximal duodenum to the liver; the hepatoduodenal ligament is its thickened free edge, conducting the portal vein, hepatic artery and bile duct.
A(iii)
The greater omentum hangs like an apron from the greater curvature of the stomach and proximal duodenum, folds back after descending and attaches to the anterior surface of the transverse colon and its mesocolon.
A(iv)
• Liver: falciform ligament (anterior wall), gastrohepatic ligament (stomach), hepatoduodenal ligament (duodenum). Stomach: gastrophrenic, gastrosplenic, gastrocolic, gastrohepatic, gastropancreatic.
• Spleen: gastrosplenic (short gastric and left gastroepiploic vessels), splenorenal (splenic vessels and tail of pancreas), phrenicosplenic, splenocolic.
B(i)
• It is large and fat laden and prevents the visceral peritoneum adhering to the parietal peritoneum lining the anterolateral wall.
• It is mobile, moving with peristalsis, and can wrap itself around an inflamed organ such as the appendix, walling it off and protecting other viscera.
• It also cushions the abdominal organs against injury and forms insulation against loss of body heat.
C(i)
• Lesser: from liver to lesser curvature and proximal duodenum, containing the hepatoduodenal ligament; greater: hangs from the greater curvature and attaches to the transverse colon.
• The anterior and posterior layers of the lesser omentum extend from the liver to the lesser curvature; the anterior layer continues as the first layer of the greater omentum, the posterior layer forms its second and third layers.
• The lesser omentum forms part of the anterior wall of the lesser sac together with the peritoneum of the posterior wall of the stomach and the anterior two layers of the greater omentum.
• The hepatoduodenal ligament forms the anterior boundary of the omental foramen.

A(i)
Muscularis and serosa:
• Muscularis: composed of an internal circular layer and an external longitudinal layer; between these muscle layers is the myenteric (Auerbach) nerve plexus, which produces peristalsis.
• Serosa: the small intestine is covered by a thin serosa.
A(ii)
Lamina propria of the small intestine:
• Composed of loose connective tissue containing extensive blood and lymph microvasculature, nerve fibers, smooth muscle cells, and lymphoid tissue.
• It penetrates the core of each intestinal villus, bringing microvasculature, lymphatics, and nerves into each villus.
• Smooth muscle fibers inside the villi are responsible for rhythmic movements important for efficient absorption.
• Contractions of the muscularis mucosae also produce local movements of the plicae circulares that help propel lymph from the lacteals into submucosal and mesenteric lymphatics.
B(i)
Submucosa — Brunner (duodenal) glands:
• Location: present in the proximal part of the duodenum; large clusters of branched tubular mucous glands with small excretory ducts opening among the intestinal crypts.
• Type: branched tubular mucous glands.
• Product: mucus, which is alkaline (pH 8.1–9.3).
Three functions:
• Protects the mucous membrane.
• Brings the intestinal contents to the optimum pH for pancreatic enzyme action.
• Neutralises chyme entering the duodenum from the pylorus.
B(ii)
Lacteals:
• Lymph vessels of the intestine beginning as closed tubes in the cores of villi.
• They run to the region of the lamina propria above the muscularis mucosae, where they form a plexus.
• From there they are directed to the submucosa, where they surround lymphoid nodules; they anastomose repeatedly and leave the intestine along with blood vessels.
• Function: especially important for lipid absorption.
• Absorptive state: when absorption is taking place after a meal, the lacteals are dilated and prominent; at other times they are collapsed and not prominent.

A(ii) Describe the lamina propria of the small intestine, including its composition, its role in each intestinal villus, and the role of smooth muscle fibers within the villi.

B(ii) Describe the lacteals of the small intestine: what they are, where they begin, their course, their function, and how they change in appearance depending on the absorptive state of the intestine.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
The cubital fossa is a triangular space, a shallow depression on the anterior surface of the elbow region, located anterior to the elbow joint, formed between two forearm muscles (brachioradialis and pronator teres).
A(ii)
Boundaries: base (superior) — an imaginary horizontal line connecting the medial and lateral epicondyles; medial (ulnar) wall — lateral border of pronator teres; lateral (radial) wall — medial border of brachioradialis; apex — directed inferiorly, where the medial and lateral boundaries meet; floor — brachialis and supinator; roof — continuity of brachial and antebrachial (deep) fascia, reinforced by the bicipital aponeurosis, superficial fascia and skin.
A(iii)
The major contents, from medial to lateral, are the median nerve, the brachial artery (which bifurcates near the apex into the radial and ulnar arteries), deep accompanying veins of the arteries, and the tendon of biceps brachii.
B
• The median cubital vein, cephalic vein and basilic vein are present in the area but are usually considered superficial to the cubital fossa and not part of its contents.
• During blood pressure measurement the stethoscope is placed over the brachial artery in the cubital fossa, and the fossa is also used to palpate the brachial pulse.
• The area just superficial to the cubital fossa is often used for venous access (phlebotomy), since it is superficial and accessible.
• The bicipital aponeurosis forms the roof of the fossa and was historically called the "grace of God" tendon because it protected the brachial artery and median nerve during blood-letting.
C
• The radial nerve is in the vicinity of the cubital fossa, located between brachialis and brachioradialis, but is often, though not always, considered part of the cubital fossa's contents.
• This differs from the median nerve and brachial artery, which are consistently listed as major contents of the fossa.
• The superficial veins similarly lie in the roof/superficial region and are related to, rather than contained within, the fossa proper.
• Venipuncture therefore uses the superficial veins overlying the fossa, while palpation of the brachial pulse and auscultation for blood pressure use the deeper true content, the brachial artery.
• This distinction between superficial and deep structures is the basis for choosing the correct site for a given clinical procedure at the elbow.
questions.question:
Describe the cubital fossa:
A(i) Location and shape
A(ii) Boundaries (base, medial wall, lateral wall, apex, floor, roof)
A(iii) Contents
B. Explain the clinical basis for distinguishing the true "contents" of the cubital fossa from structures that are merely superficial to it.
C. Distinguish the position of the radial nerve in relation to the cubital fossa from that of the median nerve and brachial artery.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Boundaries: superiorly — inguinal ligament; medially — medial border of adductor longus; laterally — medial border of sartorius; apex — where adductor longus and sartorius cross. Roof: fascia lata (deep fascia) pierced by the great saphenous vein at the saphenous opening (fossa ovalis). Floor: formed by iliopsoas laterally and pectineus medially. Contents from lateral to medial: femoral nerve, femoral artery, femoral vein (the mnemonic 'NAVY' — from lateral: Nerve, Artery, Vein, Y-fronts/lymphatics). The femoral pulse can be palpated as it enters the femoral triangle, midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis — the mid-inguinal point.
A(ii)
The femoral artery divides to give the profunda femoris 5 cm below the inguinal ligament. Branches of the femoral artery (mnemonic: 'Does She Scream During Poking Sessions?'): Deep external pudendal arteries, Superficial epigastric, Superficial external pudendal, Descending genicular artery, Profunda femoris artery, Superficial circumflex iliac. Profunda femoris arises from the posterolateral aspect of the femoral artery; it gives: (1) Perforating branches — 3 or 4 arteries that perforate adductor magnus, contributing to medial and posterior thigh. (2) Lateral femoral circumflex artery — wraps around anterior and lateral side of femur, supplying muscles on lateral aspect of thigh. (3) Medial femoral circumflex artery — wraps around posterior side of femur, supplying its neck and head; in a fracture of the femoral neck this artery can easily be damaged and avascular necrosis of the femoral head can occur.
B(i)
The adductor canal is a passageway in the medial thigh. The adductor hiatus is an opening between the aponeurotic distal attachment of the adductor part of adductor magnus and the tendinous distal attachment of the hamstring part. The hiatus transmits the femoral artery and vein from the adductor canal in the thigh to the popliteal fossa posterior to the knee. It is located just lateral and superior to the adductor tubercle of the femur.
B(ii)
Femoral pulse: palpated at mid-inguinal point (midway between ASIS and pubic symphysis). In femoral artery occlusion, the profunda femoris artery is the main collateral channel because the superior muscular branches of the popliteal artery have clinically important anastomoses with the terminal part of the profunda femoris and gluteal arteries, maintaining perfusion to the leg.
C(i)
The posterior division of the obturator nerve supplies both the hip and the knee joint; therefore, pain from hip pathology is referred along this common nerve pathway to present as knee pain. This is the basis of Hilton's law applied to the hip: 'the nerve supplying the joint also supplies the muscles moving the joint and the skin covering the insertion of these muscles.' The femoral nerve also supplies the hip joint via intermediate and cutaneous branches and the knee via branches of obturator and femoral nerves.
questions.question:
Describe the femoral triangle and adductor canal under the following headings, state how they relate to common pathologies, and explain the anatomical basis of referred pain to the knee from the hip.
A(i) Boundaries, roof, and floor of the femoral triangle; contents from lateral to medial
A(ii) Femoral artery — branches within the femoral triangle, including the profunda femoris and its branches
B(i) Adductor canal — boundaries, contents, and where it terminates
B(ii) Clinical basis: femoral pulse palpation and profunda femoris in femoral artery occlusion
C(i) Explain why hip joint disease causes referred pain at the knee, based on the nerve supply of both joints

questions.answerText:
A(i)
The phrenic nerve is formed in the neck within the cervical plexus and contains fibres from spinal roots C3, C4 and C5.
A(ii)
• Its long course from the neck follows the embryological migration of the diaphragm from the cervical region: the septum transversum is carried ventrally and caudally, and the cervical myotomes and nerves contribute the muscle and nerve supply.
• It passes through the superior and middle mediastinum: the right phrenic descends on the right side of the SVC and heart; the left phrenic descends on the left side of the heart.
A(iii)
Both nerves terminate in the diaphragm: terminal branches of the right phrenic pass through the caval opening (T8) in the central tendon, and the left phrenic pierces the left dome.
A(iv)
• Motor: the sole motor supply of the diaphragm; the right nerve supplies the right half up to the right margin of the oesophageal opening and the left nerve the left half up to the left margin.
• Sensory: the central part of the diaphragm and the related pleura and peritoneum, and sensory fibres to the pleurae and pericardium (mediastinal pleura, fibrous and parietal pericardium); the peripheral part receives sensory fibres from the lower 6 or 7 intercostal and subcostal nerves.
C(i)
• Sectioning or injury of a phrenic nerve in the neck causes complete paralysis and eventual atrophy of the muscular part of the corresponding half of the diaphragm, except in persons who have an accessory phrenic nerve.
• Causes of injury: mechanical trauma (ligation or damage during surgery) and compression by a tumour within the chest cavity; myopathies (e.g. myasthenia gravis) and neuropathies (e.g. diabetic neuropathy) also interrupt the supply.
• The paralysed half is elevated and shows paradoxical movement: it moves upwards during inspiration (forced up by abdominal viscera) and downwards during expiration; only one half is affected because each dome has a separate nerve supply.
• Unilateral paralysis is usually asymptomatic and an incidental finding on X-ray; if both sides are paralysed there is poor exercise tolerance, orthopnoea and fatigue, and lung function tests show a restrictive deficit.
• Irritation of the diaphragmatic pleura or of the peritoneum under the diaphragm (pleurisy, subphrenic pus or blood) refers pain to the shoulder tip, because the central diaphragm sends sensory fibres in the phrenic nerve (C3-5) and the shoulder skin is supplied by the supraclavicular nerve (C3,4).

questions.answerText:
A(i)
• The longest lymphatic duct, conveying lymph to the circulatory system.
• It begins as the upward continuation of the cisterna chyli, a dilated sac formed by the union of the left and right lumbar trunks and the intestinal trunk, in front of L1 (also stated at T12).
A(ii)
• It enters the thorax through the aortic opening of the diaphragm and ascends in the posterior mediastinum, on the right side of and behind the oesophagus, with the oesophagus lying in front of it.
• It veers to the left at the level of T5 and ascends in the superior mediastinum to the left of the oesophagus.
• At the root of the neck it turns laterally, arches forwards and descends to enter the left venous angle.
A(iii)
• Before termination it receives the left jugular, left subclavian and left bronchomediastinal trunks; it ends in the left brachiocephalic vein.
• It contains many valves, with no valve at its termination.
A(iv)
• It drains lymph from the lower limbs, pelvic cavity, abdominal cavity, left half of the thorax and left side of the head, neck and upper limb (all the body except the right side of the head, neck, thorax and upper limb).
• The right lymphatic duct, formed by the union of the right jugular, subclavian and bronchomediastinal trunks, drains the right half of the head, neck, thorax and upper limb, right lung, right side of the heart and right surface of the liver, and ends in the right brachiocephalic vein.
• The lymph trunks are the right and left jugular, subclavian, bronchomediastinal and lumbar trunks and the intestinal trunk; the left brachiocephalic vein receives the thoracic duct, the right brachiocephalic vein the right lymphatic duct.

Describe the gross anatomy of the clavicle:
A(i) Shape and articulations
A(ii) Surface features
A(iii) Functions
B. State how a particular part of the clavicle relates to a common fracture pattern.
C. Explain how injury at this region may involve a distant structure, causing a functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The clavicle forms the anterior portion of the shoulder girdle; it is curved like the italic letter "f" and lies nearly horizontally at the upper and anterior part of the thorax, immediately above the first rib. It articulates medially with the manubrium sterni and laterally with the acromion of the scapula.
A(ii)
The upper surface is flat, rough, and marked by impressions for the attachment of deltoid in front and trapezius behind; the bone has no medullary cavity.
A(iii)
Its functions are to transmit forces from the upper limb to the axial skeleton, to act as a strut holding the arm free from the trunk (supported principally by trapezius), and to provide attachment for muscles.
B
• The weakest point along the clavicle is the junction of the middle and outer thirds.
• Transmission of forces to the axial skeleton in falls on the shoulder or hand may exceed the strength of the bone at this site, and this indirect force commonly results in fracture there.
• Clavicle fracture is caused by landing on the hand from a fall with the arm rigidly outstretched, or by a direct blow.
C
• The clavicle has important deep relations that make it clinically significant beyond the bone itself.
• The third parts of the subclavian vessels and the trunks of the brachial plexus pass behind the medial third of the shaft of the clavicle, separated only by the thin subclavius muscle.
• At the sternal end, behind the sternoclavicular joints, lie the common carotid artery on the left and the bifurcation of the brachiocephalic artery on the right, with the internal jugular vein lying a little more laterally; these vessels are separated from the bone only by the strap muscles (sternohyoid and sternothyroid).
• Because these major vessels and the brachial plexus trunks lie in such close proximity to the clavicle, deep or displaced injury involving the bone can threaten them.
• Compromise of the subclavian vessels can produce vascular insufficiency of the upper limb, while injury to the brachial plexus trunks passing behind the medial clavicle can produce motor and sensory deficits in the limb.
• This illustrates how a skeletal injury at the clavicle can spread to affect distant neurovascular structures, producing a functional deficit beyond the fracture site itself.

A
Most of the muscles of the larynx receive their innervation via the recurrent laryngeal branch of the vagus nerve; the exception is the cricothyroid muscle, which receives its innervation via the external laryngeal nerve. Motor supply to the muscles is from the nucleus ambiguus via the cranial accessory: to the cricothyroid via the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, and to all other laryngeal muscles, including the upper oesophagus and cricopharyngeus, via the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
B
Sensory innervation of the larynx is via branches of the vagus nerve: above the vocal folds it is via the internal laryngeal nerve, and below the vocal folds it is by way of branches of the recurrent laryngeal nerve; parasympathetic innervation of the larynx is mainly by way of branches of the vagus nerve. Lymphatic drainage similarly follows this division: above the cords to the upper deep cervical nodes, and below the cords to the lower deep cervical nodes.

A(i) Define the diaphragm and describe its shape, position and relations.
A(ii) Describe its origin (sternal, costal and vertebral, including the crura and arcuate ligaments) and its insertion.
A(iii) Describe its openings, their vertebral levels and the structures transmitted.
A(iv) Describe its blood supply.
A(v) Describe its nerve supply and lymphatic drainage.
B(i) Explain the anatomical basis of referred shoulder pain from irritation of the diaphragm.
B(ii) Explain why acquired herniae occur through the oesophageal opening and name the two types.
B(iii) Explain hiccup.
C(i) Distinguish between the right and the left crus of the diaphragm.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
A double-domed, thin fibromuscular (musculotendinous) partition between the thoracic and abdominal cavities and the main muscle of respiration; convex superior surface faces the thorax (covered by diaphragmatic pleura, lungs fit the domes, fibrous pericardium on the central tendon), concave inferior surface faces the abdomen (parietal peritoneum; liver, kidneys, suprarenals, stomach, spleen); higher on the right because of the liver (in expiration the right dome reaches the 5th rib, the left the 5th intercostal space); level varies with respiration, posture and abdominal distension, and the domes flatten in maximal inspiration.
A(ii)
Sternal: 2 slips from the posterior xiphoid process; costal: deep surfaces of the lower 6 ribs and costal cartilages (forms the domes); vertebral: the crura and 3 arcuate ligaments - medial (thickened psoas fascia, from the body of L2 to the tip of the L1 transverse process), lateral (thickened quadratus lumborum fascia, from the L1 transverse process to the lower border of the 12th rib) and median (joins the crura across the front of the aorta). Insertion: trefoil central tendon, no bony attachments, partly fused with the fibrous pericardium (pericardiophrenic ligament).
A(iii)
• Caval opening (T8; the only opening in the central tendon): IVC, terminal branches of the right phrenic nerve, a few lymphatics. Oesophageal opening (T10; in the right crus): oesophagus, anterior and posterior vagal trunks, oesophageal branches of the left gastric vessels, a few lymphatics. Aortic opening (T12; lowest and most posterior, between the crura): aorta, thoracic duct, sometimes azygos and hemiazygos veins.
• Smaller openings: greater and lesser splanchnic nerves pierce each crus; hemiazygos vein pierces the left crus; left phrenic nerve pierces the left dome; sympathetic trunks pass behind the diaphragm deep to the medial arcuate ligament; subcostal vessels and nerve pass behind the lateral arcuate ligament; superior epigastric vessels pass between the sternal and costal origins; 7th-11th intercostal neurovascular bundles pass through the costal origin.
A(iv)
Arteries: pericardiophrenic and musculophrenic (from the internal thoracic) and superior phrenic (from the thoracic aorta) to the superior surface; inferior phrenic (first branches of the abdominal aorta) to the inferior surface. Veins: pericardiophrenic and musculophrenic to the internal thoracic vein; superior phrenic vein (right) and right inferior phrenic vein to the IVC; the left inferior phrenic vein drains to the IVC and the left suprarenal vein.
A(v)
• Motor: phrenic nerves (C3-5) only - the right nerve to the right half up to the right margin of the oesophageal opening, the left to the left half. Sensory: central part (with related pleura and peritoneum) via the phrenic nerves; peripheral part via the lower 6 or 7 intercostal and subcostal nerves.
• Lymph: thoracic surface to anterior and posterior diaphragmatic nodes (anterior on to parasternal nodes; posterior to phrenic and posterior mediastinal nodes); abdominal surface to anterior diaphragmatic, phrenic and superior lumbar (caval/aortic) nodes.
B(i)
The central diaphragm is supplied sensorily by the phrenic nerve (C3-5) and the shoulder skin by the supraclavicular nerve (C3,4); so pain from irritation of pleura or pericardium over the central diaphragm, or of the peritoneum under it by subphrenic pus or blood, is referred to the shoulder tip.
B(ii)
Acquired herniae occur in middle-aged people with weak musculature around the oesophageal opening; they are either sliding or paraoesophageal (rolling, alongside the oesophagus).
B(iii)
Hiccup is an involuntary spasmodic contraction of the diaphragm with approximation of the vocal folds and closure of the glottis; common after eating or drinking from gastric irritation of vagus nerve endings; it may be due to pleurisy, peritonitis or pericarditis.
C(i)
• Right crus: larger and longer, arises from the upper 3 lumbar vertebrae (L1-L3) and their intervertebral discs; some of its fibres pass up to the left and loop round the oesophageal orifice as a physiological sphincter preventing reflux of gastric contents.
• Left crus: smaller, arises from the side of the bodies of the upper 2 (L1-L2) lumbar vertebrae and their discs; each crus is attached to the medial and lateral arcuate ligaments, and the medial borders of the two crura unite in front of T12 as the median arcuate ligament over the aorta.

A(i)
Molecular composition: The cell membrane consists of amphipathic phospholipids arranged so that the hydrophobic tails face inward (away from water) and the more hydrophilic head regions associate with the cytosolic and extracellular environments, forming a spherical lipid bilayer. The phospholipid bilayer was proposed by Gorter and Grendel in 1925. It also includes integral membrane proteins and peripheral membrane proteins (almost half of the total mass of the membrane), a network of tiny microfilaments of the cytoskeleton, and the lipid molecule cholesterol, which stabilizes and makes the cell membrane more rigid. Functions: structural support; semi-permeable membrane (controls what molecules enter and leave the cell); establishes and maintains an electrochemical gradient; contains receptors that recognize and respond to molecular signals; supports cell adhesion and cell communication. Membrane transport mechanisms: passive (osmosis, diffusion, simple diffusion), facilitated transport, active transport (primary and secondary), and vesicular transport (endocytosis: pinocytosis and phagocytosis; exocytosis).
A(ii)
Several diseases have been implicated with defective membrane receptors. Pseudohypoparathyroidism is associated with defective parathyroid and growth hormone receptors. In these conditions, the glands produce the respective hormones, but the target cells do not respond because they lack normal receptors. Signal transduction can be hindered and cause diseases when mutations occur in the genes that encode and regulate receptor proteins.
B(i)
Integral membrane proteins: are directly incorporated within the lipid bilayer; most are transmembrane proteins passing through the entire membrane; inserted into the lipid bilayer. Functions: transport, signal transduction, structural support. Peripheral membrane proteins: exhibit a looser association with the membrane; bound to the membrane indirectly by protein-protein interactions; located on the cytosolic face. Plasma membrane contains proteins called integrins that are linked to cytoplasmic molecules; through these linkages there is a connection between the extracellular matrix and cytoplasm, mediating cell adhesion and cell communication.

A(ii) Explain the clinical basis of diseases caused by defective membrane receptors.
B(i) Distinguish between integral (transmembrane) membrane proteins and peripheral membrane proteins, stating the function of each.

questions.answerText:
(i)
• The arteries of the stomach are derived from branches of the coeliac artery. The left gastric artery arises from the coeliac artery, passes upward and to the left to reach the oesophagus, then descends along the lesser curvature, supplying the lower third of the oesophagus and the upper right part of the stomach. The right gastric artery arises from the hepatic artery at the upper border of the pylorus and runs left along the lesser curvature, supplying the lower right part of the stomach.
• The short gastric arteries arise from the splenic artery at the hilum of the spleen and pass forward in the gastrosplenic omentum to supply the fundus. The left gastro-omental (gastroepiploic) artery arises from the splenic artery at the hilum of the spleen and passes forward in the gastrosplenic omentum to supply the stomach along the upper part of the greater curvature. The right gastro-omental artery arises from the gastroduodenal branch of the hepatic artery and passes left to supply the stomach along the lower part of the greater curvature.
(iii)
• The left and right gastric veins drain directly into the portal vein.
• The short gastric veins and the left gastroepiploic vein join the splenic vein.
• The right gastroepiploic vein joins the superior mesenteric vein.
• All venous drainage of the stomach therefore ultimately enters the portal circulation, via the portal vein, splenic vein or superior mesenteric vein, before passing through the liver.
• This portal route explains why bleeding from portal-systemic anastomoses, such as oesophageal varices, is related to the portal venous system.

(A) Describe the urinary bladder under the headings: A(i) parts A(ii) trigone A(iii) peritoneal/ligamentous relations.
(B) Explain the clinical basis of why the trigone remains an important fixed landmark during bladder filling.
(C) Distinguish the male urethra from the female urethra.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• The urinary bladder is a musculomembranous sac composed of a body, which collects urine, and a neck, a funnel-shaped extension passing inferiorly to join the urethra; it is divided into apex, fundus and body, with superior, posterior (base) and two inferolateral surfaces.
• The apex points towards the pubic symphysis and continues as the median umbilical ligament, a remnant of the embryonic urachus, up to the umbilicus; the base faces posteroinferiorly, with the two ureters entering at its upper corners and the urethra draining from its lower corner.
A(ii)
The trigone is the smooth, posteroinferior triangular area of the bladder wall formed by imaginary lines connecting the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice; it has four tunics, mucosa, submucosa, muscularis (detrusor muscle) and adventitia.
A(iii)
• Except for its superior surface, which is covered by peritoneum, the bladder is connected to surrounding structures by fibroareolar tissue (true ligaments): the lateral true ligaments, the puboprostatic or pubovesical ligaments anteriorly, the median umbilical ligament at the apex, and a posterior ligament.
• In the male, the upper posterior surface is related to the rectovesical pouch, and the lower part relates to the seminal vesicles and vas deferens; in the female, the posterior surface is related to the anterior wall of the vagina.
B
• The trigone remains immovable as the bladder fills and empties, and functions as a funnel that directs urine into the urethra as the bladder wall (detrusor) contracts.
• This fixed relationship of the ureteric and urethral orifices at the trigone is why it is used as a constant anatomical landmark despite the changing size and shape of the rest of the bladder.
C
• The male urethra is about 20 cm long and is divided into four parts: intramural (preprostatic), prostatic, membranous, and spongy (penile) parts, opening at the end of the penis.
• The male urethra passes through the prostate, the deep perineal pouch/urogenital diaphragm as the membranous urethra, and then the length of the penis as the spongy urethra, bending twice along its course.
• The female urethra is much shorter, about 3-4 cm long, corresponding to the prostatic part of the male urethra proximal to the prostatic utricle.
• The female urethra begins at the internal urethral orifice about 5 cm behind the pubic symphysis, runs downward embedded in the anterior wall of the vagina, traverses the urogenital diaphragm, and ends at the external urethral orifice in the vestibule, receiving the paraurethral (Skene's) glands.
• Both sexes have an internal, smooth muscle, involuntary urethral sphincter continuous with the detrusor muscle, and an external, skeletal muscle, voluntary sphincter innervated by the pudendal nerve, located inferior to the prostate in males and at the bladder's distal inferior end in females.

(i)
• The renal arteries arise from the aorta at the level of the L1/L2 intervertebral disc; the right renal artery passes posterior to the inferior vena cava.
• Each renal artery divides at the hilum into anterior and posterior branches; these give rise to segmental arteries.
• Four segmental arteries, apical, anterosuperior, anteroinferior and inferior, arise from the anterior branch, and the posterior branch itself constitutes the posterior segmental artery.
• Each segmental artery further gives lobar arteries, one for each renal pyramid, which give two or three interlobar arteries running toward the cortex on each side of the pyramid.
• Interlobar arteries give arcuate arteries at the corticomedullary junction, which give several interlobular arteries, from which afferent glomerular arterioles arise.
• The renal veins lie anterior to their respective arteries; each renal vein drains into the inferior vena cava, and the left renal vein additionally receives the left suprarenal and left gonadal veins before crossing anterior to the aorta.
(ii)
• The segmental arteries of the kidney are described as end arteries, meaning they do not anastomose with one another.
• Because each segmental artery supplies its own renal segment without collateral supply from adjacent segmental arteries, the renal parenchyma is divided into distinct vascular segments.
(iii)
• Since the segmental arteries are end arteries, occlusion or injury of one segmental artery cuts off blood supply to its corresponding renal segment.
• This lack of anastomosis means the affected segment cannot receive compensatory blood flow from neighbouring segments.
• Lymphatic drainage of the kidney is to the right and left lumbar lymph nodes, and nerve supply is via the renal plexus (vagus and abdominopelvic splanchnic nerves), so a segmental vascular injury is an isolated event within the kidney rather than one shared with adjacent segments.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Continuation of the sigmoid colon at S3; ends as the anal canal one inch below and in front of the tip of the coccyx; about 12 to 13 cm (5 inches); lower end dilated as the ampulla; lacks mesentery, taeniae coli, sacculations and appendices epiploicae.
• Two anteroposterior curves (sacral posterior; perineal anterior at puborectalis) and three lateral curves (upper convex to right, middle convex to left and most prominent, lower convex to right).
A(ii)
Upper third: front and sides covered; middle third: front only; lower third: none; posterior surface: none. Male: recto-vesical pouch 7.5 cm from anus; female: recto-uterine pouch of Douglas 5.5 cm from anus.
A(iii)
Four permanent horizontal Houston's valves (1st and 3rd constant); the 3rd at S5, 5 cm above the anus, if completely encircling forms Nelaton's sphincter, and divides an upper chamber (faeces without reflex to defecate) from a lower sensitive chamber; valves support faecal weight; cannulae/rectal washing are given in left lateral position to avoid injury to the 3rd valve.
A(iv)
Wall: serous, muscular (outer longitudinal, inner circular), submucosa, mucosa. Arteries: superior rectal (main, from inferior mesenteric), middle rectal (anterior division of internal iliac), inferior rectal (internal pudendal), median sacral (aorta), inferior gluteal.
B(i)
Superior rectal vein drains to inferior mesenteric then portal vein; middle rectal to internal iliac and inferior rectal to internal pudendal (systemic). Internal haemorrhoids (superior rectal tributaries, above Hilton's line, painless); external (inferior rectal, below, painful).
B(ii)
Support: puborectal sling, Waldeyer fascia, lateral ligaments, pelvirectal and ischiorectal fat. Upper third lateral: pararectal fossa (sigmoid colon, small intestine); middle third: pelvirectal space; lower third: ischioanal fossa.
B(iii)
Sympathetic (L1, L2) is vasomotor, stimulates the internal anal sphincter and inhibits the rest of the musculature; parasympathetic (S2 to S4) is secretomotor, stimulates peristalsis and relaxes sphincters.
C(i)
Lymph: upper half via superior rectal to left common iliac and pararectal nodes; middle half to internal iliac nodes; lower part to anal valves to internal iliac nodes; below the anal valves to superficial inguinal nodes.
C(ii)
Portal-systemic anastomosis: superior rectal (portal) with middle and inferior rectal veins (systemic); gut lymph follows arteries to pre-aortic nodes.
C(iii)
Male: anterior sigmoid colon, small intestine, seminal vesicles, ampulla of vas, posterior bladder and prostate; female: posterior vaginal wall; posterior: sacrum, sacral plexus, coccyx, and piriformis, coccygeus, levator ani.
C(iv)
Hindgut origin (endoderm), sympathetic least splanchnic (T12, L1) plus hypogastric (S2 to S4), inferior mesenteric artery (L3); mucosa above the 3rd valve from pre-allantoic hindgut, below from cloaca; muscle from splanchnic mesoderm.
