A. Describe the gross anatomy of the tongue under the following headings: division into anterior and posterior parts, and the intrinsic and extrinsic muscles.
B. State how the different regions of the tongue relate to common developmental and pathological conditions.
C. Explain why disease affecting one region of the tongue can produce a functional deficit at a distant site, based on its lymphatic drainage pattern.
questions.answerText:
A
A V-shaped groove, the sulcus terminalis, demarcates the anterior two-thirds of the tongue from the posterior one-third. The intrinsic muscles of the tongue are the superior longitudinal, inferior longitudinal, transverse, and vertical muscles. The extrinsic muscles are the genioglossus, styloglossus, palatoglossus, and hyoglossus. The mucosa of the anterior two-thirds is formed into papillae (filiform, fungiform, circumvallate, foliate), which contain taste buds.
B
Clinical correlates involving the tongue include loss of taste sensation, bifid tongue, tongue tie (ankyloglossia), microglossia/macroglossia, and lingual carcinoma. Nerve supply differs by region: in the anterior two-thirds, motor supply to the muscles is via CN XII (except palatoglossus, supplied by the pharyngeal plexus of the vagus nerve), sensory supply to the mucous membrane is via the lingual nerve (a branch of CN V3), and special (taste) sensory supply is via the chorda tympani nerve (a branch of CN VII); in the posterior one-third, motor supply is via CN XII, and sensory supply (general and special) is via the lingual branch of CN IX and the internal laryngeal nerve (a branch of CN X).
C
Lymphatic drainage of the tongue takes 4 routes: the posterior third drains to the superior deep cervical lymph nodes; the medial part of the anterior two-thirds drains to the inferior deep cervical lymph nodes; the lateral parts of the anterior two-thirds drain to the submandibular lymph nodes; and the apex of the tongue drains to the submental lymph nodes - with the posterior third and the area near the midline draining bilaterally. Because disease (such as lingual carcinoma) arising in a particular region of the tongue follows that region's specific lymphatic drainage route, it can spread to produce nodal or functional deficits at lymph node groups that are anatomically distant from the primary site, with the pattern of spread differing depending on which part of the tongue is affected, and bilateral drainage from the posterior third and midline region meaning disease there can involve lymph nodes on both sides of the neck.

questions.question:
A. Describe the gross anatomy of the larynx under the following headings: the three zones/compartments and the folds that demarcate them.
B. State how the zones of the larynx and the vocal folds relate to laryngeal function and clinical assessment (e.g. on laryngoscopy).
C. Explain how disease/infection at a site distant from the larynx can spread to compromise laryngeal or lower respiratory function, and the functional deficit that results from disordered laryngeal muscle action.
questions.answerText:
A
The larynx is demarcated by the vestibular fold (containing fibrous tissue, forming the false vocal cord on each side) and the vocal fold (the true vocal cord, containing the vocal ligament) into 3 zones: the supraglottic compartment (vestibule), above the false cords; the glottic compartment, between the false and true cords; and the subglottic compartment, between the true cords and the first ring of the trachea. The space between the vocal cords is the rima glottidis.
B
The mucosa is firmly adherent to the vocal ligament without any intervening submucosa, which accounts for the pearly white, avascular appearance of the vocal cords as seen on laryngoscopy; regulation of vocal cord tension (and therefore pitch of the voice) is accomplished primarily by pivoting the thyroid cartilage forward or backward at the cricothyroid joint, via the cricothyroid muscle, which is the only laryngeal muscle that tightens the cords, is supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (not the recurrent laryngeal nerve), and is the only intrinsic laryngeal muscle situated on the outside of the larynx.
C
Sensory innervation is via the internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve above the cords and via the recurrent laryngeal nerve below the cords; motor supply to the muscles is from the nucleus ambiguus via the cranial accessory, with the cricothyroid supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve and all other laryngeal muscles (including the upper oesophagus and cricopharyngeus) supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve. Lymphatic drainage above the cords is to the upper deep cervical nodes and below the cords to the lower deep cervical nodes; a disease process at either level can therefore spread along its corresponding drainage route to functionally distant lymph node groups. Movements which close off the entrance to the larynx during swallowing involve the epiglottis being pulled down and the arytenoid cartilages being pulled forward toward the epiglottis; the larynx is also raised, along with the pharynx, by contraction of the longitudinal muscles of the pharynx, and the epiglottis acts partly as a passive barrier, so disordered laryngeal muscle action compromises this protective closure mechanism.

A(i)
The great saphenous vein (GSV) is the longest vein in the body. It is formed by the union of the dorsal vein of the great toe and the dorsal venous arch of the foot. It ascends anterior to the medial malleolus, passes posterior to the medial condyle of the femur (about a hand's breadth posterior to the medial border of the patella), anastomoses freely with the small saphenous vein, traverses the saphenous opening in the fascia lata, and empties into the femoral vein.
A(ii)
The GSV has 10–12 valves, which are more numerous in the leg than in the thigh; these valves are usually located just inferior to the perforating veins. Perforating veins also have their own valves. Tributaries in the anterior and lateral part of the thighs converge to form the accessory saphenous vein (ASV), which communicates the GSV with the small saphenous vein. Just before emptying into the femoral vein, the GSV receives tributaries from the superficial circumflex iliac, superficial epigastric, and external pudendal veins.
B(i)
The small saphenous vein (SSV) arises on the lateral side of the foot from the union of the dorsal vein of the little toe with the dorsal venous arch. It ascends posterior to the lateral malleolus as a continuation of the lateral marginal vein, passes along the lateral border of the calcaneal tendon, inclines to the midline of the fibula and penetrates the deep fascia, ascends between the heads of the gastrocnemius muscle, and empties into the popliteal vein in the popliteal fossa.
B(ii)
There are four main pulse points in the lower limb: femoral (palpated midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and pubic symphysis — the mid-inguinal point); popliteal (deep in the popliteal fossa, requires deep palpation, best with slight knee flexion); dorsalis pedis (on the dorsum of the foot, just lateral to extensor hallucis longus tendon); and posterior tibial (inferoposteriorly to the medial malleolus). The GSV anterior to the medial malleolus is the classic site for venous cut-down; the GSV at the medial condyle of the femur is another accessible site.
C(i)
Superficial veins (GSV and SSV) are unaccompanied, lie in the superficial fascia, and their varicosity is visible. Deep veins of the lower limb accompany the arteries (read-up). Deep vein thrombosis involves the deep system and poses a risk of pulmonary embolism because the deep veins drain directly into the popliteal, femoral, and iliac veins and thence to the inferior vena cava. Superficial varicosity alone rarely embolises unless thrombosis extends through a perforating vein into the deep system.
questions.question:
Describe the great saphenous vein and small saphenous vein under the following headings, and explain the clinical basis of their use in surgery.
A(i) Origin, course, and termination of the great saphenous vein
A(ii) Tributaries and valves of the great saphenous vein
B(i) Origin, course, and termination of the small saphenous vein
B(ii) Clinical basis: pulse points of the lower limb and sites of venepuncture or cut-down
C(i) Distinguish varicosity from deep vein thrombosis based on the anatomical differences between the superficial and deep venous systems

Describe the popliteal fossa under the following headings and explain its clinical importance.
A(i) Boundaries
A(ii) Roof and floor
B(i) Contents, naming structures from superficial to deep
B(ii) Clinical basis for why popliteal aneurysm can produce neurological features
C(i) Distinguish the tibial nerve from the common fibular nerve with respect to origin, course, and consequences of injury within the fossa
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The popliteal fossa is a diamond-shaped depression in the posterior aspect of the knee. Superolateral border: biceps femoris. Superomedial border: semimembranosus and semitendinosus. Inferolateral border: lateral head of gastrocnemius. Inferomedial border: medial head of gastrocnemius.
A(ii)
Roof (posteriorly): skin and fascia — the popliteal fascia is a strong sheet of deep fascia continuous superiorly with the fascia lata and inferiorly with the deep fascia of the leg. Floor (anteriorly): popliteal surface of femur, capsule of knee joint, oblique popliteal ligament, and popliteal fascia over popliteus.
B(i)
From superficial to deep: posterior cutaneous nerve of thigh; tibial nerve (most superficial of the neurovascular bundle); popliteal vein; popliteal artery (deepest structure in the fossa, running close to the articular capsule of the knee joint); popliteal lymph nodes and lymphatic vessels. The small saphenous vein and three cutaneous nerves (posterior cutaneous nerve of thigh, medial sural cutaneous nerve, lateral sural cutaneous nerve) lie in the superficial fascia.
B(ii)
The popliteal artery is the deepest structure and lies in close proximity to the tibial nerve. An aneurysm (dilation of the artery beyond 50% of its normal diameter) causes compression of the tibial nerve. The tibial nerve is particularly susceptible to this compression; the major features include weakened or absent plantarflexion, paraesthesia of the foot and posterolateral leg, and paralysis of flexor muscles in the leg and intrinsic muscles of the sole.
C(i)
The tibial nerve is the medial and larger branch of the sciatic nerve; it bisects the fossa passing from the superior to the inferior angle and gives muscular branches to soleus, gastrocnemius, plantaris, and popliteus, and the medial sural cutaneous nerve. The common fibular nerve is the lateral, smaller terminal branch; it begins at the superior angle, closely follows the medial border of biceps femoris, exits the fossa by passing superficial to the lateral head of gastrocnemius, then winds around the neck of fibula where it divides into terminal branches. Injury to the tibial nerve causes inability to plantarflex the ankle or flex the toes and loss of sensation on the sole of the foot.

questions.question:
Describe the arches of the foot under the following headings and explain their clinical relevance.
A(i) Name and constituent bones of each arch, identifying the keystone of each
A(ii) Factors maintaining the arches — ligaments, muscles, and bony factor for each arch
B(i) Functions of the foot arches in weight-bearing and locomotion
B(ii) Deformities of the foot — name and define pes planus, pes cavus, talipes equinovarus, and talipes calcaneovalgus
C(i) Explain why the medial longitudinal arch is more dynamic and more clinically vulnerable than the lateral longitudinal arch
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Medial longitudinal arch: formed by calcaneus, talus (keystone — its superior articular facet is the summit), navicular, 3 cuneiform bones, and 1st, 2nd, and 3rd metatarsals; found on medial aspect of foot; larger, with greatest height, higher, more mobile, and more resilient. Lateral longitudinal arch: formed by calcaneus, cuboid, and the 4th and 5th metatarsals; summit is the subtalar articulation; flat, contains relatively fewer bones, hence more rigid; bears body weight before the medial arch comes into play. Transverse arch: formed proximally by 3 cuneiforms and cuboid, and distally by the bases of 5 metatarsals; it is a partial arch (each foot represents a half dome); the intermediate and lateral cuneiforms are wedge-shaped (bony factor).
A(ii)
Medial longitudinal arch: Ligaments — spring ligament, deltoid ligament, plantar aponeurosis, interosseous ligaments, long and short plantar ligaments. Muscles — tibialis posterior, tibialis anterior, flexor hallucis longus, flexor digitorum longus, and short muscles of the big toe. Bony factor — the shape and constitution of the bones. Lateral longitudinal arch: Ligaments — plantar aponeurosis, interosseous ligaments, long and short plantar ligaments. Muscles — peroneus longus and brevis, flexor digitorum longus, and short muscles of the little toe. Bony factor — shape and constitution of the bones. Transverse arch: Bony factor — intermediate and lateral cuneiforms are wedge-shaped. Ligaments — deep transverse ligament and interosseous ligaments (dorsal and plantar). Muscles — peroneus longus and brevis, transverse head of adductor hallucis, and slips of tibialis posterior.
B(i)
The human foot supports the body weight and serves as a lever to propel the body forward during locomotion. Functions carried out by arches: (1) Foot acts as a segmented lever with multiple joints and adapts to uneven surfaces. (2) Long flexors and intrinsic muscles assist propulsive action of gastrocnemius and soleus. (3) Arches are springs that absorb shock and store energy — elastic arches present between weight-bearing points can flatten and recoil back to normal.
B(ii)
Pes planus (flat foot): rotation of the calcaneus, eversion of the plantar surface, slipping down of the talus and navicular, lengthening of the medial longitudinal arch, and abduction of the forefoot; caused by excess weight on medial side, relaxation of ligaments, or muscular imbalance. Pes cavus (high-arched foot): exaggeration of the longitudinal arch; toes dorsiflexed at metatarsophalangeal joints and plantarflexed at interphalangeal joints — claw foot. Talipes equinovarus: plantar flexion, inversion, and adduction of the foot (clubfoot). Talipes calcaneovalgus: dorsiflexion, eversion, and abduction of the foot.
C(i)
The medial longitudinal arch is higher, more mobile, and more resilient — it is dynamic, changes most during movement, and requires active muscular support (particularly tibialis posterior, flexor hallucis longus, and the spring ligament). The lateral longitudinal arch is lower, more stable, built to transmit weight to the ground, makes more contact with the ground, has limited mobility, and depends more on bony and ligamentous rather than muscular support. The medial arch is therefore more clinically vulnerable to collapse (pes planus) when muscles weaken or ligaments stretch.

(i)
• The spleen is an ovoid, highly vascular, reddish-purple organ, on average about 12 cm long, 7 cm broad, 3 cm thick and weighing about 150 g, related to the 9th to 11th ribs on the left side.
• It has two ends, an expanded anterior end and a rounded posterior end resting on the upper pole of the left kidney, three borders (superior, inferior and intermediate), and two surfaces (diaphragmatic and visceral).
• The diaphragmatic surface is convex and related to the diaphragm, left lung and pleura, and the 9th-11th ribs; the visceral surface is concave and bears gastric, renal, colic and pancreatic impressions.
• The hilum lies on the inferomedial part of the gastric impression and transmits the splenic vessels and nerves, giving attachment to the gastrosplenic and splenorenal ligaments; the phrenicocolic ligament supports, but is not attached to, the anterior end of the spleen.
(ii)
• The gastric impression, related to the fundus of the stomach, is the largest impression; the renal impression relates to the left kidney and sometimes the suprarenal gland; the colic impression relates to the splenic flexure of the colon; the pancreatic impression relates to the tail of the pancreas.
• The gastrosplenic ligament contains the short gastric vessels supplying the stomach, and the splenorenal ligament contains the tail of the pancreas and splenic vessels, so disease or surgery at the spleen can affect the stomach, kidney, colon or pancreas through these relations.
(iii)
• Although protected by the 9th to 12th ribs, the spleen is the most frequently injured organ in the abdomen.
• Severe blows to the left side may fracture ribs, producing sharp fragments that lacerate the spleen, and blunt trauma elsewhere that raises intra-abdominal pressure can also rupture it because its capsule is thin and the pulp soft.
• If ruptured, the spleen bleeds profusely because it is a highly vascular organ receiving the splenic artery, the largest branch of the coeliac trunk.
• This produces severe intraperitoneal haemorrhage and shock, a systemic and distant functional deficit in circulation arising from a local splenic injury.
• Repair of a ruptured spleen is difficult, so splenectomy or subtotal splenectomy is often performed to prevent the patient from bleeding to death.
• Even after total splenectomy, most splenic functions are assumed by other reticuloendothelial organs such as the liver and bone marrow, though susceptibility to certain bacterial infections increases.
questions.question:
(i) Describe the gross anatomy of the spleen - measurements, external features (ends, borders, surfaces, hilum) and peritoneal ligaments.
(ii) Relate the surfaces/impressions of the spleen to organs it may affect in disease.
(iii) Explain why splenic rupture produces a distant, life-threatening functional deficit.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
• The sacrum is formed by the union of 5 sacral vertebrae (fusion begins at 16 to 18 years, usually complete by 30); wedge-shaped; concave anterior surface with four transverse lines and four pairs of anterior sacral foramina.
• Dorsally a median sacral crest and posterior foramina; the sacral canal is continuous with the vertebral canal; an auricular surface forms the sacroiliac joint; structures emerge at the sacral hiatus.
A(ii)
• Each hip bone is three bones (ilium, pubis, ischium) separated by cartilage in the newborn and fused at puberty in the acetabulum; the ilium is the largest, with ala, body, crest, spines, greater sciatic notch, iliac fossa, auricular surface and arcuate line.
• Ischium: body, ramus, spine, lesser sciatic notch and tuberosity; pubis: superior and inferior rami, body, crest, tubercle, iliopectineal line; ischium and pubis surround the obturator foramen.
A(iii)
Two hip bones united at the pubic symphysis and with the sacrum at the sacroiliac joints; the girdle moves as a unit and supports and protects lower abdominal and pelvic organs; the pelvic brim divides true and false pelves.
B(i)
• The female pelvis serves for childbearing and easier delivery; it is bigger and wider, with a large oval brim and a wider outlet.
• The sacral promontory, the superior border of the anterior sacral surface, is an important obstetric landmark for pelvic measurements.
• The sacral index is about 105 in males and 115 in females, and the sacrovertebral angle is more prominent in females.
C(i)
• Male: smaller, narrower, heavier and thicker bone; deep false pelvis; pubic arch V-shaped and less than 90°; acetabulum larger, facing laterally; coccyx immovable; brim smaller and heart-shaped; outlet narrower.
• Male: narrower greater sciatic notch, round obturator foramen, longer narrower sacrum, more vertical ilium, ischial tuberosities longer, close together and laterally projecting.
• Female: shallow false pelvis; wider pubic arch greater than 90°; acetabulum smaller, facing anteriorly; coccyx movable; large oval brim; wider outlet.
• Female: wider greater sciatic notch, oval obturator foramen, less vertical ilium, ischial tuberosities shorter, farther apart and projecting medially.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the five functions of the epithelial lining of the digestive tract.
A(ii) Describe the submucosal (Meissner) plexus and the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus together as the local enteric nervous system: name the layers of the GIT wall each is found in, state the ganglia they are composed of, what the number of ganglia depends on, and what system they function independently of.
B(i) Describe the muscularis mucosae: its composition, its location, and the two functions attributed to it.
B(ii) Explain the immunological backup to the thin epithelial barrier of the GIT, and identify what the digestive tract normally contains that makes this backup essential.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Five functions of the epithelial lining:
• Provide a selectively permeable barrier between the contents of the tract and the tissues of the body.
• Facilitate the transport and digestion of food.
• Promote the absorption of the products of digestion.
• Produce hormones that affect the activity of the digestive system.
• Produce mucus for lubrication and protection.
A(ii)
Local enteric nervous system:
• The submucosal (Meissner) plexus is located in the submucosa; the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus is located in the connective tissue between the circular and longitudinal muscle sublayers of the muscularis.
• Together they constitute the local enteric nervous system of the digestive tract.
• This system functions independently of the CNS.
• Both plexuses are composed mainly of nerve cell aggregates forming small parasympathetic ganglia.
• The number of ganglia along the digestive tract is variable — numerous in the regions of greatest motility.
B(i)
Muscularis mucosae:
• Composition: thin layer of smooth muscle.
• Location: usually separates the mucosa from the submucosa.
• Functions: (1) allows local movements of the mucosa independent of other movements of the digestive tract, helping to increase contact of the lining with food; (2) its contractions contribute to mixing and propelling food (the plexuses coordinate the contractions of the muscularis to mix and propel food).
B(ii)
Immunological backup:
• The mucosa-associated immune defense system (MALT) provides an essential backup to the thin physical barrier of the epithelial lining.
• The lamina propria (just below the epithelium) is a zone rich in macrophages and lymphocytes, some of which actively produce IgA antibodies.
• The digestive tract normally contains thousands of microbial species, including both useful gut inhabitants and potential pathogens ingested with food and drink, making this immune backup essential.

A(i)
The hip joint is a multiaxial ball-and-socket type of synovial joint. It is the largest joint in the human body and the 2nd largest weight-bearing joint. Articular surfaces: the lunate surface of the acetabulum (covered by hyaline cartilage except at the fovea) and the spherical head of femur (which forms 2/3 of a sphere, covered by hyaline cartilage except at the fovea capitis). The acetabulum is deepened by the fibrocartilaginous acetabular labrum; it is deficient inferiorly as the acetabular notch, bridged by the transverse acetabular ligament.
A(ii)
Capsule: strong and thick; medially attached to margin of acetabulum, transverse acetabular ligament, and adjacent margin of obturator foramen; laterally attached to the intertrochanteric line anteriorly. Ligaments: (1) Iliofemoral ligament (ligament of Bigelow) — one of the strongest in the body, Y-shaped; apex at inferior iliac spine, base to intertrochanteric line; prevents overextension and prevents trunk from falling backwards while standing. (2) Pubofemoral ligament — triangular; attached superiorly to iliopubic eminence and obturator crest, inferiorly merges with capsule; limits extension and abduction. (3) Ischiofemoral ligament — reinforces posterior aspect; medially attached to ischium posteroinferior to acetabulum, laterally to greater trochanter deep to the iliofemoral ligament; limits extension. Fibers of all three spiral so they become taut in extension, stabilizing the joint and reducing muscle energy needed for standing. Ligament teres (round ligament): flat triangular band from fovea to acetabular notch and transverse ligament; ensheathed by synovial membrane; transmits arteries to head of femur.
B(i)
By Hilton's law: the nerve supplying the joint also supplies the muscles moving the joint and the skin covering the insertion of those muscles. Nerve supply: femoral nerve, anterior division of obturator nerve, nerve to rectus femoris, nerve to quadratus femoris, sciatic nerve, and superior gluteal nerve. The posterior division of the obturator nerve supplies both the hip and the knee joint.
B(ii)
Flexion (120–140°): iliopsoas, sartorius, rectus femoris, tensor fasciae latae. Extension: gluteus maximus, semimembranosus, semitendinosus, biceps femoris. Abduction (60–80°): gluteus medius, minimus, tensor fasciae latae. Adduction: pectineus, adductor longus, brevis, magnus, gracilis. Medial rotation: gluteus medius, minimus, tensor fasciae latae. Lateral rotation: obturator internus and externus, gemellus superior and inferior, quadratus femoris, piriformis, posterior fibres of gluteus medius and minimus, superior fibres of gluteus maximus.
C(i)
The posterior division of the obturator nerve supplies both the hip and knee joints; pain from hip pathology is therefore referred along this common nerve pathway to the knee joint. Coxa valga follows congenital dislocation of the head of femur; coxa vara follows fracture of the neck of femur.
questions.question:
Describe the hip joint under the following headings and explain its clinical correlates.
A(i) Type and articular surfaces
A(ii) Capsule, ligaments — name, attachments and function of each
B(i) Nerve supply, applying Hilton's law
B(ii) Movements and muscles responsible for each movement
C(i) Explain why referred pain from the hip can present at the knee, and distinguish coxa valga from coxa vara

questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Formed by the ventral rami of L1, L2, L3 and the upper part of L4; the lower part of L4 joins L5 to form the lumbosacral trunk.
• The rami emerge from the intervertebral foramina, enter psoas, give branches to psoas and quadratus lumborum, then form the plexus within the substance of psoas major.
A(ii)
• Iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal: L1; genitofemoral: L1, L2; lateral femoral cutaneous: L2, L3 (posterior division).
• Femoral: L2, L3, L4 (posterior division); obturator: L2, L3, L4 (anterior division); sometimes an accessory obturator L3, L4.
A(iii)
• From the lateral border of psoas major: iliohypogastric, ilioinguinal, lateral femoral cutaneous, femoral.
• Through psoas anteriorly: genitofemoral; from the medial border: obturator.
A(iv)
• It innervates part of the lower abdominal wall but chiefly supplies skin and muscle 'borrowed from the trunk by the lower limb'.
• The genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve supplies the cremasteric muscle; the ilioinguinal nerve runs in the inguinal canal.
B(i)
The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve normally passes deep to the lateral end of the inguinal ligament; sometimes it passes through the substance of the ligament.
C(i)
• Entrapment causes pain along its distribution (meralgia paresthetica).
• Psoas major is supplied by ventral rami L1 to L4, psoas minor by L1, quadratus lumborum by upper lumbar and subcostal nerves, iliacus by the femoral nerve.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the nasal septum and the cartilages of the external nose under the following headings: the quadrangular cartilage, the upper lateral cartilages, and the lower lateral (alar) cartilages.
A(ii) Describe the blood supply to the nasal septum.
B. Explain the clinical basis for why the anteroinferior third of the nasal septum is the commonest site of nosebleeds (epistaxis).
C. Distinguish between the upper lateral cartilages and the lower lateral (alar) cartilages of the nose.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The quadrangular cartilaginous septum extends from the nasal bones in the midline above to the bony septum in the midline posteriorly, then down along the bony floor. Its upper half is flanked by two triangular-to-trapezoidal cartilages, the upper lateral cartilages, which are fused to the dorsal septum in the midline and attached to the bony margin of the pyriform aperture laterally by loose ligaments; the inferior ends of the upper lateral cartilages are free. Beneath the upper lateral cartilages lie the lower lateral cartilages; the paired lower lateral cartilages swing out from medial attachments to the caudal septum in the midline (the medial crura), through an intermediate crus area, finally flaring out superolaterally as the lateral crura; these cartilages are frequently mobile, in contradistinction to the upper lateral cartilages. The internal area or angle formed by the septum and upper lateral cartilage constitutes the internal valve.
A(ii)
The nasal septum is supplied from the sphenopalatine artery (posterior septal branch) and the anterior and posterior ethmoid arteries, with contribution of the superior labial artery (anteriorly) and the greater palatine artery (posteriorly).
B
The Kiesselbach plexus, or Little's area, represents a region in the anteroinferior third of the nasal septum where all 3 of the chief blood supplies to the internal nose converge, which is the clinical basis for this being a common site of nosebleeds; venous blood leaving the region drains into the facial, ophthalmic and sphenopalatine veins, and these veins are significant for their direct communication with the cavernous sinus and for their lack of valves, features that potentiate the intracranial spread of infection.
C
The upper lateral cartilages are fused to the dorsal septum in the midline and attached to the bony margin of the pyriform aperture laterally by loose ligaments, with their inferior ends free; they are relatively fixed. The lower lateral (alar) cartilages, by contrast, swing out from medial attachments to the caudal septum (the medial crura) to flare out superolaterally as the lateral crura, and are frequently mobile, unlike the upper lateral cartilages.

questions.question:
Describe the gross anatomy of the brachial plexus:
A(i) Formation (roots)
A(ii) Trunks, divisions, cords
A(iii) Five main terminal branches
B. State how injury at each level (trunk/cord) of the plexus relates to a specific clinical pathology.
C. Explain how injury at the level of a trunk or cord spreads to affect distant structures (individual peripheral nerves), causing specific functional deficits.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The brachial plexus is formed by the union of the C5, C6, C7 and C8 ventral rami and the greater part of the 1st thoracic ventral ramus, with contribution sometimes from C4 (giving a "prefixed" plexus) or T2 (giving a "postfixed" plexus); the roots emerge from the transverse processes of the cervical vertebrae, immediately posterior to the vertebral artery, and lie between the scalene muscles.
A(ii)
C5 and C6 unite to form the upper trunk, C7 continues as the middle trunk, and C8 and T1 unite to form the lower trunk, lying in the posterior triangle of the neck; each trunk bifurcates behind the clavicle into an anterior and a posterior division. The anterior divisions of the upper and middle trunks unite to form the lateral cord; the anterior division of the lower trunk continues as the medial cord; the posterior divisions of all three trunks unite to form the posterior cord, lying in the axilla below pectoralis minor.
A(iii)
The five main terminal branches are the musculocutaneous nerve and the lateral root of the median nerve (from the lateral cord), the ulnar nerve and the medial root of the median nerve (from the medial cord), and the axillary and radial nerves (from the posterior cord).
B
• Injury to the upper trunk (C5, C6), at "Erb's point," produces Erb's paralysis, from causes such as birth injury, a fall on the shoulder, or during anaesthesia, affecting the axillary, musculocutaneous and suprascapular nerves.
• Injury to the lower trunk (C8, T1), from causes such as undue abduction of the arm, produces Klumpke's paralysis, with paralysis of the intrinsic hand muscles and ulnar wrist/finger flexors, and possible Horner's syndrome from associated sympathetic fibre injury.
C
• Erb's paralysis paralyses biceps, deltoid, brachialis, brachioradialis, supraspinatus, infraspinatus and supinator, producing the "Policeman's/Porter's tip hand": the arm hangs adducted and medially rotated, the forearm extended and pronated, with loss of abduction/lateral rotation of the shoulder and flexion/supination of the forearm.
• Klumpke's paralysis produces a claw hand from unopposed long flexors/extensors, plus cutaneous anaesthesia along the ulnar border of the limb.
• Injury to the lateral cord (e.g. from dislocation of the humerus) involves the musculocutaneous nerve and the lateral root of the median nerve, paralysing biceps, coracobrachialis and the median-supplied forearm muscles, producing a midprone forearm with loss of elbow and wrist flexion and sensory loss on the radial side of the forearm.
• Injury to the medial cord (e.g. from subcoracoid dislocation of the humerus) involves the ulnar nerve and the medial root of the median nerve, producing claw hand with sensory loss on the ulnar side of the forearm and hand.
• Injury to the posterior cord involves the upper and lower subscapular nerves, the thoracodorsal nerve, the axillary nerve, and the radial nerve (the largest and most frequently injured branch of the plexus).
• This weakens elbow, wrist and metacarpophalangeal joint extension via the radial nerve, and shoulder abduction via the axillary nerve.
• In this way, a single lesion at the level of a trunk or cord of the brachial plexus spreads its effect along the several peripheral nerves derived from it, each producing its own characteristic and distant functional deficit in the arm, forearm or hand.

A(i)
A thin serous membrane lining the walls of the abdominal and pelvic cavities and covering the organs within; two layers: parietal and visceral.
A(ii)
• The cavity is the potential space between the layers, contains no organs and a thin layer of fluid, and is a closed sac in males; it is divided into greater and lesser sacs that communicate through the epiploic foramen.
• The fluid lubricates the surfaces so viscera move without friction, contains leukocytes and antibodies, and is absorbed by lymphatics on the inferior surface of the diaphragm.
A(iii)
• Provides a slippery surface for movement of viscera; phagocytic cells protect viscera; can store large amounts of fat.
• Mesothelial cells transform into fibroblasts, promoting healing; the mesothelium acts as a semi-permeable membrane.
A(iv)
Intraperitoneal organs are completely surrounded (stomach, spleen, small intestine); retroperitoneal organs are covered partially on their anterior surfaces only (kidney, ureter).
B(i)
• In the female the cavity communicates with the exterior through the uterine tubes, uterus and vagina, a potential pathway of infection.
• Because the mesothelium is semi-permeable, urea can be removed from blood by circulating fluids through the cavity: peritoneal dialysis.
C(i)
• Parietal: lines the inner surface of abdominal and pelvic walls and lower surface of diaphragm; loosely attached by extraperitoneal connective tissue; pain sensitive; nerve supply same as the overlying body wall.
• Visceral: lines the outer surface of viscera; cannot be stripped; nerve supply is that of the underlying viscera (sympathetic), with receptors sensitive to overdistension, traction on mesenteries, spasm and ischaemia.
• Blood supply: parietal from lumbar vessels, inferior and superior epigastric, musculophrenic and deep circumflex arteries; visceral from the arteries supplying the appropriate viscera.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the gross histology of bone under the following headings: chemical composition and properties, cell types and their functions, and types of bone.
A(ii) State how the Haversian system (osteon) is organised and relate this to bone function.
B(i) Explain how blood calcium levels are regulated through bone, naming the hormones involved and their actions.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Chemical composition and properties: Bone is a connective tissue mineralized by calcium phosphate in the form of crystals very similar to hydroxyapatite. The minerals are both in the type I collagen fibers (which constitute about 95% of the matrix) and in the ground substance. Bone is both resilient and hard. Its resilience is due to the organic matter (collagen); its hardness is due to the inorganic minerals (calcium phosphate, calcium carbonate, calcium fluoride, calcium hydroxide, and citrate). Cell types: Osteocytes — maintain calcium and phosphate ion levels in the blood, are essentially stress sensors, and are osteoblasts that have been trapped in their own matrix in lacunae. Osteoblasts — synthesize the organic matrix (osteoid). Osteoclasts — multinucleated giant cells involved in resorption and remodeling of bone; they are also chondrocytes during bone healing and remodeling. Osteoid is the matrix secreted by osteoblasts and osteocytes prior to mineralization. Types of bone: compact bone (also called dense bone, cortical bone, or lamellar bone) and spongy bone (also called cancellous bone, trabecular bone, and medullary bone).
A(ii)
Compact bone is organized into structures called osteons or Haversian systems: concentric lamellae surrounding a central canal called the Haversian canal, which contains blood vessels, nerves, loose connective tissue, and endosteum. Between lamellae are lacunae, each with one osteocyte interconnected by canaliculi containing the cells' dendritic processes. Canals called Volkmann's canals link Haversian canals with one another and with the marrow cavity. Metabolic exchanges between osteocytes and blood capillaries depend on communication through the canaliculi.
B(i)
Blood calcium levels are regulated by the hormones parathormone (parathyroid hormone), which raises blood calcium levels by stimulating bone resorption, and calcitonin, which reduces blood calcium by suppressing bone resorption and increasing osteoid calcification.

questions.question:
Describe the adductor group of the medial compartment of the thigh under the following headings, explaining the anatomical basis of the pes anserinus and its clinical importance.
A(i) Name all 5 adductor muscles; give origin, insertion, innervation, and action for each
A(ii) Why all adductor muscles are supplied by the obturator nerve except the hamstring part of adductor magnus — state its nerve supply and embryologic basis
B(i) The adductor hiatus — its boundaries and the structures it transmits
B(ii) The pes anserinus — its composition and function
C(i) Distinguish the gracilis from the other adductor muscles based on its unique anatomical features; name the other two compartments' muscles that join it to form the pes anserinus and their common innervation
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Adductor longus: origin — anterior surface of body of pubis, inferior to pubic crest and lateral to pubic symphysis; insertion — middle third of medial lip of linea aspera of femur; innervation — obturator nerve, anterior division (L2, L3, L4); action — adducts thigh. It is the most anteriorly placed muscle of the adductor group, large and fan-shaped. Adductor brevis: origin — body and inferior ramus of pubis; insertion — pectineal line and proximal part of linea aspera of femur; innervation — obturator nerve, anterior division (L2, L3, L4); action — adducts thigh and to an extent flexes it; it is short and lies deep to pectineus and adductor longus. Adductor magnus: largest, most powerful, most posterior muscle in the group; has an adductor part and a hamstring part. Origin — adductor part from inferior ramus of pubis and ramus of ischium; hamstring part from ischial tuberosity. Insertion — adductor part to gluteal tuberosity, linea aspera, medial supracondylar line; hamstring part to adductor tubercle of femur. Innervation — adductor part: obturator nerve (L2, L3, L4); hamstring part: tibial nerve. Action — adducts thigh; adductor part flexes, hamstring part extends. Gracilis: origin — body and inferior ramus of pubis; insertion — superior part of medial surface of tibia; innervation — obturator nerve (L2, L3); action — adducts thigh, flexes leg, helps rotate leg medially. Obturator externus: origin — margins of obturator foramen and obturator membrane; insertion — trochanteric fossa of femur; innervation — obturator nerve (L2, L3); action — laterally rotates thigh, steadies head of femur in acetabulum.
A(ii)
All adductor muscles are supplied by the obturator nerve except the hamstring part of adductor magnus and part of pectineus. The hamstring part of adductor magnus is supplied by the tibial nerve — because embryologically the hamstring part shares the same developmental origin as the true hamstrings (which arise from the ischial tuberosity and are all innervated by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve).
B(i)
The adductor hiatus is an opening between the aponeurotic distal attachment of the adductor part of adductor magnus and the tendinous distal attachment of the hamstring part. It transmits the femoral artery and vein from the adductor canal in the thigh to the popliteal fossa posterior to the knee. It is located just lateral and superior to the adductor tubercle of the femur.
B(ii)
The pes anserinus consists of the conjoined tendons of the sartorius, gracilis, and semitendinosus muscles; they insert into the superior part of the medial surface of the tibia. It acts as a secondary valgus restraint, augmenting the medial supporting structures of the knee. Bursitis of the pes anserinus bursa causes medial knee pain, especially in osteoarthritis.
C(i)
Gracilis is unique among the adductor group: it is a long strap-like muscle, the most medial and most superficial of the adductors, and the weakest member; it is the only member of the adductor group to cross both the hip and knee joints. It joins with sartorius (from the anterior compartment, supplied by femoral nerve) and semitendinosus (from the posterior compartment, supplied by tibial nerve) to form the pes anserinus — three muscles from three different compartments with three different nerve supplies share a common insertion.

A(i)
The surface marking of the base of the appendix is McBurney's point, at the junction of the lateral one-third and medial two-thirds of a line drawn from the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus. The appendix is attached to the cecum below the ileocaecal valve, and the teniae coli of the cecum converge at the root of the appendix.
A(ii)
The appendix is one of the intraperitoneal parts of the large intestine, suspended by its own mesentery, the mesoappendix.
A(iii)
The appendix opens at the posteromedial aspect of the cecum, about one inch below the ileocaecal junction; its positions include retrocecal, the most common, pelvic, subcecal, preileal, and postileal, the least common.
B
• Deep tenderness at McBurney's point, McBurney's sign, is the clinical sign used to localise inflammation of the appendix, that is, acute appendicitis.
• The appendix is described as an intestinal tonsil because of the abundant lymphatic nodules in its lamina propria, which extend into the submucosa and give it an immune function, similar to the tonsils.
C
• Grossly, the appendix has no teniae coli and shows various shapes and positions, whereas the rest of the colon shows three longitudinal teniae coli, free, mesocolic and omental, which converge at the root of the appendix.
• The colon has haustra (sacculations), because the teniae are shorter than the length of the gut wall, appendices epiploicae (fat-filled peritoneal pouches), and semilunar folds; the appendix lacks these features.
• Microscopically, the appendix has no villi and its crypts (of Lieberkuhn) are less abundant than in the colon.
• The colon's mucosa shows enterocytes with no digestive enzyme production, water and electrolyte reabsorption, deep crypts, a thick mucin layer, and goblet cells that increase in number caudally.
• The appendix has prominent lymphatic nodules in the lamina propria extending into the submucosa, which are far less prominent in the general colon.
• Both the appendix and colon lack villi, unlike the small intestine, but only the appendix is described as functioning analogously to the tonsils.
questions.question:
(A) Describe the vermiform appendix under the headings: A(i) surface anatomy/position A(ii) peritoneal relations A(iii) opening and possible positions.
(B) Explain the clinical basis of tenderness at McBurney's point in appendicitis.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Immunological defense system:
• Name: Mucosa-Associated Lymphoid Tissue (MALT).
• Layers occupied: the mucosa (especially the lamina propria located just below the epithelium) and the submucosal layers.
• Cell types: macrophages and lymphocytes (some of which actively produce antibodies); also free immune cells and lymphoid nodules.
• Antibody produced: mainly immunoglobulin A (IgA).
A(ii)
IgA protection mechanism:
• IgA antibodies undergo transcytosis into the intestinal lumen, bound to the secretory protein produced by epithelial cells.
• This complex (secretory IgA) protects against viral and bacterial pathogens.
• IgA is resistant to proteolytic enzymes and can therefore coexist with the proteases present in the lumen, making it effective even in the enzyme-rich intestinal environment.
B(i)
Stratified squamous epithelium lines the oral cavity, esophagus, and anal canal (not vulnerable simple columnar). The rest of the GIT (except these three regions) is lined by a simple thin vulnerable epithelium. Because the rest of the GIT is lined by this vulnerable epithelium and normally contains thousands of microbial species (including potential pathogens), the MALT provides an essential backup to the thin physical barrier.
B(ii)
The enteric nervous system (submucosal/Meissner and myenteric/Auerbach plexuses) provides an anatomic basis for the well-known actions of emotional stress on the stomach and other regions of the GIT. These plexuses are interconnected with the autonomic nervous system and CNS.
questions.question:

A(ii) Explain the complete mechanism by which IgA protects the lumen of the GIT from pathogens, including the role of the secretory protein and the property that makes IgA effective.

B(ii) Explain the clinical and anatomical basis for the well-known effects of emotional stress on the stomach and other regions of the GIT.

questions.answerText:
(i)
• The heart has four chambers, the right and left atria (receiving chambers) and the right and left ventricles (discharging chambers), enclosed in the double-walled pericardial sac, and rests on its diaphragmatic (inferior) surface.
• It has an apex, formed by the inferolateral part of the left ventricle and lying posterior to the 5th intercostal space where the apex beat is felt, a base, formed mainly by the left atrium and part of the right atrium, four borders and three surfaces.
• The right border is formed mainly by the right atrium; the left border by the left ventricle and left auricle; the inferior border by the right ventricle mainly and the left ventricle; the superior border by both atria, auricles and the great vessels.
• The anterior (sternocostal) surface consists chiefly of the right ventricle; the inferior (diaphragmatic) surface consists chiefly of the left ventricle and a small part of the right ventricle; the left (pulmonary) surface is formed mainly by the left ventricle.
• The right atrium receives venous blood from the SVC, IVC and coronary sinus, has a smooth sinus venarum and a rough muscular wall with pectinate muscles, and communicates with the right ventricle via the right atrioventricular (tricuspid) orifice.
• The left atrium receives the four pulmonary veins and communicates with the left ventricle via the left atrioventricular (mitral) orifice; the right ventricle has a tricuspid valve and leads to the pulmonary trunk via the conus arteriosus, while the left ventricle, with twice the wall thickness, has the mitral valve and leads to the aorta via the aortic vestibule and aortic valve.
(ii)
• Valvular insufficiency results from valve leaflets not completely sealing when a valve is closed, so regurgitation of blood occurs into the proximal chamber, generating a characteristic heart murmur.
• Positional and septal anomalies include dextrocardia, atrial septal defects and ventricular septal defects.
• Aortic dissection, a tear in the inner wall of the aorta associated with high blood pressure, and aortic aneurysm, dilation of an artery greater than 50% of its normal diameter, are pathologies of the great vessel arising from the left ventricle.
(iii)
• The conducting system, the SA node in the posterior wall of the right atrium, the AV node in the floor of the right atrium, the AV bundle and Purkinje fibres, initiates and coordinates the heartbeat; damage to a coronary artery supplying these nodes can disturb heart rhythm.
• Cardiac afferent fibres carrying pain from ischaemic myocardium travel via sympathetic afferents in the cardiac plexus to spinal cord segments T1-T5 shared with dermatomes of the chest wall and upper limb, so the central nervous system perceives cardiac pain as coming from the body wall.
• This explains why myocardial ischaemia is felt as pain in the mid or left chest that radiates to the left jaw and left arm, a distant somatic sensation produced by a cardiac (visceral) problem.
questions.question:
(i) Describe the gross anatomy of the heart under the headings: chambers, borders and surfaces.
(ii) Relate the chambers/valves of the heart to a recognised pathology.

Describe the gross anatomy of the proximal carpal row/wrist region:
A(i) Bones forming the proximal row and their articulation with the radius
A(ii) The scaphoid's distinguishing feature
B. State how the scaphoid and lunate each relate to common wrist pathologies.
C. Explain how pathology at the lunate spreads to affect a distant structure, causing a functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The wrist (radiocarpal) joint is formed distally by the proximal row of carpal bones — the scaphoid, lunate and triquetrum, excluding the pisiform — and proximally by the distal end of the radius and the articular disk; the ulna is not part of the wrist joint, being prevented from articulating with the carpal bones by this fibrocartilaginous articular disk, and instead articulates with the radius at the distal radioulnar joint.
A(ii)
The scaphoid has a unique blood supply that runs from distal to proximal, unlike most bones.
B
• The scaphoid is the carpal bone most commonly fractured, more so in the younger population, typically from a blow to the wrist such as falling on an outstretched hand, when it takes most of the force.
• Because of its distal-to-proximal blood supply, a scaphoid fracture can disrupt supply to the proximal fragment; this is considered an emergency, and failure to revascularise can lead to avascular necrosis and future arthritis.
• The lunate is prone to anterior dislocation, which is uncommon but can occur by falling on a dorsiflexed wrist, forcing the lunate anteriorly.
• The lunate can also undergo avascular necrosis, so it too requires immediate clinical attention when injured.
C
• Anterior dislocation of the lunate compresses the carpal tunnel, since the lunate lies immediately related to the floor of this tunnel region.
• This compression of the carpal tunnel affects the median nerve, which lies within it.
• The resulting clinical picture manifests as paraesthesia in the sensory distribution of the median nerve.
• There is also weakness of the thenar muscles, which are supplied by the median nerve's recurrent branch.
• This produces the symptoms of carpal tunnel syndrome, even though the primary pathology (lunate dislocation) is a distinct injury from the usual causes of carpal tunnel syndrome.
• This illustrates how a purely skeletal injury at the wrist can spread to compromise an adjacent soft-tissue structure, producing a functional/sensorimotor deficit in the hand.

A(i)
The tibia is the large weight-bearing medial bone of the leg; it articulates with femoral condyles superiorly and the head of fibula laterally. It has an expanded upper end, a shaft, and a smaller lower end. Upper end (see A(ii)). Shaft: triangular in cross-section; 3 borders and 3 surfaces (borders and surfaces are named by opposites); anterior border forms the shin; soleal line on the posterior surface is for soleus. Lower end: expanded; saddle-shaped articular surface for talus; prolonged downwards medially to form the medial malleolus; the medial surface is subcutaneous from the medial malleolus to the medial condyle above.
A(ii)
The upper end has tibial plateaus (lateral and medial condyles); the lateral and medial menisci; anterior and posterior intercondylar areas separate the tibial plateaus; the intercondylar eminence; an articular facet for the head of fibula; and a groove on the medial condyle for semimembranosus. The anterior intercondylar area of the tibia is where the ACL attaches (just posterior to attachment of medial meniscus); the posterior intercondylar area is where the PCL attaches.
B(i)
The nutrient artery (medullary artery) is the main artery of the diaphysis. It is directed obliquely away from the epiphyseal end. When there is an epiphysis at both ends (tibia is one of the 5 bones unique in having epiphyseal plates at both ends — viz: femur, tibia, fibula, humerus, and radius), the nutrient canal is directed away from the more actively growing end. Hughes: 'to the elbow I go, from the knee I flee'. Fracture of the middle third of the tibia lies in a 'watershed' zone between the nutrient artery (supplying the upper 2/3) and the periosteal vessels (supplying the lower 1/3), making this zone most susceptible to avascular non-union.
B(ii)
Proximal tibia: tibial plateau fractures (high-energy trauma), associated with meniscal and ligamentous tears. Mid-shaft tibia: most common site of delayed or non-union, stress fractures (runners), and compartment syndrome (anterior compartment syndrome). Distal tibia (ankle): Pott's fracture involving the malleolus; ankle sprains; avulsion fractures.
C(i)
Tibia: large weight-bearing medial bone; articulates with femoral condyles, fibula head, and talus; contributes the roof (inferior surface of tibia) and the medial malleolus (wall) of the ankle mortise; the medial surface is subcutaneous. Fibula: not a weight-bearing bone; does not articulate with the femur or patella at the knee (only serves as attachment for knee joint structures); contributes the lateral malleolus (wall of ankle mortise) from fibula. At the ankle: lateral malleolar wall is from fibula and medial malleolar wall is from tibia.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
• The thoracoabdominal nerves are the abdominal portions of the anterior rami of T7 to T12 (T7 to T11 thoracoabdominal, T12 subcostal); their distal portions lie in the rectus sheath.
• External oblique: T7 to T11 and T12; internal oblique and transversus abdominis: T7 to T11, T12 and branches of the lumbar plexus; rectus abdominis: T7 to T11; pyramidalis: subcostal T12.
A(ii)
• The lumbar plexus (ventral rami L1 to L4, formed within psoas major) innervates part of the lower abdominal wall.
• The iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves (L1) emerge from the lateral border of psoas major.
A(iii)
• The umbilicus is the segmental landmark with dermatome T10, the same root that innervates the appendix, so appendicular referred pain is felt there.
• The segmental innervation applies to both the anterior abdominal skin and musculature.
B(i)
• The TAP block is a peripheral nerve block that anaesthetises the nerves of the abdominal wall.
• It is performed by injecting anaesthetic into the fascial plane between transversus abdominis and internal oblique muscles.
C(i)
• The ilioinguinal, iliohypogastric and inferior thoracic nerves are spread across the abdominal wall and so are prone to injury.
• Their injury results in muscle weakness of the abdominal wall.
• In entrapment (ACNES) the Carnett sign is positive at the lateral border of the rectus abdominis, with altered skin sensation.

A(i)
It has cervical, thoracic and abdominal parts and is not a straight structure: it lies to the left in the neck, returns to the midline at the thoracic inlet, lies to the left in the superior mediastinum, returns to the midline in the posterior mediastinum and deviates to the left as it pierces the diaphragm at T10.
A(ii)
Cervical part lies in front of the prevertebral fascia, behind the trachea; the thoracic part is crossed on the right by the azygos vein and on the left by the aorta; in the posterior mediastinum it lies behind the left main bronchus and left pulmonary artery and in front of the thoracic duct; it is the most posterior tube of the superior mediastinum and the most anterior structure of the posterior mediastinum, with the vagus nerves around it, the azygos vein behind and to the right and the descending aorta behind and to the left.
A(iii)
Four constrictions: at its origin (C6), 15 cm from the incisor teeth; where the arch of the aorta lies in front of it, 22 cm; where the left main bronchus lies in front of it (tracheal bifurcation), 27 cm; at the diaphragm (T10), 38-40 cm.
A(iv)
• Arteries: inferior thyroid artery, oesophageal branches of the descending thoracic aorta, and the left gastric artery.
• Veins: upper part to the brachiocephalic vein, middle part to the azygos vein, lower part to the portal vein.
• Lymphatics: upper part to deep cervical nodes, middle part to tracheobronchial nodes, lower part to preaortic nodes.
• Nerves: upper third is striated, supplied by the recurrent laryngeal branch of the vagus, with sympathetics from the middle cervical ganglion; lower two-thirds is smooth, receiving sympathetics from the sympathetic trunk and greater splanchnic nerve, and parasympathetic secretomotor fibres from the vagus to the oesophageal glands.
B(i)
• Upper part: inferior thyroid artery, brachiocephalic vein, deep cervical nodes, striated muscle with recurrent laryngeal supply, related to the trachea and prevertebral fascia in the neck.
• Middle and lower parts: middle drains to the azygos vein and tracheobronchial nodes and is crossed by the azygos vein, arch of the aorta and left main bronchus; lower part has aortic and left gastric arteries, portal venous drainage, preaortic nodes and smooth muscle, and passes through the diaphragm at T10.
C(i)
• Venous routes: upper part to the brachiocephalic vein, middle part to the azygos vein (which empties into the SVC and forms a communication between the SVC and IVC), lower part to the portal vein.
• Lymphatic routes: upper part to deep cervical nodes, middle part to tracheobronchial nodes, lower part to preaortic nodes.

A(ii) Describe its relations.

A(i) Describe the histological features of the four stomach regions — cardia, fundus, body, and pylorus — under the headings: surface epithelium, gland type, gastric pit length, and principal secretion.
A(ii) Explain the complete structure and function of the gastric glands of the fundus/body, including the isthmus, neck, and base, and what cells are found in each part.
B(i) Explain the full role of mucous neck cells in the gastric gland, comparing their secretion to that of surface mucous cells.
B(ii) Describe where intrinsic factor is produced, what it is chemically, what it does, and how its deficiency leads to anaemia.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Four stomach regions:
• Cardia and pylorus are histologically similar: tubular glands with long pits usually branching into coiled secretory portions (cardiac and pyloric glands respectively); pits are longer in the pylorus; lack both parietal and chief cells; major secretion is abundant mucus.
• Fundus and body are histologically identical: simple columnar epithelium invaginates to form gastric pits leading into long, branched, tubular gastric glands; 3 to 7 glands usually open into the bottom of each gastric pit; contain all four secretory cell types; involved in secretion of acidic gastric juice.
A(ii)
Structure of fundic/body glands:
• Each gland has three named parts: isthmus, neck, and base.
• Isthmus: the region of stem cells (between the gastric pit and gland); the pluripotent stem cells divide asymmetrically and can move upward or downward to replace epithelial cells.
• Neck: contains mucous neck cells (MNCs) in clusters or singly; also contains parietal cells.
• Base: predominantly chief (zymogen) cells; also contains enteroendocrine cells.
B(i)
Mucous neck cells (MNCs):
• Present in clusters or singly in the necks of gastric glands.
• Less columnar than surface mucous cells; irregular in shape with round nucleus and apical secretory granules.
• Their mucous secretion is less alkaline than that of the surface epithelial mucous cells; they secrete acidic fluid containing mucin (not mucus, which implies alkaline content).
B(ii)
Intrinsic factor:
• Produced by: parietal (oxyntic) cells.
• Chemical nature: a glycoprotein.
• Function: required for the uptake of vitamin B12 in the small intestine.
• Deficiency and anaemia: if parietal cells are damaged, insufficient quantities of intrinsic factor are secreted; without adequate intrinsic factor, vitamin B12 is not absorbed adequately; low levels of vitamin B12 reduce the proliferation of erythroblasts, resulting in pernicious anaemia.

A(i)
A thin, double-layered serous membrane that envelops each lung and lines the thoracic cavity, made of visceral and parietal layers with the intervening pleural cavity; the two pleural cavities are totally separate.
A(ii)
Thicker outer layer lining the thoracic wall, mediastinum, diaphragm and neck, and can be stripped; 4 parts: costal (ribs, costal cartilages, intercostal spaces, sides of vertebral bodies, back of sternum, separated from them by endothoracic fascia), diaphragmatic, mediastinal (encloses the hilum structures, continuous with visceral pleura at the hilum, and below the hilum forms the pulmonary ligament) and cervical (cupola, 2.5-4 cm above the medial third of the clavicle, attached to the suprapleural membrane).
A(iii)
Visceral pleura: closely adherent to the lung including its fissures, cannot be stripped, smooth and slippery, continuous with the parietal pleura at the hilum; the pleural cavity is a potential space with a small amount of lubricating pleural fluid that reduces friction and helps prevent lung collapse.
A(iv)
Sternal (costal to mediastinal anteriorly): from behind the sternoclavicular joints to the midline at the 2nd costal cartilage, then the right edge passes vertically to the 6th costal cartilage while the left arches laterally at the 4th costal cartilage (because of the heart) to the 6th. Costal (costal to diaphragmatic): crosses the 8th rib in the midclavicular line, the 10th rib in the midaxillary line and the 12th rib at the lateral border of erector spinae. Vertebral: rounded reflections in the paravertebral planes from T1 to T12.
A(v)
Recesses are spaces not occupied by lung that lung enters only on forced deep respiration: costodiaphragmatic (between costal and diaphragmatic pleura, shallow in inspiration and deeper in expiration) and costomediastinal (behind the sternum where costal pleura becomes mediastinal pleura, more conspicuous on the left near the heart).
A(vi)
• Blood supply: visceral pleura from bronchial and pulmonary arteries, veins to the pulmonary vein; parietal pleura from the vessels of the structures covered - cervical and costal from intercostal vessels, diaphragmatic outer part from intercostal and inner part from pericardiophrenic vessels, mediastinal from pericardiophrenic vessels.
• Nerve supply: costal pleura by intercostal nerves; diaphragmatic pleura by phrenic nerves centrally and intercostal nerves peripherally; mediastinal pleura by the phrenic nerve; the visceral pleura is described as having no nerve supply and as receiving vasomotor supply from autonomic nerves (pulmonary plexuses).
• Lymph: visceral to the pulmonary plexus in interlobar and peribronchial spaces; parietal costal, mediastinal and cervical to the internal thoracic (anterior) and intercostal (posterior) chains; diaphragmatic to retrosternal, mediastinal and sometimes coeliac nodes.
B(i)
The cervical pleura reaches about 1 inch (2.5 cm) above the clavicle because of the oblique slope of the first rib, so it can be wounded (pneumothorax) by a stab wound, a surgeon's knife or an anaesthetist's needle above the clavicle; the lower edge descends just below the 12th rib medially (below the 11th if the 12th is short), so it may be opened in a loin incision.
B(ii)
The costodiaphragmatic recess is the larger recess and the clinically more important one, providing the space where fluid collects in disease (pneumothorax with air, haemothorax with blood, empyema with pus, effusion); fluid is drained with a needle just above a rib, or through the space between the 7th costal cartilage and the xiphoid process.
C(i)
• Parietal: thicker, outer, lines wall, diaphragm, mediastinum and neck, named regionally, can be stripped, supplied by intercostal and phrenic nerves (so pleural irritation refers pain along the thoracic and anterior abdominal wall, and to the shoulder from the central diaphragm).
• Visceral: inner layer closely adherent to the lung surface and fissures, cannot be stripped, smooth and slippery so the lung moves freely, supplied by bronchial and pulmonary vessels; pleurisy is inflammation of the pleura, usually with pneumonia or other lung infection.

Describe the axillary artery:
A(i) Origin, extent and continuation
A(ii) Division into three parts by pectoralis minor
A(iii) Branches of each part
B. State the safe site associated with clinical control of bleeding from the axillary artery.
C. Explain the anatomical basis for the scapular anastomosis providing a collateral circulation if the artery is occluded.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The axillary artery is a continuation of the subclavian artery; it begins at the lateral border of the first rib and ends at the lower border of teres major, continuing thereafter as the brachial artery. It is closely related to the cords of the brachial plexus and is enclosed with them in the axillary sheath.
A(ii)
Pectoralis minor divides the axillary artery into three parts: the first part extends from the lateral border of the first rib to the upper border of pectoralis minor; the second part lies behind pectoralis minor; the third part extends from the lower border of pectoralis minor to the lower border of teres major.
A(iii)
The first part gives one branch, the superior (highest) thoracic artery; the second part gives two branches, the thoracoacromial and lateral thoracic arteries; the third part gives three branches, the subscapular artery and the anterior and posterior circumflex humeral arteries.
B
• The inferior part of the axillary artery can be palpated in the inferior part of the lateral wall of the axilla.
• This part can be compressed against the humerus to control profuse bleeding.
C
• The scapular anastomosis is a system of arteries connecting the subclavian artery and the corresponding axillary artery, forming an anastomosis around the scapula, occurring in the subscapular, supraspinatus and infraspinatus fossae.
• It is formed by the suprascapular artery (a branch of the thyrocervical trunk from the subclavian artery), the deep branch of the transverse cervical artery (another branch of the thyrocervical trunk), and the circumflex scapular artery (a branch of the subscapular artery arising from the third part of the axillary artery).
• These vessels anastomose the first part of the subclavian artery with the third part of the axillary artery, allowing blood to flow past the shoulder joint regardless of the position of the arm.
• A further anastomosis occurs over the acromion process, formed by the acromial branch of the thoracoacromial artery, the acromial branch of the suprascapular artery, and the acromial branch of the posterior circumflex humeral artery, linking the subclavian with the second and third parts of the axillary artery.
• The arterial anastomoses around the scapula thus provide a collateral circulation through which blood can continue to flow to the limb when the distal part of the subclavian artery or the proximal part of the axillary artery is blocked or occluded.
• This collateral circulation is clinically important because it allows blood to continue circulating to the upper limb even if the main line of supply is obstructed.
• This anatomical arrangement explains why proximal occlusion of the axillary or subclavian artery does not necessarily result in complete loss of blood supply to the limb.

A(i)
The deep cervical fascia consists of areolar tissue that supports the muscles, vessels and viscera of the neck; it is condensed to form well-defined fibrous sheets, labelled as: (1) the investing layer (superficial), (2) the pretracheal fascia, (3) the prevertebral fascia, (4) the carotid sheath, and (5) the axillary fascia. More generally, deep fascia is the membranous investment of structures deep to the superficial fascia, containing cells (fibroblasts), fibres (collagen, elastic) and matrix; being subjected to tensile strains, the collagen forms parallel fibre bundles, with the cells flattened. Deep fascia is best marked in the limbs and neck, where it is wrapped around the muscles, veins and nerves like a bandage, the fibres being mainly circularly arranged; around the thorax and abdomen, which require to expand and contract, there is merely a film of areolar tissue but no true deep fascia.
A(ii)
The pretracheal fascia is found only in the anterior region; superiorly it is attached to the thyroid and cricoid cartilage, and inferiorly it extends into the thorax to blend with the fibrous pericardium; laterally it blends with the carotid sheath and with the investing layer of the deep cervical fascia beneath sternocleidomastoid. The prevertebral fascia is attached superiorly to the base of the skull, and inferiorly enters the thorax and blends with the anterior longitudinal ligament of the vertebral column; it covers the prevertebral muscles (longus capitis and longus cervicis), passes round the neck, attaches to the ligamentum nuchae, and in the posterior triangle forms the fascial floor, covering the muscles scalenus anterior, scalenus medius, scalenus posterior, levator scapulae and splenius capitis.
B
Penetration of the fascia during instrumentation of the pretracheal fascia can lead to collection of infectious substances (pus) in the retropharyngeal space (the space between the pharynx and the prevertebral fascia); whiplash injury of the neck can cause quadriplegia, stabbing injury of the neck can cause vascular/nervous injury, and a tumour blocking the airway may necessitate insertion of a tracheostomy tube. The deep cervical fascia will necessarily be pierced during tracheostomy.
C
The pretracheal fascia surrounds the thyroid gland completely, forming a sheath for it, binds the thyroid gland to the larynx, encloses the parathyroid gland, invests the infrahyoid muscles, and encloses the visceral components of the neck (larynx and trachea, pharynx and oesophagus, and the thyroid and parathyroid glands). The prevertebral fascia, in contrast, surrounds the vertebral column and its associated muscles, extending from the base of the skull to approximately the T3 vertebra, and extends laterally as the axillary sheaths.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Fixation: to achieve a permanent section, tissues must be fixed to preserve the structure and molecular composition; fixation prevents autolysis (self-digestion by enzymes present in the cells) and destruction by bacteria. Dehydration and clearing: tissues are progressed in graded steps to 100% alcohol to remove water; after the solvent replaces the alcohol, the tissue becomes transparent in xylene (clearing). Embedding: once the tissue is impregnated with the solvent, it is placed in a hard medium (e.g., wax); heat causes the solvent to evaporate, and the spaces within the tissue are filled by the embedding medium. Sectioning: tissues are sectioned by the microtome's steel or glass blade; this method allows stained sections to be prepared rapidly for study of specimens. Mounting: sections are mounted on a supportive structure (e.g., slide) that can be placed on a microscope stage. Staining: stains are applied to differentiate tissue components.
A(ii)
The most commonly used stains are hematoxylin and eosin (H & E). Hematoxylin stains basic (acidic) structures — the most acidic components are DNA and RNA; therefore, the nucleus and cytoplasmic RNA stain blue/purple (basophilic). Eosin stains acidophilic (basic) structures — many cytoplasmic constituents stain pinkish (eosinophilic/acidophilic). Reason: differential staining is based on the acid-base chemistry of cell components; acidic cell components bind basic dyes (hematoxylin) and basic components bind acidic dyes (eosin).
B(i)
Light microscopy: the standard technique; produces images of tissue sections examined by transmitted light; maximum resolving power is 0.2 micrometers (two marks 0.2 micrometers apart can be seen as two distinct entities). Types include brightfield, phase contrast, differential interference contrast (DIC), fluorescence, and confocal. Preferred for: routine tissue examination, diagnosis of pathology, overview of cell and tissue structure. Electron microscopy: has extended the detail at which subcellular structures can be studied; reveals ultrastructural details such as organelles, myelin sheaths, and synapse morphology. Preferred for: study of subcellular structures, ultrastructural detail, and molecular architecture of cell membranes.
