A(i) Describe the parotid gland under the following headings: location, external features, and capsule.
A(ii) Describe the parotid duct, and list the structures within the substance of the gland from superficial to deep, and the other structures found within the gland.
B. Explain the clinical basis for why the parotid gland is particularly vulnerable to nerve injury during surgery, and describe the syndrome that can follow such injury.
C. Distinguish between the parotid gland and the submandibular gland in terms of their ducts and ganglia associated with their secretomotor supply.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The parotid gland is the largest salivary gland (para = around, otic = ear); it is situated below the external acoustic meatus, in front of the sternomastoid, and also projects forward onto the surface of masseter. It is pyramidal in shape with the apex pointing downward, has 4 surfaces (superior/base, lateral/superficial, anteromedial, posteromedial) separated by 3 borders (anterior, posterior, medial), and has 1 main lobe and 1 accessory lobe (a small detached part called the accessory parotid gland or Socia Parotidis, lying on masseter between the zygomatic arch and the parotid duct). The capsule has a false capsule, formed by the investing layer of deep cervical fascia, and a true capsule, formed by condensation of the stroma.
A(ii)
The parotid duct is about 5 cm long, arises from the anterior border of the gland, runs on masseter, and at the anterior border of masseter runs medially to pierce buccinator and the mucosa, opening into the vestibule of the mouth opposite the crown of the upper 2nd molar tooth; its surface anatomy corresponds to the middle third of a line from the lower border of the tragus to a point midway between the nasal ala and the upper labial margin. From superficial to deep within the substance of the gland are: the facial nerve and its branches; the retromandibular vein and its two divisions (maxillary vein, superficial temporal vein); and the external carotid artery and its two terminal branches. Other structures within the gland are the auriculotemporal nerve, the posterior auricular artery, and the preauricular lymph nodes.
B
Within the gland, the facial nerve radiates like a goose's foot (Pes Anserinus) through the anterior border of the gland into its branches (temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular, cervical); because the facial nerve runs through the substance of the gland, it is at risk during parotid surgery or trauma. Frey's syndrome (also known as gustatory sweating or auriculo-temporal nerve syndrome) commonly occurs after parotid surgery or trauma, from injury of the auriculotemporal and great auricular nerves; during healing, secretomotor fibres of the auriculotemporal nerve join with the great auricular nerve and reach the sweat glands of facial skin, so that sweating, warmth and redness of the face occur as a result of salivary stimulation by the smell or taste of food.
C
The parotid gland's secretomotor (parasympathetic) supply is via the auriculotemporal nerve, producing a watery secretion, with sympathetic supply producing a mucous-rich, sticky secretion derived from the plexus around the external carotid artery. In contrast, the submandibular gland's duct is the submandibular duct (Wharton's duct), and its nerve supply is via branches from the submandibular ganglion, through which it receives parasympathetic fibres from the chorda tympani, sensory fibres from the lingual branch of the mandibular nerve, and sympathetic fibres from the plexus on the facial artery.

A(i)
A fibroserous sac that encloses the heart and the roots of the great vessels; it lies behind the body of the sternum and the 2nd-6th costal cartilages and in front of the T5-T8 vertebrae; it is attached to the central tendon of the diaphragm (pericardiophrenic ligament).
A(ii)
The outer fibrous tissue layer, enclosing the heart and the roots of the great vessels (the IVC excepted, as stated); its base is attached to the central tendon of the diaphragm.
A(iii)
Thin, elastic tissue lining the fibrous pericardium, made of a parietal layer (lines and fuses with the fibrous pericardium) and a visceral layer (forms the epicardium of the heart and encloses the aorta and pulmonary trunk); between them lies the pericardial cavity containing pericardial fluid.
A(iv)
Transverse sinus: formed by a tear in the dorsal mesocardium; lies behind the aorta and pulmonary trunk, in front of the SVC on the right and the left atrium on the left.
A(v)
Oblique sinus: a blind sac (cul-de-sac) formed as a result of the entrance of the 4 pulmonary veins and the IVC into the heart; lies behind the 2 left pulmonary veins and in front of the 2 right pulmonary veins and the IVC.
A(vi)
• Blood supply: fibrous pericardium from the pericardiophrenic and musculophrenic arteries; serous pericardium from the coronary arteries; veins drain to the azygos system, and the pericardiophrenic vein drains to the internal thoracic vein.
• Nerve supply: the fibrous and parietal pericardium by the phrenic nerve; the visceral pericardium by autonomic nerves.
B(i)
• Draining of pericardial fluid is done between the 7th costal cartilage and the xiphoid process.
• In pulmonary embolectomy a temporary ligature is passed through the transverse sinus to occlude the aorta and pulmonary trunk; the oblique sinus allows for pulsation of the left atrium.
B(ii)
Pain from irritation of the pleura or pericardium covering the central part of the diaphragm may be referred to the shoulder, because the phrenic nerve (C3,4,5) supplies the central diaphragm and the pericardium, and the supraclavicular nerve (C3,4) supplies the shoulder skin; pericarditis may also cause hiccup.
C(i)
• The transverse sinus is a passage formed by a tear in the dorsal mesocardium, lying behind the great arteries and used for the ligature; the oblique sinus is a blind sac formed by the entry of the pulmonary veins and IVC, allowing pulsation of the left atrium.
• The fibrous pericardium is the outer fibrous layer with phrenic nerve and pericardiophrenic/musculophrenic arterial supply; the serous pericardium is thin and elastic, with a parietal layer fused to the fibrous layer and a visceral layer forming the epicardium, supplied by coronary arteries and autonomic nerves.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
The most common sites of ulnar nerve entrapment around the elbow are: above the elbow, in the region of the intermuscular septum; the medial epicondylar region; the epicondylar (ulnar) groove; the region of the cubital tunnel; and the point where the nerve exits from flexor carpi ulnaris, where the usual cause of compression is the deep flexor-pronator aponeurosis.
A(ii)
Medially, in relation to the elbow joint, the ulnar nerve passes behind the medial epicondyle and crosses the medial collateral ligament of the joint.
B
• The medial epicondyle of the humerus bears a groove on its posterior aspect specifically for the ulnar nerve, and the medial epicondyle is the larger of the two epicondyles, extending more distally.
• This places the ulnar nerve in a relatively superficial, subcutaneous position as it passes behind the medial epicondyle and through the cubital tunnel region, making it vulnerable to direct trauma and to compression at each of the sites listed above.
• Ulnar nerve injuries are recognised as a distinct item of applied anatomy at the elbow, alongside subluxation/dislocation of the radial head, the carrying angle, olecranon bursitis, avulsion of the medial epicondyle, and dislocation with Volkmann's ischaemic contracture.
C
• The ulnar nerve's entrapment region at the elbow lies behind the medial epicondyle of the humerus, where it crosses the medial collateral ligament of the elbow joint, and where compression is often caused by the deep flexor-pronator aponeurosis as the nerve exits between the heads of flexor carpi ulnaris.
• The median nerve's tunnel at the wrist, the carpal tunnel, differs in that it has a defined bony floor — the carpal sulcus, bounded laterally by the scaphoid and trapezium and medially by the hook of hamate and pisiform — roofed by the fibrous flexor retinaculum.
• The carpal tunnel additionally transmits eight flexor tendons and the tendon of flexor pollicis longus alongside the median nerve, whereas other tendons sharing the ulnar nerve's entrapment site at the elbow are not described.
• Both regions, however, are sites where a single major nerve is placed in a confined space adjacent to bone, predisposing it to compression.
• At the elbow, injury or entrapment of the ulnar nerve is associated with claw hand and sensory/motor deficits in the ulnar nerve distribution of the hand and forearm.
• At the wrist, compression of the median nerve within the carpal tunnel produces carpal tunnel syndrome, with sensory disturbance in the lateral three and a half digits and weakness of the thenar muscles.
• The comparison illustrates a shared anatomical principle, nerve entrapment at a narrow passage, applied to two different nerves at two different levels of the upper limb.

A(i) Describe the cell cycle under the following headings: definition, phases (G1, S, G2, M), and the two key regulatory molecules that control progression through the cycle.
A(ii) Explain the clinical consequences of errors in mitosis, naming three chromosomal abnormalities that can result.
B(i) Distinguish between apoptosis and necrosis, giving the distinguishing morphological changes and clinical consequences of each.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Definition: The cell cycle, or cell-division cycle, is the series of events that takes place in a cell leading to its division and duplication (replication). In cells with a nucleus (eukaryotes), the cell cycle can be divided into two brief periods: interphase (during which the cell grows, accumulates nutrients needed for mitosis and duplicates its DNA) and the mitosis (M) phase (during which the cell splits itself into two distinct cells, often called daughter cells). Phases: G1 (Gap 1) — cell grows; S phase (synthesis) — chromosomes are replicated; G2 (Gap 2) — cell grows more and prepares for mitosis; M phase (mitosis and cytokinesis) — cell division. Cells that have temporarily or reversibly stopped dividing are said to have entered the G0 phase (quiescence). Two key regulatory molecules: cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs), which determine a cell's progress through the cell cycle.
A(ii)
In non-disjunction, a chromosome may fail to separate during anaphase: one daughter cell will receive both sister chromosomes (leading to trisomy — three copies) and the other will receive none (leading to monosomy — one copy). These cells are considered aneuploid, a condition often associated with cancer. Other chromosomal abnormalities: deletion — an arm of the chromosome may be broken and the fragment lost. Translocation — the fragment incorrectly reattaches to another, non-homologous chromosome. Inversion — the fragment reattaches to the original chromosome in reverse orientation. The effect may range from no noticeable effect to cancer induction or organism death.
B(i)
Apoptosis (programmed cell death): biochemical events lead to characteristic cell changes including blebbing, loss of cell membrane asymmetry and attachment, cell shrinkage, nuclear fragmentation, chromatin condensation, and chromosomal DNA fragmentation. Apoptosis differs from necrosis in that the cellular debris does not damage the organism. Necrosis: a form of traumatic cell death that results from acute cellular injury; cellular debris can damage the organism. Clinical consequences: excessive apoptosis causes atrophy (e.g., ischemic damage); insufficient apoptosis results in uncontrolled cell proliferation such as cancer.

A(i)
A wide tube about 10 cm long and 2 cm wide, lying in the superior mediastinum and extending from C6 (lower border of the cricoid cartilage) to T4, where it divides into the right and left main bronchi; it has cervical and thoracic parts, the cervical part measuring 5 cm.
A(ii)
• The cervical part is in contact posteriorly with the oesophagus and anteriorly with the isthmus of the thyroid gland; it is palpable in the suprasternal notch midway between the heads of the clavicles; it ends at the sternal angle (T4/5) just to the right of the midline (at T6 in the erect position in full inspiration).
• At the bifurcation the azygos vein arches over the right main bronchus (T4) and the left main bronchus lies in front of the oesophagus (27 cm from the incisor teeth); the cardiac plexus lies on the lowest part of the trachea behind the arch of the aorta.
A(iii)
Right main bronchus: 2.5 cm long, shorter, wider and vertically oriented; left main bronchus: 5 cm long, longer, narrower and horizontally oriented.
A(iv)
• Right main bronchus divides into upper (outside the hilum), middle and lower lobar bronchi, giving 10 bronchopulmonary segments; the left divides within the hilum into 2 lobar bronchi, giving 8 segments; segmental (third-order) bronchi supply the segments.
• The U-shaped cartilage bars of the trachea are replaced by irregular plates in smaller bronchi; the smallest bronchi give bronchioles (under 1 mm), then terminal bronchioles and respiratory bronchioles (about 0.5 mm, with outpouchings where gas exchange occurs), then alveolar ducts, alveolar sacs and alveoli surrounded by capillaries.
A(v)
Trachea: lymphatics drain to the deep cervical and paratracheal lymph nodes; the mucous membrane is supplied by the vagus, which also gives the parasympathetic supply. Lung and bronchi: pulmonary plexuses with vagal (bronchoconstrictor, secretomotor) and sympathetic (bronchodilator) fibres.
B(i)
• The wider, more vertical right main bronchus allows foreign particles to enter it easily; asthma (dyspnoea); pneumonia (bacterial or viral infection of the lung); pulmonary embolism (pulmonary artery obstructed by air, blood clot, fat, tumour cells or foreign particles).
• Abscesses are commoner in the posterior segment of the upper lobe and the apical segment of the lower lobe (most dependent supine); septa between segments limit infection but carcinoma and tuberculosis break through; fibrosis reduces compliance and emphysema reduces elasticity.
C(i)
• Lymph from lung and bronchi passes to the bronchopulmonary (hilar) nodes, then to the superior and inferior tracheobronchial nodes (above and below the tracheal bifurcation), then to the right and left bronchomediastinal trunks.
• The trunks usually end at the junction of the subclavian and internal jugular veins; the right trunk may join other trunks to form the right lymphatic duct and the left may end in the thoracic duct.

A(i) Describe the orbit under the following headings: shape, the bones forming it, and its average dimensions.
A(ii) Describe the three openings into the orbital cavity and the structures transmitted through each, and describe the connective tissue planes of the orbit.
B. Explain the clinical basis for why orbital trauma can result in double vision and in a rise of intraocular pressure.
C. Distinguish between the superior orbital fissure and the inferior orbital fissure in terms of the structures each transmits.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The orbit is shaped like a pear or quadrilateral pyramid, with its base in the plane of the orbital rim and its pyramidal cavity base in front and apex behind; it protects, supports and maximises the function of the eye, and seven bones conjoin to form the orbital structure. The average dimensions of the orbit are: height of orbital margin 40 mm, width of orbital margin 35 mm, depth of orbit 40-50 mm, interorbital distance 25 mm, and volume of orbit 30 cm³; 20% of this space is occupied by the eyeball, and about one-sixth of the eye is exposed, the remainder being protected by the walls of the orbit.
A(ii)
The major nerves and vessels to the orbit and globe enter through 3 openings. The superior orbital fissure, bounded by the lesser and greater wings of the sphenoid, transmits cranial nerves III, IV and VI, the lacrimal nerve, frontal nerve, nasociliary nerve, orbital branch of the middle meningeal artery, recurrent branch of the lacrimal artery, superior orbital vein and superior ophthalmic vein. The inferior orbital fissure, bounded by the greater wing of the sphenoid, the maxilla and the palatine bones, transmits the infraorbital nerve, zygomatic nerve, parasympathetics to the lacrimal gland, infraorbital artery, infraorbital vein, and the inferior ophthalmic vein branch to the pterygoid plexus. The optic canal, at the apex of the orbit within the sphenoid bone, transmits the optic nerve, ophthalmic artery, and central retinal vein. The connective tissue boundaries of the orbit are divided into 4 main units: the bulbar (Tenon) fascia, surrounding and protecting the globe and providing a barrier between the globe and retrobulbar fat; multiple connective tissue septa extending from the globe to the periorbita like spokes on a wheel; the individual connective tissue sheath of each extraocular muscle, which fuses to form a confluent muscle sheath and the medial and lateral check ligaments; and the periosteal lining of the orbit, which can be elevated in surgery to expose the bony orbit.
B
Clinical correlates of the orbit include eye trauma with blow-out fracture, due to blunt trauma, which displaces the orbital walls; paralysis of the extraocular muscles results in double vision. Obstruction of the flow of aqueous humor results in a rise in intraocular pressure called glaucoma, leading to degenerative changes in the retina with consequent blindness.
C
The superior orbital fissure transmits cranial nerves III, IV and VI, the lacrimal, frontal and nasociliary nerves, the orbital branch of the middle meningeal artery, the recurrent branch of the lacrimal artery, and the superior orbital and superior ophthalmic veins. The inferior orbital fissure, in contrast, transmits the infraorbital nerve, the zygomatic nerve, parasympathetics to the lacrimal gland, the infraorbital artery and vein, and the inferior ophthalmic vein branch to the pterygoid plexus.

A(i)
The femur is the long bone of the thigh; the longest and strongest bone in the body (Latin: femur = thigh); it accounts for approximately one-quarter of a person's total height and averages 45 cm. It has a shaft (body) and 2 expanded ends. Parts: (1) proximal end — consisting of head, neck, and the trochanters; (2) shaft; (3) distal end — consisting of the femoral condyles. It articulates superiorly with the acetabulum to form the hip joint, and inferiorly with the patella and tibia to form the knee joint.
A(ii)
The neck is the curved upper end of the shaft; it connects the head to the shaft and passes downward, backward, and laterally, obliquely placed to the long axis of the shaft. The angle of inclination (neck–shaft angle) is approximately 135 degrees; reduction of this angle is coxa vara and follows fracture of the neck of femur. The angle of anteversion (torsion) — the forward relationship of head and neck — is normally 12–15 degrees; wide variation in anteversion of the femoral neck means that during total hip arthroplasty, orientation of the femoral neck osteotomy in correct anteversion must be assessed after hip dislocation with reference to the shaft of femur with knee flexed at 90 degrees, or an inaccurate cut and malposition of the prosthesis may result.
B(i)
The fovea capitis on the head of femur transmits blood from the obturator artery via the ligament of the head of femur (ligamentum teres). The main blood supply travels retinacularly along the intracapsular neck from the medial femoral circumflex artery (which wraps around the posterior side of the femur supplying its neck and head). In an intracapsular fracture, these retinacular vessels are disrupted; the obturator artery contribution via ligamentum teres is insufficient to sustain the head, and avascular necrosis results.
B(ii)
The linea aspera is a posterior ridge on the shaft of femur; it diverges superiorly and inferiorly. The inferior divergence ends as the medial supracondylar ridge to the adductor tubercle and the lateral supracondylar ridge. The linea aspera gives origin to many muscles: adductor longus inserts into the middle third of its medial lip; adductor magnus into the gluteal tuberosity, linea aspera, and medial supracondylar line; the vastus lateralis arises from its lateral lip.
C(i)
Pressure epiphyses are formed at joints and bear compressive forces (e.g., head of femur — a pressure epiphysis; femoral condyles). Traction epiphyses are pulled by muscles (e.g., greater trochanter — traction epiphysis for gluteus medius which draws it upward, medially, and backward; lesser trochanter — traction epiphysis for iliopsoas, the great flexor of the hip joint). The nutrient artery is directed obliquely away from the epiphyseal end; when there is an epiphysis at both ends, the nutrient canal is directed away from the more actively growing end (as per Hughes's rule: 'to the elbow I go, from the knee I flee'). Surgically, the nutrient canal direction matters during intramedullary nail insertion, as the nail must not block the nutrient foramen.

questions.answerText:
A(ii)
The aortic hiatus lies posterior to the diaphragm, between the two crura, at the level of the lower border of the T12 vertebra; it transmits the aorta, the thoracic duct and sometimes the azygos and hemiazygos veins. Because the aorta does not pierce the diaphragm itself, movements of the diaphragm during respiration do not affect blood flow through it.
A(iii)
The caval opening lies in the central tendon of the diaphragm at the level of T8; it transmits the inferior vena cava, terminal branches of the right phrenic nerve, and a few hepatic lymphatic vessels. The inferior vena cava is adherent to the margin of this opening, so diaphragmatic contraction during inspiration widens the opening and dilates the inferior vena cava, aiding venous return to the heart.
B
• The right and left crura arise from the bodies of the L1-L3 vertebrae, the anterior longitudinal ligament and the intervertebral discs; the oesophageal hiatus lies within the right crus, to the left of the midline, superior to and to the left of the aortic hiatus. Diaphragmatic hernia (sliding and paraoesophageal types) and diaphragmatic rupture are clinical considerations related to weakness or defects around these openings.
• In most individuals, about 70%, both margins of the oesophageal hiatus are formed by muscular bundles of the right crus; in others the left crus contributes to the right margin, and such variation can affect the sphincter-like action around the oesophagus.
C
• The oesophageal hiatus is a muscular opening in the right crus at the level of T10 that actively constricts around the oesophagus with diaphragmatic contraction, contributing to prevention of reflux.
• The aortic hiatus is a non-muscular, fibrous opening bounded by the crura and the median arcuate ligament at the lower border of T12, so diaphragmatic contraction does not compress or affect flow through the aorta.
• The oesophageal hiatus transmits the oesophagus and vagal trunks, whereas the aortic hiatus transmits the aorta and thoracic duct, reflecting their different anatomical roles.
questions.question:
(A) Describe the three main openings of the diaphragm - A(i) oesophageal hiatus A(ii) aortic hiatus A(iii) caval opening - including their vertebral levels and the structures each transmits.
(B) Explain the clinical basis of diaphragmatic (hiatus) hernia.
(C) Distinguish between the oesophageal hiatus and the aortic hiatus.

(A) Describe the duodenum under the headings: A(i) parts and dimensions A(ii) peritoneal relations A(iii) visceral relations.
(B) Explain the clinical basis for the duodenum's common site of ulceration and for paraduodenal hernia.
(C) Distinguish between the jejunum and the ileum.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The duodenum is the first, shortest (about 25 cm) and widest part of the small intestine; it is C-shaped and mostly retroperitoneal, made up of four parts - superior (5 cm), descending (7.5-8 cm), horizontal (6-10 cm) and ascending (2.5 cm).
A(ii)
The proximal 2.5 cm of the superior part is movable and intraperitoneal, attached to the lesser omentum above and greater omentum below; the rest of the duodenum is retroperitoneal, covered by peritoneum only on its anterior aspect.
A(iii)
The superior part is anteriorly related to the quadrate lobe of the liver and gallbladder, and posteriorly to the gastroduodenal artery, bile duct, portal vein and inferior vena cava; the descending part is related medially to the head of pancreas and bile duct, laterally to the right colic flexure, and rests on the right kidney, ureter, psoas major and renal vessels, and receives the major duodenal papilla; the horizontal part crosses the inferior vena cava, aorta and L3 vertebra and is crossed anteriorly by the superior mesenteric vessels; the ascending part rises to the duodenojejunal flexure.
B
• The proximal (superior) part of the duodenum is the most common site of duodenal ulcer.
• The duodenojejunal flexure is fixed by the suspensory muscle of the duodenum (ligament of Treitz), which passes posterior to the pancreas and splenic vein and anterior to the left renal vein; a weakness near this fixed flexure is the anatomical basis for a paraduodenal hernia.
C
• The jejunum lies mainly in the left upper (infracolic) quadrant, has thicker, more vascular walls and a wider, often empty lumen, with long and few vasa recta, one or two layers of arterial arcades, numerous circular mucosal folds, and large, thick, abundant villi.
• The ileum lies predominantly in the right lower quadrant and pelvis, has thinner, less vascular walls and a narrower, often loaded lumen, with short and numerous vasa recta and multiple layers of arterial arcades.
• The ileum has smaller and sparser circular mucosal folds and shorter, thinner villi than the jejunum, but the terminal ileum has numerous Peyer's patches and more numerous solitary lymphatic follicles, which are absent or scanty in the jejunum.
• The jejunum has mesenteric windows and less abundant mesenteric fat, whereas the ileum has no windows and more abundant mesenteric fat.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the origin, structural components, and classification of neurons under the following headings: cell body (soma), dendrites, axon, myelin sheath, nodes of Ranvier, and neurilemma.
A(ii) State the basis of why local anaesthetics block nerve impulse transmission.
B(i) Explain the anatomical basis of why nerve fibers within the CNS do not regenerate after injury, while peripheral nerve fibers may regenerate.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Cell body (soma): The neuronal cell body is similar to other cell types; it has a nucleus with at least one nucleolus and many typical cytoplasmic organelles. It lacks centrioles, which is consistent with the amitotic nature of neurons. Dendrites: Dendrites are cytoplasmic extensions that project from the cell body; they are usually short and branching, increasing their surface area to receive signals from other neurons. The number of dendrites varies. They are called afferent processes because they transmit impulses to the neuron cell body. Axon: There is only one axon projecting from each cell body; it is usually elongated and carries impulses away from the cell body, so it is called an efferent process. Axons may have infrequent branches called axon collaterals; these terminate in short branches or telodendria, whose distal ends are slightly enlarged to form synaptic bulbs. Myelin sheath: Many axons are surrounded by a segmented, white, fatty substance called myelin or myelin sheath. Myelinated fibers make up the white matter in the CNS, while cell bodies and unmyelinated fibers make the gray matter. Nodes of Ranvier: The unmyelinated regions between myelin segments are called nodes of Ranvier. Neurilemma: In the peripheral nervous system, myelin is produced by Schwann cells. The cytoplasm, nucleus, and outer cell membrane of the Schwann cell form a tight covering around the myelin and around the axon at the nodes of Ranvier — this covering is the neurilemma, which plays an important role in regeneration of nerve fibers.
A(ii)
Most local anesthetics are low-molecular-weight molecules that bind to the voltage-gated sodium channels of the axolemma, interfering with sodium ion influx and, consequently, inhibiting the action potential responsible for the nerve impulse.
B(i)
In the CNS, oligodendrocytes produce myelin, but there is no neurilemma. It is the neurilemma that plays an important role in regeneration of nerve fibers; therefore fibers within the CNS do not regenerate because they lack neurilemma.

A(i)
Skeletal muscle: contains bundles of very long, multinucleated cells with cross-striations; contraction is quick, forceful, and usually under voluntary control. Connective tissue: endomysium surrounds individual muscle fibers (nerve fibers and capillaries form a rich network in the endomysium); perimysium surrounds fascicles; epimysium (deep fascia) surrounds the whole muscle belly and connects to tendons. Distinguishing feature: cross-striations; multinucleated; sarcomeres extending from Z disc to Z disc (~2.5 µm long in resting muscle). The A bands are anisotropic (dark); I bands are isotropic (light); each I band is bisected by the Z disc. Smooth muscle: consists of collections of fusiform cells that lack striations and have slow, involuntary contractions; elongated and spindle-shaped; single nucleus at the widest point; contain actin and myosin filaments but lack sarcomeres. Prominent locations: wall of GI tract, walls of arteries and veins, around glands. Distinguishing feature: no striations; slow, sustained contractions; non-voluntary. Cardiac muscle: cross-striations; composed of elongated, often branched cells; bound by intercalated discs unique to cardiac muscle; contraction is involuntary, vigorous, and rhythmic. Central nuclei; high cytoplasm-to-nucleus ratio. Distinguishing feature: intercalated discs; branching cells; involuntary continuous rhythmic contraction.
A(ii)
Skeletal muscle fibers show cross-striations of alternating light and dark bands. The sarcomere extends from Z disc to Z disc. During contraction, shortening of myofibrils (shortening of sarcomeres) is transmitted through the connective tissue (endomysium, perimysium, epimysium) and via tendons to bone, producing bodily movements.
B(i)
Cardiac muscle cells contain numerous mitochondria; a large proportion of cell volume is occupied by mitochondria. Fatty acids, transported by lipoproteins, are stored as triglycerides in numerous lipid droplets in cardiac muscle cells — this supports the extremely rich capillary network and strong continuous activity. Cardiac muscle has limited regenerative capacity; spaces left after infarction are filled by connective tissue forming dense irregular scar tissue, because cardiac muscle cells do not go through mitosis.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the origin, course, and distribution of the three types of muscle tissue under the following headings: structural features at the light microscope level, connective tissue organization (endomysium, perimysium, epimysium), and characteristic distinguishing feature of each type.
A(ii) State the safe structural basis of how skeletal muscle contraction is transmitted to produce movement.
B(i) Explain the anatomical and histological basis of why cardiac muscle does not fatigue and cannot be replaced after infarction.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
The thenar space lies on the thumb side of the septum that joins the border of the palmar aponeurosis to the palmar border of the third metacarpal bone; it contains the first lumbrical muscle and is overlaid by the flexor tendons to the index finger.
A(ii)
The compartments and fascial spaces of the hand include the dorsal spaces, hypothenar space, midpalmar space, thenar space, web spaces and pulp spaces, all bounded by connective tissue.
A(iii)
The space of Parona extends from the proximal margin of the carpal tunnel to the mid-forearm; its roof is formed distally by the flexor digitorum profundus tendons and proximally by the belly of flexor digitorum superficialis (whose origin forms the proximal boundary), it is limited medially by flexor carpi ulnaris and laterally by flexor pollicis longus, and its floor is formed by pronator quadratus distally and the interosseous membrane in its proximal two-thirds.
B
• These fascial spaces allow mobility of the hand structures but, being bounded by connective tissue, offer little resistance to the spread of infection.
• Infection within the thenar space can readily break into the connective tissue canals surrounding the ulnar three lumbricals.
• For practical purposes the thenar space may therefore be considered continuous distally with these lumbrical canals, and thus distally communicates with the web spaces.
• The thenar space also communicates proximally with the space of Parona.
• Infection of these deep spaces, including the space of Parona, can be difficult to diagnose.
C
• The thenar space lies on the thumb (radial) side of the septum joining the palmar aponeurosis to the third metacarpal, contains the first lumbrical, and is overlaid by the flexor tendons of the index finger.
• The midpalmar space, by contrast, lies on the ulnar side of this septum, related to the tendons for the middle, ring and little fingers and to adductor pollicis, separated from the thenar space by the lateral palmar septum.
• The thenar space communicates proximally with the space of Parona and distally with the lumbrical canals/web spaces, reflecting its position along the flexor tendon of the index finger.
• This anatomical separation by the lateral palmar septum explains why infection in one compartment tends initially to remain localised to that space before spreading along its own specific communicating pathway.

A(iii) Space of Parona

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Skeletal muscle — longitudinal section: cross-striations of alternating dark (A bands, anisotropic) and light (I bands, isotropic) bands; each I band bisected by a dark transverse Z disc; multinucleated fibers at periphery. Cross-section: peripheral nuclei; high cytoplasm-to-nucleus ratio. Smooth muscle — longitudinal section: meshwork appearance; no striations; elongated spindle-shaped cells; elongated and central nuclei. Cross-section: central nuclei; low cytoplasm-to-nucleus ratio. Cardiac muscle — longitudinal section: striations; branching cells; intercalated discs. Cross-section: central nuclei; high cytoplasm-to-nucleus ratio.
A(ii)
Skeletal muscle: troponin subunits (troponin I and troponin T) are integral to muscle contraction; mutations in cardiac troponin subunits can result in cardiomyopathies. Smooth muscle: smooth muscle cells are able to undergo cell division (unlike cardiac and skeletal muscle). Cardiac muscle: atrial myocytes secrete atrial natriuretic peptide; kidneys respond to this to cause sodium and water loss (natriuresis and diuresis); when natriuretic peptide levels fall, kidneys result in sodium and water conservation.
B(i)
Cardiac muscle cells act as a syncytium through gap junctions in intercalated discs, which provide ionic continuity between adjacent cells, allowing the signal to contract to pass throughout the organ. The blood supply to the heart is through three main coronary arteries prone to atheroma. Acute coronary arterial occlusion involving nearly the entire area at risk causes necrosis of the myocardium. Because the cardiac muscle acts as a syncytium and is continuously active, obstruction of coronary blood flow rapidly leads to widespread ischemia and necrosis of the myocardium.
questions.question:

A(ii) Relate the structural differences of each muscle type to their specific pathological conditions.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
The brachial artery provides the main arterial supply to the arm and is the continuation of the axillary artery; it begins at the inferior border of teres major and ends in the cubital fossa opposite the neck of the radius.
A(ii)
Under cover of the bicipital aponeurosis, it divides into the radial and ulnar arteries.
A(iii)
Its branches include the deep brachial (profunda brachii) artery, which accompanies the radial nerve, the superior ulnar collateral artery, which accompanies the ulnar nerve, and the inferior ulnar collateral artery.
B
During blood pressure measurement, the stethoscope is placed over the brachial artery in the cubital fossa, and the cubital fossa is the site used to palpate the brachial pulse.
C
• Volkmann's ischaemic contracture is a deformity of the hand, fingers and wrist caused by injury to the muscles of the forearm.
• The classical presentation is a supracondylar fracture of the humerus, although fracture of the arm or elbow may also result in this deformity; the artery involved is the brachial artery.
• The contracture occurs when there is a lack of blood flow (ischaemia) to the forearm, usually from increased pressure resulting from swelling (compartment syndrome).
• Because there is very little room within each fascial compartment of the arm and forearm, haemorrhage or oedema following injury to the brachial artery can cause secondary vascular compression: veins are affected first, and later the arteries, resulting in ischaemia of the affected part.
• The classical presentation of the resulting acute compartment syndrome is remembered by "the five P's": pulselessness, paraesthesia, poikilothermia, paralysis and pallor.
• There are three levels of severity of the resulting Volkmann's contracture: the mildest involves flexion contracture of only two or three fingers with no or limited loss of sensation; a more severe form involves all fingers flexed with the thumb stuck in the palm and some sensory loss.
• The most severe form involves all the muscles in the forearm that flex and extend the wrist and fingers, producing a severely disabling condition.
• This progression illustrates how injury to the brachial artery at the elbow can produce a graded functional deficit distally in the hand and fingers.

Describe the brachial artery:
A(i) Origin and termination
A(ii) Course

A. Describe the course, relations and branches of the facial nerve within the parotid gland, and its termination pattern.
B. State the structures/procedures for which knowledge of the facial nerve's branching is clinically important.
C. Explain the anatomical/functional basis of the deformity that results when this nerve is injured.
questions.answerText:
A
Within the substance of the parotid gland, from superficial to deep are found the facial nerve and its branches, the retromandibular vein and its two divisions, and the external carotid artery and its two terminal branches. The facial nerve radiates through the anterior border of the gland like a goose's foot, termed the Pes Anserinus, giving off the temporal branch, the zygomatic branch, the buccal branch, the marginal mandibular branch, and the cervical branch.
B
Frey's syndrome commonly occurs after parotid surgery or trauma, from injury of the auriculo-temporal nerve and great auricular nerve; the facial nerve's course through the parotid gland is therefore clinically important in parotid surgery, where the nerve and its branches are structures to be identified and preserved.
C
Bell's palsy is associated with drooping of the mouth, reflecting facial nerve dysfunction; facial laceration is also noted as a clinical correlate involving this nerve's territory. Because the facial nerve, once it has divided within the parotid gland into its temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular and cervical branches, supplies the muscles of facial expression, injury to the trunk or a branch of the nerve produces the drooping and loss of movement seen in facial nerve palsy.

A(i)
It arises from the external iliac artery.
A(ii)
• It enters the rectus sheath at the arcuate line.
• It lies beneath the lateral umbilical fold on the internal surface of the anterolateral abdominal wall.
A(iii)
• Branches: cremasteric artery (to the cremasteric muscle) and pubic branch.
• Median umbilical fold covers the remnant of the urachus; medial umbilical folds cover the obliterated umbilical arteries; lateral umbilical folds cover the inferior epigastric vessels.
A(iv)
• It anastomoses with the superior epigastric artery, the terminal branch of the internal thoracic that descends in the rectus sheath posterior to the muscle.
• Veins: the external iliac vein receives the epigastric and deep circumflex iliac veins; the superior epigastric vein drains to the brachiocephalic vein.
B(i)
• The deep inguinal ring lies lateral to it, about ½ inch above the inguinal ligament at the midinguinal point; the opening to the canal is located laterally to it.
• Indirect hernias enter the canal lateral to the vessels; direct hernias bulge through the posterior wall medial to the artery.
C(i)
The lateral umbilical folds cover the inferior epigastric vessels, which bleed if cut.

A(i)
The space between two ribs; with 12 ribs on each side there are 11 intercostal spaces; each space contains intercostal muscles, the intercostal neurovascular bundle and lymphatics.
A(ii)
• Three muscles (external, internal, innermost; transversus thoracis, subcostalis and levator costarum are also listed), supplied by the corresponding intercostal nerves, that pull the ribs nearer to each other and strengthen the space. External intercostal: most superficial, fibres downward and forward, origin lower border of the rib above, insertion upper border of the rib below, from the rib tubercle behind to the costochondral junction in front, replaced anteriorly by the anterior intercostal membrane.
• Internal intercostal: intermediate layer, fibres downward and backward, origin subcostal groove of the rib above, insertion upper border of the rib below, from the sternum in front to the angle of the rib behind, replaced posteriorly by the posterior intercostal membrane.
A(iii)
Innermost intercostal: deepest, incomplete layer divided into 3 portions, its fibres cross more than one space; related externally to the intercostal nerve and vessels and internally to the endothoracic fascia. Endothoracic fascia: extrapleural fascia lining the chest wall between the muscles and bones and the parietal pleura, extending over the pleural apex as the suprapleural membrane and forming a thin layer between diaphragm and pleura.
A(iv)
The neurovascular bundle lies between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles, high in the space in relation to the subcostal groove of the rib above; strict order from above downwards: vein, artery, nerve (VAN); because the innermost layer is incomplete it is generally covered on the inside by endothoracic fascia.
A(v)
Each space has a single posterior and 2 anterior intercostal arteries, giving branches to muscles, skin, parietal pleura and breast. Posterior: upper 2 spaces from the superior intercostal artery (costocervical trunk of the subclavian artery), lower 9 spaces from the thoracic aorta. Anterior: upper 6 spaces from the internal thoracic artery, lower 5 from the musculophrenic artery; they anastomose with the posterior arteries.
A(vi)
Veins accompany the arteries and nerves (11 posterior intercostal and 1 subcostal vein); valves direct blood posteriorly. Right side: 1st space to the brachiocephalic vein, the rest to the azygos vein. Left side: upper 3 spaces to the left brachiocephalic vein, the rest to the hemiazygos and accessory hemiazygos veins, which drain to the azygos vein. Anterior veins: upper 6 spaces to the internal thoracic vein, lower 5 to the musculophrenic vein.
A(vii)
12 pairs, the anterior primary rami of the thoracic spinal nerves and mixed nerves; nerves 1-6 are distributed in the intercostal spaces, 7-11 supply the anterior abdominal wall, and the 12th runs forward in the abdomen as the subcostal nerve; they supply skin, muscles of the space and abdomen, parietal pleura and parietal peritoneum. Branches: rami communicantes, collateral (muscular), lateral cutaneous, anterior cutaneous, pleural and peritoneal (7th-11th).
A(viii)
Deep lymphatics follow the arteries: anteriorly they drain into the anterior intercostal (parasternal) nodes along the internal thoracic artery; posteriorly they drain into the posterior intercostal nodes in the posterior mediastinum.
B(i)
• A needle or drain is passed immediately above the upper border of the rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle (vein, artery, nerve from above downwards) running under the rib above in the subcostal groove.
• Intercostal spaces are access points for surgical procedures (e.g. resection of part of the lung), for percussion and auscultation of the heart and lung, and for sampling pleural fluid or draining pus or blood from the pleural cavity; disease in the thorax may cause pain in the anterior abdominal wall because the intercostal nerves supply both the thoracic and abdominal wall and the parietal pleura.
C(i)
Typical nerves are T3-6. T1 is atypical: no anterior cutaneous branch, joined to the brachial plexus by a large branch corresponding to the lateral cutaneous branch. T2 is atypical: its lateral cutaneous branch is the intercostobrachial nerve, which joins the medial cutaneous nerve of the arm through the brachial plexus.

A. Describe the course of the maxillary nerve, from its origin to its continuation on the face, and list its branches.
B. State the clinically relevant procedure and the region associated with this nerve.
questions.answerText:
A
The maxillary nerve passes through the pterygopalatine fossa, where it is one of the contents (along with the terminal part of the maxillary artery, the maxillary vein, and the pterygopalatine ganglion); nerve structures enter the fossa through its posterior wall. Its branches include the superior alveolar nerves (anterior, posterior and middle), the middle meningeal nerve, the infraorbital nerve, the zygomatic nerve, the inferior palpebral nerve, the superior labial nerve, the pharyngeal nerve, the greater and lesser palatine nerves, and the nasopalatine nerve. The infraorbital nerve continues from the maxillary nerve onto the face via the infraorbital groove and canal, situated on the floor of the orbit in the orbital plate of the maxilla, and via the infraorbital foramen.
B
Clinical correlates of this region include maxillary nerve block, and the pterygopalatine ganglion is also referred to as the "hay fever ganglion".

questions.question:
Describe the axilla under the following headings:
A(i) Shape and apex
A(ii) Base
A(iii) Walls
A(iv) Contents
B. Explain the clinical basis for the axillary vein being particularly vulnerable to injury in this region.
C. Distinguish between the quadrangular space and the triangular interval found in the posterior wall of the axilla.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The axilla is a pyramid-shaped space between the upper part of the arm and the side of the upper chest; its apex is the cervicoaxillary canal, bounded by the 1st rib, clavicle, and superior edge of the scapula, forming the passageway between the neck and axilla.
A(ii)
The base is formed by concave skin, subcutaneous tissue, and the axillary (deep) fascia.
A(iii)
Anterior wall: pectoralis major and minor, subclavius, and clavipectoral fascia. Posterior wall: scapula and subscapularis above, teres major and latissimus dorsi below. Medial wall: upper ribs, intercostal muscles, and serratus anterior. Lateral wall: narrow and bony, formed by the intertubercular groove of the humerus.
A(iv)
Contents: the axillary artery and its branches, the axillary vein and its tributaries, the infraclavicular part of the brachial plexus, axillary lymph nodes, and loose areolar/adipose tissue, all enclosed with the plexus in the axillary sheath.
B
• The axillary vein is large and lies in an exposed, superficial position within the axilla.
• Wounds to the axilla therefore often involve the axillary vein because of its large size and exposed position.
• A wound to the proximal part of the axillary vein is especially dangerous because of the risk of air entering the vessel (air embolism).
C
• The quadrangular space lies in the posterior wall of the axilla and transmits the axillary nerve and the posterior circumflex humeral artery and vein.
• The triangular interval also lies in the posterior wall and transmits the radial nerve and the profunda brachii artery.
• Both spaces are related to the long head of triceps brachii and the teres major muscle in their boundaries.
• The quadrangular space thus carries the nerve/vessels supplying the deltoid and teres minor region, while the triangular interval carries those continuing into the posterior compartment of the arm.
• This distinction explains why injury near the surgical neck of the humerus threatens the axillary nerve, whereas injury lower down at the spiral groove threatens the radial nerve instead.

questions.question:
A. Describe the gross anatomy of the cranial base under the following headings: the anterior cranial fossa, the middle cranial fossa, and the posterior cranial fossa, and their main foramina and contents.
B. State how fractures involving the different regions of the skull base relate to specific clinical presentations.
C. Explain why disease/infection or trauma involving one region of the skull base can produce a functional deficit at a distant site, such as the nasal cavity or the brain itself.
questions.answerText:
A
In the anterior cranial fossa, the foramen caecum transmits a nasal emissary vein (in 1% of the population), the cribriform foramina in the cribriform plate transmit axons of olfactory cells forming the olfactory nerves, and the anterior and posterior ethmoidal foramina transmit vessels and nerves of the same names. In the middle cranial fossa, the optic canals transmit the optic nerves (CN II) and ophthalmic arteries; the superior orbital fissure transmits ophthalmic veins, the ophthalmic nerve (CN V1), CN III, IV and VI, and sympathetic fibres; the foramen rotundum transmits the maxillary nerve (CN V2); the foramen ovale transmits the mandibular nerve (CN V3), the accessory meningeal artery, the lesser petrosal nerve and an emissary vein; the foramen spinosum transmits the middle meningeal artery and vein and the meningeal branch of CN V3; and the foramen lacerum transmits the deep petrosal nerve and some meningeal arterial branches and small veins. In the posterior cranial fossa, the foramen magnum transmits the medulla and meninges, vertebral arteries, CN XI, dural veins, and the anterior and posterior spinal arteries; the jugular foramen transmits CN IX, X and XI, the superior bulb of the internal jugular vein, the inferior petrosal and sigmoid sinuses, and meningeal branches of the ascending pharyngeal and occipital arteries; the hypoglossal canal transmits the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII); the condylar canal transmits an emissary vein from the sigmoid sinus to the vertebral veins in the neck; and the mastoid foramen transmits a mastoid emissary vein from the sigmoid sinus and a meningeal branch of the occipital artery.
B
Fractures of the calvaria are classified as depressed, linear, comminuted, or basilar fractures; fractures of the maxillae and associated bones are termed Le Fort fractures; and there are also fractures of the mandible.
C
The close relation of the frontal sinus to the frontal lobe of the brain explains how infection of this sinus may result in development of a frontal lobe abscess; a fracture involving the sinus, severe enough to tear the dura and pia-arachnoid, will place the subarachnoid space in communication with the nasal cavity, so that CSF may be detected trickling through the nostril (CSF rhinorrhoea), usually on the affected side, although a contralateral leak can occur since these sinuses may communicate. Similarly, infection of the ethmoid sinuses (ethmoiditis) may result in a frontal cerebral abscess, and an ethmoidal fracture may cause CSF leakage into the nasal cavity, because the ethmoid sinuses lie on each side of the cribriform plate and are related above to the frontal lobes of the brain.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the processes of digestion, naming all eight steps in order.
A(ii) Describe the four main functions of the GI tract, distinguishing between the role of the small intestine and the role of the large intestine in absorption.
B(i) Describe the composition and function of the serosa, including the structures it is continuous with and how it differs between organs within the abdominal cavity and the esophagus.
B(ii) Explain why the enteric nervous system provides the anatomical basis for the effects of emotional stress on the GIT, and name the two diseases that demonstrate the clinical consequences of plexus destruction.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Eight processes of digestion (in order):
• Ingestion
• Mastication
• Peristalsis / motility
• Secretions
• Hormone release
• Chemical digestion
• Absorption
• Elimination
A(ii)
Four main functions of the GI tract:
• Macromolecules (proteins, complex carbohydrates, nucleic acids, and fat) obtained from ingested food are broken down into smaller subunits for easy absorption through the lining of the small intestine during digestion.
• These smaller subunits are required for the release of energy, maintenance, and growth.
• Most of the water and electrolytes are absorbed in the large intestine.
• The inner layer of the entire GI tract forms an important protective barrier between the contents of the tract and the tissues of the body.
B(i)
Serosa:
• Composition: a thin sheet of loose connective tissue covered with mesothelium (a simple squamous covering epithelium); rich in blood vessels, lymphatics, and adipose tissue.
• Function: the outermost covering of GIT organs within the abdominal cavity.
• Continuity: the serosa of the small and large intestines is continuous with parts of the mesentery (a large fold of adipose connective tissue covered on both sides by mesothelium, which suspends the intestines and is continuous with the peritoneum).
• Esophagus: because the esophagus is bound directly to adjacent structures and not suspended in a cavity, it has a thick adventitia instead of a serosa; the adventitia consists of connective tissue containing vessels and nerves, lacking mesothelium.
B(ii)
• The enteric nervous system (submucosal and myenteric plexuses) functions independently of the CNS; because it is anatomically connected to the autonomic nervous system, it provides the anatomical basis for the well-known actions of emotional stress on the stomach and other regions of the GIT.
Two diseases demonstrating clinical consequences of plexus destruction:
• Hirschsprung disease (congenital aganglionic megacolon): caused by absence or severely injured plexuses in parts or all of the large intestine; disturbs motility and produces dilation, causing difficulty passing stool.
• Chagas disease / trypanosomiasis (infection with Trypanosoma cruzi): the protozoan destroys the enteric plexuses, producing similar motility disturbance.

questions.question:
A. Describe the gross anatomy of the paranasal sinuses under the following headings: the four pairs of sinuses, their development, and their general function.
B. State how each of the paranasal sinuses relates to a specific clinical complication when infected or fractured.
C. Explain why disease of the paranasal sinuses can spread to produce a functional deficit in a distant structure, namely the brain or the nasal cavity.
questions.answerText:
A
The nasal sinuses are air-containing sacs lined by ciliated epithelium, communicating with the nasal cavity through narrow, easily occluded channels; they develop as outgrowths from the nasal cavity. There are 4 pairs: the maxillary antrum, sphenoid, frontal and ethmoid sinuses. The maxillary antrum and ethmoid sinuses are present in a rudimentary state at birth, while the rest become evident at about the 7th year of life. The lining of the sinuses is continuous with the nasal mucosa; their function is obscure, but they provide resonance to the voice, shape to the face, and some degree of warmth and humidification to inspired air. The paranasal sinuses are supplied by branches of the ophthalmic and maxillary nerves.
B
The frontal sinuses' posterosuperior wall lies adjacent to the frontal lobe of the brain, and their floor abuts the ethmoid cells, nasal fossa roof and orbit; infection here may cause a frontal lobe abscess, and fracture severe enough to tear the dura and pia-arachnoid causes CSF rhinorrhoea. The maxillary sinus (antrum) may become infected from the nasal cavity or from caries of the upper molar teeth, whose roots are separated from the sinus floor only by a thin, sometimes deficient, layer of bone. The ethmoid sinuses lie on each side of the cribriform plate, related above to the frontal lobes; infection (ethmoiditis) may result in a frontal cerebral abscess, and ethmoidal fracture may cause CSF leakage into the nasal cavity. The sphenoid sinuses lie within the body of the sphenoid and may extend laterally into the greater wing of the sphenoid or backward into the basal part of the occipital bone; each drains into the nasal cavity above the superior concha (the sphenoethmoidal recess).
C
Because the frontal and ethmoid sinuses are directly related anatomically to the frontal lobes of the brain (posterosuperior wall of the frontal sinus, and the region above the cribriform plate for the ethmoid sinuses), infection at either site can spread directly to produce a frontal lobe or frontal cerebral abscess; and because fracture of either sinus, if severe enough to tear the dura and pia-arachnoid, places the subarachnoid space in communication with the nasal cavity, CSF rhinorrhoea (leakage of CSF into the nose) results, sometimes even on the contralateral side since the sinuses may communicate with one another.

questions.question:
Describe the gluteal region under the following headings.
A(i) Boundaries and bony landmarks
A(ii) Fascia — superficial and deep; name all 9 muscles and give their OCIANA (origin, course, insertion, action, nerve, artery)
B(i) Nerves of the gluteal region — name all 6 nerves
B(ii) Arteries — name all 4 arteries; describe the trochanteric anastomosis and cruciate anastomosis fully
C(i) Functions of the sacrotuberous and sacrospinous ligaments; explain the formation and roles of the greater and lesser sciatic foramina
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The gluteal region is the region of the buttock. Bony landmarks — surface anatomy: iliac crest, gluteus medius, tip of greater trochanter, gluteus maximus (fold of buttock), ischial tuberosity, tip of coccyx, natal cleft, posterior superior iliac spine (PSIS), sciatic nerve. Bones: os coxae (ilium, ischium, pubis) and femur.
A(ii)
Superficial fascia: thick in women; impregnated with large quantities of fat, hence the prominence of the buttock. Deep fascia: continuous with fascia lata of the thigh. The 9 muscles: gluteus maximus, gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, tensor fasciae latae (superficial layer); piriformis, obturator internus, gemellus superior, gemellus inferior, quadratus femoris (deep layer). Deep layer muscles all have distal attachments on or adjacent to the intertrochanteric crest of the femur; they are lateral rotators of the thigh and stabilise the hip joint. Obturator internus, superior gemellus, and inferior gemellus form the triceps coxae of the hip.
B(i)
6 nerves of the gluteal region: sciatic nerve (L4, 5; S1, 2, 3); posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh; superior gluteal nerve; inferior gluteal nerve; nerve to quadratus femoris; pudendal nerve. (Nerve to obturator internus also exits here.) The sciatic nerve curves downward midway between the tuber ischii and the greater trochanter.
B(ii)
4 arteries: superior gluteal artery (SGA), inferior gluteal artery (IGA), medial femoral circumflex artery (MFCA), lateral femoral circumflex artery (LFCA). Trochanteric anastomosis (TA) — main blood supply to the head of femur: SGA, IGA, MFCA, LFCA. Cruciate anastomosis (CA) — situated at the level of the lesser trochanter: IGA, MFCA, LFCA, and 1st perforating branch of profunda femoris. The CA jointly with the TA provides a connection between the femoral arteries and the internal iliac arteries.
C(i)
Sacrotuberous ligament (STL) and sacrospinous ligament (SSL): (1) both stabilise the sacrum and prevent its rotation at the sacroiliac joint by the weight of the vertebral column; (2) in conjunction with bones, they form the greater sciatic foramen (GSF) and lesser sciatic foramen (LSF). Functions of GSF and LSF: GSF provides an exit from the pelvis into the gluteal region. LSF (1) provides an entrance into the perineum from the gluteal region; (2) enables nerves and vessels that left the pelvis through the GSF above the pelvic floor to enter the perineum below the pelvic floor.

questions.question:
Describe the muscles of the posterior compartment of the leg under the following headings and explain why disease of tibialis posterior leads to collapse of the medial longitudinal arch.
A(i) Classify muscles into superficial and deep groups; give origin, insertion, innervation, and action of each
A(ii) The calcaneal (Achilles) tendon — formation, course, and clinical significance
B(i) The tibial nerve — course in the posterior compartment, branches, safe site for tarsal tunnel block
B(ii) How tibialis posterior supports the medial longitudinal arch and why its dysfunction causes pes planus
C(i) Distinguish the actions of gastrocnemius from soleus, explaining the anatomical basis of their different clinical testing
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Superficial group (3 muscles): Gastrocnemius — lateral head from lateral aspect of lateral condyle of femur; insertion: posterior surface of calcaneus via calcaneal tendon; innervation: tibial nerve (S1, S2); action: plantarflexes ankle when knee is extended, raises heel during walking, flexes leg at knee joint. Soleus — posterior aspect of head and superior quarter of posterior surface of fibula; soleal line and middle third of medial border of tibia; tendinous arch; insertion: posterior surface of calcaneus via calcaneal tendon; innervation: tibial nerve (S1, S2); action: plantarflexes ankle independent of position of knee, steadies leg on foot. Plantaris — inferior end of lateral supracondylar line of femur, oblique popliteal ligament; insertion: posterior surface of calcaneus via calcaneal tendon; innervation: tibial nerve (S1, S2); action: weakly assists gastrocnemius in plantarflexing ankle. Deep group (4 muscles): Popliteus — lateral surface of lateral condyle of femur and lateral meniscus; posterior surface of tibia superior to soleal line; tibial nerve (L4, L5, S1); weakly flexes knee, unlocks it by rotating femur 5° on fixed tibia, and medially rotates tibia of unplanted limb. Flexor hallucis longus — inferior 2/3 of posterior surface of fibula; base of distal phalanx of great toe; tibial nerve (S2, S3); flexes great toe at all joints, weakly plantarflexes ankle, supports medial longitudinal arch. Flexor digitorum longus — medial part of posterior surface of tibia inferior to soleal line; bases of distal phalanges of lateral 4 digits; tibial nerve (S2, S3); flexes lateral 4 digits, plantarflexes ankle, supports longitudinal arches. Tibialis posterior — interosseous membrane, posterior tibia inferior to soleal line, posterior fibula; tuberosity of navicular, cuneiform, cuboid, sustentaculum tali of calcaneus, bases of 2nd, 3rd, and 4th metatarsals; tibial nerve (L4, L5); plantarflexes ankle and inverts foot.
A(ii)
The calcaneal tendon is formed by the union of the tendons of gastrocnemius, soleus, and plantaris; it inserts into the posterior surface of the calcaneus. It is the largest and strongest tendon in the body. Clinical significance: rupture of the Achilles tendon (commonly felt as a 'pop' and tested by Thompson's squeeze test) results in inability to plantarflex the foot.
B(i)
The posterior tibial artery enters the sole of the foot through the tarsal tunnel, accompanying the tibial nerve. The tibial nerve enters the sole of the foot via the tarsal tunnel and then splits into the lateral and medial plantar arteries. For a tarsal tunnel block, the posterior tibial pulse can be palpated inferoposteriorly to the medial malleolus, where the artery turns to enter the foot — the tibial nerve lies adjacent.
B(ii)
Tibialis posterior inserts into the tuberosity of the navicular, cuneiform, cuboid, sustentaculum tali of calcaneus, and the bases of the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th metatarsals — the very bones that form the medial longitudinal arch. It plantarflexes the ankle and inverts the foot; by pulling the navicular and cuneiforms downward and inward it actively maintains the height of the medial longitudinal arch. Dysfunction (e.g., from tenosynovitis or rupture) leads to eversion of the calcaneus, slipping down of the talus and navicular, and pes planus — collapse of the medial longitudinal arch.
C(i)
Gastrocnemius spans the knee joint (arising from the femoral condyle) and the ankle joint; it plantarflexes the ankle only when the knee is extended and also flexes the knee. It is tested with the knee extended. Soleus arises entirely from the tibia and fibula (below the knee) and plantarflexes the ankle independent of the position of the knee. It is tested by single-leg heel raise with the knee flexed to 90°, which eliminates gastrocnemius from the movement and isolates soleus.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the mucosa of the stomach under the following headings: surface epithelium and gastric pits; the isthmus and stem cells; the lamina propria; and the muscularis mucosae.
A(ii) Name and describe all four secretory epithelial cell types found in the gastric glands of the fundus and body, including the characteristics of each cell and what it secretes.
B(i) Distinguish between the mucosa of the fundus/body and the mucosa of the cardia/pylorus under the headings: gland type, cell types present, and principal secretion.
B(ii) Explain what rugae are and the physiological condition under which they disappear.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Stomach mucosa:
• Surface epithelium and gastric pits: consists of a simple columnar epithelium that invaginates into the lamina propria forming gastric pits. Millions of gastric pits each open into the lumen of the stomach; the gastric pits lead into long, branched, tubular glands extending through the thickness of the lamina propria; between each gastric pit and gastric gland is the isthmus (region of stem cells).
• Isthmus and stem cells: the pluripotent stem cells divide asymmetrically producing progenitor cells for all other epithelial cells; they can move upwards to replace surface mucous cells or downwards to replace other secretory cells.
• Lamina propria: highly vascularised; supports pits and glands; contains smooth muscle fibers, capillaries, lymphatics, and lymphoid cells.
• Muscularis mucosae: layer of smooth muscle separating the mucosa from the underlying submucosa.
A(ii)
Four secretory cell types of fundic/body glands:
• Mucous neck cells (MNCs): less columnar than surface mucous cells; irregular in shape with round nucleus and apical secretory granules; secrete acidic fluid containing mucin (less alkaline than surface mucous cells).
• Parietal (oxyntic) cells: large, rounded or pyramidal cells; one central spherical nucleus; intensely eosinophilic cytoplasm due to high density of mitochondria; secrete hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor.
• Chief (zymogen) cells: predominate in lower regions; abundant RER and numerous apical secretory granules (characteristics of protein-secreting cells); secrete pepsinogen (converted to pepsin at pH < 5), lipase, and leptin.
• Enteroendocrine cells: scattered throughout the gastric mucosa; secrete hormones with endocrine or paracrine functions (e.g., serotonin in fundus; gastrin from G cells in pylorus).
B(i)
• Fundus/body: long branched tubular gastric glands (3 to 7 per pit); each gland has an isthmus, neck, and base; contains all four cell types above; secretes acidic gastric juice.
• Cardia/pylorus: tubular glands with long pits, usually branching into coiled secretory portions (cardiac/pyloric glands); lack parietal and chief cells; major secretion is abundant mucus.
B(ii)
Rugae are longitudinally directed folds of the mucosa and submucosa of the empty stomach. They flatten when the stomach is full with food.

A(i)
General characteristics: epithelial tissue consists of closely packed cells arranged in one or more layers; these cells are specialized and fill roles such as protection, secretion, and absorption; the cells are tightly packed together with very little extracellular matrix and almost no intercellular substance; they rest on a basement membrane (a basal lamina containing the glycoprotein laminin). Morphological classification by cell shape: squamous (flat), cuboidal (square or cube-like), columnar (tall and thin). By number of layers: simple epithelium (one cell thick) — can be simple squamous, simple cuboidal, or simple columnar; stratified epithelium (multiple layers — described as heterogeneous); pseudostratified epithelium — appears stratified but all cells contact the basal lamina. Transitional epithelium: recognized by its appearance — when the bladder is empty (relaxed), the epithelium appears thicker and has more layers than when the bladder is full. Basement membrane: contains the glycoprotein laminin; the border between epithelia and the underlying connective tissue is sharp and distinct.
A(ii)
Simple squamous epithelium: lines blood vessels (endothelium) and body cavities. Simple cuboidal epithelium: lines many small ducts in the body. Simple columnar epithelium: lines the gallbladder, larger ducts near the urinary papilla; also found in the jejunum (with goblet cells). Ciliated columnar epithelium: found in the respiratory tract and fallopian tubes; goblet cells (glandular epithelium) are present, making it heterogeneous. Stratified squamous epithelium (keratinized): forms the outer layer of skin; contains the protective protein keratin; a keratinized (dry) epithelium. Transitional epithelium: lines the urinary bladder.
B(i)
Epithelial tissue is avascular (contains no blood vessels); the lamina propria (underlying connective tissue) supplies the necessary nutrients and metabolites, which are transported to and from epithelial cells by diffusion through the basement membrane. If the basement membrane is disrupted (e.g., in cancer invasion or severe inflammation), the barrier between epithelium and connective tissue is lost, allowing unrestricted cell invasion into the underlying stroma; epithelial cells in contact with the environment are constantly subjected to mechanical damage and must show many dividing cells (mitoses) to replace lost cells; disruption of this repair mechanism contributes to disease progression.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the gross anatomy of epithelial tissue under the following headings: general characteristics, morphological classification (by cell shape and number of layers), and the basement membrane.
A(ii) Relate specific epithelial types to their common locations in the body, giving one example each of simple squamous, simple cuboidal, simple columnar, ciliated columnar, stratified squamous, and transitional epithelium.
B(i) Explain why epithelial tissue is avascular, how it receives nutrients, and state the clinical consequence when the basement membrane is disrupted in disease.

questions.answerText:
(i)
• The liver has two surfaces - a convex diaphragmatic surface (anterior, superior, posterior and right lateral) and a relatively flat, posteroinferior visceral surface.
• It is divided into a large right lobe and a smaller left lobe by the falciform ligament, with the caudate and quadrate lobes arising from the right lobe on the visceral surface.
• Two sagittally oriented fissures (for the ligamentum teres and ligamentum venosum on the left, and the gallbladder fossa and IVC groove on the right) are linked by the transverse porta hepatis, forming an H on the visceral surface.
• Ligaments include the falciform ligament, the coronary ligament with the right and left triangular ligaments, and the lesser omentum (hepatogastric and hepatoduodenal ligaments).
• The porta hepatis transmits the hepatic ducts, hepatic artery and portal vein branches, and hepatic nerves and lymph nodes.
(ii)
• The bare area of the diaphragmatic surface has no peritoneal covering, so infection there can track through the diaphragm to posterior mediastinal lymph nodes.
• The subphrenic and subhepatic spaces, and Morison's pouch between the liver and right kidney, are recesses where pathological fluid such as pus, blood or ascites collects.
• Liver fissures serve as surgical landmarks, such as Cantlie's line, which divides the liver into functional right and left lobes along the middle hepatic vein.
• Because the liver is large, fixed in position and friable, it is vulnerable to rupture, often from a fractured rib perforating the diaphragm, causing haemorrhage and right upper quadrant pain.
(iii)
• In cirrhosis, hepatocytes are destroyed and replaced by fibrous tissue that impedes blood flow through the liver, causing portal hypertension.
• This opens portal-systemic anastomoses at the lower oesophagus, anal canal, paraumbilical region, retroperitoneum and intrahepatic sites, producing distant complications such as bleeding oesophageal varices.
• Distension of Glisson's capsule from an enlarged liver produces sharp, well-localised pain via the lower intercostal nerves, illustrating how a hepatic process produces a distant sensory effect.
questions.question:
(i) Describe the gross anatomy of the liver under the headings: surfaces, lobes, fissures and peritoneal ligaments.
(ii) Relate the lobes/fissures of the liver to common hepatic pathology.
(iii) Explain how liver disease can spread its effects to a distant structure, producing a functional deficit there.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Oblique, tunnel-shaped passage through the lower part of the anterior abdominal wall just above the medial half of the inguinal ligament, present in both sexes; about 4 cm (1½ inches) long in adults, directed downwards, forwards and medially.
A(ii)
It extends from the deep inguinal ring to the superficial inguinal ring; in the newborn the deep ring lies almost directly posterior to the superficial ring.
A(iii)
• Anterior wall: external oblique aponeurosis, reinforced laterally by internal oblique. Posterior wall: transversalis fascia, reinforced medially by the conjoint tendon.
• Roof: arching lowest fibres of internal oblique and transversus abdominis with transversalis fascia. Floor: inguinal ligament, reinforced medially by the lacunar ligament.
A(iv)
Spermatic cord (male) or round ligament of uterus (female); processus vaginalis remnant; 3 fasciae; 3 arteries (artery to vas, cremasteric, testicular); 3 nerves (ilio-inguinal L1, genital branch of genitofemoral L2, sympathetic); vas, pampiniform plexus, lymphatics.
B(i)
• It is a potential weakness in the abdominal wall. The posterior wall is weak laterally at the deep ring, but the anterior wall opposite is reinforced by internal oblique, so a hernia through the deep ring must travel along the canal.
• The anterior wall is weak medially at the superficial ring, but the posterior wall opposite is reinforced by the conjoint tendon; weakness there leads to direct hernias.
B(ii)
In the male it allows spermatic cord structures to pass to and from the testis (normal spermatogenesis needs the cooler scrotum) while preventing intestine entering the scrotum; in the female the smaller canal carries the round ligament of the uterus to the labium majus.
C(i)
• Deep ring: oval opening in the transversalis fascia, about ½ inch (1.3 cm) above the inguinal ligament at the midinguinal point, lateral to the inferior epigastric artery; margins give attachment to internal spermatic fascia; entrance of the cord.
• Superficial ring: triangular defect in the external oblique aponeurosis, immediately above and medial to the pubic tubercle; its medial and lateral crura give attachment to the external spermatic fascia; it is the exit of the cord from the canal.

questions.question:
A(i) State the origin of the posterior intercostal arteries.
A(ii) Describe their course and relations in the intercostal space.
A(iii) State their branches, distribution and venous and lymphatic companions.
B(i) State the safe site and the danger site for passing a needle or drain through an intercostal space and the anatomical basis.
C(i) Explain the anatomical basis of the rib deformity seen on radiographs in coarctation of the aorta.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Each intercostal space has a single posterior and two anterior intercostal arteries.
• In the upper two spaces the posterior intercostal arteries arise from the superior intercostal artery (branch of the costocervical trunk of the subclavian artery); in the lower nine spaces they arise from the thoracic aorta (9 pairs, plus 1 pair of subcostal arteries from the posterior surface of the descending thoracic aorta).
A(ii)
Course and branching follow the intercostal nerves: each artery runs forward in the subcostal groove, high in the space between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles, in the order vein, artery, nerve from above downwards, and anastomoses with the anterior intercostal artery.
A(iii)
• Branches go to adjacent muscles, skin, parietal pleura, spinal cord and breast (branches in the 3rd and 4th spaces supply the breast); the 3rd right posterior intercostal artery gives the right bronchial artery.
• Distribution: the posterior and lateral parts of the intercostal spaces.
• Veins accompany the arteries and contain valves that direct blood posteriorly; on the right the 1st space drains to the brachiocephalic vein and the rest to the azygos vein; on the left the upper 3 spaces drain to the left brachiocephalic vein and the rest to the hemiazygos and accessory hemiazygos veins, which drain to the azygos vein.
• Lymphatics: deep lymphatics follow the arteries; posteriorly they drain to the posterior intercostal nodes in the posterior mediastinum.
B(i)
• Safe site: a needle or drain is passed immediately above the upper border of a rib; it is dangerous to pass it immediately below a rib.
• Basis: the intercostal vessels lie immediately below their corresponding ribs (vein above artery) in the subcostal groove, so a needle just above the lower rib avoids the neurovascular bundle; in thoracotomy the periosteum over a segment of the 5th or 6th rib is elevated, protecting the bundle.
C(i)
• In coarctation of the aorta the intercostal arteries derived from the aorta receive blood from the superior intercostals, from the anterior intercostal branches of the internal thoracic artery and from arteries anastomosing around the scapula.
• Together with the communication between the internal thoracic and inferior epigastric arteries, these are the principal collaterals between the aorta above and below the block.
• The intercostal arteries dilate and become tortuous and erode the lower borders of the corresponding ribs, giving the characteristic irregular notching of the ribs that helps radiographic confirmation.

A(i)
Formed behind the neck of the pancreas by the union of the superior mesenteric and splenic veins.
A(ii)
• Large but short, about 5 cm; in front of the opening of the lesser sac it passes to the porta hepatis where it divides into right and left terminal branches.
