• At the porta hepatis the order from behind forwards is portal vein branches, proper hepatic artery, hepatic ducts; in the hepatoduodenal ligament it lies with the hepatic artery and bile duct.
A(iii)
Drains poorly oxygenated but nutrient-rich blood from the GI tract (lower oesophagus to upper anal canal), pancreas, gallbladder, bile ducts and spleen to the liver.
A(iv)
Direct route: through the liver to the IVC via the hepatic veins; alternative routes exist and the portal vein and its tributaries have no valves.
B(i)
Portasystemic shunts join the portal vein to the IVC or join the splenic vein to the left renal vein after splenectomy.
C(i)
• Portal hypertension: cirrhosis scarring and fibrosis obstruct the portal vein, pressure mounts, and blood forced through collaterals dilates veins into varices, potentially fatal.
• Lower third of oesophagus: left gastric branches with oesophageal veins to the azygos: oesophageal varices.
• Anal canal: superior rectal with middle and inferior rectal veins: haemorrhoids (mucosa with normally dilated submucosal veins prolapses).
• Anterior abdominal wall: paraumbilical with superficial epigastric veins: caput medusae, veins radiating like small snakes from the umbilicus.
• Retroperitoneal: colic twig veins of ascending and descending colon, duodenum, pancreas and liver with renal, lumbar and phrenic veins.

A(i)
Autonomic nerve supply:
• Vessels and nerves enter the large salivary glands at the hilum and gradually branch into the lobules; a rich vascular and nerve plexus surrounds the secretory and ductal components of each lobule.
• The capillaries surrounding the secretory end pieces are important for saliva secretion, stimulated by the autonomic nervous system.
• Parasympathetic stimulation (usually through smell or taste of food): promotes vasodilation and a copious watery secretion.
• Sympathetic stimulation: produces small amounts of viscous saliva, rich in organic material. NOTE: dry mouth sensation in stressful situations (sympathetic predominance).
A(ii)
Immunological secretory mechanism:
• Plasma cells (in the connective tissue around the glands) secrete IgA.
• IgA forms a complex with a secretory component synthesized by the serous acinar cells, intercalated duct cells, and striated duct cells.
• The IgA-rich secretory complex released into the saliva is resistant to enzymatic digestion and constitutes an immunological defense mechanism against pathogens in the oral cavity.
B(i)
Parotid vs pancreatic tissue:
• Both resemble each other histologically.
• Parotid gland: has adipocytes (fat cells) in its parenchyma.
• Pancreatic tissue: has islets of Langerhans (endocrine clusters) and centroacinar cells.
B(ii)
• Minor salivary glands by location and secretion: von Ebner's glands of tongue (posterior dorsal and lateral): serous acini only.
• Palate, base and lateral border of tongue: predominantly mucous acini.
• Lip, cheek, apex of tongue: mixed serous and mucous acini.
• Minor glands secrete 10% of the total volume of saliva but account for approximately 70% of the mucus secreted.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the autonomic nerve supply to the salivary glands, including which division of the autonomic nervous system produces each type of secretory response and what type of saliva each produces.
A(ii) Describe the full immunological secretory mechanism of the large salivary glands, identifying the cell type that secretes IgA and the cell types that synthesise the secretory component.
B(i) The parotid gland resembles pancreatic tissue but can be distinguished from it. State the distinguishing features of each gland.
B(ii) Classify all minor salivary glands by location and secretion type, and state what proportion of total saliva volume and mucus the minor glands produce.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Protective coverings: the nervous system contains very little collagen or fibrous tissue; it is relatively soft and easily damaged by injuries affecting the cranium or vertebral bones. It is covered by three connective tissue layers — the meninges: dura mater (thickest and toughest layer, contains sinuses to collect venous blood), arachnoid membrane (middle web-like covering; cerebrospinal fluid flows in the web-like spaces), and pia mater (thin delicate layer that follows the contour of the brain and spinal cord). Gray matter and white matter: myelinated fibers make up the white matter in the CNS; cell bodies and unmyelinated fibers make the gray matter. Glial cells in CNS: Oligodendrocytes — produce myelin in CNS. Microglia — part of the MPS (CNS macrophages). Astrocytes and other glial cells — support, nourish, and protect neurons; they are far more numerous than neurons; unlike neurons, they are capable of mitosis.
A(ii)
Dura mater — thickest and toughest layer; contains sinuses to collect venous blood. Arachnoid membrane — middle web-like covering; cerebrospinal fluid flows in the web-like (subarachnoid) spaces. Pia mater — thin delicate layer that follows the contour of brain and spinal cord. CSF flows within the subarachnoid spaces of the arachnoid.
B(i)
The optic nerve and retina arise in the embryo as an outgrowth of the diencephalon (forebrain); the optic nerve is therefore not a true peripheral nerve like the other cranial nerves. Its myelin is produced by oligodendrocytes (not by Schwann cells). Because the optic nerve is part of the CNS (produced by oligodendrocytes and without neurilemma), it is associated with multiple sclerosis — a demyelinating disease. Demyelination of the optic nerve disrupts the action potential transmission from the retinal ganglion cells, causing visual symptoms. The retinal ganglion cells communicate with the cerebrum through the optic nerve and extend into the brain.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the gross histology of the nervous tissue of the brain under the following headings: protective coverings (meninges), gray matter and white matter, types of glial cells in the CNS and their functions.
A(ii) Relate the three meningeal layers to their specific functions and state how cerebrospinal fluid flows.
B(i) Explain why a demyelinating disease of the optic nerve causes visual symptoms and state the histological basis of the link between the retina, optic nerve, and the CNS.

A(i) Describe connective tissue under the following headings: definition and function, major constituent and its components, classification.
A(ii) Explain the clinical basis of edema in connective tissue.
B(i) Distinguish between loose connective tissue and dense connective tissue, giving two examples of each.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Definition and function: Connective tissue derives its name from its function in connecting or binding cells and tissues; it maintains the form of organs throughout the body. Unlike other tissue types (epithelium, muscle, nerve) which consist mainly of cells, the major constituent of connective tissue is the extracellular matrix. The extracellular matrix is composed of protein fibers (collagen, elastic, and reticular fibers), ground substance (a jelly-like, amorphous, anionic, hydrophilic complex of proteoglycans, glycosaminoglycans, and multiadhesive glycoproteins such as laminin and fibronectin), and tissue fluid. Classification: connective tissue is classified as connective tissue proper (loose: areolar, adipose, reticular; dense: regular, irregular, elastic) and specialized connective tissue (blood, cartilage, bone).
A(ii)
The amount of tissue fluid (interstitial fluid) is fairly constant and there is an equilibrium between water entering and leaving the intercellular substance. In pathological conditions (traumatic injury and inflammation), fluid may accumulate in the connective tissue, a condition known as edema.
B(i)
Loose connective tissue: irregularly arranged tissue with abundant ground substance, capable of withstanding stress from many directions; present in dermis, capsules of joints, and submucosa of the alimentary tract. Examples: areolar tissue, adipose tissue. Dense connective tissue: tissue in which fibers predominate; it is organized to withstand forces in specific directions. Dense regular: present in tendons and ligaments. Dense irregular: present in the dermis of skin and capsules of organs.

A(i)
The greater sac is the main larger part; the lesser sac (omental bursa) lies posterior to the stomach, adjoining structures and lesser omentum; an incision through the anterolateral wall enters the greater sac; the sacs communicate through the epiploic foramen.
A(ii)
• The transverse mesocolon divides the cavity into supracolic and infracolic compartments; the infracolic lies posterior to the greater omentum and is divided by the mesentery of the small intestine into right and left infracolic spaces.
• Right space: triangular, between the root of the mesentery, ascending colon and right two-thirds of transverse colon; left: between the root, descending colon and left one-third of transverse colon, widening below into the pelvis.
A(iii)
Right paracolic gutter lies lateral to the ascending colon and communicates with the hepatorenal recess and pelvic cavity; the left, lateral to the descending colon, is separated from the splenic area by the phrenicocolic ligament.
A(iv)
• Lesser sac: superior wall peritoneum over the caudate lobe and diaphragm; anterior lesser omentum, peritoneum of the posterior stomach and anterior two layers of greater omentum; posterior the posterior two layers, transverse colon and mesocolon, peritoneum over pancreas, left kidney and suprarenal gland.
• Omental foramen (of Winslow), behind the hepatoduodenal ligament, admits 2 fingers: liver superiorly, first part of duodenum inferiorly, hepatoduodenal ligament anteriorly, IVC and right crus posteriorly.
B(i)
Median umbilical fold covers the urachal remnant, medial folds the obliterated umbilical arteries, lateral folds the inferior epigastric vessels; the supravesical fossa is a site for external supravesical hernia, the medial inguinal fossa for the less common direct hernia, the lateral inguinal fossa for the most common indirect hernia.
B(ii)
Blockage of the uterine tubes (hysterosalpingography), peritonitis, ascites, paracentesis and intraperitoneal injection, flow of exudates in the paracolic gutters, and adhesions with adhesiotomy in intestinal obstruction.
C(i)
• The right paracolic gutter provides a route for spread of infection between the pelvic and upper abdominal regions, and the supracolic and infracolic compartments communicate freely through the gutters.
• In the female the cavity communicates with the exterior via the uterine tubes, uterus and vagina.
• Parietal peritoneum is supplied by the nerves of the adjacent body wall and diaphragm; visceral peritoneum by sympathetic nerves of the underlying viscus.
• Receptors respond to overdistension, traction on mesenteries, spasm of smooth muscle and ischaemia.

A(i)
The knee joint is primarily a hinge type of synovial joint. It is the largest and very complex joint in the body. Articulations: femur with tibia (tibiofemoral joint) and femur with patella (patellofemoral joint). Articular bones: (1) Femur — enlarged medial and lateral femoral condyles. (2) Tibia — enlarged medial and lateral tibial condyles (tibial plateaus), which are the receptacles for the femoral condyles; tibia bears most of the weight. (3) Patella — a true sesamoid bone embedded in the quadriceps and patellar tendon; serves as a pulley improving the angle of pull. Fibula is not part of the knee joint and does not articulate with the femur or patella; it only serves as attachment for knee joint structures.
A(ii)
Extracapsular ligaments (5): (1) Patellar ligament — distal part of quadriceps tendon; strong, thick fibrous band passing from apex of patella to tibial tuberosity. (2) Fibular (lateral) collateral ligament — strong, rounded, cordlike; extends from lateral epicondyle of femur to head of fibula; tendon of popliteus passes deep to it, separating it from the lateral meniscus. (3) Tibial (medial) collateral ligament — strong flat band from medial epicondyle of femur to medial condyle and superior part of tibia; firmly attached to medial meniscus; weaker and more often damaged than the fibular collateral ligament. (4) Oblique popliteal ligament — expansion of tendon of semimembranosus; strengthens fibrous capsule posteriorly. (5) Arcuate popliteal ligament — arises from posterior aspect of fibular head; passes superomedially over tendon of popliteus; strengthens fibrous capsule posteriorly. Intra-articular ligaments (3): (1) ACL — from anterior intercondylar area of tibia to lateral condyle of femur; weaker; slack when flexed, taut when extended; prevents posterior displacement of femur on tibia and hyperextension. (2) PCL — from posterior intercondylar area of tibia to medial condyle of femur; stronger; taut during flexion; prevents anterior displacement of femur on tibia; main stabilizing factor in weight-bearing flexed knee. (3) Menisci — crescentic plates of fibrocartilage that deepen the surface and act as shock absorbers.
B(i)
Flexion — hamstrings. Extension — quadriceps. Medial rotation — popliteus, semitendinosus, semimembranosus. Lateral rotation — biceps femoris. Locking: when fully extended with foot on ground, the knee locks because of medial rotation of femur on tibia. Unlocking: popliteus contracts rotating femur laterally so flexion can occur.
B(ii)
Blood supply: genicular branches of femoral artery, popliteal artery, anterior and posterior recurrent branches of anterior tibial recurrent artery, and anterior and posterior branches of circumflex fibular arteries. The middle genicular branches of the popliteal artery penetrate the fibrous capsule and supply the cruciate ligaments, synovial membrane, and peripheral margins of the menisci. Nerve supply: branches of obturator nerve, femoral nerve, tibial nerve, and common fibular nerve.
C(i)
Medial meniscus: C-shaped, broader posteriorly; anterior end attaches to anterior intercondylar area of tibia anterior to ACL; posterior end to posterior intercondylar area anterior to PCL; firmly adheres to tibial collateral ligament. Lateral meniscus: almost circular, smaller and more freely movable; tendon of popliteus separates it from fibular collateral ligament; attached posteriorly via the posterior meniscofemoral ligament to PCL and medial femoral condyle. The medial meniscus is more frequently injured because its firm attachment to the tibial collateral ligament makes it immobile and liable to being trapped and torn when the ligament is stressed; the lateral meniscus is protected by its free mobility.
questions.question:
Describe the knee joint under the following headings and explain its clinical importance.
A(i) Type, articular surfaces, and articular bones
A(ii) Ligaments — classify as extracapsular or intra-articular; describe each fully
B(i) Movements and muscles responsible
B(ii) Blood supply and nerve supply of the knee joint
C(i) Distinguish the medial from the lateral meniscus, and explain the anatomical basis of why the medial meniscus is more frequently injured

Describe the gross anatomy of the humerus:
A(i) Upper end
A(ii) Shaft
A(iii) Lower end
B. State how different parts of the humerus relate to common fracture patterns.
C. Explain how injury at each of these parts may spread to affect a distant structure, causing a functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• The upper end has a large, rounded head joined to the shaft by a constricted surgical neck, and greater and lesser tubercles.
• The tubercles are separated by the intertubercular (bicipital) groove, which lodges the long tendon of biceps brachii and transmits a branch of the anterior humeral circumflex artery to the shoulder joint.
A(ii)
The shaft is circular in section above and flattened in its lower part, bears the deltoid tuberosity, and its posterior aspect shows the spiral groove, which demarcates the origins of the medial and lateral heads of triceps and between which the radial nerve and profunda vessels wind.
A(iii)
The lower end bears the rounded capitulum laterally, for articulation with the radial head, and the spool-shaped trochlea medially, for articulation with the trochlear notch of the ulna; the medial and lateral epicondyles are extracapsular, the medial being the larger, extending more distally and bearing a groove on its posterior aspect for the ulnar nerve.
B
• Fractures of the surgical neck of the humerus are especially common in elderly people with osteoporosis, usually from a minor fall on the hand with the force transmitted up the extended limb.
• Transverse fractures of the shaft frequently result from a direct blow to the arm.
• Fracture of the distal humerus, near the supracondylar ridges, is a supracondylar fracture.
C
• Because the axillary, radial and ulnar nerves are in close contact with the humerus, they may be damaged when the associated part of the bone is fractured.
• Fracture at the surgical neck threatens the axillary nerve, producing deltoid paralysis with loss of abduction and sensory loss over the regimental badge area.
• Fracture through the radial (spiral) groove of the shaft threatens the radial nerve, producing wrist drop.
• Fracture at the medial epicondyle at the lower end threatens the ulnar nerve, while injury at the distal humerus (supracondylar region) threatens the median nerve.
• Fractures of the humeral neck, midshaft and lower end are therefore each associated with a characteristic pattern of nerve injury and resultant functional deficit.

questions.question:
Describe the carpal tunnel:
A(i) Bony wall (carpal arch/sulcus)
A(ii) Fibrous wall (flexor retinaculum)
A(iii) Contents
B. Explain the clinical basis for the median nerve being the structure most adversely affected in carpal tunnel syndrome.
C. Distinguish between the tendons of flexor digitorum profundus and flexor digitorum superficialis as they lie within the tunnel.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The bony wall is the carpal sulcus, formed by the concavity on the anterior aspect of the carpal bones, forming the base and sides of the tunnel; it is bounded laterally by the scaphoid and trapezium tubercles and medially by the hook of the hamate and the pisiform.
A(ii)
The fibrous wall is the flexor retinaculum, a thick connective tissue band that stretches over the carpal sulcus, converting it into the carpal tunnel by bridging the space between the medial and lateral parts of the arch, spanning from the hook of hamate and pisiform medially to the scaphoid and trapezium laterally.
A(iii)
Contents: four tendons of flexor digitorum profundus (the deepest structures), four tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis lying anterior to those of profundus (all eight enclosed in a common synovial sheath), the tendon of flexor pollicis longus occupying the lateral angle of the compartment with its own synovial sheath, and the median nerve, which lies anterior to the tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis, deep to the flexor retinaculum.
B
• Carpal tunnel syndrome may occur following inflammatory reactions (synovitis) in the synovial sheath of the tendons traversing the tunnel.
• Excess fluid, such as follows inflammation of the synovial sheaths, compresses the structures within the confined tunnel.
• The median nerve is the structure most adversely affected, since it lies anterior to the crowded flexor tendons, immediately deep to the unyielding flexor retinaculum, leaving it particularly exposed to any rise in pressure within the tunnel.
• Compression of the median nerve produces sensory disturbance (hypoesthesia or anaesthesia) in the skin of the lateral three and a half fingers on their palmar aspect.
• Weakness or paralysis of the thenar muscles also occurs, because the recurrent branch of the median nerve that supplies these muscles arises in the hand and is also compressed.
C
• Within the tunnel, the tendons of flexor digitorum profundus are the deepest structures.
• The tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis lie anterior to (more superficial than) those of profundus.
• Both sets of four tendons are enclosed together in a single common synovial sheath, whereas the tendon of flexor pollicis longus lies separately at the lateral angle of the compartment, enclosed in its own distinct synovial sheath.
• This layered arrangement of tendons deep to the median nerve means the nerve is the most superficial of the tunnel's principal contents, most exposed to the flexor retinaculum's unyielding roof.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the temporomandibular joint (TMJ) under the following headings: articular surfaces, articular capsule, and synovial membranes/compartments.
A(ii) Describe the ligaments of the TMJ.
B. Explain the clinical basis for why TMJ dislocation is commoner in the aged and in females.
C. Distinguish between the intrinsic (lateral) ligament and the extrinsic ligaments (sphenomandibular and stylomandibular) of the TMJ.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The articular surfaces of the TMJ are the condyle of the mandible (inferior) and the articular tubercle/mandibular fossa of the temporal bone (squamous part). The articular capsule is loose and fibrous, attaching to the margins of the articular area on the temporal bone and around the neck of the mandible. The superior synovial membrane lines the fibrous capsule superior to the articular disc, and the inferior synovial membrane lines the capsule inferior to the disc; the joint is divided into two compartments (superior and inferior) by an articular disc of fibrocartilage.
A(ii)
The ligaments of the TMJ are divided into an intrinsic ligament and extrinsic ligaments. The intrinsic ligament, also known as the lateral ligament, is the thick part of the articular capsule, strengthens the TMJ laterally, and prevents posterior dislocation of the TMJ. The extrinsic ligaments are the sphenomandibular ligament, which runs from the spine of the sphenoid to the lingula of the mandible and is the primary passive support of the mandible, and the stylomandibular ligament, a thickening of the fibrous capsule of the parotid gland, extending from the styloid process of the temporal bone to the angle of the mandible, which does not contribute significantly to the strength of the joint.
B
Dislocation of the TMJ is common in aged persons and females, due to wearing and resorption of the articular eminence and reducing muscle tone with advancing age.
C
The intrinsic (lateral) ligament is the thick part of the articular capsule, strengthens the joint laterally and prevents posterior dislocation. The sphenomandibular ligament, by contrast, runs from the spine of the sphenoid to the lingula of the mandible and is the primary passive support of the mandible, while the stylomandibular ligament is a thickening of the fibrous capsule of the parotid gland, running from the styloid process to the angle of the mandible, and does not contribute significantly to the strength of the joint.

questions.question:
Describe the ulnar nerve:
A(i) Origin
A(ii) Course and common entrapment sites
A(iii) Muscles innervated (forearm and hand)
A(iv) Sensory distribution
C. Explain the anatomical basis of the deformity seen after ulnar nerve injury.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The ulnar nerve is an extension of the medial cord of the brachial plexus.
A(ii)
The most common sites of ulnar nerve entrapment are: above the elbow in the region of the intermuscular septum; the medial epicondylar region; the epicondylar (ulnar) groove; the region of the cubital tunnel; and the region where the nerve exits from flexor carpi ulnaris, where compression is usually caused by the deep flexor-pronator aponeurosis.
A(iii)
• In the forearm it supplies flexor carpi ulnaris and the medial (3rd & 4th) part of flexor digitorum profundus.
• In the hand it supplies the hypothenar muscles, adductor pollicis, flexor pollicis brevis, the palmar and dorsal interossei, the 3rd and 4th lumbricals, and the muscles of digiti minimi (abductor, opponens, flexor digiti minimi).
A(iv)
It provides sensation to the medial surface of the hand and the medial half of the 4th and 5th digits, on both palmar and dorsal aspects, through its superficial branch; its motor functions include finger adduction and abduction other than the thumb, thumb adduction, flexion of digits 4 and 5, and wrist flexion and adduction.
C
• Injury to the ulnar nerve, or to the medial cord/lower trunk from which it derives, produces a claw hand deformity.
• This deformity arises from the unopposed action of the long flexors and extensors of the fingers once the ulnar-innervated intrinsic muscles (interossei, medial lumbricals) are paralysed.
• In a claw hand there is hyperextension at the metacarpophalangeal joints and flexion at the interphalangeal joints.
• Where the injury occurs at the level of the medial cord (e.g. from subcoracoid dislocation of the humerus), the ulnar nerve and medial root of median nerve are both involved.
• This produces sensory loss on the ulnar side of the forearm and hand, along with vasomotor and trophic changes.
• The claw hand deformity, together with the specific pattern of muscle paralysis, thus reflects the level and combination of nerve fibres interrupted along the course of the ulnar nerve or its parent cord/trunk.

questions.question:
Describe the median nerve:
A(i) Formation (roots)
A(ii) Relations in the cubital fossa and at the wrist
A(iii) Branches
A(iv) Distribution
C. Explain the anatomical basis of the deformity seen after a low (wrist-level) injury to the median nerve.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The median nerve is formed by the union of a lateral root from the lateral cord (C5, C6, C7) and a medial root from the medial cord (C8, T1) of the brachial plexus.
A(ii)
In the cubital fossa the median nerve is the most medial of the major vertical contents, lying medial to the brachial artery and the tendon of biceps brachii; at the wrist it lies anterior to the tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis, deep to the flexor retinaculum, within the carpal tunnel.
A(iii)
It gives a palmar cutaneous branch that arises in the forearm, proximal to the flexor retinaculum, and a recurrent branch that arises in the hand to supply the thenar muscles.
A(iv)
It supplies flexor carpi radialis, palmaris longus, pronator teres, pronator quadratus and the digital flexors, producing thumb flexion and opposition, flexion of digits 2 and 3, wrist flexion and abduction, and forearm pronation; it also supplies sensation to the anterolateral surface of the hand.
C
• A low (wrist-level) median nerve injury produces an "ape-like hand."
• There is flattening of the thenar eminence because the recurrent branch supplying abductor pollicis brevis and flexor pollicis brevis, which arises in the hand, is affected.
• Opposition and abduction of the thumb become impossible, so the pincer-like action of the hand is lost, causing difficulty with fine manual tasks such as buttoning.
• Adductor pollicis, being supplied by the ulnar nerve, is unopposed, further contributing to the deformity.
• This contrasts with an elbow-level injury, where flexion of the index and middle fingers is lost (flexor digitorum superficialis and the lateral half of profundus are affected), the ring and little fingers weakly flex, and flexion of the distal phalanx of the thumb is lost, while the interosseous muscles are unaffected, being supplied by the ulnar nerve.
• The median nerve can be torn partially or fully, or compressed, at the elbow, from fracture, other trauma, or compression from fluid build-up following injury.
• The most common site of median nerve injury overall is at the wrist, within the carpal tunnel.

A(i)
The radial nerve is a terminal branch of the posterior cord of the brachial plexus; it courses posteromedially with the axillary vessels and enters the posterior compartment of the arm under teres major, where it winds around the spiral (radial) groove of the humerus, accompanied by the profunda brachii artery.
A(ii)
• It pierces the lateral intermuscular septum to enter the anterior compartment of the arm, passes to the forearm at the level of the elbow joint, enters the cubital fossa, and there divides into a superficial and a deep branch.
• The superficial branch courses toward the wrist lateral to the radial artery and enters the hand, dividing into dorsal digital cutaneous branches; the deep branch gives off the posterior interosseous nerve, which passes between the heads of supinator to enter the posterior compartment of the forearm and terminates near the wrist joint.
A(iii)
Branches include muscular twigs in the arm to triceps brachii and anconeus, the posterior interosseous nerve to the forearm extensors, the superficial (cutaneous) branch, and articular twigs to the elbow and wrist joints.
A(iv)
The deep branch/posterior interosseous nerve supplies the extensor muscles in the forearm as well as brachioradialis; the superficial branch supplies cutaneous sensation to the dorsal aspect of the hand, the dorsal aspect of the first to third digits, and the dorsolateral aspect of the fourth finger.
C
• Injury to the radial nerve produces "wrist drop."
• Because the nerve's deep branch/posterior interosseous nerve supplies the extensor muscles of the forearm, injury interrupts the motor supply to the wrist and finger extensors.
• The nerve can be injured at any level — axilla, spiral groove, radial tunnel, posterior interosseous, or superficial radial.
• Injury may result from fracture of the body (shaft) of the humerus, where the nerve lies in close contact with the bone in the spiral groove.
• "Saturday Night Palsy" describes compression of the nerve in the axilla, such as from using improperly adjusted crutches, which similarly interrupts its motor function.
• With the extensors paralysed and unopposed flexor tone at the wrist, the hand falls into flexion at the wrist, producing the characteristic wrist drop.
questions.question:
Describe the radial nerve:
A(i) Origin and course in the arm
A(ii) Course/division in the cubital fossa and forearm
A(iii) Branches
A(iv) Distribution
C. Explain the anatomical basis of the deformity ("wrist drop") seen after radial nerve injury.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
• 12 pairs of intercostal (thoracic) nerves, the anterior primary rami of the thoracic spinal nerves; they are mixed nerves; T3-6 are typical and T1 and T2 are atypical.
• Atypical nerves: T1 has no anterior cutaneous branch and is joined to the brachial plexus by a large branch corresponding to the lateral cutaneous branch; the lateral cutaneous branch of T2 is the intercostobrachial nerve, joined to the medial cutaneous nerve of the arm.
A(ii)
A typical nerve lies in the neurovascular bundle between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles, high in the space in relation to the subcostal groove of the rib above, below the artery (vein, artery, nerve from above downwards); nerves 1-6 are distributed in the intercostal spaces, 7-11 pass to the anterior abdominal wall, and the anterior ramus of the 12th runs forward in the abdomen as the subcostal nerve.
A(iii)
Branches: rami communicantes, collateral (muscular) branches, lateral cutaneous branch, anterior cutaneous branch, muscular branches, pleural branch and peritoneal branches (7th-11th).
A(iv)
They supply the skin, the muscles of the intercostal space and abdomen, and the parietal pleura and parietal peritoneum; cutaneous supply of the anterior wall is by supraclavicular nerves (C4) above the sternal angle and by the anterior and lateral cutaneous branches below it; the posterior wall is supplied by the posterior rami of the thoracic spinal nerves.
B(i)
• Local anaesthesia of an intercostal space is easily produced by infiltration around the intercostal nerve trunk and its collateral branch (intercostal nerve block).
• A needle or drain is passed immediately above the upper border of a rib, to avoid the neurovascular bundle lying under the rib above.
• In a conventional posterolateral thoracotomy the incision is along the 5th or 6th rib; the periosteum over a segment of the rib is elevated, protecting the neurovascular bundle, and the rib is excised to reach the lung or mediastinum through the intercostal space.
C(i)
• Local irritation of the intercostal nerves (e.g. by Pott's disease, tuberculosis of the thoracic vertebrae) gives pain referred to the front of the chest or abdomen, in the region of the peripheral termination of the nerves.
• Pus from the region of the vertebral column tracks around the thorax along the neurovascular bundle and points at the three sites of exit of the cutaneous branches: lateral to erector spinae, in the midaxillary line and just lateral to the sternum.
• A rib fracture is extremely painful because the periosteum of the rib is supplied by the intercostal nerves above and below the rib; the parietal pleura is segmentally supplied by the intercostal nerves, so pleural disease refers pain along the thoracic wall and anterior abdominal wall.
questions.question:
A(i) State the nature and number of the intercostal nerves and distinguish the typical from the atypical nerves.
A(ii) Describe the course and relations of a typical intercostal nerve.
A(iii) State its branches.
A(iv) Describe its distribution, including the cutaneous supply of the thoracic wall.
B(i) State the safe method and site for anaesthetising an intercostal space and for passing a needle or drain.
C(i) Explain the anatomical basis of the effects of irritation or injury of the intercostal nerves.

A(i) Define the mediastinum and state its extent and boundaries.
A(ii) State its divisions and the plane that separates them.
A(iii) Describe the boundaries and contents of each division.
A(iv) List the structures that occupy more than one division.
B(i) Explain the importance of the level of T4 in relation to the mediastinum.
B(ii) Explain why the mediastinum is vulnerable when the chest wall is severely injured.
C(i) Distinguish between the superior and the inferior mediastinum.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
A highly mobile, bulky connective tissue septum (thick movable partition) in the midline between the right and left pleural cavities and their lungs, containing the heart and great vessels, oesophagus, trachea and its bifurcation, thoracic duct, and vagus and phrenic nerves; superior: root of the neck (thoracic outlet: manubrium, 1st rib, T1); inferior: diaphragm; anterior: sternum; posterior: thoracic vertebrae; lateral: lungs and pleurae.
A(ii)
A horizontal plane from the sternal angle to the lower border of T4 divides it into the superior mediastinum (above) and the inferior mediastinum (below), the latter subdivided into anterior (in front of the heart), middle (containing the heart) and posterior (behind the heart) parts.
A(iii)
• Superior: bounded by the thoracic outlet above, the T4 plane below, the manubrium in front and T1-T4 vertebrae behind; contents from superficial to deep: thymus; right and left brachiocephalic veins and SVC; arch of the aorta with brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid and left subclavian arteries; right and left vagus and phrenic nerves; trachea and oesophagus (most posterior); thoracic duct beside the oesophagus; lymph nodes.
• Anterior: bounded by the T4 plane above, the diaphragm below, the body of the sternum in front and the pericardium/heart behind; contains the thymus, fatty tissue and lymph nodes.
• Middle: lies between the anterior and posterior mediastina; contains the pericardium and heart, ascending aorta, pulmonary trunk, SVC and IVC, right and left pulmonary veins, main bronchi, part of the phrenic nerves and lymph nodes.
• Posterior: bounded by the T4 plane above, the heart/middle mediastinum and diaphragm in front, and the T5 (lower border of T4) to T12 vertebrae behind; contains the oesophagus (most anterior), right and left vagus nerves around it, thoracic duct behind it, azygos vein (behind and to the right), descending aorta (behind and to the left), sympathetic trunks and lymph nodes.
A(iv)
Six structures lie in more than one division: thoracic duct, oesophagus and vagus nerves (superior and posterior); phrenic nerves and SVC (superior and middle); thymus (superior and anterior); lymph nodes are present in all regions.
B(i)
The T4 level marks the sternal angle and the 2nd costal cartilage, the bifurcation of the trachea, the bifurcation of the pulmonary trunk, and the beginning and termination of the arch of the aorta.
B(ii)
The mediastinum is highly mobile; in a stove-in chest the loose chest wall segment produces swinging movements of the mediastinum that cause severe shock.
C(i)
• Superior mediastinum: one part above the T4 plane, bounded in front by the manubrium and behind by T1-T4, containing thymus, great veins, aortic arch and its branches, trachea, oesophagus, thoracic duct, vagus and phrenic nerves.
• Inferior mediastinum: three parts below the T4 plane down to the diaphragm - anterior (thymus and fat, in front of the heart), middle (heart, pericardium, ascending aorta, pulmonary trunk) and posterior (oesophagus, descending aorta, azygos system, thoracic duct, sympathetic trunks).
• Nerves differ by position: the right vagus descends on the right of the trachea, forms the posterior oesophageal plexus and continues as the posterior gastric nerve; the left vagus descends between the left common carotid and left subclavian arteries and forms the anterior oesophageal plexus; the right phrenic descends on the right of the SVC and heart, the left on the left side of the heart.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the complete path of blood flow through the renal blood vessels, from the aorta to the peritubular capillaries or vasa recta.
A(ii) State the nerve supply to the kidneys and name the source.
B(i) Distinguish between the capillary beds associated with cortical nephrons and those associated with juxtamedullary nephrons.
B(ii) Explain the anatomical basis for high blood pressure in the glomerulus.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Path of blood flow:
• Aorta → Renal artery → Segmental artery → Interlobar artery → Arcuate artery → Cortical radiate artery → Afferent arteriole → Glomerulus (capillaries) → Efferent arteriole → Peritubular capillaries (cortical nephrons) or Vasa recta (juxtamedullary nephrons) → Cortical radiate vein → Arcuate vein → Interlobar vein → Renal vein → Inferior vena cava.
• Renal arteries deliver approximately one-quarter (1,200 ml) of cardiac output to the kidneys each minute.
A(ii)
Nerve supply is via sympathetic fibers from the renal plexus.
B(i)
• Cortical nephrons (85% of nephrons): efferent arteriole supplies peritubular capillaries — low-pressure, porous capillaries adapted for absorption of water and solutes; they cling to adjacent renal tubules in the cortex and empty into venules.
• Juxtamedullary nephrons: efferent arteriole supplies vasa recta — long, thin-walled vessels parallel to the long nephron loops; important in formation of concentrated urine.
B(ii)
Blood pressure in the glomerulus is high because:
• Afferent arterioles are larger in diameter than efferent arterioles.
• Arterioles are high-resistance vessels.
• The glomerulus is fed and drained by arterioles (not venules), which maintains the high filtration pressure. The glomerulus is also specialized for filtration, with fenestrated endothelium that is highly porous, allowing filtrate formation.

A(i)
The oesophagus has four constrictions: at 15 cm (cricopharyngeus, upper oesophageal sphincter), at 22.5 cm (crossed by the aortic arch) and 27.5 cm (crossed by the left main bronchus) from the upper incisor teeth, and at 40 cm, where it passes through the right crus of the diaphragm (oesophageal hiatus).
A(ii)
The upper oesophageal sphincter is an anatomical sphincter formed by the cricopharyngeus muscle at the pharyngo-oesophageal junction.
A(iii)
• The lower oesophageal sphincter is a physiological sphincter at the gastro-oesophageal junction with no true muscular thickening.
• It is maintained by the acute angle of entry of the oesophagus into the stomach, compression of the intra-abdominal oesophagus by positive intra-abdominal pressure, prominent mucosal folds at the junction, and the pinch-cock effect of the right crus of the diaphragm.
B
• The constrictions are clinically important because they are sites where swallowed foreign bodies commonly impact.
• They are prone to trauma during instrumentation such as rigid oesophagoscopy.
• They are common sites for stricture formation following ingestion of corrosive substances.
• They are also common sites of oesophageal carcinoma.
C
• The upper oesophageal sphincter is a true anatomical (muscular) sphincter formed by the cricopharyngeus, located at 15 cm from the incisor teeth.
• The lower oesophageal sphincter is a physiological sphincter maintained by mechanical factors at the gastro-oesophageal junction and prevents gastric reflux, rather than a distinct muscular ring controlling food passage.
questions.question:
(A) Describe the oesophagus under the following headings: A(i) its four constrictions along its length A(ii) the upper oesophageal sphincter A(iii) the lower oesophageal sphincter.
(B) Explain the clinical basis of why the areas of constriction are important.
(C) Distinguish between the upper oesophageal sphincter and the lower oesophageal sphincter.

(i) Describe the gross anatomy of the kidney, including its shape, coverings, and internal structure (cortex, medulla, pyramids, sinus, calyces).
(ii) Relate the parts of the kidney to a common renal pathology.
(iii) Explain how disease/obstruction of the kidney or its drainage system can produce a functional deficit at a distance.
questions.answerText:
(i)
• The kidneys are bean-shaped, retroperitoneal organs lying on the posterior abdominal wall from about the T12 to L3 vertebral level, each about 10 cm long, 5 cm wide and 2.5 cm thick, with the right kidney slightly lower due to the liver.
• Each kidney has a superior pole bearing the suprarenal gland, an inferior pole, a convex lateral border, and a concave medial border indented by the renal hilum.
• Coverings, from within outward, are the fibrous (renal) capsule, perirenal fat, renal fascia, and pararenal fat.
• Internally, a dark brown outer cortex surrounds a lighter medulla composed of about a dozen renal pyramids, each with its base toward the cortex and its apex (renal papilla) projecting into a minor calyx; cortex extends between pyramids as renal columns.
• At the hilum, the renal vein lies anterior to the renal artery, which lies anterior to the renal pelvis; the hilum leads into the renal sinus, which contains the pelvis, calyces, vessels, nerves and fat.
• The renal pelvis, a funnel-shaped expansion of the ureter, receives two or three major calyces, each dividing into two or three minor calyces.
(ii)
• Renal (kidney) stones are a clinical consideration associated with the kidney and relate to the calyceal and pelvic system where urine collects before draining into the ureter.
• The renal pyramids and papillae are the sites from which urine is excreted into the minor calyces, so pathology of the papillae or pyramids affects urine drainage.
(iii)
• The ureter has three points of constriction - the pelviureteric junction, where it crosses the pelvic brim, and its intramural (intravesical) course - which are potential sites of obstruction by ureteric stones.
• Obstruction at any of these constrictions causes back-pressure on the kidney, from the collecting system through the pelvis to the pyramids, producing a functional deficit in urine drainage from that kidney.
• Ureteric pain from such obstruction is referred to the ipsilateral lower quadrant of the anterior abdominal wall and especially the groin, showing how a renal or ureteric problem produces a distant clinical effect.
• This referred pain reflects the segmental (T11-T12) sympathetic innervation shared by the ureter and the abdominal wall/groin dermatomes.

questions.question:
A. Describe the gross anatomy of the pterygopalatine fossa under the following headings: description/location, boundaries, and contents.
B. State the communications of the pterygopalatine fossa and relate these to how disease may spread from this region.
C. Explain why disease or infection arising near the pterygopalatine fossa can spread to distant structures such as the orbit, the nasal cavity, the middle cranial fossa or the pharynx, and the functional deficit that could result.
questions.answerText:
A
The pterygopalatine fossa is an inverted pyramidal-shaped, fat-filled space located on the lateral side of the skull, between the infratemporal fossa and the nasopharynx; it is antero-posteriorly between the maxilla/palatine bone and the pterygoid process, and laterally between the infratemporal fossa and nasopharynx. Its boundaries are: anterior - posterior surface of maxilla below the floor of the orbit; posterior - lateral pterygoid plate and part of the medial plate; medial - perpendicular plate of the palatine bone; lateral - pterygomaxillary fissure; superior - undersurface of the greater wing of the sphenoid; inferior - absent (the posterior wall meets the anterior wall, and between them is the greater palatine canal). Its contents are the terminal (third/pterygoid) part of the maxillary artery and the initial parts of its branches, the maxillary vein, the maxillary nerve, and the pterygopalatine ganglion (a parasympathetic ganglion, one of four parasympathetic ganglia of the head and neck, the others being the submandibular, otic and ciliary ganglia).
B
The pterygopalatine fossa is described as a major neurovascular crossroad between the orbit, the nasal cavity, the nasopharynx, the oral cavity, the infratemporal fossa and the cranial fossa. Its communications are: laterally with the infratemporal fossa through the pterygomaxillary fissure; medially with the nasal cavity through the sphenopalatine foramen; anterosuperiorly with the orbit through the inferior orbital fissure; posterosuperiorly with the middle cranial fossa through the foramen rotundum and pterygoid canal; with the palate through the greater and lesser palatine canals and foramina; and with the pharynx through the pterygoid canal and palatovaginal canal - in general, vascular structures enter the fossa through its lateral wall, while nerve structures enter through its posterior wall.
C
Because the pterygopalatine fossa communicates directly with the orbit (via the inferior orbital fissure), the nasal cavity (via the sphenopalatine foramen), the middle cranial fossa (via the foramen rotundum and pterygoid canal), and the pharynx (via the pterygoid canal and palatovaginal canal), disease or infection arising in or near the fossa has multiple direct anatomical routes by which it can spread to these distant sites; clinical correlates noted for this region include hay fever affecting the ganglion here (the pterygopalatine ganglion is also known as the hay fever ganglion), and maxillary nerve block is performed in relation to this fossa.

A(i)
Five lumbar vertebrae (1 to 4 typical, 5 atypical); largest and strongest of the column because supported weight increases inferiorly; superior facets face medially, inferior facets laterally; thick broad spines.
A(ii)
• Large kidney-shaped body, deeper anteriorly; triangular foramen (larger than thoracic, smaller than cervical); short strong pedicles; short thick broad laminae; spine a vertical quadrilateral plate.
• Transverse processes thin and tapering (accessory process); superior articular facets concave facing medially and backwards with the mammillary process; inferior facets convex facing laterally and forwards.
A(iii)
L5: thick short pyramidal transverse processes; largest body, anterior deeper than posterior, creating the sharp lumbosacral angle; small short rounded spine; inferior articular distance equal to or more than the superior.
A(iv)
Joints: intervertebral discs (symphysis) between bodies; synovial joints between arches. Ligaments: anterior and posterior longitudinal, ligamentum flavum, interspinous, supraspinous; iliolumbar ligaments strengthen the L5 to S1 lumbosacral joint.
B(i)
• A lumbar vertebra ossifies from three primary centres (body and each half of the neural arch) appearing in the third month of fetal life; the halves of the arch fuse posteriorly in the first year.
• Failure of fusion of the two halves of the neural arch results in spina bifida; if one primary centre of the body fails, hemivertebra.
B(ii)
• Lumbar spinal stenosis: thought hereditary, a narrow vertebral foramen in one or several vertebrae.
• Excessive lumbar lordosis: abnormal anterior curvature with anterior tilting of the pelvis.
C(i)
• The canal formed by L1 and L2 contains the conus medullaris; the lower three contain the cauda equina; all contain the spinal meninges.
• Stenosis can compress the spinal cord and exiting nerves; the pedicles are related above and below to spinal nerves.
• The right crus of the diaphragm attaches to the upper three lumbar vertebrae and the left crus to the upper two; psoas major arises from the vertebral borders.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the origin, types, and functions of cells found in connective tissue under the following headings: cells of fixed (resident) population and cells of wandering (transient) population.
A(ii) State where the mesenchymal stem-like cells persist in adults and state their clinical significance.
B(i) Explain the anatomical and histological basis of why connective tissue of the head region differs in embryological origin from the rest of the body, and state the clinical implication.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Fixed (resident) cells: Mesenchyme cells — embryonic source of all connective tissue cells; only found in embryos, but some mesenchyme-like cells persist in adult connective tissue. Fibroblasts — most common cell type in connective tissue; elongated, spindle-shaped cells with many cell processes; have oval, pale-staining, regular nuclei with prominent nucleoli; abundant rough endoplasmic reticulum and active Golgi bodies; synthesize collagen, reticular and elastic fibers, and amorphous extracellular substance. Fibrocytes — quiescent fibroblasts; smaller, darker nucleus; less rough ER. Chondroblasts/osteoblasts — synthesize cartilage and bone matrices. Adipocytes — energy storage, thermal insulation. Wandering (transient) cells: Macrophages — ingestion by phagocytosis; antigen presentation; secretion of enzymes and cytokines; long-lived (several months); originate from monocytes in bone marrow. Plasma cells — defense and immune function. Lymphocytes — immune function. Neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils — immune function. Mast cells — immune function. All connective tissue cells are derived from mesenchymal cells.
A(ii)
Mesenchyme-like cells (pericytes) persist in adult connective tissue, including that of tooth pulp and some adipose tissue. These mesenchyme-like cells retain their capacity to differentiate into other connective tissue cells in response to injury (e.g., pericytes — perivascular cells of blood capillaries). They are being investigated as possible sources of stem cells for therapeutic repair and organ regeneration. Some multipotent stem cells potentially useful in regenerative medicine after grafting to replace damaged tissue in certain patients.
B(i)
All connective tissue cells are derived from mesenchymal cells; mesenchyme cells are for the most part derived from the mesoderm. However, several of the connective tissues of the head region are derived from the neural crest cells (ectodermal origin). Endothelial cells lining blood vessels are derived from mesenchyme. The clinical implication is that connective tissue tumors or developmental disorders in the head may follow patterns distinct from those in the rest of the body due to this different embryological derivation.

questions.question:
(i) Describe the gross anatomy of the pancreas - location, shape, and its four parts (head, neck, body, tail) with their relations.
(ii) Relate the parts of the pancreas to pathology (annular pancreas, pancreatitis).
(iii) Explain how pancreatic disease can produce a functional deficit in a distant organ/system.
questions.answerText:
(i)
• The pancreas is a soft, lobulated, J- or retort-shaped gland lying retroperitoneally, except for the tail, and transversely across the posterior abdominal wall at the level of L1-L2, posterior to the stomach, between the duodenum on the right and the spleen on the left; it is about 15-20 cm long and weighs about 90 g.
• The head is disc-shaped, enlarged, and lies within the concavity of the duodenum; the uncinate process projects from its lower part, posterior to the superior mesenteric vessels.
• The neck is the constricted portion connecting the head to the body and overlies the superior mesenteric vessels.
• The body is centrally located, crossing the midline behind the stomach, with anterior, posterior and inferior surfaces; the posterior surface contacts the aorta, splenic vein, left kidney and vessels, left suprarenal gland, origin of the superior mesenteric artery, and the crura of the diaphragm.
• The tail is narrow, lies at the level of T12, ends within the splenic hilum in the splenophrenic ligament, and is the only intraperitoneal part of the pancreas; it may be injured during splenectomy, causing a pancreatic fistula.
• The main pancreatic duct, of Wirsung, begins in the tail and runs to the head, usually joining the bile duct to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla, which opens at the major duodenal papilla; the accessory duct, of Santorini, drains the upper head via the minor duodenal papilla.
(ii)
• Annular pancreas is a rare congenital defect in which the pancreas encircles the duodenum; ectopic pancreatic tissue outside the gastrointestinal tract is a very common anomaly.
• Due to its deep retroperitoneal position, the pancreas is not easily accessible for direct clinical examination, so diagnosis of pancreatic disease relies on ultrasound, CT scan, special investigations of the pancreatic and biliary ducts, and biochemical tests.
• Acute necrotizing pancreatitis results when proenzymes are prematurely activated and digest pancreatic tissue, from causes including infection, gallstones, alcoholism, drugs and trauma.
(iii)
• The endocrine part of the pancreas, the islets of Langerhans, secretes insulin and glucagon into the blood; lack of insulin production by the beta cells, or defective insulin receptors, causes diabetes mellitus, a hyperglycaemic metabolic disorder affecting the whole body.
• Because the exocrine pancreas secretes digestive enzymes and bicarbonate essential for neutralising gastric acid and digesting food in the duodenum, pancreatic disease impairing exocrine secretion produces a functional deficit in intestinal digestion, a distant effect of pancreatic pathology.
• In extreme malnutrition, acinar cell atrophy further reduces digestive enzyme production, compounding this distant digestive deficit.

questions.question:
(i) Describe the origin, course, branches and distribution of the splenic artery.
(ii) State the anatomical basis that makes subtotal (partial) splenectomy a safe surgical option.
(iii) Explain the anatomical basis of the complications that can follow injury to the spleen and its vasculature.
questions.answerText:
(i)
• The spleen receives its arterial supply from the splenic artery, the largest branch of the coeliac trunk.
• The splenic artery runs laterally along the superior aspect of the pancreas, within the splenorenal ligament.
• As it reaches the spleen it branches into about five vessels, each supplying a different vascular segment of the spleen.
• Along its course it also gives off the short gastric and left gastroepiploic arteries to the stomach, and pancreatic branches to the pancreas.
• Venous drainage is through the splenic vein, which combines with the superior mesenteric vein to form the hepatic portal vein.
(ii)
• The terminal arterial branches of the splenic artery do not anastomose with one another, so each supplies an independent vascular segment of the spleen.
• This segmental (end-arterial) arrangement allows a surgeon to remove one diseased or injured segment (subtotal splenectomy) without compromising the blood supply of the remaining segments.
(iii)
• The tail of the pancreas lies within the splenorenal ligament, close to the splenic vessels at the hilum, and may be injured during splenectomy, producing a pancreatic fistula.
• The spleen is the most frequently injured organ in the abdomen despite protection by the 9th to 12th ribs.
• Severe blows to the left side may fracture ribs, producing sharp fragments that lacerate the spleen.
• Blunt trauma elsewhere that suddenly raises intra-abdominal pressure can also rupture the spleen because its capsule is thin and its pulp is soft and pulpy.
• A ruptured spleen bleeds profusely, causing severe intraperitoneal haemorrhage and shock, so splenectomy or subtotal splenectomy is often required to prevent the patient from bleeding to death.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the gross and microscopic structure of the large salivary glands under the following headings: capsule and septa; parenchyma (secretory end pieces); cell types in the secretory end pieces; the duct system in sequence from secretory unit to oral cavity.
A(ii) State the type of secretion produced by each of the three pairs of major salivary glands and by the minor glands.
B(i) Distinguish between striated ducts and intercalated ducts, including location, epithelium, and function.
B(ii) Explain how saliva is modified as it passes through the duct system.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Structure:
• Capsule and septa: a capsule of connective tissue rich in collagen fibers surrounds the large salivary glands; septa of connective tissue originate from the capsule and divide the glands into lobules; each lobule contains numerous secretory units (acini).
• Parenchyma: consists of secretory end pieces and a branching duct system arranged in lobules separated by septae of connective tissue from the capsule. Vessels and nerves enter at the hilum and gradually branch into the lobules.
• Cell types in secretory end pieces: serous cells (polarized protein-secreting cells, pyramidal in shape, round nuclei, well-stained RER, apical secretory granules; joined apically by tight and adherent junctions; form a spherical unit called an acinus with a very small central lumen; secrete enzymes and other proteins); mucous cells; and nonsecretory myoepithelial cells.
• Duct system in sequence: secretory end pieces → intercalated ducts (lined by simple low cuboidal epithelium, surrounded by myoepithelial cells) → striated ducts (intralobular) → interlobular (excretory/striated ducts drain into these) → interlobar ducts → main duct (opens into the oral cavity, lined with nonkeratinized-stratified squamous epithelium).
A(ii)
Secretion types:
• Parotid gland: serous and watery.
• Submandibular and sublingual glands: seromucous secretion.
• Minor glands: mostly mucous.
• Type depends on content of glycoprotein mucin: serous, seromucous, or mucous.
B(i)
• Intercalated ducts: several short intercalated ducts join to form striated ducts; they are lined by cuboidal epithelial cells that have the ability to divide and differentiate into secretory or ductal cells; also called intralobular ducts.
• Striated ducts: characterized by radial striations that extend from the bases of the cells to the level of the central nuclei; striations consist of infoldings of the basal plasma membrane with numerous elongated mitochondria aligned parallel to the infolded membranes (characteristic of ion-transporting cells); they have a folded basal membrane enabling active transport; also called intralobular ducts.
B(ii)
Saliva is modified by the cells of the duct system draining the secretory units: much Na+ and Cl- is reabsorbed while certain growth factors and digestive enzymes are added. Water resorption and ion secretion in the striated ducts make saliva hypotonic (reduced Na and Cl ions; increased carbonate and potassium ions).

A(i)
• The vagus is the 10th cranial nerve.
• The right vagus descends on the right side of the trachea, forms the posterior oesophageal plexus and continues in the abdomen as the posterior gastric nerve.
• The left vagus descends between the left common carotid and left subclavian arteries, forms the anterior oesophageal plexus and continues in the abdomen as the anterior gastric nerve.
A(ii)
• The vagus nerves lie in both the superior and the posterior mediastinum; in the posterior mediastinum the right and left vagi lie around the oesophagus and pass through the oesophageal opening of the diaphragm (T10) as the anterior and posterior vagal trunks.
• The left recurrent laryngeal branch of the vagus winds round the ligamentum arteriosus, which connects the inferior concave surface of the arch of the aorta to the left pulmonary artery.
A(iii)
• Branches: recurrent laryngeal branches on both sides and superior and inferior cervical cardiac branches (the right has both, the left has the inferior branch) to the cardiac plexus; pulmonary plexuses to the lungs; oesophageal plexuses.
• Cardiac plexus: the superficial part lies in front of the ligamentum arteriosus (inferior cervical cardiac branch of the left vagus); the deep part lies in front of the left bronchus and at the bifurcation of the pulmonary trunk, behind the arch of the aorta on the lowest part of the trachea; parasympathetic fibres relay in the heart.
A(iv)
• Heart: through the cardiac plexus to the SA and AV nodes and the AV bundle; parasympathetics decrease the rate of impulse generation, sympathetics increase it.
• Lungs and visceral pleura (via the pulmonary plexuses): bronchoconstrictor, vasodilator to pulmonary vessels and secretomotor to glands; the vagal efferents mediate the cough reflex that clears secretions and dust.
• Oesophagus and trachea: recurrent laryngeal branch to the striated upper third of the oesophagus, parasympathetic secretomotor fibres to the oesophageal glands; vagus to the mucous membrane and parasympathetics of the trachea; gastric irritation of vagus nerve endings may cause hiccup.
questions.question:
A(i) State the nature of the vagus nerve and describe its course in the thorax on the right and left.
A(ii) Describe its relations in the mediastinum.
A(iii) State its branches and plexuses in the thorax.
A(iv) Describe its distribution to thoracic structures.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Quadriceps femoris forms the main bulk of the anterior thigh muscles; it collectively constitutes the largest and one of the most powerful muscles of the body. It covers almost all the anterior aspect and sides of the femur. It is the great extensor of the leg. It consists of 4 muscles: rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, vastus medialis, and vastus intermedius. The tendons of the four parts unite in the distal portion of the thigh to form a single, strong, broad tendon — the quadriceps tendon; this continues as the patellar ligament (in which the patella is embedded) and is attached to the tibial tuberosity.
A(ii)
Rectus femoris — origin: anterior inferior iliac spine and ilium superior to acetabulum; insertion: via common quadriceps tendon and patellar ligament to tibial tuberosity; innervation: femoral nerve (L2, L3, L4); action: extends leg at knee joint, steadies hip joint, and helps iliopsoas flex thigh. It is the only part of the quadriceps that crosses the hip joint, named because it runs straight down the thigh. Vastus lateralis — origin: greater trochanter and lateral lip of linea aspera of femur; same insertion and innervation; action: extends leg at knee joint; it is the largest component. Vastus medialis — origin: intertrochanteric line and medial lip of linea aspera of femur; same insertion and innervation; action: extends leg at knee joint; inferior fibres are particularly important in stabilising the knee joint. Vastus intermedius — origin: anterior and lateral surfaces of shaft of femur; same insertion and innervation; action: extends leg at knee joint; lies deep to rectus femoris between the vastus medialis and lateralis.
B(i)
The quadriceps is the primary extensor of the knee — the most important movement for standing, walking, climbing stairs, and rising from a chair. Stability of the knee joint depends on the strength and action of surrounding muscles and tendons; the quadriceps femoris is most important in stabilising the knee joint. Paralysis means the patient cannot extend the knee or control descent on stairs, rendering them unable to walk safely without a brace.
B(ii)
All four components of the quadriceps are innervated by the femoral nerve (L2, L3, L4). The femoral nerve also supplies the hip joint via intermediate and cutaneous branches and the skin of the front and medial side of the thigh (Hilton's law). Loss of knee extension eliminates the ability to straighten or stabilise the knee against gravity — the most critical functional deficit for bipedal locomotion.
C(i)
Quadriceps femoris: origin from femur and ilium; action — extends the knee (and rectus femoris also flexes the hip); nerve supply — femoral nerve (L2, L3, L4). Hamstrings (semitendinosus, semimembranosus, biceps femoris): origin from ischial tuberosity (long head of biceps femoris and both semi-muscles) and linea aspera (short head of biceps femoris); action — extend the thigh, flex the leg, and rotate it (semitendinosus and semimembranosus medially, biceps femoris laterally); nerve supply — tibial division of sciatic nerve for semitendinosus, semimembranosus, and long head of biceps femoris; common fibular division of sciatic nerve for short head of biceps femoris. The quadriceps is 3 times stronger than its antagonist muscle group (the hamstrings).
questions.question:
Describe the quadriceps femoris muscle fully under the following headings, explain why its paralysis causes the most profound disability of any single muscle in the lower limb, and distinguish it from the hamstrings.
A(i) General features: number of components, collective description, and composite tendon
A(ii) Origin, insertion, innervation, and action of each component
B(i) Why paralysis of the quadriceps femoris produces more functional disability than paralysis of the hamstrings
B(ii) The femoral nerve — its role in supplying the quadriceps and why knee extension is the most critical movement lost
C(i) Distinguish the quadriceps femoris from the hamstrings with respect to origin, action, and nerve supply; state the numerical strength ratio

questions.answerText:
A(i)
The anterior branch of the abdominal aorta supplying the midgut; it arises immediately below the celiac artery, anterior to the lower part of vertebra LI.
A(ii)
• It is crossed anteriorly by the splenic vein and the neck of the pancreas; posterior to it are the left renal vein, the uncinate process of the pancreas and the inferior part of the duodenum.
• The middle colic artery arises as it emerges from beneath the pancreas.
A(iii)
• First branch: inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery, dividing into anterior and posterior branches that anastomose with the superior pancreaticoduodenal arteries.
• Left side: numerous jejunal and ileal arteries passing between the two layers of the mesentery to form arcades, whose number increases distally.
• Vasa recta: long, close together and narrow windows in the jejunum; short, far apart and low broad windows in the ileum.
• Right side: middle colic (transverse mesocolon; anastomoses with left colic), right colic (inconsistent, retroperitoneal) and ileocolic arteries.
• The ileocolic divides into superior and inferior branches; the inferior gives colic, cecal, appendicular (in the mesoappendix free margin) and ileal branches.
A(iv)
• Midgut: duodenum below the major papilla, jejunum, ileum, cecum, appendix, ascending colon and right two-thirds of the transverse colon.
• The midgut ends at the junction of the proximal two-thirds and distal one-third of the transverse colon.

A(i)
Collagen fibers: protein fibers that form the bulk of connective tissue fibers. Major types and distribution: Type I collagen — fibril-forming; found in bone, dermis, tendon, ligaments, and cornea; produced by fibroblasts, osteoblasts, odontoblasts. Type II collagen — fibril-forming; found in cartilage and vitreous body of the eye; produced by chondrocytes and retinal cells. Type III collagen — fibril-forming; found in loose connective tissue and reticular fibers in lungs, liver, and spleen; produced by fibroblasts and reticular cells. Type IV collagen — network-forming; found in basement membranes; produced by epithelial and endothelial cells. Type XI collagen — fibrillar; found in cartilage. Elastic fibers: present in elastic connective tissue; provide elasticity. Reticular fibers: fine fibers present in reticular connective tissue; form reticular (meshwork) framework of organs.
A(ii)
Dense regular connective tissue is present in tendons and ligaments because it is organized to withstand forces from specific directions; the regular parallel arrangement of collagen type I fibers allows maximum tensile strength along the axis of the tendon or ligament.
B(i)
The regenerative capacity of connective tissue is clearly observed in organs damaged by ischemia, inflammation, or traumatic injury. Spaces left after such injuries, especially in tissues whose cells divide poorly or not at all (e.g., cardiac muscle), are filled by connective tissue, forming dense irregular scar tissue. The healing of surgical incisions and other wounds depends on the reparative capacity of connective tissue and the activity of fibroblasts. Fibroblasts synthesize collagen, reticular and elastic fibers, and the amorphous extracellular substance. In some rapidly closing wounds, a cell called the myofibroblast (with features of both fibroblasts and smooth muscle cells) is observed. Myofibroblasts have most of the morphologic characteristics of fibroblasts but contain increased amounts of actin microfilaments and myosin and behave like smooth muscle cells. Their activity is responsible for wound contraction (wound closure after tissue injury).
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the origin, composition, and classification of connective tissue fibers under the following headings: collagen fibers (types and tissue distribution), elastic fibers, and reticular fibers.
A(ii) State the safe structural principle that makes collagen type I dominant in tendons and ligaments.
B(i) Explain the anatomical basis of scar formation after organ injury, with specific reference to fibroblasts and myofibroblasts.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Three tunics: The eye has three layers. Outer tunic: the sclera and cornea; the sclera serves primarily as a structural support for the optic apparatus. Middle layer (vascular layer, uvea): the choroid, ciliary body, and iris. The iris functions as a contractile diaphragm (the aperture of the eye). Inner tunic: the retina — a double-layered epithelium consisting of an outer pigmented layer and an inner neural retina; it is subdivided into 10 recognizable layers. The outermost layer (closest to the choriocapillaris) contains the photoreceptors whose outer segments are in close contact with pigmented epithelial cells. Contents: the vitreous body fills the space between the lens and retina; the aqueous humor is in the anterior and posterior chambers; the lens is a transparent biconvex structure that, along with the cornea, focuses light on the retina. Photoreceptors: rods — more sensitive to light, primarily used in dim light. Cones — require more intense lighting; conical in shape. There are also bipolar cells, horizontal cells, amacrine cells, and Müller glia cells, and a retinal ganglion cell layer.
A(ii)
Cataract: when the lens becomes opaque, the condition is termed cataract, which may also be caused by excessive exposure to ultraviolet radiation. Histological changes: the lens has three principal components — lens capsule (corresponds to a thick, elastic basal lamina), subcapsular epithelium, and lens fibers. Opacification of the lens fibers makes them less transparent; this is the basis of cataract. A myopic (short-sighted) eye can be corrected by wearing glasses with concave lenses; a hyperopic eye with convex lenses.
B(i)
Retinal pigment epithelium (RPE): the outer cell layer is pigmented; it lies between the choroid and the neural retina; Bruch's membrane is located between the choroid and the RPE. Tight junctions between RPE cells establish a blood-retina barrier. Neural retina: the inner cell layer; it is a multi-layered structure containing photoreceptors (rods and cones), neurons, and glial cells. The optic nerve (and the retina) arises in the embryo as an outgrowth of the diencephalon (forebrain); thus the optic nerve is not a true peripheral nerve — its myelin is produced by oligodendrocytes (not Schwann cells), and it is associated with multiple sclerosis.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the histology of the eye under the following headings: three tunics (layers) of the eyeball, contents of each layer, and the photoreceptor cell types in the retina.
A(ii) Explain the clinical basis of cataract and state the histological changes in the lens.
B(i) Distinguish between the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and the neural retina, stating the function of each and their embryological origin.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
• A strong, incomplete fibrous compartment of the rectus abdominis and pyramidalis, formed by the aponeuroses of the three flat muscles.
• The linea alba separates the right and left rectus abdominis; the linea semilunaris marks the lateral border; tendinous intersections and linea alba give the 'six packs'.
A(ii)
It has an anterior and posterior wall for most of its length: anterior wall from the aponeuroses of external oblique and half of internal oblique; posterior wall from the aponeuroses of half of internal oblique and transversus abdominis.
A(iii)
• Superior and inferior epigastric arteries and veins, lymphatic vessels and the distal portions of the thoracoabdominal nerves (anterior rami of T7 to T12).
• Superior epigastric: terminal branch of internal thoracic, descends posterior to the muscle, anastomoses with inferior epigastric; inferior epigastric: from external iliac, enters the sheath at the arcuate line.
A(iv)
A strong expandable support; protects viscera from injury such as a low blow in boxing; compresses the abdominal contents; maintains or increases intra-abdominal pressure; moves the trunk and maintains posture.
B(i)
• In anterior cutaneous nerve entrapment syndrome (ACNES), 12 of 95 adolescents with chronic abdominal pain had it; the Carnett sign was positive at the lateral border of rectus abdominis in all 12.
• Altered skin sensation was present in 11 of 12; the distal thoracoabdominal nerves run in the rectus sheath.
• After treatment (1 to 3 injections, n = 5; neurectomy, n = 7) pain was absent in 11; the conclusion was that ACNES is present in 1 of 8 such adolescents.
C(i)
• Rectus abdominis: long paired muscle split by the linea alba, origin pubic crest, insertion xiphoid process and costal cartilages of ribs 5 to 7, nerve T7 to T11, stabilises the pelvis in walking and depresses the ribs.
• Pyramidalis: small triangular muscle superficial to rectus, base on the pubis and apex on the linea alba, origin pubic crest and symphysis, insertion linea alba, tenses the linea alba; nerve supply is the subcostal nerve (T12).

A(i)
Basic architecture:
• Capsule: the outer surface of the liver is composed of a fibrous/connective tissue capsule (Glisson's capsule); the outermost surface is covered by a thin layer of mesothelial cells that arise from the peritoneum.
• Parenchyma: the capsule surrounds the liver parenchyma, composed of hepatocytes — large polygonal cells with eosinophilic (pink) cytoplasm, round nuclei, and prominent nucleoli.
• Bile canaliculi: spaces present between the plasma membranes of adjacent liver cells.
• Perisinusoidal space of Disse: separates the surface of the liver cell from the endothelial lining of the sinusoid.
A(ii)
Three models:
• Classic (hepatic) lobule: based on blood flow; organised as hexagons, with the central vein (CV) in the centre and portal tracts (PTs) at the periphery (corners of the hexagon). Each PT consists of hepatic artery (HA), portal vein (PV), and bile duct (BD).
• Portal lobule: based on bile flow; organised as triangles, with a portal tract at the centre and central veins at the periphery (corners of the triangle). Flow of bile is in the opposite direction to blood flow.
• Hepatic acinus (acinus of Rappaport): based on blood perfusion; organised as a diamond, with portal tracts at the corners of the short axis and central veins at the corners of the long axis.
B(i)
Zones of the hepatic acinus:
• Zone 1: receives the most oxygenated blood and nutrients.
• Zone 2: intermediate oxygenation and nutrient supply.
• Zone 3: receives the least oxygenated blood and nutrients.
B(ii)
Bile flow pathway:
• Bile canaliculi → Canals of Hering → Bile ductules → Interlobular bile ducts → Intrahepatic ducts → Right and left hepatic ducts → Common hepatic duct → joins with cystic duct to form the common bile duct → Duodenum.
questions.question:

A(ii) There are three different ways to represent the microscopic organisation of the liver parenchyma. Name and describe each model, stating the geometric shape used and the central and peripheral reference points for each.
B(i) Describe the three zones of the hepatic acinus (acinus of Rappaport), stating what distinguishes each zone.
