A(i) Describe the gross anatomy of the pancreas, including its nature as a gland, its retroperitoneal position, its capsular covering, and how its parenchyma is organised into lobules.
A(ii) Describe the two functional components of the pancreas (exocrine and endocrine), including the cell types involved and the products of each.
B(i) Describe the exocrine secretory acini of the pancreas, including the arrangement around the acini and the volume of juice produced.
B(ii) Explain the role of the pancreas in digestion and hormonal regulation, and contrast this with the role of the liver and the gallbladder.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Gross anatomy of the pancreas:
• Nature: a mixed exocrine-endocrine gland that produces both digestive enzymes and hormones.
• Position: retroperitoneally positioned on the posterior wall of the abdominal cavity at the level of the 2nd and 3rd lumbar vertebrae.
• Capsular covering: it has no distinct capsule, but is covered by a thin layer of loose connective tissue, from which septa extend to cover the larger vessels and ducts and to separate the parenchyma into lobules.
A(ii)
Two functional components:
• Exocrine: produces digestive enzymes that act in the small intestine; secretory acini produce about 1.6 litres of pancreatic juice every day.
• Endocrine: involves primarily smaller cells similar to enteroendocrine cells located in variously sized clusters called the pancreatic islets (islets of Langerhans); secretes hormones such as insulin and glucagon into the bloodstream, which are very important for the metabolism of absorbed nutrients.
B(i)
Exocrine acini:
• The secretory acini are surrounded by a basal lamina that is supported only by a delicate sheath of reticular fibers with a rich capillary network.
• The exocrine part produces about 1.6 litres of pancreatic juice every day.
B(ii)
• Pancreas: produces digestive enzymes that act in the small intestine; secretes insulin and glucagon, both important for metabolism of absorbed nutrients.
• Liver: produces bile, an important fluid in the digestion of fats; plays a major role in lipid, carbohydrate, and protein metabolism; inactivates and metabolizes many toxic substances and drugs; participates in iron metabolism and the synthesis of blood proteins and factors necessary for blood coagulation.
• Gallbladder: absorbs water from bile and stores bile in a concentrated form.

A
The only artery supplying structures in the orbit is the ophthalmic artery, which is a branch of the internal carotid artery; it enters the orbit with the optic nerve through the optic foramen (canal). Its branches include the lacrimal artery (to the lacrimal gland and upper eyelid), muscular branches to the muscles, long posterior ciliary arteries (to the ciliary body), short posterior ciliary arteries (to the choroid and part of the optic nerve), and medial palpebral arteries (to the eyelids).
B
The ophthalmic artery gives rise to the very important branch, the central artery of the retina; because the ophthalmic artery is the only artery supplying orbital structures, and the central retinal artery is its branch, the retina is dependent on this single arterial source, so the optic nerve is covered by dura, arachnoid and pia from the sclera to the canal, where the dura is continuous with the periosteum of the orbit, and venous drainage (superior and inferior ophthalmic veins) communicates with the cavernous sinus, giving direct communication between the skin of the face and the cavernous sinus (the danger triangle).

• 3.8 cm long, an anteroposterior slit; anterior wall shorter, posterior longer; begins one inch below and in front of the tip of the coccyx at the recto-anal junction, runs down and backwards, ends at the anus.
• Relations: laterally the ischioanal fossa; posteriorly the anococcygeal raphe; anteriorly the perineal body with bulb of penis and spongy urethra (male), or perineal body and posterior vaginal wall (female).

• The pectinate (dentate) line is the mucocutaneous junction at the level of the anal valves; Hilton's white line lies at the lower end of the internal sphincter.
• Upper area 15 mm (columns, valves, papillae, sinuses, glands); intermediate area 15 mm (pecten, stratified squamous without sebaceous or sweat glands); lower area 8 mm (true skin).
A(iii)
Internal sphincter: thickened involuntary circular muscle around the upper three-quarters, sympathetic L1, L2 and parasympathetic S2 to S4. External sphincter: striated voluntary, whole length, subcutaneous, superficial and deep parts, supplied by the inferior rectal nerve (pudendal) and perineal branch of S4.
B(i)
Internal haemorrhoids: above Hilton's line, tributaries of the superior rectal vein, painless (primary piles at 3, 7 and 11 o'clock); external: below the line, inferior rectal vein, painful.
B(ii)
Anal sinuses are recesses above the anal columns where foreign bodies may impact and cause infection; infection of the anal glands in the sinus floors may lead to anal fistula; rupture of an anal valve with a tag is a sentinel pile.
B(iii)
Anal columns of Morgagni (6 to 10 folds with superior rectal vein radicles); anal valves of Ball form the pectinate line; anal papillae are remnants of the anal membrane.
C(i)
Above: superior rectal artery with drainage by the superior rectal vein (portal); below: inferior rectal artery (internal pudendal) with the middle rectal artery, draining to the internal iliac vein (systemic).
C(ii)
Above the pectinate line lymph goes to the internal iliac nodes; below it to the superficial inguinal nodes.
C(iii)
Above the line the fibres are autonomic and pain-insensitive to stretch; below, the inferior rectal nerve is sensitive to pain and touch.
C(iv)
Above the line is hindgut/endodermal with columnar epithelium; below is cloacal membrane/ectodermal with stratified epithelium; the lower third has somatic supply (inferior rectal nerves).

questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Mucosa: consists of an epithelial lining, lamina propria (zone of loose connective tissue rich in blood vessels, lymphatics, lymphocytes, smooth muscle cells, and sometimes small glands), and muscularis mucosae (thin layer of smooth muscle that separates the mucosa from the submucosa and allows local movements of the mucosa).
• Submucosa: denser connective tissue containing larger blood and lymph vessels, the submucosal (Meissner) plexus of autonomic nerves, and possibly glands and lymphoid tissue.
• Muscularis (muscularis externa): thick layer of smooth muscle organized into an internal circular sublayer and an external longitudinal sublayer; connective tissue between them contains blood vessels, lymph vessels, and the myenteric (Auerbach) nerve plexus.
• Serosa: outermost layer; a thin sheet of loose connective tissue covered with mesothelium (simple squamous covering epithelium); rich in blood vessels, lymphatics, and adipose tissue.
A(ii)
• Submucosal (Meissner) plexus: located in the submucosa between the submucosa and the muscularis; together with the myenteric plexus constitutes the local enteric nervous system.
• Myenteric (Auerbach) plexus: located in the connective tissue between the circular and longitudinal muscle sublayers; responsible for local contraction of the muscularis, mixing and propelling the contents of the lumen (peristalsis).
• Both plexuses together form the local enteric nervous system, which functions independently of the CNS; they are composed mainly of nerve cell aggregates forming small parasympathetic ganglia, numerous in regions of greatest motility.
B(i)
The esophagus is not suspended in a cavity but is bound directly to adjacent structures, so instead of a serosa it has a thick adventitia. The adventitia consists of connective tissue containing vessels and nerves but lacks mesothelium, whereas the serosa is covered by mesothelium.
B(ii)
The serosa of the small and large intestines is continuous with parts of the mesentery. The mesentery is a large fold of adipose connective tissue covered on both sides by mesothelium; it suspends the intestines and is continuous with the peritoneum (the serous membrane lining the abdominal cavity).

questions.answerText:
A(i)
• A pear-shaped fibromuscular sac that stores and concentrates bile, in the gallbladder fossa on the inferior surface of the right lobe of the liver, 7 to 10 cm long, 3 cm broad and 30 to 50 ml in capacity.
• Fundus: projects beyond the inferior border of the liver, covered by peritoneum on all sides. Body: superior surface adherent to the liver and devoid of peritoneum. Neck: upper narrow part ending in the cystic duct, with a spiral fold.
• The fundus is related to the anterior abdominal wall and transverse colon; the body's inferior surface to the transverse colon and the 1st and 2nd parts of the duodenum.
A(ii)
• Right and left hepatic ducts emerge at the porta hepatis; the common hepatic duct (3 to 4 cm) is joined by the cystic duct (3 to 4 cm, spiral folds of Heister) to form the common bile duct.
• The common bile duct (about 8 cm, 6 mm wide) has supraduodenal, retroduodenal, infraduodenal and intraduodenal parts, joining the main pancreatic duct at the hepatopancreatic ampulla.
A(iii)
• Cystic artery (from the right hepatic artery) is the chief supply, with the cystic vein to the portal vein; the posterior superior pancreaticoduodenal branches supply the lower bile duct.
• Sympathetic nerves come from the celiac plexus and parasympathetic from the vagus.
B(i)
The posteromedial wall of the neck may dilate as Hartmann's pouch, where gallstones may lodge.
B(ii)
Calot's triangle (liver inferior surface, common hepatic duct, cystic duct) locates the cystic artery in laparoscopic cholecystectomy; Lund's node enlarges in cholecystitis or cholangitis and may be removed.
B(iii)
Gallbladder muscle and the sphincter of Oddi have reciprocal innervation (gallbladder contracts, sphincter relaxes); disruption is biliary dyskinesia.
C(i)
• Inflammation irritates the subdiaphragmatic parietal peritoneum supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3, 4, 5), referred to the right shoulder tip supplied by the supraclavicular nerve (C3, C4).
• In Murphy's sign the inflamed gallbladder descends on deep inspiration and contacts the palpating hand at the right costal margin, causing pain and a caught breath.

(i) Describe the origin, course, branches and distribution of the right and left coronary arteries.
(ii) State which artery gives off the posterior interventricular artery in most individuals (arterial dominance).
(iii) Explain the anatomical basis for the pattern of myocardial damage that follows occlusion of a particular coronary artery.
questions.answerText:
(i)
• The right and left coronary arteries are the first branches of the aorta, arising from the corresponding right and left aortic sinuses at the proximal ascending aorta.
• The right coronary artery runs in the atrioventricular (coronary) groove and gives off the SA nodal branch, right marginal branch, AV nodal branch, and posterior interventricular branch, which anastomoses with the anterior interventricular branch of the left coronary artery.
• The right coronary artery typically supplies the right atrium, most of the right ventricle, part of the left ventricle, the posterior third of the AV septum, the SA node in 60% of people and the AV node in 80% of people.
• The left coronary artery arises from the left aortic sinus, runs in the AV groove, and divides into the circumflex and anterior interventricular branches.
• The left coronary artery typically supplies the left atrium, most of the left ventricle, part of the right ventricle, most of the interventricular septum and the SA node in 40% of people.
• Venous drainage is mainly through the coronary sinus, which receives the great, middle and small cardiac veins and the left posterior ventricular and left marginal veins.
(ii)
Arterial dominance is defined by which artery gives rise to the posterior interventricular artery; right dominance is typical, the left is dominant in about 10% of people, and co-dominance occurs in about 15% of people.
(iii)
• Because the right coronary artery mainly supplies the right atrium, right ventricle and, in most people, the SA and AV nodes, its occlusion can damage right-sided myocardium and disturb the conduction system.
• Because the left coronary artery mainly supplies the left atrium, left ventricle and interventricular septum, its occlusion tends to damage the left ventricle, which performs more work than the right, and the septum.
• Damage to the region supplying the SA or AV node can disturb the heart's conducting system, since the SA and AV nodes are the pacesetters of the heart.
• Tissue damage from reduced blood flow in the territory of the affected artery causes the chest pain of ischaemia/infarction, which can radiate as referred pain to the jaw and left arm.

A(i)
The glenohumeral (shoulder) joint is a multiaxial synovial joint of the ball-and-socket variety, formed by articulation between the head of the humerus and the glenoid cavity of the scapula; due to the very limited interface between humerus and scapula, it is the most mobile joint in the human body.
A(ii)
The joint capsule is a fibrous sheath enclosing the joint structures; it is thin and lax to allow a wide range of movement (particularly abduction), is strengthened by muscles and ligaments, but is weakest inferiorly, placing it at risk of dislocation in that direction. It is lined by synovial membrane and forms a tubular sheath around the tendon of the long head of biceps, and a number of bursae aid mobility.
A(iii)
• Factors contributing to mobility are the ball-and-socket joint type, the shallow glenoid cavity against the large humeral head (a 1:4 disproportion, likened to a golf ball and tee), and laxity of the joint capsule.
• Factors contributing to stability are the rotator cuff muscles, whose resting tone pulls the humeral head into the glenoid cavity, the glenoid labrum, which deepens the cavity and reduces dislocation risk, and the ligaments, which reinforce the capsule and form the coraco-acromial arch.
B
• The glenohumeral joint is the most commonly dislocated joint in the body, accounting for approximately 95% of all shoulder dislocations, and anterior dislocations are the most prevalent.
• An anterior dislocation is usually caused by excessive extension and lateral rotation of the humerus, which forces the humeral head anteriorly and inferiorly into the weakest (inferior) part of the joint capsule.
• Tearing of the joint capsule during dislocation is associated with an increased risk of future (recurrent) dislocations.
C
• The axillary nerve runs in close proximity to the shoulder joint and can be damaged during dislocation.
• Injury to the axillary nerve causes paralysis of the deltoid muscle, with loss of sensation over the "regimental badge" area of skin overlying the deltoid.
• A dislocation can also stretch the radial nerve, since it is tightly bound within the radial (spiral) groove of the humerus.
• These nerve injuries represent the spread of the joint pathology to distant neurological structures.
• The resulting functional deficits include loss of shoulder abduction and sensory loss from axillary nerve injury, reflecting how a purely mechanical joint injury can produce a distinct neurological deficit at a distance from the joint itself.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Tibialis anterior: origin — lateral condyle and superior half of lateral surface of tibia and interosseous membrane; insertion — medial and inferior surfaces of medial cuneiform and base of 1st metatarsal; innervation — deep fibular nerve (L4, L5); action — dorsiflexes ankle and inverts foot. Extensor digitorum longus: origin — lateral condyle of tibia and superior 3/4 of medial surface of fibula and interosseous membrane; insertion — middle and distal phalanges of lateral 4 digits; innervation — deep fibular nerve (L4, L5); action — extends lateral 4 digits and dorsiflexes ankle. Extensor hallucis longus: origin — middle part of anterior surface of fibula and interosseous membrane; insertion — dorsal aspect of base of distal phalanx of great toe; innervation — deep fibular nerve (L4, L5); action — extends great toe and dorsiflexes ankle. Fibularis tertius: origin — inferior 3rd of anterior surface of fibula and interosseous membrane; insertion — dorsum of base of 5th metatarsal; innervation — deep fibular nerve (L4, L5); action — dorsiflexes ankle and aids in eversion of foot.
A(ii)
The dorsalis pedis artery begins as the anterior tibial artery enters the foot. It passes over the dorsal aspect of the tarsal bones, then moves inferiorly towards the sole of the foot. It then anastomoses with the lateral plantar artery to form the deep plantar arch. It supplies the tarsal bones and the dorsal aspect of the metatarsals; via the deep plantar arch, it also contributes to the supply of the toes. The dorsalis pedis pulse is found by palpating on the dorsum of the foot, just lateral to extensor hallucis longus tendon.
B(i)
The common fibular nerve is the lateral, smaller terminal branch of the sciatic nerve; it begins at the superior angle of the popliteal fossa, closely follows the medial border of biceps femoris, exits the fossa superficial to the lateral head of gastrocnemius, passes over the posterior aspect of the head of fibula, and winds around the neck of fibula where it divides into its terminal branches — the deep fibular nerve and superficial fibular nerve. The deep fibular nerve supplies all 4 muscles of the anterior compartment (tibialis anterior, extensor digitorum longus, extensor hallucis longus, fibularis tertius) and the foot.
B(ii)
At the neck of fibula the common fibular nerve is subcutaneous and directly palpable, making it vulnerable to direct trauma, compression, or traction. Injury here interrupts the deep fibular nerve before it reaches the anterior compartment. All 4 anterior compartment muscles (which perform dorsiflexion and toe extension) are paralysed. The result is foot drop: the foot hangs in plantarflexion and inversion (because the unopposed plantarflexors — gastrocnemius, soleus — and invertor — tibialis posterior — continue to act), and the patient develops a high-stepping gait to clear the dragging toe.
C(i)
Tibialis anterior: dorsiflexes the ankle AND inverts the foot; supplied by the deep fibular nerve (L4, L5). Fibularis tertius: dorsiflexes the ankle AND aids eversion of the foot; supplied by the deep fibular nerve (L4, L5). Both share the same nerve supply but perform opposite movements about the subtalar axis (inversion vs. eversion), reflecting their positions on opposite sides of the interosseous membrane.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Shape of a clenched fist; base to apex 12 cm in males and 10 cm in females, anteroposterior 6 cm and 5 cm, transverse 9 cm and 8 cm; weight 280-340 g in males and 230-280 g in females; lies behind the body of the sternum, in front of T5-T8, with a base, an apex, 3 surfaces and 4 borders.
• Base: posterior, mostly left atrium, receives the 4 pulmonary veins; ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk emerge from it; separated from the diaphragmatic surface by the coronary sulcus. Apex: inferolateral, mostly left ventricle, behind the 5th left intercostal space. Surfaces: sternocostal (mostly right ventricle), diaphragmatic (concave), pulmonary (left ventricle, fitting the cardiac notch of the left lung). Borders: right (right atrium), left (mostly left ventricle with the left auricle), superior (auricles and upper right ventricle), inferior (right atrium and right ventricle).
A(ii)
Right border: 3rd to 6th right costal cartilage; left border: 5th left intercostal space (apex beat, 9 cm from the midline) up to the 2nd costal cartilage; superior border: 2nd left to 3rd right costal cartilage; inferior border: 6th right costal cartilage to the 5th left intercostal space.
A(iii)
• Four chambers: atria separated by the interatrial septum, ventricles by the interventricular septum, atria from ventricles by the right and left coronary (AV) sulci. Right atrium: forms the right border, lies between SVC and IVC, has the right auricle; rough part (musculi pectinati) and smooth part (from the right horn of the sinus venosus) separated by the sulcus terminalis (crista terminalis); receives SVC, IVC and coronary sinus.
• Right ventricle: forms the sternocostal and diaphragmatic surfaces and inferior border; trabeculae carneae including the septomarginal trabecula (carries part of the AV bundle) and anterior, posterior and septal papillary muscles joined by chordae tendineae to the tricuspid valve (3 cusps, admits 3 fingertips), the chordae preventing the cusps being driven into the right atrium; pulmonary orifice about 2.5 cm with 3 semilunar cusps (anterior, left, right).
• Left atrium: posterior, forms the base, receives 4 valveless pulmonary veins; left auricle forms the upper left border; smooth wall except the auricle. Mitral (bicuspid) valve: anterior and posterior cusps, admits 2 fingertips, overlaps the tricuspid and lies slightly higher. Left ventricle: aortic orifice about 2.5 cm at the right upper part with 3 semilunar cusps (posterior, right, left); numerous trabeculae carneae; anterior and posterior papillary muscles with chordae to the mitral valve.
A(iv)
SA node: natural pacemaker, first conducting cell, below the opening of the SVC in the right atrium, contains pacemaker P-cells, autonomic supply from the cardiac plexus (sympathetics increase and parasympathetics decrease the rate of impulse generation). AV node: slow conducting tissue in the posterior and inferior interatrial septum, allows complete atrial contraction before ventricular contraction. AV bundle of His: Purkinje fibres in the membranous part of the interventricular septum, the only bridge between atrial and ventricular muscle; right branch to papillary muscles and moderator band, left branch to the left papillary muscles.
A(v)
Arteries: right and left coronary arteries from the ascending aorta run in the right and left AV sulci; the right gives posterior interventricular and marginal arteries, the left gives anterior interventricular and circumflex arteries (the circumflex gives a marginal branch). Veins: the coronary sinus (posterior part of the AV sulcus, valve at its opening, empties into the right atrium) receives the great, small and middle cardiac veins, posterior vein of the left ventricle and oblique vein of the left atrium; the anterior cardiac vein opens into the right atrium and venae cordis minimae open into the chambers. Nerve supply: cardiac plexus.
B(i)
• The heart has a poor anastomotic network, so blockage of one coronary artery (coronary thrombosis) leads to myocardial infarction; the heart wall has 3 layers (epicardium, myocardium, endocardium) and the serous pericardium receives the coronary arteries.
• Angina pectoris: chest pain originating from the heart, caused by insufficient supply of oxygen to the heart muscle.
C(i)
• Irritation of the pleura or pericardium covering the central part of the diaphragm is referred to the shoulder, because the central diaphragm is supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3-5) and the shoulder skin by the supraclavicular nerve (C3,4); the fibrous and parietal pericardium are supplied by the phrenic nerve.
• Hiccup: involuntary spasmodic contraction of the diaphragm with approximation of the vocal folds and closure of the glottis; it may be due to pleurisy, peritonitis or pericarditis.

A. Describe the course and distribution of the lingual nerve, including its relationship to the submandibular duct.
B. State the site at which the lingual nerve crosses the submandibular duct, which is relevant to procedures in this region.
C. Explain the functional deficit that would be anticipated from injury to the lingual nerve, based on the sensory territory it supplies.
questions.answerText:
A
The lingual nerve is a branch of the mandibular nerve (CN V3). It provides sensory supply to the mucous membrane of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. In its course, the submandibular duct (Wharton's duct) runs forwards on hyoglossus, between the lingual and hypoglossal nerves.
B
At the anterior border of hyoglossus, the submandibular duct is crossed by the lingual nerve; this crossing relationship is anatomically relevant, since a stone in the submandibular duct can be felt bimanually in the floor of the mouth, and surgery/removal in this region places the lingual nerve at risk, along with the hypoglossal nerve, given their close relationship to the duct on hyoglossus.
C
Sensory supply to the mucous membrane of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is via the lingual nerve (a branch of CN V3), while special (taste) sensory supply to the same region is via the chorda tympani nerve (a branch of CN VII); injury to the lingual nerve would therefore be expected to impair general sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, distinct from a taste deficit, which would instead follow injury to the chorda tympani.

A(i)
Fibularis longus: origin — head and superior 2/3 of lateral surface of fibula; insertion — base of 1st metatarsal and medial cuneiform; innervation — superficial fibular nerve (L5, S1, S2); action — everts foot and weakly plantarflexes ankle. Fibularis brevis: origin — inferior 2/3 of lateral surface of fibula; insertion — dorsal surface of tuberosity on lateral side of base of 5th metatarsal; innervation — superficial fibular nerve (L5, S1, S2); action — everts foot and weakly plantarflexes ankle. Arterial supply: both are supplied by the fibular (peroneal) artery.
A(ii)
The common fibular nerve is the lateral, smaller terminal branch of the sciatic nerve; it begins at the superior angle of the popliteal fossa, closely follows the medial border of biceps femoris and its tendon, exits the fossa by passing superficial to the lateral head of gastrocnemius, then over the posterior aspect of the head of fibula, winds around the neck of fibula, and divides into the superficial fibular nerve (to the lateral compartment) and the deep fibular nerve (to the anterior compartment). The superficial fibular nerve runs in the lateral compartment to supply fibularis longus and brevis; its cutaneous distribution supplies the dorsum of the foot (lateral side of leg and ankle, as the sural nerve — formed by medial sural cutaneous nerve joined by the sural communicating branch of the common fibular nerve — supplies the lateral side of leg and ankle).
B(i)
Fibularis longus inserts onto the base of the 1st metatarsal and medial cuneiform on the plantar aspect of the foot — it therefore acts as a stirrup, pulling the medial forefoot downward and laterally, producing eversion and weak plantarflexion. Fibularis brevis inserts onto the tuberosity of the base of the 5th metatarsal on the lateral side of the foot — it abducts the forefoot and everts the foot. The lateral longitudinal arch (made of calcaneus, cuboid, and 4th and 5th metatarsals) is supported by peroneus longus and brevis; muscles of the lateral arch include peroneus longus and brevis, flexor digitorum longus, and short muscles of the little toe.
B(ii)
The transverse arch muscles include peroneus longus and brevis, transverse head of adductor hallucis, and slips of tibialis posterior. Fibularis longus, by crossing under the foot from the lateral side to insert medially at the base of the 1st metatarsal, acts as a dynamic tie-beam, pulling the medial and lateral borders of the foot together and maintaining the curvature of the transverse arch; adductor hallucis transverse head also assists by pulling metatarsals medially.
C(i)
Superficial fibular nerve injury (at fibular neck): loss of eversion of the foot (fibularis longus and brevis paralysed); weakness of plantarflexion; sensory loss on dorsum of foot. Deep fibular nerve injury (at fibular neck): loss of dorsiflexion (tibialis anterior paralysed) and toe extension (extensor digitorum longus, extensor hallucis longus paralysed); loss of eversion contribution of fibularis tertius; result is foot drop with the foot held in plantarflexion and inversion; sensory loss is limited to the 1st web space (between 1st and 2nd toes). Injury to the common fibular nerve at the fibular neck produces both effects combined — foot drop with loss of both dorsiflexion and eversion.

questions.answerText:
(i)
• The anterior vagal trunk is formed mainly in the thorax from the left vagus nerve; it enters the abdomen on the anterior surface of the oesophagus and divides into branches that supply the anterior surface of the stomach. A large hepatic branch of the anterior vagal trunk passes up to the liver, and from this a pyloric branch passes down to the pylorus.
• The posterior vagal trunk is formed mainly from the right vagus nerve; it enters the abdomen on the posterior surface of the oesophagus and divides into branches supplying mainly the posterior surface of the stomach. A large branch of the posterior vagal trunk passes to the coeliac and superior mesenteric plexuses and is distributed to the intestine as far as the splenic flexure and to the pancreas.
(ii)
At the opening in the diaphragm (the oesophageal hiatus), the oesophagus is accompanied by the two vagal trunks, branches of the left gastric vessels, and lymphatic vessels, with fibres of the right crus forming a sling around the oesophagus. Inferior to the root of the lungs, the vagus nerves leave the pulmonary plexus and join sympathetic nerves to form the oesophageal plexus, from which the anterior trunk (left vagus, anterior) and posterior trunk (right vagus, posterior) are derived.
(iii)
• The vagal (parasympathetic) fibres are secretomotor to the gastric glands and motor to the muscular wall of the stomach, and the pyloric sphincter receives inhibitory fibres from the vagus.
• Vagotomy is a recognised surgical option for peptic ulcer disease; division of the vagal trunks reduces the vagal secretomotor drive to the gastric glands, decreasing acid secretion.
• Since the hepatic branch arises from the anterior vagal trunk and the coeliac/pancreatic branch from the posterior trunk, a truncal vagotomy also interrupts vagal input to the liver, pancreas and intestine as far as the splenic flexure.
• Loss of vagal inhibitory input to the pyloric sphincter can alter pyloric motor function, which is why vagotomy for peptic ulcer disease is often combined with a drainage procedure such as pyloroplasty.
questions.question:
(i) Describe the origin, course and distribution of the anterior and posterior vagal trunks in the abdomen.
(ii) State where the vagal trunks lie in relation to the oesophageal hiatus.
(iii) Explain the anatomical basis of the effect of vagal injury (vagotomy) on the stomach and related viscera.

A(i) Describe the cell body (soma), types of neurons by structure, and the glial cells of the nervous system under the following headings: cell types, function, and capacity for mitosis.
A(ii) Explain the clinical significance of neurons being amitotic.
B(i) Distinguish between the central nervous system (CNS) and peripheral nervous system (PNS) structurally and functionally.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Cell body (soma): The neuronal cell body has a nucleus with at least one nucleolus and typical cytoplasmic organelles; it lacks centrioles, consistent with the amitotic nature of neurons. Types of neurons by structure: Unipolar (pseudounipolar) neurons — sensory neurons with only a single process or fiber that divides close to the cell body into two main branches (axon and dendrite); the longer branch extends to a peripheral ending and the other toward the CNS. Multipolar neurons — motor neurons and interneurons with numerous cell processes (an axon and many dendrites). Bipolar neurons — spindle-shaped, with a dendrite at one end and an axon at the other; found in the light-sensitive retina of the eye. Anaxonic neurons — have many dendrites but no true axon; do not produce action potentials, but regulate electrical changes of adjacent neurons. Glial cells (neuroglia): Neuroglia is a special type of connective tissue for the nervous system. Glial cells are nonconductive; they provide a support system for neurons; they support, nourish, and protect neurons. They are far more numerous than neurons and, unlike neurons, are capable of mitosis. Types include oligodendrocytes (produce myelin in CNS), Schwann cells and satellite cells (in PNS), and microglia.
A(ii)
Neurons are highly specialized and amitotic: if a neuron is destroyed, it cannot be replaced because neurons do not go through mitosis. This means that neuronal loss (e.g., in injury or disease) is permanent and irreplaceable.
B(i)
CNS consists of the brain and spinal cord; it is covered by three connective tissue layers called meninges (dura, arachnoid, and pia maters); it contains very little collagen or fibrous tissue and is relatively soft, easily damaged by injuries affecting the cranium or vertebral bones. The PNS is composed of nerves and ganglia. Functionally, the CNS is the master control unit while the PNS is the body's link to the outside world. Sensory (afferent) and motor (efferent) are the functional categories.

A(i)
Gross anatomy of the kidney:
• Renal cortex: granular-appearing superficial region.
• Renal medulla: composed of cone-shaped medullary (renal) pyramids; pyramids are separated by renal columns (inward extensions of cortical tissue).
• Structures in frontal section: renal hilum, renal cortex, renal medulla, major calyx, papilla of pyramid, renal pelvis, minor calyx, ureter, renal pyramid in renal medulla, renal column, fibrous capsule.
A(ii)
Seven functions of the kidney:
• Regulating total water volume and total solute concentration in water.
• Regulating ECF ion concentrations.
• Ensuring long-term acid-base balance.
• Removal of metabolic wastes, toxins, and drugs.
• Endocrine functions: renin (regulation of blood pressure) and erythropoietin (regulation of RBC production).
• Activation of vitamin D.
• Gluconeogenesis during prolonged fasting.
B(i)
Comparison of nephron types:
• Cortical nephrons: 85% of nephrons; short nephron loop; glomerulus further from the cortex-medulla junction; efferent arteriole supplies peritubular capillaries.
• Juxtamedullary nephrons: long nephron loops that deeply invade the medulla; glomerulus closer to the cortex-medulla junction; efferent arteriole supplies vasa recta; ascending limbs have thick and thin segments; important in production of concentrated urine.
B(ii)
Two collecting duct cell types:
• Principal cells: sparse, short microvilli; maintain water and Na+ balance.
• Intercalated cells (A and B types): cuboidal cells with abundant microvilli; both types help maintain acid-base balance of blood.
• Collecting ducts receive filtrate from many nephrons; run through medullary pyramids giving them a striped appearance; fuse together to deliver urine through papillae into minor calyces.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the gross anatomy of the kidney, naming its outer and inner regions and the structures visible in a frontal section.
A(ii) State all seven functions of the kidney.
B(i) Compare cortical nephrons and juxtamedullary nephrons under the headings: proportion, loop length, glomerulus position, and capillary bed supplied by the efferent arteriole.
B(ii) Describe the two cell types in the collecting ducts, including their microscopic features and functions, and describe how the collecting ducts contribute to urine delivery.

A(i) Describe the development, structure, shape and position of the female breast.
A(ii) Describe the nipple and areola.
A(iii) Describe the internal structure of the breast.
A(iv) Describe the arterial supply, venous drainage and nerve supply.
B(i) Relate the parts and structures of the breast to common pathologies and to surgical incisions.
B(ii) Describe the developmental anomalies of the breast.
C(i) Explain how breast disease spreads through the lymphatics, naming the drainage routes and the axillary node groups, and its effect on distant structures.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• A modified sweat gland of ectodermal origin, non-capsulated, present in both sexes (rudimentary in males), starting to develop at puberty in females with most development in late pregnancy and lactation; lies in the superficial fascia; shape and size vary with genetics, race, diet, age, parity and menopausal status (hemispherical, conical, pendulous, piriform, flattened).
• Base extends vertically from the 2nd to the 6th rib and transversely from the sternal edge to the midaxillary line; two-thirds of the base lie on pectoralis major and the inferolateral third on serratus anterior and external oblique; the axillary tail (of Spence) passes into the axilla; the retromammary space (loose areolar tissue) separates it from the deep fascia.
A(ii)
Nipple: at the greatest prominence, opposite the 4th intercostal space (about 10 cm from the midline in men and young nulliparous women); carries 15-20 pores of the lactiferous ducts; circular and radial smooth muscle causes erection with cold, tactile or emotional stimuli; devoid of fat, hair and sweat glands. Areola: pigmented skin (22-60 mm) with sebaceous glands and glands of Montgomery; darkening in the 2nd month of pregnancy is permanent.
A(iii)
Glandular tissue (15-20 lobes made of lobules of alveoli/acini and alveolar ducts converging on 15-20 lactiferous ducts, each with a lactiferous sinus deep to the areola), stroma (fibrous strands, the suspensory ligaments of Astley Cooper, connecting the skin with the deep fascia of pectoralis major) and adipose tissue (determines form and size).
A(iv)
Arteries: internal thoracic (medial mammary and perforating branches of the 2nd-4th spaces, the 2nd largest; about 60% of flow, mainly medial), lateral thoracic and thoraco-acromial pectoral branch (axillary), lateral mammary branches of posterior intercostal arteries, anterior intercostal branches. Veins correspond, with a circular venous plexus at the base of the nipple draining to the axillary and internal thoracic veins. Nerves: anterior and lateral cutaneous branches of the 4th-6th intercostal nerves (sensory to skin, sympathetic to vessels and the smooth muscle of skin and nipple).
B(i)
Cancer of the breast is a common surgical condition, about 60% arising in the upper lateral quadrant; the lactiferous ducts are radial, so incisions are made radially; infiltration of the ligaments of Cooper shortens them and gives peau d'orange; fibroadenoma is also listed.
B(ii)
Polymastia, polythelia and amastia; the mammary ridge extends from the axilla to the inguinal region and disappears in humans except in the pectoral region, so accessory breasts or nipples can occur along it (axillary and inguinal); the male breast stays rudimentary (small ducts without lobules or alveoli).
C(i)
• About 75% of lymph drains to the axillary nodes (central and lateral parts to the pectoral group, upper part to the apical group), about 20% (medial part) to the internal thoracic (parasternal) chain, and the lower quadrants to the inferior phrenic (abdominal) nodes.
• Axillary nodes lie in 5 groups: pectoral (anterior), subscapular (posterior), brachial (lateral), central and apical; levels 1-3 and Rotter's nodes between pectoralis minor and major; the subclavian lymph trunk from the apical group opens into the subclavian vein (left side usually the thoracic duct).
• Other routes: lymphatics follow vessels through pectoralis major to parasternal nodes, cross the median plane to the opposite breast, and reach the sheath of rectus abdominis and the subperitoneal and subhepatic plexuses.
• Nodes below and above the clavicle, and axillary and cervical nodes, communicate freely; cancer of one breast can affect the other breast and the opposite axillary nodes through the anastomosing lymphatics.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the general features of the lung (shape, appearance, weight, right compared with left) and its apex, base, surfaces and borders.
A(ii) Describe the lobes and fissures and the surface marking of the lower border of the lung.
A(iii) Compare the hilum and roots of the right and left lungs.
A(iv) Describe the bronchopulmonary segments of the right and left lungs and the features of a bronchopulmonary segment.
A(v) Describe the blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of the lung.
B(i) Relate the parts and segments of the lung to the sites and spread of common pathologies.
C(i) Explain how disease of the lung and pleura may involve distant structures and produce referred pain or a functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Conical, soft, spongy, elastic and pinkish in health (brown in the young, mottled black in adults and dark in city dwellers from deposited dust and carbon particles); right lung about 600 g, left about 550 g; the right is larger, heavier, shorter and wider. Each has an apex, a base, 3 surfaces (costal convex, mediastinal with the hilum, diaphragmatic concave), 3 borders (anterior, posterior, inferior) and a root; the posterior surface lies in the paravertebral gutter.
• Apex: rounded, extends into the root of the neck 2.5-4 cm above the sternal end of the 1st rib, covered by cervical pleura and suprapleural membrane. Base: broad, concave, rests on the diaphragm, which separates the right lung from the right lobe of the liver and the left lung from the left lobe of the liver, stomach and spleen. Anterior border: where costal and mediastinal surfaces meet, with the cardiac notch on the left; posterior border from C7 to T10; inferior border separates the base from the costal and mediastinal surfaces.
A(ii)
Right lung: 3 lobes (upper, middle, lower) by oblique and horizontal fissures; left lung: 2 lobes (upper and smaller lower) by the oblique fissure, with the lingula below the cardiac notch; visceral pleura extends into the fissures so the lobes move freely. Lower border (neutral position) crosses the 6th rib in the midclavicular line, the 8th rib in the midaxillary line and reaches the 10th rib posteriorly.
A(iii)
Hilum: wedge-shaped area on the mediastinal surface; root lies opposite T5-T7. Right root: in the groove of the arch of the azygos vein; eparterial and hyparterial bronchi, right pulmonary artery, 2 right pulmonary veins, hilar lymph nodes. Left root: in the concavity of the arch of the aorta; left main bronchus, left pulmonary artery, 2 left pulmonary veins, hilar lymph nodes. Both also contain bronchial vessels, nerves and lymphatics enclosed by pleura.
A(iv)
• Right lung, 10 segments: upper lobe apical, posterior, anterior; middle lobe lateral, medial; lower lobe superior (apical), medial basal, anterior basal, lateral basal, posterior basal. Left lung, 8 segments: upper lobe apicoposterior, anterior, superior lingula, inferior lingula; lower lobe superior (apical), medial basal, anterior basal, lateral basal, posterior basal.
• Each segment is pyramidal (apex to the hilum, base to the surface), separated from its neighbours by connective tissue septa, with the segmental bronchus, bronchial vessels and a pulmonary artery branch central; little arterial anastomosis between segments; intersegmental pulmonary vein tributaries guide separation; it has its own lymphatics and autonomic supply and is the smallest part that can be removed without affecting adjacent lung.
A(v)
• Arteries: 2 left bronchial arteries from the descending thoracic aorta and 1 right bronchial artery from the 3rd right posterior intercostal supply the bronchial tree down to the respiratory bronchioles; pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood to the alveoli and anastomose with the bronchial arteries at the precapillary level. Veins: 4 pulmonary veins to the left atrium; right bronchial vein to the azygos vein, left to the accessory hemiazygos vein.
• Lymph: superficial plexus (deep to the visceral pleura) and deep plexus (peribronchial) drain to pulmonary then bronchopulmonary (hilar) nodes, then superior and inferior tracheobronchial nodes, then the bronchomediastinal trunks to the junction of subclavian and internal jugular veins (right trunk may form the right lymphatic duct; left may end in the thoracic duct). Nerves: pulmonary plexuses; vagus is bronchoconstrictor, vasodilator and secretomotor, sympathetic has the opposite actions.
B(i)
• Connective tissue septa between segments are a natural barrier to the spread of infection, but carcinoma and tuberculosis break through; abscesses are commoner in the posterior segment of the upper lobe and the apical segment of the lower lobe because these are the most dependent segments in the supine position.
• Other pathologies: foreign particles enter the right main bronchus easily (wider, more vertical); pulmonary embolism (pulmonary artery obstructed by air, blood clot, fat, tumour cells or foreign particles); asthma (dyspnoea); fibrosis reduces compliance and emphysema reduces elasticity; lobectomy or pneumonectomy is used in lung cancer.
C(i)
• Costal pleura is supplied by intercostal nerves, so pleural or lung disease may cause referred pain along the thoracic wall and anterior abdominal wall; irritation over the central diaphragm refers pain to the shoulder through the phrenic nerve (C3-5).
• Lymphatic spread passes from the hilar nodes to the tracheobronchial nodes and bronchomediastinal trunks; a tumour within the chest cavity may compress the phrenic nerve and cause diaphragmatic paralysis with paradoxical movement (functional deficit).

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the three parts of the renal tubule, including the cell type lining each part, distinguishing microscopic features, and the primary function (reabsorption vs. secretion) attributed to each part.
A(ii) Describe the two parts of the nephron loop, including the type of epithelium lining each limb and any variation across nephron types.
B(i) Describe the renal corpuscle, naming its two components, the two layers of the glomerular capsule, and the specialised features of the visceral layer.
B(ii) For the proximal convoluted tubule, explain how its structure is adapted for its function.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Three parts of the renal tubule:
• Proximal convoluted tubule (PCT): cuboidal cells with dense microvilli (brush border — increase surface area); large mitochondria; functions in reabsorption and secretion; confined to the cortex.
• Nephron loop: descending and ascending limbs; distal descending limb = descending thin limb — simple squamous epithelium; thick ascending limb — cuboidal to columnar cells (thin in some nephrons).
• Distal convoluted tubule (DCT): cuboidal cells with very few microvilli; functions more in secretion than reabsorption; confined to the cortex.
A(ii)
Nephron loop:
• Descending limb: proximal descending limb is continuous with the proximal tubule; distal descending limb (thin limb) is lined by simple squamous epithelium.
• Thick ascending limb: cuboidal to columnar cells; may be thin in some nephrons.
B(i)
Renal corpuscle:
• Two components: glomerulus and glomerular (Bowman's) capsule.
• Glomerulus: tuft of capillaries with fenestrated endothelium (highly porous) allowing filtrate formation.
Glomerular capsule: cup-shaped, hollow structure surrounding the glomerulus; has two layers:
• Parietal layer: simple squamous epithelium.
• Visceral layer: branching epithelial podocytes; extensions terminate in foot processes that cling to the basement membrane; filtration slits between foot processes allow filtrate to pass into the capsular space.
B(ii)
Structural adaptations of the PCT:
• Dense microvilli (brush border) greatly increase the apical surface area for reabsorption.
• Large mitochondria provide energy (ATP) for active transport processes.
• Highly infolded basolateral membrane increases surface area for solute exchange at the basolateral side.
• These features together support the PCT's role in reabsorption and secretion.

questions.question:
Describe the popliteal artery and its branches, stating the safe site for popliteal pulse palpation, and explain the anatomical basis of the deformity and functional deficit after tibial nerve injury in the popliteal fossa.
A(i) Origin, course, and relations of the popliteal artery
A(ii) All branches of the popliteal artery — genicular and muscular
B(i) Termination and continuation of the popliteal artery into the leg and foot
B(ii) Safe site for popliteal pulse palpation and clinical technique
C(i) Anatomical basis of the deformity and functional deficit after tibial nerve injury in the popliteal fossa
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The popliteal artery is the continuation of the femoral artery; it begins when the femoral artery passes through the adductor hiatus. It descends through the fossa, passing inferolaterally and is the deepest structure in the fossa — it runs in close proximity to the articular capsule of the knee joint. It terminates at the inferior border of the popliteus by dividing into the anterior and posterior tibial arteries.
A(ii)
Five genicular branches participate in the genicular anastomosis (a network of vessels surrounding the knee providing collateral circulation capable of maintaining blood supply to the leg during full knee flexion): superior lateral genicular artery, superior medial genicular artery, middle genicular artery (penetrates the fibrous capsule and supplies the cruciate ligaments, synovial membrane, and peripheral margins of the menisci), inferior lateral genicular artery, and inferior medial genicular artery. Muscular branches supply the hamstring, gastrocnemius, soleus, and plantaris muscles. The superior muscular branches have clinically important anastomoses with the terminal part of the profunda femoris and gluteal arteries.
B(i)
Termination: the popliteal artery divides into the anterior tibial artery and the tibioperoneal trunk; the tibioperoneal trunk divides into the posterior tibial artery and fibular (peroneal) artery. Anterior tibial artery: passes anterior to the interosseous membrane between tibia and fibula; supplies muscles of anterior compartment; continues as the dorsalis pedis artery in the foot, supplying tarsal bones and dorsal metatarsals, and anastomoses with the lateral plantar artery to form the deep plantar arch. Posterior tibial artery: continues inferiorly along surface of deep posterior leg muscles; enters the sole of the foot via the tarsal tunnel; splits into lateral and medial plantar arteries supplying the plantar foot.
B(ii)
The popliteal artery is the hardest pulse to find, lying deep in the popliteal fossa; it requires deep palpation. To make it easier, the patient should slightly flex the leg — this relaxes the fascia around the popliteal fossa. An aneurysm of the popliteal artery can be detected by an obvious palpable pulsation in the popliteal fossa; an arterial bruit may be heard on auscultation.
C(i)
The tibial nerve is the medial and larger branch of the sciatic nerve and the most superficial of the neurovascular bundle. Injury causes: paralysis of flexor muscles in the leg and intrinsic muscles in the sole of the foot; inability to plantarflex the ankles or flex the toes; and loss of sensation on the sole of the foot. The resulting deformity is a calcaneovalgus posture — unopposed dorsiflexion with loss of plantarflexion, the foot assuming a dorsiflexed position because the antagonist muscles remain intact. Weakened or absent plantarflexion and paraesthesia of the foot and posterolateral leg are the major features of tibial nerve compression.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Otosclerosis is abnormal middle-ear bone remodelling, an inherited disorder causing mild to severe hearing impairment but rarely total deafness; it cannot be cured but can be managed.
• Risks: previous measles, osteogenesis imperfecta, stress fractures, immune disorders, family history, female sex (twice as often), vitamin deficiency, focal infection, pregnancy.
• Normal bone is absorbed and replaced by vascular, spongy osteoid; later the bone thickens and becomes less vascular, with new bone at the annular ligament of the oval window fixing the stapes.

(b)
• A fixed stapes cannot vibrate, producing conductive deafness.
• The change spreads to the stapes footplate and the labyrinth's bony capsule, resulting in sensorineural deafness.

(c)
• Manifestations: hearing loss starting in one ear then the other, balance problems, vertigo, tinnitus, dizziness, monotonous soft speech.
• Diagnosis: audiogram (conductive or mixed loss, higher bone-conduction threshold at 2000 Hz), tympanogram, CT.
• Nursing diagnoses: disturbed auditory perception, impaired verbal communication, anxiety about surgery and prognosis.
• Management: hearing aid for mild cases; stapedectomy with prosthesis (about 80% restored, 10% slight, 5% worse).
• Nursing: cerumen management, hearing device support, communication strategies; Rinne and Weber tests.
• After surgery: keep operated ear upward for 24 hours, head elevated, avoid lifting, straining, bending and nose-blowing for three weeks.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the pathophysiology and stages of otosclerosis.
(b) State how its stages relate to the types of hearing loss.
(c) Explain how the disorder may spread, the resulting functional deficit, and the related nursing management and health education.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Retinal detachment: separation of the retinal pigment epithelium from the sensory layer; risk factors include age, myopia, eye surgery and trauma; types are rhegmatogenous, traction, combined and exudative.
• Procedures for eye assessment include ophthalmoscopy (direct and indirect), slit-lamp examination, colour fundus test, ultrasonography and perimetry.

(b)
Surgery reattaches the sensory retina to the retinal pigment epithelium; vitrectomy is also used.

(c)
Nursing care includes comfort care.

(d)
Complications to teach about: raised IOP, endophthalmitis, retinal detachment, cataract and loss of eye turgor.

(e)
Teach about these complications.
questions.question:
A patient reports a sudden curtain-like shadow across the vision of one eye with floaters, bright flashes of light and blurred vision but no pain, and retinal detachment is suspected.
(a) Identify the condition and the relevant diagnostic procedures.
(b) Describe the intra-operative care and surgical options.
(c) Describe the post-operative nursing care.
(d) State the complications to monitor for and their prevention.
(e) Outline patient education and discharge planning.

Describe HIV infection under the following headings:
(a) Pathophysiology
(b) Progression and stages
State how the stages relate to the common complications (opportunistic infections).
(c) Link the stages of immunodeficiency to the infections.
Explain how the disorder may affect distant body systems, the resulting functional deficit and the related nursing management and health education.
(d) Distant effects and deficit
(e) Nursing management
(f) Health education
questions.answerText:
(a)
HIV is a retrovirus whose genetic information is RNA; its enzyme reverse transcriptase makes DNA from the RNA template, and it infects cells carrying the CD4 protein.

(b)
• An acute illness may occur 2-6 weeks after infection (fever, myalgia, arthralgia, headache, diarrhoea, sore throat, lymphadenopathy, rash); antibodies become detectable after about 3 months, sometimes 6 months or longer, by ELISA confirmed with Western blot.
• Most infected people eventually become severely immunosuppressed (AIDS); first signs are fever, night sweats, rashes, diarrhoea, unexplained weight loss or respiratory symptoms, depending on the degree of immunodeficiency.

(c)
• Opportunistic infections: Pneumocystis carinii (lungs: dry cough, breathlessness, fever), Toxoplasma gondii (brain), Cryptosporidium (profuse diarrhoea), Candida (mouth, oesophagus), Cryptococcus (brain, lungs), cytomegalovirus (retinitis) and herpes simplex (skin sores).
• Various cancers also occur in AIDS.

(d)
• Brain: headache, seizures, neurological deficits, dementia; eyes: loss of vision; spinal cord: paraparesis; gut: dehydration and debility; lungs: cough and dyspnoea.
• Children may show failure to thrive, developmental delay, recurrent infections and thrush; in women, recurrent yeast infections and gynaecological problems.

(e)
• Pre-test counselling gives information, explores risks and benefits, builds a plan and assesses support; the counsellor is a confidential listener and links to support groups.
• Treat opportunistic infections (e.g. co-trimoxazole, pentamidine, sulfadiazine with pyrimethamine, nystatin, fluconazole, acyclovir).

(f)
• Education: safer sex and safer drug use, risks of sharing needles, meaning of positive and negative antibody results, and that early treatment can delay onset of AIDS.
• A positive test means the person is infectious and can pass on the virus but does not mean the person has AIDS or is immune.
• A negative test does not mean immunity; antibodies may not yet have formed.

(a)
Hyperthyroidism is increased secretion of thyroid hormones; basal metabolic rate rises 60-100%; it is the second most prevalent endocrine disorder after diabetes.

(b)
Causes: Graves' disease (autoimmune, most common), thyroid adenoma, thyroiditis and excessive ingestion of thyroid hormone.

(c)
In Graves' disease antibodies mimic TSH and bind its receptors, causing hypersecretion; high hormone levels suppress TSH, so TSH is low or almost zero.

(d)
Heat intolerance, sweating, weight loss, diarrhoea, muscle weakness, nervousness, insomnia, tremor, toxic goitre, oligomenorrhoea or amenorrhoea, exophthalmos, polycythaemia, tachycardia and atrial fibrillation.

(e)
Women are affected eight times more than men; also family history of thyroid or autoimmune disease, age above 60, type 1 diabetes, thyroid surgery and goitre.

(f)
• Hypothyroidism: reduced hormone output, BMR falls 20-40%; causes include Hashimoto's disease (major), iodine deficiency, age-related atrophy and infiltrative disease.
• In primary hypothyroidism low T3 and T4 raise TSH; secondary is pituitary, tertiary hypothalamic (TRH), central both.
• Susceptibility: age 30-60, women five times more than men, previous hyperthyroid treatment (surgery, antithyroid drugs, radioactive iodine), lithium, iodine compounds, head and neck radiotherapy.
• Manifestations: fatigue, dry scaly skin, brittle nails, hair loss, menorrhagia, anaemia, husky voice; advanced: weight gain, constipation, cold intolerance, subnormal temperature and pulse, masklike face, dullness.
• TSH above 0.4-6.15 microunits/mL indicates primary hypothyroidism, low TSH indicates hyperthyroidism.
• Advanced hypothyroidism brings abnormal sensitivity to sedatives, opioids and anaesthetics; myxoedema coma is the extreme stage with hypothermia, unconsciousness and depressed respiratory drive.
• Contrast: hyperthyroid shows heat intolerance, weight loss, diarrhoea and tachycardia; hypothyroid shows cold intolerance, weight gain and constipation.
questions.question:
(a) Define hyperthyroidism.
(b) State its causes.
(c) Describe its pathophysiology.
(d) List its clinical manifestations.
(e) Explain why certain people are more susceptible.
(f) Distinguish hyperthyroidism from hypothyroidism.

(a) Describe the drugs used to treat Alzheimer's disease: indications, classes and monitoring.
(b) State the safety and supportive practice points.
(c) Explain the rationale behind the nursing actions and describe the care and family support required.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Goals of drug therapy: preserve cognitive and functional abilities, minimise behavioural disturbance and slow progression.
• Acetylcholine, vital for memory, falls as neurons degenerate; raising it may improve memory symptoms.
• Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (galantamine, rivastigmine, donepezil) raise brain acetylcholine and are used for mild to moderate disease; monitor nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea and weight loss.
• Memantine, an NMDA antagonist, blocks glutamate and is used for moderate to severe disease; monitor headache, constipation, confusion and dizziness.
• Olanzapine and quetiapine (dopamine and serotonin antagonists) treat delusions, hallucinations, agitation and combativeness; monitor mental status, orthostatic hypotension and somnolence.
• Sertraline and citalopram (SSRIs) inhibit serotonin uptake with little effect on other neurotransmitters.

(b)
• At best, drugs only temporarily slow decline; as the disease advances, non-pharmacological management of behaviour increasingly dominates.
• Give the patient an ID card or bracelet, speak calmly, give simple instructions and provide a quiet environment.

(c)
• Rationale: overstimulation is poorly tolerated; complicated instructions frustrate; the patient may wander and lack judgment for driving, appliances or finances.
• Maintain nutrition (the patient may not eat unless reminded), assist with dressing and toileting, plan daily activities including music therapy.
• Teach family, refer to a support group and discuss power of attorney.

(a)
• Parkinson's disease is a slowly progressing, chronic degenerative disease of the basal ganglia, substantia nigra and corpus striatum with dopamine deficiency; it affects men more, starting in the fifth decade.
• Causes: unknown; toxins (carbon monoxide, manganese), genetic factors, vascular changes, viral infection; iatrogenic forms follow major tranquilisers, methyldopa and reserpine and reverse within about 2 weeks of stopping.
• Degeneration of dopamine cells in the substantia nigra leaves excess acetylcholine relative to dopamine; symptoms appear only after 60% of neurons are lost and striatal dopamine is down 80%.
• Cardinal signs: resting pill-rolling tremor (disappears with purposeful movement and in sleep), rigidity (lead-pipe or cogwheel), bradykinesia or akinesia, postural instability with forward-bent posture and propulsive gait.

(b)
Gait and postural instability raise fall risk; dysphagia leads to malnutrition and aspiration; immobility causes infection, skin breakdown and pneumonia, and death is usually from complications of immobility.

(c)
• Autonomic effects: sweating, drooling, flushing, orthostatic hypotension, constipation, dysphagia, frequent urination; psychiatric effects: depression, anxiety, dementia, delirium, hallucinations.
• Diagnosis is clinical (two of four cardinal signs), often confirmed by a levodopa trial.
• Levodopa with carbidopa is the mainstay; others include trihexyphenidyl, amantadine, pramipexole, selegiline, entacapone; within 5-10 years dyskinesia and on-off responses develop; deep brain stimulation has largely replaced ablative surgery.
• Nursing: physical, occupational and speech therapy; prevent infection, malnutrition, aspiration, falls, depression and isolation; adapt the home; use an electric shaver.
• Give education and support to client and family; care is mostly at home.
• Surgery gives symptom relief but does not alter the disease course.

questions.answerText:

• CT provides a three-dimensional cross-sectional view and a computer-constructed picture of tissue densities; it is most useful for viewing tumors of the chest, abdominal cavity and brain.
• There are brain, cardiac, thoracic, bone, abdomen and pelvic types; angiography or myelography can be done by CT, and it is most often used to detect pulmonary emboli.

(b)
• Explain the procedure, obtain informed consent, remove wigs, hairpins and clips for head CT, and keep the client nothing by mouth for 8 hours before the scan.
• Assess for iodine allergy and check for claustrophobia.

(c)
• Observe for signs of anaphylaxis if dye is used.
• Inform the client that the test takes about 45 minutes to 1 hour and that they must lie still on a hard, flat table and pass through a large machine.

(d)
Anaphylaxis to the dye is the main complication.

(e)
Assess iodine allergy before dye, watch for anaphylaxis, check claustrophobia, and schedule barium tests after or 4 or more days before the scan.

(f)
• Barium interferes with the test, which is why studies using barium are timed after or 4 or more days before the scan.
• Anaphylaxis is the main danger with dye, so allergy assessment and observation are emphasized.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Acute angle-closure glaucoma, a form of angle-closure (pupillary block) glaucoma.

(b)
• Complete or partial closure of the angle, from forward shift of the peripheral iris against the trabecula, obstructs aqueous humour outflow and raises IOP.
• High IOP damages the optic nerve by direct mechanical injury at the nerve head and by ischaemic compression of its microcirculation, leading to optic atrophy and visual loss.

(c)
Assessment: ocular and medical history, tonometry (IOP), ophthalmoscopy (optic nerve), gonioscopy (filtration angle) and perimetry (visual fields).

(d)
• Medical: drugs that lower IOP, both topical and systemic: miotics, adrenergic agonists, beta-blockers, alpha2-agonists, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, prostaglandins.
• Start with the lowest topical dose and increase until the target IOP is reached; one eye is treated first with the other as a control.
• Surgical: laser trabeculoplasty or iridotomy when medication fails; trabeculectomy (filtering), drainage implant or shunt; trabectome for refractory cases.
• Therapy is lifelong because glaucoma cannot be cured; follow-up checks IOP, optic nerve, visual fields and drug side effects.

questions.question:
Describe insulin therapy and oral hypoglycemic agents under the following headings:
(a) Indications
(b) Preparation and types
(c) Nursing responsibilities

(e) List the safety points.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Type 1 diabetes needs exogenous insulin for life; in type 2, insulin may be needed long term if meal planning and oral agents are ineffective.
• Oral hypoglycemics are not insulin and supplement, not replace, diet and exercise; they treat type 2 diabetes.

(b)
• Insulin by action duration: rapid-acting (lispro, aspart), short-acting (regular), intermediate-acting (NPH) and long-acting (glargine, detemir).
• Oral classes: biguanides, sulfonylureas, meglitinide derivatives and alpha-glucosidase inhibitors.

(c)
Teach self-monitoring of blood glucose, insulin self-injection (rotating sites), diet, exercise, foot care, and avoiding smoking and alcohol; assess barriers such as limited income or language.

(d)
Hypoglycemia is the life-threatening complication; hyperglycemia symptoms and treatment are also taught before discharge.

(e)
• Do not exercise when insulin is peaking; best time is 60-90 minutes after a meal; always carry a quick source of sugar and wear proper footwear.
• Self-monitoring aims to achieve glycemic control and prevent hypoglycemia.

(f)
• Insulin lets cells absorb glucose and store it as glycogen, so excess insulin or missed food lowers blood glucose.
• Neglect produces hypoglycemia (diminished consciousness, cool clammy skin); treat with orange juice if conscious or IV dextrose 50% or glucagon if unconscious, retest in 10-15 minutes and notify the provider.

questions.question:
A patient has a slow, unilateral resting tremor of the hand (pill-rolling) that disappears with purposeful movement and during sleep, muscle rigidity with jerky cogwheel movement, slowed active movement, and stands with the head bent forward and a propulsive gait.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Parkinson's disease, a chronic degenerative disease of the basal ganglia, substantia nigra and corpus striatum with dopamine deficiency.

(b)
• Unknown cause; toxins (carbon monoxide, manganese), genetic factors, vascular changes, viral infection; it affects men more, usually in the fifth decade.
• Drug-induced forms: major tranquilisers, methyldopa, reserpine, phenothiazines; generally reversible within 2 weeks of stopping.

(c)
• Degeneration of dopamine storage cells in the substantia nigra leaves more excitatory acetylcholine than inhibitory dopamine, disturbing voluntary movement.
• Symptoms appear after 60% of neurons are lost and striatal dopamine falls 80%; extrapyramidal tracts are impaired while the motor cortex and pyramidal tracts are spared.

(d)
• Physical, occupational and speech therapy; education and support for client and family.
• Prevent infection from skin breakdown, immobility and pneumonia; prevent and manage malnutrition from dysphagia; prevent aspiration, depression and isolation.
• Adapt the home environment, prevent falls and use an electric shaver to avoid cuts.

(a)
• Glaucoma is a leading cause of blindness, often silent until irreversible damage; it cannot be cured but can be controlled.
• Raised IOP damages the optic nerve by direct mechanical injury and by ischaemic compression of its microcirculation, usually both.
• In open-angle glaucoma the anterior chamber angle is open and looks normal; it is usually bilateral, though one eye may be worse.
• Primary open-angle: optic nerve damage, visual field defects, IOP above 21 mm Hg with fluctuation; usually no symptoms but possible ocular pain, headache and halos.
• Variants: normal-tension glaucoma (optic nerve damage and field defects) and ocular hypertension (raised IOP).

(b)
• Risk: age above 40, diabetes, African Americans, family history, previous eye trauma or surgery, long-term steroids.
• Initiating events include illness, emotional stress, congenital narrow angles, corticosteroids and mydriatics.

(c)
• Angle-closure: aqueous outflow is obstructed by angle closure from forward shift of the peripheral iris against the trabecula, raising IOP.
• Acute: rapid visual loss, periocular pain, hyperaemia, nausea, vomiting, bradycardia, sweating, severely raised IOP, corneal oedema, vertically oval fixed semidilated pupil.
• Subacute: transient blurring, halos, temporal headache; chronic: cupping and significant field loss, IOP normal or raised.
• Diagnosis for both: tonometry, ophthalmoscopy, gonioscopy, perimetry.
• Treatment for both: lifelong pressure-lowering drugs, laser, trabeculectomy, drainage implants.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• A progressive, irreversible deterioration from irreversible loss of large numbers of nephrons; remaining nephrons enlarge to compensate, then become sclerotic and stop working.
• Protein waste products accumulate; uremia develops and affects every system; the kidneys function until about 70% of nephrons are destroyed.

(b)
• Stage 1, reduced renal reserve: 40-75% nephron loss, usually no symptoms.
• Stage 2, renal insufficiency: 75-90% loss; creatinine and BUN rise, urine concentration is lost, anemia develops, with polyuria and nocturia.
• Stage 3, ESRD: under 10% nephron function; regulatory, excretory and hormonal functions severely impaired, electrolyte imbalance; dialysis is usually indicated.

(c)
• Anemia appears by stage 2; in stage 3 fluid overload, edema, hypertension, oliguria and hyperkalemic cardiac problems occur; uremic symptoms are largely reversible with dialysis.
• Long-term complications: atherosclerotic disease, heart failure, renal osteodystrophy and gastric ulcers.

(d)
• GI: nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, anorexia; skin: pruritus, dryness, uremic fetor; CNS: drowsiness, headache, muscle twitching, seizures; cardiorespiratory: hypertension, shortness of breath and hyperkalemic cardiac problems.
• The patient may appear critically ill and lethargic.

(e)
Monitor edema and weigh daily; reduce protein and increase carbohydrate and fat; fall safety and reorientation; assess bleeding, prevent infection and monitor labs; provide emotional support.

(f)
Explain tests and what is happening to the patient; dietary management is a collaboration of nurses, dieticians and physicians.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Respiratory acidosis: interference with pulmonary gas exchange causes CO2 retention and raised carbonic acid; normal values: pH 7.35-7.45, PaCO2 35-45 mm Hg, HCO3 22-26.

(b)
• Ventilation and gas exchange are reduced (hypoventilation); causes include respiratory arrest, head trauma, pneumonia, sedation or anesthesia, atelectasis, Guillain-Barre syndrome, COPD and CNS depression.
• The kidneys compensate by adjusting bicarbonate, the slowest response (2-3 days); acidosis moves potassium out of cells.

(c)
Metabolic acidosis (low bicarbonate, Kussmaul breathing); respiratory alkalosis (hyperventilation in fever or anxiety; dizziness, tingling, tetany); metabolic alkalosis (high bicarbonate after vomiting or NG suction; hypoventilation, tetany).

(d)
• Assessment: early signs weakness, headache, fatigue, anxiety, tremors; progressive dehydration and confusion, ultimately coma; ABGs and pulse oximetry.
• Diagnoses: ineffective breathing pattern related to decreased respiratory depth from anesthesia, immobility and guarding with painful incision; potential alteration in respiratory function from inactivity or omitted deep breathing.
• Implementation: find the cause, give bicarbonate, antibiotics for pneumonia, naloxone hydrochloride for oversedation and replace potassium chloride.
questions.question:

questions.answerText:
(a)
• For an acute attack: NSAIDs, corticosteroid and colchicine; for prevention of chronic attacks: allopurinol (Zyloprim).
• Colchicine is used for both acute relief and prevention; it reduces swelling and uric acid level.
• Allopurinol prevents gout attacks and does not treat an acute attack; NSAIDs and colchicine are best for inflammation and pain during an attack.
• Colchicine toxicity shows as tingling or numbness in fingers and toes, gray lips and muscle pain.
• Allopurinol can cause vision changes.

(b)
• Do not take colchicine with grapefruit juice because it increases toxicity.
• Give annual eye examinations to patients on allopurinol; avoid large doses of vitamin C because of the risk of renal calculi.
• Avoid aspirin, which can raise uric acid, and avoid alcohol, dehydration and high-fructose drinks.

(c)
• Nursing responsibilities: administer medications, monitor vital signs, urine output, intake and output, uric acid and ESR, and assess joint pain, oedema and ROM.
• Keep the patient hydrated (2-3 litres per day; diet therapy 3,000 mL/day) and on a low-purine diet; dehydration increases uric acid build-up and alcohol competes with uric acid for kidney excretion.
• If neglected, chronic high uric acid leads to repeated attacks, tophi, joint damage, bone deformity and uric acid kidney stones; patients with chronic renal failure are especially at risk.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Transient ischaemic attack: temporary focal loss of function from ischaemia of a brain vascular territory, lasting minutes to hours; it may warn of an impending CVA.
• Tests: carotid Doppler, echocardiogram, CT or MRI, and cerebral angiogram for vessel patency and collateral circulation.

(b)
• Medical management controls the cause: drugs for atrial fibrillation and hypertension, warfarin for clot-prone patients, antiplatelets (ticlopidine or aspirin).
• Atherosclerosis is the commonest cause, most often at the carotid bifurcation; emboli may also lodge in cerebral vessels.

(c)
If carotid stenosis exceeds 70%, carotid endarterectomy opens the artery and removes plaque; balloon angioplasty is under investigation.

(d)
Nursing care focuses on careful neurological assessment for signs of deterioration related to ischaemia.

(e)
• Complications: falls (fractures, abrasions, lacerations, cerebral haematomas, especially on anticoagulants) and motor vehicle accidents from visual or cognitive impairment; no long-term complications of TIA itself.
• Prevention is by treating the cause.

(a) Identify the condition and name the diagnostic tests.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• A bacterial infection of the renal pelvis, tubules and interstitial tissue of one or both kidneys (upper urinary tract infection).
• Causes: ureterovesical reflux and urinary tract obstruction (stones, tumors, strictures, benign prostatic hyperplasia).

(b)
An incompetent ureterovesical valve lets urine back up into the ureters during voiding; kidneys enlarge with interstitial inflammatory infiltrates, abscesses on the capsule and corticomedullary junction, and atrophy and destruction of tubules and glomeruli.

(c)
Acutely ill, chills and fever, leukocytosis, bacteriuria and pyuria, flank pain, costovertebral angle tenderness, with dysuria and frequency.

(d)
• Ultrasound or CT to find obstruction and relieve it; urine culture; 2 weeks of antibiotics for outpatients (ciprofloxacin, gentamicin with or without ampicillin, or a third-generation cephalosporin); hospitalize pregnant women.
• Follow-up urine culture 2 weeks after treatment; nursing: monitor intake and output, temperature every 4 hours, 3-4 L fluids daily and teach perineal hygiene.

(e)
• Women, people over 65, pregnant women, immunosuppressed patients, people with diabetes and those with obstruction are at greater risk of urinary tract infection; catheterization or instrumentation is a precipitating cause.
• Obstruction increases susceptibility of the kidneys to infection.

(f)
• Chronic pyelonephritis follows repeated acute bouts; kidneys become scarred, contracted and nonfunctioning, and there are usually no infection symptoms unless an acute exacerbation occurs.
• Chronic symptoms: fatigue, headache, poor appetite, polyuria, excessive thirst and weight loss.
• Chronic complications: end-stage renal disease, hypertension and kidney stones; tests: creatinine clearance, BUN, creatinine, culture and sensitivity.
• Chronic treatment follows the culture; nitrofurantoin or TMP-SMZ suppresses bacteria if urine cannot be sterilized; antibiotics up to 6 weeks if relapse.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Hyperthyroidism (most commonly Graves' disease, an autoimmune disorder); other causes: thyroid adenoma, thyroiditis, excess thyroid hormone ingestion.

(b)
• In Graves' disease antibodies mimic TSH and bind its receptors, causing hypersecretion; high hormone levels suppress TSH, so TSH is low; BMR rises 60-100%.
• Excess thyroxine explains heat intolerance, sweating (vasodilatation), weight loss (fat mobilisation), diarrhoea (GI motility), weakness (protein catabolism) and nervousness (CNS stimulation).

(c)
Inspect and palpate the thyroid for size, shape, consistency, symmetry and tenderness; auscultate an enlarged gland for a bruit and refer.

(d)
• Radioactive iodine destroys overactive thyroid cells (commonest in the elderly), inevitably leading to hypothyroidism.
• Antithyroid drugs (propylthiouracil, methimazole) until euthyroid; potassium iodide, Lugol's solution or SSKI with beta-blockers prepare for surgery.
• Subtotal thyroidectomy (about five-sixths of tissue) is reserved for pregnant women allergic to antithyroid drugs, large goitres, or those unable to take antithyroid agents.
questions.question:
