questions.answerText:
(a)
• Thyroid cancer (malignancy is suggested by a single, hard, fixed lesion or cervical lymphadenopathy); risk factors are female gender and external irradiation of the head, neck or chest in infancy and childhood.
• Diagnosis: needle or aspiration biopsy, thyroid function tests, ultrasound, MRI, CT, thyroid scans, radioactive iodine uptake and thyroid suppression tests.

(b)
Inform the patient of the purpose of preoperative tests and what preparations to expect; demonstrate how to support the neck with the hands after surgery to prevent stress on the incision.

(c)
• Intra-operative: treatment of choice is total or near-total thyroidectomy (radical neck dissection if nodes are involved).
• Post-operative: assess and reinforce surgical dressings, observe for bleeding, monitor pulse and blood pressure for internal bleeding, assess respiratory status, assess pain and give analgesics.

(d)
Monitor for hemorrhage, hematoma formation, edema of the glottis and injury to the recurrent laryngeal nerve; surgery risks damage to the vocal cords and parathyroid glands (calcium control).

(e)
• Teach patient and family the signs and symptoms of complications to report; strategies for managing pain at home and increasing humidification.
• Explain the need for rest, relaxation and nutrition; activities can resume once recovered; refer for home care if indicated.
• Radioactive iodine eradicates residual tissue; suppressive thyroid hormone lowers TSH; lifelong thyroxine is required if remaining tissue is inadequate.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Epidural haemorrhage (haematoma) as a secondary head injury, with raised intracranial pressure.

(b)
• A temporal bone fracture tears the middle meningeal artery, causing arterial bleeding between the dura and the skull.
• Expanding bleeding raises ICP; bleeding within the cerebrum can lead to raised ICP and permanent damage, and herniation can follow.

(c)
• Vital signs and neurological assessment every 15 minutes until stable, with LOC by Glasgow Coma Scale; a cervical collar is kept until cervical injury is ruled out; CT scan guides diagnosis.
• Start IV therapy with strict intake and output; keep the airway patent and ventilation adequate (hypoxaemia and hypercapnia raise ICP); elevate the head of the bed as prescribed.
• Provide a safe, quiet, dimly lit environment, seizure precautions and emergency equipment nearby; watch for excessive urine output (diabetes insipidus) or fluid retention (SIADH).

(d)
• Clots are removed surgically and haematomas evacuated; a ventricular drain is placed if hydrocephalus is present.
• Supportive care: drug therapy for raised ICP, intubation and mechanical ventilation, invasive haemodynamic and ICP monitoring.
• Continue bed rest with appropriate positioning, nutrition and emotional support for patient and family.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Otitis externa (swimmer's ear): inflammation or infection of the external auditory canal, the auricle or both; acute (under 6 weeks) or chronic (over 3 months); bacterial infection is the commonest cause.

(b)
• Trauma or devices (cotton swabs, earplugs, hearing aids), eczema and psoriasis, narrow canals, cerumen or foreign body obstruction, stress, humidity, immunocompromise, diabetes and swimming.
• Other causes: irritation, fungal infection, allergies and water in the ear too long; it peaks at ages 7-14.

(c)
• Cerumen forms a protective, acidic barrier; disruption of pH and protective factors damages the epithelium, removes wax and traps moisture, raising pH and allowing bacterial growth.
• Severity: mild (itching, discomfort, canal oedema), moderate (canal partly occluded), severe (canal fully occluded, intense pain, lymphadenopathy, fever).

(d)
• Assess for fever and pain; give analgesics, antibiotics and antipyretics as prescribed; facilitate drainage and keep the external ear clean and dry.
• Educate patient and family to avoid swimming and keep water out; never put objects in the ear; after swimming tip the head to drain and dry only the outer ear gently.
• Medical: analgesic, otic antibiotics (for example ciprofloxacin, gentamicin, dexamethasone drops) and oral antibiotics; nursing diagnosis: acute pain related to inflammation and pressure in the outer ear.
questions.question:
A patient with recent swimming has redness of the outer ear, a swollen ear canal, ear pain, hearing loss, fever and ear discharge that was clear but has become purulent and foul-smelling.
(a) Identify the condition.
(b) State the predisposing factors.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Separation of the retinal pigment epithelium from the sensory layer; it is serious, usually of sudden onset, and can lead to blindness if not treated.
• Risk factors: age, myopia, eye surgery or trauma.

(b)
• Rhegmatogenous: tear of the sensory retina with seepage of vitreous humour causing detachment.
• Traction: separation from pulling tension. Combined rhegmatogenous and traction. Exudative: serous fluid under the retina from the choroid.

(c)
• Rhegmatogenous detachment is linked to myopia, trauma and surgery; traction to diabetic retinopathy and vitreous hemorrhage; exudative to uveitis and wet macular degeneration.
• Complications to teach about: raised IOP, endophthalmitis, recurrent retinal detachment, cataract and loss of eye turgor.

(d)
• Partial vision loss with a curtain-like shade across one eye, sudden floaters or cobwebs, bright flashes and blurred vision, without pain.
• Blindness or low vision needs emotional, physical and social adaptation and magnification or vision aids.

(e)
• Treatment is surgery to reattach the sensory retina to the retinal pigment epithelium, including vitrectomy; nursing provides comfort care.
• For visual loss, promote coping, spatial orientation and mobility, and home and community-based care.

(f)
Teach the patient about the possible complications.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• UTI is most common in women and more common over 65 years; at risk are pregnant women, immunosuppressed patients, people with diabetes and patients with obstruction.
• In most hospital-acquired UTIs instrumentation or catheterization is the precipitating cause; complicated UTIs occur with urologic abnormalities or recent catheterization.

(b)
Upper tract involvement (pyelonephritis, interstitial nephritis, renal abscess); repeated pyelonephritis can lead to chronic pyelonephritis with hypertension, kidney stones and end-stage renal disease.

(c)
• Nursing: monitor intake and output; encourage 3-4 L fluids daily unless contraindicated; check temperature every 4 hours and give antipyretics and antibiotics as prescribed.
• Teach adequate fluids, regular bladder emptying, perineal hygiene, taking antimicrobials exactly as prescribed and keeping follow-up appointments.
• Nursing diagnoses: ineffective health maintenance, acute pain, disturbed sleep pattern from frequency, and impaired urinary elimination; urine culture and sensitivity guides therapy.

(d)
Taking antimicrobials exactly as prescribed is stressed, because persistent and recurring infection can produce progressive kidney scarring and renal failure.
questions.question:
A 65-year-old post-menopausal woman with an indwelling urinary catheter reports burning on urination, frequency and urgency, and urinary tract infection is suspected.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Alzheimer's disease (dementia of the Alzheimer's type), a progressive, irreversible disorder of the cerebral cortex; the nervous system is affected.

(b)
• Plaques appear first in the hippocampus (short-term memory), then the cerebral cortex (language and reasoning); acetylcholine falls and neurons die, impairing memory and judgment.
• Later loss of self-care skills, speech, swallowing and voluntary movement.

(c)
Diagnosis is made after other dementia-producing conditions are ruled out; a definitive diagnosis needs neuritic plaques and tangles at postmortem.

(d)
• Safety first: ID card or bracelet, safe environment, possible home care aide, since judgment for driving, appliances and finances is lost.
• Then nutrition (may not eat unless reminded), help with dressing and toileting, calm friendly tone, simple instructions, quiet environment, music therapy and stretching.
• Medicines: cholinesterase inhibitors (mild to moderate), memantine (moderate to severe); monitor side effects.
• Inform and support family, refer to a support group, discuss power of attorney early.
questions.question:
A patient shows recent memory loss, difficulty finding words, inability to learn new information, personality and mood changes and progressive difficulty with activities of daily living. Other dementia-producing conditions have been ruled out.
(a) Identify the condition and the body system affected.
(b) State the organs or functions compromised.
(c) State how the diagnosis is made.
(d) Explain the nursing reasoning and prioritisation of care.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Haemorrhage is escape of blood from vessels, internal or external; causes are direct injury to the vessel wall, disease of the vessel wall (infection, malignancy) or disease of the blood (e.g. haemophilia).
• Natural strategies to limit loss: blood pressure falls, a clot forms, and the vessel wall turns in to hold the clot.

(b)
• By situation: external (visible) and internal (into a cavity, organ or tissue, e.g. a bruise or hematoma).
• By source: arterial (bright red, spurting, under pressure), venous (dark red, steady stream, part of wound farthest from heart), capillary (oozing).
• By time: primary (at injury or operation), reactionary (within 24 hours) and secondary (7-10 days). Types include: antepartum, cerebral, primary and secondary postpartum.

(c)
• Secondary haemorrhage is slow to develop, often due to infection and extremely dangerous, which shows the importance of keeping wounds absolutely clean.
• Reactionary bleeding can recur up to 24 hours after injury or operation as the body's control relaxes.

(d)
Skin becomes pale, cold and clammy with subnormal temperature; pulse is rapid and weak; respiration shows 'air hunger'; the brain suffers hypoxia (blurred vision, ringing ears, dilated pupils, confusion); thirst follows fluid loss.

(e)
• Lie flat with head lowered, reassure, loosen clothing, keep warm; for external bleeding cover the wound, raise the limb, apply pressure or digital pressure at pressure points (temporal, facial, brachial, radial, femoral).
• A tourniquet is the last resort: tight, with material beneath, not over 15 minutes, marked T with the time; dangers include nerve, muscle and skin damage and death of the part.
• Internal haemorrhage may need blood transfusion and surgery.
questions.question:
Describe haemorrhage under the following headings:
(a) Pathophysiology and causes
(b) Classification
State how the types relate to the common complications.
(c) Link the types to complications.
Explain how haemorrhage affects distant body systems, the resulting functional deficit and the related management and health education.
(d) Distant effects and deficit
(e) First aid and nursing management

An unconscious elderly patient has intense thirst, flushed dry skin, sticky mucous membranes, raised temperature and restlessness; serum sodium is above 147 mEq/L and urine specific gravity is above 1.030.
(a) State the risk factors for this condition.
(b) Outline the complications.
(c) Describe the nursing and medical management options.
(d) Justify the priority intervention.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Hypernatremia usually reflects a relative ECF water deficit; causes: decreased water intake from inability to respond to thirst (unconscious state, less efficient thirst centre in the elderly).
• Other causes: severe hypotonic fluid loss through the GI and respiratory tracts, osmotic diuresis, diabetes insipidus, and excess sodium from concentrated electrolyte mixtures.

(b)
• Agitation, restlessness, excitement, convulsions, decreased reflexes, oliguria or anuria; elevated temperature and loss of skin turgor.
• Rapid reduction of serum sodium may lead to cerebral edema, seizures or death.

(c)
• Medical: replace water by mouth if serum sodium is below 160 mEq/L, or IV hypotonic fluid (5% dextrose in water) if above 160; diuretics with plain water; repeat serum sodium at about 6-hour intervals.
• Nursing: monitor vital signs and intake and output, assess skin turgor and mucous membranes, check urine specific gravity and serum sodium, and encourage or give prescribed fluids.
• Assess sensorium, institute seizure precautions and notify the doctor of significant findings.

(d)
Gradual water replacement to restore normal sodium is the priority, because the goal is normal sodium concentration and correcting too rapidly risks cerebral edema, seizures or death.

questions.question:
Describe hyperkalemia under the following headings:
(a) Definition and causes
(b) Pathophysiology
(c) Clinical manifestations
(d) Management
Explain the clinical basis for why certain people are more susceptible.
(e) Give the reasons for vulnerability.
Distinguish between hyperkalemia and hypokalemia.
(f) State the differences in causes, features and management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Serum potassium above 5.0 mmol/L; causes: decreased excretion (renal failure, Addison's disease), tissue breakdown (crush, burns, surgery, hemolysis, GI bleeding), excess potassium administration or potassium-sparing diuretics, and massive transfusion of stored blood.

(b)
Potassium is the major intracellular cation, essential for neuromuscular function and cellular water; only 2% is extracellular, it is not stored, and the kidneys do not conserve it; metabolic acidosis shifts potassium out of cells.

(c)
Neuromuscular irritability, weakness, paresthesia, paralysis, nausea, diarrhoea, bradycardia and ventricular fibrillation; ECG shows tall peaked T-waves and wide QRS complexes; serum potassium repeatedly above 5.6 mmol/L.

(d)
• IV calcium gluconate or chloride, IV sodium bicarbonate, hypertonic glucose with insulin, dialysis and treatment of the underlying disease.
• Nursing: assess respirations, monitor ECG and serial potassium, notify the doctor above 6.0-6.6 mmol/L, and teach limiting dietary potassium.

(e)
• Patients with renal failure or adrenal insufficiency cannot excrete potassium; burns, crush injury and major surgery release intracellular potassium.
• Excess potassium supplements, potassium-sparing diuretics, high-dose penicillin in renal failure and massive stored blood transfusions add potassium, and excess does not usually develop if renal function is normal.

(f)
• Hypokalemia is serum potassium below 3.5 mEq/L; causes: GI losses (diarrhoea, vomiting, NG suction), urinary losses (diuretics, corticosteroids, osmotic diuresis) and inadequate intake.
• Hypokalemia features: fatigue, muscle weakness, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, decreased bowel sounds, paralytic ileus and arrhythmias; ECG: prolonged PR interval, flattened or inverted T waves, ST depression, prominent U wave.
• Hypokalemia treatment replaces potassium without causing hyperkalemia: potassium-rich foods or oral supplements with about 4 ounces of water or juice, and IV potassium chloride if severe.
• Nursing in hypokalemia: monitor vital signs, cardiac rate and rhythm and serum potassium; notify the doctor below 3.5 mmol/L.
• Hyperkalemia needs potassium removed or antagonized, whereas hypokalemia needs potassium replaced.

(a)
• Type 1 (formerly insulin-dependent or juvenile-onset) is one in which the immune system attacks the insulin-producing pancreatic cells and more than 90% are permanently destroyed, so little or no insulin is produced.
• Only 5-10% of all people with diabetes have type 1; most develop it before age 30 though it can develop later.

(b)
The exact cause is unknown; the immune system destroys the pancreatic insulin-producing cells, and an environmental factor (possibly a viral infection or a nutritional factor in childhood or early adulthood) is thought to trigger this.

(c)
• Insulin (from beta cells, an anabolic hormone) moves glucose from blood into muscle, liver and fat cells; with little or no insulin, sugar builds up in the bloodstream instead of entering cells.
• Without insulin the body burns fat for fuel, forming ketones that build up in blood and appear in urine (diabetic ketoacidosis).

(d)
• The three Ps: polyuria and polydipsia (osmotic diuresis) and polyphagia (catabolic state from insulin deficiency); also fatigue, weakness, sudden vision changes, tingling or numbness, dry skin, weight loss, irritability, slow-healing wounds and recurrent infections.
• Onset may include sudden weight loss, nausea, vomiting or abdominal pain if ketoacidosis has developed.

(e)
• Family history (parent or sibling), environmental factors such as viral illness, and the presence of auto antibodies raise risk, although not everyone with auto antibodies develops diabetes.
• Geography: countries such as Finland and Sweden have higher rates; a genetic predisposition makes some people more susceptible to the environmental factor.

(f)
• Type 2 (formerly non-insulin-dependent or adult-onset): the pancreas often continues to make insulin, sometimes above normal early on, but the body is resistant to it; production falls as the disease progresses.
• Type 2 risk is linked to being overweight, inactivity, age, family history and ethnicity, and it usually begins after age 30.
• Ketoacidosis mainly affects type 1; the hyperosmolar nonketotic syndrome mainly affects type 2 because some insulin remains to use glucose before fat.
questions.question:
(a) Define type 1 diabetes mellitus.
(b) State its causes.
(c) Describe its pathophysiology.
(d) List the clinical manifestations.
(e) Explain why some people are more susceptible to type 1 diabetes.
(f) Distinguish type 1 from type 2 diabetes.

A patient has headache, fever, vomiting and focal neurological deficits such as weakness and decreasing vision, with decreasing level of consciousness and seizures from raised intracranial pressure. Predisposing factors are otitis media and rhinosinusitis.
(a) Identify the condition and the diagnostic tests.
(b) Describe the pre-operative management.
(c) Describe the surgical procedures.
(d) Describe the post-operative nursing care.
(e) Name the complication to monitor and its prevention.
(f) Describe the assessment of the family's coping and support.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Brain abscess: pus enclosed in brain tissue from bacterial or fungal infection; tests: MRI (preferred, more sensitive), contrast CT, aspiration, blood cultures and chest X-ray for lung infection.
• Stages: early cerebritis (1-3 days), late cerebritis (4-9), early capsule (10-13), late capsule (beyond 14 days).

(b)
• Before encapsulation give antimicrobial therapy with measures to control ICP; verify the abscess size and number by contrast CT or MRI.
• Corticosteroid use is controversial (can retard encapsulation, reduce antibiotic penetration and raise risk of ventricular rupture).

(c)
• Emergent surgery for a single abscess: over 2.5 cm excised or aspirated; under 2.5 cm or at cerebritis stage aspirated for diagnosis only.
• Needle aspiration through a bur hole, often stereotactic with ultrasound or CT guidance and preferably before antibiotics, is preferred; craniotomy allows complete excision.

(d)
Continue neurological assessment, give medications, assess treatment response and provide supportive care and safety.

(e)
With corticosteroids, monitor blood glucose and serum potassium; insulin or electrolyte replacement may be needed; ongoing assessment detects rising ICP.

(f)
Assess the family's ability to express distress, cope and obtain support.

questions.question:
Describe glaucoma under the following headings:
(a) Definition
(b) Types and causes
(c) Pathophysiology
(d) Clinical manifestations and management
Explain the clinical basis for why certain people are more susceptible.
(e) Give the reasons for vulnerability.
Distinguish between open-angle and angle-closure glaucoma.
(f) State the differences.
questions.answerText:
(a)
An ocular condition with optic nerve damage due to raised intraocular pressure from congestion of aqueous humor; it is the leading cause of irreversible blindness and has no cure.

(b)
• Types: open-angle, angle-closure (chronic or acute), low-tension (normal-tension), ocular hypertension, congenital and secondary glaucoma.
• Secondary glaucoma arises from diabetes, hypertension, cataracts, uveitis, medication or trauma.

(c)
IOP (normal 10-21 mmHg) depends on aqueous production, resistance to drainage and episcleral venous pressure; about 90% drains via the canal of Schlemm and episcleral veins and 10% via the ciliary body and suprachoroidal space.

(d)
• Eye pain is associated with acute closed-angle glaucoma.
• Goal is to prevent optic nerve damage: medication (topical or systemic) and surgery (laser trabeculoplasty, laser iridotomy, filtering procedure, trabeculectomy, drainage implant); treatment is lifelong and cannot reverse damage.

(e)
• It is prevalent in people over 40 years and more in men than women.
• Low blood pressure is a risk factor for low-tension glaucoma; diabetes, hypertension, cataracts, uveitis, drugs and trauma predispose to secondary glaucoma.

(f)
• Open-angle glaucoma is the most common type: the drainage angle looks normal but aqueous fluid exits too slowly.
• Angle-closure glaucoma is less common: complete or partial closure of the drainage angle obstructs outflow; it can be chronic or acute (angle narrows or closes suddenly).
• Low-tension glaucoma has optic nerve damage and vision loss despite normal IOP, whereas ocular hypertension has elevated IOP.
• Diagnosis uses tonometry, gonioscopy and perimetry; nursing management is patient teaching.

(a)
Hyperparathyroidism (endocrine system): overproduction of parathormone with raised calcium; primary form occurs two to four times more often in women and is most common at 60-70 years.

(b)
Bones (decalcification, deep bone pain, pathologic fractures) and kidneys (calcium stones, nephrolithiasis, obstruction, pyelonephritis and kidney injury); hypercalcemia also causes anorexia, nausea, lethargy, stupor and personality changes.

(c)
• Diabetes mellitus (thirst, polyuria), diabetes insipidus (lack of antidiuretic hormone, water loss), hypoparathyroidism (low calcium: cramps, tetany) and secondary hyperparathyroidism in chronic kidney failure.
• Diagnosis: persistent elevated serum calcium with elevated parathormone; the double-antibody PTH test separates it from malignancy as a cause of hypercalcemia.

(d)
• Assessment and diagnosis: monitor serial serum calcium, intake and output; altered urinary elimination related to renal calculi.
• Implementation: encourage early mobility, ROM and turning every 2 hours; encourage oral fluids; strain all urine for stones; teach avoiding high-calcium foods and calcium-containing antacids.
• Medical: saline infusion with diuretics, restrict calcium, steroids, calcitonin.
• Evaluation: the patient relates return of a normal voiding pattern.
questions.question:
A 67-year-old woman complains of sleeping more, increased urination, anorexia, weakness, irritability, depression and bone pain that interferes with her going outdoors.
(a) Identify the condition or affected body system.
(b) State the organs or functions compromised.
(c) Give differential conditions.
(d) Apply the nursing process.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Risk factors: family history; age (type 1 usually in children and young adults, type 2 from 45 years, gestational above 25); race; obesity; sedentary lifestyle; polycystic ovary syndrome; adrenaline-raising exercise.
• Tests: fasting plasma glucose 126 mg/dL or more, 2-hour OGTT 200 mg/dL or more, HbA1c 6.5% or more, random glucose 200 mg/dL or more with symptoms, and urine glucose; diagnosis rests on two different tests.

(b)
Complications: eye disease, foot problems, gum and dental disease, heart disease and stroke, kidney disease, neuropathy, sexual and bladder problems, and skin conditions.

(c)
• Diet: control calories and body weight; carbohydrate 60%, protein 20%, fat 20%; sodium 1000 mg per 1000 kcal; limit alcohol. Oral hypoglycemics (type 2) supplement, not replace, diet and exercise.
• Insulin: lifelong in type 1 (rapid, short, intermediate, long-acting); self-monitoring of blood glucose; exercise 60-90 minutes after a meal, not when insulin peaks, carrying a quick sugar source.
• Nursing: teach foot care, insulin self-injection, nutrition and exercise; urge no smoking and no alcohol; encourage pneumonia and influenza vaccination; assess barriers such as limited income or language.

(d)
Hypoglycemia is one of the most common life-threatening conditions and needs immediate nursing management: orange juice if conscious, IV dextrose 50% or glucagon if unconscious, retest in 10-15 minutes and notify the provider.
questions.question:
A 32-year-old man complains of increasing thirst, frequent urination, constant hunger, tingling and numbness of the extremities, cloudy vision, early tiredness and a slow-healing wound on his right knee.
(a) State the risk factors for this condition and the diagnostic tests.
(b) Outline its complications.
(c) Describe the nursing and medical management options.
(d) Justify the priority intervention.

A patient wakes at night with sudden swelling, redness and severe pain in the big toe; even the pressure of bed linens greatly increases the pain. Contributing factors include decreased uric acid excretion, chronic renal failure, high-purine foods, alcohol, diuretics, dehydration and being overweight.
(a) Identify the risk factors.
(b) Explain the pathophysiology and the complications of chronic disease.
(c) State the nursing and medical management options.
(d) Justify the priority intervention.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Gout: risk factors are genetics, decreased uric acid excretion, chronic renal failure, myxoedema, polycythaemia vera, hyperparathyroidism; organ meats, red meat, seafood, beer; aspirin, cyclosporine, diuretics, dehydration, BMI above 25 and physical stress.

(b)
• Uric acid (end product of purine metabolism) rises in blood because urinary excretion falls or production is excessive; it precipitates where blood flow is slowest; needle-like crystals form in joints.
• Acute attack: sudden, lasts 1-2 weeks, pain intensifies within 4-24 hours, no long-term joint damage; chronic gout: repeated attacks, joint damage, tophi, bone deformity, itching or peeling skin and uric acid kidney stones.

(c)
• Medical: NSAIDs, corticosteroid and colchicine for acute attack; allopurinol to prevent chronic attacks; low-purine diet, fluids 3,000 mL/day, avoid shellfish, liver, sardines, anchovies and kidneys; monitor uric acid and ESR.
• Nursing: assess joint pain, oedema and ROM; teach avoidance of purine-rich foods, aspirin, alcohol, dehydration and high-fructose drinks; cold or warm compress if tolerated; hydrate 2-3 litres; bed rest with cradle or footboard; weight loss; skin care; allay anxiety.

(d)
• Priority is relief of inflammation and pain with NSAIDs and colchicine, because they treat the acute attack while allopurinol does not.
• Protect the affected extremity from pressure with a cradle or footboard, because any pressure, even bed linens, worsens pain.

questions.question:
An older patient complains of painless blurring of vision, sensitivity to glare, halos around lights, difficulty seeing at night and fading of colours, and cataract is suspected.
(a) Identify the condition and the relevant diagnostic tests or procedures.
(b) Describe the pre-operative care.
(c) Describe the intra-operative care and surgical options.
(d) State the complications to monitor for and their prevention.
(e) Outline patient education and discharge planning.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Cataract: opacity or cloudiness of the lens, the most common cause of visual impairment and a preventable cause of blindness; risk factors include ageing, diabetes, corticosteroids, smoking, trauma and ultraviolet radiation.
• Assessment procedures include: Snellen chart visual acuity, direct and indirect ophthalmoscopy and slit-lamp examination.

(b)
Provide pre-operative care and withhold anticoagulants.

(c)
There is no non-surgical treatment; surgery: intracapsular extraction, extracapsular extraction, phacoemulsification (ultrasonic liquefaction of nucleus and cortex) and lens replacement.

(d)
Complications: hemorrhage, rupture of the posterior capsule, acute bacterial endophthalmitis, malposition of the lens and suture-related problems.

(e)
Teach self-care to promote home care; early-stage measures include proper lighting and positioning to reduce glare and facilitate reading.

(a)
• Meningitis, inflammation of the meninges and subarachnoid space; septic (bacterial, mainly Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis in adults) or aseptic (viral, or secondary to cancer or weak immunity such as HIV).
• Signs: nuchal rigidity, positive Kernig sign, positive Brudzinski sign (more sensitive), photophobia, and a rash in about half of meningococcal cases.

(b)
• The organism enters the bloodstream (or spreads directly after facial trauma or invasive procedures), crosses the blood-brain barrier and multiplies in CSF; the immune response releases cell wall fragments and lipopolysaccharides, inflaming the subarachnoid space and pia mater.
• The cranial vault has little room, so inflammation raises ICP. Bacterial CSF: opening pressure 200-500 mm H2O, leukocytes 100-5000, neutrophils 80% or more, protein 100-500 mg/dL, glucose below 40 mg/dL; Gram stain and culture of CSF and blood identify the organism.

(c)
• Hourly neurological examination and vital signs to detect raised ICP (first signs: decreased LOC and focal motor deficits), hyperthermia, hydrocephalus and shock; use pulse oximetry and ABGs to detect need for respiratory support.
• Apply infection control precautions until 24 hours after antibiotics start; provide a quiet, dimly lit room, pain relief, antipyretics or cooling blankets, hydration and nutritional support (enteral if needed).
• Position, care for skin and do ROM exercises to prevent immobility complications; give emotional support and refer for rehabilitation if deficits are permanent.

(d)
• Early IV antibiotic that crosses the blood-brain barrier: penicillin G with a cephalosporin (ceftriaxone or cefotaxime), optimally within 30 minutes of hospital arrival.
• Dexamethasone adjunct 15-20 minutes before the first antibiotic dose, then every 6 hours for 4 days; fluid expanders for dehydration and shock; anticonvulsants for seizures; treat raised ICP.
• Prevention: meningococcal conjugate vaccine at 11-12 years with booster at 16; contacts get rifampin, ciprofloxacin or ceftriaxone prophylaxis.
questions.question:
A patient presents with headache and fever, a stiff and painful neck, inability to fully extend the leg when the thigh is flexed on the abdomen, flexion of the knees and hips when the neck is flexed, photophobia, disorientation and a petechial rash.
(a) Identify the condition and its classification.
(b) Explain the pathophysiological basis and the expected CSF findings.
(c) State the priority nursing assessment and immediate interventions.
(d) Outline the definitive medical management and prevention.

A 42-year-old man with a history of Hashimoto's thyroiditis and type 1 diabetes, who was diagnosed with an adrenal disorder six months ago and takes hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone, presents with three weeks of worsening fatigue, vomiting, excessive sweating, weakness, weight loss and abdominal pain. BP 90/60 mmHg, heart rate 100/min, respiratory rate 20/min, temperature 37°C. He has hyperpigmentation of the face, neck and hands and right upper quadrant tenderness. Na+ 128 mmol/L, K+ 3.1 mmol/L, Cl- 91 mmol/L, serum cortisol 2 mcg/dL; cortisol did not rise significantly after an ACTH stimulation test.
(a) Identify the condition.
(b) Explain the pathophysiological basis.
(c) State the priority nursing assessment and immediate interventions.
(d) Outline the definitive medical management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Adrenal crisis due to Addison's disease (primary adrenal insufficiency / adrenocortical insufficiency).
• Supporting cues: BP 90/60, heart rate 100, hyperpigmentation, Na+ 128, serum cortisol 2 mcg/dL, no significant cortisol rise on ACTH stimulation.

(b)
• The adrenal cortex is damaged or destroyed, so cortisol and aldosterone production fall; the most common cause is autoimmune disease.
• Low or absent cortisol reduces glucose release from the liver, causing profound hypoglycemia that can lead to shock, coma and death.
• Low or absent aldosterone causes sodium and fluid loss, then hypovolemia, dehydration and hypotension, leading to shock or coma.

(c)
• Monitor daily weight, intake and output, urine specific gravity and serum electrolytes to detect fluid and electrolyte change early.
• Administer prescribed fluid replacement, restore fluid balance, and monitor and manage the addisonian crisis.
• Avoid unnecessary activity and stress that could precipitate hypotensive episodes; encourage simple, non-exerting activities.

(d)
• Replace cortisol with a synthetic glucocorticoid (e.g. hydrocortisone, prednisone, dexamethasone) and aldosterone with fludrocortisone.
• Give fluids to replace losses; a vasopressor may be required if hypotension persists.
• If the gland does not regain function, lifelong corticosteroid and mineralocorticoid replacement is needed; extra glucocorticoids during other significant illness and dietary salt during vomiting/diarrhoea.
• Educate the patient on the disease process, medication management and signs and symptoms of complications.

questions.question:
A patient with chronic renal and heart disease has elevated blood pressure, a bounding pulse, distended neck veins, weight gain, dyspnea, crackles in the lungs and pretibial and sacral edema.
(a) Identify the condition or disturbance and the body system affected.
(b) State the organs or functions compromised.
(c) Give differential conditions.
(d) Apply the nursing process.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Hypervolemia (fluid volume excess): the extracellular fluid compartment is expanded with a surplus of circulating fluid and near-normal electrolyte proportions.

(b)
Kidneys cannot excrete excess water (chronic renal or liver disease, heart failure); if overload exceeds left ventricular pumping capacity, pulmonary edema results; gas exchange is impaired by tissue hypoxia.

(c)
Hypovolemia (flattened neck veins, postural hypotension, poor skin turgor, reduced urine output), hypernatremia, hyponatremia and other forms of edema (localized, pulmonary, cerebral, ascites).

(d)
• Assess vital signs, intake and output, daily weight, irregular pulse (possible hypokalemia) and edema, which may not show until 5-10 pounds of fluid are retained; check sacral areas in bed-rest patients.
• Diagnosis and objective: fluid volume excess with edema; weight reduced by 1 kg within 3 days; also impaired gas exchange related to pulmonary edema.
• Implement fluid and sodium restriction, diuretics, potassium replacement and potassium-rich foods; semi-Fowler's position and deep-breathing exercises; dialysis for renal failure or life-threatening overload.
• Evaluation: the patient's weight has reduced by 1 kg.

questions.question:
(a) Define Cushing's syndrome.
(b) State its causes.
(c) Describe its pathophysiology.
(d) List its clinical manifestations.
(e) Explain why certain people are more susceptible.
(f) Distinguish Cushing's disease from exogenous Cushing's syndrome.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Cushing's syndrome is chronic hypercortisolism from endogenous cortisol overproduction or exogenous glucocorticoids.

(b)
Endogenous: pituitary adenoma (Cushing's disease, about 70%), adrenal tumours (15-20%), ectopic ACTH tumours (5-10%, e.g. small cell lung cancer), familial (under 1%).

(c)
Excess cortisol disrupts negative feedback; it causes protein breakdown (muscle wasting, thin skin), gluconeogenesis (hyperglycaemia), fat redistribution and immunosuppression.

(d)
Moon face, buffalo hump, central obesity, purple striae, easy bruising, muscle weakness, hypertension, hyperglycaemia, osteoporosis, mood disturbances, menstrual irregularity, hirsutism, infections and delayed healing.

(e)
• It is commoner in adults aged 20-50 and in females; Cushing's disease typically affects women aged 20-40.
• People on long-term glucocorticoids for asthma, rheumatoid arthritis or lupus are susceptible.

(f)
• Cushing's disease: ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma overstimulates the adrenals to make cortisol.
• Exogenous (iatrogenic or factitious): long-term glucocorticoid therapy or intentional or accidental ingestion, with no tumour source.
• Other forms: pseudo-Cushing's (alcoholism, depression, obesity, pregnancy) and cyclical Cushing's.
• Diagnosis: 24-hour urinary free cortisol, late-night salivary cortisol, low-dose dexamethasone suppression, imaging, petrosal sinus sampling.
• Management: steroidogenesis inhibitors (ketoconazole, metyrapone, osilodrostat), surgery for tumours.
• After adrenalectomy prevent adrenal insufficiency with glucocorticoid replacement.

questions.question:
An adolescent has whiteheads and blackheads with tender red papules, pustules and painful nodules on the face, back, shoulders, neck and chest.
(a) Identify the condition.
(b) State the predisposing factors.
(c) Explain the pathophysiology.
(d) Outline the nursing management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Acne vulgaris, a long-term skin condition where dead cells and oil clog hair follicles; lesions include comedones, papules, pustules, nodules and cysts, graded mild, moderate or severe.

(b)
Genetics (family history), age (12-35, especially puberty), both sexes, slightly earlier onset in girls, hormonal changes including before menstruation.

(c)
Androgens stimulate enlargement of sebaceous glands at puberty; sebum plugs pilosebaceous ducts in a heightened response, forming comedones, then inflammation.

(d)
• Give benzoyl peroxide, vitamin A acid and antibiotics such as tetracycline as prescribed.
• Teach that heat, humidity and perspiration worsen acne, and that uncleanliness, diet and menstrual cycle are myths; results take 4-6 weeks.
• Wash gently twice daily with mild soap, do not scrub, squeeze blackheads, prop hands on or rub the face; wash hair daily and keep it off the face; use cosmetics cautiously.
• Female clients should tell their provider if possibly pregnant.
• Medical: combination therapy, hormone therapy (combined oral contraceptives), surgery (comedo extraction, corticosteroid injection, incision and drainage, cryosurgery).

(a)
• Cushing's syndrome: exposure to excess cortisol; causes include excess ACTH or corticosteroid administration, a pituitary tumor producing ACTH, adrenal hyperplasia and ectopic ACTH from malignancy (bronchogenic carcinoma most common).
• Tests: 24-hour urinary cortisol, low-dose dexamethasone suppression test, late-night salivary cortisol, MRI, ultrasound, CT, electrolyte and blood tests.

(b)
Nursing care includes preparation for surgery, decreasing risk of injury and infection, encouraging rest and activity, promoting skin integrity and improving body image and thought process.

(c)
Surgical options: adrenalectomy, transsphenoidal hypophysectomy, subtotal hypophysectomy and microsurgical resection of the ACTH-producing tumor; drugs include ketoconazole, mitotane, metyrapone and mifepristone.

(d)
• Complications: heart attack, stroke, hypertension; depression and memory loss; unhealthy cholesterol; pulmonary blood clots and lung infections; bone loss and fractures; insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes.
• Nursing management includes managing and monitoring potential complications.
questions.question:
A patient presents with weight gain in the face and back of the neck, a red round face, easy bruising, purplish striae, hypertension, mood swings and menstrual disturbance. Cushing's syndrome is suspected and surgery is planned.
(a) Identify the condition and the relevant diagnostic tests.
(b) Describe the pre-operative nursing care.
(c) Describe the intra-operative and post-operative nursing care and the surgical options.
(d) State the complications to monitor for and their prevention.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Rheumatoid arthritis: an autoimmune, systemic, symmetrical peripheral polyarthritis of the synovium with remissions and exacerbations and great potential for disability.

(b)
Cause unknown: autoimmune and genetic; it can occur at any age (20-60).

(c)
• Stages: synovial inflammation, pannus formation, ankylosis; congestion and oedema, reactive hyperplasia, vasodilation (warmth, redness) and capillary permeability (swelling) follow.
• Pannus destroys cartilage, capsule and bone, becomes fibrotic and calcified causing subluxation, and may produce ankylosis.

(d)
• Assess neuromuscular status and joints for swelling, pain and redness; maintain joints in extension; provide ROM and warm compresses as ordered.
• Monitor vital signs, urine output, intake and output and labs (ESR, WBC); give medications; provide skin care; minimise environmental stress.
• Encourage expression of feelings about body changes and self-esteem.
• Drugs: aspirin, NSAIDs, steroids, DMARDs; splints, assistive devices, heat or cold, physical therapy.
questions.question:
A patient has soft, tender, warm, stiff, swollen joints of the fingers and wrists on both sides of the body, with pain worse in the morning for more than 30 minutes, fatigue and subcutaneous nodules.
(a) Identify the condition.
(b) State the predisposing factors.
(c) Explain the pathophysiology.
(d) Outline the nursing management.

(a) Describe the drug therapy of glaucoma: indications, classes and monitoring.
(b) State the safe practice points and teaching.
(c) Explain the rationale behind the nursing actions and what follows when they are neglected.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The aim of all glaucoma treatment is to prevent optic nerve damage; therapy is almost always lifelong because glaucoma is not curable.
• Topical and systemic drugs lower IOP: miotics, adrenergic agonists, beta-blockers, alpha2-agonists, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, prostaglandins.
• Therapy considers the patient's health and stage; begin with the lowest topical dose and increase until the desired IOP is reached and maintained.
• One eye is treated first, with the other as a control for efficacy.

(b)
• Periodic follow-up checks IOP, optic nerve appearance, visual fields and drug side effects.
• Create a teaching plan on the disease and strict adherence to medication.
• Review medications, especially interactions between glaucoma drugs and other drugs.
• Explain that miotics and sympathomimetics alter focus.

(c)
• Rationale: adherence protects the optic nerve; stopping allows pressure to rise and optic nerve atrophy and visual loss to progress.
• Refer for ADL help, low vision and rehabilitation services, and legal blindness agencies.
• Surgical options when drugs fail: laser trabeculoplasty or iridotomy, trabeculectomy, drainage implants, trabectome.

(a)
• Outcome depends on early antibiotic that crosses the blood-brain barrier in enough concentration to halt bacterial multiplication.
• Penicillin G with a cephalosporin (ceftriaxone or cefotaxime) is given IV, optimally within 30 minutes of hospital arrival.
• Dexamethasone is adjunct therapy 15-20 minutes before the first antibiotic dose and every 6 hours for 4 days; research shows it improves outcome and does not raise GI bleeding risk.
• Other: fluid expanders for dehydration and shock, anticonvulsants, treatment of raised ICP (mannitol, Lasix), pain medicines, acyclovir for viral causes.
• Gram stain of CSF and blood allows rapid identification of the bacteria and appropriate antibiotic choice.

(b)
• Hourly neurological examination and vital signs; infection control precautions until 24 hours after antibiotics begin (oral and nasal discharge is infectious).
• Contacts receive rifampin, ciprofloxacin or ceftriaxone prophylaxis; vaccination is an adjunct.

(c)
• Early detection of raised ICP, hyperthermia, hydrocephalus and shock prevents complications; pulse oximetry and ABGs identify respiratory support needs.
• Quiet, dimly lit room prevents seizures and eases photophobia; antipyretics or cooling blankets treat fever; hydration and nutrition maintain immunity and balance.
• Positioning, skin care and ROM prevent contractures, muscle wasting, pneumonia and pressure ulcers.
• Neglect risks: death within hours, seizures, raised ICP, permanent deficits needing rehabilitation.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• The only treatment for hypothyroidism is thyroid extract or pure thyroxine by mouth; synthetic levothyroxine is preferred and also suppresses nontoxic goitres.
• The dose is based on serum TSH concentration.
• Indication: hypothyroidism from Hashimoto's disease, iodine deficiency, age-related atrophy or infiltrative thyroid disease.

(b)
• Two things to watch: cardiac function (angina and dysrhythmias) and drug interactions.
• Thyroxine interacts with anticoagulants, indomethacin and phenytoin.
• Advanced hypothyroidism makes patients abnormally sensitive to sedatives, opioids and anaesthetics.

(c)
• Angina and dysrhythmias arise from the tissues' increased oxygen need and the heart's inability to pump enough because of atherosclerosis.
• Serum TSH (normal 0.4-6.15 microunits/mL), free T4 (0.9-1.7 ng/dL) and total T4 (4.5-11.5 micrograms/dL) guide monitoring.
• Untreated disease progresses: myxoedema with thickened skin, hypothermia and slowed mentation, then myxoedema coma with unconsciousness and CO2 retention.
• Cardiac effects of untreated disease include reduced output, raised cholesterol, atherosclerosis and poor left ventricular function.
• Nursing responsibilities: observe cardiac response, check interactions, and monitor TSH.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Above 44 °C proteins lose their shape, causing cell and tissue damage; skin functions (sensation, prevention of evaporative water loss, temperature control) are lost.
• Burns over 30% TBSA cause inflammatory capillary leak, edema and loss of plasma volume; catecholamines and cortisol rise, producing a hypermetabolic state that may last years.

(b)
• First degree: epidermis only, red, intact, painful, heals without scarring. Second degree: into the dermis, pink, moist, very painful, with blisters. Third degree: full thickness, white or leathery, needs skin grafting. Fourth degree: involves fascia, muscle and bone and needs extensive debridement.
• Rule of nines (adult): 9% head and each arm, 18% each leg and each trunk surface, 1% perineum; Lund and Browder is used in children (infant head 18%, lower limbs 14%).
• Minor: under 15% TBSA in adults (under 10% in children); moderate: 15-20%; major: over 23% in young adults, full-thickness burns of 10% or more, or burns of face, hands, ears and perineum.

(c)
• Deeper and larger burns bring infection and sepsis, dehydration, low body temperature, contractures, muscle and tissue damage and emotional problems.
• Scars: hypertrophic (red, raised), contracture (tighten skin and joints) and keloid (shiny, hairless bumps); third-degree burns may need compression garments and grafting.

(d)
• Poor blood flow to kidney and gut may cause kidney failure and stomach ulcers; inhalation injury (about 6%) causes shortness of breath, hoarseness, stridor or wheezing; hypermetabolism brings fast heart rate and poor immunity.
• Contractures limit movement, and large scars cause emotional distress.

(e)
• First aid: stop burning, cool running water, no ice, no paste or oil; resuscitation with ABCD, wide-bore IV and Parkland formula; urine output, pain control, tetanus cover, nutrition, antibiotics and wound care.
• Principles of management: revive, restore, repair, rehabilitate; physical therapy exercises help regain motion.

(f)
Prevention: cook where children cannot reach, better house design, do not leave epileptic children and infants near fire, store kerosene, petrol and gas properly, put out candles and teach fire extinguisher use.

A patient aged 45 years presents with marked hypertension together with headache, excessive sweating and palpitations, tremor, flushing, anxiety and hyperglycemia.
(a) Identify the condition.
(b) State the predisposing factors.
(c) Explain the pathophysiology and the characteristic findings that support the diagnosis.
(d) Describe the nursing and medical management, including complications to watch for.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Pheochromocytoma, a rare, usually benign tumor arising from the chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla.

(b)
• It may occur at any age, peaks between 40 and 50 years, and affects men and women equally.
• It may be familial as part of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 and is considered in patients with medullary thyroid carcinoma and parathyroid hyperplasia or tumor.

(c)
• Manifestations depend on the relative proportions of epinephrine and norepinephrine secreted.
• The typical triad is headache, diaphoresis and palpitations in a hypertensive patient; suspect it when sympathetic overactivity occurs with marked blood pressure elevation (the 'five Hs': hypertension, headache, hyperhidrosis, hypermetabolism, hyperglycemia).
• Definitive diagnostic studies: urinalysis and imaging (CT, MRI, ultrasonography).

(d)
• Monitor until stable with special attention to ECG changes, arterial pressures, fluid and electrolyte balance and blood glucose levels.
• Complications: cardiac arrhythmias, dissecting aneurysm, stroke and acute kidney failure.
• Pharmacologic: low-dose alpha-adrenergic blocker (phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin) for 10-14 days or longer before surgery; calcium channel blockers (nifedipine) as alternative or supplement; metyrosine inhibits catecholamine synthesis.
• Definitive treatment is surgical removal of the tumor, usually by adrenalectomy.

(a)
Major burn injury; flame is the most common cause (44%); in young adults, burns over 23% TBSA (or full-thickness burns of 10% or more) are classed as major.

(b)
• Above 44 °C proteins lose their shape, causing cell and tissue damage; skin functions (sensation, prevention of evaporative water loss, temperature control) are lost.
• Over 30% TBSA an inflammatory response causes capillary leak and tissue edema, loss of plasma volume with hemoconcentration, poor kidney and GI blood flow (kidney failure, stomach ulcers), and raised catecholamines and cortisol causing a hypermetabolic state.

(c)
• Stop the burning process (remove clothing, irrigate, cool running water); do ABCD with primary and secondary survey, expose the patient and set up wide-bore IV access.
• Parkland formula: adult 2-4 mL/kg/% TBSA of Ringer's lactate: 4 x 30 x 70 = 8400 mL in 24 hours; half (4200 mL) in the first 8 hours from injury, less the 1000 mL already given = 3200 mL.
• Catheterize and aim for urine output of 0.3 mL/kg/hr or 50 mL/hr; pass an NG tube; prioritize pain management after the surveys; give ATS or tetanus toxoid; vital signs every 30 minutes; record all measures.

(d)
• Wound care after resuscitation: exposure method, wound dressing, excision and skin grafting (third-degree burns need grafting unless small enough to heal by contraction).
• Nutritional support (adult 100 J/kg plus 160 J per % burn; protein 2-3 g/kg) and antibiotics; for inhalation injury: early bronchoscopy, open airway with oxygen, suction and early physiotherapy.
• Management principles: revive, restore, repair, rehabilitate.
questions.question:
A 25-year-old man weighing 70 kg sustains a 30% total body surface area flame burn at 3 pm and is admitted at 4 pm, having already received 1000 mL of fluid from the emergency services.
(a) Identify the condition and its severity.
(b) Explain the pathophysiological basis.

A patient has left gaze preference, right visual field deficit, right hemiparesis and right hemisensory loss; another patient has nausea, vomiting, diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, vertigo and truncal or gait ataxia; a third has headache, neck pain, light intolerance and decreased level of consciousness. A CT scan is done.
(a) Identify the condition and affected areas.
(b) State the functions compromised.
(c) State the differential conditions.
(d) Explain the nursing reasoning and prioritisation (nursing process).
questions.answerText:
(a)
Stroke syndromes: the first pattern is the left (dominant) hemisphere; right hemisphere gives right gaze preference, left field deficit, left hemiparesis, left sensory loss and neglect; brainstem and cerebellum signs as described.

(b)
Language and voluntary motor control, vision, swallowing, balance and coordination, consciousness and respiration (hiccups, abnormal respirations in brainstem stroke).

(c)
• Ischaemic stroke (blocked vessel) versus haemorrhagic (ruptured vessel, headache, neck pain, light intolerance, decreased LOC); a TIA resolves within 24 hours.
• Symptoms lasting over 24 hours without permanent change are RIND; CT shows infarct size and location and whether haemorrhagic.

(d)
• Assessment: ABCs, oxygenation, blood glucose, last known well time, FAST or Cincinnati scale, neurological assessment and vital signs at least every 30 minutes.
• Planning and implementation: load-and-go to an acute stroke centre; rt-PA within 1 hour of ED arrival if eligible (3-4.5 hour window with screening).
• Nurses should watch for unusual presentations because symptoms evolve over minutes to hours.
• After thrombolysis: neurological checks every 15 minutes during infusion, every 30 minutes for 6 hours, hourly for 16 hours.

(a)
Acute renal failure of the renal system: an abrupt decline in renal function with falling GFR; BUN and creatinine rise and the patient can go from normal to uremia in a week; most forms are reversible if correctly diagnosed.

(b)
• Excretion of toxic wastes fails; potassium cannot be removed (hyperkalemia incompatible with cardiac function), sodium loss causes hyponatremia, acidosis develops, and confusion, convulsions and coma follow.
• Renal failure disrupts endocrine, metabolic, fluid, electrolyte and acid-base function; it is a systemic disease.

(c)
• Chronic renal failure (progressive, irreversible loss of nephrons) is the main differential; other causes of acute failure include: MI, shock, peritonitis, volume depletion, nephrotoxic drugs (gentamicin, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors), hemorrhage, burns, trauma, DIC.
• Four phases: initiation, oliguria (hyperkalemia, uremic phase), diuresis (gradual rise in urine output) and recovery (3-12 months).

(d)
• Assessment: monitor phase-related urine output, observe closely for dehydration during diuresis, and follow BUN, creatinine, potassium, sodium and ABGs.
• Planning and implementation: monitor edema and weigh daily, protein-restricted diet with more carbohydrate and fat, safety and reorientation, bleeding and infection prevention, emotional support; treat hypovolemia with 0.45% saline, nephrotoxicity with mannitol or loop diuretics, and use dialysis if medication fails.
questions.question:
A patient who developed hypotension and sepsis now has a sharp fall in urine output, rising BUN and creatinine, confusion and a high serum potassium.
(a) Identify the condition and the body system affected.

A patient reports hearing loss that started in one ear and then moved to the other, with tinnitus, vertigo, dizziness and balance problems, and speaks with a monotonous, soft voice.
(a) Identify the condition and the diagnostic tests.
(b) Describe the pre-operative nursing diagnoses and care.
(c) Describe the surgical procedure.
(d) Describe the post-operative nursing care.
(e) State the complication to monitor, the related patient education and the nursing interventions.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Otosclerosis: abnormal middle-ear bone remodelling, inherited; the stapes becomes fixed, giving conductive loss, which can spread to the labyrinth capsule and cause sensorineural loss.
• Tests: audiogram (higher bone-conduction threshold at 2000 Hz), tympanogram, CT scan; nursing assessment includes Rinne and Weber tests.

(b)
Nursing diagnoses: disturbed auditory sensory perception, impaired verbal communication and anxiety related to surgery and prognosis; no effective drug exists, and mild cases use a hearing aid.

(c)
• Stapedectomy: a prosthesis is placed in the middle ear to bypass the stapes, done under a microscope with local or (more often) general anaesthesia.
• Results: hearing restored in almost 80%, slight improvement in about 10%, worse in about 5%.

(d)
• Expect dizziness, nausea, vomiting and nystagmus (from perilymph disturbance); keep the operated ear upward for 24 hours, head elevated on 2-3 pillows, monitor vital signs, and reduce sudden movements.
• Place a Vaseline-coated cotton ball in the ear canal to keep it dry during a head bath; assist out of bed.

(e)
• Complication: worsened hearing (about 5%); avoid heavy lifting, straining or bending and do not blow the nose for three weeks after surgery.
• Nursing interventions: cerumen management, hearing device support and communication strategies.

(a)
Haemorrhage: escape of blood from the blood vessels, internal or external; it may come from an artery (bright red, spurting), a vein (dark red, steady stream) or capillaries (oozing).

(b)
• Causes: direct injury to the vessel wall, disease of the vessel wall (infection, malignancy) or disease of the blood itself (e.g. haemophilia).
• Superficial vessels constrict (pale, cold, clammy skin, subnormal temperature, rapid weak pulse); the brain suffers hypoxia (blurred vision, buzzing in the ears, dilated pupils, confusion); thirst arises as fluid is withdrawn from tissues into the blood.

(c)
• Lie the patient flat with the head lowered, reassure, loosen tight clothing, keep warm, keep the crowd away and contact a doctor; transfer to hospital with minimal handling if severe.
• External bleeding: cover the wound with a clean dressing, raise the limb, apply firm pressure with a pad, or digital pressure on the artery supplying the part.
• A tourniquet is a last resort: tight enough, with material between it and the skin, not left on longer than 15 minutes, and marked with the letter T and the time on the forehead; it can damage nerves, muscles and skin.

(d)
Internal haemorrhage: blood transfusion and surgery may be indicated; shock is managed with fluid replacement, oxygenation and close monitoring.
questions.question:
A patient with a severe wound is brought in with pale, cold, clammy skin, a rapid weak pulse, 'air hunger', anxiety and restlessness, blurred vision, ringing in the ears and thirst.
(a) Identify the condition.
(b) Explain the pathophysiological basis.
(c) State the priority nursing assessment and immediate interventions.
(d) Outline the definitive management.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Inflammation of the thyroid gland, characterized by inflammation, fibrosis or lymphocytic infiltration; it is acute, subacute or chronic.

(b)
• Acute thyroiditis is rare and caused by infection with bacteria, fungi, mycobacteria or parasites, most commonly Staphylococcus aureus.
• Subacute forms are granulomatous (de Quervain's) or painless (silent, lymphocytic); chronic thyroiditis is Hashimoto's disease (chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis).

(c)
• Acute: anterior neck pain and swelling, fever, dysphagia and dysphonia, often with pharyngeal pain.
• Chronic: painless enlargement of the gland with possible dysphagia; early overproduction of hormone causes irritability, nervousness, insomnia and weight loss.

(d)
• Diagnosis: serum thyroid hormone, TSH, radioactive iodine uptake and needle biopsy.
• Treatment: acute, antimicrobials and fluids with incision and drainage of abscess; subacute, NSAIDs, beta blockers (propranolol) and corticosteroids if severe.

(e)
Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis predominantly affects women aged 40-50; chronic thyroiditis occurs most often in women aged 30-50.

(f)
• Acute thyroiditis is infective and painful; chronic thyroiditis is usually not accompanied by pain and is diagnosed from the histologic appearance of the inflamed gland.
• In chronic thyroiditis thyroid function is usually normal or low, and untreated it eventually leads to hypothyroidism.
• Chronic thyroiditis is treated with thyroid hormone supplementation to prevent hypothyroidism and suppress TSH secretion.

(a) Definition and types
(b) Causes

(d) Diagnosis and treatment
Explain the clinical basis for why certain people are more susceptible.
(e) Give the reasons for vulnerability.

A patient has recurring seizures. Causes of epilepsy include head injury, infections, brain tumours, metabolic disorders, fever and drug or alcohol intoxication; one seizure is a generalised tonic-clonic episode with tongue chewing and incontinence.
(a) State the risk factors.
(b) State the complications.
(c) Outline the nursing, medical and surgical management options.
(d) Justify the priority intervention.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Idiopathic causes, birth trauma, asphyxia neonatorum, head injuries, infections, toxicity (carbon monoxide, lead), circulatory problems, fever, metabolic disorders, intoxication, tumours, abscesses, congenital malformations.

(b)
• Injury during seizures; status epilepticus (series of seizures without recovery, or seizures lasting 30 minutes or more), precipitated by interrupted anticonvulsants, fever, infection or illness.
• In status epilepticus, vigorous contractions impose heavy metabolic demand, interfere with breathing, and cause hypoxia, cerebral anoxia and oedema, possibly irreversible fatal brain damage.

(c)
• Medical: anticonvulsants (carbamazepine, clonazepam, phenobarbital, phenytoin, valproate) control 70-80%, starting with one drug, monitoring blood levels.
• Surgical: for tumours, abscesses, cysts, vascular anomalies or intractable seizures; removal of a circumscribed focus may give long-term control.
• Nursing during seizure: ease to floor, pad head, loosen clothing, clear furniture, side-lying with head flexed forward, suction if needed; after: side-lying, reorient, guide gently.

(d)
• Priority is preventing injury and keeping the airway safe: do not pry jaws or restrain.
• In status epilepticus, stopping seizures quickly and ensuring cerebral oxygenation come first, with IV diazepam, lorazepam or phenytoin and intubation if unresponsive.

(a)
• Immobile people are at highest risk; ICU patients have increased risk, and patients aged 71-80 form the largest affected age group.
• Other contributors: shear, friction, and microclimate (moisture from incontinence, perspiration or exudates and raised skin temperature).
• The Braden scale predicts risk using 6 areas: sensory perception, immobility, inactivity, moisture, nutrition and friction/shear.

(b)
• Prolonged compression causes ischemia that can lead to tissue necrosis if untreated.
• Complications of chronic injury: malignant transformation, autonomic dysreflexia, osteomyelitis, pyarthrosis, sepsis, urethral fistula, amyloidosis and anemia.

(c)
• Remove all pressure from the affected area and keep it clean; pain needs continual assessment, documentation and treatment.
• Basic treatment is debridement, cleansing and dressing to give a moist healing environment; nonsurgical debridement is mechanical, enzymatic or autolytic, and surgical debridement is for sepsis, cellulitis or extensive eschar.
• Cleanse by irrigation (30 mL syringe with 18-gauge needle, 1.81-6.8 kg per square inch, 250 mL normal saline); dressings include hydrogel, polyurethane film, hydrocolloid, biological, alginate or cotton gauze.
• Give antibiotics according to culture and sensitivity; treat the worst colour (black, yellow, red) present first; beefy red wound is a healing wound.

(d)
Pressure removal comes first because external pressure above arterial capillary pressure (32 mmHg) and venous closing pressure (8-12 mmHg) impairs blood flow and starts the spiral toward necrosis and ulceration.
questions.question:
A bedridden elderly patient in an intensive care unit has lain in one position for a long time. The patient is immobile, has moist skin from incontinence and perspiration, poor nutrition, and a localized area of nonblanchable erythema over intact sacral skin.
(a) State the risk factors predisposing this patient to pressure injury and the tool used to predict the risk.
(b) Outline the complications that may follow if the injury progresses.
