Describe inflammation under the following headings:
(a) Pathophysiology
(b) Causes, exudates and classification
State how the types of exudate and outcomes relate to the common complications.
(c) Link the types to complications.
Explain how inflammation may spread or affect distant body systems, the resulting functional deficit and the related nursing management and health education.
(d) Distant effects and deficit
(e) Nursing management
(f) Health education and emotional support
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Local response: brief vasoconstriction (about five minutes) then vasodilatation within thirty minutes, hyperaemia (redness, heat), exudation of plasma and cells (swelling, firmness), pain from pressure on nerve endings and leucocyte migration (diapedesis).
• Bacterial inflammation often forms an abscess; pus forms after phagocytes engulf bacteria and necrotic tissue.

(b)
• Causes: chemical, biological (bacteria, fungi, viruses), immunological, mechanical and thermal agents.
• Exudates: serous (mild, clear), fibrinous or serosanguinous (severe) and purulent (pyogenic infection). Termination: resolution, spontaneous rupture, surgical incision and drainage, or ulcer/erosion.

(c)
• Bacterial origin leads to abscess and suppuration; severe inflammation gives fibrinous exudate; pyogenic organisms give purulent exudate; a superficial erosion differs from a deeper ulcer.
• Premature or improper opening of an abscess interferes with the body's limiting of spread and leads to widespread dissemination.

(d)
• Systemic effects: leucocytosis, raised ESR, toxaemia with malaise, loss of appetite, headache, fever, lethargy and weakness; fever can destroy organisms but may cause cellular damage or fluid and electrolyte imbalance.
• Pain and swelling account for loss of function in the affected area.

(e)
• Rest (splints, slings), elevation, heat or cold compresses, increased calories, protein and vitamin C, antibiotics after sensitivity tests, incision and drainage of pus, and fluid replacement.
• Maintain medical and surgical asepsis, hand washing and careful disposal of dressings, protect oneself from pus and avoid contact with surrounding skin.

(f)
• Emotional support and reassurance are given.
• Antibiotics only sterilize pus; healing does not occur until the pus is removed.

questions.question:
Describe bronchoscopy under the following headings:
(a) Indications
(b) Preparation
(c) Nursing responsibilities
(d) Complications
State the safety precautions or safe practice points.
(e) List the safety points.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Bronchoscopy is direct visual examination of the bronchi through a fiber-optic scope.
• It is used to remove foreign bodies, for aggressive pulmonary cleansing and to obtain sputum and tissue specimens; in atelectasis it visualizes the obstruction and obtains specimens, and in lung cancer it confirms the diagnosis.

(b)
• Obtain written informed consent per facility policy and explain the procedure to the client.
• Keep the client nothing by mouth for at least 6 hours; pre-procedure sedation is given if ordered, and IV access is obtained for sedation during the procedure.

(c)
• After the procedure, frequently assess vital signs and respiratory status.
• Assess for unusual amounts of bleeding and tell the client sputum may be blood-tinged initially.
• Maintain the client side-lying until the gag reflex returns and withhold all food and fluids until the client is fully awake with a gag reflex.

(d)
Bleeding (unusual amounts) is the main complication to assess for.

(e)
Safe practice: written consent, explanation, fasting for at least 6 hours, side-lying position until gag reflex returns, withholding oral intake until fully awake, and frequent vital sign and respiratory monitoring.

(a)
• MS is an immune-mediated, progressive demyelinating disease of the CNS; destruction of myelin impairs nerve impulse transmission.
• The disease waxes and wanes for up to 30 years; in perhaps half of cases it steadily progresses to severe disability and premature death; there is no cure.

(b)
• Relapse triggers: febrile states, emotional stress, pregnancy, physical exertion and fatigue, and warm showers or baths; it is more common in temperate climates.
• Goals: delay progression, manage chronic symptoms and treat acute exacerbations.

(c)
• Spasticity: painful spasms in limbs; remove irritants, physical therapy, baclofen, diazepam, dantrolene.
• Paroxysmal phenomena (trigeminal neuralgia, pain, tonic seizures): carbamazepine, Neurontin, phenytoin.
• Fatigue: energy conservation, amantadine; depression: antidepressants.
• Sexual dysfunction (cannot produce or sustain erection): behavioural therapy and drugs; urinary urgency, frequency and retention: Detrol, Ditropan, Botox.
• Interferon beta-1a and beta-1b reduce relapse frequency by 30%; glatiramer acetate reduces lesions and relapse rate.
• Health promotion: protect the eyes, guard against aspiration and respiratory collapse, refer to home health agencies when needed.
• Ataxia also needs intervention.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the pathophysiology of multiple sclerosis and its course.
(b) State how the disease pattern relates to common complications and triggers.
(c) Explain how it affects body systems, the resulting functional deficit, and the related nursing management and health education.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Radioactive iodine (123I or 131I) aims to destroy overactive thyroid cells and is the commonest treatment in elderly patients.
• Almost all retained iodine concentrates in the thyroid, destroying thyroid cells without jeopardising other radiosensitive tissues.
• Over several weeks thyroid cells are destroyed, reducing hyperthyroidism and inevitably producing hypothyroidism.
• Antithyroid drugs (propylthiouracil, methimazole) inhibit hormone synthesis or release and reduce thyroid tissue, continued until the patient is euthyroid.

(b)
• Potassium iodide, Lugol's solution or SSKI, with antithyroid drugs or beta-blockers, prepare the patient for surgery by reducing hormone activity and gland vascularity.
• Subtotal thyroidectomy (about five-sixths of tissue) is reserved for pregnant women allergic to antithyroid drugs, large goitres, or patients unable to take antithyroid agents.

(c)
• Monitoring uses TSH (low in hyperthyroidism) and T3, the more accurate indicator; radioactive iodine uptake test measures thyroid iodine uptake rate.
• Post-thyroidectomy care is directed at detecting early hypocalcaemia; positive Trousseau or Chvostek signs suggest latent tetany.
• Neglect may lead to untreated hyperthyroid effects: tachycardia, atrial fibrillation, exophthalmos, weight loss and heat intolerance.
• Hypothyroidism after radioactive iodine requires recognition and hormone replacement.
• Hypocalcaemia with tetany after thyroidectomy needs immediate treatment.
questions.question:
(a) Describe radioactive iodine and antithyroid drug therapy for hyperthyroidism: indications and action.
(b) State the safety precautions and adjunctive measures.
(c) Explain the rationale behind the nursing actions and the complications that follow when they are neglected.

(a) Describe the pathophysiology and classification of diabetes mellitus.
(b) State how the types relate to common acute and chronic complications.
(c) Explain how diabetes affects distant body systems, the resulting functional deficit, and the related nursing management and health education.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Diabetes is a metabolic disease in which insulin is deficient or ineffective; types: prediabetes, type 1, type 2 and gestational diabetes.
• Insulin (beta-cell, anabolic) moves glucose into muscle, liver and fat cells; without it sugar builds up in the blood and chronic hyperglycaemia damages nerves and blood vessels.
• Diagnosis: A1C 6.5% or more on two tests (5.7-6.4% prediabetes), random glucose 200 mg/dL or more, fasting glucose categories.

(b)
• Hypoglycaemia (below 50-60 mg/dL) from too much insulin or agents, too little food or excess activity.
• Diabetic ketoacidosis mainly in type 1 (fat burned, ketones); hyperosmolar nonketotic syndrome mainly in type 2 (residual insulin).

(c)
• Heart: narrowed, clogged vessels, high blood pressure, heart attack, stroke.
• Eyes: diabetic retinopathy; nerves: diabetic neuropathy; kidneys: nephropathy.
• Manifestations: polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, fatigue, vision changes, numbness, slow-healing wounds, recurrent infections.
• Nursing assessment: sitting and standing blood pressure, BMI, visual acuity, foot, skin, nervous system and mouth examination.
• Management: normalise insulin activity, intensive insulin, nutrition, weight loss of 5-10% in obese type 2 patients, alcohol and sweetener guidance.
• Prevention: for prediabetes, losing 5-10% of body weight by diet and exercise significantly reduces risk.

questions.question:
A patient is found to be HIV positive on an ELISA test confirmed by Western blot and presents with fever, night sweats, diarrhoea and unexplained weight loss.
(a) State the risk factors and modes of transmission.
(b) Outline the complications.
(c) Describe the nursing, medical and counselling management options.
(d) Justify the priority intervention.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Risk is determined by behaviours: sexual intercourse, sharing injecting equipment, infected blood or blood products, tissue transplantation, and mother-to-baby transmission through the placenta, delivery or breast milk.
• Risk to healthcare workers after exposure is under 1%, about 0.3% (one case per 300 needlestick injuries) with percutaneous exposure.

(b)
• Most infected people eventually become severely immunosuppressed (AIDS) with opportunistic infections and cancers; a debilitating syndrome of weight loss, diarrhoea, fever and night sweats may occur.
• Opportunistic infections: Pneumocystis carinii (lungs), Toxoplasma gondii (brain), Cryptosporidium (GI), Candida, Cryptococcus, cytomegalovirus and herpes simplex.

(c)
• Pre-test counselling gives information, explores risks and benefits, builds a plan and assesses support; support groups are available; promote safer sex and safer drug use.
• Opportunistic infections are treated with agents such as co-trimoxazole, pentamidine, sulfadiazine with pyrimethamine, nystatin, fluconazole and acyclovir.

(d)
Testing with counselling is the priority because early treatment can delay onset of AIDS and knowing status lets the individual protect partners; a negative result may reflect antibodies not yet produced (weeks to months).

(a)
Hyperkalemia (potassium above 5.0 mmol/L), with ECG changes that can culminate in ventricular fibrillation or asystole.

(b)
• Potassium is the major intracellular cation and is essential for neuromuscular function; it is not stored and the kidneys do not conserve it, so excess does not usually develop when renal function is normal.
• Causes: decreased excretion (renal failure, Addison's disease); tissue breakdown (crush injury, burns, major surgery, rhabdomyolysis, hemolysis, GI bleeding); excessive potassium administration or potassium-sparing diuretics; massive stored-blood transfusion; shift out of cells in metabolic acidosis.
• Effects: neuromuscular irritability, weakness, respiratory muscle paralysis, bradycardia and ventricular fibrillation.

(c)
• Assess respiratory character, rate and depth; reposition every 2 hours, elevate the head of bed, encourage deep breathing and coughing, and suction if unable to expectorate.
• Monitor ECG, cardiac rate and rhythm and serial serum potassium; notify the doctor if potassium exceeds 6.0-6.6 mmol/L.
• Give IV calcium gluconate or calcium chloride (5-10 mL of 10% solution) to antagonize the toxic neuromuscular and cardiac effects.

(d)
• Temporary redistribution: IV sodium bicarbonate, or hypertonic glucose with regular insulin; give prescribed IV or oral fluids and ion-exchange resins.
• Dialysis removes potassium from the blood, and the underlying disease must be treated.
• Teach the patient to limit dietary potassium and about potassium-sparing diuretics.
questions.question:
A patient with renal failure presents with muscle weakness, paresthesia, nausea and diarrhoea and a slow heart rate. Repeated serum potassium is above 5.6 mmol/L and the ECG shows tall, peaked T-waves with widening QRS complexes.
(a) Identify the condition.
(b) Explain the pathophysiological basis.
(c) State the priority nursing assessment and immediate interventions.
(d) Outline the definitive medical management.

A patient suddenly develops numbness, weakness or paralysis of one side of the face and one arm or leg, with trouble understanding or speaking coherently, vision changes and impaired coordination or balance. A CT scan is requested.
(a) Identify the condition and its subtypes.
(b) Explain the pathophysiological basis, including the ischemic cascade and the factors that influence the extent of injury.
(c) State the priority nursing assessment and the immediate interventions in the first hours.
(d) Outline the definitive medical and surgical management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Ischemic stroke (cerebrovascular accident) is infarction of brain tissue from disrupted blood flow; ischemic strokes (about 85%) result from vascular occlusion and hypoperfusion and are subdivided into thrombotic and embolic.

(b)
• Obstruction of a cerebral vessel starts the ischemic cascade when cerebral blood flow falls below 25 mL/100 g/min; neurons can no longer maintain aerobic respiration.
• The penumbra (low-flow ischemic tissue around the infarct) can be salvaged with timely intervention; if the cascade continues, cell membranes are destroyed and more calcium and glutamate are released.
• Extent of injury depends on rate of onset and duration, collateral circulation, systemic circulation (hypotension), hypercoagulable state, elevated temperature, and hyper- or hypoglycaemia.

(c)
• Establish the 'last known well time', the single most important determinant of treatment options; assess ABCs, oxygenation and blood glucose; use FAST or the Cincinnati scale in the field.
• In the ED, carry out neurological assessment, vital signs and temperature not less than every 30 minutes; rt-PA treatment is targeted within 1 hour of ED arrival, and eligible patients can be treated in the 3-4.5 hour window after careful screening for exclusions.

(d)
• Medical: thrombolytic therapy (streptokinase, urokinase, tissue plasminogen activator) only after intracerebral haemorrhage is ruled out; airway management and control of hypertension.
• If an embolism is the cause, anticoagulants may be prescribed, with PT/INR monitored and warfarin dose adjusted.
• rt-PA is given at 0.9 mg/kg: 10% as a bolus over 1 minute, the rest over 1 hour, maximum 90 mg.
• Surgical: craniotomy to remove an embolus or thrombus or repair an aneurysm; endarterectomy or balloon angioplasty if carotid blockage is the cause.
• Surgery must be done within a few hours of the ischemic event to have any chance of preventing permanent neurological deficit.

questions.question:
(a) Define head trauma and classify its primary and secondary injuries.
(b) Describe the pathophysiology of each type.
(c) State how the types relate to common complications such as raised intracranial pressure and herniation.
(d) Explain how head trauma may affect distant body systems, the resulting functional deficits, and the related nursing management and health education.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Head trauma is a general term for injuries to the head, from minor concussion to life-threatening haematoma and herniation; it is a leading cause of disability.

(b)
• Primary: concussion (sudden blow, brief cerebral paralysis, recovery usually within 12 hours, possible post-concussion syndrome of poor concentration, fatigue, headache, photophobia); contusion (acceleration-deceleration bruising, coup or contrecoup); laceration (tearing of cortical surface from high-velocity or penetrating trauma).
• Secondary: epidural haematoma (middle meningeal artery torn by temporal fracture, arterial bleeding, loss of consciousness, lucid period, then deterioration); subdural (venous bleeding; acute within 48 hours, subacute 2-14 days, chronic 2 weeks or more); subarachnoid; intracerebral.

(c)
• Intracerebral haemorrhage may lead to raised ICP and permanent neurological damage; raised ICP shows as bradycardia, posturing, focal signs, headache, raised BP, pupillary changes, reduced LOC, seizures, vomiting and widened pulse pressure.
• Herniation: cerebellar (tonsils through foramen magnum, compressing medulla), supratentorial central (compressing diencephalon and midbrain), uncal (temporal lobe across tentorium, compressing midbrain and brainstem); CSF leak shows as frequent swallowing, otorrhoea, rhinorrhoea.
• Diagnosis: skull X-ray, CT of head and cervical spine, MRI, lumbar puncture, cerebral angiography, EEG; a cervical collar stays until cervical injury is ruled out.

(d)
• Distant effects: excessive urine output may mean diabetes insipidus from pituitary damage (treated with vasopressin); fluid retention may mean SIADH (fluid restriction); watch for acute respiratory distress syndrome, traumatic delirium, and meningitis or brain abscess after open injury.
• Deficits include motor and sensory changes, pupillary changes, reduced LOC and seizures; the patient may need extensive rehabilitation and the injury may be fatal or alter lifestyle.
• Nursing: vital signs and neurological assessment (Glasgow Coma Scale) every 15 minutes until stable; IV therapy with strict intake and output; airway care, since hypoxaemia and hypercapnia raise ICP.
• Quiet, dimly lit environment; seizure precautions; head of bed elevated as prescribed (early elevation after infratentorial craniotomy raises herniation risk); frequent repositioning and ROM unless raised ICP contraindicates.
• Nutritional support (enteral or parenteral) with cough and gag reflex checks to prevent aspiration; emotional support for patient and family.

(a)
• Retinal detachment: separation of the neurosensory retina from the retinal pigment epithelium (types: rhegmatogenous, traction, combined, exudative); no pain is associated.
• Examinations: visual acuity, pupillary examination, visual field testing, tonometry, then dilated fundus examination with indirect ophthalmoscope and Goldmann three-mirror.

(b)
Nursing diagnoses: disturbed sensory perception related to retinal tear, and risk for injury from impaired vision.

(c)
Rhegmatogenous and traction detachments need surgery: pneumatic retinopexy (gas bubble with cryotherapy or laser, head positioned to tamponade the tear), scleral buckle (silicone band around the globe, done in the operating room), pars plana vitrectomy.

(d)
• Gas tamponade requires the patient to lie face down or on the side for days; prepare patient and family beforehand; many cases are outpatient with next-day follow-up.
• Complications: increased IOP, endophthalmitis, further detachments, cataract, loss of eye turgor.
• Prevention: serial dilated fundus examinations, often yearly, for diabetic and sickle cell patients; protective eyewear for high myopia in contact sports.

(e)
Teach signs of raised IOP (eye pain, nausea, vomiting, headache) and infection (pain, redness, swelling).
questions.question:
A patient reports a sensation of a shade or curtain coming across the vision of one eye, partial vision loss, bright flashes of light, areas of darkness in the visual field and suddenly seeing many floaters, with no pain.
(a) Identify the condition and name the diagnostic examinations.
(b) State the nursing diagnoses.
(c) State the surgical procedures.
(d) Describe the post-operative nursing care and complications to monitor, with prevention.
(e) Outline patient education.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Interference with pulmonary gas exchange causes CO2 retention and raised carbonic acid; causes include respiratory arrest, head or brain trauma, pneumonia, sedation or anesthesia, atelectasis, Guillain-Barre syndrome and COPD.

(b)
Body pH is held at 7.35-7.45 by buffers, the respiratory response and the renal response; in respiratory acidosis pH falls with raised PaCO2, bicarbonate rises to buffer, and kidney compensation is slowest (2-3 days).

(c)
Early: weakness, headache, fatigue, anxiety and tremors; progressive: dehydration and confusion, leading to coma if untreated.

(d)
• Find the cause; give bicarbonate; antibiotics for pneumonia; naloxone for oversedation; replace potassium chloride.
• Nursing diagnoses: ineffective breathing pattern from decreased depth due to anesthesia, immobility and incision guarding; potential alteration in respiratory function from inactivity or omitted deep breathing.

(e)
• Susceptible are patients with CNS depression or obstructive pulmonary disease, those oversedated or anesthetized, immobile patients and those guarding a painful incision.
• Hypoventilation is more dangerous than hyperventilation because it causes retention of excess carbon dioxide.

(f)
• Metabolic acidosis is high fixed acid content in ECF with low bicarbonate; causes: cardiac arrest, renal failure, ketoacidosis, acidic ingestion, or loss of base in diarrhoea.
• Metabolic acidosis features: Kussmaul's respirations, dehydration, lethargy, nausea and vomiting, headache, shortness of breath, vasodilatation, tremors, coma; urine becomes acidic.
• Metabolic acidosis treatment: glucose, insulin or IV potassium chloride for ketoacidosis, fluid replacement, bicarbonate, low-protein high-carbohydrate diet in renal failure, phosphate replacement.
• Respiratory acidosis is a disorder of ventilation (raised CO2), while metabolic acidosis is a disorder of acid or bicarbonate balance.
• Metabolic acidosis nursing: monitor intake and output, glucose, potassium, ECG and sensorium and use seizure precautions.
questions.question:
Describe respiratory acidosis under the following headings:
(a) Definition and causes

Describe thoracentesis under the following headings:
(a) Indications
(b) Preparation
(c) Nursing responsibilities
(d) Complications
State the safety precautions or safe practice points.
(e) List the safety points.
(f) State the key sign that must be reported immediately after the procedure.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Thoracentesis is removal of pleural fluid for diagnostic purposes; it may also obtain a biopsy, instill medications and remove fluid for comfort and safety.
• In pleural effusion, pleurisy or atelectasis it removes trapped air or fluid; a chest x-ray shows pleural effusions of 250 mL or more.

(b)
• Explain the procedure and obtain written informed consent.
• Position the client upright and sitting, leaning forward with arms resting on an overbed table; explain that the area will be anesthetized.

(c)
• Instruct the client to hold as still as possible during needle insertion and assist the physician.
• Deliver the specimen to the laboratory as soon as possible and observe the site for bleeding afterwards.
• Assess breath sounds before and after the procedure and report absent breath sounds immediately.

(d)
Bleeding at the site and absent breath sounds are the problems to watch for.

(e)
Safe practice: written consent, correct positioning, keeping still during needle insertion, timely specimen delivery, bleeding checks and before-and-after breath sound assessment.

(f)
Absent breath sounds must be reported immediately.

(a)
Hypothyroidism: a hypometabolic state from deficiency of T4 and T3; other features include menorrhagia or amenorrhea, hypothermia and, in severe cases, sleep apnea.

(b)
The most common cause is disease of the thyroid itself; others: iodine deficiency, radiation therapy of the head and neck, thyroidectomy, atrophy related to aging, drugs such as lithium and antithyroid medications, and chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis.

(c)
• Production and release of T4 and T3 is deficient; a normal thyroid (15-20 g) produces about 90-100 µg of T4 and 30-35 µg of T3 daily, and these hormones influence basal metabolic processes.
• Inadequate secretion in fetal and neonatal life causes stunted physical and mental growth (cretinism); in adults it causes lethargy, slow mentation and slowing of body functions.
• Diagnosis: serum TSH immunoassay and total and free T4 and T3 measurements; treatment is synthetic levothyroxine.

(d)
• Encourage activity such as exercise; provide warm clothing because of cold intolerance; monitor vital signs; give emotional support; encourage adequate diet.
• Teach self-care because most treatment occurs at home, and follow up patients receiving home care.
questions.question:
A patient reports puffiness of the face and hands, weight gain, cold intolerance, a hoarse voice, hair loss, brittle nails, lethargy and slow thinking.
(a) Identify the condition.
(b) State the predisposing factors.
(c) Explain the pathophysiology.
(d) Describe the nursing management.

A patient has central obesity, a moon-shaped face, buffalo hump, purple striae, easy bruising, muscle wasting, hypertension and hyperglycaemia. Causes include a pituitary adenoma, adrenal tumours, ectopic ACTH-producing tumours and long-term glucocorticoid therapy.
(a) State the risk factors.
(b) State the complications.
(c) Outline the medical and surgical management options.
(d) Justify the priority intervention.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Endogenous: pituitary adenoma (Cushing's disease, about 70%, mostly women aged 20-40), adrenal tumours (15-20%), ectopic ACTH tumours such as small cell lung cancer (5-10%), familial (under 1%).
• Exogenous: long-term glucocorticoid therapy (for example prednisone for asthma, rheumatoid arthritis or lupus) or glucocorticoid abuse; it is commoner in women aged 20-50.

(b)
Hyperglycaemia and insulin resistance, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, osteoporosis and fracture risk, avascular necrosis of the femoral head, mood disturbance, infections and delayed wound healing.

(c)
• Diagnosis: 24-hour urinary free cortisol, late-night salivary cortisol, low-dose dexamethasone suppression test, imaging, petrosal sinus sampling.
• Medical: steroidogenesis inhibitors (ketoconazole, metyrapone, osilodrostat), glucocorticoid receptor antagonists; surgery for tumours: transsphenoidal surgery, adrenalectomy, ectopic tumour removal, bilateral adrenalectomy in refractory cases.

(d)
• Priority for a tumour cause is surgery, followed by preventing adrenal insufficiency: sudden cortisol withdrawal can cause life-threatening hypotension, fatigue and hypoglycaemia.
• Give glucocorticoid replacement and taper as needed; teach the signs of adrenal crisis and stress-dose steroids during illness or surgery; monitor for CSF leak or infection after transsphenoidal surgery.

questions.question:
A patient with diabetes mellitus on insulin has a diminished level of consciousness with cool, clammy, moist skin.
(a) Identify the condition.
(b) State the predisposing factors.
(c) Explain the pathophysiology.
(d) Describe the nursing management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Hypoglycemia, one of the most common life-threatening conditions in diabetes that requires immediate nursing management.

(b)
It occurs when the body has too much insulin; insulin therapy and oral hypoglycemic agents are the treatments used, and exercise should not be done when insulin is peaking.

(c)
Insulin lets cells absorb glucose and promotes glycogen storage; excess insulin lowers blood glucose, and when glucose is low alpha cells secrete glucagon to raise it.

(d)
• Monitor blood sugar and recognize altered glucose levels (diminished level of consciousness, cool and clammy skin).
• Conscious patient: orange juice; unconscious patient: IV dextrose 50% or glucagon injection; retest blood glucose in 10-15 minutes and notify the healthcare provider.
• Teach self-monitoring of blood glucose, which prevents hypoglycemia, and carrying a quick source of sugar when exercising.

(a)
Meningitis is inflammation of the meninges and subarachnoid space; septic meningitis is bacterial, aseptic is viral or secondary to other disease.

(b)
Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis cause most adult bacterial cases; Haemophilus influenzae also; aseptic causes: viruses, lymphoma, leukaemia, brain abscess; a non-infectious irritant such as myelogram dye can also cause it.

(c)
Organisms reach the meninges by blood or direct spread, cross the blood-brain barrier and multiply in CSF; the immune response releases cell wall fragments and lipopolysaccharides, inflaming the subarachnoid space and pia mater and raising ICP.

(d)
Headache, fever, nuchal rigidity, positive Kernig and Brudzinski signs, photophobia, rash (petechial to ecchymosis), cranial nerve effects, disorientation, seizures, decreased LOC; death may occur within hours.

(e)
• Tobacco use and viral upper respiratory infection (more droplets), otitis media, mastoiditis, sinusitis, head trauma with basilar skull fracture, neurosurgery, systemic sepsis.
• Immune depression (steroids, chemotherapy, radiation, malnutrition) and dense groups such as college campuses and military installations; meningococcal peaks in winter and early spring.

(f)
• Aseptic meningitis occurs more often in summer and early fall.
• Bacterial CSF: opening pressure 200-500 mm H2O, leukocytes 100-5000, neutrophils 80% or more, protein 100-500 mg/dL, glucose below 40 mg/dL.
• Viral CSF: pressure up to 250, leukocytes 50-1000, neutrophils under 40%, protein under 200, glucose above 45; normal CSF is 100-180, 0-5, 18-45 and 45-80 mg/dL glucose.
• Bacterial needs early antibiotics crossing the blood-brain barrier (penicillin G with a cephalosporin) and adjunct dexamethasone; acyclovir is used for viral cases.
• Prevention: meningococcal conjugate vaccine, vaccination against H. influenzae and S. pneumoniae in at-risk people, chemoprophylaxis for contacts.
• Droplet precautions and infection control continue until 24 hours after antibiotics begin.
questions.question:
(a) Define bacterial meningitis.
(b) State its causes.
(c) Describe its pathophysiology.
(d) List its clinical manifestations.
(e) Explain why certain people are more susceptible.
(f) Distinguish bacterial from viral (aseptic) meningitis.

(a) Define gout arthritis.
(b) State its causes.
(c) Describe its pathophysiology.
(d) List its manifestations.
(e) Explain why certain people are susceptible.
(f) Distinguish an acute gout attack from chronic gout.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Gout is an inflammatory joint disease from uric acid crystal deposits: accumulated uric acid forms needlelike joint crystals.

(b)
Genetics, decreased uric acid excretion, chronic renal failure, myxoedema, polycythaemia vera, hyperparathyroidism; purine-rich foods, alcohol (especially beer), aspirin, cyclosporine, diuretics, dehydration.

(c)
Uric acid is the end product of purine metabolism; abnormal purine metabolism lowers urinary urate excretion and raises blood levels; it precipitates where blood flow is slowest; a genetic defect can overproduce it.

(d)
• Joint pain, redness and swelling, tophi (great toe, ankle, outer ear), malaise, tachycardia and raised skin temperature.
• Tests: raised ESR and uric acid; sodium urate crystals in synovial fluid.

(e)
• Overweight (above 25), physical stress (illness, hospitalisation), dehydration, diuretics and alcohol (kidneys excrete alcohol and leave uric acid behind).
• Chronic renal failure patients cannot remove uric acid and are at risk of chronic gout.

(f)
• Acute: random sudden attack lasting 1-2 weeks, months or years apart, no long-term damage, starts in big toe, pain peaks in 4-24 hours, very sensitive to pressure.
• Chronic: persistently high uric acid causes repeated attacks and joint damage.
• Chronic: tophi (white or yellowish nodules) form in elbows, toes, ear helix, fingers, bursae and bone, causing deformity.
• Chronic: itching, peeling skin and uric acid kidney stones.
• Treatment: acute uses NSAIDs, corticosteroid, colchicine; chronic prevention uses allopurinol.

(a)
• A brain abscess is a collection of pus enclosed in brain tissue from bacterial or fungal infection; it may complicate infection, trauma or surgery, and is rare in immunocompetent people.
• Predisposing: otitis media and rhinosinusitis; spread from lungs, gums, tongue, heart, wounds or intra-abdominal infection.
• Organisms include Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA), streptococci, Prevotella, Fusobacterium, B. fragilis, Enterobacteriaceae and Pseudomonas.
• Infection enters the intracranial compartment directly or indirectly, collects in brain tissue, raises ICP and forms the abscess.
• Stages: early cerebritis (1-3 days), late cerebritis (4-9, pus formation), early capsule (10-13), late capsule (beyond 14 days, dense collagenous capsule).

(b)
• Before encapsulation, antimicrobial therapy with ICP control is essential; abscesses over 2.5 cm are excised or aspirated, smaller ones or cerebritis-stage lesions aspirated for diagnosis.
• Steroids may delay encapsulation, increase necrosis, reduce antibiotic penetration and raise ventricular rupture risk.

(c)
• Manifestations: headache, fever (50%), vomiting, focal deficits (weakness, reduced vision), raised ICP (decreasing LOC, seizures).
• Diagnosis: MRI (preferred), CT, aspiration, blood cultures, chest X-ray to exclude lung infection.
• Antibiotics: penicillin, chloramphenicol, metronidazole and third- or fourth-generation cephalosporins; aminoglycosides penetrate poorly.
• Nursing: continued neurological assessment for ICP change, medication and response, safety; monitor glucose and potassium with corticosteroids; assess family coping.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the pathophysiology and stages of brain abscess.
(b) State how the stages relate to management and complications.
(c) Explain how a brain abscess arises from and affects other body systems, the resulting deficits, and the related nursing management.

Describe Cushing's syndrome under the following headings:
(a) Definition and causes
(b) Pathophysiology
(c) Clinical manifestations and complications
(d) Management
Explain the clinical basis for why certain people are more susceptible.
(e) Give the reasons for vulnerability.
Distinguish between Cushing's syndrome and Addison's disease.
(f) State the differences.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• A disorder from exposure to excess cortisol affecting all tissues; it results from excessive rather than deficient adrenocortical activity.
• Causes: excessive ACTH or corticosteroid administration, adrenal cortex hyperplasia, a pituitary tumor producing ACTH, and ectopic ACTH from malignancy (bronchogenic carcinoma most common).

(b)
Normal feedback control of the adrenal cortex becomes ineffective and the usual diurnal cortisol pattern is lost.

(c)
• Fat gain in the face, above the collarbone and back of neck; red round face; vertigo and blurred vision; mood swings, depression, hypertension; weakness; easy bruising and purplish striae; amenorrhea; reduced fertility.
• Complications: heart attack, stroke, unhealthy cholesterol, pulmonary blood clots and lung infections, bone loss and fractures, insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes.

(d)
Drugs: ketoconazole, mitotane, metyrapone, mifepristone; surgery: adrenalectomy, transsphenoidal or subtotal hypophysectomy; nursing: reduce risk of injury and infection, promote skin integrity and body image.

(e)
People given excess ACTH or corticosteroids, or with a pituitary ACTH tumor or an ACTH-producing malignancy, are susceptible because feedback no longer limits cortisol.

(f)
• Addison's disease is primary adrenal insufficiency: too little cortisol and aldosterone, most often autoimmune damage to the adrenal cortex.
• Addison's features: fatigue, poor appetite, dizziness, hypotension, salt cravings, skin darkening, depression, hyponatremia and hyperkalemia; Cushing's gives hypertension and striae.
• Addison's is treated by replacing hormones (hydrocortisone, fludrocortisone) and fluids; Cushing's by drugs or surgery to reduce cortisol.
• Addisonian crisis: low cortisol causes hypoglycemia, low aldosterone causes hypovolemia and shock.

(a)
• Opacity or cloudiness of the lens from gradual progressive thickening; it is the most common cause of visual impairment and a preventable cause of blindness; extent of impairment depends on size, density and location of the opacity.
• Risk factors: ageing, ocular conditions, corticosteroids, chemicals, smoking, poor antioxidants and nutrition, obesity, dehydration, trauma, ultraviolet radiation.

(b)
• Nuclear: centre of lens, initially myopia with improved near vision, then impaired vision. Cortical: edges of lens, little effect except worse with glare.
• Posterior subcapsular: younger people, linked to corticosteroids, inflammation or trauma; impaired near vision and halos. Congenital: infection in pregnancy or inherited.

(c)
• Surgical complications include hemorrhage, rupture of the posterior capsule, acute bacterial endophthalmitis, malposition of the lens and suture-related problems.
• Surgery: intracapsular extraction, extracapsular extraction, phacoemulsification and lens replacement; there is no non-surgical treatment.

(d)
• Systemic diseases associated: diabetes, Down syndrome, renal disorders, lipid metabolism disorders and musculoskeletal disorders.
• Functional deficit: painless blurring, glare sensitivity, reduced acuity, poor night vision, double vision, halos and fading of colours.

(e)
• Pre-operative care includes withholding anticoagulants.
• Early-stage help: vision aids, proper lighting and positioning to reduce glare, and short-term mydriatics.

(f)
Self-care teaching to promote home care.

(a) Pathophysiology
