A patient presents with sudden severe eye pain and marked redness of the eye with a sudden visual disturbance, and acute angle-closure glaucoma is suspected.
(a) Identify the condition.
(b) Explain the pathophysiological basis.
(c) State the priority nursing assessment and immediate interventions.
(d) Outline the definitive medical and surgical management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Acute angle-closure glaucoma, a type in which the drainage angle narrows or closes suddenly; eye pain is associated with acute closed-angle glaucoma.

(b)
• Glaucoma is optic nerve damage from raised intraocular pressure caused by congestion of aqueous humor; obstruction of outflow follows complete or partial closure of the drainage angle.
• IOP depends on aqueous production, resistance to drainage and episcleral venous pressure; about 90% drains via the canal of Schlemm.

(c)
• Take a history (sudden visual disturbance, marked redness, eye pain) using SOCRATES; tonometry measures IOP (normal 10-21 mmHg); also consider gonioscopy, perimetry and ophthalmoscopy.
• Topical or systemic medication is given to prevent optic nerve damage.

(d)
• Goal: prevent optic nerve damage by medical therapy, surgery or both; surgery: laser trabeculoplasty, laser iridotomy, filtering procedure, trabeculectomy and drainage implant.
• Treatment is lifelong and cannot reverse damage but can prevent further damage; nursing management centres on patient teaching.

questions.question:
Describe acute renal failure under the following headings:
(a) Pathophysiology and causes
(b) Phases
State how the phases relate to the common complications.
(c) Link the phases to complications.
Explain how the disorder affects distant body systems, the resulting functional deficit and the related management and health education.
(d) Distant effects and deficit
(e) Medical and nursing management
questions.answerText:
(a)
• An abrupt decline in renal function with falling GFR; the kidneys cannot excrete toxic wastes, BUN and creatinine rise, and the patient can reach uremia in a week; most forms are reversible if correctly diagnosed.
• Causes: myocardial infarction, hypotension, sepsis, shock, peritonitis, volume depletion, nephrotoxic drugs (gentamicin, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors), hemorrhage, burns, trauma and DIC.
• Nephrons cannot exchange potassium, so hyperkalemia develops; sodium loss causes hyponatremia and hydrogen retention causes acidosis.

(b)
• Initiation: from the initial insult until oliguria begins.
• Oliguria: urea, creatinine, uric acid, organic acids, potassium and magnesium rise (uremic phase, hyperkalemia).
• Diuresis: urine output gradually rises, signalling GFR recovery; labs stop rising. Recovery: improvement over 3 to 12 months.

(c)
• Oliguria brings hyperkalemia and uremia; in diuresis renal function may still be markedly abnormal with uremic symptoms present and dehydration can worsen uremia.
• A 1-3% GFR reduction in recovery is common but not clinically significant.

(d)
Rising wastes cause confusion, convulsions and coma; high potassium threatens cardiac function; renal failure disrupts endocrine, metabolic, fluid, electrolyte and acid-base function.

(e)
• Treat hypovolemia with 0.45% saline and nephrotoxicity with mannitol or loop diuretics; dialysis when medications fail (rising potassium, fluid overload, impending pulmonary edema, acidosis, pericarditis, severe confusion).
• Nursing: monitor edema and daily weight, protein-reduced diet, safety, bleeding and infection prevention, emotional support; observe closely for dehydration in diuresis.

(a)
• Shock is an abnormal physiological state of widespread, serious reduction of tissue perfusion with fall in blood pressure that, if prolonged, impairs cellular function.
• Reduced cardiac output and arterial pressure trigger compensation; when it fails, shock progresses; cells swell, membranes become permeable, mitochondria and lysosomes are damaged and the cell dies.

(b)
• Hypovolaemic: blood volume loss (hemorrhage, vomiting, diarrhoea, burns, diuretics). Cardiogenic: pump failure (heart failure, pulmonary embolism, myocardial infarction).
• Neurogenic: loss of sympathetic tone with vasodilatation. Circulatory or distributive: septic (widespread infection) and anaphylactic (antigen-antibody reaction with histamine); these show dry warm skin and bradycardia rather than cool moist skin.

(c)
• Complications of shock: metabolic acidosis, cardiac failure, arrhythmias, shock lung, uremia, cerebral damage, susceptibility to infection and hemorrhage.
• Fluid replacement carries the risks of cardiovascular overload and pulmonary edema.

(d)
• Skin is pale, cold, clammy and cyanosed; respiration rises then depresses, with atelectasis, pulmonary emboli and edema 3-6 days later; the gut develops paralytic ileus and stress ulcers; urine output falls.
• Immobility brings thrombosis, circulatory stasis, pressure ulcers, contractures and atelectasis.

(e)
• Restoring tissue perfusion with IV fluids takes precedence, then oxygenation with a patent airway; vasoactive drugs, nutritional support (over 3000 calories daily) and an NG tube for ileus.
• Monitor blood pressure and pulse every 15 minutes, respirations every 15-30 minutes, hourly urine (report under 30 mL), change position every 1-2 hours and give IV analgesia watching for respiratory depression.

(f)
• Patients with known allergies need to understand the consequences of later exposure to the antigen.
• First aid teaching: stop bleeding, lay the patient flat or head lower, keep warm, reassure and transport quickly.
questions.question:
Describe shock under the following headings:
(a) Pathophysiology
(b) Types and classification
(c) State the complications of shock and of fluid replacement.
Explain how shock affects distant body systems, the resulting functional deficit and the related nursing management and health education.
(d) Distant effects and deficit
(e) Nursing management
(f) Health education

questions.answerText:
(a)
Multiple sclerosis: an immune-mediated, progressive demyelinating disease of the CNS, in which destruction of myelin impairs nerve impulse transmission.

(b)
Motor (spasticity, ataxia), pain pathways (trigeminal neuralgia, tonic seizures), energy (fatigue), mood, sexual and urinary function; the eyes, swallowing and breathing need protection.

(c)
• Assessment: known stressors that trigger relapse: febrile states, emotional stress, pregnancy, exertion, fatigue, warm shower or bath.
• Planning: delay progression, manage chronic symptoms, treat acute exacerbations; intervene for spasticity, fatigue, bladder dysfunction and ataxia.
• Implementation: remove irritants and use physical therapy with baclofen, diazepam or dantrolene for spasticity; carbamazepine, Neurontin or phenytoin for paroxysmal pain; energy conservation and amantadine for fatigue.
• Antidepressants for depression; behavioural therapy for sexual dysfunction; Detrol, Ditropan or Botox for urinary problems.
• Interferon beta-1a and 1b cut relapse frequency by 30%; glatiramer acetate reduces lesions and relapses; protect eyes, prevent aspiration and respiratory collapse; refer to home health.
questions.question:
A patient has painful spasms in the limbs, fatigue, depression, urinary urgency, frequency and retention, sexual dysfunction and trigeminal neuralgia; symptoms worsen after a warm shower, fever or emotional stress.
(a) Identify the condition and the system affected.
(b) State the organs or functions compromised.
(c) Explain the nursing reasoning and prioritisation (nursing process).

A 38-year-old woman has had six months of increased heart rate, weight loss, nervousness, irritability, heat intolerance, sweating and difficulty sleeping; her eyes have become bulgy and red, affecting her vision. Her thyroid is enlarged and tender. T3 220 ng/dL (normal 80-200), T4 15 µg/dL (normal 5-12), TSH <0.01 µIU/mL (normal 0.5-5); radioactive iodine uptake is increased; ultrasound shows an enlarged thyroid with multiple nodules.
(a) Identify the condition and the body system affected.
(b) State the organs or functions compromised.
(c) Give differential conditions.
(d) Apply the nursing process: assessment, diagnosis, planning, implementation and evaluation.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Graves' disease (hyperthyroidism) of the endocrine system: overproduction of T3 and T4; low TSH because the pituitary decreases TSH when hormone levels are high.

(b)
Metabolism is greatly increased; the heart (fast or irregular rate, palpitations), nervous system (nervousness, tremor), skin (warm, sweating), muscles, GI tract, sleep, and the eyes (redness, dryness, vision problems).

(c)
Other forms of hyperthyroidism: toxic adenoma, TSH-secreting pituitary tumor, subacute or silent thyroiditis and some thyroid cancers; Hashimoto's thyroiditis may initially overproduce hormone.

(d)
• Assessment: monitor vital signs (especially BP and pulse), ask about chest pain, listen for murmurs, obtain ECG because atrial arrhythmias may occur.
• Diagnosis: risk for decreased cardiac output (increased heart rate); fatigue related to irritability; risk for impaired tissue integrity (impaired eyelid closure).
• Planning: maintain adequate cardiac output within 30 minutes; increase energy level within 24 hours; protect the eyes and reduce inflammation within 24 hours.
• Implementation: cool environment, limit bed linens, IV normal saline, atenolol; quiet cool room with restricted activity and bed rest; elevate head of bed, dark glasses, tape eyelids shut during sleep, prednisone.

questions.question:
Describe hypothyroidism under the following headings:
(a) Definition and causes
(b) Pathophysiology
(c) Clinical manifestations
(d) Management
Explain the clinical basis for why certain people are more susceptible.
(e) Give the reasons for increased vulnerability.
Distinguish between hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism.
(f) State the differences in metabolism, features and treatment.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• A hypometabolic state from deficiency of T4 and T3; the most common cause is disease of the thyroid itself.
• Other causes: iodine deficiency, radiation of the head and neck, thyroidectomy, age-related atrophy, lithium and antithyroid drugs, chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis.

(b)
Production and release of T4 and T3 is deficient; a normal gland makes about 90-100 µg of T4 and 30-35 µg of T3 daily, and these hormones drive basal metabolic processes.

(c)
• Hair loss, brittle nails, dry hair, husky voice, menorrhagia or amenorrhea, weight gain, hypothermia and sleep apnea in severe disease.
• Adults show lethargy and slow mentation; deficiency in fetal and neonatal life causes stunted physical and mental growth (cretinism).

(d)
Diagnosis by serum TSH and thyroid hormone immunoassay; treatment is synthetic levothyroxine; nursing gives warm clothing, encourages exercise, monitors vital signs, gives emotional support and teaches self-care.

(e)
• Susceptible are people with thyroid disease, previous thyroidectomy or head and neck radiation, aging thyroid atrophy and those taking lithium or antithyroid drugs.
• Iodine deficiency lowers hormone levels, so pituitary TSH rises and causes compensatory goiter.

(f)
• Hyperthyroidism is overproduction of T3 and T4 with greatly increased metabolic rate; Graves' disease is the most common form.
• Hyperthyroidism features: nervousness, heat sensitivity, weight loss despite appetite, palpitations, tremor, warm sweaty skin, diarrhoea, goiter and eye problems; hypothyroidism features weight gain and cold intolerance.
• Hyperthyroidism: low TSH; antithyroid drugs (methimazole, propylthiouracil), beta blockers, radioiodine or thyroidectomy; thyroid storm is an emergency.
• Hyperthyroid nursing: monitor heart rate and blood pressure, ask about chest pain, listen for murmurs, obtain ECG and teach relaxation.

questions.question:
A patient with uncontrolled diabetes mellitus and diarrhoea has deep, rapid breathing, lethargy, nausea, headache and dehydration, and the urine is acidic.
(a) Identify the condition.
(b) State the predisposing factors.
(c) Explain the pathophysiology.
(d) Describe the nursing management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Metabolic acidosis: high acid content in extracellular fluid with low bicarbonate, shown by Kussmaul (deep, rapid) breathing as the lungs blow off CO2 and the kidneys excrete hydrogen, making the urine acidic.

(b)
Build-up of fixed acids (cardiac arrest, renal failure, ketoacidosis, acidic substances) or loss of base (diarrhoea); also seen with vomiting and diabetes mellitus.

(c)
• Fixed acids arise from diet, lactic acid in anaerobic metabolism, and ketoacids from fatty acid oxidation in insulin-deficient states such as diabetes.
• Body pH (7.35-7.45) is held by buffers (carbonic acid/bicarbonate), respiratory response and the renal response, which is the slowest (2-3 days).
• Signs: Kussmaul respirations, dehydration, lethargy, malaise, fatigue, nausea/vomiting, headache, shortness of breath, vasodilatation, tremors and coma.

(d)
• Medical: find the cause; in ketoacidosis give glucose, insulin or IV potassium chloride; replace fluids; give bicarbonate; in renal failure give low-protein, high-carbohydrate diet and replace phosphates.
• Nursing diagnosis: fluid volume deficit related to abnormal losses; monitor intake and output, vital signs, glucose and potassium, and ECG for dysrhythmias.
• Assess for dehydration and decreased sensorium, test urine pH and specific gravity, encourage fluids or give IV lactate and NaHCO3 as prescribed, and institute seizure precautions if sensorium decreases.

questions.question:
(a) Define ischaemic stroke and describe thrombotic and embolic stroke (causes, pathophysiology, manifestations).
(b) Explain why certain people are more susceptible.
(c) Distinguish thrombotic from embolic stroke.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Ischaemic stroke results from partial or complete arterial occlusion and is about 85% of strokes; thrombotic stroke is clot formation at an injured vessel, embolic stroke is an embolus lodging in a cerebral artery.
• Thrombotic causes: atherosclerosis (hypertension, heart disease, diabetes, smoking, hyperlipidaemia, family history), hypercoagulable state, fibromuscular dysplasia; minor factors are obesity, inactivity and alcohol.
• Embolic causes: atrial fibrillation, myocardial infarction, infective endocarditis, atrial septal defects, rheumatic heart disease; less commonly fat or air from long bone fracture.
• Thrombotic: plaques develop over months to years from subintimal lipid deposition; ulceration disrupts the intima and starts coagulation; common at bifurcations; 61% of strokes, and 30-50% are preceded by a TIA.
• Embolic: emboli mostly arise in the endocardium, travel upward and lodge where vessels narrow or bifurcate, causing infarction and oedema; second most common.
• Manifestations: changes in LOC, fever, headache, vomiting, seizures, one-sided numbness, weakness or paralysis, speech and vision problems, poor coordination.

(b)
• Non-modifiable risks: age, gender, race, heredity.
• Modifiable risks: hypertension, obesity, oral contraceptives, sickle cell disease, inactivity, smoking, hyperlipidaemia, heavy alcohol, heart disease, diabetes, hypercoagulation and cocaine.

(c)
• Thrombotic develops on atherosclerotic vessels, extent depending on speed of onset, lesion size and collateral circulation.
• Embolic has rapid onset of severe symptoms, and prognosis relates to the amount of brain tissue deprived of blood.
• Lacunar infarcts involve small deep penetrating arteries (basal ganglia, thalamus, internal capsule, pons), causing hemiplegia and facial weakness.
• CT shows infarct size and location; if embolism is suspected, cardiac tests seek the source.

questions.question:
Describe diabetes mellitus under the following headings:
(a) Definition and types
(b) Risk factors
(c) Pathophysiology
(d) Clinical manifestations
Explain the clinical basis for why certain people are more susceptible to the disease.
(e) Give the reasons for increased susceptibility.
Distinguish between type 1 diabetes mellitus and type 2 diabetes mellitus.
(f) State the differences in cause, onset, insulin status and treatment.
questions.answerText:
(a)
A metabolic disorder of multiple etiology with chronic hyperglycemia and disturbed carbohydrate, fat and protein metabolism from a defect in insulin secretion, insulin action or both; the three major types are type 1, type 2 and gestational.

(b)
Risk factors: family history, age, race, obesity, sedentary lifestyle, polycystic ovary syndrome, and adrenaline-raising exercise that stimulates the liver to release glucose.

(c)
• Type 1: autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells causes insulin deficiency, and alpha-cell function is abnormal with excess glucagon.
• Type 2: inadequate insulin or insulin resistance, where muscle, liver and fat cells fail to respond to insulin even when levels are high.

(d)
• Polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, unintentional weight loss, fatigue and blurred vision.
• Slow wound healing, numbness and tingling of hands and feet, recurrent infections and skin changes.

(e)
• Obesity: adipose tissue releases non-esterified fatty acids, glycerol, hormones and pro-inflammatory cytokines that contribute to insulin resistance.
• Sedentary lifestyle: long sitting changes metabolism including insulin resistance; women with PCOS are insulin resistant; type 2 is more common from age 45 years and in certain racial groups.

(f)
• Type 1: insulin-dependent, once called juvenile-onset, autoimmune, may be genetic, often begins in childhood, and needs exogenous insulin for life.
• Type 2: once called non-insulin-dependent or adult-onset, about 90% of cases, the pancreas usually makes some insulin but not enough or it is not used well; increasingly seen in overweight children and teens.
• Type 2 is treated with diet, exercise and oral agents; insulin is used long term if meal planning and oral agents are ineffective.
• Gestational diabetes arises from pregnancy-related insulin resistance, is spotted in middle or late pregnancy and is a greater risk to the baby than to the mother.

(a)
• Hypocalcemia: repeated serum calcium below 4.5 mEq/L or 8.5 mg/dL (albumin normal); ECG shows prolonged Q-T interval.
• Findings: numbness and tingling around the mouth (early indicator), muscle cramps, paresthesia, tetany (twitching, facial spasms, painful tonic spasms), carpopedal spasm; hypotension and bleeding if severe.

(b)
• Predisposing factor: loss of calcium-rich secretions through diarrhoea or wound exudates.
• Serum calcium is controlled by the parathyroid glands and is inversely related to phosphate; calcium is needed for bones and teeth, blood clotting, nerve impulse transmission and muscle contraction, and needs vitamin D and protein; about half is bound to albumin.

(c)
• Nursing diagnosis: potential for injury from increased seizure risk; give prescribed calcium, vitamin D and magnesium supplements and teach about calcium-containing foods.
• Observe for tingling and tetany, assess carpopedal spasm and lip/cheek spasm on facial nerve tap, monitor serum calcium and notify the doctor of significant findings.
• Medical: IV 10% calcium gluconate 10-20 mL over 10-15 minutes in acute symptomatic cases, then 600-800 mg in 1000 mL D5W titrated until oral therapy suffices; oral calcium in less acute cases; vitamin D enhances absorption.
questions.question:
A patient with prolonged diarrhoea and wound exudate complains of muscle cramps and numbness and tingling around the mouth and fingers. Tapping the facial nerve produces spasm of the lip and cheek, and reduced blood supply to the hand produces spasm of the hand.
(a) Identify the condition.
(b) State the predisposing factors and the pathophysiological basis.
(c) Describe the nursing management.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Medication is indicated in epilepsy to control, not cure, seizures; it is selected on seizure type, effectiveness and safety.
• Properly prescribed and taken, medication controls seizures in 70-80% of patients.
• Treatment starts with a single drug; starting dose and rate of increase depend on side effects; blood levels are monitored because absorption varies between patients.
• Change drug if control fails or toxicity blocks dose increase; adjust for concurrent illness, weight change or stress; examples: carbamazepine, clonazepam, phenobarbital, phenytoin, valproate.
• In status epilepticus, IV diazepam, lorazepam or phenytoin is given slowly, and phenytoin or phenobarbital later maintains control; an endotracheal tube is inserted if the patient stays unresponsive.

(b)
• During a seizure ease the patient to the floor, protect the head with a pad, loosen tight clothing, remove eyeglasses and clear furniture; in bed remove pillows and raise side rails.
• Do not pry open the jaws or insert anything in the mouth, and do not restrain the patient.
• Place the patient on one side with head flexed forward; suction if needed; afterwards keep on one side, reorient, and guide a confused patient gently.

(c)
• Rationale: prying causes broken teeth and injury to lips and tongue; restraint injures because contractions are strong; side-lying lets the tongue fall forward and drains saliva and mucus.
• Nursing diagnoses include risk for injury, fear, ineffective coping and deficient knowledge about anticonvulsants.
• Neglect: interrupted anticonvulsant medication (with fever or infection) can precipitate status epilepticus, where cerebral anoxia and oedema may cause irreversible, fatal brain damage.
questions.question:
(a) Describe antiepileptic drug therapy: indications, selection, monitoring and complications.
(b) State the safety precautions and safe practice points during a seizure.
(c) Explain the rationale behind the nursing actions and the complications that follow when they are neglected.

(a) Describe the diagnostic measurement and therapy of acute ischemic stroke using tissue plasminogen activator (rt-PA): indications and dosing.
(b) State the nursing responsibilities before and during administration.
(c) State the safety precautions.
(d) Explain the rationale for the assessment schedule and the complications that follow if these are neglected.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• rt-PA is the only FDA-approved drug for acute ischemic stroke; it is indicated for eligible ischemic stroke patients, with intracerebral haemorrhage ruled out first by CT.
• Dosing is 0.9 mg/kg: 10% bolus over 1 minute, the remaining 90% over 1 hour, with a maximum dose of 90 mg.
• Target treatment within 1 hour of ED arrival; eligible patients can be treated in the 3-4.5 hour window when carefully screened for exclusions.

(b)
• Determine the 'last known well time', the single most important determinant of treatment options.
• rt-PA is a crystalline powder reconstituted with sterile water; calculate the dose by weight.
• Make sure all invasive lines (for example endotracheal tube and indwelling urinary catheter) are in place before giving rt-PA.

(c)
• Waste the unused amount with another nurse before administering, to prevent accidental overdose.
• Neurological assessment and vital signs (except temperature) every 15 minutes during the infusion, then every 30 minutes for 6 hours, then hourly for 16 hours (24 hours total).

(d)
• Blood pressure checks should be more frequent if systolic stays at 180 mm Hg or diastolic at 105 mm Hg; temperature every 4 hours, treating temperatures above 37.6 degrees C with acetaminophen.
• Non-thrombolysis patients: hourly neurological checks in ICU, or at minimum every 4 hours in a non-ICU setting.
• Rationale for close monitoring: stroke symptoms can evolve over minutes to hours; intracerebral haemorrhage must be excluded before thrombolysis.

(a)
Shock, a widespread serious reduction in tissue perfusion with fall in blood pressure; in this patient, hypovolaemic shock from blood or fluid loss (circulatory system).

(b)
Skin (pale, cold, clammy, cyanosed); pulse (rapid and thready, later slow and irregular); respiration (hyperventilation then depression, atelectasis, pulmonary emboli, edema); kidneys (oliguria, uremia); GI tract (paralytic ileus, stress ulcer); brain; cells swell and die.

(c)
Other types: cardiogenic (pump failure), neurogenic (loss of sympathetic tone; dry warm skin, bradycardia), septic, anaphylactic (antigen-antibody reaction with histamine) and circulatory/distributive shock.

(d)
• Assessment: blood pressure and pulse every 15 minutes, respirations every 15-30 minutes, skin, urine output (report less than 30 mL/hr in adults).
• Diagnoses: altered nutrition, impaired mobility, fluid volume deficit, altered comfort, altered urinary output, ineffective breathing pattern.
• Priority: restore tissue perfusion with IV fluids (Ringer's lactate or normal saline, then colloids), then oxygenation with a patent airway; vasoactive drugs; nutritional support (over 3000 calories daily).
• Nothing by mouth (NG tube for ileus; oral feeding only with bowel sounds); turn every 1-2 hours; indwelling catheter; IV analgesic with watch for respiratory depression; stress ulcer prophylaxis.
• Evaluation: monitor for metabolic acidosis, cardiac failure, arrhythmias, shock lung, uremia, cerebral damage, infection and hemorrhage.
questions.question:
A patient who has lost a large volume of blood and fluid is restless and apathetic, with cold clammy skin, a rapid thready pulse, low blood pressure, rapid shallow respirations, subnormal temperature, cyanosis and very little urine.
(a) Identify the condition and body system affected.
(b) State the organs or functions compromised.
(c) Give differential conditions.
(d) Apply the nursing process, prioritizing care.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Encephalitis, inflammation of the brain tissue; the central nervous system is affected.

(b)
• Primary (acute viral) encephalitis is direct viral infection of brain and spinal cord, focal or diffuse; secondary (post-infective) encephalitis follows a current or earlier infection or immunisation, appearing 2-3 weeks later.
• Viruses are the commonest cause (West Nile from ticks or mosquitoes, mononucleosis, mumps); herpes simplex is the commonest non-insect-borne virus; other causes are parasites, toxins, bacteria, vaccines and fungi.

(c)
Brain function: consciousness, motor control (hemiparesis, ataxia, tremors), reflexes, vision (light sensitivity) and seizure threshold; herpes encephalitis causes local necrotising haemorrhage, then oedema, with progressive nerve cell deterioration.

(d)
Differentials from the same material: meningitis (septic or aseptic, with Kernig and Brudzinski signs and CSF changes) and brain abscess (pus collection with headache, fever, vomiting and focal deficits).

(e)
• No specific treatment exists for insect-borne encephalitis; careful neurological assessment and symptomatic care prevent complications and improve survival; give analgesics and antipyretics and anticonvulsants.
• IV acyclovir for herpes simplex encephalitis as soon as possible after diagnosis; give emotional support and ongoing teaching to significant others.
• Complications: cognitive disabilities, personality changes, ongoing seizures, motor deficits, blindness.
questions.question:
A patient has headache, fever, nausea, vomiting and malaise, then develops nuchal rigidity, confusion, decreased level of consciousness, seizures, sensitivity to light, ataxia, tremors, hemiparesis and abnormal deep tendon reflexes. CT scan, lumbar puncture for CSF and EEG are ordered.
(a) Identify the condition and the body system affected.
(b) Explain the types and causes.
(c) State the organs or functions compromised.
(d) Name the differential conditions.
(e) Give the nursing care priorities and the complications to watch for.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Chronic renal failure (ESRD) can result from glomerular, vascular or tubular disease, congenital anomalies (e.g. polycystic kidney disease), infection and obstructive disease of the urinary system.
• Repeated acute pyelonephritis can lead to chronic pyelonephritis and end-stage renal disease; hypertension and diabetes are related chronic diseases that cause renal disease.
• Remaining nephrons enlarge to compensate, then become sclerotic; the kidneys function until about 70% of nephrons are destroyed.

(b)
• Uremia affects every system: nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, anorexia, pruritus, fluid overload (shortness of breath, edema, hypertension), oliguria, cardiac problems from hyperkalemia, uremic fetor, drowsiness, headache, muscle twitching and seizures.
• Dialysis-related problems include atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, hypertriglyceridemia, heart failure, anemia, renal osteodystrophy (bone pain, fractures) and gastric ulcers.

(c)
• Stages: 40-75% nephron loss (reduced renal reserve), 75-90% (renal insufficiency) and less than 10% (ESRD), when dialysis is usually indicated.
• Medical: treatment depends on the cause; dialysis is required when medications fail; dietary management is most important.
• Nursing: monitor edema and weigh daily; decrease protein and increase carbohydrates and fats; fall safety and reorientation; assess for bleeding, prevent infection, monitor labs; give emotional support and explain tests.

(d)
Dialysis is the priority when there is hyperkalemia, fluid overload unresponsive to diuretics and fluid restriction, or pericardial friction rub (urgent), because many uremic symptoms are reversible with dialysis.
questions.question:
A patient has progressive, irreversible loss of kidney function with uremia after long-standing glomerular and obstructive kidney disease.
(a) State the risk factors or causes of the condition.
(b) Outline the complications.
(c) Describe the nursing and medical management options.
(d) Justify the priority intervention.

(a) Define epilepsy.
(b) State its causes.
(c) Describe its pathophysiology.
(d) Describe its clinical manifestations.
(e) Explain why certain people are more susceptible.
(f) Distinguish epilepsy from a seizure.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Epilepsy (ILAE) is at least two unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart; a group of syndromes of unprovoked, recurring seizures affecting about 3% of people, mostly children and older adults.

(b)
Idiopathic; birth trauma, asphyxia neonatorum, head injury, infections, toxicity (carbon monoxide, lead), circulatory problems, fever, metabolic and nutritional disorders, drug or alcohol intoxication, tumours, abscesses, congenital malformations.

(c)
Neurons keep firing after a task is finished; unwanted discharges make controlled body parts act erratically; repeated discharges constitute an epileptic syndrome.

(d)
Generalised tonic-clonic: rigidity then alternating contraction and relaxation, epileptic cry, tongue chewing, incontinence; after 1-2 minutes deep coma with noisy breathing, then postictal confusion and sleep for hours.

(e)
• Better treatment of cerebrovascular disorders, head injury, tumours, meningitis and encephalitis has increased the number of survivors at risk of seizures.
• Head injury is a main preventable cause, through highway and occupational safety.

(f)
• A seizure is an episode of abnormal motor, sensory, autonomic or psychic activity from sudden excessive cerebral neuron discharge, in part or all of the brain.
• Seizure causes include cerebrovascular disease, hypoxaemia, childhood fever, hypertension, CNS infections, hyponatraemia, hypocalcaemia, hypoglycaemia, brain tumour, drug and alcohol withdrawal.
• Types: generalised, focal (one hemisphere) and unknown; range from staring (absence) to prolonged convulsions; an aura may warn.
• Diagnosis: MRI for structural lesions, EEG (and telemetry) for diagnosis and classification, biochemical, haematologic and serologic studies.
• Medication controls seizures in 70-80% of patients; surgery is for tumours, abscesses, cysts, vascular anomalies or intractable seizures.
• Status epilepticus is a series of seizures without recovery of consciousness, or seizures lasting at least 30 minutes.

(a)
• Type 2 risk factors: weight, inactivity, family history, race/ethnicity (Black, Hispanic, American Indian, Asian American), age (usually over 30), gestational diabetes, birth of a baby over 9 pounds, polycystic ovary syndrome, blood pressure over 140/90, low HDL and high triglycerides.
• Obesity is the chief risk factor: the more fatty tissue, the more resistant cells become to insulin; 80-90% of people with type 2 are overweight or obese and need very large amounts of insulin.

(b)
• Short-term: hypoglycaemia (glucose below 50-60 mg/dL from too much insulin or agents, too little food or excess activity); diabetic ketoacidosis (mainly type 1, fat burned and ketones form); hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic nonketotic syndrome (mainly type 2, rarely ketones).
• Long-term: heart problems (narrowed, clogged vessels, high blood pressure, heart attack, stroke), diabetic retinopathy, neuropathy, and nephropathy.

(c)
• Medical: normalise insulin activity and blood glucose to reduce vascular and neuropathic complications; intensive treatment is 3-4 insulin injections daily or an insulin pump with frequent glucose monitoring, done with thorough education.
• Management has five components, with constant assessment and daily therapy adjustments by the patient.
• Nutrition: meal planning and weight control are the foundation; a dietitian leads; consistent meal intervals with snacks as needed; soluble fibre lowers glucose and lipids.
• Alcohol: moderate intake is one drink daily for women and two for men; alcohol on an empty stomach raises hypoglycaemia likelihood.
• Nursing assessment: history, glucose monitoring results, adherence; sitting and standing blood pressure, BMI, visual acuity, and examination of foot, skin, nervous system and mouth.

(d)
• Priority is weight loss with nutritional management: it is the key treatment for obese type 2 patients, and a 5-10% loss of body weight may significantly improve glucose levels.
• Rationale: it directly targets insulin resistance, the underlying mechanism of type 2 diabetes.
questions.question:
A patient with diabetes mellitus has risk factors that include being overweight, inactivity, family history, older age, high blood pressure over 140/90 mm Hg, and abnormal cholesterol and triglyceride levels.
(a) Identify the risk factors for type 2 diabetes present in this patient and explain why obesity matters.
(b) State the short-term and long-term complications.
(c) Outline the nursing, medical and nutritional management options.
(d) Justify the priority intervention.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Acute pyelonephritis: a bacterial infection of the renal pelvis, tubules and interstitial tissue of one or both kidneys (an upper urinary tract infection).

(b)
• It is frequently secondary to ureterovesical reflux, where an incompetent valve lets urine back up into the ureters during voiding; obstruction (stones, tumors, strictures, prostatic hypertrophy) increases susceptibility.
• The kidneys are enlarged with interstitial inflammatory infiltrates, abscesses on the capsule and corticomedullary junction, and atrophy and destruction of tubules and glomeruli.

(c)
• Monitor fluid intake and output; check temperature every 4 hours and give antipyretics and antibiotics; encourage 3-4 L of fluid a day unless contraindicated to dilute urine, ease burning and prevent dehydration.
• Send urine culture and sensitivity; ultrasound or CT locates obstruction, and relief of obstruction is essential to save the kidney.

(d)
• Outpatient treatment (if not dehydrated, no nausea or vomiting, no sepsis): 2-week antibiotic course such as ciprofloxacin, gentamicin with or without ampicillin, or a third-generation cephalosporin, used cautiously in renal or liver dysfunction.
• Hospitalize others, including all pregnant women, for 2-3 days of parenteral therapy, then oral agents once afebrile; up to 6 weeks if relapse; repeat urine culture 2 weeks after treatment.
• Teach adequate fluids, regular bladder emptying, perineal hygiene, taking antimicrobials exactly as prescribed and keeping follow-up appointments.
questions.question:
A woman presents acutely ill with chills, fever, flank pain, costovertebral angle tenderness, dysuria and urinary frequency; investigations show leukocytosis, bacteriuria and pyuria.
(a) Identify the condition.
(b) Explain the pathophysiological basis.
(c) State the priority nursing assessment and immediate interventions.
(d) Outline the definitive medical management.

A patient shows restlessness and anxiety that progress to decreased wakefulness, confusion, disorientation and agitation; the pupils become sluggish and later fixed, and the patient does not open the eyes, speak or move the extremities. A Glasgow Coma Scale, CT, MRI, EEG and tests of blood glucose, electrolytes, serum ammonia, blood urea nitrogen, calcium and clotting times are ordered.
(a) Identify the condition and the body system affected.
(b) State the organs and functions compromised.
(c) List the differential causes.
(d) Explain the nursing reasoning: assessment, nursing diagnoses and planning.
(e) State the priority nursing interventions and the evaluation of care.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Altered level of consciousness: being less responsive to and aware of the environment, on a continuum from alert through confused, lethargic, obtunded and stuporous to comatose; the nervous system is affected (cells, neurotransmitters or brain anatomy disrupted).

(b)
Pupillary response, eye opening, verbal and motor responses are compromised; complications include respiratory failure, pneumonia, pressure ulcers and aspiration; cornea, thermoregulation, bladder and bowel control also suffer.

(c)
• Differentials: structural (trauma, stroke, infection such as meningitis, encephalitis, abscess, tumours), metabolic (hypoglycaemia, ketoacidosis, hyperosmolar state, uraemia, hepatic encephalopathy, hyponatraemia, myxoedema, hypoxic states), toxins (heavy metals, carbon monoxide, opiates, barbiturates, alcohol), temperature extremes, seizures.
• The Glasgow Coma Scale (eye opening, verbal, motor) scores 3 (deep coma) to 15 (normal).

(d)
• Assess responsiveness, orientation, eye opening, motor response (including decorticate or decerebrate posturing), respiratory pattern, eye signs, corneal reflex, facial symmetry, swallowing and deep tendon reflexes.
• Diagnoses: ineffective airway clearance, risk of injury, deficient fluid volume, impaired oral mucosa, risk of impaired skin integrity, impaired corneal tissue integrity, ineffective thermoregulation, impaired urinary elimination, bowel incontinence, disturbed sensory perception, interrupted family processes.

(e)
• Airway first: remove secretions, raise head of bed to 30 degrees, lateral or semiprone position, suction with hyperoxygenation, chest physiotherapy, auscultate at least every 8 hours, monitor ABGs.
• Protect: padded raised side rails, avoid injury from lines and equipment, preserve dignity; give IV fluids slowly for intracranial conditions and restrict fluids to limit cerebral oedema; enteral feeding; mouth care.
• Turn regularly without dragging, use splints or foam boots, eye care with saline and artificial tears every 2 hours; persistent hyperthermia without infection signals brain stem damage, and the room may be cooled to 18.3 degrees C.
• Palpate or scan the bladder; use an indwelling or intermittent catheter as needed.

(a)
• Traction is a mechanical pulling force applied to overcome muscle spasm so a fracture can be reduced.
• It reduces pain and allows more joint and muscle exercise; it also corrects or prevents deformity such as contracture in non-fracture patients.
• It is used temporarily to disengage fragments and continuously to maintain alignment.
• Types: manual (by hand, directly to bone), skin traction (applied to skin, acting indirectly on bone) and skeletal traction (directly to bone using Kirschner wire, Steinmann pin or Crutchfield tongs).

(b)
• Counter-traction is needed, made by elevating the foot or head of the bed or adding weight; sometimes patient weight is enough.
• Nurses assess neurovascular and respiratory status, maintain traction, provide pin care and check pin sites for infection.

(c)
• Keep side rails up, provide a trapeze, maintain body alignment, and turn every 2 hours to the unaffected side.
• Assess pressure areas, use antiembolic stockings, give incentive spirometry, prevent constipation and increase fluids.

(d)
• Active and passive ROM exercises on unaffected limbs prevent muscle atrophy and joint stiffness; diversional activity prevents boredom.
• Possible complications if care fails: DVT, pulmonary embolism, fat embolism, pneumonia, UTI, renal calculi, pressure ulcer, compartment syndrome, nonunion, osteomyelitis.
• Skin, pin and cast care and monitoring of vital signs, intake and output and laboratory studies are part of general interventions.
questions.question:
(a) Describe traction as a treatment for fracture: indications, types and benefits.
(b) State the nursing responsibilities and possible complications.
(c) State the safe practice points.
(d) Explain the rationale behind the nursing actions and the complications that follow when they are neglected.

A patient has a fracture. Possible causes include trauma, osteoporosis, bone tumours, steroid therapy, Cushing's syndrome and ageing; findings include pain aggravated by motion, tenderness, loss of function, oedema, crepitus, deformity and a shortened leg in a fractured hip.
(a) State the risk factors and pathophysiology.
(b) List the complications.
(c) Outline the nursing, medical and surgical management options.
(d) Justify the priority intervention.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Causes: trauma, osteoporosis, multiple myeloma, bone tumours, immobility, malnutrition, Cushing's syndrome, osteomyelitis, steroid therapy, ageing; fracture is a break in bone continuity and may be open or closed.
• Bleeding follows injury to vessels and periosteum; an aseptic inflammatory response causes swelling; nerve compression causes pain; periosteal stripping cuts blood supply and kills bone cells; muscles are flaccid for 10-40 minutes and then spasm.

(b)
Complications: DVT, anaemia, fat embolism, pulmonary embolism, renal calculi, pneumonia, UTI, compartment syndrome, hypovolaemic shock, nonunion, osteomyelitis, avascular necrosis of the femoral head, decubitus ulcer.

(c)
• Principles: first aid, reduction, immobilisation, rehabilitation; reduction is closed (external manipulation) or open (surgical, when closed fails, fragments overlap or tissue lies between bone ends).
• Immobilisation by cast (plaster of Paris), splint covering joints above and below, or traction; surgery: open reduction with internal fixation, or external fixation.
• Nursing: neurovascular and respiratory assessment, elevate the limb, cast, pin and skin care, turn every 2 hours, pulmonary toilet, antiembolic stockings, pin-site checks, prevent constipation, diversional activity.
• Rehabilitation: physiotherapy, passive and active exercise to prevent atrophy and stiffness, properly fitted crutches or canes.

(d)
Priority is life-saving measures: establish respiration, arrest haemorrhage and immobilise the part; respiratory insufficiency, bleeding or shock are treated before the fracture.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the pathophysiology and stages of rheumatoid arthritis.
(b) State how the stages relate to common complications.
(c) Explain how the disease affects distant body systems, the resulting functional deficit, and the related nursing management and health education.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• RA is an autoimmune, systemic inflammatory disease of the synovial lining, a symmetrical peripheral polyarthritis with chronicity, remissions and exacerbations; cause unknown (autoimmune, genetic).
• Stages: 1 synovial inflammation; 2 pannus formation; 3 ankylosis; congestion and oedema develop, the synovium shows reactive hyperplasia, vasodilation causes warmth and redness, and capillary permeability causes swelling.
• Pannus (destructive vascular granulation tissue) destroys adjacent cartilage, joint capsule and bone.

(b)
• Pannus becomes fibrotic and calcified, causing subluxation; pannus between joint margins reduces mobility and leads to ankylosis (joint immobility).
• X-ray shows joint space narrowing and bone erosion; labs: raised ESR, WBC, platelets, CRP, IgM and IgG; positive rheumatoid factor.

(c)
• Systemic features: fatigue, anorexia, malaise, raised temperature, subcutaneous nodules, pericarditis, splenomegaly, leukopenia, enlarged lymph nodes, paraesthesias of hands and feet.
• Deficit: painful swollen joints, morning stiffness, limited ROM, with great potential for disability.
• Medical: analgesics (aspirin), NSAIDs, steroids, DMARDs (hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate, sulfasalazine); surgery (joint replacement, synovectomy); physical therapy, splints, heat or cold, plasmapheresis.
• Nursing: assess neuromuscular status and joints for swelling, pain, redness; maintain joints in extension; ROM; warm compresses as ordered; skin care; minimise environmental stress.
• Monitor vital signs, urine output, intake and output and labs; give medications; encourage expression of feelings about body changes and self-esteem.
• Differences from OA: RA affects fingers and wrists, is symmetrical, with morning pain over 30 minutes.

questions.question:
(a) Define otitis externa.
(b) State its causes.
(c) Describe its pathophysiology.
(d) List its manifestations and complications.
(e) Explain why certain people are more susceptible.
(f) Distinguish it from otitis media.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Otitis externa is inflammation or infection of the external auditory canal, auricle or both; acute under 6 weeks, chronic over 3 months; called swimmer's ear.

(b)
Bacterial infection (commonest), irritation, fungal infection, allergies and water retained in the ear; associated with eczema and psoriasis.

(c)
Cerumen gives an acidic protective barrier; disrupted pH, epithelial damage, wax loss and moisture raise pH and allow bacterial growth.

(d)
• Redness, swollen canal, hearing loss, fever, otalgia, tinnitus, discharge (clear, then purulent and foul) and facial or neck cellulitis.
• Complications: temporary hearing loss, chronic otitis externa, cellulitis, and rare skull base osteomyelitis that can spread to brain or nerves.

(e)
• Risks: swabs, earplugs, hearing aids, eczema, psoriasis, narrow canals, obstruction, stress, humidity, immunocompromise, diabetes and swimming; skull base osteomyelitis risk is higher in older adults and diabetics.
• Prevention: keep ears dry, dry only the outer ear gently, avoid inserting objects.

(f)
• Otitis media is inflammation or infection of the middle ear, often after a cold blocks the Eustachian tube; main bacteria: S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis.
• Susceptibility: immature immune system, genetics, palate abnormalities, Eustachian tube dysfunction; in children the tube is short, straight and wide; breastfeeding protects.
• Otitis media features: ear pain, drainage, fever, hearing loss; canal looks normal, no pain with auricle movement, eardrum red and bulging, conductive hearing loss.
• Types: acute (under 6 weeks), serous, chronic; treatment: broad-spectrum antibiotics, myringotomy, ventilating tubes.
• Otitis externa treatment: analgesics and otic or oral antibiotics, with the canal kept clean and dry.

(a)
Acute pancreatitis, sudden inflammation of the pancreas; tests: ultrasound, CT, MRI, abdominal X-ray, ERCP and genetic testing.

(b)
• Injury to the acinar cell impairs secretion of zymogen granules; triggers include alcohol, gallstones and certain drugs; intracellular digestive enzyme activation and calcium signalling are involved.
• Ductal cell injury can delay enzyme secretion (for example CFTR gene mutation); other causes: high triglycerides, hypercalcaemia, abdominal surgery, trauma, ERCP.

(c)
• Assess nutritional status and metabolic needs, fluid and electrolyte status, and sources of fluid and electrolyte loss.
• Give bed rest, hydration, a low-fat diet, no alcohol, and prescribed analgesics and antibiotics; these patients need intensive care.

(d)
• Initial supportive care: fluid resuscitation and nutritional support; antibiotics (imipenem class) only for infected necrosis, not routinely for fever.
• Surgery: cholecystectomy for gallstone pancreatitis; drain, stent or (refractory) distal pancreatectomy or Whipple for duct disruption; pseudocysts often need nothing, large ones aspiration or surgery.
• Infected necrosis: image-guided aspiration and necrosectomy; abscess: catheter drainage and antibiotics, then debridement if no response.
questions.question:
A patient presents with severe abdominal pain, fever, rapid pulse, nausea, vomiting, abdominal tenderness or swelling and jaundice.
(a) Identify the condition and its diagnostic tests.
(b) Explain the pathophysiological basis.
(c) State the priority nursing assessment and immediate interventions.
(d) Outline the definitive medical and surgical management.

(a) Describe the pharmacological treatment of osteoarthritis: indications and drug classes.
(b) State the safe practice points.
(c) Explain the rationale behind the nursing actions and the complications when they are neglected.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Drugs manage symptoms and pain and are used with non-pharmacological strategies, which are the mainstay.
• Initial analgesic is acetaminophen.
• Some respond to nonselective NSAIDs; patients at higher GI bleeding risk use COX-2 agents.
• Others: opioids, intra-articular corticosteroids (oral steroids are not effective because OA is within the joint), topical capsaicin and methylsalicylate.
• Glucosamine and chondroitin are thought to improve tissue function and retard cartilage breakdown.
• Viscosupplementation: hyaluronic acid (Hyalgan, Synvisc) acts as a lubricant, stimulates synoviocytes; three to five weekly injections; relief up to 6 months.

(b)
• Choose medicines by the patient's needs, stage and risk of side effects.
• Plan exercise for when pain is least or after an analgesic; adequate pain control makes exercise succeed.

(c)
• Non-drug measures first: weight loss, walking, water aerobics, stationary bike, strength training, ROM; avoid running, jump rope and tennis.
• Rationale: patients are older with other health problems, often overweight and sedentary; obesity increases pain.
• Tidal knee lavage gives pain relief for up to 6 months in some.

questions.question:
Describe peritoneal dialysis under the following headings:
(a) Indications and benefits
(b) Procedure and preparation
(c) Nursing responsibilities
(d) Complications
State the safety precautions or safe practice points.
(e) List the safety points.
Explain the rationale behind the nursing actions and the complications that follow when they are neglected.
(f) Give the rationale and consequences of neglect.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Dialysate is placed in the peritoneal cavity, where the peritoneal capillaries and membrane act as a semipermeable membrane; dialysis is needed when the kidneys cannot remove fluid and uremic wastes; it can be continuous (up to 36 hours) or intermittent.
• Benefits: home self-dialysis by continuous cyclic treatment, steady blood chemistry, no machine needed, and fewer dietary restrictions with a high-protein diet allowed because of dialysate protein loss.

(b)
A small incision below the umbilicus takes a multilumen catheter; warmed sterile dialysate runs in rapidly, is clamped for 20-30 minutes for osmosis and diffusion, then unclamped to drain by gravity; repeated several times.

(c)
• Diagnoses: ineffective breathing pattern (dialysate pressure), impaired comfort (instillation, dialysate temperature), impaired home maintenance, deficient knowledge, chronic sorrow and ineffective coping.
• Also: risk for unstable blood glucose (glucose in dialysate), risk for imbalanced fluid volume, risk for infection and risk for powerlessness.

(d)
Complications: peritonitis, bleeding and leakages.

(e)
• Use warmed sterile dialysate and aseptic handling because the catheter, invasive procedure and dialysate create infection risk.
• Monitor breathing, blood glucose and fluid balance.

(f)
• Dialysate is warmed for comfort; glucose in the dialysate is why blood glucose is monitored; teaching supports safe self-care at home.
• Neglecting asepsis leads to peritonitis; poor monitoring can leave glucose and fluid imbalance or breathing difficulty unrecognized.
• Bleeding and leakage are recognised complications.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the pathophysiology and types of stroke.
(b) State how the types relate to common complications.
(c) Explain how stroke affects other body systems, the resulting functional deficit, and the related nursing management and health education.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Stroke: ischaemic (about 85%, occlusion and hypoperfusion) or haemorrhagic (about 15%, blood extravasation); the ischaemic cascade begins when flow falls below 25 mL/100 g/min, with a salvageable penumbra.
• Haemorrhagic: intracerebral (primary ~80%, mainly uncontrolled hypertension; secondary from AVMs, aneurysms, anticoagulants, amphetamines, trauma, tumours, coagulation disorders) and subarachnoid (leaking aneurysm or AVM).
• Sudden arterial rupture abruptly raises ICP, causing severe headache, impaired consciousness and focal deficit.

(b)
• Subarachnoid haemorrhage: rebleeding (until repaired), hydrocephalus and vasospasm (most long-term complications); blood pressure kept systolic 120-160.
• Ischaemic stroke: raised ICP with further brain damage and repeated strokes.

(c)
• Respiratory compromise and aspiration from reduced consciousness or impaired swallowing; dysphagia can cause aspiration pneumonia and death.
• Motor: hemiplegia on the side opposite the infarct (flaccid if no tone); emotional lability; aphasia (expressive, receptive, global); unilateral neglect; homonymous hemianopsia; impaired judgment.
• Right-brain damage: left weakness, left neglect, spatial deficits, impulsiveness; left-brain damage: right weakness, language impairment, depression and anxiety, slow cautious behaviour.
• Nursing: neurological assessment and vital signs at least every 30 minutes in the ED; last known well time; rt-PA when eligible; protect from injury given poor judgment.
• Rehabilitation: most patients learn to walk (some with walker or cane), speech therapy, self-care; some drive and work again.
• Health education: controlling modifiable risk factors is the most effective way to reduce stroke burden.

(a)
• Curative surgery removes a diseased body part to restore function; surgery is a stressor producing anxiety, fear and neuroendocrine stress reactions.
• Tests: chest X-ray if ordered; ECG (age 40 or older); CBC and electrolytes; typing and cross-matching if major blood loss is likely; liver function tests, BUN, creatinine, urinalysis; pregnancy test for women of childbearing age.

(b)
• Psychosocial assessment; health history including allergies (drugs, adhesive tape, latex, betadine, soap), preexisting illness, implants and medications; obtain informed consent before pre-anesthesia medication.
• Teach: no smoking or alcohol for 48 hours, nothing by mouth for at least 6 hours, cough and deep breathing, hair removal by clippers or depilatory cream rather than shaving.

(c)
The intra-operative phase runs from transfer to the table to transfer to the PACU; universal protocol prevents wrong-site, wrong-procedure and wrong-patient errors; strict asepsis; general, regional or local anesthesia.

(d)
Verify identity and position the patient; assess airway, respirations, lung sounds and oxygen; notify the practitioner if saturation is not above 90% or PaO2 not above 80 mm Hg; check vital signs, LOC, dressings, drains, IV, pain and bowel sounds; keep nothing by mouth until peristalsis.

(e)
Wound infection: prevented by rigorous surgical asepsis and sterile supplies; also monitor fluid balance (tachycardia or hypotension suggests fluid volume deficit) and manage vomiting with antiemetics and aspiration prevention.

(f)
Teach care and continued recovery after discharge, arrange home health referral if needed, and give psychosocial support and referral to support groups.
questions.question:
A patient aged 45 years is scheduled for curative surgery (for example cholecystectomy) and is anxious about the operation.
(a) Identify the type of surgery and the relevant pre-operative tests.
(b) Describe the pre-operative nursing care.
(c) Describe the intra-operative care.
(d) Describe the post-operative nursing care.
(e) State a complication to monitor for and its prevention.
(f) Outline patient education and discharge planning.

Describe pressure injury under the following headings:
(a) Pathophysiology
(b) Stages and classification
(c) State the complications of chronic pressure injury and the common sites.
Explain how the injury may affect distant body systems, the resulting functional deficit and the related nursing management and health education.
(d) Distant effects and deficit
(e) Nursing management
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Constant pressure impairs local blood flow when it exceeds arterial capillary pressure (32 mmHg) and venous closing pressure (8-12 mmHg); shear, friction and moist, warm skin add to the risk.
• Tissue withstands high pressure briefly, but prolonged pressure slightly above capillary filling pressure starts a downward spiral to necrosis and ulceration; skin metabolic demand rises 13% per 1 °C.

(b)
• Stage 1: intact skin with localized nonblanchable erythema. Stage 2: partial-thickness loss with exposed dermis, pink or red and moist, or a serum-filled blister.
• Stage 3: full-thickness skin loss with visible fat, granulation tissue and rolled edges; undermining and tunneling may occur. Stage 4: exposed fascia, muscle, tendon, ligament, cartilage or bone.
• Unstageable: depth hidden by slough or eschar. Deep tissue injury: persistent nonblanchable deep red, maroon or purple discoloration or blood-filled blister.

(c)
• Complications of chronic injury include malignant transformation, autonomic dysreflexia, osteomyelitis, pyarthrosis, sepsis, urethral fistula, amyloidosis and anemia.
• Common sites: back of the hand, ear, shoulder, scapula, sacrum, hip, knee, heels, ankle, toe and elbows.

(d)
• Distant effects include sepsis, anemia, amyloidosis and autonomic dysreflexia; most patients have pain at the site.
• Contractures or spasticity mark additional areas at risk.

(e)
• Predict risk with the Braden scale; remove pressure, keep clean, debride, cleanse and dress the wound; culture and sensitivity guide antibiotics; assess pain, nutrition and mental status.
• Treat the worst colour present first; a beefy red wound is healing; biopsy if the wound does not heal.

questions.question:
A patient reports clouded, blurred or dim vision, increasing difficulty seeing at night, sensitivity to light and glare, halos around lights, fading or yellowing of colours and frequent changes in eyeglass prescription.
(a) Identify the condition and name the diagnostic tests.
(b) Describe the pre-operative nursing care.
(c) Describe the surgical approaches and timing of surgery.
(d) Name the complications to monitor for and the preventive measures.
(e) Outline patient education and discharge planning.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Cataract: opacity or clouding of the normally clear lens, the leading cause of blindness worldwide; tests are Snellen visual acuity (reduced acuity is proportional to cataract density), ophthalmoscopy and slit-lamp biomicroscopy.

(b)
• Pre-operative: assess medical history to decide on tests, stable vital signs, visual acuity results; withhold anticoagulants to reduce retrobulbar haemorrhage risk; CBC, ECG and urinalysis only if indicated.
• Provide night light and adequate lighting, large print, move furniture to the walls and remove rugs; instruct patient and family about the procedure.
• Drugs: dilating drops every 10 minutes for four doses at least 1 hour before surgery; prophylactic antibiotics; IV sedation to lessen anxiety.

(c)
• Approaches: extracapsular extraction (anterior lens and cortex removed, posterior capsule intact), intracapsular extraction (whole lens in intact capsule), phacoemulsification, lens replacement.
• Surgery depends on functional and visual status; if both eyes are affected, one is done first with weeks to months between operations to assess results and allow recovery.

(d)
• Complications: retrobulbar haemorrhage (from anaesthetic injection reaching the short ciliary artery), acute bacterial endophthalmitis (about 1 in 1000 cases), toxic anterior segment syndrome (non-infectious inflammation).
• Prevention of cataract: avoid smoking, wear sunglasses; prophylactic antibiotics are given to prevent post-operative infection and inflammation.

(e)
Nursing diagnoses include deficient knowledge about coping with altered abilities and anxiety about loss of vision or independence.

(a)
• Glaucoma is a leading cause of blindness; most cases are asymptomatic until extensive irreversible damage; no cure but it can be controlled.
• Two theories: direct mechanical damage to the retinal layer at the optic nerve head, and indirect ischaemic compression of optic nerve microcirculation; usually both.
• Stages: 1 initiating events (illness, stress, narrow angles, long-term corticosteroids, mydriatics); 2 structural alterations in aqueous outflow; 3 functional alterations (raised IOP, impaired blood flow).
• Stage 4 optic nerve damage (atrophy, loss of nerve fibres and blood supply); stage 5 visual loss with field defects.

(b)
Open-angle (primary, normal tension, ocular hypertension), angle-closure (acute, subacute, chronic), congenital, and glaucoma associated with other conditions.

(c)
• Primary open-angle: usually bilateral, often no symptoms but possible pain, headache and halos; acute angle-closure: rapid visual loss, periocular pain, nausea, vomiting, bradycardia, sweating, severely raised IOP, corneal oedema and a semidilated fixed pupil.
• Risk: age above 40, diabetes, African Americans, family history, eye trauma or surgery, long-term steroids; chronic angle-closure causes cupping and significant field loss.

(d)
• Effects: blurred vision, halos, difficulty focusing and adjusting in low light, loss of peripheral vision, aching around the eyes.
• Diagnosis: tonometry, ophthalmoscopy, gonioscopy, perimetry.
• Treatment is lifelong: miotics, adrenergic agonists, beta-blockers, alpha2-agonists, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, prostaglandins; laser trabeculoplasty or iridotomy, trabeculectomy, drainage implants.
• Teach the disease and strict adherence to medication; review drug interactions; explain that miotics and sympathomimetics alter focus.
• Refer for help with ADLs, low vision and rehabilitation, and agencies for legal blindness.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the pathophysiology and stages of glaucoma.
(b) State its classification.
(c) State how the types relate to common complications and symptoms.
(d) Explain how glaucoma affects vision and daily function, and state the related nursing management and health education.

(a) Describe the pathophysiology and stages of Alzheimer's disease.
(b) State how the stages relate to common complications and risk.
(c) Explain how the disease affects the brain and function, and state the related nursing management and health education.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Alzheimer's disease is a progressive, irreversible degenerative disorder of the cerebral cortex and the most common dementia, with brain cell atrophy, reduced acetylcholine, enlarged ventricles, neuritic plaques and neurofibrillary tangles.
• Changes: amyloid plaques (beta-amyloid cleaved from amyloid precursor protein), neurofibrillary tangles, loss of neuronal connections and neuron death; overproduction of beta-amyloid is a key risk factor.
• Cause unknown: abnormal protein, environmental toxins, genetic factors (apolipoprotein E variant), inadequate cerebral blood flow; risks include age above 65, family history and female gender.
• Early stage: recent memory loss, inability to learn new information, difficulty finding words, personality and mood changes, progressive difficulty with ADLs.
• Intermediate stage: cannot learn or recall new information, reduced memory of past events, more ADL help, wandering, agitation, hostility or aggression, disorientation, bladder and bowel incontinence.

(b)
End stage: inability to walk, total incontinence, no memory, inability to swallow and eat, no intelligible speech; wandering and poor judgment create safety risks (driving, appliances, finances).

(c)
• Plaques form first in the hippocampus (memory), later the cerebral cortex (language and reasoning); anomia, aphasia, rigidity, myoclonic jerks and restlessness may occur; dementia eventually results in death.
• Diagnosis is by excluding other causes; definitive only by plaques and tangles at postmortem.
• Drugs: cholinesterase inhibitors (galantamine, rivastigmine, donepezil) for mild to moderate, memantine for moderate to severe, antipsychotics and SSRIs for behaviour; they only temporarily slow decline.
• Nursing: ID bracelet, calm friendly tone, simple instructions, quiet environment, nutrition help, dressing and toileting help, music therapy, safe environment and possible home care aide.
• Education: inform patient and family, refer to a support group, discuss power of attorney as soon as diagnosis is made.
• Give emotional support and affection, since the family may be exhausted and frustrated.

(a)
Skin tests help establish cause and effect when a patient may be allergic to several things; desensitization is used because there is no real cure for allergy.

(b)
• Take a careful, detailed history; scratch the skin first and, if negative, inject a small amount of antigen intradermally.
• Wait 20 minutes; a positive test is a wheal surrounded by erythema.

(c)
• Observe for reactions within 20 minutes and keep epinephrine 1:1000 ready.
• Desensitization injects very small allergen doses into the skin in gradually increasing amounts until tolerance develops, preventing histamine release.
• Drugs: antihistamines relieve short-lived symptoms such as drug sensitivity or hay fever; epinephrine relaxes bronchiolar smooth muscle; corticosteroids are given briefly for severe symptoms.

(d)
A severe reaction, including anaphylactic shock, is the danger.

(e)
Keep epinephrine 1:1000 ready, observe for 20 minutes, take the same precautions with desensitization, and advise avoiding or minimizing allergen contact.

(f)
• Antihistamines inhibit histamine action, and epinephrine counteracts histamine effects on bronchioles, which is why they are used.
• Immediate reactions occur within seconds or minutes and may become systemic, so ready epinephrine and observation matter.
• Neglect risks anaphylactic shock, with widespread vasodilation and relative hypovolemia.
questions.question:
Describe allergy skin testing, desensitization and drug therapy under the following headings:

questions.answerText:
(a)
A tourniquet is a last resort in external haemorrhage, used only after other measures (clean dressing, raising the limb, firm pressure, digital pressure) have failed.

(b)
It must be tight enough and there must be a piece of material between the tourniquet and the skin.

(c)
• Do not leave it on longer than 15 minutes.
• Make its presence obvious by writing the letter T and the time of application on the patient's forehead.

(d)
• Dangers: damage to nerves and muscles, damage to the skin, and death of the affected part if kept on longer than 20 minutes.
• If not tight enough it may limit only venous flow and not stop arterial blood flow.

(e)
• First stop the bleeding by covering the wound, raising and immobilizing the limb, and applying direct or digital pressure at a pressure point (temporal, facial, brachial, radial, femoral).
• Use the tourniquet only as a last resort, padded, time-limited and clearly marked.

(f)
• The time mark lets others see how long it has been applied, limiting the tissue damage from prolonged use.
• Neglect leads to nerve, muscle and skin damage, or loss of the limb; inadequate tightness fails to stop arterial bleeding.

(a) Indications

A patient has fatigue, dry scaly skin, brittle nails, hair loss, a husky voice, constipation, weight gain without increased food intake and feeling cold even in a warm environment. Serum TSH is raised and free T4 is reduced.
(a) Identify the condition and the body system affected.
(b) State the organs or functions compromised.
(c) List the differential types or conditions.
(d) Give the nursing reasoning and prioritisation of care using the nursing process.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Hypothyroidism (for example Hashimoto's disease, where autoimmune destruction lowers T3 and T4 and raises TSH); the endocrine system (thyroid, pituitary, hypothalamus) is affected.
• Serum TSH is the best single screening test (normal 0.4-6.15 microunits/mL; above this indicates primary hypothyroidism); normal free T4 is 0.9-1.7 ng/dL.

(b)
• Metabolism (BMR falls 20-40%), cardiovascular function (reduced rate, force, output, raised cholesterol, atherosclerosis), skin, GI (constipation), nervous system (dullness, apathy, dementia-like change), menstrual function, hearing, respiratory muscles.
• Severe disease: myxoedema, pleural and pericardial effusion, subnormal temperature and pulse, expressionless face.

(c)
Primary (thyroid), secondary (pituitary, TSH disturbed), tertiary (hypothalamus, TRH disturbed) and central (both) hypothyroidism; hyperthyroidism shows low TSH; myxoedema coma is the most extreme stage.

(d)
• Assess: thyroid gland palpation for size, shape, consistency, symmetry and tenderness, plus thyroid function tests and radioactive iodine uptake.
• Priorities: give levothyroxine (dose set by serum TSH), watch cardiac function (angina, dysrhythmias) and drug interactions (anticoagulants, indomethacin, phenytoin).
• Advanced disease: the patient is hypothermic and abnormally sensitive to sedatives, opioids and anaesthetics; in myxoedema coma, respiratory drive is depressed with CO2 retention.
• Evaluation: monitor serum TSH, which guides the replacement dose.

questions.question:
(a) Define osteoarthritis.
(b) State its causes and risk factors.
(c) Describe its pathophysiology.
(d) List its clinical manifestations.
(e) Explain why certain people are more susceptible to osteoarthritis.
(f) Distinguish osteoarthritis from rheumatoid arthritis (tissue affected, joints, symmetry, systemic features, stiffness, age).
questions.answerText:
(a)
Osteoarthritis is the most common arthritis; it develops from deterioration of the hyaline cartilage (not the synovium), leading to bone breakdown, sclerosis and osteophyte (bone spur) formation; it may be primary (idiopathic) or secondary to joint injury or inflammatory disease.

(b)
Risk factors: old age, being overweight (BMI above 25), repeated injuries to weight-bearing joints, and genetics.

(c)
It affects articular cartilage, subchondral bone and synovium: cartilage degradation, bone stiffening and reactive synovial inflammation occur; it is more than simple wear and tear, and repetitive pressure reduces the cartilage's protective ability.

(d)
• Main manifestations are pain, stiffness and functional impairment; stiffness is usually in the morning, lasts under 30 minutes and lessens with movement; painless bony nodes may be present.
• X-ray shows joint space narrowing with osteophytes; only 30-50% of patients with X-ray changes report symptoms.

(e)
• Age: OA often begins at 40, and by age 75 about 85% have X-ray or clinical evidence, though only 15-25% have significant symptoms.
• Congenital and developmental hip disorders (congenital subluxation-dislocation, acetabular dysplasia, Legg-Calve-Perthes disease, slipped capital femoral epiphysis) predispose to hip OA.
• Obesity is a well-recognised risk factor and also increases the pain and discomfort of the disease.

(f)
• OA is not systemic (no fever or anaemia), is asymmetrical, and pain and stiffness are worst at the end of the day; it mainly affects weight-bearing joints in older people.
• RA is an autoimmune, systemic, symmetrical inflammation of the synovium affecting mainly fingers and wrists, with morning pain lasting over 30 minutes.
• RA can occur at any age (20-60) and inflammation is the destructive type (pannus); in OA inflammation is not the destructive type seen in RA.
• RA is not aggravated by extreme temperature and gives a positive rheumatoid factor (latex fixation test); OA pain is due to inflamed synovium, stretched capsule or ligaments and irritated periosteal nerve endings over osteophytes.

questions.question:
A patient has pain, stiffness and functional impairment of weight-bearing joints, with painless bony nodes on the fingers and morning stiffness lasting less than 30 minutes. Contributors include old age, being overweight, repeated joint injury and genetics.
(a) State the risk factors.
(b) State the complications or effects.
(c) Outline the nursing, medical and surgical management options.
(d) Justify the priority intervention.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Old age, BMI above 25, repeated injury to weight-bearing joints, genetics, and congenital hip disorders; obesity also increases pain.

(b)
Progressive loss of joint cartilage (joint space narrowing), osteophytes, bony nodes, pain, stiffness and functional impairment from limited motion.

(c)
• Conservative: weight reduction, heat, joint rest, orthotic devices, isometric and postural exercises, aerobic exercise, occupational and physical therapy.
• Drugs: acetaminophen first; nonselective NSAIDs; COX-2 agents for those at GI bleeding risk; opioids; intra-articular corticosteroids (oral steroids not effective); capsaicin or methylsalicylate topicals; glucosamine and chondroitin.
• Surgical: osteotomy, arthroplasty, hyaluronic acid viscosupplementation (3-5 weekly injections, relief up to 6 months), tidal lavage of the knee.
• Nursing: walking, water aerobics, stationary bike, strength training and ROM; avoid high-impact exercise (running, jump rope, tennis); canes or assistive devices; exercise when pain is least or after an analgesic.

(d)
• Priority is non-pharmacological care first (mainstay) with pain management and optimising function, since no treatment halts degeneration.
• Weight loss and aerobic activity with quadriceps strengthening are key to pain management in patients who are older, often overweight and sedentary.

(a)
An immediate allergic reaction (occurring within seconds or minutes), which may become systemic as anaphylactic shock.

(b)
• Allergy follows abnormal antibody formation to agents not usually antigenic; causes include inhalants (dust, feathers, pollen), ingestants (egg, seafood, nuts), contactants (wool, dye, cosmetics) and drugs (penicillin, ASA, quinine, chloroquine).
• Anaphylactic shock occurs in patients already exposed to the antigen who have developed antibodies to it.

(c)
• Effects trace to suddenly released histamine: vasodilatation (flush, headache), increased capillary permeability (wheals, laryngeal edema, nasal congestion), smooth muscle contraction in bronchioles (breathing difficulty), and exocrine stimulation (epigastric distress, vomiting, diarrhoea, secretions).
• Anaphylaxis: mast cells release histamine or bradykinin causing widespread vasodilation and capillary permeability.

(d)
• Avoid or minimize contact with the allergen; keep epinephrine 1:1000 ready, which relaxes bronchiolar smooth muscle; antihistamines give symptomatic relief; corticosteroids for brief periods if severe.
• After skin testing, observe for reactions within 20 minutes; desensitization gradually raises allergen doses and needs the same precautions; take a careful, detailed history.
• Shock care: fluid replacement, vasoactive medications, airway and oxygen, and close monitoring.
questions.question:
Minutes after receiving a drug to which he was previously exposed, a patient develops skin flushing with wheals and intense itching, nasal congestion and difficulty breathing.
(a) Identify the condition.
(b) State the predisposing factors.
(c) Explain the pathophysiology.
(d) Describe the nursing management.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Herpes zoster (shingles), a viral disease caused by varicella zoster virus, the same virus that causes chickenpox; the virus stays dormant after chickenpox and can reactivate years later.

(b)
Predisposing factors: advanced age (usually after 50), emotional stress, immunosuppressants such as steroids, cancer (especially leukaemia and lymphoma), bone marrow transplantation, diabetes, HIV/AIDS, and intrauterine exposure to the virus.

(c)
• After varicella resolves, the virus establishes latency in the trigeminal and dorsal root ganglia, held in check by the immune system; age, stress or immunocompromise trigger reactivation.
• The reactivated virus multiplies in the ganglion causing neuronal necrosis and intense inflammation, and travels down the nerve to the skin it supplies, causing local inflammation and blistering.
• Dermatomes affected: thoracic 55%, cranial 20%, lumbar 15%, sacral 5%; skin reddens, papules become vesicles then pustules, crusts form, then healing; scarring may occur in the immunocompromised.
• A prodrome of 2-5 days with burning pain, itching or tenderness, malaise, headache, chills and GI disturbance precedes the eruption.

(d)
• Shingles itself cannot be passed on, but the virus can spread from active blisters to a person with no immunity by direct contact or inhaling droplets, causing chickenpox not shingles.
• The person is highly contagious until the rash has crusted, infectious for the first 2-3 days after eruption, and not infectious before blisters appear or during postherpetic neuralgia; incubation is 10-21 days.
questions.question:
A patient is seen with a burning, painful rash on the trunk that began with skin redness, followed by grouped papules that became vesicles and pustules, after a short prodrome of malaise and headache. The patient has a history of chickenpox.
(a) Identify the condition.
(b) State the predisposing factors.
(c) Explain the pathophysiology.
