questions.answerText:
(a)
IV fluids provide water, electrolytes and nutrients for daily needs, replace water and correct electrolyte deficits, and deliver medications and blood products when no other route is available.

(b)
• Verify the prescription, label and patient identity, explain the procedure, perform hand hygiene and wear gloves; apply a tourniquet 4-6 inches above the site and use distal veins of hands and arms first.
• The vein should feel firm, elastic, engorged and round; use 20-22 gauge for most fluids and 14-18 gauge for blood, trauma and surgery; ask about latex or iodine allergy and clip excess hair.

(c)
Observe the site hourly, anchor the cannula well and use aseptic technique; flow rises with the height of the container and tubing diameter, and falls with longer tubing and more viscous fluids.

(d)
Local and systemic complications: fluid overload, air embolism, febrile reaction and septicemia, infiltration or extravasation, phlebitis and hematoma.

(e)
• Avoid pulsating vessels, palpating for arterial pulsation even with the tourniquet on; do not let the tip rest in a flexion area such as the antecubital fossa.
• Use an appropriate cannula size; give strongly hypertonic dextrose into central veins so rapid blood flow dilutes it; maintain asepsis because infection is a major risk.

(f)
• Careful checking avoids serious errors, explanation increases comfort and cooperation, and asepsis prevents infection and exposure to blood.
• Neglect: air embolism (dyspnea, cyanosis, hypotension, loss of consciousness) needs immediate clamping and left-side Trendelenburg; fluid overload gives crackles, edema, weight gain and dyspnea.
• Phlebitis (red warm swelling) needs the IV removed and resited with warm moist compress; hematoma needs pressure, ice for 24 hours then warm compress.
• Septicemia shows abrupt temperature rise, chills and malaise and may progress to septic shock; infiltration shows edema, coolness, leakage and slowed flow.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• The ECF compartment is expanded with a surplus of circulating fluid and near-normal electrolyte proportions.
• Causes: kidneys unable to excrete water and electrolytes (chronic renal or liver disease, heart failure), IV fluids given beyond renal capacity, and corticosteroid-induced aldosterone fluid retention.

(b)
Expanded extracellular volume; if overload exceeds the pumping capacity of the left ventricle, pulmonary edema results; serum osmolality is unchanged, sodium is often unaffected and hematocrit may be decreased.

(c)
Elevated BP, bounding pulse, distended neck veins, weight gain, dyspnea, crackles, and pretibial and sacral edema.

(d)
Restrict fluid and sodium, give diuretics (e.g. Lasix), replace potassium losses, and dialysis for renal failure or life-threatening overload; nursing: daily weight, intake and output, semi-Fowler's position.

(e)
• Infants and the elderly are vulnerable: an infant's body contains more water and needs large fluid intake, and in the elderly respiratory, renal, cardiac or GI breakdown leads to imbalance.
• IV fluids beyond renal capacity are especially risky in patients with impaired kidney function, infants and elderly people.

(f)
• Hypovolemia is depletion of ECF from water and sodium loss, one third from vascular and two thirds from interstitial space, with no water shift because osmolarity is unchanged.
• Causes: GI losses, urinary losses, third-spacing (burns, peritonitis, ascites, pancreatitis), profuse sweating and blood loss.
• Features: postural hypotension, weak tachycardic pulse, flattened neck veins, poor turgor, reduced urine, raised BUN, hematocrit and urine specific gravity.
• Treatment: isotonic fluids (Lactated Ringer's, 0.9% saline) and blood in severe shock; nursing: monitor vital signs and daily weight, oral hygiene, supine with foot elevated.
• Hypervolemia needs restriction and diuresis, whereas hypovolemia needs fluid replacement.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Bronchoscopy is direct visual examination of the bronchi through a fiber-optic scope, used to remove foreign bodies, cleanse the lungs and obtain sputum and tissue specimens; it confirms lung cancer and visualizes the obstruction in atelectasis.

(b)
Obtain written informed consent per facility policy; explain the procedure; nothing by mouth for at least 6 hours; IV access is obtained and pre-procedure sedation given if ordered.

(c)
Sedation is given through the IV during the procedure.

(d)
Frequently assess vital signs and respiratory status; keep the patient side-lying until the gag reflex returns; withhold all food and fluids until fully awake with a gag reflex.

(e)
Assess for unusual amounts of bleeding; sputum may be blood-tinged initially.

(f)
Explaining the procedure, sedation and expected blood-tinged sputum forms the teaching.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Psoriasis, a long-lasting, noncontagious autoimmune skin disease; types: plaque (about 90%), guttate, pustular, inverse and erythrodermic.

(b)
• Genetics (immune genes, MHC, T cells); lifestyle (chronic infections, stress, season and climate change, hot water, scratching, dryness, alcohol, smoking, obesity); HIV; infections (strep throat, Staphylococcus aureus, Malassezia, Candida).
• Drugs that aggravate it: beta blockers, lithium, antimalarials, NSAIDs, terbinafine, calcium channel blockers, captopril, glyburide; corticosteroid withdrawal causes rebound.

(c)
Epidermal cells are made six to nine times faster than normal and replaced every 3-5 days instead of 28-30; dendritic cells, macrophages and T cells release cytokines (IL-36 gamma, TNF-alpha, IL-1 beta, IL-6, IL-22) that make keratinocytes mature prematurely, producing scales and plaques.

(d)
• Assess skin colour and for infection; monitor vital signs; do not pinch or scratch; keep area clean; bath oil to reduce scales; avoid vigorous scrubbing.
• After phototherapy stay out of the sun that day and wear UVA-screening sunglasses for 24 hours; teach correct use of ointments, creams and lotions with written instructions.
• Help the patient cope, since stress worsens psoriasis; encourage high-calorie, high-protein nutrition; enhance skin integrity, prevent infection, and teach patient and family.
• No specific diagnostic test exists; diagnosis is by examination and sometimes biopsy; no cure, but treatment reduces symptoms, with gentle scale removal the key principle.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Subarachnoid haemorrhage, most commonly from a leaking aneurysm near the circle of Willis or a congenital AVM; tests: CT scan and cerebral angiogram.
• The angiogram can frighten a patient facing a life-threatening illness; sedation may be needed if neurological status prevents cooperation.

(b)
Care is in ICU with an arterial line and CVP catheter; blood pressure is monitored closely (high risks rerupture, low risks ischaemia), systolic kept between 120 and 160 with vasoactive drugs.

(c)
• Craniotomy exposes the aneurysm, and a berry aneurysm neck is clamped with a metal clip.
• Inoperable aneurysms: a tiny metallic coil or fibrin glue causes a thrombus that occludes the aneurysm.

(d)
Post-operative care continues ICU monitoring with neurological assessment.

(e)
• Rebleeding (risk until repaired), hydrocephalus (blood blocks CSF flow) and vasospasm (intensified headaches, decreased responsiveness, confusion, disorientation).
• Prevention: repair or occlusion of the aneurysm and blood pressure control.

Describe hemodialysis under the following headings:
(a) Indications
(b) Alternatives when hemodialysis cannot be used
(c) Principles, preparation and access
(d) Nursing responsibilities
(e) Complications
State the safety precautions or safe practice points.

Explain the rationale behind the nursing actions and the complications that follow when they are neglected.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Acute indications: high rising potassium, fluid overload, impending pulmonary edema, increasing acidosis, pericarditis, severe confusion, and removal of drugs or toxins.
• Chronic indications: uremic symptoms (nausea, vomiting, anorexia, lethargy, confusion), hyperkalemia, and fluid overload unresponsive to diuretics; pericardial friction rub is urgent.

(b)
Continuous renal replacement therapy is recommended for patients too unstable for hemodialysis.

(c)
• Blood is taken out, diffused across a semipermeable dialyzer and returned; principles are diffusion, osmosis and ultrafiltration (negative pressure removes water).
• Access: short-term dual-lumen catheter in a central vein; long-term surgically created fistula between peripheral artery and vein (radial artery and cephalic vein).

(d)
The dialysis nurse monitors, supports, assesses and educates; diagnoses include excess fluid volume, risk for deficient fluid volume, electrolyte imbalance, infection (hepatitis B or C), injury from access clotting and impaired tissue integrity from the fistula.

(e)
• Atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, hypertriglyceridemia, heart failure, anemia and fatigue, dialyzer clotting, gastric ulcers and renal osteodystrophy (bone pain, fractures).
• Other problems: hypotension, cramping, vomiting, blood leaks, contamination and access complications.

(f)
A reliable access to the bloodstream is essential; monitor for excessive fluid removal, infection from blood exposure and clotting of the access.

(g)
• Ultrafiltration is needed because diseased kidneys cannot excrete water; excessive removal causes fluid deficit and hypotension.
• Neglecting infection control risks infection and hepatitis; neglecting access care risks clotting and injury; poor monitoring leaves electrolyte imbalance undetected.

questions.question:
Describe pulmonary function tests under the following headings:
(a) Indications
(b) Preparation

State the safety precautions or safe practice points.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• A group of studies that evaluate ventilatory function, measured directly by spirometer or calculated from spirometer results.
• Significance: asthma shows abnormal flow rate and lung volume; emphysema shows decreased expiratory volume.

(b)
Explain the procedure to the client; do not perform the test within 1-2 hours after a meal; bronchodilators may be used during the study.

(c)
• Tidal volume is 500 mL at rest; inspiratory reserve volume 2100-3200 mL; expiratory reserve volume 1000-1200 mL.
• Residual volume cannot be measured directly; vital capacity = tidal volume + IRV + ERV; functional residual capacity and inspiratory capacity are also measured.
• Alveolar ventilation = (tidal volume - anatomical dead space) x respiratory rate, e.g. (500 - 150) x 15 = 5.25 litres per minute.

(d)
Fatigue may follow the test.

(e)
Avoid testing within 1-2 hours of a meal, monitor respiratory status after the test and advise the client to rest.

(f)
After the test, respiratory status is monitored and activity avoided because fatigue may result.

questions.question:
Describe oedema under the following headings:
(a) Definition and causes
(b) Pathophysiology
(c) Clinical manifestations
(d) Nursing care
Explain the clinical basis for why certain people are more susceptible.
(e) Give the reasons for vulnerability.
Distinguish between oedema and dehydration.
(f) State the differences.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Excess fluid retained in the interstitial space, localized or generalized, from blood plasma; causes: arteriolar dilatation, venous obstruction, protein malnutrition, kidney disease, burns, hypoxia, sodium retention and local trauma.

(b)
It results from raised capillary blood pressure that increases fluid production and/or reduced plasma protein osmotic pressure that reduces reabsorption; histamine after trauma damages capillaries.

(c)
• Weight gain, tissue swelling, puffy eyelids, reduced output, amber-dark urine, lowered hematocrit, hemoglobin and RBC count, weakness, anorexia, confusion and apathy.
• Types: pitting, dependent, cerebral, pulmonary and ascites.

(d)
Skin and pressure-area care, fluid restriction, accurate intake and output, daily weight, elevate foot of bed, cardiac position for pulmonary edema, turn sacral edema patients regularly.

(e)
• Pregnant women (baby presses on pelvic veins), limbs with tight casts or bandages, heart failure patients, and people with malnutrition, kidney disease or burns are susceptible.
• Loss of serum albumin lets fluid leave the blood into tissue because the main force holding water in vessels is lost.

(f)
• Dehydration is deprivation of body water, with loss of 10% or more; causes are insufficient intake, sweating, vomiting and diarrhoea; the effect is more acute in the young, elderly or poorly patients.
• Dehydration signs: sunken eyes, weight loss, poor skin turgor, thirst, reduced and concentrated urine, raised hematocrit, weakness and malaise.
• Dehydration care: fluid intake about 3 litres daily, skin and mouth care, intake and output record, rest and temperature monitoring.
• Oedema involves excess interstitial fluid and dilution (low hematocrit); dehydration involves fluid deficit and hemoconcentration.
• Oedema care restricts fluid, whereas dehydration care increases fluid.

questions.explanation: A test dose with adrenaline is used to identify inadvertent intravascular placement of the epidural catheter before the full therapeutic dose is given, since intravascular injection of the full dose could cause systemic toxicity or high spinal block if the catheter had migrated intrathecally. A significant rise in maternal heart rate signals a positive test. This simple safety step is standard practice in obstetric epidural management.
options: To reduce the total volume of drug required
To detect accidental intravascular catheter placement
To speed up the onset of analgesia
To reduce fetal heart rate variability
questions.question: Why is a test dose containing a small amount of adrenaline given before the main epidural dose in obstetric patients?

questions.explanation: The WHO ladder clearly prescribes escalation to Step 3 (strong opioids: morphine, oxycodone, hydromorphone, fentanyl) when Step 2 analgesia is inadequate. The weak opioid (codeine, tramadol) is discontinued → not combined with a strong opioid, as there is no additive benefit in combining weak and strong opioids. Oral morphine is the first-line Step 3 agent and remains the gold standard for moderate-to-severe cancer pain globally.
questions.question: In managing cancer pain with the WHO ladder, a patient on Step 2 (weak opioids) continues to have moderate pain. The MOST appropriate NEXT step is:
options: Add a NSAID and reduce the weak opioid to avoid addiction risk
Switch to a different weak opioid at the same dose before escalating further
Step 3: start strong opioid (e.g., morphine), stop weak opioid
Add an adjuvant analgesic and observe for 4 weeks before considering opioids
Prescribe a benzodiazepine to address the anxiety component of pain
The maximum tissue concentration before systemic toxicity begins
The concentration at which 50% of patients develop a motor block
The plasma concentration producing CNS excitatory symptoms
Minimum concentration to produce complete block of a given nerve
The equi-analgesic concentration ratio between ester and amide LAs
questions.explanation: Critical concentration (Cm) is the minimum LA concentration that produces impulse block in a nerve → analogous to MAC for volatile anaesthetics. Concentrations above Cm produce complete block; concentrations below Cm may produce partial or differential block. Factors lowering Cm (increasing sensitivity) include smaller nerve diameter, lower pH, decreased temperature, and slower firing rate. This concept underlies the calculation of LA doses needed for clinical nerve blocks.
questions.question: The critical concentration of local anaesthetic refers to:

questions.explanation: Pre-oxygenation with 100% oxygen (denitrogenation) fills the functional residual capacity with oxygen, creating a reservoir that extends the safe apnea time during intubation from approximately 12 minutes (breathing room air) to 810 minutes in healthy adults. This provides critical buffer time during difficult laryngoscopy attempts.
options: To improve cardiac output based on typical clinical findings
To create an oxygen reservoir to extend safe apnea time
To activate the CO2 absorber in the majority of documented cases
questions.question: Pre-oxygenation before intubation is performed with 100% oxygen for what primary purpose?
Halothane is classified as a halogenated alkane, while most modern volatile agents (isoflurane, desflurane, sevoflurane, enflurane) are classified as:
questions.explanation: Halothane (CF3CHClBr) is a halogenated alkane (halogenated ethane derivative), while isoflurane, desflurane, sevoflurane, and enflurane are all halogenated ethers. The ether linkage (R-O-R) in these modern agents contributes to their greater stability, lower flammability, and reduced arrhythmogenicity compared to halothane. This structural distinction is fundamental to understanding their differing pharmacological profiles.

PDPH results from CSF leakage through the dural puncture hole, causing intracranial hypotension. The reduced CSF pressure allows gravitational descent of the brain on upright posture, stretching pain-sensitive intracranial structures (meninges, bridging veins). The headache is classically positionalworse on sitting/standing, relieved by lying flat. Risk factors include larger needle gauge, cutting (Quincke) tip needles, young age, female sex, and obstetric patients. Treatment includes bed rest, hydration, analgesics, caffeine, and epidural blood patch for severe cases.
options: Local anaesthetic neurotoxicity causing meningeal irritation
Air entry into the subarachnoid space during injection
Vasodilation from sympathetic block causing intracranial hypertension
questions.question: Post-dural puncture headache (PDPH) following spinal anaesthesia is caused by which mechanism?
Halothane sensitizes the heart to catecholamines. This is most likely to manifest clinically when:
questions.explanation: Halothane sensitizes the myocardium to catecholamines, which can cause serious arrhythmias (tachycardia, ventricular extrasystoles, or even cardiac arrest) when adrenaline-containing local anesthetic solutions are injected concurrently. This catecholamine sensitization is dose-dependent and is less pronounced with isoflurane and absent with sevoflurane.
options: Used with nitrous oxide based on typical clinical findings
Local infiltration with adrenaline is done concurrently
Used at less than 0.5 MAC in the majority of documented cases

questions.question: The clinical goal of supplemental oxygen therapy targeting vital end-organ tissues is achieved through which THREE mechanisms?
questions.explanation: The three clinical goals of supplemental oxygen therapy are: (1) treating hypoxemia to correct inadequate tissue oxygenation, (2) decreasing the work of breathing by improving oxygen delivery per breath, and (3) decreasing myocardial work by reducing the cardiac compensatory response to hypoxemia. These goals are achieved by administering oxygen at concentrations higher than atmospheric (21%).
options: Preventing PONV, reducing pain, improving cardiac rate in most clinical presentations
Reducing acidosis, preventing infection, improving ventilation under standard examination conditions
Treating hypoxemia, decreasing work of breathing, decreasing myocardial work
Replacing blood, stimulating respiration, lowering CO2
Improving mucociliary clearance, reducing secretions, bronchodilation

questions.question: A patient presents with hoarseness after prolonged intubation, with the tube cuff pressing against the vocal folds. Which epithelial change would explain later granuloma formation?
questions.explanation: Prolonged mucosal pressure from the tube or cuff at the vocal process causes squamous metaplasia and ulceration, which can progress to granuloma formation. The larynx above the cords is normally lined by stratified squamous epithelium, making it more prone to this change under pressure. This is a recognised cause of post-intubation hoarseness.

options: Presence of a significant beard obscuring the face
questions.question: Which finding on preoperative airway examination is most predictive of difficult mask ventilation rather than difficult intubation?
questions.explanation: Difficult mask ventilation is associated with specific factors including a beard preventing a good facial seal, obesity, edentulousness, snoring history and advanced age, which are somewhat distinct from predictors of difficult laryngoscopy such as reduced mouth opening or a high Mallampati score. Recognising these separate risk factors is important because a patient can be difficult to ventilate but easy to intubate, or vice versa. A comprehensive assessment considers both sets of predictors.

ASA class II describes a patient with mild systemic disease without substantive functional limitation, which fits well-controlled hypertension and diabetes without evidence of end-organ complications. ASA I is reserved for entirely healthy patients, while ASA III and above describe more severe or poorly controlled systemic disease with functional limitation. This classification helps communicate overall perioperative risk among the surgical team, though it does not itself predict outcome with complete precision.
options: ASA I with no modification needed
ASA IV due to systemic disease
ASA V regardless of control status
questions.question: A patient with well-controlled hypertension and type 2 diabetes without end-organ damage is being classified preoperatively. Which ASA physical status class best describes this patient?

options: Propofol infusion used for ICU sedation
Haloperidol combined with azithromycin and ondansetron
Furosemide infusion for diuresis in fluid overload
Insulin infusion for tight glycaemic control
questions.explanation: QT-prolonging drugs are common in ICU polypharmacy: antipsychotics (haloperidol, quetiapine), antibiotics (azithromycin, fluoroquinolones, metronidazole), antiemetics (ondansetron, metoclopramide), antifungals (fluconazole), and vasopressors. The combination of multiple QT-prolonging agents → particularly haloperidol  azithromycin  ondansetron → creates additive risk of QTc prolongation beyond 500 ms, the threshold for torsades de pointes (TdP). Serial QTc monitoring and drug review are mandatory. Hypomagnesaemia and hypokalaemia potentiate QT prolongation.
questions.question: In the ICU, which medication is MOST frequently implicated as the cause of iatrogenic QT prolongation, risking torsades de pointes ventricular arrhythmia?

questions.explanation: Substance P released from peripheral nociceptor terminals promotes vasodilation and increased vascular permeability, producing local swelling and redness known as neurogenic inflammation. This process contributes to the flare response seen around an injury site. It is a peripheral, not central, mechanism of pain amplification.
options: Rapid clot formation at the site
questions.question: A patient sustains tissue injury, and substance P is released from primary afferent nerve terminals into the periphery. What local effect does this co-released neuropeptide PRIMARILY produce?

options: Sciatic nerve at the buttock only
Common peroneal nerve at the fibular head
Femoral nerve at the inguinal ligament
questions.question: A patient undergoing prolonged surgery in the lithotomy position develops postoperative calf pain and reduced sensation in the lower leg. This complication is most likely related to compression of which structure?
questions.explanation: The common peroneal nerve winds superficially around the fibular head and is particularly vulnerable to compression against poorly padded leg supports in the lithotomy position, and injury classically produces foot drop and sensory loss over the lateral lower leg and dorsum of the foot.

questions.question: For arterial blood gas (ABG) sampling, the most preferred artery is the radial artery. All of the following arteries are acceptable alternatives EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Acceptable arteries for ABG sampling include the radial (preferred), brachial, dorsalis pedis, and femoral arteries. The internal carotid artery is absolutely NOT used for ABG sampling as it is an intracranial vessel with catastrophic consequences if mishandled. Allen's test is performed before radial artery sampling. Each ABG sample requires 1 mL of heparinized blood in a syringe.

options: Higher intraoperative blood loss due to arterial vasodilation from fluid loading
Increased transfusion requirements from avoiding crystalloid haemodilution
Reduced postoperative complications including renal failure, ileus, and hospital stay
Longer ICU stay due to more complex haemodynamic monitoring requirements
Greater postoperative nausea from aggressive crystalloid administration
questions.question: Goal-directed fluid therapy (GDFT) in perioperative care is MOST associated with which outcome compared to liberal or restrictive fixed-volume fluid strategies?
questions.explanation: GDFT uses cardiac output monitoring (oesophageal Doppler, pulse contour analysis, transoesophageal echo) to titrate fluid administration to stroke volume or flow-based endpoints. Multiple RCTs demonstrate that GDFT reduces postoperative complications → ileus, acute kidney injury, wound infection → and length of stay in major abdominal, cardiac, and orthopaedic surgery compared to liberal or fixed fluid regimens. It avoids both under-filling (tissue hypoperfusion) and over-filling (oedema, gut dysfunction). options: Increased glomerular filtration increasing drug dose requirements as commonly encountered in practice
Accelerated gastric emptying reducing aspiration risk
Reduced FRC, difficult airway, sleep apnoea, and cardiovascular comorbidities
Enhanced respiratory muscle strength reducing ventilation problems during routine ophthalmic assessment
Increased cardiac reserve from habitual physical exertion
questions.explanation: Obesity causes reduced functional residual capacity (FRC) and faster oxygen desaturation during apnoea, difficult airway anatomy (fat neck, large tongue, limited neck extension), obstructive sleep apnoea requiring careful post-operative monitoring, and associated cardiovascular comorbidities (hypertension, coronary disease, cardiomyopathy). Gastric emptying is delayed and aspiration risk is increased. Drug dosing is complex because the volume of distribution differs for lipophilic and hydrophilic drugs. Positioning difficulties and pressure sore risk add further challenges.
questions.question: Obesity significantly increases anaesthetic risk primarily through which pathophysiological combination?

options: Achieving rapid heart rate to increase output
Encouraging profound vasodilation for the procedure
Maintaining adequate preload and avoiding tachycardia
questions.explanation: Patients with severe aortic stenosis have a fixed, obstructed outflow and depend on adequate preload and a slower heart rate to allow sufficient time for ventricular filling and ejection through the narrowed valve. Sudden vasodilation, hypotension or tachycardia can precipitate severe haemodynamic collapse because the heart cannot compensate by increasing output through the fixed stenotic orifice. Careful, gradual induction with close haemodynamic monitoring is essential in this population.
questions.question: Which anaesthetic goal is most important when managing a patient with severe aortic stenosis undergoing surgery?

questions.explanation: A rightward shift of the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve (increased P50) reduces hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen, facilitating greater oxygen release to hypoxic, acidotic, hypercarbic tissues. This is physiologically beneficial in exercising or ischemic tissue where CO2 and H+ are elevated (Bohr effect). However, this same shift impairs oxygen loading in the pulmonary capillaries.
options: Improves loading of O2 in the lungs in most clinical presentations
Increases total hemoglobin concentration under standard examination conditions
Facilitates unloading of O2 from hemoglobin to hypoxic tissues
questions.question: The oxygen dissociation curve shift to the RIGHT by increased 2,3-DPG, hypercapnia, and acidosis is clinically beneficial at the tissue level because it:

questions.explanation: Transduction is the first step of pain processing: noxious stimuli (heat, pressure, chemicals) activate nociceptor ion channels (TRPV1, TRPA1, ASICs), converting stimuli into electrical action potentials. Transmission moves the signal centrally via afferent fibres. Modulation occurs in the dorsal horn and descending pathways. Perception is the conscious cortical experience of pain. Understanding each step guides targeted pharmacological intervention.
questions.question: Which process describes the conversion of a noxious mechanical, thermal, or chemical stimulus into an electrical signal in peripheral nociceptors?
For a patient in haemorrhagic shock requiring emergency lower abdominal surgery, spinal anaesthesia is contraindicated primarily because:
questions.explanation: In haemorrhagic shock, the body compensates for reduced circulating volume through intense sympathetic-mediated vasoconstriction. Spinal or epidural anaesthesia abolishes this compensatory sympathetic tone, removing the only mechanism maintaining blood pressure in a hypovolaemic patient and potentially causing precipitous cardiovascular collapse. Hypovolaemia/shock is therefore a contraindication to neuraxial block. General anaesthesia (with agents that maintain cardiovascular function) or resuscitation to near-normal haemodynamic status before neuraxial block are appropriate alternatives.
options: LA will not work in hypovolaemic patients
Coagulopathy from blood loss prevents safe spinal
Splanchnic vasodilation will cause gut ischaemia
CSF pressure drops make dural puncture impossible
Sympathetic block will worsen hypotension catastrophically

questions.explanation: Tricyclic antidepressants such as amitriptyline modulate descending inhibitory pain pathways through serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibition, making them an established adjuvant option for neuropathic pain, including diabetic peripheral neuropathy, when initial anticonvulsant therapy is inadequate. They are often combined with, rather than simply substituted for, the anticonvulsant already in use. Side effects such as sedation and anticholinergic effects require careful dose titration, particularly in older patients.
questions.question: A patient with chronic neuropathic pain from diabetic peripheral neuropathy has failed to respond adequately to gabapentin alone. Which class of drug is a recognised next-line adjuvant option?
options: A tricyclic antidepressant such as amitriptyline
A weak opioid used alone indefinitely

questions.explanation: Rapid sequence induction uses a predetermined dose of induction agent immediately followed by a fast-acting muscle relaxant, minimising the time between loss of airway reflexes and securing the trachea, while avoiding positive pressure mask ventilation that could insufflate the stomach. Cricoid pressure is traditionally applied throughout this sequence. This combination is designed specifically to reduce the window of aspiration risk in patients presumed to have a full stomach.
questions.question: A patient with a full stomach requires emergency surgery. Which airway management strategy best minimises aspiration risk during induction?
options: Slow titrated induction with mask ventilation first
Rapid sequence induction with cricoid pressure
Standard induction followed by gentle bag ventilation
Deep inhalational induction over several minutes
Continue spraying to complete the procedure
Administer a second local anaesthetic agent
Stop further dosing and monitor for toxicity
questions.question: A patient receiving repeated topical lidocaine sprays for awake intubation becomes drowsy and reports circumoral numbness. What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.explanation: Circumoral numbness and drowsiness after repeated topical dosing are early signs of systemic local anaesthetic absorption approaching toxic levels, since mucosal surfaces absorb local anaesthetic efficiently. Further dosing should stop immediately and the patient should be monitored closely for progression to seizures or cardiovascular effects. Cumulative topical doses must always be calculated as part of the total safe dose.

options: Reduces the risk of mask fogging
Allows room air entry if oxygen supply fails
Prevents bacterial contamination of the mask
questions.explanation: The deliberate absence of a one-way valve on one exhalation port allows the patient to entrain room air if the oxygen supply is interrupted, preventing suffocation from a fully sealed mask with no gas source. This is a safety feature rather than a means to increase FiO2. Both exhalation ports being valved would risk asphyxiation if oxygen flow stopped.
questions.question: A patient uses a non-rebreather mask with a reservoir bag at high flow. The one-way valve is deliberately absent from one exhalation port. What is the safety rationale for this design?
Sugammadex is contraindicated or used with extreme caution in patients with:
questions.explanation: The sugammadex-rocuronium (or vecuronium) complex is excreted unchanged in the urine. In patients with severe renal impairment (eGFR <30 mL/min), this complex may not be cleared efficiently, and there is a theoretical risk of the complex slowly dissociating to release free rocuronium, potentially causing recurarisation. Sugammadex is therefore not recommended in severe renal failure except as a last resort. In moderate renal impairment (eGFR 3080), a single dose is acceptable but repeat dosing is not.

questions.question: A labouring patient self-administers a 50% nitrous oxide and 50% oxygen mixture for analgesia. What is the PRIMARY limitation of this inhalational technique?
questions.explanation: Entonox provides only partial, variable analgesia and is generally less effective than neuraxial techniques for moderate to severe labour pain, though it remains popular for its simplicity and self-administered control. It does not cause loss of consciousness or protective airway reflexes when used correctly. It is a useful adjunct rather than a complete analgesic solution for labour.
options: Cannot be used in any setting

questions.explanation: Suxamethonium's rapid onset of action (3060 seconds) is largely attributed to its low lipid solubility and small molecular size. Low lipid solubility means it remains in the aqueous plasma phase and rapidly distributes to the NMJ without significant tissue sequestration. As drug concentration at the receptor rises quickly, intubating conditions are achieved faster than with most non-depolarising agents. This rapid distribution to the NMJ is the key pharmacokinetic property explaining its clinical utility for RSI.
options: Low lipid solubility enabling rapid distribution
Extensive hepatic metabolism before reaching the NMJ
Lipid-soluble diffusion across the blood-brain barrier
questions.question: Onset of action after intravenous suxamethonium administration is primarily attributed to its:

questions.explanation: Epidural anaesthesia requires approximately 10 times more local anaesthetic than spinal block because the drug must diffuse across the dural sleeve and intervertebral foramina to reach the nerve roots, traversing a much larger anatomical space. In spinal anaesthesia, a small volume of concentrated drug is injected directly into the CSF surrounding nerve roots at high concentration. Epidural drug absorption into the epidural venous plexus also reduces bioavailability at the target site.
questions.question: Which of the following best explains why larger volumes of local anaesthetic are needed for epidural block compared to spinal (subarachnoid) block?
options: The epidural space has a higher fat content absorbing more drug
Greater nerve-root distance, lower drug concentration at target
Epidural local anaesthetics have higher pKa values than spinal preparations
Spinal needles deliver drug closer to the cord
Epidural technique requires higher drug potency

questions.explanation: Ex-premature infants (born before 37 weeks gestation) have immature respiratory centres with blunted hypoxic and hypercapnic ventilatory responses, and are at high risk of postoperative apnoea (defined as cessation of breathing for >20 seconds) after general anaesthesia up to 60 weeks post-conceptual age (gestational age at birth + weeks since birth). Procedures in this group require overnight admission with apnoea monitoring. Regional anaesthesia without general anaesthesia or sedation is preferred when feasible, as it significantly reduces postoperative apnoea risk.
questions.question: In neonatal anaesthesia, the risk of apnoea after general anaesthesia is most significant in which patient group?
options: Full-term neonates under 48 hours of age
Ex-premature infants less than 60 weeks post-conceptual age
Neonates over 4 kg with no respiratory comorbidities
All neonates regardless of gestational age or birth history

questions.question: When considering organ effects of isoflurane, it is preferred for cardiac and neurosurgery because it:
questions.explanation: Isoflurane is preferred for cardiac and neurosurgery because it maintains cardiac output, heart rate, and rhythm with minimal cardiac depression, and has the fewest adverse cardiovascular effects among the volatile agents. In patients with hepatic or renal compromise, it is also preferred due to its minimal metabolism (0.2%) and low hepatorenal toxicity risk.
options: Increases cardiac output and cerebral perfusion as commonly encountered in practice
Eliminates all risk of hepatorenal toxicity during routine ophthalmic assessment
Increases heart rate and causes bronchodilation
Maintains cardiac output and has fewest adverse cardiovascular effects
Has the most potent analgesic effect

questions.explanation: Halothane is the volatile agent with the greatest catecholamine-sensitizing effect, causing myocardial sensitization to catecholamines leading to arrhythmiasespecially dangerous when adrenaline-containing local anesthetics are used. Isoflurane, sevoflurane, desflurane, and nitrous oxide have minimal to no clinically significant catecholamine sensitization. Sevoflurane specifically has no myocardial sensitization to catecholamines.
questions.question: The ideal volatile anesthetic should have no cardiac irritability. Halothane fails this criterion because it sensitizes the heart to catecholamines. All of the following agents have MINIMAL catecholamine sensitization EXCEPT:

options: PaO2 target is irrelevant if conscious
questions.question: A patient in acute respiratory failure requires correction of hypoxaemia as the immediate priority. What target is generally used when initiating oxygen therapy?
questions.explanation: In acute respiratory failure, oxygen therapy aims to correct hypoxaemia to a PaO2 above roughly 60 mmHg or SaO2 above 90%, which is generally sufficient to ensure adequate tissue oxygenation without unnecessary hyperoxia. Aiming for 100% saturation is not required and may risk oxygen toxicity with prolonged high concentrations. This target should be individualised in chronic CO2 retainers, where lower saturation targets are used.

Propofol reliably reduces intraocular pressure and provides smooth induction conditions, minimising the risk of extrusion of intraocular contents in open-globe injury. Ketamine, in contrast, may raise intraocular pressure and is generally avoided. Adequate depth of anaesthesia and avoidance of coughing or straining are equally important.
questions.question: A patient with an open-globe injury requires emergency induction of general anaesthesia. Which intravenous agent is preferred because it reliably lowers intraocular pressure?

options: Most potent analgesic effect during routine ophthalmic assessment
Causes selective basal ganglia stimulation as commonly encountered in practice
Epileptogenic with excitatory muscular effects on EEG
questions.explanation: Enflurane is uniquely epileptogenic among modern volatile anesthetic agents and can cause excitatory muscular activity and spike-and-dome patterns on EEG, particularly at high concentrations or in combination with hypocapnia. This makes it absolutely contraindicated in patients with epilepsy or seizure disorders. All other modern volatile agents (isoflurane, desflurane, sevoflurane) are not epileptogenic and isoflurane is even sometimes used in refractory status epilepticus.
questions.question: Enflurane (colour code ORANGE) has which unique CNS property that distinguishes it from all other modern volatile agents?

options: Complete inertness preventing any systemic absorption
High solubility reducing the risk of significant gas embolism
questions.question: A patient undergoing general anaesthesia for a laparoscopic procedure requires pneumoperitoneum with carbon dioxide insufflation. This gas is preferred over other gases for insufflation primarily because of which property?
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide is highly soluble in blood compared with less soluble gases such as air or nitrous oxide, meaning that any small amount inadvertently entering the circulation is more readily absorbed and eliminated, substantially reducing the clinical risk and severity of gas embolism compared with using a less soluble insufflating gas.

questions.question: A patient with a head injury is assessed using the Glasgow Coma Scale. Which three domains does this scale specifically evaluate to quantify level of consciousness?
questions.explanation: The Glasgow Coma Scale quantifies consciousness by scoring eye-opening, verbal, and motor responses, generating a total score used to communicate severity of impaired consciousness. It is widely used in trauma and critical care settings to track neurological status over time. It does not directly assess pupillary or vital sign parameters, which are evaluated separately.

Myasthenia gravis reduces the number of functional postjunctional nicotinic receptors due to autoantibody-mediated destruction, markedly increasing sensitivity to non-depolarising neuromuscular blockers, so these patients require substantially reduced doses and close monitoring to avoid prolonged, exaggerated block.
options: Exaggerated and prolonged block at reduced doses
Normal response identical to healthy patients
questions.question: A patient with myasthenia gravis undergoing thymectomy requires neuromuscular blockade. Compared to a healthy patient, this patient would be expected to show which altered response to a standard dose of a non-depolarising agent?

questions.explanation: The massive skeletal muscle breakdown (rhabdomyolysis) occurring in MH releases large quantities of myoglobin into the bloodstream. Myoglobin is nephrotoxic and precipitates in renal tubules in acidic, low-flow conditions, causing acute tubular necrosis and acute renal failure. Maintaining high urine output (>1-2 mL/kg/hr) through aggressive IV fluid hydration and, in some protocols, urine alkalinisation with sodium bicarbonate (to reduce myoglobin precipitation) are important supportive measures for renal protection in the MH crisis management bundle.
questions.question: Rhabdomyolysis in malignant hyperthermia leads to which serious renal complication?
options: Haemolytic uraemic syndrome from complement activation in most clinical presentations
Myoglobinuria causing acute tubular necrosis and acute renal failure
Membranous nephropathy from immune complex deposition under standard examination conditions
Papillary necrosis from renal artery vasospasm

questions.question: Which of the following is a standard basic monitor required to be continuously available and functioning during every anaesthetic?
questions.explanation: The pulse oximeter is a mandatory standard basic monitor for all anaesthetic procedures, providing continuous non-invasive measurement of arterial oxygen saturation and heart rate. Other standard basic monitors include the oxygen analyser (continuous), capnograph (continuous), ECG (continuous), and non-invasive blood pressure device. Transoesophageal echocardiography, pulmonary artery catheters, cerebral oximetry, and ICP monitors are specialised devices used only in specific high-risk or complex surgical or critical care settings.

questions.question: Which physical property of a local anaesthetic agent MOST directly determines its potency?
questions.explanation: Lipid solubility is the primary determinant of LA potency because the drug must penetrate lipid-rich nerve membranes to reach the sodium channel. Higher lipid solubility (partition coefficient) → greater membrane penetration → lower concentration required for effective block → higher potency. Bupivacaine's high lipid solubility explains its much greater potency than procaine. pKa determines onset; protein binding determines duration.

Rocuronium at a high (RSI) dose of 1.2 mg/kg provides intubating conditions comparable to suxamethonium 1.5 mg/kg within approximately 60 seconds at the vocal cords. This makes it the only non-depolarising agent that can match suxamethonium's onset for RSI. The major trade-off is that its duration of action at this dose is approximately 6090 minutes, requiring adequate sugammadex availability for rapid reversal in a failed intubation scenario.
questions.question: Rocuronium is the only non-depolarising agent used as an alternative to suxamethonium for RSI. At what dose is it used for RSI, and what is its approximate onset time?

questions.explanation: Chronic steroid use suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, impairing the cortisol stress response to surgery. Failure to supplement with stress-dose corticosteroids (e.g., hydrocortisone 100 mg IV) can lead to life-threatening adrenal insufficiency (Addisonian crisis). Abrupt discontinuation before surgery is dangerous and inadequate without steroid coverage.
options: Tapering corticosteroids over 6 weeks before the operation
Discontinuing steroids 48 hours before the surgical procedure
Administer stress-dose hydrocortisone to prevent adrenal crisis
Substituting prednisolone with aspirin for anti-inflammatory effect
Increasing the patient's regular dose after surgery is completed
questions.question: A patient on long-term oral corticosteroids presents for major elective surgery. Which perioperative management is MOST critical?

questions.explanation: Delivering oxygen via nasal cannula during the apnoeic period of laryngoscopy, known as apnoeic oxygenation, extends the time available before desaturation occurs by maintaining oxygen diffusion into the alveoli. It does not replace adequate pre-oxygenation but supplements it during the intubation attempt itself. This technique is particularly valuable in patients with reduced oxygen reserve.
questions.question: A patient undergoing rapid sequence induction desaturates before laryngoscopy is attempted, despite adequate pre-oxygenation. What technique can extend the safe apnoea time during the attempt?

options: Phenytoin IV as the first-line antiepileptic for all seizure types
Propofol infusion to terminate status epilepticus immediately
Diazepam IV followed immediately by phenobarbitone loading dose
IV or IM benzodiazepine (lorazepam IV or midazolam IM)
Valproate sodium as the sole first-line agent in all adults
questions.explanation: Current status epilepticus guidelines (NICE, Epilepsy Foundation) recommend benzodiazepines as first-line treatment: IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg (max 4 mg/dose) if IV access available, or IM midazolam 10 mg (0.2 mg/kg) if no IV access → both equally effective (RAMPART trial). Benzodiazepines potentiate GABA-A receptors, rapidly terminating seizure activity. If seizures persist after 2 doses, second-line agents (levetiracetam, valproate, phenytoin) are added. Propofol is reserved for refractory status epilepticus with anaesthetic monitoring.
questions.question: In the management of status epilepticus lasting >5 minutes, which drug is the RECOMMENDED FIRST-LINE treatment?

options: Visceral and somatic afferents converge onto shared dorsal horn neurons
Axonal sprouting from damaged nerves that innervate distant uninjured skin
Descending facilitation from the PAG amplifying signals from uninvolved dermatomes
Sympathetic nervous system activation causing distant vasospasm and ischaemia
Cross-sensitization between adjacent dermatomal segments at cortical level
questions.question: Referred pain → pain perceived at a site distant from the actual pathological source → occurs PRIMARILY because of which neuroanatomical mechanism?
questions.explanation: Referred pain (e.g., myocardial infarction causing left arm pain, diaphragmatic irritation causing shoulder pain) arises because visceral and somatic afferents converge onto the same second-order neurons (wide-dynamic-range neurons) in the dorsal horn. The brain misinterprets the origin as the somatic structure sharing that spinal segment. This viscero-somatic convergence is the anatomical basis of all referred pain patterns in clinical medicine.

options: The total daily infusion volume alone
The concentration of drug in the syringe
The type of intravenous cannula used
The background continuous infusion rate alone
questions.question: Which patient-controlled analgesia parameter is specifically designed to prevent opioid overdose from repeated demands?
questions.explanation: The lockout interval is a programmed minimum time that must elapse between successive patient-triggered doses, preventing the patient from receiving another bolus before the previous dose has had time to exert its peak effect. This safety feature is central to the design of patient-controlled analgesia systems in preventing cumulative overdose. Adjusting the lockout interval, alongside the bolus dose, allows individualised titration of analgesia while maintaining safety.

Hyperkalemia produces a classic ECG progression: tall peaked (tented) T waves → PR prolongation → P wave flattening/disappearance → QRS widening → sine wave pattern → VF or asystole. Emergency treatment includes IV calcium (membrane stabilization), insulin + glucose (intracellular K+ shift), sodium bicarbonate, salbutamol nebulization, and dialysis. In cardiac arrest, sodium bicarbonate is given early.
options: Delta waves and wide QRS based on typical clinical findings
ST depression and flat T waves in the majority of documented cases
Tall peaked T waves progressing to wide QRS and sine wave pattern
questions.question: Potassium disturbances (both hyperkalemia and hypokalemia) can precipitate cardiac arrest. Hyperkalemia most characteristically causes which ECG change leading to VF?

options: Normal saline is acidic (pH 5.0) and directly lowers plasma pH without metabolic effects
Dilutional effect on serum bicarbonate from adding a neutral sodium chloride solution
Saline reduces aldosterone secretion, impairing renal hydrogen ion excretion
Chloride load from normal saline exceeds renal excretion, reducing plasma bicarbonate and causing acidosis
Chloride in saline competitively inhibits carbonic anhydrase in the renal proximal tubule
questions.explanation: Normal saline contains 154 mEq/L of chloride (supraphysiological vs. plasma 100 mEq/L). Large-volume infusion delivers a massive chloride load. To maintain electroneutrality, renal tubular bicarbonate reabsorption is reduced (Stewart's strong ion difference theory) and urinary bicarbonate excretion increases, lowering serum bicarbonate and causing non-anion gap hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis. This is a well-established complication of large-volume saline resuscitation.
questions.question: Which principle BEST explains why infusion of large volumes of normal saline (0.9% NaCl) can cause a non-anion gap metabolic acidosis (hyperchloraemic acidosis)?

options: Legal requirement regardless of clinical necessity
Unknown infectious status of the trauma patient
Requirement for sterile technique in all trauma cases
questions.question: A healthcare worker performing trauma resuscitation observes universal precautions throughout the procedure. This practice is recommended primarily because of which specific patient care consideration?
questions.explanation: Universal precautions are applied in trauma resuscitation because the infectious status of an acutely injured patient is typically unknown at the time of presentation, and the resuscitation environment often involves exposure to blood and body fluids, making standard barrier precautions essential to protect all members of the healthcare team.

options: Catheters are routinely placed for both spinal and epidural anaesthesia
Spinal catheters are preferred for obstetric analgesia
Epidural catheters are never used beyond 24 hours
More common in epidural than spinal, for top-up dosing
Both techniques use identical Tuohy needles
questions.explanation: Epidural catheters are routinely placed during epidural block to allow repeated bolus doses or continuous infusion, enabling prolonged anaesthesia or analgesia (e.g., labour epidural, post-thoracotomy analgesia). Spinal block is traditionally a single-shot technique, though continuous spinal catheters exist but carry higher risk of neurological complications and post-dural puncture headache. The Tuohy needle (large gauge, curved tip) is used specifically for epidural catheter insertion; spinal needles are smaller gauge.
questions.question: In comparing spinal and epidural block, which statement about catheter placement is most accurate?
Which local anaesthetic agent is specifically known for its use in topical anaesthesia of the upper airway (nose, pharynx, larynx) before awake fibre-optic intubation?
options: Bupivacaine 0.5% alone for topical mucosal application
Ropivacaine 2% spray applied to the nasal mucosa
questions.explanation: Lidocaine 4% is the standard topical LA for awake fibreoptic intubation → applied by spray, nebulisation, or nerve block (glossopharyngeal, superior laryngeal nerve, transtracheal) to anaesthetize the upper airway. Total dose must not exceed 9 mg/kg topically. Cocaine 4–10% is also used for nasal anaesthesia with the added benefit of vasoconstriction. Bupivacaine and ropivacaine have insufficient mucosal penetration for reliable topical effect.

Pregnancy causes generalised mucosal oedema, including of the airway and larynx, along with breast enlargement and reduced functional residual capacity, all of which combine to make both visualisation and instrumentation of the airway more difficult and less forgiving of delay. This contributes to obstetric general anaesthesia carrying a higher documented failed intubation rate than the general surgical population. These factors underlie the strong preference for regional techniques in obstetric anaesthesia where feasible.
questions.question: Why is general anaesthesia associated with a higher risk of failed intubation in obstetric patients compared with the general surgical population?
options: Pregnant patients require larger endotracheal tubes always
Obstetric general anaesthesia never uses muscle relaxants
Pregnancy causes airway oedema and reduced functional reserve
Pregnant patients have improved laryngoscopic views generally
Pregnancy reduces the need for airway assessment

questions.question: Which preoperative assessment finding represents a relative contraindication to neuraxial anaesthesia that requires careful individualised risk-benefit analysis?
questions.explanation: Prior back surgery at the proposed injection site is a relative contraindication because scar tissue, altered anatomy, and instrumentation may make needle placement difficult, increase the risk of failed block, and potentially alter the pattern of drug spread or increase the risk of neurological complications. The decision to proceed requires careful consideration of the surgical anatomy, imaging review if available, and discussion with the patient about the increased risk of failed or patchy block. Spinal anaesthesia after previous lumbar laminectomy may still be feasible with skilled technique.

questions.question: Intravenous Regional Anaesthesia (IVRA, Bier's block) is most commonly performed for surgical procedures on which body region?
questions.explanation: IVRA (Bier's block) is most commonly applied to the upper limb, involving injection of local anaesthetic into a vein of an exsanguinated, tourniquet-occluded limb. The drug diffuses to peripheral nerves within the isolated limb, producing anaesthesia for the duration of significant drug concentration. Common indications include ganglion excision, fracture reduction, and lipoma excision in the forearm, wrist, or hand.

Differential nerve blockade follows the order: small myelinated A-delta fibres (carrying acute pain and temperature) are blocked first, followed by unmyelinated C fibres (dull pain, temperature, autonomic), then A-beta fibres (touch, pressure), and finally large myelinated A-alpha motor fibres last. This differential sequence explains why pain and temperature are lost early in a regional block while motor function is preserved until higher local anaesthetic concentrations are achieved, enabling awake patients to remain mobile while pain-free.
options: All fibre types are blocked simultaneously
questions.question: During onset of a peripheral nerve block, which nerve fibres are blocked FIRST?

questions.explanation: Documented details from a previous anaesthetic, including the laryngoscopic grade achieved and devices used, provide the most reliable guide to planning management in a patient with known airway difficulty. Bedside predictors alone may be normal despite a truly difficult airway. This history should always be actively sought before repeat anaesthesia.
questions.question: A patient with a history of previous difficult intubation is scheduled for elective surgery. What is the single most useful source of information for planning the airway?

questions.explanation: Traces of the maxillary and sphenoid sinuses are present in the newborn at birth. The frontal and ethmoidal sinuses are not well developed until approximately 78 years of age. This has clinical implications for the diagnosis of sinusitis in young children.
questions.question: In a newborn baby, which paranasal sinuses are already present at birth?
Pre-operative assessment reveals a patient has a haemoglobin of 7.2 g/dL before major elective orthopaedic surgery. The MOST appropriate action is:
questions.explanation: Preoperative anaemia (Hb <8 g/dL) significantly increases perioperative morbidity and mortality from inadequate oxygen delivery. Elective surgery should be postponed to investigate the cause (iron deficiency, haemolysis, chronic disease) and optimize haemoglobin via iron therapy, EPO, or transfusion. Proceeding without optimization exposes the patient to avoidable risk in an elective setting.
options: Proceed immediately with intraoperative cell salvage alone
Cancel surgery indefinitely until haemoglobin exceeds 15 g/dL
Administer a single unit of red blood cells one hour pre-operatively
Postpone surgery, investigate anaemia aetiology, and optimize haematologically
Accept and proceed, planning for liberal intraoperative transfusion
Radiofrequency ablation of dorsal root ganglia
Peripheral nerve cryoablation for chronic pain
questions.question: Which non-pharmacological pain management technique uses electrical impulses applied to the skin over peripheral nerves to reduce pain perception, consistent with the gate control theory?
questions.explanation: TENS applies low-voltage electrical impulses through surface electrodes to stimulate large Aß fibres, activating inhibitory interneurons in the dorsal horn → 'closing the gate' on C-fibre nociceptive transmission. High-frequency TENS (conventional) activates gate control mechanisms; low-frequency TENS activates endorphin release. TENS is safe, non-invasive, and effective for musculoskeletal, labour, and neuropathic pain as a component of multimodal management.

options: The flow rate delivers insufficient FiO2 because it is below the minimum required
Lower flows cause direct mucosal damage from concentrated oxygen
2 L/min is too fast for comfortable mask delivery
Simple masks require at least 10 L/min for any benefit
2 L/min causes CO2 rebreathing in the mask reservoir space, worsening hypercapnia
questions.explanation: A simple face mask requires a minimum flow rate of 4 L/min (not 2 L/min) to prevent rebreathing of exhaled CO2 that accumulates in the mask's dead space reservoir (100250 mL). At 2 L/min, fresh oxygen flow is insufficient to continuously flush exhaled gases from the mask cavity, causing the patient to rebreathe CO2 and potentially worsening hypercapnia. Nasal prongs are appropriate for low flow rates (16 L/min).
questions.question: A medical student is observed applying oxygen via a simple face mask at 2 L/min to a patient in moderate respiratory distress. Why is this flow rate inadequate for a simple face mask?

questions.explanation: Septic shock is a distributive shock characterised by a hyperdynamic circulatory state in the early (compensated) phase: high cardiac output, low systemic vascular resistance (SVR), warm peripheral circulation, and bounding pulses due to massive vasodilation from inflammatory mediators (cytokines, endotoxins). This distinguishes it from cardiogenic and hypovolaemic shock, which are characterised by low cardiac output and high SVR (cold, clammy shock). Late septic shock may progress to a low cardiac output state as myocardial depression develops.
options: Low cardiac output with high SVR (cold shock)
Low cardiac output with low SVR
Normal cardiac output with very high SVR
High cardiac output with very high SVR
High output, low SVR (warm, distributive shock)
questions.question: Septic shock is characterised by which pattern of haemodynamic disturbance?

options: Corner of mouth to angle of jaw
Center of the mouth to the earlobe
Tip of nose to angle of jaw
questions.question: The oropharyngeal (Guedel) airway size is measured from the:
questions.explanation: The oropharyngeal airway size is measured from the corner of the mouth to the angle of the jaw. It is inserted with the curve directed toward the roof of the mouth, then rotated 180 degrees as it passes the posterior pharynx, allowing the curve to follow the tongue's contour. Sizes range from 0 to 6.

options: PABA is an active metabolite that enhances local anaesthetic potency
PABA is associated with allergic hypersensitivity reactions including anaphylaxis
PABA accumulates in patients with renal failure causing neurotoxicity
PABA prevents folate synthesis in bacteria, causing antibiotic interactions
PABA has antifibrinolytic properties reducing perioperative blood loss
questions.question: Para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA) is a breakdown product of ester local anaesthetics that is CLINICALLY significant because:
questions.explanation: Ester LA hydrolysis produces PABA (para-aminobenzoic acid), which is highly immunogenic and responsible for the higher incidence of allergic reactions → including anaphylaxis → associated with ester LAs compared to amides. This is the reason ester LAs have largely been superseded by amides in clinical practice. True allergy to amide LAs is exceptionally rare; reactions usually result from preservatives (methylparaben, which itself metabolizes to PABA).

questions.question: A postoperative patient in the ICU is noted to have an irregularly irregular pulse with absent P waves on ECG occurring in the early postoperative period. Which cardiovascular complication does this MOST likely represent?
questions.explanation: An irregularly irregular rhythm without discernible P waves is characteristic of atrial fibrillation, one of the most common postoperative cardiac complications, particularly after major or cardiothoracic surgery. Rate or rhythm control strategies, along with correction of precipitating factors such as electrolyte disturbance, form the mainstay of management. Anticoagulation consideration depends on duration and underlying risk factors.

questions.question: A patient with ankylosing spondylitis has severely restricted neck extension noted on pre-anaesthetic examination. This finding MOST directly predicts difficulty with which step of airway management?
questions.explanation: Adequate atlanto-occipital extension is required to align the oral, pharyngeal, and laryngeal axes for a direct laryngoscopic view of the glottis. Fixed flexion deformities from ankylosing spondylitis severely restrict this alignment. Awake fibre-optic intubation is often planned in such patients.

questions.question: Which of the following CORRECTLY describes the mechanism of action of paracetamol (acetaminophen) that distinguishes it from NSAIDs?
options: Paracetamol irreversibly acetylates COX enzymes like aspirin
Paracetamol competitively blocks prostaglandin synthase peripherally
Inhibits central COX-3 and activates endocannabinoid system; minimal peripheral effect
Paracetamol inhibits thromboxane synthesis reducing platelet aggregation
Paracetamol is a selective COX-2 inhibitor with minimal gastric side effects
questions.explanation: Paracetamol's exact mechanism remains debated but it is believed to act predominantly centrally: inhibition of a central COX-3 variant, activation of the serotonergic descending inhibitory system, and indirect endocannabinoid system potentiation (via TRPV1 desensitization). Unlike NSAIDs, paracetamol has minimal peripheral anti-inflammatory activity and does not inhibit peripheral COX-1/COX-2 meaningfully → explaining its lack of gastric and renal side effects at therapeutic doses.

questions.question: In the Heimlich maneuver for a responsive adult with foreign body airway obstruction (FBAO), the hands are positioned between the:
questions.explanation: In the Heimlich maneuver for responsive adults, the rescuer stands behind the victim, wraps arms around the waist, makes a fist with the thumb side placed between the navel and the xiphisternum, and delivers 5 quick upward thrusts. This creates a sudden increase in intrathoracic pressure to expel the foreign body. SUBTOPIC 3: INHALATIONAL ANAESTHESIA

options: It has rapid onset enabling quick depth adjustment
It causes no cardiovascular effects at any dose
It has the lowest MAC of all agents
Signs of respiratory depression precede serious cardiac depression
It eliminates entirely unchanged via the lungs
questions.explanation: Diethyl ether has a wide therapeutic index because respiratory depression (a warning sign) precedes serious cardiac depression, unlike agents such as halothane where cardiac toxicity occurs at lower concentrations. Ether also maintains blood pressure and has no tendency to cause arrhythmias. These properties made it relatively safer in resource-limited settings with less monitoringbut its flammability limits its use.
questions.question: Diethyl ether is described as having a 'wide safety margin,' making it relatively safe in the hands of less experienced anaesthetists. This is primarily because:

options: Increased functional residual capacity from abdominal fat as commonly encountered in practice
Obesity-induced myocardial depression reducing pulmonary blood flow during routine ophthalmic assessment
Excess fat loading the chest wall, reducing ventilatory reserve and causing hypoventilation
questions.explanation: Obesity hypoventilation syndrome (Pickwickian syndrome) occurs because excessive adipose tissue loading of the chest wall and abdomen reduces thoracic compliance and diaphragmatic excursion. This decreases functional residual capacity and alveolar ventilation, causing chronic hypoventilation and CO2 retention (Type II failure). It is listed alongside Guillain-Barré, myasthenia gravis, and kyphoscoliosis as causes of Type II failure.
questions.question: Morbid obesity (severe) can cause Type II respiratory failure through the Pickwickian syndrome. The mechanism involves:
Which volatile agent has the colour code YELLOW on its vaporizer filling collar?
questions.explanation: Sevoflurane has the colour code YELLOW on its keyed filling system collar. The internationally standardized colour codes prevent accidental filling of the wrong vaporizer: halothane = red, enflurane = orange, isoflurane = purple/violet, sevoflurane = yellow, desflurane = blue. N2O cylinders have a French blue body with blue and white quartered shoulders. These colour codes are a critical patient safety system.

options: Better if defibrillation energy is increased
questions.question: In an unwitnessed cardiac arrest with delayed BLS and defibrillation, the chance of successful resuscitation is:
questions.explanation: Patients who suffer unwitnessed cardiac arrests and have delayed BLS and defibrillation as a result usually have unsuccessful resuscitation in most cases. This underscores the critical importance of the chain of survival, particularly early recognition and bystander CPR. Each minute of delay without CPR reduces the chance of survival by 27%, and without defibrillation for shockable rhythms, by a similar margin.

Glycopyrrolate has an onset of action that closely matches that of neostigmine, providing better temporal coupling of the anticholinergic and anticholinesterase effects and reducing the transient bradycardia that can occur if the muscarinic effects of neostigmine begin before the anticholinergic effect takes hold, as can happen with atropine's more rapid onset mismatch.
options: Longer duration of action than atropine
Better matched onset time reducing transient bradycardia
questions.question: A patient requires reversal of a moderate non-depolarising block. Neostigmine is combined with glycopyrrolate rather than atropine in this context primarily because glycopyrrolate offers which advantage?

options: Prolonged postoperative antibiotic courses for all surgical patients
Routine preoperative bowel preparation for all abdominal surgeries
Maintaining hyperoxia (FiO2 1.0) throughout the entire surgical procedure
Appropriate timing and selection of prophylactic antibiotics before incision
Avoiding all blood transfusion during the perioperative period
questions.question: The most important single measure to reduce perioperative surgical site infections is:
questions.explanation: Appropriate surgical antibiotic prophylaxis  selecting the correct antibiotic active against the likely pathogens, administering it within 60 minutes before surgical incision (within 120 minutes for vancomycin/fluoroquinolones), and re-dosing for prolonged procedures  is the most evidence-based single intervention for reducing surgical site infections. Additional measures include hair removal by clipping (not shaving), maintaining normothermia, optimising blood glucose, and antiseptic skin preparation, but none matches the evidence base of correctly timed prophylaxis.

options: Right infraclavicular and left lateral chest at nipple level
Left side of sternum and right axilla
Both sides of the chest symmetrically
Anterior chest and posterior infrascapular (anterior-posterior position is required for all defibrillations)
Left anterior and right posterior positions are mandatory
questions.question: Which of the following CORRECTLY identifies the standard paddle positions for defibrillation (STERNAL-APEX position)?
questions.explanation: Standard defibrillator paddle (or pad) placement uses the STERNAL-APEX position: the STERNAL paddle/pad is placed to the right of the sternum below the right clavicle (avoiding placement directly over the sternum where bone reduces current delivery), and the APEX paddle/pad is placed laterally to the left breast at the nipple line (V4V6 position), maximising current flow through the myocardium. Alternative positions (anterior-posterior, anterior-left infrascapular, anterior-right infrascapular) are used when standard positioning is impractical.

questions.question: In nutritional support for critically ill patients, enteral nutrition (EN) is preferred over total parenteral nutrition (TPN) for which primary reason?
options: EN is cheaper and more readily available
EN requires no monitoring of blood glucose
TPN is only available in specialised centres
Maintains gut integrity, prevents translocation, preserves immunity
questions.explanation: Enteral nutrition is preferred over TPN because gut feeding maintains intestinal mucosal integrity by stimulating enterocyte turnover and preserving tight junctions between cells, preventing bacterial translocation (movement of gut bacteria across the mucosal barrier into the bloodstream). EN also preserves gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT) immune function, reduces infections, maintains biliary secretion (preventing cholestasis), and is associated with fewer metabolic complications than TPN. The principle 'if the gut works, use it' guides nutritional decision-making.

Infected tissues have a low pH due to bacterial and cellular metabolic acid production. This acidic environment shifts the local anaesthetic equilibrium towards the ionised (protonated) form, significantly reducing the proportion in the lipid-soluble un-ionised free base form available to cross the nerve membrane. Since only the free base form penetrates the axolemma, less drug enters the nerve, resulting in unreliable or failed block. Practically, higher doses or alternative anaesthetic approaches are needed in infected tissues.
options: Increased vascularity washes the drug away before it can act in most clinical presentations
Inflamed tissue has thickened nerve sheaths that block drug access under standard examination conditions
Local anaesthetics are inactivated by inflammatory enzymes
Tissue acidosis traps the drug in ionised form, reducing membrane penetration
Elevated tissue temperature denatures the local anaesthetic molecule
questions.question: Why is local anaesthetic block unreliable and difficult to achieve in infected or inflamed tissues?

questions.explanation: Hypothermia impairs coagulation primarily through two mechanisms: the temperature-dependent enzymatic reactions of the coagulation cascade (serine proteases such as factors VII, VIII, IX, X) slow significantly below 35°C, reducing thrombin generation; and platelet aggregation and granule release are impaired at lower temperatures, reducing primary haemostasis. These effects compound coagulopathy from dilution by crystalloids, consumption by injury, and fibrinolysis. Laboratory coagulation tests (PT, APTT) performed at 37°C in the lab will appear normal in a hypothermic patient, underestimating actual in vivo coagulopathy.
options: Temperature-dependent coagulation and platelet enzyme activity
Synthesis of fibrinogen in the liver
questions.question: Hypothermia in trauma patients is defined as a core temperature below 35°C. Which coagulation mechanism is specifically impaired by hypothermia?
Which of the following clinical signs is an adequate test for reversal of neuromuscular block before extubation, according to traditional (non-quantitative) assessment?
questions.explanation: A sustained head lift for 5 seconds has traditionally been used as a clinical sign of adequate reversal of neuromuscular block, correlating approximately with a TOF ratio of 0.70.8. However, it is now known that pharyngeal and airway protective reflexes may still be impaired at this TOF level. Despite its limitations, the 5-second head lift test remains commonly used in clinical practice alongside other signs. Quantitative monitoring with TOF ratio ≥0.9 is superior and should be used whenever possible.
options: Patient able to open eyes on command

questions.question: A structural feature that distinguishes neuromuscular blocking agents from acetylcholine is that they are quaternary ammonium compounds. What clinical implication follows from this structural feature?
questions.explanation: Quaternary ammonium compounds carry a permanent positive charge and are therefore highly ionised at physiological pH, resulting in poor lipid solubility. Consequently, they cannot cross lipid barriers such as the blood-brain barrier, the placenta significantly, or intestinal mucosa. This is why neuromuscular blocking agents must be administered intravenously and do not produce CNS effects or dependence.
options: They freely cross the blood-brain barrier
They are absorbed well via the oral route
They are highly lipid-soluble and extensively protein-bound
Cannot cross lipid membranes; given IV
They undergo extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism

questions.explanation: Patients with undiagnosed muscular dystrophies have widespread upregulation of extrajunctional acetylcholine receptors across muscle membranes, so suxamethonium triggers massive potassium efflux from an abnormally large receptor population, precipitating life-threatening hyperkalaemia and cardiac arrest even in a seemingly healthy young patient presenting for routine surgery.
questions.question: During rapid sequence induction, a patient develops sudden hyperkalaemic cardiac arrest minutes after suxamethonium administration. Which underlying condition most likely predisposed to this outcome?

options: Hyperthermia through increased basal metabolic rate
No clinically significant effect on body temperature
questions.question: Temperature monitoring during anaesthesia is critically important because anaesthetic agents primarily cause which thermoregulatory effect?
questions.explanation: General anaesthetic agents impair thermoregulation by widening the interthreshold range (the temperature band triggering no response), effectively disabling the vasoconstriction and shivering responses that normally prevent core temperature from falling. Heat is redistributed from the warm core to cooler peripheral tissues, causing a characteristic 1-2°C drop in core temperature in the first hour. Hypothermia causes coagulation dysfunction, delayed drug metabolism, increased wound infection risk, and cardiac arrhythmias.

questions.question: A pregnant patient at term undergoes physiological changes that significantly affect anaesthetic management for Caesarean section. Which combination of changes is MOST clinically relevant to the anaesthetist?
questions.explanation: Pregnancy reduces functional residual capacity while increasing oxygen consumption, predisposing to rapid desaturation during apnoea, and also increases aspiration risk through delayed gastric emptying and reduced sphincter tone. These combined changes necessitate careful preoxygenation and airway protection strategies during general anaesthesia. Cardiac output and blood volume actually increase in pregnancy, contrary to some common misconceptions.
options: Decreased cardiac output with reduced oxygen demand
Increased plasma cholinesterase with prolonged drug action
Reduced blood volume with lower cardiac output
Decreased minute ventilation with reduced oxygen requirement
Reduced functional residual capacity with increased aspiration risk

questions.question: During verification of endotracheal tube placement, which finding is MOST reliable as a confirmatory step?
questions.explanation: Direct visualization of the endotracheal tube passing through the vocal cords is the most reliable primary confirmation method. At least two forms of placement verification are required; the esophageal detector device (EDD) provides mechanical confirmation. Auscultation, capnography, and SpO2 improvement are secondary confirmatory tools.
options: Absence of gurgling over epigastrium in the majority of documented cases
Direct visualization of tube passing through cords
