It is identical to its elimination half-life regardless of infusion duration
It is shorter than thiopentone after equivalent infusion duration
It is unaffected by hepatic blood flow or liver enzyme activity
It remains relatively short even after prolonged infusion due to continued clearance
questions.question: Which statement MOST accurately describes the context-sensitive half-time of propofol after prolonged infusion?
questions.explanation: Propofol has a relatively favourable context-sensitive half-time because of its very high clearance (even after 8-hour infusions, recovery remains predictable). Unlike thiopentone, which accumulates in fat and has a markedly prolonged context-sensitive half-time with infusion, propofol's high hepatic extraction ratio ensures continued clearance despite compartment saturation. This property makes propofol suitable for TIVA and sedation.

options: Encourage the infant to cry forcefully
questions.explanation: In infants, abdominal thrusts are avoided due to the risk of visceral injury, and back blows alternated with chest thrusts are used instead to relieve foreign body airway obstruction. This reflects the infant's smaller and more vulnerable abdominal organs compared to older children and adults. The universal choking sign and adult Heimlich technique are not applied at this young age.
questions.question: A choking infant under one year old is being managed for foreign body airway obstruction. What technique is recommended instead of abdominal thrusts?

options: Direct antagonism of NMDA receptors only
Inhibition of serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake
Selective blockade of sodium channels only
questions.question: Tramadol is sometimes preferred as a step-two analgesic because of its dual mechanism of action, which includes what additional effect beyond weak opioid activity?
questions.explanation: Tramadol combines weak mu opioid receptor agonism with inhibition of serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake, giving it a dual mechanism that contributes to analgesia through both opioid and monoaminergic pathways. This combination can make it effective for certain pain types but also raises the risk of serotonin syndrome when combined with other serotonergic drugs. Awareness of this dual mechanism is important for safe prescribing alongside other medications.

options: Opioids have no effect on MAC
Opioids only affect intravenous induction agents
Opioids increase blood:gas solubility of volatiles
questions.explanation: Concurrent opioid administration decreases the MAC of volatile anaesthetic agents, reducing the concentration needed to prevent movement to a surgical stimulus, since opioids contribute to analgesia and blunt nociceptive responses. This synergy allows lower volatile concentrations to be used safely in balanced anaesthesia. Recognising this interaction helps avoid unintended anaesthetic overdose.
questions.question: A patient receiving chronic opioid therapy requires a lower volatile agent concentration than an opioid-naive patient during the same procedure. What best explains this reduced requirement?

options: Ligamentous/periosteal trauma from needle insertion and positioning
Permanent dural injury from the Tuohy needle
Nerve root compression from catheter placement
questions.explanation: Postoperative backache after epidural anaesthesia is common and usually benign, resulting from localised inflammatory response and muscle spasm caused by needle trauma to periosteum, ligaments, or paraspinous muscles at the injection site. Prolonged positioning under anaesthesia in unusual postures can also strain paraspinal muscles and ligaments. The backache is typically mild, localised, and resolves within days with analgesics and anti-inflammatory agents. However, it is important to distinguish benign backache from the progressive and more serious back pain of epidural haematoma or abscess.
questions.question: Postoperative backache following epidural anaesthesia is most commonly attributed to:

options: Use of inhalational induction rather than intravenous agents under standard examination conditions
Performance of the entire induction sequence by a single practitioner in most clinical presentations
Application of cricoid pressure and avoidance of bag-mask ventilation before intubation
Administration of neuromuscular blocker before the induction agent
questions.explanation: RSI is characterised by pre-oxygenation, rapid IV induction, immediate administration of fast-onset neuromuscular blocker (suxamethonium or high-dose rocuronium), application of Sellick's cricoid pressure (compressing the oesophagus against the cervical vertebra), and avoidance of bag-mask ventilation before intubation, to minimise the risk of gastric regurgitation and pulmonary aspiration in patients with a full stomach. The cricoid pressure and avoidance of positive-pressure ventilation are the defining features distinguishing RSI from routine induction.
questions.question: Rapid Sequence Induction (RSI) is specifically distinguished from routine induction by which critical manoeuvre?

options: Level 4 ICU for highly specialized quaternary care
questions.explanation: Level 3 ICU (tertiary/quaternary centre) provides the highest level of critical care: all complex organ support (renal replacement, ECMO, high-frequency ventilation), invasive monitoring, complex imaging (CT/MRI at bedside or nearby), dedicated full-time intensivists, trainees, critical care nurses, and allied health professionals. Level 2 (regional) provides prolonged ventilation but not complex life support. Level 1/HDU provides short-term ventilation and close monitoring. Level 0 is standard ward care.
questions.question: Which ICU level of care is defined as providing ALL aspects of ICU management including complex investigations, multi-organ support, and staffed by dedicated intensivists?

questions.explanation: Local anaesthetics block nerve fibres based on diameter and myelination → smaller fibres with shorter internodal distances are blocked first. The correct sequence from most to least sensitive: B fibres (autonomic, small myelinated) → C fibres (unmyelinated, pain/temp) → Ad fibres (small myelinated, pain/temp) → Aß (touch/pressure) → Aa (large myelinated, motor). This explains the classic clinical sequence: autonomic block → sensory block → motor block.
questions.question: Which of the following CORRECTLY describes the order of nerve fibre sensitivity to local anaesthetic blockade from MOST to LEAST sensitive?
options: Large myelinated Aa motor → Aß touch → Ad pain → C fibres → autonomic B
Autonomic B → small C → Ad → Aß → Aa motor fibres
Ad pain fibres are blocked before C fibres because of their thin myelin sheath
All fibre types are blocked simultaneously because LA acts on all sodium channels equally
Motor Aa fibres are blocked first as they are exposed directly to injected drug

questions.question: A child requires suxamethonium for emergency airway management. Prior administration of atropine is considered primarily to prevent which specific complication in this age group?
questions.explanation: Children are particularly susceptible to suxamethonium-induced bradycardia and even asystole due to heightened vagal tone and cardiac muscarinic receptor sensitivity, so pretreatment with an anticholinergic such as atropine is a recognised precaution before administering the drug in this population.

Low-dose opioids (morphine 2.5–5 mg oral q4h, or parenteral equivalent) are the most effective pharmacological treatment for dyspnoea in palliative patients → they reduce the subjective awareness of breathlessness by central mechanisms (µ-receptor modulation of the respiratory centre sensitivity to hypercapnia and hypoxia) without causing proportionally equivalent respiratory depression at analgesic doses. Evidence does NOT support nebulised opioids for dyspnoea. Oxygen only helps if the patient is hypoxaemic.
options: Low-dose oral or parenteral morphine titrated to relieve dyspnoea
High-flow oxygen at 15 L/min via non-rebreather mask continuously
Intubation and mechanical ventilation for respiratory support
Benzodiazepine alone without any opioid for dyspnoea management
Nebulised morphine as the most effective route for dyspnoea relief
questions.question: A terminal cancer patient develops severe dyspnoea despite maximum bronchodilator therapy. The MOST effective pharmacological intervention for palliation of dyspnoea is:

questions.explanation: In chronic hypercapnic respiratory failure, the kidneys compensate over several days to weeks by retaining bicarbonate, which buffers the increased CO2 and normalizes pH to near-normal levels. This renal compensation is the basis for the classification: acute hypercapnia shows pH < 7.3, while chronic hypercapnia shows only slight pH decrease despite high PaCO2, with elevated serum bicarbonate.
options: Respiratory compensation by hyperventilation in the majority of documented cases
Buffering by serum albumin based on typical clinical findings
Renal compensation with increased bicarbonate retention
questions.question: In acute hypercapnic respiratory failure, the arterial pH is typically less than 7.3. In chronic hypercapnic failure, the pH is near-normal because of:

questions.question: A patient receiving gentamicin for a severe infection develops unexpectedly prolonged neuromuscular block after a standard dose of vecuronium. Aminoglycosides potentiate neuromuscular block primarily through which mechanism?

questions.explanation: The classic LMA cannot be used for pulmonary toilet (tracheal suctioning) because it does not provide direct access to the trachea. It sits over (not in) the glottis and cannot isolate the trachea for suctioning. It also cannot protect against aspiration. The Pro-Seal LMA with its esophageal conduit allows gastric tube passage but still not tracheal suctioning. Only an endotracheal tube allows reliable pulmonary toilet.

Reducing anesthesia requirements compared to ETT
questions.question: The LMA was designed by Dr. Archie Brain in 1981 and is specified in difficult airway management. It CANNOT be used for which of the following purposes?
A child of 5 years requires suxamethonium for emergency intubation. What key practical precaution should be taken prior to administration?
questions.explanation: Children are more susceptible than adults to bradycardia and even asystole following a single dose of suxamethonium, due to the higher vagal tone in the paediatric population and the muscarinic agonist activity of the drug. Prophylactic atropine (1020 mcg/kg IV) is recommended before suxamethonium in all children to prevent this potentially fatal bradycardia. The risk is greatest with repeat doses but is present even with the first dose in small children.
options: Administer a precurarising dose of pancuronium first
Ensure the child is deeply anaesthetised to reduce fasciculations
Give prophylactic atropine to prevent bradycardia

questions.question: Which premedication agent MOST effectively prevents the increase in intragastric pressure and aspiration risk in a morbidly obese patient?
options: Intravenous fentanyl 100 mcg administered at induction
Intramuscular morphine 10 mg given 90 minutes pre-induction
Intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg given before skin incision
Oral midazolam 7.5 mg given 30 minutes pre-induction
questions.explanation: Sodium citrate is a non-particulate oral antacid that rapidly (within minutes) neutralizes gastric acid, raising pH above 2.5 to reduce Mendelson's syndrome severity if aspiration occurs. It is the fastest-acting, most reliable means of lowering aspiration injury risk immediately pre-induction. Its effects are transient; hence timing 15–30 minutes pre-induction is critical for its effectiveness.

options: Hypertension and tachycardia from inadequate analgesia based on typical clinical findings
Hypoventilation and hypoxaemia from impaired respiratory muscle function
Emergence delirium from persistent anaesthetic blood levels in the majority of documented cases
Nausea and vomiting from vestibular stimulation
questions.explanation: Residual neuromuscular blockade (TOF ratio <0.9) impairs the function of the diaphragm, intercostal muscles, and upper airway muscles, resulting in hypoventilation, hypercapnia, and hypoxaemia in the postoperative period. Partial blockade of the pharyngeal muscles also impairs upper airway patency and swallowing, increasing aspiration risk. This is one of the most preventable causes of postoperative respiratory complications and death, underscoring the importance of quantitative TOF monitoring before extubation.
questions.question: During recovery from general anaesthesia in the post-anaesthesia care unit (PACU), which complication is caused by residual neuromuscular blockade?
Which of the following is the RECOMMENDED nil per os (NPO) fasting guideline for clear fluids in an adult patient before elective general anaesthesia, per current evidence-based guidelines?
questions.explanation: Current evidence-based guidelines (ASA, ESAIC) recommend a minimum 2-hour fast for clear fluids (water, clear juices, carbonated drinks) before elective anaesthesia in adults. Prolonged fasting beyond 2 hours for liquids is not supported and increases patient discomfort and dehydration. Solids require 6 hours and breast milk 4 hours.

options: Oxygen source and delivery devices during routine ophthalmic assessment
Monitoring equipment (BP, ECG, pulse oximetry) as commonly encountered in practice
Operating table with surgical lighting for minor procedures
questions.explanation: The PACU requires oxygen delivery systems, comprehensive monitoring (blood pressure, ECG, pulse oximetry, temperature), suction equipment, airway devices, warming equipment, IV consumables, emergency drugs, and defibrillators  all directed at managing the patient through the critical recovery phase from anaesthesia. An operating table with surgical lighting is part of the operating theatre, not the PACU, which is a recovery and monitoring environment rather than a surgical facility.
questions.question: The PACU should have all of the following essential equipment EXCEPT:

options: Proceeding with a different amide agent
Using a higher dose of the same amide
Using an untested ester without evaluation
questions.question: A patient scheduled for spinal anaesthesia has a known allergy to amide local anaesthetics confirmed on testing. What is the most appropriate alternative approach?
questions.explanation: True allergy to amide local anaesthetics is rare but, once confirmed, cross-reactivity among amides means switching to another amide is unsafe without further allergy testing. General anaesthesia avoiding the implicated drug class, guided by allergist input, is the safer approach for definitive surgical management. Ester agents may be considered only after appropriate allergy evaluation given their different chemical structure.

options: Greater potency for equivalent lipid solubility
Reduced systemic toxicity regardless of dose
questions.question: A local anaesthetic with high plasma protein binding would be expected to demonstrate which pharmacological property?
questions.explanation: High plasma protein binding is associated with a longer duration of action because the drug is retained at the site of action and released more slowly from the nerve membrane binding sites, whereas onset of action is more closely related to the pKa and resulting unionised fraction rather than to protein binding.

questions.question: The supraclavicular brachial plexus block specifically does NOT reliably anaesthetise which territory, limiting its use for shoulder surgery?
questions.explanation: The supraclavicular block does not reliably anaesthetise the axillary nerve and suprascapular nerve territories, which are formed at the upper trunk level and leave the plexus before the supraclavicular fossa where the block is performed. This means the shoulder (deltoid and supraspinous muscles, glenohumeral joint capsule) is incompletely blocked, making this approach unsuitable for shoulder surgery. The block is however excellent for elbow, forearm, wrist, and hand procedures.

questions.question: Nutritional support in critically ill patients is aimed at preventing which nutritional complication of prolonged fasting during serious illness?
questions.explanation: Critical illness triggers a hypermetabolic catabolic state driven by counter-regulatory hormones (cortisol, glucagon, catecholamines) and inflammatory cytokines, causing accelerated protein catabolism, muscle wasting, impaired immune function, and compromised wound healing. Without nutritional support, patients develop rapid malnutrition, which prolongs ICU stay, increases susceptibility to infection, impairs respiratory muscle function, and delays weaning from ventilation. Enteral nutrition (preferred over parenteral when gut function permits) maintains gut mucosal integrity and reduces bacterial translocation.

questions.question: A patient suffers cardiac arrest from accidental electrocution. What safety priority must the rescuer address before beginning resuscitation?
options: Begin chest compressions immediately regardless of danger
Apply defibrillation pads before checking the scene
Ensure the power source is disconnected
Perform a pulse check before any other action
Administer rescue breaths before scene safety is confirmed
questions.explanation: In electrocution, the rescuer's first priority is ensuring the electrical source is switched off or the patient is safely separated from it, since approaching a live current risks becoming a second casualty. Only once scene safety is confirmed should standard resuscitation measures begin. This precaution takes priority even over immediate initiation of compressions.

questions.question: A patient scheduled for elective surgery discloses recreational cocaine use two days prior. The MOST critical perioperative concern is:
options: Prolonged drug clearance requiring delayed induction for 7 days
Requirement for mandatory urine toxicology before any anaesthesia
Development of postoperative cocaine withdrawal seizures after surgery
Risk of severe hypertension, coronary vasospasm, and arrhythmias
Excessive intraoperative hypotension due to catecholamine depletion
questions.explanation: Cocaine blocks catecholamine re-uptake, causing sympathomimetic hyperactivation → severe hypertension, tachycardia, coronary vasospasm, and ventricular arrhythmias → which are dramatically exacerbated by anaesthetic agents and surgical stimulation. Recent use (within 24–72 hours) significantly elevates cardiovascular risk perioperatively. Elective procedures should ideally be postponed; emergency cases require invasive monitoring and haemodynamic control. SUBTOPIC 2: INTRAVENOUS ANAESTHETIC AGENTS

options: Oral morphine titrated to maximum dose as first-line treatment
Surgical stabilization of the bone with prophylactic internal fixation
Palliative radiotherapy targeting the specific metastatic lesion
Bisphosphonate infusion (zoledronic acid) given monthly for 6 months
Intrathecal morphine pump for refractory bone pain from all metastases
questions.question: In palliative care for cancer patients with bone pain from metastasis, which analgesic intervention provides the MOST effective and lasting pain relief for a single metastatic bone lesion?
questions.explanation: Palliative radiotherapy provides effective, durable pain relief in 60–80% of patients with painful bone metastases → a single fraction (8 Gy) is as effective as multifraction regimens for pain control. It directly targets the metastasis, reducing inflammatory mediators and tumour mass on periosteum/nerves. Bisphosphonates prevent skeletal events but are not analgesics. Oral opioids are concurrently used for breakthrough pain. Surgical stabilization is indicated for impending pathological fracture, not primarily for analgesia.

Neostigmine inhibits acetylcholinesterase non-selectively, increasing acetylcholine at both nicotinic neuromuscular junctions, which is desired, and muscarinic receptors elsewhere, which can cause bradycardia, excessive salivation and bronchospasm. Co-administering an antimuscarinic agent such as glycopyrrolate blocks these unwanted muscarinic effects while preserving the beneficial nicotinic reversal action. This combination allows safe and effective reversal of residual neuromuscular blockade.
questions.question: Why is neostigmine typically co-administered with an antimuscarinic agent such as glycopyrrolate when reversing non-depolarising neuromuscular blockade?
options: To increase the speed of neuromuscular reversal itself
To counteract muscarinic side effects such as bradycardia
To prevent residual neuromuscular blockade entirely
To reduce the total dose of neostigmine needed
To prevent postoperative nausea and vomiting only

questions.explanation: Labour analgesia requires a technique that can be maintained for the highly variable, unpredictable duration of labour (hours to days), adjusted as needed for different stages of labour and converted rapidly to surgical block if emergency Caesarean section becomes necessary. The epidural catheter uniquely meets all these requirements: it allows dose titration, top-up boluses for dense surgical anaesthesia, and continuous infusions for maintenance. Single-shot spinal provides an excellent dense block but its fixed duration makes it unsuitable for labour analgesia.
questions.question: Epidural analgesia via a catheter is specifically preferred over single-shot spinal anaesthesia for which clinical indication?
options: Emergency Caesarean section where rapid dense surgical block is needed immediately
Short outpatient urological procedures under anaesthesia
Single-dose analgesia after appendicectomy in ASA I patients
Labour analgesia requiring prolonged and adjustable block throughout unpredictable labour duration
Hospital-acquired pneumonia treated with empirical antibiotics
Acute myocardial infarction requiring immediate ECG and troponin
Pneumothorax from the epidural catheter insertion on admission
Pericarditis presenting with pleuritic pain and pericardial rub
Pulmonary embolism requiring immediate CT pulmonary angiography
questions.explanation: Day 5 post-hip replacement is a peak time for DVT/PE, with major orthopaedic surgery being the highest VTE-risk surgical procedure. The clinical triad of sudden pleuritic chest pain, dyspnoea, and tachycardia, in conjunction with the clinical context, mandates immediate PE workup: bilateral lower limb Doppler ultrasonography, D-dimer (if low pre-test probability), and CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) as the gold standard. Immediate anticoagulation should not await imaging in patients with high clinical probability and no bleeding contraindication.
questions.question: A post-operative patient develops sudden onset pleuritic chest pain, dyspnoea, and tachycardia on day 5 post-elective hip replacement. Which diagnosis should be IMMEDIATELY suspected and investigated?

questions.explanation: The lethal triad of trauma describes the mutually reinforcing combination of hypothermia, metabolic acidosis, and coagulopathy, each of which worsens the others in a vicious cycle that significantly increases mortality in severely injured patients, making early recognition and correction of all three a central goal of damage control resuscitation.
questions.question: A trauma patient develops the lethal triad during prolonged resuscitation. Which three physiological derangements together constitute this life-threatening combination?

questions.explanation: Cocaine is unique among local anaesthetics in blocking noradrenaline reuptake at sympathetic nerve terminals, producing intrinsic vasoconstriction in addition to its local anaesthetic effect, which is particularly valuable for nasal surgery where it simultaneously reduces mucosal bleeding and provides surface anaesthesia without needing a separate vasoconstrictor.
questions.question: A patient undergoing ENT surgery receives topical cocaine to the nasal mucosa. Cocaine is uniquely useful in this setting because it combines local anaesthesia with which additional property?

options: Using only inhalational agents at high concentration during routine ophthalmic assessment
Combination of drugs and techniques to achieve hypnosis, analgesia, and relaxation
Using spinal block alongside general anaesthesia in every case as commonly encountered in practice
Administering equal doses of opioids and sedatives
questions.question: Balanced anaesthesia is best defined as which approach to achieving the triad of anaesthesia?
questions.explanation: Balanced anaesthesia uses a combination of different pharmacological agents and techniques, each targeting a specific component of the anaesthetic triad (hypnosis, analgesia, muscle relaxation), allowing lower doses of each drug to be used. By exploiting pharmacological synergism, balanced anaesthesia achieves better haemodynamic stability and fewer side effects than using a single high-dose agent. This remains the dominant philosophy in modern anaesthetic practice.

options: The prongs become dislodged at high flows during routine ophthalmic assessment
The anatomical dead space becomes the limiting factor as commonly encountered in practice
Nasal mucosal drying causes mouth breathing that dilutes inspired O2
CO2 rebreathing prevents further O2 increase
questions.question: Nasal prongs provide a maximum useful FiO2 increase of only up to flow rates of 6 L/min. Above 6 L/min there is no further increase in FiO2 primarily because:
questions.explanation: Above 6 L/min via nasal prongs, there is no significant increase in FiO2 because high-flow oxygen causes nasal mucosal drying and irritation, prompting patients to mouth-breathe. This mouth breathing entrains room air that dilutes the inspired oxygen concentration. Additionally, the anatomical nasopharyngeal reservoir is already saturated with oxygen at 6 L/min.

questions.question: Clonidine added to intrathecal bupivacaine for spinal anaesthesia can prolong the block. Which is its most significant unwanted effect in this context?
questions.explanation: Intrathecal clonidine prolongs both sensory and motor block from spinal anaesthesia and provides post-operative analgesia. Its main drawbacks are dose-dependent sedation (from alpha-2 receptor activation in the brain via systemic absorption) and hypotension (from central sympatholysis). These effects limit the dose used clinically to approximately 1575 mcg intrathecally. Bradycardia may also occur. Clonidine does not cause significant respiratory depression (unlike intrathecal opioids), which is a notable advantage in outpatient spinal anaesthesia.

questions.question: A patient with chronic non-specific low back pain and no evidence of nerve root compression on imaging is being started on pharmacotherapy. Which agent represents the MOST evidence-based first-line choice?
questions.explanation: For non-specific low back pain without radicular features, NSAIDs are recommended as first-line pharmacological therapy, combined with physical activity and education. Opioids are generally reserved for short-term use when other measures fail due to limited long-term benefit and dependence risk. Gabapentinoids have not shown consistent benefit in the absence of a neuropathic component.

questions.question: Which of the following clinical conditions is associated with ACQUIRED reduction in plasma cholinesterase activity, prolonging suxamethonium action?
questions.explanation: Plasma cholinesterase is synthesised in the liver, so liver disease reduces its production and activity, prolonging suxamethonium effect. Pregnancy also reduces plasma cholinesterase activity by approximately 25% due to haemodilution and altered synthesis. Other acquired causes include carcinomatosis, hypothyroidism, malnutrition, and exposure to organophosphate pesticides. Despite reduced enzyme levels in pregnancy, the dose-response is not clinically significantly changed because of the increased volume of distribution.

questions.question: EMLA cream, used for topical anaesthesia prior to venous cannulation, is a eutectic mixture of which two agents?
questions.explanation: EMLA (Eutectic Mixture of Local Anaesthetics) contains lignocaine 2.5% and prilocaine 2.5% in a eutectic mixture that exists as a liquid oil at room temperature, improving skin penetration compared to either agent alone. Applied under occlusion for a minimum of 60 minutes, it achieves adequate dermal anaesthesia for venous cannulation, lumbar puncture, and minor dermatological procedures. The prilocaine component requires caution regarding methaemoglobinaemia in neonates when applied to large areas.

questions.question: A patient requires an alternative airway after two failed intubation attempts, and rapid ventilation without visualising the cords is needed. Which device is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: The laryngeal mask airway is a supraglottic device that can be inserted blindly to establish ventilation quickly when intubation has failed, without requiring visualisation of the cords. It sits above the larynx rather than within the trachea. Basic airways such as oropharyngeal or nasopharyngeal devices do not provide a sealed ventilation circuit.

Referred pain occurs because visceral and somatic afferent fibres converge on the same spinal dorsal horn neurons, so the brain misattributes visceral pain to a corresponding somatic dermatome. Diaphragmatic irritation from gallbladder disease commonly refers pain to the shoulder tip via the phrenic nerve's shared segmental origin. This convergence explains many classic patterns of referred pain.
options: Direct nerve damage to the shoulder
Convergence of visceral and somatic afferents
questions.question: A patient with gallbladder disease reports pain felt in the right shoulder tip rather than the abdomen. Which mechanism BEST explains this distant pain location?

questions.explanation: For symptomatic bradycardia (not cardiac arrest), atropine is given at 0.51 mg IV and may be repeated. In cardiac arrest with asystole, a single dose of 3 mg is given to completely block vagal tone. Doses below 0.5 mg can paradoxically worsen bradycardia by causing a central vagomimetic effect. Doses above 3 mg provide no additional benefit and may cause atropine toxicity.
options: 3 mg IV as a single dose
questions.question: In symptomatic bradycardia during resuscitation (not cardiac arrest), atropine is given at which dose per administration?
Which pharmacokinetic feature of local anaesthetics is MOST relevant when performing a caudal block in a 2-year-old child for inguinal hernia repair?
options: Children have lower protein binding, requiring lower mg/kg doses than adults
Higher volume of distribution and faster absorption require weight-based dose calculations
Hepatic enzyme maturity is complete by 6 months, making clearance identical to adults
Children have higher plasma cholinesterase activity, accelerating ester LA metabolism
Neonates and infants have thicker nerve sheaths, requiring higher LA concentrations
questions.explanation: In young children, higher Vd for LAs (larger water compartments, lower protein binding in neonates) means faster systemic absorption and higher peak plasma concentrations per dose. Simultaneously, hepatic LA metabolism is immature in infants (<6 months). These pharmacokinetic differences necessitate: strict weight-based dosing, reduced maximum doses (especially for bupivacaine: 2 mg/kg without adrenaline vs 3 mg/kg in adults), and caution with repeated doses or infusions in the youngest patients. Caudal bupivacaine 0.25% at 0.5 mL/kg provides reliable sacral-lumbar blockade for inguinal surgery.

options: The lowest mortality among the major shock categories
The highest mortality among the major shock categories
Mortality equivalent to hypovolaemic shock only
No significant mortality risk if treated promptly
Mortality only relevant in elderly patients
questions.explanation: Cardiogenic shock carries the highest reported mortality among the major categories of shock, often exceeding 50 percent even with modern treatment, reflecting the severity of the underlying pump failure and the limited physiological reserve available to compensate for a critically reduced cardiac output.
questions.question: A patient develops shock following a large myocardial infarction with acute pump failure. Compared with other forms of shock, cardiogenic shock is associated with which of the following mortality characteristics?

options: Check for a pulse before resuming compressions
Wait sixty seconds before continuing CPR
Reassess the rhythm before resuming compressions
questions.question: A patient in ventricular fibrillation receives a first defibrillation attempt. What should happen immediately after the shock is delivered?
questions.explanation: After a defibrillation attempt, chest compressions should resume immediately without pausing to check for a pulse or rhythm, since even a successfully defibrillated heart typically takes time to generate an effective pulse. Rhythm and pulse are reassessed after the next cycle of compressions, usually after two minutes. This minimises interruption to circulation during the critical post-shock period.

options: Patient airway is secured with an ETT
All personnel clear, no contact with patient or bed
CPR has been in progress for exactly 2 minutes
questions.question: Before administering a defibrillation shock, the operator must ensure which specific safety check to protect bystanders?
questions.explanation: Before delivering a defibrillation shock, the operator must verify that all personnel are completely clear of the patient, bed, and any connected equipment. Current conducted through a rescuer in contact with the patient can cause injury or cardiac arrest in the bystander. The standard safety check involves the operator shouting 'I'm clear, you're clear, everybody's clear, oxygen clear' while visually confirming no one is in contact. Oxygen flow near the patient must also be stopped or moved away to prevent fire or explosion risk from the electrical discharge.

The pre-anaesthetic visit aims to establish rapport, assess fitness for anaesthesia, prescribe premedication, and optimize the patient before surgery. It is the anaesthetist's core tool for risk stratification. Obtaining surgical consent is the surgeon's responsibility, not the anaesthetist's primary objective.
options: Establish rapport and assess patient fitness for anaesthesia
To obtain informed consent for the surgical procedure
To administer prophylactic antibiotics before surgery
To  determine the surgical approach for the operation
To review the patient's insurance and billing status
questions.question: Which of the following is the PRIMARY objective of a pre-anaesthetic visit?

questions.explanation: Estimated blood volume (EBV) varies with age: Neonates (0–1 month): 85–95 mL/kg (approximately 90 mL/kg standard); Infants (1–12 months): 85 mL/kg; Children (1–10 years): 75 mL/kg; Adults: 65–75 mL/kg. For a 3 kg neonate: EBV → 90–95 mL/kg × 3 kg → 285 mL. Allowable blood loss (ABL) = EBV × (starting Hct - minimum acceptable Hct) / starting Hct → this calculation guides intraoperative transfusion decisions in paediatric surgery.
options: Estimated blood volume = 95 mL/kg × 3 kg = 285 mL
Estimated blood volume = 75 mL/kg × 3 kg = 225 mL
Estimated blood volume = 70 mL/kg × 3 kg = 210 mL
Estimated blood volume = 60 mL/kg × 3 kg = 180 mL
Estimated blood volume = 85 mL/kg × 3 kg = 255 mL
questions.question: Which of the following describes the CORRECT technique for calculating the correct blood volume in a neonate weighing 3 kg?
A patient with severe LAST-induced ventricular arrhythmia fails to respond to standard resuscitation and lipid emulsion. What additional measure should be considered?
questions.explanation: When severe cardiovascular collapse from local anaesthetic toxicity is refractory to lipid emulsion and standard advanced life support, extracorporeal support such as cardiopulmonary bypass may be required to sustain circulation while the drug redistributes and is metabolised. This reflects the prolonged receptor binding of agents like bupivacaine. Early recognition and preparation for prolonged resuscitation are essential.

options: Make a fourth attempt with a different blade in the majority of documented cases
Call for senior help only and wait
Turn patient prone and attempt blind nasotracheal intubation based on typical clinical findings
Administer more succinylcholine and retry immediately
Declare failed intubation and implement rescue plan: supraglottic airway or surgical airway
questions.question: An anesthetist attempts intubation and after the third failed attempt lasting 12 minutes, the patient's SpO2 begins to drop. According to the difficult airway algorithm, the next step is:
questions.explanation: After 3 consecutive failed intubation attempts or prolonged attempts exceeding 10 minutes, failed intubation should be declared and a rescue plan implemented. This includes supraglottic airway insertion (LMA as rescue device) or escalation to a surgical airway (cricothyrotomy) in the 'cannot intubate, cannot oxygenate' scenario. Persisting with further laryngoscopy attempts risks complete airway loss from trauma and oedema.

questions.question: A patient with myasthenia gravis requires general anaesthesia. Which statement correctly describes the expected response to non-depolarising NMBs?
questions.explanation: Myasthenic patients have reduced numbers of functional post-junctional nicotinic receptors due to autoantibody-mediated destruction and downregulation. Their neuromuscular transmission already operates with a reduced safety margin. Non-depolarising agents, which compete with ACh at these scarce receptors, produce profound block at much lower doses than normal. Even small test doses can produce significant block, requiring careful dose titration with continuous neuromuscular monitoring.
options: Normal sensitivity due to normal receptor number
Phase II block develops faster in myasthenic patients
Suxamethonium is preferred over non-depolarising agents
Markedly increased sensitivity from reduced receptor reserve

questions.question: A patient with kyphoscoliosis develops Type II respiratory failure over years. The primary mechanism is:
questions.explanation: Severe kyphoscoliosis causes chest wall deformity that reduces thoracic compliance and lung volumes. The restricted thoracic movement limits tidal volume and minute ventilation, reducing alveolar ventilation and causing CO2 retention (Type II respiratory failure). Concomitant hypoxemia and hypercapnia occur. The condition worsens progressively and may require nocturnal non-invasive ventilation.
options: Phrenic nerve injury from spinal deformity based on typical clinical findings
Cor pulmonale from pulmonary hypoxic vasoconstriction causing hypoventilation in the majority of documented cases
Chest wall deformity reducing total lung compliance and minute ventilation

questions.explanation: At concentrations above 1 MAC, isoflurane (and other volatile agents) causes cerebral vasodilation, increasing CBF and ICP. This is problematic in patients with intracranial mass lesions, traumatic brain injury, or elevated ICP, where further ICP increases can cause herniation. However, isoflurane at < 1 MAC maintains CBF. Halothane is most strongly contraindicated in intracranial mass lesions due to its greater ICP-increasing effect.
questions.question: Isoflurane at concentrations above 1 MAC causes an increase in cerebral blood flow (CBF) and intracranial pressure (ICP). This property makes isoflurane relatively CONTRAINDICATED (use with caution) in patients with:
options: Coronary artery disease based on typical clinical findings
Asthmatic patients with bronchospasm in the majority of documented cases
Intracranial mass lesions with raised ICP

questions.question: Which of the following is a recognized RISK FACTOR for developing LA systemic toxicity, independent of total drug dose administered?
questions.explanation: Accidental intravascular injection is the MOST common cause of LAST, bypassing tissue uptake kinetics and delivering the full dose directly into the circulation. Even within the maximum 'safe' dose limit, intravascular injection can cause immediate, catastrophic systemic toxicity. Ultrasound guidance and incremental injection with intermittent aspiration reduce but cannot eliminate this risk. Adrenaline actually reduces toxicity by slowing absorption.
options: Young patient age with higher glomerular filtration rate
Use of alkalinized LA solutions for faster nerve block onset
Addition of adrenaline to the LA solution for vasoconstriction
Block performance under ultrasound guidance at all times
Accidental intravascular injection during nerve block performance

questions.question: A patient with a known history of porphyria requires general anaesthesia. Which commonly used induction agent should be avoided?
questions.explanation: Barbiturates such as thiopentone are potent inducers of hepatic aminolevulinic acid synthase, the rate-limiting enzyme in haem synthesis, and can precipitate a life-threatening acute porphyric crisis in susceptible patients. Propofol, ketamine and etomidate are generally considered safer alternatives in porphyria. A careful drug history and consultation of porphyria-safe drug lists is essential before anaesthetising these patients.

Sodium bicarbonate is the priority treatment in tricyclic antidepressant overdose causing cardiac arrest or wide-complex arrhythmia, as it counteracts the sodium channel blockade responsible for the cardiotoxicity. Calcium gluconate is instead used in hyperkalaemia and would not address this mechanism. Naloxone and flumazenil are reversal agents for opioid and benzodiazepine toxicity respectively, not tricyclic overdose.
questions.question: A patient with tricyclic antidepressant overdose develops cardiac arrest with a wide QRS complex. What specific treatment is prioritised in this special circumstance?

questions.explanation: Precordial and oesophageal stethoscopes provide simple, inexpensive continuous auscultation of breath and heart sounds, detecting changes such as bronchospasm, secretions, air entry asymmetry, oesophageal intubation, and arrhythmias in real time. In paediatric anaesthesia, where electronic monitoring systems may have size or access limitations, and where rapid changes in airway status are common, the precordial stethoscope provides an invaluable continuous auditory monitor that needs no calibration or maintenance.
options: Continuous auscultation of breath and heart sounds at the bedside
Measuring cardiac output by acoustic cardiography
Detecting venous air embolism in neurosurgical procedures in most clinical presentations
Confirming spinal block level by auscultatory method under standard examination conditions
Measuring intracranial pressure by acoustic waves
questions.question: The precordial stethoscope is particularly valuable during paediatric anaesthesia for which type of monitoring?

questions.explanation: Morphine is a mu opioid receptor agonist, and activation of this receptor in the central nervous system produces its characteristic analgesic, sedative and respiratory depressant effects. Other opioid receptor subtypes contribute to a lesser extent to its overall pharmacological profile. Understanding this receptor basis explains both morphine's efficacy and its recognised side effect profile including constipation and respiratory depression.
questions.question: Morphine produces its analgesic effect primarily through action on which receptor?

questions.explanation: Shoulder dystocia management follows the HELPERR mnemonic. McRoberts manoeuvre (maternal thigh hyperflexion onto abdomen) is the first-line intervention → it flattens lumbar lordosis, rotates the pubic symphysis superiorly, increases the relative AP diameter of the pelvis, and facilitates delivery of the impacted anterior shoulder. Combined with suprapubic pressure (downward on the fetal posterior shoulder to dislodge it), this resolves >50% of shoulder dystocia cases without additional manoeuvres. Fundal pressure is absolutely CONTRAINDICATED as it worsens impaction.
options: McRoberts manoeuvre (hyperflexion of maternal thighs) combined with suprapubic pressure
Fundal pressure applied by an assistant to accelerate delivery
Immediate general anaesthesia for emergency Caesarean delivery
Routine episiotomy in all patients anticipated to have shoulder dystocia
Emergency symphysiotomy as first-line management of shoulder dystocia
questions.question: Which evidence-based intervention has MOST significantly reduced obstetric brachial plexus injury during shoulder dystocia management?

questions.explanation: Neuraxial anaesthesia blocks the sacral parasympathetic nerves (S2S4) that innervate the detrusor muscle and promote bladder contraction, as well as sympathetic pathways that modulate urethral sphincter tone. This combined effect causes detrusor inhibition (preventing contraction) and urethral sphincter dysfunction (inhibiting normal voluntary relaxation). Recovery of bladder function lags behind sensory and motor recovery, and urinary retention may persist for 48 hours after the block has otherwise worn off. Catheterisation may be required.
options: Femoral nerve causing impaired voiding position
questions.question: Urinary retention as a complication of spinal and epidural anaesthesia results from blockade of which nerve pathway?

questions.explanation: Pulmonary oxygen toxicity begins with tracheobronchitis, followed by damage to type II pneumocytes (reducing surfactant production), alveolar flooding, hyaline membrane formation, and progressive pulmonary fibrosis. Reactive oxygen species (superoxide, hydroxyl radicals, hydrogen peroxide) mediate lung injury. This is clinically similar to ARDS. Free radical scavengers (vitamins C, E) may be partially protective.
questions.question: Pulmonary oxygen toxicity (Lorrain-Smith effect) affects the lungs with prolonged FiO2 > 60%. The initial lung changes include:
options: Airway smooth muscle hypertrophy as commonly encountered in practice
Alveolar flooding and type II pneumocyte damage
Pulmonary arterial hypertension only during routine ophthalmic assessment

questions.explanation: The LMA is removed while the child is still deeply anesthetized to prevent laryngospasm and bronchospasm that commonly occurs when the LMA is removed in a lightly anesthetized or awake child. Coughing and laryngospasm during emergence from anesthesia can cause severe desaturation in children, who have smaller functional residual capacity and oxygen reserves than adults. In adults, awake removal is preferred to maintain protective airway reflexes.
options: Awake children are more likely to cough, causing laryngospasm and desaturation on LMA removal
Children have higher oxygen reserve and can tolerate apnea as commonly encountered in practice
Children require the LMA for longer post-operative periods during routine ophthalmic assessment
Airway reflexes are absent in deeply anesthetized children
Deep removal prevents postoperative agitation in children
questions.question: The LMA is removed 'awake in adults and deep in children.' The rationale for removing the LMA deep in children is:

options: A single nurse escort with a portable pulse oximeter only
Disconnection from the ventilator with a manual Ambu bag alone
Removing IV infusions 30 minutes before transfer to simplify logistics
Sedation reduction to a spontaneously breathing state before transport
Portable ventilator, monitoring, IV access, emergency drugs, and trained escort
questions.explanation: Critically ill intrahospital transport requires maintaining ICU-equivalent care: a portable ICU-grade ventilator (not transport Ambu bag alone for ventilator-dependent patients), continuous monitoring (SpO2, ETCO2, ECG, invasive BP for haemodynamically unstable), patent IV access, infusion pumps running, emergency medications (adrenaline, atropine, sedative, muscle relaxant), and an experienced escort (senior nurse  doctor for highest-risk patients). The 'transport ICU' principle → ICU care doesn't stop at the bedside → prevents adverse events en route.
questions.question: Transport of a critically ill ICU patient to the CT scanner should include which MINIMUM safety provision to maintain standards of care during transfer?
The correct sequential steps of general anaesthesia from start to finish are:
questions.explanation: The sequential steps of general anaesthesia are: pre-anaesthetic assessment, premedication and preparation, induction of anaesthesia with or without intubation, maintenance of anaesthesia with monitoring, and finally termination, reversal of neuromuscular blockade, and extubation or airway removal. Each step must occur in order to ensure patient safety and optimal anaesthetic conditions. Deviation from this sequence is a common source of anaesthetic complications and adverse events.

questions.question: A parturient undergoing elective Caesarean section under spinal anaesthesia requires a rapid, dense sensory block to the T4 dermatomal level. Which drug combination is MOST commonly used to achieve this?
questions.explanation: Hyperbaric bupivacaine combined with a lipophilic opioid such as fentanyl is the standard intrathecal combination for Caesarean section, providing rapid onset, dense sensory block to T4, and improved intraoperative analgesia. The addition of opioid reduces the required local anaesthetic dose and associated hypotension. This combination remains the most widely used technique for elective Caesarean delivery worldwide.

questions.question: A ventilated patient with ARDS is managed using lung-protective ventilation. Which combination of ventilator parameters reflects this evidence-based strategy?
questions.explanation: Lung-protective ventilation uses low tidal volumes of approximately 6 mL/kg predicted body weight combined with a plateau pressure limit, typically below 30 cmH2O, to minimise ventilator-induced lung injury in ARDS. This strategy has been shown to reduce mortality compared with traditional higher tidal volume ventilation. Appropriate positive end-expiratory pressure is titrated alongside these limits.
options: Low tidal volume with limited plateau pressure
High tidal volume with zero positive pressure
Unlimited plateau pressure with low volume
High tidal volume with high plateau pressure
Low respiratory rate with high tidal volume

questions.explanation: The lethal triad of trauma consists of hypothermia, metabolic acidosis, and coagulopathythree interconnected derangements that mutually worsen each other. Hypothermia impairs enzymatic coagulation cascade reactions and platelet function. Acidosis (from lactic acidosis of shock) impairs coagulation factor function and reduces myocardial responsiveness to catecholamines. Coagulopathy causes uncontrolled haemorrhage, worsening hypovolaemia and shock, which deepens acidosis and hypothermia. Damage control resuscitation focuses on breaking this vicious cycle.
questions.question: The 'lethal triad' of trauma refers to three interconnected physiological derangements that are mutually exacerbating. Which combination correctly identifies all three elements?

A patient under general anaesthesia with a volatile agent shows enhanced neuromuscular block from a standard dose of a non-depolarising relaxant. Which volatile agent produces the greatest degree of this potentiation?
questions.explanation: Volatile anaesthetic agents, particularly the more potent ethers such as desflurane and sevoflurane, potentiate non-depolarising neuromuscular block through central and peripheral mechanisms including reduced acetylcholine release and altered postjunctional receptor sensitivity, an effect that is greater than with intravenous agents such as propofol.

CPAP reduces the need for intubation in cardiogenic pulmonary edema by: (1) maintaining alveolar patency and improving oxygenation, (2) reducing preload and afterload through positive intrathoracic pressure (reducing venous return and cardiac transmural pressure), and (3) recruiting collapsed alveoli. Multiple trials show CPAP reduces intubation rates and mortality in acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema.
questions.question: Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP) is effective in cardiogenic pulmonary edema primarily because it:
options: Reduces intubation rate by improving FiO2 delivery and reducing pulmonary edema via positive pressure
Reduces heart rate and cardiac preload through reflex mechanisms in the majority of documented cases
Removes excess fluid from alveoli by osmotic pressure based on typical clinical findings
Increases respiratory rate to improve minute ventilation

questions.explanation: H2 receptor antagonists such as ranitidine reduce gastric acid secretion, raising gastric pH above the critical threshold of 2.5. This reduces the severity of chemical pneumonitis (Mendelson's syndrome) should pulmonary aspiration occur. They are particularly used in at-risk patients: full stomach, obesity, pregnancy, and gastrointestinal reflux disease.
questions.question: The purpose of prescribing H2 blockers (e.g., ranitidine) as premedication is PRIMARILY to:
options: Provide pre-emptive analgesia for postoperative pain control
Reduce the incidence of postoperative nausea and vomiting
Decrease the minimum alveolar concentration of inhalational agents
Reduce risk and severity of pulmonary aspiration injury

questions.question: An endotracheal tube is inserted and, on auscultation, gurgling is heard over the epigastrium with no breath sounds in the chest. What does this indicate?
questions.explanation: Gurgling over the epigastrium with absent chest breath sounds is a classic sign that the tube has been passed into the oesophagus rather than the trachea. This should prompt immediate removal and reintubation under direct or video-assisted vision. Capnography, where available, provides a more reliable confirmation than auscultation alone.

questions.question: In the treatment of acute respiratory failure, the most life-threatening facet that must be corrected FIRST is:
questions.explanation: Hypoxemia is the most life-threatening facet of acute respiratory failure and must be corrected first. The goal is to assure adequate oxygen delivery to tissues, targeting PaO2 > 60 mmHg or SaO2 > 90%. Hypercapnia and acidosis, while important, are generally better tolerated acutely (permissive hypercapnia is sometimes intentional in ventilated patients) compared to the immediate cellular damage from hypoxia.

A-delta fibres are small, thinly myelinated afferents that conduct rapidly, mediating sharp, well-localised 'first' pain and the associated withdrawal reflex. C fibres are unmyelinated and conduct the slower, dull 'second' pain. This distinction underlies the double pain sensation felt after acute injury.
questions.question: A patient sustains a crush injury and immediately withdraws the limb before consciously perceiving pain. Which fibre type is responsible for transmitting this rapid 'first' pain sensation?

options: Maintaining airway patency with positioning, suction, oropharyngeal airway, or intubation as indicated
Routine nasogastric tube insertion in all unconscious patients for medication delivery
Prophylactic tracheostomy within 24 hours of ICU admission for all comatose patients
Initiating mechanical ventilation exclusively through a tracheostomy tube
Avoiding suctioning of secretions to prevent vagal stimulation and bradycardia
questions.explanation: The unconscious patient cannot protect their airway from aspiration, obstruction, and desaturation. Airway management is the absolute first priority: lateral recovery position for self-ventilating patients, oropharyngeal airway for partial obstruction, jaw thrust and bag-mask ventilation if needed, and endotracheal intubation for definitive airway protection in deeply unconscious (GCS ≤8) or haemodynamically unstable patients. Regular oral suctioning prevents secretion aspiration. Airway precedence over all other interventions.
questions.question: The CARE of the UNCONSCIOUS patient in the ICU includes which PRIORITY airway management consideration?

options: Enhancement of GABA-A receptor-mediated chloride ion influx
Blockade of NMDA glutamate receptors reducing excitatory transmission
Activation of mu-opioid receptors producing profound analgesia
Inhibition of sodium channels preventing action potential generation
Potentiation of glycine receptors in the brainstem and spinal cord
questions.explanation: Propofol potentiates GABA-A receptors, the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter in the CNS, by increasing the frequency and duration of chloride channel opening → producing CNS depression, hypnosis, and anaesthesia. Most IV anaesthetics (thiopentone, etomidate, benzodiazepines) share this GABA-A mechanism. Ketamine is unique in primarily blocking NMDA receptors.
questions.question: The PRIMARY mechanism of action of propofol as a general anaesthetic agent is:

options: Its boiling point is close to room temperature
Its high potency requiring low concentrations
Its property of triggering malignant hyperthermia
questions.explanation: Desflurane has a boiling point of approximately 22.8 degrees Celsius, close to ambient room temperature, meaning a standard variable-bypass vaporizer cannot reliably control its vapour output. A specially heated and pressurised vaporizer is required to deliver a controlled, predictable concentration. This is a unique physical property among currently used volatile agents.
questions.question: A vaporizer designed for desflurane must be electronically heated and pressurised. What property of desflurane necessitates this specialised design?
Oxygen toxicity can cause pathological changes in the CNS, lungs, and eyes. FiO2 > 100% for longer than how many hours risks toxicity?
questions.explanation: Oxygen toxicity: FiO2 > 100% for longer than 12 hours, FiO2 > 80% for longer than 24 hours, and FiO2 > 60% for longer than 36 hours risk toxicity. This can cause retrolental fibroplasia (in neonates), absorption atelectasis, pulmonary oxygen toxicity (Lorrain-Smith effect), and CNS toxicity (Paul Bert effect). Drying of mucous membranes and suppression of hypoxic drive in COPD patients also occur.

options: Pure nociceptive bone pain without inflammatory component based on typical clinical findings
Nerve compression pain, raised ICP headache, and hepatic capsule stretch pain
Pure neuropathic pain from chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy
Opioid-refractory visceral pain from bowel obstruction
Procedural pain from dressing changes and tumour debridement in the majority of documented cases
questions.explanation: Dexamethasone is a potent glucocorticoid with anti-inflammatory and anti-oedema properties making it specifically effective for: nerve compression pain (reducing perineural oedema), raised intracranial pressure headache from cerebral metastases (reducing vasogenic oedema), and hepatic capsule pain from liver metastases (reducing capsular inflammation and oedema). It also has general appetite-stimulating and mood-elevating effects benefiting cachexia and anorexia. Short-term high-dose regimens (4-16 mg/day) can produce rapid, dramatic pain relief in these specific pain syndromes, though long-term use carries significant side effects.
questions.question: The analgesic adjuvant dexamethasone is particularly effective for which types of cancer-related pain?

questions.explanation: The SSC 1-hour bundle (2018): (1) Measure lactate → repeat if >2 mmol/L; (2) Obtain blood cultures BEFORE antibiotics; (3) Administer broad-spectrum antibiotics; (4) Begin 30 mL/kg IV crystalloid for hypotension/lactate ≥4; (5) Vasopressors if hypotensive during/after fluids to maintain MAP ≥65 mmHg. Each hour of antibiotic delay in septic shock increases mortality by 7–10%. Blood cultures are taken BEFORE antibiotics to guide de-escalation, but antibiotic administration must NOT be delayed >1 hour.
options: Obtain blood cultures and administer broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour
Insert a pulmonary artery catheter before initiating fluid resuscitation
Wait for culture results before starting antibiotics to optimize antimicrobial selection
Administer hydrocortisone 200 mg IV as the first priority before antibiotics
Perform CT imaging to identify the infection source before any treatment
questions.question: The 'surviving sepsis campaign' 1-hour bundle recommends which IMMEDIATE action as the highest priority in a patient with septic shock?
In which patient group is premedication with benzodiazepines MOST likely to cause clinically significant respiratory depression?
questions.explanation: Elderly patients with COPD have reduced respiratory reserve and heightened sensitivity to CNS depressants. Benzodiazepines blunt the hypercapnic ventilatory drive, risking CO2 retention and acute-on-chronic respiratory failure. In this population, doses must be greatly reduced or the agents avoided. Healthy ASA I adults tolerate standard benzodiazepine premedication safely.
options: Young adults undergoing elective appendicectomy under general anaesthesia
Paediatric patients aged 2–5 years given intranasal midazolam
Elderly patients with severe COPD and borderline respiratory reserve
Non-obese adults with ASA I status undergoing minor day surgery
Paediatric patients above 12 years scheduled for tonsillectomy

questions.question: Regarding suxamethonium and the full-stomach patient, which of the following is the PRIMARY reason it remains favoured for rapid sequence induction despite its side effects?
options: Restores spontaneous breathing rapidly if intubation fails
It is the only agent compatible with cricoid pressure
It provides amnesia if anaesthesia is inadequate
questions.explanation: The principal reason suxamethonium remains preferred for RSI is that its ultrashort duration of action (35 minutes) means spontaneous ventilation resumes quickly in the event of a failed intubation or cannot-intubate-cannot-oxygenate scenario. No other available intubating dose of a relaxant provides comparable recovery time. While rocuronium with sugammadex offers a reversible alternative, immediate sugammadex availability is required to match suxamethonium's safety profile in failed airway situations.

options: Sedative medications to reduce consciousness in a dying patient with refractory intolerable symptoms
Administration of opioids at doses intended to hasten death in cancer patients
General anaesthesia for all procedures performed in palliative care patients
Benzodiazepine therapy to manage anxiety without reducing consciousness
Routine sedation for all ICU patients at end of life regardless of symptoms
questions.question: The term 'palliative sedation' refers to which specific clinical practice in end-of-life care?
questions.explanation: Palliative sedation (PS) is the intentional use of sedative drugs (midazolam, propofol, phenobarbital) to reduce consciousness in imminently dying patients when all other interventions have failed to relieve refractory, intolerable suffering (pain, dyspnoea, delirium, existential distress). It is ethically justified by the doctrine of double effect, patient/family consent, and multidisciplinary agreement. It is distinct from euthanasia: the intent is symptom relief, not death. Proportionate PS (lightest effective sedation) is preferred; continuous deep sedation (CDS) is the deepest form.

The 'cannot intubate, cannot ventilate' scenario is a true anaesthetic emergency requiring immediate front-of-neck access, typically via emergency cricothyroidotomy, to restore oxygenation before irreversible hypoxic injury occurs. Repeating a failed technique or further paralysis wastes critical time without addressing the obstruction. Difficult airway algorithms specifically escalate to surgical airway access as the definitive rescue step in this situation.
options: Repeat the same failed laryngoscopy technique
Wait several minutes before further action
questions.question: A patient cannot be intubated or ventilated after induction of general anaesthesia despite optimal positioning and equipment. What is the most appropriate next step?

questions.explanation: In an unresponsive patient without suspected cervical spine injury, head-tilt/chin-lift is the first and most effective basic airway maneuver. It opens the airway by extending the atlanto-occipital joint and lifting the tongue from the posterior pharynx. Jaw thrust is preferred when spinal injury is suspected.
questions.question: Which airway maneuver is most appropriate as the FIRST intervention in an unresponsive patient without suspected spinal injury?

questions.explanation: The retroperitoneal pelvic space can accommodate 34 litres or more of blood before tamponade pressure limits further haemorrhage. This massive concealed haemorrhage explains why pelvic fracture patients may present in profound shock with no obvious external bleeding. The diagnosis requires a high index of suspicion in hypotensive trauma patients without obvious haemorrhage source. Pelvic binders, external fixation, and haemostatic interventional radiology (angioembolisation) are key haemorrhage control strategies for unstable pelvic fractures.
questions.question: Pelvic fractures in trauma can cause massive concealed haemorrhage. What volume of blood can the pelvis accommodate before external tamponade occurs?

questions.explanation: The dermatomal height of a spinal (or epidural) block is assessed by sensory testing using pin-prick (sharp/dull discrimination) or cold (ethyl chloride spray) applied along dermatomes from the feet cephalad until the patient can no longer distinguish the sensation. This determines the highest level of sensory blockade, which guides the anaesthetist's assessment of whether the block is adequate for surgery (e.g., T10 needed for lower abdominal surgery, T4 for Caesarean section) and whether the patient is at risk from high block complications.
options: Asking the patient to move their toes
Pin-prick testing for highest sensory loss level
questions.question: The height of a spinal block is assessed by which method?
Which of the following is a RELATIVE contraindication to the use of adrenaline-containing local anaesthetics?
questions.explanation: Adrenaline-containing local anaesthetics are relatively contraindicated in areas supplied by end-arteries with no collateral circulation, including digital nerve blocks of fingers and toes, penile nerve blocks, and blocks of the tip of the nose and ear lobes. Vasoconstriction in end-artery areas can cause ischaemia and gangrene. Plain local anaesthetics must be used for digital and penile nerve blocks. Modern evidence suggests low concentrations of adrenaline (1:200,000) may be safe for digital blocks, but this remains cautious clinical practice.
options: Brachial plexus block for upper limb surgery
Ring block of finger or penis (end-artery)
Reduced need for aspiration before injection
Prolonged duration and reduced systemic absorption
Reduced total local anaesthetic dose needed
Faster onset of sensory block only
questions.question: A patient undergoing a dental block receives lignocaine with adrenaline rather than plain lignocaine. The primary clinical benefit of adding adrenaline in this context is which effect?
questions.explanation: Adrenaline causes local vasoconstriction that reduces vascular uptake of the local anaesthetic, prolonging its duration of action at the injection site and simultaneously reducing peak plasma concentrations, thereby lowering the risk of systemic toxicity compared with plain solutions.

Isoflurane is an isomer of enflurane (1-chloro-2,2,2-trifluoroethyl difluoromethyl ether vs enflurane's 2-chloro-1,1,2-trifluoroethyl difluoromethyl ether) and was introduced in 1981. Despite being isomers with the same molecular formula, isoflurane has different propertiesnotably lower hepatic metabolism (0.2%) and no epileptogenic activity. Halothane was introduced in 1956.
questions.question: Which inhalational agent is the isomer of enflurane and was introduced into clinical practice in 1981?
A patient with a burn injury develops exaggerated pain response to a normally mild painful stimulus around the wound. Which mechanism BEST explains this peripheral change?
questions.explanation: Tissue injury releases inflammatory mediators such as prostaglandins and bradykinin that lower the activation threshold of peripheral nociceptors, producing hyperalgesia at the site of injury. This peripheral sensitization amplifies pain signalling from an otherwise mild stimulus. It differs from central sensitization, which occurs within the spinal cord and brain.

questions.question: Anticonvulsant drugs (gabapentin, pregabalin, carbamazepine) are used as analgesic adjuvants specifically for pain with which characteristics?
questions.explanation: Anticonvulsant analgesics (gabapentinoids and sodium channel blockers like carbamazepine) are specifically indicated for neuropathic pain  pain arising from nerve damage or dysfunction  characterised by burning, shooting, stabbing, electric shock-like, or allodynia (pain from normally non-painful stimuli) qualities. Carbamazepine is first-line specifically for trigeminal neuralgia (lancinating facial pain). These drugs stabilise neuronal membranes and reduce ectopic discharge from damaged nerves. They are not effective for nociceptive (inflammatory, ischaemic, visceral) pain and are not interchangeable with traditional analgesics for these pain types.
options: Inflammatory joint pain with morning stiffness and swelling as commonly encountered in practice
Neuropathic pain with burning, stabbing, or electric shock-like qualities
Visceral pain from hollow organ distension or spasm during routine ophthalmic assessment
Ischaemic pain from peripheral vascular insufficiency
Somatic pain from bone metastases in cancer patients

questions.explanation: CO2-saturated local anaesthetic solutions have a faster onset because CO2 diffuses rapidly across the lipid nerve membrane. Once inside the axon, CO2 lowers the intracellular pH, shifting the equilibrium towards the ionised cationic form of the local anaesthetic within the axon (ion trapping). Since the ionised form binds sodium channels with higher affinity and cannot easily diffuse back out of the nerve, the effective concentration inside the axon is increased, accelerating onset and intensifying block.
questions.question: What is the mechanism by which carbonated (CO2-saturated) local anaesthetic solutions produce faster onset of block compared to standard preparations?
options: CO2 enters the axon, lowers pH, traps ionised drug inside
CO2 increases tissue pH, shifting more drug to un-ionised form
CO2 acts as a vasoconstrictor reducing absorption
CO2 increases the lipid solubility of the local anaesthetic

questions.question: A patient loses consciousness within one arm-brain circulation time after an intravenous bolus of propofol. Which receptor action MOST directly explains this rapid effect?
questions.explanation: Propofol enhances chloride ion influx by potentiating GABA-A receptor activity, producing rapid, dose-dependent central nervous system depression. This mechanism accounts for its swift onset of unconsciousness. It differs from ketamine, which acts primarily through NMDA receptor antagonism.

Ketamine indirectly stimulates the sympathetic nervous system, typically increasing heart rate, blood pressure, and cardiac output, unlike other induction agents that tend to cause cardiovascular depression. This property makes it valuable in hypovolaemic or shocked patients. Direct myocardial depression can still emerge in catecholamine-depleted critically ill patients.
questions.question: A trauma patient with hypovolaemic shock requires anaesthesia induction. Ketamine is chosen because, unlike other intravenous agents, it characteristically produces which effect on the cardiovascular system?
During thoracic surgery requiring one-lung ventilation, the dependent (ventilated) lung must receive which specific ventilation strategy?
questions.explanation: During one-lung ventilation for thoracic surgery, the ventilated (dependent) lung receives the entire tidal volume and is at high risk of ventilator-induced lung injury (VILI) from barotrauma and volutrauma. Protective ventilation using low tidal volumes (5-6 mL/kg ideal body weight), PEEP of 5-8 cmH2O, and intermittent recruitment manoeuvres minimises this risk. Permissive hypercapnia (accepting PaCO2 up to 50-55 mmHg) reduces the need for injuriously high ventilator pressures. Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction in the non-ventilated lung helps maintain oxygenation.
options: Protective lung ventilation: low tidal volumes and PEEP to prevent ventilator-induced injury
High tidal volumes (15 mL/kg) to maximise ventilation of the single lung
Maximum positive pressure ventilation to maintain normocapnia at all times
Zero PEEP to prevent hyperinflation of the single dependent lung
Pressure-controlled ventilation at the highest possible rate to maximise oxygenation

questions.explanation: At term, the gravid uterus compresses the aorta (reducing uteroplacental perfusion) and inferior vena cava (reducing venous return to the heart → supine hypotension syndrome) in the fully supine position. A 15° left lateral tilt (right hip wedge) displaces the uterus leftward, relieving aortocaval compression and restoring cardiac output. This is mandatory positioning during spinal anaesthesia for Caesarean section and intraoperative management. Full left lateral decubitus is used for severe supine hypotension.
options: Head-up tilt of 30° (semi-Fowler's position) throughout surgery
Manual compression of the aorta by the surgeon during surgery
Tight thigh-high compression stockings for venous return enhancement
Intravenous adrenaline 10 mcg boluses to maintain maternal blood pressure
Left lateral tilt 15° with wedge under right hip
questions.question: Aortocaval compression in the supine pregnant patient at term is MOST effectively prevented by:

options: Significantly reduced risk of hepatotoxicity and less cardiac sensitisation to catecholamines
More pleasant smell enabling smooth inhalational induction during routine ophthalmic assessment
Higher potency (lower MAC) at room temperature
Complete absence of cardiovascular side effects
Faster onset and offset due to lower blood-gas solubility as commonly encountered in practice
questions.explanation: Isoflurane largely replaced halothane for maintenance of anaesthesia because its risk of hepatotoxicity (halothane hepatitis) is orders of magnitude lower than halothane, and it does not sensitise the myocardium to catecholamine-induced arrhythmias to the same degree as halothane. Isoflurane has a pungent smell precluding inhalational induction, but for maintenance delivered via an endotracheal tube or LMA, it offers superior safety. Newer agents (sevoflurane, desflurane) have since superseded isoflurane for induction.
questions.question: Isoflurane was widely used as a maintenance volatile agent primarily because of which advantage over halothane?

questions.explanation: Chronic phenytoin use produces resistance to non-depolarising NMBs through two mechanisms: pharmacodynamic upregulation of acetylcholine receptors (similar to denervation) and pharmacokinetic acceleration of drug metabolism through hepatic cytochrome P450 enzyme induction. As a result, patients on long-term phenytoin require up to 50% larger doses of aminosteroid NMBs to achieve comparable block. This resistance may persist for weeks after phenytoin withdrawal.
options: Resistance from receptor upregulation and faster metabolism
Potentiates the block by inhibiting hepatic metabolism
Converts non-depolarising block to Phase II block
questions.question: A patient on long-term phenytoin (anticonvulsant) therapy requires NMB for surgery. How does phenytoin affect non-depolarising NMB?

questions.explanation: A fractured cribriform plate creates a direct communication between the nasal cavity and the anterior cranial fossa. Blind nasogastric or nasotracheal tube passage risks intracranial penetration through this defect. Oral routes for gastric tubes and airway devices are preferred in suspected basal skull fracture.
questions.question: A patient with a fractured cribriform plate requires oxygen supplementation. Why should a nasogastric tube be avoided in this patient?

questions.explanation: Blood pressure can be maintained within a normal range through compensatory mechanisms such as increased systemic vascular resistance even while tissue perfusion remains critically inadequate, so combining blood pressure with markers of end-organ perfusion such as lactate clearance and urine output provides a more comprehensive assessment of resuscitation adequacy.
questions.question: A patient in shock is monitored using a combination of blood pressure, urine output, lactate clearance, and central venous oxygen saturation. This multimodal approach is preferred over blood pressure alone primarily because blood pressure can remain normal despite which underlying problem?
options: Adequate oxygen delivery in all cases

questions.explanation: In a cannot-intubate, cannot-ventilate scenario with worsening hypoxia, the priority is to proceed promptly to an emergency surgical airway such as cricothyroidotomy rather than repeating failed techniques. Delaying for further attempts or awaiting review risks irreversible hypoxic injury. This represents the final rescue step of the difficult airway algorithm.
questions.question: An anaesthetist is unable to intubate or adequately ventilate a paralysed patient after multiple attempts, with falling oxygen saturation. What is the immediate priority?

options: Head-to-toe exam after primary survey and resuscitation
The reassessment of vital signs every 15 minutes
The handover from pre-hospital to emergency team
questions.explanation: The secondary survey is a systematic head-to-toe physical examination conducted after the primary survey (ABCDE) and initial life-saving resuscitation have been completed and the patient is haemodynamically stable. It aims to identify all injuries including occult injuries that were not apparent during the primary survey. It includes a detailed examination of the head, neck, thorax, abdomen, pelvis, spine, and extremities, along with appropriate radiological investigations (FAST ultrasound, plain X-rays, CT scanning) and a complete history (AMPLE: Allergies, Medications, Past history, Last meal, Events).
questions.question: The secondary survey in trauma management is defined as:

questions.explanation: Felypressin is a synthetic vasopressin analogue that produces vasoconstriction through V1 receptors without adrenergic activity. It is preferred over adrenaline in patients with cardiovascular disease, those on tricyclic antidepressants (which potentiate catecholamine effects), and patients with hyperthyroidism where exogenous catecholamines carry elevated cardiovascular risks. It is available in combination with prilocaine (Citanest with Octapressin) for dental use and does not carry the arrhythmia risk associated with adrenaline. SUBTOPIC 6: REGIONAL, SPINAL, AND EPIDURAL ANAESTHESIA
questions.question: A vasopressor used in combination with local anaesthetics for dental and minor surgical procedures that is specifically preferred in hypertensive patients and those on tricyclic antidepressants due to its lack of beta-adrenergic activity is:
