Increases the non-ionized base fraction, accelerating onset of block
Increases protein binding and prolongs the duration of the block
Raises tissue pH to prevent methaemoglobinaemia from prilocaine
Prevents bacterial contamination of the LA solution in the syringe
questions.question: Alkalinization of a local anaesthetic solution with sodium bicarbonate IMMEDIATELY before injection PRIMARILY achieves which pharmacological effect?

questions.explanation: COPD patients with type 2 respiratory failure (hypercapnia) have chronic CO2 retention and depend partly on hypoxic drive for ventilation. Raising SpO2 above 92–93% by high-flow oxygen abolishes hypoxic drive, worsens hypercapnia (Haldane effect), and may cause respiratory arrest. Target SpO2 88–92% maintains adequate oxygenation (O2 saturation on steep part of haemoglobin dissociation curve) while preserving the hypoxic ventilatory stimulus. Controlled oxygen therapy is mandatory in COPD exacerbation.
options: SpO2 =98% with high-flow oxygen to maximise tissue oxygenation
SpO2 100% maintained continuously by all available oxygen delivery means
SpO2 80–85% accepted as adequate in all COPD patients on oxygen
SpO2 94–98% identical to the target for all non-COPD ICU patients
SpO2 88–92% to avoid suppression of hypoxic respiratory drive
questions.question: In ICU management of acute respiratory failure, which oxygenation target is appropriate in a patient with COPD-associated type 2 respiratory failure?

options: Wider glottic opening relative to body size than adults
Anterior and superior larynx at the level of C4 (same as adults)
Epiglottis identical in shape and mobility to adult epiglottis
Trachea identical in relative length and diameter to adults
Narrowest airway at the cricoid ring (subglottic), not at the glottis
questions.explanation: In children under 2 years, the narrowest point of the upper airway is at the cricoid ring (subglottis) rather than at the glottis, as in adults. This critical difference means that an endotracheal tube that passes the vocal cords may still cause a pressure seal at the subglottis, potentially causing subglottic oedema and post-extubation stridor with even a small excess in tube diameter. This is why traditionally uncuffed tubes were used in young children, though modern high-volume low-pressure cuffed tubes are now acceptable if cuff pressure is carefully monitored.
questions.question: Paediatric anaesthesia differs from adult anaesthesia in that children under 2 years have which critical airway anatomical difference?

questions.explanation: When oxygen delivery fails to meet cellular metabolic demand during shock, cells shift from aerobic to anaerobic metabolism, producing lactate as a byproduct and generating far less ATP per glucose molecule, ultimately leading to cellular energy failure, membrane pump dysfunction, and, if prolonged, irreversible cell injury.
questions.question: A patient in shock develops evidence of cellular hypoxia at the tissue level. Prolonged inadequate perfusion at the cellular level most directly leads to which biochemical consequence?

options: Heart rate of 75 beats/min in a patient on beta-blocker therapy
SpO2 of 98% on room air in a healthy adult non-smoker
Mild residual cough 6 weeks after a fully resolved upper respiratory infection
Uncontrolled hypertension with BP 200/120 mmHg on day of surgery
ASA Class II with well-controlled asthma on inhaled salbutamol
questions.explanation: A BP of ≥180/110 mmHg on the day of surgery is generally considered a threshold for postponing elective procedures, as it dramatically increases the risk of perioperative stroke, myocardial infarction, and haemodynamic instability. Optimization is required before proceeding safely. Well-controlled conditions (beta-blocked HR, cleared URI, controlled asthma) are not grounds for postponement.
questions.question: When recording a pre-anaesthetic physical examination, which finding is an indication for POSTPONING elective surgery?

questions.explanation: Emergence agitation (EA) occurs in 25–80% of children following sevoflurane, manifesting as inconsolable crying, purposeless movements, and self-harm risk. Effective pharmacological prevention includes: a small propofol dose at surgery end (1 mg/kg), dexmedetomidine (0.5 mcg/kg IV over 10 minutes), ketamine (0.25–0.5 mg/kg IV), or fentanyl. Non-pharmacological strategies include: parental presence at emergence, minimizing noxious stimuli, maintaining pacifier/comfort items. EA is distinct from pain and resolves within 5–15 minutes in most cases.
questions.question: Emergence agitation (EA) in children following sevoflurane anaesthesia is MOST effectively prevented by which intervention?
options: Administering high-dose benzodiazepine premedication routinely to all paediatric patients before induction
Switch to propofol at end of case, or give dexmedetomidine or ketamine
Using isoflurane rather than sevoflurane for all paediatric maintenance anaesthesia routinely
Performing all paediatric surgery exclusively under regional anaesthesia without any general anaesthetic
Increasing sevoflurane concentration at emergence to prevent agitation

questions.explanation: The Modified Aldrete Score assesses five parameters: Activity (limb movement: 0-2), Respiration (effort and depth: 0-2), Circulation (blood pressure within 20% of preoperative: 0-2), Consciousness (fully awake, arousable, or unresponsive: 0-2), and Oxygen Saturation (SpO2 >92% on room air, with supplemental O2, or <90%: 0-2). A score of 9 or 10 out of 10 is required for safe transfer from PACU to the ward. This score has replaced the original Aldrete score by adding oxygen saturation as the fifth parameter.
questions.question: The Modified Aldrete Score used for discharge from the PACU assesses which five physiological parameters?
options: Pain, nausea, bleeding, activity, and consciousness
Activity, respiration, circulation, consciousness, and oxygen saturation
Temperature, pain, blood pressure, respiration, and consciousness
Urine output, activity, blood pressure, pain, and temperature
Consciousness, reflexes, colour, breathing, and cardiac rhythm

questions.explanation: For neostigmine-based reversal to achieve reliable recovery to TOF ratio ≥0.9 within approximately 15 minutes, a PTC of at least 10 (and return of at least 12 TOF twitches) is typically required. Attempting neostigmine reversal at very deep block levels (PTC <5) with no TOF twitches is likely to be inadequate and may delay recovery unpredictably. If the PTC is below 10 and urgent reversal is needed, sugammadex 4 mg/kg (for aminosteroid agents) provides reliable reversal.
questions.question: What is the minimum post-tetanic count (PTC) value that generally allows reversal of deep block with neostigmine to achieve adequate recovery within a clinically acceptable time?

questions.explanation: Tension pneumothorax causing cardiac arrest is treated with immediate needle decompression or thoracostomy to relieve the trapped intrathoracic pressure and restore venous return. Fluids and adrenaline may support circulation but do not address the underlying mechanical cause. Pericardiocentesis is instead the treatment for cardiac tamponade, a separate reversible cause.
questions.question: A patient in cardiac arrest is found to have tension pneumothorax as the underlying cause. What is the immediate definitive treatment?
The primary aim of Basic Life Support (BLS) is to:
options: Administer adrenaline as quickly as possible as commonly encountered in practice
Defibrillate the heart within 2 minutes during routine ophthalmic assessment
Maintain adequate circulation and ventilation until definitive treatment
questions.explanation: The primary aim of BLS is to maintain an adequate circulation and ventilation to vital organsparticularly the brainuntil the underlying cause of cardiac arrest can be reversed or definitive treatment initiated. BLS slows deterioration from VF to asystole, may improve the probability of successful defibrillation, and leads to significantly increased survival.

questions.question: Pre-operative fasting for solids is recommended for a minimum of how many hours before elective anaesthesia in adult patients?
questions.explanation: The current standard guideline recommends 6 hours of fasting from solids (light meal) before elective anaesthesia in adults. This allows adequate gastric emptying of food particles, reducing the risk and volume of aspiration. Clear fluids require only 2 hours, while fatty meals may require up to 8 hours. Dairy products and non-clear juices are considered solids/semi-solids.

questions.question: A patient in ARDS is distinguished from cardiogenic pulmonary oedema primarily by which key diagnostic feature?
questions.explanation: Acute respiratory distress syndrome is defined by bilateral pulmonary infiltrates and hypoxaemia occurring in the absence of elevated left atrial pressure, distinguishing it from cardiogenic pulmonary oedema where elevated pulmonary capillary wedge pressure reflects the underlying cardiac cause of fluid accumulation in the lungs.
options: Normal pulmonary capillary wedge pressure with bilateral infiltrates
Continue antibiotics for 5–7 days post-operatively to prevent wound infection
Reserve the most broad-spectrum antibiotics for all routine surgical prophylaxis
Prescribe antibiotics only after documented surgical site infection develops
Narrow-spectrum antibiotic within 60 min pre-incision; stop within 24 hr post-op
Use the same antibiotic regardless of surgical site or organism susceptibility
questions.question: Which principle guides antibiotic prescribing for prophylaxis in surgical patients to minimise resistance while providing effective coverage?
questions.explanation: Evidence-based surgical antibiotic prophylaxis (SAP): use the narrowest effective antibiotic for the likely contaminating organisms at that surgical site (e.g., first-generation cephalosporin for clean/skin surgery); administer within 60 minutes before incision (30 minutes for fluoroquinolones/vancomycin); redose every two half-lives during prolonged surgery; STOP within 24 hours postoperatively (no benefit beyond this, resistance risk increases). Prolonged courses provide no additional benefit and dramatically increase C. difficile risk and antimicrobial resistance.

options: Anaphylaxis to the local anaesthetic agent
Idiopathic generalised epilepsy unrelated to the block
questions.question: A patient develops perioral numbness, tinnitus, metallic taste, and then convulsions after a peripheral nerve block. This presentation is most consistent with:
questions.explanation: The classic prodromal and progression sequence of local anaesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST) comprises perioral numbness, metallic taste, tinnitus, light-headedness, visual disturbances, then muscle twitching and convulsions, progressing to cardiovascular collapse if untreated. LAST results from inadvertent intravascular injection or excessive systemic absorption. Treatment includes immediate cessation of drug, airway management, seizure control with benzodiazepines, and 20% intravenous lipid emulsion as the specific antidote.

options: Direct LA absorption into the gut wall reducing motility
Hypotension causing gut ischaemia and nausea
Vagal hyperperistalsis from unopposed parasympathetic activity
questions.explanation: Neuraxial block abolishes sympathetic outflow to the gastrointestinal tract (T6L2) while leaving the parasympathetic vagal innervation intact. This sympathectomy creates unopposed parasympathetic (vagal) activity, causing hyperperistalsis with increased bowel tone and contractile activity. The resulting nausea and vomiting affect approximately 20% of patients having spinal or epidural anaesthesia. Treatment includes ensuring adequate blood pressure (hypotension is also emetogenic) and antiemetics such as ondansetron or metoclopramide.
questions.question: The physiological effects of neuraxial block on gastrointestinal function include nausea and vomiting in up to 20% of patients. The mechanism is:
Which spinal level is the PRIMARY entry point of pain signals from abdominal viscera and the site of intervention for coeliac plexus nerve blocks?
options: L1?L3 via the lumbar plexus and genitofemoral nerve
S2?S4 via the pelvic splanchnic nerves from the sacral parasympathetics
C3?C4 via phrenic nerve for referred diaphragmatic pain
T1?T4 via cardiac accelerator fibres from the stellate ganglion
T5?T12 via thoracic splanchnic nerves converging at the coeliac plexus
questions.explanation: Visceral afferents from the upper abdominal organs (stomach, pancreas, liver, gallbladder, proximal bowel) travel with sympathetic fibres via the greater (T5?T9) and lesser (T10?T11) splanchnic nerves to the coeliac plexus, then centrally. Coeliac plexus neurolysis using alcohol is an evidence-based intervention for pancreatic cancer pain (VAS reduction >50% in ~80% of patients). The coeliac plexus sits around the coeliac artery origin at T12?L1.

questions.question: Calcium, calmodulin, and magnesium all influence acetylcholine release at the NMJ. Which statement best describes magnesium's specific role?
questions.explanation: Magnesium ions compete with calcium at the voltage-gated calcium channels in the motor nerve terminal and thereby inhibit calcium-dependent acetylcholine release. This mechanism explains why hypermagnesaemia potentiates both depolarising and non-depolarising neuromuscular blockade. Clinically, magnesium sulphate used in obstetrics for eclampsia can significantly prolong neuromuscular blockade and requires careful dose adjustment.

options: Between the rectus abdominis muscle and its posterior sheath
Anterior to the rectus muscle only
questions.explanation: The rectus sheath block deposits local anaesthetic in the plane between the posterior surface of the rectus abdominis muscle and its posterior sheath, targeting the terminal branches of the intercostal nerves as they pierce the muscle to supply the periumbilical skin and underlying tissue, providing effective analgesia for midline umbilical incisions.
questions.question: A patient receiving a rectus sheath block for umbilical hernia repair has local anaesthetic injected into which specific location?

options: Repeated oral intubation attempts with increasingly smaller tubes
Emergency front-of-neck airway (surgical cricothyrotomy or needle cricothyrotomy)
Immediate administration of sugammadex to reverse neuromuscular blockade
Placement of a nasopharyngeal airway and continued mask ventilation
Fibreoptic bronchoscopy as the only safe option in CICO
questions.explanation: The can't intubate, can't oxygenate (CICO) emergency is the most critical airway crisis in anaesthesia, representing imminent death from hypoxia. The only definitive life-saving intervention is an immediate emergency front-of-neck airway  either surgical cricothyrotomy (incising the cricothyroid membrane and inserting a cuffed tube) or needle cricothyrotomy with jet insufflation as a bridge. All other airway manoeuvres should have been exhausted before this point. The 2022 Difficult Airway Society guidelines recommend scalpel cricothyrotomy as the first-choice rescue technique.
questions.question: The 'can't intubate, can't oxygenate' (CICO) emergency during anaesthesia is most definitively managed by which intervention?
Persistent VF after multiple defibrillation attempts is treated with antiarrhythmic drugs. Before considering antiarrhythmic drugs, at least how many shocks should be delivered?
questions.explanation: It is recommended that the defibrillation sequence be followed for at least 912 shocks before consideration is given to the use of antiarrhythmic drugs (amiodarone or lidocaine) for persistent VF. These shocks take priority over any continuing attempts at securing the airway or establishing IV access. Persistent VF is treated with further sequential 360J shocks (monophasic) as required.
options: No minimumgive drugs after first failed shock

questions.question: Which of the following is a recognised indication for awake fibreoptic intubation followed by regional anaesthesia in a trauma patient?
questions.explanation: A patient with suspected cervical spine injury and a full stomach who also has an anticipated difficult airway (e.g., from jaw fractures, neck haematoma, or limited neck extension due to collar) requires awake fibreoptic intubation to secure the airway before either general or regional anaesthesia. The airway must be secured first in all trauma patients with potential airway compromise. Regional anaesthesia alone is insufficient if airway protection cannot be guaranteed, particularly with full stomach and consciousness-impairing injuries.
options: Isolated lower limb fracture without airway concern
Difficult airway from C-spine injury, full stomach
Minor scalp laceration requiring wound closure
Closed head injury without respiratory compromise

questions.explanation: The Combitube's oesophageal balloon inflates within the oesophagus and can rupture oesophageal varices, causing catastrophic bleeding, making known oesophageal disease a contraindication. This is distinct from its more common contraindication of caustic ingestion. Alternative airway devices that avoid oesophageal instrumentation are preferred in this situation.
options: Risk of variceal rupture from oesophageal cuff
questions.question: A patient known to have oesophageal varices requires emergency airway management. Why should a Combitube be avoided in this patient?
The concept of 'opioid-induced hyperalgesia' (OIH) describes which paradoxical phenomenon?
questions.explanation: Opioid-induced hyperalgesia (OIH) is the paradoxical phenomenon whereby prolonged high-dose opioid therapy causes progressive sensitisation of nociceptive pathways, resulting in increased pain sensitivity (lower pain threshold) and diffuse pain spreading beyond the original pain site  the opposite of analgesic tolerance. The mechanism involves NMDA receptor activation by opioid metabolites, downregulation of inhibitory neurotransmitter systems, and activation of pronociceptive pathways. OIH is managed by opioid dose reduction, opioid rotation, adding NMDA antagonists (ketamine, methadone), or switching to non-opioid analgesics.
options: Opioids become less effective over time due to receptor downregulation
Opioids cause acute pain at the injection site from histamine release
Chronic high-dose opioids sensitise pain pathways, causing increased pain sensitivity
Opioids cross-react with prostaglandin pathways increasing inflammation
High-dose opioids cause peripheral sensitisation identical to NSAIDs withdrawal

questions.question: Regarding fasting guidelines before elective anaesthesia, the minimum fasting time for clear fluids in adults is:
questions.explanation: Current evidence-based fasting guidelines (ASA, NICE, ESAIC) specify a minimum fasting time of 2 hours for clear fluids (water, clear apple juice, black tea or coffee without milk, sports drinks) before elective anaesthesia in adults and children over 1 year. Solid food, milk, and milky drinks require 6 hours fasting. The traditional 'nil-by-mouth after midnight' practice has been replaced by these more permissive fluid guidelines, which reduce patient discomfort, dehydration, and hypoglycaemia without increasing aspiration risk when standard risk factors are absent.
options: 4 hours for clear fluids regardless of content
6 hours for all fluids including water
8 hours for all oral intake including water
No fasting required for clear fluids in adults

questions.explanation: Naloxone is a competitive antagonist at opioid receptors, displacing agonist opioids and rapidly reversing respiratory depression and sedation. Its action is short-lived compared with many opioids, so repeat dosing or infusion may be needed to prevent re-narcotisation. It has no direct effect on the respiratory centre itself.
questions.question: A patient develops severe respiratory depression after an opioid overdose in the recovery room. Naloxone is administered and rapidly reverses the depression. By which mechanism does naloxone act?

questions.explanation: Phenylephrine is now regarded as first-line for treating spinal anaesthesia-induced hypotension in obstetric patients, providing effective vasoconstriction with a more favourable fetal acid-base profile than older agents such as ephedrine when used appropriately. Prompt treatment of hypotension protects uteroplacental perfusion and reduces maternal nausea associated with hypotension. Left lateral tilt and adequate co-loading with fluids remain important adjuncts.
questions.question: A patient becomes profoundly hypotensive shortly after spinal anaesthesia for Caesarean section, with associated maternal nausea. Which drug is FIRST-LINE for treating this specific complication?

questions.explanation: Slowly acting IV agents (basal narcotics) include ketamine (phencyclidine derivative) and benzodiazepines, which have a slower onset and are not used as rapid primary induction agents in standard practice. They are used for sedation, co-induction, and procedural anaesthesia. Rapidly acting primary induction agents (thiopentone, propofol, etomidate) achieve hypnosis within one arm-brain circulation time.
questions.question: Which of the following correctly classifies intravenous anaesthetic agents as 'slowly acting agents' (basal narcotics) rather than primary induction agents?
options: Thiopentone and methohexitone as barbiturate induction agents
Propofol and etomidate as rapidly acting hypnotic induction drugs
Propanidid and althesin as eugenols and steroid anaesthetics
Alfentanil and remifentanil as ultra-short-acting opioids

questions.question: Pregabalin (and gabapentin) achieve their analgesic effect in neuropathic pain through which mechanism?
options: Blocking alpha-2-delta subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels, reducing neurotransmitter release
GABA-A receptor potentiation producing spinal inhibition
Sodium channel blockade in dorsal root ganglion neurons in the majority of documented cases
Serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibition in the spinal cord based on typical clinical findings
questions.explanation: Gabapentin and pregabalin bind to the alpha-2-delta (a2d) regulatory subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord and dorsal root ganglia, reducing calcium influx at the presynaptic terminal and thereby decreasing release of excitatory neurotransmitters (glutamate, substance P, noradrenaline) involved in pain sensitisation. Despite their name, they do not act on GABA receptors. This mechanism specifically reduces central sensitisation, making them effective for neuropathic pain, fibromyalgia, and as perioperative analgesic adjuvants.

options: Resistance to both classes of agent
Increased sensitivity to both classes of agent
No change in sensitivity to either class
questions.explanation: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome results from autoantibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels, reducing acetylcholine release and lowering the safety margin of neuromuscular transmission, which produces heightened sensitivity to both depolarising and non-depolarising neuromuscular blocking agents, requiring cautious dose reduction and titration.
questions.question: A patient with Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome requires general anaesthesia with muscle relaxation. Compared with typical patients, this condition produces which characteristic response to both depolarising and non-depolarising agents?

options: Epidural analgesia universally doubles the total duration of the first stage of active labour
Epidural analgesia always increases Caesarean section rates by at least 50%
Epidural analgesia eliminates all maternal pushing effort during the second stage
Epidural analgesia reduces the second stage duration by completely relieving pain
Low-dose epidurals do not prolong the first stage but may slightly extend the second
questions.question: Which statement MOST accurately describes the effect of epidural labour analgesia on the progress of labour?
questions.explanation: Contemporary evidence (Cochrane reviews, large RCTs) demonstrates that low-concentration epidurals (≤0.1% bupivacaine with opioid) do not significantly increase Caesarean section rates and do not meaningfully prolong the first stage. The second stage may be modestly prolonged (by ~15–20 minutes) as motor function is partially preserved, but this is clinically acceptable. Earlier dogma suggesting epidurals increase C-section rates was based on high-concentration epidurals that caused motor block and ineffective pushing.

questions.question: A patient develops fever, rigors, and hypotension five days after insertion of a central venous catheter, with no other identifiable source of infection. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: New fever, rigors, and hypotension without another clear source in a patient with an indwelling central venous catheter strongly suggest catheter-related bloodstream infection. Paired blood cultures from the catheter and a peripheral vein help confirm the diagnosis. Prompt catheter removal and targeted antimicrobial therapy are usually required.

Cisatracurium (the 1R-cis 1'R-cis isomer of atracurium) undergoes similar Hofmann degradation but at one-fifth the dose of atracurium required for equipotent effect, producing approximately five times less laudanosine per unit effect. Critically, it does not cause histamine release even at high doses, making it preferred over atracurium in patients at risk from histamine effects such as those with reactive airway disease or haemodynamic instability. It shares atracurium's organ-independent elimination.
questions.question: Cisatracurium is a stereoisomer of atracurium with which distinct advantage over its parent compound?

questions.explanation: Coronary perfusion pressure (CPP) during CPR = Aortic diastolic pressure - Right atrial pressure (diastolic). Since coronary arteries fill during diastole (between compressions), raising aortic diastolic pressure (via adrenaline's alpha-1 vasoconstriction) increases CPP and enhances myocardial blood flow. A CPP > 15 mmHg is associated with improved likelihood of ROSC during CPR.
options: Aortic diastolic pressure minus right atrial pressure
Mean arterial pressure minus pulmonary artery pressure
Heart rate multiplied by stroke volume
questions.question: The pharmacological rationale for giving adrenaline during CPR is its alpha-1 adrenergic effect causing peripheral vasoconstriction, which raises aortic diastolic pressure. This is important because coronary perfusion pressure during CPR depends on:

questions.explanation: In response to reduced blood pressure and renal perfusion, renin is released from juxtaglomerular cells, which cleaves angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, converted to angiotensin II by ACE. Angiotensin II causes vasoconstriction (raising SVR) and stimulates aldosterone release from the adrenal cortex. Aldosterone acts on the renal distal tubule and collecting duct to promote sodium and water retention, increasing circulating volume over hours. This compensatory mechanism preserves BP in early shock but is overwhelmed in severe haemorrhage.
options: Vasodilation to improve renal blood flow
Increased erythropoiesis to compensate for blood loss
questions.question: The primary goal in managing the compensatory physiological response to shock is to restore perfusion before irreversible cellular damage occurs. The renin-angiotensin system's contribution to this compensation involves:

questions.explanation: Current regional anaesthesia guidelines recommend a minimum interval of at least 24 hours between a therapeutic dose of low molecular weight heparin and neuraxial needle or catheter placement to minimise the risk of spinal epidural haematoma, a substantially longer interval than that required after prophylactic dosing.
questions.question: A patient scheduled for elective surgery on long-term warfarin therapy requires bridging with low molecular weight heparin before a planned spinal anaesthetic. The minimum recommended interval between the last therapeutic dose of low molecular weight heparin and spinal needle placement is best described as which timeframe?

options: No accumulation in renal failure due to exclusively hepatic metabolism in the majority of documented cases
Ultra-short half-life enabling easy dose titration
NMDA receptor antagonism providing additional benefit in neuropathic and opioid-tolerant pain
Complete absence of constipation as a side effect based on typical clinical findings
No risk of respiratory depression at therapeutic doses
questions.question: Methadone is used in advanced cancer pain management and has which specific pharmacological advantage over other strong opioids?
questions.explanation: Methadone is unique among opioid analgesics in having both mu-opioid receptor agonism and NMDA receptor antagonism. The NMDA antagonism prevents and reverses central sensitisation and opioid-induced hyperalgesia, making methadone particularly effective in neuropathic pain, opioid-tolerant patients, and pain states involving central sensitisation where pure opioids have insufficient efficacy. Additionally, methadone is not metabolised to active metabolites and has no known dose ceiling. Its very long and variable half-life (15-55 hours) makes dose titration complex and requires specialist experience to avoid accumulation toxicity.

Chronic respiratory diseases such as emphysema and chronic bronchitis are classic indications for spinal anaesthesia as they avoid the respiratory depression of general anaesthesia, endotracheal intubation, and mechanical ventilation. Other indications include full stomach, renal/hepatic/metabolic disturbances, and eclampsia. Contraindications include patient refusal, coagulopathy, hypovolaemia/shock, local sepsis at the puncture site, and raised intracranial pressure.
questions.question: Spinal anaesthesia is indicated for which of the following clinical scenarios?
options: A patient with severe coagulopathy requiring lower limb surgery
A patient who refuses the procedure after counselling
A patient with chronic bronchitis requiring inguinal hernia repair
A patient with untreated hypovolaemia requiring emergency appendicectomy
A patient with local sepsis overlying the L4/5 interspace

questions.explanation: Naloxone is a competitive opioid receptor antagonist that rapidly reverses opioid-induced respiratory depression and sedation by displacing the opioid from its receptor. Its duration of action is often shorter than that of the opioid it is reversing, particularly with longer-acting agents like morphine, so repeated dosing or an infusion may be required with close monitoring for re-sedation. Titrating the dose carefully avoids precipitating severe pain or withdrawal-like symptoms in opioid-tolerant patients.
questions.question: A patient develops progressive respiratory depression and reduced consciousness in the recovery room after receiving intraoperative morphine. What is the specific antagonist used to reverse this effect?

questions.explanation: 'D' in the ATLS primary survey stands for Disability, referring to a rapid neurological assessment. This includes assessment of the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score (eye, verbal, motor responses), pupil size and reactivity, and gross limb movement (spontaneously or in response to stimulus). The AVPU scale (Alert, responds to Voice, responds to Pain, Unresponsive) may be used as a quick alternative. Findings guide the urgency of neurosurgical review and the need for immediate airway protection in patients with GCS <9.
questions.question: The ATLS primary survey follows the ABCDE sequence. What does 'D' in the primary survey specifically assess?

options: H2 receptor blockade reducing gastric acid secretion
Direct antacid neutralization of gastric hydrochloric acid
Dopamine receptor antagonism accelerating gastric emptying
Serotonin 5-HT3 antagonism in the chemoreceptor trigger zone
questions.explanation: Metoclopramide acts as a dopamine D2 antagonist in the gut and centrally, enhancing gastric motility and accelerating emptying. It also raises lower oesophageal sphincter tone, reducing regurgitation risk. This dual action makes it valuable premedication for patients with delayed gastric emptying (diabetics, opioid users, obese). H2 blockers reduce acid secretion; antacids neutralize existing acid.
questions.question: Metoclopramide, when used as a premedication agent, exerts its gastric benefit PRIMARILY through which mechanism?

questions.explanation: At high altitude, although the fractional concentration of oxygen in air remains 21%, the reduced barometric pressure lowers the partial pressure of inspired oxygen, reducing the gradient driving oxygen into the blood. This represents hypoxic hypoxia due to the environment rather than a problem with the lungs or blood itself. Acclimatisation over time partially compensates through increased ventilation and haemoglobin production.
questions.question: A patient at high altitude develops hypoxia despite breathing 21% oxygen. What mechanism explains this?
options: Reduced barometric pressure lowering inspired oxygen partial pressure
Increased haemoglobin oxygen affinity at altitude
Increased alveolar carbon dioxide at altitude

questions.question: Colloids such as albumin and hydroxyethyl starch (HES) expand intravascular volume MORE efficiently than crystalloids PRIMARILY because:
questions.explanation: Colloids contain large molecules (proteins: albumin; polysaccharides: starch, dextran; gelatins) that generate colloid osmotic (oncotic) pressure within the vascular compartment, opposing the hydrostatic pressure driving fluid out of capillaries. This retains infused volume intravascularly longer. Crystalloids rapidly equilibrate across the endothelial and capillary membranes → only 25–30% of infused normal saline remains intravascular after 30 minutes, whereas 80–100% of colloid remains acutely.
options: Colloids are hypertonic, drawing water from the intracellular compartment into vessels
Large molecules exert oncotic pressure limiting vascular fluid egress
Colloids directly stimulate aldosterone, increasing renal sodium and water retention
Crystalloids are preferentially distributed to the intracellular space rather than vessels
Colloids contain more sodium than crystalloids, enhancing osmotic retention

questions.question: Which feature of the axon determines the minimum length of nerve that must be exposed to local anaesthetic for conduction block to occur (the 'critical length' or minimum blocking length)?
options: The diameter of the axon only
The length of the Schwann cell only
The number of voltage-gated sodium channels per millimetre
Internodal distance; needs 2-3 nodes of Ranvier blocked
The resting membrane potential of the axon
questions.explanation: In myelinated nerves, where action potential propagation occurs by saltatory conduction from one node of Ranvier to the next, complete conduction block requires that at least 23 successive nodes be blocked simultaneously (because the action potential can 'skip' over one blocked node). This means the critical length of nerve exposure to local anaesthetic must encompass at least 23 internodal segments. Shorter exposures may fail to block conduction even if individual nodes are blocked, explaining why the length of LA contact matters clinically. questions.question: Which IV induction agent produces the HIGHEST incidence of excitatory phenomena (myoclonus, hiccups, involuntary movements) on induction?
questions.explanation: Etomidate produces myoclonic movements (involuntary muscle jerking) in 10–80% of patients without premedication during induction. These are not seizure activity but subcortical disinhibition phenomena. Hiccups and eye movements are also common. These excitatory phenomena can be reduced by premedication with opioids or benzodiazepines. Propofol and thiopentone have much lower incidence of excitatory movements.

questions.question: A patient with known pheochromocytoma undergoes surgery. Which volatile agent should be AVOIDED due to the highest risk of catecholamine-induced arrhythmias?
questions.explanation: Halothane must be avoided in pheochromocytoma surgery because it sensitizes the myocardium to endogenous catecholamines more than any other volatile agent. In pheochromocytoma, catecholamine surges during tumor handling can cause life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias if halothane is used. Isoflurane, desflurane, and sevoflurane have minimal catecholamine-sensitizing effects and are safe alternatives.

options: Intravenous lipid emulsion (Intralipid 20%) given as a bolus and infusion
High-dose adrenaline (1 mg repeated every 3 minutes as in standard CPR)
Early cardioversion to treat bupivacaine-induced ventricular fibrillation
Sodium bicarbonate administration to alkalinize plasma and reverse sodium channel blockade
Immediate surgical exploration to prevent further drug absorption at the site
questions.question: In the management of local anaesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST) with cardiovascular collapse, which treatment has TRANSFORMED resuscitation outcomes in recent years?
questions.explanation: Intravenous lipid emulsion (ILE) → such as Intralipid 20% → is now the cornerstone of LAST management. The 'lipid sink' theory proposes it sequesters lipid-soluble LA molecules (especially bupivacaine) in a lipid compartment, reducing free drug concentration at cardiac tissues. The bolus (1.5 mL/kg) followed by infusion protocol has dramatically improved survival from bupivacaine cardiac arrest. All cardiac anaesthetic areas should stock lipid emulsion.

CGRP is a potent vasodilator peptide co-released with substance P from peripheral nociceptor terminals (antidromic activation). It causes vasodilation and increases vascular permeability (plasma extravasation), producing the neurogenic component of peripheral inflammation → flare, oedema, and hypersensitivity. CGRP is also the key mediator in migraine pathophysiology; monoclonal antibodies against CGRP or its receptor (erenumab, fremanezumab) are now approved preventive migraine therapies.
questions.question: Which neurotransmitter, co-released with substance P from primary afferent nociceptors, is responsible for 'neurogenic inflammation' → vasodilation and plasma extravasation at peripheral injury sites?
options: Glutamate released from Ad terminals in the dorsal horn
Serotonin released from activated platelets at injury sites
Adenosine triphosphate (ATP) from damaged tissue cells
Prostaglandin E2 from COX-2 activation in macrophages

questions.explanation: NSAIDs inhibit cyclo-oxygenase enzymes (COX-1 and COX-2), blocking the conversion of arachidonic acid to prostaglandins. Prostaglandins sensitise peripheral nociceptors (peripheral sensitisation) and facilitate central pain signal amplification (central sensitisation), particularly at sites of tissue injury and inflammation. By reducing prostaglandin synthesis, NSAIDs reduce both peripheral and central pain sensitisation, providing analgesic, anti-inflammatory, and antipyretic effects. Their opioid-sparing effect (reducing opioid requirements by 20-40%) makes them valuable components of multimodal perioperative analgesia.
questions.question: The role of NSAIDs in multimodal analgesia includes which primary mechanism?
options: Mu-opioid receptor agonism producing spinal analgesia
GABA-A receptor potentiation reducing central pain processing
Inhibition of cyclo-oxygenase enzymes reducing prostaglandin synthesis
Alpha-2 adrenoceptor agonism modulating descending inhibition
NMDA receptor antagonism preventing central sensitisation

questions.explanation: COPD patients have prolonged expiratory time constants due to airflow obstruction; if the next breath is delivered before expiration is complete, dynamic hyperinflation (gas trapping) and intrinsic PEEP develop, increasing the risk of pneumothorax, reduced cardiac output, and haemodynamic instability. Ventilation strategy must use a prolonged I:E ratio (1:3 or more), low respiratory rate (8-10 breaths/min), and moderate tidal volumes (7-8 mL/kg) to allow adequate time for full exhalation. Permissive hypercapnia accepts elevated PaCO2 to avoid these barotraumatic complications.
options: High respiratory rate with short expiratory times to maintain normocapnia
Prolonged expiratory time, low respiratory rate, and moderate tidal volumes
Maximum tidal volumes to overcome airway resistance
Zero PEEP in all COPD patients to prevent air trapping
Pressure-controlled ventilation at the highest pressure tolerated
questions.question: In patients with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) requiring general anaesthesia, which ventilation strategy prevents dynamic hyperinflation?

questions.explanation: Atropine is the first-line drug for symptomatic bradycardia with haemodynamic compromise, acting to block vagal tone and increase heart rate. If atropine fails, transcutaneous pacing or an adrenaline or dopamine infusion may be considered as next steps. Amiodarone and calcium gluconate are not indicated for isolated symptomatic bradycardia.
questions.question: A patient develops symptomatic bradycardia with hypotension during resuscitation, not in full cardiac arrest. What is the first-line pharmacological treatment?
A patient has surgical emphysema tracking from the neck into the mediastinum after a penetrating tracheal injury. Which anatomical continuity explains this spread?
questions.explanation: The pretracheal fascia is continuous from the neck down into the superior mediastinum, allowing air from a tracheal injury to track along this plane into the chest. This explains why neck trauma can produce mediastinal emphysema without direct pleural breach. Recognising this tracking pattern raises suspicion of tracheobronchial injury.

options: Cauda equina syndrome from LA neurotoxicity
Post-dural puncture headache from intracranial hypotension
questions.explanation: Epidural haematoma (usually in coagulopathic patients) or epidural abscess (from infection) can develop after neuraxial block and present as new or worsening back pain, radicular pain, and progressive motor weakness or sensory loss. Both represent neurosurgical emergencies requiring urgent MRI diagnosis and decompression within 68 hours to prevent permanent neurological damage (paraplegia). Any new back pain or neurological symptoms after neuraxial block must be urgently investigated.
questions.question: Complications of central neuraxial blockade include neurological injury. Which serious complication can result from an expanding space-occupying lesion in the epidural space presenting with back pain and progressive neurological deficit?

A patient develops sudden severe paraplegia 4 hours after uneventful labour epidural removal while on therapeutic LMWH. MRI confirms epidural haematoma. What is the definitive treatment and its time window for recovery?
options: Reversal of LMWH and observation for 48 hours
Emergency laminectomy and haematoma evacuation within 6-8 hours
Epidural blood patch to tamponade bleeding
questions.explanation: Spinal epidural haematoma causing cord compression is a neurosurgical emergency. Permanent neurological deficit (paraplegia) is highly likely if decompression is not achieved within 68 hours of symptom onset. Immediate MRI confirms the diagnosis and level of compression, followed by emergency surgical laminectomy with haematoma evacuation. LMWH should be reversed (protamine if unfractionated heparin) but this alone does not decompress the cord. Outcome is directly correlated with the severity of deficit at presentation and the time to surgery.

questions.question: Which ICU monitoring parameter BEST reflects tissue oxygen delivery adequacy and guides resuscitation in septic shock?
options: Central venous pressure maintained between 8–12 mmHg at all times
Lactate clearance >10% per 2 hr, or normalization to <2 mmol/L
Urine output above 0.5 mL/kg/hr as the sole resuscitation endpoint
Mean arterial pressure maintained above 65 mmHg as the only target
Mixed venous oxygen saturation (SvO2) measured by pulmonary artery catheter
questions.explanation: Serial lactate measurement and clearance are the current Surviving Sepsis Campaign guideline-recommended endpoints for sepsis resuscitation. Elevated lactate reflects anaerobic metabolism from tissue hypoperfusion. Lactate clearance ≥10% per 2 hours or normalization to <2 mmol/L indicates improved tissue oxygen delivery and predicts survival. CVP (8–12 mmHg) was historically recommended but is no longer considered a reliable resuscitation endpoint due to multiple confounders.

options: The lethal triad of hypothermia, acidosis, and coagulopathy
questions.question: A trauma patient undergoes damage control surgery rather than definitive repair of all injuries in a single prolonged operation. This staged approach is chosen primarily to avoid worsening which physiological state?
questions.explanation: Damage control surgery prioritises rapid control of haemorrhage and contamination with abbreviated initial surgery, deferring definitive repair to a later staged operation once physiology has been optimised in intensive care, specifically to prevent further deterioration of the lethal triad that would occur with a single prolonged definitive procedure in a physiologically unstable patient.

options: A target used only in neonates
questions.question: A patient with known chronic obstructive pulmonary disease develops acute type 2 respiratory failure in the ICU. Which oxygen saturation target is MOST appropriate to avoid worsening hypercapnia?
questions.explanation: In patients with chronic type 2 respiratory failure, a lower controlled oxygen saturation target, typically around 88 to 92%, is used to avoid suppressing hypoxic respiratory drive and worsening carbon dioxide retention. Excessive oxygen administration in this population can precipitate dangerous hypercapnia. Careful titration with arterial blood gas monitoring guides oxygen therapy.

questions.question: During defibrillation, oxygen should be removed from the patient by at least how much distance to prevent fire risk?
questions.explanation: During defibrillation, any oxygen source (face mask, nasal cannula) should be removed at least 1 meter (>1 m) from the patient to prevent sparks from the electrical shock igniting the oxygen-enriched atmosphere. If the patient is intubated, the tracheal tube is left connected to the oxygen source (closed circuit) and the operator stands clear. This fire prevention measure is critical in resuscitation safety.

questions.question: Which of the following is the largest paranasal sinus?
questions.explanation: The maxillary sinuses, also known as the antrum of Highmore, are the largest of the four paired paranasal sinuses. They are located in the maxillary bones beneath the eyes. They are innervated by the maxillary nerve (V2).

questions.question: A patient receiving a non-depolarising muscle relaxant is monitored with a peripheral nerve stimulator using train-of-four. A ratio below 0.9 at the end of surgery indicates what?
questions.explanation: A train-of-four ratio below 0.9, comparing the fourth twitch response to the first, indicates clinically significant residual neuromuscular blockade even if the patient appears to be breathing adequately. Residual block increases the risk of postoperative respiratory complications including hypoxaemia and aspiration. Objective neuromuscular monitoring helps guide the timing and adequacy of reversal before extubation.

questions.question: For laparoscopic surgery, specific complications of CO2 pneumoperitoneum include which physiological effects?
questions.explanation: CO2 pneumoperitoneum for laparoscopic surgery causes: hypercapnia from CO2 absorption (requiring increased minute ventilation to maintain normocapnia), raised intra-abdominal pressure reducing venous return and cardiac output, increased systemic vascular resistance from CO2 absorption and intra-abdominal pressure, raised ICP and intraocular pressure, and shoulder-tip pain from diaphragmatic irritation by CO2 (referred via phrenic nerve). Trendelenburg positioning (head-down) for lower abdominal laparoscopy exacerbates venous pooling, ICP, and respiratory compromise.
options: Hypocapnia, reduced ICP, and improved venous return in most clinical presentations
Hypercapnia, increased ICP, reduced venous return, and shoulder-tip pain
Hypoxia from CO2 displacing oxygen in alveoli under standard examination conditions
Bradycardia from peritoneal CO2 absorption only
Peripheral vasodilation from systemic CO2 absorption

questions.question: Which cardiovascular parameter defines functional capacity as 4 METs, the MINIMUM threshold for clearing moderate-risk surgery without further cardiac testing?
questions.explanation: 4 METs (metabolic equivalents) corresponds to climbing one flight of stairs, walking uphill, or light housework without symptoms. Patients who cannot achieve 4 METs on history are at increased cardiac risk and may require further functional or imaging cardiac assessment before non-cardiac surgery. It is the guideline-recommended screening threshold from ACC/AHA cardiac perioperative risk evaluation.
options: Lying at rest with oxygen saturation of 98% on room air
Climbing one flight of stairs without dyspnoea or chest pain
Walking on level ground at 2 mph without any symptoms
Performing heavy gardening or vigorous exercise like jogging
Resting comfortably for 30 minutes after 5 minutes of slow walking

questions.explanation: Suxamethonium's ultrashort duration relates to its rapid hydrolysis by plasma pseudocholinesterase. As the plasma concentration falls after initial bolus, suxamethonium diffuses away from the NMJ down its concentration gradient back into the plasma where it is then metabolised. This diffusion-limited termination of action, dependent on maintaining a low plasma concentration through enzymatic hydrolysis, explains why pseudocholinesterase deficiency profoundly prolongs its effect. SUBTOPIC 3: NON-DEPOLARIZING NEUROMUSCULAR BLOCKING AGENTS
questions.question: Which of the following BEST explains why suxamethonium is classified as an ultra-short acting agent despite being resistant to acetylcholinesterase?
options: It binds to plasma proteins extensively and is inactive
It diffuses away from the NMJ faster than ACh
It is excreted unchanged by the kidneys within 60 seconds
It undergoes Hofmann degradation in plasma
Hydrolysed by plasma cholinesterase before reaching the NMJ

questions.explanation: PEA is defined by organized electrical activity on the ECGin the absence of any palpable pulseand can mimic any organized rhythm including sinus rhythm, atrial fibrillation, complete heart block, idioventricular, or any other organized electrical pattern. The critical point is that despite the presence of organized ECG complexes, there is no mechanical cardiac output generating a pulse. Clinical pulse check is mandatory alongside ECG interpretation.
questions.question: On a standard ECG, the QRS complex represents ventricular depolarization. Pulseless Electrical Activity (PEA) can display a QRS complex that looks identical to:

options: Reduces local blood flow, slowing absorption and prolonging block duration
Reduces the pKa of the local anaesthetic agent
Increases lipid solubility of the local anaesthetic
Enhances sodium channel receptor binding affinity
Converts ester agents to amide class to reduce allergy risk
questions.explanation: Adrenaline causes local vasoconstriction at the injection site by stimulating alpha-1 adrenoceptors on blood vessel walls, reducing vascular absorption of the local anaesthetic. This prolongs the duration of sensory and motor block, intensifies the block density, reduces peak plasma concentrations (lowering systemic toxicity risk), and reduces local bleeding. It also effectively increases the maximum safe dose of local anaesthetic that can be administered. Adrenaline is contraindicated in end-artery areas (e.g., digits, penis, nose).
questions.question: Adding adrenaline (epinephrine) to a local anaesthetic solution primarily achieves which pharmacological benefit?

questions.explanation: The gate control theory proposed by Melzack and Wall in 1965 states that a neural 'gate' exists in the substantia gelatinosa of the spinal cord dorsal horn. Non-nociceptive large-diameter A-beta fibre activity (touch, vibration, pressure) can close this gate, reducing transmission of nociceptive signals carried by small A-delta and C fibres to the brain. This explains why rubbing a hurt area reduces pain, and forms the scientific basis for transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS), spinal cord stimulation, and acupuncture as pain management techniques.
questions.question: The gate control theory of pain (Melzack and Wall, 1965) proposes that pain transmission is modulated at which location?
options: Peripheral nociceptors where prostaglandins open the pain gate as commonly encountered in practice as commonly encountered in practice
Thalamus where consciousness determines pain perception
Dorsal horn of the spinal cord, where non-nociceptive input can close the 'gate' to pain signals
Cerebral cortex where past experience interprets pain signals during routine ophthalmic assessment during routine ophthalmic assessment
Periaqueductal grey where descending inhibition originates

questions.explanation: Fever, neck stiffness, and severe headache in a patient with a neuraxial catheter should raise urgent concern for an infective complication such as meningitis or epidural abscess rather than being attributed to a benign post-dural puncture headache, warranting prompt clinical assessment, imaging, and consideration of catheter removal with appropriate cultures and antibiotics.
questions.question: A patient undergoing surgery with an epidural catheter in place develops a sudden severe headache, neck stiffness, and fever several days postoperatively. This presentation should raise concern for which serious complication requiring urgent investigation?

questions.explanation: In severe aortic stenosis, the left ventricle must generate supraphysiological pressures to maintain forward flow across the stenotic valve, and cardiac output is relatively fixed (cannot increase rapidly). Any sudden reduction in systemic vascular resistance (e.g., from spinal anaesthesia, propofol, or volatile agents) is not compensated by an increase in cardiac output, causing precipitous hypotension, reduced coronary perfusion of the hypertrophied left ventricle, and cardiovascular collapse. Spinal anaesthesia is relatively contraindicated; slow careful induction with haemodynamic monitoring is essential.
questions.question: Patients with severe aortic stenosis are particularly vulnerable to which anaesthetic-induced haemodynamic change?
options: Peripheral oedema from IV fluid administration

questions.explanation: In adults, the spinal cord terminates at the lower border of L1 or upper border of L2 (the conus medullaris), beyond which the cauda equina (nerve roots) continues within the dural sac. The dural sac extends to S2, where the meninges fuse with the filum terminale. All lumbar punctures and spinal anaesthetic injections are performed below the L2 level (typically L3-L4 or L4-L5 interspaces) to avoid direct needle trauma to the spinal cord.
options: Cord ends at L1-L2; dural sac extends to S2
Cord ends at L4; dural sac extends to S4
Cord ends at T12; dural sac extends to S1
Cord ends at L3; dural sac extends to S3
Cord ends at L1; dural sac ends at L5
questions.question: In adults, the spinal cord ends at approximately which vertebral level, and the dural sac extends to which level?
Before delivering a defibrillation shock during resuscitation, the operator must perform which specific safety check to protect the resuscitation team?
questions.explanation: Before delivering any defibrillation shock, the operator must visually confirm that no member of the resuscitation team or bystander remains in contact with the patient or the bed to prevent inadvertent shock transmission to a rescuer, a critical safety step performed immediately before pressing the shock button.
options: Visually confirm no one is in contact with the patient
Confirm intravenous access is in place

questions.question: Pain assessment in the non-verbal, mechanically ventilated ICU patient can be performed using which validated behavioural scale?
questions.explanation: The BPS and CPOT are validated behavioural pain assessment tools for non-verbal mechanically ventilated adult ICU patients. BPS scores facial expression (1–4), upper limb movements (1–4), and compliance with ventilator (1–4) → range 3–12. CPOT scores facial expression, body movements, muscle tension, and compliance/vocalisation → range 0–8. BPS ≥5 or CPOT ≥3 indicates significant pain. Self-report scales (NRS, VAS) are only used when the patient is communicative and can self-report reliably.
options: Numerical Rating Scale (NRS) requesting self-report from the intubated patient
Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) shown to intubated patients on a clipboard
FLACC scale validated exclusively for mechanically ventilated neonates
Ramsay Sedation Scale assessing the depth of sedation not pain
Behavioural Pain Scale (BPS) or Critical-Care Pain Observation Tool (CPOT)

questions.question: A patient in haemorrhagic shock from a ruptured ectopic pregnancy requires emergency induction of anaesthesia. Etomidate is selected over propofol PRIMARILY because it:
questions.explanation: Etomidate causes minimal depression of myocardial contractility and vascular tone, making it the preferred induction agent in haemodynamically unstable or shocked patients. Propofol, in contrast, commonly causes significant vasodilation and hypotension. Etomidate does, however, carry the disadvantage of transient adrenocortical suppression.

Anterior mediastinal masses (thymoma, lymphoma, teratoma, germ cell tumour) may compress the trachea or major bronchi; this compression worsens dramatically during general anaesthesia when muscle relaxation removes the protective tone of the airway muscles and positive pressure ventilation shifts mediastinal structures. Life-threatening airway obstruction occurring after induction when the airway can no longer be maintained is the primary danger. Pre-anaesthetic CT scanning to assess tracheal cross-sectional area, upright patient positioning, and maintaining spontaneous ventilation are critical risk mitigation strategies.
questions.question: Which specific clinical feature of an anterior mediastinal mass presents the greatest anaesthetic hazard under general anaesthesia?
options: Tracheal or bronchial compression worsening under muscle relaxation and positive pressure
Superior vena cava obstruction causing facial oedema only in most clinical presentations
Pericardial effusion with minimal haemodynamic significance
Cervical lymphadenopathy limiting neck extension for intubation under standard examination conditions
Better protection against aspiration during eye surgery in most clinical presentations
Reduces the need for muscle relaxants entirely under standard examination conditions
Prevents surgical emphysema around the eye
Minimal rise in intraocular pressure during insertion and removal
questions.explanation: A specific advantage of LMA over ETT relevant to ophthalmic surgery is the minimal rise in intraocular pressure (IOP) during insertion and removal. ETT intubation and extubation cause significant IOP spikes from coughing, straining, and the hemodynamic response to laryngoscopyall dangerous after intraocular procedures. The less stimulating LMA placement and removal avoids these IOP spikes, protecting surgical outcomes.
questions.question: The LMA is less stimulating than the ETT, resulting in reduced cough on emergence. An additional advantage of LMA over ETT that directly benefits ophthalmic surgical patients is:

questions.explanation: Cocaine is the only local anaesthetic that causes vasoconstriction in addition to sensory block, by inhibiting the reuptake of noradrenaline at sympathetic nerve terminals. This unique combination of topical anaesthesia and vasoconstriction makes it particularly valuable for endoscopic nasal procedures, where bleeding reduction is as important as pain relief. All other local anaesthetics cause peripheral vasodilation and require a separate vasoconstrictor (e.g., adrenaline or xylometazoline) to achieve this combined effect.
questions.question: Cocaine is uniquely valuable as a topical nasal anaesthetic in ENT surgery because it combines which two properties not shared by any other single local anaesthetic?
options: Rapid onset and absence of vasoconstriction
Anaesthesia and vasoconstriction via noradrenaline reuptake inhibition
Deep tissue penetration and no CNS effects

questions.question: A patient receiving a continuous suxamethonium infusion during a prolonged procedure develops a train-of-four pattern showing fade, similar to a non-depolarising block. This transition is termed which phenomenon?
questions.explanation: Prolonged or repeated administration of suxamethonium can cause the block to transition from a typical depolarising Phase I pattern to a Phase II block, which mimics non-depolarising block with fade on train-of-four and tetanic stimulation, and may even be partially reversible with anticholinesterase agents, unlike classic Phase I block.

questions.question: Massive transfusion is defined as replacement of approximately one blood volume within 24 hours. Which metabolic complication is MOST commonly associated with rapid administration of large volumes of stored blood?
options: Hyperkalaemia from acidosis driving potassium into the extracellular space
Hyponatraemia from dilutional effect of large volumes of IV saline
Hypocalcaemia from citrate chelation of ionised calcium
Metabolic alkalosis from excess bicarbonate in stored blood
Hypothermia from cold blood administered without a blood warmer
questions.explanation: Stored blood contains citrate as an anticoagulant. During massive transfusion, citrate is delivered faster than the liver can metabolize it, chelating ionised calcium (Ca²⁺) and causing significant hypocalcaemia → manifesting as hypotension, prolonged QT, coagulopathy, and tetany. Ionised calcium should be monitored and calcium chloride/gluconate given. While hypothermia, hyperkalaemia, and acidosis also occur in massive transfusion, hypocalcaemia from citrate is the MOST directly transfusion-specific metabolic complication.

questions.question: Which drug combination is most effective at attenuating the sympathetic pressor response to laryngoscopy?
questions.explanation: The combination of IV lignocaine (1-1.5 mg/kg given 90 seconds before laryngoscopy) and an opioid (e.g., fentanyl 1-2 mcg/kg) or esmolol (0.5-1 mg/kg) is the most established pharmacological strategy for attenuating the sympathetic response to laryngoscopy. Lignocaine blunts afferent nociceptive transmission both peripherally and centrally; opioids suppress the nociceptive brainstem response; esmolol blocks the beta-adrenergic response to catecholamines. This combination is particularly important before laryngoscopy in hypertensive and cardiac patients.
options: IV propofol followed by IV nitrous oxide only
Intramuscular opioid given 30 minutes before induction
Topical throat spray without systemic pretreatment
Pre-induction oral antihypertensive tablets taken same morning
IV lignocaine plus IV opioid or beta-blocker

questions.question: Airway trauma during laryngoscopy and intubation is most effectively prevented by which combination of measures?
questions.explanation: Prevention of airway trauma requires adequate neuromuscular blockade (eliminating active patient resistance to the laryngoscope), application of correct laryngoscopic technique (gentle, appropriate blade curve and depth), selection of an appropriately sized endotracheal tube (too large causes subglottic trauma; too small impairs ventilation and seal), ensuring adequate anaesthetic depth before manipulation, and limiting the number of attempts. These measures together minimise the risk of vocal cord injury, arytenoid dislocation, tracheal laceration, and post-intubation subglottic stenosis.
options: Pre-treatment with adrenaline to reduce mucosal vascularity
Adequate muscle relaxation, correct technique, and appropriate ETT size selection
Deliberate use of the smallest possible ETT diameter in all cases
Limiting laryngoscopy attempts to exactly 30 seconds duration
Routine topical cocaine spray to the larynx before intubation

questions.question: Intralipid (20% lipid emulsion) is used in the management of LAST due to bupivacaine. Its proposed mechanism includes:
options: Extracts lipid-soluble bupivacaine from cardiac tissue ('lipid sink')
Reversing sodium channel block by competition
Alkalinising plasma pH to favour ionisation of bupivacaine
questions.explanation: Intralipid (20% lipid emulsion therapy) acts as a 'lipid sink': the large lipid phase absorbs the highly lipid-soluble bupivacaine from cardiac tissue and plasma, reducing the myocardial concentration. Additionally, it may provide fatty acid energy substrate for the ischaemic myocardium and have direct cardioprotective effects. The recommended dose is 1.5 mL/kg IV bolus over 1 minute followed by a 0.25 mL/kg/min infusion (maximum cumulative dose 12 mL/kg) concurrent with standard ACLS resuscitation.

questions.question: A child develops laryngospasm immediately following extubation in the PACU. The MOST appropriate immediate management is:
options: Immediate reintubation without any pharmacological intervention
Allow the child to self-resolve the laryngospasm fully without any clinical intervention
Administer intravenous propofol 3 mg/kg immediately without any airway manoeuvres
Continuous positive pressure 100% O2, jaw thrust, and suxamethonium if laryngospasm persists
Perform Heimlich manoeuvre to clear presumed foreign body obstruction
questions.explanation: Laryngospasm is complete closure of the vocal cords causing total airway obstruction → a paediatric anaesthetic emergency. Immediate management: (1) Remove stimulus, suction oropharynx; (2) Apply CPAP 20–30 cmH2O with 100% O2 via tight-fitting mask and jaw thrust → positive pressure may break partial laryngospasm; (3) If complete/unresponsive: suxamethonium 1–2 mg/kg IV (or 4 mg/kg IM/IO if no IV access) to achieve immediate vocal cord relaxation; (4) Re-intubate if needed. Larson's point (firm pressure behind mandibular ramus) may break partial laryngospasm.

questions.question: Implantable devices (pacemakers or AICDs) may be damaged during defibrillation. The correct practice is to:
questions.explanation: During defibrillation in patients with implantable pacemakers or AICDs, pads or paddles should not be placed directly over the implanted device to minimize damage. The standard anterolateral or anteroposterior pad positions should be modified to be at least 8 cm away from the device. After resuscitation, the device should be checked for programming changes or damage.
options: Avoid placing pads directly over the device
Avoid defibrillation entirely in these patients
Use lower energy to protect the device
Position both pads on the same side
The minimum mouth opening for its use
An opening too small for insertion
The ideal opening for a Classic LMA
The opening needed for nasal intubation only
questions.question: An Intubating LMA (Fastrach) is used to secure the airway in a patient with a mouth opening of exactly 20 mm. What does this represent?
questions.explanation: The Intubating LMA is specifically designed to allow blind intubation through it with a mouth opening as small as 20 mm, making it valuable when opening is restricted. This is narrower than typically required for direct laryngoscopy. It combines supraglottic ventilation with a conduit for tube passage.

options: Patients with acute postoperative pain requiring rapid dose titration
Opioid-naive patients starting strong opioid therapy for the first time
Patients requiring immediate-release analgesia for breakthrough pain
Patients with intermittent, unpredictable pain spikes only
Patients with stable, chronic pain requiring steady-state 24-hour opioid delivery
questions.question: Transdermal fentanyl patches are specifically appropriate for which type of patient in chronic pain management?
questions.explanation: Transdermal fentanyl patches deliver a constant, predictable rate of fentanyl absorption through the skin over 72 hours, making them ideal for patients with stable chronic pain requiring steady-state round-the-clock opioid delivery. They are particularly valuable in patients who cannot swallow oral medications, have nausea limiting oral intake, have compliance issues with multiple daily doses, or prefer the convenience of 3-day dosing intervals. They are inappropriate for opioid-naive patients (risk of fatal respiratory depression), acute pain, or conditions where rapid dose titration is needed.

questions.question: Which of the following lists contains ONLY ester-class local anaesthetic agents?
questions.explanation: Ester-class agents include cocaine, procaine, chloroprocaine, amethocaine, benzocaine, and tetracaine; they share a -COO- linking group. Amide agents include lignocaine, prilocaine, mepivacaine, bupivacaine, levobupivacaine, etidocaine, ropivacaine, and cinchocaine. The distinction is clinically important: allergy to ester agents is related to their PABA metabolite and does not extend to amide agents, which makes amide agents the preferred choice in patients with known ester allergy.

options: Salbutamol nebulised via the endotracheal tube
questions.explanation: Morphine promotes histamine release from mast cells, which causes bronchoconstriction, bronchial mucosal oedema, and increased secretions, potentially worsening intraoperative bronchospasm and therefore should be avoided. Other natural opioids (codeine) also release histamine; synthetic opioids (fentanyl, alfentanil, remifentanil) are safer in reactive airway disease. First-line bronchospasm management includes 100% oxygen, inhaled beta-2 agonists (salbutamol), deepening volatile anaesthesia, IV ketamine, IV corticosteroids, and IV magnesium sulphate.
questions.question: In managing severe intraoperative bronchospasm, which drug should be AVOIDED as it may worsen bronchoconstriction?

questions.explanation: Retrolental fibroplasia (retinopathy of prematurity) is a serious ocular complication of high-concentration oxygen therapy in premature neonates. Hyperoxia causes retinal vasoconstriction and subsequent fibrovascular proliferation that can lead to retinal detachment and blindness. Target SpO2 in premature infants is 9195% to balance the risk of hypoxia against oxygen toxicity.
questions.question: Retrolental fibroplasia (retinopathy of prematurity) is a specific complication of oxygen therapy in which patient population?

options: Aortic stenosis under standard examination conditions
Coronary artery disease in most clinical presentations
questions.explanation: Right ventricular failure is most commonly caused by prior LV failure, which increases pulmonary venous pressure, leading to pulmonary arterial hypertension and eventually RV pressure overload and failure. Other direct causes include tricuspid regurgitation, mitral stenosis, primary pulmonary hypertension, multiple pulmonary emboli, pulmonary artery or valve stenosis, and RV infarction.
questions.question: Right ventricular failure is most commonly secondary to which primary condition?
The nasopharynx communicates with the oropharynx through which structure?
questions.explanation: The nasopharynx communicates with the oropharynx through the pharyngeal isthmus, which can be closed by elevation of the soft palate during swallowing. The isthmus faucium connects the oral cavity to the oropharynx. The choanae connect the nasal cavity to the nasopharynx.

options: To achieve the fastest possible onset of block
To reduce the total drug cost of the infusion
To eliminate any risk of hypotension
To shorten the overall duration of labour
To achieve sensory block with minimal motor blockade
questions.explanation: Labour analgesia aims to relieve pain from uterine contractions while preserving enough motor function for the mother to move and push effectively during the second stage. Dilute local anaesthetic solutions selectively block smaller sensory fibres before larger motor fibres, achieving this differential block. Higher concentrations used for operative anaesthesia are avoided in labour because they produce excessive motor blockade.
questions.question: What is the primary rationale for using a lower concentration, larger volume local anaesthetic solution for epidural analgesia in labour compared to that used for surgical anaesthesia?

options: Maintaining minimally adequate perfusion while limiting clot disruption
Achieving supranormal blood pressure to maximise organ perfusion
Restoring completely normal blood pressure immediately
Rapidly correcting haemoglobin to normal before surgery
questions.question: A trauma patient with uncontrolled internal haemorrhage is managed with permissive hypotension prior to definitive surgical control. This strategy aims to achieve which balance?
questions.explanation: Permissive hypotension involves targeting a lower than normal blood pressure sufficient to maintain vital organ perfusion while avoiding aggressive fluid resuscitation that could dislodge early clot formation and worsen ongoing haemorrhage, a strategy used until definitive surgical or interventional control of the bleeding source is achieved.

options: It is a transient complication fully reversible within 72 hours in all patients
It is caused exclusively by accidental intrathecal injection of chlorhexidine antiseptic
It is prevented by using large-gauge spinal needles (16G) for rapid drug distribution
Neurotoxic LA pooling around sacral roots causes permanent perineal deficits
It presents exclusively as upper motor neuron signs with hyperreflexia
questions.question: Which of the following statements about cauda equina syndrome as a complication of spinal anaesthesia is MOST accurate?
questions.explanation: Cauda equina syndrome (CES) after spinal anaesthesia results from accumulation of neurotoxic concentrations of LA (classically hyperbaric lidocaine or chloroprocaine) around the sacral nerve roots. High concentrations cause direct neurotoxicity, producing irreversible lower motor neuron deficits: bilateral leg weakness, saddle anaesthesia, bladder and bowel dysfunction. Risk factors include continuous spinal catheters (micro-catheters) that allow drug pooling and repeated dosing.

questions.question: A patient undergoing emergency surgery for bowel obstruction has a nasogastric tube inserted and aspirated before induction of anaesthesia. This step is performed primarily to reduce which specific risk?
questions.explanation: Decompressing the stomach with a nasogastric tube before induction reduces the volume of gastric contents present, thereby lowering the potential volume available for regurgitation and pulmonary aspiration during induction of anaesthesia in a patient at high risk due to bowel obstruction and a full stomach.
options: Volume of gastric contents available for aspiration
Corner of the mouth as commonly encountered in practice
Angle of the jaw during routine ophthalmic assessment
questions.explanation: The nasopharyngeal airway is measured from the tip of the nose to the corner of the patient's ear to determine the correct length. It ranges from 1726 cm in length with 69 mm internal diameter. It can be used in patients with an intact gag reflex but is absolutely contraindicated when basilar skull fracture is suspected.
