questions.question: According to the WHO analgesic ladder approach, a patient with mild pain not controlled on paracetamol alone should next receive which category of drug?

questions.explanation: Lung-protective ventilation in ARDS uses low tidal volumes, typically around 6 millilitres per kilogram of predicted body weight, to minimise alveolar overdistension and ventilator-induced lung injury, generally combined with appropriate positive end-expiratory pressure to maintain alveolar recruitment, even if this requires tolerating a degree of permissive hypercapnia.
questions.question: A patient with ARDS is managed with lung-protective ventilation. This strategy is centred primarily on which ventilatory parameter?
options: Permissive hypercapnia avoidance at all costs
High tidal volumes to maximise oxygenation
Low tidal volumes to limit alveolar overdistension
Severely impaired with reduced EF as commonly encountered in practice
May be entirely normal despite HF symptoms
Always reduced EF < 40% during routine ophthalmic assessment
questions.explanation: Volume overload states (e.g., massive blood transfusion, severe renal failure with fluid overload, large AV fistulas) can simulate heart failure by causing increased systemic venous pressure and pulmonary congestion, yet myocardial function may be entirely normal. This is 'high-output heart failure' or volume-overload syndrome. Treatment addresses the volume overload rather than myocardial contractility.
questions.question: Volume overload can simulate heart failure by causing myocardial dysfunction with increased systemic venous pressure. In this condition, what is characteristic about myocardial function?
Transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI) is MOST likely caused by which mechanism?
questions.explanation: TRALI is characterised by acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure within 6 hours of transfusion. The dominant mechanism is immune-mediated: donor anti-HLA or anti-HNA (neutrophil antigen) antibodies bind recipient neutrophils, causing complement activation, neutrophil sequestration in pulmonary capillaries, endothelial damage, and non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema. Transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO) is volume-mediated (hydrostatic oedema) and is distinguished by elevated NT-proBNP and echocardiographic evidence of fluid overload.
options: Volume overload from rapid transfusion causing hydrostatic pulmonary oedema
Bacterial contamination of platelets causing septic shock and ARDS
ABO incompatibility causing haemolysis and subsequent ARDS
Iron overload from repeated blood transfusions damaging the pulmonary vascular endothelium
Donor antibodies react with recipient neutrophil antigens causing pulmonary sequestration

questions.question: A patient in septic shock requires vasopressor support after adequate fluid resuscitation. Which agent is recommended as the FIRST-LINE vasopressor in current guidelines?
questions.explanation: Noradrenaline is recommended as first-line vasopressor in septic shock because it produces potent alpha-adrenergic vasoconstriction with relatively less tachyarrhythmia risk compared with dopamine. Vasopressin or adrenaline are typically added as second-line agents if the target blood pressure is not achieved. Early, appropriately titrated vasopressor use, alongside fluids, forms a core component of septic shock management.

questions.question: Levobupivacaine is the single S-enantiomer of bupivacaine. Its clinical advantage over racemic bupivacaine is primarily:
questions.explanation: Levobupivacaine (S-bupivacaine) has demonstrably lower cardiotoxicity and CNS toxicity than the racemic mixture because the R-enantiomer has preferential affinity for cardiac sodium channels and causes greater myocardial depression. Levobupivacaine has an equivalent clinical analgesic and anaesthetic profile to racemic bupivacaine with a safer toxicity profile. Similarly, ropivacaine (also S-enantiomer of a different propyl compound) offers improved safety. These agents are now preferred for high-volume regional techniques.

questions.question: The oxygen delivered from a cylinder at high pressure (137 bar) must be reduced by a pressure-reducing valve to which working pressure before patient delivery?
questions.explanation: Oxygen cylinders store gas at high pressure (approximately 137 bar / 2000 psi). A pressure-reducing valve regulates and reduces this to approximately 4 bar, which is a safe working pressure for delivery to the patient. A flowmeter then controls the final delivery rate in liters per minute (015 L/min depending on the device). Humidifiers may be added to prevent mucosal drying.

options: Five-moment hand hygiene with alcohol-based hand rub or soap and water
Routine glove use eliminating the need for hand hygiene between patients
Contact precautions only for patients with MRSA or VRE colonisation
N95 respirator for all patient interactions regardless of infection status
Daily environmental cleaning with quaternary ammonium compounds only
questions.explanation: WHO five-moment hand hygiene → before patient contact, before aseptic procedure, after body fluid exposure, after patient contact, after contact with patient surroundings → is universally recognised as the single most effective HAI prevention intervention. Hand hygiene compliance is critically low (<50% without intervention in most ICUs). Alcohol-based hand rub (ABHR) is faster and more effective than soap/water for non-visibly soiled hands. Gloves reduce but do NOT eliminate pathogen transmission and must not replace hand hygiene.
questions.question: Which infection control practice is the SINGLE most important intervention for preventing healthcare-associated infections (HAI) in the ICU?

questions.explanation: Morton performed the landmark demonstration on 16th October 1846 at Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston, with surgeon John Collins Warren operating on a patient named Edward Gilbert Abbot. The patient regained consciousness at the end with no pain, disproving earlier critics who had labelled similar demonstrations 'humbug.' This date is now celebrated annually as World Anaesthesia Day.
questions.question: William T.G. Morton publicly and successfully demonstrated ether anaesthesia for the first time on which specific date?
A patient is induced with propofol and immediately develops apnoea, hypotension and loss of eyelash reflex. Which stage of anaesthesia has been reached?
questions.explanation: Loss of eyelash reflex, regular respiration transitioning to controlled ventilation, and haemodynamic changes mark the transition into stage III, the plane of surgical anaesthesia where most procedures are performed. Stage II is characterised by excitement and irregular breathing, which modern rapid intravenous induction agents largely bypass. Stage IV represents dangerous medullary depression with cardiovascular collapse and must be avoided.

Severe head injury with GCS below 9 is a primary indication for ICU admission following trauma because these patients require continuous airway protection (endotracheal tube and mechanical ventilation), ICP monitoring and management, neuroprotective care (euvolaemia, normocapnia, head elevation, avoidance of hypotension and hypoxia), and close neurological monitoring for clinical deterioration or neurosurgical intervention. Other ICU admission criteria include severe chest injury, multi-system trauma requiring ventilatory support, haemodynamic instability, and massive transfusion.
options: Severe head injury with ICP-directed airway management needed
Established aspiration pneumonia requiring prolonged ventilatory support care
questions.question: A trauma patient with GCS <9 and inability to protect the airway undergoes RSI. Post-intubation, which ICU admission criteria is directly related to the severity of the head injury?

questions.explanation: The adductor pollicis muscle, stimulated via the ulnar nerve at the wrist, is the standard monitoring site because of its superficial, easily accessible position, its large and reliable twitch response, and the ability to isolate the hand for neuromuscular assessment without interference. Its response characteristics are well-characterised relative to clinical endpoints. The facial nerve/orbicularis oculi site recovers faster than peripheral muscles and thus may give falsely reassuring readings.
options: Adductor pollicis via ulnar nerve, for accessibility and reliable response
Diaphragm, because it reflects respiratory muscle recovery best
Masseter, because it is easy to access during anaesthesia
Orbicularis oculi via facial nerve, as it is the most sensitive indicator of block
Tibialis anterior via common peroneal nerve, as it has the largest twitch response
questions.question: At which muscle group is neuromuscular block monitoring most commonly performed, and why is it a preferred monitoring site?

questions.explanation: Masseter spasm following suxamethonium may be an early warning sign of malignant hyperthermia susceptibility, so the safest course is to discontinue all potential triggering agents, switch to a total intravenous anaesthetic technique, and closely monitor for signs of an evolving hypermetabolic crisis rather than persisting with volatile agents.
options: Administer additional volatile agent to deepen anaesthesia
Give a second dose of suxamethonium immediately
Abandon triggering agents and switch to a total intravenous technique while monitoring
Give neostigmine to reverse the spasm
questions.question: A patient develops masseter muscle rigidity immediately after suxamethonium during inhalational induction, making laryngoscopy difficult. The most appropriate immediate management is which action?
Which of the following properties BEST explains why ropivacaine has a BETTER cardiac safety profile than bupivacaine at equivalent concentrations?
questions.explanation: Ropivacaine is the pure S(-)-enantiomer of propivacaine. The S-enantiomer of long-acting LAs has lower affinity for cardiac sodium channels and potassium channels compared to the R()-enantiomer (present in racemic bupivacaine). This stereoselectivity accounts for ropivacaine's lower risk of cardiac arrhythmias and ventricular fibrillation at equivalent analgesic concentrations. Levobupivacaine (pure S-bupivacaine) similarly has less cardiac toxicity than racemic bupivacaine.
options: Ropivacaine has a lower pKa resulting in faster onset and lower peak plasma levels
Ropivacaine is metabolized more rapidly by plasma cholinesterase than bupivacaine
Ropivacaine binds less to plasma proteins and is removed more rapidly
Ropivacaine (S-enantiomer) has less affinity for cardiac sodium channels than bupivacaine (racemic)
Ropivacaine does not cross the blood-brain barrier and therefore has no CNS toxicity

questions.question: Normal sinus rhythm has a rate of 60100 bpm. Sinus tachycardia is defined as a rate above:
questions.explanation: Sinus tachycardia is defined as a regular sinus rhythm at a rate greater than 100 beats per minute. In sinus tachycardia, the P waves are present and precede each QRS complex at a normal PR interval. Common causes include fever, pain, hypovolemia, anemia, anxiety, hyperthyroidism, and drugs. Unlike VT or AF, sinus tachycardia is an appropriate compensatory response.

options: High oxygen consumption with low functional residual capacity
questions.question: An anaesthetist notes that a neonate desaturates far more rapidly than an older child during a brief period of apnoea. Which respiratory physiological feature MOST explains this vulnerability?
questions.explanation: Neonates have a high metabolic rate and oxygen consumption relative to their small functional residual capacity, meaning their oxygen reserve is rapidly depleted during apnoea, leading to swift desaturation. This makes careful preoxygenation and minimising apnoeic time critical during airway management in this age group. The relatively higher closing capacity further predisposes to early airway closure and hypoxaemia.

options: Avoidance of difficult airway risk, reduced aspiration risk, and safer for the neonate
Faster onset of surgical block compared to general anaesthesia in most clinical presentations
Complete elimination of postoperative pain for 24 hours postoperatively under standard examination conditions
Reduced need for postoperative monitoring compared to general anaesthesia
Avoidance of all haemodynamic instability during the procedure
questions.explanation: Spinal anaesthesia for Caesarean section is preferred because it avoids the risks of general anaesthesia in the difficult obstetric airway (failed intubation risk is 1:300 in obstetrics vs. 1:2000 general surgical), reduces pulmonary aspiration risk (the patient remains awake with intact laryngeal reflexes), avoids neonatal exposure to general anaesthetic agents that cross the placenta, and allows the mother to remain awake for birth. The main disadvantage is spinal hypotension, which is managed with lateral tilt, IV fluid co-loading, and prophylactic vasopressors (phenylephrine infusion).
questions.question: Spinal anaesthesia for Caesarean section is preferred over general anaesthesia primarily for which reason?
According to anaesthetic monitoring principles, monitors with alarms serve which purpose in relation to the anaesthetist's own vigilance?
options: To replace direct clinical observation in modern automated theatres under standard examination conditions
To serve as the sole safety mechanism during surgical procedures in most clinical presentations
To substitute for the anaesthetist's presence during brief absences
To document findings without influencing active clinical decision-making
To enhance vigilance, not replace it, as clinical observation remains paramount
questions.explanation: The foundational principle of anaesthetic monitoring is that appropriate monitoring devices with alarms are designed to enhance  not replace  the vigilance of the qualified anaesthesia practitioner. Physical examination, clinical observation, and situational awareness remain the most important diagnostic tools available. Monitors provide objective quantitative data that supplements clinical assessment but cannot replace the integrative judgment, pattern recognition, and immediate therapeutic intervention capability of a skilled anaesthetist.

Suxamethonium can activate muscarinic (M2) receptors in the sinoatrial node in addition to nicotinic receptors, particularly with repeated doses. This muscarinic stimulation causes bradycardia, junctional rhythms, and in some cases sinus arrest. Children are more susceptible to bradycardia with a single dose. Prophylactic atropine (10 mcg/kg IV) is recommended before repeat doses of suxamethonium to prevent this bradycardia.
options: Nicotinic receptors in the sinoatrial node
Muscarinic receptors in the sinoatrial node
questions.question: Bradycardia following repeated doses of suxamethonium is mediated through which receptor mechanism?

questions.explanation: Electrocautery generates electromagnetic interference that can disrupt the light-based signal processing of pulse oximetry, producing artefactual or dampened waveforms during its use. This is a recognised technical limitation rather than a true physiological change in the patient. Clinical assessment and other monitoring parameters should be used to corroborate oxygenation status when this interference occurs.
questions.question: A patient's pulse oximeter waveform becomes dampened and unreliable during a case using electrocautery. What is the most likely cause?
options: Failure of the anaesthesia machine circuit
Electromagnetic interference from the diathermy device
Maintaining blood glucose below 4 mmol/L to prevent hyperglycaemia
Avoiding all insulin administration perioperatively to prevent hypoglycaemia
Maintaining blood glucose between 6-10 mmol/L (108-180 mg/dL)
Achieving normoglycaemia (3.5-5.5 mmol/L) throughout the procedure
Allowing glucose to rise up to 20 mmol/L to avoid all hypoglycaemia risk
questions.question: In diabetic patients undergoing surgery, the primary perioperative metabolic goal is:
questions.explanation: Perioperative blood glucose target is 6-10 mmol/L (108-180 mg/dL), balancing the risks of hypoglycaemia (which cannot be detected under anaesthesia and causes irreversible brain injury) against the risks of hyperglycaemia (impaired wound healing, increased infection, dehydration). Strict normoglycaemia (3.5-5.5 mmol/L) increases hypoglycaemia risk under anaesthesia and is not currently recommended. Hourly glucose monitoring during major surgery guides titration of glucose-insulin-potassium infusions or insulin infusions.

questions.question: Spinal anaesthesia achieves surgical anaesthesia by injecting local anaesthetic into which anatomical compartment?
questions.explanation: Spinal anaesthesia (subarachnoid block) involves injecting local anaesthetic directly into the subarachnoid space, where it mixes with cerebrospinal fluid and bathes the nerve roots emerging from the spinal cord. This produces a rapid, dense block of sensory, motor, and autonomic fibres. Injections are restricted to the lumbar region below L2 to prevent direct needle trauma to the spinal cord, which ends at the L1/L2 vertebral level in adults.

Morphine is hepatically glucuronidated to morphine-6-glucuronide (M6G), a potent active opioid metabolite excreted renally. In renal impairment, M6G accumulates, causing prolonged and exaggerated CNS depression and respiratory failure. Atracurium's breakdown via Hofmann elimination is renal-independent → it is actually the preferred muscle relaxant in renal failure precisely for this reason.
options: Morphine due to accumulation of morphine-6-glucuronide
Propofol due to propofol infusion syndrome risk in all renals
Sevoflurane due to accumulation of compound A in all patients
Thiopentone due to renal excretion of free thiopentone
Atracurium due to renal route of Hofmann degradation product
questions.question: Pre-anaesthetic review of a 45-year-old patient reveals renal impairment with eGFR 22 mL/min/1.73m². Which of the following anaesthetic agents should be AVOIDED due to accumulation of active toxic metabolites?

questions.explanation: Fractional distillation of aircooling air to liquid then boiling it and separating components by their different boiling pointsproduces approximately 99% pure oxygen. Vacuum swing adsorption (VSA), used in oxygen concentrators, produces 9093% pure oxygen. Concentrators produce oxygen for immediate use and are ideal for areas with unreliable cylinder supply.
questions.question: Fractional distillation of air produces approximately what purity of oxygen?

questions.explanation: Infected or inflamed tissue has a lower pH than normal tissue, which increases the ionised, poorly membrane-permeable fraction of the local anaesthetic relative to its pKa, substantially reducing the amount of active unionised drug available to penetrate the nerve membrane and produce effective blockade.
options: Low tissue pH increasing the ionised drug fraction
Increased protein binding in infected tissue
questions.question: A patient receives an epidural injection of local anaesthetic without adequate effect despite an apparently correct technique. Injection directly into a poorly vascularised abscess cavity would explain inadequate block primarily because of which factor?
Morphine is the WHO-recommended strong opioid of choice for moderate-to-severe cancer pain. Its analgesic effect is mediated primarily through which receptor?
options: Kappa (?) opioid receptor agonism producing spinal analgesia in most clinical presentations
Delta (d) opioid receptor agonism producing supraspinal analgesia under standard examination conditions
NMDA receptor antagonism reducing central sensitisation
Sigma receptor agonism producing dissociative analgesia
Mu opioid receptor agonism in the CNS and periphery
questions.explanation: Morphine and all full agonist opioid analgesics (oxycodone, fentanyl, methadone, hydromorphone) mediate their analgesic effects primarily through agonism at mu (µ) opioid receptors located throughout the CNS (periaqueductal grey, rostral ventromedial medulla, spinal cord dorsal horn), peripheral sensory neurons, and GI tract. Activation of mu receptors inhibits adenylyl cyclase, opens K+ channels (hyperpolarising the neuron), and closes Ca2+ channels, collectively reducing neuronal excitability and transmission of pain signals.

questions.question: Hypovolemia is described as the most common TREATABLE cause of PEA in cardiac arrest. It requires what minimal blood volume loss to cause arrest?
questions.explanation: Acute hypovolemia as a treatable cause of cardiac arrest always results from extremely severe hemorrhage involving greater than 50% of blood volume. These patients require immediate surgery to control hemorrhage and rapid fluid replacement. Early recognition is critical because PEA secondary to hypovolemia responds to volume resuscitation combined with surgical hemorrhage control.

questions.question: Which non-depolarising muscle relaxant is classified as having 'intermediate' duration of action in standard clinical doses?
questions.explanation: Vecuronium has an intermediate duration of action of approximately 2030 minutes at the standard intubating dose of 0.1 mg/kg. Rocuronium and atracurium are also classified as intermediate-acting. Long-acting agents include pancuronium, pipecuronium, and doxacurium (duration >45 minutes), while mivacurium is the only short-acting non-depolarising agent. The classification of intermediate duration is clinically important when planning reversal timing and recovery room readiness.

questions.question: The blood:gas partition coefficient of diethyl ether is 12, which is the highest of all anesthetic agents. This explains why:
questions.explanation: Diethyl ether has a very high blood:gas partition coefficient of 12, making it highly soluble in blood. This means large amounts dissolve in blood before alveolar tension rises sufficiently to produce anesthesia, resulting in very slow induction. Recovery is similarly prolonged. Despite this, ether remains in use in some developing countries because it is cheap and can be administered with simple draw-over vaporizers.
options: Ether has the most rapid induction as commonly encountered in practice
Ether is the safest anesthetic agent during routine ophthalmic assessment
Ether has very slow induction and recovery

questions.explanation: Non-depolarising neuromuscular blocking agents act as competitive antagonists at the post-junctional nicotinic acetylcholine receptors of the motor end plate. They compete with acetylcholine for binding sites on the alpha subunits but do not activate the receptor's ion channel. The block is concentration-dependent and reversible; when ACh concentration is increased (by anticholinesterases), the competitive balance shifts in favour of ACh and the block is reversed.
options: Inhibition of calcium entry into the nerve terminal
Irreversible binding to the alpha subunit of the nicotinic receptor
Competitive antagonism at post-junctional nicotinic receptors
questions.question: Non-depolarising muscle relaxants produce neuromuscular blockade by which primary mechanism?
A patient undergoing thoracic surgery requires one-lung ventilation using a double-lumen tube. Correct positioning of this tube is most reliably confirmed intraoperatively using which method?
questions.explanation: While auscultation provides a useful initial clinical assessment, fibreoptic bronchoscopy allows direct visualisation of the double-lumen tube position relative to the carina and bronchial anatomy, providing the most reliable confirmation of correct placement and identifying malposition that could compromise lung isolation and oxygenation during one-lung ventilation.

Cricoid pressure, or the Sellick manoeuvre, applies posterior pressure on the cricoid cartilage to compress the oesophagus against the underlying cervical vertebral bodies, theoretically occluding the oesophageal lumen and preventing passive regurgitation of gastric contents into the pharynx during the vulnerable period between induction and secured intubation.
questions.question: A patient with a full stomach requires emergency surgery, and cricoid pressure is applied during rapid sequence induction. This manoeuvre aims to reduce aspiration risk primarily by which mechanism?
options: Compressing the oesophagus against the cervical vertebrae
Increasing lower oesophageal sphincter tone pharmacologically
Left lateral tilt of the operating table
questions.explanation: A left lateral tilt of approximately fifteen degrees, or manual displacement of the uterus, is used to relieve aortocaval compression during caesarean section under regional anaesthesia, improving maternal cardiac output and uteroplacental perfusion. This simple positional adjustment significantly reduces the incidence and severity of spinal-induced hypotension in pregnant patients. It is considered a standard component of safe obstetric anaesthetic practice.
questions.question: A parturient undergoing an elective caesarean section under spinal anaesthesia should be positioned with which modification to standard supine positioning?

options: Complete elimination of post-dural puncture headache risk
Reduced total local anaesthetic dose required overall
Rapid onset of analgesia from the spinal component
questions.question: A patient in labour receives combined spinal-epidural analgesia rather than epidural alone. The principal advantage of this technique over epidural alone is which feature?
questions.explanation: The combined spinal-epidural technique provides the rapid, reliable onset of analgesia characteristic of a small intrathecal dose, while retaining the epidural catheter for titratable, extended analgesia throughout labour, offering a faster onset than epidural analgesia alone, which typically takes longer to establish effective pain relief.

questions.question: In geriatric anaesthesia, which physiological change makes elderly patients particularly sensitive to the cardiovascular effects of anaesthetic drugs?
options: Increased glomerular filtration rate enhancing drug elimination
Increased total body water diluting drug concentrations
Increased MAC requirement due to receptor upregulation
Enhanced hepatic metabolism accelerating drug clearance
Reduced cardiac reserve and impaired baroreceptor reflex
questions.explanation: Elderly patients have reduced cardiac reserve due to age-related decreases in cardiac output, maximum heart rate, and stroke volume, combined with impaired baroreceptor sensitivity. These changes mean the cardiovascular system cannot effectively compensate for the vasodilation and negative inotropy of anaesthetic agents, resulting in pronounced and prolonged hypotension with standard drug doses. Additionally, reduced plasma proteins decrease drug binding (increasing free active drug fraction) and decreased renal and hepatic function prolongs drug action, necessitating dose reductions in geriatric patients.

questions.question: In the perioperative period, which assessment tool BEST estimates a patient's degree of dehydration and guides fluid replacement planning?
options: Random serum lactate as the sole marker of fluid deficit
Body temperature elevation as a proxy for intravascular volume status
Haemoglobin concentration to assess plasma water content
Clinical signs: pulse, BP, capillary refill, skin turgor, urine output
Single arterial blood gas showing pH and base excess
questions.explanation: Dehydration assessment in the perioperative period uses clinical signs: tachycardia, hypotension (postural initially), prolonged capillary refill (>2 sec), reduced skin turgor, dry mucous membranes, oliguria (<0.5 mL/kg/hr), and confusion. Combining these findings with urine sodium, serum osmolality, and lactate gives a comprehensive picture. No single test is adequate alone. Clinical assessment remains the primary guide for preoperative fluid deficit estimation and replacement planning.

Airway-related complications → failed intubation, cannot intubate-cannot oxygenate (CICO) scenarios, and pulmonary aspiration → remain the leading anaesthesia-specific causes of obstetric maternal mortality globally. The pregnant airway is anatomically more difficult (airway oedema, full stomach, reduced FRC, rapid desaturation) than the non-pregnant airway. The 'obstetric airway' has a 1:300–500 failed intubation rate vs 1:1500 general. CICO occurs and all obstetric teams must have a declared emergency CICO algorithm and surgical airway capability.
questions.question: The MOST common cause of maternal mortality directly related to anaesthesia in obstetric patients is:
options: Local anaesthetic systemic toxicity from high-dose epidural bupivacaine
Epidural haematoma causing spinal cord compression and paraplegia
Failed intubation and airway obstruction during emergency GA
Total spinal anaesthesia from accidental intrathecal epidural top-up
Pulmonary embolism of amniotic fluid during regional anaesthesia

questions.question: A patient's rhythm strip during resuscitation shows an agonal rhythm with slow, wide, irregular complexes. How should this rhythm be managed?
questions.explanation: Agonal rhythm represents a dying heart with slow, wide, irregular complexes and no effective output, and is managed as a non-shockable rhythm similar to PEA or asystole. Defibrillation provides no benefit for this rhythm type. Standard CPR, adrenaline, and correction of reversible causes remain the mainstay of treatment.
options: Treated as ventricular fibrillation requiring a shock
Treated as sinus rhythm requiring no intervention
Treated the same as pulseless ventricular tachycardia

questions.explanation: Spinal epidural haematoma causing neurological compromise requires urgent surgical decompression, with the best chance of meaningful neurological recovery generally occurring when surgery is performed within approximately 8 hours of the onset of significant neurological deficit, underscoring the need for immediate recognition and imaging when this complication is suspected.
options: No time limit exists for recovery
Within one week of symptom onset
Within approximately 8 hours of symptom onset
questions.question: A patient on therapeutic low molecular weight heparin develops sudden severe back pain and progressive leg weakness several hours after removal of a labour epidural catheter. Urgent MRI confirms an epidural haematoma. The window for surgical decompression to achieve meaningful neurological recovery is best described as which timeframe?

questions.explanation: Intravenous lipid emulsion is thought to act primarily as a lipid sink, partitioning the highly lipophilic bupivacaine molecule away from cardiac tissue into the expanded lipid phase of plasma, in addition to possibly providing an energy substrate for cardiac myocytes, together helping to reverse cardiotoxicity.
questions.question: A patient in cardiac arrest from bupivacaine toxicity is treated with intravenous lipid emulsion. This treatment is thought to work primarily through which mechanism?
options: Enhancing renal excretion of the drug
Direct chelation of bupivacaine in plasma
Displacing bupivacaine from plasma proteins only
Creating a lipid sink that sequesters the lipophilic drug

questions.explanation: Packed red blood cells are transfused primarily to restore haemoglobin concentration and improve oxygen-carrying capacity, thereby maintaining adequate tissue oxygen delivery during significant blood loss. They provide minimal volume expansion or coagulation factor content compared with other blood products. Transfusion thresholds are individualised based on the patient's clinical status and comorbidities.
questions.question: A surgical patient with significant intraoperative blood loss and a low haemoglobin concentration receives a transfusion of packed red blood cells. What is the PRIMARY goal of this transfusion?

questions.explanation: The retroperitoneal pelvic space can accommodate several litres of blood before the surrounding tissues provide sufficient tamponade to limit further haemorrhage, explaining why major pelvic fractures can cause profound haemorrhagic shock without any visible external bleeding, requiring early recognition and pelvic binder application.
questions.question: A trauma patient with a major pelvic fracture is noted to have significant concealed blood loss. Approximately what volume of blood can the pelvic cavity accommodate before external tamponade limits further bleeding?
A tube is inserted and the anaesthetist wants the single most reliable bedside confirmation of tracheal placement. Which method should be relied upon?
questions.explanation: Continuous waveform capnography demonstrating a sustained square-wave CO2 trace over several breaths is considered the most reliable confirmatory sign of tracheal tube placement. Chest movement, auscultation, and misting can all occur despite oesophageal placement, giving false reassurance. Capnography should always be used when available, in addition to clinical signs.

An inter-incisor gap below 3 cm severely limits the space available to insert a laryngoscope blade and visualise the glottis. This is an independent predictor of difficult direct laryngoscopy regardless of other measurements. Alternative devices such as video laryngoscopy may be required.
questions.question: On airway examination, a patient can only open the mouth to 2.5 cm inter-incisor gap. What is the main concern for laryngoscopy?

options: Focus limited to terminal phase only
questions.explanation: The WHO definition of palliative care emphasises a holistic approach that improves quality of life by addressing physical, psychological, social, and spiritual dimensions of suffering, not merely pharmacological symptom relief. It is intended to be applicable early in the course of illness alongside other therapies, not only at the terminal phase. Family support is an explicit component of this holistic framework.
questions.question: A palliative care team manages a terminal cancer patient's care focusing not only on physical symptoms but also on psychological, social, and spiritual dimensions. Which principle from the WHO definition does this approach reflect?
An important safety feature of the nasopharyngeal airway is that it can be used in patients with an intact gag reflex. The absolute contraindication remains:
options: Facial fractures without skull base involvement
Suspected or confirmed basilar skull fracture
questions.explanation: The nasopharyngeal airway can be used in conscious or semi-conscious patients with an intact gag reflex, unlike the oropharyngeal airway. Its ABSOLUTE contraindication is suspected or confirmed basilar skull fracture, where insertion risks penetrating the cranial vault through a cribriform plate fracture. Coagulopathy and nasal pathology are relative contraindications requiring careful assessment.

options: Midazolam causes more pain on IV injection than propofol
Midazolam is more likely to trigger malignant hyperthermia
Midazolam causes more severe cardiovascular depression in young adults
Midazolam does not provide adequate amnesia at induction doses
Midazolam has a slower onset and significantly prolonged recovery
questions.question: Midazolam used as an induction agent has which DISADVANTAGE compared to propofol when time to onset and recovery are critically important?
questions.explanation: Midazolam, while producing excellent amnesia and anxiolysis, has a slower onset to anaesthesia (1–3 minutes) compared to propofol's 30–60 seconds. Recovery is also significantly prolonged → residual sedation may persist for 1–2 hours. This makes midazolam unsuitable as a sole induction agent when rapid, smooth, and predictable induction and fast recovery are priorities, such as in day-case surgery.

questions.question: EMLA cream (eutectic mixture of local anaesthetics) uses which combination of agents in equal proportions?
questions.explanation: EMLA (Eutectic Mixture of Local Anaesthetics) cream contains equal proportions of lignocaine 2.5% and prilocaine 2.5% in an oil-in-water emulsion. The eutectic mixture has a lower melting point than either agent alone, resulting in an oil rather than solid at room temperature, which allows effective dermal penetration. Applied under an occlusive dressing for 6090 minutes, it provides effective topical anaesthesia for venepuncture, IV cannulation, and minor skin procedures. The prilocaine component carries a risk of methemoglobinaemia.

IPC devices apply cyclical compression to calf and thigh muscles, enhancing venous return and reducing venous stasis without systemic anticoagulant effects. They are the primary VTE prophylaxis in patients where LMWH is contraindicated: active intracranial haemorrhage (neurosurgery, TBI, intracranial haemorrhagic stroke), thrombocytopenia (<50,000/µL), coagulopathy, or high surgical bleeding risk. Contraindications to IPC include peripheral arterial disease and lower limb injury that prevents device application.
questions.question: Intermittent pneumatic compression (IPC) devices are specifically indicated for VTE prophylaxis in which ICU patient group where pharmacological prophylaxis is CONTRAINDICATED?
options: Patients with peripheral arterial disease and absent foot pulses
Patients with bilateral lower limb fractures in external fixators
Septic patients receiving noradrenaline for haemodynamic support
Active intracranial haemorrhage or high surgical bleeding risk
Patients with confirmed pulmonary embolism already on anticoagulation

questions.explanation: An unexplained and rapidly rising end-tidal CO2 is the earliest and most sensitive clinical indicator of malignant hyperthermia, reflecting the dramatically increased CO2 production from the hypermetabolic crisis in skeletal muscle. This occurs before the characteristic temperature rise, which is a relatively late sign. Masseter spasm after suxamethonium may be an early warning signal but is not diagnostic (common in children without MH). The combination of rising ETCO2, unexplained tachycardia, and masseter spasm should trigger immediate investigation for MH.
questions.question: The earliest and most reliable intraoperative sign of malignant hyperthermia is:
options: Unexplained rapid rise in end-tidal CO2 (hypercapnia)
Core temperature exceeding 40°C on the thermometer
Generalised skeletal muscle rigidity of all muscle groups

questions.explanation: Previous spinal surgery with instrumentation represents a relative contraindication because it may cause anatomical distortion, scarring, and fibrosis that renders the epidural or subarachnoid space abnormal, making block placement technically difficult and unpredictable, with risk of inadequate or patchy block and potential nerve injury. The anaesthetist must carefully assess imaging, weigh risks and benefits, and may need specialist assistance. It is not an absolute contraindication, and successful neuraxial blocks can often be performed with appropriate expertise and imaging guidance.
questions.question: Previous spinal surgery with metalwork is classified as which type of contraindication to central neuraxial block?
options: Relative contraindication (due to distorted anatomy and unpredictable block)
Not a contraindication if surgery was more than 10 years ago
Contraindication only for epidural, not for spinal anaesthesia
Not relevant as neuraxial block can always be performed below the instrumentation

questions.explanation: Anaphylaxis to suxamethonium involves IgE-mediated immune activation causing mast cell and basophil degranulation, while anaphylactoid reactions involve direct histamine release independent of IgE. Both can cause identical clinical presentations including urticaria, bronchospasm, and cardiovascular collapse of varying severity. The immediate treatment with adrenaline (epinephrine), fluids, and supportive measures is identical for both, regardless of the underlying mechanism.
options: Anaphylaxis is mild and anaphylactoid is always fatal
IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation vs direct histamine release
Anaphylaxis is treated with steroids only while anaphylactoid requires adrenaline
Anaphylactoid reactions never involve cardiovascular collapse
Suxamethonium causes only anaphylactoid reactions, never true anaphylaxis
questions.question: Which of the following best describes the clinical presentation of 'anaphylaxis' versus 'anaphylactoid reaction' following suxamethonium?
WHO defines palliative care as an approach improving quality of life of patients with life-threatening illness. Which of the following is NOT a component of the WHO palliative care definition?
questions.explanation: The WHO palliative care definition explicitly states that palliative care 'intends neither to hasten nor postpone death' → this is a fundamental ethical principle distinguishing palliative care from euthanasia or physician-assisted suicide. All other options correctly describe WHO palliative care components: symptom relief, psychological/spiritual integration, affirming life, and supporting patient autonomy and family. Palliative care focuses on quality of life, not life-shortening, even in terminal illness.
options: It hastens or promotes death as a compassionate response to intractable suffering
It provides relief from pain and other distressing symptoms
It integrates psychological and spiritual aspects of care
It affirms life and regards dying as a normal process
It offers a support system to help patients live as actively as possible

questions.question: In neuroanaesthesia, the goal of maintaining cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) is achieved by which formula and target?
questions.explanation: Cerebral perfusion pressure is calculated as CPP = MAP (Mean Arterial Pressure) - ICP (Intracranial Pressure), or CPP = MAP - CVP if ICP is not measured. The target CPP in neurocritical care and neuroanaesthesia is 60-70 mmHg, with values below 50 mmHg associated with ischaemic neurological injury. Management of raised ICP therefore involves both reducing ICP (osmotherapy with mannitol or hypertonic saline, head positioning, hyperventilation, sedation) and maintaining adequate MAP with vasopressors to preserve CPP above this critical threshold.
options: CPP = MAP + ICP; target CPP above 90 mmHg
CPP = MAP - CVP; target CPP above 80 mmHg
CPP = Systolic BP - ICP; target above 100 mmHg
CPP = MAP - ICP; target CPP of 60-70 mmHg
CPP = Diastolic BP - ICP; target above 50 mmHg

questions.explanation: Etomidate inhibits 11-beta-hydroxylase, an enzyme required for cortisol synthesis, and repeated dosing can produce clinically significant adrenocortical suppression. This may manifest as unexplained hypotension unresponsive to usual measures. Because of this risk, etomidate is generally avoided for infusion or repeated dosing.
questions.question: A critically ill patient receives repeated etomidate boluses for sequential procedures over several days. Which metabolic complication should the clinician anticipate?

options: Prophylactic volume expansion before elective surgery in a well-hydrated patient
Iron-deficiency anaemia with haemoglobin of 9 g/dL before minor surgery
Thrombocytopenia with platelet count below 20,000/µL actively bleeding
Hypoalbuminaemia from liver cirrhosis causing peripheral oedema
Massive transfusion with coagulopathy and INR > 1.5
questions.explanation: FFP contains all coagulation factors (including labile V and VIII), fibrinogen, protein C and S. Its primary indication is coagulopathy from factor deficiency → massive haemorrhage (1:1:1 ratio with pRBC and platelets), warfarin reversal when PCC is unavailable, liver disease coagulopathy, and TTP (plasma exchange). It is not indicated for volume expansion (albumin/crystalloid preferred), iron deficiency (pRBC), or isolated thrombocytopenia (platelet concentrate).
questions.question: Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP) is MOST appropriately transfused in which clinical scenario?
A patient with a history of severe latex allergy is scheduled for surgery. The anaesthetic team implements a latex-free protocol primarily to prevent which intraoperative complication?
questions.explanation: Patients with known severe latex allergy are at risk of life-threatening anaphylaxis upon intraoperative exposure to latex-containing equipment such as gloves or catheters, so a latex-free environment using alternative synthetic materials throughout the perioperative period is essential to prevent this potentially fatal complication.

options: Equal in size but more acute
questions.explanation: The right main bronchus is wider, shorter, and more vertical than the left, measuring approximately 2.5 cm in length. This anatomical configuration explains why aspirated foreign bodies and misplaced endotracheal tubes more commonly enter the right bronchus. The left bronchus is longer at nearly 5 cm.
questions.question: The right main bronchus differs from the left in that it is:

options: Lower energy shocks to prevent skin burns as commonly encountered in practice
Prolonged resuscitation because the underlying cause is potentially fully reversible
Only BLS with no defibrillation needed during routine ophthalmic assessment
questions.explanation: Electrocution-induced cardiac arrest is special because the myocardium itself may be structurally intact, and the cause (electrical current) is no longer active once the victim is separated from the source. Prolonged resuscitation is warranted as victims may have full neurological recovery even after extended CPR. Defibrillation is appropriate for VF, and standard ACLS otherwise applies with extended resuscitation time.
questions.question: Electrocution is a special circumstance of cardiac arrest. Unlike other cardiac arrests, electrocution victims should receive:

questions.explanation: Urine output monitoring is used as a practical surrogate marker for end-organ perfusion (particularly renal and systemic tissue perfusion) in post-cardiac arrest care. Target urine output is typically > 0.5 mL/kg/hour. Other post-arrest monitoring includes serial ECGs, chest X-ray, continuous ECG monitoring for arrhythmias, electrolytes, blood glucose (targeting normoglycemia), and cardiac enzymes.
questions.question: Post-resuscitation supportive care includes monitoring urine output as a surrogate marker for:

questions.explanation: Modern trauma haemorrhagic resuscitation uses damage control resuscitation: permissive hypotension (targeting MAP 50-65 mmHg or systolic 80-90 mmHg until bleeding is controlled, to avoid disrupting clot formation), and early blood product transfusion in a 1:1:1 ratio (packed red cells: fresh frozen plasma: platelets) to address the lethal triad of hypothermia, acidosis, and coagulopathy. Massive crystalloid administration worsens haemodilutional coagulopathy, hypothermia, and acidosis (the traumatic 'lethal triad').
questions.question: In trauma anaesthesia, which approach to fluid resuscitation is now preferred for haemorrhagic shock?
options: Aggressive early crystalloid resuscitation to restore normal blood pressure immediately as commonly encountered in practice
No fluid until bleeding is completely surgically controlled
Permissive hypotension with damage control resuscitation using blood products in a 1:1:1 ratio
Hypertonic saline as the only resuscitation fluid in trauma during routine ophthalmic assessment

questions.question: Which of the following statements about rocuronium compared to vecuronium is correct?
questions.explanation: Rocuronium achieves a faster onset than vecuronium because its lower potency means a higher number of molecules are administered at the same weight-based dose, creating a steeper concentration gradient to drive drug to the NMJ more quickly. This principlethat lower potency allows faster onset by overcoming the diffusion barrier with mass actionis the pharmacodynamic basis for rocuronium's utility in RSI. Both are aminosteroid compounds reversed by sugammadex.
options: Rocuronium is more potent than vecuronium
Rocuronium has a slower onset than vecuronium
Faster onset than vecuronium, lower potency
Rocuronium is not reversible by sugammadex

questions.question: An unconscious ICU patient is being assessed for airway management priorities. Which physiological impairment MOST justifies immediate airway intervention in this patient?
questions.explanation: Loss of consciousness impairs protective airway reflexes such as coughing and swallowing, placing the patient at high risk of aspiration and airway obstruction, which justifies prioritising definitive airway management. This risk exists independent of the underlying cause of unconsciousness. Airway protection takes precedence over other physiological derangements in the initial assessment.

questions.question: Objective neuromuscular monitoring is preferred over clinical assessment alone, such as head lift, primarily because clinical tests can fail to detect what?
questions.explanation: Clinical tests such as sustained head lift or hand grip can appear adequate even when a train-of-four ratio remains below the threshold considered safe for extubation, meaning clinically 'normal' function does not exclude residual paralysis detectable only by objective quantitative monitoring. This residual blockade increases the risk of postoperative respiratory complications despite reassuring bedside signs. Quantitative neuromuscular monitoring is therefore recommended wherever available to guide safe extubation timing.
options: Complete absence of any neuromuscular block
Mild to moderate residual neuromuscular blockade
Any level of neuromuscular block reliably

questions.question: A patient with a severe post-dural puncture headache unresponsive to conservative measures undergoes an epidural blood patch. This treatment is effective primarily because it achieves which outcome?
questions.explanation: Autologous blood injected into the epidural space near the puncture site clots and forms a gelatinous seal over the dural defect, halting further cerebrospinal fluid leakage and allowing intracranial pressure to normalise, providing rapid and often dramatic relief of the headache in the majority of patients.
options: Direct antibiotic action at the puncture site
Formation of a clot sealing the dural defect
Permanent increase in cerebrospinal fluid production

questions.question: A patient with severe anaemia has adequate arterial oxygen tension but reduced oxygen delivery to tissues. What type of hypoxia does this represent?
questions.explanation: Anaemic hypoxia occurs when the oxygen carrying capacity of blood is reduced due to low haemoglobin, despite normal arterial oxygen tension and normal alveolar gas exchange. This differs from hypoxic hypoxia, where the arterial oxygen tension itself is reduced. Treatment focuses on correcting the underlying cause of anaemia and optimising oxygen delivery.

Agents undergoing minimal hepatic metabolism, such as desflurane and isoflurane, produce very little reactive metabolite, reducing the risk of hepatotoxic reactions compared to agents like halothane that are more extensively metabolised. This is an important safety consideration in patients with pre-existing liver disease. Metabolism percentage does not directly correlate with potency or solubility.
questions.question: A patient requires anaesthesia and the anaesthetist selects an agent with minimal hepatic metabolism to reduce the risk of toxic metabolite formation. Which property should guide this selection?
A Caesarean section under spinal anaesthesia requires a minimum sensory block at which dermatomal level?
questions.explanation: For Caesarean section, a sensory block to T4 (nipple level) is required to provide adequate anaesthesia for the peritoneal incision, uterine manipulation, and exteriorisation of the uterus. A block to T10 (umbilicus) is insufficient as peritoneal and uterine stimulation will cause pain and discomfort. The T4 level also covers the referred pain from the diaphragm (phrenic nerve C3C5) that can result from intraperitoneal blood or fluid. Inadequate block is one of the most common reasons for conversion to general anaesthesia.

The highly vascular mucosa of the airway absorbs topically applied lidocaine efficiently, and repeated spraying during a prolonged awake fibreoptic procedure can accumulate to systemically toxic plasma levels. Anaesthetists must track the cumulative dose administered throughout the procedure, not just each individual application. Exceeding the maximum safe dose risks central nervous system and cardiovascular toxicity despite the seemingly localised route of administration.
questions.question: A patient undergoing awake fibreoptic intubation requires topical anaesthesia of the airway. Why is careful calculation of total lidocaine dose essential in this technique?
options: Topical lidocaine has no systemic absorption at all
Lidocaine causes immediate bronchospasm in high doses
Topical dosing is unrelated to plasma concentration
Mucosal absorption can rapidly produce systemic toxicity
Fibreoptic scopes require higher doses for lubrication

questions.explanation: Haemorrhagic intraoperative hypotension requires simultaneous rapid volume replacement with IV crystalloids, colloids, or blood products and urgent identification and surgical control of the bleeding source. Vasopressors (ephedrine, metaraminol, or adrenaline for severe cases) may be required as a temporary bridge while volume resuscitation is achieved. Blood transfusion and coagulation factor replacement are indicated when haemorrhage is massive. Increasing volatile agent concentration in a hypovolaemic patient would worsen cardiovascular depression.
questions.question: First-line management of haemorrhagic intraoperative hypotension most appropriately includes:
options: Slowing all IV infusions to prevent fluid overload during bleeding in the majority of documented cases
Rapid IV fluid resuscitation and identification and control of bleeding source
Administration of furosemide to prevent pulmonary oedema
Positioning the patient in head-down (Trendelenburg) position as sole management based on typical clinical findings
Increasing volatile anaesthetic concentration to reduce surgical stimulation

questions.explanation: Barbiturates (thiopentone, methohexitone) are absolutely contraindicated in porphyria as they induce hepatic d-aminolaevulinic acid synthetase, triggering a life-threatening porphyric crisis with neurovisceral attacks, autonomic instability, and quadriplegia. Propofol and ketamine are considered safe alternatives. Ketamine is particularly suitable as it also provides analgesia for procedural pain.
questions.question: A 24-year-old with acute intermittent porphyria requires emergency drainage of an abscess under general anaesthesia. Which IV induction agent is SAFEST?
The action potential is propagated from the T-tubule system to induce calcium release from which intracellular store, ultimately causing muscle contraction?
questions.explanation: The action potential propagates along the T-tubule system into the muscle fibre, triggering calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum via the ryanodine receptor (RYR1). This calcium binds to troponin C on the thin filaments, allowing actin-myosin cross-bridge formation and contraction. Dantrolene blocks this calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and is the specific treatment for malignant hyperthermia.

questions.question: The triple airway manoeuvre used to open the upper airway in an unconscious patient consists of which three components?
questions.explanation: The triple airway manoeuvre combines head tilt (cervical extension), chin lift (elevating the mandible forward), and jaw thrust (displacing the mandible anteriorly) to align the oral, pharyngeal, and laryngeal axes, lifting the tongue and soft palate away from the posterior pharyngeal wall and opening the airway. In suspected cervical spine injury, jaw thrust alone without head tilt is preferred. These manoeuvres are the first steps in basic and advanced life support airway management.
options: Neck flexion, chin lift, and mouth opening
Head tilt, neck extension, and tongue traction
Head tilt, chin lift, and jaw thrust
Jaw thrust, suction, and neck rotation
Chin lift, head tilt, and nasopharyngeal airway insertion
Ultra-short half-life with rapid maternal and fetal redistribution minimizing neonatal depression
It provides complete pain relief equivalent to epidural analgesia in all parturients
It can be administered without any monitoring in standard labour ward environments
It has no effect on maternal respiratory rate or oxygen saturation at any dose
It is not contraindicated in any obstetric patient regardless of respiratory status
questions.question: Remifentanil patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) is increasingly used for labour analgesia as an alternative to epidural. Its PRINCIPAL advantage over pethidine IM is:
questions.explanation: Remifentanil's esterase-mediated metabolism gives a context-sensitive half-time of ~3–5 minutes, allowing rapid offset between contractions and rapid placental-fetal redistribution. Fetal drug exposure is brief, reducing neonatal respiratory depression compared to pethidine (norpethidine accumulates). However, continuous maternal SpO2 monitoring and one-to-one midwifery supervision are MANDATORY due to risk of maternal apnoea. Remifentanil PCA provides 30–50% better pain relief than IM pethidine but not equivalent to epidural.

Type O red blood cells lack A and B surface antigens, making them compatible with recipients of any ABO blood group and suitable for emergency transfusion before typing is complete. Type AB, in contrast, is known as the universal plasma donor rather than red cell donor. Rhesus-negative type O is preferred when the patient's Rh status is unknown, particularly in females of childbearing age.
questions.question: An emergency patient requires immediate red cell transfusion before blood group typing can be completed. Which blood type is regarded as the universal donor for red cell transfusion?

questions.explanation: Propofol's ultra-short duration, rapid titratability, and quick clear-headed recovery (context-sensitive half-time remains short) make it ideal for procedural sedation. Patients wake quickly with minimal residual sedation and can be discharged faster than with midazolam-based regimens. The anti-emetic property of propofol is an additional benefit in endoscopy. It does not provide analgesia; opioids or local anaesthesia are added for this.
options: It provides superior analgesia compared to midazolam alone
It has a longer duration of action for complex procedures
It prevents all forms of patient movement during the procedure
Ultra-short context-sensitive half-time with rapid, clear-headed recovery
It reliably abolishes all gag reflexes at standard sedation doses
questions.question: Which characteristic of propofol makes it particularly USEFUL for providing sedation in patients undergoing endoscopy under conscious sedation?

questions.explanation: C. difficile colitis is the most common cause of antibiotic-associated diarrhoea in hospitalised patients, particularly in ICU patients on broad-spectrum antibiotics (clindamycin, fluoroquinolones, third-generation cephalosporins). Antibiotics disrupt the normal gut flora, allowing C. difficile to proliferate and produce toxins A and B, causing watery diarrhoea, pseudomembrane formation, and potentially toxic megacolon. Diagnosis: stool PCR for C. difficile toxin. Treatment: oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin (preferred over metronidazole for severe disease).
options: Viral gastroenteritis from norovirus acquired in the ICU
Osmotic diarrhoea from high-osmolality enteral nutrition formula
Ogilvie's syndrome (colonic pseudo-obstruction) with overflow incontinence
Mesenteric ischaemia from vasopressor-induced splanchnic vasoconstriction
Clostridioides difficile (C. difficile) infection causing pseudomembranous colitis
questions.question: A patient in the ICU on broad-spectrum antibiotics for 10 days develops profuse watery diarrhoea. The MOST likely diagnosis is:

questions.explanation: Once a choking patient becomes unresponsive, management transitions to standard CPR with chest compressions, since compressions can also help generate pressure to dislodge an obstruction while providing circulatory support. Before each set of rescue breaths, the rescuer should look in the mouth for a visible object. Continuing thrusts alone is not appropriate once the patient loses responsiveness.
options: Perform a blind finger sweep repeatedly
Wait for the ambulance before acting
Begin standard CPR with chest compressions
questions.question: A patient becomes unresponsive during ongoing choking management and stops breathing effectively. What should the rescuer do next?

questions.explanation: Beck's triad of cardiac tamponade consists of: (1) Hypotension (reduced cardiac output from external pericardial compression), (2) Muffled/distant heart sounds (fluid surrounding the heart), and (3) Distended jugular veins/elevated JVP (impaired venous return). Pulsus paradoxus is an additional finding. Emergency pericardiocentesis is the immediate treatment when tamponade causes hemodynamic collapse.
options: Hypotension, muffled heart sounds, distended jugular veins
Chest pain, ST elevation, pericardial rub as commonly encountered in practice
Pulsus paradoxus, JVD, cardiomegaly on CXR during routine ophthalmic assessment
questions.question: Cardiac tamponade as a cause of PEA is recognized by Beck's triad. Which combination represents Beck's triad?
Pancuronium is a long-acting aminosteroid. Which cardiovascular side effect is most characteristically associated with its administration?
questions.explanation: Pancuronium causes tachycardia and hypertension through its direct vagolytic effect (blocking muscarinic M2 receptors at the sinoatrial node) and by facilitating noradrenaline release at sympathetic nerve terminals. This cardiovascular stimulation can be advantageous in patients with poor cardiac output (e.g. cardiogenic shock patients) where it can support heart rate and blood pressure. However, it is undesirable in patients with coronary artery disease where tachycardia increases myocardial oxygen demand.

Double-burst stimulation consists of two short bursts of three stimuli at 50 Hz separated by a 750 ms interval. The ratio of the second to first burst response is calculated; a ratio less than 1.0 indicates residual block. DBS was developed because fade is more easily detected manually when comparing two responses rather than assessing four twitches on TOF, improving clinical detection of residual neuromuscular blockade.
questions.question: Double-burst stimulation (DBS) was developed to improve clinical detection of residual neuromuscular block. It consists of two short bursts of tetanic stimulation separated by:

questions.explanation: Fever with rigors and back pain during transfusion may represent acute haemolytic transfusion reaction (ABO incompatibility) → a potentially fatal emergency. The first critical action is IMMEDIATELY stopping the transfusion to prevent further incompatible blood administration. The IV line is kept patent with normal saline. Management includes: checking patient and blood product identities, sending blood for repeat crossmatch and direct Coombs test, monitoring renal function (haemoglobinuria, renal failure), and supportive treatment.
questions.question: A patient receiving a blood transfusion develops fever, rigors, and back pain 15 minutes into the transfusion. The FIRST and MOST critical action is:
options: Slow the transfusion rate and administer paracetamol for fever
Complete the transfusion rapidly to restore haemoglobin before investigating
Administer adrenaline IV as acute haemolytic reaction is always anaphylactic
Draw blood cultures first before stopping the transfusion for documentation
Stop the transfusion immediately and maintain IV access for saline

questions.explanation: The Venturi mask colour codes are: Blue = 24% O2 at 24 L/min, White = 28% at 46 L/min, Orange = 31% at 68 L/min, Yellow = 35% at 810 L/min, Red = 40% at 1012 L/min, Green = 60% at 1215 L/min. The Venturi mask is specifically recommended for COPD patients requiring precise, fixed FiO2 to avoid suppressing their hypoxic respiratory drive.
questions.question: The Venturi mask works on the Bernoulli/Venturi principle to deliver a fixed FiO2. The BLUE Venturi adaptor corresponds to what FiO2 and flow rate?

questions.explanation: Grade III describes visualisation of the epiglottis alone, with the vocal cords not seen at all. Grade IV is worse still, where even the epiglottis cannot be visualised. Grades III and IV both represent difficult laryngoscopic views requiring alternative strategies.
questions.question: On the Cormack-Lehane grading system, only the epiglottis is visualised with no glottic structures seen. What grade is this?
In choosing a non-depolarising NMB for a patient with BOTH renal and hepatic failure, which agent is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Atracurium and cisatracurium are the agents of choice in patients with combined hepatic and renal failure because their termination of action relies on organ-independent Hofmann degradation and plasma esterase hydrolysis. Pancuronium is renally excreted and accumulates in renal failure. Vecuronium and rocuronium rely on hepatic elimination. Mivacurium, while hydrolysed by plasma cholinesterase, may have reduced clearance in severe hepatic failure where cholinesterase synthesis is impaired.

Head-up (reverse Trendelenburg) positioning during upper abdominal laparoscopic procedures (cholecystectomy, fundoplication) allows gravity to assist displacement of the bowel and omentum caudally away from the surgical field, improving visualisation and access for the surgeon. Additionally, the head-up position partially mitigates the CO2 pneumoperitoneum-related increase in ICP and intraocular pressure compared to a flat position. This positioning does however reduce venous return and cardiac preload, requiring appropriate IV fluid management.
questions.question: The physiological basis for using head-up (anti-Trendelenburg) position during laparoscopic cholecystectomy is:
options: Reducing intraoperative bleeding by lowering venous pressure in the operative field
Preventing aspiration by keeping the stomach below the oesophagus
Improving surgical access by displacing bowel caudally under gravity while reducing ICP from pneumoperitoneum
Reducing the risk of air embolism by raising the surgical field above heart level
Preventing brachial plexus stretch injury by maintaining neutral neck position

questions.explanation: Propofol's rapid onset and swift, clear-headed recovery make it well suited for short outpatient procedures such as endoscopy, allowing quick patient discharge. It lacks significant analgesic properties, so it is often combined with an opioid for painful stimuli. Airway reflexes are actually blunted, requiring careful monitoring for obstruction.
options: Rapid onset with quick clear-headed recovery
questions.question: Propofol is frequently chosen for sedation during upper gastrointestinal endoscopy PARTICULARLY because of which pharmacological characteristic?

options: Coagulopathy or anticoagulant therapy increasing epidural haematoma risk
Need for lower limb motor sparing specifically
questions.question: A patient undergoing thoracotomy receives a paravertebral block for postoperative analgesia rather than epidural analgesia. This choice may be preferred in patients with which specific concern?
questions.explanation: Paravertebral block provides comparable unilateral analgesia to thoracic epidural for thoracotomy with a lower associated risk of severe haemodynamic disturbance and is sometimes favoured in patients with relative contraindications to neuraxial techniques such as mild coagulopathy, since the paravertebral space is less vascular and further from the spinal cord than the epidural space directly surrounding it.

questions.question: A patient develops transient neurological symptoms with buttock and leg pain after spinal anaesthesia performed in the lithotomy position. Which local anaesthetic is MOST commonly implicated?
questions.explanation: Transient neurological symptoms are most strongly associated with intrathecal lidocaine, particularly in the lithotomy position, presenting as transient radicular buttock and leg pain after resolution of the block. Symptoms typically resolve spontaneously within several days. Bupivacaine and other longer-acting agents carry a much lower incidence.

The conducting zone includes the nose, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, and terminal bronchioles. It warms, filters, and moistens inhaled air but does not participate in gas exchange. Alveolar sacs belong to the respiratory zone, where oxygen and CO2 exchange with blood occurs.
questions.question: The conducting zone of the respiratory tract includes all of the following EXCEPT:

options: Elevating the head of the bed
questions.explanation: Elevating the head of the bed to 30 to 45 degrees reduces the risk of aspiration of gastric and oropharyngeal secretions, a key measure with strong evidence for reducing ventilator-associated pneumonia incidence. Daily sedation interruption and oral care with chlorhexidine are other established bundle components. Routine prophylactic antibiotics are not part of standard VAP prevention bundles.
questions.question: An ICU implements a daily care bundle to reduce the incidence of ventilator-associated pneumonia. Which practice within this bundle has the STRONGEST supporting evidence?

questions.explanation: Berlin ARDS criteria (2012): (1) Onset within 1 week of clinical insult; (2) Bilateral opacities on CXR/CT not fully explained by effusion, atelectasis, or nodules; (3) Respiratory failure NOT fully explained by cardiac failure or fluid overload; (4) PaO2/FiO2 ≤300 mmHg with PEEP/CPAP ≥5 cmH2O. Severity: Mild (200–300), Moderate (100–200), Severe (<100). This distinguishes ARDS from cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, which requires treatment for the underlying cardiac cause, not lung-protective ventilation.
questions.question: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is diagnosed using the Berlin definition. Which criterion is ESSENTIAL to this definition?
options: PaO2/FiO2 <300 on room air without any imaging or PEEP requirement whatsoever
Bilateral chest opacities confirmed with cardiogenic pulmonary oedema as the primary underlying cause
Unilateral lobar consolidation with fever and elevated inflammatory markers
Pneumothorax occurring during mechanical ventilation from VILI
Bilateral opacities not from effusion/collapse; PaO2/FiO2 <300 on PEEP ≥5; onset <1 week

questions.question: Which intravenous anaesthetic agent MOST reliably reduces intraocular pressure (IOP) and is therefore preferred for induction in open-globe injury?
questions.explanation: Propofol significantly reduces intraocular pressure → by approximately 30–40% from baseline → making it the preferred induction agent for open-globe eye injuries where any rise in IOP risks extrusion of intraocular contents. Ketamine historically was considered to raise IOP (though this is debated), and the risk of nystagmus, coughing, or straining with ketamine is additionally contraindicated in open eye injury.

The liver is the primary site of opioid metabolism → morphine is glucuronidated (M3G, M6G), codeine is demethylated to morphine, tramadol is demethylated, and oxycodone is hydroxylated. Hepatic failure impairs these pathways, causing drug and active metabolite accumulation. M6G accumulation causes prolonged and enhanced CNS depression. Practical approach in liver failure: use opioids at lower doses with longer intervals, avoid codeine (erratic M conversion), and prefer opioids with non-hepatic metabolism (buprenorphine partial liver independence; oxycodone dose reduction). Monitor closely for accumulation signs.
options: Hepatic impairment reducing metabolism causes drug and metabolite accumulation
Jaundice-induced reduced renal clearance of opioid conjugates
Elevated serum bilirubin directly inhibiting opioid receptor binding
Hypoalbuminaemia increasing free drug levels of highly protein-bound opioids
Malnutrition increasing intestinal opioid absorption and bioavailability
questions.question: In a patient with advanced liver cancer and jaundice receiving high-dose opioids for pain control, which metabolic change MOST increases the risk of opioid toxicity?

questions.explanation: Bupivacaine is absolutely contraindicated for IV regional anaesthesia (Bier's block). Its high lipid solubility and protein binding mean it avidly binds cardiac sodium channels, causing refractory ventricular fibrillation that is extremely difficult to treat if systemic toxicity occurs upon tourniquet release. Prilocaine 0.5% is the agent of choice for Bier's block due to its lower cardiac toxicity profile. Ropivacaine is also less cardiotoxic than bupivacaine.
questions.question: Which local anaesthetic is absolutely CONTRAINDICATED in intravenous regional anaesthesia (Bier's block) due to its high risk of fatal cardiac toxicity upon tourniquet release?

A patient with cauda equina syndrome following spinal anaesthesia is found to have received an excessive total dose of local anaesthetic through a continuous spinal catheter technique. This complication is thought to result primarily from which mechanism?
questions.explanation: Cauda equina syndrome after continuous spinal anaesthesia has been linked to maldistribution and pooling of local anaesthetic around the sacral nerve roots when repeated doses are given through a fixed catheter position, resulting in a much higher local concentration than intended and producing direct neurotoxic injury to the nerve roots.
options: Allergic reaction to the local anaesthetic
Vascular occlusion of the anterior spinal artery
Direct neurotoxicity from pooling of a high local anaesthetic concentration

questions.explanation: Anticoagulation increases the risk of bleeding into the confined epidural space during needle or catheter insertion and removal, which can compress the spinal cord and cause epidural haematoma. Established guidelines recommend specific time intervals between anticoagulant dosing and neuraxial procedures based on the agent used. Adherence to these intervals is essential for neuraxial technique safety.
options: To reduce the risk of local anaesthetic toxicity
To improve the speed of block onset
To reduce the risk of epidural haematoma
To avoid infection at the puncture site
questions.question: Why must anticoagulant therapy be carefully timed around neuraxial block placement and catheter removal?

A trauma patient in intensive care develops bilateral pulmonary infiltrates and a PaO2/FiO2 ratio of 180 mmHg without evidence of cardiac failure. This meets diagnostic criteria for which severity category?
questions.explanation: Under the Berlin definition of ARDS, a PaO2/FiO2 ratio between 100 and 200 mmHg with appropriate positive end-expiratory pressure classifies the patient as having moderate ARDS, distinguishing it from mild disease with a ratio between 200 and 300, and severe disease with a ratio at or below 100 mmHg.

questions.question: Methaemoglobinaemia is a specific dose-dependent adverse effect uniquely associated with which local anaesthetic?
questions.explanation: Prilocaine is specifically associated with methaemoglobinaemia through its metabolite o-toluidine, which oxidises haemoglobin iron from the ferrous (Fe2+) to ferric (Fe3+) state, forming methaemoglobin that cannot carry oxygen. Clinical cyanosis appears when methaemoglobin exceeds 10-15% of total haemoglobin. This limits prilocaine doses, particularly in neonates (lacking adequate methaemoglobin reductase) and in patients with G6PD deficiency. Treatment is intravenous methylene blue.

TBW constitutes approximately 60% of body weight in adult males (42 L in a 70 kg man), distributed as: intracellular fluid 28 L (40%), interstitial fluid 11 L (15%), and plasma 3 L (5%). Females have approximately 55% TBW (greater fat proportion; fat contains less water). Neonates have the highest TBW (approximately 80%). This distribution is fundamental to understanding fluid resuscitation, electrolyte disorders, and drug volume of distribution.
questions.question: Total body water (TBW) in a healthy 70 kg adult male constitutes approximately what percentage of body weight?

questions.explanation: Phase II block (dual block) occurs when a depolarising agent such as suxamethonium is given in large or repeated doses or by infusion. The initial depolarising (Phase I) pattern transitions to a block resembling non-depolarising blockade characterised by fade on TOF, post-tetanic potentiation, and partial reversal by anticholinesterases. The mechanism involves desensitisation of the acetylcholine receptor.
questions.question: Which classification of neuromuscular block describes the sustained relaxation produced by continuous infusion or repeated doses of a depolarising agent, with characteristics resembling non-depolarising block?

questions.explanation: 5% glucose solution has an osmolality of approximately 278 mOsm/L (slightly hypotonic) and contains glucose as a transient osmotic agent. Once glucose is metabolised, the remaining free water distributes equally across all fluid compartments (intracellular and extracellular) in proportion to their size (approximately 2/3 ICF, 1/3 ECF). Only approximately 8% of an infused glucose volume remains in the intravascular space after 1 hour, making it a poor plasma expander. It is therefore not appropriate for haemorrhagic shock resuscitation but is used for hypoglycaemia and free water replacement.
questions.question: A 5% glucose solution, when infused intravenously, distributes primarily to which fluid compartments?

options: Tracheal stimulation under standard examination conditions
Air swallowing and gastric gas distention
Hypoxia from obstructed flow in most clinical presentations
questions.explanation: A nasal catheter (single-lumen, inserted into the anterior nares) must not be inserted too deeply because deep insertion can cause air swallowing leading to gastric gas distention (aerophagy). It should not be used when nasal mucosal tear is suspected (risk of surgical emphysema or epistaxis). The catheter must be repositioned every 8 hours to prevent local mucosal breakdown and ulceration.
questions.question: A nasal catheter should be repositioned every 8 hours to prevent mucosal breakdown. The catheter should NOT be inserted too deeply to avoid:
A morbidly obese patient desaturates rapidly during induction despite adequate pre-oxygenation. What physiological feature explains this rapid desaturation?
questions.explanation: Obesity reduces functional residual capacity due to a restrictive chest wall effect and abdominal splinting of the diaphragm, shrinking the oxygen reserve available during apnoea. Combined with an increased metabolic rate and oxygen consumption, this leads to much faster desaturation than in a non-obese patient. Positioning in a ramped or head-up position and using apnoeic oxygenation help offset this risk.

questions.question: Why is temperature monitoring considered an essential part of intraoperative monitoring during prolonged general anaesthesia?
