(a) Describe the Bradford method for protein estimation under the headings: principle, preparation of reagent, and colour development.
(b) Explain the clinical significance/advantages that make the Bradford method suitable for rapid protein analysis.
(c) Distinguish between the Bradford method and Immunoturbidimetry/Nephelometry as protein assays.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Principle: relies on interaction between proteins and Coomassie Brilliant Blue G-250 dye; binding of the dye to proteins shifts its absorbance maximum and changes colour from red-brown to blue, measured spectrophotometrically.
• Reagent preparation: Coomassie Brilliant Blue G-250 dye is prepared in a solution typically containing phosphoric acid, methanol and water to form the Bradford reagent.
• Colour development: as the dye binds basic amino acid residues in proteins, a complex forms that absorbs light in the visible spectrum, with blue colour intensity proportional to protein concentration.
(b)
Advantages: the Bradford method is faster than some other protein assays, has a broad dynamic range for various applications, and is relatively tolerant of certain detergents.
(c)
• Bradford relies on dye binding to basic amino acid residues, while immunoturbidimetry/nephelometry rely on antigen-antibody complex formation and turbidity/light scattering.
• Immunoturbidimetry and nephelometry are used for specific proteins such as immunoglobulins and CRP with high sensitivity and specificity, whereas Bradford lacks specificity for certain proteins.
• Immunoturbidimetry/nephelometry can be automated for high-throughput clinical analysis but instruments can be expensive;
• Bradford is simpler and less costly but limited to total protein estimation.
• Limitations of Bradford include interference from reducing agents and detergents, while immunoturbidimetry/nephelometry can be affected by substances interfering with antigen-antibody complex formation.

questions.question:
(a) A patient's Creatine Kinase-MB (CK-MB) isoenzyme result is reported as markedly elevated. Interpret what this finding suggests.
(b) State how CK isoenzymes are classified/reported.
(c) State what this specific isoenzyme elevation indicates clinically.
(d) State the follow-up action.
questions.answerText:
(a)
A markedly elevated CK-MB suggests tissue damage involving the myocardium, since CK-MB is more specific for the myocardium (heart) among the CK isoenzymes.
(b)
CK exists as isoenzymes CK-MM (predominant in skeletal and heart muscle), CK-MB (more specific for myocardium), and CK-BB (predominantly in brain), reflecting the dimeric M and B subunits encoded by separate genetic loci.
(c)
• Total CK elevations are seen after any kind of muscular injury or trauma, and acute myocardial infarction increases total CK;
• CK-MB elevation specifically points toward myocardial (heart) muscle injury such as myocardial infarction, since it is not increased in neurogenic muscle diseases such as myasthenia gravis.
(d)
The finding should be interpreted alongside the clinical picture, since serum CK activity is also influenced by physiologic variations such as sex, age, race, muscle mass and physical activity; correlation with other clinical/laboratory findings and possibly repeat testing is appropriate.

questions.question:
(a) Describe standard solutions and primary standards under the headings: preparation of standard solutions, and characteristics of a primary standard.
(b) Explain the significance of reference materials in the analytical/laboratory process.
(c) Distinguish between primary reference materials and secondary reference materials.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Preparation: a standard solution is prepared by dissolving an accurate weight of a pure material (a primary standard) and diluting to an accurately known volume in a volumetric flask; if the material is not pure, the solution is prepared to an approximate concentration and standardized by titrating a weighed quantity of a primary standard.
• Characteristics of a primary standard: it should be 100% pure; stable to drying temperatures and stable indefinitely at room temperature (it is always dried before weighing); easily and readily available; and should have a high formula weight so that a relatively large amount is weighed, reducing relative weighing error.
(b)
Reference materials are of prime importance in establishing metrologic transferability, defined as the property whereby a measurement result can be related to a reference through a documented unbroken chain of calibrations; they are used for calibrating instruments, validating methods, assigning values to materials, and evaluating comparability of results.
(c)
• Primary reference materials are highly purified chemicals directly weighed or measured to produce a solution of exactly known concentration, with IUPAC proposing a purity degree of 99.98% for primary reference materials.
• Secondary reference materials are solutions whose concentrations cannot be prepared by weighing the solute and dissolving a known amount into a volume of solution.
• The concentration of secondary reference materials is usually determined by analysis of an aliquot of the solution by an acceptable reference method, using a primary reference material to calibrate the method.
• Thus primary reference materials establish concentration directly by weighing, while secondary reference materials require standardization against a primary reference material.

(a)
This is the Biuret method for total protein determination.
(b)
The principle involves complexation of proteins with copper ions in an alkaline environment; coordination of peptide bonds in proteins with copper ions leads to formation of a violet-coloured complex.
(c)
The Biuret reagent (copper sulfate, sodium potassium tartrate, sodium hydroxide) is mixed with the protein sample, initiating the complexation reaction in the alkaline environment; the colour is then quantified spectrophotometrically.
(d)
The intensity of the violet colour is directly proportional to the concentration of protein in the sample, so the measured absorbance is compared against a standard/calibration to determine total protein concentration; the method demonstrates a linear response over a wide range of protein concentrations, allowing accurate quantification, though interference from reducing/chelating agents or non-protein peptide-bond-containing substances should be considered.
questions.question:
(a) A serum sample is treated with an alkaline copper sulfate reagent and develops a violet colour whose intensity is measured spectrophotometrically for total protein estimation. Identify the test being performed.
(b) State the underlying biochemical principle of this test.
(c) Describe the correct procedure/next action after colour development.
(d) State how the result is interpreted.

(a) Describe the general methods of enzyme purification under the headings: precipitation, chromatography (including affinity chromatography), and physical separation methods (ultracentrifugation, gel filtration, ultrafiltration, electrophoresis).
(b) Explain the objectives of enzyme purification.
(c) Distinguish between "salting out" and affinity (ligand-based) purification.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Precipitation: changes in pH, ionic strength or dielectric constant alter solubility (salting out); the salt concentration at which a protein precipitates differs from protein to protein, so salting out can fractionate proteins or concentrate diluted protein.
• Chromatography: includes ion-exchange chromatography (columns of charged beads separating cationic enzymes on anionic columns and vice versa), hydrophobic interaction chromatography (HIC, using matrices such as octyl- or phenyl-Sepharose), and affinity chromatography, which takes advantage of an enzyme's high affinity for a specific chemical group by covalently attaching the group to a column, adding the protein mixture, washing away unbound protein, then eluting the desired protein with a high concentration of the soluble affinity group or altered conditions.
• Physical separation methods: ultracentrifugation spins samples at forces of 100,000-1,000,000 x g to separate molecules by size, mass, density or anisotropy; gel filtration (size-exclusion) separates by molecular size using a gel medium; ultrafiltration uses semipermeable membranes with specific molecular weight cutoffs to retain the enzyme while smaller molecules pass through;; electrophoresis (e.g. SDS-PAGE) separates proteins with migration distance inversely proportional to molecular weight.
(b)
Objectives: to obtain maximum possible yield, maximum catalytic activity, and maximum possible purity; purification is also important for studying an enzyme in a simple system to understand its structure, kinetics, mechanisms and regulation, and for using pure enzyme for medical and industrial purposes.
(c)
• Salting out relies on solubility-based separation: high salt concentrations (commonly ammonium sulfate) promote precipitation as proteins interact via hydrophobic patches while competing with salt for residual water, with different proteins precipitating at different salt concentrations ("cuts").
• Affinity purification relies on the specific binding affinity of the enzyme for a chemical group attached to a chromatography column, rather than general solubility changes.
• Ammonium sulfate is preferred for salting out because it preserves protein activity and promotes precipitation at lower concentrations than other salts, whereas affinity chromatography's key strength is high specificity for the target enzyme.
• Salting out is typically an early, relatively crude fractionation step, while affinity chromatography can achieve high purity in fewer steps due to its specific ligand-based mechanism.

(a)
This is a discrete analyzer; sample identification is usually done by reading the bar code (information can also be entered manually), and the laboratory information system (LIS) then communicates to the analyzer which test(s) have been ordered.
(b)
Discrete analysis is the separation of each sample and its accompanying reagents in a separate container/cuvette; discrete analyzers can run multiple tests on one sample at a time, or multiple samples for one test, and have almost completely replaced continuous-flow and centrifugal analyzers.
(c)
Steps: sample identification and determination of tests to perform; reagent system dispensing into the reaction cuvette; specimen measurement and delivery (a small aliquot introduced into the cuvette); the chemical reaction phase (sample and reagents mixed and incubated); the measurement phase (optical readings initiated before or after all reagents have been added); and signal processing/data handling.
(d)
The analyte concentration is estimated from a calibration curve stored in the analyzer; even with automation, laboratory personnel must still perform specimen preparation/labelling, program the instrument, and observe quality assurance and quality control.
questions.question:
(a) A blood sample is loaded onto an automated discrete clinical chemistry analyzer, and its identity is read by bar code before testing. Identify the type of analyzer and the first steps in its operation.
(b) State the underlying operating principle of this type of analyzer.
(c) Describe the sequence of steps the analyzer follows to produce a result.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Key terms: the substrate is the reactant which binds to the enzyme; the enzyme-substrate complex is a temporary association of enzyme and substrate; the active site is the enzyme's catalytic site into which the substrate fits; the product is the end result of the reaction.
• Steps of the catalytic cycle: (1) the substrate approaches the active site;
• (2) the enzyme-substrate complex is formed;; (3) the substrate transforms into products;; (4) products are released;; (5) the enzyme is recycled; The substrate binds to the enzyme at its active catalytic site to form an activated intermediate enzyme-substrate complex, which is then cleaved into products and the original enzyme.
(b)
The two theories of enzyme-substrate binding are the Lock and Key theory and the Induced Fit theory, both describing how the substrate interacts with the enzyme's active site.
(c)
• The Lock and Key theory, proposed by Fischer in 1894, holds that the active site of the enzyme has a shape complementary (fitting) to the shape of the substrate, similar to a key fitting only its own lock.
• The Induced Fit theory, proposed by Koshland in 1958, is a more flexible model where the catalytic site is not fully formed/complementary to the substrate at first; binding of the substrate induces changes in the shape of the active site, making it more fit for the substrate.
• In the Lock and Key model the enzyme shape is fixed and pre-complementary, whereas in the Induced Fit model the enzyme changes shape upon substrate binding.
• Both theories aim to explain the same catalytic outcome (formation of the enzyme-substrate complex leading to product formation) but differ in whether the active site shape is rigid or flexible/adaptive.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the mechanism of enzyme action under the headings: key terms (substrate, enzyme-substrate complex, active site, product) and the steps of the catalytic cycle.
(b) Explain the two theories of enzyme-substrate binding.
(c) Distinguish between the Lock and Key theory and the Induced Fit theory.

questions.answerText:
(a)
In voltammetry, the magnitude of the limiting current is related to the concentration of the analyte.
(b)
By using standard solutions, or internal standard and standard addition techniques, a quantitative evaluation of the analyte may be carried out from the measured current.
(c)
The current reading indicates the concentration of the analyte (e.g. metal, metal complex, or organic compound) present in the sample, since analytical signal in these electrochemical techniques derives from current.
(d)
The measured current should be compared against standard solutions or evaluated using standard addition/internal standard techniques to determine the actual analyte concentration in the sample.
questions.question:
(a) A voltammetric measurement gives a current reading related to the analyte's concentration. Interpret what this current reading represents.
(b) State how the reading is used to quantitatively evaluate the analyte.
(c) State what the reading indicates about the sample.

(a) Describe the three main types of automated clinical chemistry analyzers (continuous flow, centrifugal, and discrete) under the headings: mechanism of operation.
(b) Explain why automation is used in the clinical chemistry laboratory.
(c) Distinguish between continuous flow analyzers and discrete analyzers.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Continuous flow analyzers: samples are aspirated into tubing, reagent is introduced, a chemical reaction occurs, and the chromogen solution is pumped into a flow-through cuvette for spectrophotometric analysis; the first "AutoAnalyzer" was a continuous-flow, single-channel, sequential batch analyzer providing about 40 samples per hour, and later multi-channel analyzers produced 6 or 12 results simultaneously at 360-720 tests per hour.
• Centrifugal analyzers: discrete aliquots of specimens and reagents are pipetted into discrete chambers in a rotor; specimens are analysed in parallel by spinning the rotor, using centrifugal force to transfer and mix aliquots into radially located cuvettes, with rotary motion moving the cuvettes through the optical path; Discrete analyzers: separate each sample and its reagents in a separate container/cuvette/cell/slide/well, disposed of after analysis;; they can run multiple tests on one sample or multiple samples on one test, and have almost completely replaced continuous-flow and centrifugal analyzers.
(b)
Reasons for automation: increase the number of tests performed by one person in a given period; minimize variations in results from one person to another; minimize errors found in manual analyses (e.g. equipment/pipette variations); and use less sample and reagent for each test.
(c)
• Continuous flow analyzers use tubing to flow reagents and patient samples together, with the major drawbacks of significant carry-over problems and wasteful continuous reagent flow that contributed to their eventual decline.
• Discrete analyzers keep sample reactions discrete through separate reaction cuvettes, cells, slides or wells that are disposed of after analysis, minimizing sample and reaction carryover but increasing cost per test due to disposable products.
• Discrete analyzers have the capability of running multiple tests on one sample at a time or multiple samples on one test, whereas continuous flow analyzers process samples sequentially through shared tubing/channels.
• Even with automation, basic steps remain: specimen preparation and identification (e.g. by bar code), labelling, instrument programming, and laboratory personnel performing quality assurance and quality control.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the Beer-Lambert law under the headings: derivation/components (Beer's law and Lambert's law), and the equation and its terms.
(b) Explain the significance/applications of the Beer-Lambert law in analytical work.
(c) Distinguish between absorbance (transmission) photometry and reflectance photometry.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Components: the Beer-Lambert law is a combination of two laws;
• Beer's law states that concentration and absorbance are directly proportional, while Lambert's law states that absorbance and path length are directly proportional.
• When monochromatic radiation passes through a homogeneous medium, the rate of decrease in intensity of transmitted radiation with increasing thickness and concentration of the solution varies directly with the intensity of incident radiation.
• Equation: A = εbc, where A = absorption, ε = molar absorption coefficient (molar absorptivity), b = thickness of the medium in cm, and c = molar concentration.
(b)
The Beer-Lambert law is used in modern-day laboratories for testing medicines, organic chemistry and quantification tests, helping define the relationship between the intensity of visible/UV radiation and the exact quantity of substance present.
(c)
• The electro-optical components used in reflectance photometry are essentially the same as those required for absorbance photometry, except that the geometry is modified so that the light source and detector are located next to each other on one side of the sample, as opposed to on opposite sides of the sample cuvette as in absorption photometry.
• In reflectance photometry, diffuse reflected light is measured: the reaction mixture in a carrier is illuminated with diffused light, and the intensity of light reflected from the chromogen is compared with light reflected from a reference surface, expressed as %R = Is/Ir x R.
• Absorbance (transmission) photometry measures light transmitted through the sample in a cuvette, following the Beer-Lambert relationship between absorbance, concentration and path length.
• Reflectance photometry is the principle underlying dry/solid-phase chemistry reagent slides, while absorbance photometry underlies conventional wet chemistry reactions.

(a)
• Enzyme activation refers to enzymes becoming more active or catalytically efficient in response to certain conditions or stimuli, and its clinical measurement is used as a diagnostic tool to assess organ function.
• Examples: protein kinase activation in cell signalling pathways (growth, proliferation, apoptosis); coagulation cascade activation involving enzymes such as thrombin and factor Xa forming blood clots; digestive enzyme activation (proteases, lipases, amylases) breaking down food;; immune system enzyme activation (proteases and reactive oxygen species generators in neutrophils, macrophages, natural killer cells) killing invading microorganisms;; and metabolic enzyme activation (e.g. hexokinase, glucokinase, lipoprotein lipase) regulating glucose and lipid metabolism.
(b)
• Abnormal activation of protein kinases is implicated in diseases including cancer, and targeted therapies such as tyrosine kinase inhibitors rely on manipulating these pathways.
• Dysregulation of the coagulation cascade can lead to thrombotic disorders such as deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism, managed with anticoagulants like heparin or warfarin.
• Dysfunction or insufficient activation of digestive enzymes can lead to pancreatic insufficiency or lactose intolerance, managed with enzyme replacement therapy.
• Dysregulated immune enzyme activation can contribute to tissue damage in inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis or inflammatory bowel disease; Dysregulated metabolic enzyme activation or deficiency can lead to diabetes mellitus or hyperlipidaemia.
(c)
• Enzyme activation is a process where enzymes become more active or catalytically efficient in response to conditions or stimuli, while enzyme repression is a regulatory mechanism involving inhibition or reduction of enzyme synthesis or activity in response to certain signals or conditions.
• Enzyme repression occurs in response to cellular environment signals and often involves downregulation of enzyme synthesis at the level of gene expression, whereas activation examples given involve post-translational or signalling-mediated increases in enzyme activity (e.g. Akt activation via insulin receptor binding).
• Both processes are essential for physiological homeostasis: activation increases enzymatic output when needed (e.g. digestion, coagulation, immune defence), while repression reduces enzymatic output to prevent overproduction or adapt to changing conditions.
• Both mechanisms are used clinically/diagnostically: activation is assessed to evaluate organ function and disease response, while repression concepts such as feedback inhibition help explain conditions like diabetes and chronic liver disease.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the general characteristics of enzyme activation as a regulatory mechanism, giving examples from different physiological systems.
(b) Explain how abnormal/dysregulated activation in these systems relates to specific diseases.
(c) Distinguish between enzyme activation and enzyme repression as regulatory mechanisms.

(a) A mixture of proteins needs to be separated based on differing molecular size using porous beads in a column. Identify the appropriate technique.
(b) State its underlying principle.
(c) State the materials/stationary phase required.
(d) State common sources of error or limitations of this technique.
(e) State a precaution to ensure effective separation.
questions.answerText:
(a)
This is gel filtration (size-exclusion/molecular-sieve) chromatography.
(b)
Principle: separation is based on the differing ability of molecules to enter the pores of the gel-filtration medium, due to differing molecular size; molecules larger than the pores move quickly through the column, while smaller molecules enter the pores and move more slowly, eluting in order of decreasing molecular size.
(c)
Materials: the stationary phase consists of beads of a hydrated, sponge-like cross-linked polymer material (e.g. Dextran/Sephadex for small peptides and globular proteins, or Agarose for large globular proteins/long linear molecules), with pores of molecular dimensions and a narrow range of sizes.
(d)
Limitations: because none of the proteins is retained by the column, the absence of binding limits the resolution of the chromatography, which is at the same time a weakness of the technique (although it is a strength for not damaging fragile protein function).
(e)
The correct type of gel should be selected according to the molecular weight range of the target protein, since the pore size (and hence exclusion limit) differs between gel types such as Sephadex and Agarose.

questions.question:
(a) A urine specimen is tested on a reagent pad impregnated with glucose oxidase, peroxidase, potassium iodide, and a blue dye. Identify the test performed and its principle.
(b) State the materials/reagents present on the pad.
(c) State common sources of error with this test.
(d) State a precaution to be observed when performing this test.
questions.answerText:
(a)
This is the dry-chemistry reagent-strip test for measurement of glucose in urine; the reaction employs glucose oxidase and peroxidase to produce hydrogen peroxide, which is subsequently reduced with concurrent oxidation of potassium iodide to release iodine; the free iodine blends with the background colour to produce a range of colours from green to dark brown.
(b)
Materials/reagents: the reagent pad is impregnated with glucose oxidase, peroxidase, potassium iodide, and a blue dye.
(c)
Sources of error: the urine sample must be fresh, as with all reagent strip testing; the general precautions for reagent strip testing apply (mixing well before testing, complete but brief immersion of reagent areas, and avoiding contamination between adjacent reagent pads).
(d)
Testing should be performed on fresh urine collected in a clean, dry container, and the strip should be handled and read according to the standard precautions (horizontal handling, immediate removal after immersion) to avoid inaccurate colour development.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the classification of proteins/enzymes according to organic and inorganic cofactors, distinguishing coenzymes from prosthetic groups.
(b) Explain the general role/function of a coenzyme.
(c) Distinguish between simple protein enzymes and complex protein enzymes (apoenzyme, cofactor, holoenzyme).
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Some enzymes require no chemical groups for activity other than their amino acid residues; others require an additional non-protein chemical component called a cofactor.
• Cofactors are divided into organic cofactors (such as flavin or heme, with molecular mass typically <1000 Da, loosely or tightly bound and directly participating in the reaction) and inorganic cofactors (such as metal ions Mg2+, Cu2+, Mn2+, or iron-sulfur clusters).
• Loosely bound organic cofactors are termed coenzymes: freely diffusing organic compounds that function as cofactors in promoting metabolic reactions, bound to the enzyme's active site to aid function; coenzymes directly involved and altered in the reaction are considered a type of secondary substrate; A prosthetic group, by contrast (as described in enzyme mechanism content), is inorganic, thermo-stable, and firmly attached to the enzyme (e.g. Ca, Zn), whereas a coenzyme is organic, thermo-labile and loosely attached (e.g. vitamin derivatives such as FAD, NAD).
(b)
The function of coenzymes is to transport chemical groups between enzymes: hydride ions carried by coenzymes such as NAD, phosphate groups carried by coenzymes such as ATP, and acetyl groups carried by coenzymes such as coenzyme A; the coenzyme is essential for the biological activity of the enzyme, since a coenzyme is a low molecular weight organic substance without which the enzyme cannot exhibit any reaction, and one molecule of coenzyme can convert a large number of substrate molecules with the help of the enzyme.
(c)
• Simple protein enzymes are made up of only proteins.
• Complex protein enzymes are made up of protein and a non-protein part; the protein part is known as the apoenzyme, the non-protein part is known as the cofactor, and the whole (protein plus cofactor) is known as the holoenzyme.
• The cofactor of a complex protein enzyme may itself be a coenzyme or a prosthetic group.
• Enzymes are also classified according to the theory of enzyme-substrate binding: simple lock-and-key binding (Fischer, 1894, where the active site shape is complementary to the substrate) versus induced-fit binding (Koshland, 1958, where substrate binding induces a shape change in the active site to make it more fit for the substrate).

questions.question:
(a) Describe enzyme repression under the headings: regulation of enzyme synthesis, feedback inhibition, and transcriptional repression.
(b) Explain how enzyme repression contributes to metabolic regulation and cellular adaptation, with a clinical example.
(c) Distinguish between inducible enzyme systems and constitutively repressed systems as described for enzyme repression.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Regulation of enzyme synthesis: enzyme repression involves downregulation of synthesis of specific enzymes at the level of gene expression, where genetic information for producing enzymes is inhibited or reduced; example given is insulin promoting glucose uptake via GLUT4 and activation of protein kinase B (Akt), and in diabetes mellitus reduced insulin causes impaired glucose uptake.
• Feedback inhibition: the end product of a metabolic pathway acts as an inhibitor of an earlier enzyme in that pathway; when the end product accumulates it binds to the allosteric site of the enzyme, causing a conformational change that inhibits activity, preventing overproduction and maintaining homeostasis;; in diabetes, elevated blood glucose triggers increased insulin production, which inhibits enzymes involved in gluconeogenesis; Transcriptional repression: occurs when regulatory proteins or repressor molecules bind specific DNA sequences near the gene of interest, hindering recruitment or activity of RNA polymerase, and can involve chromatin remodelling (making DNA packaging less accessible) and co-repressor proteins that enhance the inhibitory effect.
(b)
• Enzyme repression allows cells to adapt to changing environmental conditions by optimizing metabolic pathways according to substrate availability and demand.
• Example: in chronic liver disease, destruction of liver cells leads to fibrosis and loss of liver function; in response to chronic injury, enzymes are repressed, leading to reduced albumin and coagulation factor synthesis, and transcriptional repression in hepatocytes can decrease albumin synthesis, contributing to hypoalbuminaemia affecting fluid regulation and metabolic function.
(c)
• Inducible systems are those where the presence of a specific substrate induces synthesis of the enzymes required for its metabolism; example given is drug metabolism by cytochrome P450, where regular exposure to a drug (its substrate) induces hepatic synthesis of the enzyme.
• Conversely, when the substrate is not available or is in excess, repression mechanisms may prevent unnecessary enzyme production.
• Feedback inhibition is a related repression mechanism where accumulation of an end product represses an earlier pathway enzyme, differing from substrate-induced systems where the substrate's presence increases (induces) enzyme synthesis rather than repressing it.
• Enzyme repression is described as important in lipid metabolism, e.g. in atherosclerosis where cholesterol accumulation may lead to repression of enzymes involved in cholesterol synthesis to prevent further plaque formation, illustrating a further example of feedback-type regulation.

(a)
This is potentiometry; the principle is that potentiometry measures the potential developed by a cell consisting of an indicator electrode and a reference electrode, with the indicator electrode response measuring the activity of the analyte, and the cell potential measured under negligible current flow (currents around 1 picoampere with modern potentiometers) to avoid significant changes in analyte concentration.
(b)
Materials/electrodes: an indicator (working) electrode sensitive to the analyte's activity, and a reference/counter electrode whose potential ideally remains constant so that any change in overall cell potential is attributed to the working electrode; in dynamic conditions, a separate reference electrode (no current flow) and auxiliary electrode (carries current) may be used instead of a simple counter electrode.
(c)
A source of error would arise if the reference/counter electrode's potential changes over time (as can happen in dynamic methods where passage of current changes species concentrations in the cell), causing inaccurate attribution of potential change to the working electrode.
(d)
This problem is eliminated by replacing a simple counter electrode with two electrodes: a reference electrode through which no current flows and whose potential remains constant, and an auxiliary electrode that completes the circuit and carries the current.
questions.question:
(a) A serum sample's pH is measured using an electrode system consisting of an indicator electrode and a reference electrode, under negligible current flow. Identify the technique and its principle.
(b) State the materials/electrodes required.
(c) State a source of error in this measurement.
(d) State a precaution to reduce this error.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• A solution is a homogeneous mixture of one or more solutes dispersed molecularly in a sufficient quantity of a dissolving solvent, and may be gaseous, liquid or solid; in laboratory practice, solutes are typically measured and are frequently referred to as analytes or measurands.
• A mole is a unit defined for the amount of substance (SI unit "mol"), representing the mass of a substance containing the same number of fundamental units (atoms, molecules or formula units) as in 12.0 grams of ¹²C; it is the basis of stoichiometry; Normality (N) is the equivalent concentration of a solution, described as the number of gram or mole equivalents of solute present in one litre of solution, mainly used for reactive species and acid-base/titration reactions.
(b)
Many analyses in the clinical laboratory concern the presence or concentration of substances in solutions such as blood, serum, urine, or spinal fluid; a meaningful measurement is expressed with both a number and a unit, where the unit identifies the dimension (mass, volume, or concentration) and the number indicates how many units are contained; factors affecting the analytical process and clinical laboratory operation include knowledge of the concept of solute and solvent, units of measurement, chemicals, reference materials and basic techniques.
(c)
• Molality describes the moles of solute in relation to the mass of a solvent, while molarity is concerned with the moles of solute in relation to the volume of a solution; the primary difference between molarity and molality comes down to mass versus volume.
• Molarity of a solution is the number of moles of solute present in one litre of its solution (Molarity = number of moles of solute / volume of solution in litres).
• Normality is described as the number of gram or mole equivalents of solute present in one litre of solution, mainly used as a measure of reactive species during titration reactions, particularly acid-base chemistry.
• Thus molarity, molality and normality all express concentration but differ in their reference quantity: volume of solution (molarity), mass of solvent (molality), or gram-equivalents of reactive species per litre (normality).
questions.question:
(a) Describe the general characteristics/classification of solutions and the units used to express their concentration (mole, molarity, molality, normality).
(b) Explain why understanding solute/solvent concepts and units of measurement is important to the clinical laboratory analytical process.
(c) Distinguish between molarity and molality, and between molarity and normality.

questions.answerText:
(a)
The endpoint is the point at which the reaction between the titrant and analyte is essentially finished; the volume of titrant added corresponds to the endpoint, which is an approximation of the true equivalence point, and is used to calculate the amount of analyte.
(b)
The analyte concentration is calculated using the formula Ca = Ct x Vt x M / Va, where Ct is the titrant concentration, Vt is the volume of titrant used, M is the mole ratio of the analyte, and Va is the volume of the analyte.
(c)
The calculated concentration (Ca) indicates the amount/concentration of the unknown analyte originally present in the specimen.
(d)
Because a single drop of titrant can make the difference between a permanent and transitory colour change and other sources of error (temperature, calibration) can affect precision, the titration should ideally be repeated to confirm the result and check reproducibility.
questions.question:
(a) At the end of a titration, the volume of titrant used to reach the colour-change endpoint is recorded. Interpret what this endpoint volume represents.
(b) State the formula used to calculate the analyte concentration from this reading.
(c) State what the result indicates about the specimen.
(d) State the follow-up action for confirming the result.

questions.answerText:
(a)
This is gel/zone electrophoresis; the principle is that charged molecules in solution (chiefly proteins and nucleic acids) migrate in response to an electrical field, with rate of migration depending on field strength, net charge, size and shape of the molecules, and the ionic strength, viscosity and temperature of the medium.
(b)
Materials/apparatus: cellulose or polymeric gel as the supporting medium, an enclosed tank with electrodes and buffer reservoirs, and a dc power supply; suitable buffers include Tris Borate EDTA (TBE), Tris Acetate EDTA (TAE), Tris Phosphate EDTA (TPE) for DNA, or sodium phosphate buffer for RNA.
(c)
Molecules collect or form bands in the gel according to their speed of migration, which depends on charge, size, shape and the medium; in SDS-PAGE, the distance a protein migrates is inversely proportional to its molecular weight, so band position can be used to characterise or identify the separated proteins or nucleic acids.
questions.question:
(a) A protein sample is subjected to electrophoresis, and separated bands are visualised under an applied electric field. Identify the technique and its principle.
(b) State the materials/apparatus required.
(c) State how the result (the position/pattern of bands) is interpreted.

questions.answerText:
(a)
This is volumetric titration (titrimetric analysis); its principle is that the standard solution is added gradually to the sample containing an unknown concentration of reactant until the reactant is consumed at the equivalence point, with indicators used to identify the endpoint.
(b)
Materials/apparatus: burette, pipette, measuring flasks, measuring cylinders, flask for general titration, beaker, tile, glass rod, funnel, weighing bottle, wash bottle, and a weighing machine with a chemical balance.
(c)
Sources of error: changes in temperature cause changes in the volume of glass apparatus and liquids (e.g. an ordinary 1000ml glass flask increases by 0.025ml per °C); there may be errors of calibration where the marked volume is not the true volume; pH, temperature and humidity may affect results since it is an open system; and human error may occur during processing.
(d)
These errors can be eliminated only by recalibrating the apparatus, and care should be taken to add the titrant in small amounts near the expected endpoint, since a single drop or less can make the difference between a permanent and a transitory colour change.
questions.question:
(a) A specimen containing an unknown analyte concentration is analysed by adding a standard titrant from a burette until a colour-change endpoint is reached. Identify the technique and its principle.
(b) State the materials/apparatus required.
(c) State common sources of error in this procedure.
(d) State a precaution taken to minimize these errors.

(a) Describe polarography under the headings: principle, and instrumentation (the three electrodes involved).
(b) Explain the applications and disadvantages of polarography.
(c) Distinguish between polarography and potentiometry.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Principle: involves measurement of the current flowing in an electrolysis cell due to oxidation-reduction reactions of the analyte, usually occurring at the surface of one electrode; the current produced is directly proportional to the concentration of the analyte.
• Instrumentation: the working electrode (a dropping mercury electrode, DME) is where oxidation/reduction of the analyte occurs; the reference electrode is a silver-silver chloride (Ag/AgCl) type electrode crucial for controlling the working electrode's potential; the auxiliary (counter) electrode carries the bulk of the current, placed in a separate chamber with a fritted glass disc to allow electrical contact without diffusion of undesirable species to the working electrode.
(b)
• Applications: widely used for quantitative and qualitative determination of metals, metal complexes, and organic compounds at trace levels.
• Disadvantages: measurements are very sensitive to solution composition, dissolved oxygen and capillary characteristics; impurities in the background electrolyte also affect sensitivity.
(c)
• Polarography measures current resulting from redox reactions at the dropping mercury electrode as a function of applied potential, whereas potentiometry measures potential under negligible current flow using an indicator and reference electrode.
• Polarography's principal analytical signal is current, while potentiometry's principal analytical signal is potential.
• Polarography uses a background (excess) electrolyte to bring the electrode process potential to the desired range and eliminate interference, a feature not emphasised in basic potentiometric setups.
• Both are interfacial electrochemical methods, but potentiometry is a static method (no current flows) while polarography is a dynamic method in which current passage changes concentrations in the cell.

(a)
• Principle: based on the reduction of Folin-Ciocalteu reagent by amino acid residues in proteins under alkaline conditions, leading to formation of a blue colour measured spectrophotometrically.
• Reagent preparation: made by mixing copper sulfate, sodium potassium tartrate, and Folin-Ciocalteu phenol reagent to form the working reagent.
• Procedure: protein sample is mixed with the Lowry reagent and incubated at room temperature; the reduction of Folin-Ciocalteu reagent produces a blue colour proportional to protein concentration.
• Advantages/limitations: more sensitive than the Biuret method and broadly applicable to various sample types for routine and research purposes; limitations include interference from detergents and reducing agents, and time-consuming reagent preparation.
(b)
The Lowry method is more sensitive than the Biuret method, allowing detection of lower protein concentrations, and its broad applicability makes it suitable for both routine and research purposes.
(c)
• The Bradford method relies on the interaction between proteins and Coomassie Brilliant Blue G-250 dye, producing a colour shift from red-brown to blue, whereas Lowry depends on reduction of Folin-Ciocalteu reagent producing a blue colour.
• Bradford is faster than other protein assays and has a broad dynamic range, while Lowry reagent preparation is time-consuming.
• Bradford is relatively tolerant of certain detergents, whereas detergents interfere with the Lowry reaction.
• Both methods lack full protein specificity, but Bradford's dye-binding lacks specificity for certain proteins leading to variable responses among protein types.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the Lowry method for protein determination under the headings: principle, reagent preparation, procedure, and advantages/limitations.
(b) Explain why the Lowry method is preferred for certain applications in protein estimation.
(c) Distinguish between the Lowry method and the Bradford method.

questions.answerText:
(a)
This is the dry-chemistry reagent-strip test for detection of hemoglobin in urine; the reagent pad impregnated with buffered tetramethylbenzidine (TMB) and an organic peroxide reacts to give a colour change ranging from orange to pale to dark green in the presence of hemoglobin.
(b)
Procedure: collect a fresh urine specimen in a clean, dry, labelled container; mix well immediately before testing; completely immerse the reagent areas of the strip in the fresh urine and remove immediately to avoid dissolving out the reagent; hold the strip horizontally to prevent mixing of chemicals from adjacent reagent pads or contamination of hands with urine.
(c)
The test detects red cells or free hemoglobin together with myoglobin, and is equally sensitive to hemoglobin and myoglobin, so a negative result excludes myoglobinuria; water must not be used as a negative control with this test, as a false-positive result will be obtained.
questions.question:
(a) A fresh urine specimen is tested on a reagent strip pad impregnated with buffered tetramethylbenzidine (TMB) and an organic peroxide, producing a colour change from orange toward green. Identify the test and its principle.
(b) Describe the correct procedure for performing this test.
(c) State how the result should be interpreted, including an important exclusion the test allows.

questions.answerText:
(a)
The likely underlying process is hepatocellular destruction/damage, since AST and ALT are enzymes reflecting hepatocellular injury, such as viral hepatitis.
(b)
• AST catalyses the reversible transfer of an alpha-amino group between aspartate and glutamate, and ALT catalyses the reversible transfer of an alpha-amino group between alanine and glutamate;
• AST and ALT are cytosolic/tissue enzymes whose levels rise in serum when hepatocyte membrane integrity is disrupted, releasing these enzymes; elevated levels are often seen before patients develop symptoms and are usually elevated in multiples of the upper limit of normal.
(c)
AST and ALT are measured as part of the liver function test (LFT) panel, with quantification methods described as commonly using spectrophotometric enzyme assays (per general enzyme measurement principles), and ALT has greater specificity for liver disease than AST since AST is also found in the liver, kidney, skeletal muscle, myocardium, pancreas and red blood cells.
(d)
An AST/ALT ratio >5 is associated with extrahepatic causes; a ratio >2 is associated with alcoholic hepatitis; the associated conditions listed also include hepatocellular carcinoma and early-stage viral hepatitis; because ALT is more liver-specific, the pattern and ratio of AST and ALT together help refine the differential diagnosis of the hepatic condition.
questions.question:
(a) A liver function test panel shows elevated ALT and AST in a patient, with the AST/ALT ratio calculated. Identify the likely underlying process.
(b) State the biochemical basis for the enzyme elevation.
(c) State the test/assay principle used to measure these enzymes.
(d) Interpret the result using the stated AST/ALT ratio associations.

(a) Describe volumetric titration (titrimetric analysis) under the headings: principle, types of titrations, and procedure.
(b) Explain the advantages and disadvantages of volumetric titration.
(c) Distinguish between volumetric titrimetry and gravimetric/coulometric titrimetry.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Principle: the standard solution is added gradually to the sample containing an unknown concentration of reactant until the reactant is consumed (stoichiometric completion, the equivalence point); indicators are used to identify the endpoint, and titrations are commonly used in acid-base reactions to determine the amount of analyte.
• Types: titration is divided into four types depending on the nature of the chemical reaction: acid-base/neutralization methods, oxidation-reduction (redox) methods, precipitation methods, and complexometric titrations.
• Other classifications include simple titration, back titration, and double titration; Procedure: an accurately weighed sample is analysed;; the correct titrant is chosen;; small amounts of titrant are added to the analyte and indicator until colour change occurs at the endpoint;; titration continues until the reaction is finished;; molarity of the standard solution is used to calculate moles present;; the endpoint volume is used with the formula Ca = Ct x Vt x M / Va to calculate analyte concentration.
(b)
Advantages: simple and cost-effective; does not require sophisticated skill; rapid and gives accurate results; the reaction can be identified visually at the endpoint; Disadvantages: pH, temperature and humidity may affect results (open system);; human error may occur;; an indicator is required;; it can produce large volumes of chemical waste;; reactions must occur in the liquid phase.
(c)
• Volumetric titration determines the amount of analyte by measuring the volume of a standard solution needed for a quantitative reaction with the analyte, whereas the titrimetric method more broadly includes volumetric, gravimetric and coulometric titrimetry.
• Volumetric titration relies on volume measurement and a visible/instrumental endpoint, while gravimetric methods (such as electrogravimetry, an electrochemical method) rely on weighing the substance deposited from a reaction.
• Coulometric titrimetry belongs to the electrochemical methods where the analyte is determined by quantitative reaction at an electrode during electrolysis (coulometry), rather than by volume of titrant.
• Volumetric analysis was first devised by Jean-Baptiste-André Dumas and remains commonly used due to its high precision, accuracy, ease of use and low cost compared to these other titrimetric approaches.

(a)
• Coenzymes involved in hydrogen transfer reactions include nicotinamide nucleotides (NAD+ and NADP+), which are coenzymes of dehydrogenases catalysing oxidation-reduction reactions, all reversible.
• Coenzymes involved in group transfer include biotin (belonging to the vitamin B group), an essential growth factor for yeast and other microorganisms and also required by higher organisms, which is water-soluble and participates in transfer of the carboxyl group.
• Other important coenzymes named are Coenzyme A, Flavin Adenine Dinucleotide (FAD), and Adenosine Triphosphate (ATP).
(b)
Salient features: coenzymes are heat stable; they are low-molecular-weight substances; they combine loosely with the enzyme molecule and so can be separated easily by dialysis; when the reaction is completed, the coenzyme is released from the apoenzyme and goes to another reaction site; Relationship to vitamins: many coenzymes are closely related to vitamins and are important growth factors;; coenzymes are the precursors of vitamins, and a vitamin is a main component of a coenzyme endowed with biocatalytic functions.
(c)
• NAD (Nicotinamide Adenine Dinucleotide) is composed of two nucleotides, adenine and nicotinamide, held together by a pair of phosphate groups and bonded to a ribose sugar each; its function is to carry electrons from one enzyme-controlled reaction to another, existing as NAD+ (oxidizing agent, accepts electrons) or NADH (reducing agent, donates electrons).
• FAD (Flavin Adenine Dinucleotide) is composed of an adenine nucleotide, a ribose sugar and two phosphate groups; it can also exist as a monophosphate called flavin adenine mononucleotide (FMN); like NAD it is involved in redox reactions and can exist in two redox states, FAD and FADH; Both NAD and FAD are organic cofactors involved in electron/hydrogen transfer in redox reactions catalysed by dehydrogenases, but they differ in their nucleotide composition (nicotinamide-based versus flavin-based); An example of a NAD-dependent enzyme is alcohol dehydrogenase, which uses NAD+ as coenzyme to convert ethanol to ethanal, removing two hydrogen ions and two electrons from ethanol and converting NAD+ to NADH + H+.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the general classification of coenzymes according to the chemical group they transfer, giving named examples.
(b) Explain the salient features of coenzymes and their relationship to vitamins.
(c) Distinguish between NAD/NADP and FAD as hydrogen-transferring coenzymes.

(a) Describe isoelectric precipitation and solvent precipitation as protein fractionation methods under the headings: mechanism and relevant examples.
(b) Explain the significance of the isoelectric point in protein solubility and electrophoretic behaviour.
(c) Distinguish between solvent precipitation and heat treatment as methods of selective protein removal.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Isoelectric precipitation: solubility of proteins depends on ionic strength and pH; if pH approaches the pI of a protein the net charge goes to zero, and in the absence of electrostatic repulsion, weak electrostatic attractive forces may lead to aggregation and precipitation; this tendency can be promoted by reducing ionic strength or adding organic solvent.
• Example: the milk protein β-lactoglobulin has a pI of about 5.3; at or below this pH behaviour changes markedly in solubility.
• Solvent precipitation: used historically in early protein isolation, especially fractionation of plasma proteins, using ethanol or acetone;; the mechanism is reduction of water activity (availability of water for protein solvation), most likely to occur at the pI;; the order of precipitation is largely determined by protein size; Disadvantages include flammability (acetone) and easy denaturation of proteins at temperatures above 0°C;; a variant is PEG precipitation (20%, molecular weight 4000 or greater).
(b)
Protein is unable to migrate in an electrical field (electrophoresis) since it exhibits electrical neutrality at its isoelectric point; at pH above the pI the protein takes on a negative charge (excess hydroxide removes protein from the amino radical, net charge -1), while at pH below the pI the excess proton protonates the carboxyl group (net charge +1); solubility is minimal at the isoelectric point due to electrostatic and van der Waals interactions promoting clumping.
(c)
• Solvent precipitation reduces water activity using organic solvents such as ethanol or acetone, most likely acting near the protein's isoelectric point, and can easily denature proteins if conducted above 0°C.
• Heat treatment brings about selective denaturation of contaminant proteins in isolated cases, using heat, extremes of pH, and organic solvents (e.g. isolation of calmodulin from brain extracts by boiling).
• Heat treatment may result in chemical modification of the desired protein and is therefore not recommended, whereas solvent precipitation's main risk is denaturation from elevated temperature during the procedure rather than the heat itself being the separating agent.
• Both are precipitation-based fractionation techniques, but solvent precipitation is a variant historically popular for plasma protein fractionation, while heat treatment is used only in selected/isolated cases due to its denaturation risk.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the "salting out" (ammonium sulfate precipitation) technique for protein fractionation under the headings: mechanism, choice of salt, and procedure.
(b) Explain the significance of this technique in fractionating proteins in solution.
(c) Distinguish between salting out and isoelectric precipitation.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Mechanism: high salt concentrations promote precipitation; with increasing ionic strength, proteins begin to interact via hydrophobic patches on their surface as proteins and salt compete for residual water.
• Choice of salt: ammonium sulfate is the salt of choice since it preserves protein activity and promotes precipitation at lower concentrations than other salts; phosphate is theoretically better but ruled out because trivalent phosphate occurs only at extremely low pH, sodium sulfate and many potassium salts are not sufficiently soluble, many multivalent cations are toxic, and potassium phosphate at fairly low concentration is too dense to allow the precipitate to settle.
• Procedure: increasing amounts of ammonium sulfate are added to the extract with intermittent centrifugation steps, referred to as ammonium sulfate "cuts";; solid ammonium sulfate should be added slowly while stirring, in powdered form, to allow uniform concentration increase and rapid equilibration.
(b)
This procedure takes advantage of the differential solubility of proteins under varying conditions and the high protein concentration of the solution, permitting protein aggregates to form over minutes to hours; precipitation of one group of proteins permits their separation from other proteins remaining in solution by low-speed centrifugation.
(c)
• Salting out precipitates proteins by increasing ionic strength so that proteins compete with salt for water and interact via hydrophobic patches, whereas isoelectric precipitation occurs when pH approaches a protein's isoelectric point (pI), where net charge goes to zero and weak electrostatic attractive forces lead to aggregation.
• Isoelectric precipitation tendency can be promoted by reducing ionic strength or adding organic solvent, whereas salting out specifically requires increasing salt concentration.
• At very low ionic strength, like-charged particles repel strongly and unlike-charged particles attract strongly; as ionic strength increases, the counterion atmosphere shrinks and screening becomes effective, explaining why increasing salt concentration ("salting in") can actually increase solubility even at the isoelectric point.
• Solubility of a protein is minimal at its isoelectric point due to these electrostatic interactions and van der Waals forces causing clumping, which is the basis of isoelectric precipitation, distinct from the competitive dehydration mechanism of salting out.

(a)
• Reaction scheme: E + S ⇌ ES → E + P, where E is enzyme, S is substrate, ES is the enzyme-substrate complex, P is product, k1 is the rate constant for the forward reaction, k-1 for breakdown of ES back to substrate, and k2 for formation of products.
• Assumptions: the ES complex is in rapid equilibrium with free enzyme; breakdown of ES to form product is slower than formation of the ES complex and breakdown of ES back to E and S; the reaction quickly achieves a steady state in which [ES] remains approximately constant over time (the steady-state assumption, Briggs and Haldane 1925), following an initial pre-steady-state period lasting microseconds; Equation: V0 = Vmax[S] / (Km + [S]), where V0 is initial reaction velocity, Vmax is maximum reaction velocity when all active sites are saturated, [S] is substrate concentration, and Km is the substrate concentration at which V0 = Vmax/2, reflecting the enzyme's affinity for its substrate.
(b)
Significance: quantifies enzyme-substrate interactions and how reaction rate depends on substrate concentration; determines kinetic parameters Vmax and Km, offering insight into enzyme efficiency and substrate binding affinity; predicts enzyme behaviour with changing substrate concentration; forms a basis for enzyme classification by Km values and mechanisms;; and is important in drug design and enzyme inhibition, since drugs can target active sites or modulate Km.
(c)
• The Michaelis-Menten plot is a curve showing reaction velocity versus substrate concentration at a fixed enzyme concentration, showing saturation kinetics approaching Vmax.
• The Lineweaver-Burk plot is a linear representation obtained by taking the reciprocal of both sides of the Michaelis-Menten equation, expressed as 1/v = (Km/Vmax)(1/[S]) + 1/Vmax.
• The Lineweaver-Burk (double reciprocal) plot is described as more accurate and convenient for determining Vmax and Km than reading them from the curved Michaelis-Menten plot.
• Both describe the same underlying kinetic relationship, but the linear Lineweaver-Burk form facilitates graphical determination of the kinetic constants.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the Michaelis-Menten model of enzyme kinetics under the headings: the reaction scheme, assumptions, and the equation with its terms.
(b) Explain the significance of the Michaelis-Menten equation in enzyme kinetics.
(c) Distinguish between the Michaelis-Menten plot and the Lineweaver-Burk (double reciprocal) plot.

(a) Describe the factors influencing the rate of enzyme-catalysed reactions, focusing on enzyme concentration and substrate concentration.
(b) Explain the effects of temperature and pH on enzyme activity.
(c) Distinguish between first-order and zero-order kinetics as they apply to enzyme-catalysed reactions at low versus high substrate concentration.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Enzyme concentration: the equilibrium reaction between enzyme and substrate is assumed to be rapid compared with breakdown of ES into free enzyme and product; the rate of reaction is proportional to the concentration of the ES complex; in the presence of excess substrate, adding more enzyme increases the ES complex concentration and overall reaction rate, forming the basis for quantitative determination of enzymes by measuring reaction rates.
• Substrate concentration: when enzyme concentration is fixed and substrate concentration is varied, at low substrate concentration the rate is almost directly proportional to substrate concentration (first order);; at high substrate concentration the reaction becomes zero order, as the entire enzyme is bound to substrate and the maximum possible velocity (Vmax) has been reached, so no further increase in complex concentration or rate is possible.
(b)
Temperature: reaction rate is proportional to reaction temperature because increased temperature increases molecular motion and the number of reactions; however, temperature that is too high denatures the enzyme's protein structure and slows or stops the reaction; enzymes are most active at an optimum temperature, usually 37°C in humans, show little activity at low temperature, and lose activity at high temperature due to denaturation. pH: the rate of enzyme-catalysed reactions depends on pH;; many enzymes function best at a neutral pH around 7, though some work better in more acidic or alkaline environments (e.g. pepsin at pH 1.5-2.2, arginase at pH 9.5-9.9);; enzyme assays should be carried out at the pH of optimal activity, and pH effects can be controlled by adding buffer;; a small variation in pH causes a minimal change in enzyme activity.
(c)
• At low substrate concentration, the rate of reaction is almost directly proportional to substrate concentration; this is known as first order kinetics.
• At high substrate concentration, the reaction rate becomes a zero-order reaction, meaning there is no increase in the rate of the reaction when more substrate is added.
• In zero-order kinetics the entire enzyme is present as the ES complex, so the maximum possible velocity for the reaction (Vmax) has been reached and no further increase in complex concentration or reaction rate is possible; This transition from first-order to zero-order behaviour as substrate concentration increases is the essential feature of enzyme saturation described in enzyme kinetics.

(a)
• Hemoglobin test: the reagent pad is impregnated with buffered tetramethylbenzidine (TMB) and an organic peroxide, detecting hemoglobin, red cells, and myoglobin.
• Glucose test: the reagent pad is impregnated with glucose oxidase, peroxidase, potassium iodide, and a blue dye. pH test: uses methyl red (red below pH 4.2, yellow above pH 6.2) and bromothymol blue (yellow below pH 6.0, blue above pH 7.6).
• Albumin (protein) test: the test area is impregnated with tetrabromophenol blue.
(b)
• In the hemoglobin test, the colour changes from orange to pale to dark green as hemoglobin/myoglobin react with the reagent; the test is equally sensitive to hemoglobin and myoglobin, so a negative result excludes myoglobinuria.
• In the glucose test, glucose oxidase and peroxidase produce hydrogen peroxide which oxidizes potassium iodide to release free iodine, which blends with the background colour to give colours from green to dark brown, proportional to glucose present.
• In the pH test, urine pH tends to rise on standing because of loss of carbon dioxide and production of ammonia from urea by bacterial growth, which the indicator dyes reflect through colour change; In the albumin test, the area is yellow in the absence of protein but changes to green/blue in the presence of protein depending on type and concentration, and is read on a plus system from negative/trace to 1+ through 4+.
(c)
• Urine samples for reagent strip testing should be collected in sterile containers and tested on fresh urine; the strip should be mixed well immediately before testing, and reagent areas should be completely immersed then removed immediately to avoid dissolving the reagent out; failure to follow this can compromise results.
• The strip should be held horizontally to prevent possible mixing of chemicals from adjacent reagent pads or contamination of the hands with urine, since cross-contamination would invalidate individual pad readings; Water must not be used as a negative control for the hemoglobin test, as this will give a false-positive result, illustrating how the wrong control choice invalidates the result; On standing, urine pH tends to rise due to bacterial breakdown of urea to ammonia and loss of carbon dioxide, so delayed testing of a urine specimen can give a falsely elevated pH reading rather than the true value at collection.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the general classification of dry-phase (reagent strip) urine tests according to the analyte/condition each detects (hemoglobin, glucose, pH, albumin).
(b) Explain how each test's chemical reaction relates to the condition it is designed to detect.
(c) Explain how improper technique or handling of these reagent strips (e.g. contamination, wrong negative control, timing) leads to an inaccurate/invalid laboratory result.

questions.answerText:
(a)
This is the dry-chemistry measurement of creatinine; creatinine deaminase catalyzes the conversion of creatinine to N-methylhydantoin and ammonia.
(b)
Ammonia diffuses through a semipermeable and optically opaque layer and reacts with bromophenol blue, producing an increase in absorbance at 600nm; the colour produced in the film is quantitated by reflectance.
(c)
The magnitude of the reflectance signal (proportional colour change) indicates the concentration of creatinine present in the blood specimen, since the amount of ammonia generated - and hence the colour produced - is proportional to the amount of creatinine originally present.
questions.question:
(a) A blood specimen is analysed on a dry-slide (reflectance) system for creatinine, and an increase in absorbance at 600nm is recorded within the film. Identify the test and its underlying principle.
(b) State how the colour/signal produced is quantitated.
(c) State what the reading indicates about the specimen.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Serum amylase and lipase are the appropriate tests.
• Amylase catalyses hydrolysis of 1,4-alpha-glucosidic linkages in polysaccharides (produced in the acinar cells of the pancreas and salivary glands), while lipase hydrolyzes glycerol esters of long-chain fatty acids (produced by the pancreas, among other sites such as the mouth and stomach).
(b)
These enzymes are measured through enzyme activity assays as part of routine clinical enzymology testing; amylase reference interval is stated as 31-107U/L, and lipase upper reference limit is 45U/L (diglyceride assay) or 64U/L (methylresorufin assay).
(c)
Amylase rises 5-8 hours post-abdominal pain, peaks by 12-24 hours, and persists 3-4 days in acute pancreatitis, but can also rise in ruptured ectopic pregnancy, salpingitis, or perforated peptic ulcer; lipase rises 4-8 hours post-abdominal pain, peaks by 24 hours, and decreases within 7-14 days, and can likewise rise in ruptured ectopic pregnancy, salpingitis, or perforated peptic ulcer.
(d)
Because both enzymes can be elevated by conditions other than pancreatitis, lipase is recommended alongside amylase to diagnose acute pancreatitis, and results should be interpreted together with the timing of onset of pain and the overall clinical picture.
questions.question:
(a) A patient presents with abdominal pain, and serum amylase and lipase are requested for suspected acute pancreatitis. State the appropriate test(s) and their underlying principle.
(b) State the materials/reagents/equipment basis for measuring these enzymes.
(c) State sources of error/other conditions that could cause a similar rise in these enzymes.
(d) State the precaution/appropriate interpretation to be applied.

(a) Describe absorption, adsorption, and desorption as defined for chromatographic separation.
(b) Explain the mechanism of adsorption and give examples of good adsorbents.
(c) Distinguish between absorption and adsorption using their defining criteria (phenomenon, heat exchange, temperature effect, rate of reaction, and concentration).
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Absorption is a physical or chemical effect/mechanism in which electrons, molecules or ions join some bulk phase (solid or liquid substance).
• Adsorption is the adhesion of molecules (or ions and atoms) to the surface of a solid or liquid, where molecules accumulate only at the surface and do not enter the bulk of the adsorbing material; the substance whose molecules get adsorbed is the adsorbate, and the substance on whose surface adsorption occurs is the adsorbent.
• Desorption is the reverse process in which the adsorbed substance is removed from the surface of the adsorbent.
(b)
• Mechanism: adsorption arises because forces acting on surface particles of a substance are not the same as those acting on the bulk material; particles on the exposed surface are not surrounded by atoms on all sides, so forces on the surface are unbalanced and have a tendency to attract adsorbate particles; at a given temperature and pressure, the greater the surface area of adsorbent, the higher the extent of adsorption.
• Examples of good adsorbents: alumina gel, silica gel, zeolites, activated carbon, and graphite.
(c)
• Absorption is a bulk phenomenon (assimilation throughout the bulk of the solid or liquid medium), whereas adsorption is a surface phenomenon (accumulation of molecular species at the surface).
• Absorption is an endothermic process, whereas adsorption is an exothermic process.
• Temperature has no effect on absorption, whereas adsorption is influenced by low temperature; absorption occurs at a uniform rate, whereas the rate of adsorption increases steadily and reaches equilibrium; Concentration is constant throughout the medium in absorption, whereas in adsorption the concentration at the adsorbent surface differs from that in the bulk.

(a)
This is the Bradford method for protein estimation.
(b)
Principle: the method relies on the interaction between proteins and Coomassie Brilliant Blue G-250 dye; binding of the dye to proteins results in a shift in absorbance maximum and a colour change from red-brown to blue, measured spectrophotometrically and proportional to protein concentration.
(c)
Materials/reagents: Coomassie Brilliant Blue G-250 dye prepared in a reagent solution typically containing phosphoric acid, methanol, and water (the Bradford reagent).
(d)
Sources of error: the assay lacks specificity for certain proteins, like many dye-binding methods, potentially leading to variability in response among different protein types; some substances such as reducing agents and detergents may interfere with the reaction, affecting accuracy.
(e)
Precaution: because the assay is relatively tolerant of certain detergents (a stated advantage), this feature should be used appropriately for detergent-containing samples, while being aware that reducing agents may still interfere and should be avoided or accounted for.
questions.question:
(a) A serum sample is submitted for total protein determination using a dye-binding method employing Coomassie Brilliant Blue G-250. Identify the assay.
(b) State its underlying principle.
(c) List the materials/reagents required.
(d) State common sources of error/interference with this assay.
(e) State a precaution to minimize error.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Laboratory chemicals are available in a variety of grades; the solutes and solvents used in analytical work are reagent grade chemicals, among which water is a solvent of primary importance.
• Chemicals that meet specifications of the American Chemical Society (ACS) are described as reagent or analytical reagent (AR) grade, and these specifications have become de facto standards for chemicals used in many high-purity applications.
(b)
The quality of analytical results produced by the laboratory is a direct indication of the purity of the chemicals used as analytical reagents; the availability and quality of reference materials used to calibrate assays and monitor analytical performance are also important, since reference materials establish metrologic transferability so that a measurement result can be related to a reference through an unbroken chain of calibrations.
(c)
• Reagent/AR grade chemicals are available in two forms: lot-analyzed reagents and maximum-impurities reagents.
• Lot-analyzed reagents are those in which each individual lot is analyzed and the actual amount of impurity is reported.
• Maximum-impurities reagents are those for which only maximum impurities are listed, without reporting the actual amount present in a given lot.
• Both forms fall under the reagent/analytical reagent grade category meeting ACS specifications, but lot-analyzed reagents give more precise, lot-specific impurity information than maximum-impurities reagents.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the classification of laboratory chemicals and reagent grades used in the clinical laboratory.
(b) Explain why the purity/quality of reagents and reference materials matters for analytical results.
(c) Distinguish between lot-analyzed reagents and maximum-impurities reagents within the reagent/analytical reagent (AR) grade category.

(a) Describe paper chromatography under the headings: principle, apparatus required, and procedure.
(b) Explain the clinical/laboratory significance and applications of paper chromatography.
(c) Distinguish between partition chromatography and adsorption chromatography as principles underlying paper chromatography.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Principle: separation of mixture components by partition between two phases (water held in pores of the filter paper as stationary phase, and a mobile phase passing through the paper), or by adsorption between solid and liquid phases.
• Apparatus: chromatography jar, liquid-impregnated paper (stationary phase), capillary tube to apply sample mixture, and mobile phase (e.g. chloroform, methanol, acetone, ethanol).
• Procedure: prepare a clean dry jar saturated with solvent vapour, add mobile phase, mark baseline, spot sample with capillary tube and air-dry, place paper in jar to develop, dry the paper, detect coloured or UV-visualised spots, and calculate the Rf value.
(b)
Applications: studying fermentation/ripening, checking purity of pharmaceuticals, inspecting cosmetics, detecting adulterants and contaminants in foods/drinks, examining reaction mixtures in biochemical laboratories, and determining dopes/drugs in humans and animals.
(c)
• Partition chromatography occurs because substances are partitioned or distributed between two liquid phases: water held in the paper's pores and a mobile liquid phase.
• Compounds separate according to differences in affinity for stationary and mobile phase solvents under capillary action.
• Adsorption chromatography occurs between solid and liquid phases, where the solid surface of the paper is the stationary phase and the liquid is the mobile phase.
• Separation in partition chromatography depends on differing partition coefficients, while adsorption chromatography depends on differential adhesion of molecules to the solid adsorbent surface.

(a)
• Definition: an isoenzyme is a variant form of an enzyme that catalyzes the same reaction but differs in amino acid sequence, often with distinct properties; isoenzymes are multiple forms of an enzyme found within an organism.
• Basis of differences: they may be produced by different genes (encoded by distinct structural genes) or arise through post-translational modifications of a single gene product.
• Distinguishing properties: differences in physical properties such as electrophoretic migration, resistance to thermal inactivation, and resistance to chemical inactivation, as well as quantifiable differences in catalytic properties.
(b)
• Different isoenzymes are often associated with specific tissues or organs: Creatine Kinase isoenzymes CK-MM (skeletal/heart muscle), CK-MB (more specific for myocardium/heart), and CK-BB (predominantly brain);
• Lactate Dehydrogenase isoenzymes LD-1 to LD-5 (subunit combinations of H and M chains) found in various tissues such as heart, liver, kidneys and muscles;
• Alkaline Phosphatase isoforms found in liver, bone, kidney and other tissues, with elevations indicating liver or bone disorders;
• ALT and AST as indicators of liver function;
• GGT associated with liver and bile ducts;; and Amylase and Lipase associated with the pancreas, elevated in pancreatic disorders.
(c)
• Qualitative methods include electrophoresis (separating molecules by charge and size to visualize distinct bands, commonly used for LDH and CK isoenzymes), immunoprecipitation (using antibodies to isolate specific isoenzymes such as CK-MB), and chromatography (e.g. HPLC, separating isoenzymes by different properties).
• Quantitative methods include enzyme activity assays (measuring catalytic activity, e.g. CK activity in U/L), immunoassays such as ELISA (using antibodies to specifically quantify isoenzymes), spectrophotometry (measuring absorbance of substrates/products, commonly used for ALT and AST), real-time PCR (quantifying mRNA levels, more applicable in research), and mass spectrometry (offering high sensitivity/specificity by measuring mass-to-charge ratios).
• Qualitative methods primarily identify and visualize distinct isoenzyme forms, whereas quantitative methods measure the actual amount or activity level of specific isoenzymes.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the general characteristics of isoenzymes under the headings: definition, basis of differences (genetic/post-translational origin), and physical/catalytic properties used to distinguish them.
(b) Explain how different types of isoenzymes relate to specific tissues and diseases, giving examples of clinically important isoenzymes.
(c) Distinguish between qualitative and quantitative methods of measuring isoenzymes.

(a) During enzyme purification, ammonium sulfate is added stepwise to an enzyme extract with intermittent centrifugation. Identify this step and its underlying principle.
(b) Describe the correct procedure for carrying out this step.
(c) State how the outcome (precipitate at each "cut") is interpreted.
questions.answerText:
(a)
This step is "salting out" using ammonium sulfate precipitation; its principle is that high salt concentrations promote precipitation, as increasing ionic strength causes proteins to interact via hydrophobic patches on their surface while proteins and salt compete for residual water; the salt concentration at which a protein precipitates differs from protein to protein.
(b)
Procedure: increasing amounts of ammonium sulfate are added to the extract with intermittent centrifugation steps, referred to as ammonium sulfate "cuts"; solid ammonium sulfate should be added slowly, while the solution is stirring, and in powdered form, to allow a uniform increase in concentration and ensure rapid equilibration.
(c)
