Because the salt concentration at which a given protein precipitates differs from one protein to another, each "cut" precipitates a different subset of proteins; this stepwise approach can therefore be used to fractionate proteins or concentrate a diluted protein of interest, with ammonium sulfate chosen because it preserves protein activity and promotes precipitation at lower concentrations than other salts.

(a)
• Solubility-based separation exploits changes in pH, ionic strength or dielectric constant to change solubility (salting out); the salt concentration at which a protein precipitates differs from protein to protein.
• Size-based separation includes gel filtration (differing ability of molecules to enter gel pores based on size), ultrafiltration (semipermeable membranes with molecular weight cutoffs), and ultracentrifugation (separation by size, mass, density, or anisotropy at very high centrifugal forces).
• Polarity/charge-based separation includes ion-exchange chromatography (cationic enzymes separated on anionic columns and vice versa) and considerations of net charge, charge density and hydrophobic interactions (e.g. hydrophobic interaction chromatography using octyl- or phenyl-Sepharose).
(b)
Purification and separation of enzymes are generally based on solubility, size, polarity, and binding affinity; choosing the proper separation method requires considering the production scale, the timeline, and the properties of the enzyme, all of which should be considered when selecting a purification method.
(c)
• Objectives of purification are maximum possible yield, maximum catalytic activity, and maximum possible purity; failure to consider enzyme properties, production scale and timeline when choosing a method can compromise these objectives.
• Assessment of purity is done via SDS polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis, and units of enzyme activity (activity, specific activity, enrichment, % purity, % recovery/yield) are used to monitor the enzyme's activity and purity at each step; failure to monitor these at each purification step means unsuccessful purification or loss of yield may not be detected in time to adjust the process.
• Throughout the purification process it is essential to monitor the enzyme's activity and purity at each step to gauge success and make necessary adjustments, since an inappropriate step (e.g. wrong salt, wrong gel pore size, or unsuitable ion-exchange resin for the enzyme's charge) will fail to isolate the enzyme from other proteins, nucleic acids and small molecules effectively.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the classification of enzyme purification approaches by the physicochemical property exploited: solubility-based, size-based, and polarity/charge-based separation.
(b) Explain how the choice of separation method relates to the properties of the enzyme being purified and to practical considerations (production scale, timeline).
(c) Explain how an error/poor choice in method or handling leads to low yield, poor purity, or invalid results in enzyme purification.

(a) Describe the basic analytic disciplines/techniques used in a modern clinical chemistry laboratory.
(b) Explain the significance of miniaturization and point-of-care testing (POCT) devices in modern analytical chemistry.
(c) Distinguish between spectrometry and luminescence as basic analytic disciplines.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The majority of techniques fall into four basic disciplines within analytic chemistry: spectrometry (including spectrophotometry, atomic absorption, and mass spectrometry); luminescence (including fluorescence, chemiluminescence, and nephelometry); electroanalytic methods (including electrophoresis, potentiometry, and amperometry); and chromatography (including gas, liquid, and thin-layer).
(b)
With improvements in optics, electronics, and computerization, instrumentation has become miniaturized; this miniaturization has enabled development of point-of-care testing (POCT) devices that produce results as accurate as those provided by large laboratory-based instrumentation.
(c)
• Spectrometry includes spectrophotometry, atomic absorption, and mass spectrometry (MS), techniques generally based on measurement of absorption or mass-to-charge properties of a sample.
• Luminescence includes fluorescence, chemiluminescence, and nephelometry, techniques based on emitted or scattered light from the sample rather than absorbed light.
• Nephelometry, listed under luminescence, measures scattered light from particles in a sample, distinguishing it from spectrometric absorption-based techniques.
• Both disciplines provide the analytic foundation for measurements in the modern clinical chemistry laboratory, alongside electroanalytic methods and chromatography.

questions.question:
(a) A sample mixture is spotted on filter paper for separation by paper chromatography. Identify the technique and its underlying principle.
(b) Describe the correct step-by-step procedure for developing the chromatogram.
(c) State how the result is interpreted after development.
questions.answerText:
(a)
This is paper chromatography, based on partition chromatography (substances partitioned/distributed between water held in the pores of the filter paper as one phase and a mobile phase passing through the paper) or adsorption chromatography (solid surface of the paper as stationary phase, liquid as mobile phase).
(b)
Procedure: take a clean, dry chromatography jar and saturate its environment with solvent vapour; add mobile phase to about 0.5-1cm from the bottom; close the jar and allow it to attain equilibrium; mark the baseline on the paper; apply the sample to the paper using a capillary tube and air-dry the spot; place the paper in the jar and close it; allow the solvent to move some distance from the baseline; remove the paper and dry it; detect coloured spots in ordinary light or colourless spots under a UV lamp; store the chromatogram; calculate the Rf value.
(c)
If sample components separate showing colours, they are examined in ordinary light; colourless components are examined under UV light; the position of the separated spots and their calculated Rf values are used to identify/characterize the compounds in the mixture, based on differences in their affinity for the stationary and mobile phases.

questions.question:
(a) A tissue homogenate is being processed to purify a protein known to be localized in the nucleus. Identify the appropriate initial approach.
(b) State the principle behind the sequence of centrifugation steps used.
(c) State the materials/equipment required.
(d) State a source of error that could compromise this fractionation.
(e) State a precaution to avoid this error.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The appropriate approach is fractionation of the homogenate by differential centrifugation, first preparing nuclei and extracting them, since it is desirable to isolate the specific subcellular fraction where the desired protein resides.
(b)
Principle: a low-speed centrifugation separates nuclei from the remainder of the homogenate; the post-nuclear supernatant is then centrifuged at intermediate speed to sediment mitochondria; finally the post-mitochondrial supernatant is fractionated in the ultracentrifuge into a ribosomal fraction and a post-ribosomal supernatant containing all soluble proteins.
(c)
Materials/equipment: a homogenizer to prepare the homogenate, and a centrifuge capable of low-speed, intermediate-speed, and ultracentrifuge (up to very high g-forces) steps.
(d)
A source of error would be using an incorrect centrifugation speed at any stage, which could fail to properly separate nuclei, mitochondria, and ribosomal fractions from each other, leading to cross-contamination of fractions.
(e)
The correct low, intermediate, and ultracentrifuge speeds must be applied at each successive step in the correct order to achieve proper separation of the subcellular components.

questions.question:
(a) Describe Immunoturbidimetry and Nephelometry as protein assay techniques under the headings: principle, and applications.
(b) Explain the clinical significance of these techniques, including their advantages and limitations.
(c) Distinguish between Immunoturbidimetry and Nephelometry.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Principle: both methods quantify specific proteins in biological samples based on turbidity and light scattering, commonly used for immunoglobulins, C-reactive protein (CRP) and other proteins forming antigen-antibody complexes.
• Applications: commonly used for quantification of specific proteins including immunoglobulins, CRP, and other analytes in clinical diagnostics; particularly sensitive for detecting proteins at low concentrations.
(b)
• Advantages: high sensitivity allowing detection at low concentrations; specificity for the target protein providing accurate, selective measurements; automated analyzers allow high-throughput analysis.
• Limitations: certain substances in the sample may interfere with antigen-antibody complex formation, affecting accuracy; instruments can be expensive, limiting availability in smaller laboratories.
(c)
• In immunoturbidimetry, a specific antibody is added to the sample, forming antigen-antibody complexes if the target protein is present, and the resulting increased turbidity (cloudiness/haziness caused by suspended particles) is measured.
• In nephelometry, a beam of light is directed through the sample and particles such as antigen-antibody complexes scatter the light.
• Nephelometry detects the amount of scattered light at a specific angle, with intensity proportional to particle concentration, whereas immunoturbidimetry measures the degree of turbidity/cloudiness of the sample.
• Both are used for the same class of specific protein assays but differ in the optical phenomenon measured: turbidity (cloudiness) versus light scattering at an angle.

(a)
• Principle/definition: a type of liquid-solid chromatography specially applicable to ionic species; it is the exchange of ions between two electrolytes or an electrolyte solution and a complex, enabling separation of similar molecules by manipulating the charge carried through changes in buffer pH; it is also known as adsorption chromatography.
• Properties: the ion exchanger should be almost insoluble in water and organic solvents, should be complex/polymeric in nature, and should contain active or counter ions that allow reversible exchange without substantial change to the material.
• Advantages: useful for detection of inorganic salts and organic ions with poor UV absorptivity; preparative separations are preferred due to availability of volatile buffers; useful for resolving complex samples and biological mixtures;; provides long resin life, cheap maintenance and is environmentally friendly.
(b)
Ion-exchange chromatography is a popular method for purification of proteins and other charged molecules, allowing analysis of a wide range of molecules in pharmaceutical, biotechnology, environmental and agricultural applications, from water purification to separation of antibiotics.
(c)
• Ion-exchange chromatography separates ionizable molecules based on total charge using a column of charged beads, whereas gel electrophoresis separates charged molecules in solution that migrate in response to an applied electric field on a gel medium.
• In electrophoresis, migration rate depends on the strength of the field, net charge, size and shape of molecules, and on ionic strength, viscosity and temperature of the medium, while in ion-exchange chromatography separation depends on manipulation of buffer pH and charge on the stationary phase.
• Electrophoresis uses gel/buffer systems such as Tris Borate EDTA (TBE) or Tris Acetate EDTA (TAE), while ion-exchange chromatography uses resin columns with active counter-ions.
• Electrophoresis can be used analytically or preparatively and is simple, rapid and highly sensitive, while ion-exchange chromatography is valued for high resolving power, versatility and low-cost preparative separations.
questions.question:
(a) Describe ion-exchange chromatography under the headings: principle/definition, properties of ion exchangers, and advantages.
(b) Explain the clinical/laboratory significance of ion-exchange chromatography.
(c) Distinguish between ion-exchange chromatography and gel electrophoresis.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Principle: complexation of proteins with copper ions in an alkaline environment; coordination of peptide bonds with copper ions forms a violet-coloured complex, quantified spectrophotometrically.
• Reagent: prepared by mixing copper sulfate with sodium potassium tartrate and sodium hydroxide, giving an alkaline copper-ion solution.
• Procedure: the protein sample is mixed with Biuret reagent in an alkaline environment; colour changes from blue to violet, and colour intensity is directly proportional to protein concentration.
• Advantages/limitations: shows a linear response over a wide range of protein concentrations and is more sensitive than the Kjeldahl method; however it is not specific to proteins (can react with other peptide-bond-containing substances) and reducing/chelating agents may interfere.
(b)
Estimating plasma protein levels is a crucial aspect of clinical diagnostics, providing valuable information about an individual's health and potential underlying medical conditions.
(c)
• The Lowry method is based on reduction of Folin-Ciocalteu reagent by amino acid residues in proteins under alkaline conditions, forming a blue colour, whereas the Biuret method depends on complexation of copper ions with peptide bonds forming a violet colour.
• The Lowry method is more sensitive than the Biuret method, allowing detection of lower protein concentrations.
• Biuret reagent is copper sulfate, sodium potassium tartrate and sodium hydroxide, while the Lowry reagent additionally includes Folin-Ciocalteu phenol reagent.
• Both are colorimetric assays measured spectrophotometrically, but interferents differ: Biuret is affected by reducing/chelating agents, while Lowry is affected by detergents and reducing agents, and Lowry reagent preparation is more time-consuming.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the Biuret method for total protein determination in serum under the following headings: principle, preparation of reagent, procedure (sample addition and colour development), and advantages/limitations.
(b) Explain the clinical or diagnostic significance of estimating plasma protein levels.
(c) Distinguish between the Biuret method and the Lowry method for total protein determination.

(a) Describe gel electrophoresis under the headings: principle, buffers used, and uses.
(b) Explain the clinical/laboratory significance of electrophoresis as an analytical tool.
(c) Distinguish between electrophoresis performed via zone/capillary methods and chromatographic separation methods generally.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Principle: charged molecules in solution (chiefly proteins and nucleic acids) migrate in response to an electrical field; the rate of migration depends on field strength, net charge, size and shape of the molecules, and on ionic strength, viscosity and temperature of the medium; molecules are impeded by the gel and collect into bands according to migration speed.
• Buffers: Tris Borate EDTA (TBE), Tris Acetate EDTA (TAE), Tris Phosphate EDTA (TPE) used most often for DNA, and sodium phosphate buffer used for RNA.
• Uses: as an analytical tool it is simple, rapid and highly sensitive, used to study properties of a single charged species or mixtures of molecules, and can also be used preparatively as a separating technique.
(b)
Electrophoresis finds application in the qualitative characterization of biologically active materials where charged amino acids and other biomolecules need separation, and is highly useful for clinical and forensic work involving small amounts of complex samples.
(c)
• In electrophoresis, under an electric field, ions of opposite charge migrate in different directions and become separated, while ions of like charge migrating in the same direction separate due to different migration rates; the medium used is usually cellulose or gel.
• In chromatography, separation depends on partition, adsorption, or size-exclusion between a stationary and a mobile phase rather than an applied electric field.
• Electrophoresis gives less precision for quantitative work and its mobility is very sensitive to the supporting medium chosen, while chromatographic techniques such as gel filtration are less affected by such conditions.
• Both are used to separate proteins/biomolecules, but electrophoresis relies on charge-driven migration while chromatography relies on differential partition, adsorption or molecular sieving.

(a)
• Coenzyme A: a prominent coenzyme that transfers the acyl group of carboxylic acid; it plays an important role in metabolism of proteins, carbohydrates and fats, and is required for oxidation of pyruvate in the citric acid cycle.
• ATP: composed of an adenine nucleotide base, a ribose sugar and three phosphate groups; its function is to transport chemical energy within cells for metabolism, and is often referred to as the energy currency of cells; energy is released when the terminal phosphate group is hydrolysed, because the energy of ATP is held in the bonds between phosphate groups.
(b)
Coenzyme A is important in the synthesis of cholesterol and steroid hormones, and is required for the detoxification of a range of harmful drugs that can accumulate in the liver; it is essential for reactions that allow energy from food to be released.
(c)
• Cofactors, including coenzymes, are described as "helper molecules" that assist proteins (commonly enzymes) in biochemical transformations; coenzymes are freely diffusing organic compounds that bind loosely to enzyme active sites and are considered a type of secondary substrate when altered in the course of the reaction.
• Coenzymes lose or gain chemical groups (hydride ions via NAD, phosphate groups via ATP, acetyl groups via coenzyme A) in the course of the reaction, and are often reformed in the same metabolic pathway (e.g. NAD+ used in glycolysis and the citric acid cycle is replenished in the electron transport chain).
• As growth factors/vitamin precursors, coenzymes are closely related to vitamins and are described as precursors of vitamins, with a vitamin being a main component of a coenzyme endowed with biocatalytic functions; biotin, for example, is described as an essential growth factor for yeast and other microorganisms; Thus the same coenzyme molecule functions repeatedly as a chemical-group carrier within reactions (helper-molecule role) while also being biochemically linked to dietary vitamin requirements (growth-factor/precursor role).
questions.question:
(a) Describe Coenzyme A and Adenosine Triphosphate (ATP) under the headings: composition, and biochemical function.
(b) Explain the clinical/biochemical significance of Coenzyme A in metabolism.
(c) Distinguish between the roles of coenzymes as "helper molecules" (cofactors) versus their role as growth factors/vitamin precursors.

(a) Describe the general classification of clinically important enzymes according to tissue of origin (muscle, liver, pancreatic, and bone enzymes).
(b) Explain how disturbances/damage in each tissue type relate to elevations in the corresponding enzyme(s), with reference intervals where stated.
(c) Distinguish between how AST and ALT are used to differentiate the cause of liver disease using the AST/ALT ratio.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Muscle enzymes: creatine kinase (CK) and aldolase.
• Liver enzymes: AST, ALT, glutamate dehydrogenase, glutathione S-transferase, ALP, GGT, and 5'-nucleotidase.
• Pancreatic enzymes: lipase, amylase, trypsin.
• Bone enzymes: ALP and ACP; Others include LDH, cholinesterase, and PAPP-A.
(b)
• CK catalyses reversible phosphorylation of creatine by ATP; its clinical utilities include myopathy, muscular dystrophy, myositis, rhabdomyolysis, and myocardial infarction (reference interval M 46-171U/L, F 34-145U/L).
• Aldolase catalyses splitting of F1,6DP to G3P and DHAP, elevated in muscular dystrophy and polymyositis (reference interval 2.5-10U/L).
• AST catalyses transfer of an amino group between aspartate and glutamate;; clinical utilities include hepatitis, myocardial infarction, muscle injury, haemolytic disease and pulmonary embolism (reference interval M 0-35U/L); ALT catalyses transfer of an amino group between alanine and glutamate (reference interval M 0-60U/L, F 0-42U/L); Glutamate dehydrogenase interconverts glutamate and 2-oxoglutarate and is elevated in centrilobular necrosis, e.g. halothane toxicity or ischaemia; ALP hydrolyses phosphate esters at alkaline pH and is elevated in active bone growth, osteogenic sarcoma, Paget's disease, hyperparathyroidism, and cholestatic liver disorders (reference interval 33-98U/L premenopausal female, 43-115U/L male); Amylase and lipase rise in acute pancreatitis (amylase rises 5-8 hours post-abdominal pain, peaks 12-24 hours, persists 3-4 days;; lipase rises 4-8 hours, peaks by 24 hours, decreases within 7-14 days).
(c)
• An AST/ALT ratio >5 is associated with extrahepatic causes.
• An AST/ALT ratio >2 is associated with alcoholic hepatitis.
• Hepatocellular carcinoma and early-stage viral hepatitis are also associated conditions listed in relation to AST/ALT ratio interpretation.
• ALT has greater specificity for liver disease than AST, since AST is also found in the heart, skeletal muscle and other tissues, whereas ALT is more predominantly hepatic.

questions.question:
(a) Describe partition chromatography under the headings: principle and general characteristics.
(b) Explain the significance/advantages of partition chromatography as an analytical technique.
(c) Distinguish between partition chromatography and gel filtration chromatography in terms of the property exploited for separation.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Principle: separation of components from a sample mixture is carried out by partition of the components between two liquid phases; an immiscible solid surface coated with liquid on the stationary phase is in the mobile phase, and the liquid surface is immobilized by a stationary phase; the mobile phase moves and components get separated, with separation depending on different partition coefficients.
• General characteristics: partition chromatography is a technique for separating soluble mixtures by taking advantage of their different rates of migration; it is inexpensive, simple, and requires only small quantities of sample.
(b)
It provides a technique for separating soluble mixtures based on differing migration rates, and is applied (for example in paper chromatography) for quantitative determination of enzymes, hormones, proteins, lipids, trace elements, and non-protein nitrogen (thin film technology/immobilized enzyme analytical techniques).
(c)
• Partition chromatography separates components based on their differing partition coefficients between two liquid phases (stationary liquid coating and mobile liquid phase).
• Gel filtration chromatography separates molecules based on their differing molecular size and ability to enter the pores of a gel medium (a size-exclusion mechanism), not on partitioning between two liquid phases.
• Partition chromatography is inexpensive, simple, and requires only a small quantity of sample, while gel filtration is described as unique in that fractionation is based purely on relative protein size without the protein being retained/bound by the column.
• Both are chromatographic separation techniques, but the underlying separating principle differs: partition coefficient versus molecular size exclusion.

questions.question:
(a) During enzyme purification, the specific activity of an enzyme fraction is compared before and after a purification step. Interpret what an increase in specific activity indicates.
(b) State the formula/term used to express this improvement.
(c) State what this reading indicates about the purification process.
(d) State the follow-up action based on this reading.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Specific activity is the amount of product produced per unit time per mg of protein; an increase in specific activity after a purification step indicates that the enzyme has become more concentrated relative to total protein, i.e. it is becoming purer.
(b)
This improvement is expressed as enrichment: specific activity of the fraction divided by specific activity of the starting material.
(c)
This reading indicates the degree of purification achieved so far; percent purity is calculated as actual enrichment divided by maximum possible enrichment, while percent recovery (yield) is the total activity of the fraction divided by the total starting activity.
(d)
The enzyme's activity and purity should be monitored at each purification step to gauge the success of purification and to make any necessary adjustments, working towards the objectives of maximum yield, maximum catalytic activity, and maximum possible purity.

courses.title: Geriatric Physiotherapy
courses.objectives:
Health Promotion, Communication & Ageing Physiology: Q1–65

questions.explanation: Both the concentrating and diluting ability of the kidneys slowly deteriorate with age. This decline contributes to increased susceptibility to dehydration and hyponatraemia in older patients. It is one of several renal changes with direct clinical relevance.
questions.question: Which of the following best explains why older adults are more prone to dehydration and hyponatraemia?
options: Increased renal blood flow with age
Declining concentrating and diluting ability of the kidneys
Reduced sodium intake in all elderly diets

questions.question: A physiotherapist is treating an elderly patient with generalised joint stiffness attributed to collagen cross-linking changes with age. Which two clinical features are most directly linked to this connective tissue change?
questions.explanation: Because the number of collagen crosslinks increases with age, two observable clinical changes become manifest: decreased range of motion and increased tissue stiffness. Increased crosslinking also raises passive tension within tissues. Recognising this underlying mechanism helps guide stretching and mobility interventions.
options: Increased range of motion and reduced stiffness
Improved shock absorption and increased flexibility
Decreased range of motion and increased tissue stiffness
Increased muscle mass and reduced joint pain
Screw fixation permits immediate return to competitive sport with no precautions
Both approaches support early physiotherapy, with differing precautions
Hemiarthroplasty patients must remain completely non-weight-bearing indefinitely
Only screw fixation patients require any physiotherapy input
Precautions are identical regardless of the surgical technique used
questions.explanation: Regardless of whether fixation is achieved through percutaneous screws or hemiarthroplasty, physical therapy should begin immediately after surgery, though specific hip precautions may vary depending on the surgical approach used. Understanding the particular procedure performed helps the physiotherapist tailor safe, procedure-specific rehabilitation. This individualised approach supports optimal recovery while minimising complication risk.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is treating a patient following surgical fixation of a non-displaced femoral neck fracture using percutaneous cannulated screws. Compared with a displaced fracture treated with hemiarthroplasty, what should the physiotherapist anticipate regarding early rehabilitation approach?

questions.explanation: Loss of control of the internal and external anal sphincters in older adults often results in faecal incontinence. This is usually an emotionally traumatic and demeaning experience for those with intact cognition. The cause is reported to be loss of tone of the external rectal sphincter.
questions.question: Loss of tone of the external rectal sphincter in older adults with normal cognitive function most commonly results in which distressing complaint?

options: A loose rug on the floor
Wet floor tiles in the bathroom
Age-related physiologic changes in balance and gait
An electrical cord across the walkway
questions.explanation: Intrinsic factors relate to the individual, such as age-related physiologic changes in balance and gait, cognitive impairment, and medication use. Extrinsic factors instead relate to the environment, such as loose rugs, poor lighting or wet floors. Distinguishing these categories helps target the most relevant component of a falls prevention plan.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is asked to distinguish between intrinsic and extrinsic factors contributing to an older patient's recent fall. Which of the following is an example of an intrinsic factor?

options: Complete absence of pain in women after menopause
Identical pain and disability outcomes in men and women
Lower pain intensity reported by women compared with men
No gender differences in any pain condition
Greater pain-related disability in women compared with men
questions.question: A physiotherapist is educating a group of older women about their relatively higher prevalence of persistent back pain and fibromyalgia compared with men. According to geriatric pain teaching, gender is associated with which additional pain-related outcome?
questions.explanation: Female gender is associated with greater pain intensity, more pain locations, and greater pain-related disability compared with men, alongside higher prevalence of conditions such as persistent back pain, fibromyalgia and arthritis. Recognising these gender-based patterns can inform more individualised pain management approaches. This does not mean male patients experience no significant pain, but rather that population-level differences exist.

options: Bladder control and bowel control exclusively
Visual acuity and colour discrimination exclusively
Hearing threshold and speech articulation exclusively
questions.explanation: Evaluation of sitting and standing balance is important for assessing independence with transfers and, subsequently, ambulation. Poor balance in these positions directly impacts a patient's ability to move safely and independently. This makes balance assessment a foundational component of functional mobility evaluation.
questions.question: A physiotherapist notes a patient has particular difficulty with sitting and standing balance following a stroke, affecting her transfer ability. Which two functional components does this observation link to independence?

options: Assume the patient will remember complex multi-step instructions unaided
Ignore the score since it is not physiotherapy's concern
Simplify instructions and involve a caregiver in supervising the programme
questions.explanation: A score of 23 or lower on the MMSE indicates cognitive impairment, which may affect the patient's ability to recall and safely follow complex multi-step home exercise instructions. Simplifying instructions and involving a caregiver in supervision helps ensure safety and adherence. This does not mean physiotherapy should be withheld, but rather adapted.
questions.question: A patient's Mini-Mental Status Examination score is 21 out of 30. Based on this result, what should the physiotherapist do before proceeding with a complex, multi-step home exercise programme?

questions.explanation: Gait can be objectively assessed as the patient walks in, often revealing a cautious pattern with slower speed and reduced step length. This complements balance testing and self-reported ADL and IADL information as key elements of functional status. Together these elements guide appropriate treatment planning.
options: Basic self-care ADLs only via self-report
questions.question: Among the four elements of physical functional status evaluated in a comprehensive geriatric assessment, which is assessed objectively as the patient walks into the clinic?

questions.explanation: Subdural haematoma, common in the elderly after a fall, can produce symptoms similar to dementia and is potentially reversible with treatment. Other reversible causes include infections, metabolic problems, nutritional deficiencies and medication side effects. Recognising reversible causes is essential before assuming an irreversible dementia diagnosis.
questions.question: Which of the following conditions can produce dementia-like symptoms that are potentially reversible with treatment?

questions.explanation: Specific interventions such as sit-to-stand practice, resisted exercise repetitions and gait training distances represent tactics used to achieve the broader short-term and long-term goals of treatment. This detailed prescription operationalises the care plan into measurable, trackable actions. Clear tactics support consistent delivery and monitoring of progress.
options: Tactics to reach short and long-term goals
Diagnosis of the underlying medical condition
Prognosis for a full clinical recovery
Referral criteria used for discharge planning
Billing codes used for insurance purposes
questions.question: An elderly patient's rehabilitation plan includes sit-to-stand practice, resisted lower limb exercises with ankle weights, and gait training with a walker, prescribed as specific sets and repetitions. What term describes this type of detailed prescription within the goal-setting framework?

questions.explanation: Multimorbidity refers to the presence of complex, multiple and interdependent health problems common among geriatric patients, which can present nonspecifically as vague complaints like general weakness. This makes assessment more challenging than in younger patients with a single medical problem. Recognising multimorbidity supports a broader, multidisciplinary approach to diagnosis and treatment planning.
questions.question: A physiotherapist identifies that an elderly patient's chief complaint of 'general weakness' may actually reflect multiple underlying pathologies rather than a single diagnosis. What broader clinical concept does this scenario illustrate?
options: An entirely psychological cause requiring no physical assessment
A diagnosis that requires no further systems review
A presentation unique to institutionalised patients only

questions.question: Which walk test requires an indoor walking area recommended by the American Thoracic Society to be approximately how long, with marks every 3 metres?
questions.explanation: The American Thoracic Society recommends an indoor walking area of 30 metres with marks every 3 metres for timed walk tests such as the 6-minute walk test. Shorter or longer walkways have also been used in practice. Standardised distance and instructions are important for valid, comparable results.

questions.question: Which dementia subtype is characterised by pronounced fluctuations in alertness, recurrent visual hallucinations, and parkinsonian motor symptoms?
questions.explanation: Lewy body dementia features progressive cognitive decline combined with pronounced fluctuations in alertness, recurrent visual hallucinations, and parkinsonian motor symptoms such as rigidity. Abnormal balloonlike protein clumps called Lewy bodies are found in affected brains. This condition is one of the more common progressive dementias.

Published TUG norms show a mean of around 8.1 seconds for ages 60 to 69 years, so a score of 9.5 seconds falls within an expected range for her age group and is well under the 12-second community mobility threshold. This suggests reasonably preserved mobility rather than significant impairment. Comparing individual results against age-based norms supports accurate clinical interpretation.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is asked to interpret a TUG score of 9.5 seconds in a 68-year-old community-dwelling client compared with published age-based norms. What does this result most likely indicate?
options: A result indicating she needs a wheelchair immediately
A result suggesting significant cognitive impairment
A result consistent with expected mobility for her age group
Any deliberate sitting down onto the floor for exercise
A controlled slide down a wall while resting
Tripping while running competitively as an athlete
Unintentionally resting on the ground, without a major intrinsic cause
Fainting during a scheduled medical procedure
questions.explanation: A fall is defined as unintentionally coming to rest on the ground, not as a result of a major intrinsic event such as stroke or syncope, or an overwhelming hazard. Falls are a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in older adults. Most falls are multifactorial, combining host and environmental causes.
questions.question: A fall is best defined for geriatric assessment purposes as which of the following?
A 75-year-old retiree insists on maintaining hobbies, socialising and staying busy because she believes remaining active keeps her feeling young. This best illustrates which theory of ageing?
questions.explanation: Activity theory holds that remaining active helps maintain life satisfaction and a positive self-concept in older age. It assumes it is better to be active than inactive and that the individual is the best judge of their own success. This theory encourages continued participation rather than withdrawal.

questions.question: Using the Garden classification, a complete but non-displaced femoral neck fracture is classified as which type?
questions.explanation: In the Garden classification, Type I is an incomplete, valgus impacted, non-displaced fracture, while Type II is a complete but non-displaced fracture. Type III is a complete fracture with partial displacement, and Type IV is complete with full displacement. For treatment purposes, this is often simplified into non-displaced (Types I and II) versus displaced fractures.

questions.question: Which of the following frequently presents atypically in older adults as a manifestation of an adverse drug reaction, sometimes described as a 'geriatric giant'?
questions.explanation: Adverse drug reactions in older adults often present atypically and nonspecifically as a geriatric giant, including confusion, delirium, dementia, depression, falls and incontinence. Drugs should always be considered as a potential cause of any new symptom in this population. This atypical presentation can delay recognition of drug toxicity.

options: Document the withdrawal as expected disengagement and take no action
Use assessment tools to further investigate before assuming normal ageing behaviour
Discharge the patient from further group sessions
Ignore the behaviour since it is a personal choice
Reduce contact with the patient to respect autonomy
questions.explanation: Withdrawal by older adults may signal a deeper problem such as depression rather than mere disengagement. Physiotherapists should use assessment skills and specific tools to investigate further. Appropriate interventions can then be planned based on findings rather than assumptions.
questions.question: A physiotherapist notices that an elderly patient's withdrawal from group exercise sessions may actually reflect an underlying mood disorder rather than simple disengagement with age. What is the most appropriate initial action?

A physiotherapist works with an older patient whose functional decline cannot be fully reversed despite maximal rehabilitation effort. According to the conclusions drawn in geriatric physiotherapy teaching, what should remain the therapist's focus in such cases?
questions.explanation: In some situations, neither improvement nor even maintenance of functional mobility can be achieved. In these particular cases, physiotherapists can still make a difference by helping older people to be comfortable and pain free. This reflects a person-centred, compassionate approach even when full functional recovery is not possible.
options: Discontinuing all further contact with the patient
Insisting on continued aggressive rehabilitation regardless of patient wishes
Focusing solely on documentation rather than patient care
Helping the patient stay comfortable and pain free
Referring the patient exclusively to psychiatric services
No measurable benefit compared with general changes
questions.explanation: Interventions that target a specific aspect of the home environment related to a functional ability have greater impact than more general interventions. The more intense and skilled the home modification, the greater the observed improvement. This underlines the value of individualised environmental assessment.
questions.question: A physical environment intervention that targets a specific functional ability, rather than a broad general modification, tends to have which outcome for older adults?

A physiotherapist is asked to assess an elderly patient's aerobic capacity in a home setting where a long, unobstructed corridor is unavailable. Which walk test would be the most practical alternative to the 6-minute walk test?
questions.explanation: The 2-minute walk test requires a shorter measured corridor and has been used to measure exercise capacity in individuals with moderate-to-severe cardiopulmonary disease or frailty, making it more practical when space is limited. The 400-metre walk test requires considerably more space. Shuttle runs and treadmill stress tests are not appropriate for frail elderly assessment.

questions.question: A physiotherapist is asked to summarise the overarching goals of physiotherapy treatment in older adults, beyond addressing a single presenting complaint. Which set of goals best reflects this broader purpose?
questions.explanation: Treatment goals serve to give direction and purpose to treatment, minimise the final losses associated with ageing, disease and disability, and assist in maximising the older adult's available capabilities. This broader framing shapes both short-term and long-term goal setting. It reflects a realistic, function-focused philosophy rather than an expectation of complete symptom elimination in every case.
options: Focusing exclusively on eliminating all symptoms immediately
Ensuring the patient never requires further medical review
Giving direction while minimising losses and maximising capability
Achieving identical outcomes for every older patient regardless of condition
Prioritising discharge speed above all other considerations
The patient has definitively normal balance function
The test result should be disregarded as clinically meaningless
The patient demonstrates impaired balance, gait and mobility warranting further intervention
The finding indicates a permanent, untreatable condition
The test can only be interpreted by a psychologist
questions.question: A physiotherapist notices that an elderly patient's Tandem Walk Test performance shows repeated stepping off the gait line and loss of balance. What is the most appropriate clinical interpretation of this finding?
questions.explanation: The Tandem Walk Test measures balance, gait and mobility by requiring the patient to walk heel-to-toe along a marked line, with errors including stepping off the line or losing balance. Repeated errors suggest impaired balance and mobility requiring further assessment and intervention. This is a quick, equipment-light test suitable for many clinical settings.

questions.question: Which risk factor is specifically identified as predisposing women to more disability in old age compared with men, despite women's longer life expectancy?
questions.explanation: Women experience more disability in old age than men, even though women generally survive longer with a longer life expectancy. This paradox is attributed partly to differing patterns of chronic disease and frailty between sexes. Gender is therefore listed among the predisposing factors for disability in old age.

options: That cognitively impaired patients never experience pain
That pain assessment tools are unnecessary in this population
The particular challenge that cognitive impairment poses to accurate pain assessment
That verbal scales are always superior regardless of cognition
That pain management should be abandoned in dementia
questions.question: A physiotherapist working with a cognitively impaired elderly patient with significant pain finds standard verbal rating scales difficult to use reliably. What does this scenario best illustrate?
questions.explanation: Accurately assessing pain is particularly challenging in patients with significant cognitive impairment, yet accurate assessment remains key to appropriate pain management. Alternative observational pain scales may be more appropriate in this group. Abandoning pain management is inappropriate, since pain is often undertreated in patients with dementia.

options: A single one-off balance assessment only
Long-term exercise with gait and balance training
Complete bed rest until balance normalises
Strict avoidance of any walking practice
questions.explanation: Older people who have had recurrent falls should be offered long-term exercise focused on gait and balance training, since balance exercises have been shown to reduce fall risk over a period of months. A single assessment alone is insufficient, and inactivity worsens deconditioning and fall risk. Ongoing structured exercise is the recommended core intervention.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is planning a falls prevention exercise programme for a group of community-dwelling elderly clients who have had recurrent falls. According to the evidence discussed in geriatric physiotherapy teaching, which intervention type should form the core of this programme?

questions.explanation: Firearms accounted for 71 percent of suicides among persons aged 65 years or older, followed by overdose and suffocation at 11 percent each. Older adults who attempt suicide die from the attempt more often than any other age group. Risk factors differ from younger populations, including greater social isolation.
questions.question: Which method of suicide is reported as most common among persons aged 65 years or older?
According to the International Association for the Study of Pain definition referenced in geriatric teaching, pain is best described as which of the following?
options: A purely physical sensation without emotional component
An experience that only occurs after visible tissue injury
A symptom exclusive to psychiatric disorders
An unpleasant sensory and emotional experience from tissue damage
A sensation that always indicates malingering in older adults
questions.explanation: Pain is defined as an unpleasant sensory and emotional experience associated with actual or potential tissue damage, or described in terms of such damage. It has biological, psychological and social components producing individualised responses. It is the patient's report that defines the presence of pain, not the clinician's judgement.

The ICF emphasises environmental factors in creating disability, marking the main difference from the earlier International Classification of Impairments, Disabilities and Handicaps. It categorises human functioning problems into impairments, activity limitations and participation restrictions. The ICF also adopts neutral language without distinguishing physical from mental health causes.
questions.question: The International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) differs from the earlier ICIDH mainly by emphasising which factor in creating disability?

options: Restricting healthcare access for people over 70
Strategic prevention plans and geriatric medicine training
Removing gerontology training from professional curricula
questions.explanation: Prevention strategies include developing strategic preventive plans at national and community levels and promoting training in gerontology and geriatric medicine for relevant professionals. Programmes should also help older people cope with disability risk factors and manage chronic illness. Benefits from exercise accrue even when started later in life, helping to postpone disability.
questions.question: Which strategy is emphasised as a national-level intervention to prevent disability in old age, alongside individual lifestyle changes?
Which of the following is classified as a cause of acute rather than persistent incontinence?
questions.explanation: Acute incontinence can be caused by delirium, restricted mobility, infection, polyuria, inflammation, impaction or medications. Persistent incontinence is instead classified into stress, urge, overflow and functional types. Distinguishing acute from persistent causes guides appropriate management.

options: High-heeled shoes with soft cushioned soles
Thick platform soles with high heels
Low-heeled, hard-soled shoes with low resistance
questions.question: A physiotherapist evaluating footwear as part of a falls risk assessment should recommend which type of shoe sole for optimal safety in elderly clients?
questions.explanation: Falls prevention advice includes checking footwear, recommending low-heeled and hard-soled shoes with low resistance as safer options. High heels, backless slippers and slick or platform soles all increase instability and fall risk. Simple footwear modification is a low-cost but effective falls prevention strategy.

options: Weight in kilograms multiplied by height in metres
Height in metres divided by weight in kilograms
Weight in pounds divided by height in inches
Waist circumference divided by hip circumference
Weight in kilograms divided by height in metres squared
questions.question: Body Mass Index (BMI) is calculated using which formula?
questions.explanation: BMI is calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in metres squared, or alternatively weight in pounds divided by height in inches squared multiplied by 704.5. It is used to diagnose obesity but may be affected by muscular composition and body frame. It is one of several anthropometric characteristics assessed in older adults.

Humanitarian skills are required for the therapist to judge when to treat, converse with, listen to, coax, or leave an older patient in peace, reflecting sensitivity to the individual's emotional and physical state. This differs from purely technical skills such as goniometry or exercise prescription parameters. Both technical and humanitarian skills are needed for holistic geriatric care.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is asked to justify the inclusion of humanitarian skills as a core competency in geriatric physiotherapy practice. Which scenario best exemplifies the application of this skill?
options: Calculating the precise angle of a goniometric measurement
Selecting the correct billing code for an insurance claim
Choosing the appropriate resistance band colour for exercise
Determining the exact repetitions for a strengthening set
Deciding when to converse versus allow quiet rest

questions.explanation: The most obvious consequence of connective tissue water loss with age is body shrinking or height loss, primarily due to water loss from the intervertebral discs. Articular cartilage also loses water, becoming more susceptible to breakdown. This explains the characteristic pattern of trunk height loss seen with advancing age.
options: Increased bone length in the long bones
Water loss from the intervertebral discs
Increased muscle mass in the trunk
questions.question: An elderly patient reports a noticeable reduction in height over the past decade, most prominent in the trunk. Which tissue change is primarily responsible for this pattern of height loss?

questions.explanation: Gait speed of 1.2 to 1.3 metres per second is considered usual adult walking speed, while 0.5 metres per second is sufficient only for limited community mobility. Speeds below 1.0 metre per second are associated with high risk of health-related outcomes. These norms allow clinicians to interpret an individual's measured gait speed meaningfully.
options: Speed sufficient only for limited community mobility
Speed indicating high risk of health-related outcomes
questions.question: Gait speed values around 1.2 to 1.3 metres per second are generally interpreted as representing which level of function?

questions.explanation: Maximum lung function gradually declines with age, including decreases in vital capacity and weakening of the respiratory muscles. These changes contribute to a reduced ability to perform vigorous aerobic exercise such as running or biking. In healthy people these changes seldom produce symptoms at rest.
options: Weak respiratory muscles and reduced vital capacity
questions.question: Which of the following age-related respiratory changes contributes most directly to a reduced ability to perform vigorous aerobic exercise?
An elderly nursing home resident spends over 20 hours per day lying in bed or sitting indoors. What long-term musculoskeletal consequence is this pattern most likely to accelerate?
questions.explanation: Older women who spend excessive hours lying in bed or sitting inside are at unusually high risk for fracture, becoming more osteoporotic, frail and predisposed to falling and bone breakage. Contracting muscles naturally maintain bone mineral density, so inactivity accelerates its loss. This underlines the value of structured mobility programmes in institutional settings.
options: Improved bone mineral density from reduced mechanical stress
Increased osteoporosis and predisposition to falls and fracture
Reduced risk of pressure ulcers from prolonged rest

questions.question: A physiotherapist is evaluating range of motion in an elderly wheelchair user who relies on her arms for transfers. Which specific joints should receive particular attention during this assessment?
questions.explanation: Shoulder and elbow range of motion restrictions are particularly significant for patients who need to use their arms for transfers and manual wheelchair mobility. Limiting these restrictions helps preserve functional independence in this population. This differs from lower limb priorities relevant to ambulatory patients.

options: Complete joint immobilisation in a rigid cast
Strict bed rest until pain resolves fully
High-impact running to distract from the pain
Therapeutic exercise, joint mobilisation and heat or TENS
Withholding all treatment until pain reaches zero
questions.question: An 80-year-old woman with knee osteoarthritis reports pain that limits her ability to attend physiotherapy sessions. Which combination of physical therapy interventions is most appropriate according to geriatric pain management principles?
questions.explanation: Physical therapy interventions for pain in older adults include therapeutic exercise such as flexibility and strengthening work, joint mobilisation, and modalities such as heat, cryotherapy or TENS. Complete immobilisation or bed rest would worsen deconditioning and stiffness. A multimodal, active approach is preferred over passive avoidance of movement.

options: Decline in total glomeruli number per kidney
questions.question: Which structural change in the ageing kidney is most directly responsible for the observed decline in creatinine clearance?
questions.explanation: A decline in the total number of glomeruli per kidney with age results in decreased creatinine clearance. This is an important indicator for balancing fluid and electrolytes in older patients. By the ninth decade, renal size is roughly seventy percent of that in the third decade.

Upper extremity work requires higher arterial blood pressure and heart rate for a given oxygen consumption compared with leg work. This is relevant when prescribing exercise for patients who rely heavily on their arms for transfers or wheelchair mobility. Awareness of this difference helps guide safe exercise intensity and monitoring.
options: Upper extremity work always uses less oxygen than leg work
Arm muscles have no cardiovascular demand at all
Arm work needs higher blood pressure and heart rate than leg work
Leg work always produces higher blood pressure than arm work
There is no physiological difference between arm and leg exercise
questions.question: A physiotherapist is asked why upper extremity exercise may be more cardiovascularly demanding than lower extremity exercise of similar intensity in an elderly patient using a wheelchair. Which physiological explanation applies?

A physiotherapist is asked to identify why an older adult must first understand and agree that a rehabilitation goal is important before treatment planning proceeds. What is the primary reason this step is emphasised in geriatric goal setting?
questions.explanation: The older adult must first understand the goal, agree that it is important, and be able to relate treatment to the goal, since patient cooperation is essential for effective rehabilitation. Encouraging participation in planning and frequently checking for understanding supports this cooperative process. This patient-centred approach improves the likelihood of successful goal achievement.
options: Understanding the goal is legally required only for patients under 65
Patient agreement has no bearing on treatment success
Patient understanding and agreement support cooperation and successful goal achievement
Goals can be achieved effectively without patient understanding
This step exists only to satisfy documentation requirements
Dementia and normal ageing produce identical severity of memory loss
Normal ageing produces worse memory loss than dementia
Dementia causes forgetting of whole events and daily-task difficulty
Dementia only affects language, never memory
There is no clinically useful distinction between the two
questions.question: How does the severity of cognitive decline in dementia typically differ from that seen in normal ageing?
questions.explanation: In normal ageing, people may misplace items or forget minor details, whereas people with dementia forget entire events. Dementia is also associated with difficulty in performing activities of daily living and disorientation to place and time. This marks dementia as a disorder rather than a feature of normal ageing.

Assessment tools should have strong psychometric properties, be easy to perform across settings and between different physiotherapists, and be responsive to change if used as an outcome measure. This ensures reliable and valid interpretation of results in diverse clinical contexts. Choosing well-validated tools supports sound clinical decision-making rather than replacing clinical judgement.
options: To make the tool more expensive and exclusive to specialist centres
To ensure the tool reliably measures the intended construct
To ensure the tool cannot be used by physiotherapists
To guarantee every patient receives an identical numerical score regardless of condition
To eliminate the need for clinical judgement entirely
questions.question: A physiotherapist is asked to identify why comprehensive geriatric assessment tools should ideally have strong psychometric properties before being adopted into routine clinical practice. What is the primary reason for this requirement?

questions.explanation: Depression in older adults can mask itself in physical symptoms, with patients denying sadness but complaining of tiredness or low motivation. Increased anxiety, irritability, weight loss and insomnia may also be present. Recognising this masked presentation is important because depression is commonly related to suicide risk.
options: Older adults never experience clinical depression
Depression in older adults always presents identically to younger adults
Physical complaints exclude the possibility of depression
Fatigue in the elderly always indicates dementia rather than mood disorder
Depression may be masked by physical complaints in older people
questions.question: An older adult with depression denies feeling sad but instead reports low energy, fatigue and low motivation. This pattern reflects which recognised feature of depression in older adults?

questions.explanation: Femoral neck fractures in the elderly are associated with low energy falls, in contrast to younger patients where high-energy trauma such as motor vehicle accidents is the usual cause. Risk factors include female gender, decreased mobility and low bone density. This distinction is important for both diagnosis and prevention strategies.
questions.question: Femoral neck fractures in elderly patients are most commonly associated with which mechanism of injury?

questions.explanation: Changes in vascular circulation and loss of subcutaneous tissue in older individuals impair thermal sensitivity and reduce the ability to cope with extreme temperatures. This commonly makes older adults feel cold even in environments that feel comfortable to younger people. Clinicians should consider room temperature and clothing when treating older patients.
options: A side effect of regular strength training
Age-related loss of subcutaneous fat and reduced thermal sensitivity
An early sign of active infection in all cases
questions.question: An 84-year-old man reports feeling cold and uncomfortable even on a warm day, and struggles to tolerate the air conditioning in the clinic. Which physiological explanation best accounts for this complaint?

options: Random accumulation of cellular replication errors
Wear and tear from repeated mechanical use
questions.question: Non-stochastic theories of biological ageing attribute changes such as menopause and greying of hair mainly to which underlying mechanism?
questions.explanation: Non-stochastic theories attribute ageing to an inherent, predetermined and timed programme, often called the biological clock theory. Events such as menopause and greying hair are viewed as normal programmed changes rather than pathology. Gene theory and immunity theory are subdivisions of this approach.

questions.question: The Mini-Mental Status Examination (MMSE) score range that is generally considered indicative of cognitive impairment is:
questions.explanation: The MMSE has a potential range of 0 to 30, with lower scores indicating poorer cognitive status. A score of 24 or higher generally identifies individuals who are cognitively intact, while scores of 23 or lower are indicative of cognitive impairment. The tool does not, however, indicate the specific cause of any impairment found.

Patients who have fallen, especially those on four or more medications, should have their medications reviewed in light of their falls risk. While physiotherapists cannot alter prescriptions themselves, liaising with the prescriber is an essential part of a multidisciplinary falls prevention approach. Independently stopping or altering medication is outside physiotherapy scope and could be dangerous.
options: Ignore medications since they are outside physiotherapy scope entirely
Increase her exercise intensity to compensate for drug effects
Advise her to double her diuretic dose to reduce swelling
Liaise with the prescribing physician to review and possibly rationalise her medications
questions.question: An 80-year-old woman on four or more medications, including a diuretic and a benzodiazepine, reports two recent unexplained falls. What is the most appropriate physiotherapy action regarding her drug regimen?

questions.explanation: Nocturnal urgency linked to diuretic use should prompt review of medication timing in collaboration with the prescribing physician, since diuretics are a recognised contributing factor to incontinence in the elderly. Physiotherapists play a role in identifying such contributing factors even though they do not prescribe medication. This supports a coordinated, multidisciplinary approach to bladder management.
options: Restricting all fluid intake throughout the entire day
Recommending an indwelling catheter as the first-line solution
Reviewing the timing of diuretic administration in collaboration with the prescribing physician
Advising complete cessation of physiotherapy sessions
Ignoring the medication list since it is outside physiotherapy's role
questions.question: A physiotherapist notices that an elderly patient's medication list includes a loop diuretic and observes she reports urinary urgency mainly at night. Which management step is most directly relevant to this presentation?
Multimorbidity in geriatric patients is best described as which of the following?
options: The presence of exactly one chronic disease
The presence of complex, multiple and interdependent health problems
A condition found only in institutionalised elderly patients
A term used exclusively for psychiatric conditions
A term describing only post-surgical complications
questions.explanation: Geriatric patients often have complex, multiple and interdependent problems, described as multimorbidity, which makes their care more challenging than for younger people with a single medical problem. This complexity necessitates comprehensive assessment leading to a coordinated problem list and management plan. Multimorbidity is a central concept underlying comprehensive geriatric assessment.

questions.question: A physiotherapist is reviewing systems as part of a geriatric examination and notes reduced chest expansion and an abnormal breathing pattern. Under which systems review category should this finding be recorded?
questions.explanation: Pulmonary systems review includes assessment of breathing rate, breathing pattern and ease of respiration. This differs from integumentary review, which covers skin condition, and neuromuscular review, which covers tone, spasticity and reflexes. Correct categorisation supports clear, standardised clinical documentation.

Completely impaired ADL capacity describes a patient who needs help throughout the day and night to carry out activities of daily living. This is the most dependent category on the summarised ADL scale. Recognising this level of dependency is essential for appropriate discharge and care planning.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is scoring a patient who needs help throughout both day and night with most activities of daily living. According to the ADL capacity classification, this represents which category?
Which professional is specifically listed as part of the multidisciplinary team for geriatric assessment, alongside the physician, nurse, and physical therapist?
questions.explanation: The multidisciplinary team for geriatric assessment described in geriatric physiotherapy teaching includes the physician, physical therapist, ophthalmologist, nurse and psychologist. Each professional contributes a different perspective to the comprehensive evaluation. This teamwork approach reflects the multiple, interdependent problems common in older patients.

options: Checkups are unnecessary once a person feels well
Checkups are only relevant for people already diagnosed with illness
Checkups have no role in promoting healthy ageing
Regular checkups are solely for administrative record-keeping
Checkups can detect subclinical problems before major decline
questions.question: An older patient asks the physiotherapist why regular medical checkups are emphasised as part of healthy ageing, despite feeling generally well. What is the most appropriate response?
questions.explanation: Regular medical checkups are recommended as part of healthy habits and positive lifestyles for older persons, supporting early detection of health problems before they cause significant functional decline. This proactive approach aligns with broader disease prevention goals in geriatric care. Feeling generally well does not eliminate the value of routine preventive health monitoring.

The standard patient care elements in geriatric physiotherapy practice follow the sequence of examination, evaluation, diagnosis, prognosis, and then intervention and plan of care. Skipping examination or evaluation risks an inaccurate diagnosis and inappropriate intervention. Following this structured sequence supports sound, evidence-based clinical reasoning.
options: Intervention first, followed by examination and diagnosis
Examination, evaluation, diagnosis, prognosis, then intervention and plan of care
Prognosis first, followed by intervention with no examination
Plan of care first, followed by examination afterward
questions.question: A physiotherapist is asked to prioritise physiotherapy assessment components for a newly admitted geriatric patient with multiple comorbidities. Which sequence best reflects the standard patient care elements described in geriatric physiotherapy teaching?

questions.explanation: Depression can commonly and dramatically affect the response to rehabilitation, with hopelessness, apathy and withdrawal making active participation more challenging. Recognising and addressing depression, potentially alongside pharmacological or psychological treatment, supports better rehabilitation engagement. This does not mean physiotherapy should be withheld, but rather that mood should be actively considered in the treatment plan.
questions.question: A physiotherapist notices that an elderly patient with major depression shows hopelessness, apathy and withdrawal during rehabilitation sessions after a stroke. How does this presentation most directly affect the rehabilitation process?
options: It can make active participation in rehabilitation more challenging
It has no measurable effect on rehabilitation outcomes
It guarantees faster recovery due to reduced anxiety
It automatically disqualifies the patient from physiotherapy
It indicates the stroke diagnosis was incorrect
Proceed immediately at maximum walking pace
Ask the patient to run rather than walk
Skip pre-test vital signs entirely next time
Exercise caution and consider deferring or modifying the test
Double the test duration to compensate
questions.question: Before beginning a 6-minute walk test with an older patient, the physiotherapist records a resting heart rate of 145 beats per minute. What is the most appropriate action?
questions.explanation: Caution should be exercised before beginning a 6-minute walk test if the resting heart rate exceeds 130 beats per minute, since this is one of several safety threshold parameters. Proceeding at full pace despite this finding could pose a cardiovascular risk. The physiotherapist should reassess the patient and consider medical review before continuing.

Overflow, or neurogenic, incontinence presents as frequent dribbling of urine, often after stroke or benign prostatic hyperplasia. It results from mechanical forces on an overdistended bladder or from urinary retention effects on the bladder and sphincter. This is distinct from functional incontinence caused by impaired mobility or cognition.
questions.question: Frequent dribbling of urine following a stroke or benign prostatic hyperplasia, resulting from mechanical forces on an overdistended bladder, describes which type of incontinence?

options: Increase the volume of the television for familiarity
Minimise noise and distraction during the session
Invite additional visitors to provide reassurance
Conduct the session in the busiest room of the house
Ignore the noise since it cannot be modified
questions.explanation: Environmental modification during geriatric assessment and treatment should minimise noise and distraction, such as those from television or intercoms. This is particularly important for patients with cognitive impairment who may become overwhelmed. A calm, quiet environment supports better participation and reduces agitation.
questions.question: An older patient with dementia becomes increasingly agitated during a home physiotherapy visit due to background television noise and multiple family members talking. What environmental adjustment should the physiotherapist recommend first?

options: Avoid electric heating pads because they can cause burns
Always use the highest available heat setting
Apply heat directly without any barrier for maximum effect
Heat should be applied for at least three hours continuously
No precautions are needed regardless of skin condition
questions.explanation: Geriatric pain management guidance specifically advises avoiding electric heating pads, which can cause burns, particularly in patients with reduced sensation and thinner skin. Alternative modalities or careful supervised use with barriers and time limits are safer options. This reflects the broader principle of protecting fragile ageing skin during physical modalities.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is choosing a heat modality for an elderly patient with reduced skin sensitivity and thin skin. Which caution is most important?

A physiotherapist is designing a strengthening programme for a sarcopenic but otherwise healthy 76-year-old. Which principle should guide exercise prescription based on the distinction between sarcopenia and cachexia?
questions.explanation: Sarcopenic muscle, unlike cachectic muscle, is amenable to change and responds to strength training exercise. Progressive resistance training is therefore an appropriate and evidence-based intervention for sarcopenia. This distinction is clinically important because cachectic muscle typically does not respond to the same exercise approach.
options: Complete rest, since sarcopenic muscle cannot recover
Only passive range of motion, avoiding all resistance
Avoidance of exercise until cachexia is ruled out surgically
Progressive resistance training, since sarcopenic muscle responds to strength training

questions.explanation: Physical examination after a fall should look for an orthostatic blood pressure drop, reported to occur in about 25 percent of patients who fall. Checking blood pressure in both sitting and lying, or lying and standing, positions is essential. A significant drop signals increased falls risk requiring further cardiovascular evaluation.
questions.question: During assessment of an older patient after a fall, the physiotherapist checks for a drop in blood pressure when moving from lying to standing. What condition is this test specifically screening for?

options: Training effective coughing and airway clearance techniques
Recommending complete avoidance of any physical activity
Advising rapid, shallow breathing during all exercise
Restricting all activity to bed rest for lung protection
questions.question: A physiotherapist is treating an elderly patient with reduced vital capacity and weakened respiratory muscles. Which intervention listed in geriatric physiotherapy teaching is specifically recommended to support respiratory changes?
questions.explanation: Ways to support age-related respiratory changes include planning activities with shorter durations, training airway clearance techniques, and training effective coughing. This helps offset weakened respiratory muscles and declining lung defence mechanisms. It supports safer participation in rehabilitation without overburdening the respiratory system.

options: Loss of normal sleep-wake circadian rhythms
questions.question: Decreased melatonin levels with advancing age are most directly associated with which functional change?
questions.explanation: Decreased melatonin levels with ageing result in loss of normal sleep-wake cycles, or circadian rhythms. This is one of several nervous system changes that affect daily function in older adults. Sleep disturbance can further compound other age-related problems such as fatigue and falls risk.

options: Increased intra-abdominal fat consistent with obesity
Severe malnutrition requiring urgent feeding support
Significant muscle hypertrophy from strength training
A measurement error requiring no further consideration
questions.question: A physiotherapist measures an elderly man's waist circumference at 108 centimetres. According to anthropometric norms discussed in geriatric assessment, what does this finding suggest?
questions.explanation: In men, a waist circumference greater than 102 centimetres is considered indicative of obesity and increased intra-abdominal fat. This finding should prompt consideration of cardiovascular risk factors and appropriate lifestyle counselling as part of the broader rehabilitation plan. It is not consistent with malnutrition or simple muscle hypertrophy.

questions.question: Chronic or persistent pain is defined as pain lasting for what minimum duration?
questions.explanation: Chronic or persistent pain refers to an unresolved pain problem lasting more than three months, continuing due to factors other than the original injury. Acute pain, by contrast, usually resolves within three months through the healing process. This distinction guides different management approaches.

options: Impaired capacity for dual-tasking, associated with increased fall risk
A sign of intact frontal executive function only
questions.question: An older patient who stops walking whenever asked a question during a clinic corridor test demonstrates which recognised clinical sign relevant to fall risk?
questions.explanation: Elderly persons who stop walking while talking demonstrate a recognised sign linked to impaired dual-tasking and increased fall risk, reflecting reduced frontal executive reserve. This 'stops walking when talking' sign is a simple bedside indicator used in falls assessment. It should prompt further cognitive and gait evaluation.

There is a gradual decrease in kidney volume and weight with ageing, so that by the ninth decade renal size is about 70 percent of that in the third decade. This accompanies a decline in glomerular number and filtration capacity. These changes have direct implications for drug dosing in the elderly.
questions.question: By the ninth decade of life, renal size is approximately what percentage of its size in the third decade?

An elderly patient reports feeling persistently tired and unmotivated but denies feeling sad, despite family concern about her mood. Which condition should the physiotherapist consider, prompting appropriate referral?
options: Definite normal ageing requiring no further action
Confirmed vitamin C deficiency requiring dietary change alone
Confirmed hearing loss requiring only a hearing aid referral
questions.explanation: Depression in older adults can present atypically, with patients denying sadness while reporting tiredness, low energy or low motivation. Recognising this pattern should prompt appropriate referral for further assessment, since a physiotherapist should not diagnose depression outright but can flag concerning features. Early recognition supports timely and effective management.

questions.question: Menopause is fundamentally caused by which underlying physiological process?
options: Sudden failure of the pituitary gland
Complete cessation of adrenal hormone production
Disappearance of oocytes through ovulation and atresia
questions.explanation: Menopause occurs because of the disappearance of oocytes from the ovary through ovulation and atresia. The exact mechanism of ovarian atresia, whether primary ovarian failure or secondary to hypothalamic-pituitary changes, is not fully understood. Vasomotor symptoms are one well-known consequence.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes 'handicap' as distinguished from impairment and disability in older adults?
options: Handicap is identical in meaning to impairment
Handicap is purely an imagined experience without real effect
The effect is felt at the person or society level
questions.explanation: Concerning handicap in the elderly population, the effect is felt at the person or societal level rather than at the organ level, unlike impairment.
