B. State how fractures involving the different regions of the skull base relate to specific clinical presentations.
C. Explain why disease/infection or trauma involving one region of the skull base can produce a functional deficit at a distant site, such as the nasal cavity or the brain itself.
questions.answerText:
A
In the anterior cranial fossa, the foramen caecum transmits a nasal emissary vein (in 1% of the population), the cribriform foramina in the cribriform plate transmit axons of olfactory cells forming the olfactory nerves, and the anterior and posterior ethmoidal foramina transmit vessels and nerves of the same names. In the middle cranial fossa, the optic canals transmit the optic nerves (CN II) and ophthalmic arteries; the superior orbital fissure transmits ophthalmic veins, the ophthalmic nerve (CN V1), CN III, IV and VI, and sympathetic fibres; the foramen rotundum transmits the maxillary nerve (CN V2); the foramen ovale transmits the mandibular nerve (CN V3), the accessory meningeal artery, the lesser petrosal nerve and an emissary vein; the foramen spinosum transmits the middle meningeal artery and vein and the meningeal branch of CN V3; and the foramen lacerum transmits the deep petrosal nerve and some meningeal arterial branches and small veins. In the posterior cranial fossa, the foramen magnum transmits the medulla and meninges, vertebral arteries, CN XI, dural veins, and the anterior and posterior spinal arteries; the jugular foramen transmits CN IX, X and XI, the superior bulb of the internal jugular vein, the inferior petrosal and sigmoid sinuses, and meningeal branches of the ascending pharyngeal and occipital arteries; the hypoglossal canal transmits the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII); the condylar canal transmits an emissary vein from the sigmoid sinus to the vertebral veins in the neck; and the mastoid foramen transmits a mastoid emissary vein from the sigmoid sinus and a meningeal branch of the occipital artery.
B
Fractures of the calvaria are classified as depressed, linear, comminuted, or basilar fractures; fractures of the maxillae and associated bones are termed Le Fort fractures; and there are also fractures of the mandible.
C
The close relation of the frontal sinus to the frontal lobe of the brain explains how infection of this sinus may result in development of a frontal lobe abscess; a fracture involving the sinus, severe enough to tear the dura and pia-arachnoid, will place the subarachnoid space in communication with the nasal cavity, so that CSF may be detected trickling through the nostril (CSF rhinorrhoea), usually on the affected side, although a contralateral leak can occur since these sinuses may communicate. Similarly, infection of the ethmoid sinuses (ethmoiditis) may result in a frontal cerebral abscess, and an ethmoidal fracture may cause CSF leakage into the nasal cavity, because the ethmoid sinuses lie on each side of the cribriform plate and are related above to the frontal lobes of the brain.

A
Most of the muscles of the larynx receive their innervation via the recurrent laryngeal branch of the vagus nerve; the exception is the cricothyroid muscle, which receives its innervation via the external laryngeal nerve. Motor supply to the muscles is from the nucleus ambiguus via the cranial accessory: to the cricothyroid via the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, and to all other laryngeal muscles, including the upper oesophagus and cricopharyngeus, via the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
B
Sensory innervation of the larynx is via branches of the vagus nerve: above the vocal folds it is via the internal laryngeal nerve, and below the vocal folds it is by way of branches of the recurrent laryngeal nerve; parasympathetic innervation of the larynx is mainly by way of branches of the vagus nerve. Lymphatic drainage similarly follows this division: above the cords to the upper deep cervical nodes, and below the cords to the lower deep cervical nodes.
questions.question:
A. Describe the nerve supply of the larynx, including the origin and distribution of the recurrent laryngeal nerve and the exception to its motor supply.
B. State how the sensory innervation of the larynx is divided in relation to the vocal folds.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
The phrenic nerve is formed in the neck within the cervical plexus and contains fibres from spinal roots C3, C4 and C5.
A(ii)
• Its long course from the neck follows the embryological migration of the diaphragm from the cervical region: the septum transversum is carried ventrally and caudally, and the cervical myotomes and nerves contribute the muscle and nerve supply.
• It passes through the superior and middle mediastinum: the right phrenic descends on the right side of the SVC and heart; the left phrenic descends on the left side of the heart.
A(iii)
Both nerves terminate in the diaphragm: terminal branches of the right phrenic pass through the caval opening (T8) in the central tendon, and the left phrenic pierces the left dome.
A(iv)
• Motor: the sole motor supply of the diaphragm; the right nerve supplies the right half up to the right margin of the oesophageal opening and the left nerve the left half up to the left margin.
• Sensory: the central part of the diaphragm and the related pleura and peritoneum, and sensory fibres to the pleurae and pericardium (mediastinal pleura, fibrous and parietal pericardium); the peripheral part receives sensory fibres from the lower 6 or 7 intercostal and subcostal nerves.
C(i)
• Sectioning or injury of a phrenic nerve in the neck causes complete paralysis and eventual atrophy of the muscular part of the corresponding half of the diaphragm, except in persons who have an accessory phrenic nerve.
• Causes of injury: mechanical trauma (ligation or damage during surgery) and compression by a tumour within the chest cavity; myopathies (e.g. myasthenia gravis) and neuropathies (e.g. diabetic neuropathy) also interrupt the supply.
• The paralysed half is elevated and shows paradoxical movement: it moves upwards during inspiration (forced up by abdominal viscera) and downwards during expiration; only one half is affected because each dome has a separate nerve supply.
• Unilateral paralysis is usually asymptomatic and an incidental finding on X-ray; if both sides are paralysed there is poor exercise tolerance, orthopnoea and fatigue, and lung function tests show a restrictive deficit.
• Irritation of the diaphragmatic pleura or of the peritoneum under the diaphragm (pleurisy, subphrenic pus or blood) refers pain to the shoulder tip, because the central diaphragm sends sensory fibres in the phrenic nerve (C3-5) and the shoulder skin is supplied by the supraclavicular nerve (C3,4).
questions.question:
A(i) State the origin and root value of the phrenic nerve.
A(ii) Describe its course, relations and embryological basis of its long course on the right and left.
A(iii) Describe its termination and the points at which it reaches the diaphragm.
A(iv) Describe its distribution (motor and sensory).
C(i) Explain the anatomical basis of the deformity and other consequences after injury or section of the nerve.

A(i) State the origin of the posterior intercostal arteries.
A(ii) Describe their course and relations in the intercostal space.
A(iii) State their branches, distribution and venous and lymphatic companions.
B(i) State the safe site and the danger site for passing a needle or drain through an intercostal space and the anatomical basis.
C(i) Explain the anatomical basis of the rib deformity seen on radiographs in coarctation of the aorta.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Each intercostal space has a single posterior and two anterior intercostal arteries.
• In the upper two spaces the posterior intercostal arteries arise from the superior intercostal artery (branch of the costocervical trunk of the subclavian artery); in the lower nine spaces they arise from the thoracic aorta (9 pairs, plus 1 pair of subcostal arteries from the posterior surface of the descending thoracic aorta).
A(ii)
Course and branching follow the intercostal nerves: each artery runs forward in the subcostal groove, high in the space between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles, in the order vein, artery, nerve from above downwards, and anastomoses with the anterior intercostal artery.
A(iii)
• Branches go to adjacent muscles, skin, parietal pleura, spinal cord and breast (branches in the 3rd and 4th spaces supply the breast); the 3rd right posterior intercostal artery gives the right bronchial artery.
• Distribution: the posterior and lateral parts of the intercostal spaces.
• Veins accompany the arteries and contain valves that direct blood posteriorly; on the right the 1st space drains to the brachiocephalic vein and the rest to the azygos vein; on the left the upper 3 spaces drain to the left brachiocephalic vein and the rest to the hemiazygos and accessory hemiazygos veins, which drain to the azygos vein.
• Lymphatics: deep lymphatics follow the arteries; posteriorly they drain to the posterior intercostal nodes in the posterior mediastinum.
B(i)
• Safe site: a needle or drain is passed immediately above the upper border of a rib; it is dangerous to pass it immediately below a rib.
• Basis: the intercostal vessels lie immediately below their corresponding ribs (vein above artery) in the subcostal groove, so a needle just above the lower rib avoids the neurovascular bundle; in thoracotomy the periosteum over a segment of the 5th or 6th rib is elevated, protecting the bundle.
C(i)
• In coarctation of the aorta the intercostal arteries derived from the aorta receive blood from the superior intercostals, from the anterior intercostal branches of the internal thoracic artery and from arteries anastomosing around the scapula.
• Together with the communication between the internal thoracic and inferior epigastric arteries, these are the principal collaterals between the aorta above and below the block.
• The intercostal arteries dilate and become tortuous and erode the lower borders of the corresponding ribs, giving the characteristic irregular notching of the ribs that helps radiographic confirmation.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the extent, length and parts of the trachea.
A(ii) Describe the relations of the trachea and its level of bifurcation.
A(iii) Compare the right and left main bronchi.
A(iv) Describe the lobar and segmental divisions of the bronchi and the terminal airways.
A(v) Describe the lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of the trachea and bronchi.
B(i) Relate the parts of the bronchial tree to common pathologies.
C(i) Explain how disease of the bronchial tree may spread to distant structures through the lymphatics.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
A wide tube about 10 cm long and 2 cm wide, lying in the superior mediastinum and extending from C6 (lower border of the cricoid cartilage) to T4, where it divides into the right and left main bronchi; it has cervical and thoracic parts, the cervical part measuring 5 cm.
A(ii)
• The cervical part is in contact posteriorly with the oesophagus and anteriorly with the isthmus of the thyroid gland; it is palpable in the suprasternal notch midway between the heads of the clavicles; it ends at the sternal angle (T4/5) just to the right of the midline (at T6 in the erect position in full inspiration).
• At the bifurcation the azygos vein arches over the right main bronchus (T4) and the left main bronchus lies in front of the oesophagus (27 cm from the incisor teeth); the cardiac plexus lies on the lowest part of the trachea behind the arch of the aorta.
A(iii)
Right main bronchus: 2.5 cm long, shorter, wider and vertically oriented; left main bronchus: 5 cm long, longer, narrower and horizontally oriented.
A(iv)
• Right main bronchus divides into upper (outside the hilum), middle and lower lobar bronchi, giving 10 bronchopulmonary segments; the left divides within the hilum into 2 lobar bronchi, giving 8 segments; segmental (third-order) bronchi supply the segments.
• The U-shaped cartilage bars of the trachea are replaced by irregular plates in smaller bronchi; the smallest bronchi give bronchioles (under 1 mm), then terminal bronchioles and respiratory bronchioles (about 0.5 mm, with outpouchings where gas exchange occurs), then alveolar ducts, alveolar sacs and alveoli surrounded by capillaries.
A(v)
Trachea: lymphatics drain to the deep cervical and paratracheal lymph nodes; the mucous membrane is supplied by the vagus, which also gives the parasympathetic supply. Lung and bronchi: pulmonary plexuses with vagal (bronchoconstrictor, secretomotor) and sympathetic (bronchodilator) fibres.
B(i)
• The wider, more vertical right main bronchus allows foreign particles to enter it easily; asthma (dyspnoea); pneumonia (bacterial or viral infection of the lung); pulmonary embolism (pulmonary artery obstructed by air, blood clot, fat, tumour cells or foreign particles).
• Abscesses are commoner in the posterior segment of the upper lobe and the apical segment of the lower lobe (most dependent supine); septa between segments limit infection but carcinoma and tuberculosis break through; fibrosis reduces compliance and emphysema reduces elasticity.
C(i)
• Lymph from lung and bronchi passes to the bronchopulmonary (hilar) nodes, then to the superior and inferior tracheobronchial nodes (above and below the tracheal bifurcation), then to the right and left bronchomediastinal trunks.
• The trunks usually end at the junction of the subclavian and internal jugular veins; the right trunk may join other trunks to form the right lymphatic duct and the left may end in the thoracic duct.

A(i)
Stomach mucosa:
• Surface epithelium and gastric pits: consists of a simple columnar epithelium that invaginates into the lamina propria forming gastric pits. Millions of gastric pits each open into the lumen of the stomach; the gastric pits lead into long, branched, tubular glands extending through the thickness of the lamina propria; between each gastric pit and gastric gland is the isthmus (region of stem cells).
• Isthmus and stem cells: the pluripotent stem cells divide asymmetrically producing progenitor cells for all other epithelial cells; they can move upwards to replace surface mucous cells or downwards to replace other secretory cells.
• Lamina propria: highly vascularised; supports pits and glands; contains smooth muscle fibers, capillaries, lymphatics, and lymphoid cells.
• Muscularis mucosae: layer of smooth muscle separating the mucosa from the underlying submucosa.
A(ii)
Four secretory cell types of fundic/body glands:
• Mucous neck cells (MNCs): less columnar than surface mucous cells; irregular in shape with round nucleus and apical secretory granules; secrete acidic fluid containing mucin (less alkaline than surface mucous cells).
• Parietal (oxyntic) cells: large, rounded or pyramidal cells; one central spherical nucleus; intensely eosinophilic cytoplasm due to high density of mitochondria; secrete hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor.
• Chief (zymogen) cells: predominate in lower regions; abundant RER and numerous apical secretory granules (characteristics of protein-secreting cells); secrete pepsinogen (converted to pepsin at pH < 5), lipase, and leptin.
• Enteroendocrine cells: scattered throughout the gastric mucosa; secrete hormones with endocrine or paracrine functions (e.g., serotonin in fundus; gastrin from G cells in pylorus).
B(i)
• Fundus/body: long branched tubular gastric glands (3 to 7 per pit); each gland has an isthmus, neck, and base; contains all four cell types above; secretes acidic gastric juice.
• Cardia/pylorus: tubular glands with long pits, usually branching into coiled secretory portions (cardiac/pyloric glands); lack parietal and chief cells; major secretion is abundant mucus.
B(ii)
Rugae are longitudinally directed folds of the mucosa and submucosa of the empty stomach. They flatten when the stomach is full with food.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the mucosa of the stomach under the following headings: surface epithelium and gastric pits; the isthmus and stem cells; the lamina propria; and the muscularis mucosae.
A(ii) Name and describe all four secretory epithelial cell types found in the gastric glands of the fundus and body, including the characteristics of each cell and what it secretes.
B(i) Distinguish between the mucosa of the fundus/body and the mucosa of the cardia/pylorus under the headings: gland type, cell types present, and principal secretion.
B(ii) Explain what rugae are and the physiological condition under which they disappear.

A(i) Define the diaphragm and describe its shape, position and relations.
A(ii) Describe its origin (sternal, costal and vertebral, including the crura and arcuate ligaments) and its insertion.
A(iii) Describe its openings, their vertebral levels and the structures transmitted.
A(iv) Describe its blood supply.
A(v) Describe its nerve supply and lymphatic drainage.
B(i) Explain the anatomical basis of referred shoulder pain from irritation of the diaphragm.
B(ii) Explain why acquired herniae occur through the oesophageal opening and name the two types.
B(iii) Explain hiccup.
C(i) Distinguish between the right and the left crus of the diaphragm.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
A double-domed, thin fibromuscular (musculotendinous) partition between the thoracic and abdominal cavities and the main muscle of respiration; convex superior surface faces the thorax (covered by diaphragmatic pleura, lungs fit the domes, fibrous pericardium on the central tendon), concave inferior surface faces the abdomen (parietal peritoneum; liver, kidneys, suprarenals, stomach, spleen); higher on the right because of the liver (in expiration the right dome reaches the 5th rib, the left the 5th intercostal space); level varies with respiration, posture and abdominal distension, and the domes flatten in maximal inspiration.
A(ii)
Sternal: 2 slips from the posterior xiphoid process; costal: deep surfaces of the lower 6 ribs and costal cartilages (forms the domes); vertebral: the crura and 3 arcuate ligaments - medial (thickened psoas fascia, from the body of L2 to the tip of the L1 transverse process), lateral (thickened quadratus lumborum fascia, from the L1 transverse process to the lower border of the 12th rib) and median (joins the crura across the front of the aorta). Insertion: trefoil central tendon, no bony attachments, partly fused with the fibrous pericardium (pericardiophrenic ligament).
A(iii)
• Caval opening (T8; the only opening in the central tendon): IVC, terminal branches of the right phrenic nerve, a few lymphatics. Oesophageal opening (T10; in the right crus): oesophagus, anterior and posterior vagal trunks, oesophageal branches of the left gastric vessels, a few lymphatics. Aortic opening (T12; lowest and most posterior, between the crura): aorta, thoracic duct, sometimes azygos and hemiazygos veins.
• Smaller openings: greater and lesser splanchnic nerves pierce each crus; hemiazygos vein pierces the left crus; left phrenic nerve pierces the left dome; sympathetic trunks pass behind the diaphragm deep to the medial arcuate ligament; subcostal vessels and nerve pass behind the lateral arcuate ligament; superior epigastric vessels pass between the sternal and costal origins; 7th-11th intercostal neurovascular bundles pass through the costal origin.
A(iv)
Arteries: pericardiophrenic and musculophrenic (from the internal thoracic) and superior phrenic (from the thoracic aorta) to the superior surface; inferior phrenic (first branches of the abdominal aorta) to the inferior surface. Veins: pericardiophrenic and musculophrenic to the internal thoracic vein; superior phrenic vein (right) and right inferior phrenic vein to the IVC; the left inferior phrenic vein drains to the IVC and the left suprarenal vein.
A(v)
• Motor: phrenic nerves (C3-5) only - the right nerve to the right half up to the right margin of the oesophageal opening, the left to the left half. Sensory: central part (with related pleura and peritoneum) via the phrenic nerves; peripheral part via the lower 6 or 7 intercostal and subcostal nerves.
• Lymph: thoracic surface to anterior and posterior diaphragmatic nodes (anterior on to parasternal nodes; posterior to phrenic and posterior mediastinal nodes); abdominal surface to anterior diaphragmatic, phrenic and superior lumbar (caval/aortic) nodes.
B(i)
The central diaphragm is supplied sensorily by the phrenic nerve (C3-5) and the shoulder skin by the supraclavicular nerve (C3,4); so pain from irritation of pleura or pericardium over the central diaphragm, or of the peritoneum under it by subphrenic pus or blood, is referred to the shoulder tip.
B(ii)
Acquired herniae occur in middle-aged people with weak musculature around the oesophageal opening; they are either sliding or paraoesophageal (rolling, alongside the oesophagus).
B(iii)
Hiccup is an involuntary spasmodic contraction of the diaphragm with approximation of the vocal folds and closure of the glottis; common after eating or drinking from gastric irritation of vagus nerve endings; it may be due to pleurisy, peritonitis or pericarditis.
C(i)
• Right crus: larger and longer, arises from the upper 3 lumbar vertebrae (L1-L3) and their intervertebral discs; some of its fibres pass up to the left and loop round the oesophageal orifice as a physiological sphincter preventing reflux of gastric contents.
• Left crus: smaller, arises from the side of the bodies of the upper 2 (L1-L2) lumbar vertebrae and their discs; each crus is attached to the medial and lateral arcuate ligaments, and the medial borders of the two crura unite in front of T12 as the median arcuate ligament over the aorta.

A(i)
• Shape of a clenched fist; base to apex 12 cm in males and 10 cm in females, anteroposterior 6 cm and 5 cm, transverse 9 cm and 8 cm; weight 280-340 g in males and 230-280 g in females; lies behind the body of the sternum, in front of T5-T8, with a base, an apex, 3 surfaces and 4 borders.
• Base: posterior, mostly left atrium, receives the 4 pulmonary veins; ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk emerge from it; separated from the diaphragmatic surface by the coronary sulcus. Apex: inferolateral, mostly left ventricle, behind the 5th left intercostal space. Surfaces: sternocostal (mostly right ventricle), diaphragmatic (concave), pulmonary (left ventricle, fitting the cardiac notch of the left lung). Borders: right (right atrium), left (mostly left ventricle with the left auricle), superior (auricles and upper right ventricle), inferior (right atrium and right ventricle).
A(ii)
Right border: 3rd to 6th right costal cartilage; left border: 5th left intercostal space (apex beat, 9 cm from the midline) up to the 2nd costal cartilage; superior border: 2nd left to 3rd right costal cartilage; inferior border: 6th right costal cartilage to the 5th left intercostal space.
A(iii)
• Four chambers: atria separated by the interatrial septum, ventricles by the interventricular septum, atria from ventricles by the right and left coronary (AV) sulci. Right atrium: forms the right border, lies between SVC and IVC, has the right auricle; rough part (musculi pectinati) and smooth part (from the right horn of the sinus venosus) separated by the sulcus terminalis (crista terminalis); receives SVC, IVC and coronary sinus.
• Right ventricle: forms the sternocostal and diaphragmatic surfaces and inferior border; trabeculae carneae including the septomarginal trabecula (carries part of the AV bundle) and anterior, posterior and septal papillary muscles joined by chordae tendineae to the tricuspid valve (3 cusps, admits 3 fingertips), the chordae preventing the cusps being driven into the right atrium; pulmonary orifice about 2.5 cm with 3 semilunar cusps (anterior, left, right).
• Left atrium: posterior, forms the base, receives 4 valveless pulmonary veins; left auricle forms the upper left border; smooth wall except the auricle. Mitral (bicuspid) valve: anterior and posterior cusps, admits 2 fingertips, overlaps the tricuspid and lies slightly higher. Left ventricle: aortic orifice about 2.5 cm at the right upper part with 3 semilunar cusps (posterior, right, left); numerous trabeculae carneae; anterior and posterior papillary muscles with chordae to the mitral valve.
A(iv)
SA node: natural pacemaker, first conducting cell, below the opening of the SVC in the right atrium, contains pacemaker P-cells, autonomic supply from the cardiac plexus (sympathetics increase and parasympathetics decrease the rate of impulse generation). AV node: slow conducting tissue in the posterior and inferior interatrial septum, allows complete atrial contraction before ventricular contraction. AV bundle of His: Purkinje fibres in the membranous part of the interventricular septum, the only bridge between atrial and ventricular muscle; right branch to papillary muscles and moderator band, left branch to the left papillary muscles.
A(v)
Arteries: right and left coronary arteries from the ascending aorta run in the right and left AV sulci; the right gives posterior interventricular and marginal arteries, the left gives anterior interventricular and circumflex arteries (the circumflex gives a marginal branch). Veins: the coronary sinus (posterior part of the AV sulcus, valve at its opening, empties into the right atrium) receives the great, small and middle cardiac veins, posterior vein of the left ventricle and oblique vein of the left atrium; the anterior cardiac vein opens into the right atrium and venae cordis minimae open into the chambers. Nerve supply: cardiac plexus.
B(i)
• The heart has a poor anastomotic network, so blockage of one coronary artery (coronary thrombosis) leads to myocardial infarction; the heart wall has 3 layers (epicardium, myocardium, endocardium) and the serous pericardium receives the coronary arteries.
• Angina pectoris: chest pain originating from the heart, caused by insufficient supply of oxygen to the heart muscle.
C(i)
• Irritation of the pleura or pericardium covering the central part of the diaphragm is referred to the shoulder, because the central diaphragm is supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3-5) and the shoulder skin by the supraclavicular nerve (C3,4); the fibrous and parietal pericardium are supplied by the phrenic nerve.
• Hiccup: involuntary spasmodic contraction of the diaphragm with approximation of the vocal folds and closure of the glottis; it may be due to pleurisy, peritonitis or pericarditis.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the size, shape, position, base, apex, surfaces and borders of the heart.
A(ii) Describe the surface marking of the heart.
A(iii) Describe the chambers and valves of the heart.
A(iv) Describe the conducting system of the heart.
A(v) Describe the blood supply, venous drainage and nerve supply of the heart.
B(i) Relate the arterial supply and structure of the heart to common cardiac pathologies.
C(i) Explain how disease of the heart coverings and neighbouring structures may cause pain or disturbance in a distant structure.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Three parts of the renal tubule:
• Proximal convoluted tubule (PCT): cuboidal cells with dense microvilli (brush border — increase surface area); large mitochondria; functions in reabsorption and secretion; confined to the cortex.
• Nephron loop: descending and ascending limbs; distal descending limb = descending thin limb — simple squamous epithelium; thick ascending limb — cuboidal to columnar cells (thin in some nephrons).
• Distal convoluted tubule (DCT): cuboidal cells with very few microvilli; functions more in secretion than reabsorption; confined to the cortex.
A(ii)
Nephron loop:
• Descending limb: proximal descending limb is continuous with the proximal tubule; distal descending limb (thin limb) is lined by simple squamous epithelium.
• Thick ascending limb: cuboidal to columnar cells; may be thin in some nephrons.
B(i)
Renal corpuscle:
• Two components: glomerulus and glomerular (Bowman's) capsule.
• Glomerulus: tuft of capillaries with fenestrated endothelium (highly porous) allowing filtrate formation.
Glomerular capsule: cup-shaped, hollow structure surrounding the glomerulus; has two layers:
• Parietal layer: simple squamous epithelium.
• Visceral layer: branching epithelial podocytes; extensions terminate in foot processes that cling to the basement membrane; filtration slits between foot processes allow filtrate to pass into the capsular space.
B(ii)
Structural adaptations of the PCT:
• Dense microvilli (brush border) greatly increase the apical surface area for reabsorption.
• Large mitochondria provide energy (ATP) for active transport processes.
• Highly infolded basolateral membrane increases surface area for solute exchange at the basolateral side.
• These features together support the PCT's role in reabsorption and secretion.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the three parts of the renal tubule, including the cell type lining each part, distinguishing microscopic features, and the primary function (reabsorption vs. secretion) attributed to each part.
A(ii) Describe the two parts of the nephron loop, including the type of epithelium lining each limb and any variation across nephron types.
B(i) Describe the renal corpuscle, naming its two components, the two layers of the glomerular capsule, and the specialised features of the visceral layer.
B(ii) For the proximal convoluted tubule, explain how its structure is adapted for its function.

questions.answerText:
(i)
• The right and left coronary arteries are the first branches of the aorta, arising from the corresponding right and left aortic sinuses at the proximal ascending aorta.
• The right coronary artery runs in the atrioventricular (coronary) groove and gives off the SA nodal branch, right marginal branch, AV nodal branch, and posterior interventricular branch, which anastomoses with the anterior interventricular branch of the left coronary artery.
• The right coronary artery typically supplies the right atrium, most of the right ventricle, part of the left ventricle, the posterior third of the AV septum, the SA node in 60% of people and the AV node in 80% of people.
• The left coronary artery arises from the left aortic sinus, runs in the AV groove, and divides into the circumflex and anterior interventricular branches.
• The left coronary artery typically supplies the left atrium, most of the left ventricle, part of the right ventricle, most of the interventricular septum and the SA node in 40% of people.
• Venous drainage is mainly through the coronary sinus, which receives the great, middle and small cardiac veins and the left posterior ventricular and left marginal veins.
(ii)
Arterial dominance is defined by which artery gives rise to the posterior interventricular artery; right dominance is typical, the left is dominant in about 10% of people, and co-dominance occurs in about 15% of people.
(iii)
• Because the right coronary artery mainly supplies the right atrium, right ventricle and, in most people, the SA and AV nodes, its occlusion can damage right-sided myocardium and disturb the conduction system.
• Because the left coronary artery mainly supplies the left atrium, left ventricle and interventricular septum, its occlusion tends to damage the left ventricle, which performs more work than the right, and the septum.
• Damage to the region supplying the SA or AV node can disturb the heart's conducting system, since the SA and AV nodes are the pacesetters of the heart.
• Tissue damage from reduced blood flow in the territory of the affected artery causes the chest pain of ischaemia/infarction, which can radiate as referred pain to the jaw and left arm.
questions.question:
(i) Describe the origin, course, branches and distribution of the right and left coronary arteries.
(ii) State which artery gives off the posterior interventricular artery in most individuals (arterial dominance).
(iii) Explain the anatomical basis for the pattern of myocardial damage that follows occlusion of a particular coronary artery.

Describe the femur under the following headings and explain how its zones relate to common pathologies.
A(i) General features, parts, and gross anatomy of the femur
A(ii) The neck of femur — angles of inclination and torsion, and why fracture here causes coxa vara
B(i) Blood supply of the head of femur and why avascular necrosis occurs after intracapsular fracture
B(ii) The linea aspera — muscular and bony attachments, and clinical significance
C(i) Distinguish pressure epiphysis from traction epiphysis with examples from the femur, and explain why the nutrient canal direction matters surgically
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The femur is the long bone of the thigh; the longest and strongest bone in the body (Latin: femur = thigh); it accounts for approximately one-quarter of a person's total height and averages 45 cm. It has a shaft (body) and 2 expanded ends. Parts: (1) proximal end — consisting of head, neck, and the trochanters; (2) shaft; (3) distal end — consisting of the femoral condyles. It articulates superiorly with the acetabulum to form the hip joint, and inferiorly with the patella and tibia to form the knee joint.
A(ii)
The neck is the curved upper end of the shaft; it connects the head to the shaft and passes downward, backward, and laterally, obliquely placed to the long axis of the shaft. The angle of inclination (neck–shaft angle) is approximately 135 degrees; reduction of this angle is coxa vara and follows fracture of the neck of femur. The angle of anteversion (torsion) — the forward relationship of head and neck — is normally 12–15 degrees; wide variation in anteversion of the femoral neck means that during total hip arthroplasty, orientation of the femoral neck osteotomy in correct anteversion must be assessed after hip dislocation with reference to the shaft of femur with knee flexed at 90 degrees, or an inaccurate cut and malposition of the prosthesis may result.
B(i)
The fovea capitis on the head of femur transmits blood from the obturator artery via the ligament of the head of femur (ligamentum teres). The main blood supply travels retinacularly along the intracapsular neck from the medial femoral circumflex artery (which wraps around the posterior side of the femur supplying its neck and head). In an intracapsular fracture, these retinacular vessels are disrupted; the obturator artery contribution via ligamentum teres is insufficient to sustain the head, and avascular necrosis results.
B(ii)
The linea aspera is a posterior ridge on the shaft of femur; it diverges superiorly and inferiorly. The inferior divergence ends as the medial supracondylar ridge to the adductor tubercle and the lateral supracondylar ridge. The linea aspera gives origin to many muscles: adductor longus inserts into the middle third of its medial lip; adductor magnus into the gluteal tuberosity, linea aspera, and medial supracondylar line; the vastus lateralis arises from its lateral lip.
C(i)
Pressure epiphyses are formed at joints and bear compressive forces (e.g., head of femur — a pressure epiphysis; femoral condyles). Traction epiphyses are pulled by muscles (e.g., greater trochanter — traction epiphysis for gluteus medius which draws it upward, medially, and backward; lesser trochanter — traction epiphysis for iliopsoas, the great flexor of the hip joint). The nutrient artery is directed obliquely away from the epiphyseal end; when there is an epiphysis at both ends, the nutrient canal is directed away from the more actively growing end (as per Hughes's rule: 'to the elbow I go, from the knee I flee'). Surgically, the nutrient canal direction matters during intramedullary nail insertion, as the nail must not block the nutrient foramen.

A(i)
Five lumbar vertebrae (1 to 4 typical, 5 atypical); largest and strongest of the column because supported weight increases inferiorly; superior facets face medially, inferior facets laterally; thick broad spines.
A(ii)
• Large kidney-shaped body, deeper anteriorly; triangular foramen (larger than thoracic, smaller than cervical); short strong pedicles; short thick broad laminae; spine a vertical quadrilateral plate.
• Transverse processes thin and tapering (accessory process); superior articular facets concave facing medially and backwards with the mammillary process; inferior facets convex facing laterally and forwards.
A(iii)
L5: thick short pyramidal transverse processes; largest body, anterior deeper than posterior, creating the sharp lumbosacral angle; small short rounded spine; inferior articular distance equal to or more than the superior.
A(iv)
Joints: intervertebral discs (symphysis) between bodies; synovial joints between arches. Ligaments: anterior and posterior longitudinal, ligamentum flavum, interspinous, supraspinous; iliolumbar ligaments strengthen the L5 to S1 lumbosacral joint.
B(i)
• A lumbar vertebra ossifies from three primary centres (body and each half of the neural arch) appearing in the third month of fetal life; the halves of the arch fuse posteriorly in the first year.
• Failure of fusion of the two halves of the neural arch results in spina bifida; if one primary centre of the body fails, hemivertebra.
B(ii)
• Lumbar spinal stenosis: thought hereditary, a narrow vertebral foramen in one or several vertebrae.
• Excessive lumbar lordosis: abnormal anterior curvature with anterior tilting of the pelvis.
C(i)
• The canal formed by L1 and L2 contains the conus medullaris; the lower three contain the cauda equina; all contain the spinal meninges.
• Stenosis can compress the spinal cord and exiting nerves; the pedicles are related above and below to spinal nerves.
• The right crus of the diaphragm attaches to the upper three lumbar vertebrae and the left crus to the upper two; psoas major arises from the vertebral borders.

A(i)
The great saphenous vein (GSV) is the longest vein in the body. It is formed by the union of the dorsal vein of the great toe and the dorsal venous arch of the foot. It ascends anterior to the medial malleolus, passes posterior to the medial condyle of the femur (about a hand's breadth posterior to the medial border of the patella), anastomoses freely with the small saphenous vein, traverses the saphenous opening in the fascia lata, and empties into the femoral vein.
A(ii)
The GSV has 10–12 valves, which are more numerous in the leg than in the thigh; these valves are usually located just inferior to the perforating veins. Perforating veins also have their own valves. Tributaries in the anterior and lateral part of the thighs converge to form the accessory saphenous vein (ASV), which communicates the GSV with the small saphenous vein. Just before emptying into the femoral vein, the GSV receives tributaries from the superficial circumflex iliac, superficial epigastric, and external pudendal veins.
B(i)
The small saphenous vein (SSV) arises on the lateral side of the foot from the union of the dorsal vein of the little toe with the dorsal venous arch. It ascends posterior to the lateral malleolus as a continuation of the lateral marginal vein, passes along the lateral border of the calcaneal tendon, inclines to the midline of the fibula and penetrates the deep fascia, ascends between the heads of the gastrocnemius muscle, and empties into the popliteal vein in the popliteal fossa.
B(ii)
There are four main pulse points in the lower limb: femoral (palpated midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and pubic symphysis — the mid-inguinal point); popliteal (deep in the popliteal fossa, requires deep palpation, best with slight knee flexion); dorsalis pedis (on the dorsum of the foot, just lateral to extensor hallucis longus tendon); and posterior tibial (inferoposteriorly to the medial malleolus). The GSV anterior to the medial malleolus is the classic site for venous cut-down; the GSV at the medial condyle of the femur is another accessible site.
C(i)
Superficial veins (GSV and SSV) are unaccompanied, lie in the superficial fascia, and their varicosity is visible. Deep veins of the lower limb accompany the arteries (read-up). Deep vein thrombosis involves the deep system and poses a risk of pulmonary embolism because the deep veins drain directly into the popliteal, femoral, and iliac veins and thence to the inferior vena cava. Superficial varicosity alone rarely embolises unless thrombosis extends through a perforating vein into the deep system.
questions.question:
Describe the great saphenous vein and small saphenous vein under the following headings, and explain the clinical basis of their use in surgery.
A(i) Origin, course, and termination of the great saphenous vein
A(ii) Tributaries and valves of the great saphenous vein
B(i) Origin, course, and termination of the small saphenous vein
B(ii) Clinical basis: pulse points of the lower limb and sites of venepuncture or cut-down
C(i) Distinguish varicosity from deep vein thrombosis based on the anatomical differences between the superficial and deep venous systems

(A) Describe the oesophagus under the following headings: A(i) its four constrictions along its length A(ii) the upper oesophageal sphincter A(iii) the lower oesophageal sphincter.
(B) Explain the clinical basis of why the areas of constriction are important.
(C) Distinguish between the upper oesophageal sphincter and the lower oesophageal sphincter.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The oesophagus has four constrictions: at 15 cm (cricopharyngeus, upper oesophageal sphincter), at 22.5 cm (crossed by the aortic arch) and 27.5 cm (crossed by the left main bronchus) from the upper incisor teeth, and at 40 cm, where it passes through the right crus of the diaphragm (oesophageal hiatus).
A(ii)
The upper oesophageal sphincter is an anatomical sphincter formed by the cricopharyngeus muscle at the pharyngo-oesophageal junction.
A(iii)
• The lower oesophageal sphincter is a physiological sphincter at the gastro-oesophageal junction with no true muscular thickening.
• It is maintained by the acute angle of entry of the oesophagus into the stomach, compression of the intra-abdominal oesophagus by positive intra-abdominal pressure, prominent mucosal folds at the junction, and the pinch-cock effect of the right crus of the diaphragm.
B
• The constrictions are clinically important because they are sites where swallowed foreign bodies commonly impact.
• They are prone to trauma during instrumentation such as rigid oesophagoscopy.
• They are common sites for stricture formation following ingestion of corrosive substances.
• They are also common sites of oesophageal carcinoma.
C
• The upper oesophageal sphincter is a true anatomical (muscular) sphincter formed by the cricopharyngeus, located at 15 cm from the incisor teeth.
• The lower oesophageal sphincter is a physiological sphincter maintained by mechanical factors at the gastro-oesophageal junction and prevents gastric reflux, rather than a distinct muscular ring controlling food passage.

A(i)
The orbit is shaped like a pear or quadrilateral pyramid, with its base in the plane of the orbital rim and its pyramidal cavity base in front and apex behind; it protects, supports and maximises the function of the eye, and seven bones conjoin to form the orbital structure. The average dimensions of the orbit are: height of orbital margin 40 mm, width of orbital margin 35 mm, depth of orbit 40-50 mm, interorbital distance 25 mm, and volume of orbit 30 cm³; 20% of this space is occupied by the eyeball, and about one-sixth of the eye is exposed, the remainder being protected by the walls of the orbit.
A(ii)
The major nerves and vessels to the orbit and globe enter through 3 openings. The superior orbital fissure, bounded by the lesser and greater wings of the sphenoid, transmits cranial nerves III, IV and VI, the lacrimal nerve, frontal nerve, nasociliary nerve, orbital branch of the middle meningeal artery, recurrent branch of the lacrimal artery, superior orbital vein and superior ophthalmic vein. The inferior orbital fissure, bounded by the greater wing of the sphenoid, the maxilla and the palatine bones, transmits the infraorbital nerve, zygomatic nerve, parasympathetics to the lacrimal gland, infraorbital artery, infraorbital vein, and the inferior ophthalmic vein branch to the pterygoid plexus. The optic canal, at the apex of the orbit within the sphenoid bone, transmits the optic nerve, ophthalmic artery, and central retinal vein. The connective tissue boundaries of the orbit are divided into 4 main units: the bulbar (Tenon) fascia, surrounding and protecting the globe and providing a barrier between the globe and retrobulbar fat; multiple connective tissue septa extending from the globe to the periorbita like spokes on a wheel; the individual connective tissue sheath of each extraocular muscle, which fuses to form a confluent muscle sheath and the medial and lateral check ligaments; and the periosteal lining of the orbit, which can be elevated in surgery to expose the bony orbit.
B
Clinical correlates of the orbit include eye trauma with blow-out fracture, due to blunt trauma, which displaces the orbital walls; paralysis of the extraocular muscles results in double vision. Obstruction of the flow of aqueous humor results in a rise in intraocular pressure called glaucoma, leading to degenerative changes in the retina with consequent blindness.
C
The superior orbital fissure transmits cranial nerves III, IV and VI, the lacrimal, frontal and nasociliary nerves, the orbital branch of the middle meningeal artery, the recurrent branch of the lacrimal artery, and the superior orbital and superior ophthalmic veins. The inferior orbital fissure, in contrast, transmits the infraorbital nerve, the zygomatic nerve, parasympathetics to the lacrimal gland, the infraorbital artery and vein, and the inferior ophthalmic vein branch to the pterygoid plexus.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the orbit under the following headings: shape, the bones forming it, and its average dimensions.
A(ii) Describe the three openings into the orbital cavity and the structures transmitted through each, and describe the connective tissue planes of the orbit.
B. Explain the clinical basis for why orbital trauma can result in double vision and in a rise of intraocular pressure.
C. Distinguish between the superior orbital fissure and the inferior orbital fissure in terms of the structures each transmits.

A. Describe the course and distribution of the lingual nerve, including its relationship to the submandibular duct.
B. State the site at which the lingual nerve crosses the submandibular duct, which is relevant to procedures in this region.
C. Explain the functional deficit that would be anticipated from injury to the lingual nerve, based on the sensory territory it supplies.
questions.answerText:
A
The lingual nerve is a branch of the mandibular nerve (CN V3). It provides sensory supply to the mucous membrane of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. In its course, the submandibular duct (Wharton's duct) runs forwards on hyoglossus, between the lingual and hypoglossal nerves.
B
At the anterior border of hyoglossus, the submandibular duct is crossed by the lingual nerve; this crossing relationship is anatomically relevant, since a stone in the submandibular duct can be felt bimanually in the floor of the mouth, and surgery/removal in this region places the lingual nerve at risk, along with the hypoglossal nerve, given their close relationship to the duct on hyoglossus.
C
Sensory supply to the mucous membrane of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is via the lingual nerve (a branch of CN V3), while special (taste) sensory supply to the same region is via the chorda tympani nerve (a branch of CN VII); injury to the lingual nerve would therefore be expected to impair general sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, distinct from a taste deficit, which would instead follow injury to the chorda tympani.

questions.question:
Describe the axillary artery:
A(i) Origin, extent and continuation
A(ii) Division into three parts by pectoralis minor
A(iii) Branches of each part
B. State the safe site associated with clinical control of bleeding from the axillary artery.
C. Explain the anatomical basis for the scapular anastomosis providing a collateral circulation if the artery is occluded.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The axillary artery is a continuation of the subclavian artery; it begins at the lateral border of the first rib and ends at the lower border of teres major, continuing thereafter as the brachial artery. It is closely related to the cords of the brachial plexus and is enclosed with them in the axillary sheath.
A(ii)
Pectoralis minor divides the axillary artery into three parts: the first part extends from the lateral border of the first rib to the upper border of pectoralis minor; the second part lies behind pectoralis minor; the third part extends from the lower border of pectoralis minor to the lower border of teres major.
A(iii)
The first part gives one branch, the superior (highest) thoracic artery; the second part gives two branches, the thoracoacromial and lateral thoracic arteries; the third part gives three branches, the subscapular artery and the anterior and posterior circumflex humeral arteries.
B
• The inferior part of the axillary artery can be palpated in the inferior part of the lateral wall of the axilla.
• This part can be compressed against the humerus to control profuse bleeding.
C
• The scapular anastomosis is a system of arteries connecting the subclavian artery and the corresponding axillary artery, forming an anastomosis around the scapula, occurring in the subscapular, supraspinatus and infraspinatus fossae.
• It is formed by the suprascapular artery (a branch of the thyrocervical trunk from the subclavian artery), the deep branch of the transverse cervical artery (another branch of the thyrocervical trunk), and the circumflex scapular artery (a branch of the subscapular artery arising from the third part of the axillary artery).
• These vessels anastomose the first part of the subclavian artery with the third part of the axillary artery, allowing blood to flow past the shoulder joint regardless of the position of the arm.
• A further anastomosis occurs over the acromion process, formed by the acromial branch of the thoracoacromial artery, the acromial branch of the suprascapular artery, and the acromial branch of the posterior circumflex humeral artery, linking the subclavian with the second and third parts of the axillary artery.
• The arterial anastomoses around the scapula thus provide a collateral circulation through which blood can continue to flow to the limb when the distal part of the subclavian artery or the proximal part of the axillary artery is blocked or occluded.
• This collateral circulation is clinically important because it allows blood to continue circulating to the upper limb even if the main line of supply is obstructed.
• This anatomical arrangement explains why proximal occlusion of the axillary or subclavian artery does not necessarily result in complete loss of blood supply to the limb.

A(i)
The gluteal region is the region of the buttock. Bony landmarks — surface anatomy: iliac crest, gluteus medius, tip of greater trochanter, gluteus maximus (fold of buttock), ischial tuberosity, tip of coccyx, natal cleft, posterior superior iliac spine (PSIS), sciatic nerve. Bones: os coxae (ilium, ischium, pubis) and femur.
A(ii)
Superficial fascia: thick in women; impregnated with large quantities of fat, hence the prominence of the buttock. Deep fascia: continuous with fascia lata of the thigh. The 9 muscles: gluteus maximus, gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, tensor fasciae latae (superficial layer); piriformis, obturator internus, gemellus superior, gemellus inferior, quadratus femoris (deep layer). Deep layer muscles all have distal attachments on or adjacent to the intertrochanteric crest of the femur; they are lateral rotators of the thigh and stabilise the hip joint. Obturator internus, superior gemellus, and inferior gemellus form the triceps coxae of the hip.
B(i)
6 nerves of the gluteal region: sciatic nerve (L4, 5; S1, 2, 3); posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh; superior gluteal nerve; inferior gluteal nerve; nerve to quadratus femoris; pudendal nerve. (Nerve to obturator internus also exits here.) The sciatic nerve curves downward midway between the tuber ischii and the greater trochanter.
B(ii)
4 arteries: superior gluteal artery (SGA), inferior gluteal artery (IGA), medial femoral circumflex artery (MFCA), lateral femoral circumflex artery (LFCA). Trochanteric anastomosis (TA) — main blood supply to the head of femur: SGA, IGA, MFCA, LFCA. Cruciate anastomosis (CA) — situated at the level of the lesser trochanter: IGA, MFCA, LFCA, and 1st perforating branch of profunda femoris. The CA jointly with the TA provides a connection between the femoral arteries and the internal iliac arteries.
C(i)
Sacrotuberous ligament (STL) and sacrospinous ligament (SSL): (1) both stabilise the sacrum and prevent its rotation at the sacroiliac joint by the weight of the vertebral column; (2) in conjunction with bones, they form the greater sciatic foramen (GSF) and lesser sciatic foramen (LSF). Functions of GSF and LSF: GSF provides an exit from the pelvis into the gluteal region. LSF (1) provides an entrance into the perineum from the gluteal region; (2) enables nerves and vessels that left the pelvis through the GSF above the pelvic floor to enter the perineum below the pelvic floor.
questions.question:
Describe the gluteal region under the following headings.
A(i) Boundaries and bony landmarks
A(ii) Fascia — superficial and deep; name all 9 muscles and give their OCIANA (origin, course, insertion, action, nerve, artery)
B(i) Nerves of the gluteal region — name all 6 nerves
B(ii) Arteries — name all 4 arteries; describe the trochanteric anastomosis and cruciate anastomosis fully
C(i) Functions of the sacrotuberous and sacrospinous ligaments; explain the formation and roles of the greater and lesser sciatic foramina

questions.answerText:
A(i)
• The thoracoabdominal nerves are the abdominal portions of the anterior rami of T7 to T12 (T7 to T11 thoracoabdominal, T12 subcostal); their distal portions lie in the rectus sheath.
• External oblique: T7 to T11 and T12; internal oblique and transversus abdominis: T7 to T11, T12 and branches of the lumbar plexus; rectus abdominis: T7 to T11; pyramidalis: subcostal T12.
A(ii)
• The lumbar plexus (ventral rami L1 to L4, formed within psoas major) innervates part of the lower abdominal wall.
• The iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves (L1) emerge from the lateral border of psoas major.
A(iii)
• The umbilicus is the segmental landmark with dermatome T10, the same root that innervates the appendix, so appendicular referred pain is felt there.
• The segmental innervation applies to both the anterior abdominal skin and musculature.
B(i)
• The TAP block is a peripheral nerve block that anaesthetises the nerves of the abdominal wall.
• It is performed by injecting anaesthetic into the fascial plane between transversus abdominis and internal oblique muscles.
C(i)
• The ilioinguinal, iliohypogastric and inferior thoracic nerves are spread across the abdominal wall and so are prone to injury.
• Their injury results in muscle weakness of the abdominal wall.
• In entrapment (ACNES) the Carnett sign is positive at the lateral border of the rectus abdominis, with altered skin sensation.

questions.question:
(A) Describe the duodenum under the headings: A(i) parts and dimensions A(ii) peritoneal relations A(iii) visceral relations.
(B) Explain the clinical basis for the duodenum's common site of ulceration and for paraduodenal hernia.
(C) Distinguish between the jejunum and the ileum.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The duodenum is the first, shortest (about 25 cm) and widest part of the small intestine; it is C-shaped and mostly retroperitoneal, made up of four parts - superior (5 cm), descending (7.5-8 cm), horizontal (6-10 cm) and ascending (2.5 cm).
A(ii)
The proximal 2.5 cm of the superior part is movable and intraperitoneal, attached to the lesser omentum above and greater omentum below; the rest of the duodenum is retroperitoneal, covered by peritoneum only on its anterior aspect.
A(iii)
The superior part is anteriorly related to the quadrate lobe of the liver and gallbladder, and posteriorly to the gastroduodenal artery, bile duct, portal vein and inferior vena cava; the descending part is related medially to the head of pancreas and bile duct, laterally to the right colic flexure, and rests on the right kidney, ureter, psoas major and renal vessels, and receives the major duodenal papilla; the horizontal part crosses the inferior vena cava, aorta and L3 vertebra and is crossed anteriorly by the superior mesenteric vessels; the ascending part rises to the duodenojejunal flexure.
B
• The proximal (superior) part of the duodenum is the most common site of duodenal ulcer.
• The duodenojejunal flexure is fixed by the suspensory muscle of the duodenum (ligament of Treitz), which passes posterior to the pancreas and splenic vein and anterior to the left renal vein; a weakness near this fixed flexure is the anatomical basis for a paraduodenal hernia.
C
• The jejunum lies mainly in the left upper (infracolic) quadrant, has thicker, more vascular walls and a wider, often empty lumen, with long and few vasa recta, one or two layers of arterial arcades, numerous circular mucosal folds, and large, thick, abundant villi.
• The ileum lies predominantly in the right lower quadrant and pelvis, has thinner, less vascular walls and a narrower, often loaded lumen, with short and numerous vasa recta and multiple layers of arterial arcades.
• The ileum has smaller and sparser circular mucosal folds and shorter, thinner villi than the jejunum, but the terminal ileum has numerous Peyer's patches and more numerous solitary lymphatic follicles, which are absent or scanty in the jejunum.
• The jejunum has mesenteric windows and less abundant mesenteric fat, whereas the ileum has no windows and more abundant mesenteric fat.

A(i)
General characteristics: epithelial tissue consists of closely packed cells arranged in one or more layers; these cells are specialized and fill roles such as protection, secretion, and absorption; the cells are tightly packed together with very little extracellular matrix and almost no intercellular substance; they rest on a basement membrane (a basal lamina containing the glycoprotein laminin). Morphological classification by cell shape: squamous (flat), cuboidal (square or cube-like), columnar (tall and thin). By number of layers: simple epithelium (one cell thick) — can be simple squamous, simple cuboidal, or simple columnar; stratified epithelium (multiple layers — described as heterogeneous); pseudostratified epithelium — appears stratified but all cells contact the basal lamina. Transitional epithelium: recognized by its appearance — when the bladder is empty (relaxed), the epithelium appears thicker and has more layers than when the bladder is full. Basement membrane: contains the glycoprotein laminin; the border between epithelia and the underlying connective tissue is sharp and distinct.
A(ii)
Simple squamous epithelium: lines blood vessels (endothelium) and body cavities. Simple cuboidal epithelium: lines many small ducts in the body. Simple columnar epithelium: lines the gallbladder, larger ducts near the urinary papilla; also found in the jejunum (with goblet cells). Ciliated columnar epithelium: found in the respiratory tract and fallopian tubes; goblet cells (glandular epithelium) are present, making it heterogeneous. Stratified squamous epithelium (keratinized): forms the outer layer of skin; contains the protective protein keratin; a keratinized (dry) epithelium. Transitional epithelium: lines the urinary bladder.
B(i)
Epithelial tissue is avascular (contains no blood vessels); the lamina propria (underlying connective tissue) supplies the necessary nutrients and metabolites, which are transported to and from epithelial cells by diffusion through the basement membrane. If the basement membrane is disrupted (e.g., in cancer invasion or severe inflammation), the barrier between epithelium and connective tissue is lost, allowing unrestricted cell invasion into the underlying stroma; epithelial cells in contact with the environment are constantly subjected to mechanical damage and must show many dividing cells (mitoses) to replace lost cells; disruption of this repair mechanism contributes to disease progression.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the gross anatomy of epithelial tissue under the following headings: general characteristics, morphological classification (by cell shape and number of layers), and the basement membrane.
A(ii) Relate specific epithelial types to their common locations in the body, giving one example each of simple squamous, simple cuboidal, simple columnar, ciliated columnar, stratified squamous, and transitional epithelium.
B(i) Explain why epithelial tissue is avascular, how it receives nutrients, and state the clinical consequence when the basement membrane is disrupted in disease.

A(i) Define the thoracic duct and state its origin.
A(ii) Describe its course and relations.
A(iii) State its tributaries and termination.
A(iv) Describe the area it drains and compare it with the right lymphatic duct.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• The longest lymphatic duct, conveying lymph to the circulatory system.
• It begins as the upward continuation of the cisterna chyli, a dilated sac formed by the union of the left and right lumbar trunks and the intestinal trunk, in front of L1 (also stated at T12).
A(ii)
• It enters the thorax through the aortic opening of the diaphragm and ascends in the posterior mediastinum, on the right side of and behind the oesophagus, with the oesophagus lying in front of it.
• It veers to the left at the level of T5 and ascends in the superior mediastinum to the left of the oesophagus.
• At the root of the neck it turns laterally, arches forwards and descends to enter the left venous angle.
A(iii)
• Before termination it receives the left jugular, left subclavian and left bronchomediastinal trunks; it ends in the left brachiocephalic vein.
• It contains many valves, with no valve at its termination.
A(iv)
• It drains lymph from the lower limbs, pelvic cavity, abdominal cavity, left half of the thorax and left side of the head, neck and upper limb (all the body except the right side of the head, neck, thorax and upper limb).
• The right lymphatic duct, formed by the union of the right jugular, subclavian and bronchomediastinal trunks, drains the right half of the head, neck, thorax and upper limb, right lung, right side of the heart and right surface of the liver, and ends in the right brachiocephalic vein.
• The lymph trunks are the right and left jugular, subclavian, bronchomediastinal and lumbar trunks and the intestinal trunk; the left brachiocephalic vein receives the thoracic duct, the right brachiocephalic vein the right lymphatic duct.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the parotid gland under the following headings: location, external features, and capsule.
A(ii) Describe the parotid duct, and list the structures within the substance of the gland from superficial to deep, and the other structures found within the gland.
B. Explain the clinical basis for why the parotid gland is particularly vulnerable to nerve injury during surgery, and describe the syndrome that can follow such injury.
C. Distinguish between the parotid gland and the submandibular gland in terms of their ducts and ganglia associated with their secretomotor supply.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The parotid gland is the largest salivary gland (para = around, otic = ear); it is situated below the external acoustic meatus, in front of the sternomastoid, and also projects forward onto the surface of masseter. It is pyramidal in shape with the apex pointing downward, has 4 surfaces (superior/base, lateral/superficial, anteromedial, posteromedial) separated by 3 borders (anterior, posterior, medial), and has 1 main lobe and 1 accessory lobe (a small detached part called the accessory parotid gland or Socia Parotidis, lying on masseter between the zygomatic arch and the parotid duct). The capsule has a false capsule, formed by the investing layer of deep cervical fascia, and a true capsule, formed by condensation of the stroma.
A(ii)
The parotid duct is about 5 cm long, arises from the anterior border of the gland, runs on masseter, and at the anterior border of masseter runs medially to pierce buccinator and the mucosa, opening into the vestibule of the mouth opposite the crown of the upper 2nd molar tooth; its surface anatomy corresponds to the middle third of a line from the lower border of the tragus to a point midway between the nasal ala and the upper labial margin. From superficial to deep within the substance of the gland are: the facial nerve and its branches; the retromandibular vein and its two divisions (maxillary vein, superficial temporal vein); and the external carotid artery and its two terminal branches. Other structures within the gland are the auriculotemporal nerve, the posterior auricular artery, and the preauricular lymph nodes.
B
Within the gland, the facial nerve radiates like a goose's foot (Pes Anserinus) through the anterior border of the gland into its branches (temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular, cervical); because the facial nerve runs through the substance of the gland, it is at risk during parotid surgery or trauma. Frey's syndrome (also known as gustatory sweating or auriculo-temporal nerve syndrome) commonly occurs after parotid surgery or trauma, from injury of the auriculotemporal and great auricular nerves; during healing, secretomotor fibres of the auriculotemporal nerve join with the great auricular nerve and reach the sweat glands of facial skin, so that sweating, warmth and redness of the face occur as a result of salivary stimulation by the smell or taste of food.
C
The parotid gland's secretomotor (parasympathetic) supply is via the auriculotemporal nerve, producing a watery secretion, with sympathetic supply producing a mucous-rich, sticky secretion derived from the plexus around the external carotid artery. In contrast, the submandibular gland's duct is the submandibular duct (Wharton's duct), and its nerve supply is via branches from the submandibular ganglion, through which it receives parasympathetic fibres from the chorda tympani, sensory fibres from the lingual branch of the mandibular nerve, and sympathetic fibres from the plexus on the facial artery.

A(i)
Fibularis longus: origin — head and superior 2/3 of lateral surface of fibula; insertion — base of 1st metatarsal and medial cuneiform; innervation — superficial fibular nerve (L5, S1, S2); action — everts foot and weakly plantarflexes ankle. Fibularis brevis: origin — inferior 2/3 of lateral surface of fibula; insertion — dorsal surface of tuberosity on lateral side of base of 5th metatarsal; innervation — superficial fibular nerve (L5, S1, S2); action — everts foot and weakly plantarflexes ankle. Arterial supply: both are supplied by the fibular (peroneal) artery.
A(ii)
The common fibular nerve is the lateral, smaller terminal branch of the sciatic nerve; it begins at the superior angle of the popliteal fossa, closely follows the medial border of biceps femoris and its tendon, exits the fossa by passing superficial to the lateral head of gastrocnemius, then over the posterior aspect of the head of fibula, winds around the neck of fibula, and divides into the superficial fibular nerve (to the lateral compartment) and the deep fibular nerve (to the anterior compartment). The superficial fibular nerve runs in the lateral compartment to supply fibularis longus and brevis; its cutaneous distribution supplies the dorsum of the foot (lateral side of leg and ankle, as the sural nerve — formed by medial sural cutaneous nerve joined by the sural communicating branch of the common fibular nerve — supplies the lateral side of leg and ankle).
B(i)
Fibularis longus inserts onto the base of the 1st metatarsal and medial cuneiform on the plantar aspect of the foot — it therefore acts as a stirrup, pulling the medial forefoot downward and laterally, producing eversion and weak plantarflexion. Fibularis brevis inserts onto the tuberosity of the base of the 5th metatarsal on the lateral side of the foot — it abducts the forefoot and everts the foot. The lateral longitudinal arch (made of calcaneus, cuboid, and 4th and 5th metatarsals) is supported by peroneus longus and brevis; muscles of the lateral arch include peroneus longus and brevis, flexor digitorum longus, and short muscles of the little toe.
B(ii)
The transverse arch muscles include peroneus longus and brevis, transverse head of adductor hallucis, and slips of tibialis posterior. Fibularis longus, by crossing under the foot from the lateral side to insert medially at the base of the 1st metatarsal, acts as a dynamic tie-beam, pulling the medial and lateral borders of the foot together and maintaining the curvature of the transverse arch; adductor hallucis transverse head also assists by pulling metatarsals medially.
C(i)
Superficial fibular nerve injury (at fibular neck): loss of eversion of the foot (fibularis longus and brevis paralysed); weakness of plantarflexion; sensory loss on dorsum of foot. Deep fibular nerve injury (at fibular neck): loss of dorsiflexion (tibialis anterior paralysed) and toe extension (extensor digitorum longus, extensor hallucis longus paralysed); loss of eversion contribution of fibularis tertius; result is foot drop with the foot held in plantarflexion and inversion; sensory loss is limited to the 1st web space (between 1st and 2nd toes). Injury to the common fibular nerve at the fibular neck produces both effects combined — foot drop with loss of both dorsiflexion and eversion.
questions.question:
Describe the lateral compartment muscles of the leg under the following headings, explain the anatomical basis of their action, and distinguish the consequences of superficial fibular nerve injury from deep fibular nerve injury.
A(i) Name both muscles, giving full OCIANA (origin, course, insertion, action, nerve, artery) for each
A(ii) The superficial fibular nerve — its origin, course in the lateral compartment, and cutaneous distribution
B(i) The mechanical basis of eversion and plantarflexion — how fibularis longus and brevis produce their actions based on their insertions
B(ii) The role of fibularis longus in maintaining the transverse arch of the foot
C(i) Distinguish the clinical effects of superficial fibular nerve injury from those of deep fibular nerve injury at the fibular neck, and state which movements are lost in each

(i) Describe the gross anatomy of the kidney, including its shape, coverings, and internal structure (cortex, medulla, pyramids, sinus, calyces).
(ii) Relate the parts of the kidney to a common renal pathology.
(iii) Explain how disease/obstruction of the kidney or its drainage system can produce a functional deficit at a distance.
questions.answerText:
(i)
• The kidneys are bean-shaped, retroperitoneal organs lying on the posterior abdominal wall from about the T12 to L3 vertebral level, each about 10 cm long, 5 cm wide and 2.5 cm thick, with the right kidney slightly lower due to the liver.
• Each kidney has a superior pole bearing the suprarenal gland, an inferior pole, a convex lateral border, and a concave medial border indented by the renal hilum.
• Coverings, from within outward, are the fibrous (renal) capsule, perirenal fat, renal fascia, and pararenal fat.
• Internally, a dark brown outer cortex surrounds a lighter medulla composed of about a dozen renal pyramids, each with its base toward the cortex and its apex (renal papilla) projecting into a minor calyx; cortex extends between pyramids as renal columns.
• At the hilum, the renal vein lies anterior to the renal artery, which lies anterior to the renal pelvis; the hilum leads into the renal sinus, which contains the pelvis, calyces, vessels, nerves and fat.
• The renal pelvis, a funnel-shaped expansion of the ureter, receives two or three major calyces, each dividing into two or three minor calyces.
(ii)
• Renal (kidney) stones are a clinical consideration associated with the kidney and relate to the calyceal and pelvic system where urine collects before draining into the ureter.
• The renal pyramids and papillae are the sites from which urine is excreted into the minor calyces, so pathology of the papillae or pyramids affects urine drainage.
(iii)
• The ureter has three points of constriction - the pelviureteric junction, where it crosses the pelvic brim, and its intramural (intravesical) course - which are potential sites of obstruction by ureteric stones.
• Obstruction at any of these constrictions causes back-pressure on the kidney, from the collecting system through the pelvis to the pyramids, producing a functional deficit in urine drainage from that kidney.
• Ureteric pain from such obstruction is referred to the ipsilateral lower quadrant of the anterior abdominal wall and especially the groin, showing how a renal or ureteric problem produces a distant clinical effect.
• This referred pain reflects the segmental (T11-T12) sympathetic innervation shared by the ureter and the abdominal wall/groin dermatomes.

A(i)
Collagen fibers: protein fibers that form the bulk of connective tissue fibers. Major types and distribution: Type I collagen — fibril-forming; found in bone, dermis, tendon, ligaments, and cornea; produced by fibroblasts, osteoblasts, odontoblasts. Type II collagen — fibril-forming; found in cartilage and vitreous body of the eye; produced by chondrocytes and retinal cells. Type III collagen — fibril-forming; found in loose connective tissue and reticular fibers in lungs, liver, and spleen; produced by fibroblasts and reticular cells. Type IV collagen — network-forming; found in basement membranes; produced by epithelial and endothelial cells. Type XI collagen — fibrillar; found in cartilage. Elastic fibers: present in elastic connective tissue; provide elasticity. Reticular fibers: fine fibers present in reticular connective tissue; form reticular (meshwork) framework of organs.
A(ii)
Dense regular connective tissue is present in tendons and ligaments because it is organized to withstand forces from specific directions; the regular parallel arrangement of collagen type I fibers allows maximum tensile strength along the axis of the tendon or ligament.
B(i)
The regenerative capacity of connective tissue is clearly observed in organs damaged by ischemia, inflammation, or traumatic injury. Spaces left after such injuries, especially in tissues whose cells divide poorly or not at all (e.g., cardiac muscle), are filled by connective tissue, forming dense irregular scar tissue. The healing of surgical incisions and other wounds depends on the reparative capacity of connective tissue and the activity of fibroblasts. Fibroblasts synthesize collagen, reticular and elastic fibers, and the amorphous extracellular substance. In some rapidly closing wounds, a cell called the myofibroblast (with features of both fibroblasts and smooth muscle cells) is observed. Myofibroblasts have most of the morphologic characteristics of fibroblasts but contain increased amounts of actin microfilaments and myosin and behave like smooth muscle cells. Their activity is responsible for wound contraction (wound closure after tissue injury).
questions.question:

A(ii) State the safe structural principle that makes collagen type I dominant in tendons and ligaments.
B(i) Explain the anatomical basis of scar formation after organ injury, with specific reference to fibroblasts and myofibroblasts.

questions.answerText:
A(ii)
The aortic hiatus lies posterior to the diaphragm, between the two crura, at the level of the lower border of the T12 vertebra; it transmits the aorta, the thoracic duct and sometimes the azygos and hemiazygos veins. Because the aorta does not pierce the diaphragm itself, movements of the diaphragm during respiration do not affect blood flow through it.
A(iii)
The caval opening lies in the central tendon of the diaphragm at the level of T8; it transmits the inferior vena cava, terminal branches of the right phrenic nerve, and a few hepatic lymphatic vessels. The inferior vena cava is adherent to the margin of this opening, so diaphragmatic contraction during inspiration widens the opening and dilates the inferior vena cava, aiding venous return to the heart.
B
• The right and left crura arise from the bodies of the L1-L3 vertebrae, the anterior longitudinal ligament and the intervertebral discs; the oesophageal hiatus lies within the right crus, to the left of the midline, superior to and to the left of the aortic hiatus. Diaphragmatic hernia (sliding and paraoesophageal types) and diaphragmatic rupture are clinical considerations related to weakness or defects around these openings.
• In most individuals, about 70%, both margins of the oesophageal hiatus are formed by muscular bundles of the right crus; in others the left crus contributes to the right margin, and such variation can affect the sphincter-like action around the oesophagus.
C
• The oesophageal hiatus is a muscular opening in the right crus at the level of T10 that actively constricts around the oesophagus with diaphragmatic contraction, contributing to prevention of reflux.
• The aortic hiatus is a non-muscular, fibrous opening bounded by the crura and the median arcuate ligament at the lower border of T12, so diaphragmatic contraction does not compress or affect flow through the aorta.
• The oesophageal hiatus transmits the oesophagus and vagal trunks, whereas the aortic hiatus transmits the aorta and thoracic duct, reflecting their different anatomical roles.
