questions.answerText:
(i)
• The liver has two surfaces - a convex diaphragmatic surface (anterior, superior, posterior and right lateral) and a relatively flat, posteroinferior visceral surface.
• It is divided into a large right lobe and a smaller left lobe by the falciform ligament, with the caudate and quadrate lobes arising from the right lobe on the visceral surface.
• Two sagittally oriented fissures (for the ligamentum teres and ligamentum venosum on the left, and the gallbladder fossa and IVC groove on the right) are linked by the transverse porta hepatis, forming an H on the visceral surface.
• Ligaments include the falciform ligament, the coronary ligament with the right and left triangular ligaments, and the lesser omentum (hepatogastric and hepatoduodenal ligaments).
• The porta hepatis transmits the hepatic ducts, hepatic artery and portal vein branches, and hepatic nerves and lymph nodes.
(ii)
• The bare area of the diaphragmatic surface has no peritoneal covering, so infection there can track through the diaphragm to posterior mediastinal lymph nodes.
• The subphrenic and subhepatic spaces, and Morison's pouch between the liver and right kidney, are recesses where pathological fluid such as pus, blood or ascites collects.
• Liver fissures serve as surgical landmarks, such as Cantlie's line, which divides the liver into functional right and left lobes along the middle hepatic vein.
• Because the liver is large, fixed in position and friable, it is vulnerable to rupture, often from a fractured rib perforating the diaphragm, causing haemorrhage and right upper quadrant pain.
(iii)
• In cirrhosis, hepatocytes are destroyed and replaced by fibrous tissue that impedes blood flow through the liver, causing portal hypertension.
• This opens portal-systemic anastomoses at the lower oesophagus, anal canal, paraumbilical region, retroperitoneum and intrahepatic sites, producing distant complications such as bleeding oesophageal varices.
• Distension of Glisson's capsule from an enlarged liver produces sharp, well-localised pain via the lower intercostal nerves, illustrating how a hepatic process produces a distant sensory effect.
questions.question:

(ii) Relate the lobes/fissures of the liver to common hepatic pathology.
(iii) Explain how liver disease can spread its effects to a distant structure, producing a functional deficit there.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
The hip joint is a multiaxial ball-and-socket type of synovial joint. It is the largest joint in the human body and the 2nd largest weight-bearing joint. Articular surfaces: the lunate surface of the acetabulum (covered by hyaline cartilage except at the fovea) and the spherical head of femur (which forms 2/3 of a sphere, covered by hyaline cartilage except at the fovea capitis). The acetabulum is deepened by the fibrocartilaginous acetabular labrum; it is deficient inferiorly as the acetabular notch, bridged by the transverse acetabular ligament.
A(ii)
Capsule: strong and thick; medially attached to margin of acetabulum, transverse acetabular ligament, and adjacent margin of obturator foramen; laterally attached to the intertrochanteric line anteriorly. Ligaments: (1) Iliofemoral ligament (ligament of Bigelow) — one of the strongest in the body, Y-shaped; apex at inferior iliac spine, base to intertrochanteric line; prevents overextension and prevents trunk from falling backwards while standing. (2) Pubofemoral ligament — triangular; attached superiorly to iliopubic eminence and obturator crest, inferiorly merges with capsule; limits extension and abduction. (3) Ischiofemoral ligament — reinforces posterior aspect; medially attached to ischium posteroinferior to acetabulum, laterally to greater trochanter deep to the iliofemoral ligament; limits extension. Fibers of all three spiral so they become taut in extension, stabilizing the joint and reducing muscle energy needed for standing. Ligament teres (round ligament): flat triangular band from fovea to acetabular notch and transverse ligament; ensheathed by synovial membrane; transmits arteries to head of femur.
B(i)
By Hilton's law: the nerve supplying the joint also supplies the muscles moving the joint and the skin covering the insertion of those muscles. Nerve supply: femoral nerve, anterior division of obturator nerve, nerve to rectus femoris, nerve to quadratus femoris, sciatic nerve, and superior gluteal nerve. The posterior division of the obturator nerve supplies both the hip and the knee joint.
B(ii)
Flexion (120–140°): iliopsoas, sartorius, rectus femoris, tensor fasciae latae. Extension: gluteus maximus, semimembranosus, semitendinosus, biceps femoris. Abduction (60–80°): gluteus medius, minimus, tensor fasciae latae. Adduction: pectineus, adductor longus, brevis, magnus, gracilis. Medial rotation: gluteus medius, minimus, tensor fasciae latae. Lateral rotation: obturator internus and externus, gemellus superior and inferior, quadratus femoris, piriformis, posterior fibres of gluteus medius and minimus, superior fibres of gluteus maximus.
C(i)
The posterior division of the obturator nerve supplies both the hip and knee joints; pain from hip pathology is therefore referred along this common nerve pathway to the knee joint. Coxa valga follows congenital dislocation of the head of femur; coxa vara follows fracture of the neck of femur.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
The axilla is a pyramid-shaped space between the upper part of the arm and the side of the upper chest; its apex is the cervicoaxillary canal, bounded by the 1st rib, clavicle, and superior edge of the scapula, forming the passageway between the neck and axilla.
A(ii)
The base is formed by concave skin, subcutaneous tissue, and the axillary (deep) fascia.
A(iii)
Anterior wall: pectoralis major and minor, subclavius, and clavipectoral fascia. Posterior wall: scapula and subscapularis above, teres major and latissimus dorsi below. Medial wall: upper ribs, intercostal muscles, and serratus anterior. Lateral wall: narrow and bony, formed by the intertubercular groove of the humerus.
A(iv)
Contents: the axillary artery and its branches, the axillary vein and its tributaries, the infraclavicular part of the brachial plexus, axillary lymph nodes, and loose areolar/adipose tissue, all enclosed with the plexus in the axillary sheath.
B
• The axillary vein is large and lies in an exposed, superficial position within the axilla.
• Wounds to the axilla therefore often involve the axillary vein because of its large size and exposed position.
• A wound to the proximal part of the axillary vein is especially dangerous because of the risk of air entering the vessel (air embolism).
C
• The quadrangular space lies in the posterior wall of the axilla and transmits the axillary nerve and the posterior circumflex humeral artery and vein.
• The triangular interval also lies in the posterior wall and transmits the radial nerve and the profunda brachii artery.
• Both spaces are related to the long head of triceps brachii and the teres major muscle in their boundaries.
• The quadrangular space thus carries the nerve/vessels supplying the deltoid and teres minor region, while the triangular interval carries those continuing into the posterior compartment of the arm.
• This distinction explains why injury near the surgical neck of the humerus threatens the axillary nerve, whereas injury lower down at the spiral groove threatens the radial nerve instead.

A(i) Define the intercostal space and state the number of spaces and their contents.
A(ii) Describe the intercostal muscles, including the fibre direction, attachments and extent of the external and internal intercostals.
A(iii) Describe the innermost intercostal muscle and the endothoracic fascia.
A(iv) Describe the intercostal neurovascular bundle and the order of its components.
A(v) Describe the arteries of the intercostal space.
A(vi) Describe the veins of the intercostal space.
A(vii) Describe the intercostal nerves and their branches.
A(viii) Describe the lymphatic drainage of the intercostal space.
B(i) Explain why a needle or drain is passed immediately above the upper border of a rib and state the other clinical uses of the intercostal spaces.
C(i) Distinguish between a typical and an atypical intercostal nerve.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The space between two ribs; with 12 ribs on each side there are 11 intercostal spaces; each space contains intercostal muscles, the intercostal neurovascular bundle and lymphatics.
A(ii)
• Three muscles (external, internal, innermost; transversus thoracis, subcostalis and levator costarum are also listed), supplied by the corresponding intercostal nerves, that pull the ribs nearer to each other and strengthen the space. External intercostal: most superficial, fibres downward and forward, origin lower border of the rib above, insertion upper border of the rib below, from the rib tubercle behind to the costochondral junction in front, replaced anteriorly by the anterior intercostal membrane.
• Internal intercostal: intermediate layer, fibres downward and backward, origin subcostal groove of the rib above, insertion upper border of the rib below, from the sternum in front to the angle of the rib behind, replaced posteriorly by the posterior intercostal membrane.
A(iii)
Innermost intercostal: deepest, incomplete layer divided into 3 portions, its fibres cross more than one space; related externally to the intercostal nerve and vessels and internally to the endothoracic fascia. Endothoracic fascia: extrapleural fascia lining the chest wall between the muscles and bones and the parietal pleura, extending over the pleural apex as the suprapleural membrane and forming a thin layer between diaphragm and pleura.
A(iv)
The neurovascular bundle lies between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles, high in the space in relation to the subcostal groove of the rib above; strict order from above downwards: vein, artery, nerve (VAN); because the innermost layer is incomplete it is generally covered on the inside by endothoracic fascia.
A(v)
Each space has a single posterior and 2 anterior intercostal arteries, giving branches to muscles, skin, parietal pleura and breast. Posterior: upper 2 spaces from the superior intercostal artery (costocervical trunk of the subclavian artery), lower 9 spaces from the thoracic aorta. Anterior: upper 6 spaces from the internal thoracic artery, lower 5 from the musculophrenic artery; they anastomose with the posterior arteries.
A(vi)
Veins accompany the arteries and nerves (11 posterior intercostal and 1 subcostal vein); valves direct blood posteriorly. Right side: 1st space to the brachiocephalic vein, the rest to the azygos vein. Left side: upper 3 spaces to the left brachiocephalic vein, the rest to the hemiazygos and accessory hemiazygos veins, which drain to the azygos vein. Anterior veins: upper 6 spaces to the internal thoracic vein, lower 5 to the musculophrenic vein.
A(vii)
12 pairs, the anterior primary rami of the thoracic spinal nerves and mixed nerves; nerves 1-6 are distributed in the intercostal spaces, 7-11 supply the anterior abdominal wall, and the 12th runs forward in the abdomen as the subcostal nerve; they supply skin, muscles of the space and abdomen, parietal pleura and parietal peritoneum. Branches: rami communicantes, collateral (muscular), lateral cutaneous, anterior cutaneous, pleural and peritoneal (7th-11th).
A(viii)
Deep lymphatics follow the arteries: anteriorly they drain into the anterior intercostal (parasternal) nodes along the internal thoracic artery; posteriorly they drain into the posterior intercostal nodes in the posterior mediastinum.
B(i)
• A needle or drain is passed immediately above the upper border of the rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle (vein, artery, nerve from above downwards) running under the rib above in the subcostal groove.
• Intercostal spaces are access points for surgical procedures (e.g. resection of part of the lung), for percussion and auscultation of the heart and lung, and for sampling pleural fluid or draining pus or blood from the pleural cavity; disease in the thorax may cause pain in the anterior abdominal wall because the intercostal nerves supply both the thoracic and abdominal wall and the parietal pleura.
C(i)
Typical nerves are T3-6. T1 is atypical: no anterior cutaneous branch, joined to the brachial plexus by a large branch corresponding to the lateral cutaneous branch. T2 is atypical: its lateral cutaneous branch is the intercostobrachial nerve, which joins the medial cutaneous nerve of the arm through the brachial plexus.

A(i)
• A strong, incomplete fibrous compartment of the rectus abdominis and pyramidalis, formed by the aponeuroses of the three flat muscles.
• The linea alba separates the right and left rectus abdominis; the linea semilunaris marks the lateral border; tendinous intersections and linea alba give the 'six packs'.
A(ii)
It has an anterior and posterior wall for most of its length: anterior wall from the aponeuroses of external oblique and half of internal oblique; posterior wall from the aponeuroses of half of internal oblique and transversus abdominis.
A(iii)
• Superior and inferior epigastric arteries and veins, lymphatic vessels and the distal portions of the thoracoabdominal nerves (anterior rami of T7 to T12).
• Superior epigastric: terminal branch of internal thoracic, descends posterior to the muscle, anastomoses with inferior epigastric; inferior epigastric: from external iliac, enters the sheath at the arcuate line.
A(iv)
A strong expandable support; protects viscera from injury such as a low blow in boxing; compresses the abdominal contents; maintains or increases intra-abdominal pressure; moves the trunk and maintains posture.
B(i)
• In anterior cutaneous nerve entrapment syndrome (ACNES), 12 of 95 adolescents with chronic abdominal pain had it; the Carnett sign was positive at the lateral border of rectus abdominis in all 12.
• Altered skin sensation was present in 11 of 12; the distal thoracoabdominal nerves run in the rectus sheath.
• After treatment (1 to 3 injections, n = 5; neurectomy, n = 7) pain was absent in 11; the conclusion was that ACNES is present in 1 of 8 such adolescents.
C(i)
• Rectus abdominis: long paired muscle split by the linea alba, origin pubic crest, insertion xiphoid process and costal cartilages of ribs 5 to 7, nerve T7 to T11, stabilises the pelvis in walking and depresses the ribs.
• Pyramidalis: small triangular muscle superficial to rectus, base on the pubis and apex on the linea alba, origin pubic crest and symphysis, insertion linea alba, tenses the linea alba; nerve supply is the subcostal nerve (T12).

questions.question:
Describe the tibia under the following headings, state how its zones relate to common pathologies, and explain why fracture of the middle third is at highest risk of delayed union.
A(i) General features, upper end, shaft, and lower end of the tibia
A(ii) How the upper end of the tibia relates to the knee joint — tibial plateaus, menisci, and intercondylar areas
B(i) Blood supply of the tibia and the significance of nutrient artery direction
B(ii) Common pathologies related to zones of the tibia — proximal, mid-shaft, and distal
C(i) Distinguish tibia from fibula with respect to weight-bearing function, articulations, and nerve–vessel relations at each malleolus
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The tibia is the large weight-bearing medial bone of the leg; it articulates with femoral condyles superiorly and the head of fibula laterally. It has an expanded upper end, a shaft, and a smaller lower end. Upper end (see A(ii)). Shaft: triangular in cross-section; 3 borders and 3 surfaces (borders and surfaces are named by opposites); anterior border forms the shin; soleal line on the posterior surface is for soleus. Lower end: expanded; saddle-shaped articular surface for talus; prolonged downwards medially to form the medial malleolus; the medial surface is subcutaneous from the medial malleolus to the medial condyle above.
A(ii)
The upper end has tibial plateaus (lateral and medial condyles); the lateral and medial menisci; anterior and posterior intercondylar areas separate the tibial plateaus; the intercondylar eminence; an articular facet for the head of fibula; and a groove on the medial condyle for semimembranosus. The anterior intercondylar area of the tibia is where the ACL attaches (just posterior to attachment of medial meniscus); the posterior intercondylar area is where the PCL attaches.
B(i)
The nutrient artery (medullary artery) is the main artery of the diaphysis. It is directed obliquely away from the epiphyseal end. When there is an epiphysis at both ends (tibia is one of the 5 bones unique in having epiphyseal plates at both ends — viz: femur, tibia, fibula, humerus, and radius), the nutrient canal is directed away from the more actively growing end. Hughes: 'to the elbow I go, from the knee I flee'. Fracture of the middle third of the tibia lies in a 'watershed' zone between the nutrient artery (supplying the upper 2/3) and the periosteal vessels (supplying the lower 1/3), making this zone most susceptible to avascular non-union.
B(ii)
Proximal tibia: tibial plateau fractures (high-energy trauma), associated with meniscal and ligamentous tears. Mid-shaft tibia: most common site of delayed or non-union, stress fractures (runners), and compartment syndrome (anterior compartment syndrome). Distal tibia (ankle): Pott's fracture involving the malleolus; ankle sprains; avulsion fractures.
C(i)
Tibia: large weight-bearing medial bone; articulates with femoral condyles, fibula head, and talus; contributes the roof (inferior surface of tibia) and the medial malleolus (wall) of the ankle mortise; the medial surface is subcutaneous. Fibula: not a weight-bearing bone; does not articulate with the femur or patella at the knee (only serves as attachment for knee joint structures); contributes the lateral malleolus (wall of ankle mortise) from fibula. At the ankle: lateral malleolar wall is from fibula and medial malleolar wall is from tibia.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the gross histology of the three types of muscle tissue (skeletal, smooth, and cardiac) as seen in longitudinal section and cross-section under the light microscope.
A(ii) Relate the structural differences of each muscle type to their specific pathological conditions.
B(i) Explain how the histological organization of cardiac muscle facilitates rapid spread of the signal to contract, and state why blockage of the coronary arteries leads to widespread myocardial damage.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Skeletal muscle — longitudinal section: cross-striations of alternating dark (A bands, anisotropic) and light (I bands, isotropic) bands; each I band bisected by a dark transverse Z disc; multinucleated fibers at periphery. Cross-section: peripheral nuclei; high cytoplasm-to-nucleus ratio. Smooth muscle — longitudinal section: meshwork appearance; no striations; elongated spindle-shaped cells; elongated and central nuclei. Cross-section: central nuclei; low cytoplasm-to-nucleus ratio. Cardiac muscle — longitudinal section: striations; branching cells; intercalated discs. Cross-section: central nuclei; high cytoplasm-to-nucleus ratio.
A(ii)
Skeletal muscle: troponin subunits (troponin I and troponin T) are integral to muscle contraction; mutations in cardiac troponin subunits can result in cardiomyopathies. Smooth muscle: smooth muscle cells are able to undergo cell division (unlike cardiac and skeletal muscle). Cardiac muscle: atrial myocytes secrete atrial natriuretic peptide; kidneys respond to this to cause sodium and water loss (natriuresis and diuresis); when natriuretic peptide levels fall, kidneys result in sodium and water conservation.
B(i)
Cardiac muscle cells act as a syncytium through gap junctions in intercalated discs, which provide ionic continuity between adjacent cells, allowing the signal to contract to pass throughout the organ. The blood supply to the heart is through three main coronary arteries prone to atheroma. Acute coronary arterial occlusion involving nearly the entire area at risk causes necrosis of the myocardium. Because the cardiac muscle acts as a syncytium and is continuously active, obstruction of coronary blood flow rapidly leads to widespread ischemia and necrosis of the myocardium.

A(i)
It has cervical, thoracic and abdominal parts and is not a straight structure: it lies to the left in the neck, returns to the midline at the thoracic inlet, lies to the left in the superior mediastinum, returns to the midline in the posterior mediastinum and deviates to the left as it pierces the diaphragm at T10.
A(ii)
Cervical part lies in front of the prevertebral fascia, behind the trachea; the thoracic part is crossed on the right by the azygos vein and on the left by the aorta; in the posterior mediastinum it lies behind the left main bronchus and left pulmonary artery and in front of the thoracic duct; it is the most posterior tube of the superior mediastinum and the most anterior structure of the posterior mediastinum, with the vagus nerves around it, the azygos vein behind and to the right and the descending aorta behind and to the left.
A(iii)
Four constrictions: at its origin (C6), 15 cm from the incisor teeth; where the arch of the aorta lies in front of it, 22 cm; where the left main bronchus lies in front of it (tracheal bifurcation), 27 cm; at the diaphragm (T10), 38-40 cm.
A(iv)
• Arteries: inferior thyroid artery, oesophageal branches of the descending thoracic aorta, and the left gastric artery.
• Veins: upper part to the brachiocephalic vein, middle part to the azygos vein, lower part to the portal vein.
• Lymphatics: upper part to deep cervical nodes, middle part to tracheobronchial nodes, lower part to preaortic nodes.
• Nerves: upper third is striated, supplied by the recurrent laryngeal branch of the vagus, with sympathetics from the middle cervical ganglion; lower two-thirds is smooth, receiving sympathetics from the sympathetic trunk and greater splanchnic nerve, and parasympathetic secretomotor fibres from the vagus to the oesophageal glands.
B(i)
• Upper part: inferior thyroid artery, brachiocephalic vein, deep cervical nodes, striated muscle with recurrent laryngeal supply, related to the trachea and prevertebral fascia in the neck.
• Middle and lower parts: middle drains to the azygos vein and tracheobronchial nodes and is crossed by the azygos vein, arch of the aorta and left main bronchus; lower part has aortic and left gastric arteries, portal venous drainage, preaortic nodes and smooth muscle, and passes through the diaphragm at T10.
C(i)
• Venous routes: upper part to the brachiocephalic vein, middle part to the azygos vein (which empties into the SVC and forms a communication between the SVC and IVC), lower part to the portal vein.
• Lymphatic routes: upper part to deep cervical nodes, middle part to tracheobronchial nodes, lower part to preaortic nodes.

A(i) Describe the parts and the course of the oesophagus.
A(ii) Describe its relations.
A(iii) State its constrictions and their distances from the incisor teeth.
A(iv) Describe its arterial supply, venous drainage, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
The greater sac is the main larger part; the lesser sac (omental bursa) lies posterior to the stomach, adjoining structures and lesser omentum; an incision through the anterolateral wall enters the greater sac; the sacs communicate through the epiploic foramen.
A(ii)
• The transverse mesocolon divides the cavity into supracolic and infracolic compartments; the infracolic lies posterior to the greater omentum and is divided by the mesentery of the small intestine into right and left infracolic spaces.
• Right space: triangular, between the root of the mesentery, ascending colon and right two-thirds of transverse colon; left: between the root, descending colon and left one-third of transverse colon, widening below into the pelvis.
A(iii)
Right paracolic gutter lies lateral to the ascending colon and communicates with the hepatorenal recess and pelvic cavity; the left, lateral to the descending colon, is separated from the splenic area by the phrenicocolic ligament.
A(iv)
• Lesser sac: superior wall peritoneum over the caudate lobe and diaphragm; anterior lesser omentum, peritoneum of the posterior stomach and anterior two layers of greater omentum; posterior the posterior two layers, transverse colon and mesocolon, peritoneum over pancreas, left kidney and suprarenal gland.
• Omental foramen (of Winslow), behind the hepatoduodenal ligament, admits 2 fingers: liver superiorly, first part of duodenum inferiorly, hepatoduodenal ligament anteriorly, IVC and right crus posteriorly.
B(i)
Median umbilical fold covers the urachal remnant, medial folds the obliterated umbilical arteries, lateral folds the inferior epigastric vessels; the supravesical fossa is a site for external supravesical hernia, the medial inguinal fossa for the less common direct hernia, the lateral inguinal fossa for the most common indirect hernia.
B(ii)
Blockage of the uterine tubes (hysterosalpingography), peritonitis, ascites, paracentesis and intraperitoneal injection, flow of exudates in the paracolic gutters, and adhesions with adhesiotomy in intestinal obstruction.
C(i)
• The right paracolic gutter provides a route for spread of infection between the pelvic and upper abdominal regions, and the supracolic and infracolic compartments communicate freely through the gutters.
• In the female the cavity communicates with the exterior via the uterine tubes, uterus and vagina.
• Parietal peritoneum is supplied by the nerves of the adjacent body wall and diaphragm; visceral peritoneum by sympathetic nerves of the underlying viscus.
• Receptors respond to overdistension, traction on mesenteries, spasm of smooth muscle and ischaemia.

A(i)
Cell body (soma): The neuronal cell body has a nucleus with at least one nucleolus and typical cytoplasmic organelles; it lacks centrioles, consistent with the amitotic nature of neurons. Types of neurons by structure: Unipolar (pseudounipolar) neurons — sensory neurons with only a single process or fiber that divides close to the cell body into two main branches (axon and dendrite); the longer branch extends to a peripheral ending and the other toward the CNS. Multipolar neurons — motor neurons and interneurons with numerous cell processes (an axon and many dendrites). Bipolar neurons — spindle-shaped, with a dendrite at one end and an axon at the other; found in the light-sensitive retina of the eye. Anaxonic neurons — have many dendrites but no true axon; do not produce action potentials, but regulate electrical changes of adjacent neurons. Glial cells (neuroglia): Neuroglia is a special type of connective tissue for the nervous system. Glial cells are nonconductive; they provide a support system for neurons; they support, nourish, and protect neurons. They are far more numerous than neurons and, unlike neurons, are capable of mitosis. Types include oligodendrocytes (produce myelin in CNS), Schwann cells and satellite cells (in PNS), and microglia.
A(ii)
Neurons are highly specialized and amitotic: if a neuron is destroyed, it cannot be replaced because neurons do not go through mitosis. This means that neuronal loss (e.g., in injury or disease) is permanent and irreplaceable.
B(i)
CNS consists of the brain and spinal cord; it is covered by three connective tissue layers called meninges (dura, arachnoid, and pia maters); it contains very little collagen or fibrous tissue and is relatively soft, easily damaged by injuries affecting the cranium or vertebral bones. The PNS is composed of nerves and ganglia. Functionally, the CNS is the master control unit while the PNS is the body's link to the outside world. Sensory (afferent) and motor (efferent) are the functional categories.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the cell body (soma), types of neurons by structure, and the glial cells of the nervous system under the following headings: cell types, function, and capacity for mitosis.
A(ii) Explain the clinical significance of neurons being amitotic.
B(i) Distinguish between the central nervous system (CNS) and peripheral nervous system (PNS) structurally and functionally.

A(i) Describe the immunological defence system of the gastrointestinal tract, including: the name of the tissue system; the layers of the GIT wall it occupies; the cell types it contains; and the antibody it produces.
A(ii) Explain the complete mechanism by which IgA protects the lumen of the GIT from pathogens, including the role of the secretory protein and the property that makes IgA effective.
B(i) State which regions of the GIT are lined by stratified squamous epithelium rather than the simple thin vulnerable epithelium lining the rest of the tract, and explain the significance of this difference in the context of microbial defense.
B(ii) Explain the clinical and anatomical basis for the well-known effects of emotional stress on the stomach and other regions of the GIT.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Immunological defense system:
• Name: Mucosa-Associated Lymphoid Tissue (MALT).
• Layers occupied: the mucosa (especially the lamina propria located just below the epithelium) and the submucosal layers.
• Cell types: macrophages and lymphocytes (some of which actively produce antibodies); also free immune cells and lymphoid nodules.
• Antibody produced: mainly immunoglobulin A (IgA).
A(ii)
IgA protection mechanism:
• IgA antibodies undergo transcytosis into the intestinal lumen, bound to the secretory protein produced by epithelial cells.
• This complex (secretory IgA) protects against viral and bacterial pathogens.
• IgA is resistant to proteolytic enzymes and can therefore coexist with the proteases present in the lumen, making it effective even in the enzyme-rich intestinal environment.
B(i)
Stratified squamous epithelium lines the oral cavity, esophagus, and anal canal (not vulnerable simple columnar). The rest of the GIT (except these three regions) is lined by a simple thin vulnerable epithelium. Because the rest of the GIT is lined by this vulnerable epithelium and normally contains thousands of microbial species (including potential pathogens), the MALT provides an essential backup to the thin physical barrier.
B(ii)
The enteric nervous system (submucosal/Meissner and myenteric/Auerbach plexuses) provides an anatomic basis for the well-known actions of emotional stress on the stomach and other regions of the GIT. These plexuses are interconnected with the autonomic nervous system and CNS.

A(i)
• Continuation of the sigmoid colon at S3; ends as the anal canal one inch below and in front of the tip of the coccyx; about 12 to 13 cm (5 inches); lower end dilated as the ampulla; lacks mesentery, taeniae coli, sacculations and appendices epiploicae.
• Two anteroposterior curves (sacral posterior; perineal anterior at puborectalis) and three lateral curves (upper convex to right, middle convex to left and most prominent, lower convex to right).
A(ii)
Upper third: front and sides covered; middle third: front only; lower third: none; posterior surface: none. Male: recto-vesical pouch 7.5 cm from anus; female: recto-uterine pouch of Douglas 5.5 cm from anus.
A(iii)
Four permanent horizontal Houston's valves (1st and 3rd constant); the 3rd at S5, 5 cm above the anus, if completely encircling forms Nelaton's sphincter, and divides an upper chamber (faeces without reflex to defecate) from a lower sensitive chamber; valves support faecal weight; cannulae/rectal washing are given in left lateral position to avoid injury to the 3rd valve.
A(iv)
Wall: serous, muscular (outer longitudinal, inner circular), submucosa, mucosa. Arteries: superior rectal (main, from inferior mesenteric), middle rectal (anterior division of internal iliac), inferior rectal (internal pudendal), median sacral (aorta), inferior gluteal.
B(i)
Superior rectal vein drains to inferior mesenteric then portal vein; middle rectal to internal iliac and inferior rectal to internal pudendal (systemic). Internal haemorrhoids (superior rectal tributaries, above Hilton's line, painless); external (inferior rectal, below, painful).
B(ii)
Support: puborectal sling, Waldeyer fascia, lateral ligaments, pelvirectal and ischiorectal fat. Upper third lateral: pararectal fossa (sigmoid colon, small intestine); middle third: pelvirectal space; lower third: ischioanal fossa.
B(iii)
Sympathetic (L1, L2) is vasomotor, stimulates the internal anal sphincter and inhibits the rest of the musculature; parasympathetic (S2 to S4) is secretomotor, stimulates peristalsis and relaxes sphincters.
C(i)
Lymph: upper half via superior rectal to left common iliac and pararectal nodes; middle half to internal iliac nodes; lower part to anal valves to internal iliac nodes; below the anal valves to superficial inguinal nodes.
C(ii)
Portal-systemic anastomosis: superior rectal (portal) with middle and inferior rectal veins (systemic); gut lymph follows arteries to pre-aortic nodes.
C(iii)
Male: anterior sigmoid colon, small intestine, seminal vesicles, ampulla of vas, posterior bladder and prostate; female: posterior vaginal wall; posterior: sacrum, sacral plexus, coccyx, and piriformis, coccygeus, levator ani.
C(iv)
Hindgut origin (endoderm), sympathetic least splanchnic (T12, L1) plus hypogastric (S2 to S4), inferior mesenteric artery (L3); mucosa above the 3rd valve from pre-allantoic hindgut, below from cloaca; muscle from splanchnic mesoderm.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Mucosa: consists of an epithelial lining, lamina propria (zone of loose connective tissue rich in blood vessels, lymphatics, lymphocytes, smooth muscle cells, and sometimes small glands), and muscularis mucosae (thin layer of smooth muscle that separates the mucosa from the submucosa and allows local movements of the mucosa).
• Submucosa: denser connective tissue containing larger blood and lymph vessels, the submucosal (Meissner) plexus of autonomic nerves, and possibly glands and lymphoid tissue.
• Muscularis (muscularis externa): thick layer of smooth muscle organized into an internal circular sublayer and an external longitudinal sublayer; connective tissue between them contains blood vessels, lymph vessels, and the myenteric (Auerbach) nerve plexus.
• Serosa: outermost layer; a thin sheet of loose connective tissue covered with mesothelium (simple squamous covering epithelium); rich in blood vessels, lymphatics, and adipose tissue.
A(ii)
• Submucosal (Meissner) plexus: located in the submucosa between the submucosa and the muscularis; together with the myenteric plexus constitutes the local enteric nervous system.
• Myenteric (Auerbach) plexus: located in the connective tissue between the circular and longitudinal muscle sublayers; responsible for local contraction of the muscularis, mixing and propelling the contents of the lumen (peristalsis).
• Both plexuses together form the local enteric nervous system, which functions independently of the CNS; they are composed mainly of nerve cell aggregates forming small parasympathetic ganglia, numerous in regions of greatest motility.
B(i)
The esophagus is not suspended in a cavity but is bound directly to adjacent structures, so instead of a serosa it has a thick adventitia. The adventitia consists of connective tissue containing vessels and nerves but lacks mesothelium, whereas the serosa is covered by mesothelium.
B(ii)
The serosa of the small and large intestines is continuous with parts of the mesentery. The mesentery is a large fold of adipose connective tissue covered on both sides by mesothelium; it suspends the intestines and is continuous with the peritoneum (the serous membrane lining the abdominal cavity).
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the four main layers of the gastrointestinal tract wall, giving the composition of each layer.
A(ii) For the muscularis layer, name the two nerve plexuses associated with it, state where each is located, and explain the function of each.
B(i) Explain why the esophagus has an adventitia instead of a serosa, and state the structural difference between these two outermost coverings.
B(ii) Distinguish between the serosa and the mesentery, naming the structures each is continuous with.

(i) Describe the gross anatomy of the heart under the headings: chambers, borders and surfaces.
(ii) Relate the chambers/valves of the heart to a recognised pathology.
(iii) Explain how a cardiac problem can produce a functional deficit or sensation felt at a distant site.
questions.answerText:
(i)
• The heart has four chambers, the right and left atria (receiving chambers) and the right and left ventricles (discharging chambers), enclosed in the double-walled pericardial sac, and rests on its diaphragmatic (inferior) surface.
• It has an apex, formed by the inferolateral part of the left ventricle and lying posterior to the 5th intercostal space where the apex beat is felt, a base, formed mainly by the left atrium and part of the right atrium, four borders and three surfaces.
• The right border is formed mainly by the right atrium; the left border by the left ventricle and left auricle; the inferior border by the right ventricle mainly and the left ventricle; the superior border by both atria, auricles and the great vessels.
• The anterior (sternocostal) surface consists chiefly of the right ventricle; the inferior (diaphragmatic) surface consists chiefly of the left ventricle and a small part of the right ventricle; the left (pulmonary) surface is formed mainly by the left ventricle.
• The right atrium receives venous blood from the SVC, IVC and coronary sinus, has a smooth sinus venarum and a rough muscular wall with pectinate muscles, and communicates with the right ventricle via the right atrioventricular (tricuspid) orifice.
• The left atrium receives the four pulmonary veins and communicates with the left ventricle via the left atrioventricular (mitral) orifice; the right ventricle has a tricuspid valve and leads to the pulmonary trunk via the conus arteriosus, while the left ventricle, with twice the wall thickness, has the mitral valve and leads to the aorta via the aortic vestibule and aortic valve.
(ii)
• Valvular insufficiency results from valve leaflets not completely sealing when a valve is closed, so regurgitation of blood occurs into the proximal chamber, generating a characteristic heart murmur.
• Positional and septal anomalies include dextrocardia, atrial septal defects and ventricular septal defects.
• Aortic dissection, a tear in the inner wall of the aorta associated with high blood pressure, and aortic aneurysm, dilation of an artery greater than 50% of its normal diameter, are pathologies of the great vessel arising from the left ventricle.
(iii)
• The conducting system, the SA node in the posterior wall of the right atrium, the AV node in the floor of the right atrium, the AV bundle and Purkinje fibres, initiates and coordinates the heartbeat; damage to a coronary artery supplying these nodes can disturb heart rhythm.
• Cardiac afferent fibres carrying pain from ischaemic myocardium travel via sympathetic afferents in the cardiac plexus to spinal cord segments T1-T5 shared with dermatomes of the chest wall and upper limb, so the central nervous system perceives cardiac pain as coming from the body wall.
• This explains why myocardial ischaemia is felt as pain in the mid or left chest that radiates to the left jaw and left arm, a distant somatic sensation produced by a cardiac (visceral) problem.

questions.question:
Describe the femoral triangle and adductor canal under the following headings, state how they relate to common pathologies, and explain the anatomical basis of referred pain to the knee from the hip.
A(i) Boundaries, roof, and floor of the femoral triangle; contents from lateral to medial
A(ii) Femoral artery — branches within the femoral triangle, including the profunda femoris and its branches
B(i) Adductor canal — boundaries, contents, and where it terminates
B(ii) Clinical basis: femoral pulse palpation and profunda femoris in femoral artery occlusion
C(i) Explain why hip joint disease causes referred pain at the knee, based on the nerve supply of both joints
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Boundaries: superiorly — inguinal ligament; medially — medial border of adductor longus; laterally — medial border of sartorius; apex — where adductor longus and sartorius cross. Roof: fascia lata (deep fascia) pierced by the great saphenous vein at the saphenous opening (fossa ovalis). Floor: formed by iliopsoas laterally and pectineus medially. Contents from lateral to medial: femoral nerve, femoral artery, femoral vein (the mnemonic 'NAVY' — from lateral: Nerve, Artery, Vein, Y-fronts/lymphatics). The femoral pulse can be palpated as it enters the femoral triangle, midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis — the mid-inguinal point.
A(ii)
The femoral artery divides to give the profunda femoris 5 cm below the inguinal ligament. Branches of the femoral artery (mnemonic: 'Does She Scream During Poking Sessions?'): Deep external pudendal arteries, Superficial epigastric, Superficial external pudendal, Descending genicular artery, Profunda femoris artery, Superficial circumflex iliac. Profunda femoris arises from the posterolateral aspect of the femoral artery; it gives: (1) Perforating branches — 3 or 4 arteries that perforate adductor magnus, contributing to medial and posterior thigh. (2) Lateral femoral circumflex artery — wraps around anterior and lateral side of femur, supplying muscles on lateral aspect of thigh. (3) Medial femoral circumflex artery — wraps around posterior side of femur, supplying its neck and head; in a fracture of the femoral neck this artery can easily be damaged and avascular necrosis of the femoral head can occur.
B(i)
The adductor canal is a passageway in the medial thigh. The adductor hiatus is an opening between the aponeurotic distal attachment of the adductor part of adductor magnus and the tendinous distal attachment of the hamstring part. The hiatus transmits the femoral artery and vein from the adductor canal in the thigh to the popliteal fossa posterior to the knee. It is located just lateral and superior to the adductor tubercle of the femur.
B(ii)
Femoral pulse: palpated at mid-inguinal point (midway between ASIS and pubic symphysis). In femoral artery occlusion, the profunda femoris artery is the main collateral channel because the superior muscular branches of the popliteal artery have clinically important anastomoses with the terminal part of the profunda femoris and gluteal arteries, maintaining perfusion to the leg.
C(i)
The posterior division of the obturator nerve supplies both the hip and the knee joint; therefore, pain from hip pathology is referred along this common nerve pathway to present as knee pain. This is the basis of Hilton's law applied to the hip: 'the nerve supplying the joint also supplies the muscles moving the joint and the skin covering the insertion of these muscles.' The femoral nerve also supplies the hip joint via intermediate and cutaneous branches and the knee via branches of obturator and femoral nerves.

A(i)
Fixation: to achieve a permanent section, tissues must be fixed to preserve the structure and molecular composition; fixation prevents autolysis (self-digestion by enzymes present in the cells) and destruction by bacteria. Dehydration and clearing: tissues are progressed in graded steps to 100% alcohol to remove water; after the solvent replaces the alcohol, the tissue becomes transparent in xylene (clearing). Embedding: once the tissue is impregnated with the solvent, it is placed in a hard medium (e.g., wax); heat causes the solvent to evaporate, and the spaces within the tissue are filled by the embedding medium. Sectioning: tissues are sectioned by the microtome's steel or glass blade; this method allows stained sections to be prepared rapidly for study of specimens. Mounting: sections are mounted on a supportive structure (e.g., slide) that can be placed on a microscope stage. Staining: stains are applied to differentiate tissue components.
A(ii)
The most commonly used stains are hematoxylin and eosin (H & E). Hematoxylin stains basic (acidic) structures — the most acidic components are DNA and RNA; therefore, the nucleus and cytoplasmic RNA stain blue/purple (basophilic). Eosin stains acidophilic (basic) structures — many cytoplasmic constituents stain pinkish (eosinophilic/acidophilic). Reason: differential staining is based on the acid-base chemistry of cell components; acidic cell components bind basic dyes (hematoxylin) and basic components bind acidic dyes (eosin).
B(i)
Light microscopy: the standard technique; produces images of tissue sections examined by transmitted light; maximum resolving power is 0.2 micrometers (two marks 0.2 micrometers apart can be seen as two distinct entities). Types include brightfield, phase contrast, differential interference contrast (DIC), fluorescence, and confocal. Preferred for: routine tissue examination, diagnosis of pathology, overview of cell and tissue structure. Electron microscopy: has extended the detail at which subcellular structures can be studied; reveals ultrastructural details such as organelles, myelin sheaths, and synapse morphology. Preferred for: study of subcellular structures, ultrastructural detail, and molecular architecture of cell membranes.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the tissue preparation process used in histology under the following headings: fixation, dehydration and clearing, embedding, sectioning, and staining.
A(ii) State the most commonly used stain in histology, explain what structures it stains and the colors produced, and give the reason for the differential staining.
B(i) Distinguish between light microscopy and electron microscopy in histology, stating what each reveals and an example of when each is preferred.

Describe the popliteal artery and its branches, stating the safe site for popliteal pulse palpation, and explain the anatomical basis of the deformity and functional deficit after tibial nerve injury in the popliteal fossa.
A(i) Origin, course, and relations of the popliteal artery
A(ii) All branches of the popliteal artery — genicular and muscular
B(i) Termination and continuation of the popliteal artery into the leg and foot
B(ii) Safe site for popliteal pulse palpation and clinical technique
C(i) Anatomical basis of the deformity and functional deficit after tibial nerve injury in the popliteal fossa
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The popliteal artery is the continuation of the femoral artery; it begins when the femoral artery passes through the adductor hiatus. It descends through the fossa, passing inferolaterally and is the deepest structure in the fossa — it runs in close proximity to the articular capsule of the knee joint. It terminates at the inferior border of the popliteus by dividing into the anterior and posterior tibial arteries.
A(ii)
Five genicular branches participate in the genicular anastomosis (a network of vessels surrounding the knee providing collateral circulation capable of maintaining blood supply to the leg during full knee flexion): superior lateral genicular artery, superior medial genicular artery, middle genicular artery (penetrates the fibrous capsule and supplies the cruciate ligaments, synovial membrane, and peripheral margins of the menisci), inferior lateral genicular artery, and inferior medial genicular artery. Muscular branches supply the hamstring, gastrocnemius, soleus, and plantaris muscles. The superior muscular branches have clinically important anastomoses with the terminal part of the profunda femoris and gluteal arteries.
B(i)
Termination: the popliteal artery divides into the anterior tibial artery and the tibioperoneal trunk; the tibioperoneal trunk divides into the posterior tibial artery and fibular (peroneal) artery. Anterior tibial artery: passes anterior to the interosseous membrane between tibia and fibula; supplies muscles of anterior compartment; continues as the dorsalis pedis artery in the foot, supplying tarsal bones and dorsal metatarsals, and anastomoses with the lateral plantar artery to form the deep plantar arch. Posterior tibial artery: continues inferiorly along surface of deep posterior leg muscles; enters the sole of the foot via the tarsal tunnel; splits into lateral and medial plantar arteries supplying the plantar foot.
B(ii)
The popliteal artery is the hardest pulse to find, lying deep in the popliteal fossa; it requires deep palpation. To make it easier, the patient should slightly flex the leg — this relaxes the fascia around the popliteal fossa. An aneurysm of the popliteal artery can be detected by an obvious palpable pulsation in the popliteal fossa; an arterial bruit may be heard on auscultation.
C(i)
The tibial nerve is the medial and larger branch of the sciatic nerve and the most superficial of the neurovascular bundle. Injury causes: paralysis of flexor muscles in the leg and intrinsic muscles in the sole of the foot; inability to plantarflex the ankles or flex the toes; and loss of sensation on the sole of the foot. The resulting deformity is a calcaneovalgus posture — unopposed dorsiflexion with loss of plantarflexion, the foot assuming a dorsiflexed position because the antagonist muscles remain intact. Weakened or absent plantarflexion and paraesthesia of the foot and posterolateral leg are the major features of tibial nerve compression.

A(i)
Chemical composition and properties: Bone is a connective tissue mineralized by calcium phosphate in the form of crystals very similar to hydroxyapatite. The minerals are both in the type I collagen fibers (which constitute about 95% of the matrix) and in the ground substance. Bone is both resilient and hard. Its resilience is due to the organic matter (collagen); its hardness is due to the inorganic minerals (calcium phosphate, calcium carbonate, calcium fluoride, calcium hydroxide, and citrate). Cell types: Osteocytes — maintain calcium and phosphate ion levels in the blood, are essentially stress sensors, and are osteoblasts that have been trapped in their own matrix in lacunae. Osteoblasts — synthesize the organic matrix (osteoid). Osteoclasts — multinucleated giant cells involved in resorption and remodeling of bone; they are also chondrocytes during bone healing and remodeling. Osteoid is the matrix secreted by osteoblasts and osteocytes prior to mineralization. Types of bone: compact bone (also called dense bone, cortical bone, or lamellar bone) and spongy bone (also called cancellous bone, trabecular bone, and medullary bone).
A(ii)
Compact bone is organized into structures called osteons or Haversian systems: concentric lamellae surrounding a central canal called the Haversian canal, which contains blood vessels, nerves, loose connective tissue, and endosteum. Between lamellae are lacunae, each with one osteocyte interconnected by canaliculi containing the cells' dendritic processes. Canals called Volkmann's canals link Haversian canals with one another and with the marrow cavity. Metabolic exchanges between osteocytes and blood capillaries depend on communication through the canaliculi.
B(i)
Blood calcium levels are regulated by the hormones parathormone (parathyroid hormone), which raises blood calcium levels by stimulating bone resorption, and calcitonin, which reduces blood calcium by suppressing bone resorption and increasing osteoid calcification.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the gross histology of bone under the following headings: chemical composition and properties, cell types and their functions, and types of bone.
A(ii) State how the Haversian system (osteon) is organised and relate this to bone function.
B(i) Explain how blood calcium levels are regulated through bone, naming the hormones involved and their actions.

(i) Describe the gross anatomy of the pancreas - location, shape, and its four parts (head, neck, body, tail) with their relations.
(ii) Relate the parts of the pancreas to pathology (annular pancreas, pancreatitis).
(iii) Explain how pancreatic disease can produce a functional deficit in a distant organ/system.
questions.answerText:
(i)
• The pancreas is a soft, lobulated, J- or retort-shaped gland lying retroperitoneally, except for the tail, and transversely across the posterior abdominal wall at the level of L1-L2, posterior to the stomach, between the duodenum on the right and the spleen on the left; it is about 15-20 cm long and weighs about 90 g.
• The head is disc-shaped, enlarged, and lies within the concavity of the duodenum; the uncinate process projects from its lower part, posterior to the superior mesenteric vessels.
• The neck is the constricted portion connecting the head to the body and overlies the superior mesenteric vessels.
• The body is centrally located, crossing the midline behind the stomach, with anterior, posterior and inferior surfaces; the posterior surface contacts the aorta, splenic vein, left kidney and vessels, left suprarenal gland, origin of the superior mesenteric artery, and the crura of the diaphragm.
• The tail is narrow, lies at the level of T12, ends within the splenic hilum in the splenophrenic ligament, and is the only intraperitoneal part of the pancreas; it may be injured during splenectomy, causing a pancreatic fistula.
• The main pancreatic duct, of Wirsung, begins in the tail and runs to the head, usually joining the bile duct to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla, which opens at the major duodenal papilla; the accessory duct, of Santorini, drains the upper head via the minor duodenal papilla.
(ii)
• Annular pancreas is a rare congenital defect in which the pancreas encircles the duodenum; ectopic pancreatic tissue outside the gastrointestinal tract is a very common anomaly.
• Due to its deep retroperitoneal position, the pancreas is not easily accessible for direct clinical examination, so diagnosis of pancreatic disease relies on ultrasound, CT scan, special investigations of the pancreatic and biliary ducts, and biochemical tests.
• Acute necrotizing pancreatitis results when proenzymes are prematurely activated and digest pancreatic tissue, from causes including infection, gallstones, alcoholism, drugs and trauma.
(iii)
• The endocrine part of the pancreas, the islets of Langerhans, secretes insulin and glucagon into the blood; lack of insulin production by the beta cells, or defective insulin receptors, causes diabetes mellitus, a hyperglycaemic metabolic disorder affecting the whole body.
• Because the exocrine pancreas secretes digestive enzymes and bicarbonate essential for neutralising gastric acid and digesting food in the duodenum, pancreatic disease impairing exocrine secretion produces a functional deficit in intestinal digestion, a distant effect of pancreatic pathology.
• In extreme malnutrition, acinar cell atrophy further reduces digestive enzyme production, compounding this distant digestive deficit.

questions.question:
Describe the deep fascial spaces of the hand:
A(i) Thenar space
A(ii) The list of compartments/fascial spaces of the hand
A(iii) Space of Parona
B. Explain the clinical basis for infection spreading between these compartments.
C. Distinguish between the thenar space and the midpalmar space.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The thenar space lies on the thumb side of the septum that joins the border of the palmar aponeurosis to the palmar border of the third metacarpal bone; it contains the first lumbrical muscle and is overlaid by the flexor tendons to the index finger.
A(ii)
The compartments and fascial spaces of the hand include the dorsal spaces, hypothenar space, midpalmar space, thenar space, web spaces and pulp spaces, all bounded by connective tissue.
A(iii)
The space of Parona extends from the proximal margin of the carpal tunnel to the mid-forearm; its roof is formed distally by the flexor digitorum profundus tendons and proximally by the belly of flexor digitorum superficialis (whose origin forms the proximal boundary), it is limited medially by flexor carpi ulnaris and laterally by flexor pollicis longus, and its floor is formed by pronator quadratus distally and the interosseous membrane in its proximal two-thirds.
B
• These fascial spaces allow mobility of the hand structures but, being bounded by connective tissue, offer little resistance to the spread of infection.
• Infection within the thenar space can readily break into the connective tissue canals surrounding the ulnar three lumbricals.
• For practical purposes the thenar space may therefore be considered continuous distally with these lumbrical canals, and thus distally communicates with the web spaces.
• The thenar space also communicates proximally with the space of Parona.
• Infection of these deep spaces, including the space of Parona, can be difficult to diagnose.
C
• The thenar space lies on the thumb (radial) side of the septum joining the palmar aponeurosis to the third metacarpal, contains the first lumbrical, and is overlaid by the flexor tendons of the index finger.
• The midpalmar space, by contrast, lies on the ulnar side of this septum, related to the tendons for the middle, ring and little fingers and to adductor pollicis, separated from the thenar space by the lateral palmar septum.
• The thenar space communicates proximally with the space of Parona and distally with the lumbrical canals/web spaces, reflecting its position along the flexor tendon of the index finger.
• This anatomical separation by the lateral palmar septum explains why infection in one compartment tends initially to remain localised to that space before spreading along its own specific communicating pathway.

questions.question:
Describe the brachial artery:
A(i) Origin and termination
A(ii) Course
A(iii) Branches
B. State the safe site associated with clinical use of the brachial artery.
C. Explain the anatomical basis of the deformity/complication (Volkmann's ischaemic contracture) that can follow injury to this artery.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The brachial artery provides the main arterial supply to the arm and is the continuation of the axillary artery; it begins at the inferior border of teres major and ends in the cubital fossa opposite the neck of the radius.
A(ii)
Under cover of the bicipital aponeurosis, it divides into the radial and ulnar arteries.
A(iii)
Its branches include the deep brachial (profunda brachii) artery, which accompanies the radial nerve, the superior ulnar collateral artery, which accompanies the ulnar nerve, and the inferior ulnar collateral artery.
B
During blood pressure measurement, the stethoscope is placed over the brachial artery in the cubital fossa, and the cubital fossa is the site used to palpate the brachial pulse.
C
• Volkmann's ischaemic contracture is a deformity of the hand, fingers and wrist caused by injury to the muscles of the forearm.
• The classical presentation is a supracondylar fracture of the humerus, although fracture of the arm or elbow may also result in this deformity; the artery involved is the brachial artery.
• The contracture occurs when there is a lack of blood flow (ischaemia) to the forearm, usually from increased pressure resulting from swelling (compartment syndrome).
• Because there is very little room within each fascial compartment of the arm and forearm, haemorrhage or oedema following injury to the brachial artery can cause secondary vascular compression: veins are affected first, and later the arteries, resulting in ischaemia of the affected part.
• The classical presentation of the resulting acute compartment syndrome is remembered by "the five P's": pulselessness, paraesthesia, poikilothermia, paralysis and pallor.
• There are three levels of severity of the resulting Volkmann's contracture: the mildest involves flexion contracture of only two or three fingers with no or limited loss of sensation; a more severe form involves all fingers flexed with the thumb stuck in the palm and some sensory loss.
• The most severe form involves all the muscles in the forearm that flex and extend the wrist and fingers, producing a severely disabling condition.
• This progression illustrates how injury to the brachial artery at the elbow can produce a graded functional deficit distally in the hand and fingers.

A(i)
• The vagus is the 10th cranial nerve.
• The right vagus descends on the right side of the trachea, forms the posterior oesophageal plexus and continues in the abdomen as the posterior gastric nerve.
• The left vagus descends between the left common carotid and left subclavian arteries, forms the anterior oesophageal plexus and continues in the abdomen as the anterior gastric nerve.
A(ii)
• The vagus nerves lie in both the superior and the posterior mediastinum; in the posterior mediastinum the right and left vagi lie around the oesophagus and pass through the oesophageal opening of the diaphragm (T10) as the anterior and posterior vagal trunks.
• The left recurrent laryngeal branch of the vagus winds round the ligamentum arteriosus, which connects the inferior concave surface of the arch of the aorta to the left pulmonary artery.
A(iii)
• Branches: recurrent laryngeal branches on both sides and superior and inferior cervical cardiac branches (the right has both, the left has the inferior branch) to the cardiac plexus; pulmonary plexuses to the lungs; oesophageal plexuses.
• Cardiac plexus: the superficial part lies in front of the ligamentum arteriosus (inferior cervical cardiac branch of the left vagus); the deep part lies in front of the left bronchus and at the bifurcation of the pulmonary trunk, behind the arch of the aorta on the lowest part of the trachea; parasympathetic fibres relay in the heart.
A(iv)
• Heart: through the cardiac plexus to the SA and AV nodes and the AV bundle; parasympathetics decrease the rate of impulse generation, sympathetics increase it.
• Lungs and visceral pleura (via the pulmonary plexuses): bronchoconstrictor, vasodilator to pulmonary vessels and secretomotor to glands; the vagal efferents mediate the cough reflex that clears secretions and dust.
• Oesophagus and trachea: recurrent laryngeal branch to the striated upper third of the oesophagus, parasympathetic secretomotor fibres to the oesophageal glands; vagus to the mucous membrane and parasympathetics of the trachea; gastric irritation of vagus nerve endings may cause hiccup.
questions.question:
A(i) State the nature of the vagus nerve and describe its course in the thorax on the right and left.
A(ii) Describe its relations in the mediastinum.
A(iii) State its branches and plexuses in the thorax.
A(iv) Describe its distribution to thoracic structures.

A(i) Describe the gross anatomy of the pancreas, including its nature as a gland, its retroperitoneal position, its capsular covering, and how its parenchyma is organised into lobules.
A(ii) Describe the two functional components of the pancreas (exocrine and endocrine), including the cell types involved and the products of each.
B(i) Describe the exocrine secretory acini of the pancreas, including the arrangement around the acini and the volume of juice produced.
B(ii) Explain the role of the pancreas in digestion and hormonal regulation, and contrast this with the role of the liver and the gallbladder.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Gross anatomy of the pancreas:
• Nature: a mixed exocrine-endocrine gland that produces both digestive enzymes and hormones.
• Position: retroperitoneally positioned on the posterior wall of the abdominal cavity at the level of the 2nd and 3rd lumbar vertebrae.
• Capsular covering: it has no distinct capsule, but is covered by a thin layer of loose connective tissue, from which septa extend to cover the larger vessels and ducts and to separate the parenchyma into lobules.
A(ii)
Two functional components:
• Exocrine: produces digestive enzymes that act in the small intestine; secretory acini produce about 1.6 litres of pancreatic juice every day.
• Endocrine: involves primarily smaller cells similar to enteroendocrine cells located in variously sized clusters called the pancreatic islets (islets of Langerhans); secretes hormones such as insulin and glucagon into the bloodstream, which are very important for the metabolism of absorbed nutrients.
B(i)
Exocrine acini:
• The secretory acini are surrounded by a basal lamina that is supported only by a delicate sheath of reticular fibers with a rich capillary network.
• The exocrine part produces about 1.6 litres of pancreatic juice every day.
B(ii)
• Pancreas: produces digestive enzymes that act in the small intestine; secretes insulin and glucagon, both important for metabolism of absorbed nutrients.
• Liver: produces bile, an important fluid in the digestion of fats; plays a major role in lipid, carbohydrate, and protein metabolism; inactivates and metabolizes many toxic substances and drugs; participates in iron metabolism and the synthesis of blood proteins and factors necessary for blood coagulation.
• Gallbladder: absorbs water from bile and stores bile in a concentrated form.

A(i)
Medial longitudinal arch: formed by calcaneus, talus (keystone — its superior articular facet is the summit), navicular, 3 cuneiform bones, and 1st, 2nd, and 3rd metatarsals; found on medial aspect of foot; larger, with greatest height, higher, more mobile, and more resilient. Lateral longitudinal arch: formed by calcaneus, cuboid, and the 4th and 5th metatarsals; summit is the subtalar articulation; flat, contains relatively fewer bones, hence more rigid; bears body weight before the medial arch comes into play. Transverse arch: formed proximally by 3 cuneiforms and cuboid, and distally by the bases of 5 metatarsals; it is a partial arch (each foot represents a half dome); the intermediate and lateral cuneiforms are wedge-shaped (bony factor).
A(ii)
Medial longitudinal arch: Ligaments — spring ligament, deltoid ligament, plantar aponeurosis, interosseous ligaments, long and short plantar ligaments. Muscles — tibialis posterior, tibialis anterior, flexor hallucis longus, flexor digitorum longus, and short muscles of the big toe. Bony factor — the shape and constitution of the bones. Lateral longitudinal arch: Ligaments — plantar aponeurosis, interosseous ligaments, long and short plantar ligaments. Muscles — peroneus longus and brevis, flexor digitorum longus, and short muscles of the little toe. Bony factor — shape and constitution of the bones. Transverse arch: Bony factor — intermediate and lateral cuneiforms are wedge-shaped. Ligaments — deep transverse ligament and interosseous ligaments (dorsal and plantar). Muscles — peroneus longus and brevis, transverse head of adductor hallucis, and slips of tibialis posterior.
B(i)
The human foot supports the body weight and serves as a lever to propel the body forward during locomotion. Functions carried out by arches: (1) Foot acts as a segmented lever with multiple joints and adapts to uneven surfaces. (2) Long flexors and intrinsic muscles assist propulsive action of gastrocnemius and soleus. (3) Arches are springs that absorb shock and store energy — elastic arches present between weight-bearing points can flatten and recoil back to normal.
B(ii)
Pes planus (flat foot): rotation of the calcaneus, eversion of the plantar surface, slipping down of the talus and navicular, lengthening of the medial longitudinal arch, and abduction of the forefoot; caused by excess weight on medial side, relaxation of ligaments, or muscular imbalance. Pes cavus (high-arched foot): exaggeration of the longitudinal arch; toes dorsiflexed at metatarsophalangeal joints and plantarflexed at interphalangeal joints — claw foot. Talipes equinovarus: plantar flexion, inversion, and adduction of the foot (clubfoot). Talipes calcaneovalgus: dorsiflexion, eversion, and abduction of the foot.
C(i)
The medial longitudinal arch is higher, more mobile, and more resilient — it is dynamic, changes most during movement, and requires active muscular support (particularly tibialis posterior, flexor hallucis longus, and the spring ligament). The lateral longitudinal arch is lower, more stable, built to transmit weight to the ground, makes more contact with the ground, has limited mobility, and depends more on bony and ligamentous rather than muscular support. The medial arch is therefore more clinically vulnerable to collapse (pes planus) when muscles weaken or ligaments stretch.
questions.question:
Describe the arches of the foot under the following headings and explain their clinical relevance.
A(i) Name and constituent bones of each arch, identifying the keystone of each
A(ii) Factors maintaining the arches — ligaments, muscles, and bony factor for each arch
B(i) Functions of the foot arches in weight-bearing and locomotion
B(ii) Deformities of the foot — name and define pes planus, pes cavus, talipes equinovarus, and talipes calcaneovalgus
C(i) Explain why the medial longitudinal arch is more dynamic and more clinically vulnerable than the lateral longitudinal arch

(A) Describe the urinary bladder under the headings: A(i) parts A(ii) trigone A(iii) peritoneal/ligamentous relations.
(B) Explain the clinical basis of why the trigone remains an important fixed landmark during bladder filling.
(C) Distinguish the male urethra from the female urethra.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• The urinary bladder is a musculomembranous sac composed of a body, which collects urine, and a neck, a funnel-shaped extension passing inferiorly to join the urethra; it is divided into apex, fundus and body, with superior, posterior (base) and two inferolateral surfaces.
• The apex points towards the pubic symphysis and continues as the median umbilical ligament, a remnant of the embryonic urachus, up to the umbilicus; the base faces posteroinferiorly, with the two ureters entering at its upper corners and the urethra draining from its lower corner.
A(ii)
The trigone is the smooth, posteroinferior triangular area of the bladder wall formed by imaginary lines connecting the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice; it has four tunics, mucosa, submucosa, muscularis (detrusor muscle) and adventitia.
A(iii)
• Except for its superior surface, which is covered by peritoneum, the bladder is connected to surrounding structures by fibroareolar tissue (true ligaments): the lateral true ligaments, the puboprostatic or pubovesical ligaments anteriorly, the median umbilical ligament at the apex, and a posterior ligament.
• In the male, the upper posterior surface is related to the rectovesical pouch, and the lower part relates to the seminal vesicles and vas deferens; in the female, the posterior surface is related to the anterior wall of the vagina.
B
• The trigone remains immovable as the bladder fills and empties, and functions as a funnel that directs urine into the urethra as the bladder wall (detrusor) contracts.
• This fixed relationship of the ureteric and urethral orifices at the trigone is why it is used as a constant anatomical landmark despite the changing size and shape of the rest of the bladder.
C
• The male urethra is about 20 cm long and is divided into four parts: intramural (preprostatic), prostatic, membranous, and spongy (penile) parts, opening at the end of the penis.
• The male urethra passes through the prostate, the deep perineal pouch/urogenital diaphragm as the membranous urethra, and then the length of the penis as the spongy urethra, bending twice along its course.
• The female urethra is much shorter, about 3-4 cm long, corresponding to the prostatic part of the male urethra proximal to the prostatic utricle.
• The female urethra begins at the internal urethral orifice about 5 cm behind the pubic symphysis, runs downward embedded in the anterior wall of the vagina, traverses the urogenital diaphragm, and ends at the external urethral orifice in the vestibule, receiving the paraurethral (Skene's) glands.
• Both sexes have an internal, smooth muscle, involuntary urethral sphincter continuous with the detrusor muscle, and an external, skeletal muscle, voluntary sphincter innervated by the pudendal nerve, located inferior to the prostate in males and at the bladder's distal inferior end in females.

questions.question:
Describe the gross anatomy of the brachial plexus:
A(i) Formation (roots)
A(ii) Trunks, divisions, cords
A(iii) Five main terminal branches
B. State how injury at each level (trunk/cord) of the plexus relates to a specific clinical pathology.
C. Explain how injury at the level of a trunk or cord spreads to affect distant structures (individual peripheral nerves), causing specific functional deficits.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The brachial plexus is formed by the union of the C5, C6, C7 and C8 ventral rami and the greater part of the 1st thoracic ventral ramus, with contribution sometimes from C4 (giving a "prefixed" plexus) or T2 (giving a "postfixed" plexus); the roots emerge from the transverse processes of the cervical vertebrae, immediately posterior to the vertebral artery, and lie between the scalene muscles.
A(ii)
C5 and C6 unite to form the upper trunk, C7 continues as the middle trunk, and C8 and T1 unite to form the lower trunk, lying in the posterior triangle of the neck; each trunk bifurcates behind the clavicle into an anterior and a posterior division. The anterior divisions of the upper and middle trunks unite to form the lateral cord; the anterior division of the lower trunk continues as the medial cord; the posterior divisions of all three trunks unite to form the posterior cord, lying in the axilla below pectoralis minor.
A(iii)
The five main terminal branches are the musculocutaneous nerve and the lateral root of the median nerve (from the lateral cord), the ulnar nerve and the medial root of the median nerve (from the medial cord), and the axillary and radial nerves (from the posterior cord).
B
• Injury to the upper trunk (C5, C6), at "Erb's point," produces Erb's paralysis, from causes such as birth injury, a fall on the shoulder, or during anaesthesia, affecting the axillary, musculocutaneous and suprascapular nerves.
• Injury to the lower trunk (C8, T1), from causes such as undue abduction of the arm, produces Klumpke's paralysis, with paralysis of the intrinsic hand muscles and ulnar wrist/finger flexors, and possible Horner's syndrome from associated sympathetic fibre injury.
C
• Erb's paralysis paralyses biceps, deltoid, brachialis, brachioradialis, supraspinatus, infraspinatus and supinator, producing the "Policeman's/Porter's tip hand": the arm hangs adducted and medially rotated, the forearm extended and pronated, with loss of abduction/lateral rotation of the shoulder and flexion/supination of the forearm.
• Klumpke's paralysis produces a claw hand from unopposed long flexors/extensors, plus cutaneous anaesthesia along the ulnar border of the limb.
• Injury to the lateral cord (e.g. from dislocation of the humerus) involves the musculocutaneous nerve and the lateral root of the median nerve, paralysing biceps, coracobrachialis and the median-supplied forearm muscles, producing a midprone forearm with loss of elbow and wrist flexion and sensory loss on the radial side of the forearm.
• Injury to the medial cord (e.g. from subcoracoid dislocation of the humerus) involves the ulnar nerve and the medial root of the median nerve, producing claw hand with sensory loss on the ulnar side of the forearm and hand.
• Injury to the posterior cord involves the upper and lower subscapular nerves, the thoracodorsal nerve, the axillary nerve, and the radial nerve (the largest and most frequently injured branch of the plexus).
• This weakens elbow, wrist and metacarpophalangeal joint extension via the radial nerve, and shoulder abduction via the axillary nerve.
• In this way, a single lesion at the level of a trunk or cord of the brachial plexus spreads its effect along the several peripheral nerves derived from it, each producing its own characteristic and distant functional deficit in the arm, forearm or hand.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the deep cervical fascia under the following headings: composition, and the named fibrous sheets into which it is condensed.
A(ii) Describe the attachments of the pretracheal fascia and the prevertebral fascia.
B. Explain the clinical basis for why infection can spread within specific fascial planes/spaces of the neck.
C. Distinguish between the pretracheal fascia and the prevertebral fascia in terms of what each surrounds/encloses.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The deep cervical fascia consists of areolar tissue that supports the muscles, vessels and viscera of the neck; it is condensed to form well-defined fibrous sheets, labelled as: (1) the investing layer (superficial), (2) the pretracheal fascia, (3) the prevertebral fascia, (4) the carotid sheath, and (5) the axillary fascia. More generally, deep fascia is the membranous investment of structures deep to the superficial fascia, containing cells (fibroblasts), fibres (collagen, elastic) and matrix; being subjected to tensile strains, the collagen forms parallel fibre bundles, with the cells flattened. Deep fascia is best marked in the limbs and neck, where it is wrapped around the muscles, veins and nerves like a bandage, the fibres being mainly circularly arranged; around the thorax and abdomen, which require to expand and contract, there is merely a film of areolar tissue but no true deep fascia.
A(ii)
The pretracheal fascia is found only in the anterior region; superiorly it is attached to the thyroid and cricoid cartilage, and inferiorly it extends into the thorax to blend with the fibrous pericardium; laterally it blends with the carotid sheath and with the investing layer of the deep cervical fascia beneath sternocleidomastoid. The prevertebral fascia is attached superiorly to the base of the skull, and inferiorly enters the thorax and blends with the anterior longitudinal ligament of the vertebral column; it covers the prevertebral muscles (longus capitis and longus cervicis), passes round the neck, attaches to the ligamentum nuchae, and in the posterior triangle forms the fascial floor, covering the muscles scalenus anterior, scalenus medius, scalenus posterior, levator scapulae and splenius capitis.
B
Penetration of the fascia during instrumentation of the pretracheal fascia can lead to collection of infectious substances (pus) in the retropharyngeal space (the space between the pharynx and the prevertebral fascia); whiplash injury of the neck can cause quadriplegia, stabbing injury of the neck can cause vascular/nervous injury, and a tumour blocking the airway may necessitate insertion of a tracheostomy tube. The deep cervical fascia will necessarily be pierced during tracheostomy.
C
The pretracheal fascia surrounds the thyroid gland completely, forming a sheath for it, binds the thyroid gland to the larynx, encloses the parathyroid gland, invests the infrahyoid muscles, and encloses the visceral components of the neck (larynx and trachea, pharynx and oesophagus, and the thyroid and parathyroid glands). The prevertebral fascia, in contrast, surrounds the vertebral column and its associated muscles, extending from the base of the skull to approximately the T3 vertebra, and extends laterally as the axillary sheaths.

A(i)
The anterior branch of the abdominal aorta supplying the midgut; it arises immediately below the celiac artery, anterior to the lower part of vertebra LI.
A(ii)
• It is crossed anteriorly by the splenic vein and the neck of the pancreas; posterior to it are the left renal vein, the uncinate process of the pancreas and the inferior part of the duodenum.
