• The middle colic artery arises as it emerges from beneath the pancreas.
A(iii)
• First branch: inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery, dividing into anterior and posterior branches that anastomose with the superior pancreaticoduodenal arteries.
• Left side: numerous jejunal and ileal arteries passing between the two layers of the mesentery to form arcades, whose number increases distally.
• Vasa recta: long, close together and narrow windows in the jejunum; short, far apart and low broad windows in the ileum.
• Right side: middle colic (transverse mesocolon; anastomoses with left colic), right colic (inconsistent, retroperitoneal) and ileocolic arteries.
• The ileocolic divides into superior and inferior branches; the inferior gives colic, cecal, appendicular (in the mesoappendix free margin) and ileal branches.
A(iv)
• Midgut: duodenum below the major papilla, jejunum, ileum, cecum, appendix, ascending colon and right two-thirds of the transverse colon.
• The midgut ends at the junction of the proximal two-thirds and distal one-third of the transverse colon.

A(i)
Skeletal muscle: contains bundles of very long, multinucleated cells with cross-striations; contraction is quick, forceful, and usually under voluntary control. Connective tissue: endomysium surrounds individual muscle fibers (nerve fibers and capillaries form a rich network in the endomysium); perimysium surrounds fascicles; epimysium (deep fascia) surrounds the whole muscle belly and connects to tendons. Distinguishing feature: cross-striations; multinucleated; sarcomeres extending from Z disc to Z disc (~2.5 µm long in resting muscle). The A bands are anisotropic (dark); I bands are isotropic (light); each I band is bisected by the Z disc. Smooth muscle: consists of collections of fusiform cells that lack striations and have slow, involuntary contractions; elongated and spindle-shaped; single nucleus at the widest point; contain actin and myosin filaments but lack sarcomeres. Prominent locations: wall of GI tract, walls of arteries and veins, around glands. Distinguishing feature: no striations; slow, sustained contractions; non-voluntary. Cardiac muscle: cross-striations; composed of elongated, often branched cells; bound by intercalated discs unique to cardiac muscle; contraction is involuntary, vigorous, and rhythmic. Central nuclei; high cytoplasm-to-nucleus ratio. Distinguishing feature: intercalated discs; branching cells; involuntary continuous rhythmic contraction.
A(ii)
Skeletal muscle fibers show cross-striations of alternating light and dark bands. The sarcomere extends from Z disc to Z disc. During contraction, shortening of myofibrils (shortening of sarcomeres) is transmitted through the connective tissue (endomysium, perimysium, epimysium) and via tendons to bone, producing bodily movements.
B(i)
Cardiac muscle cells contain numerous mitochondria; a large proportion of cell volume is occupied by mitochondria. Fatty acids, transported by lipoproteins, are stored as triglycerides in numerous lipid droplets in cardiac muscle cells — this supports the extremely rich capillary network and strong continuous activity. Cardiac muscle has limited regenerative capacity; spaces left after infarction are filled by connective tissue forming dense irregular scar tissue, because cardiac muscle cells do not go through mitosis.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the origin, course, and distribution of the three types of muscle tissue under the following headings: structural features at the light microscope level, connective tissue organization (endomysium, perimysium, epimysium), and characteristic distinguishing feature of each type.
A(ii) State the safe structural basis of how skeletal muscle contraction is transmitted to produce movement.
B(i) Explain the anatomical and histological basis of why cardiac muscle does not fatigue and cannot be replaced after infarction.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
The knee joint is primarily a hinge type of synovial joint. It is the largest and very complex joint in the body. Articulations: femur with tibia (tibiofemoral joint) and femur with patella (patellofemoral joint). Articular bones: (1) Femur — enlarged medial and lateral femoral condyles. (2) Tibia — enlarged medial and lateral tibial condyles (tibial plateaus), which are the receptacles for the femoral condyles; tibia bears most of the weight. (3) Patella — a true sesamoid bone embedded in the quadriceps and patellar tendon; serves as a pulley improving the angle of pull. Fibula is not part of the knee joint and does not articulate with the femur or patella; it only serves as attachment for knee joint structures.
A(ii)
Extracapsular ligaments (5): (1) Patellar ligament — distal part of quadriceps tendon; strong, thick fibrous band passing from apex of patella to tibial tuberosity. (2) Fibular (lateral) collateral ligament — strong, rounded, cordlike; extends from lateral epicondyle of femur to head of fibula; tendon of popliteus passes deep to it, separating it from the lateral meniscus. (3) Tibial (medial) collateral ligament — strong flat band from medial epicondyle of femur to medial condyle and superior part of tibia; firmly attached to medial meniscus; weaker and more often damaged than the fibular collateral ligament. (4) Oblique popliteal ligament — expansion of tendon of semimembranosus; strengthens fibrous capsule posteriorly. (5) Arcuate popliteal ligament — arises from posterior aspect of fibular head; passes superomedially over tendon of popliteus; strengthens fibrous capsule posteriorly. Intra-articular ligaments (3): (1) ACL — from anterior intercondylar area of tibia to lateral condyle of femur; weaker; slack when flexed, taut when extended; prevents posterior displacement of femur on tibia and hyperextension. (2) PCL — from posterior intercondylar area of tibia to medial condyle of femur; stronger; taut during flexion; prevents anterior displacement of femur on tibia; main stabilizing factor in weight-bearing flexed knee. (3) Menisci — crescentic plates of fibrocartilage that deepen the surface and act as shock absorbers.
B(i)
Flexion — hamstrings. Extension — quadriceps. Medial rotation — popliteus, semitendinosus, semimembranosus. Lateral rotation — biceps femoris. Locking: when fully extended with foot on ground, the knee locks because of medial rotation of femur on tibia. Unlocking: popliteus contracts rotating femur laterally so flexion can occur.
B(ii)
Blood supply: genicular branches of femoral artery, popliteal artery, anterior and posterior recurrent branches of anterior tibial recurrent artery, and anterior and posterior branches of circumflex fibular arteries. The middle genicular branches of the popliteal artery penetrate the fibrous capsule and supply the cruciate ligaments, synovial membrane, and peripheral margins of the menisci. Nerve supply: branches of obturator nerve, femoral nerve, tibial nerve, and common fibular nerve.
C(i)
Medial meniscus: C-shaped, broader posteriorly; anterior end attaches to anterior intercondylar area of tibia anterior to ACL; posterior end to posterior intercondylar area anterior to PCL; firmly adheres to tibial collateral ligament. Lateral meniscus: almost circular, smaller and more freely movable; tendon of popliteus separates it from fibular collateral ligament; attached posteriorly via the posterior meniscofemoral ligament to PCL and medial femoral condyle. The medial meniscus is more frequently injured because its firm attachment to the tibial collateral ligament makes it immobile and liable to being trapped and torn when the ligament is stressed; the lateral meniscus is protected by its free mobility.
questions.question:
Describe the knee joint under the following headings and explain its clinical importance.
A(i) Type, articular surfaces, and articular bones
A(ii) Ligaments — classify as extracapsular or intra-articular; describe each fully
B(i) Movements and muscles responsible
B(ii) Blood supply and nerve supply of the knee joint
C(i) Distinguish the medial from the lateral meniscus, and explain the anatomical basis of why the medial meniscus is more frequently injured

Describe the carpal tunnel:
A(i) Bony wall (carpal arch/sulcus)
A(ii) Fibrous wall (flexor retinaculum)
A(iii) Contents
B. Explain the clinical basis for the median nerve being the structure most adversely affected in carpal tunnel syndrome.
C. Distinguish between the tendons of flexor digitorum profundus and flexor digitorum superficialis as they lie within the tunnel.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The bony wall is the carpal sulcus, formed by the concavity on the anterior aspect of the carpal bones, forming the base and sides of the tunnel; it is bounded laterally by the scaphoid and trapezium tubercles and medially by the hook of the hamate and the pisiform.
A(ii)
The fibrous wall is the flexor retinaculum, a thick connective tissue band that stretches over the carpal sulcus, converting it into the carpal tunnel by bridging the space between the medial and lateral parts of the arch, spanning from the hook of hamate and pisiform medially to the scaphoid and trapezium laterally.
A(iii)
Contents: four tendons of flexor digitorum profundus (the deepest structures), four tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis lying anterior to those of profundus (all eight enclosed in a common synovial sheath), the tendon of flexor pollicis longus occupying the lateral angle of the compartment with its own synovial sheath, and the median nerve, which lies anterior to the tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis, deep to the flexor retinaculum.
B
• Carpal tunnel syndrome may occur following inflammatory reactions (synovitis) in the synovial sheath of the tendons traversing the tunnel.
• Excess fluid, such as follows inflammation of the synovial sheaths, compresses the structures within the confined tunnel.
• The median nerve is the structure most adversely affected, since it lies anterior to the crowded flexor tendons, immediately deep to the unyielding flexor retinaculum, leaving it particularly exposed to any rise in pressure within the tunnel.
• Compression of the median nerve produces sensory disturbance (hypoesthesia or anaesthesia) in the skin of the lateral three and a half fingers on their palmar aspect.
• Weakness or paralysis of the thenar muscles also occurs, because the recurrent branch of the median nerve that supplies these muscles arises in the hand and is also compressed.
C
• Within the tunnel, the tendons of flexor digitorum profundus are the deepest structures.
• The tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis lie anterior to (more superficial than) those of profundus.
• Both sets of four tendons are enclosed together in a single common synovial sheath, whereas the tendon of flexor pollicis longus lies separately at the lateral angle of the compartment, enclosed in its own distinct synovial sheath.
• This layered arrangement of tendons deep to the median nerve means the nerve is the most superficial of the tunnel's principal contents, most exposed to the flexor retinaculum's unyielding roof.

questions.question:
Describe the quadriceps femoris muscle fully under the following headings, explain why its paralysis causes the most profound disability of any single muscle in the lower limb, and distinguish it from the hamstrings.
A(i) General features: number of components, collective description, and composite tendon
A(ii) Origin, insertion, innervation, and action of each component
B(i) Why paralysis of the quadriceps femoris produces more functional disability than paralysis of the hamstrings
B(ii) The femoral nerve — its role in supplying the quadriceps and why knee extension is the most critical movement lost
C(i) Distinguish the quadriceps femoris from the hamstrings with respect to origin, action, and nerve supply; state the numerical strength ratio
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Quadriceps femoris forms the main bulk of the anterior thigh muscles; it collectively constitutes the largest and one of the most powerful muscles of the body. It covers almost all the anterior aspect and sides of the femur. It is the great extensor of the leg. It consists of 4 muscles: rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, vastus medialis, and vastus intermedius. The tendons of the four parts unite in the distal portion of the thigh to form a single, strong, broad tendon — the quadriceps tendon; this continues as the patellar ligament (in which the patella is embedded) and is attached to the tibial tuberosity.
A(ii)
Rectus femoris — origin: anterior inferior iliac spine and ilium superior to acetabulum; insertion: via common quadriceps tendon and patellar ligament to tibial tuberosity; innervation: femoral nerve (L2, L3, L4); action: extends leg at knee joint, steadies hip joint, and helps iliopsoas flex thigh. It is the only part of the quadriceps that crosses the hip joint, named because it runs straight down the thigh. Vastus lateralis — origin: greater trochanter and lateral lip of linea aspera of femur; same insertion and innervation; action: extends leg at knee joint; it is the largest component. Vastus medialis — origin: intertrochanteric line and medial lip of linea aspera of femur; same insertion and innervation; action: extends leg at knee joint; inferior fibres are particularly important in stabilising the knee joint. Vastus intermedius — origin: anterior and lateral surfaces of shaft of femur; same insertion and innervation; action: extends leg at knee joint; lies deep to rectus femoris between the vastus medialis and lateralis.
B(i)
The quadriceps is the primary extensor of the knee — the most important movement for standing, walking, climbing stairs, and rising from a chair. Stability of the knee joint depends on the strength and action of surrounding muscles and tendons; the quadriceps femoris is most important in stabilising the knee joint. Paralysis means the patient cannot extend the knee or control descent on stairs, rendering them unable to walk safely without a brace.
B(ii)
All four components of the quadriceps are innervated by the femoral nerve (L2, L3, L4). The femoral nerve also supplies the hip joint via intermediate and cutaneous branches and the skin of the front and medial side of the thigh (Hilton's law). Loss of knee extension eliminates the ability to straighten or stabilise the knee against gravity — the most critical functional deficit for bipedal locomotion.
C(i)
Quadriceps femoris: origin from femur and ilium; action — extends the knee (and rectus femoris also flexes the hip); nerve supply — femoral nerve (L2, L3, L4). Hamstrings (semitendinosus, semimembranosus, biceps femoris): origin from ischial tuberosity (long head of biceps femoris and both semi-muscles) and linea aspera (short head of biceps femoris); action — extend the thigh, flex the leg, and rotate it (semitendinosus and semimembranosus medially, biceps femoris laterally); nerve supply — tibial division of sciatic nerve for semitendinosus, semimembranosus, and long head of biceps femoris; common fibular division of sciatic nerve for short head of biceps femoris. The quadriceps is 3 times stronger than its antagonist muscle group (the hamstrings).

A(i)
A thin serous membrane lining the walls of the abdominal and pelvic cavities and covering the organs within; two layers: parietal and visceral.
A(ii)
• The cavity is the potential space between the layers, contains no organs and a thin layer of fluid, and is a closed sac in males; it is divided into greater and lesser sacs that communicate through the epiploic foramen.
• The fluid lubricates the surfaces so viscera move without friction, contains leukocytes and antibodies, and is absorbed by lymphatics on the inferior surface of the diaphragm.
A(iii)
• Provides a slippery surface for movement of viscera; phagocytic cells protect viscera; can store large amounts of fat.
• Mesothelial cells transform into fibroblasts, promoting healing; the mesothelium acts as a semi-permeable membrane.
A(iv)
Intraperitoneal organs are completely surrounded (stomach, spleen, small intestine); retroperitoneal organs are covered partially on their anterior surfaces only (kidney, ureter).
B(i)
• In the female the cavity communicates with the exterior through the uterine tubes, uterus and vagina, a potential pathway of infection.
• Because the mesothelium is semi-permeable, urea can be removed from blood by circulating fluids through the cavity: peritoneal dialysis.
C(i)
• Parietal: lines the inner surface of abdominal and pelvic walls and lower surface of diaphragm; loosely attached by extraperitoneal connective tissue; pain sensitive; nerve supply same as the overlying body wall.
• Visceral: lines the outer surface of viscera; cannot be stripped; nerve supply is that of the underlying viscera (sympathetic), with receptors sensitive to overdistension, traction on mesenteries, spasm and ischaemia.
• Blood supply: parietal from lumbar vessels, inferior and superior epigastric, musculophrenic and deep circumflex arteries; visceral from the arteries supplying the appropriate viscera.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the gross anatomy of cartilage under the following headings: definition, histogenesis (development from mesenchyme), growth mechanisms, and nutrient supply.
A(ii) Relate the three types of cartilage to their specific locations and collagen types, explaining why each is suited to its location.
B(i) Explain why articular cartilage degenerates with age and state the role of exercise in cartilage health.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Definition: Cartilage is a connective tissue in which the cells are relatively sparse and embedded in a large amount of firm characteristic matrix. It is a specialized form of connective tissue in which the firm consistency of the extracellular matrix allows the tissue to bear mechanical stresses without permanent distortion. Histogenesis: Cartilage is derived from the mesenchyme. The first modification observed is the rounding up of mesenchymal cells, which retract their extensions, multiply rapidly, and form mesenchymal condensations of chondroblasts (cells with ribosome-rich basophilic cytoplasm). Synthesis and deposition of matrix then begin to separate chondroblasts from one another. Differentiation takes place from center outward: central cells have characteristics of chondrocytes, peripheral cells are typical chondroblasts. The superficial mesenchyme develops into the perichondrium. Growth mechanisms: interstitial growth (from mitotic division of preexisting chondrocytes, expanding from within) and appositional growth (from differentiation of perichondrial cells, expanding from the outside). Nutrient supply: Cartilage is avascular; nourished by diffusion of nutrients from capillaries in adjacent connective tissue (perichondrium) or by synovial fluid. It has no lymphatic vessels or nerves. Chondrocytes exhibit low metabolic activity.
A(ii)
Hyaline cartilage: most common form; collagen type II is the principal collagen; found in nose, trachea, bronchi, rib-sternal joints, and synovial joints; resilient and shock absorbing. Elastic cartilage: contains abundant elastic fibers in addition to collagen type II; found in auricle of ear, external auditory canals, eustachian tubes, epiglottis, and cuneiform cartilage in larynx; elastic fibers allow flexibility. Fibrocartilage: rich in collagen type I (acidophilic matrix); found in intervertebral disks, attachments of certain ligaments to cartilaginous surfaces, and symphysis pubis; dense collagen provides strength for high-load sites.
B(i)
Articular cartilage is devoid of perichondrium and is sustained by diffusion of oxygen and nutrients from synovial fluid; this limited supply combined with low metabolic activity of chondrocytes means repair is slow. Hyaline cartilage is more susceptible to degenerative aging processes; calcification of the matrix, preceded by an increase in size and volume of chondrocytes followed by their death, leads to osteoarthritis. Role of exercise: participation in sports involving torsional loading, fast acceleration/deceleration, repetitive high impact increases risk of osteoarthritis. However, some levels of loading and exercise are beneficial: exercise enhances production of matrix molecules, which can have a positive effect on joint health. Exercise has both beneficial and detrimental effects on cartilage.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the five functions of the epithelial lining of the digestive tract.
A(ii) Describe the submucosal (Meissner) plexus and the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus together as the local enteric nervous system: name the layers of the GIT wall each is found in, state the ganglia they are composed of, what the number of ganglia depends on, and what system they function independently of.
B(i) Describe the muscularis mucosae: its composition, its location, and the two functions attributed to it.
B(ii) Explain the immunological backup to the thin epithelial barrier of the GIT, and identify what the digestive tract normally contains that makes this backup essential.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Five functions of the epithelial lining:
• Provide a selectively permeable barrier between the contents of the tract and the tissues of the body.
• Facilitate the transport and digestion of food.
• Promote the absorption of the products of digestion.
• Produce hormones that affect the activity of the digestive system.
• Produce mucus for lubrication and protection.
A(ii)
Local enteric nervous system:
• The submucosal (Meissner) plexus is located in the submucosa; the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus is located in the connective tissue between the circular and longitudinal muscle sublayers of the muscularis.
• Together they constitute the local enteric nervous system of the digestive tract.
• This system functions independently of the CNS.
• Both plexuses are composed mainly of nerve cell aggregates forming small parasympathetic ganglia.
• The number of ganglia along the digestive tract is variable — numerous in the regions of greatest motility.
B(i)
Muscularis mucosae:
• Composition: thin layer of smooth muscle.
• Location: usually separates the mucosa from the submucosa.
• Functions: (1) allows local movements of the mucosa independent of other movements of the digestive tract, helping to increase contact of the lining with food; (2) its contractions contribute to mixing and propelling food (the plexuses coordinate the contractions of the muscularis to mix and propel food).
B(ii)
Immunological backup:
• The mucosa-associated immune defense system (MALT) provides an essential backup to the thin physical barrier of the epithelial lining.
• The lamina propria (just below the epithelium) is a zone rich in macrophages and lymphocytes, some of which actively produce IgA antibodies.
• The digestive tract normally contains thousands of microbial species, including both useful gut inhabitants and potential pathogens ingested with food and drink, making this immune backup essential.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the nasal septum and the cartilages of the external nose under the following headings: the quadrangular cartilage, the upper lateral cartilages, and the lower lateral (alar) cartilages.
A(ii) Describe the blood supply to the nasal septum.
B. Explain the clinical basis for why the anteroinferior third of the nasal septum is the commonest site of nosebleeds (epistaxis).
C. Distinguish between the upper lateral cartilages and the lower lateral (alar) cartilages of the nose.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The quadrangular cartilaginous septum extends from the nasal bones in the midline above to the bony septum in the midline posteriorly, then down along the bony floor. Its upper half is flanked by two triangular-to-trapezoidal cartilages, the upper lateral cartilages, which are fused to the dorsal septum in the midline and attached to the bony margin of the pyriform aperture laterally by loose ligaments; the inferior ends of the upper lateral cartilages are free. Beneath the upper lateral cartilages lie the lower lateral cartilages; the paired lower lateral cartilages swing out from medial attachments to the caudal septum in the midline (the medial crura), through an intermediate crus area, finally flaring out superolaterally as the lateral crura; these cartilages are frequently mobile, in contradistinction to the upper lateral cartilages. The internal area or angle formed by the septum and upper lateral cartilage constitutes the internal valve.
A(ii)
The nasal septum is supplied from the sphenopalatine artery (posterior septal branch) and the anterior and posterior ethmoid arteries, with contribution of the superior labial artery (anteriorly) and the greater palatine artery (posteriorly).
B
The Kiesselbach plexus, or Little's area, represents a region in the anteroinferior third of the nasal septum where all 3 of the chief blood supplies to the internal nose converge, which is the clinical basis for this being a common site of nosebleeds; venous blood leaving the region drains into the facial, ophthalmic and sphenopalatine veins, and these veins are significant for their direct communication with the cavernous sinus and for their lack of valves, features that potentiate the intracranial spread of infection.
C
The upper lateral cartilages are fused to the dorsal septum in the midline and attached to the bony margin of the pyriform aperture laterally by loose ligaments, with their inferior ends free; they are relatively fixed. The lower lateral (alar) cartilages, by contrast, swing out from medial attachments to the caudal septum (the medial crura) to flare out superolaterally as the lateral crura, and are frequently mobile, unlike the upper lateral cartilages.

A(i)
• Formed by the ventral rami of L1, L2, L3 and the upper part of L4; the lower part of L4 joins L5 to form the lumbosacral trunk.
• The rami emerge from the intervertebral foramina, enter psoas, give branches to psoas and quadratus lumborum, then form the plexus within the substance of psoas major.
A(ii)
• Iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal: L1; genitofemoral: L1, L2; lateral femoral cutaneous: L2, L3 (posterior division).
• Femoral: L2, L3, L4 (posterior division); obturator: L2, L3, L4 (anterior division); sometimes an accessory obturator L3, L4.
A(iii)
• From the lateral border of psoas major: iliohypogastric, ilioinguinal, lateral femoral cutaneous, femoral.
• Through psoas anteriorly: genitofemoral; from the medial border: obturator.
A(iv)
• It innervates part of the lower abdominal wall but chiefly supplies skin and muscle 'borrowed from the trunk by the lower limb'.
• The genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve supplies the cremasteric muscle; the ilioinguinal nerve runs in the inguinal canal.
B(i)
The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve normally passes deep to the lateral end of the inguinal ligament; sometimes it passes through the substance of the ligament.
C(i)
• Entrapment causes pain along its distribution (meralgia paresthetica).
• Psoas major is supplied by ventral rami L1 to L4, psoas minor by L1, quadratus lumborum by upper lumbar and subcostal nerves, iliacus by the femoral nerve.

A(i)
Protective coverings: the nervous system contains very little collagen or fibrous tissue; it is relatively soft and easily damaged by injuries affecting the cranium or vertebral bones. It is covered by three connective tissue layers — the meninges: dura mater (thickest and toughest layer, contains sinuses to collect venous blood), arachnoid membrane (middle web-like covering; cerebrospinal fluid flows in the web-like spaces), and pia mater (thin delicate layer that follows the contour of the brain and spinal cord). Gray matter and white matter: myelinated fibers make up the white matter in the CNS; cell bodies and unmyelinated fibers make the gray matter. Glial cells in CNS: Oligodendrocytes — produce myelin in CNS. Microglia — part of the MPS (CNS macrophages). Astrocytes and other glial cells — support, nourish, and protect neurons; they are far more numerous than neurons; unlike neurons, they are capable of mitosis.
A(ii)
Dura mater — thickest and toughest layer; contains sinuses to collect venous blood. Arachnoid membrane — middle web-like covering; cerebrospinal fluid flows in the web-like (subarachnoid) spaces. Pia mater — thin delicate layer that follows the contour of brain and spinal cord. CSF flows within the subarachnoid spaces of the arachnoid.
B(i)
The optic nerve and retina arise in the embryo as an outgrowth of the diencephalon (forebrain); the optic nerve is therefore not a true peripheral nerve like the other cranial nerves. Its myelin is produced by oligodendrocytes (not by Schwann cells). Because the optic nerve is part of the CNS (produced by oligodendrocytes and without neurilemma), it is associated with multiple sclerosis — a demyelinating disease. Demyelination of the optic nerve disrupts the action potential transmission from the retinal ganglion cells, causing visual symptoms. The retinal ganglion cells communicate with the cerebrum through the optic nerve and extend into the brain.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the gross histology of the nervous tissue of the brain under the following headings: protective coverings (meninges), gray matter and white matter, types of glial cells in the CNS and their functions.
A(ii) Relate the three meningeal layers to their specific functions and state how cerebrospinal fluid flows.
B(i) Explain why a demyelinating disease of the optic nerve causes visual symptoms and state the histological basis of the link between the retina, optic nerve, and the CNS.

A(i) Describe the three named regions of the male urethra, giving the length and relations of each.
A(ii) Describe the two urethral sphincters — their type of muscle, location, and the mechanism by which each controls urinary continence.
B(i) Describe the female urethra, including its length, relations, and the location of its external orifice.
B(ii) State the layers visible in the structure of the urinary bladder wall.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Three regions of the male urethra:
• Prostatic urethra (2.5 cm): located within the prostate.
• Intermediate part of the urethra (membranous urethra) (2 cm): passes through the urogenital diaphragm from the prostate to the beginning of the penis.
• Spongy urethra (15 cm): passes through the penis and opens via the external urethral orifice.
• The male urethra carries both semen and urine.
A(ii)
Two sphincters:
• Internal urethral sphincter: involuntary (smooth muscle) at the bladder-urethra junction; contracts to open (its contraction, paradoxically, opens the sphincter as described — 'contracts to open').
• External urethral sphincter: voluntary (skeletal muscle) surrounding the urethra as it passes through the pelvic floor.
B(i)
Female urethra:
• Length: 3–4 cm.
• Relations: tightly bound to the anterior vaginal wall.
• External urethral orifice: anterior to the vaginal opening and posterior to the clitoris.
B(ii)
Layers of the urinary bladder wall:
• Peritoneum, rugae, detrusor (muscle), adventitia, ureteric orifices, trigone of bladder, bladder neck, internal urethral sphincter.

A(i)
Tibialis anterior: origin — lateral condyle and superior half of lateral surface of tibia and interosseous membrane; insertion — medial and inferior surfaces of medial cuneiform and base of 1st metatarsal; innervation — deep fibular nerve (L4, L5); action — dorsiflexes ankle and inverts foot. Extensor digitorum longus: origin — lateral condyle of tibia and superior 3/4 of medial surface of fibula and interosseous membrane; insertion — middle and distal phalanges of lateral 4 digits; innervation — deep fibular nerve (L4, L5); action — extends lateral 4 digits and dorsiflexes ankle. Extensor hallucis longus: origin — middle part of anterior surface of fibula and interosseous membrane; insertion — dorsal aspect of base of distal phalanx of great toe; innervation — deep fibular nerve (L4, L5); action — extends great toe and dorsiflexes ankle. Fibularis tertius: origin — inferior 3rd of anterior surface of fibula and interosseous membrane; insertion — dorsum of base of 5th metatarsal; innervation — deep fibular nerve (L4, L5); action — dorsiflexes ankle and aids in eversion of foot.
A(ii)
The dorsalis pedis artery begins as the anterior tibial artery enters the foot. It passes over the dorsal aspect of the tarsal bones, then moves inferiorly towards the sole of the foot. It then anastomoses with the lateral plantar artery to form the deep plantar arch. It supplies the tarsal bones and the dorsal aspect of the metatarsals; via the deep plantar arch, it also contributes to the supply of the toes. The dorsalis pedis pulse is found by palpating on the dorsum of the foot, just lateral to extensor hallucis longus tendon.
B(i)
The common fibular nerve is the lateral, smaller terminal branch of the sciatic nerve; it begins at the superior angle of the popliteal fossa, closely follows the medial border of biceps femoris, exits the fossa superficial to the lateral head of gastrocnemius, passes over the posterior aspect of the head of fibula, and winds around the neck of fibula where it divides into its terminal branches — the deep fibular nerve and superficial fibular nerve. The deep fibular nerve supplies all 4 muscles of the anterior compartment (tibialis anterior, extensor digitorum longus, extensor hallucis longus, fibularis tertius) and the foot.
B(ii)
At the neck of fibula the common fibular nerve is subcutaneous and directly palpable, making it vulnerable to direct trauma, compression, or traction. Injury here interrupts the deep fibular nerve before it reaches the anterior compartment. All 4 anterior compartment muscles (which perform dorsiflexion and toe extension) are paralysed. The result is foot drop: the foot hangs in plantarflexion and inversion (because the unopposed plantarflexors — gastrocnemius, soleus — and invertor — tibialis posterior — continue to act), and the patient develops a high-stepping gait to clear the dragging toe.
C(i)
Tibialis anterior: dorsiflexes the ankle AND inverts the foot; supplied by the deep fibular nerve (L4, L5). Fibularis tertius: dorsiflexes the ankle AND aids eversion of the foot; supplied by the deep fibular nerve (L4, L5). Both share the same nerve supply but perform opposite movements about the subtalar axis (inversion vs. eversion), reflecting their positions on opposite sides of the interosseous membrane.
questions.question:
Describe the anterior compartment muscles of the leg and the dorsum of the foot under the following headings, and explain why injury to the deep fibular nerve causes foot drop.
A(i) Name all 4 muscles of the anterior compartment; give origin, insertion, innervation, and action for each
A(ii) The dorsalis pedis artery — origin, course, and branches
B(i) The deep fibular nerve — its origin, course, and distribution in the anterior compartment and the foot
B(ii) Explain the anatomical basis of foot drop following injury to the deep fibular nerve at the fibular neck
C(i) Distinguish the actions of tibialis anterior and fibularis tertius; state which muscle inverts and which everts the foot, and name the nerve supplying each

Describe the gross anatomy of the clavicle:
A(i) Shape and articulations
A(ii) Surface features
A(iii) Functions
B. State how a particular part of the clavicle relates to a common fracture pattern.
C. Explain how injury at this region may involve a distant structure, causing a functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The clavicle forms the anterior portion of the shoulder girdle; it is curved like the italic letter "f" and lies nearly horizontally at the upper and anterior part of the thorax, immediately above the first rib. It articulates medially with the manubrium sterni and laterally with the acromion of the scapula.
A(ii)
The upper surface is flat, rough, and marked by impressions for the attachment of deltoid in front and trapezius behind; the bone has no medullary cavity.
A(iii)
Its functions are to transmit forces from the upper limb to the axial skeleton, to act as a strut holding the arm free from the trunk (supported principally by trapezius), and to provide attachment for muscles.
B
• The weakest point along the clavicle is the junction of the middle and outer thirds.
• Transmission of forces to the axial skeleton in falls on the shoulder or hand may exceed the strength of the bone at this site, and this indirect force commonly results in fracture there.
• Clavicle fracture is caused by landing on the hand from a fall with the arm rigidly outstretched, or by a direct blow.
C
• The clavicle has important deep relations that make it clinically significant beyond the bone itself.
• The third parts of the subclavian vessels and the trunks of the brachial plexus pass behind the medial third of the shaft of the clavicle, separated only by the thin subclavius muscle.
• At the sternal end, behind the sternoclavicular joints, lie the common carotid artery on the left and the bifurcation of the brachiocephalic artery on the right, with the internal jugular vein lying a little more laterally; these vessels are separated from the bone only by the strap muscles (sternohyoid and sternothyroid).
• Because these major vessels and the brachial plexus trunks lie in such close proximity to the clavicle, deep or displaced injury involving the bone can threaten them.
• Compromise of the subclavian vessels can produce vascular insufficiency of the upper limb, while injury to the brachial plexus trunks passing behind the medial clavicle can produce motor and sensory deficits in the limb.
• This illustrates how a skeletal injury at the clavicle can spread to affect distant neurovascular structures, producing a functional deficit beyond the fracture site itself.

A(i)
The glenohumeral (shoulder) joint is a multiaxial synovial joint of the ball-and-socket variety, formed by articulation between the head of the humerus and the glenoid cavity of the scapula; due to the very limited interface between humerus and scapula, it is the most mobile joint in the human body.
A(ii)
The joint capsule is a fibrous sheath enclosing the joint structures; it is thin and lax to allow a wide range of movement (particularly abduction), is strengthened by muscles and ligaments, but is weakest inferiorly, placing it at risk of dislocation in that direction. It is lined by synovial membrane and forms a tubular sheath around the tendon of the long head of biceps, and a number of bursae aid mobility.
A(iii)
• Factors contributing to mobility are the ball-and-socket joint type, the shallow glenoid cavity against the large humeral head (a 1:4 disproportion, likened to a golf ball and tee), and laxity of the joint capsule.
• Factors contributing to stability are the rotator cuff muscles, whose resting tone pulls the humeral head into the glenoid cavity, the glenoid labrum, which deepens the cavity and reduces dislocation risk, and the ligaments, which reinforce the capsule and form the coraco-acromial arch.
B
• The glenohumeral joint is the most commonly dislocated joint in the body, accounting for approximately 95% of all shoulder dislocations, and anterior dislocations are the most prevalent.
• An anterior dislocation is usually caused by excessive extension and lateral rotation of the humerus, which forces the humeral head anteriorly and inferiorly into the weakest (inferior) part of the joint capsule.
• Tearing of the joint capsule during dislocation is associated with an increased risk of future (recurrent) dislocations.
C
• The axillary nerve runs in close proximity to the shoulder joint and can be damaged during dislocation.
• Injury to the axillary nerve causes paralysis of the deltoid muscle, with loss of sensation over the "regimental badge" area of skin overlying the deltoid.
• A dislocation can also stretch the radial nerve, since it is tightly bound within the radial (spiral) groove of the humerus.
• These nerve injuries represent the spread of the joint pathology to distant neurological structures.
• The resulting functional deficits include loss of shoulder abduction and sensory loss from axillary nerve injury, reflecting how a purely mechanical joint injury can produce a distinct neurological deficit at a distance from the joint itself.
questions.question:
Describe the gross anatomy of the glenohumeral (shoulder) joint:
A(i) Articular surfaces and classification
A(ii) Capsule
A(iii) Factors contributing to its mobility and stability
B. State how a part of the joint capsule relates to the common direction of shoulder dislocation.
C. Explain how shoulder dislocation may spread to affect a distant structure (nerve), causing a functional deficit.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Conical, soft, spongy, elastic and pinkish in health (brown in the young, mottled black in adults and dark in city dwellers from deposited dust and carbon particles); right lung about 600 g, left about 550 g; the right is larger, heavier, shorter and wider. Each has an apex, a base, 3 surfaces (costal convex, mediastinal with the hilum, diaphragmatic concave), 3 borders (anterior, posterior, inferior) and a root; the posterior surface lies in the paravertebral gutter.
• Apex: rounded, extends into the root of the neck 2.5-4 cm above the sternal end of the 1st rib, covered by cervical pleura and suprapleural membrane. Base: broad, concave, rests on the diaphragm, which separates the right lung from the right lobe of the liver and the left lung from the left lobe of the liver, stomach and spleen. Anterior border: where costal and mediastinal surfaces meet, with the cardiac notch on the left; posterior border from C7 to T10; inferior border separates the base from the costal and mediastinal surfaces.
A(ii)
Right lung: 3 lobes (upper, middle, lower) by oblique and horizontal fissures; left lung: 2 lobes (upper and smaller lower) by the oblique fissure, with the lingula below the cardiac notch; visceral pleura extends into the fissures so the lobes move freely. Lower border (neutral position) crosses the 6th rib in the midclavicular line, the 8th rib in the midaxillary line and reaches the 10th rib posteriorly.
A(iii)
Hilum: wedge-shaped area on the mediastinal surface; root lies opposite T5-T7. Right root: in the groove of the arch of the azygos vein; eparterial and hyparterial bronchi, right pulmonary artery, 2 right pulmonary veins, hilar lymph nodes. Left root: in the concavity of the arch of the aorta; left main bronchus, left pulmonary artery, 2 left pulmonary veins, hilar lymph nodes. Both also contain bronchial vessels, nerves and lymphatics enclosed by pleura.
A(iv)
• Right lung, 10 segments: upper lobe apical, posterior, anterior; middle lobe lateral, medial; lower lobe superior (apical), medial basal, anterior basal, lateral basal, posterior basal. Left lung, 8 segments: upper lobe apicoposterior, anterior, superior lingula, inferior lingula; lower lobe superior (apical), medial basal, anterior basal, lateral basal, posterior basal.
• Each segment is pyramidal (apex to the hilum, base to the surface), separated from its neighbours by connective tissue septa, with the segmental bronchus, bronchial vessels and a pulmonary artery branch central; little arterial anastomosis between segments; intersegmental pulmonary vein tributaries guide separation; it has its own lymphatics and autonomic supply and is the smallest part that can be removed without affecting adjacent lung.
A(v)
• Arteries: 2 left bronchial arteries from the descending thoracic aorta and 1 right bronchial artery from the 3rd right posterior intercostal supply the bronchial tree down to the respiratory bronchioles; pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood to the alveoli and anastomose with the bronchial arteries at the precapillary level. Veins: 4 pulmonary veins to the left atrium; right bronchial vein to the azygos vein, left to the accessory hemiazygos vein.
• Lymph: superficial plexus (deep to the visceral pleura) and deep plexus (peribronchial) drain to pulmonary then bronchopulmonary (hilar) nodes, then superior and inferior tracheobronchial nodes, then the bronchomediastinal trunks to the junction of subclavian and internal jugular veins (right trunk may form the right lymphatic duct; left may end in the thoracic duct). Nerves: pulmonary plexuses; vagus is bronchoconstrictor, vasodilator and secretomotor, sympathetic has the opposite actions.
B(i)
• Connective tissue septa between segments are a natural barrier to the spread of infection, but carcinoma and tuberculosis break through; abscesses are commoner in the posterior segment of the upper lobe and the apical segment of the lower lobe because these are the most dependent segments in the supine position.
• Other pathologies: foreign particles enter the right main bronchus easily (wider, more vertical); pulmonary embolism (pulmonary artery obstructed by air, blood clot, fat, tumour cells or foreign particles); asthma (dyspnoea); fibrosis reduces compliance and emphysema reduces elasticity; lobectomy or pneumonectomy is used in lung cancer.
C(i)
• Costal pleura is supplied by intercostal nerves, so pleural or lung disease may cause referred pain along the thoracic wall and anterior abdominal wall; irritation over the central diaphragm refers pain to the shoulder through the phrenic nerve (C3-5).

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Definition: The cell cycle, or cell-division cycle, is the series of events that takes place in a cell leading to its division and duplication (replication). In cells with a nucleus (eukaryotes), the cell cycle can be divided into two brief periods: interphase (during which the cell grows, accumulates nutrients needed for mitosis and duplicates its DNA) and the mitosis (M) phase (during which the cell splits itself into two distinct cells, often called daughter cells). Phases: G1 (Gap 1) — cell grows; S phase (synthesis) — chromosomes are replicated; G2 (Gap 2) — cell grows more and prepares for mitosis; M phase (mitosis and cytokinesis) — cell division. Cells that have temporarily or reversibly stopped dividing are said to have entered the G0 phase (quiescence). Two key regulatory molecules: cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs), which determine a cell's progress through the cell cycle.
A(ii)
In non-disjunction, a chromosome may fail to separate during anaphase: one daughter cell will receive both sister chromosomes (leading to trisomy — three copies) and the other will receive none (leading to monosomy — one copy). These cells are considered aneuploid, a condition often associated with cancer. Other chromosomal abnormalities: deletion — an arm of the chromosome may be broken and the fragment lost. Translocation — the fragment incorrectly reattaches to another, non-homologous chromosome. Inversion — the fragment reattaches to the original chromosome in reverse orientation. The effect may range from no noticeable effect to cancer induction or organism death.
B(i)
Apoptosis (programmed cell death): biochemical events lead to characteristic cell changes including blebbing, loss of cell membrane asymmetry and attachment, cell shrinkage, nuclear fragmentation, chromatin condensation, and chromosomal DNA fragmentation. Apoptosis differs from necrosis in that the cellular debris does not damage the organism. Necrosis: a form of traumatic cell death that results from acute cellular injury; cellular debris can damage the organism. Clinical consequences: excessive apoptosis causes atrophy (e.g., ischemic damage); insufficient apoptosis results in uncontrolled cell proliferation such as cancer.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
The median nerve is formed by the union of a lateral root from the lateral cord (C5, C6, C7) and a medial root from the medial cord (C8, T1) of the brachial plexus.
A(ii)
In the cubital fossa the median nerve is the most medial of the major vertical contents, lying medial to the brachial artery and the tendon of biceps brachii; at the wrist it lies anterior to the tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis, deep to the flexor retinaculum, within the carpal tunnel.
A(iii)
It gives a palmar cutaneous branch that arises in the forearm, proximal to the flexor retinaculum, and a recurrent branch that arises in the hand to supply the thenar muscles.
A(iv)
It supplies flexor carpi radialis, palmaris longus, pronator teres, pronator quadratus and the digital flexors, producing thumb flexion and opposition, flexion of digits 2 and 3, wrist flexion and abduction, and forearm pronation; it also supplies sensation to the anterolateral surface of the hand.
C
• A low (wrist-level) median nerve injury produces an "ape-like hand."
• There is flattening of the thenar eminence because the recurrent branch supplying abductor pollicis brevis and flexor pollicis brevis, which arises in the hand, is affected.
• Opposition and abduction of the thumb become impossible, so the pincer-like action of the hand is lost, causing difficulty with fine manual tasks such as buttoning.
• Adductor pollicis, being supplied by the ulnar nerve, is unopposed, further contributing to the deformity.
• This contrasts with an elbow-level injury, where flexion of the index and middle fingers is lost (flexor digitorum superficialis and the lateral half of profundus are affected), the ring and little fingers weakly flex, and flexion of the distal phalanx of the thumb is lost, while the interosseous muscles are unaffected, being supplied by the ulnar nerve.
• The median nerve can be torn partially or fully, or compressed, at the elbow, from fracture, other trauma, or compression from fluid build-up following injury.
• The most common site of median nerve injury overall is at the wrist, within the carpal tunnel.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Definition and function: Connective tissue derives its name from its function in connecting or binding cells and tissues; it maintains the form of organs throughout the body. Unlike other tissue types (epithelium, muscle, nerve) which consist mainly of cells, the major constituent of connective tissue is the extracellular matrix. The extracellular matrix is composed of protein fibers (collagen, elastic, and reticular fibers), ground substance (a jelly-like, amorphous, anionic, hydrophilic complex of proteoglycans, glycosaminoglycans, and multiadhesive glycoproteins such as laminin and fibronectin), and tissue fluid. Classification: connective tissue is classified as connective tissue proper (loose: areolar, adipose, reticular; dense: regular, irregular, elastic) and specialized connective tissue (blood, cartilage, bone).
A(ii)
The amount of tissue fluid (interstitial fluid) is fairly constant and there is an equilibrium between water entering and leaving the intercellular substance. In pathological conditions (traumatic injury and inflammation), fluid may accumulate in the connective tissue, a condition known as edema.
B(i)
Loose connective tissue: irregularly arranged tissue with abundant ground substance, capable of withstanding stress from many directions; present in dermis, capsules of joints, and submucosa of the alimentary tract. Examples: areolar tissue, adipose tissue. Dense connective tissue: tissue in which fibers predominate; it is organized to withstand forces in specific directions. Dense regular: present in tendons and ligaments. Dense irregular: present in the dermis of skin and capsules of organs.

A(i)
The articular surfaces of the TMJ are the condyle of the mandible (inferior) and the articular tubercle/mandibular fossa of the temporal bone (squamous part). The articular capsule is loose and fibrous, attaching to the margins of the articular area on the temporal bone and around the neck of the mandible. The superior synovial membrane lines the fibrous capsule superior to the articular disc, and the inferior synovial membrane lines the capsule inferior to the disc; the joint is divided into two compartments (superior and inferior) by an articular disc of fibrocartilage.
A(ii)
The ligaments of the TMJ are divided into an intrinsic ligament and extrinsic ligaments. The intrinsic ligament, also known as the lateral ligament, is the thick part of the articular capsule, strengthens the TMJ laterally, and prevents posterior dislocation of the TMJ. The extrinsic ligaments are the sphenomandibular ligament, which runs from the spine of the sphenoid to the lingula of the mandible and is the primary passive support of the mandible, and the stylomandibular ligament, a thickening of the fibrous capsule of the parotid gland, extending from the styloid process of the temporal bone to the angle of the mandible, which does not contribute significantly to the strength of the joint.
B
Dislocation of the TMJ is common in aged persons and females, due to wearing and resorption of the articular eminence and reducing muscle tone with advancing age.
C
The intrinsic (lateral) ligament is the thick part of the articular capsule, strengthens the joint laterally and prevents posterior dislocation. The sphenomandibular ligament, by contrast, runs from the spine of the sphenoid to the lingula of the mandible and is the primary passive support of the mandible, while the stylomandibular ligament is a thickening of the fibrous capsule of the parotid gland, running from the styloid process to the angle of the mandible, and does not contribute significantly to the strength of the joint.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Molecular composition: The cell membrane consists of amphipathic phospholipids arranged so that the hydrophobic tails face inward (away from water) and the more hydrophilic head regions associate with the cytosolic and extracellular environments, forming a spherical lipid bilayer. The phospholipid bilayer was proposed by Gorter and Grendel in 1925. It also includes integral membrane proteins and peripheral membrane proteins (almost half of the total mass of the membrane), a network of tiny microfilaments of the cytoskeleton, and the lipid molecule cholesterol, which stabilizes and makes the cell membrane more rigid. Functions: structural support; semi-permeable membrane (controls what molecules enter and leave the cell); establishes and maintains an electrochemical gradient; contains receptors that recognize and respond to molecular signals; supports cell adhesion and cell communication. Membrane transport mechanisms: passive (osmosis, diffusion, simple diffusion), facilitated transport, active transport (primary and secondary), and vesicular transport (endocytosis: pinocytosis and phagocytosis; exocytosis).
A(ii)
Several diseases have been implicated with defective membrane receptors. Pseudohypoparathyroidism is associated with defective parathyroid and growth hormone receptors. In these conditions, the glands produce the respective hormones, but the target cells do not respond because they lack normal receptors. Signal transduction can be hindered and cause diseases when mutations occur in the genes that encode and regulate receptor proteins.
B(i)
Integral membrane proteins: are directly incorporated within the lipid bilayer; most are transmembrane proteins passing through the entire membrane; inserted into the lipid bilayer. Functions: transport, signal transduction, structural support. Peripheral membrane proteins: exhibit a looser association with the membrane; bound to the membrane indirectly by protein-protein interactions; located on the cytosolic face. Plasma membrane contains proteins called integrins that are linked to cytoplasmic molecules; through these linkages there is a connection between the extracellular matrix and cytoplasm, mediating cell adhesion and cell communication.

Describe the popliteal fossa under the following headings and explain its clinical importance.
A(i) Boundaries
A(ii) Roof and floor

questions.answerText:
A(i)
The popliteal fossa is a diamond-shaped depression in the posterior aspect of the knee. Superolateral border: biceps femoris. Superomedial border: semimembranosus and semitendinosus. Inferolateral border: lateral head of gastrocnemius. Inferomedial border: medial head of gastrocnemius.
A(ii)
Roof (posteriorly): skin and fascia — the popliteal fascia is a strong sheet of deep fascia continuous superiorly with the fascia lata and inferiorly with the deep fascia of the leg. Floor (anteriorly): popliteal surface of femur, capsule of knee joint, oblique popliteal ligament, and popliteal fascia over popliteus.
B(i)
From superficial to deep: posterior cutaneous nerve of thigh; tibial nerve (most superficial of the neurovascular bundle); popliteal vein; popliteal artery (deepest structure in the fossa, running close to the articular capsule of the knee joint); popliteal lymph nodes and lymphatic vessels. The small saphenous vein and three cutaneous nerves (posterior cutaneous nerve of thigh, medial sural cutaneous nerve, lateral sural cutaneous nerve) lie in the superficial fascia.
B(ii)
The popliteal artery is the deepest structure and lies in close proximity to the tibial nerve. An aneurysm (dilation of the artery beyond 50% of its normal diameter) causes compression of the tibial nerve. The tibial nerve is particularly susceptible to this compression; the major features include weakened or absent plantarflexion, paraesthesia of the foot and posterolateral leg, and paralysis of flexor muscles in the leg and intrinsic muscles of the sole.
C(i)
The tibial nerve is the medial and larger branch of the sciatic nerve; it bisects the fossa passing from the superior to the inferior angle and gives muscular branches to soleus, gastrocnemius, plantaris, and popliteus, and the medial sural cutaneous nerve. The common fibular nerve is the lateral, smaller terminal branch; it begins at the superior angle, closely follows the medial border of biceps femoris, exits the fossa by passing superficial to the lateral head of gastrocnemius, then winds around the neck of fibula where it divides into terminal branches. Injury to the tibial nerve causes inability to plantarflex the ankle or flex the toes and loss of sensation on the sole of the foot.

questions.question:
Describe the radial nerve:
A(i) Origin and course in the arm
A(ii) Course/division in the cubital fossa and forearm
A(iii) Branches
A(iv) Distribution
C. Explain the anatomical basis of the deformity ("wrist drop") seen after radial nerve injury.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The radial nerve is a terminal branch of the posterior cord of the brachial plexus; it courses posteromedially with the axillary vessels and enters the posterior compartment of the arm under teres major, where it winds around the spiral (radial) groove of the humerus, accompanied by the profunda brachii artery.
A(ii)
• It pierces the lateral intermuscular septum to enter the anterior compartment of the arm, passes to the forearm at the level of the elbow joint, enters the cubital fossa, and there divides into a superficial and a deep branch.
• The superficial branch courses toward the wrist lateral to the radial artery and enters the hand, dividing into dorsal digital cutaneous branches; the deep branch gives off the posterior interosseous nerve, which passes between the heads of supinator to enter the posterior compartment of the forearm and terminates near the wrist joint.
A(iii)
Branches include muscular twigs in the arm to triceps brachii and anconeus, the posterior interosseous nerve to the forearm extensors, the superficial (cutaneous) branch, and articular twigs to the elbow and wrist joints.
A(iv)
The deep branch/posterior interosseous nerve supplies the extensor muscles in the forearm as well as brachioradialis; the superficial branch supplies cutaneous sensation to the dorsal aspect of the hand, the dorsal aspect of the first to third digits, and the dorsolateral aspect of the fourth finger.
C
• Injury to the radial nerve produces "wrist drop."
• Because the nerve's deep branch/posterior interosseous nerve supplies the extensor muscles of the forearm, injury interrupts the motor supply to the wrist and finger extensors.
• The nerve can be injured at any level — axilla, spiral groove, radial tunnel, posterior interosseous, or superficial radial.
• Injury may result from fracture of the body (shaft) of the humerus, where the nerve lies in close contact with the bone in the spiral groove.
• "Saturday Night Palsy" describes compression of the nerve in the axilla, such as from using improperly adjusted crutches, which similarly interrupts its motor function.
• With the extensors paralysed and unopposed flexor tone at the wrist, the hand falls into flexion at the wrist, producing the characteristic wrist drop.

A(i)
Fixed (resident) cells: Mesenchyme cells — embryonic source of all connective tissue cells; only found in embryos, but some mesenchyme-like cells persist in adult connective tissue. Fibroblasts — most common cell type in connective tissue; elongated, spindle-shaped cells with many cell processes; have oval, pale-staining, regular nuclei with prominent nucleoli; abundant rough endoplasmic reticulum and active Golgi bodies; synthesize collagen, reticular and elastic fibers, and amorphous extracellular substance. Fibrocytes — quiescent fibroblasts; smaller, darker nucleus; less rough ER. Chondroblasts/osteoblasts — synthesize cartilage and bone matrices. Adipocytes — energy storage, thermal insulation. Wandering (transient) cells: Macrophages — ingestion by phagocytosis; antigen presentation; secretion of enzymes and cytokines; long-lived (several months); originate from monocytes in bone marrow. Plasma cells — defense and immune function. Lymphocytes — immune function. Neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils — immune function. Mast cells — immune function. All connective tissue cells are derived from mesenchymal cells.
A(ii)
Mesenchyme-like cells (pericytes) persist in adult connective tissue, including that of tooth pulp and some adipose tissue. These mesenchyme-like cells retain their capacity to differentiate into other connective tissue cells in response to injury (e.g., pericytes — perivascular cells of blood capillaries). They are being investigated as possible sources of stem cells for therapeutic repair and organ regeneration. Some multipotent stem cells potentially useful in regenerative medicine after grafting to replace damaged tissue in certain patients.
B(i)
All connective tissue cells are derived from mesenchymal cells; mesenchyme cells are for the most part derived from the mesoderm. However, several of the connective tissues of the head region are derived from the neural crest cells (ectodermal origin). Endothelial cells lining blood vessels are derived from mesenchyme. The clinical implication is that connective tissue tumors or developmental disorders in the head may follow patterns distinct from those in the rest of the body due to this different embryological derivation.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
The most common sites of ulnar nerve entrapment around the elbow are: above the elbow, in the region of the intermuscular septum; the medial epicondylar region; the epicondylar (ulnar) groove; the region of the cubital tunnel; and the point where the nerve exits from flexor carpi ulnaris, where the usual cause of compression is the deep flexor-pronator aponeurosis.
A(ii)
Medially, in relation to the elbow joint, the ulnar nerve passes behind the medial epicondyle and crosses the medial collateral ligament of the joint.
B
• The medial epicondyle of the humerus bears a groove on its posterior aspect specifically for the ulnar nerve, and the medial epicondyle is the larger of the two epicondyles, extending more distally.
• This places the ulnar nerve in a relatively superficial, subcutaneous position as it passes behind the medial epicondyle and through the cubital tunnel region, making it vulnerable to direct trauma and to compression at each of the sites listed above.
• Ulnar nerve injuries are recognised as a distinct item of applied anatomy at the elbow, alongside subluxation/dislocation of the radial head, the carrying angle, olecranon bursitis, avulsion of the medial epicondyle, and dislocation with Volkmann's ischaemic contracture.
C
• The ulnar nerve's entrapment region at the elbow lies behind the medial epicondyle of the humerus, where it crosses the medial collateral ligament of the elbow joint, and where compression is often caused by the deep flexor-pronator aponeurosis as the nerve exits between the heads of flexor carpi ulnaris.
• The median nerve's tunnel at the wrist, the carpal tunnel, differs in that it has a defined bony floor — the carpal sulcus, bounded laterally by the scaphoid and trapezium and medially by the hook of hamate and pisiform — roofed by the fibrous flexor retinaculum.
• The carpal tunnel additionally transmits eight flexor tendons and the tendon of flexor pollicis longus alongside the median nerve, whereas other tendons sharing the ulnar nerve's entrapment site at the elbow are not described.
• Both regions, however, are sites where a single major nerve is placed in a confined space adjacent to bone, predisposing it to compression.
• At the elbow, injury or entrapment of the ulnar nerve is associated with claw hand and sensory/motor deficits in the ulnar nerve distribution of the hand and forearm.
• At the wrist, compression of the median nerve within the carpal tunnel produces carpal tunnel syndrome, with sensory disturbance in the lateral three and a half digits and weakness of the thenar muscles.
• The comparison illustrates a shared anatomical principle, nerve entrapment at a narrow passage, applied to two different nerves at two different levels of the upper limb.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Gross anatomy of the kidney:
• Renal cortex: granular-appearing superficial region.
• Renal medulla: composed of cone-shaped medullary (renal) pyramids; pyramids are separated by renal columns (inward extensions of cortical tissue).
• Structures in frontal section: renal hilum, renal cortex, renal medulla, major calyx, papilla of pyramid, renal pelvis, minor calyx, ureter, renal pyramid in renal medulla, renal column, fibrous capsule.
A(ii)
Seven functions of the kidney:
• Regulating total water volume and total solute concentration in water.
• Regulating ECF ion concentrations.
• Ensuring long-term acid-base balance.
• Removal of metabolic wastes, toxins, and drugs.
• Endocrine functions: renin (regulation of blood pressure) and erythropoietin (regulation of RBC production).
• Activation of vitamin D.
• Gluconeogenesis during prolonged fasting.
B(i)
Comparison of nephron types:
• Cortical nephrons: 85% of nephrons; short nephron loop; glomerulus further from the cortex-medulla junction; efferent arteriole supplies peritubular capillaries.
• Juxtamedullary nephrons: long nephron loops that deeply invade the medulla; glomerulus closer to the cortex-medulla junction; efferent arteriole supplies vasa recta; ascending limbs have thick and thin segments; important in production of concentrated urine.
B(ii)
Two collecting duct cell types:
• Principal cells: sparse, short microvilli; maintain water and Na+ balance.
• Intercalated cells (A and B types): cuboidal cells with abundant microvilli; both types help maintain acid-base balance of blood.
• Collecting ducts receive filtrate from many nephrons; run through medullary pyramids giving them a striped appearance; fuse together to deliver urine through papillae into minor calyces.
