A
The pterygopalatine fossa is an inverted pyramidal-shaped, fat-filled space located on the lateral side of the skull, between the infratemporal fossa and the nasopharynx; it is antero-posteriorly between the maxilla/palatine bone and the pterygoid process, and laterally between the infratemporal fossa and nasopharynx. Its boundaries are: anterior - posterior surface of maxilla below the floor of the orbit; posterior - lateral pterygoid plate and part of the medial plate; medial - perpendicular plate of the palatine bone; lateral - pterygomaxillary fissure; superior - undersurface of the greater wing of the sphenoid; inferior - absent (the posterior wall meets the anterior wall, and between them is the greater palatine canal). Its contents are the terminal (third/pterygoid) part of the maxillary artery and the initial parts of its branches, the maxillary vein, the maxillary nerve, and the pterygopalatine ganglion (a parasympathetic ganglion, one of four parasympathetic ganglia of the head and neck, the others being the submandibular, otic and ciliary ganglia).
B
The pterygopalatine fossa is described as a major neurovascular crossroad between the orbit, the nasal cavity, the nasopharynx, the oral cavity, the infratemporal fossa and the cranial fossa. Its communications are: laterally with the infratemporal fossa through the pterygomaxillary fissure; medially with the nasal cavity through the sphenopalatine foramen; anterosuperiorly with the orbit through the inferior orbital fissure; posterosuperiorly with the middle cranial fossa through the foramen rotundum and pterygoid canal; with the palate through the greater and lesser palatine canals and foramina; and with the pharynx through the pterygoid canal and palatovaginal canal - in general, vascular structures enter the fossa through its lateral wall, while nerve structures enter through its posterior wall.
C
Because the pterygopalatine fossa communicates directly with the orbit (via the inferior orbital fissure), the nasal cavity (via the sphenopalatine foramen), the middle cranial fossa (via the foramen rotundum and pterygoid canal), and the pharynx (via the pterygoid canal and palatovaginal canal), disease or infection arising in or near the fossa has multiple direct anatomical routes by which it can spread to these distant sites; clinical correlates noted for this region include hay fever affecting the ganglion here (the pterygopalatine ganglion is also known as the hay fever ganglion), and maxillary nerve block is performed in relation to this fossa.

A
The larynx is demarcated by the vestibular fold (containing fibrous tissue, forming the false vocal cord on each side) and the vocal fold (the true vocal cord, containing the vocal ligament) into 3 zones: the supraglottic compartment (vestibule), above the false cords; the glottic compartment, between the false and true cords; and the subglottic compartment, between the true cords and the first ring of the trachea. The space between the vocal cords is the rima glottidis.
B
The mucosa is firmly adherent to the vocal ligament without any intervening submucosa, which accounts for the pearly white, avascular appearance of the vocal cords as seen on laryngoscopy; regulation of vocal cord tension (and therefore pitch of the voice) is accomplished primarily by pivoting the thyroid cartilage forward or backward at the cricothyroid joint, via the cricothyroid muscle, which is the only laryngeal muscle that tightens the cords, is supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (not the recurrent laryngeal nerve), and is the only intrinsic laryngeal muscle situated on the outside of the larynx.
C
Sensory innervation is via the internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve above the cords and via the recurrent laryngeal nerve below the cords; motor supply to the muscles is from the nucleus ambiguus via the cranial accessory, with the cricothyroid supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve and all other laryngeal muscles (including the upper oesophagus and cricopharyngeus) supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve. Lymphatic drainage above the cords is to the upper deep cervical nodes and below the cords to the lower deep cervical nodes; a disease process at either level can therefore spread along its corresponding drainage route to functionally distant lymph node groups. Movements which close off the entrance to the larynx during swallowing involve the epiglottis being pulled down and the arytenoid cartilages being pulled forward toward the epiglottis; the larynx is also raised, along with the pharynx, by contraction of the longitudinal muscles of the pharynx, and the epiglottis acts partly as a passive barrier, so disordered laryngeal muscle action compromises this protective closure mechanism.
questions.question:
A. Describe the gross anatomy of the larynx under the following headings: the three zones/compartments and the folds that demarcate them.
B. State how the zones of the larynx and the vocal folds relate to laryngeal function and clinical assessment (e.g. on laryngoscopy).
C. Explain how disease/infection at a site distant from the larynx can spread to compromise laryngeal or lower respiratory function, and the functional deficit that results from disordered laryngeal muscle action.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
• The sacrum is formed by the union of 5 sacral vertebrae (fusion begins at 16 to 18 years, usually complete by 30); wedge-shaped; concave anterior surface with four transverse lines and four pairs of anterior sacral foramina.
• Dorsally a median sacral crest and posterior foramina; the sacral canal is continuous with the vertebral canal; an auricular surface forms the sacroiliac joint; structures emerge at the sacral hiatus.
A(ii)
• Each hip bone is three bones (ilium, pubis, ischium) separated by cartilage in the newborn and fused at puberty in the acetabulum; the ilium is the largest, with ala, body, crest, spines, greater sciatic notch, iliac fossa, auricular surface and arcuate line.
• Ischium: body, ramus, spine, lesser sciatic notch and tuberosity; pubis: superior and inferior rami, body, crest, tubercle, iliopectineal line; ischium and pubis surround the obturator foramen.
A(iii)
Two hip bones united at the pubic symphysis and with the sacrum at the sacroiliac joints; the girdle moves as a unit and supports and protects lower abdominal and pelvic organs; the pelvic brim divides true and false pelves.
B(i)
• The female pelvis serves for childbearing and easier delivery; it is bigger and wider, with a large oval brim and a wider outlet.
• The sacral promontory, the superior border of the anterior sacral surface, is an important obstetric landmark for pelvic measurements.
• The sacral index is about 105 in males and 115 in females, and the sacrovertebral angle is more prominent in females.
C(i)
• Male: smaller, narrower, heavier and thicker bone; deep false pelvis; pubic arch V-shaped and less than 90°; acetabulum larger, facing laterally; coccyx immovable; brim smaller and heart-shaped; outlet narrower.
• Male: narrower greater sciatic notch, round obturator foramen, longer narrower sacrum, more vertical ilium, ischial tuberosities longer, close together and laterally projecting.
• Female: shallow false pelvis; wider pubic arch greater than 90°; acetabulum smaller, facing anteriorly; coccyx movable; large oval brim; wider outlet.
• Female: wider greater sciatic notch, oval obturator foramen, less vertical ilium, ischial tuberosities shorter, farther apart and projecting medially.

A(i)
The cubital fossa is a triangular space, a shallow depression on the anterior surface of the elbow region, located anterior to the elbow joint, formed between two forearm muscles (brachioradialis and pronator teres).
A(ii)
Boundaries: base (superior) — an imaginary horizontal line connecting the medial and lateral epicondyles; medial (ulnar) wall — lateral border of pronator teres; lateral (radial) wall — medial border of brachioradialis; apex — directed inferiorly, where the medial and lateral boundaries meet; floor — brachialis and supinator; roof — continuity of brachial and antebrachial (deep) fascia, reinforced by the bicipital aponeurosis, superficial fascia and skin.
A(iii)
The major contents, from medial to lateral, are the median nerve, the brachial artery (which bifurcates near the apex into the radial and ulnar arteries), deep accompanying veins of the arteries, and the tendon of biceps brachii.
B
• The median cubital vein, cephalic vein and basilic vein are present in the area but are usually considered superficial to the cubital fossa and not part of its contents.
• During blood pressure measurement the stethoscope is placed over the brachial artery in the cubital fossa, and the fossa is also used to palpate the brachial pulse.
• The area just superficial to the cubital fossa is often used for venous access (phlebotomy), since it is superficial and accessible.
• The bicipital aponeurosis forms the roof of the fossa and was historically called the "grace of God" tendon because it protected the brachial artery and median nerve during blood-letting.
C
• The radial nerve is in the vicinity of the cubital fossa, located between brachialis and brachioradialis, but is often, though not always, considered part of the cubital fossa's contents.
• This differs from the median nerve and brachial artery, which are consistently listed as major contents of the fossa.
• The superficial veins similarly lie in the roof/superficial region and are related to, rather than contained within, the fossa proper.
• Venipuncture therefore uses the superficial veins overlying the fossa, while palpation of the brachial pulse and auscultation for blood pressure use the deeper true content, the brachial artery.
• This distinction between superficial and deep structures is the basis for choosing the correct site for a given clinical procedure at the elbow.
questions.question:
Describe the cubital fossa:
A(i) Location and shape
A(ii) Boundaries (base, medial wall, lateral wall, apex, floor, roof)
A(iii) Contents
B. Explain the clinical basis for distinguishing the true "contents" of the cubital fossa from structures that are merely superficial to it.
C. Distinguish the position of the radial nerve in relation to the cubital fossa from that of the median nerve and brachial artery.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Adductor longus: origin — anterior surface of body of pubis, inferior to pubic crest and lateral to pubic symphysis; insertion — middle third of medial lip of linea aspera of femur; innervation — obturator nerve, anterior division (L2, L3, L4); action — adducts thigh. It is the most anteriorly placed muscle of the adductor group, large and fan-shaped. Adductor brevis: origin — body and inferior ramus of pubis; insertion — pectineal line and proximal part of linea aspera of femur; innervation — obturator nerve, anterior division (L2, L3, L4); action — adducts thigh and to an extent flexes it; it is short and lies deep to pectineus and adductor longus. Adductor magnus: largest, most powerful, most posterior muscle in the group; has an adductor part and a hamstring part. Origin — adductor part from inferior ramus of pubis and ramus of ischium; hamstring part from ischial tuberosity. Insertion — adductor part to gluteal tuberosity, linea aspera, medial supracondylar line; hamstring part to adductor tubercle of femur. Innervation — adductor part: obturator nerve (L2, L3, L4); hamstring part: tibial nerve. Action — adducts thigh; adductor part flexes, hamstring part extends. Gracilis: origin — body and inferior ramus of pubis; insertion — superior part of medial surface of tibia; innervation — obturator nerve (L2, L3); action — adducts thigh, flexes leg, helps rotate leg medially. Obturator externus: origin — margins of obturator foramen and obturator membrane; insertion — trochanteric fossa of femur; innervation — obturator nerve (L2, L3); action — laterally rotates thigh, steadies head of femur in acetabulum.
A(ii)
All adductor muscles are supplied by the obturator nerve except the hamstring part of adductor magnus and part of pectineus. The hamstring part of adductor magnus is supplied by the tibial nerve — because embryologically the hamstring part shares the same developmental origin as the true hamstrings (which arise from the ischial tuberosity and are all innervated by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve).
B(i)
The adductor hiatus is an opening between the aponeurotic distal attachment of the adductor part of adductor magnus and the tendinous distal attachment of the hamstring part. It transmits the femoral artery and vein from the adductor canal in the thigh to the popliteal fossa posterior to the knee. It is located just lateral and superior to the adductor tubercle of the femur.
B(ii)
The pes anserinus consists of the conjoined tendons of the sartorius, gracilis, and semitendinosus muscles; they insert into the superior part of the medial surface of the tibia. It acts as a secondary valgus restraint, augmenting the medial supporting structures of the knee. Bursitis of the pes anserinus bursa causes medial knee pain, especially in osteoarthritis.
C(i)
Gracilis is unique among the adductor group: it is a long strap-like muscle, the most medial and most superficial of the adductors, and the weakest member; it is the only member of the adductor group to cross both the hip and knee joints. It joins with sartorius (from the anterior compartment, supplied by femoral nerve) and semitendinosus (from the posterior compartment, supplied by tibial nerve) to form the pes anserinus — three muscles from three different compartments with three different nerve supplies share a common insertion.
questions.question:

A(i) Name all 5 adductor muscles; give origin, insertion, innervation, and action for each
A(ii) Why all adductor muscles are supplied by the obturator nerve except the hamstring part of adductor magnus — state its nerve supply and embryologic basis
B(i) The adductor hiatus — its boundaries and the structures it transmits
B(ii) The pes anserinus — its composition and function
C(i) Distinguish the gracilis from the other adductor muscles based on its unique anatomical features; name the other two compartments' muscles that join it to form the pes anserinus and their common innervation

questions.answerText:
(i)
• The anterior vagal trunk is formed mainly in the thorax from the left vagus nerve; it enters the abdomen on the anterior surface of the oesophagus and divides into branches that supply the anterior surface of the stomach. A large hepatic branch of the anterior vagal trunk passes up to the liver, and from this a pyloric branch passes down to the pylorus.
• The posterior vagal trunk is formed mainly from the right vagus nerve; it enters the abdomen on the posterior surface of the oesophagus and divides into branches supplying mainly the posterior surface of the stomach. A large branch of the posterior vagal trunk passes to the coeliac and superior mesenteric plexuses and is distributed to the intestine as far as the splenic flexure and to the pancreas.
(ii)
At the opening in the diaphragm (the oesophageal hiatus), the oesophagus is accompanied by the two vagal trunks, branches of the left gastric vessels, and lymphatic vessels, with fibres of the right crus forming a sling around the oesophagus. Inferior to the root of the lungs, the vagus nerves leave the pulmonary plexus and join sympathetic nerves to form the oesophageal plexus, from which the anterior trunk (left vagus, anterior) and posterior trunk (right vagus, posterior) are derived.
(iii)
• The vagal (parasympathetic) fibres are secretomotor to the gastric glands and motor to the muscular wall of the stomach, and the pyloric sphincter receives inhibitory fibres from the vagus.
• Vagotomy is a recognised surgical option for peptic ulcer disease; division of the vagal trunks reduces the vagal secretomotor drive to the gastric glands, decreasing acid secretion.
• Since the hepatic branch arises from the anterior vagal trunk and the coeliac/pancreatic branch from the posterior trunk, a truncal vagotomy also interrupts vagal input to the liver, pancreas and intestine as far as the splenic flexure.
• Loss of vagal inhibitory input to the pyloric sphincter can alter pyloric motor function, which is why vagotomy for peptic ulcer disease is often combined with a drainage procedure such as pyloroplasty.
questions.question:
(i) Describe the origin, course and distribution of the anterior and posterior vagal trunks in the abdomen.
(ii) State where the vagal trunks lie in relation to the oesophageal hiatus.
(iii) Explain the anatomical basis of the effect of vagal injury (vagotomy) on the stomach and related viscera.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Eight processes of digestion (in order):
• Ingestion
• Mastication
• Peristalsis / motility
• Secretions
• Hormone release
• Chemical digestion
• Absorption
• Elimination
A(ii)
Four main functions of the GI tract:
• Macromolecules (proteins, complex carbohydrates, nucleic acids, and fat) obtained from ingested food are broken down into smaller subunits for easy absorption through the lining of the small intestine during digestion.
• These smaller subunits are required for the release of energy, maintenance, and growth.
• Most of the water and electrolytes are absorbed in the large intestine.
• The inner layer of the entire GI tract forms an important protective barrier between the contents of the tract and the tissues of the body.
B(i)
Serosa:
• Composition: a thin sheet of loose connective tissue covered with mesothelium (a simple squamous covering epithelium); rich in blood vessels, lymphatics, and adipose tissue.
• Function: the outermost covering of GIT organs within the abdominal cavity.
• Continuity: the serosa of the small and large intestines is continuous with parts of the mesentery (a large fold of adipose connective tissue covered on both sides by mesothelium, which suspends the intestines and is continuous with the peritoneum).
• Esophagus: because the esophagus is bound directly to adjacent structures and not suspended in a cavity, it has a thick adventitia instead of a serosa; the adventitia consists of connective tissue containing vessels and nerves, lacking mesothelium.
B(ii)
• The enteric nervous system (submucosal and myenteric plexuses) functions independently of the CNS; because it is anatomically connected to the autonomic nervous system, it provides the anatomical basis for the well-known actions of emotional stress on the stomach and other regions of the GIT.
Two diseases demonstrating clinical consequences of plexus destruction:
• Hirschsprung disease (congenital aganglionic megacolon): caused by absence or severely injured plexuses in parts or all of the large intestine; disturbs motility and produces dilation, causing difficulty passing stool.
• Chagas disease / trypanosomiasis (infection with Trypanosoma cruzi): the protozoan destroys the enteric plexuses, producing similar motility disturbance.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the processes of digestion, naming all eight steps in order.
A(ii) Describe the four main functions of the GI tract, distinguishing between the role of the small intestine and the role of the large intestine in absorption.
B(i) Describe the composition and function of the serosa, including the structures it is continuous with and how it differs between organs within the abdominal cavity and the esophagus.
B(ii) Explain why the enteric nervous system provides the anatomical basis for the effects of emotional stress on the GIT, and name the two diseases that demonstrate the clinical consequences of plexus destruction.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Path of blood flow:
• Aorta → Renal artery → Segmental artery → Interlobar artery → Arcuate artery → Cortical radiate artery → Afferent arteriole → Glomerulus (capillaries) → Efferent arteriole → Peritubular capillaries (cortical nephrons) or Vasa recta (juxtamedullary nephrons) → Cortical radiate vein → Arcuate vein → Interlobar vein → Renal vein → Inferior vena cava.
• Renal arteries deliver approximately one-quarter (1,200 ml) of cardiac output to the kidneys each minute.
A(ii)
Nerve supply is via sympathetic fibers from the renal plexus.
B(i)
• Cortical nephrons (85% of nephrons): efferent arteriole supplies peritubular capillaries — low-pressure, porous capillaries adapted for absorption of water and solutes; they cling to adjacent renal tubules in the cortex and empty into venules.
• Juxtamedullary nephrons: efferent arteriole supplies vasa recta — long, thin-walled vessels parallel to the long nephron loops; important in formation of concentrated urine.
B(ii)
Blood pressure in the glomerulus is high because:
• Afferent arterioles are larger in diameter than efferent arterioles.
• Arterioles are high-resistance vessels.
• The glomerulus is fed and drained by arterioles (not venules), which maintains the high filtration pressure. The glomerulus is also specialized for filtration, with fenestrated endothelium that is highly porous, allowing filtrate formation.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the complete path of blood flow through the renal blood vessels, from the aorta to the peritubular capillaries or vasa recta.
A(ii) State the nerve supply to the kidneys and name the source.
B(i) Distinguish between the capillary beds associated with cortical nephrons and those associated with juxtamedullary nephrons.
B(ii) Explain the anatomical basis for high blood pressure in the glomerulus.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Muscularis and serosa:
• Muscularis: composed of an internal circular layer and an external longitudinal layer; between these muscle layers is the myenteric (Auerbach) nerve plexus, which produces peristalsis.
• Serosa: the small intestine is covered by a thin serosa.
A(ii)
Lamina propria of the small intestine:
• Composed of loose connective tissue containing extensive blood and lymph microvasculature, nerve fibers, smooth muscle cells, and lymphoid tissue.
• It penetrates the core of each intestinal villus, bringing microvasculature, lymphatics, and nerves into each villus.
• Smooth muscle fibers inside the villi are responsible for rhythmic movements important for efficient absorption.
• Contractions of the muscularis mucosae also produce local movements of the plicae circulares that help propel lymph from the lacteals into submucosal and mesenteric lymphatics.
B(i)
Submucosa — Brunner (duodenal) glands:
• Location: present in the proximal part of the duodenum; large clusters of branched tubular mucous glands with small excretory ducts opening among the intestinal crypts.
• Type: branched tubular mucous glands.
• Product: mucus, which is alkaline (pH 8.1–9.3).
Three functions:
• Protects the mucous membrane.
• Brings the intestinal contents to the optimum pH for pancreatic enzyme action.
• Neutralises chyme entering the duodenum from the pylorus.
B(ii)
Lacteals:
• Lymph vessels of the intestine beginning as closed tubes in the cores of villi.
• They run to the region of the lamina propria above the muscularis mucosae, where they form a plexus.
• From there they are directed to the submucosa, where they surround lymphoid nodules; they anastomose repeatedly and leave the intestine along with blood vessels.
• Function: especially important for lipid absorption.
• Absorptive state: when absorption is taking place after a meal, the lacteals are dilated and prominent; at other times they are collapsed and not prominent.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the muscularis and serosa of the small intestine, naming the layers of the muscularis, the nerve plexus between them, and the covering of the serosa.
A(ii) Describe the lamina propria of the small intestine, including its composition, its role in each intestinal villus, and the role of smooth muscle fibers within the villi.
B(i) Describe the submucosa of the small intestine, giving particular attention to the Brunner (duodenal) glands: location, type of gland, product, pH, and all three functions.
B(ii) Describe the lacteals of the small intestine: what they are, where they begin, their course, their function, and how they change in appearance depending on the absorptive state of the intestine.

A. Describe the course of the maxillary nerve, from its origin to its continuation on the face, and list its branches.
B. State the clinically relevant procedure and the region associated with this nerve.
questions.answerText:
A
The maxillary nerve passes through the pterygopalatine fossa, where it is one of the contents (along with the terminal part of the maxillary artery, the maxillary vein, and the pterygopalatine ganglion); nerve structures enter the fossa through its posterior wall. Its branches include the superior alveolar nerves (anterior, posterior and middle), the middle meningeal nerve, the infraorbital nerve, the zygomatic nerve, the inferior palpebral nerve, the superior labial nerve, the pharyngeal nerve, the greater and lesser palatine nerves, and the nasopalatine nerve. The infraorbital nerve continues from the maxillary nerve onto the face via the infraorbital groove and canal, situated on the floor of the orbit in the orbital plate of the maxilla, and via the infraorbital foramen.
B
Clinical correlates of this region include maxillary nerve block, and the pterygopalatine ganglion is also referred to as the "hay fever ganglion".

(i)
• The renal arteries arise from the aorta at the level of the L1/L2 intervertebral disc; the right renal artery passes posterior to the inferior vena cava.
• Each renal artery divides at the hilum into anterior and posterior branches; these give rise to segmental arteries.
• Four segmental arteries, apical, anterosuperior, anteroinferior and inferior, arise from the anterior branch, and the posterior branch itself constitutes the posterior segmental artery.
• Each segmental artery further gives lobar arteries, one for each renal pyramid, which give two or three interlobar arteries running toward the cortex on each side of the pyramid.
• Interlobar arteries give arcuate arteries at the corticomedullary junction, which give several interlobular arteries, from which afferent glomerular arterioles arise.
• The renal veins lie anterior to their respective arteries; each renal vein drains into the inferior vena cava, and the left renal vein additionally receives the left suprarenal and left gonadal veins before crossing anterior to the aorta.
(ii)
• The segmental arteries of the kidney are described as end arteries, meaning they do not anastomose with one another.
• Because each segmental artery supplies its own renal segment without collateral supply from adjacent segmental arteries, the renal parenchyma is divided into distinct vascular segments.
(iii)
• Since the segmental arteries are end arteries, occlusion or injury of one segmental artery cuts off blood supply to its corresponding renal segment.
• This lack of anastomosis means the affected segment cannot receive compensatory blood flow from neighbouring segments.
• Lymphatic drainage of the kidney is to the right and left lumbar lymph nodes, and nerve supply is via the renal plexus (vagus and abdominopelvic splanchnic nerves), so a segmental vascular injury is an isolated event within the kidney rather than one shared with adjacent segments.
questions.question:
(i) Describe the origin, course, branches and distribution of the renal artery.
(ii) State why the segmental arteries of the kidney are described as end arteries.
(iii) Explain the anatomical basis of the consequence of injury or occlusion of a segmental renal artery.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Four stomach regions:
• Cardia and pylorus are histologically similar: tubular glands with long pits usually branching into coiled secretory portions (cardiac and pyloric glands respectively); pits are longer in the pylorus; lack both parietal and chief cells; major secretion is abundant mucus.
• Fundus and body are histologically identical: simple columnar epithelium invaginates to form gastric pits leading into long, branched, tubular gastric glands; 3 to 7 glands usually open into the bottom of each gastric pit; contain all four secretory cell types; involved in secretion of acidic gastric juice.
A(ii)
Structure of fundic/body glands:
• Each gland has three named parts: isthmus, neck, and base.
• Isthmus: the region of stem cells (between the gastric pit and gland); the pluripotent stem cells divide asymmetrically and can move upward or downward to replace epithelial cells.
• Neck: contains mucous neck cells (MNCs) in clusters or singly; also contains parietal cells.
• Base: predominantly chief (zymogen) cells; also contains enteroendocrine cells.
B(i)
Mucous neck cells (MNCs):
• Present in clusters or singly in the necks of gastric glands.
• Less columnar than surface mucous cells; irregular in shape with round nucleus and apical secretory granules.
• Their mucous secretion is less alkaline than that of the surface epithelial mucous cells; they secrete acidic fluid containing mucin (not mucus, which implies alkaline content).
B(ii)
Intrinsic factor:
• Produced by: parietal (oxyntic) cells.
• Chemical nature: a glycoprotein.
• Function: required for the uptake of vitamin B12 in the small intestine.
• Deficiency and anaemia: if parietal cells are damaged, insufficient quantities of intrinsic factor are secreted; without adequate intrinsic factor, vitamin B12 is not absorbed adequately; low levels of vitamin B12 reduce the proliferation of erythroblasts, resulting in pernicious anaemia.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the histological features of the four stomach regions — cardia, fundus, body, and pylorus — under the headings: surface epithelium, gland type, gastric pit length, and principal secretion.
A(ii) Explain the complete structure and function of the gastric glands of the fundus/body, including the isthmus, neck, and base, and what cells are found in each part.
B(i) Explain the full role of mucous neck cells in the gastric gland, comparing their secretion to that of surface mucous cells.
B(ii) Describe where intrinsic factor is produced, what it is chemically, what it does, and how its deficiency leads to anaemia.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Superficial group (3 muscles): Gastrocnemius — lateral head from lateral aspect of lateral condyle of femur; insertion: posterior surface of calcaneus via calcaneal tendon; innervation: tibial nerve (S1, S2); action: plantarflexes ankle when knee is extended, raises heel during walking, flexes leg at knee joint. Soleus — posterior aspect of head and superior quarter of posterior surface of fibula; soleal line and middle third of medial border of tibia; tendinous arch; insertion: posterior surface of calcaneus via calcaneal tendon; innervation: tibial nerve (S1, S2); action: plantarflexes ankle independent of position of knee, steadies leg on foot. Plantaris — inferior end of lateral supracondylar line of femur, oblique popliteal ligament; insertion: posterior surface of calcaneus via calcaneal tendon; innervation: tibial nerve (S1, S2); action: weakly assists gastrocnemius in plantarflexing ankle. Deep group (4 muscles): Popliteus — lateral surface of lateral condyle of femur and lateral meniscus; posterior surface of tibia superior to soleal line; tibial nerve (L4, L5, S1); weakly flexes knee, unlocks it by rotating femur 5° on fixed tibia, and medially rotates tibia of unplanted limb. Flexor hallucis longus — inferior 2/3 of posterior surface of fibula; base of distal phalanx of great toe; tibial nerve (S2, S3); flexes great toe at all joints, weakly plantarflexes ankle, supports medial longitudinal arch. Flexor digitorum longus — medial part of posterior surface of tibia inferior to soleal line; bases of distal phalanges of lateral 4 digits; tibial nerve (S2, S3); flexes lateral 4 digits, plantarflexes ankle, supports longitudinal arches. Tibialis posterior — interosseous membrane, posterior tibia inferior to soleal line, posterior fibula; tuberosity of navicular, cuneiform, cuboid, sustentaculum tali of calcaneus, bases of 2nd, 3rd, and 4th metatarsals; tibial nerve (L4, L5); plantarflexes ankle and inverts foot.
A(ii)
The calcaneal tendon is formed by the union of the tendons of gastrocnemius, soleus, and plantaris; it inserts into the posterior surface of the calcaneus. It is the largest and strongest tendon in the body. Clinical significance: rupture of the Achilles tendon (commonly felt as a 'pop' and tested by Thompson's squeeze test) results in inability to plantarflex the foot.
B(i)
The posterior tibial artery enters the sole of the foot through the tarsal tunnel, accompanying the tibial nerve. The tibial nerve enters the sole of the foot via the tarsal tunnel and then splits into the lateral and medial plantar arteries. For a tarsal tunnel block, the posterior tibial pulse can be palpated inferoposteriorly to the medial malleolus, where the artery turns to enter the foot — the tibial nerve lies adjacent.
B(ii)
Tibialis posterior inserts into the tuberosity of the navicular, cuneiform, cuboid, sustentaculum tali of calcaneus, and the bases of the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th metatarsals — the very bones that form the medial longitudinal arch. It plantarflexes the ankle and inverts the foot; by pulling the navicular and cuneiforms downward and inward it actively maintains the height of the medial longitudinal arch. Dysfunction (e.g., from tenosynovitis or rupture) leads to eversion of the calcaneus, slipping down of the talus and navicular, and pes planus — collapse of the medial longitudinal arch.
C(i)
Gastrocnemius spans the knee joint (arising from the femoral condyle) and the ankle joint; it plantarflexes the ankle only when the knee is extended and also flexes the knee. It is tested with the knee extended. Soleus arises entirely from the tibia and fibula (below the knee) and plantarflexes the ankle independent of the position of the knee. It is tested by single-leg heel raise with the knee flexed to 90°, which eliminates gastrocnemius from the movement and isolates soleus.
questions.question:
Describe the muscles of the posterior compartment of the leg under the following headings and explain why disease of tibialis posterior leads to collapse of the medial longitudinal arch.
A(i) Classify muscles into superficial and deep groups; give origin, insertion, innervation, and action of each
A(ii) The calcaneal (Achilles) tendon — formation, course, and clinical significance
B(i) The tibial nerve — course in the posterior compartment, branches, safe site for tarsal tunnel block
B(ii) How tibialis posterior supports the medial longitudinal arch and why its dysfunction causes pes planus
C(i) Distinguish the actions of gastrocnemius from soleus, explaining the anatomical basis of their different clinical testing

A(i) Describe the development, structure, shape and position of the female breast.
A(ii) Describe the nipple and areola.
A(iii) Describe the internal structure of the breast.
A(iv) Describe the arterial supply, venous drainage and nerve supply.
B(i) Relate the parts and structures of the breast to common pathologies and to surgical incisions.
B(ii) Describe the developmental anomalies of the breast.
C(i) Explain how breast disease spreads through the lymphatics, naming the drainage routes and the axillary node groups, and its effect on distant structures.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• A modified sweat gland of ectodermal origin, non-capsulated, present in both sexes (rudimentary in males), starting to develop at puberty in females with most development in late pregnancy and lactation; lies in the superficial fascia; shape and size vary with genetics, race, diet, age, parity and menopausal status (hemispherical, conical, pendulous, piriform, flattened).
• Base extends vertically from the 2nd to the 6th rib and transversely from the sternal edge to the midaxillary line; two-thirds of the base lie on pectoralis major and the inferolateral third on serratus anterior and external oblique; the axillary tail (of Spence) passes into the axilla; the retromammary space (loose areolar tissue) separates it from the deep fascia.
A(ii)
Nipple: at the greatest prominence, opposite the 4th intercostal space (about 10 cm from the midline in men and young nulliparous women); carries 15-20 pores of the lactiferous ducts; circular and radial smooth muscle causes erection with cold, tactile or emotional stimuli; devoid of fat, hair and sweat glands. Areola: pigmented skin (22-60 mm) with sebaceous glands and glands of Montgomery; darkening in the 2nd month of pregnancy is permanent.
A(iii)
Glandular tissue (15-20 lobes made of lobules of alveoli/acini and alveolar ducts converging on 15-20 lactiferous ducts, each with a lactiferous sinus deep to the areola), stroma (fibrous strands, the suspensory ligaments of Astley Cooper, connecting the skin with the deep fascia of pectoralis major) and adipose tissue (determines form and size).
A(iv)
Arteries: internal thoracic (medial mammary and perforating branches of the 2nd-4th spaces, the 2nd largest; about 60% of flow, mainly medial), lateral thoracic and thoraco-acromial pectoral branch (axillary), lateral mammary branches of posterior intercostal arteries, anterior intercostal branches. Veins correspond, with a circular venous plexus at the base of the nipple draining to the axillary and internal thoracic veins. Nerves: anterior and lateral cutaneous branches of the 4th-6th intercostal nerves (sensory to skin, sympathetic to vessels and the smooth muscle of skin and nipple).
B(i)
Cancer of the breast is a common surgical condition, about 60% arising in the upper lateral quadrant; the lactiferous ducts are radial, so incisions are made radially; infiltration of the ligaments of Cooper shortens them and gives peau d'orange; fibroadenoma is also listed.
B(ii)
Polymastia, polythelia and amastia; the mammary ridge extends from the axilla to the inguinal region and disappears in humans except in the pectoral region, so accessory breasts or nipples can occur along it (axillary and inguinal); the male breast stays rudimentary (small ducts without lobules or alveoli).
C(i)
• About 75% of lymph drains to the axillary nodes (central and lateral parts to the pectoral group, upper part to the apical group), about 20% (medial part) to the internal thoracic (parasternal) chain, and the lower quadrants to the inferior phrenic (abdominal) nodes.
• Axillary nodes lie in 5 groups: pectoral (anterior), subscapular (posterior), brachial (lateral), central and apical; levels 1-3 and Rotter's nodes between pectoralis minor and major; the subclavian lymph trunk from the apical group opens into the subclavian vein (left side usually the thoracic duct).
• Other routes: lymphatics follow vessels through pectoralis major to parasternal nodes, cross the median plane to the opposite breast, and reach the sheath of rectus abdominis and the subperitoneal and subhepatic plexuses.
• Nodes below and above the clavicle, and axillary and cervical nodes, communicate freely; cancer of one breast can affect the other breast and the opposite axillary nodes through the anastomosing lymphatics.

(i)
• The spleen is an ovoid, highly vascular, reddish-purple organ, on average about 12 cm long, 7 cm broad, 3 cm thick and weighing about 150 g, related to the 9th to 11th ribs on the left side.
• It has two ends, an expanded anterior end and a rounded posterior end resting on the upper pole of the left kidney, three borders (superior, inferior and intermediate), and two surfaces (diaphragmatic and visceral).
• The diaphragmatic surface is convex and related to the diaphragm, left lung and pleura, and the 9th-11th ribs; the visceral surface is concave and bears gastric, renal, colic and pancreatic impressions.
• The hilum lies on the inferomedial part of the gastric impression and transmits the splenic vessels and nerves, giving attachment to the gastrosplenic and splenorenal ligaments; the phrenicocolic ligament supports, but is not attached to, the anterior end of the spleen.
(ii)
• The gastric impression, related to the fundus of the stomach, is the largest impression; the renal impression relates to the left kidney and sometimes the suprarenal gland; the colic impression relates to the splenic flexure of the colon; the pancreatic impression relates to the tail of the pancreas.
• The gastrosplenic ligament contains the short gastric vessels supplying the stomach, and the splenorenal ligament contains the tail of the pancreas and splenic vessels, so disease or surgery at the spleen can affect the stomach, kidney, colon or pancreas through these relations.
(iii)
• Although protected by the 9th to 12th ribs, the spleen is the most frequently injured organ in the abdomen.
• Severe blows to the left side may fracture ribs, producing sharp fragments that lacerate the spleen, and blunt trauma elsewhere that raises intra-abdominal pressure can also rupture it because its capsule is thin and the pulp soft.
• If ruptured, the spleen bleeds profusely because it is a highly vascular organ receiving the splenic artery, the largest branch of the coeliac trunk.
• This produces severe intraperitoneal haemorrhage and shock, a systemic and distant functional deficit in circulation arising from a local splenic injury.
• Repair of a ruptured spleen is difficult, so splenectomy or subtotal splenectomy is often performed to prevent the patient from bleeding to death.
• Even after total splenectomy, most splenic functions are assumed by other reticuloendothelial organs such as the liver and bone marrow, though susceptibility to certain bacterial infections increases.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
The surface marking of the base of the appendix is McBurney's point, at the junction of the lateral one-third and medial two-thirds of a line drawn from the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus. The appendix is attached to the cecum below the ileocaecal valve, and the teniae coli of the cecum converge at the root of the appendix.
A(ii)
The appendix is one of the intraperitoneal parts of the large intestine, suspended by its own mesentery, the mesoappendix.
A(iii)
The appendix opens at the posteromedial aspect of the cecum, about one inch below the ileocaecal junction; its positions include retrocecal, the most common, pelvic, subcecal, preileal, and postileal, the least common.
B
• Deep tenderness at McBurney's point, McBurney's sign, is the clinical sign used to localise inflammation of the appendix, that is, acute appendicitis.
• The appendix is described as an intestinal tonsil because of the abundant lymphatic nodules in its lamina propria, which extend into the submucosa and give it an immune function, similar to the tonsils.
C
• Grossly, the appendix has no teniae coli and shows various shapes and positions, whereas the rest of the colon shows three longitudinal teniae coli, free, mesocolic and omental, which converge at the root of the appendix.
• The colon has haustra (sacculations), because the teniae are shorter than the length of the gut wall, appendices epiploicae (fat-filled peritoneal pouches), and semilunar folds; the appendix lacks these features.
• Microscopically, the appendix has no villi and its crypts (of Lieberkuhn) are less abundant than in the colon.
• The colon's mucosa shows enterocytes with no digestive enzyme production, water and electrolyte reabsorption, deep crypts, a thick mucin layer, and goblet cells that increase in number caudally.
• The appendix has prominent lymphatic nodules in the lamina propria extending into the submucosa, which are far less prominent in the general colon.
• Both the appendix and colon lack villi, unlike the small intestine, but only the appendix is described as functioning analogously to the tonsils.
questions.question:
(A) Describe the vermiform appendix under the headings: A(i) surface anatomy/position A(ii) peritoneal relations A(iii) opening and possible positions.
(B) Explain the clinical basis of tenderness at McBurney's point in appendicitis.

Describe the gross anatomy of the proximal carpal row/wrist region:
A(i) Bones forming the proximal row and their articulation with the radius
A(ii) The scaphoid's distinguishing feature
B. State how the scaphoid and lunate each relate to common wrist pathologies.
C. Explain how pathology at the lunate spreads to affect a distant structure, causing a functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The wrist (radiocarpal) joint is formed distally by the proximal row of carpal bones — the scaphoid, lunate and triquetrum, excluding the pisiform — and proximally by the distal end of the radius and the articular disk; the ulna is not part of the wrist joint, being prevented from articulating with the carpal bones by this fibrocartilaginous articular disk, and instead articulates with the radius at the distal radioulnar joint.
A(ii)
The scaphoid has a unique blood supply that runs from distal to proximal, unlike most bones.
B
• The scaphoid is the carpal bone most commonly fractured, more so in the younger population, typically from a blow to the wrist such as falling on an outstretched hand, when it takes most of the force.
• Because of its distal-to-proximal blood supply, a scaphoid fracture can disrupt supply to the proximal fragment; this is considered an emergency, and failure to revascularise can lead to avascular necrosis and future arthritis.
• The lunate is prone to anterior dislocation, which is uncommon but can occur by falling on a dorsiflexed wrist, forcing the lunate anteriorly.
• The lunate can also undergo avascular necrosis, so it too requires immediate clinical attention when injured.
C
• Anterior dislocation of the lunate compresses the carpal tunnel, since the lunate lies immediately related to the floor of this tunnel region.
• This compression of the carpal tunnel affects the median nerve, which lies within it.
• The resulting clinical picture manifests as paraesthesia in the sensory distribution of the median nerve.
• There is also weakness of the thenar muscles, which are supplied by the median nerve's recurrent branch.
• This produces the symptoms of carpal tunnel syndrome, even though the primary pathology (lunate dislocation) is a distinct injury from the usual causes of carpal tunnel syndrome.
• This illustrates how a purely skeletal injury at the wrist can spread to compromise an adjacent soft-tissue structure, producing a functional/sensorimotor deficit in the hand.

questions.question:
A. Describe the gross anatomy of the gallbladder and the extrahepatic bile ducts under the following headings:
A(i) location, shape, dimensions and parts;
A(ii) the ducts and course of the common bile duct;
A(iii) blood and nerve supply.
B(i) State how the neck relates to gallstones.
B(ii) State how Calot's triangle and its lymph node relate to surgery and inflammation.
B(iii) State how the sphincters relate to biliary dyskinesia.
C(i) Explain why gallbladder inflammation may cause pain at the right shoulder tip and a positive Murphy's sign.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• A pear-shaped fibromuscular sac that stores and concentrates bile, in the gallbladder fossa on the inferior surface of the right lobe of the liver, 7 to 10 cm long, 3 cm broad and 30 to 50 ml in capacity.
• Fundus: projects beyond the inferior border of the liver, covered by peritoneum on all sides. Body: superior surface adherent to the liver and devoid of peritoneum. Neck: upper narrow part ending in the cystic duct, with a spiral fold.
• The fundus is related to the anterior abdominal wall and transverse colon; the body's inferior surface to the transverse colon and the 1st and 2nd parts of the duodenum.
A(ii)
• Right and left hepatic ducts emerge at the porta hepatis; the common hepatic duct (3 to 4 cm) is joined by the cystic duct (3 to 4 cm, spiral folds of Heister) to form the common bile duct.
• The common bile duct (about 8 cm, 6 mm wide) has supraduodenal, retroduodenal, infraduodenal and intraduodenal parts, joining the main pancreatic duct at the hepatopancreatic ampulla.
A(iii)
• Cystic artery (from the right hepatic artery) is the chief supply, with the cystic vein to the portal vein; the posterior superior pancreaticoduodenal branches supply the lower bile duct.
• Sympathetic nerves come from the celiac plexus and parasympathetic from the vagus.
B(i)
The posteromedial wall of the neck may dilate as Hartmann's pouch, where gallstones may lodge.
B(ii)
Calot's triangle (liver inferior surface, common hepatic duct, cystic duct) locates the cystic artery in laparoscopic cholecystectomy; Lund's node enlarges in cholecystitis or cholangitis and may be removed.
B(iii)
Gallbladder muscle and the sphincter of Oddi have reciprocal innervation (gallbladder contracts, sphincter relaxes); disruption is biliary dyskinesia.
C(i)
• Inflammation irritates the subdiaphragmatic parietal peritoneum supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3, 4, 5), referred to the right shoulder tip supplied by the supraclavicular nerve (C3, C4).
• In Murphy's sign the inflamed gallbladder descends on deep inspiration and contacts the palpating hand at the right costal margin, causing pain and a caught breath.

A(i)
An omentum is a double-layered extension or fold passing from the stomach and proximal duodenum to adjacent organs or to the abdominal wall; there are two types, lesser and greater.
A(ii)
The lesser omentum is a two-layered fold connecting the lesser curvature of the stomach and proximal duodenum to the liver; the hepatoduodenal ligament is its thickened free edge, conducting the portal vein, hepatic artery and bile duct.
A(iii)
The greater omentum hangs like an apron from the greater curvature of the stomach and proximal duodenum, folds back after descending and attaches to the anterior surface of the transverse colon and its mesocolon.
A(iv)
• Liver: falciform ligament (anterior wall), gastrohepatic ligament (stomach), hepatoduodenal ligament (duodenum). Stomach: gastrophrenic, gastrosplenic, gastrocolic, gastrohepatic, gastropancreatic.
• Spleen: gastrosplenic (short gastric and left gastroepiploic vessels), splenorenal (splenic vessels and tail of pancreas), phrenicosplenic, splenocolic.
B(i)
• It is large and fat laden and prevents the visceral peritoneum adhering to the parietal peritoneum lining the anterolateral wall.
• It is mobile, moving with peristalsis, and can wrap itself around an inflamed organ such as the appendix, walling it off and protecting other viscera.
• It also cushions the abdominal organs against injury and forms insulation against loss of body heat.
C(i)
• Lesser: from liver to lesser curvature and proximal duodenum, containing the hepatoduodenal ligament; greater: hangs from the greater curvature and attaches to the transverse colon.
• The anterior and posterior layers of the lesser omentum extend from the liver to the lesser curvature; the anterior layer continues as the first layer of the greater omentum, the posterior layer forms its second and third layers.
• The lesser omentum forms part of the anterior wall of the lesser sac together with the peritoneum of the posterior wall of the stomach and the anterior two layers of the greater omentum.
• The hepatoduodenal ligament forms the anterior boundary of the omental foramen.

A(i)
Structure:
• Capsule and septa: a capsule of connective tissue rich in collagen fibers surrounds the large salivary glands; septa of connective tissue originate from the capsule and divide the glands into lobules; each lobule contains numerous secretory units (acini).
• Parenchyma: consists of secretory end pieces and a branching duct system arranged in lobules separated by septae of connective tissue from the capsule. Vessels and nerves enter at the hilum and gradually branch into the lobules.
• Cell types in secretory end pieces: serous cells (polarized protein-secreting cells, pyramidal in shape, round nuclei, well-stained RER, apical secretory granules; joined apically by tight and adherent junctions; form a spherical unit called an acinus with a very small central lumen; secrete enzymes and other proteins); mucous cells; and nonsecretory myoepithelial cells.
• Duct system in sequence: secretory end pieces → intercalated ducts (lined by simple low cuboidal epithelium, surrounded by myoepithelial cells) → striated ducts (intralobular) → interlobular (excretory/striated ducts drain into these) → interlobar ducts → main duct (opens into the oral cavity, lined with nonkeratinized-stratified squamous epithelium).
A(ii)
Secretion types:
• Parotid gland: serous and watery.
• Submandibular and sublingual glands: seromucous secretion.
• Minor glands: mostly mucous.
• Type depends on content of glycoprotein mucin: serous, seromucous, or mucous.
B(i)
• Intercalated ducts: several short intercalated ducts join to form striated ducts; they are lined by cuboidal epithelial cells that have the ability to divide and differentiate into secretory or ductal cells; also called intralobular ducts.
• Striated ducts: characterized by radial striations that extend from the bases of the cells to the level of the central nuclei; striations consist of infoldings of the basal plasma membrane with numerous elongated mitochondria aligned parallel to the infolded membranes (characteristic of ion-transporting cells); they have a folded basal membrane enabling active transport; also called intralobular ducts.
B(ii)
Saliva is modified by the cells of the duct system draining the secretory units: much Na+ and Cl- is reabsorbed while certain growth factors and digestive enzymes are added. Water resorption and ion secretion in the striated ducts make saliva hypotonic (reduced Na and Cl ions; increased carbonate and potassium ions).
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the gross and microscopic structure of the large salivary glands under the following headings: capsule and septa; parenchyma (secretory end pieces); cell types in the secretory end pieces; the duct system in sequence from secretory unit to oral cavity.
A(ii) State the type of secretion produced by each of the three pairs of major salivary glands and by the minor glands.
B(i) Distinguish between striated ducts and intercalated ducts, including location, epithelium, and function.
B(ii) Explain how saliva is modified as it passes through the duct system.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
• 12 pairs of intercostal (thoracic) nerves, the anterior primary rami of the thoracic spinal nerves; they are mixed nerves; T3-6 are typical and T1 and T2 are atypical.
• Atypical nerves: T1 has no anterior cutaneous branch and is joined to the brachial plexus by a large branch corresponding to the lateral cutaneous branch; the lateral cutaneous branch of T2 is the intercostobrachial nerve, joined to the medial cutaneous nerve of the arm.
A(ii)
A typical nerve lies in the neurovascular bundle between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles, high in the space in relation to the subcostal groove of the rib above, below the artery (vein, artery, nerve from above downwards); nerves 1-6 are distributed in the intercostal spaces, 7-11 pass to the anterior abdominal wall, and the anterior ramus of the 12th runs forward in the abdomen as the subcostal nerve.
A(iii)
Branches: rami communicantes, collateral (muscular) branches, lateral cutaneous branch, anterior cutaneous branch, muscular branches, pleural branch and peritoneal branches (7th-11th).
A(iv)
They supply the skin, the muscles of the intercostal space and abdomen, and the parietal pleura and parietal peritoneum; cutaneous supply of the anterior wall is by supraclavicular nerves (C4) above the sternal angle and by the anterior and lateral cutaneous branches below it; the posterior wall is supplied by the posterior rami of the thoracic spinal nerves.
B(i)
• Local anaesthesia of an intercostal space is easily produced by infiltration around the intercostal nerve trunk and its collateral branch (intercostal nerve block).
• A needle or drain is passed immediately above the upper border of a rib, to avoid the neurovascular bundle lying under the rib above.
• In a conventional posterolateral thoracotomy the incision is along the 5th or 6th rib; the periosteum over a segment of the rib is elevated, protecting the neurovascular bundle, and the rib is excised to reach the lung or mediastinum through the intercostal space.
C(i)
• Local irritation of the intercostal nerves (e.g. by Pott's disease, tuberculosis of the thoracic vertebrae) gives pain referred to the front of the chest or abdomen, in the region of the peripheral termination of the nerves.
• Pus from the region of the vertebral column tracks around the thorax along the neurovascular bundle and points at the three sites of exit of the cutaneous branches: lateral to erector spinae, in the midaxillary line and just lateral to the sternum.
• A rib fracture is extremely painful because the periosteum of the rib is supplied by the intercostal nerves above and below the rib; the parietal pleura is segmentally supplied by the intercostal nerves, so pleural disease refers pain along the thoracic wall and anterior abdominal wall.
questions.question:

A(ii) Describe the course and relations of a typical intercostal nerve.
A(iii) State its branches.
A(iv) Describe its distribution, including the cutaneous supply of the thoracic wall.
B(i) State the safe method and site for anaesthetising an intercostal space and for passing a needle or drain.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Formed behind the neck of the pancreas by the union of the superior mesenteric and splenic veins.
A(ii)
• Large but short, about 5 cm; in front of the opening of the lesser sac it passes to the porta hepatis where it divides into right and left terminal branches.
• At the porta hepatis the order from behind forwards is portal vein branches, proper hepatic artery, hepatic ducts; in the hepatoduodenal ligament it lies with the hepatic artery and bile duct.
A(iii)
Drains poorly oxygenated but nutrient-rich blood from the GI tract (lower oesophagus to upper anal canal), pancreas, gallbladder, bile ducts and spleen to the liver.
A(iv)
Direct route: through the liver to the IVC via the hepatic veins; alternative routes exist and the portal vein and its tributaries have no valves.
B(i)
Portasystemic shunts join the portal vein to the IVC or join the splenic vein to the left renal vein after splenectomy.
C(i)
• Portal hypertension: cirrhosis scarring and fibrosis obstruct the portal vein, pressure mounts, and blood forced through collaterals dilates veins into varices, potentially fatal.
• Lower third of oesophagus: left gastric branches with oesophageal veins to the azygos: oesophageal varices.
• Anal canal: superior rectal with middle and inferior rectal veins: haemorrhoids (mucosa with normally dilated submucosal veins prolapses).
• Anterior abdominal wall: paraumbilical with superficial epigastric veins: caput medusae, veins radiating like small snakes from the umbilicus.
• Retroperitoneal: colic twig veins of ascending and descending colon, duodenum, pancreas and liver with renal, lumbar and phrenic veins.

A
The only artery supplying structures in the orbit is the ophthalmic artery, which is a branch of the internal carotid artery; it enters the orbit with the optic nerve through the optic foramen (canal). Its branches include the lacrimal artery (to the lacrimal gland and upper eyelid), muscular branches to the muscles, long posterior ciliary arteries (to the ciliary body), short posterior ciliary arteries (to the choroid and part of the optic nerve), and medial palpebral arteries (to the eyelids).
B
The ophthalmic artery gives rise to the very important branch, the central artery of the retina; because the ophthalmic artery is the only artery supplying orbital structures, and the central retinal artery is its branch, the retina is dependent on this single arterial source, so the optic nerve is covered by dura, arachnoid and pia from the sclera to the canal, where the dura is continuous with the periosteum of the orbit, and venous drainage (superior and inferior ophthalmic veins) communicates with the cavernous sinus, giving direct communication between the skin of the face and the cavernous sinus (the danger triangle).
questions.question:
A. Describe the origin, course, and branches/distribution of the ophthalmic artery.
B. State why the ophthalmic artery and its central retinal branch are of particular functional importance to the orbit.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
A thin, double-layered serous membrane that envelops each lung and lines the thoracic cavity, made of visceral and parietal layers with the intervening pleural cavity; the two pleural cavities are totally separate.
A(ii)
Thicker outer layer lining the thoracic wall, mediastinum, diaphragm and neck, and can be stripped; 4 parts: costal (ribs, costal cartilages, intercostal spaces, sides of vertebral bodies, back of sternum, separated from them by endothoracic fascia), diaphragmatic, mediastinal (encloses the hilum structures, continuous with visceral pleura at the hilum, and below the hilum forms the pulmonary ligament) and cervical (cupola, 2.5-4 cm above the medial third of the clavicle, attached to the suprapleural membrane).
A(iii)
Visceral pleura: closely adherent to the lung including its fissures, cannot be stripped, smooth and slippery, continuous with the parietal pleura at the hilum; the pleural cavity is a potential space with a small amount of lubricating pleural fluid that reduces friction and helps prevent lung collapse.
A(iv)
Sternal (costal to mediastinal anteriorly): from behind the sternoclavicular joints to the midline at the 2nd costal cartilage, then the right edge passes vertically to the 6th costal cartilage while the left arches laterally at the 4th costal cartilage (because of the heart) to the 6th. Costal (costal to diaphragmatic): crosses the 8th rib in the midclavicular line, the 10th rib in the midaxillary line and the 12th rib at the lateral border of erector spinae. Vertebral: rounded reflections in the paravertebral planes from T1 to T12.
A(v)
Recesses are spaces not occupied by lung that lung enters only on forced deep respiration: costodiaphragmatic (between costal and diaphragmatic pleura, shallow in inspiration and deeper in expiration) and costomediastinal (behind the sternum where costal pleura becomes mediastinal pleura, more conspicuous on the left near the heart).
A(vi)
• Blood supply: visceral pleura from bronchial and pulmonary arteries, veins to the pulmonary vein; parietal pleura from the vessels of the structures covered - cervical and costal from intercostal vessels, diaphragmatic outer part from intercostal and inner part from pericardiophrenic vessels, mediastinal from pericardiophrenic vessels.
• Nerve supply: costal pleura by intercostal nerves; diaphragmatic pleura by phrenic nerves centrally and intercostal nerves peripherally; mediastinal pleura by the phrenic nerve; the visceral pleura is described as having no nerve supply and as receiving vasomotor supply from autonomic nerves (pulmonary plexuses).
• Lymph: visceral to the pulmonary plexus in interlobar and peribronchial spaces; parietal costal, mediastinal and cervical to the internal thoracic (anterior) and intercostal (posterior) chains; diaphragmatic to retrosternal, mediastinal and sometimes coeliac nodes.
B(i)
The cervical pleura reaches about 1 inch (2.5 cm) above the clavicle because of the oblique slope of the first rib, so it can be wounded (pneumothorax) by a stab wound, a surgeon's knife or an anaesthetist's needle above the clavicle; the lower edge descends just below the 12th rib medially (below the 11th if the 12th is short), so it may be opened in a loin incision.
B(ii)
The costodiaphragmatic recess is the larger recess and the clinically more important one, providing the space where fluid collects in disease (pneumothorax with air, haemothorax with blood, empyema with pus, effusion); fluid is drained with a needle just above a rib, or through the space between the 7th costal cartilage and the xiphoid process.
C(i)
• Parietal: thicker, outer, lines wall, diaphragm, mediastinum and neck, named regionally, can be stripped, supplied by intercostal and phrenic nerves (so pleural irritation refers pain along the thoracic and anterior abdominal wall, and to the shoulder from the central diaphragm).
• Visceral: inner layer closely adherent to the lung surface and fissures, cannot be stripped, smooth and slippery so the lung moves freely, supplied by bronchial and pulmonary vessels; pleurisy is inflammation of the pleura, usually with pneumonia or other lung infection.

questions.answerText:
(i)
• The spleen receives its arterial supply from the splenic artery, the largest branch of the coeliac trunk.
• The splenic artery runs laterally along the superior aspect of the pancreas, within the splenorenal ligament.
• As it reaches the spleen it branches into about five vessels, each supplying a different vascular segment of the spleen.
• Along its course it also gives off the short gastric and left gastroepiploic arteries to the stomach, and pancreatic branches to the pancreas.
• Venous drainage is through the splenic vein, which combines with the superior mesenteric vein to form the hepatic portal vein.
(ii)
• The terminal arterial branches of the splenic artery do not anastomose with one another, so each supplies an independent vascular segment of the spleen.
• This segmental (end-arterial) arrangement allows a surgeon to remove one diseased or injured segment (subtotal splenectomy) without compromising the blood supply of the remaining segments.
(iii)
• The tail of the pancreas lies within the splenorenal ligament, close to the splenic vessels at the hilum, and may be injured during splenectomy, producing a pancreatic fistula.
• The spleen is the most frequently injured organ in the abdomen despite protection by the 9th to 12th ribs.
• Severe blows to the left side may fracture ribs, producing sharp fragments that lacerate the spleen.
• Blunt trauma elsewhere that suddenly raises intra-abdominal pressure can also rupture the spleen because its capsule is thin and its pulp is soft and pulpy.
• A ruptured spleen bleeds profusely, causing severe intraperitoneal haemorrhage and shock, so splenectomy or subtotal splenectomy is often required to prevent the patient from bleeding to death.

A fibroserous sac that encloses the heart and the roots of the great vessels; it lies behind the body of the sternum and the 2nd-6th costal cartilages and in front of the T5-T8 vertebrae; it is attached to the central tendon of the diaphragm (pericardiophrenic ligament).
A(ii)
The outer fibrous tissue layer, enclosing the heart and the roots of the great vessels (the IVC excepted, as stated); its base is attached to the central tendon of the diaphragm.
A(iii)
Thin, elastic tissue lining the fibrous pericardium, made of a parietal layer (lines and fuses with the fibrous pericardium) and a visceral layer (forms the epicardium of the heart and encloses the aorta and pulmonary trunk); between them lies the pericardial cavity containing pericardial fluid.
A(iv)
Transverse sinus: formed by a tear in the dorsal mesocardium; lies behind the aorta and pulmonary trunk, in front of the SVC on the right and the left atrium on the left.
A(v)
Oblique sinus: a blind sac (cul-de-sac) formed as a result of the entrance of the 4 pulmonary veins and the IVC into the heart; lies behind the 2 left pulmonary veins and in front of the 2 right pulmonary veins and the IVC.
A(vi)
• Blood supply: fibrous pericardium from the pericardiophrenic and musculophrenic arteries; serous pericardium from the coronary arteries; veins drain to the azygos system, and the pericardiophrenic vein drains to the internal thoracic vein.
• Nerve supply: the fibrous and parietal pericardium by the phrenic nerve; the visceral pericardium by autonomic nerves.
B(i)
• Draining of pericardial fluid is done between the 7th costal cartilage and the xiphoid process.
• In pulmonary embolectomy a temporary ligature is passed through the transverse sinus to occlude the aorta and pulmonary trunk; the oblique sinus allows for pulsation of the left atrium.
B(ii)
Pain from irritation of the pleura or pericardium covering the central part of the diaphragm may be referred to the shoulder, because the phrenic nerve (C3,4,5) supplies the central diaphragm and the pericardium, and the supraclavicular nerve (C3,4) supplies the shoulder skin; pericarditis may also cause hiccup.
C(i)
• The transverse sinus is a passage formed by a tear in the dorsal mesocardium, lying behind the great arteries and used for the ligature; the oblique sinus is a blind sac formed by the entry of the pulmonary veins and IVC, allowing pulsation of the left atrium.
• The fibrous pericardium is the outer fibrous layer with phrenic nerve and pericardiophrenic/musculophrenic arterial supply; the serous pericardium is thin and elastic, with a parietal layer fused to the fibrous layer and a visceral layer forming the epicardium, supplied by coronary arteries and autonomic nerves.

A(i) Describe the origin, structural components, and classification of neurons under the following headings: cell body (soma), dendrites, axon, myelin sheath, nodes of Ranvier, and neurilemma.
A(ii) State the basis of why local anaesthetics block nerve impulse transmission.
B(i) Explain the anatomical basis of why nerve fibers within the CNS do not regenerate after injury, while peripheral nerve fibers may regenerate.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Cell body (soma): The neuronal cell body is similar to other cell types; it has a nucleus with at least one nucleolus and many typical cytoplasmic organelles. It lacks centrioles, which is consistent with the amitotic nature of neurons. Dendrites: Dendrites are cytoplasmic extensions that project from the cell body; they are usually short and branching, increasing their surface area to receive signals from other neurons. The number of dendrites varies. They are called afferent processes because they transmit impulses to the neuron cell body. Axon: There is only one axon projecting from each cell body; it is usually elongated and carries impulses away from the cell body, so it is called an efferent process. Axons may have infrequent branches called axon collaterals; these terminate in short branches or telodendria, whose distal ends are slightly enlarged to form synaptic bulbs. Myelin sheath: Many axons are surrounded by a segmented, white, fatty substance called myelin or myelin sheath. Myelinated fibers make up the white matter in the CNS, while cell bodies and unmyelinated fibers make the gray matter. Nodes of Ranvier: The unmyelinated regions between myelin segments are called nodes of Ranvier. Neurilemma: In the peripheral nervous system, myelin is produced by Schwann cells. The cytoplasm, nucleus, and outer cell membrane of the Schwann cell form a tight covering around the myelin and around the axon at the nodes of Ranvier — this covering is the neurilemma, which plays an important role in regeneration of nerve fibers.
A(ii)
Most local anesthetics are low-molecular-weight molecules that bind to the voltage-gated sodium channels of the axolemma, interfering with sodium ion influx and, consequently, inhibiting the action potential responsible for the nerve impulse.
B(i)
In the CNS, oligodendrocytes produce myelin, but there is no neurilemma. It is the neurilemma that plays an important role in regeneration of nerve fibers; therefore fibers within the CNS do not regenerate because they lack neurilemma.

questions.question:
Describe the ulnar nerve:
A(i) Origin
A(ii) Course and common entrapment sites
A(iii) Muscles innervated (forearm and hand)
A(iv) Sensory distribution
C. Explain the anatomical basis of the deformity seen after ulnar nerve injury.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The ulnar nerve is an extension of the medial cord of the brachial plexus.
A(ii)
The most common sites of ulnar nerve entrapment are: above the elbow in the region of the intermuscular septum; the medial epicondylar region; the epicondylar (ulnar) groove; the region of the cubital tunnel; and the region where the nerve exits from flexor carpi ulnaris, where compression is usually caused by the deep flexor-pronator aponeurosis.
A(iii)
• In the forearm it supplies flexor carpi ulnaris and the medial (3rd & 4th) part of flexor digitorum profundus.
• In the hand it supplies the hypothenar muscles, adductor pollicis, flexor pollicis brevis, the palmar and dorsal interossei, the 3rd and 4th lumbricals, and the muscles of digiti minimi (abductor, opponens, flexor digiti minimi).
A(iv)
It provides sensation to the medial surface of the hand and the medial half of the 4th and 5th digits, on both palmar and dorsal aspects, through its superficial branch; its motor functions include finger adduction and abduction other than the thumb, thumb adduction, flexion of digits 4 and 5, and wrist flexion and adduction.
C
• Injury to the ulnar nerve, or to the medial cord/lower trunk from which it derives, produces a claw hand deformity.
• This deformity arises from the unopposed action of the long flexors and extensors of the fingers once the ulnar-innervated intrinsic muscles (interossei, medial lumbricals) are paralysed.
• In a claw hand there is hyperextension at the metacarpophalangeal joints and flexion at the interphalangeal joints.
• Where the injury occurs at the level of the medial cord (e.g. from subcoracoid dislocation of the humerus), the ulnar nerve and medial root of median nerve are both involved.
• This produces sensory loss on the ulnar side of the forearm and hand, along with vasomotor and trophic changes.
• The claw hand deformity, together with the specific pattern of muscle paralysis, thus reflects the level and combination of nerve fibres interrupted along the course of the ulnar nerve or its parent cord/trunk.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Exercise assessment includes exercise stress testing (maximal or submaximal), activity and endurance evaluation, and functional status testing, most commonly the 6-minute walk test (6MWT) and 12-minute walk test (12MWT), alongside skin testing for other purposes.
A(i) For reduced exercise tolerance, problem identification includes disease profile and history, mobility status, distance mobilised on the ward, stair-climbing ability, requirement for oxygen, and results of the 6-minute walk test and shuttle walk test.
A(ii) These tests are used as outcome measures/tools across multiple respiratory conditions, including COPD (6-minute, 12-minute and shuttle walk tests), bronchiectasis (6-minute walk test/shuttle walk test), pulmonary oedema, pleural effusion and lung cancer (6-minute walk test).
A(ii) Goals set from these tests are typically SMART, for example: mobilise a set distance with assistance within a set number of days, climb a set number of flights of stairs independently within a set number of days, or walk/jog at a set pace for a set duration.
B. Reduced walking distance or reduced performance on the 6-minute walk test/shuttle walk test relates to conditions with impaired oxygen transport, such as COPD, bronchiectasis, pulmonary oedema, pleural effusion and lung cancer, where reduced exercise tolerance is a shared problem.
B. In COPD specifically, exercise capacity and physical activity level (6-minute walk test, 12-minute walk test, shuttle walk test) are grouped as functional outcomes alongside symptomatic outcomes such as dyspnoea.
B. The requirement for supplemental oxygen during exercise testing is also a marker of the degree of functional impairment relevant to reduced exercise tolerance.
C. Reduced exercise tolerance represents a functional deficit that limits the patient's mobility, functional independence and quality of life, and can extend to other systems as reduced cardiovascular endurance in conditions such as pulmonary oedema.
C. Physiotherapy addresses this deficit through a physiological hierarchy that includes mobilisation and exercise, body positioning, breathing control manoeuvres and coughing manoeuvres, since immobility and recumbence are major factors contributing to impaired oxygen transport.
C. Treatment plans for reduced exercise tolerance include a graduated mobilisation programme (twice a day or as a daily routine), walking aids, oxygen therapy, home programmes and strengthening programmes.
C. Mobilisation is prescribed based on the exercise testing protocol and metabolic equivalents (METs), setting intensity within safe limits of the patient's oxygen transport capacity and combining body positions (especially upright) with various manoeuvres.
C. Progression is based on the patient's response (changes in measures/indices of oxygen transport) rather than time alone, with the intensity or duration of the mobilisation stimulus increased as tolerated, in the absence of distress.
