questions.answerText:
A(i) The pleura consists of the visceral pleura (covering the lung surface) and the parietal pleura (lining the thoracic wall), separated by the pleural space containing pleural fluid, a dynamic layer between the two pleural surfaces.
A(i) Two forces hold the thoracic wall and lungs in close apposition, stretching the lungs to fill the large thoracic cavity: intrapleural fluid cohesiveness (the polarity of water attracting wet surfaces) and the transmural pressure gradient, since atmospheric pressure (760mmHg) is greater than intrapleural pressure (756mmHg).
A(ii) Intrapulmonary pressure and intrapleural pressure fluctuate with the phases of breathing; intrapulmonary pressure always eventually equalises with atmospheric pressure, while intrapleural pressure is always less than both intrapulmonary pressure and atmospheric pressure.
A(ii) This pressure relationship keeps the lung stretched against the thoracic wall, so that any change in the pressure gradient across the pleura directly affects lung expansion.
B. Clinically, large pleural effusions are listed as a contraindication for airway clearance techniques, since excess pleural fluid limits lung expansion and increases risk with positional and manual techniques.
B. An upright posture, which is generally encouraged since functional residual capacity varies with body position, is also relevant in patients with pleural pathology who are often more comfortable and better able to breathe when sitting upright rather than lying flat.
B. In pleural effusion, physiotherapy management includes breathing control, thoracic expansion exercises and incentive spirometry to increase lung volumes and control breathing, aiding chest fluid drainage where possible.
C. Pleural effusion is the excessive accumulation of fluid in the pleural space, resulting from an imbalance between production and clearance of pleural fluid, and is a reflection of underlying pathology in the lung, pleura, or a systemic condition rather than a specific disease itself.
C. It may arise from altered permeability of the pleural membranes, reduction in intravascular oncotic pressure, increased capillary hydrostatic pressure, reduced pressure in the pleural space (trapped lung), decreased lymphatic drainage or thoracic duct obstruction, increased peritoneal fluid, or movement of fluid from pulmonary oedema across the visceral pleura.
C. Pleural fluid is classified by origin (hydrothorax, haemothorax, chylothorax, pyothorax/empyema, urinothorax) or by pathophysiology as transudative (e.g. from congestive heart failure, cirrhosis, atelectasis) or exudative (e.g. from malignancy, pulmonary embolism, tuberculosis, trauma).
C. The excess fluid in the pleural space obstructs breathing by limiting the expansion of the lungs, presenting clinically as chest pain worse with breathing, diminished chest expansion and a stony dull percussion note.
C. Similarly, air entering the pleural space (pneumothorax) is described as producing abnormal ventilating lungs with altered compliance.

A patient develops pleural effusion secondary to an underlying malignancy.
(i) State the likely type of effusion and its causes.
(ii) Explain the pathogenesis of this condition.
(iii) State the key assessment/clinical findings expected.
(iv) List the physiotherapy goals.
(v) Outline the physiotherapy management.
questions.answerText:
(i) Exudative pleural effusion; causes include malignancy, pulmonary embolism, tuberculosis, trauma, sarcoidosis, fungal infection, pericardial disease and radiation pleuritis, resulting from inflammatory processes of the pleura and/or decreased lymphatic drainage.
(ii) Altered permeability of the pleural membranes, reduction in intravascular oncotic pressure, increased capillary hydrostatic pressure, reduction of pleural space pressure (trapped lung), decreased lymphatic drainage or thoracic duct obstruction, increased peritoneal fluid, or movement of fluid from pulmonary oedema across the visceral pleura.
(iii) Chest pain especially with breathing, diminished chest expansion, breathing difficulties, and cough (dry or productive); the excess fluid obstructs breathing by limiting expansion of the lungs.
(iv) Short-term goals: relieving pain associated with breathing, improving chest excursion, increasing lung volumes, controlling breathing, aiding chest fluid drainage and clearing chest secretions if any; long-term goals: increasing cardiopulmonary endurance, increasing functional capacity, improving quality of life.
(v) Breathing control, thoracic expansion exercises, incentive spirometry, airway clearance techniques (if necessary), assisted cough, graded exercises, and patient education and counselling.

questions.question:
Describe the Active Cycle of Breathing Technique (ACBT) under the following headings: A(i) definition, A(ii) indications, A(iii) contraindications, A(iv) procedure, A(v) physiological effects.
B. Explain the clinical basis for how ACBT mobilises secretions.
C. Distinguish between ACBT and Autogenic Drainage.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Active Cycle of Breathing Technique (ACBT) is a combination of breathing control, thoracic expansion exercises and the forced expiratory technique (FET) performed in cycles to enhance cephalad airflow bias and mobilise secretions.
A(ii) It is indicated as an airway clearance technique for conditions such as cystic fibrosis, atelectasis, asthma, respiratory muscle weakness, bronchiectasis and mechanical ventilation.
A(iii) General contraindications for airway clearance techniques apply, including untreated pneumothorax, active haemoptysis, active haemorrhage with haemodynamic instability, large pleural effusions and recent spinal surgery.
A(iv) Breathing control uses diaphragmatic or gentle lower-chest breathing, with the upper chest and shoulders relaxed at a normal tidal volume and rate, forming the default relaxed breathing manoeuvre between active components.
A(iv) Thoracic expansion exercises are active inspirations with larger-than-normal breaths followed by relaxed expiration, typically limited to cycles of 3 to 4 deep breaths to avoid fatigue and hyperventilation.
A(v) The forced expiratory technique consists of 1 or 2 huffs from middle to low lung volume with the mouth and glottis open, active but not violent or explosive, combined with a period of controlled breathing.
B. The larger lung volume from thoracic expansion increases airflow through peripheral airways and collateral ventilation channels, increasing the gas volume available to mobilise secretions during expiration.
B. The huff creates a shear force on the mucus without the fatigue of repeated coughing, while interspersed breathing control periods prevent bronchospasm and hyperventilation between active manoeuvres.
C. Autogenic drainage is a self-drainage technique described by Jean Chevaillier in 1967, using controlled expiratory airflow (tidal breathing) to mobilise secretions, and is generally practised in sitting.
C. It consists of three phases: un-sticking (a big breath out, small breath in, mobilising secretions in the small airways), collecting (middle-sized breaths in and out, moving secretions into the main airways), and evacuating (taking in as much air as possible then slowly sighing out to bring secretions to the throat).
C. The urge to cough is suppressed until the evacuating phase, when gentle active huffs are used to remove secretions from the mouth, unlike ACBT which uses active huffing (FET) throughout its cycle.
C. Autogenic drainage does not require postural drainage positions, generally takes 30-40 minutes up to an hour and 10-20 hours to learn from trained staff (from age 8-12 years), whereas ACBT is simpler to learn and can be combined with postural drainage.

A(i) Sputum is a normal secretion, about 100mL produced daily in normal adults and cleared subconsciously by coughing or huffing; it may contain mucus, cellular debris, microorganisms, blood and foreign particles, and questioning should determine its colour, consistency, odour, taste and the quantity produced each day.
A(ii) Miller's (1968) sputum grading classifies sputum as M1 (mucoid, no suspicion of pus), M2 (predominantly mucoid, suspicious of pus), P1 (one-third purulent, two-thirds mucoid), P2 (two-thirds purulent, one-third mucoid) and P3 (more than two-thirds purulent); in clinical practice sputum is usually simply classified as mucoid, mucopurulent or purulent.
A(ii) Sputum cast may be seen in asthma and bronchiectasis, and haemoptysis (blood in sputum) is a further finding to be noted; sputum culture identifies causative organisms, such as tubercle bacilli in tuberculosis.
A(ii) Sputum volume is used quantitatively: more than 30mL in 24 hours for at least 3 months of the year for 2 consecutive years defines the cough of chronic bronchitis, while sputum exceeding 500mL a day may be seen in bronchiectasis.
B. Copious purulent sputum relates to bronchiectasis, where secretions may exceed 500mL a day and haemoptysis occurs in about half of cases; excessive mucus secretion also relates to chronic bronchitis, where sputum is thick and obstructs airflow.
B. Sputum culture positive for tubercle bacilli relates to pulmonary tuberculosis, alongside other investigation findings such as chest X-ray consolidation and cavity formation.
B. Moist cough with sputum expectorated, alongside coarse or fine crackles on auscultation and consolidation on chest X-ray, relates to the problem of retention of secretions requiring airway clearance.
C. Excessive, retained or purulent sputum represents a functional deficit in airway clearance that obstructs airflow, provides a medium for infection, and can extend to systemic effects such as raised temperature and altered gas exchange if secretions are not cleared.
C. In bronchiectasis, retained purulent secretions in bronchiectatic segments reduce expiratory volume and vital capacity and reduce quality of life, extending the deficit to functional and respiratory capacity.
C. Postural drainage is used specifically when sputum production exceeds 30cc a day (as noted for COPD), directing gravity-assisted drainage of the affected segments.
C. Physiotherapy addresses sputum-related problems through positioning, manual techniques (percussion, vibration), and airway clearance techniques (ACBT, autogenic drainage, forced expiratory technique), aiming for independent expectoration and reduction of sputum volume as treatment goals.
C. Monitoring sputum volume, colour and consistency, alongside sputum culture results where infection is suspected, guides both the intensity of airway clearance physiotherapy and the need for urgent referral for appropriate antibiotic treatment.
questions.question:

A(ii) State the sputum grading system used and other sputum-related findings.
B. State how sputum findings relate to common respiratory conditions.

Describe Positive Expiratory Pressure (PEP) therapy under the following headings: A(i) definition, A(ii) indications, A(iii) contraindications/precautions, A(iv) procedure, A(v) physiological effects.
B. Explain the clinical basis of airway oscillation devices as a form of PEP therapy.
C. Distinguish between the Flutter device and the Acapella device.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Positive expiratory pressure (PEP) therapy involves active expiration through a one-way valve against a variable flow resistor, delivered via a facemask or mouthpiece, and was developed in Denmark in the late 1970s.
A(ii) It is indicated for airway clearance in conditions requiring secretion mobilisation, and can be incorporated into the thoracic expansion phase of the Active Cycle of Breathing Technique.
A(iii) Precautions include untreated pneumothorax, severe haemoptysis, facial fractures or surgery, sinusitis or ear problems, and hyper-reactive airways (which may provoke early uncontrolled coughing).
A(iv) The patient exhales at an expiratory pressure of 10-20cmH2O during the middle phase of exhalation, with breaths of tidal volume or slightly larger and an inspiration:expiration ratio of 1:3 to 1:4, for 5-20 breaths repeated 4-6 times over a 10-20 minute session.
A(v) Resistance to expiratory flow limits compression of compliant airways and facilitates collateral airflow between ventilated and atelectatic alveoli through the pores of Kohn, generating flow behind obstructing mucus to expel it.
B. Airway oscillation devices add an oscillating pressure within the airway to standard PEP; the oscillations reduce the viscoelasticity of mucus and provide short bursts of increased expiratory airflow that help mobilise secretions.
B. The Flutter is a pipe-shaped airway oscillation device, developed in Switzerland in the early 1990s, containing a steel ball resting in an angled, upward-widening bowl.
B. On exhalation into the Flutter, the ball oscillates at approximately 15Hz (range 8-26Hz), providing 5-25cmH2O resistance; the patient takes a deep breath with a 2-3 second hold, then exhales fully, adjusting the device's angle and flow rate to attain optimal vibration.
C. The Flutter is gravity-dependent, requiring the device to be held at a specific angle for the ball to oscillate, which makes it difficult to combine with postural drainage; the Acapella uses a counterweighted plug and magnet to achieve valve closure and is therefore not gravity-dependent.
C. This means the Acapella can be used in virtually any position, allowing patients to move freely and sit, stand or recline, unlike the Flutter which needs a set orientation.
C. The Acapella, designed by Smiths Medical, combines the benefits of PEP therapy and airway vibration and is available in low-flow, high-flow and choice models with adjustable frequency and flow resistance.
C. The Acapella additionally allows inhalation and exhalation without removing it from the mouth, can be fitted with an inline nebulizer adapter, and may be used after a short-acting bronchodilator to enhance effectiveness, giving it greater practical flexibility than the Flutter.

A(i) The muscles of respiration are of two types: inspiratory and expiratory muscles.
A(i) The primary inspiratory muscles are the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles, while accessory inspiratory muscles are the sternocleidomastoid, scalene, serratus anterior, levator scapulae, erector spinae, and pectoralis major and minor.
A(i) The primary muscle of expiration is the internal intercostal muscles, while the accessory muscles of expiration are the abdominal muscles.
A(ii) The diaphragm is a large, dome-shaped muscle at the base of the chest cavity and, with the intercostal muscles between the ribs, is under the precise control of the central nervous system, generating the pumping action that moves air in and out of the lungs.
A(ii) During inspiration the diaphragm contracts and flattens while the intercostal muscles contract, lifting the rib cage up and out, increasing thoracic cavity volume and decreasing intrapulmonary pressure so air rushes in down its pressure gradient.
A(ii) During expiration the diaphragm relaxes and returns to its dome shape while the intercostals relax, allowing the rib cage to move down and in, decreasing thoracic volume and increasing intrapulmonary pressure so air is forced out.
B. Clinically, the use of accessory muscles of breathing (e.g. scalenes, sternocleidomastoids) signifies some element of respiratory difficulty and should be observed for during patient assessment.
B. In physiotherapy, facilitation of the accessory muscles of respiration - pectoralis major, sternocleidomastoid, trapezius and serratus anterior - is used as a technique to facilitate ventilation pattern in patients with respiratory dysfunction.
B. Body positioning to mobilise the thorax and facilitate accessory muscle use is combined with breathing techniques such as diaphragmatic breathing to optimise the patient's ventilation pattern.
C. Normally, descent of the diaphragm pushes intra-abdominal contents downward and the abdominal wall outward during inspiration.
C. In cases of severe diaphragmatic flattening (as in emphysema) or diaphragmatic paralysis, the abdominal wall may instead move inward during inspiration, a phenomenon referred to as paradoxical breathing, which can be accentuated by placing a hand on the patient's abdomen while they breathe.
C. When the primary muscles fail or are overloaded, the body increasingly recruits the accessory muscles of respiration, and their visible use during assessment is therefore a sign of increased work of breathing and respiratory compromise.

questions.answerText:
(i) The patient requires mechanical ventilation, as these are the concerning findings indicating the patient cannot maintain an airway or adequate oxygenation/ventilation.
(ii) Indications include prophylactic (pre-existing lung disease, site of surgery, obesity), intra-operative (adverse effects during surgery) and therapeutic bases (respiratory failure type 1, 2 or 3); mechanical ventilation should be considered based on clinical judgement of the entire clinical situation and not delayed until the patient is in extreme condition.
(iii) Level of ventilatory support and mode, route of ventilation, level of cardiovascular support and consciousness (GCS), vital sign charts (temperature, heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate), airway pressure, auscultation, and arterial blood gases (normal pH 7.35-7.45, PaCO2 35-45mmHg, PaO2 80-100mmHg, HCO3 22-26mmol/l).
(iv) Problems relate to retention of secretions, increased work of breathing, decreased lung volume and reduced exercise tolerance; goals include independent expectoration, reduced perceived breathlessness/exertion, resolution of chest X-ray and auscultation findings, and increased mobilisation distance as appropriate.
(v) Positioning in side lying, manual techniques, airway clearing techniques and nasopharyngeal suction for secretion retention; manual hyperinflation to aid secretion removal and reinflate atelectatic segments; mobilisation once stable, progressing toward weaning from mechanical ventilation.

A patient with known lung cancer develops bone pain, enlarged supraclavicular nodes, hepatomegaly and neurological symptoms.
(i) Identify the pathological process suggested by these findings.
(ii) State the differential clinical features associated with lung cancer.
(iii) Explain the clinical reasoning for physiotherapy technique selection given the multisystem involvement.
questions.answerText:
(i) These findings suggest local and distant spread of the lung cancer (invasion of nearby tissues and involvement of other systems), consistent with cancer being a disease in which abnormal cells divide without control and can invade nearby tissues.
(ii) Differential clinical features include cough, dyspnoea, chest pain, haemoptysis, weight loss/anorexia, hoarse voice, anaemia, bone pain, clubbing of the fingers, supraclavicular nodes, pleural effusion, hepatomegaly and neurological symptoms/signs.
(iii) Because the problem list includes pain, reduced chest excursion/lung volumes, excessive/retained secretion, altered arterial blood gases, general body weakness, poor posture, fatigue and reduced functional capacity, physiotherapy reasoning favours a combination of positioning, breathing exercises, incentive spirometry, airway clearance techniques, mobilization, muscle strengthening, postural re-education and functional training to address the multiple systems affected.

questions.question:
A patient presents with orthopnoea, difficulty breathing, peripheral oedema, reduced exercise tolerance, dyspnoea, pale skin, anxiety, a crackling heart sound and weight gain.
(i) State the most likely diagnosis.
(ii) Name the physiotherapy techniques indicated for this condition.
(iii) State the positioning principle applied.
(iv) State the progression and outcome measures used.
questions.answerText:
(i) Pulmonary oedema.
(ii) Relaxation exercises, breathing exercises, oedema massage and aerobic exercises.
(iii) An upright posture is encouraged since functional residual capacity varies with body position; severely dyspnoeic patients often need to sit completely upright, while those with less severe distress may find a semi-upright position suitable.
(iv) Progression is guided by improvement in breathing pattern and reduction of oedema; outcome measures include spirometry, BODE score, circumferential measurement and the 6-minute walk test.

A(i) Manual hyperinflation (bagging) was originally defined as inflating the lungs with oxygen and manual compression to a tidal volume of 1 litre requiring a peak inspiratory pressure of 20-40cmH2O; more recent definitions describe delivering a tidal volume 50% greater than that delivered via the ventilator.
A(ii) It is indicated to aid removal of secretions, aid reinflation of atelectatic segments, and to assess or improve lung compliance.
A(iii) Contraindications include undrained pneumothorax, potential or severe bronchospasm, gross cardiovascular instability causing arrhythmias and hypovolaemia, unexplained haemoptysis, and patients on high PEEP.
A(iv) The technique involves slow deep inspiration, an inspiratory hold at full inspiration, a fast expiratory release, and hand-held pressure support.
A(v) Advantages include reversal of atelectasis and improvement in oxygen saturation, lung compliance and sputum clearance, though disadvantages include haemodynamic and metabolic upset, risk of barotrauma, and discomfort and anxiety.
B. Incentive spirometry is listed as a treatment option for decreased lung volume, alongside positioning, thoracic expansion exercises, intermittent positive pressure breathing (IPPB) and mobilisation, and its readings are also used as a goal/outcome to demonstrate resolution of volume loss.
B. Increasing functional residual capacity, which incentive spirometry aims to achieve, has been found to contribute to the prevention and reversal of atelectasis; when incentive spirometry alone does not open the patient's airways, options can be expanded with devices such as EzPAP.
C. Manual hyperinflation is an externally delivered technique performed by a therapist (or ventilator/bagging circuit) on an intubated or dependent patient, whereas incentive spirometry is a self-directed, voluntary deep-breathing exercise performed by a spontaneously breathing, cooperative patient.
C. Manual hyperinflation directly manipulates airway pressure and tidal volume through external compression and carries risks such as barotrauma and cardiovascular instability.
C. Incentive spirometry instead relies on the patient's own inspiratory effort against a visual/flow target device to sustain lung expansion, with its role being to increase functional residual capacity.
C. Both aim to reverse or prevent atelectasis and increase lung volume, but manual hyperinflation is reserved for patients unable to generate adequate spontaneous breaths.
C. Incentive spirometry is used in spontaneously breathing patients as a first-line lung expansion measure before considering devices like EzPAP.
questions.question:
Describe manual hyperinflation (bagging) under the following headings: A(i) definition, A(ii) indications, A(iii) contraindications, A(iv) procedure, A(v) physiological effects (advantages/disadvantages).
B. Explain the clinical basis for the use of incentive spirometry as an alternative lung-expansion technique.
C. Distinguish between manual hyperinflation and incentive spirometry.

A(i) Describe the procedure for inspection/observation of a breathing patient.
A(ii) State the breathing patterns and chest shape abnormalities identifiable on inspection.
B. State how inspection/observation findings relate to common respiratory conditions.
C. Explain how these observational findings represent a functional deficit and how physiotherapy addresses it.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Inspection/observation gathers information simply by watching the patient breathe, paying attention to general comfort and breathing pattern, colour (particularly around the lips and nail beds), the patient's position, breathing through pursed lips, ability to speak, audible noises associated with breathing, direction of abdominal wall movement during inspiration, and any chest or spine deformities.
A(i) Comfort and breathing pattern are assessed by noting whether the patient appears distressed, diaphoretic or laboured, whether breaths are regular and deep, and whether accessory muscles of breathing (e.g. scalenes, sternocleidomastoids) are being used, which signifies respiratory difficulty.
A(ii) Breathing patterns observed include normal breathing, prolonged expiration, pursed-lip breathing, apnoea, hypopnoea, Kussmaul respiration, Cheyne-Stokes breathing, ataxic breathing and apneustic breathing; chest shape observations include kyphosis, kyphoscoliosis, pectus excavatum, pectus carinatum and hyperinflation.
A(ii) Ability to speak is assessed by noting how many words the patient can speak per breath (the fewer words, the worse the problem), and audible noises such as wheezing or gurgling from secretions in large airways may occasionally be heard without a stethoscope.
B. Those with extreme pulmonary dysfunction will often sit upright, and in cases of real distress lean forward resting their hands on their knees in the tripod position, as seen in patients with emphysema.
B. Breathing through pursed lips is often seen in cases of emphysema, and normally the descent of the diaphragm pushes intra-abdominal contents down and the abdominal wall outward during inspiration.
B. In cases of severe diaphragmatic flattening (as in emphysema) or paralysis, the abdominal wall may instead move inward during inspiration, known as paradoxical breathing, accentuated by placing a hand on the patient's abdomen while they breathe.
C. The tripod position, pursed-lip breathing and paradoxical breathing are findings that relate to severe pulmonary dysfunction, particularly emphysema, reflecting the functional deficit of severely compromised ventilatory mechanics.
C. Barrel chest (increased anterior-posterior diameter with diaphragmatic flattening) also relates to emphysema, while pectus excavatum, kyphosis and scoliosis are deformities that can impair a patient's ability to breathe normally, whether congenital, acquired, or resulting from chronic lung disease.
C. Cyanosis, particularly of the nail beds, indicates a functional deficit in oxygenation and is described in assessment as 'blue is bad'.
C. These observational findings extend beyond the respiratory system to functional impact, since reduced ability to speak in full sentences and use of the tripod position reflect a degree of functional impairment significant enough to limit normal activity and conversation.
C. Physiotherapy uses these observations to guide immediate management, such as positioning the severely dyspnoeic patient upright, teaching pursed-lip breathing (as already adopted spontaneously by many emphysema patients) and addressing accessory muscle overuse through breathing control and relaxation techniques.

questions.question:
Describe non-invasive ventilation (NIV) under the following headings: A(i) definition, A(ii) indications, A(iii) contraindications, A(iv) advantages, A(v) physiological effects.
B. Explain the clinical basis and indications for invasive mechanical ventilation.
C. Distinguish between NIV and invasive mechanical ventilation.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Non-invasive ventilation (NIV), also called non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (NPPV), delivers mechanical ventilatory support using various types of face masks rather than an artificial airway, allowing relatively unrestricted breathing and improved comfort of ventilation.
A(ii) Indications for NIV include prevention of intubation in a patient who is not immediately deteriorating, early management of immunocompromised patients with acute respiratory failure, post-operative acute respiratory failure, palliation for dyspnoea in terminal conditions such as cancer, prevention of post-extubation respiratory failure, and COPD with hypercapnia.
A(iii) Absolute contraindications for NIV are facial trauma/burns, fixed upper airway obstruction, active vomiting, and respiratory or cardiac arrest; relative contraindications include recent facial, upper airway or upper gastrointestinal surgery, altered mental status and haemodynamic instability.
A(iv) NIV reduces the use of sedatives and relaxants compared with invasive ventilation, since the patient can continue to breathe with less restriction while still receiving positive pressure support.
A(v) Physiologically, NIV reduces the patient's work of breathing while avoiding the risks associated with an artificial airway, as long as the patient can protect their own airway.
B. Invasive mechanical ventilation involves endotracheal intubation (or tracheostomy) and positive pressure ventilation, and is indicated for airway compromise (reduced consciousness, dynamic airway, airway obstruction), hypoventilation (impaired central drive, respiratory muscle weakness, restrictive ventilatory defects), hypoxaemic respiratory failure (alveolar filling or diffusion defects, pulmonary vascular defects) and increased ventilatory demand (severe sepsis, shock, severe metabolic acidosis).
B. Complications of invasive ventilation include pulmonary barotrauma/alveolar rupture, infection, oxygen toxicity, respiratory muscle weakness, laryngeal/tracheal trauma, and decreased cardiac output due to increased intrathoracic pressure and reduced venous return.
B. Selection and use of either technique requires understanding of respiratory mechanics, and invasive ventilation is usually handled by the anaesthetist/intensivist.
C. NIV uses a mask interface and preserves the patient's own airway, whereas invasive ventilation bypasses the natural airway with an endotracheal or tracheostomy tube.
C. Because it avoids an artificial airway, NIV carries a lower risk of airway trauma and typically requires less sedation than invasive ventilation, but it depends on the patient being able to protect their airway and cooperate with the mask.
C. Invasive ventilation is required when airway protection is compromised, when hypoventilation or hypoxaemic failure is severe, or when absolute contraindications to NIV exist (e.g. facial trauma, active vomiting, respiratory/cardiac arrest).
C. NIV is generally reserved for patients who are not immediately deteriorating and can be managed non-invasively (e.g. COPD with hypercapnia, palliative dyspnoea), while invasive ventilation is used for more severe, unstable, or airway-compromised presentations.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the procedure for palpating symmetric chest expansion.
A(ii) Describe the procedure for assessing tactile fremitus and other palpation findings.
B. State how palpation findings relate to common respiratory conditions.
C. Explain how reduced chest expansion represents a functional deficit and how physiotherapy addresses it.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Palpation is performed separately on the anterior and posterior chest, beginning with the posterior chest, assessing symmetric chest expansion and tactile fremitus.
A(i) For symmetric expansion, the examiner stands behind the patient, places hands parallel over the lower ribcage on both sides with thumbs at T9 or T10, moves the thumbs medially to pinch some skin, and asks the patient to inhale deeply while watching the thumbs move; normally the thumbs move apart symmetrically about 1.5 to 2 inches.
A(ii) For tactile fremitus, the patient folds their arms in front of the chest (moving the scapula out of the way), the examiner places the base of the hands symmetrically beginning at the lung apex and asks the patient to say '99' (a phrase creating strong vibration), feeling for symmetric vibrations while moving down the chest at five locations.
A(ii) General palpation uses the fingertips to gently feel for lumps, masses or tenderness over the ribs and intercostal spaces, avoiding breast tissue; the anterior chest is palpated similarly, with thumbs placed at the costal margins pointing toward the xiphoid process.
B. Reduced or asymmetric chest expansion on palpation relates to conditions that limit lung expansion on one side, such as pleural effusion (diminished chest expansion is a listed clinical feature) and post-surgical pulmonary complications.
B. Palpation of chest movement patterns (pump-handle and bucket-handle movement) and tactile/focal fremitus is part of the objective respiratory assessment used alongside inspection, percussion and auscultation.
B. Pathology that increases lung density (such as consolidation) enhances transmission of vibrations/voice sounds through the chest wall, which is the same principle underlying changes detected on tactile fremitus and voice sound testing.
C. Reduced chest expansion on the affected side represents a functional deficit in ventilation of that area, contributing to reduced lung volumes and, if secretions or fluid are present, impaired gas exchange.
C. This deficit is reflected in the problem lists of conditions such as pleural effusion (diminished chest expansion, breathing difficulties) and decreased lung volume (shallow breathing pattern).
C. Physiotherapy directs thoracic expansion exercises and positioning specifically toward the side or segment found to have reduced expansion on palpation, aiming to increase lung volumes on that side.
C. Increasing chest excursion is a stated short-term physiotherapy goal in pleural effusion, monitored in part by reassessing symmetric expansion on palpation.
C. Palpation findings therefore both localise the functional deficit and provide a simple bedside measure that physiotherapists can reassess to track improvement in chest expansion following treatment.

questions.question:
A COPD patient produces more than 30cc of sputum per day and has reduced exercise tolerance.
(i) Name the physiotherapy technique(s) indicated for secretion clearance.
(ii) State the criterion given for using postural drainage in this condition.
(iii) State the precautions relevant to airway clearance techniques.
(iv) State the progression/outcome measures for this patient.
questions.answerText:
(i) Postural drainage, chest percussion and vibration, along with breathing exercises and airway clearing techniques.
(ii) Postural drainage is used if sputum production exceeds 30cc per day.
(iii) Contraindications for airway clearance techniques include intracranial pressure above 20mmHg, active haemorrhage with haemodynamic instability, recent spinal surgery, active haemoptysis, empyema, broncho-pleural fistula, large pleural effusions, pulmonary embolism, and aged, confused or anxious patients.
(iv) Progression includes rehabilitation with exercise reconditioning to increase endurance, exercise tolerance and maximal oxygen consumption; outcome measures include lung volumes (TV, FVC, FEV1, FEV1/FVC, PEFR), exercise capacity (6-minute walk test, 12-minute walk test, shuttle walk test), dyspnoea scales (Borg, MRC, BDI/TDI) and health status questionnaires (St George's Respiratory Questionnaire, SF-36) as well as the BODE index.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the role and use of chest X-ray as an investigative tool in respiratory assessment.
A(ii) State the chest and spine deformities/abnormal findings identifiable on chest X-ray.
B. State how chest X-ray findings relate to common respiratory conditions.
C. Explain how these findings represent a functional deficit and how physiotherapy addresses it.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Chest X-ray is a good adjunct for respiratory assessment, used alongside auscultation and other investigations; in the intensive care unit an AP radiograph may magnify certain structures such as the heart, and limited optimal positioning of the patient can make interpretation difficult, so day-to-day comparison is used only as a guide.
A(i) Chest X-ray is also used to identify the position of the diaphragm, fissures and the trachea in relation to skeletal landmarks as part of a normal chest radiograph.
A(ii) Chest X-ray is used to identify chest and spine deformities: pectus excavatum shows a subtle concave appearance of the lower sternum, barrel chest shows increased anterior-posterior diameter with diaphragmatic flattening, and kyphosis/scoliosis show extreme spinal curvature, more pronounced on X-ray than clinically.
A(ii) In decreased lung volume/atelectasis, chest X-ray shows a raised diaphragm or collapse (raised hemi-diaphragm); in pulmonary tuberculosis, it shows consolidation, cavity formation, soft spreading apical shadowing and pleural effusion.
B. A raised hemi-diaphragm or area of collapse on chest X-ray relates to decreased lung volume/atelectasis, often correlating with bronchial breathing and fine crackles on auscultation and a shallow breathing pattern.
B. Consolidation, cavity formation and apical shadowing on chest X-ray relate to pulmonary tuberculosis, while consolidation/infiltrates also relate to the problem of retention of secretions, alongside a moist cough and coarse crackles.
B. Barrel chest with diaphragmatic flattening on chest X-ray relates to emphysema, while pectus excavatum and kyphoscoliosis are structural deformities that can impair a patient's ability to breathe normally.
C. These chest X-ray findings indicate a functional deficit in lung expansion or aeration, whether through collapse, consolidation, cavitation, hyperinflation or structural deformity, each compromising ventilation and, in some cases, gas exchange.
C. Where the deficit is localised (e.g. collapse of a specific lobe), the chest X-ray finding is used to direct physiotherapy positioning, such as postural drainage aimed at the affected bronchopulmonary segment.
C. Resolution of chest X-ray findings is itself listed as a treatment goal in problems such as retention of secretions and decreased lung volume, alongside resolution of auscultation findings.
C. Physiotherapy management directed at these findings includes positioning, thoracic expansion exercises, incentive spirometry, airway clearance techniques and mobilisation, aimed at re-expanding collapsed areas and clearing consolidative secretions.
C. Because interpretation in the ICU can be limited by positioning and radiographic magnification, physiotherapists use chest X-ray findings alongside auscultation, percussion and clinical assessment rather than in isolation when planning treatment.

(i) Retention of secretions (secretion retention leading to consolidation).
(ii) Predisposing factors relate to disease profile and history that impair secretion clearance, such as inability to expectorate and ineffective cough.
(iii) Inability to expectorate and an ineffective cough lead to accumulation of secretions, which is identified by a moist cough, coarse or fine crackles on auscultation or bronchial breathing, altered gas exchange and raised temperature, with chest X-ray showing consolidation/infiltrates.
(iv) Positioning in side lying, nasopharyngeal suction, manual techniques and airway clearing techniques; goals are independent expectoration within a set number of days, resolution of chest X-ray findings and resolution of auscultation findings.
questions.question:
A patient presents with a moist productive cough, coarse crackles on auscultation, raised temperature and chest X-ray findings of consolidation.
(i) What is the physiotherapy problem identified?
(ii) State the predisposing factors typically associated with this presentation.
(iii) Explain the pathophysiology of this problem.
(iv) Outline the physiotherapy management.

A(i) Describe the pressure relationships involved in the mechanics of breathing.
A(ii) Explain how these pressure changes produce inspiration and expiration.
B. State the application of body positioning based on these mechanics in physiotherapy practice.
C. Explain the physiological basis of the dysfunction that results when lung compliance is altered.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Boyle's law describes the inverse relationship between the pressure and volume of a gas (P1V1 = P2V2): as pressure decreases, volume increases, and as volume decreases, pressure increases.
A(i) Intrapulmonary pressure (within the alveoli) is about 760mmHg and always eventually equalises with atmospheric pressure, while intrapleural pressure (within the pleural cavity) is about 756mmHg and is always less than both intrapulmonary and atmospheric pressure.
A(ii) During inspiration, the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles contract, the rib cage rises, the lungs stretch and intrapulmonary volume increases, so intrapulmonary pressure drops below atmospheric pressure (about -1mmHg) and air flows in down its pressure gradient until pressures equalise.
A(ii) During expiration, the inspiratory muscles relax, the rib cage descends due to gravity, thoracic cavity volume decreases and the elastic lungs recoil passively, so intrapulmonary pressure rises above atmospheric pressure (about +1mmHg) and gases flow out until pressure equalises.
A(ii) Compliance is the ease with which the lungs can be expanded, expressed as the change in volume divided by the change in pressure, and is determined mainly by the distensibility of the lung tissue and thoracic cage and by the surface tension of the alveoli.
B. Functional residual capacity is known to vary with body position, so an upright posture is encouraged in patients with respiratory difficulty.
B. Severely dyspnoeic people often need to sit completely upright, while people with less severe respiratory distress may find a semi-upright position suitable, in line with the physiological hierarchy for treatment of impaired oxygen transport in which body positioning is a key early intervention.
B. Frequently changing position also causes secretions to move within the tracheobronchial tree, preventing pooling of secretions and stimulating coughing.
C. Elastic recoil is the tendency of the lung to return to its resting volume when the stretching force is released, and elastance is a measure of how readily the lungs rebound after being stretched; high compliance means the lung stretches easily, while low compliance requires more force to expand.
C. In an abnormally ventilating lung, such as in a left pneumothorax, the normal relationship between pressure changes and volume changes seen in a healthy lung is disrupted, altering compliance.
C. Where compliance changes, for a set pressure delivered to the lung, tidal volume will change accordingly; and for a set volume of gas delivered, airway pressure will change according to the altered compliance.
C. Since surfactant reduces alveolar surface tension and helps keep the alveoli from collapsing, any disruption of surfactant or of lung tissue distensibility directly alters compliance and therefore the pressure-volume relationship that drives normal breathing.

A(i) Percussion of the lung fields starts at the apices, comparing side to side all the way down the lung region, avoiding the damping effect of the scapulae and ribs.
A(i) The lower lung border is mapped both in expiration and inspiration: the patient exhales and holds while the examiner percusses down the scapular line until the sound changes from resonant to dull, marking the spot; the patient then takes a deep breath and holds while percussion continues to where the sound again changes to dull, this level being marked and normally equal bilaterally, measuring about 3-5cm.
A(ii) Resonance predominates over normal lung tissue; hyperresonance is heard as in emphysema or pneumothorax; a dull note is heard as in atelectasis.
A(ii) In the intensive care setting, percussion note is used to differentiate pathologies: a stony dull note suggests pleural effusion, a dull note suggests atelectasis or consolidation, and a hyperresonant note suggests pneumothorax.
B. A hyperresonant percussion note relates to conditions with increased air content or trapped air in the thorax, such as emphysema (with hyperinflation) or pneumothorax (air in the pleural space).
B. A dull percussion note relates to conditions with reduced air content or increased density in the underlying lung, such as atelectasis (collapse) or consolidation (e.g. pneumonia, retained secretions).
B. A stony dull percussion note relates specifically to fluid accumulation in the pleural space, as in pleural effusion, which obstructs breathing by limiting lung expansion.
C. Percussion findings therefore reflect a functional deficit in lung aeration: hyperresonance reflects excess air (over-distension or a free air space), while dullness reflects reduced air content (collapse, consolidation or fluid).
C. This functional deficit affects ventilation and, in conditions like consolidation and collapse, will also alter gas exchange, contributing to the problem of decreased lung volume or increased work of breathing.
C. Physiotherapy uses the percussion finding to guide technique selection: a dull note over an area of collapse or consolidation supports use of positioning, thoracic expansion exercises and airway clearance techniques to re-expand the lung and mobilise secretions.
C. A hyperresonant note associated with pneumothorax is instead a caution/contraindication for certain airway clearance techniques, such as manual hyperinflation, until the pneumothorax is treated/drained.
C. Similarly, a stony dull note from a large pleural effusion is a contraindication for airway clearance techniques, so management is directed instead at breathing control and thoracic expansion exercises to improve lung volumes.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the procedure for performing chest percussion as an assessment technique.
A(ii) State the percussion notes obtained and their classification.
B. State how percussion findings relate to common respiratory conditions.
C. Explain how these findings represent a functional deficit and how physiotherapy addresses it.

A patient with bronchiectasis has excessive purulent secretions localised to the lower lobes.
(i) Name the physiotherapy technique indicated for clearing these secretions.
(ii) Describe the positioning principle used and the lung segments most frequently requiring this technique.
(iii) State the precautions/contraindications relevant to this technique.
(iv) State the progression and outcome measures used to monitor treatment.
questions.answerText:
(i) Postural drainage combined with facilitating airway clearance through effective coughing techniques.
(ii) Postural drainage is the gravitational clearance of secretions from specific bronchial segments using one or more positions, so that gravity moves secretions to the trachea to be coughed up; the lower lobes require drainage most frequently because the upper lobes drain by gravity, and positioning is scheduled two to three times daily, best before meals and before bedtime, with the client remaining in the desired position for 10 to 15 minutes if tolerated.
(iii) Contraindications relevant to airway clearance techniques include intracranial pressure above 20mmHg, active haemorrhage with haemodynamic instability, recent spinal surgery, active haemoptysis, empyema, broncho-pleural fistula, large pleural effusions, pulmonary embolism, and rib fracture with or without flail chest.
(iv) Progression follows the patient's tolerance and clinical response; outcome measures/tools include spirometry (lung function), the 6-minute walk test/shuttle walk test (exercise capacity), and the Baseline Dyspnoea Index/Transition Dyspnoea Index for dyspnoea.

A(i) Chest percussion involves striking the chest wall over the area being drained, with the hand held in a rigid, dome-shaped (cupped) position, in a rhythmic pattern, to loosen pulmonary secretions for easier expectoration.
A(ii) It is indicated for patients with retained secretions requiring mobilisation, typically combined with postural drainage positioning, and may be taught to patients for self-percussion of the anterior chest.
A(iii) Cupping (percussion) is never done on bare skin or performed over surgical incisions, below the ribs, over the spine, or over the breasts, because of the danger of tissue damage; clapping should also avoid the liver, spleen, scapula, clavicle and sternum.
A(iv) The patient is positioned in supine or prone without pain, and each area is percussed for 30-60 seconds several times a day, or 3-5 minutes several times a day if secretions are tenacious (5 minutes per segment in cystic fibrosis, 1-2 minutes in other conditions), instructed to use diaphragmatic breathing throughout.
A(v) Percussion increases the shearing action on the mucosal layer by mechanically loosening secretions adherent to the airway walls, aiding their movement toward the central airways.
B. Vibration and shaking consist of intermittent chest wall compression performed throughout the expiratory phase, immediately over the area of secretions, which is thought to reinforce expiratory gas flow and increase shearing action on the mucosal layer.
B. For vibration, the therapist places one hand on top of the other (or one hand on each side of the rib cage), tenses the hand muscles while applying moderate downward pressure, and vibrates the arms and hands as the patient exhales slowly through pursed lips, relieving pressure on inhalation.
B. After three or four vibrations the patient is encouraged to cough using the abdominal muscles, allowed to rest, and breath sounds are checked with a stethoscope; the percussion and vibration cycle is repeated according to tolerance and clinical response, usually for 15-30 minutes.
C. Vibration is a less intense form of chest shaking, performed using the therapist's hands and arms to create oscillations of small amplitude and high frequency (about 200 per minute).
C. Shaking, in contrast, uses the therapist's arms and body to create oscillations of large amplitude and lower frequency than vibration.
C. Percussion differs from both in that it is a rhythmic striking action with a cupped hand rather than a sustained oscillatory compression, and is avoided over the breasts, spine, sternum and rib cage similarly to vibration.
C. Vibration and shaking are both never performed over the patient's breasts, spine, sternum and rib cage, and can also be taught to family members or achieved with a mechanical device, unlike percussion which is usually performed by a trained person or the patient on their own anterior chest.
questions.question:
Describe chest percussion under the following headings: A(i) definition, A(ii) indications, A(iii) contraindications, A(iv) procedure, A(v) physiological effects.
B. Explain the clinical basis and detailed procedure of vibration and shaking as adjunct manual techniques.
C. Distinguish between percussion, vibration and shaking.

questions.answerText:
(i) Bronchiectasis.
(ii) Chronic inflammatory secretions and microbes cause permanent dilation and distortion of the airway walls; inflammation, infection and obstruction of the bronchioles lead to accumulated secretions, airway blockage, further breakdown of the airways and loss of tone in the bronchial walls, in a vicious cycle of infection and inflammation.
(iii) Clinical features include persistent/recurrent cough with purulent sputum (may exceed 500ml/day), haemoptysis (about 50% of cases), clubbing of the fingers, dyspnoea, wheezing and pleuritic chest pain; problem list findings include reduced expiratory volume and vital capacity, a bronchiectatic segment with purulent secretions, hypersecretion of the airways in the morning or with change of position, stress incontinence, reduced lung function and reduced quality of life.
(iv) Short-term goals: pain relief, improved breathing pattern, increased lung function (volumes and capacities), and clearing the airway of secretions; long-term goals: increased lung function, improved exercise capacity and improved quality of life.
(v) Breathing control, airway clearance, facilitating airway clearance with effective coughing techniques and graded exercises; outcome measures include spirometry, the 6-minute/shuttle walk tests, and the Baseline/Transition Dyspnoea Index.
questions.question:
A patient presents with persistent cough productive of purulent sputum exceeding 500ml a day, occasional streaks of blood in sputum, clubbing of the fingers, dyspnoea, wheezing and pleuritic chest pain that worsens with position change.
(i) State the most likely diagnosis.
(ii) Explain the pathophysiological basis of this condition.
(iii) State the key assessment findings/clinical features and problem-list findings expected.
(iv) List the physiotherapy goals.
(v) Outline the physiotherapy management.

A patient recovering from pulmonary tuberculosis has reduced spirometric measures and reduced exercise capacity.
(i) Name the physiotherapy techniques indicated.
(ii) State the precaution associated with applying airway clearance techniques in suspected/active tuberculosis.
(iii) State the outcome measures used to monitor progression.
questions.answerText:
(i) Self-assisted coughing, breathing control, thoracic expansion exercises, incentive spirometry, respiratory muscle training and graded exercise programmes.
(ii) Suspected pulmonary tuberculosis is listed as a caution for airway clearance techniques.
(iii) Pain intensity (VAS/numerical rating scale), perceived exertion (Borg's/MRC scale), lung function (spirometer), sputum volume, body mass index, quality of life (SF-36) and functional performance (Karnofsky Performance Scale).

A(i) Diaphragmatic (belly/abdominal) breathing is a breathing control manoeuvre in which the patient breathes using the diaphragm and lower chest, with attention to the position of the therapist's hands and the patient's hands to guide the movement, using an inspiration:expiration time ratio of about 1:2-3.
A(ii) It is indicated as a breathing control/re-education technique, used as the default relaxed breathing manoeuvre between more active airway clearance techniques and as part of post-surgical breathing exercise regimens.
A(iii) During diaphragmatic breathing, the upper chest and shoulders are relaxed while the subject breathes at a relatively normal tidal volume and rate; a swelling is felt around the waist during inspiration as the descending diaphragm displaces abdominal contents, subsiding with exhalation.
A(iv) Physiologically, this pattern optimises the descent of the diaphragm and use of the lower chest for ventilation, forming the resting/default breathing pattern between active manoeuvres in the breathing techniques used for airway clearance.
B. Pursed-lip breathing involves breathing slowly and completely for a comfortable length of time through pursed lips, and is often seen in and taught to patients with emphysema.
B. It is used together with diaphragmatic breathing, breathing control and deep breathing as part of the breathing exercise components of post-surgical pulmonary complication management.
B. Clinically, pursed-lip breathing is adopted because patients with severe diaphragmatic flattening or emphysema often develop it spontaneously as a strategy to manage their breathing difficulty.
C. Diaphragmatic breathing emphasises the direction and depth of abdominal wall movement, using lower chest and diaphragm action with a controlled inspiration:expiration ratio, and is used as the relaxed baseline breathing pattern.
C. Pursed-lip breathing instead emphasises the manner of exhalation - slow and complete through pursed lips - and is particularly associated with emphysema, where it helps patients manage their breathing pattern.
C. Both are breathing control manoeuvres used to assure maximal use of respiratory function and allow patients to get the most out of their available respiratory capacity, and both are taught as part of a structured breathing exercise programme.
C. In practice they are often combined with breathing control and deep breathing (as in post-surgical management) rather than used in isolation, since together they address both diaphragmatic movement pattern and exhalation technique.
questions.question:
Describe diaphragmatic (belly/abdominal) breathing under the following headings: A(i) definition, A(ii) indications, A(iii) procedure, A(iv) physiological effects.
B. Explain the clinical basis of pursed-lip breathing as a related breathing control manoeuvre.
C. Distinguish between diaphragmatic breathing and pursed-lip breathing.

A patient is being managed for pulmonary tuberculosis.
(i) State the pathological process/risk factors leading to this presentation.
(ii) State the problems/complications that arise from this condition.
(iii) Outline the physiotherapy management options and justify the most appropriate.
questions.answerText:
(i) The pathology follows formation of a "tuberculous follicle", a caseation process, cavity formation and calcification, caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis irritating the mucous lining of the bronchioles or alveoli.
(ii) Problem list of cough, chest pain, dyspnoea and reduced exercise tolerance, alongside clinical features of weight loss, loss of appetite, fever, night sweats, fatigue, malaise and haemoptysis.
(iii) Options include self-assisted coughing, breathing control, thoracic expansion exercises, incentive spirometry, respiratory muscle training and graded exercise programmes; breathing control and thoracic expansion exercises with incentive spirometry are most appropriate first as they address the short-term goals of relieving pain, increasing spirometric measures and reducing work of breathing before progressing to graded exercise for long-term fitness goals.

questions.question:
A patient's chest X-ray shows a raised hemi-diaphragm, and auscultation reveals bronchial breathing with fine crackles over the affected area; breathing pattern is shallow.
(i) Identify the physiotherapy problem and the structures/area likely affected.
(ii) State the differential auscultation findings that may be found as the condition changes.
(iii) Explain the clinical reasoning for selecting the physiotherapy technique.
questions.answerText:
(i) Decreased lung volume with an anatomical area collapsed (atelectasis, e.g. lower lobe collapse), identified by a raised hemi-diaphragm on chest X-ray and a shallow breathing pattern on observation.
(ii) Auscultation changes may progress through stages from bronchial breathing to fine crackles, with altered breath sounds; altered gas exchange may be reflected on arterial blood gas or oxygen saturation readings and confirmed on spirometry.
(iii) As the goals are auscultation changes toward normal, chest X-ray resolution and improved incentive spirometry readings, positioning, thoracic expansion exercises, incentive spirometry, IPPB and mobilisation are selected, guided by how much the individual can do and whether associated problems are present.

(i) Indications include airway compromise (reduced consciousness, dynamic airway, airway obstruction), hypoventilation (impaired central drive, respiratory muscle weakness, restrictive ventilatory defects), hypoxaemic respiratory failure (alveolar filling defects e.g. pneumonia/pulmonary oedema, pulmonary vascular defects, diffusion defects), and increased ventilatory demand (severe sepsis, shock, severe metabolic acidosis); concerning findings include respiratory rate >30/min, inability to maintain SaO2 >90% on FiO2 >0.60, and PaCO2 >50mmHg with pH <7.25.
(ii) Pulmonary barotrauma/alveolar rupture, infection, oxygen toxicity, respiratory muscle weakness, laryngeal/tracheal trauma, and decreased cardiac output due to increased intrathoracic pressure and reduced venous return.
(iii) Options include airway clearance techniques (indicated in mechanical ventilation), manual hyperinflation/bagging to aid removal of secretions and reinflate atelectatic segments, and positioning with suctioning; manual hyperinflation is most appropriate here as it aids secretion removal, reverses atelectasis and improves oxygen saturation and lung compliance, though hazards such as reduced blood pressure and raised intracranial pressure must be monitored.
questions.question:
A patient in the intensive care unit is intubated and mechanically ventilated for hypoxaemic respiratory failure.
(i) State the risk factors/indications that could lead to this patient requiring mechanical ventilation.
(ii) State the complications that can arise from invasive mechanical ventilation.
(iii) Outline the physiotherapy management options available for this patient and justify the most appropriate one.

questions.answerText:
(i) Asthma; the bronchial wall and airway smooth muscle are affected, with reversible airway inflammation, swelling of the mucosal layer, thickening of the muscle layer, hypersecretion of mucus and bronchoconstriction by the surrounding smooth muscle.
(ii) Differential pathological findings include bronchial wall thickening, mucus stasis in the bronchioles, constrictive bronchiolitis, hyperinflation of the parenchyma and emphysema.
(iii) Since asthma involves bronchospasm, mucus hypersecretion and airway hyper-responsiveness, techniques such as positioning, breathing techniques, physical training (respiratory muscle training, chest expansion exercises), manual techniques (percussion, shaking, vibration), postural drainage, and coughing and huffing are selected to relieve bronchospasm, reduce breathing difficulty and facilitate removal of excess secretions, in line with the short-term goals of the first weeks of treatment.
questions.question:
On examination, a patient has widespread wheeze on auscultation, tachypnoea and tachycardia, with hyperinflation of the lung parenchyma noted.
(i) Identify the pathology and structures affected.
(ii) State the differential pathological findings that may coexist.
(iii) Explain the clinical reasoning for selecting an appropriate physiotherapy technique in this condition.

A(i) Describe the concept of ventilation-perfusion matching.
A(ii) Explain the mechanism of ventilation-perfusion coupling.
B. State the application of body positioning in relation to ventilation-perfusion matching in physiotherapy practice.
C. Explain the physiological basis of the dysfunction that results when ventilation and perfusion are mismatched.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Ventilation is the amount of gas reaching the alveoli, and perfusion is the blood flow reaching the alveoli; ventilation and perfusion must be tightly regulated for efficient gas exchange to occur.
A(i) This ventilation-perfusion coupling relies on a permeable alveolar-capillary membrane and adequate pulmonary and systemic circulation.
A(ii) Changes in alveolar PCO2 cause changes in the diameter of the pulmonary arterioles: when alveolar CO2 is high and O2 is low, vasoconstriction occurs; when alveolar CO2 is low and O2 is high, vasodilation occurs.
A(ii) In response to decreased pO2, the systemic circulation responds with vasodilation (allowing more time for gas exchange), whereas the pulmonary circulation responds with vasoconstriction, shunting blood to better-ventilated areas of lung.
B. Body positioning affects the matching of ventilation and perfusion, an effect noted under ventilation/perfusion matching.
B. Because gravity influences both regional ventilation and regional blood flow differently, positioning is used clinically as part of the physiological hierarchy of treatment (body positioning, breathing control, coughing manoeuvres, mobilisation) to optimise oxygen transport.
B. Ventilation-perfusion imbalance is listed among the common problems in respiratory disorders that physiotherapy management addresses through the problem-oriented approach.
C. Disruption in perfusion can arise from alteration in systemic blood flow, changes in haemoglobin, pulmonary shunting, or damaged alveoli, all of which impair the matching of ventilation to perfusion.
C. During anaesthesia and surgery, ventilation-perfusion mismatch is one of the effects contributing to post-surgical pulmonary complications, alongside altered CNS regulation of breathing and reduction in lung capacities.
C. When ventilation is reduced relative to perfusion (e.g. in atelectasis or secretion retention), poorly ventilated but still perfused alveoli act as a shunt, allowing under-oxygenated blood to reach the systemic circulation.
C. When perfusion is reduced relative to ventilation (e.g. pulmonary embolism), ventilated alveoli receive too little blood flow, wasting ventilation as alveolar dead space.
C. Physiotherapy techniques that improve secretion clearance, lung expansion and positioning aim to restore matched ventilation and perfusion, thereby improving gas exchange and reducing the work of breathing associated with V/Q imbalance.

(i) Exercise, cold air, climate change, emotions, medications (aspirin, NSAIDs, beta-blockers), respiratory infection, irritant inhalation, environmental pollutants, stress and allergic reaction.
(ii) Bronchial wall thickening, mucus stasis in the bronchioles, constrictive bronchiolitis, hyperinflation of the parenchyma and emphysema.
(iii) Options include education, positioning, breathing techniques, physical training (respiratory muscle training, chest expansion exercises), manual techniques (percussion, shaking, vibration), postural drainage, coughing and huffing, and range of motion exercises; relieving bronchospasm and reducing breathing difficulty through positioning and breathing techniques is most appropriate in the acute phase since the short-term goals include relief of bronchospasm and reduction of breathing difficulties within the first week of treatment.
questions.question:
A known asthmatic reports recurrent attacks triggered by cold air and stressful situations.
(i) State the triggers for an asthma attack.
(ii) State the pathological findings/complications that can develop from recurrent attacks.
(iii) Outline the physiotherapy management options and justify the most appropriate for the acute phase.

questions.answerText:
(i) Bronchiectasis.
(ii) It is an acquired obstructive lung disease resulting from chronic inflammatory secretions and microbes, with pathogenesis described as distinct phases of infection and chronic inflammation that establish a vicious circle destroying the bronchi and producing the clinical symptoms.
(iii) Inflammation, infection and obstruction of bronchioles with accumulated secretions, airway blockage and further breakdown of the airways, and loss of tone in bronchial walls, leading to permanent dilation and distortion of airway walls and recurrent infection.
(iv) Breathing control, airway clearance, facilitating airway clearance with effective coughing techniques, and graded exercises; short-term goals are pain relief, improved breathing pattern, increased lung function and clearing airway secretions, while long-term goals are increased lung function, improved exercise capacity and improved quality of life.
questions.question:
A patient presents with persistent cough productive of large amounts of purulent sputum that may exceed 500ml a day, occasional haemoptysis, clubbing of the fingers, dyspnoea, wheezing and pleuritic chest pain.
(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) State the predisposing pathogenesis of this condition.
(iii) Describe the pathological findings.
(iv) Outline the physiotherapy management.

A patient with a long history of cigarette smoking is being evaluated for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
(i) State the major and minor risk factors for this condition.
(ii) State the complications that can arise.
(iii) Outline the physiotherapy management options and justify the most appropriate one for this patient.
questions.answerText:
(i) Major risk factors: cigarette smoking (worldwide the most common), severe alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, occupational hazards and indoor pollution (biogas burning), age, male gender and existing impaired lung function; Minor risk factors: air pollution, alcohol, race, nutritional status, family history and bronchial reactivity.
(ii) Pulmonary hypertension, acute respiratory failure, infections and polycythaemia.
(iii) Options include chest physiotherapy (postural drainage if sputum exceeds 30cc/day, chest percussion and vibration), breathing exercises, rehabilitation (exercise reconditioning, energy conservation, nutrition, psychosocial management), and smoking cessation (group therapy, drugs, hypnosis); smoking cessation is most appropriate as smoking is the major risk factor and its discontinuation prevents further progressive tissue degeneration, while chest physiotherapy addresses the existing secretion and airflow problems.

A(i) The dorsal respiratory group (DRG), or inspiratory centre, in the medulla contains inspiratory neurons thought to set the basic rhythm (now believed to be the pre-Botzinger complex), exciting the inspiratory muscles and setting eupnoea at 12-15 breaths per minute, ceasing firing during expiration.
A(i) The ventral respiratory group (VRG) contains both inspiratory and expiratory neurons, remains inactive during quiet breathing, becomes active when demand is high, and is involved in forced inspiration and expiration, controlled via the phrenic and intercostal nerves.
A(ii) The pontine respiratory group (PRG) modifies medullary activity to smooth the transition between inspiration and expiration: the pneumotaxic centre sends impulses to switch off inspiratory neurons, limiting the duration of inspiration, while the apneustic centre prevents inspiratory inhibition to increase inspiratory drive when needed, with the pneumotaxic centre normally dominating to allow expiration to occur.
A(ii) Inspiratory depth is determined by how actively the respiratory centre stimulates the respiratory muscles, while the rate of respiration is determined by how long the inspiratory centre remains active; peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies sense changes in PO2, pH and PCO2.
B. Cortical controls send direct signals from the cerebral motor cortex that bypass medullary controls (e.g. voluntary breath-holding or taking a deep breath), while hypothalamic controls act through the limbic system to modify rate and depth of respiration, for example a rise in body temperature increasing respiratory rate.
B. The Hering-Breuer inflation reflex sends inhibitory signals from stretch receptors to the medullary inspiration centre upon lung inflation, ending inhalation and allowing expiration; pulmonary irritant reflexes promote reflexive constriction of the air passages.
B. Clinically, altered breathing patterns are recognised as deviations from normal quiet breathing (eupnoea): tachypnoea (increased rate), bradypnoea (decreased rate), apnoea (temporary arrest of breathing), hyperpnoea (increased ventilation from increased rate or force), hyperventilation (abnormal increase in rate and force, often with dizziness or chest pain), hypoventilation (decreased rate and force) and dyspnoea (difficulty breathing).
C. Control of breathing at rest is regulated by hydrogen ion concentration in the brain, changes in which are monitored via changing PCO2 levels sensed by brain-stem chemoreceptors; as PCO2 rises it diffuses into the cerebrospinal fluid, is hydrated to carbonic acid, and dissociates to release hydrogen ions, decreasing pH and increasing the depth and rate of breathing.
C. Hyperventilation quickly flushes carbon dioxide from the blood in response to hypercapnia, while hypoventilation is slow, shallow breathing due to abnormally low PCO2 levels, and apnoea may occur until PCO2 levels rise again.
C. Substantial drops in arterial PO2 (to about 60mmHg) are normally needed before oxygen levels become a major stimulus for increased ventilation, since PCO2/pH is the primary driver at rest.
C. If carbon dioxide is not adequately removed, as in emphysema and chronic bronchitis, the chemoreceptors become unresponsive to PCO2 chemical stimuli, and PO2 levels become the principal respiratory stimulus, a state known as the hypoxic drive.
C. This dysfunction of central chemoreceptor sensitivity explains why some chronic respiratory patients rely on hypoxaemia rather than hypercapnia to drive their breathing, a consideration physiotherapists must be aware of when managing oxygen therapy and ventilatory support in such patients.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the medullary and pontine respiratory centres that control breathing.
A(ii) Explain the chemical and reflex mechanisms regulating the rate and depth of breathing.
B. State the application of recognising altered breathing patterns in clinical practice.
C. Explain the physiological basis of the dysfunction that results when chemoreceptor sensitivity is altered.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Outcome measures document treatment efficacy across respiratory conditions and include pain scales (Visual Analogue Scale, Numerical Pain Rating Scale, Short Form McGill Pain Questionnaire), dyspnoea scales (Borg scale, Medical Research Council scale, Baseline/Transition Dyspnoea Index, Dyspnoea-12), and health status questionnaires (St George's Respiratory Questionnaire, Chronic Respiratory Disease Questionnaire, Short Form 36).
A(i) Further tools include the BODE multidimensional scoring system (BMI, airflow Obstruction, Dyspnoea, Exercise capacity), the Karnofsky Performance Scale, the Dyspnoea Management Questionnaire (DMQ), Oxford muscle grading, goniometry, and the Pulmonary Functional Status and Dyspnoea Questionnaire-Modified (PFSDQ-M).
A(ii) In COPD, outcomes are grouped as physiologic (lung function tests for airflow, gas exchange and diffusion; respiratory work via minute ventilation and spirometry), symptomatic (patient/physician dyspnoea assessment), functional (exercise tolerance, work capacity/oxygen consumption, 12-minute walk test), and other measures (hospitalisation, disease stability and response to therapy).
A(ii) In asthma, outcome tools include the British Medical Research Council scale and American Thoracic Society scale for the dyspnoea threshold, electrocardiograph for tachycardia, and the American Thoracic Society scale for level of impairment.
B. In bronchiectasis, outcome measures include spirometry (lung function), the 6-minute walk test/shuttle walk test (exercise capacity), the Baseline/Transition Dyspnoea Index (both scales), and health status tools such as the St George's Respiratory Questionnaire, Chronic Respiratory Disease Questionnaire and the BODE score.
B. In pleural effusion, outcome tools include the Visual Analogue Scale/SF-MPQ for pain, the Baseline Dyspnoea Index/Modified Borg Scale/Dyspnoea-12 for breathlessness, the spirometer (TV, FVC) for lung function, and the 6-minute walk/shuttle walk test for functional exercise capacity.
B. In tuberculosis and lung cancer, outcome tools include the VAS/numerical rating scale and numerical pain rating scale for pain, the Borg's/MRC scale for perceived exertion, spirometric measures for lung function, sputum volume, body mass index, SF-36 for quality of life, and the Karnofsky Performance Scale/Extended Activities of Daily Living scale for functional performance.
B. In post-surgical pulmonary complications, generic outcome tools include a functional status questionnaire, functional independence measures, SF-36, Numerical Pain Rating Scale, Oxford muscle grading and goniometry, while specific tools include the Dyspnoea Management Questionnaire and PFSDQ-M.
C. These outcome measures relate to specific functional deficits: dyspnoea scales relate to breathlessness/increased work of breathing, exercise tests relate to reduced exercise tolerance, health status questionnaires relate to reduced quality of life, and pain scales relate to conditions with chest pain such as pleural effusion or post-surgical patients.
C. The BODE index relates to overall COPD severity across nutritional status, airflow limitation, breathlessness and exercise capacity, reflecting how the respiratory functional deficit extends to systemic effects such as nutritional decline.
C. Physiotherapy uses these outcome measures both to establish a baseline of patient performance and to guide evaluation and management, since they document whether an intervention has produced the intended change.
C. By reassessing these measures over the course of treatment, physiotherapists can document efficacy of the intervention, adjust treatment plans, and demonstrate progress toward the short- and long-term goals set for each condition.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the general categories of outcome measures used in respiratory physiotherapy.
A(ii) State the specific outcome tools used across various respiratory conditions.
B. State how these outcome measures relate to specific respiratory conditions.
C. Explain how the underlying functional deficits are addressed and monitored by physiotherapy using these measures.

Describe Assist Control (AC) ventilation under the following headings: A(i) definition, A(ii) indications, A(iii) complications, A(iv) procedure/settings, A(v) physiological effects.
B. Explain the clinical basis of Synchronised Intermittent Mandatory Ventilation (SIMV) as an alternative mode.
C. Distinguish between Assist Control and SIMV.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Assist control (AC) ventilation is a mode in which the ventilator assists every breath the patient takes; a minimum respiratory rate and tidal volume are set, and if the patient's own rate falls below the preset value the ventilator takes over and delivers the set number of breaths per minute.
A(ii) It is indicated for full ventilatory support, including in paralysed or heavily sedated patients (as controlled mandatory ventilation) and in patients needing every breath supported to a fixed tidal volume.
A(iii) Complications relevant to any mode of invasive ventilation include pulmonary barotrauma/alveolar rupture, infection, oxygen toxicity, respiratory muscle weakness, laryngeal/tracheal trauma, and decreased cardiac output from increased intrathoracic pressure and reduced venous return.
A(iv) In volume-control assist-control ventilation, each inspiratory effort beyond a set sensitivity threshold triggers delivery of the fixed tidal volume; if the patient does not trigger the ventilator often enough, the ventilator initiates a breath to ensure the desired minimum rate; typical settings are a tidal volume of 6-8 to 8-10 ml/kg, rate of 10-12 breaths/min, FiO2 kept below 0.5, and PEEP 5-15cmH2O.
A(v) Because every breath (mandatory or patient-triggered) is delivered at the same fixed tidal volume, AC provides the most complete ventilatory support of the common modes.
B. Synchronised Intermittent Mandatory Ventilation (SIMV) delivers mandatory breaths at a set rate and volume in synchrony with the patient's inspiratory effort; if no inspiratory effort is detected, the ventilator delivers a mandatory breath at a set time.
B. Between the machine-delivered breaths, the patient is allowed to breathe spontaneously; patient efforts above the set respiratory rate are unassisted (though the intake valve opens to allow the breath), and spontaneous breaths may not reach the preset tidal volume, with only pressure support added.
B. The set minute ventilation equals the set respiratory rate multiplied by the set tidal volume, while total respiratory rate equals the set rate plus the patient's spontaneous rate.
C. In AC, every breath the patient initiates receives the full preset tidal volume, so the ventilator does virtually all the work of breathing for each breath.
C. In SIMV, only the mandatory breaths receive the full preset tidal volume; spontaneous breaths taken between mandatory breaths are largely the patient's own effort, assisted only by pressure support if set.
C. Consequently, SIMV provides less complete ventilatory support than AC and, despite remaining a popular mode, does not facilitate liberating the patient from mechanical ventilation nor improve patient comfort any better than AC.
