C. AC is therefore preferred when full respiratory support is required (e.g. paralysed or very sedated patients), while SIMV allows a degree of spontaneous breathing between mandatory breaths, which can be used progressively during weaning.

A(i) Forced expiratory technique (FET), first described by Thompson and Thompson (1968), consists of 1 or 2 forced expirations (huffs) from middle to low lung volumes, combined with a period of controlled, relaxed diaphragmatic breathing with slow deep breaths.
A(ii) It is indicated, like other airway clearance techniques, in conditions such as cystic fibrosis, atelectasis, asthma, bronchiectasis and respiratory muscle weakness where secretions need mobilising.
A(iii) Contraindications are the general cautions for airway clearance techniques, including untreated pneumothorax, active haemoptysis, large pleural effusions and hyper-reactive airways which may trigger uncontrolled coughing.
A(iv) The huff is performed with the mouth and glottis open, rapidly squeezing out air by contracting the chest wall and abdominal muscles; the huff should be active but not violent or explosive, and subsequent huffs may start at higher lung volumes.
A(v) By keeping the glottis open, FET mobilises secretions from middle to lower lung volumes toward the central airways with less fatigue than repeated coughing.
B. The effective cough, by contrast, requires a slow deep inspiration to open the trachea and inflate the lungs, quick tight closure of the glottis (a Valsalva manoeuvre), and contraction of the intercostal and abdominal muscles.
B. At peak intrathoracic pressure the glottis opens, creating a pressure difference between the higher-pressure abdomen and lower-pressure thorax that pushes the diaphragm upward, producing a violent, explosive current of air.
B. Facilitating measures for effective coughing include changing position, increasing activity level, prolonging exhalation, vibrations/end-expiratory assist, sips of water, manually stimulated cough and splinting with a pillow.
C. FET and coughing both aim to mobilise and expel secretions, but FET is performed with the glottis kept open throughout, avoiding the explosive glottal closure and release that characterises a true cough.
C. Because it avoids glottal closure, FET generates less airway collapse, less fatigue and lower bronchospasm risk than repeated forceful coughing, making it useful in patients with hyper-reactive or unstable airways.
C. A true cough, using the Valsalva manoeuvre and glottal closure, generates a much more forceful, higher-velocity expulsion of air, useful for clearing secretions from larger central airways once they have been mobilised.
C. In practice, FET is often used to mobilise secretions from smaller airways to the central airways, after which coughing (self-assisted, manual or directed) is used to expel the mobilised secretions from the mouth.
questions.question:
Describe the Forced Expiratory Technique (FET) under the following headings: A(i) definition, A(ii) indications, A(iii) contraindications, A(iv) procedure, A(v) physiological effects.
B. Explain the clinical basis of the effective cough manoeuvre.
C. Distinguish between FET and true coughing as airway clearance manoeuvres.

questions.answerText:
A(i) The mucociliary escalator and cough reflex maintain optimal function of the respiratory system by removing secretions and preventing airway obstruction; in health, 10-100mL of airway secretions are continuously produced and cleared by the centripetal movement of the mucociliary escalator, aided by transient increases in expiratory airflow.
A(i) Cilia are microscopic, hair-like projections lining the nasal passages, numerous and covering the nasal cavity, exhibiting independent, coordinated, rhythmic wave-like movement, and are embedded in mucus produced by goblet cells to form the mucociliary escalator.
A(ii) The escalator's functions include trapping inhaled particles (dust, pollen, smoke, bacteria, viruses, debris) in mucus, propelling mucus posteriorly toward the throat from the front of the nose and superiorly toward the throat from the lower respiratory tract, clearing debris by swallowing (neutralised in the stomach), and humidifying inhaled air.
A(ii) Factors that can interfere with this defence mechanism, making it difficult to mobilise and evacuate secretions, include the aging process, tobacco use and environmental exposures, all of which reduce ciliary structure and function.
B. Airway clearance techniques are indicated for individuals whose mucociliary escalator function and/or cough mechanics are altered and whose ability to mobilise and expectorate airway secretions is compromised.
B. These techniques use physical or mechanical means (breathing manoeuvres, gravity-assisted drainage, manual techniques and/or mechanical devices) to manipulate airflow, aid mobilisation of tracheobronchial phlegm cephalad, and facilitate evacuation by coughing.
B. Efficient airway clearance techniques aim to remove the most sputum in the shortest time with the least energy expended, and are usually performed by the patient themselves.
C. A number of disease processes can impair ciliary function, alter secretion production and mucus rheology, and interfere with the cough reflex: progressive neurodegenerative conditions inhibit the normal cough reflex, pulmonary disorders such as cystic fibrosis, COPD and bronchiectasis alter mucus production and composition, and mucociliary clearance disorders such as primary ciliary dyskinesia reduce ciliary efficacy.
C. Secretions that accumulate or become stagnant obstruct the conducting airways, act as conduits for bacterial colonisation and infection, evoke an inflammatory response, and contribute to airway and parenchymal damage.
C. This recurring cycle of secretion retention, infection and inflammatory change results in airway obstruction and structural damage to the airways and lung parenchyma.
C. In the problem-oriented approach, this presents as the problem of retention of secretions, identified by an inability to expectorate, ineffective cough, and, if consolidation develops, coarse crackles on auscultation and chest X-ray changes.
C. Physiotherapy addresses this dysfunction through positioning, manual techniques and airway clearing techniques aimed at restoring the mobilisation and expectoration function that the impaired mucociliary escalator and cough reflex can no longer achieve alone.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the mucociliary escalator and its structures.
A(ii) Explain the mechanism by which it clears secretions from the respiratory tract.
B. State the application/indication of airway clearance techniques when this mechanism is compromised.
C. Explain the physiological basis of the dysfunction that results when the mucociliary escalator and cough reflex fail.

A patient has a cough producing more than 30 ml of sputum in 24 hours, occurring for at least 3 months of the year for 2 consecutive years, with frequent chest infections, progressive and incomplete airflow obstruction, wheeze and diminished breath sounds. The patient is overweight.
(i) What is the most likely diagnosis, and which type of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease does it represent?
(ii) Explain the pathophysiological basis of this condition.
(iii) State the key assessment findings expected on observation, palpation, auscultation and investigation.
(iv) List the physiotherapy problem list and the short- and long-term goals for this patient.
(v) Outline the physiotherapy management for this patient.
questions.answerText:
(i) Chronic bronchitis, a type of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD); described as the "blue bloater" pattern.
(ii) Inhalation of noxious particles activates neutrophils, macrophages and CD8+ lymphocytes releasing chemical mediators; this causes vasodilation, congestion, mucosal oedema and goblet cell hypertrophy with excessive mucus production; recurrent infections reduce ciliary/phagocytic activity, weaken defences and destroy small bronchioles; gas exchange becomes impaired causing exertional dyspnoea, and sustained hypoxaemia with rising PaCO2 can desensitise the brain's respiratory centre.
(iii) Observation: overweight build, mild dyspnoea, barrel chest, possible cor pulmonale; Auscultation: wheezing and abnormal/diminished breath sounds; Investigation: copious sputum, frequent infections, hypoxaemia; spirometry shows progressive and incomplete airflow obstruction.
(iv) Problem list: exertional breathlessness, chronic cough, increased work of breathing, reduced exercise tolerance, regular sputum production, frequent winter bronchitis or wheeze; Goals: short-term - reduce airway limitation, alleviate respiratory symptoms, prevent secondary complications; long-term - improve quality of life and well-being, increase exercise tolerance and functional activities, reduce anxiety and depression, smoking cessation.
(v) Oxygen therapy, breathing exercises, airway clearing technique, relaxation techniques, strength and endurance exercise, patient education, nicotine chewing gum; postural drainage if sputum exceeds 30cc/day, chest percussion and vibration, and rehabilitation with exercise reconditioning.

(i) Pleural effusion (excessive accumulation of fluid in the pleural space).
(ii) It arises from altered permeability of pleural membranes, reduction in intravascular oncotic pressure, increased capillary hydrostatic pressure in the systemic and/or pulmonary circulation, reduction of pleural space pressure (trapped lung), decreased lymphatic drainage or thoracic duct obstruction, increased peritoneal fluid, or movement of fluid from pulmonary oedema across the visceral pleura; it is not a specific disease but reflects underlying pathology in the lung, pleura or systemic circulation.
(iii) Observation: breathing difficulties; Palpation/percussion: diminished chest expansion, stony dull percussion note; Problem list/clinical features: chest pain worse with breathing, diminished chest expansion, breathing difficulties, dry or productive cough.
(iv) Short-term goals: relieve pain associated with breathing, improve chest excursion, increase lung volumes, control breathing, aid chest fluid drainage, and clear chest secretions if present; long-term goals: increase cardiopulmonary endurance, increase functional capacity and improve quality of life.
(v) Breathing control, thoracic expansion exercises, incentive spirometry, airway clearance techniques (if necessary), assisted cough, graded exercises, and patient education and counselling; outcome measures include the Visual Analogue Scale/SF-MPQ for pain, Baseline Dyspnoea Index/Modified Borg Scale/Dyspnoea-12 for breathlessness, spirometry, and the 6-minute walk/shuttle walk tests for functional exercise capacity.
questions.question:
A patient presents with chest pain that worsens with breathing, diminished chest expansion on the affected side, breathing difficulties and a dry cough. Chest examination reveals a stony dull percussion note over the lower zone.
(i) State the most likely diagnosis.
(ii) Explain the pathogenesis of this condition.
(iii) State the key assessment findings on observation, palpation/percussion and the clinical/problem-list features.
(iv) List the physiotherapy goals.
(v) Outline the physiotherapy management.

questions.answerText:
(i) Increased work of breathing, involving the use of accessory muscles of respiration in addition to the primary muscles of respiration.
(ii) Disease profile and history, increased respiration rate, altered respiratory pattern, breathlessness and altered arterial blood gases.
(iii) Since the goals are to reduce perceived breathlessness/exertion on the Borg scale, decrease respiration rate and eliminate visible use of accessory muscles, the reasoned treatment options are positioning, relaxation and breathing re-education/control, progressing from rest to moving.
questions.question:
A patient is observed using accessory muscles of breathing, with an increased respiratory rate and altered arterial blood gases.
(i) Identify the physiotherapy problem and the structures involved.
(ii) State the differential findings that support this problem.
(iii) Explain the clinical reasoning for the physiotherapy technique selected.

A(i) Describe the transport of oxygen in the blood.
A(ii) Explain the oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve and the factors affecting it.
B. State the application of oxygen transport principles in physiotherapy/clinical practice.
C. Explain the physiological basis of the dysfunction that results when oxygen delivery to tissues is impaired.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Oxygen is transported from the alveoli to the tissues in two forms: as a simple physical solution in plasma (important during conditions like muscular exercise, to meet excess tissue oxygen demand) and in combination with haemoglobin as oxyhaemoglobin (the major form, carrying about 97% of transported oxygen).
A(i) The oxygen-carrying capacity of blood is about 201mL O2 per litre in males (150g Hb/L x 1.34mL O2/g Hb) and about 174mL O2 per litre in females (130g Hb/L x 1.34mL O2/g Hb); saturated haemoglobin has all four haem groups bound to oxygen, while partially saturated haemoglobin has one to three haem groups bound.
A(ii) The rate at which haemoglobin binds and releases oxygen is regulated by PO2, temperature, blood pH, PCO2 and 2,3-DPG (an organic chemical produced by red blood cell metabolism when environmental oxygen levels are low).
A(ii) The oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve shows that at a PO2 of 100mmHg, haemoglobin is 98% saturated, and haemoglobin is almost completely saturated at a PO2 as low as 70mmHg, so further increases in PO2 produce only small increases in oxygen binding.
B. Because saturation changes little above a PO2 of 70mmHg, hyperventilation has little effect on arterial oxygen levels, and oxygen loading and delivery to tissues remain adequate even when PO2 is somewhat below normal.
B. In practice, oxygen therapy is applied clinically as part of the management of conditions such as COPD, and pulse oximetry (a non-invasive monitoring method) is used to continuously assess oxygen saturation.
B. As arterial blood flows through the capillaries, about 5mL of oxygen per decilitre is normally released; only 20-25% of bound oxygen is unloaded during one systemic circulation, leaving a reserve that can be drawn on when tissue oxygen demand rises.
C. If oxygen levels in the tissues drop, more oxygen dissociates from haemoglobin and is used by the cells without necessarily requiring an increase in respiratory rate or cardiac output.
C. Increases in temperature, hydrogen ion concentration, PCO2 and 2,3-DPG decrease haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen and enhance oxygen unloading from the blood; hydrogen ions and carbon dioxide modify the structure of haemoglobin in what is known as the Bohr effect.
C. When gas exchange or perfusion is impaired (as in various respiratory conditions), tissue oxygen delivery falls, and clinically this may present as cyanosis, particularly noted around the lips and nail beds, where blue discolouration is an abnormal finding.
C. Chronic hypoxaemia, as may be sustained in some respiratory disorders, can also contribute to complications such as polycythaemia, listed as a complication of COPD.
C. Because hypoxaemia results in increasing PaCO2, if sustained, the brain's respiratory control centre and central chemoreceptors can become desensitised, so compensatory action to correct hypoxaemia does not occur, worsening the dysfunction.

questions.question:
A patient develops pulmonary oedema.
(i) State the pathological process/underlying factors leading to this condition.
(ii) State the associated clinical/pathological findings.
(iii) Outline the physiotherapy management options and justify the most appropriate.
questions.answerText:
(i) Pulmonary oedema is caused by transudation of fluid into the pulmonary interstitium and alveoli, occurring when the net flux of fluid from the vasculature into the interstitial space increases.
(ii) Increased interstitial pressure, fluid retention in pulmonary tissues, reduced venous return, peripheral oedema (pitting) and raised jugular venous pressure, with clinical features of orthopnoea, difficulty breathing, reduced exercise tolerance, dyspnoea, pale skin, anxiety, a crackling heart sound/third heart sound and weight gain.
(iii) Options are relaxation exercises, breathing exercises, oedema massage and aerobic exercises; breathing exercises are most appropriate initially since the short-term goals are to improve breathing pattern and reduce work of breathing, before progressing to aerobic exercise to improve cardiovascular endurance and exercise tolerance as long-term goals.

(i) Lung cancer.
(ii) The development of cancer reduces lung function; abnormal cells divide without control and can invade nearby tissues, and surgical intervention (if performed) may reduce respiratory function or result in pulmonary complications.
(iii) Chest X-ray, lung function tests, sputum cytology, bronchoscopy or percutaneous biopsy, spirometry and blood gas analysis.
(iv) Positioning, breathing exercises, incentive spirometry, airway clearance techniques, mobilization, muscle strengthening, postural re-education and functional training; short-term goals are to reduce pain, improve breathing pattern, increase vital capacity, improve/reduce mucus secretion and improve muscle power, while long-term goals are to improve respiratory function, cardiopulmonary fitness and functional capacity.
questions.question:
A patient presents with a persistent cough, haemoptysis, unexplained weight loss, hoarseness of voice, clubbing of the fingers and enlarged supraclavicular nodes.
(i) What is the most likely diagnosis?
(ii) State the pathogenesis of this condition.
(iii) State the investigations that would be used to confirm the diagnosis.
(iv) Outline the physiotherapy management.

A patient recovering from upper abdominal surgery has reduced lung volumes, pain on breathing and difficulty clearing secretions.
(i) Name the physiotherapy techniques indicated.
(ii) State the positioning and breathing techniques used.
(iii) State the precautions to consider.
(iv) State the expected progression and outcome measures.
questions.answerText:
(i) Electro-analgesia, breathing exercises, incentive spirometry, airway clearance techniques (huffing, ACBT, autogenic drainage) and coughing techniques (assisted coughing, directed cough), together with exercise therapy.
(ii) Positioning; breathing control, diaphragmatic breathing, pursed lip breathing and deep breathing; early and graduated mobilization, range of motion exercises, strengthening exercises and endurance exercises.
(iii) Precautions specific to post-surgical patients are not detailed beyond the general problem list of pain, muscle atrophy/weakness, loss of range of motion, impaired air clearance, reduced lung volume, reduced exercise tolerance, and risk of skin breakdown, infection and deep vein thrombosis, all of which should guide safe progression.
(iv) Short-term goals guiding progression: reduce pain, increase lung volumes, improve joint range of motion, improve breathing pattern, remove secretion/clear airway, improve arterial blood gas profile and preserve muscle bulk; outcome measures include functional status questionnaire, Short Form 36, Numerical Pain Rating Scale, Oxford muscle grading, goniometry, dyspnoea management questionnaire and spirometric measures.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the procedure for performing chest auscultation.
A(ii) State the normal and adventitious breath sounds and voice sounds assessed.
B. State how auscultation findings relate to common respiratory conditions.
C. Explain how abnormal auscultation findings represent a functional deficit and how physiotherapy addresses it.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Auscultation is performed by instructing the patient to breathe through the mouth, deeper than usual, using the flat diaphragm of the stethoscope, with side-to-side comparison being most important, listening posteriorly from the apices at C7 to the bases at T10, and laterally from the axilla down to the 7th or 8th rib.
A(i) The passage of air creates a characteristic set of noises audible through the chest wall, which may be modified by obstruction within the respiratory passageways or by changes in the lung parenchyma, pleura or chest wall.
A(ii) Normal breath sounds include bronchial, bronchovesicular and vesicular sounds; adventitious breath sounds include crackle, wheeze, rhonchus and pleural friction rub; voice sounds tested include bronchophony, whispered pectoriloquy and egophony, all normally soft, muffled and indistinct, but enhanced when lung density increases.
A(ii) For bronchophony the patient repeats '99' while the examiner listens over the chest wall; for egophony the patient phonates an 'ee' sound (normally heard as 'eeeeee'); for whispered pectoriloquy the patient whispers a phrase such as 'one-two-three', normally faint, muffled and inaudible.
B. Coarse crackles, fine crackles or bronchial breathing on auscultation, together with a moist cough, are findings used to identify retention of secretions, which may progress from bronchial breathing to fine crackles.
B. In decreased lung volume/atelectasis, auscultation reveals bronchial breathing, fine crackles or diminished breath sounds, correlating with a raised hemi-diaphragm on chest X-ray.
B. In chronic bronchitis and emphysema, abnormal breath sounds including wheezing and diminished breath sounds are clinical features, while in tuberculosis, rales and bronchial breath sounds are noted.
B. In asthma, wheezing is a clinical feature reflecting bronchoconstriction and airway inflammation, and occasionally wheezing or gurgling from secretions in large airways may even be audible to the naked ear.
C. Abnormal auscultation findings indicate a functional deficit such as impaired ventilation, retained secretions, or reduced/absent air entry, which can extend to impaired gas exchange (altered arterial blood gases) if unaddressed.
C. Physiotherapy uses auscultation both before and after treatment (e.g. following chest physiotherapy) to guide the choice of technique and to compare findings against baseline data.
C. Physiotherapy addresses the underlying causes of abnormal breath sounds through positioning, percussion and vibration, and airway clearance techniques directed at mobilising secretions or re-expanding collapsed lung tissue.
C. Resolution of auscultation findings (e.g. crackles clearing or breath sounds normalising) is itself used as a goal and outcome measure of successful physiotherapy management, for example in retention of secretions and decreased lung volume problems.

A(i) Arterial blood gas (ABG) analysis is used to ascertain the state of a patient's respiratory and metabolic function, measured from a blood sample taken via an arterial line, with trends over time giving more meaningful conclusions than a single reading.
A(i) ABG values (or oxygen saturation) are used as part of the objective assessment for decreased lung volume, increased work of breathing (altered ABG), and post-surgical pulmonary complications (impaired gas exchange, altered arterial blood gases).
A(ii) Normal values are pH 7.35-7.45, PaCO2 35-45mmHg, PaO2 80-100mmHg, HCO3 22-26mmol/L and base excess -2 to +2.
A(ii) Concerning findings that may indicate the need for mechanical ventilation include a respiratory rate greater than 30 breaths/minute, inability to maintain arterial oxygen saturation above 90% with FiO2 above 0.60, and PaCO2 above 50mmHg with pH below 7.25.
B. In chronic bronchitis, hypoxaemia is a common finding, and if hypoxaemia is sustained it results in increasing PaCO2; in emphysema, hypercapnoea and respiratory acidosis are uncommon because breathing imbalance is compensated for by an increase in respiratory rate.
B. In lung disease where carbon dioxide is not adequately removed, as in emphysema and chronic bronchitis, chemoreceptors can become desensitised to PCO2, so PO2 becomes the principal respiratory stimulus (hypoxic drive).
B. Altered arterial blood gases are listed as part of the problem list in lung cancer, reflecting compromised respiratory function from the disease process or its treatment.
C. Abnormal ABG values indicate a functional deficit in gas exchange or ventilation, ranging from mild hypoxaemia to severe respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilatory support.
C. If sustained, hypoxaemia and hypercapnia can desensitise the brain's respiratory control centre and central chemoreceptors so compensatory action to correct the imbalance does not occur, extending the dysfunction beyond the respiratory system alone.
C. In post-surgical pulmonary complications, improving the arterial blood gas profile is a specific short-term physiotherapy goal, addressed through breathing exercises, incentive spirometry, airway clearance techniques and early mobilisation.
C. In more severe presentations, physiotherapy techniques such as manual hyperinflation and positioning are used together with oxygen therapy to improve oxygenation and lung compliance, monitored by serial ABG measurements.
C. Physiotherapists therefore use ABG trends to judge the severity and direction of change of a patient's respiratory status and to guide the intensity and choice of intervention, including recognising when a patient's status may be approaching the concerning findings that indicate a need for ventilatory support.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the procedure and purpose of arterial blood gas (ABG) analysis.
A(ii) State the normal ABG values and the concerning findings that indicate a need for ventilatory support.
B. State how ABG findings relate to common respiratory conditions.
C. Explain how abnormal ABG findings represent a functional deficit and how physiotherapy addresses it.

A(i) Describe the physical laws and structures governing gas exchange across the respiratory membrane.
A(ii) Explain the mechanism of gas diffusion between the alveoli and the blood.
B. State the application of posture and positioning as a factor affecting gas exchange.
C. Explain the physiological basis of the dysfunction that results when the respiratory membrane is damaged.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Dalton's law states that the total pressure exerted by a mixture of gases is the sum of the pressures exerted independently by each gas, with each gas's partial pressure proportional to its percentage in the mixture; for example, air is 20.93% oxygen, so at a total pressure of 760mmHg the partial pressure of oxygen (PO2) is 159mmHg.
A(i) Henry's law states that when a mixture of gases is in contact with a liquid, each gas dissolves in proportion to its partial pressure and its solubility; carbon dioxide is the most soluble, oxygen is about 1/20th as soluble as carbon dioxide, and nitrogen is practically insoluble in plasma.
A(ii) Fick's law of diffusion states that the rate of gas diffusion is proportional to the tissue area and the diffusion coefficient of the gas and the partial pressure difference across the tissue, and inversely proportional to the tissue thickness.
A(ii) The respiratory membrane is only 0.5 to 1 micrometre thick, allowing efficient gas exchange, has a total surface area of about 60 square metres in males, and is composed of alveolar walls (a single layer of Type I epithelial cells) and capillary walls.
B. Because of gas exchange, humidification of air, and mixing of alveolar gas with each breath, alveolar gas composition differs from atmospheric air, with the partial pressure of alveolar oxygen about 100mmHg and alveolar carbon dioxide about 40mmHg.
B. The partial pressure of oxygen in venous blood is about 40mmHg against about 100mmHg in the alveoli, a steep gradient that allows equilibrium to be reached rapidly (about 0.25 seconds); posture and positioning are listed among the pathophysiological factors affecting external respiration/gas exchange.
B. Although carbon dioxide has a lower partial pressure gradient (40 to 46mmHg) than oxygen, it is about 20 times more soluble in plasma, allowing it to diffuse in equal amounts to oxygen.
C. Pulmonary perfusion requires adequate blood volume, intact pulmonary capillaries and efficient pumping by the heart, and the respiratory membrane must remain thin and intact for efficient diffusion.
C. When the alveolar walls are inflamed (as in pneumonia or emphysema), scarred (as in emphysema or tuberculosis), infected, or filled with fluid, pus or blood (as in pneumonia, pulmonary oedema or ARDS), the gas exchange surface is compromised and diffusion efficiency falls.
C. Overdistention of the alveoli (e.g. from mechanical ventilation) and surfactant dysfunction (as in infant respiratory distress syndrome) also impair the ability of the alveoli to inflate properly and exchange gas efficiently.
C. Because the diffusion rate depends on tissue thickness and area (Fick's law), any thickening or reduction of the respiratory membrane's surface area directly reduces the rate of oxygen and carbon dioxide diffusion between alveoli and blood.
C. Clinically, this manifests as hypoxaemia, and where CO2 retention also occurs (as in emphysema and chronic bronchitis), the chemoreceptors can become unresponsive to PCO2 and PO2 levels become the principal respiratory stimulus (hypoxic drive).

A(i) Postural drainage is the gravitational clearance of secretions from specific bronchial segments using one or more positions so that gravity moves secretions to the trachea to be coughed up more readily.
A(ii) It is used when secretions are localised to specific lobes/segments, most frequently the lower lobes, since the upper lobes drain by gravity; a bronchodilator or nebuliser may be given beforehand to loosen secretions.
A(iii) Contraindications include intracranial pressure above 20mmHg, active haemorrhage with haemodynamic instability, recent spinal surgery, active haemoptysis, empyema, broncho-pleural fistula, large pleural effusions, pulmonary embolism, and rib fracture with or without flail chest.
A(iv) Positioning is scheduled two to three times daily (before breakfast, before lunch, in the late afternoon and before bedtime, avoiding times shortly after meals), and the client remains in the desired position for 10 to 15 minutes if tolerated.
A(iv) The sequence for chest physiotherapy is positioning, percussion, vibration, and removal of secretions by coughing or suction, after which the lungs are auscultated and findings documented.
A(v) The goal is to move bronchial secretions to the central airways via gravity and external manipulation of the chest so they can be eliminated by cough or aspiration, improving ventilation-perfusion matching and normalising functional residual capacity.
B. Percussion and vibration are effective because air moving over a thick layer of mucus creates a shear force on the liquid layer; when this shear force exceeds the surface tension in the mucus layer, the mucus begins to move, and mucus flow is higher when airflow is higher.
B. Percussion involves striking the chest wall with a rigid, dome-shaped (cupped) hand in a rhythmic pattern for 30 to 60 seconds, or 3 to 5 minutes if secretions are tenacious, avoiding the spine, breasts, below the ribs and surgical incisions.
B. Vibration and shaking are intermittent chest wall compressions performed throughout the expiratory phase, thought to reinforce expiratory gas flow and increase the shearing action on the mucosal layer, avoiding the breasts, spine, sternum and rib cage.
C. Postural drainage relies purely on gravity and positioning of the affected bronchial segment above the trachea to drain secretions, requiring no manual contact with the chest wall.
C. Percussion and vibration are manual techniques applied directly over the area of secretions to mechanically loosen and mobilise mucus, and are typically combined with postural drainage rather than used alone.
C. Vibration itself differs from shaking in that vibration uses the therapist's hands and arms to create small-amplitude, high-frequency oscillations (about 200 per minute), while shaking uses the arms and body to create large-amplitude, lower-frequency oscillations.
questions.question:
Describe postural drainage under the following headings: A(i) definition, A(ii) indications, A(iii) contraindications, A(iv) procedure, A(v) physiological effects.
B. Explain the clinical basis of chest percussion and vibration as adjuncts to postural drainage.
C. Distinguish between postural drainage and the manual techniques of percussion and vibration, and between vibration and shaking.

questions.answerText:
(i) Post-surgical pulmonary complications (PPC), e.g. atelectasis or hypoxaemia, common after upper abdominal or chest surgery due to severe and prolonged alteration in pulmonary mechanics.
(ii) Prior health status (pre-existing respiratory/cardiovascular disorders, poor immune system), effects of anaesthesia (ventilation-perfusion mismatch, CNS regulation of breathing, immunosuppressive and drug effects, reduction in lung capacities, neuromuscular blocking agents), and surgical trauma (post-operative pain, disruption of respiratory muscles, reflex inhibition of the phrenic nerve).
(iii) Clinical features: pain, difficulty coughing, accumulation of secretion, dyspnoea, reduced lung volume, impaired gas exchange, respiratory muscle dysfunction and postural abnormalities; investigations: spirometry, plethysmography/chest excursion, respiratory muscle strength, arterial blood gas assessment, sputum culture, chest X-ray and ECG.
(iv) Problem list: pain, breathing problems, muscle atrophy and weakness, loss of range of motion, impaired air clearance, reduced lung volume, reduced exercise tolerance, functional limitation, reduced quality of life, skin breakdown/infection and deep vein thrombosis; short-term goals: reduce pain, increase lung volumes, improve joint range of motion, improve breathing pattern, remove secretion/clear airway, improve arterial blood gas profile and preserve muscle bulk and strength.
(v) Electro-analgesia, positioning, breathing exercises (breathing control, diaphragmatic breathing, pursed lip breathing, deep breathing), incentive spirometry, airway clearance (huffing, ACBT, autogenic drainage), exercise therapy (early graduated mobilization, ROM, strengthening, endurance) and coughing (assisted coughing techniques, directed cough).
questions.question:
A patient recently underwent upper abdominal surgery and now has pain on coughing, accumulation of secretions, dyspnoea and reduced lung volume.
(i) State the likely diagnosis/category of complication.
(ii) Explain the pathogenesis of this condition.
(iii) State the key assessment findings/investigations expected.
(iv) List the physiotherapy problem list and goals.
(v) Outline the physiotherapy management.

A ventilated patient in the intensive care unit has retained secretions and reduced lung compliance.
(i) Name the physiotherapy technique indicated.
(ii) Describe the technique.
(iii) State the precautions/contraindications.
(iv) State the progression/outcome expected.
questions.answerText:
(i) Bagging/manual hyperinflation (MHI).
(ii) The technique involves slow deep inspiration, an inspiratory hold at full inspiration, a fast expiratory release, and hand-held pressure support, using a tidal volume greater than the baseline tidal volume (about 50% greater than that delivered via the ventilator).
(iii) Contraindications include undrained pneumothorax, potential or severe bronchospasm, gross cardiovascular instability causing arrhythmias and hypovolaemia, unexplained haemoptysis, and patients on high PEEP; hazards include reduction in blood pressure, reduced saturation, raised intracranial pressure and reduced respiratory drive.
(iv) Advantages/expected progression include reversal of atelectasis and improvement in oxygen saturation, lung compliance and sputum clearance, supporting progression toward weaning from mechanical ventilation.

questions.question:
A ventilated patient in the intensive care unit develops a sudden rise in peak inspiratory pressure and a dull percussion note over one lung base.
(i) Identify the possible pathology and structures affected.
(ii) State the differential causes of the elevated airway pressure.
(iii) Explain the clinical reasoning for the physiotherapy technique selected.
questions.answerText:
(i) A dull percussion note suggests atelectasis or consolidation of the affected lung base; elevated peak inspiratory pressure reflects reduced lung compliance.
(ii) Elevated peak inspiratory pressure could be due to reduced compliance, fibrosis, ARDS, pulmonary oedema, sputum plugging or bronchospasm.
(iii) Since sputum plugging is a likely reversible cause and secretion retention worsens compliance and gas exchange, airway clearance techniques and manual hyperinflation are reasoned choices, as manual hyperinflation aids removal of secretions, aids reinflation of atelectatic segments, and can assess and improve lung compliance.

questions.question:
A known asthmatic presents with wheezing, dyspnoea, persistent cough, tachypnoea and tachycardia during an acute episode.
(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) Define this condition as presented.
(iii) State the pathogenesis.
(iv) Outline the physiotherapy management.
questions.answerText:
(i) Bronchial asthma (acute exacerbation).
(ii) Asthma is a reversible chronic inflammatory airway disease characterised by bronchial hyper-responsiveness of the airways to various stimuli, leading to widespread bronchoconstriction, airflow limitation and inflammation of the bronchi causing cough, wheeze, chest tightness and dyspnoea.
(iii) Release of inflammatory mediators causes reversible airway inflammation, swelling of the mucosa layer, thickening of the muscle layer, hypersecretion of mucus and bronchoconstriction by the surrounding smooth muscle.
(iv) Education, positioning, breathing techniques, physical training, manual techniques (percussion, shaking, vibration), postural drainage, coughing and huffing, and range of motion exercises; short-term goals include relief of bronchospasm and reduction of breathing difficulties within the first week.

A(i) Carbon dioxide is transported in the blood in three forms: dissolved in plasma (about 7-10%), chemically bound to haemoglobin as carbaminohaemoglobin in red blood cells (about 20%), and as bicarbonate ion in plasma (about 70%, the major transport form).
A(i) Carbon dioxide diffuses into red blood cells and combines with water to form carbonic acid, a reaction reversibly catalysed by carbonic anhydrase, and the carbonic acid quickly dissociates into hydrogen ions and bicarbonate ions.
A(ii) The carbonic acid-bicarbonate buffer system resists blood pH changes: if hydrogen ion concentration rises, excess hydrogen ions are removed by combining with bicarbonate; if hydrogen ion concentration falls, carbonic acid dissociates, releasing hydrogen ions.
A(ii) At the tissues, bicarbonate diffuses from red blood cells into the plasma, and to counterbalance the loss of negative bicarbonate ions, chloride ions move from the plasma into the erythrocytes (the chloride shift); at the lungs these processes reverse, with bicarbonate moving back into red blood cells to reform carbonic acid, which is split to release carbon dioxide for diffusion into the alveoli.
B. The Haldane effect describes how removing oxygen from haemoglobin increases haemoglobin's ability to pick up carbon dioxide and the hydrogen ions generated from it; the Haldane and Bohr effects work together, so at the tissues more oxygen dissociates from haemoglobin while more carbon dioxide and bicarbonate are formed, a situation reversed in the pulmonary circulation.
B. Clinically, arterial blood gas analysis applies these transport and buffer principles: normal values are pH 7.35-7.45, PaCO2 35-45mmHg, PaO2 80-100mmHg, HCO3 22-26mmol/L and base excess -2 to +2, and trends over time give more meaningful conclusions than a single reading.
B. Control of breathing rate and depth is used to regulate arterial pH: if pH is low, the respiratory system attempts to raise it by increasing the rate and depth of breathing; if pH is high, it attempts to lower it by decreasing the rate and depth of breathing.
C. Acidosis may reflect carbon dioxide retention, accumulation of lactic acid, or excess fatty acids in patients with diabetes mellitus, and increased ventilation in response to falling pH is mediated by peripheral chemoreceptors.
C. When carbon dioxide is not adequately removed, as in emphysema and chronic bronchitis, the chemoreceptors can become unresponsive to PCO2 as a stimulus, and PO2 levels become the principal respiratory stimulus (hypoxic drive).
C. Sustained hypoxaemia results in increasing PaCO2, and if this is sustained the brain's respiratory control centre and central chemoreceptors are desensitised, so compensatory action to correct the imbalance does not occur.
C. This underlies the risk of hypercapnia and respiratory acidosis seen in chronic respiratory conditions such as COPD, where impaired gas exchange and chronic CO2 retention overwhelm the buffering and compensatory capacity of the system.
C. Recognising abnormal arterial blood gas values (e.g. low pH with high PaCO2) therefore helps identify respiratory acidosis and guides physiotherapy decisions about airway clearance and ventilatory support needs.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the transport of carbon dioxide in the blood.
A(ii) Explain the carbonic acid-bicarbonate buffer system and the chloride shift.
B. State the application of these principles in interpreting arterial blood gases in practice.
C. Explain the physiological basis of the dysfunction that results when CO2 is not adequately removed.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Static lung volumes include tidal volume (TV, about 500mL, the volume breathed in a single normal quiet respiration), inspiratory reserve volume (IRV, the additional volume that can be inspired forcefully after normal inspiration, about 3000mL), expiratory reserve volume (ERV, the additional volume that can be expired forcefully after normal expiration, about 1100mL), and residual volume (RV, the volume remaining after the most forceful expiration, about 1200mL).
A(i) Static lung capacities combine two or more volumes: inspiratory capacity (IC = TV + IRV = 3500mL), vital capacity (VC = IRV + TV + ERV = 4600mL), functional residual capacity (FRC = ERV + RV = 2300mL), and total lung capacity (TLC = IRV + TV + ERV + RV = 5800mL).
A(ii) Dead space comprises anatomical dead space (the volume of the conducting respiratory passages, about 150mL), alveolar dead space (alveoli that cease to act in gas exchange due to collapse or obstruction), and total dead space (the sum of both).
A(ii) Pulmonary ventilation (respiratory minute volume) equals tidal volume multiplied by respiratory rate (500mL x 12 breaths/min = 6000mL/min), while alveolar ventilation equals (tidal volume minus dead space) multiplied by respiratory rate ((500-150)mL x 12 breaths/min = 4200mL/min).
B. Pulmonary function tests apply these volumes and capacities to evaluate lung function, assessing airflow, gas exchange, diffusion capacity, airway resistance and distribution of ventilation, and require client preparation and a defined bedside testing procedure.
B. Because functional residual capacity varies with body position, an upright posture is used clinically to optimise FRC, and incentive spirometry is applied to increase FRC as a means of preventing and reversing atelectasis.
B. Spirometry, one of the outcome measures/tools used in respiratory conditions, records values such as tidal volume, forced vital capacity, FEV1, FEV1/FVC ratio and peak expiratory flow rate.
C. Reduced lung volumes is listed among the common problems in respiratory disorders that physiotherapy addresses, since a reduction in effective lung volume compromises ventilation and gas exchange.
C. When an anatomical area of lung collapses (atelectasis), this presents as decreased volume, identified by a raised hemi-diaphragm on chest X-ray, altered breath sounds and a shallow breathing pattern, together with altered gas exchange.
C. An increase in total or alveolar dead space (e.g. through alveolar collapse or airway obstruction) reduces the effective alveolar ventilation available for gas exchange even if pulmonary ventilation (minute volume) remains unchanged, so alveolar ventilation is the more physiologically relevant measure of gas exchange.
C. Treatment options for decreased lung volume - positioning, thoracic expansion exercises, incentive spirometry, IPPB and mobilisation - are therefore directed at restoring functional residual capacity and vital capacity toward normal.
C. Resolution is monitored by improved spirometry readings, auscultation changes and chest X-ray findings, which together are used as goals to demonstrate the reversal of the decreased volume problem.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the static lung volumes and capacities.
A(ii) Explain the concept of dead space and its relation to ventilation.
B. State the application of these measures in pulmonary function testing/practice.
C. Explain the physiological basis of the dysfunction that results when lung volume is reduced.

A patient diagnosed with lung cancer is being assessed for physiotherapy input.
(i) State the risk/pathogenic factors associated with reduced respiratory function in this condition.
(ii) State the problems/complications that arise as a result.
(iii) Outline the physiotherapy management options and justify the most appropriate one.
questions.answerText:
(i) The development of lung cancer itself reduces lung function; for other cancers, the disease may reduce physical activity, and surgical intervention may reduce respiratory function or result in pulmonary complications.
(ii) Pain, reduced chest excursion/lung volumes, excessive/retained secretions, altered arterial blood gases, general body weakness, poor posture, fatigue/tiredness and reduced functional capacity.
(iii) Options include positioning, breathing exercises, incentive spirometry, airway clearance techniques, mobilization, muscle strengthening, postural re-education and functional training; airway clearance techniques combined with breathing exercises are most appropriate where excessive/retained secretions and reduced chest excursion are the dominant problems, aiming to increase vital capacity and improve/reduce mucus secretion as a short-term goal.

(i) Pulmonary oedema; fluid accumulates in the tissues near/within the lungs due to transudation of fluid into the pulmonary interstitium and alveoli, with increased interstitial pressure, fluid retention in pulmonary tissues and reduced venous return.
(ii) Supporting features include peripheral oedema (pitting), raised jugular venous pressure, hepatomegaly, reduced exercise tolerance, pale skin, anxiety and weight gain.
(iii) Since the problem list includes difficulty breathing (especially with postural changes), peripheral oedema, reduced cardiovascular endurance and reduced exercise/functional capacity, management is directed at relaxation exercises and breathing exercises to reduce work of breathing and improve breathing pattern, oedema massage to reduce oedema, and aerobic exercises to improve cardiovascular endurance and exercise tolerance.
questions.question:
A patient presents with orthopnoea, pitting peripheral oedema, raised jugular venous pressure, a third heart sound and crackling heart sounds on auscultation.
(i) Identify the pathology and the structures/tissues affected.
(ii) State the differential clinical features that support the diagnosis.
(iii) Explain the clinical reasoning behind the choice of physiotherapy management.

A(i) Describe pulmonary function tests and the spirometric measures obtained.
A(ii) State the classification of COPD severity based on these measures.
B. State how spirometric findings relate to common respiratory conditions.
C. Explain how a reduced spirometric measure represents a functional deficit and how physiotherapy addresses it.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Pulmonary function tests evaluate lung volumes and capacities, flow rates, diffusion capacity, gas exchange, airway resistance and distribution of ventilation, and require client preparation and a defined procedure for performing the tests at the bedside.
A(i) Spirometric measures commonly recorded include tidal volume, forced vital capacity (FVC), FEV1, the FEV1/FVC ratio and peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR).
A(ii) COPD is classified by severity using these measures: Stage 1 (mild) has FEV1/FVC below 70% with FEV1 above 80% predicted; Stage 2 (moderate) has FEV1/FVC 50-70% with FEV1 below 80% predicted; Stage 3 (severe) has FEV1/FVC 30-70% with FEV1 below 50% predicted; Stage 4 (very severe) has FEV1/FVC below 70% with FEV1 below 30% predicted, or FEV1 below 50% predicted with respiratory failure.
A(ii) Severity of COPD is further determined by severity of symptoms, severity of airway limitation, frequency and severity of exacerbations, presence of complications, presence of respiratory insufficiency, comorbidity, general health status and number of medications needed.
B. Spirometric outcome measures (lung volumes: TV, FVC, FEV1, FEV1/FVC, PEFR) are used to monitor COPD, and spirometry is also listed as an outcome measure/tool in bronchiectasis, pleural effusion, pulmonary oedema, pulmonary tuberculosis and lung cancer.
B. In pleural effusion, the spirometer is specifically used to measure tidal volume and forced vital capacity as part of monitoring functional exercise capacity and lung function.
B. In tuberculosis and lung cancer, spirometric measures are among the outcome measures/tools used alongside pain, exertion, sputum volume and quality-of-life measures.
C. A reduced FEV1/FVC ratio and reduced FEV1 percentage predicted indicate a functional deficit of airflow limitation, the pulmonary component that characterises COPD and determines its stage of severity.
C. This airflow limitation contributes to exertional breathlessness, increased work of breathing and reduced exercise tolerance, which extend the functional deficit beyond the lungs to overall functional capacity and quality of life.
C. Physiotherapy addresses this deficit through airway clearing techniques, breathing exercises and strength and endurance exercise, as part of the means of treatment for COPD, aiming to reduce airway limitation and improve exercise tolerance.
C. In other conditions such as bronchiectasis, pleural effusion, pulmonary oedema, tuberculosis and lung cancer, physiotherapy management (breathing control, thoracic expansion exercises, incentive spirometry, graded exercise) similarly aims to increase lung function as reflected by improving spirometric measures.
C. Because spirometric measures are used as outcome measures across nearly all these conditions, they provide an objective way for physiotherapists to document whether their intervention has increased lung function and to progress treatment accordingly.

questions.question:
Describe Positive End-Expiratory Pressure (PEEP) under the following headings: A(i) definition, A(ii) indications, A(iii) complications, A(iv) settings/application, A(v) related pressure-support component.
B. Explain the clinical basis of Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP)/Pressure Support Ventilation (PSV) as a spontaneous breathing mode.
C. Distinguish between PEEP and CPAP/PSV.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) maintains airway pressure during expiration at a constant positive value; it is functionally similar to CPAP but is applied specifically at the end of expiration.
A(ii) PEEP is indicated to splint airways open to prevent atelectasis, increase end-expiratory lung volume (FRC), and increase gas exchange/oxygenation; it is kept at about 5cmH2O for prophylaxis and higher for therapeutic use, within a normal range of 5-15cmH2O.
A(iii) The main complication of PEEP is decreased cardiac output, via increased intrathoracic pressure and decreased venous return.
A(iv) PEEP is the pressure required to keep the airway open at the end of expiration and can be applied together with mandatory modes (such as SIMV) or with spontaneous breathing modes.
A(v) Pressure support (PS) supports spontaneous breaths only, delivering gas to the airway during inspiration according to a pre-set level (normal range 5-20cmH2O), and is used to increase the patient's spontaneous tidal volume and decrease work of breathing; it can work together with CPAP, SIMV(V) or PCV.
B. Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP), also referred to as Pressure Support Ventilation (PSV) in this context, is used for spontaneously breathing patients with an intact respiratory drive who initiate all their own breaths.
B. A constant positive pressure is applied during both inspiration (as pressure support) and expiration (as PEEP), and it is available on non-invasive devices as well as invasive ventilators.
B. CPAP/PSV helps prevent alveolar collapse, increases functional residual capacity and increases oxygenation, and is commonly used for patients being weaned from mechanical ventilation, hence also called the spontaneous breathing mode; peak airway pressure (PIP) equals the pressure support plus the PEEP (PIP = PS + PEEP).
C. PEEP by itself is only the expiratory-phase pressure component and can be combined with fully mandatory modes (e.g. AC, SIMV) where the ventilator also controls inspiration.
C. CPAP/PSV, in contrast, is a spontaneous breathing mode: the patient triggers and largely controls their own breathing, with the ventilator providing constant background pressure (PEEP) and inspiratory assistance (pressure support) rather than mandatory breaths.
C. Thus PEEP is a pressure setting applicable across ventilator modes, whereas CPAP/PSV is a specific mode built from a PEEP component (expiration) and a pressure-support component (inspiration).
C. CPAP/PSV is used mainly for spontaneously breathing or weaning patients, whereas PEEP alone can be applied even to fully ventilator-dependent patients on mandatory modes.

questions.question:
On chest examination, a patient has diminished chest expansion on one side, a dry cough, chest pain worse on breathing, and a stony dull note on percussion over the lower zone.
(i) What is the most likely diagnosis?
(ii) State the possible causes of this condition.
(iii) State the physiotherapy problem list.
(iv) Outline the physiotherapy management.
questions.answerText:
(i) Pleural effusion.
(ii) By pathophysiology it may be transudative (caused by congestive heart failure, cirrhosis/hepatic hydrothorax, atelectasis, cerebrospinal fluid leaks to the pleura, or peritoneal dialysis/nephrotic syndrome) or exudative (caused by malignancy, pulmonary embolism, tuberculosis, trauma, sarcoidosis, fungal infection, pericardial disease or radiation pleuritis).
(iii) Chest pain especially with breathing, diminished chest expansion and breathing difficulties, and cough (dry or productive).
(iv) Breathing control, thoracic expansion exercises, incentive spirometry, airway clearance techniques if necessary, assisted cough, graded exercises, and patient education and counselling.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Superficial group (3 muscles): Gastrocnemius — lateral head from lateral aspect of lateral condyle of femur; insertion: posterior surface of calcaneus via calcaneal tendon; innervation: tibial nerve (S1, S2); action: plantarflexes ankle when knee is extended, raises heel during walking, flexes leg at knee joint. Soleus — posterior aspect of head and superior quarter of posterior surface of fibula; soleal line and middle third of medial border of tibia; tendinous arch; insertion: posterior surface of calcaneus via calcaneal tendon; innervation: tibial nerve (S1, S2); action: plantarflexes ankle independent of position of knee, steadies leg on foot. Plantaris — inferior end of lateral supracondylar line of femur, oblique popliteal ligament; insertion: posterior surface of calcaneus via calcaneal tendon; innervation: tibial nerve (S1, S2); action: weakly assists gastrocnemius in plantarflexing ankle. Deep group (4 muscles): Popliteus — lateral surface of lateral condyle of femur and lateral meniscus; posterior surface of tibia superior to soleal line; tibial nerve (L4, L5, S1); weakly flexes knee, unlocks it by rotating femur 5° on fixed tibia, and medially rotates tibia of unplanted limb. Flexor hallucis longus — inferior 2/3 of posterior surface of fibula; base of distal phalanx of great toe; tibial nerve (S2, S3); flexes great toe at all joints, weakly plantarflexes ankle, supports medial longitudinal arch. Flexor digitorum longus — medial part of posterior surface of tibia inferior to soleal line; bases of distal phalanges of lateral 4 digits; tibial nerve (S2, S3); flexes lateral 4 digits, plantarflexes ankle, supports longitudinal arches. Tibialis posterior — interosseous membrane, posterior tibia inferior to soleal line, posterior fibula; tuberosity of navicular, cuneiform, cuboid, sustentaculum tali of calcaneus, bases of 2nd, 3rd, and 4th metatarsals; tibial nerve (L4, L5); plantarflexes ankle and inverts foot.
A(ii)
The calcaneal tendon is formed by the union of the tendons of gastrocnemius, soleus, and plantaris; it inserts into the posterior surface of the calcaneus. It is the largest and strongest tendon in the body. Clinical significance: rupture of the Achilles tendon (commonly felt as a 'pop' and tested by Thompson's squeeze test) results in inability to plantarflex the foot.
B(i)
The posterior tibial artery enters the sole of the foot through the tarsal tunnel, accompanying the tibial nerve. The tibial nerve enters the sole of the foot via the tarsal tunnel and then splits into the lateral and medial plantar arteries. For a tarsal tunnel block, the posterior tibial pulse can be palpated inferoposteriorly to the medial malleolus, where the artery turns to enter the foot — the tibial nerve lies adjacent.
B(ii)
Tibialis posterior inserts into the tuberosity of the navicular, cuneiform, cuboid, sustentaculum tali of calcaneus, and the bases of the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th metatarsals — the very bones that form the medial longitudinal arch. It plantarflexes the ankle and inverts the foot; by pulling the navicular and cuneiforms downward and inward it actively maintains the height of the medial longitudinal arch. Dysfunction (e.g., from tenosynovitis or rupture) leads to eversion of the calcaneus, slipping down of the talus and navicular, and pes planus — collapse of the medial longitudinal arch.
C(i)
Gastrocnemius spans the knee joint (arising from the femoral condyle) and the ankle joint; it plantarflexes the ankle only when the knee is extended and also flexes the knee. It is tested with the knee extended. Soleus arises entirely from the tibia and fibula (below the knee) and plantarflexes the ankle independent of the position of the knee. It is tested by single-leg heel raise with the knee flexed to 90°, which eliminates gastrocnemius from the movement and isolates soleus.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
The quadrangular cartilaginous septum extends from the nasal bones in the midline above to the bony septum in the midline posteriorly, then down along the bony floor. Its upper half is flanked by two triangular-to-trapezoidal cartilages, the upper lateral cartilages, which are fused to the dorsal septum in the midline and attached to the bony margin of the pyriform aperture laterally by loose ligaments; the inferior ends of the upper lateral cartilages are free. Beneath the upper lateral cartilages lie the lower lateral cartilages; the paired lower lateral cartilages swing out from medial attachments to the caudal septum in the midline (the medial crura), through an intermediate crus area, finally flaring out superolaterally as the lateral crura; these cartilages are frequently mobile, in contradistinction to the upper lateral cartilages. The internal area or angle formed by the septum and upper lateral cartilage constitutes the internal valve.
A(ii)
The nasal septum is supplied from the sphenopalatine artery (posterior septal branch) and the anterior and posterior ethmoid arteries, with contribution of the superior labial artery (anteriorly) and the greater palatine artery (posteriorly).
B
The Kiesselbach plexus, or Little's area, represents a region in the anteroinferior third of the nasal septum where all 3 of the chief blood supplies to the internal nose converge, which is the clinical basis for this being a common site of nosebleeds; venous blood leaving the region drains into the facial, ophthalmic and sphenopalatine veins, and these veins are significant for their direct communication with the cavernous sinus and for their lack of valves, features that potentiate the intracranial spread of infection.
C
The upper lateral cartilages are fused to the dorsal septum in the midline and attached to the bony margin of the pyriform aperture laterally by loose ligaments, with their inferior ends free; they are relatively fixed. The lower lateral (alar) cartilages, by contrast, swing out from medial attachments to the caudal septum (the medial crura) to flare out superolaterally as the lateral crura, and are frequently mobile, unlike the upper lateral cartilages.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the nasal septum and the cartilages of the external nose under the following headings: the quadrangular cartilage, the upper lateral cartilages, and the lower lateral (alar) cartilages.
A(ii) Describe the blood supply to the nasal septum.
B. Explain the clinical basis for why the anteroinferior third of the nasal septum is the commonest site of nosebleeds (epistaxis).

Describe the popliteal artery and its branches, stating the safe site for popliteal pulse palpation, and explain the anatomical basis of the deformity and functional deficit after tibial nerve injury in the popliteal fossa.
A(i) Origin, course, and relations of the popliteal artery
A(ii) All branches of the popliteal artery — genicular and muscular
B(i) Termination and continuation of the popliteal artery into the leg and foot
B(ii) Safe site for popliteal pulse palpation and clinical technique
C(i) Anatomical basis of the deformity and functional deficit after tibial nerve injury in the popliteal fossa
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The popliteal artery is the continuation of the femoral artery; it begins when the femoral artery passes through the adductor hiatus. It descends through the fossa, passing inferolaterally and is the deepest structure in the fossa — it runs in close proximity to the articular capsule of the knee joint. It terminates at the inferior border of the popliteus by dividing into the anterior and posterior tibial arteries.
A(ii)
Five genicular branches participate in the genicular anastomosis (a network of vessels surrounding the knee providing collateral circulation capable of maintaining blood supply to the leg during full knee flexion): superior lateral genicular artery, superior medial genicular artery, middle genicular artery (penetrates the fibrous capsule and supplies the cruciate ligaments, synovial membrane, and peripheral margins of the menisci), inferior lateral genicular artery, and inferior medial genicular artery. Muscular branches supply the hamstring, gastrocnemius, soleus, and plantaris muscles. The superior muscular branches have clinically important anastomoses with the terminal part of the profunda femoris and gluteal arteries.
B(i)
Termination: the popliteal artery divides into the anterior tibial artery and the tibioperoneal trunk; the tibioperoneal trunk divides into the posterior tibial artery and fibular (peroneal) artery. Anterior tibial artery: passes anterior to the interosseous membrane between tibia and fibula; supplies muscles of anterior compartment; continues as the dorsalis pedis artery in the foot, supplying tarsal bones and dorsal metatarsals, and anastomoses with the lateral plantar artery to form the deep plantar arch. Posterior tibial artery: continues inferiorly along surface of deep posterior leg muscles; enters the sole of the foot via the tarsal tunnel; splits into lateral and medial plantar arteries supplying the plantar foot.
B(ii)
The popliteal artery is the hardest pulse to find, lying deep in the popliteal fossa; it requires deep palpation. To make it easier, the patient should slightly flex the leg — this relaxes the fascia around the popliteal fossa. An aneurysm of the popliteal artery can be detected by an obvious palpable pulsation in the popliteal fossa; an arterial bruit may be heard on auscultation.
C(i)
The tibial nerve is the medial and larger branch of the sciatic nerve and the most superficial of the neurovascular bundle. Injury causes: paralysis of flexor muscles in the leg and intrinsic muscles in the sole of the foot; inability to plantarflex the ankles or flex the toes; and loss of sensation on the sole of the foot. The resulting deformity is a calcaneovalgus posture — unopposed dorsiflexion with loss of plantarflexion, the foot assuming a dorsiflexed position because the antagonist muscles remain intact. Weakened or absent plantarflexion and paraesthesia of the foot and posterolateral leg are the major features of tibial nerve compression.

questions.question:
A. Describe the origin, course, and branches/distribution of the ophthalmic artery.
B. State why the ophthalmic artery and its central retinal branch are of particular functional importance to the orbit.
questions.answerText:
A
The only artery supplying structures in the orbit is the ophthalmic artery, which is a branch of the internal carotid artery; it enters the orbit with the optic nerve through the optic foramen (canal). Its branches include the lacrimal artery (to the lacrimal gland and upper eyelid), muscular branches to the muscles, long posterior ciliary arteries (to the ciliary body), short posterior ciliary arteries (to the choroid and part of the optic nerve), and medial palpebral arteries (to the eyelids).
B
The ophthalmic artery gives rise to the very important branch, the central artery of the retina; because the ophthalmic artery is the only artery supplying orbital structures, and the central retinal artery is its branch, the retina is dependent on this single arterial source, so the optic nerve is covered by dura, arachnoid and pia from the sclera to the canal, where the dura is continuous with the periosteum of the orbit, and venous drainage (superior and inferior ophthalmic veins) communicates with the cavernous sinus, giving direct communication between the skin of the face and the cavernous sinus (the danger triangle).

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the parts and the course of the oesophagus.
A(ii) Describe its relations.
A(iii) State its constrictions and their distances from the incisor teeth.
A(iv) Describe its arterial supply, venous drainage, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply.
B(i) Relate the upper, middle and lower parts of the oesophagus to their differing supply and relations.
C(i) Explain how disease may spread from the oesophagus to distant structures through its venous and lymphatic drainage.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
It has cervical, thoracic and abdominal parts and is not a straight structure: it lies to the left in the neck, returns to the midline at the thoracic inlet, lies to the left in the superior mediastinum, returns to the midline in the posterior mediastinum and deviates to the left as it pierces the diaphragm at T10.
A(ii)
Cervical part lies in front of the prevertebral fascia, behind the trachea; the thoracic part is crossed on the right by the azygos vein and on the left by the aorta; in the posterior mediastinum it lies behind the left main bronchus and left pulmonary artery and in front of the thoracic duct; it is the most posterior tube of the superior mediastinum and the most anterior structure of the posterior mediastinum, with the vagus nerves around it, the azygos vein behind and to the right and the descending aorta behind and to the left.
A(iii)
Four constrictions: at its origin (C6), 15 cm from the incisor teeth; where the arch of the aorta lies in front of it, 22 cm; where the left main bronchus lies in front of it (tracheal bifurcation), 27 cm; at the diaphragm (T10), 38-40 cm.
A(iv)
• Arteries: inferior thyroid artery, oesophageal branches of the descending thoracic aorta, and the left gastric artery.
• Veins: upper part to the brachiocephalic vein, middle part to the azygos vein, lower part to the portal vein.
• Lymphatics: upper part to deep cervical nodes, middle part to tracheobronchial nodes, lower part to preaortic nodes.
• Nerves: upper third is striated, supplied by the recurrent laryngeal branch of the vagus, with sympathetics from the middle cervical ganglion; lower two-thirds is smooth, receiving sympathetics from the sympathetic trunk and greater splanchnic nerve, and parasympathetic secretomotor fibres from the vagus to the oesophageal glands.
B(i)
• Upper part: inferior thyroid artery, brachiocephalic vein, deep cervical nodes, striated muscle with recurrent laryngeal supply, related to the trachea and prevertebral fascia in the neck.
• Middle and lower parts: middle drains to the azygos vein and tracheobronchial nodes and is crossed by the azygos vein, arch of the aorta and left main bronchus; lower part has aortic and left gastric arteries, portal venous drainage, preaortic nodes and smooth muscle, and passes through the diaphragm at T10.
C(i)
• Venous routes: upper part to the brachiocephalic vein, middle part to the azygos vein (which empties into the SVC and forms a communication between the SVC and IVC), lower part to the portal vein.
• Lymphatic routes: upper part to deep cervical nodes, middle part to tracheobronchial nodes, lower part to preaortic nodes.

A(i)
Oblique, tunnel-shaped passage through the lower part of the anterior abdominal wall just above the medial half of the inguinal ligament, present in both sexes; about 4 cm (1½ inches) long in adults, directed downwards, forwards and medially.
A(ii)
It extends from the deep inguinal ring to the superficial inguinal ring; in the newborn the deep ring lies almost directly posterior to the superficial ring.
A(iii)
• Anterior wall: external oblique aponeurosis, reinforced laterally by internal oblique. Posterior wall: transversalis fascia, reinforced medially by the conjoint tendon.
• Roof: arching lowest fibres of internal oblique and transversus abdominis with transversalis fascia. Floor: inguinal ligament, reinforced medially by the lacunar ligament.
A(iv)
Spermatic cord (male) or round ligament of uterus (female); processus vaginalis remnant; 3 fasciae; 3 arteries (artery to vas, cremasteric, testicular); 3 nerves (ilio-inguinal L1, genital branch of genitofemoral L2, sympathetic); vas, pampiniform plexus, lymphatics.
B(i)
• It is a potential weakness in the abdominal wall. The posterior wall is weak laterally at the deep ring, but the anterior wall opposite is reinforced by internal oblique, so a hernia through the deep ring must travel along the canal.
• The anterior wall is weak medially at the superficial ring, but the posterior wall opposite is reinforced by the conjoint tendon; weakness there leads to direct hernias.
B(ii)
In the male it allows spermatic cord structures to pass to and from the testis (normal spermatogenesis needs the cooler scrotum) while preventing intestine entering the scrotum; in the female the smaller canal carries the round ligament of the uterus to the labium majus.
C(i)
• Deep ring: oval opening in the transversalis fascia, about ½ inch (1.3 cm) above the inguinal ligament at the midinguinal point, lateral to the inferior epigastric artery; margins give attachment to internal spermatic fascia; entrance of the cord.
• Superficial ring: triangular defect in the external oblique aponeurosis, immediately above and medial to the pubic tubercle; its medial and lateral crura give attachment to the external spermatic fascia; it is the exit of the cord from the canal.

A(i)
An omentum is a double-layered extension or fold passing from the stomach and proximal duodenum to adjacent organs or to the abdominal wall; there are two types, lesser and greater.
A(ii)
The lesser omentum is a two-layered fold connecting the lesser curvature of the stomach and proximal duodenum to the liver; the hepatoduodenal ligament is its thickened free edge, conducting the portal vein, hepatic artery and bile duct.
A(iii)
The greater omentum hangs like an apron from the greater curvature of the stomach and proximal duodenum, folds back after descending and attaches to the anterior surface of the transverse colon and its mesocolon.
A(iv)
• Liver: falciform ligament (anterior wall), gastrohepatic ligament (stomach), hepatoduodenal ligament (duodenum). Stomach: gastrophrenic, gastrosplenic, gastrocolic, gastrohepatic, gastropancreatic.
• Spleen: gastrosplenic (short gastric and left gastroepiploic vessels), splenorenal (splenic vessels and tail of pancreas), phrenicosplenic, splenocolic.
B(i)
• It is large and fat laden and prevents the visceral peritoneum adhering to the parietal peritoneum lining the anterolateral wall.
• It is mobile, moving with peristalsis, and can wrap itself around an inflamed organ such as the appendix, walling it off and protecting other viscera.
• It also cushions the abdominal organs against injury and forms insulation against loss of body heat.
C(i)
• Lesser: from liver to lesser curvature and proximal duodenum, containing the hepatoduodenal ligament; greater: hangs from the greater curvature and attaches to the transverse colon.
• The anterior and posterior layers of the lesser omentum extend from the liver to the lesser curvature; the anterior layer continues as the first layer of the greater omentum, the posterior layer forms its second and third layers.
• The lesser omentum forms part of the anterior wall of the lesser sac together with the peritoneum of the posterior wall of the stomach and the anterior two layers of the greater omentum.
• The hepatoduodenal ligament forms the anterior boundary of the omental foramen.

A(i)
• The longest lymphatic duct, conveying lymph to the circulatory system.
• It begins as the upward continuation of the cisterna chyli, a dilated sac formed by the union of the left and right lumbar trunks and the intestinal trunk, in front of L1 (also stated at T12).
A(ii)
• It enters the thorax through the aortic opening of the diaphragm and ascends in the posterior mediastinum, on the right side of and behind the oesophagus, with the oesophagus lying in front of it.
• It veers to the left at the level of T5 and ascends in the superior mediastinum to the left of the oesophagus.
• At the root of the neck it turns laterally, arches forwards and descends to enter the left venous angle.
A(iii)
• Before termination it receives the left jugular, left subclavian and left bronchomediastinal trunks; it ends in the left brachiocephalic vein.
• It contains many valves, with no valve at its termination.
A(iv)
• It drains lymph from the lower limbs, pelvic cavity, abdominal cavity, left half of the thorax and left side of the head, neck and upper limb (all the body except the right side of the head, neck, thorax and upper limb).
• The right lymphatic duct, formed by the union of the right jugular, subclavian and bronchomediastinal trunks, drains the right half of the head, neck, thorax and upper limb, right lung, right side of the heart and right surface of the liver, and ends in the right brachiocephalic vein.
• The lymph trunks are the right and left jugular, subclavian, bronchomediastinal and lumbar trunks and the intestinal trunk; the left brachiocephalic vein receives the thoracic duct, the right brachiocephalic vein the right lymphatic duct.
questions.question:
A(i) Define the thoracic duct and state its origin.
A(ii) Describe its course and relations.
A(iii) State its tributaries and termination.
A(iv) Describe the area it drains and compare it with the right lymphatic duct.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Gross anatomy of the pancreas:
• Nature: a mixed exocrine-endocrine gland that produces both digestive enzymes and hormones.
• Position: retroperitoneally positioned on the posterior wall of the abdominal cavity at the level of the 2nd and 3rd lumbar vertebrae.
• Capsular covering: it has no distinct capsule, but is covered by a thin layer of loose connective tissue, from which septa extend to cover the larger vessels and ducts and to separate the parenchyma into lobules.
A(ii)
Two functional components:
• Exocrine: produces digestive enzymes that act in the small intestine; secretory acini produce about 1.6 litres of pancreatic juice every day.
• Endocrine: involves primarily smaller cells similar to enteroendocrine cells located in variously sized clusters called the pancreatic islets (islets of Langerhans); secretes hormones such as insulin and glucagon into the bloodstream, which are very important for the metabolism of absorbed nutrients.
B(i)
Exocrine acini:
• The secretory acini are surrounded by a basal lamina that is supported only by a delicate sheath of reticular fibers with a rich capillary network.
• The exocrine part produces about 1.6 litres of pancreatic juice every day.
B(ii)
• Pancreas: produces digestive enzymes that act in the small intestine; secretes insulin and glucagon, both important for metabolism of absorbed nutrients.
• Liver: produces bile, an important fluid in the digestion of fats; plays a major role in lipid, carbohydrate, and protein metabolism; inactivates and metabolizes many toxic substances and drugs; participates in iron metabolism and the synthesis of blood proteins and factors necessary for blood coagulation.
• Gallbladder: absorbs water from bile and stores bile in a concentrated form.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the gross anatomy of the pancreas, including its nature as a gland, its retroperitoneal position, its capsular covering, and how its parenchyma is organised into lobules.
A(ii) Describe the two functional components of the pancreas (exocrine and endocrine), including the cell types involved and the products of each.
B(i) Describe the exocrine secretory acini of the pancreas, including the arrangement around the acini and the volume of juice produced.
B(ii) Explain the role of the pancreas in digestion and hormonal regulation, and contrast this with the role of the liver and the gallbladder.

Describe the radial nerve:
A(i) Origin and course in the arm
A(ii) Course/division in the cubital fossa and forearm
A(iii) Branches
A(iv) Distribution
C. Explain the anatomical basis of the deformity ("wrist drop") seen after radial nerve injury.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The radial nerve is a terminal branch of the posterior cord of the brachial plexus; it courses posteromedially with the axillary vessels and enters the posterior compartment of the arm under teres major, where it winds around the spiral (radial) groove of the humerus, accompanied by the profunda brachii artery.
A(ii)
• It pierces the lateral intermuscular septum to enter the anterior compartment of the arm, passes to the forearm at the level of the elbow joint, enters the cubital fossa, and there divides into a superficial and a deep branch.
• The superficial branch courses toward the wrist lateral to the radial artery and enters the hand, dividing into dorsal digital cutaneous branches; the deep branch gives off the posterior interosseous nerve, which passes between the heads of supinator to enter the posterior compartment of the forearm and terminates near the wrist joint.
A(iii)
