Branches include muscular twigs in the arm to triceps brachii and anconeus, the posterior interosseous nerve to the forearm extensors, the superficial (cutaneous) branch, and articular twigs to the elbow and wrist joints.
A(iv)
The deep branch/posterior interosseous nerve supplies the extensor muscles in the forearm as well as brachioradialis; the superficial branch supplies cutaneous sensation to the dorsal aspect of the hand, the dorsal aspect of the first to third digits, and the dorsolateral aspect of the fourth finger.
C
• Injury to the radial nerve produces "wrist drop."
• Because the nerve's deep branch/posterior interosseous nerve supplies the extensor muscles of the forearm, injury interrupts the motor supply to the wrist and finger extensors.
• The nerve can be injured at any level — axilla, spiral groove, radial tunnel, posterior interosseous, or superficial radial.
• Injury may result from fracture of the body (shaft) of the humerus, where the nerve lies in close contact with the bone in the spiral groove.
• "Saturday Night Palsy" describes compression of the nerve in the axilla, such as from using improperly adjusted crutches, which similarly interrupts its motor function.
• With the extensors paralysed and unopposed flexor tone at the wrist, the hand falls into flexion at the wrist, producing the characteristic wrist drop.

A(i)
Fibularis longus: origin — head and superior 2/3 of lateral surface of fibula; insertion — base of 1st metatarsal and medial cuneiform; innervation — superficial fibular nerve (L5, S1, S2); action — everts foot and weakly plantarflexes ankle. Fibularis brevis: origin — inferior 2/3 of lateral surface of fibula; insertion — dorsal surface of tuberosity on lateral side of base of 5th metatarsal; innervation — superficial fibular nerve (L5, S1, S2); action — everts foot and weakly plantarflexes ankle. Arterial supply: both are supplied by the fibular (peroneal) artery.
A(ii)
The common fibular nerve is the lateral, smaller terminal branch of the sciatic nerve; it begins at the superior angle of the popliteal fossa, closely follows the medial border of biceps femoris and its tendon, exits the fossa by passing superficial to the lateral head of gastrocnemius, then over the posterior aspect of the head of fibula, winds around the neck of fibula, and divides into the superficial fibular nerve (to the lateral compartment) and the deep fibular nerve (to the anterior compartment). The superficial fibular nerve runs in the lateral compartment to supply fibularis longus and brevis; its cutaneous distribution supplies the dorsum of the foot (lateral side of leg and ankle, as the sural nerve — formed by medial sural cutaneous nerve joined by the sural communicating branch of the common fibular nerve — supplies the lateral side of leg and ankle).
B(i)
Fibularis longus inserts onto the base of the 1st metatarsal and medial cuneiform on the plantar aspect of the foot — it therefore acts as a stirrup, pulling the medial forefoot downward and laterally, producing eversion and weak plantarflexion. Fibularis brevis inserts onto the tuberosity of the base of the 5th metatarsal on the lateral side of the foot — it abducts the forefoot and everts the foot. The lateral longitudinal arch (made of calcaneus, cuboid, and 4th and 5th metatarsals) is supported by peroneus longus and brevis; muscles of the lateral arch include peroneus longus and brevis, flexor digitorum longus, and short muscles of the little toe.
B(ii)
The transverse arch muscles include peroneus longus and brevis, transverse head of adductor hallucis, and slips of tibialis posterior. Fibularis longus, by crossing under the foot from the lateral side to insert medially at the base of the 1st metatarsal, acts as a dynamic tie-beam, pulling the medial and lateral borders of the foot together and maintaining the curvature of the transverse arch; adductor hallucis transverse head also assists by pulling metatarsals medially.
C(i)
Superficial fibular nerve injury (at fibular neck): loss of eversion of the foot (fibularis longus and brevis paralysed); weakness of plantarflexion; sensory loss on dorsum of foot. Deep fibular nerve injury (at fibular neck): loss of dorsiflexion (tibialis anterior paralysed) and toe extension (extensor digitorum longus, extensor hallucis longus paralysed); loss of eversion contribution of fibularis tertius; result is foot drop with the foot held in plantarflexion and inversion; sensory loss is limited to the 1st web space (between 1st and 2nd toes). Injury to the common fibular nerve at the fibular neck produces both effects combined — foot drop with loss of both dorsiflexion and eversion.
questions.question:
Describe the lateral compartment muscles of the leg under the following headings, explain the anatomical basis of their action, and distinguish the consequences of superficial fibular nerve injury from deep fibular nerve injury.
A(i) Name both muscles, giving full OCIANA (origin, course, insertion, action, nerve, artery) for each
A(ii) The superficial fibular nerve — its origin, course in the lateral compartment, and cutaneous distribution
B(i) The mechanical basis of eversion and plantarflexion — how fibularis longus and brevis produce their actions based on their insertions
B(ii) The role of fibularis longus in maintaining the transverse arch of the foot
C(i) Distinguish the clinical effects of superficial fibular nerve injury from those of deep fibular nerve injury at the fibular neck, and state which movements are lost in each

A(i) Describe the processes of digestion, naming all eight steps in order.
A(ii) Describe the four main functions of the GI tract, distinguishing between the role of the small intestine and the role of the large intestine in absorption.
B(i) Describe the composition and function of the serosa, including the structures it is continuous with and how it differs between organs within the abdominal cavity and the esophagus.
B(ii) Explain why the enteric nervous system provides the anatomical basis for the effects of emotional stress on the GIT, and name the two diseases that demonstrate the clinical consequences of plexus destruction.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Eight processes of digestion (in order):
• Ingestion
• Mastication
• Peristalsis / motility
• Secretions
• Hormone release
• Chemical digestion
• Absorption
• Elimination
A(ii)
Four main functions of the GI tract:
• Macromolecules (proteins, complex carbohydrates, nucleic acids, and fat) obtained from ingested food are broken down into smaller subunits for easy absorption through the lining of the small intestine during digestion.
• These smaller subunits are required for the release of energy, maintenance, and growth.
• Most of the water and electrolytes are absorbed in the large intestine.
• The inner layer of the entire GI tract forms an important protective barrier between the contents of the tract and the tissues of the body.
B(i)
Serosa:
• Composition: a thin sheet of loose connective tissue covered with mesothelium (a simple squamous covering epithelium); rich in blood vessels, lymphatics, and adipose tissue.
• Function: the outermost covering of GIT organs within the abdominal cavity.
• Continuity: the serosa of the small and large intestines is continuous with parts of the mesentery (a large fold of adipose connective tissue covered on both sides by mesothelium, which suspends the intestines and is continuous with the peritoneum).
• Esophagus: because the esophagus is bound directly to adjacent structures and not suspended in a cavity, it has a thick adventitia instead of a serosa; the adventitia consists of connective tissue containing vessels and nerves, lacking mesothelium.
B(ii)
• The enteric nervous system (submucosal and myenteric plexuses) functions independently of the CNS; because it is anatomically connected to the autonomic nervous system, it provides the anatomical basis for the well-known actions of emotional stress on the stomach and other regions of the GIT.
Two diseases demonstrating clinical consequences of plexus destruction:
• Hirschsprung disease (congenital aganglionic megacolon): caused by absence or severely injured plexuses in parts or all of the large intestine; disturbs motility and produces dilation, causing difficulty passing stool.
• Chagas disease / trypanosomiasis (infection with Trypanosoma cruzi): the protozoan destroys the enteric plexuses, producing similar motility disturbance.

A(i)
The anterior branch of the abdominal aorta supplying the midgut; it arises immediately below the celiac artery, anterior to the lower part of vertebra LI.
A(ii)
• It is crossed anteriorly by the splenic vein and the neck of the pancreas; posterior to it are the left renal vein, the uncinate process of the pancreas and the inferior part of the duodenum.
• The middle colic artery arises as it emerges from beneath the pancreas.
A(iii)
• First branch: inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery, dividing into anterior and posterior branches that anastomose with the superior pancreaticoduodenal arteries.
• Left side: numerous jejunal and ileal arteries passing between the two layers of the mesentery to form arcades, whose number increases distally.
• Vasa recta: long, close together and narrow windows in the jejunum; short, far apart and low broad windows in the ileum.
• Right side: middle colic (transverse mesocolon; anastomoses with left colic), right colic (inconsistent, retroperitoneal) and ileocolic arteries.
• The ileocolic divides into superior and inferior branches; the inferior gives colic, cecal, appendicular (in the mesoappendix free margin) and ileal branches.
A(iv)
• Midgut: duodenum below the major papilla, jejunum, ileum, cecum, appendix, ascending colon and right two-thirds of the transverse colon.
• The midgut ends at the junction of the proximal two-thirds and distal one-third of the transverse colon.

questions.question:
Describe the femoral triangle and adductor canal under the following headings, state how they relate to common pathologies, and explain the anatomical basis of referred pain to the knee from the hip.
A(i) Boundaries, roof, and floor of the femoral triangle; contents from lateral to medial
A(ii) Femoral artery — branches within the femoral triangle, including the profunda femoris and its branches
B(i) Adductor canal — boundaries, contents, and where it terminates
B(ii) Clinical basis: femoral pulse palpation and profunda femoris in femoral artery occlusion
C(i) Explain why hip joint disease causes referred pain at the knee, based on the nerve supply of both joints
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Boundaries: superiorly — inguinal ligament; medially — medial border of adductor longus; laterally — medial border of sartorius; apex — where adductor longus and sartorius cross. Roof: fascia lata (deep fascia) pierced by the great saphenous vein at the saphenous opening (fossa ovalis). Floor: formed by iliopsoas laterally and pectineus medially. Contents from lateral to medial: femoral nerve, femoral artery, femoral vein (the mnemonic 'NAVY' — from lateral: Nerve, Artery, Vein, Y-fronts/lymphatics). The femoral pulse can be palpated as it enters the femoral triangle, midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis — the mid-inguinal point.
A(ii)
The femoral artery divides to give the profunda femoris 5 cm below the inguinal ligament. Branches of the femoral artery (mnemonic: 'Does She Scream During Poking Sessions?'): Deep external pudendal arteries, Superficial epigastric, Superficial external pudendal, Descending genicular artery, Profunda femoris artery, Superficial circumflex iliac. Profunda femoris arises from the posterolateral aspect of the femoral artery; it gives: (1) Perforating branches — 3 or 4 arteries that perforate adductor magnus, contributing to medial and posterior thigh. (2) Lateral femoral circumflex artery — wraps around anterior and lateral side of femur, supplying muscles on lateral aspect of thigh. (3) Medial femoral circumflex artery — wraps around posterior side of femur, supplying its neck and head; in a fracture of the femoral neck this artery can easily be damaged and avascular necrosis of the femoral head can occur.
B(i)
The adductor canal is a passageway in the medial thigh. The adductor hiatus is an opening between the aponeurotic distal attachment of the adductor part of adductor magnus and the tendinous distal attachment of the hamstring part. The hiatus transmits the femoral artery and vein from the adductor canal in the thigh to the popliteal fossa posterior to the knee. It is located just lateral and superior to the adductor tubercle of the femur.
B(ii)
Femoral pulse: palpated at mid-inguinal point (midway between ASIS and pubic symphysis). In femoral artery occlusion, the profunda femoris artery is the main collateral channel because the superior muscular branches of the popliteal artery have clinically important anastomoses with the terminal part of the profunda femoris and gluteal arteries, maintaining perfusion to the leg.
C(i)
The posterior division of the obturator nerve supplies both the hip and the knee joint; therefore, pain from hip pathology is referred along this common nerve pathway to present as knee pain. This is the basis of Hilton's law applied to the hip: 'the nerve supplying the joint also supplies the muscles moving the joint and the skin covering the insertion of these muscles.' The femoral nerve also supplies the hip joint via intermediate and cutaneous branches and the knee via branches of obturator and femoral nerves.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the general features of the lung (shape, appearance, weight, right compared with left) and its apex, base, surfaces and borders.
A(ii) Describe the lobes and fissures and the surface marking of the lower border of the lung.
A(iii) Compare the hilum and roots of the right and left lungs.
A(iv) Describe the bronchopulmonary segments of the right and left lungs and the features of a bronchopulmonary segment.
A(v) Describe the blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of the lung.
B(i) Relate the parts and segments of the lung to the sites and spread of common pathologies.
C(i) Explain how disease of the lung and pleura may involve distant structures and produce referred pain or a functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Conical, soft, spongy, elastic and pinkish in health (brown in the young, mottled black in adults and dark in city dwellers from deposited dust and carbon particles); right lung about 600 g, left about 550 g; the right is larger, heavier, shorter and wider. Each has an apex, a base, 3 surfaces (costal convex, mediastinal with the hilum, diaphragmatic concave), 3 borders (anterior, posterior, inferior) and a root; the posterior surface lies in the paravertebral gutter.
• Apex: rounded, extends into the root of the neck 2.5-4 cm above the sternal end of the 1st rib, covered by cervical pleura and suprapleural membrane. Base: broad, concave, rests on the diaphragm, which separates the right lung from the right lobe of the liver and the left lung from the left lobe of the liver, stomach and spleen. Anterior border: where costal and mediastinal surfaces meet, with the cardiac notch on the left; posterior border from C7 to T10; inferior border separates the base from the costal and mediastinal surfaces.
A(ii)
Right lung: 3 lobes (upper, middle, lower) by oblique and horizontal fissures; left lung: 2 lobes (upper and smaller lower) by the oblique fissure, with the lingula below the cardiac notch; visceral pleura extends into the fissures so the lobes move freely. Lower border (neutral position) crosses the 6th rib in the midclavicular line, the 8th rib in the midaxillary line and reaches the 10th rib posteriorly.
A(iii)
Hilum: wedge-shaped area on the mediastinal surface; root lies opposite T5-T7. Right root: in the groove of the arch of the azygos vein; eparterial and hyparterial bronchi, right pulmonary artery, 2 right pulmonary veins, hilar lymph nodes. Left root: in the concavity of the arch of the aorta; left main bronchus, left pulmonary artery, 2 left pulmonary veins, hilar lymph nodes. Both also contain bronchial vessels, nerves and lymphatics enclosed by pleura.
A(iv)
• Right lung, 10 segments: upper lobe apical, posterior, anterior; middle lobe lateral, medial; lower lobe superior (apical), medial basal, anterior basal, lateral basal, posterior basal. Left lung, 8 segments: upper lobe apicoposterior, anterior, superior lingula, inferior lingula; lower lobe superior (apical), medial basal, anterior basal, lateral basal, posterior basal.
• Each segment is pyramidal (apex to the hilum, base to the surface), separated from its neighbours by connective tissue septa, with the segmental bronchus, bronchial vessels and a pulmonary artery branch central; little arterial anastomosis between segments; intersegmental pulmonary vein tributaries guide separation; it has its own lymphatics and autonomic supply and is the smallest part that can be removed without affecting adjacent lung.
A(v)
• Arteries: 2 left bronchial arteries from the descending thoracic aorta and 1 right bronchial artery from the 3rd right posterior intercostal supply the bronchial tree down to the respiratory bronchioles; pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood to the alveoli and anastomose with the bronchial arteries at the precapillary level. Veins: 4 pulmonary veins to the left atrium; right bronchial vein to the azygos vein, left to the accessory hemiazygos vein.
• Lymph: superficial plexus (deep to the visceral pleura) and deep plexus (peribronchial) drain to pulmonary then bronchopulmonary (hilar) nodes, then superior and inferior tracheobronchial nodes, then the bronchomediastinal trunks to the junction of subclavian and internal jugular veins (right trunk may form the right lymphatic duct; left may end in the thoracic duct). Nerves: pulmonary plexuses; vagus is bronchoconstrictor, vasodilator and secretomotor, sympathetic has the opposite actions.
B(i)
• Connective tissue septa between segments are a natural barrier to the spread of infection, but carcinoma and tuberculosis break through; abscesses are commoner in the posterior segment of the upper lobe and the apical segment of the lower lobe because these are the most dependent segments in the supine position.
• Other pathologies: foreign particles enter the right main bronchus easily (wider, more vertical); pulmonary embolism (pulmonary artery obstructed by air, blood clot, fat, tumour cells or foreign particles); asthma (dyspnoea); fibrosis reduces compliance and emphysema reduces elasticity; lobectomy or pneumonectomy is used in lung cancer.
C(i)
• Costal pleura is supplied by intercostal nerves, so pleural or lung disease may cause referred pain along the thoracic wall and anterior abdominal wall; irritation over the central diaphragm refers pain to the shoulder through the phrenic nerve (C3-5).
• Lymphatic spread passes from the hilar nodes to the tracheobronchial nodes and bronchomediastinal trunks; a tumour within the chest cavity may compress the phrenic nerve and cause diaphragmatic paralysis with paradoxical movement (functional deficit).

A(i)
Adductor longus: origin — anterior surface of body of pubis, inferior to pubic crest and lateral to pubic symphysis; insertion — middle third of medial lip of linea aspera of femur; innervation — obturator nerve, anterior division (L2, L3, L4); action — adducts thigh. It is the most anteriorly placed muscle of the adductor group, large and fan-shaped. Adductor brevis: origin — body and inferior ramus of pubis; insertion — pectineal line and proximal part of linea aspera of femur; innervation — obturator nerve, anterior division (L2, L3, L4); action — adducts thigh and to an extent flexes it; it is short and lies deep to pectineus and adductor longus. Adductor magnus: largest, most powerful, most posterior muscle in the group; has an adductor part and a hamstring part. Origin — adductor part from inferior ramus of pubis and ramus of ischium; hamstring part from ischial tuberosity. Insertion — adductor part to gluteal tuberosity, linea aspera, medial supracondylar line; hamstring part to adductor tubercle of femur. Innervation — adductor part: obturator nerve (L2, L3, L4); hamstring part: tibial nerve. Action — adducts thigh; adductor part flexes, hamstring part extends. Gracilis: origin — body and inferior ramus of pubis; insertion — superior part of medial surface of tibia; innervation — obturator nerve (L2, L3); action — adducts thigh, flexes leg, helps rotate leg medially. Obturator externus: origin — margins of obturator foramen and obturator membrane; insertion — trochanteric fossa of femur; innervation — obturator nerve (L2, L3); action — laterally rotates thigh, steadies head of femur in acetabulum.
A(ii)
All adductor muscles are supplied by the obturator nerve except the hamstring part of adductor magnus and part of pectineus. The hamstring part of adductor magnus is supplied by the tibial nerve — because embryologically the hamstring part shares the same developmental origin as the true hamstrings (which arise from the ischial tuberosity and are all innervated by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve).
B(i)
The adductor hiatus is an opening between the aponeurotic distal attachment of the adductor part of adductor magnus and the tendinous distal attachment of the hamstring part. It transmits the femoral artery and vein from the adductor canal in the thigh to the popliteal fossa posterior to the knee. It is located just lateral and superior to the adductor tubercle of the femur.
B(ii)
The pes anserinus consists of the conjoined tendons of the sartorius, gracilis, and semitendinosus muscles; they insert into the superior part of the medial surface of the tibia. It acts as a secondary valgus restraint, augmenting the medial supporting structures of the knee. Bursitis of the pes anserinus bursa causes medial knee pain, especially in osteoarthritis.
C(i)
Gracilis is unique among the adductor group: it is a long strap-like muscle, the most medial and most superficial of the adductors, and the weakest member; it is the only member of the adductor group to cross both the hip and knee joints. It joins with sartorius (from the anterior compartment, supplied by femoral nerve) and semitendinosus (from the posterior compartment, supplied by tibial nerve) to form the pes anserinus — three muscles from three different compartments with three different nerve supplies share a common insertion.
questions.question:
Describe the adductor group of the medial compartment of the thigh under the following headings, explaining the anatomical basis of the pes anserinus and its clinical importance.
A(i) Name all 5 adductor muscles; give origin, insertion, innervation, and action for each
A(ii) Why all adductor muscles are supplied by the obturator nerve except the hamstring part of adductor magnus — state its nerve supply and embryologic basis
B(i) The adductor hiatus — its boundaries and the structures it transmits
B(ii) The pes anserinus — its composition and function
C(i) Distinguish the gracilis from the other adductor muscles based on its unique anatomical features; name the other two compartments' muscles that join it to form the pes anserinus and their common innervation

A(i) Define the mediastinum and state its extent and boundaries.
A(ii) State its divisions and the plane that separates them.
A(iii) Describe the boundaries and contents of each division.
A(iv) List the structures that occupy more than one division.
B(i) Explain the importance of the level of T4 in relation to the mediastinum.
B(ii) Explain why the mediastinum is vulnerable when the chest wall is severely injured.
C(i) Distinguish between the superior and the inferior mediastinum.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
A highly mobile, bulky connective tissue septum (thick movable partition) in the midline between the right and left pleural cavities and their lungs, containing the heart and great vessels, oesophagus, trachea and its bifurcation, thoracic duct, and vagus and phrenic nerves; superior: root of the neck (thoracic outlet: manubrium, 1st rib, T1); inferior: diaphragm; anterior: sternum; posterior: thoracic vertebrae; lateral: lungs and pleurae.
A(ii)
A horizontal plane from the sternal angle to the lower border of T4 divides it into the superior mediastinum (above) and the inferior mediastinum (below), the latter subdivided into anterior (in front of the heart), middle (containing the heart) and posterior (behind the heart) parts.
A(iii)
• Superior: bounded by the thoracic outlet above, the T4 plane below, the manubrium in front and T1-T4 vertebrae behind; contents from superficial to deep: thymus; right and left brachiocephalic veins and SVC; arch of the aorta with brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid and left subclavian arteries; right and left vagus and phrenic nerves; trachea and oesophagus (most posterior); thoracic duct beside the oesophagus; lymph nodes.
• Anterior: bounded by the T4 plane above, the diaphragm below, the body of the sternum in front and the pericardium/heart behind; contains the thymus, fatty tissue and lymph nodes.
• Middle: lies between the anterior and posterior mediastina; contains the pericardium and heart, ascending aorta, pulmonary trunk, SVC and IVC, right and left pulmonary veins, main bronchi, part of the phrenic nerves and lymph nodes.
• Posterior: bounded by the T4 plane above, the heart/middle mediastinum and diaphragm in front, and the T5 (lower border of T4) to T12 vertebrae behind; contains the oesophagus (most anterior), right and left vagus nerves around it, thoracic duct behind it, azygos vein (behind and to the right), descending aorta (behind and to the left), sympathetic trunks and lymph nodes.
A(iv)
Six structures lie in more than one division: thoracic duct, oesophagus and vagus nerves (superior and posterior); phrenic nerves and SVC (superior and middle); thymus (superior and anterior); lymph nodes are present in all regions.
B(i)
The T4 level marks the sternal angle and the 2nd costal cartilage, the bifurcation of the trachea, the bifurcation of the pulmonary trunk, and the beginning and termination of the arch of the aorta.
B(ii)
The mediastinum is highly mobile; in a stove-in chest the loose chest wall segment produces swinging movements of the mediastinum that cause severe shock.
C(i)
• Superior mediastinum: one part above the T4 plane, bounded in front by the manubrium and behind by T1-T4, containing thymus, great veins, aortic arch and its branches, trachea, oesophagus, thoracic duct, vagus and phrenic nerves.
• Inferior mediastinum: three parts below the T4 plane down to the diaphragm - anterior (thymus and fat, in front of the heart), middle (heart, pericardium, ascending aorta, pulmonary trunk) and posterior (oesophagus, descending aorta, azygos system, thoracic duct, sympathetic trunks).
• Nerves differ by position: the right vagus descends on the right of the trachea, forms the posterior oesophageal plexus and continues as the posterior gastric nerve; the left vagus descends between the left common carotid and left subclavian arteries and forms the anterior oesophageal plexus; the right phrenic descends on the right of the SVC and heart, the left on the left side of the heart.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the development, structure, shape and position of the female breast.
A(ii) Describe the nipple and areola.
A(iii) Describe the internal structure of the breast.
A(iv) Describe the arterial supply, venous drainage and nerve supply.
B(i) Relate the parts and structures of the breast to common pathologies and to surgical incisions.
B(ii) Describe the developmental anomalies of the breast.
C(i) Explain how breast disease spreads through the lymphatics, naming the drainage routes and the axillary node groups, and its effect on distant structures.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• A modified sweat gland of ectodermal origin, non-capsulated, present in both sexes (rudimentary in males), starting to develop at puberty in females with most development in late pregnancy and lactation; lies in the superficial fascia; shape and size vary with genetics, race, diet, age, parity and menopausal status (hemispherical, conical, pendulous, piriform, flattened).
• Base extends vertically from the 2nd to the 6th rib and transversely from the sternal edge to the midaxillary line; two-thirds of the base lie on pectoralis major and the inferolateral third on serratus anterior and external oblique; the axillary tail (of Spence) passes into the axilla; the retromammary space (loose areolar tissue) separates it from the deep fascia.
A(ii)
Nipple: at the greatest prominence, opposite the 4th intercostal space (about 10 cm from the midline in men and young nulliparous women); carries 15-20 pores of the lactiferous ducts; circular and radial smooth muscle causes erection with cold, tactile or emotional stimuli; devoid of fat, hair and sweat glands. Areola: pigmented skin (22-60 mm) with sebaceous glands and glands of Montgomery; darkening in the 2nd month of pregnancy is permanent.
A(iii)
Glandular tissue (15-20 lobes made of lobules of alveoli/acini and alveolar ducts converging on 15-20 lactiferous ducts, each with a lactiferous sinus deep to the areola), stroma (fibrous strands, the suspensory ligaments of Astley Cooper, connecting the skin with the deep fascia of pectoralis major) and adipose tissue (determines form and size).
A(iv)
Arteries: internal thoracic (medial mammary and perforating branches of the 2nd-4th spaces, the 2nd largest; about 60% of flow, mainly medial), lateral thoracic and thoraco-acromial pectoral branch (axillary), lateral mammary branches of posterior intercostal arteries, anterior intercostal branches. Veins correspond, with a circular venous plexus at the base of the nipple draining to the axillary and internal thoracic veins. Nerves: anterior and lateral cutaneous branches of the 4th-6th intercostal nerves (sensory to skin, sympathetic to vessels and the smooth muscle of skin and nipple).
B(i)
Cancer of the breast is a common surgical condition, about 60% arising in the upper lateral quadrant; the lactiferous ducts are radial, so incisions are made radially; infiltration of the ligaments of Cooper shortens them and gives peau d'orange; fibroadenoma is also listed.
B(ii)
Polymastia, polythelia and amastia; the mammary ridge extends from the axilla to the inguinal region and disappears in humans except in the pectoral region, so accessory breasts or nipples can occur along it (axillary and inguinal); the male breast stays rudimentary (small ducts without lobules or alveoli).
C(i)
• About 75% of lymph drains to the axillary nodes (central and lateral parts to the pectoral group, upper part to the apical group), about 20% (medial part) to the internal thoracic (parasternal) chain, and the lower quadrants to the inferior phrenic (abdominal) nodes.
• Axillary nodes lie in 5 groups: pectoral (anterior), subscapular (posterior), brachial (lateral), central and apical; levels 1-3 and Rotter's nodes between pectoralis minor and major; the subclavian lymph trunk from the apical group opens into the subclavian vein (left side usually the thoracic duct).
• Other routes: lymphatics follow vessels through pectoralis major to parasternal nodes, cross the median plane to the opposite breast, and reach the sheath of rectus abdominis and the subperitoneal and subhepatic plexuses.
• Nodes below and above the clavicle, and axillary and cervical nodes, communicate freely; cancer of one breast can affect the other breast and the opposite axillary nodes through the anastomosing lymphatics.

A(i)
• Formed by the ventral rami of L1, L2, L3 and the upper part of L4; the lower part of L4 joins L5 to form the lumbosacral trunk.
• The rami emerge from the intervertebral foramina, enter psoas, give branches to psoas and quadratus lumborum, then form the plexus within the substance of psoas major.
A(ii)
• Iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal: L1; genitofemoral: L1, L2; lateral femoral cutaneous: L2, L3 (posterior division).
• Femoral: L2, L3, L4 (posterior division); obturator: L2, L3, L4 (anterior division); sometimes an accessory obturator L3, L4.
A(iii)
• From the lateral border of psoas major: iliohypogastric, ilioinguinal, lateral femoral cutaneous, femoral.
• Through psoas anteriorly: genitofemoral; from the medial border: obturator.
A(iv)
• It innervates part of the lower abdominal wall but chiefly supplies skin and muscle 'borrowed from the trunk by the lower limb'.
• The genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve supplies the cremasteric muscle; the ilioinguinal nerve runs in the inguinal canal.
B(i)
The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve normally passes deep to the lateral end of the inguinal ligament; sometimes it passes through the substance of the ligament.
C(i)
• Entrapment causes pain along its distribution (meralgia paresthetica).
• Psoas major is supplied by ventral rami L1 to L4, psoas minor by L1, quadratus lumborum by upper lumbar and subcostal nerves, iliacus by the femoral nerve.

A(i)
Definition: Cartilage is a connective tissue in which the cells are relatively sparse and embedded in a large amount of firm characteristic matrix. It is a specialized form of connective tissue in which the firm consistency of the extracellular matrix allows the tissue to bear mechanical stresses without permanent distortion. Histogenesis: Cartilage is derived from the mesenchyme. The first modification observed is the rounding up of mesenchymal cells, which retract their extensions, multiply rapidly, and form mesenchymal condensations of chondroblasts (cells with ribosome-rich basophilic cytoplasm). Synthesis and deposition of matrix then begin to separate chondroblasts from one another. Differentiation takes place from center outward: central cells have characteristics of chondrocytes, peripheral cells are typical chondroblasts. The superficial mesenchyme develops into the perichondrium. Growth mechanisms: interstitial growth (from mitotic division of preexisting chondrocytes, expanding from within) and appositional growth (from differentiation of perichondrial cells, expanding from the outside). Nutrient supply: Cartilage is avascular; nourished by diffusion of nutrients from capillaries in adjacent connective tissue (perichondrium) or by synovial fluid. It has no lymphatic vessels or nerves. Chondrocytes exhibit low metabolic activity.
A(ii)
Hyaline cartilage: most common form; collagen type II is the principal collagen; found in nose, trachea, bronchi, rib-sternal joints, and synovial joints; resilient and shock absorbing. Elastic cartilage: contains abundant elastic fibers in addition to collagen type II; found in auricle of ear, external auditory canals, eustachian tubes, epiglottis, and cuneiform cartilage in larynx; elastic fibers allow flexibility. Fibrocartilage: rich in collagen type I (acidophilic matrix); found in intervertebral disks, attachments of certain ligaments to cartilaginous surfaces, and symphysis pubis; dense collagen provides strength for high-load sites.
B(i)
Articular cartilage is devoid of perichondrium and is sustained by diffusion of oxygen and nutrients from synovial fluid; this limited supply combined with low metabolic activity of chondrocytes means repair is slow. Hyaline cartilage is more susceptible to degenerative aging processes; calcification of the matrix, preceded by an increase in size and volume of chondrocytes followed by their death, leads to osteoarthritis. Role of exercise: participation in sports involving torsional loading, fast acceleration/deceleration, repetitive high impact increases risk of osteoarthritis. However, some levels of loading and exercise are beneficial: exercise enhances production of matrix molecules, which can have a positive effect on joint health. Exercise has both beneficial and detrimental effects on cartilage.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the gross anatomy of cartilage under the following headings: definition, histogenesis (development from mesenchyme), growth mechanisms, and nutrient supply.
A(ii) Relate the three types of cartilage to their specific locations and collagen types, explaining why each is suited to its location.
B(i) Explain why articular cartilage degenerates with age and state the role of exercise in cartilage health.

(A) Describe the urinary bladder under the headings: A(i) parts A(ii) trigone A(iii) peritoneal/ligamentous relations.
(B) Explain the clinical basis of why the trigone remains an important fixed landmark during bladder filling.
(C) Distinguish the male urethra from the female urethra.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• The urinary bladder is a musculomembranous sac composed of a body, which collects urine, and a neck, a funnel-shaped extension passing inferiorly to join the urethra; it is divided into apex, fundus and body, with superior, posterior (base) and two inferolateral surfaces.
• The apex points towards the pubic symphysis and continues as the median umbilical ligament, a remnant of the embryonic urachus, up to the umbilicus; the base faces posteroinferiorly, with the two ureters entering at its upper corners and the urethra draining from its lower corner.
A(ii)
The trigone is the smooth, posteroinferior triangular area of the bladder wall formed by imaginary lines connecting the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice; it has four tunics, mucosa, submucosa, muscularis (detrusor muscle) and adventitia.
A(iii)
• Except for its superior surface, which is covered by peritoneum, the bladder is connected to surrounding structures by fibroareolar tissue (true ligaments): the lateral true ligaments, the puboprostatic or pubovesical ligaments anteriorly, the median umbilical ligament at the apex, and a posterior ligament.
• In the male, the upper posterior surface is related to the rectovesical pouch, and the lower part relates to the seminal vesicles and vas deferens; in the female, the posterior surface is related to the anterior wall of the vagina.
B
• The trigone remains immovable as the bladder fills and empties, and functions as a funnel that directs urine into the urethra as the bladder wall (detrusor) contracts.
• This fixed relationship of the ureteric and urethral orifices at the trigone is why it is used as a constant anatomical landmark despite the changing size and shape of the rest of the bladder.
C
• The male urethra is about 20 cm long and is divided into four parts: intramural (preprostatic), prostatic, membranous, and spongy (penile) parts, opening at the end of the penis.
• The male urethra passes through the prostate, the deep perineal pouch/urogenital diaphragm as the membranous urethra, and then the length of the penis as the spongy urethra, bending twice along its course.
• The female urethra is much shorter, about 3-4 cm long, corresponding to the prostatic part of the male urethra proximal to the prostatic utricle.
• The female urethra begins at the internal urethral orifice about 5 cm behind the pubic symphysis, runs downward embedded in the anterior wall of the vagina, traverses the urogenital diaphragm, and ends at the external urethral orifice in the vestibule, receiving the paraurethral (Skene's) glands.
• Both sexes have an internal, smooth muscle, involuntary urethral sphincter continuous with the detrusor muscle, and an external, skeletal muscle, voluntary sphincter innervated by the pudendal nerve, located inferior to the prostate in males and at the bladder's distal inferior end in females.

A(i)
Formed behind the neck of the pancreas by the union of the superior mesenteric and splenic veins.
A(ii)
• Large but short, about 5 cm; in front of the opening of the lesser sac it passes to the porta hepatis where it divides into right and left terminal branches.
• At the porta hepatis the order from behind forwards is portal vein branches, proper hepatic artery, hepatic ducts; in the hepatoduodenal ligament it lies with the hepatic artery and bile duct.
A(iii)
Drains poorly oxygenated but nutrient-rich blood from the GI tract (lower oesophagus to upper anal canal), pancreas, gallbladder, bile ducts and spleen to the liver.
A(iv)
Direct route: through the liver to the IVC via the hepatic veins; alternative routes exist and the portal vein and its tributaries have no valves.
B(i)
Portasystemic shunts join the portal vein to the IVC or join the splenic vein to the left renal vein after splenectomy.
C(i)
• Portal hypertension: cirrhosis scarring and fibrosis obstruct the portal vein, pressure mounts, and blood forced through collaterals dilates veins into varices, potentially fatal.
• Lower third of oesophagus: left gastric branches with oesophageal veins to the azygos: oesophageal varices.
• Anal canal: superior rectal with middle and inferior rectal veins: haemorrhoids (mucosa with normally dilated submucosal veins prolapses).
• Anterior abdominal wall: paraumbilical with superficial epigastric veins: caput medusae, veins radiating like small snakes from the umbilicus.
• Retroperitoneal: colic twig veins of ascending and descending colon, duodenum, pancreas and liver with renal, lumbar and phrenic veins.

A(i)
The hip joint is a multiaxial ball-and-socket type of synovial joint. It is the largest joint in the human body and the 2nd largest weight-bearing joint. Articular surfaces: the lunate surface of the acetabulum (covered by hyaline cartilage except at the fovea) and the spherical head of femur (which forms 2/3 of a sphere, covered by hyaline cartilage except at the fovea capitis). The acetabulum is deepened by the fibrocartilaginous acetabular labrum; it is deficient inferiorly as the acetabular notch, bridged by the transverse acetabular ligament.
A(ii)
Capsule: strong and thick; medially attached to margin of acetabulum, transverse acetabular ligament, and adjacent margin of obturator foramen; laterally attached to the intertrochanteric line anteriorly. Ligaments: (1) Iliofemoral ligament (ligament of Bigelow) — one of the strongest in the body, Y-shaped; apex at inferior iliac spine, base to intertrochanteric line; prevents overextension and prevents trunk from falling backwards while standing. (2) Pubofemoral ligament — triangular; attached superiorly to iliopubic eminence and obturator crest, inferiorly merges with capsule; limits extension and abduction. (3) Ischiofemoral ligament — reinforces posterior aspect; medially attached to ischium posteroinferior to acetabulum, laterally to greater trochanter deep to the iliofemoral ligament; limits extension. Fibers of all three spiral so they become taut in extension, stabilizing the joint and reducing muscle energy needed for standing. Ligament teres (round ligament): flat triangular band from fovea to acetabular notch and transverse ligament; ensheathed by synovial membrane; transmits arteries to head of femur.
B(i)
By Hilton's law: the nerve supplying the joint also supplies the muscles moving the joint and the skin covering the insertion of those muscles. Nerve supply: femoral nerve, anterior division of obturator nerve, nerve to rectus femoris, nerve to quadratus femoris, sciatic nerve, and superior gluteal nerve. The posterior division of the obturator nerve supplies both the hip and the knee joint.
B(ii)
Flexion (120–140°): iliopsoas, sartorius, rectus femoris, tensor fasciae latae. Extension: gluteus maximus, semimembranosus, semitendinosus, biceps femoris. Abduction (60–80°): gluteus medius, minimus, tensor fasciae latae. Adduction: pectineus, adductor longus, brevis, magnus, gracilis. Medial rotation: gluteus medius, minimus, tensor fasciae latae. Lateral rotation: obturator internus and externus, gemellus superior and inferior, quadratus femoris, piriformis, posterior fibres of gluteus medius and minimus, superior fibres of gluteus maximus.
C(i)
The posterior division of the obturator nerve supplies both the hip and knee joints; pain from hip pathology is therefore referred along this common nerve pathway to the knee joint. Coxa valga follows congenital dislocation of the head of femur; coxa vara follows fracture of the neck of femur.
questions.question:
Describe the hip joint under the following headings and explain its clinical correlates.
A(i) Type and articular surfaces
A(ii) Capsule, ligaments — name, attachments and function of each
B(i) Nerve supply, applying Hilton's law
B(ii) Movements and muscles responsible for each movement
C(i) Explain why referred pain from the hip can present at the knee, and distinguish coxa valga from coxa vara

questions.answerText:
A(i)
The ulnar nerve is an extension of the medial cord of the brachial plexus.
A(ii)
The most common sites of ulnar nerve entrapment are: above the elbow in the region of the intermuscular septum; the medial epicondylar region; the epicondylar (ulnar) groove; the region of the cubital tunnel; and the region where the nerve exits from flexor carpi ulnaris, where compression is usually caused by the deep flexor-pronator aponeurosis.
A(iii)
• In the forearm it supplies flexor carpi ulnaris and the medial (3rd & 4th) part of flexor digitorum profundus.
• In the hand it supplies the hypothenar muscles, adductor pollicis, flexor pollicis brevis, the palmar and dorsal interossei, the 3rd and 4th lumbricals, and the muscles of digiti minimi (abductor, opponens, flexor digiti minimi).
A(iv)
It provides sensation to the medial surface of the hand and the medial half of the 4th and 5th digits, on both palmar and dorsal aspects, through its superficial branch; its motor functions include finger adduction and abduction other than the thumb, thumb adduction, flexion of digits 4 and 5, and wrist flexion and adduction.
C
• Injury to the ulnar nerve, or to the medial cord/lower trunk from which it derives, produces a claw hand deformity.
• This deformity arises from the unopposed action of the long flexors and extensors of the fingers once the ulnar-innervated intrinsic muscles (interossei, medial lumbricals) are paralysed.
• In a claw hand there is hyperextension at the metacarpophalangeal joints and flexion at the interphalangeal joints.
• Where the injury occurs at the level of the medial cord (e.g. from subcoracoid dislocation of the humerus), the ulnar nerve and medial root of median nerve are both involved.
• This produces sensory loss on the ulnar side of the forearm and hand, along with vasomotor and trophic changes.
• The claw hand deformity, together with the specific pattern of muscle paralysis, thus reflects the level and combination of nerve fibres interrupted along the course of the ulnar nerve or its parent cord/trunk.
questions.question:
Describe the ulnar nerve:
A(i) Origin
A(ii) Course and common entrapment sites
A(iii) Muscles innervated (forearm and hand)
A(iv) Sensory distribution
C. Explain the anatomical basis of the deformity seen after ulnar nerve injury.

A(i) Describe the histological features of the four stomach regions — cardia, fundus, body, and pylorus — under the headings: surface epithelium, gland type, gastric pit length, and principal secretion.
A(ii) Explain the complete structure and function of the gastric glands of the fundus/body, including the isthmus, neck, and base, and what cells are found in each part.
B(i) Explain the full role of mucous neck cells in the gastric gland, comparing their secretion to that of surface mucous cells.
B(ii) Describe where intrinsic factor is produced, what it is chemically, what it does, and how its deficiency leads to anaemia.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Four stomach regions:
• Cardia and pylorus are histologically similar: tubular glands with long pits usually branching into coiled secretory portions (cardiac and pyloric glands respectively); pits are longer in the pylorus; lack both parietal and chief cells; major secretion is abundant mucus.
• Fundus and body are histologically identical: simple columnar epithelium invaginates to form gastric pits leading into long, branched, tubular gastric glands; 3 to 7 glands usually open into the bottom of each gastric pit; contain all four secretory cell types; involved in secretion of acidic gastric juice.
A(ii)
Structure of fundic/body glands:
• Each gland has three named parts: isthmus, neck, and base.
• Isthmus: the region of stem cells (between the gastric pit and gland); the pluripotent stem cells divide asymmetrically and can move upward or downward to replace epithelial cells.
• Neck: contains mucous neck cells (MNCs) in clusters or singly; also contains parietal cells.
• Base: predominantly chief (zymogen) cells; also contains enteroendocrine cells.
B(i)
Mucous neck cells (MNCs):
• Present in clusters or singly in the necks of gastric glands.
• Less columnar than surface mucous cells; irregular in shape with round nucleus and apical secretory granules.
• Their mucous secretion is less alkaline than that of the surface epithelial mucous cells; they secrete acidic fluid containing mucin (not mucus, which implies alkaline content).
B(ii)
Intrinsic factor:
• Produced by: parietal (oxyntic) cells.
• Chemical nature: a glycoprotein.
• Function: required for the uptake of vitamin B12 in the small intestine.
• Deficiency and anaemia: if parietal cells are damaged, insufficient quantities of intrinsic factor are secreted; without adequate intrinsic factor, vitamin B12 is not absorbed adequately; low levels of vitamin B12 reduce the proliferation of erythroblasts, resulting in pernicious anaemia.

A(i)
Collagen fibers: protein fibers that form the bulk of connective tissue fibers. Major types and distribution: Type I collagen — fibril-forming; found in bone, dermis, tendon, ligaments, and cornea; produced by fibroblasts, osteoblasts, odontoblasts. Type II collagen — fibril-forming; found in cartilage and vitreous body of the eye; produced by chondrocytes and retinal cells. Type III collagen — fibril-forming; found in loose connective tissue and reticular fibers in lungs, liver, and spleen; produced by fibroblasts and reticular cells. Type IV collagen — network-forming; found in basement membranes; produced by epithelial and endothelial cells. Type XI collagen — fibrillar; found in cartilage. Elastic fibers: present in elastic connective tissue; provide elasticity. Reticular fibers: fine fibers present in reticular connective tissue; form reticular (meshwork) framework of organs.
A(ii)
Dense regular connective tissue is present in tendons and ligaments because it is organized to withstand forces from specific directions; the regular parallel arrangement of collagen type I fibers allows maximum tensile strength along the axis of the tendon or ligament.
B(i)
The regenerative capacity of connective tissue is clearly observed in organs damaged by ischemia, inflammation, or traumatic injury. Spaces left after such injuries, especially in tissues whose cells divide poorly or not at all (e.g., cardiac muscle), are filled by connective tissue, forming dense irregular scar tissue. The healing of surgical incisions and other wounds depends on the reparative capacity of connective tissue and the activity of fibroblasts. Fibroblasts synthesize collagen, reticular and elastic fibers, and the amorphous extracellular substance. In some rapidly closing wounds, a cell called the myofibroblast (with features of both fibroblasts and smooth muscle cells) is observed. Myofibroblasts have most of the morphologic characteristics of fibroblasts but contain increased amounts of actin microfilaments and myosin and behave like smooth muscle cells. Their activity is responsible for wound contraction (wound closure after tissue injury).
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the origin, composition, and classification of connective tissue fibers under the following headings: collagen fibers (types and tissue distribution), elastic fibers, and reticular fibers.
A(ii) State the safe structural principle that makes collagen type I dominant in tendons and ligaments.
B(i) Explain the anatomical basis of scar formation after organ injury, with specific reference to fibroblasts and myofibroblasts.

A(i) Define the pleura and describe its parts.
A(ii) Describe the parietal pleura and its parts.
A(iii) Describe the visceral pleura and the pleural cavity.
A(iv) Describe the lines of pleural reflection with their surface markings.
A(v) Describe the pleural recesses.
A(vi) Describe the blood supply, nerve supply and lymphatic drainage of the pleura.
B(i) Explain why the cervical pleura and the lower pleural margin are vulnerable to injury.
B(ii) Explain why the costodiaphragmatic recess is the clinically more important recess.
C(i) Distinguish between the parietal and the visceral pleura.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
A thin, double-layered serous membrane that envelops each lung and lines the thoracic cavity, made of visceral and parietal layers with the intervening pleural cavity; the two pleural cavities are totally separate.
A(ii)
Thicker outer layer lining the thoracic wall, mediastinum, diaphragm and neck, and can be stripped; 4 parts: costal (ribs, costal cartilages, intercostal spaces, sides of vertebral bodies, back of sternum, separated from them by endothoracic fascia), diaphragmatic, mediastinal (encloses the hilum structures, continuous with visceral pleura at the hilum, and below the hilum forms the pulmonary ligament) and cervical (cupola, 2.5-4 cm above the medial third of the clavicle, attached to the suprapleural membrane).
A(iii)
Visceral pleura: closely adherent to the lung including its fissures, cannot be stripped, smooth and slippery, continuous with the parietal pleura at the hilum; the pleural cavity is a potential space with a small amount of lubricating pleural fluid that reduces friction and helps prevent lung collapse.
A(iv)
Sternal (costal to mediastinal anteriorly): from behind the sternoclavicular joints to the midline at the 2nd costal cartilage, then the right edge passes vertically to the 6th costal cartilage while the left arches laterally at the 4th costal cartilage (because of the heart) to the 6th. Costal (costal to diaphragmatic): crosses the 8th rib in the midclavicular line, the 10th rib in the midaxillary line and the 12th rib at the lateral border of erector spinae. Vertebral: rounded reflections in the paravertebral planes from T1 to T12.
A(v)
Recesses are spaces not occupied by lung that lung enters only on forced deep respiration: costodiaphragmatic (between costal and diaphragmatic pleura, shallow in inspiration and deeper in expiration) and costomediastinal (behind the sternum where costal pleura becomes mediastinal pleura, more conspicuous on the left near the heart).
A(vi)
• Blood supply: visceral pleura from bronchial and pulmonary arteries, veins to the pulmonary vein; parietal pleura from the vessels of the structures covered - cervical and costal from intercostal vessels, diaphragmatic outer part from intercostal and inner part from pericardiophrenic vessels, mediastinal from pericardiophrenic vessels.
• Nerve supply: costal pleura by intercostal nerves; diaphragmatic pleura by phrenic nerves centrally and intercostal nerves peripherally; mediastinal pleura by the phrenic nerve; the visceral pleura is described as having no nerve supply and as receiving vasomotor supply from autonomic nerves (pulmonary plexuses).
• Lymph: visceral to the pulmonary plexus in interlobar and peribronchial spaces; parietal costal, mediastinal and cervical to the internal thoracic (anterior) and intercostal (posterior) chains; diaphragmatic to retrosternal, mediastinal and sometimes coeliac nodes.
B(i)
The cervical pleura reaches about 1 inch (2.5 cm) above the clavicle because of the oblique slope of the first rib, so it can be wounded (pneumothorax) by a stab wound, a surgeon's knife or an anaesthetist's needle above the clavicle; the lower edge descends just below the 12th rib medially (below the 11th if the 12th is short), so it may be opened in a loin incision.
B(ii)
The costodiaphragmatic recess is the larger recess and the clinically more important one, providing the space where fluid collects in disease (pneumothorax with air, haemothorax with blood, empyema with pus, effusion); fluid is drained with a needle just above a rib, or through the space between the 7th costal cartilage and the xiphoid process.
C(i)
• Parietal: thicker, outer, lines wall, diaphragm, mediastinum and neck, named regionally, can be stripped, supplied by intercostal and phrenic nerves (so pleural irritation refers pain along the thoracic and anterior abdominal wall, and to the shoulder from the central diaphragm).
• Visceral: inner layer closely adherent to the lung surface and fissures, cannot be stripped, smooth and slippery so the lung moves freely, supplied by bronchial and pulmonary vessels; pleurisy is inflammation of the pleura, usually with pneumonia or other lung infection.

A(i)
The greater sac is the main larger part; the lesser sac (omental bursa) lies posterior to the stomach, adjoining structures and lesser omentum; an incision through the anterolateral wall enters the greater sac; the sacs communicate through the epiploic foramen.
A(ii)
• The transverse mesocolon divides the cavity into supracolic and infracolic compartments; the infracolic lies posterior to the greater omentum and is divided by the mesentery of the small intestine into right and left infracolic spaces.
• Right space: triangular, between the root of the mesentery, ascending colon and right two-thirds of transverse colon; left: between the root, descending colon and left one-third of transverse colon, widening below into the pelvis.
A(iii)
Right paracolic gutter lies lateral to the ascending colon and communicates with the hepatorenal recess and pelvic cavity; the left, lateral to the descending colon, is separated from the splenic area by the phrenicocolic ligament.
A(iv)
• Lesser sac: superior wall peritoneum over the caudate lobe and diaphragm; anterior lesser omentum, peritoneum of the posterior stomach and anterior two layers of greater omentum; posterior the posterior two layers, transverse colon and mesocolon, peritoneum over pancreas, left kidney and suprarenal gland.
• Omental foramen (of Winslow), behind the hepatoduodenal ligament, admits 2 fingers: liver superiorly, first part of duodenum inferiorly, hepatoduodenal ligament anteriorly, IVC and right crus posteriorly.
B(i)
Median umbilical fold covers the urachal remnant, medial folds the obliterated umbilical arteries, lateral folds the inferior epigastric vessels; the supravesical fossa is a site for external supravesical hernia, the medial inguinal fossa for the less common direct hernia, the lateral inguinal fossa for the most common indirect hernia.
B(ii)
Blockage of the uterine tubes (hysterosalpingography), peritonitis, ascites, paracentesis and intraperitoneal injection, flow of exudates in the paracolic gutters, and adhesions with adhesiotomy in intestinal obstruction.
C(i)
• The right paracolic gutter provides a route for spread of infection between the pelvic and upper abdominal regions, and the supracolic and infracolic compartments communicate freely through the gutters.
• In the female the cavity communicates with the exterior via the uterine tubes, uterus and vagina.
• Parietal peritoneum is supplied by the nerves of the adjacent body wall and diaphragm; visceral peritoneum by sympathetic nerves of the underlying viscus.
• Receptors respond to overdistension, traction on mesenteries, spasm of smooth muscle and ischaemia.

A(i)
The oesophagus has four constrictions: at 15 cm (cricopharyngeus, upper oesophageal sphincter), at 22.5 cm (crossed by the aortic arch) and 27.5 cm (crossed by the left main bronchus) from the upper incisor teeth, and at 40 cm, where it passes through the right crus of the diaphragm (oesophageal hiatus).
A(ii)
The upper oesophageal sphincter is an anatomical sphincter formed by the cricopharyngeus muscle at the pharyngo-oesophageal junction.
A(iii)
• The lower oesophageal sphincter is a physiological sphincter at the gastro-oesophageal junction with no true muscular thickening.
• It is maintained by the acute angle of entry of the oesophagus into the stomach, compression of the intra-abdominal oesophagus by positive intra-abdominal pressure, prominent mucosal folds at the junction, and the pinch-cock effect of the right crus of the diaphragm.
B
• The constrictions are clinically important because they are sites where swallowed foreign bodies commonly impact.
• They are prone to trauma during instrumentation such as rigid oesophagoscopy.
• They are common sites for stricture formation following ingestion of corrosive substances.
• They are also common sites of oesophageal carcinoma.
C
• The upper oesophageal sphincter is a true anatomical (muscular) sphincter formed by the cricopharyngeus, located at 15 cm from the incisor teeth.
• The lower oesophageal sphincter is a physiological sphincter maintained by mechanical factors at the gastro-oesophageal junction and prevents gastric reflux, rather than a distinct muscular ring controlling food passage.
questions.question:
(A) Describe the oesophagus under the following headings: A(i) its four constrictions along its length A(ii) the upper oesophageal sphincter A(iii) the lower oesophageal sphincter.
(B) Explain the clinical basis of why the areas of constriction are important.
(C) Distinguish between the upper oesophageal sphincter and the lower oesophageal sphincter.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
• A strong, incomplete fibrous compartment of the rectus abdominis and pyramidalis, formed by the aponeuroses of the three flat muscles.
• The linea alba separates the right and left rectus abdominis; the linea semilunaris marks the lateral border; tendinous intersections and linea alba give the 'six packs'.
A(ii)
It has an anterior and posterior wall for most of its length: anterior wall from the aponeuroses of external oblique and half of internal oblique; posterior wall from the aponeuroses of half of internal oblique and transversus abdominis.
A(iii)
• Superior and inferior epigastric arteries and veins, lymphatic vessels and the distal portions of the thoracoabdominal nerves (anterior rami of T7 to T12).
• Superior epigastric: terminal branch of internal thoracic, descends posterior to the muscle, anastomoses with inferior epigastric; inferior epigastric: from external iliac, enters the sheath at the arcuate line.
A(iv)
A strong expandable support; protects viscera from injury such as a low blow in boxing; compresses the abdominal contents; maintains or increases intra-abdominal pressure; moves the trunk and maintains posture.
B(i)
• In anterior cutaneous nerve entrapment syndrome (ACNES), 12 of 95 adolescents with chronic abdominal pain had it; the Carnett sign was positive at the lateral border of rectus abdominis in all 12.
• Altered skin sensation was present in 11 of 12; the distal thoracoabdominal nerves run in the rectus sheath.
• After treatment (1 to 3 injections, n = 5; neurectomy, n = 7) pain was absent in 11; the conclusion was that ACNES is present in 1 of 8 such adolescents.
C(i)
• Rectus abdominis: long paired muscle split by the linea alba, origin pubic crest, insertion xiphoid process and costal cartilages of ribs 5 to 7, nerve T7 to T11, stabilises the pelvis in walking and depresses the ribs.
• Pyramidalis: small triangular muscle superficial to rectus, base on the pubis and apex on the linea alba, origin pubic crest and symphysis, insertion linea alba, tenses the linea alba; nerve supply is the subcostal nerve (T12).

questions.question:
Describe the tibia under the following headings, state how its zones relate to common pathologies, and explain why fracture of the middle third is at highest risk of delayed union.
A(i) General features, upper end, shaft, and lower end of the tibia
A(ii) How the upper end of the tibia relates to the knee joint — tibial plateaus, menisci, and intercondylar areas
B(i) Blood supply of the tibia and the significance of nutrient artery direction
B(ii) Common pathologies related to zones of the tibia — proximal, mid-shaft, and distal
C(i) Distinguish tibia from fibula with respect to weight-bearing function, articulations, and nerve–vessel relations at each malleolus
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The tibia is the large weight-bearing medial bone of the leg; it articulates with femoral condyles superiorly and the head of fibula laterally. It has an expanded upper end, a shaft, and a smaller lower end. Upper end (see A(ii)). Shaft: triangular in cross-section; 3 borders and 3 surfaces (borders and surfaces are named by opposites); anterior border forms the shin; soleal line on the posterior surface is for soleus. Lower end: expanded; saddle-shaped articular surface for talus; prolonged downwards medially to form the medial malleolus; the medial surface is subcutaneous from the medial malleolus to the medial condyle above.
A(ii)
The upper end has tibial plateaus (lateral and medial condyles); the lateral and medial menisci; anterior and posterior intercondylar areas separate the tibial plateaus; the intercondylar eminence; an articular facet for the head of fibula; and a groove on the medial condyle for semimembranosus. The anterior intercondylar area of the tibia is where the ACL attaches (just posterior to attachment of medial meniscus); the posterior intercondylar area is where the PCL attaches.
B(i)
The nutrient artery (medullary artery) is the main artery of the diaphysis. It is directed obliquely away from the epiphyseal end. When there is an epiphysis at both ends (tibia is one of the 5 bones unique in having epiphyseal plates at both ends — viz: femur, tibia, fibula, humerus, and radius), the nutrient canal is directed away from the more actively growing end. Hughes: 'to the elbow I go, from the knee I flee'. Fracture of the middle third of the tibia lies in a 'watershed' zone between the nutrient artery (supplying the upper 2/3) and the periosteal vessels (supplying the lower 1/3), making this zone most susceptible to avascular non-union.
B(ii)
Proximal tibia: tibial plateau fractures (high-energy trauma), associated with meniscal and ligamentous tears. Mid-shaft tibia: most common site of delayed or non-union, stress fractures (runners), and compartment syndrome (anterior compartment syndrome). Distal tibia (ankle): Pott's fracture involving the malleolus; ankle sprains; avulsion fractures.
C(i)
Tibia: large weight-bearing medial bone; articulates with femoral condyles, fibula head, and talus; contributes the roof (inferior surface of tibia) and the medial malleolus (wall) of the ankle mortise; the medial surface is subcutaneous. Fibula: not a weight-bearing bone; does not articulate with the femur or patella at the knee (only serves as attachment for knee joint structures); contributes the lateral malleolus (wall of ankle mortise) from fibula. At the ankle: lateral malleolar wall is from fibula and medial malleolar wall is from tibia.

A(i)
Muscularis and serosa:
• Muscularis: composed of an internal circular layer and an external longitudinal layer; between these muscle layers is the myenteric (Auerbach) nerve plexus, which produces peristalsis.
• Serosa: the small intestine is covered by a thin serosa.
A(ii)
Lamina propria of the small intestine:
• Composed of loose connective tissue containing extensive blood and lymph microvasculature, nerve fibers, smooth muscle cells, and lymphoid tissue.
• It penetrates the core of each intestinal villus, bringing microvasculature, lymphatics, and nerves into each villus.
• Smooth muscle fibers inside the villi are responsible for rhythmic movements important for efficient absorption.
• Contractions of the muscularis mucosae also produce local movements of the plicae circulares that help propel lymph from the lacteals into submucosal and mesenteric lymphatics.
B(i)
Submucosa — Brunner (duodenal) glands:
• Location: present in the proximal part of the duodenum; large clusters of branched tubular mucous glands with small excretory ducts opening among the intestinal crypts.
• Type: branched tubular mucous glands.
• Product: mucus, which is alkaline (pH 8.1–9.3).
Three functions:
• Protects the mucous membrane.
• Brings the intestinal contents to the optimum pH for pancreatic enzyme action.
• Neutralises chyme entering the duodenum from the pylorus.
B(ii)
Lacteals:
• Lymph vessels of the intestine beginning as closed tubes in the cores of villi.
• They run to the region of the lamina propria above the muscularis mucosae, where they form a plexus.
• From there they are directed to the submucosa, where they surround lymphoid nodules; they anastomose repeatedly and leave the intestine along with blood vessels.
• Function: especially important for lipid absorption.
• Absorptive state: when absorption is taking place after a meal, the lacteals are dilated and prominent; at other times they are collapsed and not prominent.
questions.question:

A(ii) Describe the lamina propria of the small intestine, including its composition, its role in each intestinal villus, and the role of smooth muscle fibers within the villi.
B(i) Describe the submucosa of the small intestine, giving particular attention to the Brunner (duodenal) glands: location, type of gland, product, pH, and all three functions.
B(ii) Describe the lacteals of the small intestine: what they are, where they begin, their course, their function, and how they change in appearance depending on the absorptive state of the intestine.

A(i) Describe the gross histology of the nervous tissue of the brain under the following headings: protective coverings (meninges), gray matter and white matter, types of glial cells in the CNS and their functions.
A(ii) Relate the three meningeal layers to their specific functions and state how cerebrospinal fluid flows.
B(i) Explain why a demyelinating disease of the optic nerve causes visual symptoms and state the histological basis of the link between the retina, optic nerve, and the CNS.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Protective coverings: the nervous system contains very little collagen or fibrous tissue; it is relatively soft and easily damaged by injuries affecting the cranium or vertebral bones. It is covered by three connective tissue layers — the meninges: dura mater (thickest and toughest layer, contains sinuses to collect venous blood), arachnoid membrane (middle web-like covering; cerebrospinal fluid flows in the web-like spaces), and pia mater (thin delicate layer that follows the contour of the brain and spinal cord). Gray matter and white matter: myelinated fibers make up the white matter in the CNS; cell bodies and unmyelinated fibers make the gray matter. Glial cells in CNS: Oligodendrocytes — produce myelin in CNS. Microglia — part of the MPS (CNS macrophages). Astrocytes and other glial cells — support, nourish, and protect neurons; they are far more numerous than neurons; unlike neurons, they are capable of mitosis.
A(ii)
Dura mater — thickest and toughest layer; contains sinuses to collect venous blood. Arachnoid membrane — middle web-like covering; cerebrospinal fluid flows in the web-like (subarachnoid) spaces. Pia mater — thin delicate layer that follows the contour of brain and spinal cord. CSF flows within the subarachnoid spaces of the arachnoid.
B(i)
The optic nerve and retina arise in the embryo as an outgrowth of the diencephalon (forebrain); the optic nerve is therefore not a true peripheral nerve like the other cranial nerves. Its myelin is produced by oligodendrocytes (not by Schwann cells). Because the optic nerve is part of the CNS (produced by oligodendrocytes and without neurilemma), it is associated with multiple sclerosis — a demyelinating disease. Demyelination of the optic nerve disrupts the action potential transmission from the retinal ganglion cells, causing visual symptoms. The retinal ganglion cells communicate with the cerebrum through the optic nerve and extend into the brain.

A(i)
• Shape of a clenched fist; base to apex 12 cm in males and 10 cm in females, anteroposterior 6 cm and 5 cm, transverse 9 cm and 8 cm; weight 280-340 g in males and 230-280 g in females; lies behind the body of the sternum, in front of T5-T8, with a base, an apex, 3 surfaces and 4 borders.
• Base: posterior, mostly left atrium, receives the 4 pulmonary veins; ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk emerge from it; separated from the diaphragmatic surface by the coronary sulcus. Apex: inferolateral, mostly left ventricle, behind the 5th left intercostal space. Surfaces: sternocostal (mostly right ventricle), diaphragmatic (concave), pulmonary (left ventricle, fitting the cardiac notch of the left lung). Borders: right (right atrium), left (mostly left ventricle with the left auricle), superior (auricles and upper right ventricle), inferior (right atrium and right ventricle).
A(ii)
Right border: 3rd to 6th right costal cartilage; left border: 5th left intercostal space (apex beat, 9 cm from the midline) up to the 2nd costal cartilage; superior border: 2nd left to 3rd right costal cartilage; inferior border: 6th right costal cartilage to the 5th left intercostal space.
A(iii)
• Four chambers: atria separated by the interatrial septum, ventricles by the interventricular septum, atria from ventricles by the right and left coronary (AV) sulci. Right atrium: forms the right border, lies between SVC and IVC, has the right auricle; rough part (musculi pectinati) and smooth part (from the right horn of the sinus venosus) separated by the sulcus terminalis (crista terminalis); receives SVC, IVC and coronary sinus.
• Right ventricle: forms the sternocostal and diaphragmatic surfaces and inferior border; trabeculae carneae including the septomarginal trabecula (carries part of the AV bundle) and anterior, posterior and septal papillary muscles joined by chordae tendineae to the tricuspid valve (3 cusps, admits 3 fingertips), the chordae preventing the cusps being driven into the right atrium; pulmonary orifice about 2.5 cm with 3 semilunar cusps (anterior, left, right).
• Left atrium: posterior, forms the base, receives 4 valveless pulmonary veins; left auricle forms the upper left border; smooth wall except the auricle. Mitral (bicuspid) valve: anterior and posterior cusps, admits 2 fingertips, overlaps the tricuspid and lies slightly higher. Left ventricle: aortic orifice about 2.5 cm at the right upper part with 3 semilunar cusps (posterior, right, left); numerous trabeculae carneae; anterior and posterior papillary muscles with chordae to the mitral valve.
A(iv)
SA node: natural pacemaker, first conducting cell, below the opening of the SVC in the right atrium, contains pacemaker P-cells, autonomic supply from the cardiac plexus (sympathetics increase and parasympathetics decrease the rate of impulse generation). AV node: slow conducting tissue in the posterior and inferior interatrial septum, allows complete atrial contraction before ventricular contraction. AV bundle of His: Purkinje fibres in the membranous part of the interventricular septum, the only bridge between atrial and ventricular muscle; right branch to papillary muscles and moderator band, left branch to the left papillary muscles.
A(v)
Arteries: right and left coronary arteries from the ascending aorta run in the right and left AV sulci; the right gives posterior interventricular and marginal arteries, the left gives anterior interventricular and circumflex arteries (the circumflex gives a marginal branch). Veins: the coronary sinus (posterior part of the AV sulcus, valve at its opening, empties into the right atrium) receives the great, small and middle cardiac veins, posterior vein of the left ventricle and oblique vein of the left atrium; the anterior cardiac vein opens into the right atrium and venae cordis minimae open into the chambers. Nerve supply: cardiac plexus.
B(i)
• The heart has a poor anastomotic network, so blockage of one coronary artery (coronary thrombosis) leads to myocardial infarction; the heart wall has 3 layers (epicardium, myocardium, endocardium) and the serous pericardium receives the coronary arteries.
• Angina pectoris: chest pain originating from the heart, caused by insufficient supply of oxygen to the heart muscle.
C(i)
• Irritation of the pleura or pericardium covering the central part of the diaphragm is referred to the shoulder, because the central diaphragm is supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3-5) and the shoulder skin by the supraclavicular nerve (C3,4); the fibrous and parietal pericardium are supplied by the phrenic nerve.
• Hiccup: involuntary spasmodic contraction of the diaphragm with approximation of the vocal folds and closure of the glottis; it may be due to pleurisy, peritonitis or pericarditis.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
The glenohumeral (shoulder) joint is a multiaxial synovial joint of the ball-and-socket variety, formed by articulation between the head of the humerus and the glenoid cavity of the scapula; due to the very limited interface between humerus and scapula, it is the most mobile joint in the human body.
A(ii)
The joint capsule is a fibrous sheath enclosing the joint structures; it is thin and lax to allow a wide range of movement (particularly abduction), is strengthened by muscles and ligaments, but is weakest inferiorly, placing it at risk of dislocation in that direction. It is lined by synovial membrane and forms a tubular sheath around the tendon of the long head of biceps, and a number of bursae aid mobility.
A(iii)
• Factors contributing to mobility are the ball-and-socket joint type, the shallow glenoid cavity against the large humeral head (a 1:4 disproportion, likened to a golf ball and tee), and laxity of the joint capsule.
• Factors contributing to stability are the rotator cuff muscles, whose resting tone pulls the humeral head into the glenoid cavity, the glenoid labrum, which deepens the cavity and reduces dislocation risk, and the ligaments, which reinforce the capsule and form the coraco-acromial arch.
B
• The glenohumeral joint is the most commonly dislocated joint in the body, accounting for approximately 95% of all shoulder dislocations, and anterior dislocations are the most prevalent.
• An anterior dislocation is usually caused by excessive extension and lateral rotation of the humerus, which forces the humeral head anteriorly and inferiorly into the weakest (inferior) part of the joint capsule.
• Tearing of the joint capsule during dislocation is associated with an increased risk of future (recurrent) dislocations.
C
• The axillary nerve runs in close proximity to the shoulder joint and can be damaged during dislocation.
• Injury to the axillary nerve causes paralysis of the deltoid muscle, with loss of sensation over the "regimental badge" area of skin overlying the deltoid.
• A dislocation can also stretch the radial nerve, since it is tightly bound within the radial (spiral) groove of the humerus.
• These nerve injuries represent the spread of the joint pathology to distant neurological structures.
• The resulting functional deficits include loss of shoulder abduction and sensory loss from axillary nerve injury, reflecting how a purely mechanical joint injury can produce a distinct neurological deficit at a distance from the joint itself.
questions.question:

A(iii) Factors contributing to its mobility and stability
