questions.answerText:
A(i)
Fixation: to achieve a permanent section, tissues must be fixed to preserve the structure and molecular composition; fixation prevents autolysis (self-digestion by enzymes present in the cells) and destruction by bacteria. Dehydration and clearing: tissues are progressed in graded steps to 100% alcohol to remove water; after the solvent replaces the alcohol, the tissue becomes transparent in xylene (clearing). Embedding: once the tissue is impregnated with the solvent, it is placed in a hard medium (e.g., wax); heat causes the solvent to evaporate, and the spaces within the tissue are filled by the embedding medium. Sectioning: tissues are sectioned by the microtome's steel or glass blade; this method allows stained sections to be prepared rapidly for study of specimens. Mounting: sections are mounted on a supportive structure (e.g., slide) that can be placed on a microscope stage. Staining: stains are applied to differentiate tissue components.
A(ii)
The most commonly used stains are hematoxylin and eosin (H & E). Hematoxylin stains basic (acidic) structures — the most acidic components are DNA and RNA; therefore, the nucleus and cytoplasmic RNA stain blue/purple (basophilic). Eosin stains acidophilic (basic) structures — many cytoplasmic constituents stain pinkish (eosinophilic/acidophilic). Reason: differential staining is based on the acid-base chemistry of cell components; acidic cell components bind basic dyes (hematoxylin) and basic components bind acidic dyes (eosin).
B(i)
Light microscopy: the standard technique; produces images of tissue sections examined by transmitted light; maximum resolving power is 0.2 micrometers (two marks 0.2 micrometers apart can be seen as two distinct entities). Types include brightfield, phase contrast, differential interference contrast (DIC), fluorescence, and confocal. Preferred for: routine tissue examination, diagnosis of pathology, overview of cell and tissue structure. Electron microscopy: has extended the detail at which subcellular structures can be studied; reveals ultrastructural details such as organelles, myelin sheaths, and synapse morphology. Preferred for: study of subcellular structures, ultrastructural detail, and molecular architecture of cell membranes.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the tissue preparation process used in histology under the following headings: fixation, dehydration and clearing, embedding, sectioning, and staining.
A(ii) State the most commonly used stain in histology, explain what structures it stains and the colors produced, and give the reason for the differential staining.
B(i) Distinguish between light microscopy and electron microscopy in histology, stating what each reveals and an example of when each is preferred.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Medial longitudinal arch: formed by calcaneus, talus (keystone — its superior articular facet is the summit), navicular, 3 cuneiform bones, and 1st, 2nd, and 3rd metatarsals; found on medial aspect of foot; larger, with greatest height, higher, more mobile, and more resilient. Lateral longitudinal arch: formed by calcaneus, cuboid, and the 4th and 5th metatarsals; summit is the subtalar articulation; flat, contains relatively fewer bones, hence more rigid; bears body weight before the medial arch comes into play. Transverse arch: formed proximally by 3 cuneiforms and cuboid, and distally by the bases of 5 metatarsals; it is a partial arch (each foot represents a half dome); the intermediate and lateral cuneiforms are wedge-shaped (bony factor).
A(ii)
Medial longitudinal arch: Ligaments — spring ligament, deltoid ligament, plantar aponeurosis, interosseous ligaments, long and short plantar ligaments. Muscles — tibialis posterior, tibialis anterior, flexor hallucis longus, flexor digitorum longus, and short muscles of the big toe. Bony factor — the shape and constitution of the bones. Lateral longitudinal arch: Ligaments — plantar aponeurosis, interosseous ligaments, long and short plantar ligaments. Muscles — peroneus longus and brevis, flexor digitorum longus, and short muscles of the little toe. Bony factor — shape and constitution of the bones. Transverse arch: Bony factor — intermediate and lateral cuneiforms are wedge-shaped. Ligaments — deep transverse ligament and interosseous ligaments (dorsal and plantar). Muscles — peroneus longus and brevis, transverse head of adductor hallucis, and slips of tibialis posterior.
B(i)
The human foot supports the body weight and serves as a lever to propel the body forward during locomotion. Functions carried out by arches: (1) Foot acts as a segmented lever with multiple joints and adapts to uneven surfaces. (2) Long flexors and intrinsic muscles assist propulsive action of gastrocnemius and soleus. (3) Arches are springs that absorb shock and store energy — elastic arches present between weight-bearing points can flatten and recoil back to normal.
B(ii)
Pes planus (flat foot): rotation of the calcaneus, eversion of the plantar surface, slipping down of the talus and navicular, lengthening of the medial longitudinal arch, and abduction of the forefoot; caused by excess weight on medial side, relaxation of ligaments, or muscular imbalance. Pes cavus (high-arched foot): exaggeration of the longitudinal arch; toes dorsiflexed at metatarsophalangeal joints and plantarflexed at interphalangeal joints — claw foot. Talipes equinovarus: plantar flexion, inversion, and adduction of the foot (clubfoot). Talipes calcaneovalgus: dorsiflexion, eversion, and abduction of the foot.
C(i)
The medial longitudinal arch is higher, more mobile, and more resilient — it is dynamic, changes most during movement, and requires active muscular support (particularly tibialis posterior, flexor hallucis longus, and the spring ligament). The lateral longitudinal arch is lower, more stable, built to transmit weight to the ground, makes more contact with the ground, has limited mobility, and depends more on bony and ligamentous rather than muscular support. The medial arch is therefore more clinically vulnerable to collapse (pes planus) when muscles weaken or ligaments stretch.
questions.question:
Describe the arches of the foot under the following headings and explain their clinical relevance.
A(i) Name and constituent bones of each arch, identifying the keystone of each
A(ii) Factors maintaining the arches — ligaments, muscles, and bony factor for each arch
B(i) Functions of the foot arches in weight-bearing and locomotion
B(ii) Deformities of the foot — name and define pes planus, pes cavus, talipes equinovarus, and talipes calcaneovalgus
C(i) Explain why the medial longitudinal arch is more dynamic and more clinically vulnerable than the lateral longitudinal arch

A. Describe the gross anatomy of the cranial base under the following headings: the anterior cranial fossa, the middle cranial fossa, and the posterior cranial fossa, and their main foramina and contents.
B. State how fractures involving the different regions of the skull base relate to specific clinical presentations.
C. Explain why disease/infection or trauma involving one region of the skull base can produce a functional deficit at a distant site, such as the nasal cavity or the brain itself.
questions.answerText:
A
In the anterior cranial fossa, the foramen caecum transmits a nasal emissary vein (in 1% of the population), the cribriform foramina in the cribriform plate transmit axons of olfactory cells forming the olfactory nerves, and the anterior and posterior ethmoidal foramina transmit vessels and nerves of the same names. In the middle cranial fossa, the optic canals transmit the optic nerves (CN II) and ophthalmic arteries; the superior orbital fissure transmits ophthalmic veins, the ophthalmic nerve (CN V1), CN III, IV and VI, and sympathetic fibres; the foramen rotundum transmits the maxillary nerve (CN V2); the foramen ovale transmits the mandibular nerve (CN V3), the accessory meningeal artery, the lesser petrosal nerve and an emissary vein; the foramen spinosum transmits the middle meningeal artery and vein and the meningeal branch of CN V3; and the foramen lacerum transmits the deep petrosal nerve and some meningeal arterial branches and small veins. In the posterior cranial fossa, the foramen magnum transmits the medulla and meninges, vertebral arteries, CN XI, dural veins, and the anterior and posterior spinal arteries; the jugular foramen transmits CN IX, X and XI, the superior bulb of the internal jugular vein, the inferior petrosal and sigmoid sinuses, and meningeal branches of the ascending pharyngeal and occipital arteries; the hypoglossal canal transmits the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII); the condylar canal transmits an emissary vein from the sigmoid sinus to the vertebral veins in the neck; and the mastoid foramen transmits a mastoid emissary vein from the sigmoid sinus and a meningeal branch of the occipital artery.
B
Fractures of the calvaria are classified as depressed, linear, comminuted, or basilar fractures; fractures of the maxillae and associated bones are termed Le Fort fractures; and there are also fractures of the mandible.
C
The close relation of the frontal sinus to the frontal lobe of the brain explains how infection of this sinus may result in development of a frontal lobe abscess; a fracture involving the sinus, severe enough to tear the dura and pia-arachnoid, will place the subarachnoid space in communication with the nasal cavity, so that CSF may be detected trickling through the nostril (CSF rhinorrhoea), usually on the affected side, although a contralateral leak can occur since these sinuses may communicate. Similarly, infection of the ethmoid sinuses (ethmoiditis) may result in a frontal cerebral abscess, and an ethmoidal fracture may cause CSF leakage into the nasal cavity, because the ethmoid sinuses lie on each side of the cribriform plate and are related above to the frontal lobes of the brain.

questions.question:
(i) Describe the origin, course, branches and distribution of the renal artery.
(ii) State why the segmental arteries of the kidney are described as end arteries.
(iii) Explain the anatomical basis of the consequence of injury or occlusion of a segmental renal artery.
questions.answerText:
(i)
• The renal arteries arise from the aorta at the level of the L1/L2 intervertebral disc; the right renal artery passes posterior to the inferior vena cava.
• Each renal artery divides at the hilum into anterior and posterior branches; these give rise to segmental arteries.
• Four segmental arteries, apical, anterosuperior, anteroinferior and inferior, arise from the anterior branch, and the posterior branch itself constitutes the posterior segmental artery.
• Each segmental artery further gives lobar arteries, one for each renal pyramid, which give two or three interlobar arteries running toward the cortex on each side of the pyramid.
• Interlobar arteries give arcuate arteries at the corticomedullary junction, which give several interlobular arteries, from which afferent glomerular arterioles arise.
• The renal veins lie anterior to their respective arteries; each renal vein drains into the inferior vena cava, and the left renal vein additionally receives the left suprarenal and left gonadal veins before crossing anterior to the aorta.
(ii)
• The segmental arteries of the kidney are described as end arteries, meaning they do not anastomose with one another.
• Because each segmental artery supplies its own renal segment without collateral supply from adjacent segmental arteries, the renal parenchyma is divided into distinct vascular segments.
(iii)
• Since the segmental arteries are end arteries, occlusion or injury of one segmental artery cuts off blood supply to its corresponding renal segment.
• This lack of anastomosis means the affected segment cannot receive compensatory blood flow from neighbouring segments.
• Lymphatic drainage of the kidney is to the right and left lumbar lymph nodes, and nerve supply is via the renal plexus (vagus and abdominopelvic splanchnic nerves), so a segmental vascular injury is an isolated event within the kidney rather than one shared with adjacent segments.

A
A V-shaped groove, the sulcus terminalis, demarcates the anterior two-thirds of the tongue from the posterior one-third. The intrinsic muscles of the tongue are the superior longitudinal, inferior longitudinal, transverse, and vertical muscles. The extrinsic muscles are the genioglossus, styloglossus, palatoglossus, and hyoglossus. The mucosa of the anterior two-thirds is formed into papillae (filiform, fungiform, circumvallate, foliate), which contain taste buds.
B
Clinical correlates involving the tongue include loss of taste sensation, bifid tongue, tongue tie (ankyloglossia), microglossia/macroglossia, and lingual carcinoma. Nerve supply differs by region: in the anterior two-thirds, motor supply to the muscles is via CN XII (except palatoglossus, supplied by the pharyngeal plexus of the vagus nerve), sensory supply to the mucous membrane is via the lingual nerve (a branch of CN V3), and special (taste) sensory supply is via the chorda tympani nerve (a branch of CN VII); in the posterior one-third, motor supply is via CN XII, and sensory supply (general and special) is via the lingual branch of CN IX and the internal laryngeal nerve (a branch of CN X).
C
Lymphatic drainage of the tongue takes 4 routes: the posterior third drains to the superior deep cervical lymph nodes; the medial part of the anterior two-thirds drains to the inferior deep cervical lymph nodes; the lateral parts of the anterior two-thirds drain to the submandibular lymph nodes; and the apex of the tongue drains to the submental lymph nodes - with the posterior third and the area near the midline draining bilaterally. Because disease (such as lingual carcinoma) arising in a particular region of the tongue follows that region's specific lymphatic drainage route, it can spread to produce nodal or functional deficits at lymph node groups that are anatomically distant from the primary site, with the pattern of spread differing depending on which part of the tongue is affected, and bilateral drainage from the posterior third and midline region meaning disease there can involve lymph nodes on both sides of the neck.
questions.question:
A. Describe the gross anatomy of the tongue under the following headings: division into anterior and posterior parts, and the intrinsic and extrinsic muscles.
B. State how the different regions of the tongue relate to common developmental and pathological conditions.
C. Explain why disease affecting one region of the tongue can produce a functional deficit at a distant site, based on its lymphatic drainage pattern.

questions.answerText:
A
The nasal sinuses are air-containing sacs lined by ciliated epithelium, communicating with the nasal cavity through narrow, easily occluded channels; they develop as outgrowths from the nasal cavity. There are 4 pairs: the maxillary antrum, sphenoid, frontal and ethmoid sinuses. The maxillary antrum and ethmoid sinuses are present in a rudimentary state at birth, while the rest become evident at about the 7th year of life. The lining of the sinuses is continuous with the nasal mucosa; their function is obscure, but they provide resonance to the voice, shape to the face, and some degree of warmth and humidification to inspired air. The paranasal sinuses are supplied by branches of the ophthalmic and maxillary nerves.
B
The frontal sinuses' posterosuperior wall lies adjacent to the frontal lobe of the brain, and their floor abuts the ethmoid cells, nasal fossa roof and orbit; infection here may cause a frontal lobe abscess, and fracture severe enough to tear the dura and pia-arachnoid causes CSF rhinorrhoea. The maxillary sinus (antrum) may become infected from the nasal cavity or from caries of the upper molar teeth, whose roots are separated from the sinus floor only by a thin, sometimes deficient, layer of bone. The ethmoid sinuses lie on each side of the cribriform plate, related above to the frontal lobes; infection (ethmoiditis) may result in a frontal cerebral abscess, and ethmoidal fracture may cause CSF leakage into the nasal cavity. The sphenoid sinuses lie within the body of the sphenoid and may extend laterally into the greater wing of the sphenoid or backward into the basal part of the occipital bone; each drains into the nasal cavity above the superior concha (the sphenoethmoidal recess).
C
Because the frontal and ethmoid sinuses are directly related anatomically to the frontal lobes of the brain (posterosuperior wall of the frontal sinus, and the region above the cribriform plate for the ethmoid sinuses), infection at either site can spread directly to produce a frontal lobe or frontal cerebral abscess; and because fracture of either sinus, if severe enough to tear the dura and pia-arachnoid, places the subarachnoid space in communication with the nasal cavity, CSF rhinorrhoea (leakage of CSF into the nose) results, sometimes even on the contralateral side since the sinuses may communicate with one another.
questions.question:
A. Describe the gross anatomy of the paranasal sinuses under the following headings: the four pairs of sinuses, their development, and their general function.
B. State how each of the paranasal sinuses relates to a specific clinical complication when infected or fractured.
C. Explain why disease of the paranasal sinuses can spread to produce a functional deficit in a distant structure, namely the brain or the nasal cavity.

Describe the axilla under the following headings:
A(i) Shape and apex
A(ii) Base
A(iii) Walls
A(iv) Contents
B. Explain the clinical basis for the axillary vein being particularly vulnerable to injury in this region.
C. Distinguish between the quadrangular space and the triangular interval found in the posterior wall of the axilla.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The axilla is a pyramid-shaped space between the upper part of the arm and the side of the upper chest; its apex is the cervicoaxillary canal, bounded by the 1st rib, clavicle, and superior edge of the scapula, forming the passageway between the neck and axilla.
A(ii)
The base is formed by concave skin, subcutaneous tissue, and the axillary (deep) fascia.
A(iii)
Anterior wall: pectoralis major and minor, subclavius, and clavipectoral fascia. Posterior wall: scapula and subscapularis above, teres major and latissimus dorsi below. Medial wall: upper ribs, intercostal muscles, and serratus anterior. Lateral wall: narrow and bony, formed by the intertubercular groove of the humerus.
A(iv)
Contents: the axillary artery and its branches, the axillary vein and its tributaries, the infraclavicular part of the brachial plexus, axillary lymph nodes, and loose areolar/adipose tissue, all enclosed with the plexus in the axillary sheath.
B
• The axillary vein is large and lies in an exposed, superficial position within the axilla.
• Wounds to the axilla therefore often involve the axillary vein because of its large size and exposed position.
• A wound to the proximal part of the axillary vein is especially dangerous because of the risk of air entering the vessel (air embolism).
C
• The quadrangular space lies in the posterior wall of the axilla and transmits the axillary nerve and the posterior circumflex humeral artery and vein.
• The triangular interval also lies in the posterior wall and transmits the radial nerve and the profunda brachii artery.
• Both spaces are related to the long head of triceps brachii and the teres major muscle in their boundaries.
• The quadrangular space thus carries the nerve/vessels supplying the deltoid and teres minor region, while the triangular interval carries those continuing into the posterior compartment of the arm.
• This distinction explains why injury near the surgical neck of the humerus threatens the axillary nerve, whereas injury lower down at the spiral groove threatens the radial nerve instead.

questions.question:
A. Describe the gross anatomy of the gallbladder and the extrahepatic bile ducts under the following headings:
A(i) location, shape, dimensions and parts;
A(ii) the ducts and course of the common bile duct;
A(iii) blood and nerve supply.
B(i) State how the neck relates to gallstones.
B(ii) State how Calot's triangle and its lymph node relate to surgery and inflammation.
B(iii) State how the sphincters relate to biliary dyskinesia.
C(i) Explain why gallbladder inflammation may cause pain at the right shoulder tip and a positive Murphy's sign.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• A pear-shaped fibromuscular sac that stores and concentrates bile, in the gallbladder fossa on the inferior surface of the right lobe of the liver, 7 to 10 cm long, 3 cm broad and 30 to 50 ml in capacity.
• Fundus: projects beyond the inferior border of the liver, covered by peritoneum on all sides. Body: superior surface adherent to the liver and devoid of peritoneum. Neck: upper narrow part ending in the cystic duct, with a spiral fold.
• The fundus is related to the anterior abdominal wall and transverse colon; the body's inferior surface to the transverse colon and the 1st and 2nd parts of the duodenum.
A(ii)
• Right and left hepatic ducts emerge at the porta hepatis; the common hepatic duct (3 to 4 cm) is joined by the cystic duct (3 to 4 cm, spiral folds of Heister) to form the common bile duct.
• The common bile duct (about 8 cm, 6 mm wide) has supraduodenal, retroduodenal, infraduodenal and intraduodenal parts, joining the main pancreatic duct at the hepatopancreatic ampulla.
A(iii)
• Cystic artery (from the right hepatic artery) is the chief supply, with the cystic vein to the portal vein; the posterior superior pancreaticoduodenal branches supply the lower bile duct.
• Sympathetic nerves come from the celiac plexus and parasympathetic from the vagus.
B(i)
The posteromedial wall of the neck may dilate as Hartmann's pouch, where gallstones may lodge.
B(ii)
Calot's triangle (liver inferior surface, common hepatic duct, cystic duct) locates the cystic artery in laparoscopic cholecystectomy; Lund's node enlarges in cholecystitis or cholangitis and may be removed.
B(iii)
Gallbladder muscle and the sphincter of Oddi have reciprocal innervation (gallbladder contracts, sphincter relaxes); disruption is biliary dyskinesia.
C(i)
• Inflammation irritates the subdiaphragmatic parietal peritoneum supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3, 4, 5), referred to the right shoulder tip supplied by the supraclavicular nerve (C3, C4).
• In Murphy's sign the inflamed gallbladder descends on deep inspiration and contacts the palpating hand at the right costal margin, causing pain and a caught breath.

A(i)
Structure:
• Capsule and septa: a capsule of connective tissue rich in collagen fibers surrounds the large salivary glands; septa of connective tissue originate from the capsule and divide the glands into lobules; each lobule contains numerous secretory units (acini).
• Parenchyma: consists of secretory end pieces and a branching duct system arranged in lobules separated by septae of connective tissue from the capsule. Vessels and nerves enter at the hilum and gradually branch into the lobules.
• Cell types in secretory end pieces: serous cells (polarized protein-secreting cells, pyramidal in shape, round nuclei, well-stained RER, apical secretory granules; joined apically by tight and adherent junctions; form a spherical unit called an acinus with a very small central lumen; secrete enzymes and other proteins); mucous cells; and nonsecretory myoepithelial cells.
• Duct system in sequence: secretory end pieces → intercalated ducts (lined by simple low cuboidal epithelium, surrounded by myoepithelial cells) → striated ducts (intralobular) → interlobular (excretory/striated ducts drain into these) → interlobar ducts → main duct (opens into the oral cavity, lined with nonkeratinized-stratified squamous epithelium).
A(ii)
Secretion types:
• Parotid gland: serous and watery.
• Submandibular and sublingual glands: seromucous secretion.
• Minor glands: mostly mucous.
• Type depends on content of glycoprotein mucin: serous, seromucous, or mucous.
B(i)
• Intercalated ducts: several short intercalated ducts join to form striated ducts; they are lined by cuboidal epithelial cells that have the ability to divide and differentiate into secretory or ductal cells; also called intralobular ducts.
• Striated ducts: characterized by radial striations that extend from the bases of the cells to the level of the central nuclei; striations consist of infoldings of the basal plasma membrane with numerous elongated mitochondria aligned parallel to the infolded membranes (characteristic of ion-transporting cells); they have a folded basal membrane enabling active transport; also called intralobular ducts.
B(ii)
Saliva is modified by the cells of the duct system draining the secretory units: much Na+ and Cl- is reabsorbed while certain growth factors and digestive enzymes are added. Water resorption and ion secretion in the striated ducts make saliva hypotonic (reduced Na and Cl ions; increased carbonate and potassium ions).
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the gross and microscopic structure of the large salivary glands under the following headings: capsule and septa; parenchyma (secretory end pieces); cell types in the secretory end pieces; the duct system in sequence from secretory unit to oral cavity.
A(ii) State the type of secretion produced by each of the three pairs of major salivary glands and by the minor glands.
B(i) Distinguish between striated ducts and intercalated ducts, including location, epithelium, and function.
B(ii) Explain how saliva is modified as it passes through the duct system.

Describe the deep fascial spaces of the hand:
A(i) Thenar space
A(ii) The list of compartments/fascial spaces of the hand
A(iii) Space of Parona
B. Explain the clinical basis for infection spreading between these compartments.
C. Distinguish between the thenar space and the midpalmar space.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The thenar space lies on the thumb side of the septum that joins the border of the palmar aponeurosis to the palmar border of the third metacarpal bone; it contains the first lumbrical muscle and is overlaid by the flexor tendons to the index finger.
A(ii)
The compartments and fascial spaces of the hand include the dorsal spaces, hypothenar space, midpalmar space, thenar space, web spaces and pulp spaces, all bounded by connective tissue.
A(iii)
The space of Parona extends from the proximal margin of the carpal tunnel to the mid-forearm; its roof is formed distally by the flexor digitorum profundus tendons and proximally by the belly of flexor digitorum superficialis (whose origin forms the proximal boundary), it is limited medially by flexor carpi ulnaris and laterally by flexor pollicis longus, and its floor is formed by pronator quadratus distally and the interosseous membrane in its proximal two-thirds.
B
• These fascial spaces allow mobility of the hand structures but, being bounded by connective tissue, offer little resistance to the spread of infection.
• Infection within the thenar space can readily break into the connective tissue canals surrounding the ulnar three lumbricals.
• For practical purposes the thenar space may therefore be considered continuous distally with these lumbrical canals, and thus distally communicates with the web spaces.
• The thenar space also communicates proximally with the space of Parona.
• Infection of these deep spaces, including the space of Parona, can be difficult to diagnose.
C
• The thenar space lies on the thumb (radial) side of the septum joining the palmar aponeurosis to the third metacarpal, contains the first lumbrical, and is overlaid by the flexor tendons of the index finger.
• The midpalmar space, by contrast, lies on the ulnar side of this septum, related to the tendons for the middle, ring and little fingers and to adductor pollicis, separated from the thenar space by the lateral palmar septum.
• The thenar space communicates proximally with the space of Parona and distally with the lumbrical canals/web spaces, reflecting its position along the flexor tendon of the index finger.
• This anatomical separation by the lateral palmar septum explains why infection in one compartment tends initially to remain localised to that space before spreading along its own specific communicating pathway.

A
The larynx is demarcated by the vestibular fold (containing fibrous tissue, forming the false vocal cord on each side) and the vocal fold (the true vocal cord, containing the vocal ligament) into 3 zones: the supraglottic compartment (vestibule), above the false cords; the glottic compartment, between the false and true cords; and the subglottic compartment, between the true cords and the first ring of the trachea. The space between the vocal cords is the rima glottidis.
B
The mucosa is firmly adherent to the vocal ligament without any intervening submucosa, which accounts for the pearly white, avascular appearance of the vocal cords as seen on laryngoscopy; regulation of vocal cord tension (and therefore pitch of the voice) is accomplished primarily by pivoting the thyroid cartilage forward or backward at the cricothyroid joint, via the cricothyroid muscle, which is the only laryngeal muscle that tightens the cords, is supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (not the recurrent laryngeal nerve), and is the only intrinsic laryngeal muscle situated on the outside of the larynx.
C
Sensory innervation is via the internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve above the cords and via the recurrent laryngeal nerve below the cords; motor supply to the muscles is from the nucleus ambiguus via the cranial accessory, with the cricothyroid supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve and all other laryngeal muscles (including the upper oesophagus and cricopharyngeus) supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve. Lymphatic drainage above the cords is to the upper deep cervical nodes and below the cords to the lower deep cervical nodes; a disease process at either level can therefore spread along its corresponding drainage route to functionally distant lymph node groups. Movements which close off the entrance to the larynx during swallowing involve the epiglottis being pulled down and the arytenoid cartilages being pulled forward toward the epiglottis; the larynx is also raised, along with the pharynx, by contraction of the longitudinal muscles of the pharynx, and the epiglottis acts partly as a passive barrier, so disordered laryngeal muscle action compromises this protective closure mechanism.
questions.question:
A. Describe the gross anatomy of the larynx under the following headings: the three zones/compartments and the folds that demarcate them.
B. State how the zones of the larynx and the vocal folds relate to laryngeal function and clinical assessment (e.g. on laryngoscopy).
C. Explain how disease/infection at a site distant from the larynx can spread to compromise laryngeal or lower respiratory function, and the functional deficit that results from disordered laryngeal muscle action.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Skeletal muscle — longitudinal section: cross-striations of alternating dark (A bands, anisotropic) and light (I bands, isotropic) bands; each I band bisected by a dark transverse Z disc; multinucleated fibers at periphery. Cross-section: peripheral nuclei; high cytoplasm-to-nucleus ratio. Smooth muscle — longitudinal section: meshwork appearance; no striations; elongated spindle-shaped cells; elongated and central nuclei. Cross-section: central nuclei; low cytoplasm-to-nucleus ratio. Cardiac muscle — longitudinal section: striations; branching cells; intercalated discs. Cross-section: central nuclei; high cytoplasm-to-nucleus ratio.
A(ii)
Skeletal muscle: troponin subunits (troponin I and troponin T) are integral to muscle contraction; mutations in cardiac troponin subunits can result in cardiomyopathies. Smooth muscle: smooth muscle cells are able to undergo cell division (unlike cardiac and skeletal muscle). Cardiac muscle: atrial myocytes secrete atrial natriuretic peptide; kidneys respond to this to cause sodium and water loss (natriuresis and diuresis); when natriuretic peptide levels fall, kidneys result in sodium and water conservation.
B(i)
Cardiac muscle cells act as a syncytium through gap junctions in intercalated discs, which provide ionic continuity between adjacent cells, allowing the signal to contract to pass throughout the organ. The blood supply to the heart is through three main coronary arteries prone to atheroma. Acute coronary arterial occlusion involving nearly the entire area at risk causes necrosis of the myocardium. Because the cardiac muscle acts as a syncytium and is continuously active, obstruction of coronary blood flow rapidly leads to widespread ischemia and necrosis of the myocardium.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the gross histology of the three types of muscle tissue (skeletal, smooth, and cardiac) as seen in longitudinal section and cross-section under the light microscope.
A(ii) Relate the structural differences of each muscle type to their specific pathological conditions.
B(i) Explain how the histological organization of cardiac muscle facilitates rapid spread of the signal to contract, and state why blockage of the coronary arteries leads to widespread myocardial damage.

A(i) Describe the autonomic nerve supply to the salivary glands, including which division of the autonomic nervous system produces each type of secretory response and what type of saliva each produces.
A(ii) Describe the full immunological secretory mechanism of the large salivary glands, identifying the cell type that secretes IgA and the cell types that synthesise the secretory component.
B(i) The parotid gland resembles pancreatic tissue but can be distinguished from it. State the distinguishing features of each gland.
B(ii) Classify all minor salivary glands by location and secretion type, and state what proportion of total saliva volume and mucus the minor glands produce.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Autonomic nerve supply:
• Vessels and nerves enter the large salivary glands at the hilum and gradually branch into the lobules; a rich vascular and nerve plexus surrounds the secretory and ductal components of each lobule.
• The capillaries surrounding the secretory end pieces are important for saliva secretion, stimulated by the autonomic nervous system.
• Parasympathetic stimulation (usually through smell or taste of food): promotes vasodilation and a copious watery secretion.
• Sympathetic stimulation: produces small amounts of viscous saliva, rich in organic material. NOTE: dry mouth sensation in stressful situations (sympathetic predominance).
A(ii)
Immunological secretory mechanism:
• Plasma cells (in the connective tissue around the glands) secrete IgA.
• IgA forms a complex with a secretory component synthesized by the serous acinar cells, intercalated duct cells, and striated duct cells.
• The IgA-rich secretory complex released into the saliva is resistant to enzymatic digestion and constitutes an immunological defense mechanism against pathogens in the oral cavity.
B(i)
Parotid vs pancreatic tissue:
• Both resemble each other histologically.
• Parotid gland: has adipocytes (fat cells) in its parenchyma.
• Pancreatic tissue: has islets of Langerhans (endocrine clusters) and centroacinar cells.
B(ii)
• Minor salivary glands by location and secretion: von Ebner's glands of tongue (posterior dorsal and lateral): serous acini only.
• Palate, base and lateral border of tongue: predominantly mucous acini.
• Lip, cheek, apex of tongue: mixed serous and mucous acini.
• Minor glands secrete 10% of the total volume of saliva but account for approximately 70% of the mucus secreted.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the gross anatomy of the kidney, naming its outer and inner regions and the structures visible in a frontal section.
A(ii) State all seven functions of the kidney.
B(i) Compare cortical nephrons and juxtamedullary nephrons under the headings: proportion, loop length, glomerulus position, and capillary bed supplied by the efferent arteriole.
B(ii) Describe the two cell types in the collecting ducts, including their microscopic features and functions, and describe how the collecting ducts contribute to urine delivery.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Gross anatomy of the kidney:
• Renal cortex: granular-appearing superficial region.
• Renal medulla: composed of cone-shaped medullary (renal) pyramids; pyramids are separated by renal columns (inward extensions of cortical tissue).
• Structures in frontal section: renal hilum, renal cortex, renal medulla, major calyx, papilla of pyramid, renal pelvis, minor calyx, ureter, renal pyramid in renal medulla, renal column, fibrous capsule.
A(ii)
Seven functions of the kidney:
• Regulating total water volume and total solute concentration in water.
• Regulating ECF ion concentrations.
• Ensuring long-term acid-base balance.
• Removal of metabolic wastes, toxins, and drugs.
• Endocrine functions: renin (regulation of blood pressure) and erythropoietin (regulation of RBC production).
• Activation of vitamin D.
• Gluconeogenesis during prolonged fasting.
B(i)
Comparison of nephron types:
• Cortical nephrons: 85% of nephrons; short nephron loop; glomerulus further from the cortex-medulla junction; efferent arteriole supplies peritubular capillaries.
• Juxtamedullary nephrons: long nephron loops that deeply invade the medulla; glomerulus closer to the cortex-medulla junction; efferent arteriole supplies vasa recta; ascending limbs have thick and thin segments; important in production of concentrated urine.
B(ii)
Two collecting duct cell types:
• Principal cells: sparse, short microvilli; maintain water and Na+ balance.
• Intercalated cells (A and B types): cuboidal cells with abundant microvilli; both types help maintain acid-base balance of blood.
• Collecting ducts receive filtrate from many nephrons; run through medullary pyramids giving them a striped appearance; fuse together to deliver urine through papillae into minor calyces.

questions.question:
A(i) State the nature of the vagus nerve and describe its course in the thorax on the right and left.
A(ii) Describe its relations in the mediastinum.
A(iii) State its branches and plexuses in the thorax.
A(iv) Describe its distribution to thoracic structures.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• The vagus is the 10th cranial nerve.
• The right vagus descends on the right side of the trachea, forms the posterior oesophageal plexus and continues in the abdomen as the posterior gastric nerve.
• The left vagus descends between the left common carotid and left subclavian arteries, forms the anterior oesophageal plexus and continues in the abdomen as the anterior gastric nerve.
A(ii)
• The vagus nerves lie in both the superior and the posterior mediastinum; in the posterior mediastinum the right and left vagi lie around the oesophagus and pass through the oesophageal opening of the diaphragm (T10) as the anterior and posterior vagal trunks.
• The left recurrent laryngeal branch of the vagus winds round the ligamentum arteriosus, which connects the inferior concave surface of the arch of the aorta to the left pulmonary artery.
A(iii)
• Branches: recurrent laryngeal branches on both sides and superior and inferior cervical cardiac branches (the right has both, the left has the inferior branch) to the cardiac plexus; pulmonary plexuses to the lungs; oesophageal plexuses.
• Cardiac plexus: the superficial part lies in front of the ligamentum arteriosus (inferior cervical cardiac branch of the left vagus); the deep part lies in front of the left bronchus and at the bifurcation of the pulmonary trunk, behind the arch of the aorta on the lowest part of the trachea; parasympathetic fibres relay in the heart.
A(iv)
• Heart: through the cardiac plexus to the SA and AV nodes and the AV bundle; parasympathetics decrease the rate of impulse generation, sympathetics increase it.
• Lungs and visceral pleura (via the pulmonary plexuses): bronchoconstrictor, vasodilator to pulmonary vessels and secretomotor to glands; the vagal efferents mediate the cough reflex that clears secretions and dust.
• Oesophagus and trachea: recurrent laryngeal branch to the striated upper third of the oesophagus, parasympathetic secretomotor fibres to the oesophageal glands; vagus to the mucous membrane and parasympathetics of the trachea; gastric irritation of vagus nerve endings may cause hiccup.

questions.question:
(i) Describe the gross anatomy of the kidney, including its shape, coverings, and internal structure (cortex, medulla, pyramids, sinus, calyces).
(ii) Relate the parts of the kidney to a common renal pathology.
(iii) Explain how disease/obstruction of the kidney or its drainage system can produce a functional deficit at a distance.
questions.answerText:
(i)
• The kidneys are bean-shaped, retroperitoneal organs lying on the posterior abdominal wall from about the T12 to L3 vertebral level, each about 10 cm long, 5 cm wide and 2.5 cm thick, with the right kidney slightly lower due to the liver.
• Each kidney has a superior pole bearing the suprarenal gland, an inferior pole, a convex lateral border, and a concave medial border indented by the renal hilum.
• Coverings, from within outward, are the fibrous (renal) capsule, perirenal fat, renal fascia, and pararenal fat.
• Internally, a dark brown outer cortex surrounds a lighter medulla composed of about a dozen renal pyramids, each with its base toward the cortex and its apex (renal papilla) projecting into a minor calyx; cortex extends between pyramids as renal columns.
• At the hilum, the renal vein lies anterior to the renal artery, which lies anterior to the renal pelvis; the hilum leads into the renal sinus, which contains the pelvis, calyces, vessels, nerves and fat.
• The renal pelvis, a funnel-shaped expansion of the ureter, receives two or three major calyces, each dividing into two or three minor calyces.
(ii)
• Renal (kidney) stones are a clinical consideration associated with the kidney and relate to the calyceal and pelvic system where urine collects before draining into the ureter.
• The renal pyramids and papillae are the sites from which urine is excreted into the minor calyces, so pathology of the papillae or pyramids affects urine drainage.
(iii)
• The ureter has three points of constriction - the pelviureteric junction, where it crosses the pelvic brim, and its intramural (intravesical) course - which are potential sites of obstruction by ureteric stones.
• Obstruction at any of these constrictions causes back-pressure on the kidney, from the collecting system through the pelvis to the pyramids, producing a functional deficit in urine drainage from that kidney.
• Ureteric pain from such obstruction is referred to the ipsilateral lower quadrant of the anterior abdominal wall and especially the groin, showing how a renal or ureteric problem produces a distant clinical effect.
• This referred pain reflects the segmental (T11-T12) sympathetic innervation shared by the ureter and the abdominal wall/groin dermatomes.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the orbit under the following headings: shape, the bones forming it, and its average dimensions.
A(ii) Describe the three openings into the orbital cavity and the structures transmitted through each, and describe the connective tissue planes of the orbit.
B. Explain the clinical basis for why orbital trauma can result in double vision and in a rise of intraocular pressure.
C. Distinguish between the superior orbital fissure and the inferior orbital fissure in terms of the structures each transmits.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The orbit is shaped like a pear or quadrilateral pyramid, with its base in the plane of the orbital rim and its pyramidal cavity base in front and apex behind; it protects, supports and maximises the function of the eye, and seven bones conjoin to form the orbital structure. The average dimensions of the orbit are: height of orbital margin 40 mm, width of orbital margin 35 mm, depth of orbit 40-50 mm, interorbital distance 25 mm, and volume of orbit 30 cm³; 20% of this space is occupied by the eyeball, and about one-sixth of the eye is exposed, the remainder being protected by the walls of the orbit.
A(ii)
The major nerves and vessels to the orbit and globe enter through 3 openings. The superior orbital fissure, bounded by the lesser and greater wings of the sphenoid, transmits cranial nerves III, IV and VI, the lacrimal nerve, frontal nerve, nasociliary nerve, orbital branch of the middle meningeal artery, recurrent branch of the lacrimal artery, superior orbital vein and superior ophthalmic vein. The inferior orbital fissure, bounded by the greater wing of the sphenoid, the maxilla and the palatine bones, transmits the infraorbital nerve, zygomatic nerve, parasympathetics to the lacrimal gland, infraorbital artery, infraorbital vein, and the inferior ophthalmic vein branch to the pterygoid plexus. The optic canal, at the apex of the orbit within the sphenoid bone, transmits the optic nerve, ophthalmic artery, and central retinal vein. The connective tissue boundaries of the orbit are divided into 4 main units: the bulbar (Tenon) fascia, surrounding and protecting the globe and providing a barrier between the globe and retrobulbar fat; multiple connective tissue septa extending from the globe to the periorbita like spokes on a wheel; the individual connective tissue sheath of each extraocular muscle, which fuses to form a confluent muscle sheath and the medial and lateral check ligaments; and the periosteal lining of the orbit, which can be elevated in surgery to expose the bony orbit.
B
Clinical correlates of the orbit include eye trauma with blow-out fracture, due to blunt trauma, which displaces the orbital walls; paralysis of the extraocular muscles results in double vision. Obstruction of the flow of aqueous humor results in a rise in intraocular pressure called glaucoma, leading to degenerative changes in the retina with consequent blindness.
C
The superior orbital fissure transmits cranial nerves III, IV and VI, the lacrimal, frontal and nasociliary nerves, the orbital branch of the middle meningeal artery, the recurrent branch of the lacrimal artery, and the superior orbital and superior ophthalmic veins. The inferior orbital fissure, in contrast, transmits the infraorbital nerve, the zygomatic nerve, parasympathetics to the lacrimal gland, the infraorbital artery and vein, and the inferior ophthalmic vein branch to the pterygoid plexus.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the parotid gland under the following headings: location, external features, and capsule.
A(ii) Describe the parotid duct, and list the structures within the substance of the gland from superficial to deep, and the other structures found within the gland.
B. Explain the clinical basis for why the parotid gland is particularly vulnerable to nerve injury during surgery, and describe the syndrome that can follow such injury.
C. Distinguish between the parotid gland and the submandibular gland in terms of their ducts and ganglia associated with their secretomotor supply.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The parotid gland is the largest salivary gland (para = around, otic = ear); it is situated below the external acoustic meatus, in front of the sternomastoid, and also projects forward onto the surface of masseter. It is pyramidal in shape with the apex pointing downward, has 4 surfaces (superior/base, lateral/superficial, anteromedial, posteromedial) separated by 3 borders (anterior, posterior, medial), and has 1 main lobe and 1 accessory lobe (a small detached part called the accessory parotid gland or Socia Parotidis, lying on masseter between the zygomatic arch and the parotid duct). The capsule has a false capsule, formed by the investing layer of deep cervical fascia, and a true capsule, formed by condensation of the stroma.
A(ii)
The parotid duct is about 5 cm long, arises from the anterior border of the gland, runs on masseter, and at the anterior border of masseter runs medially to pierce buccinator and the mucosa, opening into the vestibule of the mouth opposite the crown of the upper 2nd molar tooth; its surface anatomy corresponds to the middle third of a line from the lower border of the tragus to a point midway between the nasal ala and the upper labial margin. From superficial to deep within the substance of the gland are: the facial nerve and its branches; the retromandibular vein and its two divisions (maxillary vein, superficial temporal vein); and the external carotid artery and its two terminal branches. Other structures within the gland are the auriculotemporal nerve, the posterior auricular artery, and the preauricular lymph nodes.
B
Within the gland, the facial nerve radiates like a goose's foot (Pes Anserinus) through the anterior border of the gland into its branches (temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular, cervical); because the facial nerve runs through the substance of the gland, it is at risk during parotid surgery or trauma. Frey's syndrome (also known as gustatory sweating or auriculo-temporal nerve syndrome) commonly occurs after parotid surgery or trauma, from injury of the auriculotemporal and great auricular nerves; during healing, secretomotor fibres of the auriculotemporal nerve join with the great auricular nerve and reach the sweat glands of facial skin, so that sweating, warmth and redness of the face occur as a result of salivary stimulation by the smell or taste of food.
C
The parotid gland's secretomotor (parasympathetic) supply is via the auriculotemporal nerve, producing a watery secretion, with sympathetic supply producing a mucous-rich, sticky secretion derived from the plexus around the external carotid artery. In contrast, the submandibular gland's duct is the submandibular duct (Wharton's duct), and its nerve supply is via branches from the submandibular ganglion, through which it receives parasympathetic fibres from the chorda tympani, sensory fibres from the lingual branch of the mandibular nerve, and sympathetic fibres from the plexus on the facial artery.

questions.question:
Describe the popliteal fossa under the following headings and explain its clinical importance.
A(i) Boundaries
A(ii) Roof and floor
B(i) Contents, naming structures from superficial to deep
B(ii) Clinical basis for why popliteal aneurysm can produce neurological features
C(i) Distinguish the tibial nerve from the common fibular nerve with respect to origin, course, and consequences of injury within the fossa
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The popliteal fossa is a diamond-shaped depression in the posterior aspect of the knee. Superolateral border: biceps femoris. Superomedial border: semimembranosus and semitendinosus. Inferolateral border: lateral head of gastrocnemius. Inferomedial border: medial head of gastrocnemius.
A(ii)
Roof (posteriorly): skin and fascia — the popliteal fascia is a strong sheet of deep fascia continuous superiorly with the fascia lata and inferiorly with the deep fascia of the leg. Floor (anteriorly): popliteal surface of femur, capsule of knee joint, oblique popliteal ligament, and popliteal fascia over popliteus.
B(i)
From superficial to deep: posterior cutaneous nerve of thigh; tibial nerve (most superficial of the neurovascular bundle); popliteal vein; popliteal artery (deepest structure in the fossa, running close to the articular capsule of the knee joint); popliteal lymph nodes and lymphatic vessels. The small saphenous vein and three cutaneous nerves (posterior cutaneous nerve of thigh, medial sural cutaneous nerve, lateral sural cutaneous nerve) lie in the superficial fascia.
B(ii)
The popliteal artery is the deepest structure and lies in close proximity to the tibial nerve. An aneurysm (dilation of the artery beyond 50% of its normal diameter) causes compression of the tibial nerve. The tibial nerve is particularly susceptible to this compression; the major features include weakened or absent plantarflexion, paraesthesia of the foot and posterolateral leg, and paralysis of flexor muscles in the leg and intrinsic muscles of the sole.
C(i)
The tibial nerve is the medial and larger branch of the sciatic nerve; it bisects the fossa passing from the superior to the inferior angle and gives muscular branches to soleus, gastrocnemius, plantaris, and popliteus, and the medial sural cutaneous nerve. The common fibular nerve is the lateral, smaller terminal branch; it begins at the superior angle, closely follows the medial border of biceps femoris, exits the fossa by passing superficial to the lateral head of gastrocnemius, then winds around the neck of fibula where it divides into terminal branches. Injury to the tibial nerve causes inability to plantarflex the ankle or flex the toes and loss of sensation on the sole of the foot.

(i)
• The liver has two surfaces - a convex diaphragmatic surface (anterior, superior, posterior and right lateral) and a relatively flat, posteroinferior visceral surface.
• It is divided into a large right lobe and a smaller left lobe by the falciform ligament, with the caudate and quadrate lobes arising from the right lobe on the visceral surface.
• Two sagittally oriented fissures (for the ligamentum teres and ligamentum venosum on the left, and the gallbladder fossa and IVC groove on the right) are linked by the transverse porta hepatis, forming an H on the visceral surface.
• Ligaments include the falciform ligament, the coronary ligament with the right and left triangular ligaments, and the lesser omentum (hepatogastric and hepatoduodenal ligaments).
• The porta hepatis transmits the hepatic ducts, hepatic artery and portal vein branches, and hepatic nerves and lymph nodes.
(ii)
• The bare area of the diaphragmatic surface has no peritoneal covering, so infection there can track through the diaphragm to posterior mediastinal lymph nodes.
• The subphrenic and subhepatic spaces, and Morison's pouch between the liver and right kidney, are recesses where pathological fluid such as pus, blood or ascites collects.
• Liver fissures serve as surgical landmarks, such as Cantlie's line, which divides the liver into functional right and left lobes along the middle hepatic vein.
• Because the liver is large, fixed in position and friable, it is vulnerable to rupture, often from a fractured rib perforating the diaphragm, causing haemorrhage and right upper quadrant pain.
(iii)
• In cirrhosis, hepatocytes are destroyed and replaced by fibrous tissue that impedes blood flow through the liver, causing portal hypertension.
• This opens portal-systemic anastomoses at the lower oesophagus, anal canal, paraumbilical region, retroperitoneum and intrahepatic sites, producing distant complications such as bleeding oesophageal varices.
• Distension of Glisson's capsule from an enlarged liver produces sharp, well-localised pain via the lower intercostal nerves, illustrating how a hepatic process produces a distant sensory effect.
questions.question:
(i) Describe the gross anatomy of the liver under the headings: surfaces, lobes, fissures and peritoneal ligaments.
(ii) Relate the lobes/fissures of the liver to common hepatic pathology.
(iii) Explain how liver disease can spread its effects to a distant structure, producing a functional deficit there.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
The great saphenous vein (GSV) is the longest vein in the body. It is formed by the union of the dorsal vein of the great toe and the dorsal venous arch of the foot. It ascends anterior to the medial malleolus, passes posterior to the medial condyle of the femur (about a hand's breadth posterior to the medial border of the patella), anastomoses freely with the small saphenous vein, traverses the saphenous opening in the fascia lata, and empties into the femoral vein.
A(ii)
The GSV has 10–12 valves, which are more numerous in the leg than in the thigh; these valves are usually located just inferior to the perforating veins. Perforating veins also have their own valves. Tributaries in the anterior and lateral part of the thighs converge to form the accessory saphenous vein (ASV), which communicates the GSV with the small saphenous vein. Just before emptying into the femoral vein, the GSV receives tributaries from the superficial circumflex iliac, superficial epigastric, and external pudendal veins.
B(i)
The small saphenous vein (SSV) arises on the lateral side of the foot from the union of the dorsal vein of the little toe with the dorsal venous arch. It ascends posterior to the lateral malleolus as a continuation of the lateral marginal vein, passes along the lateral border of the calcaneal tendon, inclines to the midline of the fibula and penetrates the deep fascia, ascends between the heads of the gastrocnemius muscle, and empties into the popliteal vein in the popliteal fossa.
B(ii)
There are four main pulse points in the lower limb: femoral (palpated midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and pubic symphysis — the mid-inguinal point); popliteal (deep in the popliteal fossa, requires deep palpation, best with slight knee flexion); dorsalis pedis (on the dorsum of the foot, just lateral to extensor hallucis longus tendon); and posterior tibial (inferoposteriorly to the medial malleolus). The GSV anterior to the medial malleolus is the classic site for venous cut-down; the GSV at the medial condyle of the femur is another accessible site.
C(i)
Superficial veins (GSV and SSV) are unaccompanied, lie in the superficial fascia, and their varicosity is visible. Deep veins of the lower limb accompany the arteries (read-up). Deep vein thrombosis involves the deep system and poses a risk of pulmonary embolism because the deep veins drain directly into the popliteal, femoral, and iliac veins and thence to the inferior vena cava. Superficial varicosity alone rarely embolises unless thrombosis extends through a perforating vein into the deep system.
questions.question:
Describe the great saphenous vein and small saphenous vein under the following headings, and explain the clinical basis of their use in surgery.
A(i) Origin, course, and termination of the great saphenous vein
A(ii) Tributaries and valves of the great saphenous vein
B(i) Origin, course, and termination of the small saphenous vein
B(ii) Clinical basis: pulse points of the lower limb and sites of venepuncture or cut-down
C(i) Distinguish varicosity from deep vein thrombosis based on the anatomical differences between the superficial and deep venous systems

questions.answerText:
A(i)
A double-domed, thin fibromuscular (musculotendinous) partition between the thoracic and abdominal cavities and the main muscle of respiration; convex superior surface faces the thorax (covered by diaphragmatic pleura, lungs fit the domes, fibrous pericardium on the central tendon), concave inferior surface faces the abdomen (parietal peritoneum; liver, kidneys, suprarenals, stomach, spleen); higher on the right because of the liver (in expiration the right dome reaches the 5th rib, the left the 5th intercostal space); level varies with respiration, posture and abdominal distension, and the domes flatten in maximal inspiration.
A(ii)
Sternal: 2 slips from the posterior xiphoid process; costal: deep surfaces of the lower 6 ribs and costal cartilages (forms the domes); vertebral: the crura and 3 arcuate ligaments - medial (thickened psoas fascia, from the body of L2 to the tip of the L1 transverse process), lateral (thickened quadratus lumborum fascia, from the L1 transverse process to the lower border of the 12th rib) and median (joins the crura across the front of the aorta). Insertion: trefoil central tendon, no bony attachments, partly fused with the fibrous pericardium (pericardiophrenic ligament).
A(iii)
• Caval opening (T8; the only opening in the central tendon): IVC, terminal branches of the right phrenic nerve, a few lymphatics. Oesophageal opening (T10; in the right crus): oesophagus, anterior and posterior vagal trunks, oesophageal branches of the left gastric vessels, a few lymphatics. Aortic opening (T12; lowest and most posterior, between the crura): aorta, thoracic duct, sometimes azygos and hemiazygos veins.
• Smaller openings: greater and lesser splanchnic nerves pierce each crus; hemiazygos vein pierces the left crus; left phrenic nerve pierces the left dome; sympathetic trunks pass behind the diaphragm deep to the medial arcuate ligament; subcostal vessels and nerve pass behind the lateral arcuate ligament; superior epigastric vessels pass between the sternal and costal origins; 7th-11th intercostal neurovascular bundles pass through the costal origin.
A(iv)
Arteries: pericardiophrenic and musculophrenic (from the internal thoracic) and superior phrenic (from the thoracic aorta) to the superior surface; inferior phrenic (first branches of the abdominal aorta) to the inferior surface. Veins: pericardiophrenic and musculophrenic to the internal thoracic vein; superior phrenic vein (right) and right inferior phrenic vein to the IVC; the left inferior phrenic vein drains to the IVC and the left suprarenal vein.
A(v)
• Motor: phrenic nerves (C3-5) only - the right nerve to the right half up to the right margin of the oesophageal opening, the left to the left half. Sensory: central part (with related pleura and peritoneum) via the phrenic nerves; peripheral part via the lower 6 or 7 intercostal and subcostal nerves.
• Lymph: thoracic surface to anterior and posterior diaphragmatic nodes (anterior on to parasternal nodes; posterior to phrenic and posterior mediastinal nodes); abdominal surface to anterior diaphragmatic, phrenic and superior lumbar (caval/aortic) nodes.
B(i)
The central diaphragm is supplied sensorily by the phrenic nerve (C3-5) and the shoulder skin by the supraclavicular nerve (C3,4); so pain from irritation of pleura or pericardium over the central diaphragm, or of the peritoneum under it by subphrenic pus or blood, is referred to the shoulder tip.
B(ii)
Acquired herniae occur in middle-aged people with weak musculature around the oesophageal opening; they are either sliding or paraoesophageal (rolling, alongside the oesophagus).
B(iii)
Hiccup is an involuntary spasmodic contraction of the diaphragm with approximation of the vocal folds and closure of the glottis; common after eating or drinking from gastric irritation of vagus nerve endings; it may be due to pleurisy, peritonitis or pericarditis.
C(i)
• Right crus: larger and longer, arises from the upper 3 lumbar vertebrae (L1-L3) and their intervertebral discs; some of its fibres pass up to the left and loop round the oesophageal orifice as a physiological sphincter preventing reflux of gastric contents.
• Left crus: smaller, arises from the side of the bodies of the upper 2 (L1-L2) lumbar vertebrae and their discs; each crus is attached to the medial and lateral arcuate ligaments, and the medial borders of the two crura unite in front of T12 as the median arcuate ligament over the aorta.

A(ii) Describe its origin (sternal, costal and vertebral, including the crura and arcuate ligaments) and its insertion.
A(iii) Describe its openings, their vertebral levels and the structures transmitted.
A(iv) Describe its blood supply.
A(v) Describe its nerve supply and lymphatic drainage.
B(i) Explain the anatomical basis of referred shoulder pain from irritation of the diaphragm.

A(i) Describe the immunological defence system of the gastrointestinal tract, including: the name of the tissue system; the layers of the GIT wall it occupies; the cell types it contains; and the antibody it produces.
A(ii) Explain the complete mechanism by which IgA protects the lumen of the GIT from pathogens, including the role of the secretory protein and the property that makes IgA effective.
B(i) State which regions of the GIT are lined by stratified squamous epithelium rather than the simple thin vulnerable epithelium lining the rest of the tract, and explain the significance of this difference in the context of microbial defense.
B(ii) Explain the clinical and anatomical basis for the well-known effects of emotional stress on the stomach and other regions of the GIT.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Immunological defense system:
• Name: Mucosa-Associated Lymphoid Tissue (MALT).
• Layers occupied: the mucosa (especially the lamina propria located just below the epithelium) and the submucosal layers.
• Cell types: macrophages and lymphocytes (some of which actively produce antibodies); also free immune cells and lymphoid nodules.
• Antibody produced: mainly immunoglobulin A (IgA).
A(ii)
IgA protection mechanism:
• IgA antibodies undergo transcytosis into the intestinal lumen, bound to the secretory protein produced by epithelial cells.
• This complex (secretory IgA) protects against viral and bacterial pathogens.
• IgA is resistant to proteolytic enzymes and can therefore coexist with the proteases present in the lumen, making it effective even in the enzyme-rich intestinal environment.
B(i)
Stratified squamous epithelium lines the oral cavity, esophagus, and anal canal (not vulnerable simple columnar). The rest of the GIT (except these three regions) is lined by a simple thin vulnerable epithelium. Because the rest of the GIT is lined by this vulnerable epithelium and normally contains thousands of microbial species (including potential pathogens), the MALT provides an essential backup to the thin physical barrier.
B(ii)
The enteric nervous system (submucosal/Meissner and myenteric/Auerbach plexuses) provides an anatomic basis for the well-known actions of emotional stress on the stomach and other regions of the GIT. These plexuses are interconnected with the autonomic nervous system and CNS.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the cell body (soma), types of neurons by structure, and the glial cells of the nervous system under the following headings: cell types, function, and capacity for mitosis.
A(ii) Explain the clinical significance of neurons being amitotic.
B(i) Distinguish between the central nervous system (CNS) and peripheral nervous system (PNS) structurally and functionally.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Cell body (soma): The neuronal cell body has a nucleus with at least one nucleolus and typical cytoplasmic organelles; it lacks centrioles, consistent with the amitotic nature of neurons. Types of neurons by structure: Unipolar (pseudounipolar) neurons — sensory neurons with only a single process or fiber that divides close to the cell body into two main branches (axon and dendrite); the longer branch extends to a peripheral ending and the other toward the CNS. Multipolar neurons — motor neurons and interneurons with numerous cell processes (an axon and many dendrites). Bipolar neurons — spindle-shaped, with a dendrite at one end and an axon at the other; found in the light-sensitive retina of the eye. Anaxonic neurons — have many dendrites but no true axon; do not produce action potentials, but regulate electrical changes of adjacent neurons. Glial cells (neuroglia): Neuroglia is a special type of connective tissue for the nervous system. Glial cells are nonconductive; they provide a support system for neurons; they support, nourish, and protect neurons. They are far more numerous than neurons and, unlike neurons, are capable of mitosis. Types include oligodendrocytes (produce myelin in CNS), Schwann cells and satellite cells (in PNS), and microglia.
A(ii)
Neurons are highly specialized and amitotic: if a neuron is destroyed, it cannot be replaced because neurons do not go through mitosis. This means that neuronal loss (e.g., in injury or disease) is permanent and irreplaceable.
B(i)
CNS consists of the brain and spinal cord; it is covered by three connective tissue layers called meninges (dura, arachnoid, and pia maters); it contains very little collagen or fibrous tissue and is relatively soft, easily damaged by injuries affecting the cranium or vertebral bones. The PNS is composed of nerves and ganglia. Functionally, the CNS is the master control unit while the PNS is the body's link to the outside world. Sensory (afferent) and motor (efferent) are the functional categories.

questions.question:
Describe the gross anatomy of the brachial plexus:
A(i) Formation (roots)
A(ii) Trunks, divisions, cords
A(iii) Five main terminal branches
B. State how injury at each level (trunk/cord) of the plexus relates to a specific clinical pathology.
C. Explain how injury at the level of a trunk or cord spreads to affect distant structures (individual peripheral nerves), causing specific functional deficits.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The brachial plexus is formed by the union of the C5, C6, C7 and C8 ventral rami and the greater part of the 1st thoracic ventral ramus, with contribution sometimes from C4 (giving a "prefixed" plexus) or T2 (giving a "postfixed" plexus); the roots emerge from the transverse processes of the cervical vertebrae, immediately posterior to the vertebral artery, and lie between the scalene muscles.
A(ii)
C5 and C6 unite to form the upper trunk, C7 continues as the middle trunk, and C8 and T1 unite to form the lower trunk, lying in the posterior triangle of the neck; each trunk bifurcates behind the clavicle into an anterior and a posterior division. The anterior divisions of the upper and middle trunks unite to form the lateral cord; the anterior division of the lower trunk continues as the medial cord; the posterior divisions of all three trunks unite to form the posterior cord, lying in the axilla below pectoralis minor.
A(iii)
The five main terminal branches are the musculocutaneous nerve and the lateral root of the median nerve (from the lateral cord), the ulnar nerve and the medial root of the median nerve (from the medial cord), and the axillary and radial nerves (from the posterior cord).
B
• Injury to the upper trunk (C5, C6), at "Erb's point," produces Erb's paralysis, from causes such as birth injury, a fall on the shoulder, or during anaesthesia, affecting the axillary, musculocutaneous and suprascapular nerves.
• Injury to the lower trunk (C8, T1), from causes such as undue abduction of the arm, produces Klumpke's paralysis, with paralysis of the intrinsic hand muscles and ulnar wrist/finger flexors, and possible Horner's syndrome from associated sympathetic fibre injury.
C
• Erb's paralysis paralyses biceps, deltoid, brachialis, brachioradialis, supraspinatus, infraspinatus and supinator, producing the "Policeman's/Porter's tip hand": the arm hangs adducted and medially rotated, the forearm extended and pronated, with loss of abduction/lateral rotation of the shoulder and flexion/supination of the forearm.
• Klumpke's paralysis produces a claw hand from unopposed long flexors/extensors, plus cutaneous anaesthesia along the ulnar border of the limb.
• Injury to the lateral cord (e.g. from dislocation of the humerus) involves the musculocutaneous nerve and the lateral root of the median nerve, paralysing biceps, coracobrachialis and the median-supplied forearm muscles, producing a midprone forearm with loss of elbow and wrist flexion and sensory loss on the radial side of the forearm.
• Injury to the medial cord (e.g. from subcoracoid dislocation of the humerus) involves the ulnar nerve and the medial root of the median nerve, producing claw hand with sensory loss on the ulnar side of the forearm and hand.
• Injury to the posterior cord involves the upper and lower subscapular nerves, the thoracodorsal nerve, the axillary nerve, and the radial nerve (the largest and most frequently injured branch of the plexus).
• This weakens elbow, wrist and metacarpophalangeal joint extension via the radial nerve, and shoulder abduction via the axillary nerve.
• In this way, a single lesion at the level of a trunk or cord of the brachial plexus spreads its effect along the several peripheral nerves derived from it, each producing its own characteristic and distant functional deficit in the arm, forearm or hand.

A(i)
The space between two ribs; with 12 ribs on each side there are 11 intercostal spaces; each space contains intercostal muscles, the intercostal neurovascular bundle and lymphatics.
A(ii)
• Three muscles (external, internal, innermost; transversus thoracis, subcostalis and levator costarum are also listed), supplied by the corresponding intercostal nerves, that pull the ribs nearer to each other and strengthen the space. External intercostal: most superficial, fibres downward and forward, origin lower border of the rib above, insertion upper border of the rib below, from the rib tubercle behind to the costochondral junction in front, replaced anteriorly by the anterior intercostal membrane.
• Internal intercostal: intermediate layer, fibres downward and backward, origin subcostal groove of the rib above, insertion upper border of the rib below, from the sternum in front to the angle of the rib behind, replaced posteriorly by the posterior intercostal membrane.
A(iii)
Innermost intercostal: deepest, incomplete layer divided into 3 portions, its fibres cross more than one space; related externally to the intercostal nerve and vessels and internally to the endothoracic fascia. Endothoracic fascia: extrapleural fascia lining the chest wall between the muscles and bones and the parietal pleura, extending over the pleural apex as the suprapleural membrane and forming a thin layer between diaphragm and pleura.
A(iv)
The neurovascular bundle lies between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles, high in the space in relation to the subcostal groove of the rib above; strict order from above downwards: vein, artery, nerve (VAN); because the innermost layer is incomplete it is generally covered on the inside by endothoracic fascia.
A(v)
Each space has a single posterior and 2 anterior intercostal arteries, giving branches to muscles, skin, parietal pleura and breast. Posterior: upper 2 spaces from the superior intercostal artery (costocervical trunk of the subclavian artery), lower 9 spaces from the thoracic aorta. Anterior: upper 6 spaces from the internal thoracic artery, lower 5 from the musculophrenic artery; they anastomose with the posterior arteries.
A(vi)
Veins accompany the arteries and nerves (11 posterior intercostal and 1 subcostal vein); valves direct blood posteriorly. Right side: 1st space to the brachiocephalic vein, the rest to the azygos vein. Left side: upper 3 spaces to the left brachiocephalic vein, the rest to the hemiazygos and accessory hemiazygos veins, which drain to the azygos vein. Anterior veins: upper 6 spaces to the internal thoracic vein, lower 5 to the musculophrenic vein.
A(vii)
12 pairs, the anterior primary rami of the thoracic spinal nerves and mixed nerves; nerves 1-6 are distributed in the intercostal spaces, 7-11 supply the anterior abdominal wall, and the 12th runs forward in the abdomen as the subcostal nerve; they supply skin, muscles of the space and abdomen, parietal pleura and parietal peritoneum. Branches: rami communicantes, collateral (muscular), lateral cutaneous, anterior cutaneous, pleural and peritoneal (7th-11th).
A(viii)
Deep lymphatics follow the arteries: anteriorly they drain into the anterior intercostal (parasternal) nodes along the internal thoracic artery; posteriorly they drain into the posterior intercostal nodes in the posterior mediastinum.
B(i)
• A needle or drain is passed immediately above the upper border of the rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle (vein, artery, nerve from above downwards) running under the rib above in the subcostal groove.
• Intercostal spaces are access points for surgical procedures (e.g. resection of part of the lung), for percussion and auscultation of the heart and lung, and for sampling pleural fluid or draining pus or blood from the pleural cavity; disease in the thorax may cause pain in the anterior abdominal wall because the intercostal nerves supply both the thoracic and abdominal wall and the parietal pleura.
C(i)
Typical nerves are T3-6. T1 is atypical: no anterior cutaneous branch, joined to the brachial plexus by a large branch corresponding to the lateral cutaneous branch. T2 is atypical: its lateral cutaneous branch is the intercostobrachial nerve, which joins the medial cutaneous nerve of the arm through the brachial plexus.

A(ii) Describe the intercostal muscles, including the fibre direction, attachments and extent of the external and internal intercostals.
A(iii) Describe the innermost intercostal muscle and the endothoracic fascia.
A(iv) Describe the intercostal neurovascular bundle and the order of its components.
