questions.answerText:
(i)
• The spleen is an ovoid, highly vascular, reddish-purple organ, on average about 12 cm long, 7 cm broad, 3 cm thick and weighing about 150 g, related to the 9th to 11th ribs on the left side.
• It has two ends, an expanded anterior end and a rounded posterior end resting on the upper pole of the left kidney, three borders (superior, inferior and intermediate), and two surfaces (diaphragmatic and visceral).
• The diaphragmatic surface is convex and related to the diaphragm, left lung and pleura, and the 9th-11th ribs; the visceral surface is concave and bears gastric, renal, colic and pancreatic impressions.
• The hilum lies on the inferomedial part of the gastric impression and transmits the splenic vessels and nerves, giving attachment to the gastrosplenic and splenorenal ligaments; the phrenicocolic ligament supports, but is not attached to, the anterior end of the spleen.
(ii)
• The gastric impression, related to the fundus of the stomach, is the largest impression; the renal impression relates to the left kidney and sometimes the suprarenal gland; the colic impression relates to the splenic flexure of the colon; the pancreatic impression relates to the tail of the pancreas.
• The gastrosplenic ligament contains the short gastric vessels supplying the stomach, and the splenorenal ligament contains the tail of the pancreas and splenic vessels, so disease or surgery at the spleen can affect the stomach, kidney, colon or pancreas through these relations.
(iii)
• Although protected by the 9th to 12th ribs, the spleen is the most frequently injured organ in the abdomen.
• Severe blows to the left side may fracture ribs, producing sharp fragments that lacerate the spleen, and blunt trauma elsewhere that raises intra-abdominal pressure can also rupture it because its capsule is thin and the pulp soft.
• If ruptured, the spleen bleeds profusely because it is a highly vascular organ receiving the splenic artery, the largest branch of the coeliac trunk.
• This produces severe intraperitoneal haemorrhage and shock, a systemic and distant functional deficit in circulation arising from a local splenic injury.
• Repair of a ruptured spleen is difficult, so splenectomy or subtotal splenectomy is often performed to prevent the patient from bleeding to death.
• Even after total splenectomy, most splenic functions are assumed by other reticuloendothelial organs such as the liver and bone marrow, though susceptibility to certain bacterial infections increases.
questions.question:
(i) Describe the gross anatomy of the spleen - measurements, external features (ends, borders, surfaces, hilum) and peritoneal ligaments.
(ii) Relate the surfaces/impressions of the spleen to organs it may affect in disease.
(iii) Explain why splenic rupture produces a distant, life-threatening functional deficit.

A(i) Describe the three named regions of the male urethra, giving the length and relations of each.
A(ii) Describe the two urethral sphincters — their type of muscle, location, and the mechanism by which each controls urinary continence.
B(i) Describe the female urethra, including its length, relations, and the location of its external orifice.
B(ii) State the layers visible in the structure of the urinary bladder wall.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Three regions of the male urethra:
• Prostatic urethra (2.5 cm): located within the prostate.
• Intermediate part of the urethra (membranous urethra) (2 cm): passes through the urogenital diaphragm from the prostate to the beginning of the penis.
• Spongy urethra (15 cm): passes through the penis and opens via the external urethral orifice.
• The male urethra carries both semen and urine.
A(ii)
Two sphincters:
• Internal urethral sphincter: involuntary (smooth muscle) at the bladder-urethra junction; contracts to open (its contraction, paradoxically, opens the sphincter as described — 'contracts to open').
• External urethral sphincter: voluntary (skeletal muscle) surrounding the urethra as it passes through the pelvic floor.
B(i)
Female urethra:
• Length: 3–4 cm.
• Relations: tightly bound to the anterior vaginal wall.
• External urethral orifice: anterior to the vaginal opening and posterior to the clitoris.
B(ii)
Layers of the urinary bladder wall:
• Peritoneum, rugae, detrusor (muscle), adventitia, ureteric orifices, trigone of bladder, bladder neck, internal urethral sphincter.

questions.question:
Describe the gross anatomy of the clavicle:
A(i) Shape and articulations
A(ii) Surface features
A(iii) Functions
B. State how a particular part of the clavicle relates to a common fracture pattern.
C. Explain how injury at this region may involve a distant structure, causing a functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The clavicle forms the anterior portion of the shoulder girdle; it is curved like the italic letter "f" and lies nearly horizontally at the upper and anterior part of the thorax, immediately above the first rib. It articulates medially with the manubrium sterni and laterally with the acromion of the scapula.
A(ii)
The upper surface is flat, rough, and marked by impressions for the attachment of deltoid in front and trapezius behind; the bone has no medullary cavity.
A(iii)
Its functions are to transmit forces from the upper limb to the axial skeleton, to act as a strut holding the arm free from the trunk (supported principally by trapezius), and to provide attachment for muscles.
B
• The weakest point along the clavicle is the junction of the middle and outer thirds.
• Transmission of forces to the axial skeleton in falls on the shoulder or hand may exceed the strength of the bone at this site, and this indirect force commonly results in fracture there.
• Clavicle fracture is caused by landing on the hand from a fall with the arm rigidly outstretched, or by a direct blow.
C
• The clavicle has important deep relations that make it clinically significant beyond the bone itself.
• The third parts of the subclavian vessels and the trunks of the brachial plexus pass behind the medial third of the shaft of the clavicle, separated only by the thin subclavius muscle.
• At the sternal end, behind the sternoclavicular joints, lie the common carotid artery on the left and the bifurcation of the brachiocephalic artery on the right, with the internal jugular vein lying a little more laterally; these vessels are separated from the bone only by the strap muscles (sternohyoid and sternothyroid).
• Because these major vessels and the brachial plexus trunks lie in such close proximity to the clavicle, deep or displaced injury involving the bone can threaten them.
• Compromise of the subclavian vessels can produce vascular insufficiency of the upper limb, while injury to the brachial plexus trunks passing behind the medial clavicle can produce motor and sensory deficits in the limb.
• This illustrates how a skeletal injury at the clavicle can spread to affect distant neurovascular structures, producing a functional deficit beyond the fracture site itself.

questions.question:
(i) Describe the gross anatomy of the heart under the headings: chambers, borders and surfaces.
(ii) Relate the chambers/valves of the heart to a recognised pathology.
(iii) Explain how a cardiac problem can produce a functional deficit or sensation felt at a distant site.
questions.answerText:
(i)
• The heart has four chambers, the right and left atria (receiving chambers) and the right and left ventricles (discharging chambers), enclosed in the double-walled pericardial sac, and rests on its diaphragmatic (inferior) surface.
• It has an apex, formed by the inferolateral part of the left ventricle and lying posterior to the 5th intercostal space where the apex beat is felt, a base, formed mainly by the left atrium and part of the right atrium, four borders and three surfaces.
• The right border is formed mainly by the right atrium; the left border by the left ventricle and left auricle; the inferior border by the right ventricle mainly and the left ventricle; the superior border by both atria, auricles and the great vessels.
• The anterior (sternocostal) surface consists chiefly of the right ventricle; the inferior (diaphragmatic) surface consists chiefly of the left ventricle and a small part of the right ventricle; the left (pulmonary) surface is formed mainly by the left ventricle.
• The right atrium receives venous blood from the SVC, IVC and coronary sinus, has a smooth sinus venarum and a rough muscular wall with pectinate muscles, and communicates with the right ventricle via the right atrioventricular (tricuspid) orifice.
• The left atrium receives the four pulmonary veins and communicates with the left ventricle via the left atrioventricular (mitral) orifice; the right ventricle has a tricuspid valve and leads to the pulmonary trunk via the conus arteriosus, while the left ventricle, with twice the wall thickness, has the mitral valve and leads to the aorta via the aortic vestibule and aortic valve.
(ii)
• Valvular insufficiency results from valve leaflets not completely sealing when a valve is closed, so regurgitation of blood occurs into the proximal chamber, generating a characteristic heart murmur.
• Positional and septal anomalies include dextrocardia, atrial septal defects and ventricular septal defects.
• Aortic dissection, a tear in the inner wall of the aorta associated with high blood pressure, and aortic aneurysm, dilation of an artery greater than 50% of its normal diameter, are pathologies of the great vessel arising from the left ventricle.
(iii)
• The conducting system, the SA node in the posterior wall of the right atrium, the AV node in the floor of the right atrium, the AV bundle and Purkinje fibres, initiates and coordinates the heartbeat; damage to a coronary artery supplying these nodes can disturb heart rhythm.
• Cardiac afferent fibres carrying pain from ischaemic myocardium travel via sympathetic afferents in the cardiac plexus to spinal cord segments T1-T5 shared with dermatomes of the chest wall and upper limb, so the central nervous system perceives cardiac pain as coming from the body wall.
• This explains why myocardial ischaemia is felt as pain in the mid or left chest that radiates to the left jaw and left arm, a distant somatic sensation produced by a cardiac (visceral) problem.

A
The lingual nerve is a branch of the mandibular nerve (CN V3). It provides sensory supply to the mucous membrane of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. In its course, the submandibular duct (Wharton's duct) runs forwards on hyoglossus, between the lingual and hypoglossal nerves.
B
At the anterior border of hyoglossus, the submandibular duct is crossed by the lingual nerve; this crossing relationship is anatomically relevant, since a stone in the submandibular duct can be felt bimanually in the floor of the mouth, and surgery/removal in this region places the lingual nerve at risk, along with the hypoglossal nerve, given their close relationship to the duct on hyoglossus.
C
Sensory supply to the mucous membrane of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is via the lingual nerve (a branch of CN V3), while special (taste) sensory supply to the same region is via the chorda tympani nerve (a branch of CN VII); injury to the lingual nerve would therefore be expected to impair general sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, distinct from a taste deficit, which would instead follow injury to the chorda tympani.
questions.question:
A. Describe the course and distribution of the lingual nerve, including its relationship to the submandibular duct.
B. State the site at which the lingual nerve crosses the submandibular duct, which is relevant to procedures in this region.
C. Explain the functional deficit that would be anticipated from injury to the lingual nerve, based on the sensory territory it supplies.

A(i) Describe the origin, structural components, and classification of neurons under the following headings: cell body (soma), dendrites, axon, myelin sheath, nodes of Ranvier, and neurilemma.
A(ii) State the basis of why local anaesthetics block nerve impulse transmission.
B(i) Explain the anatomical basis of why nerve fibers within the CNS do not regenerate after injury, while peripheral nerve fibers may regenerate.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Cell body (soma): The neuronal cell body is similar to other cell types; it has a nucleus with at least one nucleolus and many typical cytoplasmic organelles. It lacks centrioles, which is consistent with the amitotic nature of neurons. Dendrites: Dendrites are cytoplasmic extensions that project from the cell body; they are usually short and branching, increasing their surface area to receive signals from other neurons. The number of dendrites varies. They are called afferent processes because they transmit impulses to the neuron cell body. Axon: There is only one axon projecting from each cell body; it is usually elongated and carries impulses away from the cell body, so it is called an efferent process. Axons may have infrequent branches called axon collaterals; these terminate in short branches or telodendria, whose distal ends are slightly enlarged to form synaptic bulbs. Myelin sheath: Many axons are surrounded by a segmented, white, fatty substance called myelin or myelin sheath. Myelinated fibers make up the white matter in the CNS, while cell bodies and unmyelinated fibers make the gray matter. Nodes of Ranvier: The unmyelinated regions between myelin segments are called nodes of Ranvier. Neurilemma: In the peripheral nervous system, myelin is produced by Schwann cells. The cytoplasm, nucleus, and outer cell membrane of the Schwann cell form a tight covering around the myelin and around the axon at the nodes of Ranvier — this covering is the neurilemma, which plays an important role in regeneration of nerve fibers.
A(ii)
Most local anesthetics are low-molecular-weight molecules that bind to the voltage-gated sodium channels of the axolemma, interfering with sodium ion influx and, consequently, inhibiting the action potential responsible for the nerve impulse.
B(i)
In the CNS, oligodendrocytes produce myelin, but there is no neurilemma. It is the neurilemma that plays an important role in regeneration of nerve fibers; therefore fibers within the CNS do not regenerate because they lack neurilemma.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the cell cycle under the following headings: definition, phases (G1, S, G2, M), and the two key regulatory molecules that control progression through the cycle.
A(ii) Explain the clinical consequences of errors in mitosis, naming three chromosomal abnormalities that can result.
B(i) Distinguish between apoptosis and necrosis, giving the distinguishing morphological changes and clinical consequences of each.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Definition: The cell cycle, or cell-division cycle, is the series of events that takes place in a cell leading to its division and duplication (replication). In cells with a nucleus (eukaryotes), the cell cycle can be divided into two brief periods: interphase (during which the cell grows, accumulates nutrients needed for mitosis and duplicates its DNA) and the mitosis (M) phase (during which the cell splits itself into two distinct cells, often called daughter cells). Phases: G1 (Gap 1) — cell grows; S phase (synthesis) — chromosomes are replicated; G2 (Gap 2) — cell grows more and prepares for mitosis; M phase (mitosis and cytokinesis) — cell division. Cells that have temporarily or reversibly stopped dividing are said to have entered the G0 phase (quiescence). Two key regulatory molecules: cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs), which determine a cell's progress through the cell cycle.
A(ii)
In non-disjunction, a chromosome may fail to separate during anaphase: one daughter cell will receive both sister chromosomes (leading to trisomy — three copies) and the other will receive none (leading to monosomy — one copy). These cells are considered aneuploid, a condition often associated with cancer. Other chromosomal abnormalities: deletion — an arm of the chromosome may be broken and the fragment lost. Translocation — the fragment incorrectly reattaches to another, non-homologous chromosome. Inversion — the fragment reattaches to the original chromosome in reverse orientation. The effect may range from no noticeable effect to cancer induction or organism death.
B(i)
Apoptosis (programmed cell death): biochemical events lead to characteristic cell changes including blebbing, loss of cell membrane asymmetry and attachment, cell shrinkage, nuclear fragmentation, chromatin condensation, and chromosomal DNA fragmentation. Apoptosis differs from necrosis in that the cellular debris does not damage the organism. Necrosis: a form of traumatic cell death that results from acute cellular injury; cellular debris can damage the organism. Clinical consequences: excessive apoptosis causes atrophy (e.g., ischemic damage); insufficient apoptosis results in uncontrolled cell proliferation such as cancer.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the origin, types, and functions of cells found in connective tissue under the following headings: cells of fixed (resident) population and cells of wandering (transient) population.
A(ii) State where the mesenchymal stem-like cells persist in adults and state their clinical significance.
B(i) Explain the anatomical and histological basis of why connective tissue of the head region differs in embryological origin from the rest of the body, and state the clinical implication.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Fixed (resident) cells: Mesenchyme cells — embryonic source of all connective tissue cells; only found in embryos, but some mesenchyme-like cells persist in adult connective tissue. Fibroblasts — most common cell type in connective tissue; elongated, spindle-shaped cells with many cell processes; have oval, pale-staining, regular nuclei with prominent nucleoli; abundant rough endoplasmic reticulum and active Golgi bodies; synthesize collagen, reticular and elastic fibers, and amorphous extracellular substance. Fibrocytes — quiescent fibroblasts; smaller, darker nucleus; less rough ER. Chondroblasts/osteoblasts — synthesize cartilage and bone matrices. Adipocytes — energy storage, thermal insulation. Wandering (transient) cells: Macrophages — ingestion by phagocytosis; antigen presentation; secretion of enzymes and cytokines; long-lived (several months); originate from monocytes in bone marrow. Plasma cells — defense and immune function. Lymphocytes — immune function. Neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils — immune function. Mast cells — immune function. All connective tissue cells are derived from mesenchymal cells.
A(ii)
Mesenchyme-like cells (pericytes) persist in adult connective tissue, including that of tooth pulp and some adipose tissue. These mesenchyme-like cells retain their capacity to differentiate into other connective tissue cells in response to injury (e.g., pericytes — perivascular cells of blood capillaries). They are being investigated as possible sources of stem cells for therapeutic repair and organ regeneration. Some multipotent stem cells potentially useful in regenerative medicine after grafting to replace damaged tissue in certain patients.
B(i)
All connective tissue cells are derived from mesenchymal cells; mesenchyme cells are for the most part derived from the mesoderm. However, several of the connective tissues of the head region are derived from the neural crest cells (ectodermal origin). Endothelial cells lining blood vessels are derived from mesenchyme. The clinical implication is that connective tissue tumors or developmental disorders in the head may follow patterns distinct from those in the rest of the body due to this different embryological derivation.

A(i)
Three parts of the renal tubule:
• Proximal convoluted tubule (PCT): cuboidal cells with dense microvilli (brush border — increase surface area); large mitochondria; functions in reabsorption and secretion; confined to the cortex.
• Nephron loop: descending and ascending limbs; distal descending limb = descending thin limb — simple squamous epithelium; thick ascending limb — cuboidal to columnar cells (thin in some nephrons).
• Distal convoluted tubule (DCT): cuboidal cells with very few microvilli; functions more in secretion than reabsorption; confined to the cortex.
A(ii)
Nephron loop:
• Descending limb: proximal descending limb is continuous with the proximal tubule; distal descending limb (thin limb) is lined by simple squamous epithelium.
• Thick ascending limb: cuboidal to columnar cells; may be thin in some nephrons.
B(i)
Renal corpuscle:
• Two components: glomerulus and glomerular (Bowman's) capsule.
• Glomerulus: tuft of capillaries with fenestrated endothelium (highly porous) allowing filtrate formation.
Glomerular capsule: cup-shaped, hollow structure surrounding the glomerulus; has two layers:
• Parietal layer: simple squamous epithelium.
• Visceral layer: branching epithelial podocytes; extensions terminate in foot processes that cling to the basement membrane; filtration slits between foot processes allow filtrate to pass into the capsular space.
B(ii)
Structural adaptations of the PCT:
• Dense microvilli (brush border) greatly increase the apical surface area for reabsorption.
• Large mitochondria provide energy (ATP) for active transport processes.
• Highly infolded basolateral membrane increases surface area for solute exchange at the basolateral side.
• These features together support the PCT's role in reabsorption and secretion.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the three parts of the renal tubule, including the cell type lining each part, distinguishing microscopic features, and the primary function (reabsorption vs. secretion) attributed to each part.
A(ii) Describe the two parts of the nephron loop, including the type of epithelium lining each limb and any variation across nephron types.
B(i) Describe the renal corpuscle, naming its two components, the two layers of the glomerular capsule, and the specialised features of the visceral layer.
B(ii) For the proximal convoluted tubule, explain how its structure is adapted for its function.

A(i) State the origin of the posterior intercostal arteries.
A(ii) Describe their course and relations in the intercostal space.
A(iii) State their branches, distribution and venous and lymphatic companions.
B(i) State the safe site and the danger site for passing a needle or drain through an intercostal space and the anatomical basis.
C(i) Explain the anatomical basis of the rib deformity seen on radiographs in coarctation of the aorta.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Each intercostal space has a single posterior and two anterior intercostal arteries.
• In the upper two spaces the posterior intercostal arteries arise from the superior intercostal artery (branch of the costocervical trunk of the subclavian artery); in the lower nine spaces they arise from the thoracic aorta (9 pairs, plus 1 pair of subcostal arteries from the posterior surface of the descending thoracic aorta).
A(ii)
Course and branching follow the intercostal nerves: each artery runs forward in the subcostal groove, high in the space between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles, in the order vein, artery, nerve from above downwards, and anastomoses with the anterior intercostal artery.
A(iii)
• Branches go to adjacent muscles, skin, parietal pleura, spinal cord and breast (branches in the 3rd and 4th spaces supply the breast); the 3rd right posterior intercostal artery gives the right bronchial artery.
• Distribution: the posterior and lateral parts of the intercostal spaces.
• Veins accompany the arteries and contain valves that direct blood posteriorly; on the right the 1st space drains to the brachiocephalic vein and the rest to the azygos vein; on the left the upper 3 spaces drain to the left brachiocephalic vein and the rest to the hemiazygos and accessory hemiazygos veins, which drain to the azygos vein.
• Lymphatics: deep lymphatics follow the arteries; posteriorly they drain to the posterior intercostal nodes in the posterior mediastinum.
B(i)
• Safe site: a needle or drain is passed immediately above the upper border of a rib; it is dangerous to pass it immediately below a rib.
• Basis: the intercostal vessels lie immediately below their corresponding ribs (vein above artery) in the subcostal groove, so a needle just above the lower rib avoids the neurovascular bundle; in thoracotomy the periosteum over a segment of the 5th or 6th rib is elevated, protecting the bundle.
C(i)
• In coarctation of the aorta the intercostal arteries derived from the aorta receive blood from the superior intercostals, from the anterior intercostal branches of the internal thoracic artery and from arteries anastomosing around the scapula.
• Together with the communication between the internal thoracic and inferior epigastric arteries, these are the principal collaterals between the aorta above and below the block.
• The intercostal arteries dilate and become tortuous and erode the lower borders of the corresponding ribs, giving the characteristic irregular notching of the ribs that helps radiographic confirmation.

A(i)
Three tunics: The eye has three layers. Outer tunic: the sclera and cornea; the sclera serves primarily as a structural support for the optic apparatus. Middle layer (vascular layer, uvea): the choroid, ciliary body, and iris. The iris functions as a contractile diaphragm (the aperture of the eye). Inner tunic: the retina — a double-layered epithelium consisting of an outer pigmented layer and an inner neural retina; it is subdivided into 10 recognizable layers. The outermost layer (closest to the choriocapillaris) contains the photoreceptors whose outer segments are in close contact with pigmented epithelial cells. Contents: the vitreous body fills the space between the lens and retina; the aqueous humor is in the anterior and posterior chambers; the lens is a transparent biconvex structure that, along with the cornea, focuses light on the retina. Photoreceptors: rods — more sensitive to light, primarily used in dim light. Cones — require more intense lighting; conical in shape. There are also bipolar cells, horizontal cells, amacrine cells, and Müller glia cells, and a retinal ganglion cell layer.
A(ii)
Cataract: when the lens becomes opaque, the condition is termed cataract, which may also be caused by excessive exposure to ultraviolet radiation. Histological changes: the lens has three principal components — lens capsule (corresponds to a thick, elastic basal lamina), subcapsular epithelium, and lens fibers. Opacification of the lens fibers makes them less transparent; this is the basis of cataract. A myopic (short-sighted) eye can be corrected by wearing glasses with concave lenses; a hyperopic eye with convex lenses.
B(i)
Retinal pigment epithelium (RPE): the outer cell layer is pigmented; it lies between the choroid and the neural retina; Bruch's membrane is located between the choroid and the RPE. Tight junctions between RPE cells establish a blood-retina barrier. Neural retina: the inner cell layer; it is a multi-layered structure containing photoreceptors (rods and cones), neurons, and glial cells. The optic nerve (and the retina) arises in the embryo as an outgrowth of the diencephalon (forebrain); thus the optic nerve is not a true peripheral nerve — its myelin is produced by oligodendrocytes (not Schwann cells), and it is associated with multiple sclerosis.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the histology of the eye under the following headings: three tunics (layers) of the eyeball, contents of each layer, and the photoreceptor cell types in the retina.
A(ii) Explain the clinical basis of cataract and state the histological changes in the lens.
B(i) Distinguish between the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and the neural retina, stating the function of each and their embryological origin.

Describe the cubital fossa:
A(i) Location and shape
A(ii) Boundaries (base, medial wall, lateral wall, apex, floor, roof)
A(iii) Contents
B. Explain the clinical basis for distinguishing the true "contents" of the cubital fossa from structures that are merely superficial to it.
C. Distinguish the position of the radial nerve in relation to the cubital fossa from that of the median nerve and brachial artery.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The cubital fossa is a triangular space, a shallow depression on the anterior surface of the elbow region, located anterior to the elbow joint, formed between two forearm muscles (brachioradialis and pronator teres).
A(ii)
Boundaries: base (superior) — an imaginary horizontal line connecting the medial and lateral epicondyles; medial (ulnar) wall — lateral border of pronator teres; lateral (radial) wall — medial border of brachioradialis; apex — directed inferiorly, where the medial and lateral boundaries meet; floor — brachialis and supinator; roof — continuity of brachial and antebrachial (deep) fascia, reinforced by the bicipital aponeurosis, superficial fascia and skin.
A(iii)
The major contents, from medial to lateral, are the median nerve, the brachial artery (which bifurcates near the apex into the radial and ulnar arteries), deep accompanying veins of the arteries, and the tendon of biceps brachii.
B
• The median cubital vein, cephalic vein and basilic vein are present in the area but are usually considered superficial to the cubital fossa and not part of its contents.
• During blood pressure measurement the stethoscope is placed over the brachial artery in the cubital fossa, and the fossa is also used to palpate the brachial pulse.
• The area just superficial to the cubital fossa is often used for venous access (phlebotomy), since it is superficial and accessible.
• The bicipital aponeurosis forms the roof of the fossa and was historically called the "grace of God" tendon because it protected the brachial artery and median nerve during blood-letting.
C
• The radial nerve is in the vicinity of the cubital fossa, located between brachialis and brachioradialis, but is often, though not always, considered part of the cubital fossa's contents.
• This differs from the median nerve and brachial artery, which are consistently listed as major contents of the fossa.
• The superficial veins similarly lie in the roof/superficial region and are related to, rather than contained within, the fossa proper.
• Venipuncture therefore uses the superficial veins overlying the fossa, while palpation of the brachial pulse and auscultation for blood pressure use the deeper true content, the brachial artery.
• This distinction between superficial and deep structures is the basis for choosing the correct site for a given clinical procedure at the elbow.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the basic architectural components of the liver, including the capsule, parenchyma, and the spaces between liver cells.
A(ii) There are three different ways to represent the microscopic organisation of the liver parenchyma. Name and describe each model, stating the geometric shape used and the central and peripheral reference points for each.
B(i) Describe the three zones of the hepatic acinus (acinus of Rappaport), stating what distinguishes each zone.
B(ii) Describe the complete pathway of bile flow from bile canaliculi to the duodenum.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Basic architecture:
• Capsule: the outer surface of the liver is composed of a fibrous/connective tissue capsule (Glisson's capsule); the outermost surface is covered by a thin layer of mesothelial cells that arise from the peritoneum.
• Parenchyma: the capsule surrounds the liver parenchyma, composed of hepatocytes — large polygonal cells with eosinophilic (pink) cytoplasm, round nuclei, and prominent nucleoli.
• Bile canaliculi: spaces present between the plasma membranes of adjacent liver cells.
• Perisinusoidal space of Disse: separates the surface of the liver cell from the endothelial lining of the sinusoid.
A(ii)
Three models:
• Classic (hepatic) lobule: based on blood flow; organised as hexagons, with the central vein (CV) in the centre and portal tracts (PTs) at the periphery (corners of the hexagon). Each PT consists of hepatic artery (HA), portal vein (PV), and bile duct (BD).
• Portal lobule: based on bile flow; organised as triangles, with a portal tract at the centre and central veins at the periphery (corners of the triangle). Flow of bile is in the opposite direction to blood flow.
• Hepatic acinus (acinus of Rappaport): based on blood perfusion; organised as a diamond, with portal tracts at the corners of the short axis and central veins at the corners of the long axis.
B(i)
Zones of the hepatic acinus:
• Zone 1: receives the most oxygenated blood and nutrients.
• Zone 2: intermediate oxygenation and nutrient supply.
• Zone 3: receives the least oxygenated blood and nutrients.
B(ii)
Bile flow pathway:
• Bile canaliculi → Canals of Hering → Bile ductules → Interlobular bile ducts → Intrahepatic ducts → Right and left hepatic ducts → Common hepatic duct → joins with cystic duct to form the common bile duct → Duodenum.

questions.question:
A. Describe the gross anatomy of the pterygopalatine fossa under the following headings: description/location, boundaries, and contents.
B. State the communications of the pterygopalatine fossa and relate these to how disease may spread from this region.
C. Explain why disease or infection arising near the pterygopalatine fossa can spread to distant structures such as the orbit, the nasal cavity, the middle cranial fossa or the pharynx, and the functional deficit that could result.
questions.answerText:
A
The pterygopalatine fossa is an inverted pyramidal-shaped, fat-filled space located on the lateral side of the skull, between the infratemporal fossa and the nasopharynx; it is antero-posteriorly between the maxilla/palatine bone and the pterygoid process, and laterally between the infratemporal fossa and nasopharynx. Its boundaries are: anterior - posterior surface of maxilla below the floor of the orbit; posterior - lateral pterygoid plate and part of the medial plate; medial - perpendicular plate of the palatine bone; lateral - pterygomaxillary fissure; superior - undersurface of the greater wing of the sphenoid; inferior - absent (the posterior wall meets the anterior wall, and between them is the greater palatine canal). Its contents are the terminal (third/pterygoid) part of the maxillary artery and the initial parts of its branches, the maxillary vein, the maxillary nerve, and the pterygopalatine ganglion (a parasympathetic ganglion, one of four parasympathetic ganglia of the head and neck, the others being the submandibular, otic and ciliary ganglia).
B
The pterygopalatine fossa is described as a major neurovascular crossroad between the orbit, the nasal cavity, the nasopharynx, the oral cavity, the infratemporal fossa and the cranial fossa. Its communications are: laterally with the infratemporal fossa through the pterygomaxillary fissure; medially with the nasal cavity through the sphenopalatine foramen; anterosuperiorly with the orbit through the inferior orbital fissure; posterosuperiorly with the middle cranial fossa through the foramen rotundum and pterygoid canal; with the palate through the greater and lesser palatine canals and foramina; and with the pharynx through the pterygoid canal and palatovaginal canal - in general, vascular structures enter the fossa through its lateral wall, while nerve structures enter through its posterior wall.
C
Because the pterygopalatine fossa communicates directly with the orbit (via the inferior orbital fissure), the nasal cavity (via the sphenopalatine foramen), the middle cranial fossa (via the foramen rotundum and pterygoid canal), and the pharynx (via the pterygoid canal and palatovaginal canal), disease or infection arising in or near the fossa has multiple direct anatomical routes by which it can spread to these distant sites; clinical correlates noted for this region include hay fever affecting the ganglion here (the pterygopalatine ganglion is also known as the hay fever ganglion), and maxillary nerve block is performed in relation to this fossa.

A(i)
The deep cervical fascia consists of areolar tissue that supports the muscles, vessels and viscera of the neck; it is condensed to form well-defined fibrous sheets, labelled as: (1) the investing layer (superficial), (2) the pretracheal fascia, (3) the prevertebral fascia, (4) the carotid sheath, and (5) the axillary fascia. More generally, deep fascia is the membranous investment of structures deep to the superficial fascia, containing cells (fibroblasts), fibres (collagen, elastic) and matrix; being subjected to tensile strains, the collagen forms parallel fibre bundles, with the cells flattened. Deep fascia is best marked in the limbs and neck, where it is wrapped around the muscles, veins and nerves like a bandage, the fibres being mainly circularly arranged; around the thorax and abdomen, which require to expand and contract, there is merely a film of areolar tissue but no true deep fascia.
A(ii)
The pretracheal fascia is found only in the anterior region; superiorly it is attached to the thyroid and cricoid cartilage, and inferiorly it extends into the thorax to blend with the fibrous pericardium; laterally it blends with the carotid sheath and with the investing layer of the deep cervical fascia beneath sternocleidomastoid. The prevertebral fascia is attached superiorly to the base of the skull, and inferiorly enters the thorax and blends with the anterior longitudinal ligament of the vertebral column; it covers the prevertebral muscles (longus capitis and longus cervicis), passes round the neck, attaches to the ligamentum nuchae, and in the posterior triangle forms the fascial floor, covering the muscles scalenus anterior, scalenus medius, scalenus posterior, levator scapulae and splenius capitis.
B
Penetration of the fascia during instrumentation of the pretracheal fascia can lead to collection of infectious substances (pus) in the retropharyngeal space (the space between the pharynx and the prevertebral fascia); whiplash injury of the neck can cause quadriplegia, stabbing injury of the neck can cause vascular/nervous injury, and a tumour blocking the airway may necessitate insertion of a tracheostomy tube. The deep cervical fascia will necessarily be pierced during tracheostomy.
C
The pretracheal fascia surrounds the thyroid gland completely, forming a sheath for it, binds the thyroid gland to the larynx, encloses the parathyroid gland, invests the infrahyoid muscles, and encloses the visceral components of the neck (larynx and trachea, pharynx and oesophagus, and the thyroid and parathyroid glands). The prevertebral fascia, in contrast, surrounds the vertebral column and its associated muscles, extending from the base of the skull to approximately the T3 vertebra, and extends laterally as the axillary sheaths.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the deep cervical fascia under the following headings: composition, and the named fibrous sheets into which it is condensed.
A(ii) Describe the attachments of the pretracheal fascia and the prevertebral fascia.
B. Explain the clinical basis for why infection can spread within specific fascial planes/spaces of the neck.
C. Distinguish between the pretracheal fascia and the prevertebral fascia in terms of what each surrounds/encloses.

A. Describe the course, relations and branches of the facial nerve within the parotid gland, and its termination pattern.
B. State the structures/procedures for which knowledge of the facial nerve's branching is clinically important.
C. Explain the anatomical/functional basis of the deformity that results when this nerve is injured.
questions.answerText:
A
Within the substance of the parotid gland, from superficial to deep are found the facial nerve and its branches, the retromandibular vein and its two divisions, and the external carotid artery and its two terminal branches. The facial nerve radiates through the anterior border of the gland like a goose's foot, termed the Pes Anserinus, giving off the temporal branch, the zygomatic branch, the buccal branch, the marginal mandibular branch, and the cervical branch.
B
Frey's syndrome commonly occurs after parotid surgery or trauma, from injury of the auriculo-temporal nerve and great auricular nerve; the facial nerve's course through the parotid gland is therefore clinically important in parotid surgery, where the nerve and its branches are structures to be identified and preserved.
C
Bell's palsy is associated with drooping of the mouth, reflecting facial nerve dysfunction; facial laceration is also noted as a clinical correlate involving this nerve's territory. Because the facial nerve, once it has divided within the parotid gland into its temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular and cervical branches, supplies the muscles of facial expression, injury to the trunk or a branch of the nerve produces the drooping and loss of movement seen in facial nerve palsy.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the gross histology of bone under the following headings: chemical composition and properties, cell types and their functions, and types of bone.
A(ii) State how the Haversian system (osteon) is organised and relate this to bone function.
B(i) Explain how blood calcium levels are regulated through bone, naming the hormones involved and their actions.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Chemical composition and properties: Bone is a connective tissue mineralized by calcium phosphate in the form of crystals very similar to hydroxyapatite. The minerals are both in the type I collagen fibers (which constitute about 95% of the matrix) and in the ground substance. Bone is both resilient and hard. Its resilience is due to the organic matter (collagen); its hardness is due to the inorganic minerals (calcium phosphate, calcium carbonate, calcium fluoride, calcium hydroxide, and citrate). Cell types: Osteocytes — maintain calcium and phosphate ion levels in the blood, are essentially stress sensors, and are osteoblasts that have been trapped in their own matrix in lacunae. Osteoblasts — synthesize the organic matrix (osteoid). Osteoclasts — multinucleated giant cells involved in resorption and remodeling of bone; they are also chondrocytes during bone healing and remodeling. Osteoid is the matrix secreted by osteoblasts and osteocytes prior to mineralization. Types of bone: compact bone (also called dense bone, cortical bone, or lamellar bone) and spongy bone (also called cancellous bone, trabecular bone, and medullary bone).
A(ii)
Compact bone is organized into structures called osteons or Haversian systems: concentric lamellae surrounding a central canal called the Haversian canal, which contains blood vessels, nerves, loose connective tissue, and endosteum. Between lamellae are lacunae, each with one osteocyte interconnected by canaliculi containing the cells' dendritic processes. Canals called Volkmann's canals link Haversian canals with one another and with the marrow cavity. Metabolic exchanges between osteocytes and blood capillaries depend on communication through the canaliculi.
B(i)
Blood calcium levels are regulated by the hormones parathormone (parathyroid hormone), which raises blood calcium levels by stimulating bone resorption, and calcitonin, which reduces blood calcium by suppressing bone resorption and increasing osteoid calcification.

questions.question:
Describe the quadriceps femoris muscle fully under the following headings, explain why its paralysis causes the most profound disability of any single muscle in the lower limb, and distinguish it from the hamstrings.
A(i) General features: number of components, collective description, and composite tendon
A(ii) Origin, insertion, innervation, and action of each component
B(i) Why paralysis of the quadriceps femoris produces more functional disability than paralysis of the hamstrings
B(ii) The femoral nerve — its role in supplying the quadriceps and why knee extension is the most critical movement lost
C(i) Distinguish the quadriceps femoris from the hamstrings with respect to origin, action, and nerve supply; state the numerical strength ratio
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Quadriceps femoris forms the main bulk of the anterior thigh muscles; it collectively constitutes the largest and one of the most powerful muscles of the body. It covers almost all the anterior aspect and sides of the femur. It is the great extensor of the leg. It consists of 4 muscles: rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, vastus medialis, and vastus intermedius. The tendons of the four parts unite in the distal portion of the thigh to form a single, strong, broad tendon — the quadriceps tendon; this continues as the patellar ligament (in which the patella is embedded) and is attached to the tibial tuberosity.
A(ii)
Rectus femoris — origin: anterior inferior iliac spine and ilium superior to acetabulum; insertion: via common quadriceps tendon and patellar ligament to tibial tuberosity; innervation: femoral nerve (L2, L3, L4); action: extends leg at knee joint, steadies hip joint, and helps iliopsoas flex thigh. It is the only part of the quadriceps that crosses the hip joint, named because it runs straight down the thigh. Vastus lateralis — origin: greater trochanter and lateral lip of linea aspera of femur; same insertion and innervation; action: extends leg at knee joint; it is the largest component. Vastus medialis — origin: intertrochanteric line and medial lip of linea aspera of femur; same insertion and innervation; action: extends leg at knee joint; inferior fibres are particularly important in stabilising the knee joint. Vastus intermedius — origin: anterior and lateral surfaces of shaft of femur; same insertion and innervation; action: extends leg at knee joint; lies deep to rectus femoris between the vastus medialis and lateralis.
B(i)
The quadriceps is the primary extensor of the knee — the most important movement for standing, walking, climbing stairs, and rising from a chair. Stability of the knee joint depends on the strength and action of surrounding muscles and tendons; the quadriceps femoris is most important in stabilising the knee joint. Paralysis means the patient cannot extend the knee or control descent on stairs, rendering them unable to walk safely without a brace.
B(ii)
All four components of the quadriceps are innervated by the femoral nerve (L2, L3, L4). The femoral nerve also supplies the hip joint via intermediate and cutaneous branches and the skin of the front and medial side of the thigh (Hilton's law). Loss of knee extension eliminates the ability to straighten or stabilise the knee against gravity — the most critical functional deficit for bipedal locomotion.
C(i)
Quadriceps femoris: origin from femur and ilium; action — extends the knee (and rectus femoris also flexes the hip); nerve supply — femoral nerve (L2, L3, L4). Hamstrings (semitendinosus, semimembranosus, biceps femoris): origin from ischial tuberosity (long head of biceps femoris and both semi-muscles) and linea aspera (short head of biceps femoris); action — extend the thigh, flex the leg, and rotate it (semitendinosus and semimembranosus medially, biceps femoris laterally); nerve supply — tibial division of sciatic nerve for semitendinosus, semimembranosus, and long head of biceps femoris; common fibular division of sciatic nerve for short head of biceps femoris. The quadriceps is 3 times stronger than its antagonist muscle group (the hamstrings).

questions.question:
A(i) State the origin and root value of the phrenic nerve.
A(ii) Describe its course, relations and embryological basis of its long course on the right and left.
A(iii) Describe its termination and the points at which it reaches the diaphragm.
A(iv) Describe its distribution (motor and sensory).
C(i) Explain the anatomical basis of the deformity and other consequences after injury or section of the nerve.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The phrenic nerve is formed in the neck within the cervical plexus and contains fibres from spinal roots C3, C4 and C5.
A(ii)
• Its long course from the neck follows the embryological migration of the diaphragm from the cervical region: the septum transversum is carried ventrally and caudally, and the cervical myotomes and nerves contribute the muscle and nerve supply.
• It passes through the superior and middle mediastinum: the right phrenic descends on the right side of the SVC and heart; the left phrenic descends on the left side of the heart.
A(iii)
Both nerves terminate in the diaphragm: terminal branches of the right phrenic pass through the caval opening (T8) in the central tendon, and the left phrenic pierces the left dome.
A(iv)
• Motor: the sole motor supply of the diaphragm; the right nerve supplies the right half up to the right margin of the oesophageal opening and the left nerve the left half up to the left margin.
• Sensory: the central part of the diaphragm and the related pleura and peritoneum, and sensory fibres to the pleurae and pericardium (mediastinal pleura, fibrous and parietal pericardium); the peripheral part receives sensory fibres from the lower 6 or 7 intercostal and subcostal nerves.
C(i)
• Sectioning or injury of a phrenic nerve in the neck causes complete paralysis and eventual atrophy of the muscular part of the corresponding half of the diaphragm, except in persons who have an accessory phrenic nerve.
• Causes of injury: mechanical trauma (ligation or damage during surgery) and compression by a tumour within the chest cavity; myopathies (e.g. myasthenia gravis) and neuropathies (e.g. diabetic neuropathy) also interrupt the supply.
• The paralysed half is elevated and shows paradoxical movement: it moves upwards during inspiration (forced up by abdominal viscera) and downwards during expiration; only one half is affected because each dome has a separate nerve supply.
• Unilateral paralysis is usually asymptomatic and an incidental finding on X-ray; if both sides are paralysed there is poor exercise tolerance, orthopnoea and fatigue, and lung function tests show a restrictive deficit.
• Irritation of the diaphragmatic pleura or of the peritoneum under the diaphragm (pleurisy, subphrenic pus or blood) refers pain to the shoulder tip, because the central diaphragm sends sensory fibres in the phrenic nerve (C3-5) and the shoulder skin is supplied by the supraclavicular nerve (C3,4).

A(i)
• The sacrum is formed by the union of 5 sacral vertebrae (fusion begins at 16 to 18 years, usually complete by 30); wedge-shaped; concave anterior surface with four transverse lines and four pairs of anterior sacral foramina.
• Dorsally a median sacral crest and posterior foramina; the sacral canal is continuous with the vertebral canal; an auricular surface forms the sacroiliac joint; structures emerge at the sacral hiatus.
A(ii)
• Each hip bone is three bones (ilium, pubis, ischium) separated by cartilage in the newborn and fused at puberty in the acetabulum; the ilium is the largest, with ala, body, crest, spines, greater sciatic notch, iliac fossa, auricular surface and arcuate line.
• Ischium: body, ramus, spine, lesser sciatic notch and tuberosity; pubis: superior and inferior rami, body, crest, tubercle, iliopectineal line; ischium and pubis surround the obturator foramen.
A(iii)
Two hip bones united at the pubic symphysis and with the sacrum at the sacroiliac joints; the girdle moves as a unit and supports and protects lower abdominal and pelvic organs; the pelvic brim divides true and false pelves.
B(i)
• The female pelvis serves for childbearing and easier delivery; it is bigger and wider, with a large oval brim and a wider outlet.
• The sacral promontory, the superior border of the anterior sacral surface, is an important obstetric landmark for pelvic measurements.
• The sacral index is about 105 in males and 115 in females, and the sacrovertebral angle is more prominent in females.
C(i)
• Male: smaller, narrower, heavier and thicker bone; deep false pelvis; pubic arch V-shaped and less than 90°; acetabulum larger, facing laterally; coccyx immovable; brim smaller and heart-shaped; outlet narrower.
• Male: narrower greater sciatic notch, round obturator foramen, longer narrower sacrum, more vertical ilium, ischial tuberosities longer, close together and laterally projecting.
• Female: shallow false pelvis; wider pubic arch greater than 90°; acetabulum smaller, facing anteriorly; coccyx movable; large oval brim; wider outlet.
• Female: wider greater sciatic notch, oval obturator foramen, less vertical ilium, ischial tuberosities shorter, farther apart and projecting medially.

questions.question:
(i) Describe the gross anatomy of the pancreas - location, shape, and its four parts (head, neck, body, tail) with their relations.
(ii) Relate the parts of the pancreas to pathology (annular pancreas, pancreatitis).
(iii) Explain how pancreatic disease can produce a functional deficit in a distant organ/system.
questions.answerText:
(i)
• The pancreas is a soft, lobulated, J- or retort-shaped gland lying retroperitoneally, except for the tail, and transversely across the posterior abdominal wall at the level of L1-L2, posterior to the stomach, between the duodenum on the right and the spleen on the left; it is about 15-20 cm long and weighs about 90 g.
• The head is disc-shaped, enlarged, and lies within the concavity of the duodenum; the uncinate process projects from its lower part, posterior to the superior mesenteric vessels.
• The neck is the constricted portion connecting the head to the body and overlies the superior mesenteric vessels.
• The body is centrally located, crossing the midline behind the stomach, with anterior, posterior and inferior surfaces; the posterior surface contacts the aorta, splenic vein, left kidney and vessels, left suprarenal gland, origin of the superior mesenteric artery, and the crura of the diaphragm.
• The tail is narrow, lies at the level of T12, ends within the splenic hilum in the splenophrenic ligament, and is the only intraperitoneal part of the pancreas; it may be injured during splenectomy, causing a pancreatic fistula.
• The main pancreatic duct, of Wirsung, begins in the tail and runs to the head, usually joining the bile duct to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla, which opens at the major duodenal papilla; the accessory duct, of Santorini, drains the upper head via the minor duodenal papilla.
(ii)
• Annular pancreas is a rare congenital defect in which the pancreas encircles the duodenum; ectopic pancreatic tissue outside the gastrointestinal tract is a very common anomaly.
• Due to its deep retroperitoneal position, the pancreas is not easily accessible for direct clinical examination, so diagnosis of pancreatic disease relies on ultrasound, CT scan, special investigations of the pancreatic and biliary ducts, and biochemical tests.
• Acute necrotizing pancreatitis results when proenzymes are prematurely activated and digest pancreatic tissue, from causes including infection, gallstones, alcoholism, drugs and trauma.
(iii)
• The endocrine part of the pancreas, the islets of Langerhans, secretes insulin and glucagon into the blood; lack of insulin production by the beta cells, or defective insulin receptors, causes diabetes mellitus, a hyperglycaemic metabolic disorder affecting the whole body.
• Because the exocrine pancreas secretes digestive enzymes and bicarbonate essential for neutralising gastric acid and digesting food in the duodenum, pancreatic disease impairing exocrine secretion produces a functional deficit in intestinal digestion, a distant effect of pancreatic pathology.
• In extreme malnutrition, acinar cell atrophy further reduces digestive enzyme production, compounding this distant digestive deficit.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the origin, course, and distribution of the three types of muscle tissue under the following headings: structural features at the light microscope level, connective tissue organization (endomysium, perimysium, epimysium), and characteristic distinguishing feature of each type.
A(ii) State the safe structural basis of how skeletal muscle contraction is transmitted to produce movement.
B(i) Explain the anatomical and histological basis of why cardiac muscle does not fatigue and cannot be replaced after infarction.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Skeletal muscle: contains bundles of very long, multinucleated cells with cross-striations; contraction is quick, forceful, and usually under voluntary control. Connective tissue: endomysium surrounds individual muscle fibers (nerve fibers and capillaries form a rich network in the endomysium); perimysium surrounds fascicles; epimysium (deep fascia) surrounds the whole muscle belly and connects to tendons. Distinguishing feature: cross-striations; multinucleated; sarcomeres extending from Z disc to Z disc (~2.5 µm long in resting muscle). The A bands are anisotropic (dark); I bands are isotropic (light); each I band is bisected by the Z disc. Smooth muscle: consists of collections of fusiform cells that lack striations and have slow, involuntary contractions; elongated and spindle-shaped; single nucleus at the widest point; contain actin and myosin filaments but lack sarcomeres. Prominent locations: wall of GI tract, walls of arteries and veins, around glands. Distinguishing feature: no striations; slow, sustained contractions; non-voluntary. Cardiac muscle: cross-striations; composed of elongated, often branched cells; bound by intercalated discs unique to cardiac muscle; contraction is involuntary, vigorous, and rhythmic. Central nuclei; high cytoplasm-to-nucleus ratio. Distinguishing feature: intercalated discs; branching cells; involuntary continuous rhythmic contraction.
A(ii)
Skeletal muscle fibers show cross-striations of alternating light and dark bands. The sarcomere extends from Z disc to Z disc. During contraction, shortening of myofibrils (shortening of sarcomeres) is transmitted through the connective tissue (endomysium, perimysium, epimysium) and via tendons to bone, producing bodily movements.
B(i)
Cardiac muscle cells contain numerous mitochondria; a large proportion of cell volume is occupied by mitochondria. Fatty acids, transported by lipoproteins, are stored as triglycerides in numerous lipid droplets in cardiac muscle cells — this supports the extremely rich capillary network and strong continuous activity. Cardiac muscle has limited regenerative capacity; spaces left after infarction are filled by connective tissue forming dense irregular scar tissue, because cardiac muscle cells do not go through mitosis.

A(i)
The articular surfaces of the TMJ are the condyle of the mandible (inferior) and the articular tubercle/mandibular fossa of the temporal bone (squamous part). The articular capsule is loose and fibrous, attaching to the margins of the articular area on the temporal bone and around the neck of the mandible. The superior synovial membrane lines the fibrous capsule superior to the articular disc, and the inferior synovial membrane lines the capsule inferior to the disc; the joint is divided into two compartments (superior and inferior) by an articular disc of fibrocartilage.
A(ii)
The ligaments of the TMJ are divided into an intrinsic ligament and extrinsic ligaments. The intrinsic ligament, also known as the lateral ligament, is the thick part of the articular capsule, strengthens the TMJ laterally, and prevents posterior dislocation of the TMJ. The extrinsic ligaments are the sphenomandibular ligament, which runs from the spine of the sphenoid to the lingula of the mandible and is the primary passive support of the mandible, and the stylomandibular ligament, a thickening of the fibrous capsule of the parotid gland, extending from the styloid process of the temporal bone to the angle of the mandible, which does not contribute significantly to the strength of the joint.
B
Dislocation of the TMJ is common in aged persons and females, due to wearing and resorption of the articular eminence and reducing muscle tone with advancing age.
C
The intrinsic (lateral) ligament is the thick part of the articular capsule, strengthens the joint laterally and prevents posterior dislocation. The sphenomandibular ligament, by contrast, runs from the spine of the sphenoid to the lingula of the mandible and is the primary passive support of the mandible, while the stylomandibular ligament is a thickening of the fibrous capsule of the parotid gland, running from the styloid process to the angle of the mandible, and does not contribute significantly to the strength of the joint.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
• The thoracoabdominal nerves are the abdominal portions of the anterior rami of T7 to T12 (T7 to T11 thoracoabdominal, T12 subcostal); their distal portions lie in the rectus sheath.
• External oblique: T7 to T11 and T12; internal oblique and transversus abdominis: T7 to T11, T12 and branches of the lumbar plexus; rectus abdominis: T7 to T11; pyramidalis: subcostal T12.
A(ii)
• The lumbar plexus (ventral rami L1 to L4, formed within psoas major) innervates part of the lower abdominal wall.
• The iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves (L1) emerge from the lateral border of psoas major.
A(iii)
• The umbilicus is the segmental landmark with dermatome T10, the same root that innervates the appendix, so appendicular referred pain is felt there.
• The segmental innervation applies to both the anterior abdominal skin and musculature.
B(i)
• The TAP block is a peripheral nerve block that anaesthetises the nerves of the abdominal wall.
• It is performed by injecting anaesthetic into the fascial plane between transversus abdominis and internal oblique muscles.
C(i)
• The ilioinguinal, iliohypogastric and inferior thoracic nerves are spread across the abdominal wall and so are prone to injury.

questions.question:
Describe the median nerve:
A(i) Formation (roots)
A(ii) Relations in the cubital fossa and at the wrist
A(iii) Branches
A(iv) Distribution
C. Explain the anatomical basis of the deformity seen after a low (wrist-level) injury to the median nerve.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The median nerve is formed by the union of a lateral root from the lateral cord (C5, C6, C7) and a medial root from the medial cord (C8, T1) of the brachial plexus.
A(ii)
In the cubital fossa the median nerve is the most medial of the major vertical contents, lying medial to the brachial artery and the tendon of biceps brachii; at the wrist it lies anterior to the tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis, deep to the flexor retinaculum, within the carpal tunnel.
A(iii)
It gives a palmar cutaneous branch that arises in the forearm, proximal to the flexor retinaculum, and a recurrent branch that arises in the hand to supply the thenar muscles.
A(iv)
It supplies flexor carpi radialis, palmaris longus, pronator teres, pronator quadratus and the digital flexors, producing thumb flexion and opposition, flexion of digits 2 and 3, wrist flexion and abduction, and forearm pronation; it also supplies sensation to the anterolateral surface of the hand.
C
• A low (wrist-level) median nerve injury produces an "ape-like hand."
• There is flattening of the thenar eminence because the recurrent branch supplying abductor pollicis brevis and flexor pollicis brevis, which arises in the hand, is affected.
• Opposition and abduction of the thumb become impossible, so the pincer-like action of the hand is lost, causing difficulty with fine manual tasks such as buttoning.
• Adductor pollicis, being supplied by the ulnar nerve, is unopposed, further contributing to the deformity.
• This contrasts with an elbow-level injury, where flexion of the index and middle fingers is lost (flexor digitorum superficialis and the lateral half of profundus are affected), the ring and little fingers weakly flex, and flexion of the distal phalanx of the thumb is lost, while the interosseous muscles are unaffected, being supplied by the ulnar nerve.
• The median nerve can be torn partially or fully, or compressed, at the elbow, from fracture, other trauma, or compression from fluid build-up following injury.
• The most common site of median nerve injury overall is at the wrist, within the carpal tunnel.

A(i)
Five lumbar vertebrae (1 to 4 typical, 5 atypical); largest and strongest of the column because supported weight increases inferiorly; superior facets face medially, inferior facets laterally; thick broad spines.
A(ii)
• Large kidney-shaped body, deeper anteriorly; triangular foramen (larger than thoracic, smaller than cervical); short strong pedicles; short thick broad laminae; spine a vertical quadrilateral plate.
• Transverse processes thin and tapering (accessory process); superior articular facets concave facing medially and backwards with the mammillary process; inferior facets convex facing laterally and forwards.
A(iii)
L5: thick short pyramidal transverse processes; largest body, anterior deeper than posterior, creating the sharp lumbosacral angle; small short rounded spine; inferior articular distance equal to or more than the superior.
A(iv)
Joints: intervertebral discs (symphysis) between bodies; synovial joints between arches. Ligaments: anterior and posterior longitudinal, ligamentum flavum, interspinous, supraspinous; iliolumbar ligaments strengthen the L5 to S1 lumbosacral joint.
B(i)
• A lumbar vertebra ossifies from three primary centres (body and each half of the neural arch) appearing in the third month of fetal life; the halves of the arch fuse posteriorly in the first year.
• Failure of fusion of the two halves of the neural arch results in spina bifida; if one primary centre of the body fails, hemivertebra.
B(ii)
• Lumbar spinal stenosis: thought hereditary, a narrow vertebral foramen in one or several vertebrae.
• Excessive lumbar lordosis: abnormal anterior curvature with anterior tilting of the pelvis.
C(i)
• The canal formed by L1 and L2 contains the conus medullaris; the lower three contain the cauda equina; all contain the spinal meninges.
• Stenosis can compress the spinal cord and exiting nerves; the pedicles are related above and below to spinal nerves.
• The right crus of the diaphragm attaches to the upper three lumbar vertebrae and the left crus to the upper two; psoas major arises from the vertebral borders.

A(i)
Molecular composition: The cell membrane consists of amphipathic phospholipids arranged so that the hydrophobic tails face inward (away from water) and the more hydrophilic head regions associate with the cytosolic and extracellular environments, forming a spherical lipid bilayer. The phospholipid bilayer was proposed by Gorter and Grendel in 1925. It also includes integral membrane proteins and peripheral membrane proteins (almost half of the total mass of the membrane), a network of tiny microfilaments of the cytoskeleton, and the lipid molecule cholesterol, which stabilizes and makes the cell membrane more rigid. Functions: structural support; semi-permeable membrane (controls what molecules enter and leave the cell); establishes and maintains an electrochemical gradient; contains receptors that recognize and respond to molecular signals; supports cell adhesion and cell communication. Membrane transport mechanisms: passive (osmosis, diffusion, simple diffusion), facilitated transport, active transport (primary and secondary), and vesicular transport (endocytosis: pinocytosis and phagocytosis; exocytosis).
A(ii)
Several diseases have been implicated with defective membrane receptors. Pseudohypoparathyroidism is associated with defective parathyroid and growth hormone receptors. In these conditions, the glands produce the respective hormones, but the target cells do not respond because they lack normal receptors. Signal transduction can be hindered and cause diseases when mutations occur in the genes that encode and regulate receptor proteins.
B(i)
Integral membrane proteins: are directly incorporated within the lipid bilayer; most are transmembrane proteins passing through the entire membrane; inserted into the lipid bilayer. Functions: transport, signal transduction, structural support. Peripheral membrane proteins: exhibit a looser association with the membrane; bound to the membrane indirectly by protein-protein interactions; located on the cytosolic face. Plasma membrane contains proteins called integrins that are linked to cytoplasmic molecules; through these linkages there is a connection between the extracellular matrix and cytoplasm, mediating cell adhesion and cell communication.

A(i)
The brachial artery provides the main arterial supply to the arm and is the continuation of the axillary artery; it begins at the inferior border of teres major and ends in the cubital fossa opposite the neck of the radius.
A(ii)
Under cover of the bicipital aponeurosis, it divides into the radial and ulnar arteries.
A(iii)
Its branches include the deep brachial (profunda brachii) artery, which accompanies the radial nerve, the superior ulnar collateral artery, which accompanies the ulnar nerve, and the inferior ulnar collateral artery.
B
During blood pressure measurement, the stethoscope is placed over the brachial artery in the cubital fossa, and the cubital fossa is the site used to palpate the brachial pulse.
C
• Volkmann's ischaemic contracture is a deformity of the hand, fingers and wrist caused by injury to the muscles of the forearm.
• The classical presentation is a supracondylar fracture of the humerus, although fracture of the arm or elbow may also result in this deformity; the artery involved is the brachial artery.
• The contracture occurs when there is a lack of blood flow (ischaemia) to the forearm, usually from increased pressure resulting from swelling (compartment syndrome).
• Because there is very little room within each fascial compartment of the arm and forearm, haemorrhage or oedema following injury to the brachial artery can cause secondary vascular compression: veins are affected first, and later the arteries, resulting in ischaemia of the affected part.
• The classical presentation of the resulting acute compartment syndrome is remembered by "the five P's": pulselessness, paraesthesia, poikilothermia, paralysis and pallor.
• There are three levels of severity of the resulting Volkmann's contracture: the mildest involves flexion contracture of only two or three fingers with no or limited loss of sensation; a more severe form involves all fingers flexed with the thumb stuck in the palm and some sensory loss.
• The most severe form involves all the muscles in the forearm that flex and extend the wrist and fingers, producing a severely disabling condition.
• This progression illustrates how injury to the brachial artery at the elbow can produce a graded functional deficit distally in the hand and fingers.

A(i)
The bony wall is the carpal sulcus, formed by the concavity on the anterior aspect of the carpal bones, forming the base and sides of the tunnel; it is bounded laterally by the scaphoid and trapezium tubercles and medially by the hook of the hamate and the pisiform.
A(ii)
The fibrous wall is the flexor retinaculum, a thick connective tissue band that stretches over the carpal sulcus, converting it into the carpal tunnel by bridging the space between the medial and lateral parts of the arch, spanning from the hook of hamate and pisiform medially to the scaphoid and trapezium laterally.
A(iii)
Contents: four tendons of flexor digitorum profundus (the deepest structures), four tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis lying anterior to those of profundus (all eight enclosed in a common synovial sheath), the tendon of flexor pollicis longus occupying the lateral angle of the compartment with its own synovial sheath, and the median nerve, which lies anterior to the tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis, deep to the flexor retinaculum.
B
• Carpal tunnel syndrome may occur following inflammatory reactions (synovitis) in the synovial sheath of the tendons traversing the tunnel.
• Excess fluid, such as follows inflammation of the synovial sheaths, compresses the structures within the confined tunnel.
• The median nerve is the structure most adversely affected, since it lies anterior to the crowded flexor tendons, immediately deep to the unyielding flexor retinaculum, leaving it particularly exposed to any rise in pressure within the tunnel.
• Compression of the median nerve produces sensory disturbance (hypoesthesia or anaesthesia) in the skin of the lateral three and a half fingers on their palmar aspect.
• Weakness or paralysis of the thenar muscles also occurs, because the recurrent branch of the median nerve that supplies these muscles arises in the hand and is also compressed.
C
• Within the tunnel, the tendons of flexor digitorum profundus are the deepest structures.
• The tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis lie anterior to (more superficial than) those of profundus.
• Both sets of four tendons are enclosed together in a single common synovial sheath, whereas the tendon of flexor pollicis longus lies separately at the lateral angle of the compartment, enclosed in its own distinct synovial sheath.
• This layered arrangement of tendons deep to the median nerve means the nerve is the most superficial of the tunnel's principal contents, most exposed to the flexor retinaculum's unyielding roof.

A(i)
The gluteal region is the region of the buttock. Bony landmarks — surface anatomy: iliac crest, gluteus medius, tip of greater trochanter, gluteus maximus (fold of buttock), ischial tuberosity, tip of coccyx, natal cleft, posterior superior iliac spine (PSIS), sciatic nerve. Bones: os coxae (ilium, ischium, pubis) and femur.
A(ii)
Superficial fascia: thick in women; impregnated with large quantities of fat, hence the prominence of the buttock. Deep fascia: continuous with fascia lata of the thigh. The 9 muscles: gluteus maximus, gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, tensor fasciae latae (superficial layer); piriformis, obturator internus, gemellus superior, gemellus inferior, quadratus femoris (deep layer). Deep layer muscles all have distal attachments on or adjacent to the intertrochanteric crest of the femur; they are lateral rotators of the thigh and stabilise the hip joint. Obturator internus, superior gemellus, and inferior gemellus form the triceps coxae of the hip.
B(i)
6 nerves of the gluteal region: sciatic nerve (L4, 5; S1, 2, 3); posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh; superior gluteal nerve; inferior gluteal nerve; nerve to quadratus femoris; pudendal nerve. (Nerve to obturator internus also exits here.) The sciatic nerve curves downward midway between the tuber ischii and the greater trochanter.
B(ii)
4 arteries: superior gluteal artery (SGA), inferior gluteal artery (IGA), medial femoral circumflex artery (MFCA), lateral femoral circumflex artery (LFCA). Trochanteric anastomosis (TA) — main blood supply to the head of femur: SGA, IGA, MFCA, LFCA. Cruciate anastomosis (CA) — situated at the level of the lesser trochanter: IGA, MFCA, LFCA, and 1st perforating branch of profunda femoris. The CA jointly with the TA provides a connection between the femoral arteries and the internal iliac arteries.
C(i)
Sacrotuberous ligament (STL) and sacrospinous ligament (SSL): (1) both stabilise the sacrum and prevent its rotation at the sacroiliac joint by the weight of the vertebral column; (2) in conjunction with bones, they form the greater sciatic foramen (GSF) and lesser sciatic foramen (LSF). Functions of GSF and LSF: GSF provides an exit from the pelvis into the gluteal region. LSF (1) provides an entrance into the perineum from the gluteal region; (2) enables nerves and vessels that left the pelvis through the GSF above the pelvic floor to enter the perineum below the pelvic floor.
