Describe the gross anatomy of the humerus:
A(i) Upper end
A(ii) Shaft
A(iii) Lower end
B. State how different parts of the humerus relate to common fracture patterns.
C. Explain how injury at each of these parts may spread to affect a distant structure, causing a functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• The upper end has a large, rounded head joined to the shaft by a constricted surgical neck, and greater and lesser tubercles.
• The tubercles are separated by the intertubercular (bicipital) groove, which lodges the long tendon of biceps brachii and transmits a branch of the anterior humeral circumflex artery to the shoulder joint.
A(ii)
The shaft is circular in section above and flattened in its lower part, bears the deltoid tuberosity, and its posterior aspect shows the spiral groove, which demarcates the origins of the medial and lateral heads of triceps and between which the radial nerve and profunda vessels wind.
A(iii)
The lower end bears the rounded capitulum laterally, for articulation with the radial head, and the spool-shaped trochlea medially, for articulation with the trochlear notch of the ulna; the medial and lateral epicondyles are extracapsular, the medial being the larger, extending more distally and bearing a groove on its posterior aspect for the ulnar nerve.
B
• Fractures of the surgical neck of the humerus are especially common in elderly people with osteoporosis, usually from a minor fall on the hand with the force transmitted up the extended limb.
• Transverse fractures of the shaft frequently result from a direct blow to the arm.
• Fracture of the distal humerus, near the supracondylar ridges, is a supracondylar fracture.
C
• Because the axillary, radial and ulnar nerves are in close contact with the humerus, they may be damaged when the associated part of the bone is fractured.
• Fracture at the surgical neck threatens the axillary nerve, producing deltoid paralysis with loss of abduction and sensory loss over the regimental badge area.
• Fracture through the radial (spiral) groove of the shaft threatens the radial nerve, producing wrist drop.
• Fracture at the medial epicondyle at the lower end threatens the ulnar nerve, while injury at the distal humerus (supracondylar region) threatens the median nerve.
• Fractures of the humeral neck, midshaft and lower end are therefore each associated with a characteristic pattern of nerve injury and resultant functional deficit.

(i)
• The arteries of the stomach are derived from branches of the coeliac artery. The left gastric artery arises from the coeliac artery, passes upward and to the left to reach the oesophagus, then descends along the lesser curvature, supplying the lower third of the oesophagus and the upper right part of the stomach. The right gastric artery arises from the hepatic artery at the upper border of the pylorus and runs left along the lesser curvature, supplying the lower right part of the stomach.
• The short gastric arteries arise from the splenic artery at the hilum of the spleen and pass forward in the gastrosplenic omentum to supply the fundus. The left gastro-omental (gastroepiploic) artery arises from the splenic artery at the hilum of the spleen and passes forward in the gastrosplenic omentum to supply the stomach along the upper part of the greater curvature. The right gastro-omental artery arises from the gastroduodenal branch of the hepatic artery and passes left to supply the stomach along the lower part of the greater curvature.
(iii)
• The left and right gastric veins drain directly into the portal vein.
• The short gastric veins and the left gastroepiploic vein join the splenic vein.
• The right gastroepiploic vein joins the superior mesenteric vein.
• All venous drainage of the stomach therefore ultimately enters the portal circulation, via the portal vein, splenic vein or superior mesenteric vein, before passing through the liver.
• This portal route explains why bleeding from portal-systemic anastomoses, such as oesophageal varices, is related to the portal venous system.

A. Describe the course of the maxillary nerve, from its origin to its continuation on the face, and list its branches.
B. State the clinically relevant procedure and the region associated with this nerve.
questions.answerText:
A
The maxillary nerve passes through the pterygopalatine fossa, where it is one of the contents (along with the terminal part of the maxillary artery, the maxillary vein, and the pterygopalatine ganglion); nerve structures enter the fossa through its posterior wall. Its branches include the superior alveolar nerves (anterior, posterior and middle), the middle meningeal nerve, the infraorbital nerve, the zygomatic nerve, the inferior palpebral nerve, the superior labial nerve, the pharyngeal nerve, the greater and lesser palatine nerves, and the nasopalatine nerve. The infraorbital nerve continues from the maxillary nerve onto the face via the infraorbital groove and canal, situated on the floor of the orbit in the orbital plate of the maxilla, and via the infraorbital foramen.
B
Clinical correlates of this region include maxillary nerve block, and the pterygopalatine ganglion is also referred to as the "hay fever ganglion".

questions.question:
(i) Describe the origin, course and distribution of the anterior and posterior vagal trunks in the abdomen.
(ii) State where the vagal trunks lie in relation to the oesophageal hiatus.
(iii) Explain the anatomical basis of the effect of vagal injury (vagotomy) on the stomach and related viscera.
questions.answerText:
(i)
• The anterior vagal trunk is formed mainly in the thorax from the left vagus nerve; it enters the abdomen on the anterior surface of the oesophagus and divides into branches that supply the anterior surface of the stomach. A large hepatic branch of the anterior vagal trunk passes up to the liver, and from this a pyloric branch passes down to the pylorus.
• The posterior vagal trunk is formed mainly from the right vagus nerve; it enters the abdomen on the posterior surface of the oesophagus and divides into branches supplying mainly the posterior surface of the stomach. A large branch of the posterior vagal trunk passes to the coeliac and superior mesenteric plexuses and is distributed to the intestine as far as the splenic flexure and to the pancreas.
(ii)
At the opening in the diaphragm (the oesophageal hiatus), the oesophagus is accompanied by the two vagal trunks, branches of the left gastric vessels, and lymphatic vessels, with fibres of the right crus forming a sling around the oesophagus. Inferior to the root of the lungs, the vagus nerves leave the pulmonary plexus and join sympathetic nerves to form the oesophageal plexus, from which the anterior trunk (left vagus, anterior) and posterior trunk (right vagus, posterior) are derived.
(iii)
• The vagal (parasympathetic) fibres are secretomotor to the gastric glands and motor to the muscular wall of the stomach, and the pyloric sphincter receives inhibitory fibres from the vagus.
• Vagotomy is a recognised surgical option for peptic ulcer disease; division of the vagal trunks reduces the vagal secretomotor drive to the gastric glands, decreasing acid secretion.
• Since the hepatic branch arises from the anterior vagal trunk and the coeliac/pancreatic branch from the posterior trunk, a truncal vagotomy also interrupts vagal input to the liver, pancreas and intestine as far as the splenic flexure.
• Loss of vagal inhibitory input to the pyloric sphincter can alter pyloric motor function, which is why vagotomy for peptic ulcer disease is often combined with a drainage procedure such as pyloroplasty.

A(i)
• Continuation of the sigmoid colon at S3; ends as the anal canal one inch below and in front of the tip of the coccyx; about 12 to 13 cm (5 inches); lower end dilated as the ampulla; lacks mesentery, taeniae coli, sacculations and appendices epiploicae.
• Two anteroposterior curves (sacral posterior; perineal anterior at puborectalis) and three lateral curves (upper convex to right, middle convex to left and most prominent, lower convex to right).
A(ii)
Upper third: front and sides covered; middle third: front only; lower third: none; posterior surface: none. Male: recto-vesical pouch 7.5 cm from anus; female: recto-uterine pouch of Douglas 5.5 cm from anus.
A(iii)
Four permanent horizontal Houston's valves (1st and 3rd constant); the 3rd at S5, 5 cm above the anus, if completely encircling forms Nelaton's sphincter, and divides an upper chamber (faeces without reflex to defecate) from a lower sensitive chamber; valves support faecal weight; cannulae/rectal washing are given in left lateral position to avoid injury to the 3rd valve.
A(iv)
Wall: serous, muscular (outer longitudinal, inner circular), submucosa, mucosa. Arteries: superior rectal (main, from inferior mesenteric), middle rectal (anterior division of internal iliac), inferior rectal (internal pudendal), median sacral (aorta), inferior gluteal.
B(i)
Superior rectal vein drains to inferior mesenteric then portal vein; middle rectal to internal iliac and inferior rectal to internal pudendal (systemic). Internal haemorrhoids (superior rectal tributaries, above Hilton's line, painless); external (inferior rectal, below, painful).
B(ii)
Support: puborectal sling, Waldeyer fascia, lateral ligaments, pelvirectal and ischiorectal fat. Upper third lateral: pararectal fossa (sigmoid colon, small intestine); middle third: pelvirectal space; lower third: ischioanal fossa.
B(iii)
Sympathetic (L1, L2) is vasomotor, stimulates the internal anal sphincter and inhibits the rest of the musculature; parasympathetic (S2 to S4) is secretomotor, stimulates peristalsis and relaxes sphincters.
C(i)
Lymph: upper half via superior rectal to left common iliac and pararectal nodes; middle half to internal iliac nodes; lower part to anal valves to internal iliac nodes; below the anal valves to superficial inguinal nodes.
C(ii)
Portal-systemic anastomosis: superior rectal (portal) with middle and inferior rectal veins (systemic); gut lymph follows arteries to pre-aortic nodes.
C(iii)
Male: anterior sigmoid colon, small intestine, seminal vesicles, ampulla of vas, posterior bladder and prostate; female: posterior vaginal wall; posterior: sacrum, sacral plexus, coccyx, and piriformis, coccygeus, levator ani.
C(iv)
Hindgut origin (endoderm), sympathetic least splanchnic (T12, L1) plus hypogastric (S2 to S4), inferior mesenteric artery (L3); mucosa above the 3rd valve from pre-allantoic hindgut, below from cloaca; muscle from splanchnic mesoderm.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Five functions of the epithelial lining:
• Provide a selectively permeable barrier between the contents of the tract and the tissues of the body.
• Facilitate the transport and digestion of food.
• Promote the absorption of the products of digestion.
• Produce hormones that affect the activity of the digestive system.
• Produce mucus for lubrication and protection.
A(ii)
Local enteric nervous system:
• The submucosal (Meissner) plexus is located in the submucosa; the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus is located in the connective tissue between the circular and longitudinal muscle sublayers of the muscularis.
• Together they constitute the local enteric nervous system of the digestive tract.
• This system functions independently of the CNS.
• Both plexuses are composed mainly of nerve cell aggregates forming small parasympathetic ganglia.
• The number of ganglia along the digestive tract is variable — numerous in the regions of greatest motility.
B(i)
Muscularis mucosae:
• Composition: thin layer of smooth muscle.
• Location: usually separates the mucosa from the submucosa.
• Functions: (1) allows local movements of the mucosa independent of other movements of the digestive tract, helping to increase contact of the lining with food; (2) its contractions contribute to mixing and propelling food (the plexuses coordinate the contractions of the muscularis to mix and propel food).
B(ii)
Immunological backup:
• The mucosa-associated immune defense system (MALT) provides an essential backup to the thin physical barrier of the epithelial lining.
• The lamina propria (just below the epithelium) is a zone rich in macrophages and lymphocytes, some of which actively produce IgA antibodies.
• The digestive tract normally contains thousands of microbial species, including both useful gut inhabitants and potential pathogens ingested with food and drink, making this immune backup essential.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the five functions of the epithelial lining of the digestive tract.
A(ii) Describe the submucosal (Meissner) plexus and the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus together as the local enteric nervous system: name the layers of the GIT wall each is found in, state the ganglia they are composed of, what the number of ganglia depends on, and what system they function independently of.
B(i) Describe the muscularis mucosae: its composition, its location, and the two functions attributed to it.
B(ii) Explain the immunological backup to the thin epithelial barrier of the GIT, and identify what the digestive tract normally contains that makes this backup essential.

A(i) Describe the gross anatomy of epithelial tissue under the following headings: general characteristics, morphological classification (by cell shape and number of layers), and the basement membrane.
A(ii) Relate specific epithelial types to their common locations in the body, giving one example each of simple squamous, simple cuboidal, simple columnar, ciliated columnar, stratified squamous, and transitional epithelium.
B(i) Explain why epithelial tissue is avascular, how it receives nutrients, and state the clinical consequence when the basement membrane is disrupted in disease.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
General characteristics: epithelial tissue consists of closely packed cells arranged in one or more layers; these cells are specialized and fill roles such as protection, secretion, and absorption; the cells are tightly packed together with very little extracellular matrix and almost no intercellular substance; they rest on a basement membrane (a basal lamina containing the glycoprotein laminin). Morphological classification by cell shape: squamous (flat), cuboidal (square or cube-like), columnar (tall and thin). By number of layers: simple epithelium (one cell thick) — can be simple squamous, simple cuboidal, or simple columnar; stratified epithelium (multiple layers — described as heterogeneous); pseudostratified epithelium — appears stratified but all cells contact the basal lamina. Transitional epithelium: recognized by its appearance — when the bladder is empty (relaxed), the epithelium appears thicker and has more layers than when the bladder is full. Basement membrane: contains the glycoprotein laminin; the border between epithelia and the underlying connective tissue is sharp and distinct.
A(ii)
Simple squamous epithelium: lines blood vessels (endothelium) and body cavities. Simple cuboidal epithelium: lines many small ducts in the body. Simple columnar epithelium: lines the gallbladder, larger ducts near the urinary papilla; also found in the jejunum (with goblet cells). Ciliated columnar epithelium: found in the respiratory tract and fallopian tubes; goblet cells (glandular epithelium) are present, making it heterogeneous. Stratified squamous epithelium (keratinized): forms the outer layer of skin; contains the protective protein keratin; a keratinized (dry) epithelium. Transitional epithelium: lines the urinary bladder.
B(i)
Epithelial tissue is avascular (contains no blood vessels); the lamina propria (underlying connective tissue) supplies the necessary nutrients and metabolites, which are transported to and from epithelial cells by diffusion through the basement membrane. If the basement membrane is disrupted (e.g., in cancer invasion or severe inflammation), the barrier between epithelium and connective tissue is lost, allowing unrestricted cell invasion into the underlying stroma; epithelial cells in contact with the environment are constantly subjected to mechanical damage and must show many dividing cells (mitoses) to replace lost cells; disruption of this repair mechanism contributes to disease progression.

questions.question:
A. Describe the nerve supply of the larynx, including the origin and distribution of the recurrent laryngeal nerve and the exception to its motor supply.
B. State how the sensory innervation of the larynx is divided in relation to the vocal folds.
questions.answerText:
A
Most of the muscles of the larynx receive their innervation via the recurrent laryngeal branch of the vagus nerve; the exception is the cricothyroid muscle, which receives its innervation via the external laryngeal nerve. Motor supply to the muscles is from the nucleus ambiguus via the cranial accessory: to the cricothyroid via the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, and to all other laryngeal muscles, including the upper oesophagus and cricopharyngeus, via the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
B
Sensory innervation of the larynx is via branches of the vagus nerve: above the vocal folds it is via the internal laryngeal nerve, and below the vocal folds it is by way of branches of the recurrent laryngeal nerve; parasympathetic innervation of the larynx is mainly by way of branches of the vagus nerve. Lymphatic drainage similarly follows this division: above the cords to the upper deep cervical nodes, and below the cords to the lower deep cervical nodes.

questions.question:
(A) Describe the duodenum under the headings: A(i) parts and dimensions A(ii) peritoneal relations A(iii) visceral relations.
(B) Explain the clinical basis for the duodenum's common site of ulceration and for paraduodenal hernia.
(C) Distinguish between the jejunum and the ileum.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The duodenum is the first, shortest (about 25 cm) and widest part of the small intestine; it is C-shaped and mostly retroperitoneal, made up of four parts - superior (5 cm), descending (7.5-8 cm), horizontal (6-10 cm) and ascending (2.5 cm).
A(ii)
The proximal 2.5 cm of the superior part is movable and intraperitoneal, attached to the lesser omentum above and greater omentum below; the rest of the duodenum is retroperitoneal, covered by peritoneum only on its anterior aspect.
A(iii)
The superior part is anteriorly related to the quadrate lobe of the liver and gallbladder, and posteriorly to the gastroduodenal artery, bile duct, portal vein and inferior vena cava; the descending part is related medially to the head of pancreas and bile duct, laterally to the right colic flexure, and rests on the right kidney, ureter, psoas major and renal vessels, and receives the major duodenal papilla; the horizontal part crosses the inferior vena cava, aorta and L3 vertebra and is crossed anteriorly by the superior mesenteric vessels; the ascending part rises to the duodenojejunal flexure.
B
• The proximal (superior) part of the duodenum is the most common site of duodenal ulcer.
• The duodenojejunal flexure is fixed by the suspensory muscle of the duodenum (ligament of Treitz), which passes posterior to the pancreas and splenic vein and anterior to the left renal vein; a weakness near this fixed flexure is the anatomical basis for a paraduodenal hernia.
C
• The jejunum lies mainly in the left upper (infracolic) quadrant, has thicker, more vascular walls and a wider, often empty lumen, with long and few vasa recta, one or two layers of arterial arcades, numerous circular mucosal folds, and large, thick, abundant villi.
• The ileum lies predominantly in the right lower quadrant and pelvis, has thinner, less vascular walls and a narrower, often loaded lumen, with short and numerous vasa recta and multiple layers of arterial arcades.
• The ileum has smaller and sparser circular mucosal folds and shorter, thinner villi than the jejunum, but the terminal ileum has numerous Peyer's patches and more numerous solitary lymphatic follicles, which are absent or scanty in the jejunum.
• The jejunum has mesenteric windows and less abundant mesenteric fat, whereas the ileum has no windows and more abundant mesenteric fat.

A(i)
• Mucosa: consists of an epithelial lining, lamina propria (zone of loose connective tissue rich in blood vessels, lymphatics, lymphocytes, smooth muscle cells, and sometimes small glands), and muscularis mucosae (thin layer of smooth muscle that separates the mucosa from the submucosa and allows local movements of the mucosa).
• Submucosa: denser connective tissue containing larger blood and lymph vessels, the submucosal (Meissner) plexus of autonomic nerves, and possibly glands and lymphoid tissue.
• Muscularis (muscularis externa): thick layer of smooth muscle organized into an internal circular sublayer and an external longitudinal sublayer; connective tissue between them contains blood vessels, lymph vessels, and the myenteric (Auerbach) nerve plexus.
• Serosa: outermost layer; a thin sheet of loose connective tissue covered with mesothelium (simple squamous covering epithelium); rich in blood vessels, lymphatics, and adipose tissue.
A(ii)
• Submucosal (Meissner) plexus: located in the submucosa between the submucosa and the muscularis; together with the myenteric plexus constitutes the local enteric nervous system.
• Myenteric (Auerbach) plexus: located in the connective tissue between the circular and longitudinal muscle sublayers; responsible for local contraction of the muscularis, mixing and propelling the contents of the lumen (peristalsis).
• Both plexuses together form the local enteric nervous system, which functions independently of the CNS; they are composed mainly of nerve cell aggregates forming small parasympathetic ganglia, numerous in regions of greatest motility.
B(i)
The esophagus is not suspended in a cavity but is bound directly to adjacent structures, so instead of a serosa it has a thick adventitia. The adventitia consists of connective tissue containing vessels and nerves but lacks mesothelium, whereas the serosa is covered by mesothelium.
B(ii)
The serosa of the small and large intestines is continuous with parts of the mesentery. The mesentery is a large fold of adipose connective tissue covered on both sides by mesothelium; it suspends the intestines and is continuous with the peritoneum (the serous membrane lining the abdominal cavity).

(A) Describe the vermiform appendix under the headings: A(i) surface anatomy/position A(ii) peritoneal relations A(iii) opening and possible positions.
(B) Explain the clinical basis of tenderness at McBurney's point in appendicitis.
(C) Distinguish the appendix from the rest of the large intestine (colon) in gross and microscopic structure.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The surface marking of the base of the appendix is McBurney's point, at the junction of the lateral one-third and medial two-thirds of a line drawn from the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus. The appendix is attached to the cecum below the ileocaecal valve, and the teniae coli of the cecum converge at the root of the appendix.
A(ii)
The appendix is one of the intraperitoneal parts of the large intestine, suspended by its own mesentery, the mesoappendix.
A(iii)
The appendix opens at the posteromedial aspect of the cecum, about one inch below the ileocaecal junction; its positions include retrocecal, the most common, pelvic, subcecal, preileal, and postileal, the least common.
B
• Deep tenderness at McBurney's point, McBurney's sign, is the clinical sign used to localise inflammation of the appendix, that is, acute appendicitis.
• The appendix is described as an intestinal tonsil because of the abundant lymphatic nodules in its lamina propria, which extend into the submucosa and give it an immune function, similar to the tonsils.
C
• Grossly, the appendix has no teniae coli and shows various shapes and positions, whereas the rest of the colon shows three longitudinal teniae coli, free, mesocolic and omental, which converge at the root of the appendix.
• The colon has haustra (sacculations), because the teniae are shorter than the length of the gut wall, appendices epiploicae (fat-filled peritoneal pouches), and semilunar folds; the appendix lacks these features.
• Microscopically, the appendix has no villi and its crypts (of Lieberkuhn) are less abundant than in the colon.
• The colon's mucosa shows enterocytes with no digestive enzyme production, water and electrolyte reabsorption, deep crypts, a thick mucin layer, and goblet cells that increase in number caudally.
• The appendix has prominent lymphatic nodules in the lamina propria extending into the submucosa, which are far less prominent in the general colon.
• Both the appendix and colon lack villi, unlike the small intestine, but only the appendix is described as functioning analogously to the tonsils.

questions.question:
Describe the region of the ulnar nerve at the elbow:
A(i) Common sites of entrapment
A(ii) Relation to the elbow joint
B. Explain the clinical basis for the ulnar nerve being vulnerable at the elbow.
C. Distinguish between the ulnar nerve's entrapment region at the elbow and the median nerve's carpal tunnel at the wrist.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The most common sites of ulnar nerve entrapment around the elbow are: above the elbow, in the region of the intermuscular septum; the medial epicondylar region; the epicondylar (ulnar) groove; the region of the cubital tunnel; and the point where the nerve exits from flexor carpi ulnaris, where the usual cause of compression is the deep flexor-pronator aponeurosis.
A(ii)
Medially, in relation to the elbow joint, the ulnar nerve passes behind the medial epicondyle and crosses the medial collateral ligament of the joint.
B
• The medial epicondyle of the humerus bears a groove on its posterior aspect specifically for the ulnar nerve, and the medial epicondyle is the larger of the two epicondyles, extending more distally.
• This places the ulnar nerve in a relatively superficial, subcutaneous position as it passes behind the medial epicondyle and through the cubital tunnel region, making it vulnerable to direct trauma and to compression at each of the sites listed above.
• Ulnar nerve injuries are recognised as a distinct item of applied anatomy at the elbow, alongside subluxation/dislocation of the radial head, the carrying angle, olecranon bursitis, avulsion of the medial epicondyle, and dislocation with Volkmann's ischaemic contracture.
C
• The ulnar nerve's entrapment region at the elbow lies behind the medial epicondyle of the humerus, where it crosses the medial collateral ligament of the elbow joint, and where compression is often caused by the deep flexor-pronator aponeurosis as the nerve exits between the heads of flexor carpi ulnaris.
• The median nerve's tunnel at the wrist, the carpal tunnel, differs in that it has a defined bony floor — the carpal sulcus, bounded laterally by the scaphoid and trapezium and medially by the hook of hamate and pisiform — roofed by the fibrous flexor retinaculum.
• The carpal tunnel additionally transmits eight flexor tendons and the tendon of flexor pollicis longus alongside the median nerve, whereas other tendons sharing the ulnar nerve's entrapment site at the elbow are not described.
• Both regions, however, are sites where a single major nerve is placed in a confined space adjacent to bone, predisposing it to compression.
• At the elbow, injury or entrapment of the ulnar nerve is associated with claw hand and sensory/motor deficits in the ulnar nerve distribution of the hand and forearm.
• At the wrist, compression of the median nerve within the carpal tunnel produces carpal tunnel syndrome, with sensory disturbance in the lateral three and a half digits and weakness of the thenar muscles.
• The comparison illustrates a shared anatomical principle, nerve entrapment at a narrow passage, applied to two different nerves at two different levels of the upper limb.

A(i)
Definition and function: Connective tissue derives its name from its function in connecting or binding cells and tissues; it maintains the form of organs throughout the body. Unlike other tissue types (epithelium, muscle, nerve) which consist mainly of cells, the major constituent of connective tissue is the extracellular matrix. The extracellular matrix is composed of protein fibers (collagen, elastic, and reticular fibers), ground substance (a jelly-like, amorphous, anionic, hydrophilic complex of proteoglycans, glycosaminoglycans, and multiadhesive glycoproteins such as laminin and fibronectin), and tissue fluid. Classification: connective tissue is classified as connective tissue proper (loose: areolar, adipose, reticular; dense: regular, irregular, elastic) and specialized connective tissue (blood, cartilage, bone).
A(ii)
The amount of tissue fluid (interstitial fluid) is fairly constant and there is an equilibrium between water entering and leaving the intercellular substance. In pathological conditions (traumatic injury and inflammation), fluid may accumulate in the connective tissue, a condition known as edema.
B(i)
Loose connective tissue: irregularly arranged tissue with abundant ground substance, capable of withstanding stress from many directions; present in dermis, capsules of joints, and submucosa of the alimentary tract. Examples: areolar tissue, adipose tissue. Dense connective tissue: tissue in which fibers predominate; it is organized to withstand forces in specific directions. Dense regular: present in tendons and ligaments. Dense irregular: present in the dermis of skin and capsules of organs.

It arises from the external iliac artery.
A(ii)
• It enters the rectus sheath at the arcuate line.
• It lies beneath the lateral umbilical fold on the internal surface of the anterolateral abdominal wall.
A(iii)
• Branches: cremasteric artery (to the cremasteric muscle) and pubic branch.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the complete path of blood flow through the renal blood vessels, from the aorta to the peritubular capillaries or vasa recta.
A(ii) State the nerve supply to the kidneys and name the source.
B(i) Distinguish between the capillary beds associated with cortical nephrons and those associated with juxtamedullary nephrons.
B(ii) Explain the anatomical basis for high blood pressure in the glomerulus.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Path of blood flow:
• Aorta → Renal artery → Segmental artery → Interlobar artery → Arcuate artery → Cortical radiate artery → Afferent arteriole → Glomerulus (capillaries) → Efferent arteriole → Peritubular capillaries (cortical nephrons) or Vasa recta (juxtamedullary nephrons) → Cortical radiate vein → Arcuate vein → Interlobar vein → Renal vein → Inferior vena cava.
• Renal arteries deliver approximately one-quarter (1,200 ml) of cardiac output to the kidneys each minute.
A(ii)
Nerve supply is via sympathetic fibers from the renal plexus.
B(i)
• Cortical nephrons (85% of nephrons): efferent arteriole supplies peritubular capillaries — low-pressure, porous capillaries adapted for absorption of water and solutes; they cling to adjacent renal tubules in the cortex and empty into venules.
• Juxtamedullary nephrons: efferent arteriole supplies vasa recta — long, thin-walled vessels parallel to the long nephron loops; important in formation of concentrated urine.
B(ii)
Blood pressure in the glomerulus is high because:
• Afferent arterioles are larger in diameter than efferent arterioles.
• Arterioles are high-resistance vessels.
• The glomerulus is fed and drained by arterioles (not venules), which maintains the high filtration pressure. The glomerulus is also specialized for filtration, with fenestrated endothelium that is highly porous, allowing filtrate formation.

questions.question:
Describe the knee joint under the following headings and explain its clinical importance.
A(i) Type, articular surfaces, and articular bones
A(ii) Ligaments — classify as extracapsular or intra-articular; describe each fully
B(i) Movements and muscles responsible
B(ii) Blood supply and nerve supply of the knee joint
C(i) Distinguish the medial from the lateral meniscus, and explain the anatomical basis of why the medial meniscus is more frequently injured
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The knee joint is primarily a hinge type of synovial joint. It is the largest and very complex joint in the body. Articulations: femur with tibia (tibiofemoral joint) and femur with patella (patellofemoral joint). Articular bones: (1) Femur — enlarged medial and lateral femoral condyles. (2) Tibia — enlarged medial and lateral tibial condyles (tibial plateaus), which are the receptacles for the femoral condyles; tibia bears most of the weight. (3) Patella — a true sesamoid bone embedded in the quadriceps and patellar tendon; serves as a pulley improving the angle of pull. Fibula is not part of the knee joint and does not articulate with the femur or patella; it only serves as attachment for knee joint structures.
A(ii)
Extracapsular ligaments (5): (1) Patellar ligament — distal part of quadriceps tendon; strong, thick fibrous band passing from apex of patella to tibial tuberosity. (2) Fibular (lateral) collateral ligament — strong, rounded, cordlike; extends from lateral epicondyle of femur to head of fibula; tendon of popliteus passes deep to it, separating it from the lateral meniscus. (3) Tibial (medial) collateral ligament — strong flat band from medial epicondyle of femur to medial condyle and superior part of tibia; firmly attached to medial meniscus; weaker and more often damaged than the fibular collateral ligament. (4) Oblique popliteal ligament — expansion of tendon of semimembranosus; strengthens fibrous capsule posteriorly. (5) Arcuate popliteal ligament — arises from posterior aspect of fibular head; passes superomedially over tendon of popliteus; strengthens fibrous capsule posteriorly. Intra-articular ligaments (3): (1) ACL — from anterior intercondylar area of tibia to lateral condyle of femur; weaker; slack when flexed, taut when extended; prevents posterior displacement of femur on tibia and hyperextension. (2) PCL — from posterior intercondylar area of tibia to medial condyle of femur; stronger; taut during flexion; prevents anterior displacement of femur on tibia; main stabilizing factor in weight-bearing flexed knee. (3) Menisci — crescentic plates of fibrocartilage that deepen the surface and act as shock absorbers.
B(i)
Flexion — hamstrings. Extension — quadriceps. Medial rotation — popliteus, semitendinosus, semimembranosus. Lateral rotation — biceps femoris. Locking: when fully extended with foot on ground, the knee locks because of medial rotation of femur on tibia. Unlocking: popliteus contracts rotating femur laterally so flexion can occur.
B(ii)
Blood supply: genicular branches of femoral artery, popliteal artery, anterior and posterior recurrent branches of anterior tibial recurrent artery, and anterior and posterior branches of circumflex fibular arteries. The middle genicular branches of the popliteal artery penetrate the fibrous capsule and supply the cruciate ligaments, synovial membrane, and peripheral margins of the menisci. Nerve supply: branches of obturator nerve, femoral nerve, tibial nerve, and common fibular nerve.
C(i)
Medial meniscus: C-shaped, broader posteriorly; anterior end attaches to anterior intercondylar area of tibia anterior to ACL; posterior end to posterior intercondylar area anterior to PCL; firmly adheres to tibial collateral ligament. Lateral meniscus: almost circular, smaller and more freely movable; tendon of popliteus separates it from fibular collateral ligament; attached posteriorly via the posterior meniscofemoral ligament to PCL and medial femoral condyle. The medial meniscus is more frequently injured because its firm attachment to the tibial collateral ligament makes it immobile and liable to being trapped and torn when the ligament is stressed; the lateral meniscus is protected by its free mobility.

(i)
• The right and left coronary arteries are the first branches of the aorta, arising from the corresponding right and left aortic sinuses at the proximal ascending aorta.
• The right coronary artery runs in the atrioventricular (coronary) groove and gives off the SA nodal branch, right marginal branch, AV nodal branch, and posterior interventricular branch, which anastomoses with the anterior interventricular branch of the left coronary artery.
• The right coronary artery typically supplies the right atrium, most of the right ventricle, part of the left ventricle, the posterior third of the AV septum, the SA node in 60% of people and the AV node in 80% of people.
• The left coronary artery arises from the left aortic sinus, runs in the AV groove, and divides into the circumflex and anterior interventricular branches.
• The left coronary artery typically supplies the left atrium, most of the left ventricle, part of the right ventricle, most of the interventricular septum and the SA node in 40% of people.
• Venous drainage is mainly through the coronary sinus, which receives the great, middle and small cardiac veins and the left posterior ventricular and left marginal veins.
(ii)
Arterial dominance is defined by which artery gives rise to the posterior interventricular artery; right dominance is typical, the left is dominant in about 10% of people, and co-dominance occurs in about 15% of people.
(iii)
• Because the right coronary artery mainly supplies the right atrium, right ventricle and, in most people, the SA and AV nodes, its occlusion can damage right-sided myocardium and disturb the conduction system.
• Because the left coronary artery mainly supplies the left atrium, left ventricle and interventricular septum, its occlusion tends to damage the left ventricle, which performs more work than the right, and the septum.
• Damage to the region supplying the SA or AV node can disturb the heart's conducting system, since the SA and AV nodes are the pacesetters of the heart.
• Tissue damage from reduced blood flow in the territory of the affected artery causes the chest pain of ischaemia/infarction, which can radiate as referred pain to the jaw and left arm.

A(ii)
The aortic hiatus lies posterior to the diaphragm, between the two crura, at the level of the lower border of the T12 vertebra; it transmits the aorta, the thoracic duct and sometimes the azygos and hemiazygos veins. Because the aorta does not pierce the diaphragm itself, movements of the diaphragm during respiration do not affect blood flow through it.
A(iii)
The caval opening lies in the central tendon of the diaphragm at the level of T8; it transmits the inferior vena cava, terminal branches of the right phrenic nerve, and a few hepatic lymphatic vessels. The inferior vena cava is adherent to the margin of this opening, so diaphragmatic contraction during inspiration widens the opening and dilates the inferior vena cava, aiding venous return to the heart.
B
• The right and left crura arise from the bodies of the L1-L3 vertebrae, the anterior longitudinal ligament and the intervertebral discs; the oesophageal hiatus lies within the right crus, to the left of the midline, superior to and to the left of the aortic hiatus. Diaphragmatic hernia (sliding and paraoesophageal types) and diaphragmatic rupture are clinical considerations related to weakness or defects around these openings.
• In most individuals, about 70%, both margins of the oesophageal hiatus are formed by muscular bundles of the right crus; in others the left crus contributes to the right margin, and such variation can affect the sphincter-like action around the oesophagus.
C
• The oesophageal hiatus is a muscular opening in the right crus at the level of T10 that actively constricts around the oesophagus with diaphragmatic contraction, contributing to prevention of reflux.
• The aortic hiatus is a non-muscular, fibrous opening bounded by the crura and the median arcuate ligament at the lower border of T12, so diaphragmatic contraction does not compress or affect flow through the aorta.
• The oesophageal hiatus transmits the oesophagus and vagal trunks, whereas the aortic hiatus transmits the aorta and thoracic duct, reflecting their different anatomical roles.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Tibialis anterior: origin — lateral condyle and superior half of lateral surface of tibia and interosseous membrane; insertion — medial and inferior surfaces of medial cuneiform and base of 1st metatarsal; innervation — deep fibular nerve (L4, L5); action — dorsiflexes ankle and inverts foot. Extensor digitorum longus: origin — lateral condyle of tibia and superior 3/4 of medial surface of fibula and interosseous membrane; insertion — middle and distal phalanges of lateral 4 digits; innervation — deep fibular nerve (L4, L5); action — extends lateral 4 digits and dorsiflexes ankle. Extensor hallucis longus: origin — middle part of anterior surface of fibula and interosseous membrane; insertion — dorsal aspect of base of distal phalanx of great toe; innervation — deep fibular nerve (L4, L5); action — extends great toe and dorsiflexes ankle. Fibularis tertius: origin — inferior 3rd of anterior surface of fibula and interosseous membrane; insertion — dorsum of base of 5th metatarsal; innervation — deep fibular nerve (L4, L5); action — dorsiflexes ankle and aids in eversion of foot.
A(ii)
The dorsalis pedis artery begins as the anterior tibial artery enters the foot. It passes over the dorsal aspect of the tarsal bones, then moves inferiorly towards the sole of the foot. It then anastomoses with the lateral plantar artery to form the deep plantar arch. It supplies the tarsal bones and the dorsal aspect of the metatarsals; via the deep plantar arch, it also contributes to the supply of the toes. The dorsalis pedis pulse is found by palpating on the dorsum of the foot, just lateral to extensor hallucis longus tendon.
B(i)
The common fibular nerve is the lateral, smaller terminal branch of the sciatic nerve; it begins at the superior angle of the popliteal fossa, closely follows the medial border of biceps femoris, exits the fossa superficial to the lateral head of gastrocnemius, passes over the posterior aspect of the head of fibula, and winds around the neck of fibula where it divides into its terminal branches — the deep fibular nerve and superficial fibular nerve. The deep fibular nerve supplies all 4 muscles of the anterior compartment (tibialis anterior, extensor digitorum longus, extensor hallucis longus, fibularis tertius) and the foot.
B(ii)
At the neck of fibula the common fibular nerve is subcutaneous and directly palpable, making it vulnerable to direct trauma, compression, or traction. Injury here interrupts the deep fibular nerve before it reaches the anterior compartment. All 4 anterior compartment muscles (which perform dorsiflexion and toe extension) are paralysed. The result is foot drop: the foot hangs in plantarflexion and inversion (because the unopposed plantarflexors — gastrocnemius, soleus — and invertor — tibialis posterior — continue to act), and the patient develops a high-stepping gait to clear the dragging toe.
C(i)
Tibialis anterior: dorsiflexes the ankle AND inverts the foot; supplied by the deep fibular nerve (L4, L5). Fibularis tertius: dorsiflexes the ankle AND aids eversion of the foot; supplied by the deep fibular nerve (L4, L5). Both share the same nerve supply but perform opposite movements about the subtalar axis (inversion vs. eversion), reflecting their positions on opposite sides of the interosseous membrane.
questions.question:
Describe the anterior compartment muscles of the leg and the dorsum of the foot under the following headings, and explain why injury to the deep fibular nerve causes foot drop.

A(ii) The dorsalis pedis artery — origin, course, and branches

questions.answerText:
A(i)
A wide tube about 10 cm long and 2 cm wide, lying in the superior mediastinum and extending from C6 (lower border of the cricoid cartilage) to T4, where it divides into the right and left main bronchi; it has cervical and thoracic parts, the cervical part measuring 5 cm.
A(ii)
• The cervical part is in contact posteriorly with the oesophagus and anteriorly with the isthmus of the thyroid gland; it is palpable in the suprasternal notch midway between the heads of the clavicles; it ends at the sternal angle (T4/5) just to the right of the midline (at T6 in the erect position in full inspiration).
• At the bifurcation the azygos vein arches over the right main bronchus (T4) and the left main bronchus lies in front of the oesophagus (27 cm from the incisor teeth); the cardiac plexus lies on the lowest part of the trachea behind the arch of the aorta.
A(iii)
Right main bronchus: 2.5 cm long, shorter, wider and vertically oriented; left main bronchus: 5 cm long, longer, narrower and horizontally oriented.
A(iv)
• Right main bronchus divides into upper (outside the hilum), middle and lower lobar bronchi, giving 10 bronchopulmonary segments; the left divides within the hilum into 2 lobar bronchi, giving 8 segments; segmental (third-order) bronchi supply the segments.
• The U-shaped cartilage bars of the trachea are replaced by irregular plates in smaller bronchi; the smallest bronchi give bronchioles (under 1 mm), then terminal bronchioles and respiratory bronchioles (about 0.5 mm, with outpouchings where gas exchange occurs), then alveolar ducts, alveolar sacs and alveoli surrounded by capillaries.
A(v)
Trachea: lymphatics drain to the deep cervical and paratracheal lymph nodes; the mucous membrane is supplied by the vagus, which also gives the parasympathetic supply. Lung and bronchi: pulmonary plexuses with vagal (bronchoconstrictor, secretomotor) and sympathetic (bronchodilator) fibres.
B(i)
• The wider, more vertical right main bronchus allows foreign particles to enter it easily; asthma (dyspnoea); pneumonia (bacterial or viral infection of the lung); pulmonary embolism (pulmonary artery obstructed by air, blood clot, fat, tumour cells or foreign particles).
• Abscesses are commoner in the posterior segment of the upper lobe and the apical segment of the lower lobe (most dependent supine); septa between segments limit infection but carcinoma and tuberculosis break through; fibrosis reduces compliance and emphysema reduces elasticity.
C(i)
• Lymph from lung and bronchi passes to the bronchopulmonary (hilar) nodes, then to the superior and inferior tracheobronchial nodes (above and below the tracheal bifurcation), then to the right and left bronchomediastinal trunks.
• The trunks usually end at the junction of the subclavian and internal jugular veins; the right trunk may join other trunks to form the right lymphatic duct and the left may end in the thoracic duct.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the extent, length and parts of the trachea.
A(ii) Describe the relations of the trachea and its level of bifurcation.
A(iii) Compare the right and left main bronchi.
A(iv) Describe the lobar and segmental divisions of the bronchi and the terminal airways.
A(v) Describe the lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of the trachea and bronchi.
B(i) Relate the parts of the bronchial tree to common pathologies.

Describe the femur under the following headings and explain how its zones relate to common pathologies.
A(i) General features, parts, and gross anatomy of the femur
A(ii) The neck of femur — angles of inclination and torsion, and why fracture here causes coxa vara
B(i) Blood supply of the head of femur and why avascular necrosis occurs after intracapsular fracture
B(ii) The linea aspera — muscular and bony attachments, and clinical significance
C(i) Distinguish pressure epiphysis from traction epiphysis with examples from the femur, and explain why the nutrient canal direction matters surgically
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The femur is the long bone of the thigh; the longest and strongest bone in the body (Latin: femur = thigh); it accounts for approximately one-quarter of a person's total height and averages 45 cm. It has a shaft (body) and 2 expanded ends. Parts: (1) proximal end — consisting of head, neck, and the trochanters; (2) shaft; (3) distal end — consisting of the femoral condyles. It articulates superiorly with the acetabulum to form the hip joint, and inferiorly with the patella and tibia to form the knee joint.
A(ii)
The neck is the curved upper end of the shaft; it connects the head to the shaft and passes downward, backward, and laterally, obliquely placed to the long axis of the shaft. The angle of inclination (neck–shaft angle) is approximately 135 degrees; reduction of this angle is coxa vara and follows fracture of the neck of femur. The angle of anteversion (torsion) — the forward relationship of head and neck — is normally 12–15 degrees; wide variation in anteversion of the femoral neck means that during total hip arthroplasty, orientation of the femoral neck osteotomy in correct anteversion must be assessed after hip dislocation with reference to the shaft of femur with knee flexed at 90 degrees, or an inaccurate cut and malposition of the prosthesis may result.
B(i)
The fovea capitis on the head of femur transmits blood from the obturator artery via the ligament of the head of femur (ligamentum teres). The main blood supply travels retinacularly along the intracapsular neck from the medial femoral circumflex artery (which wraps around the posterior side of the femur supplying its neck and head). In an intracapsular fracture, these retinacular vessels are disrupted; the obturator artery contribution via ligamentum teres is insufficient to sustain the head, and avascular necrosis results.
B(ii)
The linea aspera is a posterior ridge on the shaft of femur; it diverges superiorly and inferiorly. The inferior divergence ends as the medial supracondylar ridge to the adductor tubercle and the lateral supracondylar ridge. The linea aspera gives origin to many muscles: adductor longus inserts into the middle third of its medial lip; adductor magnus into the gluteal tuberosity, linea aspera, and medial supracondylar line; the vastus lateralis arises from its lateral lip.
C(i)
Pressure epiphyses are formed at joints and bear compressive forces (e.g., head of femur — a pressure epiphysis; femoral condyles). Traction epiphyses are pulled by muscles (e.g., greater trochanter — traction epiphysis for gluteus medius which draws it upward, medially, and backward; lesser trochanter — traction epiphysis for iliopsoas, the great flexor of the hip joint). The nutrient artery is directed obliquely away from the epiphyseal end; when there is an epiphysis at both ends, the nutrient canal is directed away from the more actively growing end (as per Hughes's rule: 'to the elbow I go, from the knee I flee'). Surgically, the nutrient canal direction matters during intramedullary nail insertion, as the nail must not block the nutrient foramen.

questions.question:
A(i) State the nature and number of the intercostal nerves and distinguish the typical from the atypical nerves.
A(ii) Describe the course and relations of a typical intercostal nerve.
A(iii) State its branches.
A(iv) Describe its distribution, including the cutaneous supply of the thoracic wall.
B(i) State the safe method and site for anaesthetising an intercostal space and for passing a needle or drain.
C(i) Explain the anatomical basis of the effects of irritation or injury of the intercostal nerves.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• 12 pairs of intercostal (thoracic) nerves, the anterior primary rami of the thoracic spinal nerves; they are mixed nerves; T3-6 are typical and T1 and T2 are atypical.
• Atypical nerves: T1 has no anterior cutaneous branch and is joined to the brachial plexus by a large branch corresponding to the lateral cutaneous branch; the lateral cutaneous branch of T2 is the intercostobrachial nerve, joined to the medial cutaneous nerve of the arm.
A(ii)
A typical nerve lies in the neurovascular bundle between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles, high in the space in relation to the subcostal groove of the rib above, below the artery (vein, artery, nerve from above downwards); nerves 1-6 are distributed in the intercostal spaces, 7-11 pass to the anterior abdominal wall, and the anterior ramus of the 12th runs forward in the abdomen as the subcostal nerve.
A(iii)
Branches: rami communicantes, collateral (muscular) branches, lateral cutaneous branch, anterior cutaneous branch, muscular branches, pleural branch and peritoneal branches (7th-11th).
A(iv)
They supply the skin, the muscles of the intercostal space and abdomen, and the parietal pleura and parietal peritoneum; cutaneous supply of the anterior wall is by supraclavicular nerves (C4) above the sternal angle and by the anterior and lateral cutaneous branches below it; the posterior wall is supplied by the posterior rami of the thoracic spinal nerves.
B(i)
• Local anaesthesia of an intercostal space is easily produced by infiltration around the intercostal nerve trunk and its collateral branch (intercostal nerve block).
• A needle or drain is passed immediately above the upper border of a rib, to avoid the neurovascular bundle lying under the rib above.
• In a conventional posterolateral thoracotomy the incision is along the 5th or 6th rib; the periosteum over a segment of the rib is elevated, protecting the neurovascular bundle, and the rib is excised to reach the lung or mediastinum through the intercostal space.
C(i)
• Local irritation of the intercostal nerves (e.g. by Pott's disease, tuberculosis of the thoracic vertebrae) gives pain referred to the front of the chest or abdomen, in the region of the peripheral termination of the nerves.
• Pus from the region of the vertebral column tracks around the thorax along the neurovascular bundle and points at the three sites of exit of the cutaneous branches: lateral to erector spinae, in the midaxillary line and just lateral to the sternum.
• A rib fracture is extremely painful because the periosteum of the rib is supplied by the intercostal nerves above and below the rib; the parietal pleura is segmentally supplied by the intercostal nerves, so pleural disease refers pain along the thoracic wall and anterior abdominal wall.

questions.question: What is the mechanism of richter transformation?
options: CLL transformation to aggressive large B-cell lymphoma
CLL progression to higher Rai stage
questions.explanation: Richter transformation is the development of aggressive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma in CLL patients, occurring in 2-10%. It manifests as rapidly enlarging lymph nodes, B symptoms, elevated LDH, and extranodal disease. Prognosis is poor with median survival <1 year.

questions.question: Which cells are found within the endosteal lining of bone marrow cavities?
questions.explanation: Osteoblasts and osteoclasts are specifically found within the endosteal lining along with bone-lining cells. These cells play crucial roles in bone remodeling and maintenance of the hematopoietic microenvironment. The endosteal lining provides structural support and participates in regulating hematopoietic stem cell activity.

questions.question: During fetal development, the primary site of haemopoiesis from 2-7 months gestation is:
questions.explanation: The liver and spleen are the main sites of haemopoiesis from 2-7 months of gestation. The yolk sac is the primary site from 0-2 months, while bone marrow becomes dominant from 5 months onward. This sequential pattern of haemopoietic site migration is essential for normal fetal development.

The t(15;17) translocation creating PML-RARa fusion is diagnostic of APL (AML-M3). This fusion protein blocks myeloid differentiation at promyelocyte stage. All-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) degrades the fusion protein, inducing differentiation and cure.
questions.question: Which translocation is pathognomonic for acute promyelocytic leukemia?

questions.explanation: G6PD A- affects approximately 15% of African Americans and is a Class III variant with 10-60% residual enzyme activity. It causes episodic moderate hemolysis with oxidative triggers. G6PD A+ is the normal variant in this population.
questions.question: Which G6PD variant is most common in African Americans?
What percentage of CML patients present in chronic phase?
questions.explanation: Approximately 85-90% of CML patients present in chronic phase, often diagnosed incidentally on routine blood counts. Accelerated phase occurs in 10% and blast crisis in <5% at diagnosis. Chronic phase can last years without treatment.

T lymphocytes produce interferon, which induces non-specific resistance to viral infection by inhibiting protein synthesis and inactivating viral RNA. Interferon also enhances phagocytic and cytotoxic activity of immune cells. Multiple interferon types exist with overlapping functions.
questions.question: Which cells produce interferon?

options: Deletion of all four alpha-globin genes
questions.explanation: Deletion of all four alpha genes (--/--) causes Hb Bart's hydrops fetalis, incompatible with life. Only ?4 tetramers (Hb Bart's) form, which have extremely high oxygen affinity, causing severe tissue hypoxia. Affected fetuses develop hydrops (severe anemia, heart failure, edema) and die in utero or shortly after birth.
questions.question: What causes hydrops fetalis in alpha-thalassemia?

questions.explanation: The WHO 2016 classification defines AML by the presence of greater than or equal to 20% blasts in bone marrow or peripheral blood, replacing the FAB threshold of 30%. Exceptions include AML with certain recurrent genetic abnormalities (t(8;21), inv(16), t(15;17)) which are diagnosed regardless of blast percentage.
options: Greater than 10% blasts on two separate occasions
Greater than or equal to 30% as per FAB classification
Greater than 5% with an abnormal karyotype present
Greater than or equal to 20% in all AML subtypes
Greater than 15% with multilineage dysplastic features
questions.question: What percentage of bone marrow blasts by WHO 2016 criteria defines acute myeloid leukaemia?

questions.explanation: Precursor B-ALL shows: CD19+ (pan-B marker), cytoplasmic CD22+, TdT+ (terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase), with variable CD10 (CALLA). Subtyped based on differentiation: early pre-B (CD10-), common ALL (CD10+), pre-B (cytoplasmic µ+). Surface immunoglobulin indicates mature B-cell neoplasm (Burkitt), not precursor ALL.
questions.question: Which immunophenotype indicates precursor B-cell ALL?

questions.explanation: Newborn MCV is elevated (100-120 fL, mean ~108) due to predominance of fetal haemoglobin and rapid cell division. MCV gradually decreases, reaching adult values (80-100 fL) by adolescence. This physiological macrocytosis should not be confused with pathological causes. Understanding age-related normal values prevents unnecessary investigation.
questions.question: Mean corpuscular volume (MCV) in newborns is approximately:

questions.explanation: Hydroxyurea increases HbF production which doesn't participate in sickling, reducing vaso-occlusive crises, acute chest syndrome, and transfusion requirements. Mechanisms include: cytotoxicity to erythroid precursors selecting F-cell producing clones, nitric oxide donation (vasodilation), reduced leucocyte/platelet counts (anti-inflammatory). Side effects include cytopenias (dose-dependent), rarely leg ulcers. Monitoring requires regular blood counts.
questions.question: Hydroxyurea therapy in sickle cell disease works primarily by:

options: To prevent CNS relapse with intrathecal agents
To treat steroid resistance identified after induction
To increase platelet count before maintenance phase
To prepare the patient for bone marrow transplant
To eliminate minimal residual disease below morphological threshold
questions.explanation: Morphological remission (blasts <5%) still leaves approximately 10^8–10^9 leukaemic cells below the detection threshold. Consolidation therapy uses high-dose chemotherapy to eradicate this minimal residual disease burden. Without consolidation, these residual cells are the principal source of eventual relapse. MRD-directed consolidation intensity has become standard in contemporary ALL protocols.
questions.question: A child with ALL achieves morphological remission after induction. What is the rationale for consolidation chemotherapy?
Which intervention reduces hemolytic disease of the newborn?
questions.explanation: Rh immune globulin (RhIG, RhoGAM) given to Rh-negative mothers at 28 weeks gestation and within 72 hours of delivery (if infant Rh-positive) prevents maternal sensitization to fetal Rh-positive cells, reducing hemolytic disease of newborn from 13% to <1%. Also given after miscarriage, abortion, amniocentesis, or any fetal-maternal hemorrhage. Established antibodies cannot be prevented/treated; fetal monitoring and intrauterine transfusion may be needed.

options: Aspirin at therapeutic doses usually safe
questions.explanation: Primaquine (antimalarial), dapsone (antibiotic), rasburicase (uric acid oxidase), and sulfonamides cause severe hemolysis in G6PD deficiency. Many drugs previously thought harmful (aspirin at therapeutic doses, acetaminophen) are actually safe. Fava beans cause severe hemolysis in Mediterranean variant. Comprehensive drug lists are available; avoid oxidant drugs during acute illness.
questions.question: Which medication should be avoided in G6PD deficiency?

questions.explanation: The knee is the most common target joint in hemophilia, followed by ankles and elbows. Recurrent hemarthroses cause chronic synovitis, cartilage damage, and eventually debilitating arthropathy. Prophylactic factor replacement prevents this complication.
questions.question: Which joint is most commonly affected by hemophilic arthropathy?

questions.explanation: Lymphoblasts typically have: scanty agranular basophilic cytoplasm, high nuclear:cytoplasmic ratio, condensed chromatin, and inconspicuous nucleoli. Myeloblasts have: more abundant cytoplasm, fine chromatin, prominent nucleoli, and may contain azurophilic granules or Auer rods (pathognomonic for myeloid lineage). Immunophenotyping definitively distinguishes them.
questions.question: What distinguishes lymphoblasts from myeloblasts morphologically?
What is the role of ADAMTS-13 in VWF metabolism?
options: Cleavage of ultra-large multimers to smaller forms
Synthesis of VWF multimers in endothelial cells
Enhancement of VWF binding to Factor VIII
Promotion of VWF release from Weibel-Palade bodies
Protection of VWF from premature degradation
questions.explanation: ADAMTS-13 is a metalloprotease that cleaves ultra-large VWF multimers at the Tyr1605-Met1606 bond. This regulates multimer size and prevents spontaneous platelet aggregation. ADAMTS-13 deficiency causes thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura from uncleaved ultra-large multimers.

questions.question: What percentage of Castleman disease cases are multicentric?
questions.explanation: Castleman disease can be either unicentric (localized to one lymph node region) or multicentric (affecting several nodal areas) with variable distribution. The multicentric form has worse prognosis and systemic symptoms. HHV-8 association is stronger in multicentric disease.

Haemorrhagic disease of newborn results from vitamin K deficiency (factors II, VII, IX, X). Newborns have low vitamin K (poor placental transfer, sterile gut, low breast milk content). Classic form (days 2-7) and late form (weeks 2-12, breastfed infants) occur. Prevented by prophylactic vitamin K at birth (IM preferred over oral). Presents with bleeding, prolonged PT/aPTT.
questions.question: Neonatal haemorrhagic disease results from deficiency of:

options: Increased toxicity for better tumor kill
Reduced toxicity for older patients, GVL-reliant
questions.question: What is the role of reduced-intensity conditioning in transplant?
questions.explanation: Reduced-intensity conditioning (RIC, "mini-transplant") uses lower-dose chemotherapy/radiation sufficient for engraftment but relying on graft-versus-malignancy effect for disease control rather than pre-transplant cytoreduction. Advantages: lower toxicity, permits transplant in older patients (>60-70) or those with comorbidities. Disadvantages: higher relapse risk (especially in aggressive diseases), mixed chimerism more common. Best for diseases sensitive to GVL effect.

options: M-protein level and plasma cell percentage
Number of bone lesions on imaging
questions.explanation: ISS uses serum beta-2 microglobulin and albumin: Stage I (β2M <3.5 mg/L, albumin ≥3.5 g/dL), Stage II (neither I nor III), Stage III (β2M ≥5.5 mg/L). Revised ISS adds cytogenetics and LDH. These reflect tumor burden and prognosis.
questions.question: What does the International Staging System (ISS) for myeloma use?
What is the normal platelet count range?
questions.explanation: Normal platelet count is 150,000-450,000/µL (150-450 × 10⁹/L). Thrombocytopenia is <150,000/µL. Spontaneous bleeding risk increases markedly when platelets fall below 20,000/µL. Thrombocytosis is >450,000/µL, which may be reactive or clonal.

Transient erythroblastopenia of childhood (TEC) is acquired temporary red cell aplasia in previously healthy children aged 1-4 years, often post-viral. Presents with severe anaemia, reticulocytopenia, absent erythroid precursors. Distinguishing from Diamond-Blackfan: TEC has later onset, normal HbF/MCV, no congenital abnormalities. Spontaneous recovery in 1-2 months; transfusion only if symptomatic. Differentiation from parvovirus requires serology.
questions.question: Transient erythroblastopenia of childhood typically occurs at what age?

options: Von Willebrand disease; normal ristocetin aggregation rules out VWD
Glanzmann thrombasthenia; absent aggregation from GpIIb/IIIa deficiency
Bernard-Soulier syndrome; confirms deficiency of GpIb-IX-V complex
Platelet storage pool disease; absent dense granule ADP release causing aggregation failure
Afibrinogenaemia; fibrinogen required for platelet-platelet bridging via GpIIb/IIIa
questions.question: A 19-year-old woman has lifelong mucocutaneous bleeding, platelet count 280 × 10⁹/L, normal PT and APTT, and platelet aggregation showing absent aggregation with ADP, collagen, arachidonic acid, and adrenaline but normal aggregation with ristocetin. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Glanzmann thrombasthenia is an autosomal recessive disorder of quantitative or qualitative deficiency of platelet GpIIb/IIIa (integrin alphaIIbbeta3), the receptor that binds fibrinogen to mediate platelet-platelet aggregation. Without GpIIb/IIIa, platelets adhere to injured vessel walls normally (GpIb-IX-V is intact - hence normal ristocetin aggregation, which tests GpIb/VWF interaction) but cannot aggregate with each other regardless of the agonist used. All agonists (ADP, collagen, arachidonic acid, adrenaline) require GpIIb/IIIa for the final aggregation step. Treatment for major bleeds uses recombinant FVIIa or platelet transfusion; HLA-matched platelets are preferred to avoid alloimmunisation.

questions.question: Which JAK2 inhibitor is FDA-approved for myelofibrosis?
questions.explanation: Ruxolitinib, a JAK1/2 inhibitor, is FDA-approved for intermediate-2 and high-risk myelofibrosis, reducing spleen size and improving symptoms in ~50% regardless of JAK2 mutation status. It doesn't reverse fibrosis or alter disease natural history but significantly improves quality of life. Fedratinib is a second JAK2 inhibitor option.

questions.question: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia is characterized by accumulation of which cell type?
questions.explanation: CLL involves clonal proliferation of mature-appearing small B lymphocytes accumulating in blood, bone marrow, lymph nodes, and spleen. Cells express CD5, CD19, CD20, and CD23. The disease is often asymptomatic and found incidentally on routine blood counts showing absolute lymphocytosis. Smudge cells on blood film are characteristic.

questions.question: A patient with iron deficiency anaemia is started on oral ferrous sulphate. Which finding confirms an adequate response at 2 weeks?
questions.explanation: The earliest objective marker of response to iron therapy is a reticulocytosis, typically peaking around 7-10 days. Haemoglobin and MCV normalise more slowly over weeks, and ferritin should not be checked early as it is an acute phase reactant.

Phlebotomy (venesection) is first-line treatment for hemochromatosis, removing 500 ml blood weekly (containing 200-250 mg iron) until iron depletion. Treatment continues until ferritin <50 mcg/L and transferrin saturation <50%. Iron chelation is reserved for anemic patients.
questions.question: What is first-line treatment for hemochromatosis?
Osmotic fragility testing is abnormal in:
questions.explanation: Osmotic fragility test incubates red cells in decreasing saline concentrations. Spherocytes (reduced surface/volume ratio) lyse at higher concentrations than normal cells. Increased osmotic fragility occurs in hereditary spherocytosis, confirming diagnosis. Eosin-5-maleimide (EMA) binding flow cytometry is more sensitive. Thalassaemia shows decreased fragility (flatter cells).

questions.question: A patient with HbSC disease undergoes a routine eye examination. Which complication is this genotype particularly prone to compared to HbSS disease?
questions.explanation: Despite generally milder systemic disease, HbSC disease carries a higher relative risk of proliferative sickle retinopathy than HbSS disease, possibly related to higher haemoglobin and blood viscosity. Regular ophthalmological screening is therefore important.

The Rai staging system (0-IV) is used in the United States: Stage 0 (lymphocytosis only), I (lymphadenopathy), II (splenomegaly/hepatomegaly), III (anemia Hb<11), IV (thrombocytopenia <100,000). Binet staging (A-C) is used in Europe. Both predict prognosis.
questions.question: Which staging system is used for CLL in the United States?
What is the mechanism of renal failure in myeloma?
options: Tubular damage from light chain casts
questions.explanation: Myeloma kidney (cast nephropathy) results from filtered free light chains precipitating with Tamm-Horsfall protein in distal tubules, forming casts that obstruct tubules and cause inflammation. Light chains are also directly toxic to tubular cells. Additional factors include hypercalcemia, dehydration, and NSAIDs.

Cold agglutinin disease features IgM antibodies that bind red cells maximally at 4°C, causing agglutination and complement-mediated hemolysis. Direct Coombs test shows complement (C3d) coating. Mycoplasma infection or lymphoproliferative disorders may trigger production.
questions.question: What characterizes cold agglutinin disease?

questions.explanation: Inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-1, TNF-α) stimulate hepatic hepcidin production in ACD. Elevated hepcidin binds ferroportin causing its degradation, blocking iron export from macrophages and enterocytes. This creates functional iron deficiency despite adequate stores, contributing significantly to anaemia. Hepcidin is the master regulator linking inflammation to iron metabolism.
questions.question: The primary mediator of functional iron deficiency in anaemia of chronic disease is:
Febrile neutropenia is defined as neutrophil count below:
questions.explanation: Febrile neutropenia is neutrophils <0.5×10⁹/L (or <1.0 expected to fall <0.5) with fever ≥38.3°C once or ≥38.0°C sustained >1 hour. Medical emergency requiring immediate empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics (antipseudomonal β-lactam ± aminoglycoside) after cultures. Mortality risk stratified by MASCC score. G-CSF in high-risk patients. Common in chemotherapy; prevention includes primary G-CSF prophylaxis for high-risk regimens.

Hydroxyurea increases HbF production, which doesn't participate in HbS polymerization, thereby reducing sickling. Additional benefits include reduced leucocyte count (anti-inflammatory effect), increased red cell hydration, decreased adhesiveness, and nitric oxide release causing vasodilatation. It significantly reduces painful crises, acute chest syndrome, and transfusion requirements.
questions.question: Hydroxyurea benefits sickle cell disease primarily by:
Scurvy (vitamin C deficiency) causes which haematological abnormality?
questions.explanation: Vitamin C deficiency impairs collagen synthesis causing capillary fragility, bleeding (gums, skin, joints), and defective iron absorption (vitamin C enhances non-haem iron absorption). Anaemia results from bleeding and impaired iron utilization. Features include perifollicular haemorrhages, corkscrew hairs, bleeding gums, poor wound healing. Diagnosis is clinical (dietary history, signs). Treatment is vitamin C supplementation with rapid response.

questions.question: A woman with beta-thalassaemia major requires pre-transfusion haemoglobin maintenance. What is the optimal pre-transfusion haemoglobin target?
questions.explanation: The pre-transfusion haemoglobin target in thalassaemia major is 9–10.5 g/dL. This level adequately suppresses ineffective erythropoiesis (preventing bone marrow expansion, skeletal deformity, and extramedullary haematopoiesis) while minimising the total volume of blood transfused and associated iron loading. Keeping haemoglobin consistently above 9 g/dL has been shown to normalise growth and quality of life without causing excessive iron overload from over-transfusion.
options: 5–6 g/dL to minimise total transfusion requirements
7–8 g/dL to maintain basic growth and development
11–12 g/dL to achieve completely normal haemoglobin levels
9–10.5 g/dL to optimally suppress ineffective erythropoiesis
13–14 g/dL to suppress all bone marrow erythropoiesis

questions.explanation: Ankyrin deficiency is the most common molecular cause of hereditary spherocytosis, accounting for approximately 50% of cases with autosomal dominant inheritance. Ankyrin provides the critical vertical linkage anchoring spectrin to Band 3 (the major integral membrane protein) in the lipid bilayer. Loss of this vertical support causes membrane lipid loss as the bilayer detaches from the skeleton, reducing surface area and transforming the biconcave disc into a rigid sphere. Spherocytes have increased osmotic fragility and are trapped and destroyed in the splenic red pulp.
options: Ankyrin deficiency disrupting vertical spectrin-Band 3 linkage
Glycophorin C loss reducing lateral membrane support
Protein 4.2 deficiency impairing ion channel anchoring
Alpha-spectrin mutation causing asymmetric membrane bending
Spectrin dimer-dimer self-association failure reducing horizontal stability
questions.question: A 7-year-old Northern European boy has spherocytes on blood film, mild jaundice, splenomegaly, positive osmotic fragility, and reticulocytes 8%. Which structural protein defect is most commonly responsible?
A 52-year-old woman with TRALI (transfusion-related acute lung injury) developed after receiving a blood transfusion. Which is the most specific laboratory finding that confirms TRALI?
questions.explanation: Transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI) is caused by passive transfer of donor anti-HLA class I/II antibodies or anti-neutrophil antibodies (anti-HNA antibodies) that bind to recipient leucocytes in the pulmonary vasculature, triggering neutrophil activation, endothelial damage, and non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema within 6 hours of transfusion. Demonstration of donor-specific anti-HLA or anti-HNA antibodies in the implicated donor blood product that match recipient HLA antigens (or neutrophil antigens) is the most specific confirmatory finding. TRALI is a leading cause of transfusion-related fatality; the blood service should be notified and the donor investigated.
options: Elevated BNP and troponin confirming cardiac involvement
Anti-HLA class I/II or anti-neutrophil antibodies in the implicated donor blood
Elevated ferritin and D-dimer confirming systemic inflammatory activation
CD4+ T-cell lymphocytosis in the BAL fluid confirming T-cell-mediated injury
Positive Coombs test on recipient cells confirming antibody-mediated damage

questions.question: A 60-year-old with MDS has Hb 7.5 g/dL and serum EPO 150 U/L. Which treatment is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Lower-risk MDS with anemia, EPO <500 U/L, and lower transfusion burden may respond to ESA (+ G-CSF). EPO 150 U/L suggests likely response. Alternative: lenalidomide if del(5q). Supportive transfusions if ESA fails. Transplant reserved for higher-risk or younger fit patients. Regular transfusions require iron chelation monitoring.
options: Red cell transfusions without other therapy

questions.question: What percentage of AML cases show clonal chromosomal abnormalities?
questions.explanation: Clonal chromosomal abnormalities are detected in 80-90% of acute myeloid leukemia patients using conventional cytogenetics and molecular techniques. These abnormalities have prognostic and therapeutic implications. The detection rate increases with more sensitive molecular methods.

questions.question: How much iron is lost during menstruation?
questions.explanation: Women lose 15-40 mg of iron per menstruation, significantly increasing their iron requirements compared to men. Pregnancy requires approximately 500 mg additional iron. These physiological losses predispose women to iron deficiency.

questions.question: What ABO blood group is the universal plasma donor for emergency fresh frozen plasma transfusion?
options: Group AB with no anti-A or anti-B antibodies
Group A with low-titre anti-B antibodies only
Group B with low-titre anti-A antibodies only
Group O with only anti-A and anti-B of IgM class
Group O with high-titre anti-A and anti-B
questions.explanation: Group AB plasma contains no anti-A or anti-B antibodies, making it safe for transfusion to any ABO group recipient without risk of haemolytic reaction. This makes AB plasma the universal donor for FFP and other plasma products. This is the opposite of red cell universal donation (Group O), because it is the PLASMA antibodies (not red cell antigens) that are relevant for plasma products. Many trauma centres maintain stocks of AB-positive FFP for emergency use.

options: Factor VIII inhibitor causing acquired hemophilia
Factor IX deficiency from inherited mutation
Von Willebrand disease with Factor VIII reduction
questions.question: A 28-year-old presents with extensive DVT and family history of thrombosis. Mixing studies fail to correct prolonged aPTT. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Lupus anticoagulant causes in vitro prolongation of aPTT that fails to correct with mixing studies, but paradoxically increases thrombosis risk in vivo. This is characteristic of antiphospholipid syndrome. The family history and thrombosis exclude bleeding disorders.

options: Hepatocytes and bone marrow megakaryocytes exclusively
Bone marrow stromal cells and fibroblasts
Splenic macrophages and liver Kupffer cells
questions.question: Where is von Willebrand factor synthesized?
questions.explanation: VWF is synthesized exclusively in endothelial cells (where it's stored in Weibel-Palade bodies) and megakaryocytes (stored in alpha granules). Endothelial synthesis provides the major circulating pool. Platelet VWF is released at sites of vascular injury.

questions.question: Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria diagnosis is confirmed by:
questions.explanation: Flow cytometry detecting deficiency of GPI-anchored proteins (CD55, CD59) on red cells, granulocytes, monocytes is diagnostic standard for PNH. Sensitive, specific, quantifies clone size. Ham's test and sucrose lysis (historical) are obsolete, less sensitive. PNH results from acquired PIG-A mutation causing absent GPI anchor synthesis.
