options: ABO/Rh typing if not previously done
questions.question: Which test is performed before EVERY transfusion?
questions.explanation: An immediate-spin crossmatch (or computer crossmatch if antibody screen negative) is performed before EVERY transfusion to confirm ABO compatibility. This rapid test (5-10 minutes) detects ABO incompatibility. Full crossmatch (37°C incubation, antiglobulin phase) is done if antibody screen is positive.

questions.question: A patient develops fever and rigors within 30 minutes of starting a blood transfusion, without haemoglobinuria or hypotension. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Febrile non-haemolytic transfusion reactions are the most common transfusion reaction, caused by cytokines from donor white cells or platelets. They present with fever and rigors without the haemodynamic instability or haemoglobinuria seen in haemolytic reactions.

Red bone marrow constitutes approximately 80% of bone tissue in adults, with yellow marrow comprising the remaining 20%. Red marrow is the hematopoietically active component containing stem cells and developing blood cells. Yellow marrow primarily stores fat.
questions.question: What percentage of bone marrow is red (hematopoietic) marrow?
An elderly patient is found incidentally to have lymphocytosis with smudge cells on blood film and no symptoms. What is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.explanation: Early-stage, asymptomatic chronic lymphocytic leukaemia is typically managed with active surveillance, as early treatment has not shown survival benefit. Treatment is reserved for progressive, symptomatic, or advanced-stage disease.

As little as 10-20 ml of ABO-incompatible blood can cause fatal acute hemolytic reaction. Severity increases with volume transfused. Clerical errors are the commonest cause. Stringent identification procedures at bedside prevent most cases.
questions.question: What volume of incompatible blood can cause fatal reaction?
A toddler with pica and lethargy has Hb 7.2 g/dL, MCV 65 fL, and a raised blood lead level. Which mechanism links lead toxicity to this anaemia?
questions.explanation: Lead inhibits ferrochelatase and ALA dehydratase, key enzymes in haem biosynthesis, producing a microcytic anaemia resembling iron deficiency. Pica increases lead ingestion risk in children. Basophilic stippling on blood film supports this diagnosis.

questions.question: Which complication is specific to acute promyelocytic leukemia treatment?
options: Tumor lysis syndrome from rapid cell death
questions.explanation: Differentiation syndrome (formerly called retinoic acid syndrome) occurs in 15-25% of APL patients treated with ATRA. It manifests as fever, respiratory distress, pulmonary infiltrates, pleural/pericardial effusions, and renal failure. High-dose steroids are treatment. It can be fatal if unrecognized.

questions.question: What is the role of C3a and C5a?
questions.explanation: C3a and C5a are anaphylatoxins that cause massive mobilization of neutrophils and macrophages to injury sites through chemotaxis. They also activate mast cells and basophils, releasing histamine and heparin. These fragments potentiate inflammation.

questions.question: A 52-year-old woman has macro-ovalocytes, hypersegmented neutrophils (>5 lobes in >5% of cells), and MCV 112 fL. Serum B12 is 89 pg/mL with no dietary restriction or GI disease. What is the most likely cause?
options: Dietary vitamin B12 deficiency from strict veganism over many years
Terminal ileal Crohn's disease impairing B12 absorption
Pernicious anaemia from autoimmune gastric parietal cell destruction
Metformin-induced B12 malabsorption from ileal receptor inhibition
Chronic alcoholism suppressing B12 utilisation in bone marrow cells
questions.explanation: Pernicious anaemia (PA) is the most common cause of vitamin B12 deficiency in developed countries. PA is an autoimmune condition where gastric parietal cell destruction (anti-parietal cell antibodies in ~90%, anti-intrinsic factor antibodies in ~50%) eliminates intrinsic factor, the glycoprotein essential for ileal absorption of B12. The megaloblastic picture results from impaired DNA synthesis, producing large oval cells and hypersegmented neutrophils. Treatment is lifelong intramuscular hydroxocobalamin injections, as no intrinsic factor means oral supplements cannot be reliably absorbed.

Heinz bodies and blister cells are characteristic findings during hemolytic crisis in G6PD deficiency. These represent denatured hemoglobin precipitates that form under oxidative stress. The blood film may also show contracted and fragmented cells.
questions.question: Which cells are characteristically seen in G6PD deficiency during crisis?
What defines high-risk ALL in children?
questions.explanation: High-risk features in pediatric ALL include: age <1 or >10 years, WBC >50,000/µL, T-cell phenotype, CNS/testicular involvement, poor early response, and adverse genetics (Ph+, MLL-rearranged, hypodiploidy). These factors guide treatment intensification.

The RH locus is located on chromosome 1, consisting of two closely linked genes: RHD and RHCE. The alleles of RHCE are CE, Ce, ce, and cE. Deletions or mutations of the RHD gene result in Rh-negative phenotype.
questions.question: What chromosome carries the RH gene locus?

questions.explanation: Normal haemoglobin for adult males is 13.0-17.0 g/dL (130-170 g/L). For females, it's 12.0-16.0 g/dL (120-160 g/L). Values below these ranges define anaemia according to WHO criteria. These sex differences reflect androgen effects on erythropoiesis and differences in blood volume.
questions.question: The normal reference range for haemoglobin in adult males is:

questions.explanation: HbH disease (--/-α) results from deletion of three α-genes, leaving only one functional gene. Excess β-chains form β4 tetramers (HbH), which precipitate causing haemolysis and ineffective erythropoiesis. Patients have moderate haemolytic anaemia, splenomegaly, and require occasional transfusions. "Golf ball" cells with multiple HbH inclusions appear with supravital staining.
questions.question: HbH disease results from deletion of how many β-globin genes?

questions.explanation: Fetal hemoglobin (HbF) consists of two alpha and two gamma chains (α2γ2). HbF has higher oxygen affinity than adult hemoglobin, facilitating placental oxygen transfer. Gamma chain synthesis decreases after birth as beta chain production increases.
questions.question: Which globin chains are present in fetal hemoglobin?

questions.explanation: Rouleaux formation is not characteristic of hyposplenism and instead suggests increased plasma proteins or inflammation. Hyposplenism shows target cells, acanthocytes, Howell-Jolly bodies, Pappenheimer bodies, and sometimes lymphocytosis and thrombocytosis. These inclusions normally removed by functioning spleen.
questions.question: Which finding is NOT characteristic of hyposplenism?

options: Slow growth rate requiring minimal therapy
questions.explanation: Burkitt leukemia/lymphoma is characterized by t(8;14)(80%) or variant translocations t(2;8), t(8;22) that place MYC adjacent to immunoglobulin loci, causing MYC overexpression. This causes extremely rapid proliferation. Intensive short-duration chemotherapy is curative in most children.
questions.question: Which feature distinguishes Burkitt leukemia/lymphoma?

options: Cladribine (2-CdA); purine analogue achieving durable complete remission in >80%
Rituximab monotherapy; anti-CD20 antibody achieves remission in most HCL patients
Splenectomy; historically first-line treatment before modern chemotherapy
Interferon-alpha; the historical treatment still used for pregnant patients with HCL
Pentostatin (2'-deoxycoformycin); equally effective but more toxic than cladribine
questions.question: A 38-year-old man with hairy cell leukaemia has pancytopenia and a dry tap on bone marrow aspiration. Trephine shows mononuclear cells with abundant pale cytoplasm (fried-egg appearance) and positive TRAP stain. What is the first-line treatment?
questions.explanation: Hairy cell leukaemia (HCL) is a rare indolent B-cell malignancy named for the cytoplasmic hair-like projections on leukaemic cells, with characteristic TRAP stain positivity and BRAF V600E mutation in >95%. The bone marrow typically shows fried-egg infiltration (cells with abundant pale cytoplasm separated by clear spaces) and causes a dry tap due to fibrosis. Cladribine (2-chlorodeoxyadenosine, 2-CdA) is the treatment of choice: a single 5-7 day course achieves complete remission in >80% of patients with 10-year relapse-free survival >80%, making it one of the most effective treatments in oncology. Rituximab is added for refractory or relapsed cases.

Severe haemophilia A (factor VIII <1%) causes spontaneous joint bleeds; acute haemarthrosis requires prompt factor VIII concentrate replacement to achieve 50-80% factor VIII activity for joint bleeds (80-100% for life-threatening bleeds). Recombinant factor VIII concentrates are preferred where available. DDAVP raises factor VIII by releasing endothelial vWF stores - it is only effective in mild-moderate haemophilia A (not severe, as these patients have essentially no factor VIII to release). Cryoprecipitate and FFP contain factor VIII but in variable and lower concentrations; factor concentrates are the standard of care.
options: Desmopressin (DDAVP) to increase endogenous factor VIII release from endothelium
Factor VIII concentrate to achieve 50-80% factor VIII activity levels
Recombinant FVIIa to bypass the intrinsic pathway factor VIII deficiency
Cryoprecipitate as first-line replacement for acute haemophilia A bleeds
Fresh frozen plasma as the most rapidly available source of factor VIII
questions.question: A 40-year-old man with severe haemophilia A (FVIII <1%) has acute haemarthrosis of the left knee. What is the correct immediate treatment?
A blood film from a patient shows a positive DAT (IgG). On crossmatch with a blood unit, the crossmatch is incompatible. What is the most appropriate next step in the blood bank?
questions.explanation: A positive DAT indicates IgG or complement is coating the patient's red cells in vivo. Elution removes the coating antibodies from the patient's red cells by heating or acid treatment, concentrating them for identification. The eluate is then tested against a panel of group O red cells with known antigen profiles to identify the specificity - revealing whether this is an autoantibody (AIHA) or an alloantibody (delayed haemolytic transfusion reaction). Additionally, the patient's serum must be adsorbed to remove the autoantibody before testing for clinically significant alloantibodies. A positive DAT causing an incompatible crossmatch is most commonly due to AIHA.
options: Report ABO incompatibility error; send both donor and recipient samples for repeat ABO typing
Perform antibody elution and identification from the patient's DAT-positive red cells
Immediately provide uncrossmatched O negative blood as no compatible blood can be found
Type the patient's cells with anti-A and anti-B only; DAT positivity is irrelevant to ABO typing
Crossmatch with the intended unit first; if compatible, no further investigation needed

questions.explanation: RAEB-2 is defined as 10-19% blasts in bone marrow or 5-19% in blood (RAEB-1 is 5-9% in marrow, 2-4% in blood). At ≥20% blasts, diagnosis changes to acute myeloid leukemia by WHO criteria. RAEB has higher transformation risk (~25% at 2 years) and worse prognosis than lower-risk MDS.
questions.question: What defines refractory anemia with excess blasts-2 (RAEB-2)?
options: Any blast percentage with Auer rods

questions.explanation: R-CHOP (rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisone) every 21 days for 6-8 cycles is standard treatment. Addition of rituximab improved cure rates from 45% to 60-70%. R-CHOP cures most limited-stage and approximately half of advanced-stage DLBCL.
questions.question: What is the standard treatment for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma?
A patient with severe haemophilia A develops a target joint with recurrent haemarthrosis. What is the most appropriate long-term preventive strategy?
questions.explanation: Prophylactic regular factor VIII replacement reduces the frequency of joint bleeds and prevents progressive haemophilic arthropathy, compared to on-demand treatment which is reserved for milder disease or where prophylaxis is unavailable.

questions.question: What characterizes hemophilia A?
questions.explanation: Hemophilia A results from factor VIII deficiency due to X-linked recessive inheritance. Severity correlates with factor level: severe (<1%), moderate (1-5%), mild (5-40%). Bleeding into joints (hemarthrosis) and muscles characterizes severe disease.

questions.question: A 34-year-old man donates 470 mL of whole blood and feels faint. Which physiological mechanism initially maintains his blood pressure in the first minutes after donation?
questions.explanation: The immediate cardiovascular response to acute blood volume loss is baroreceptor (carotid sinus and aortic arch) detection of reduced arterial stretch, triggering sympathetic nervous system activation: increased heart rate, increased myocardial contractility, and peripheral vasoconstriction - all to maintain cardiac output and blood pressure. Plasma volume restitution begins within minutes but takes 24-72 hours for full compensation. Hepatic albumin synthesis takes days; EPO-stimulated erythropoiesis takes 5-7 days to increase reticulocyte count. After whole blood donation, haemoglobin takes 4-8 weeks to fully recover.
options: EPO-mediated stimulation of erythropoiesis within 30 minutes of donation
Rapid plasma volume replacement from hepatic albumin synthesis
Baroreceptor-mediated sympathetic activation causing vasoconstriction and tachycardia
Activation of the renin-angiotensin system promoting renal sodium retention
Splenic contraction releasing stored red cells into the general circulation

questions.question: A 55-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes has normochromic normocytic anaemia (Hb 9.4 g/dL), low reticulocytes, normal iron studies, elevated ferritin 460 ng/mL, ESR 88 mm/hr, and elevated CRP. What is the mechanism of her anaemia?
questions.explanation: Anaemia of chronic disease (ACD) or anaemia of inflammation results from chronic inflammatory state: inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-1, TNF-alpha) stimulate hepatic hepcidin production (the master iron regulator), which degrades ferroportin on duodenal enterocytes and macrophages, blocking both intestinal iron absorption and release of iron from macrophage stores. This creates functional iron restriction - iron is trapped in macrophages (ferritin elevated) while insufficient iron reaches erythroid precursors. IL-6, IL-13, and IFN-gamma also directly suppress erythropoiesis and EPO production. The result is normochromic normocytic anaemia with low reticulocytes, elevated ferritin, low TIBC, and low transferrin saturation.
options: Iron deficiency masked by elevated ferritin from concurrent hepatic inflammation
Renal anaemia from diabetic nephropathy reducing erythropoietin synthesis
Anaemia of chronic disease from inflammatory cytokines suppressing erythropoiesis and causing functional iron restriction
Haemolysis from elevated haemolytic markers in the inflammatory state
Bone marrow suppression from chronic hyperglycaemia impairing erythropoiesis

questions.question: What is the most important laboratory test to monitor during ATRA treatment for APL?
options: Factor VIII levels for haemostatic monitoring purposes
WBC count to detect differentiation syndrome development early
Retinoic acid syndrome markers such as LDH and uric acid
Bone marrow blasts percentage assessed weekly during therapy
Fibrinogen for DIC occurring during blast differentiation
questions.explanation: Differentiation syndrome occurs in up to 25% of APL patients receiving ATRA or arsenic trioxide. It results from cytokine release by differentiating APL cells causing fluid retention, respiratory failure, and renal impairment. The earliest warning sign is a rising WBC above 10,000/µL, which prompts prophylactic dexamethasone. All patients are monitored with daily WBC counts during early APL treatment.

Hemoglobinuria (free hemoglobin in urine causing dark red/brown color) indicates acute intravascular hemolysis. Other findings: fever, chills, back/chest/abdominal pain, hypotension, bleeding (DIC), renal failure. Laboratory: positive DAT, hemoglobinemia, decreased haptoglobin, elevated LDH and indirect bilirubin. Clerical check reveals ABO incompatibility.
options: Shortness of breath from fluid overload
questions.question: Which finding indicates acute hemolytic transfusion reaction?

questions.explanation: Glanzmann thrombasthenia is autosomal recessive deficiency of GPIIb/IIIa (integrin αIIbβ3), the fibrinogen receptor, preventing platelet aggregation. Platelet count and morphology are normal but aggregation studies show absent response to all agonists except ristocetin. Features include mucocutaneous bleeding, prolonged bleeding time. Treatment includes platelet transfusions, antifibrinolytics, recombinant factor VIIa.
questions.question: Glanzmann thrombasthenia involves deficiency of which platelet glycoprotein?
Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) characteristically presents with:
questions.explanation: Visceral leishmaniasis presents with fever, massive splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, pancytopenia (bone marrow infiltration, hypersplenism), hypergammaglobulinaemia. Endemic in South Asia, East Africa, Mediterranean, South America. Diagnosis: amastigotes in bone marrow/splenic aspirate, serology, PCR. Treatment: liposomal amphotericin B, miltefosine. Untreated mortality is high. Post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis occurs after treatment.

questions.question: Where does the majority of hemoglobin synthesis occur?
questions.explanation: Approximately 65% of hemoglobin synthesis occurs in erythroblasts, with the remaining 35% in reticulocytes. This distribution reflects the cellular capacity for protein synthesis at different maturation stages. Mature erythrocytes cannot synthesize hemoglobin.

Lead and other heavy metals inhibit both ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase in heme synthesis. This dual inhibition causes accumulation of intermediates and impaired hemoglobin production. Lead poisoning manifests with basophilic stippling and anemia.
questions.question: Heavy metals primarily inhibit which heme synthesis enzymes?
A 65-year-old woman with AML receives high-dose cytarabine (HiDAC) as consolidation. What mechanism makes high-dose cytarabine more effective than standard dose in AML?
options: HiDAC saturates intracellular deaminase enzymes preventing cytarabine inactivation
HiDAC saturates the nucleoside transport system ensuring maximum intracellular accumulation
HiDAC bypasses MDR1-mediated drug efflux by non-transporter-dependent entry at high concentrations
HiDAC increases ara-CTP (active metabolite) accumulation by saturating deoxycytidine kinase
HiDAC causes more extensive DNA strand breaks activating irreversible apoptosis
questions.explanation: Cytarabine (ara-C) must be converted intracellularly to its active triphosphate form (ara-CTP) by deoxycytidine kinase (dCK). At standard doses, the limited dCK enzyme activity is not saturated, and much cytarabine is inactivated by cytidine deaminase. At high doses (>=1-3 g/m2), dCK is saturated, maximising ara-CTP formation and achieving intracellular concentrations that are difficult to metabolise. The high ara-CTP competes more effectively with dCTP for incorporation into DNA, causing chain termination and DNA strand breaks that overwhelm repair mechanisms. HiDAC achieves better responses in refractory AML and is standard for consolidation in favourable-risk AML due to superior CNS penetration.

questions.question: Which finding indicates CML transformation to accelerated phase?
questions.explanation: Accelerated phase is defined by: blasts 10-19%, basophils ≥20%, persistent thrombocytopenia (<100,000/µL) unrelated to therapy, thrombocytosis unresponsive to therapy, or cytogenetic evolution. This transitional phase often precedes blast crisis.

Bone marrow failure is defined as failure to carry out blood cell production, leading to decreased production of one or more hematopoietic cell lineages. It can affect single (monolineage) or multiple lineages (multilineage). The condition may be inherited or acquired.
questions.question: What defines bone marrow failure?
Which finding suggests acute hemolytic transfusion reaction?
questions.explanation: Hypotension, hemoglobinuria, flank/back pain, and DIC suggest acute hemolytic reaction. Hemoglobin rises initially then falls. Free hemoglobin in plasma and urine confirms intravascular hemolysis. Oliguria and acute renal failure may develop.

IPSS uses: blast percentage (< 5%, 5-10%, 11-20%), karyotype (good, intermediate, poor), and number of cytopenias (0-1, 2-3) to categorize patients into risk groups (low, INT-1, INT-2, high) predicting survival and AML transformation. Revised IPSS (IPSS-R) includes additional variables for refined prognostication.
questions.question: What is the International Prognostic Scoring System (IPSS) for MDS based on?
options: Patient age and performance status only

questions.explanation: ESAs (epoetin alfa, darbepoetin) reduce transfusion needs in chemotherapy-induced anemia but have risks: hypertension, thrombosis, potential tumor progression (controversial). Restricted use: Hb <10 g/dL due to chemotherapy, target Hb 10-12 g/dL (not normal), use lowest effective dose, discontinue at chemotherapy completion. Many guidelines recommend transfusion over ESAs due to risks.
options: Routine use to maintain normal hemoglobin at all times
Contraindicated in all cancer types always
Preferred over all transfusions in every case
When Hb below 10 g/dL to minimize transfusion requirements
questions.question: What is the role of erythropoiesis-stimulating agents in cancer?

questions.explanation: Haemoglobin synthesis begins predominantly in the polychromatic (intermediate) normoblast stage, giving the cytoplasm a gray-blue color from mixed RNA (basophilia) and haemoglobin (acidophilia). This is the last mitotic stage. Subsequent stages show progressively more haemoglobin and less RNA, with increasing cytoplasmic eosinophilia.
questions.question: Hemoglobin synthesis predominantly begins in which erythroid stage?
Which hematologic malignancy is compatible with pregnancy?
options: All can be observed without treatment
Chronic myeloid leukemia in chronic phase
questions.explanation: CML in chronic phase can often be observed during pregnancy (especially if diagnosed late pregnancy) with delivery followed by treatment, as hydroxyurea/interferon have fetal risks and TKIs are teratogenic (class D). Leukapheresis controls counts if needed. Acute leukemia requires urgent treatment (cannot delay); many chemotherapy agents can be given after first trimester with acceptable fetal outcomes. Hodgkin lymphoma treatment may be modified or delayed depending on stage/trimester.

questions.question: What ABO type is the universal plasma donor?
options: Type A plasma for all recipients
Type O plasma containing both antibodies
questions.explanation: Type AB plasma lacks anti-A and anti-B antibodies (isoagglutinins), making it compatible with all recipients (universal plasma donor). In emergencies (massive transfusion), AB plasma is preferred. Type O plasma contains anti-A and anti-B, potentially causing hemolysis if given to A, B, or AB recipients.

CLL characteristically shows CD5+, CD19+, CD20+(dim), CD23+, weak surface immunoglobulin (sIg), with ? or ? light chain restriction. The co-expression of CD5 (T-cell marker) with B-cell markers is diagnostic. Strong sIg suggests other lymphoproliferative disorders.
options: CD5+, CD19+, CD23+, weak surface immunoglobulin
questions.question: What is chronic lymphocytic leukemia's most common immunophenotype?

questions.explanation: Approximately 80% of most populations are secretors, possessing the dominant Se gene (SeSe or Sese genotypes). Secretors express ABH antigens in body fluids including saliva, plasma and other secretions. Non-secretors (sese genotype) lack soluble antigens but express them on red cells.
questions.question: What percentage of individuals are typically secretors?
In anaemia of chronic disease, serum iron is low while bone marrow iron stores are:
questions.explanation: ACD paradoxically shows low serum iron despite normal or increased marrow iron stores because hepcidin elevation blocks iron release from macrophages. Iron remains sequestered and unavailable for erythropoiesis. Bone marrow examination with Prussian blue staining demonstrates normal or increased haemosiderin, distinguishing ACD from true iron deficiency.

questions.question: What defines chronic GVHD temporally and clinically?
questions.explanation: Chronic GVHD is now defined by distinctive manifestations (e.g., sclerosis, lichen planus-like features, fasciitis, bronchiolitis obliterans) regardless of timing, rather than strict >100-day onset. Can occur without prior acute GVHD or as progression from acute. Multi-organ involvement common. Requires prolonged immunosuppression. Quality of life impact substantial. Risk factors: prior acute GVHD, peripheral blood stem cells, HLA mismatch, older age.

Conditioning (preparative regimen) is high-dose chemotherapy ± total body irradiation given before stem cell infusion to: (1) eradicate malignancy, (2) create marrow space for donor cells, and (3) in allogeneic transplant, provide immunosuppression to prevent graft rejection. Intensity ranges from myeloablative to reduced-intensity.
questions.question: What is conditioning regimen in transplantation?
options: Physical therapy preparing patient for procedure

questions.question: What is first-line treatment for warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia?
questions.explanation: Corticosteroids (prednisone 1 mg/kg/day) are first-line, inducing remission in 70-85% by reducing antibody production and macrophage Fc receptor activity. Gradual taper over 2-3 months follows response. Rituximab (anti-CD20) is increasingly used as second-line or combined with steroids initially. Splenectomy reserved for refractory cases.

questions.question: Which malignancy has highest risk of CNS involvement?
options: Acute lymphoblastic leukemia and Burkitt lymphoma
questions.explanation: ALL (especially T-cell, mature B-cell/Burkitt) and Burkitt lymphoma have high CNS involvement risk (30-50% without prophylaxis). CNS sanctuary site: poor chemotherapy penetration allows CNS relapse. CNS prophylaxis (intrathecal chemotherapy ± cranial radiation for high-risk) is standard. High-risk features: high WBC, certain immunophenotypes/cytogenetics, testicular involvement. Aggressive NHL also requires CNS prophylaxis.

Temperature increase ≥1°C (some definitions ≥2°C) from baseline suggests transfusion reaction (FNHTR or hemolytic). Other concerning signs: rig ors, hypotension (>30 mmHg drop), tachycardia (>120 bpm), respiratory distress, urticaria. Vital signs should be checked pre-transfusion, 15 minutes after starting, then per protocol. Any concerning change warrants stopping transfusion and investigation.
questions.question: Which vital sign change suggests transfusion reaction?

questions.explanation: Neutrophil engraftment (sustained neutrophil count >0.5 × 10⁹/L for three consecutive days) typically occurs 3-4 weeks (21-28 days) after uncomplicated allogeneic bone marrow transplantation. Peripheral blood stem cell transplants engraft faster (10-14 days) due to greater numbers of infused CD34+ progenitor cells. Cord blood transplants engraft more slowly (4-6 weeks). G-CSF can shorten the neutropenic period by 3-5 days. During the neutropenic window patients are at extreme risk of bacterial and fungal infections, requiring protective isolation and prophylactic antimicrobials until engraftment is confirmed.
questions.question: A 45-year-old man with aplastic anaemia failed two courses of immunosuppressive therapy and undergoes matched sibling allogeneic bone marrow transplantation. On day 14 his neutrophil count is 0.2 × 10⁹/L. When is neutrophil engraftment typically expected?
options: Day 21-28 post-transplant in uncomplicated allogeneic bone marrow SCT
Day 7-10 post-transplant in uncomplicated engraftment scenarios
Day 10-14 post-transplant in matched sibling transplants specifically
Day 35-42 post-transplant in all allogeneic transplant types
Day 5-7 post-transplant with modern growth factor support protocols

questions.explanation: Excess unpaired β-chains precipitate in erythroid precursors in β-thalassaemia major, causing their death in bone marrow (ineffective erythropoiesis). This, along with peripheral haemolysis from precipitated β-chains in mature cells, causes severe anaemia. The ineffective erythropoiesis drives bone marrow expansion and extramedullary haemopoiesis.
questions.question: In β-thalassaemia major, ineffective erythropoiesis results from:

questions.explanation: Priapism in sickle cell disease results from veno-occlusion within the corpora cavernosa by sickled red cells. The obstruction prevents venous drainage, causing sustained erection that is painful and ultimately ischaemic. If untreated beyond 4–6 hours, ischaemia causes cavernosal fibrosis and permanent erectile dysfunction. Management includes hydration, analgesia, aspiration of corpora, and exchange transfusion for recurrent episodes.
questions.question: A 22-year-old with sickle cell disease presents with persistent painful erection lasting 4 hours. What is the mechanism?
options: Autonomic nerve damage from chronic neuropathy
Arterial vasodilation causing increased penile inflow
Medication side effects from long-term opioid analgesics
Psychological factors during a concurrent pain crisis

questions.question: Which coagulation factor has the shortest half-life?
questions.explanation: Factor VII has the shortest half-life (4-6 hours), explaining why prothrombin time (which measures VII) abnormalizes first in liver disease or warfarin therapy. Other factors have longer half-lives: II (60 hours), V (12-36 hours), X (40-60 hours).

questions.question: A 19-year-old West African man develops acute haemolytic anaemia 48 hours after starting primaquine. Blood film shows bite cells and Heinz bodies on supravital staining. Which red cell enzymatic defect underlies this presentation?
options: Pyruvate kinase deficiency causing ATP depletion in erythrocytes
G6PD deficiency causing failure to regenerate NADPH
Hexokinase deficiency impairing anaerobic glycolysis pathway
Glutathione synthetase deficiency reducing oxidant buffering capacity
questions.explanation: G6PD deficiency (X-linked recessive) prevents regeneration of NADPH via the pentose phosphate pathway; without NADPH, reduced glutathione cannot be maintained, leaving haemoglobin vulnerable to oxidative denaturation by primaquine's hydroxylamine metabolites. The denatured haemoglobin precipitates as Heinz bodies; affected red cells are then pitted or destroyed by the spleen, producing the characteristic bite cells on blood film. This is the most common inherited red cell enzyme disorder globally, with highest prevalence in malaria-endemic regions.

questions.question: What causes pernicious anemia?
questions.explanation: Pernicious anemia results from autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells with intrinsic factor deficiency, preventing B12 absorption. Anti-intrinsic factor and anti-parietal cell antibodies are present. Achlorhydria and atrophic gastritis occur. Lifelong B12 replacement is required.

questions.question: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia type II (HIT) typically develops after how many days of heparin exposure?
questions.explanation: HIT type II develops 5-10 days after starting heparin due to antibodies against heparin-platelet factor 4 complexes, causing platelet activation and consumption. Features include thrombocytopenia (usually >50% decrease) and paradoxical thrombosis (arterial or venous). 4T score assesses probability. Treatment requires immediate heparin cessation and alternative anticoagulation (argatroban, bivalirudin).

options: Factors VIII, VWF, fibrinogen, XIII, and fibronectin
Factor IX and prothrombin complex concentrate components
Immunoglobulins and albumin in high concentration
Platelets and red cells suspended in plasma protein
All clotting factors in concentrated equal quantities
questions.question: Cryoprecipitate is transfused to a patient with fibrinogen of 0.8 g/L after massive haemorrhage. What are the main haemostatic components in cryoprecipitate?
questions.explanation: Cryoprecipitate is prepared from fresh frozen plasma by slow thaw at 1–6°C and contains concentrated fibrinogen (the primary indication), factor VIII, von Willebrand factor, factor XIII, and fibronectin. Each unit contains approximately 150–300 mg fibrinogen. It does not contain factors II, VII, IX, or X and is specifically indicated for fibrinogen replacement in DIC and massive haemorrhage.

MGUS is characterized by monoclonal protein presence without clinical or laboratory features of plasma cell disorder or lymphoproliferative disease. M-protein is typically less than 30 g/L with bone marrow plasma cells less than 10%. Annual transformation risk to myeloma is approximately 1%.
questions.question: What defines monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS)?

questions.explanation: MCV typically ranges between 50 and 70 fL in hereditary pyropoikilocytosis, reflecting microspherocytosis and fragmentation. This microcytosis is more pronounced than in typical hereditary elliptocytosis. The low MCV helps distinguish HPP from other hemolytic disorders.
questions.question: What is the typical MCV range in hereditary pyropoikilocytosis?

questions.explanation: Transferrin saturation = (serum iron/TIBC) × 100 = (30/450) × 100 = 6.7%, rounded to 7%. Values below 15% indicate iron deficiency, with lower percentages reflecting more severe depletion. This calculation demonstrates inadequate iron availability for erythropoiesis despite increased binding capacity.
questions.question: A patient with chronic iron deficiency has a total iron binding capacity of 450 µg/dL and serum iron of 30 µg/dL. What is the transferrin saturation?
Malaria parasites are visualized on blood film as:
questions.explanation: Malaria parasites (Plasmodium species) appear as intraerythrocytic organisms on Giemsa-stained thick/thin films. Thick films screen for parasites; thin films identify species and quantify parasitaemia. P. falciparum: ring forms, crescentic gametocytes, no schizonts (sequestered); P. vivax/ovale: enlarged cells, Schuffner's dots; P. malariae: band forms. Severe disease: >2% parasitaemia, schizonts in peripheral blood.

questions.question: What is the doubling time threshold indicating progressive CLL?
questions.explanation: Lymphocyte doubling time <6 months indicates rapidly progressive disease and is an indication for treatment in otherwise asymptomatic patients. Slow doubling time (>12 months) suggests indolent disease that can be observed. This marker reflects disease biology.

questions.question: Which finding would establish smoldering myeloma rather than active myeloma?
questions.explanation: Smoldering myeloma has M-protein ≥3 g/dL and/or bone marrow plasma cells 10-60% WITHOUT end-organ damage (CRAB criteria) or other myeloma-defining events. These patients are observed without treatment until progression. Risk of progression is ~10% per year for first 5 years.
options: Presence of lytic bone lesions on imaging
M-protein ≥3 g/dL or bone marrow plasma cells ≥10%

questions.explanation: Bleomycin causes dose-dependent pulmonary fibrosis (incidence 10%, mortality 1-2%). Risk increases with cumulative dose >400 units, age >70, renal dysfunction, high FiO2, chest radiation. Presents with dyspnea, cough, restrictive pattern, reduced DLCO, reticular infiltrates. No effective treatment once established; prevention requires dose limits, monitoring (PFTs, symptoms), avoiding high oxygen. Discontinue bleomycin if toxicity develops.
questions.question: What defines bleomycin pulmonary toxicity?

questions.explanation: Classical HL Reed-Sternberg cells characteristically express CD30 and CD15 but lack typical B-cell markers (CD20 usually negative, PAX5 weakly positive). They've lost expression of B-cell transcription factors. This aberrant phenotype distinguishes HL from non-Hodgkin lymphomas.
questions.question: What is the typical immunophenotype of classical Hodgkin lymphoma?

options: Second most immunogenic after ABO antigens
questions.question: What is the Rh(D) antigen significance?
questions.explanation: Rh(D) is the second most important blood group antigen after ABO. About 85% are Rh-positive (D+), 15% Rh-negative (D-). Unlike ABO, anti-D is not naturally occurring but develops after exposure (transfusion/pregnancy). It causes delayed hemolytic reactions and hemolytic disease of newborn, not immediate reactions.

questions.question: Mycosis fungoides is a type of:
questions.explanation: Mycosis fungoides is the most common cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, presenting with patches, plaques, then tumors over years. Sezary syndrome is leukaemic variant with erythroderma and circulating Sezary cells (cerebriform nuclei). Diagnosis requires skin biopsy showing epidermotropism. Treatment ranges from topical therapy (early stages) to systemic chemotherapy (advanced disease).

questions.question: A 70-year-old with polycythemia vera has hematocrit 52%. What is the target hematocrit with phlebotomy?
options: Maintain hematocrit at 50 percent as normal
Hematocrit below 45 percent men, 42 percent women
Reduce hematocrit below 40 percent in all
No target set; avoid phlebotomy always
questions.explanation: Target hematocrit <45% in men, <42% in women reduces thrombotic risk by approximately 50% (CYTO-PV trial). Phlebotomy is first-line for all PV patients. Remove 250-500 mL initially (adjust for elderly/cardiac disease), repeat every 2-3 days until target reached, then as needed to maintain target. Add hydroxyurea for: high-risk (age >60, prior thrombosis), symptomatic splenomegaly, progressive leukocytosis/thrombocytosis, poor venous access.

questions.question: What is the target INR for most indications on warfarin?
questions.explanation: Target INR is 2.0-3.0 for most indications including atrial fibrillation, venous thromboembolism, and post-myocardial infarction. Higher target (2.5-3.5) is used for mechanical heart valves and recurrent thrombosis. INR monitoring guides dose adjustments.

questions.question: Which vaccines are recommended after splenectomy?
questions.explanation: Polyvalent pneumococcal, Haemophilus influenzae type B, and meningococcal vaccines are recommended after splenectomy. These protect against encapsulated bacteria causing overwhelming post-splenectomy infection. Vaccination should occur pre-operatively when possible, supplemented by lifelong penicillin prophylaxis.

Splenomegaly in MPNs results from extramedullary haemopoiesis as splenic red pulp resumes fetal haemopoietic function. Most marked in myelofibrosis (massive splenomegaly), also occurs in PV, ET, CML. Complications include hypersplenism (cytopenias), splenic infarction (pain), and rupture. Splenectomy may be needed for symptomatic splenomegaly but has significant morbidity/mortality.
questions.question: Splenomegaly in myeloproliferative neoplasms results primarily from:
What is the first-line treatment for chronic ITP?
questions.explanation: Corticosteroids are first-line therapy for ITP, inducing remission in 60-80% initially (though many relapse). They work by reducing antibody production and macrophage function. IVIG provides rapid but temporary increase for emergencies. Thrombopoietin agonists, rituximab, and splenectomy are second-line options.

options: FEIBA providing activated coagulation bypass factors
Fresh frozen plasma providing all clotting factors
Cryoprecipitate enriched with factor VIII antigen
Desmopressin releasing stored endogenous factor VIII
Recombinant factor VIII at double the normal dose
questions.question: A haemophilia A patient requires urgent surgery but has a high-titre inhibitor. Which product bypasses factor VIII?
questions.explanation: FEIBA (Factor Eight Inhibitor Bypassing Activity) contains activated factors II, VII, IX, and X that generate thrombin independently of factor VIII, bypassing the inhibitor-blocked step. Recombinant factor VIII would be neutralised by the inhibitor immediately. FEIBA and recombinant FVIIa are the two main bypassing agents for high-titre inhibitor patients.

questions.question: What indicates functional iron deficiency?
questions.explanation: Functional iron deficiency shows low serum iron despite adequate or elevated ferritin (storage iron), common in chronic inflammation/infection. Iron is sequestered in macrophages, unavailable for erythropoiesis. Transferrin saturation is low. Anemia of chronic disease exemplifies this.

ABO incompatibility (group O mother, group A/B infant) is most common but usually mild. Maternal IgG anti-A or anti-B crosses placenta causing haemolysis, jaundice, rarely severe anaemia. Rh disease (Rh-negative mother, Rh-positive infant) is less common but more severe, preventable with anti-D immunoglobulin. Exchange transfusion may be needed for severe hyperbilirubinaemia preventing kernicterus.
questions.question: Haemolytic disease of the newborn most commonly results from:

questions.explanation: β-thalassaemia major shows predominantly HbF (70-95%) with variable HbA2 and absent or minimal HbA. The high HbF partially compensates for absent β-chain production as β-chains pair with β-chains. This pattern distinguishes β-thalassaemia major from other haemoglobinopathies and guides diagnosis and genetic counseling.
questions.question: In β-thalassaemia major, the predominant haemoglobin on electrophoresis is:

questions.explanation: EBV is detected in ~40% of classical HL overall, but association is strongest (up to 90%) in mixed cellularity subtype, developing countries, extremes of age, and HIV+ patients. EBV+ cases may have different pathogenesis and response to therapy.
questions.question: Which Epstein-Barr virus association is strongest in Hodgkin lymphoma?

options: Inhibition of DNA synthesis in dividing cells
Promotion of CML cell apoptosis non-specifically
questions.explanation: TKIs competitively inhibit ATP binding to the BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase domain, inactivating the enzyme. This blocks downstream signaling pathways (RAS/MAPK, PI3K/AKT, JAK/STAT) that drive proliferation and survival. The result is selective CML cell death.
questions.question: What is the mechanism of action of tyrosine kinase inhibitors?
What is the significance of flow cytometry detection of MRD after ALL induction?
options: MRD positivity confirms relapse requiring salvage therapy
MRD below 0.01% guarantees cure without further treatment
MRD level has no impact on treatment decisions in ALL
MRD positivity only matters in adult not paediatric ALL
MRD level predicts relapse risk and guides therapy intensity
questions.explanation: Minimal residual disease (MRD) assessment by flow cytometry or PCR after ALL induction is a powerful independent prognostic factor that guides therapy intensity in modern protocols. MRD negativity (typically below 0.01%) after induction correlates with excellent prognosis and may allow therapy de-escalation. Persistent MRD positivity or late MRD conversion to positive predicts high relapse risk and may prompt intensification (high-dose therapy, transplantation, or novel agents like blinatumomab).

Eculizumab is a monoclonal antibody inhibiting complement C5, preventing formation of membrane attack complex (C5b-9) that lyses PNH cells. It dramatically reduces intravascular hemolysis, transfusion needs, thrombosis risk, and improves quality of life. Patients require meningococcal vaccination (increased meningococcal infection risk) and prophylactic antibiotics. Ravulizumab is longer-acting C5 inhibitor.
options: Complement C5 inhibition preventing MAC formation
questions.question: What is the mechanism of eculizumab in PNH treatment?

questions.explanation: Infection during the profound neutropenic period between conditioning and engraftment (typically days 0–30) is the most common cause of early non-relapse mortality after allogeneic SCT. Bacterial, fungal (Aspergillus), and viral (CMV, adenovirus) infections are all major threats. This is why comprehensive antimicrobial prophylaxis (antibacterial, antifungal, antiviral), surveillance, and prompt empirical therapy for febrile neutropenia are essential components of post-transplant care.
options: Infection during the neutropenic engraftment period
Severe acute GVHD unresponsive to corticosteroids
Hepatic veno-occlusive disease from conditioning regimen
Primary graft failure preventing normal haematopoiesis
questions.question: What is the most common cause of non-relapse mortality in the first 100 days after allogeneic stem cell transplantation?
What percentage of cancers does multiple myeloma represent?
questions.explanation: Multiple myeloma accounts for approximately 1% of all cancers and 10% of hematological malignancies. It predominantly affects elderly patients with median age of 65-70 years. Slight male predominance exists.

Age is the most important prognostic factor in childhood ALL: infants <1 year and older children >10 years have worse prognosis than those aged 1-10 years. Other adverse factors include high white count (>50×10⁹/L), T-cell phenotype, CNS involvement, and certain cytogenetic abnormalities (Philadelphia chromosome, MLL rearrangements). Modern therapy achieves >85% cure rates.
questions.question: In acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, the most important prognostic factor in children is:

questions.explanation: Donor T lymphocytes mediate GVL by recognizing minor histocompatibility antigens or tumor-associated antigens on leukemic cells. This allogeneic immune response is the major curative mechanism in allogeneic transplant. Donor lymphocyte infusions can induce remissions in relapsed CML, demonstrating GVL potency. NK cells may also contribute.
options: Donor T lymphocytes recognizing tumor antigens
questions.question: Which cells mediate graft-versus-leukemia effect?
Which transfusion reaction occurs most frequently?
questions.explanation: Febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reactions occur most frequently, in 1-3% of transfusions. Cytokines from donor leukocytes or recipient anti-leukocyte antibodies cause fever. Leukocyte-reduced blood products reduce incidence. Antipyretics provide symptomatic relief.

questions.question: A patient with chronic lymphocytic leukaemia develops Coombs-positive haemolytic anaemia. What is the most likely underlying mechanism?
questions.explanation: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia is associated with autoimmune complications, including warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, due to dysregulated immune function and production of autoantibodies against red cell antigens, confirmed by a positive direct antiglobulin test.

questions.question: What is the principle of flow cytometry?
questions.explanation: Flow cytometry identifies and quantifies cells based on fluorescence from antibody-fluorochrome conjugates binding specific cell surface or intracellular antigens. Multiple parameters analyzed simultaneously. Applications include immunophenotyping leukemias/lymphomas, CD4 counts, PNH detection.

Patients with SCD lose splenic function by 2–4 years of age, making them functionally asplenic and highly susceptible to encapsulated bacteria, especially Streptococcus pneumoniae. The landmark PROPS study showed that prophylactic oral penicillin starting at age 2–3 months reduced pneumococcal sepsis by 84%. Pneumococcal vaccination alongside penicillin prophylaxis has dramatically reduced early childhood mortality in SCD.
options: Prophylactic penicillin starting from age 2 months
Meningococcal conjugate vaccination at 2 years of age
Transcranial Doppler screening to detect stroke risk
Haemophilus influenzae type b vaccination in early infancy
Annual influenza vaccination from age 6 months onwards
questions.question: Which preventive measure in sickle cell disease has most reduced mortality from pneumococcal infection?

questions.explanation: Platelets form the primary haemostatic plug at sites of vessel injury through adhesion, activation, and aggregation. They also provide phospholipid surface for coagulation factor activation, release procoagulant factors, and contract to stabilize the clot. Normal platelet count is 150-400×10⁹/L; lifespan is 7-10 days.
questions.question: The primary function of platelets in haemostasis is:

questions.explanation: Pulmonary artery pressure increases only when more than 30-50 percent of the total cross-sectional area is occluded. This reflects the lung's substantial vascular reserve. Lesser degrees of occlusion are compensated without hemodynamic compromise.
options: 80-90 percent needed for right heart failure
Complete occlusion necessary for pressure rise
questions.question: What percentage of total cross-sectional pulmonary arterial bed must be occluded before pulmonary artery pressure rises?

questions.explanation: Follicular lymphoma is characterised by t(14;18)(q32;q21), juxtaposing BCL-2 to the immunoglobulin heavy chain promoter, causing constitutive BCL-2 overexpression. BCL-2 is an anti-apoptotic protein preventing programmed cell death, allowing follicular centre cells to accumulate. This explains the indolent but incurable nature of follicular lymphoma with standard therapy.
questions.question: What translocation is characteristic of follicular lymphoma and what is its molecular consequence?
options: t(14;18) causing BCL-2 overexpression blocking apoptosis
t(11;14) causing cyclin D1 overexpression in mantle cell
t(2;5) creating NPM-ALK fusion in T-cell lymphoma
t(9;22) creating BCR-ABL proliferative kinase fusion
t(8;14) juxtaposing MYC to immunoglobulin heavy chain

questions.question: What is the primary mechanism by which TFPI inhibits coagulation?
options: Direct neutralization of thrombin at activation sites
Enhancement of protein C anticoagulant activity
Inhibition of Factor Xa-FVIIa/tissue factor complex
Promotion of fibrinolysis through plasminogen activation
Sequestration of Factor V from prothrombinase complex
questions.explanation: TFPI inhibits coagulation by forming a quaternary complex with Factor Xa, Factor VIIa, and tissue factor. At lower concentrations, it specifically inhibits the FXa-FVIIa/TF complex, while at higher concentrations it directly inhibits Factor VIIa-TF. This reversible inhibition differs from SERPIN mechanisms.

Severe malnutrition (kwashiorkor, marasmus) causes bone marrow hypocellularity with serous atrophy (fat replaced by gelatinous material), resembling aplastic anaemia morphologically. Haematological effects include anaemia (normocytic or microcytic), lymphopenia, impaired cell-mediated immunity, increased infections. Bone marrow recovers with nutritional rehabilitation. Distinguishing from primary aplastic anaemia requires clinical context.
questions.question: Severe protein-energy malnutrition causes which bone marrow change?

questions.explanation: Massive transfusion protocols recommend giving red cells, fresh frozen plasma, and platelets in a balanced ratio, approximately 1:1:1, to replace lost clotting factors and platelets alongside oxygen-carrying capacity, reducing dilutional coagulopathy in major haemorrhage.
questions.question: A patient requires massive blood transfusion following major trauma. What ratio of blood products is generally recommended to reduce coagulopathy?

questions.explanation: Persistently elevated D-dimer after stopping anticoagulation strongly predicts recurrent VTE, with hazard ratios of 2-3 fold. This marker reflects ongoing coagulation activation. It helps guide decisions about extended anticoagulation duration.
options: Age over 65 years at first event
questions.question: Which factor most strongly predicts recurrent VTE after stopping anticoagulation?

questions.explanation: Treatment-free remission (TFR) - discontinuing TKI therapy while maintaining molecular remission - is achievable in approximately 40-50% of CML patients who meet strict eligibility criteria (typically: chronic phase CML, >=5 years TKI therapy total, >=2 years sustained MR4 or MR4.5 undetectable BCR-ABL1). The STIM, EURO-SKI, DESTINY, and EURO-TFR trials established this paradigm. Molecular relapse occurs in the remaining 50-60%, typically within the first 6-12 months, requiring TKI resumption - with >95% regaining remission after restarting. Patients attempting TFR require monthly PCR monitoring for the first 12 months. TFR offers avoidance of long-term TKI side effects and treatment cost.
options: Imatinib must be taken lifelong; stopping always causes molecular relapse within 3 months
TFR attempts are only safe with second-generation TKIs; imatinib-treated patients cannot stop
MR4.5 is insufficient; BCR-ABL1 must remain undetectable for 5 years before stopping safely
All CML patients in molecular remission should stop imatinib as continued treatment causes cumulative toxicity
TFR is achievable in ~40-50% of patients with sustained deep molecular remission after stopping TKI
questions.question: A 45-year-old man with CML (BCR-ABL1+) has been in sustained deep molecular remission (MR4.5, BCR-ABL1 undetectable) for 3 years on imatinib. He asks about stopping treatment. What does current evidence say about treatment-free remission (TFR) in CML?

questions.explanation: Elevated INR without bleeding: hold warfarin, give oral vitamin K (dose depends on INR level - 2.5-5 mg for INR 5-9, 5-10 mg for >9). Avoid IV vitamin K (anaphylaxis risk) unless life-threatening bleeding. FFP reserved for serious bleeding or urgent procedure. Recheck INR in 24 hours. Resume warfarin at lower dose when INR therapeutic. For major bleeding: IV vitamin K + 4-factor PCC or FFP.
options: Withhold warfarin, administer oral vitamin K
questions.question: A patient on warfarin for atrial fibrillation presents with INR 9.0 without bleeding. What is appropriate management?

questions.explanation: The sickle mutation involves substitution of valine for glutamic acid at position 6 of the β-globin chain (β6Glu→Val). This single nucleotide change (GAG→GTG) alters the haemoglobin's physiochemical properties, causing polymerization under deoxygenated conditions. This specific location on the surface of the haemoglobin molecule is critical for the sickling phenomenon.
questions.question: In sickle cell anaemia, the amino acid substitution in the β-globin chain occurs at position:

questions.explanation: Salmonella species are the most common cause of osteomyelitis in SCD, though Staphylococcus aureus is also frequent. Bone infarction from vaso-occlusion creates necrotic tissue susceptible to infection. Distinguishing osteomyelitis from vaso-occlusive bone pain is challenging, requiring imaging and cultures for definitive diagnosis.
questions.question: Osteomyelitis in sickle cell disease is most commonly caused by:
Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia occurs in all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: MAHA results from red cell fragmentation passing through damaged microvasculature (TTP, HUS, DIC, malignant hypertension, prosthetic valves, HELLP syndrome). Schistocytes on blood film, elevated LDH, low haptoglobin, negative Coombs. Hereditary spherocytosis is extravascular haemolysis with spherocytes (not schistocytes). Treatment addresses underlying condition. Plasma exchange for TTP, delivery for HELLP, blood pressure control for malignant hypertension.

Bernard-Soulier syndrome is autosomal recessive deficiency of GPIb/IX/V complex, causing defective platelet adhesion and thrombocytopenia with giant platelets (size of red cells). Platelets cannot bind vWF. Bleeding time is prolonged out of proportion to platelet count. Treatment requires platelet transfusions.
options: Gray platelet syndrome lacking alpha granules
Storage pool disease with dense granule deficiency
questions.question: Which inherited platelet disorder shows giant platelets and thrombocytopenia?

questions.explanation: Tissue hypoxia stimulates erythropoietin (EPO) production by renal peritubular interstitial cells (~90%) and liver (~10%). Hypoxia stabilizes hypoxia-inducible factors (HIF) which activate EPO gene transcription. EPO stimulates proliferation and differentiation of erythroid progenitors (BFU-E, CFU-E), increasing red cell mass to improve oxygen delivery.
questions.question: Erythropoietin is primarily produced in response to:

questions.explanation: Burkitt lymphoma shows t(8;14) in 80% of cases, translocating MYC oncogene to immunoglobulin heavy chain locus, causing MYC overexpression. Variants include t(2;8) and t(8;22). Endemic (African, EBV-associated), sporadic, and immunodeficiency-associated forms exist. Highly aggressive but chemotherapy-curable. "Starry sky" appearance from tingible body macrophages is characteristic.
questions.question: Burkitt lymphoma is characteristically associated with translocation involving which chromosomes?
A 4-year-old with sickle cell disease presents with fever and is found to have pneumococcal bacteraemia. What is the underlying reason for this susceptibility?
questions.explanation: Repeated splenic infarction in sickle cell disease leads to functional hyposplenism from early childhood, impairing clearance of encapsulated organisms like Streptococcus pneumoniae. This is why penicillin prophylaxis and pneumococcal vaccination are essential in these children.

Autologous transplantation uses the patient's own stem cells harvested before conditioning. Cells are processed and cryopreserved until needed. Most patients without compatible donors undergo autologous transplantation.
questions.question: What characterizes autologous stem cell transplantation?

questions.explanation: Cold agglutinins are IgM antibodies that bind red cells optimally at low temperatures, causing agglutination and complement-mediated haemolysis in cooler peripheral body areas. Avoiding cold exposure reduces triggering of this process.
questions.question: A patient with cold agglutinin disease is advised to avoid cold exposure. What is the underlying reason for this advice?

questions.explanation: The normal M:E ratio (2-12:1) reverses in conditions with erythroid hyperplasia like haemolytic anaemia, haemorrhage, or response to haematinics. The ratio increases in infections, myeloid leukaemias. In megaloblastic anaemia, erythroid hyperplasia occurs but the M:E ratio may not reverse due to ineffective erythropoiesis.
questions.question: The bone marrow myeloid to erythroid (M:E) ratio is reversed in:

questions.explanation: Serum ferritin >1000 ng/mL suggests iron overload, though ferritin is an acute phase reactant and can be elevated in inflammation without overload. Transferrin saturation >45% supports overload. Liver biopsy or MRI quantifies hepatic iron definitively.
questions.question: What serum ferritin level suggests iron overload?
A 42-year-old man with haemophilia A also has HIV. His factor VIII activity was previously consistently 3% but is now measured at 45%. What is the most likely explanation?
questions.explanation: Von Willebrand factor (VWF) is an acute-phase reactant synthesised by endothelial cells; it rises significantly in inflammatory states, infection (including HIV), and following antiretroviral therapy commencement with immune reconstitution. VWF is the plasma carrier and stabiliser of factor VIII - it protects FVIII from premature clearance and proteolysis, extending its plasma half-life. In a patient with mild haemophilia A (baseline FVIII 3%), a marked VWF elevation from HIV-related inflammation can substantially raise the measured FVIII level by increasing FVIII-VWF complex stability and reducing clearance. This pseudo-normalisation of FVIII activity during acute illness is temporary; FVIII levels should be measured during a quiescent period to determine the true baseline.
options: Laboratory artefact from antiretroviral drugs interfering with the clotting assay
Eradication of high-titre FVIII inhibitor by HIV-induced immunosuppression
Antiretroviral therapy-induced immune reconstitution increasing FVIII half-life
HIV-associated VWF elevation increasing FVIII binding and stability in plasma
HIV itself upregulates factor VIII synthesis as an acute-phase reactant

questions.question: What characterizes MDS-associated dysplasia in erythroid lineage?
questions.explanation: Ring sideroblasts (erythroblasts with iron-laden mitochondria forming ring around nucleus, visible with Prussian blue stain) characterize MDS with ring sideroblasts (MDS-RS). They result from abnormal heme synthesis. When isolated, prognosis is better. SF3B1 mutation is common in MDS-RS.
options: Microcytic hypochromic cells from iron deficiency

questions.explanation: Approximately 45% of severe hemophilia A cases result from intron 22 inversion of the factor VIII gene. This common mutation disrupts gene function, causing severe factor VIII deficiency. Other mutations include deletions, insertions and point mutations.
questions.question: What percentage of hemophilia A cases involve gene inversion?
What defines Burkitt lymphoma immunophenotype?
questions.explanation: Burkitt lymphoma shows: CD10+, BCL6+, BCL2- (distinguishes from follicular), surface IgM+, extremely high proliferation (Ki-67 >95%). Molecular signature: MYC translocation t(8;14) or variants. The extremely high proliferation rate (doubling time 24-48 hours) causes high tumor lysis risk but also sensitivity to intensive chemotherapy. Cure rates are 80-90% in children.

ABO-incompatible transfusion from clerical/identification errors remains the most common cause of fatal transfusion reactions despite being entirely preventable. It causes acute hemolytic transfusion reaction with DIC, renal failure, shock. Prevention requires meticulous patient identification and labeling at bedside.
questions.question: What is the most common cause of fatal transfusion reactions?
Which phospholipid is preferentially located in the inner membrane leaflet?
questions.explanation: Phosphatidylserine is preferentially located in the inner leaflet of the lipid bilayer along with phosphatidylethanolamine and phosphatidylinositol. This asymmetric distribution is actively maintained and prevents premature cell removal. Externalization of phosphatidylserine signals macrophage recognition.

questions.question: Which patients require rasburicase rather than allopurinol?
questions.explanation: Rasburicase is preferred for high TLS risk: bulky/rapidly proliferative tumors (Burkitt lymphoma, ALL with high WBC, bulky DLBCL), baseline hyperuricemia, or renal insufficiency. It rapidly reduces uric acid (hours vs. days for allopurinol). Contraindicated in G6PD deficiency (causes severe hemolysis). Single dose (0.2 mg/kg) often sufficient. Expensive; reserved for high-risk situations.
options: High TLS risk or pre-existing hyperuricemia

questions.question: What causes tropical splenomegaly syndrome?
questions.explanation: Tropical splenomegaly syndrome (hyperimmune malarial syndrome) results from continuous exposure to malarial antigens in endemic zones. Abnormal host immune response produces reactive lymphoproliferation affecting the spleen. The condition is a diagnosis of exclusion.

questions.question: What is the primary indication for G-CSF in chemotherapy patients?
options: Treatment of established neutropenic fever episodes
Routine use in all chemotherapy regimens
Prophylaxis when febrile neutropenia risk exceeds 20 percent
questions.explanation: G-CSF (filgrastim, pegfilgrastim) is indicated for primary prophylaxis when chemotherapy regimen carries >20% risk of febrile neutropenia, reducing duration/severity of neutropenia. It's also used for mobilizing stem cells for collection. Not routinely recommended for established fever (no proven benefit). Started 24-72 hours post-chemotherapy, continued until ANC recovery.

questions.question: Which antibody is naturally occurring without prior exposure?
questions.explanation: Anti-A and anti-B are naturally occurring antibodies present from early infancy without prior exposure to foreign red cells. They're IgM antibodies that activate complement, causing immediate hemolytic reactions if incompatible blood is transfused. All other antibodies require alloimmunization through transfusion or pregnancy.

questions.question: What distinguishes polycythemia vera from secondary erythrocytosis?
questions.explanation: PV is distinguished by: (1) low EPO (vs. elevated in secondary erythrocytosis from hypoxia/EPO-secreting tumors), (2) splenomegaly (rare in secondary), (3) JAK2 mutation (absent in secondary), (4) elevated red cell mass (vs. apparent polycythemia from reduced plasma volume). Bone marrow shows panmyelosis.

ET diagnosis requires sustained platelet count ≥50×10⁹/L, bone marrow showing megakaryocytic proliferation, and exclusion of other myeloproliferative neoplasms or reactive causes. JAK2 V617F (~55%), CALR (~25%), or MPL (~5%) mutations support diagnosis. Complications include thrombosis and bleeding (especially if platelets >1000). Treatment includes aspirin, hydroxyurea if high-risk, or anagrelide.
questions.question: Essential thrombocythemia diagnostic criteria include platelet count greater than:
Staging of multiple myeloma traditionally uses which system?
questions.explanation: Traditional Durie-Salmon staging uses hemoglobin, calcium, bone lesions, and M-protein levels. International Staging System (ISS) uses β2-microglobulin and albumin, correlating better with survival. Revised ISS incorporates cytogenetics and LDH. Staging guides prognosis and treatment decisions. Modern risk stratification includes FISH abnormalities (del17p, t(4;14), t(14;16) are high-risk).

TP53 mutations (or del17p deleting TP53) occur in 5-10% of CLL at diagnosis, increasing with disease progression, conferring extremely poor prognosis with chemo-immunotherapy resistance. Median survival <3 years with conventional treatment. These patients require novel agents (venetoclax BCL2 inhibitor, ibrutinib BTK inhibitor) or allogeneic transplant. TP53 testing mandatory before treatment initiation. IGHV mutational status also prognostic (mutated favorable).
questions.question: TP53 mutations in chronic lymphocytic leukaemia predict:

options: Absence of GPI-anchored complement regulatory proteins
Inherited spectrin deficiency causing spherocyte formation
Oxidative haemoglobin denaturation causing Heinz body formation
Mechanical fragmentation from cardiac valve turbulence
Warm autoantibody IgG coating red cells for destruction
questions.explanation: Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria results from a somatic PIG-A gene mutation impairing GPI anchor synthesis. GPI-anchored proteins CD55 (DAF) and CD59 (protectin) normally protect red cells from complement attack. Their absence allows uninhibited terminal complement activation and MAC-mediated intravascular haemolysis. Haemoglobinuria results from intravascular lysis, and thrombosis is driven by platelet complement activation.
questions.question: A patient with PNH has recurrent thrombosis despite anticoagulation and haemoglobinuria. What is the mechanism of haemolysis?
A child with iron deficiency anaemia has a diet consisting mainly of unmodified cow's milk before 12 months of age. What is the likely mechanism?
questions.explanation: Early introduction of whole cow's milk in infants is associated with occult gastrointestinal blood loss, likely from a heat-labile protein effect on the immature gut mucosa, contributing to iron deficiency. Cow's milk is also low in bioavailable iron.

questions.question: What percentage of the general population has VWF levels suggesting possible VWD?
questions.explanation: Approximately 1% of the general population has low VWF levels consistent with possible VWD. However, clinically significant bleeding occurs in only about 1:1000, as many with low levels remain asymptomatic. Diagnosis requires both laboratory findings and bleeding history.

The red cell storage lesion includes progressive ATP depletion from glycolytic inhibition at 4°C, impairing Na-K-ATPase activity and membrane cytoskeletal function. ATP depletion causes loss of discocyte shape (echinocyte formation), increased membrane rigidity, and loss of normal biconcave deformability required to traverse the splenic sinusoids. Rigid, ATP-depleted stored red cells are more rapidly cleared by the spleen (reduced 24-hour in-vivo recovery), reducing the expected post-transfusion haemoglobin increment. Additionally, 2,3-DPG falls during storage, potassium leaks out (hyperkalaemia concern in massive transfusion), and microparticles are released. Units stored longer show a more pronounced storage lesion.
questions.question: A 58-year-old man receives red cells 8 days after collection and has a poor post-transfusion haemoglobin increment (0.4 g/dL per unit instead of expected 1 g/dL). Which storage lesion most directly accounts for reduced in-vivo survival?
options: Potassium leak from stored red cells causing electrolyte imbalance on infusion
Accumulated 2,3-DPG reducing oxygen delivery capacity in stored red cells
Decreased pH in additive solution causing stored red cell haemolysis in vitro
ATP depletion in stored red cells causing membrane rigidity and accelerated splenic clearance
Microaggregate formation from stored platelets causing microvascular sludging

questions.explanation: Natural killer cells are large lymphoid cells lacking characteristic surface markers of mature T and B lymphocytes. They are non-adherent and non-phagocytic but possess innate cytotoxicity against tumor cells and virus-infected cells. NK cells provide rapid immune response.
questions.question: What do natural killer cells lack?

questions.explanation: Antihistamines (diphenhydramine) given prophylactically may prevent/reduce mild allergic (urticarial) reactions in patients with history of such reactions. However, routine premedication isn't recommended as it may mask serious reactions. Acetaminophen may prevent/reduce FNHTR but doesn't prevent other reactions. No premedication prevents serious hemolytic or TRALI reactions.
questions.question: Which medication can be given to prevent urticarial reactions?
What is the mechanism of action of eculizumab in treating paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria?
questions.explanation: Eculizumab is a monoclonal antibody that binds complement protein C5, preventing its cleavage into C5a and C5b. This blocks assembly of the membrane attack complex (MAC) on GPI-deficient red cells, preventing intravascular haemolysis. It dramatically reduces haemolysis, transfusion requirements, and thrombotic events in PNH. It does not correct the underlying PIG-A mutation but effectively controls the complement-mediated haemolysis.
options: Immunosuppression reducing antibody production against RBCs
Stimulation of normal clone expansion to dilute PNH cells
Complement C5 inhibition preventing MAC formation on red cells
Chelation of iron released from intravascular haemolysis
Replacement of deficient GPI-anchored proteins on red cells

questions.question: What confirms heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT)?
questions.explanation: Anti-platelet factor 4/heparin antibodies confirm HIT diagnosis. Platelet count typically falls to 50-150 × 10⁹/L. Paradoxical thrombosis occurs despite thrombocytopenia. Heparin must be stopped immediately; alternative anticoagulation started.

questions.question: What is the most immunogenic red cell antigen after A and B?
questions.explanation: The D antigen is the most immunogenic after A and B, readily inducing anti-D antibodies in D-negative individuals. Approximately 80% of D-negative persons develop anti-D after exposure to D-positive red cells. This explains Rh incompatibility importance in pregnancy and transfusion.

Cord blood has the lowest GVHD risk due to immunological naivety of neonatal T cells. The immature immune system causes less severe immunological complications. This advantage allows greater HLA disparity tolerance.
questions.question: Which stem cell source has lowest GVHD risk?

questions.explanation: Normal reticulocyte percentage ranges from 0.5-2.5%, reflecting daily red cell turnover. Absolute reticulocyte count is 50-100 × 10⁹/L. Increased reticulocytes indicate marrow response to anemia or hemolysis.
questions.question: What is the normal reticulocyte percentage?

questions.explanation: FISH uses fluorescent probes hybridizing to specific DNA sequences, detecting chromosomal translocations, deletions, or duplications. Advantages include rapid results (24-48 hours versus days for conventional cytogenetics) and detection in non-dividing cells. Used for Philadelphia chromosome, PML-RARA in APL, IGH rearrangements in lymphomas, and 17p deletion in CLL/myeloma. Complements conventional cytogenetics and molecular studies.
questions.question: Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) is used to detect:

questions.explanation: Factor VIII is primarily synthesized by hepatic sinusoidal endothelial cells, with additional production by endothelial cells throughout the vascular system. This explains successful liver transplant correction of hemophilia A. Megakaryocytes do not produce Factor VIII.
questions.question: What is the primary site of Factor VIII synthesis?

questions.explanation: Hereditary spherocytosis results from mutations in membrane proteins (spectrin, ankyrin, band 3, protein 4.2) causing loss of membrane surface area relative to volume, forming spherocytes. Spherocytes are less deformable and trapped in splenic cords, undergoing extravascular hemolysis. Inheritance is usually autosomal dominant.
questions.question: What is the pathophysiology of hereditary spherocytosis?

questions.explanation: Permanent tooth extraction requires factor replacement to achieve >50% levels before procedure and maintenance for 2-3 days. Antifibrinolytic agents (EACA or tranexamic acid) supplement coverage. Simple fillings may not require replacement in mild hemophilia.
questions.question: Which dental procedure requires factor replacement in hemophilia?
options: Simple cleaning with no gingival trauma

questions.explanation: Beta-thalassaemia trait (heterozygous beta-thalassaemia) presents with mild microcytic hypochromic anaemia and characteristically elevated HbA2 (>3.5%, normal <3.2%) because with reduced beta chain synthesis, excess alpha chains combine with delta chains to form HbA2 (alpha2delta2) in increased proportions. Iron stores are normal, excluding iron deficiency. Alpha-thalassaemia trait causes similar morphological changes but HbA2 is normal or low. The diagnosis of beta-thalassaemia trait is essential for genetic counselling, particularly before pregnancy, as two carriers risk having a child with beta-thalassaemia major.
options: Alpha-thalassaemia trait reducing alpha chain production
Beta-thalassaemia trait causing reduced beta chain synthesis
HbC trait producing microcytosis and target cells
Sideroblastic anaemia from impaired haem ring iron incorporation
Iron deficiency anaemia with coincidentally elevated HbA2
questions.question: A 28-year-old woman has microcytic hypochromic anaemia (MCV 64 fL, Hb 9.2 g/dL) with normal serum iron and ferritin but elevated HbA2 (4.8%) on haemoglobin electrophoresis. What is the diagnosis?

questions.explanation: The Kell system (especially K antigen) is highly immunogenic after ABO and Rh. Anti-K can cause severe hemolytic transfusion reactions and hemolytic disease of the newborn. K-negative blood is often provided to women of childbearing potential and previously transfused patients to prevent alloimmunization.
questions.question: Which antigen system, after ABO and Rh, is most immunogenic?

questions.explanation: Approximately 50% of multiple myeloma patients develop renal failure at some point. Causes include light chain deposition, hypercalcemia, hyperuricemia, dehydration and contrast nephropathy. Renal function affects prognosis and treatment options.
questions.question: What percentage of myeloma patients have renal involvement?

questions.explanation: Breast milk has low iron content, and infant iron stores from birth typically deplete by 6 months. Exclusive prolonged breastfeeding without iron-fortified weaning foods or supplementation predisposes to iron deficiency anaemia in this age group.
questions.question: A 6-month-old exclusively breastfed infant develops microcytic anaemia. What is the most likely contributing factor?
The bone marrow accounts for what percentage of body weight in humans?
questions.explanation: The bone marrow comprises approximately 5% of total body weight in humans, making it the fourth largest organ by weight. This significant proportion reflects its crucial role in continuous blood cell production throughout life. The marrow's extensive distribution ensures adequate hematopoietic capacity to meet physiological demands.

options: Azacitidine incorporates into DNA, inhibiting DNMT and reversing hypermethylation of tumour suppressors
Azacitidine inhibits ribonucleotide reductase reducing dNTP pool for MDS blast proliferation
Azacitidine directly cross-links DNA, causing double-strand breaks in MDS blast cells
Azacitidine activates p53 through nucleoside analogue DNA damage signalling
Azacitidine is an immunomodulator increasing NK cell killing of myelodysplastic blasts
questions.explanation: Azacitidine (5-azacytidine) is a hypomethylating agent: after incorporation into DNA during replication, it covalently traps DNA methyltransferases (DNMTs), causing their depletion and inhibiting cytosine methylation. In MDS, aberrant promoter CpG hypermethylation silences tumour suppressor genes (p15/CDKN2B, CDH1, SOCS1) that would otherwise control cell cycle, apoptosis, and differentiation. Azacitidine reverses this hypermethylation, reactivating silenced tumour suppressors and partially restoring normal haematopoietic differentiation. The AZA-001 trial showed azacitidine prolongs survival (24.5 months vs 15 months) versus conventional care in high-risk MDS.
questions.question: A 78-year-old man with high-risk MDS (RAEB-2, 16% marrow blasts) is started on azacitidine. What is the mechanism of azacitidine's anti-leukaemic activity in MDS?

questions.explanation: MDS is predominantly disease of elderly (median age 70 years). Elderly patients have worse outcomes due to: adverse cytogenetics, more comorbidities, poorer performance status, decreased tolerance of intensive therapy. Allogeneic SCT (only cure) has higher mortality risk in elderly. Treatment often focuses on supportive care, quality of life, and less intensive approaches (azacitidine, decitabine, lenalidomide for del(5q)).
questions.question: What characterizes myelodysplastic syndrome in elderly patients?
options: Age >70 years associates with poor prognosis

questions.explanation: CLL does not require immediate treatment in most patients at diagnosis. The watch-and-wait approach is standard for early-stage asymptomatic CLL, as early treatment does not improve survival. Treatment is initiated when active disease criteria are met: progressive lymphocytosis, symptomatic lymphadenopathy, cytopenias, constitutional symptoms, or lymphocyte doubling time under 6 months.
options: Start ibrutinib immediately upon confirmed diagnosis
