What is the significance of t(4;11) in infant acute leukemia?
questions.explanation: t(4;11) and other 11q23 (MLL/KMT2A) rearrangements occur in 70-80% of infant ALL (<1 year) and confer poor prognosis. MLL fusion proteins cause aberrant gene expression driving leukemogenesis. These leukemias often present with high WBC, CNS involvement, and mixed-lineage phenotype. Intensive therapy and transplant may be needed.

Antiphospholipid syndrome is characterised by recurrent thrombosis or pregnancy morbidity in association with persistent antiphospholipid antibodies, including lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin antibodies, despite a paradoxically prolonged clotting time in vitro.
questions.question: A patient on long-term anticoagulation for recurrent thrombosis is found to have lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin antibodies. What syndrome does this most likely represent?
What is the daily iron requirement for menstruating women?
questions.explanation: Menstruating women require approximately 18 mg dietary iron daily versus 8 mg for men. Menstrual losses average 15-40 mg per period. Pregnancy requires 27 mg daily. Requirements decrease postmenopausally.

options: Deficient dense granules with content deficiency
Normal platelet function with count deficiency
questions.explanation: Glanzmann thrombasthenia is autosomal recessive deficiency of GPIIb/IIIa (integrin aIIbβ3), preventing platelet aggregation. Platelets cannot bind fibrinogen. Platelet count and size are normal but aggregation is absent to all agonists except ristocetin (tests GPIb). Severe bleeding requires platelet transfusions or recombinant Factor VIIa.
questions.question: What characterizes Glanzmann thrombasthenia?

questions.explanation: Rising BCR-ABL suggests: non-compliance (most common - assess adherence), resistance (kinase domain mutations - perform mutation analysis), inadequate dosing (drug interactions, poor absorption). Options: dose escalation (imatinib 600-800 mg if tolerated), switch to second-generation TKI (dasatinib, nilotinib) if mutations or intolerance, ponatinib if T315I mutation. Transplant considered for blast crisis or multiple TKI failures.
options: Continue same dose and monitor counts closely
Check adherence, escalate dose, or test mutations
Stop all TKI therapy without assessment
questions.question: A patient with CML on imatinib for 1 year has rising BCR-ABL levels. What is the next appropriate step?
What is the hallmark cytogenetic abnormality in chronic myeloid leukemia?
questions.explanation: The Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22)(q34;q11) creates BCR-ABL1 fusion oncogene and is present in >95% of CML cases. This balanced translocation was the first consistent chromosomal abnormality linked to a specific cancer. It drives the pathogenesis of CML.

Hemarthrosis requires Factor VIII levels of 40-50% for adequate treatment. More severe joint bleeding may require 50% or higher. Treatment should begin at first symptom before objective signs develop. RICE (rest, ice, compression, elevation) supplements factor replacement.
questions.question: What is the recommended Factor VIII level for mild hemarthrosis treatment?

questions.explanation: Gamma irradiation (25-50 Gy) prevents transfusion-associated GVHD (TA-GVHD) by inactivating donor T lymphocytes that could engraft and attack recipient tissues. Indicated for immunocompromised patients, HLA-matched products, and blood from relatives. TA-GVHD is rare but highly fatal (>90% mortality).
questions.question: What is irradiation of blood components intended to prevent?

questions.explanation: Thalidomide and lenalidomide significantly increase VTE risk in myeloma, particularly when combined with dexamethasone or chemotherapy. The mechanism involves multiple pathways: upregulation of endothelial adhesion molecules (VCAM-1, E-selectin) promoting hypercoagulability; increased tissue factor expression on monocytes and tumour cells; reduced levels of natural anticoagulants; and direct pro-aggregatory platelet effects. The combination with dexamethasone is particularly thrombogenic (3-6-fold increased VTE risk vs controls). Current guidelines mandate VTE prophylaxis for all myeloma patients on thalidomide/lenalidomide-based regimens: low-risk patients receive aspirin; high-risk patients receive LMWH.
questions.question: A 68-year-old man with multiple myeloma started on thalidomide-dexamethasone develops deep vein thrombosis three weeks later. What pharmacological property of thalidomide explains the increased VTE risk?
options: Thalidomide directly activates platelet aggregation via thromboxane A2
Thalidomide causes immobility from peripheral neuropathy increasing stasis-related thrombosis
Thalidomide inhibits natural anticoagulants (protein C and S) at the hepatic level
Thalidomide promotes a procoagulant state by increasing endothelial adhesion molecule expression and tissue factor
Dexamethasone-thalidomide combination induces factor VIII synthesis in myeloma cells

questions.question: A patient with CLL develops rapidly enlarging lymph node, fever, and elevated LDH. Biopsy shows large cells. What occurred?
questions.explanation: Richter transformation: CLL transformation to aggressive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (90%) or Hodgkin lymphoma (10%). Occurs in 2-10% of CLL patients. Clinical clues: rapid single-node enlargement, B symptoms, elevated LDH, extranodal disease, hypercalcemia. Diagnosis requires biopsy. Poor prognosis (median survival <1 year with chemotherapy). Consider clinical trial, intensive chemotherapy, or allogeneic transplant in fit patients.

Infections cause most deaths in first 100 days: bacterial (neutropenic phase), fungal (Aspergillus, Candida during prolonged neutropenia), viral (CMV, adenovirus with immunosuppression). Pneumonia is leading infectious cause. Other early causes include VOD, acute GVHD, organ toxicity. Later (>100 days), chronic GVHD, infections (encapsulated bacteria, varicella zoster), relapse predominate. Prophylactic antimicrobials reduce but don't eliminate infection risk.
questions.question: The most common cause of death in the first 100 days post-transplant is:

options: Mutations in VWF promoter reducing transcription
Large deletions removing entire VWF gene
Increased clearance from clearance receptor polymorphisms
questions.question: Which genetic abnormality is associated with Type 1 VWD in some cases?
questions.explanation: Type 1 VWD results from various mechanisms: reduced synthesis (promoter mutations), impaired secretion (misfolding), or increased clearance (receptor polymorphisms). The phenotype is proportionate reduction of all multimers. Genetic heterogeneity explains variable severity and family patterns.

Deferoxamine requires subcutaneous infusion over 8-12 hours (usually overnight), 5-7 nights weekly, or continuous IV infusion. This route is necessary due to short half-life. It effectively removes iron but poor compliance is common. Oral agents (deferasirox once daily, deferiprone three times daily) improve compliance. Combination therapy enhances iron removal.
questions.question: Which chelator is administered via subcutaneous infusion overnight?

options: Hip joint from weight-bearing locomotor trauma
Knee joint from weight-bearing and full range of motion
Elbow joint from repetitive upper extremity use
Shoulder joint from daily overhead activity loads
Ankle joint from frequent minor soft tissue injury
questions.explanation: The knee is the most frequently affected joint in haemophilic arthropathy due to its biomechanics, range of motion, and vulnerability to minor trauma in active patients. Repeated haemarthroses cause synovial hypertrophy, iron deposition, cartilage degradation, and progressive arthropathy. Early prophylactic factor replacement specifically aims to protect knee joints alongside ankles and elbows.
questions.question: What is the most likely joint to develop chronic haemophilic arthropathy in severe untreated haemophilia A?

questions.explanation: The contact pathway (Factor XII activation) is important for in vitro clotting (aPTT test) but not physiologic hemostasis. Factor XII deficiency causes prolonged aPTT but no bleeding. This pathway involves high molecular weight kininogen and prekallikrein. TF pathway is physiologically important.
options: Important for in vitro aPTT prolongation
questions.question: What characterizes the contact activation pathway?

options: Increased hemoglobin F production reducing HbS percentage
Improved red cell hydration preventing polymerization
questions.explanation: Hydroxyurea's benefits involve multiple mechanisms: increased HbF (primary effect), increased red cell hydration and MCV, reduced leukocyte and platelet counts (reducing inflammation), increased nitric oxide bioavailability, and direct anti-adhesive effects. It reduces crisis frequency by 50%, mortality, and acute chest syndrome. It's standard therapy for adults and children.
questions.question: What is the mechanism of hydroxyurea benefit in sickle cell disease?

options: Deletion of all four alpha genes
questions.explanation: Hemoglobin H disease (--/-a) results from three alpha-gene deletions, causing excess beta chains that form unstable β4 tetramers (HbH). It presents with moderate hemolytic anemia (Hb 7-10 g/dL), splenomegaly, and microcytosis. HbH is detectable on electrophoresis and forms inclusions with supravital staining. Transfusions occasionally needed during infections/pregnancy.
questions.question: What is hemoglobin H disease?
Clopidogrel prevents platelet aggregation by blocking:
questions.explanation: Clopidogrel irreversibly blocks P2Y12 ADP receptor, preventing ADP-mediated platelet activation and aggregation. It's a prodrug requiring hepatic activation by CYP2C19. Used for secondary prevention of cardiovascular events, often combined with aspirin (dual antiplatelet therapy) after acute coronary syndrome or stenting. Prasugrel and ticagrelor are alternative P2Y12 inhibitors.

WHO criteria define acute leukemia as ≥20% blasts in bone marrow, reduced from FAB's 30%. However, certain cytogenetic abnormalities (t(8;21), inv(16), t(15;17)) establish AML diagnosis regardless of blast percentage. This reflects recognition of distinct biological entities.
questions.question: What percentage of bone marrow blasts defines acute leukemia by WHO criteria?
Which laboratory test monitors myeloma response to treatment?
questions.explanation: Serial serum and urine protein electrophoresis/immunofixation tracks M-protein levels, the most sensitive and practical response marker. Serum free light chains supplement monitoring, especially in light chain or oligosecretory myeloma. Bone marrow biopsy confirms complete response. Imaging assesses structural bone disease.

questions.question: What is the typical cause of maternal sensitization to D antigen?
questions.explanation: Maternal sensitization to D antigen usually results from previous pregnancy with D-positive fetus or past transfusion with D-positive blood. Fetomaternal hemorrhage during pregnancy allows fetal cells into maternal circulation, triggering antibody formation. Even small volumes can sensitize.

options: Antibody formation against protein C-warfarin complex
Direct toxic effect of warfarin on dermal vessels
Rapid depletion of protein C before clotting factors
Enhanced platelet aggregation from warfarin metabolites
Increased tissue factor expression in skin
questions.question: Which mechanism explains warfarin-induced skin necrosis in protein C deficiency?
questions.explanation: Protein C has a shorter half-life (6-8 hours) than vitamin K-dependent clotting factors (24-60 hours). Warfarin initiation rapidly depletes protein C before factors II, VII, IX, and X, creating transient hypercoagulability. This causes dermal vessel thrombosis in deficient patients.

Heinz bodies are denatured hemoglobin precipitates attached to red cell membrane, seen in G6PD deficiency during oxidative stress. They're visible with supravital stains (crystal violet) but not Wright-Giemsa. Splenic pitting creates "bite cells" when Heinz bodies are removed.
questions.question: What do Heinz bodies represent?
What percentage of body's platelets are stored in the spleen?
questions.explanation: Approximately one-third (33%) of total body platelets are stored in the spleen and can be released into circulation when needed. This platelet pool is in continuous exchange with circulating platelets. Splenomegaly can sequester even more platelets.

questions.question: Which cells produce EBV-specific antibodies in infectious mononucleosis?
questions.explanation: Plasma cells produce EBV-specific antibodies detectable by the Paul-Bunnell test (heterophile antibodies). Atypical lymphocytes seen on blood film are activated T cells responding to infected B cells. The immune response drives lymphocytosis.

questions.question: Which lymphoma may develop after EBV infection?
questions.explanation: Burkitt lymphoma is associated with EBV infection, particularly endemic African cases. EBV infection of B lymphocytes can lead to malignant transformation. Other EBV-associated malignancies include Hodgkin lymphoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

questions.question: A neonate develops jaundice within 24 hours of birth. Mother is blood group O, baby is group A, direct Coombs is weakly positive. Hb is 13.8 g/dL. What is the most likely mechanism?
options: Maternal IgM anti-A antibodies crossing the placenta and haemolysing A cells
Neonatal G6PD deficiency triggered by ABO blood group antigen difference
Group O maternal IgG anti-A antibodies crossing placenta and destroying neonatal A cells
ABO-incompatible transfusion given to the mother intrapartum
Complement-mediated intravascular haemolysis from alternative pathway activation
questions.explanation: ABO haemolytic disease of the newborn occurs when a group O mother has IgG class anti-A (or anti-B) antibodies that cross the placenta - in contrast to naturally occurring IgM isoagglutinins, which cannot cross the placenta. Group O individuals frequently have IgG anti-A antibodies that are transplacental and haemolyse fetal/neonatal group A (or B) red cells. ABO HDN is generally milder than Rh HDN because A and B antigens are incompletely developed at birth and expressed on many body tissues, diluting the antibody. First pregnancies can be affected, unlike Rh disease.

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman has petechiae, purpura, and platelet count of 8,000/µL. Bone marrow biopsy shows increased megakaryocytes. What is the mechanism?
questions.explanation: Increased megakaryocytes confirm adequate platelet production, ruling out hypoproliferative causes. The combination of peripheral thrombocytopenia, increased megakaryocytes, and isolated thrombocytopenia in a young woman is classic ITP. Anti-platelet IgG antibodies (against GPIIb/IIIa or GPIb) cause Fc receptor-mediated splenic destruction of opsonised platelets.
options: Reduced platelet production from bone marrow failure
Platelet consumption in disseminated intravascular coagulation
Dilutional thrombocytopenia from massive fluid replacement
Splenic trapping without peripheral immune destruction

questions.question: A CLL patient with unmutated IGHV and del(17p) has progressive disease. Why does FCR chemotherapy perform poorly?
questions.explanation: Del(17p) results in loss of TP53, which induces apoptosis in response to DNA damage from cytotoxic chemotherapy like FCR. Without functional p53, CLL cells cannot undergo apoptosis when DNA damage is inflicted by fludarabine or cyclophosphamide. These patients require p53-independent therapies such as BTK inhibitors (ibrutinib) or BCL-2 inhibitors (venetoclax).
options: FCR causes excessive myelosuppression in 17p deletion
Fludarabine metabolism is impaired in 17p deletion
TP53 mutation prevents DNA damage-induced apoptosis
FCR activates anti-apoptotic BCL-2 through 17p loss
Rituximab cannot penetrate lymph nodes containing CLL

questions.explanation: Polycythaemia vera shows JAK2 V617F mutation in >95% of cases, or JAK2 exon 12 mutations in remainder. This causes constitutive activation of JAK-STAT pathway, driving erythrocytosis independent of erythropoietin. Diagnostic criteria include elevated Hct (>49% males, >48% females), bone marrow hypercellularity, low EPO, and JAK2 mutation. Treatment includes phlebotomy, aspirin, hydroxyurea.

questions.explanation: Chronic haemolysis in sickle cell disease increases bilirubin turnover, predisposing to pigment gallstones composed mainly of calcium bilirubinate, which occur at a much higher frequency and younger age than in the general population.
questions.question: A patient with sickle cell disease is found to have asymptomatic gallstones on ultrasound. What is the most likely composition of these stones?

options: 25,000 to 100,000 daltons for Factor VIII binding
questions.explanation: VWF exists as multimers ranging from 600,000 to over 20 million daltons. The largest multimers are most effective in platelet adhesion. ADAMTS-13 cleaves ultra-large multimers released from endothelial cells into smaller, circulating forms.

options: Factor VIII concentrate before all procedures and during heavy bleeds
Platelet transfusions for major bleeds in this platelet dysfunction disorder
Fresh frozen plasma as the most readily available VWF source
Recombinant FVIIa to bypass the VWF-dependent haemostatic pathway
Tranexamic acid and DDAVP to treat von Willebrand disease type 1
questions.question: A 35-year-old woman has menorrhagia since menarche, mildly prolonged APTT, normal PT, normal platelet count, VWF antigen 28%, and reduced ristocetin cofactor activity. What is the first-line treatment for her menorrhagia?
questions.explanation: Von Willebrand disease type 1 is the most common inherited bleeding disorder, caused by quantitative reduction in vWF. Treatment for menorrhagia and minor bleeds includes DDAVP (intranasal or IV) which releases stored vWF from endothelial Weibel-Palade bodies, raising vWF levels 2-5-fold, combined with tranexamic acid (antifibrinolytic) to prevent clot dissolution. The APTT is mildly prolonged because vWF stabilises factor VIII; PT is unaffected. VWF concentrate is reserved for type 2/3 VWD or DDAVP non-responders.

Among CRAB criteria, hypercalcaemia is the most immediately life-threatening, causing polyuria, dehydration, confusion, cardiac arrhythmia, and coma if untreated. Urgent management includes aggressive IV hydration and bisphosphonates. While renal impairment is also serious, acute symptomatic hypercalcaemia above 11 mg/dL with symptoms takes immediate priority.
options: Anaemia with haemoglobin below 10 g/dL threshold
Hypercalcaemia causing confusion and acute dehydration
M-spike requiring bone marrow biopsy confirmation
Bone pain from osteolytic lesions needing analgesia
Renal impairment from light chain cast nephropathy
questions.question: A 62-year-old has back pain, anaemia, serum calcium 11.8 mg/dL, creatinine 2.1 mg/dL, and an M-spike on SPEP. Which immediate complication requires most urgent management?

options: Normal protein C level with functional deficiency
Prolonged dilute Russell viper venom time
Failure of APC to prolong aPTT appropriately
Elevated Factor V antigen with normal activity
questions.question: Which laboratory finding best distinguishes Factor V Leiden from other causes of APC resistance?
questions.explanation: Molecular detection of the specific G1691A mutation definitively diagnoses Factor V Leiden. Functional APC resistance assays can be abnormal in other conditions. Genetic testing distinguishes true Factor V Leiden from acquired causes of APC resistance.

options: CLL remains in remission for months as ibrutinib's effect persists through tissue binding
CLL is eliminated because ibrutinib has induced complete molecular remission
CLL transforms to AML following ibrutinib discontinuation due to clonal evolution
CLL becomes sensitive to FCR chemotherapy after BTK inhibitor exposure
CLL may flare rapidly with lymphocytosis and lymphadenopathy within days to weeks
questions.question: A 67-year-old man with CLL has biopsy-confirmed Richter's transformation to DLBCL and his ibrutinib is stopped. What typically happens to his underlying CLL after stopping ibrutinib?
questions.explanation: Ibrutinib (a covalent BTK inhibitor) redistributes CLL cells from lymph nodes and bone marrow into the blood during the first weeks of treatment (causing transient lymphocytosis), then gradually reduces the CLL clone over months to years. This redistribution effect and BTK inhibition are reversible upon drug discontinuation; abrupt ibrutinib cessation can cause rapid disease rebound - CLL cells re-traffic from blood back into lymph nodes and proliferate aggressively, sometimes causing a fulminant lymphocytosis or lymphadenopathy flare within days to weeks. In Richter's transformation, stopping BTK inhibitor to pursue DLBCL-directed therapy can unmask rapid CLL disease acceleration.

The pronormoblast (proerythroblast) is the earliest morphologically recognizable erythroid precursor, with fine nuclear chromatin, nucleoli, and basophilic cytoplasm. Earlier stages (BFU-E, CFU-E) are committed progenitors identifiable only by culture, not morphology. One pronormoblast undergoes ~4 mitotic divisions producing 16 mature red cells.

questions.explanation: Normal activated partial thromboplastin time ranges from 30-40 seconds. APTT evaluates intrinsic and common coagulation pathways. Prolongation suggests deficiency of factors VIII, IX, XI, XII or presence of inhibitors.
questions.question: What is the normal APTT range?

questions.explanation: Riboflavin deficiency impairs iron mobilization and utilization, causing normocytic or microcytic anaemia despite adequate iron stores. Riboflavin is cofactor for flavoproteins in iron metabolism. Clinical features include angular stomatitis, glossitis, cheilosis, seborrheic dermatitis. Rare in developed countries; occurs in malabsorption, alcoholism, strict dietary restrictions. Treatment is riboflavin supplementation.
questions.question: Riboflavin (vitamin B2) deficiency causes anaemia through:
A patient with sickle cell disease develops priapism lasting more than 4 hours. What is the most appropriate immediate management approach?
questions.explanation: Prolonged priapism beyond 4 hours is a urological emergency requiring prompt aspiration and irrigation, sometimes with intracavernosal phenylephrine, alongside hydration and analgesia, to prevent corporal fibrosis and permanent erectile dysfunction.

questions.question: Hereditary persistence of fetal haemoglobin is characterized by:
questions.explanation: HPFH is benign condition with continued HbF production into adulthood (10-30% in heterozygotes, 100% in homozygotes) due to deletions or point mutations preventing γ to β-chain switch. Individuals are asymptomatic with normal haemoglobin, slight microcytosis. Clinical importance: ameliorates sickle cell disease and β-thalassaemia when coinherited. Pancellular (all cells) versus heterocellular (some cells) distribution distinguishes types.

options: Co-amoxiclav; best coverage for Haemophilus influenzae and Moraxella catarrhalis
Flucloxacillin IV; Staphylococcus aureus is the most common pathogen in SCD sepsis
Gentamicin IV; gram-negative cover for UTI as the likely source in SCD children
Azithromycin; covers atypical organisms causing pneumonia in SCD-related ACS
Ceftriaxone IV; covers encapsulated bacteria causing sepsis in functionally asplenic children
questions.question: A 3-year-old child with sickle cell disease (HbSS) has fever 39.1°C, respiratory rate 40/min, and appears toxic. WBC is 28 × 10⁹/L. What is the most important immediate antibiotic and why?
questions.explanation: Children with sickle cell disease develop functional hyposplenism from repeated splenic infarction (autosplenectomy) by age 3-5 years, eliminating the spleen's role in clearing encapsulated bacteria (Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Neisseria meningitidis). Without a functional spleen, overwhelming infection occurs with high mortality. Febrile SCD children under 3 years with temperature >38.5°C are a medical emergency; ceftriaxone (third-generation cephalosporin) covers pneumococcus - the most dangerous pathogen - and gram-negative organisms. Penicillin prophylaxis (from birth) and pneumococcal vaccination are lifelong preventive measures.

questions.question: How many red cell surface antigens are recognized by ISBT?
questions.explanation: The International Society of Blood Transfusion recognizes 347 red cell surface antigens, with 308 belonging to 36 blood group systems. Each system represents single genes or closely linked homologous genes. The remaining antigens lack adequate genetic classification evidence.

questions.question: Which mechanism causes immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP)?
questions.explanation: ITP results from autoantibodies (usually IgG) against platelet surface antigens (GPIIb/IIIa, GPIb/IX), causing premature platelet destruction by splenic macrophages. Bone marrow shows increased megakaryocytes (compensatory). It's a diagnosis of exclusion after ruling out other causes of thrombocytopenia.
options: Bone marrow failure reducing platelet production

questions.explanation: Between 3 and 4 months of fetal development, embryonic hemoglobins (Gower I, Gower II, Portland) are replaced by fetal hemoglobin (HbF). The major switch from fetal to adult hemoglobin occurs 3-6 months after birth. This sequential switching reflects developmental gene regulation.
questions.question: At what fetal age do embryonic hemoglobins switch to fetal hemoglobin?
Between which fetal months does the spleen perform hematopoiesis?
questions.explanation: The spleen serves as a hematopoietic organ between 3 and 7 months of fetal development. This function ceases before birth but can resume in adulthood when needed. Extramedullary hematopoiesis occurs in myelofibrosis, severe hemolysis and myeloid metaplasia.

questions.question: A 55-year-old man with chronic transfusion-dependent MDS has serum ferritin 5,200 ng/mL and normal renal function. Which iron chelating agent is most suitable as a once-daily oral option?
questions.explanation: Deferasirox (Exjade, Jadenu) is a once-daily oral tridentate iron chelator that forms stable 2:1 complexes with ferric iron, predominantly eliminated via biliary/faecal excretion (>80%), making it suitable for patients with normal or mildly impaired renal function. Its oral once-daily dosing dramatically improves compliance over deferoxamine (which requires 8-12 hour subcutaneous infusions 5-7 nights per week). Deferasirox has demonstrated efficacy in reducing serum ferritin and liver iron concentration in chronically transfused patients. Monitoring for renal impairment, hepatotoxicity, and auditory/ocular toxicity is required. Deferiprone is most effective specifically for cardiac iron but requires three-times-daily dosing.
options: Deferasirox; once-daily oral tablet with predominantly biliary excretion
Deferoxamine; the gold standard chelator given subcutaneously over 8-12 hours nightly
Deferiprone; oral three-times-daily chelator with specific cardiac iron removal
Phlebotomy; the most effective method of iron removal in transfused patients
Erythrocytapheresis; removes iron-laden red cells while returning plasma

questions.question: What is the normal myeloid to erythroid ratio in bone marrow?
questions.explanation: The normal myeloid to erythroid (M:E) ratio in bone marrow ranges from 2:1 to 12:1, typically around 3:1 to 4:1. This ratio reflects the relative proportions of granulocytic and erythroid precursors. Altered ratios indicate various pathological conditions.

Platelets have an average lifespan of approximately 10 days and must be continuously replaced by bone marrow megakaryocytes. White blood cells survive only hours to days while red cells last about 120 days. These varying lifespans necessitate differential production rates.
questions.question: What is the average lifespan of platelets?
What percentage of blast cells defines acute leukemia?
questions.explanation: Acute leukemia is defined by 20% or more blast cells in bone marrow or peripheral blood (WHO classification). Exception is acute promyelocytic leukemia with t(15;17) which is diagnosed regardless of blast percentage. Blast morphology and immunophenotype determine subtype.

questions.question: Which antimicrobial prophylaxis is standard during neutropenia?
options: No prophylaxis; treat infections when they occur
questions.explanation: Fluoroquinolone prophylaxis (levofloxacin or ciprofloxacin) is recommended for high-risk neutropenia (expected ANC <500/µL for >7 days) reducing bacterial infections and infection-related mortality. Antifungal prophylaxis (fluconazole or broader agent) is added for prolonged neutropenia (>14 days). Viral prophylaxis (acyclovir/valacyclovir) for herpes-seropositive patients receiving intensive chemotherapy.

questions.question: How many globin genes do humans normally carry?
questions.explanation: Humans normally carry 8 functional globin genes arranged in two clusters. The beta-like cluster on chromosome 11 includes epsilon, two gamma, delta and beta genes. The alpha-like cluster on chromosome 16 includes zeta and two alpha genes.

questions.question: What is the normal bleeding time by template method?
questions.explanation: Normal bleeding time by template method is 2.5-9.5 minutes. Ivy's method has range of 2-7 minutes. Prolonged bleeding time indicates platelet dysfunction or vascular abnormality. The test is operator-dependent.

TRALI is non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema developing within 6 hours of transfusion, caused by donor antibodies (anti-HLA, anti-HNA) activating recipient neutrophils in pulmonary capillaries. It resembles ARDS. Treatment is supportive (oxygen, ventilation). Most cases resolve within 48-96 hours. Prevention involves using plasma from male donors.
options: Cardiogenic pulmonary edema from volume overload
Chronic pulmonary disease from iron deposition
questions.question: What characterizes transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI)?

questions.explanation: Hydroxyurea (hydroxycarbamide) causes macrocytosis and megaloblastic morphological changes by inhibiting ribonucleotide reductase, the enzyme converting ribonucleoside diphosphates to deoxyribonucleoside diphosphates - reducing the dNTP pool available for DNA synthesis. The resulting impairment in DNA replication mimics megaloblastic changes (large red cells, macro-ovalocytes, hypersegmented neutrophils, large platelets) without true folate or B12 deficiency. This is a recognisable and expected side effect of hydroxyurea therapy. Serum B12 and folate are normal in hydroxyurea-induced megaloblastosis, distinguishing it from nutritional deficiency. No treatment beyond dose adjustment is required if clinically significant cytopenias develop.
questions.question: A 60-year-old man on hydroxyurea for polycythaemia vera has macro-ovalocytes, hypersegmented neutrophils, large platelets, and MCV 108 fL on blood film. Serum B12 and folate are normal. What explains this megaloblastic morphology?
options: Hydroxyurea; inhibits ribonucleotide reductase causing megaloblastic morphology
Omeprazole reduces B12 absorption by raising gastric pH and inhibiting intrinsic factor
Phenytoin; impairs intestinal folate absorption through brush border enzyme inhibition
Methotrexate; inhibits dihydrofolate reductase depleting tetrahydrofolate
Trimethoprim; acts as a dihydrofolate reductase inhibitor at therapeutic doses

questions.explanation: VOD/SOS prevention strategies: ursodeoxycholic acid (reduces hepatotoxicity), defibrotide (protects endothelium), avoiding hepatotoxic drugs. High-risk patients (prior VOD, intensive conditioning, iron overload, hepatitis, gemtuzumab ozogamicin exposure) may receive prophylactic defibrotide. Once VOD develops, treatment is supportive (fluid management, avoiding nephrotoxins/hepatotoxins); severe cases receive therapeutic defibrotide (only approved treatment). Mortality in severe VOD exceeds 80% without defibrotide.
questions.question: What is the mechanism of veno-occlusive disease prevention?

questions.explanation: HbSC disease (compound heterozygote for HbS and HbC) has intermediate severity between HbSS and trait. Hemoglobin is higher (10-12 g/dL), sickling less frequent, but complications still occur: vaso-occlusive crises, acute chest syndrome, proliferative retinopathy (more common than HbSS), avascular necrosis. Treatment principles similar to HbSS.
questions.question: What characterizes hemoglobin SC disease?
options: Milder than HbSS with intermediate severity

questions.explanation: Cold agglutinin disease involves IgM antibodies that bind red cells optimally at 4°C, causing agglutination and complement-mediated haemolysis. Clinical features include haemolysis exacerbated by cold exposure, acrocyanosis, and Raynaud phenomenon. It may be idiopathic or secondary to Mycoplasma pneumonia, infectious mononucleosis, or lymphoproliferative disorders.
questions.question: Cold agglutinin disease is associated with antibodies of which immunoglobulin class?

questions.explanation: Factor V Leiden mutation (G1691A) causes replacement of arginine with glutamine at position 506, creating resistance to activated protein C. This is the most common inherited thrombophilia causing APC resistance. The mutant Factor V remains active longer, promoting hypercoagulability.
options: Prothrombin G20210A causing elevated factor levels
Protein C Leiden affecting activation site
Antithrombin Cambridge with reduced heparin binding
Factor V Leiden with arginine to glutamine substitution
Thrombomodulin mutation reducing protein C activation
questions.question: A patient with recurrent DVT has normal protein C and S levels but demonstrates APC resistance. What mutation is most likely?

options: Factor levels always normal exceeding 50 percent
Factor levels average 50 percent with range 25-75 percent
Identical bleeding phenotype to affected males
Normal coagulation tests excluding carrier status
questions.question: What characterizes hemophilia carrier state in females?
questions.explanation: Female carriers typically have factor levels around 50% (range 25-75%) due to random X-inactivation (lyonization). Most are asymptomatic, but those with levels <30% may have bleeding. Extreme lyonization can produce hemophilia in carriers.

questions.question: A patient with combined iron and B12 deficiency presents with a normal MCV. What is the most likely explanation for this finding?
questions.explanation: Iron deficiency causes microcytosis while B12 deficiency causes macrocytosis. When both occur together, their opposing effects on red cell size can cancel out, producing a deceptively normal MCV despite significant underlying anaemia and combined deficiency.

questions.question: Folate deficiency develops within what time period of inadequate intake?
questions.explanation: Folate stores (5-10 mg) are exhausted within 2-3 months of inadequate intake, causing megaloblastic anaemia. Rapid turnover occurs because daily requirements (~400 µg) are high relative to stores. Contrasts with B12 (stores last 3-4 years). Causes include poor diet (elderly, alcoholics), malabsorption, increased demand (pregnancy, haemolysis), drugs (methotrexate). Treatment is oral folic acid 5 mg daily.

questions.question: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) is elevated in all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: ESR decreases in polycythaemia (increased Hct reduces settling), sickle cell disease (abnormal shape prevents rouleaux), heart failure, and hypofibrinogenaemia. ESR increases with inflammation (elevated fibrinogen, immunoglobulins), anaemia, pregnancy, age, and paraproteins promoting rouleaux formation. Normal values: males 2-10, females 2-12 mm/hr, higher in pregnancy (<48).

options: Spontaneous de novo AML with no relationship to prior lymphoma treatment
Therapy-related AML from alkylating agent (cyclophosphamide) and topoisomerase II inhibitor (doxorubicin)
Richter's transformation of residual DLBCL clone into myeloid lineage
EBV-driven myeloid transformation following rituximab-induced immunosuppression
MDS progression to AML unrelated to prior treatment in this ageing patient
questions.explanation: Therapy-related AML (t-AML) develops in 1-3% of patients treated with alkylating agents and/or topoisomerase II inhibitors, typically 5-10 years after exposure. Cyclophosphamide (alkylating agent in CHOP) causes deletion of chromosomes 5 and 7 (or 5q and 7q), creating a characteristic cytogenetic profile for alkylating agent-related t-AML. Doxorubicin (topoisomerase II inhibitor) causes balanced translocations (typically MLL gene rearrangements at 11q23) presenting earlier (1-3 years). The 6-year latency and complex karyotype with del(5) and del(7) are classic for alkylator-related t-AML. Therapy-related AML has poor prognosis with complex karyotype conferring further adverse risk.
questions.question: A 66-year-old man in complete remission 6 years after R-CHOP for DLBCL is found to have new AML with complex karyotype including chromosome 5 and 7 deletions. What is the most likely explanation?

options: Hepatic vein thrombosis causing liver dysfunction
questions.explanation: Budd-Chiari syndrome (hepatic vein thrombosis) causes hepatomegaly, ascites, liver dysfunction. MPNs (especially PV) are the most common cause of Budd-Chiari in Western countries. Many patients with "idiopathic" Budd-Chiari have undiagnosed MPN (often JAK2+). Screening for MPN is mandatory in unusual thrombosis sites.
questions.question: What is Budd-Chiari syndrome in MPN context?

questions.explanation: Haploidentical transplant uses half-matched (typically 5/10) family donor (parent, child, half-sibling). Everyone has a haploidentical donor (parents, children, ~50% siblings). Post-transplant cyclophosphamide eliminates alloreactive T-cells, permitting engraftment with acceptable GVHD rates. This expands donor access.
options: Perfect HLA match from family member
Autologous cells with minimal HLA matching
questions.question: What characterizes haploidentical transplantation?
Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura in adults is best treated initially with:
questions.explanation: First-line treatment for ITP in adults is corticosteroids (prednisone 1 mg/kg/day), which suppress antibody production and reduce macrophage clearance. Most patients respond within 2-4 weeks. IVIG is reserved for severe bleeding or urgent situations. Splenectomy is considered for refractory cases after 3-6 months. Platelet transfusions are generally ineffective except life-threatening bleeding.

questions.question: Which test assesses platelet function?
questions.explanation: Platelet aggregometry measures platelet aggregation in response to agonists (ADP, collagen, epinephrine, arachidonic acid, ristocetin). Different patterns identify specific defects. PFA-100 (closure time) is a screening test. Bleeding time is obsolete. Flow cytometry assesses surface receptors.

options: Asymptomatic (smouldering) myeloma; start chemotherapy to prevent progression
Stage I multiple myeloma; initiate bortezomib-dexamethasone immediately
Systemic AL amyloidosis; echocardiogram and organ biopsy needed urgently
Solitary plasmacytoma; local radiotherapy to the affected bone lesion
Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS); monitor without treatment
questions.explanation: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) is defined by: paraprotein <30 g/L, bone marrow plasma cells <10%, and absence of CRAB features (hypercalcaemia, renal failure, anaemia, bone lesions) or other myeloma-related end-organ damage. MGUS is a precursor to myeloma with 1% annual progression risk; it does not itself require treatment. Management is observation: repeat paraprotein and FBC at 3-6 months, then annually if stable. Risk stratification (Mayo MGUS model) uses paraprotein concentration, isotype (non-IgG = higher risk), and serum free light chain ratio to guide monitoring intervals.
questions.question: A 70-year-old man has paraprotein 18 g/L (IgG kappa), bone marrow 8% plasma cells, normal skeletal survey, and normal calcium, creatinine, and haemoglobin. What is this condition and the appropriate management?
A patient with thalassaemia intermedia who is not on a regular transfusion programme still develops iron overload. What is the primary mechanism?
questions.explanation: Ineffective erythropoiesis in thalassaemia suppresses hepcidin, the key regulator that normally limits intestinal iron absorption. This causes progressive iron overload even without transfusion, through chronically increased gut iron absorption.

questions.question: Thrombophilia screening is most appropriately performed in:
questions.explanation: Thrombophilia testing is indicated for unprovoked VTE at young age (<50), recurrent VTE, unusual site thrombosis, strong family history, or VTE during pregnancy/OCPs. Testing doesn't affect acute management and should occur after completing 3-6 months anticoagulation (to avoid false results). Results influence anticoagulation duration but rarely change immediate management.

Peripheral blood stem cells are easily collected by apheresis without general anesthesia. Higher CD34+ cell yields are achieved, especially after G-CSF mobilization. Faster engraftment occurs with quicker myeloid and platelet recovery.
questions.question: What is the advantage of peripheral blood stem cells?

questions.explanation: Chronic transfusions cause iron deposition in the heart (cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias), liver (cirrhosis, fibrosis), and endocrine glands (diabetes, hypothyroidism, hypogonadism, growth failure). Each unit of blood contains ~250 mg iron, which accumulates without physiological excretion mechanism. Iron chelation therapy is essential to prevent organ damage and death.
questions.question: Iron overload in transfusion-dependent thalassaemia primarily affects which organs?

questions.explanation: HbSC disease is generally milder than HbSS because HbC interacts less readily with HbS in polymer formation than another HbS molecule. However, it is not benign and patients still experience vaso-occlusive crises, though less frequently. Complications like proliferative retinopathy may actually be more common in HbSC disease.
questions.question: In HbSC disease compared to HbSS disease, the clinical course is generally:

questions.explanation: Partial response (PR) in myeloma requires a 50% or greater reduction in serum M-protein AND a 90% or greater reduction in 24-hour urine M-protein. Very good partial response (VGPR) requires 90% or greater serum M-protein reduction. Complete response requires M-protein undetectable by immunofixation with bone marrow plasma cells below 5%. These standardised response criteria guide treatment decisions and prognostic assessment.
questions.question: A patient with multiple myeloma achieves partial response to bortezomib-based therapy. What defines partial response?
options: M-protein reduction greater than 25% from baseline
M-protein reduction greater than or equal to 50%
M-protein reduction greater than 90% from baseline
Resolution of all CRAB criteria from treatment response
Bone marrow plasma cells reducing to below 20%

questions.explanation: B12 bound to intrinsic factor (IF) is absorbed in the terminal ileum via cubilin-amnionless receptors. Ileal resection (>60 cm) or Crohn's disease affecting terminal ileum causes B12 malabsorption requiring lifelong parenteral replacement. Fish tapeworm (Diphyllobothrium latum) competing for B12 or bacterial overgrowth in blind loops also cause deficiency. Total gastrectomy removes IF source.
questions.question: Vitamin B12 is absorbed in which part of the gastrointestinal tract?
What is the role of tissue factor in coagulation?
options: Inhibition of coagulation at intact endothelium
Initiation of coagulation at injury sites
questions.explanation: Tissue factor (TF) exposed at sites of vascular injury binds Factor VIIa, forming the TF-VIIa complex that initiates coagulation by activating Factors IX and X. This extrinsic pathway is the primary physiologic initiator. TF is constitutively expressed in subendothelial cells, normally separated from circulating factors.

Digestive enzymes do not regulate bone marrow function. Regulation involves humoral factors like erythropoietin, growth factors, colony stimulating factors, interleukins, hormones, nutritional status and various physiological stresses. These factors coordinate to maintain appropriate blood cell production.
questions.question: Which factors do NOT regulate bone marrow function?
What is the mechanism of warfarin anticoagulation?
questions.explanation: Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKORC1), preventing regeneration of reduced vitamin K required for gamma-carboxylation of Factors II, VII, IX, X, and proteins C and S. This impairs their calcium-dependent binding to phospholipid surfaces. Effect is delayed until existing factors are depleted.
options: Inhibition of vitamin K epoxide reductase

questions.explanation: CNS leukemia presents with: headache (increased intracranial pressure), nausea/vomiting, cranial nerve palsies (especially VI, VII), papilledema, seizures, altered mental status. Lumbar puncture shows: elevated protein, decreased glucose, blasts on cytospin. Treatment: intrathecal chemotherapy (methotrexate, cytarabine, hydrocortisone) or systemic high-dose chemotherapy penetrating CNS, ± cranial radiation. Prevention (prophylaxis) is standard in high-risk ALL.
questions.question: What characterizes central nervous system leukemia clinically?
Neural tube defects in newborns are most strongly associated with maternal deficiency of:
questions.explanation: Folate deficiency during the first trimester, particularly around conception and neural tube closure (weeks 3-4), significantly increases neural tube defect risk. Supplementation with 400-800 µg daily before conception and during early pregnancy reduces this risk by up to 70%. This critical period often occurs before pregnancy recognition.

questions.question: What is the antidote for methotrexate toxicity?
questions.explanation: Leucovorin (folinic acid) is reduced folate bypassing methotrexate's dihydrofolate reductase inhibition, rescuing normal cells from toxicity. Given 24 hours after high-dose methotrexate, continued until methotrexate level <0.05 µmol/L. Dose/duration adjusted based on methotrexate levels. For severe toxicity with renal failure, glucarpidase (enzyme cleaving methotrexate) rapidly reduces levels. Aggressive hydration and alkalinization prevent precipitation.

All Ph-negative MPNs (PV, ET, PMF) can: transform to AML (2-5% at 10 years for ET/PV, higher for MF), progress to myelofibrosis (10-15% of PV/ET), cause thrombosis/bleeding, and potentially require allogeneic SCT (currently only curative option for MF). Evolution reflects clonal progression with additional mutations.
questions.question: Which complication can occur in all Philadelphia-negative MPNs?
What is the most serious transfusion reaction?
questions.explanation: Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction is most serious, usually from ABO incompatibility due to clerical errors. Intravascular hemolysis, DIC, acute renal failure and death can occur. Reaction severity depends on volume transfused. Immediate cessation and supportive care are critical.

questions.question: The most appropriate haemoglobin target for patients with chronic kidney disease on dialysis is:
questions.explanation: Target Hb 10-12 g/dL in CKD patients balances benefits (reduced symptoms, transfusions) versus risks of higher targets (>13 g/dL: hypertension, thrombosis, stroke, mortality). Studies showed harm with targeting normal Hb. Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs: epoetin, darbepoetin) plus iron supplementation achieve target. Iron status must be adequate (ferritin >100, TSAT >20%) for ESA response. Individualize based on symptoms, cardiovascular disease.

HTLV-1 causes adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma (ATL) years after infection, presenting with lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, skin lesions, hypercalcemia, leucocytosis with characteristic "flower cells" (multilobulated nuclei). Endemic in Japan, Caribbean, West Africa. Also causes tropical spastic paraparesis. Poor prognosis; treatment includes chemotherapy, zidovudine-interferon, allogenic transplant. Screening blood donors in endemic areas prevents transmission.
questions.question: Human T-lymphotropic virus (HTLV-1) is associated with which malignancy?

questions.explanation: Bone marrow accounts for 4-5% of total body weight, making it the fourth largest organ by weight. This substantial mass reflects its critical role in continuous hematopoiesis throughout life. The marrow is widely distributed in axial and long bones.
questions.question: What percentage of body weight does bone marrow constitute?

options: Core binding factor abnormalities: t(8;21), inv(16)
questions.explanation: Favorable-risk cytogenetics: t(8;21), inv(16)/t(16;16), normal karyotype with NPM1 mutation without FLT3-ITD. Intermediate-risk: normal karyotype, various single abnormalities. Adverse-risk: complex karyotype (≥3 abnormalities), monosomy 5 or 7, deletion 5q, inv(3)/t(3;3), t(6;9), t(9;22), MLL-rearranged (except t(9;11)), TP53 mutation. Cytogenetics/molecular markers guide treatment intensity and transplant decisions.
questions.question: What defines favorable-risk cytogenetics in AML?

questions.explanation: Splenomegaly results from extramedullary hematopoiesis (spleen attempts to compensate for ineffective marrow production) and accelerated destruction of defective red cells. Massive splenomegaly causes hypersplenism, increasing transfusion requirements. Splenectomy reduces transfusion needs but increases infection risk and thrombotic complications. It's reserved for hypersplenism or mechanical symptoms.
options: Extramedullary hematopoiesis and red cell destruction
questions.question: What causes splenomegaly in thalassemia?
Which first-line therapy combination shows high efficacy in fit CLL patients?
questions.explanation: FCR (fludarabine, cyclophosphamide, rituximab) was the standard first-line therapy for fit CLL patients, achieving complete remissions in 70% with prolonged remissions in IGHV-mutated cases. However, targeted agents (ibrutinib, venetoclax combinations) are increasingly preferred due to better tolerability.

questions.question: In sickle cell disease, acute chest syndrome is most commonly precipitated by:
questions.explanation: Acute chest syndrome results from infection (Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, pneumococcus) or fat embolism from bone marrow. Infection is more common in children while fat embolism occurs more in adults, especially following painful crises. Vaso-occlusion in pulmonary vasculature, hypoxia, and widespread sickling can lead to multiorgan failure.

Ankyrin deficiency is the most common protein abnormality in hereditary spherocytosis, accounting for majority of cases. Band 3 protein deficiency accounts for approximately 25% of cases. These defects disrupt vertical interactions between the membrane skeleton and lipid bilayer.
questions.question: Which protein deficiency is most common in hereditary spherocytosis?

questions.explanation: PNH results from acquired mutation in PIG-A gene causing deficiency of GPI-anchored proteins including CD55 and CD59 which protect against complement-mediated lysis. Affected cells undergo intravascular haemolysis, especially at night (acidosis activates complement). Features include haemoglobinuria, pancytopenia, thrombosis, and evolution to aplastic anaemia or leukaemia.
questions.question: Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria results from deficiency of:
What characterizes rouleaux formation?
questions.explanation: Rouleaux formation shows red cells arranged like stacked coins due to increased plasma proteins (immunoglobulins, fibrinogen). Occurs in multiple myeloma, chronic inflammation, and macroglobulinemia. Saline dilution disperses rouleaux, distinguishing it from true agglutination.

Anaerobic glycolysis via the Embden-Meyerhof pathway is the primary energy source for red cells, generating ATP. This pathway accounts for 90% of ATP production since mature red cells lack mitochondria. The process converts glucose to pyruvate and lactate.
questions.question: What is the primary energy source for red blood cells?
G-CSF (granulocyte colony-stimulating factor) primarily stimulates the production of:
questions.explanation: G-CSF is a lineage-specific growth factor that stimulates proliferation and differentiation of neutrophil precursors. It is used clinically to prevent febrile neutropenia during chemotherapy and to mobilize stem cells for collection. Unlike GM-CSF which affects multiple lineages, G-CSF specifically targets the neutrophil lineage.

questions.question: What is the hallmark of Hodgkin lymphoma histology?
questions.explanation: Reed-Sternberg cells are the hallmark of classical Hodgkin lymphoma, representing malignant cells in inflammatory background. These large binucleated or multinucleated cells have prominent nucleoli ("owl's eye" appearance). Different subtypes show varying inflammatory cell composition.

questions.question: What is the hallmark immunophenotype of mantle cell lymphoma?
questions.explanation: Mantle cell lymphoma characteristically shows CD5+, CD10-, CD20+, CD23-, cyclin D1+ (from t(11;14)). The combination of CD5 positivity (unusual for B-cells) with cyclin D1 overexpression is diagnostic. MCL has intermediate prognosis between indolent and aggressive lymphomas.

questions.question: Leucodepletion of blood components primarily reduces:
questions.explanation: Leucodepletion (filtration removing >99.9% leucocytes) reduces febrile non-haemolytic transfusion reactions, HLA alloimmunization, and CMV transmission. It's universal in many countries. Benefits include reduced platelet refractoriness and possibly decreased immunomodulation. Doesn't prevent allergic reactions or TRALI. Most blood components are now prestorage leucodepleted.

Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22) creating BCR-ABL1 fusion is present in >95% of CML cases. This constitutively active tyrosine kinase drives the chronic phase characterized by leucocytosis with left shift, splenomegaly. Tyrosine kinase inhibitors (imatinib, dasatinib, nilotinib) targeting BCR-ABL1 transform CML from fatal to chronic disease. Ph chromosome also occurs in some ALL cases (poor prognosis).
questions.question: The Philadelphia chromosome is diagnostic of:

questions.explanation: Plasma exchange (daily until remission) removes autoantibody against ADAMTS-13 and replaces enzyme. Without treatment, mortality exceeds 90%; with treatment, survival is 80-90%. Caplacizumab (anti-vWF antibody preventing platelet adhesion) accelerates response. Platelets are contraindicated (may worsen thrombosis). Rituximab prevents relapses. Immunosuppression for refractory cases.
questions.question: What is the treatment of choice for thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura?

questions.explanation: The classical pathway is activated by antibody (IgG or IgM) binding to antigen, initiating the complement cascade via C1q. This pathway provides specific immune recognition. The alternative and lectin pathways activate without antibodies.
questions.question: Which pathway activates complement via antibody binding?
What is the inheritance pattern of pyruvate kinase deficiency?
questions.explanation: Pyruvate kinase deficiency follows autosomal recessive inheritance, affecting individuals who are homozygous or compound heterozygous for PKLR mutations. Both parents are typically asymptomatic carriers. Consanguinity increases the risk.

options: Fall in white cell count below 5 × 10⁹/L indicating adequate myelosuppression
Reduction in reticulocyte count indicating improved red cell survival
Rise in haemoglobin F (HbF) percentage above 15-20% of total haemoglobin
Reduction in LDH level confirming decreased intravascular haemolysis
Increase in MCV above 100 fL indicating macrocytosis from hydroxyurea
questions.explanation: The primary therapeutic mechanism of hydroxyurea in SCD is HbF induction; HbF (alpha2gamma2) dilutes HbS and inhibits its polymerisation. A rise in HbF to >=15-20% is the most direct indicator of adequate therapeutic effect, correlating with reduced painful crises, acute chest syndrome frequency, and hospitalisation rates. In practice, MCV increase (macrocytosis from ribonucleotide reductase inhibition) serves as an early, easily monitored surrogate for hydroxyurea activity and compliance before HbF levels rise. Dose is titrated to maximum tolerated dose (targeting ANC 2-4 × 10⁹/L) to maximise HbF induction while avoiding excessive myelosuppression.
questions.question: A 22-year-old woman with sickle cell disease (HbSS) had 6 hospitalisations for painful crises this year and is started on hydroxyurea. Which laboratory parameter most directly indicates hydroxyurea is having its intended therapeutic effect?
Which complication manifests as bronchiolitis obliterans post-transplant?
questions.explanation: Bronchiolitis obliterans (BO) is a manifestation of chronic pulmonary GVHD, characterized by progressive airflow obstruction (FEV1 decline, obstructive pattern on PFTs). Results from immune-mediated injury to bronchioles causing fibrosis. Presents with progressive dyspnea, cough, wheezing. Poor prognosis; treatment (high-dose steroids, immunosuppression, azithromycin) minimally effective. Prevention through adequate chronic GVHD prophylaxis/treatment is key.

questions.question: How much elemental iron does one blood unit contain?
questions.explanation: Each unit of blood contains approximately 200 mg of elemental iron. Multiple transfusions easily lead to iron overload as iron elimination routes are limited. Chronically transfused patients like thalassemia require iron chelation therapy.

questions.question: Which finding distinguishes acute promyelocytic leukemia-associated DIC from other causes?
questions.explanation: APL cells release procoagulant substances from abnormal primary granules, activating the coagulation cascade and causing consumption coagulopathy. This mechanism is specific to M3 AML and explains the high DIC incidence. Other features occur in various DIC causes.
options: Release of procoagulant from abnormal granules
Isolated prolongation of PT without aPTT changes

questions.question: A cardiac surgery patient on unfractionated heparin develops platelet count drop from 280,000 to 55,000/µL on day 8. Anti-PF4/heparin antibodies are positive. What is the immediate treatment?
questions.explanation: HIT type II is an immune-mediated disorder where antibodies against heparin-PF4 complexes activate platelets, causing paradoxical thrombosis. Management requires immediate cessation of ALL heparin and substitution with a non-heparin anticoagulant (argatroban or bivalirudin). LMWH is contraindicated as cross-reactivity occurs in approximately 90% of HIT cases; platelet transfusion may fuel thrombosis.
options: Stop heparin and start a direct thrombin inhibitor
Administer IV immunoglobulin to slow platelet destruction
Reduce heparin dose and monitor counts daily closely
Transfuse platelets to prevent haemorrhagic complications
Switch to low molecular weight heparin prophylaxis instead

questions.question: Sickle cell disease patients undergoing surgery require:
questions.explanation: Preoperative transfusion (simple or exchange) reduces HbS percentage (<30%), decreasing perioperative vaso-occlusive complications. Aggressive hydration, oxygenation, normothermia, adequate analgesia essential. Regional anesthesia preferred when appropriate. Surgery triggers crises through hypoxia, hypothermia, dehydration, stress. Even minor procedures (dental) warrant precautions. Some recommend transfusion for moderate-major procedures only, individualize based on patient/procedure risk.

questions.question: A pregnant woman with sickle cell disease is at increased risk of which obstetric complication compared to the general population?
questions.explanation: Pregnancy in sickle cell disease carries increased risk of pre-eclampsia, intrauterine growth restriction, and vaso-occlusive crises due to the hypercoagulable and hypoxic placental environment. Close multidisciplinary monitoring is required throughout pregnancy.

High-titre FVIII inhibitors (>5 Bethesda Units) neutralise any administered factor VIII and cannot be overcome by dose escalation alone - bypassing agents that generate thrombin independently of factor VIII are required. Recombinant FVIIa (NovoSeven) activates the extrinsic pathway at high local tissue factor concentrations on platelet surfaces, generating sufficient thrombin for haemostasis bypassing the intrinsic pathway deficiency. Activated prothrombin complex concentrate (aPCC; FEIBA) similarly bypasses factor VIII. Emicizumab (bispecific antibody mimicking FVIII co-factor function) is given as weekly/monthly subcutaneous prophylaxis in inhibitor patients, not for acute bleed treatment. Immune tolerance induction (ITI) with daily high-dose FVIII is the long-term strategy to eradicate inhibitors.
options: Give high-dose factor VIII to overwhelm the inhibitor titre
Use a bypassing agent: recombinant FVIIa or activated prothrombin complex concentrate
Use emicizumab subcutaneously for acute bleed management in inhibitor patients
Plasmapheresis to rapidly remove the inhibitor antibodies before factor VIII infusion
Cryoprecipitate contains factor VIII and avoids the problem of isolated FVIII products
questions.question: A 25-year-old man with haemophilia A (FVIII 2%) has high-titre anti-FVIII inhibitors (28 Bethesda units) and a major knee bleed. How should this bleed be managed?

questions.explanation: Zinc deficiency impairs cell-mediated immunity (T-cell function), causing increased infections. Also causes dermatitis (acrodermatitis enteropathica), diarrhea, alopecia, growth retardation, delayed wound healing. Occurs in malabsorption, parenteral nutrition without supplementation, acrodermatitis enteropathica (genetic). Haematological effects include thymic atrophy, lymphopenia. Treatment is zinc supplementation; genetic form requires lifelong treatment.
questions.question: Zinc deficiency causes which haematological problem?

questions.explanation: Type 3 VWD is autosomal recessive, occurring in homozygotes or compound heterozygotes for VWF mutations. Patients have undetectable VWF (<5%) and very low Factor VIII (usually <10%). Parents are obligate carriers with intermediate VWF levels.
options: Autosomal recessive requiring two mutant alleles
questions.question: What is the inheritance pattern of Type 3 von Willebrand disease?

options: Complete haematological response with normal blood counts
Complete cytogenetic response with zero Ph-positive cells
Undetectable BCR-ABL transcripts by standard PCR testing
Major molecular response with BCR-ABL below 0.1% IS
Partial cytogenetic response with fewer than 35% Ph cells
questions.explanation: The ELN 2020 guidelines define optimal response milestones in CML on TKI therapy. At 12 months, the target is at least a major molecular response (MMR), defined as BCR-ABL below 0.1% on the international scale (IS). Failure to achieve BCR-ABL below 1% at 3 months, below 1% at 6 months, or MMR at 12 months prompts evaluation for resistance or switch to a second-generation TKI. Complete cytogenetic response should ideally be achieved by 6 months.
questions.question: A 55-year-old man has WBC 120,000/µL with myelocytes, metamyelocytes, and basophilia on blood film. BCR-ABL is detected. He is started on imatinib. What is the target response at 12 months?
Which patient population should receive CMV-negative blood products?
questions.explanation: CMV-negative products (or leukoreduced, which achieves similar risk reduction) are indicated for: CMV-negative transplant candidates, intrauterine transfusions, premature/low-birth-weight infants, CMV-negative pregnant women, and HIV+ patients. This prevents transfusion-transmitted CMV, which can be severe in immunocompromised recipients.

options: Mild microcytic anemia with normal mentum
questions.question: What characterizes alpha-thalassemia trait (deletion of 2 genes)?
questions.explanation: Alpha-thalassemia trait (--/aa or -a/-a) causes mild microcytic anemia (Hb 10-13 g/dL), often misdiagnosed as iron deficiency. Hemoglobin electrophoresis is usually normal (no HbH at steady state). Diagnosis requires DNA analysis or exclusion of other causes of microcytosis. It's clinically benign but important for genetic counseling.

questions.question: Tumour lysis syndrome is characterized by all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Tumour lysis syndrome shows hypocalcaemia (not hypercalcaemia) from phosphate binding calcium, plus hyperuricaemia, hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia, and acute kidney injury. Occurs with rapid cell lysis during chemotherapy (high-grade lymphomas, leukaemias with high WBC). Prevention includes hydration, allopurinol/rasburicase, monitoring electrolytes. Treatment addresses electrolyte abnormalities, maintaining urine output, rarely dialysis.

questions.question: Which zone in bone marrow contains the most dormant HSCs?
questions.explanation: The endosteal niche contains the most dormant HSCs as shown by label-retaining cell assays. This niche serves as a quiescent-storage area or self-renewing niche for long-term HSC maintenance. HSCs in this location demonstrate minimal proliferative activity.

In adults, active haemopoiesis occurs in the vertebrae, ribs, sternum, skull, sacrum, pelvis, and proximal ends of femur. Childhood haemopoiesis extends to all bones, but fatty marrow replaces haemopoietic marrow in peripheral skeleton with age. During increased demand, haemopoietic tissue can expand into fatty marrow areas.
questions.question: In adults, which bones are the primary sites of active haemopoiesis?
Which protein interaction provides the second major vertical linkage?
questions.explanation: Glycophorin C and protein 4.1 provide the second major vertical interaction through linkage with actin. This differs from the band 3-ankyrin-spectrin complex which is the primary vertical interaction. Both pathways are essential for membrane stability.

Folic acid (1 mg daily) is recommended to support high erythroid turnover from chronic hemolysis. Though megaloblastic anemia from folate deficiency is rare, supplementation ensures adequate folate for DNA synthesis during accelerated erythropoiesis. It doesn't prevent crises or increase HbF but supports bone marrow function.
questions.question: What is the role of folic acid supplementation in sickle cell disease?
Which drug combination is commonly used for myeloma?
questions.explanation: Melphalan plus prednisolone (MP) is a traditional myeloma treatment regimen. Modern regimens include bortezomib, lenalidomide and dexamethasone. Autologous stem cell transplantation is considered for eligible patients.

questions.question: What characterizes target cells?
questions.explanation: Target cells show bull's eye or target appearance with central hemoglobin surrounded by pallor then peripheral rim of hemoglobin. They occur in thalassemia, hemoglobin C disease, liver disease, post-splenectomy, and iron deficiency. Increased surface area-to-volume ratio causes morphology.

options: Start bortezomib-based chemotherapy immediately to reduce plasma cell mass
Arrange autologous stem cell transplant as definitive first-line treatment
Start dexamethasone alone to rapidly suppress the myeloma clone
Treat hypercalcaemia with IV fluids and zoledronic acid bisphosphonate
Initiate dialysis immediately for acute kidney injury from myeloma
questions.explanation: Hypercalcaemia (CRAB: calcium, renal failure, anaemia, bone lesions) is a myeloma emergency requiring immediate treatment before starting definitive anti-myeloma therapy. Aggressive IV hydration (0.9% saline 3-4 L/day) corrects dehydration and promotes renal calcium excretion; zoledronic acid inhibits osteoclast-mediated bone resorption driving hypercalcaemia within 24-48 hours. Uncorrected hypercalcaemia causes renal failure, cardiac arrhythmias, and altered consciousness. Once calcium and renal function are stabilised, systemic anti-myeloma therapy (bortezomib-dexamethasone ± cyclophosphamide) can be safely commenced.
questions.question: A 68-year-old man with myeloma (35% marrow plasma cells, calcium 3.1 mmol/L, creatinine 210 μmol/L) presents before starting chemotherapy. What is the immediate priority?
Which virus causes post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder?
questions.explanation: Post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD) results from EBV-driven uncontrolled B-cell proliferation in immunosuppressed transplant recipients (solid organ > allogeneic HSCT). Risk highest with T-cell depletion, ATG/alemtuzumab use, EBV-seronegative recipient with EBV+ donor. Spectrum: polyclonal early lesions to monomorphic B-cell lymphoma. Treatment: reduce immunosuppression, rituximab, chemotherapy if aggressive. EBV monitoring permits preemptive therapy.

Relapse is the major cause of treatment failure in AML, occurring in 50-70% of patients achieving initial remission. Primary resistance occurs in 20-30%. Improving relapse rates requires better minimal residual disease detection and targeted therapies.
questions.question: What is the primary cause of treatment failure in AML?

questions.explanation: Parenteral iron is preferred in late pregnancy with moderate anaemia to rapidly replenish stores before delivery. Oral iron may not adequately restore iron levels in the limited time remaining. While oral iron is generally preferred, the timing and severity warrant parenteral administration to prevent maternal and fetal complications.
questions.question: A pregnant woman at 32 weeks gestation has Hb 9.5 g/dL, MCV 76 fL, and ferritin 10 µg/L. What is the most appropriate initial management?
A neonate is found to have Hb Bart's at a low percentage on newborn screening with no clinical symptoms. What does this most likely represent?
questions.explanation: A small amount of Hb Bart's on newborn screening, without clinical disease, typically indicates alpha thalassaemia trait (one or two gene deletions), which is usually asymptomatic and only becomes apparent through screening or family studies.

questions.question: What is the most common chromosomal loss in myeloma?
questions.explanation: Loss of chromosome 13 or deletion of 13q is the most frequently observed chromosomal abnormality in myeloma, detectable by FISH. This abnormality confers poor prognosis and is found in approximately 50% of cases. Other common abnormalities include IGH translocations.

questions.question: What is the mechanism of imatinib resistance in CML?
options: Decreased drug absorption from GI tract
BCR-ABL kinase domain mutations preventing binding
questions.explanation: Imatinib resistance mechanisms: BCR-ABL kinase domain mutations (most common, especially T315I completely resistant to imatinib, dasatinib, nilotinib), BCR-ABL amplification/overexpression, alternative signaling pathway activation (SRC family kinases), decreased drug levels (poor compliance, increased efflux pumps, decreased influx). T315I requires ponatinib (third-generation TKI) or alternative approaches. Mutation analysis guides TKI selection.

questions.question: What is the treatment for severe hemophilia A bleeding?
questions.explanation: Recombinant factor VIII concentrate is first-line treatment for severe hemophilia A bleeding episodes. Dose and duration depend on bleeding severity and location. Prophylactic factor replacement prevents bleeding in severe cases. Gene therapy shows promise.

questions.question: Copper deficiency can cause anaemia resembling:
questions.explanation: Copper deficiency (gastric bypass, excessive zinc, Menkes disease) causes anaemia with ring sideroblasts, neutropenia resembling MDS. Copper is cofactor for hephaestin (iron export) and ceruloplasmin. Features include cytopenias, neuropathy, myelopathy. Bone marrow shows vacuolated precursors, ring sideroblasts. Serum copper/ceruloplasmin low. Treatment is copper supplementation. Unlike MDS, copper deficiency is reversible.

questions.question: The inheritance pattern for a couple both with β-thalassaemia trait having a child with β-thalassaemia major is:
questions.explanation: Each pregnancy has a 25% chance of homozygous inheritance (β-thalassaemia major), 50% chance of trait, and 25% chance of being unaffected. This autosomal recessive inheritance pattern applies to each conception independently. Genetic counseling and prenatal diagnosis options should be offered to at-risk couples.

Elevated homocysteine with normal MMA indicates folate deficiency rather than B12 deficiency. Both deficiencies elevate homocysteine, but only B12 deficiency elevates MMA. Vegans typically have adequate folate from vegetables but this patient's diet appears deficient, possibly from overcooking vegetables.
questions.question: A 45-year-old vegan presents with Hb 8.0 g/dL, MCV 118 fL, and normal methylmalonic acid but elevated homocysteine. What is the deficiency?
Primary myelofibrosis is characterized by bone marrow showing:
questions.explanation: Primary myelofibrosis shows bone marrow fibrosis with reticulin and collagen deposition, making aspiration difficult ("dry tap"). Peripheral blood shows leucoerythroblastic picture with tear-drop cells. Splenomegaly from extramedullary haematopoiesis is prominent. JAK2, CALR, or MPL mutations present in ~90%. Median survival 5-7 years; allogenic transplant is only cure.

options: Immunocompromised patients at risk for TA-GvHD
Elderly patients over 70 years as standard practice
Trauma patients receiving massive transfusion protocols
Patients with autoimmune haemolytic anaemia only
All patients with anaemia from any cause routinely
questions.explanation: Irradiation of blood products prevents transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease (TA-GvHD) by inactivating donor lymphocytes. It is indicated for severely immunocompromised patients (SCT recipients, SCID, DiGeorge syndrome), premature neonates, intrauterine transfusions, Hodgkin lymphoma patients, and transfusions from blood relatives. TA-GvHD has greater than 90% mortality and prevention by irradiation is essential; leukodepletion alone is insufficient to prevent it.
questions.question: Which patients specifically require irradiated blood products to prevent transfusion-associated GvHD?

questions.explanation: Decreased expression of the iron regulatory hormone hepcidin causes increased dietary iron absorption in hereditary hemochromatosis. Altered HFE protein function leads to inappropriate hepcidin suppression. Total body iron may reach 20-60 grams versus normal 3-4 grams.
questions.question: What causes increased iron absorption in hereditary hemochromatosis?

options: Poor G-CSF mobilizers or high-risk patients
questions.explanation: Plerixafor (CXCR4 antagonist) disrupts SDF-1/CXCR4 interaction, mobilizing stem cells from marrow niches. Used with G-CSF for: poor mobilizers (inadequate CD34+ cells with G-CSF alone), high risk for poor mobilization (multiple prior therapies, prior pelvic radiation, diagnosis like NHL or Hodgkin lymphoma). Given evening before apheresis. Expensive; reserved for specific indications. Significantly improves CD34+ cell yield in poor mobilizers.
questions.question: What is the indication for plerixafor in stem cell mobilization?

questions.explanation: Beta-thalassaemia intermedia (now termed non-transfusion-dependent thalassaemia, NTDT) results from beta-thalassaemia mutations of moderate severity producing sufficient residual beta-chain output to maintain Hb 7-10 g/dL without regular transfusions. The skull hair-on-end appearance reflects expansion of erythropoietically active bone marrow attempting to compensate for ineffective erythropoiesis. HbA2 markedly elevated (6.2%) confirms beta-thalassaemia in a homozygous or compound heterozygous state. Unlike thalassaemia major (Hb <7 g/dL, transfusion-dependent from infancy), intermedia patients survive without regular transfusions but may develop iron overload, extramedullary haematopoiesis, hypersplenism, and thrombotic complications.
options: Severe iron deficiency anaemia with secondary haemolytic component
Beta-thalassaemia major presenting in adulthood with transfusion dependence
Beta-thalassaemia intermedia with moderate haemolytic anaemia
Sickle cell disease with HbAS causing severe sickling crisis
questions.question: A 42-year-old man has Hb 7.8 g/dL, MCV 56 fL, target cells, elevated HbA2 (6.2%), and skull X-ray showing a hair-on-end appearance. What is the diagnosis?
A patient with beta thalassaemia major develops cardiac failure despite regular chelation therapy. Which investigation best assesses cardiac iron burden?
questions.explanation: Cardiac T2-star MRI directly quantifies myocardial iron deposition and correlates with risk of heart failure, making it superior to serum ferritin, which reflects total body iron but not specifically cardiac burden, for guiding chelation intensity.

options: Morphologic bone marrow examination only done
Clinical symptoms and examination for diagnosis
Flow cytometry or PCR for submicroscopic disease
CT and imaging for disease masses
Complete blood count alone for monitoring
questions.question: What characterizes minimal residual disease monitoring in ALL?
questions.explanation: MRD monitoring uses flow cytometry (sensitivity 10⁴, 1 cell in 10,000) or PCR for fusion transcripts/IG/TCR rearrangements (sensitivity 10⁵ to 10⁶) to detect submicroscopic leukemia. MRD negativity at end-induction predicts superior outcomes. MRD positivity indicates high relapse risk, prompting treatment intensification or transplant. Standardized time points (post-induction, post-consolidation) optimize risk stratification. Particularly valuable in pediatric ALL.

questions.question: What percentage of follicular lymphomas show t(14;18)?
questions.explanation: The t(14;18) translocation is found in 70-90% of follicular small cleaved cell lymphomas. This translocation juxtaposes the BCL2 gene to the immunoglobulin heavy chain locus, deregulating BCL2 expression. It also occurs in 20% of diffuse large B-cell lymphomas.

questions.question: A 44-year-old woman receiving her sixth cycle of chemotherapy (including carboplatin) has platelets 6 × 10⁹/L with mucosal bleeding. No fever or sepsis. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
options: Stop all chemotherapy permanently; severe thrombocytopenia precludes further treatment
Transfuse one pool of single-donor apheresis platelets to maintain platelets above 10 × 10⁹/L
Transfuse red cells to correct anaemia; platelet transfusion is ineffective here
Start eltrombopag for chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia management
Administer G-CSF to stimulate neutrophil and platelet production simultaneously
questions.explanation: Prophylactic platelet transfusion threshold in haematology oncology is <10 × 10⁹/L (or <20 × 10⁹/L with active bleeding). At 6 × 10⁹/L with mucosal bleeding, platelet transfusion is immediately indicated. Each pool of apheresis platelets (or 4 units of random-donor platelets) raises the platelet count by approximately 20-40 × 10⁹/L. Single-donor apheresis platelets reduce donor exposures and alloimmunisation risk. G-CSF stimulates neutrophil production but not platelet production; thrombopoietin agonists take weeks to act and are not used for acute thrombocytopenia.
