questions.question: A patient with inherited giant platelets and severely reduced GPIb expression has prolonged bleeding time but normal platelet count. What is the diagnosis?
options: Grey platelet syndrome from alpha-granule absence
May-Hegglin anomaly with Döhle body inclusions
Storage pool disease from dense granule deficiency
Bernard-Soulier syndrome from GPIb complex deficiency
questions.explanation: Bernard-Soulier syndrome is caused by GPIb-IX-V complex deficiency, the VWF receptor essential for platelet adhesion to subendothelium. Features include giant platelets (the largest of the inherited platelet disorders), moderate thrombocytopenia, severely prolonged bleeding time, and failure of ristocetin-induced aggregation. Glanzmann thrombasthenia affects aggregation via GPIIb/IIIa with normal platelet size and no thrombocytopenia.

questions.question: A patient undergoing allogeneic stem cell transplantation develops a skin rash, diarrhoea, and deranged liver function 3 weeks post-transplant. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Acute graft-versus-host disease classically affects skin, gut, and liver, presenting with rash, diarrhoea, and abnormal liver function within the first 100 days post-transplant, resulting from donor T-cell recognition of recipient tissue antigens.

questions.question: In the absorption of vitamin B12, intrinsic factor is secreted by which gastric cells?
questions.explanation: Parietal cells in the gastric fundus and body secrete both hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor. Intrinsic factor binds B12 in the duodenum after pancreatic proteases cleave the B12-R protein complex. This IF-B12 complex is then absorbed in the terminal ileum via cubilin and amnionless receptors.

questions.question: A child with sickle cell disease presents with severe abdominal pain, a rapidly enlarging spleen, and Hb dropping from 8 to 4 g/dL within hours. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Splenic sequestration occurs when sickled cells trap within the spleen, causing rapid splenic enlargement and a precipitous fall in haemoglobin, sometimes with hypovolaemic shock. It is a paediatric emergency requiring urgent transfusion and is a major cause of early childhood mortality in sickle cell disease.

questions.question: Cryoglobulinaemia is associated with which infection?
questions.explanation: Hepatitis C causes mixed cryoglobulinaemia (type II: monoclonal IgM with polyclonal IgG) presenting with purpura, arthralgia, glomerulonephritis, neuropathy. Cryoglobulins precipitate in cold, causing vasculitis. Diagnosis: cryoglobulin presence (sample kept warm), low C4, rheumatoid factor, HCV serology/PCR. Treatment: antiviral therapy (DAAs) treats HCV and cryoglobulinaemia. Severe manifestations may require rituximab, plasmapheresis. Type I cryoglobulinaemia (monoclonal, lymphoproliferative); Type III (polyclonal, autoimmune).

Prophylactic platelet transfusion threshold is 10×10⁹/L in stable patients without bleeding, fever, sepsis, or coagulopathy. Higher thresholds apply for: active bleeding (>50), minor procedures (>50), major surgery/neurosurgery (>80-100). Each adult therapeutic dose should increase platelet count by 30-60×10⁹/L. ABO-compatible platelets preferred but not mandatory.
questions.question: Platelet transfusion threshold for prophylaxis in stable haematology patients is:

questions.explanation: SVC syndrome from mediastinal lymphadenopathy compressing SVC causes facial/arm swelling, dyspnoea, headache, prominent chest veins. Most common in aggressive NHL (lymphoblastic, DLBCL) and Hodgkin lymphoma. Emergency: maintain airway, elevate head, steroids if lymphoma suspected, urgent tissue diagnosis (biopsy not contraindicated despite swelling), specific treatment (chemotherapy/radiotherapy). Stenting for severe symptoms.
questions.question: Superior vena cava syndrome in haematological malignancies most commonly results from:

options: At least 30 percent for initial hemostasis
At least 50 percent sustained for 10-14 days
At least 75 percent to ensure safety
questions.question: What is the target Factor VIII level for major surgery?
questions.explanation: Major surgery and life-threatening bleeding require Factor VIII levels >50% maintained for 10-14 days post-surgery. Joint replacement or major orthopedic surgery may need 3 weeks of coverage. Daily monitoring ensures adequate levels during critical healing period.

Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) is the most common childhood malignancy (~25% of childhood cancers, peak age 2-5 years). Presents with anaemia, infections, bleeding, bone pain, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly. Morphology, immunophenotype, and cytogenetics classify subtypes guiding prognosis/treatment. Modern therapy achieves >85% cure rates. Favorable: age 1-10, low WBC, hyperdiploidy, t(12;21). Unfavorable: infant, high WBC, Philadelphia chromosome, MLL rearrangements.
questions.question: The most common childhood cancer is:

questions.explanation: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia is a prothrombotic disorder despite low platelets, requiring immediate cessation of all heparin products and substitution with a non-heparin anticoagulant, since continuing heparin risks severe thrombotic complications.
questions.question: A patient develops heparin-induced thrombocytopenia with a falling platelet count 7 days after starting heparin. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Continue heparin at a reduced dose

questions.explanation: For young patients (<40 years) with severe aplastic anaemia and HLA-matched sibling donor, allogeneic transplant is first-line treatment offering 70-90% long-term survival and cure. Older patients or those without matched donors receive immunosuppressive therapy (ATG plus cyclosporine) with 60-70% response. Age >40 increases transplant mortality, making immunosuppression preferable first-line. Matched unrelated donor transplant is option if immunosuppression fails.
questions.question: The major indication for allogeneic stem cell transplantation in severe aplastic anaemia is:

questions.explanation: The carrier rate for hemochromatosis mutations is 1 in 7-10 Caucasians, making it very common. Disease incidence is 1 in 200-400 Caucasians. The high carrier frequency likely reflects historical selection advantage.
questions.question: What is the carrier rate for hemochromatosis mutations?
Which chromosome carries the factor VIII gene?
questions.explanation: The factor VIII gene is located on the long arm of the X chromosome (Xq28). Hemophilia A results from mutations in this gene. The X-linked recessive inheritance means males are affected while females are carriers.

Follicular lymphoma has t(14;18) in ~90%, translocating BCL2 to IGH locus, preventing apoptosis. It's an indolent B-cell NHL presenting with painless lymphadenopathy, often disseminated at diagnosis. Transforms to aggressive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma in 30%. Treatment is observation if asymptomatic, or rituximab-based therapy. Cure is rare but median survival exceeds 10 years.
questions.question: Follicular lymphoma is associated with which chromosomal translocation?
Which factor triggers sickling of red blood cells?
questions.explanation: Deoxygenation triggers HbS polymerization, forming tactoids that distort red cells into rigid sickle shapes. Factors promoting sickling include: hypoxia, acidosis, dehydration, fever, and increased 2,3-DPG. Sickling is initially reversible but repeated cycles cause irreversible membrane damage and permanent sickle cells.

questions.question: Which thrombophilia has the highest relative risk for first VTE?
questions.explanation: Antithrombin deficiency carries the highest thrombotic risk among inherited thrombophilias, with 15-20 fold increased risk of first VTE. This reflects antithrombin's critical role in inhibiting multiple activated factors. Protein C and S deficiencies have intermediate risk.
options: Factor V Leiden heterozygosity with 5-fold increase

questions.question: How long does thawing cryoprecipitate take?
questions.explanation: Cryoprecipitate thawing takes approximately 20 minutes just before use. Once thawed, it must be stored at room temperature and infused within 4 hours. Cryoprecipitate contains fibrinogen, von Willebrand factor, factor VIII, factor XIII and fibronectin.

options: Immunosuppression with anti-thymocyte globulin and cyclosporin
Allogeneic stem cell transplantation from the matched sibling
Supportive care with transfusions and growth factors
Danazol as an androgen to stimulate haematopoiesis
Eltrombopag as thrombopoietin receptor agonist therapy
questions.explanation: For patients with severe aplastic anaemia (SAA) under 40 years with an HLA-matched sibling donor, allogeneic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) is the treatment of choice, offering long-term cure rates of 80–90%. Immunosuppressive therapy (ATG plus cyclosporin) is first-line for patients without a matched donor or those over 40 years (higher transplant-related mortality). Eltrombopag has emerged as an important addition to IST but does not match HSCT cure rates in young patients with matched donors.
questions.question: What is the most appropriate management for a patient with severe aplastic anaemia under 40 years old who has an HLA-matched sibling donor?
What is the main function of 2,3-DPG in red cells?
questions.explanation: 2,3-DPG regulates the oxygen affinity of hemoglobin by stabilizing the deoxygenated form, facilitating oxygen release to tissues. It is produced through the Rapoport-Luebering shunt from 1,3-DPG. Levels adapt to maintain optimal oxygen delivery.

Target pre-transfusion Hb is 9-10 g/dL (post-transfusion 13-14 g/dL) to suppress ineffective erythropoiesis, prevent marrow expansion, ensure normal growth/development, and minimize iron loading (by reducing transfusion frequency). Lower targets (7-8 g/dL) don't adequately suppress erythropoiesis; higher targets increase iron burden without additional benefit.
questions.question: What is the target pre-transfusion hemoglobin in thalassemia major?
A patient with G6PD deficiency develops acute haemolysis after eating fava beans. What is the underlying biochemical mechanism?
questions.explanation: G6PD deficiency impairs the hexose monophosphate shunt, reducing NADPH and glutathione regeneration needed to protect red cells from oxidative stress. Fava beans contain oxidant compounds that trigger haemolysis in vulnerable G6PD-deficient cells.

questions.question: Which cytogenetic finding in adult ALL mandates tyrosine kinase inhibitor addition to chemotherapy?
questions.explanation: Philadelphia chromosome-positive ALL arising from t(9;22) BCR-ABL fusion is high-risk and historically had poor outcomes. Addition of tyrosine kinase inhibitors (imatinib, dasatinib) to chemotherapy dramatically improves outcomes. This targeted approach is mandatory in all Ph-positive adult ALL patients, transforming a previously lethal entity.
options: t(9;22) Philadelphia chromosome BCR-ABL fusion gene
t(12;21) translocation TEL-AML1 fusion gene product
Deletion 9p affecting CDKN2A tumour suppressor gene
Autosomal recessive requiring two mutant alleles
questions.question: What is the inheritance pattern of sickle cell disease?
questions.explanation: Sickle cell disease is autosomal recessive. HbSS requires inheritance of βS from both parents. Each parent is usually HbAS (sickle trait). Two carrier parents have 25% chance of HbSS offspring, 50% HbAS, 25% HbAA per pregnancy. Compound heterozygotes (HbSC, HbS-thal) also cause disease.

options: Hypomethylation of silenced tumour suppressor gene promoters
Inhibition of ribonucleotide reductase like hydroxyurea
BCL-2 inhibition restoring the apoptotic pathway function
Proteasome inhibition causing toxic protein accumulation
Direct cytotoxicity killing rapidly dividing blast cells
questions.explanation: Azacitidine is a hypomethylating agent that inhibits DNA methyltransferase after incorporation into DNA, preventing methylation of CpG islands. In MDS, tumour suppressor genes are epigenetically silenced by promoter hypermethylation; azacitidine reverses this, re-expressing these genes. Unlike cytarabine, azacitidine acts through epigenetic reprogramming and improves overall survival in high-risk MDS.
questions.question: What is the mechanism of action of azacitidine in MDS treatment?

questions.explanation: GVHD prophylaxis (typically calcineurin inhibitor [tacrolimus or cyclosporine] + methotrexate or mycophenolate) prevents donor T-cells from recognizing and attacking recipient tissues. Challenge is preventing GVHD while preserving GVL effect. Too much immunosuppression increases infection/relapse; too little causes severe GVHD.
options: Prevention of donor T-cells attacking recipient
questions.question: What is the purpose of GVHD prophylaxis post-transplant?
A 2-year-old presents with severe anaemia, massive splenomegaly, and chipmunk facies. Haemoglobin electrophoresis shows HbF 95%, HbA2 3%, and no HbA. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Beta-thalassaemia major results from homozygous beta-globin mutations abolishing HbA production. Patients present in infancy with absent HbA, elevated HbF, slightly raised HbA2, and severe microcytic anaemia requiring transfusion. Chipmunk facies results from marrow expansion attempting to compensate for severe anaemia through ineffective erythropoiesis. Diagnosis is confirmed by haemoglobin electrophoresis showing no HbA.
options: Sickle cell disease presenting in early childhood
Beta-thalassaemia major requiring chronic transfusion support
Hereditary spherocytosis with severe compensated haemolysis

questions.question: Which reverses warfarin effect most rapidly?
questions.explanation: Prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) most rapidly reverses warfarin, providing immediate factor replacement. FFP also works but requires larger volumes. Intravenous vitamin K takes 12-24 hours. PCC is preferred for major bleeding.

Cytogenetic analysis requires viable dividing cells, best obtained from heparinized bone marrow or blood (never EDTA which inhibits cell division). Cells are cultured, arrested in metaphase, and chromosomes analyzed for numerical/structural abnormalities. Conventional cytogenetics detects balanced translocations missed by FISH but requires dividing cells and takes 2-3 weeks. FISH and molecular methods complement cytogenetics.
questions.question: The most appropriate specimen for cytogenetic analysis is:

questions.explanation: Partial response requires ≥50% reduction in serum M-protein and/or ≥90% reduction in urine M-protein. Very good partial response (VGPR) is ≥90% reduction in serum M-protein or M-protein detectable only by immunofixation. Response criteria (IMWG) standardize treatment efficacy assessment.
questions.question: What percentage reduction in M-protein defines partial response?
What is the principle behind T-cell depletion of donor graft?
options: GVHD reduction by removing donor T-cells
questions.explanation: T-cell depletion (ex vivo removal or in vivo depletion with alemtuzumab/ATG) dramatically reduces GVHD by eliminating donor T-cells that mediate tissue attack. However, it also eliminates GVL, increases relapse, delays immune reconstitution, increases infections, and risks graft rejection. Optimal T-cell dose balances these competing risks.

questions.question: Which cells are found in splenic PALS?
questions.explanation: The periarteriolar lymphatic sheath (PALS) contains T lymphocytes, predominantly CD4+ subtype. B cells are located in follicles and marginal zones. This spatial organization optimizes antigen presentation and immune response.

options: Independent inactivation of Factors Va and VIIIa
Cofactor enhancing activated protein C function
Direct activation of protein C at endothelium
Inhibition of tissue factor pathway independently
Promotion of thrombomodulin expression on endothelium
questions.question: In protein C pathway, what is the role of protein S?
questions.explanation: Protein S acts as a cofactor for activated protein C, forming a calcium-dependent complex on phospholipid surfaces. This complex enhances APC's ability to inactivate Factors Va and VIIIa. Free protein S is the functional form.

MDS features ineffective haematopoiesis with dysplastic changes in bone marrow despite normal or increased cellularity, leading to peripheral cytopenias. Dysplasia affects multiple lineages. Risk of transformation to AML varies by subtype. Diagnosis requires bone marrow examination showing dysplasia and excluding other causes. Management includes supportive care, growth factors, or stem cell transplantation.
questions.question: Myelodysplastic syndromes are characterized by:

questions.explanation: No proven intervention prevents chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN) from platinum agents, vinca alkaloids, taxanes, or bortezomib. Management: dose reduction/discontinuation if severe (grade 3-4), symptomatic treatment (duloxetine has most evidence, gabapentin/pregabalin for neuropathic pain), physical therapy. Most cases partially improve months-years after stopping causative agent, but some neuropathy persists.
questions.question: Which supportive care intervention prevents chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy?

questions.explanation: Splanchnic vein thrombosis in an otherwise unexplained context should prompt screening for acquired thrombophilic states. In addition to the JAK2 mutation already diagnosed, testing for antiphospholipid antibodies (the most important acquired thrombophilia), factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A, and protein C/S deficiency identifies co-existing risk factors that significantly influence the duration and intensity of anticoagulation needed. Long-term anticoagulation is generally recommended for splanchnic vein thrombosis in PV regardless of co-morbid thrombophilia, but identifying additional risk factors guides intensity and duration of anticoagulation decisions.
options: JAK2 V617F allele burden quantification to assess thrombotic risk level
Thrombophilia screen for factor V Leiden, prothrombin mutation, antiphospholipid antibodies
Spleen size measurement by ultrasound to plan elective splenectomy
Red cell mass measurement by isotope dilution to confirm true erythrocytosis
Bone marrow biopsy to exclude transformation to myelofibrosis or blast phase
questions.question: A 48-year-old man with PV has a splenic vein thrombosis on imaging. He is on hydroxyurea and aspirin. Which additional investigation is most important to guide long-term anticoagulation decisions?

questions.explanation: Fresh frozen plasma must be stored at less than -30°C to preserve coagulation factor activity. Once thawed, it must be used within 24 hours if kept at 4°C or 4 hours at room temperature. Freezing occurs within 6 hours of collection.
questions.question: At what temperature should fresh frozen plasma be stored?
What is the treatment for unicentric Castleman disease?
questions.explanation: Surgical excision is the treatment for unicentric Castleman disease, often providing cure. The multicentric form requires chemotherapy and/or radiotherapy due to widespread involvement. Complete resection of localized disease has excellent prognosis.

questions.question: A 35-year-old male with recurrent DVT has APC resistance on functional testing. Which molecular test confirms Factor V Leiden?
options: Prolonged dilute Russell viper venom time result
Reduced factor V antigen by ELISA assay method
Failure of APC to prolong aPTT appropriately
Elevated factor V activity with reduced protein level
Detection of the G1691A point mutation
questions.explanation: Factor V Leiden results from a specific G1691A point mutation substituting arginine with glutamine at the primary APC cleavage site. Molecular genetic testing for this specific mutation is the gold standard for confirmation. Functional APC resistance testing may be falsely abnormal due to other causes, making molecular testing definitive and specific.

Chloramphenicol causes two types of bone marrow toxicity: dose-related reversible suppression (common) and idiosyncratic irreversible aplastic anaemia (rare, 1:30,000). Aplastic anaemia may occur weeks-months after exposure, unrelated to dose. Due to this risk, chloramphenicol is reserved for serious infections (typhoid, bacterial meningitis) where alternatives inadequate. Monitoring blood counts doesn't prevent aplastic anaemia.
questions.question: Chloramphenicol can cause which serious haematological complication?

Leucostasis in acute leukaemia with hyperleucoc

ytosis primarily affects which organs?
questions.explanation: Leucostasis (WBC >100×10⁹/L causing hyperviscosity) affects brain (confusion, stroke, coma) and lungs (dyspnoea, hypoxia), rarely other organs. More common in AML (blast rigidity) than ALL. Emergency treatment includes leucopheresis, hydroxyurea, hydration (cautiously), initiating chemotherapy. Avoid transfusion increasing viscosity unless severe anaemia causes symptoms. Tumour lysis prophylaxis essential.

HIV causes cytopenias through multiple mechanisms: bone marrow suppression (virus, medications, opportunistic infections), peripheral destruction (ITP, TTP), ineffective haemopoiesis, nutritional deficiencies (B12, folate). Anaemia is most common, also neutropenia, thrombocytopenia. Antiretroviral therapy improves cytopenias but some drugs (zidovudine) cause anaemia/neutropenia. Thrombocytopenia may respond to HAART, IVIG, or corticosteroids.
questions.question: HIV infection commonly causes which haematological abnormality?
A patient with sickle cell disease who has never been transfused requires an urgent blood transfusion for severe anaemia. What additional testing is most important before transfusion?
questions.explanation: Patients with sickle cell disease have a high risk of alloimmunisation due to multiple transfusions over their lifetime and differing red cell antigen frequencies between donor and patient populations. Extended phenotyping before the first transfusion helps select better-matched blood and reduce future alloimmunisation.

questions.question: Fresh frozen plasma should be thawed and transfused within:
questions.explanation: Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) must be transfused within 24 hours of thawing to maintain labile coagulation factors (V, VIII). It's indicated for coagulation factor deficiency with bleeding/pre-procedure when specific factor concentrates unavailable, massive transfusion, warfarin reversal (with vitamin K), and TTP (plasma exchange). ABO-compatible plasma should be used.

Corrected reticulocyte count = (patient Hct/normal Hct) × reticulocyte %, adjusting for the degree of anaemia. Without correction, reticulocytes appear falsely elevated in severe anaemia as each reticulocyte represents a larger percentage of total cells. This correction provides accurate assessment of marrow response.
questions.question: The corrected reticulocyte count formula accounts for:
What type of drainage does bone marrow lack?
questions.explanation: The marrow does not have lymphatic drainage, as documented by Munka and Gregor in 1965. This absence distinguishes bone marrow from most other tissues and affects how immune responses are coordinated. The lack of lymphatic vessels means cellular trafficking occurs primarily through blood vessels.

questions.question: What characterizes trisomy 8 in myeloproliferative neoplasms?
questions.explanation: Trisomy 8 is a common finding in myeloproliferative neoplasms, occurring in polycythemia vera, essential thrombocythemia and primary myelofibrosis. It represents clonal expansion. The additional chromosome 8 contributes to disease pathogenesis.

Helicobacter pylori chronic gastritis precedes gastric MALT lymphoma development. H. pylori eradication with antibiotics causes lymphoma regression in 60-80% of cases limited to gastric wall. This represents the first example of cancer cure with antibiotics alone.
questions.question: Which gastric infection is associated with MALT lymphoma?
Bone marrow trephine biopsy provides information on all EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Trephine biopsy provides overall architecture, cellularity, fibrosis, and detects focal lesions (granulomas, metastases, lymphoma). Individual cell morphology is better assessed on aspirate smears. Trephine is essential when aspiration yields "dry tap" (fibrosis, packed marrow) or when architecture assessment is needed. Both aspirate and trephine are complementary investigations.

Nodular lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin lymphoma (NLPHL) has excellent prognosis with >90% 10-year survival. The malignant cells ("popcorn" or LP cells) are CD20+, unlike classical HL. It often presents as localized disease amenable to radiation alone.
questions.question: Which Hodgkin lymphoma subtype shows best prognosis?

questions.explanation: The Rai staging system classifies CLL by: Stage 0 (lymphocytosis only, median survival >10 years), Stage I (lymphadenopathy), Stage II (hepatosplenomegaly), Stage III (anaemia, Hb <11 g/dL), Stage IV (thrombocytopenia, platelets <100,000/µL). This patient has thrombocytopenia below 100,000/µL, placing them in Rai Stage IV (high risk), which along with Stage III typically requires treatment initiation regardless of other criteria.
options: Rai stage I with lymphocytosis and lymphadenopathy
Rai stage II with hepatomegaly or splenomegaly
Rai stage IV with thrombocytopenia below 100,000/µL
Rai stage III with anaemia from marrow infiltration
questions.question: A 65-year-old with CLL has progressive lymphadenopathy, haemoglobin 9 g/dL, and platelets 60,000/µL. What Rai stage applies?
What is the normal prothrombin time range?
questions.explanation: Normal prothrombin time ranges from 11-16 seconds, though laboratory-specific reference ranges vary. PT assesses extrinsic and common coagulation pathways. Prolongation indicates deficiency of factors II, V, VII, X or fibrinogen.

Idiopathic causes account for the majority of acquired aplastic anemia cases where etiology cannot be identified. Other secondary causes include drugs, chemicals, ionizing radiation, viruses and immune disorders. The idiopathic category likely includes unrecognized immune-mediated cases.
questions.question: What is the most common secondary cause of aplastic anemia?
A 38-year-old Nigerian woman with sickle cell disease (HbSS) is 16 weeks pregnant. What is the single most important medication to prescribe specifically for this pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Although penicillin prophylaxis is standard lifelong treatment for SCD due to functional asplenia, folic acid 5 mg daily is specifically the most important prescription to emphasise and maintain during pregnancy in SCD. The increased erythropoietic demand of both sickle cell disease (reduced red cell lifespan requiring compensatory increased production) and pregnancy dramatically raises folate requirements; deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia superimposed on haemolytic anaemia and increases risk of neural tube defects. All pregnant women with SCD should take high-dose folic acid (5 mg, not the standard 400 mcg pregnancy dose) throughout pregnancy. Hydroxyurea is contraindicated in pregnancy due to teratogenicity.
options: Penicillin V 250 mg twice daily to prevent pneumococcal sepsis
Hydroxyurea to reduce HbS polymerisation through HbF induction
Low-molecular weight heparin throughout pregnancy to prevent VTE
Folic acid 5 mg daily to prevent megaloblastic anaemia and neural tube defects
High-dose vitamin D and calcium to prevent cortical bone damage

questions.explanation: Following splenectomy, patients lose an important defence against encapsulated organisms. Lifelong vaccination against pneumococcus, along with continued penicillin prophylaxis where appropriate, is essential to reduce the risk of overwhelming post-splenectomy infection.
questions.question: A patient with sickle cell disease undergoes splenectomy for recurrent sequestration crises. What is the most important subsequent preventive measure?

questions.explanation: Acute promyelocytic leukaemia (APL) with t(15;17) produces the PML-RARA fusion protein that blocks differentiation at the promyelocyte stage. ATRA binds the RARA moiety, overcoming this differentiation block and driving blast cells to mature neutrophils. This makes APL uniquely responsive to differentiation therapy, transforming it from the most lethal to the most curable acute leukaemia subtype.
questions.question: A patient with AML has t(15;17). Treatment with ATRA causes blast differentiation. What is the specific molecular target?
options: PML-RARA fusion receptor driving differentiation block
FLT3-ITD mutation causing uncontrolled cell signalling
NPM1 mutation causing abnormal cytoplasmic protein export
BCR-ABL fusion kinase blocking myeloid proliferation

questions.question: Which anticoagulant is used for blood counts?
questions.explanation: EDTA (ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid) is the anticoagulant of choice for complete blood counts. It preserves cell morphology, prevents platelet clumping, and doesn't affect cell size. Concentration is 1.5 mg/ml blood. Purple-top tubes contain EDTA.

Delta storage pool disease involves deficiency of dense (δ) granules containing ADP, ATP, serotonin, and calcium. It occurs in Hermansky-Pudlak and Chediak-Higashi syndromes. Features include mild bleeding, prolonged bleeding time, normal platelet count, and absent second wave on aggregation studies. Electron microscopy confirms absent/reduced dense granules. Treatment includes desmopressin and antifibrinolytics.
questions.question: Delta storage pool disease affects which platelet component?

questions.explanation: Erythropoietin is primarily synthesized by peritubular cells in the kidney, not by osteoblastic cells. Osteoblastic cells produce jagged, thrombopoietin, angiopoietin and osteopontin which contribute to HSC maintenance and regulation. These molecules are crucial for the endosteal niche function.
questions.question: Which molecule is NOT synthesized by osteoblastic cells?

questions.explanation: ALL accounts for approximately 75% of childhood leukemias, peaking at ages 2-5 years. AML comprises most remaining cases. Childhood ALL has much better prognosis than adult ALL, with cure rates exceeding 85% in favorable subtypes.
options: Chronic myeloid leukemia in blast crisis
questions.question: What is the most common acute leukemia in children?

questions.explanation: Diamond-Blackfan anemia presents at birth or early infancy (versus TEC at 6 months-4 years), doesn't spontaneously recover, and frequently has congenital anomalies (craniofacial, thumb, cardiac). Elevated HbF and adenosine deaminase distinguish DBA. Ribosomal protein mutations are causative.
questions.question: What distinguishes Diamond-Blackfan anemia from TEC?

options: Autoantibody-mediated platelet destruction in spleen and liver
Dilutional thrombocytopenia from massive blood transfusion
Splenic sequestration of normal platelets without destruction
Platelet consumption in disseminated intravascular coagulation
Bone marrow failure reducing megakaryocyte platelet production
questions.question: What is the mechanism of immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) in adults?
questions.explanation: In ITP, autoantibodies (usually IgG) directed against platelet surface glycoproteins (predominantly GPIIb/IIIa or GPIb-IX) coat circulating platelets. These antibody-coated platelets are recognised by Fc receptors on splenic macrophages and reticuloendothelial cells, leading to phagocytosis and destruction. Autoantibodies also impair megakaryocyte platelet production. The bone marrow shows increased megakaryocytes as a compensatory response.

Fetal cells >0.5% (fetomaternal hemorrhage >30 ml) requires additional Rh immunoglobulin beyond standard 300 mcg dose. Each 300 mcg dose covers approximately 30 ml fetal blood. Calculate additional doses based on estimated hemorrhage volume.
questions.question: What Kleihauer-Betke result requires additional Rh immunoglobulin?

options: Development of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
questions.explanation: Follicular lymphoma transforms to aggressive diffuse large B-cell lymphoma in 2-3% per year (Richter transformation for FL). Clinical clues: rapidly enlarging node (often single site), B symptoms, elevated LDH, extranodal disease. Biopsy shows large cells. Mechanism involves additional genetic events (MYC, TP53 mutations). Prognosis post-transformation is poor (median survival <1 year).
questions.question: Which finding indicates transformation of follicular lymphoma?

A 21-year-old woman has mild anaemia (Hb 10.8 g/dL), thrombocytopenia (62 × 10⁹/L), positive Ham's test, and flow cytometry showing CD55 and CD59 deficiency on red cells and neutrophils. What is this condition and its most dangerous complication?
options: Evans syndrome; both autoimmune haemolytic anaemia and ITP occurring together
Aplastic anaemia with secondary PNH clone from immune escape
Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria (PNH); major thrombotic events are most lethal
Hereditary complement deficiency causing membrane attack complex overactivation
Systemic lupus erythematosus causing complement consumption and cytopenias
questions.explanation: Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria (PNH) results from a somatic PIGA gene mutation causing deficiency of GPI-anchored complement regulatory proteins CD55 and CD59 on blood cell surfaces. Without these inhibitors, complement alternative pathway activity continuously attacks the cell membrane. The most lethal complication is thrombosis (hepatic vein - Budd-Chiari syndrome, cerebral sinus, portal vein, peripheral arteries) occurring in 40% of patients and causing 50% of deaths, driven by platelet activation from complement and haemolysis-released cell-free haemoglobin scavenging nitric oxide. Eculizumab (anti-C5 complement inhibitor) dramatically reduces haemolysis and thrombosis. Allogeneic SCT is curative.

Deferoxamine is associated with dose-related ototoxicity and ocular toxicity, particularly when used in patients with relatively low iron burden or at excessive doses. Regular audiometric and ophthalmological monitoring is recommended during chelation therapy.
questions.question: A patient on long-term deferoxamine chelation for thalassaemia develops high-frequency hearing loss and visual disturbance. What is the most likely cause?
Hemophilia B (Christmas disease) involves deficiency of factor:
questions.explanation: Haemophilia B is X-linked recessive deficiency of factor IX, clinically indistinguishable from haemophilia A. Laboratory shows prolonged aPTT with normal PT and specific factor IX assay confirms diagnosis. Treatment involves factor IX replacement (recombinant or plasma-derived). Haemophilia B is less common than haemophilia A (1:30,000 vs 1:5,000 males).

questions.question: Langerhans cell histiocytosis bone marrow involvement shows:
questions.explanation: Langerhans cell histiocytosis (histiocytosis X) involves abnormal proliferation of Langerhans cells (dendritic cells) affecting bones, skin, pituitary, lungs, liver, marrow. Bone marrow shows Langerhans cell infiltrates (CD1a+, S100+, Langerin+, Birbeck granules on EM). Presentation varies: localized bone lesions (eosinophilic granuloma) to disseminated disease (Letterer-Siwe). BRAF V600E mutation in ~50%. Treatment ranges from observation/local therapy to chemotherapy depending on extent/organs involved.

questions.question: A patient with suspected haemophilia A has a prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time that corrects with mixing studies. What does this correction indicate?
questions.explanation: In mixing studies, correction of a prolonged clotting time after adding normal plasma indicates a factor deficiency, as the normal plasma supplies the missing factor. Failure to correct suggests an inhibitor, such as an autoantibody against a clotting factor.

questions.question: Aplastic anaemia is characterized by bone marrow showing:
questions.explanation: Aplastic anaemia shows marked bone marrow hypocellularity (<25% cellularity) with fat replacement and reduced haematopoietic cells. Peripheral blood shows pancytopenia. Residual haematopoietic cells appear morphologically normal, distinguishing it from MDS. Causes include idiosyncratic drug reactions, viruses (hepatitis, parvovirus), radiation, or idiopathic autoimmune destruction.

questions.question: A patient with multiple myeloma presents with bone pain, anaemia, renal impairment, and hypercalcaemia. Which investigation is most useful to confirm a monoclonal protein?
questions.explanation: Serum protein electrophoresis identifies the monoclonal paraprotein band characteristic of multiple myeloma, supporting the diagnosis alongside bone marrow plasma cell infiltration and the clinical features of the CRAB criteria (calcium, renal, anaemia, bone).

DIC involves widespread activation of coagulation consuming platelets and clotting factors, with secondary fibrinolysis. Laboratory findings include thrombocytopenia, prolonged PT/aPTT, low fibrinogen, elevated D-dimers, and schistocytes. Causes include sepsis, malignancy, obstetric complications, and trauma. Treatment addresses underlying cause plus supportive replacement of consumed factors.
questions.question: Disseminated intravascular coagulation is characterized by consumption of:

questions.explanation: Flow cytometry analyzes cell surface and intracellular markers using fluorescent-labeled antibodies, essential for immunophenotyping leukaemias and lymphomas. It distinguishes lineage (B-cell, T-cell, myeloid), maturity, and aberrant antigen expression guiding diagnosis and classification. Also used for CD4 counts (HIV), PNH clone detection, platelet function testing, and minimal residual disease monitoring.
questions.question: Flow cytometry is most useful for:
What defines the neoplastic cell in multiple myeloma?
options: Mature B lymphocytes in lymph nodes
questions.explanation: Multiple myeloma is a plasma cell neoplasm characterized by clonal proliferation of malignant plasma cells in bone marrow. These cells produce monoclonal immunoglobulin (M-protein) detectable in serum/urine. Plasma cells are the terminally differentiated B-cell stage.

questions.question: The Rh blood group system most commonly refers to which antigen?
questions.explanation: Rh refers primarily to D antigen; Rh-positive individuals express D, Rh-negative lack it. D is highly immunogenic; Rh-negative individuals receiving Rh-positive blood develop anti-D, risking haemolytic transfusion reactions and haemolytic disease of newborn. Prevention involves Rh-negative women receiving anti-D immunoglobulin after exposure to Rh-positive blood.

options: Deep muscle hematomas after minor trauma
questions.question: What characterizes the bleeding pattern in platelet disorders?
questions.explanation: Platelet disorders cause mucocutaneous bleeding: petechiae, purpura, epistaxis, gingival bleeding, menorrhagia, and GI bleeding. Bleeding is immediate after trauma. This differs from coagulation disorders causing deep tissue bleeding (muscles, joints) with delayed onset. Pattern recognition aids diagnosis.

Howell-Jolly bodies are DNA remnants (nuclear fragments) normally removed by splenic pitting. They appear as single purple inclusions in red cells. Multiple Howell-Jolly bodies indicate hyposplenism or asplenia. Also seen in severe hemolysis and megaloblastic anemia.
questions.question: What do Howell-Jolly bodies represent?

options: Reduced Factor VIII with normal VWF in Type 2N
Presence of bleeding in females with Type 2N
questions.explanation: Type 2N VWD shows reduced Factor VIII binding, mimicking mild hemophilia A with Factor VIII levels of 5-35%. However, it's autosomal recessive (affecting both sexes) versus X-linked hemophilia A. Specific Factor VIII binding assays distinguish them.
questions.question: What distinguishes Type 2N VWD from mild hemophilia A?

questions.explanation: Lenalidomide maintenance post-autologous SCT for myeloma improves progression-free survival and overall survival (multiple trials). Started 2-3 months post-transplant, continued until progression or intolerance. Dose: 10-15 mg days 1-21 of 28-day cycles. Toxicity: myelosuppression, increased second primary malignancy risk (benefit exceeds risk). Alternative: observation with early relapse treatment (individualized decision).
questions.question: A patient post-autologous transplant for myeloma achieves CR. What is appropriate maintenance therapy?
Which feature distinguishes thalassaemia trait from iron deficiency anaemia on laboratory testing?
questions.explanation: Alpha- and beta-thalassaemia trait characteristically show microcytic hypochromic anaemia with a normal or elevated red cell count despite low MCV — the opposite of iron deficiency where red cell count falls. The Mentzer index (MCV/RBC) less than 13 suggests thalassaemia; greater than 13 suggests iron deficiency. Serum ferritin and iron studies are normal in thalassaemia trait unlike true iron deficiency.
options: Reduced serum ferritin in thalassaemia trait only
Normal MCV in thalassaemia despite low haemoglobin
Elevated total iron-binding capacity in thalassaemia trait
Hypochromic macrocytosis specific to thalassaemia trait
Elevated red cell count with low MCV in thalassaemia

questions.question: What inheritance pattern characterizes G6PD deficiency?
questions.explanation: G6PD deficiency follows X-linked recessive inheritance, predominantly affecting males while females serve as carriers. The gene is located on the X chromosome, explaining the sex-linked pattern. Hemizygous males and homozygous females manifest the condition.

options: Lenalidomide acts as an immunomodulator increasing NK cell killing of dysplastic cells
Lenalidomide directly inhibits VEGF pathway reducing del(5q) clone angiogenesis
Lenalidomide restores the deleted RPS14 gene product via epigenetic upregulation
Lenalidomide suppresses TNF-alpha from marrow stroma rescuing erythropoiesis
Lenalidomide activates CRBN E3 ligase to degrade CK1A1, selectively toxic to del(5q) cells
questions.explanation: Lenalidomide is a cereblon (CRBN)-modulating immunomodulatory drug; it acts as a molecular glue that enhances E3 ubiquitin ligase (CRL4-CRBN) activity, promoting ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of casein kinase 1A1 (CK1alpha). The CK1A gene maps to chromosome 5q32 (within the commonly deleted region); del(5q) MDS cells have only one copy and are exquisitely sensitive to further CK1alpha reduction, leading to selective apoptosis of the abnormal clone while sparing normal haematopoiesis. This explains lenalidomide's >60% transfusion independence rate and cytogenetic remission specifically in del(5q) MDS.
questions.question: A 58-year-old man with MDS with del(5q) has transfusion-dependent anaemia and is prescribed lenalidomide. Through which mechanism does lenalidomide specifically target the del(5q) MDS clone?
What is the pathophysiology of vaso-occlusive crisis?
questions.explanation: Vaso-occlusive crisis results from sickled red cells, leukocytes, and platelets adhering to vascular endothelium and obstructing microcirculation. This causes tissue ischemia and infarction, manifesting as severe pain in bones, chest, abdomen. Inflammation amplifies the process. It's the most common acute complication of sickle cell disease.
options: Increased red cell production overwhelming circulation
Sickled cells obstructing microvasculature causing ischemia
Iron deficiency from chronic blood loss
Thrombosis in unusual sites (hepatic, cerebral veins)
questions.question: Which complication is unique to paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria?
questions.explanation: Thrombosis in unusual sites (hepatic veins causing Budd-Chiari, cerebral veins, mesenteric, dermal) occurs in 40% of PNH patients and is a leading cause of death. Mechanism involves complement activation on platelets/endothelium and release of procoagulant microparticles. Anticoagulation may be needed. Eculizumab reduces thrombotic risk.

questions.question: The most common cause of acquired thrombophilia is:
questions.explanation: Antiphospholipid syndrome is the most common acquired thrombophilia, characterized by venous/arterial thrombosis, recurrent pregnancy loss, and persistent antiphospholipid antibodies (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, anti-β2-glycoprotein I). May be primary or secondary (SLE). Diagnosis requires clinical events plus positive antibodies on two occasions ≥12 weeks apart. Treatment involves anticoagulation.

Factor V Leiden is the most common inherited cause of activated protein C resistance, resulting from a point mutation that makes factor V resistant to cleavage by activated protein C, predisposing to venous thromboembolism.
questions.question: A patient is found to have an unprovoked deep vein thrombosis and activated protein C resistance on testing. What is the most likely underlying genetic cause?
A child with β-thalassaemia major typically presents with severe anaemia at what age?
questions.explanation: Symptoms of β-thalassaemia major appear at 3-6 months when fetal haemoglobin (HbF) production declines and β-chain synthesis becomes critical. At birth, HbF predominates and compensates for deficient β-chain production. As the normal switch from γ to β-globin occurs, severe anaemia develops requiring regular transfusions.

questions.question: In the body, what percentage of total iron is normally present as haemoglobin?
questions.explanation: Approximately 65% of body iron is incorporated into haemoglobin in circulating red blood cells. Storage iron (ferritin and haemosiderin) comprises about 30%, transport iron 1%, and tissue iron (myoglobin, enzymes) 4%. This distribution reflects the primary role of iron in oxygen transport.

Autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA) occurs in 10-15% of CLL patients, mediated by warm antibodies (positive direct Coombs test). It requires corticosteroids and may need rituximab or other immunosuppression. Red cell transfusions are supportive. Immune thrombocytopenia also occurs.
questions.question: Which CLL complication requires transfusion support and may need corticosteroids?

options: Factor X activated by extrinsic and intrinsic
Factor IX activated by both pathways
questions.explanation: Factor X is activated by both extrinsic (TF-VIIa complex) and intrinsic (IXa-VIIIa complex) pathways, representing the convergence to the common pathway. Activated Factor X (Xa) with Factor Va forms the prothrombinase complex that converts prothrombin to thrombin.
questions.question: Which factor is in both intrinsic and common pathways?
Which chromosome carries the ABO gene locus?
questions.explanation: The ABO gene locus is located on chromosome 9, inherited in Mendelian patterns. The gene produces glycosyltransferases that determine A and B antigen expression. The O allele produces an inactive enzyme.

TP53 abnormalities (deletion 17p13 and/or TP53 mutation) confer worst prognosis with median survival <3 years and resistance to standard chemotherapy. These patients require novel agents (ibrutinib, venetoclax) rather than chemoimmunotherapy. TP53 testing is mandatory before treatment.
questions.question: Which CLL prognostic marker indicates poorest outcome?
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole commonly causes which haematological abnormality?
questions.explanation: Trimethoprim inhibits dihydrofolate reductase causing megaloblastic changes (macrocytosis, hypersegmented neutrophils) especially with prolonged use or underlying folate deficiency. Sulfamethoxazole can cause haemolysis in G6PD deficiency. Also causes neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, rarely aplastic anaemia. Common in HIV patients (cotrimoxazole for PCP prophylaxis). Folinic acid supplementation reverses megaloblastic changes without compromising antibacterial activity.

questions.question: What is the pathophysiology of paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria?
questions.explanation: PNH results from acquired somatic mutation in PIG-A gene in hematopoietic stem cell, causing deficiency of GPI-anchored proteins including CD55 and CD59 (complement regulatory proteins). This makes cells susceptible to complement-mediated lysis, causing chronic intravascular hemolysis, hemoglobinuria (especially morning), thrombosis, and marrow failure.

questions.question: A patient on maintenance 6-mercaptopurine for ALL develops hepatotoxicity and myelosuppression at standard dosing. Which pharmacogenomic test predicts this toxicity?
questions.explanation: 6-Mercaptopurine is a thiopurine metabolised by thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT). Patients with TPMT deficiency accumulate thioguanine nucleotides at toxic levels, causing severe myelosuppression and hepatotoxicity at standard doses. TPMT genotyping before thiopurine initiation identifies patients requiring dose reduction. NUDT15 variants, particularly in Asian populations, also predict thiopurine toxicity through a distinct but related mechanism.
options: CYP2D6 genotyping for opioid analgesic metabolism
HLA-B*5701 testing for abacavir hypersensitivity reactions
TPMT or NUDT15 genotyping for thiopurine metabolism
DPYD mutation testing for fluorouracil neurotoxicity risk
UGT1A1 genotyping for irinotecan chemotherapy tolerance

questions.explanation: Physiological anaemia of infancy occurs at 2-3 months when haemoglobin reaches nadir (~11 g/dL in term infants, lower in preterm). Results from decreased erythropoiesis as HbF (high oxygen affinity) is replaced by HbA, suppressing EPO production. Bone marrow erythropoiesis resumes when haemoglobin falls sufficiently. No treatment needed in healthy infants; distinguishing from pathological anaemia is important.
questions.question: Physiological anaemia of infancy typically occurs at what age?

options: Direct synthesis of new Factor VIII molecules
Inhibition of Factor VIII clearance mechanisms
Release of stored Factor VIII from endothelium
Enhancement of residual Factor VIII activity
Suppression of Factor VIII inhibitor antibodies
questions.explanation: DDAVP stimulates release of endogenous Factor VIII stored in endothelial cells via V2 receptor activation. This raises Factor VIII levels 2-5 fold, often sufficient for mild hemophilia A. It's ineffective in severe hemophilia (no factor to release).
questions.question: What mechanism explains desmopressin efficacy in mild hemophilia A?

questions.explanation: Desmopressin acts on V2 receptors of vascular endothelium to release pre-formed VWF stored in Weibel-Palade bodies. This transiently raises plasma VWF levels 2–5 fold. It is effective in Type 1 VWD but not in Type 3 (absent stores) or most Type 2 variants where qualitative defects persist despite VWF release.
options: Stimulation of VWF gene transcription in hepatocytes
Inhibition of ADAMTS-13 preventing multimer cleavage
Release of stored VWF from endothelial Weibel-Palade bodies
Direct increase of factor VIII synthesis in endothelial cells
Enhancement of platelet GPIb receptor surface expression
questions.question: Desmopressin is given to a patient with Type 1 VWD before a dental extraction. What is the mechanism of its haemostatic effect?
What characterizes the most severe form of Rh HDN?
questions.explanation: Hydrops fetalis represents the most severe manifestation of Rh HDN, with severe anemia, hepatosplenomegaly, ascites and anasarca. Most hydropic fetuses die in utero. Live-born hydropic infants show profound anemia and cardiorespiratory compromise.

Type 2B VWD involves a gain-of-function mutation that increases VWF affinity for platelet GPIb. This causes spontaneous platelet agglutination and removal of both platelets and high-molecular-weight multimers from circulation, resulting in mild thrombocytopenia. This distinguishes Type 2B from Type 2A where GPIb binding is actually reduced.
options: Enhanced GPIb binding causing spontaneous platelet clumping
Autoimmune platelet destruction by VWF antibodies
Bone marrow suppression from the VWF gene mutation
Splenic sequestration from hepatic VWF overproduction
Increased ADAMTS-13 activity cleaving large multimers
questions.question: A patient with Type 2B von Willebrand disease has mild thrombocytopenia. What is the mechanism?
What is the most common primary cause of aplastic anemia?
questions.explanation: Fanconi anemia is the most common inherited cause of aplastic anemia, though the condition is predominantly acquired (secondary). Other inherited bone marrow failure syndromes include dyskeratosis congenita, Shwachman-Diamond syndrome and Diamond-Blackfan anemia. Fanconi anemia is autosomal recessive.

questions.question: What is the most common cause of DIC?
questions.explanation: Sepsis, especially gram-negative bacteremia, is the most common DIC cause. Endotoxin triggers widespread coagulation activation. Other causes include obstetric emergencies, malignancy, trauma, and severe tissue injury. Treatment addresses underlying cause.

questions.question: What characterizes nodular sclerosis Hodgkin lymphoma?
options: Absence of fibrosis in lymph node
questions.explanation: Nodular sclerosis HL is characterized by broad collagen bands dividing lymph node into nodules containing lacunar variant RS cells. It's the most common subtype (60-70%), often affects young adults with mediastinal involvement, and has good prognosis.

questions.question: A patient with sickle cell disease is being assessed before elective surgery requiring general anaesthesia. What is the most important perioperative measure to reduce sickling risk?
questions.explanation: Hypoxia, dehydration, acidosis, and hypothermia all promote sickling. Perioperative care focuses on maintaining adequate hydration, oxygenation, normothermia, and avoiding acidosis to reduce the risk of perioperative vaso-occlusive crisis and acute chest syndrome.

options: Febrile neutropenic pneumonia; broad-spectrum antibiotics immediately
Pulmonary embolism from hypercoagulable state; anticoagulate with LMWH
Leukaemic infiltration causing pulmonary leukaemostasis; urgent leukapheresis or cytoreduction
Alveolar haemorrhage from thrombocytopenia; platelet transfusion and steroids
Cardiogenic pulmonary oedema from leukaemic myocardial infiltration
questions.explanation: Pulmonary leukaemostasis (symptomatic hyperleukocytosis) occurs when WBC exceeds 100 × 10⁹/L (particularly myeloid blasts, which are larger and more rigid than mature granulocytes), causing leukaemic aggregates to plug pulmonary microvessels. The massive WBC mass increases blood viscosity and oxygen consumption while impairing gas exchange in pulmonary capillaries. Treatment requires urgent cytoreduction: leukapheresis provides rapid mechanical removal of circulating blasts (reducing WBC by 30-50% in hours), while chemotherapy is initiated simultaneously. Hydroxyurea reduces WBC in AML/ALL over 24-48 hours as a bridge. Avoiding red cell transfusion (which worsens hyperviscosity) is important while reducing WBC.
questions.question: A 20-year-old man with acute leukaemia has WBC 380 × 10⁹/L and respiratory distress with bilateral pulmonary infiltrates and oxygen saturation 87%. What is the most likely pulmonary complication and its immediate management?
A patient with multiple myeloma has serum calcium 13.5 mg/dL. What is the immediate management priority?
questions.explanation: Severe hypercalcemia (>13 mg/dL) requires urgent treatment: aggressive IV hydration (200-300 mL/hour normal saline, monitoring fluid status), bisphosphonate (zoledronic acid 4 mg IV or pamidronate 90 mg IV - lowers calcium in 2-4 days), calcitonin (rapid but temporary effect), treat underlying myeloma. Avoid thiazides, vitamin D, calcium. Loop diuretics AFTER adequate hydration. Severe symptoms (>14 mg/dL) may require dialysis.

questions.question: Priapism in sickle cell disease most commonly affects males in which age group?
questions.explanation: Priapism has peak incidence in the second and third decades, affecting two-thirds of males with SCD. Episodes can be stuttering (brief) or prolonged (>3 hours), resulting from vaso-occlusion obstructing penile venous drainage. Recurrent episodes lead to fibrosis and eventual impotence, significantly impacting quality of life.

questions.question: What is chronic GVHD analogous to?
questions.explanation: Chronic GVHD resembles autoimmune diseases, affecting skin (scleroderma-like), eyes (sicca), mouth (lichen planus-like), liver (cholestasis), lungs (bronchiolitis obliterans), and other organs. It occurs in 30-70% of allogeneic transplant recipients. Treatment includes corticosteroids, calcineurin inhibitors, and other immunosuppressants. Quality of life impact is substantial.

Properdin (Factor P) stabilizes the alternative pathway by conserving C3 and C5 convertases. It also ensures efficient uptake of immune complexes. Properdin deficiency increases infection susceptibility, particularly to Neisseria species.
questions.question: What stabilizes the alternative complement pathway?
What causes transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO)?
questions.explanation: TACO results from volume overload in patients with limited cardiac reserve (elderly, heart failure, renal failure). It causes pulmonary edema within 6 hours, but unlike TRALI, has elevated BNP, response to diuretics, and cardiogenic features. Prevention involves slow transfusion rate, diuretics, monitoring fluid balance.

options: Milder than major, occasional transfusions needed
Identical to thalassemia major requiring transfusion
questions.question: What is thalassemia intermedia?
questions.explanation: Thalassemia intermedia describes patients with moderate anemia (Hb 7-10 g/dL) who don't require regular transfusions but need occasional support during infections, pregnancy, or growth spurts. Genotypes include mild β+ mutations, β/normal with additional modifiers, or β-thal with hereditary persistence of HbF. Complications include extramedullary hematopoiesis, leg ulcers, pulmonary hypertension.

questions.question: What percentage of individuals are Rh D-positive in India?
questions.explanation: Approximately 95% of the Indian population is Rh D-positive, with only 5% being Rh D-negative. This frequency varies significantly across different populations and geographical regions. The high D-positive prevalence reduces Rh disease incidence.

Severe aplastic anemia is defined by neutrophils less than 0.5 × 10⁹/L plus two other criteria: platelets <20 × 10⁹/L and reticulocytes <1%, with marrow hypocellularity. Very severe disease has neutrophils <0.2 × 10⁹/L. These criteria predict prognosis.
questions.question: What neutrophil count defines severe aplastic anemia?
The FIP1L1-PDGFRA fusion gene responds to treatment with:
questions.explanation: FIP1L1-PDGFRA fusion (from cryptic deletion in chromosome 4) causes hypereosinophilic syndrome/chronic eosinophilic leukaemia, responding dramatically to low-dose imatinib (100 mg daily). Detection by RT-PCR or FISH is crucial as these patients would otherwise receive toxic chemotherapy unnecessarily. Other PDGFRA/PDGFRB rearrangements also imatinib-sensitive. Represents paradigm for targeted therapy based on molecular pathogenesis. Durable remissions common; molecular monitoring guides therapy.

questions.question: A patient on phenytoin for epilepsy develops macrocytic anaemia. What is the most likely mechanism?
questions.explanation: Anticonvulsants such as phenytoin interfere with folate absorption and metabolism, producing macrocytic anaemia. Folate supplementation is often required during long-term therapy, though it must be balanced against theoretical concerns of reduced seizure control.

questions.question: What characterizes immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP)?
questions.explanation: ITP presents as isolated thrombocytopenia without identifiable cause after excluding other disorders. Antiplatelet antibodies cause peripheral destruction. Bone marrow shows normal or increased megakaryocytes. Splenomegaly is absent, distinguishing it from other causes.

Splenectomy should be deferred until the child is at least 6 years old despite severe disease. This minimizes the lifelong risk of overwhelming post-splenectomy infection from encapsulated bacteria. The risk is particularly high in younger children with immature immune systems.
questions.question: When should splenectomy be performed in hereditary spherocytosis children?

options: Recipient antibodies against donor HLA/neutrophil antigens
questions.explanation: FNHTR results from recipient antibodies against donor leukocyte antigens (HLA, HNA) or cytokines accumulated during storage. It causes fever (≥1°C rise) and/or chills during or within 4 hours of transfusion without hemolysis. Leukoreduction of blood components has dramatically reduced FNHTR incidence.
questions.question: What is the mechanism of febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reaction (FNHTR)?

questions.explanation: Normally 5-10% of dietary iron is absorbed, increasing to 20-30% in iron deficiency. Heme iron (meat) is better absorbed than non-heme iron (plants). Vitamin C enhances non-heme iron absorption. Tea, calcium, and phytates inhibit absorption.
questions.question: What percentage of dietary iron is absorbed normally?
Which cytogenetic abnormality confers poor prognosis in myeloma?
questions.explanation: High-risk cytogenetics include del(17p), t(4;14), t(14;16), t(14;20), and del(1p). Deletion 17p (TP53 loss) is particularly adverse, conferring resistance to therapy and short survival. Standard-risk includes hyperdiploidy and t(11;14). Cytogenetics guide treatment intensity.

Reduced-intensity conditioning (RIC) uses lower-dose chemotherapy/radiation (e.g., fludarabine + low-dose busulfan or melphalan) to allow engraftment while relying on GVL for disease control. It permits transplant in older patients (>60-70 years) or those with comorbidities who cannot tolerate myeloablative conditioning.
questions.question: Which preparative regimen is used for reduced-intensity transplant?

questions.explanation: TRALI (non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema) occurs from leucocyte antibody-mediated neutrophil activation in pulmonary vasculature, while TACO is cardiogenic from volume overload. BNP is normal or minimally elevated in TRALI (no cardiac failure) but significantly elevated in TACO. Diuretics benefit TACO but not TRALI. Echocardiography showing normal cardiac function supports TRALI diagnosis.
questions.question: What is the distinguishing diagnostic feature differentiating TRALI from TACO in a patient who develops acute dyspnoea during transfusion?
options: TRALI occurs after 24 hours unlike early-onset TACO
TACO has bilateral infiltrates while TRALI affects one lung
TRALI shows normal or low BNP while TACO shows elevated BNP
TACO has unilateral infiltrates while TRALI is bilateral
TRALI responds to diuresis well unlike TACO treatment

questions.explanation: Approximately 60-70% of younger adults achieve complete remission with standard induction. Older patients (>60 years) have lower rates (40-50%) due to adverse biology, comorbidities, and treatment-related mortality. Remission is necessary but not sufficient for cure.
questions.question: What percentage of adult AML patients achieve complete remission with induction?

questions.explanation: By teenage years, bone marrow is primarily found in axial bones including chest, ribs, spine, collar bone, shoulder blades, skull and pelvic bones. Long bones contain marrow mainly in proximal femur and humerus. This distribution optimizes hematopoietic capacity.
questions.question: Which bones primarily contain bone marrow in adults?
CEBPA mutations in acute myeloid leukaemia confer:
questions.explanation: Biallelic CEBPA mutations (3-5% of AML) define favorable-risk category with good response to chemotherapy, potentially avoiding transplant in first remission. CEBPA encodes transcription factor regulating myeloid differentiation. Monoallelic mutations lack favorable prognosis. Often occurs with normal karyotype. Included in WHO classification as provisional entity "AML with biallelic CEBPA mutation." NGS panels detect these mutations during diagnostic workup.

Fanconi anemia is inherited in autosomal recessive pattern, requiring mutations in both alleles for disease manifestation. Thirteen genes (FANCA through FANCN) have been identified. Parents are typically asymptomatic carriers, and consanguinity increases risk.
questions.question: What is the inheritance pattern of Fanconi anemia?
A patient with haemolysis has haemoglobinuria but normal serum haptoglobin. Which type of haemolysis does this combination most suggest?
questions.explanation: Haptoglobin binds free haemoglobin released during intravascular haemolysis and becomes depleted when this process is significant. Haemoglobinuria with preserved haptoglobin is unusual and should prompt review, though mild or early intravascular haemolysis can sometimes present this way before haptoglobin depletion occurs.

questions.question: Autologous stem cell transplantation differs from allogeneic by:
questions.explanation: Autologous transplant uses patient's own stem cells (collected during remission), re-infused after high-dose chemotherapy. No GVHD risk (no immunological difference), no HLA matching needed, faster immune reconstitution. Used for lymphomas, myeloma, some solid tumors. Limitation: potential tumor cell contamination, no graft-versus-tumor effect. Allogeneic uses donor cells, risks GVHD but provides graft-versus-tumor benefit.

questions.question: Hairy cell leukaemia cells are characteristically positive for which stain?
questions.explanation: Hairy cells strongly express tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (TRAP), distinguishing them from other lymphoproliferative disorders. These B-cell neoplasms show cytoplasmic projections ("hairs") on phase contrast microscopy. Treatment with cladribine or pentostatin achieves high response rates. Flow cytometry shows CD19, CD20, CD11c, and CD103 expression.

options: Bone marrow plasma cells below 10 percent
questions.explanation: Complete response requires: negative immunofixation of serum/urine, disappearance of soft tissue plasmacytomas, and <5% plasma cells in bone marrow. Stringent CR adds normal free light chain ratio and absence of clonal cells by flow cytometry. Depth of response correlates with survival.
questions.question: What defines complete response in multiple myeloma?

options: Absence of neutrophil engraftment by day 28
Mixed chimerism with recipient cells present
questions.explanation: Primary graft failure is absence of neutrophil engraftment (ANC <500/µL) by day 28. Secondary graft failure is loss of previously established graft. Causes include inadequate stem cell dose, HLA mismatch, infections, drugs, recipient antibodies. Treatment requires salvage transplant with different donor if possible.
questions.question: What defines graft failure?

questions.explanation: APL characterized by t(15;17) creating PML-RARA fusion protein blocking myeloid differentiation at promyelocyte stage. All-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) induces differentiation by degrading fusion protein. Combined ATRA-arsenic trioxide achieves >90% cure without chemotherapy in low/intermediate-risk APL. Variant translocations involving RARA with other partners (~5%) may not respond to ATRA. RT-PCR monitoring detects molecular relapse enabling preemptive treatment.
questions.question: PML-RARA fusion in acute promyelocytic leukaemia results from translocation:
Which ALL subtype requires tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy?
options: Early pre-B ALL with MLL rearrangement
questions.explanation: Ph+ ALL (BCR-ABL1 positive, 3-5% of pediatric, 25% of adult ALL) requires tyrosine kinase inhibitor (imatinib, dasatinib) combined with chemotherapy. This combination dramatically improved outcomes from historically worst to potentially curable with allogeneic transplant.

questions.question: Which chromosome carries the beta-like globin gene cluster?
questions.explanation: The beta-like globin genes cluster on the short arm of chromosome 11, including epsilon, gamma, delta and beta genes. The alpha-like globin genes are located on chromosome 16. This chromosomal organization allows coordinated regulation of globin expression.

Cold agglutinin disease management includes avoiding cold (triggers agglutination/haemolysis), treating underlying lymphoproliferative disorder if present. Rituximab (anti-CD20) effective for chronic severe cases (targets B-cell clone producing IgM). Corticosteroids minimally effective unlike warm AIHA. Transfusions must use blood warmer. Splenectomy ineffective (haemolysis is intravascular/hepatic). Complement inhibitors (eculizumab, sutimlimab) show promise for refractory disease.
questions.question: Cold agglutinin disease is optimally managed by:

questions.explanation: Aplastic crisis in hereditary spherocytosis (and other hemolytic anemias) results from parvovirus B19 infection suppressing erythropoiesis. Reticulocytopenia with worsening anemia (Hb can drop severely). Usually self-limited (7-10 days); supportive care with transfusions if needed. Parvovirus testing confirms. Distinguish from hemolytic crisis (reticulocytosis) and folate deficiency (macrocytic cells, hypersegmented neutrophils).
questions.question: A patient with hereditary spherocytosis develops sudden worsening anemia with reticulocyte count <1%. What complication occurred?

questions.explanation: Post-PV myelofibrosis (spent phase) represents PV evolution with marrow fibrosis, declining hematocrit (often requiring transfusions instead of phlebotomy), progressive splenomegaly, leukoerythroblastic picture, and constitutional symptoms. It complicates 10-15% of PV cases. Prognosis resembles primary myelofibrosis. Allogeneic SCT may be considered.
options: Conversion of PV to fibrotic phase
Declining red cell requirement with anemia
questions.question: What characterizes post-polycythemic myelofibrosis?

questions.explanation: Direct antiglobulin test (DAT/Coombs test) detects IgG and/or C3 on red cell surface, confirming immune-mediated hemolysis. Pattern helps classify: IgG alone (warm AIHA), C3 alone (cold agglutinin disease), both (warm with complement). DAT-negative AIHA occurs (low-affinity antibodies below detection threshold); diagnosis requires clinical suspicion.
options: Direct antiglobulin test detecting cell-bound antibodies
Indirect antiglobulin test detecting plasma antibodies
questions.question: Which test is positive in autoimmune hemolytic anemia?
What percentage of HLA match is required for matched unrelated donor transplant?
questions.explanation: Modern matched unrelated donor (MUD) transplants aim for 10/10 HLA match (high-resolution typing at HLA-A, B, C, DRB1, DQB1). Higher matching improves outcomes (survival, reduces GVHD). One-antigen mismatch (9/10) is acceptable if no better match exists. Matching reduces allorecognition and immune complications.
options: 8/8 match at A, B, C, DR
10/10 match at A, B, C, DR, DQ
Perfect match at all loci required

questions.question: Which cardiac complication is the leading cause of death in thalassemia?
questions.explanation: Cardiac iron overload causing cardiomyopathy, heart failure, and arrhythmias is the leading cause of death (>50%) in inadequately chelated thalassemia major patients. Cardiac MRI T2 measurement quantifies cardiac iron. Intensive chelation (deferiprone crosses into myocardium better than deferoxamine) can reverse cardiac iron. Prevention through adequate chelation is crucial.

This is classic heparin-induced thrombocytopenia type 2 (HIT): platelet fall >50% occurring 5-10 days after heparin initiation with paradoxical thrombosis, confirmed by positive anti-PF4/heparin antibodies. HIT is an immune-mediated disorder where IgG antibodies bind PF4-heparin complexes on platelet surfaces, causing Fc receptor-mediated platelet activation, thrombosis, and platelet consumption. All heparin (including flushes and LMWH, which cross-reacts) must be stopped immediately. Direct thrombin inhibitors (argatroban in renal impairment, bivalirudin) or fondaparinux are the alternatives. Platelet transfusion is contraindicated as it fuels further thrombosis.
options: Increase heparin dose; thrombocytopenia indicates underdosing with ongoing clot
Switch to LMWH; less likely to cause HIT than unfractionated heparin
Stop all heparin immediately and switch to a direct thrombin inhibitor
Add aspirin and continue heparin until warfarin reaches therapeutic INR
Transfuse platelets to prevent further thrombosis in this setting
questions.question: A 60-year-old post-CABG man on unfractionated heparin has platelets fall from 250 to 42 × 10⁹/L on day 8, with a new DVT despite anticoagulation. What is the immediate management?

questions.explanation: TLS prevention: aggressive hydration (2-3 L/m²/day) maintaining urine output >100 mL/m²/hr; allopurinol (xanthine oxidase inhibitor preventing uric acid formation) OR rasburicase (uric acid oxidase converting uric acid to soluble allantoin - preferred for high risk). Avoid potassium/phosphate. Monitor electrolytes, uric acid, creatinine frequently. Alkalinization controversial (may worsen calcium-phosphate precipitation).
questions.question: What is the mechanism of tumor lysis syndrome prevention?
Which compensatory mechanism increases oxygen delivery in chronic anaemia?
questions.explanation: Right shift of the oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve occurs through increased red cell 2,3-DPG, facilitating oxygen release to tissues. This compensates for reduced oxygen-carrying capacity in chronic anaemia. Other compensations include increased cardiac output, tachycardia, and enhanced oxygen extraction by tissues.

questions.question: Which laboratory test is diagnostic for hemophilia?
questions.explanation: Specific factor VIII or IX assay definitively diagnoses hemophilia and determines severity. aPTT is prolonged but nonspecific. Mixing studies show correction distinguishing from inhibitors. Factor assay quantifies deficiency and guides replacement therapy.
options: Prolonged aPTT correcting with mixing study
Normal bleeding time despite factor deficiency
Specific factor VIII or IX assay

questions.explanation: Severe aortic stenosis causes high shear stress that mechanically cleaves large VWF multimers. Valve replacement corrects the abnormality. This acquired defect causes bleeding despite normal VWF synthesis, distinguishing it from inherited VWD.
options: Mechanical shearing of large VWF multimers
Antibody formation against VWF causing clearance
Increased ADAMTS-13 activity from turbulent flow
questions.question: What characterizes acquired von Willebrand syndrome in aortic stenosis?

questions.explanation: The adult spleen normally weighs between 150-250 grams with length of 5-13 cm. Splenic size varies with age, immunologic and nutritional status. The spleen becomes palpable when enlarged beyond 14 cm.
questions.question: What is the normal weight range of adult spleen?

questions.explanation: Normal adult hemoglobin (HbA) consists of four polypeptide chains: two alpha and two beta chains (α2β2), each with its own heme group. This tetrameric structure is essential for cooperative oxygen binding and release. Each chain contains approximately 140-150 amino acids.
questions.question: How many polypeptide chains comprise normal adult hemoglobin?

questions.explanation: Imatinib (Gleevec), introduced in 2001, revolutionized CML treatment by specifically inhibiting BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase. It induces complete cytogenetic response in 80-90% of chronic phase patients. Annual mortality dropped from 10-20% to <2%, converting CML to a manageable chronic disease.
questions.question: Which medication transformed CML from fatal to manageable disease?

questions.explanation: Folate has minimal body stores compared to B12 and is rapidly depleted without adequate supplementation, particularly during high cell turnover states. Parenteral nutrition regimens must include folate to prevent megaloblastic anaemia developing within weeks.
questions.question: A patient receiving total parenteral nutrition for several weeks without micronutrient supplementation develops macrocytic anaemia. What is the most likely cause?

questions.explanation: Early pre-B ALL (pro-B ALL) is CD19+, cytoplasmic CD22+, but CD10-negative. This subtype is common in infants and associated with MLL rearrangements. It carries poorer prognosis than common ALL (CD10+).
questions.question: Which immunophenotype characterizes early precursor B-ALL?
Acute haemolytic transfusion reaction most commonly results from:
questions.explanation: ABO incompatibility from clerical error causes acute intravascular haemolysis within minutes-hours, presenting with fever, rigors, chest/back pain, hypotension, DIC, and renal failure. IgM anti-A or anti-B activate complement destroying incompatible cells. This is a medical emergency requiring immediate transfusion cessation, supportive care, and investigation. Most are preventable with proper identification procedures.

questions.question: Which condition shows normal PT, normal APTT, prolonged bleeding time?
questions.explanation: Von Willebrand disease typically shows normal PT, normal or prolonged APTT, and prolonged bleeding time from platelet dysfunction. VWF deficiency impairs platelet adhesion. Factor VIII levels may be reduced as VWF carries factor VIII.

questions.question: Which empiric antibiotic regimen covers neutropenic fever adequately?
questions.explanation: Empiric therapy requires anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam: cefepime, piperacillin-tazobactam, meropenem, or imipenem. Vancomycin added if: suspected catheter infection, skin/soft tissue infection, pneumonia, hemodynamic instability, or known MRSA colonization. Aminoglycoside adds gram-negative coverage in critically ill. Antifungal added if fever persists >4-7 days despite antibiotics.

Acute erythroid leukemia (AML-M6) requires ≥50% erythroid precursors in marrow AND ≥20% myeloblasts among non-erythroid cells (or pure erythroid leukemia with ≥80% immature erythroid cells). Erythroblasts show dysplastic features, are PAS-positive, and express glycophorin A. It typically has poor prognosis with complex karyotype.
questions.question: Which finding suggests acute erythroid leukemia?
A 27-year-old man with ALL started on L-asparaginase develops severe abdominal pain, vomiting, and serum amylase 2,800 U/L. What is the mechanism of this complication?
questions.explanation: L-asparaginase depletes circulating asparagine by converting it to aspartate and ammonia; while ALL blasts are auxotrophic for asparagine, normal cells including pancreatic acinar cells also depend on extracellular asparagine for protein synthesis during high secretory demand. Asparagine depletion in pancreatic cells impairs synthesis of secretory proteins and zymogen packaging, disrupting normal compartmentalisation of digestive enzymes and triggering premature intracellular activation, leading to acute pancreatitis. This occurs in 2-10% of patients receiving L-asparaginase. Triglyceride elevation (from impaired lipoprotein lipase synthesis) also contributes to pancreatitis risk.
options: L-asparaginase inhibits protein synthesis in pancreatic cells impairing enzyme compartmentalisation
L-asparaginase depletion of asparagine in pancreatic cells causes autodigestive enzyme release
L-asparaginase induces acute pancreatitis by directly damaging pancreatic acinar cell DNA
L-asparaginase activates trypsinogen directly in pancreatic ductal cells
L-asparaginase causes hypertriglyceridaemia from lipoprotein lipase inhibition precipitating pancreatitis

questions.question: When should liver biopsy be considered in hemochromatosis?
