Only trained athletes use multiple systems
Systems alternate strictly every ten seconds
questions.question: A physiology lecturer reminds students that the three energy systems rarely operate in total isolation from one another during real exercise. Which statement best reflects this principle?
questions.explanation: The three energy systems do not work in complete isolation from one another across the spectrum of exercise intensities and durations. From very short, intense efforts to light, prolonged activity, all three systems make some contribution, although typically one or two predominate depending on the demand. This integrated view explains why athletes can transition smoothly between energy pathways as exercise intensity changes.

questions.question: Exercise is described as increasing oxygen pickup in the lungs and increasing greater extraction of oxygen at which level of the body?
questions.explanation: Among the physiological benefits of exercise, it increases oxygen pickup in the lungs and increases greater extraction of oxygen at the peripheral level, where working tissues utilise the oxygen delivered to them. This benefit works together with increased oxygen supply to the heart muscles to support overall cardiovascular efficiency. These combined respiratory and circulatory adaptations underlie much of the improved exercise capacity seen with regular training.

Understanding that PCr plus ADP yields creatine plus ATP explains why maximal sprint performance declines after 8-10 seconds as PCr stores deplete and inorganic phosphate accumulates. Inorganic phosphate accumulation itself inhibits cross-bridge cycling and contributes to early fatigue. In sprint rehabilitation, this explains why repeated sprints with insufficient recovery intervals produce progressive performance decline, informing rest-to-work ratio prescriptions.
questions.question: Understanding that phosphocreatine breakdown frees inorganic phosphate that combines with ADP is most clinically relevant when a physiotherapist is:
options: Designing endurance training for a cardiac patient
Explaining early fatigue mechanisms in sprint rehabilitation
Prescribing flexibility exercises for joint mobility
Advising on carbohydrate timing for marathon runners
Assessing breathing patterns during aerobic exercise

questions.explanation: Psychological benefits of exercise include improved self-esteem and confidence, reduction in stress, anxiety, and depression, improved mood and sense of well-being, improved concentration, and enhanced memory and learning ability. Reduced feelings of fatigue and improved sleep are also recognised psychological benefits. These outcomes complement the physiological benefits to support comprehensive patient well-being.
questions.question: Among the psychological benefits of exercise, improved concentration is listed alongside which other cognitive benefit?
In body composition assessment, lean body mass differs from fat-free body mass in that lean body mass:
questions.explanation: Fat-free body mass includes all body components except all fat, including essential fat. Lean body mass is a clinically useful concept that includes essential fat (located in nerve tissue, bone marrow, and organ membranes) because this fat is not removable without compromising function. Lean body mass therefore equals fat-free body mass plus essential fat. This distinction matters when setting minimal body fat targets in athletes and patients.
options: Includes the essential fat within adipose cells
Excludes all adipose tissue from measurement
Excludes bone mineral from total calculation
Is measured exclusively by DEXA scanning

questions.question: A patient's accelerometer shows a high step count but prolonged sedentary bouts of 90-120 minutes between walks. The most evidence-based physiotherapy intervention is to:
options: Increase daily step count target by 2000 steps
Replace sedentary time with high-intensity exercise
Introduce regular activity breaks every 30 minutes
Reduce step count and focus on aerobic intensity
questions.explanation: Emerging evidence demonstrates that prolonged uninterrupted sedentary bouts carry independent metabolic risk even in physically active individuals who meet step count targets. Breaking up sedentary time with brief activity breaks every 20-30 minutes reduces postprandial glucose, blood pressure, and triglycerides. This directly addresses the sedentary behaviour pattern identified in the accelerometer data rather than simply adding more structured exercise.

questions.question: Girth measurement as a predictor of body fat percentage is described as best suited to which population group, based on accuracy and reliability considerations?
questions.explanation: Girth measurements as a predictor of body fat percentage are best suited to individuals with average or above-average body fat percentages, since girth tends to increase significantly with fat gain in this population. In lean individuals, girth measurements do not decrease significantly even with further fat loss, reducing their sensitivity in this group. This limitation should be considered when selecting girth measurement as an assessment tool for athletic or very lean populations.

Ketosis is a metabolic state that develops when the body burns fat instead of glucose for fuel, typically as a consequence of carbohydrate deficiency. Symptoms include bad breath, mental fatigue, headache, nausea, painful joint swelling, and dehydration. It arises as a downstream consequence of the hypoglycemia that occurs when carbohydrate intake is insufficient.
questions.question: When carbohydrate intake is chronically inadequate, the body increasingly relies on fat breakdown for fuel, producing a metabolic state characterised by bad breath and headache. This state is called?

questions.explanation: The agonist, or prime mover, is the muscle whose concentric contraction is primarily responsible for producing a specific joint motion. During elbow flexion, the biceps brachii acts as the agonist. The triceps brachii must relax to permit this motion, functioning as the antagonist.
questions.question: During elbow flexion against a held dumbbell, the biceps brachii is the prime mover responsible for producing the motion. Which functional role does the biceps brachii play in this action?
A muscle has fascicles running diagonally off only one side of a central tendon, producing a feather-like appearance similar to the biceps femoris. This is an example of which arrangement?
questions.explanation: In a unipennate arrangement, the muscle fibres run diagonally off only one side of the central tendon, giving a feather-like appearance. The biceps femoris, semimembranosus, and tibialis posterior are examples of unipennate muscles. This arrangement contrasts with bipennate muscles, whose fibres run diagonally from both sides of the tendon.

questions.question: The oxidative energy system is more appropriate than the glycolytic system for long-duration physiotherapy exercise because:
questions.explanation: Complete oxidative metabolism of one glucose molecule through glycolysis, Krebs cycle, and electron transport chain generates approximately 30-32 ATP, compared to only 2 net ATP from glycolysis alone. This far greater efficiency per substrate molecule allows the oxidative system to sustain energy production for prolonged periods without depleting fuel stores. However, the rate of ATP production is slower, making it unsuitable for high-intensity efforts.
options: It produces lactate more slowly than glycolysis
It requires less oxygen than glycolytic metabolism
It only metabolises fat, sparing muscle glycogen
It produces energy at a faster rate than glycolysis
It generates far more ATP per glucose molecule

questions.explanation: WHO BMI classification defines overweight as BMI 25.0-29.9 kg/m2. A BMI of 28.5 falls within this range, indicating overweight status with increased risk for type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and musculoskeletal disorders. Obesity Class I begins at BMI 30.0 or above. Physiotherapists should recognise overweight classification to appropriately address weight management within their scope of practice.
questions.question: A patient's BMI is 28.5 kg/m2. According to standard WHO classification, this patient is best categorised as:

questions.explanation: The kidneys perform the final hydroxylation step converting 25-hydroxyvitamin D to the active form 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D. Chronic kidney disease impairs this activation, leading to secondary hyperparathyroidism, impaired calcium absorption, and renal osteodystrophy. Physiotherapists treating this population must account for increased fracture risk and bone pain when prescribing weight-bearing and resistance exercise.
questions.question: A patient with chronic kidney disease is at risk for which metabolic bone condition related to impaired vitamin D metabolism?
options: Renal osteodystrophy from impaired vitamin D activation

questions.question: During dynamic whole-body exercise such as running, systolic blood pressure rises noticeably while diastolic blood pressure barely changes. What is the main physiological reason for this difference?
questions.explanation: During dynamic exercise, blood is pumped more forcefully and rapidly out of the heart, which raises systolic blood pressure, the pressure recorded during the contraction phase of the cardiac cycle. Diastolic blood pressure, recorded during the relaxation phase, barely changes because peripheral vasodilation in the working muscles offsets the increased cardiac output. A normal resting blood pressure is commonly cited as approximately one hundred and twenty over eighty millimetres of mercury.

questions.question: The principle of fat-free body mass in body composition is most accurately applied when a physiotherapist is:
questions.explanation: Basal metabolic rate is predominantly determined by metabolically active fat-free mass (primarily skeletal muscle and organ mass) rather than total body weight. Using fat-free body mass to estimate BMR provides more accurate energy expenditure calculations than total body weight, particularly in obese individuals where excess fat mass is metabolically less active. This allows physiotherapists to more accurately prescribe caloric targets when supporting weight management programmes.
options: Estimating basal metabolic rate from lean mass
Setting ideal weight targets for obese patients
Comparing patient data to population norms
Estimating drug dosing per unit body weight
Macro minerals are more important for muscle function
Macro minerals are required in gram amounts daily
Trace minerals are found exclusively in animal foods
Trace minerals have no role in energy metabolism
Macro minerals are stored only in bone tissue
questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes macro from trace minerals in the context of exercise physiology?
questions.explanation: The distinction between macro and trace minerals is based on the quantity required daily: macrominerals are required in amounts greater than 100 mg per day, while trace minerals are needed in milligram to microgram quantities. This classification does not indicate relative biological importance, as some trace minerals are critical for energy metabolism and immune function.

options: Determine the need for dietary modification
Establish BMI targets for the programme
Determine the frequency of physiotherapy sessions
Identify appropriate exercise intensity and safety limits
questions.explanation: Pre-exercise fitness assessment in cardiac rehabilitation establishes baseline functional capacity, identifies exercise-limiting symptoms, determines appropriate training heart rate zones, and flags contraindications to exercise progression. Exercise prescription in cardiac rehabilitation must be precisely individualised based on objective fitness assessment to minimise risk and maximise rehabilitation efficacy. This is a fundamental safety and effectiveness requirement of evidence-based cardiac physiotherapy.
questions.question: The most critical reason to assess physical fitness before designing a post-cardiac event rehabilitation programme is to:

questions.explanation: Skinfold measurements are taken using a caliper at standard anatomical sites including the triceps, biceps, subscapular, suprailiac, abdomen, thigh, and chest. This is one of the indirect anthropometric methods commonly used in physiotherapy practice to estimate relative body fatness. The technique requires minimal equipment, making it practical and inexpensive compared with laboratory-based body composition methods.
questions.question: A physiotherapist measures subcutaneous fat thickness at the triceps, biceps, subscapular, and suprailiac sites using a handheld instrument. Which instrument is being used in this assessment?

Before performing a graded exercise test, a patient must be informed about the test procedure, associated risks and discomforts, and expected benefits, and must freely agree to proceed. What is this process called?
questions.explanation: Informed consent for graded exercise testing requires explanation of the test, disclosure of risks and discomforts, clarification of participant responsibilities, description of expected benefits, an opportunity for questions, and confirmation of the participant's freedom to consent. This ethical and legal requirement ensures the patient fully understands the procedure before undergoing it. It is a mandatory step regardless of whether the test is being performed for diagnostic or screening purposes.

questions.question: Regular physical exercise has been shown to increase the brain's production of which substance, often described as the body's own natural opiates?
questions.explanation: Exercise increases the production of endorphins by the brain, which are described as nature's own opiates and contribute to an emotional lift following physical activity. Physical exercise also has a positive influence on psychological functioning more broadly, reducing anxiety and depression and elevating mood. These psychological benefits occur alongside the wide range of physiological benefits produced by regular exercise.

Acute myocardial infarction within the past two weeks is listed as a contraindication to the Naughton protocol stress test, since testing during this period can increase the risk of further cardiac damage. In such cases, the test should be postponed until the patient's condition has stabilised sufficiently, as judged by the supervising healthcare professional. This precaution reflects the broader principle that graded exercise testing should never be performed when the risk of harm outweighs the diagnostic benefit.
options: only the warm-up stage is skipped
only the recovery stage is skipped
questions.question: A patient who suffered a myocardial infarction within the past two weeks is scheduled for Naughton protocol stress testing. How should this scenario be managed according to standard contraindication guidelines?

questions.explanation: The flat, parallel fibre arrangement is thin and broad, originating from sheet-like aponeuroses that spread the generated force over a larger area. The rectus abdominis and external oblique are classic examples of this shape. This contrasts with fusiform muscles, which have a spindle-shaped central belly tapering to tendons.
questions.question: A flat, broad muscle such as the external oblique originates from a sheet-like aponeurosis and spreads force over a wide area. Which fibre arrangement does this describe?
Among recommendations for incorporating exercise into a busy work schedule for stress management, joining a group is suggested to provide which benefit?
questions.explanation: Recommendations for successfully incorporating exercise into a stress management routine include deciding to exercise and staying focused, joining a group to provide encouragement, starting small, and making activity regular. Hospital policy supporting workplace exercise facilities, along with short pauses for stretching during work hours, is also suggested as a practical strategy. These recommendations emphasise consistency and social support as key factors in sustaining a stress-reducing exercise habit.

Published reference values for fat-free mass hydration are relatively consistent with measured values in healthy infants and children, showing relatively low between-individual variability. This consistency supports the reasonable accuracy of isotope dilution for estimating fat-free mass in healthy populations. In disease states, however, variability in hydration may be substantially higher due to overhydration or underhydration, reducing the accuracy of this assumption.
questions.question: In healthy individuals, isotope dilution methods for estimating fat-free mass are described as relatively accurate because published reference hydration values show what characteristic across measured populations?

questions.explanation: Elasticity is the ability of a muscle fibre to return to its resting length once a stretch has been removed. This property is determined mainly by the connective tissue within the muscle rather than by the contractile fibrils themselves. Together with extensibility, it protects the muscle and maintains its structural integrity.
questions.question: After a stretch is released, a muscle fibre returns to its original resting length mainly because of which property?

A simple objective device counts the number of times a certain acceleration threshold is exceeded to provide an overall estimate of steps taken, but cannot capture activities such as cycling or swimming. Which device is this?
questions.explanation: Pedometers count the number of times a certain acceleration threshold is exceeded, or the number of zero crossings in the acceleration waveform, to provide an overall estimate of steps taken. A key limitation is that pedometers cannot capture non-ambulatory activities such as cycling or swimming, and cannot assess intensity in a caloric sense. This makes them less comprehensive than accelerometers or combined sensor devices for assessing overall physical activity.

Potassium is the predominant intracellular cation and is essential for maintaining the resting membrane potential of muscle and nerve cells. Hypokalaemia impairs membrane repolarisation, causing muscle weakness, cramps, and cardiac conduction disturbances including arrhythmias. These are clinically significant findings requiring medical referral before continuing exercise prescription. Calcium deficiency primarily causes tetany through different mechanisms.
options: Sodium required for action potential generation
questions.question: A physiotherapist assessing mineral status finds that a patient has muscle cramps, weakness, and cardiac arrhythmia during supervised exercise. The mineral most likely deficient is:
In prescribing exercise for a patient with type 2 diabetes, moderate-intensity exercise primarily enhances which metabolic pathway for glycaemic management?
questions.explanation: Moderate-intensity aerobic exercise predominantly engages the oxidative system, which increases insulin-independent glucose uptake into skeletal muscle via GLUT4 transporter translocation. This mechanism acutely lowers blood glucose and, with regular training, improves insulin sensitivity. The ATP-PCr and anaerobic systems are minimal contributors at moderate intensities and do not promote the sustained glucose uptake central to diabetes management.

questions.question: The warm-up stage of the Naughton protocol typically lasts how long and is designed to gradually increase heart rate and blood flow to the muscles?
questions.explanation: The warm-up stage of the Naughton protocol typically lasts three to five minutes and is designed to gradually increase the patient's heart rate and blood flow to the muscles. During this stage, the patient begins exercising at a slow pace, such as walking on a treadmill or pedalling slowly on a stationary bike. This gradual onset helps prepare the cardiovascular system before progressing to the more demanding main exercise stage.

Among the listed benefits of exercise, it improves resistance to cold, increases basal metabolic rate, and decreases load on the heart. These benefits reflect the broader cardiovascular efficiency gained through regular training, allowing the heart to perform its pumping function with less relative strain. This reduced cardiac workload is particularly relevant when considering exercise as part of managing cardiovascular risk.
questions.question: Regular exercise is described as improving resistance to cold and decreasing load on which organ specifically?

questions.explanation: Exercise is one of the first management strategies advised for newly diagnosed diabetes mellitus patients, used together with diet and behaviour modifications. This combined approach helps control weight, lower blood pressure, lower harmful cholesterol and triglycerides, strengthen muscles and bones, and improve general well-being. Exercise specifically helps counter the effects of diabetes mellitus by lowering blood glucose and boosting insulin sensitivity.
questions.question: Exercise is recommended as one of the first management strategies for newly diagnosed diabetes mellitus, used together with diet and which other intervention?

questions.explanation: The resting electrocardiogram usually precedes graded exercise testing as an important baseline study confirming the person can safely engage in the procedure. This baseline allows comparison with the exercise electrocardiogram to detect new abnormalities that emerge only under the stress of physical exertion. Without this baseline, it would be difficult to attribute electrocardiographic changes specifically to the exercise stress itself.
questions.question: Prior to performing graded exercise testing, an important baseline study is typically obtained to confirm that a person can safely engage in the test. Which baseline study is this?

options: A proton gradient (chemiosmotic potential) across the membrane
Direct phosphorylation of ADP by substrate molecules
Oxygen combining directly with ADP and phosphate
Heat released during electron transfer reactions
questions.question: The electron transport chain produces the majority of cellular ATP. The driving force for ATP synthesis is:
questions.explanation: The electron transport chain uses energy from NADH and FADH2 oxidation to pump protons from the mitochondrial matrix to the intermembrane space, creating a proton gradient. Protons flow back through ATP synthase down this electrochemical gradient, driving the mechanical rotation of ATP synthase that catalyses ADP phosphorylation to ATP. This chemiosmotic mechanism generates approximately 28-30 of the 32 ATP produced per glucose molecule.

Subjective assessment methods include questionnaires, interviews, activity diaries, and direct observation, and are particularly useful for assessing physical activity in controlled situations or as a validation criterion. Their accuracy is influenced by the participant's ability to accurately recall relevant details, as well as their own perceptions and opinions. This contrasts with objective methods, which measure physiological or biomechanical parameters directly rather than relying on self-report.
questions.question: A researcher uses questionnaires, interviews, and activity diaries to assess a participant's physical activity level, relying on the participant's recall of their own behaviour. Which broad category of assessment is this?

questions.explanation: The lowest risk of cardiovascular complications associated with BMI is generally found within the range of twenty to twenty-five, with risk increasing progressively as BMI rises above this range. The highest risk is associated with a BMI over forty. This curvilinear relationship between BMI and all-cause mortality underlies its widespread clinical use, despite its limitations in distinguishing fat mass from lean mass.
questions.question: The lowest risk of cardiovascular complications associated with rising Body Mass Index is generally cited as occurring within which range?
A component of fitness is measured by how much force a person can exert and how much weight can be lifted for a short period, typically developed through resistance training. Which component is this?
questions.explanation: Muscular strength relates to a person's ability to move and lift objects, measured by how much force can be exerted and how much weight can be lifted over a short duration. It is developed through resistance training such as weightlifting, bodyweight exercises, and resistance band exercises. This is distinct from muscular endurance, which concerns the ability to sustain repeated contractions over a longer period.

During severe caloric restriction, blood glucose falls and gluconeogenesis increases to maintain glucose supply to the brain and obligate glucose-dependent tissues. Amino acids from skeletal muscle protein catabolism serve as gluconeogenic substrates, leading to muscle wasting alongside fat loss. Resistance exercise during caloric restriction preserves muscle by providing an anabolic stimulus that reduces the proportion of weight loss attributable to muscle protein catabolism.
questions.question: A physiotherapist explains to a patient why severe caloric restriction without exercise causes loss of both fat and muscle. The most accurate metabolic explanation is:
options: Fat stores are insufficient for metabolic needs
The Krebs cycle cannot function without dietary carbohydrate
Muscle protein is catabolised for gluconeogenesis
Insulin deficiency prevents adipose tissue mobilisation

questions.question: Which energy system characteristic is most important for a physiotherapist designing rehabilitation for a 100-metre sprinter with a hamstring injury?
options: Maximal oxidative capacity for sustained effort
Fat oxidation efficiency for energy storage
ATP-PCr capacity for explosive power output
Krebs cycle rate for recovery between efforts
questions.explanation: Sprinting 100 metres is almost entirely dependent on the ATP-PCr system and fast glycolysis, lasting approximately 10-12 seconds at elite level. Rehabilitation for a 100-metre sprinter must include high-intensity explosive plyometric and sprint progressions that specifically load and develop ATP-PCr system capacity in the recovering hamstring. Oxidative and fat-burning capacity are irrelevant at 100-metre sprint intensities.

BMI cannot distinguish fat mass from lean mass. Athletes with high skeletal muscle mass may have elevated BMI values, incorrectly classifying them as overweight or obese despite having low body fat percentages. This is a well-documented limitation in sports physiotherapy and occupational health settings. Sarcopenic obesity paradoxically may show normal BMI despite excess fat and low muscle mass.
options: Athletes with high lean muscle mass
questions.question: Body Mass Index (BMI) systematically overestimates adiposity in which patient group most commonly encountered in physiotherapy practice?

questions.explanation: Recommendations for physician supervision during graded exercise testing depend on the individual's risk classification, distinguishing between apparently healthy individuals, those at higher risk, and those with known disease, as well as whether the test is submaximal or maximal. Lower-risk, apparently healthy individuals generally require less direct physician supervision than higher-risk individuals or those with diagnosed disease. This risk-stratified approach helps balance patient safety with the practical resources required to conduct testing.
options: testing must always be maximal type
supervision requirement depends on risk classification
testing must always be submaximal type
supervision is never required at all
questions.question: A patient undergoing graded exercise testing is found to have controlled, stable hypertension with no other contraindicating features. Which decision regarding physician supervision is most appropriate for this lower-risk scenario?

options: The cellular location of glucose breakdown
The type of glucose molecule metabolised
The availability of oxygen for pyruvate processing
The number of ATP molecules initially consumed
The hormonal regulation of glycolytic enzymes
questions.question: The physiological process by which fast glycolysis differs from slow glycolysis is primarily determined by:
questions.explanation: Both fast and slow glycolysis occur in the cytoplasm and process glucose identically to pyruvate. The distinction lies in oxygen availability: in fast (anaerobic) glycolysis, limited oxygen means pyruvate is converted to lactate, regenerating NAD+ to sustain glycolysis. In slow glycolysis, adequate oxygen allows pyruvate to enter mitochondria as acetyl-CoA for complete oxidation via the Krebs cycle.

Piezoelectric pedometers use crystal elements that generate electrical signals in response to mechanical deformation from acceleration, making them more sensitive and accurate than spring-lever mechanisms. The electrical signal output allows more precise step detection at varying speeds. GPS, heart rate, and altitude monitoring are features of separate or combined device technologies.
questions.question: Piezoelectric pedometers improve upon mechanical spring-lever designs primarily by:
A general guideline identifies increased risk of heart disease when waist girth exceeds a specific threshold in men compared with women. What is the commonly cited threshold for men?
questions.explanation: A commonly cited risk threshold identifies increased risk of heart disease when waist girth exceeds 102 centimetres in men, compared with a threshold of 88 centimetres in women. These guidelines are used alongside waist-to-hip ratio as general risk indicators based on girth measurement. Such thresholds reflect the association between central fat accumulation and elevated cardiovascular risk discussed in relation to waist circumference.

questions.question: A hospital is considering supporting workplace exercise among staff to address occupational stress. Which institutional-level recommendation is specifically suggested to facilitate this?
questions.explanation: Among recommendations for managing work-related stress through exercise, supportive hospital policy is suggested as a facilitator, such as providing a dedicated facility for exercise within the hospital. Short pauses for stretches and exercise during work hours are also suggested to help relieve stress among health workers. This institutional-level recommendation recognises that individual motivation alone may be insufficient without supportive organisational structures.

questions.question: A physiotherapist notes elevated creatine kinase (CK) in a patient after high-intensity resistance training. Elevated CK most directly reflects:
questions.explanation: Creatine kinase is an intracellular enzyme located in muscle cytoplasm and mitochondria. Elevated serum CK after high-intensity exercise indicates sarcolemmal (muscle cell membrane) disruption from mechanical stress and eccentric loading, releasing intracellular contents including CK into circulation. This is the biochemical marker of exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD) and the precursor to DOMS. Markedly elevated CK may indicate rhabdomyolysis requiring urgent medical assessment.
options: Muscle membrane disruption from high-intensity work
Liver enzyme elevation from exercise metabolism

questions.explanation: BMI in children and adolescents is not interpreted using fixed adult cut-offs because body composition changes substantially with age and differs between sexes during development. Age- and sex-specific BMI percentile charts are used, with overweight defined as at or above the 85th percentile and obesity at or above the 95th percentile for age and sex. Adult cut-offs applied to adolescents would misclassify many individuals.
options: Applying the same BMI cut-offs as adults
Using age- and sex-specific BMI percentiles
Calculating body fat from bioelectrical impedance
questions.question: A physiotherapist conducting body composition assessment for a 16-year-old athlete should interpret BMI differently from adults by:

questions.explanation: Carbohydrates are one of the three macronutrients in the diet, the other two being proteins and fats. Macronutrients are required by the body in relatively large amounts to supply energy and support growth and repair. Carbohydrates specifically contribute the major source of readily available metabolic energy for both plants and animals.
questions.question: Carbohydrates belong to one of the three major classes of macronutrients in the human diet, alongside which other two nutrient classes?

questions.explanation: The fast glycolytic system becomes the dominant contributor after the first ten to fifteen seconds of exercise and continues to power activity for up to around forty-five seconds. It breaks down glucose anaerobically, producing pyruvate that is converted to lactic acid when oxygen supply is insufficient. Eight hundred metre runners rely heavily on this pathway because the event duration exceeds the capacity of the ATP-PCr system.
questions.question: An 800-metre runner sustains near-maximal effort for close to two minutes, producing significant lactic acid as the dominant by-product of ATP regeneration. Which energy system is chiefly responsible?

questions.explanation: Storage fat is the fat accumulated within adipose tissue, comprising both visceral and subcutaneous adipose deposits, and represents about twelve percent of body mass in men and fifteen percent in women. Unlike essential fat, storage fat serves primarily as an energy reserve rather than a structural or functional requirement. This is the component of body fat most readily targeted through weight management interventions.
questions.question: Fat accumulated in adipose tissue, consisting of both visceral and subcutaneous deposits, is reported to constitute approximately 12 percent of body mass in men and 15 percent in women. What is this fat category termed?

questions.explanation: The acinus is the functional gas exchange unit of the lung, comprising the respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, alveolar sacs, and alveoli. It is at this level that oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged between inspired air and pulmonary capillary blood. Efficient function of the acinus is therefore essential to the overall respiratory response to exercise.
questions.question: The gas exchange unit of the lung, comprising respiratory bronchioles leading to alveolar ducts, alveolar sacs, and alveoli, is collectively known as the?

options: Subcutaneous fat correlates with visceral fat
Subcutaneous fat represents a fixed body fat fraction
Muscle thickness is inversely related to skin folds
Hydration does not influence skinfold readings
questions.question: A physiotherapist uses skinfold measurements to estimate body composition. The underlying principle of this method relies on which relationship?
questions.explanation: Skinfold measurement assumes that subcutaneous fat represents a predictable proportion of total body fat, typically estimated at about one-third in reference populations. By measuring multiple standardised skinfold sites, regression equations estimate total body fat percentage. The assumption of a fixed subcutaneous-to-total-fat relationship is population-specific, which is why different prediction equations exist for different age, sex, and ethnic groups.

questions.question: Aerobic capability is reported to be largely genetically determined, accounting for up to what proportion of the variance in VO2 max between individuals?
questions.explanation: Genetics accounts for up to twenty-five to fifty percent of the variance in aerobic capability between individuals, although training can still substantially improve VO2 max regardless of genetic predisposition. This means that while genetic factors set a baseline potential, structured training remains an important modifiable contributor to aerobic fitness. Age, body size, gender, and training status are additional extrinsic factors that interact with genetic potential to determine overall aerobic capacity.

questions.question: A device estimates physical activity intensity or energy expenditure based on the assumption of a linear relationship between a physiological parameter and energy expenditure, performing best at moderate to vigorous intensities. Which device is this?
questions.explanation: Heart rate monitors estimate physical activity intensity or energy expenditure based on the assumed linear relationship between heart rate and energy expenditure, and are most useful at moderate and vigorous intensity levels. A key limitation is reduced accuracy at lower levels of activity intensity, where the heart rate response is less linearly related to energy expenditure. Despite this limitation, heart rate monitors remain a widely used objective tool in physical activity assessment.

questions.question: A method of indirect body composition assessment involves submerging an individual in water to estimate body density based on water displacement. What is this technique called?
questions.explanation: Hydrostatic weighing is an indirect method of body composition assessment that estimates body density based on underwater weight relative to weight on land. It is grouped alongside anthropometry and measures of stature and mass as indirect techniques used when direct chemical analysis is not feasible. While more accurate than simple field methods, it requires specialised equipment not typically available in routine physiotherapy practice.

Psychological signs of stress include difficulty concentrating, worrying, anxiety, and trouble remembering, distinguishing them from emotional signs such as anger, irritation, or frustration. Physical signs include high blood pressure and changes in weight, while behavioural signs include poor self-care or reliance on substances to cope. Recognising which category a given sign of stress falls into helps guide a more comprehensive clinical assessment.
questions.question: Among the signs of stress, difficulty concentrating, worrying, and trouble remembering are classified as which category of sign?

questions.explanation: Direct behavioural observation has evolved from real-time manual coding systems to include video recording with computerised coding software, enabling retrospective analysis, improved inter-rater reliability, and more detailed behavioural categorisation. This technological evolution allows observation to be conducted without requiring observers to be present during activity, reduces observer-induced reactivity, and enables multiple observers to code the same recordings for reliability assessment.
questions.question: A physiotherapist conducts direct behavioural observation in a paediatric rehabilitation setting. The modern evolution of this method includes which technological enhancement?
options: Use of validated questionnaires for children
Video recording and computerised coding systems
Remote observation via wearable cameras only
Using GPS tracking as a primary observation tool

questions.explanation: The whole body level represents the fifth and most practically applied level of the multi-component model, encompassing techniques such as skinfold thickness, girth measurement, densitometry, and segment volume. These methods are widely used in physiotherapy and sports science settings because they are accessible and require minimal equipment. They provide indirect estimates of the underlying atomic, molecular, cellular, and tissue components.
questions.question: Skinfold thickness, girth measurement, densitometry, and segment volume are practical assessment techniques applied at which level of body composition?

questions.explanation: Iron is essential for haemoglobin synthesis, which transports oxygen to working muscles. Iron deficiency anaemia directly impairs oxygen-carrying capacity, reducing VO2 max and causing early fatigue at submaximal exercise intensities. Muscular strength is less affected than aerobic capacity. Proprioception and blood pressure are not primarily impaired by iron deficiency.
questions.question: An athlete presents with iron deficiency anaemia. The physiotherapist should anticipate which primary impairment during submaximal exercise testing?
options: Impaired oxygen delivery and early fatigue

questions.explanation: Glycolysis is fast or anaerobic when the final product is lactic acid, occurring when oxygen supply cannot keep pace with demand. It is slow or aerobic when the final product is pyruvate, which can then proceed into the Krebs cycle. The distinction reflects the rate of glucose breakdown relative to the availability of oxygen in the working tissue.
questions.question: A biochemistry tutorial explains that glycolysis can yield either pyruvate or lactic acid as its final product, depending on oxygen availability in the working muscle. Which condition favours lactic acid as the end product?

options: a sign of low insulin sensitivity
a need for a small snack only
a normal value requiring no action
questions.explanation: A blood glucose level above 240 mg/dL before exercise indicates a risk of serious complications that requires immediate treatment, according to special considerations for diabetic patients engaging in physical activity. This contrasts with a level below 100 mg/dL, which instead calls for eating a small snack before proceeding with exercise. Checking blood sugar before activity is therefore an essential safety step for diabetic patients.
questions.question: A diabetic patient checks their blood sugar before exercising and finds it to be 260 mg/dL. According to special considerations for exercise in diabetes management, what does this finding indicate?

questions.explanation: Body composition is listed as one of the five health-related components of physical fitness, alongside cardiorespiratory endurance, muscular strength, muscular endurance, and flexibility. This component directly overlaps with the body composition assessment techniques covered separately, such as skinfold thickness, girth measurement, and Body Mass Index. Its inclusion reflects the recognised link between favourable body composition and overall physical fitness.
questions.question: A health-related fitness component already discussed under body composition assessment overlaps directly with one of the five components of physical fitness. Which component is this overlap referring to?
A large polysaccharide containing up to ten thousand linked monosaccharide units is stored in the liver and muscle as the body's main reserve of carbohydrate energy. What is this storage form called?
questions.explanation: Polysaccharides represent most of the structural and energy-reserve carbohydrates found in nature, and may contain as many as ten thousand linked monosaccharide units. Glycogen is the primary polysaccharide used by the body to store excess glucose in the liver and muscle. This storage process is known as glycogenesis and provides a readily mobilisable carbohydrate reserve.

questions.question: Excess circulating glucose that is not immediately required for energy is converted and stored in the liver and muscle through a process distinct from glycolysis. What is this storage process called?
questions.explanation: Glycogenesis is the process by which excess circulating glucose is converted and stored as glycogen in the liver and muscle. This stored glycogen acts as a readily available carbohydrate reserve that can later be broken down to supply glucose during periods of increased demand, such as exercise. It is distinct from glycolysis, which describes the breakdown rather than the storage of glucose.

questions.question: A 300-level physiotherapy student defines exercise physiology to a junior colleague as the branch of science primarily concerned with which of the following?
questions.explanation: Exercise physiology is defined as the study of how the human body responds and adjusts to exercise, both acutely and over time. It examines the physiological interactions and adjustments that occur before, during, and after exercise. This distinguishes it from general physiology, which deals broadly with function rather than the specific stimulus of exercise.

questions.question: When glucose combines with fructose through a glycosidic bond, the resulting double sugar commonly known as table sugar is formed. What is this disaccharide called?
questions.explanation: Sucrose, commonly known as table sugar, is formed when one molecule of glucose links with one molecule of fructose via a glycosidic bond. All disaccharides, including sucrose, contain at least one glucose molecule. Lactose, by contrast, is formed from glucose and galactose, while maltose is formed from two glucose molecules.

Multi-site skinfold measurement using validated regression equations provides a reasonably accurate field estimate of percent body fat when performed by a trained tester with calibrated callipers. While inferior to DEXA or underwater weighing, multi-site skinfold equations outperform BMI and circumference measures in distinguishing fat from lean tissue.
questions.question: A physiotherapist working in a weight management clinic measures a patient's percent body fat. The most accurate non-laboratory method is:
options: Calculating BMI from height and weight
Measuring waist circumference at the umbilicus
Estimating from visual inspection of body shape
Applying height-weight tables from population data

questions.question: Exercises recommended for managing diabetes mellitus are described as needing to be of moderate intensity and drawn from two specific categories. Which two categories are these?
questions.explanation: Exercises useful in managing diabetes mellitus are required to be of moderate intensity and are drawn from two broad categories: aerobic exercises and resistance exercises. Examples of moderate intensity aerobic activities include brisk walking, dancing, swimming, and cycling. This combination of aerobic and resistance training reflects current best practice for supporting glycaemic control in diabetic patients.

options: Heart rate response during outdoor activities
Step count accuracy in outdoor environments
questions.question: Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) are incorporated into physical activity assessment primarily to measure which dimension not captured by accelerometers?
questions.explanation: GNSS/GPS technology in physical activity monitors tracks geographic position and movement patterns, providing information on location, route, and speed of travel not available from accelerometers alone. This is particularly valuable for outdoor rehabilitation assessment, fall prevention in community settings, and understanding environmental context of physical activity. Accelerometers better quantify movement intensity, while GNSS adds spatial and contextual dimensions.

The muscle pump describes how rhythmic skeletal muscle contraction compresses surrounding veins, helping propel blood back toward the heart and increasing venous return during exercise. This mechanism works alongside the respiratory pump and venoconstriction to enhance the volume of blood returned to be reoxygenated. Increased venous return is essential to sustaining the elevated stroke volume required during sustained physical activity.
questions.question: During exercise, increased venous return is facilitated by rhythmic contraction of skeletal muscle around veins, assisting blood flow back toward the heart. This mechanism is known as the?

options: A young female athlete with menstrual dysfunction
A competitive bodybuilder in off-season conditioning
A distance runner during peak training load
An elderly patient with mild sarcopenic changes
A swimmer with high training volume demands
questions.explanation: A young female athlete with body fat below essential fat levels presenting with menstrual dysfunction is showing two components of the female athlete triad (or RED-S), indicating energy deficiency with potentially irreversible consequences for bone health, reproductive function, and cardiovascular status. Physiotherapists are well-positioned to identify this clinical pattern and require mandatory referral to sports medicine and dietitian services. This is a medical urgency requiring immediate multi-disciplinary intervention.
questions.question: The assessment finding of very low body fat percentage well below essential fat levels is most clinically urgent in which physiotherapy context?

Behavioural signs of stress are described as including poor self-care and reliance on substances to cope, in contrast to which category of sign that includes high blood pressure and changes in weight?
questions.explanation: Physical signs of stress include high blood pressure, changes in weight, frequent colds or infections, and changes in the menstrual cycle and libido. Behavioural signs, by contrast, include poor self-care, not having time for enjoyable activities, or relying on drugs, alcohol, caffeine, or energy drinks to cope. This categorisation into psychological, emotional, physical, and behavioural signs provides a structured framework for recognising stress in patients and colleagues.

questions.question: A region of the sarcomere is occupied only by thin filaments and is bisected by the Z disk, becoming shorter as the muscle contracts. Which region is this?
questions.explanation: The I band is the lightest region of the sarcomere, occupied only by thin filaments, and is bisected by the Z disk. Half of each I band belongs to one sarcomere and the other half to the neighbouring sarcomere. Like the H zone, the I band shortens progressively as the muscle contracts.

questions.question: A long-distance cyclist maintains a steady, low-to-moderate intensity pace for over an hour, deriving most of the required ATP from fat oxidation in the presence of oxygen. Which system is primarily supplying this energy?
questions.explanation: The oxidative system, also known as the Krebs cycle or aerobic system, is used for exercise lasting longer than about three minutes and requires oxygen throughout. It is the slowest system to activate but has by far the greatest energy capacity, using fat as its primary substrate during sustained low to moderate intensity work. Long-distance cycling and jogging are classic examples of activities powered predominantly by this pathway.

questions.question: The concept that 'energy systems do not work independently' is most practically demonstrated in physiotherapy by which exercise scenario?
options: A patient resting between exercise sets
questions.explanation: Interval training involves repeated high-intensity bouts separated by rest periods, simultaneously engaging the ATP-PCr system during high-intensity intervals, glycolytic system during sub-maximal periods, and oxidative system during recovery intervals. This concurrent engagement demonstrates the overlapping and interdependent nature of all three energy systems. A single maximal isometric contraction is predominantly ATP-PCr, while prolonged moderate-intensity activity is predominantly oxidative.

Diffusion is the movement of oxygen and carbon dioxide along their concentration gradients between the alveoli of the lungs and the surrounding capillaries, as well as between the muscle capillaries and the tissue. During exercise, increased diffusion allows a greater volume of oxygen to move into the blood for transport to working muscles. Gas exchange at the level of the alveoli is a critical step linking pulmonary ventilation to the delivery of oxygen to active tissue.
questions.question: The movement of oxygen and carbon dioxide between the alveoli and the pulmonary capillaries, occurring from an area of high concentration to an area of low concentration, is termed?
A patient with iodine deficiency presenting with an enlarged thyroid gland would also be expected to show which clinical sign most relevant to physiotherapy assessment?
options: Peripheral oedema in the lower limbs
questions.explanation: Iodine deficiency impairs thyroid hormone synthesis, leading to hypothyroidism characterised by reduced metabolic rate and consequently reduced aerobic exercise tolerance. Physiotherapists may observe fatigue, reduced exercise capacity, and cold intolerance. Oedema, skin changes, and hypertension are not primary consequences of iodine deficiency-related thyroid dysfunction.

questions.question: The biceps brachii has a spindle-shaped central belly that tapers into tendons on both ends, transmitting force to small bony attachment sites. This describes which fibre shape?
questions.explanation: The fusiform fibre arrangement is spindle-shaped, with a central belly tapering to tendons at each end, allowing force transmission to small bony sites. The biceps brachii, brachialis, and brachioradialis are typical examples of this shape. This parallel arrangement favours a greater range of shortening and movement velocity.

questions.question: In a patient with uncontrolled type 2 diabetes, prolonged moderate exercise may lead to which potentially dangerous metabolic scenario during the session?
questions.explanation: During moderate-intensity exercise, muscle glucose uptake increases via insulin-independent GLUT4 translocation. In diabetic patients on insulin or sulphonylureas, this additive glucose-lowering effect can cause hypoglycaemia, particularly when exercise duration extends beyond 30-45 minutes. Physiotherapists must monitor blood glucose before, during, and after exercise in insulin-treated diabetes and have carbohydrate sources available to manage hypoglycaemic episodes.

questions.question: During the oxidative process, slow glycolysis produces pyruvic acid that is subsequently converted into a compound used to enter the Krebs cycle for further aerobic energy production. What is this entry compound called?
questions.explanation: Slow glycolysis within the oxidative process produces pyruvic acid as its end product, which is then converted into acetyl coenzyme A. This compound enters the Krebs cycle to be further oxidised for aerobic ATP production. This pathway contrasts with fast anaerobic glycolysis, in which pyruvate is instead converted to lactic acid when oxygen is insufficient.

questions.question: A male patient's BMI is 33 but his waist-to-height ratio is 0.62. Together these findings most strongly indicate risk for:
questions.explanation: A BMI of 33 (obese Class I) combined with a waist-to-height ratio of 0.62 (above 0.5 threshold for elevated risk) indicates both overall and central obesity, a combination most strongly associated with cardiometabolic risk including hypertension, dyslipidaemia, and coronary artery disease. The waist-to-height ratio is a validated predictor of cardiometabolic risk independent of BMI. Physiotherapists should integrate both measures in pre-exercise risk stratification.
options: Osteoporotic fracture from obesity-related bone loss
Sleep apnoea from upper airway soft tissue excess
Type 1 diabetes from pancreatic adipose deposition
Peripheral neuropathy from adipose nerve compression
Cardiac disease from central adiposity and obesity

questions.question: The most clinically relevant reason for a physiotherapist to assess body composition rather than BMI alone in a post-bariatric surgery patient is that:
options: BMI cannot be calculated after surgery
BMI overestimates fat in post-surgical patients
Post-surgical weight loss may include significant muscle loss
questions.explanation: Rapid weight loss following bariatric surgery often includes significant skeletal muscle loss alongside fat loss, a condition termed sarcopenic obesity where low muscle mass coexists with remaining adiposity. BMI normalisation does not reflect this unfavourable body composition change. Physiotherapists need body composition data to guide resistance training programmes that preserve or rebuild muscle mass during the post-surgical period, which BMI alone cannot provide.

questions.question: The World Health Organization defines stress as any type of change that causes which combination of strain on an individual?
questions.explanation: The World Health Organization defines stress as any type of change that causes physical, emotional, or psychological strain. Stress can be described more generally as the individual body's reaction to a challenge or demand, arising from any event or thought that produces feelings of frustration, anger, or nervousness. This broad definition encompasses both the triggering event and the individual's physiological and emotional response to it.

Many enzymes require specific minerals as cofactors or activators to achieve their catalytically active conformation. Examples include zinc in over 300 enzymes including matrix metalloproteinases (relevant to tissue remodelling), magnesium required by all ATP-dependent enzymes in energy metabolism, and copper in superoxide dismutase for antioxidant defence. Mineral deficiency impairs enzymatic activity, reducing metabolic efficiency relevant to physiotherapy rehabilitation outcomes.
options: Enzymes cannot be replaced once degraded by exercise
Only trace minerals are required for enzymatic activity
Mineral supplements can replace enzyme deficiencies
Minerals act as structural cofactors for enzyme function
questions.question: Which statement most accurately describes the clinical relevance of essential minerals being required for enzyme production in physiotherapy rehabilitation?

questions.explanation: Trained athletes typically develop a larger resting stroke volume as a result of cardiac adaptations to endurance training, allowing the same resting cardiac output to be achieved with fewer beats per minute. This is why trained athletes characteristically display a lower resting heart rate, sometimes termed training bradycardia. Resting cardiac output itself does not decrease, since the reduced heart rate is compensated for by the increased stroke volume.
questions.question: A trained athlete is noted to have a lower resting heart rate than an untrained individual of similar age and body size. Which adaptation most directly accounts for this finding?

When the body works persistently in emergency mode, the autonomic nervous system becomes dysregulated, affecting three anatomically distinct divisions. Which three divisions make up the autonomic nervous system?
questions.explanation: The autonomic nervous system is a component of the peripheral nervous system that regulates involuntary physiological processes including heart rate, blood pressure, respiration, digestion, and sexual arousal. It contains three anatomically distinct divisions: sympathetic, parasympathetic, and enteric. Working persistently in emergency mode can cause this system to become dysregulated, contributing to the harmful effects of chronic stress.

questions.question: When a physiotherapist interprets accelerometer data showing high sedentary time alongside elevated BMI, the most clinically relevant next action is to:
options: Design a progressive activity break programme
questions.explanation: Accelerometer data revealing prolonged sedentary time with elevated BMI indicates combined deconditioning and metabolic risk. A structured programme targeting sedentary time reduction through regular activity breaks is the most evidence-based physiotherapy intervention. Resistance training alone would not adequately address the sedentary behaviour pattern identified.

Exercise strengthens the tendons, ligaments, muscles, and other tissues around joints while lubricating joint cartilages and capsules, maintaining proper joint flexibility. Greater flexibility of joints is associated with a lower chance of injury during physical activity. This musculoskeletal benefit complements the cardiovascular and metabolic adaptations also produced by regular exercise.
questions.question: Regular exercise lubricates joint cartilages and capsules while strengthening tendons and ligaments around joints, leading to which functional benefit?

questions.explanation: In short bursts, stress can be positive, helping a person avoid danger or meet a deadline, an experience common to everyone. Chronic stress, by contrast, is described as harmful to health, distinguishing it clearly from the more adaptive short-term stress response. This distinction underlies the importance of managing prolonged stress exposure rather than viewing all stress as inherently harmful.
questions.question: Short bursts of stress are described as potentially positive, such as when they help a person avoid danger or meet a deadline, but which form of stress is described as harmful to health?

Treadmill testing, ergometer testing, and step testing are examples of physical fitness assessment conducted in a controlled setting requiring specialised equipment. Which broad category does this represent?
questions.explanation: Laboratory methods of physical fitness assessment include treadmill testing, ergometer testing, and step testing, all of which require specialised equipment typically only available in a controlled clinical or research setting. These contrast with field methods such as the twelve-minute walk-run test, which can be performed with minimal equipment outside a laboratory. The choice between laboratory and field methods often depends on equipment availability and the population being assessed.

questions.question: Stroke volume increases progressively with rising exercise intensity but then plateaus once exercise reaches approximately what percentage of maximum intensity?
questions.explanation: Stroke volume increases with exercise intensity but plateaus once intensity reaches roughly forty to sixty percent of maximum, after which further increases in cardiac output rely mainly on rising heart rate. This plateau occurs because diastolic filling time shortens at higher heart rates, limiting further increases in the volume ejected per beat. Trained individuals typically achieve a higher stroke volume both at rest and during exercise compared with untrained individuals.

questions.question: Although blood pressure rises acutely during a single bout of exercise, what is the long-term effect of regular exercise on resting blood pressure?
options: it only affects pressure in athletes
questions.explanation: Blood pressure rises acutely during a bout of exercise, but in the long run regular exercise decreases resting blood pressure. This long-term reduction is one of the key physiological benefits underlying the use of exercise in managing hypertension. This distinction between the acute exercise response and the chronic training adaptation is an important concept in exercise physiology.

options: Vitamin D and calcium causing rickets
Vitamin K reducing bone protein synthesis
questions.explanation: Rickets is caused by vitamin D and/or calcium deficiency during skeletal development, leading to impaired bone mineralisation. Vitamin D is required for intestinal calcium and phosphorus absorption; deficiency results in inadequate mineralisation of growth plates and cortical bone, producing the characteristic bowing deformity, dental hypoplasia, and growth retardation that physiotherapists encounter in paediatric practice.
questions.question: A 5-year-old child presents with bowed legs, dental abnormalities, and delayed growth. The physiotherapist should recognise this as consistent with deficiency of:

questions.explanation: Cadaver analysis is considered the gold standard for body composition analysis, since no in vivo technique can match its accuracy for directly measuring body components. Because cadaver analysis is not feasible in living individuals, multicomponent models are instead considered the most accurate reference or criterion methods available for living subjects. All other techniques, including DXA and hydrostatic weighing, are validated against these more accurate reference standards.
questions.question: A clinician notes that the gold standard for body composition analysis, against which all other techniques should ideally be evaluated, is which method?
During nutrition counselling, a patient asks why vegans specifically need vitamin B12 supplementation. The correct explanation is:
options: Vitamin B12 is found only in animal-derived foods
Vegans need more B12 due to higher metabolic demands
Plant foods contain B12 inhibitors reducing absorption
Vegans have lower gastric acid for B12 absorption
Plant foods have B12 in a non-bioavailable form
questions.explanation: Vitamin B12 is synthesised exclusively by bacteria and archaea and is found in the food supply only through animal products where it accumulates via intestinal bacterial synthesis or dietary ingestion by animals. Plant foods do not naturally contain bioavailable B12. Vegans must supplement or consume B12-fortified foods to prevent deficiency, which physiotherapists should incorporate in nutritional counselling for athletic populations.

options: Iron or vitamin B12 causing anaemia
Vitamin C deficiency causing poor immunity
questions.question: A patient with persistent fatigue despite adequate sleep is referred to physiotherapy. The physiotherapist should recommend assessment for which nutritional deficiency as a priority?
questions.explanation: Persistent fatigue without adequate explanation is a cardinal symptom of anaemia, most commonly caused by iron or vitamin B12 deficiency. Both deficiencies impair red blood cell production, reducing oxygen delivery to tissues and causing fatigue even at rest. Physiotherapists should flag this for medical investigation before progressing exercise programmes, as anaemia significantly affects exercise tolerance.

questions.question: The overall process in which absorbed food substances, including carbohydrates, are chemically broken down within the body to release usable energy is broadly termed?
questions.explanation: Catabolism is the process in which food substances, including carbohydrates, are broken down to release energy after digestion and absorption have occurred. This is part of the broader process of metabolism, which encompasses all the chemical and energy transformations that food substances undergo in the body. Catabolism ensures that energy is constantly supplied to living cells to sustain physiological function.

options: a state of reduced metabolic rate
questions.explanation: Exercise activates the sympathetic nervous system and puts the whole body on the alert, reflecting the heightened physiological readiness associated with physical exertion. This activation also contributes to increased gastrointestinal tone, another listed benefit of regular exercise. These autonomic nervous system effects illustrate how exercise influences body systems well beyond the muscles directly involved in movement.
questions.question: Exercise is reported to activate the sympathetic nervous system, putting the whole body into which state?
While lowering into a squat under control against gravity, the quadriceps lengthens while still generating tension to decelerate the movement. Which type of contraction is occurring?
questions.explanation: Eccentric contraction occurs when a muscle lengthens while still activated, with its points of insertion moving further apart, typically while controlling movement against gravity. It decelerates body segments and provides shock absorption, and is referred to as negative work. The controlled descent into a squat is a classic example of eccentric quadriceps activity.

Maintaining good physical fitness can help prevent several chronic conditions, including hypertension, diabetes, colon cancer, and cardiovascular disease. With regular exercise, body composition can also improve even without significant changes in total body weight. These broad health benefits underline the importance of incorporating physical fitness assessment and promotion into routine physiotherapy practice.
questions.question: Maintaining good physical fitness is associated with prevention of several chronic conditions, including hypertension, diabetes, and colon cancer, in addition to which major disease category?

options: Step count from a mechanical pedometer
questions.explanation: Doubly labelled water combined with indirect calorimetry is the gold standard for measuring physical activity energy expenditure, providing accurate assessment over days to weeks without affecting behaviour. Questionnaires are prone to recall bias in clinical populations. Pedometers measure steps without energy cost quantification, and BMI reflects body composition rather than energy expenditure.
questions.question: A physiotherapist assessing physical activity energy expenditure (PAEE) in a patient with cardiac disease most accurately estimates PAEE using:

courses.title: Pain Management

options: Anchoring the ribs to provide upper body stability
Forming the back of the pelvis for weight transfer
Providing attachment for ligaments as a tailbone remnant
Supporting the head and allowing a wide range of motion
Bearing most of the body's weight directly
questions.explanation: The cervical spine, with 7 vertebrae, supports the head and allows for a wide range of motion. The thoracic spine anchors the ribs, the lumbar spine bears most of the body's weight, and the sacrum and coccyx serve pelvic and ligament-attachment roles. The distractors describe functions of these other spinal regions rather than the cervical spine's head-support and mobility role.
questions.question: The cervical spine, consisting of 7 vertebrae, is primarily responsible for:

options: Immediately refer to a psychologist and end the physiotherapy session
Continue with the planned physical treatment to maintain session structure
Perform a detailed trauma history to fully understand the background
Document the trauma disclosure and inform the patient's GP only
Provide validation, choice, and control within the current session
questions.explanation: Trauma-informed care in physiotherapy requires recognising trauma's effects, creating safety, and restoring a sense of control and choice — not trauma processing (which requires specialist training) or immediate referral that might feel rejecting. The immediate response to emotional disclosure is to acknowledge and validate the patient's experience, slow down, check in about continuing, offer choices (positioning, pacing, what to focus on), and adjust the session to restore the patient's sense of control and safety. This approach maintains the therapeutic relationship and applies trauma-informed principles within the physiotherapist's scope, while also facilitating appropriate ongoing support through collaborative care pathways.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is treating a patient with chronic pain who becomes emotional during the session, revealing significant personal trauma. The physiotherapist recognises signs of trauma and wishes to provide trauma-informed care. Which is the most important immediate response?

questions.explanation: Melzack and Wall proposed the Gate Control Theory of pain in 1965, explaining how transmission across the dorsal horn synapse can be modulated. The theory has since been modified but remains a valid foundation for understanding pain modulation. The other named pairs are associated with different topics, such as nociception processes or stages of dying, not the gate theory.
questions.question: The Gate Control Theory of pain was proposed in 1965 by:

options: Dorsal column pathway for fine touch
questions.explanation: The spinoreticular pathway synapses in the brainstem reticular formation, where arousal, attention and sleep-waking cycles are modulated, explaining why severe pain interferes with sleep. This is distinct from the spinothalamic pathway's discriminative role and the spinolimbic pathway's emotional role. The spinomesencephalic pathway instead governs orienting eye and head movements toward the source of pain.
questions.question: Arousal, attention and sleep-wake cycle modulation in response to severe pain are mediated mainly through the:

options: Only acute nociceptive pain immediately after surgery
Only psychogenic pain without any physical cause
Only mild transient pain from minor everyday cuts
Only pain associated with active bleeding wounds
Neuropathic, cancer, labour and chronic nociceptive pain
questions.explanation: The guide to selection of modalities recommends electro-analgesic currents (TENS and Interferential Current) for neuropathic pain, cancer pain, labour pain, and chronic nociceptive pain. This broad range reflects the multiple mechanisms, segmental and hormonal, through which electro-analgesic currents can modulate different pain types. The distractors restrict the indication to pain types not specifically listed for this modality.
questions.question: Electro-analgesic currents such as TENS and Interferential Current are recommended in the modality selection guide mainly for which pain types?

options: Pain neurophysiology education correcting threat beliefs
Providing detailed anatomical explanation of neck structures
Reassuring the patient to avoid all painful movements
Prescribing stronger analgesic medication before exercise
Advising complete rest until pain fully resolves
questions.question: A physiotherapist is explaining pain neurophysiology to a patient with chronic neck pain who believes further damage is occurring when they exercise. Which educational approach is most evidence-based for reducing this pain catastrophising?
questions.explanation: Pain Neurophysiology Education (PNE) — also called Explain Pain — directly targets the patient's conceptual model of pain, shifting it from a structural damage model to an understanding of nervous system sensitisation. Evidence shows PNE reduces pain catastrophising, fear of movement (kinesiophobia), disability, and pain intensity. Simply reassuring the patient to avoid pain or prescribing stronger medication reinforces the threat model and increases long-term disability. PNE combined with graded exposure exercise is the evidence-based approach for chronic pain rehabilitation.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT part of the multidimensional approach to pain assessment?
options: Severity or intensity of the pain
Quality and contributing or alleviating factors
Location, distribution or mechanism of injury
questions.explanation: The multidimensional approach to pain assessment includes chronicity, severity or intensity, quality, contributing or aggravating/alleviating factors, location or distribution, and mechanism of injury. These dimensions together provide a comprehensive picture beyond a single pain rating number. Income level is not a recognised dimension of this multidimensional pain assessment framework.

options: Motivational interviewing to explore ambivalence to change
Behavioural activation to increase pleasant activities
Activity scheduling to promote exercise adherence
Relaxation training for autonomic arousal reduction
Cognitive restructuring of pain-threat appraisal thoughts
questions.explanation: Pain catastrophising involves specific cognitive distortions: magnification of pain threat, rumination on pain, and helplessness about coping. Cognitive restructuring is the specific behaviour change technique that directly targets these cognitive distortions by helping patients identify, challenge, and modify the automatic catastrophic appraisals they make about pain. In physiotherapy, this may be partially addressed through Pain Neurophysiology Education (challenging the structural damage belief) and collaborative pain reappraisal. More intensive cognitive work is delivered by psychologists within multidisciplinary programmes. However, physiotherapists skilled in cognitive behavioural approaches can apply Socratic questioning and evidence-based restructuring within their scope.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is designing a rehabilitation programme for a patient with chronic pain who has high levels of pain catastrophising. Which behaviour change technique is most directly targeted at reducing catastrophising?

options: Dismissing the patient's pain as not having a physical basis
Justifying avoidance of further imaging investigations
Convincing the patient that their MRI is normal
Encouraging the patient to self-manage without physiotherapy
Reducing structural threat beliefs driving pain and avoidance
questions.explanation: Showing patients research demonstrating a high prevalence of structural findings (disc bulges, degeneration, meniscal tears) in completely asymptomatic individuals directly challenges the structural threat model — the belief that the radiological finding is causing pain and is dangerous. This evidence-based strategy reduces the catastrophic appraisal of the structural finding, reducing fear and avoidance behaviours associated with movement. The goal is not to deny the physical finding but to recontextualise its significance within a more accurate neurophysiological model where structure does not equal pain, and pain does not equal damage.
questions.question: A physiotherapist uses therapeutic neuroscience education (TNE) with a patient who attributes all their pain to a disc bulge seen on MRI. The therapist shows the patient research demonstrating disc bulges in asymptomatic individuals. What is the primary clinical purpose of this evidence presentation?

questions.explanation: For acute on chronic bone pain, additional medications recommended are strong opioids and NSAIMs, beyond the standard WHO Ladder steps. For acute or chronic neuropathic pain, tricyclic antidepressants or anticonvulsants are instead recommended as additional medications. The distractors mismatch the additional medications with the wrong pain presentation.
questions.question: For acute on chronic bone pain in cancer patients, additional medications recommended alongside the WHO Ladder steps include:

options: Abbey Pain Scale for behavioural pain indicators
Visual Analogue Scale with large print format
McGill Pain Questionnaire short form verbally administered
Numeric Pain Rating Scale adapted with visual cues
Brief Pain Inventory for comprehensive pain characterisation
questions.explanation: The Abbey Pain Scale was specifically designed and validated for assessing pain in patients with dementia who are non-verbal or have severe cognitive impairment. It assesses six behavioural indicators: vocalisation (whimpering, crying), facial expression (grimacing, looking frightened), change in body language (fidgeting, rocking), behavioural change (increased confusion), physiological change (pallor, diaphoresis), and physical changes (skin tears, pressure areas). This behavioural observation tool provides reliable pain assessment when self-report is not possible. NRS, VAS, and MPQ all require verbal or motor self-report, making them inappropriate for non-verbal dementia patients.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is performing a pain assessment on a non-verbal patient with dementia. Which validated assessment tool is most appropriate for this population?

options: Primary somatosensory cortex projecting to dorsal horn
Reticular formation projecting to peripheral nerves
Thalamic relay nuclei projecting to spinal cord
Amygdala projecting directly to nociceptors peripherally
Periaqueductal grey matter projecting to the dorsal horn
