questions.explanation: The spinomesencephalic tract carries nociceptive information to the midbrain, including the superior colliculus and periaqueductal grey, involved in turning the eyes and head toward noxious input. It also activates descending tracts that help control pain, distinguishing it from the other three ascending pain pathways. The distractors describe the discriminative, arousal, or emotional functions of the other named pathways instead.
questions.question: Turning the eyes and head toward the source of a noxious stimulus is a function most associated with the:

options: It opens the gate, enhancing pain perception
It closes the gate, diminishing pain perception
It opens the gate, but only for somatic pain
It closes the gate, but only for visceral pain
It has no measurable effect on the gate mechanism
questions.explanation: Stimulation of small fibre input inhibits the substantia gelatinosa cells, opening the gate, which enhances transmission of impulses and pain perception. This is the opposite effect to stimulation of larger Aa and Aß fibres, which closes the gate and diminishes pain. The distractors reverse this relationship or wrongly restrict the effect to a single pain type.
questions.question: Stimulation of small fibre input (C fibres), in contrast to large fibre input, has which effect on the pain gate?

options: A purely physical injury with no emotional dimension
A reaction that always resolves within a fixed short time
A behaviour exhibited only by professional caregivers
The natural reactions following the death of someone close
An entirely abnormal psychiatric reaction requiring treatment
questions.explanation: Grief is the name given to the natural reactions experienced after the death of someone who has been close, similar to the recovery process after physical injury. This recovery and healing process cannot be rushed and varies from individual to individual. The distractors wrongly pathologise grief, deny its emotional nature, fix its duration, or misattribute it to caregivers only.
questions.question: Grief is best described as:

questions.explanation: Serotonin and norepinephrine are the main neurotransmitters of the descending pathway, which can be modulated pharmacologically (e.g. by antidepressants) and physiotherapeutically. This explains the rationale for using both medications and physical modalities together in comprehensive pain management. Glutamate, substance P, bradykinin, histamine and prostaglandin are excitatory or peripheral mediators, not the descending pathway's main neurotransmitters.
questions.question: The main neurotransmitters of the descending analgesic pathway, which can be modulated both pharmacologically and physiotherapeutically, are:

options: Increased lumbar extension and upright posture
Lateral trunk lean toward the symptomatic side
Increased walking speed to reduce claudication time
Walking with forward trunk lean or using a shopping trolley
questions.explanation: Neurogenic claudication in lumbar spinal stenosis is relieved by lumbar flexion, which enlarges the spinal canal and reduces neural compression. Walking with a forward trunk lean (flexed lumbar spine) or using a shopping trolley (which encourages lumbar flexion through forward lean) provides immediate symptomatic relief by maintaining the canal in a more open position. Extension (standing upright or leaning back) narrows the canal and worsens symptoms. This position-dependent pattern distinguishes neurogenic claudication from vascular claudication and guides both physiotherapy and activity modification advice.
questions.question: A patient with lumbar spinal stenosis reports pain and heaviness in both legs after walking 200 metres, relieved by sitting or leaning forward. A physiotherapist suspects neurogenic claudication. Which gait position modification is most likely to provide immediate relief during walking?

questions.explanation: For acute or chronic neuropathic pain, tricyclic antidepressants or anticonvulsants are recommended as additional medications alongside the standard WHO Ladder steps. This differs from acute on chronic bone pain, for which strong opioids and NSAIMs are instead recommended. The distractors mismatch the additional medications with the wrong pain presentation.
questions.question: For acute or chronic neuropathic pain occurring in cancer patients, additional medications recommended alongside the WHO Ladder include:

questions.explanation: Progressive resistance training combined with balance training has the strongest evidence in osteoporosis management, addressing both pain and fracture prevention through multiple mechanisms: resistance training stimulates osteogenic loading and improves bone mineral density; balance training reduces fall risk (the proximate cause of most osteoporotic fractures); and improved paraspinal muscle strength provides vertebral protection. Spinal flexion exercises are relatively contraindicated in vertebral osteoporosis as they increase compressive forces on the anterior vertebral body. High-impact exercises risk fracture in established osteoporosis. Aquatic exercise is beneficial for pain but provides minimal osteogenic stimulus.
options: Aquatic exercise in warm pool for joint offloading
Progressive resistance and balance training programme
Spinal flexion exercises for paraspinal strengthening
High-impact aerobics for bone density stimulation
Passive stretching for flexibility and pain relief
questions.question: A physiotherapist is reviewing evidence on pain management for a patient with osteoporotic vertebral fracture. Which exercise type has the strongest evidence for managing pain and preventing further fractures in osteoporosis?

options: Sudden traumatic injury to the vertebrae
Direct bacterial infection of the spine
questions.explanation: Pregnancy contributes to low back pain mainly through increased load on the spine and altered posture as the pregnancy progresses. This mechanical and postural change distinguishes pregnancy-related back pain from infective, traumatic, or genetic causes. The distractors describe causes unrelated to the load and posture changes specifically attributed to pregnancy in this context.
questions.question: Pregnancy is listed as a risk factor for low back pain mainly due to:

options: A gradual onset unrelated to any stimulus
An abrupt onset with a foreseeable end
A fleeting sensation from everyday minor cuts
A vague onset persisting beyond tissue healing
An onset with no identifiable precipitating cause
questions.question: Acute pain, as distinguished from transient pain, is best characterised by:
questions.explanation: Acute pain begins abruptly and has a foreseeable end, representing the body's natural response to an adverse chemical, thermal or mechanical stimulus. This differs from transient pain, which is more fleeting and minor, and from chronic pain, which persists beyond expected healing. The distractors describe transient or chronic pain features rather than the defining abruptness and foreseeable resolution of acute pain.

options: A descending pathway of noradrenergic and serotonergic fibres
Descending fibres themselves activated by opioid peptides
Reflex stimulation of sympathetic neurones in the anterior horn
Direct activation of motor neurones in the anterior horn for voluntary movement
Local interneurones releasing opioid peptides such as enkephalin
questions.question: Pain physiology in the cord involves three principal pathways at the first synapse. Which of these is NOT one of them?
questions.explanation: At the first synapse in the cord, modulation occurs through local opioid-releasing interneurones, a descending noradrenergic/serotonergic pathway, and descending fibres activated by opioid peptides, alongside a separate sympathetic reflex pathway. Voluntary movement via direct motor neurone activation is not part of the described pain modulation pathways at this synapse. The correct answer therefore describes a motor function unrelated to the recognised pain modulation mechanisms in the cord.

questions.question: The lumbar spine, consisting of 5 vertebrae, is significant in low back pain mainly because it:
questions.explanation: The lumbar spine, with 5 vertebrae, bears most of the body's weight and is a common site for low back pain. This weight-bearing role distinguishes it from the cervical spine's head support function and the thoracic spine's rib-anchoring role. The distractors describe functions of other spinal regions rather than the lumbar spine's primary weight-bearing role.
options: Bears most of the body's weight
Anchors the ribs to the upper body
Supports the head's wide range of motion
Forms the back of the pelvis only
Serves only as a tailbone ligament attachment

questions.question: Paracetamol and opioids are noted to act primarily at which site of pain medication action?
questions.explanation: Paracetamol, opioids and tramadol are noted to work primarily at the brain as their site of action. This differs from local anaesthetics and NSAIMs, which act primarily at the periphery, or amitriptyline and clonidine, acting on descending pathways. The distractors describe other sites of action that are not the primary site listed for paracetamol and opioids.
options: The periphery, at the site of injury only

questions.question: Low back pain lasting less than six weeks is classified as:
questions.explanation: Low back pain is classified as acute when it lasts less than six weeks, according to the back hygiene material. Subacute low back pain lasts from six weeks to three months, and chronic low back pain persists beyond three months. The distractors use classification terms that correspond to longer durations or are not part of this specific three-tier classification.

The cognitive-evaluative aspect of the pain matrix refers to the meaning ascribed to pain, such as viewing it as punishment, an unfair burden, or a sign of life-threatening illness. Focusing exclusively on and worrying about pain within this dimension can increase distress and amplify the overall pain experience. The discriminative and motivational-affective dimensions instead concern spatial localisation and emotional arousal respectively, not interpreted meaning.
options: The reflexive dimension for autonomic responses
The peripheral transduction dimension for nociceptors
The discriminative dimension for tissue localisation
questions.question: The meaning a patient ascribes to their pain, such as viewing it as punishment or a sign of serious illness, reflects which dimension of the pain matrix?
Ketamine and clonidine are grouped together under which drug category in pain management?
questions.explanation: Ketamine and clonidine are grouped under the 'Others' category, distinct from the simple analgesics, opioids, TCAs, anticonvulsants and local anaesthetics already classified. Ketamine blocks NMDA receptors while clonidine increases descending inhibitory signals, giving each a unique mechanism within this miscellaneous category. The distractors place these drugs into categories that do not match their actual classification as 'Others'.

questions.question: During pain assessment, a physiotherapist distinguishes between primary and secondary hyperalgesia. Which statement correctly characterises the mechanism of secondary hyperalgesia?
questions.explanation: Primary hyperalgesia occurs at the site of tissue injury and results from peripheral sensitisation — inflammatory mediators (bradykinin, prostaglandins, substance P) lowering the activation threshold of peripheral nociceptors at the injury site. Secondary hyperalgesia occurs in areas surrounding but separate from the injury site, and results from central sensitisation in the dorsal horn — increased excitability of spinal nociceptive neurons that respond to a broader receptive field. Secondary hyperalgesia is therefore a central phenomenon, extending beyond the peripheral injury, and its presence indicates significant central sensitisation requiring centrally-directed management strategies.
options: Increased sensitivity beyond the injury site from central sensitisation
Increased sensitivity at the injury site from peripheral sensitisation
Reduced sensitivity away from injury from gate control mechanisms
Increased sensitivity from peripheral prostaglandin accumulation
Reduced pain threshold at the injury site from C-fibre wind-up
Absence of pain to normally painful stimuli
Pain perceived distant from its actual origin
Pain from a stimulus that is not normally painful
Excessive pain response to a painful stimulus
Delayed pain response after initial nerve injury
questions.explanation: Allodynia is defined as pain elicited by a stimulus that does not normally produce pain — for example, light touch, clothing contact, or gentle temperature changes causing severe pain. It reflects central sensitisation in the dorsal horn, where nociceptive threshold is dramatically lowered and non-nociceptive inputs gain access to pain-processing circuits. This must be distinguished from hyperalgesia (exaggerated response to a normally painful stimulus), which has different clinical implications for CRPS management.
questions.question: A 45-year-old patient with complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS) reports allodynia in the affected limb. How should the physiotherapist define allodynia?

options: Experiencing sudden, unexpected loss with no warning
Recovering fully from an unrelated personal injury
Celebrating a loved one's full recovery from illness
Witnessing a stranger's unrelated bereavement experience
Observing a loved one die slowly from a terminal illness
questions.question: Anticipatory grief is best described as grief experienced by someone who is:
questions.explanation: Anticipatory grief is usually experienced by someone observing a loved one die slowly from a terminal illness or unexpected injury. During this period, some people prematurely separate and withdraw from their dying loved one. The distractors describe sudden loss, recovery, or unrelated experiences that do not match the anticipatory nature described.

Step 1 of the WHO Ladder, for mild pain, recommends use of simple analgesics as the initial treatment. If pain progresses to moderate, codeine or tramadol are added at Step 2, and a strong opioid is added at Step 3 for severe pain. The distractors list medications introduced at later steps of the ladder, not the appropriate starting point for mild pain.
questions.question: A patient with mild cancer pain who is started on Step 1 of the WHO Ladder should receive:
options: A mild opioid such as codeine or tramadol
A strong opioid such as morphine

questions.explanation: Maladaptive structural beliefs (spine is 'crumbling', 'out of place', 'fragile') are common drivers of fear-avoidance and catastrophising in low back pain. Pain neurophysiology education directly addresses these beliefs by providing accurate, evidence-based information about spinal structures (which are very strong and resilient), the normal prevalence of degenerative findings in asymptomatic people, and the neurophysiological rather than structural basis of chronic pain. Prescribing a lumbar support or referring for imaging validates and reinforces the structural threat belief, worsening outcomes. Education correcting inaccurate beliefs is the evidence-based approach.
questions.question: A physiotherapist identifies that a patient with persistent low back pain has a strong belief that their spine is 'crumbling' and 'fragile'. Which intervention most directly addresses this maladaptive structural belief?
options: Immediate imaging to confirm or deny the belief
Pain neurophysiology education with accurate anatomical context
Avoiding all discussion of spinal anatomy with the patient
Referral to orthopaedic specialist for structural assessment
Prescribing a lumbar support to validate the structural concern

questions.explanation: Level II dorsal horn antinociception via the counterirritant effect is achieved using high-frequency, low-intensity TENS, alongside superficial heat. This contrasts with the low-frequency, high-intensity stimulation used to engage C fibres and the hormonal Level IV mechanism for more lasting effects. The other parameter combinations do not match the specific counterirritant mechanism described for Level II.
options: Low frequency with low intensity stimulation only
Variable frequency with no set intensity
High frequency with low intensity stimulation
Low frequency with high intensity stimulation
High frequency with high intensity stimulation only
questions.question: A patient receives a TENS treatment intended to activate Level II dorsal horn mechanisms via a counterirritant effect. Which parameter combination is most appropriate?
Which of the following is listed among the feelings associated with bereavement and grief?
questions.explanation: Feelings associated with bereavement and grief listed include numbness, loneliness, sadness, guilt, shock, anxiety, depression, anger and agitation. These feelings reflect the broad emotional impact of loss across multiple dimensions of a person's wellbeing. The distractors list positive or neutral emotional states that are not among the recognised grief-associated feelings.

Musculoskeletal chest wall pain from CPR-related rib fractures or costochondral injuries is distinguished from cardiac chest pain by its mechanical characteristics: reproduction by palpation of specific chest wall sites, reproduction by resisted movements (isometric chest compression, rotation), modification with respiratory position, and localised tenderness. Cardiac pain is typically constant or exertional, not reproducible by palpation or movement. However, three days post-MI, the physiotherapist must exercise extreme caution — any cardiac-pattern features (rest pain, radiation, diaphoresis, haemodynamic changes) require immediate medical reassessment before proceeding with musculoskeletal assessment or treatment.
options: High-dose analgesic trial to determine pain source
Mechanical testing reproducing pain with palpation and movement
Musculoskeletal pain is always present with bone tenderness
Cardiac pain always radiates to the left arm and jaw
NRS score above 7/10 indicates cardiac rather than musculoskeletal
questions.question: A physiotherapist is treating a patient at three days post-acute myocardial infarction who is also experiencing chest wall musculoskeletal pain from resuscitation. Which pain assessment approach is most appropriate to differentiate musculoskeletal from cardiac chest pain?
Placebo antinociception is notable because it activates:
questions.explanation: Placebo antinociception activates the same higher-order cognitive and brainstem regions that are activated by opiate drugs, occurring at the cortical Level V. This demonstrates that expectation and belief can engage genuine physiological antinociceptive pathways, not merely a psychological illusion. The distractors wrongly restrict the effect to peripheral, spinal, unrelated, or purely autonomic mechanisms.
options: Only the spinal dorsal horn interneurons exclusively
A completely separate pathway unrelated to opioids
Only the autonomic nervous system reflex arcs
The same brainstem and cognitive regions activated by opiate drugs
Only peripheral nociceptors directly at the injury site
The primary weight-bearing structure of the spine
The structure anchoring the ribs to the spine
The structure supporting head movement directly
The structure forming the main pelvic weight transfer point
A remnant of the tailbone providing ligament and muscle attachment
questions.explanation: The coccyx, formed of 4 fused vertebrae, is a remnant of the tailbone, providing attachments for ligaments and muscles. This is distinct from the sacrum's role in pelvic formation and weight transfer, and from the lumbar spine's primary weight-bearing function. The distractors describe functions of other spinal regions rather than the coccyx's ligament-attachment role.
questions.question: The coccyx, consisting of 4 fused vertebrae, is best described as functioning mainly as:

questions.explanation: Level III is the fast-acting neuronal descending system, involving the periaqueductal grey (PAG), rostral ventromedial medulla, and locus coeruleus. This differs from Level IV, the hormonal system, which involves the periventricular grey and the pituitary gland. The substantia gelatinosa and postcentral gyrus are structures relevant to other levels of pain processing, not this fast descending system.
questions.question: Level III antinociception, the fast-acting neuronal descending system, involves the PAG, rostral ventromedial medulla and:

questions.explanation: Melzack's neuromatrix theory expanded beyond gate control by proposing that pain is an active output of the brain's widely distributed neurosignature (neuromatrix) — not simply a passive response to incoming signals. The neuromatrix integrates nociceptive input with somatosensory memory, emotional state, cognitive appraisal, past experience, immune function, and endocrine signals to construct the pain experience. This multidimensional model explains phantom limb pain (pain without peripheral input), central sensitisation, and why the same nociceptive input produces different pain experiences in different individuals — none of which gate control theory (focused on spinal gating) adequately explained.
options: Pain as an output of the brain influenced by multiple inputs
The role of A-delta fibres in rapid pain transmission
Peripheral sensitisation at the level of nociceptors
Spinal gating mechanism in the substantia gelatinosa
The role of prostaglandins in peripheral inflammation
questions.question: A physiotherapist reviews the neuromatrix theory of pain proposed by Melzack. Which key concept of the neuromatrix theory most expanded on the original gate control theory?

questions.explanation: Poor healthcare refers to multiple and conflicting diagnoses that are thought to contribute to the maintenance of persistent pain. This mechanism is system-related, unlike sensitivity, memory, representation and emotion, which are patient-centred neurological or psychological mechanisms. Distinguishing this external contributor from the internal mechanisms is important for comprehensive chronic pain management.
options: Representation on the cortical body map
Emotion affecting mood and activity level
questions.question: Multiple and conflicting diagnoses contributing to the maintenance of persistent pain best illustrates which mechanism?
Carbamazepine, sodium valproate, gabapentin and pregabalin are classified as:
questions.explanation: Carbamazepine, sodium valproate, gabapentin and pregabalin are classified as anticonvulsants used in pain control, particularly for neuropathic pain. They are described as 'membrane stabilisers' that probably work by reducing abnormal firing of pain nerves. The distractors place these drugs into incorrect categories that do not match their anticonvulsant classification.

options: Monofilament testing for touch threshold assessment
Pinprick testing for sharp pain threshold
Vibration testing with tuning fork only
Quantitative sensory testing with thermomode device
questions.question: A physiotherapist assesses cold allodynia and cold hyperalgesia in a patient with neuropathic pain. Which sensory testing modality should be used for formal quantitative assessment?
questions.explanation: Quantitative Sensory Testing (QST) using a calibrated thermomode device applies precisely controlled temperature stimuli to assess cold detection, warmth detection, cold pain threshold, and heat pain threshold. This allows systematic quantification of thermal sensory loss and gain (allodynia, hyperalgesia) across the sensory profile. QST is the gold standard for characterising neuropathic pain sensory phenotypes, enabling mechanism-based treatment selection and research stratification. Monofilament and pinprick testing assess touch and sharp pain but cannot characterise the thermal sensory dysfunction characteristic of cold-related neuropathic symptoms.

questions.question: Amitriptyline and nortriptyline belong to which drug class used in pain control?
questions.explanation: Amitriptyline and nortriptyline are tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs), used particularly for neuropathic and chronic pain management. TCAs work mainly by increasing descending inhibitory signals in the spinal cord rather than acting directly on opioid receptors. The distractors place these drugs in incorrect categories that do not match their classification as TCAs.

questions.question: Clonidine's mechanism of analgesic action is best described as:
questions.explanation: Clonidine increases descending inhibitory signals in the spinal cord, similar in general effect to amitriptyline and tramadol but via a different receptor mechanism. This differentiates it from ketamine, which instead blocks NMDA receptors, and from NSAIMs, which act peripherally on prostaglandins. The distractors attribute mechanisms belonging to other drug classes to clonidine incorrectly.
options: Acting strongly on opioid receptors in the brain
Providing complete local nerve blockade at the injury site
Increasing descending inhibitory signals in the spinal cord
Blocking NMDA receptors in the dorsal horn
Changing prostaglandin levels in the periphery

questions.question: A major limitation shared by the visual analogue scale, numerical scale and verbal rating scale is that they:
questions.explanation: The limitation shared by these psychometrically sound scales is that they measure only one quality of pain, which is its intensity. This means they do not capture quality, location, or psychosocial dimensions of the pain experience. The distractors describe limitations not attributed to these scales in the source material, such as cost, exclusivity, or condition restriction.
options: Measure only one quality of pain, namely intensity
Cannot be used in any chronic pain condition
Require expensive specialised equipment to administer
Can only be completed by a trained physician
Are valid only for cancer-related pain assessment

questions.question: Prolonged or massive input from a C fibre producing a progressive build-up of excitability in the dorsal horn is termed:
questions.explanation: Wind-up describes the progressive build-up of dorsal horn excitability following massive or prolonged C fibre input, similar to tetanus in muscle. It can progress toward central sensitisation, but the two terms describe related yet distinct stages of the process. Hyperalgesia, allodynia and transduction are consequences or earlier steps rather than the build-up phenomenon itself.
options: Transduction of mechanical stimuli into impulses
Central sensitisation from NMDA receptor activation

questions.explanation: Allodynia is pain evoked by stimuli that are not normally painful, such as light touch on sunburnt skin. This differs from hyperalgesia, an increased response to a stimulus that is already painful. The other distractors describe analgesia, hypoalgesia and hypoesthesia respectively, which are distinct pain terms.
questions.question: Allodynia is most accurately described as:
options: A diminished response to a normally painful stimulus
A complete loss of sensation excluding special senses
Pain evoked by a stimulus that is not normally painful
An absence of pain to a normally painful stimulus
An exaggerated response to a normally painful stimulus

questions.explanation: To be bereaved usually means to lose someone loved through death, resulting in great longing and a period of adjustment that may take years. All parts of being may be affected, including emotional, physical, spiritual and social dimensions, with intense pain or grief as the overriding feeling. The distractors understate the duration, wrongly medicalise it, or restrict it inappropriately to a single population.
options: An exclusively physical reaction without emotional component
A condition limited strictly to elderly patients
The loss of someone loved through death, with a period of adjustment
A brief instance of sadness lasting only a few hours
A medical diagnosis requiring pharmacological treatment
questions.question: Bereavement is best defined as:

questions.explanation: McCaffery and Pasero (1999) describe four basic processes of nociception occurring in the order: transduction, transmission, modulation, and perception. Transduction converts noxious stimuli into electrical signals, transmission carries them centrally, modulation alters the signal, and perception creates conscious awareness. The distractors rearrange this sequence incorrectly, which would misrepresent the physiological order of events.
questions.question: According to McCaffery and Pasero (1999), the four basic processes involved in nociception, in correct order, are:

options: Hyperalgesia limited to the original injury site
Paradoxical worsening of pain with opioid dose increases
Improved pain control with increasing opioid doses
Pain specifically relieved by opioid rotation to methadone
Tolerance developing to opioid analgesic effects
questions.question: A physiotherapist works with a patient who has opioid-induced hyperalgesia (OIH). Which clinical feature most distinguishes OIH from inadequately treated pain?
questions.explanation: Opioid-induced hyperalgesia is paradoxically characterised by increased pain sensitivity (hyperalgesia and allodynia) that worsens with increasing opioid doses, rather than improving. This contrasts with simple tolerance (reduced analgesic effect at same dose without hyperalgesia) and inadequately treated pain (which responds to dose increases). OIH results from central sensitisation driven by opioid-induced activation of pronociceptive systems (NMDA receptor activation, dynorphin release). Recognition is critical because the appropriate management is opioid tapering, not dose escalation, combined with non-opioid pain strategies.

A herniated disc is described as a bulging or ruptured disc pressing on spinal nerves, a distinct structural cause of low back pain. This differs from degenerative disc disease, which is wear and tear of spinal discs with aging, and from osteoporosis or osteoarthritis. The distractors describe other structural or soft tissue causes rather than the specific bulging/rupture described for a herniated disc.
questions.question: A bulging or ruptured disc pressing on spinal nerves is best described as:
In the stepwise physiotherapy management of pain, Step 2 involves analysis of underlying factors such as inflammation, muscle spasm and:
options: History of previous surgical procedures only
Family history of unrelated chronic disease
Soft tissue tightness and slight mal-alignment
Patient's annual income and occupation only
questions.explanation: Step 2 analyses underlying factors and presenting symptoms including inflammation, muscle spasm, soft tissue tightness, slight mal-alignment, and loss of range of motion and function. This step bridges identification of pain type (Step 1) with selection of an appropriate modality (Step 3). The distractors list factors unrelated to the physical underlying factors specified in this assessment step.

questions.question: A physiotherapist uses the Patient-Specific Functional Scale (PSFS) to monitor progress in a patient with chronic shoulder pain. The patient rates three activities: 0, 2, and 4 out of 10 at baseline. What does the PSFS specifically measure that the NRS alone cannot?
options: Overall tissue healing and structural recovery
questions.explanation: The Patient-Specific Functional Scale uniquely captures the patient's own identified functional activity limitations — the activities that matter most to that individual — rather than therapist-selected impairment measures. The patient nominates 3–5 activities they cannot perform or have difficulty with, and rates each from 0 (unable to perform) to 10 (able to perform at pre-injury level). This patient-centred approach is more sensitive to meaningful functional change than generic measures, and the activities selected reflect the patient's individual goals, improving therapeutic engagement and goal-oriented rehabilitation planning.

questions.question: A physiotherapist observes a patient guarding their lumbar spine, wincing, and dramatically limping during a pain assessment. Which assessment tool specifically quantifies these observable pain behaviours?
questions.explanation: The Photograph Series of Daily Activities (PHODA) and the Modified Pain Behaviour Assessment tools specifically capture observable pain behaviours — physical signs such as guarding, bracing, rubbing, facial grimacing, and sighing — which are distinct from self-reported pain intensity or quality. Observable pain behaviours can be reinforced operantly by environmental responses and may not correlate with subjective pain intensity. Systematic assessment of pain behaviours guides understanding of operant factors in chronic pain and informs behavioural modification strategies in rehabilitation.
options: Numerical Rating Scale for pain intensity
Modified PHODA for observed pain behaviours
McGill Pain Questionnaire for pain quality

questions.explanation: Nociceptive pain is proportionate to tissue loading, position, and movement — it is provoked by activity or postures that mechanically stress the involved tissue and relieved by unloading or optimal positioning. This proportionate mechanical relationship with tissue behaviour distinguishes nociceptive pain from neuropathic pain (burning, shooting, electrical quality; positive neurodynamic tests; allodynia at distant sites) and nociplastic pain (disproportionate, multisystem). Accurate pain classification guides mechanism-specific treatment selection.
options: Pain proportionate to tissue loading and position
Allodynia and hyperalgesia at distant sites
Spontaneous pain at rest without provocation
questions.question: A physiotherapist documents a patient's pain as nociceptive rather than neuropathic. Which feature most supports a nociceptive classification?
Hyperalgesia refers to:
questions.explanation: Hyperalgesia is an increased response to a stimulus that is normally painful, producing an exaggerated pain reaction. This is distinguished from allodynia, where a non-painful stimulus becomes painful, and from analgesia or hypoalgesia, which describe reduced pain. The distractors describe these other related but distinct pain terms.
options: An increased response to a normally painful stimulus
Pain produced by a stimulus that is not normally painful
An absence of pain to a stimulus that should hurt
A reduced sensitivity to touch excluding special senses
A diminished pain response to a normally painful stimulus

questions.question: A physiotherapist observes that a patient's pain flares are consistently preceded by psychosocial stress at work. Which pain science concept explains this observation?
questions.explanation: Allostatic load — the cumulative neurobiological burden of chronic stress — drives stress-induced hyperalgesia through sustained activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis and sympathetic nervous system. Chronic stress elevates cortisol (initially analgesic but eventually pronociceptive), activates spinal microglia, and reduces activity in descending inhibitory pathways, lowering the pain threshold. Work-related psychosocial stress systematically triggers neurobiological changes that amplify nociceptive processing, explaining the consistent relationship between work stress and pain flares. This finding implicates occupational stress management as a necessary component of the rehabilitation plan.
options: Nocebo effect from negative treatment expectations
Secondary gain maintaining pain behaviour patterns
Somatisation of psychological distress into physical symptoms
Gate control mechanism activated by emotional arousal

questions.explanation: Neuritis is inflammation of a nerve or nerves, an underlying pathological process rather than the symptom of pain itself. Neuralgia, by contrast, describes pain in the distribution of a nerve, which may or may not involve inflammation. The distractors describe pain, threshold change or sensory loss rather than the inflammatory process defining neuritis.
options: Pain felt along the course of a nerve
Increased threshold for pain within a nerve territory
Abnormal spontaneous sensation arising from a nerve
Loss of touch sensation along a nerve pathway
Inflammation of a nerve or nerves
questions.question: Neuritis differs from neuralgia in that neuritis specifically denotes:

A physiotherapist treats a patient with post-surgical persistent pain three months following lumbar fusion. Which factor most specifically distinguishes persistent post-surgical pain (PPSP) from expected post-operative pain?
options: Presence of scar tissue at the surgical site
Pain intensity above 5/10 on a numerical scale
Pain beyond expected healing time in the surgical area
Requirement for opioid analgesics at three months
Radiological evidence of adjacent segment disease
questions.explanation: Persistent Post-Surgical Pain (PPSP) is defined by the IASP as pain developing after a surgical procedure, lasting beyond the normal healing period (typically three months), located in the surgical area or projected to the innervation territory of a nerve in the area, excluding other causes. The key distinguishing feature is pain persisting beyond the expected healing time in the anatomical region of surgery. PPSP has significant central sensitisation, psychological, and neuroplastic components beyond any residual tissue pathology. Identifying PPSP as distinct from expected recovery guides treatment toward central sensitisation management rather than tissue-directed interventions.

questions.question: External nociceptors, as opposed to internal ones, are found mainly in which tissues?
options: Lymph nodes, spleen and bone marrow
Muscles, joints and the digestive tract
questions.explanation: External nociceptors are located in tissues exposed to the external environment such as the skin, corneas, and mucosa. Internal nociceptors, by contrast, are found in organs such as muscles, joints, the bladder and the gut. The distractors list internal organ sites or unrelated tissues, not the external locations described for external nociceptors.

options: Cases managed successfully with physical therapy alone
Structural issues unresponsive to conservative management
Any first presentation of mild low back pain
Routine cases of postural muscle strain only
All cases regardless of symptom severity
questions.question: Surgical options for low back pain are reserved specifically for cases involving:
questions.explanation: Surgical options are reserved for cases with structural issues, such as a herniated disc or spinal stenosis, that do not respond to conservative management. This positions surgery as a later-line treatment after rest, physical therapy, medication, injections, or chiropractic care have been tried. The distractors wrongly suggest surgery is a first-line or routine option for mild or successfully managed cases.

options: A greater sense of loss at the time of death
A lesser sense of loss at the time of death
No measurable difference in the grief experience
Complete avoidance of any grieving process
An immediate resolution of all grief symptoms
questions.question: Maintaining a strong sense of closeness to a dying loved one throughout the anticipatory grief period tends to result in:
questions.explanation: At other times, a person feels a strong sense of closeness to the loved one during the anticipatory grief period, leading to a greater sense of loss at the time of death. This contrasts with premature withdrawal, which can instead lessen the eventual impact of the loss. The distractors either reverse this relationship or wrongly claim no effect or complete avoidance of grief.

options: The anterior horn of the spinal cord
questions.question: Perception, the final stage of nociception, occurs primarily in which brain region?
questions.explanation: Perception is the interpretation of sensations into meaningful forms and occurs in the cerebrum, completing the nociceptive process. It is described as an active process involving interaction between the brain and the environment. The cerebellum, medulla, spinal anterior horn and peripheral ganglion are not the principal sites for conscious pain perception.

Psychogenic pain is pain for which there is no known physical cause, but in which disturbed processing of sensory information in the CNS is implicated. This contrasts with somatogenic pain, which has a usually known cause localised within body tissue. Nociceptive, neuropathic and visceral pain are all somatogenic categories with identifiable tissue or nerve origins.
questions.question: Pain for which there is no known physical cause, but disturbed processing of sensory information in the CNS is suspected, is termed:
options: Visceral pain from internal organ disease
Somatogenic pain localised in body tissue
Nociceptive pain from normal receptor activity
Neuropathic pain from a nerve lesion

questions.question: The clinical device whose development was a direct consequence of the Gate Control Theory is the:
questions.explanation: The development of Transcutaneous Electrical Nerve Stimulation (TENS) was the clinical consequence of the gate control phenomenon described by Melzack and Wall. TENS works by stimulating large-diameter afferent fibres to close the gate and reduce pain perception. The other devices, while used in pain or rehabilitation management, are not specifically the clinical outcome of the gate theory.

questions.question: Clinical signs of withdrawal, psychomotor retardation, sleep disturbance and possible suicidal ideation in a dying patient are characteristic of the stage of:
questions.explanation: The depression stage shows clinical signs such as withdrawal, psychomotor retardation, sleep disturbances, hopelessness and possibly suicidal ideation. This may reflect a reaction to the illness's effects on the patient's life or anticipation of approaching death. Denial, anger, bargaining and acceptance are other stages with distinct emotional and behavioural presentations.

questions.question: Physical therapy for low back pain primarily focuses on exercises to strengthen core muscles and improve:
questions.explanation: Physical therapy for low back pain focuses on exercises to strengthen core muscles and improve posture, addressing modifiable mechanical contributors to pain. This functional, exercise-based approach differs from pharmacological, injection-based, chiropractic, or surgical treatment categories. The distractors describe outcomes not specifically targeted by the exercise and posture focus of physical therapy as described.

The vertebral column is described as consisting of 33 vertebrae divided into five regions: cervical, thoracic, lumbar, sacrum and coccyx. This total includes the fused vertebrae of the sacrum and coccyx, not just the individually mobile vertebrae. The distractors use incorrect total vertebral counts that do not match the figure given in the material.
questions.question: How many vertebrae in total make up the human vertebral column according to the back care material?

questions.explanation: Ketamine blocks NMDA receptors in the brain and spinal cord, particularly in the dorsal horn, providing its analgesic effect. This differs from clonidine, which instead increases descending inhibitory signals in the spinal cord. The distractors describe mechanisms attributed to other drugs, such as TCAs, NSAIMs, codeine, or local anaesthetics.
questions.question: Ketamine's analgesic mechanism is primarily described as:
options: Changing prostaglandin levels in the periphery
Acting weakly on opioid receptors in the brain
Temporarily blocking signalling in peripheral pain nerves
Blocking NMDA receptors in the brain and spinal cord
Increasing descending inhibitory signals in the spinal cord

questions.explanation: In the effectiveness table, morphine is rated '-' (not useful, may be harmful) specifically for acute nociceptive mild pain. For acute nociceptive severe pain and chronic cancer pain, morphine is instead rated highly effective (+++). The distractors list pain types for which morphine is actually rated as useful rather than potentially harmful.
questions.question: In the medication effectiveness table, morphine is rated as not useful, and possibly harmful, for which type of pain?
options: Acute on chronic bone pain episodes

questions.question: Which class of drugs includes paracetamol and the non-steroidal anti-inflammatory medicines such as aspirin and ibuprofen?
questions.explanation: Simple analgesics include paracetamol/acetaminophen and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory medicines (NSAIMs) such as aspirin, ibuprofen and diclofenac. This is the first and most basic class in the classification of analgesic drugs used for pain control. Opioids, TCAs, anticonvulsants and local anaesthetics are separate drug classes used for different pain mechanisms.

A biopsychosocial pain assessment must capture biological (pain intensity, location, quality), psychological (catastrophising, anxiety, depression, fear-avoidance, sleep), and social (work factors, social support, relationships, disability) dimensions. The combination of a pain intensity scale (NRS/VAS), disability measure (PSFS, PDQ), psychological screening (PHQ-4, GAD-7), and pain catastrophising (PCS) provides a comprehensive biopsychosocial profile that guides individualised treatment planning across all relevant domains. Imaging and physiological measures provide structural or biological data only and miss the psychological and social drivers of chronic pelvic pain that are often primary drivers of disability and chronicity.
options: Pain intensity, disability, psychological screens, and catastrophising
MRI and ultrasound for structural pathology identification
NRS only for pain intensity measurement
Physiological measures of muscle tension and autonomic function
Patient history and clinical examination only
questions.question: A physiotherapist is using a multidimensional approach to pain assessment with a patient who has chronic pelvic pain. Which combination of assessment tools most comprehensively evaluates the biopsychosocial pain experience for this patient?

questions.explanation: The medication effectiveness table notes that combinations of medications are usually required, with paracetamol plus morphine given as an example for severe acute nociceptive pain. Morphine alone is rated highly effective (+++) for acute nociceptive severe pain, while paracetamol adds further benefit. The distractors combine drugs not specifically highlighted together for this severe acute nociceptive pain scenario.
questions.question: According to the medication effectiveness table, which combination is recommended for severe acute nociceptive pain?

questions.explanation: Contemporary guidelines for exercise in joint pain and tendinopathy allow up to 4–5/10 pain during therapeutic exercise, provided it does not worsen during the session and settles to baseline within 24 hours. This monitoring framework (traffic light approach: green 0–4/10, amber 4–5/10, red >5/10) permits therapeutic loading that drives adaptation without causing prolonged sensitisation. A rating of 4/10 is at the upper acceptable boundary — the appropriate response is to maintain current load for this session and assess the 24-hour response before deciding whether to progress, maintain, or reduce in the next session.
questions.question: A physiotherapist treating a patient with patellofemoral pain syndrome is attempting to load the knee joint progressively. The patient reports 4/10 pain during a step-down exercise. Based on current pain management guidelines for tendinopathy and joint pain, how should the therapist respond?
options: Continue at current load and reassess the following day
Increase load immediately as the patient can clearly tolerate pain
Stop immediately as any pain is contraindicated during exercise
Switch to a completely pain-free alternative exercise
Administer NSAID and ice before continuing the session

questions.question: People over the age of 30 are more likely to experience back pain mainly because:
questions.explanation: Age is a risk factor for back pain because vertebral disks wear away with age, and as they weaken and wear down, pain and stiffness can result. This age-related disk wear is distinct from acute injury or other risk factors such as weight or occupation. The distractors describe physiological changes that do not accurately reflect the age-related disk degeneration described as the underlying mechanism.
options: Vertebral disks wear away with age
Bone density always increases sharply after 30
Muscle mass typically peaks only after age 30
Spinal nerve conduction velocity increases with age
Cartilage regenerates more rapidly after age 30

questions.question: Which behaviour is specifically listed as being associated with bereavement and grief?
questions.explanation: Behaviours associated with bereavement and grief listed include crying, insomnia, restlessness, and withdrawal. These behavioural changes often accompany the emotional feelings of numbness, sadness, guilt and anxiety described alongside grief. The distractors list behaviours that are not identified as associated with the grieving process in this material.

options: Somatic pain from skin and tissue
Transient pain from a minor cut
Acute pain from a surgical incision
questions.explanation: Visceral pain arises from internal organs and is typically diffuse, poorly localised, and often referred to another body region. This contrasts with somatic pain, which is usually well localised because it arises from skin or musculoskeletal tissue. Neuropathic, transient and acute pain are classified by different criteria such as nerve origin or duration, not visceral origin.
questions.question: Pain arising from internal organs that is usually diffuse, poorly localised and often referred is termed:

questions.explanation: Neuralgia refers specifically to pain occurring in the distribution of a nerve or nerves. This is distinct from neuritis, which is inflammation of a nerve, even though both terms relate to nerve pathology. The other distractors describe sensory loss or abnormal sensation rather than the defining pain distribution of neuralgia.
options: Reduced pain threshold within a nerve territory
Pain in the distribution of one or more nerves
Inflammation occurring within one or more nerves
Loss of sensation along a nerve distribution
Abnormal spontaneous sensation along a nerve pathway
questions.question: Neuralgia is best described as:

questions.explanation: Sensitivity refers to changes in nerves carrying pain messages, which can become hyperexcitable so that even light touch is interpreted as pain. This is a peripheral and central nervous system change distinct from memory-based or cortical-mapping mechanisms. The other options describe separate contributing mechanisms to chronic pain rather than nerve hyperexcitability itself.
options: Representation on the cortical body map
questions.question: Nerves becoming hyperexcitable so that even light touch is interpreted as pain reflects which mechanism of chronic pain?

questions.explanation: Factors affecting the intensity and length of grieving include the kind of relationship one had with the deceased, the circumstances of their death, and one's own life experiences. These personal and relational factors explain why grief reactions vary so widely between individuals. The distractors list factors that are not identified as influencing grief intensity or length in this material.
options: The exact time of day the death occurred
The geographic distance from a hospital
The number of years of formal education completed
The kind of relationship one had with the deceased
The blood type of the bereaved individual
questions.question: Which of the following is listed as a factor affecting the intensity and length of grieving?

questions.explanation: Hyperpathia is a painful syndrome characterised by an abnormally painful reaction to a stimulus, especially repetitive stimulation, combined with an increased threshold. It combines features of both a raised threshold and an exaggerated painful response, distinguishing it from simple hyperalgesia or allodynia. The other options describe single, simpler phenomena that do not capture both features together.
questions.question: A clinician notes a patient has an abnormally painful reaction to repetitive stimulation along with a raised threshold. This best describes:
options: Hypoalgesia from a raised pain threshold alone
Hyperalgesia from a single noxious stimulus

questions.question: A physiotherapist applies transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) for acute post-surgical pain. Which neurophysiological mechanism best explains the analgesic effect of conventional high-frequency TENS?
options: Endogenous opioid release from descending inhibition
Large diameter fibre activation closing the spinal gate
Prostaglandin inhibition at the peripheral nociceptor
Direct muscle relaxation reducing local ischaemia
questions.explanation: Conventional (high-frequency, low-intensity) TENS activates large-diameter A-beta sensory fibres, which, according to Melzack and Wall's gate control theory, activate inhibitory interneurons in the substantia gelatinosa of the spinal cord dorsal horn. These interneurons close the gate to incoming nociceptive signals from small-diameter A-delta and C fibres, reducing pain transmission to the brain. This mechanism explains why TENS works quickly — within minutes — without requiring endogenous opioid release.

Paracetamol works mainly by changing prostaglandin levels in the brain, distinguishing its central mechanism from the peripheral action of NSAIMs. NSAIMs instead mainly change prostaglandin levels in the periphery, thereby reducing inflammation at the injury site. The distractors list other substances not described as paracetamol's primary mechanism of action.
questions.question: Paracetamol is described as working mainly by changing which substance's level in the brain?
Weak, brittle bones leading to fractures, as a cause of low back pain, is best described as:
questions.explanation: Osteoporosis is described specifically as weak, brittle bones leading to fractures, a distinct cause of low back pain among those listed. This differs from osteoarthritis, which is breakdown of cartilage in the spine, and from degenerative disc disease, which affects the discs themselves. The distractors describe other structural causes that do not match the bone fragility described for osteoporosis.

questions.question: The three Ds that must be addressed in managing chronic pain are distress, disability and:
questions.explanation: The three Ds of chronic pain that must be addressed are distress, disuse, and disability. These reflect the psychological, physical inactivity, and functional impact dimensions of persistent pain that compound the original nociceptive problem. The distractors substitute terms that are not part of this recognised triad.

questions.question: A patient with shoulder impingement syndrome reports that their pain has gradually shifted from being activity-related only (6 months ago) to now being present at rest and at night. Which pain science concept best explains this temporal evolution?
questions.explanation: The progression from activity-related (nociceptive, mechanical) pain to rest pain and night pain represents a temporal evolution from primarily peripheral nociceptive pain toward central sensitisation. Prolonged, repeated nociceptive input from the shoulder sensitises dorsal horn neurons (central sensitisation), expanding their receptive fields and lowering their thresholds to the point where ongoing afferent input is no longer required to maintain pain — pain becomes self-sustaining centrally. This evolution necessitates a management strategy shift from purely local shoulder treatment to include central sensitisation management: pain education, sleep management, and desensitisation alongside local shoulder rehabilitation.
options: Disease progression causing additional structural damage
Central sensitisation developing from prolonged nociception
Natural history of shoulder impingement worsening inevitably

questions.explanation: The anger stage is marked by frustration and irritability, with the patient commonly asking 'Why me?' and sometimes displacing anger onto hospital staff or doctors. This follows the initial denial stage and precedes bargaining in the Kubler-Ross sequence. Denial, bargaining, depression and acceptance describe different emotional responses occurring at other points in the model.
questions.question: In the Kubler-Ross model, a patient who becomes frustrated and irritable, asking 'Why me?', and may displace blame onto hospital staff, is in the stage of:
In the table of chemicals released by tissue damage, bradykinin is primarily sourced from:
questions.explanation: Bradykinin is sourced from plasma following tissue damage, distinguishing it from potassium and prostaglandins, which originate from damaged cells. Serotonin is sourced from platelets, histamine from mast cells, and substance P from primary nerve afferents, according to the chemical mediator table. The distractors assign bradykinin to the wrong source, mixing up the origins of the various algesic chemicals.

questions.question: In Step 2 of the WHO Ladder for moderate cancer pain, simple analgesics are continued and which medication(s) are added?
questions.explanation: Step 2 of the WHO Ladder, for moderate pain, continues simple analgesics and adds codeine or tramadol as mild opioids. Step 3, for severe pain, then continues simple analgesics and adds a strong opioid, usually morphine. The distractors list strong opioids or other drug classes not specified as the Step 2 addition.

The sacrum, formed of 5 fused vertebrae, forms the back of the pelvis and supports weight transfer to the lower limbs. This differs from the coccyx, a remnant of the tailbone providing ligament and muscle attachment, and from the lumbar spine's direct weight-bearing role. The distractors describe functions of other spinal regions rather than the sacrum's pelvic and weight-transfer role.
questions.question: The sacrum, formed of 5 fused vertebrae, primarily functions to:
options: Anchor the ribs and provide upper body stability
Bear most of the body's weight directly as discs
Provide a remnant tailbone attachment for ligaments
Form the back of the pelvis and support weight transfer to the lower limbs
Support the head and allow a wide range of motion

questions.question: Codeine and tramadol are classified together as:
questions.explanation: Codeine and tramadol are classified as mild opioids, distinguished from strong opioids such as morphine, pethidine and oxycodone. Tramadol is further noted to also act on descending inhibitory pathways, giving it an additional mechanism beyond simple opioid receptor activity. The distractors place these drugs in incorrect categories that do not match their classification as mild opioids.

options: Medium frequency 20 to 40 hertz for 10 minutes
Low frequency 2 to 7 hertz for 20 to 40 minutes
High frequency 80 to 150 hertz for 5 minutes
Low frequency 2 to 7 hertz for 2 to 5 minutes
High frequency 80 to 150 hertz for 60 minutes
questions.explanation: Endorphin release is associated with pulsed rhythmical motor stimulation at a low frequency of 2 to 7 hertz applied for a long duration of 20 to 40 minutes. This parameter combination distinguishes it from the high-frequency, short-duration stimulation typically used for the segmental gate mechanism. The distractors mismatch either the frequency range or duration from the parameters described for endorphin-mediated antinociception.
questions.question: The stimulation characteristics associated with endorphin release via afferent nerve fibres include pulsed rhythmical motor stimulation at a frequency and duration of approximately:

questions.explanation: Distraction reduces pain awareness, while isolation and inactivity increase pain awareness and foster self-preoccupation. This highlights the importance of engaging patients in activity and attention-shifting strategies in chronic pain management. The distractors reverse this relationship or wrongly minimise the established effect of distraction on pain awareness.
options: Distraction has no measurable effect on awareness
Distraction only affects awareness of visceral pain
questions.question: Distraction is reported to have which effect on pain awareness, in contrast to isolation and inactivity?

questions.explanation: By temporal classification, acute pain is defined as pain lasting three months or less, while chronic pain lasts three months or more. This three-month cut-off is the standard boundary used to separate the two temporal categories. The distractors use incorrect durations that do not match this classification.
options: One month or less from onset
Three months or more from onset
Twelve months or less from onset
Six months or less from onset
questions.question: By temporal classification, acute pain is generally defined as pain lasting:

questions.explanation: Referred pain occurs when nociceptive fibres from the skin converge onto the same second-order neurons in the spinal cord or thalamus as visceral afferents. The central neurons become sensitised, so pain originating viscerally is misinterpreted as arising from the corresponding skin area. The distractors propose mechanisms, such as direct cutaneous activation or demyelination, that are not the convergence explanation given.
options: Increased conduction velocity in visceral C fibres
Loss of inhibitory control purely at the cortical level
Convergence of nociceptive afferents onto shared second-order neurons
Direct activation of cutaneous nociceptors at the distant site
Selective demyelination of visceral afferent nerve fibres
questions.question: Referred pain is best explained physiologically by which mechanism?

options: The periphery, at the site of injury
questions.question: NSAIMs and local anaesthetics are noted to act primarily at which site of pain medication action?
questions.explanation: NSAIMs and local anaesthetics are noted to work at the periphery, at the site of injury, as their primary site of action. This contrasts with paracetamol and opioids, which act mainly in the brain, and amitriptyline and clonidine, acting on descending pathways. The distractors describe other sites of action that are not the primary site listed for NSAIMs and local anaesthetics.

options: Because long-term use carries risks that must be weighed against benefit
Because NSAIMs are completely ineffective for this pain type
Because NSAIMs cannot be administered orally at all
Because NSAIMs are classified as strong opioids
Because NSAIMs have no documented side effect profile
questions.question: In chronic non-cancer pain management, why must potential side effects of long-term NSAIM administration be considered?
questions.explanation: It is important to consider the potential side effects of long-term administration of medications such as NSAIMs in chronic non-cancer pain. This reflects the general principle that prolonged use of any medication requires ongoing risk-benefit evaluation, especially in chronic conditions. The distractors misrepresent NSAIMs as ineffective, non-oral, opioid-classified, or free of side effects, none of which is accurate.

questions.question: Wear and tear of spinal discs occurring with the aging process is best described as:
questions.explanation: Degenerative disc disease is described as the wear and tear of spinal discs that occurs with aging, a distinct cause of low back pain. This differs from a herniated disc, which involves bulging or rupture, and from osteoporosis, which involves weak, brittle bones. The distractors describe other distinct causes that do not match the gradual wear-and-tear process of degenerative disc disease.

questions.question: Which of these is listed among the non-electrical modalities used for pain modulation, alongside cryotherapy and thermotherapy?
questions.explanation: Listed modalities for pain modulation include cryotherapy, thermotherapy, electrical stimulation, counter irritants such as analgesic balms, and massage. These are physical and physiotherapeutic interventions rather than pharmacological or surgical treatments. Surgery, opioids, antidepressants and corticosteroid injections are medical or surgical interventions, not the physical modalities being described.

options: Only pain associated with active infection
Only neuropathic pain of central origin
Only labour pain during active delivery
Acute pain, along with certain chronic pain
Only chronic pain with muscle spasm
questions.question: Cold therapy is recommended in the modality guide mainly for pain relief and inflammation control in:
questions.explanation: Cold therapy is recommended for pain relief and inflammation control in acute pain, for reduction of swelling, and in certain chronic pain presentations. This differs from heat therapy, which is instead recommended primarily for chronic pain and relief of muscle spasm. The distractors restrict cold therapy's indication to pain types not specifically listed for this modality.

questions.question: An abnormal sensation, whether spontaneous or evoked, that is not necessarily unpleasant, is termed:
questions.explanation: Paraesthesia is an abnormal sensation, whether spontaneous or evoked, such as tingling, that is not inherently unpleasant or painful. This distinguishes it from allodynia and hyperalgesia, both of which specifically describe abnormal pain responses. Hypoesthesia and neuralgia also describe different phenomena, namely reduced sensitivity and nerve-distribution pain respectively.

options: Pure nociceptive mechanical low back pain
Inflammatory pain from discal annular tear
questions.question: A physiotherapist uses the DN4 questionnaire to assess a patient with leg pain following lumbar disc herniation. A DN4 score of 5/10 is recorded. What does this score indicate?
questions.explanation: The Douleur Neuropathique 4 (DN4) questionnaire screens for neuropathic pain using seven symptom descriptors (burning, painful cold, electric shocks, tingling, pins and needles, numbness, itching) and three physical signs (hypoaesthesia to touch, hypoaesthesia to pinprick, brush allodynia). A score of 4/10 or above indicates a probable neuropathic pain component. A score of 5/10 strongly suggests neuropathic pain, indicating that in addition to the disc-mediated mechanical pain, there is nerve root sensitisation contributing to the leg pain symptoms. This finding guides the addition of neuropathic-specific interventions to the management plan.

Sensation refers to the awareness of stimuli from the senses, while perception is the interpretation of that sensation into a meaningful form, occurring in the cerebrum. Perception is an active process involving interaction between the brain and the environment. The distractors reverse these roles or wrongly locate both processes in the periphery rather than centrally for perception.
options: Sensation is voluntary; perception is an involuntary reflex action
Sensation is awareness of stimuli; perception is its interpretation
Sensation occurs in the cerebrum; perception occurs in receptors
Sensation interprets stimuli; perception merely detects raw stimuli
Sensation and perception both occur exclusively in peripheral nerves
questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes sensation from perception?
A dying patient who attempts to negotiate with physicians or God, promising to fulfil certain obligations in exchange for a cure, is demonstrating the stage of:
questions.explanation: Bargaining involves the patient attempting to negotiate with physicians, friends, or God, promising actions such as charitable giving in return for a cure. This stage follows anger and precedes depression in the Kubler-Ross sequence of dying. Denial, anger, depression and acceptance describe other distinct emotional stages, not this negotiating behaviour.

questions.question: A patient who realises death is inevitable and can talk about it courageously while facing the unknown is in the stage of:
questions.explanation: Acceptance is the stage in which the patient realises death is inevitable and accepts the universality of the experience, often facing it courageously. People with strong religious beliefs may find particular comfort during this final stage. Denial, anger, bargaining and depression are earlier stages preceding this final acceptance stage.

options: Immobilisation to protect the affected limb from damage
High-dose opioid analgesia to control severe pain
Exclusive use of passive physical therapy modalities
Surgical sympathectomy to interrupt pain pathways
Graded exposure and desensitisation within a multidisciplinary framework
questions.explanation: Graded exposure and desensitisation — progressively reintroducing normal sensory inputs, movement, and functional loading to the affected limb within a multidisciplinary framework — is the cornerstone of CRPS management at all stages. Immobilisation is contraindicated as it worsens central sensitisation, cortical reorganisation, and physical deconditioning. High-dose opioids have limited evidence and significant harm in CRPS. Graded desensitisation (brushing, different textures, temperature) and graded motor imagery combined with functional rehabilitation address the central and peripheral mechanisms simultaneously, which is required for comprehensive CRPS management.
questions.question: A physiotherapist completes a comprehensive pain assessment on a patient with complex regional pain syndrome. Following assessment, an individualised management plan is developed. Which component is essential for all CRPS management plans at any stage?

questions.explanation: Osteoarthritis is described as breakdown of cartilage in the spine, distinct from osteoporosis, which involves weak and brittle bone rather than cartilage. Degenerative disc disease instead refers to wear and tear of the intervertebral discs rather than the cartilage of the joints. The distractors describe other structural causes that do not match the cartilage breakdown described for osteoarthritis.
questions.question: Breakdown of cartilage in the spine, as a cause of low back pain, is best described as:

questions.explanation: In the gate control circuit diagram, the projection neuron carrying the nociceptive signal ascends via the spinothalamic tract toward the brain. This is the same ascending pathway responsible for conscious pain perception described elsewhere in pain physiology. The corticospinal, spinocerebellar, dorsal column and rubrospinal tracts are not the pathway used by the projection neuron in this circuit.
questions.question: In the gate control circuit, the projection neuron that carries the nociceptive signal toward the brain communicates through which tract?
Morphine, pethidine and oxycodone are classified together as:
questions.explanation: Morphine, pethidine (Demerol) and oxycodone are classified as strong opioids, distinct from the mild opioids codeine and tramadol. Strong opioids act on opioid receptors in both the brain and spinal cord, used for more severe pain presentations. The distractors misclassify these drugs into categories such as mild opioids or unrelated drug classes.

options: Mirror therapy, laterality recognition, imagined movements
Laterality recognition, explicit motor imagery, mirror therapy
Explicit motor imagery, mirror therapy, laterality recognition
Mirror therapy, explicit motor imagery, laterality recognition
Imagined movements, mirror therapy, explicit motor imagery
questions.question: A physiotherapist applies graded motor imagery (GMI) to a patient with CRPS of the right hand. What is the correct sequence of the three stages of GMI?
questions.explanation: Graded Motor Imagery follows a specific three-stage sequence designed to progressively activate cortical motor areas without triggering pain: (1) Laterality Discrimination — recognising left or right body images to normalise cortical representation without movement; (2) Explicit Motor Imagery — imagining movements without actually performing them; (3) Mirror Therapy — using mirror visual feedback of the intact limb to provide normalised sensory feedback while movements are performed. This sequence gradually increases cortical activation, reducing central sensitisation while avoiding the pain responses that movement itself would trigger in CRPS.

options: Increase exercise volume by 20% each session
Reduce exercise to zero during any flare occurrence
Advance based on time quota, not pain or symptom response
Only increase exercise when completely pain-free at rest
Add maximum resistance as quickly as possible for gains
questions.explanation: Time-contingent graded activity advances exercise based on pre-planned, agreed schedules (time quotas) rather than pain or symptom levels. This approach prevents the operant conditioning trap where pain controls behaviour — patients on pain-contingent exercise learn to rest when in pain, reinforcing avoidance. Time-contingent quotas are agreed collaboratively, starting well below the patient's pain threshold, and increased systematically regardless of symptom fluctuation. This evidence-based approach from operant conditioning models has strong evidence in chronic pain rehabilitation.
questions.question: A physiotherapist applies a progressive exercise programme for a patient with chronic widespread pain. The patient reports post-exercise pain flares. Which graded activity principle should guide progression?

questions.explanation: Correct lifting technique recommends bending at the hips and knees, not the back, while keeping objects close to the body. Twisting the spine during lifting should also be avoided; pivoting the feet instead is recommended. The distractors list joints not specifically identified as the recommended bending points for safe lifting technique.
questions.question: Correct lifting technique, as part of back hygiene, recommends bending at which joints rather than the back?

questions.explanation: The periaqueductal grey, locus coeruleus, and raphe nucleus magnus are identified as major sites of descending pain modulation in the dorsal horn and higher levels. These structures use norepinephrine, serotonin and dopamine to send descending inhibitory signals that reduce incoming pain transmission. The distractors list structures more associated with movement, memory or emotion rather than descending pain modulation specifically.
questions.question: Which structures are identified as major sites of descending pain modulation?
options: Cerebellum, basal ganglia and hippocampus only
Substantia nigra, globus pallidus and putamen
Primary motor cortex and supplementary motor area
Periaqueductal grey, locus coeruleus and raphe nucleus magnus

questions.question: A physiotherapist treating a patient with chronic pain notices the patient has strong negative beliefs about pain and recovery. Which psychological construct is most important to screen for, given its strong prediction of disability outcomes?
questions.explanation: Pain catastrophising — measured with the Pain Catastrophising Scale (PCS) — is the single strongest psychological predictor of pain-related disability, healthcare utilisation, and poor treatment outcomes across pain conditions. It comprises three components: magnification (exaggerating the threat value of pain), rumination (inability to divert attention away from pain), and helplessness (feeling unable to cope). High PCS scores predict transition from acute to chronic pain, poor surgical outcomes, and reduced rehabilitation benefit. PCS screening should be routine in physiotherapy assessments to identify those needing targeted psychological co-intervention.

options: Increased progressively regardless of clinical response
Frequently reassessed, as they may not be particularly effective
Maintained indefinitely without any further reassessment
questions.question: In acute, severe neuropathic pain, the use of strong opioids should be:
questions.explanation: In acute, severe, neuropathic pain, strong opioids are occasionally helpful but may not be particularly effective, so their use should be frequently reassessed. This reflects the generally limited and inconsistent efficacy of strong opioids in neuropathic, compared with nociceptive, pain. The distractors describe inappropriate, absolute approaches that contradict the recommended cautious and reassessed use.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT typically listed as an example of chronic pain in physiotherapy practice?
questions.explanation: A fresh surgical incision produces acute, not chronic, pain, since it has a recent identifiable cause and expected healing course. Trigeminal neuralgia, fibromyalgia, phantom limb pain and chronic low back pain are all listed examples of chronic pain conditions. The distractors therefore represent genuine chronic pain examples, while the correct answer is the odd one out as an acute pain example.
options: Chronic low back pain persisting for months
Trigeminal neuralgia as a neuropathic pain
Fibromyalgia as a widespread pain condition

questions.explanation: The disconnect between pain intensity ratings and functional capacity illustrates that pain intensity and disability are not linearly correlated. A patient can have high pain ratings yet maintain high function — reflecting good pain self-efficacy, acceptance, and adaptive coping strategies. Conversely, some patients with lower pain ratings have severe disability due to fear-avoidance or catastrophising. This concept is fundamental to pain assessment, highlighting the need to assess function, disability, and psychological factors independently from pain intensity, and to set functional outcomes (rather than pain reduction alone) as primary rehabilitation goals.
questions.question: A physiotherapist notes that a patient with chronic knee pain consistently rates pain at 7/10 but reports no functional limitations and plays recreational football. Which pain assessment concept does this illustrate?
options: Disconnect between pain intensity and disability
Pain catastrophising as the primary driver
Measurement error in the NRS assessment tool

questions.explanation: Topical diclofenac (a topical NSAID) works through peripheral cyclo-oxygenase (COX) inhibition, reducing prostaglandin synthesis at the application site. Prostaglandins are key peripheral sensitisers that lower nociceptor thresholds at sites of inflammation and tissue injury. By inhibiting their production locally, topical diclofenac reduces peripheral sensitisation without significant systemic absorption, avoiding the gastrointestinal and renal adverse effects of oral NSAIDs. This makes it particularly appropriate for localised musculoskeletal pain (osteoarthritis, tendinopathy, soft tissue injury) in patients with systemic NSAID contraindications.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is reviewing the pharmacological basis of topical analgesics used for localised musculoskeletal pain. Which mechanism of action is specific to topical diclofenac?
options: Peripheral cyclo-oxygenase inhibition reducing prostaglandin synthesis
Local anaesthetic blocking voltage-gated sodium channels
Capsaicin receptor activation depleting substance P
