A medicinal chemist modifies a hypnotic 5,5-disubstituted barbituric acid by (A) alkylating one imide nitrogen, (B) alkylating both nitrogens, (C) replacing one oxygen by sulphur and (D) replacing two or all the oxygens by sulphur, and also varies the C5 substituents.
(a) Predict the effect of (A) on lipid solubility, onset, duration and anticonvulsant activity.
(b) Predict the effect of (B).
(c) Predict the effect of (C) and the resulting use.
(d) Predict the effect of (D).
(e) Justify the C5 requirements through SAR.
(f) Explain why acidity decides whether a barbituric acid is active.
(g) Explain how the partition coefficient affects the hypnotic effect.
(h) State the rationale for such modifications and name the duration classes of the resulting drugs.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Alkylating the imide hydrogen increases lipid solubility, giving a quicker onset and shorter duration; as the alkyl size increases (CH3 < C2H5 < C3H7) lipid solubility increases and hydrophilic character decreases beyond the limits; large alkyl groups, starting from C2H5, impart anticonvulsant properties.
(b)
Alkyl substituents on both nitrogens render the drug non-acidic and therefore inactive (1,3,5,5-tetrasubstituted), although its metabolite, a 1,5,5-trisubstituted barbituric acid, is active.
(c)
Replacing one oxygen by sulphur increases lipid solubility so maximal brain levels are reached quickly and onset is rapid, which makes the thiobarbiturates useful as intravenous anaesthetics (thiopental is the thiobarbiturate example named alongside pentobarbital).
(d)
Replacing two or all of the oxygens by sulphur decreases hydrolytic properties beyond the required limits, destroying hypnotic activity.
(e)
The sum of the carbons of both C5 substituents should be 6 to 10; branched isomers are more active than straight-chain isomers (pentobarbital, branching closer to the ring, versus amobarbital); alicyclic and aromatic groups, and unsaturated groups, give greater potency than saturated aliphatic groups; halogen in a 5-alkyl group increases potency; polar groups (OH, NH2, RNH, CO, COOH, SO3H) destroy potency; stereoisomers have about the same potency.
(f)
Barbituric acid (acidic hydrogen, pH 4.8) exists as lactam-lactim tautomers; 5,5-disubstituted, 5,5-disubstituted thio and 1,5,5-trisubstituted derivatives are weakly acidic and active, whereas 1-, 5-, 1,3- and 1,5-substituted derivatives are strongly acidic (ionize completely) and inactive.
(g)
Within the active class, the lipid/water partition coefficient determines duration of hypnotic activity: the higher the lipid solubility, the higher the percentage absorbed and the greater the hypnotic activity.
(h)
Modification aims to adjust onset, duration and activity; long-acting: barbital, mephobarbital, phenobarbital; intermediate: butabarbital, cyclobarbital, pentobarbital, amobarbital; short-acting: hexobarbital (intermediate or short depending on dose).

(a)
Meprobamate (Equanil), 2-methyl-2-propyl-1,3-propanediol dicarbamate; mainly a muscle relaxant and antianxiety agent, a sedative-hypnotic in large doses; now rarely useful for anxiety and less effective than the benzodiazepines.
(b)
Substitution of a butyl group in place of a hydrogen on one of the carbamoyl groups gives tybamate, N-butyl-2-methyl-2-propyl-1,3-propanediol dicarbamate.
(c)
The carbamoyl (carbamate) groups; carbamates are generally described as resistant to hydrolysis.
(d)
Tybamate is short acting (half-life about 3 hours) against about 10 hours for meprobamate; the two are chemically related with similar activity and are used in anxiety and tension.
(e)
Oxanamide (Quiactin) and carbromal (Bromadol).
questions.question:
A propanediol dicarbamate anxiolytic has a half-life of about 10 hours and peak plasma concentration about 3 hours after oral ingestion. Substituting a butyl group for a hydrogen on one carbamoyl group gives a related, shorter-acting drug with a half-life of about 3 hours.
(a) Identify the parent drug and its properties.
(b) State the synthetic change that gives the analogue.
(c) Identify the site at risk.
(d) State the effect of the structural variant on the profile.
(e) Name other related acyclic nitrogen-containing hypnotics.

Discuss the barbiturates under the headings below.
(a) State the classification of the barbiturates.
(b) State the general structure and tautomerism.
(c) State the requirements for hypnotic activity.
(d) State the mechanism of action.
(e) Explain the C5 structure-activity relationships.
(f) Explain the effect of nitrogen modification.
(g) Explain the effect of oxygen modification.
(h) Describe metabolism, synthesis and the qualitative test.
(i) Distinguish the hypnotic class from the inactive class.
(j) Distinguish pentobarbital from amobarbital.
(k) Distinguish barbiturates from thiobarbiturates.
(l) Distinguish long-, intermediate- and short-acting members on partition behaviour.
questions.answerText:
(a)
By structure: active hypnotic class (5,5-disubstituted, 5,5-disubstituted thio and 1,5,5-trisubstituted barbituric acids) and inactive class (1-, 5-, 1,3- and 1,5-substituted acids, strongly acidic; 1,3,5,5-tetrasubstituted, non-acidic); by duration: long (barbital, mephobarbital, phenobarbital), intermediate (butabarbital, cyclobarbital, pentobarbital, amobarbital) and short (hexobarbital, which acts as intermediate or short depending on dose).
(b)
Barbituric acid has three lactam groups and exists in aqueous solution in equilibrium among barbituric acid, monolactim and dilactim forms, the most common tautomer being the tri-keto form; the acidic hydrogen (pH 4.8) is related to the lactam-lactim tautomerism.
(c)
The compound must be a weak acid and must have a lipid/water partition coefficient between certain limits.
(d)
Barbiturates depress the cerebrospinal axis and neuronal, skeletal, smooth and cardiac muscle activity depending on compound, dose and route, producing depression, sedation, hypnosis or anaesthesia, and decrease oxidative metabolic processes and functional activity of the brain.
(e)
The sum of carbons in both C5 substituents should be 6 to 10; branched isomers are more active than straight chains (pentobarbital over amobarbital); stereoisomers have about the same potency; alicyclic and aromatic substituents are more potent than aliphatic; unsaturated more than saturated; halogen increases potency; polar groups (OH, NH2, RNH, CO, COOH, SO3H) destroy it.
(f)
Alkylating the imide hydrogen increases lipid solubility with quicker onset and shorter duration, larger groups (CH3, C2H5, C3H7) increase it further and reduce hydrophilicity, groups from C2H5 upward confer anticonvulsant properties, and alkylation on both nitrogens makes the drug non-acidic and inactive.
(g)
Replacing one oxygen by sulphur increases lipid solubility so brain levels are reached quickly and onset is rapid (useful as intravenous anaesthetics); replacing two or all oxygens decreases hydrolytic properties beyond limits and destroys hypnotic activity.
(h)
Hepatic metabolism lowers lipophilicity and so cerebral concentration and activity, by oxidation of C5 substituents, hydrolytic cleavage of the ring, desulphuration of 2-thiobarbiturates and N-dealkylation; synthesis is by condensation reactions in alkaline, neutral or acidic medium; test: 5 mg in hot 0.2% cobalt(II) acetate in methanol with powdered sodium tetraborate gives a blue-violet colour.
(i)
The hypnotic class is weakly acidic and active, whereas the inactive class is strongly acidic (ionises completely) or non-acidic (tetrasubstituted), although the 1,5,5-trisubstituted metabolites of the latter are active.
(j)
Both are intermediate-acting; pentobarbital has branching closer to the ring than amobarbital and branched isomers are more active than straight-chain isomers.
(k)
Thiobarbiturates (for example thiopental) have higher lipid solubility, rapid onset and use as intravenous anaesthetics, but replacing two or all oxygens by sulphur destroys hypnotic activity.
(l)
The partition coefficient determines duration of hypnotic activity: the higher the lipid solubility the higher the percentage absorbed and the greater the hypnotic activity.

questions.question:
Discuss flufenamic acid and its N-phenylanthranilate analogues as AKR1C3 inhibitors under the headings below.
(a) State the lead and its names.
(b) State the structure and the five classes.
(c) State the properties of the lead.
(d) State the synthesis and assay.
(e) Explain the class 1 structure-activity relationships.
(f) Explain the class 2 and 3 relationships.
(g) Explain the class 4 and 5 relationships.
(h) Explain the electronic basis.
(i) Explain why selectivity over related enzymes is required.
(j) State the toxicity avoided.
(k) State the loss of activity with structural change.
(l) State the advantage over abiraterone acetate.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Flufenamic acid (FLU), 2-{[3-(trifluoromethyl)phenyl]amino}benzoic acid, an N-phenylanthranilate NSAID used as the lead compound.
(b)
Ring A is the benzoic acid ring and ring B the N-phenyl ring: class 1 B-ring variants; class 2 4-OCH3 on ring A; class 3 5-COCH3 on ring A; class 4 carboxyl moved from ortho to meta; class 5 carboxyl moved to para.
(c)
AKR1C3 IC50 51 nM with selectivity ratio AKR1C2:AKR1C3 of 7; COX-1 IC50 2.23 micromolar and COX-2 16 nM.
(d)
Buchwald-Hartwig C-N coupling (Pd(OAc)2, BINAP, Cs2CO3, toluene, 120 degrees C) followed by KOH saponification of the methyl ester (EtOH/water, 100 degrees C) and acidification to pH 2; screened by inhibition of NADP+-dependent oxidation of S-tetralol by AKR1C3 and AKR1C2, selectivity being the ratio of IC50 values.
(e)
Removing CF3 (1b) gave a 30-fold loss of AKR1C3 potency and reversed selectivity; potency returned with B-ring substituents; p-t-butyl (1o, 38 nM, 28-fold selective) and o-NO2/p-OMe (1q) were best.
(f)
Class 2 (4-OCH3) kept potency (2a 60 nM) while class 3 (5-COCH3) lost 14-fold; neither gave much selectivity apart from 3y (56-fold); A-ring substitution is known to remove COX inhibition.
(g)
Class 4 (meta carboxyl) lost 6-fold AKR1C3 and 43-fold AKR1C2 potency giving 50-fold selectivity; para B-ring substituents were best (CF3 ortho, meta, para gave 560, 319 and 62 nM); class 5 gave only modest potency changes, with 5a (500 nM) the most potent and 5r (57-fold) most selective.
(h)
Electron-withdrawing B-ring groups gave better inhibitors than electron-donating groups, NO2 being most potent; Hammett correlations were found (R2 0.81 para, 0.90 meta); the carboxyl anchors in the oxyanion hole of AKR1C3.
(i)
AKR1C1 and AKR1C2 inactivate 5-alpha-dihydrotestosterone, so their inhibition would remove a safeguard; AKR1C1 and AKR1C2 are 98% identical, so AKR1C2 was used as a surrogate.
(j)
Chronic COX inhibition carries gastrointestinal and cardiovascular adverse effects; the lead compounds showed little or no COX-1 or COX-2 inhibition at 100 micromolar (except 4m).
(k)
Losing CF3 reduced potency 30-fold, adding 5-COCH3 reduced it 14-fold, and para-carboxyl (class 5) analogues were about 100-fold less potent than class 1 counterparts; dicarboxylic and m,m-disubstituted analogues were weak.
(l)
Abiraterone acetate (a CYP17 inhibitor) must be given with a glucocorticoid to prevent build-up of desoxycorticosterone, with chronic risks of Cushing's syndrome, immunosuppression and diabetes; AKR1C3 acts downstream, so no glucocorticoid is needed; the leads blocked testosterone formation in LNCaP-AKR1C3 cells.

questions.question:
Discuss the antimetabolite approach under the headings below.
(a) Define an antimetabolite.
(b) State the general nature.
(c) State the classes.
(d) State the role in toxicity and optimisation.
(e) Explain the sulfonamide example.
(f) Give the structure-activity basis for sulfanilamide.
(g) Give the anticancer examples.
(h) State the selectivity logic.
(i) Explain why it improves the therapeutic index.
(j) State the limitation from target change.
(k) State the toxicity trade-off.
(l) State the examples of side effects exploited.
questions.answerText:
(a)
A compound sufficiently similar in chemistry to a metabolite that it can inhibit or completely replace it in a biological system but cannot carry out the metabolite's normal function, producing deficiency of the metabolite and eventually death of the organism (for example PABA and sulfanilamide).
(b)
Structural analogues of naturally occurring substances needed for specific biochemical reactions; they substitute fraudulently for purines or pyrimidines or inhibit critical enzymes of nucleic acid synthesis, affecting protein synthesis and DNA and RNA replication.
(c)
Folate antagonists, pyrimidine antagonists and purine antagonists.
(d)
The approach is used in toxicity reduction and optimisation, using molecules that mimic natural metabolites and disrupt pathways.
(e)
Bacteria synthesise folic acid in two steps; the first enzyme is not very specific and uses the sulphonamide in place of PABA to give a pteridine-sulfa product, and the final step needing PABA and glutamic acid is inhibited so no folic acid is produced.
(f)
Groups must be para, the NH2 must be free or regenerated in vivo, benzene ring changes decrease or abolish activity, and SO2NR2 gives inactive compounds.
(g)
Methotrexate, a folic acid antagonist that inhibits DNA synthesis in cancer cells, and 5-fluorouracil, a pyrimidine antagonist that disrupts RNA and DNA synthesis.
(h)
Selectivity arises from targeting a bacterial enzyme not present in mammals or with significant structural differences from the mammalian enzyme.
(i)
By exploiting a pathway essential to the pathogen but absent in the host, it achieves selective toxicity, the aim of Ehrlich's chemotherapeutic index.
(j)
A target may lose sensitivity over time, as when the penicillin-binding protein of Staphylococcus aureus evolved a mutant form that no longer recognises penicillin.
(k)
An anticancer drug should ideally target tumour cells without affecting normal cells, since selectivity reduces adverse drug reactions.
(l)
Side effects of sulphonamides gave diuretics, hypoglycaemics, antithyroids and a uricosuric, showing the value of the lead.

questions.question:
A benzodiazepine marketed as Valium (Roche) is hardly ever seen as a syrup because it is prepared for immediate use. It is also used in tetanus and is a drug of choice in status epilepticus.
(a) Identify the drug and its class, and state the history of the class.
(b) State the physicochemical and stability properties and the assay.
(c) Describe the metabolic pathway and the metabolites.
(d) State the clinical consequence of the active metabolites.
(e) Explain the mechanism and the basis for its use in tetanus.
(f) State the uses and the adverse-effect concern, and the reversal agent.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Diazepam, a benzodiazepine; the first compound in the class was chlordiazepoxide (Librium) and structural modification of it gave many congeners; they are mostly antianxiety drugs with sedative, hypnotic and muscle relaxant action.
(b)
It is unstable in solution and on exposure to UV light isomerisation occurs with reduced activity; it is phototoxic and kept in well-closed containers protected from light; assay is by non-aqueous titration with 0.1 M perchloric acid, UV/visible spectrophotometry and HPLC.
(c)
Benzodiazepines are metabolised by hydrolysis, hydroxylation, dealkylation, reduction, oxidation and conjugation to active or inactive compounds; medazepam → (oxidation) diazepam → (N-demethylation) desmethyldiazepam; diazepam → (hydroxylation) temazepam → (N-demethylation) oxazepam; desmethyldiazepam → (hydroxylation) oxazepam.
(d)
Anxiolytic benzodiazepines have half-lives and durations (of the drug and its active metabolites) longer than those used as hypnotics, because of many active metabolites, in particular desmethyldiazepam and oxazepam; midazolam, used as an anaesthetic, has a short half-life of about 2 to 3 hours.
(e)
Benzodiazepines depress the limbic system and act most prominently on the spinal cord, facilitating release of GABA; Clostridium tetani acts presynaptically in the spinal cord and prevents GABA release, and diazepam antagonises this presynaptic block and restores GABA-ergic transmission, which is the basis of its use in tetanus.
(f)
Anxiety, convulsions, status epilepticus, tetanus and muscle relaxation; long-term treatment should be avoided because of psychic and physical dependence; flumazenil competitively displaces benzodiazepines from their receptors and reverses their effects.

(a)
They determine absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion and toxicity (ADMET) and so whether a drug is effective and safe.
(b)
Drugs must be sufficiently soluble in aqueous fluids to be absorbed; lipophilicity is measured by logP (octanol/water); high logP gives membrane penetration but fat accumulation and poor solubility, low logP gives solubility but poor penetration.
(c)
logD accounts for ionisation at a given pH; pKa is the pH at which 50% is ionised; ionised forms are more water soluble but less permeable, unionised forms cross membranes more easily; weak acids absorb in acidic stomach and weak bases in the intestine.
(d)
Targets are chiral so 3D arrangement affects binding (thalidomide enantiomers); covalent bonds are strong and sometimes toxic (organophosphates), noncovalent bonds are reversible, chelation reduces absorption (tetracyclines with calcium); molecular weight, hydrogen bond donors and acceptors and chemical stability also matter.
(e)
Molecular weight below 500 Da, logP below 5, fewer than 5 hydrogen bond donors and fewer than 10 acceptors for good oral drugs.
(f)
Veber: polar surface area at most 140 square angstroms and at most 10 rotatable bonds favour oral bioavailability; Egan's egg model plots logP against PSA to predict intestinal absorption and brain penetration (the BOILED-Egg of swissADME).
(g)
Type of ionisation centre (phenolic, enolic, carboxylic, ureide) and its chemical environment, including neighbouring atoms; the same substituent can shift pKa differently for different centres through different intramolecular hydrogen bonding.
(h)
Hydrogen bonding can weaken the electron-withdrawing effect of NO2, so a carboxylic acid is less acidic than predicted and the experimental proton-donor pKa is lower than calculated.
(i)
Calculated values can differ from experiment because some 3D details are not well represented in the algorithms.
(j)
Ionisation raises solubility but lowers permeability, so the unionised fraction governs membrane crossing (chlorpromazine pKa 9.2 is only 1.6% unionised at pH 7.4).
(k)
Proximal factors (steric hindrance, electron density, delocalisation, stereochemistry) affect rate and binding; global factors (pKa, logP and logD, 3D geometry) regulate penetration into enzyme compartments, recognition and binding mode.
(l)
Intra-individual factors (food, alcohol, tobacco, physiological and pathological state) and inter-individual factors (genetics, species, sex, polymorphisms) vary widely, so reliable prediction needs complex systems-biology modelling.
questions.question:
Discuss physicochemical properties in drug design under the headings below.
(a) State why the properties matter.
(b) State solubility and lipophilicity.
(c) State logD, ionisation and pKa.
(d) State stereochemistry, bonding and other properties.
(e) State Lipinski's rule.
(f) State Veber's rule and Egan's model.
(g) State the pKa factors.
(h) State the hydrogen-bond example.
(i) State the limitation of calculated properties.
(j) State the trade-off of ionisation.
(k) State metabolic prediction factors.
(l) State why biological factors complicate prediction.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Isosteres have the same number and arrangement of electrons (identical peripheral electron layers) and similar physical properties; bioisosteres are groups with similar chemical or physical properties that produce similar biological properties; bioisosterism is synthesis of analogues of a lead by replacing an atom or group with another of similar electronic and steric character, as a special process of molecular modification (concept of isosterism first developed by Langmuir).
(b)
The lead compound should have a well-known structure and mechanism of action, if possible at the level of receptor interaction, including knowledge of all its pharmacophoric groups.
(c)
Classical (monovalent, divalent, trivalent, tetrasubstituted atoms or groups and ring equivalents) and non-classical, which do not have the same number of atoms and do not fit the steric and electronic rules but have similar biological activity.
(d)
To maintain similar biological properties and to resolve biological problems (potency, side effects, separation of biological activities, duration of action), correcting a poor drug profile such as poor bioavailability, side effects, inability to cross barriers or poor pharmacokinetics.
(e)
NH2 and OH (isosteric, both able to hydrogen bond; descending the table H atoms are added to keep the same number of valence electrons, and OH and SH are isoelectronic); the amino acids serine and cysteine, tyrosine and histidine; the bases cytosine and uracil, adenine and guanine; the xanthines caffeine and theophylline; benzene replaced by pyridine.
(f)
A pyrrole ring as a bioisostere in antipsychotics; acetylsalicylic acid and mefenamic acid as NSAID classes; antihistamine analogues A, B and C where A has twice the activity of C and many times that of B; pentobarbital and thiopental (oxygen replaced by sulphur).
(g)
Factors are structural (size, shape, hydrogen bonding), receptor interactions (all except lipid and water solubility), pharmacokinetics (lipophilicity, hydrophilicity, pKa, hydrogen bonding) and metabolism (chemical reactivity), allowing the designer to adjust the parameter needed to increase potency or reduce toxicity.
(h)
In the cimetidine programme the thiourea group of metiamide, linked to agranulocytosis, was replaced by a cyanoguanidine moiety to give cimetidine.
(i)
NH2 and OH are isosteric and both hydrogen bond, but their acidity and basicity differ, so their behaviour in biological systems and pharmacokinetics differ greatly.
(j)
Isosteric replacements have different effects (for example benzene to pyridine) and it is difficult to generalise between different biological systems.
(k)
Multiple alterations may be necessary: if a modification for receptor binding decreases lipophilicity, a different part of the molecule may need a lipophilic group.
(l)
The strategy is widely used to discover analogues of therapeutic innovations (me-too drugs) and as a tool in molecular modification of bioactive compounds, and it can attenuate toxicity, modify lead activity and alter pharmacokinetics.
questions.question:
Discuss bioisosterism as a drug-design principle under the headings below.
(a) Define isosteres, bioisosteres and bioisosterism.
(b) State the requirements for applying it to a lead.
(c) State the types of bioisostere.

(e) Give examples of classical bioisosteres.

(g) Explain how replacement changes properties.
(h) Give a clinical example from lead optimisation.

Discuss the cinchona alkaloids (quinine) under the headings below.
(a) State the source and names.
(b) State the structure.
(c) State the source.
(d) State the pharmacological basis of use.
(e) State the congeners derived from this lead.
(f) State the role of this lead in drug discovery.
(g) State the toxicity.
(h) State the replacement of the natural drug.
(i) Illustrate how a drug target can lose sensitivity (resistance).
(j) Distinguish quinine from quinidine.
questions.answerText:
(a)
From Cinchona succirubra (Cinchona officinalis bark): the quinoline alkaloids quinine and quinidine, the two major ones.
(b)
Quinoline alkaloids with an unusual quinuclidine ring.
(c)
They are obtained from the bark.
(d)
Quinine is used to treat malaria and, as a skeletal muscle relaxant, in nocturnal leg cramps; quinidine is used for cardiac arrhythmias.
(e)
Antimalarial 4-aminoquinolines (chloroquine, amodiaquine, piperaquine) and 8-aminoquinolines (primaquine, pamaquine) are congeners of quinine.
(f)
It illustrates plant-derived leads, whose compounds provide drugs and prototypes that can be modified to be more effective or less toxic.
(g)
Overdoses lead to temporary loss of hearing, impaired sight and tinnitus.
(h)
It has been replaced by synthetic hydroxyquinolines.
(i)
A target may lose sensitivity, as shown for penicillin, where the penicillin-binding protein of Staphylococcus aureus has evolved a mutant form that no longer recognises the drug.
(j)
Both are quinoline alkaloids of cinchona: quinine is used for malaria and nocturnal leg cramps, whereas quinidine is used for cardiac arrhythmias.

questions.question:
A research team starts from flufenamic acid, 2-{[3-(trifluoromethyl)phenyl]amino}benzoic acid, and wants to prepare N-phenylanthranilic acid analogues carrying different substituents on the N-phenyl ring (B-ring) as selective inhibitors of the enzyme AKR1C3.
(a) State the synthetic route and the named reaction involved.
(b) State the reagents and conditions of the coupling step.
(c) State the reagents, intermediate and work-up of the second step.
(d) Identify the functional group at risk and explain its importance.
(e) Describe the structural variants that were made (classes) and the effect of moving the carboxyl group.
(f) State the optimal B-ring substituents and the electronic and positional rules.
(g) State the biological rationale and outcome for the lead compounds.
questions.answerText:
(a)
A two-step route: Buchwald-Hartwig C-N coupling of the aniline with the aryl bromide (or triflate) of the methyl ester, followed by saponification of the methyl ester formed.
(b)
Aniline (1.2 equiv), Cs2CO3 (1.4 equiv), BINAP (0.08 equiv) and Pd(OAc)2 (0.05 equiv) added to the aryl bromide or triflate (1 equiv) in toluene (0.1 M), stirred at 120 degrees C for 4 to 48 h and followed by TLC; the mixture is diluted with EtOAc, washed with 2 M HCl and brine, dried over sodium sulphate and purified on silica gel.
(c)
The purified methyl ester (the N-aryl anthranilate intermediate) in EtOH (0.2 M) is treated with KOH (2 equiv per ester) in water and stirred at 100 degrees C for 1 to 6 h; EtOH is evaporated, the solution is cooled to 0 degrees C and acidified to pH 2 with 2 M HCl, and the acid usually crystallises and is collected by vacuum filtration; products are characterised by NMR and high-resolution mass spectrometry.
(d)
The carboxylic acid, which is masked as the methyl ester during coupling and released by saponification; the carboxyl group is essential for anchoring N-phenylanthranilates to the oxyanion hole of AKR1C3, and its ortho position relative to the amine is essential for COX inhibition.
(e)
Class 1: flufenamic acid analogues with varied B-ring substituents; class 2: 4-OCH3 on the benzoic acid ring; class 3: 5-COCH3 on that ring (ring substitution is known to eliminate COX inhibition); class 4: carboxyl moved from ortho to meta; class 5: carboxyl moved to para; moving to meta (4a, m-CF3) caused 6-fold and 43-fold losses of AKR1C3 and AKR1C2 potency, giving 50-fold selectivity versus 7 for flufenamic acid.
(f)
Electron-withdrawing groups gave better AKR1C3 inhibitors than electron-donating groups at every position, and NO2 gave the most potent compounds (IC50 150, 290 and 33 nM at ortho, meta and para); para was best (CF3 at ortho, meta and para gave IC50 560, 319 and 62 nM and selectivity 27, 50 and 249); the p-COCH3 compound 4n was the most selective (50 nM versus 19.5 micromolar, 364-fold); a Hammett relationship was found (R2 0.81 para, 0.90 meta).
(g)
Selectivity is needed because AKR1C1 and AKR1C2 inactivate 5-alpha-dihydrotestosterone; flufenamic acid inhibits COX-1 (2.23 micromolar) and COX-2 (16 nM) but the leads showed little or no COX inhibition at 100 micromolar (except 4m), which minimises gastrointestinal and cardiovascular adverse effects; they blocked testosterone formation in LNCaP-AKR1C3 cells.

(a)
British approved name adrenaline (from the adrenal gland), American name epinephrine (excreted by the nephrons); abbreviation ADREN; systematic name (R)-1-(3,4-dihydroxyphenyl)-2-methylaminoethanol, the IUPAC name carrying the stereochemical configuration; only the laevorotatory form is official.
(b)
A catechol (3,4-dihydroxyphenyl) ring with a beta-hydroxyl on the ethylene linkage and an N-methyl secondary amine, C9H13NO3, CAS Registry number 51-43-4.
(c)
White or creamy-white crystalline powder that darkens in air and light; sparingly soluble in water, insoluble in ethanol (96%) and ether; freely soluble in mineral acids, NaOH and KOH but not in ammonia or alkali carbonates (amino group gives solubility in mineral acids, phenolic OH groups in strong alkali); turns red litmus blue (secondary amino group); melts with decomposition at about 212 degrees C; specific rotation -50 to -53.5 degrees in a 1 in 50 solution in dilute HCl.
(d)
Obtained from the medulla of suprarenal glands (usually pigs) substantially freed of noradrenaline, or by synthesis; content not less than 98.5% and not more than 101.0% of C9H13NO3 (dried substance, a range that is not symmetrical); assay by non-aqueous titration with crystal violet indicator and 0.1 M perchloric acid, each mL equivalent to 0.01832 g of C9H13NO3.
(e)
The catechol 3,4-dihydroxy pattern gives both alpha and beta activity, the R beta-hydroxyl gives full activity and the secondary amine gives good adrenergic activity; it binds alpha1, alpha2, beta1, beta2 and beta3 receptors, so is potent at all.
(f)
Catecholamines are destroyed by COMT and MAO and are not effective orally; oral use has been described as a pivalic acid prodrug to prevent first-pass metabolism.
(g)
Sympathomimetic, bronchodilator and antiasthmatic; prevents bleeding in surgery by vasoconstriction; combined with local anaesthetics to prolong their effect at smaller doses; treatment of heart block, circulatory collapse and open-angle glaucoma; drug of choice in acute allergic disorders, anaphylaxis and anaphylactic shock.
(h)
Ferric chloride colour test for phenolic OH, infrared spectrum identical to the BP reference, UV absorption lambda max 280 nm; limit of adrenalone (synthetic drug) not more than 0.2% by UV; limit of noradrenaline (natural drug) by a red or purple colour with sodium naphthaquinone sulphonate compared with a noradrenaline standard.
(i)
The catechol ring system is light sensitive and easily oxidised in air; the darkening is due to formation of adrenochrome, and a pink to brown colour indicates oxidative breakdown.
(j)
Solutions are stabilised with a reducing agent such as sodium bisulphite; the drug is kept in well-closed airtight containers, preferably filled with nitrogen and protected from light.
(k)
The S isomer has decreased activity; removing the p-hydroxyl gives alpha selectivity (phenylephrine), enlarging the N-alkyl gives beta selectivity (isoproterenol, salbutamol) and a resorcinol ring gives beta-2 selectivity with decreased COMT metabolism (terbutaline).
(l)
Noradrenaline lacks the N-methyl group, is potent at alpha receptors (less potent than adrenaline) with effect on beta1 but none on beta2, and is used in local anaesthetic dental solutions and as an intravenous infusion in hypotension and myocardial shock; it also becomes coloured on exposure to air and light.
questions.question:
Discuss adrenaline (epinephrine) as a monograph drug under the headings below.
(a) State the approved names, abbreviation and systematic name.
(b) State the structure and formula.
(c) State the physical and chemical properties.
(d) State the source, content limits and assay.
(e) Explain the structural basis of activity.
(f) Explain the metabolic basis of its pharmacokinetic limitation.
(g) State the uses.
(h) State the identification and impurity tests.
(i) Explain the oxidative loss of quality.
(j) State the protection against oxidation.
(k) State the effect of structural changes on activity.
(l) Distinguish adrenaline from noradrenaline.

Discuss the sympathomimetic agents under the headings below.
(a) State the chemical and mechanistic classification.
(b) State the general structure.
(c) State the pharmacophore requirements.
(d) State the mechanisms of action.
(e) Explain the receptor potency order of the catecholamines.
(f) Explain the metabolic basis of the oral limitation.
(g) Explain the effect of ring, chain and nitrogen changes.
(h) State the adverse-effect limitations.
(i) Distinguish epinephrine from norepinephrine.
(j) Distinguish phenylephrine from the imidazolines.
(k) Distinguish ephedrine from pseudoephedrine.
(l) Distinguish isoproterenol, salbutamol and dobutamine.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Chemical: catecholamines (norepinephrine, epinephrine, dopamine, dobutamine, isoproterenol) and non-catecholamines (phenylephrine, hydroxyamphetamine, ephedrine, salbutamol, naphazoline, terbutaline); mechanistic: direct acting (for example norepinephrine, epinephrine, phenylephrine, dobutamine, terbutaline, salbutamol, clonidine, methyldopa), indirect acting (hydroxyamphetamine, propylhexedrine) and mixed acting (ephedrine, pseudoephedrine, metaraminol).
(b)
Many contain beta-phenylethylamine as the parent structure, with substitution possible on the catechol ring, the ethylene linkage and the amino group.
(c)
A 3-hydroxyl for alpha activity, a 4-hydroxyl for beta activity (3,4-dihydroxy for both), a hydroxyl on the beta carbon (R form active) and a primary or secondary amine for good adrenergic activity.
(d)
Direct agonists bind adrenergic receptors (epinephrine, norepinephrine, isoproterenol, phenylephrine); indirect agonists displace norepinephrine from stores (amphetamine, hydroxyamphetamine, tyramine), block its uptake (cocaine, tricyclic antidepressants, SNRIs) or inhibit its breakdown (MAO inhibitors such as phenelzine); mixed agents (ephedrine, pseudoephedrine) do both.
(e)
Isoproterenol beta1 = beta2 = beta3 >>> alpha1 = alpha2; norepinephrine alpha1 = alpha2 = beta1 = beta3 >>> beta2; epinephrine acts on all five; dopamine DA1 > beta1 > alpha1.
(f)
Catecholamines are rapidly destroyed by COMT and MAO (in the neuron and gut wall), are not effective orally and penetrate the CNS poorly; non-catecholamines are not destroyed by COMT, MAO deactivation is limited, so they have longer half-lives and better CNS penetration through lipid solubility.
(g)
A resorcinol ring or meta-hydroxyl replacement gives beta-2 selectivity and COMT resistance (terbutaline, salbutamol); removing the p-hydroxyl gives alpha selectivity (phenylephrine); an alpha methyl lowers MAO metabolism (amphetamine); a larger N-alkyl gives beta selectivity (isoprenaline).
(h)
Amphetamines and cocaine cause CNS effects (confusion, insomnia, tremor, psychosis), cardiovascular effects (palpitations, arrhythmias, hypertension) and gastrointestinal effects; beta-2 agonists cause nervousness, tremor, tachycardia and, systemically, hypokalaemia and hyperglycaemia; alpha-1 agonists cause hypertension, nervousness and headache.
(i)
Epinephrine is potent at alpha1, beta1 and beta2 and is used in anaphylaxis, with local anaesthetics and in heart block; norepinephrine is a potent alpha agonist with beta1 action but none at beta2, is a strong vasoconstrictor used in dental local anaesthetic solutions and to support blood pressure in hypotension and shock.
(j)
Phenylephrine is a selective alpha1 agonist (parenteral, nasal or eye use); naphazoline (2-(1-naphthylmethyl)-2-imidazoline) is essentially ionised at physiological pH (pKa 9 to 10) and stimulates alpha1 and alpha2; oxymetazoline binds alpha1 and selectively alpha2; xylometazoline is a partial agonist at alpha2 and selective at alpha1.
(k)
Ephedrine has two asymmetric carbons (four isomers), is naturally occurring, acts directly and indirectly on alpha and beta receptors and is used as bronchodilator, nasal decongestant and in orthostatic hypotension; pseudoephedrine is its optically active isomer, stimulates alpha and beta receptors and the CNS and is a vasoconstrictor for nasal and sinus congestion.
(l)
Isoproterenol is a non-selective beta agonist (beta1 raises cardiac output, beta2 bronchodilation) used in bronchial asthma; salbutamol is a COMT-resistant non-catecholamine beta2 agonist and the drug of choice in bronchial asthma; dobutamine is mainly beta1 with some alpha1 and is used in congestive heart failure and cardiogenic shock.

questions.question:
Discuss acetylcholine under the headings below.
(a) State the name, class and role.
(b) State the structure.
(c) State the physicochemical properties.
(d) State the biosynthesis.
(e) Explain the structure-activity relationships.
(f) Explain the metabolic basis of weak action.
(g) State the muscarinic actions.
(h) State the nicotinic actions.
(i) State the effect of changing the quaternary nitrogen or its methyl groups.
(j) Explain resistance to the enzyme after a structural change.
(k) State the toxicity of excess ACh.
(l) Distinguish the designed analogues.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Acetylcholine (ACh) is the key neurotransmitter of the parasympathetic nervous system and the cholinergic system; the same molecule binds muscarinic and nicotinic receptors using different conformations.
(b)
The ester of acetic acid and choline: an acetoxy group, an ethylene group and a quaternary trimethylammonium group.
(c)
Soluble in water because of the salt form at nitrogen; stable as a solid but in solution the ester hydrolyses to acid and alcohol, very quickly in the presence of acid or base, which prevents oral dosing.
(d)
Serine is converted to choline (serine decarboxylase), methylated by choline-N-methyl transferase with S-adenosylmethionine until the amine is quaternary, then acetylated by choline acetyltransferase (ChAT) in the cytosol using acetyl-CoA, and transported into vesicles.
(e)
A quaternary nitrogen with three methyls (sulphur, arsenic or phosphorus lower activity), a two-carbon chain, acetyl not larger, oxygen in the ester region, beta methyl for muscarinic selectivity and alpha methyl for nicotinic selectivity.
(f)
Butyrylcholinesterase significantly degrades injected ACh, giving a weak response; AChE hydrolyses it to acetic acid and choline; the ionic ammonium prevents penetration of the lipophilic cell wall and the lack of selectivity makes it a weak agonist.
(g)
Bradycardia, decreased atrioventricular conduction and atrial contractile force; nitric oxide release dilating vessels; increased intestinal tone (nausea, vomiting), ureter tone, bronchoconstriction, increased salivary, bronchial, sweat and lacrimal secretions and miosis, which can lower intra-ocular pressure.
(h)
Nerve transmission in the autonomic system; at the neuromuscular junction low doses allow skeletal muscle movement and high doses cause paralysis; cholinergic deficiency in the brain causes Alzheimer's disease.
(i)
Replacing nitrogen by sulphur, arsenic or phosphorus reduces activity; changing methyl to ethyl gives an antagonist, to propyl or higher gives inactive compounds, and hydrogen progressively reduces activity.
(j)
AChE is acylated during hydrolysis and must be hydrolysed by water to regenerate; replacing the acetyl ester by a carbamate (or a phosphate) resists this hydrolysis, so carbamates resist AChE and acid and can be given orally.
(k)
Cholinergic crisis, over-stimulation at the neuromuscular junction from excess ACh (nerve gas such as sarin, insecticides), causing muscle paralysis and respiratory failure.
(l)
Methacholine (beta methyl) is as potent and muscarinic selective, carbachol is a non-selective carbamate and bethanechol is a stable, muscarinic-selective carbamate with a beta methyl; the alpha-methyl isomer is nicotinic selective and not used clinically.

(a)
Enalaprilat (the active diacid) and enalapril (its mono-ester prodrug); both are ACE inhibitors used to treat hypertension.
(b)
Enalaprilat has high polarity because it carries two COOH groups, so it was not orally bioavailable and needed injection; the ester enalapril is orally bioavailable.
(c)
Esters are the most commonly employed prodrugs and numerous catalytic esterases in vivo hydrolyse simple esters; enalapril is bioactivated by hydrolysis to enalaprilat after oral administration.
(d)
The ester allows oral administration of an ACE inhibitor for hypertension, avoiding the need for injection.
(e)
Prodrugs may be designed for solubility, absorption, biostability and prolonged release; other examples are chloramphenicol palmitate, proguanil (to cycloguanil), L-dopa (to dopamine), aspirin (to salicylic acid), chloral hydrate (to trichloroethanol) and bitolterol (to colterol).
(f)
Prodrugs are inactive compounds metabolised chemically or enzymatically, in a controlled or predictable manner, to the parent active drug inside the body; they can enhance efficacy or reduce adverse effects through increased solubility, improved permeability and bioavailability, prolonged half-life and tissue-targeted delivery.
questions.question:
A dicarboxylic acid inhibitor of angiotensin converting enzyme, first discovered for hypertension, was highly polar and had to be given by injection. Its mono-ester, supplied as the maleate salt (Vasotec), is orally bioavailable.
(a) Identify the compounds and the relationship between them.
(b) State the physicochemical properties that govern oral availability.
(c) Describe the metabolic activation.
(d) State the clinical consequence.
(e) State the general aims of the prodrug approach with other examples.
(f) Define a prodrug and state how prodrugs improve therapy.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Sedatives reduce excitement and calm the patient; hypnotics produce sleep resembling normal sleep; both are CNS depressants with somewhat differing time-action and dose-action relationships, quicker onset, shorter duration and a steeper dose-response curve being preferred in hypnotics, and slower action with a flatter curve in sedatives.
(b)
Inorganic substances; alcohols and aldehydes; acetylene derivatives; acyclic hypnotics containing nitrogen; piperidinediones and quinazolinones; benzodiazepines; barbiturates.
(c)
Sodium and potassium bromides; chloral hydrate and paraldehyde (a cyclic polyether of acetaldehyde); methylpentynol (3-methyl-1-pentyn-3-ol) and ethclorvynol (1-chloro-3-ethyl-1-penten-4-yn-3-ol); meprobamate, oxanamide and carbromal; methylprylon (3,3-diethyl-5-methyl-2,4-piperidinedione), glutethimide (2-ethyl-2-phenylglutarimide), methaqualone (2-methyl-3-o-tolyl-4(3H)-quinazolinone) and thalidomide (3-phthalimidopiperidine-2,6-dione); chlordiazepoxide and diazepam; barbital, phenobarbital and others.
(d)
Benzodiazepines depress the limbic system and act most on the spinal cord, facilitating release of GABA; barbiturates depress the cerebrospinal axis and decrease oxidative metabolic processes and functional activity of the brain; chloral hydrate acts through its reduced metabolite trichloroethanol and methylpentynol acts like chloral hydrate.
(e)
The linear slope typical of barbiturates and alcohols means a dose above that needed for hypnosis may lead to general anaesthesia, and at still higher doses depression of the respiratory and vasomotor centres in the medulla, leading to coma and death.
(f)
The curve deviates from linearity, so proportionately greater dose increments are needed to achieve CNS depression more profound than hypnosis; this is also the case for certain newer hypnotics with a similar mechanism.
(g)
Bromides accumulate in the body and cause brominism (dermatitis, gastrointestinal disorders, mental disturbances); chloral hydrate is stable because of the electron-withdrawing effect of its halogenated group, is hygroscopic and therefore given as a solution rather than a tablet, and is a prodrug of trichloroethanol.
(h)
Methaqualone and related drugs cause delusions, hallucinations, disorientation with confusion and even convulsions and are contraindicated in pregnancy and in patients with suicidal tendencies; thalidomide causes phocomelia (absence of arms and legs) and is strongly contraindicated in pregnancy.
(i)
Chloral hydrate has less dependency than the barbiturates, causes no hangover and produces very little depression of vasomotor and respiratory centres, but has little anticonvulsant activity; very large doses can depress those centres.
(j)
Paraldehyde is a volatile colourless liquid with a bad smell and taste that decomposes in air and light to toxic acetic acid, is given as a freshly prepared 10% solution, has appreciable anticonvulsant activity (a drug of choice in status epilepticus) and is metabolised to CO2 and H2O; chloral hydrate is a hygroscopic crystalline solid and a prodrug with little anticonvulsant activity.
(k)
Methylpentynol acts similarly to chloral hydrate; ethclorvynol (Placidyl) is a mild hypnotic with quick onset and short duration, useful as a daytime sedative, and carries a chlorine and an additional unsaturation.
(l)
Glutethimide (Doriden) is a very active non-barbiturate hypnotic and safer than phenobarbitone; methylprylon (Noludar) is a piperidinedione; methaqualone (Parest) is a quinazolinone; they are useful for patients who cannot tolerate barbiturates.
questions.question:
Discuss the sedative-hypnotic agents under the headings below.
(a) Define sedatives and hypnotics and state how their time-action and dose-response relationships differ.
(b) Give the classification of sedative and hypnotic agents.
(c) Give examples of each class with their structures.
(d) State the mechanisms of action of the main classes.
(e) Explain the dose-response behaviour of the older sedative-hypnotics.
(f) Explain the dose-response behaviour of the benzodiazepines.
(g) State the chemical basis of the limitation of the inorganic agents and of chloral hydrate formulation.
(h) State the toxicity limitations of the piperidinedione and quinazolinone group.

An azaspirodecanedione anxiolytic marketed as Buspa has efficacy comparable to diazepam, yet it alleviates anxiety without causing sedation or functional impairment.
(a) Identify the drug and its class.
(b) State the structural features of the class.
(c) State the mechanism of action.
(d) State the therapeutic use.
(e) State the adverse-effect profile.
(f) Differentiate it from the other minor tranquillisers.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Buspirone, an azaspirodecanedione and a minor tranquilliser; it is a novel anxiolytic unrelated to the benzodiazepines in structure or pharmacological properties.
(b)
The class carries an azaspirodecanedione ring system.
(c)
For minor tranquillisers generally, the anxiolytic action is probably in the limbic system and may involve potentiation of GABA inhibition and reduced turnover of norepinephrine or other monoamines.
(d)
Anxiety, with antianxiety effects but limited sedative properties and efficacy comparable to diazepam.
(e)
It does not promote abuse or physical dependence and does not cause sedation or functional impairment.
(f)
Benzodiazepines are sedative and muscle relaxant and long-term use may lead to psychic and physical dependence; meprobamate is less effective than the benzodiazepines; hydroxyzine produces marked sedation at 400 mg per day; chlormezanone is less effective than diazepam and meprobamate but equal to chlordiazepoxide in mild anxiety.

(a)
Chloral hydrate, formed when chloral is treated with water (chloral + H2O → chloral hydrate) or ethanol.
(b)
It is a crystalline halogenated aliphatic alcohol, stable because of the electron-withdrawing effect of its halogenated group, and hygroscopic, so it is usually given as a solution and not available as a tablet.
(c)
It is absorbed from the stomach and intestine, metabolized by the liver and kidney and excreted by the kidney; trichloroethanol (TCE) is the major metabolite and is the active compound, so chloral hydrate is a prodrug; TCE is conjugated with glucuronic acid and excreted in urine.
(d)
It produces sedation and hypnosis with no hangover effect and very little depression of the vasomotor and respiratory centres, dependency is less prevalent than with barbiturates, and it has little anticonvulsant activity; very large doses can depress the vasomotor and respiratory centres.
(e)
Contraindicated in peptic ulcer (irritant to the GIT) and in liver and kidney diseases because metabolism is impaired, leading to prolonged action and toxicity; it is not used as an anaesthetic because of its long duration of action.
(f)
Treatment of infantile spasm and as a hypnotic in elderly people.
(g)
Dichloral phenazone, triclofos (Trichonyl), chloral betaine (Somilan), and others such as chlorobutanol, carbochloral, chloral salicylamide and chlorhexadol; the derivatives lack the undesirable side effects of chloral hydrate.
questions.question:
A crystalline halogenated aliphatic alcohol, formed when chloral is treated with water or ethanol and stable because of the electron-withdrawing effect of its halogenated group, is a sedative-hypnotic with onset of action of about 30 minutes and duration of about 6 hours.
(a) Identify the compound and state how it is formed.
(b) State its physicochemical properties and the formulation consequence.
(c) Describe its metabolic pathway and the nature of the metabolites.
(d) State the clinical effects that follow from its profile.
(e) State the contraindications and explain them from its chemistry and metabolism.
(f) State its therapeutic uses.
(g) Name the derivatives and state their advantage.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Quantitative models relating biological activity to properties calculated in 3D space, considering the whole molecule rather than individual substituents; structures come from 2D, databases, X-ray or NMR and are optimised to a lowest-energy structure.
(b)
Developed by Cramer in 1988; bioactive conformations are aligned, steric (Lennard-Jones) and electrostatic (Coulombic) fields are sampled on a 3D grid with a probe (usually a methyl group and a proton), and differences in activity are related to differences in noncovalent fields, displayed as contour maps.
(c)
CoMSIA uses a Gaussian function to evaluate similarity in space, avoiding the steep Lennard-Jones and Coulomb potentials, and adds hydrophobic and hydrogen bond donor and acceptor fields.
(d)
Molecular shape analysis, distance geometry, binding site model, COMPASS, molecular similarity and genetically evolved receptor models.
(e)
Correlation coefficient r and r squared (explained variance, for example r = 0.8 gives 66.4%), standard error of the estimate S (smaller is better, degrees of freedom n - k - 1) and the F-value.
(f)
PRESS (sum of squared differences between actual and predicted values) and cross-validated q squared = 1 - sum(Ypred - Yobs) squared / sum(Yobs - Ymean) squared, usually smaller than r squared.
(g)
Simple linear, multiple linear (one variable per five molecules), stepwise, partial least squares (when data are collinear or N is less than 5M, the method of choice in 3D-QSAR), genetic function approximation, genetic partial least squares and principal component analysis.
(h)
Cross-validation (omitting rows and re-predicting), outlier detection (residual greater than two standard deviations) and bootstrapping.
(i)
They account for spatial arrangement and interaction fields, avoiding pitfalls of classical methods and permitting a hypothetical receptor model, with high-dimensional (3D, 4D, 5D) analyses developed for this reason.
(j)
The steep potentials produce singularities near atoms, require arbitrary cutoffs and scaling and can lose information about one field, which CoMSIA was designed to overcome.
(k)
Alignment depends on the supposed binding mode, many descriptors can give perfect but over-fitted correlations (so cross-validation is required), and the ligand-receptor structure may be unavailable.
(l)
A good CoMFA model needs conformational analysis, establishing the bioactive conformation, superimposition, lattice and force-field choice, and interpretation of contour plots.
questions.question:
Discuss three-dimensional QSAR and the statistics of QSAR models under the headings below.
(a) Define 3D-QSAR.
