Methylcellulose as suspending agent significantly retards the transformation; the sodium salt is the usual form in clinical usage; balance the stability of the stable crystal form (resistant to chemical degradation, preferred for suspensions) against the higher bioavailability of the metastable form.
(d)
If conversion to the stable form is so slow as to be negligible during shelf life, the metastable form's greater solubility can be exploited; here conversion occurs within shelf life, so the amorphous suspension cannot be relied on and the sodium salt or a methylcellulose-stabilised product is chosen; pre-formulation evaluation of crystal structure is advised.
questions.question:
An aqueous suspension of novobiocin made with its bioactive amorphous form loses activity on standing within its shelf life, and blood levels after oral dosing fall.
(a) Identify the instability involved (physical, chemical or microbial).
(b) Explain the degradation pathway and the factors that promote it.
(c) State the stabilisation measures and suitable alternatives.
(d) Reason to the shelf-life, storage or handling decision.

(a) Define creams and classify them (types by emulsion, function and characteristic properties).
(b) State the advantages, limitations and routes of administration of creams.
(c) Explain the formulation basis: the components of the oil and water phases and the function of each excipient.
(d) Distinguish between oil-in-water and water-in-oil creams, with vanishing and cold creams as examples.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Creams are homogeneous semi-solid or viscous preparations of relatively fluid consistency, intended for external application to the skin or certain mucous membranes for protective, therapeutic or prophylactic purposes where an occlusive effect is not necessary; they are semi-solid emulsions of oil and water.
• Types: oil-in-water (small oil droplets in a continuous aqueous phase) and water-in-oil (water droplets in a continuous oily phase); classified by function (cleansing, foundation, massage), by characteristic properties (cold, vanishing) and by emulsion type.
(b)
• Advantages: easy to apply and easy to remove compared with ointments and pastes; cleansing, moisturising and protective uses, and healing of cuts, burns and wounds; safe; avoid first-pass metabolism.
• Limitations: skin irritation or dermatitis from drug or excipients, allergic reactions, slow absorption, most drugs have high molecular weight and are poorly lipid soluble so are not absorbed, and only suit drugs needing very small plasma concentrations; route: skin and certain mucous membranes.
(c)
• The oil phase contains waxes, emollients and lubricants (mineral oils such as light and heavy liquid paraffin; glyceride oils such as almond, arachis, castor, coconut and olive oil; waxes such as beeswax, carnauba wax, ceresin and spermaceti, which prevent emulsion separation and aid adherence; fats as thickeners; lanolin as lubricant and emulsion aid).
• The water phase contains emulsifying, stabilising and thickening agents, preservatives and colorants; water is the most important raw material and is used as solvent; active ingredients are dispersed in either phase or added after emulsification and cooling.
• Emollients soften skin and increase its ability to hold water; humectants (glycerin, betaine, sodium PCA) absorb or retain moisture; vitamins A, B, C and E, perfumes (to impart scent) and colours are also used.
• Preservatives (organic acids, parabens, aldehyde releasers, quaternary ammonium compounds, biguanides) prevent microbial alteration and antioxidants protect against oxygen.
(d)
• O/W creams (make-up creams, vanishing creams) have more water than oil; vanishing creams are stearic acid based and seem to disappear on rubbing, leaving a dry but tacky film with a drying effect.
• W/O creams (cleansing creams; winter or cold creams) have more oil than water; cold creams are moisturisers that must be emollient, give a cooling sensation and leave a non-occlusive oil film; they are used for chapped and dry skin.
• Type is shown by the dye-staining test: a water-soluble dye stains the globules blue in w/o creams, whereas a coloured background with colourless globules indicates o/w.

questions.question:
Medicated suppositories prepared by pour moulding with a low-viscosity fatty base show settling of drug particles, some suppositories are brittle and fracture, and others have a hole at the open end with weight variation between units.
(a) Identify the problems and their causes.
(b) Explain the formulation or processing factors responsible.
(c) State the corrective measures.
(d) Name the evaluation tests that detect them and the limits given.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Sedimentation of drug (low viscosity of the melted base, so suspended particles settle, and a wide gap between melting and solidifying points leaves the base liquid at low temperature while the apex collects the drug); brittleness; and holes and weight variation from volume contraction and trapped air.
(b)
• Synthetic fatty bases with a high degree of hydrogenation, high stearate content and high solid content at room temperature are brittle, and synthetic hard fats become brittle if cooled rapidly; melted synthetic fats are less viscous than cocoa butter, and sedimentation leads to non-uniform drug distribution and localised irritancy.
• On solidification the mass contracts; a hole forms at the open end if the mass contracts while setting, and trapped air forms holes; weight depends on drug concentration, mould volume, specific gravity of the base and mould variation.
(c)
• Sedimentation: use a base with a narrower melting range closer to body temperature, add about 2% aluminium monostearate, or add cetyl, stearyl or myristyl alcohols or stearic acid for consistency.
• Brittleness: keep the temperature difference between melted base and mould minimal, avoid refrigeration, and add small amounts of Tween 80, castor oil, glycerin or propylene glycol for plasticity.
• Holes and weight variation: pour the mass slightly above its congealing temperature into a mould warmed to about the same temperature, or overfill the moulds and scrape off the excess containing the contraction hole; calibrate the mould with the specific base.
(d)
• Surface appearance and shape (fissuring, migration of active, pitting, fat blooming); weight uniformity of 20 suppositories (not more than 2 differ from the average by more than 5%, none by more than 10%); breaking test for brittleness (600 g then 200 g increments each minute).
• Melting range test (37°C), softening time and dissolution (time versus release) tests; the upper weight variation limit is 5%.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the types of instability and the formulation problems of suppositories, including hygroscopicity, incompatibilities, rancidity, brittleness, viscosity and use of water.
(b) State the stabilisation methods, containers, packaging and storage conditions for suppositories.
(c) Explain the chemical or physical basis of rancidity, blooming, hardening on storage and polymorphism in fatty bases.
(d) State the consequences for storage, shelf-life and use, including the tests that follow stability.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Water: causes oxidation of fats, evaporates at high temperature leaving drug to crystallise, favours drug-excipient interaction and bacterial growth, so a preservative may be needed; hygroscopicity: glycero-gelatin loses moisture in dry climates and absorbs it in humid conditions, and PEG bases are hygroscopic (less so as molecular weight rises).
• Incompatibilities: PEG with silver salts, tannic acid, aminopyrine, quinine, ichthammol, aspirin, benzocaine and sulphonamides; sodium barbital, salicylic acid and camphor crystallise out of PEG; high salicylic acid softens PEG; penicillin G is stable in fatty bases but decomposes in PEG; fatty bases with significant hydroxyl value may react with acidic ingredients.
• Viscosity: low-viscosity melted bases allow sedimentation of suspended drug; brittleness: cocoa butter suppositories are elastic but synthetic fats with high hydrogenation, high stearate content and high solids are brittle.
• Volume contraction may leave a hole at the open end and cause weight variation; weight depends on drug concentration, mould volume, specific gravity of the base and mould variation (upper weight variation limit 5%).
(b)
• Stabilisation: 2% aluminium monostearate raises viscosity and keeps solids suspended; cetyl, stearyl or myristyl alcohols or stearic acid improve consistency; Tween 80, castor oil, glycerin or propylene glycol add plasticity; antioxidants such as hydroquinone or B-naphtholquinone resist rancidity; beeswax (4%) offsets softening by volatile oils, phenols or chloral hydrate.
• Containers: aluminium (tin), paper or plastic; they must not touch each other; poor packing causes staining, breakage or deformation by melting; cocoa butter and glycerinated gelatin suppositories are stored preferably in a refrigerator, PEG suppositories at usual room temperature, protected from heat; glycerinated gelatin needs well-sealed containers in a cool place.
• Soap glycerin bases are very hygroscopic and need wrapping in waxed paper or aluminium foil.
(c)
• Rancidity: auto-oxidation and decomposition of unsaturated fats into low and medium molecular weight aldehydes, ketones and acids with strong unpleasant odour; the lower the unsaturated fatty acid content, the higher the resistance; a higher iodine value raises the chance of decomposition by moisture, acids and oxygen.
• Cocoa butter exists in four crystalline states (alpha, gamma and beta-prime unstable; beta stable); over-heating then cooling yields unstable gamma (melts about 15°C) or alpha (about 20°C) crystals that return to the stable form after at least 4 days; unstable forms have low melting points and conversion to the stable form raises the melting range.
• On storage cocoa butter suppositories bloom (white powdery deposit), avoided by storing at uniform cool temperatures and wrapping in foils; fat-based suppositories harden because slow crystallisation to the more stable polymorph shifts the melting range upwards.
(d)
• Heat just below the melting range soon after manufacture speeds the ageing process; the softening time test and differential scanning calorimetry are stability-indicating methods.
• Consequences: store cool and wrapped, away from heat (refrigerate fatty and glycero-gelatin suppositories), prevent over-heating during preparation, and avoid PEG with incompatible drugs.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the principle of immediate-release, extended-release and delayed-release oral dosage forms.
(b) Relate each system to the examples and terms given (suffixes, enteric polymers, pellet mixtures).
(c) Explain how modified release improves duration of action, dosing frequency and patient compliance.
(d) State the limitations and trade-offs of these systems.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Immediate release: the drug is released rapidly, plasma concentration peaks soon after administration then falls as metabolism and excretion dominate, so levels are not kept within the therapeutic range for long and the duration of action is short.
• Extended release: the drug is released slowly over an extended time to maintain therapeutic blood levels for a prolonged period; the terms extended-, sustained- and slow-release are used interchangeably, while controlled release means delivery at a predetermined rate for a defined time.
• Delayed release: designed to target release to a specific site; the FDA defines it as releasing a drug at a time other than promptly after administration; there is a lag time and the systems may be combined with immediate release or other modified-release technologies.
(b)
• Product designations: CR (controlled release), LA (long-acting), ER, XL and XR (extended release); compressed tablets can be formulated for extended, sustained, prolonged or delayed release; an example of delayed release is the enteric coated Bisacodyl tablet.
• Delay is achieved with an enteric polymeric film (polyacids with carboxyl groups, pH-dependent solubility): intact in the low-pH stomach, dissolving when ionised in the small intestine; polymers include cellulose acetate phthalate (soluble from about pH 5.2), polyvinyl acetate phthalate, acrylic derivatives and HPMC phthalate.
• In capsules, sustained release uses pellets: a mixture might contain 30% uncoated pellets for immediate release, 30% each of coated pellets releasing at 4 hours and 8 hours, and 10% neutral pellets used to fill the capsule; each batch is coloured differently and receives a different coating thickness.
(c)
• The traditional dose three or four times a day gives periods of excess and deficiency in blood concentration; extended-release systems reduce dosing frequency and remove fluctuations in blood concentration.
• The common goal of modified release is to enhance therapeutic benefit, minimise side-effects and improve overall disease management; multiple dosing of immediate-release forms may be tolerated for short-term treatment but is not desirable for chronic conditions.
• Delayed release protects drug from acid, protects the stomach from irritation and favours absorption distal to the stomach; fewer doses per day is the stated benefit.
(d)
• Extended-release systems have a slower onset of action than immediate release (but a longer duration).
• Delayed-release systems give no drug release immediately (a lag time); in capsules, coating requires considerable formulation skill and quality control equipment found in manufacturing facilities.
• Film coating polymer solubility must be chosen: highly soluble for immediate release and lowly soluble for controlled release.

(a)
Tablet: compressed solid dosage form with additives; hard gelatin capsule: two-piece shell (cap and body) filled with powder or pellets; soft gelatin capsule: one-piece plasticized gelatin shell filled with liquid, semi-solid or paste (capsules are solid preparations enclosed in a soft or hard soluble shell).
(b)
• Tablet: dose precision, lowest cost, greatest stability, but drugs with poor wettability and slow dissolution are hard to formulate with full bioavailability, and some resist compression.
• Hard capsule: easy to swallow, tasteless, odourless, elegant, no secondary coating needed; utilisation exceeds soft capsules about 10-fold; capsule shells are sensitive to moisture (13-16% moisture), and gelatin carries a risk of transmissible spongiform encephalopathy.
• Soft capsule: flexible plasticized shell; bioavailability of hydrophobic drugs can be significantly increased; suits lipid solutions, suspensions and pastes and gives better absorption than a tablet or powder; masks unpleasant taste and odour; avoids tableting problems such as poor compaction and weight or content non-uniformity; improves stability of oxidation-prone drugs.
• Soft capsule limits: the shell is a more dynamic system (moisture, plasticizer, drug or volatile components can migrate), so shelf-life programmes must test leakage, brittleness and pellicle formation.
(c)
Tablets: hardness, friability, weight variation, thickness, disintegration, dissolution, assay; capsules: weight variation (10 capsules), content uniformity, disintegration, dissolution, moisture content (Karl Fischer), leakage and integrity inspection, microbial content, moisture permeation.
(d)
The soft gelatin capsule (or a liquid-filled hard capsule) is chosen for the poorly soluble drug because it enhances solubility and absorption; development of soft gels is of growing interest for BCS class II or IV compounds.
questions.question:
A poorly water-soluble drug (a BCS class II or IV compound) must be given orally. The choice is between a tablet, a powder-filled hard gelatin capsule and a soft gelatin capsule (lipid solution or suspension).
(a) Identify each dosage form.
(b) Compare their advantages and limitations and their release or absorption behaviour.
(c) State the evaluation tests that differentiate them.
(d) Justify the final choice.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Loss of water solubility of the gelatin shell: the capsules develop a skin or pellicle, show retarded dissolution and may fail the USP dissolution specification; the decrease in solubility is presumed to result from gelatin cross-linking caused by impurities such as formaldehyde.
(b)
• Exposure to high humidity and temperature or to trace aldehydes cross-links gelatin; gelatin is a protein and is unstable from a chemical viewpoint; moisture transfer between shell and contents depends on relative hygroscopicity and can also retard disintegration.
• Drug absorption and physiological availability depend on the drug being dissolved at the site of absorption, so retarded dissolution reduces availability.
(c)
• Protect from humidity and temperature extremes (relative humidity 40-60%; empty shells at 15-25°C and 35-65% relative humidity); equilibrate shell and contents to the same relative humidity before filling; use moisture-protective strip or blister packs with desiccant.
• Non-gelatin shells (HPMC, starch capsules) are described as non-cross-linking: HPMC capsules were developed as a non-cross-linking shell with gelatin-like dissolution and starch capsules show no cross-linking.
(d)
• Dissolution test (rate and extent of dissolution; ensures similar release between batches and with the clinically effective batch); disintegration test (basket-rack 30 cycles per minute, 37 ± 2°C).
• Moisture content by Karl Fischer titration; moisture permeation test; stability testing and shelf-life testing, which observe dissolution and pellicle formation.
questions.question:
Hard gelatin capsules that were exposed to high humidity and temperature, and to trace aldehydes, develop a skin during dissolution testing, dissolve slowly and fail the dissolution specification.
(a) Identify the problem and its cause.
(b) Explain the formulation or processing factor responsible.
(c) State the corrective measure.
(d) Name the evaluation tests that detect it.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Film-coated tablet: tablet covered by a thin polymer layer sprayed as a coating liquid (polymer, plasticizer, colorant, solvent) in a rotating coating pan; sugar-coated tablet: successive application of sucrose solutions in stages (sealing, sub-coating, smoothing, colouring, polishing, printing); both are coated tablets taken orally (film coated e.g. metronidazole, sugar coated e.g. multivitamin).
(b)
• Film coating: better mechanical strength, little weight increase (2-3% or 2-5%), retains embossed markings, logo or breakline, avoids sugar, single stage and one piece of equipment, batch time 1.5-2 hours, easily adaptable for modified release, and less likely to be mistaken for candy; polymers include HPMC, methylcellulose, hydroxypropylcellulose and methacrylate amino ester copolymer.
• Sugar coating: elegant, rounded, highly glossed and highly coloured, but weight increase of 50-100%, no breaklines (logo only by printing), multiple stages and several pieces of equipment, difficult on a small scale, more than 8 hours (could be days), and mostly immediate release unless special treatment is given at the sealing stage.
• For gastric protection, enteric coating is possible for both film and sugar coating; enteric polymers (cellulose acetate phthalate, polyvinyl acetate phthalate, acrylic derivatives, HPMC phthalate) are insoluble at low pH and dissolve from about pH 5.2, preventing disintegration in the stomach (pH 1.5-3.5).
(c)
Weight variation or weight gain by coating (2-3% versus 50-100%); appearance (retains contour versus rounded and polished); disintegration (coated tablets 1-2 hours; uncoated 5-30 minutes); dissolution (basket or paddle); thickness and diameter; hardness; assay.
(d)
Film coating is the choice when markings or a breakline, a thin coat and modified or enteric release are needed; sugar coating is chosen mainly for elegance and gloss with immediate release.
questions.question:
A patient needs a coated tablet of a drug. The choice is between a film-coated tablet and a sugar-coated tablet, and the tablet may need to protect the drug from gastric acid.
(a) Identify each dosage form and its coating process.
(b) Compare their advantages, limitations and release behaviour.
(c) State the evaluation tests that differentiate them.
(d) Justify the final choice for the patient.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Cocoa butter (theobroma oil) and synthetic hard fats (Suppocire, Witepsol, Fattibase) are fatty bases; macrogols (PEGs, Carbowax) and glycero-gelatin bases are water-miscible and water-soluble bases.
(b)
• Cocoa butter: melts at 30-35°C and at body temperature, non-reactive and seldom irritant, but melts readily in warm weather, goes rancid, over-heating gives unstable polymorphs, adheres to moulds, has a low water number and may leak.
• Synthetic hard fats: solidifying point unaffected by overheating, good oxidation resistance, small melting-setting gap so they set quickly, graded melting ranges to suit climatic conditions, good water absorption and no mould lubricant needed; but brittle if cooled rapidly, less viscous (greater sedimentation risk).
• Macrogols: melting point often around 50°C (above body temperature), so cool storage is not critical and they suit hot climates; drug release depends on dissolving, sustained effect, high viscosity so less leakage, no laxative effect, less microbial contamination; but hygroscopic (dip in water before insertion), poor bioavailability from drug retention, incompatibilities (e.g. benzocaine, penicillin) and brittleness.
• Glycero-gelatin: does not melt but dissolves in rectal secretion; disadvantages are laxative osmotic effect, rectal irritation, unpredictable solution time, hygroscopicity, likely microbial contamination, long preparation and the need to lubricate the mould.
(c)
Melting range, solidification point, solid fat index, hydroxyl, saponification, iodine, water and acid values of the base; for suppositories the melting range test at 37°C, liquefaction (softening) time, breaking test, dissolution test and stability test.
(d)
For a hot climate the macrogol base (or a synthetic hard fat grade chosen for the climate) is preferred over cocoa butter, which melts readily in warm weather; PEG suppositories are stored at usual room temperature without refrigeration, while cocoa butter and glycero-gelatin suppositories are stored preferably in a refrigerator; compatibility with the drug must be checked, since some drugs are incompatible with PEG.
questions.question:
A patient living in a hot climate needs a suppository for the same drug. The choice is between cocoa butter, a synthetic hard fat, a macrogol (PEG) base and a glycero-gelatin base.
(a) Identify each base and its class.
(b) Compare their advantages, limitations and release behaviour.
(c) State the evaluation tests that differentiate them.
(d) Justify the final choice for the patient.

questions.answerText:
(a)
The base has dried out and cracked because water is the external phase and evaporates; the thinning is the base losing viscosity and turning essentially into a lotion once the amount of added liquid reaches a critical amount.
(b)
• O/W emulsifying bases contain emulsifiers and water, so they can have compatibility issues, chemical stability issues and microbial contamination risk; they can absorb only limited amounts of water or alcohol, and are less protective, less emollient and less occlusive than w/o emulsions.
• If the volume of oil to be incorporated exceeds what the internal phase can emulsify, the emulsion is overloaded; emulsifying bases are anionic, cationic or non-ionic according to the emulsifying agent.
(c)
• Store the base in a tight container and add humectants, which hold on to water and slow dehydration (glycerin, hydroxyethyl urea, betaine, sodium PCA, sodium-L-lactate are examples given); do not exceed the capacity for added liquid or oil; extra emulsifiers such as polysorbate or Tween 80 can be added when too much oil is to be emulsified.
• Preservatives (e.g. organic acids, parabens) and antioxidants protect against microbial and oxidative alteration.
(d)
• Organoleptic properties (colour, odour, texture); pH with a digital pH meter; spreadability (two glass slides, 100 g for 5 minutes, S = m x l / t); viscosity (Brookfield viscometer); homogeneity (visual and touch); ease of removal by washing with tap water.
• Emulsion type by dye staining under the microscope; irritancy study (1 sq. cm area, up to 24 h); content uniformity; in-vitro skin penetration (Franz diffusion cell) and rate of release.
(e)
Creams: well-closed containers with closures that minimise microbial contamination, or collapsible metal or plastic tubes; label the name and concentration of any added antimicrobial preservative and the storage conditions; store below 25°C unless otherwise directed and do not freeze.
questions.question:
An oil-in-water emulsifying ointment base kept in a loosely closed container has dried out and cracked. In another batch so much aqueous liquid was added that the base thinned and no longer stays where it is applied.
(a) Identify the problems and their cause.
(b) Explain the formulation factors responsible.
(c) State the corrective measures.
(d) Name the evaluation tests that detect such defects.
(e) State the packaging, labelling and storage conditions given for such semisolids.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Rectal suppository (solid dosage form inserted into a body orifice, melting, softening or dissolving to act locally or systemically); a fatty (oleaginous) base, cocoa butter; adult rectal suppositories weigh 2 g and infant ones 1 g, usually 32 mm long, cylindrical with one or both ends tapered.
(b)
• Pour moulding, the most common method: melt the base on a water bath, suspend or emulsify the drug in it, and pour into cooled metal (chrome or nickel plated) or plastic moulds.
• Calibrate the mould with the specific base, since densities differ (cocoa butter 0.86 g/mL gives 1.72 g in a 2 mL cavity; PEG 400 at 1.125 g/mL gives 2.25 g).
• Displacement: 1.5 g boric acid displaces 1 g cocoa butter, so 0.5 g boric acid displaces 0.3 g of cocoa butter; the base weight is reduced by this amount per suppository; prepare an excess.
(c)
• Cocoa butter shows polymorphism: melting at not more than 36°C and slow cooling gives the stable beta form, whereas over-heating gives unstable forms melting at about 15-20°C that revert over about 4 days or more.
• Cocoa butter sticks to the mould (little contraction), so a water-soluble lubricant (different in nature from the base) is used; air trapped can leave holes, avoided by pouring slightly above the congealing temperature into a warm mould or overfilling and scraping off the excess.
(d)
Suppositories must not touch each other; pack in aluminium, paper or plastic, or in cardboard boxes or plastic containers with compartments for 6 or 12; protect from heat, preferably in a refrigerator (cocoa butter melts easily and goes rancid).
(e)
Keep the suppository in the lower part of the rectum (the upper haemorrhoidal vein drains into the portal circulation); an evacuation enema may be given before insertion; a patient who is not well positioned may leak the melted base.
questions.question:
A pharmacist receives an order for rectal suppositories containing 0.5 g of boric acid each in a cocoa butter base. Boric acid is available as bulk powder with a displacement factor of 1.5 in cocoa butter.
(a) Identify the dosage form and its type or class.
(b) Outline the step-by-step preparation, including the displacement calculation.
(c) Identify the incompatibility or special precautions with this base.
(d) State the container, labelling and storage requirements.
(e) Give the patient counselling points.

(a) Define microencapsulation and describe the structures of microcapsules.
(b) State the objectives of encapsulation.
(c) Describe the three steps of an encapsulation process and the methods of dispersion and stabilisation.
(d) Describe encapsulation by coating, agglomeration and layering.
(e) Relate these parts to the examples and applications that are known for them.
(f) Explain how microencapsulation improves a property of a product and the limitations or trade-offs that result.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Entrapment of a compound or system inside a dispersed material for immobilization, protection, controlled release, structuration and functionalization; the active may be a solution, suspension or emulsion, ranging from small molecules to peptides, drugs, DNA and cells.
• A true microcapsule is a liquid core surrounded by a membrane; structures range from hollow molecules (cyclodextrin), nanocapsules, nanospheres and liposomes to hydrogel beads and solid microspheres of 2-3 mm; below a few micrometres is nanoencapsulation and above 1 mm macroencapsulation.
(b)
Five objectives: immobilization or entrapment; protection (vitamins, polyunsaturated fatty acids, drugs destroyed in gastric transit); controlled release (a drug delivered with well-defined kinetics, limited or made more rapid); structuration (liquid converted to powder, pharmacy dosage forms); functionalisation (e.g. permeability regulated by pH).
(c)
• Three steps: incorporate the active in the core (liquid or solid); a mechanical operation (liquid-in-air dropping or spraying, or emulsification; spraying solution on agitated solid particles); stabilisation by chemical (polymerisation), physicochemical (gelation, coacervation) or physical (drying, solidification) processes.
• Dispersion: prilling (laminar flow, size dispersion below 10%; electrostatic generators to 20 micrometres at 10 kV, nozzle resonance, jet cutter for high viscosity, spinning disks); spraying (high productivity, size dispersion often above 30%); emulsification (low shear, static mixers); microemulsification (sub-micrometre droplets).
• Stabilisation: solidification (hot-melt prilling, spray cooling), evaporation (spray drying, solvent evaporation), gelation (alginate in calcium ions, agarose by cooling), polymerisation (interfacial, in situ), coacervation (simple with one polymer, complex with two), micellar (liposomes).
(d)
Coating needs agitation (fluid bed or pan), spraying (top spray, bottom spray or Wurster) and solidification (hot air drying, hot-melt coating, dry powder technology); spraying too fast causes agglomeration; layering builds active layers on small particles.
(e)
Examples: alginate dropped in a calcium bath forms hydrogel beads; agarose gels on cooling; coating brown sugar with crystalline sugar gives a flowing powder; industrial enzymes are sold encapsulated to avoid allergic problems; iron is encapsulated to protect fatty acids from oxidation.
(f)
• Improvement: fragile ingredients are protected from oxygen, shear and gastric transit and released with defined kinetics; a first encapsulation ensures immobilization and stabilisation while a coating controls protection and release.
• Trade-offs: encapsulation is costly and must be justified; spray and emulsification give wide size dispersion; prilling requires low flow rates; electrostatic generation yields only a few millilitres per hour; nozzle resonance is damped if viscosity is too high.
• Microcapsules are generally a technique to overcome process limitations rather than an end-product; engineered systems remain inferior to biological cells.
• Many challenges and opportunities remain in the field.

questions.question:
(a) Describe microcapsules: definition, parts, size range and the types.
(b) Describe the mechanisms of drug release from microcapsules.
(c) Describe the core and coating materials, the factors influencing the properties of microcapsules and the techniques of preparation.
(d) Relate these parts to the examples and applications given.
(e) Explain how microcapsules improve a property of a drug product and the limitations or trade-offs that result.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Microencapsulation encloses a substance inside a miniature capsule; a microcapsule is a small sphere with a uniform wall; the inner material is the core or internal phase and the wall is the shell or coating; size range 1 micrometre to 7 mm; solids, liquids and gases can be encapsulated; a solid or crystalline core gives irregular capsules, a liquid core gives simple spheres.
• Types: mononuclear (single core), polynuclear (multiple core) and matrix type.
(b)
• Four release mechanisms: diffusion through pores of the wall (most common, monolithic system following the Higuchi equation, depending on dissolution rate and on penetration of fluid and escape of dissolved drug); dissolution of the polymer coat (depends on solubility and coat thickness); degradation-controlled monolithic release; erosion by pH or enzymatic hydrolysis of the coat.
• Release depends on size, shape, core solubility, diffusibility, partition coefficient and coat thickness and porosity; it follows zero-order kinetics (constant release rate), while monolithic types show release dependent on the square root of time for the first half of release.
(c)
• Core may be solid (active, stabilisers, diluents, excipients, release retardants) or liquid; coating should give controlled release, be flexible, strong, impermeable, stable, film-forming, chemically compatible and non-reactive with the core.
• Higher polymer concentration raises encapsulation efficiency, a viscous dispersed phase lowers porosity and sustains release, a larger continuous phase volume speeds solidification and raises particle size, and a rapid temperature rise during solvent removal gives a thin wall and large hollow core with burst release, whereas stepwise heating gives controlled release.
• Physical methods: air suspension coating, coacervation, pan coating (particles above 600 micrometres), centrifugal extrusion (liquids or slurries, 400-2000 micrometres), spray drying and congealing; chemical methods: solvent evaporation, interfacial polymerisation, interfacial cross-linking, in situ polymerisation (0.2-75 micrometres), matrix polymerisation; physicochemical: coacervation phase separation and ionotropic gelation (alginate with calcium, zinc, iron or aluminium).
(d)
Examples: vitamins A and K protected from moisture and oxygen; the Lucrin depot (lyophilised lactic acid polymer with a leuprolide acetate core for prostate cancer, breast cancer and endometriosis) reduces multiple dosing; protection of drugs from humidity, light, oxygen or heat.
(e)
• Improvement: sustained or prolonged release, controlled release rate, increased stability, masking of taste and odour, better patient compliance, conversion of liquid drugs to free-flowing powder, reduced toxicity and gastric irritation, and an altered site of absorption.
• Trade-offs: drug release from microcapsules is complex and depends on physical form, core properties and coat properties; a rapid temperature rise causes burst release; spray drying is only suited to heat-sensitive drugs; centrifugal extrusion suits only liquids or slurries and pan coating only particles above 600 micrometres.
• Microcapsules were reported to be a better delivery system for sustaining release and targeting a specific site, reducing toxicity and adverse effects.

questions.question:
A drug is degraded by acid at low pH, irritates the stomach and is preferentially absorbed distal to the stomach. A tablet that releases the drug only after it leaves the stomach is needed (an enteric-coated Bisacodyl tablet is an example of this class).
(a) Identify the most suitable dosage form and the tablet class it belongs to.
(b) Justify the choice with reference to route, stomach and intestinal pH, absorption and patient factors.
(c) List the additives required in the tablet and the function of each, and name the coating polymers.
(d) Outline the method of preparation.
(e) State the key evaluation tests with the limits given for them.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Enteric-coated tablet, a delayed-release compressed tablet taken orally (e.g. enteric coated Bisacodyl tablet); a delayed-release form releases the drug at a time other than promptly after administration and shows a lag time to target a specific site.
(b)
• The enteric coating prevents disintegration in the acidic stomach (pH 1.5 to 3.5) and allows release in the small intestine (pH 5.5 to 7.5).
• Reasons: prevents acid attack on the active at low pH, protects the stomach from drug irritation, and facilitates absorption of a drug preferentially absorbed distal to the stomach; enteric polymers are polyacids with carboxyl groups whose film stays intact at low pH and dissolves when ionised at higher pH.
• Patient factor: tablets are difficult to swallow for children and unconscious patients; tablets are the most popular dosage form (about 70% of medicines dispensed).
(c)
• Diluent (bulking agent, e.g. lactose, the most common); binder (e.g. acacia, gelatin 10-20% solution, starch paste 10-20%, PVP 2%) for cohesion; disintegrant (starch 5-20% of tablet weight, or superdisintegrants croscarmellose, crospovidone, sodium starch glycolate) to break up the tablet.
• Lubricant (stearic acid, magnesium stearate, talc) prevents sticking to dies and punches; glidant (talc 5%, colloidal silica 0.25-3%) improves flow; colouring and flavouring agents are also used as additives.
• Enteric polymers: cellulose acetate phthalate (soluble from about pH 5.2), polyvinyl acetate phthalate, acrylic derivatives, hydroxypropyl methylcellulose phthalate; enteric coating is possible for both film and sugar coating; a film coat contains polymer, plasticizer, colorant and solvent.
(d)
• Wet granulation: weigh and blend, add liquid binder to form a damp mass, screen the damp mass (6 or 8 mesh), dry the granules, dry screen (12-20 mesh), lubricate and blend, then compress.
• Coating: tablets are agitated in the coating apparatus, the coating solution is sprayed on, warm air removes the solvent and leaves a solid film.
(e)
• Appearance and markings; weight variation (20 tablets); thickness and diameter; hardness (4-8 kg acceptable for uncoated tablets); friability (accepted if loss is 1% or less).
• Disintegration (USP basket, 37°C; coated tablets 1-2 hours); dissolution (basket or paddle apparatus at 37 ± 0.5°C); assay/content uniformity (9 of 10 tablets within 85-115% of label claim, none outside 75-125%).

questions.question:
(a) Describe the methods of preparing ointments (incorporation, fusion, emulsification), with steps, equipment and critical control points.
(b) Describe how the choice of method and the order of addition depend on the ingredients.
(c) State the finished-product evaluation tests for ointments, with the procedures and limits given.
(d) Explain the faults that can arise in semisolid bases and how each is prevented or corrected.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Both on a large and small scale ointments are prepared by three general methods, the choice depending primarily on the nature of the ingredients: incorporation, fusion and emulsification.
• Incorporation: components are mixed by various means until uniform; on a small scale in a mortar with a pestle, or with a spatula and an ointment slab (a large glass or porcelain plate) to triturate the ingredients.
• Fusion: all or some components are melted together and cooled with constant stirring until congealed; components not melted are added to the congealing mixture while it is cooled and stirred.
• Emulsification: melt the water-immiscible components (oils, waxes) in a steam bath at about 70-75°C; heat an aqueous solution of heat-stable water-soluble components to the same temperature; add it slowly with constant mechanical stirring, hold the temperature for 5-10 minutes to prevent crystallisation of waxes, and cool slowly with stirring until congealed.
(b)
• Heat-labile substances and volatile components are added last, when the mixture is cool enough to avoid decomposition or volatilisation; mineral oil is used as a levigating substance to wet and incorporate solids into oleaginous bases.
• Some waxes solidify if the aqueous solution is colder than the oleaginous melt, so both are brought to the same temperature before mixing.
(c)
• Content uniformity (assay of a known weight); penetration (rubbing on skin and weighing unabsorbed ointment; in-vitro Franz diffusion cell or flow-through cell with mouse or human cadaver skin between donor and receptor compartments); rate of release (zone of inhibition on seeded nutrient agar, e.g. Staphylococcus aureus, or smeared test tubes with saline or serum).
• Absorption in blood stream (in vivo only; drug estimated in plasma or urine); irritant effect (rabbit skin and eyes or human skin; read at 24, 48, 72 and 96 hours; patches within 2 weeks indicate irritancy).
• Draize eye test: test material in one eye of each of six albino rabbits with the other eye as control, not washed and examined at 24, 48 and 72 hours; positive if ulceration, corneal opacity, iris inflammation or conjunctival swelling occurs; irritant if up to four of the six rabbits are positive, non-irritant if none or only one is positive.
(d)
• O/W bases dry out and crack when water evaporates (prevented by a tight container and humectants); too much added liquid thins the base into a lotion; too much oil beyond emulsifying capacity needs extra emulsifier such as polysorbate or Tween 80.
• Water-soluble (macrogol) bases soften greatly with water so aqueous solutions are not effectively incorporated, and macrogols reduce the activity of phenolic antiseptics; emulsifying bases may have chemical stability and microbial contamination issues; hydrocarbon bases only take small amounts of aqueous preparations.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the types of instability and deterioration affecting creams and the factors that promote them.
(b) State the stabilisation methods, including the classes and examples of antimicrobial preservatives, antioxidants, humectants and waxes.
(c) State the containers, closures, labelling and storage conditions for creams.
(d) Explain the chemical or physical basis of these instabilities.
(e) State the consequence for storage, shelf-life and use.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Microbial instability: all products containing water and organic or inorganic compounds under suitable physicochemical conditions are exposed to microbial contamination and need protection against microbial proliferation and degradation, in the closed pack until use and in an open container throughout use.
• Oxidative instability: exposure to oxygen can alter the product; physical instability: separation of oil and liquid components of the emulsion, and drying out of o/w bases through evaporation of the external water phase, which can crack.
(b)
• Preservation systems may be intrinsic or extrinsic; classes of antimicrobial preservatives: organic acids (benzoic, propionic, salicylic, sorbic, dehydroacetic, formic, undecylenic, citric); alcohols and phenols (parabens, triclosan, chlorobutanol, chlorocresol, chloroxylenol, phenoxyethanol, benzyl alcohol).
• Aldehydes and formaldehyde releasers (imidazolidinyl urea, diazolidinyl urea, DMDM hydantoin, bronopol, methenamine); quaternary ammonium compounds, which are cationic surfactants (benzalkonium chloride, cetrimonium bromide); biguanides (chlorhexidine, polyaminopropyl biguanide); synthetic preservatives work effectively at low concentration.
• Antioxidants protect against alteration by oxygen; waxes (beeswax, carnauba wax, ceresin, spermaceti) help keep an emulsion from separating and increase thickness and adherence; humectants (glycerin and others) absorb or retain moisture and slow dehydration.
(c)
• Pack in well-closed containers with closures that minimise contamination with micro-organisms, or in collapsible tubes of suitable metal or plastic (aluminium collapsible tubes remain collapsed as product is removed; metal containers can react with the product, which is prevented by lacquer coating); label the name and concentration of any added antimicrobial preservative and the storage conditions.
• Store at temperatures below 25°C unless otherwise directed and do not freeze.
(d)
• Water, nutrients and organic compounds support microbial growth; the FDA position is that cosmetics need not be sterile, but must not be contaminated with pathogenic micro-organisms and non-pathogens must be low.
• In an o/w cream water is the continuous phase, so evaporation dries the product and, if enough water is lost, it cracks; humectants hold water against this loss.
• In a w/o cream water droplets are dispersed in an oily continuous phase and the oil content exceeds the water content; oxygen exposure alters oxidisable ingredients, which antioxidants protect.
(e)
Preserved creams in closed, well-closed or tubed packs remain protected until opened; once opened, the preservative system must protect in use; storage below 25°C and no freezing preserve the emulsion.

(a)
• Semi-solid dosage forms have a semi-solid consistency and are applied to skin or mucous membranes for therapeutic (local or systemic), protective or cosmetic purposes; types are suppositories and dermatologicals (ointments, creams, pastes, gels); a revised ointment definition is a viscous, oleaginous or polymeric semi-solid of soft hydrocarbon (e.g. white petrolatum).
• Ointment bases are classified by level of action (epidermatic, endodermatic, diadermic) and by components (hydrocarbon, fats and fixed oils, silicones, absorption, emulsifying and water-soluble bases); general classes are organogels, hydrogels and emulsion-type bases.
(b)
• Advantages of ointments: site-specific application, avoid first-pass metabolism, suitable for unconscious patients and bitter drugs, chemically more stable than liquids; limitations: staining and less aesthetic, finger contamination, bulky, dose accuracy depends on quantity applied, physico-chemically less stable than solids.
• Routes of semi-solid dosage forms: skin, cornea, rectal tissue, nasal mucosa, vagina, buccal tissue, urethral membrane and external ear lining.
(c)
• Ideal properties: smooth, elegant, non-dehydrating, non-gritty, non-greasy, non-staining, non-irritating, miscible with skin secretion, low sensitisation index, easily applied with efficient drug release, washable; base choice depends on release rate, absorption enhancement, occlusion, drug stability, drug influence on consistency and patient factors.
• Hydrocarbon bases: petrolatum, paraffin (stiffens), liquid paraffin (viscosity adjustment), mineral oil (levigating agent); absorption bases such as hydrophilic petrolatum and wool fat take up water to form w/o emulsions, and Simple Ointment BP (wool fat, hard paraffin, cetostearyl alcohol, soft paraffin) absorbs 15% of its weight of water.
• Emulsifying bases: Emulsifying Ointment BP (anionic: cetostearyl alcohol, sodium lauryl sulphate, white soft paraffin, liquid paraffin), Cetrimide Emulsifying Ointment BP (cationic) and Cetomacrogol Emulsifying Ointment BP (non-ionic); water-soluble bases are macrogols, which are washable and absorb serous discharges, but reduce the activity of phenolic antiseptics.
• Beeswax and spermaceti are weak surfactants used to stabilise o/w emulsifying ointments; humectants slow drying of o/w bases; polysorbate or Tween 80 is added when too much oil is to be emulsified.
(d)
• Pastes are homogeneous semi-solid preparations containing a high concentration (20% w/w or more) of insoluble powder (starch, zinc oxide, calcium carbonate) dispersed in a suitable base; they are very thick and stiff, less greasy and more absorptive than ointments, adhere well, do not melt at normal temperature and are applied with a spatula or spread on lint.
• Ointments are soft semisolid preparations with medicaments dissolved, suspended or emulsified in the base; they are more greasy, are simply applied, soften or liquefy on application but do not melt, serve as protective or emollient agents and are more macerating, whereas pastes form a protective coating, are porous so perspiration can escape and are less macerating.
• Pastes are mostly applied over moist lesions and do not interfere with non-infected skin, but are mostly unsuitable for the scalp; ointments are indicated in chronic dry lesions and contraindicated in weeping lesions.
• Paste bases: hydrocarbon (soft and liquid paraffin), water-miscible (emulsifying ointment, glycerin) or water-soluble (high and low molecular weight PEGs); pastes are prepared by trituration (liquid or semisolid base) or fusion (semi-solid or solid base).
questions.question:
(a) Define ointments and semi-solid dosage forms, and classify the types and the ointment bases.
(b) State the advantages, limitations and routes of semi-solid dosage forms and ointments.
(c) Explain the formulation basis: the ideal properties, the factors in base selection and the function of each type of base and ingredient.
(d) Distinguish between pastes and ointments.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Hard gelatin capsules hold an equilibrium moisture content of 13-16%; below 12% the shell is brittle and may crack, above 18% it is too soft and may lose shape; the bulk of shell moisture is physically bound and transfers readily between shell and contents depending on their relative hygroscopicity.
• Moisture removal can cause splitting or cracking; moisture transfer to powder contents (reported for deliquescent potassium acetate and sodium cromoglycate) may cause caking and retarded disintegration; high humidity and temperature, or trace aldehydes, cause loss of shell water solubility with a skin or pellicle and retarded dissolution.
• Soft gelatin capsules are a more dynamic system than tablets: atmospheric moisture can permeate the shell or fill, drug or fill liquid may migrate into the shell, plasticizer or residual water may migrate into the fill, and volatile components may escape.
(b)
• Avoid extremes of temperature and keep relative humidity at 40-60% when handling and storing; equilibrate shell and contents to the same relative humidity before filling; empty shells are stored at 15-25°C and 35-65% relative humidity to limit moisture gain or loss.
• Hard capsules are protected in strip packs (hermetically sealed in aluminium foil or plastic film) or blister packs; an ideal film is heat stable, impermeable to moisture, water vapour, air and odours, strong enough for machine handling and easy to tear; desiccants such as silica gel are used with capsules sensitive to humidity.
• Light-resistant containers (amber glass, co-extruded two-layer HDPE bottles with a black inner and white outer layer) suit tablets and capsules; recommended storage conditions are stated on the label, and heat-sensitive products are stored at a lower temperature (e.g. 30°C versus 40°C may be justified).
(c)
Cross-linking of gelatin by impurities such as formaldehyde makes the shell less soluble; gelatin is a protein that is chemically unstable; the plasticizer and water in the shell give flexibility, so loss or gain of these changes brittleness or softness; opacifier (titanium dioxide) reduces light penetration for photosensitive drugs.
(d)
• Capsules are stored within the stated humidity and temperature limits and in moisture-resistant packs so that moisture content stays within 13-16% and dissolution is not retarded.
• Stability testing (stress, long-term and accelerated) determines the storage conditions and anticipated shelf life; soft gelatin capsule testing covers appearance (including brittleness), colour, odour, assay, degradation products, dissolution, microbial content, pH, leakage and pellicle formation, and fill precipitation or cloudiness.
• The moisture permeation test packages the unit with a colour-revealing desiccant pellet at known humidity and compares weights before and after.
• Moisture content is measured by Karl Fischer titration to correlate water content with degradation or release.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the types of instability affecting hard and soft gelatin capsules and the factors affecting them.
(b) State the stabilisation methods, containers, packaging, storage conditions and labelled conditions.
(c) Explain the chemical or physical basis of the instabilities.
(d) State the consequences for storage, shelf-life and use, including the stability testing involved.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Soft gelatin capsule (one-piece, plasticized gelatin shell) with a liquid, semi-solid or paste fill, given orally.
(b)
• The bioavailability of hydrophobic drugs can be significantly increased; absorption is better than from a tablet or powder; useful for poorly water-soluble (BCS class II or IV) compounds; it gives high content uniformity for low-dose drugs, improved stability for highly oxidation-susceptible drugs, and the tasteless gelatin shell masks unpleasant taste and odour.
• Patient and safety factors: easy to swallow, available in many sizes for dosing flexibility, and reduced operator and environmental contamination with highly potent compounds; problems of tableting such as poor compaction and weight or content non-uniformity are avoided.
(c)
• Shell: gelatin (usually alkali-processed type B, about 40% of wet gel) forms the film; plasticizer (glycerol; sorbitol, mannitol) gives flexibility by lowering glass transition temperature and retaining moisture; water 30-40% of wet gel (0.7-1.3 parts per part gelatin) aids manufacture and flexibility.
• Preservatives (potassium sorbate, methyl, ethyl and propyl hydroxybenzoate) prevent bacterial and mould growth; colourant and opacifier (titanium dioxide) give appearance and light protection; EDTA chelates free metals such as iron that catalyse oxidation; flavours and sweeteners improve palatability.
• Fill vehicles: water-immiscible liquids (vegetable and aromatic oils, hydrocarbons, esters, alcohols); water-miscible non-volatile liquids (polyethylene glycols, polysorbate 80); propylene glycol and isopropyl alcohol, depending on concentration and packaging.
(d)
Rotary die process: two plasticized gelatin ribbons are fed continuously and simultaneously with the fill between the rollers; injection swells the ribbons into the die pockets, and the converging dies seal and cut the filled capsules, which fall into a cooled solvent bath so they do not adhere.
(e)
• In-process: gel ribbon thickness and uniformity, seal thickness, fill weight and variation, shell weight and variation, shell moisture before and after drying; finished: leakage by visual inspection, potency and impurities, weight variation (10 capsules cut open, washed), content uniformity (9 of 10 within 85-115%, none outside 75-125%).
• Disintegration (basket-rack 30 cycles per minute, 37 ± 2°C), dissolution, moisture content (Karl Fischer), moisture permeation, microbial content; shelf-life tests cover appearance including brittleness, colour, odour, assay, degradation products, pH, leakage and pellicle formation, and fill precipitation or cloudiness.
questions.question:
A low-dose, poorly water-soluble drug that is susceptible to oxidation and has an unpleasant taste is to be given orally in a form that gives high content uniformity and improved absorption.
(a) Identify the most suitable dosage form.
(b) Justify the choice (route, bioavailability, patient factors).
(c) List the shell components and fill vehicles required and the function of each.
(d) Outline the method of preparation.
(e) State the key in-process, finished-product and shelf-life tests.

questions.explanation: The micromassage effect arises as longitudinal ultrasound waves alternately compress and decompress cells, affecting tissue fluid movement within the interstitial space. This mechanical action contributes to sclerolytic effects and the release of contractures and adhesions. It represents a distinctly mechanical, rather than thermal, therapeutic mechanism.
questions.question: The micromassage effect of ultrasound results from longitudinal waves producing which mechanical action on cells?

questions.explanation: Mercury vapor UV lamps require 5-10 minutes warm-up before output stabilizes and clinical dosimetry measurements are taken, because as mercury vapor temperature increases within the lamp tube during warm-up, vapour pressure rises progressively, altering the proportion of UV wavelengths emitted and total lamp output. Taking dosimetry readings before thermal equilibrium is reached produces inaccurate measurements that would lead to erroneous patient exposure calculations. Regular dosimetry measurement with a calibrated UV meter is essential for safe UV phototherapy, as lamp output decreases progressively with use due to tridymite formation on the lamp envelope.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is calibrating a mercury vapor UV lamp. The lamp output should be tested after a minimum warm-up period of:

questions.explanation: Attenuation refers to the gradual reduction in ultrasound beam intensity as it travels further into tissue, resulting from absorption, reflection, and scattering. As more energy is absorbed superficially, less remains available for deeper tissue effects. This principle underlies the selection of frequency based on target tissue depth.
questions.question: Attenuation of an ultrasound beam describes which overall phenomenon as the wave travels deeper into tissue?

questions.explanation: Delayed Onset Muscle Soreness, occurring after vigorous exercise and typically lasting one to two days, is listed among the injuries treated with phonophoresis. Tendonitis, bursitis, and adhesive capsulitis are also included in this list. The combination of ultrasound and topical medication addresses both inflammation and discomfort in these conditions.
questions.question: Delayed Onset Muscle Soreness is listed among the conditions treated with which combined therapy technique?

questions.explanation: A modest 1 degree Celsius rise in tissue temperature during ultrasound is associated mainly with increased metabolic rate. Larger temperature increases of 2 to 3 degrees are needed to reduce pain and spasm. A 4 degree rise is required to meaningfully increase tissue extensibility and decrease joint stiffness.
questions.question: A tissue temperature increase of approximately 1 degree Celsius during continuous ultrasound primarily produces which thermal effect?

options: Electrical shock from ground fault currents
questions.explanation: Shortwave diathermy generates intense electromagnetic fields at 27.12 MHz that can interfere with nearby electronic equipment including other SWD machines, electromedical devices, patient monitors, infusion pumps, and hearing aids. This electromagnetic interference can cause malfunction of life-critical monitoring equipment and implanted electronic devices including cardiac pacemakers, neurostimulators, and cochlear implants. Physiotherapy departments must maintain SWD equipment at safe distances from electronic devices, install electromagnetic shielding where possible, and ensure patients wearing electronic implants are identified before treatment to prevent potentially fatal device interference.
questions.question: When applying shortwave diathermy near electronic equipment, the physiotherapist must be aware that the primary risk is:

questions.explanation: Paraffin bath therapy delivers superficial conductive heat through direct contact between the paraffin-oil mixture and skin surface. Paraffin wax has a high specific heat capacity and low thermal conductivity, allowing it to hold a large amount of heat energy that transfers gradually through conduction. This sustained superficial heating increases skin and periarticular tissue temperature, improving joint extensibility and reducing pain stiffness. The physiotherapist exploits the therapeutic temperature range of 47-54°C to achieve tissue warming while keeping the burn risk low due to paraffin's low conductivity.
questions.question: A physiotherapist applies a paraffin bath for a patient with hand osteoarthritis. The therapeutic mechanism primarily utilized is:

questions.explanation: Ultrasound travels at approximately 1500 metres per second through saline solution, considerably faster than the roughly 350 metres per second observed in air. Sound generally travels more rapidly through denser media. Tissue velocity is thought to closely approximate that of saline.
questions.question: The velocity of ultrasound through saline solution is approximately how many metres per second?

questions.explanation: Air-activated heat wraps use the exothermic oxidation of iron powder when exposed to atmospheric oxygen, generating heat at approximately 40°C sustained for up to eight hours. This prolonged low-level heat delivery provides sustained muscle relaxation, pain relief, and increased tissue extensibility without burning risk, making these devices suitable for home use between clinical sessions. The extended heating duration is clinically significant because chronic musculoskeletal pain conditions benefit from sustained rather than brief heat exposure, and eight hours of treatment during sleep or daily activities extends physiotherapy beyond clinic attendance.
questions.question: A physiotherapist applies air-activated heat wraps for musculoskeletal pain management. These devices maintain temperature at approximately:
For acute injuries, ultrasound treatment frequency is generally recommended at what schedule?
questions.explanation: Acute injuries are generally treated with ultrasound one to two times daily, reflecting the more frequent treatment needs of early-stage tissue conditions. Subacute conditions are typically treated daily, while chronic conditions are treated less often. Treatment frequency should be continually reassessed based on patient response.

questions.question: Ensuring the skin is well moistened and avoiding areas of dry skin is a preparation step specific to which technique?
questions.explanation: Phonophoresis preparation specifically calls for ensuring the skin is well moistened, while avoiding dry skin areas that could impair medication diffusion. Adequate moisture supports effective transdermal transport during ultrasound exposure. This preparation detail reflects the technique's reliance on optimal skin permeability.

questions.question: Tendonitis and bursitis are both listed as conditions appropriately managed using which ultrasound-based combined technique?
questions.explanation: Tendonitis and bursitis are both listed among the injuries treated using phonophoresis, reflecting its role in managing inflammatory soft tissue conditions. The combination of ultrasound and topical anti-inflammatory medication addresses both the mechanical and chemical aspects of these conditions. This combined approach can enhance outcomes compared to ultrasound alone.

questions.question: Which type of topical medication used with phonophoresis is specifically described as blocking pain receptors?
questions.explanation: Anesthetics such as lidocaine block pain receptors and are listed among the categories of topical drugs used in phonophoresis. Counter-irritants like menthol work through a different mechanism, causing localized skin inflammation to relieve pain elsewhere. Steroidal and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory medications represent yet another distinct category used in this technique.

The ultrasound applicator should be cleaned with an alcohol-based swab between treatments rather than simply wiped with tissue. This practice minimises potential transmission of microbial agents between patients. Proper applicator hygiene is an important infection control measure in ultrasound therapy.
questions.question: Care of the ultrasound applicator between patients should include cleaning with which type of preparation?

questions.explanation: Acoustic impedance is calculated as tissue density multiplied by the speed of sound transmission through that tissue. Greater differences in acoustic impedance between adjacent tissues result in greater reflection of ultrasound energy at their interface. This principle explains why bone and air interfaces reflect significantly more energy than soft tissue interfaces.
questions.question: Acoustic impedance of a tissue is mathematically defined as the product of tissue density and which other property?
Treatment parameters that should be documented after ultrasound therapy include duty cycle, intensity, and which other essential value?
questions.explanation: Proper documentation after ultrasound treatment includes output frequency, intensity, duration, and duty cycle. This record ensures continuity of treatment across sessions and allows tracking of the total number of treatments given for a condition. Comprehensive documentation supports both clinical reasoning and accountability.

questions.question: In the dip and wrap method, a hand or foot is typically re-immersed in wax how many times to build adequate thickness?
questions.explanation: The dip and wrap technique requires repeated immersion, typically 6 to 12 times, allowing thin wax layers to build up to roughly 2 to 3 millimetres thick. Each dip is followed by brief cooling before re-immersion. Insufficient repetitions fail to produce adequate insulating thickness.

Standard shortwave diathermy treatment sessions last 15-20 minutes, which provides sufficient time to achieve the desired tissue temperature elevation and maintain therapeutic temperature levels long enough for physiological effects including increased tissue extensibility, enhanced metabolic activity, and pain relief. Shorter sessions may not raise deep tissue temperature adequately, while sessions exceeding 20-30 minutes risk tissue overheating, patient fatigue, and diminishing returns as tissues reach thermal equilibrium. The physiotherapist monitors patient comfort and skin appearance throughout the treatment session.
questions.question: The appropriate duration for a shortwave diathermy treatment session in a typical clinical protocol is:
Increased enzyme activity following ultrasound exposure is listed under which category of physiological effect?
questions.explanation: Increased enzyme activity is listed among the thermal effects produced by continuous mode ultrasound at therapeutic intensities. This effect accompanies increased blood flow and tissue perfusion following meaningful temperature rise. Together these thermal changes support the tissue healing process targeted by ultrasound therapy.

questions.question: Laser therapy following radiotherapy should be avoided for a minimum period of:
questions.explanation: Laser therapy should be avoided for a minimum of 4-6 months following radiotherapy in the irradiated field because radiation-damaged tissue has severely compromised vascular supply, reduced cellular repair capacity, and increased susceptibility to radiation recall reactions. Photobiomodulation stimulating cellular metabolism and proliferation in post-radiation tissue may accelerate any residual malignant cells that survived irradiation, and the compromised vasculature cannot support the increased metabolic demands stimulated by laser therapy. After 4-6 months, the acute radiation effects have resolved sufficiently that laser therapy can be cautiously applied for radiation-induced fibrosis and wound management with oncological clearance.

questions.question: Which form of energy is described as the kinetic energy arising from motion of atoms and molecules?
questions.explanation: Heat or thermal energy results directly from the constant motion of atoms and molecules within a substance. Faster molecular motion corresponds to higher temperature. This kinetic basis distinguishes heat from stored potential energy.

questions.question: Lewis's Hunting Reaction describes which physiological response following prolonged cold exposure?
questions.explanation: Lewis's Hunting Reaction describes a reflex vasoconstriction followed by periodic vasodilation as the body attempts to prevent tissue damage from prolonged cold. Sympathetic fibres and direct vascular effects mediate this cyclical response. This mechanism protects tissue during extended cold exposure.

questions.question: The two most common modes of heat transfer involved in cold application are conduction and which other mechanism?
questions.explanation: Cold therapy primarily removes heat from tissue through conduction and evaporation. Conduction occurs through direct contact with the cooling agent, while evaporation contributes when agents like vapocoolant sprays are used. These mechanisms together account for the cooling effect observed clinically.

options: Pulsed mode is more effective at deep structures
Pulsed mode prevents any tissue heating
Pulsed mode delivers lower mean power with non-thermal effects
Pulsed mode eliminates all electromagnetic fields
Pulsed mode only stimulates nerve regeneration
questions.question: A physiotherapist selects pulsed shortwave diathermy over continuous SWD for a patient in the subacute inflammatory phase because:
questions.explanation: Pulsed SWD allows heat generated during each pulse to dissipate between pulses, delivering electromagnetic energy below the cumulative threshold required for significant tissue temperature elevation while still providing the non-thermal electromagnetic effects on cell membranes, calcium transport, and inflammatory mediator production. In the subacute inflammatory phase, significant additional heating may increase inflammatory activity and pain, making the non-thermal effects of pulsed SWD more appropriate for reducing edema, modulating inflammation, and promoting tissue repair. The physiotherapist adjusts pulse duration, repetition rate, and peak power to remain within non-thermal energy delivery ranges.

options: Even heating throughout the entire region
Greater heating under the larger electrode
No differential heating effect between electrodes
Greater heating concentrated under the smaller electrode
Risk of electrical shock from unequal sizes
questions.explanation: When electrode sizes are unequal in shortwave diathermy application, the electromagnetic field density is greater under the smaller electrode because the same total field energy is concentrated over a smaller surface area, producing greater energy density and therefore greater heating under the smaller electrode. This principle allows the physiotherapist to selectively concentrate heating over a small target structure (such as a small joint or localized trigger point) by placing the smaller electrode directly over the target, while the larger electrode disperses field energy over a broader reference area. This technique is particularly useful for small joint treatment where precision heating is required.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is assessing which electrode size to use for shortwave diathermy over a patient's small wrist joint. Using a smaller electrode over the target area than the opposite larger electrode will produce:
What primary vascular response occurs in skin and soft tissue when local temperature is increased?
questions.explanation: Raising tissue temperature triggers vasodilatation of local blood vessels, increasing regional blood flow. This response is mediated by cutaneous thermoreceptors and chemical vasodilators. Increased blood flow delivers oxygen and nutrients to the heated area.

options: No precaution is necessary at any age
Avoid all patients under 25 years entirely
Use only at maximum intensity settings
Use caution due to the growth plate's sensitivity
questions.explanation: Caution is advised when applying ultrasound over the epiphyseal plates of growing bone, given the sensitivity of this developing tissue. This precaution reflects concern for potential effects on normal growth processes. Such areas require careful clinical judgement regarding intensity and duration of treatment.
questions.question: Which precaution applies specifically to applying ultrasound near the epiphyseal plates of growing bone?

questions.explanation: Fluidotherapy units typically operate between 113 and 117 degrees Fahrenheit, delivering dry heat through circulating cellulose particles. This temperature range allows active range of motion exercises to be performed safely during treatment. The dry heat mechanism differs from the moist heat delivered by hydrocollator packs.
questions.question: Fluidotherapy is typically operated within which approximate dry heat temperature range?

questions.explanation: Luminous infrared generators, which use tungsten filaments heated to high temperatures, emit approximately 70% of their output as short-wave (near) infrared radiation in the 760-1500 nm range, with the remainder as visible light and some long-wave infrared. Short-wave infrared penetrates to 5-10 mm depth, reaching superficial dermis and subcutaneous tissues. Non-luminous generators produce predominantly long-wave (far) infrared with wavelengths of 3000-4000+ nm that penetrates only 1-3 mm, heating almost exclusively the skin surface. This difference determines which generator type is selected for specific therapeutic objectives.
questions.question: A physiotherapist selects a luminous infrared generator for treatment. Compared to non-luminous generators, luminous generators:

options: Converting one form of energy into another
Storing thermal energy for later use
questions.question: A transducer is best defined as a device performing which general function?
questions.explanation: A transducer is broadly defined as a device capable of converting one form of energy into another. In ultrasound therapy, the piezoelectric transducer converts electrical energy into mechanical ultrasonic energy and vice versa. This bidirectional conversion underlies both generation and detection of ultrasound.

questions.question: A physiotherapist applying cryotherapy to an acute ankle sprain should expect the PRIMARY initial vascular response to be:
questions.explanation: The initial vascular response to cold application is vasoconstriction, which reduces blood flow, decreases capillary hydrostatic pressure, and limits fluid extravasation into injured tissues. This mechanism directly reduces acute post-traumatic edema and hemorrhage in the acute sprain phase. Physiotherapists exploit this vasoconstriction therapeutically within the first 48 hours to limit secondary hypoxic injury caused by expanding hematoma compressing adjacent healthy tissue.

questions.question: The pulse repetition rate in pulsed shortwave diathermy typically ranges from:
questions.explanation: Pulsed SWD pulse repetition rates range from 15 to 800 Hz, allowing the physiotherapist to vary the mean power delivered to tissues while maintaining constant peak power. Higher repetition rates deliver more energy per unit time and are used when greater therapeutic effect is desired, while lower rates allow more complete tissue heat dissipation between pulses for non-thermal applications. The combination of adjustable pulse duration (25-500 microseconds) and variable repetition rate gives the physiotherapist precise control over mean power delivered, enabling tailoring of thermal versus non-thermal dosimetry for individual patients.

Because wax is less dense than water, pouring water onto a wax fire causes the burning wax to float and spread rather than be extinguished. A fire blanket or foam extinguisher should be used instead. This is a critical safety precaution in any paraffin treatment area.
options: Wax floats on water and spreads the fire
Water causes wax to solidify safely
Water reacts explosively with mineral oil
questions.question: Why is pouring water onto an overheated paraffin wax fire considered dangerous and ineffective?

questions.explanation: Quartz is a classic example of a crystal exhibiting piezoelectric properties used in ultrasound transducer construction. Other materials such as lead zirconate, barium titanate, and nickel cobalt are also used in modern transducers. These crystals deform mechanically when an alternating current is applied.
questions.question: Which crystal material is classically cited as an example used to generate the piezoelectric effect?
Sound energy beyond the upper limit of human hearing, roughly above 20,000 Hz, is classified as what?
questions.explanation: The normal human hearing range extends from about 16 Hz to 15,000 to 20,000 Hz. Mechanical vibration beyond this upper limit is termed ultrasound rather than audible sound. Therapeutic ultrasound operates well above this threshold, typically between 0.75 and 3 MHz.

options: Higher temperature tolerance enabling more heat
Greater patient comfort from reduced contact
Ability to exercise and perform desensitization simultaneously
Lower infection risk than water-based treatment
questions.question: A physiotherapist selects fluidotherapy over hot packs for a patient with hand burns and hypersensitivity. The specific advantage for this patient is:
questions.explanation: Fluidotherapy uniquely combines convective heat delivery with the ability to perform active movement and desensitization within the treatment chamber simultaneously. For burn patients with hypersensitivity, the gentle flowing cellulose particles provide progressive tactile desensitization while the therapeutic heat improves tissue extensibility and reduces scar stiffness that limits hand function. Active exercise within the heated fluidotherapy chamber achieves simultaneous desensitization, heat therapy, and therapeutic exercise that would require separate treatment episodes with other modalities, making fluidotherapy particularly efficient for patients with hand burns and sensory hypersensitivity.

questions.question: Which of the following is classified as a psychological rather than physical contraindication to ice treatment?
questions.explanation: Psychological factors such as a patient's intolerance or fear of cold are recognised as a distinct contraindication category, separate from physical conditions. Effective cryotherapy requires the patient's receptiveness to the modality for therapeutic benefit. Forcing cold application on an unreceptive patient may reduce treatment effectiveness and compliance.
options: Patient intolerance or fear of cold

questions.question: Elevation of muscle temperature to around 42 degrees Celsius decreases the firing rate of which spindle fibre type?
questions.explanation: Heating to approximately 42 degrees Celsius decreases firing of type II muscle spindle fibres and gamma efferents. This reduces afferent signalling from the spindle and lowers alpha motor neuron activity. The combined effect reduces muscle spasm and promotes relaxation.

When a treatment area exceeds the recommended limit relative to the sound head size, it should be divided into smaller zones treated sequentially. This maintains adequate energy delivery across the entire region. Attempting to treat an oversized area without dividing it risks under-dosing significant portions of tissue.
options: Divide the area into smaller treatment zones
questions.question: For larger treatment areas exceeding the recommended maximum relative to the sound head size, what approach is recommended?

questions.explanation: Infrared-induced erythema (erythema ab igne) produced during therapeutic application persists for approximately 30-60 minutes after treatment cessation, reflecting the vasodilatory response of dermal capillaries during and after heating. This duration distinguishes infrared erythema from ultraviolet erythema, which develops with a latency of several hours and persists for 24-48 hours or more. The temporary nature of infrared erythema without the DNA-damaging and persistent inflammatory mechanisms of UV erythema makes infrared a safer repeated thermal treatment.
