• The organism is a Trypanosoma species (African trypanosome, of the Trypanosoma brucei complex); the wavy membrane described is the "undulating membrane" along which the single free flagellum runs, and the deep-red dot at the posterior end is the "kinetoplast", with the large central nucleus being the trophonucleus.
(b)
• In early stages the trypanosomes may be present in scanty numbers, especially in T. gambiense infection, so a thick film preparation is advocated, stained by Leishman's stain as for malarial diagnosis; wet preparations of the blood may also be used to advantage.
(c)
• The finding is recorded as trypanosomes seen on the peripheral blood film, noting the characteristic undulating membrane and kinetoplast used to identify the organism.
(d)
• A low-grade parasitaemia can be pursued with a concentration method: 5 mL venous blood is mixed with 20 mL of 1% sodium citrate solution, centrifuged at 1000 rpm for 10 minutes, and the plasma supernatant and "buffy-coat" layer are carefully transferred and re-centrifuged (repeated two or three times), examining the deposit each time by making stained films; smears of aspirates from lymph nodes, bone marrow or CSF may also be examined.
questions.question:
Question 55
A thick blood film stained with Leishman's stain from a patient with fever and enlarged posterior cervical lymph nodes shows elongated, sky-blue, flagellate organisms measuring about 15-30 by 1.5-3.5 µm, with a large central reddish-purple nucleus, a single free flagellum running back along a wavy membrane, and a deep-red dot at the posterior end.
(a) Identify the organism and the specific structures described.
(b) State the basic technique used to detect this organism when parasitaemia is low.
(c) State how the finding should be recorded/reported.
(d) State the follow-up practical step(s) that may be taken if the organism is not seen on the film.

Question 47
(a) Describe the basic structure of protozoa, including their locomotor organelles and modes of reproduction.
(b) State the identifying characteristics that distinguish the trophozoite form from the cyst form.
(c) State the standard classification setting in which these structural features are used to group protozoa.
(d) Explain the basic reasoning behind the precaution of examining a fresh/warm specimen when looking for trophozoites.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Protozoa are unicellular organisms able to perform all vital functions of life independently; locomotion takes place by means of three basic types of organelles - flagella, cilia, and pseudopodia - and most activities such as nutrition, respiration and excretion occur through osmosis.
• Reproduction may be asexual (binary fission - transverse in ciliates or longitudinal in flagellates; multiple fission/schizogony as in Plasmodium; or endodyogeny as in Toxoplasma) or sexual (conjugation, as in ciliates; or syngamy/gametogony, as in sporozoa).
(b)
• The trophozoite is the motile, proliferative, labile (actively feeding and moving) form, while encystation is the cellular differentiation from this motile trophozoite form to the dormant, resistant cyst form, which deals with adverse external environmental changes and is an integral part of disease transmission.
(c)
• The shape, size, mode of reproduction and type of locomotive organelle are used to divide protozoa into four major classes: Sarcodina (Rhizopods/Amoebae), Ciliophora (Ciliates), Mastigophora (Flagellates), and Coccidia (Sporozoa).
(d)
• Because the trophozoite is the motile, labile and actively feeding form, it is fragile and loses its distinguishing motility soon after passage; examining the specimen fresh and warm (as with a stool sample passed into a warmed bedpan) gives the best chance of observing the actively motile trophozoite before it degenerates, whereas the more resistant cyst form can withstand some delay.

questions.question:
Question 59
A high vaginal swab is collected from a woman with a foul-smelling vaginal discharge, genital itching and painful urination, in whom Trichomonas vaginalis infection is suspected.
(a) Identify the specimen and the preparation used to detect the organism.
(b) State the principle behind this method of examination.
(c) Describe the step-by-step procedure, including how the specimen should be handled and transported.
(d) State the expected observed result and its interpretation if positive.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The specimen is a vaginal swab, and the preparation used is a "hanging drop" preparation made from the moist swab.
(b)
• The method relies on direct visualization of the organism's characteristic motility, since Trichomonas vaginalis is easily recognized as a motile, pear-shaped flagellate on this preparation.
(c)
• The swab should be placed in a tube so that it is partially covered by warm saline; the tube should be delivered immediately to the laboratory and, if it cannot be examined at once, may be left temporarily in a 37°C incubator; a hanging drop preparation is then made from the moist swab for examination (urethral discharge from a male, or material from prostatic massage, may be examined similarly).
(d)
• A positive result shows a motile, pear-shaped flagellate organism with a single nucleus, four anterior flagella and an undulating membrane running along part of the body length, confirming Trichomonas vaginalis infection.

questions.question:
Question 34
A specimen for viral diagnosis is collected from a patient who is currently in the recovery phase of the illness. Virus is not detected in the specimen, but specific antibody is detected.
(a) Interpret this combination of findings in relation to the phase of illness.
(b) State how this result should be recorded/reported.
(c) State what this result indicates about the appropriateness of the timing of specimen collection for virus isolation versus serology.
(d) State the follow-up action that should have been taken earlier, or should now be taken, based on this timing.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• This combination (virus rarely detected, antibody often detected) is consistent with the recovery phase of the disease, based on the relationship between the phase/stage of disease and the likelihood of detecting virus in the specimen versus detecting specific antibody: during the incubation period virus is rarely present and antibody is undetectable; in the early stage virus is often present and antibody seldom detected; in the acute phase both are often detected; in recovery virus is rarely present but antibody is often detected; and in convalescence virus is rarely present but antibody is usually detected.
(b)
• The result is recorded as virus not isolated, specific antibody detected, with the phase of illness (recovery) noted as the likely explanation.
(c)
• This indicates that specimen collection for virus isolation was not optimally timed, since specimens for virus isolation should be collected as early as possible during the course of illness (when virus is more likely to be present), whereas the recovery/convalescent phase is more suited to detecting antibody.
(d)
• For future or repeat sampling, specimens intended for virus isolation should be collected early in the illness (incubation, early stage, or acute phase), while a convalescent serum sample can be relied upon for serological (antibody) testing at this later recovery stage.

questions.question:
Question 39
A Gram-stained smear prepared from a yeast colony shows Gram-positive oval cells, some of which show budding.
(a) Identify the organism most consistent with this Gram-stain appearance.
(b) State the basic technique used to obtain this observation.
(c) State how this finding should be recorded/reported.
(d) State a follow-up test that can be used to confirm the species identity of the organism.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The appearance of Gram-positive oval cells showing budding is consistent with Candida, seen on Gram staining as Gram positive oval cells that are budding.
(b)
• The basic technique used is Gram staining of a smear prepared from the yeast colony/growth.
(c)
• The finding is recorded as Gram-positive budding oval (yeast) cells seen on smear, consistent with a Candida species.
(d)
• A germ tube test (growth in human or sheep serum at 37°C for about 3 hours, detected as filamentous outgrowth on wet mount) or demonstration of chlamydospores on cornmeal agar can be used as follow-up to confirm identification of the isolate as Candida albicans specifically.

(a)
• The trophozoite is the growing and feeding stage; its shape is not fixed because of constantly changing position, it ranges from 18-40 µm (average 20-30 µm) in size, its cytoplasm is divided into a clear transparent ectoplasm and a granular endoplasm (which contains ingested red blood cells, tissue granules and food materials), and it is actively motile with the help of pseudopodia; it is an anaerobic parasite present in the large intestine.
• The precyst is the intermediate stage between trophozoite and cyst, smaller in size (10-20 µm), round or slightly ovoid with a blunt pseudopodium projecting from the periphery, and no red blood cells or food materials are found in its endoplasm.
• The cyst is the infective form of the parasite, round or oval in shape, 12-15 µm in diameter, surrounded by a highly retractile membrane (the cyst wall) that resists digestion by gastric juice; its cytoplasm shows chromatoidal bars and glycogen masses, but no red blood cells or food particles.
(b)
• The trophozoite's nucleus is single, spherical, 4-6 µm in size, containing a central karyosome and fine peripheral chromatin; the mature cyst is quadrinucleated, and cysts from different strains vary in size (5-20 µm) with one to four nuclear structures, each containing a central karyosome, and one or two chromatoidal bodies (about 2 by 4 µm) may be present within the cyst.
(c)
• These stages are examined diagnostically in stool samples, with the actively motile trophozoite best collected in a specimen passed into a warmed bedpan and examined with as little delay as possible, and the cyst best demonstrated with an iodine (Lugol's iodine) preparation, or with iron haematoxylin stains for the sharpest picture of chromatoidal bodies and nuclei.
(d)
• The cyst wall is resistant to digestion by gastric juice in the human stomach, allowing the mature (quadrinucleated) cyst passed in stool to survive the acidic stomach environment of a new host after ingestion, whereas the trophozoite is the more fragile, motile feeding form found within the large intestine; this is why the mature cyst, not the trophozoite, is the infective form responsible for transmission via contaminated food or water.
questions.question:
Question 58
(a) Describe the basic structure of the trophozoite, precyst and cyst stages of Entamoeba histolytica.
(b) State the identifying nuclear and size characteristics of each stage.
(c) State the standard diagnostic method/setting in which these stages are examined in practice.
(d) Explain the basic reasoning behind the precaution that a mature cyst, rather than the trophozoite, is the form responsible for transmission of infection.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Specimens for fungal diagnosis depend on the site of infection and include pus, CSF, sputum, bronchial washings, tissue biopsies, skin scrapings, nail clippings, blood, and swabs; hair and nails should be sent in a dry envelope inside a proper container, body fluids in sterile containers, and cultures for transport are preferably set up on tubed media rather than plates.
(b)
• Tubed media are preferred to plate media because there is less chance of spore release into the environment, less chance of dehydration, and easier storage of the culture.
(c)
• Nails are cleaned as for skin and usually clipped, and need to be finely minced before inoculation onto media; sputum and bronchial aspiration specimens must be fresh and may be refrigerated for up to 2 hours; tissue specimens are examined for pus, caseous material or granules, then minced aseptically and inoculated onto media.
(d)
• Types of tests carried out on the processed specimens include microscopy, culture, antifungal susceptibility testing, serology/antigen detection, and molecular diagnosis, with preliminary identification based on the differential growth pattern seen on the various media used.
questions.question:
Question 44
A patient with a suspected systemic fungal infection has several types of specimen sent to the laboratory: sputum, a tissue biopsy, and nail clippings from a separate skin lesion.
(a) Identify the range of specimens that may be collected for fungal diagnosis and the apparatus/container in which each should be prepared for transport.
(b) State the principle behind why tubed media are preferred over plates for the cultures set up from these specimens.
(c) Describe how each of the three named specimens should be collected/processed before culture.
(d) State the expected outcome once the specimens are processed and the appropriate tests are performed.

Question 38
(a) State the general morphological classification of fungi and the systematic classification into phyla, with examples of each.
(b) State how each type/phylum is applied or recognized in laboratory identification.
(c) Explain why a basic error in culture temperature or interpretation leads to an inaccurate identification for a group of fungi.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Morphologically, fungi are classified into Yeasts (unicellular, reproduce by budding, e.g; Candida albicans, Cryptococcus neoformans), Moulds (multicellular, filamentous, produce hyphae forming mycelia, e.g; Aspergillus flavus, Microsporum canis), and Dimorphic fungi (exist as either mould phase at 25°C/in soil or yeast phase at 37°C/in host tissue, e.g; Histoplasma capsulatum, Blastomyces dermatitidis).
• Systematically, based on sexual spore formation, medically important fungi fall into four phyla: Glomerulomycota (e.g. Rhizopus, Mucor), Ascomycota (includes yeasts and filamentous fungi, e.g. Penicillium, Aspergillus, Histoplasma), Basidiomycota (e.g. Cryptococcus), and Deuteromycota/fungi imperfecti, whose sexual phases are not identified (e.g. Candida, Sporothrix, Coccidioides).
(b)
• Yeasts are recognized by their spherical or oval unicellular form and budding reproduction and grow optimally at 37°C, while moulds are recognized by production of hyphae/mycelia and grow optimally at 25°C; dimorphic fungi are applied/selected as a group requiring examination in both mould and yeast form depending on incubation temperature.
• Glomerulomycota are recognized by broad, non-septate hyphae and asexual sporangiospores in a sporangium; Ascomycota by narrow, septate hyphae and conidia; Basidiomycota by a club-shaped basidium bearing basidiospores; Deuteromycota (fungi imperfecti) by an asexual conidial stage only, since their sexual phase is unidentified.
(c)
• Since most fungi causing systemic infections are dimorphic, growing as moulds (filaments) at 25°C in soil/culture media but as yeasts at 37°C in host tissue, incubating or interpreting a culture at only one temperature, or misreading the phase seen, can lead to a wrong identification of the organism because the same fungus presents differently depending on temperature.

questions.question:
Question 54
(a) State the principle behind using thick and thin blood films for malaria diagnosis.
(b) State the materials/apparatus (stain) used.
(c) Describe how each type of film is used in the diagnostic procedure.
(d) State a precaution relevant to this technique.
(e) State how the result is reported.
(f) Explain why the thick film method is preferred in endemic areas.
(g) Distinguish the thin film from the thick film in terms of what each is best suited to show.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The clinical diagnosis of malaria is substantiated by finding the parasites in the peripheral blood; both thick and thin films rely on Romanowsky staining of the blood film to visualize the parasite within or in relation to red blood cells.
(b)
• An ordinary Romanowsky-stained thin film is used, and in endemic areas the thick film method is also used, being a more rapid and efficient means of diagnosis.
(c)
• The thin film is examined for parasite morphology and species characteristics within individual red cells; the thick film, which concentrates a larger volume of blood in a smaller area, is examined to increase the chance of detecting scanty parasites.
(d)
• A rapid diagnostic test employing antigen-antibody reaction is commonly used as an initial/screening step, but confirmation is by thin or thick blood film examination.
(e)
• The result is reported as parasites seen or not seen, with the stages identified (e.g. rings, schizonts, gametocytes) noted on the film.
(f)
• The thick film method is preferred in endemic areas because it provides a more rapid and efficient means of diagnosis than the ordinary thin film, being useful where a large number of specimens must be screened for the presence of parasites.
(g)
• The thin film, in which red cells are spread in a single layer, is quite satisfactory for demonstrating parasite morphology and species identification, whereas the thick film concentrates parasites from a larger blood volume into a smaller viewing area, making it more efficient specifically for detecting the presence of parasites, especially when numbers are low.

questions.question:
Question 7
(a) Describe the basic nature/structure of a bacteriophage and of a plasmid as genetic elements in bacteria.
(b) State the identifying characteristics/types of plasmids.
(c) State the standard setting in which plasmids are used in practice.
(d) Explain the basic reasoning behind the precaution that elimination of a prophage can change a bacterium's virulence.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• A bacteriophage is a virus infecting bacteria; a plasmid is extrachromosomal genetic material in the cytoplasm that replicates independently of the bacterial chromosome, while the bacterial chromosome itself carries properties like virulence, pathogenicity and resistance.
• Plasmids are circular DNA molecules; an episome is a plasmid DNA integrated with chromosomal DNA.
(b)
• Types of plasmids include the R plasmid (drug resistance, consisting of RTF plus r determinant) and the F plasmid (maleness), the latter of which is determined by the presence of a plasmid that codes for sex pili, also called the sex factor or fertility factor.
(c)
• Plasmids are used in practice as important vectors in genetic engineering, since they are circular DNA molecules that can carry and transfer genetic material such as drug resistance genes between bacteria.
(d)
• Bacteriophages have two types of life cycle: the lytic (virulent) cycle, in which progeny viruses build up inside the host bacterium and rupture it to be released, and the temperate (nonlytic/lysogenic) cycle, in which the host bacterium is unharmed and the phage DNA (prophage) behaves as an additional segment of the bacterial chromosome, coding for new characteristics (lysogenic conversion); by lysogenic conversion, diphtheria bacilli acquire toxigenicity and therefore virulence, and elimination of the phage renders a toxigenic strain non-toxigenic, so the presence or loss of a prophage can directly change the pathogenic potential of the bacterium.

questions.question:
Question 52
(a) Describe the different stages of Plasmodium seen during its life cycle in the human host.
(b) State the identifying features that distinguish sporozoites, merozoites, schizonts and gametocytes.
(c) State the standard method by which these stages are examined in practice.
(d) Explain the basic reasoning behind the precaution that Plasmodium vivax and P. ovale infections can relapse after apparent cure.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The female Anopheles mosquito injects sporozoites into the bloodstream during a blood meal; these are rapidly taken up by liver cells, where they develop to form schizonts (the multinucleate stage during asexual reproduction), from which several thousand merozoites develop.
• When liver cells rupture, merozoites are released into the bloodstream and rapidly invade red blood cells, where they replicate asexually; a small percentage of merozoites differentiate into male and female gametocytes, which are taken up by the mosquito in a subsequent blood meal to continue the cycle of transmission.
(b)
• Sporozoites are the form injected by the mosquito and taken up by liver cells; schizonts are the multinucleate asexual stage from which merozoites develop; merozoites are released on rupture of liver or red cells and invade further red blood cells; gametocytes are the sexual forms that cause the cycle of transmission to continue back to the mosquito.
(c)
• These blood-stage forms are examined by Romanowsky-stained thin blood film (satisfactory for diagnosis), or by the thick film method, which provides a more rapid and efficient means of diagnosis in endemic areas.
(d)
• In Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium ovale only, a proportion of the liver-stage parasites, known as hypnozoites, remain dormant in the hepatocytes and can remain dormant for months or years; this stage can initiate a further cycle of asexual reproduction causing clinical symptoms in the absence of a new mosquito bite, giving P. vivax infection the name "relapsing malaria", so a patient may need to be monitored for relapse even after apparent clearance of the blood-stage infection.

questions.question:
Question 3
(a) State the classification of bacteria by their pathogenic potential, and the characteristics of pathogenic bacteria, with an example of each type.
(b) State how these characteristics/types are applied in understanding how a bacterium causes disease.
(c) Explain why treating an opportunistic organism as inherently harmless would be a basic error in an immunocompromised patient.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• By pathogenic potential, bacteria are classified as: intracellular bacteria (pathogenic bacteria that always cause disease when they enter the human body), opportunistic bacteria (do not normally cause disease but will if the patient has a compromised immune system), and true pathogens (cause disease in healthy individuals, associated with a recognizable and specific disease).
• The characteristics of pathogenic bacteria are: transmissibility, adherence to host cells, invasion of host cells and tissue, evasion of the host immune system, and toxigenicity; a bacterium may cause disease by destroying tissue (invasiveness), producing toxins (toxigenicity), or stimulating an overwhelming host immune response.
(b)
• Pathogenesis refers to both the mechanism of infection and the mechanism by which disease develops; steps in bacterial infection include entry (at the portal of entry, the site of first contact of microbe to host tissue), attachment by adherence (via fimbriae, hooks, and adhesive capsules), becoming established by surviving host defences, an incubation period, invasion (multiplication at high level with signs and symptoms), and a convalescent phase.
• Specific adherence (biochemical interaction between bacterial surface ligands/adhesins and host cell receptors) and tissue tropism (bacterial preference for certain tissues) explain why particular bacteria colonize particular sites and cause disease at those sites.
(c)
• Because opportunistic bacteria do not normally cause disease but will do so specifically if a patient has a compromised immune system, treating such an organism as inherently harmless without considering the patient's immune status is a basic error that could delay recognition of an infection that the same organism would not have caused in a healthy host.

(a)
• Mutation is a random, undirected heritable variation caused by a change in the nucleotide base sequence of DNA; types of mutation include point mutation (addition, deletion or substitution of one or more bases, further divided into transition and transversion, and resulting in missense or nonsense mutations), frameshift mutation (deletion or insertion of a base, changing all downstream codons), lethal mutation (a nonviable mutation, e.g. a temperature-sensitive mutant that can live only at a permissive temperature), and suppressor mutation (reversal of a mutant phenotype by a second mutation at a distinct position).
• Mechanisms of transfer or exchange of genetic material include transformation (transfer of genetic information by free DNA, direct uptake of donor DNA by the recipient, as demonstrated by Griffith's pneumococcus experiment), transduction (transfer of DNA from one bacterium to another by a bacteriophage, either generalized or restricted), lysogenic conversion (the phage DNA itself becomes the new genetic element via the lysogenic cycle), conjugation (a donor/male bacterium passes DNA directly to a recipient/female bacterium via a conjugation tube/sex pili, first described by Lederberg and Tatum), and transposition (a transposon, a DNA segment that can move between chromosome and plasmid, discovered by Barbara McClintock).
(b)
• Transformation is recognized when free DNA released from one bacterium is taken up directly by another; transduction is recognized when a bacteriophage carries host DNA between bacteria (any group of bacteria for which bacteriophages exist can be subjected to transduction, and it is the most widely used mechanism of gene transfer among prokaryotes); conjugation is recognized by direct cell-to-cell transfer via a sex pilus, requiring a donor (F+) and recipient (F-) cell.
(c)
• Because R (resistance) factors can be transferred by conjugation, while resistance genes can also move as part of a bacteriophage-mediated transduction event or be integrated as a transposon that jumps between chromosome and plasmid, assuming that a resistant strain must have arisen by only one of these mechanisms (for example conjugation alone) without considering transduction or transposition could give an incorrect account of how the resistance spread between bacteria.

(a) State the classification of bacterial mutation types and the mechanisms of genetic transfer/exchange, with an example of each.
(b) State how each mechanism is applied/recognized as a means by which bacteria acquire new characteristics.
(c) Explain why confusing one mechanism of gene transfer for another could lead to an incorrect understanding of how a resistant strain arose.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Methods of diagnosis of parasitic infections include: direct demonstration of adult parasites (e.g. Ascaris) or segments (e.g. Taenia); microscopic examination of body fluids and tissues for early stages such as ova, trophozoites, larvae and cysts; cultural methods xenodiagnosis; animal inoculation; histopathology; immunodiagnosis/serology, including skin reaction; and radiological and scanning techniques.
(b)
• Direct demonstration is applied when the adult worm or a recognizable segment is passed or recovered; microscopic examination of body fluids/tissues is applied for early developmental stages such as ova, trophozoites, larvae and cysts, as in stool examination for Entamoeba histolytica or blood film examination for Plasmodium and Trypanosoma.
• Xenodiagnosis and animal inoculation are applied particularly in chronic or low-parasitaemia cases, such as chronic Chagas disease, where the organism is not reliably found by direct examination; immunodiagnosis/serology is applied as a further tool, for example the precipitin band screening method used to select cases of African trypanosomiasis for further investigation.
(c)
• Because different methods are suited to detecting different stages or levels of infection (for example, peripheral blood examination for Trypanosoma cruzi is generally unreliable except in very early infection, in contrast to xenodiagnosis for chronic disease, and virus/antibody detection differs by phase of illness for viral infections), relying on only one diagnostic method risks missing an infection that method is not suited to detect, so complementary methods are used depending on the parasite and stage.
questions.question:
Question 49
(a) State the classification of the general methods used for the diagnosis of parasitic infections.
(b) State how each method is applied/selected depending on the parasite or the stage of infection being investigated.

Question 56
(a) Describe the basic structure of the trypanosome as seen in a stained blood smear.
(b) State the identifying features that distinguish the amastigote form from the trypanosomal (trypomastigote) form of Trypanosoma cruzi.
(c) State the standard method/setting in which trypanosome morphology is used for diagnosis.
(d) Explain the basic reasoning behind the precaution of examining marrow/lymph node aspirates when trypanosomes are not found in peripheral blood.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• In Romanowsky-stained blood smears, African trypanosomes are seen as elongated sky-blue cytoplasmic protozoa measuring 15 to 30 by 1.5 to 3.5 µm; there is a large, red or reddish-purple nucleus (trophonucleus) in the centre, with a single free flagellum projecting from the anterior end that runs back along the edge of a wavy "undulating membrane" to end in a deep red dot known as the "kinetoplast", situated at the posterior end of the body.
(b)
• For Trypanosoma cruzi, two forms are recognized: the amastigote form, which is a small oval or round body occurring in heart, muscle and brain cells, and the trypanosomal (trypomastigote) form found in the blood during the febrile phase, seen as typical C- or U-shaped forms with a central nucleus and a characteristically large kinetoplast at the extreme posterior position.
(c)
• This morphology is used for diagnosis by examination of peripheral blood (thick film preparation, stained by Leishman's stain as for malarial diagnosis, since parasites may be scanty especially in T. gambiense infection) and by examination of aspirates from lymph nodes, liver biopsy material, bone marrow, or centrifuged CSF deposits.
(d)
• The parasites are most numerous in the blood in the early or septicaemic phase; because in man the parasites also live in the tissue spaces and lymphatics of the lymph nodes, brain, and spleen, smears of aspirated marrow or of aspirates from enlarged lymph nodes are usually diagnostic and yield a high percentage of positive diagnoses, so these sites should be examined when peripheral blood is negative.

(a)
• Moist heat may be used in three forms: dry saturated steam - autoclaving boiling water/steam at atmospheric pressure; and hot water below boiling point.
• Pasteurization uses the holding method (63°C for 30 minutes) or flash pasteurization (72°C for 15 seconds, after which the fluid is kept below 10°C to minimize subsequent bacterial growth) boiling at 100°C for 30 minutes kills most non-spore-forming bacteria, and 100°C for 5-10 minutes kills all non-sporing organisms except Clostridium tetani, which may survive boiling for 1-3 hours.
(b)
• Autoclaving (dry saturated steam under pressure) is applied where full sterility, including destruction of spores, is required, using 121°C or 132°C for the stated minimum exposure times; the pasteurization holding method (63°C/30 min) is applied to fluids such as milk to reduce bacterial numbers/eliminate pathogens present in small numbers and improve shelf life, destroying non-spore-forming pathogens such as M. tuberculosis, B. abortus and Salmonellae; boiling/steaming at 100°C is applied to items such as pipettes, measuring cylinders, and culture media such as broth and nutrient agar.
(c)
• Boiling at 100°C for even 5-10 minutes kills all non-sporing organisms except Clostridium tetani, which may survive boiling for 1-3 hours, whereas autoclaving (dry saturated steam under pressure) is sporicidal; using boiling instead of autoclaving for an item that may harbour Clostridium tetani spores would therefore fail to achieve sterility and could leave viable, infective spores on the item.
questions.question:
Question 9
(a) State the classification of the forms in which moist heat may be used to achieve microbial inactivation, with the temperature/time conditions for each.

Question 37
A tubed Sabouraud's dextrose agar (SDA) culture from a nail clipping specimen, incubated at room temperature, develops a mould colony after some days. A wet mount of the colony is prepared using lactophenol cotton blue.
(a) Identify the technique used for the microscopic evaluation and what feature of the fungus it demonstrates.
(b) State the basic technique(s) used to obtain the growth being examined.
(c) State how the colony and microscopic findings should be recorded.
(d) State a follow-up practical step that gives an undisturbed view of the fungal microscopic morphology.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The technique is a lactophenol cotton blue (LPCB) wet mount, used for quick evaluation of fungal structures; it stains the chitin in the cell walls of fungi, allowing the hyphae, spore-bearing structures and spores to be examined.
(b)
• The specimen (nail clipping, finely minced before inoculation) was cultured on Sabouraud's dextrose agar, a classic selective medium recommended for most fungal studies; tubed media rather than plates are preferred as fungal culture media because there is less chance of spore release into the environment, less chance of dehydration, and easier storage, and cultures are generally held for at least 4 weeks and examined every other day.
(c)
• Findings are recorded under colony morphology (surface topography, surface texture such as cottony/woolly, granular, chalky, velvety, powdery, silky, glabrous or waxy, and pigmentation) and under microscopic evaluation (hyphae structure - septate versus non-septate, and spore type seen).
(d)
• A slide culture can be set up as a follow-up step, as it gives an undisturbed view of the microscopic morphology of the fungus, compared with a teased preparation or cellophane tape preparation.

(a)
• In the laboratory, susceptibility is often measured using a disk diffusion test, based on comparing the zones of inhibition produced by an antibiotic around a test organism and around a known sensitive control organism.
(b)
• Antibiotic solutions of particular concentrations are dried onto filter paper disks; these are applied to a mat of the microbes under test that has been inoculated previously on an appropriate solid medium (Mueller-Hinton Agar).
(c)
• In the Stokes controlled sensitivity test, a control organism is inoculated on part of the plate and the test organism is plated on the remainder disks are placed at the interface, the plate is incubated, and the zones of inhibition around the control and test organisms are then compared.
(d)
• A precaution is that the control and test organisms must be applied to the same plate under the same conditions, so that the zones produced are genuinely comparable.
(e)
• If the test organism grows up to the disk (no zone), it is reported as resistant to that drug; a clear zone comparable to the control indicates the organism is susceptible.
(f)
• The use of a sensitive control shows that the antibiotic is active, so that a lack of zone around the test organism can be confidently interpreted as resistance rather than an inactive/expired antibiotic disk.
(g)
• The disk diffusion test gives a qualitative (susceptible/resistant) result based on zone comparison on solid medium, whereas the MIC/MBC method uses a series of broths with serially diluted antibiotic and a standard inoculum to give a quantitative concentration value: the MIC is the lowest concentration inhibiting visible growth, and the MBC is the lowest concentration giving no visible growth on subculture to drug-free medium.

(a) State the principle of the disk diffusion (Stokes' controlled sensitivity) susceptibility test.
(b) State the apparatus/materials used.
(c) Describe the step-by-step procedure.

Question 22
A bacterial suspension is serially diluted ten-fold several times, and 0.1 mL from one of the dilution tubes is spread onto a nutrient agar plate and incubated; 150 colonies are counted on the plate after incubation.
(a) Interpret what this colony count represents in terms of the technique being performed.
(b) State how such a plate count result should be recorded/reported.
(c) State what the result indicates about the concentration of viable microorganisms in the original suspension.
(d) State the follow-up/repeat action that may be needed if the number of colonies makes accurate counting difficult.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The 150 colonies counted represent the outcome of the plate count method, in which the result reflects the number of microbial colonies capable of emerging under the given physical and chemical conditions (pH, temperature, available nutrients, presence of growth-inhibitory compounds, etc.) after growth from the diluted inoculum.
(b)
• The result is recorded as the colony count obtained on the plate together with the dilution factor used, since serial dilution (log dilution) was carried out to lower the bacterial concentration to a level that would make the colonies easier to count on the agar plate.
(c)
• Combined with the known dilution factor, the colony count indicates the concentration of viable microorganisms present in the original bacterial suspension.
(d)
• If colonies are too numerous or too few to count accurately at a given dilution, the serial dilution and plating should be repeated using a different (more appropriate) dilution so that a countable number of colonies is obtained; alternative methods such as the Most Probable Number (MPN) technique or use of a spectrophotometer to estimate the total bacterial number may also be used.

(a)
• A positive indole test (deamination of tryptophan by tryptophanase to indole) together with a positive Methyl Red test and a negative Voges-Proskauer test is the pattern described for Escherichia coli, which follows the mixed acid fermentation pathway and is Methyl Red test positive; this differs from organisms such as Enterobacter aerogenes, which follow the 2,3-butanediol pathway and are Voges-Proskauer test positive.
(b)
• The results are recorded as the individual reactions obtained for each test performed (indole positive, Methyl Red positive, Voges-Proskauer negative) alongside any Triple Sugar Iron (lactose, sucrose, glucose and ferrous sulphate) reaction, which is used for differentiation of enteric pathogens such as Salmonella.
(c)
• The pattern indicates that the organism ferments glucose via the mixed acid fermentation pathway (glucose/lactose/mannitol through glycolysis to pyruvate to fermentation products), consistent with mixed acid end products rather than 2,3-butanediol.
(d)
• Once this biochemical pattern is obtained, it is used together with the Triple Sugar Iron reaction and other biochemical tests to identify the enteric organism among the Enterobacteriaceae.
questions.question:
Question 20
An unknown Gram-negative rod isolated from a stool sample is tested biochemically. It gives a positive indole test and a positive Methyl Red test, but a negative Voges-Proskauer test.
(a) Interpret this biochemical reaction pattern in terms of the likely organism.
(b) State how such biochemical results are typically recorded/reported in the laboratory.
(c) State what this pattern indicates about the organism's fermentation pathway.
