questions.answerText:
(a)
• For the endoscope, 2% glutaraldehyde is a suitable agent (also used to sterilize cystoscopes, bronchoscopes, centrifuges and anaesthetic equipment); for the clinical thermometer, isopropyl alcohol is suitable, as it is used to disinfect clinical thermometers.
(b)
• Aldehydes such as glutaraldehyde act through alkylation of amino-, carboxyl- or hydroxyl groups and probably damage nucleic acids, killing all microorganisms including spores; alcohols such as isopropyl alcohol act by dehydrating cells, disrupting membranes and causing coagulation of protein.
(c)
• An exposure of at least 3 hours at alkaline pH is required for action by glutaraldehyde on the endoscope; isopropyl alcohol, which is preferred to ethanol and can also be used to disinfect surfaces, is applied to the thermometer for disinfection.
(d)
• A 70% aqueous alcohol solution is more effective at killing microbes than absolute alcohol, and alcohols have the disadvantage of being skin irritants, volatile (evaporating rapidly) and inflammable; glutaraldehyde requires the stated minimum exposure time at alkaline pH to be effective.
questions.question:
Question 16
A flexible endoscope, which cannot withstand heat sterilization, needs to be disinfected between uses, and a clinical thermometer also needs routine disinfection.
(a) Identify a suitable chemical agent for each item.
(b) State the principle/mode of action of the agent(s) identified.
(c) Describe how each agent should be applied/used.
(d) State a precaution or limitation associated with the agent(s) used.

Question 26
(a) State the classification of the major mechanisms by which bacteria develop resistance to antibiotics, with an example for each.
(b) State how each mechanism is applied/recognized in explaining resistance to a particular class of antibiotic.
(c) Explain why assuming resistance is always due to genetic mutation, without considering the other mechanisms, could lead to an incorrect understanding of an organism's resistance.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The major mechanisms of antibiotic resistance are: genetic alterations leading to drug resistance, through spontaneous mutation or acquired gain/alteration of genetic information moving from one organism to another modification of target sites, such as alteration of penicillin-binding proteins in S. pneumoniae, decreasing binding of beta-lactam antibiotics to their target decreased accumulation, through decreased uptake or increased efflux (e.g. gram-negative organisms limiting penetration of beta-lactams, tetracyclines and chloramphenicol via altered porins, or via efflux pumps); and (4) enzymic inactivation, such as beta-lactamases that hydrolytically inactivate the beta-lactam ring, acetyltransferases that inactivate chloramphenicol or aminoglycosides, and esterases that hydrolyze the lactone ring of macrolides.
(b)
• Modification of target sites is applied to explain beta-lactam resistance arising from altered penicillin-binding proteins; decreased accumulation/efflux is applied to explain resistance to beta-lactams, tetracyclines and chloramphenicol in gram-negative organisms due to altered porins or efflux pumps; enzymic inactivation is applied to explain resistance to penicillins/cephalosporins (via beta-lactamases), chloramphenicol/aminoglycosides (via acetyltransferases), and macrolides (via esterases).
• There are also four major mechanisms specific to beta-lactam resistance: inactivation of the beta-lactam ring, alteration of penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs), reduction of antibiotic access to PBPs, and elaboration of antibiotic efflux mechanisms.
(c)
• Because resistance can arise not only from genetic mutation but also from target site modification, decreased drug accumulation (via porin alteration or efflux pumps), and enzymic inactivation of the drug itself, assuming that resistance in a given organism is necessarily due to mutation alone, without testing for enzyme production (e.g. beta-lactamase) or accumulation defects, could lead to an incorrect understanding of the resistance mechanism actually operating in that organism.

questions.question:
Question 2
(a) State the classification of bacteria based on their mode of nutrition, their oxygen (atmosphere) requirement, and their temperature requirement, with an example organism for each type.
(b) State how each type is applied/selected in choosing appropriate incubation conditions for a specimen.
(c) Explain why incubating a specimen under the wrong atmospheric or temperature condition could lead to a false-negative culture result.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Based on mode of nutrition, bacteria are Autotrophic (carbon obtained from CO2 during photosynthesis) or Heterotrophic (carbon obtained from organic compounds through metabolic pathways); Based on oxygen requirement, bacteria are: strict/obligate aerobes, requiring O2 for growth (e.g; Pseudomonas aeruginosa); strict/obligate anaerobes, growing in the absence of O2 and possibly dying on exposure to it (e.g. Clostridium tetani); microaerophilic organisms, growing best with low oxygen levels (e.g. Campylobacter spp, Helicobacter spp, Haemophilus); and facultative anaerobes, aerobic but also able to grow without O2 (e.g. Staphylococcus spp).
• Based on temperature requirement, bacteria are: Mesophilic, growing best between 25°C and 40°C (most bacterial pathogens)
• Psychrophilic (cold-loving), growing best below 25°C (e.g. Flavobacterium spp); and Thermophilic, growing best at high temperatures of 55-58°C (e.g. Bacillus stearothermophilus).
(b)
• The optimum temperature for growth of most pathogenic bacteria is 37°C, so specimens suspected to contain typical pathogens are incubated near this temperature, while an organism suspected to be microaerophilic (e.g. Campylobacter, Helicobacter) requires incubation under low-oxygen conditions rather than standard aerobic incubation.
• H-ion concentration is also selected according to the organism: a neutral or slightly alkaline pH (7.2-7.6) suits most bacteria, an acidic pH suits Lactobacilli, and an alkaline pH suits Vibrio cholerae.
(c)
• Because strict anaerobes such as Clostridium tetani may die on exposure to oxygen, and microaerophilic organisms such as Campylobacter or Helicobacter grow best only under low oxygen levels, incubating a specimen containing such an organism under ordinary aerobic conditions (or at the wrong temperature range for a psychrophilic or thermophilic organism) can fail to support its growth, giving a false-negative culture result even though the organism is present in the specimen.

questions.question:
Question 17
(a) State the principle behind using a biological indicator to monitor sterilization.
(b) State the apparatus/organism used for steam sterilization monitoring.
(c) Describe how biological indicators differ for the different sterilization methods.
(d) State a precaution relevant to this monitoring technique.
(e) State how the result of biological indicator testing is reported/used.
(f) Explain why periodic biological indicator testing is necessary even when the correct temperature/time settings are used.
(g) Distinguish the biological indicator used for dry-heat sterilization from that used for steam sterilization.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• A biological indicator uses spores of a known, highly heat/agent-resistant organism placed through the sterilization process if the process is effective, the spores are killed, confirming that the process achieved sterilization.
(b)
• For steam sterilization, spores of Bacillus stearothermophilus are used; autoclaves should be tested periodically with this biological indicator to ensure proper function.
(c)
• Different biological indicator organisms are used for different sterilization methods: Bacillus stearothermophilus for steam sterilization, Bacillus subtilis for dry-heat sterilization, Bacillus subtilis for gas sterilization, and Bacillus pumilus for ionizing radiation sterilization.
(d)
• A precaution is that the correct indicator organism for the specific method being used (steam, dry heat, gas, or radiation) must be selected, since different organisms are used to validate each method.
(e)
• The result is used to confirm (or fail to confirm) proper function of the sterilizing equipment, so that the equipment's continued use for critical or semi-critical items can be relied upon.
(f)
• Periodic testing with a biological indicator is necessary because it directly demonstrates that the sterilizing conditions (steam, pressure, temperature and time in the case of autoclaving) actually achieved the destruction of a resistant test organism, rather than relying only on the display of correct settings on the equipment.
(g)
• Steam sterilization is monitored with Bacillus stearothermophilus spores, whereas dry-heat sterilization is monitored with Bacillus subtilis spores, reflecting the different resistance profiles of these organisms to the two different sterilization mechanisms.

questions.question:
Question 24
(a) State the general classification of antimicrobial agents based on their mechanism of action, with an example drug class for each.
(b) State how the mechanism of action is used/selected when choosing an antimicrobial agent for therapy.
(c) Explain why ignoring whether an agent is bactericidal or bacteriostatic can lead to an inappropriate treatment choice.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Antimicrobial agents are classified, based on chemical structure and mechanism of action, as: agents that inhibit synthesis of bacterial cell walls (e.g. beta-lactams such as penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems, and also vancomycin, bacitracin) agents acting directly on the cell membrane (e.g. polymyxin, polyene antifungals such as nystatin and amphotericin B, and daptomycin) agents that reversibly inhibit protein synthesis via the 30S or 50S ribosomal subunit, generally bacteriostatic (e.g. chloramphenicol, tetracyclines, erythromycin) agents that bind the 30S subunit and alter protein synthesis, generally bactericidal (e.g. aminoglycosides) agents affecting nucleic acid metabolism (e.g. rifamycins, which inhibit RNA polymerase, and quinolones, which inhibit topoisomerases); and antimetabolites (e.g. trimethoprim and sulfonamides) blocking folate metabolism enzymes.
(b)
• Selection of an antimicrobial agent for therapy is influenced by pharmacological and microbiological factors, including determination of the organism's antibiotic susceptibility using the disk diffusion or broth (dilution) method, so that an agent whose mechanism matches a susceptible target in the identified organism is chosen.
(c)
• Antimicrobial drugs are classified as either bacteriostatic or bactericidal; a bacteriostatic drug's effects are reversible upon removal of the drug, so bacterial growth resumes when a bacteriostatic drug is withdrawn, whereas a cidal drug kills the bacteria.
• Choosing a bacteriostatic agent where a bactericidal effect is clinically required (or vice versa, without regard to the site and severity of infection) can therefore lead to an inappropriate treatment outcome, since the mechanism of action determines whether organisms are killed outright or merely have their growth halted while the host's own defences act.

questions.question:
Question 33
(a) State the principle behind using embryonated eggs for virus cultivation.
(b) State the apparatus/materials (routes of inoculation) used.
(c) Describe the step-by-step procedure, including the precautionary check done before inoculation.
(d) State a precaution associated with the choice of inoculation route.
(e) State how growth of virus in the egg is reported/detected.
(f) Explain why the embryonated egg method is convenient/economical compared with animal inoculation.
(g) Distinguish embryonated egg inoculation from the tissue culture method of virus cultivation.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The cultivation of virus is an essential prerequisite for their isolation, since viruses are obligate intracellular parasites that can only replicate in cells; although not all viruses can be grown in an embryonated egg, many viruses are cultivated in this host, and eggs are used for rapid isolation of viruses and also for vaccine or antigen production.
(b)
• Embryonated eggs may be infected by various routes: amniotic, allantoic, chorio-allantoic, yolk sac, and, in special cases, intravenous and intra-embryonal routes.
(c)
• Before inoculation, eggs are candled to check that the embryo is alive; the specimen is then introduced by the chosen route, which depends on the ability of that tissue to support virus replication.
(d)
• A precaution is that the choice of a particular route depends on the ability of the tissue at that route to support virus replication, so an inappropriate route may fail to demonstrate virus growth even if virus is present in the specimen.
(e)
• The presence of virus in the inoculated egg is detected by mortality, deformities and haemorrhage of the embryo, lesions in the form of pocks, oedema of the developing membrane, or the presence of specific antigen in the fluid as shown by the HI test, SN test, FAT and other serological tests.
(f)
• This method is more economical and convenient than animal inoculation, which is why eggs are used for rapid isolation of a few viruses as well as for vaccine or antigen production.
(g)
• Embryonated egg inoculation grows the virus within the living tissues of a developing embryo, detected by embryo mortality/lesions or antigen tests, whereas tissue culture grows the virus in cells (primary culture, continuous cell line, monolayer or suspension culture) maintained in vitro in nutrient media, with growth recognized by the cytopathic effect, metabolic effect, plaque formation, or interference.

questions.question:
Question 10
A batch of wrapped surgical instruments is brought to the laboratory for sterilization before re-use on patients.
(a) Identify the apparatus and the physical method that should be used for this batch.
(b) State the principle on which this method destroys microorganisms.
(c) Describe the step-by-step procedure, including the temperature-time combinations that may be used.
(d) State the expected result if the process was successful and how this would be confirmed.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The apparatus is the autoclave, using moist heat (dry saturated steam under pressure) sterilization.
(b)
• In the presence of moisture, microorganisms are destroyed at a lower temperature; steam, pressure, temperature and time are the four parameters, with pressure serving as the means of obtaining the high temperature needed to kill microorganisms quickly.
(c)
• The wrapped instruments are loaded into the autoclave and exposed to dry saturated steam.
• Two common steam-sterilizing temperatures are used: 121°C (250°F) or 132°C (270°F).
• The recognized minimum exposure period is 30 minutes at 121°C in a gravity displacement sterilizer, or 4 minutes at 132°C in a pre-vacuum sterilizer.
• Sterilization time varies with the type of item (metal versus rubber/plastic or items with lumens), whether wrapped or unwrapped, and the sterilizer type.
(d)
• A successful run destroys all viable organisms and their spores, rendering the instruments free of biological contamination.
• This is confirmed periodically by testing the autoclave with a biological indicator such as spores of Bacillus stearothermophilus.

(a)
• The organism is Candida albicans; the filamentous outgrowth seen after growth in serum is the germ tube, and the thick-walled resting spore seen on cornmeal agar is the chlamydospore.
(b)
• The germ tube is detected by the germ tube test, in which the yeast is grown in human or sheep serum at 37°C for about 3 hours and detected with wet mounts as a filamentous outgrowth extending from the yeast cell; the chlamydospore is detected by inoculating the yeast onto an appropriate agar such as cornmeal agar and observing for chlamydospore production.
(c)
• Both findings are recorded as positive: germ tube test positive, and chlamydospore production positive on cornmeal agar.
(d)
• The germ tube test is used to differentiate Candida albicans from other Candida species, and a positive chlamydospore demonstration on cornmeal agar is likewise positive specifically in Candida albicans, so both findings together support identification of the isolate as Candida albicans.
questions.question:
Question 40
A yeast isolate recovered from an oral swab is grown in human serum at 37°C for about 3 hours; filamentous outgrowths are seen extending from some yeast cells on a wet mount. The same isolate, when inoculated onto cornmeal agar, later shows thick-walled resting spores.
(a) Identify the organism and the two structures/observations described.
(b) State the basic technique used to detect each of these two findings.
(c) State how the results should be recorded/reported.
(d) State the follow-up significance of these findings for identification of the isolate.

Question 60
(a) Describe the basic structure of Trichomonas vaginalis.
(b) State the identifying features that distinguish it on a hanging drop preparation.
(c) State the standard method/setting in which this organism is examined in practice.
(d) Explain the basic reasoning behind the precaution of keeping the specimen warm and examining it promptly.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Trichomonas vaginalis is a flagellated protozoan parasite found in the genitourinary tract of humans, found only as a trophozoite (it has no cyst stage), measuring about 12 to 26 µm long and pear-shaped.
• There are four anterior flagella and an undulating membrane running on one side of the organism for about half the body length; a single nucleus and a slender axostyle in a granular cytoplasm complete the anatomy.
(b)
• On a hanging drop preparation, Trichomonas vaginalis is easily recognized as a motile, pear-shaped flagellate, distinguished by its characteristic jerky motility driven by the four anterior flagella and undulating membrane.
(c)
• The organism is examined by taking a vaginal swab (or urethral discharge from a male, or material from prostatic massage), which is placed in a tube partially covered by warm saline and delivered immediately to the laboratory for a hanging drop preparation.
(d)
• If the specimen cannot be examined at once, it may be left temporarily in a 37°C incubator, because identification of Trichomonas vaginalis on a hanging drop preparation depends on observing its characteristic motility; motility declines as the specimen cools or dries, so keeping the swab warm in saline and examining it promptly preserves the feature needed for identification.

(a)
• Filtration works by physical removal of microorganisms in a liquid or gas by adsorption on the filter medium; it does not destroy but removes microorganisms.
(b)
• Equipment used is filters of pore size 0.75µ or less; types of filters include earthenware candles (e.g. porcelain filters, siliceous earth filters), sintered glass filters, asbestos filters (e.g. Seitz filters), and cellulose membrane filters (e.g. millipore, 1.7cm to 14cm).
(c)
• The pore size of the filter used determines the kinds of microbes removed, so filtration is used for both clarification and sterilization of liquids and gases, since it can prevent the passage of both viable and non-viable particles.
(d)
• A limitation is that filtration removes rather than destroys the microorganisms, so it must be used with appropriately sized filters and is restricted to liquids/gases that can pass through the filter medium.
(e)
• It is used for heat-sensitive materials, toxins, serum and antibiotic solutions.
(f)
• Heat-based methods can destroy heat-labile materials such as toxins, serum, and antibiotic solutions, so filtration is preferred for these materials since it achieves sterilization without heat.
(g)
• Filtration physically removes microorganisms by passage through a filter medium of a given pore size, whereas radiation sterilization uses electromagnetic radiation (gamma rays, UV light) or particulate radiation (accelerated electrons) whose major target is microbial DNA, with gamma rays/electrons causing ionization and free radical production and UV light causing excitation, so radiation destroys the organism rather than physically removing it.
questions.question:
Question 13
(a) State the principle of filtration as a sterilization method.
(b) State the apparatus/equipment (filter types) used.
(c) Describe how filtration is applied/carried out.
(d) State a precaution/limitation of the method.
(e) State the materials for which filtration sterilization is reported/used.
(f) Explain why filtration is preferred for certain materials over heat-based methods.
(g) Distinguish filtration sterilization from radiation (UV/ionizing) sterilization.

Question 50
(a) State the principle behind examining a stool specimen for intestinal parasites.
(b) State the materials/reagents used for direct microscopy of the specimen.
(c) Describe the step-by-step approach to collecting and examining the specimen.
(d) State a precaution relevant to this technique.
(e) State how the findings are reported.
(f) Explain why blood-stained mucus in the stool should specifically be selected for examination.
(g) Distinguish the use of iodine preparation from iron haematoxylin staining in this examination.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Since the trophozoite of Entamoeba histolytica is actively motile, examination relies on prompt collection and microscopy of a fresh, warm specimen to catch the parasite before it degenerates, while the more resistant cyst form can be demonstrated even after some delay.
(b)
• Materials used include iodine (Lugol's iodine) for direct wet preparation of cysts, and iron haematoxylin stain for fixed faecal smears; several culture media are also available for culture of the parasitic amoebae.
(c)
• It is advantageous to collect a stool sample passed into a warmed bedpan and examine it with as little delay as possible; blood-stained particles of mucus in the stool offer the best chance of success in the search for the parasites, and a preparation with iodine is made to look for cysts, or the smear is fixed and stained with iron haematoxylin.
(d)
• A precaution is the need for prompt examination of the specimen while still warm, since the diagnostic trophozoite form is actively motile and fragile.
(e)
• Findings are reported as trophozoites and/or cysts seen (or not seen), noting the stain/preparation used to demonstrate them.
(f)
• Blood-stained particles of mucus in the stool offer the best chance of success in the search for the parasites, since Entamoeba histolytica causes ulceration of the large intestine and amoebic dysentery, so these particles are more likely to contain the actively invasive trophozoite form.
(g)
• An iodine (Lugol's iodine) preparation is a direct wet-mount method advantageous for demonstrating cysts, whereas iron haematoxylin stains of fixed faecal smears give the sharpest pictures of the cysts, by which the chromatoidal bodies and nuclei are shown more clearly than with the iodine wet mount.

questions.question:
Question 53
A Romanowsky-stained peripheral blood film from a febrile patient shows red cells containing small ring-shaped structures, together with some cells containing a multinucleate stage and others containing rounded bodies that are taken up when a mosquito feeds.
(a) Identify the organism and the stages being described.
(b) State the basic technique used to detect this organism in blood.
(c) State how the finding should be recorded/reported.
(d) State the follow-up practical step once parasites are demonstrated.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The organism is Plasmodium (the malaria parasite)
• The multinucleate stage described is the schizont, and the stage taken up by the mosquito during a blood meal to continue transmission is the gametocyte; the ring-shaped structures are the early blood-stage parasites within red cells.
(b)
• An ordinary Romanowsky-stained thin film is satisfactory for detecting the parasite, while in endemic areas the thick film method provides a more rapid and efficient means of diagnosis; a rapid diagnostic test based on antigen-antibody reaction may also be used but confirmation is by thin or thick blood film.
(c)
• The finding is recorded as a positive blood film for malaria parasites, noting the stages of the parasite that are seen (e.g. rings, schizonts, gametocytes) as observed on the stained film.
(d)
• Because the clinical diagnosis is substantiated by finding the parasites in the peripheral blood, the positive film supports and confirms the clinical suspicion of malaria in the febrile patient.

questions.question:
Question 8
(a) State the general classification of the methods by which sterilization can be attained.
(b) State how each type of method is applied/selected in the laboratory, with an example of equipment or agent for each.
(c) Explain why a basic error in exposure time, concentration, or method choice leads to an inaccurate or invalid (non-sterile) result.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Sterilization can be attained by physical, chemical and gaseous means.
• Physical methods are further divided into thermal (heat) methods, radiation methods, and filtration methods, while chemical and gaseous methods make up the other two broad categories.
(b)
• Thermal methods are applied using dry heat (160-180°C, e.g. hot air oven, incineration, flaming) for thermostable/moisture-sensitive materials, and moist heat (121-134°C, e.g. autoclave) for moisture-resistant materials.
• Radiation methods use electromagnetic radiation (gamma rays, UV light) or particulate radiation (accelerated electrons), with UV light applied for air and surface sterilization due to poor penetrability, and gamma rays (from a cobalt-60 source) applied to articles in the dry state such as sutures and plastic syringes.
• Filtration is applied to heat-sensitive materials such as toxins, serum and antibiotic solutions, using filters of pore size 0.75µ or less, and it removes rather than destroys microorganisms.
• Chemical and gaseous methods, such as ethylene oxide (for thermolabile plastics/polymers) and liquid chemical sterilants (e.g. peracetic acid, hydrogen peroxide), are selected for items that cannot tolerate heat.
(c)
• Recognized minimum exposure periods (e.g. 30 minutes at 121°C, or 4 minutes at 132°C for autoclaving) must be maintained for the minimal required time to kill microorganisms; a shortened exposure fails to reach the microbicidal endpoint and leaves viable organisms.
• At constant temperatures, sterilization times vary depending on the type of item, whether wrapped or unwrapped, and the sterilizer type, so applying a generic exposure without regard to these factors can leave an item non-sterile even though the correct general method was chosen.

questions.question:
Question 18
(a) State the classification of disinfectants based on their mechanism of action, with an example agent for each mechanism.
(b) State how disinfectants are also classified and selected based on spectrum of activity and consistency.
(c) Explain why using a disinfectant at an incorrect dilution or against the wrong spectrum of organism could lead to failed disinfection.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Based on mechanism of action, disinfectants are classified as: acting on the cell membrane (e.g. alcohol, detergent) causing denaturation of cellular proteins (e.g. alcohol, phenol) oxidation of essential sulphydryl groups of enzymes (e.g. hydrogen peroxide, halogens) alkylation of amino-, carboxyl- and hydroxyl groups (e.g. formaldehyde); and damage to nucleic acids (e.g. formaldehyde).
(b)
• Disinfectants are also classified based on consistency, as liquid (e.g. alcohols, phenols) or gaseous (e.g. formaldehyde vapour), and based on spectrum of activity, as high level, intermediate level, or low level.
• An ideal antiseptic/disinfectant should have a wide spectrum of activity, be able to destroy microbes within a practical period of time, be active in the presence of organic matter, make effective contact and be wettable, be active at any pH, be stable, have a long shelf life, be speedy, have high penetrating power, be non-toxic, non-allergenic, non-irritative or non-corrosive, have no bad odour, leave no non-volatile residue or stain, retain efficacy on reasonable dilution, and not be expensive.
(c)
• Because efficacy should not be lost on reasonable dilution but can still be compromised if diluted beyond the recommended concentration (for example, the requirement for a 70% aqueous alcohol solution being more effective than absolute alcohol, or a 2% gluteraldehyde solution needing at least 3 hours exposure at alkaline pH), and because agents are bactericidal, fungicidal or mycobactericidal but inactive against spores and most viruses at low concentration (as with phenols), applying the wrong concentration or expecting activity outside an agent's spectrum will fail to achieve disinfection.

(a)
• In the presence of moisture, microorganisms are destroyed at a lower temperature; sterilization is nontoxic, inexpensive, rapidly microbicidal and sporicidal, and rapidly heats and penetrates materials.
(b)
• The equipment used is the autoclave.
(c)
• The four parameters of steam sterilization are steam, pressure, temperature and time; the two common steam-sterilizing temperatures are 121°C (250°F) and 132°C (270°F).
• Recognized minimum exposure periods are 30 minutes at 121°C in a gravity displacement sterilizer, or 4 minutes at 132°C in a pre-vacuum sterilizer, with times varying by item type and whether wrapped or unwrapped.
(d)
• The method cannot be used for oily preparations (oil-based ointments) or for moisture-sensitive preparations.
(e)
• Autoclaves should be tested periodically with biological indicators such as spores of Bacillus stearothermophilus to ensure proper function.
(f)
• Moist heat destroys enzymes and other essential cell constituents, and the process is more effective in the hydrated state, where under conditions of high humidity, hydrolysis and denaturation occur more readily.
• It is rapid, inexpensive, effective and can sterilize large volumes, unlike methods restricted to dry or heat-sensitive materials.
(g)
• Dry heat sterilization (160-180°C) is applied to thermostable products, while moisture-resistant materials use moist heat at the lower range of 121-134°C.
• Dry heat has good penetrability and a non-corrosive nature, making it suitable for glassware and metal instruments, and it also destroys bacterial endotoxins/pyrogens, unlike moist heat, so the two methods are chosen for different categories of material.
questions.question:
Question 11
(a) State the principle of autoclaving.
(b) State the apparatus/equipment used.
(c) Describe the procedure, including the temperature-time combinations used.
(d) State a precaution associated with the technique.
(e) State how the effectiveness of the process is monitored/reported.
(f) Explain why moist heat sterilization is preferred over other heat methods for most laboratory and hospital items.
(g) Distinguish autoclaving from dry heat (hot air oven) sterilization.

Question 31
A monolayer cell culture inoculated with a clinical specimen is examined under the inverted microscope several days later. Formation of giant cells, complete destruction of some cells, and the presence of inclusion bodies are observed, and the colour of the culture medium has changed.
(a) Identify what these observed changes are collectively called and what they indicate.
(b) State the basic technique used to grow the cells in which these changes are seen.
(c) State how such findings should be recorded/reported.
(d) State a further practical step that can be used to localize and visualize the pattern of viral spread in the monolayer.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• These changes (giant cell formation, complete cell destruction, and inclusion bodies) are collectively called the cytopathic effect (CPE); this is the morphological evidence of cell damage caused by many viruses that kill cells, and it is visible with the inverted microscope, indicating that the virus has grown/multiplied in the culture.
(b)
• The cells were grown as a monolayer cell culture, in which sheets of cells only one cell thick are grown on the surface of a glass or plastic vessel, in a nutrient medium consisting of a balanced salt solution, glucose, vitamin, coenzyme, amino acids, serum, sodium bicarbonate and phenol red.
(c)
• The findings are recorded as cytopathic effect positive, noting the specific features observed (giant cell formation, cell destruction, inclusion bodies) together with the metabolic effect seen as a change in the colour of the medium (from red to yellow, through orange, due to the change in pH of the medium).
(d)
• A plaque formation technique can be used as a follow-up step, in which the virus is inoculated into a monolayer culture with the late addition of a semisolid overlay agar, which localizes the viral spread and produces a plaque.

questions.question:
Question 43
(a) State the principle of the germ tube test.
(b) State the materials/apparatus used.
(c) Describe the step-by-step procedure for the germ tube test and for chlamydospore demonstration.
(d) State a precaution in performing the test.
(e) State how the result is reported.
(f) Explain why this test is preferred for rapid identification of Candida albicans.
(g) Distinguish the germ tube test from chlamydospore demonstration as identification methods.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The germ tube test relies on the fact that when Candida is grown in human or sheep serum at 37°C for about 3 hours, it forms a germ tube (a filamentous outgrowth extending from the yeast cell), and this feature differentiates Candida albicans from other Candida species.
(b)
• Human or sheep serum is used as the growth medium for the germ tube test; cornmeal agar is used as the medium for chlamydospore demonstration.
(c)
• For the germ tube test, the yeast is inoculated into human or sheep serum and incubated at 37°C for about 3 hours, then detected with a wet mount as a filamentous outgrowth extending from the yeast cell; for chlamydospore demonstration, the yeast is inoculated in an appropriate agar (e.g. cornmeal agar) and observed for chlamydospore production.
(d)
• A precaution is that the germ tube test requires the correct incubation time (about 3 hours) and temperature (37°C), as the germ tube is a specific, time-dependent morphological feature.
(e)
• The result is reported as germ tube test positive or negative, and separately as chlamydospore production positive or negative on cornmeal agar.
(f)
• The germ tube test is preferred for rapid identification because the germ tube is detected by a simple wet mount after only about 3 hours of incubation, differentiating Candida albicans from other Candida species without requiring lengthier biochemical or culture-based methods.
(g)
• The germ tube test demonstrates a filamentous outgrowth from the yeast cell after growth in serum at 37°C, whereas chlamydospore demonstration shows a thick-walled resting spore formed within the hypha after growth on cornmeal agar; both are positive specifically in Candida albicans but detect different morphological structures.

questions.question:
Question 12
(a) State the principle of dry heat (hot air oven) sterilization.
(b) State the apparatus used and the materials it is applied to.
(c) Describe the procedure, including the temperature range used.
(d) State a precaution/limitation of the method.
(e) State a benefit of the method relevant to reporting/use of the sterilized item.
(f) Explain why dry heat is preferred for glassware and metal surgical instruments.
(g) Distinguish dry heat sterilization from moist heat (autoclave) sterilization.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Heat sterilization involves destruction of enzymes and other essential cell constituents; dry heat sterilization is applied to thermostable products.
(b)
• The apparatus is the hot air oven, and methods under dry heat also include incineration, red heat, and flaming.
(c)
• Dry heat (160-180°C) sterilization is used, unlike moisture-resistant materials which use 121-134°C moist heat.
(d)
• A limitation is that dry heat is applied to thermostable products, so it is less suited than filtration or gaseous methods for materials that cannot withstand these higher temperatures.
(e)
• The benefit relevant to reporting is that dry heat destroys bacterial endotoxins (pyrogens), which are difficult to eliminate by other means, so glass bottles sterilized this way are suitable to be filled aseptically.
(f)
• The benefit of dry heat includes good penetrability and a non-corrosive nature, which makes it applicable for sterilizing glassware and metal surgical instruments, and it is also used for sterilizing non-aqueous thermostable liquids and thermostable powders.
(g)
• Heat sterilization is more effective in the hydrated state, where under conditions of high humidity, hydrolysis and denaturation occur; dry heat therefore requires a higher temperature range (160-180°C) than moist heat (121-134°C) to achieve the same microbicidal effect, and moist heat in the form of saturated steam under pressure (autoclaving) is the most widely used and dependable form of moist heat sterilization.

questions.question:
Question 41
(a) Describe the basic structure/formation of the main types of asexual fungal spores.
(b) State the identifying characteristics that distinguish the main types of sexual fungal spores.
(c) State the standard setting in which spore type is used to classify fungi.
(d) Explain the basic reasoning behind the precaution needed when handling fungal cultures because of how spores are formed and dispersed.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Types of asexual spores include: conidiospores (multiple, in chains, or single spores formed at the end of an aerial hypha, not enclosed within a sac, e.g. Aspergillus, Penicillium), arthrospores/arthroconidia (formed from fragmentation of hyphae into single thick cells, e.g. Coccidioides), blastospores/blastoconidia (buds coming from the parent cell, e.g. Candida), chlamydospores (a thick-walled spore formed within the hypha, a way of producing a substantial resting spore quickly, e.g. Candida albicans), and sporangiospores (hundreds of spores formed within a sac, the sporangium, at the end of an aerial hypha, e.g. Rhizopus, Mucor).
(b)
• Sexual spores are relatively rare compared with asexual sporulation and develop through three phases: plasmogamy, karyogamy and meiosis; sexual spores are used to classify fungi into the divisions Glomerulomycota (zygospore), Ascomycota (ascospores within a sac-like ascus, 4 to 8 per ascus), and Basidiomycota (basidiospores borne on a club-shaped basidium).
(c)
• Sexual spore formation is used as the basis of the systematic classification of medically important fungi into the four phyla Glomerulomycota, Ascomycota, Basidiomycota, and Deuteromycota (fungi imperfecti, whose sexual phase is not identified).
(d)
• Sporulation is the principal way by which fungi reproduce and spread; fungal spores are metabolically dormant, protected cells released by the mycelium in enormous numbers and borne by air or water to new sites, where they germinate and establish new colonies, which is why handling fungal cultures (for example, preferring tubed rather than plate media) is done with care to reduce the chance of spore release into the laboratory environment.

questions.question:
Question 51
(a) State the principle of xenodiagnosis.
(b) State the apparatus/organism used.
(c) Describe the step-by-step procedure.
(d) State a precaution relevant to this technique.
(e) State how a positive result is reported.
(f) Explain why xenodiagnosis is used in the diagnosis of chronic Chagas disease specifically.
(g) Distinguish xenodiagnosis from direct examination of peripheral blood as diagnostic techniques for Trypanosoma cruzi.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Xenodiagnosis is a technique employed in the diagnosis of chronic cases of trypanosomiasis; it relies on allowing the vector insect to feed on the patient's blood, so that if the patient is infected, the parasite will multiply within the insect and can then be demonstrated.
(b)
• Laboratory-bred triatomid bugs are the apparatus/organism used.
(c)
• The laboratory-bred triatomid bugs are allowed to feed on the blood of the patient suspected of having the disease; if the patient is infected, the trypanosomes will multiply rapidly in the intestine of the bug.
(d)
• A precaution is that the bugs used must be laboratory-bred (to ensure they were not already carrying trypanosomes from another source) before being allowed to feed on the patient.
(e)
• A positive result is reported when examination of the intestinal content of the bug reveals the presence of infective metacyclic forms of the parasite.
(f)
• Xenodiagnosis is used for chronic cases because examination of peripheral blood is generally unreliable for routine diagnosis of Trypanosoma cruzi infection, as the organism can only be detected in very early infections by direct blood examination.
(g)
• Direct examination of peripheral blood looks for the trypanosomal form directly in a blood film, which is generally unreliable except in very early infection, whereas xenodiagnosis instead uses the multiplication of the parasite within a feeding vector insect to amplify and then demonstrate an infection that may not be directly detectable in the patient's own blood.

(a)
• The use of a sensitive control organism shows that the antibiotic itself is active; because the test organism grew up to the disk (no zone of inhibition around it) while the control organism showed a zone, it may safely be assumed that the test organism is resistant to that drug.
(b)
• The result for that antibiotic is recorded as "resistant" for the test organism, based on comparison of its zone (absent) with the zone produced around the sensitive control organism on the same plate.
(c)
• For the other disks where the test organism does show a clear zone of inhibition, comparable to that of the control organism, the organism is indicated to be susceptible to those antibiotics.
(d)
• A more precise measure of susceptibility can be obtained by determining the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) and the minimum bactericidal concentration (MBC), using a series of broths mixed with serially diluted antibiotic solutions and a standard inoculum of the organism.
questions.question:
Question 25
In a Stokes' controlled sensitivity test set up on Mueller-Hinton agar, a control (known-sensitive) organism is inoculated on part of the plate and the test organism on the remainder, with antibiotic disks placed at the interface. After incubation, the test organism is found to have grown right up to the edge of one of the disks, while a clear zone of inhibition is seen around the control organism for the same disk.
(a) Interpret what this pattern of growth means for the test organism and that antibiotic.
(b) State how this result should be recorded.
(c) State what the result indicates about further antibiotics tested on the same plate that show a clear zone around the test organism.
(d) State the follow-up action that can be taken to obtain a more precise measure of susceptibility.

Question 21
(a) State the general classification of culture media used in the microbiology laboratory, with an example of each.
(b) State how each type of medium is applied/selected for a given purpose in the laboratory.
(c) Explain why choosing the wrong type of medium for a specimen would lead to an inaccurate or invalid laboratory result.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Media are classified, based on nutrient content and consistency, as: Basal Media (e.g. nutrient broth, nutrient agar), Enriched Media (e.g. blood agar), Selective Media (e.g. MacConkey agar, Lowenstein-Jensen media), Differential (Indicator) Media (e.g. MacConkey agar, which contains the dye neutral red), Transport Media (e.g. Stuart medium, Cary-Blair medium), and Storage Media (e.g. egg saline medium, chalk-cooked meat broth).
(b)
• Basal media are used for culturing bacteria (such as Staphylococcus and Enterobacteriaceae) that do not need enrichment.
• Enriched media, comprising complex organic substances such as blood or serum, are used where specific species require this for growth.
• Selective media favour the growth of selected bacteria while inhibiting undesirable bacteria.
• Differential media allow growth of several different organisms that show visible differences (e.g. MacConkey agar is yellow when neutral and red/pink when acidic, due to the neutral red dye).
• Transport media are used where specimens cannot be cultured soon after collection, so that the organism survives until it reaches the laboratory.
• Storage media are used when bacteria are to be kept viable for a long period.
(c)
• Because selective and differential media are formulated to favour or visually distinguish particular organisms, using an unsuitable medium (for example, a basal medium instead of a selective medium for a mixed specimen, or omitting a transport medium for a delayed specimen) can allow overgrowth of unwanted organisms, failure of the pathogen to survive transport, or loss of the differential colour reaction needed for identification, giving an inaccurate or invalid result.

questions.question:
Question 57
In a simple screening method for African trypanosomiasis, a patient's serum is tested in a gel containing antiserum against IgM and beta-2 macroglobulins, and precipitin bands are formed.
(a) Interpret what the formation of these precipitin bands indicates.
(b) State how this screening result should be recorded/reported.
(c) State what this result indicates about the need for further investigation of the patient.
(d) State the follow-up action/technique that should follow a positive screening result.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The formation of precipitin bands by the patient's serum in a gel containing antiserum against IgM and beta-2 macroglobulins is apparently a feature of trypanosomal infection, and this reaction is used as a simple method of selecting cases for further investigation.
(b)
• The result is recorded as a positive screening test for trypanosomal infection, based on the precipitin band formation described.
(c)
• A positive result indicates that the patient should be selected for further laboratory investigation to confirm African trypanosomiasis, since the screening test alone is a selection method and not a definitive diagnosis.
(d)
• Follow-up should proceed to examination of the peripheral blood (thick film stained by Leishman's stain, with a concentration method if parasitaemia is low), examination of aspirates from lymph nodes or CSF, or animal inoculation, so that the trypanosomes themselves can be demonstrated.

(a)
• Radiation is energy emitted from atomic activities, dispersed at high velocity through matter or space, and it usually destroys or distorts nucleic acids; the major target for radiation is microbial DNA.
(b)
• Equipment used includes the ultraviolet lamp, and ionization sources (beta rays, gamma rays, X-rays) gamma ray sterilization uses a gamma ray sterilizer with rays usually derived from a cobalt-60 source.
(c)
• For UV light, articles/areas are exposed to the ultraviolet lamp; for gamma rays, articles being sterilized are passed through the irradiation chamber on a conveyor belt and move around the raised source.
(d)
• Disadvantages of radiation sterilization include the requirement for highly specialized equipment, and the effect of irradiation on the products and their containers.
(e)
• Radiation sterilization is generally applied to articles in the dry state, including surgical instruments, sutures, prostheses, unit-dose ointments, and plastic syringes.
(f)
• UV light has much lower energy and poor penetrability compared with gamma rays and electrons, but this makes it useful in the sterilization of air, surface sterilization of aseptic work areas, and treatment of manufacturing-grade water, and it is used in operating areas and bacteriological cabinets to reduce cross infection.
(g)
• Gamma rays and electrons cause ionization and free radical production, while UV light causes excitation rather than ionization; gamma rays, with much greater penetrability, are applied to dry-state articles such as sutures and plastic syringes passed through an irradiation chamber, whereas UV light, with poor penetrability, is limited to surface and air sterilization.
questions.question:
Question 14
(a) State the principle of radiation sterilization.
(b) State the apparatus/equipment used.
(c) Describe how UV light and gamma ray sterilization are each carried out.
(d) State a precaution/disadvantage of the method.
(e) State the type of items for which radiation sterilization is reported/used.
(f) Explain why UV light is preferred for air and surface sterilization of aseptic work areas.
(g) Distinguish gamma ray sterilization from UV light sterilization.

Question 15
(a) State the principle/mechanism of action of ethylene oxide gaseous sterilization.
(b) State the apparatus/equipment and conditions (pressure, temperature) used.
(c) Describe the materials/items to which this method is applied.
(d) State a precaution/disadvantage of the method.
(e) State how the method's use is reported/recorded in practice.
(f) Explain why ethylene oxide is preferred for certain thermolabile items.
(g) Distinguish ethylene oxide gaseous sterilization from hydrogen peroxide sterilization.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The mechanism of antimicrobial action of ethylene oxide (and formaldehyde) is through alkylation of sulphydryl, amino, hydroxyl and carboxyl groups on proteins and amino groups of nucleic acids; ethylene oxide is a colourless, odourless and flammable gas that possesses biocidal activity.
(b)
• The equipment is a special oven for admission of gas and humidity, using ethylene oxide-carbon dioxide at a pressure of 30 psi and a temperature of 20-55°C.
(c)
• It is applied to thermolabile powder, plastic/polymer materials, ophthalmic preparations, subcutaneous and vaginal inserts, plastic syringes, and tubing sets.
(d)
• Disadvantages include explosive hazard, toxicity, and unsuitability for solutions.
(e)
• Its use is reported/recorded as ethylene oxide sterilization at the stated pressure and temperature for the specific thermolabile item processed.
(f)
• Because ethylene oxide sterilization is carried out at a relatively low temperature range (20-55°C), it is preferred for thermolabile powders, plastics/polymers and other heat-sensitive items that would be damaged by heat-based sterilization methods.
(g)
• Ethylene oxide acts through alkylation and is applied in a special gas-admitting oven at 30 psi and 20-55°C to thermolabile plastics and polymers, whereas hydrogen peroxide sterilization disperses a hydrogen peroxide solution in a vacuum chamber to create a plasma cloud that sterilizes by oxidizing key cellular components, at a temperature range of 40-50°C, making it well suited for heat- and moisture-sensitive medical devices.

questions.question:
Question 29
(a) Describe the basic structure and composition of a virus, including its nucleic acid, capsid, and envelope.
(b) State the identifying/distinguishing features of enveloped versus naked viruses and of the different capsid symmetries.
(c) State the standard setting/method in which the structural features of a virus are used in practice.
(d) Explain the basic reasoning behind the common precaution that enveloped viruses become non-infectious if their membrane is destroyed.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Viruses are made up of proteins and nucleic acid; the viral nucleic acid, which is either DNA or RNA but never both, is enclosed in a capsid made up of protein subunits called protomeres.
• The capsid accounts for most of the virion mass, protects the nucleic acid, and in naked viruses also provides attachment; some viruses have an envelope, an amorphous structure of lipid, protein and carbohydrate lying outside the capsid, from which glycoprotein spikes with enzymatic, absorptive, haemagglutinating and/or antigenic activity arise.
(b)
• A naked virus is one without an envelope; the morphology of a virus is determined by the arrangement of the protomeres into icosahedral (cubic, 20 equal triangular faces, 12 apices), helical (protomeres aggregated into a capped tube around one axis of symmetry), or complex forms.
• Icosahedral symmetry shows structural units on faces giving morphological capsomeres (pentons with 5-fold symmetry, hexons), with 3-fold symmetry through the face and 2-fold through the edge, while helical symmetry has multiple structural units along a single central axis.
(c)
• These structural features (nature of nucleic acid, capsid symmetry, presence/absence of envelope, and dimensions of virion and capsid) are the four main characteristics used in the Hierarchical virus classification system to group viruses according to their shared properties down to the level of family, genus, and species/strain.
(d)
• Since the envelope's lipid component is host-derived and forms an amorphous layer outside the capsid, disruption of this membrane structurally compromises the intact virion the mechanism of attachment, entry, assembly and release depends on the intact envelope and its spikes, so destruction of the envelope renders the virus noninfectious.

(a)
• The organism is Entamoeba histolytica, and the actively motile form containing ingested red blood cells in its granular endoplasm is the trophozoite (the growing and feeding stage of the parasite).
(b)
• Since the trophozoite is actively motile, the stool sample should be examined with as little delay as possible; cysts, which are also passed in stool, are best seen by making a preparation with iodine (Lugol's iodine), while iron haematoxylin stains of faecal smears give the sharpest pictures of cysts, showing the chromatoidal bodies and nuclei more clearly.
(c)
• The finding is recorded as trophozoites of Entamoeba histolytica seen, noting the presence of ingested red blood cells, which is consistent with invasive amoebic dysentery.
(d)
• Because blood-stained particles of mucus in the stool offer the best chance of finding the parasites, such particles should specifically be selected for examination; cultural methods, for which several media are available, may also be used for the culture of the parasitic amoebae.
questions.question:
Question 48
A fresh, blood-stained, mucus-containing stool sample from a patient with suspected amoebic dysentery is examined under the microscope. Actively motile amoeboid organisms about 20-30 µm in size, with a clear ectoplasm and granular endoplasm containing ingested red blood cells, are seen.
(a) Identify the organism and the stage observed.
(b) State the basic technique(s) used to detect and better visualize this organism and its cyst stage in stool.
(c) State how the finding should be recorded/reported.
(d) State the follow-up practical step suggested for such a specimen.

Question 27
A series of broths containing serially diluted concentrations of an antibiotic are each inoculated with a standard amount of a test bacterium and incubated. Growth (turbidity) is inhibited from the 8 µg/mL tube upward, but when these tubes are subsequently subcultured onto drug-free medium, visible growth appears from the 8 µg/mL and 16 µg/mL subcultures, with no growth only from the 32 µg/mL subculture onward.
(a) Interpret these results in terms of the MIC and the MBC of the antibiotic for this organism.
(b) State how these values should be recorded/reported.
(c) State what the relationship between the MIC and MBC values indicates about whether the drug is acting as a cidal or a static agent for this organism.
(d) State the follow-up action indicated by this relationship.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The MIC (minimum inhibitory concentration) is the lowest concentration at which growth of the organism has been inhibited, which is 8 µg/mL in this case; the MBC (minimum bactericidal concentration) is the lowest concentration at which no visible growth is observed on subculture onto drug-free medium, which is 32 µg/mL in this case.
(b)
• The result is recorded as MIC = 8 µg/mL and MBC = 32 µg/mL for this organism against this antibiotic.
(c)
• Because the MBC is higher than the MIC (rather than close to it), this indicates a static rather than a cidal action for this organism; with static agents the MIC is much lower than the MBC, since once the bacteria are removed from the drug they can grow again on drug-free medium at most concentrations, whereas cidal drugs have MBC values close to the MIC value.
(d)
• This static relationship is taken into account in selecting or continuing the antimicrobial agent, since a cidal drug that kills the organism outright would be indicated by an MBC close to the MIC rather than several dilutions above it.

(a)
• DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) stores information for protein synthesis; its double helix structure, proposed by Watson and Crick, is composed of two chains of polynucleotides, each chain having a backbone of deoxyribose sugar and phosphate residues arranged alternately, with four nitrogenous bases - adenine and guanine (purines), and thymine and cytosine (pyrimidines).
• RNA (ribonucleic acid) is involved in transcription and translation of information for protein synthesis, following the central dogma: DNA to RNA to protein; there are three types of RNA - messenger RNA (mRNA), transfer RNA (tRNA), and ribosomal RNA (rRNA).
(b)
• RNA is structurally similar to DNA except for two major differences: RNA has a ribose sugar (instead of deoxyribose) and uses uracil in place of thymine as one of its bases.
(c)
• The gene, a segment of DNA specifying a particular polypeptide, is the unit of heredity, and bacterial genetics is used as a model to understand DNA replication, genetic characters, and how these characters change and are transferred to the next generation.
(d)
• Genotype is the genetic constitution of a cell that is transmitted to its progeny, whereas phenotype is the physical expression of the genotype in a given environment; because phenotypic variations are influenced by the environment and are temporary and not heritable, while genotypic variations are not influenced by the environment and are stable and heritable, a bacterium's observed (phenotypic) characteristic must not automatically be assumed to be a stable, heritable genetic change unless it is shown to be genotypic.
questions.question:
Question 5
(a) Describe the basic structure of DNA and RNA as the nucleic acids carrying genetic information in bacteria.
(b) State the identifying features that distinguish RNA structurally from DNA.
(c) State the standard setting/model in which the structure of DNA is used to explain heredity.
(d) Explain the basic reasoning behind the precaution of understanding genotype versus phenotype when interpreting a bacterium's observed characteristics.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• For culturing a microorganism, a small sample is introduced into a culture medium, usually with the help of a platinum wire probe streaked across its surface; the growth observed on or in the medium is the culture.
(b)
• A heat-sterilized loop or a micropipette with sterilized tips is the most common apparatus used for spreading/inoculating the sample; the pour plate method, spread plate method, and streak plate method are all included among the inoculation techniques.
(c)
• The five basic microbiology laboratory procedures are Inoculation, Incubation, Isolation, Inspection (Observation), and Identification; once inoculation is done, the agar or broth containing the inoculum is kept in the incubator at a certain temperature for the required time to support optimum bacterial growth.
(d)
• A precaution is the use of an aseptic technique throughout, to avert contamination of laboratory personnel, cultures, and equipment during manipulation of the specimen.
(e)
• Bacterial numbers may be further reported/quantified by serial dilution (to lower bacterial concentration to a countable level), plate counts (reflecting the number of colonies capable of emerging under the given conditions), the Most Probable Number (MPN) technique (for estimating viable microorganism concentration by replicate liquid broth dilutions), or use of a spectrophotometer (to estimate total bacterial number during growth studies).
(f)
• Good Microbiological Practice, comprising aseptic techniques, is of utmost importance to prevent contamination of the laboratory when handling microorganisms, keeping the research/diagnostic material in a safe place without contact with other organisms, and keeping the safety of people around in mind, so that the result is obtained without adulteration or contamination.
(g)
• The streak, pour and spread plate methods are inoculation techniques used to introduce and distribute the organism on/in the medium so that isolated colonies can grow and be observed, whereas serial dilution is a separate step used specifically to lower the bacterial concentration to a level at which colonies (or MPN tubes) can be accurately counted for enumeration purposes.
questions.question:
Question 19
(a) State the principle behind the basic culture technique used to grow and examine bacteria in the laboratory.
(b) State the apparatus/materials used for inoculation.
(c) Describe the sequence of the five basic microbiology laboratory procedures used to examine and characterize microbes.
(d) State a precaution relevant to this technique.
(e) State how bacterial numbers may be further reported/quantified from such a culture.
(f) Explain why aseptic technique (Good Microbiological Practice) is important throughout this process.
(g) Distinguish the streak/pour/spread plate inoculation methods from the use of serial dilution for enumeration.

Question 45
(a) State the general classification of host-parasite (symbiotic) relationships, and the classification of parasites by their level of dependence on the host, with an example of each.
(b) State how recognizing each type is applied/useful in understanding a given infection.
(c) Explain why classifying a parasite as purely commensal without considering the host's immune status could be a basic error.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Symbiotic relationships include: Commensalism (one organism benefits while the other remains unaffected, e.g. Entamoeba gingivalis and Trichomonas tenax in the mouth), Mutualism (both partners benefit), Parasitism (one organism benefits at the cost of the host - the group of disease-causing organisms), and Opportunism (if the host's normal defences are weakened, a commensal parasite may cause disease, e.g. Isospora belli, Cryptosporidium).
• By level of dependence on the host, parasites are classified as: Obligate parasites (must spend at least part of their life cycle in/on a host, e.g. the malaria parasite), Facultative parasites (normally free-living but can obtain nutrients from a host, e.g. Naegleria fowleri, Acanthamoeba), Accidental parasites (attack an unusual host, e.g. Toxocara canis/catis), and Aberrant parasites (reach a site in a host, during migration, where they cannot live or develop further).
(b)
• Recognizing a relationship as commensal versus parasitic helps explain why an organism such as Entamoeba gingivalis is generally harmless, whereas recognizing an organism as an obligate parasite (e.g. Plasmodium) explains why it must always be found in association with a host at some stage of its life cycle.
(c)
• Because opportunism means that a normally commensal or weakly pathogenic parasite (e.g. Isospora belli, Cryptosporidium) may cause disease specifically when the host's normal defences are weakened, assuming an organism is harmless purely because it is usually commensal, without considering whether the host is immunocompromised, is a basic error that could result in a missed or delayed diagnosis of opportunistic parasitic disease.

(a)
• Methods for growing cells in vitro include cell culture (the growing of cells in vitro, including single-cell culture), comprising suspension culture (some cell lines adapted to grow in suspension in continuously stirred and aerated vessels) and monolayer cell culture (sheets of cells, only one cell thick, grown on the surface of glass or plastic vessels), and organ culture (growth of tissue or part of an organ in vitro).
• Types of culture include primary cell culture (started from cells, tissues or organs taken directly from an animal, regarded as primary until first subcultured) and continuous cell lines (cells of a single type capable of indefinite propagation in vitro).
(b)
• Recognition of viral growth in culture includes: Cytopathic Effect (CPE - morphological evidence of cell damage visible with the inverted microscope, such as giant cell formation, complete destruction of cells, presence of inclusion bodies, and syncytium formation), metabolism effect (change in colour of the medium from red to yellow through orange, reflecting a change in pH), plaque formation (inoculation of virus into monolayer culture with late addition of a semisolid overlay agar, which localizes viral spread and produces a plaque), and interference (multiplication of one virus in the cells often inhibiting subsequent multiplication of another virus).
(c)
• The nutrient medium used for these cultures usually consists of a balanced salt solution, glucose, vitamin, coenzyme, amino acids, serum, sodium bicarbonate and phenol red.
(d)
• The ideal animal host for study of a virus is the natural host, though this is not always possible or practical; the animal used should be Specific Pathogen Free, because an intercurrent infection could contaminate the propagated virus, and the animal must also have no prior immunity to the particular virus being studied, since prior immunity would prevent successful propagation/study of that virus.
questions.question:
Question 32
(a) Describe the basic types of cell/tissue culture systems used to grow viruses in vitro.
(b) State the identifying features used to recognize viral growth in these culture systems.
(c) State the standard nutrient components used to maintain these cultures in practice.
(d) Explain the basic reasoning behind the precaution that a laboratory animal used for virus study should be Specific Pathogen Free.

Question 42
Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) is received from a patient with suspected fungal meningitis and is to be examined for encapsulated yeasts.
(a) Identify the specimen and the reagent/preparation used for direct demonstration of the capsule.
(b) State the principle behind this preparation.
(c) Describe the step-by-step procedure for preparing and examining the slide.
(d) State the expected observed result and its interpretation if positive.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The specimen is cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), and the preparation used is an India ink preparation, used for demonstration of the capsule of Cryptococcus neoformans in CSF specimens.
(b)
• India ink induces negative staining by creating a black, semi-opaque background, which makes the capsule of the yeast cell clearly visible against the dark background.
(c)
• One drop of cerebrospinal fluid is mixed with a drop of India ink on a clean slide; a cover slip is placed over it and the sample is then examined by microscopy.
(d)
• A positive result shows an unstained wide capsule surrounding a budding yeast cell, consistent with Cryptococcus neoformans, whose characteristic thick capsule surrounds the budding yeast cell.

questions.question:
Question 30
A clinical specimen suspected to contain a virus is to be isolated by inoculation into embryonated hen's eggs.
(a) Identify the apparatus/host system and the routes by which the egg may be inoculated.
(b) State the principle behind checking the egg before inoculation.
(c) Describe the step-by-step procedure, including what is done to confirm viral growth after inoculation.
(d) State the expected result and its interpretation if virus is present.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The host system is the embryonated egg; it may be infected by various routes including the amniotic, allantoic, chorio-allantoic, and yolk sac routes, and in special cases the intravenous and intra-embryonal routes, with the choice of route depending on the ability of the tissue to support virus replication.
(b)
• Before inoculation, eggs are candled to check that the embryo is alive, since the egg method is used for rapid isolation of viruses and is more economical and convenient than animal inoculation.
(c)
• The chosen route of inoculation is used to introduce the specimen into the egg; the presence of virus in the inoculated egg is then detected by mortality, deformities and haemorrhage of the embryo, lesions in the form of pocks, oedema of the developing membrane, or the presence of specific antigen in the fluid as shown by the haemagglutination inhibition (HI) test, serum neutralization (SN) test, fluorescent antibody test (FAT) and other serological tests.
(d)
• If virus is present, one or more of these changes (embryo mortality, deformity, haemorrhage, pock lesions, membrane oedema, or detectable specific antigen) will be observed, confirming successful isolation of the virus in the egg.

(a)
• A prokaryotic cell has five essential structural components: a nucleoid (DNA), ribosomes, a cell membrane, a cell wall, and a surface layer, which may or may not be an inherent part of the wall.
• Bacteria are typically unicellular, microscopic, prokaryotic organisms whose cells lack a nucleus or any other organelle, and they reproduce by binary fission.
(b)
• Most members of the Bacteria domain have a cell wall containing peptidoglycan, a substance not found anywhere else but in bacteria, and this feature, together with the absence of a nucleus, distinguishes them from Archaea and Eukarya in the Three Domain Classification (based on rRNA sequences, first proposed by Carl Woese).
(c)
• Identification of bacteria in the laboratory is based on media (e.g. selective media such as MacConkey for lactose and non-lactose fermenters, and blood agar which can accommodate almost all bacteria), colonial morphology, Gram reaction (Gram-positive and Gram-negative), and biochemical reactions such as catalase, other enzymes and coagulase.
(d)
• An aseptic technique is a procedure performed under sterile conditions to prevent the introduction of unwanted organisms or bacterial contaminants into an environment.
• This is an important microbiological lab technique to avert contamination of laboratory personnel, cultures, and equipment, so that the research/diagnostic result is obtained without adulteration or contamination, which is the ultimate goal of Good Microbiological Practice (GMP).
questions.question:
Question 1
(a) Describe the basic structure and composition of a bacterial (prokaryotic) cell.
(b) State the identifying characteristics that distinguish the Bacteria domain from other microbial groups.
(c) State the standard method/setting in which bacterial structural and staining features are used in practice for identification.
(d) Explain the basic reasoning behind the precaution of using aseptic technique when handling bacterial cultures.

Question 36
A patient presents with an itching, scaling patch on the skin suspected to be a dermatophyte infection. Skin scrapings are to be collected and examined in the laboratory.
(a) Identify the specimen and the reagent/mount used for direct examination of this type of specimen.
(b) State the principle behind the use of this reagent.
(c) Describe how the specimen should be collected and processed before examination.
(d) State the expected microscopic finding and its interpretation if the test is positive.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The specimen is a skin scraping, and the direct examination is done as a KOH (potassium hydroxide) mount.
(b)
• KOH clears the tissue cells so that fungal elements may be seen more clearly, allowing direct examination of the specimen for spores, hyphae and other mycelial elements.
(c)
• The skin should first be cleaned with 70% alcohol to remove dirt, oil and surface saprophytes before the scraping is taken; skin, nails and hair are examined by direct exam following the KOH preparation.
(d)
• A positive result shows fungal elements such as hyphae or spores/mycelial elements on direct microscopy, supporting a diagnosis of a dermatophyte (cutaneous mycosis) infection.

questions.question:
Question 35
(a) Describe the basic structure and composition of the fungal cell wall and cell membrane.
(b) State the identifying characteristics that distinguish fungal cell composition from that of bacteria and of mammalian cells.
(c) State the standard setting/method in which this structural difference is used in practice.
(d) Explain the basic reasoning behind why antifungal agents can be selectively toxic to fungi.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The fungal cell wall contains chitin, which provides rigidity and support, and also contains polysaccharides the major polysaccharides of the cell wall matrix consist of glucans such as mannans, chitosan, and galactans.
• The fungal cell membrane is similar to the mammalian plasma membrane, but the cytoplasmic membrane contains ergosterol rather than cholesterol, and it regulates passage of materials into and out of the cell by being selectively permeable.
(b)
• The fungal cell wall lacks peptidoglycan, glycerol and ribitol teichoic acid, and lipopolysaccharide (features found in bacterial cell walls), and its membrane sterol is ergosterol rather than the cholesterol found in mammalian cell membranes.
(c)
• The ergosterol-containing cell membrane is the target of action of antifungal agents, and the cell wall glucan is important for a class of newer antifungal agents, so these structural differences from mammalian cells are used in practice as the basis for antifungal drug targets.
(d)
• Because fungal cell membranes contain ergosterol rather than the cholesterol found in human cell membranes, and the fungal cell wall (containing chitin and glucans) has no equivalent structure in human cells, agents that target ergosterol or the cell wall components can act on the fungus while causing comparatively less harm to the human host's own cells.

(a)
• Helminths are divided into two major phyla: Platyhelminthes (flat worms), which includes the classes Trematoda (flukes, e.g. Schistosoma, Fasciola) and Cestoda (tapeworms, e.g. Taenia, Diphyllobothrium, Hymenolepis); and Nemathelminthes (round worms), class Nematoda (e.g. Ascaris, Ancylostoma, Necator, Enterobius, Wuchereria).
(b)
• Trematodes and cestodes are recognized by their flattened body form and, in the case of cestodes, a segmented tapeworm structure, while nematodes are recognized by their rounded, unsegmented body form identification in the laboratory rests on features such as the outer cuticle/integument (tough, may be armed with spines or hooks, resistant to intestinal digestion), and the eggs or larvae recovered from a specimen.
• Helminths generally do not possess organs of locomotion (movement is by muscular contraction and relaxation), have an absent or rudimentary digestive system and a primitive nervous system, but a very well-developed reproductive system, so identification often focuses on the distinctive reproductive structures (eggs, proglottids) rather than locomotor features.
(c)
• Helminths, by and large, do not multiply in the human body, so a single infection does not by itself lead to disease, even though eggs are produced in enormous numbers by the adult worm; assuming that because eggs are abundant the worm burden (and therefore disease severity) is necessarily high would be a basic error, since disease depends on the adult worm burden established from the original infecting dose, not from multiplication within the host.
questions.question:
Question 46
(a) State the general classification of helminths into phyla and classes, with an example genus for each.
(b) State how each class is applied/recognized in identifying a helminth infection.
(c) Explain why a basic error in recognizing the general features of helminths (e.g. their reproductive capacity) could lead to a wrong assumption about disease severity.

Question 4
(a) Describe the composition of the normal bacterial flora at different anatomical sites of the body.
(b) State the identifying characteristic organisms found at the mouth, skin, and large intestine.
(c) State the standard setting in which knowledge of normal flora composition is applied in practice.
(d) Explain the basic reasoning behind the precaution that normal flora can cause disease in an immunocompromised host or when transferred to another site.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The normal flora of humans consist mainly of bacteria, but other organisms such as fungi can also be found; it has been calculated that a human adult houses about 10^12 bacteria on the skin, 10^10 in the mouth, and 10^14 in the gastrointestinal tract.
• The mixture of organisms regularly found at any anatomical site is referred to as the normal flora, and this composition may be influenced by genetics, age, sex, climate, stress, migration, diet, and the environment.
(b)
• The mouth flora includes Staphylococcus aureus, Staphylococcus epidermidis, viridans streptococci, Micrococcus spp, Corynebacterium spp, Lactobacillus sp, Bacteroides sp, Haemophilus spp, Neisseria spp, Branhamella spp and Enterobacteriaceae; skin flora includes Staphylococcus epidermidis, Micrococcus spp and Corynebacterium spp; the large intestine and lower ileum flora includes Enterococci, Lactobacillus spp, Clostridium spp, Bacteroides spp, Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Candida albicans among other organisms.
(c)
• Knowledge of normal flora composition at each anatomical site is applied when interpreting a culture result from a clinical specimen, so that organisms that are part of the expected normal flora of that site can be distinguished from unexpected or pathogenic isolates.
(d)
• The relationship between the normal flora and the host may be mutual, commensal, or parasitic; some normal flora are pathogenic and cause endogenous infections in immunocompromised patients (opportunistic infections), or when transferred from their original site to another site in the body (e.g. during endotracheal intubation), where they are no longer restricted or tolerated by host defences.

questions.explanation: NK cells are lymphocytes capable of destroying tumour cells without prior sensitisation, thus providing the first line of defence against tumour cells. After activation with IL-2 and IL-15, NK cells can lyse a wide range of human tumours. T cells, NK cells, and macrophages may collaborate in antitumour reactivity because interferon-?, secreted by T cells and NK cells, is a potent activator of macrophages.
questions.question: Natural killer (NK) cells contribute to antitumour immunity by:
options: Destroying tumour cells without prior sensitisation, providing a first line of defence
Presenting tumour antigens to cytotoxic T cells in lymph nodes
Producing specific antibodies against tumour-specific antigens
Secreting pro-inflammatory cytokines that activate macrophages exclusively
Producing complement proteins that lyse tumour cells by membrane attack

questions.explanation: The hyperinflammatory state initiated by sepsis can activate counter-regulatory immunosuppressive mechanisms, which may involve both innate and adaptive immunity.
