This immune suppression following the initial hyperinflammatory phase makes septic patients vulnerable to secondary infections and inability to clear the primary infection. This is one of the four major factors contributing to the pathophysiology of septic shock.
options: Antibiotic-induced reduction in microbial antigens stimulating immunity
Cytokine-induced corticosteroid excess suppressing lymphocyte function
Gram-positive toxin–mediated destruction of natural killer cells
Bone marrow failure from DIC-induced vascular damage
Counter-regulatory immunosuppressive mechanisms activated by the hyperinflammatory state
questions.question: In septic shock, immune suppression is triggered by:

questions.explanation: The prognosis varies with the origin and duration of shock. Greater than 90% of young, otherwise healthy patients with hypovolemic shock survive with appropriate management. In comparison, septic shock or cardiogenic shock associated with extensive myocardial infarction can have substantially worse mortality rates even with optimal care. The nature and extent of the precipitating insult significantly determines outcome.
questions.question: Prognosis in shock varies with its origin. Which statement CORRECTLY reflects this?
options: Septic shock has the best prognosis with aggressive antibiotic therapy
Cardiogenic shock from large MI has better mortality than hypovolemic shock in young patients
Neurogenic shock carries the highest mortality of all shock types
All types of shock have similar mortality rates with optimal care
Greater than 90% of young otherwise healthy patients with hypovolemic shock survive with appropriate management

questions.explanation: Squamous metaplasia in the respiratory tract of smokers represents an adaptive response that initially provides a more resistant epithelial lining against chronic irritant injury, but if the offending stimulus persists, the metaplastic epithelium can progress through dysplasia toward malignant transformation. This dual nature, protective in the short term but potentially precancerous with continued exposure, is an important concept in understanding how chronic injury can eventually lead to cancer. Smoking cessation is therefore critical to halt this progression before irreversible dysplastic or malignant change occurs.
questions.question: A patient with chronic bronchitis from occupational dust exposure develops squamous metaplasia of the bronchial lining, and continued exposure eventually leads to dysplastic changes. This progression illustrates that squamous metaplasia in smokers is an example of which adaptational response category?
options: An entirely harmless adaptation with no long-term risk
A protective but potentially precancerous adaptation
An irreversible malignant transformation from onset
A purely regenerative process unrelated to injury

questions.explanation: Metaplasia is a reversible change in which one differentiated cell type is replaced by another differentiated cell type better able to withstand the adverse stress, commonly seen when columnar epithelium is replaced by more durable squamous epithelium. It represents an adaptive substitution of cell type rather than a disordered proliferation. Persistent metaplasia may progress to dysplasia if the stimulus continues.
questions.question: A heavy smoker's bronchial ciliated columnar epithelium is replaced by stratified squamous epithelium on biopsy. This reversible change is best termed:

questions.explanation: The four classes of normal regulatory genes targeted by genetic damage in carcinogenesis are growth-promoting proto-oncogenes, growth-inhibiting tumour suppressor genes, genes regulating programmed cell death, and genes involved in DNA repair. Damage to any of these gene classes can disrupt the normal balance of cell proliferation, survival, and genomic stability, contributing to the multistep process of malignant transformation. Understanding these categories provides a framework for classifying the molecular abnormalities found across different human cancers.
questions.question: A pathologist studying carcinogenesis identifies that damage to four broad classes of normal regulatory genes underlies malignant transformation. Which class listed is one of these four?
The role of macrophages in the proliferative phase of wound healing includes:
questions.explanation: Macrophages are key cellular constituents of tissue repair. By 48-96 hours, neutrophils are largely replaced by macrophages in the wound. Macrophages clear extracellular debris, fibrin, and other foreign material at the repair site, and promote angiogenesis and ECM deposition. They are essential for wound healing — wounds in macrophage-depleted animals heal poorly.
options: Formation of the initial fibrin-rich blood clot sealing the wound
First-line phagocytosis of bacteria within the first 24 hours
Synthesising type I collagen to provide tensile strength to the scar
Clearing extracellular debris, fibrin, and foreign material while promoting angiogenesis and ECM deposition
Contracting the wound margins to reduce the wound surface area

questions.question: A worker exposed to a carcinogenic chemical develops an irreversible genetic alteration in a lung epithelial cell, but no tumour develops until years later after repeated exposure to a second agent. This initial genetic alteration is termed:
questions.explanation: Initiation refers to the irreversible genetic alteration produced in a cell by exposure to a carcinogenic agent, rendering the cell susceptible to subsequent neoplastic transformation, though initiation alone is insufficient to produce a tumour. A second, promoting stimulus is typically required to drive the clonal expansion of the initiated cell into a detectable neoplasm. This two-stage model explains why cancer often develops only after prolonged or repeated exposure to carcinogenic influences over many years.

questions.question: Recovery of tensile strength in a healing wound depends PRIMARILY on:
options: Formation of granulation tissue with abundant new blood vessels
Wound contraction by myofibroblasts closing the wound margins
Net collagen accumulation from increased synthesis and decreased degradation
Macrophage-mediated clearance of dead tissue debris
questions.explanation: Recovery of tensile strength depends on fibrillar collagens (mostly type I collagen), which form a major portion of connective tissue in repair sites. Net collagen accumulation depends not only on increased collagen synthesis but also on decreased degradation. The degradation of collagen is achieved by matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) — a balance between synthesis and degradation determines the final tensile strength.

options: Any capacity for wound healing whatsoever
Circulating blood supply to the limb
Peripheral nerve supply to the limb
Basic cellular metabolism in limb tissue
questions.explanation: Mammals have lost the capacity for limb regeneration seen in some amphibians because they lack the specialised blastema-forming programme, a population of dedifferentiated progenitor cells capable of reforming complex limb structures, relying instead on scar-forming repair processes. This evolutionary difference explains why humans heal wounds through fibrous repair rather than true regeneration of complex lost structures. Understanding this gap has driven interest in regenerative medicine research aimed at potentially reactivating dormant regenerative pathways in mammalian tissue.
questions.question: A researcher studying limb regeneration in amphibians compares this capacity with the very limited regenerative ability of human limbs. The loss of this regenerative capacity in mammals is attributed to the ABSENCE of:

questions.explanation: Research on stem cells is at the forefront of modern biomedical investigation and stands at the core of a new field called regenerative medicine. The enthusiasm derives from findings that challenge established views about cell differentiation, and from the hope that stem cells may one day be used to repair damaged human tissues such as heart, brain, liver, and skeletal muscle — tissues currently incapable of significant regeneration.
questions.question: Regenerative medicine derives its enthusiasm from findings that challenge which established views?
options: The inability of any mammalian tissue to regenerate after injury
The requirement for immunosuppression before stem cell transplantation
The universal applicability of growth factor therapy for organ regeneration
The conclusion that scar formation is always preferable to regeneration
Established views about cell differentiation, with hope that stem cells may repair damaged human tissues

questions.explanation: Prognosis in shock varies significantly according to its underlying cause, with septic shock generally carrying a higher mortality than uncomplicated hypovolaemic shock, reflecting the complex combination of vasodilation, capillary leak, myocardial depression, and coagulation derangements involved in sepsis. Hypovolaemic shock, if recognised and treated promptly with volume replacement, often has a more favourable outcome. This variation highlights the importance of identifying the specific type of shock to guide targeted management.
questions.question: Two patients present in shock, one from acute haemorrhage and one from overwhelming sepsis with multi-organ dysfunction. Which statement CORRECTLY reflects how prognosis varies with the origin of shock?
options: All forms of shock carry an identical prognosis regardless of cause
Hypovolaemic shock is always more lethal than septic shock
Neurogenic shock has the highest mortality of all shock types
Septic shock generally carries a worse prognosis than uncomplicated hypovolaemic shock
Cardiogenic shock always resolves without specific intervention

questions.question: The three phases of cutaneous wound healing in order are:
questions.explanation: Cutaneous wound healing is divided into three phases: (1) inflammation — initial platelet adhesion, aggregation, clot formation; (2) proliferation — formation of granulation tissue, proliferation and migration of connective tissue cells, and re-epithelialisation; and (3) maturation — ECM deposition, tissue remodelling, and wound contraction. These phases overlap and their separation is somewhat arbitrary.
options: Clot formation, re-epithelialisation, and scar formation

questions.question: Which clinical condition is classified under 'arteriolar dilation' as a cause of increased hydrostatic pressure?
options: Congestive heart failure from myocardial infarction
Heat causing vasodilation increasing capillary hydrostatic pressure
Deep vein thrombosis causing venous obstruction
Prolonged dependency of the lower extremities
questions.explanation: Arteriolar dilation is listed as a cause of increased hydrostatic pressure leading to oedema. Specific examples under this category include heat (causing vasodilation) and neurohumoral dysregulation. Vasodilation increases blood flow into capillaries, raising capillary hydrostatic pressure and promoting fluid extravasation. This can occur in hot environments or with inflammatory vasodilation.

options: Fibronectin, complement C3b, and fibrin as the initial scaffold
Collagen type I, proteoglycans, and endothelial growth factors
Fibrin, fibronectin, complement components, and entrapped red cells
Hyaluronan, elastin, and laminin as the provisional matrix
Platelet-derived growth factor, VEGF, and EGF released from endothelium
questions.explanation: Wounding causes rapid activation of coagulation pathways, resulting in formation of a blood clot on the wound surface. In addition to entrapped red cells, the clot contains fibrin, fibronectin, and complement components. The clot serves to stop bleeding and also as a scaffold for migrating cells, which are attracted by growth factors, cytokines, and chemokines released into the area.
questions.question: Platinum-based formation of the initial blood clot in wound healing primarily involves:

questions.explanation: Quiescent (stable) tissues normally have a low level of replication; however, cells from these tissues can undergo rapid division in response to stimuli and are capable of reconstituting the tissue of origin. Examples include parenchymal cells of liver, kidneys, and pancreas; mesenchymal cells (fibroblasts, smooth muscle); vascular endothelial cells; and lymphocytes. The liver's capacity to regenerate after partial hepatectomy exemplifies stable tissue regeneration.
questions.question: Quiescent (stable) tissues are BEST characterised by:
options: Cells that have permanently lost the capacity for mitotic division
Continuously proliferating cells replacing dead cells throughout life
Low level of replication at rest but capable of rapid division in response to stimuli
Cells capable only of hypertrophy without any potential for division
Terminally differentiated cells with no regenerative capacity

questions.explanation: The overall aim of general and cellular pathology for nurses is to enable understanding of cellular events leading to diseases — from cellular response to stress and noxious substances, to cell injury and death, wound healing, oedema, shock, and cancer. Understanding these events underpins sound clinical decision-making and nursing care.
questions.question: A nurse who understands pathology well is BEST positioned to:
options: Perform complex surgical procedures with confidence
Prescribe appropriate antibiotics for infectious diseases
Administer radiotherapy to patients with cancer
Conduct advanced molecular genetic testing independently
Understand the cellular events underlying the disease process
Abnormal exogenous substance from environmental exposure
Mutated endogenous protein unable to be secreted
Normal cellular constituent (lipid) accumulating at a rate exceeding metabolism
Lysosomal enzyme products from inherited storage diseases
Calcium salts from hypercalcaemia-induced metastatic calcification
questions.explanation: Fatty change in the liver represents accumulation of lipid vacuoles in the cytoplasm when lipid production exceeds the rate of removal and metabolism. This is an example of normal cellular constituent (lipid) produced at increased rate or with inadequate metabolism. It is seen in hypoxic, toxic, or metabolic injuries and is most prominent in cells dependent on fat metabolism like hepatocytes.
questions.question: Fatty change (steatosis) occurring in the liver is an example of intracellular accumulation of:

questions.explanation: An abnormal increase in interstitial fluid within tissues is called oedema. Fluid collections in different body cavities are variously designated: hydrothorax (pleural space), hydropericardium (pericardial space), and hydroperitoneum/ascites (peritoneal cavity). Anasarca is severe generalised oedema with widespread subcutaneous tissue swelling. Oedema occurs when fluid movement into tissues exceeds lymphatic drainage.
options: Generalised accumulation of fluid in all body compartments equally
Excess fluid in the intravascular compartment causing hypertension
Fluid accumulation exclusively in the pleural and pericardial spaces
Abnormal increase in interstitial fluid within tissues or body cavities
Accumulation of lymph fluid within the lymphatic channels
questions.question: Oedema is MOST accurately defined as:
Monoclonal antibody against CD20 (a B-cell surface antigen) is used therapeutically for treatment of:
options: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung
Gastric adenocarcinoma from H. pylori infection
questions.explanation: Although there is no evidence for protective effects of antitumour antibodies against spontaneous tumours, administration of monoclonal antibodies against tumour cells can be therapeutically effective. A monoclonal antibody against CD20, a B-cell surface antigen, is widely used for treatment of lymphomas (e.g., rituximab). This represents an example of successful immunotherapy using antibodies targeting tumour-specific surface markers.

questions.question: A patient with cirrhosis and low serum sodium is placed on a low-salt diet to reduce fluid retention. Sodium and water retention contribute to oedema through which two combined mechanisms?
options: Reduced hydrostatic pressure and increased osmotic pressure
Increased hydrostatic pressure and reduced plasma osmotic pressure
Increased red cell mass and reduced plasma volume
questions.explanation: Retained sodium and water expand the intravascular volume, which raises capillary hydrostatic pressure, while the accompanying dilution of plasma proteins reduces plasma colloid osmotic pressure, together favouring net fluid movement into the interstitium. This dual mechanism compounds oedema formation in conditions of chronic sodium retention such as cirrhosis and renal disease. Dietary sodium restriction is therefore a key intervention to limit further fluid accumulation.

options: Immediate immune destruction of avascular tumour cells
Diffusion limits of oxygen and nutrients from existing vessels
Complete loss of tumour cell proliferative capacity
Mandatory apoptosis triggered at a fixed tumour size
Loss of genetic material beyond a certain cell number
questions.explanation: Solid tumours cannot grow beyond approximately one to two millimetres in diameter without developing their own blood supply, because oxygen and nutrients can only diffuse a limited distance from existing vessels to sustain viable tumour cells. Angiogenesis, the formation of new blood vessels, is therefore essential for continued tumour growth beyond this size and also facilitates access to the circulation for metastatic spread. This dependence on angiogenesis has made it an important target for anticancer therapies.
questions.question: A solid tumour on imaging is found to have a central area of necrosis where the tumour has outgrown its blood supply. Angiogenesis is essential for further tumour growth because solid tumours cannot enlarge beyond a certain size without it due to:
Vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) in wound healing PRIMARILY promotes:
options: Collagen synthesis by fibroblasts at the wound site
Keratinocyte migration and re-epithelialisation of the wound surface
Monocyte chemotaxis to the wound from peripheral blood
Increased vascular permeability and mitogenesis for endothelial cells (angiogenesis)
Platelet aggregation and initial haemostasis at the wound site
questions.explanation: VEGF (vascular endothelial growth factor) increases vascular permeability and is mitogenic for endothelial cells, thus promoting angiogenesis. In the wound healing context, VEGF is listed under the angiogenesis step in the growth factors table. Collagen synthesis is stimulated by TGF-ß and PDGF; keratinocyte replication by HB-EGF, FGF-7, HGF; and monocyte chemotaxis by chemokines, TNF, PDGF, FGF, TGF-ß.

Oedema caused by increased hydrostatic pressure or reduced plasma protein is typically a protein-poor fluid called a transudate. This type of oedema is seen in patients with heart failure, renal failure, hepatic failure, and certain forms of malnutrition. In contrast, inflammatory oedema is a protein-rich exudate resulting from increased vascular permeability.
questions.question: Oedema caused by increased hydrostatic pressure or reduced plasma protein is typically:
options: A protein-rich exudate from inflammatory vascular permeability
A mucinous fluid from mesothelial cell secretion
A lymphatic fluid with high lipid content (chyle)
A bloody haemorrhagic effusion from vascular injury
A protein-poor fluid called a transudate
Platelets, macrophages, saliva, urine, milk, and plasma
Fibroblasts in the wound stroma exclusively
Mast cells and basophils in the inflammatory infiltrate
Endothelial cells lining the new blood vessels in granulation tissue
Keratinocytes at the wound margin undergoing re-epithelialisation
questions.question: EGF (Epidermal Growth Factor) in wound healing is PRIMARILY sourced from:
questions.explanation: EGF (Epidermal Growth Factor) is sourced from platelets, macrophages, saliva, urine, milk, and plasma. It is mitogenic for keratinocytes and fibroblasts, and stimulates keratinocyte migration and granulation tissue formation. It is a key growth factor in the proliferative phase of wound healing. TGF-a, similar to EGF, comes from macrophages, T lymphocytes, keratinocytes, and many tissues.

questions.question: The thoracic duct plays which role in preventing tissue oedema?
questions.explanation: A small residual amount of fluid left in the interstitium after capillary filtration is drained by lymphatic vessels, ultimately returning to the bloodstream via the thoracic duct. When fluid movement into tissues exceeds lymphatic drainage capacity, fluid accumulates as oedema. The thoracic duct is the major lymphatic vessel that returns lymph (including interstitial fluid) from most of the body to the venous circulation.
options: Returning interstitial fluid drained by lymphatics to the bloodstream
Directly absorbing plasma proteins from the interstitium into blood
Regulating hydrostatic pressure in the thoracic cavity
Filtering interstitial fluid before returning it to lymph nodes
Producing lymph from blood filtration at the thoracic level

questions.question: In congestive heart failure, systemic oedema results from:
questions.explanation: Generalised increases in venous pressure with resulting systemic oedema occur most commonly in congestive heart failure, where compromised right ventricular function leads to pooling of blood on the venous side of the circulation. This increases capillary hydrostatic pressure, driving fluid into the interstitium. Regional increases in hydrostatic pressure (e.g., from deep venous thrombosis) cause localised oedema.
options: Compromised right ventricular function leading to venous pooling
Lymphatic obstruction by cardiac tumour metastases
Reduced plasma albumin from hepatic dysfunction
Increased capillary permeability from cardiac inflammatory cytokines
Renal sodium retention from adrenal tumour secreting aldosterone

questions.question: A patient found unconscious for several hours after a myocardial infarction shows biochemical evidence of hypoxic myocyte injury before any visible microscopic changes appear. This delay between injury and detectable morphology is BEST explained by:
options: Absence of any cellular response to hypoxia
Delayed arrival of inflammatory cells only
questions.explanation: Following an injurious stimulus, biochemical derangements such as ATP depletion and enzyme leakage occur rapidly, but morphological evidence of injury under light or electron microscopy takes hours to become apparent. In myocardial infarction, this lag explains why early infarcts may appear grossly and microscopically normal despite ongoing irreversible damage. Recognising this lag is clinically important because biomarkers can detect injury before structural changes are visible.

options: The study exclusively of benign tumour classification
The study limited to surgical tumour removal techniques
The study of the causes, development, and management of neoplasms
The study focused only on tumour genetics in isolation
The study of infectious diseases affecting glandular tissue
questions.question: A patient's biopsy of a firm neck mass is diagnosed as a malignant tumour arising from glandular epithelial tissue. Oncology, the study of tumours, would classify the overall scientific approach to this diagnosis as:
questions.explanation: Oncology is defined as the branch of medicine concerned with the study of tumours, encompassing their causes, mechanisms of development, diagnosis, and treatment across both benign and malignant neoplasms. This comprehensive scope distinguishes oncology from narrower disciplines focused solely on surgical technique or genetics in isolation. A thorough understanding of oncology therefore integrates pathology, molecular biology, and clinical management to guide patient care.

Circulatory status modulates wound healing. Inadequate blood supply, usually caused by arteriosclerosis or venous abnormalities (varicose veins) that retard venous drainage, also impairs healing. Poor circulation reduces the delivery of oxygen, nutrients, growth factors, and repair cells (fibroblasts, macrophages) to the wound site, slowing or preventing healing.
questions.question: Inadequate blood supply to a wound, caused by arteriosclerosis or varicose veins, impairs healing because:
options: It reduces delivery of oxygen, nutrients, and repair cells to the wound
It directly inhibits collagen synthesis by wound fibroblasts
It prevents neutrophil migration into the wound site
It allows bacterial colonisation by reducing antimicrobial factors
It prevents scar maturation by blocking MMP enzyme delivery
Loss in the uniformity of individual cells
Loss in architectural orientation of cells
Abundant and abnormally located mitotic figures
Complete penetration through the basement membrane
questions.question: Dysplasia in epithelium is characterised by all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Dysplasia is characterised by: loss in uniformity of individual cells; loss in architectural orientation; pleomorphism with large hyperchromatic nuclei and high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio; and more abundant mitotic figures (often in abnormal locations). When dysplastic changes are marked and involve the entire thickness of the epithelium but remain confined by the basement membrane, it is called carcinoma in situ — not invasive cancer.

options: Symptom complexes that cannot readily be explained by local tumour spread, metastasis, or indigenous hormone elaboration
Symptoms and signs directly caused by local tumour expansion or distant metastasis
Endocrine syndromes from tumours arising in recognised endocrine glands
Systemic effects of cancer treatment (surgery, chemotherapy, radiotherapy)
Inflammatory reactions to tumour necrosis causing fever and weight loss
questions.question: Paraneoplastic syndromes are MOST accurately described as:
questions.explanation: Paraneoplastic syndromes are symptom complexes in cancer-bearing individuals that cannot readily be explained, either by the local or distant spread of the tumour or by elaboration of hormones indigenous to the tissue from which the tumour arose. They occur in about 10% of persons with malignant disease and are important because: they may be the earliest manifestation of an occult neoplasm; they may represent significant clinical problems or be lethal; and they may mimic metastatic disease.

questions.question: FGF (Fibroblast Growth Factor) stimulates which processes during wound healing?
options: Platelet aggregation and initial haemostasis at the wound site
Monocyte chemotaxis and macrophage activation exclusively
Keratinocyte migration, angiogenesis, wound contraction, and matrix deposition
Collagen degradation by activating matrix metalloproteinases
Complement activation and opsonisation of wound bacteria
questions.explanation: FGF (Fibroblast Growth Factor — including FGF-1 acidic, FGF-2 basic, and family members) is sourced from macrophages, mast cells, T lymphocytes, endothelial cells, and fibroblasts. Its functions in wound healing include: chemotaxis for fibroblasts; mitogenesis for fibroblasts and keratinocytes; stimulation of keratinocyte migration; angiogenesis; wound contraction; and matrix deposition. FGF-7 (KGF) specifically stimulates keratinocyte migration, proliferation, and differentiation.

questions.question: A patient with tertiary syphilis has a biopsy of a soft, rubbery mass with a central area of necrosis surrounded by plasma cells and fibrous tissue. This lesion is:
questions.explanation: A gumma is the characteristic granulomatous lesion of tertiary syphilis, consisting of a central area of necrosis surrounded by macrophages, plasma cells, and dense fibrous tissue. It differs from tuberculous caseating granulomas by its greater fibrous encapsulation and prominent plasma cell infiltrate. Recognising the gumma pattern helps distinguish syphilitic granulomatous disease from other infectious and noninfectious causes of granuloma formation.

questions.question: Basement membranes are composed PRIMARILY of which constituents?
options: Nonfibrillar collagen type IV, laminin, heparan sulfate, and proteoglycans
Fibrillar collagen type I, fibronectin, and elastin
Hyaluronan, versican, and aggrecan proteoglycans exclusively
Type III collagen, vitronectin, and tenascin
Fibrin, fibronectin, and complement C3 components
questions.explanation: Basement membranes are closely associated with cell surfaces and consist of nonfibrillar collagen (mostly type IV), laminin, heparan sulfate, and proteoglycans. The basement membrane acts as a boundary between epithelium and underlying connective tissue, and forms part of the filtration apparatus in the kidney. Disruption of the basement membrane scaffold leads to collagen deposition and scar formation rather than regeneration.

options: Reduced plasma oncotic pressure from albumin loss
Elevated venous pressure from heart failure
questions.explanation: Nephrotic syndrome causes massive urinary loss of albumin, resulting in hypoalbuminaemia that reduces plasma colloid osmotic pressure and allows fluid to shift from the vasculature into the interstitial space, producing generalised oedema. This mechanism is distinct from the hydrostatic pressure-driven oedema seen in heart failure. The resulting drop in effective circulating volume can also secondarily activate the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, further worsening fluid retention.
questions.question: A patient with nephrotic syndrome has generalised oedema and heavy proteinuria. Oedema PRIMARILY develops in this condition through:

questions.explanation: In habitual cigarette smokers, normal ciliated columnar epithelial cells of the trachea and bronchi are often replaced by stratified squamous epithelial cells — this is columnar to squamous metaplasia. While the more rugged squamous epithelium can survive chronic irritation, the protective mechanisms (mucus secretion and ciliary action) are lost. Persistent metaplasia-inducing influences may initiate malignant transformation.
questions.question: Squamous metaplasia in the respiratory tract of cigarette smokers is an example of which adaptational change?
options: Hyperplasia replacing ciliated columnar cells with stratified squamous cells
Dysplasia indicating preinvasive squamous cell carcinoma
Atrophy of ciliated cells from reduced respiratory demands
Metaplasia in which ciliated columnar cells are replaced by stratified squamous epithelium
Hypertrophy of bronchial mucous glands from chronic irritation

questions.explanation: In syphilis caused by Treponema pallidum, the tissue reaction is a gumma — a microscopic to grossly visible lesion enclosing a wall of histiocytes with plasma cell infiltrate and central cells that are necrotic without loss of cellular outline. This is distinct from the caseous necrosis of tuberculosis and the noncaseating granulomas of sarcoidosis.
questions.question: The characteristic appearance of granuloma in syphilis (gumma) includes which finding?
options: Noncaseating granulomas with abundant activated macrophages
Rounded stellate granuloma with recognisable neutrophils and giant cells
Microscopic to grossly visible lesion with plasma cell infiltrate and central necrosis without cellular outline loss
Occasional noncaseating granulomas in the intestinal wall

questions.question: A tumour biopsy shows mutation of a gene found altered in the majority of human cancers, with loss of normal apoptotic response to DNA damage. This gene is:
questions.explanation: p53 is a tumour suppressor gene mutated in the majority of human cancers, and its normal function includes inducing cell cycle arrest or apoptosis in response to DNA damage, thereby preventing propagation of genetically damaged cells. Loss of functional p53 allows cells with damaged DNA to continue dividing, contributing to genomic instability and tumour progression. Because of its central role across many cancer types, p53 is often referred to as the guardian of the genome.

Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome refers to adrenal necrosis due to DIC. Although sepsis is initially associated with an acute surge in glucocorticoid production, this phase is frequently followed by adrenal insufficiency and a functional deficit of glucocorticoids. This may stem from depression of the synthetic capacity of intact adrenal glands or frank adrenal necrosis due to DIC — named Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome.
questions.question: Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome in septic shock refers to:
options: Renal cortical necrosis from severe hypovolaemia
Hepatic failure from cytokine-induced hepatocyte damage
Adrenal necrosis due to DIC causing functional glucocorticoid deficit
Cerebral oedema from septic emboli causing brain infarction
Pulmonary haemorrhage from DIC damaging alveolar capillaries

questions.question: A tumour biopsy shows overexpression of a cell cycle regulatory protein that drives cells prematurely through the G1 to S phase checkpoint. This regulatory oncogene is:
questions.explanation: Cyclin D is a cell cycle regulatory protein that, together with its associated cyclin-dependent kinases, drives progression through the G1 to S phase checkpoint, and its overexpression can push cells through this checkpoint inappropriately, contributing to uncontrolled proliferation in several human cancers. This differs from tumour suppressor genes such as p53 and RB1, which normally restrain rather than promote cell cycle progression. Cyclin D overexpression is a recognised mechanism of oncogene activation in cancers including breast cancer and lymphoma.

questions.question: A woman with a strong family history of breast and ovarian cancer undergoes genetic testing revealing a mutation in a DNA repair-associated tumour suppressor gene. This gene is MOST likely:
questions.explanation: BRCA1 and BRCA2 are tumour suppressor genes involved in DNA double-strand break repair, and inherited mutations in either gene significantly increase the lifetime risk of breast and ovarian cancer due to accumulating unrepaired DNA damage and genomic instability. Their role in DNA repair distinguishes them functionally from cell cycle regulators such as RB1 or growth-signalling oncogenes such as RAS. Genetic counselling and testing for these mutations is important for at-risk families to guide surveillance and preventive strategies.

Primary renal failure causes oedema through both increased hydrostatic pressure (from sodium and fluid retention increasing intravascular volume) and reduced colloid osmotic pressure (from loss of protein in glomerulonephritis/nephrotic syndrome or dilution). The figure in the document shows pathways from primary renal failure leading to systemic oedema through both these mechanisms simultaneously.
options: Hypoproteinaemia from increased glomerular permeability alone
Direct aldosterone secretion from the kidney causing sodium retention
Lymphatic obstruction from renal inflammation affecting inguinal nodes
Increased hydrostatic pressure from fluid retention AND reduced colloid osmotic pressure
Inflammatory vascular permeability from immune complex deposition
questions.question: The oedema pathway in primary renal failure involves:
Immune-mediated inflammatory disease is classified as a cause of:
options: Chronic inflammation through sustained immune reaction
questions.explanation: Immune-mediated inflammatory diseases are one of the three main causes of chronic inflammation. These involve immune reactions including autoimmune diseases and hypersensitivity reactions. Examples include rheumatoid arthritis, Crohn disease, and atherosclerosis. They cause sustained chronic inflammatory responses that lead to progressive tissue damage.

questions.question: Increased intracellular calcium causes cell injury through all of the following mechanisms EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Increased intracellular Ca2+ causes injury by: opening the mitochondrial permeability transition pore (failure of ATP generation); activating phospholipases (membrane damage), proteases (membrane and cytoskeletal protein breakdown), endonucleases (DNA fragmentation), and ATPases (ATP depletion); and inducing apoptosis via caspase activation and increased mitochondrial permeability. It does NOT increase protein synthesis.
options: Opening mitochondrial permeability transition pore causing ATP generation failure
Activating endonucleases causing DNA and chromatin fragmentation
Increasing protein synthesis to compensate for membrane damage
Activating caspases and increasing mitochondrial permeability leading to apoptosis

questions.question: A patient with a mediastinal mass is found to have a tumour associated with a virus also implicated in nasopharyngeal carcinoma and Burkitt lymphoma. This virus is:
questions.explanation: Epstein-Barr virus has been implicated in the pathogenesis of several human malignancies including Burkitt lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and certain Hodgkin lymphomas, through mechanisms involving viral gene products that promote B-lymphocyte or epithelial cell proliferation. Its broad association across multiple tumour types distinguishes it from more narrowly associated oncogenic viruses such as human T-cell lymphotropic virus. Recognising these associations aids in understanding the aetiology of these specific malignancies in affected patient populations.

Complications in wound healing can arise from abnormalities in any of the basic components of the repair process. Deficient scar formation — inadequate formation of granulation tissue or assembly of a scar — can lead to two types of complications: wound dehiscence (separation of wound edges) and ulceration. Excessive formation of repair components leads to hypertrophic scars and keloids.
options: Deficient scar formation from inadequate granulation tissue assembly
Formation of contracture from exaggerated wound contraction
Keloid formation from overactive collagen synthesis
Secondary infection complicating the proliferative phase
questions.question: Wound dehiscence and ulceration are complications of which category of wound healing pathology?

questions.explanation: Neurogenic shock occurs in the setting of anaesthetic accident or spinal cord injury. It results from loss of vascular tone and peripheral pooling of blood, causing tissue hypoperfusion and hypoxia. This is classified as a less common type of shock, distinct from the three major categories (cardiogenic, hypovolemic, and septic shock).
options: Overwhelming microbial infection causing systemic immune activation
Intrinsic myocardial damage from coronary artery occlusion
Massive haemorrhage from ruptured aortic aneurysm
Loss of vascular tone and peripheral pooling from anaesthetic accident or spinal cord injury
IgE-mediated systemic vasodilation from allergic reaction
questions.question: Neurogenic shock occurs due to:
A patient with pleural effusion has fluid analysis showing high protein content, elevated specific gravity, and numerous leukocytes. This fluid is best classified as:
questions.explanation: An exudate is an inflammatory extravascular fluid with high protein content and cellularity, resulting from increased vascular permeability caused by inflammatory mediators. This contrasts with a transudate, which is a protein-poor ultrafiltrate of plasma caused by hydrostatic or osmotic imbalance without increased permeability. The presence of numerous leukocytes and high protein strongly favours an inflammatory exudative process over a simple transudate.

questions.question: A patient with advanced liver cirrhosis develops abdominal distension with a fluid wave on examination. This accumulation of fluid within the peritoneal cavity is termed:
questions.explanation: Ascites refers specifically to the accumulation of excess fluid within the peritoneal cavity, most commonly resulting from portal hypertension and hypoalbuminaemia in liver cirrhosis. It is distinguished from anasarca, which describes severe, generalised subcutaneous oedema throughout the body rather than fluid confined to a body cavity. Recognising the specific compartment of fluid accumulation guides appropriate diagnostic and management approaches.

Tumour promotion involves the induction of cell proliferation in cells that have already been genetically initiated, and unlike initiation, promotional agents are typically reversible in their effects and do not themselves cause permanent DNA mutation. Continued exposure to a promoting agent increases the likelihood that an initiated cell will accumulate the additional changes needed for malignant transformation. This distinction is important because removing a promoting agent can reduce cancer risk even after initiation has already occurred.
questions.question: A worker repeatedly exposed to a substance that stimulates cell proliferation in previously initiated cells, without itself causing permanent genetic mutation, is experiencing which phase of carcinogenesis?

options: Plasma cells, dendritic cells, and basophils primarily
Mast cells and natural killer cells as the principal components
Macrophages and lymphocytes predominantly, with plasma cells
Neutrophils and fibrin deposits as the primary features
questions.explanation: Chronic inflammation is characterised by infiltration with mononuclear cells — predominantly macrophages, lymphocytes, and plasma cells, along with eosinophils and mast cells. In contrast, acute inflammation is characterised by vascular changes, oedema, and predominantly neutrophilic infiltration. Macrophages are the predominant cellular component in chronic inflammation.
questions.question: Chronic inflammation is characterised by which cellular infiltrate?

questions.explanation: Continuously dividing (labile) tissues proliferate throughout life, replacing those that are destroyed. They include surface epithelia (stratified squamous of skin, oral cavity, vagina, cervix), lining mucosa of excretory ducts, columnar epithelium of GI tract and uterus, transitional epithelium of the urinary tract, and bone marrow and haematopoietic tissues. In these tissues, mature cells derive from adult stem cells.
questions.question: Which tissues are classified as 'labile' (continuously dividing)?
options: Cardiac muscle cells and skeletal muscle fibres
Neurons in the central nervous system and peripheral ganglia
Fibroblasts and smooth muscle cells of vessel walls
Hepatocytes, renal tubular cells, and pancreatic acinar cells
Surface epithelia of skin, GI tract, bone marrow and haematopoietic tissues

questions.explanation: Tuberculous granulomas are classically distinguished by central caseous necrosis, an amorphous, cheese-like debris surrounded by a rim of epithelioid macrophages, lymphocytes, and multinucleated Langhans giant cells. This caseating pattern differs from the noncaseating granulomas of sarcoidosis, which lack central necrosis. Special stains for acid-fast bacilli are used to confirm Mycobacterium tuberculosis as the causative organism.
questions.question: A patient with disseminated tuberculosis has lymph node granulomas showing central structureless eosinophilic debris surrounded by epithelioid cells and Langhans giant cells. This necrotic centre is:

A retinoblastoma patient's tumour biopsy shows loss of function of both alleles of a growth-regulating gene. Tumour suppressor genes differ from oncogenes in that their cancer-promoting effect requires:
questions.explanation: Tumour suppressor genes normally restrain cell proliferation, and their cancer-promoting loss of function typically requires inactivation of both alleles, consistent with the two-hit hypothesis, unlike oncogenes which can promote cancer through activation of a single mutant allele acting dominantly. This recessive-at-the-cellular-level behaviour explains why hereditary cancer syndromes often involve inheritance of one already-mutated allele, requiring only a single additional somatic hit to lose complete tumour suppressor function. Retinoblastoma is the classic example illustrating this two-hit mechanism.
options: Loss of function of both gene copies
Activation of a single mutant gene copy
Amplification of a normal gene copy
Overexpression of a single wild-type allele

questions.explanation: Oedema is defined as an increase in interstitial fluid volume within tissue, resulting from an imbalance in the forces governing fluid movement between the vascular and interstitial compartments. In congestive heart failure, raised venous hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid out of capillaries faster than it can be reabsorbed, producing dependent swelling. This differs from ascites and hydrothorax, which refer specifically to fluid accumulation within the peritoneal and pleural cavities respectively.
questions.question: A patient with congestive heart failure develops bilateral pitting ankle swelling due to fluid accumulation in the interstitial tissue. This finding is best defined as:

options: Collagen fibres providing tensile strength to skin and tendons
Fibronectin connecting cells to fibronectin receptors (integrins)
Basement membrane acting as boundary between epithelium and connective tissue and forming part of kidney filtration apparatus
Proteoglycans lubricating joint surfaces reducing wear
Elastin providing recoil allowing tissues to return to original shape
questions.question: The ECM function of 'establishment of tissue microenvironments' is exemplified by:
questions.explanation: The establishment of tissue microenvironments function of ECM is exemplified by the basement membrane acting as a boundary between epithelium and underlying connective tissue, and also forming part of the filtration apparatus in the kidney (glomerular basement membrane). The basement membrane creates distinct compartments that define tissue architecture and regulate movement of cells and molecules between tissue compartments.

questions.question: Which mechanism of cell injury is associated with membrane permeability defects?
questions.explanation: Mechanisms of membrane damage include: reactive oxygen species causing lipid peroxidation; decreased phospholipid synthesis (due to reduced oxygen and substrate availability); increased phospholipid breakdown (from phospholipase activation by elevated Ca2+); and cytoskeletal abnormalities (cytoskeletal damage allows membrane detachment from cytoskeleton). Early loss of selective membrane permeability is a consistent feature of most forms of cell injury.
options: Reactive oxygen species, decreased phospholipid synthesis, and cytoskeletal abnormalities
Mitochondrial DNA mutation causing respiratory chain failure
Lysosomal swelling from excessive glycogen accumulation
Nucleolar enlargement from increased ribosomal RNA synthesis

questions.question: A benign tumour is distinguished from a malignant tumour by its ability to:
options: Grow rapidly with frequent mitotic figures
Show marked anaplasia and loss of differentiation
Remain localised without invasion or metastasis, generally amenable to surgical removal
Cause systemic manifestations through paraneoplastic syndromes
Produce extensive necrosis and haemorrhage at the tumour centre
questions.explanation: A tumour is said to be benign when it will remain localised, cannot spread to other sites, and is generally amenable to local surgical removal — the patient generally survives. Malignant tumours (cancers) can invade and destroy adjacent structures and spread to distant sites (metastasize) to cause death. Benign tumours are well-differentiated with rare normal mitotic figures; malignant tumours show anaplasia and may have numerous abnormal mitoses.

Barrett's oesophagus is an example of metaplasia in which the normal squamous epithelium of the distal oesophagus is replaced by columnar epithelium better adapted to withstand chronic acid exposure from reflux disease. While metaplasia itself is a reversible adaptive change, this particular metaplastic epithelium carries an increased risk of progressing through dysplasia to adenocarcinoma if the underlying stimulus persists. This makes it an important condition for endoscopic surveillance in patients with chronic reflux disease.
questions.question: A patient with chronic gastro-oesophageal reflux disease develops columnar metaplasia of the distal oesophagus, a change recognised as a precursor lesion for adenocarcinoma. This adaptational response is:
options: Simple hyperplasia without cell type change
Metaplasia in response to chronic acid injury

questions.explanation: The initial haemostatic response to wounding involves platelet aggregation at the site of vascular injury, followed by activation of the coagulation cascade to form a fibrin meshwork that stabilises the platelet plug and provides a provisional matrix. This clot also serves as a reservoir of growth factors that initiate subsequent phases of healing. Only after this initial haemostatic phase do inflammatory cells and later fibroblasts populate the wound.
options: Platelet aggregation and fibrin meshwork formation
questions.question: A patient's wound shows an initial platelet plug forming within minutes of injury, initiating the clotting cascade. This initial blood clot formation PRIMARILY involves:

questions.explanation: In ischaemia of the myocardium, cell swelling (reversible morphologic change) may occur within minutes and may progress to irreversibility within an hour or two. However, unmistakable light microscopic changes of cell death may not be seen until 4 to 12 hours after total ischaemia. This illustrates that morphologic manifestations of necrosis take more time to develop than those of reversible damage.
questions.question: In ischaemic myocardial injury, unmistakable light microscopic changes of cell death appear:
options: At 4 to 12 hours after total ischaemia
Within 5 to 30 minutes of total ischaemia
At 24 to 48 hours after the ischaemic event
Only after 72 hours when necrosis is fully established

questions.explanation: Promoters can induce tumours in initiated cells, but are nontumorigenic by themselves. The cellular changes resulting from promoters do not affect DNA directly and are reversible (unlike the permanent changes from initiators). That effects of promoters are reversible is further documented by the finding that tumours fail to develop in initiated cells if the time between multiple applications of the promoter is sufficiently extended.
questions.question: Tumour promotion differs from tumour initiation in that promotional effects are:
options: Permanent and irreversible with memory of prior exposure
Sufficient alone to produce tumours without prior initiation
Effective when applied before, rather than after, the initiating agent
Mutagenic causing permanent DNA damage in initiated cells
Reversible and enhance proliferation of initiated cells without directly affecting DNA

questions.question: A tumour marker used to monitor a patient with hepatocellular carcinoma is normally expressed only during fetal development. This category of tumour antigen is termed:
questions.explanation: Oncofetal antigens are proteins normally expressed only during fetal development that become re-expressed in certain tumours, with alpha-fetoprotein in hepatocellular carcinoma being a classic clinical example used for monitoring disease. Their re-emergence reflects a partial reversion of tumour cells toward a less differentiated, embryonic-like gene expression pattern. Measuring these markers in blood can aid in diagnosis, monitoring treatment response, and detecting tumour recurrence.

questions.question: A patient with acute bacterial cellulitis has a wound swab showing a predominance of a specific leukocyte type within the first 24 hours. This predominant cell is:
questions.explanation: Neutrophils are the predominant leukocyte in the earliest hours of acute inflammation because they are the most abundant circulating white cell and respond rapidly to chemotactic signals. They arrive within the first six to twenty-four hours and are progressively replaced by monocytes and macrophages as the response evolves. This early neutrophilic infiltrate is a hallmark used to distinguish acute from chronic inflammation histologically.

CD20 is a surface antigen expressed on B lymphocytes, including most malignant B cells in non-Hodgkin lymphoma, and monoclonal antibodies directed against CD20 are used therapeutically to selectively target and destroy these malignant cells while sparing many other cell types. This targeted immunotherapy approach represented a significant advance in the treatment of B-cell lymphomas. Its selective mechanism illustrates how understanding tumour cell surface markers can be translated into effective, targeted cancer therapies.
questions.question: A patient with B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma is treated with a monoclonal antibody that targets a specific surface antigen expressed on malignant B cells. This antigen is:

questions.explanation: Shock is characterised by systemic hypotension due either to reduced cardiac output or to reduced effective circulating blood volume. The consequences are impaired tissue perfusion and cellular hypoxia. At the outset cellular injury is reversible; however, prolonged shock leads to irreversible tissue injury that often proves fatal. Shock is the final common pathway for several potentially lethal clinical events.
questions.question: Shock is BEST defined as:
options: Severe anaemia from acute blood loss causing organ hypoperfusion
Cardiac arrest with cessation of all organ perfusion
Systemic hypotension due to reduced cardiac output or reduced effective circulating blood volume
Inflammatory response to severe infection causing widespread tissue damage
Severe hypertension causing end-organ damage to kidneys and brain
Has not yet begun to form
Is completely replaced by mature scar
Has fully regained normal tensile strength
Fills the wound space and continues to mature
questions.explanation: By five to seven days, granulation tissue has typically become well established, filling the wound space with proliferating fibroblasts and new capillaries, though it continues to mature and remodel over subsequent weeks. At this stage tensile strength remains far below normal, and the tissue has not yet been replaced by mature collagenous scar. This timeline is clinically useful for anticipating the expected appearance of a healing wound at follow-up assessment.
questions.question: A patient's surgical wound is examined one week after injury and shows an established bed of new vessels and fibroblasts filling the defect. By five to seven days after wounding, granulation tissue:

questions.explanation: Small incisional wounds heal faster than large excisional wounds primarily because they require less granulation tissue formation, less wound contraction, and a smaller area of epithelium to regenerate to achieve closure. The overall time and biological resources needed for repair scale with the volume and surface area of tissue that must be replaced. This is why deep but narrow wounds typically heal more quickly than broad, shallow ones.
questions.question: A patient asks why a small facial laceration heals faster than a large excisional surgical wound of similar depth. The BEST explanation is:
options: Facial skin regenerates through mitosis unlike other skin
Small wounds bypass the inflammatory phase entirely
Smaller wounds require less new tissue formation and epithelial coverage
Excisional wounds heal exclusively by primary intention
Large wounds have greater intrinsic blood supply

questions.explanation: Hypovolemic shock results from low cardiac output due to loss of blood or plasma volume. Examples include massive haemorrhage, or fluid loss from severe burns, vomiting, diarrhoea, or trauma. The loss of circulating volume reduces venous return, cardiac preload, and cardiac output, leading to impaired tissue perfusion and cellular hypoxia.
options: Loss of vascular tone from spinal cord injury
Bacterial toxin–induced endothelial activation and vasodilation
Massive haemorrhage or fluid loss from burns, vomiting, or diarrhoea
IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation causing vasodilation
questions.question: Hypovolemic shock is caused by:

questions.explanation: High-risk human papillomavirus types produce viral oncoproteins, E6 and E7, that bind and inactivate the tumour suppressor proteins p53 and retinoblastoma protein respectively, disabling key cell cycle checkpoints and promoting uncontrolled proliferation of infected cervical epithelial cells. Persistent infection with these high-risk types, rather than transient infection, is what drives progression to dysplasia and eventually invasive cervical cancer. This mechanism underlies the rationale for HPV vaccination as a cervical cancer prevention strategy.
questions.question: A cervical biopsy from a woman with persistent high-risk viral infection shows dysplastic changes progressing toward malignancy. High-risk HPV types associated with cervical cancer PRIMARILY act by:
options: Inactivating tumour suppressor proteins p53 and RB
Suppressing bone marrow stem cell function

questions.explanation: Atrophy is a reduction in cell size and metabolic activity due to decreased functional demand, resulting in a smaller but viable cell. Disuse atrophy from immobilisation is a classic physiologic example, mediated by reduced protein synthesis and increased protein degradation. Unlike necrosis or apoptosis, atrophic cells remain alive, only diminished in size and function.
questions.question: An elderly bedridden patient develops shrinkage of quadriceps muscle mass following prolonged immobilisation. This cellular change is:

questions.explanation: Granulation tissue is a specialised type of tissue formed 24-72 hours after injury by fibroblast and vascular endothelial cell proliferation. The term derives from its pink, soft, granular appearance on wound surfaces. Its characteristic histological feature is the presence of new small blood vessels (angiogenesis) and proliferation of fibroblasts. New granulation tissue is often oedematous due to leaky new vessels.
questions.question: Granulation tissue is BEST described as:
options: A specialised tissue with new small blood vessels (angiogenesis) and proliferating fibroblasts
The fibrin-rich exudate forming the initial wound clot
The calcium-rich matrix deposited during pathological calcification
Dense collagen scar replacing the original granulation tissue scaffold
Acellular connective tissue replacing parenchymal cells after injury

questions.question: The interstitial matrix of the ECM is found in spaces between which cell types?
questions.explanation: The interstitial matrix is found in spaces between epithelial, endothelial, and smooth muscle cells, as well as in connective tissue. It consists mostly of fibrillar and nonfibrillar collagen, elastin, fibronectin, proteoglycans, and hyaluronan. The basement membrane, in contrast, is closely associated with cell surfaces and consists of nonfibrillar collagen (mostly type IV), laminin, heparan sulfate, and proteoglycans.
options: Exclusively between bone marrow cells and haematopoietic progenitors
Between epithelial, endothelial, and smooth muscle cells, and in connective tissue
Only between glomerular podocytes and endothelial cells in the kidney
Between neurons and glial cells in the central nervous system
Between hepatocytes and sinusoidal endothelium in the liver

questions.question: Cyclin D overexpression as a cell cycle regulator oncogene is associated with:
questions.explanation: Cyclin D is listed in the cell cycle regulators oncogene table with translocation as its mode of activation and mantle cell lymphoma as the associated human tumour. Cyclin D amplification is also associated with breast and esophageal cancers. Cyclins are cell cycle regulators that, when constitutively overexpressed, allow cells to bypass normal cell cycle checkpoints and proliferate uncontrollably.
options: Chronic myeloid leukaemia from BCR-ABL fusion
Retinoblastoma from RB1 loss of function
Mantle cell lymphoma from cyclin D translocation

questions.explanation: Immune surveillance is the theory that the immune system continuously monitors the body for emerging neoplastic cells and eliminates them through mechanisms such as natural killer cell and cytotoxic T lymphocyte activity before they can develop into clinically detectable tumours. This concept helps explain the increased incidence of certain cancers in immunosuppressed individuals, such as transplant recipients. Evasion of immune surveillance is now recognised as one of the key steps that allows malignant cells to progress to overt cancer.
questions.question: A researcher studying the immune system's role in cancer proposes that the immune system continuously identifies and eliminates emerging malignant cells before they become clinically apparent tumours. This concept is known as:

questions.explanation: Complete resolution occurs when the injurious agent is eliminated and the tissue has the capacity to regenerate, restoring the site to its normal structure and function without scarring. It requires minimal tissue destruction and a tissue type capable of regeneration, such as superficial epidermis. This is the most favourable outcome compared with fibrosis, abscess formation, or progression to chronic inflammation, all of which leave some form of permanent alteration.
questions.question: A patient recovering from a minor superficial abrasion heals with no residual scar and normal tissue architecture. This favourable outcome of acute inflammation is:

A pathologist reviewing multiple tumour specimens from the same patient over several biopsies notes an increasing insensitivity to signals that would normally halt proliferation. This hallmark of cancer specifically involves resistance to which class of molecules?
questions.explanation: Insensitivity to growth-inhibitory signals is a hallmark of cancer in which tumour cells become resistant to molecules that normally restrain proliferation, such as transforming growth factor beta, often through mutation or loss of the receptors and downstream signalling components that mediate these inhibitory effects. This resistance allows malignant cells to continue proliferating despite the presence of signals that would normally halt the cell cycle in healthy tissue. Combined with self-sufficiency in growth signals, this loss of growth inhibition contributes to the characteristic uncontrolled proliferation of cancer cells.
options: Digestive enzymes released by the pancreas
Signals such as transforming growth factor beta

questions.question: The initial nonprogressive phase of shock is characterised by:
options: Tissue hypoperfusion with worsening metabolic acidosis
Reflex compensatory mechanisms being activated to maintain vital organ perfusion
Irreversible cellular injury despite haemodynamic correction
Multiple organ failure from prolonged inadequate perfusion
Progressive circulatory and metabolic imbalances causing acidosis
questions.explanation: Shock tends to evolve through three phases: (1) An initial nonprogressive phase during which reflex compensatory mechanisms are activated and perfusion of vital organs is maintained; (2) A progressive stage characterised by tissue hypoperfusion and onset of worsening circulatory and metabolic imbalances, including acidosis; and (3) An irreversible stage where cellular and tissue injury is so severe that survival is not possible even if haemodynamic defects are corrected.

questions.question: Ionising radiation carcinogenesis is BEST demonstrated by which historical evidence?
options: Increased leukaemia and solid tumours in atomic bomb survivors from Hiroshima and Nagasaki
Skin cancers in chimney sweeps from soot exposure
Gastric cancer from H. pylori infection in Japanese population
Mesothelioma in asbestos workers from occupational exposure
Lung cancer from polycyclic hydrocarbon inhalation in smokers
questions.explanation: The most compelling evidence for ionising radiation carcinogenesis comes from follow-up of survivors of the atomic bombs dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki. Initially there was a marked increase in leukaemia (principally acute and chronic myelogenous) after an average latent period of about 7 years. Subsequently, solid tumours with longer latent periods (breast, colon, thyroid, lung) increased. Many early x-ray pioneers also developed skin cancers.

Sarcoidosis is listed as having unknown aetiology in the granuloma table. It is characterised by noncaseating granulomas with abundant activated macrophages. In contrast, tuberculosis is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, leprosy by Mycobacterium leprae, cat-scratch disease by a gram-negative bacillus, and syphilis by Treponema pallidum.
questions.question: Which disease in the granuloma table is caused by an UNKNOWN aetiology?
A neoplasm, as defined by Willis, is BEST described as:
questions.explanation: According to Willis, a neoplasm is 'an abnormal mass of tissue, the growth of which exceeds and is uncoordinated with that of the normal tissues and persists in the same excessive manner after cessation of the stimuli which evoked the change.' The persistence of tumours after the inciting stimulus results from genetic alterations passed to tumour cell progeny, allowing autonomous excessive growth.
options: An abnormal mass of tissue with uncoordinated growth exceeding normal tissue and persisting after stimulus removal
Any swelling resulting from tissue inflammation or infection
A physiological response to chronic tissue damage requiring surgical excision
A benign overgrowth of normal tissue in response to hormonal stimulation
Any rapidly growing mass regardless of its histological characteristics

questions.question: In pathology, 'morphologic changes' refer to:
questions.explanation: Morphologic changes refer to the biochemical and structural alterations induced in the cells and organs of the body by disease. In the context of Plasmodium falciparum infection, haemolysis represents the morphologic/molecular change. These changes are distinct from aetiology, pathogenesis, and clinical manifestations.
options: The causative agents responsible for disease development
The mechanisms by which disease progressively develops
The biochemical and structural alterations induced in cells and organs by disease
The symptoms and signs that patients experience and display
The body's response and adaptation to physiological stress

questions.explanation: Pathology uses molecular, microbiologic, immunologic, and morphologic techniques to explain the whys and wherefores of signs and symptoms. Epidemiological survey techniques are tools of public health and epidemiology, not among the techniques traditionally used in pathological analysis of disease at the cellular and tissue level.
questions.question: Techniques used in pathology to explain disease processes include all of the following EXCEPT:
A patient with septic shock develops widespread microvascular thrombosis and consumption of clotting factors, leading to spontaneous bleeding. This feared coagulation complication is:
questions.explanation: Septic shock can trigger widespread activation of the coagulation cascade, consuming platelets and clotting factors while simultaneously causing microvascular thrombosis, a combination known as disseminated intravascular coagulation. This paradoxical state of simultaneous clotting and bleeding can cause both organ ischaemia from microthrombi and life-threatening haemorrhage from factor depletion. It is one of the most feared complications of severe sepsis due to its association with multi-organ failure and high mortality.

questions.question: The 'point of no return' in cell injury — when damage becomes irreversible — is associated with:
questions.explanation: The 'point of no return' — when damage becomes irreversible — is still largely undefined, with no reliable morphologic or biochemical correlates. However, two phenomena consistently characterise irreversibility: (1) inability to reverse mitochondrial dysfunction (lack of oxidative phosphorylation and ATP generation) even after resolution of the original injury; and (2) profound disturbances in membrane function.
options: Cellular swelling visible under light microscopy within minutes of injury
First appearance of fatty change in the cytoplasm of hepatocytes
Nuclear pyknosis detectable on standard haematoxylin and eosin staining
Irreversible mitochondrial dysfunction and profound membrane function disturbance
Activation of heat shock proteins in response to protein unfolding
Platelets, macrophages, endothelial cells, keratinocytes, and smooth muscle cells
Mast cells and basophils in the inflammatory infiltrate
Fibroblasts exclusively in the wound stroma
Bone marrow stem cells recruited to the wound
questions.question: PDGF (Platelet-Derived Growth Factor) in wound healing is sourced from which cells?
questions.explanation: PDGF (Platelet-Derived Growth Factor) is sourced from platelets, macrophages, endothelial cells, keratinocytes, and smooth muscle cells. Its functions include being chemotactic for PMNs, macrophages, fibroblasts, and smooth muscle cells; activating PMNs, macrophages, and fibroblasts; being mitogenic for fibroblasts, endothelial cells, and smooth muscle cells; stimulating MMPs, fibronectin, and HA production; and stimulating angiogenesis and wound contraction.

options: Small wounds have a higher concentration of growth factors per unit area
Incisional wounds have richer vascular supply than excisional wounds
Incisional wounds bypass the inflammatory phase of healing entirely
Small wounds undergo regeneration while large wounds only repair
Small incisional injuries heal with less intense inflammation and less scar formation than large excisional or blunt trauma wounds
questions.explanation: Small incisional injuries heal faster and with less scar formation than large excisional wounds or wounds caused by blunt trauma. Small surgical incisions (healing by primary intention) involve limited cell death, minimal disruption, thin scar formation, and a relatively thin re-epithelialisation. Large excisional wounds (healing by secondary intention) require more intense inflammation, abundant granulation tissue, and extensive collagen deposition leading to substantial scarring.
questions.question: Small incisional injuries heal faster than large excisional wounds because:

options: Reduced plasma osmotic pressure from hypoproteinaemia
Increased hydrostatic pressure from arteriolar dilation
Sodium retention from increased tubular reabsorption via renin-angiotensin-aldosterone
Inflammatory oedema from angiogenesis in chronic inflammation
questions.question: Which cause of oedema results from renal hypoperfusion triggering the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system?
questions.explanation: Sodium retention is listed as a cause of oedema, including through renal hypoperfusion (as occurs in heart failure) triggering increased renin-angiotensin-aldosterone secretion, which causes increased tubular reabsorption of sodium. The resulting sodium and water retention increases intravascular volume and hydrostatic pressure, while diluting plasma proteins and reducing colloid osmotic pressure.

options: Focal bacterial infections with neutrophilic exudate
Pancreatic fat destruction from lipase enzyme release
Ischaemic injury to the myocardium following coronary occlusion
Immune reactions involving blood vessels with antigen-antibody complex deposition
Tuberculous infection with central caseous necrosis
questions.question: Fibrinoid necrosis is typically seen in:
questions.explanation: Fibrinoid necrosis is a special form of necrosis usually seen in immune reactions involving blood vessels. This pattern typically occurs when complexes of antigens and antibodies are deposited in the walls of arteries. The immune complexes leak plasma proteins (including fibrin) into the vessel wall, giving it a bright pink, structureless 'fibrinoid' appearance on histology.

Septic shock triggers an initial hyperinflammatory response that is often followed by a compensatory anti-inflammatory phase, during which excessive apoptosis of lymphocytes and dendritic cells, together with release of anti-inflammatory mediators, produces a state of immune suppression. This immunosuppressed state increases the patient's vulnerability to secondary nosocomial infections during recovery from the initial septic insult. Understanding this biphasic immune response has informed strategies aimed at modulating immune function in critically ill septic patients.
options: Complete absence of any inflammatory mediator production
Isolated bone marrow failure unrelated to sepsis
Direct bacterial destruction of the spleen
Permanent loss of innate immune receptors
Excessive apoptosis of immune cells combined with anti-inflammatory mediator release
questions.question: A patient in septic shock is found to have suppressed lymphocyte function alongside ongoing infection, increasing susceptibility to secondary infections. This immune suppression in septic shock is triggered by:

options: Inhibits keratinocyte proliferation and MMP production
Inhibits fibroblast migration into the wound site
Inhibits endothelial cell chemotaxis reducing angiogenesis
Inhibits platelet aggregation and clot formation
Inhibits monocyte chemotaxis to the wound site
questions.question: TGF-ß (Transforming Growth Factor beta) in wound healing has which specific inhibitory action?
questions.explanation: According to the wound healing growth factors table, TGF-ß inhibits production of MMPs (matrix metalloproteinases) and keratinocyte proliferation. While TGF-ß stimulates TIMP synthesis, angiogenesis, and fibroplasia, it simultaneously inhibits MMP production and keratinocyte proliferation — a regulatory balance ensuring appropriate collagen accumulation and controlled re-epithelialisation during repair.

options: It causes renal sodium retention exacerbating systemic oedema
It always leads to permanent intellectual disability
It leads to irreversible loss of myelin from osmotic damage
It triggers severe inflammatory reaction destroying brain tissue
It can cause herniation through the foramen magnum or compression of brain stem vascular supply, causing death
questions.question: Brain oedema is particularly dangerous because:
questions.explanation: Brain oedema is life-threatening. If severe, brain substance can herniate (extrude) through the foramen magnum, or the brain stem vascular supply can be compressed. Either condition can injure the medullary centres and cause death. This is why pulmonary oedema and brain oedema represent the most serious consequences of oedema — the former impedes oxygen diffusion, the latter can be immediately fatal.

options: Complete resolution of all inflammatory processes
Acute respiratory distress syndrome and progressive organ dysfunction
Isolated recovery of renal function only
Rapid return to full physical health
questions.question: A patient recovers from the initial hypotensive phase of septic shock but subsequently develops progressive respiratory failure requiring ventilatory support. This second phase following initial shock is dominated by:
questions.explanation: Patients who survive the initial hypotensive phase of shock may enter a second phase characterised by progressive multi-organ dysfunction, with acute respiratory distress syndrome being a particularly common and serious manifestation due to diffuse alveolar capillary injury. This phase reflects the ongoing systemic inflammatory response and microvascular injury that persists even after initial haemodynamic stabilisation. Recognising this risk allows clinicians to anticipate and monitor for evolving organ dysfunction during recovery from the acute shock episode.

questions.question: Pathology is BEST defined as the study of:
options: Surgical procedures used to correct organ defects
Clinical signs and laboratory investigations of illness
Structural, biochemical, and functional changes in cells caused by disease
questions.explanation: Pathology is defined as the study of structural, biochemical, and functional changes in cells, tissues, and organs that underlie disease. It uses molecular, microbiologic, immunologic, and morphologic techniques to explain disease processes. Pathology bridges basic sciences and clinical practice, forming the scientific foundation of medicine.

options: Haemolysis of the infected red blood cells
Invasion and multiplication of the parasite within red cells
The mosquito bite that transmitted the infection
questions.explanation: Aetiology refers to the cause of the disease. In Plasmodium falciparum malaria, the aetiological agent is the Plasmodium falciparum parasite itself. The mosquito bite is the mode of transmission, invasion and multiplication in RBCs is the pathogenesis, haemolysis is the morphologic change, and anaemia is the clinical manifestation.
questions.question: Which of the following CORRECTLY represents the cause (aetiology) in Plasmodium falciparum malaria?

questions.explanation: Tumour necrosis factor is a cytokine primarily sourced from activated macrophages that plays a dual role, contributing to normal wound healing processes while also being implicated in the systemic wasting seen in cancer cachexia when chronically elevated. Its pleiotropic effects illustrate how the same signalling molecule can have both beneficial local roles in tissue repair and detrimental systemic effects when persistently overexpressed. Understanding this dual role has informed research into cytokine-targeted therapies for both wound healing complications and cancer-related wasting syndromes.
questions.question: A cachectic cancer patient has elevated levels of a cytokine known to contribute to systemic muscle wasting and is also implicated as a key growth factor sourced from macrophages during wound healing. This cytokine is:
A patient with chronic gastric inflammation and peptic ulcer disease is found to have a bacterial infection linked to increased risk of gastric cancer. This organism is:
questions.explanation: Helicobacter pylori is classified as a carcinogen because chronic infection is strongly associated with the development of gastric adenocarcinoma and gastric mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma, through mechanisms involving chronic inflammation and epithelial cell damage. It was the first bacterium to be formally classified as a carcinogen by international cancer research authorities. Eradication of Helicobacter pylori infection has been shown to reduce the risk of developing these associated malignancies.

questions.question: A patient with meningococcal septicaemia develops bilateral adrenal haemorrhage and acute adrenal insufficiency. This syndrome is known as:
questions.explanation: Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome refers to acute adrenal insufficiency caused by bilateral adrenal haemorrhage, classically associated with fulminant meningococcal septicaemia and disseminated intravascular coagulation. The resulting loss of cortisol production compounds the haemodynamic instability already present in septic shock, worsening the patient's prognosis. Recognising this syndrome is important because it requires urgent corticosteroid replacement in addition to standard septic shock management.

Healing by secondary intention occurs in wounds with significant tissue loss or infection where edges cannot be approximated, requiring more extensive granulation tissue formation, prolonged inflammation, and wound contraction to close the defect.
