questions.explanation: Because polymyositis involves inflammation and weakness of the muscles, exercise intensity should be guided by the degree of muscle weakness and fatigue present, avoiding overexertion that could exacerbate symptoms. It does not cause muscle hypertrophy or increased flexibility, which would be inconsistent with an inflammatory myopathy. Sensory loss is not a typical feature of polymyositis, which primarily affects motor function.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is teaching a patient with polymyositis appropriate exercise precautions. Which specific muscular symptom should guide exercise intensity?
options: Complete absence of any muscular symptoms
Muscle weakness and fatigue from ongoing inflammation
Total loss of all sensory function
Rest and elevate the affected joint
Perform passive stretching to end range
questions.question: What is the immediate physiotherapy advice for a patient during an acute gout flare of the knee?
questions.explanation: During an acute flare, uric acid crystals can damage the joint surface with vigorous movement, so rest and elevation are recommended alongside ice application. Exercise and stretching are deferred until the flare resolves. Heat is avoided in acute inflammatory episodes.

options: Symmetrical involvement of the MCP and wrist joints
Asymmetrical involvement of the DIP and first CMC joints
Systemic fever and significant weight loss
Subcutaneous nodules near the affected joints
Morning stiffness lasting over one hour
questions.explanation: Osteoarthritis typically shows asymmetrical involvement of joints such as the distal interphalangeal and first carpometacarpal joints, along with brief morning stiffness. Symmetrical MCP and wrist involvement, systemic symptoms, prolonged stiffness, and nodules are instead characteristic of rheumatoid arthritis. Recognising this distribution pattern helps guide appropriate clinical assessment and referral.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is asked to identify which joint pattern would help clinically distinguish osteoarthritis from rheumatoid arthritis during an initial assessment. Which finding favours osteoarthritis?

questions.explanation: This triad is classic for the arthritis-dermatitis syndrome of disseminated gonococcal infection, which should be considered in sexually active young patients. Osteoarthritis and DISH are degenerative, non-infectious conditions unrelated to this presentation. Ankylosing spondylitis presents with axial, not migratory peripheral, symptoms.
questions.question: A sexually active young woman presents with a triad of dermatitis, migratory polyarthralgia, and tenosynovitis. Which diagnosis should be prioritised?
Which joint is most commonly affected by septic arthritis in adults?
questions.explanation: The knee is the most commonly affected joint in adult septic arthritis, followed by the hip, elbow, shoulder, and ankle in decreasing frequency. This pattern helps guide clinical suspicion when a patient presents with an acutely swollen joint. Hip involvement is instead more common in children.

options: No follow-up testing is ever required after treatment
Reinfection is biologically impossible after one gonococcal episode
Retesting approximately three months after treatment due to high reinfection risk
Retesting is only needed if symptoms never improve
Partners never require evaluation regardless of symptoms
questions.question: A patient recovering from disseminated gonococcal infection asks about the risk of reinfection. What follow-up advice is appropriate?
questions.explanation: Patients treated for gonorrhoea have a high incidence of reinfection and should be retested around three months after treatment, with sexual partners also referred for evaluation since they are often asymptomatic. Reinfection is biologically possible and common, not impossible. Partner evaluation is recommended regardless of the index patient's symptom resolution.

options: Transfer training and basic gait training with support
Passive range of motion exercises exclusively
Complete bed rest with no mobility work
questions.explanation: In the subacute phase of autoimmune encephalitis rehabilitation, therapy progresses to active-assisted ROM, sitting balance, transfer training, and basic gait training using parallel bars or a walker as appropriate. Passive ROM alone and ICU-focused chest physiotherapy reflect the earlier acute phase. Community reintegration is instead a goal of the later recovery/rehabilitation phase.
questions.question: A patient with autoimmune encephalitis is in the subacute recovery phase, sitting independently but requiring assistance to stand. Which physiotherapy focus is most appropriate at this stage?
Which physical examination finding would prompt a physiotherapist to specifically suspect an attempt by the body to immobilise a traumatised or acutely inflamed joint?
options: Full painless active range of motion
Palpable muscle spasm around the joint
A cool, dry, normally coloured limb
questions.explanation: Palpable muscle spasm around a joint might indicate an attempt by the body to immobilise a traumatised or inflamed joint, providing a protective splinting effect. Full painless ROM and normal muscle bulk would instead suggest an unaffected, healthy joint. Recognising spasm as a protective mechanism helps guide gentle, graded treatment progression.

options: The device eliminates all sensation in the joint
The device increases the overall load on the hip joint
The device has no measurable biomechanical effect
The device works only by providing a placebo effect
The device shares body weight, lowering hip joint reaction force by up to 50%
questions.explanation: Holding a quadripod (four-point) assistive device redistributes body weight through the upper limb, reducing hip joint loading by approximately 50% during ambulation, a specific and measurable biomechanical effect. It does not eliminate sensation or increase joint load. This mechanical unloading effect is the rationale for recommending such devices in hip arthropathy.
questions.question: A physiotherapist explains to a patient with an arthropathy why holding a quadripod cane reduces stress on the hip joint. What is the underlying biomechanical principle?

questions.explanation: Large knee effusions in reactive arthritis can develop into popliteal cysts, and rupture of such a cyst may cause a pseudo-phlebitis syndrome mimicking deep vein thrombosis, which the physiotherapist should be alert to as a potential complication. This is not a benign or inconsequential finding to be dismissed. It does not mean physiotherapy is permanently contraindicated, but this specific complication should be recognised and appropriately referred if suspected.
questions.question: A physiotherapist notes a large knee effusion in a patient with reactive arthritis, exceeding 100mL, with a palpable popliteal swelling. What could this finding potentially indicate if it were to rupture?
options: A completely benign finding requiring no further consideration
Immediate resolution of the underlying reactive arthritis
Guaranteed improvement in joint range of motion
A pseudo-phlebitis syndrome from a ruptured popliteal cyst
A sign that physiotherapy is absolutely contraindicated forever

questions.explanation: Allopurinol and febuxostat are xanthine oxidase inhibitors that reduce uric acid production for long-term prevention of gout flares. Probenecid instead works by increasing renal excretion of urate. Colchicine, indomethacin, and prednisolone only manage acute symptoms rather than lowering serum urate.
questions.question: A patient with recurrent gout is started on a xanthine oxidase inhibitor for long-term prevention. Which drug is this?
A 45-year-old man presents with sudden severe pain at the first metatarsophalangeal joint. Which crystal is responsible for this presentation?
questions.explanation: The first metatarsophalangeal joint (podagra) is the classic site for acute gouty arthritis. Gout results from deposition of monosodium urate crystals following sustained hyperuricaemia. The other crystals listed cause pseudogout and calcific tendinitis, not gout.

During an acute gout flare, rest and elevation of the joint combined with ice application are recommended, as exercise during this period can be detrimental due to the risk of uric acid crystals damaging the joint surface during extreme motion. Stretching, resistance training, heat, and weight-bearing exercise are all deferred until the flare resolves. This approach protects the inflamed joint while managing pain.
options: Rest, elevation, and application of ice
Full weight-bearing exercise on a treadmill
questions.question: A physiotherapist is treating a patient during an acute gout flare of the ankle. Which treatment approach is most appropriate at this stage?

questions.explanation: After antibiotic treatment, progressive physiotherapy focusing on strengthening, increasing range of motion, decreasing pain and stiffness, and improving cardiovascular fitness is vital for preserving joint function. Permanent immobilisation would cause unnecessary disability. High-impact activity is not an early-stage goal.
options: Permanent immobilisation of the affected joint
Preservation of function through progressive strengthening and ROM
Discouraging any patient education on joint protection
questions.question: Which of the following physiotherapy goals is prioritised following antibiotic treatment for gonococcal arthritis?

options: Water increases uric acid excretion directly
Chlorine in pools dissolves urate crystals
Buoyancy reduces joint loading, making movement less painful
Aquatic exercise eliminates the need for medication
Cold water triggers anti-inflammatory hormone release
questions.explanation: Aquatic exercise reduces mechanical loading on joints through buoyancy, making stretching and strengthening more comfortable for gout patients. This is combined with, not a replacement for, pharmacological urate-lowering therapy. Water itself has no direct effect on uric acid metabolism.
questions.question: Why is aquatic exercise particularly recommended for patients managing chronic gout between flares?

options: Avoidance of prolonged static positioning to protect joints
Maximising joint loading for strength gains
questions.explanation: Frequent position changes prevent prolonged static loading of joints, which is part of the broader joint protection principles used in rheumatoid arthritis management. This is combined with balancing rest and activity to avoid fatigue. It does not involve maximising joint stress or encouraging deforming positions.
questions.question: A rheumatoid arthritis patient is advised to change position every 20 to 30 minutes during the day. What principle does this reflect?
What distinguishes secondary osteoarthritis from primary osteoarthritis?
questions.explanation: Secondary osteoarthritis arises from an identifiable cause such as previous trauma, infection, gout, or congenital hip dislocation, whereas primary OA has an unknown aetiology linked mainly to the ageing process. Both forms involve cartilage breakdown. Radiological features are present in both types.
options: Secondary OA only affects the spine
Secondary OA has an identifiable underlying cause
Secondary OA never involves cartilage loss
Secondary OA cannot be diagnosed radiologically

questions.explanation: Compression gloves provide gentle pressure that reduces joint swelling at the wrist, hand, and fingers, used at hourly intervals or at night in patients with hand or finger inflammation. They do not cure the underlying disease or regenerate cartilage. They are an adjunct, not a replacement, for other joint protection strategies.
options: Complete resolution of the underlying disease
Complete elimination of the need for splinting
Reduced joint swelling at the wrist, hand, and fingers
questions.question: What benefit do compression gloves provide for patients with hand or finger joint inflammation?
A patient with viral arthritis reports symmetrical joint pain and morning stiffness resembling rheumatoid arthritis. Which additional clinical clue points toward a viral cause?
options: Recent history of fever, myalgia, and fatigue preceding joint symptoms
Positive rheumatoid factor at high titres for years
Gradual insidious onset over several years
Bilateral hand nodules present for a decade
questions.explanation: A preceding or coincident systemic viral illness with fever, muscle ache, and fatigue is a key clue suggesting viral rather than rheumatoid arthritis. Long-standing deformity and chronically elevated rheumatoid factor instead suggest established RA. Viral arthritis has an acute, not insidious, onset.

options: Complete elimination of the surgical scar
Guaranteed prevention of any future joint replacement
Immediate full return to competitive sport
Elimination of the need for any rehabilitation exercise
questions.explanation: TENS therapy following knee joint arthroplasty has been shown to reduce the need for analgesic drugs alongside reducing hospital stay, reflecting its value as an adjunct in postoperative pain control. It does not eliminate scarring, guarantee against future surgery, or replace the need for rehabilitation exercise. This makes it a useful complementary, not standalone, intervention.
questions.question: A physiotherapist wants to reduce postoperative pain and hospital stay following knee arthroplasty using a specific electrotherapy modality. What additional patient benefit is associated with this modality's use?
A synovial joint that permits gliding movement between numerous small, relatively flat articular surfaces, such as the carpal bones, is classified as which joint type?
questions.explanation: Plane or gliding joints have flat or nearly flat articular surfaces that glide over one another, exemplified by the intercarpal joints and the acromioclavicular joint, with movement limited by a tight capsule. Hinge joints instead allow flexion and extension in a single plane, such as the knee. Ball and socket joints permit multiaxial movement, as at the hip.

Hyaluronate injections provide symptomatic relief and improved function mainly in the knee, but require a series of injections and lack evidence of long-term benefit, and are expensive. Corticosteroid injections instead provide good short-term pain relief but carry infection risk with frequent use. Oral glucosamine and topical agents are non-injectable alternatives.
questions.question: Which intra-articular therapy for osteoarthritis is limited mainly to the knee and requires a series of injections without proven long-term benefit?

options: Apply deep heat directly to the septic joint
Ignore the laboratory report and continue as planned
Defer physiotherapy and ensure medical management of the infection is underway
questions.question: A physiotherapist reviews a patient's synovial fluid report showing WBC count over 50,000/mm3 and a positive culture before starting treatment. What is the most appropriate clinical action?
questions.explanation: A synovial WBC count above 50,000/mm3 with a positive culture indicates septic arthritis, meaning physiotherapy should be deferred until appropriate medical management, typically antibiotics with or without drainage, is underway. Aggressive mobilisation, heat, or resistance exercise on an actively septic joint could worsen the infection and joint damage. Recognising this laboratory pattern is essential for physiotherapist safety and appropriate referral.

options: To permanently cure the underlying cartilage degeneration
To increase the Q-angle to abnormal levels intentionally
To eliminate the need for any exercise therapy
To replace the function of the anterior cruciate ligament
To alter joint loading and reduce mechanical stress on the affected compartment
questions.explanation: Lateral-wedged insoles are used as part of non-pharmacological OA management to alter knee joint loading patterns and reduce mechanical stress on the affected compartment. They do not cure the underlying cartilage pathology or replace the ACL's function. They are used alongside, not instead of, exercise therapy.
questions.question: A patient with knee osteoarthritis has been prescribed a lateral-wedged insole. What is the primary mechanical rationale for this intervention?

options: To replace all future physiotherapy appointments
To serve as the sole treatment without any exercise
To provide entertainment unrelated to the condition
To reinforce patient understanding and encourage self-management skills
To eliminate the need for medical diagnosis
questions.question: A physiotherapist provides a self-management booklet to a newly diagnosed rheumatic disease patient. What is the primary purpose of this educational resource?
questions.explanation: Self-management programmes with informative booklets are encouraged to support patient understanding of their condition and reinforce self-management skills alongside ongoing physiotherapy and medical care. They do not replace appointments or serve as a standalone treatment. This educational approach is a recognised component of comprehensive rheumatic disease management.

An abrupt hard stop with a grating sensation from roughened articular surfaces is an abnormal bony end-feel, indicating pathology such as loose bodies, degenerative joint disease, or fracture. A normal bony end-feel instead occurs painlessly, such as at elbow extension. This distinction alerts the therapist to underlying joint pathology.
questions.question: A physiotherapist measures a patient's knee passively and feels an abrupt hard stop with a bony grating sensation. Which end-feel category does this represent?

options: Long bone, due to its tubular shape
Flat bone, due to its plate-like shape
Short bone, due to its cuboidal shape
Irregular bone, due to its complex, variable shape
Sesamoid bone, due to its tendon location
questions.explanation: The vertebra is classified as an irregular bone because of its complex, variable shape that does not fit the tubular, plate-like, or cuboidal patterns of long, flat, or short bones. Long bones such as the femur are tubular for weight-bearing, while flat bones like the skull provide protection. This classification reflects the vertebra's specialised structural role in supporting and protecting the spinal cord.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is asked to classify the vertebra during a practical class exercise on bone types. Which classification is most accurate, and why?

questions.explanation: Heat modalities are avoided in the acute phase of septic arthritis prior to antibiotic initiation because increased local temperature could theoretically promote bacterial activity and worsen inflammation. Once treatment is underway, modalities such as ice, hydrotherapy, and TENS become appropriate. This is not a universal contraindication across all rheumatological conditions.
options: Heat causes immediate anaphylaxis in septic patients
Heat is contraindicated in all rheumatological conditions
Heat may increase bacterial metabolic activity and worsen the infection
questions.question: What is the physiotherapy rationale for avoiding heat modalities in the acute phase of septic arthritis before antibiotic treatment begins?
Which of the following is the most appropriate reason for delaying resistance exercise during an acute flare of an inflammatory arthropathy?
questions.explanation: During an acute inflammatory flare, resistance exercise can increase mechanical stress on already inflamed joints and worsen symptoms, so gentle isometrics and rest are favoured until the flare subsides. Resistance training is not contraindicated at every disease stage, only during acute exacerbations. Delaying exercise during a flare does not cause permanent joint fusion.
options: Resistance loading can increase joint stress and worsen inflammation
Resistance exercise cures the disease if delayed long enough
Resistance exercise is contraindicated in every stage of arthritis
Delaying exercise guarantees permanent joint fusion
Resistance training has no effect on joint pain

questions.explanation: Seronegative describes a patient whose rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibody levels are too low to be detected on blood testing, even though clinical features of RA may still be present. As disease progresses, antibody levels may rise enough to become seropositive. This term does not describe disease severity or treatment response.
questions.question: A patient with rheumatoid factor levels too low to detect is best described using which term?

questions.explanation: Connective tissue is made up of collagen, found in tendons, ligaments, and cartilage, and elastin, a stretchy protein found in ligaments and skin. In connective tissue disease, these proteins become inflamed, harming the structures they connect. Actin, myosin, keratin, and haemoglobin are unrelated structural or functional proteins.
questions.question: Which two proteins make up the connective tissue that becomes inflamed and damaged in connective tissue disease?

options: Non-erosive arthritis that is rarely deforming
Erosive symmetrical arthritis with severe deformity
Isolated monoarthritis of the great toe
questions.question: Which joint manifestation is most characteristic of systemic lupus erythematosus?
questions.explanation: Arthritis in systemic lupus erythematosus is the most common musculoskeletal manifestation but is typically non-erosive and rarely deforming, occasionally producing Jaccoud's deformity from ligamentous laxity rather than bone erosion. This differs from the erosive joint destruction of rheumatoid arthritis. Ankylosis and chondrocalcinosis are unrelated findings from other conditions.

When both active and passive range of motion are equally limited, this suggests a joint or capsular restriction rather than isolated muscle weakness, since even an external force cannot move the joint further. Full passive ROM with limited active ROM instead points toward muscle weakness, as previously established. Comparing active and passive ROM is a standard and necessary part of differentiating these two causes of limitation.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is asked to compare active and passive ROM to determine whether a patient's shoulder limitation is due to muscle weakness or joint restriction. Which finding would suggest joint restriction rather than muscle weakness?
options: Passive ROM is full while active ROM is limited
Only active ROM is tested, passive ROM is never assessed
Both active and passive ROM are equally limited
Neither active nor passive ROM can ever be compared

questions.explanation: For elbow flexion and extension, the goniometer fulcrum is centred over the lateral epicondyle, with the stationary arm aligned to the humerus toward the acromion and the moving arm aligned with the radius toward the radial styloid. The olecranon process is instead used as the fulcrum for measuring forearm rotation. The acromion and greater trochanter are landmarks for the shoulder and hip respectively.
questions.question: Where should the fulcrum of the goniometer be placed to accurately measure elbow flexion and extension?

questions.explanation: A boggy end-feel sensation indicates the presence of synovitis or soft tissue oedema within or around the joint, an abnormal pathological finding. This differs from the firm, springy quality of a normal capsular or ligamentous end-feel. Recognising this finding helps the therapist identify active inflammation requiring caution during treatment.
questions.question: A therapist palpates a joint during passive movement and feels a 'boggy' sensation at the end of range. What does this most likely indicate?

questions.explanation: Immunoglobulin M and G testing helps determine how recent or established a viral infection is, since IgM rises early and IgG later, aiding in tracking infection stage. Rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP are used to rule out rheumatoid arthritis rather than confirm viral aetiology. Gram stain is used for suspected bacterial infection.
questions.question: Which laboratory test specifically helps track the stage and duration of a viral infection causing arthritis?
options: Immunoglobulin M and G antibody testing

questions.explanation: Sesamoid bones, such as the patella, develop within certain tendons where they cross the ends of long bones, protecting the tendon from excessive wear and altering the angle of tendon attachment. Long bones like the femur are tubular and weight-bearing. Flat and irregular bones serve protective or variable structural roles instead.
questions.question: Which bone classification includes the patella, a bone that forms within a tendon to protect it from wear?

questions.explanation: Arthrocentesis carries rare potential complications including cartilage damage from needle insertion, bleeding, iatrogenic haemarthrosis, and reaccumulation of joint effusion. It does not cause joint fusion or guaranteed future osteoarthritis. Loss of proprioception is not a recognised complication of this procedure.
questions.question: Which complication of arthrocentesis, though rare, involves damage to the articular cartilage from needle insertion?
A synovial fluid sample shows a white cell count of 4,000/mm3 with translucent-opaque clarity. Which category does this most likely represent?
questions.explanation: A white cell count in the 2,000 to 10,000/mm3 range with translucent-opaque clarity is typical of inflammatory synovial fluid, as seen in crystal arthropathies or spondyloarthropathy. Normal and non-inflammatory fluid have much lower counts, while septic fluid typically exceeds 50,000/mm3. Haemorrhagic fluid would show blood staining rather than opacity alone.

questions.question: Which physiotherapy modality is used specifically to break up calcific deposits before saline flushing of the subacromial space?
questions.explanation: Needling combined with lavage mechanically disrupts calcific deposits, after which the subacromial space is flushed with saline to remove fragments. This differs from purely symptomatic modalities like cryotherapy. Traction and continuous passive motion machines play no role in calcific tendinitis management.

questions.question: Which frequency of TENS is described as most beneficial for pain management in arthropathies?
questions.explanation: A TENS frequency of 70 Hz has been described as the most beneficial for analgesia in arthropathy management, reducing swelling and inflammation in acute arthritis. TENS is a short-acting therapy lasting roughly 6 to 24 hours. The much higher or lower frequencies listed are not the cited optimal setting.

Rheumatoid arthritis classically begins in the small joints, most commonly the proximal interphalangeal joints of the hands and feet, with a symmetrical distribution. The distal interphalangeal joints are typically spared, unlike in osteoarthritis. Large weight-bearing joints tend to become involved later in disease progression.
options: Large weight-bearing joints such as the hip
Distal interphalangeal joints of the fingers
Small proximal joints of the hands and feet
questions.question: Which joints are classically first affected by the early inflammatory changes of rheumatoid arthritis?
A physiotherapist is asked to select an appropriate outcome measure for a patient with temporomandibular joint dysfunction secondary to an inflammatory arthropathy. Which tool should be used?
options: Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score
questions.explanation: The TMJ Disability Index Questionnaire is specifically designed to assess disability related to temporomandibular joint dysfunction, making it the most appropriate outcome measure in this scenario. The Oswestry, Neck Disability Index, SPADI, and KOOS instead assess the low back, neck, shoulder, and knee respectively, none of which are relevant to TMJ dysfunction. Choosing the region-specific tool ensures the assessment accurately reflects the patient's condition.

options: Using a standard pillow at night
Use of a quadripod walking aid
questions.explanation: Holding a quadripod (four-point) walking aid can reduce loading over the hip joint by approximately 50%, helping to protect the joint during ambulation. This is a specific biomechanical effect of assistive device use. The other listed items do not influence hip joint loading during walking.
questions.question: Which assistive device modification can reduce hip joint loading by up to 50% during ambulation?

options: Exactly 15 degrees of elbow flexion only
Zero degrees of any joint motion
Approximately 140 degrees of elbow flexion combined with adequate shoulder motion
Only wrist motion, disregarding the elbow and shoulder entirely
Maximal hyperextension of the elbow beyond normal limits
questions.explanation: Reaching the back of the head to comb hair requires approximately 140 degrees of elbow flexion working together with adequate shoulder motion, providing a specific functional ROM target for the physiotherapist when restoring overhead reaching after joint recovery. Minimal flexion values or ignoring relevant joints would not reflect the functional demand of this task. Hyperextension beyond normal limits is neither necessary nor appropriate for this activity.
questions.question: A physiotherapist working with a patient recovering from septic arthritis of the shoulder wants to restore functional overhead reaching. Which specific ROM value should guide the therapist's functional goal for combing hair at the back of the head?

A patient with dermatomyositis reports skin involvement around the eyes and hands alongside proximal muscle weakness. Which practical adaptation might the physiotherapist need to consider during a therapy session?
options: Ignoring the skin findings entirely since they are unrelated to therapy
Applying maximal friction massage directly over the affected skin
Protecting fragile, affected skin during handling and exercise equipment use
Using only equipment with abrasive surfaces regardless of skin condition
Assuming skin involvement has no bearing on physiotherapy technique
questions.explanation: Given the skin involvement seen in dermatomyositis, physiotherapists should adapt handling techniques and consider skin protection during exercise and equipment use to avoid causing further irritation or damage. Applying friction massage or abrasive equipment directly over affected skin would risk harm. Skin findings are clinically relevant to session planning, not something to disregard.

Pseudogout, or calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease, results from deposition of calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate crystals in articular cartilage and fibrocartilage. This differs from gout, which involves monosodium urate. Calcium hydroxyapatite instead causes calcific tendinitis.
questions.question: Which crystal type is deposited in the joints of a patient diagnosed with pseudogout?
Which route of joint infection is most common overall in septic arthritis?
options: Direct spread from adjacent osteomyelitis only
Haematogenous spread from a distant infection site
Spread through intact skin without a wound
questions.explanation: Haematogenous spread is the most common route by which bacteria reach the joint in septic arthritis, particularly in patients with underlying medical problems. Direct inoculation and spread from adjacent bone are recognised but less common routes. Intact skin without any breach is not a described mechanism.

Asymptomatic hyperuricaemia is the earliest stage, where elevated serum urate exists without any clinical arthritis. Acute gouty arthritis follows once crystal-induced inflammation occurs. Intercritical gout refers to symptom-free periods between flares rather than an entirely pre-clinical state.
questions.question: Which stage of gout is characterised by radiographic crystal deposits without any clinical symptoms?

questions.explanation: Osteoarthritis is a degenerative joint disease characterised by breakdown of articular cartilage along with proliferative changes of the surrounding bone, without systemic involvement. This differs from the autoimmune synovial attack of rheumatoid arthritis. Crystal deposition and bacterial invasion characterise other arthropathies, not primary OA.
questions.question: Which pathological process best defines primary osteoarthritis?
options: Autoimmune destruction of the synovial membrane
Deposition of monosodium urate crystals in cartilage
Bacterial invasion of the joint space
Breakdown of articular cartilage with proliferative bony changes
Deposition of calcium pyrophosphate crystals only

questions.explanation: The carrying (cubital) angle is measured using a goniometer with the patient standing in anatomical position, aligning the arms along the upper arm and forearm respectively. A tape measure, stethoscope, or reflex hammer would not provide the angular measurement required. Comparing both elbows with the goniometer is recommended since the carrying angle varies between individuals.
questions.question: Which measurement tool is required to accurately assess the carrying angle of the elbow?

questions.explanation: A hard, abrupt stop as bone contacts bone, such as at full elbow or knee extension in some individuals, represents a normal physiological end-feel when it occurs painlessly at the expected anatomical limit. A boggy sensation, springy rebound, or pain-limited early stopping are all abnormal pathological findings instead. Correctly distinguishing normal from abnormal end-feel is essential for accurate clinical interpretation.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is assessing whether a patient's knee joint shows a 'normal' or 'abnormal' end-feel during passive extension. Which finding would be classified as a normal physiological end-feel at this joint?
options: A springy rebound suggesting internal derangement
Pain occurring well before any mechanical resistance
A hard, abrupt stop as bone meets bone at full extension
No sensation at all followed by severe pain

questions.explanation: Acetic acid iontophoresis uses an electrical current to drive acetic acid ions through the skin, and is used as an adjunct physiotherapy modality in calcific tendinitis to help resolve calcium deposits. Ultrasound and cryotherapy work through different physical mechanisms without transdermal drug delivery. TENS and static stretching also do not deliver medication transdermally.
questions.question: Which physiotherapy modality specifically uses electrical current to drive medication such as acetic acid through the skin for calcific tendinitis?

questions.explanation: Splints and orthoses are used to diminish pain and inflammation, prevent deformity development, reduce joint stress, support joints, and decrease stiffness. They complement rather than replace exercise therapy. They are not designed to increase ROM beyond normal or to affect sensation.
questions.question: What is the main purpose of orthoses and splinting in the management of arthropathies?
options: To permanently fuse the joint surgically
To increase joint range of motion beyond normal limits
To diminish pain, prevent deformity, and reduce joint stress
To replace the need for any exercise therapy
To eliminate all sensation in the joint

questions.explanation: Using the same outcome measure consistently at each visit allows the physiotherapist to make valid comparisons and track meaningful change in the patient's condition over the course of treatment. Constantly switching measures would undermine this comparability. Reassessment complements, rather than replaces, ongoing physical examination and has genuine clinical value beyond administrative record-keeping.
options: To give the patient something different to complete at every visit
To replace the need for any physical examination
To satisfy administrative requirements with no clinical value
To provide a consistent, comparable measure of change in the patient's condition over time
To ensure the therapist never has to re-examine the patient
questions.question: A physiotherapist is asked to explain why reassessment using the same outcome measure at each visit is important when managing a patient with an arthropathy. What is the primary purpose of this practice?

questions.explanation: Synovial fluid analysis must be interpreted cautiously because the presence of gout crystals, for example, does not exclude a concurrent septic process, and multiple aetiologies may coexist. Assuming mutual exclusivity could lead to a missed infection. This is why culture and crystal analysis are both performed on aspirated fluid.
options: Synovial fluid can only ever show one diagnosis
Crystals and infection are mutually exclusive findings
The presence of crystals does not rule out a concurrent joint infection
Synovial fluid analysis is never useful in gout
Infected joints never contain any crystals at all
questions.question: Why is it important to remember that multiple pathologies can coexist when interpreting synovial fluid analysis?

questions.explanation: In chronic arthritis, low-impact conditioning exercises such as swimming, walking, and cycling with adequate rest periods are recommended to increase muscle endurance and aerobic capacity while minimising joint stress. High-impact and contact activities risk further joint damage. Maximal strength testing is not an appropriate conditioning method in this population.
questions.question: Which type of exercise is recommended in chronic arthritis to improve aerobic capacity while minimising joint stress?
options: Low-impact conditioning exercise such as swimming and cycling
Prolonged static holding at end-range stretch
No obvious structural cause in a patient under 45
A clear traumatic fracture seen on X-ray
Back pain resolving completely with simple rest
An isolated muscular strain from heavy lifting
Back pain confined to one dermatome only
questions.explanation: Clinicians are advised to actively ask about spondyloarthritis features as part of the history in patients under 45 years with no obvious structural cause for their back pain, since early diagnosis improves treatment response. A clear traumatic fracture or simple muscular strain points toward a mechanical rather than inflammatory cause. Dermatomal pain instead suggests nerve root involvement.
questions.question: Which finding on examination of a patient with suspected spondyloarthritis and chronic low back pain should raise suspicion, according to current recommendations?

questions.explanation: Dermatomyositis is distinguished from polymyositis by the additional presence of a skin rash, alongside shared features of muscle weakness, fatigue, and difficulty swallowing. Osteogenesis imperfecta and Marfan syndrome are structural, not inflammatory muscle, disorders. Reactive arthritis primarily affects joints rather than producing myositis.
questions.question: Which musculoskeletal disease characterised by muscle inflammation also involves a skin rash when present?

questions.explanation: Seropositive rheumatoid arthritis patients commonly develop firm subcutaneous rheumatoid nodules near affected joints, a feature generally absent in seronegative patients. Symmetrical involvement, morning stiffness, swelling, and elevated ESR can occur in both groups. Nodules therefore serve as a distinguishing clinical clue.
questions.question: Which extra-articular feature distinguishes seropositive from seronegative rheumatoid arthritis patients?
options: Presence of firm rheumatoid nodules near affected joints

questions.explanation: Once the acute inflammatory phase has settled, heat application is used to help alleviate the residual joint stiffness associated with viral arthritis. Cryotherapy is instead reserved for the earlier acute swelling phase. Surgery and long-term corticosteroids are not standard interventions for self-limiting viral arthritis, and continued immobilisation would worsen stiffness.
questions.question: A patient recovering from viral arthritis reports residual joint stiffness once acute swelling has resolved. Which modality is then appropriate to help alleviate this stiffness?
Which synovial fluid component is primarily responsible for boundary lubrication of cartilage surfaces?
questions.explanation: Lubricin is a surface-active glycoprotein secreted into synovial fluid that coats cartilage and provides boundary lubrication while preventing cell and protein adhesion. Collagenases and proteinases instead break down proteins rather than lubricate surfaces. Prostaglandins mediate inflammation rather than joint lubrication.

Measuring at the same time of day, along with duplicating positions and removing restrictive clothing, helps control factors that can affect reliability of ROM measurement, such as diurnal variation in joint stiffness. This is a specific reliability consideration, not a claim that joints only move properly at certain times. Goniometers do not malfunction based on time of day, and repeat assessment is a standard, expected part of monitoring progress.
options: Because joints only move properly in the morning
Because afternoon measurements are always inaccurate
Because the goniometer malfunctions at certain times of day
Because patients cannot be assessed twice under any circumstance
To improve reliability by controlling for factors that affect ROM throughout the day
questions.question: A physiotherapist is asked why goniometric measurements should be taken at the same time of day when reassessing a patient's ROM. What is the primary rationale?

questions.explanation: The plan section of a SOAP note should include the immediate treatment to be given, frequency and duration of treatments, evaluation standards for progress, ongoing patient education, and criteria for discharge. Subjective pain descriptions and palpation findings belong to earlier sections of the note. Irrelevant personal details such as family members or restaurant preferences have no place in clinical documentation.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is completing the 'plan' section of a SOAP note for a patient with an arthropathy. Which of the following should be included in this section?
options: The patient's subjective description of pain alone
The frequency and duration of prescribed treatments and criteria for discharge
The examiner's observed findings from palpation alone
A list of the patient's family members
Delay in diagnosis has no effect on joint outcome
Antibiotics work equally well regardless of timing
Cartilage regenerates fully no matter how late treatment starts
Only the skin is affected by delayed treatment
Cartilage destruction from bacterial and inflammatory enzymes progresses rapidly with time
questions.question: Which statement best explains why septic arthritis carries a worse prognosis when diagnosis is delayed?
questions.explanation: The longer septic arthritis goes untreated, the more cartilage is destroyed by bacterial enzymes and the host inflammatory response, worsening long-term joint outcomes. This is why septic arthritis is treated as an emergency requiring prompt antibiotics and drainage. Cartilage does not regenerate fully once significantly destroyed, unlike the claim in the distractor.

questions.question: Which metabolic condition shows a significant association with the development of diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis?
questions.explanation: DISH shows a significant association with metabolic disorders including diabetes mellitus, obesity, hyperinsulinemia, dyslipidaemia, and hyperuricaemia. Iron deficiency anaemia, vitamin C deficiency, hypothyroidism, and folate deficiency are not established associations of DISH. This metabolic link is important when considering comorbidities in an affected patient.

questions.question: Which cardiac manifestation of systemic lupus erythematosus involves non-infective valvular vegetations?
questions.explanation: Libman-Sacks endocarditis is a non-infective, verrucous valvular lesion associated with systemic lupus erythematosus, distinct from infective or rheumatic valve disease. Aortic dissection is instead a classic complication of Marfan syndrome. Tophi-related embolism is not a recognised cardiac complication of any connective tissue disease.

The periosteum is the connective tissue sleeve covering bone that nourishes it, lays down new bone, and provides attachment sites for tendons and ligaments. The endosteum instead lines the medullary canal and contains osteoclasts responsible for bone resorption. Synovium and perichondrium line joints and cartilage, not the bone shaft surface.
questions.question: Which layer of connective tissue covering bone is primarily responsible for nourishing bone and providing attachment for tendons and ligaments?

questions.explanation: Normal hip flexion measured in supine is approximately 0 to 125 degrees, providing a reference range against which a patient's restricted or hypermobile hip can be compared. Values dramatically outside normal physiological limits, such as 220 or 300 degrees, are not anatomically possible. Recognising the expected normal range helps identify clinically significant restriction from arthropathy.
questions.question: Which normal range of hip flexion should a physiotherapist expect when goniometrically assessing a healthy adult hip in supine?

A patient with widespread joint pain from an arthropathy struggles to exercise on land due to weakness. Which modality allows the patient to exercise more comfortably by reducing effective body weight?
questions.explanation: Hydrotherapy reduces effective body weight by 50% to 90% depending on immersion depth, allowing patients with muscle weakness or widespread joint pain to exercise more comfortably than on land. Iontophoresis, TENS, and compression gloves serve different therapeutic purposes rather than mechanically unloading the joints. Static stretching alone does not provide the buoyancy-related unloading effect.

Holding a cane in the hand opposite the affected knee creates a more effective reduction in joint loading during the stance phase of gait, following normal reciprocal arm-leg movement patterns. Holding it on the same side as the affected knee would be less biomechanically effective at unloading the joint. This principle is a standard component of gait aid education in osteoarthritis management.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is teaching a patient with osteoarthritis of the knee how to use a cane correctly. In which hand should the cane be held to most effectively reduce joint loading?
options: In the hand on the same side as the affected knee
In the hand opposite the affected knee
In either hand, since side makes no difference
Held in front of the body with both hands
Behind the back regardless of the affected side
Compliance has no bearing on treatment outcomes
Only the therapist's preferences matter in exercise design
Compliance is only relevant for surgical patients
Exercise programmes are effective regardless of patient adherence
Poor compliance can limit the effectiveness of even a well-designed programme
questions.explanation: Patient compliance is a key factor influencing exercise prescription because even a well-designed programme will have limited effectiveness if the patient does not adhere to it, making individualisation essential. This factor is relevant across arthropathies, not limited to surgical patients. Recognising the role of compliance encourages therapists to consider patient preferences and barriers when designing programmes.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is asked why patient compliance should be considered before prescribing an exercise programme for an arthropathy. Which statement best explains this consideration?
Which enzyme system does allopurinol inhibit to reduce uric acid production?
questions.explanation: Allopurinol works by inhibiting xanthine oxidase, the enzyme responsible for converting purines into uric acid, thereby lowering serum urate levels over the long term. Cyclooxygenase is instead the target of NSAIDs, not urate-lowering agents. ACE and monoamine oxidase inhibition are unrelated to uric acid metabolism.

options: No walking aid under any circumstances
A walking aid to relieve pressure on the affected joint
Ankle weights to increase joint loading
Resistance bands around the affected foot
questions.question: Which walking aid recommendation is appropriate for a patient experiencing a gout flare of the first metatarsophalangeal joint?
questions.explanation: Using a walking aid during a gout flare helps relieve pressure on the affected joint, reducing pain during ambulation until the acute episode resolves. Increasing joint loading through ankle weights or resistance bands would worsen symptoms. Treadmill incline training is inappropriate during an acute painful flare.

questions.question: A physiotherapist recommends splinting for a patient with active rheumatoid arthritis of the wrist. What is the primary purpose of this intervention?
options: To permanently fuse the wrist joint
To completely replace the need for medication
To diminish pain and prevent deformity development
To increase range of motion beyond normal limits
To eliminate the need for any future physiotherapy
questions.explanation: Splinting in active rheumatoid arthritis aims to diminish pain and inflammation, prevent development of deformity, decrease joint stress, and support the joint during the acute period. It is not intended to fuse the joint permanently or replace medical treatment. It also does not aim to increase ROM beyond normal, as this could risk instability.

questions.question: Which position is recommended for measuring hip extension using a goniometer?
questions.explanation: Hip extension is measured with the patient side-lying and the knee flexed to 90 degrees, allowing the femur to move independently of the pelvis for accurate measurement. Supine positioning with hips flexed would not allow extension to be assessed. Standing or unsupported prone rotation would introduce compensatory pelvic movement, reducing measurement accuracy.
options: Side-lying with the knee flexed to 90 degrees
Supine with both hips fully flexed
Prone with the pelvis unsupported and rotated
Sitting with the hip flexed to 90 degrees

questions.explanation: The synovial membrane lines the joint capsule except where hyaline cartilage covers the articular surfaces, and it secretes synovial fluid to lubricate and nourish the joint. The periosteum instead covers the external bone shaft. The meniscus is an intra-articular fibrocartilage disc, not a membrane lining.
questions.question: Which structure lines the entire synovial joint capsule except for the areas covered by hyaline cartilage?

questions.explanation: Because viral arthritis typically resolves within about six weeks, physiotherapy treatment planning and patient education should reflect this expected short-term course rather than the chronic, lifelong management approach used in rheumatoid arthritis. It does not require disease-modifying therapy or joint replacement in typical cases. Physiotherapy can still play a role in symptomatic management during the self-limited course.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is treating a patient with viral arthritis affecting multiple joints symmetrically. Which practical distinction should guide the treatment timeline compared with rheumatoid arthritis?
options: Viral arthritis requires lifelong disease-modifying therapy
Viral arthritis always requires joint replacement surgery
Viral arthritis never responds to any physiotherapy input
Viral arthritis is expected to resolve within about six weeks
Viral arthritis requires identical long-term management to RA

questions.question: A physiotherapist working with a patient with mixed connective tissue disease notices signs of Raynaud's phenomenon during a cold clinic environment. What immediate practical adjustment should be made to the treatment session?
options: Open windows to increase cold air exposure
Ensure the treatment area is warm and encourage the patient to keep extremities covered
Apply ice packs directly to the fingers
Ignore the temperature of the treatment room entirely
Ask the patient to remove gloves and socks throughout
questions.explanation: Since cold exposure can trigger Raynaud's phenomenon in mixed connective tissue disease, ensuring a warm treatment environment and encouraging the patient to keep extremities covered is a simple, practical adjustment to reduce symptom triggering during the session. Increasing cold exposure or applying ice would directly provoke vasospasm. Removing protective clothing would similarly increase the risk of triggering symptoms.

Because reactive arthritis frequently involves enthesitis, such as Achilles tendonitis or pain at the patellar tendon insertion, specifically assessing for these features before beginning treatment ensures the exercise plan accounts for potentially painful and vulnerable tendon insertion sites. The other listed factors are administrative or preference-based and do not affect clinical assessment. Identifying enthesitis helps the physiotherapist select appropriately graded loading strategies.
options: The colour of the patient's exercise clothing
The patient's preferred time of day for appointments
The patient's favourite type of music
Presence of enthesitis such as Achilles tendonitis or heel pain
questions.question: A physiotherapist is developing an individualised exercise plan for a patient with newly diagnosed reactive arthritis affecting the knee and ankle. Which clinical feature should specifically be assessed before beginning treatment?

questions.explanation: Posture exercises emphasising upper back hyperextension, avoiding lumbar hyperextension, combined with range-of-motion exercises for the hips and knees, help prevent and address the excessive kyphosis and flexion contractures common in ankylosing spondylitis. Aggressive lumbar hyperextension is specifically avoided. Prolonged static postures would instead worsen these deformities.
options: Complete avoidance of any spinal extension exercise
Upper back hyperextension exercises and hip/knee ROM exercises
Prolonged static seated postures without breaks
questions.question: A patient with ankylosing spondylitis has significant thoracic kyphosis and hip flexion contractures. Which combination of exercises addresses these specific deformities?

questions.explanation: Pain occurring before resistance during passive movement suggests an acute injury, whereas pain occurring together with resistance suggests a sub-acute injury, and pain following resistance suggests a chronic injury. This sequence helps the therapist grade irritability and select an appropriate treatment intensity. Recognising an acute pattern guides the therapist toward gentler initial handling.
questions.question: During passive ROM assessment, a therapist notes pain occurring before any resistance is felt. According to the pain-resistance sequence, what type of injury does this suggest?
Which connective tissue disorder results from an autosomal dominant mutation in the fibrillin-1 (FBN1) gene?
questions.explanation: Marfan syndrome is inherited through an autosomal dominant mutation of the FBN1 gene encoding fibrillin-1, which affects the strength and elasticity of connective tissue microfibrils. This differs from the acquired autoimmune mechanisms of lupus, Sjögren's syndrome, and rheumatoid arthritis. Reactive arthritis is triggered by infection, not genetic mutation.

options: Passive positioning to prevent contractures only
questions.explanation: Coordination exercises are specifically included in the subacute phase of autoimmune encephalitis rehabilitation to address cerebellar involvement affecting balance and movement control. Chest physiotherapy and contracture-prevention positioning are relevant to the earlier acute phase, while community reintegration belongs to a later stage. Medication titration is a medical rather than physiotherapy intervention.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is treating a patient with cerebellar involvement following autoimmune encephalitis. Which intervention specifically targets this deficit during the subacute phase?
Which radiographic feature is NOT typically found in early osteoarthritis but may appear as the disease progresses?
questions.explanation: Subchondral bone cysts develop as osteoarthritis progresses, alongside joint space narrowing, osteophytes, and subchondral sclerosis, but are not typical of early-stage disease. Early OA may show a relatively preserved joint space. Absence of osteophytes and normal cartilage would be expected only in the earliest or pre-radiographic stage.

options: Complete surgical fusion as a routine first step
questions.question: Which type of physical therapy intervention is 'conditionally recommended' over passive modalities such as massage and ultrasound in the management of ankylosing spondylitis, according to current guidelines?
questions.explanation: Current guidelines conditionally recommend active physical therapy in the form of supervised exercise over passive interventions such as massage, ultrasound, and other thermal modalities for ankylosing spondylitis. Bed rest and passive-only treatment would not achieve the mobility and functional goals of AS management. Surgical fusion is reserved for specific complications, not routine first-line management.

Glucocorticoids, especially when injected intra-articularly, must not be given until joint infection is excluded because they can worsen an underlying septic process. This is a critical safety consideration when managing undifferentiated acute monoarthritis. The other listed options carry no comparable risk of worsening joint infection.
questions.question: Which drug class is specifically noted to worsen an existing joint infection if given before septic arthritis is excluded in an acute monoarthritis presentation?
A physiotherapist is planning a home exercise programme for a patient with ankylosing spondylitis. Which primary treatment goal should guide the programme design?
options: Achieving complete spinal fusion as quickly as possible
Increasing spinal mobility and correcting postural deformities
Eliminating the need for any medical follow-up
Maximising sedentary rest throughout the day
Avoiding all forms of physical activity
questions.explanation: Physical therapy goals in ankylosing spondylitis include alleviating pain, increasing spinal mobility, improving functional capacity, reducing morning stiffness, and correcting postural deformities. Encouraging fusion or promoting inactivity would work against these aims. Regular physical activity is instead strongly recommended to slow disease progression.

questions.question: Which breathing exercise focus is emphasised in ankylosing spondylitis physiotherapy management?
options: Abdominothoracic breathing to maintain rib cage excursion
Pursed-lip breathing to reduce oxygen saturation

questions.question: A physiotherapist compares active range of motion between a patient's affected and unaffected shoulder to grossly evaluate coordination and functional ability. Which type of ROM assessment does this best represent?
questions.explanation: Active range of motion assessment grossly evaluates coordination of movement and functional ability, since it requires the patient to generate the movement through voluntary muscle contraction. questions.explanation: Physiotherapy management of reactive arthritis includes core stabilisation exercises, cryoanalgesia, electroanalgesia, iontophoresis, soft tissue release, mobilisation techniques, muscle energy techniques, and functional retraining. questions.question: A physiotherapist palpates warmth over a patient's knee joint during examination. What does this finding most likely suggest?
questions.explanation: Warmth over a joint on palpation often indicates active inflammation, whereas coldness can instead indicate vascular compromise. Recognising warmth as a sign of inflammation helps guide clinical reasoning toward an inflammatory or infective differential.

questions.question: Which term describes joint pain localised to a single joint?
questions.explanation: Joint pain confined to a single joint is termed monoarthralgia, while involvement of two or three joints is oligoarthralgia, and four or more joints is polyarthralgia. questions.question: During passive shoulder flexion, a patient reports pain that stops the movement well before the normal anatomical end-range, with no resistance felt beforehand. What does this finding suggest?

Complete absence of rib cage movement would be an extreme and unusual finding, not the typical presentation.
questions.question: A patient with ankylosing spondylitis is assessed for chest expansion as part of a respiratory physiotherapy assessment. Which finding would be expected due to the disease process?
A physiotherapist recommends an elevated toilet seat and widened gripping handles for an elderly patient with hand and hip arthropathy. What is the primary aim of this intervention?
questions.explanation: Adaptive equipment such as elevated toilet seats and widened gripping handles is provided to facilitate activities of daily living, achieve joint protection, and support patient independence and self-efficiency. It does not cure the underlying disease or replace exercise therapy. It is intended to reduce, not increase, joint loading during daily tasks.
options: To permanently cure the underlying arthropathy
To facilitate activities of daily living and maintain independence
To replace the need for any exercise programme
To increase joint loading during daily tasks
To eliminate the need for any medical review

questions.question: A patient recovering from gonococcal arthritis of the wrist has been cleared for hydrotherapy. What is the primary benefit of this modality in the described physiotherapy plan?
questions.explanation: Hydrotherapy is listed among the physiotherapy treatments for gonococcal arthritis recovery, providing reduced joint loading that supports early rehabilitation exercise. It does not replace the need for completing prescribed antibiotic therapy. It serves a therapeutic exercise role rather than a diagnostic or preventive antimicrobial function.
options: It allows exercise with reduced joint loading during early rehabilitation
It replaces the need for any antibiotic completion
It is used only to measure joint temperature
It permanently prevents any future joint infection
It is used exclusively for diagnostic purposes
They have no analgesic properties whatsoever
They cause permanent joint destruction in all cases
They can mask or worsen the underlying viral disease
They immediately cure the viral infection
questions.explanation: Corticosteroids are generally avoided in viral arthritis because immunosuppression may mask symptoms or allow the underlying viral illness to worsen. NSAIDs and simple analgesics are preferred instead for symptomatic relief. This precaution does not apply to their general pharmacological properties.
questions.question: Why are corticosteroids generally avoided in the routine treatment of viral arthritis?

questions.explanation: During remission or intercritical periods, physiotherapists can focus on maintaining range of motion, strength, and function while helping the patient build a suitable long-term exercise routine. Complete cessation of exercise or bed rest would encourage deconditioning even during a quiet disease phase. Ongoing assessment and outcome tracking remain valuable to detect early signs of flare.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is developing a home exercise programme for a patient with early rheumatoid arthritis in remission. Which exercise focus best reflects appropriate management during this stable period?
options: Maintenance of ROM, strength, and general function
Complete cessation of all exercise since disease is inactive
Maximal contact sport participation with no precautions
Exclusive bed rest to conserve energy
Avoidance of any assessment or outcome tracking

questions.question: What is the normal range of ankle dorsiflexion according to standard goniometric measurement?
questions.explanation: Normal ankle dorsiflexion measures 0 to 20 degrees, typically assessed with the patient supine and the knee flexed 20 to 30 degrees and supported on a pillow. Plantarflexion has a larger normal range of 0 to 45 degrees. This distinction is important when interpreting restricted ankle mobility in a patient with an arthropathy.

Because ankylosing spondylitis can restrict costovertebral joint mobility and reduce rib cage excursion, abdominothoracic breathing exercises are taught to help maintain or increase chest expansion. This addresses restricted, not excessive, rib cage mobility. The exercises support functional respiratory capacity rather than address unconsciousness or absent muscle function.
options: Restricted rib cage and costovertebral joint excursion
Complete loss of consciousness during exercise
Excessive rib cage mobility beyond normal
Total absence of any respiratory muscle function
Overactive diaphragmatic movement with no restriction
questions.question: A physiotherapist teaches a patient with ankylosing spondylitis abdominothoracic breathing exercises. What specific physiological limitation is this intended to address?

questions.explanation: Combining objective goniometric ROM measurement with a relevant lower limb outcome measure provides a comprehensive, measurable picture of functional improvement following treatment for reactive arthritis affecting the knee and ankle. Relying on mood alone, personal opinion without measurement, blood pressure, or skin colour would not provide meaningful functional data. This combined objective approach supports evidence-based monitoring of treatment progress.
questions.question: A physiotherapist wants to objectively document improvement in a patient's functional mobility after a course of treatment for reactive arthritis affecting the knee and ankle. Which combination of assessment tools would provide the most complete picture?
options: The therapist's personal opinion without any measurement
The colour of the patient's skin alone
Goniometric ROM measurement combined with a relevant lower limb outcome measure

questions.explanation: Caution is necessary when applying heat or cold therapy in patients with sensorial deficits and impaired vascular circulation in the hands and feet, due to an increased risk of burns or tissue injury. Patients with normal sensation and circulation do not carry this heightened risk. Lifestyle factors such as diet and exercise habits are unrelated to this specific safety precaution.
questions.question: Which patient population requires particular caution when applying heat or cold therapy to the hands or feet due to burn risk?
options: Patients with normal sensation and intact circulation
Patients with sensory deficits and impaired vascular circulation

questions.question: What is the first-line CDC-recommended antibiotic regimen for disseminated gonococcal infection?
options: Ceftriaxone plus a single dose of azithromycin
questions.explanation: The CDC recommends ceftriaxone 1g given intramuscularly or intravenously every 24 hours plus a single oral dose of azithromycin for disseminated gonococcal infection. This dual regimen also covers possible coinfection with Chlamydia trachomatis. Fluoroquinolone monotherapy is no longer recommended due to resistance.

questions.question: A patient with hypermobile joints from an underlying connective tissue disorder is at increased risk of which type of joint problem, according to standard joint assessment principles?
questions.explanation: Hypermobile joints, with increased range of motion, are more susceptible to recurrent injury, sprains, early degenerative joint changes, and tendinitis resulting from muscular imbalance. This differs from hypomobile joints, which are instead more prone to muscular strains, overuse tendinitis, and nerve entrapment. Recognising this distinction guides appropriate joint protection advice for hypermobile patients.
options: Complete joint fusion with no mobility at all
Total absence of any injury risk
Recurrent sprains and early degenerative changes
Permanent loss of all joint sensation
Tying a shoelace, which requires only about 15 degrees
Walking on a flat, level surface
Combing the back of the head, which requires about 140 degrees
questions.question: A physiotherapist measuring elbow flexion notes the patient can only achieve 90 degrees actively but reaches 140 degrees passively. Which functional activity is likely to be impaired given standard functional ROM requirements?
questions.explanation: Reaching the back of the head to comb hair requires approximately 140 degrees of elbow flexion, so a patient limited to 90 degrees actively would struggle with this specific task despite adequate passive range. Tying a shoelace requires much less flexion, around 15 degrees, and would likely remain unaffected. Standing balance, walking, and swallowing are unrelated to elbow flexion range.

questions.question: A physiotherapist is treating a patient with confirmed calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease (pseudogout) of the wrist. Which joint is described as commonly affected alongside the wrist in this condition?
questions.explanation: Pseudogout commonly affects the knee, along with the wrist, elbow, and ankle, distinguishing its typical joint distribution from the classic first metatarsophalangeal joint predilection of gout. The temporomandibular, sacroiliac, and acromioclavicular joints are not the classic sites described for pseudogout. Recognising this joint pattern assists in clinical differentiation between the two crystal arthropathies.

questions.question: Mixed connective tissue disease (Sharp syndrome) is best described as a condition with features of which combination of diseases?
options: Ankylosing spondylitis and reactive arthritis only
questions.explanation: Mixed connective tissue disease presents with overlapping features of systemic lupus erythematosus, scleroderma, and polymyositis or dermatomyositis, and may also show features of Raynaud's phenomenon. This distinguishes it from purely crystal-induced or infective arthropathies. It is not a combination of osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis.

options: TENS cannot treat every painful joint simultaneously
TENS instantly cures all forms of arthritis
TENS must always be applied for 24 continuous hours
TENS is only effective in monoarticular disease and never polyarticular disease
TENS cannot be used on any joint in the body
questions.explanation: A recognised practical disadvantage of TENS is that it cannot be applied to every painful joint simultaneously, posing a challenge in patients with polyarticular involvement. It is a short-acting therapy lasting 6 to 24 hours rather than requiring continuous 24-hour application. TENS can be used on various joints, just not all of them at once.
questions.question: Before applying TENS as an analgesic modality for a patient with polyarticular arthropathy, what practical limitation should the physiotherapist consider?
Calcific tendinitis of the shoulder most commonly involves deposition of crystals in which structure?
questions.explanation: Calcific tendinitis most frequently affects the supraspinatus tendon due to calcium hydroxyapatite crystal deposition, often related to subacromial impingement. Other rotator cuff tendons can be involved but far less often. The labrum and acromioclavicular ligament are not the classic sites.

questions.question: Which outcome measure is specifically designed for assessing hip osteoarthritis-related dysfunction?
options: Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index for the shoulder
Disability of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand Index
Hip Dysfunction and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (HOOS)
questions.explanation: The HOOS is specifically validated for assessing hip dysfunction related to osteoarthritis, capturing pain, symptoms, and function relevant to the hip joint. The Roland Morris and Oswestry indices instead assess low back pain, while the Neck Disability and Northwick Park questionnaires target cervical spine dysfunction. DASH assesses upper limb disability, not the hip.

questions.question: A physiotherapist is measuring shoulder abduction using a goniometer. Where should the fulcrum be placed?
questions.explanation: For shoulder abduction and adduction, the goniometer fulcrum is placed close to the anterior aspect of the acromion, with the stationary arm aligned to the midline of the anterior sternum and the moving arm aligned with the humerus. The olecranon and radial styloid are instead used for elbow and forearm measurements. The medial malleolus and tibial tuberosity relate to ankle and knee measurements.
options: Close to the anterior aspect of the acromion

questions.explanation: Resting splints in active RA are designed to provide non-deforming, functional positioning of the involved joint, helping to diminish pain and prevent deformity while allowing appropriate rest. Forcing full flexion or excessive tightness could itself contribute to deformity or vascular compromise. Immobilising unaffected joints unnecessarily would not follow the principle of joint-specific protection.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is fitting a resting splint for a patient with actively inflamed MCP joints. What key principle should guide the splint's positioning?
options: The splint should force the joint into full flexion at all times
The splint should be applied only during vigorous exercise
The splint should be as tight as physically possible
The splint should immobilise the entire limb including unaffected joints
The splint should hold the joint in a non-deforming, functional position

questions.question: A child presents with an antalgic limp, hip held in flexion and external rotation, fever, and raised inflammatory markers. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Transient synovitis of the hip only
questions.explanation: Fever with markedly raised inflammatory markers and an irritable, guarded hip strongly suggests septic arthritis rather than the more benign transient synovitis. Prompt investigation and treatment are essential to prevent joint destruction. The other conditions typically lack the acute febrile, markedly elevated inflammatory picture.

questions.question: Which condition should be considered when antibiotic-responsive, culture-negative acute arthritis occurs in a sexually active young adult?
questions.explanation: Antibiotic-responsive, culture-negative acute arthritis in a sexually active young person is most often caused by disseminated gonococcal infection, since synovial cultures are frequently negative despite active infection. Osteoarthritis and DISH are degenerative rather than infective, and Marfan syndrome is a structural connective tissue disorder unrelated to arthritis of this type. Gout would typically show crystals rather than an antibiotic-responsive course.

Glucocorticoids, particularly intra-articular injections, must not be given until septic arthritis has been excluded because they can worsen an underlying joint infection. NSAIDs and colchicine are standard first-line options once infection is ruled out. Simple analgesics and cold therapy carry no such risk.
questions.question: During an acute gout flare, which class of drug is generally avoided until infection has been excluded?

questions.explanation: Rheumatoid arthritis can produce extra-articular pathological changes such as rheumatoid nodules, muscle atrophy, and fibrosis, contributing to progressive functional decline. Aortic root dilation is instead a hallmark of Marfan syndrome, and malar rash is characteristic of lupus. Chondrocalcinosis is associated with CPPD, not RA.
questions.question: Which extra-articular pathological change can occur in rheumatoid arthritis alongside joint involvement?
options: Aortic root dilation as the primary feature
Malar butterfly rash as the defining sign
Rheumatoid nodules with muscle atrophy and fibrosis

questions.question: A patient develops sudden polyarticular joint pain a week after a parvovirus B19 infection acquired from close contact with children. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Parvovirus B19 is a recognised cause of sudden-onset polyarticular viral arthritis, especially in adults frequently exposed to children. Viral arthritis is usually self-limiting, unlike the chronic autoimmune course of rheumatoid arthritis. Septic and gouty arthritis typically present as monoarthritis rather than symmetrical polyarthritis.

The assessment section of the SOAP format is where the examiner analyses and interprets the individual's status and prognosis following the objective evaluation, including setting long- and short-term goals. The subjective and objective sections instead record patient-reported and examiner-observed findings. The plan section outlines the treatment approach going forward.
questions.question: In the SOAP documentation format, which section includes the therapist's analysis of the patient's status and prognosis after examination?

questions.explanation: The pseudo-rheumatoid pattern of CPPD presents with symmetrical inflammation of the proximal interphalangeal and metacarpophalangeal joints, mimicking rheumatoid arthritis. This pattern occurs in about 5% of CPPD patients. The great toe pattern instead suggests gout rather than pseudogout.
questions.question: Which joint pattern is most characteristic of pseudo-rheumatoid presentation of CPPD?
options: Asymmetrical involvement of the great toe only
Symmetrical inflammation of PIP and MCP joints
Symmetrical involvement of the cervical facets only
High fever with marked systemic toxicity
Loss of hip flexion, abduction, and external rotation
Excessive spontaneous kicking of the affected leg
Painless full range of motion at the hip
questions.explanation: Neonates with septic hip arthritis classically show loss of the normal resting position of flexion, abduction, and external rotation, along with irritability and reluctance to feed. Fever may actually be absent in neonates, unlike in older children. Painless full ROM would be inconsistent with an infected joint.
questions.question: In a neonate with septic arthritis of the hip, which clinical sign is classically described?

options: The colour of the patient's clothing
The time of day the assessment occurs
The name of the referring physician
The specific end-feel quality assessed at the limit of passive range
questions.question: A physiotherapist is asked to identify which finding on passive shoulder ROM testing indicates a capsular pattern of restriction rather than a non-capsular pattern. What examination feature helps determine this?
questions.explanation: Determining whether a capsular or non-capsular pattern of movement restriction is present relies on assessing the specific end-feel quality at the limit of passive range of motion. Irrelevant factors such as shoe size, clothing colour, appointment time, or referral source have no bearing on this clinical determination. This end-feel assessment is a key component of passive ROM examination.

Comparing soft tissue between the affected and unaffected sides helps the physiotherapist detect localised atrophy or swelling, as well as differences in colour, texture, and temperature that may indicate pathology. This comparison is unrelated to assessing age, cardiac function, blood pressure, or vision. Bilateral comparison is a standard principle in musculoskeletal examination.
