questions.explanation: In neonates and infants with hip infection, the joint is positioned abducted and flexed at approximately 30 degrees on traction to prevent dislocation while managing the infection. Full extension and adduction would not provide this protective positioning. This specific positioning reflects the vulnerability of the immature hip joint during active infection.

questions.question: A patient with suspected inflammatory arthritis reports morning stiffness lasting over an hour with symmetrical hand swelling. Based on joint assessment principles, which additional finding would most support a rheumatoid rather than osteoarthritic process?
options: Bony hard end-feel with painless crepitus
Pain that only occurs with heavy mechanical loading
Boggy synovitis end-feel on palpation of the MCP joints
Normal inflammatory markers on blood testing
questions.explanation: A boggy end-feel on palpation reflects synovitis and soft tissue oedema, consistent with the active synovial inflammation seen in rheumatoid arthritis. A bony hard end-feel with brief stiffness and normal inflammatory markers would instead favour a degenerative process such as osteoarthritis. This physical examination finding helps corroborate the clinical suspicion raised by the history.

questions.question: Which type of autoimmune encephalitis is most strongly associated with ovarian teratomas in young women?
questions.explanation: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis is the most common type of autoimmune encephalitis and is frequently linked to ovarian teratomas in young women, presenting with behavioural change, psychosis, and seizures. Anti-LGI1 and anti-CASPR2 encephalitis instead typically affect older men and are less associated with tumours. Hashimoto's encephalopathy is linked to thyroid autoimmunity rather than tumours.

options: Passive range-of-motion exercise within pain limits
Use of splints for joint protection
Heavy resistance exercise causing joint stress
questions.question: Which of the following is a contraindication during the acute inflammatory period of rheumatoid arthritis management?
questions.explanation: Heavy resistance exercise that stresses inflamed joints is specifically contraindicated during the acute phase of rheumatoid arthritis, along with joint stretching that could worsen inflammation. Passive ROM within pain limits, splinting, education, and gentle massage are all appropriate. This distinction protects fragile, actively inflamed joint structures.

Pain that occurs after resistance is felt during passive range of motion testing suggests a chronic injury, whereas pain before resistance suggests an acute injury and pain occurring together with resistance suggests a sub-acute injury. This sequence provides useful information about tissue irritability and guides appropriate treatment intensity. Complete absence of pain or resistance would not fit any of these injury categories.
options: Pain occurring after resistance is felt during passive movement
Pain occurring before any resistance is felt
Complete absence of any pain or resistance
Pain occurring only with active movement, never passive
questions.question: A physiotherapist is asked to differentiate between an acute and chronic joint injury during assessment. Which finding is most consistent with a chronic injury based on the pain-resistance sequence?
Which synovial cell type is primarily responsible for phagocytosing debris within the joint cavity?
questions.explanation: Type A synoviocytes are macrophage-like cells derived from the monocyte lineage that remove debris from synovial fluid through phagocytosis. Type B synoviocytes instead synthesise extracellular matrix components such as hyaluronic acid. Chondrocytes, osteoclasts, and osteoblasts are found in cartilage and bone, not primarily within the synovial lining.

questions.question: A physiotherapist is asked to differentiate a 'firm' end-feel from a 'soft' end-feel during passive ROM assessment. Which statement correctly describes the firm end-feel?
questions.explanation: A firm end-feel has a springy, elastic quality resulting from stretching of the joint capsule, ligament, or muscle, such as normally felt at the limit of hip flexion with the knee extended. A soft end-feel instead results from soft tissue approximation, and a hard end-feel results from bone contacting bone. Complete absence of resistance or early pain-limited stopping represent different, abnormal findings rather than a normal firm end-feel.
options: A soft, mushy stop from tissue approximation
A springy, elastic resistance from stretching of the joint capsule or ligament
A hard, bony stop from bone contacting bone
Complete absence of any resistance whatsoever
Pain occurring well before resistance is reached

questions.question: Following medical treatment for septic arthritis, a physiotherapist notices the patient is reluctant to move the joint at all despite reduced pain. What educational focus is most appropriate at this stage?
questions.explanation: Patient education about properly protecting the joint while gradually reintroducing movement is emphasised once infection is well managed, since current evidence supports physiotherapy achieving maximum post-infection functioning. Complete avoidance of movement or permanent weight-bearing restriction would not support recovery of function. This reflects the described aim of restoring physiological joint function after infection resolves.
options: Insisting on immediate return to unrestricted heavy manual labour
Telling the patient that further movement is unnecessary permanently
Educating the patient on how to protect and gradually reintroduce movement to the joint
Avoiding any communication about the recovery process
Discouraging the patient from ever bearing weight again

questions.question: Which classic triad characterises the arthritis-dermatitis syndrome of disseminated gonococcal infection?
questions.explanation: The arthritis-dermatitis syndrome of disseminated gonococcal infection classically presents with dermatitis, tenosynovitis, and migratory polyarthritis. This is distinct from the conjunctivitis-urethritis-arthritis triad of reactive arthritis. Cardiac and ocular features are not part of this classic triad.

Organ meats, along with seafood such as anchovies and sardines, are extremely high in purines and are broken down into uric acid. Low-fat dairy has actually been associated with a reduced gout risk. Grains, vegetables, and citrus fruits are comparatively low in purines.
questions.question: Which of the following foods carries the highest purine load and should be limited in gout management?

questions.explanation: Allopurinol is a xanthine oxidase inhibitor that reduces uric acid production, whereas probenecid is a uricosuric agent that increases renal excretion of urate. Both are long-term urate-lowering strategies rather than acute analgesics. Neither drug treats infection directly.
options: Allopurinol increases urate production, probenecid reduces excretion
Both drugs act identically on xanthine oxidase
Allopurinol treats infection, probenecid treats inflammation
Both drugs are used only for acute flare pain relief
Allopurinol reduces urate production, probenecid increases urate excretion
questions.question: Which statement correctly differentiates the pharmacological target of allopurinol from that of probenecid in gout management?

questions.explanation: Disseminated gonococcal infection is the most common cause of infectious arthritis among sexually active, previously healthy young people. Skin lesions occur in about 75% of patients with bacteraemia. This differs from typical non-gonococcal septic arthritis, which favours the elderly and immunocompromised.
questions.question: Disseminated gonococcal infection most commonly causes septic arthritis in which population?
options: Sexually active, previously healthy young adults

questions.question: A young man presents with asymmetric oligoarthritis of the lower limbs, a swollen 'sausage' toe, and heel pain from enthesitis. Which diagnosis is most likely?
questions.explanation: Asymmetric lower-limb oligoarthritis with dactylitis (sausage digit) and enthesitis such as Achilles tendonitis or heel pain is characteristic of reactive arthritis. Gout more typically presents as monoarthritis with tophi in chronic disease. DISH and Marfan syndrome do not produce this inflammatory enthesitic pattern.

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: frostbite (ice burn/snow burn) - a thermal burn caused by exposure of the skin to cold for an extended period, typically below -0.55°C (31°F); can also be caused iatrogenically by applying ice or cold packs directly against the skin.
(ii) Pathophysiology: leads to ice crystal formation - water in the cells of the skin and underlying tissue freezes and crystallizes, causing direct cellular injury; indirect injury occurs when tissues become ischaemic; the extremities (fingers, toes, ears, nose, lips) are most likely affected, and if frostbite penetrates deeper skin layers, impacting tissue and bone, it can cause permanent damage.
(iii) Acute assessment/management: assess severity and depth of tissue involvement; rewarming must be gradual; prevention includes protective clothing against prolonged exposure to freezing temperatures, snow, or high-velocity winds.
(iv) Rehabilitation plan: severe cases may require or lead to amputation; where tissue is salvageable, general burn rehabilitation principles apply - maintaining joint ROM, splinting/positioning as needed, and monitoring for further tissue damage progression.
questions.question:
A patient presents after prolonged exposure of the fingers to extreme cold (below -0.55°C/31°F), with tissue changes affecting the digits.
(i) State the diagnosis/classification.
(ii) Explain the pathophysiology.
(iii) Outline the acute assessment and management.
(iv) Outline the definitive/long-term rehabilitation plan.

A 4-year-old child is brought in after a domestic accident in which hot water spilled onto the anterior trunk and thigh. The wound is bright pink/red, wet, with blisters present, and is very painful to touch.
(i) State the diagnosis/classification of this burn.
(ii) Explain the pathophysiological basis of the injury using the relevant burn wound model.
(iii) Outline the acute assessment and physiotherapy management.
(iv) Outline the definitive/long-term rehabilitation plan.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: a superficial partial-thickness (second-degree A) burn - epidermis and part of the dermis (papillary dermis) affected; caused by a scald, a thermal burn from a hot liquid; domestic accidents involving hot water are a major cause, seen more commonly in children.
(ii) Pathophysiology (Jackson's burn wound model): the wound has a zone of coagulation (irreversible cell death), a zone of stasis (reversible if capillary flow is restored), and a zone of hyperaemia (recovers well); fluid slips between epidermal layers to form blisters, and blanching (capillary refill) is present.
(iii) Acute assessment/management: estimate total burn surface area (rule of nines/rule of palms); perform the blanch test (refill should be 3 seconds or less); initiate fluid resuscitation guidelines if TBSA exceeds 20% using the Parkland formula. Physiotherapy: clear airways, position to prevent contractures, elevate to reduce oedema, gentle active ROM, hydrotherapy for wound cleansing, and splinting in an anti-deformity position; manage pain.
(iv) Rehabilitation plan: progress from active to passive ROM and static stretching with goniometry; apply pressure garments once the wound is closed and stable to reduce scar thickness and prevent hypertrophic scarring; scar massage and desensitization; chest/breathing exercises; functional re-integration using tools such as the FIM; education and distraction techniques; monitor for hypertrophic scarring since burns over 30% TBSA are prone to scarring.

(i) Diagnosis: a chronic wound - one that fails to heal within a typical timeframe (4-12 weeks) despite appropriate treatment, with disruption occurring mainly in the inflammatory and proliferative phases.
(ii) PT intervention: high-voltage pulsed current (HVPC) electrical stimulation.
(iii) Assessment findings/protocol: indicated for Stage II-IV pressure ulcers, diabetic ulcers, and venous leg ulcers; protocol is 30-60 minutes per day, 5-7 days per week; polarity is negative (cathode) initially to attract neutrophils, then switched to positive (anode) to promote epithelialization.
(iv) Precautions/contraindications: malignancy near the wound site, active bleeding, untreated osteomyelitis, pacemakers (for electrical modalities), pregnancy (caution over the abdomen/pelvis), and sensory impairments requiring close monitoring.
(v) Prevention: intensity is kept at a comfortable sensory level with no muscle contraction, and treatment is integrated with standard wound care under the TIME principle with individualized patient assessment.
questions.question:
A patient with a chronic, non-healing diabetic pressure ulcer is referred for physical agent therapy.
(i) State the diagnosis.
(ii) Name the physiotherapy intervention indicated.
(iii) State the assessment findings/protocol guiding its use.
(iv) State the precautions/contraindications.
(v) State how complications are prevented.

An elderly patient with a history of intermittent claudication develops a painful ulcer on the toes.
(i) State the risk factors for this ulcer.
(ii) State the possible complications.
(iii) Outline the physiotherapy management options, and justify the use of one.
questions.answerText:
(i) Risk factors: chronic arterial insufficiency associated with arteriosclerosis obliterans, atheroembolism, and a history of minor nonhealing trauma.
(ii) Complications: pain is often severe with intermittent claudication progressing to pain at rest; skin changes include trophic changes (thin, shiny, atrophic skin) and loss of hair on the foot and toes with thickened nails; gangrene (black, gangrenous skin adjacent to the ulcer) can develop.
(iii) PT management options: the initial workup should include ABI measurement and palpation of pulses; wound management otherwise follows the TIME principle, except that tissue debridement is applied in all cases except arterial ulcers. Justification: aggressive debridement or compression is avoided in this case because, given the compromised arterial blood supply, tissue debridement is specifically excluded from the TIME framework for arterial ulcers, and blood flow must first be assessed before other physical interventions are applied.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the zone of coagulation.
A(ii) Describe the zone of stasis (ischaemia).
A(iii) Describe the zone of hyperaemia.
B(i) Explain the clinical basis for why the zone of stasis is the critical focus of burn wound care.
B(ii) Distinguish between the zone of stasis and the zone of hyperaemia.
questions.answerText:
A(i) The zone of coagulation is the central area of a burn injury and has experienced the greatest tissue damage; it is characterised by complete destruction of the capillaries leading to cell death, and is irreversible because there is no capillary refill.
A(ii) The zone of stasis (or zone of ischaemia) is the area adjacent to the zone of coagulation, where there is slowing of circulating blood due to the damage; it corresponds to areas of deep partial-thickness burns or burns of indeterminate depth.
This zone can usually be saved with correct wound care, but its capillaries are often compromised by oedema due to hypovolemia and/or vasoconstrictive mediators responding to the injury, so it is reversible only if capillary flow can be restored.
A(iii) The zone of hyperaemia is located around the edge of the zone of stasis and is characterised by superficial and superficial partial-thickness burns with a robust capillary refill.
It represents an area of increased circulation caused by vasodilators such as histamine released in response to the burn injury, and this tissue will completely recover without intervention unless complications such as severe sepsis or prolonged hypoperfusion occur.
B(i) Clinically, the zone of stasis is the critical focus of burn wound care because, unlike the zone of coagulation which is already irreversibly dead, or the zone of hyperaemia which recovers well regardless, the zone of stasis can go either way.
With correct wound care and restoration of capillary flow it can be saved, but if oedema and vasoconstriction are allowed to persist, it can progress to further tissue death, effectively extending the zone of coagulation.
This is why early, correct wound care and fluid management are prioritized in acute burn management, since they directly determine how much of the zone of stasis survives.
B(ii) Distinguishing the two zones: the zone of stasis lies adjacent to the zone of coagulation and shows slowed circulation from capillary compromise due to oedema and vasoconstrictive mediators, corresponding to deep partial-thickness or indeterminate-depth burns.
The zone of hyperaemia lies further out, at the edge of the injury, and shows a robust capillary refill from vasodilators such as histamine, corresponding to superficial and superficial partial-thickness burns.
The zone of stasis is reversible only if capillary flow is actively restored, whereas the zone of hyperaemia has a good recovery rate and will heal on its own unless complications develop.
This difference in prognosis is why the zone of stasis, rather than the zone of hyperaemia, is the zone that clinical intervention aims to rescue.

questions.question:
A patient with diabetes presents with a plantar foot ulcer and reduced sensation in the foot.
(i) State the risk factors for this ulcer.
(ii) State the possible complications.
(iii) Outline the physiotherapy management options, and justify the use of one.
questions.answerText:
(i) Risk factors: diabetic foot ulcers are caused by a combination of underlying neuropathy, peripheral arterial disease, and structural deformities that cause increased pressure on affected areas of the foot; diabetes is associated with arterial disease and peripheral neuropathy, and repetitive trauma occurs on insensitive skin.
(ii) Complications: diabetic ulcers are the most common cause of lower extremity amputation; early intervention is essential given the high mortality rate after amputation; sepsis is common and gangrene may develop, with absent ankle jerks reflecting the neuropathy.
(iii) PT management options: wound management following the TIME principle (tissue debridement, infection control, moisture balance, edges); electrical stimulation, indicated for diabetic ulcers; patient education on daily foot inspection. Justification: electrical stimulation is justified because it is supported by strong evidence for pressure/diabetic ulcer healing, promoting fibroblast activity and angiogenesis that lead to epithelial migration and wound closure.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the hemostasis phase of wound healing.
A(ii) Describe the inflammatory phase.
A(iii) Describe the proliferative phase.
A(iv) Describe the maturation/remodeling phase.
B(i) Explain the clinical basis for why delayed healing can lead to a chronic wound.
B(ii) Distinguish between an acute wound and a chronic wound.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Hemostasis (immediate, lasting minutes to about 2 hours): goal is to stop bleeding through vasoconstriction, platelet aggregation, and clot/fibrin-mesh formation; key cells are platelets.
A(ii) Inflammation (about 0-4/1-5 days): goal is to remove pathogens and debris; vasodilation causes redness and swelling, neutrophils and macrophages clean the wound, and cytokines/growth factors are released; signs include pain, heat and oedema.
A(iii) Proliferation (about 4-21 days): goal is to rebuild tissue; fibroblasts produce Type III collagen forming granulation tissue, angiogenesis restores blood supply, and epithelial cells close the wound; key cells are fibroblasts, endothelial cells and keratinocytes.
A(iv) Maturation/Remodeling (21 days to up to 2 years): goal is to strengthen and reorganize tissue; Type III collagen is replaced by stronger Type I collagen, and wound tensile strength improves but never reaches 100% of the original.
B(i) Clinically, aggressive physical therapy should be avoided during inflammation, gentle mobilization is supported during proliferation, and scar management, stretching and strength training are appropriate during maturation.
Delays caused by factors such as diabetes, infection, or poor nutrition can prevent a wound from progressing normally and can lead to a chronic wound.
In a chronic wound, the disruption to the normal, timely healing sequence occurs mainly in the inflammatory and proliferative phases.
This disruption shows as alterations in protease activity, changes in cytokine profile and inflammatory response, changes in cellular profile and activity, and changes in the composition of the extracellular matrix.
It also involves the presence of free radicals and nitric oxide, accumulation of necrotic tissue and slough, presence of microorganisms, and disease-specific pathological change.
B(ii) An acute wound follows a predictable and timely healing process, typically resolving within weeks to a few months, as seen with a surgical incision that heals without complication.
A chronic wound, by contrast, fails to progress through the normal stages of healing in a timely manner and often persists for months or years.
Chronic wounds are frequently linked to underlying conditions such as diabetes or poor circulation, infection, or repeated trauma, as seen in pressure ulcers, diabetic foot ulcers, and venous leg ulcers.

(i) Diagnosis: full-thickness (third-degree) burn requiring skin grafting - epidermis, dermis and other underlying tissues destroyed; presents as black, white or yellow eschar; the skin is dead, so no analgesic is needed, and escharotomy/debridement may be required.
(ii) PT intervention: post-grafting positioning/splinting with a monitored, delayed mobilization protocol.
(iii) Assessment findings/landmarks: before starting an intervention, note whether the graft/flap has adhered ("taken") to the recipient site; a period of 5-7 days is allowed for this before movement of the grafted area is encouraged.
(iv) Precautions/structures at risk: movement of the grafted area is not encouraged during this adherence period; skin grafts fail or do not "take" if there is wound infection, shear stress, or inadequate blood supply to the wound bed.
(v) Prevention: the graft should be stable and placed over bleeding, healthy tissue to ensure adequate vascularity; the area should be immobilized in an anti-deformity position to prevent shearing forces; exercise is discontinued for 3-5 days postgrafting to allow the graft to heal, and pressure garments are applied once the wound is closed and stable to prevent hypertrophic scarring or keloid formation.

A patient with a darker skin tone develops a raised, itchy scar that extends beyond the boundaries of a healed wound on the shoulder.
(i) State the risk factors for this presentation.
(ii) State the possible complications.
(iii) Outline the physiotherapy management options, and justify the use of one.
questions.answerText:
(i) Risk factors: genetic/family history predisposition to keloids; darker skin tones (Fitzpatrick IV-VI are more prone to keloids); high-tension/high-movement areas such as the shoulders; larger or deeper wounds; infection delaying healing; poor wound care; younger age (thicker scars from robust collagen production).
(ii) Complications: contractures limiting joint ROM; adhesions binding the scar to underlying tissue and restricting movement; neuropathic pain or hyperesthesia; itching or tenderness; psychological distress or low self-esteem from visible scarring.
(iii) PT management options: circular frictional massage to break adhesions/improve pliability/reduce sensitivity; stretching and mobilization to prevent contractures; soft tissue techniques (myofascial release); ultrasound to promote collagen realignment; low-level laser therapy to reduce inflammation/scar thickness. Justification: massage is justified here because it directly breaks down adhesions, improves pliability, and reduces sensitivity of the keloid, addressing both the itching and the restricted movement described in this presentation.

questions.question:
A stroke survivor with right hemiplegia and left-sided neglect is found to have redness over the sacrum and the heel of the affected limb.
(i) Identify the likely finding and its significance.
(ii) State the affected structures and functional limitations contributing to this presentation.
(iii) State the differential consideration for assessment.
(iv) Give the clinical reasoning for treatment priorities.
questions.answerText:
(i) Identification: early pressure ulcer risk/skin change over the sacrum and heel; the heel of the paretic limb may remain compressed against the mattress without the patient noticing.
(ii) Affected structures/functional limitations: hemiplegia/hemiparesis weakness limits repositioning and independent mobility; sensory impairment prevents perceiving pressure on the affected side; neglect (in right hemisphere strokes) causes ignoring of one side of the body; cognitive impairment reduces compliance with pressure-relief strategies; dysphagia and malnutrition delay tissue repair.
(iii) Differential consideration: distinguish simple erythema/Stage 1 pressure injury from deeper tissue injury by its non-blanchable nature and persistence.
(iv) Clinical reasoning: prioritize early mobilization, frequent repositioning, bed and chair positioning, ROM exercises, and sitting balance training; always inspect the heel of the paretic limb specifically, as it may remain compressed against the mattress unnoticed.

(i) Diagnosis: herpetic whitlow.
(ii) Predisposing factors: HIV infection; nail-biting habit; wounded finger with exposed skin surface; a career in the healthcare profession.
(iii) Pathophysiology: caused by the Herpes Simplex Virus (type 1 or 2); occurs when wounded and exposed skin comes into contact with body fluids contaminated with HSV; may also be caused by bacterial fingertip infection.
(iv) Management: not much research has been done on physiotherapy and whitlow; management includes topical analgesic to reduce pain and itching, antiviral medications, analgesics to reduce pain and fever, and electrotherapy; the disease is self-limiting and usually resolves within two to three weeks.

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis/risk: risk of claw hand (intrinsic minus position) deformity following a dorsal hand burn.
(ii) PT intervention: a resting hand splint positioned in the intrinsic plus position.
(iii) Assessment findings/landmarks: the common deformity of the hand after burn is claw hand (intrinsic minus position); splinting should stress wrist extension (15°), MP flexion (70°), PIP and DIP extension, and thumb abduction (the intrinsic plus position).
(iv) Precautions/structures at risk: graft/flap adherence should be checked before mobilizing, since a period of 5-7 days is allowed for the graft to "take"; movement of the grafted area is not encouraged during this period; watch for shear stress or inadequate blood supply, which can cause graft failure.
(v) Prevention: combine splinting with progression from active to passive ROM and static stretching with goniometry, apply pressure garments once the wound is closed and stable, and use scar massage to minimize hypertrophic scarring and contracture.

A(i) Describe the structure and growth cycle of hair.
A(ii) Describe the structure of nails.
A(iii) Describe the sebaceous glands.
A(iv) Describe the sudoriferous (sweat) glands.
B(i) Explain the clinical basis of hirsutism and of hair-color change in severe malnutrition.
B(ii) Distinguish between eccrine and apocrine sweat glands.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Hair: a modified epidermal structure and organ of sensation and protection, made up of the shaft (visible portion), root (within the follicle), hair follicle, hair papilla (contains blood vessels nourishing growth), and the arrector pili muscle (produces "goose bumps") with an associated hair root plexus for touch sensation.
Hair grows in cycles: anagen (growth phase, 3-7 years), catagen (transitional phase, 2-4 months), and telogen (resting phase, 3-4 months); disorders include hirsutism (excessive hair growth in women in a male pattern) and alopecia (hair loss).
A(ii) Nails: made of plates of tightly packed, hard, keratinized epidermal cells, with a nail body, free edge, nail root, lunula and cuticle; nails grow about 1 mm per week.
A(iii) Sebaceous glands: oil glands connected to hair follicles that secrete sebum, which prevents excessive water loss, keeps skin soft, coats hair, and inhibits some bacterial growth.
A(iv) Sudoriferous (sweat) glands: there are 3-4 million of them, of two types - eccrine and apocrine sweat glands.
Eccrine sweat glands secrete cooling sweat directly onto the skin, help regulate body temperature and aid waste removal, and contain water, ions, urea and uric acid.
Apocrine sweat glands are stimulated by stress, secrete into the hair follicles of the axilla and groin, begin functioning at puberty, and produce a slightly more viscous secretion containing the same components as eccrine sweat plus lipids and proteins.
B(i) Clinically, hirsutism is typically the result of excessive male hormone (androgen) levels in a woman, producing hair growth in a male pattern.
Severe malnutrition, particularly severe protein deficiency (as in Kwashiorkor), can cause naturally dark brown or black hair to turn red or blonde.
This occurs alongside bloating of the belly and body, which is itself a sign of severe malnutrition.
B(ii) Distinguishing the two sweat gland types: eccrine glands are widely distributed over the body, open directly onto the skin surface, and function mainly in cooling and temperature regulation.
Apocrine glands, in contrast, are restricted to the axilla and groin, open into hair follicles rather than directly onto the skin, only become active at puberty, are triggered by emotional stress rather than temperature, and produce a more viscous secretion because it additionally contains lipids and proteins.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the epidermis.
A(ii) Describe the dermis.
A(iii) Describe the subcutaneous layer (hypodermis).
A(iv) State the functions of the integumentary system.
B(i) Explain the clinical basis for why the palms, soles and fingertips differ in epidermal structure from the rest of the body.
B(ii) Distinguish between the epidermis and the dermis.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Epidermis: superficial, thinner, epithelial tissue; keratinized stratified squamous epithelium.
Has 4 key cells - keratinocytes (~90%), melanocytes (~8%), Langerhans cells, Merkel cells; avascular, nourished by diffusion from the dermis.
Arranged in strata: basale, spinosum, granulosum, corneum in thin skin; lucidum also present in thick skin (palms/soles).
A(ii) Dermis: deeper, thicker connective tissue with collagen and elastic fibers; highly vascular.
Two layers - papillary (areolar tissue, dermal papillae) and reticular (dense irregular connective tissue).
A(iii) Subcutaneous layer (hypodermis): deep to the dermis, not part of the skin; areolar and adipose tissue; attaches skin to underlying structures.
A(iv) Functions: body temperature regulation (sweat release; altering blood flow through dermal vessels).
Protection (keratin resists abrasion/heat/microbes; fats resist water loss; melanin protects against UV; acidic sweat slows bacterial growth); sensation (touch, pressure, vibration, temperature, pain).
Excretion (water, fatty substances, ions); absorption (fat-soluble vitamins A, E, K and hormones); synthesis of vitamin D.
B(i) Clinical basis: fingertips, palms and soles are exposed to greater friction and have five epidermal strata (thick skin) including the stratum lucidum, versus four strata elsewhere (thin skin).
Constant friction on these areas can cause a callus - an abnormal thickening of the stratum corneum.
B(ii) Distinguish: the epidermis is the superficial, avascular epithelial layer nourished by diffusion; the dermis is the deeper, vascular connective-tissue layer containing collagen/elastic fibers, vessels and nerves; the two are joined by the basement membrane.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe open wounds and their types.
A(ii) Describe closed wounds and their types.
A(iii) Describe the classification of wounds by duration.
B(i) Explain the clinical basis for why puncture wounds are considered dangerous.
B(ii) Distinguish between a laceration and an incision.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Open wounds involve a break in the skin or mucous membrane exposing underlying tissue and include abrasions (superficial scrapes from friction, involving epidermis and sometimes superficial dermis, e.g. a skinned knee), lacerations (irregular, jagged tearing wounds of variable depth), punctures (created by a sharp, pointed object, small externally but potentially deep), incisions (clean, straight cuts from a sharp-edged object), and avulsions (a portion of tissue forcibly torn away, as in a degloving injury).
A(ii) Closed wounds do not involve a break in the skin, with the injury occurring beneath the surface, and include contusions (bruises from blunt trauma damaging capillaries and causing discoloration that changes from red/purple to blue, green and yellow) and hematomas (a more severe, significant collection of blood forming a palpable lump).
A(iii) By duration, acute wounds follow a predictable and timely healing process, typically resolving within weeks to a few months, such as a surgical incision that heals without complication.
Chronic wounds fail to progress through the normal stages of healing in a timely manner, often persisting for months or years, as seen in pressure ulcers, diabetic foot ulcers and venous leg ulcers, usually because of underlying medical conditions, infection or repeated trauma.
B(i) Clinically, puncture wounds are particularly dangerous because their deceptive appearance means the external wound may look small while the depth is considerable, creating a risk of internal organ damage and deep tissue infection such as tetanus.
This is why an apparently minor injury, such as stepping on a nail or being pricked by a needle, still requires careful assessment.
B(ii) A laceration is an irregular, jagged wound caused by tearing or crushing forces, typically with uneven edges and variable depth that can involve muscle, tendon or even bone, such as from a fall onto a sharp, uneven object or a machinery accident.
An incision, by contrast, is a clean, straight cut caused by a sharp-edged object such as a surgical scalpel or a knife.
Incisions have well-defined edges and bleed freely due to the clean severance of blood vessels, whereas lacerations have uneven, torn edges.
Surgical incisions are a controlled, precise form of this wound type designed for planned access to underlying structures.
An accidental cut from a kitchen knife is also an example of an incision, while a deep, irregular wound from an arm caught in machinery is an example of a laceration.
The clean edges of an incision typically heal faster and with less scarring than the irregular, more traumatized edges of a laceration.

A Physiotherapy's overall approach to laser therapy uses the unique properties of monochromaticity, coherence and collimation that allow non-invasive skin penetration, applied via either the grid method (treatment area divided into 1cm squares, probe in light contact) or the scanning method (probe held 5-10mm from the skin without contact).
Laser therapy is used therapeutically for wound healing, removal of scar tissue, pain relief, fracture healing/bone remodelling, and healing of connective tissues, working through primary (photon absorption), secondary (amplified metabolic/cellular) and tertiary (systemic) effects.
B(i) Wavelength choice depends on the lasing medium and depth of the lesion: visible red laser is used for superficial conditions like wounds and ulcers, infrared laser for deeper muscle and bone conditions, and cluster probes for larger areas of soft tissue.
Dosage (energy density) must be matched to the tissue: doses such as 4-5 J/cm² have been shown to stimulate fibroblast/mitochondrial activity and wound closure, whereas a dose of around 10 J/cm² was associated with cellular and molecular damage, so too low a dose is negligible and too high a dose is biosuppressive.
Frequency of treatment also depends on wound type: acute wounds are treated daily while chronic wounds are treated only 1-2 times a week, and infected wounds are treated with the probe held close in non-contact mode and cleaned between uses to reduce contamination.
B(ii) Complications of inappropriate laser parameters include a biosuppressive or inhibitory effect from excessive dosing, and photosensitivity reactions in patients on certain medications, who should be patch-tested before full treatment.
Laser must not be applied directly to the eyes (risk of eye damage), over cancerous growths (risk of accelerating growth/metastasis), or directly over a pregnant uterus (risk of abnormal growth).
C(i) A distant or systemic effect of laser therapy is the tertiary effect, in which treatment of one lesion can stimulate the healing of both the directly treated lesion and other lesions the patient may have, through cytokine- and growth-factor-mediated communication between cells.
This systemic effect also includes activation of T-lymphocytes, macrophages and mast cells, increasing the overall immune response.
C(ii) Functionally, laser therapy contributes to pain relief, improved absorption of interstitial fluid (anti-oedematous effect), increased lymphatic circulation and drainage, and better tissue regeneration.
It also improves local and systemic blood circulation and can restore normal pigment in abnormally coloured cutaneous lesions.
This shows why correct parameter selection determines whether laser therapy produces these beneficial local and systemic effects or instead causes tissue damage or harm.

B(i) State how laser parameters relate to treatment choice.
B(ii) State the complications of inappropriate laser use.

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: psoriasis (plaque psoriasis), the most prevalent type, accounting for 80-90% of cases.
(ii) Predisposing/precipitating factors: hereditary etiological factors and association with immune disorders and certain drugs; precipitating factors include trauma, infection, pregnancy and endocrine changes, cold weather, smoking, anxiety and stress.
(iii) Pathophysiology: psoriasis is a chronic, non-infectious inflammatory disease in which epidermal cells are produced about six to nine times faster than normal; the cells in the basal layer divide too quickly and the newly formed cells move so rapidly to the skin surface that they become evident as profuse scales or plaques.
(iv) PT management: phototherapy using ultraviolet light mimics sunlight exposure to trigger biologic processes that reduce inflammation and prevent skin cells from growing too fast; long-wave UV light can be combined with oral photosensitizing drugs (psoralens); ultrasound can also be used, since it treats conditions with an increased tendency to new tissue formation.
questions.question:
A patient presents with raised, red plaques covered with silvery-white scales on the elbows, knees and scalp, with itching and pitting of the nails.

A(i) Describe the Wallace Rule of Nines.
A(ii) Describe the Rule of Palms.
A(iii) Describe the Lund and Browder scale.
B(i) Explain the clinical basis for why accurate TBSA estimation matters.
B(ii) Distinguish between the Rule of Nines and the Lund-Browder scale.
questions.answerText:
A(i) The Wallace Rule of Nines divides the adult body surface into 13 areas for estimating burn size: head and neck 9%, anterior trunk 18%, posterior trunk 18%, each upper limb 9%, each lower limb 18%, and the perineum 1%.
A(ii) The Rule of Palms uses the surface of the patient's own palm, which represents approximately 1% of body surface area, and is particularly helpful for estimating the area of small or scattered burns.
A(iii) The Lund and Browder scale is commonly used for infants and children and uses different percentages from the adult rule because the surface area of the head and neck relative to the limbs is typically larger in children.
In this scale, a child under one year has 9% redistributed from the lower extremities to the head and neck region, and 1% is returned to the lower extremities for each year of life until age nine, when the head is considered proportionally the same as an adult's.
B(i) Clinically, accurate TBSA estimation matters because it directly affects prognosis: percentage chance of survival is calculated as 100 minus the sum of age in years and percentage TBSA.
TBSA also determines fluid resuscitation needs; this is initiated when TBSA is greater than 20% and guided by the Parkland formula, using 4 mL of lactated Ringer's solution per kilogram of body weight per percentage TBSA in adults (half in the first 8 hours, the rest over the next 16 hours) and 3 mL/kg/%TBSA in paediatric patients.
TBSA and depth together also determine burn severity classification: critical burns involve 10% or more third-degree and 30% or more second-degree burns, moderate burns less than 10% third-degree and 15-30% second-degree, and minor burns less than 2% third-degree and 15% second-degree.
B(ii) Distinguishing the two main methods: the Rule of Nines allows only a gross approximation of the percentage of body area burned and does not account for age-related differences in body proportion, and its percentages are intended for adult patients.
The Lund and Browder chart is more accurate, particularly for infants and children, because it adjusts the percentage assigned to the head/neck and lower extremities according to the child's age.
This is necessary because a young child's head and neck make up a proportionally larger share of total body surface area than an adult's, a difference the Rule of Nines does not capture.
As the child grows, the Lund-Browder chart gradually shifts percentage back to the lower extremities until, by age nine, the head is considered to have the same proportion as in an adult.
Using the age-appropriate method is therefore essential for guiding fluid resuscitation and prognosis correctly.

(i) Diagnosis: venous ulcer (venous stasis ulcer) - the most common type of chronic wound, typically shallow, located on the medial supramalleolar aspect of the lower extremity.
(ii) Predisposing factors: chronic venous insufficiency; valvular incompetence; history of deep venous thrombosis (DVT); venous hypertension.
(iii) Pathophysiology: venous hypertension due to incompetent veins or venous obstruction distends the superficial veins, causing wall damage, exudation of fluid into the interstitial space, and oedema of venous insufficiency.
(iv) PT management: compression therapy (wraps, stockings, or compression pump) to facilitate movement of excess fluid from the lower extremity; leg elevation and exercise (ankle pumps); appropriate wound dressings and electrotherapeutic modalities as part of general wound care; oedema management.
questions.question:
A patient presents with a wet lower-leg wound near the medial malleolus, with large amounts of exudate, surrounding hyperpigmentation, and aching pain relieved by leg elevation.
(i) State the diagnosis.
(ii) State the predisposing factors.
(iii) Explain the pathophysiology.
(iv) State the physiotherapy management.

Two patients present with lower-leg ulcers. Patient A has an irregular, dark-pigmented, wet wound near the medial malleolus with palpable pedal pulses and pain relieved by leg elevation. Patient B has an irregular, smooth-edged, dry wound on the toes with absent pedal pulses, cool skin, hair loss, and severe pain relieved only by dependency.
(i) Identify the likely skin/vascular condition in each patient.
(ii) State the affected structures and functional limitations in each case.
(iii) State the key differential features between the two conditions.
(iv) Give the clinical reasoning for treatment priorities in each.
questions.answerText:
(i) Patient A shows features of a venous ulcer (venous insufficiency with dark pigmentation, oedema, stasis dermatitis); Patient B shows features of an arterial ulcer (arterial insufficiency with trophic, ischaemic skin changes).
(ii) Patient A: superficial veins and valves are incompetent, causing oedema and skin thickening that can limit ankle mobility. Patient B: arterioles/capillaries are compromised, causing intermittent claudication progressing to pain at rest, which limits walking distance.
(iii) Differential features: aetiology - venous (valvular incompetence, venous hypertension) vs arterial (arteriosclerosis obliterans, atheroembolism); pulses - usually present in venous, decreased/absent in arterial; pain - little/aching in venous (worse dependent), painful/severe in arterial (worse on elevation, eased by dependency); drainage - moderate/large in venous, minimal in arterial; gangrene - may be present in arterial, absent in venous; skin changes - pigmentation/stasis dermatitis in venous, pallor on elevation and dusky rubor on dependency with trophic changes in arterial.
(iv) Clinical reasoning: for the venous ulcer, prioritize compression therapy and leg elevation since these address venous hypertension; for the arterial ulcer, the initial workup should include ABI measurement and palpation of pulses, and aggressive compression is avoided because blood flow must first be assessed given the compromised arterial supply.

questions.question:
A(i) State the aetiology of psoriasis.
A(ii) Explain the pathophysiology.
A(iii) Describe the clinical features and types.
A(iv) State how psoriasis is assessed.
B(i) State the physiotherapy techniques used.
B(ii) State the precautions to be observed.
B(iii) State the indications for phototherapy.
C(i) Explain the basis of functional loss if psoriasis is left untreated.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Aetiology: psoriasis has hereditary etiological factors and is associated with immune disorders and certain drugs; precipitating factors include trauma, infection, pregnancy and endocrine changes, cold weather, smoking, anxiety and stress.
A(ii) Pathophysiology: psoriasis is a chronic, non-infectious inflammatory disease in which epidermal cells are produced about six to nine times faster than normal; basal layer cells divide too quickly and the newly formed cells move rapidly to the surface, becoming evident as profuse scales or plaques.
A(iii) Clinical features: common presentations include red spots, dry, swollen and inflamed patches covered with silvery-white flakes, raised and thickened skin, pain, itching and burning, restricted joint motion, cracked and bleeding skin, dandruff, pus-filled blisters, genital lesions in males, and pitting of the nails.
Types include plaque psoriasis (raised red patches with silvery scales on elbows, knees, scalp and lower back), guttate psoriasis (small red drop-shaped spots, often after strep infection), inverse psoriasis (smooth red patches in skin folds), pustular psoriasis (pus-filled bumps), and erythrodermic psoriasis (severe, widespread redness and shedding).
A(iv) Assessment: psoriasis commonly affects the scalp, ears, elbows, knees, umbilicus and nails, follows a variable course of exacerbations and remissions, and may be associated with psoriatic arthritis and joint pain, particularly of the small distal joints.
B(i) PT techniques: phototherapy using ultraviolet light mimics sunlight exposure to trigger biologic processes that reduce inflammation and slow abnormal skin cell growth; long-wave UV light may be combined with oral photosensitizing drugs (psoralens); ultrasound can also be used because of the tendency toward new tissue formation in psoriasis.
B(ii) Precautions: psoriasis follows a variable, relapsing-remitting course that should be monitored, and there is no cure, so management is aimed at symptom control rather than resolution.
B(iii) Indications: phototherapy is indicated for the treatment of psoriasis and is also used for vitiligo, eczema, mycosis fungoides and acne vulgaris.
C(i) If untreated, psoriasis may be associated with the development of psoriatic arthritis and joint pain, particularly affecting the small distal joints.
This joint involvement can restrict joint motion, adding a musculoskeletal functional deficit to the skin condition.
The chronic, relapsing itching and pain from dry, cracked lesions can also affect a person's daily comfort and activity.
This combination of skin and joint involvement underlines why psoriasis needs ongoing, individualized management rather than a single course of treatment.

A(i) Aetiology: dermatitis/eczema can be allergic or contact (from poison ivy, harsh soaps, chemicals, adhesive tape), actinic (photosensitivity/reaction to sunlight or ultraviolet light), or atopic (etiology unknown, associated with allergic, hereditary or psychological disorders); atopic dermatitis often begins in early childhood, runs in families, and forms part of the "atopic triad" with asthma and allergic rhinitis.
A(ii) Pathophysiology: inflammation causes itching, redness and skin lesions; in atopic eczema, genetic defects such as filaggrin gene mutations weaken the skin barrier, allowing allergens and microbes to enter and trigger an exaggerated immune response.
The resulting inflammation causes itching, which leads to scratching and further skin damage, and microbial colonization such as Staphylococcus aureus worsens the inflammation in a self-perpetuating cycle.
A(iii) Clinical features/stages: the acute stage shows a red, oozing, crusting rash with extensive erosions, exudate and pruritic vesicles; the subacute stage shows erythematous, scaling skin with scattered plaques; the chronic stage shows thickened skin from scratching, fibrotic papules and nodules, and postinflammatory pigmentation changes, and the course can be relapsing.
A(iv) Assessment: identifying which stage (acute, subacute or chronic) the presentation is in, and noting any precautions or contraindications for physical therapy modalities.
B(i) PT techniques: physical therapy can improve the appearance of the skin, reduce itching and inflammation, and speed healing, using methods such as phototherapy (ultraviolet light), iontophoresis (electrical current to drive ionized anti-inflammatory or analgesic drugs through the skin), ultrasound, and laser therapy.
B(ii) Precautions: some physical therapy modalities should be avoided or used cautiously, and use of alcohol should be avoided; medical management is aimed at the inflammation using topical or systemic therapy.
B(iii) Indications: phototherapy is indicated for eczema as well as psoriasis, vitiligo, mycosis fungoides and acne vulgaris; iontophoresis is indicated for inflammatory skin lesions and contact dermatitis.
C(i) If untreated, the chronic stage of eczema leads to thickened skin (lichenification) and increased skin marking from repeated scratching.
Fibrotic papules and nodules and postinflammatory pigmentation changes can also develop, and the condition can follow a relapsing course.
Daily care with hydration and lubrication of the skin is therefore emphasized to help prevent this progression to chronic, thickened, pigmented skin changes.
This underlines why an accurate stage-based assessment guides both medical and physiotherapy management.
questions.question:
A(i) State the aetiology of dermatitis/eczema.
A(ii) Explain the pathophysiology.
A(iii) Describe the clinical features/stages.
A(iv) State how it is assessed.
B(i) State the physiotherapy techniques used.
B(ii) State the precautions to be observed.
B(iii) State the indications for phototherapy/iontophoresis.
C(i) Explain the basis of chronic skin damage if eczema is left untreated.

A(i) State the aetiology of skin cancer.
A(ii) Explain the pathophysiology of the main types.
A(iii) Describe the clinical features.
A(iv) State how skin cancer is assessed.
B(i) State the precautions to be observed.
C(i) Explain the basis of functional/systemic loss if skin cancer is left untreated.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Aetiology: skin cancers develop due to DNA damage, often from ultraviolet radiation from the sun or tanning beds, which triggers mutations leading to rapid, uncontrolled skin cell multiplication; risk factors include excessive sun or tanning-bed exposure, fair skin that burns easily, a family or personal history of skin cancer, a weakened immune system, older age, and the presence of many or atypical moles.
A(ii) Pathophysiology: basal cell carcinoma develops in the basal cells of the lower epidermis, grows slowly and rarely spreads but can damage surrounding tissue; squamous cell carcinoma arises from squamous cells in the outer skin layer and is more likely than basal cell carcinoma to spread if untreated; melanoma begins in the melanocytes and is fast-growing and more likely to spread to other organs.
A(iii) Clinical features: basal cell carcinoma appears as a pearly or waxy bump, a flat scar-like area, or a sore that bleeds and does not heal; squamous cell carcinoma appears as a scaly red patch, open sore, or wart-like growth with poorly defined margins; melanoma may develop in an existing mole or as a new dark spot.
A(iv) Assessment: diagnosis is made by skin examination and biopsy; suspicious pigmented lesions are examined using the ABCDE rule - Asymmetry (uneven edges), Border irregularity (poorly defined, notching), Color variation (especially mixtures of black, blue or red), Diameter greater than 6mm, and Elevation (usually raised, but may be flat).
Lesions showing new swelling, redness, scaling, oozing or bleeding are considered suspicious and should be assessed further.
B(i) Precautions: laser acts as a photobiostimulatory agent, so its use should be avoided directly over an area of known or suspected cancerous growth, because this exposure can accelerate tumor growth and metastasis.
This precaution applies broadly to physical agents that stimulate cellular activity, since promoting tissue growth in a malignant lesion would be harmful rather than beneficial.
C(i) If untreated, suspicious lesions should be referred to a dermatologist for evaluation and biopsy, because prognosis depends on the extent of invasion.
Untreated squamous cell carcinoma is more likely than basal cell carcinoma to metastasize, and untreated melanoma is fast-growing and more likely to spread to other organs.
Early detection is therefore critical for survival, underscoring why any suspicious skin lesion warrants prompt medical evaluation rather than being treated with stimulating physical modalities.

A(i) Surgical debridement removes non-viable and necrotic tissue but causes considerable trauma and excessive bleeding and is non-selective in what it removes.
A(ii) Mechanical debridement is a non-selective method that includes wound irrigation, whirlpool, scraping with a scalpel/curette edge (recommended for infected wounds), and wet-to-dry dressings, where moistened gauze is removed once dry, pulling away devitalized tissue but also some healthy granulation tissue; it can be painful.
A(iii) Autolytic debridement is a natural, selective process in which the body's own phagocytic cells and proteolytic enzymes break down necrotic tissue; it is recommended for non-infected wounds, is contraindicated in immunocompromised patients, and is facilitated by dressings such as hydrocolloids, hydrogel or medical-grade honey.
A(iv) Biological (larval/maggot) debridement uses sterile fly larvae applied directly to the wound; the larvae release proteolytic enzymes that dissolve necrotic tissue, ingest bacteria, and release ammonia that raises wound pH to inhibit bacterial growth; it is painless, selective, rapid, and can reach areas difficult to access by other methods.
A(v) Enzymatic debridement uses topical proteolytic or collagenolytic enzyme preparations to promote liquefaction of necrotic tissue and is indicated for moist necrotic wounds or eschar after cross-hatching, but is contraindicated in ischaemic wounds of undetermined vascular status or dry gangrene.
A(vi) Sharp debridement uses sterile instruments (scalpel, scissors, forceps, silver nitrate stick) to sequentially remove only necrotic tissue with little or no bleeding of viable tissue, and is indicated for scoring or excising leathery eschar, but is contraindicated in clean wounds or in patients on anticoagulant therapy.
B(i) Clinically, the selective methods (autolytic, enzymatic, biological, sharp) are chosen when only necrotic tissue should be removed or when the patient cannot tolerate more aggressive methods, whereas the non-selective methods (mechanical, surgical) are used when a large amount of necrotic tissue needs rapid removal, accepting some risk to healthy tissue.
This is why, for example, autolytic debridement is preferred for a clean but slow-healing wound, while surgical debridement is reserved for advancing cellulitis or sepsis threatening the individual's life.
B(ii) Autolytic debridement is a selective method that relies on the body's own endogenous phagocytic cells and proteolytic enzymes, working under an occlusive or semi-occlusive moisture-retentive dressing, and only affects necrotic tissue.
Mechanical debridement, by contrast, is a non-selective method that uses external physical forces such as wound irrigation, whirlpool, or wet-to-dry gauze dressings.
Because mechanical debridement is non-selective, the loosened devitalized tissue removed with a wet-to-dry dressing can also carry away adherent healthy granulation tissue, making it more painful and less discriminating than autolytic debridement.
Autolytic debridement is therefore reserved for non-infected wounds in medically stable individuals, while mechanical debridement suits a larger amount of moist necrotic tissue or foreign material.

questions.answerText:
A The overall physiotherapy approach to burn rehabilitation has the aims of clearing the airways, maintaining joint range of motion, maintaining soft tissue length, maintaining muscle strength, regaining maximum function, minimizing scarring, and helping the patient gain independence and return to their lifestyle.
The means used include splinting (static/dynamic) and positioning to prevent contractures, elevation, strengthening exercises, active progressing to passive range-of-motion exercises and static stretching with goniometry, pressure garments, chest or breathing exercises, scar massage with desensitization, education and distraction techniques, and functional re-integration measured with tools such as the Functional Independence Measure.
B(i) Treatment choice is guided by burn degree: first-degree burns heal in 3-5 days without scarring and need minimal intervention.
Superficial partial-thickness (second-degree) burns heal in 10-14 days typically without scarring or grafting, while deep partial-thickness burns heal in 14-21 days or longer and scar if the burn exceeds 30% TBSA, sometimes requiring surgical closure.
Full-thickness (third-degree) burns require skin grafting and carry a risk of scarring and contractures, while subdermal (fourth-degree) burns require excision, possible amputation, and cause significant functional impairment.
B(ii) Common complications of burn injury include hypovolemic shock, infection, gastrointestinal problems such as Curling's ulcer and liver damage, cardiopulmonary/inhalation injury (ARDS, pneumonia, atelectasis), vascular complications such as DVT, and psychiatric manifestations.
Further complications include deformities and contractures, hypertrophic scarring, keloid formation, compartmental syndrome, and multi-system organ dysfunction including acute kidney injury.
C(i) A major distant/systemic problem is burn shock, a medical emergency in which body tissues and organs are deprived of adequate oxygenated blood.
Burn shock results from fluid loss and oedema formation, accompanied by loss of protein and electrolyte imbalance, which triggers release of inflammatory substances such as histamines, cytokines and prostaglandins, leading to renal failure, sepsis, pulmonary problems, and Curling's ulcer.
C(ii) The functional deficit from unmanaged burns includes deformities and contractures affecting joints distant from the original burn site if anti-deformity positioning is not maintained.
Hypertrophic scarring and keloid formation can further restrict movement and affect appearance long after the acute injury has resolved.
This shows why burn rehabilitation must address both the immediate systemic risks and the longer-term functional and cosmetic consequences.

A patient presents with an itchy, red, scaly rash between the toes, with peeling and cracked skin and a bad odor.
(i) State the diagnosis.
(ii) State the predisposing factors.
(iii) Explain the pathophysiology.
(iv) State the management, including any physiotherapy relevance.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: athlete's foot (tinea pedis).
(ii) Predisposing factors: warm, moist environments (sweaty feet, tight shoes) promote fungal growth; transmission is person-to-person or animal-to-person.
(iii) Pathophysiology: a fungal infection of the feet, especially between the toes, caused by dermatophytes, most commonly Trichophyton rubrum; fungal spores invade the keratinized tissue of the skin, and dermatophytes digest keratin, causing inflammation and scaling.
(iv) Management: treated with antifungal creams; standard precautions should be observed since it can spread to other parts of the body or to surfaces like showers and floors; if untreated it can progress to bacterial infections and cellulitis.

(i) Diagnosis: electrical burn - an injury caused by heat produced when an electrical current passes through the body; typically presents with an entrance and an exit wound.
(ii) Pathophysiology: severity depends on the pathway of the current, the resistance of the current in the tissues, and the strength and duration of the flow; damage may be deeper than what is visible and can affect muscles and organs; electricians and illegal electrical connections are noted occupational causes.
(iii) Acute assessment/management: monitor for complications such as hypovolemic shock, infection, cardiopulmonary/inhalation injury, vascular complications (e.g. DVT), and compartmental syndrome. Physiotherapy: clear airways, positioning and splinting in anti-deformity positions, elevation to decrease oedema, and gentle ROM once medically stable; monitor for eschar formation, which may require escharotomy if circumferential and causing impaired circulation.
(iv) Rehabilitation plan: as with other burns - progress active to passive ROM and static stretching with goniometry, strengthening exercises, pressure garments once wound closed/stable, scar massage/desensitization, chest/breathing exercises, and functional re-integration; the goal is to return the individual to society with unaltered appearance, abilities and potentials while minimizing scarring.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Aetiology: burns are caused by heat, electricity, chemicals, friction or radiation, arising from fire, cold, scald, chemical, electrical, frictional, inhalation or irradiation exposure.
A(ii) Pathophysiology (Jackson's burn wound model): zone of coagulation - irreversible complete capillary destruction and cell death; zone of stasis/ischaemia - reversible with correct wound care, compromised by oedema; zone of hyperaemia - increased circulation from vasodilators, recovers well.
A(iii) Clinical features: first-degree burns are pink/red, dry, painful, blanch, and heal in 3-5 days with no scarring.
Second-degree superficial partial-thickness burns are bright pink/red, wet with blisters, painful, blanch, and heal in 10-14 days without scarring; deep partial-thickness burns are red/waxy white, wet, have variable sensation and diminished blanching, and heal in 14-21+ days with scarring if burns exceed 30% TBSA.
Third-degree (full-thickness) burns are white/red/tan, dry and leathery with reduced sensation and absent blanching, needing skin grafting; fourth-degree (subdermal) burns are black and charred with absent sensation and blanching, needing excision or amputation.
A(iv) Assessment: total burn surface area is estimated using the Wallace rule of nines, the rule of palms, or the Lund and Browder scale (for infants/children); the blanch test checks capillary refill (should be 3 seconds or less); percentage survival chance = 100 - (age in years + percentage TBSA).
B(i) PT techniques: splinting (static/dynamic) and positioning in anti-deformity positions, elevation, active progressing to passive ROM and static stretching with goniometry, strengthening exercises, pressure garments, chest/breathing exercises, scar massage/desensitization, education and distraction, functional re-integration.
B(ii) Precautions: before starting intervention, check whether a graft/flap has adhered ("taken") to the recipient site; a period of 5-7 days is allowed for this before movement of the grafted area is encouraged, to avoid disrupting circulation.
Graft failure can occur from wound infection, shear stress, or inadequate blood supply to the wound bed, so shearing forces must be avoided.
B(iii) Indications: the goals are to return the individual to society with unaltered appearance, abilities and potentials, increase functional mobility, prevent pulmonary complications, decrease oedema, and initiate proper positioning.
C(i) If untreated, burns lead to deformities and contractures as complications, alongside hypertrophic scarring and keloid formation.
Typical untreated deformities include shoulder adduction/internal rotation, elbow flexion/pronation, claw hand, hip flexion/adduction, knee flexion, and ankle plantarflexion, arising from lack of anti-deformity positioning and stretching.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Aetiology: scar tissue is fibrous tissue that replaces normal skin or connective tissue after injury, surgery or trauma, forming through hemostasis, inflammation, proliferation and remodeling.
Intrinsic factors influencing scar formation include age (younger skin heals faster but may form thicker scars), genetics/family history of keloids, and skin type (darker Fitzpatrick IV-VI skin is more prone to keloids); extrinsic factors include larger/deeper wounds, infection, high-tension or high-movement locations, and poor wound care.
A(ii) Pathophysiology: scar tissue is composed primarily of collagen and is less elastic than normal tissue; scarring occurs mainly in the dermis, where fibroblasts first produce Type III collagen (granulation tissue) which is later replaced by stronger Type I collagen during remodeling, leaving a flatter, paler but less flexible scar.
A(iii) Clinical features/types: normal scars are flat and pale; hypertrophic scars are raised, red and confined to the wound borders; keloid scars are raised, extend beyond the wound borders and are often itchy or painful; atrophic scars are sunken/pitted; contracture scars are tight and restrict movement, often after burns.
A(iv) Assessment: visual inspection of color, texture and size; palpation for scar mobility, adhesions and tenderness; functional assessment of ROM by goniometry and impact on ADLs; the Vancouver Scar Scale scores pigmentation, vascularity, pliability and height, alongside patient-reported pain scales such as the VAS.
B(i) PT techniques: circular frictional massage to break adhesions, improve pliability and reduce sensitivity; gentle stretching and mobilization to prevent contractures (e.g. passive knee flexion for post-surgical scars); myofascial release for adhesions between scar and deeper tissue; ultrasound to promote collagen realignment; low-level laser therapy to reduce inflammation and scar thickness.
B(ii) Precautions: contractures require aggressive stretching while keloids need pain management, and hypertrophic scars that restrict joint mobility require targeted interventions matched to the specific scar type.
B(iii) Indications: early, evidence-based physiotherapy is indicated to prevent complications and optimize recovery, with interventions tailored to the scar type and patient needs.
C(i) If untreated, contractures limit joint range of motion, such as elbow flexion contracture following a burn.
Adhesions can also bind the scar to underlying tissues, further restricting movement.
Neuropathic pain, hyperesthesia and itching or tenderness (especially with keloids) may persist and add to functional loss.
Visible, unmanaged scars may also cause psychological distress and low self-esteem, compounding the overall functional and emotional impact.

A Physiotherapy's overall approach to chronic wounds uses physical agents whose goals are to promote wound healing, improve local circulation, control infection, reduce pain and inflammation, maintain a moist wound environment, and facilitate debridement and tissue regeneration.
Common physical agents used include electrical stimulation, low-frequency ultrasound, pulsed electromagnetic field therapy, and low-level laser therapy, often combined with massage and integrated with standard wound care under a multidisciplinary team.
B(i) Venous ulcers, the most common chronic wound type, are typically shallow and located on the medial supramalleolar area and are managed with the general TIME principle plus compression/elevation.
Arterial ulcers are typically located on distal extremities and may be deep with tendon or bone exposed; initial workup includes ABI measurement and pulse palpation, and tissue debridement is not applied to arterial ulcers within the TIME framework.
Diabetic foot ulcers, caused by neuropathy, peripheral arterial disease and structural deformity causing increased pressure, are the most common cause of lower extremity amputation and need early intervention.
Pressure ulcers, usually over a bony prominence, are staged using the National Pressure Ulcer Advisory Panel classification, and treatment (debridement, dressing, pressure relief) is matched to the stage.
All chronic wounds are treated according to the TIME principle: tissue debridement (in all cases except arterial ulcers), infection control, moisture balance, and attention to the edges of the wound.
B(ii) Common complications across chronic wound types include infection, cellulitis, delayed healing, gangrene (in arterial disease), and sepsis in advanced cases.
C(i) A distant or systemic problem that can arise from a chronic, non-healing wound is malignant transformation into a Marjolin's ulcer, listed among the complications of wounds.
Diabetic foot ulcers left untreated can also progress to a systemic threat through infection spreading.
They are also the leading cause of lower-extremity amputation, which carries a high mortality rate.
C(ii) The functional deficit from an unresolved chronic wound can therefore include loss of a limb through amputation, with major impact on mobility and independence, showing why individualized assessment and correct classification are critical before selecting physical agents.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Aetiology: herpetic whitlow is caused by the Herpes Simplex Virus (type 1 or 2) when wounded, exposed skin contacts HSV-contaminated body fluids, or by bacterial fingertip infection; risk factors include HIV infection, a nail-biting habit, a wounded finger, and a career in healthcare.
Boils are most often caused by Staphylococcus aureus bacteria, which many healthy people carry on their skin or in their nose, entering through a scrape, cut or splinter that breaks the skin; a carbuncle forms when several boils join together beneath the skin and lies deeper, taking longer to heal.
A(ii) Pathophysiology: herpetic whitlow is a self-limiting viral disease of the thumb and fingertips (rarely the toes/nail cuticle), of which the herpetic type is more prevalent than the melanotic type; a boil begins as a red lump that fills with pus as white blood cells fight the infection.
A(iii) Clinical features: whitlow presents locally with tingling, itchy feeling, burning sensation, blisters, redness, warmth or swelling, and systemically with fever, lymphangitis, blisters/sores elsewhere, and enlarged lymph nodes, with high fever and confusion suggesting serious progression.
Boils are pea- to golf-ball-sized with swelling, redness, pain, a white or yellow center or tip, and weeping, oozing or crusting, sometimes with general ill health, fatigue or fever.
A(iv) Differential diagnosis: whitlow must be distinguished from paronychia (a localized bacterial abscess in the nail fold) and bacterial felon (a digital pulp abscess), while a boil must be distinguished from folliculitis (an earlier, less deep and less painful inflammation of the hair follicle).
B(i) PT techniques: little research exists specifically on physiotherapy for whitlow, though electrotherapy has been used; for carbuncles, physiotherapy focuses on heat therapy to encourage drainage, ultrasound to reduce inflammation, manual therapy to enhance local circulation, and education on proper skin hygiene, always as an adjunct to medical care.
B(ii) Precautions: a boil or carbuncle should never be squeezed or pricked, as this can spread the infection; professional medical drainage (incision and drainage) or antibiotics are usually still required.
B(iii) Indications: heat therapy is indicated to ease discomfort from swelling and pressure and to encourage drainage, manual techniques to enhance blood flow and promote faster healing, and post-incision physiotherapy to assist with scar management and improving skin mobility.
C(i) If untreated, whitlow can lead to scarring, numbness, recurrent infection, spread of infection, skin ulceration, pain and discomfort, and rarely encephalitis, meningitis or tenosynovitis.
If a boil-related skin infection spreads or fails to improve after two to three days of antibiotics, a resistant infection such as MRSA should be suspected.
Recurrent boils may also require additional treatment aimed at reducing staphylococcal bacteria throughout the body.

(i) Diagnosis/risk: burn scar contracture of the shoulder from an axillary burn.
(ii) PT intervention: splinting (static/dynamic), specifically an airplane splint, with positioning in abduction, flexion and external rotation.
(iii) Assessment findings/landmarks: the common deformity at the shoulder after burn is adduction and internal rotation; therefore ROM and goniometry should be monitored to detect early loss of abduction/external rotation; graft/flap adherence should also be checked before mobilizing.
(iv) Precautions/structures at risk: a graft or flap must be allowed 5-7 days to "take" before movement is encouraged; movement of the grafted area during this period is not encouraged; graft failure can occur from wound infection, shear stress, or inadequate blood supply to the wound bed.
(v) Prevention: use pressure garments once the wound is closed and stable to reduce scar thickness and prevent hypertrophic scarring; maintain the anti-deformity (airplane splint) position; progress active to passive ROM and stretching with goniometry to monitor and prevent progression of the deformity.

An elderly, bedridden and incontinent patient with reduced sensation develops non-blanchable redness over the sacrum after prolonged immobility.
(i) State the risk factors for this condition.
(ii) State the possible complications if this progresses untreated.
(iii) Outline the physiotherapy management options, and justify the use of one.
questions.answerText:
(i) Risk factors: immobility; incontinence (skin becomes vulnerable with extended exposure to urine/stool); lack of sensory perception (cannot feel pressure/discomfort or the need to change position); poor nutrition and hydration; medical conditions affecting blood flow (e.g. diabetes, vascular disease); age over 70.
(ii) Complications: infection (cellulitis, osteomyelitis); delayed healing; pain; sepsis in advanced cases.
(iii) PT management options: pressure relief strategies (repositioning every 2 hours); pressure-relieving devices (air mattresses, cushions); patient and caregiver education; functional training to improve mobility; ROM exercises to prevent contractures; electrical stimulation in some cases to promote healing. Justification: repositioning every 2 hours is prioritized because pressure ulcers result from constant pressure sufficient to impair local blood flow for an extended period; regular repositioning interrupts this sustained pressure before tissue ischaemia and necrosis can develop.

A The overall approach to wound dressing selection is to create and maintain a moist wound environment, remove non-viable tissue, control infection, promote granulation and epithelialization, manage exudate effectively, protect the peri-wound skin, and promote patient comfort and mobility.
Wound cleaning itself aims to reduce microbial load and remove debris, using solutions such as normal saline (preferred), sterile water, or antiseptics only when infection is suspected, and the dressing choice is guided by wound depth/size, exudate level, infection status, tissue type in the wound bed, and the need for protection or debridement.
B(i) Hydrocolloid dressings are used for partial-thickness wounds with mild exudate and support autolytic debridement of necrosis or slough.
Hydrogels are used for dry wounds with necrotic tissue, transparent films for superficial wounds needing visual monitoring and autolysis, and foam dressings for moderate to heavy exudate.
Alginates are used for heavily exuding wounds because they can absorb large amounts of drainage and fill dead space, gauze dressings provide basic, inexpensive coverage, and antimicrobial dressings such as silver are used for infected wounds.
B(ii) Choosing the wrong dressing category can cause complications: hydrocolloids may leave a characteristic odor and yellow exudate on removal, hydrogels can macerate surrounding skin or promote growth of pseudomonas or yeast, and gauze used improperly can be painful to remove and delay healing.
In general, dressings that do not adequately balance moisture or control bacterial load can worsen exudate, channeling, or infection risk instead of promoting healing.
C(i) If wound infection is not controlled through correct dressing selection and the TIME principle, it can progress to a distant or systemic problem.
Complications of unmanaged wounds include wound infection progressing to systemic infection, chronic non-healing wounds and ulcers, and the development of sepsis.
C(ii) Poor dressing choice and unresolved infection therefore delay wound closure, prolonging the associated pain, immobility, and functional deficit for the patient.
This can also mean a prolonged period before interventions such as exercise or positioning can be safely progressed.
Matching the dressing category correctly to the wound's exudate level, infection status and tissue type is therefore essential to prevent this progression from local wound to systemic complication.
