questions.answerText:
(i) Identification: post-burn pruritus (itching sensations on or around the burn, graft, or donor site), affecting up to 93% of individuals by the day of discharge, alongside a developing scar that could be hypertrophic (raised, red, remains within wound boundaries) or keloid (extends beyond boundaries, more common in darker skin/younger women).
(ii) Affected structures/functional limitations: pruritus can cause distress, affect quality of life, and patients may traumatize the wound by scratching, delaying healing; hypertrophic/keloid scarring can restrict joint ROM and cause functional impairment via contractures.
(iii) Differential consideration: a hypertrophic scar stays within the boundaries of the original wound and is characteristically red, raised and firm, whereas a keloid scar extends beyond the boundaries of the original wound, is also red, raised and firm, and is more common in young women and those with dark skin.
(iv) Clinical reasoning: manage pruritus first, since current treatments have not shown clinically significant benefit but options include pressure therapy, massage therapy, moisturisers, and cold compresses in the subacute phase; prioritize pressure garment therapy since it addresses both oedema and scar management, reducing scar thickness by encouraging reorientation of collagen fibers into a uniform parallel pattern instead of the whorled pattern seen in untreated/hypertrophic scars.

questions.answerText:
A Overall PT approach to pressure ulcers includes pressure relief strategies such as repositioning every 2 hours, use of pressure-relieving devices (static devices like foam/water/gel/air mattresses; dynamic devices such as alternating-pressure or low-air-loss surfaces).
It also includes patient and caregiver education, functional training to improve mobility, range of motion exercises to prevent contractures, and electrical stimulation in some cases to promote healing.
B(i) Stage 1 (non-blanchable erythema, epidermis only, skin intact) is managed mainly with pressure relief and repositioning.
Stage 2 (partial-thickness skin loss, shallow open wound or blister) requires continued pressure relief plus appropriate wound dressings.
Stage 3 (full-thickness skin loss extending into subcutaneous tissue, may expose fat) requires debridement and more advanced dressings in addition to pressure relief.
Stage 4 (full-thickness loss with exposed muscle, tendon or bone) requires more extensive wound care and often surgical input; unstageable ulcers (obscured by slough/eschar) require debridement before staging and treatment can be finalized.
B(ii) Common complications across stages include infection (cellulitis, osteomyelitis), delayed healing, pain, and sepsis in advanced cases.
C(i) A distant or systemic problem that can result is sepsis, which is a serious, potentially life-threatening complication of an infected pressure ulcer.
Osteomyelitis (bone infection) can also occur when deep ulcers extend to exposed bone, representing spread of infection beyond the local wound.
C(ii) Functional deficits include contractures from prolonged immobility and poor positioning, and prolonged hospitalization due to slow, complicated healing.
Pain associated with pressure ulcers can also limit mobility, further compounding functional loss.
Overall, without proper staging-based treatment and prevention, pressure ulcers can progress from a mild, reversible skin change to a life-threatening systemic infection with lasting functional impairment.

questions.answerText:
(i) Identification: Stage 1 pressure ulcer - intact skin with non-blanchable erythema, affecting the epidermis only; a Stage 1 redness over the ischial tuberosity in a paraplegic patient should be treated as an urgent warning sign.
(ii) Affected structures/functional limitations: SCI patients have loss of sensation (cannot feel pressure, pain, heat or tissue damage), paralysis that prevents spontaneous repositioning, muscle atrophy of the gluteal and thigh muscles that reduces natural cushioning over bony prominences, autonomic dysfunction that can impair skin health, and prolonged wheelchair sitting that sustains pressure on the ischial tuberosities, sacrum and greater trochanters.
(iii) Differential consideration: deep tissue pressure injury (persistent non-blanchable deep red, maroon, or purple discoloration) must be distinguished from a simple Stage 1 ulcer (non-blanchable erythema with intact skin only).
(iv) Clinical reasoning: prioritize pressure relief every 15-30 minutes, wheelchair cushion assessment, daily skin inspection education, transfer training, and upper-limb strengthening, because the combined loss of sensation and paralysis removes the natural protective repositioning behaviors that would otherwise prevent tissue breakdown.

A. Describe the overall physiotherapy approach to scar management, including multidisciplinary collaboration.
B(i) State how scar type relates to treatment choice.
B(ii) State the common complications across scar types.
C(i) Explain how scarring can lead to a problem extending beyond the local tissue.
C(ii) State the resulting functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
A Physiotherapists assess and treat scars to restore mobility and quality of life, using circular frictional massage to break adhesions, improve pliability and reduce sensitivity, gentle stretching and mobilization to prevent contractures, myofascial release for adhesions between scar and deeper tissue, and modalities such as ultrasound (to promote collagen realignment) and low-level laser therapy (to reduce inflammation and scar thickness), together with patient education.
This is combined with multidisciplinary collaboration: dermatologists manage keloids with corticosteroid injections or laser therapy, plastic surgeons perform scar revision for severe cases, occupational therapists provide splints or ADL training for contractures, and psychologists address the emotional impact of visible scars.
B(i) The scar type guides treatment choice: contracture scars require aggressive stretching because they restrict movement and affect underlying muscles and joints.
Keloid scars, which are raised and extend beyond the wound borders and are often itchy or painful, need pain management as part of their treatment.
Hypertrophic scars, which are raised, red and confined to the original wound borders, may restrict joint mobility and require targeted interventions, while normal, flat, pale scars generally need minimal intervention.
B(ii) Complications common across scar types include functional impairments such as contractures limiting joint range of motion (e.g. elbow flexion after a burn) and adhesions that bind the scar to underlying tissue, restricting movement.
Pain and sensitivity, such as neuropathic pain, hyperesthesia, and itching or tenderness in keloids, are also common complications.
C(i) A problem that extends beyond the local tissue is the psychological impact of scarring: visible scars may cause distress or low self-esteem, affecting the person as a whole rather than only the scarred area.
C(ii) Functionally, contractures and adhesions can limit activities of daily living, such as difficulty dressing due to scar tightness, which is assessed as part of a thorough scar examination.
Untreated hypertrophic or keloid scarring can therefore progress from a local cosmetic issue to a source of ongoing pain, restricted joint movement, and psychological distress.
This is why physiotherapy assessment includes visual inspection, palpation for mobility and adhesions, and functional assessment of ROM and ADL impact, alongside tools such as the Vancouver Scar Scale.
Early, tailored, evidence-based physiotherapy intervention is therefore important to prevent both the physical and the psychological complications of scarring.

(i) Diagnosis: chemical burn - an injury caused by the skin coming into direct contact with a chemical agent; classified by chemical type (acid vs alkali), since the effect depends on the concentration of the chemical, site of contact, ingestion or inhalation, volume of chemical, and duration of exposure.
(ii) Pathophysiology: alkaline substances cause liquefaction necrosis - the tissue softens and becomes viscous, causing the burn to spread deeper than originally thought; this differs from acids, which cause coagulation necrosis, where blood flow is slowed or stopped, causing ischaemia and cell death.
(iii) Acute assessment/management: water irrigation is the primary treatment; damage continues until the chemical is removed, so specialized, early care is required to limit severity and prevent progressive tissue damage; protective measures should prevent further exposure.
(iv) Rehabilitation plan: as with general burn rehabilitation - splinting/positioning in an anti-deformity position, active-to-passive ROM exercises, pressure garments once the wound is closed and stable, and scar massage; monitor closely for delayed tissue damage, scarring and contractures given the tendency of alkaline burns to spread deeper than initially apparent.
questions.question:
A worker is exposed to a strong alkali (e.g., lye) on the forearm during an industrial task.
(i) State the diagnosis/classification.
(ii) Explain the pathophysiology.
(iii) Outline the acute assessment and management.
(iv) Outline the definitive/long-term rehabilitation plan.

A(i) State the aetiology of common infectious skin disorders.
A(ii) Explain the pathophysiology.
A(iii) Describe the clinical features.
A(iv) State how these infections are assessed.
B(i) State the physiotherapy-related techniques used.
B(ii) State the precautions to be observed.
B(iii) State the indications for physical modalities.
C(i) Explain the basis of complications if these infections are left untreated.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Aetiology: infectious skin disorders are caused by bacteria (e.g. impetigo from Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes, cellulitis), viruses (herpes simplex, herpes zoster, warts from HPV), fungi (tinea pedis/ringworm from dermatophytes such as Trichophyton rubrum), and parasites (scabies mites, lice).
A(ii) Pathophysiology: bacteria enter through breaks in the skin and multiply in the superficial epidermis, triggering fluid and pus accumulation; herpes viruses enter via mucous membranes or broken skin, replicate in epithelial cells causing ulceration, then travel to sensory nerve ganglia where they remain latent and reactivate with stress or illness.
Dermatophytes digest keratin in warm, moist conditions to cause inflammation and scaling, while scabies mites burrow into the upper skin layer to lay eggs, causing inflammation and itching.
A(iii) Clinical features: impetigo shows red sores/blisters that burst into honey-colored crusts with itching and, in severe cases, swollen lymph nodes; herpes simplex causes painful blisters preceded by tingling/itching/burning, with fever and swollen lymph nodes during primary infection and recurrence afterward.
Herpes zoster causes pain and tingling along a nerve dermatome followed by red papules progressing to vesicles, fever, chills and malaise, with possible ocular complications if cranial nerves III or V are involved.
Athlete's foot causes an itchy, red, scaly rash between the toes with peeling and odor.
A(iv) Assessment: identifying lesion type, distribution and site, together with history of contact/exposure; contagious infections are managed with standard precautions to prevent transmission.
B(i) PT techniques: management of skin infections is mostly medical, though electrotherapy has been used for painful conditions such as whitlow.
B(ii) Precautions: heat or ultrasound is contraindicated in herpes zoster because it can increase the severity of symptoms; standard precautions should be observed to avoid person-to-person or contact/sexual transmission of viral and parasitic infections.
B(iii) Indications: physical modalities may be used adjunctively for symptomatic relief of pain and itching, alongside medical antiviral, antibiotic, antifungal or scabicide treatment and patient education on hygiene.
C(i) If untreated, impetigo can progress to lymphangitis, gangrene, abscess formation and sepsis; untreated herpes zoster can lead to postherpetic neuralgia lasting weeks to years and, with cranial nerve involvement, ocular complications including corneal damage and loss of vision.
Untreated whitlow can cause scarring, numbness, recurrent infection, spread of infection, skin ulceration, and rarely encephalitis, meningitis or tenosynovitis, while untreated athlete's foot can progress to bacterial infection and cellulitis.

questions.question:
Describe the adductor group of the medial compartment of the thigh under the following headings, explaining the anatomical basis of the pes anserinus and its clinical importance.
A(i) Name all 5 adductor muscles; give origin, insertion, innervation, and action for each
A(ii) Why all adductor muscles are supplied by the obturator nerve except the hamstring part of adductor magnus — state its nerve supply and embryologic basis
B(i) The adductor hiatus — its boundaries and the structures it transmits
B(ii) The pes anserinus — its composition and function
C(i) Distinguish the gracilis from the other adductor muscles based on its unique anatomical features; name the other two compartments' muscles that join it to form the pes anserinus and their common innervation
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Adductor longus: origin — anterior surface of body of pubis, inferior to pubic crest and lateral to pubic symphysis; insertion — middle third of medial lip of linea aspera of femur; innervation — obturator nerve, anterior division (L2, L3, L4); action — adducts thigh. It is the most anteriorly placed muscle of the adductor group, large and fan-shaped. Adductor brevis: origin — body and inferior ramus of pubis; insertion — pectineal line and proximal part of linea aspera of femur; innervation — obturator nerve, anterior division (L2, L3, L4); action — adducts thigh and to an extent flexes it; it is short and lies deep to pectineus and adductor longus. Adductor magnus: largest, most powerful, most posterior muscle in the group; has an adductor part and a hamstring part. Origin — adductor part from inferior ramus of pubis and ramus of ischium; hamstring part from ischial tuberosity. Insertion — adductor part to gluteal tuberosity, linea aspera, medial supracondylar line; hamstring part to adductor tubercle of femur. Innervation — adductor part: obturator nerve (L2, L3, L4); hamstring part: tibial nerve. Action — adducts thigh; adductor part flexes, hamstring part extends. Gracilis: origin — body and inferior ramus of pubis; insertion — superior part of medial surface of tibia; innervation — obturator nerve (L2, L3); action — adducts thigh, flexes leg, helps rotate leg medially. Obturator externus: origin — margins of obturator foramen and obturator membrane; insertion — trochanteric fossa of femur; innervation — obturator nerve (L2, L3); action — laterally rotates thigh, steadies head of femur in acetabulum.
A(ii)
All adductor muscles are supplied by the obturator nerve except the hamstring part of adductor magnus and part of pectineus. The hamstring part of adductor magnus is supplied by the tibial nerve — because embryologically the hamstring part shares the same developmental origin as the true hamstrings (which arise from the ischial tuberosity and are all innervated by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve).
B(i)
The adductor hiatus is an opening between the aponeurotic distal attachment of the adductor part of adductor magnus and the tendinous distal attachment of the hamstring part. It transmits the femoral artery and vein from the adductor canal in the thigh to the popliteal fossa posterior to the knee. It is located just lateral and superior to the adductor tubercle of the femur.
B(ii)
The pes anserinus consists of the conjoined tendons of the sartorius, gracilis, and semitendinosus muscles; they insert into the superior part of the medial surface of the tibia. It acts as a secondary valgus restraint, augmenting the medial supporting structures of the knee. Bursitis of the pes anserinus bursa causes medial knee pain, especially in osteoarthritis.
C(i)
Gracilis is unique among the adductor group: it is a long strap-like muscle, the most medial and most superficial of the adductors, and the weakest member; it is the only member of the adductor group to cross both the hip and knee joints. It joins with sartorius (from the anterior compartment, supplied by femoral nerve) and semitendinosus (from the posterior compartment, supplied by tibial nerve) to form the pes anserinus — three muscles from three different compartments with three different nerve supplies share a common insertion.

questions.question:
(i) Describe the origin, course, branches and distribution of the splenic artery.
(ii) State the anatomical basis that makes subtotal (partial) splenectomy a safe surgical option.
(iii) Explain the anatomical basis of the complications that can follow injury to the spleen and its vasculature.
questions.answerText:
(i)
• The spleen receives its arterial supply from the splenic artery, the largest branch of the coeliac trunk.
• The splenic artery runs laterally along the superior aspect of the pancreas, within the splenorenal ligament.
• As it reaches the spleen it branches into about five vessels, each supplying a different vascular segment of the spleen.
• Along its course it also gives off the short gastric and left gastroepiploic arteries to the stomach, and pancreatic branches to the pancreas.
• Venous drainage is through the splenic vein, which combines with the superior mesenteric vein to form the hepatic portal vein.
(ii)
• The terminal arterial branches of the splenic artery do not anastomose with one another, so each supplies an independent vascular segment of the spleen.
• This segmental (end-arterial) arrangement allows a surgeon to remove one diseased or injured segment (subtotal splenectomy) without compromising the blood supply of the remaining segments.
(iii)
• The tail of the pancreas lies within the splenorenal ligament, close to the splenic vessels at the hilum, and may be injured during splenectomy, producing a pancreatic fistula.
• The spleen is the most frequently injured organ in the abdomen despite protection by the 9th to 12th ribs.
• Severe blows to the left side may fracture ribs, producing sharp fragments that lacerate the spleen.
• Blunt trauma elsewhere that suddenly raises intra-abdominal pressure can also rupture the spleen because its capsule is thin and its pulp is soft and pulpy.
• A ruptured spleen bleeds profusely, causing severe intraperitoneal haemorrhage and shock, so splenectomy or subtotal splenectomy is often required to prevent the patient from bleeding to death.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the origin, course, and distribution of the three types of muscle tissue under the following headings: structural features at the light microscope level, connective tissue organization (endomysium, perimysium, epimysium), and characteristic distinguishing feature of each type.
A(ii) State the safe structural basis of how skeletal muscle contraction is transmitted to produce movement.
B(i) Explain the anatomical and histological basis of why cardiac muscle does not fatigue and cannot be replaced after infarction.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Skeletal muscle: contains bundles of very long, multinucleated cells with cross-striations; contraction is quick, forceful, and usually under voluntary control. Connective tissue: endomysium surrounds individual muscle fibers (nerve fibers and capillaries form a rich network in the endomysium); perimysium surrounds fascicles; epimysium (deep fascia) surrounds the whole muscle belly and connects to tendons. Distinguishing feature: cross-striations; multinucleated; sarcomeres extending from Z disc to Z disc (~2.5 µm long in resting muscle). The A bands are anisotropic (dark); I bands are isotropic (light); each I band is bisected by the Z disc. Smooth muscle: consists of collections of fusiform cells that lack striations and have slow, involuntary contractions; elongated and spindle-shaped; single nucleus at the widest point; contain actin and myosin filaments but lack sarcomeres. Prominent locations: wall of GI tract, walls of arteries and veins, around glands. Distinguishing feature: no striations; slow, sustained contractions; non-voluntary. Cardiac muscle: cross-striations; composed of elongated, often branched cells; bound by intercalated discs unique to cardiac muscle; contraction is involuntary, vigorous, and rhythmic. Central nuclei; high cytoplasm-to-nucleus ratio. Distinguishing feature: intercalated discs; branching cells; involuntary continuous rhythmic contraction.
A(ii)
Skeletal muscle fibers show cross-striations of alternating light and dark bands. The sarcomere extends from Z disc to Z disc. During contraction, shortening of myofibrils (shortening of sarcomeres) is transmitted through the connective tissue (endomysium, perimysium, epimysium) and via tendons to bone, producing bodily movements.
B(i)
Cardiac muscle cells contain numerous mitochondria; a large proportion of cell volume is occupied by mitochondria. Fatty acids, transported by lipoproteins, are stored as triglycerides in numerous lipid droplets in cardiac muscle cells — this supports the extremely rich capillary network and strong continuous activity. Cardiac muscle has limited regenerative capacity; spaces left after infarction are filled by connective tissue forming dense irregular scar tissue, because cardiac muscle cells do not go through mitosis.

questions.question:
A(i) Define the pericardium and state its position and relations.
A(ii) Describe the fibrous pericardium.
A(iii) Describe the serous pericardium and the pericardial cavity.
A(iv) Describe the transverse sinus.
A(v) Describe the oblique sinus.
A(vi) Describe the blood supply, venous drainage and nerve supply of the pericardium.
B(i) Explain the clinical importance of the pericardial sinuses and of the site for draining pericardial fluid.
B(ii) Explain why pericardial irritation may cause pain or disturbance in a distant structure.
C(i) Distinguish between the transverse and the oblique sinus, and between the fibrous and the serous pericardium.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
A fibroserous sac that encloses the heart and the roots of the great vessels; it lies behind the body of the sternum and the 2nd-6th costal cartilages and in front of the T5-T8 vertebrae; it is attached to the central tendon of the diaphragm (pericardiophrenic ligament).
A(ii)
The outer fibrous tissue layer, enclosing the heart and the roots of the great vessels (the IVC excepted, as stated); its base is attached to the central tendon of the diaphragm.
A(iii)
Thin, elastic tissue lining the fibrous pericardium, made of a parietal layer (lines and fuses with the fibrous pericardium) and a visceral layer (forms the epicardium of the heart and encloses the aorta and pulmonary trunk); between them lies the pericardial cavity containing pericardial fluid.
A(iv)
Transverse sinus: formed by a tear in the dorsal mesocardium; lies behind the aorta and pulmonary trunk, in front of the SVC on the right and the left atrium on the left.
A(v)
Oblique sinus: a blind sac (cul-de-sac) formed as a result of the entrance of the 4 pulmonary veins and the IVC into the heart; lies behind the 2 left pulmonary veins and in front of the 2 right pulmonary veins and the IVC.
A(vi)
• Blood supply: fibrous pericardium from the pericardiophrenic and musculophrenic arteries; serous pericardium from the coronary arteries; veins drain to the azygos system, and the pericardiophrenic vein drains to the internal thoracic vein.
• Nerve supply: the fibrous and parietal pericardium by the phrenic nerve; the visceral pericardium by autonomic nerves.
B(i)
• Draining of pericardial fluid is done between the 7th costal cartilage and the xiphoid process.
• In pulmonary embolectomy a temporary ligature is passed through the transverse sinus to occlude the aorta and pulmonary trunk; the oblique sinus allows for pulsation of the left atrium.
B(ii)
Pain from irritation of the pleura or pericardium covering the central part of the diaphragm may be referred to the shoulder, because the phrenic nerve (C3,4,5) supplies the central diaphragm and the pericardium, and the supraclavicular nerve (C3,4) supplies the shoulder skin; pericarditis may also cause hiccup.
C(i)
• The transverse sinus is a passage formed by a tear in the dorsal mesocardium, lying behind the great arteries and used for the ligature; the oblique sinus is a blind sac formed by the entry of the pulmonary veins and IVC, allowing pulsation of the left atrium.
• The fibrous pericardium is the outer fibrous layer with phrenic nerve and pericardiophrenic/musculophrenic arterial supply; the serous pericardium is thin and elastic, with a parietal layer fused to the fibrous layer and a visceral layer forming the epicardium, supplied by coronary arteries and autonomic nerves.

A(i)
A highly mobile, bulky connective tissue septum (thick movable partition) in the midline between the right and left pleural cavities and their lungs, containing the heart and great vessels, oesophagus, trachea and its bifurcation, thoracic duct, and vagus and phrenic nerves; superior: root of the neck (thoracic outlet: manubrium, 1st rib, T1); inferior: diaphragm; anterior: sternum; posterior: thoracic vertebrae; lateral: lungs and pleurae.
A(ii)
A horizontal plane from the sternal angle to the lower border of T4 divides it into the superior mediastinum (above) and the inferior mediastinum (below), the latter subdivided into anterior (in front of the heart), middle (containing the heart) and posterior (behind the heart) parts.
A(iii)
• Superior: bounded by the thoracic outlet above, the T4 plane below, the manubrium in front and T1-T4 vertebrae behind; contents from superficial to deep: thymus; right and left brachiocephalic veins and SVC; arch of the aorta with brachiocephalic trunk, left common carotid and left subclavian arteries; right and left vagus and phrenic nerves; trachea and oesophagus (most posterior); thoracic duct beside the oesophagus; lymph nodes.
• Anterior: bounded by the T4 plane above, the diaphragm below, the body of the sternum in front and the pericardium/heart behind; contains the thymus, fatty tissue and lymph nodes.
• Middle: lies between the anterior and posterior mediastina; contains the pericardium and heart, ascending aorta, pulmonary trunk, SVC and IVC, right and left pulmonary veins, main bronchi, part of the phrenic nerves and lymph nodes.
• Posterior: bounded by the T4 plane above, the heart/middle mediastinum and diaphragm in front, and the T5 (lower border of T4) to T12 vertebrae behind; contains the oesophagus (most anterior), right and left vagus nerves around it, thoracic duct behind it, azygos vein (behind and to the right), descending aorta (behind and to the left), sympathetic trunks and lymph nodes.
A(iv)
Six structures lie in more than one division: thoracic duct, oesophagus and vagus nerves (superior and posterior); phrenic nerves and SVC (superior and middle); thymus (superior and anterior); lymph nodes are present in all regions.
B(i)
The T4 level marks the sternal angle and the 2nd costal cartilage, the bifurcation of the trachea, the bifurcation of the pulmonary trunk, and the beginning and termination of the arch of the aorta.
B(ii)
The mediastinum is highly mobile; in a stove-in chest the loose chest wall segment produces swinging movements of the mediastinum that cause severe shock.
C(i)
• Superior mediastinum: one part above the T4 plane, bounded in front by the manubrium and behind by T1-T4, containing thymus, great veins, aortic arch and its branches, trachea, oesophagus, thoracic duct, vagus and phrenic nerves.
• Inferior mediastinum: three parts below the T4 plane down to the diaphragm - anterior (thymus and fat, in front of the heart), middle (heart, pericardium, ascending aorta, pulmonary trunk) and posterior (oesophagus, descending aorta, azygos system, thoracic duct, sympathetic trunks).
• Nerves differ by position: the right vagus descends on the right of the trachea, forms the posterior oesophageal plexus and continues as the posterior gastric nerve; the left vagus descends between the left common carotid and left subclavian arteries and forms the anterior oesophageal plexus; the right phrenic descends on the right of the SVC and heart, the left on the left side of the heart.
questions.question:
A(i) Define the mediastinum and state its extent and boundaries.
A(ii) State its divisions and the plane that separates them.
A(iii) Describe the boundaries and contents of each division.
A(iv) List the structures that occupy more than one division.
B(i) Explain the importance of the level of T4 in relation to the mediastinum.
B(ii) Explain why the mediastinum is vulnerable when the chest wall is severely injured.
C(i) Distinguish between the superior and the inferior mediastinum.

A(i) Describe connective tissue under the following headings: definition and function, major constituent and its components, classification.
A(ii) Explain the clinical basis of edema in connective tissue.
B(i) Distinguish between loose connective tissue and dense connective tissue, giving two examples of each.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Definition and function: Connective tissue derives its name from its function in connecting or binding cells and tissues; it maintains the form of organs throughout the body. Unlike other tissue types (epithelium, muscle, nerve) which consist mainly of cells, the major constituent of connective tissue is the extracellular matrix. The extracellular matrix is composed of protein fibers (collagen, elastic, and reticular fibers), ground substance (a jelly-like, amorphous, anionic, hydrophilic complex of proteoglycans, glycosaminoglycans, and multiadhesive glycoproteins such as laminin and fibronectin), and tissue fluid. Classification: connective tissue is classified as connective tissue proper (loose: areolar, adipose, reticular; dense: regular, irregular, elastic) and specialized connective tissue (blood, cartilage, bone).
A(ii)
The amount of tissue fluid (interstitial fluid) is fairly constant and there is an equilibrium between water entering and leaving the intercellular substance. In pathological conditions (traumatic injury and inflammation), fluid may accumulate in the connective tissue, a condition known as edema.
B(i)
Loose connective tissue: irregularly arranged tissue with abundant ground substance, capable of withstanding stress from many directions; present in dermis, capsules of joints, and submucosa of the alimentary tract. Examples: areolar tissue, adipose tissue. Dense connective tissue: tissue in which fibers predominate; it is organized to withstand forces in specific directions. Dense regular: present in tendons and ligaments. Dense irregular: present in the dermis of skin and capsules of organs.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the five functions of the epithelial lining of the digestive tract.
A(ii) Describe the submucosal (Meissner) plexus and the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus together as the local enteric nervous system: name the layers of the GIT wall each is found in, state the ganglia they are composed of, what the number of ganglia depends on, and what system they function independently of.
B(i) Describe the muscularis mucosae: its composition, its location, and the two functions attributed to it.
B(ii) Explain the immunological backup to the thin epithelial barrier of the GIT, and identify what the digestive tract normally contains that makes this backup essential.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Five functions of the epithelial lining:
• Provide a selectively permeable barrier between the contents of the tract and the tissues of the body.
• Facilitate the transport and digestion of food.
• Promote the absorption of the products of digestion.
• Produce hormones that affect the activity of the digestive system.
• Produce mucus for lubrication and protection.
A(ii)
Local enteric nervous system:
• The submucosal (Meissner) plexus is located in the submucosa; the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus is located in the connective tissue between the circular and longitudinal muscle sublayers of the muscularis.
• Together they constitute the local enteric nervous system of the digestive tract.
• This system functions independently of the CNS.
• Both plexuses are composed mainly of nerve cell aggregates forming small parasympathetic ganglia.
• The number of ganglia along the digestive tract is variable — numerous in the regions of greatest motility.
B(i)
Muscularis mucosae:
• Composition: thin layer of smooth muscle.
• Location: usually separates the mucosa from the submucosa.
• Functions: (1) allows local movements of the mucosa independent of other movements of the digestive tract, helping to increase contact of the lining with food; (2) its contractions contribute to mixing and propelling food (the plexuses coordinate the contractions of the muscularis to mix and propel food).
B(ii)
Immunological backup:
• The mucosa-associated immune defense system (MALT) provides an essential backup to the thin physical barrier of the epithelial lining.
• The lamina propria (just below the epithelium) is a zone rich in macrophages and lymphocytes, some of which actively produce IgA antibodies.
• The digestive tract normally contains thousands of microbial species, including both useful gut inhabitants and potential pathogens ingested with food and drink, making this immune backup essential.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the parts and the course of the oesophagus.
A(ii) Describe its relations.
A(iii) State its constrictions and their distances from the incisor teeth.
A(iv) Describe its arterial supply, venous drainage, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply.
B(i) Relate the upper, middle and lower parts of the oesophagus to their differing supply and relations.
C(i) Explain how disease may spread from the oesophagus to distant structures through its venous and lymphatic drainage.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
It has cervical, thoracic and abdominal parts and is not a straight structure: it lies to the left in the neck, returns to the midline at the thoracic inlet, lies to the left in the superior mediastinum, returns to the midline in the posterior mediastinum and deviates to the left as it pierces the diaphragm at T10.
A(ii)
Cervical part lies in front of the prevertebral fascia, behind the trachea; the thoracic part is crossed on the right by the azygos vein and on the left by the aorta; in the posterior mediastinum it lies behind the left main bronchus and left pulmonary artery and in front of the thoracic duct; it is the most posterior tube of the superior mediastinum and the most anterior structure of the posterior mediastinum, with the vagus nerves around it, the azygos vein behind and to the right and the descending aorta behind and to the left.
A(iii)
Four constrictions: at its origin (C6), 15 cm from the incisor teeth; where the arch of the aorta lies in front of it, 22 cm; where the left main bronchus lies in front of it (tracheal bifurcation), 27 cm; at the diaphragm (T10), 38-40 cm.
A(iv)
• Arteries: inferior thyroid artery, oesophageal branches of the descending thoracic aorta, and the left gastric artery.
• Veins: upper part to the brachiocephalic vein, middle part to the azygos vein, lower part to the portal vein.
• Lymphatics: upper part to deep cervical nodes, middle part to tracheobronchial nodes, lower part to preaortic nodes.
• Nerves: upper third is striated, supplied by the recurrent laryngeal branch of the vagus, with sympathetics from the middle cervical ganglion; lower two-thirds is smooth, receiving sympathetics from the sympathetic trunk and greater splanchnic nerve, and parasympathetic secretomotor fibres from the vagus to the oesophageal glands.
B(i)
• Upper part: inferior thyroid artery, brachiocephalic vein, deep cervical nodes, striated muscle with recurrent laryngeal supply, related to the trachea and prevertebral fascia in the neck.
• Middle and lower parts: middle drains to the azygos vein and tracheobronchial nodes and is crossed by the azygos vein, arch of the aorta and left main bronchus; lower part has aortic and left gastric arteries, portal venous drainage, preaortic nodes and smooth muscle, and passes through the diaphragm at T10.
C(i)
• Venous routes: upper part to the brachiocephalic vein, middle part to the azygos vein (which empties into the SVC and forms a communication between the SVC and IVC), lower part to the portal vein.
• Lymphatic routes: upper part to deep cervical nodes, middle part to tracheobronchial nodes, lower part to preaortic nodes.

questions.question:
Describe the knee joint under the following headings and explain its clinical importance.
A(i) Type, articular surfaces, and articular bones
A(ii) Ligaments — classify as extracapsular or intra-articular; describe each fully
B(i) Movements and muscles responsible
B(ii) Blood supply and nerve supply of the knee joint
C(i) Distinguish the medial from the lateral meniscus, and explain the anatomical basis of why the medial meniscus is more frequently injured
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The knee joint is primarily a hinge type of synovial joint. It is the largest and very complex joint in the body. Articulations: femur with tibia (tibiofemoral joint) and femur with patella (patellofemoral joint). Articular bones: (1) Femur — enlarged medial and lateral femoral condyles. (2) Tibia — enlarged medial and lateral tibial condyles (tibial plateaus), which are the receptacles for the femoral condyles; tibia bears most of the weight. (3) Patella — a true sesamoid bone embedded in the quadriceps and patellar tendon; serves as a pulley improving the angle of pull. Fibula is not part of the knee joint and does not articulate with the femur or patella; it only serves as attachment for knee joint structures.
A(ii)
Extracapsular ligaments (5): (1) Patellar ligament — distal part of quadriceps tendon; strong, thick fibrous band passing from apex of patella to tibial tuberosity. (2) Fibular (lateral) collateral ligament — strong, rounded, cordlike; extends from lateral epicondyle of femur to head of fibula; tendon of popliteus passes deep to it, separating it from the lateral meniscus. (3) Tibial (medial) collateral ligament — strong flat band from medial epicondyle of femur to medial condyle and superior part of tibia; firmly attached to medial meniscus; weaker and more often damaged than the fibular collateral ligament. (4) Oblique popliteal ligament — expansion of tendon of semimembranosus; strengthens fibrous capsule posteriorly. (5) Arcuate popliteal ligament — arises from posterior aspect of fibular head; passes superomedially over tendon of popliteus; strengthens fibrous capsule posteriorly. Intra-articular ligaments (3): (1) ACL — from anterior intercondylar area of tibia to lateral condyle of femur; weaker; slack when flexed, taut when extended; prevents posterior displacement of femur on tibia and hyperextension. (2) PCL — from posterior intercondylar area of tibia to medial condyle of femur; stronger; taut during flexion; prevents anterior displacement of femur on tibia; main stabilizing factor in weight-bearing flexed knee. (3) Menisci — crescentic plates of fibrocartilage that deepen the surface and act as shock absorbers.
B(i)
Flexion — hamstrings. Extension — quadriceps. Medial rotation — popliteus, semitendinosus, semimembranosus. Lateral rotation — biceps femoris. Locking: when fully extended with foot on ground, the knee locks because of medial rotation of femur on tibia. Unlocking: popliteus contracts rotating femur laterally so flexion can occur.
B(ii)
Blood supply: genicular branches of femoral artery, popliteal artery, anterior and posterior recurrent branches of anterior tibial recurrent artery, and anterior and posterior branches of circumflex fibular arteries. The middle genicular branches of the popliteal artery penetrate the fibrous capsule and supply the cruciate ligaments, synovial membrane, and peripheral margins of the menisci. Nerve supply: branches of obturator nerve, femoral nerve, tibial nerve, and common fibular nerve.
C(i)
Medial meniscus: C-shaped, broader posteriorly; anterior end attaches to anterior intercondylar area of tibia anterior to ACL; posterior end to posterior intercondylar area anterior to PCL; firmly adheres to tibial collateral ligament. Lateral meniscus: almost circular, smaller and more freely movable; tendon of popliteus separates it from fibular collateral ligament; attached posteriorly via the posterior meniscofemoral ligament to PCL and medial femoral condyle. The medial meniscus is more frequently injured because its firm attachment to the tibial collateral ligament makes it immobile and liable to being trapped and torn when the ligament is stressed; the lateral meniscus is protected by its free mobility.

questions.question:
Describe the muscles of the posterior compartment of the leg under the following headings and explain why disease of tibialis posterior leads to collapse of the medial longitudinal arch.
A(i) Classify muscles into superficial and deep groups; give origin, insertion, innervation, and action of each
A(ii) The calcaneal (Achilles) tendon — formation, course, and clinical significance
B(i) The tibial nerve — course in the posterior compartment, branches, safe site for tarsal tunnel block
B(ii) How tibialis posterior supports the medial longitudinal arch and why its dysfunction causes pes planus
C(i) Distinguish the actions of gastrocnemius from soleus, explaining the anatomical basis of their different clinical testing
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Superficial group (3 muscles): Gastrocnemius — lateral head from lateral aspect of lateral condyle of femur; insertion: posterior surface of calcaneus via calcaneal tendon; innervation: tibial nerve (S1, S2); action: plantarflexes ankle when knee is extended, raises heel during walking, flexes leg at knee joint. Soleus — posterior aspect of head and superior quarter of posterior surface of fibula; soleal line and middle third of medial border of tibia; tendinous arch; insertion: posterior surface of calcaneus via calcaneal tendon; innervation: tibial nerve (S1, S2); action: plantarflexes ankle independent of position of knee, steadies leg on foot. Plantaris — inferior end of lateral supracondylar line of femur, oblique popliteal ligament; insertion: posterior surface of calcaneus via calcaneal tendon; innervation: tibial nerve (S1, S2); action: weakly assists gastrocnemius in plantarflexing ankle. Deep group (4 muscles): Popliteus — lateral surface of lateral condyle of femur and lateral meniscus; posterior surface of tibia superior to soleal line; tibial nerve (L4, L5, S1); weakly flexes knee, unlocks it by rotating femur 5° on fixed tibia, and medially rotates tibia of unplanted limb. Flexor hallucis longus — inferior 2/3 of posterior surface of fibula; base of distal phalanx of great toe; tibial nerve (S2, S3); flexes great toe at all joints, weakly plantarflexes ankle, supports medial longitudinal arch. Flexor digitorum longus — medial part of posterior surface of tibia inferior to soleal line; bases of distal phalanges of lateral 4 digits; tibial nerve (S2, S3); flexes lateral 4 digits, plantarflexes ankle, supports longitudinal arches. Tibialis posterior — interosseous membrane, posterior tibia inferior to soleal line, posterior fibula; tuberosity of navicular, cuneiform, cuboid, sustentaculum tali of calcaneus, bases of 2nd, 3rd, and 4th metatarsals; tibial nerve (L4, L5); plantarflexes ankle and inverts foot.
A(ii)
The calcaneal tendon is formed by the union of the tendons of gastrocnemius, soleus, and plantaris; it inserts into the posterior surface of the calcaneus. It is the largest and strongest tendon in the body. Clinical significance: rupture of the Achilles tendon (commonly felt as a 'pop' and tested by Thompson's squeeze test) results in inability to plantarflex the foot.
B(i)
The posterior tibial artery enters the sole of the foot through the tarsal tunnel, accompanying the tibial nerve. The tibial nerve enters the sole of the foot via the tarsal tunnel and then splits into the lateral and medial plantar arteries. For a tarsal tunnel block, the posterior tibial pulse can be palpated inferoposteriorly to the medial malleolus, where the artery turns to enter the foot — the tibial nerve lies adjacent.
B(ii)
Tibialis posterior inserts into the tuberosity of the navicular, cuneiform, cuboid, sustentaculum tali of calcaneus, and the bases of the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th metatarsals — the very bones that form the medial longitudinal arch. It plantarflexes the ankle and inverts the foot; by pulling the navicular and cuneiforms downward and inward it actively maintains the height of the medial longitudinal arch. Dysfunction (e.g., from tenosynovitis or rupture) leads to eversion of the calcaneus, slipping down of the talus and navicular, and pes planus — collapse of the medial longitudinal arch.
C(i)
Gastrocnemius spans the knee joint (arising from the femoral condyle) and the ankle joint; it plantarflexes the ankle only when the knee is extended and also flexes the knee. It is tested with the knee extended. Soleus arises entirely from the tibia and fibula (below the knee) and plantarflexes the ankle independent of the position of the knee. It is tested by single-leg heel raise with the knee flexed to 90°, which eliminates gastrocnemius from the movement and isolates soleus.

questions.question:
A(i) State the origin and root value of the phrenic nerve.
A(ii) Describe its course, relations and embryological basis of its long course on the right and left.
A(iii) Describe its termination and the points at which it reaches the diaphragm.
A(iv) Describe its distribution (motor and sensory).
C(i) Explain the anatomical basis of the deformity and other consequences after injury or section of the nerve.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The phrenic nerve is formed in the neck within the cervical plexus and contains fibres from spinal roots C3, C4 and C5.
A(ii)
• Its long course from the neck follows the embryological migration of the diaphragm from the cervical region: the septum transversum is carried ventrally and caudally, and the cervical myotomes and nerves contribute the muscle and nerve supply.
• It passes through the superior and middle mediastinum: the right phrenic descends on the right side of the SVC and heart; the left phrenic descends on the left side of the heart.
A(iii)
Both nerves terminate in the diaphragm: terminal branches of the right phrenic pass through the caval opening (T8) in the central tendon, and the left phrenic pierces the left dome.
A(iv)
• Motor: the sole motor supply of the diaphragm; the right nerve supplies the right half up to the right margin of the oesophageal opening and the left nerve the left half up to the left margin.
• Sensory: the central part of the diaphragm and the related pleura and peritoneum, and sensory fibres to the pleurae and pericardium (mediastinal pleura, fibrous and parietal pericardium); the peripheral part receives sensory fibres from the lower 6 or 7 intercostal and subcostal nerves.
C(i)
• Sectioning or injury of a phrenic nerve in the neck causes complete paralysis and eventual atrophy of the muscular part of the corresponding half of the diaphragm, except in persons who have an accessory phrenic nerve.
• Causes of injury: mechanical trauma (ligation or damage during surgery) and compression by a tumour within the chest cavity; myopathies (e.g. myasthenia gravis) and neuropathies (e.g. diabetic neuropathy) also interrupt the supply.
• The paralysed half is elevated and shows paradoxical movement: it moves upwards during inspiration (forced up by abdominal viscera) and downwards during expiration; only one half is affected because each dome has a separate nerve supply.
• Unilateral paralysis is usually asymptomatic and an incidental finding on X-ray; if both sides are paralysed there is poor exercise tolerance, orthopnoea and fatigue, and lung function tests show a restrictive deficit.
• Irritation of the diaphragmatic pleura or of the peritoneum under the diaphragm (pleurisy, subphrenic pus or blood) refers pain to the shoulder tip, because the central diaphragm sends sensory fibres in the phrenic nerve (C3-5) and the shoulder skin is supplied by the supraclavicular nerve (C3,4).

A(i)
The gluteal region is the region of the buttock. Bony landmarks — surface anatomy: iliac crest, gluteus medius, tip of greater trochanter, gluteus maximus (fold of buttock), ischial tuberosity, tip of coccyx, natal cleft, posterior superior iliac spine (PSIS), sciatic nerve. Bones: os coxae (ilium, ischium, pubis) and femur.
A(ii)
Superficial fascia: thick in women; impregnated with large quantities of fat, hence the prominence of the buttock. Deep fascia: continuous with fascia lata of the thigh. The 9 muscles: gluteus maximus, gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, tensor fasciae latae (superficial layer); piriformis, obturator internus, gemellus superior, gemellus inferior, quadratus femoris (deep layer). Deep layer muscles all have distal attachments on or adjacent to the intertrochanteric crest of the femur; they are lateral rotators of the thigh and stabilise the hip joint. Obturator internus, superior gemellus, and inferior gemellus form the triceps coxae of the hip.
B(i)
6 nerves of the gluteal region: sciatic nerve (L4, 5; S1, 2, 3); posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh; superior gluteal nerve; inferior gluteal nerve; nerve to quadratus femoris; pudendal nerve. (Nerve to obturator internus also exits here.) The sciatic nerve curves downward midway between the tuber ischii and the greater trochanter.
B(ii)
4 arteries: superior gluteal artery (SGA), inferior gluteal artery (IGA), medial femoral circumflex artery (MFCA), lateral femoral circumflex artery (LFCA). Trochanteric anastomosis (TA) — main blood supply to the head of femur: SGA, IGA, MFCA, LFCA. Cruciate anastomosis (CA) — situated at the level of the lesser trochanter: IGA, MFCA, LFCA, and 1st perforating branch of profunda femoris. The CA jointly with the TA provides a connection between the femoral arteries and the internal iliac arteries.
C(i)
Sacrotuberous ligament (STL) and sacrospinous ligament (SSL): (1) both stabilise the sacrum and prevent its rotation at the sacroiliac joint by the weight of the vertebral column; (2) in conjunction with bones, they form the greater sciatic foramen (GSF) and lesser sciatic foramen (LSF). Functions of GSF and LSF: GSF provides an exit from the pelvis into the gluteal region. LSF (1) provides an entrance into the perineum from the gluteal region; (2) enables nerves and vessels that left the pelvis through the GSF above the pelvic floor to enter the perineum below the pelvic floor.

A(ii) Fascia — superficial and deep; name all 9 muscles and give their OCIANA (origin, course, insertion, action, nerve, artery)

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Path of blood flow:
• Aorta → Renal artery → Segmental artery → Interlobar artery → Arcuate artery → Cortical radiate artery → Afferent arteriole → Glomerulus (capillaries) → Efferent arteriole → Peritubular capillaries (cortical nephrons) or Vasa recta (juxtamedullary nephrons) → Cortical radiate vein → Arcuate vein → Interlobar vein → Renal vein → Inferior vena cava.
• Renal arteries deliver approximately one-quarter (1,200 ml) of cardiac output to the kidneys each minute.
A(ii)
Nerve supply is via sympathetic fibers from the renal plexus.
B(i)
• Cortical nephrons (85% of nephrons): efferent arteriole supplies peritubular capillaries — low-pressure, porous capillaries adapted for absorption of water and solutes; they cling to adjacent renal tubules in the cortex and empty into venules.
• Juxtamedullary nephrons: efferent arteriole supplies vasa recta — long, thin-walled vessels parallel to the long nephron loops; important in formation of concentrated urine.
B(ii)
Blood pressure in the glomerulus is high because:
• Afferent arterioles are larger in diameter than efferent arterioles.
• Arterioles are high-resistance vessels.
• The glomerulus is fed and drained by arterioles (not venules), which maintains the high filtration pressure. The glomerulus is also specialized for filtration, with fenestrated endothelium that is highly porous, allowing filtrate formation.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the complete path of blood flow through the renal blood vessels, from the aorta to the peritubular capillaries or vasa recta.
A(ii) State the nerve supply to the kidneys and name the source.
B(i) Distinguish between the capillary beds associated with cortical nephrons and those associated with juxtamedullary nephrons.
B(ii) Explain the anatomical basis for high blood pressure in the glomerulus.

A. Describe the gross anatomy of the paranasal sinuses under the following headings: the four pairs of sinuses, their development, and their general function.
B. State how each of the paranasal sinuses relates to a specific clinical complication when infected or fractured.
C. Explain why disease of the paranasal sinuses can spread to produce a functional deficit in a distant structure, namely the brain or the nasal cavity.
questions.answerText:
A
The nasal sinuses are air-containing sacs lined by ciliated epithelium, communicating with the nasal cavity through narrow, easily occluded channels; they develop as outgrowths from the nasal cavity. There are 4 pairs: the maxillary antrum, sphenoid, frontal and ethmoid sinuses. The maxillary antrum and ethmoid sinuses are present in a rudimentary state at birth, while the rest become evident at about the 7th year of life. The lining of the sinuses is continuous with the nasal mucosa; their function is obscure, but they provide resonance to the voice, shape to the face, and some degree of warmth and humidification to inspired air. The paranasal sinuses are supplied by branches of the ophthalmic and maxillary nerves.
B
The frontal sinuses' posterosuperior wall lies adjacent to the frontal lobe of the brain, and their floor abuts the ethmoid cells, nasal fossa roof and orbit; infection here may cause a frontal lobe abscess, and fracture severe enough to tear the dura and pia-arachnoid causes CSF rhinorrhoea. The maxillary sinus (antrum) may become infected from the nasal cavity or from caries of the upper molar teeth, whose roots are separated from the sinus floor only by a thin, sometimes deficient, layer of bone. The ethmoid sinuses lie on each side of the cribriform plate, related above to the frontal lobes; infection (ethmoiditis) may result in a frontal cerebral abscess, and ethmoidal fracture may cause CSF leakage into the nasal cavity. The sphenoid sinuses lie within the body of the sphenoid and may extend laterally into the greater wing of the sphenoid or backward into the basal part of the occipital bone; each drains into the nasal cavity above the superior concha (the sphenoethmoidal recess).
C
Because the frontal and ethmoid sinuses are directly related anatomically to the frontal lobes of the brain (posterosuperior wall of the frontal sinus, and the region above the cribriform plate for the ethmoid sinuses), infection at either site can spread directly to produce a frontal lobe or frontal cerebral abscess; and because fracture of either sinus, if severe enough to tear the dura and pia-arachnoid, places the subarachnoid space in communication with the nasal cavity, CSF rhinorrhoea (leakage of CSF into the nose) results, sometimes even on the contralateral side since the sinuses may communicate with one another.

A(i)
Cell body (soma): The neuronal cell body has a nucleus with at least one nucleolus and typical cytoplasmic organelles; it lacks centrioles, consistent with the amitotic nature of neurons. Types of neurons by structure: Unipolar (pseudounipolar) neurons — sensory neurons with only a single process or fiber that divides close to the cell body into two main branches (axon and dendrite); the longer branch extends to a peripheral ending and the other toward the CNS. Multipolar neurons — motor neurons and interneurons with numerous cell processes (an axon and many dendrites). Bipolar neurons — spindle-shaped, with a dendrite at one end and an axon at the other; found in the light-sensitive retina of the eye. Anaxonic neurons — have many dendrites but no true axon; do not produce action potentials, but regulate electrical changes of adjacent neurons. Glial cells (neuroglia): Neuroglia is a special type of connective tissue for the nervous system. Glial cells are nonconductive; they provide a support system for neurons; they support, nourish, and protect neurons. They are far more numerous than neurons and, unlike neurons, are capable of mitosis. Types include oligodendrocytes (produce myelin in CNS), Schwann cells and satellite cells (in PNS), and microglia.
A(ii)
Neurons are highly specialized and amitotic: if a neuron is destroyed, it cannot be replaced because neurons do not go through mitosis. This means that neuronal loss (e.g., in injury or disease) is permanent and irreplaceable.
B(i)
CNS consists of the brain and spinal cord; it is covered by three connective tissue layers called meninges (dura, arachnoid, and pia maters); it contains very little collagen or fibrous tissue and is relatively soft, easily damaged by injuries affecting the cranium or vertebral bones. The PNS is composed of nerves and ganglia. Functionally, the CNS is the master control unit while the PNS is the body's link to the outside world. Sensory (afferent) and motor (efferent) are the functional categories.
questions.question:

A(ii) Explain the clinical significance of neurons being amitotic.
B(i) Distinguish between the central nervous system (CNS) and peripheral nervous system (PNS) structurally and functionally.

Describe the gross anatomy of the glenohumeral (shoulder) joint:
A(i) Articular surfaces and classification
A(ii) Capsule
A(iii) Factors contributing to its mobility and stability
B. State how a part of the joint capsule relates to the common direction of shoulder dislocation.
C. Explain how shoulder dislocation may spread to affect a distant structure (nerve), causing a functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The glenohumeral (shoulder) joint is a multiaxial synovial joint of the ball-and-socket variety, formed by articulation between the head of the humerus and the glenoid cavity of the scapula; due to the very limited interface between humerus and scapula, it is the most mobile joint in the human body.
A(ii)
The joint capsule is a fibrous sheath enclosing the joint structures; it is thin and lax to allow a wide range of movement (particularly abduction), is strengthened by muscles and ligaments, but is weakest inferiorly, placing it at risk of dislocation in that direction. It is lined by synovial membrane and forms a tubular sheath around the tendon of the long head of biceps, and a number of bursae aid mobility.
A(iii)
• Factors contributing to mobility are the ball-and-socket joint type, the shallow glenoid cavity against the large humeral head (a 1:4 disproportion, likened to a golf ball and tee), and laxity of the joint capsule.
• Factors contributing to stability are the rotator cuff muscles, whose resting tone pulls the humeral head into the glenoid cavity, the glenoid labrum, which deepens the cavity and reduces dislocation risk, and the ligaments, which reinforce the capsule and form the coraco-acromial arch.
B
• The glenohumeral joint is the most commonly dislocated joint in the body, accounting for approximately 95% of all shoulder dislocations, and anterior dislocations are the most prevalent.
• An anterior dislocation is usually caused by excessive extension and lateral rotation of the humerus, which forces the humeral head anteriorly and inferiorly into the weakest (inferior) part of the joint capsule.
• Tearing of the joint capsule during dislocation is associated with an increased risk of future (recurrent) dislocations.
C
• The axillary nerve runs in close proximity to the shoulder joint and can be damaged during dislocation.
• Injury to the axillary nerve causes paralysis of the deltoid muscle, with loss of sensation over the "regimental badge" area of skin overlying the deltoid.
• A dislocation can also stretch the radial nerve, since it is tightly bound within the radial (spiral) groove of the humerus.
• These nerve injuries represent the spread of the joint pathology to distant neurological structures.
• The resulting functional deficits include loss of shoulder abduction and sensory loss from axillary nerve injury, reflecting how a purely mechanical joint injury can produce a distinct neurological deficit at a distance from the joint itself.

A(i)
Formed behind the neck of the pancreas by the union of the superior mesenteric and splenic veins.
A(ii)
• Large but short, about 5 cm; in front of the opening of the lesser sac it passes to the porta hepatis where it divides into right and left terminal branches.
• At the porta hepatis the order from behind forwards is portal vein branches, proper hepatic artery, hepatic ducts; in the hepatoduodenal ligament it lies with the hepatic artery and bile duct.
A(iii)
Drains poorly oxygenated but nutrient-rich blood from the GI tract (lower oesophagus to upper anal canal), pancreas, gallbladder, bile ducts and spleen to the liver.
A(iv)
Direct route: through the liver to the IVC via the hepatic veins; alternative routes exist and the portal vein and its tributaries have no valves.
B(i)
Portasystemic shunts join the portal vein to the IVC or join the splenic vein to the left renal vein after splenectomy.
C(i)
• Portal hypertension: cirrhosis scarring and fibrosis obstruct the portal vein, pressure mounts, and blood forced through collaterals dilates veins into varices, potentially fatal.
• Lower third of oesophagus: left gastric branches with oesophageal veins to the azygos: oesophageal varices.
• Anal canal: superior rectal with middle and inferior rectal veins: haemorrhoids (mucosa with normally dilated submucosal veins prolapses).
• Anterior abdominal wall: paraumbilical with superficial epigastric veins: caput medusae, veins radiating like small snakes from the umbilicus.
• Retroperitoneal: colic twig veins of ascending and descending colon, duodenum, pancreas and liver with renal, lumbar and phrenic veins.

A(i)
• Continuation of the sigmoid colon at S3; ends as the anal canal one inch below and in front of the tip of the coccyx; about 12 to 13 cm (5 inches); lower end dilated as the ampulla; lacks mesentery, taeniae coli, sacculations and appendices epiploicae.
• Two anteroposterior curves (sacral posterior; perineal anterior at puborectalis) and three lateral curves (upper convex to right, middle convex to left and most prominent, lower convex to right).
A(ii)
Upper third: front and sides covered; middle third: front only; lower third: none; posterior surface: none. Male: recto-vesical pouch 7.5 cm from anus; female: recto-uterine pouch of Douglas 5.5 cm from anus.
A(iii)
Four permanent horizontal Houston's valves (1st and 3rd constant); the 3rd at S5, 5 cm above the anus, if completely encircling forms Nelaton's sphincter, and divides an upper chamber (faeces without reflex to defecate) from a lower sensitive chamber; valves support faecal weight; cannulae/rectal washing are given in left lateral position to avoid injury to the 3rd valve.
A(iv)
Wall: serous, muscular (outer longitudinal, inner circular), submucosa, mucosa. Arteries: superior rectal (main, from inferior mesenteric), middle rectal (anterior division of internal iliac), inferior rectal (internal pudendal), median sacral (aorta), inferior gluteal.
B(i)
Superior rectal vein drains to inferior mesenteric then portal vein; middle rectal to internal iliac and inferior rectal to internal pudendal (systemic). Internal haemorrhoids (superior rectal tributaries, above Hilton's line, painless); external (inferior rectal, below, painful).
B(ii)
Support: puborectal sling, Waldeyer fascia, lateral ligaments, pelvirectal and ischiorectal fat. Upper third lateral: pararectal fossa (sigmoid colon, small intestine); middle third: pelvirectal space; lower third: ischioanal fossa.
B(iii)
Sympathetic (L1, L2) is vasomotor, stimulates the internal anal sphincter and inhibits the rest of the musculature; parasympathetic (S2 to S4) is secretomotor, stimulates peristalsis and relaxes sphincters.
C(i)
Lymph: upper half via superior rectal to left common iliac and pararectal nodes; middle half to internal iliac nodes; lower part to anal valves to internal iliac nodes; below the anal valves to superficial inguinal nodes.
C(ii)
Portal-systemic anastomosis: superior rectal (portal) with middle and inferior rectal veins (systemic); gut lymph follows arteries to pre-aortic nodes.
C(iii)
Male: anterior sigmoid colon, small intestine, seminal vesicles, ampulla of vas, posterior bladder and prostate; female: posterior vaginal wall; posterior: sacrum, sacral plexus, coccyx, and piriformis, coccygeus, levator ani.
C(iv)
Hindgut origin (endoderm), sympathetic least splanchnic (T12, L1) plus hypogastric (S2 to S4), inferior mesenteric artery (L3); mucosa above the 3rd valve from pre-allantoic hindgut, below from cloaca; muscle from splanchnic mesoderm.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
The popliteal artery is the continuation of the femoral artery; it begins when the femoral artery passes through the adductor hiatus. It descends through the fossa, passing inferolaterally and is the deepest structure in the fossa — it runs in close proximity to the articular capsule of the knee joint. It terminates at the inferior border of the popliteus by dividing into the anterior and posterior tibial arteries.
A(ii)
Five genicular branches participate in the genicular anastomosis (a network of vessels surrounding the knee providing collateral circulation capable of maintaining blood supply to the leg during full knee flexion): superior lateral genicular artery, superior medial genicular artery, middle genicular artery (penetrates the fibrous capsule and supplies the cruciate ligaments, synovial membrane, and peripheral margins of the menisci), inferior lateral genicular artery, and inferior medial genicular artery. Muscular branches supply the hamstring, gastrocnemius, soleus, and plantaris muscles. The superior muscular branches have clinically important anastomoses with the terminal part of the profunda femoris and gluteal arteries.
B(i)
Termination: the popliteal artery divides into the anterior tibial artery and the tibioperoneal trunk; the tibioperoneal trunk divides into the posterior tibial artery and fibular (peroneal) artery. Anterior tibial artery: passes anterior to the interosseous membrane between tibia and fibula; supplies muscles of anterior compartment; continues as the dorsalis pedis artery in the foot, supplying tarsal bones and dorsal metatarsals, and anastomoses with the lateral plantar artery to form the deep plantar arch. Posterior tibial artery: continues inferiorly along surface of deep posterior leg muscles; enters the sole of the foot via the tarsal tunnel; splits into lateral and medial plantar arteries supplying the plantar foot.
B(ii)
The popliteal artery is the hardest pulse to find, lying deep in the popliteal fossa; it requires deep palpation. To make it easier, the patient should slightly flex the leg — this relaxes the fascia around the popliteal fossa. An aneurysm of the popliteal artery can be detected by an obvious palpable pulsation in the popliteal fossa; an arterial bruit may be heard on auscultation.
C(i)
The tibial nerve is the medial and larger branch of the sciatic nerve and the most superficial of the neurovascular bundle. Injury causes: paralysis of flexor muscles in the leg and intrinsic muscles in the sole of the foot; inability to plantarflex the ankles or flex the toes; and loss of sensation on the sole of the foot. The resulting deformity is a calcaneovalgus posture — unopposed dorsiflexion with loss of plantarflexion, the foot assuming a dorsiflexed position because the antagonist muscles remain intact. Weakened or absent plantarflexion and paraesthesia of the foot and posterolateral leg are the major features of tibial nerve compression.

A(i) Describe the cell cycle under the following headings: definition, phases (G1, S, G2, M), and the two key regulatory molecules that control progression through the cycle.
A(ii) Explain the clinical consequences of errors in mitosis, naming three chromosomal abnormalities that can result.
B(i) Distinguish between apoptosis and necrosis, giving the distinguishing morphological changes and clinical consequences of each.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Definition: The cell cycle, or cell-division cycle, is the series of events that takes place in a cell leading to its division and duplication (replication). In cells with a nucleus (eukaryotes), the cell cycle can be divided into two brief periods: interphase (during which the cell grows, accumulates nutrients needed for mitosis and duplicates its DNA) and the mitosis (M) phase (during which the cell splits itself into two distinct cells, often called daughter cells). Phases: G1 (Gap 1) — cell grows; S phase (synthesis) — chromosomes are replicated; G2 (Gap 2) — cell grows more and prepares for mitosis; M phase (mitosis and cytokinesis) — cell division. Cells that have temporarily or reversibly stopped dividing are said to have entered the G0 phase (quiescence). Two key regulatory molecules: cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs), which determine a cell's progress through the cell cycle.
A(ii)
In non-disjunction, a chromosome may fail to separate during anaphase: one daughter cell will receive both sister chromosomes (leading to trisomy — three copies) and the other will receive none (leading to monosomy — one copy). These cells are considered aneuploid, a condition often associated with cancer. Other chromosomal abnormalities: deletion — an arm of the chromosome may be broken and the fragment lost. Translocation — the fragment incorrectly reattaches to another, non-homologous chromosome. Inversion — the fragment reattaches to the original chromosome in reverse orientation. The effect may range from no noticeable effect to cancer induction or organism death.
B(i)
Apoptosis (programmed cell death): biochemical events lead to characteristic cell changes including blebbing, loss of cell membrane asymmetry and attachment, cell shrinkage, nuclear fragmentation, chromatin condensation, and chromosomal DNA fragmentation. Apoptosis differs from necrosis in that the cellular debris does not damage the organism. Necrosis: a form of traumatic cell death that results from acute cellular injury; cellular debris can damage the organism. Clinical consequences: excessive apoptosis causes atrophy (e.g., ischemic damage); insufficient apoptosis results in uncontrolled cell proliferation such as cancer.

A(i)
Tibialis anterior: origin — lateral condyle and superior half of lateral surface of tibia and interosseous membrane; insertion — medial and inferior surfaces of medial cuneiform and base of 1st metatarsal; innervation — deep fibular nerve (L4, L5); action — dorsiflexes ankle and inverts foot. Extensor digitorum longus: origin — lateral condyle of tibia and superior 3/4 of medial surface of fibula and interosseous membrane; insertion — middle and distal phalanges of lateral 4 digits; innervation — deep fibular nerve (L4, L5); action — extends lateral 4 digits and dorsiflexes ankle. Extensor hallucis longus: origin — middle part of anterior surface of fibula and interosseous membrane; insertion — dorsal aspect of base of distal phalanx of great toe; innervation — deep fibular nerve (L4, L5); action — extends great toe and dorsiflexes ankle. Fibularis tertius: origin — inferior 3rd of anterior surface of fibula and interosseous membrane; insertion — dorsum of base of 5th metatarsal; innervation — deep fibular nerve (L4, L5); action — dorsiflexes ankle and aids in eversion of foot.
A(ii)
The dorsalis pedis artery begins as the anterior tibial artery enters the foot. It passes over the dorsal aspect of the tarsal bones, then moves inferiorly towards the sole of the foot. It then anastomoses with the lateral plantar artery to form the deep plantar arch. It supplies the tarsal bones and the dorsal aspect of the metatarsals; via the deep plantar arch, it also contributes to the supply of the toes. The dorsalis pedis pulse is found by palpating on the dorsum of the foot, just lateral to extensor hallucis longus tendon.
B(i)
The common fibular nerve is the lateral, smaller terminal branch of the sciatic nerve; it begins at the superior angle of the popliteal fossa, closely follows the medial border of biceps femoris, exits the fossa superficial to the lateral head of gastrocnemius, passes over the posterior aspect of the head of fibula, and winds around the neck of fibula where it divides into its terminal branches — the deep fibular nerve and superficial fibular nerve. The deep fibular nerve supplies all 4 muscles of the anterior compartment (tibialis anterior, extensor digitorum longus, extensor hallucis longus, fibularis tertius) and the foot.
B(ii)
At the neck of fibula the common fibular nerve is subcutaneous and directly palpable, making it vulnerable to direct trauma, compression, or traction. Injury here interrupts the deep fibular nerve before it reaches the anterior compartment. All 4 anterior compartment muscles (which perform dorsiflexion and toe extension) are paralysed. The result is foot drop: the foot hangs in plantarflexion and inversion (because the unopposed plantarflexors — gastrocnemius, soleus — and invertor — tibialis posterior — continue to act), and the patient develops a high-stepping gait to clear the dragging toe.
C(i)
Tibialis anterior: dorsiflexes the ankle AND inverts the foot; supplied by the deep fibular nerve (L4, L5). Fibularis tertius: dorsiflexes the ankle AND aids eversion of the foot; supplied by the deep fibular nerve (L4, L5). Both share the same nerve supply but perform opposite movements about the subtalar axis (inversion vs. eversion), reflecting their positions on opposite sides of the interosseous membrane.

A(i) Describe the extent, length and parts of the trachea.
A(ii) Describe the relations of the trachea and its level of bifurcation.
A(iii) Compare the right and left main bronchi.
A(iv) Describe the lobar and segmental divisions of the bronchi and the terminal airways.
A(v) Describe the lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of the trachea and bronchi.
B(i) Relate the parts of the bronchial tree to common pathologies.
C(i) Explain how disease of the bronchial tree may spread to distant structures through the lymphatics.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
A wide tube about 10 cm long and 2 cm wide, lying in the superior mediastinum and extending from C6 (lower border of the cricoid cartilage) to T4, where it divides into the right and left main bronchi; it has cervical and thoracic parts, the cervical part measuring 5 cm.
A(ii)
• The cervical part is in contact posteriorly with the oesophagus and anteriorly with the isthmus of the thyroid gland; it is palpable in the suprasternal notch midway between the heads of the clavicles; it ends at the sternal angle (T4/5) just to the right of the midline (at T6 in the erect position in full inspiration).
• At the bifurcation the azygos vein arches over the right main bronchus (T4) and the left main bronchus lies in front of the oesophagus (27 cm from the incisor teeth); the cardiac plexus lies on the lowest part of the trachea behind the arch of the aorta.
A(iii)
Right main bronchus: 2.5 cm long, shorter, wider and vertically oriented; left main bronchus: 5 cm long, longer, narrower and horizontally oriented.
A(iv)
• Right main bronchus divides into upper (outside the hilum), middle and lower lobar bronchi, giving 10 bronchopulmonary segments; the left divides within the hilum into 2 lobar bronchi, giving 8 segments; segmental (third-order) bronchi supply the segments.
• The U-shaped cartilage bars of the trachea are replaced by irregular plates in smaller bronchi; the smallest bronchi give bronchioles (under 1 mm), then terminal bronchioles and respiratory bronchioles (about 0.5 mm, with outpouchings where gas exchange occurs), then alveolar ducts, alveolar sacs and alveoli surrounded by capillaries.
A(v)
Trachea: lymphatics drain to the deep cervical and paratracheal lymph nodes; the mucous membrane is supplied by the vagus, which also gives the parasympathetic supply. Lung and bronchi: pulmonary plexuses with vagal (bronchoconstrictor, secretomotor) and sympathetic (bronchodilator) fibres.
B(i)
• The wider, more vertical right main bronchus allows foreign particles to enter it easily; asthma (dyspnoea); pneumonia (bacterial or viral infection of the lung); pulmonary embolism (pulmonary artery obstructed by air, blood clot, fat, tumour cells or foreign particles).
• Abscesses are commoner in the posterior segment of the upper lobe and the apical segment of the lower lobe (most dependent supine); septa between segments limit infection but carcinoma and tuberculosis break through; fibrosis reduces compliance and emphysema reduces elasticity.
C(i)
• Lymph from lung and bronchi passes to the bronchopulmonary (hilar) nodes, then to the superior and inferior tracheobronchial nodes (above and below the tracheal bifurcation), then to the right and left bronchomediastinal trunks.
• The trunks usually end at the junction of the subclavian and internal jugular veins; the right trunk may join other trunks to form the right lymphatic duct and the left may end in the thoracic duct.

A
Most of the muscles of the larynx receive their innervation via the recurrent laryngeal branch of the vagus nerve; the exception is the cricothyroid muscle, which receives its innervation via the external laryngeal nerve. Motor supply to the muscles is from the nucleus ambiguus via the cranial accessory: to the cricothyroid via the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, and to all other laryngeal muscles, including the upper oesophagus and cricopharyngeus, via the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
B
Sensory innervation of the larynx is via branches of the vagus nerve: above the vocal folds it is via the internal laryngeal nerve, and below the vocal folds it is by way of branches of the recurrent laryngeal nerve; parasympathetic innervation of the larynx is mainly by way of branches of the vagus nerve. Lymphatic drainage similarly follows this division: above the cords to the upper deep cervical nodes, and below the cords to the lower deep cervical nodes.
