questions.answerText:
A(i)
• 3.8 cm long, an anteroposterior slit; anterior wall shorter, posterior longer; begins one inch below and in front of the tip of the coccyx at the recto-anal junction, runs down and backwards, ends at the anus.
• Relations: laterally the ischioanal fossa; posteriorly the anococcygeal raphe; anteriorly the perineal body with bulb of penis and spongy urethra (male), or perineal body and posterior vaginal wall (female).
A(ii)
• The pectinate (dentate) line is the mucocutaneous junction at the level of the anal valves; Hilton's white line lies at the lower end of the internal sphincter.
• Upper area 15 mm (columns, valves, papillae, sinuses, glands); intermediate area 15 mm (pecten, stratified squamous without sebaceous or sweat glands); lower area 8 mm (true skin).
A(iii)
Internal sphincter: thickened involuntary circular muscle around the upper three-quarters, sympathetic L1, L2 and parasympathetic S2 to S4. External sphincter: striated voluntary, whole length, subcutaneous, superficial and deep parts, supplied by the inferior rectal nerve (pudendal) and perineal branch of S4.
B(i)
Internal haemorrhoids: above Hilton's line, tributaries of the superior rectal vein, painless (primary piles at 3, 7 and 11 o'clock); external: below the line, inferior rectal vein, painful.
B(ii)
Anal sinuses are recesses above the anal columns where foreign bodies may impact and cause infection; infection of the anal glands in the sinus floors may lead to anal fistula; rupture of an anal valve with a tag is a sentinel pile.
B(iii)
Anal columns of Morgagni (6 to 10 folds with superior rectal vein radicles); anal valves of Ball form the pectinate line; anal papillae are remnants of the anal membrane.
C(i)
Above: superior rectal artery with drainage by the superior rectal vein (portal); below: inferior rectal artery (internal pudendal) with the middle rectal artery, draining to the internal iliac vein (systemic).
C(ii)
Above the pectinate line lymph goes to the internal iliac nodes; below it to the superficial inguinal nodes.
C(iii)
Above the line the fibres are autonomic and pain-insensitive to stretch; below, the inferior rectal nerve is sensitive to pain and touch.
C(iv)
Above the line is hindgut/endodermal with columnar epithelium; below is cloacal membrane/ectodermal with stratified epithelium; the lower third has somatic supply (inferior rectal nerves).

questions.answerText:
A(i)
A thin serous membrane lining the walls of the abdominal and pelvic cavities and covering the organs within; two layers: parietal and visceral.
A(ii)
• The cavity is the potential space between the layers, contains no organs and a thin layer of fluid, and is a closed sac in males; it is divided into greater and lesser sacs that communicate through the epiploic foramen.
• The fluid lubricates the surfaces so viscera move without friction, contains leukocytes and antibodies, and is absorbed by lymphatics on the inferior surface of the diaphragm.
A(iii)
• Provides a slippery surface for movement of viscera; phagocytic cells protect viscera; can store large amounts of fat.
• Mesothelial cells transform into fibroblasts, promoting healing; the mesothelium acts as a semi-permeable membrane.
A(iv)
Intraperitoneal organs are completely surrounded (stomach, spleen, small intestine); retroperitoneal organs are covered partially on their anterior surfaces only (kidney, ureter).
B(i)
• In the female the cavity communicates with the exterior through the uterine tubes, uterus and vagina, a potential pathway of infection.
• Because the mesothelium is semi-permeable, urea can be removed from blood by circulating fluids through the cavity: peritoneal dialysis.
C(i)
• Parietal: lines the inner surface of abdominal and pelvic walls and lower surface of diaphragm; loosely attached by extraperitoneal connective tissue; pain sensitive; nerve supply same as the overlying body wall.
• Visceral: lines the outer surface of viscera; cannot be stripped; nerve supply is that of the underlying viscera (sympathetic), with receptors sensitive to overdistension, traction on mesenteries, spasm and ischaemia.
• Blood supply: parietal from lumbar vessels, inferior and superior epigastric, musculophrenic and deep circumflex arteries; visceral from the arteries supplying the appropriate viscera.

questions.question:
Describe the cubital fossa:
A(i) Location and shape
A(ii) Boundaries (base, medial wall, lateral wall, apex, floor, roof)
A(iii) Contents
B. Explain the clinical basis for distinguishing the true "contents" of the cubital fossa from structures that are merely superficial to it.
C. Distinguish the position of the radial nerve in relation to the cubital fossa from that of the median nerve and brachial artery.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The cubital fossa is a triangular space, a shallow depression on the anterior surface of the elbow region, located anterior to the elbow joint, formed between two forearm muscles (brachioradialis and pronator teres).
A(ii)
Boundaries: base (superior) — an imaginary horizontal line connecting the medial and lateral epicondyles; medial (ulnar) wall — lateral border of pronator teres; lateral (radial) wall — medial border of brachioradialis; apex — directed inferiorly, where the medial and lateral boundaries meet; floor — brachialis and supinator; roof — continuity of brachial and antebrachial (deep) fascia, reinforced by the bicipital aponeurosis, superficial fascia and skin.
A(iii)
The major contents, from medial to lateral, are the median nerve, the brachial artery (which bifurcates near the apex into the radial and ulnar arteries), deep accompanying veins of the arteries, and the tendon of biceps brachii.
B
• The median cubital vein, cephalic vein and basilic vein are present in the area but are usually considered superficial to the cubital fossa and not part of its contents.
• During blood pressure measurement the stethoscope is placed over the brachial artery in the cubital fossa, and the fossa is also used to palpate the brachial pulse.
• The area just superficial to the cubital fossa is often used for venous access (phlebotomy), since it is superficial and accessible.
• The bicipital aponeurosis forms the roof of the fossa and was historically called the "grace of God" tendon because it protected the brachial artery and median nerve during blood-letting.
C
• The radial nerve is in the vicinity of the cubital fossa, located between brachialis and brachioradialis, but is often, though not always, considered part of the cubital fossa's contents.
• This differs from the median nerve and brachial artery, which are consistently listed as major contents of the fossa.
• The superficial veins similarly lie in the roof/superficial region and are related to, rather than contained within, the fossa proper.
• Venipuncture therefore uses the superficial veins overlying the fossa, while palpation of the brachial pulse and auscultation for blood pressure use the deeper true content, the brachial artery.
• This distinction between superficial and deep structures is the basis for choosing the correct site for a given clinical procedure at the elbow.

A(i)
Molecular composition: The cell membrane consists of amphipathic phospholipids arranged so that the hydrophobic tails face inward (away from water) and the more hydrophilic head regions associate with the cytosolic and extracellular environments, forming a spherical lipid bilayer. The phospholipid bilayer was proposed by Gorter and Grendel in 1925. It also includes integral membrane proteins and peripheral membrane proteins (almost half of the total mass of the membrane), a network of tiny microfilaments of the cytoskeleton, and the lipid molecule cholesterol, which stabilizes and makes the cell membrane more rigid. Functions: structural support; semi-permeable membrane (controls what molecules enter and leave the cell); establishes and maintains an electrochemical gradient; contains receptors that recognize and respond to molecular signals; supports cell adhesion and cell communication. Membrane transport mechanisms: passive (osmosis, diffusion, simple diffusion), facilitated transport, active transport (primary and secondary), and vesicular transport (endocytosis: pinocytosis and phagocytosis; exocytosis).
A(ii)
Several diseases have been implicated with defective membrane receptors. Pseudohypoparathyroidism is associated with defective parathyroid and growth hormone receptors. In these conditions, the glands produce the respective hormones, but the target cells do not respond because they lack normal receptors. Signal transduction can be hindered and cause diseases when mutations occur in the genes that encode and regulate receptor proteins.
B(i)
Integral membrane proteins: are directly incorporated within the lipid bilayer; most are transmembrane proteins passing through the entire membrane; inserted into the lipid bilayer. Functions: transport, signal transduction, structural support. Peripheral membrane proteins: exhibit a looser association with the membrane; bound to the membrane indirectly by protein-protein interactions; located on the cytosolic face. Plasma membrane contains proteins called integrins that are linked to cytoplasmic molecules; through these linkages there is a connection between the extracellular matrix and cytoplasm, mediating cell adhesion and cell communication.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the histology of the cell membrane (plasma membrane) under the following headings: molecular composition (phospholipid bilayer and proteins), functions, and membrane transport mechanisms.
A(ii) Explain the clinical basis of diseases caused by defective membrane receptors.
B(i) Distinguish between integral (transmembrane) membrane proteins and peripheral membrane proteins, stating the function of each.

A(i) Describe the basic architectural components of the liver, including the capsule, parenchyma, and the spaces between liver cells.
A(ii) There are three different ways to represent the microscopic organisation of the liver parenchyma. Name and describe each model, stating the geometric shape used and the central and peripheral reference points for each.
B(i) Describe the three zones of the hepatic acinus (acinus of Rappaport), stating what distinguishes each zone.
B(ii) Describe the complete pathway of bile flow from bile canaliculi to the duodenum.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Basic architecture:
• Capsule: the outer surface of the liver is composed of a fibrous/connective tissue capsule (Glisson's capsule); the outermost surface is covered by a thin layer of mesothelial cells that arise from the peritoneum.
• Parenchyma: the capsule surrounds the liver parenchyma, composed of hepatocytes — large polygonal cells with eosinophilic (pink) cytoplasm, round nuclei, and prominent nucleoli.
• Bile canaliculi: spaces present between the plasma membranes of adjacent liver cells.
• Perisinusoidal space of Disse: separates the surface of the liver cell from the endothelial lining of the sinusoid.
A(ii)
Three models:
• Classic (hepatic) lobule: based on blood flow; organised as hexagons, with the central vein (CV) in the centre and portal tracts (PTs) at the periphery (corners of the hexagon). Each PT consists of hepatic artery (HA), portal vein (PV), and bile duct (BD).
• Portal lobule: based on bile flow; organised as triangles, with a portal tract at the centre and central veins at the periphery (corners of the triangle). Flow of bile is in the opposite direction to blood flow.
• Hepatic acinus (acinus of Rappaport): based on blood perfusion; organised as a diamond, with portal tracts at the corners of the short axis and central veins at the corners of the long axis.
B(i)
Zones of the hepatic acinus:
• Zone 1: receives the most oxygenated blood and nutrients.
• Zone 2: intermediate oxygenation and nutrient supply.
• Zone 3: receives the least oxygenated blood and nutrients.
B(ii)
Bile flow pathway:
• Bile canaliculi → Canals of Hering → Bile ductules → Interlobular bile ducts → Intrahepatic ducts → Right and left hepatic ducts → Common hepatic duct → joins with cystic duct to form the common bile duct → Duodenum.

questions.question:
Describe the gross anatomy of the proximal carpal row/wrist region:
A(i) Bones forming the proximal row and their articulation with the radius
A(ii) The scaphoid's distinguishing feature
B. State how the scaphoid and lunate each relate to common wrist pathologies.
C. Explain how pathology at the lunate spreads to affect a distant structure, causing a functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The wrist (radiocarpal) joint is formed distally by the proximal row of carpal bones — the scaphoid, lunate and triquetrum, excluding the pisiform — and proximally by the distal end of the radius and the articular disk; the ulna is not part of the wrist joint, being prevented from articulating with the carpal bones by this fibrocartilaginous articular disk, and instead articulates with the radius at the distal radioulnar joint.
A(ii)
The scaphoid has a unique blood supply that runs from distal to proximal, unlike most bones.
B
• The scaphoid is the carpal bone most commonly fractured, more so in the younger population, typically from a blow to the wrist such as falling on an outstretched hand, when it takes most of the force.
• Because of its distal-to-proximal blood supply, a scaphoid fracture can disrupt supply to the proximal fragment; this is considered an emergency, and failure to revascularise can lead to avascular necrosis and future arthritis.
• The lunate is prone to anterior dislocation, which is uncommon but can occur by falling on a dorsiflexed wrist, forcing the lunate anteriorly.
• The lunate can also undergo avascular necrosis, so it too requires immediate clinical attention when injured.
C
• Anterior dislocation of the lunate compresses the carpal tunnel, since the lunate lies immediately related to the floor of this tunnel region.
• This compression of the carpal tunnel affects the median nerve, which lies within it.
• The resulting clinical picture manifests as paraesthesia in the sensory distribution of the median nerve.
• There is also weakness of the thenar muscles, which are supplied by the median nerve's recurrent branch.
• This produces the symptoms of carpal tunnel syndrome, even though the primary pathology (lunate dislocation) is a distinct injury from the usual causes of carpal tunnel syndrome.
• This illustrates how a purely skeletal injury at the wrist can spread to compromise an adjacent soft-tissue structure, producing a functional/sensorimotor deficit in the hand.

questions.question:
A. Describe the origin, course, and branches/distribution of the ophthalmic artery.
B. State why the ophthalmic artery and its central retinal branch are of particular functional importance to the orbit.
questions.answerText:
A
The only artery supplying structures in the orbit is the ophthalmic artery, which is a branch of the internal carotid artery; it enters the orbit with the optic nerve through the optic foramen (canal). Its branches include the lacrimal artery (to the lacrimal gland and upper eyelid), muscular branches to the muscles, long posterior ciliary arteries (to the ciliary body), short posterior ciliary arteries (to the choroid and part of the optic nerve), and medial palpebral arteries (to the eyelids).
B
The ophthalmic artery gives rise to the very important branch, the central artery of the retina; because the ophthalmic artery is the only artery supplying orbital structures, and the central retinal artery is its branch, the retina is dependent on this single arterial source, so the optic nerve is covered by dura, arachnoid and pia from the sclera to the canal, where the dura is continuous with the periosteum of the orbit, and venous drainage (superior and inferior ophthalmic veins) communicates with the cavernous sinus, giving direct communication between the skin of the face and the cavernous sinus (the danger triangle).

A(i)
• Formed by the ventral rami of L1, L2, L3 and the upper part of L4; the lower part of L4 joins L5 to form the lumbosacral trunk.
• The rami emerge from the intervertebral foramina, enter psoas, give branches to psoas and quadratus lumborum, then form the plexus within the substance of psoas major.
A(ii)
• Iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal: L1; genitofemoral: L1, L2; lateral femoral cutaneous: L2, L3 (posterior division).
• Femoral: L2, L3, L4 (posterior division); obturator: L2, L3, L4 (anterior division); sometimes an accessory obturator L3, L4.
A(iii)
• From the lateral border of psoas major: iliohypogastric, ilioinguinal, lateral femoral cutaneous, femoral.
• Through psoas anteriorly: genitofemoral; from the medial border: obturator.
A(iv)
• It innervates part of the lower abdominal wall but chiefly supplies skin and muscle 'borrowed from the trunk by the lower limb'.
• The genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve supplies the cremasteric muscle; the ilioinguinal nerve runs in the inguinal canal.
B(i)
The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve normally passes deep to the lateral end of the inguinal ligament; sometimes it passes through the substance of the ligament.
C(i)
• Entrapment causes pain along its distribution (meralgia paresthetica).
• Psoas major is supplied by ventral rami L1 to L4, psoas minor by L1, quadratus lumborum by upper lumbar and subcostal nerves, iliacus by the femoral nerve.

A(i)
The radial nerve is a terminal branch of the posterior cord of the brachial plexus; it courses posteromedially with the axillary vessels and enters the posterior compartment of the arm under teres major, where it winds around the spiral (radial) groove of the humerus, accompanied by the profunda brachii artery.
A(ii)
• It pierces the lateral intermuscular septum to enter the anterior compartment of the arm, passes to the forearm at the level of the elbow joint, enters the cubital fossa, and there divides into a superficial and a deep branch.
• The superficial branch courses toward the wrist lateral to the radial artery and enters the hand, dividing into dorsal digital cutaneous branches; the deep branch gives off the posterior interosseous nerve, which passes between the heads of supinator to enter the posterior compartment of the forearm and terminates near the wrist joint.
A(iii)
Branches include muscular twigs in the arm to triceps brachii and anconeus, the posterior interosseous nerve to the forearm extensors, the superficial (cutaneous) branch, and articular twigs to the elbow and wrist joints.
A(iv)
The deep branch/posterior interosseous nerve supplies the extensor muscles in the forearm as well as brachioradialis; the superficial branch supplies cutaneous sensation to the dorsal aspect of the hand, the dorsal aspect of the first to third digits, and the dorsolateral aspect of the fourth finger.
C
• Injury to the radial nerve produces "wrist drop."
• Because the nerve's deep branch/posterior interosseous nerve supplies the extensor muscles of the forearm, injury interrupts the motor supply to the wrist and finger extensors.
• The nerve can be injured at any level — axilla, spiral groove, radial tunnel, posterior interosseous, or superficial radial.
• Injury may result from fracture of the body (shaft) of the humerus, where the nerve lies in close contact with the bone in the spiral groove.
• "Saturday Night Palsy" describes compression of the nerve in the axilla, such as from using improperly adjusted crutches, which similarly interrupts its motor function.
• With the extensors paralysed and unopposed flexor tone at the wrist, the hand falls into flexion at the wrist, producing the characteristic wrist drop.
questions.question:
Describe the radial nerve:
A(i) Origin and course in the arm
A(ii) Course/division in the cubital fossa and forearm
A(iii) Branches
A(iv) Distribution
C. Explain the anatomical basis of the deformity ("wrist drop") seen after radial nerve injury.

Describe the hip joint under the following headings and explain its clinical correlates.
A(i) Type and articular surfaces
A(ii) Capsule, ligaments — name, attachments and function of each
B(i) Nerve supply, applying Hilton's law
B(ii) Movements and muscles responsible for each movement
C(i) Explain why referred pain from the hip can present at the knee, and distinguish coxa valga from coxa vara
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The hip joint is a multiaxial ball-and-socket type of synovial joint. It is the largest joint in the human body and the 2nd largest weight-bearing joint. Articular surfaces: the lunate surface of the acetabulum (covered by hyaline cartilage except at the fovea) and the spherical head of femur (which forms 2/3 of a sphere, covered by hyaline cartilage except at the fovea capitis). The acetabulum is deepened by the fibrocartilaginous acetabular labrum; it is deficient inferiorly as the acetabular notch, bridged by the transverse acetabular ligament.
A(ii)
Capsule: strong and thick; medially attached to margin of acetabulum, transverse acetabular ligament, and adjacent margin of obturator foramen; laterally attached to the intertrochanteric line anteriorly. Ligaments: (1) Iliofemoral ligament (ligament of Bigelow) — one of the strongest in the body, Y-shaped; apex at inferior iliac spine, base to intertrochanteric line; prevents overextension and prevents trunk from falling backwards while standing. (2) Pubofemoral ligament — triangular; attached superiorly to iliopubic eminence and obturator crest, inferiorly merges with capsule; limits extension and abduction. (3) Ischiofemoral ligament — reinforces posterior aspect; medially attached to ischium posteroinferior to acetabulum, laterally to greater trochanter deep to the iliofemoral ligament; limits extension. Fibers of all three spiral so they become taut in extension, stabilizing the joint and reducing muscle energy needed for standing. Ligament teres (round ligament): flat triangular band from fovea to acetabular notch and transverse ligament; ensheathed by synovial membrane; transmits arteries to head of femur.
B(i)
By Hilton's law: the nerve supplying the joint also supplies the muscles moving the joint and the skin covering the insertion of those muscles. Nerve supply: femoral nerve, anterior division of obturator nerve, nerve to rectus femoris, nerve to quadratus femoris, sciatic nerve, and superior gluteal nerve. The posterior division of the obturator nerve supplies both the hip and the knee joint.
B(ii)
Flexion (120–140°): iliopsoas, sartorius, rectus femoris, tensor fasciae latae. Extension: gluteus maximus, semimembranosus, semitendinosus, biceps femoris. Abduction (60–80°): gluteus medius, minimus, tensor fasciae latae. Adduction: pectineus, adductor longus, brevis, magnus, gracilis. Medial rotation: gluteus medius, minimus, tensor fasciae latae. Lateral rotation: obturator internus and externus, gemellus superior and inferior, quadratus femoris, piriformis, posterior fibres of gluteus medius and minimus, superior fibres of gluteus maximus.
C(i)
The posterior division of the obturator nerve supplies both the hip and knee joints; pain from hip pathology is therefore referred along this common nerve pathway to the knee joint. Coxa valga follows congenital dislocation of the head of femur; coxa vara follows fracture of the neck of femur.

questions.question:
A(i) Define the diaphragm and describe its shape, position and relations.
A(ii) Describe its origin (sternal, costal and vertebral, including the crura and arcuate ligaments) and its insertion.
A(iii) Describe its openings, their vertebral levels and the structures transmitted.
A(iv) Describe its blood supply.
A(v) Describe its nerve supply and lymphatic drainage.
B(i) Explain the anatomical basis of referred shoulder pain from irritation of the diaphragm.
B(ii) Explain why acquired herniae occur through the oesophageal opening and name the two types.
B(iii) Explain hiccup.
C(i) Distinguish between the right and the left crus of the diaphragm.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
A double-domed, thin fibromuscular (musculotendinous) partition between the thoracic and abdominal cavities and the main muscle of respiration; convex superior surface faces the thorax (covered by diaphragmatic pleura, lungs fit the domes, fibrous pericardium on the central tendon), concave inferior surface faces the abdomen (parietal peritoneum; liver, kidneys, suprarenals, stomach, spleen); higher on the right because of the liver (in expiration the right dome reaches the 5th rib, the left the 5th intercostal space); level varies with respiration, posture and abdominal distension, and the domes flatten in maximal inspiration.
A(ii)
Sternal: 2 slips from the posterior xiphoid process; costal: deep surfaces of the lower 6 ribs and costal cartilages (forms the domes); vertebral: the crura and 3 arcuate ligaments - medial (thickened psoas fascia, from the body of L2 to the tip of the L1 transverse process), lateral (thickened quadratus lumborum fascia, from the L1 transverse process to the lower border of the 12th rib) and median (joins the crura across the front of the aorta). Insertion: trefoil central tendon, no bony attachments, partly fused with the fibrous pericardium (pericardiophrenic ligament).
A(iii)
• Caval opening (T8; the only opening in the central tendon): IVC, terminal branches of the right phrenic nerve, a few lymphatics. Oesophageal opening (T10; in the right crus): oesophagus, anterior and posterior vagal trunks, oesophageal branches of the left gastric vessels, a few lymphatics. Aortic opening (T12; lowest and most posterior, between the crura): aorta, thoracic duct, sometimes azygos and hemiazygos veins.
• Smaller openings: greater and lesser splanchnic nerves pierce each crus; hemiazygos vein pierces the left crus; left phrenic nerve pierces the left dome; sympathetic trunks pass behind the diaphragm deep to the medial arcuate ligament; subcostal vessels and nerve pass behind the lateral arcuate ligament; superior epigastric vessels pass between the sternal and costal origins; 7th-11th intercostal neurovascular bundles pass through the costal origin.
A(iv)
Arteries: pericardiophrenic and musculophrenic (from the internal thoracic) and superior phrenic (from the thoracic aorta) to the superior surface; inferior phrenic (first branches of the abdominal aorta) to the inferior surface. Veins: pericardiophrenic and musculophrenic to the internal thoracic vein; superior phrenic vein (right) and right inferior phrenic vein to the IVC; the left inferior phrenic vein drains to the IVC and the left suprarenal vein.
A(v)
• Motor: phrenic nerves (C3-5) only - the right nerve to the right half up to the right margin of the oesophageal opening, the left to the left half. Sensory: central part (with related pleura and peritoneum) via the phrenic nerves; peripheral part via the lower 6 or 7 intercostal and subcostal nerves.
• Lymph: thoracic surface to anterior and posterior diaphragmatic nodes (anterior on to parasternal nodes; posterior to phrenic and posterior mediastinal nodes); abdominal surface to anterior diaphragmatic, phrenic and superior lumbar (caval/aortic) nodes.
B(i)
The central diaphragm is supplied sensorily by the phrenic nerve (C3-5) and the shoulder skin by the supraclavicular nerve (C3,4); so pain from irritation of pleura or pericardium over the central diaphragm, or of the peritoneum under it by subphrenic pus or blood, is referred to the shoulder tip.
B(ii)
Acquired herniae occur in middle-aged people with weak musculature around the oesophageal opening; they are either sliding or paraoesophageal (rolling, alongside the oesophagus).
B(iii)
Hiccup is an involuntary spasmodic contraction of the diaphragm with approximation of the vocal folds and closure of the glottis; common after eating or drinking from gastric irritation of vagus nerve endings; it may be due to pleurisy, peritonitis or pericarditis.
C(i)
• Right crus: larger and longer, arises from the upper 3 lumbar vertebrae (L1-L3) and their intervertebral discs; some of its fibres pass up to the left and loop round the oesophageal orifice as a physiological sphincter preventing reflux of gastric contents.
• Left crus: smaller, arises from the side of the bodies of the upper 2 (L1-L2) lumbar vertebrae and their discs; each crus is attached to the medial and lateral arcuate ligaments, and the medial borders of the two crura unite in front of T12 as the median arcuate ligament over the aorta.

A(i)
Cell body (soma): The neuronal cell body is similar to other cell types; it has a nucleus with at least one nucleolus and many typical cytoplasmic organelles. It lacks centrioles, which is consistent with the amitotic nature of neurons. Dendrites: Dendrites are cytoplasmic extensions that project from the cell body; they are usually short and branching, increasing their surface area to receive signals from other neurons. The number of dendrites varies. They are called afferent processes because they transmit impulses to the neuron cell body. Axon: There is only one axon projecting from each cell body; it is usually elongated and carries impulses away from the cell body, so it is called an efferent process. Axons may have infrequent branches called axon collaterals; these terminate in short branches or telodendria, whose distal ends are slightly enlarged to form synaptic bulbs. Myelin sheath: Many axons are surrounded by a segmented, white, fatty substance called myelin or myelin sheath. Myelinated fibers make up the white matter in the CNS, while cell bodies and unmyelinated fibers make the gray matter. Nodes of Ranvier: The unmyelinated regions between myelin segments are called nodes of Ranvier. Neurilemma: In the peripheral nervous system, myelin is produced by Schwann cells. The cytoplasm, nucleus, and outer cell membrane of the Schwann cell form a tight covering around the myelin and around the axon at the nodes of Ranvier — this covering is the neurilemma, which plays an important role in regeneration of nerve fibers.
A(ii)
Most local anesthetics are low-molecular-weight molecules that bind to the voltage-gated sodium channels of the axolemma, interfering with sodium ion influx and, consequently, inhibiting the action potential responsible for the nerve impulse.
B(i)
In the CNS, oligodendrocytes produce myelin, but there is no neurilemma. It is the neurilemma that plays an important role in regeneration of nerve fibers; therefore fibers within the CNS do not regenerate because they lack neurilemma.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the origin, structural components, and classification of neurons under the following headings: cell body (soma), dendrites, axon, myelin sheath, nodes of Ranvier, and neurilemma.
A(ii) State the basis of why local anaesthetics block nerve impulse transmission.
B(i) Explain the anatomical basis of why nerve fibers within the CNS do not regenerate after injury, while peripheral nerve fibers may regenerate.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Four stomach regions:
• Cardia and pylorus are histologically similar: tubular glands with long pits usually branching into coiled secretory portions (cardiac and pyloric glands respectively); pits are longer in the pylorus; lack both parietal and chief cells; major secretion is abundant mucus.
• Fundus and body are histologically identical: simple columnar epithelium invaginates to form gastric pits leading into long, branched, tubular gastric glands; 3 to 7 glands usually open into the bottom of each gastric pit; contain all four secretory cell types; involved in secretion of acidic gastric juice.
A(ii)
Structure of fundic/body glands:
• Each gland has three named parts: isthmus, neck, and base.
• Isthmus: the region of stem cells (between the gastric pit and gland); the pluripotent stem cells divide asymmetrically and can move upward or downward to replace epithelial cells.
• Neck: contains mucous neck cells (MNCs) in clusters or singly; also contains parietal cells.
• Base: predominantly chief (zymogen) cells; also contains enteroendocrine cells.
B(i)
Mucous neck cells (MNCs):
• Present in clusters or singly in the necks of gastric glands.
• Less columnar than surface mucous cells; irregular in shape with round nucleus and apical secretory granules.
• Their mucous secretion is less alkaline than that of the surface epithelial mucous cells; they secrete acidic fluid containing mucin (not mucus, which implies alkaline content).
B(ii)
Intrinsic factor:
• Produced by: parietal (oxyntic) cells.
• Chemical nature: a glycoprotein.
• Function: required for the uptake of vitamin B12 in the small intestine.
• Deficiency and anaemia: if parietal cells are damaged, insufficient quantities of intrinsic factor are secreted; without adequate intrinsic factor, vitamin B12 is not absorbed adequately; low levels of vitamin B12 reduce the proliferation of erythroblasts, resulting in pernicious anaemia.

A(ii) Explain the complete structure and function of the gastric glands of the fundus/body, including the isthmus, neck, and base, and what cells are found in each part.
B(i) Explain the full role of mucous neck cells in the gastric gland, comparing their secretion to that of surface mucous cells.
B(ii) Describe where intrinsic factor is produced, what it is chemically, what it does, and how its deficiency leads to anaemia.

Describe the median nerve:
A(i) Formation (roots)
A(ii) Relations in the cubital fossa and at the wrist
A(iii) Branches
A(iv) Distribution
C. Explain the anatomical basis of the deformity seen after a low (wrist-level) injury to the median nerve.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The median nerve is formed by the union of a lateral root from the lateral cord (C5, C6, C7) and a medial root from the medial cord (C8, T1) of the brachial plexus.
A(ii)
In the cubital fossa the median nerve is the most medial of the major vertical contents, lying medial to the brachial artery and the tendon of biceps brachii; at the wrist it lies anterior to the tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis, deep to the flexor retinaculum, within the carpal tunnel.
A(iii)
It gives a palmar cutaneous branch that arises in the forearm, proximal to the flexor retinaculum, and a recurrent branch that arises in the hand to supply the thenar muscles.
A(iv)
It supplies flexor carpi radialis, palmaris longus, pronator teres, pronator quadratus and the digital flexors, producing thumb flexion and opposition, flexion of digits 2 and 3, wrist flexion and abduction, and forearm pronation; it also supplies sensation to the anterolateral surface of the hand.
C
• A low (wrist-level) median nerve injury produces an "ape-like hand."
• There is flattening of the thenar eminence because the recurrent branch supplying abductor pollicis brevis and flexor pollicis brevis, which arises in the hand, is affected.
• Opposition and abduction of the thumb become impossible, so the pincer-like action of the hand is lost, causing difficulty with fine manual tasks such as buttoning.
• Adductor pollicis, being supplied by the ulnar nerve, is unopposed, further contributing to the deformity.
• This contrasts with an elbow-level injury, where flexion of the index and middle fingers is lost (flexor digitorum superficialis and the lateral half of profundus are affected), the ring and little fingers weakly flex, and flexion of the distal phalanx of the thumb is lost, while the interosseous muscles are unaffected, being supplied by the ulnar nerve.
• The median nerve can be torn partially or fully, or compressed, at the elbow, from fracture, other trauma, or compression from fluid build-up following injury.
• The most common site of median nerve injury overall is at the wrist, within the carpal tunnel.

questions.question:
(i) Describe the gross anatomy of the heart under the headings: chambers, borders and surfaces.
(ii) Relate the chambers/valves of the heart to a recognised pathology.
(iii) Explain how a cardiac problem can produce a functional deficit or sensation felt at a distant site.
questions.answerText:
(i)
• The heart has four chambers, the right and left atria (receiving chambers) and the right and left ventricles (discharging chambers), enclosed in the double-walled pericardial sac, and rests on its diaphragmatic (inferior) surface.
• It has an apex, formed by the inferolateral part of the left ventricle and lying posterior to the 5th intercostal space where the apex beat is felt, a base, formed mainly by the left atrium and part of the right atrium, four borders and three surfaces.
• The right border is formed mainly by the right atrium; the left border by the left ventricle and left auricle; the inferior border by the right ventricle mainly and the left ventricle; the superior border by both atria, auricles and the great vessels.
• The anterior (sternocostal) surface consists chiefly of the right ventricle; the inferior (diaphragmatic) surface consists chiefly of the left ventricle and a small part of the right ventricle; the left (pulmonary) surface is formed mainly by the left ventricle.
• The right atrium receives venous blood from the SVC, IVC and coronary sinus, has a smooth sinus venarum and a rough muscular wall with pectinate muscles, and communicates with the right ventricle via the right atrioventricular (tricuspid) orifice.
• The left atrium receives the four pulmonary veins and communicates with the left ventricle via the left atrioventricular (mitral) orifice; the right ventricle has a tricuspid valve and leads to the pulmonary trunk via the conus arteriosus, while the left ventricle, with twice the wall thickness, has the mitral valve and leads to the aorta via the aortic vestibule and aortic valve.
(ii)
• Valvular insufficiency results from valve leaflets not completely sealing when a valve is closed, so regurgitation of blood occurs into the proximal chamber, generating a characteristic heart murmur.
• Positional and septal anomalies include dextrocardia, atrial septal defects and ventricular septal defects.
• Aortic dissection, a tear in the inner wall of the aorta associated with high blood pressure, and aortic aneurysm, dilation of an artery greater than 50% of its normal diameter, are pathologies of the great vessel arising from the left ventricle.
(iii)
• The conducting system, the SA node in the posterior wall of the right atrium, the AV node in the floor of the right atrium, the AV bundle and Purkinje fibres, initiates and coordinates the heartbeat; damage to a coronary artery supplying these nodes can disturb heart rhythm.
• Cardiac afferent fibres carrying pain from ischaemic myocardium travel via sympathetic afferents in the cardiac plexus to spinal cord segments T1-T5 shared with dermatomes of the chest wall and upper limb, so the central nervous system perceives cardiac pain as coming from the body wall.
• This explains why myocardial ischaemia is felt as pain in the mid or left chest that radiates to the left jaw and left arm, a distant somatic sensation produced by a cardiac (visceral) problem.

A(i)
The surface marking of the base of the appendix is McBurney's point, at the junction of the lateral one-third and medial two-thirds of a line drawn from the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus. The appendix is attached to the cecum below the ileocaecal valve, and the teniae coli of the cecum converge at the root of the appendix.
A(ii)
The appendix is one of the intraperitoneal parts of the large intestine, suspended by its own mesentery, the mesoappendix.
A(iii)
The appendix opens at the posteromedial aspect of the cecum, about one inch below the ileocaecal junction; its positions include retrocecal, the most common, pelvic, subcecal, preileal, and postileal, the least common.
B
• Deep tenderness at McBurney's point, McBurney's sign, is the clinical sign used to localise inflammation of the appendix, that is, acute appendicitis.
• The appendix is described as an intestinal tonsil because of the abundant lymphatic nodules in its lamina propria, which extend into the submucosa and give it an immune function, similar to the tonsils.
C
• Grossly, the appendix has no teniae coli and shows various shapes and positions, whereas the rest of the colon shows three longitudinal teniae coli, free, mesocolic and omental, which converge at the root of the appendix.
• The colon has haustra (sacculations), because the teniae are shorter than the length of the gut wall, appendices epiploicae (fat-filled peritoneal pouches), and semilunar folds; the appendix lacks these features.
• Microscopically, the appendix has no villi and its crypts (of Lieberkuhn) are less abundant than in the colon.
• The colon's mucosa shows enterocytes with no digestive enzyme production, water and electrolyte reabsorption, deep crypts, a thick mucin layer, and goblet cells that increase in number caudally.
• The appendix has prominent lymphatic nodules in the lamina propria extending into the submucosa, which are far less prominent in the general colon.
• Both the appendix and colon lack villi, unlike the small intestine, but only the appendix is described as functioning analogously to the tonsils.

(A) Describe the vermiform appendix under the headings: A(i) surface anatomy/position A(ii) peritoneal relations A(iii) opening and possible positions.
(B) Explain the clinical basis of tenderness at McBurney's point in appendicitis.
(C) Distinguish the appendix from the rest of the large intestine (colon) in gross and microscopic structure.

questions.answerText:
A
The pterygopalatine fossa is an inverted pyramidal-shaped, fat-filled space located on the lateral side of the skull, between the infratemporal fossa and the nasopharynx; it is antero-posteriorly between the maxilla/palatine bone and the pterygoid process, and laterally between the infratemporal fossa and nasopharynx. Its boundaries are: anterior - posterior surface of maxilla below the floor of the orbit; posterior - lateral pterygoid plate and part of the medial plate; medial - perpendicular plate of the palatine bone; lateral - pterygomaxillary fissure; superior - undersurface of the greater wing of the sphenoid; inferior - absent (the posterior wall meets the anterior wall, and between them is the greater palatine canal). Its contents are the terminal (third/pterygoid) part of the maxillary artery and the initial parts of its branches, the maxillary vein, the maxillary nerve, and the pterygopalatine ganglion (a parasympathetic ganglion, one of four parasympathetic ganglia of the head and neck, the others being the submandibular, otic and ciliary ganglia).
B
The pterygopalatine fossa is described as a major neurovascular crossroad between the orbit, the nasal cavity, the nasopharynx, the oral cavity, the infratemporal fossa and the cranial fossa. Its communications are: laterally with the infratemporal fossa through the pterygomaxillary fissure; medially with the nasal cavity through the sphenopalatine foramen; anterosuperiorly with the orbit through the inferior orbital fissure; posterosuperiorly with the middle cranial fossa through the foramen rotundum and pterygoid canal; with the palate through the greater and lesser palatine canals and foramina; and with the pharynx through the pterygoid canal and palatovaginal canal - in general, vascular structures enter the fossa through its lateral wall, while nerve structures enter through its posterior wall.
C
Because the pterygopalatine fossa communicates directly with the orbit (via the inferior orbital fissure), the nasal cavity (via the sphenopalatine foramen), the middle cranial fossa (via the foramen rotundum and pterygoid canal), and the pharynx (via the pterygoid canal and palatovaginal canal), disease or infection arising in or near the fossa has multiple direct anatomical routes by which it can spread to these distant sites; clinical correlates noted for this region include hay fever affecting the ganglion here (the pterygopalatine ganglion is also known as the hay fever ganglion), and maxillary nerve block is performed in relation to this fossa.
questions.question:
A. Describe the gross anatomy of the pterygopalatine fossa under the following headings: description/location, boundaries, and contents.
B. State the communications of the pterygopalatine fossa and relate these to how disease may spread from this region.
C. Explain why disease or infection arising near the pterygopalatine fossa can spread to distant structures such as the orbit, the nasal cavity, the middle cranial fossa or the pharynx, and the functional deficit that could result.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
The bony wall is the carpal sulcus, formed by the concavity on the anterior aspect of the carpal bones, forming the base and sides of the tunnel; it is bounded laterally by the scaphoid and trapezium tubercles and medially by the hook of the hamate and the pisiform.
A(ii)
The fibrous wall is the flexor retinaculum, a thick connective tissue band that stretches over the carpal sulcus, converting it into the carpal tunnel by bridging the space between the medial and lateral parts of the arch, spanning from the hook of hamate and pisiform medially to the scaphoid and trapezium laterally.
A(iii)
Contents: four tendons of flexor digitorum profundus (the deepest structures), four tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis lying anterior to those of profundus (all eight enclosed in a common synovial sheath), the tendon of flexor pollicis longus occupying the lateral angle of the compartment with its own synovial sheath, and the median nerve, which lies anterior to the tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis, deep to the flexor retinaculum.
B
• Carpal tunnel syndrome may occur following inflammatory reactions (synovitis) in the synovial sheath of the tendons traversing the tunnel.
• Excess fluid, such as follows inflammation of the synovial sheaths, compresses the structures within the confined tunnel.
• The median nerve is the structure most adversely affected, since it lies anterior to the crowded flexor tendons, immediately deep to the unyielding flexor retinaculum, leaving it particularly exposed to any rise in pressure within the tunnel.
• Compression of the median nerve produces sensory disturbance (hypoesthesia or anaesthesia) in the skin of the lateral three and a half fingers on their palmar aspect.
• Weakness or paralysis of the thenar muscles also occurs, because the recurrent branch of the median nerve that supplies these muscles arises in the hand and is also compressed.
C
• Within the tunnel, the tendons of flexor digitorum profundus are the deepest structures.
• The tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis lie anterior to (more superficial than) those of profundus.
• Both sets of four tendons are enclosed together in a single common synovial sheath, whereas the tendon of flexor pollicis longus lies separately at the lateral angle of the compartment, enclosed in its own distinct synovial sheath.
• This layered arrangement of tendons deep to the median nerve means the nerve is the most superficial of the tunnel's principal contents, most exposed to the flexor retinaculum's unyielding roof.
questions.question:

A(i) Bony wall (carpal arch/sulcus)

A(iii) Contents

questions.answerText:
A(i)
The quadrangular cartilaginous septum extends from the nasal bones in the midline above to the bony septum in the midline posteriorly, then down along the bony floor. Its upper half is flanked by two triangular-to-trapezoidal cartilages, the upper lateral cartilages, which are fused to the dorsal septum in the midline and attached to the bony margin of the pyriform aperture laterally by loose ligaments; the inferior ends of the upper lateral cartilages are free. Beneath the upper lateral cartilages lie the lower lateral cartilages; the paired lower lateral cartilages swing out from medial attachments to the caudal septum in the midline (the medial crura), through an intermediate crus area, finally flaring out superolaterally as the lateral crura; these cartilages are frequently mobile, in contradistinction to the upper lateral cartilages. The internal area or angle formed by the septum and upper lateral cartilage constitutes the internal valve.
A(ii)
The nasal septum is supplied from the sphenopalatine artery (posterior septal branch) and the anterior and posterior ethmoid arteries, with contribution of the superior labial artery (anteriorly) and the greater palatine artery (posteriorly).
B
The Kiesselbach plexus, or Little's area, represents a region in the anteroinferior third of the nasal septum where all 3 of the chief blood supplies to the internal nose converge, which is the clinical basis for this being a common site of nosebleeds; venous blood leaving the region drains into the facial, ophthalmic and sphenopalatine veins, and these veins are significant for their direct communication with the cavernous sinus and for their lack of valves, features that potentiate the intracranial spread of infection.
C
The upper lateral cartilages are fused to the dorsal septum in the midline and attached to the bony margin of the pyriform aperture laterally by loose ligaments, with their inferior ends free; they are relatively fixed. The lower lateral (alar) cartilages, by contrast, swing out from medial attachments to the caudal septum (the medial crura) to flare out superolaterally as the lateral crura, and are frequently mobile, unlike the upper lateral cartilages.
questions.question:

A(ii) Describe the blood supply to the nasal septum.
B. Explain the clinical basis for why the anteroinferior third of the nasal septum is the commonest site of nosebleeds (epistaxis).
