questions.answerText:
A
A V-shaped groove, the sulcus terminalis, demarcates the anterior two-thirds of the tongue from the posterior one-third. The intrinsic muscles of the tongue are the superior longitudinal, inferior longitudinal, transverse, and vertical muscles. The extrinsic muscles are the genioglossus, styloglossus, palatoglossus, and hyoglossus. The mucosa of the anterior two-thirds is formed into papillae (filiform, fungiform, circumvallate, foliate), which contain taste buds.
B
Clinical correlates involving the tongue include loss of taste sensation, bifid tongue, tongue tie (ankyloglossia), microglossia/macroglossia, and lingual carcinoma. Nerve supply differs by region: in the anterior two-thirds, motor supply to the muscles is via CN XII (except palatoglossus, supplied by the pharyngeal plexus of the vagus nerve), sensory supply to the mucous membrane is via the lingual nerve (a branch of CN V3), and special (taste) sensory supply is via the chorda tympani nerve (a branch of CN VII); in the posterior one-third, motor supply is via CN XII, and sensory supply (general and special) is via the lingual branch of CN IX and the internal laryngeal nerve (a branch of CN X).
C
Lymphatic drainage of the tongue takes 4 routes: the posterior third drains to the superior deep cervical lymph nodes; the medial part of the anterior two-thirds drains to the inferior deep cervical lymph nodes; the lateral parts of the anterior two-thirds drain to the submandibular lymph nodes; and the apex of the tongue drains to the submental lymph nodes - with the posterior third and the area near the midline draining bilaterally. Because disease (such as lingual carcinoma) arising in a particular region of the tongue follows that region's specific lymphatic drainage route, it can spread to produce nodal or functional deficits at lymph node groups that are anatomically distant from the primary site, with the pattern of spread differing depending on which part of the tongue is affected, and bilateral drainage from the posterior third and midline region meaning disease there can involve lymph nodes on both sides of the neck.
questions.question:
A. Describe the gross anatomy of the tongue under the following headings: division into anterior and posterior parts, and the intrinsic and extrinsic muscles.
B. State how the different regions of the tongue relate to common developmental and pathological conditions.
C. Explain why disease affecting one region of the tongue can produce a functional deficit at a distant site, based on its lymphatic drainage pattern.

Describe the gross anatomy of the humerus:
A(i) Upper end
A(ii) Shaft
A(iii) Lower end
B. State how different parts of the humerus relate to common fracture patterns.
C. Explain how injury at each of these parts may spread to affect a distant structure, causing a functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• The upper end has a large, rounded head joined to the shaft by a constricted surgical neck, and greater and lesser tubercles.
• The tubercles are separated by the intertubercular (bicipital) groove, which lodges the long tendon of biceps brachii and transmits a branch of the anterior humeral circumflex artery to the shoulder joint.
A(ii)
The shaft is circular in section above and flattened in its lower part, bears the deltoid tuberosity, and its posterior aspect shows the spiral groove, which demarcates the origins of the medial and lateral heads of triceps and between which the radial nerve and profunda vessels wind.
A(iii)
The lower end bears the rounded capitulum laterally, for articulation with the radial head, and the spool-shaped trochlea medially, for articulation with the trochlear notch of the ulna; the medial and lateral epicondyles are extracapsular, the medial being the larger, extending more distally and bearing a groove on its posterior aspect for the ulnar nerve.
B
• Fractures of the surgical neck of the humerus are especially common in elderly people with osteoporosis, usually from a minor fall on the hand with the force transmitted up the extended limb.
• Transverse fractures of the shaft frequently result from a direct blow to the arm.
• Fracture of the distal humerus, near the supracondylar ridges, is a supracondylar fracture.
C
• Because the axillary, radial and ulnar nerves are in close contact with the humerus, they may be damaged when the associated part of the bone is fractured.
• Fracture at the surgical neck threatens the axillary nerve, producing deltoid paralysis with loss of abduction and sensory loss over the regimental badge area.
• Fracture through the radial (spiral) groove of the shaft threatens the radial nerve, producing wrist drop.
• Fracture at the medial epicondyle at the lower end threatens the ulnar nerve, while injury at the distal humerus (supracondylar region) threatens the median nerve.
• Fractures of the humeral neck, midshaft and lower end are therefore each associated with a characteristic pattern of nerve injury and resultant functional deficit.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the orbit under the following headings: shape, the bones forming it, and its average dimensions.
A(ii) Describe the three openings into the orbital cavity and the structures transmitted through each, and describe the connective tissue planes of the orbit.
B. Explain the clinical basis for why orbital trauma can result in double vision and in a rise of intraocular pressure.
C. Distinguish between the superior orbital fissure and the inferior orbital fissure in terms of the structures each transmits.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The orbit is shaped like a pear or quadrilateral pyramid, with its base in the plane of the orbital rim and its pyramidal cavity base in front and apex behind; it protects, supports and maximises the function of the eye, and seven bones conjoin to form the orbital structure. The average dimensions of the orbit are: height of orbital margin 40 mm, width of orbital margin 35 mm, depth of orbit 40-50 mm, interorbital distance 25 mm, and volume of orbit 30 cm³; 20% of this space is occupied by the eyeball, and about one-sixth of the eye is exposed, the remainder being protected by the walls of the orbit.
A(ii)
The major nerves and vessels to the orbit and globe enter through 3 openings. The superior orbital fissure, bounded by the lesser and greater wings of the sphenoid, transmits cranial nerves III, IV and VI, the lacrimal nerve, frontal nerve, nasociliary nerve, orbital branch of the middle meningeal artery, recurrent branch of the lacrimal artery, superior orbital vein and superior ophthalmic vein. The inferior orbital fissure, bounded by the greater wing of the sphenoid, the maxilla and the palatine bones, transmits the infraorbital nerve, zygomatic nerve, parasympathetics to the lacrimal gland, infraorbital artery, infraorbital vein, and the inferior ophthalmic vein branch to the pterygoid plexus. The optic canal, at the apex of the orbit within the sphenoid bone, transmits the optic nerve, ophthalmic artery, and central retinal vein. The connective tissue boundaries of the orbit are divided into 4 main units: the bulbar (Tenon) fascia, surrounding and protecting the globe and providing a barrier between the globe and retrobulbar fat; multiple connective tissue septa extending from the globe to the periorbita like spokes on a wheel; the individual connective tissue sheath of each extraocular muscle, which fuses to form a confluent muscle sheath and the medial and lateral check ligaments; and the periosteal lining of the orbit, which can be elevated in surgery to expose the bony orbit.
B
Clinical correlates of the orbit include eye trauma with blow-out fracture, due to blunt trauma, which displaces the orbital walls; paralysis of the extraocular muscles results in double vision. Obstruction of the flow of aqueous humor results in a rise in intraocular pressure called glaucoma, leading to degenerative changes in the retina with consequent blindness.
C
The superior orbital fissure transmits cranial nerves III, IV and VI, the lacrimal, frontal and nasociliary nerves, the orbital branch of the middle meningeal artery, the recurrent branch of the lacrimal artery, and the superior orbital and superior ophthalmic veins. The inferior orbital fissure, in contrast, transmits the infraorbital nerve, the zygomatic nerve, parasympathetics to the lacrimal gland, the infraorbital artery and vein, and the inferior ophthalmic vein branch to the pterygoid plexus.

questions.question:
Describe the region of the ulnar nerve at the elbow:
A(i) Common sites of entrapment
A(ii) Relation to the elbow joint
B. Explain the clinical basis for the ulnar nerve being vulnerable at the elbow.
C. Distinguish between the ulnar nerve's entrapment region at the elbow and the median nerve's carpal tunnel at the wrist.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The most common sites of ulnar nerve entrapment around the elbow are: above the elbow, in the region of the intermuscular septum; the medial epicondylar region; the epicondylar (ulnar) groove; the region of the cubital tunnel; and the point where the nerve exits from flexor carpi ulnaris, where the usual cause of compression is the deep flexor-pronator aponeurosis.
A(ii)
Medially, in relation to the elbow joint, the ulnar nerve passes behind the medial epicondyle and crosses the medial collateral ligament of the joint.
B
• The medial epicondyle of the humerus bears a groove on its posterior aspect specifically for the ulnar nerve, and the medial epicondyle is the larger of the two epicondyles, extending more distally.
• This places the ulnar nerve in a relatively superficial, subcutaneous position as it passes behind the medial epicondyle and through the cubital tunnel region, making it vulnerable to direct trauma and to compression at each of the sites listed above.
• Ulnar nerve injuries are recognised as a distinct item of applied anatomy at the elbow, alongside subluxation/dislocation of the radial head, the carrying angle, olecranon bursitis, avulsion of the medial epicondyle, and dislocation with Volkmann's ischaemic contracture.
C
• The ulnar nerve's entrapment region at the elbow lies behind the medial epicondyle of the humerus, where it crosses the medial collateral ligament of the elbow joint, and where compression is often caused by the deep flexor-pronator aponeurosis as the nerve exits between the heads of flexor carpi ulnaris.
• The median nerve's tunnel at the wrist, the carpal tunnel, differs in that it has a defined bony floor — the carpal sulcus, bounded laterally by the scaphoid and trapezium and medially by the hook of hamate and pisiform — roofed by the fibrous flexor retinaculum.
• The carpal tunnel additionally transmits eight flexor tendons and the tendon of flexor pollicis longus alongside the median nerve, whereas other tendons sharing the ulnar nerve's entrapment site at the elbow are not described.
• Both regions, however, are sites where a single major nerve is placed in a confined space adjacent to bone, predisposing it to compression.
• At the elbow, injury or entrapment of the ulnar nerve is associated with claw hand and sensory/motor deficits in the ulnar nerve distribution of the hand and forearm.
• At the wrist, compression of the median nerve within the carpal tunnel produces carpal tunnel syndrome, with sensory disturbance in the lateral three and a half digits and weakness of the thenar muscles.
• The comparison illustrates a shared anatomical principle, nerve entrapment at a narrow passage, applied to two different nerves at two different levels of the upper limb.

(i)
• The liver has two surfaces - a convex diaphragmatic surface (anterior, superior, posterior and right lateral) and a relatively flat, posteroinferior visceral surface.
• It is divided into a large right lobe and a smaller left lobe by the falciform ligament, with the caudate and quadrate lobes arising from the right lobe on the visceral surface.
• Two sagittally oriented fissures (for the ligamentum teres and ligamentum venosum on the left, and the gallbladder fossa and IVC groove on the right) are linked by the transverse porta hepatis, forming an H on the visceral surface.
• Ligaments include the falciform ligament, the coronary ligament with the right and left triangular ligaments, and the lesser omentum (hepatogastric and hepatoduodenal ligaments).
• The porta hepatis transmits the hepatic ducts, hepatic artery and portal vein branches, and hepatic nerves and lymph nodes.
(ii)
• The bare area of the diaphragmatic surface has no peritoneal covering, so infection there can track through the diaphragm to posterior mediastinal lymph nodes.
• The subphrenic and subhepatic spaces, and Morison's pouch between the liver and right kidney, are recesses where pathological fluid such as pus, blood or ascites collects.
• Liver fissures serve as surgical landmarks, such as Cantlie's line, which divides the liver into functional right and left lobes along the middle hepatic vein.
• Because the liver is large, fixed in position and friable, it is vulnerable to rupture, often from a fractured rib perforating the diaphragm, causing haemorrhage and right upper quadrant pain.
(iii)
• In cirrhosis, hepatocytes are destroyed and replaced by fibrous tissue that impedes blood flow through the liver, causing portal hypertension.
• This opens portal-systemic anastomoses at the lower oesophagus, anal canal, paraumbilical region, retroperitoneum and intrahepatic sites, producing distant complications such as bleeding oesophageal varices.
• Distension of Glisson's capsule from an enlarged liver produces sharp, well-localised pain via the lower intercostal nerves, illustrating how a hepatic process produces a distant sensory effect.
questions.question:
(i) Describe the gross anatomy of the liver under the headings: surfaces, lobes, fissures and peritoneal ligaments.
(ii) Relate the lobes/fissures of the liver to common hepatic pathology.
(iii) Explain how liver disease can spread its effects to a distant structure, producing a functional deficit there.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Collagen fibers: protein fibers that form the bulk of connective tissue fibers. Major types and distribution: Type I collagen — fibril-forming; found in bone, dermis, tendon, ligaments, and cornea; produced by fibroblasts, osteoblasts, odontoblasts. Type II collagen — fibril-forming; found in cartilage and vitreous body of the eye; produced by chondrocytes and retinal cells. Type III collagen — fibril-forming; found in loose connective tissue and reticular fibers in lungs, liver, and spleen; produced by fibroblasts and reticular cells. Type IV collagen — network-forming; found in basement membranes; produced by epithelial and endothelial cells. Type XI collagen — fibrillar; found in cartilage. Elastic fibers: present in elastic connective tissue; provide elasticity. Reticular fibers: fine fibers present in reticular connective tissue; form reticular (meshwork) framework of organs.
A(ii)
Dense regular connective tissue is present in tendons and ligaments because it is organized to withstand forces from specific directions; the regular parallel arrangement of collagen type I fibers allows maximum tensile strength along the axis of the tendon or ligament.
B(i)
The regenerative capacity of connective tissue is clearly observed in organs damaged by ischemia, inflammation, or traumatic injury. Spaces left after such injuries, especially in tissues whose cells divide poorly or not at all (e.g., cardiac muscle), are filled by connective tissue, forming dense irregular scar tissue. The healing of surgical incisions and other wounds depends on the reparative capacity of connective tissue and the activity of fibroblasts. Fibroblasts synthesize collagen, reticular and elastic fibers, and the amorphous extracellular substance. In some rapidly closing wounds, a cell called the myofibroblast (with features of both fibroblasts and smooth muscle cells) is observed. Myofibroblasts have most of the morphologic characteristics of fibroblasts but contain increased amounts of actin microfilaments and myosin and behave like smooth muscle cells. Their activity is responsible for wound contraction (wound closure after tissue injury).
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the origin, composition, and classification of connective tissue fibers under the following headings: collagen fibers (types and tissue distribution), elastic fibers, and reticular fibers.
A(ii) State the safe structural principle that makes collagen type I dominant in tendons and ligaments.
B(i) Explain the anatomical basis of scar formation after organ injury, with specific reference to fibroblasts and myofibroblasts.

A(i) Describe the general features of the lung (shape, appearance, weight, right compared with left) and its apex, base, surfaces and borders.
A(ii) Describe the lobes and fissures and the surface marking of the lower border of the lung.
A(iii) Compare the hilum and roots of the right and left lungs.
A(iv) Describe the bronchopulmonary segments of the right and left lungs and the features of a bronchopulmonary segment.
A(v) Describe the blood supply, lymphatic drainage and nerve supply of the lung.
B(i) Relate the parts and segments of the lung to the sites and spread of common pathologies.
C(i) Explain how disease of the lung and pleura may involve distant structures and produce referred pain or a functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Conical, soft, spongy, elastic and pinkish in health (brown in the young, mottled black in adults and dark in city dwellers from deposited dust and carbon particles); right lung about 600 g, left about 550 g; the right is larger, heavier, shorter and wider. Each has an apex, a base, 3 surfaces (costal convex, mediastinal with the hilum, diaphragmatic concave), 3 borders (anterior, posterior, inferior) and a root; the posterior surface lies in the paravertebral gutter.
• Apex: rounded, extends into the root of the neck 2.5-4 cm above the sternal end of the 1st rib, covered by cervical pleura and suprapleural membrane. Base: broad, concave, rests on the diaphragm, which separates the right lung from the right lobe of the liver and the left lung from the left lobe of the liver, stomach and spleen. Anterior border: where costal and mediastinal surfaces meet, with the cardiac notch on the left; posterior border from C7 to T10; inferior border separates the base from the costal and mediastinal surfaces.
A(ii)
Right lung: 3 lobes (upper, middle, lower) by oblique and horizontal fissures; left lung: 2 lobes (upper and smaller lower) by the oblique fissure, with the lingula below the cardiac notch; visceral pleura extends into the fissures so the lobes move freely. Lower border (neutral position) crosses the 6th rib in the midclavicular line, the 8th rib in the midaxillary line and reaches the 10th rib posteriorly.
A(iii)
Hilum: wedge-shaped area on the mediastinal surface; root lies opposite T5-T7. Right root: in the groove of the arch of the azygos vein; eparterial and hyparterial bronchi, right pulmonary artery, 2 right pulmonary veins, hilar lymph nodes. Left root: in the concavity of the arch of the aorta; left main bronchus, left pulmonary artery, 2 left pulmonary veins, hilar lymph nodes. Both also contain bronchial vessels, nerves and lymphatics enclosed by pleura.
A(iv)
• Right lung, 10 segments: upper lobe apical, posterior, anterior; middle lobe lateral, medial; lower lobe superior (apical), medial basal, anterior basal, lateral basal, posterior basal. Left lung, 8 segments: upper lobe apicoposterior, anterior, superior lingula, inferior lingula; lower lobe superior (apical), medial basal, anterior basal, lateral basal, posterior basal.
• Each segment is pyramidal (apex to the hilum, base to the surface), separated from its neighbours by connective tissue septa, with the segmental bronchus, bronchial vessels and a pulmonary artery branch central; little arterial anastomosis between segments; intersegmental pulmonary vein tributaries guide separation; it has its own lymphatics and autonomic supply and is the smallest part that can be removed without affecting adjacent lung.
A(v)
• Arteries: 2 left bronchial arteries from the descending thoracic aorta and 1 right bronchial artery from the 3rd right posterior intercostal supply the bronchial tree down to the respiratory bronchioles; pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood to the alveoli and anastomose with the bronchial arteries at the precapillary level. Veins: 4 pulmonary veins to the left atrium; right bronchial vein to the azygos vein, left to the accessory hemiazygos vein.
• Lymph: superficial plexus (deep to the visceral pleura) and deep plexus (peribronchial) drain to pulmonary then bronchopulmonary (hilar) nodes, then superior and inferior tracheobronchial nodes, then the bronchomediastinal trunks to the junction of subclavian and internal jugular veins (right trunk may form the right lymphatic duct; left may end in the thoracic duct). Nerves: pulmonary plexuses; vagus is bronchoconstrictor, vasodilator and secretomotor, sympathetic has the opposite actions.
B(i)
• Connective tissue septa between segments are a natural barrier to the spread of infection, but carcinoma and tuberculosis break through; abscesses are commoner in the posterior segment of the upper lobe and the apical segment of the lower lobe because these are the most dependent segments in the supine position.
• Other pathologies: foreign particles enter the right main bronchus easily (wider, more vertical); pulmonary embolism (pulmonary artery obstructed by air, blood clot, fat, tumour cells or foreign particles); asthma (dyspnoea); fibrosis reduces compliance and emphysema reduces elasticity; lobectomy or pneumonectomy is used in lung cancer.
C(i)
• Costal pleura is supplied by intercostal nerves, so pleural or lung disease may cause referred pain along the thoracic wall and anterior abdominal wall; irritation over the central diaphragm refers pain to the shoulder through the phrenic nerve (C3-5).
• Lymphatic spread passes from the hilar nodes to the tracheobronchial nodes and bronchomediastinal trunks; a tumour within the chest cavity may compress the phrenic nerve and cause diaphragmatic paralysis with paradoxical movement (functional deficit).

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the development, structure, shape and position of the female breast.
A(ii) Describe the nipple and areola.
A(iii) Describe the internal structure of the breast.
A(iv) Describe the arterial supply, venous drainage and nerve supply.
B(i) Relate the parts and structures of the breast to common pathologies and to surgical incisions.
B(ii) Describe the developmental anomalies of the breast.
C(i) Explain how breast disease spreads through the lymphatics, naming the drainage routes and the axillary node groups, and its effect on distant structures.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• A modified sweat gland of ectodermal origin, non-capsulated, present in both sexes (rudimentary in males), starting to develop at puberty in females with most development in late pregnancy and lactation; lies in the superficial fascia; shape and size vary with genetics, race, diet, age, parity and menopausal status (hemispherical, conical, pendulous, piriform, flattened).
• Base extends vertically from the 2nd to the 6th rib and transversely from the sternal edge to the midaxillary line; two-thirds of the base lie on pectoralis major and the inferolateral third on serratus anterior and external oblique; the axillary tail (of Spence) passes into the axilla; the retromammary space (loose areolar tissue) separates it from the deep fascia.
A(ii)
Nipple: at the greatest prominence, opposite the 4th intercostal space (about 10 cm from the midline in men and young nulliparous women); carries 15-20 pores of the lactiferous ducts; circular and radial smooth muscle causes erection with cold, tactile or emotional stimuli; devoid of fat, hair and sweat glands. Areola: pigmented skin (22-60 mm) with sebaceous glands and glands of Montgomery; darkening in the 2nd month of pregnancy is permanent.
A(iii)
Glandular tissue (15-20 lobes made of lobules of alveoli/acini and alveolar ducts converging on 15-20 lactiferous ducts, each with a lactiferous sinus deep to the areola), stroma (fibrous strands, the suspensory ligaments of Astley Cooper, connecting the skin with the deep fascia of pectoralis major) and adipose tissue (determines form and size).
A(iv)
Arteries: internal thoracic (medial mammary and perforating branches of the 2nd-4th spaces, the 2nd largest; about 60% of flow, mainly medial), lateral thoracic and thoraco-acromial pectoral branch (axillary), lateral mammary branches of posterior intercostal arteries, anterior intercostal branches. Veins correspond, with a circular venous plexus at the base of the nipple draining to the axillary and internal thoracic veins. Nerves: anterior and lateral cutaneous branches of the 4th-6th intercostal nerves (sensory to skin, sympathetic to vessels and the smooth muscle of skin and nipple).
B(i)
Cancer of the breast is a common surgical condition, about 60% arising in the upper lateral quadrant; the lactiferous ducts are radial, so incisions are made radially; infiltration of the ligaments of Cooper shortens them and gives peau d'orange; fibroadenoma is also listed.
B(ii)
Polymastia, polythelia and amastia; the mammary ridge extends from the axilla to the inguinal region and disappears in humans except in the pectoral region, so accessory breasts or nipples can occur along it (axillary and inguinal); the male breast stays rudimentary (small ducts without lobules or alveoli).
C(i)
• About 75% of lymph drains to the axillary nodes (central and lateral parts to the pectoral group, upper part to the apical group), about 20% (medial part) to the internal thoracic (parasternal) chain, and the lower quadrants to the inferior phrenic (abdominal) nodes.
• Axillary nodes lie in 5 groups: pectoral (anterior), subscapular (posterior), brachial (lateral), central and apical; levels 1-3 and Rotter's nodes between pectoralis minor and major; the subclavian lymph trunk from the apical group opens into the subclavian vein (left side usually the thoracic duct).
• Other routes: lymphatics follow vessels through pectoralis major to parasternal nodes, cross the median plane to the opposite breast, and reach the sheath of rectus abdominis and the subperitoneal and subhepatic plexuses.
• Nodes below and above the clavicle, and axillary and cervical nodes, communicate freely; cancer of one breast can affect the other breast and the opposite axillary nodes through the anastomosing lymphatics.

questions.question:
Describe the ulnar nerve:
A(i) Origin
A(ii) Course and common entrapment sites
A(iii) Muscles innervated (forearm and hand)
A(iv) Sensory distribution
C. Explain the anatomical basis of the deformity seen after ulnar nerve injury.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The ulnar nerve is an extension of the medial cord of the brachial plexus.
A(ii)
The most common sites of ulnar nerve entrapment are: above the elbow in the region of the intermuscular septum; the medial epicondylar region; the epicondylar (ulnar) groove; the region of the cubital tunnel; and the region where the nerve exits from flexor carpi ulnaris, where compression is usually caused by the deep flexor-pronator aponeurosis.
A(iii)
• In the forearm it supplies flexor carpi ulnaris and the medial (3rd & 4th) part of flexor digitorum profundus.
• In the hand it supplies the hypothenar muscles, adductor pollicis, flexor pollicis brevis, the palmar and dorsal interossei, the 3rd and 4th lumbricals, and the muscles of digiti minimi (abductor, opponens, flexor digiti minimi).
A(iv)
It provides sensation to the medial surface of the hand and the medial half of the 4th and 5th digits, on both palmar and dorsal aspects, through its superficial branch; its motor functions include finger adduction and abduction other than the thumb, thumb adduction, flexion of digits 4 and 5, and wrist flexion and adduction.
C
• Injury to the ulnar nerve, or to the medial cord/lower trunk from which it derives, produces a claw hand deformity.
• This deformity arises from the unopposed action of the long flexors and extensors of the fingers once the ulnar-innervated intrinsic muscles (interossei, medial lumbricals) are paralysed.
• In a claw hand there is hyperextension at the metacarpophalangeal joints and flexion at the interphalangeal joints.
• Where the injury occurs at the level of the medial cord (e.g. from subcoracoid dislocation of the humerus), the ulnar nerve and medial root of median nerve are both involved.
• This produces sensory loss on the ulnar side of the forearm and hand, along with vasomotor and trophic changes.
• The claw hand deformity, together with the specific pattern of muscle paralysis, thus reflects the level and combination of nerve fibres interrupted along the course of the ulnar nerve or its parent cord/trunk.

A(i)
A thin, double-layered serous membrane that envelops each lung and lines the thoracic cavity, made of visceral and parietal layers with the intervening pleural cavity; the two pleural cavities are totally separate.
A(ii)
Thicker outer layer lining the thoracic wall, mediastinum, diaphragm and neck, and can be stripped; 4 parts: costal (ribs, costal cartilages, intercostal spaces, sides of vertebral bodies, back of sternum, separated from them by endothoracic fascia), diaphragmatic, mediastinal (encloses the hilum structures, continuous with visceral pleura at the hilum, and below the hilum forms the pulmonary ligament) and cervical (cupola, 2.5-4 cm above the medial third of the clavicle, attached to the suprapleural membrane).
A(iii)
Visceral pleura: closely adherent to the lung including its fissures, cannot be stripped, smooth and slippery, continuous with the parietal pleura at the hilum; the pleural cavity is a potential space with a small amount of lubricating pleural fluid that reduces friction and helps prevent lung collapse.
A(iv)
Sternal (costal to mediastinal anteriorly): from behind the sternoclavicular joints to the midline at the 2nd costal cartilage, then the right edge passes vertically to the 6th costal cartilage while the left arches laterally at the 4th costal cartilage (because of the heart) to the 6th. Costal (costal to diaphragmatic): crosses the 8th rib in the midclavicular line, the 10th rib in the midaxillary line and the 12th rib at the lateral border of erector spinae. Vertebral: rounded reflections in the paravertebral planes from T1 to T12.
A(v)
Recesses are spaces not occupied by lung that lung enters only on forced deep respiration: costodiaphragmatic (between costal and diaphragmatic pleura, shallow in inspiration and deeper in expiration) and costomediastinal (behind the sternum where costal pleura becomes mediastinal pleura, more conspicuous on the left near the heart).
A(vi)
• Blood supply: visceral pleura from bronchial and pulmonary arteries, veins to the pulmonary vein; parietal pleura from the vessels of the structures covered - cervical and costal from intercostal vessels, diaphragmatic outer part from intercostal and inner part from pericardiophrenic vessels, mediastinal from pericardiophrenic vessels.
• Nerve supply: costal pleura by intercostal nerves; diaphragmatic pleura by phrenic nerves centrally and intercostal nerves peripherally; mediastinal pleura by the phrenic nerve; the visceral pleura is described as having no nerve supply and as receiving vasomotor supply from autonomic nerves (pulmonary plexuses).
• Lymph: visceral to the pulmonary plexus in interlobar and peribronchial spaces; parietal costal, mediastinal and cervical to the internal thoracic (anterior) and intercostal (posterior) chains; diaphragmatic to retrosternal, mediastinal and sometimes coeliac nodes.
B(i)
The cervical pleura reaches about 1 inch (2.5 cm) above the clavicle because of the oblique slope of the first rib, so it can be wounded (pneumothorax) by a stab wound, a surgeon's knife or an anaesthetist's needle above the clavicle; the lower edge descends just below the 12th rib medially (below the 11th if the 12th is short), so it may be opened in a loin incision.
B(ii)
The costodiaphragmatic recess is the larger recess and the clinically more important one, providing the space where fluid collects in disease (pneumothorax with air, haemothorax with blood, empyema with pus, effusion); fluid is drained with a needle just above a rib, or through the space between the 7th costal cartilage and the xiphoid process.
C(i)
• Parietal: thicker, outer, lines wall, diaphragm, mediastinum and neck, named regionally, can be stripped, supplied by intercostal and phrenic nerves (so pleural irritation refers pain along the thoracic and anterior abdominal wall, and to the shoulder from the central diaphragm).
• Visceral: inner layer closely adherent to the lung surface and fissures, cannot be stripped, smooth and slippery so the lung moves freely, supplied by bronchial and pulmonary vessels; pleurisy is inflammation of the pleura, usually with pneumonia or other lung infection.
questions.question:
A(i) Define the pleura and describe its parts.
A(ii) Describe the parietal pleura and its parts.
A(iii) Describe the visceral pleura and the pleural cavity.
A(iv) Describe the lines of pleural reflection with their surface markings.
A(v) Describe the pleural recesses.
A(vi) Describe the blood supply, nerve supply and lymphatic drainage of the pleura.
B(i) Explain why the cervical pleura and the lower pleural margin are vulnerable to injury.
B(ii) Explain why the costodiaphragmatic recess is the clinically more important recess.
C(i) Distinguish between the parietal and the visceral pleura.

(i) Describe the gross anatomy of the spleen - measurements, external features (ends, borders, surfaces, hilum) and peritoneal ligaments.
(ii) Relate the surfaces/impressions of the spleen to organs it may affect in disease.
(iii) Explain why splenic rupture produces a distant, life-threatening functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
(i)
• The spleen is an ovoid, highly vascular, reddish-purple organ, on average about 12 cm long, 7 cm broad, 3 cm thick and weighing about 150 g, related to the 9th to 11th ribs on the left side.
• It has two ends, an expanded anterior end and a rounded posterior end resting on the upper pole of the left kidney, three borders (superior, inferior and intermediate), and two surfaces (diaphragmatic and visceral).
• The diaphragmatic surface is convex and related to the diaphragm, left lung and pleura, and the 9th-11th ribs; the visceral surface is concave and bears gastric, renal, colic and pancreatic impressions.
• The hilum lies on the inferomedial part of the gastric impression and transmits the splenic vessels and nerves, giving attachment to the gastrosplenic and splenorenal ligaments; the phrenicocolic ligament supports, but is not attached to, the anterior end of the spleen.
(ii)
• The gastric impression, related to the fundus of the stomach, is the largest impression; the renal impression relates to the left kidney and sometimes the suprarenal gland; the colic impression relates to the splenic flexure of the colon; the pancreatic impression relates to the tail of the pancreas.
• The gastrosplenic ligament contains the short gastric vessels supplying the stomach, and the splenorenal ligament contains the tail of the pancreas and splenic vessels, so disease or surgery at the spleen can affect the stomach, kidney, colon or pancreas through these relations.
(iii)
• Although protected by the 9th to 12th ribs, the spleen is the most frequently injured organ in the abdomen.
• Severe blows to the left side may fracture ribs, producing sharp fragments that lacerate the spleen, and blunt trauma elsewhere that raises intra-abdominal pressure can also rupture it because its capsule is thin and the pulp soft.
• If ruptured, the spleen bleeds profusely because it is a highly vascular organ receiving the splenic artery, the largest branch of the coeliac trunk.
• This produces severe intraperitoneal haemorrhage and shock, a systemic and distant functional deficit in circulation arising from a local splenic injury.
• Repair of a ruptured spleen is difficult, so splenectomy or subtotal splenectomy is often performed to prevent the patient from bleeding to death.
• Even after total splenectomy, most splenic functions are assumed by other reticuloendothelial organs such as the liver and bone marrow, though susceptibility to certain bacterial infections increases.

questions.question:
(i) Describe the origin, course and distribution of the anterior and posterior vagal trunks in the abdomen.
(ii) State where the vagal trunks lie in relation to the oesophageal hiatus.
(iii) Explain the anatomical basis of the effect of vagal injury (vagotomy) on the stomach and related viscera.
questions.answerText:
(i)
• The anterior vagal trunk is formed mainly in the thorax from the left vagus nerve; it enters the abdomen on the anterior surface of the oesophagus and divides into branches that supply the anterior surface of the stomach. A large hepatic branch of the anterior vagal trunk passes up to the liver, and from this a pyloric branch passes down to the pylorus.
• The posterior vagal trunk is formed mainly from the right vagus nerve; it enters the abdomen on the posterior surface of the oesophagus and divides into branches supplying mainly the posterior surface of the stomach. A large branch of the posterior vagal trunk passes to the coeliac and superior mesenteric plexuses and is distributed to the intestine as far as the splenic flexure and to the pancreas.
(ii)
At the opening in the diaphragm (the oesophageal hiatus), the oesophagus is accompanied by the two vagal trunks, branches of the left gastric vessels, and lymphatic vessels, with fibres of the right crus forming a sling around the oesophagus. Inferior to the root of the lungs, the vagus nerves leave the pulmonary plexus and join sympathetic nerves to form the oesophageal plexus, from which the anterior trunk (left vagus, anterior) and posterior trunk (right vagus, posterior) are derived.
(iii)
• The vagal (parasympathetic) fibres are secretomotor to the gastric glands and motor to the muscular wall of the stomach, and the pyloric sphincter receives inhibitory fibres from the vagus.
• Vagotomy is a recognised surgical option for peptic ulcer disease; division of the vagal trunks reduces the vagal secretomotor drive to the gastric glands, decreasing acid secretion.
• Since the hepatic branch arises from the anterior vagal trunk and the coeliac/pancreatic branch from the posterior trunk, a truncal vagotomy also interrupts vagal input to the liver, pancreas and intestine as far as the splenic flexure.
• Loss of vagal inhibitory input to the pyloric sphincter can alter pyloric motor function, which is why vagotomy for peptic ulcer disease is often combined with a drainage procedure such as pyloroplasty.

A(i)
The brachial plexus is formed by the union of the C5, C6, C7 and C8 ventral rami and the greater part of the 1st thoracic ventral ramus, with contribution sometimes from C4 (giving a "prefixed" plexus) or T2 (giving a "postfixed" plexus); the roots emerge from the transverse processes of the cervical vertebrae, immediately posterior to the vertebral artery, and lie between the scalene muscles.
A(ii)
C5 and C6 unite to form the upper trunk, C7 continues as the middle trunk, and C8 and T1 unite to form the lower trunk, lying in the posterior triangle of the neck; each trunk bifurcates behind the clavicle into an anterior and a posterior division. The anterior divisions of the upper and middle trunks unite to form the lateral cord; the anterior division of the lower trunk continues as the medial cord; the posterior divisions of all three trunks unite to form the posterior cord, lying in the axilla below pectoralis minor.
A(iii)
The five main terminal branches are the musculocutaneous nerve and the lateral root of the median nerve (from the lateral cord), the ulnar nerve and the medial root of the median nerve (from the medial cord), and the axillary and radial nerves (from the posterior cord).
B
• Injury to the upper trunk (C5, C6), at "Erb's point," produces Erb's paralysis, from causes such as birth injury, a fall on the shoulder, or during anaesthesia, affecting the axillary, musculocutaneous and suprascapular nerves.
• Injury to the lower trunk (C8, T1), from causes such as undue abduction of the arm, produces Klumpke's paralysis, with paralysis of the intrinsic hand muscles and ulnar wrist/finger flexors, and possible Horner's syndrome from associated sympathetic fibre injury.
C
• Erb's paralysis paralyses biceps, deltoid, brachialis, brachioradialis, supraspinatus, infraspinatus and supinator, producing the "Policeman's/Porter's tip hand": the arm hangs adducted and medially rotated, the forearm extended and pronated, with loss of abduction/lateral rotation of the shoulder and flexion/supination of the forearm.
• Klumpke's paralysis produces a claw hand from unopposed long flexors/extensors, plus cutaneous anaesthesia along the ulnar border of the limb.
• Injury to the lateral cord (e.g. from dislocation of the humerus) involves the musculocutaneous nerve and the lateral root of the median nerve, paralysing biceps, coracobrachialis and the median-supplied forearm muscles, producing a midprone forearm with loss of elbow and wrist flexion and sensory loss on the radial side of the forearm.
• Injury to the medial cord (e.g. from subcoracoid dislocation of the humerus) involves the ulnar nerve and the medial root of the median nerve, producing claw hand with sensory loss on the ulnar side of the forearm and hand.
• Injury to the posterior cord involves the upper and lower subscapular nerves, the thoracodorsal nerve, the axillary nerve, and the radial nerve (the largest and most frequently injured branch of the plexus).
• This weakens elbow, wrist and metacarpophalangeal joint extension via the radial nerve, and shoulder abduction via the axillary nerve.
• In this way, a single lesion at the level of a trunk or cord of the brachial plexus spreads its effect along the several peripheral nerves derived from it, each producing its own characteristic and distant functional deficit in the arm, forearm or hand.
questions.question:

A(iii) Five main terminal branches

C. Explain how injury at the level of a trunk or cord spreads to affect distant structures (individual peripheral nerves), causing specific functional deficits.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Three regions of the male urethra:
• Prostatic urethra (2.5 cm): located within the prostate.
• Intermediate part of the urethra (membranous urethra) (2 cm): passes through the urogenital diaphragm from the prostate to the beginning of the penis.
• Spongy urethra (15 cm): passes through the penis and opens via the external urethral orifice.
• The male urethra carries both semen and urine.
A(ii)
Two sphincters:
• Internal urethral sphincter: involuntary (smooth muscle) at the bladder-urethra junction; contracts to open (its contraction, paradoxically, opens the sphincter as described — 'contracts to open').
• External urethral sphincter: voluntary (skeletal muscle) surrounding the urethra as it passes through the pelvic floor.
B(i)
Female urethra:
• Length: 3–4 cm.
• Relations: tightly bound to the anterior vaginal wall.
• External urethral orifice: anterior to the vaginal opening and posterior to the clitoris.
B(ii)
Layers of the urinary bladder wall:
• Peritoneum, rugae, detrusor (muscle), adventitia, ureteric orifices, trigone of bladder, bladder neck, internal urethral sphincter.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Medial longitudinal arch: formed by calcaneus, talus (keystone — its superior articular facet is the summit), navicular, 3 cuneiform bones, and 1st, 2nd, and 3rd metatarsals; found on medial aspect of foot; larger, with greatest height, higher, more mobile, and more resilient. Lateral longitudinal arch: formed by calcaneus, cuboid, and the 4th and 5th metatarsals; summit is the subtalar articulation; flat, contains relatively fewer bones, hence more rigid; bears body weight before the medial arch comes into play. Transverse arch: formed proximally by 3 cuneiforms and cuboid, and distally by the bases of 5 metatarsals; it is a partial arch (each foot represents a half dome); the intermediate and lateral cuneiforms are wedge-shaped (bony factor).
A(ii)
Medial longitudinal arch: Ligaments — spring ligament, deltoid ligament, plantar aponeurosis, interosseous ligaments, long and short plantar ligaments. Muscles — tibialis posterior, tibialis anterior, flexor hallucis longus, flexor digitorum longus, and short muscles of the big toe. Bony factor — the shape and constitution of the bones. Lateral longitudinal arch: Ligaments — plantar aponeurosis, interosseous ligaments, long and short plantar ligaments. Muscles — peroneus longus and brevis, flexor digitorum longus, and short muscles of the little toe. Bony factor — shape and constitution of the bones. Transverse arch: Bony factor — intermediate and lateral cuneiforms are wedge-shaped. Ligaments — deep transverse ligament and interosseous ligaments (dorsal and plantar). Muscles — peroneus longus and brevis, transverse head of adductor hallucis, and slips of tibialis posterior.
B(i)
The human foot supports the body weight and serves as a lever to propel the body forward during locomotion. Functions carried out by arches: (1) Foot acts as a segmented lever with multiple joints and adapts to uneven surfaces. (2) Long flexors and intrinsic muscles assist propulsive action of gastrocnemius and soleus. (3) Arches are springs that absorb shock and store energy — elastic arches present between weight-bearing points can flatten and recoil back to normal.
B(ii)
Pes planus (flat foot): rotation of the calcaneus, eversion of the plantar surface, slipping down of the talus and navicular, lengthening of the medial longitudinal arch, and abduction of the forefoot; caused by excess weight on medial side, relaxation of ligaments, or muscular imbalance. Pes cavus (high-arched foot): exaggeration of the longitudinal arch; toes dorsiflexed at metatarsophalangeal joints and plantarflexed at interphalangeal joints — claw foot. Talipes equinovarus: plantar flexion, inversion, and adduction of the foot (clubfoot). Talipes calcaneovalgus: dorsiflexion, eversion, and abduction of the foot.
C(i)
The medial longitudinal arch is higher, more mobile, and more resilient — it is dynamic, changes most during movement, and requires active muscular support (particularly tibialis posterior, flexor hallucis longus, and the spring ligament). The lateral longitudinal arch is lower, more stable, built to transmit weight to the ground, makes more contact with the ground, has limited mobility, and depends more on bony and ligamentous rather than muscular support. The medial arch is therefore more clinically vulnerable to collapse (pes planus) when muscles weaken or ligaments stretch.
questions.question:
Describe the arches of the foot under the following headings and explain their clinical relevance.
A(i) Name and constituent bones of each arch, identifying the keystone of each
A(ii) Factors maintaining the arches — ligaments, muscles, and bony factor for each arch
B(i) Functions of the foot arches in weight-bearing and locomotion
B(ii) Deformities of the foot — name and define pes planus, pes cavus, talipes equinovarus, and talipes calcaneovalgus
C(i) Explain why the medial longitudinal arch is more dynamic and more clinically vulnerable than the lateral longitudinal arch

A(i) Describe the gross histology of the nervous tissue of the brain under the following headings: protective coverings (meninges), gray matter and white matter, types of glial cells in the CNS and their functions.
A(ii) Relate the three meningeal layers to their specific functions and state how cerebrospinal fluid flows.
B(i) Explain why a demyelinating disease of the optic nerve causes visual symptoms and state the histological basis of the link between the retina, optic nerve, and the CNS.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Protective coverings: the nervous system contains very little collagen or fibrous tissue; it is relatively soft and easily damaged by injuries affecting the cranium or vertebral bones. It is covered by three connective tissue layers — the meninges: dura mater (thickest and toughest layer, contains sinuses to collect venous blood), arachnoid membrane (middle web-like covering; cerebrospinal fluid flows in the web-like spaces), and pia mater (thin delicate layer that follows the contour of the brain and spinal cord). Gray matter and white matter: myelinated fibers make up the white matter in the CNS; cell bodies and unmyelinated fibers make the gray matter. Glial cells in CNS: Oligodendrocytes — produce myelin in CNS. Microglia — part of the MPS (CNS macrophages). Astrocytes and other glial cells — support, nourish, and protect neurons; they are far more numerous than neurons; unlike neurons, they are capable of mitosis.
A(ii)
Dura mater — thickest and toughest layer; contains sinuses to collect venous blood. Arachnoid membrane — middle web-like covering; cerebrospinal fluid flows in the web-like (subarachnoid) spaces. Pia mater — thin delicate layer that follows the contour of brain and spinal cord. CSF flows within the subarachnoid spaces of the arachnoid.
B(i)
The optic nerve and retina arise in the embryo as an outgrowth of the diencephalon (forebrain); the optic nerve is therefore not a true peripheral nerve like the other cranial nerves. Its myelin is produced by oligodendrocytes (not by Schwann cells). Because the optic nerve is part of the CNS (produced by oligodendrocytes and without neurilemma), it is associated with multiple sclerosis — a demyelinating disease. Demyelination of the optic nerve disrupts the action potential transmission from the retinal ganglion cells, causing visual symptoms. The retinal ganglion cells communicate with the cerebrum through the optic nerve and extend into the brain.

A(i)
The clavicle forms the anterior portion of the shoulder girdle; it is curved like the italic letter "f" and lies nearly horizontally at the upper and anterior part of the thorax, immediately above the first rib. It articulates medially with the manubrium sterni and laterally with the acromion of the scapula.
A(ii)
The upper surface is flat, rough, and marked by impressions for the attachment of deltoid in front and trapezius behind; the bone has no medullary cavity.
A(iii)
Its functions are to transmit forces from the upper limb to the axial skeleton, to act as a strut holding the arm free from the trunk (supported principally by trapezius), and to provide attachment for muscles.
B
• The weakest point along the clavicle is the junction of the middle and outer thirds.
• Transmission of forces to the axial skeleton in falls on the shoulder or hand may exceed the strength of the bone at this site, and this indirect force commonly results in fracture there.
• Clavicle fracture is caused by landing on the hand from a fall with the arm rigidly outstretched, or by a direct blow.
C
• The clavicle has important deep relations that make it clinically significant beyond the bone itself.
• The third parts of the subclavian vessels and the trunks of the brachial plexus pass behind the medial third of the shaft of the clavicle, separated only by the thin subclavius muscle.
• At the sternal end, behind the sternoclavicular joints, lie the common carotid artery on the left and the bifurcation of the brachiocephalic artery on the right, with the internal jugular vein lying a little more laterally; these vessels are separated from the bone only by the strap muscles (sternohyoid and sternothyroid).
• Because these major vessels and the brachial plexus trunks lie in such close proximity to the clavicle, deep or displaced injury involving the bone can threaten them.
• Compromise of the subclavian vessels can produce vascular insufficiency of the upper limb, while injury to the brachial plexus trunks passing behind the medial clavicle can produce motor and sensory deficits in the limb.
• This illustrates how a skeletal injury at the clavicle can spread to affect distant neurovascular structures, producing a functional deficit beyond the fracture site itself.

A(iii) Functions

questions.answerText:
A(i)
• The thoracoabdominal nerves are the abdominal portions of the anterior rami of T7 to T12 (T7 to T11 thoracoabdominal, T12 subcostal); their distal portions lie in the rectus sheath.
• External oblique: T7 to T11 and T12; internal oblique and transversus abdominis: T7 to T11, T12 and branches of the lumbar plexus; rectus abdominis: T7 to T11; pyramidalis: subcostal T12.
A(ii)
• The lumbar plexus (ventral rami L1 to L4, formed within psoas major) innervates part of the lower abdominal wall.
• The iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves (L1) emerge from the lateral border of psoas major.
A(iii)
• The umbilicus is the segmental landmark with dermatome T10, the same root that innervates the appendix, so appendicular referred pain is felt there.
• The segmental innervation applies to both the anterior abdominal skin and musculature.
B(i)
• The TAP block is a peripheral nerve block that anaesthetises the nerves of the abdominal wall.
• It is performed by injecting anaesthetic into the fascial plane between transversus abdominis and internal oblique muscles.
C(i)
• The ilioinguinal, iliohypogastric and inferior thoracic nerves are spread across the abdominal wall and so are prone to injury.
• Their injury results in muscle weakness of the abdominal wall.
• In entrapment (ACNES) the Carnett sign is positive at the lateral border of the rectus abdominis, with altered skin sensation.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the muscularis and serosa of the small intestine, naming the layers of the muscularis, the nerve plexus between them, and the covering of the serosa.
A(ii) Describe the lamina propria of the small intestine, including its composition, its role in each intestinal villus, and the role of smooth muscle fibers within the villi.
B(i) Describe the submucosa of the small intestine, giving particular attention to the Brunner (duodenal) glands: location, type of gland, product, pH, and all three functions.
B(ii) Describe the lacteals of the small intestine: what they are, where they begin, their course, their function, and how they change in appearance depending on the absorptive state of the intestine.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Muscularis and serosa:
• Muscularis: composed of an internal circular layer and an external longitudinal layer; between these muscle layers is the myenteric (Auerbach) nerve plexus, which produces peristalsis.
• Serosa: the small intestine is covered by a thin serosa.
A(ii)
Lamina propria of the small intestine:
• Composed of loose connective tissue containing extensive blood and lymph microvasculature, nerve fibers, smooth muscle cells, and lymphoid tissue.
• It penetrates the core of each intestinal villus, bringing microvasculature, lymphatics, and nerves into each villus.
• Smooth muscle fibers inside the villi are responsible for rhythmic movements important for efficient absorption.
• Contractions of the muscularis mucosae also produce local movements of the plicae circulares that help propel lymph from the lacteals into submucosal and mesenteric lymphatics.
B(i)
Submucosa — Brunner (duodenal) glands:
• Location: present in the proximal part of the duodenum; large clusters of branched tubular mucous glands with small excretory ducts opening among the intestinal crypts.
• Type: branched tubular mucous glands.
• Product: mucus, which is alkaline (pH 8.1–9.3).
Three functions:
• Protects the mucous membrane.
• Brings the intestinal contents to the optimum pH for pancreatic enzyme action.
• Neutralises chyme entering the duodenum from the pylorus.
B(ii)
Lacteals:
• Lymph vessels of the intestine beginning as closed tubes in the cores of villi.
• They run to the region of the lamina propria above the muscularis mucosae, where they form a plexus.
• From there they are directed to the submucosa, where they surround lymphoid nodules; they anastomose repeatedly and leave the intestine along with blood vessels.
• Function: especially important for lipid absorption.
• Absorptive state: when absorption is taking place after a meal, the lacteals are dilated and prominent; at other times they are collapsed and not prominent.

A(i)
Fibularis longus: origin — head and superior 2/3 of lateral surface of fibula; insertion — base of 1st metatarsal and medial cuneiform; innervation — superficial fibular nerve (L5, S1, S2); action — everts foot and weakly plantarflexes ankle. Fibularis brevis: origin — inferior 2/3 of lateral surface of fibula; insertion — dorsal surface of tuberosity on lateral side of base of 5th metatarsal; innervation — superficial fibular nerve (L5, S1, S2); action — everts foot and weakly plantarflexes ankle. Arterial supply: both are supplied by the fibular (peroneal) artery.
A(ii)
The common fibular nerve is the lateral, smaller terminal branch of the sciatic nerve; it begins at the superior angle of the popliteal fossa, closely follows the medial border of biceps femoris and its tendon, exits the fossa by passing superficial to the lateral head of gastrocnemius, then over the posterior aspect of the head of fibula, winds around the neck of fibula, and divides into the superficial fibular nerve (to the lateral compartment) and the deep fibular nerve (to the anterior compartment). The superficial fibular nerve runs in the lateral compartment to supply fibularis longus and brevis; its cutaneous distribution supplies the dorsum of the foot (lateral side of leg and ankle, as the sural nerve — formed by medial sural cutaneous nerve joined by the sural communicating branch of the common fibular nerve — supplies the lateral side of leg and ankle).
B(i)
Fibularis longus inserts onto the base of the 1st metatarsal and medial cuneiform on the plantar aspect of the foot — it therefore acts as a stirrup, pulling the medial forefoot downward and laterally, producing eversion and weak plantarflexion. Fibularis brevis inserts onto the tuberosity of the base of the 5th metatarsal on the lateral side of the foot — it abducts the forefoot and everts the foot. The lateral longitudinal arch (made of calcaneus, cuboid, and 4th and 5th metatarsals) is supported by peroneus longus and brevis; muscles of the lateral arch include peroneus longus and brevis, flexor digitorum longus, and short muscles of the little toe.
B(ii)
The transverse arch muscles include peroneus longus and brevis, transverse head of adductor hallucis, and slips of tibialis posterior. Fibularis longus, by crossing under the foot from the lateral side to insert medially at the base of the 1st metatarsal, acts as a dynamic tie-beam, pulling the medial and lateral borders of the foot together and maintaining the curvature of the transverse arch; adductor hallucis transverse head also assists by pulling metatarsals medially.
C(i)
Superficial fibular nerve injury (at fibular neck): loss of eversion of the foot (fibularis longus and brevis paralysed); weakness of plantarflexion; sensory loss on dorsum of foot. Deep fibular nerve injury (at fibular neck): loss of dorsiflexion (tibialis anterior paralysed) and toe extension (extensor digitorum longus, extensor hallucis longus paralysed); loss of eversion contribution of fibularis tertius; result is foot drop with the foot held in plantarflexion and inversion; sensory loss is limited to the 1st web space (between 1st and 2nd toes). Injury to the common fibular nerve at the fibular neck produces both effects combined — foot drop with loss of both dorsiflexion and eversion.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
The oesophagus has four constrictions: at 15 cm (cricopharyngeus, upper oesophageal sphincter), at 22.5 cm (crossed by the aortic arch) and 27.5 cm (crossed by the left main bronchus) from the upper incisor teeth, and at 40 cm, where it passes through the right crus of the diaphragm (oesophageal hiatus).
A(ii)
The upper oesophageal sphincter is an anatomical sphincter formed by the cricopharyngeus muscle at the pharyngo-oesophageal junction.
A(iii)
• The lower oesophageal sphincter is a physiological sphincter at the gastro-oesophageal junction with no true muscular thickening.
• It is maintained by the acute angle of entry of the oesophagus into the stomach, compression of the intra-abdominal oesophagus by positive intra-abdominal pressure, prominent mucosal folds at the junction, and the pinch-cock effect of the right crus of the diaphragm.
B
• The constrictions are clinically important because they are sites where swallowed foreign bodies commonly impact.
• They are prone to trauma during instrumentation such as rigid oesophagoscopy.
• They are common sites for stricture formation following ingestion of corrosive substances.
• They are also common sites of oesophageal carcinoma.
C
• The upper oesophageal sphincter is a true anatomical (muscular) sphincter formed by the cricopharyngeus, located at 15 cm from the incisor teeth.
• The lower oesophageal sphincter is a physiological sphincter maintained by mechanical factors at the gastro-oesophageal junction and prevents gastric reflux, rather than a distinct muscular ring controlling food passage.
questions.question:
(A) Describe the oesophagus under the following headings: A(i) its four constrictions along its length A(ii) the upper oesophageal sphincter A(iii) the lower oesophageal sphincter.
(B) Explain the clinical basis of why the areas of constriction are important.
(C) Distinguish between the upper oesophageal sphincter and the lower oesophageal sphincter.

A(i) Describe the gross histology of bone under the following headings: chemical composition and properties, cell types and their functions, and types of bone.
A(ii) State how the Haversian system (osteon) is organised and relate this to bone function.
B(i) Explain how blood calcium levels are regulated through bone, naming the hormones involved and their actions.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Chemical composition and properties: Bone is a connective tissue mineralized by calcium phosphate in the form of crystals very similar to hydroxyapatite. The minerals are both in the type I collagen fibers (which constitute about 95% of the matrix) and in the ground substance. Bone is both resilient and hard. Its resilience is due to the organic matter (collagen); its hardness is due to the inorganic minerals (calcium phosphate, calcium carbonate, calcium fluoride, calcium hydroxide, and citrate). Cell types: Osteocytes — maintain calcium and phosphate ion levels in the blood, are essentially stress sensors, and are osteoblasts that have been trapped in their own matrix in lacunae. Osteoblasts — synthesize the organic matrix (osteoid). Osteoclasts — multinucleated giant cells involved in resorption and remodeling of bone; they are also chondrocytes during bone healing and remodeling. Osteoid is the matrix secreted by osteoblasts and osteocytes prior to mineralization. Types of bone: compact bone (also called dense bone, cortical bone, or lamellar bone) and spongy bone (also called cancellous bone, trabecular bone, and medullary bone).
A(ii)
Compact bone is organized into structures called osteons or Haversian systems: concentric lamellae surrounding a central canal called the Haversian canal, which contains blood vessels, nerves, loose connective tissue, and endosteum. Between lamellae are lacunae, each with one osteocyte interconnected by canaliculi containing the cells' dendritic processes. Canals called Volkmann's canals link Haversian canals with one another and with the marrow cavity. Metabolic exchanges between osteocytes and blood capillaries depend on communication through the canaliculi.
B(i)
Blood calcium levels are regulated by the hormones parathormone (parathyroid hormone), which raises blood calcium levels by stimulating bone resorption, and calcitonin, which reduces blood calcium by suppressing bone resorption and increasing osteoid calcification.

questions.question:
A. Describe the gross anatomy of the larynx under the following headings: the three zones/compartments and the folds that demarcate them.
B. State how the zones of the larynx and the vocal folds relate to laryngeal function and clinical assessment (e.g. on laryngoscopy).
C. Explain how disease/infection at a site distant from the larynx can spread to compromise laryngeal or lower respiratory function, and the functional deficit that results from disordered laryngeal muscle action.
questions.answerText:
A
The larynx is demarcated by the vestibular fold (containing fibrous tissue, forming the false vocal cord on each side) and the vocal fold (the true vocal cord, containing the vocal ligament) into 3 zones: the supraglottic compartment (vestibule), above the false cords; the glottic compartment, between the false and true cords; and the subglottic compartment, between the true cords and the first ring of the trachea. The space between the vocal cords is the rima glottidis.
B
The mucosa is firmly adherent to the vocal ligament without any intervening submucosa, which accounts for the pearly white, avascular appearance of the vocal cords as seen on laryngoscopy; regulation of vocal cord tension (and therefore pitch of the voice) is accomplished primarily by pivoting the thyroid cartilage forward or backward at the cricothyroid joint, via the cricothyroid muscle, which is the only laryngeal muscle that tightens the cords, is supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (not the recurrent laryngeal nerve), and is the only intrinsic laryngeal muscle situated on the outside of the larynx.
C
Sensory innervation is via the internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve above the cords and via the recurrent laryngeal nerve below the cords; motor supply to the muscles is from the nucleus ambiguus via the cranial accessory, with the cricothyroid supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve and all other laryngeal muscles (including the upper oesophagus and cricopharyngeus) supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve. Lymphatic drainage above the cords is to the upper deep cervical nodes and below the cords to the lower deep cervical nodes; a disease process at either level can therefore spread along its corresponding drainage route to functionally distant lymph node groups. Movements which close off the entrance to the larynx during swallowing involve the epiglottis being pulled down and the arytenoid cartilages being pulled forward toward the epiglottis; the larynx is also raised, along with the pharynx, by contraction of the longitudinal muscles of the pharynx, and the epiglottis acts partly as a passive barrier, so disordered laryngeal muscle action compromises this protective closure mechanism.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the temporomandibular joint (TMJ) under the following headings: articular surfaces, articular capsule, and synovial membranes/compartments.
A(ii) Describe the ligaments of the TMJ.
B. Explain the clinical basis for why TMJ dislocation is commoner in the aged and in females.
C. Distinguish between the intrinsic (lateral) ligament and the extrinsic ligaments (sphenomandibular and stylomandibular) of the TMJ.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The articular surfaces of the TMJ are the condyle of the mandible (inferior) and the articular tubercle/mandibular fossa of the temporal bone (squamous part). The articular capsule is loose and fibrous, attaching to the margins of the articular area on the temporal bone and around the neck of the mandible. The superior synovial membrane lines the fibrous capsule superior to the articular disc, and the inferior synovial membrane lines the capsule inferior to the disc; the joint is divided into two compartments (superior and inferior) by an articular disc of fibrocartilage.
A(ii)
The ligaments of the TMJ are divided into an intrinsic ligament and extrinsic ligaments. The intrinsic ligament, also known as the lateral ligament, is the thick part of the articular capsule, strengthens the TMJ laterally, and prevents posterior dislocation of the TMJ. The extrinsic ligaments are the sphenomandibular ligament, which runs from the spine of the sphenoid to the lingula of the mandible and is the primary passive support of the mandible, and the stylomandibular ligament, a thickening of the fibrous capsule of the parotid gland, extending from the styloid process of the temporal bone to the angle of the mandible, which does not contribute significantly to the strength of the joint.
B
Dislocation of the TMJ is common in aged persons and females, due to wearing and resorption of the articular eminence and reducing muscle tone with advancing age.
C
The intrinsic (lateral) ligament is the thick part of the articular capsule, strengthens the joint laterally and prevents posterior dislocation. The sphenomandibular ligament, by contrast, runs from the spine of the sphenoid to the lingula of the mandible and is the primary passive support of the mandible, while the stylomandibular ligament is a thickening of the fibrous capsule of the parotid gland, running from the styloid process to the angle of the mandible, and does not contribute significantly to the strength of the joint.

questions.question:
A(i) State the nature of the vagus nerve and describe its course in the thorax on the right and left.
A(ii) Describe its relations in the mediastinum.
A(iii) State its branches and plexuses in the thorax.
A(iv) Describe its distribution to thoracic structures.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• The vagus is the 10th cranial nerve.
• The right vagus descends on the right side of the trachea, forms the posterior oesophageal plexus and continues in the abdomen as the posterior gastric nerve.
• The left vagus descends between the left common carotid and left subclavian arteries, forms the anterior oesophageal plexus and continues in the abdomen as the anterior gastric nerve.
A(ii)
• The vagus nerves lie in both the superior and the posterior mediastinum; in the posterior mediastinum the right and left vagi lie around the oesophagus and pass through the oesophageal opening of the diaphragm (T10) as the anterior and posterior vagal trunks.
• The left recurrent laryngeal branch of the vagus winds round the ligamentum arteriosus, which connects the inferior concave surface of the arch of the aorta to the left pulmonary artery.
A(iii)
• Branches: recurrent laryngeal branches on both sides and superior and inferior cervical cardiac branches (the right has both, the left has the inferior branch) to the cardiac plexus; pulmonary plexuses to the lungs; oesophageal plexuses.
• Cardiac plexus: the superficial part lies in front of the ligamentum arteriosus (inferior cervical cardiac branch of the left vagus); the deep part lies in front of the left bronchus and at the bifurcation of the pulmonary trunk, behind the arch of the aorta on the lowest part of the trachea; parasympathetic fibres relay in the heart.
A(iv)
• Heart: through the cardiac plexus to the SA and AV nodes and the AV bundle; parasympathetics decrease the rate of impulse generation, sympathetics increase it.
• Lungs and visceral pleura (via the pulmonary plexuses): bronchoconstrictor, vasodilator to pulmonary vessels and secretomotor to glands; the vagal efferents mediate the cough reflex that clears secretions and dust.
• Oesophagus and trachea: recurrent laryngeal branch to the striated upper third of the oesophagus, parasympathetic secretomotor fibres to the oesophageal glands; vagus to the mucous membrane and parasympathetics of the trachea; gastric irritation of vagus nerve endings may cause hiccup.

A(i)
The axillary artery is a continuation of the subclavian artery; it begins at the lateral border of the first rib and ends at the lower border of teres major, continuing thereafter as the brachial artery. It is closely related to the cords of the brachial plexus and is enclosed with them in the axillary sheath.
A(ii)
Pectoralis minor divides the axillary artery into three parts: the first part extends from the lateral border of the first rib to the upper border of pectoralis minor; the second part lies behind pectoralis minor; the third part extends from the lower border of pectoralis minor to the lower border of teres major.
A(iii)
The first part gives one branch, the superior (highest) thoracic artery; the second part gives two branches, the thoracoacromial and lateral thoracic arteries; the third part gives three branches, the subscapular artery and the anterior and posterior circumflex humeral arteries.
B
• The inferior part of the axillary artery can be palpated in the inferior part of the lateral wall of the axilla.
• This part can be compressed against the humerus to control profuse bleeding.
C
• The scapular anastomosis is a system of arteries connecting the subclavian artery and the corresponding axillary artery, forming an anastomosis around the scapula, occurring in the subscapular, supraspinatus and infraspinatus fossae.
• It is formed by the suprascapular artery (a branch of the thyrocervical trunk from the subclavian artery), the deep branch of the transverse cervical artery (another branch of the thyrocervical trunk), and the circumflex scapular artery (a branch of the subscapular artery arising from the third part of the axillary artery).
• These vessels anastomose the first part of the subclavian artery with the third part of the axillary artery, allowing blood to flow past the shoulder joint regardless of the position of the arm.
• A further anastomosis occurs over the acromion process, formed by the acromial branch of the thoracoacromial artery, the acromial branch of the suprascapular artery, and the acromial branch of the posterior circumflex humeral artery, linking the subclavian with the second and third parts of the axillary artery.
• The arterial anastomoses around the scapula thus provide a collateral circulation through which blood can continue to flow to the limb when the distal part of the subclavian artery or the proximal part of the axillary artery is blocked or occluded.
• This collateral circulation is clinically important because it allows blood to continue circulating to the upper limb even if the main line of supply is obstructed.
• This anatomical arrangement explains why proximal occlusion of the axillary or subclavian artery does not necessarily result in complete loss of blood supply to the limb.

A(iii) Branches of each part

questions.answerText:
A(i)
The tibia is the large weight-bearing medial bone of the leg; it articulates with femoral condyles superiorly and the head of fibula laterally. It has an expanded upper end, a shaft, and a smaller lower end. Upper end (see A(ii)). Shaft: triangular in cross-section; 3 borders and 3 surfaces (borders and surfaces are named by opposites); anterior border forms the shin; soleal line on the posterior surface is for soleus. Lower end: expanded; saddle-shaped articular surface for talus; prolonged downwards medially to form the medial malleolus; the medial surface is subcutaneous from the medial malleolus to the medial condyle above.
A(ii)
The upper end has tibial plateaus (lateral and medial condyles); the lateral and medial menisci; anterior and posterior intercondylar areas separate the tibial plateaus; the intercondylar eminence; an articular facet for the head of fibula; and a groove on the medial condyle for semimembranosus. The anterior intercondylar area of the tibia is where the ACL attaches (just posterior to attachment of medial meniscus); the posterior intercondylar area is where the PCL attaches.
B(i)
The nutrient artery (medullary artery) is the main artery of the diaphysis. It is directed obliquely away from the epiphyseal end. When there is an epiphysis at both ends (tibia is one of the 5 bones unique in having epiphyseal plates at both ends — viz: femur, tibia, fibula, humerus, and radius), the nutrient canal is directed away from the more actively growing end. Hughes: 'to the elbow I go, from the knee I flee'. Fracture of the middle third of the tibia lies in a 'watershed' zone between the nutrient artery (supplying the upper 2/3) and the periosteal vessels (supplying the lower 1/3), making this zone most susceptible to avascular non-union.
B(ii)
Proximal tibia: tibial plateau fractures (high-energy trauma), associated with meniscal and ligamentous tears. Mid-shaft tibia: most common site of delayed or non-union, stress fractures (runners), and compartment syndrome (anterior compartment syndrome). Distal tibia (ankle): Pott's fracture involving the malleolus; ankle sprains; avulsion fractures.
C(i)
Tibia: large weight-bearing medial bone; articulates with femoral condyles, fibula head, and talus; contributes the roof (inferior surface of tibia) and the medial malleolus (wall) of the ankle mortise; the medial surface is subcutaneous. Fibula: not a weight-bearing bone; does not articulate with the femur or patella at the knee (only serves as attachment for knee joint structures); contributes the lateral malleolus (wall of ankle mortise) from fibula. At the ankle: lateral malleolar wall is from fibula and medial malleolar wall is from tibia.
