questions.answerText:
A(i)
Autonomic nerve supply:
• Vessels and nerves enter the large salivary glands at the hilum and gradually branch into the lobules; a rich vascular and nerve plexus surrounds the secretory and ductal components of each lobule.
• The capillaries surrounding the secretory end pieces are important for saliva secretion, stimulated by the autonomic nervous system.
• Parasympathetic stimulation (usually through smell or taste of food): promotes vasodilation and a copious watery secretion.
• Sympathetic stimulation: produces small amounts of viscous saliva, rich in organic material. NOTE: dry mouth sensation in stressful situations (sympathetic predominance).
A(ii)
Immunological secretory mechanism:
• Plasma cells (in the connective tissue around the glands) secrete IgA.
• IgA forms a complex with a secretory component synthesized by the serous acinar cells, intercalated duct cells, and striated duct cells.
• The IgA-rich secretory complex released into the saliva is resistant to enzymatic digestion and constitutes an immunological defense mechanism against pathogens in the oral cavity.
B(i)
Parotid vs pancreatic tissue:
• Both resemble each other histologically.
• Parotid gland: has adipocytes (fat cells) in its parenchyma.
• Pancreatic tissue: has islets of Langerhans (endocrine clusters) and centroacinar cells.
B(ii)
• Minor salivary glands by location and secretion: von Ebner's glands of tongue (posterior dorsal and lateral): serous acini only.
• Palate, base and lateral border of tongue: predominantly mucous acini.
• Lip, cheek, apex of tongue: mixed serous and mucous acini.
• Minor glands secrete 10% of the total volume of saliva but account for approximately 70% of the mucus secreted.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the autonomic nerve supply to the salivary glands, including which division of the autonomic nervous system produces each type of secretory response and what type of saliva each produces.
A(ii) Describe the full immunological secretory mechanism of the large salivary glands, identifying the cell type that secretes IgA and the cell types that synthesise the secretory component.
B(i) The parotid gland resembles pancreatic tissue but can be distinguished from it. State the distinguishing features of each gland.
B(ii) Classify all minor salivary glands by location and secretion type, and state what proportion of total saliva volume and mucus the minor glands produce.

A(i) Describe the gross histology of the three types of muscle tissue (skeletal, smooth, and cardiac) as seen in longitudinal section and cross-section under the light microscope.
A(ii) Relate the structural differences of each muscle type to their specific pathological conditions.
B(i) Explain how the histological organization of cardiac muscle facilitates rapid spread of the signal to contract, and state why blockage of the coronary arteries leads to widespread myocardial damage.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Skeletal muscle — longitudinal section: cross-striations of alternating dark (A bands, anisotropic) and light (I bands, isotropic) bands; each I band bisected by a dark transverse Z disc; multinucleated fibers at periphery. Cross-section: peripheral nuclei; high cytoplasm-to-nucleus ratio. Smooth muscle — longitudinal section: meshwork appearance; no striations; elongated spindle-shaped cells; elongated and central nuclei. Cross-section: central nuclei; low cytoplasm-to-nucleus ratio. Cardiac muscle — longitudinal section: striations; branching cells; intercalated discs. Cross-section: central nuclei; high cytoplasm-to-nucleus ratio.
A(ii)
Skeletal muscle: troponin subunits (troponin I and troponin T) are integral to muscle contraction; mutations in cardiac troponin subunits can result in cardiomyopathies. Smooth muscle: smooth muscle cells are able to undergo cell division (unlike cardiac and skeletal muscle). Cardiac muscle: atrial myocytes secrete atrial natriuretic peptide; kidneys respond to this to cause sodium and water loss (natriuresis and diuresis); when natriuretic peptide levels fall, kidneys result in sodium and water conservation.
B(i)
Cardiac muscle cells act as a syncytium through gap junctions in intercalated discs, which provide ionic continuity between adjacent cells, allowing the signal to contract to pass throughout the organ. The blood supply to the heart is through three main coronary arteries prone to atheroma. Acute coronary arterial occlusion involving nearly the entire area at risk causes necrosis of the myocardium. Because the cardiac muscle acts as a syncytium and is continuously active, obstruction of coronary blood flow rapidly leads to widespread ischemia and necrosis of the myocardium.

A(i)
• A strong, incomplete fibrous compartment of the rectus abdominis and pyramidalis, formed by the aponeuroses of the three flat muscles.
• The linea alba separates the right and left rectus abdominis; the linea semilunaris marks the lateral border; tendinous intersections and linea alba give the 'six packs'.
A(ii)
It has an anterior and posterior wall for most of its length: anterior wall from the aponeuroses of external oblique and half of internal oblique; posterior wall from the aponeuroses of half of internal oblique and transversus abdominis.
A(iii)
• Superior and inferior epigastric arteries and veins, lymphatic vessels and the distal portions of the thoracoabdominal nerves (anterior rami of T7 to T12).
• Superior epigastric: terminal branch of internal thoracic, descends posterior to the muscle, anastomoses with inferior epigastric; inferior epigastric: from external iliac, enters the sheath at the arcuate line.
A(iv)
A strong expandable support; protects viscera from injury such as a low blow in boxing; compresses the abdominal contents; maintains or increases intra-abdominal pressure; moves the trunk and maintains posture.
B(i)
• In anterior cutaneous nerve entrapment syndrome (ACNES), 12 of 95 adolescents with chronic abdominal pain had it; the Carnett sign was positive at the lateral border of rectus abdominis in all 12.
• Altered skin sensation was present in 11 of 12; the distal thoracoabdominal nerves run in the rectus sheath.
• After treatment (1 to 3 injections, n = 5; neurectomy, n = 7) pain was absent in 11; the conclusion was that ACNES is present in 1 of 8 such adolescents.
C(i)
• Rectus abdominis: long paired muscle split by the linea alba, origin pubic crest, insertion xiphoid process and costal cartilages of ribs 5 to 7, nerve T7 to T11, stabilises the pelvis in walking and depresses the ribs.
• Pyramidalis: small triangular muscle superficial to rectus, base on the pubis and apex on the linea alba, origin pubic crest and symphysis, insertion linea alba, tenses the linea alba; nerve supply is the subcostal nerve (T12).

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the gross anatomy of cartilage under the following headings: definition, histogenesis (development from mesenchyme), growth mechanisms, and nutrient supply.
A(ii) Relate the three types of cartilage to their specific locations and collagen types, explaining why each is suited to its location.
B(i) Explain why articular cartilage degenerates with age and state the role of exercise in cartilage health.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Definition: Cartilage is a connective tissue in which the cells are relatively sparse and embedded in a large amount of firm characteristic matrix. It is a specialized form of connective tissue in which the firm consistency of the extracellular matrix allows the tissue to bear mechanical stresses without permanent distortion. Histogenesis: Cartilage is derived from the mesenchyme. The first modification observed is the rounding up of mesenchymal cells, which retract their extensions, multiply rapidly, and form mesenchymal condensations of chondroblasts (cells with ribosome-rich basophilic cytoplasm). Synthesis and deposition of matrix then begin to separate chondroblasts from one another. Differentiation takes place from center outward: central cells have characteristics of chondrocytes, peripheral cells are typical chondroblasts. The superficial mesenchyme develops into the perichondrium. Growth mechanisms: interstitial growth (from mitotic division of preexisting chondrocytes, expanding from within) and appositional growth (from differentiation of perichondrial cells, expanding from the outside). Nutrient supply: Cartilage is avascular; nourished by diffusion of nutrients from capillaries in adjacent connective tissue (perichondrium) or by synovial fluid. It has no lymphatic vessels or nerves. Chondrocytes exhibit low metabolic activity.
A(ii)
Hyaline cartilage: most common form; collagen type II is the principal collagen; found in nose, trachea, bronchi, rib-sternal joints, and synovial joints; resilient and shock absorbing. Elastic cartilage: contains abundant elastic fibers in addition to collagen type II; found in auricle of ear, external auditory canals, eustachian tubes, epiglottis, and cuneiform cartilage in larynx; elastic fibers allow flexibility. Fibrocartilage: rich in collagen type I (acidophilic matrix); found in intervertebral disks, attachments of certain ligaments to cartilaginous surfaces, and symphysis pubis; dense collagen provides strength for high-load sites.
B(i)
Articular cartilage is devoid of perichondrium and is sustained by diffusion of oxygen and nutrients from synovial fluid; this limited supply combined with low metabolic activity of chondrocytes means repair is slow. Hyaline cartilage is more susceptible to degenerative aging processes; calcification of the matrix, preceded by an increase in size and volume of chondrocytes followed by their death, leads to osteoarthritis. Role of exercise: participation in sports involving torsional loading, fast acceleration/deceleration, repetitive high impact increases risk of osteoarthritis. However, some levels of loading and exercise are beneficial: exercise enhances production of matrix molecules, which can have a positive effect on joint health. Exercise has both beneficial and detrimental effects on cartilage.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the four main layers of the gastrointestinal tract wall, giving the composition of each layer.
A(ii) For the muscularis layer, name the two nerve plexuses associated with it, state where each is located, and explain the function of each.
B(i) Explain why the esophagus has an adventitia instead of a serosa, and state the structural difference between these two outermost coverings.
B(ii) Distinguish between the serosa and the mesentery, naming the structures each is continuous with.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Mucosa: consists of an epithelial lining, lamina propria (zone of loose connective tissue rich in blood vessels, lymphatics, lymphocytes, smooth muscle cells, and sometimes small glands), and muscularis mucosae (thin layer of smooth muscle that separates the mucosa from the submucosa and allows local movements of the mucosa).
• Submucosa: denser connective tissue containing larger blood and lymph vessels, the submucosal (Meissner) plexus of autonomic nerves, and possibly glands and lymphoid tissue.
• Muscularis (muscularis externa): thick layer of smooth muscle organized into an internal circular sublayer and an external longitudinal sublayer; connective tissue between them contains blood vessels, lymph vessels, and the myenteric (Auerbach) nerve plexus.
• Serosa: outermost layer; a thin sheet of loose connective tissue covered with mesothelium (simple squamous covering epithelium); rich in blood vessels, lymphatics, and adipose tissue.
A(ii)
• Submucosal (Meissner) plexus: located in the submucosa between the submucosa and the muscularis; together with the myenteric plexus constitutes the local enteric nervous system.
• Myenteric (Auerbach) plexus: located in the connective tissue between the circular and longitudinal muscle sublayers; responsible for local contraction of the muscularis, mixing and propelling the contents of the lumen (peristalsis).
• Both plexuses together form the local enteric nervous system, which functions independently of the CNS; they are composed mainly of nerve cell aggregates forming small parasympathetic ganglia, numerous in regions of greatest motility.
B(i)
The esophagus is not suspended in a cavity but is bound directly to adjacent structures, so instead of a serosa it has a thick adventitia. The adventitia consists of connective tissue containing vessels and nerves but lacks mesothelium, whereas the serosa is covered by mesothelium.
B(ii)
The serosa of the small and large intestines is continuous with parts of the mesentery. The mesentery is a large fold of adipose connective tissue covered on both sides by mesothelium; it suspends the intestines and is continuous with the peritoneum (the serous membrane lining the abdominal cavity).

A
Within the substance of the parotid gland, from superficial to deep are found the facial nerve and its branches, the retromandibular vein and its two divisions, and the external carotid artery and its two terminal branches. The facial nerve radiates through the anterior border of the gland like a goose's foot, termed the Pes Anserinus, giving off the temporal branch, the zygomatic branch, the buccal branch, the marginal mandibular branch, and the cervical branch.
B
Frey's syndrome commonly occurs after parotid surgery or trauma, from injury of the auriculo-temporal nerve and great auricular nerve; the facial nerve's course through the parotid gland is therefore clinically important in parotid surgery, where the nerve and its branches are structures to be identified and preserved.
C
Bell's palsy is associated with drooping of the mouth, reflecting facial nerve dysfunction; facial laceration is also noted as a clinical correlate involving this nerve's territory. Because the facial nerve, once it has divided within the parotid gland into its temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular and cervical branches, supplies the muscles of facial expression, injury to the trunk or a branch of the nerve produces the drooping and loss of movement seen in facial nerve palsy.
questions.question:
A. Describe the course, relations and branches of the facial nerve within the parotid gland, and its termination pattern.
B. State the structures/procedures for which knowledge of the facial nerve's branching is clinically important.
C. Explain the anatomical/functional basis of the deformity that results when this nerve is injured.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
• A pear-shaped fibromuscular sac that stores and concentrates bile, in the gallbladder fossa on the inferior surface of the right lobe of the liver, 7 to 10 cm long, 3 cm broad and 30 to 50 ml in capacity.
• Fundus: projects beyond the inferior border of the liver, covered by peritoneum on all sides. Body: superior surface adherent to the liver and devoid of peritoneum. Neck: upper narrow part ending in the cystic duct, with a spiral fold.
• The fundus is related to the anterior abdominal wall and transverse colon; the body's inferior surface to the transverse colon and the 1st and 2nd parts of the duodenum.
A(ii)
• Right and left hepatic ducts emerge at the porta hepatis; the common hepatic duct (3 to 4 cm) is joined by the cystic duct (3 to 4 cm, spiral folds of Heister) to form the common bile duct.
• The common bile duct (about 8 cm, 6 mm wide) has supraduodenal, retroduodenal, infraduodenal and intraduodenal parts, joining the main pancreatic duct at the hepatopancreatic ampulla.
A(iii)
• Cystic artery (from the right hepatic artery) is the chief supply, with the cystic vein to the portal vein; the posterior superior pancreaticoduodenal branches supply the lower bile duct.
• Sympathetic nerves come from the celiac plexus and parasympathetic from the vagus.
B(i)
The posteromedial wall of the neck may dilate as Hartmann's pouch, where gallstones may lodge.
B(ii)
Calot's triangle (liver inferior surface, common hepatic duct, cystic duct) locates the cystic artery in laparoscopic cholecystectomy; Lund's node enlarges in cholecystitis or cholangitis and may be removed.
B(iii)
Gallbladder muscle and the sphincter of Oddi have reciprocal innervation (gallbladder contracts, sphincter relaxes); disruption is biliary dyskinesia.
C(i)
• Inflammation irritates the subdiaphragmatic parietal peritoneum supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3, 4, 5), referred to the right shoulder tip supplied by the supraclavicular nerve (C3, C4).
• In Murphy's sign the inflamed gallbladder descends on deep inspiration and contacts the palpating hand at the right costal margin, causing pain and a caught breath.

A(i) location, shape, dimensions and parts;
A(ii) the ducts and course of the common bile duct;

A(i) Describe the parotid gland under the following headings: location, external features, and capsule.
A(ii) Describe the parotid duct, and list the structures within the substance of the gland from superficial to deep, and the other structures found within the gland.
B. Explain the clinical basis for why the parotid gland is particularly vulnerable to nerve injury during surgery, and describe the syndrome that can follow such injury.
C. Distinguish between the parotid gland and the submandibular gland in terms of their ducts and ganglia associated with their secretomotor supply.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The parotid gland is the largest salivary gland (para = around, otic = ear); it is situated below the external acoustic meatus, in front of the sternomastoid, and also projects forward onto the surface of masseter. It is pyramidal in shape with the apex pointing downward, has 4 surfaces (superior/base, lateral/superficial, anteromedial, posteromedial) separated by 3 borders (anterior, posterior, medial), and has 1 main lobe and 1 accessory lobe (a small detached part called the accessory parotid gland or Socia Parotidis, lying on masseter between the zygomatic arch and the parotid duct). The capsule has a false capsule, formed by the investing layer of deep cervical fascia, and a true capsule, formed by condensation of the stroma.
A(ii)
The parotid duct is about 5 cm long, arises from the anterior border of the gland, runs on masseter, and at the anterior border of masseter runs medially to pierce buccinator and the mucosa, opening into the vestibule of the mouth opposite the crown of the upper 2nd molar tooth; its surface anatomy corresponds to the middle third of a line from the lower border of the tragus to a point midway between the nasal ala and the upper labial margin. From superficial to deep within the substance of the gland are: the facial nerve and its branches; the retromandibular vein and its two divisions (maxillary vein, superficial temporal vein); and the external carotid artery and its two terminal branches. Other structures within the gland are the auriculotemporal nerve, the posterior auricular artery, and the preauricular lymph nodes.
B
Within the gland, the facial nerve radiates like a goose's foot (Pes Anserinus) through the anterior border of the gland into its branches (temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular, cervical); because the facial nerve runs through the substance of the gland, it is at risk during parotid surgery or trauma. Frey's syndrome (also known as gustatory sweating or auriculo-temporal nerve syndrome) commonly occurs after parotid surgery or trauma, from injury of the auriculotemporal and great auricular nerves; during healing, secretomotor fibres of the auriculotemporal nerve join with the great auricular nerve and reach the sweat glands of facial skin, so that sweating, warmth and redness of the face occur as a result of salivary stimulation by the smell or taste of food.
C
The parotid gland's secretomotor (parasympathetic) supply is via the auriculotemporal nerve, producing a watery secretion, with sympathetic supply producing a mucous-rich, sticky secretion derived from the plexus around the external carotid artery. In contrast, the submandibular gland's duct is the submandibular duct (Wharton's duct), and its nerve supply is via branches from the submandibular ganglion, through which it receives parasympathetic fibres from the chorda tympani, sensory fibres from the lingual branch of the mandibular nerve, and sympathetic fibres from the plexus on the facial artery.

A(i)
Immunological defense system:
• Name: Mucosa-Associated Lymphoid Tissue (MALT).
• Layers occupied: the mucosa (especially the lamina propria located just below the epithelium) and the submucosal layers.
• Cell types: macrophages and lymphocytes (some of which actively produce antibodies); also free immune cells and lymphoid nodules.
• Antibody produced: mainly immunoglobulin A (IgA).
A(ii)
IgA protection mechanism:
• IgA antibodies undergo transcytosis into the intestinal lumen, bound to the secretory protein produced by epithelial cells.
• This complex (secretory IgA) protects against viral and bacterial pathogens.
• IgA is resistant to proteolytic enzymes and can therefore coexist with the proteases present in the lumen, making it effective even in the enzyme-rich intestinal environment.
B(i)
Stratified squamous epithelium lines the oral cavity, esophagus, and anal canal (not vulnerable simple columnar). The rest of the GIT (except these three regions) is lined by a simple thin vulnerable epithelium. Because the rest of the GIT is lined by this vulnerable epithelium and normally contains thousands of microbial species (including potential pathogens), the MALT provides an essential backup to the thin physical barrier.
B(ii)
The enteric nervous system (submucosal/Meissner and myenteric/Auerbach plexuses) provides an anatomic basis for the well-known actions of emotional stress on the stomach and other regions of the GIT. These plexuses are interconnected with the autonomic nervous system and CNS.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the immunological defence system of the gastrointestinal tract, including: the name of the tissue system; the layers of the GIT wall it occupies; the cell types it contains; and the antibody it produces.
A(ii) Explain the complete mechanism by which IgA protects the lumen of the GIT from pathogens, including the role of the secretory protein and the property that makes IgA effective.
B(i) State which regions of the GIT are lined by stratified squamous epithelium rather than the simple thin vulnerable epithelium lining the rest of the tract, and explain the significance of this difference in the context of microbial defense.
B(ii) Explain the clinical and anatomical basis for the well-known effects of emotional stress on the stomach and other regions of the GIT.

(A) Describe the duodenum under the headings: A(i) parts and dimensions A(ii) peritoneal relations A(iii) visceral relations.
(B) Explain the clinical basis for the duodenum's common site of ulceration and for paraduodenal hernia.
(C) Distinguish between the jejunum and the ileum.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The duodenum is the first, shortest (about 25 cm) and widest part of the small intestine; it is C-shaped and mostly retroperitoneal, made up of four parts - superior (5 cm), descending (7.5-8 cm), horizontal (6-10 cm) and ascending (2.5 cm).
A(ii)
The proximal 2.5 cm of the superior part is movable and intraperitoneal, attached to the lesser omentum above and greater omentum below; the rest of the duodenum is retroperitoneal, covered by peritoneum only on its anterior aspect.
A(iii)
The superior part is anteriorly related to the quadrate lobe of the liver and gallbladder, and posteriorly to the gastroduodenal artery, bile duct, portal vein and inferior vena cava; the descending part is related medially to the head of pancreas and bile duct, laterally to the right colic flexure, and rests on the right kidney, ureter, psoas major and renal vessels, and receives the major duodenal papilla; the horizontal part crosses the inferior vena cava, aorta and L3 vertebra and is crossed anteriorly by the superior mesenteric vessels; the ascending part rises to the duodenojejunal flexure.
B
• The proximal (superior) part of the duodenum is the most common site of duodenal ulcer.
• The duodenojejunal flexure is fixed by the suspensory muscle of the duodenum (ligament of Treitz), which passes posterior to the pancreas and splenic vein and anterior to the left renal vein; a weakness near this fixed flexure is the anatomical basis for a paraduodenal hernia.
C
• The jejunum lies mainly in the left upper (infracolic) quadrant, has thicker, more vascular walls and a wider, often empty lumen, with long and few vasa recta, one or two layers of arterial arcades, numerous circular mucosal folds, and large, thick, abundant villi.
• The ileum lies predominantly in the right lower quadrant and pelvis, has thinner, less vascular walls and a narrower, often loaded lumen, with short and numerous vasa recta and multiple layers of arterial arcades.
• The ileum has smaller and sparser circular mucosal folds and shorter, thinner villi than the jejunum, but the terminal ileum has numerous Peyer's patches and more numerous solitary lymphatic follicles, which are absent or scanty in the jejunum.
• The jejunum has mesenteric windows and less abundant mesenteric fat, whereas the ileum has no windows and more abundant mesenteric fat.

A(i)
Structure:
• Capsule and septa: a capsule of connective tissue rich in collagen fibers surrounds the large salivary glands; septa of connective tissue originate from the capsule and divide the glands into lobules; each lobule contains numerous secretory units (acini).
• Parenchyma: consists of secretory end pieces and a branching duct system arranged in lobules separated by septae of connective tissue from the capsule. Vessels and nerves enter at the hilum and gradually branch into the lobules.
• Cell types in secretory end pieces: serous cells (polarized protein-secreting cells, pyramidal in shape, round nuclei, well-stained RER, apical secretory granules; joined apically by tight and adherent junctions; form a spherical unit called an acinus with a very small central lumen; secrete enzymes and other proteins); mucous cells; and nonsecretory myoepithelial cells.
• Duct system in sequence: secretory end pieces → intercalated ducts (lined by simple low cuboidal epithelium, surrounded by myoepithelial cells) → striated ducts (intralobular) → interlobular (excretory/striated ducts drain into these) → interlobar ducts → main duct (opens into the oral cavity, lined with nonkeratinized-stratified squamous epithelium).
A(ii)
Secretion types:
• Parotid gland: serous and watery.
• Submandibular and sublingual glands: seromucous secretion.
• Minor glands: mostly mucous.
• Type depends on content of glycoprotein mucin: serous, seromucous, or mucous.
B(i)
• Intercalated ducts: several short intercalated ducts join to form striated ducts; they are lined by cuboidal epithelial cells that have the ability to divide and differentiate into secretory or ductal cells; also called intralobular ducts.
• Striated ducts: characterized by radial striations that extend from the bases of the cells to the level of the central nuclei; striations consist of infoldings of the basal plasma membrane with numerous elongated mitochondria aligned parallel to the infolded membranes (characteristic of ion-transporting cells); they have a folded basal membrane enabling active transport; also called intralobular ducts.
B(ii)
Saliva is modified by the cells of the duct system draining the secretory units: much Na+ and Cl- is reabsorbed while certain growth factors and digestive enzymes are added. Water resorption and ion secretion in the striated ducts make saliva hypotonic (reduced Na and Cl ions; increased carbonate and potassium ions).
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the gross and microscopic structure of the large salivary glands under the following headings: capsule and septa; parenchyma (secretory end pieces); cell types in the secretory end pieces; the duct system in sequence from secretory unit to oral cavity.
A(ii) State the type of secretion produced by each of the three pairs of major salivary glands and by the minor glands.
B(i) Distinguish between striated ducts and intercalated ducts, including location, epithelium, and function.
B(ii) Explain how saliva is modified as it passes through the duct system.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
The great saphenous vein (GSV) is the longest vein in the body. It is formed by the union of the dorsal vein of the great toe and the dorsal venous arch of the foot. It ascends anterior to the medial malleolus, passes posterior to the medial condyle of the femur (about a hand's breadth posterior to the medial border of the patella), anastomoses freely with the small saphenous vein, traverses the saphenous opening in the fascia lata, and empties into the femoral vein.
A(ii)
The GSV has 10–12 valves, which are more numerous in the leg than in the thigh; these valves are usually located just inferior to the perforating veins. Perforating veins also have their own valves. Tributaries in the anterior and lateral part of the thighs converge to form the accessory saphenous vein (ASV), which communicates the GSV with the small saphenous vein. Just before emptying into the femoral vein, the GSV receives tributaries from the superficial circumflex iliac, superficial epigastric, and external pudendal veins.
B(i)
The small saphenous vein (SSV) arises on the lateral side of the foot from the union of the dorsal vein of the little toe with the dorsal venous arch. It ascends posterior to the lateral malleolus as a continuation of the lateral marginal vein, passes along the lateral border of the calcaneal tendon, inclines to the midline of the fibula and penetrates the deep fascia, ascends between the heads of the gastrocnemius muscle, and empties into the popliteal vein in the popliteal fossa.
B(ii)
There are four main pulse points in the lower limb: femoral (palpated midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and pubic symphysis — the mid-inguinal point); popliteal (deep in the popliteal fossa, requires deep palpation, best with slight knee flexion); dorsalis pedis (on the dorsum of the foot, just lateral to extensor hallucis longus tendon); and posterior tibial (inferoposteriorly to the medial malleolus). The GSV anterior to the medial malleolus is the classic site for venous cut-down; the GSV at the medial condyle of the femur is another accessible site.
C(i)
Superficial veins (GSV and SSV) are unaccompanied, lie in the superficial fascia, and their varicosity is visible. Deep veins of the lower limb accompany the arteries (read-up). Deep vein thrombosis involves the deep system and poses a risk of pulmonary embolism because the deep veins drain directly into the popliteal, femoral, and iliac veins and thence to the inferior vena cava. Superficial varicosity alone rarely embolises unless thrombosis extends through a perforating vein into the deep system.
questions.question:
Describe the great saphenous vein and small saphenous vein under the following headings, and explain the clinical basis of their use in surgery.
A(i) Origin, course, and termination of the great saphenous vein
A(ii) Tributaries and valves of the great saphenous vein
B(i) Origin, course, and termination of the small saphenous vein
B(ii) Clinical basis: pulse points of the lower limb and sites of venepuncture or cut-down
C(i) Distinguish varicosity from deep vein thrombosis based on the anatomical differences between the superficial and deep venous systems

(A) Describe the three main openings of the diaphragm - A(i) oesophageal hiatus A(ii) aortic hiatus A(iii) caval opening - including their vertebral levels and the structures each transmits.
(B) Explain the clinical basis of diaphragmatic (hiatus) hernia.
(C) Distinguish between the oesophageal hiatus and the aortic hiatus.
questions.answerText:
A(ii)
The aortic hiatus lies posterior to the diaphragm, between the two crura, at the level of the lower border of the T12 vertebra; it transmits the aorta, the thoracic duct and sometimes the azygos and hemiazygos veins. Because the aorta does not pierce the diaphragm itself, movements of the diaphragm during respiration do not affect blood flow through it.
A(iii)
The caval opening lies in the central tendon of the diaphragm at the level of T8; it transmits the inferior vena cava, terminal branches of the right phrenic nerve, and a few hepatic lymphatic vessels. The inferior vena cava is adherent to the margin of this opening, so diaphragmatic contraction during inspiration widens the opening and dilates the inferior vena cava, aiding venous return to the heart.
B
• The right and left crura arise from the bodies of the L1-L3 vertebrae, the anterior longitudinal ligament and the intervertebral discs; the oesophageal hiatus lies within the right crus, to the left of the midline, superior to and to the left of the aortic hiatus. Diaphragmatic hernia (sliding and paraoesophageal types) and diaphragmatic rupture are clinical considerations related to weakness or defects around these openings.
• In most individuals, about 70%, both margins of the oesophageal hiatus are formed by muscular bundles of the right crus; in others the left crus contributes to the right margin, and such variation can affect the sphincter-like action around the oesophagus.
C
• The oesophageal hiatus is a muscular opening in the right crus at the level of T10 that actively constricts around the oesophagus with diaphragmatic contraction, contributing to prevention of reflux.
• The aortic hiatus is a non-muscular, fibrous opening bounded by the crura and the median arcuate ligament at the lower border of T12, so diaphragmatic contraction does not compress or affect flow through the aorta.
• The oesophageal hiatus transmits the oesophagus and vagal trunks, whereas the aortic hiatus transmits the aorta and thoracic duct, reflecting their different anatomical roles.

A(i)
The axilla is a pyramid-shaped space between the upper part of the arm and the side of the upper chest; its apex is the cervicoaxillary canal, bounded by the 1st rib, clavicle, and superior edge of the scapula, forming the passageway between the neck and axilla.
A(ii)
The base is formed by concave skin, subcutaneous tissue, and the axillary (deep) fascia.
A(iii)
Anterior wall: pectoralis major and minor, subclavius, and clavipectoral fascia. Posterior wall: scapula and subscapularis above, teres major and latissimus dorsi below. Medial wall: upper ribs, intercostal muscles, and serratus anterior. Lateral wall: narrow and bony, formed by the intertubercular groove of the humerus.
A(iv)
Contents: the axillary artery and its branches, the axillary vein and its tributaries, the infraclavicular part of the brachial plexus, axillary lymph nodes, and loose areolar/adipose tissue, all enclosed with the plexus in the axillary sheath.
B
• The axillary vein is large and lies in an exposed, superficial position within the axilla.
• Wounds to the axilla therefore often involve the axillary vein because of its large size and exposed position.
• A wound to the proximal part of the axillary vein is especially dangerous because of the risk of air entering the vessel (air embolism).
C
• The quadrangular space lies in the posterior wall of the axilla and transmits the axillary nerve and the posterior circumflex humeral artery and vein.
• The triangular interval also lies in the posterior wall and transmits the radial nerve and the profunda brachii artery.
• Both spaces are related to the long head of triceps brachii and the teres major muscle in their boundaries.
• The quadrangular space thus carries the nerve/vessels supplying the deltoid and teres minor region, while the triangular interval carries those continuing into the posterior compartment of the arm.
• This distinction explains why injury near the surgical neck of the humerus threatens the axillary nerve, whereas injury lower down at the spiral groove threatens the radial nerve instead.
questions.question:
Describe the axilla under the following headings:
A(i) Shape and apex
A(ii) Base
A(iii) Walls
A(iv) Contents
B. Explain the clinical basis for the axillary vein being particularly vulnerable to injury in this region.
C. Distinguish between the quadrangular space and the triangular interval found in the posterior wall of the axilla.

questions.answerText:
(i)
• The renal arteries arise from the aorta at the level of the L1/L2 intervertebral disc; the right renal artery passes posterior to the inferior vena cava.
• Each renal artery divides at the hilum into anterior and posterior branches; these give rise to segmental arteries.
• Four segmental arteries, apical, anterosuperior, anteroinferior and inferior, arise from the anterior branch, and the posterior branch itself constitutes the posterior segmental artery.
• Each segmental artery further gives lobar arteries, one for each renal pyramid, which give two or three interlobar arteries running toward the cortex on each side of the pyramid.
• Interlobar arteries give arcuate arteries at the corticomedullary junction, which give several interlobular arteries, from which afferent glomerular arterioles arise.
• The renal veins lie anterior to their respective arteries; each renal vein drains into the inferior vena cava, and the left renal vein additionally receives the left suprarenal and left gonadal veins before crossing anterior to the aorta.
(ii)
• The segmental arteries of the kidney are described as end arteries, meaning they do not anastomose with one another.
• Because each segmental artery supplies its own renal segment without collateral supply from adjacent segmental arteries, the renal parenchyma is divided into distinct vascular segments.
(iii)
• Since the segmental arteries are end arteries, occlusion or injury of one segmental artery cuts off blood supply to its corresponding renal segment.
• This lack of anastomosis means the affected segment cannot receive compensatory blood flow from neighbouring segments.
• Lymphatic drainage of the kidney is to the right and left lumbar lymph nodes, and nerve supply is via the renal plexus (vagus and abdominopelvic splanchnic nerves), so a segmental vascular injury is an isolated event within the kidney rather than one shared with adjacent segments.
questions.question:
(i) Describe the origin, course, branches and distribution of the renal artery.
(ii) State why the segmental arteries of the kidney are described as end arteries.
(iii) Explain the anatomical basis of the consequence of injury or occlusion of a segmental renal artery.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
The femur is the long bone of the thigh; the longest and strongest bone in the body (Latin: femur = thigh); it accounts for approximately one-quarter of a person's total height and averages 45 cm. It has a shaft (body) and 2 expanded ends. Parts: (1) proximal end — consisting of head, neck, and the trochanters; (2) shaft; (3) distal end — consisting of the femoral condyles. It articulates superiorly with the acetabulum to form the hip joint, and inferiorly with the patella and tibia to form the knee joint.
A(ii)
The neck is the curved upper end of the shaft; it connects the head to the shaft and passes downward, backward, and laterally, obliquely placed to the long axis of the shaft. The angle of inclination (neck–shaft angle) is approximately 135 degrees; reduction of this angle is coxa vara and follows fracture of the neck of femur. The angle of anteversion (torsion) — the forward relationship of head and neck — is normally 12–15 degrees; wide variation in anteversion of the femoral neck means that during total hip arthroplasty, orientation of the femoral neck osteotomy in correct anteversion must be assessed after hip dislocation with reference to the shaft of femur with knee flexed at 90 degrees, or an inaccurate cut and malposition of the prosthesis may result.
B(i)
The fovea capitis on the head of femur transmits blood from the obturator artery via the ligament of the head of femur (ligamentum teres). The main blood supply travels retinacularly along the intracapsular neck from the medial femoral circumflex artery (which wraps around the posterior side of the femur supplying its neck and head). In an intracapsular fracture, these retinacular vessels are disrupted; the obturator artery contribution via ligamentum teres is insufficient to sustain the head, and avascular necrosis results.
B(ii)
The linea aspera is a posterior ridge on the shaft of femur; it diverges superiorly and inferiorly. The inferior divergence ends as the medial supracondylar ridge to the adductor tubercle and the lateral supracondylar ridge. The linea aspera gives origin to many muscles: adductor longus inserts into the middle third of its medial lip; adductor magnus into the gluteal tuberosity, linea aspera, and medial supracondylar line; the vastus lateralis arises from its lateral lip.
C(i)
Pressure epiphyses are formed at joints and bear compressive forces (e.g., head of femur — a pressure epiphysis; femoral condyles). Traction epiphyses are pulled by muscles (e.g., greater trochanter — traction epiphysis for gluteus medius which draws it upward, medially, and backward; lesser trochanter — traction epiphysis for iliopsoas, the great flexor of the hip joint). The nutrient artery is directed obliquely away from the epiphyseal end; when there is an epiphysis at both ends, the nutrient canal is directed away from the more actively growing end (as per Hughes's rule: 'to the elbow I go, from the knee I flee'). Surgically, the nutrient canal direction matters during intramedullary nail insertion, as the nail must not block the nutrient foramen.
questions.question:
Describe the femur under the following headings and explain how its zones relate to common pathologies.
A(i) General features, parts, and gross anatomy of the femur
A(ii) The neck of femur — angles of inclination and torsion, and why fracture here causes coxa vara
B(i) Blood supply of the head of femur and why avascular necrosis occurs after intracapsular fracture
B(ii) The linea aspera — muscular and bony attachments, and clinical significance
C(i) Distinguish pressure epiphysis from traction epiphysis with examples from the femur, and explain why the nutrient canal direction matters surgically

A(i) Describe the three parts of the renal tubule, including the cell type lining each part, distinguishing microscopic features, and the primary function (reabsorption vs. secretion) attributed to each part.
A(ii) Describe the two parts of the nephron loop, including the type of epithelium lining each limb and any variation across nephron types.
B(i) Describe the renal corpuscle, naming its two components, the two layers of the glomerular capsule, and the specialised features of the visceral layer.
B(ii) For the proximal convoluted tubule, explain how its structure is adapted for its function.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Three parts of the renal tubule:
• Proximal convoluted tubule (PCT): cuboidal cells with dense microvilli (brush border — increase surface area); large mitochondria; functions in reabsorption and secretion; confined to the cortex.
• Nephron loop: descending and ascending limbs; distal descending limb = descending thin limb — simple squamous epithelium; thick ascending limb — cuboidal to columnar cells (thin in some nephrons).
• Distal convoluted tubule (DCT): cuboidal cells with very few microvilli; functions more in secretion than reabsorption; confined to the cortex.
A(ii)
Nephron loop:
• Descending limb: proximal descending limb is continuous with the proximal tubule; distal descending limb (thin limb) is lined by simple squamous epithelium.
• Thick ascending limb: cuboidal to columnar cells; may be thin in some nephrons.
B(i)
Renal corpuscle:
• Two components: glomerulus and glomerular (Bowman's) capsule.
• Glomerulus: tuft of capillaries with fenestrated endothelium (highly porous) allowing filtrate formation.
Glomerular capsule: cup-shaped, hollow structure surrounding the glomerulus; has two layers:
• Parietal layer: simple squamous epithelium.
• Visceral layer: branching epithelial podocytes; extensions terminate in foot processes that cling to the basement membrane; filtration slits between foot processes allow filtrate to pass into the capsular space.
B(ii)
Structural adaptations of the PCT:
• Dense microvilli (brush border) greatly increase the apical surface area for reabsorption.
• Large mitochondria provide energy (ATP) for active transport processes.
• Highly infolded basolateral membrane increases surface area for solute exchange at the basolateral side.
• These features together support the PCT's role in reabsorption and secretion.

A(i)
An omentum is a double-layered extension or fold passing from the stomach and proximal duodenum to adjacent organs or to the abdominal wall; there are two types, lesser and greater.
A(ii)
The lesser omentum is a two-layered fold connecting the lesser curvature of the stomach and proximal duodenum to the liver; the hepatoduodenal ligament is its thickened free edge, conducting the portal vein, hepatic artery and bile duct.
A(iii)
The greater omentum hangs like an apron from the greater curvature of the stomach and proximal duodenum, folds back after descending and attaches to the anterior surface of the transverse colon and its mesocolon.
A(iv)
• Liver: falciform ligament (anterior wall), gastrohepatic ligament (stomach), hepatoduodenal ligament (duodenum). Stomach: gastrophrenic, gastrosplenic, gastrocolic, gastrohepatic, gastropancreatic.
• Spleen: gastrosplenic (short gastric and left gastroepiploic vessels), splenorenal (splenic vessels and tail of pancreas), phrenicosplenic, splenocolic.
B(i)
• It is large and fat laden and prevents the visceral peritoneum adhering to the parietal peritoneum lining the anterolateral wall.
• It is mobile, moving with peristalsis, and can wrap itself around an inflamed organ such as the appendix, walling it off and protecting other viscera.
• It also cushions the abdominal organs against injury and forms insulation against loss of body heat.
C(i)
• Lesser: from liver to lesser curvature and proximal duodenum, containing the hepatoduodenal ligament; greater: hangs from the greater curvature and attaches to the transverse colon.
• The anterior and posterior layers of the lesser omentum extend from the liver to the lesser curvature; the anterior layer continues as the first layer of the greater omentum, the posterior layer forms its second and third layers.
• The lesser omentum forms part of the anterior wall of the lesser sac together with the peritoneum of the posterior wall of the stomach and the anterior two layers of the greater omentum.
• The hepatoduodenal ligament forms the anterior boundary of the omental foramen.

questions.question:
Describe the femoral triangle and adductor canal under the following headings, state how they relate to common pathologies, and explain the anatomical basis of referred pain to the knee from the hip.
A(i) Boundaries, roof, and floor of the femoral triangle; contents from lateral to medial
A(ii) Femoral artery — branches within the femoral triangle, including the profunda femoris and its branches
B(i) Adductor canal — boundaries, contents, and where it terminates
B(ii) Clinical basis: femoral pulse palpation and profunda femoris in femoral artery occlusion
C(i) Explain why hip joint disease causes referred pain at the knee, based on the nerve supply of both joints
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Boundaries: superiorly — inguinal ligament; medially — medial border of adductor longus; laterally — medial border of sartorius; apex — where adductor longus and sartorius cross. Roof: fascia lata (deep fascia) pierced by the great saphenous vein at the saphenous opening (fossa ovalis). Floor: formed by iliopsoas laterally and pectineus medially. Contents from lateral to medial: femoral nerve, femoral artery, femoral vein (the mnemonic 'NAVY' — from lateral: Nerve, Artery, Vein, Y-fronts/lymphatics). The femoral pulse can be palpated as it enters the femoral triangle, midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis — the mid-inguinal point.
A(ii)
The femoral artery divides to give the profunda femoris 5 cm below the inguinal ligament. Branches of the femoral artery (mnemonic: 'Does She Scream During Poking Sessions?'): Deep external pudendal arteries, Superficial epigastric, Superficial external pudendal, Descending genicular artery, Profunda femoris artery, Superficial circumflex iliac. Profunda femoris arises from the posterolateral aspect of the femoral artery; it gives: (1) Perforating branches — 3 or 4 arteries that perforate adductor magnus, contributing to medial and posterior thigh. (2) Lateral femoral circumflex artery — wraps around anterior and lateral side of femur, supplying muscles on lateral aspect of thigh. (3) Medial femoral circumflex artery — wraps around posterior side of femur, supplying its neck and head; in a fracture of the femoral neck this artery can easily be damaged and avascular necrosis of the femoral head can occur.
B(i)
The adductor canal is a passageway in the medial thigh. The adductor hiatus is an opening between the aponeurotic distal attachment of the adductor part of adductor magnus and the tendinous distal attachment of the hamstring part. The hiatus transmits the femoral artery and vein from the adductor canal in the thigh to the popliteal fossa posterior to the knee. It is located just lateral and superior to the adductor tubercle of the femur.
B(ii)
Femoral pulse: palpated at mid-inguinal point (midway between ASIS and pubic symphysis). In femoral artery occlusion, the profunda femoris artery is the main collateral channel because the superior muscular branches of the popliteal artery have clinically important anastomoses with the terminal part of the profunda femoris and gluteal arteries, maintaining perfusion to the leg.
C(i)
The posterior division of the obturator nerve supplies both the hip and the knee joint; therefore, pain from hip pathology is referred along this common nerve pathway to present as knee pain. This is the basis of Hilton's law applied to the hip: 'the nerve supplying the joint also supplies the muscles moving the joint and the skin covering the insertion of these muscles.' The femoral nerve also supplies the hip joint via intermediate and cutaneous branches and the knee via branches of obturator and femoral nerves.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the histology of the eye under the following headings: three tunics (layers) of the eyeball, contents of each layer, and the photoreceptor cell types in the retina.
A(ii) Explain the clinical basis of cataract and state the histological changes in the lens.
B(i) Distinguish between the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and the neural retina, stating the function of each and their embryological origin.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Three tunics: The eye has three layers. Outer tunic: the sclera and cornea; the sclera serves primarily as a structural support for the optic apparatus. Middle layer (vascular layer, uvea): the choroid, ciliary body, and iris. The iris functions as a contractile diaphragm (the aperture of the eye). Inner tunic: the retina — a double-layered epithelium consisting of an outer pigmented layer and an inner neural retina; it is subdivided into 10 recognizable layers. The outermost layer (closest to the choriocapillaris) contains the photoreceptors whose outer segments are in close contact with pigmented epithelial cells. Contents: the vitreous body fills the space between the lens and retina; the aqueous humor is in the anterior and posterior chambers; the lens is a transparent biconvex structure that, along with the cornea, focuses light on the retina. Photoreceptors: rods — more sensitive to light, primarily used in dim light. Cones — require more intense lighting; conical in shape. There are also bipolar cells, horizontal cells, amacrine cells, and Müller glia cells, and a retinal ganglion cell layer.
A(ii)
Cataract: when the lens becomes opaque, the condition is termed cataract, which may also be caused by excessive exposure to ultraviolet radiation. Histological changes: the lens has three principal components — lens capsule (corresponds to a thick, elastic basal lamina), subcapsular epithelium, and lens fibers. Opacification of the lens fibers makes them less transparent; this is the basis of cataract. A myopic (short-sighted) eye can be corrected by wearing glasses with concave lenses; a hyperopic eye with convex lenses.
B(i)
Retinal pigment epithelium (RPE): the outer cell layer is pigmented; it lies between the choroid and the neural retina; Bruch's membrane is located between the choroid and the RPE. Tight junctions between RPE cells establish a blood-retina barrier. Neural retina: the inner cell layer; it is a multi-layered structure containing photoreceptors (rods and cones), neurons, and glial cells. The optic nerve (and the retina) arises in the embryo as an outgrowth of the diencephalon (forebrain); thus the optic nerve is not a true peripheral nerve — its myelin is produced by oligodendrocytes (not Schwann cells), and it is associated with multiple sclerosis.

questions.question:
Describe the brachial artery:
A(i) Origin and termination
A(ii) Course
A(iii) Branches
B. State the safe site associated with clinical use of the brachial artery.
C. Explain the anatomical basis of the deformity/complication (Volkmann's ischaemic contracture) that can follow injury to this artery.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The brachial artery provides the main arterial supply to the arm and is the continuation of the axillary artery; it begins at the inferior border of teres major and ends in the cubital fossa opposite the neck of the radius.
A(ii)
Under cover of the bicipital aponeurosis, it divides into the radial and ulnar arteries.
A(iii)
Its branches include the deep brachial (profunda brachii) artery, which accompanies the radial nerve, the superior ulnar collateral artery, which accompanies the ulnar nerve, and the inferior ulnar collateral artery.
B
During blood pressure measurement, the stethoscope is placed over the brachial artery in the cubital fossa, and the cubital fossa is the site used to palpate the brachial pulse.
C
• Volkmann's ischaemic contracture is a deformity of the hand, fingers and wrist caused by injury to the muscles of the forearm.
• The classical presentation is a supracondylar fracture of the humerus, although fracture of the arm or elbow may also result in this deformity; the artery involved is the brachial artery.
• The contracture occurs when there is a lack of blood flow (ischaemia) to the forearm, usually from increased pressure resulting from swelling (compartment syndrome).
• Because there is very little room within each fascial compartment of the arm and forearm, haemorrhage or oedema following injury to the brachial artery can cause secondary vascular compression: veins are affected first, and later the arteries, resulting in ischaemia of the affected part.
• The classical presentation of the resulting acute compartment syndrome is remembered by "the five P's": pulselessness, paraesthesia, poikilothermia, paralysis and pallor.
• There are three levels of severity of the resulting Volkmann's contracture: the mildest involves flexion contracture of only two or three fingers with no or limited loss of sensation; a more severe form involves all fingers flexed with the thumb stuck in the palm and some sensory loss.
• The most severe form involves all the muscles in the forearm that flex and extend the wrist and fingers, producing a severely disabling condition.
• This progression illustrates how injury to the brachial artery at the elbow can produce a graded functional deficit distally in the hand and fingers.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the mucosa of the stomach under the following headings: surface epithelium and gastric pits; the isthmus and stem cells; the lamina propria; and the muscularis mucosae.
A(ii) Name and describe all four secretory epithelial cell types found in the gastric glands of the fundus and body, including the characteristics of each cell and what it secretes.
B(i) Distinguish between the mucosa of the fundus/body and the mucosa of the cardia/pylorus under the headings: gland type, cell types present, and principal secretion.
B(ii) Explain what rugae are and the physiological condition under which they disappear.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Stomach mucosa:
• Surface epithelium and gastric pits: consists of a simple columnar epithelium that invaginates into the lamina propria forming gastric pits. Millions of gastric pits each open into the lumen of the stomach; the gastric pits lead into long, branched, tubular glands extending through the thickness of the lamina propria; between each gastric pit and gastric gland is the isthmus (region of stem cells).
• Isthmus and stem cells: the pluripotent stem cells divide asymmetrically producing progenitor cells for all other epithelial cells; they can move upwards to replace surface mucous cells or downwards to replace other secretory cells.
• Lamina propria: highly vascularised; supports pits and glands; contains smooth muscle fibers, capillaries, lymphatics, and lymphoid cells.
• Muscularis mucosae: layer of smooth muscle separating the mucosa from the underlying submucosa.
A(ii)
Four secretory cell types of fundic/body glands:
• Mucous neck cells (MNCs): less columnar than surface mucous cells; irregular in shape with round nucleus and apical secretory granules; secrete acidic fluid containing mucin (less alkaline than surface mucous cells).
• Parietal (oxyntic) cells: large, rounded or pyramidal cells; one central spherical nucleus; intensely eosinophilic cytoplasm due to high density of mitochondria; secrete hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor.
• Chief (zymogen) cells: predominate in lower regions; abundant RER and numerous apical secretory granules (characteristics of protein-secreting cells); secrete pepsinogen (converted to pepsin at pH < 5), lipase, and leptin.
• Enteroendocrine cells: scattered throughout the gastric mucosa; secrete hormones with endocrine or paracrine functions (e.g., serotonin in fundus; gastrin from G cells in pylorus).
B(i)
• Fundus/body: long branched tubular gastric glands (3 to 7 per pit); each gland has an isthmus, neck, and base; contains all four cell types above; secretes acidic gastric juice.
• Cardia/pylorus: tubular glands with long pits, usually branching into coiled secretory portions (cardiac/pyloric glands); lack parietal and chief cells; major secretion is abundant mucus.
B(ii)
Rugae are longitudinally directed folds of the mucosa and submucosa of the empty stomach. They flatten when the stomach is full with food.

A(i)
• The urinary bladder is a musculomembranous sac composed of a body, which collects urine, and a neck, a funnel-shaped extension passing inferiorly to join the urethra; it is divided into apex, fundus and body, with superior, posterior (base) and two inferolateral surfaces.
• The apex points towards the pubic symphysis and continues as the median umbilical ligament, a remnant of the embryonic urachus, up to the umbilicus; the base faces posteroinferiorly, with the two ureters entering at its upper corners and the urethra draining from its lower corner.
A(ii)
The trigone is the smooth, posteroinferior triangular area of the bladder wall formed by imaginary lines connecting the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice; it has four tunics, mucosa, submucosa, muscularis (detrusor muscle) and adventitia.
A(iii)
• Except for its superior surface, which is covered by peritoneum, the bladder is connected to surrounding structures by fibroareolar tissue (true ligaments): the lateral true ligaments, the puboprostatic or pubovesical ligaments anteriorly, the median umbilical ligament at the apex, and a posterior ligament.
• In the male, the upper posterior surface is related to the rectovesical pouch, and the lower part relates to the seminal vesicles and vas deferens; in the female, the posterior surface is related to the anterior wall of the vagina.
B
• The trigone remains immovable as the bladder fills and empties, and functions as a funnel that directs urine into the urethra as the bladder wall (detrusor) contracts.
• This fixed relationship of the ureteric and urethral orifices at the trigone is why it is used as a constant anatomical landmark despite the changing size and shape of the rest of the bladder.
C
• The male urethra is about 20 cm long and is divided into four parts: intramural (preprostatic), prostatic, membranous, and spongy (penile) parts, opening at the end of the penis.
• The male urethra passes through the prostate, the deep perineal pouch/urogenital diaphragm as the membranous urethra, and then the length of the penis as the spongy urethra, bending twice along its course.
• The female urethra is much shorter, about 3-4 cm long, corresponding to the prostatic part of the male urethra proximal to the prostatic utricle.
• The female urethra begins at the internal urethral orifice about 5 cm behind the pubic symphysis, runs downward embedded in the anterior wall of the vagina, traverses the urogenital diaphragm, and ends at the external urethral orifice in the vestibule, receiving the paraurethral (Skene's) glands.
• Both sexes have an internal, smooth muscle, involuntary urethral sphincter continuous with the detrusor muscle, and an external, skeletal muscle, voluntary sphincter innervated by the pudendal nerve, located inferior to the prostate in males and at the bladder's distal inferior end in females.

(B) Explain the clinical basis of why the trigone remains an important fixed landmark during bladder filling.
(C) Distinguish the male urethra from the female urethra.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
• The sacrum is formed by the union of 5 sacral vertebrae (fusion begins at 16 to 18 years, usually complete by 30); wedge-shaped; concave anterior surface with four transverse lines and four pairs of anterior sacral foramina.
• Dorsally a median sacral crest and posterior foramina; the sacral canal is continuous with the vertebral canal; an auricular surface forms the sacroiliac joint; structures emerge at the sacral hiatus.
A(ii)
• Each hip bone is three bones (ilium, pubis, ischium) separated by cartilage in the newborn and fused at puberty in the acetabulum; the ilium is the largest, with ala, body, crest, spines, greater sciatic notch, iliac fossa, auricular surface and arcuate line.
• Ischium: body, ramus, spine, lesser sciatic notch and tuberosity; pubis: superior and inferior rami, body, crest, tubercle, iliopectineal line; ischium and pubis surround the obturator foramen.
A(iii)
Two hip bones united at the pubic symphysis and with the sacrum at the sacroiliac joints; the girdle moves as a unit and supports and protects lower abdominal and pelvic organs; the pelvic brim divides true and false pelves.
B(i)
• The female pelvis serves for childbearing and easier delivery; it is bigger and wider, with a large oval brim and a wider outlet.
• The sacral promontory, the superior border of the anterior sacral surface, is an important obstetric landmark for pelvic measurements.
• The sacral index is about 105 in males and 115 in females, and the sacrovertebral angle is more prominent in females.
C(i)
• Male: smaller, narrower, heavier and thicker bone; deep false pelvis; pubic arch V-shaped and less than 90°; acetabulum larger, facing laterally; coccyx immovable; brim smaller and heart-shaped; outlet narrower.
• Male: narrower greater sciatic notch, round obturator foramen, longer narrower sacrum, more vertical ilium, ischial tuberosities longer, close together and laterally projecting.
• Female: shallow false pelvis; wider pubic arch greater than 90°; acetabulum smaller, facing anteriorly; coccyx movable; large oval brim; wider outlet.
• Female: wider greater sciatic notch, oval obturator foramen, less vertical ilium, ischial tuberosities shorter, farther apart and projecting medially.

A(i)
Gross anatomy of the kidney:
• Renal cortex: granular-appearing superficial region.
• Renal medulla: composed of cone-shaped medullary (renal) pyramids; pyramids are separated by renal columns (inward extensions of cortical tissue).
• Structures in frontal section: renal hilum, renal cortex, renal medulla, major calyx, papilla of pyramid, renal pelvis, minor calyx, ureter, renal pyramid in renal medulla, renal column, fibrous capsule.
A(ii)
Seven functions of the kidney:
• Regulating total water volume and total solute concentration in water.
• Regulating ECF ion concentrations.
• Ensuring long-term acid-base balance.
• Removal of metabolic wastes, toxins, and drugs.
• Endocrine functions: renin (regulation of blood pressure) and erythropoietin (regulation of RBC production).
• Activation of vitamin D.
• Gluconeogenesis during prolonged fasting.
B(i)
Comparison of nephron types:
• Cortical nephrons: 85% of nephrons; short nephron loop; glomerulus further from the cortex-medulla junction; efferent arteriole supplies peritubular capillaries.
• Juxtamedullary nephrons: long nephron loops that deeply invade the medulla; glomerulus closer to the cortex-medulla junction; efferent arteriole supplies vasa recta; ascending limbs have thick and thin segments; important in production of concentrated urine.
B(ii)
Two collecting duct cell types:
• Principal cells: sparse, short microvilli; maintain water and Na+ balance.
• Intercalated cells (A and B types): cuboidal cells with abundant microvilli; both types help maintain acid-base balance of blood.
• Collecting ducts receive filtrate from many nephrons; run through medullary pyramids giving them a striped appearance; fuse together to deliver urine through papillae into minor calyces.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Five lumbar vertebrae (1 to 4 typical, 5 atypical); largest and strongest of the column because supported weight increases inferiorly; superior facets face medially, inferior facets laterally; thick broad spines.
A(ii)
• Large kidney-shaped body, deeper anteriorly; triangular foramen (larger than thoracic, smaller than cervical); short strong pedicles; short thick broad laminae; spine a vertical quadrilateral plate.
• Transverse processes thin and tapering (accessory process); superior articular facets concave facing medially and backwards with the mammillary process; inferior facets convex facing laterally and forwards.
A(iii)
L5: thick short pyramidal transverse processes; largest body, anterior deeper than posterior, creating the sharp lumbosacral angle; small short rounded spine; inferior articular distance equal to or more than the superior.
A(iv)
Joints: intervertebral discs (symphysis) between bodies; synovial joints between arches. Ligaments: anterior and posterior longitudinal, ligamentum flavum, interspinous, supraspinous; iliolumbar ligaments strengthen the L5 to S1 lumbosacral joint.
B(i)
• A lumbar vertebra ossifies from three primary centres (body and each half of the neural arch) appearing in the third month of fetal life; the halves of the arch fuse posteriorly in the first year.
• Failure of fusion of the two halves of the neural arch results in spina bifida; if one primary centre of the body fails, hemivertebra.
B(ii)
• Lumbar spinal stenosis: thought hereditary, a narrow vertebral foramen in one or several vertebrae.
• Excessive lumbar lordosis: abnormal anterior curvature with anterior tilting of the pelvis.
C(i)
• The canal formed by L1 and L2 contains the conus medullaris; the lower three contain the cauda equina; all contain the spinal meninges.
• Stenosis can compress the spinal cord and exiting nerves; the pedicles are related above and below to spinal nerves.
• The right crus of the diaphragm attaches to the upper three lumbar vertebrae and the left crus to the upper two; psoas major arises from the vertebral borders.

A(i)
• 12 pairs of intercostal (thoracic) nerves, the anterior primary rami of the thoracic spinal nerves; they are mixed nerves; T3-6 are typical and T1 and T2 are atypical.
• Atypical nerves: T1 has no anterior cutaneous branch and is joined to the brachial plexus by a large branch corresponding to the lateral cutaneous branch; the lateral cutaneous branch of T2 is the intercostobrachial nerve, joined to the medial cutaneous nerve of the arm.
A(ii)
A typical nerve lies in the neurovascular bundle between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles, high in the space in relation to the subcostal groove of the rib above, below the artery (vein, artery, nerve from above downwards); nerves 1-6 are distributed in the intercostal spaces, 7-11 pass to the anterior abdominal wall, and the anterior ramus of the 12th runs forward in the abdomen as the subcostal nerve.
A(iii)
Branches: rami communicantes, collateral (muscular) branches, lateral cutaneous branch, anterior cutaneous branch, muscular branches, pleural branch and peritoneal branches (7th-11th).
A(iv)
They supply the skin, the muscles of the intercostal space and abdomen, and the parietal pleura and parietal peritoneum; cutaneous supply of the anterior wall is by supraclavicular nerves (C4) above the sternal angle and by the anterior and lateral cutaneous branches below it; the posterior wall is supplied by the posterior rami of the thoracic spinal nerves.
B(i)
• Local anaesthesia of an intercostal space is easily produced by infiltration around the intercostal nerve trunk and its collateral branch (intercostal nerve block).
• A needle or drain is passed immediately above the upper border of a rib, to avoid the neurovascular bundle lying under the rib above.
• In a conventional posterolateral thoracotomy the incision is along the 5th or 6th rib; the periosteum over a segment of the rib is elevated, protecting the neurovascular bundle, and the rib is excised to reach the lung or mediastinum through the intercostal space.
C(i)
• Local irritation of the intercostal nerves (e.g. by Pott's disease, tuberculosis of the thoracic vertebrae) gives pain referred to the front of the chest or abdomen, in the region of the peripheral termination of the nerves.
• Pus from the region of the vertebral column tracks around the thorax along the neurovascular bundle and points at the three sites of exit of the cutaneous branches: lateral to erector spinae, in the midaxillary line and just lateral to the sternum.
• A rib fracture is extremely painful because the periosteum of the rib is supplied by the intercostal nerves above and below the rib; the parietal pleura is segmentally supplied by the intercostal nerves, so pleural disease refers pain along the thoracic wall and anterior abdominal wall.
