A(i) Describe the processes of digestion, naming all eight steps in order.
A(ii) Describe the four main functions of the GI tract, distinguishing between the role of the small intestine and the role of the large intestine in absorption.
B(i) Describe the composition and function of the serosa, including the structures it is continuous with and how it differs between organs within the abdominal cavity and the esophagus.
B(ii) Explain why the enteric nervous system provides the anatomical basis for the effects of emotional stress on the GIT, and name the two diseases that demonstrate the clinical consequences of plexus destruction.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Eight processes of digestion (in order):
• Ingestion
• Mastication
• Peristalsis / motility
• Secretions
• Hormone release
• Chemical digestion
• Absorption
• Elimination
A(ii)
Four main functions of the GI tract:
• Macromolecules (proteins, complex carbohydrates, nucleic acids, and fat) obtained from ingested food are broken down into smaller subunits for easy absorption through the lining of the small intestine during digestion.
• These smaller subunits are required for the release of energy, maintenance, and growth.
• Most of the water and electrolytes are absorbed in the large intestine.
• The inner layer of the entire GI tract forms an important protective barrier between the contents of the tract and the tissues of the body.
B(i)
Serosa:
• Composition: a thin sheet of loose connective tissue covered with mesothelium (a simple squamous covering epithelium); rich in blood vessels, lymphatics, and adipose tissue.
• Function: the outermost covering of GIT organs within the abdominal cavity.
• Continuity: the serosa of the small and large intestines is continuous with parts of the mesentery (a large fold of adipose connective tissue covered on both sides by mesothelium, which suspends the intestines and is continuous with the peritoneum).
• Esophagus: because the esophagus is bound directly to adjacent structures and not suspended in a cavity, it has a thick adventitia instead of a serosa; the adventitia consists of connective tissue containing vessels and nerves, lacking mesothelium.
B(ii)
• The enteric nervous system (submucosal and myenteric plexuses) functions independently of the CNS; because it is anatomically connected to the autonomic nervous system, it provides the anatomical basis for the well-known actions of emotional stress on the stomach and other regions of the GIT.
Two diseases demonstrating clinical consequences of plexus destruction:
• Hirschsprung disease (congenital aganglionic megacolon): caused by absence or severely injured plexuses in parts or all of the large intestine; disturbs motility and produces dilation, causing difficulty passing stool.
• Chagas disease / trypanosomiasis (infection with Trypanosoma cruzi): the protozoan destroys the enteric plexuses, producing similar motility disturbance.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the tissue preparation process used in histology under the following headings: fixation, dehydration and clearing, embedding, sectioning, and staining.
A(ii) State the most commonly used stain in histology, explain what structures it stains and the colors produced, and give the reason for the differential staining.
B(i) Distinguish between light microscopy and electron microscopy in histology, stating what each reveals and an example of when each is preferred.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Fixation: to achieve a permanent section, tissues must be fixed to preserve the structure and molecular composition; fixation prevents autolysis (self-digestion by enzymes present in the cells) and destruction by bacteria. Dehydration and clearing: tissues are progressed in graded steps to 100% alcohol to remove water; after the solvent replaces the alcohol, the tissue becomes transparent in xylene (clearing). Embedding: once the tissue is impregnated with the solvent, it is placed in a hard medium (e.g., wax); heat causes the solvent to evaporate, and the spaces within the tissue are filled by the embedding medium. Sectioning: tissues are sectioned by the microtome's steel or glass blade; this method allows stained sections to be prepared rapidly for study of specimens. Mounting: sections are mounted on a supportive structure (e.g., slide) that can be placed on a microscope stage. Staining: stains are applied to differentiate tissue components.
A(ii)
The most commonly used stains are hematoxylin and eosin (H & E). Hematoxylin stains basic (acidic) structures — the most acidic components are DNA and RNA; therefore, the nucleus and cytoplasmic RNA stain blue/purple (basophilic). Eosin stains acidophilic (basic) structures — many cytoplasmic constituents stain pinkish (eosinophilic/acidophilic). Reason: differential staining is based on the acid-base chemistry of cell components; acidic cell components bind basic dyes (hematoxylin) and basic components bind acidic dyes (eosin).
B(i)
Light microscopy: the standard technique; produces images of tissue sections examined by transmitted light; maximum resolving power is 0.2 micrometers (two marks 0.2 micrometers apart can be seen as two distinct entities). Types include brightfield, phase contrast, differential interference contrast (DIC), fluorescence, and confocal. Preferred for: routine tissue examination, diagnosis of pathology, overview of cell and tissue structure. Electron microscopy: has extended the detail at which subcellular structures can be studied; reveals ultrastructural details such as organelles, myelin sheaths, and synapse morphology. Preferred for: study of subcellular structures, ultrastructural detail, and molecular architecture of cell membranes.

questions.question:
Describe the deep fascial spaces of the hand:
A(i) Thenar space
A(ii) The list of compartments/fascial spaces of the hand
A(iii) Space of Parona
B. Explain the clinical basis for infection spreading between these compartments.
C. Distinguish between the thenar space and the midpalmar space.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
The thenar space lies on the thumb side of the septum that joins the border of the palmar aponeurosis to the palmar border of the third metacarpal bone; it contains the first lumbrical muscle and is overlaid by the flexor tendons to the index finger.
A(ii)
The compartments and fascial spaces of the hand include the dorsal spaces, hypothenar space, midpalmar space, thenar space, web spaces and pulp spaces, all bounded by connective tissue.
A(iii)
The space of Parona extends from the proximal margin of the carpal tunnel to the mid-forearm; its roof is formed distally by the flexor digitorum profundus tendons and proximally by the belly of flexor digitorum superficialis (whose origin forms the proximal boundary), it is limited medially by flexor carpi ulnaris and laterally by flexor pollicis longus, and its floor is formed by pronator quadratus distally and the interosseous membrane in its proximal two-thirds.
B
• These fascial spaces allow mobility of the hand structures but, being bounded by connective tissue, offer little resistance to the spread of infection.
• Infection within the thenar space can readily break into the connective tissue canals surrounding the ulnar three lumbricals.
• For practical purposes the thenar space may therefore be considered continuous distally with these lumbrical canals, and thus distally communicates with the web spaces.
• The thenar space also communicates proximally with the space of Parona.
• Infection of these deep spaces, including the space of Parona, can be difficult to diagnose.
C
• The thenar space lies on the thumb (radial) side of the septum joining the palmar aponeurosis to the third metacarpal, contains the first lumbrical, and is overlaid by the flexor tendons of the index finger.
• The midpalmar space, by contrast, lies on the ulnar side of this septum, related to the tendons for the middle, ring and little fingers and to adductor pollicis, separated from the thenar space by the lateral palmar septum.
• The thenar space communicates proximally with the space of Parona and distally with the lumbrical canals/web spaces, reflecting its position along the flexor tendon of the index finger.
• This anatomical separation by the lateral palmar septum explains why infection in one compartment tends initially to remain localised to that space before spreading along its own specific communicating pathway.

questions.question:
A. Describe the gross anatomy of the cranial base under the following headings: the anterior cranial fossa, the middle cranial fossa, and the posterior cranial fossa, and their main foramina and contents.
B. State how fractures involving the different regions of the skull base relate to specific clinical presentations.
C. Explain why disease/infection or trauma involving one region of the skull base can produce a functional deficit at a distant site, such as the nasal cavity or the brain itself.
questions.answerText:
A
In the anterior cranial fossa, the foramen caecum transmits a nasal emissary vein (in 1% of the population), the cribriform foramina in the cribriform plate transmit axons of olfactory cells forming the olfactory nerves, and the anterior and posterior ethmoidal foramina transmit vessels and nerves of the same names. In the middle cranial fossa, the optic canals transmit the optic nerves (CN II) and ophthalmic arteries; the superior orbital fissure transmits ophthalmic veins, the ophthalmic nerve (CN V1), CN III, IV and VI, and sympathetic fibres; the foramen rotundum transmits the maxillary nerve (CN V2); the foramen ovale transmits the mandibular nerve (CN V3), the accessory meningeal artery, the lesser petrosal nerve and an emissary vein; the foramen spinosum transmits the middle meningeal artery and vein and the meningeal branch of CN V3; and the foramen lacerum transmits the deep petrosal nerve and some meningeal arterial branches and small veins. In the posterior cranial fossa, the foramen magnum transmits the medulla and meninges, vertebral arteries, CN XI, dural veins, and the anterior and posterior spinal arteries; the jugular foramen transmits CN IX, X and XI, the superior bulb of the internal jugular vein, the inferior petrosal and sigmoid sinuses, and meningeal branches of the ascending pharyngeal and occipital arteries; the hypoglossal canal transmits the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII); the condylar canal transmits an emissary vein from the sigmoid sinus to the vertebral veins in the neck; and the mastoid foramen transmits a mastoid emissary vein from the sigmoid sinus and a meningeal branch of the occipital artery.
B
Fractures of the calvaria are classified as depressed, linear, comminuted, or basilar fractures; fractures of the maxillae and associated bones are termed Le Fort fractures; and there are also fractures of the mandible.
C
The close relation of the frontal sinus to the frontal lobe of the brain explains how infection of this sinus may result in development of a frontal lobe abscess; a fracture involving the sinus, severe enough to tear the dura and pia-arachnoid, will place the subarachnoid space in communication with the nasal cavity, so that CSF may be detected trickling through the nostril (CSF rhinorrhoea), usually on the affected side, although a contralateral leak can occur since these sinuses may communicate. Similarly, infection of the ethmoid sinuses (ethmoiditis) may result in a frontal cerebral abscess, and an ethmoidal fracture may cause CSF leakage into the nasal cavity, because the ethmoid sinuses lie on each side of the cribriform plate and are related above to the frontal lobes of the brain.

A(i)
It arises from the external iliac artery.
A(ii)
• It enters the rectus sheath at the arcuate line.
• It lies beneath the lateral umbilical fold on the internal surface of the anterolateral abdominal wall.
A(iii)
• Branches: cremasteric artery (to the cremasteric muscle) and pubic branch.
• Median umbilical fold covers the remnant of the urachus; medial umbilical folds cover the obliterated umbilical arteries; lateral umbilical folds cover the inferior epigastric vessels.
A(iv)
• It anastomoses with the superior epigastric artery, the terminal branch of the internal thoracic that descends in the rectus sheath posterior to the muscle.
• Veins: the external iliac vein receives the epigastric and deep circumflex iliac veins; the superior epigastric vein drains to the brachiocephalic vein.
B(i)
• The deep inguinal ring lies lateral to it, about ½ inch above the inguinal ligament at the midinguinal point; the opening to the canal is located laterally to it.
• Indirect hernias enter the canal lateral to the vessels; direct hernias bulge through the posterior wall medial to the artery.
C(i)
The lateral umbilical folds cover the inferior epigastric vessels, which bleed if cut.

A(i)
Gross anatomy of the pancreas:
• Nature: a mixed exocrine-endocrine gland that produces both digestive enzymes and hormones.
• Position: retroperitoneally positioned on the posterior wall of the abdominal cavity at the level of the 2nd and 3rd lumbar vertebrae.
• Capsular covering: it has no distinct capsule, but is covered by a thin layer of loose connective tissue, from which septa extend to cover the larger vessels and ducts and to separate the parenchyma into lobules.
A(ii)
Two functional components:
• Exocrine: produces digestive enzymes that act in the small intestine; secretory acini produce about 1.6 litres of pancreatic juice every day.
• Endocrine: involves primarily smaller cells similar to enteroendocrine cells located in variously sized clusters called the pancreatic islets (islets of Langerhans); secretes hormones such as insulin and glucagon into the bloodstream, which are very important for the metabolism of absorbed nutrients.
B(i)
Exocrine acini:
• The secretory acini are surrounded by a basal lamina that is supported only by a delicate sheath of reticular fibers with a rich capillary network.
• The exocrine part produces about 1.6 litres of pancreatic juice every day.
B(ii)
• Pancreas: produces digestive enzymes that act in the small intestine; secretes insulin and glucagon, both important for metabolism of absorbed nutrients.
• Liver: produces bile, an important fluid in the digestion of fats; plays a major role in lipid, carbohydrate, and protein metabolism; inactivates and metabolizes many toxic substances and drugs; participates in iron metabolism and the synthesis of blood proteins and factors necessary for blood coagulation.
• Gallbladder: absorbs water from bile and stores bile in a concentrated form.
questions.question:

A(ii) Describe the two functional components of the pancreas (exocrine and endocrine), including the cell types involved and the products of each.
B(i) Describe the exocrine secretory acini of the pancreas, including the arrangement around the acini and the volume of juice produced.
B(ii) Explain the role of the pancreas in digestion and hormonal regulation, and contrast this with the role of the liver and the gallbladder.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
The space between two ribs; with 12 ribs on each side there are 11 intercostal spaces; each space contains intercostal muscles, the intercostal neurovascular bundle and lymphatics.
A(ii)
• Three muscles (external, internal, innermost; transversus thoracis, subcostalis and levator costarum are also listed), supplied by the corresponding intercostal nerves, that pull the ribs nearer to each other and strengthen the space. External intercostal: most superficial, fibres downward and forward, origin lower border of the rib above, insertion upper border of the rib below, from the rib tubercle behind to the costochondral junction in front, replaced anteriorly by the anterior intercostal membrane.
• Internal intercostal: intermediate layer, fibres downward and backward, origin subcostal groove of the rib above, insertion upper border of the rib below, from the sternum in front to the angle of the rib behind, replaced posteriorly by the posterior intercostal membrane.
A(iii)
Innermost intercostal: deepest, incomplete layer divided into 3 portions, its fibres cross more than one space; related externally to the intercostal nerve and vessels and internally to the endothoracic fascia. Endothoracic fascia: extrapleural fascia lining the chest wall between the muscles and bones and the parietal pleura, extending over the pleural apex as the suprapleural membrane and forming a thin layer between diaphragm and pleura.
A(iv)
The neurovascular bundle lies between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles, high in the space in relation to the subcostal groove of the rib above; strict order from above downwards: vein, artery, nerve (VAN); because the innermost layer is incomplete it is generally covered on the inside by endothoracic fascia.
A(v)
Each space has a single posterior and 2 anterior intercostal arteries, giving branches to muscles, skin, parietal pleura and breast. Posterior: upper 2 spaces from the superior intercostal artery (costocervical trunk of the subclavian artery), lower 9 spaces from the thoracic aorta. Anterior: upper 6 spaces from the internal thoracic artery, lower 5 from the musculophrenic artery; they anastomose with the posterior arteries.
A(vi)
Veins accompany the arteries and nerves (11 posterior intercostal and 1 subcostal vein); valves direct blood posteriorly. Right side: 1st space to the brachiocephalic vein, the rest to the azygos vein. Left side: upper 3 spaces to the left brachiocephalic vein, the rest to the hemiazygos and accessory hemiazygos veins, which drain to the azygos vein. Anterior veins: upper 6 spaces to the internal thoracic vein, lower 5 to the musculophrenic vein.
A(vii)
12 pairs, the anterior primary rami of the thoracic spinal nerves and mixed nerves; nerves 1-6 are distributed in the intercostal spaces, 7-11 supply the anterior abdominal wall, and the 12th runs forward in the abdomen as the subcostal nerve; they supply skin, muscles of the space and abdomen, parietal pleura and parietal peritoneum. Branches: rami communicantes, collateral (muscular), lateral cutaneous, anterior cutaneous, pleural and peritoneal (7th-11th).
A(viii)
Deep lymphatics follow the arteries: anteriorly they drain into the anterior intercostal (parasternal) nodes along the internal thoracic artery; posteriorly they drain into the posterior intercostal nodes in the posterior mediastinum.
B(i)
• A needle or drain is passed immediately above the upper border of the rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle (vein, artery, nerve from above downwards) running under the rib above in the subcostal groove.
• Intercostal spaces are access points for surgical procedures (e.g. resection of part of the lung), for percussion and auscultation of the heart and lung, and for sampling pleural fluid or draining pus or blood from the pleural cavity; disease in the thorax may cause pain in the anterior abdominal wall because the intercostal nerves supply both the thoracic and abdominal wall and the parietal pleura.
C(i)
Typical nerves are T3-6. T1 is atypical: no anterior cutaneous branch, joined to the brachial plexus by a large branch corresponding to the lateral cutaneous branch. T2 is atypical: its lateral cutaneous branch is the intercostobrachial nerve, which joins the medial cutaneous nerve of the arm through the brachial plexus.

(i) Describe the origin, course, branches and distribution of the arteries supplying the stomach.
(iii) Explain the anatomical basis of the venous route through which gastric bleeding enters the portal circulation.
questions.answerText:
(i)
• The arteries of the stomach are derived from branches of the coeliac artery. The left gastric artery arises from the coeliac artery, passes upward and to the left to reach the oesophagus, then descends along the lesser curvature, supplying the lower third of the oesophagus and the upper right part of the stomach. The right gastric artery arises from the hepatic artery at the upper border of the pylorus and runs left along the lesser curvature, supplying the lower right part of the stomach.
• The short gastric arteries arise from the splenic artery at the hilum of the spleen and pass forward in the gastrosplenic omentum to supply the fundus. The left gastro-omental (gastroepiploic) artery arises from the splenic artery at the hilum of the spleen and passes forward in the gastrosplenic omentum to supply the stomach along the upper part of the greater curvature. The right gastro-omental artery arises from the gastroduodenal branch of the hepatic artery and passes left to supply the stomach along the lower part of the greater curvature.
(iii)
• The left and right gastric veins drain directly into the portal vein.
• The short gastric veins and the left gastroepiploic vein join the splenic vein.
• The right gastroepiploic vein joins the superior mesenteric vein.
• All venous drainage of the stomach therefore ultimately enters the portal circulation, via the portal vein, splenic vein or superior mesenteric vein, before passing through the liver.
• This portal route explains why bleeding from portal-systemic anastomoses, such as oesophageal varices, is related to the portal venous system.

A(i)
The popliteal fossa is a diamond-shaped depression in the posterior aspect of the knee. Superolateral border: biceps femoris. Superomedial border: semimembranosus and semitendinosus. Inferolateral border: lateral head of gastrocnemius. Inferomedial border: medial head of gastrocnemius.
A(ii)
Roof (posteriorly): skin and fascia — the popliteal fascia is a strong sheet of deep fascia continuous superiorly with the fascia lata and inferiorly with the deep fascia of the leg. Floor (anteriorly): popliteal surface of femur, capsule of knee joint, oblique popliteal ligament, and popliteal fascia over popliteus.
B(i)
From superficial to deep: posterior cutaneous nerve of thigh; tibial nerve (most superficial of the neurovascular bundle); popliteal vein; popliteal artery (deepest structure in the fossa, running close to the articular capsule of the knee joint); popliteal lymph nodes and lymphatic vessels. The small saphenous vein and three cutaneous nerves (posterior cutaneous nerve of thigh, medial sural cutaneous nerve, lateral sural cutaneous nerve) lie in the superficial fascia.
B(ii)
The popliteal artery is the deepest structure and lies in close proximity to the tibial nerve. An aneurysm (dilation of the artery beyond 50% of its normal diameter) causes compression of the tibial nerve. The tibial nerve is particularly susceptible to this compression; the major features include weakened or absent plantarflexion, paraesthesia of the foot and posterolateral leg, and paralysis of flexor muscles in the leg and intrinsic muscles of the sole.
C(i)
The tibial nerve is the medial and larger branch of the sciatic nerve; it bisects the fossa passing from the superior to the inferior angle and gives muscular branches to soleus, gastrocnemius, plantaris, and popliteus, and the medial sural cutaneous nerve. The common fibular nerve is the lateral, smaller terminal branch; it begins at the superior angle, closely follows the medial border of biceps femoris, exits the fossa by passing superficial to the lateral head of gastrocnemius, then winds around the neck of fibula where it divides into terminal branches. Injury to the tibial nerve causes inability to plantarflex the ankle or flex the toes and loss of sensation on the sole of the foot.

questions.answerText:
A(i)
Quadriceps femoris forms the main bulk of the anterior thigh muscles; it collectively constitutes the largest and one of the most powerful muscles of the body. It covers almost all the anterior aspect and sides of the femur. It is the great extensor of the leg. It consists of 4 muscles: rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, vastus medialis, and vastus intermedius. The tendons of the four parts unite in the distal portion of the thigh to form a single, strong, broad tendon — the quadriceps tendon; this continues as the patellar ligament (in which the patella is embedded) and is attached to the tibial tuberosity.
A(ii)
Rectus femoris — origin: anterior inferior iliac spine and ilium superior to acetabulum; insertion: via common quadriceps tendon and patellar ligament to tibial tuberosity; innervation: femoral nerve (L2, L3, L4); action: extends leg at knee joint, steadies hip joint, and helps iliopsoas flex thigh. It is the only part of the quadriceps that crosses the hip joint, named because it runs straight down the thigh. Vastus lateralis — origin: greater trochanter and lateral lip of linea aspera of femur; same insertion and innervation; action: extends leg at knee joint; it is the largest component. Vastus medialis — origin: intertrochanteric line and medial lip of linea aspera of femur; same insertion and innervation; action: extends leg at knee joint; inferior fibres are particularly important in stabilising the knee joint. Vastus intermedius — origin: anterior and lateral surfaces of shaft of femur; same insertion and innervation; action: extends leg at knee joint; lies deep to rectus femoris between the vastus medialis and lateralis.
B(i)
The quadriceps is the primary extensor of the knee — the most important movement for standing, walking, climbing stairs, and rising from a chair. Stability of the knee joint depends on the strength and action of surrounding muscles and tendons; the quadriceps femoris is most important in stabilising the knee joint. Paralysis means the patient cannot extend the knee or control descent on stairs, rendering them unable to walk safely without a brace.
B(ii)
All four components of the quadriceps are innervated by the femoral nerve (L2, L3, L4). The femoral nerve also supplies the hip joint via intermediate and cutaneous branches and the skin of the front and medial side of the thigh (Hilton's law). Loss of knee extension eliminates the ability to straighten or stabilise the knee against gravity — the most critical functional deficit for bipedal locomotion.
C(i)
Quadriceps femoris: origin from femur and ilium; action — extends the knee (and rectus femoris also flexes the hip); nerve supply — femoral nerve (L2, L3, L4). Hamstrings (semitendinosus, semimembranosus, biceps femoris): origin from ischial tuberosity (long head of biceps femoris and both semi-muscles) and linea aspera (short head of biceps femoris); action — extend the thigh, flex the leg, and rotate it (semitendinosus and semimembranosus medially, biceps femoris laterally); nerve supply — tibial division of sciatic nerve for semitendinosus, semimembranosus, and long head of biceps femoris; common fibular division of sciatic nerve for short head of biceps femoris. The quadriceps is 3 times stronger than its antagonist muscle group (the hamstrings).

questions.answerText:
A(i)
• Each intercostal space has a single posterior and two anterior intercostal arteries.
• In the upper two spaces the posterior intercostal arteries arise from the superior intercostal artery (branch of the costocervical trunk of the subclavian artery); in the lower nine spaces they arise from the thoracic aorta (9 pairs, plus 1 pair of subcostal arteries from the posterior surface of the descending thoracic aorta).
A(ii)
Course and branching follow the intercostal nerves: each artery runs forward in the subcostal groove, high in the space between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles, in the order vein, artery, nerve from above downwards, and anastomoses with the anterior intercostal artery.
A(iii)
• Branches go to adjacent muscles, skin, parietal pleura, spinal cord and breast (branches in the 3rd and 4th spaces supply the breast); the 3rd right posterior intercostal artery gives the right bronchial artery.
• Distribution: the posterior and lateral parts of the intercostal spaces.
• Veins accompany the arteries and contain valves that direct blood posteriorly; on the right the 1st space drains to the brachiocephalic vein and the rest to the azygos vein; on the left the upper 3 spaces drain to the left brachiocephalic vein and the rest to the hemiazygos and accessory hemiazygos veins, which drain to the azygos vein.
• Lymphatics: deep lymphatics follow the arteries; posteriorly they drain to the posterior intercostal nodes in the posterior mediastinum.
B(i)
• Safe site: a needle or drain is passed immediately above the upper border of a rib; it is dangerous to pass it immediately below a rib.
• Basis: the intercostal vessels lie immediately below their corresponding ribs (vein above artery) in the subcostal groove, so a needle just above the lower rib avoids the neurovascular bundle; in thoracotomy the periosteum over a segment of the 5th or 6th rib is elevated, protecting the bundle.
C(i)
• In coarctation of the aorta the intercostal arteries derived from the aorta receive blood from the superior intercostals, from the anterior intercostal branches of the internal thoracic artery and from arteries anastomosing around the scapula.
• Together with the communication between the internal thoracic and inferior epigastric arteries, these are the principal collaterals between the aorta above and below the block.
• The intercostal arteries dilate and become tortuous and erode the lower borders of the corresponding ribs, giving the characteristic irregular notching of the ribs that helps radiographic confirmation.

questions.answerText:
(i)
• The right and left coronary arteries are the first branches of the aorta, arising from the corresponding right and left aortic sinuses at the proximal ascending aorta.
• The right coronary artery runs in the atrioventricular (coronary) groove and gives off the SA nodal branch, right marginal branch, AV nodal branch, and posterior interventricular branch, which anastomoses with the anterior interventricular branch of the left coronary artery.
• The right coronary artery typically supplies the right atrium, most of the right ventricle, part of the left ventricle, the posterior third of the AV septum, the SA node in 60% of people and the AV node in 80% of people.
• The left coronary artery arises from the left aortic sinus, runs in the AV groove, and divides into the circumflex and anterior interventricular branches.
• The left coronary artery typically supplies the left atrium, most of the left ventricle, part of the right ventricle, most of the interventricular septum and the SA node in 40% of people.
• Venous drainage is mainly through the coronary sinus, which receives the great, middle and small cardiac veins and the left posterior ventricular and left marginal veins.
(ii)
Arterial dominance is defined by which artery gives rise to the posterior interventricular artery; right dominance is typical, the left is dominant in about 10% of people, and co-dominance occurs in about 15% of people.
(iii)
• Because the right coronary artery mainly supplies the right atrium, right ventricle and, in most people, the SA and AV nodes, its occlusion can damage right-sided myocardium and disturb the conduction system.
• Because the left coronary artery mainly supplies the left atrium, left ventricle and interventricular septum, its occlusion tends to damage the left ventricle, which performs more work than the right, and the septum.
• Damage to the region supplying the SA or AV node can disturb the heart's conducting system, since the SA and AV nodes are the pacesetters of the heart.
• Tissue damage from reduced blood flow in the territory of the affected artery causes the chest pain of ischaemia/infarction, which can radiate as referred pain to the jaw and left arm.

A. Describe the course of the maxillary nerve, from its origin to its continuation on the face, and list its branches.
B. State the clinically relevant procedure and the region associated with this nerve.
questions.answerText:
A
The maxillary nerve passes through the pterygopalatine fossa, where it is one of the contents (along with the terminal part of the maxillary artery, the maxillary vein, and the pterygopalatine ganglion); nerve structures enter the fossa through its posterior wall. Its branches include the superior alveolar nerves (anterior, posterior and middle), the middle meningeal nerve, the infraorbital nerve, the zygomatic nerve, the inferior palpebral nerve, the superior labial nerve, the pharyngeal nerve, the greater and lesser palatine nerves, and the nasopalatine nerve. The infraorbital nerve continues from the maxillary nerve onto the face via the infraorbital groove and canal, situated on the floor of the orbit in the orbital plate of the maxilla, and via the infraorbital foramen.
B
Clinical correlates of this region include maxillary nerve block, and the pterygopalatine ganglion is also referred to as the "hay fever ganglion".

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the origin, types, and functions of cells found in connective tissue under the following headings: cells of fixed (resident) population and cells of wandering (transient) population.
A(ii) State where the mesenchymal stem-like cells persist in adults and state their clinical significance.
B(i) Explain the anatomical and histological basis of why connective tissue of the head region differs in embryological origin from the rest of the body, and state the clinical implication.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
Fixed (resident) cells: Mesenchyme cells — embryonic source of all connective tissue cells; only found in embryos, but some mesenchyme-like cells persist in adult connective tissue. Fibroblasts — most common cell type in connective tissue; elongated, spindle-shaped cells with many cell processes; have oval, pale-staining, regular nuclei with prominent nucleoli; abundant rough endoplasmic reticulum and active Golgi bodies; synthesize collagen, reticular and elastic fibers, and amorphous extracellular substance. Fibrocytes — quiescent fibroblasts; smaller, darker nucleus; less rough ER. Chondroblasts/osteoblasts — synthesize cartilage and bone matrices. Adipocytes — energy storage, thermal insulation. Wandering (transient) cells: Macrophages — ingestion by phagocytosis; antigen presentation; secretion of enzymes and cytokines; long-lived (several months); originate from monocytes in bone marrow. Plasma cells — defense and immune function. Lymphocytes — immune function. Neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils — immune function. Mast cells — immune function. All connective tissue cells are derived from mesenchymal cells.
A(ii)
Mesenchyme-like cells (pericytes) persist in adult connective tissue, including that of tooth pulp and some adipose tissue. These mesenchyme-like cells retain their capacity to differentiate into other connective tissue cells in response to injury (e.g., pericytes — perivascular cells of blood capillaries). They are being investigated as possible sources of stem cells for therapeutic repair and organ regeneration. Some multipotent stem cells potentially useful in regenerative medicine after grafting to replace damaged tissue in certain patients.
B(i)
All connective tissue cells are derived from mesenchymal cells; mesenchyme cells are for the most part derived from the mesoderm. However, several of the connective tissues of the head region are derived from the neural crest cells (ectodermal origin). Endothelial cells lining blood vessels are derived from mesenchyme. The clinical implication is that connective tissue tumors or developmental disorders in the head may follow patterns distinct from those in the rest of the body due to this different embryological derivation.

A(i)
• The longest lymphatic duct, conveying lymph to the circulatory system.
• It begins as the upward continuation of the cisterna chyli, a dilated sac formed by the union of the left and right lumbar trunks and the intestinal trunk, in front of L1 (also stated at T12).
A(ii)
• It enters the thorax through the aortic opening of the diaphragm and ascends in the posterior mediastinum, on the right side of and behind the oesophagus, with the oesophagus lying in front of it.
• It veers to the left at the level of T5 and ascends in the superior mediastinum to the left of the oesophagus.
• At the root of the neck it turns laterally, arches forwards and descends to enter the left venous angle.
A(iii)
• Before termination it receives the left jugular, left subclavian and left bronchomediastinal trunks; it ends in the left brachiocephalic vein.
• It contains many valves, with no valve at its termination.
A(iv)
• It drains lymph from the lower limbs, pelvic cavity, abdominal cavity, left half of the thorax and left side of the head, neck and upper limb (all the body except the right side of the head, neck, thorax and upper limb).
• The right lymphatic duct, formed by the union of the right jugular, subclavian and bronchomediastinal trunks, drains the right half of the head, neck, thorax and upper limb, right lung, right side of the heart and right surface of the liver, and ends in the right brachiocephalic vein.
• The lymph trunks are the right and left jugular, subclavian, bronchomediastinal and lumbar trunks and the intestinal trunk; the left brachiocephalic vein receives the thoracic duct, the right brachiocephalic vein the right lymphatic duct.

A. Describe the course and distribution of the lingual nerve, including its relationship to the submandibular duct.
B. State the site at which the lingual nerve crosses the submandibular duct, which is relevant to procedures in this region.
C. Explain the functional deficit that would be anticipated from injury to the lingual nerve, based on the sensory territory it supplies.
questions.answerText:
A
The lingual nerve is a branch of the mandibular nerve (CN V3). It provides sensory supply to the mucous membrane of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. In its course, the submandibular duct (Wharton's duct) runs forwards on hyoglossus, between the lingual and hypoglossal nerves.
B
At the anterior border of hyoglossus, the submandibular duct is crossed by the lingual nerve; this crossing relationship is anatomically relevant, since a stone in the submandibular duct can be felt bimanually in the floor of the mouth, and surgery/removal in this region places the lingual nerve at risk, along with the hypoglossal nerve, given their close relationship to the duct on hyoglossus.
C
Sensory supply to the mucous membrane of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is via the lingual nerve (a branch of CN V3), while special (taste) sensory supply to the same region is via the chorda tympani nerve (a branch of CN VII); injury to the lingual nerve would therefore be expected to impair general sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, distinct from a taste deficit, which would instead follow injury to the chorda tympani.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the gross anatomy of epithelial tissue under the following headings: general characteristics, morphological classification (by cell shape and number of layers), and the basement membrane.
A(ii) Relate specific epithelial types to their common locations in the body, giving one example each of simple squamous, simple cuboidal, simple columnar, ciliated columnar, stratified squamous, and transitional epithelium.
B(i) Explain why epithelial tissue is avascular, how it receives nutrients, and state the clinical consequence when the basement membrane is disrupted in disease.
questions.answerText:
A(i)
General characteristics: epithelial tissue consists of closely packed cells arranged in one or more layers; these cells are specialized and fill roles such as protection, secretion, and absorption; the cells are tightly packed together with very little extracellular matrix and almost no intercellular substance; they rest on a basement membrane (a basal lamina containing the glycoprotein laminin). Morphological classification by cell shape: squamous (flat), cuboidal (square or cube-like), columnar (tall and thin). By number of layers: simple epithelium (one cell thick) — can be simple squamous, simple cuboidal, or simple columnar; stratified epithelium (multiple layers — described as heterogeneous); pseudostratified epithelium — appears stratified but all cells contact the basal lamina. Transitional epithelium: recognized by its appearance — when the bladder is empty (relaxed), the epithelium appears thicker and has more layers than when the bladder is full. Basement membrane: contains the glycoprotein laminin; the border between epithelia and the underlying connective tissue is sharp and distinct.
A(ii)
Simple squamous epithelium: lines blood vessels (endothelium) and body cavities. Simple cuboidal epithelium: lines many small ducts in the body. Simple columnar epithelium: lines the gallbladder, larger ducts near the urinary papilla; also found in the jejunum (with goblet cells). Ciliated columnar epithelium: found in the respiratory tract and fallopian tubes; goblet cells (glandular epithelium) are present, making it heterogeneous. Stratified squamous epithelium (keratinized): forms the outer layer of skin; contains the protective protein keratin; a keratinized (dry) epithelium. Transitional epithelium: lines the urinary bladder.
B(i)
Epithelial tissue is avascular (contains no blood vessels); the lamina propria (underlying connective tissue) supplies the necessary nutrients and metabolites, which are transported to and from epithelial cells by diffusion through the basement membrane. If the basement membrane is disrupted (e.g., in cancer invasion or severe inflammation), the barrier between epithelium and connective tissue is lost, allowing unrestricted cell invasion into the underlying stroma; epithelial cells in contact with the environment are constantly subjected to mechanical damage and must show many dividing cells (mitoses) to replace lost cells; disruption of this repair mechanism contributes to disease progression.

A(i)
The greater sac is the main larger part; the lesser sac (omental bursa) lies posterior to the stomach, adjoining structures and lesser omentum; an incision through the anterolateral wall enters the greater sac; the sacs communicate through the epiploic foramen.
A(ii)
• The transverse mesocolon divides the cavity into supracolic and infracolic compartments; the infracolic lies posterior to the greater omentum and is divided by the mesentery of the small intestine into right and left infracolic spaces.
• Right space: triangular, between the root of the mesentery, ascending colon and right two-thirds of transverse colon; left: between the root, descending colon and left one-third of transverse colon, widening below into the pelvis.
A(iii)
Right paracolic gutter lies lateral to the ascending colon and communicates with the hepatorenal recess and pelvic cavity; the left, lateral to the descending colon, is separated from the splenic area by the phrenicocolic ligament.
A(iv)
• Lesser sac: superior wall peritoneum over the caudate lobe and diaphragm; anterior lesser omentum, peritoneum of the posterior stomach and anterior two layers of greater omentum; posterior the posterior two layers, transverse colon and mesocolon, peritoneum over pancreas, left kidney and suprarenal gland.
• Omental foramen (of Winslow), behind the hepatoduodenal ligament, admits 2 fingers: liver superiorly, first part of duodenum inferiorly, hepatoduodenal ligament anteriorly, IVC and right crus posteriorly.
B(i)
Median umbilical fold covers the urachal remnant, medial folds the obliterated umbilical arteries, lateral folds the inferior epigastric vessels; the supravesical fossa is a site for external supravesical hernia, the medial inguinal fossa for the less common direct hernia, the lateral inguinal fossa for the most common indirect hernia.
B(ii)
Blockage of the uterine tubes (hysterosalpingography), peritonitis, ascites, paracentesis and intraperitoneal injection, flow of exudates in the paracolic gutters, and adhesions with adhesiotomy in intestinal obstruction.
C(i)
• The right paracolic gutter provides a route for spread of infection between the pelvic and upper abdominal regions, and the supracolic and infracolic compartments communicate freely through the gutters.
• In the female the cavity communicates with the exterior via the uterine tubes, uterus and vagina.
• Parietal peritoneum is supplied by the nerves of the adjacent body wall and diaphragm; visceral peritoneum by sympathetic nerves of the underlying viscus.
• Receptors respond to overdistension, traction on mesenteries, spasm of smooth muscle and ischaemia.

A(i)
The deep cervical fascia consists of areolar tissue that supports the muscles, vessels and viscera of the neck; it is condensed to form well-defined fibrous sheets, labelled as: (1) the investing layer (superficial), (2) the pretracheal fascia, (3) the prevertebral fascia, (4) the carotid sheath, and (5) the axillary fascia. More generally, deep fascia is the membranous investment of structures deep to the superficial fascia, containing cells (fibroblasts), fibres (collagen, elastic) and matrix; being subjected to tensile strains, the collagen forms parallel fibre bundles, with the cells flattened. Deep fascia is best marked in the limbs and neck, where it is wrapped around the muscles, veins and nerves like a bandage, the fibres being mainly circularly arranged; around the thorax and abdomen, which require to expand and contract, there is merely a film of areolar tissue but no true deep fascia.
A(ii)
The pretracheal fascia is found only in the anterior region; superiorly it is attached to the thyroid and cricoid cartilage, and inferiorly it extends into the thorax to blend with the fibrous pericardium; laterally it blends with the carotid sheath and with the investing layer of the deep cervical fascia beneath sternocleidomastoid. The prevertebral fascia is attached superiorly to the base of the skull, and inferiorly enters the thorax and blends with the anterior longitudinal ligament of the vertebral column; it covers the prevertebral muscles (longus capitis and longus cervicis), passes round the neck, attaches to the ligamentum nuchae, and in the posterior triangle forms the fascial floor, covering the muscles scalenus anterior, scalenus medius, scalenus posterior, levator scapulae and splenius capitis.
B
Penetration of the fascia during instrumentation of the pretracheal fascia can lead to collection of infectious substances (pus) in the retropharyngeal space (the space between the pharynx and the prevertebral fascia); whiplash injury of the neck can cause quadriplegia, stabbing injury of the neck can cause vascular/nervous injury, and a tumour blocking the airway may necessitate insertion of a tracheostomy tube. The deep cervical fascia will necessarily be pierced during tracheostomy.
C
The pretracheal fascia surrounds the thyroid gland completely, forming a sheath for it, binds the thyroid gland to the larynx, encloses the parathyroid gland, invests the infrahyoid muscles, and encloses the visceral components of the neck (larynx and trachea, pharynx and oesophagus, and the thyroid and parathyroid glands). The prevertebral fascia, in contrast, surrounds the vertebral column and its associated muscles, extending from the base of the skull to approximately the T3 vertebra, and extends laterally as the axillary sheaths.

A(i)
The anterior branch of the abdominal aorta supplying the midgut; it arises immediately below the celiac artery, anterior to the lower part of vertebra LI.
A(ii)
• It is crossed anteriorly by the splenic vein and the neck of the pancreas; posterior to it are the left renal vein, the uncinate process of the pancreas and the inferior part of the duodenum.
• The middle colic artery arises as it emerges from beneath the pancreas.
A(iii)
• First branch: inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery, dividing into anterior and posterior branches that anastomose with the superior pancreaticoduodenal arteries.
• Left side: numerous jejunal and ileal arteries passing between the two layers of the mesentery to form arcades, whose number increases distally.
• Vasa recta: long, close together and narrow windows in the jejunum; short, far apart and low broad windows in the ileum.
• Right side: middle colic (transverse mesocolon; anastomoses with left colic), right colic (inconsistent, retroperitoneal) and ileocolic arteries.
• The ileocolic divides into superior and inferior branches; the inferior gives colic, cecal, appendicular (in the mesoappendix free margin) and ileal branches.
A(iv)
• Midgut: duodenum below the major papilla, jejunum, ileum, cecum, appendix, ascending colon and right two-thirds of the transverse colon.
• The midgut ends at the junction of the proximal two-thirds and distal one-third of the transverse colon.

A(i)
Oblique, tunnel-shaped passage through the lower part of the anterior abdominal wall just above the medial half of the inguinal ligament, present in both sexes; about 4 cm (1½ inches) long in adults, directed downwards, forwards and medially.
A(ii)
It extends from the deep inguinal ring to the superficial inguinal ring; in the newborn the deep ring lies almost directly posterior to the superficial ring.
A(iii)
• Anterior wall: external oblique aponeurosis, reinforced laterally by internal oblique. Posterior wall: transversalis fascia, reinforced medially by the conjoint tendon.
• Roof: arching lowest fibres of internal oblique and transversus abdominis with transversalis fascia. Floor: inguinal ligament, reinforced medially by the lacunar ligament.
A(iv)
Spermatic cord (male) or round ligament of uterus (female); processus vaginalis remnant; 3 fasciae; 3 arteries (artery to vas, cremasteric, testicular); 3 nerves (ilio-inguinal L1, genital branch of genitofemoral L2, sympathetic); vas, pampiniform plexus, lymphatics.
B(i)
• It is a potential weakness in the abdominal wall. The posterior wall is weak laterally at the deep ring, but the anterior wall opposite is reinforced by internal oblique, so a hernia through the deep ring must travel along the canal.
• The anterior wall is weak medially at the superficial ring, but the posterior wall opposite is reinforced by the conjoint tendon; weakness there leads to direct hernias.
B(ii)
In the male it allows spermatic cord structures to pass to and from the testis (normal spermatogenesis needs the cooler scrotum) while preventing intestine entering the scrotum; in the female the smaller canal carries the round ligament of the uterus to the labium majus.
C(i)
• Deep ring: oval opening in the transversalis fascia, about ½ inch (1.3 cm) above the inguinal ligament at the midinguinal point, lateral to the inferior epigastric artery; margins give attachment to internal spermatic fascia; entrance of the cord.
• Superficial ring: triangular defect in the external oblique aponeurosis, immediately above and medial to the pubic tubercle; its medial and lateral crura give attachment to the external spermatic fascia; it is the exit of the cord from the canal.

A(i)
• Shape of a clenched fist; base to apex 12 cm in males and 10 cm in females, anteroposterior 6 cm and 5 cm, transverse 9 cm and 8 cm; weight 280-340 g in males and 230-280 g in females; lies behind the body of the sternum, in front of T5-T8, with a base, an apex, 3 surfaces and 4 borders.
• Base: posterior, mostly left atrium, receives the 4 pulmonary veins; ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk emerge from it; separated from the diaphragmatic surface by the coronary sulcus. Apex: inferolateral, mostly left ventricle, behind the 5th left intercostal space. Surfaces: sternocostal (mostly right ventricle), diaphragmatic (concave), pulmonary (left ventricle, fitting the cardiac notch of the left lung). Borders: right (right atrium), left (mostly left ventricle with the left auricle), superior (auricles and upper right ventricle), inferior (right atrium and right ventricle).
A(ii)
Right border: 3rd to 6th right costal cartilage; left border: 5th left intercostal space (apex beat, 9 cm from the midline) up to the 2nd costal cartilage; superior border: 2nd left to 3rd right costal cartilage; inferior border: 6th right costal cartilage to the 5th left intercostal space.
A(iii)
• Four chambers: atria separated by the interatrial septum, ventricles by the interventricular septum, atria from ventricles by the right and left coronary (AV) sulci. Right atrium: forms the right border, lies between SVC and IVC, has the right auricle; rough part (musculi pectinati) and smooth part (from the right horn of the sinus venosus) separated by the sulcus terminalis (crista terminalis); receives SVC, IVC and coronary sinus.
• Right ventricle: forms the sternocostal and diaphragmatic surfaces and inferior border; trabeculae carneae including the septomarginal trabecula (carries part of the AV bundle) and anterior, posterior and septal papillary muscles joined by chordae tendineae to the tricuspid valve (3 cusps, admits 3 fingertips), the chordae preventing the cusps being driven into the right atrium; pulmonary orifice about 2.5 cm with 3 semilunar cusps (anterior, left, right).
• Left atrium: posterior, forms the base, receives 4 valveless pulmonary veins; left auricle forms the upper left border; smooth wall except the auricle. Mitral (bicuspid) valve: anterior and posterior cusps, admits 2 fingertips, overlaps the tricuspid and lies slightly higher. Left ventricle: aortic orifice about 2.5 cm at the right upper part with 3 semilunar cusps (posterior, right, left); numerous trabeculae carneae; anterior and posterior papillary muscles with chordae to the mitral valve.
A(iv)
SA node: natural pacemaker, first conducting cell, below the opening of the SVC in the right atrium, contains pacemaker P-cells, autonomic supply from the cardiac plexus (sympathetics increase and parasympathetics decrease the rate of impulse generation). AV node: slow conducting tissue in the posterior and inferior interatrial septum, allows complete atrial contraction before ventricular contraction. AV bundle of His: Purkinje fibres in the membranous part of the interventricular septum, the only bridge between atrial and ventricular muscle; right branch to papillary muscles and moderator band, left branch to the left papillary muscles.
A(v)
Arteries: right and left coronary arteries from the ascending aorta run in the right and left AV sulci; the right gives posterior interventricular and marginal arteries, the left gives anterior interventricular and circumflex arteries (the circumflex gives a marginal branch). Veins: the coronary sinus (posterior part of the AV sulcus, valve at its opening, empties into the right atrium) receives the great, small and middle cardiac veins, posterior vein of the left ventricle and oblique vein of the left atrium; the anterior cardiac vein opens into the right atrium and venae cordis minimae open into the chambers. Nerve supply: cardiac plexus.
B(i)
• The heart has a poor anastomotic network, so blockage of one coronary artery (coronary thrombosis) leads to myocardial infarction; the heart wall has 3 layers (epicardium, myocardium, endocardium) and the serous pericardium receives the coronary arteries.
• Angina pectoris: chest pain originating from the heart, caused by insufficient supply of oxygen to the heart muscle.
C(i)
• Irritation of the pleura or pericardium covering the central part of the diaphragm is referred to the shoulder, because the central diaphragm is supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3-5) and the shoulder skin by the supraclavicular nerve (C3,4); the fibrous and parietal pericardium are supplied by the phrenic nerve.
• Hiccup: involuntary spasmodic contraction of the diaphragm with approximation of the vocal folds and closure of the glottis; it may be due to pleurisy, peritonitis or pericarditis.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the size, shape, position, base, apex, surfaces and borders of the heart.
A(ii) Describe the surface marking of the heart.
A(iii) Describe the chambers and valves of the heart.
A(iv) Describe the conducting system of the heart.
A(v) Describe the blood supply, venous drainage and nerve supply of the heart.
B(i) Relate the arterial supply and structure of the heart to common cardiac pathologies.
C(i) Explain how disease of the heart coverings and neighbouring structures may cause pain or disturbance in a distant structure.

questions.answerText:
(i)
• The kidneys are bean-shaped, retroperitoneal organs lying on the posterior abdominal wall from about the T12 to L3 vertebral level, each about 10 cm long, 5 cm wide and 2.5 cm thick, with the right kidney slightly lower due to the liver.
• Each kidney has a superior pole bearing the suprarenal gland, an inferior pole, a convex lateral border, and a concave medial border indented by the renal hilum.
• Coverings, from within outward, are the fibrous (renal) capsule, perirenal fat, renal fascia, and pararenal fat.
• Internally, a dark brown outer cortex surrounds a lighter medulla composed of about a dozen renal pyramids, each with its base toward the cortex and its apex (renal papilla) projecting into a minor calyx; cortex extends between pyramids as renal columns.
• At the hilum, the renal vein lies anterior to the renal artery, which lies anterior to the renal pelvis; the hilum leads into the renal sinus, which contains the pelvis, calyces, vessels, nerves and fat.
• The renal pelvis, a funnel-shaped expansion of the ureter, receives two or three major calyces, each dividing into two or three minor calyces.
(ii)
• Renal (kidney) stones are a clinical consideration associated with the kidney and relate to the calyceal and pelvic system where urine collects before draining into the ureter.
• The renal pyramids and papillae are the sites from which urine is excreted into the minor calyces, so pathology of the papillae or pyramids affects urine drainage.
(iii)
• The ureter has three points of constriction - the pelviureteric junction, where it crosses the pelvic brim, and its intramural (intravesical) course - which are potential sites of obstruction by ureteric stones.
• Obstruction at any of these constrictions causes back-pressure on the kidney, from the collecting system through the pelvis to the pyramids, producing a functional deficit in urine drainage from that kidney.
• Ureteric pain from such obstruction is referred to the ipsilateral lower quadrant of the anterior abdominal wall and especially the groin, showing how a renal or ureteric problem produces a distant clinical effect.
• This referred pain reflects the segmental (T11-T12) sympathetic innervation shared by the ureter and the abdominal wall/groin dermatomes.
questions.question:
(i) Describe the gross anatomy of the kidney, including its shape, coverings, and internal structure (cortex, medulla, pyramids, sinus, calyces).
(ii) Relate the parts of the kidney to a common renal pathology.
(iii) Explain how disease/obstruction of the kidney or its drainage system can produce a functional deficit at a distance.

questions.answerText:
(i)
• The pancreas is a soft, lobulated, J- or retort-shaped gland lying retroperitoneally, except for the tail, and transversely across the posterior abdominal wall at the level of L1-L2, posterior to the stomach, between the duodenum on the right and the spleen on the left; it is about 15-20 cm long and weighs about 90 g.
• The head is disc-shaped, enlarged, and lies within the concavity of the duodenum; the uncinate process projects from its lower part, posterior to the superior mesenteric vessels.
• The neck is the constricted portion connecting the head to the body and overlies the superior mesenteric vessels.
• The body is centrally located, crossing the midline behind the stomach, with anterior, posterior and inferior surfaces; the posterior surface contacts the aorta, splenic vein, left kidney and vessels, left suprarenal gland, origin of the superior mesenteric artery, and the crura of the diaphragm.
• The tail is narrow, lies at the level of T12, ends within the splenic hilum in the splenophrenic ligament, and is the only intraperitoneal part of the pancreas; it may be injured during splenectomy, causing a pancreatic fistula.
• The main pancreatic duct, of Wirsung, begins in the tail and runs to the head, usually joining the bile duct to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla, which opens at the major duodenal papilla; the accessory duct, of Santorini, drains the upper head via the minor duodenal papilla.
(ii)
• Annular pancreas is a rare congenital defect in which the pancreas encircles the duodenum; ectopic pancreatic tissue outside the gastrointestinal tract is a very common anomaly.
• Due to its deep retroperitoneal position, the pancreas is not easily accessible for direct clinical examination, so diagnosis of pancreatic disease relies on ultrasound, CT scan, special investigations of the pancreatic and biliary ducts, and biochemical tests.
• Acute necrotizing pancreatitis results when proenzymes are prematurely activated and digest pancreatic tissue, from causes including infection, gallstones, alcoholism, drugs and trauma.
(iii)
• The endocrine part of the pancreas, the islets of Langerhans, secretes insulin and glucagon into the blood; lack of insulin production by the beta cells, or defective insulin receptors, causes diabetes mellitus, a hyperglycaemic metabolic disorder affecting the whole body.
• Because the exocrine pancreas secretes digestive enzymes and bicarbonate essential for neutralising gastric acid and digesting food in the duodenum, pancreatic disease impairing exocrine secretion produces a functional deficit in intestinal digestion, a distant effect of pancreatic pathology.
• In extreme malnutrition, acinar cell atrophy further reduces digestive enzyme production, compounding this distant digestive deficit.
questions.question:
(i) Describe the gross anatomy of the pancreas - location, shape, and its four parts (head, neck, body, tail) with their relations.
(ii) Relate the parts of the pancreas to pathology (annular pancreas, pancreatitis).
(iii) Explain how pancreatic disease can produce a functional deficit in a distant organ/system.

questions.answerText:
1. Functions:
• The hypothalamus is the primary output node of the limbic system; it is connected with the frontal lobes, septal nuclei and brain stem reticular formation through the medial forebrain bundle and receives input from the hippocampus via the fornix and from the amygdala via the ventral amygdalofugal pathway and stria terminalis.
• It has centres for sexual, endocrine, behavioural and autonomic functions; autonomic functions are controlled through projections to the brain stem.
• Inputs: from most of the body, olfaction, the viscera and the retina; internal sensors for temperature, osmolarity, glucose and sodium; receptors for steroid hormones and for appetite signals such as leptin and orexin.
• Regions: the ventromedial nucleus is a satiety area and the lateral hypothalamic area a feeding centre; the preoptic area (greatest sexual dimorphism) with the septal nuclei projects gonadotropin releasing hormone to the median eminence; the suprachiasmatic nucleus receives direct retinal input and entrains circadian rhythms.
• The lateral hypothalamus releases orexin, which activates the arousal system; the posterior tuberomammillary hypothalamus is the source of histamine projections.
2. Distant effects:
• It controls temperature and osmolarity regulation, endocrine functions and appetite, and produces sexual responses that combine autonomic, endocrine and behavioural elements.
• Through the brain stem it influences autonomic organs, and through the median eminence it influences the gonads.
• The hypothalamus is one of the last areas of the brain to develop.
questions.question:
Answer the following on the functions of the hypothalamus:
1. Describe the functions of the hypothalamus under these headings: connections and inputs, autonomic, endocrine and behavioural functions, internal sensors, and the roles of its regions (satiety and feeding areas, preoptic area, suprachiasmatic nucleus).
2. Explain why a disturbance of the hypothalamus may affect a distant organ or system.

questions.answerText:
1. Olfactory pathway:
• The olfactory epithelium (about 5 cm2 in the roof of the nasal cavity) has 10 to 20 million bipolar olfactory sensory neurons among supporting (sustentacular) cells and basal stem cells; each neuron has a dendrite ending in a knob with 10 to 20 cilia bearing odorant receptors, covered by mucus from Bowman's glands.
• Transduction: odorants dissolve in mucus and bind G-protein-coupled receptors, which activate adenylyl cyclase and cAMP, opening cation channels; Na+ and Ca2+ enter and depolarise the cell.
• Axons pass through the cribriform plate into the olfactory bulb, where they contact mitral and tufted cell dendrites in glomeruli; mitral and tufted axons run through the intermediate and lateral olfactory striae to the olfactory cortex (anterior olfactory nucleus, olfactory tubercle, piriform cortex, amygdala, entorhinal cortex).
• There is no thalamic relay in the primary smell pathway; conscious discrimination depends on the pathway to the orbitofrontal cortex (greater on the right); the amygdala pathway gives emotional responses and the entorhinal cortex olfactory memories; olfactory cortex also projects via the hypothalamus.
2. Modifiers and adaptation:
• Rapid adaptation is mediated by Ca2+ acting through calmodulin on cyclic nucleotide-gated channels.
• The olfactory threshold increases with age: more than 75% of humans over 80 have impaired ability to identify smells; pregnancy commonly gives oversensitivity (hyperosmia).
3. Abnormalities:
• Anosmia (absence), hyposmia (diminished) and dysosmia (distorted); anosmia is associated with hypogonadism (Kallmann's syndrome).
• Causes: nasal congestion, fracture of the cribriform plate, tumours (neuroblastoma, meningioma), infections and abscesses, and Alzheimer's disease; dysosmia arises from sinus infections, partial nerve damage and poor dental hygiene.
questions.question:
Answer the following on olfaction (smell):
1. Describe the olfactory pathway as a control system: receptor cells and epithelium, transduction, olfactory bulb, olfactory tract, olfactory cortex and central connections.
2. State the normal features (numbers, adaptation), the factors that raise or lower olfactory sensitivity and the adaptation response.
3. Explain the physiological basis of the abnormalities of smell.

questions.answerText:
1. Visual pathway:
• Retina: pigment layer, rods and cones, bipolar cells (excitatory or inhibitory), horizontal cells (inhibitory, lateral inhibition to enhance contrast), amacrine cells and ganglion cells, whose axons form the optic nerve.
• After leaving the retinas impulses pass through the optic nerves; at the optic chiasm fibres from the nasal halves of the retinas cross and join the temporal fibres of the other eye to form the optic tract.
• Fibres of each tract synapse in the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus (six layers: P ganglion cells project to layers 3 to 6 and M ganglion cells to layers 1 and 2), and the geniculocalcarine fibres pass by the optic radiation to the primary visual cortex of the occipital lobe, with onward transmission to secondary visual areas.
• Other projections: fibres go from the optic tracts to the suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus to control circadian rhythm.
2. Values and adaptation:
• About 6 million cones and 120 million rods supply 1.2 million optic nerve fibres (convergence about 105:1).
• Visual acuity is tested with the Snellen chart at 20 ft (6 m); normal is 20/20, 20/15 is better than normal and 20/100 is subnormal.
• Dark adaptation is an increase in retinal sensitivity on moving to dim light, maximal in about 20 minutes, cones adapting first and rods later; retinal, opsins and vitamin A are converted back to rhodopsin.
• Light adaptation: after hours in bright light the photochemicals are reduced to retinal and opsins (and retinal to vitamin A), so sensitivity falls.
• Radiologists and pilots wear red goggles in bright light to avoid waiting 20 minutes to become dark-adapted.
3. Deficits:
• Colour blindness: dichromates lack one cone type (protanope lacks red, deuteranope green, tritanope blue) and monochromates have one type; red-green colour blindness occurs almost exclusively in males (8% of women are carriers); blue-green defects occur in people taking sildenafil.
• Nyctalopia (night blindness) is linked to the rhodopsin-retinal visual cycle; the pigment layer stores vitamin A, a precursor of rhodopsin.
• After a lesion of the pathway, fibres from the macula are spared.
questions.question:
Answer the following on the central visual pathway:
1. Describe the visual pathway as a control system: photoreceptors and retinal processing, the optic nerve, chiasm, lateral geniculate nucleus, optic radiation, visual cortex and other projections.
2. State the normal values (photoreceptor numbers, visual acuity), the factors that raise or lower retinal sensitivity and the compensatory adaptation responses.
3. Explain the physiological basis of the visual deficits when the pathway or the receptors fail.

Answer the following on blood groups:
1. Describe the ABO and RhD blood group systems under these headings: basis of the groups, antigens (agglutinogens), antibodies (agglutinins), genotypes and their resulting groups, and the clinical significance.
2. Explain the clinical basis of the disturbances associated with blood groups: why transfusion and child bearing carry risk in some states.
3. Distinguish between an agglutinogen and an agglutinin, and between group A from genotype AA and from genotype AO.
questions.answerText:
1. Blood group systems:
• Blood types are classified by the ABO system (A, B, AB, O) and the RhD system (RhD positive and negative); they are established before birth by genes inherited from the parents.
• They are identified by agglutinogens (antigens) on the surface of all your red blood cells.
• AA and AO give group A (antigen A with antibody B); BB and BO give group B (antigen B with antibody A); AB has antigens A and B and no antibody; OO has no antigen but antibodies A and B.
• Clinical significance: medical diagnosis with physical findings and history, blood transfusion and child bearing (for example haemolytic disease of the newborn); compatibility of ABO, plasma and RhD groups matters.
2. Basis of disturbances:
• Incompatible blood transfusion can cause disseminated intravascular coagulation, in which widespread clotting in intact vessels leaves residual blood unable to clot, with blockage of flow and severe bleeding.
3. Distinctions:
• Agglutinogens are the antigens on the red cell surface; agglutinins are the antibodies in plasma.
• AA and AO both give group A because both carry antigen A with antibody B; AO carries an O allele that gives no antigen.

1. Functions:
• The limbic system combines higher mental functions and primitive emotion into a single system, the emotional nervous system; its components are the amygdala, hippocampus, thalamus, hypothalamus, basal ganglia and cingulate gyrus.
• Thalamus: a sensory way-station connected with other limbic structures; hypothalamus: primary output node with endocrine, behavioural, autonomic and sexual centres; hippocampus: formation of new memories; amygdala: coordinates behavioural, autonomic and endocrine responses, mostly to fear and anxiety.
• Cingulate gyrus: focuses attention on emotionally significant events and associates memories with smells and pain, providing a pathway from the thalamus to the hippocampus.
• Ventral tegmental area: dopamine pathways responsible for pleasure.
• Basal ganglia (caudate, putamen, globus pallidus, substantia nigra): repetitive behaviours, reward and focusing attention.
• Prefrontal cortex: thinking about the future, planning, action, and the same dopamine pathways of pleasure and addiction; the olfactory cortex connects to the amygdala and hypothalamus, influencing emotional and endocrine reactions.
2. Pathologies:
• Damage to the ventral tegmental area leaves difficulty getting pleasure, and people often turn to alcohol, drugs, sweets and gambling.
• Prefrontal damage causes poor abstract reasoning, judgment and mood; depression is linked to increased medial frontal activity and decreased posterior cingulate activity.
• Amygdala lesions reduce stress responses and stimulation produces rage; hippocampal damage causes amnesia; Parkinson's disease involves degeneration of dopamine cells in the basal ganglia (substantia nigra).
3. Distant effects:
• The hypothalamus controls autonomic responses through the brain stem and endocrine functions through projections to the median eminence, so limbic changes alter organ function.
• The autonomic nervous system, with its opposing sympathetic and parasympathetic parts, plays a powerful part in emotional life.
questions.question:
Answer the following on the limbic system and emotions:
1. Describe the functions of the limbic system under these headings: components, the roles of the thalamus, hypothalamus, hippocampus and amygdala, and the related areas (cingulate gyrus, ventral tegmental area, basal ganglia, prefrontal cortex, olfactory cortex).
2. State how its components relate to common pathologies of excess and deficiency.
3. Explain why a limbic disturbance may affect a distant organ or system and cause a functional deficit.

Answer the following on the diffusion of oxygen and carbon dioxide (mechanism of gaseous exchange):
1. Describe gas exchange between the alveoli and the pulmonary capillaries under these headings: composition of inspired, alveolar and expired air, the respiratory membrane, Fick's law and the factors governing diffusing capacity, and normal diffusing capacities.
2. Explain why gas exchange is impaired in certain states (emphysema, oedema, fibrosis, removal of a lung) and how diffusing capacity increases in exercise.
3. Distinguish between alveolar air and inspired air, and between alveolar air and expired air.
questions.answerText:
1. Gas exchange:
• Air compositions: alveolar air is partially replaced by atmospheric air at each breath, oxygen constantly diffuses into the capillaries, carbon dioxide diffuses from the blood into alveolar air, and dry inspired air is humidified in the passages.
• Respiratory membrane: a fluid layer with surfactant, alveolar epithelium, epithelial basement membrane, thin interstitial space, capillary basement membrane and capillary endothelium; thickness averages about 0.6 micrometre and is as little as 0.2 micrometre in places.
• Fick's law: diffusing capacity is proportional to pressure gradient x surface area / thickness; solubility and molecular weight give the diffusion coefficient (proportional to S/square root of MW); diffusing capacity is the volume of gas that diffuses each minute for a 1 mmHg pressure difference.
• Values: for oxygen 21 ml/min/mmHg at rest, rising to about 65 (three times); for CO2 about 400 to 450 at rest, rising to about 1200 to 1300 in exercise.
• Alveoli: about 300 million alveoli of 0.3 to 0.5 mm diameter with total area about 70 square metres, each in a basket of pulmonary capillaries; type I cells allow rapid diffusion and type II cells secrete surfactant.
2. Impaired exchange and exercise:
• Removing a lung halves the surface area; in emphysema alveolar walls dissolve and area falls up to fivefold, and with a fall to one third or one quarter of normal exchange is impeded even at rest.
• Oedema and fibrosis increase membrane thickness; a thickness of two to three times normal interferes significantly with exchange.
• Exercise raises diffusing capacity by opening previously dormant capillaries or dilating open ones, increasing surface area, and by a better ventilation-perfusion ratio.
3. Distinctions:
• Alveolar versus inspired air: partial replacement per breath, continual O2 uptake, CO2 addition and humidification.
• Alveolar versus expired air: dead space air mixes with alveolar air, so expired air has higher oxygen tension and lower carbon dioxide tension than alveolar air.

1. Erythrocyte functions:
• Structure: biconcave disc (6 to 9 micrometre diameter, 1 to 2 micrometre thick), deformable to pass the smallest vessels, no nucleus or mitochondria, about 33% haemoglobin; over 97% of the dry cell is haemoglobin.
• Haemoglobin: globin (two alpha and two beta chains) bound to haem, each haem bearing an iron atom that binds one O2 reversibly, so one Hb carries four O2; one cell holds about 250 million Hb molecules; normal Hb is 13 to 18 g/100 ml in adult males, 12 to 16 in females and 14 to 20 in infants.
• Functions: transport oxygen and assist CO2 transport, regulate acid-base balance to prevent large pH changes, assist clot formation; erythrocytes are the major factor in blood viscosity.
• Production: stimulated by erythropoietin (made mainly by the kidneys) in response to tissue oxygenation; a 70 kg man produces about 2.3 x 10^6 red cells per second.
• Destruction: life span 100 to 120 days; anucleate cells cannot synthesise protein, become rigid and fragile and are trapped in the spleen (the red blood cell graveyard) and engulfed by macrophages; haem is split from globin, globin to amino acids, iron stored as ferritin or haemosiderin and haem to bilirubin, carried on albumin, taken up by liver, secreted in bile and metabolised to urobilinogen and stercobilin in faeces; spilled Hb is captured by haptoglobin.
2. Deficiency and excess:
• Anaemia: blood with abnormally low oxygen-carrying capacity, from insufficient red cells (haemorrhagic, haemolytic, aplastic), from low Hb content (iron-deficiency, pernicious) or from abnormal Hb.
• Abnormal Hb: in thalassaemia one globin chain is absent or faulty and cells are thin and deficient in Hb; in sickle-cell anaemia one of 146 amino acids in a beta chain is changed, so HbS links into stiff rods under low oxygen and cells become spiky.
• Polycythaemia: an abnormal excess of erythrocytes that increases viscosity so blood sludges; polycythaemia vera, a bone marrow cancer, has 8 to 11 million cells/microlitre and haematocrit up to 80%, with dizziness.
3. Distant effects:
• Because the erythrocyte delivers oxygen to every tissue, anaemia leaves oxygen inadequate for normal metabolism and gives fatigue, pallor, breathlessness and chilliness.
• Sickle cells interfere with oxygen delivery, leaving victims gasping for air and in extreme pain.
• Aplastic anaemia from marrow destruction (drugs, radiation, viruses) impairs formation of all formed elements, so anaemia is one sign among several.
• Sluggish flow in polycythaemia impairs circulation generally.
questions.question:
Answer the following on the erythrocyte and haemoglobin:
1. Describe the functions of the erythrocyte and haemoglobin under these headings: structure, production and its regulation, oxygen and carbon dioxide transport, acid-base role, life span and destruction.
2. State how erythrocyte and haemoglobin disorders relate to pathologies of deficiency (the anaemias) and of excess (polycythaemia), including the abnormal haemoglobins.
3. Explain why these disturbances produce effects in distant organs and a functional deficit.

questions.answerText:
1. Cough reflex:
• Stimulus: irritant agents; receptors are situated in several locations.
• Afferent fibres pass via the vagus, trigeminal, glossopharyngeal and phrenic nerves to the centre in the medulla oblongata.
• Efferent fibres arise from the medullary centre and pass through the vagus, phrenic and spinal motor nerves to activate the primary and accessory respiratory muscles; the effectors are the muscles of inspiration.
