• Definition: if a blood vessel wall breaks, a series of reactions is set in motion to accomplish haemostasis, the stoppage of bleeding; the response is fast, localized and carefully controlled, and involves clotting factors in plasma plus substances released by platelets and injured tissue cells.
• Vascular spasm: the damaged vessel constricts (vasoconstriction), reducing blood loss; triggers are direct injury to vascular smooth muscle, chemicals released by endothelial cells and platelets, and reflexes from local pain receptors.
• Platelet plug formation: intact endothelium releases nitric oxide and prostacyclin (PGI2), which prevent platelet aggregation in undamaged tissue; when the endothelium is damaged and collagen is exposed, platelets adhere to the collagen, stabilised by von Willebrand factor; platelets swell, form spiked processes, become stickier and release ADP (a potent aggregating agent), serotonin and thromboxane A2 (enhance vascular spasm and aggregation) in a positive feedback cycle; a plug is built within one minute but is loosely knit, so larger breaks need reinforcement.
• Coagulation: fibrin threads reinforce the platelet plug (the thrombin system forms fibrin, the "red clot", while the platelet plug is the "white clot"); blood changes from liquid to gel through clotting factors (procoagulants), most of them plasma proteins made by the liver, numbered I to XIII in order of discovery, all (except tissue factor) circulating in inactive form; vitamin K is required for the synthesis of four of the clotting factors.
• Phase 1: the intrinsic or extrinsic pathway converges on factor X, which with calcium ions, PF3 (platelet phosphatidylserine) and factor V forms prothrombin activator (usually the slowest step; once present the clot forms in 10 to 15 seconds).
• Phase 2: prothrombin activator converts prothrombin to the enzyme thrombin.
• Phase 3: thrombin converts soluble fibrinogen to fibrin, which polymerises into insoluble strands; with calcium ions thrombin activates factor XIII (fibrin stabilizing factor), which cross-links the fibrin into a mesh; clot formation is normally complete within 3 to 6 minutes.
• Clot retraction and repair: within 30 to 60 minutes platelets, which contain actin and myosin, contract, squeezing out serum and drawing the vessel edges together; platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF) stimulates smooth muscle cells and fibroblasts to divide and rebuild the wall, and vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) stimulates endothelial cells to restore the lining.
• Fibrinolysis: plasmin, produced when plasminogen is activated (tissue plasminogen activator from endothelial cells, activated factor XII and thrombin), digests fibrin; it begins within two days and continues over several days; without it vessels would gradually block.
• Limiting clot growth: swift removal of clotting factors and inhibition of activated clotting factors; heparin (from basophil and mast cell granules and found on endothelial cells) enhances antithrombin III, which inhibits thrombin and factors IXa, Xa, XIa and XIIa; other thrombin inhibitors are alpha2-macroglobulin, heparin cofactor II and alpha1-antitrypsin.
2. Basis of thromboembolic disorders:
• A thrombus is a clot that develops and persists in an unbroken vessel; if it breaks away and floats it is an embolus, which becomes an embolism when it lodges in a vessel too narrow to pass (pulmonary embolism impairs oxygen uptake; cerebral embolism may cause a stroke; coronary thrombosis may kill heart muscle).
• Conditions that roughen the vessel endothelium (atherosclerosis, inflammation) allow platelets to gain a foothold.
• Slowly flowing blood or stasis (bedridden patients, long economy-class flights) means clotting factors are not washed away and accumulate until a clot forms.
• Aspirin is an antiprostaglandin drug that inhibits thromboxane A2 formation, blocking platelet aggregation and plug formation; heparin binds antithrombin and enhances its inhibition of thrombin (IIa), Xa and IXa and is the anticoagulant most used in hospital; warfarin, taken orally, interferes with the action of vitamin K in the production of some procoagulants.
3. Intrinsic versus extrinsic pathway:
• Intrinsic: triggered by negatively charged surfaces such as activated platelets, collagen or glass (so it can clot blood in a test tube); called intrinsic because the factors are within the blood; slower because it has many intermediate steps; requires factors VIII, IX, X, XI, XII, prekallikrein, high-molecular-weight kininogen, calcium and platelet phospholipids.
• Extrinsic: triggered by tissue factor (TF, factor III) from beneath damaged endothelium, which is outside the blood; faster because it bypasses several intrinsic steps (clot in about 15 seconds in severe trauma); the TF-VIIa complex is a principal step.
• The two meet at the activation of factor X to Xa.

1. Nervous control of respiration:
• Voluntary control is through the motor cortex of the cerebrum, with inputs from the limbic system and hypothalamus; involuntary control is by neurons in the pons and medulla.
• Medullary respiratory centre: sets the basic rhythm; the dorsal respiratory group (DRG) integrates input from stretch receptors and peripheral chemoreceptors and maintains the rhythm by stimulating the diaphragm and intercostals (inspiration); when DRG activity ceases the muscles relax (expiration); the ventral respiratory group (VRG) generates the rhythm, is involved in forced breathing and stimulates accessory muscles of forced inspiration and expiration.
• Pontine respiratory group: the apneustic centre stimulates the DRG, controlling the depth of inspiration; the pneumotaxic centre inhibits the DRG, allowing relaxation after inspiration and controlling the overall rate.
• Efferent and effectors: phrenic and intercostal nerves stimulate the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles to contract, producing inspiration; when stimulation stops the muscles relax and expiration occurs.
• Feedback and receptors: aortic and carotid bodies monitor PCO2, PO2 and pH; the hypothalamus monitors emotional state and body temperature; proprioceptors report joint and muscle movement; the inflation reflex protects the lungs from over-inflating and pulmonary irritant reflexes protect the respiratory zones from foreign material.
2. Values, modifiers and compensation:
• Values: adult respiratory rate about 12 to 18 breaths per minute (about 18 to 30 in a 10-year-old); tidal volume 500 ml and pulmonary ventilation 12 x 500 = 6000 ml/min.
• Factors affecting respiration: exercise, temperature, smoking, quantity and quality of air, internal ratio of CO2 and O2, blood pH, respiratory disorders, and drugs including alcohol.
• Compensation in exercise: oxygen demand rises, so tidal volume and breathing rate increase; chemoreceptors (aortic arch and carotid arteries, detecting blood acidity) and proprioceptors (joint and muscle movement) send messages to the medulla oblongata.
3. Disturbance:
• The mechanisms available to protect the lungs are the cough reflex, the sneeze reflex, the inflation reflex and the pulmonary irritant reflexes.
questions.question:
Answer the following on the nervous control of respiration:
1. Describe the control pathway for breathing: receptors, afferent pathways, integrating centres in the brain, efferent nerves, effector muscles and feedback reflexes.
2. State the normal values for breathing, the factors that raise or lower ventilation and the compensatory response during exercise.
3. Explain the physiological basis of the signs and symptoms when the pathway is disturbed.

questions.answerText:
1. Functions:
• Liver: metabolic regulation (stores absorbed nutrients and vitamins and releases them as needed), haematological regulation (plasma protein production and removal of old RBCs), bile production, detoxification of toxins and heparin formation.
• Bile: secreted by liver cells at a constant rate of about 40 ml per hour; required for fat digestion and absorption; between meals the sphincter of Oddi is closed and bile is stored and concentrated in the gallbladder, then delivered to the duodenum.
• Gallbladder: a pear-shaped sac under the liver (fundus, body, neck) with capacity of 30 to 50 ml; it concentrates bile by absorbing water, stores bile, selectively absorbs bile salts, keeps the bile acid, excretes cholesterol and secretes mucus; the neck continues as the cystic duct, which joins the common hepatic duct to form the bile duct.
• The biliary system consists of the liver, gallbladder and bile ducts.
2. Pathologies:
• Most clotting factors are plasma proteins synthesised by the liver; when the liver cannot make its usual procoagulants abnormal and often severe bleeding occurs.
• Causes range from an easily resolved vitamin K deficiency (common in newborns and after systemic antibiotics) to near-total loss of liver function as in hepatitis or cirrhosis.
• Vitamin K is fat-soluble and absorbed with fats; in liver disease the failing cells make neither procoagulants nor the bile needed for fat and vitamin K absorption.
• Bilirubin and enzymes such as aspartate transaminase and alkaline phosphatase are markers of liver damage; excess bilirubin from red cell breakdown is taken up by the liver and secreted in bile.
3. Distant effects:
• Liver failure shows as bleeding because clotting factors are synthesised in the liver.
• Impaired bile flow causes vitamin K deficiency, and bacteria in the large intestine, which normally produce vitamin K, cannot compensate if fat absorption is impaired.
• Liver cirrhosis is listed as a cause of blood disorders, and the liver's failure to make plasma proteins and remove old RBCs affects the blood.
questions.question:
Answer the following on the liver and biliary system:
1. Describe the functions of the liver, bile and gallbladder under these headings: metabolic and haematological functions, synthesis and secretion of bile, storage and concentration of bile, and delivery to the duodenum.
2. State how liver and biliary function relate to pathologies of deficiency, especially of clotting and fat absorption.
3. Explain why liver disturbance may affect distant organs and cause a functional deficit.

questions.answerText:
1. Functions:
• Location: deep in the temporal lobe on its medial aspect, forming the medial wall of the lateral ventricle; an ancient cortex of three layers, shaped like a seahorse.
• Memory: essential for the formation of new memories about past experiences and for retrieval; it underlies declarative (explicit) memory of facts and events, which depends on the medial temporal lobe and the hippocampal-entorhinal relationship; implicit memory is the learning of skills and conditioned and emotional responses; it plays a critical role in short-term memory, which is necessary to establish long-term patterns.
• Spatial function: understanding spatial relations, with the dentate gyrus and dorsal hippocampus generating new adult-born granule cells that support pattern separation, and the left hippocampus involved in recall of spatial memories.
• It helps control corticosteroid production.
2. Pathologies:
• Damage usually causes profound difficulty forming new memories (anterograde amnesia) and may affect access to earlier memories (retrograde amnesia), usually extending some years before the damage.
• Alzheimer's disease is a progressive degenerative disease, mostly in the elderly, with memory loss, irritability, confusion and ultimately hallucinations and death.
3. Distant effects:
• Lesions do not affect old established memories, which involve association areas in the frontal lobe and the parieto-temporo-occipital cortex; the hippocampus becomes less important in storage over time.
• The hippocampus sends output to the hypothalamus through the fornix.
questions.question:
Answer the following on the functions of the hippocampus:
1. Describe the functions of the hippocampus under these headings: location and structure, memory (declarative and non-declarative), spatial function, and other regulatory roles.
2. State how damage to or dysfunction of the hippocampus relates to common pathologies.
3. Explain why a hippocampal disturbance may affect distant memory stores and cause a functional deficit.

Answer the following on the cardiac cycle:
1. Describe the cardiac cycle under these headings: definition of systole and diastole, phases, pressure and volume changes, and heart sounds.
2. Explain why ventricular filling remains possible when atrial contraction is lost (for example in atrial fibrillation) and how valve disease alters the pumping of the heart.
3. Distinguish between the first and second heart sounds, and between isovolumetric contraction and isovolumetric relaxation.
questions.answerText:
1. Cardiac cycle:
• Definition: the repeating pattern of contraction (systole) and relaxation (diastole); both atria contract almost simultaneously and both ventricles about 0.1 to 0.2 second later; diastolic systemic arterial pressure is about 80 mmHg.
• Isovolumetric contraction: ventricular pressure rises, the AV valves snap shut, and the ventricles neither fill nor eject.
• Ejection: when ventricular pressure exceeds aortic (about 120 mmHg) and pulmonary artery (about 25 mmHg) pressure the semilunar valves open; afterwards the semilunar valves close and arterial pressures fall to about 80 and 8 mmHg while ventricular pressure falls to about 0 mmHg; the dicrotic notch is a brief rise in aortic pressure from backflow.
• Isovolumetric relaxation: all valves are closed while ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure.
• Rapid filling: the AV valves open when ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure.
• Atrial contraction: empties the final blood into the ventricles.
• Volumes: about 80 ml at end of systole, about 130 ml after passive filling, active atrial filling adds about 25% (to 150 ml), and about 70 ml is ejected.
• Heart sounds: closing of valves gives "lub-dub".
2. Basis of disturbance:
• Passive filling dominates, which explains why filling is still possible in atrial fibrillation.
• Valve disease: regurgitation is leakage because the valve does not close completely (blood flows back into the atria or ventricles); stenosis is narrowing or stiffening that suppresses flow, so the heart pumps with increased force; mitral valve prolapse is also listed.
3. Distinctions:
• First sound ("lub"): closure of the AV valves during isovolumetric contraction at the start of systole; second sound ("dub"): closure of the semilunar valves when ventricular pressure falls below arterial pressure at the start of diastole.
• Isovolumetric contraction: pressure rises, AV valves shut, semilunar valves not yet open; isovolumetric relaxation: pressure falls, both valve sets closed.

1. Nerve impulse:
• Resting potential: the inside of the neurone is negative, about -70 mV (range -50 to -90 mV), maintained by the Na+/K+ ATPase pump (3 Na+ out for 2 K+ in) and by many more K+ channels than Na+ channels.
• Action potential: stimulation (mechanical, chemical, thermal or electrical) makes the membrane suddenly permeable to Na+, which rushes in, causing further depolarisation (positive feedback) to about +40 mV; permeability to Na+ then falls and K+ moves out slowly until repolarisation to -70 mV within about 2 ms.
• Threshold: the minimum stimulus, generally 5 to 15 mV less negative than resting potential, opens all voltage-gated Na+ channels; the all-or-none law means the amplitude does not change with stimulus size or distance, only frequency changes.
• Propagation: local circuits at the leading edge excite the next part of the axon.
• Conduction velocity: 1 to 120 m/s, increasing with fibre diameter, temperature and the presence of myelin.
2. Importance:
• The refractory period ensures impulses flow in only one direction because the region behind cannot be depolarised, and limits the frequency of impulses.
• Myelin acts as an insulator so action potentials occur only at nodes of Ranvier, giving saltatory conduction.
3. Distinctions:
• Absolute refractory period: about 1 ms during which no impulse can be propagated however intense the stimulus; relative refractory period: about 5 ms during which a new impulse needs a stimulus more intense than normal threshold.
• Myelinated fibres conduct much faster by jumping from node to node; unmyelinated fibres conduct more slowly (for example C fibres at 0.5 to 2 m/s versus A-delta at 12 to 30 m/s).
questions.question:
Answer the following on the nerve impulse:
1. Describe the nerve impulse under these headings: resting potential and how it is maintained, the action potential and its ionic basis, threshold and the all-or-none law, propagation, refractory periods and conduction velocity.
2. Explain why the refractory period is physiologically important and why conduction is faster in some fibres.
3. Distinguish between the absolute and relative refractory periods, and between conduction in myelinated and unmyelinated fibres.

Answer the following on synaptic transmission:
1. Describe synaptic transmission under these headings: types of synapse, parts of a chemical synapse, requirements, sequence of events, the receptor components and the fate of neurotransmitters.
2. Explain the clinical basis of disturbances of synaptic transmission: why neurotransmitter imbalance is important in certain diseases and drugs.
3. Distinguish between electrical and chemical synapses.
questions.answerText:
1. Synaptic transmission:
• A synapse is the junction where an axon terminal contacts another neuron or cell; the sending neuron is presynaptic and the receiving neuron postsynaptic; types are electrical, chemical and conjoint; by connectivity they are axodendritic, axosomatic or axoaxonic.
• Chemical synapse: cleft 20 to 50 nm wide; presynaptic button with synaptic vesicles (about 50 nm) and dense core vesicles (about 100 nm); active zones release transmitter and the postsynaptic density holds receptors.
• Requirements: synthesis and packing of neurotransmitter into vesicles, vesicle release in response to an action potential, an electrical or biochemical response in the postsynaptic neuron, removal of transmitter from the cleft, and all done very rapidly.
• Events: action potential enters the terminal, voltage-gated Ca2+ channels open, Ca2+ activates proteins so vesicles fuse and release transmitter by exocytosis, the transmitter binds the postsynaptic receptor, whose inner ionophore has an ion channel component (cation channels excite, anion channels inhibit) and a G-protein second messenger component (opens ion channels or activates enzymes that make second messengers).
• Fate: cleared by diffusion, enzymatic degradation, presynaptic reuptake then degradation or recycling, uptake by glia, or uptake by the postsynaptic neuron with desensitisation.
• Transmitters include acetylcholine, serotonin, GABA, dopamine, norepinephrine, endorphins and glutamate.
2. Clinical basis:
• Understanding synaptic transmission is necessary for the actions of psychoactive drugs, the causes of mental disorders and the neural basis of learning and memory; transmitters must be cleared to permit another round of transmission.
• Alzheimer's disease shows deterioration of memory, reasoning and language with low acetylcholine and loss of ACh neurons.
• Too much dopamine is involved in schizophrenia, cocaine and nicotine mimic dopamine, and loss of dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra causes Parkinson's disease.
3. Electrical versus chemical synapses:
• Electrical: direct transfer of ionic current through gap junctions, bidirectional, cells electronically coupled, very fast, common in non-neuronal cells and important in development.
• Chemical: transmitter released across a cleft, with receptors that convert the signal into a chemical or membrane potential change.

1. CO2 transport:
• About 4 ml of CO2 is transported from tissues to lungs in each 100 ml of blood: 10% dissolved, 30% combined with haemoglobin and plasma proteins as carbamino-Hb (CO2 reacts with the amino group), and 60% as HCO3-.
• In the red cell dissolved CO2 reacts with water to form carbonic acid, catalysed by carbonic anhydrase (about 5000-fold faster); carbonic acid dissociates into H+ and HCO3-; most H+ combine with haemoglobin.
• Chloride shift: bicarbonate diffuses out of the red cell into plasma while chloride diffuses in, so venous red cells contain more chloride than arterial cells.
• In the lungs the reactions reverse: as haemoglobin loads oxygen its affinity for H+ declines, H+ dissociates and combines with HCO3- entering the red cell, chloride moves out (reverse chloride shift), free CO2 is regenerated and diffuses into the alveolus, together with CO2 released from carbaminohaemoglobin and dissolved CO2.
2. Link to oxygen unloading:
• Active tissues generate extra CO2, which raises H+ and lowers pH; this shifts the oxygen-haemoglobin curve to the right (Bohr effect) and promotes oxygen availability.
• CO2 loading releases hydrogen ions in the erythrocyte, and hydrogen ions promote O2 dissociation.
3. Distinctions:
• Chloride shift occurs in the tissues (HCO3- out, Cl- in); the reverse chloride shift occurs in the lungs (Cl- out, HCO3- in).
• Carbaminohaemoglobin carries about 30% of CO2 bound to the amino group of Hb; bicarbonate carries about 60%, formed through carbonic anhydrase.
questions.question:
Answer the following on the transport of carbon dioxide in the blood:
1. Describe carbon dioxide transport under these headings: the three chemical forms, the reactions in the red cell, the chloride shift, and the reverse reactions in the lungs.
2. Explain why active tissues unload more oxygen (the link between CO2 loading, hydrogen ions and oxygen dissociation).
3. Distinguish between the chloride shift and the reverse chloride shift, and between carbaminohaemoglobin and bicarbonate transport.

Answer the following on the functions of the autonomic nervous system:
1. Describe the functions of the autonomic nervous system under these headings: position in the nervous system, sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions, their opposing actions and the neurotransmitters.
2. State how the regulatory divisions relate to common disturbances of excess and deficiency.
3. Explain why a disturbance of autonomic function may affect a distant organ and cause a functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
1. Functions:
• The autonomic nervous system is the involuntary branch of the efferent peripheral system, consisting of motor nerves only, with sympathetic, parasympathetic (and enteric) divisions; somatic fibres supply skeletal muscle (voluntary) using acetylcholine.
• Sympathetic: the "fight-or-flight" system, responding to unusual stimuli and increasing activity (the "E" division: exercise, excitement, emergency, embarrassment); it controls internal organs in high-stress activity and increases heart rate.
• Parasympathetic: "housekeeping"; conserves energy and maintains daily functions (the "D" division: digestion, defecation, diuresis); it decreases heart rate and controls organs during normal activity.
• The two divisions have opposite effects on the same organs.
• Transmitters: norepinephrine from sympathetic endings and epinephrine from the adrenal medulla; acetylcholine from parasympathetic endings.
2. Disturbances:
• If the vagus nerve were cut the heart would lose its tone and heart rate would rise by about 25 beats per minute.
• High vagal activity produces the resting bradycardia of trained athletes.
3. Distant effects:
• Sympathetic stimulation causes vasoconstriction, which raises blood pressure and reduces flow in the constricted region.
• Sympathetic and parasympathetic action on the SA node changes heart rate and cardiac output.
• Autonomic centres in the hypothalamus and medulla link emotion and organ function.

questions.question:
Answer the following on the control of micturition:
1. Describe the micturition pathway: the bladder and sphincters as effectors, the sensory input from the bladder, the nervous control and the storage and voiding phases.
2. State the normal values (bladder capacity), the factors that alter the process and the compensatory mechanism that prevents reflux.
questions.answerText:
1. Micturition:
• Micturition (voiding) is the expulsion of urine from the bladder; it is regulated by the nervous system and by the muscles of the bladder and urethra.
• Filling phase: urine passes from the kidneys along the ureters, which enter the bladder obliquely; the detrusor muscle relaxes so the bladder distends; the internal urethral sphincter (smooth muscle) and the external sphincter (skeletal muscle) are both contracted.
• Voiding phase: once storage capacity is reached the detrusor, which had been relaxing, contracts, and the bladder and urethra work together.
• Afferent input: distension of the bladder wall is an interoceptive sensation; the parasympathetic division controls defecation and diuresis.
2. Values and compensation:
• The bladder stores about 350 to 400 ml of urine before it is expelled.
• The ureteral openings are not guarded by any sphincter; their oblique passage through the bladder wall prevents urine re-entering the ureters.

questions.question:
Answer the following on the functions of the respiratory tract and lungs:
1. Describe the functions of the air passages, lungs and pulmonary circulation under these headings: pathway of air, mucus and cilia (mucociliary escalator), alveoli and surfactant, and the respiratory muscles.
2. State how the components relate to common respiratory disorders (airway, lung tissue and lung circulation disease) and the factors that cause them.
3. Explain why a respiratory disturbance may affect a distant organ or system.
questions.answerText:
1. Functions:
• Air passages: nasal cavity, pharynx, larynx, trachea, primary bronchi, secondary (lobar), tertiary (segmental) bronchi, bronchioles, terminal bronchioles (each bronchiole gives rise to 50 to 80), respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts and alveolar sacs; they filter, moisten, warm and conduct air; the conducting portion ends at the terminal bronchioles.
• Mucus from goblet cells and submucosal glands humidifies and filters air; ciliated epithelium (about 200 cilia per cell beating 10 to 20 times per second, upward in the lower tract and downward in the nose) moves trapped particles, forming the mucociliary escalator.
• Alveoli: about 300 million, area about 70 m2, each in a basket of capillaries; type I cells permit rapid diffusion and type II cells (5%) secrete surfactant that prevents collapse; the pulmonary circulation and alveoli together form the respiratory membrane.
• Muscles: diaphragm and external intercostals (inspiration); internal intercostals and abdominal muscles in forced expiration.
2. Disorders:
• Respiratory disorders are irregular or abnormal functioning, physiological or anatomical, resulting from genetics, allergies, lifestyle (smoking), air pollution and infections.
• Categories: airway disease, lung tissue disease and lung circulation disease; examples are asthma, COPD, emphysema, occupational disorders, sinusitis and lung cancer.
• Restrictive diseases (fibrosis, sarcoidosis) reduce volumes; obstructive diseases (emphysema, chronic bronchitis, asthma) increase residual volume; emphysema destroys alveolar walls.
• Drug groups: bronchodilators, antihistamines, antitussives, decongestants, expectorants, leukotriene modifiers, lung surfactants and mucolytics.
3. Distant effects:
• Impaired gas exchange reduces oxygen delivery to all tissues and reduces CO2 removal, changing blood pH.
• Pulmonary embolism dangerously impairs the ability to obtain oxygen; left heart failure backs blood into the lungs as pulmonary oedema.
• Smoking raises carbon monoxide occupancy of haemoglobin to as much as 10%.

1. Mechanics of ventilation:
• Pleura: the visceral pleura covers the lungs and the parietal pleura the chest wall, continuous with each other and forming the pleural cavity; a film of slippery pleural fluid separates them.
• Purposes of the pleural cavity: reduces friction, creates a pressure gradient (pleural pressure is lower than atmospheric), and compartmentalises thoracic organs to prevent spread of infection.
• Pressures: when no air flows all pressures in the respiratory tree equal atmospheric pressure; alveolar pressure must fall slightly below atmospheric for air to flow in; intrapleural pressure is slightly negative.
• Inspiration: motor impulses from the medulla run along the phrenic nerves to the diaphragm and intercostal nerves to the external intercostals; the diaphragm contracts downward, increasing the vertical diameter, and the external intercostals raise the ribs up and out, increasing the anteroposterior and transverse diameters; intrapleural pressure becomes more negative, the lungs expand, alveolar pressure falls below atmospheric and air enters until the pressures equalise.
• Expiration: motor impulses decrease, the muscles relax, the chest becomes smaller, the stretched elastic tissue recoils and compresses the alveoli, alveolar pressure rises above atmospheric and air leaves; expiration is normally passive in quiet breathing but forced expiration uses the internal intercostals and abdominal muscles.
2. Vulnerability:
• The pleural cavity is normally a potential space; under pathological conditions it can fill with air or liquid.
• Continual suction of excess fluid into lymphatic channels maintains slight negative pressure that keeps the lungs from collapsing and held to the chest wall.
• Type II alveolar cells secrete pulmonary surfactant, which prevents collapse of the alveoli and bronchioles.
3. Distinctions:
• Alveolar pressure is the pressure within the alveoli; intrapleural pressure is the pressure of fluid in the space between the visceral and parietal pleura and is slightly negative.
• Inspiration is the active process (diaphragm and external intercostals contract, chest enlarges, alveolar pressure falls); expiration is the passive process in quiet breathing (muscles relax, recoil raises alveolar pressure).
questions.question:
Answer the following on the mechanics of pulmonary ventilation:
1. Describe the mechanism of breathing under these headings: pleura and pressures, muscles of inspiration and expiration, inhalation, exhalation and the thoracic diameters.
2. Explain the physiological basis of the vulnerability of the lungs when the pleural space or alveolar stability is disturbed.
3. Distinguish between alveolar pressure and intrapleural pressure, and between inspiration and expiration.

questions.answerText:
1. Pathway:
• It carries sensations that must be transmitted rapidly with high temporal and spatial fidelity: touch (light torch), vibration, position, movement against the skin and pressure, in large myelinated fibres.
• First-order neurones (medial branch) pass uninterrupted to the medulla and synapse in the dorsal column nuclei (cuneate and gracile); a lateral branch re-enters the dorsal column (15%), forms the spinocervical tract or the spinocerebellar tract, and many elicit local cord reflexes.
• Second-order neurones decussate and continue through the medial lemnisci to the thalamus; fibres from the trigeminal sensory nuclei join the medial lemniscus.
• Thalamus: all fibres end in the ventrobasal complex (ventral posterolateral nucleus for medial lemniscal fibres, ventral posteromedial for trigeminal fibres).
• Third-order neurones project to the postcentral gyrus (SSA 1); because the medial lemnisci cross, the left side of the body is represented on the right thalamus and the right side on the left.
2. Values and cortex:
• Velocity 30 to 120 m/s.
• SSA 1 (Brodmann 3, 1, 2) localises sensations, judges pressure, weight, shape and texture; the association areas (Brodmann 5 and 7) decipher the sensory information.
• Removal of the association areas causes amorphosynthesis; inability to judge shape is astereognosis.
3. Damage:
• Brown-Sequard syndrome (one half of the cord transected): motor function is blocked on the side of the lesion below it; kinesthetic, position and vibration sensations, light touch, discrete localisation and two-point discrimination are lost on the same side; pain, heat and cold are lost on the opposite side.
• Thalamic damage affects the relay of tactile information to the cortex.
questions.question:
Answer the following on the dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway:
1. Describe the pathway as a control system: receptors and the sensations carried, first-, second- and third-order neurones, the thalamic relay, the cortical target and the branches of the first-order fibre.
2. State the conduction velocity, the functions of the somatic sensory cortex and the effects of removing the association areas.
3. Explain the physiological basis of the deficits when the pathway is damaged (including hemisection of the cord).

questions.answerText:
1. Brain waves:
• Origin: synchronised electrical pulses from masses of neurons communicating with each other; detected by scalp sensors with an EEG (electroencephalograph); speed is measured in Hertz.
• Gamma 40 to 100 Hz (highest): binding of senses, cognition, information processing, learning, perception, REM sleep.
• Beta 12 to 40 Hz (high, low amplitude): conscious focus, memory, problem solving; increased by caffeine and stimulants.
• Alpha 8 to 12 Hz (moderate): relaxation; bridges conscious and subconscious mind; alpha blocking occurs when stressed.
• Theta 4 to 8 Hz (slow): creativity, emotional connection, intuition, restorative sleep.
• Delta 0 to 4 Hz (slowest): deep restorative sleep, immune system, natural healing; commonest in infants and children, and less with age.
• All five appear during waking but one is dominant according to the state of consciousness.
2. Excess and deficiency:
• Gamma: too much gives anxiety, high arousal, stress; too little gives ADHD, depression, learning disabilities.
• Beta: too much gives anxiety, stress, inability to relax; too little gives ADHD, daydreaming, depression, poor cognition.
• Alpha: too much gives daydreaming and inability to focus; too little gives anxiety, high stress, insomnia, OCD.
• Theta: too much gives ADHD, depression, hyperactivity, impulsivity; too little gives anxiety, poor emotional awareness, stress.
• Delta: too much gives brain injuries, learning problems, inability to think, severe ADHD; too little gives inability to rejuvenate, poor sleep.
3. Wider effects:
• The ability to move flexibly through frequencies plays a large role in managing stress, focusing and sleeping well.
• Delta activity is involved in unconscious bodily functions such as regulating heart beat and digestion, so abnormal delta may affect body function and learning.
• No single band is better than the others; each serves a purpose.
questions.question:
Answer the following on brain waves and the EEG:
1. Describe brain waves under these headings: origin, detection by EEG, and the five bands (gamma, beta, alpha, theta, delta) with their frequency ranges and optimal functions.
2. State how excess and deficiency of each band relate to common disorders.
3. Explain why a disturbance of brain wave production may affect wider mental and bodily function.

questions.answerText:
1. Functions:
• The cerebrum (telencephalon) is the largest part of the brain, with the cortex divided into two hemispheres and subcortical structures such as the hippocampus, basal ganglia and olfactory bulb.
• The hemispheres are joined by the corpus callosum; each controls the opposite side of the body; the left hemisphere controls speech, comprehension, arithmetic and writing and the right creativity, spatial ability, artistic and musical skills; the left is dominant for hand use and language in about 92% of people.
• Lobes: frontal (attention, reward, short-term memory, motivation, planning), temporal (sensory input with emotional meaning, long-term memory, language perception), parietal (touch, spatial awareness, navigation, language) and occipital (visual processing).
• Somatosensory cortex: sensory signals from all modalities end in the cortex behind the central sulcus; SSA 1 localises sensations and judges pressure, weight, shape and texture; association areas 5 and 7 interpret them.
• Prefrontal and orbital frontal cortex: judgment, insight, motivation, mood and conditioned emotional reactions.
2. Pathologies:
• Damage to the prefrontal area causes difficulty with abstract reasoning, judgment, mood and puzzle solving, and tactless behaviour; alcohol strongly affects it; depression is associated with increased activity in the medial frontal regions.
• Inability to judge shapes is astereognosis; removal of the association areas causes amorphosynthesis.
• Stroke (interruption of blood supply), Alzheimer's disease and tumours also disturb cortical function.
3. Distant effects:
• Because each hemisphere controls the opposite side, a lesion affects the contralateral body.
• A cerebrovascular accident from a ruptured vessel kills the tissue supplied, with loss of some functions or death.
questions.question:
Answer the following on the functions of the cerebral cortex:
1. Describe the functions of the cerebrum under these headings: hemispheres and corpus callosum, lobes and their functions, somatosensory areas and the limbic (prefrontal) cortex.
2. State how regions of the cortex relate to common pathologies of excess and deficiency of function.
3. Explain why a cortical lesion may cause a functional deficit in a distant part of the body.

questions.answerText:
1. Pain modulation:
• The synaptic junctions between nociceptor fibres and dorsal horn cells are sites of plasticity where pain impulses can be modified; the dorsal horn is referred to as a gate.
• The analgesia system is the brain's capability to suppress input of pain signals; it consists of the periaqueductal grey and periventricular areas of the mesencephalon and upper pons, which project to the raphe magnus nucleus (lower pons and upper medulla) and the nucleus reticularis paragigantocellularis, which project to a pain inhibitory complex in the dorsal horns; other connections are the periventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus and the medial forebrain bundle.
• Most fibres secrete enkephalins and serotonin; painful stimulation releases substance P from afferent fibres, and this release is blocked by the descending system using axo-axonic synapses on the afferent neurone.
2. Modifiers and compensation:
• Raise pain: bradykinin, serotonin, histamine, K+, acetylcholine and substance P; tissue damage.
• Compensation: the opiate system; morphine-like agents cause analgesia when injected into any part of the analgesia system by activating opiate receptors; the opiate substances include beta-endorphin, met-enkephalin, leu-enkephalin and dynorphin.
3. Failure:
• Facilitation of transmission from a cord or thalamic lesion causes secondary hyperalgesia, and sensitised nociceptors cause primary hyperalgesia.
questions.question:
Answer the following on pain modulation (gating and the analgesia system):
1. Describe the pain modulation system as a control pathway: the dorsal horn gate, the brain and brainstem components of the analgesia system, the transmitters and the feedback onto the primary afferent.
2. State the factors that raise pain and the compensatory response, including the role of the opiate system.
3. Explain the physiological basis of the effects when the pathway fails or is overactive.

Answer the following on sensory receptors and the sensory pathway:
1. Describe the sensory system as a control pathway: the receptor as transducer, classes of receptors, the three-neuron chain to the cortex and the relay in the thalamus.
2. State the fibre and receptor properties (adaptation, receptive field, spot density) and the factors that alter receptor response.
3. Explain the physiological basis of the signs when the sensory pathway is damaged.
questions.answerText:
1. Sensory pathway:
• Receptors are biological transducers converting mechanical, thermal or other energy into electrical potentials and action potentials; structurally a receptor is a specialised dendritic ending, often encapsulated.
• General senses: exteroceptive, proprioceptive and interoceptive (for example bladder distension); special senses: sight, hearing, taste, smell, equilibrium.
• Classes by stimulus: mechanoreceptors (Merkel's discs, Meissner's, Pacinian and Ruffini corpuscles, hair follicle plexus), thermoreceptors (cold and warm), nociceptors (free endings), electromagnetic receptors (rods and cones) and chemoreceptors (taste, smell, oxygen, osmolality); teloceptors detect distant stimuli.
• Chain: first-order neuron from the receptor to the spinal cord (or medulla), second-order neuron to the thalamus, third-order neuron to the sensory cortex; all senses relay in the thalamus except olfaction.
2. Properties and modifiers:
• Fast-adapting afferents end in Meissner's corpuscles (FA1) and Pacinian corpuscles (FA2); slow-adapting afferents end in Merkel's discs (SA1) and Ruffini endings (SA2); type I units have small, well-defined receptive fields and type II wider fields.
• Cold spots are 4 to 10 times more numerous than warm spots (lips 15 to 25, fingers 3 to 5, trunk about 1 per cm2).
• Merkel's discs signal steady touch and texture, Meissner's corpuscles light touch and low-frequency vibration, Pacinian corpuscles pressure and vibration, Ruffini endings continuous deformation.
3. Damage:
• Inability to judge shape (astereognosis) and amorphosynthesis follow cortical and association area damage.
• Brown-Sequard syndrome: loss of position, vibration and light touch on the same side and of pain, heat and cold on the opposite side.

questions.question:
Answer the following on the control of heart rate:
1. Describe the control system for heart rate: receptors, afferent input, integrating centre, efferent pathway, effector and feedback, including the cellular actions of the transmitters on the pacemaker cells.
2. State the normal values for heart rate, stroke volume and cardiac output, the factors that raise or lower heart rate, and the compensatory response during exercise.
3. Explain the physiological basis of the changes seen when the autonomic supply to the heart fails or is removed.
questions.answerText:
1. Control of heart rate:
• Effector: the SA node sets the rhythm; without neural influences the heart beats according to the SA node rhythm, but sympathetic and parasympathetic fibres are continuously active and modify the rate of spontaneous depolarisation.
• Receptors and afferent input: pressure receptors (baroreceptors) in the aorta and carotid arteries give sensory feedback; higher brain centres also act on the centre.
• Integrating centre: the cardiac control centre (CCC) in the medulla oblongata coordinates autonomic activity of the heart.
• Efferent pathway: the sympathetic cardioacceleratory centre stimulates the heart and the parasympathetic cardioinhibitory centre (vagus) inhibits it.
• Sympathetic action: norepinephrine (sympathetic endings) and epinephrine (adrenal medulla) open Na+ and Ca2+ channels in SA node cells, increasing the pacemaker potential and firing rate.
• Parasympathetic action: acetylcholine opens K+ channels, hyperpolarising the SA node and slowing its firing.
• Feedback: the pace at any time is the net effect of these antagonistic influences; mechanisms that raise the rate are positive chronotropic and those that lower it are negative chronotropic; autonomic innervation of the SA node is the major means of regulating heart rate.
2. Normal values, modifiers and compensation:
• Normal values: resting heart rate about 70 beats per minute (the SA node generates about 75 impulses per minute); stroke volume about 70 to 80 ml per beat; cardiac output = SV x HR, for example 75 ml x 70 = 5,250 ml/min, about 5 L/min (normal range 4 to 6 L/min).
• Raise heart rate: sympathetic stimulation (stress, anxiety, excitement, exercise), norepinephrine, epinephrine, thyroxine, caffeine (positive chronotropic).
• Lower heart rate: acetylcholine and vagal tone, sedatives (negative chronotropic); the resting bradycardia of endurance-trained athletes is largely due to high vagus nerve activity.
• Compensation in exercise: heart rate rises first through decreased vagal inhibition of the SA node, then further through increased sympathetic stimulation; the sympatho-adrenal effect on cardiac output acts through a positive chronotropic effect on heart rate and a positive inotropic effect on contractility; intra- and extracellular ion concentrations must be maintained for normal heart function.
3. Basis of changes when the pathway fails:
• The parasympathetic (vagal) influence dominates at rest and produces vagal tone; if the vagus nerve were cut the heart would lose its tone and the heart rate would increase by about 25 beats per minute.
• In the complete absence of neural influences the SA node keeps the heart beating at its own rhythm because the conducting cells are self-exciting (automaticity).
• Loss of the sympathetic drive would remove the positive chronotropic and inotropic effects that increase cardiac output in exercise.

questions.question:
Answer the following on lung volumes and capacities:
1. Describe lung volumes and capacities under these headings: spirometry, the four volumes, the four capacities, minute and alveolar ventilation, and dead space.
2. Explain how restrictive and obstructive lung diseases alter the volumes and capacities.
3. Distinguish between anatomical and physiological dead space, and between pulmonary ventilation and alveolar ventilation.
questions.answerText:
1. Volumes and capacities:
• Spirometry measures air volumes and capacities; a volume is one phase of the respiratory cycle and a capacity is the sum of two or more volumes.
• Tidal volume about 500 ml; inspiratory reserve volume about 3000 ml; expiratory reserve volume about 1100 ml; residual volume about 1200 ml.
• Inspiratory capacity = TV + IRV = 3500 ml; vital capacity = TV + IRV + ERV = 4600 ml; functional residual capacity = RV + ERV = 2300 ml; total lung capacity = RV + ERV + TV + IRV = 5800 ml.
• Pulmonary ventilation = respiratory rate x tidal volume = 12 x 500 = 6000 ml/min; alveolar ventilation = (tidal volume - dead space) x respiratory rate = (500 - 150) x 12 per minute.
• All volumes and capacities are about 20 to 25% less in women than in men and greater in athletic persons than in small asthenic persons.
2. Disease patterns:
• Restrictive disease makes it harder to get air in: decreased VC, TLC, RV and FRC; examples are fibrosis, sarcoidosis, muscular diseases and chest wall deformities.
• Obstructive disease makes it harder to get air out: decreased VC but increased TLC, RV and FRC; examples are emphysema, chronic bronchitis and asthma.
3. Distinctions:
• Anatomical dead space is the volume of all passageways from the nose to the terminal bronchiole; physiological dead space adds non-functioning and poorly perfused alveoli, and in normal lungs the two are equal.
• Pulmonary ventilation is the total air moved per minute; alveolar ventilation is the air reaching the gas exchange areas per minute, that is with the dead space subtracted.

1. Control of filtration:
• Filtration barrier: a substance must pass through the pores between glomerular capillary endothelial cells, an acellular basement membrane and the filtration slits between the podocyte foot processes; small electrolytes and glucose are freely filtered, but the negatively charged basement membrane repels negatively charged molecules such as albumin.
• Sensing and feedback: a rise in arterial pressure raises glomerular capillary pressure and GFR, which raises tubular flow; macula densa cells are stimulated to release chemicals that cause afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction, reducing flow into the glomerulus and returning capillary pressure and GFR to normal (autoregulation).
• Effectors: vasodilators (nitric oxide, bradykinin, prostacyclin) dilate the afferent arteriole and raise volume and pressure entering the glomerulus; vasoconstrictors (epinephrine, norepinephrine, angiotensin II) do the reverse.
2. Values and modifiers:
• About 20% of plasma entering the kidney is filtered (80% leaves by the efferent arteriole); renal plasma flow is 625 ml/min and GFR 125 ml/min; about 99% of the filtrate is reabsorbed and urine flow is about 1 ml/min.
• Raise GFR: higher arterial pressure, higher glomerular hydrostatic pressure, afferent dilation; lower GFR: afferent vasoconstriction.
• GFR is measured as clearance of inulin, which is freely filtered and neither reabsorbed nor secreted; PAH clearance measures total renal blood flow because PAH is cleared by filtration and secretion.
3. Disturbance:
• GFR reflects the efficiency of the kidney in filtration and is an index of its functionality.
questions.question:
Answer the following on the control of glomerular filtration:
1. Describe the control system for glomerular filtration: the filtration barrier, the receptor (macula densa), the effector (afferent arteriole), vasoactive substances and feedback.
2. State the normal values (renal plasma flow, GFR, fraction filtered, reabsorbed, urine flow), the factors that raise or lower GFR and the compensatory response.
3. Explain the physiological basis of the changes when filtration control is disturbed.

courses.title: Systemic Toxicology

questions.explanation: Solanine, a glycoalkaloid, increases in potato tubers exposed to light or stored improperly, correlating with green coloration. This cholinesterase inhibitor causes gastrointestinal and neurological symptoms. Peeling removes most solanine concentrated near the skin. Proper storage in cool, dark conditions minimizes production.
questions.question: Naturally occurring solanine in potatoes increases with:

questions.explanation: Liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry offers exceptional sensitivity and specificity, allowing simultaneous detection and quantification of numerous structurally diverse drugs in complex biological matrices. This capability surpasses the more limited scope of single-analyte immunoassays. Despite requiring careful sample preparation and calibration, its analytical power makes it a gold standard in forensic and clinical toxicology.
questions.question: A laboratory adopts liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry for quantifying multiple drugs simultaneously in a single blood sample. The primary advantage of this technique is its:
options: High sensitivity and specificity for multiple analytes

questions.question: A patient develops predictable, dose-related sedation after taking a prescribed antihistamine at the recommended dose. This adverse reaction is best classified as:
questions.explanation: Type A adverse reactions are dose-dependent, predictable from the drug's known pharmacology, and generally reversible on dose reduction. This contrasts with Type B reactions, which are unpredictable, dose-independent, and often immune-mediated. Type A reactions account for the majority of clinically observed adverse drug events.

Poison centers provide expert guidance for healthcare professionals and public, available 24/7 free of charge. Consultation benefits unfamiliar scenarios, unusual exposures, or severity assessment. Centers track exposures contributing to surveillance. Pharmacists serve as poison information specialists in many centers, applying specialized toxicology knowledge.
questions.question: Poison control center consultation should occur when:

questions.explanation: The area under the concentration-time curve represents total systemic drug exposure over time and is the primary parameter used to compare bioavailability between formulations. Peak concentration and time to peak reflect the rate of absorption rather than total exposure. Regulatory bioequivalence standards rely heavily on comparing this AUC parameter between test and reference products.
questions.question: A pharmacokinetic report shows the total exposure of a drug over time after a single dose, used to compare bioavailability between two formulations. This measure is the:

questions.explanation: Dose-response evaluation quantifies the relationship between the amount of exposure and the probability of adverse effects occurring. This assessment generates dose-response curves that define threshold levels, slopes, and maximum responses. Understanding this relationship is fundamental for setting safe exposure limits and regulatory standards.
questions.question: A toxicologist examining the relationship between exposure magnitude and health effect probability is conducting:
Non-genotoxic carcinogens act primarily through:
questions.explanation: Non-genotoxic carcinogens cause cancer through mechanisms not involving direct DNA damage, such as hormonal effects, immunosuppression, or chronic inflammation. These agents may alter gene expression, signal transduction, or cellular proliferation without initially damaging DNA. Identifying non-genotoxic mechanisms requires different testing strategies than for genotoxic carcinogens.

Certain local anesthetics like benzocaine can oxidize hemoglobin to methemoglobin, which cannot carry oxygen effectively and produces a characteristic blue-gray skin and mucosal discoloration. This differs from the cherry-red appearance of carbon monoxide poisoning. Methylene blue is the specific antidote for symptomatic methemoglobinemia.
questions.question: A patient develops blue-gray discoloration of the skin after using a topical anesthetic spray excessively before a medical procedure. This finding should raise suspicion for:

options: Confined mainly to the vascular space
questions.explanation: A large volume of distribution means most of the drug resides in tissues rather than plasma, so removing blood-compartment drug through dialysis or diuresis achieves little overall reduction. Enhanced elimination techniques work best for toxins largely confined to the vascular and extracellular space. This pharmacokinetic property must be assessed before selecting an elimination strategy.
questions.question: A patient with severe phenobarbital poisoning is treated with a toxin that has a large volume of distribution, making enhanced elimination techniques of limited benefit. This limitation exists because the drug is:

A forensic laboratory analyzing blood alcohol content adds a specific chemical to the collection tube to prevent ongoing microbial fermentation from artificially raising ethanol levels. This preservative is:
questions.explanation: Sodium fluoride inhibits microbial and enzymatic activity that could generate ethanol postmortem or during storage, preserving the accuracy of blood alcohol measurements. Anticoagulants like heparin or EDTA prevent clotting but do not address this fermentation concern. Proper preservative selection is essential to avoid falsely elevated or altered alcohol results.

questions.question: Novel psychoactive substances (NPS) pose challenges because they:
questions.explanation: NPS constantly change chemically to circumvent legal controls, creating regulatory whack-a-mole scenarios. Limited toxicology data and unpredictable effects complicate medical management. Internet availability and deceptive marketing increase use. Broad legislative approaches and harm reduction strategies address this evolving threat.

AUC quantifies total systemic drug exposure over time, integrating both concentration and duration. This parameter is fundamental for bioequivalence assessment and dose-response relationships. AUC increases proportionally with dose for drugs exhibiting linear pharmacokinetics and reflects both extent of absorption and elimination rate.
questions.question: The area under the plasma concentration-time curve (AUC) represents:
A pathologist describes a sequence in which normal cells acquire mutations, escape growth control, and eventually invade surrounding tissue. This overall process is termed:
questions.explanation: Carcinogenesis describes the multistep transformation of normal cells into malignant ones through initiation, promotion and progression. It involves accumulated genetic and epigenetic changes conferring uncontrolled growth. This differs from apoptosis and senescence, which are regulated cell fate processes rather than malignant transformation.

questions.question: Confirmatory testing in forensic toxicology typically employs:
questions.explanation: Mass spectrometry provides definitive identification through unique molecular fragmentation patterns and mass-to-charge ratios. Coupled with chromatography (GC-MS or LC-MS), this technique offers unparalleled specificity. Confirmatory testing using different analytical principles from screening ensures result reliability.

questions.question: A patient recovering from an accidental pesticide poisoning is being discharged. Appropriate follow-up planning should specifically address:
questions.explanation: Follow-up after poisoning should focus on identifying and correcting the circumstances that led to exposure, such as improper storage or occupational practices, to prevent recurrence. This is distinct from unnecessary prolonged hospitalization or treatments not indicated by the specific poisoning. Education tailored to the exposure circumstance is central to secondary prevention.

Nanoscale materials exhibit unique physicochemical properties including high surface area-to-volume ratios, altered reactivity, and enhanced cellular uptake. These characteristics create distinct toxicological profiles from bulk material. Size, shape, surface chemistry, and agglomeration state influence biological effects. Standardized testing approaches are still developing.
questions.question: Toxicology of nanomaterials differs from bulk materials due to:
A factory worker exposed to a mutagen develops a mutation in a testicular germ cell that is later passed to his child. This type of mutation is termed:
questions.explanation: Mutations arising in sperm or egg cells can be transmitted to offspring, unlike somatic mutations confined to the exposed individual. This heritability is the defining feature distinguishing germline from somatic genotoxic events. Such mutations raise unique regulatory and ethical concerns.

Obesity increases volume of distribution for lipophilic drugs while having variable effects on hydrophilic drugs. Changes in hepatic blood flow, enzyme activity, and protein binding affect metabolism. Dosing strategies must consider these alterations, with some drugs dosed by total body weight, others by ideal or adjusted body weight.
questions.question: Obesity alters drug pharmacokinetics primarily through:

questions.explanation: Volume of distribution (Vd) represents the theoretical volume required to contain total drug amount at plasma concentration. Large Vd indicates extensive tissue distribution; small Vd suggests plasma/extracellular confinement. This parameter guides loading dose calculations and predicts dialyzability. Vd changes don't reflect actual anatomical volumes.
questions.question: The volume of distribution indicates:

options: Limited access to care and inadequate training
questions.explanation: Developing countries experience disproportionate pesticide poisoning due to limited regulation enforcement, inadequate training, unavailable protective equipment, hazardous storage practices, and limited medical care access. Agricultural workers, often women and children, face greatest risk. WHO-recommended interventions include safer pesticides, improved storage, and community education.
questions.question: The burden of pesticide poisoning in developing countries is increased by:

questions.explanation: Occupational asthma develops through workplace sensitization or irritant exposure, improving away from work and worsening upon return. Diagnosis requires clinical correlation with workplace exposure history and objective testing. Prevention through exposure elimination is paramount as continued exposure causes progression. Compensation and job modification considerations arise.
questions.question: Occupational asthma differs from other asthma by:

A patient taking a large dose of phenytoin shows a constant amount of drug eliminated per hour regardless of blood concentration, unlike most drugs that show proportional elimination. This elimination pattern is called:
questions.explanation: Zero-order elimination occurs when metabolic pathways become saturated, resulting in a constant amount of drug eliminated per unit time regardless of concentration, unlike first-order kinetics where a constant fraction is eliminated. This saturation can lead to disproportionate increases in blood levels with small dose increases. Phenytoin at higher doses classically exhibits this saturable elimination pattern.

questions.question: Long-term cannabis use in adolescents may affect:
questions.explanation: Adolescent cannabis use during critical neurodevelopmental periods may impair executive function, memory, and IQ, with effects potentially persisting after cessation. The developing brain's heightened cannabinoid receptor expression increases vulnerability. Heavy use associates with increased mental health problems. Legalization efforts must address youth access and education.

questions.question: Workplace drug testing programs primarily use which specimen?
questions.explanation: Urine testing dominates workplace programs due to established cutoffs, longer detection windows than blood, and large sample volumes for comprehensive screening. Federal guidelines specify urine testing procedures, cutoff concentrations, and quality control requirements. The non-invasive collection process facilitates large-scale testing programs.

questions.question: A patient receiving cisplatin chemotherapy develops rising creatinine with magnesium wasting, most pronounced in the distal nephron segments. This nephrotoxic pattern primarily reflects:
questions.explanation: Cisplatin characteristically damages the distal tubule and thick ascending limb, producing magnesium and potassium wasting alongside reduced glomerular filtration. This distal pattern differs from the classic proximal tubular injury caused by aminoglycosides. Adequate hydration reduces the severity of cisplatin nephrotoxicity.

Because hair grows at a relatively constant rate, sequential segmental analysis can reconstruct an approximate timeline of drug exposure over weeks to months. It is not useful for determining acute toxic blood concentrations or the precise cause of death. This chronological utility makes hair testing valuable in cases of suspected chronic or repeated exposure.
questions.question: A forensic toxicologist analyzes segments of a deceased person's hair to estimate the approximate timing of drug use over recent months. Hair analysis is primarily useful for establishing:

questions.explanation: Alkaline diuresis promotes renal elimination of weak acids like salicylates by ion trapping in alkaline urine. Maintaining urine pH above 8 through sodium bicarbonate administration enhances salicylate excretion significantly. This technique requires careful monitoring to prevent fluid overload and electrolyte disturbances.
questions.question: Alkaline diuresis enhances elimination of:

questions.explanation: Toxicology evolves continually with new drugs, emerging substances, and updated treatment approaches. Continuing education maintains competence, improves patient care, and fulfills professional obligations. Sources include literature, conferences, online modules, and professional organizations. Lifelong learning characterizes professional excellence.
questions.question: Continuing education in toxicology for pharmacists is:

questions.explanation: Aging is associated with declining hepatic blood flow and enzyme activity along with reduced glomerular filtration, both slowing drug clearance and prolonging exposure. Body composition changes, such as increased fat and decreased lean mass, further alter drug distribution. These combined physiological changes necessitate dose adjustment in elderly patients.
questions.question: An elderly patient develops toxicity on a medication dose that is well tolerated by younger adults. This increased susceptibility in the elderly is best explained by:

questions.explanation: Propofol infusion can cause a distinctive green discoloration of urine due to its phenolic metabolites, a benign but recognizable finding. This differs from rifampicin, which produces orange-red discoloration of body fluids. Recognizing characteristic color changes can provide rapid diagnostic clues in poisoning evaluation.
questions.question: A patient's urine turns green after a suspected medication overdose, prompting concern for a specific ingested agent. This discoloration is most classically associated with:

questions.explanation: Informal e-waste recycling exposes workers (often in developing countries) to lead, cadmium, mercury, brominated flame retardants, and other toxicants through burning, acid treatment, and dismantling. Children frequently work in or near these operations. Proper e-waste management through take-back programs and formal recycling protects health and environment.
options: Heavy metals and persistent organic pollutant exposure
questions.question: E-waste recycling poses toxicological concerns due to:

questions.explanation: Phenytoin is highly protein-bound, meaning little free drug circulates in a form accessible to dialysis membranes, limiting the effectiveness of enhanced elimination. Toxins amenable to dialysis are typically small, water-soluble, and weakly protein-bound. This pharmacokinetic principle guides selection of appropriate elimination interventions.
questions.question: A patient with severe phenytoin toxicity is not offered hemodialysis despite dangerous serum levels. This decision reflects that enhanced elimination techniques are most beneficial for toxins with:

questions.explanation: Limb malformation from prenatal exposure reflects a teratogenic effect on the developing embryo, distinct from mutation or cancer induction. This event led to mandatory reproductive and developmental toxicity testing before drug approval. Teratogenicity testing specifically evaluates structural and functional fetal harm.
questions.question: A drug approved without adequate animal reproductive studies caused severe limb malformations when taken by pregnant women. This historical lesson primarily established the need to test new drugs for:
Lead poisoning in children commonly presents with:
questions.explanation: Lead causes microcytic anemia through heme synthesis interference and irreversible neurodevelopmental effects, even at low levels. No safe blood lead level exists. Sources include deteriorating lead paint, contaminated soil, and water from lead pipes. Treatment includes lead removal from environment and chelation for severe cases.

questions.question: Product tampering detection and reporting involves:
questions.explanation: Pharmacists must inspect products for tampering evidence, maintaining vigilance throughout distribution. Detecting tampering requires regulatory notification, product removal, and public warning. The 1982 Tylenol cyanide murders transformed packaging with tamper-evident seals. Remaining alert protects public health.

Drugs or metabolites excreted in bile may be deconjugated by intestinal bacteria and reabsorbed, creating secondary concentration peaks. This recycling prolongs elimination half-life and drug effects. Multiple-dose activated charcoal interrupts this cycle for certain toxins. Enterohepatic circulation complicates pharmacokinetic predictions.
questions.question: Enterohepatic recirculation prolongs drug exposure through:

questions.explanation: Toxicovigilance involves systematic observation, evaluation, and reporting of toxic phenomena to guide preventive actions. These surveillance systems identify emerging problems, track trends, and evaluate intervention effectiveness. Data generated informs policy decisions and targeted prevention programs.
questions.question: Toxicovigilance systems primarily:
Polymorphism of N-acetyl transferase 2 affects metabolism of:
questions.explanation: NAT2 genetic polymorphism creates slow and rapid acetylator phenotypes affecting isoniazid metabolism and toxicity risk. Slow acetylators accumulate isoniazid, increasing peripheral neuropathy risk, while rapid acetylators may have treatment failure. Genotype-guided dosing optimizes efficacy while minimizing adverse effects.

questions.question: Enzyme induction typically requires:
questions.explanation: Enzyme induction increases metabolic capacity through enhanced enzyme synthesis, requiring days to weeks for full effect and similar time for reversal after discontinuation. This delayed response complicates clinical management. Induction reduces concentrations of affected drugs, risking therapeutic failure or requiring dose adjustments.

questions.question: Bioaccumulation in the food chain is most significant for:
questions.explanation: Lipophilic, persistent compounds like DDT and mercury bioaccumulate through food chains, reaching toxic concentrations in top predators including humans. These substances resist environmental degradation and preferentially partition into fatty tissues. Biomagnification results in exposures far exceeding environmental concentrations.

Tyramine, normally metabolized by MAO, accumulates when MAO is inhibited, causing norepinephrine release and hypertensive crisis. Aged cheeses, cured meats, and fermented foods contain high tyramine. Dietary restrictions prevent reactions. Modern selective MAO-B inhibitors pose less risk. Treatment involves blood pressure control.
questions.question: A patient taking MAO inhibitors who eats aged cheese develops hypertensive crisis due to:

questions.explanation: This presentation reflects an anticholinergic toxidrome, and physostigmine, a cholinesterase inhibitor, can reverse severe central anticholinergic toxicity when used cautiously. Atropine would worsen anticholinergic symptoms rather than treat them, making it an incorrect choice here. Physostigmine use requires careful monitoring due to risk of bradycardia and seizures.
questions.question: A patient with altered mental status is found to have dilated pupils, dry flushed skin, and urinary retention after ingesting an unknown substance. The most appropriate specific treatment, if severe, is:

questions.explanation: Grapefruit juice contains furanocoumarins that irreversibly inhibit intestinal CYP3A4, increasing bioavailability of susceptible drugs. This interaction can produce significantly elevated drug concentrations and enhanced effects lasting up to 24 hours. Patients should avoid grapefruit products when taking affected medications like calcium channel blockers.
questions.question: Grapefruit juice interactions with drugs primarily involve inhibition of:
Polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) in food result from:
questions.explanation: PCBs, banned industrial chemicals, persist in the environment, bioaccumulating in fatty tissues of fish and animals. Human exposure occurs primarily through contaminated fish, meat, and dairy. These endocrine disruptors and probable carcinogens raise developmental toxicity concerns. Fish advisories guide consumption to minimize exposure while maintaining nutritional benefits.

questions.question: Reproductive hazards in the workplace can affect:
questions.explanation: Reproductive toxicants may impair fertility, cause developmental toxicity, or affect sexual function in either sex. Pregnancy discrimination laws don't prevent informed reproductive hazard communication. Both prospective parents require protection. Some hazards preferentially affect one sex based on exposure patterns or biological susceptibility.

questions.question: A patient with fever, muscle rigidity, and elevated CK after MDMA use likely has:
questions.explanation: MDMA causes serotonin syndrome through massive serotonin release and reuptake inhibition. Features include hyperthermia, muscle rigidity, altered mental status, autonomic instability, and potentially fatal complications like rhabdomyolysis and disseminated intravascular coagulation. Treatment involves benzodiazepines, aggressive cooling, and supportive care. Cyproheptadine provides specific serotonin antagonism.

Reproductive toxicity encompasses effects on adult fertility, embryo-fetal development, and postnatal development including lactation and offspring maturation. These multigenerational studies identify potential hazards at all reproductive life stages. Timing of exposure during reproduction critically influences outcomes observed.
questions.question: The primary purpose of reproductive toxicity studies is to identify effects on:
A resident quotes Paracelsus while counselling a patient anxious about trace pesticide residues in food. The most accurate application of this principle is that:
questions.explanation: The dose-makes-the-poison principle means that quantity of exposure, not mere presence of a chemical, determines harm. Trace residues at very low doses may fall below any threshold of concern. This principle underlies the setting of acceptable daily intakes.
options: Toxicity depends on the amount absorbed
Any exposure to a toxin is harmful
Toxicity is fixed regardless of dose

questions.question: The concept of "toxicant-induced loss of tolerance" (TILT) suggests:
questions.explanation: TILT describes development of heightened sensitivity to diverse chemicals after acute or chronic toxic exposure. Affected individuals report symptoms from low-level exposures tolerated by most people. While controversial, TILT represents an important clinical observation requiring further research to elucidate mechanisms.

questions.question: Probenecid enhances penicillin activity by:
questions.explanation: Probenecid competitively inhibits active tubular secretion of penicillin in renal proximal tubules, prolonging penicillin half-life. This beneficial interaction was historically exploited to conserve expensive penicillin supplies. Understanding renal transport mechanisms enables prediction and management of similar interactions.

Acceptable daily intake specifically applies to food additives and residues, expressing a safe lifetime daily consumption level. It is derived similarly to the reference dose but is the term conventionally used in food regulatory contexts. It differs from maximum residue limits, which regulate concentration in a specific food commodity.
questions.question: A food safety panel sets the maximum amount of a preservative that can be consumed daily over a lifetime without appreciable health risk. This value for food additives is known as the:
A pharmacist is developing poison prevention materials for caregivers with limited health literacy. The most effective approach for this audience is to use:
questions.explanation: Effective health communication for low-literacy audiences relies on simple language, pictures, and clear actionable steps rather than technical jargon or dense text. Materials that assume prior medical knowledge often fail to achieve behavior change in this population. Visual, concrete messaging improves comprehension and retention of poison prevention advice.
options: Simple visual aids and plain language

questions.question: Thalidomide-induced phocomelia demonstrates the importance of testing for:
questions.explanation: The thalidomide tragedy highlighted the critical need for teratogenicity testing before drug approval. Phocomelia, characterized by severe limb malformations, occurred when thalidomide was taken during critical periods of embryonic development. This disaster revolutionized drug safety testing and regulatory requirements for developmental toxicity assessment.

questions.question: Pediatric drug dosing differs from adults primarily due to:
questions.explanation: Children exhibit age-dependent changes in absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion affecting drug disposition. Body composition, organ maturation, and enzymatic activity vary across pediatric age groups. Simple weight-based dosing may be inadequate; age-appropriate calculations or body surface area adjustments improve accuracy.

While both disciplines use similar analytical techniques, forensic toxicology serves legal purposes rather than patient care. Results are used in criminal investigations, workplace compliance, and cause of death determination rather than treatment decisions. Forensic toxicologists must maintain chain of custody and testify in legal proceedings.
questions.question: Forensic toxicology differs from clinical toxicology primarily in:

questions.explanation: Beta-blocker overdose can impair glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, leading to hypoglycemia, whereas calcium channel blocker toxicity more classically causes hyperglycemia due to impaired insulin release. Both classes cause bradycardia and hypotension, making this glucose difference a useful distinguishing clinical clue. Glucagon is a specific therapeutic option that helps bypass the blocked beta-receptor in this poisoning.
questions.question: A patient with beta-blocker overdose presents with profound bradycardia and hypotension resistant to standard fluid resuscitation. The characteristic hemodynamic feature that helps distinguish this from calcium channel blocker overdose is that beta-blocker toxicity commonly causes:

questions.explanation: MSDS provide essential hazard communication including chemical properties, health effects, exposure controls, and emergency procedures. These documents enable safe handling, storage, and emergency response. Regulatory requirements mandate MSDS availability to all potentially exposed workers.
questions.question: Material Safety Data Sheets (MSDS) must include information on:
A smoker's cyanide poisoning is more likely because:
questions.explanation: Tobacco smoke contains cyanide, causing chronic low-level exposure with potential tolerance. However, this doesn't protect against acute poisoning. Baseline cyanide levels may be elevated. Treatment remains the same. Smoking's role in fire deaths includes both carbon monoxide and cyanide from synthetic material combustion.

questions.question: A pregnant patient asks about medication safety. The appropriate response includes:
questions.explanation: Comprehensive counseling addresses known risks, gestational timing, dose considerations, and alternatives including non-pharmacologic options. Few medications are absolutely contraindicated; most decisions balance risk versus benefit. Current classification systems (pregnancy categories being replaced by more detailed labeling) guide but don't replace individualized assessment. Collaboration with prenatal care providers optimizes outcomes.

Cirrhosis reduces functional hepatocyte mass, enzyme activity, and hepatic blood flow, all of which impair drug metabolism and increase systemic exposure. Reduced hepatic protein synthesis also lowers albumin levels, increasing the free fraction of highly protein-bound drugs. These combined changes necessitate dose reduction for many hepatically cleared medications.
questions.question: A patient with hepatic cirrhosis develops exaggerated drug effects at standard doses of a highly hepatically metabolized medication. This altered metabolism in cirrhosis primarily results from:
options: Reduced hepatic enzyme activity and blood flow

questions.explanation: Cholinergic toxidrome from organophosphate or carbamate pesticide exposure causes muscarinic (SLUDGE: salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, gastrointestinal upset, emesis) and nicotinic (muscle fasciculations, weakness) effects.
