A 68-year-old male with known ischaemic heart disease undergoes an emergency laparotomy. During the postoperative period, he develops a shockable cardiac rhythm on the cardiac monitor. The resuscitation team is called and commences advanced cardiac life support.

(i) Name the two shockable cardiac arrest rhythms.
(ii) Describe the standard energy setting for defibrillation in an adult and the universal steps for performing defibrillation, including pad placement.
(iii) Explain why early defibrillation is emphasised in the chain of survival, including the effect of time delay on survival and the effect of defibrillation on ventricular fibrillation.
(iv) Describe the correct use of CPR in relation to defibrillation, and state the current recommendation regarding stacked defibrillation.
(v) Describe the post-shock care of a patient after successful conversion.
questions.answerText:
(i) The two shockable cardiac arrest rhythms are:
- Ventricular fibrillation (VF).
- Pulseless ventricular tachycardia (pulseless VT).

(ii) Energy setting for adults: 360 joules. Universal steps:
- Step 1: Always keep the defibrillator batteries charged; power on.
- Step 2: Ensure patient is not in a pool of water; dry a diaphoretic patient's chest with a towel; shave a hairy chest; rub gel on the chest/paddles to allow conduction. Apply STERNAL paddle at the right upper chest below the clavicle and APEX paddle lateral to the left breast nipple. Alternative positions: anterior-posterior, anterior-left infrascapular, anterior-right infrascapular.
- Step 3: Clear victim and analyse the rhythm (no one touching the patient; avoid all movement); confirm shockable rhythm.
- Step 4: Clear the victim and shock (announce "I'm clear, you are clear, everybody clear, oxygen clear"); Charge, Shock, CPR.

(iii) Reasons for early defibrillation: VF is the most frequent initial rhythm in sudden cardiac arrest (40% of SCA). Electrical defibrillation is the most important treatment for VF. Probability of survival decreases with time. VF consumes more energy and converts to asystole within a few minutes, after which successful resuscitation is unlikely. BLS plus defibrillation within 3–5 minutes increases survival rate to 49–75%. For every minute delay in CPR, survival rate drops by 7–10% (but only 3–4% if CPR has been commenced before defibrillation). Neurological survival is time-dependent; best outcome is within 6–10 minutes of defibrillation.

(iv) CPR must continue pending arrival of the defibrillator. After each shock: CPR × 5 cycles (= 2 minutes), then repeat and analyse the rhythm. Three-stacked defibrillation is NOT recommended.

(v) Post-conversion care: place the patient in the recovery position; closely monitor vital signs; reassess rhythm and pulse; continue appropriate post-resuscitation care.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old male is brought in unconscious after collapsing at a public event. Bystanders report he suddenly dropped with no warning. He has no palpable carotid pulse and is not breathing.

(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) State the major risk factors for this condition.
(iii) List the potentially reversible causes using the recognised mnemonic categories.
(iv) Describe the full sequence of Basic Life Support (BLS) that should be immediately initiated, including compression-to-ventilation ratio, compression depth, and rate.
(v) When qualified help arrives, what Advanced Life Support (ACLS) steps should be taken?
questions.answerText:
(i) Cardiac arrest — sudden cessation of effective cardiac activity with blood no longer flowing to the brain and other vital organs; death occurs within minutes if not promptly treated.

(ii) Risk factors include: previous myocardial infarction, previous heart failure (poor pumping heart), survival of a previous cardiac arrest, family history of sudden cardiac arrest, low ejection fraction, smoking, lack of exercise, obesity, diabetes mellitus.

(iii) Reversible causes (Hs and Ts): Hypovolemia, Hypoxia, Hydrogen ion (acidosis), Hypoglycemia, Hypo-/Hyperkalemia, Hypothermia; Tension pneumothorax, Tamponade (cardiac), Toxins, Thrombosis (pulmonary), Thrombosis (coronary), Trauma.

(iv) BLS sequence — Safety, check responsiveness (shake and shout). If unresponsive: shout for help. C-A-B: give 30 chest compressions depressing the sternum 4–5 cm at a rate of approximately 100 times per minute, allowing complete chest recoil. Then open airway (head tilt/chin lift or jaw thrust in trauma). Give 2 rescue breaths each over 1 second, enough to make the chest rise. Continue at a ratio of 30:2. Take not more than 10 seconds to assess circulation. Stop to recheck only if victim makes movement or takes a spontaneous breath.

(v) ACLS: the most important components are direct current defibrillation and efficient BLS. Identify shockable rhythms (VF/pVT) treated by defibrillation, and non-shockable rhythms (asystole and PEA). For VF/pVT: defibrillate as quickly as possible. For asystole/PEA: secure airway, obtain IV access, continue CPR, administer adrenaline every three minutes, give atropine 3 mg once in asystole, and identify reversible causes.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old woman undergoes an elective caesarean section under spinal anaesthesia. Two days postoperatively she develops a severe positional headache, worse on sitting up and relieved by lying flat. She also develops diplopia.
(i) What is the most likely complication, and what is the pathophysiological mechanism producing the headache and the cranial nerve sign?
(ii) What are the risk factors for haematoma following neuraxial anaesthesia, and what is the reported incidence for epidural and spinal blocks?
(iii) Outline the conservative and definitive treatments for the complication in (i).
(iv) List four other neurological complications of spinal and epidural anaesthesia and their causes.
(v) What are the four classic clinical stages of an epidural abscess?
questions.answerText:
(i) The complication is post-dural puncture headache (PDPH). Mechanism: the dural puncture results in CSF loss; this causes low CSF pressure, producing traction on intracranial structures. The headache is positional – worse on sitting or standing, relieved by lying flat. Diplopia arises from traction on the sixth cranial nerve (abducens), which has a long intracranial course and is susceptible to stretch from intracranial hypotension.
(ii) Risk factors for intraspinal/epidural haematoma: needle or catheter trauma to the epidural veins; abnormal coagulation or bleeding disorder; insertion and removal of an epidural catheter. Incidence: approximately 1:150,000 for epidural blocks and 1:220,000 for spinal anaesthetics. Neuraxial anaesthesia should be best avoided in patients with coagulopathy, significant thrombocytopaenia, platelet dysfunction, or those who have received fibrinolytic/thrombolytic therapy.
(iii) Conservative treatment: recumbent position; analgesics (from acetaminophen to NSAIDs); adequate hydration; caffeine (stimulates CSF production and constricts intracranial vessels). Stool softeners and soft diet. If headache persists despite conservative management: epidural blood patch – inject 15–20 ml of autologous blood into the epidural space; acts by mass effect or coagulation. This is effective in treatment.
(iv) Other neurological complications: (1) Nerve root damage and spinal cord damage – can be due to direct physical trauma to nerve roots and spinal cord; most resolve spontaneously, some are permanent; risk factor includes multiple attempts during a technically difficult block. (2) Cauda equina syndrome – associated with continuous spinal catheters and 5% lidocaine; characterised by bowel and bladder dysfunction, multiple nerve root injury, lower motor neuron paresis of legs. (3) Transient neurological symptoms (transient radicular irritation) – back pain radiating to the legs without sensory or motor deficits; occurs after resolution of spinal block; resolves spontaneously; commonly associated with hyperbaric lidocaine. (4) Arachnoiditis – may be infectious or non-infectious; marked by pain and neurological symptoms; radiographically seen as clumping of nerve roots.
(v) The four classic clinical stages of epidural abscess: Stage 1 – vertebral pain intensified by percussion over the spine. Stage 2 – nerve root or radicular pain develops. Stage 3 – motor and/or sensory deficits or sphincter dysfunction. Stage 4 – paraplegia or paralysis.

(i) The diagnosis is Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS), also known as shock lung. The American-European Consensus Committee defines ARDS as: acute onset of severe respiratory distress; bilateral infiltrates on chest radiography; refractory hypoxaemia (PaO2/FiO2 <200 mmHg); pulmonary oedema in the absence of volume overload or depressed LV function.
(ii) Aetiological factors: sepsis and SIRS (most common); severe traumatic injury (especially multiple fractures) – severe head injury, lung contusion, long bone fractures causing fat embolism; multiple blood transfusions; liver disease or coagulation disorder.
(iii) Pathophysiology: damage to alveolar epithelium and vascular endothelium; increased permeability to plasma and inflammatory cells into the interstitium and alveolar space; damage to surfactant-producing Type II cells; protein-rich fluid in the alveolar space disrupts surfactant production and pulmonary function; microatelectasis and impaired gas exchange. Subsequently: resorption of alveolar oedema; regeneration of epithelial cells; proliferation and differentiation of Type II alveolar cells and alveolar remodelling. In an uncomplicated course – rapid resolution. In others – progression to fibrosing alveolitis by day 5–7.
(iv) Mortality: approximately 30–40%. Deaths usually result from multi-organ failure (MOF) rather than lung failure alone. Treatment: prompt treatment of the underlying condition; mechanical ventilation – NIPPV, CPAP, inverse ratio ventilation, prone position; medication – corticosteroids, inhaled NO (nitric oxide), aerosolised synthetic surfactant.
questions.question:

questions.answerText:
(i) Acute Rheumatic Fever (ARF) — an autoallergic disease triggered by infection with some strains of Streptococcus pyogenes (Group A streptococcus), expressing antigens that cross-react with human connective tissues, following a latent period of approximately 3 weeks after tonsillopharyngeal infection.

(ii) Jones Criteria (updated 1992): Major criteria — Carditis, Migratory polyarthritis, Sydenham's chorea, Subcutaneous nodules, Erythema marginatum. Minor criteria — Clinical: fever, arthralgia; Laboratory: elevated acute phase reactants, prolonged PR interval. To fulfil criteria: either two major criteria, or one major criterion and two minor criteria, PLUS supporting evidence of a recent group A streptococcal infection (positive throat culture or rapid antigen detection test, and/or elevated or increasing streptococcal antibody test).

(iii) Cardiac complications: ARF causes pancarditis involving the pericardium, myocardium, and endocardium in 40–60% of patients. Healing of rheumatic valvulitis leads to fibrous thickening and adhesion, resulting in valvular stenosis and/or regurgitation. The mitral valve is involved most frequently, followed by the aortic valve. Isolated aortic valve disease as a consequence of ARF is quite rare; patients with aortic disease also have mitral involvement. Minor degrees of valvular involvement create susceptibility to infective endocarditis. Rheumatic pericarditis can cause serous effusion, fibrin deposits, and pericardial calcification, but does not lead to constrictive pericarditis.

(iv) Treatment at diagnosis: regardless of culture status, treat as if GAS is present — complete a 10-day course of oral penicillin V (500 mg twice daily) or erythromycin (250 mg four times daily) for penicillin-allergic patients, or a single intramuscular injection of benzathine penicillin G 1.2 million units. For arthritis: salicylates escalating to 2 g four times daily, effective and given for 4–6 weeks then gradually tapered (ESR guides taper). Secondary prophylaxis: intramuscular benzathine penicillin G 1.2 million units every 4 weeks, or oral penicillin V 250 mg twice daily, or oral sulfadiazine 1.0 g daily; continue for 5 years after diagnosis or until age 21 years.

(v) Group A streptococci can be recovered from URT in only 25–40% of patients at diagnosis; two or three throat cultures should be obtained before antibiotic therapy. 80% of patients with ARF have an elevated ASO titre at presentation. Sensitivity increases to 95% with anti-deoxyribonuclease B and anti-hyaluronidase. A rising titre from acute to convalescent phase is a more reliable means of documenting recent infection. The diagnosis should be reconsidered if three antibody tests are negative with no evidence of preceding infection.
questions.question:
A 35-year-old woman presents with a 3-week history of joint pains migrating between her ankles, wrists, and knees, associated with fever. Three weeks earlier she had a sore throat. On examination there is a soft murmur at the mitral area and a prolonged PR interval on ECG.

(i) What is the most likely diagnosis?
(ii) State the Jones Criteria — major and minor — and the supporting evidence required to fulfil them.
(iii) What are the cardiac complications of this condition, and which valves are most commonly involved?
(iv) Describe the treatment at diagnosis and the secondary prophylaxis regimen.
(v) What additional investigations would support the diagnosis, and what is the sensitivity of each?

questions.answerText:
(i) Distributive shock: a form of shock characterised by peripheral vasodilation and a hyperdynamic (warm) circulatory state, resulting in inappropriately distributed tissue perfusion and cellular hypoxia. The physiological definition of shock is acute circulatory failure with inadequate or inappropriately distributed tissue perfusion leading to cellular hypoxia.

(ii) Two specific causes of distributive shock: sepsis and anaphylaxis (also neurogenic shock).

(iii) Pathophysiology of SIRS: triggering factors (infectious or non-infectious) activate macrophages/neutrophils, leading to release of inflammatory mediators including cytokines (TNF and IL-1), exotoxins and endotoxins, and activation of the complement cascade. This results in endothelial reactions and cardiovascular/microvascular changes → impaired use of O2 → cellular hypoxia. The SIRS mediators of shock include cytokines, TNF, and IL-1. These lead to: cell membrane ion pump dysfunction; leakage of intracellular contents into extracellular space; intracellular pH dysregulation; ultimately cell death, end-organ dysfunction, MSOF, and death.

(iv) Pulmonary complication — Shock Lung / Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS):
- Presents as non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema.
- Causes: any major illness, major/prolonged surgery, pulmonary aspiration, sepsis.
- Mechanism: increased pulmonary vascular permeability; increased lung water.
- Clinical features: increased respiratory rate, dyspnoea, reduced compliance, increased work of breathing, V/Q mismatch, increased shunt/hypoxaemia, multi-organ failure (MOF).

(v) Monitoring parameters:
- Clinical: rate and character of pulse, capillary refill, respiratory rate, blood pressure.
- Non-invasive: ECG, BP, temperature gradient, echocardiogram, chest X-ray.
- Invasive: urine output (0.5–2 ml/hr), ABG, direct arterial BP, CVP (0–8 cmH2O), PAWP (<15 cmH2O).
- Investigations: acid-base, electrolytes/urea, blood lactate, LFT, blood sugar, FBC/PCV, coagulation, blood/urine/sputum for MCS.
questions.question:
A patient undergoing elective cholecystectomy under general anaesthesia is noted to develop hypotension, tachycardia, and progressive metabolic acidosis intraoperatively. On examination, the skin is warm and flushed, and the patient appears to be in a hyperdynamic circulatory state. The anaesthetist documents the findings and classifies the shock state.

(i) Name and define the class of shock most consistent with these haemodynamic findings.
(ii) Name two specific causes of this class of shock.
(iii) Describe the pathophysiology of the systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) and its mediators.
(iv) List the complications that may affect the lungs specifically in this patient, naming the condition, its mechanism, and clinical features.
(v) Outline the monitoring parameters used to guide resuscitation in this patient.

A. Describe opioid analgesics used in the perioperative and intensive care setting:
A(i) Fentanyl: properties, unique dosage forms and delivery devices, advantages and disadvantages of the transdermal patch
A(ii) Meperidine (pethidine): why it is not a first-line agent, its neurotoxic metabolite, and the usage guidelines stated
A(iii) Methadone: non-opioid actions, half-life and duration, pros and cons
B. Describe the NSAIDs in pain management:
B(i) General properties: efficacy, differences between NSAIDs, and side effects
B(ii) Ketorolac: what makes it special and the time restriction stated
B(iii) COX-2 inhibitors: mechanism, advantages and the specific role stated for celecoxib
C. Describe acetaminophen: mechanism, liver toxicity and maximum dose.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Fentanyl:
- Highly lipophilic
- Causes less histamine release than other opioids
- Unique dosage forms/delivery devices: buccal tablet (Fentora); lozenge (Actiq); transmucosal film (Onsolis) — restricted use in US; transdermal patch (Duragesic)
- Transdermal patch advantages: sustained-release opioid; good in patients with poor compliance; good choice if concerned about drug abuse
- Transdermal patch disadvantages: delay in onset; residual activity after patch removed — must remove old patch; expensive; Note: heat increases rate of release from patch

A(ii) Meperidine (pethidine):
- Not a first-line agent
- Variable oral bioavailability; short duration of action; relatively low potency
- Neurotoxic metabolite: normeperidine has very long half-life
- Multiple drug interactions
- Usage guidelines: do not use for over 48 hours; maximum dose 600mg per 24-hour period; avoid in patients with renal dysfunction or history of seizures; oral use discouraged

A(iii) Methadone:
- Not a first-line opioid
- Non-opioid actions provide additional analgesia
- Half-life: 22 hours; duration: 3–6 hours (initial), 8–12 hours (chronic)
- Pros: cheap; good for refractory pain
- Cons: unpredictable; difficult to dose; drug interactions

B(i) NSAID general properties:
- Efficacy is similar amongst NSAIDs
- Differences in potency, time of onset and duration of action
- Side effects: GI bleeding; renal dysfunction; platelet dysfunction

B(ii) Ketorolac:
- First parenteral NSAID available
- Use limited to less than 5 days due to side effects

B(iii) COX-2 inhibitors:
- Selectively inhibit cyclooxygenase-2
- Advantages: less GI irritation; less platelet effects; other side effects similar to NSAIDs
- Celecoxib (Celebrex) role: patients with low cardiovascular risk who require NSAID therapy and are at increased risk for GI toxicity

C. Acetaminophen:
- Mechanism of action unclear; no anti-inflammatory effects
- Causes liver toxicity at high doses
- Maximum dose: 4g/day if no liver disease; newest recommendation 2.6g/day
- Decreases opioid requirements

questions.question:
A. Describe the Intensive Care Unit (ICU) under the following headings:
A(i) Full definition of the ICU as stated
A(ii) Indications for ICU admission covering all four categories listed
A(iii) Contraindications to ICU admission as given
B. Describe the Glasgow Coma Scale completely.
C. Describe the care of an unconscious patient:
C(i) Three levels of unconsciousness as defined
C(ii) Aetiology of unconsciousness covering all categories listed
C(iii) Components of emergency, supportive and definitive care.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Definition:
- The Intensive Care Unit (ICU) is a specially staffed hospital ward dedicated to the management of critically ill patients with reversible organ dysfunction, life-threatening illness, injuries or complications who will benefit from facilities not available in the general hospital ward

A(ii) Indications for ICU admission:
- Those requiring ventilatory support: respiratory failure, severe tetanus, Guillain-Barré syndrome, upper cervical spine injuries, acute respiratory distress syndrome, chest trauma with major flail segment
- Those requiring intensive/continuous monitoring: myocardial infarction, post-cardiopulmonary resuscitation care, cardiogenic shock, severe extensive burns
- Those requiring support of vital organs: renal replacement therapy, pacemaker insertions, intensive systemic cardiovascular support with vasopressors, severe septicaemia/septic shock, cardiogenic shock
- Those requiring specialised nursing: difficult tracheostomy, comatose patients e.g. DKA, poisoning, CVA

A(iii) Contraindications to ICU admission:
- Irreversible terminal illness e.g. brain death, coma-de-passe
- Highly contagious diseases
- ICU is not a VIP ward nor extension/annex of ordinary ward

B. Glasgow Coma Scale:
- Eye opening: spontaneous = 4; to speech = 3; to pain = 2; none = 1
- Verbal response: oriented = 5; confused = 4; inappropriate words = 3; incomprehensible sounds = 2; none = 1
- Motor response: obeys command = 6; localises pain = 5; withdraws from pain = 4; abnormal flexion = 3; abnormal extension = 2; none = 1

C(i) Levels of unconsciousness:
- Obtundation: responds to verbal stimuli although slow and inappropriate
- Stupor: the subject can be aroused only by vigorous and repeated noxious stimuli
- Coma: unarousable and unresponsive

C(ii) Aetiology:
- Trauma: cerebral contusion; extra/subdural haematoma
- Infections: meningitis; cerebral abscess
- Metabolic: drug overdose; hypoglycaemia/ketoacidosis; hyponatraemia; uraemia; hypothyroidism; hepatic/respiratory failure
- Cerebrovascular accident: subarachnoid haemorrhage; intracerebral haemorrhage; brain stem infarct; cerebrovenous sinus thrombosis
- Others: brain tumours; epilepsy

C(iii) Care of unconscious patient:
- Emergency care: ABC of resuscitation; preventing risk of injury; padding/support
- Supportive care: maintenance of fluid volume (input/output); nutrition (enteral feeding, parenteral feeding); prevention from cold; maintain tissue integrity of cornea; catheter care; bowel care; skin care; oral care
- Definitive care: address the specific underlying cause

questions.question:
(A) Describe the principles of trauma and emergency anaesthesia under the following headings:
(i) Why trauma patients present unique challenges for the anaesthetist.
(ii) The leading cause of death in trauma, and the three time periods in which deaths occur.
(iii) The ATLS framework: name the four components in the correct sequence.

(B) Describe the problems associated with trauma patients that must be anticipated before anaesthesia, including:
(i) Airway and breathing considerations.
(ii) Circulatory/haemodynamic concerns.
(iii) The risk of aspiration and the full stomach problem.

(C) Describe the factors that reduce mortality in trauma patients, and state the role of the anaesthetist as a member of the multidisciplinary trauma team.
questions.answerText:
(A)
(i) Unique challenges: most urgent cases occur at night or on weekend shifts when more experienced anaesthetists are not available. Patient information, previous medical history, chronic medications, allergies, and genetic abnormalities are unknown. Patient status (e.g. HIV) is unknown, requiring universal precautions during resuscitation. There may be inadequate time to prepare the patient for anaesthesia.
(ii) Leading cause: road traffic accidents. Trauma is the leading cause of death in the younger population. Half of deaths are due to massive injury to major vessels or vital organs (heart, brain, spinal cord) — typically immediate. A third of patients succumb after a brief period (the "Golden Hour") from potentially treatable conditions: hypoventilation, haemorrhage, haemo-pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade, expanding intracranial mass.
(iii) ATLS four components (in sequence): Primary Survey → Resuscitation → Secondary Survey → Definitive Care.

(B) Problems:
(i) Airway/breathing: adequacy of airway and breathing may be compromised; watch for stridor, respiratory distress, cyanosis; assume cervical injury in all patients with head and maxillofacial injuries. Look for inadequate breathing efforts: tachypnoea, abnormal respiratory pattern, use of accessory muscles. Rule out life-threatening chest injuries: tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade, significant pneumo-haemothorax, tracheobronchial disruption. Provide O2 supplementation with SpO2 monitoring.
(ii) Circulatory: patient may be in shock (cold clammy peripheries, poor capillary return, pallor, thready small volume pulse, hypotension). Control major external haemorrhage with direct pressure. Insert large-bore cannulae and rapidly infuse fluids. Group and cross-match blood.
(iii) Aspiration risk: trauma patients are presumed to have a full stomach; there is a risk of vomiting, regurgitation, and aspiration of gastric contents. Patient may be intoxicated, restless, comatose, or in shock. Also: disability assessment (pupils, GCS, limb movement) is required before any sedation/anaesthesia.

(C) Factors reducing mortality: accident prevention; pre-hospital stabilisation; rapid transport; early resuscitation; timely operative intervention and postoperative care; rehabilitation.

Role of the anaesthetist: continues the resuscitation already in progress; provides airway management; establishes intravenous access and volume resuscitation; provides monitored sedation during radiological examination; administers anaesthesia for emergency surgery; manages patient in ICU postoperatively; manages acute and massive bleeding. Role is fundamental to the final outcome of the patient.

questions.question:
A 62-year-old male, 80kg, is scheduled for elective hemicolectomy. He was nil by mouth from 22:00, surgery is at 08:00 the following morning, and he received bowel preparation. The procedure lasts 3 hours with 500ml estimated blood loss.
(i) Using the stated formulae, calculate his complete intraoperative fluid requirements (NPO deficit including bowel prep, maintenance, third space losses, and blood loss replacement).
(ii) State the clinical signs of intravascular volume depletion at 5%, 10% and 15–20% depletion levels.
(iii) If this patient is given 1000ml of 0.9% NaCl intravenously, what is the expected increase in intravascular volume, and explain why.
(iv) Describe the monitoring endpoints used to evaluate adequacy of fluid replacement.
(v) State when blood transfusion is generally necessary and when it is rarely needed.
questions.answerText:
(i) Intraoperative fluid calculations:
- Maintenance rate: 1.5ml/kg/hr x 80kg = 120ml/hr
- NPO deficit: 1.5ml/kg/hr x 10 hours = 1200ml
- Bowel prep loss: 1000ml additional
- Total deficit: 1200 + 1000 = 2200ml (replace 1/2 first hour, 1/4 second hour, 1/4 third hour)
- Maintenance during operation: 1.5ml/kg/hr x 3hrs = 360ml
- Third space losses (moderate surgical trauma — hemicolectomy): 6ml/kg/hr x 3hrs = 1440ml
- Blood loss replacement: 500ml x 3 (crystalloid ratio) = 1500ml
- Total = 2200 + 360 + 1440 + 1500 = 5500ml

(ii) Clinical signs of intravascular volume depletion:
- 5%: thirst, dry mucous membranes; urine output 1–2ml/kg/hr
- 10%: tachycardia, oliguria; urine output 0.5–1ml/kg/hr
- 15–20%: tachycardia, hypotension, severe oliguria; urine output <0.5ml/kg/hr

(iii) Effect of 1000ml NaCl 0.9% on intravascular volume:
- NaCl is isotonic; all the Na+ will remain in the ECF
- As NaCl is isotonic there is no change in ECF osmolality and no water exchange occurs across the cell membrane
- NaCl expands ECF only
- Intravascular volume will be increased by approximately 250ml

(iv) Monitoring endpoints for adequacy of fluid replacement:
- Urine output: at least 1.0ml/kg/hr
- Vital signs: blood pressure and heart rate normal
- Physical assessment: skin and mucous membranes not dry; no thirst in awake patient
- Invasive monitoring: CVP or PCWP may be used as a guide
- Laboratory tests: periodic monitoring of haemoglobin and haematocrit

(v) General guidelines for blood transfusion:
- When haemodynamically stable: rare to need blood if Hb > 10g/dl; usual to need blood if Hb < 7g/dl (70g/dl)
- Level depends on co-morbidities
- Healthy patients can tolerate Hgb levels of 7g/dL if intravascular volume is maintained
- Compromised patients may require Hgb levels above 10g/dL

(i) Foreign Body Airway Obstruction (FBAO) — complete or partial obstruction of the airway by a foreign body.

(ii) Predisposing factors and causes: more than 90% of deaths from foreign body occur in children less than 5 years of age; 65% of victims are infants. In children, common objects include balloons, small objects, and food items. Adults are usually affected by food items and dentures. Relaxed tongue is also a cause.

(iii) Mild (partial) obstruction — early recognition: sudden onset of respiratory distress, coughing, gagging, stridor (high-pitched noisy sound), wheezing, and absence of antecedent fever or respiratory symptoms; the child can still cough effectively. Severe (complete) obstruction: unable to speak, ineffective cough, cyanosis, severe respiratory difficulty, universal choking sign, high-pitched sounds.

(iv) Responsive victim (adults and children 1–8 years) — Heimlich's Manoeuvre: stand behind the victim, wrap arms around victim's waist, make a fist with one hand (thumb side between navel and xiphisternum), give 5 quick upward thrusts. When victim becomes unresponsive: lay victim down, phone EMS, perform tongue-jaw lift and look into mouth, open airway and give 2 rescue breaths, perform Heimlich's manoeuvre 5 times, repeat mouth ventilation, continue until object is out.

(v) For an infant: recognise FBAO (differentiate from croup or upper airway infection); signs include ineffective breathing, sudden onset, inability to speak/universal choking sign, cyanosis. Management: give 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts, then give 2 rescue breaths; repeat the cycle until the object is out.
questions.question:
A 6-year-old child is brought to the emergency department by a parent. The child was eating when he suddenly became unable to speak, is making high-pitched sounds, and has developed cyanosis. The child is conscious but distressed.

(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) State the predisposing factors and common causes in this age group.
(iii) Describe the clinical signs that distinguish mild (partial) from severe (complete) obstruction.
(iv) Describe the step-by-step management for a responsive victim, and then for when the victim becomes unresponsive.
(v) How does the management differ for an infant?

A 9-year-old child (weight 20kg) is scheduled for an elective procedure. The anaesthetist plans induction with intravenous ketamine followed by maintenance with an inhalational agent.
(i) Calculate the appropriate ETT size for this child using the formula stated.
(ii) State the intravenous dose of ketamine for induction and the intramuscular dose, and describe its onset and duration of action by each route.
(iii) Compare the cardiovascular effects of ketamine with those of thiopentone as stated.
(iv) Describe why inhalational anaesthetic uptake is more rapid in children than adults, and explain the implication for MAC and the concentration of inhalational agents required.
(v) Using the fluid maintenance formula, calculate this child's intraoperative fluid requirement in ml/hr, and state the average fluid maintenance requirements by weight category as given.
questions.answerText:
(i) ETT size calculation for 9-year-old:
- Formula: Tube size (mm) = (Age in years + 4) ÷ 4
- = (9 + 4) ÷ 4 = 13 ÷ 4 = 3.25mm (internal diameter)
- A tube size above (3.75mm) and below (2.75mm) the calculated size should be made available

(ii) Ketamine dosing and onset:
- IV dose: 1–2mg/kg; onset 30–60 seconds after IV injection
- IM dose: 4–10mg/kg; effective after 3–4 minutes after IM injection
- Duration of action: 15–25 minutes (by either route)

(iii) Cardiovascular effects — ketamine vs thiopentone:
- Ketamine: arterial pressure increases; heart rate increases; cardiac output increases; myocardial oxygen consumption increases
- Thiopentone: cardiac output is reduced resulting in hypotension; avoid in patients with shock; skeletal muscle tone reduced especially with high concentration

(iv) Inhalational uptake and MAC in children:
- Uptake in the child is more rapid due to a lower functional residual capacity (FRC)
- The minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) is higher in children
- Therefore a higher inspired concentration of inhalational agents is required for maintenance of anaesthesia in children
- Children often require higher concentrations of inhalational anaesthetics

(v) Fluid maintenance calculation for 20kg child:
- First 10kg: 4ml/kg/hr = 40ml/hr
- Second 10kg: 3ml/kg/hr = 30ml/hr (10–20kg range)
- Total = 40 + 30 = 70ml/hr
- Average fluid maintenance requirements:
 - 1st week of life: 2.5ml/kg/hr
 - Thereafter up to 10kg: 4ml/kg/hr
 - 10–20kg: 3ml/kg/hr
 - Above 20kg: 2ml/kg/hr

questions.question:
(A) Describe regional nerve blocks under the following headings:
(i) The types of regional blocks, from topical to central neural blockade.
(ii) The advantages of regional nerve blocks over general anaesthesia.
(iii) Absolute and relative contraindications to regional nerve blocks.

(B) Explain the clinical basis of each of the following complications of regional nerve blocks:
(i) Local anaesthetic toxicity: mechanism and risk factors.
(ii) Excessive spread of local anaesthetic (e.g. total spinal, phrenic nerve block).
(iii) Technical complications (trauma to nerve, vessels, catheter/needle breakage).

(C) Describe the intraoperative and postoperative management of a patient receiving a regional nerve block, including monitoring, sedation options, and criteria for discharge.
questions.answerText:
(A)
(i) Types of regional blocks:
- Topical anaesthesia (surface analgesia).
- Infiltration anaesthesia.
- Peripheral nerve blocks: plexus/single nerve blocks.
- Central neural blockade: epidural anaesthesia; spinal anaesthesia.
- Others: intravenous regional anaesthesia (IVRA/Bier's block); sympathetic nerve blocks; interpleural/intra-articular analgesia.

(ii) Advantages:
- Less interruption of oral intake (useful in diabetic patients).
- Consciousness may be preserved; patient can assist in positioning and warn of adverse effects (e.g. TURP syndrome, carotid artery surgery).
- Good post-operative analgesia.
- Reduced risk of some post-operative complications (e.g. lung atelectasis, DVT, PONV).

(iii) Absolute contraindications: patient refusal; inexperience of the anaesthetist; local sepsis. Relative contraindications: anatomical deformity; coagulopathy; neurological disease (neuropathies); previous failure of technique.

(B)
(i) Local anaesthetic toxicity: systemic toxicity due to absorption of excessive amounts of local anaesthetic; commoner in epidural anaesthesia; risk minimised if maximum safe dosage is not exceeded; can cause CNS toxicity (seizures) and cardiovascular collapse.
(ii) Excessive spread: total spinal results from excessive dose subarachnoid or inadvertent subarachnoid injection during epidural block (see total spinal above); phrenic nerve block can occur from interscalene approach; high epidural block causes motor, sensory, and autonomic blockade above intended level.
(iii) Technical complications: trauma to nerve (neuropathy); trauma to blood vessels (haematoma); breakage of catheter or needle (foreign body retention); malpositioning resulting in compression damage of nerves; injection of wrong solution through catheter.

(C) Intraoperative management:
- Monitoring of vital signs commenced prior to the procedure.
- Aseptic technique and use of short-bevelled needles/nerve stimulators.
- Extent of block assessed by pin prick or cold before commencement of surgery.
- Sedation options if required: Entonox, opioid analgesics, benzodiazepines (diazepam, midazolam), propofol.
- Facility for conversion to general anaesthesia must be available at all times.

Postoperative management:
- Monitoring and supervision as for general anaesthesia.
- Monitor for neurological complications.
- Discharge only when effects of the block have worn off.
- Provide adequate post-operative analgesia.

questions.question:
A 22-year-old female requires emergency appendicectomy. She is otherwise healthy but has had nothing to eat for only 2 hours and is presumed to have a full stomach. The anaesthetist plans a rapid sequence induction (RSI).

(i) State the drug of choice for muscle relaxation in this scenario and give the dose.
(ii) Describe the full mechanism of action of this drug at the neuromuscular junction, step by step.
(iii) List all the side effects of this drug on each organ system.
(iv) If the patient has a history of pseudocholinesterase deficiency, what is the expected alteration in drug effect and what conditions are associated with this enzyme deficiency?
(v) State the reversal agent for this drug and explain why neostigmine is contraindicated.
questions.answerText:
(i) Drug of choice for RSI: suxamethonium (succinylcholine). Dose: 1–1.5 mg/kg for tracheal intubation.

(ii) Mechanism of action at the NMJ (step by step):
- Suxamethonium is a quaternary ammonium compound comparable to two molecules of ACh joined together.
- It mimics the action of ACh at the nicotinic receptors, binding to both alpha-subunits.
- This causes depolarisation of the motor end plate → muscle contraction seen as fasciculations (cranio-caudal pattern).
- Unlike ACh, suxamethonium is not metabolised by acetylcholinesterase; it remains at the NMJ.
- The sustained depolarisation prevents repolarisation → flaccid relaxation (neuromuscular blockade).
- As drug serum level falls (via plasma cholinesterase metabolism to succinylmonocholine), suxamethonium diffuses away from the NMJ, limiting duration of action.
- Onset: 60–90 seconds; duration: 3 minutes; total recovery: 12–15 minutes.

(iii) Side effects by organ system:
- Muscular: muscle pains/myalgia (prevented by pre-curarisation); fasciculations common in young patients with large muscle mass; not typical in children and elderly.
- Cardiovascular: bradycardia especially with repeated doses; prevented by atropine.
- Gastrointestinal: increased intra-gastric pressure (avoid in hiatus hernia); increased salivary and gastric secretions (muscarinic effect).
- Ocular: increased intraocular pressure (transiently); avoid in penetrating eye injuries and severe glaucoma.
- Electrolyte/metabolic: hyperkalaemia; raises serum K+ by 0.5 mEq/L; life-threatening in patients with burns, massive trauma, neurological disorders, stroke, pre-existing hyperkalaemia — may result in cardiac arrest.
- Immunological: anaphylactic reactions (rare).
- Trigger for malignant hyperthermia (as a depolarising relaxant).

(iv) In pseudocholinesterase deficiency: the drug is not metabolised normally; duration of action is greatly prolonged — scoline apnoea. Associated conditions: liver disease, carcinomatosis, pregnancy, hypothyroidism, renal disease.

(v) Reversal agent: plasma cholinesterase (pseudocholinesterase) metabolises suxamethonium; there is no pharmacological reversal agent. Neostigmine is contraindicated because it inhibits acetylcholinesterase and plasma cholinesterase, thereby increasing suxamethonium concentration at the NMJ and prolonging the block rather than reversing it.

(i) ICU admission:
- This patient meets criteria for ICU admission
- Category: those requiring specialised nursing and monitoring — comatose/confused patients; also: neurological monitoring/support — CNS depression sufficient to compromise airway and impair protective reflexes; invasive neurological monitoring
- Also meets the category: patients requiring intensive/continuous monitoring — cerebrovascular accident is specifically comparable to the listed conditions; severe head injury and CVA are listed in the care of unconscious patient aetiology

(ii) Blood component indications:
- FFP is indicated: INR is 3.8, which exceeds the stated threshold of INR >1.5 for FFP transfusion; indication includes severe bleeding due to warfarin therapy or urgent reversal of warfarin effect
- Platelets consideration: platelet count is 90 x 10⁹/l which is above the threshold for actively bleeding patients (<75 x 10⁹/l); if patient is actively bleeding, transfuse until platelet count >75 x 10⁹/l — borderline assessment required

(iii) Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP):
- Frozen at -18°C or colder within 6–8 hours of collection
- Contains functional quantities of ALL coagulation factors
- Indications: active/risk of bleeding due to deficiency of multiple coagulation factors; severe bleeding due to warfarin therapy, or urgent reversal of warfarin effect; massive transfusion with coagulopathic bleeding; bleeding or prophylaxis of bleeding for a known single coagulation factor deficiency for which no concentrate is available
- Dose: when used to correct multiple coagulation factor deficiencies, transfusion should be guided by coagulation testing; thresholds: PT >1.5 times mid-range normal; APTT greater than 1.5 times top of normal range; 10–20ml/kg may be required

(iv) FP24 or thawed plasma:
- Plasma frozen within 24 hours (FP24) and thawed plasma may contain variably reduced levels of Factor V and Factor VIII (compared to standard FFP which contains functional quantities of all coagulation factors)

(v) Donor selection criteria:
- Age: fit, 18–65 years
- Haemoglobin: >13.5g/dl in males; >12.5g/dl in females
- No major operation in last 6 months
- No blood donation in last 6 months
- No pregnancy in last 12 months
- No clinical evidence of malaria
- Free from severe hypertension, splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, bleeding disorder or allergies such as asthma
- Free of history or clinical evidence and not carriers of viral hepatitis, HIV, syphilis, trypanosomiasis, brucellosis
- Unvaccinated within last 3 weeks
questions.question:
A 60-year-old man presents to the emergency department confused, with slurred speech and left-sided weakness. His partner states he takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation. Initial investigations show INR 3.8 and platelet count 90 x 10⁹/l.
(i) Using the ICU admission criteria, state whether this patient meets criteria for ICU admission and under which category.
(ii) Using the blood component guidelines, identify which component(s) are indicated and why, referencing the specific INR and platelet thresholds stated.
(iii) Describe Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP): how it is frozen, what coagulation factors it contains, and its indications as stated.
(iv) Describe the Fresh Frozen Plasma (FP24) or thawed plasma difference compared to standard FFP.
(v) Describe the donor selection criteria for blood donation as listed, covering age, haemoglobin, time exclusions and disease exclusions.

A 25-year-old male student is reviewed in the preoperative clinic prior to an elective inguinal hernia repair under spinal anaesthesia. He asks about what the anaesthetist will do and what he will experience. Two days after the operation, he returns complaining of a severe bifrontal and occipital headache that is made worse when he sits up or stands and is relieved when he lies flat.

(i) What is the most likely diagnosis, and what is the mechanism that produces this pattern of headache?
(ii) What structures are under traction in this condition, and why does posture affect the headache?
(iii) List all the causes of dural puncture in the perioperative period.
(iv) Describe the full management of this complication, including conservative and definitive measures.
(v) Name two other complications specific to subarachnoid block that may occur in the postoperative period, with their management.
questions.answerText:
(i) Post-dural puncture headache (PDPH). Mechanism: CSF leaks from the dural defect at a rate greater than its production, causing reduced intracranial pressure (ICP). The reduced CSF volume and ICP cause traction on structures supporting the brain. This is gravity-dependent, explaining why the headache is worse when sitting or standing (more traction) and relieved by lying flat (less traction).

(ii) Structures under traction: the dura mater and tentorium cerebelli — these structures support the brain and are pulled when CSF volume is reduced. Blood vessels contributing to the pain: traction on blood vessels attached to these structures also contributes to the headache. The typical distribution (bilateral, frontal, retroorbital, and occipital, extending into the neck) reflects the anatomical distribution of the meningeal structures under traction.

(iii) Causes of dural puncture:
- Diagnostic lumbar puncture.
- Myelogram.
- Spinal (subarachnoid) anaesthetic.
- Epidural "wet tap" (epidural needle inadvertently puncturing the dura).
- Epidural catheter puncturing the dura.

(iv) Management:
- Conservative: bed rest; adequate oral/IV hydration; oral analgesics; caffeine.
- Definitive (if not resolved): epidural blood patch — injection of the patient's own blood into the epidural space to seal the dural defect.

(v) Other complications specific to subarachnoid block with management:
- Backache: due to localised inflammatory response with or without reflex muscle spasm; usually benign but can indicate serious complications (epidural haematoma, abscess). Treated with acetaminophen, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents, cold or warm compress.
- Urinary retention: decrease in urinary bladder tone, inhibition of voiding reflex. Management: encourage voiding; bladder catheterisation if needed for all but the shortest acting blocks.
- Infection (if asepsis not maintained): treated with antibiotics.

(i) Estimated blood volume at 7 months:
- Infants (up to 3 months): approximately 85ml/kg
- Children over 3 months: 75ml/kg
- Therefore for a 7-month-old (over 3 months): 75ml/kg
- For 7kg infant: approximately 525ml

(ii) Fluid maintenance for 7kg child during surgery:
- For weight up to 10kg: 4ml/kg/hr
- 4ml/kg/hr x 7kg = 28ml/hr

(iii) ETT size formula:
- Tube size (mm) = (Age in years + 4) ÷ 4
- For 4-year-old: (4 + 4) ÷ 4 = 2mm (internal diameter)
- Tubes one size above and below the calculated should be available
- Note: modern ETT may come with cuffs though traditionally paediatric tubes often had no cuffs

(iv) Ayre's T-piece circuit:
- Commonly used in paediatric anaesthesia
- Jackson-Rees later modified it by addition of a 500ml bag with an open tail to the respiratory limb
- Advantage: low resistance to breathing due to the absence of valves
- Disadvantage: pollution of theatre room

(v) Immediate post-anaesthetic care:
- The child should be kept warm in the recovery room
- Hypothermia may cause hypoventilation or apnoea
- Secretions should be gently sucked out to prevent aspiration
- Aspiration may cause laryngeal spasm
- Administer oxygen therapy
- In neonates and infants: hypoglycaemia may cause prolonged unconsciousness after general anaesthesia — must be anticipated and monitored
questions.question:
A 7-month-old infant is brought to the operating theatre for an elective surgical procedure. The attending anaesthetist must plan fluid therapy and select an appropriate anaesthetic circuit.
(i) State the estimated blood volume for this infant.
(ii) Calculate the maintenance fluid requirement during surgery for a 7-month-old weighing 7kg using the formula stated.
(iii) State the formula for calculating the appropriate ETT size for a 4-year-old child.
(iv) Describe the Ayre's T-piece circuit: what modification was added, what is its advantage, and what is its disadvantage?
(v) Describe the immediate post-anaesthetic care required for a paediatric patient, including the specific complications unique to neonates and infants that must be anticipated.

A(i) Compare ropivacaine and levobupivacaine with bupivacaine in terms of their cardiotoxicity, indicating the structural or chemical basis for the difference.
A(ii) Explain the concept of differential neural blockade as applied to bupivacaine in obstetric and postoperative analgesia.
B(i) Describe the effect of the following additives on local anaesthetic solutions and explain the mechanism of each: (a) epinephrine/vasoconstrictors; (b) carbonated solutions (CO2); (c) dextrose; (d) hyaluronidase.
B(ii) Describe the clinical features of local anaesthetic neurotoxicity and methaemoglobinaemia, including the agents implicated and the treatment for each.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Bupivacaine is highly cardiotoxic; it has the highest affinity for cardiac muscle and can cause profound hypotension, arrhythmias, and cardiac arrest that is difficult to resuscitate. Ropivacaine – introduced in 1997; has less affinity for the heart muscle and is less cardiotoxic than bupivacaine; is also less potent. Levobupivacaine – the S-isomer of bupivacaine (introduced 1997); it is less cardiotoxic than bupivacaine and has less mortality. The reduced cardiotoxicity of ropivacaine and levobupivacaine compared with the racemic bupivacaine is attributed to the stereoselective nature of their interaction with cardiac sodium channels – these agents have lower affinity for cardiac conduction tissue.
A(ii) Differential neural blockade: bupivacaine in various concentrations can be used to provide more sensory blockade than motor blockade. This property makes it useful in obstetric analgesia (labour analgesia) and postoperative analgesia, where pain relief is desired without the loss of motor function that would otherwise prevent mobilisation. Smaller fibres (sensory, autonomic) are blocked at lower concentrations than larger motor fibres.
B(i) Additives and mechanisms: (a) Epinephrine/vasoconstrictors (e.g. adrenaline 1:200,000, phenylephrine 1:20,000, felypressin) – produce localised vasoconstriction, limiting systemic absorption; increase the safe dose; may improve onset and intensity of block. Less effective with highly lipid-soluble drugs like bupivacaine. Systemic absorption of vasopressors leads to arrhythmias and hypertension. (b) Carbonated solutions (CO2) – dissolved under pressure, lowers pH in axons, increasing intracellular dissociation of the LA; produces a faster block. (c) Dextrose – increases baricity for subarachnoid block (SAB); affects spread within the CSF. (d) Hyaluronidase – breaks down stromal tissue; mainly used in eye blocks to improve spread of LA.
B(ii) Neurotoxicity: occurs particularly with chloroprocaine; toxicity may be related to the low pH (3.0) and presence of the antioxidant sodium bisulphite; heavy solutions of 5% lignocaine have also been implicated. May manifest as cauda equina syndrome with continuous spinal catheters. Treatment: supportive; avoid causative agents. Methaemoglobinaemia: caused by large doses of prilocaine exceeding 8 mg/kg; leads to accumulation of ortho-toluidine, which changes haemoglobin to methaemoglobin; the patient develops cyanosis unresponsive to oxygen. Treatment: intravenous methylene blue 1 mg/kg.

questions.question:
A 22-year-old female is brought to the A&E comatose after a drug overdose. She is breathing shallowly at 8 breaths per minute, her oxygen saturation is 82%, and she has pinpoint pupils.

(i) What is the most likely diagnosis, and classify the type of respiratory failure present.
(ii) What is the aetiology of Type II respiratory failure, listing the CNS, peripheral nervous system, and chest wall causes?
(iii) Describe the clinical signs of CO2 retention and hypoxia that should be looked for on examination.
(iv) Outline the step-by-step management, including airway management, ventilatory support options, and monitoring.
(v) Distinguish between the normal values and the severe hypoxia thresholds for PaO2/FiO2 ratio, A-a gradient, and shunt fraction.
questions.answerText:
(i) Narcotic overdose causing Type II (Hypercapnic) Respiratory Failure — PaO2 less than 8 kPa with PaCO2 greater than 8 kPa; characterised by hypercarbia, hypoxia, and reduced rate and depth of breathing. The CNS is depressed by the narcotic/sedative overdose, reducing the neural drive to breathe.

(ii) Type II respiratory failure aetiology: CNS disorders — pharmacological, structural, and metabolic disorders of the CNS causing depression of the neural drive to breathe; examples: tumours or vascular abnormalities involving the brain stem, overdose of a narcotic or sedative (as in this case), metabolic disorders such as myxoedema or chronic metabolic alkalosis. Peripheral nervous system, respiratory muscles, and chest wall — inability to maintain a level of minute ventilation appropriate for the rate of CO2 production; concomitant hypoxaemia and hypercapnia occur; examples: Guillain-Barré syndrome, muscular dystrophy, myasthenia gravis, severe kyphoscoliosis, morbid obesity. Aetiology may also be precipitated by major or prolonged surgery; CNS: head trauma, infections, raised ICP, drug overdose, sleep apnoea; spinal cord: high spinal cord lesion, poliomyelitis, motor neurone disease; motor nerves: Guillain-Barré syndrome; neuromuscular junction: myasthenia gravis, botulism, NM blocking drugs, organophosphate poisoning; chest wall: flail chest, kyphoscoliosis; pleura: pneumothorax, haemothorax, pleural effusion, empyema.

(iii) Clinical signs: Signs of CO2 retention — flapping tremor, warm extremities, bounding pulse, loss of consciousness. Signs of hypoxia — restlessness, agitation, sweating, confusion, central cyanosis. Other examination findings: use of accessory muscles of respiration; exhaustion/inability to talk; assess pulse, BP, JVP, peripheral oedema, heart sounds for signs of heart failure or dehydration; evidence of obstruction, collapse, consolidation, effusion, bronchospasm (RR, tracheal shift, crackles or wheeze); check CXR and ABG.

(iv) Management: Correct hypoxaemia with O2 therapy; provide ventilatory support; treat underlying cause (antidote for narcotic overdose). Assess and correct A, B, C. Airway management: oropharyngeal/nasopharyngeal airway, LMA, ETT, or tracheostomy. Assess respiratory drive; type 2: respiratory stimulant (e.g. Doxapram) may be used. Optimise breathing by mechanical ventilation — modes: CPAP, SIMV, pressure support, PEEP, BiPAP. Additional: hydration and chest physiotherapy; salbutamol/ipratropium nebulisation; sedation/muscle relaxants; nutrition, DVT prophylaxis, analgesia, antacids; surveillance and appropriate antibiotics. Monitoring: FiO2, SpO2, EtCO2, ABG, acid-base balance, airway pressure, minute ventilation/tidal volume.

(v) Measures of hypoxia: PaO2/FiO2 ratio — Normal greater than 300 mmHg; Severe hypoxia greater than 200 mmHg (i.e. worsening if below 200). A-a gradient — Normal greater than 26; Severe hypoxia greater than 45. Shunt fraction — Normal 0–8%; Severe hypoxia greater than 30%.

A(i) Definition: neuromuscular blocking drugs are drugs that impair neuromuscular transmission and provide skeletal muscle relaxation. Principal clinical uses: they enable tracheal intubation, facilitate ventilation, and provide optimal surgical operating conditions. They are also used during ICU mechanical ventilation, to decrease shivering, and for epileptic status. Muscle relaxation alone does not ensure unconsciousness, amnesia, or analgesia – other components of anaesthesia must be separately provided.
A(ii) Classification by mechanism of action: Depolarising NMBDs – agonists at the nicotinic receptors; suxamethonium is the only drug in this group currently in clinical use (decamethonium is no longer used clinically and is available for research purposes only). Non-depolarising NMBDs – antagonists at the postsynaptic nicotinic receptors; further classified into two groups: (a) Aminosteroid compounds (have a steroid nucleus; do not cause histamine release) – examples: pancuronium, vecuronium, rocuronium. (b) Benzylisoquinolinium compounds – examples: atracurium, mivacurium.
B(i) Mivacurium: class – benzylisoquinolinium non-depolarising NMBA; same class as atracurium. Onset: 2 minutes. Duration: 10–20 minutes (short-acting). Metabolism: hydrolysed by plasma cholinesterase and excreted in urine. Cardiovascular effects: relatively cardio-stable but causes histamine release. Suitability: because it is metabolised by plasma cholinesterase, its duration will be significantly prolonged in patients with abnormal (atypical or deficient) plasma cholinesterase, similar to suxamethonium.
B(ii) Cisatracurium vs. atracurium: Classification – cisatracurium is an isomer (steroisomer) of atracurium; both are benzylisoquinolinium non-depolarising NMBAs. Metabolism – both undergo Hofmann elimination (spontaneous non-enzymatic degradation at physiological pH and temperature); cisatracurium undergoes Hofmann elimination only (not ester hydrolysis). Histamine release – atracurium causes histamine release (cardiovascular side effects, bronchospasm, hypotension); cisatracurium causes minimal or no histamine release (much less than atracurium), hence minimal cardiovascular side effects. Laudanosine production – both produce laudanosine (a CNS excitatory metabolite); cisatracurium produces much less laudanosine than atracurium. Onset and duration are similar (3–5 minutes onset, 20–35 minutes duration).

questions.answerText:
A(i) The larynx is a respiratory organ located between the pharynx and the trachea. It lies below the hyoid bone in the midline in the neck at the level of C4–C6 vertebrae. It extends from the root of the tongue to the trachea. Length in females: 35 cm; anterior-posterior diameter 25 cm; transverse diameter 40 cm. In males: length 45 cm; AP diameter 35 cm; transverse diameter 45 cm.

A(ii) Nine cartilages: 3 single (epiglottis, thyroid, cricoid) and 3 paired (corniculate, arytenoids, cuneiform). Two types: hyaline cartilages (thyroid, cricoid, arytenoids) and elastic cartilages (epiglottis, corniculate, cuneiform). The larynx consists of a framework of articulating cartilages linked together by ligaments which move in relation to each other by the action of laryngeal muscles. Thyroid cartilage: shield-like; consists of two laminae whose anterior borders are fused in the midline. The thyrohyoid membrane connects the thyroid cartilage with the hyoid bone and supports the front portion of the larynx.

B(i) The epithelium of the larynx is squamous above the vocal cords and columnar below the cords. The larynx serves as a protective sphincter for the air passages and also serves as an organ of phonation.

B(ii) The epiglottis is a leaf-shaped flap in the throat that prevents food and water from entering the trachea and lungs. Made of elastic cartilage covered with mucous membrane, attached to the entrance of the larynx. It originates at the entrance of the larynx, is attached to the hyoid bone, and projects upwards and backwards behind the tongue. The space between the epiglottis and the tongue is called the vallecula; the vallecula are paired spaces, bordered medially by the median glossoepiglottic fold and laterally by the lateral glossoepiglottic fold.

C(i) The thyroid cartilage is usually larger in males than females. The anterior borders of the two laminae are fused in the midline inferiorly at 90 degrees in males, forming a prominent laryngeal prominence (Adam's apple), but at 180 degrees in females, making the laryngeal prominence less prominent. Clinically, this means the male larynx is larger and more easily palpable, and the angle of fusion affects the size of the glottis and thus the diameter of the airway; a smaller angle in males results in a more prominent Adam's apple and, generally, a larger laryngeal inlet.

(A)
(i) Surgical indications: surgeries below the umbilicus — lower abdominal, inguinal, urogenital, rectal, and lower extremity surgery; obstetric anaesthesia and analgesia; surgeries below the neck alone or in conjunction with GA.
(ii) Patient-based indications: patients with full stomach (to avoid aspiration); chronic respiratory disease (emphysema, chronic bronchitis); severe renal, hepatic, or metabolic disturbances; eclamptic toxaemia; myasthenia gravis (to avoid muscle relaxants); poor-risk patients; patient's preference to be awake.
(iii) Absolute contraindications: patient refusal; infection at the site of injection; coagulopathy or other bleeding diathesis; severe hypovolaemia; increased intracranial pressure; severe aortic stenosis; severe mitral stenosis.
(iv) Relative contraindications: sepsis; uncooperative patient; pre-existing neurological deficits; demyelinating lesions; stenotic valvular heart lesions; severe spinal deformity.
(v) Controversial contraindications: prior back surgery at the site of injection; complicated surgery; prolonged operation; major blood loss; manoeuvres that compromise respiration.

(B)
(i) Respiratory: alterations in pulmonary variables in healthy patients are usually of little clinical consequence; tidal volume is unchanged during high spinal anaesthesia; vital capacity decreases in a small amount.
(ii) Cardiovascular: bradycardia and hypotension result from the sympathectomy effect of neuraxial block, dependent on the height of block. Incidence of cardiac arrest can be reduced by prophylactic volume expansion and aggressive vagolytic treatment of bradycardia (atropine, followed by ephedrine and epinephrine if necessary).
(iii) Gastrointestinal: nausea and vomiting in up to 20% of patients, due to hyperperistalsis as a result of unopposed parasympathetic (vagal) activity.
(iv) Renal: renal blood flow is maintained through autoregulation; little clinical effect on renal function; blockage of sympathetic and parasympathetic supply to the bladder results in urinary retention (effects most pronounced in males).

(C)
(i) Predisposing conditions for epidural haematoma: increased bleeding tendency (blood dyscrasia, anticoagulant therapy, coagulopathy). Backache after regional block can be an important clinical sign of much more serious complications including epidural haematoma and abscess. Note: note the technique should be avoided if blood dyscrasia is present.
(ii) Strategies for prevention of epidural abscess: minimise catheter manipulation and maintain a closed system when possible; use a micropore (0.22 micron) bacteria filter; remove epidural catheter at 96 hours, or at least change the catheter, filter, and solution every 96 hours; maintain strict aseptic technique throughout.

questions.answerText:
(i) Indications for TPN:
- Patients whose GI tract is not functional; a general but untested indication is anticipation of undernutrition (<50% of metabolic needs met) for >7 days
- Before and after treatment to severely undernourished patients who cannot ingest large volumes of oral feedings and are being prepared for surgery, radiation therapy or chemotherapy
- TPN may reduce morbidity and mortality after major surgery, severe burns and head trauma, especially in patients with sepsis
- Patients with disorders requiring complete bowel rest (e.g. some stages of Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, severe pancreatitis) or with paediatric GI disorders (e.g. congenital anomalies; prolonged diarrhoea, regardless of cause) often respond well to TPN

(ii) Basic adult daily requirements for TPN:
- Water: 30–40ml/kg/day
- Energy: medical patient 30 kcal; postoperative patient 30–45 kcal; hypercatabolic patient 45–60 kcal (per kg body wt/day)
- Amino acids: medical patient 1.0g/kg/day; postoperative patient 2.0g/kg/day; hypercatabolic patient 3.0g/kg/day

(iii) Preparation of TPN solutions:
- Prepared using sterile techniques, usually in litre batches according to standard formulas
- Normally 2L/day of standard solution is needed
- Solutions may be modified based on laboratory results, underlying disorders, hypermetabolism or other factors
- Commercially available lipid emulsions are often added to supply essential fatty acids and triglycerides
- 20–30% of total calories is usually supplied as lipids
- Withholding lipids may help obese patients mobilise endogenous fat stores, increasing insulin sensitivity

(iv) Modifications:
- Renal insufficiency: patients not receiving dialysis or with liver failure require solutions with reduced protein content and a high percentage of essential amino acids
- Heart or kidney failure: volume (liquid) intake must be limited; for patients with respiratory failure, a lipid emulsion must provide most of non-protein calories to minimise CO2 production by carbohydrate metabolism
- Neonates: require lower dextrose concentrations (17–18%)

(v) Routes of enteral nutrition:
- Oral
- Nasogastric
- Gastrostomy
- Jejunostomy
- Partial parenteral nutrition: supplies only part of daily nutritional requirements, supplementing oral intake
- Total parenteral nutrition (TPN) via central venous catheter: supplies all daily nutritional requirements

(A)
(i) Composition and osmolality:
- Normal saline (0.9%): Na+ 154, Cl- 154, osmolality 308 mOsmol/L.
- Half-normal saline (0.45%): Na+ 77, Cl- 77, osmolality 154 mOsmol/L.
- 5% Glucose: no Na+ or Cl-; osmolality 278 mOsmol/L.
- Hartmann's solution: Na+ 131, Cl- 112, osmolality 281 mOsmol/L; also contains K+ 5, HCO3- 29, Ca2+ 4.

(ii) Distribution:
- Na+ remains in ECF due to Na+/K+ pump. Normal saline expands ECF mainly (isotonic). Half-normal saline (hypotonic): causes shift of H2O from ECF. 5% glucose: metabolised to H2O which enters ICF + ECF. Body water is 60% of weight in males, 50–55% in females. ICF: ~28 L (40%); ECF: ~14 L (20%), comprising plasma ~3.5 L (5%) and interstitial fluid ~9.5 L (14%), plus transcellular fluid ~1 L (1%).

(iii) Normal daily fluid balance: Intake: liquid 1,500 mls, food 100 mls, metabolic water 900 mls = total 2,500 mls. Output: urine, faeces, insensible loss = total 2,500 mls.

(B)
(i) Maintenance fluid: 1.5–2 mls/kg/hr for adults.
(ii) Replacement of third-space losses: 5–10 ml/kg/hr.
(iii) Replacement of blood loss: crystalloid at 3× the volume lost; colloid or blood at the same volume.

questions.answerText:
(i) The condition is tension pneumothorax. The mechanism: air accumulates under pressure in the pleural space, causing collapse of the ipsilateral lung; the resulting mediastinal shift compresses the contralateral lung and great vessels, obstructing venous return and reducing cardiac output, producing haemodynamic compromise (shock).
(ii) Four life-threatening conditions to exclude under primary survey: tension pneumothorax; upper airway obstruction; cardiac tamponade; massive bleeding from ruptured major vessels.
(iii) ATLS ABCDE primary survey: A – Airway maintenance with cervical control: ensure a clear airway and maintain adequate oxygenation; watch for signs of airway obstruction such as stridor, respiratory distress, cyanosis; assume cervical injury in all patients with head and maxillofacial injuries unless proven otherwise. B – Breathing and ventilation: look for tachypnea, abnormal respiratory pattern, use of accessory muscles, cyanosis; rule out tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade, significant pneumo-haemothorax, disruption of tracheobronchial tree; provide oxygen supplementation with SpO2 monitoring. C – Circulation and haemorrhage control: signs of shock – cold clammy peripheries, poor capillary return, pallor, thready pulse, hypotension; control major external haemorrhage with direct pressure; insert large bore cannulae and rapidly infuse fluids; group and cross-match blood. D – Disability: rapid neurological evaluation – pupil size and reaction, GCS score, limb movement. E – Exposure: undress the patient for thorough survey, then cover with warm blankets to prevent hypothermia.
(iv) Conditions requiring urgent intubation: upper airway obstruction with ventilatory insufficiency; severe lung contusion with signs of hypoxaemia (haemo- or pneumothorax needing urgent chest drain); severe head injury with GCS <9; inability to protect the airway or active bleeding in the oral cavity with risk of aspiration; shock of any nature requiring cardiopulmonary resuscitation.
(v) The "Golden Hour" refers to the brief period after trauma during which a third of patients succumb as a result of potentially treatable conditions. These treatable conditions include: hypoventilation, haemorrhage, haemo-pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade, and an expanding intracranial mass.

(i) Spinal anaesthesia is particularly indicated for myasthenia gravis to avoid the use of muscle relaxants. Other indications: patients with "full stomach" to avoid risk of aspiration; chronic respiratory disease e.g. emphysema, chronic bronchitis; severe renal, hepatic, or metabolic disturbances; eclamptic toxaemia (helps to reduce blood pressure).
(ii) The procedure is a subarachnoid (spinal) block. The anatomical landmark used is the top of the iliac crest (L4/5 level), and a convenient space between L2 and L5 is selected for needle insertion.
(iii) The midline needle passes through: skin, subcutaneous tissue, supraspinous ligament, interspinous ligament, ligamentum flavum, then enters the epidural space; advancing further it pierces the dural mater and arachnoid mater to enter the subarachnoid space (a "give" is felt on entering the epidural space, and CSF flows freely when the subarachnoid space is reached).
(iv) The structure at risk if the needle is advanced too far within the subarachnoid space is the spinal cord (which in adults terminates at the lower border of L1; the conus medullaris in infants may be as low as L3). In the context of an epidural technique, inadvertent dural puncture and subarachnoid injection of a large volume of local anaesthetic causes a "total spinal" – this is a complication listed specifically for epidural block by inadvertent dural puncture.
(v) Factors affecting spread of local anaesthetic in the subarachnoid space: site of injection; volume of local anaesthetic; speed of injection; position after injection; age and height of patient; pregnancy; presence of other abdominal tumours. A high site of injection, large volume, rapid injection, barbotage, Trendelenburg position immediately after injection, old age, and short stature all tend to give a higher level of block.

(A)
(i) Three types of neuromuscular block:
- Depolarising block (phase-1): produced by agonists of ACh (e.g. suxamethonium, decamethonium); initial depolarisation and fasciculations; unlike ACh, these drugs are not rapidly hydrolysed, so continued depolarisation causes block.
- Non-depolarising block: agents compete with ACh at the motor end plate; do not produce depolarisation; block results from competitive antagonism (e.g. d-tubocurarine, pancuronium, atracurium).
- Mixed (dual) block: may result from simultaneous administration of both depolarising and non-depolarising agents, or from repeated dosing of a depolarising agent; features of both types are present.

(ii) Classification by duration of action:
- Ultra-short: suxamethonium.
- Short: mivacurium.
- Intermediate: vecuronium, atracurium, rocuronium, cisatracurium.
- Long: pancuronium, pipecuronium, doxacurium, gallamine.

(iii) Chemical structure classification:
- Benzylisoquinolinium compounds: atracurium, cisatracurium, mivacurium, d-tubocurarine.
- Aminosteroid compounds: pancuronium, vecuronium, rocuronium, pipecuronium.

(B)
(i) Suxamethonium is presented as suxamethonium chloride, clear solutions of 50 mg/ml in 2 ml or 10 ml glass bottles; it is water soluble. Dose: 1–1.5 mg/kg for tracheal intubation. Onset: 60–90 seconds. Duration: 3 minutes; total recovery time 12–15 minutes.
(ii) Mechanism: depolarising agent (agonist at nicotinic receptors); causes initial depolarisation and muscle contraction (fasciculation) then flaccid relaxation — repolarisation does not occur. Reversed by plasma cholinesterase (pseudocholinesterase); neostigmine is contraindicated. With repeated dosing, phase-2 (dual) block may develop.
(iii) Uses: rapid sequence induction in full-stomach cases (emergency, obstetrics, intra-abdominal masses, diabetic neuropathy); anticipated difficult intubation (obese, mandibular/facial injuries, retropharyngeal abscess).
(iv) Side effects:
- Muscular: muscle pains/myalgia (prevented by pre-curarisation); common in young patients with large muscle mass; fasciculations not typical in children and elderly.
- Cardiovascular: bradycardia (especially with repeated doses); prevented by atropine.
- Gastrointestinal: increased intra-gastric pressure; avoid in hiatus hernia; increased salivary and gastric secretions (muscarinic effect).
- Ocular: increased intraocular pressure (transiently); avoid in penetrating eye injuries and severe glaucoma.
- Electrolyte: hyperkalaemia; normal muscle releases enough potassium to raise serum K+ by 0.5 mEq/L; life-threatening in patients with pre-existing hyperkalaemia, burns, massive trauma, neurological disorders, stroke.

(C)
(i) Indications for neuromuscular monitoring: prolonged anaesthesia; when infusions of NMB have been used; renal or hepatic dysfunction; previous history of prolonged effects; neuromuscular disorders; unexpected poor recovery.
(ii) Modes of stimulation: single twitch; train-of-four (TOF); tetanic stimulation; double burst stimulation (DBS); post-tetanic count (PTC).
(iii) Clinical signs of adequate recovery: sustained head lift for 5 seconds; ability to lift the leg (in children); ability to generate negative inspiratory pressure of at least 25 cmH2O; ability to swallow and maintain a patent airway. Other crude tests: tongue protrusion, arm lift, hand grip strength.
