(A)
(i) Superior border: foramen magnum. Inferior border: sacral hiatus. Posterior border: anterior surfaces of the vertebral laminae and ligamenta flava between the intervertebral foramina.
(ii) Contents: blood vessels (spinal arteries and the valveless venous plexus of Batson); nerves (dural sacs and spinal roots); fat; and lymphatics.
(iii) Layers traversed (midline): skin, subcutaneous tissue, supraspinous ligament, interspinous ligament, and ligamentum flavum.
(iv) Methods of identification depend on the negative pressure in the epidural space:
- Loss of resistance: when the plunger of a glass syringe containing air or liquid is gently pushed, a "give" is suddenly felt when the epidural space is entered.
- Hanging drop: a drop of liquid hanging from the hub of the epidural needle is sucked in when the epidural space is entered.
(v) Factors affecting spread: site of injection; volume of local anaesthetic; speed of injection; position after injection; age and height of patient; pregnancy; presence of abdominal tumours. A high site, large volume, rapid injection, Trendelenburg position, old age, and short stature all tend to give a higher level of block.

(B)
(i) Respiratory: alterations in pulmonary variables in healthy patients are usually of little clinical consequence; tidal volume is unchanged during high spinal anaesthesia; vital capacity decreases by a small amount.
(ii) Cardiovascular: bradycardia and hypotension, due to the sympathectomy effect; dependent on the height of block.
(iii) GI: nausea and vomiting in up to 20% of patients due to hyperperistalsis from unopposed parasympathetic (vagal) activity. Renal: renal blood flow is maintained through autoregulation; little clinical effect on renal function; blockage of sympathetic and parasympathetic supply to the bladder results in urinary retention.

(C) Epidural vs Subarachnoid:
- Ease of technique: more difficult (epidural) vs easier (subarachnoid).
- Type of needle: bigger Tuohy needle (epidural) vs smaller needle (subarachnoid).
- Dose of anaesthetic: much more (epidural) vs much less (subarachnoid).
- Onset of action: slower (epidural) vs quicker (subarachnoid).
- Control of block height: more difficult (epidural) vs easier via baricity (subarachnoid).
- Catheter placement: often placed (epidural) vs not usually placed (subarachnoid).
- Spinal headache: does not occur with epidural; may occur with subarachnoid block.

A(i) In sepsis, shock, multiple trauma, burns, and other serious illnesses such as myocardial infarction, there is an outpouring of counter-regulatory endocrine hormones, cytokines, and lymphokines. This results in changes in substrate utilisation and substance synthesis rates, as well as catabolism and hypermetabolism. Nutritional support is aimed at minimising these complications (starvation metabolism).
A(ii) Indications for TPN: patients whose GI tract is not functional; anticipation of undernutrition (less than 50% of metabolic needs met) for more than 7 days; severely undernourished patients being prepared for surgery, radiation therapy, or chemotherapy who cannot ingest large volumes of oral feedings; to reduce morbidity and mortality after major surgery, severe burns, and head trauma, especially in patients with sepsis; patients with disorders requiring complete bowel rest (e.g. some stages of Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, severe pancreatitis); patients with paediatric GI disorders (e.g. congenital anomalies, prolonged diarrhoea regardless of cause).
B(i) Basic adult daily requirements for TPN: Water – 30–40 mL/kg/day. Energy: medical patient – 30 kcal/kg; postoperative patient – 30–45 kcal/kg; hypercatabolic patient – 45–60 kcal/kg. Amino acids: medical patient – 1.0 g/kg; postoperative patient – 2.0 g/kg; hypercatabolic patient – 3.0 g/kg. Additional requirements include essential fatty acids, vitamins, and minerals (e.g. acetate/gluconate 90 mEq, calcium 15 mEq, magnesium 20 mEq, chromium 15 mcg, copper 1.5 mg).
B(ii) Routes of nutritional support: Enteral – oral, nasogastric, gastrostomy, jejunostomy. Parenteral – via central venous catheter. Partial parenteral nutrition supplies only part of daily nutritional requirements, supplementing oral intake. Total parenteral nutrition (TPN) supplies all daily nutritional requirements and can be used in the hospital or at home. TPN solutions are concentrated and can cause thrombosis of peripheral veins – therefore they require central venous catheter administration. Patients receive dextrose or amino acid solutions by this method.
questions.question:
A(i) Describe the physiological response to severe illness (sepsis, shock, multiple trauma, burns) that necessitates nutritional support, including the hormonal and metabolic changes involved.
A(ii) State the indications for total parenteral nutrition (TPN).
B(i) State the daily nutritional requirements for TPN for an adult, including water, energy (for medical, postoperative, and hypercatabolic patients), and amino acid requirements for each category.
B(ii) Describe the two routes of nutritional support (enteral and parenteral), including the types of parenteral nutrition and why TPN solutions require central venous administration.

A(i) Describe the gross physiology of neuromuscular transmission from the arrival of an action potential at the nerve terminal to the generation of muscle contraction, including the role of calcium, acetylcholine, and the motor end plate.
A(ii) Explain how acetylcholinesterase terminates the neuromuscular signal and restores the motor end plate to its resting state.
B(i) Describe the two types of neuromuscular block (depolarising and non-depolarising) and the mixed block, including which agents produce each type.
B(ii) State how the two types of block differ on nerve stimulator monitoring (single twitch, post-tetanic facilitation, and train-of-four) and explain why anticholinesterases reverse one type but potentiate the other.
questions.answerText:
A(i) The motor end plate is a specialised membrane at the NMJ. At rest it is less permeable to Na. Na is extracellular, K is intracellular, producing an electrical resting potential of about -90 mV. Impulses arriving at the end of the motor neurone increase the permeability of its endings to Ca; Ca enters the endings and triggers a marked increase in exocytosis of ACh-containing vesicles. ACh release is affected by Ca, calmodulin, and Mg. ACh is released from storage vesicles and diffuses to muscle-type nicotinic ACh receptors concentrated at the tops of the junctional folds of the motor end plate membrane. Binding of ACh to these receptors alters membrane permeability, increasing Na and K conductance with resultant Na influx and K efflux. The Na influx produces a depolarising potential – the END PLATE POTENTIAL. When the end plate potential reaches about 45 mV, an action potential is propagated, causing muscle contraction. Action potentials are generated on either side of the end plate and conducted away from the end plate in both directions along the muscle fibre.
A(ii) ACh released is rapidly hydrolysed and removed from the synaptic cleft by acetylcholinesterase, which is present in high concentrations at the NMJ. This restores the membrane impermeability to Na, allowing the motor end plate and muscle fibres to be repolarised.
B(i) Depolarising block: produced by agonists of acetylcholine; causes initial depolarisation; unlike ACh, these drugs are not as rapidly hydrolysed, so continued depolarisation causes neuromuscular block. Examples: suxamethonium and decamethonium. Non-depolarising block: agents compete with ACh for the motor end plate; they do not produce depolarisation but cause neuromuscular block. Examples: d-tubocurarine, pancuronium, gallamine, atracurium. Mixed block: may result from simultaneous administration of both depolarising and non-depolarising muscle relaxants; features of both types are present.
B(ii) On nerve stimulator monitoring: Depolarising agents – twitch height is reduced with no fade on single twitch; post-tetanic fasciculation is absent; response to tetanic stimulation is small but sustained. Non-depolarising agents – twitch height is reduced and there is fade on single twitch; post-tetanic facilitation is present; tetanic stimulation produces a response that reduces and fades (decreases in amplitude). Anticholinesterases inhibit acetylcholinesterase, increasing ACh concentration at the NMJ; the higher ACh competes with non-depolarising agents at nicotinic receptors and reverses non-depolarising block. In contrast, with depolarising block the block is increased (potentiated) because the already-elevated ACh further intensifies depolarisation.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the epidural space under the following headings: anatomical borders, contents, and the layers through which a midline epidural needle passes.
A(ii) Describe the two principal methods used to identify the epidural space and explain the anatomical basis for each method.
B(i) Distinguish between epidural and subarachnoid (spinal) blocks under the following headings: ease of technique, type of needle, dose of anaesthetic, onset of action, control of block height, catheter placement, and risk of spinal headache.
B(ii) State the indications and contraindications of spinal anaesthesia.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Anatomical borders: Superior border – foramen magnum; Inferior border – sacral hiatus; Posterior border – anterior surfaces of the vertebral laminae and ligamenta flava between the intervertebral foramina. Contents: blood vessels (spinal arteries and the valveless venous plexus of Batson), nerves (dural sacs and spinal roots), fat, and lymphatics. Layers the midline needle passes through: skin, subcutaneous tissue, supraspinous ligament, interspinous ligament, and ligamentum flavum.
A(ii) Both methods depend on the negative pressure in the epidural space. Loss of resistance: when the plunger of a glass syringe containing air or liquid is gently pushed, a "give" is suddenly felt when the epidural space is entered. Hanging drop: a drop of liquid hanging from the hub of the epidural needle is sucked in when the epidural space is entered.
B(i) Epidural vs. subarachnoid block: Ease of technique – epidural is more difficult; subarachnoid is easier. Type of needle – epidural uses a bigger needle (Tuohy); subarachnoid uses a smaller needle. Dose of anaesthetic – epidural requires much more; subarachnoid requires much less. Onset of action – epidural is slower; subarachnoid is quicker. Control of block height – more difficult with epidural; easier with subarachnoid (via baricity). Catheter placement – often placed with epidural; not usually placed with subarachnoid. Spinal headache – does not occur with epidural; may occur with subarachnoid. "Total spinal" – may occur with epidural by inadvertent dural puncture; rarely occurs with subarachnoid.
B(ii) Indications for spinal anaesthesia: patients with "full stomach" to avoid risk of aspiration; chronic respiratory disease e.g. emphysema and chronic bronchitis; severe renal, hepatic, or metabolic disturbances; eclamptic toxaemia (helps to reduce blood pressure); myasthenia gravis (to avoid use of muscle relaxants). Contraindications: lack of co-operation or refusal by patient; hypovolaemia or shock; clotting disorder or anticoagulant therapy; deformity of the spine e.g. scoliosis; skin sepsis at or near the proposed site of puncture; pre-existing neurological deficit (medicolegal implication).

questions.question:
Describe the Blood/Gas Partition Coefficient and the Blood:Gas relationship for inhalational anaesthetics under the following headings:

A(i) Definition of the blood/gas partition coefficient and what it indicates
A(ii) Relationship between blood/gas partition coefficient, induction speed, and recovery
B(i) The concentration effect and second gas effect
B(ii) How increasing fluorination of the carbon skeleton affects physical and clinical properties
C(i) Distinguish between volatile liquid anaesthetics and anaesthetic gases, giving examples of each
questions.answerText:
A(i) The blood/gas partition coefficient is the measure of the solubility of an inhalation anaesthetic in blood as compared to alveolar gas (air). It is an indication of the speed of induction and recovery for an inhalation anaesthetic agent. A low blood/gas partition coefficient means the agent is more soluble in alveolar gas than in blood at equilibrium, and is less soluble in blood.

A(ii) A lower blood/gas partition coefficient means faster expected induction and recovery, because alveolar tension of the anaesthetic builds up faster. Conversely, a high blood/gas partition coefficient (e.g. halothane at 2.5, ether at 12) means slower induction and recovery. Examples: Sevoflurane blood/gas solubility 0.69 (rapid induction); Desflurane MAC 6.35% but very low solubility giving rapid recovery; Halothane MAC 0.75% but recovery slower than other agents due to high blood/gas solubility.

B(i) Concentration effect: during GA, N2O is taken faster from alveoli to pulmonary capillary blood; as a result the concentration of other gases (e.g. halothane, O2) remaining in the alveoli increases — this phenomenon is known as the concentration effect. Second gas effect: when a 'first gas' (usually a volatile anaesthetic or O2) moves from lungs to plasma, it increases the alveolar concentration; consequently the rate of uptake into plasma of the 'second gas' (e.g. another inhalational gas) also increases. Nitrous oxide, despite being a carrier gas, can also behave as a second gas in this context.

B(ii) Increasing fluorination of the carbon skeleton: increases SVP and stability; reduces boiling point, flammability, and toxicity; also reduces both metabolism and toxicity. Solubility is reduced with lowering of molecular weight (e.g. fluoride ions are lighter than chloride and bromide, so desflurane — having fluoride ions in place of chloride — is less soluble than enflurane). Soda lime: formation of CO can occur when dry (used) soda lime comes into contact with desflurane, enflurane, and isoflurane.

C(i) Volatile liquid anaesthetics: liquids with a low boiling point and high saturated vapour pressure so that they evaporate easily; examples — desflurane, isoflurane, sevoflurane, enflurane, halothane. Anaesthetic gases: examples — nitrous oxide, cyclopropane, ethylene, xenon, argon, sulphur hexafluoride. Chloroform, ether, and nitrous oxide were the first universally accepted general anaesthetics; chloroform and ether are no longer in use.

A(i) Transduction at nociceptors:
- Nociceptors respond to noxious stimuli: strong mechanical, thermal, chemical; inflammatory agents (prostaglandins, bradykinin, 5HT, histamine, ATP, cytokines — IL, TNF — NO, free radicals, H+, K+)
- Activation of nociceptors results in pain; the process of activation is transduction
- Mechanism involves voltage-gated Na+/K+ pump
- Blockade achieved by local anaesthetics and tetrodotoxin

A(ii) Peripheral sensitisation:
- Persistent noxious stimuli lower the threshold for firing of A-delta and C-fibres
- Non-noxious stimuli can then activate nociceptors
- Role of prostaglandins (PGs) in sensitisation
- Clinical manifestations: allodynia and hyperalgesia

B(i) Opioid receptor classification:
- Mu (μ): mu-1 and mu-2 subtypes; activation responsible for supraspinal and spinal analgesia
- Kappa (κ): result in spinal analgesia
- Delta (δ): spinal analgesia (less clearly characterised in some models; delta agonists are more effective in persistent pain states)
- Sigma (σ): autonomic effects, dysphoria, hallucinations
- Orphan receptor 1998: opioid receptor-like (ORL-1); stimulated by endogenous agonist Orphanin FQ

B(ii) Clinically available opioids:
- The only opioids available for clinical use are those that act at mu and kappa receptors
- Endogenous opioids involved in nociception: enkephalins, beta-endorphins, dynorphins
- Systemically available delta opioid receptor agonists should be effective analgesics but are not yet in standard clinical use

B(iii) Clinical significance of delta receptor:
- Systemically available delta opioid receptor agonists should be effective analgesics
- Delta opioid receptor agonists are more effective in persistent pain states
- In chronic pain: mu-receptors are down-regulated and opioids are not effective in neuropathic pain; central sensitisation occurs

C(i) Gene therapy approaches:
- Cell transplantation: allogenic adrenal tissue infused into the subarachnoid space; chromaffin cells secrete a mixture of compounds producing profound analgesia; problems: rejection; secretion of other agents with deleterious effects; solution: developing specific analgesic cell lines for transplantation
- Recombinant viruses as vectors: spinal intraparenchymal or intrathecal injection of adenovirus to transfect spinal cord neurons or meningeal cells (genes encoding analgesic peptides) — express and secrete analgesic peptides
- Recombinant herpes virus as vectors to selectively alter the genome of primary afferent nociceptors

C(ii) Refinement of known mechanisms and improved formulations:
- Refinement: COX-2 selective inhibitors for NSAID class
- Improved formulation: slow-release morphine (oral morphine) for terminal pain
- Elucidation of unknown mechanism: anticonvulsants for neuropathic pain; tricyclic antidepressants (TCA)
questions.question:
A. Describe the physiology of pain modulation at the peripheral and central levels:
A(i) The process of transduction at nociceptors: stimuli, the voltage-gated channels involved, and agents that block transduction

B(i) Traditional receptor classification: mu (with subtypes), kappa, delta, sigma, and the orphan receptor identified in 1998
B(ii) Which opioids are available for clinical use and which receptors they act on

C. Describe the novel/experimental approaches to analgesia:
C(i) Gene therapy approaches: cell transplantation and recombinant viral vectors
C(ii) Refinement of known mechanisms and improved drug formulations mentioned.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Unidimensional pain scales:
- Numerical rating scale: 0 corresponds to no pain; 10 designates the worst pain possible
- Visual Analogue Scale (VAS): a 10cm horizontal line labelled 'no pain' at one end and 'worst pain imaginable' at the other end; patient marks where intensity lies; distance from 'no pain' to marked area quantifies pain; simple, efficient and minimally intrusive; correlates well with other methods
- Faces pain scale: useful in patients with communication difficulties, especially children; patient points to various facial expressions ranging from a smiling face (no pain) to an extremely unhappy one (worst possible pain)
- Verbal rating scale: short and easy to administer; non-continuous and generally unsatisfactory; examples: describing pain as none, mild, moderate or severe

A(ii) Multidimensional methods:
- McGill Pain Questionnaire (MPQ): checklist of words describing symptoms; 20 sets of descriptors divided into four major groups (sensory, affective, evaluative, miscellaneous); patient selects sets that apply; reliable; can be completed in 5–15 minutes; choice of words correlates with pain syndromes and is diagnostically useful
- Minnesota Multiphasic Personality Inventory (MMPI): psychological evaluation useful when medical evaluation fails to reveal cause, or when pain intensity is disproportionate to disease/injury; defines role of psychological or behavioural factors; 566-item true/false questionnaire attempting to define patient's personality; very lengthy and cumbersome
- Beck Depression Inventory: useful test for identifying patients with major depression; depression is very common in patients with chronic pain

B(i) Excitatory neurotransmitters in dorsal horn:
- Excitatory amino acids: glutamate — present in >1/2 of dorsal root ganglion neurons; responsible for fast pain
- Peptides: calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) — most widely distributed; substance P — follows CGRP; somatostatin — in cells with C-fibres; response to noxious thermal stimuli; vasoactive intestinal polypeptide (VIP) — numerous in thoracic and sacral spinal nerves and cranial nerves innervating viscera; galanin — present in 15% of dorsal root neurons

B(ii) Central inhibitory systems and receptor types:
- Opioid receptors
- Alpha-2 adrenergic receptors
- GABA receptors
- Glycine receptors
- Serotonin receptors
- Adenosine receptors

B(iii) Four transmitter-receptor components in dorsal horn:
- EAA-AMPA
- EAA-NMDA
- EAA-mGluR
- SP-NK1

C. Peripheral sensitisation:
- Definition: persistent noxious stimuli lower the threshold for firing of A-delta and C-fibres
- Trigger: persistent noxious stimuli; prostaglandins (PGs)
- Non-noxious stimuli can then activate nociceptors
- Clinical manifestations: allodynia (normally non-painful stimulus evokes pain) and hyperalgesia

A(i) The four unidimensional pain scales and how each works

B(i) The excitatory neurotransmitters liberated in the dorsal horn including the amino acids and peptides named

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Shock. The clinical features (hypotension, tachycardia, oliguria, metabolic acidosis, depressed sensorium, cold clammy skin) indicate cardiogenic or hypovolaemic shock with end-organ dysfunction.

(ii) Causes by class:
- Cardiogenic: CCF, MI, post-cardiac surgery, aortic incompetence, left ventricular aneurysm.
- Obstructive: cardiac tamponade, pulmonary embolism.
- Hypovolaemic: haemorrhage, dehydration.
- Distributive: sepsis, anaphylaxis, neurogenic (vascular dilation, A-V shunting).

(iii) Pathophysiology: shock represents an imbalance in oxygen supply and demand with conversion from aerobic to anaerobic metabolism. Sympathoadrenal response: increased HR, contractility, SVR and decreased venous capacitance to maintain CO and BP. Renin-angiotensin system causes sodium and water retention. Cell membrane ion pump dysfunction, leakage of intracellular contents into extracellular space, and intracellular pH dysregulation lead to cell death and end-organ dysfunction.

(iv) Complications: acute respiratory distress syndrome (shock lung); acute renal failure; disseminated intravascular coagulopathy (DIC); multi-organ failure including hepatic and GIT failure; death.

(v) Management:
- Treat the primary cause: haemorrhage → IV fluids/blood; sepsis → antibiotics; adrenocortical insufficiency → steroids; cardiogenic → inotropes.
- Support the cardiovascular system with IV fluids and inotropes (e.g. dopamine, dobutamine, adrenaline, noradrenaline); vasodilators (GTN, sodium nitroprusside) as indicated.
- Respiratory support: O2 therapy and mechanical ventilation.
- Renal support: haemofiltration/haemodialysis for renal failure.
- Haematological: blood transfusion to correct anaemia; other blood products for coagulopathy.
- Monitoring: BP, pulse rate, temperature, urine output (0.5–2 ml/hr), CVP (0–8 cmH2O), PAWP (<15 cmH2O), direct arterial BP, ABG, blood lactate.
questions.question:
A 45-year-old woman with a history of heavy smoking and hypertension develops sudden circulatory collapse during a surgical procedure. She is found to be tachycardic, hypotensive, oliguric, and has cold clammy peripheries with depressed sensorium. Her metabolic profile shows a lactic acidosis.

(i) What is the diagnosis, and what class of this condition does she most likely represent?
(ii) List the risk factors and common causes for this class of the condition.
(iii) Describe the pathophysiological sequence of events leading to her clinical state.
(iv) Outline the complications that may develop if the condition is not promptly reversed.
(v) Describe the management options available, justifying each intervention.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Definition: defibrillation is an electrical charge introduced into the myocardium which is sufficient to depolarize the entire heart and permit the normal cardiac rhythm to be established. Role in the chain of survival: basic life support is defined by the first 3 links in the chain of survival – early access, early and qualitative CPR, and early defibrillation. Reasons defibrillation must not be delayed: ventricular fibrillation is the most frequent initial rhythm (40% of sudden cardiac arrest); electrical defibrillation is the most important treatment for VF; probability of survival decreases with time; VF consumes more energy; VF converts to asystole within a few minutes, after which successful resuscitation is unlikely; BLS plus defibrillation within 3–5 minutes increases survival rate to 49–75%; neurological survival is possible within 6–10 minutes of defibrillation.
A(ii) The four cardiac arrest rhythms: ventricular fibrillation; pulseless ventricular tachycardia; asystole; pulseless electrical activity (PEA). VF characteristics: bizarre irregular waveform; no recognisable QRS complexes; random frequency and amplitude; uncoordinated electrical activity; may be coarse or fine; artefact (movement, electrical interference) must be excluded. Pulseless VT: Monomorphic VT – broad complex rhythm, rapid rate, constant QRS morphology. Polymorphic VT – torsade de pointes.
B(i) Universal steps: Step 1 – always keep the defibrillator batteries charged; power on. Step 2 – ensure that the patient is not in a pool of water; for a diaphoretic patient, dry the chest with a towel; shave hairy chest; rub gel on the chest/paddles to allow conduction.
B(ii) CPR significance: continue CPR pending the arrival of defibrillation. For every minute of delay in CPR, the survival rate drops by 7–10% (but only 3–4% if CPR is commenced before defibrillation). Three-stacked defibrillation is not recommended; CPR should continue before and after each defibrillation attempt.

A(ii) List the four cardiac arrest rhythms, and describe the electrocardiographic characteristics of ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia (both monomorphic and polymorphic forms).
B(i) Describe the universal steps for preparing a patient for defibrillation (Steps 1 and 2).

Describe the specific pharmacology of Sevoflurane and Desflurane as modern volatile inhalational agents under the following headings:

A(i) Sevoflurane — chemical name, physical properties, MAC, CVS, and respiratory effects
A(ii) Sevoflurane — CNS effects, metabolism, contraindications, and effect on soda lime
B(i) Desflurane — chemical name, physical properties, MAC, CNS, and CVS effects
B(ii) Desflurane — ADRs, elimination, contraindications, and storage requirements
C(i) Compare the ease of induction, cardiovascular stability, emergence, and cost ranking of these two agents against the other volatile agents
questions.answerText:
A(i) Sevoflurane: chemical name — fluoromethyl-2,2,2-trifluoro-1-(trifluoromethyl) ethyl ether (halogenated ether). Colour code: yellow. No preservative; supplied in brown bottle with keyed filling system collar. Non-flammable. Pleasant smell. MAC 2% (1.8 in some sources). Blood/gas solubility coefficient 0.69 (rapid induction). Stable; stored in amber-coloured bottle at room temperature away from heat. CVS: decreased heart rate, systemic vascular resistance, and blood pressure but stable cardiac output; no myocardial sensitisation to catecholamines. Respiratory: dose-dependent depression of respiratory rate and tidal volume; bronchodilatation.

A(ii) CNS: anaesthesia, no analgesia, not epileptogenic. Metabolism: 5% metabolised by cytochrome P450 (the most of the modern halogenated ethers). Soda lime: compatible, but may produce Compound A. Contraindications: risk of triggering malignant hyperthermia. Muscle relaxants potentiated; uterine relaxation in pregnancy similar to isoflurane. Elimination: predominantly via lungs.

B(i) Desflurane: chemical name — 1,2,2,2-tetrafluoroethyl difluoromethyl ether (halogenated ether). A pure agent without preservative or stabilisers; supplied in brown bottle with self-closing valve, which fits a special vaporiser. MAC 6.35% (6.6 in some sources). Stored at room temperature away from heat. CNS: anaesthesia, no analgesia, not epileptogenic. CVS: dose-dependent depression similar to isoflurane.

B(ii) ADRs: dose-dependent depression of respiration; respiratory irritant; increased secretions; stimulation of salivary secretions. Elimination: predominantly via lungs; only 0.02% metabolised in liver (least of all volatile agents). Contraindications: risk of triggering malignant hyperthermia. Soda lime: compatible, but avoid exhausted dry granules (formation of CO can occur). Storage: at room temperature away from heat in brown bottle with self-closing valve. Muscle relaxants potentiated.

C(i) Ranking of clinical properties (Worst to Best, scale 0–3): Induction: D (worst), then E/I, then H, then S (best — sevoflurane is best for induction). Cardiovascular stability: H (worst), then D/E/I, then S (best — sevoflurane is most stable). Respiratory irritation: D (worst — most irritant), then E/I, then H/S (best — halothane and sevoflurane least irritant). Ease of titration: H (worst), then E/I, then S, then D (best — desflurane easiest to titrate). Emergence: H (slowest), then I, then E/S, then D (fastest — desflurane gives fastest emergence). Metabolism/toxicity: H (worst), then E/S, then I, then D (safest). Cost (low flow): S (most expensive), then D/E/I, then H (cheapest).

questions.question:
A 40-year-old female is undergoing an elective lower limb procedure under spinal anaesthesia. The block was established uneventfully at the L4/5 interspace. Two days postoperatively, she develops back pain radiating down both legs without motor or sensory deficit. The symptoms resolve spontaneously within 4 days.

(i) Name the most likely postoperative complication and state when it was first described.
(ii) State the local anaesthetic agents most commonly associated with this complication, with the incidence for each.
(iii) Describe the anatomical location and pattern of symptoms that characterise this complication.
(iv) Name the more serious neurological complication that may present similarly but with bowel/bladder dysfunction and motor weakness, and state the conditions that predispose to it.
(v) Differentiate between transient neurological symptoms and cauda equina syndrome on the basis of: duration of symptoms, motor involvement, and associated factors.
questions.answerText:
(i) Transient neurological symptoms (TNS), also referred to as transient radicular irritation. First described in 1993.

(ii) Local anaesthetics and incidence:
- Hyperbaric lidocaine: highest incidence — up to 11.9%.
- Tetracaine: incidence 1.6%.
- Bupivacaine: incidence 1.3%.
- Also reported with: mepivacaine, prilocaine, procaine, and subarachnoid ropivacaine.

(iii) Anatomical location and pattern: back pain radiating to the legs (bilateral, typically); no sensory or motor deficits; occurs after resolution of the spinal block; resolves spontaneously within several days. Incidence is highest among outpatients undergoing surgery in the lithotomy position; lowest among inpatients in positions other than lithotomy.

(iv) More serious complication: cauda equina syndrome (CES). Predisposing conditions: associated with the use of continuous spinal catheters (prior to their withdrawal from clinical use) and 5% lidocaine. CES has also been reported after uneventful single-shot lidocaine spinal and epidural anaesthesia.

(v) Differentiation between TNS and cauda equina syndrome:
- TNS: symptoms (back pain, radiation to legs) occur after resolution of the block; resolve spontaneously within several days; no motor deficit; no bowel or bladder dysfunction.
- CES: characterised by bowel and bladder dysfunction; evidence of multiple nerve root injury; lower motor neuron type injury with paresis of legs; pain may be similar to nerve root compromise; does not resolve spontaneously and may be permanent. Duration: CES is persistent and serious, not self-limiting like TNS.

questions.question:
A(i) Describe rocuronium under the following headings: classification, onset of action, duration of action, intubating dose, cardiovascular effects, route of elimination, and use in rapid sequence induction.
A(ii) Explain how sugammadex reverses rocuronium (and other aminosteroid NMBAs) and state the order of affinity.
B(i) Describe the autonomic side effects of non-depolarising NMBAs, distinguishing between aminosteroids and benzylisoquinolines.
B(ii) State the considerations that guide the choice of muscle relaxant for clinical use.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Classification: rocuronium is a non-depolarising NMBA; it is an aminosteroid compound and an analogue of vecuronium. Onset: rapid – 1–2 minutes (onset time >60 seconds for intubation; 60–90 seconds for rapid sequence at higher dose); onset of action similar to that of succinylcholine. Duration: intermediate – 20–35 minutes (at standard dose); at 0.9–1.2 mg/kg, duration is much longer. Intubating dose: 0.45–0.9 mg/kg IV for intubation; 0.9–1.2 mg/kg for rapid-sequence induction (as alternative to suxamethonium). Cardiovascular effects: causes tachycardia when large doses are given (steroidal/vagolytic effect). Elimination: primarily by the liver with slight renal excretion. Use in rapid sequence: can be used as a substitute for suxamethonium, particularly when suxamethonium is contraindicated; 0.1 mg/kg of rocuronium prior to suxamethonium reduces fasciculation and postoperative myalgia.
A(ii) Sugammadex is a gamma-cyclodextrin derivative. It reverses aminosteroid NMBAs by encapsulating (forming a tight complex with) the drug molecule in the plasma, reducing the free concentration; the drug then diffuses away from the NMJ down the concentration gradient, allowing rapid recovery. The NMB-sugammadex complex is excreted by the kidneys. Order of affinity: rocuronium > vecuronium > pancuronium.
B(i) Autonomic side effects: Aminosteroids – vagolytic; pancuronium blocks muscarinic receptors in the SA node causing tachycardia; rocuronium causes tachycardia in large doses. Benzylisoquinolines – release histamine, causing bronchospasm, skin flushing, and hypotension from peripheral vasodilation (atracurium, mivacurium); aminosteroids (NMBDs in this class) do not cause histamine release.
B(ii) Considerations for choosing a muscle relaxant: duration of action required; route of excretion; tendency to release histamine; cardiopulmonary side effects; ability to reverse the blockade; contraindication to any specific muscle relaxant; cost.

A(i) Definition and levels of care:
- The ICU is a specially staffed hospital ward dedicated to the management of critically ill patients with reversible organ dysfunction, life-threatening illness, injuries or complications who will benefit from facilities not available in the general hospital ward
- Level 0: patients whose needs can be met at the normal ward
- Level 1 (HDU): patients at risk of deteriorating or recently relocated from higher level of care; located in district hospital with close nursing observation, ECG monitoring, immediate resuscitation and short-term (<24 hours) ventilation
- Level 2: regional general hospital ICU; access to physiotherapy, pathology and radiological services; prolonged ventilation; complex life support not normally provided e.g. renal dialysis, invasive monitoring, CT scan
- Level 3: provides all aspects of ICU care; staffed with intensivists, trainees, critical care nurses and allied healthcare professionals; supports all complex investigations and imaging

A(ii) Design requirements:
- Location: close to operating theatre, accident and emergency unit, x-ray and laboratory facilities; single entry point; end corridor; CCTV surveillance
- Size: approximately 20 square metres per bed space (25 square metres in single room); total area 2.5–3 times the patient area
- Nurse-to-patient ratio: 1:1 (HDU: 1:2)
- Usually 1–2% of total acute hospital beds
- Available areas: reception area, waiting room, patient area (open multi-bedded or single rooms), central nursing station, storage area (25–30% of floor space), unit laboratory, pharmacy, seminar room, offices

B. Categories of organ system support:
- Advanced respiratory support: mechanical ventilatory support or non-invasive ventilation; the possibility of sudden deterioration in respiratory function
- Basic respiratory support: need for inspired oxygen concentration >40%; physiotherapy to clear secretions at least 2-hourly; mask CPAP or non-invasive ventilation; recently extubated after prolonged intubation
- Circulatory support: need for vasoactive drugs; circulatory instability from hypovolaemia unresponsive to modest volume replacement; patients resuscitated after cardiac arrest
- Neurological monitoring/support: CNS depression sufficient to compromise airway and impair protective reflexes; invasive neurological monitoring
- Renal support: need for acute renal replacement therapy e.g. haemodialysis, haemofiltration

C(i) ICU types:
- Closed ICU: a director (intensivist) has full control of admission, discharge and referral
- Open ICU: provides unrestricted multiple doctors' access; specialists freely admit, manage and discharge patients
- Semi-closed ICU: team of anaesthetists in charge for day-to-day and emergency aspects but co-manage with referring specialists; line of management and responsibilities not well defined

C(ii) Advantages of closed ICU:
- Improved cost-benefit
- Better patient outcome
- Optimal knowledge and experience by the trainee

C(iii) Conditions for maximum success:
- A clearly defined line of management
- Clear job description for all members of staff
- Director in charge has overall authority over the staff and their actions
- Staff responsible to other heads

questions.answerText:
A(i) Anticholinesterases inhibit acetylcholinesterase, the enzyme that hydrolyses acetylcholine to choline and acetate. This allows more ACh to accumulate at the NMJ, competing with the non-depolarising agent at nicotinic cholinergic receptors and reversing the competitive block. They should NOT be used for suxamethonium (depolarising) block because: anticholinesterases inhibit pseudocholinesterase, which is the enzyme responsible for metabolising suxamethonium; inhibiting it prolongs suxamethonium blockade (Phase 1 block is increased, not reversed). Additionally, in Phase 2 (desensitisation) block, anticholinesterases may have unpredictable effects.
A(ii) Neostigmine: onset 2–5 minutes (onset 5–10 minutes in some sources); duration approximately 45–60 minutes; used to reverse non-depolarising neuromuscular blockade; dose 0.04–0.08 mg/kg (up to 5 mg in adults); the onset of glycopyrrolate is similar to neostigmine making it a preferred anticholinergic match. Edrophonium: most rapid onset (1–2 minutes); shortest duration (5–20 minutes); primarily used to diagnose myasthenia gravis and differentiate myasthenic crisis from cholinergic crisis; longer-acting NMBAs may outlast edrophonium's effects; in equipotent doses, edrophonium's muscarinic effects are less, requiring only half the amount of anticholinergic agent; its rapid onset matches well with atropine.
B(i) Muscarinic side effects of anticholinesterases: bradycardia, miosis, nausea, bronchospasm, increased bronchial secretions, sweating, salivation, increased intestinal motility, and blurred vision. Antimuscarinic (anticholinergic) drugs such as atropine and glycopyrrolate are administered simultaneously with anticholinesterases to block these unwanted muscarinic effects while preserving the desired nicotinic reversal at the NMJ.
B(ii) Clinical assessment of adequate reversal: strong hand grip; good cough; sustained protrusion of the tongue; ability to raise head from pillow; sustained head lift for 5 seconds; ability to generate negative inspiratory pressure of at least 25 cmH2O; ability to swallow and maintain a patent airway. Other crude tests: tongue protrusion, arm lift. Peripheral nerve stimulator criteria (more objective, usable in conscious and unconscious patients): sustained tetanus for 5 seconds in response to a 100 Hz stimulus; sustained head lift; TOF ratio indicating adequate recovery; the higher the frequency of stimulation, the greater the sensitivity (100 Hz tetany > 50 Hz or train-of-four > single-twitch height).
questions.question:

A(ii) Compare neostigmine and edrophonium under the following headings: onset, duration, primary clinical use, dose, and the appropriate anticholinergic agent to co-administer with each.

B(ii) Describe the clinical criteria used to assess adequacy of neuromuscular reversal – both clinical signs and peripheral nerve stimulator criteria.

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: residual neuromuscular blockade (inadequate reversal of non-depolarising neuromuscular block with pancuronium). Confirmation: clinical signs include inability to sustain head lift, weak hand grip, inability to maintain adequate spontaneous ventilation. Nerve stimulator findings: TOF showing 3/4 twitches with fade (fade on TOF indicates non-depolarising block; <4/4 twitches or TOF ratio <0.9 indicates clinically significant residual block).
(ii) Hierarchy of block / receptor occupancy: 99–100% occupied – no response to nerve stimulator, flaccid extreme relaxation. 95% – post-tetanic facilitation present, diaphragm moves. 90% – one of four TOF twitches present, abdominal relaxation adequate. 75% – four TOF twitches present with TOF ratio 0.7, tidal volume and vital capacity normal. 50% – 100 Hz tetanus sustained, passes inspiratory pressure test. 30% – 200 Hz tetanus sustained, head lift and hand-grip sustained. Three out of four TOF twitches with fade indicates approximately 90–95% receptor occupancy, meaning significant residual block is present; the patient cannot maintain adequate ventilation or airway protection.
(iii) Pharmacological reversal: neostigmine is the most commonly used anticholinesterase. Mechanism: inhibits acetylcholinesterase, allowing ACh to accumulate at the NMJ and compete with the non-depolarising agent for nicotinic receptors. Dose: 0.04–0.08 mg/kg (up to 5 mg in adults). Onset: 2–5 minutes, peak at 10 minutes. Duration: approximately 45–60 minutes. Recovery from neuromuscular blockade is maximally enhanced by 5–7 minutes.
(iv) Neostigmine also stimulates muscarinic receptors, causing bradycardia, excessive salivation, bronchospasm, increased intestinal motility, sweating, and bronchospasm. An anticholinergic (antimuscarinic) agent is co-administered to block these muscarinic side effects while preserving the nicotinic reversal. The onset of glycopyrrolate is similar to neostigmine, making it a better match than atropine and resulting in less tachycardia.
(v) Clinical criteria for extubation/adequacy of reversal: strong hand grip; good cough; sustained protrusion of the tongue; ability to raise head from pillow; sustained head lift for 5 seconds; ability to generate negative inspiratory pressure of at least 25 cmH2O; ability to swallow and maintain a patent airway. Peripheral nerve stimulator objective criterion: sustained tetanus for 5 seconds in response to a 100 Hz stimulus and sustained head lift.
questions.question:

(A) Describe the spinal cord and its coverings under the following headings:
(i) Extent of the spinal cord from above downwards, stating how the level of termination differs between infant and adult.
(ii) The three membranes covering the spinal cord (from within outward), with a note on the vascularity of each.
(iii) Contents of the subarachnoid space.
(iv) Boundaries and contents of the epidural space.

(B) Explain the clinical basis of the following complications of spinal and epidural anaesthesia:
(i) Post-dural puncture headache (PDPH): mechanism, typical features, and causes.
(ii) Urinary retention: mechanism and patient group most affected.
(iii) Total spinal: definition, clinical features, and management steps.

(C) Distinguish between the absolute and relative contraindications to spinal and epidural anaesthesia.
questions.answerText:
(A)
(i) The spinal cord is continuously cephalad with the brainstem at the foramen magnum and terminates distally in the conus medullaris. Termination: at L3 in the infant; at the lower border of L1 in the adult.
(ii) Three membranes (inner to outer):
- Pia mater: highly vascular membrane that closely invests the spinal cord (and brain).
- Arachnoid mater: non-vascular membrane closely attached to the outermost layer (dura).
- Dural mater: outermost layer.
(iii) Contents of the subarachnoid space (between pia and arachnoid): CSF, spinal nerves, a trabecular network between the two membranes, blood vessels that supply the spinal cord, and the dentate ligaments.
(iv) Epidural space surrounds the dura mater posteriorly, laterally, and anteriorly. Boundaries: anteriorly — posterior longitudinal ligament; laterally — pedicles and intervertebral foramina; posteriorly — ligamentum flavum. Contents: nerve roots, fat, areolar tissue, lymphatics, and blood vessels.

(B)
(i) PDPH: results from CSF leakage from the dural defect, causing reduced ICP; CSF is lost at a rate greater than production, causing traction on structures supporting the brain (particularly dura and tentorium) and on blood vessels, contributing to pain. PDPH is typically bilateral, frontal or retroorbital, and occipital, extending into the neck; it may be throbbing or constant. It can follow diagnostic lumbar puncture, myelogram, spinal anaesthesia, epidural wet tap, or epidural catheter puncturing the dura.
(ii) Urinary retention: caused by blockage of sympathetic and parasympathetic supply to the bladder, decreasing bladder tone and inhibiting voiding reflex. Epidural opioids can also interfere with voiding. Effects are most pronounced in males. Persistent bladder dysfunction can also indicate serious neural injury. Management: bladder catheterisation for all but the shortest acting blocks.
(iii) Total spinal: occurs in epidural block when there is inadvertent subarachnoid injection of a larger volume of local anaesthetic. Block extends to cervical level causing: hypotension, bradycardia, respiratory insufficiency, unconsciousness, and apnoea. Management: maintain airway and ventilation; support circulation; intubate and mechanically ventilate when respiratory insufficiency occurs; treat hypotension with vasopressors; treat cardiac arrest aggressively.

(C) Absolute contraindications: patient refusal, infection at the site of injection, coagulopathy or other bleeding diathesis, severe hypovolaemia, increased intracranial pressure, severe aortic stenosis, severe mitral stenosis. Relative contraindications: sepsis, uncooperative patient, pre-existing neurological deficits, demyelinating lesions, stenotic valvular heart lesions, severe spinal deformity. Controversial: prior back surgery at site, complicated or prolonged operation, major blood loss, manoeuvres that compromise respiration.

(A)
(i) Local anaesthetics are poorly water-soluble weak bases (pKa > 7.4) consisting of a hydrophilic tertiary amine and a hydrophobic (lipophilic) aromatic ring linked by an alkyl chain. The alkyl chain linking group determines the class:
- Esters: linked by "-COO-"; allergic reactions are common; rapidly metabolised by cholinesterase.
- Amides: linked by "NHCO"; allergic reactions are rare (may be preservative-related); metabolised by liver microsomal enzymes (N-dealkylation and hydroxylation). Presented in solutions as acidic hydrochloride salts.

(ii) Mechanism of action: reversible neural blockade from autonomic, sensory, and motor fibres. The drug obstructs/stabilises sodium channels without altering resting membrane potential. It binds fast Na+ channels in the axon membrane from within, preventing Na+ entry during depolarisation; the threshold potential is not reached and the action potential is not propagated. Local tissue acidosis increases ionisation and reduces quality of anaesthesia. LAs cross the membrane in the unionised form and dissociate within the axon to the ionised form. Smallest fibres are blocked first.

(iii) pKa: is the pH at which 50% of the drug is ionised; determines speed of onset — the lower the pKa, the faster the onset (e.g. lignocaine 7.7, bupivacaine 8.1). Lipid solubility: primary determinant of potency; higher solubility increases potency. Protein binding: determines duration; a highly protein-bound LA has longer duration (lignocaine 65%, prilocaine 55%, bupivacaine 95%, procaine 60%). Clearance: esters are hydrolysed by plasma pseudocholinesterases; amides undergo hepatic oxidative alkylation.

(B)
(i) Vasoconstrictors (e.g. adrenaline 1:200,000; phenylephrine 1:20,000; felypressin) produce localised vasoconstriction, limit absorption, and prolong block. Less effective with highly lipid-soluble drugs (e.g. bupivacaine). Systemic absorption of vasopressors leads to arrhythmias and hypertension.
(ii) Smallest fibres are blocked first. Activity is affected by extracellular pH. LAs bind to sodium channels in the open state.

(C)
(i) Ester LAs: allergic reactions are common. Amide LAs: allergic reactions are rare (may be preservative-related).
(ii) Esters: hydrolysed by plasma pseudocholinesterases. Amides: metabolised by hepatic microsomal enzymes via N-dealkylation and hydroxylation.

questions.answerText:
(i) Advantages of regional nerve blocks relevant to this patient: less interruption of oral intake (useful in diabetic patients); consciousness is preserved and the patient is able to assist in positioning and warn of adverse effects; good post-operative analgesia; reduced risk of some post-operative complications such as lung atelectasis, DVT, and PONV – particularly important in a patient with COPD.
(ii) Absolute contraindications: patient's refusal; inexperience of the anaesthetist; local sepsis. Relative contraindications: anatomical deformity; coagulopathy; neurological disease (neuropathies); previous failure of technique.
(iii) Intraoperative care: monitoring of vital signs commenced prior to starting the procedure; aseptic technique throughout; equipment – short-bevelled needles and nerve stimulators; technique may be single bolus injection or repeated boluses with catheter (e.g. epidural). The extent of block is assessed by pin prick or cold before commencement of surgery. Sedation may be required using: Entonox, opioid analgesics, benzodiazepines (diazepam, midazolam), or propofol. Facility for conversion to general anaesthesia must be available. Preoperative care: assessment and preparation as for GA (history, examination, investigations, medications, preoperative fast); informed consent; drugs and equipment for resuscitation including the drugs for the nerve blocks.
(iv) Types of regional block: topical anaesthesia (surface analgesia); infiltration anaesthesia; peripheral nerve blocks (plexus/single nerve blocks); central neural blockade – epidural anaesthesia and spinal anaesthesia; intravenous regional anaesthesia (IVRA); sympathetic nerve blocks; interpleural/intra-articular analgesia.
(v) Postoperative management: monitoring and supervision as for GA; monitor for neurological complications; discharge when effects of block have worn off; provide adequate postoperative analgesia.

questions.answerText:
A(i) 97–98% of oxygen is carried in combination with haemoglobin (2–3% dissolved in plasma). O2 Content = 1.31 × Hb × Saturation + 0.0031 × PO2. (Note: 1 gm Hb binds 1.31, though the theoretical maximum is 1.39, due to presence of iron in non-haeme form.) O2 content in 100 ml blood in a normal adult with Hb 15 g/dl is approximately 20 ml (19.4 ml as oxyHb + 0.3 ml dissolved in plasma). Oxygen delivery (DO2) = CO × (1.34 × Hb conc × SaO2 + 0.023 × PaO2).

A(ii) Factors shifting the O2 dissociation curve to the left (reduced O2 delivery to tissues): alkalosis, hypothermia, hypocarbia, reduced 2,3-DPG, foetal haemoglobin, carboxyhaemoglobin, methaemoglobin, isoflurane, propranolol. Factors shifting curve to the right (increased O2 delivery to tissues): acidosis, hyperthermia, hypercarbia, increased 2,3-DPG, high altitude, CO inhalation, pregnancy, haemoglobin S. Clinical significance: left shift means Hb holds O2 more tightly (useful for loading in lungs but reduces release to tissues); right shift means Hb releases O2 more readily to tissues.

B(i) Oxygen cascade — describes the decrease of oxygen from the atmosphere to the mitochondrion. The air we breathe contains approximately 21% oxygen. Atmospheric pressure = 760 mmHg. Dry atmospheric gas: 160 mmHg (21 kPa). Humidified tracheal gas: 150 mmHg (19.8 kPa). Alveolar gas: 106 mmHg (14 kPa). Arterial blood: 100 mmHg (13.3 kPa). Capillary blood: 45–55 mmHg (6–7 kPa). Mitochondria: 5–22 mmHg (1–5 kPa).

B(ii) Hypoxaemia: when oxygen tension in arterial blood is less than 80 mmHg (10.6 kPa). Four types of hypoxia: Hypoxic hypoxia — oxygen tension of arterial blood is reduced (hypoventilation, diffusion impairment/V/Q mismatch, shunt, high altitude). Anaemic hypoxia — arterial oxygen tension is normal but Hb available to carry oxygen is reduced (CO poisoning, anaemia, haemoglobinopathy, blood loss). Stagnant/ischaemic hypoxia — blood flow to tissues so low that oxygen is not delivered despite normal arterial O2 tension and Hb (e.g. mitral stenosis, constrictive pericarditis). Histotoxic hypoxia — oxygen is delivered but a toxic agent prevents cells from using it (e.g. cyanide poisoning).

C(i) Bohr effect: shift of O2-Hb dissociation curve to the right by increased PCO2. In the tissues: CO2 enters blood, H+ concentration increases due to increased H2CO3 concentration, shifting curve to the right — greater release of O2 due to less avid binding of O2 to Hb (O2 unloaded to tissues). In the lungs: CO2 diffuses out of blood, H+ concentration decreases, shifting curve to the left — more avid binding of O2 to Hb, increasing the quantity of O2 bound (O2 loaded). This is important to enhance oxygenation of blood in the lungs and to enhance release of O2 in the tissues.
questions.question:

A(i) How oxygen is carried in the blood — the oxygen content formula and the contribution of haemoglobin versus dissolved oxygen
A(ii) The oxygen dissociation curve — factors that shift it left and right, and their clinical significance
B(i) The oxygen cascade — describe each step from atmospheric air to the mitochondria
B(ii) Define hypoxaemia and the four types of hypoxia with their mechanisms

A 38-year-old woman returns from theatre following an emergency appendicectomy under general anaesthesia. In the PACU she is agitated, hypoxic on pulse oximetry, and has a blood pressure of 85/50 mmHg.
(i), list the possible causes of postoperative agitation.
(ii) List the possible causes of postoperative hypotension as stated.
(iii) Describe the routine recovery observations required for a patient who had general anaesthesia: the monitoring intervals and the oxygen concentration to be given.
(iv) State the full discharge criteria from the PACU as listed, including the Aldrete score mention and the specific criterion related to parenteral narcotics.
(v) Describe the management of postoperative nausea and vomiting: when it is commoner, what reduces its incidence, and the two anti-emetic agents named with dosages.
questions.answerText:
(i) Causes of postoperative agitation:
- Pain (most common cause)
- Hypoxaemia
- Acidosis
- Hypotension
- Bladder distension
- Surgical complications such as intra-abdominal haemorrhage
- Marked perioperative fear
- Adverse drug reaction e.g. ketamine

(ii) Causes of postoperative hypotension:
- Hypovolaemia
- Ventricular failure
- Septic shock
- (Note: hypertension and arrhythmias and MI are also listed under CVS complications but not specifically as causes of hypotension — these are classified as separate CVS complications)

(iii) Routine recovery observations:
- Vital signs and oxygenation checked on arrival
- Subsequent BP, PR and RR every 5 minutes for 15 minutes or until stable, then every 15 minutes thereafter
- Pulse oximetry continuously
- Anaesthetist should give a brief report about important pre-, intra- and immediate postoperative condition
- Patient should be given 30–40% oxygen

(iv) Discharge criteria from PACU:
- All patients must be evaluated by the anaesthetist and certified fit for discharge
- Before discharge, patient should have been observed for respiratory depression for at least 30 minutes after the last dose of parenteral narcotic
- Easy arousability
- Full orientation
- Ability to maintain and protect the airway
- Stable vital signs for at least 1 hour
- Ability to call for help if necessary
- No obvious surgical complications (such as bleeding)
- Patients who received regional anaesthesia should show signs of resolution of sensory and motor blockade (should resolve not more than 6 hours)
- Postanaesthetic recovery score (Aldrete score) is mentioned

(v) Postoperative nausea and vomiting:
- Common following GA and CNB; especially following opioid-based GA, intraperitoneal surgery, and strabismus surgery
- Commoner in young women
- Propofol decreases the incidence
- Metoclopramide: 0.15mg/kg
- Ondansetron: 0.05–0.1mg/kg

(i) Acute Myocardial Infarction (AMI) as part of Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS). Pathophysiology: atherosclerosis causes thickening of the arterial wall in coronary arteries with cholesterol plaque, clot, and spasm — acute closure of coronary arteries causes reduced supply (underperfusion of myocytes, ischaemia/infarction). Myocardial infarction begins to develop after 15–30 minutes of severe ischaemia when occlusion persists more than 30 minutes; continuing coronary occlusion results in progressive increase of infarct size; after about 6 hours of continuous occlusion the myocardium supplied by that artery becomes necrotic.

(ii) Modifiable risk factors: hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, diabetes, obesity, smoking, hyperhomocysteinaemia, inflammation, drug abuse, microalbuminuria. Non-modifiable risk factors: age, gender, family history of cardiovascular disease, personal history of cardiovascular disease. Note: 50% of patients may not have a recognisable risk factor.

(iii) Pre-hospital: early EMS activation (most common cause of pre-hospital death is VF; most deaths occur within one hour); have victim rest quietly. Give nitroglycerin — one tablet repeated 2–3 times at 3–5-minute intervals. Give aspirin. Early diagnosis and treatment of AMI significantly reduces mortality, improves LV function, and decreases incidence of heart failure; interventions must be administered within first few hours of symptom onset.

(iv) VF/pVT shockable rhythm: defibrillate as quickly as possible. For monophasic defibrillators: 360 joules for VF/pulseless VT. If unsuccessful, resume CPR for one minute while airway is secured and IV access achieved; administer IV adrenaline 1 mg and consider specifically treatable causes. After 10 cycles of CPR re-examine ECG. Persistent VF: further shocks of 360 J. Recommended to follow this sequence for at least 9–12 shocks before antiarrhythmic drugs.

(v) The goal of care in CPR is to restore a beating heart and functioning circulation to maintain oxygen delivery to vital organs and preserve vital function including brain viability. The heart, lungs, and brain function interdependently. Post-cardiac arrest care: identify and correct reversible causes; acute hypovolaemia is the most commonly treatable cause of asystole/PEA, always resulting from severe haemorrhage (greater than 50% blood volume), requiring immediate surgery and rapid fluid replacement. Successful management includes identification of patients at risk, early diagnosis and treatment, and correction of underlying abnormalities.
questions.question:
A 60-year-old man with a history of hypertension and smoking presents with sudden-onset crushing chest pain radiating to his jaw, sweating, nausea, and shortness of breath for 40 minutes. His BP is 90/60 mmHg.

(i) What is the most likely diagnosis, and what is the underlying pathophysiology?
(ii) List the major modifiable and non-modifiable risk factors for this condition.
(iii) What immediate pre-hospital actions and drug treatment should be initiated?
(iv) If the patient develops a shockable cardiac arrest rhythm, describe the ACLS defibrillation sequence and drug therapy.

A patient with a known seizure disorder, on phenytoin, undergoes a two-hour abdominal procedure under general anaesthesia using atracurium infusion. At the end of surgery, despite administration of neostigmine and atropine, the patient remains profoundly weak with a train-of-four ratio of 0.2 and is unable to sustain a head lift.

(i) Name the condition and state the clinical criteria that confirm adequate neuromuscular recovery has NOT yet occurred.
(ii) Explain why this patient may have an altered response to atracurium, citing the relevant drug interactions.
(iii) Describe the hierarchy of neuromuscular blockade, relating the fraction of receptors occupied to the train-of-four and whole-body signs.
(iv) List the indications for neuromuscular monitoring in this patient.
(v) Describe all the modes of nerve stimulator monitoring that can be used to guide management, and state the goal of reversal with anticholinesterases.
questions.answerText:
(i) Residual neuromuscular blockade (inadequate reversal). Clinical criteria confirming recovery has NOT occurred: inability to sustain head lift for 5 seconds; inability to generate negative inspiratory pressure of at least 25 cmH2O; inability to swallow and maintain a patent airway; TOF ratio <0.9 (the patient here has TOF ratio of 0.2). Other crude signs absent: tongue protrusion, arm lift, hand grip strength.

(ii) Altered response in this patient due to drug interactions.:
- Anticonvulsants (e.g. phenytoin): listed as drugs that alter responses to non-depolarising muscle relaxants; phenytoin induces hepatic enzymes and upregulates ACh receptors, typically causing resistance to non-depolarising NMBs, but in some cases producing unpredictable prolonged effects.
- Other drug interactions that alter responses: inhalational agents (potentiate non-depolarising blockade); intravenous anaesthetics; local anaesthetics; antibiotics; magnesium.
- Patient factors that alter responses: acid-base balance, electrolyte abnormality, age, and concurrent diseases (neurological and muscular diseases, myasthenia gravis, Eaton-Lambert syndrome, liver and kidney diseases).

(iii) Hierarchy of neuromuscular blockade (receptor occupancy → stimulator response → whole-body signs):
- 99–100%: no response to nerve stimulator; flaccid, extreme relaxation.
- 95%: post-tetanic facilitation present; diaphragm moves, hiccough possible.
- 90%: one of four TOF twitches present; abdominal relaxation adequate for most procedures.
- 75%: four TOF twitches present (TOF ratio ~0.7); tidal volume and vital capacity normal.
- 50%: 100 Hz tetanus sustained; passes inspiratory pressure test.
- 30%: 200 Hz tetanus sustained; head lift and hand-grip sustained.

(iv) Indications for neuromuscular monitoring in this patient: prolonged anaesthesia (two-hour infusion); infusion of NMB has been used; concurrent neurological disease (seizure disorder); anticonvulsant therapy (drug interaction risk); unexpected poor recovery.

(v) Modes of nerve stimulator stimulation: single twitch (single pulse, 0.2 msec); train-of-four (TOF) — series of 4 twitches, 0.2 msec long, 2 Hz frequency, administered every 10–15 seconds; tetanic stimulation; double burst stimulation (DBS); post-tetanic count (PTC). Muscular contraction is assessed by visual, tactile, mechanomyography, or electromyography.

Goal of reversal: re-establishment of spontaneous respiration and the ability to protect the airway from aspiration. Effectiveness of anticholinesterases depends on the degree of recovery present when they are administered.

(i) The clinical goal of supplemental O2 therapy is to ensure appropriate O2 delivery to vital end-organ tissues by: treating hypoxaemia, decreasing work of breathing, and decreasing myocardial work. Oxygen must be prescribed: the prescription must be written legibly by the doctor, be dated, and specify the O2 concentration, flow rate, and duration of O2 therapy. Oxygen therapy must not be withheld whenever indicated.

(ii) The Venturi mask is most appropriate for COPD patients requiring specific oxygen concentrations — to administer FiO2 but not too high, so that the hypoxic drive to breathe is not blunted; titrate to keep saturations about 88%. It is a high-flow delivery system; flow rate 4–12 L/min; FiO2 can be set specifically at 24, 28, 31, 35, or 40% with different flow rates and air ports.

(iii) Four types of hypoxia: Hypoxic hypoxia — oxygen tension of arterial blood is reduced (hypoventilation, V/Q mismatch, shunt, high altitude). Anaemic hypoxia — arterial oxygen tension is normal but haemoglobin available to carry oxygen is reduced (CO poisoning, anaemia, haemoglobinopathy, blood loss). Stagnant/ischaemic hypoxia — blood flow to tissues is so low that oxygen is not delivered despite normal arterial O2 tension and Hb (e.g. mitral stenosis, constrictive pericarditis). Histotoxic hypoxia — oxygen is delivered to tissues but a toxic agent prevents cells from using it (e.g. cyanide poisoning). This patient's primary problem is hypoxic hypoxia (COPD causing V/Q mismatch).

(iv) Complications of oxygen therapy: oxygen toxicity can occur with FiO2 greater than 60% for more than 36 hours, FiO2 greater than 80% for more than 24 hours, FiO2 greater than 100% for more than 12 hours; can cause pathological changes in CNS, lungs, and eye. Specific complications: retrolental fibroplasia, absorption atelectasis, pulmonary O2 toxicity. Other complications: drying of mucous membranes, depression of ventilation in COPD, reversal of compensatory hypoxic vasoconstriction, explosions.

(v) Cyanosis is a bluish discolouration of the tissue, seen when the reduced Hb concentration in the blood is greater than 5 g/dl. It is seen in nail beds, mucous membranes, earlobes, lips, and fingers where the skin is thin. Cyanosis does NOT occur in: anaemic hypoxia (total Hb content is low so the threshold of 5 g/dl reduced Hb is not reached), CO poisoning (the colour of reduced Hb is obscured by the cherry-red colour of COHb), or histotoxic hypoxia (blood gas content is normal).

A 38-year-old woman with a history of peripartum cardiomyopathy presents with progressive dyspnoea on exertion, orthopnoea, and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea. Examination reveals a laterally displaced apex beat, S3 gallop, and bilateral basal crepitations.

(i) What is the diagnosis, and how is heart failure defined?
(ii) State the classification of heart failure and the causes under each category.
(iii) Describe the symptoms and signs of left ventricular failure in detail.
(iv) What is acute pulmonary oedema, and what are its features?
(v) Distinguish between systolic and diastolic dysfunction as causes of heart failure.
questions.answerText:
(i) Heart failure — a pathophysiologic state in which an abnormality of cardiac function is responsible for the failure of the heart to pump blood at a rate commensurate with the requirements of the metabolising tissues, or can do so only from an abnormally elevated diastolic volume.

(ii) Classification and causes: Left ventricular (LV) failure: coronary artery disease, hypertension, most forms of cardiomyopathy, congenital defects (e.g. VSD, patent ductus arteriosus with large shunts). Right ventricular (RV) failure: commonly caused by prior LV failure (increasing pulmonary venous pressure and leading to pulmonary arterial hypertension), tricuspid regurgitation, mitral stenosis, primary pulmonary hypertension, multiple pulmonary emboli, pulmonary artery or valve stenosis, RV infarction. High output failure: anaemia, beriberi, thyrotoxicosis, pregnancy, advanced Paget's disease, arteriovenous fistula. Volume overload simulating HF: polycythaemia, overtransfusion, acute renal failure with overhydration, obstruction of either vena cava.

(iii) Signs of chronic LV failure: diffuse and laterally displaced apical impulse; palpable and audible ventricular (S3) and atrial gallops (S4); accentuated pulmonic second sound; inspiratory basilar rales; right-sided pleural effusion is common. Symptoms: tachycardia, fatigue on exertion, dyspnoea on mild exercise, intolerance to cold; paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea and nocturnal cough (due to redistribution of excess fluid into the lung with recumbent position); occasionally, bronchospasm and wheezing; cough may be prominent with pink-tinged or brownish sputum. Frank haemoptysis due to ruptured pulmonary varices may occur.

(iv) Acute pulmonary oedema: a life-threatening manifestation of acute LV failure secondary to sudden onset of pulmonary venous hypertension. A sudden rise in LV filling pressure results in rapid movement of plasma fluid through pulmonary capillaries into interstitial spaces and alveoli. Features: extreme dyspnoea, deep cyanosis, tachypnoea, hyperpnoea, restlessness, and anxiety with a sense of suffocation; pallor and diaphoresis are common; pulse may be thready; BP may be difficult to obtain.

(v) Systolic dysfunction: primarily a problem of ventricular contractile dysfunction; the heart fails to provide tissues with adequate circulatory output. Most common causes: coronary artery disease, hypertension, dilated congestive cardiomyopathy. Diastolic dysfunction: resistance to ventricular filling; not readily measurable at the bedside; accounts for 20–40% of cases of HF; generally associated with prolonged ventricular relaxation time; causes include hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, ventricular hypertrophy (e.g. hypertension, advanced aortic stenosis), amyloid infiltration of the myocardium.

questions.question:
A. Describe propofol under the following headings:
A(i) Chemical name and physical properties including formulation
A(ii) Pharmacokinetic profile: distribution, metabolism and excretion
A(iii) All systemic effects: CNS, CVS, respiratory and hepatorenal
B. Describe the classification of IV anaesthetic agents completely.
C. Describe the management of intraarterial injection of thiopentone as given, and explain what systemic effect of thiopentone on the hepatorenal system may affect the metabolism of other co-administered drugs.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Chemical name and physical properties:
- Chemical name: 2,6 diisopropyl phenol
- First identified as a potentially useful intravenous agent in 1980
- Extremely lipid soluble; insoluble in water
- Formulated in a white aqueous emulsion containing soyabean oil, glycerol and purified egg lecithin
- Ampoules contain 200mg of propofol in 20ml without preservative

A(ii) Pharmacokinetic profile:
- Propofol is distributed rapidly
- Blood concentration declines exponentially following administration
- Metabolised in the liver; extrahepatic sites of distribution also believed to exist
- Excreted by the kidneys
- Dosage: 1.5–2.5mg/kg

A(iii) Systemic effects:
- CNS: onset of action 20–40 seconds post IV administration; depresses the CNS; cerebral metabolic rate, CBF and intracranial pressure reduced; recovery of consciousness is rapid; minimal hangover effect
- CVS: causes hypotension
- Respiratory: after induction, apnoea occurs more commonly; tidal volume may reduce with infusion of propofol with associated respiratory depression; suppresses laryngeal reflexes resulting in low incidence of cough and laryngeal spasm during laryngeal mask insertion
- Hepatorenal: transient decrease in renal function; hepatic blood flow decreased by transient reduction in arterial and cardiac output

B. Classification of IV anaesthetic agents:
- Barbiturates: thiobarbiturates (e.g. thiopentone) and methyl barbiturates (e.g. methohexitone)
- Alkyl phenols: e.g. propofol
- Imidazole compounds: e.g. etomidate
- Steroids: e.g. althesin, eltanolone — no longer in use
- Eugenols: e.g. propanidid — no longer in use
- Phencyclidine derivatives: e.g. ketamine
- Others: benzodiazepines (diazepam, midazolam); large dose opioids (fentanyl, alfentanyl, remifentanyl)

C. Management of intraarterial injection and hepatorenal effect:
- Management: (1) leave needle in the artery; (2) flush with saline to dilute the injection; (3) inject procaine to relieve spasm; (4) keep hand elevated and warm
- Hepatorenal effect on co-administered drug metabolism: thiopentone induces hepatic enzymes; this may increase metabolism and elimination of other drugs administered concurrently

questions.question:
A(i) Describe the distribution of total body water, including the intracellular and extracellular compartments with their volumes and percentages, and the principal electrolytes in each compartment.
A(ii) State the osmolality and electrolyte content (Na+ and Cl-) of normal saline (0.9%), half-normal saline (0.45%), 5% glucose, and Hartmann's solution, and explain the fluid compartment each predominantly expands.
B(i) Outline the clinical causes of the four common electrolyte disturbances (hyponatraemia, hypernatraemia, hyperkalaemia, and hypokalaemia) and their treatments.
B(ii) State the indications for and methods of blood transfusion safety checks, and list the complications of massive blood transfusion.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Total body water: approximately 60% of weight in males, 50–55% in females. Intracellular fluid (ICF): 28 L (40% of body weight). Extracellular fluid (ECF): 14 L (20%) – comprising plasma (3.5 L / 5%) and interstitial fluid (9.5 L / 14%); plus transcellular fluid (1 L / 1%). Principal electrolytes: ICF – K+ 150, HCO3- 3, PO4 100, Mg 30 (mmol/L). ECF/Plasma – Na+ 140, Cl- 110, HCO3- 28–30, K+ 5 (mmol/L).
A(ii) Normal saline (0.9%): Na+ 154, Cl- 154, osmolality 308 mOsmol/L; isotonic, expands mainly ECF. Half-normal saline (0.45%): Na+ 77, Cl- 77, osmolality 154 mOsmol/L; hypotonic, causes shift of H2O from ECF. 5% Glucose: Na+ nil, Cl- nil, osmolality 278 mOsmol/L; metabolised to H2O which enters ICF and ECF. Hartmann's solution: Na+ 131, Cl- 112, osmolality 281 mOsmol/L (also contains K+ 5, HCO3- 29, Ca++ 4 as lactate); Na+ remains in ECF due to the Na+/K+ pump.
B(i) Hyponatraemia (water retention, Na+ loss) – treatment: give normal saline (0.9%) or hypertonic saline 3%; deficit = (140 – measured Na+) × weight × 0.6. Hypernatraemia (loss of body water, renal fluid loss) – treatment: water replacement. Hyperkalaemia (impaired excretion, excessive intake, burns) – treatment: frusemide 1–2 mg/kg; CaCl2 (gluconate) 10 ml of 10% slowly; insulin + 5–10% glucose 500 ml as infusion. Hypokalaemia (reduced intake, increased loss, redistribution) – treatment: IV K+ as an infusion at 20–40 mmol/L with ECG monitoring; K+ deficit = (4.5 – measured K+) × weight × 0.4.
B(ii) Blood transfusion safety checks (checked by 2 people): patient's name, hospital number, blood group, blood bag number, collection/expiry date, HIV screening; blood must be warmed and transfused through a filter. Complications of massive blood transfusion (defined as 10 units of blood within 6 hours, 5 units within 1 hour, or replacement of blood volume within 24 hours): hypervolaemia; ARDS; microembolism (use microfilters of 20–40 microns, normal filter is 170 microns). Other transfusion complications: incompatibility reactions (ABO/Rhesus); post-transfusion haemolysis; febrile reaction; anaphylactic reaction; circulatory overload; hypothermia; air embolism; coagulopathy; metabolic changes (hyperkalaemia, reduced Ca++, alkalosis from citrate overload).

A(i) Cardiovascular changes and implications:
- Changes: increased SVR, CO, HR, BP; plasma volume and RBC increase causing dilutional anaemia
- Implications: poor compensation in diseased hearts; aorto-caval compression; compromise by anaesthetic agents causing BP reduction

A(ii) Respiratory changes and implications:
- Changes: oedema of tissues (airways); BMR increases as pregnancy progresses; minute ventilation increases by 50%; pCO2 decreases; FRC decreases — rapid desaturation
- Difficult intubation risk: 1:300 in obstetric patients compared to 1:2000 in the general population
- Implications: difficult intubation; rapid desaturation; poorly tolerated apnoea

A(iii) Gastrointestinal changes and implications:
- Changes: progesterone effect reduces gastric motility and emptying time; increased gastric acidity; reduced lower oesophageal sphincter (LES) tone
- Implications: full stomach; regurgitation and aspiration; Mendelson's syndrome

B(i) Preoperative care components:
- Elective or emergent assessment
- High-risk patients to be assessed as soon as booked
- History and clinical examination (same as for other patients in general)
- Airway assessment
- Anaesthetic options discussed
- Investigations: basic haematological and special (clotting profile), E&U
- Group and crossmatch 2 units of blood

B(ii) Premedication for the obstetric patient:
- Antacid prophylaxis: reduce acidity — prescribe H2 antagonist; neutralise acids — prescribe saline antacids (e.g. sodium citrate); empty stomach — metoclopramide
- Apply medication protocols for DM, PIH, asthma if applicable

C. Contraindications to regional anaesthesia in obstetrics:
- Refusal
- Haemorrhagic disease
- Anticoagulant therapy
- Local or general sepsis
- Shock
- BP/cardiac disease
- Neurological disease
