Describe the classification of inhalational anaesthetics and the stages of anaesthesia under the following headings:

A(i) Classification of inhalational agents into volatile anaesthetics and anaesthetic gases, giving examples of each
A(ii) The stages of anaesthesia as described using diethyl ether — all four stages with their defining features
B(i) Diethyl ether — physical properties, MAC, blood/gas solubility, metabolism, and flammability
B(ii) The effects of diethyl ether on the circulatory and respiratory systems
C(i) Why has ether been largely abandoned, and which features of the ideal agent does it lack?
questions.answerText:
A(i) Classification: Volatile anaesthetics (liquids with low boiling point and high saturated vapour pressure): Diethyl Ether, Divinyl Ether, Ethyl chloride, Chloroform, Trichloroethylene, Halothane, Methoxyflurane, Enflurane, Isoflurane, Desflurane, Sevoflurane. Anaesthetic gases: Nitrous oxide, Cyclopropane, Ethylene, Xenon, Argon, Sulphur hexafluoride. The modern volatile inhalational agents in use include halothane, isoflurane, sevoflurane, enflurane, and desflurane.

A(ii) Stages of anaesthesia (described using diethyl ether): Stage I — from beginning of induction to loss of consciousness; also known as stage of analgesia. Stage II — from loss of consciousness to onset of regular breathing; also known as stage of excitement. Stage III — from onset of regular breathing to onset of diaphragmatic paralysis; this is the stage of surgical anaesthesia. Stage IV — from diaphragmatic paralysis to apnoea and death; it is the stage of anaesthetic overdose. Note: these classical stages are not as clear with current inhalational agents.

B(i) Diethyl ether (CH3CH2-O-CH2CH3): colourless, pungent volatile liquid. Blood/gas solubility 12; MAC 3.04. Relatively inert. Acetaldehyde and ether peroxide as impurities. Stored in dark cool place. 85–90% eliminated unchanged via lungs; 15% metabolised in the liver. Flammable in air and explosive in O2.

B(ii) Circulatory effects: heart rate first increased then unaltered. Blood pressure: decreased after 1st hour below phase II; vasomotor centre paralysis in deep plane. Functioning sympathetic nervous system maintains BP. Ether increases sympathetic adrenal activity. Cardiac output: lighter plane — CO increases; deep plane — CO decreases. Arrhythmia: rare; adrenaline is safer with ether than with halothane. Respiratory effects: respiratory rate increases initially, then decreases in deeper plane. Ether vapour is irritant, causing laryngospasm. Ether dilates bronchial musculature. Hence induction is gradual. CNS: induces analgesia, then excitement, then anaesthesia; medullary depression is late and precedes serious cardiac depression; CBF increases, raising CSF pressure.

C(i) Ether has been largely abandoned because: it is flammable in air and explosive in oxygen (a major hazard in the operating theatre). Features of the ideal agent it lacks: it has a pungent, unpleasant smell (not a pleasant odour); its high blood/gas solubility (12) means very slow induction and slow recovery; it irritates the airway causing laryngospasm and coughing; it provokes profuse secretions from mucous-secreting glands (premedication with anticholinergic agent is essential); and it causes myocardial depression in deep planes. These properties directly violate requirements of the ideal agent: pleasant smell, non-irritant to airways, low blood/gas solubility for rapid induction/recovery, and non-flammable.

A(i) Conducting zone: includes structures that conduct air breathed in — filtered, warmed, and moistened into lungs. Structures outside the lungs: nose, pharynx, larynx, trachea. Structures inside the lungs: bronchi, bronchioles, terminal bronchioles.

A(ii) Respiratory zone: includes respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, alveolar sacs, and alveoli. This is the site of oxygen and carbon dioxide exchange with blood. The lungs can be included in the lower respiratory tract or as a separate entity and include the respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, alveolar sacs, and alveoli.

B(i) Lower respiratory tract (lower airway): includes the portion of the larynx below the vocal folds, trachea, bronchi, and bronchioles. The lungs include the respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, alveolar sacs, and alveoli. The respiratory tract is divided into: upper airway (nose and nasal passages, paranasal sinuses, the pharynx, the portion of the larynx above the vocal folds) and lower airway (the portion of the larynx below the vocal folds, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles).

B(ii) Paranasal sinuses — four paired air-filled spaces surrounding the nasal cavity, lined with respiratory epithelium (ciliated pseudo-stratified columnar epithelium): (1) Maxillary sinuses (antrum of Highmore): the largest paranasal sinuses; located under the eyes in the maxillary bones; innervated by the maxillary nerve (V2). (2) Frontal sinuses: superior to the eyes in the frontal bone (forms the hard part of the forehead); innervated by the ophthalmic nerve (V1). (3) Ethmoidal sinuses: formed from discrete air cells within the ethmoidal bone between nose and the eyes; innervated by ethmoidal nerves (branches from nasociliary nerve of the ophthalmic nerve). (4) Sphenoidal sinuses: located in the sphenoid bone; innervated by the ophthalmic and maxillary nerves.

C(i) The conducting zone does not participate in gas exchange because its walls are too thick for diffusion and it is not supplied by the pulmonary capillaries in the same manner as the alveoli. Instead, the conducting zone serves to: filter air (nasal hair and mucus trap dust and matter breathed in); warm the air to body temperature; moisten the air to prevent drying of the lower respiratory tract; and conduct the air to the respiratory zone where gas exchange occurs.
questions.question:

A(i) The conducting zone — structures included inside and outside the lungs
A(ii) The respiratory zone — structures and their function
B(i) The lower respiratory tract — structures included, and the contribution of the lungs
B(ii) The paranasal sinuses — types, location, and innervation of each

questions.answerText:
A(i) Properties of the ideal intravenous anaesthetic agent:
- Rapid onset of action
- Rapid recovery
- Analgesia at subanaesthetic concentrations
- Minimal cardiovascular and respiratory depression
- No emetic effect
- No excitatory phenomena e.g. coughing, hiccups, involuntary movement on induction
- No emergence phenomena e.g. nightmares
- No injection pain
- No release of histamine
- No hypersensitivity reaction
- No toxic effect on other organs
- Water-soluble formulation
- Long shelf life

B(i) Thiopentone physical properties:
- Yellow powder, soluble in water
- Alkaline pH of 10.8
- Not stable for more than 24 hours
- Used as a 2.5% concentration
- Metabolised mainly in the liver; metabolites excreted by kidneys
- Dosage: usually given as 4mg/kg

B(ii) Effects on body systems:
- CNS: produces anaesthesia in less than 30 seconds after IV administration; causes hypnosis; poor analgesic effect at subanaesthetic doses
- Respiratory: causes respiratory depression; apnoea may occur
- CVS: cardiac output reduced resulting in hypotension; avoid in patients with shock
- Skeletal muscle: tone reduced especially with high concentration
- Hepatorenal: function of liver and kidney impaired transiently; hepatic enzymes induced which may increase metabolism and elimination of drugs
- Intra-arterial injection: causes arterial spasm and thrombosis which may lead to gangrene of the hand

B(iii) Contraindications to thiopentone:
- Severe hypotension/shock
- Previous hypersensitivity reaction to barbiturate
- Porphyria: barbiturates may precipitate paralysis or severe cardiovascular collapse

C(i) Mechanism, onset and duration:
- Propofol: 2,6 diisopropyl phenol; formulated in white aqueous emulsion containing soyabean oil, glycerol and purified egg lecithin; onset 20–40 seconds post IV administration; depresses CNS; cerebral metabolic rate, CBF and intracranial pressure reduced; recovery of consciousness is rapid; minimal hangover effect
- Ketamine: phencyclidine derivative; produces dissociative anaesthesia; onset 30–60 seconds after IV injection; also effective after 3–4 minutes after IM injection; duration of action 15–25 minutes; potent analgesic at subanaesthetic doses

C(ii) Specific adverse effects:
- Propofol: cardiovascular depression; respiratory depression; pain on injection occurs in 40% of patients (reduced by using large veins and prior lignocaine); allergic reactions — skin rashes occasionally; tidal volume may reduce with infusion
- Ketamine: emergence delirium with restlessness, disorientation and agitation; hallucinations; prolonged recovery; excessive salivation; increased intracranial pressure; arterial pressure, heart rate and cardiac output increase; increased intraocular pressure; myocardial oxygen consumption increases

C(iii) Indications and contraindications:
- Propofol: indicated for induction of anaesthesia, sedation during surgery, total intravenous anaesthesia, sedation in ICU; contraindicated in hypersensitivity to the drug
- Ketamine: indicated where its cardiovascular-stimulant properties are useful; contraindicated in patients with increased intracranial pressure and airway obstruction
questions.question:
A. Describe the properties of the ideal intravenous anaesthetic agent.
A(i) List all the properties as stated.
B. Describe thiopentone under the following headings:
B(i) Physical properties and preparation
B(ii) Effects on each body system
B(iii) Contraindications to its use
C. Distinguish between propofol and ketamine:
C(i) Mechanism of action, onset and duration
C(ii) Specific adverse effects unique to each agent
C(iii) Indications and contraindications for each

(A) Describe the gross anatomy of shock as a pathophysiological entity under the following headings:
(i) Definition of shock.
(ii) The three stages (phases) of the physiological response to shock.
(iii) The specific haemodynamic features of each stage.

(B) For each of the four causes of shock, state:
(i) The class and mechanism.
(ii) Named examples of conditions causing it.
(iii) The characteristic haemodynamic pattern (warm vs cold, high vs low CO).

(C) Explain why multi-organ failure (MOF) develops in untreated shock, naming the organs affected and the specific syndromes produced in each organ.
questions.answerText:
(A)
(i) Definition: shock is a physiologic state characterised by inadequate tissue perfusion; clinically manifested by haemodynamic disturbances and organ dysfunction. Also defined as acute circulatory failure with inadequate or inappropriately distributed tissue perfusion leading to cellular hypoxia.
(ii) Three stages: pre-shock (warm shock, compensated shock); shock (with initial signs of end-organ dysfunction); end-organ dysfunction (progressive irreversible dysfunction).
(iii) Haemodynamic features by stage:
- Pre-shock/Compensated:
 - Low preload shock: tachycardia, vasoconstriction, mildly decreased BP.
 - Low afterload (distributive) shock: peripheral vasodilation, hyperdynamic state.
- Shock: tachycardia, tachypnoea, metabolic acidosis, oliguria, cool and clammy skin.
- End-organ dysfunction: progressive irreversible dysfunction; oliguria or anuria; progressive acidosis and decreased CO; agitation, obtundation, and coma; patient death.

(B) Four causes of shock:
(i-iii) Cardiogenic: failure of the heart as a pump (e.g. CCF, MI, post-cardiac surgery, aortic incompetence, LV aneurysm); cold, low CO, high SVR.
Obstructive: mechanical obstruction to flow (e.g. cardiac tamponade, pulmonary embolism); cold, low CO.
Hypovolaemic: loss of circulating volume (e.g. haemorrhage, dehydration); cold, low CO, high SVR.
Distributive: abnormal distribution of blood flow (e.g. sepsis, anaphylaxis, neurogenic); warm, high CO, low SVR (hyperdynamic state).

(C) MOF in untreated shock — pathway and organ syndromes:
- Pathophysiology of MOF: imbalance in O2 supply and demand; anaerobic metabolism; cell membrane ion pump dysfunction; intracellular pH dysregulation; cell death → end-organ dysfunction → MSOF and death.
- Lung: acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS/shock lung) — non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema; increased pulmonary vascular permeability; dyspnoea, reduced compliance, V/Q mismatch, hypoxaemia.
- Kidney: acute renal failure — from haemofiltration deficit; oliguria or anuria.
- Coagulation system: disseminated intravascular coagulopathy (DIC) — coagulation cascade activated; later haemorrhagic tendency.
- Liver: hepatic failure.
- GIT: GIT failure.
- Mortality: septic shock 35–40% (1-month mortality); cardiogenic shock 60–90%; hypovolaemic shock: variable.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old woman in active labour requests epidural analgesia. The anaesthetist places the patient in the sitting position, selects an appropriate lumbar intervertebral space, and advances a Tuohy needle.
(i) What two methods can be used to identify entry into the epidural space, and what is the anatomical basis for each?
(ii) The anaesthetist inserts an epidural catheter. List the factors that will determine the spread of local anaesthetic within the epidural space.
(iii) Why does pregnancy affect the spread of epidural local anaesthetic, and what other factor in this patient's clinical condition might also increase the level of the block?
(iv) List the physiological effects of neuraxial block and the cardiovascular changes expected in this patient.
(v) What immediate treatment should be given for hypotension following epidural block?
questions.answerText:
(i) The two methods of identification depend on the negative pressure in the epidural space: Loss of resistance – when the plunger of a glass syringe containing air or liquid is gently pushed, a "give" is suddenly felt when the epidural space is entered; the negative pressure in the epidural space allows the syringe contents to flow in freely. Hanging drop – a drop of liquid hanging from the hub of the epidural needle is sucked in when the epidural space is entered; this also depends on the negative epidural pressure.
(ii) Factors affecting spread of local anaesthetic in the epidural space: site of injection; volume of local anaesthetic; speed of injection; position after injection; age and height of patient; pregnancy; presence of other abdominal tumours. A high site of injection, large volume, rapid injection, barbotage, Trendelenburg position immediately after injection, old age, and short stature all tend to give a higher level of block.
(iii) Pregnancy increases the spread of epidural local anaesthetic because the enlarged uterus compresses the epidural venous plexus, reducing the epidural space volume so that the same volume of local anaesthetic spreads over a greater number of segments. The presence of an abdominal tumour (comparable to the gravid uterus as an abdominal mass) is also listed as a factor increasing spread.
(iv) Physiological effects of neuraxial block are due to the sympathectomy effect and are dependent upon the height of the block. Respiratory effects: alterations in pulmonary variables in healthy patients are usually of little clinical consequence. Cardiovascular changes expected: sympathetic block causes peripheral vasodilation, leading to decreased SVR and potentially significant hypotension; the low-preload effect of venous pooling further reduces cardiac output.
(v) Treatment for hypotension following epidural block: intravenous fluids and vasopressor – ephedrine (for hypotension resulting from sympathetic autonomic blockade).

questions.question:
A 32-year-old male, 70kg, is scheduled for an axillary block. Only 2% plain lignocaine is available.
(i) What is the maximum safe dose of lignocaine without adrenaline for this patient, and what is the maximum with adrenaline?
(ii) If 30ml of solution is required, calculate the dose in 30ml of 2% plain lignocaine and state whether it is safe without adrenaline.
(iii) Describe the steps the anaesthetist must take to make this safe, including dilution and adrenaline calculation.
(iv) State the toxic dose thresholds for prilocaine and bupivacaine in plain solution and with adrenaline.
(v) List the CNS and CVS features of local anaesthetic toxicity and describe the management.
questions.answerText:
(i) Maximum safe doses for 70kg patient:
- Without adrenaline: lignocaine 3mg/kg = 3 x 70 = 210mg
- With adrenaline: lignocaine 7mg/kg = 7 x 70 = 490mg

(ii) Dose in 30ml of 2% plain lignocaine:
- A 2% solution contains 20mg/ml
- 30ml x 20mg/ml = 600mg
- Maximum without adrenaline is 210mg; 600mg is NOT safe without adrenaline

(iii) Steps to make safe:
- 20ml of 2% plain lignocaine contains 400mg lignocaine (within the 490mg with adrenaline limit)
- Make up to 30ml solution with 10ml Normal Saline
- Adrenaline 1:1000 contains 1mg/ml; require 1:200,000 i.e. 5 microgram/ml
- For every 20ml of LA solution add 0.1ml of 1:1000 adrenaline
- For the 30ml mixture add 0.15ml of 1:1000 adrenaline

(iv) Toxic dose thresholds (mg/kg):
- Prilocaine: plain 6mg/kg; with adrenaline 9mg/kg
- Lignocaine: plain 3mg/kg; with adrenaline 7mg/kg
- Bupivacaine: plain 2mg/kg; with adrenaline 2mg/kg

(v) Toxicity features and management:
- CNS toxicity: light-headedness, dizziness, circumoral paraesthesia; visual/auditory disturbances such as difficulty focusing and tinnitus; convulsions
- CVS toxicity: occurs at doses and blood concentrations higher than those required to produce CNS toxicity; direct effects on heart and peripheral blood vessels
- Management: maintain airway; administer oxygen; ventilate if apnoea occurs; treat convulsions with thiopentone 150–250mg IV or diazepam 10–20mg IV repeated as necessary; profound hypotension and brady-arrhythmias treated with IV atropine 0.5–1.5mg and colloid or crystalloid infusions; adrenaline may be required for severe hypotension or bradycardia; ventricular fibrillation due to bupivacaine toxicity requires CPR continued for at least 60 minutes; bretylium may facilitate cardioversion

(i) PEA (Pulseless Electrical Activity): present when the ECG shows a rhythm normally associated with an output but with no detectable central pulse. Asystole: occurs when there is no detectable electrical activity in the heart and is associated with a very poor prognosis. In PEA, there is organised (or semi-organised) electrical activity without effective mechanical contraction. In either case, the defibrillation-based treatment loop is not appropriate.

(ii) ACLS for non-shockable rhythms (asystole/PEA): follow the right-hand loop of the algorithm. Secure the airway and obtain IV access as soon as possible. Continue CPR. Administer adrenaline (epinephrine) every three minutes. Give atropine 3 mg once in asystole (not in PEA). The chance of surviving asystole is improved if a reversible cause can be identified and treated (6 Hs and 6 Ts). Any change on the ECG consistent with VF should prompt an immediate transfer to the shockable rhythm treatment loop.

(iii) Most likely reversible cause: toxins (organophosphate poisoning from pesticide exposure) — this inhibits acetylcholinesterase, causing cholinergic crisis; direct pharmacological actions on the heart can cause cardiac arrest. Other possibilities: hypoxia, hypovolaemia. Treatment of toxins (organophosphate): atropine in large doses to reverse muscarinic effects; pralidoxime if available. Acute hypovolaemia (most commonly treatable cause of asystole/PEA overall): always results from extremely severe haemorrhage (greater than 50% blood volume); requires immediate surgery to control haemorrhage and rapid fluid replacement.

(iv) Tension pneumothorax treatment: administer oxygen. Insert a large-bore needle (14-gauge or 16-gauge) into the second intercostal space (above the third rib), at the midclavicular line to decompress the tension pneumothorax. This is indicated by narrow QRS complex PEA (more likely noncardiac cause like low volume or low vascular tone), clinical signs of tension pneumothorax (absent breath sounds, tracheal deviation, haemodynamic deterioration), or confirmed by clinical examination in the context of cardiac arrest.

(v) Shockable rhythm loop (VF/pVT): when VF or pVT are diagnosed, the patient should be defibrillated as quickly as possible. The likelihood of successful defibrillation decreases 2–7% for every minute of cardiac arrest. For monophasic: three shocks of 200 J, 200 J, then 360 J; unless rhythm changes on ECG, no point checking pulse between shocks. After unsuccessful shocks: CPR for one minute, secure airway, IV access, IV adrenaline 1 mg, re-examine after 10 cycles of CPR. Persistent VF: further shocks of 360 J; this sequence for at least 9–12 shocks before antiarrhythmic drugs. This loop does NOT apply to PEA because defibrillation requires a shockable disorganised electrical rhythm (VF/pVT); PEA has organised electrical activity — defibrillating it would disrupt the existing organised rhythm without benefit, and since there is no fibrillation present, there is nothing to 'defibrillate'.
questions.question:
A 45-year-old man is brought to the resuscitation bay in cardiac arrest. The initial rhythm on the monitor is Pulseless Electrical Activity (PEA). He works as a farmer and had been using pesticides.

(i) Define PEA and distinguish it from asystole.
(ii) Describe the full ACLS algorithm for non-shockable rhythms, including drug therapy and timing.
(iii) Of the reversible causes, which is most likely in this patient and how is it treated?
(iv) Describe the steps and indications for needle decompression of tension pneumothorax as a reversible cause.
(v) Describe the defibrillation-based loop for shockable rhythms, and explain why this does not apply to PEA.

A 55-year-old male was involved in a high-speed road traffic accident and is brought to the emergency department. He is unresponsive, has stridor, cyanosis, and a distended neck with deviation of the trachea. He has a rapid thready pulse and grossly distended neck veins.

(i) Name the immediate life-threatening diagnosis and the underlying pathology.
(ii) Identify the predisposing factors for this type of injury.
(iii) Describe the pathophysiology of the haemodynamic compromise seen in this patient.
(iv) Describe the primary survey approach (ABCDE) used in the initial resuscitation of trauma patients.
(v) State the members of the multidisciplinary trauma team and the specific roles of the anaesthetist in trauma management.
questions.answerText:
(i) The immediate diagnosis is tension pneumothorax (or cardiac tamponade — the clinical signs of distended neck veins, hypotension, and tracheal deviation are consistent with obstructive shock from tension pneumothorax or tamponade). These are life-threatening chest injuries that compromise breathing and circulation and must be ruled out during primary survey. Half of trauma deaths are due to massive injury to major vessels or vital organs.

(ii) Predisposing factors for trauma deaths and the need for rapid intervention: road traffic accidents (leading cause of death in the younger population); sustained injuries that may be life-threatening, multiple, or occult (tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade); a third of patients succumb during the "Golden Hour" from potentially treatable conditions such as hypoventilation, haemorrhage, haemo-pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade, or expanding intracranial mass.

(iii) Pathophysiology: obstructive shock results in inadequate cardiac output; in tension pneumothorax, rising intra-thoracic pressure compresses the heart and great vessels, severely reducing venous return (preload); in cardiac tamponade, fluid in the pericardial sac compresses the heart; both lead to circulatory failure, cellular hypoxia, and end-organ dysfunction if untreated.

(iv) Primary survey (ABCDE):
- Airway with cervical control: ensure a clear airway and adequate oxygenation; watch for stridor, respiratory distress, cyanosis; assume cervical injury in all patients with head and maxillofacial injuries.
- Breathing and ventilation: look for tachypnoea, use of accessory muscles, cyanosis; rule out tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade, pneumo-haemothorax, tracheobronchial disruption; provide O2 with SpO2 monitoring and assess need for immediate intubation.
- Circulation and haemorrhage control: watch for cold clammy peripheries, poor capillary return, pallor, thready pulse, hypotension; control external haemorrhage with direct pressure; insert large-bore cannulae and infuse fluids rapidly; group and cross-match blood.
- Disability (rapid neurological assessment): assess pupil size and reaction to light, GCS score, and limb movement spontaneously or in response to stimulus.
- Expose patient for further assessment.

(v) Multidisciplinary trauma team: trauma surgeon, orthopaedic surgeon, radiologist, laboratory technician, blood bank technician, intensivist, and anaesthetist. Anaesthetist's roles: continue resuscitation already in progress (role is fundamental to final outcome); airway management; intravenous cannulation; volume resuscitation; monitored sedation during radiological examination; anaesthesia for emergency surgery; ICU management postoperatively; management of acute and massive bleeding.

questions.question:
A 70-year-old man undergoing total hip replacement develops significant intraoperative bleeding. The anaesthetist observes that 6 units of packed red cells have been transfused over 3 hours and the bleeding continues.
(i) Using the classification of haemorrhagic shock, at what class does this patient likely sit, and what clinical findings would confirm this?
(iii) What is the definition of massive blood transfusion and what are its specific complications?
(iii) Outline the methods available to estimate blood loss intraoperatively.
(iv) What autologous and blood conservation techniques are available as alternatives to allogeneic transfusion?
(v) List the storage requirements and preservative solutions for packed red cells, with their respective shelf lives.
questions.answerText:
(i) With blood loss consistent with the level of transfusion required, the patient may be in Class III–IV haemorrhagic shock. Class III findings: blood loss 1500–2000 ml (30–40%); pulse rate >120/min; decreased blood pressure; respiratory rate 30–40/min; urine output 5–15 ml/hour; CNS symptoms of confusion. Class IV: blood loss >2000 ml (>40%); pulse rate >140/min; decreased BP; respiratory rate >35/min; negligible urine output; lethargic/obtunded CNS state.
(ii) Massive blood transfusion is defined as: 10 units of blood within 6 hours; or 5 units of blood within 1 hour; or replacement of blood volume within 24 hours. Specific complications of massive blood transfusion: hypervolaemia; ARDS; microembolism (use microfilters of 20–40 microns; normal filter is 170 microns). Other transfusion complications include: incompatibility reactions (ABO/Rhesus); post-transfusion haemolysis; febrile reaction; anaphylactic reaction; circulatory overload; hypothermia; air embolism; coagulopathy; metabolic changes – hyperkalaemia, reduced Ca++, alkalosis (citrate overload).
(iii) Methods to estimate intraoperative blood loss: clinical observation of volume status by measurement of BP, HR, urine output; temperature gradient and capillary refill; observation and counting of used swabs; weighing of swabs; suction bottle measurement; washing of swabs/drapes with colorimetry; blood volume measurement.
(iv) Blood conservation and autologous transfusion techniques: autologous transfusion/stockpiling; perioperative autologous donation; haemodilution techniques – isovolaemic or hypervolaemic; artificial blood substitutes and plasma volume expanders – dextrans, gelofusine, haemacel, hetastarch, perfluorocarbons.
(v) Storage requirements and shelf lives: red cells stored at 2–6°C. Preservative solutions and shelf life: ACD – 21 days; CPD – 28 days; CPD-A – 35 days; SAGM – 42 days. Clotting factors decrease after 24 hours of storage. Platelets stored at 22°C (shelf life 3–5 days survival). Products include whole blood (420 ml + 70 ml CPD-A), packed red cells (PCV up to 60%), FFP, cryoprecipitate, platelets, human albumin solution, fibrinogen, factors VIII and IX concentrates, recombinant factor VII.

questions.question:
Describe the origin, pharmacological properties, clinical uses, and effects on organ systems of Halothane as an inhalational anaesthetic agent, under the following headings:

A(i) Chemical name, physical properties, and MAC
A(ii) Metabolism and elimination
B(i) Effects on the cardiovascular, respiratory, and central nervous systems
B(ii) Effects on the uterus, GIT, and liver
C(i) Contraindications and the clinical basis for avoiding repeated administration
questions.answerText:
A(i) Chemical name: 1-bromo-1-chloro-2,2,2-trifluoroethane (halogenated alkane). Colour code: red. Colourless liquid with a relatively pleasant smell. Stored in amber-coloured bottles with 0.1% thymol preservative to protect against decomposition by light, at room temperature away from heat. Compatible with soda lime. MAC 0.75. Blood/gas solubility coefficient of 2.5. Non-irritant to the airway, so inhalational induction is relatively fast. Recovery from halothane anaesthesia is slower than with other agents because of its high blood/gas solubility.

A(ii) Approximately 20% is metabolised in the liver, usually by the oxidative pathway. Major metabolite is trifluoroacetic acid, metabolised by isoenzyme of cytochrome P-450. End products are excreted in urine (metabolites excreted for several weeks). 60–80% is eliminated unchanged via lungs.

B(i) Cardiovascular: dose-dependent reduction of blood pressure due to myocardial depression; hypotension due to peripheral vasodilation; bradycardia may occur, usually reversible by atropine; arrhythmias (tachycardia, ventricular extrasystole, or even cardiac arrest) may occur with local infiltration with adrenaline — sensitisation to catecholamines. Respiratory: non-irritant and pleasant to breathe during induction; bronchodilator effect (good in asthmatics); in unpremedicated patients, associated with increased ventilatory rate and decreased tidal volume; rapid loss of pharyngeal and laryngeal reflexes; inhibition of salivary and bronchial secretions by depressing clearance of mucus, causing postoperative hypoxia and atelectasis. CNS: produces anaesthesia without analgesia; cerebral blood flow and intracranial pressure are increased; no seizure activity on EEG.

B(ii) Uterus: relaxes uterine muscle and may cause postpartum haemorrhage. GIT: minimal nausea and vomiting; gastric motility may be inhibited. Liver: halothane-induced hepatitis, especially with repeated doses; should be avoided in pre-existing liver dysfunction.

C(i) Contraindications: risk of triggering malignant hyperthermia; contraindicated if previous pyrexia or jaundice following prior administration. Clinically: repeated exposure increases risk of halothane-induced hepatitis, and the sensitisation of the myocardium to catecholamines makes its use hazardous when adrenaline is used for local infiltration.

questions.question:
A. Describe the physiology of the body fluid compartments:
A(i) Percentage of body weight that is water in males, females, infants and obese individuals
A(ii) Distribution of total body water in absolute volumes (for a 70kg adult) across all compartments
A(iii) Normal daily fluid and electrolyte losses and requirements
B. Describe the perioperative fluid management under the following headings:
B(i) The fasting policy (ASA guidelines) as stated
B(ii) The categories of perioperative fluid requirement and how maintenance is calculated using the 4-2-1 rule
B(iii) How pyrexia affects insensible losses
C. Explain the mechanism of how intraoperative and postoperative fluid balance is affected by anaesthetic technique.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Total body water percentages:
- Males: 55% of body weight (or 60% in some references)
- Females: 45% of body weight
- Infants: 80% of body weight
- Obese: less than standard values; fat contains little water

A(ii) Distribution of total body water (42L for 70kg adult):
- Total body water: 42L (body weight x 0.6)
- Intracellular fluid: 28L (body weight x 0.4)
- Extracellular fluid: 14L (body weight x 0.2)
- Intravascular fluid: 3L (body weight x 0.05)
- Interstitial fluid: 11L (body weight x 0.15)

A(iii) Normal daily requirements and losses:
- Adult losses: 2.5–3L per day (1300–1800ml urine; 1000ml insensible from lungs and skin; 100ml in faeces)
- About 200ml per day produced from metabolic processes
- Sodium: approximately 1.5mmol/kg/day (0.5–1.0mmol/kg/day electrolyte requirement)
- Potassium: approximately 1mmol/kg/day (0.5–1.0mmol/kg/day)
- Patient NPO: 1000ml 0.9% N/S + 1500–2000ml 5% dextrose + 60mmol KCl

B(i) Fasting policy (ASA guidelines):
- 6 hours for solid food, infant formula, or other milk
- 4 hours for breast milk
- 2 hours for clear (non-particulate) and non-carbonated fluids

B(ii) Perioperative fluid categories and 4-2-1 rule:
- Categories: replacement of pre-existing losses; provision of maintenance fluids; replacement of intraoperative and postoperative losses
- 4-2-1 rule: 4ml/kg/hr for first 10kg of body weight; 2ml/kg/hr for second 10kg of body weight; 1ml/kg/hr for subsequent kg of body weight
- Extra fluid for fever, tracheotomy, denuded surfaces

B(iii) Effect of pyrexia on insensible losses:
- Pyrexia increases insensible loss by 20% per degree Celsius rise in body temperature
- Normal insensible loss for an adult in temperate climate is 1000ml/day
- Fluid lost this way is exhaled water vapour and electrolyte-rich sweat

C. Anaesthetic effects on fluid balance:
- General anaesthesia causes significant vasodilatation and varying degrees of myocardial suppression
- Positive pressure ventilation will reduce venous return and cardiac output
- Vasodilatation produced by sympathetic blockade following spinal and epidural anaesthesia will also reduce preload and blood pressure
- Surgery contributes: bleeding, third space losses, evaporative losses from exposed surfaces, fluid sequestration in obstructed or adynamic bowel, patient positioning, and the neuro-hormonal or stress response

(i) ASA classification for this patient:
- Class V — a moribund patient who is not expected to survive 24 hours with or without operation; the suffix E is added for emergency operation
- Justification: the patient is septic with bowel perforation, haemodynamically unstable (hypotensive, tachycardic), febrile, and has co-existing ischaemic heart disease; he requires emergency surgery

(ii) Objectives of pre-anaesthetic visit:
- To establish rapport with the patient
- To assess the patient's fitness for anaesthesia
- To prescribe premedication as needed
- To ensure that patient is prepared correctly for operation, improving where feasible any existing factors which may increase the risks of an adverse outcome

(iii) Components of pre-anaesthetic assessment:
- History: presenting condition/complaints; past medical history and concurrent medical history; anaesthetic history; drug history/drug allergies; family and social history
- Physical examination: general examination; cardiovascular examination; respiratory system; airway examination — mouth opening, neck movements, thyromental distance, dentition, Mallampati
- Relevant laboratory investigations: full blood count/PCV; urea, creatinine and electrolytes; blood glucose; ECG; chest X-ray; liver function test

(iv) Preoperative fasting guideline:
- Called the 6-4-2 hours guideline: 6 hours for solid food; 4 hours for breast milk; 2 hours for clear non-particulate and non-carbonated fluids

(v) Objectives of premedication:
- To allay anxiety and fear
- Reduce secretions
- Enhance hypnotic effect of general anaesthesia
- Reduce postoperative nausea and vomiting
- Produce amnesia
- Reduce the volume and increase the pH of gastric contents
- Attenuate sympathoadrenal responses (tachycardia, hypertension, plasma catecholamine rise)
Drug classes: benzodiazepines (diazepam, midazolam — anxiolysis, sedation, amnesia); opioid analgesics (fentanyl, pethidine, morphine); antiemetics (ondansetron); beta blockers (esmolol); anticholinergic drugs (atropine, hyoscine, glycopyrrolate)
Anticholinergic properties: atropine and hyoscine are tertiary amines that cross the blood-brain barrier; glycopyrrolate is a quaternary amine that does not cross the blood-brain barrier; used for antisialagogue effect, sedation and amnesia (hyoscine + morphine), and prevention of reflex bradycardia
questions.question:
A 55-year-old male presents for emergency laparotomy following bowel perforation. He is tachycardic, hypotensive, and running a temperature of 39.5°C. His family reports he has a history of ischaemic heart disease.
(i) Using the ASA classification as stated, assign an ASA grade to this patient and justify using the exact criteria.
(ii) State the objectives of the pre-anaesthetic visit as listed.
(iii) List the components of a full pre-anaesthetic assessment including history, physical examination, and relevant investigations.
(iv) State the preoperative fasting guideline and what it is called.
(v) State the objectives of premedication and list the drug classes and specific agents named, including anticholinergic drugs and their distinctive properties.

questions.answerText:
(i) The diagnosis is Malignant Hyperthermia (MH). It is an inherited autosomal dominant disorder of skeletal muscle, triggered by inhalation anaesthetics and depolarising muscle relaxants such as suxamethonium. The trigger causes increased release of intracellular calcium and activation of various metabolic processes, resulting in a hypermetabolic state.
(ii) Earliest signs include: rapid rise in end-tidal CO2 (measured by capnograph), tachycardia, supraventricular or ventricular dysrhythmias, warm flushed skin, hypoxia secondary to increased O2 consumption, hyperthermia, muscle rigidity secondary to sustained muscle contracture, hyperkalaemia, and myoglobinuria secondary to muscle breakdown. Respiratory and metabolic acidosis may develop, followed later by renal failure from rhabdomyolysis and myoglobinuria. DIC from muscle necrosis, cyanosis, hypotension and cardiac arrest may ensue.
(iii) Immediate steps: stop all inhalation anaesthetics and succinylcholine; stop surgery or complete as soon as possible; maintain endotracheal intubation and hyperventilate, maintaining on 100% O2; maintain anaesthesia with IV agents e.g. propofol and fentanyl.
(iv) The specific agent is Dantrolene. Give rapid continuous IV push of dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg mixed in saline; repeat doses every 5–10 minutes until signs of MH are controlled or until the maximum dose of 10 mg/kg is given. Mortality is less than 10% if treated with dantrolene; before its use in 1979 the outcome was almost always fatal.
(v) Monitor arterial blood gases, serum electrolytes, creatinine kinase level, and urine for myoglobin. Symptomatic treatment: sodium bicarbonate given rapidly to correct metabolic acidosis; glucose and insulin to treat hyperkalaemia; IV 0.9% NaCl and frusemide to maintain a high urine output; alkalinisation of urine to prevent renal failure in patients with myoglobinuria. Additional treatment: core and surface cooling with iced saline gastric lavage and a cooling blanket; lidocaine or amiodarone to treat ventricular arrhythmias. Note: calcium-channel blockers should NOT be used for dysrhythmias as CVS collapse may occur when used with dantrolene. Observe in ICU for 24 hours because of risk of recurrence.
questions.question:
A 24-year-old male is undergoing elective surgery under general anaesthesia. Shortly after induction with an inhalation anaesthetic and suxamethonium, the anaesthetist notices a rapid rise in end-tidal CO2, tachycardia, supraventricular dysrhythmias, warm flushed skin, muscle rigidity, and hyperthermia.
(i) What is the most likely diagnosis, and what is the underlying pathophysiological mechanism?
(ii) What are the earliest clinical signs of this condition as they may present intraoperatively?
(iii) Outline the immediate resuscitation steps the anaesthetic team should take.
(iv) What is the specific pharmacological agent used in definitive treatment, and how is it administered?
(v) What monitoring should be instituted and what symptomatic treatments are required to address metabolic complications?

questions.answerText:
(A)
(i) Neostigmine is an anticholinesterase agent. Mechanism: it combines reversibly with acetylcholinesterase, inhibiting its activity. This prevents hydrolysis of ACh at the NMJ, allowing more ACh to accumulate and compete with the residual non-depolarising agent at nicotinic receptor sites, thereby reversing the non-depolarising blockade.
(ii) Onset: 3–5 minutes. Elimination half-life: 77 minutes. Dose: 0.04–0.07 mg/kg (also cited as 0.04–0.06 mg/kg).
(iii) Muscarinic side effects: bradycardia, hypersecretion (salivation, sweating), bronchospasm, increased intestinal motility, and blurred vision. Rationale for anticholinergic co-administration: to block muscarinic receptors and prevent these side effects. Agents used: atropine (dose 0.01–0.02 mg/kg), scopolamine, or glycopyrrolate.

(B)
(i) Edrophonium: also an anticholinesterase; listed as an available alternative to neostigmine for reversal of non-depolarising blockade. Specific pharmacokinetic comparison not detailed beyond listing.
(ii) Pyridostigmine: also an anticholinesterase available in clinical practice for reversal of non-depolarising NMB. No further detail is required beyond this listing.
(iii) Sugammadex: reverses rocuronium specifically. Mechanism: rocuronium is reversed by sugammadex (a modified gamma-cyclodextrin that encapsulates the drug molecule). Also stated that rocuronium is excreted by the kidneys.

(C)
(i) Patient concurrent disease factors altering responses: neurological diseases; muscular diseases; myasthenia gravis; myasthenic syndrome (Eaton-Lambert syndrome); liver diseases; kidney diseases.
(ii) Drug interaction categories: inhalational agents (potentiate non-depolarising block); intravenous anaesthetics; local anaesthetics; neuromuscular locking drugs; antibiotics; anticonvulsants; magnesium.
(iii) Physiological/environmental factors: temperature; acid-base balance; electrolyte abnormality; age.
questions.question:
(A) Describe the pharmacology of neostigmine as a reversal agent under the following headings:
(i) Class of drug and mechanism of action at the NMJ.
(ii) Onset of action, elimination half-life, and dose.

(B) Compare neostigmine with the following agents for reversal of neuromuscular blockade:
(i) Edrophonium.
(ii) Pyridostigmine.
(iii) Sugammadex (state which relaxant it reverses and its mechanism).

(C) Describe the choice criteria for muscle relaxants in clinical practice, including:

A 60-year-old debilitated, hospitalised patient develops progressive hypotension (SBP 80 mmHg), tachycardia, tachypnoea, oliguria, and a change in mental status. His skin is warm and flushed. His SVR is low with a hyperdynamic circulation.
(i) What type of shock does this presentation suggest, and what is the most likely aetiological category in this context?
(ii) What are the three stages of the physiological progression of shock?
(iii) What cellular and systemic pathophysiological processes occur in the shock stage (stage 2)?
(iv) Outline the management of this patient, including fluid, antimicrobials, vasopressors, and steroid use.
(v) What dopamine dose ranges correspond to its dopaminergic, inotropic, and vasoconstrictive effects?
questions.answerText:
(i) The presentation suggests distributive shock. The most likely aetiological category in a debilitated hospitalised patient is septic shock. Distributive shock results from a severe decrease in SVR; vasodilation reduces afterload and may be associated with increased cardiac output (hyperdynamic state).
(ii) The three stages of physiological progression: Preshock (warm shock, compensated shock) – compensatory mechanisms are active. Shock – initial signs of end organ dysfunction appear. End organ dysfunction – progressive irreversible dysfunction and patient death.
(iii) Cellular and systemic pathophysiology in the shock stage: imbalance in oxygen supply and demand; conversion from aerobic to anaerobic metabolism; cell membrane ion pump dysfunction; leakage of intracellular contents into the extracellular space; intracellular pH dysregulation. Clinical signs: tachycardia, tachypnoea, metabolic acidosis, oliguria, cool and clammy skin (though in distributive shock skin may remain warm early). SIRS/sepsis pathway: macrophage and neutrophil activation with mediator release (exotoxins, endotoxins, cytokines such as TNF and IL-1) activating the complement cascade; endothelial reaction; CVS/microvascular changes leading to impaired O2 use and cellular hypoxia.
(iv) Management: treat the primary cause – sepsis: administer antibiotics. Support the cardiovascular system with IV fluids and inotropes. Vasopressors: dopamine, dobutamine, adrenaline, noradrenaline; vasodilators (GTN, Na nitroprusside) may be used. Respiratory support: O2 therapy and mechanical ventilation. Renal support: haemofiltration/haemodialysis. Haematological: blood transfusion to correct anaemia; other blood products to correct coagulopathy. Steroids: controversial; main indication is adrenocortical failure (Addisonian crisis). Monitoring: BP, pulse rate, temperature, urine output, CVP, PCWP, CO, plasma lactate, gastrointestinal pH.
(v) Dopamine – an endogenous precursor of noradrenaline with multiple dose-related effects: Low dose (0.5–3 mcg/kg/min): beta-2 and dopaminergic effects – enhanced blood flow to renal and splanchnic beds. Moderate dose (5–10 mcg/kg/min): positive inotropic effects. High dose (>20 mcg/kg/min): alpha-actions (vasoconstriction).

(i) Physiological and fetal consequences of unrelieved labour pain:
- Psychological: suffering
- CVS: increased work of the heart
- Respiratory: marked hyperventilation
- Exhaustion, uterine atony, incoordinate uterine action
- Fetal: ischaemia and acidosis from stress responses and hypocapnia

(ii) Pharmacological options:
- Simple oral sedatives e.g. chloral hydrate, paracetamol
- Pethidine: 50–100mg not too early and not too late in labour; repeat every 4 hours; depresses the fetus; naloxone for reversal; side effects: depresses the fetus, nausea and vomiting, sedation; 60% of patients get relief
- Other opioids: morphine, pentazocine, tramadol
- Inhalation: Entonox = 50:50 nitrous oxide:oxygen; premixed; intermittent self-administration during contractions; quality of analgesia fair in first stage in >50% of patients; side effect: nausea and vomiting
- Regional analgesia: SAB, epidural block, CSEB; agents: weak solution of bupivacaine + fentanyl 1mcg/ml, or ropivacaine
- Special situations: PIH — diazepam, promethazine and barbiturates

(iii) Ideal properties of labour analgesic:
- Potent analgesic
- Only relieves pain during contractions
- No effect on mother and baby
- Allows participation in the birthing process
- Does not prolong labour
- No other side effects

(iv) Requirements for labour epidural analgesia service:
- Education of team on labour analgesia
- Written policies and protocols
- Availability of anaesthetist on 24-hour basis
- One-on-one midwife-patient ratio
- Monitors
- Resuscitation equipment

(v) Subarachnoid block technique:
- Obtain consent and ensure no contraindications
- Antacid prophylaxis
- Ensure adequacy of resus equipment and drugs
- Apply monitors: NIBP, SaO2, ECG, EtCO2
- Keep patient warm
- IV access and preload with N/S 500ml–1000ml
- Position: sitting or lateral
- Skin prep; identify L3–L4 interspinous space
- Infiltrate LA 1% lidocaine 2–5ml
- Introduce G25 or G26 pencil point spinal needle
- On free CSF flow give heavy bupivacaine 0.5% 2–2.5ml
- Addition of fentanyl 25mcg intensifies analgesia
- Position supine and place wedge under right hip to displace uterus
- Monitor every minute for next 10 minutes; correct hypotension with fluids and ephedrine
- Give oxygen by face mask
- On delivery of baby administer oxytocin 5 units
