questions.answerText:
(i) Malignant hyperthermia (MH).

(ii) MH is an inherited autosomal dominant disorder of skeletal muscle. It is triggered by inhalational anaesthetics and depolarising muscle relaxants (e.g. succinylcholine). These agents cause increased release of intracellular calcium, activating various metabolic processes resulting in a hypermetabolic state. Consequences include: tachycardia; rapid rise in end-tidal CO2; supraventricular or ventricular dysrhythmias; warm, flushed skin; hypoxia (secondary to increased O2 consumption); hyperthermia; muscle rigidity (secondary to sustained muscle contracture); hyperkalaemia; myoglobinuria (secondary to muscle breakdown); respiratory and metabolic acidosis; and later renal failure from rhabdomyolysis, DIC, cyanosis, hypotension, and cardiac arrest.

(iii) Immediate resuscitative measures:
- Stop all inhalational anaesthetics and succinylcholine immediately.
- Stop surgery or complete it as soon as possible.
- Maintain endotracheal intubation and hyperventilate on 100% O2.
- Maintain anaesthesia with IV agents (e.g. propofol and fentanyl).
- Monitor arterial blood gases, serum electrolytes, creatinine kinase, and urine for myoglobin.
- Sodium bicarbonate to correct metabolic acidosis; glucose and insulin to treat hyperkalaemia; IV 0.9% NaCl and frusemide to maintain high urine output; alkalinise urine to prevent renal failure.
- Core and surface cooling with iced saline gastric lavage and a cooling blanket.
- Lidocaine or amiodarone for ventricular arrhythmias (note: calcium-channel blockers should NOT be used as CVS collapse may occur when used with dantrolene).
- Observe in ICU for 24 hours because of risk of recurrence.

(iv) Dantrolene. Rapid continuous infusion IV push of dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg mixed in saline. Repeat doses every 5–10 minutes until signs of MH are controlled or until a maximum dose of 10 mg/kg is reached. Mortality is less than 10% if treated with dantrolene.
questions.question:
A 28-year-old male is brought to the operating theatre for an emergency laparotomy. On induction, he develops generalised muscle rigidity, a rapidly rising end-tidal CO2 level, tachycardia, hyperthermia, and muscle fasciculations. The anaesthetist suspects a life-threatening reaction to the inhalational agent and succinylcholine given at induction.

(i) What is the most likely diagnosis?
(ii) Describe the pathophysiologic basis of this condition, including the trigger agents and the metabolic consequences.
(iii) Outline the immediate resuscitative measures that must be taken in the operating theatre.
(iv) What is the specific drug used for definitive treatment, and how is it administered?

A(i) Describe the anatomy of the spinal cord relevant to spinal and epidural anaesthesia, including: the relationship of the cord to the foramen magnum and the conus medullaris (in adults vs infants), the three meningeal coverings and their characteristics, and the contents of the subarachnoid space.
A(ii) Describe the anatomy of the epidural space relevant to epidural anaesthesia, including its borders and contents.
B(i) Describe the technique of performing a subarachnoid block in a step-by-step format, including patient preparation, landmark identification, needle insertion, CSF confirmation, and injection.
B(ii) State the complications of epidural and subarachnoid blocks with their respective treatments.
questions.answerText:
A(i) The spinal cord is continuously cephalad with the brainstem at the foramen magnum and terminates distally in the conus medullaris. The termination varies from L3 in the infant to the lower border of L1 in the adult. The cord is covered by three membranes (from within to peripheral): the pia mater – a highly vascular membrane that closely invests the spinal cord (and brain); the arachnoid mater – a non-vascular membrane closely attached to the outermost layer (the dura); the dura mater (dural mater) – the outermost layer. The subarachnoid space lies between the pia and arachnoid mater. Contents of the subarachnoid space: CSF, spinal nerves, a trabecular network between the two membranes, blood vessels that supply the spinal cord, and the dentate ligaments.
A(ii) The epidural space surrounds the dura mater posteriorly, laterally, and anteriorly. Borders: anteriorly – posterior longitudinal ligament; laterally – the pedicles and the intervertebral foramina; posteriorly – ligamentum flavum. Contents: nerve roots, fat, areolar tissue, lymphatics, and blood vessels.
B(i) Technique of subarachnoid block: (i) Measure and record the baseline blood pressure and pulse rate; establish an intravenous infusion line. (ii) Place the patient in sitting or lateral position as preferred. (iii) Scrub hands, put on sterile gloves, and cleanse the puncture site. (iv) Locate a convenient space between L2 and L5 using the top of the iliac crest (L4/5) as a landmark. (v) Introduce the spinal needle through the selected space in the midline and advance until a "give" is felt. (vi) Remove the stylet and observe whether CSF comes out; if not, gently rotate the needle and slowly withdraw. If no CSF, re-insert stylet, advance further and repeat. (vii) When free flow of CSF is obtained, inject the appropriate dose of local anaesthetic, withdraw the needle, and close the puncture site with a sterile dressing. (viii) Return patient to supine position with legs slightly elevated; closely monitor vital signs; determine height of block by dermatome level using pin prick.
B(ii) Complications and treatments: Hypotension from sympathetic autonomic blockade – treatment: intravenous fluids and vasopressor (ephedrine). Backache from trauma to spinal ligaments – treatment: analgesics if severe. Haematoma if increased bleeding tendency – prevention: avoid technique if blood dyscrasia present. Urinary retention – treatment: encourage voiding; may need catheterisation. Infection if asepsis not maintained – treatment: antibiotics. Spinal headache (subarachnoid block only) from low CSF pressure – treated conservatively (recumbent position, hydration, caffeine) or definitively with epidural blood patch (15–20 ml autologous blood). "Total spinal" (epidural block only) – from unrecognised subarachnoid injection of a large volume of local anaesthetic during attempted epidural.

questions.question:
During an epidural block for a surgical procedure, a patient suddenly develops tinnitus, restlessness, slurred speech, and then generalised seizures. Shortly after, profound hypotension, ECG changes with arrhythmias, and respiratory depression occur.
(i) What is the spot diagnosis, and which local anaesthetic is most commonly implicated in the severe cardiovascular manifestation?
(ii) What are the three principal causes of this complication?
(iii) Describe the full spectrum of CNS and cardiovascular clinical features in order of progression.
(iv) Outline the management of this emergency using the ABC framework.
questions.answerText:
(i) The diagnosis is local anaesthetic (LA) systemic toxicity. Bupivacaine is most commonly implicated in severe cardiovascular toxicity, particularly the profound hypotension and arrhythmias.
(ii) The three principal causes are: inadvertent intravenous injection; injection into vascular areas; and gross overdose.
(iii) CNS features in order of progression: tinnitus, restlessness, vertigo, slurred speech, seizures, apnoea, and coma. Cardiovascular features: profound hypotension; ECG changes with arrhythmias; tachycardia or bradycardia (commoner with bupivacaine). Respiratory system: depression leading to apnoea (central effect).
(iv) Management – ABC framework: A – Oxygen via bag/mask or endotracheal tube. B – Hyperventilate with bag and mask. C – Intravenous fluids; inotropes e.g. ephedrine, dobutamine, dopamine, adrenaline; for seizures: diazepam 0.1 mg/kg or midazolam; thiopentone 0.5–2 mg/kg; suxamethonium is used to aid intubation. Additional toxicity considerations: neurotoxicity occurs particularly with chloroprocaine, related to low pH (3.0) and presence of antioxidant sodium bisulfite, with heavy solutions of 5% lignocaine also implicated. Methaemoglobinaemia occurs with large doses of prilocaine >8 mg/kg, which accumulates ortho-toluidine, changing haemoglobin to metHb – treatment is IV methylene blue 1 mg/kg. Allergic reactions are rare (<1%), commoner with esters, may be related to preservatives such as methylparaben, and there is no cross-sensitivity between esters and amides.

A(i) General: the LMA sits over the glottic opening. It is available in different sizes. A drain tube aids gastric suctioning. With some versions an endotracheal tube may be passed through to aid in intubation. The Classic LMA was designed in 1981 by Dr Archie Brain, and is specified in difficult airway management.

A(ii) Advantages of Classic LMA: rapidity and ease of placement; improved haemodynamic stability; minimal rise in intraocular pressure; reduced anaesthesia requirements; reduced cough on emergence; lower incidence of sore throat in adults; utility in difficult intubation. On insertion, the backward folding of the cuff (tip roll) causes resistance; the LMA is less stimulating than ETT; remove it awake in adults and deep in children. Disadvantages: no protection against aspiration; gastric insufflation; air leak with positive pressure ventilation; cannot protect aspiration; cannot be used for pulmonary toilet.

B(i) LMA ProSeal: expected to reduce aspiration risk (0.02%); intracuff pressure is lower and seals better than Classic LMA; less gastric insufflation; PEEP can safely be applied; more difficult to place than Classic LMA; suitable for longer duration surgeries; oesophageal conduit permits passage of a gastric tube.

B(ii) LMA Fastrach (ILMA): designed by Dr Brain; reusable, easy to use, with high success rate. Intubation may be difficult if mouth opens less than 20 mm. Better to withdraw the device after intubation. Ventilation and intubation can be successfully achieved in obese patients (BMI greater than 30). Accepted in guidelines for unanticipated difficult airway in non-obstetrical patients.

C(i) The LMA cannot protect against aspiration because it sits over (not inside) the glottis, and does not create a sealed cuff within the trachea as an endotracheal tube does. Gastric insufflation and passive regurgitation of gastric contents can occur without the patient coughing or showing warning signs. This limits LMA use in patients with a full stomach, in emergency (non-fasted) patients, in obstetric patients, and in patients with gastro-oesophageal reflux, where the risk of aspiration of gastric contents would be significant.
questions.question:
Describe the Laryngeal Mask Airway (LMA) under the following headings:

A(i) General features and design, including inventor and year
A(ii) Advantages and disadvantages of the Classic LMA
B(i) The LMA ProSeal — features distinguishing it from the Classic
B(ii) The intubating LMA (LMA Fastrach) — design features and patient suitability
C(i) Explain why the LMA cannot protect against aspiration, and in which clinical setting aspiration risk limits LMA use

questions.answerText:
(i) Oxygen production: Fractional distillation of air — method involves cooling air until it becomes liquid, then boiling the liquid air and separating its components; produces 99% pure O2. Vacuum swing adsorption process — non-cryogenic gas separation technology using adsorbents to segregate gases; produces 90–93% pure O2 (example: O2 concentrator, but the O2 produced is used immediately). O2 produced is stored in high-pressure cylinders after compression. O2 is delivered through oxygen cylinders or oxygen wall outlets.

(ii) Oxygen cylinder components: protective cap to prevent accidental force against the cylinder outlet; pressure gauge — shows the amount of oxygen in the tank; pressure reducing valve — releases oxygen safely at a desirable rate (O2 from cylinder at high pressure of 137 bars is regulated and reduced to 4 bars, delivered to the patient); flow meter — regulates control of oxygen in litres per minute; humidifier — oxygen is moistened by passing it through a humidifier to prevent mucous membranes of the respiratory tree from becoming dry.

(iii) Oxygen delivery devices: Nasal Prongs — low-flow; 1–6 L/min; FiO2 starts at 24% for 1 L/min and increases 4% for each L/min up to 44% for 6 L/min; well tolerated; greater than 6 L/min causes nasal mucosal drying; use for minimal or no respiratory distress. Simple (Hudson) Face Mask — low-flow; 5–8 L/min; FiO2: 5–6 L = 40%, 6–7 L = 50%, 7–8 L = 60%; mask does not need tight seal. Venturi Mask — high-flow; 4–12 L/min; FiO2 can be set at 24, 28, 31, 35, or 40%; use for COPD requiring specific O2 concentration. Non-Rebreather with Reservoir Bag — high-flow; 6–10 L/min; proper use at 10 L/min supplies 70% FiO2; requires tight fitting mask; use when 50% O2 required; for spontaneously breathing patients requiring highest O2 concentration. Puritan Face Mask — high-flow; greater than 10 L/min; FiO2 with single setup 35–50%, double setup 50–80+%; provides highest level of humidified oxygen; should be used when greater than 50% O2 required. Bag Valve Mask — FiO2 depends on type of bag; with good seal and correct position can achieve FiO2 up to 90%.

(iv) Hyperbaric oxygen therapy: breathing O2 at three times normal atmospheric pressure. Increases the amount of dissolved O2 in plasma from a maximum of 2 ml/100 ml to 6 ml/100 ml, resulting in an extra 200 ml/min of O2 delivery. Indicated for: decompression sickness, CO poisoning, gas gangrene, necrotizing fasciitis, skin flaps and grafts, chronic refractory osteomyelitis, thermal burns, and compartment syndrome.

(v) Heliox: mixture of 21% O2 and 79% helium with additional O2 entrainment; indicated in the treatment of acute exacerbation of obstructive pulmonary disorders. Entonox: mixture of 50% O2 and 50% N2O; for analgesia in labour and short procedures; supplied in cylinders as a gas under pressure (137 bar); liquefies at −7°C; may separate if exposed to low temperatures (0°C), in which case re-warm and invert to restore the mixture; colour code — body French blue, shoulder French blue and white quarters.
questions.question:
A 65-year-old man with a long history of COPD is brought to casualty with acute respiratory failure. You need to identify the source of his oxygen and prescribe an appropriate delivery device and flow rate.

(i) Describe the methods of oxygen production, and how oxygen is stored and delivered in a hospital.
(ii) Describe the oxygen cylinder, its components, and how pressure is regulated before delivery to the patient.
(iii) List all oxygen delivery devices mentioned and classify each as low-flow or high-flow, with their respective FiO2 and flow rate ranges.
(iv) What is hyperbaric oxygen therapy, and what conditions is it indicated for?
(v) Describe Heliox and Entonox — composition, indications, and storage considerations.

A 60-year-old male with type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension is on regular antihypertensives and metformin. He presents for elective right hemi-colectomy under general anaesthesia. During induction, the anaesthetist administers propofol and suxamethonium. The patient develops sinus bradycardia.

(i) Identify the drug responsible for the bradycardia and explain the mechanism.
(ii) List all the cardiovascular effects of this drug and their mechanisms.
(iii) Describe the risk factors in this patient that make him particularly vulnerable to dangerous hyperkalaemia from this drug.
(iv) State the other electrolyte/metabolic side effects that can occur, and which patient groups are at highest risk of cardiac arrest from electrolyte disturbance.
(v) What drug and dose should be given to prevent or treat the bradycardia, and what non-depolarising alternative could be used instead for a diabetic patient with autonomic neuropathy (anticipated difficult intubation)?
questions.answerText:
(i) Suxamethonium is responsible for the bradycardia. Mechanism: suxamethonium acts as an agonist at muscarinic (cardiac) receptors — its structural similarity to ACh means it activates muscarinic receptors in the heart, causing bradycardia. This is especially pronounced with repeated doses.

(ii) Cardiovascular effects of suxamethonium:
- Bradycardia: via muscarinic (M2) receptor stimulation at the SA node; especially common with repeated doses.
- In the context of hyperkalaemia: raised serum K+ from depolarisation of muscle membranes can cause arrhythmias and cardiac arrest.
- Increased intragastric pressure (gastrointestinal muscarinic effect): raises risk of regurgitation.

(iii) Risk factors for dangerous hyperkalaemia in this patient:
- Diabetes mellitus: associated with diabetic neuropathy (denervation injury causes upregulation of extrajunctional ACh receptors, increasing K+ released per molecule of suxamethonium).
- Pre-existing renal disease (common in longstanding type 2 diabetes) means baseline K+ may already be elevated.
- Other recognised risk conditions: burns injury, massive trauma, neurological disorders, stroke — any of these conditions cause upregulation of extrajunctional receptors. Although this particular patient's main risk is diabetic neuropathy.

(iv) Electrolyte/metabolic side effects: hyperkalaemia — normal muscles release enough potassium during suxamethonium-induced depolarisation to raise serum K+ by 0.5 mEq/L. Although usually insignificant in patients with normal baseline potassium, it can be life-threatening in patients with pre-existing hyperkalaemia. Patient groups at highest risk of cardiac arrest: those with burns injury, massive trauma, neurological disorders, and stroke.

(v) Prevention/treatment of bradycardia: atropine; dose to prevent bradycardia from repeated suxamethonium dosing is given prophylactically. Non-depolarising alternative for this patient with anticipated difficult intubation and diabetic neuropathy: rocuronium — can be used as a substitute for suxamethonium (onset time >60 seconds; duration 30–40 minutes; reversed by sugammadex).

questions.question:
A 45-year-old woman who is 32 weeks pregnant is brought to the emergency department following a road traffic accident. She has a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 9 and suspected head injury.
(i) Using the GCS components as stated, break down her GCS score of 9 to show one possible combination of eye, verbal and motor scores.
(ii) State the goals of brain protection in the ICU as listed and describe the brain protection protocol as stated.
(iii) Using the oxygen delivery device information, identify which device would be most appropriate for a spontaneously breathing patient who requires the highest possible oxygen concentration, and state its flow rate and expected FiO2.
(iv) For a patient with COPD requiring specific oxygen concentrations to avoid blunting the hypoxic drive, identify the appropriate device, its flow rates, the FiO2 options available, and the target saturation stated.
(v) Describe immediate ICU care of an unconscious patient covering all aspects of supportive care as listed.
questions.answerText:
(i) GCS score of 9 — one possible combination:
- Eye opening: to pain = 2
- Verbal response: confused = 4 (or inappropriate words = 3)
- Motor response: localises pain = 5 (or withdraws from pain = 4)
- Example: 2 + 4 + 3 = 9 (Eye to pain + confused verbal + inappropriate words is one combination)
- Multiple valid combinations exist; e.g. E2 + V2 + M5 = 9; or E3 + V2 + M4 = 9

(ii) Brain protection goals and protocol:
- Goals: patients with severe head injury; following major brain surgery
- Protocol: Give 100% O2; slight head up 15 degrees; sedation — fentanyl, propofol, midazolam; mechanical ventilation; ETCO2 is normal; prevent secondary causes of brain injury; steroids — no place in trauma but used for excision of tumour; mannitol is not contraindicated; close monitoring — ICP, CT scan, SpO2, ABG, E/U, input/output

(iii) Highest possible oxygen concentration device:
- Non-rebreather mask with reservoir bag
- Flow rate: 6–10L/min; at 10L/min supplies 70% FiO2
- Requires tight fitting mask; should be used when 50% oxygen required; use for any spontaneously breathing patient who requires highest O2 possible (carbon monoxide poisoning, trauma, etc.)

(iv) Device for COPD patient:
- Venturi Mask
- Flow rate: 4–12L/min
- FiO2 can be set specifically: 24, 28, 31, 35 and 40%
- Use: COPD patient that requires specific oxygen concentrations — to administer high FiO2 but not too high such that the hypoxic drive to breathe is blunted
- Target saturation: titrate to keep sats about 88%

(v) Supportive care of unconscious patient:
- Maintenance of fluid volume: input/output monitoring
- Nutrition: enteral feeding; parenteral feeding
- Prevention from cold
- Maintain tissue integrity of cornea
- Catheter care
- Bowel care
- Skin care
- Oral care
- Emergency care: ABC of resuscitation; preventing risk of injury; padding/support

(i) Category and likely cause:
- Category: drug reaction — hypersensitivity/anaphylactic reaction; this falls under the classification of 'other complications' which includes drug reactions (hypersensitivity reactions)
- Likely cause: allergic/anaphylactic drug reaction occurring during anaesthetic delivery

(ii) General sequence for managing intraoperative complications:
- Continual vigilance and monitoring
- Recognition of occurrence of a problem
- Creation of a list of differential diagnoses
- Choice of a working diagnosis — either the most likely or most dangerous possibility
- Treatment of working diagnosis
- Assessment of the response of the problem to the administered treatment
- Refinement of the list of differential diagnoses especially if the response has not been as expected

(iii) Respiratory complications:
- Respiratory obstruction
- Laryngospasm
- Bronchospasm
- Complications associated with intubation: difficult intubation, failed intubation, oesophageal intubation, endobronchial intubation
- Aspiration of gastric content
- Hypoxaemia
- Hypercapnia
- Apnoea
- Atelectasis: reduction in functional residual capacity and tendency to hypoventilation during general anaesthesia may cause alveolar collapse atelectasis

(iv) Cardiovascular complications:
- Hypertension: intraoperative hypertension defined as arterial pressure 25% greater than the patient's preoperative value; increases risk of ischaemia, infarction and haemorrhage in organs and brain in particular
- Hypotension: may impair perfusion and consequently oxygenation of vital organs
- Hypovolaemia
- Haemorrhage
- Disturbances of heart rate: bradycardia, tachycardia and arrhythmias
- Myocardial ischaemia
- Embolus: passage of non-mass through vascular system

(v) Neurological and regional complications:
- Awareness: recall of intraoperative events; may be very distressing especially if associated with painful experience
- Neurological/nerve injury
- Hypothermia
- Hyperthermia
- Regional anaesthesia-specific complications: hypotension; nerve injury; infections; haematoma; local anaesthetic toxicity — features: dizziness, drowsiness, confusion, tinnitus, circumoral tingling/numbness, seizures, and cardiovascular arrest
questions.question:
A patient develops sudden unexpected hypotension, bronchospasm, and urticaria thirty minutes into an elective surgical procedure under general anaesthesia.
(i) Using the classification, name this category of complication and identify its likely cause.
(ii) Describe the general sequence through which any complication should be managed intraoperatively.
(iii) List all types of respiratory complications of anaesthesia as given, including their named sub-types.
(iv) List all cardiovascular complications, including the definition of intraoperative hypertension given.
(v) Describe the neurological complications listed, and for local anaesthetic regional technique, state all regional anaesthesia-specific complications including the features of local anaesthetic toxicity.

questions.answerText:
(i) Indications for regional technique over GA in this patient:
- Chronic respiratory disease (e.g. emphysema, chronic bronchitis/COPD) — regional anaesthesia avoids respiratory depression from GA.
- Poor-risk patient.
- Patient's choice to be awake.
- Less interruption of oral intake (useful if diabetic).
- Good post-operative analgesia and reduced risk of post-op complications (lung atelectasis, DVT, PONV).
- Lack of adequate anaesthetic manpower or facilities for GA.

(ii) The most appropriate technique is spinal (subarachnoid) anaesthesia. Indications for spinal anaesthesia: surgery below the umbilicus (lower abdominal, inguinal, urogenital, rectal, lower extremity surgery); obstetric anaesthesia and analgesia; surgeries below the neck alone or in conjunction with GA; patients with full stomach (to avoid risk of aspiration); chronic respiratory disease; severe renal, hepatic, or metabolic disturbances; eclamptic toxaemia; myasthenia gravis.

(iii) Technique for subarachnoid block:
- Measure and record baseline blood pressure and pulse rate.
- Establish an IV infusion line.
- Place patient in sitting or lateral position as preferred.
- Scrub hands, put on sterile gloves, and cleanse puncture site.
- Locate a convenient space between L2 and L5 using the top of the iliac crest (L4/5) as a landmark.
- Introduce the spinal needle through the selected space in the midline and advance until a 'give' is felt.
- Remove the stylet and watch for free flow of CSF (end point); if absent, rotate needle gently and slowly withdraw, or re-insert stylet and advance further.
- When free flow of CSF is obtained: inject the appropriate dose of local anaesthetic, withdraw needle, close site with sterile dressing.
- Return patient to supine with legs slightly elevated; monitor vital signs until block is established.
- Determine height of block by pin prick.

(iv) Three contraindications: patient refusal; coagulopathy or anticoagulant therapy; hypovolaemia or shock; skin sepsis at or near puncture site; pre-existing neurological deficit; deformity of the spine (e.g. scoliosis); increased intracranial pressure (any three acceptable).

(v) Differences between subarachnoid and epidural blocks:
- Ease of technique: subarachnoid is simpler/easier; epidural is more difficult.
- Needle type: subarachnoid uses a smaller spinal needle; epidural uses a bigger Tuohy needle.
- Dose of local anaesthetic: much less for subarachnoid; much more for epidural.
- Onset: quicker for subarachnoid; slower onset for epidural.
- Control of block height: easier with subarachnoid (baricity); more difficult with epidural.
- Spinal headache: may occur with subarachnoid; does not occur with epidural.
- Total spinal: may occur with epidural via inadvertent dural puncture; rarely occurs with subarachnoid.
questions.question:
A 70-year-old female with known hypertension and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) presents for repair of an inguinal hernia. The surgical team requests that the anaesthetist consider a regional technique.

(i) State the indications for choosing a regional technique over general anaesthesia in this patient.
(ii) Name the most appropriate central neural block for this procedure and describe its indications.
(iii) Describe the step-by-step technique for performing a subarachnoid block, including preparation, patient positioning, the landmark used, and the end point for correct needle placement.
(iv) Name three contraindications to a subarachnoid block that would prevent this technique in this patient, if present.
(v) Describe the differences in technique between subarachnoid and epidural blocks, including needle type, dose of local anaesthetic, onset, and control of block height.

Describe the gross anatomy and physiology of the pharynx under the following headings:

A(i) Definition, extent, and the three parts with their limits
A(ii) The nasopharynx — contents, communications, and lymphoid tissue
B(i) The oropharynx — walls, lining, and structures
B(ii) The laryngopharynx — extent, lining, innervation, and vascular supply
C(i) Explain the role of the uvula and soft palate in preventing nasal regurgitation during swallowing, and the nerve controlling their muscles
questions.answerText:
A(i) The pharynx is a wide muscular tube which forms the common upper pathway of the respiratory and alimentary tracts. Anteriorly, it is in free communication with the nasal cavity, the mouth, and the larynx, which divide it into three parts: nasopharynx, oropharynx, and laryngopharynx. The pharynx carries food and air to the oesophagus and larynx respectively. The flap of cartilage called the epiglottis stops food from entering the larynx.

A(ii) Nasopharynx: lies behind the nasal cavity and above the soft palate. It communicates with the oropharynx through the pharyngeal isthmus. It includes the space between the internal nares and the soft palate and lies above the oral cavity. The adenoids (pharyngeal tonsils) are lymphoid tissue structures located in the posterior wall of the nasopharynx. Waldeyer's tonsillar ring is an annular arrangement of lymphoid tissue in both the nasopharynx and oropharynx. The auditory tube (connecting the middle ear to the pharynx) opens into the nasopharynx at the pharyngeal opening of the auditory tube.

B(i) Oropharynx: lies behind the oral cavity, extending from the uvula to the level of the hyoid bone. Opens anteriorly through the isthmus faucium into the mouth; lateral wall between palatoglossal arch and palatopharyngeal arch contains the palatine tonsil. Anterior wall consists of the base of the tongue and the epiglottic vallecula. Lateral wall: tonsil, tonsillar fossa, and tonsillar (faucial) pillars. Superior wall: inferior surface of the soft palate and the uvula. Lined by non-keratinized squamous stratified epithelium.

B(ii) Laryngopharynx (also known as hypopharynx): is the caudal part of the pharynx; connects to the oesophagus; lies inferior to the epiglottis and extends to where the common pathway diverges into the respiratory (laryngeal) and digestive (oesophageal) pathways. Lined with stratified squamous epithelium. Innervated by the pharyngeal plexus and by the recurrent laryngeal nerve. Vascular supply: superior thyroid artery, lingual artery, and ascending pharyngeal arteries.

C(i) The uvula is a conic projection from the back edge of the middle of the soft palate, composed of connective tissue with racemose glands and muscular fibres; also contains serous glands producing thin saliva. The muscular part of the uvula shortens and broadens the uvula, changing the contour of the posterior part of the soft palate. During swallowing, the soft palate and the uvula move together to close off the nasopharynx, preventing food from entering the nasal cavity. The muscles of the uvula are controlled by the pharyngeal branch of the vagus nerve.

A(i) Physical properties of an ideal volatile agent: liquid at room temperature; low latent heat of vaporisation; low specific heat capacity; saturated vapour pressure (SVP) sufficiently high to allow easy vaporisation; stable in light; stable at room temperature; non-flammable; inexpensive; environmentally safe (locally and globally).

A(ii) Pharmacological properties: pleasant smell; low blood/gas solubility; potent enough to provide surgical anaesthesia without supplement (low MAC); high oil/water solubility; analgesic effect; non-epileptogenic; no cardiac irritability; no cardiovascular depression; no respiratory depression; non-irritant to airways; muscle relaxation; no increase in intracranial pressure (ICP); unaffected by renal failure; unaffected by hepatic failure; minimal metabolism. None of the inhalational anaesthetic agents approaches all these standards.

B(i) Pulmonary phase — factors affecting uptake: (1) Inhaled concentration of the agent: the higher the concentration, the more rapid the induction. (2) Alveolar ventilation: uptake is proportional to alveolar ventilation; hypoventilation or airway obstruction slows induction; hyperventilation makes induction more rapid. (3) Blood/gas partition coefficient: the less soluble an anaesthetic is in blood, the more rapid induction because alveolar tension builds up faster. (4) Pulmonary blood flow: when reduced (as in shock), induction is more rapid because alveolar tension builds up faster. (5) Second gas effect: induction is faster if a second gas (e.g. nitrous oxide) is given with the inhalational agent rather than oxygen alone. (6) Alveolar membrane: diffusion and uptake will be reduced in the presence of pulmonary oedema or fibrosis.

B(ii) Circulatory phase — factors affecting uptake: (1) Cardiac output: a high cardiac output slows inhalational induction by reducing the rate of increase in alveolar tension. (2) Cerebral blood flow: a greater cerebral blood flow is associated with more rapid induction. (3) Ventilation/perfusion ratio: V/Q mismatch can slow inhalational induction.

C(i) A low blood/gas partition coefficient means the agent is less soluble in blood; therefore the alveolar tension of the anaesthetic builds up faster, equilibrating more rapidly with the brain — hence faster induction and faster recovery. In shock, pulmonary blood flow is reduced, meaning less anaesthetic is taken up into the blood from the alveoli, so alveolar tension builds up faster, paradoxically accelerating induction even though the patient is haemodynamically compromised.
questions.question:
Describe the properties of an ideal inhalational anaesthetic agent under the following headings:

A(i) Physical properties
A(ii) Pharmacological properties
B(i) Uptake of inhalational anaesthetics — pulmonary phase and the factors affecting it
B(ii) Circulatory phase and factors affecting it
C(i) Explain why a low blood/gas partition coefficient leads to faster induction, and why shock paradoxically speeds induction

During the pre-operative assessment of a patient listed for elective surgery under general anaesthesia, the anaesthetist discovers that the patient has myasthenia gravis, is on regular immunosuppressants, and has previously had an adverse reaction to suxamethonium.

(i) Name the diagnosis that explains the adverse reaction to suxamethonium and describe what likely occurred.
(ii) What are the predisposing factors and clinical conditions that prolong the duration of suxamethonium action?
(iii) Describe the mechanism by which suxamethonium causes neuromuscular blockade, including the sequence of events at the NMJ.
(iv) Outline the appropriate management approach including choice of alternative muscle relaxant, reversal agent, and monitoring of neuromuscular function.
questions.answerText:
(i) The adverse reaction is most likely prolonged neuromuscular blockade (scoline apnoea) due to deficient or atypical plasma cholinesterase (pseudocholinesterase). Suxamethonium is normally rapidly metabolised by plasma cholinesterase to succinylmonocholine; as the drug serum level falls, succinylcholine molecules diffuse from the NMJ, limiting duration of action. In patients with deficient or atypical enzyme, this process is impaired, greatly prolonging the blockade.

(ii) Predisposing conditions that prolong duration of suxamethonium: liver disease, carcinomatosis, pregnancy, hypothyroidism, renal disease, burns, massive trauma, neurological disorders, stroke, and pre-existing hyperkalaemia (in which the drug may also cause life-threatening cardiac arrest).

(iii) Mechanism: suxamethonium mimics the action of acetylcholine at nicotinic receptors; it is composed of two acetylcholine molecules joined together. On binding, it causes depolarisation of the motor end plate leading to muscle fasciculation (cranio-caudal), then flaccid relaxation — this is phase-1 (depolarising) block. Unlike acetylcholine, it is not rapidly hydrolysed by acetylcholinesterase; the drug remains at the NMJ, resulting in prolonged depolarisation and block. The neuromuscular blockade occurs within 60 seconds. With repeated dosing or infusion, a dual block (phase-2 block) may develop: no fasciculations, continuous relaxation.

(iv) Management:
- Avoid suxamethonium; use a non-depolarising agent such as rocuronium (can be substituted for suxamethonium; onset > 60 seconds) or vecuronium.
- Reversal of non-depolarising block: neostigmine (0.04–0.07 mg/kg) combined with an anticholinergic agent (atropine 0.01–0.02 mg/kg or glycopyrrolate) to counteract muscarinic side effects (bradycardia, salivation, bronchospasm, increased intestinal motility).
- Rocuronium can also be reversed by sugammadex.
- Monitor neuromuscular function using a nerve stimulator (train-of-four, post-tetanic count, double burst stimulation); clinical signs of adequate recovery: sustained head lift for 5 seconds, ability to generate negative inspiratory pressure of at least 25 cmH2O, ability to swallow and maintain a patent airway.

A(i) Chemical structure: a quaternary ammonium compound composed of two acetylcholine molecules joined back-to-back (dicholine ester of succinic acid). Mechanism of action: it binds to acetylcholine receptors, blocking access to these receptors and activating them in the process of binding. Phase 1 block – initial depolarization of the post-junctional membrane of the skeletal muscle causes muscle contraction seen as fasciculations; repolarization is inhibited. Phase 2 block (desensitization blockade) – after the drug has been present for a period of time, the motor end plate loses its sensitivity and depolarization cannot occur; this continues for several minutes even after the drug is no longer present. No pharmacological reversal is available for Phase 1 block; neostigmine is contraindicated. Onset: 60–90 seconds (30–60 seconds in some sources). Duration: approximately 3–5 minutes (total recovery 12–15 minutes), because the drug is rapidly metabolised by plasma cholinesterase.
A(ii) IV dose for tracheal intubation: 1–1.5 mg/kg (chloride salts 1 mg/kg; IM 3–4 mg/kg). Duration is prolonged when the enzyme is deficient or atypical – conditions include liver disease, carcinomatosis, pregnancy, hypothyroidism, renal disease; also with genetically aberrant enzyme (heterozygous 1:50 – duration 20–30 min; homozygous 1:3000 – duration 4–8 hours). High dose and hypothermia also prolong action.
B(i) Side effects: Muscular – fasciculations causing postoperative muscle pains (myalgia), most common in young patients with large muscle mass and less common in children and elderly. Cardiovascular – bradycardia especially after the second dose (more common in children); prevented/corrected with atropine. Gastrointestinal – increased salivary and gastric secretions (muscarinic effect); increased intragastric pressure. Ocular – transient increase in intraocular pressure; should be avoided in penetrating eye injuries and severe glaucoma. Metabolic – normal serum potassium rises by approximately 0.5 mEq/L; marked hyperkalaemia and risk of cardiac dysrhythmias including cardiac arrest in patients with burns injury, massive trauma, tetanus, motor neurone disorders, and spinal cord injuries.
B(ii) Contraindications: recent burns (safe in the first 24 hours); spinal trauma causing paraplegia (may be given immediately after but should be avoided from approximately 10–100 days after injury); raised potassium levels; severe muscle trauma; history of malignant hyperpyrexia; caution in atypical plasma cholinesterase or muscle diseases. Physiological basis of hyperkalaemia: suxamethonium causes depolarization; in denervated or injured muscle, there is upregulation of extrajunctional receptors anywhere in the muscle membrane, leading to widespread depolarization and extensive potassium release that can be life-threatening.

A. Describe the Intravenous fluids: crystalloids vs colloids:
A(i) Describe the differences in intravascular persistence, haemodynamic stabilisation, required infusion volume, risk of tissue oedema, enhancement of capillary perfusion, risk of anaphylaxis, effect on plasma colloid osmotic pressure, and cost between crystalloids and colloids.
A(ii) State the molecular weight threshold that classifies a colloid and give three examples of colloids.
B. Describe blood component therapy — platelets:
B(i) How platelets are prepared from whole blood and by apheresis
B(ii) Storage conditions, risk of bacterial infection and how this risk is reduced
B(iii) Storage temperature, anticoagulant used, and the time limit from removal from incubator to starting transfusion
B(iv) What each pack contains and the expected platelet count rise after transfusion
C. State all platelet transfusion thresholds for different clinical scenarios as given.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Crystalloids vs colloids comparison:
- Intravascular persistence: crystalloids — poor; colloids — good
- Haemodynamic stabilisation: crystalloids — transient; colloids — prolonged
- Required infusion volume: crystalloids — large; colloids — moderate
- Risk of tissue oedema: crystalloids — obvious; colloids — insignificant
- Enhancement of capillary perfusion: crystalloids — poor; colloids — good
- Risk of anaphylaxis: crystalloids — nil; colloids — low to moderate
- Plasma colloid osmotic pressure: crystalloids — reduced; colloids — maintained
- Cost: crystalloids — inexpensive; colloids — expensive

A(ii) Colloid classification and examples:
- Fluids containing molecules sufficiently large enough to prevent transfer across capillary membranes; solutions stay in the space into which they are infused; MW 40,000 Daltons (for gelatins as specified)
- Examples: hetastarch (Hespan); albumin; dextran; gelatins (gelofusine, haemaccel)

B(i) Platelet preparation:
- From whole blood: made from four whole blood donations, suspended in platelet additive solution and the plasma of one of the four donors
- By apheresis: obtained as an adult therapeutic dose from a single donor by apheresis donation
- Both can be used interchangeably

B(ii) Storage conditions and infection risk:
- Storage temperature: 22°C
- Risk of transmission of bacterial infection: 1 in 12,000 — higher than other blood components because platelets are stored at 22°C
- Risk is reduced by bacterial screening before release

B(iii) Storage specifications and time limit:
- Stored at 22°C with CPD or CPDA, with constant gentle agitation in an approved incubator
- Platelets must not be placed in a refrigerator
- Transfusion should ideally be commenced within 30 minutes of removal from the platelet storage incubator

B(iv) Pack contents and expected rise:
- Each pack contains 250–350ml
- Transfusion should lead to increase in patient's platelet count by approximately 30 x 10⁹/l
- Patient's platelet count should be repeated after transfusion

C. Platelet transfusion thresholds:
- If patient is actively bleeding: transfuse until platelet count >75 x 10⁹/l
- If patient is not bleeding:
 - Routine prophylactic use: 10 x 10⁹/l
 - Prophylactic use with additional risk factors (e.g. sepsis): 10–20 x 10⁹/l
 - Other major surgery or invasive procedures: 50 x 10⁹/l
 - Neuraxial blockade: 50 x 10⁹/l
 - Prophylactic use in closed compartment surgery (eye, brain): 100 x 10⁹/l

A(i) Chemical structure:
- Most clinically useful local anaesthetic agents consist of an aromatic ring linked by a carbonyl-containing moiety through a carbon chain to a substituted amino group

A(ii) Classification:
- Esters: cocaine, procaine, amethocaine, chloroprocaine
- Amides: lignocaine, prilocaine, mepivacaine, bupivacaine

A(iii) Differences in metabolism and hypersensitivity:
- Esters: relatively unstable in solution; rapidly hydrolysed in the body by plasma cholinesterase (and other esterases); main breakdown product is para-amino benzoate (PABA) which is associated with allergic phenomena and hypersensitivity reactions
- Amides: relatively stable in solution; slowly metabolised by hepatic amidases; hypersensitivity rare
- In current clinical practice, esters have largely been superseded by amides

B. Pharmacokinetic mechanism:
- Most LAs are tertiary amine bases (B) administered as water-soluble hydrochlorides (B.HCl)
- After injection, the tertiary amine base is liberated by the relatively alkaline pH of tissue fluids: B.HCl + HCO3 ↔ B + H2CO3 + Cl-
- In tissue fluid the LA is present in both ionised (BH+) and non-ionised form (B); relative proportions depend on pH of the solution and the pKa of the drug
- The non-ionised base (B) diffuses through the nerve to axoplasm where it partially ionises again: B + H+ ↔ BH+
- In the ionised form (BH+) the LA enters the Na+ channel from the interior of the nerve fibre resulting in channel blockade

C(i) Clinical techniques:
- Topical anaesthesia
- Infiltration anaesthesia
- Conduction anaesthesia
- Extradural anaesthesia
- Spinal anaesthesia
- Intravenous local anaesthesia (IVRA)

C(ii) Rule regarding adrenaline and end-arteries:
- Adrenaline-containing solutions must never be used near end-arteries i.e. penis, ring block of fingers or other areas with a terminal vascular supply

C(iii) Spread of extradural anaesthesia:
- Spread of LA is more extensive in elderly, pregnant, and obese patients

questions.answerText:
A(i) Pancuronium: Classification – long-acting non-depolarising NMBA; aminosteroid compound. Onset: 3–5 minutes; duration: 60–90 minutes (some sources state 40–60 minutes). Intubating dose: 0.08–0.12 mg/kg. Metabolism and excretion: metabolised by the liver (metabolic products have some neuromuscular blocking activity); excretion primarily renal (85%), with liver contributing 15%. Cardiovascular effects: causes hypertension and tachycardia (combination of vagal blockade and sympathetic stimulation; blocks muscarinic receptors in the SA node); does not cause histamine release; does not release histamine (safe in asthmatics).
A(ii) Vecuronium: Classification – intermediate-acting non-depolarising NMBA; aminosteroid compound; analogue of pancuronium. Onset: faster than pancuronium – 90 seconds in some sources; 3–5 minutes in others; duration 20–35 minutes (dose-dependent). Intubating dose: 0.08–0.12 mg/kg. Metabolism and excretion: metabolised in the liver to an active metabolite (3-desacetylvecuronium); excreted mainly in bile (60%) but also in urine (40%). Cardiovascular effects: minimal effects on BP; may cause unopposed vagal stimulation; has much less vagolytic effect than pancuronium.
B(i) Comparison: Vagolytic effect – pancuronium has direct vagolytic and sympathomimetic effects causing tachycardia and hypertension; vecuronium has much less vagolytic effect. Histamine release – neither pancuronium nor vecuronium causes histamine release (aminosteroids as a class do not). Suitability in shock – pancuronium is used in patients with shock (its cardiovascular stimulating effects help maintain BP). Liver disease – pancuronium should be avoided in patients with liver disease as it produces active metabolites; vecuronium is preferable but its action may also be prolonged in hepatic disease.
B(ii) Hierarchy of neuromuscular blockade (receptor occupancy / nerve stimulator response / whole-body signs): 99–100% – no response to nerve stimulator / flaccid, extreme relaxation. 95% – post-tetanic facilitation present / diaphragm moves, hiccough possible. 90% – one of four twitches of TOF present / abdominal relaxation adequate for most procedures. 75% – four twitches of TOF present, TOF ratio 0.7 / tidal volume and vital capacity normal. 50% – 100 Hz tetanus sustained / passes inspiratory pressure test. 30% – 200 Hz tetanus sustained / head lift and hand-grip sustained.

A 14-year-old boy is found pulseless and apnoeic in a swimming pool. Bystanders pulled him out 2 minutes ago. He remains unconscious with no spontaneous breathing.

(i) What is the diagnosis, and what pathophysiological changes occur rapidly in the absence of circulation?
(ii) Describe the BLS sequence step by step for this victim, including the CAB approach and timing.
(iii) When should BLS be stopped?
(iv) Describe the special BLS modifications for this near-drowning situation.
(v) What are the 6 Hs and 6 Ts of reversible causes that must be considered once ACLS is available?
questions.answerText:
(i) Cardiac arrest — sudden cessation of the circulation or cardiac function. Pathophysiological changes: maintenance of normal tissue metabolism relies principally on an adequate delivery of oxygen in a functioning circulation. Failure of delivery rapidly results in: hypoxia (following inadequate oxygen in blood); acidosis (anaerobic metabolism with accumulation of CO2 in tissues); release of stress hormones (catecholamines, ADH, aldosterone — increasing tendency for arrhythmias). Failure of circulation for 3–4 minutes (less if patient is initially hypoxaemic) leads to irreversible cerebral damage. CPR time frame: 0–4 minutes — brain damage unlikely; 4–6 minutes — brain damage possible; 6–10 minutes — brain damage probable; over 10 minutes — probable brain death.

(ii) BLS sequence — CAB approach: Ensure safety of rescuer and victim. Check responsiveness (shake and shout). If unresponsive: call for help. C — Circulation: check carotid pulse (not more than 10 seconds to assess). If no carotid pulse: give 30 chest compressions, depressing sternum 5 cm and releasing (100 compressions/min). A — Airway: open airway with chin lift/jaw thrust. Remove visible foreign body or secretions. B — Breathing: look for chest movement, listen for breath sounds, feel for expired air (look, listen, feel × 10 seconds). If not breathing: give 2 rescue breaths using expired air ventilation. Compression:ventilation ratio 30:2 for both 1 and 2 rescuers.

(iii) Continue BLS until: patient recovers; qualified help arrives and takes over; or rescuer becomes exhausted.

(iv) Near-drowning modification: respiratory arrest results from lack of oxygen, therefore rescue breathing is vital. Activate EMS. Begin rescue breathing immediately. Start CPR if victim is unresponsive. Check and maintain airway, remove visible obstruction. Compression-only CPR is appropriate in non-asphyxiated patients, but in near-drowning (asphyxia), rescue breaths are essential.

(v) 6 Hs: Hypovolemia, Hypoxia, Hydrogen ions (acidosis), Hyper/hypokalemia, Hypothermia, Hypoglycemia. 6 Ts: Toxins (drug overdose), Tamponade (cardiac), Tension pneumothorax, Thrombosis (coronary), Thrombosis (pulmonary), Trauma.

questions.question:
(A) Describe the neuromuscular junction (NMJ) under the following headings:
(i) The sequence of neuromuscular transmission from nerve impulse to muscle contraction.
(ii) The role of calcium, acetylcholine, and acetylcholinesterase in this process.
(iii) The resting membrane potential and the changes that lead to an action potential and muscle contraction.

(B) Explain how depolarising and non-depolarising muscle relaxants differ in their mechanism of action at the NMJ, including:
(i) The type of receptor interaction (agonist or antagonist).
(ii) The pattern of blockade produced (with reference to fasciculations, fade, post-tetanic facilitation, and dual block).

(C) Explain how anticholinesterase agents reverse non-depolarising blockade, and state the muscarinic side effects that must be co-managed.
questions.answerText:
(A)
(i) Sequence of neuromuscular transmission: a nerve terminal action potential causes Ca2+ influx via voltage-sensitive calcium channels. Acetylcholine (ACh), synthesised from choline and acetylcoenzyme A by choline acetyl transferase and stored in vesicles, is released by exocytosis. ACh diffuses to the muscle-type nicotinic cholinergic receptors concentrated at the tops of the junctional folds of the motor end plate. Binding alters membrane permeability, increasing Na+ and K+ conductance (Na+ in, K+ out), producing the end-plate potential. This depolarises the adjacent muscle membrane, and when the end-plate potential reaches about 45 mV, an action potential is propagated, causing muscle contraction. Action potentials are conducted away from the end plate in both directions along the muscle fibre. ACh is then rapidly hydrolysed by acetylcholinesterase, restoring membrane impermeability to Na+ and allowing repolarisation.

(ii) ACh release is affected by Ca2+, calmodulin, and Mg2+. Acetylcholinesterase is present in high concentrations at the NMJ and rapidly removes ACh from the synaptic cleft.

(iii) At rest, the motor end plate is less permeable to Na+ (extracellular) with K+ intracellular, producing a resting potential of about -90 mV. The arrival of the nerve impulse triggers exocytosis of ACh; ACh binding produces a depolarising Na+ influx (end-plate potential); when this reaches ~45 mV, an action potential propagates and muscle contraction occurs.

(B)
(i) Depolarising relaxants (e.g. suxamethonium): agonist at nicotinic ACh receptors — they bind both alpha-subunits, causing end-plate depolarisation. Non-depolarising relaxants: competitive antagonists at post-synaptic nicotinic receptors — they bind to only one alpha-subunit, preventing ACh binding without causing depolarisation.

(ii) Depolarising block: initial fasciculations (cranio-caudal) followed by sustained relaxation; no fade on tetanic stimulation; no post-tetanic facilitation; dual (phase-2) block may occur with repeated dosing or infusion (no fasciculations, continuous relaxation). Non-depolarising block: no fasciculations; fade on tetanic stimulation; post-tetanic facilitation present; blocked by competitive antagonism.

(C) Anticholinesterase agents (neostigmine, edrophonium, pyridostigmine) inhibit acetylcholinesterase, allowing more ACh to accumulate at the NMJ to compete with the non-depolarising agent. Neostigmine combines reversibly with acetylcholinesterase; effects last about 30 minutes. Muscarinic side effects include: bradycardia, salivation, sweating, bronchospasm, increased intestinal motility, and blurred vision. These are minimised by co-administering anticholinergics: atropine (0.01–0.02 mg/kg) or glycopyrrolate.

(i) Acute Rheumatic Fever (ARF) — an autoallergic disease triggered by infection with some strains of streptococcal pyogenes that express antigens which cross-react with those of human connective tissues. Most common cause of acquired heart disease in children and young adults worldwide. Most at risk: initial attacks occur most commonly between the ages of 6 and 15 years; RF rarely occurs before the age of 5 years. Risk is increased in populations at high risk for streptococcal pharyngitis (military recruits, persons living in crowded conditions, those in close contact with school-age children). More prevalent in developing countries. Definite family variation in susceptibility.

(ii) Jones Criteria met in this patient: Major criteria — Carditis (mitral regurgitation murmur, prolonged PR interval may be present), Migratory polyarthritis (diffuse joint pains moving between knees and ankles), Sydenham's chorea (involuntary jerky movements). Minor criteria — fever, arthralgia. Plus supporting evidence: recent group A streptococcal infection (sore throat 3 days prior). Meeting two major criteria plus evidence of streptococcal infection satisfies the Jones Criteria.

(iii) Migratory polyarthritis: present in as many as 75% of cases; affects the ankles, wrists, knees, and elbows over a period of days; does not affect the small joints of the hands or feet and seldom involves the hip joints. The difference between arthralgia (subjective joint pain) and arthritis (joint pain and swelling) must be understood — arthralgia is only a minor criterion; occasionally arthralgia is used (incorrectly) as a major criterion.

(iv) Sydenham's chorea: occurs in fewer than 10% of patients with rheumatic fever; the latent period between onset of the initiating streptococcal infection and onset of Sydenham's chorea may be as long as several months. Subcutaneous nodules and erythema marginatum: are rare major manifestations, usually present in fewer than 10% of cases; subcutaneous nodules are found over extensor surfaces of joints, seen most often in patients with long-standing rheumatic heart disease, and are extremely rare in patients experiencing an initial attack; erythema marginatum is an uncommon, evanescent macular eruption with rounded borders usually concentrated on the trunk.

(v) Long-term significance: the major importance of acute RF is its ability to cause fibrosis of heart valves, leading to crippling haemodynamic effects of chronic heart disease. Healing of rheumatic valvulitis leads to fibrous thickening and adhesion, resulting in valvular stenosis and/or regurgitation; the mitral valve is involved most frequently, followed by the aortic. Repeated attacks worsen the valvular damage. Secondary prophylaxis: intramuscular injection of 1.2 million units of benzathine penicillin G every 4 weeks, OR oral penicillin V (250 mg twice daily), OR oral sulfadiazine (1.0 g daily). Secondary prophylaxis should be given for five years after the diagnosis or until age 21 years (recommendation of both the American Heart Association and WHO).

questions.answerText:
A(i) The upper respiratory tract refers to the parts of the respiratory system lying above the sternal angle, above the vocal cords or vocal folds, or above the cricoid cartilage. It consists of the nasal cavity and paranasal sinuses, the pharynx (nasopharynx, oropharynx, and laryngopharynx), and some part of the larynx.

A(ii) Nasal cavity: divided by the nasal septum into two cavities (fossae). Lateral wall: nasal aspect of ethmoidal labyrinth above, nasal surface of maxilla below and in front, perpendicular plate of palatine bone behind. Medial wall (septum): septal cartilage, perpendicular plate of ethmoid, and vomer. Roof slopes upward to form bridge (nasal and frontal bones), then horizontal cribriform plate of ethmoid, then downward-sloping body of sphenoid. Floor: palatine process of maxilla and horizontal plate of palatine bone. Blood supply from branches of both internal and external carotid arteries: sphenopalatine and greater palatine arteries (maxillary artery); anterior and posterior ethmoidal arteries (ophthalmic artery); septal branches of superior labial artery (facial artery). Nerve supply: olfactory nerve for specialized olfactory zone; general sensory from trigeminal (V1 nasociliary/anterior ethmoidal; V2 posterior nasal branches of maxillary nerve).

B(i) The pharynx is a wide muscular tube forming the common upper pathway of respiratory and alimentary tracts. Three parts: nasopharynx (behind nasal cavity above soft palate, contains adenoids/pharyngeal tonsils, opens via pharyngeal isthmus); oropharynx (behind oral cavity from uvula to hyoid bone, lined by non-keratinized squamous stratified epithelium, contains palatine tonsils); laryngopharynx/hypopharynx (caudal part, connects to esophagus, lined with stratified squamous epithelium, innervated by pharyngeal plexus and recurrent laryngeal nerve).

B(ii) Larynx lies below hyoid bone in midline at level of C4–C6 vertebrae, between pharynx and trachea. Nine cartilages: 3 single (epiglottis, thyroid, cricoid) and 3 paired (corniculate, arytenoids, cuneiform). Types: hyaline (thyroid, cricoid, arytenoids) and elastic (epiglottis, corniculate, cuneiform). Epithelium is squamous above vocal cords and columnar below.

C(i) The vallecula are paired spaces between the root of the tongue and the anterior surface of the epiglottis, each bordered medially by the median glossoepiglottic fold and laterally by the lateral glossoepiglottic fold. It is an important reference landmark during intubation of the trachea: the blade tip of a Macintosh-style laryngoscope must be placed as far as possible into the vallecula in order to facilitate directly visualizing the glottis.

Describe the Upper Respiratory Tract under the following headings:

A(i) Definition and structures included
A(ii) The nasal cavity — walls, blood supply, and nerve supply
