A(i) Describe the clinical uses of suxamethonium, including the specific clinical scenarios where it is the agent of choice.
A(ii) Describe the physical properties and chemical structure of suxamethonium.
B(i) State all contraindications to suxamethonium, and for the hyperkalaemia-related contraindications, explain the time window of risk.
B(ii) Explain what happens when suxamethonium is used in patients with abnormal plasma cholinesterase, and list the conditions that cause enzyme deficiency or produce an atypical enzyme.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Clinical uses of suxamethonium: it is used during induction of anaesthesia; it is the agent most commonly used for tracheal (endotracheal) intubation; it is used for rapid sequence induction (RSI) in cases of "full stomach" – emergencies, likely unfasted patients, obstetric anaesthesia, intra-abdominal masses, diabetic neuropathy; for anticipated difficult intubation – obese patients, mandibular/facial injuries, retropharyngeal abscess; can be used as a continuous drip to maintain muscle relaxation during anaesthesia for caesarean sections or short surgical procedures because of its short duration; modification of fits after electroconvulsive therapy.
A(ii) Physical properties: short half-life (especially in a warm tropical climate); stored in powdered form historically but now comes in aqueous solution and needs to be refrigerated; commonly available as chloride and bromide salts. Chemical structure: dicholine ester of succinic acid – two acetylcholine molecules joined back-to-back (a quaternary ammonium compound); water-soluble. Presented as suxamethonium chloride, a clear solution of 50 mg/ml in 2 or 10 ml glass bottles.
B(i) Contraindications: patients with recent burns (it can be given in the first 24 hours, but should be avoided thereafter); spinal trauma causing paraplegia (can be given immediately after injury but should be avoided from approximately 10–100 days after the injury); raised potassium levels; severe muscle trauma; history of malignant hyperpyrexia; used with caution in patients with atypical plasma cholinesterase or muscle diseases – there may be prolonged paralysis or dangerous rises in potassium levels. Time window for spinal/burns: safe in the first 24 hours; risky from approximately 10–100 days after injury due to upregulation of extrajunctional receptors.
B(ii) When plasma cholinesterase is deficient or atypical, suxamethonium is not adequately metabolised and there is prolonged paralysis until the drug is eliminated by other slower methods. The drug is not used in patients with liver disorders. Conditions causing enzyme deficiency or atypical enzyme: liver disease; carcinomatosis; pregnancy; hypothyroidism; renal disease; genetically aberrant enzyme – heterozygous (1 in 50): duration 20–30 minutes; homozygous (1 in 3000): duration 4–8 hours.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old primigravida at 38 weeks gestation goes into spontaneous labour and delivers vaginally. Immediately after delivery, she develops heavy vaginal bleeding with an estimated blood loss of 2 litres. She becomes unresponsive with no palpable carotid pulse.

(i) What is the diagnosis, and what are the most likely reversible causes in this specific scenario?
(ii) Describe the BLS modifications required for a pregnant patient during CPR.
(iii) If resuscitation continues beyond 4 minutes without return of spontaneous circulation, what should be considered according to gestational age?
(iv) What is the role of the AED in a pregnant patient?
(v) Describe the general goal of CPR and why every minute of delay worsens outcome.
questions.answerText:
(i) Cardiac arrest in the peripartum period. Most likely reversible cause: acute hypovolaemia from severe haemorrhage (greater than 50% blood volume loss — she has lost 2 litres); this is the most commonly treatable cause of asystole/PEA and always results from extremely severe haemorrhage. These patients usually need immediate surgery to control haemorrhage and rapid fluid replacement. Other reversible causes to consider: hypoxia, thromboembolism (pulmonary embolus), tension pneumothorax, toxins (e.g. magnesium toxicity), cardiac tamponade.

(ii) BLS modifications for pregnancy: the increased weight of the uterus reduces blood flow during CPR. Improve circulation by left uterine displacement with a wedge placed under the right hip (to relieve aortocaval compression). Standard sequence: Ensure safety. Check responsiveness. Call for help. C-A-B: 30 chest compressions at 100/min, depressing sternum 5 cm. Open airway (head tilt/chin lift). Give 2 rescue breaths. Continue 30:2 ratio. In cervical spine injury: keep head, neck, and chest in neutral position; use jaw thrust rather than chin lift; assistance may be required to maintain alignment.

(iii) Gestational age considerations: less than 25 weeks — standard resuscitation without modification. 25–32 weeks — apply wedge to relieve aorto-caval compression. Greater than 32 weeks — immediate caesarean section for effective CPR (perimortem C-section to improve venous return and CPR efficacy). For planned home births, two midwives/birth attendants should be present, one for the mother and a second for the baby, both trained in appropriate resuscitation techniques for the newborn and mother.

(iv) AED in pregnancy: AED may be used without effect on the foetus. Reliable, computerised, battery-powered devices using voice and visual prompts; obtain and analyse heart rhythms; deliver electric shock to convert irregular rhythm to normal. Precautions: remove O2 masks and cannulae, place at least 1 m from patient's chest; disconnect bag-valve and airway adjuncts and remove at least 1 m away from patient; essential that no contact with casualty when defibrillating.

(v) The goal of CPR is to restore a beating heart and functioning circulation to maintain oxygen delivery to vital organs and therefore preserve vital function, including brain viability. The heart, lungs, and brain function interdependently. Every minute without CPR worsens outcome: 0–4 minutes — brain damage unlikely; 4–6 minutes — brain damage possible; 6–10 minutes — brain damage probable; over 10 minutes — probable brain death. BLS slows deterioration from VF to asystole, improves the probability of defibrillation, and leads to significantly increased survival. The likelihood of successful defibrillation decreases an estimated 2–7% for every minute of cardiac arrest.

questions.question:
Describe Minimum Alveolar Concentration (MAC) of inhalational anaesthetic agents under the following headings:

A(i) Definition and its significance as a measure of potency
A(ii) The MAC variants — MAC BAR, MAC Unconscious, and MAC Awake
B(i) Factors that increase MAC
B(ii) Factors that decrease MAC
C(i) Factors that have no effect on MAC, and the MAC values of the commonly used agents
questions.answerText:
A(i) MAC is the alveolar concentration of an inhaled anaesthetic that prevents movement in 50% of patients in response to a standardised surgical stimulus, at 1 atmosphere pressure. It is analogous to ED50. It is the best measure of anaesthetic potency as it mirrors the brain partial pressure. MAC values of different anaesthetics are roughly additive. A lower value represents a more potent volatile anaesthetic.

A(ii) MAC BAR: MAC that blunts the adrenergic response to noxious stimulus (1.5 MAC). MAC Unconscious: MAC at which the patient loses consciousness (0.4–0.5 MAC). MAC Awake: MAC at which patient opens his or her eyes to command (0.15–0.5 MAC). Roughly 1.3 MAC of any volatile anaesthetic can prevent movement in 95% of patients during surgical stimuli.

B(i) Factors that increase MAC: increased CNS metabolism, increased CNS neurotransmission, hyperthermia, chronic alcohol abuse, hyponatraemia; drugs — MAO inhibitors, amphetamine, cocaine, ephedrine, L-DOPA.

B(ii) Factors that decrease MAC: decreased CNS metabolism, decreased CNS neurotransmission, increased age, hypothermia, acute alcohol, hypotension (MAP less than 50 mmHg), hypoxaemia (less than 38 mmHg), pregnancy, narcotics, ketamine, benzodiazepines, lithium, local anaesthetics.

C(i) Factors with no effect on MAC: gender, duration of anaesthesia, hypertension, anaemia, thyroid status, hypo- or hypercarbia, metabolic alkalosis, hyperkalaemia, magnesium levels. MAC values of inhalational agents: N2O 104, Halothane 0.75, Isoflurane 1.17, Desflurane 6.6, Sevoflurane 1.8.

questions.question:
A. Describe the pharmacological agents used in pain management under the following headings:
A(i) Opioid classification and receptor types with cellular mechanism of action
A(ii) Common side effects of opioids and their management as stated
B. Describe morphine under the following headings:
B(i) Its status, half-life, duration of action, and all dosage forms available
B(ii) Why dose adjustment may be needed in renal failure
C. Describe the WHO analgesic ladder:
C(i) The three original steps with the drug classes at each step
C(ii) The adjuvant analgesics listed and their specific roles
C(iii) The fourth step and the interventional procedures it includes.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Opioid classification and receptor types:
- Natural occurring: papaveretum, papaverine
- Semi-synthetic: morphine, oxy-morphine, buprenorphine, codeine, pentazocine
- Synthetic: pethidine, fentanyl, alfentanil, sufentanil
- Classified based on action on receptors: partial agonist/antagonist (pentazocine, nalorphine); antagonist (naloxone, naltrexone)
- Receptor types: mu, delta, kappa, sigma
- Cellular action: affect ion-gated channels; close voltage-gated Ca2+ channels on presynaptic terminal thereby reducing transmitter release; hyperpolarise and inhibit postsynaptic neurons by opening K+ channels
- Sigma receptor: autonomic effects, dysphoria, hallucinations

A(ii) Common side effects and management:
- Constipation: very common; tolerance is unlikely; treat with stool softeners + stimulant +/- metoclopramide
- Nausea/vomiting: tolerance usually develops; pretreat with prochlorperazine
- Urticaria/pruritus: due to histamine release; treat with antihistamine
- Sedation: tolerance usually develops
- Delirium: rare in patients with normal renal function

B(i) Morphine:
- Gold standard of opioid therapy
- Half-life: 1.5–2 hours
- Duration: 3–5 hours
- Dosage forms: extended-release capsule/tablet (Avinza once daily; Kadian daily or q12h; MSContin/Oramorph SR q8–12h); immediate-release tablet; oral suspension (Roxanol); suppository (RMS); parenteral injection (Duramorph, Infumorph)

B(ii) Dose adjustment in renal failure:
- Morphine is metabolised to a renally excreted active metabolite
- Dose adjustment may be needed in renal failure due to accumulation of the active metabolite

C(i) WHO analgesic ladder — three original steps:
- Step 1 (mild pain): non-opioid analgesics such as NSAIDs or acetaminophen, with or without adjuvants
- Step 2 (moderate pain): weak opioids (hydrocodone, codeine, tramadol) with or without non-opioid analgesics and with or without adjuvants
- Step 3 (severe and persistent pain): potent opioids (morphine, methadone, fentanyl, oxycodone, buprenorphine, tapentadol, hydromorphone, oxymorphone) with or without non-opioid analgesics and with or without adjuvants

C(ii) Adjuvant analgesics:
- Antidepressants (TCAs such as amitriptyline and nortriptyline; SNRIs such as duloxetine and venlafaxine)
- Anticonvulsants (gabapentin and pregabalin)
- Topical anaesthetics (lidocaine patch)
- Topical therapies (capsaicin)
- Corticosteroids, bisphosphonates, cannabinoids
- May enhance analgesic activity, have independent analgesic activity for neuropathic pain, or counteract side effects

C(iii) Fourth step:
- Includes numerous non-pharmacological and interventional procedures for persistent pain
- Epidural analgesia; intrathecal administration of analgesic and local anaesthetic drugs with or without pumps; neurosurgical procedures (lumbar percutaneous adhesiolysis, cordotomy); neuromodulation (brain stimulators, spinal cord stimulation); nerve blocks; ablative procedures (alcoholisation, radiofrequency, microwave, cryoablation, laser-induced thermotherapy, irreversible electroporation, electrochemotherapy); cementoplasty; palliation radiotherapy

A(i) Combitube: a multi-lumen airway that works whether it is inserted into the oesophagus or the trachea. It either blocks the oesophagus above and below the glottic opening, or directly ventilates the trachea. It has 2 rings on the proximal end that upper teeth are situated between them. Size 37F for adults with height of 120–180 cm and 41F for taller patients. It enters the oesophagus in 95% of cases.

A(ii) Advantages: easily inserted; successfully used in CPR; does not need neck extension for insertion (only requires modest mouth opening); does not need any cervical manipulation; allows high-pressure ventilation (50 cmH2O); can be used in bleeding and aspiration situations; may be kept in place for 8 hours. Balloon volumes: distal balloon needs 10 ml; proximal balloon needs 80–100 ml of air for insufflation.

B(i) Contraindications to Combitube: patients under 5 feet tall or under 14 years old; patients who have ingested caustic substances; patients with oesophageal trauma or disease; patients with an intact gag reflex.

B(ii) Flexible LMA: similar in design to Classic LMA; non-kinkable; used mostly in ENT, head and neck, and dental surgeries. iGel: single-use thermoplastic device in sizes 3–5; there is no cuff; has gastric drainage; seals better than ProSeal and LMA (but if there is a leak, the iGel must be changed); drainage tube of iGel is smaller than ProSeal; no inflation required.

C(i) Blind insertion airways are used in difficult airway management because they do not require visualisation of the vocal cords, making them usable when direct laryngoscopy is impossible or unsuccessful. They are considered an alternative airway control device to be used when intubation is unsuccessful. The Combitube specifically is advantageous over the LMA in: CPR (successfully used in CPR); situations involving bleeding and aspiration (unlike the LMA, it can be used in these situations because it occludes the oesophagus and isolates the airway); when high-pressure ventilation is required (allows up to 50 cmH2O — unlike the LMA, which leaks with positive pressure); when neck extension is not possible (does not need neck extension or cervical manipulation, unlike laryngoscopy); and when an intact gag reflex is not present (though this is actually a shared contraindication with the LMA in its Classic form).
questions.question:
Describe the Combitube and the King Airway as blind insertion airway devices under the following headings:

A(i) Combitube — design, mechanism of ventilation whether in oesophagus or trachea
A(ii) Combitube — advantages, duration of use, and balloon volumes
B(i) Contraindications to the Combitube
B(ii) Describe the Flexible LMA and the iGel — design features and clinical applications
C(i) Explain why blind insertion airways are used in difficult airway management, and state the clinical situations in which the Combitube specifically is advantageous over an LMA

questions.answerText:
A(i) Physical properties: structure is a resonant hybrid of two forms N=N=O and N≡N-O. Critical temperature 36.5°C; critical pressure 72.6 bar. Presentation: supplied in cylinders as pure liquid (no water vapour) under pressure (44 bar); filling ratio 0.75. Colour code: cylinders French blue; rotameter knob blue; pin index 2,5. Storage: at room temperature away from extremes of heat; non-explosive; not flammable but can support combustion because it decomposes to oxygen and nitrogen above 450°C.

A(ii) CNS: analgesia, sedation; not epileptogenic. CVS: increased vascular tone, rise in blood pressure. Respiratory: decreased tidal volume, increased rate; non-irritant. Other: increased skeletal muscle activity; emetogenic. Elimination: predominantly via lungs.

B(i) Contraindications: diffuses into air-filled spaces causing expansion; prolonged use interferes with vitamin B12. N2O has a higher solubility than nitrogen in blood; it therefore diffuses into closed air-filled spaces (e.g. pneumothorax, middle ear, bowel loops) faster than nitrogen can leave, expanding those spaces and causing complications. This makes it contraindicated in bowel obstruction, pneumothorax, middle ear surgery, and intracranial air.

B(ii) Entonox: mixture of 50% O2 and 50% N2O for analgesia in labour and short procedures. Presentation: supplied in cylinders as a gas under pressure (137 bar); liquefies at −7°C; filling ratio 0.75. Colour code: cylinders — body French blue, shoulder French blue and white quarters; pin index is a specific large single pin offset from centre. Storage: at room temperature away from extremes of heat; may separate if exposed to low temperatures (0°C), in which case re-warm and invert to restore the mixture; non-explosive, not flammable but supports combustion. CNS, CVS, ADRs broadly similar to nitrous oxide. Mainly used as an inhaled analgesic (e.g. in labour). Elimination: predominantly via lungs. Contraindications: as for nitrous oxide.

C(i) Concentration effect: during GA, N2O is taken faster from alveoli to pulmonary capillary blood; as a result, the concentration of other gases (e.g. halothane, O2) remaining in the alveoli increases — this is the concentration effect. As a carrier gas, N2O constitutes a large proportion of the gas mixture, and its rapid uptake concentrates the co-administered agent. Second gas effect: when a 'first gas' moves from lungs to plasma, it increases the alveolar concentration; consequently the rate of uptake of the 'second gas' also increases. Nitrous oxide, despite being a carrier gas, can also behave as a second gas in this context, meaning its own alveolar concentration increases when another first gas is simultaneously absorbed.
questions.question:
Describe the properties, clinical uses, and effects on organ systems of Nitrous Oxide (N2O) as an anaesthetic agent under the following headings:

A(i) Physical properties, presentation, and storage
A(ii) CNS, CVS, and respiratory effects
B(i) Contraindications and the mechanism by which N2O causes problems in air-filled spaces
B(ii) Describe Entonox — composition, presentation, and clinical uses
C(i) Explain the concentration effect and why N2O is described as a carrier gas and a 'second gas'

A 19-year-old male presents with a retropharyngeal abscess and suspected difficult airway. The anaesthetist decides that rapid sequence induction is necessary to secure the airway quickly. The patient has no known drug allergies, no history of previous anaesthesia, and no family history of anaesthetic problems.

(i) State the drug of choice for this scenario and justify the choice based on known properties.
(ii) Name the procedure (RSI) and describe how the NMJ is involved in producing the conditions for intubation.
(iii) Identify all the anatomical structures the endotracheal tube will pass through from mouth to trachea, considering that this is a patient with a retropharyngeal abscess (anticipated difficult airway).
(iv) State the named monitoring approach used to assess neuromuscular block intraoperatively, and list the nerve stimulator sites described as readily accessible.
(v) If the patient develops Phase 2 block, describe what this means physiologically and how it arises.
questions.answerText:
(i) Drug of choice for RSI with anticipated difficult airway: suxamethonium. Justification: it has a rapid onset (60–90 seconds), short duration (3 minutes, total recovery 12–15 minutes), producing rapid and complete relaxation ideal for securing the airway. Its onset of action is largely due to its low lipid solubility. It is particularly indicated for: rapid sequence induction in cases of full stomach; anticipated difficult intubation (obese, mandibular/facial injuries, retropharyngeal abscess). An alternative is rocuronium (onset >60 seconds, similar to succinylcholine; reversed by sugammadex if intubation fails).

(ii) RSI involves rapidly achieving full neuromuscular blockade to create optimal intubating conditions. At the NMJ: suxamethonium binds to both alpha-subunits of the post-junctional nicotinic ACh receptor (agonist effect), causing initial end-plate depolarisation (fasciculations). As it is not hydrolysed by acetylcholinesterase and remains at the NMJ, sustained depolarisation produces flaccid paralysis. This relaxes the muscles of the jaw, neck, and pharynx, facilitating laryngoscopy and endotracheal intubation.

(iii) Anatomical structures passed by the endotracheal tube (mouth to trachea): mouth (lips, teeth, tongue); oropharynx; hypopharynx (behind the retropharyngeal space, where the abscess lies — this may distort normal anatomy and impede passage); larynx (epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, arytenoids, vocal cords); trachea. Note: this is a difficult airway because retropharyngeal abscess displaces soft tissue, potentially obstructing the laryngeal view. Cervical vertebral landmarks are also relevant if cervical injury is suspected.

(iv) Neuromuscular monitoring approach: a nerve stimulator delivering current up to 50 mA for a fraction of a millisecond is used; muscular contraction is assessed by visual or tactile means, or by mechanomyography or electromyography. Readily accessible nerve stimulator sites: ulnar nerve, facial nerve, and lateral popliteal nerve.

(v) Phase 2 (dual) block: if suxamethonium is given a second time or through an infusion pump, the character of the block changes. There is no depolarising effect (no fasciculations); instead, the block resembles a non-depolarising block with continuous relaxation and fade on train-of-four stimulation. This occurs because the sustained depolarisation alters receptor conformation. Dual block features both depolarising and non-depolarising characteristics.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old trauma patient requires emergency laparotomy. He was last seen eating 2 hours before the accident. He is agitated, haemodynamically borderline, and has suspected cervical spine injury.
(i) What specific anaesthetic problem does this patient present and why is it significant?
(ii) What are the problems associated with managing anaesthesia in trauma patients?
(iii) Describe the steps for rapid sequence induction (RSI) with airway management in this patient, including pre-oxygenation, induction agents, and airway protection.
(iv) What special precautions must be taken regarding the cervical spine during laryngoscopy and intubation, and how many providers are required?
(v) State the factors that may reduce mortality in trauma patients.
questions.answerText:
(i) The specific anaesthetic problem is the risk of a "full stomach" leading to vomiting, regurgitation, and aspiration of gastric contents during anaesthesia. This is significant because aspiration can cause severe aspiration pneumonia, ARDS, and death. There may also be inadequate time to prepare the patient for anaesthesia.
(ii) Problems associated with trauma anaesthesia: the sustained injuries may be life-threatening, multiple, or occult (e.g. tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade); adequacy of airway, breathing, and circulation may be compromised, requiring active, urgent and ongoing resuscitation; the patient may be intoxicated, restless, comatose, or in shock; it may not be possible to obtain a detailed history; patient status (such as HIV) is unknown, hence the need for universal precaution during resuscitation; patient information, previous medical history, chronic medication, allergies, and genetic abnormalities are unknown.
(iii) RSI steps: pre-oxygenate with 100% oxygen for 3–5 minutes, or instruct the patient to take 4 vital capacity breaths before induction; rapid sequence induction (RSI) of anaesthesia; secure the airway with an endotracheal tube (ETT); confirm correct placement of the tube; maintenance of anaesthesia. Equipment checks should confirm availability and functionality; drugs drawn and labelled appropriately; monitors attached: BP, invasive blood pressure, CVP or wide bore cannula, urine output, pulse oximetry, temperature.
(iv) Cervical spine precautions: blunt trauma victims must always be assumed to have an unstable cervical spine until proven otherwise. The anaesthesiologist must maintain in-line immobilisation of the cervical spine at all times, especially during laryngoscopy and intubation – failure to do so may exacerbate spinal cord injury. Use cervical collar if there is any doubt. During transport, ensure the head and neck are not subject to jerks or sudden movements. Four providers are required: 1st person – hold the neck and provide in-line cervical stabilisation; intubating physician – hold the mask, perform laryngoscopy, intubation and ventilation; 3rd person – maintain cricoid pressure; 4th person – medications.
(v) Factors that may reduce mortality: accident prevention; pre-hospital stabilisation; rapid transport; early resuscitation; timely operative intervention and postoperative care; rehabilitation.

questions.question:
A 22-year-old male arrives in the emergency department with multiple gunshot wounds to the abdomen and chest. He is haemodynamically unstable. The trauma team initiates damage control resuscitation.
(i) What is the "lethal triad of trauma" and how does each component contribute to a vicious cycle?
(ii) What specific measures are used during resuscitation to prevent or reverse hypothermia?
(iii) Explain the concept of "permissive hypotension" and state the systolic BP target used in practice.
(iv) What does damage control surgery (DCS) aim to achieve and what are its three phases?
(v) State the indications for ICU admission following trauma surgery.
questions.answerText:
(i) The lethal triad of trauma: Hypothermia – core temperature less than 35°C; as body temperature drops, there is prolongation of coagulation; temperature-dependent enzymatic reactions constituting the coagulation cascade become ineffective; platelet dysfunction also occurs. Acidosis – metabolic acidosis results from lactate overproduction from ischaemic tissues during hypovolemic shock; acidosis causes cardiac arrhythmias and inotropic unresponsiveness to catecholamines and is linked to coagulopathy. Coagulopathy – resuscitation with crystalloids and colloids dilutes coagulation factors and platelets; platelet dysfunction from hypothermia and coagulation factor inhibition from acidosis compound this. Each element worsens the others in a vicious circle that is invariably fatal.
(ii) Measures to prevent/reverse hypothermia: pre-warmed intravenous fluids and blood administered through a warming device; solutions used to wash body cavities should be warm; patient covered with warm blankets whenever possible; forced hot air warming (e.g. Bair Hugger) can be used; theatre environment should be kept warm.
(iii) Permissive hypotension is the strategy of withholding fluid or administering it in small aliquots until haemostasis is definitely achieved, rather than aggressive resuscitation which can exacerbate blood loss by disrupting haemostatic mechanisms. In practical terms, fluids are given in small aliquots to achieve a systolic BP of 80–90 mmHg – a value deemed sufficient to maintain vital organ perfusion in an adult.
(iv) Damage control surgery (DCS) aims to control all sources of haemorrhage and gastrointestinal contamination in the quickest way possible; it prevents the lethal triad. Patients who are bleeding profusely do not have the physiological reserves to survive complex and prolonged surgery. The three phases are: (1) initial laparotomy (haemorrhage and contamination control); (2) ICU resuscitation (correction of hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy); (3) definitive reconstruction.
(v) Indications for ICU admission after trauma surgery: severe head injury; severe chest injury with flail chest, lung contusion, or haemo/pneumothorax; evidence of aspiration pneumonia; old, ill ASA III–IV patients; multi-system trauma requiring ventilatory support; unstable haemodynamics requiring inotrope support; massive transfusion with evidence of DIC.

questions.question:
(A) Describe total parenteral nutrition (TPN) under the following headings:
(i) Definition of partial parenteral nutrition and TPN, and why TPN solutions must be given via central venous catheter.
(ii) The indications for TPN, including anticipation of undernutrition, surgical preparation, and specific disease categories.
(iii) The metabolic consequences of critical illness (sepsis, shock, burns, major trauma) that make nutritional support necessary.

(B) For an average adult receiving TPN, state the daily requirements for:
(i) Water (ml/kg/day) and energy (kcal/kg/day for medical, postoperative, and hypercatabolic patients).
(ii) Amino acids (g/kg/day for medical, postoperative, and hypercatabolic patients).
(iii) Three minerals (with amounts) and three vitamins (with amounts) from the standard daily requirements table.

(C) Describe the enteral routes of nutritional support available to critically ill patients, and explain the advantage of enteral over parenteral nutrition in appropriate patients.
questions.answerText:
(A)
(i) Partial parenteral nutrition: supplies only part of daily nutritional requirements, supplementing oral intake. TPN (Total Parenteral Nutrition): supplies all daily nutritional requirements. TPN solutions are concentrated and can cause thrombosis of peripheral veins; therefore they must be given via a central venous catheter. Patients receive dextrose or amino acid solutions by this method.
(ii) Indications for TPN: patients whose GI tract is not functional; anticipation of undernutrition (<50% of metabolic needs met) for >7 days; severely undernourished patients being prepared for surgery, radiation therapy, or chemotherapy; after major surgery, severe burns, and head trauma (especially with sepsis) to reduce morbidity and mortality; complete bowel rest disorders (e.g. Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, severe pancreatitis); paediatric GI disorders (congenital anomalies, prolonged diarrhoea).
(iii) Critical illness causes outpouring of counter-regulatory endocrine hormones, cytokines, and lymphokines, resulting in: changes in substrate utilisation and synthesis rates; catabolism; hypermetabolism. Nutritional support is aimed at minimising these complications (starvation metabolism).

(B)
(i) Water: 30–40 mL/kg/day. Energy: medical patient 30 kcal/kg; post-operative patient 30–45 kcal/kg; hypercatabolic patient 45–60 kcal/kg.
(ii) Amino acids: medical patient 1.0 g/kg/day; postoperative patient 2.0 g/kg/day; hypercatabolic patient 3.0 g/kg/day.
(iii) Three minerals (from standard table): Magnesium 20 mEq/day; Potassium 100 mEq/day; Phosphorus 300 mg/day. Three vitamins: Ascorbic acid (Vitamin C) 100 mg/day; Thiamin (B1) 3 mg/day; Folic acid 400 µg/day.

(C) Enteral routes: oral, nasogastric, gastrostomy, jejunostomy. Enteral nutrition is preferred over parenteral when the GI tract is functional because it: maintains gut mucosal integrity; prevents bacterial translocation; is more physiological; is associated with fewer complications (infection, thrombosis); and is less expensive than TPN.

(i) Total spinal (high spinal block). Mechanism: occurs when an excessive dose of local anaesthetic is injected subarachnoid, or due to unusual sensitivity or spread; the block extends to the cervical level causing hypotension, bradycardia, respiratory insufficiency, unconsciousness, and apnoea. In epidural block, it can occur if local anaesthetic is inadvertently injected into the subarachnoid space (inadvertent dural puncture with a full epidural dose).

(ii) Risk factors for high/total spinal: administration of excessive dose; failure to reduce standard doses in selected patients (elderly, pregnant, obese, or very short); unusual sensitivity to local anaesthetic; Trendelenburg position immediately after injection; old age; short stature; large volume of local anaesthetic; rapid injection; barbotage; presence of abdominal tumours or pregnancy.

(iii) Distinguishing features of total spinal vs ordinary hypotension: total spinal produces block up to cervical level causing respiratory insufficiency or apnoea; unconsciousness; numbness or weakness of upper extremities; nausea with or without vomiting typically precedes hypotension; profound bradycardia. Ordinary spinal hypotension is usually milder, without apnoea or loss of consciousness.

(iv) Management (in sequence):
- Reassure the patient (if conscious).
- Increase oxygen supplementation immediately.
- Maintain adequate airway and ventilation.
- If respiratory insufficiency is evident: intubate the trachea and mechanically ventilate.
- Correct bradycardia: atropine; if inadequate, ephedrine then epinephrine.
- Treat hypotension with vasopressors (e.g. ephedrine).
- Support circulation with IV fluids.
- Treat cardiac arrest with full cardiopulmonary resuscitation.

(v) Precautions: prophylactic volume expansion before block; aggressive vagolytic treatment of bradycardia; never administer excessive doses; reduce standard doses in high-risk patients (elderly, pregnant, obese, very short); careful positioning after injection; use correct baricity and volume of local anaesthetic; test dose in epidural to detect inadvertent subarachnoid placement.
questions.question:
A 32-year-old pregnant woman at 38 weeks gestation presents to the obstetric unit and is scheduled for caesarean section under spinal anaesthesia. Shortly after injection of the local anaesthetic into the subarachnoid space, she develops severe hypotension, bradycardia, dyspnoea, and loss of consciousness.

(i) Name the complication that has developed and explain its mechanism.
(ii) List the risk factors that predispose to a high or total spinal in this patient.
(iii) Describe the clinical features that distinguish this complication from ordinary hypotension following spinal anaesthesia.
(iv) Outline the full management of this patient, in sequence.
(v) State the precautions that should be taken to reduce the incidence of this complication during obstetric regional anaesthesia.

questions.answerText:
(i) Complication and mechanism:
- Complication: hypotension from sympathetic blockade following regional anaesthesia
- Mechanism: rapid development of sympathetic blockade following epidural/spinal leads to vasodilatation which reduces preload and blood pressure; vasodilatation produced by sympathetic blockade following spinal and epidural anaesthesia will also reduce preload and blood pressure
- Prevention: preloading with fluids 500–1000ml N/S
- Treatment: ephedrine 5–10mg increment; phenylephrine; avoid agents that would cause uterine vasoconstriction; uterine displacement

(ii) Full technique of obstetric subarachnoid block:
- Obtain consent and ensure no contraindications
- Antacid prophylaxis
- Ensure adequacy of resus equipment and drugs
- Apply monitors: NIBP, SaO2, ECG, EtCO2
- Keep patient warm
- IV access and preload with N/S 500–1000ml
- Position: sitting or lateral
- Skin prep; identify L3–L4 interspinous space
- Infiltrate LA 1% lidocaine 2–5ml
- Introduce G25 or G26 pencil point spinal needle; on free CSF flow give heavy bupivacaine 0.5% 2–2.5ml; fentanyl 25mcg intensifies analgesia
- Position supine and place wedge under right hip; monitor every minute for next 10 minutes; correct hypotension with fluids and ephedrine
- Give oxygen by face mask; on delivery administer oxytocin 5 units; may add 5–30 units in 500ml infusion

(iii) Physiological changes making GA risky:
- CVS: increased SVR, CO, HR, BP; plasma volume and RBC increase (dilutional anaemia); poor compensation in diseased hearts; aorto-caval compression; compromise by anaesthetic agents lowering BP
- Respiratory: oedema of tissues (airways); BMR increases as pregnancy progresses; minute ventilation increases by 50%; pCO2 decreases; FRC decreases — rapid desaturation; anaesthetic implications: difficult intubation (1:300 obstetric vs 1:2000 general population); rapid desaturation; poorly tolerated apnoea
- GIT: progesterone effect reduces gastric motility and emptying time; increased gastric acidity; reduced lower oesophageal sphincter tone; anaesthetic implications: full stomach; regurgitation and aspiration; Mendelson's syndrome

(iv) General anaesthesia technique for caesarean section:
- Preop and premed as stated; anaesthetic machine, equipment and drugs ready; informed assistant present; monitors; wedge; pre-oxygenation for 5 minutes; secure IV access and commence fluid if not yet on
- Induction: rapidly acting agent (e.g. thiopentone) 4–5.5mg/kg calculated dose; cricoid pressure as soon as unconscious
- Follow induction with suxamethonium — short-acting muscle relaxant; as soon as fasciculated, intubate with cuffed tube
- Confirm correct placement and continue anaesthesia N2O:O2 + inhalational agent (e.g. halothane or isoflurane) in low doses; atracurium or other non-depolariser for muscle relaxation; ventilate at normocarbia
- After delivery: give oxytocics and opioid analgesics; more blood loss with GA
- At end: reverse residual effects of muscle relaxants; aspirate pharynx dry; extubate awake lying in lateral position; post-op care as usual

(v) Advantages of GA in specified situations:
- Great advantage when rapid delivery is desired e.g. fetal distress
- Choice when substantial haemorrhage is anticipated
questions.question:
A labouring primigravida at term requests analgesia. After assessment, the anaesthetist decides to site an epidural. Thirty minutes after establishing the epidural, the patient's blood pressure drops from 120/80 to 70/40 mmHg.
(i) Name this complication and state the physiological mechanism responsible, using the information given about the obstetric anaesthetic context.
(ii) Describe the full technique of obstetric subarachnoid block: patient preparation, positioning, drug and dose, and post-block monitoring.
(iii) State the physiological changes of pregnancy that make general anaesthesia in the obstetric patient uniquely risky, covering CVS, respiratory, and GIT systems.
(iv) Describe the complete general anaesthesia technique for a caesarean section as stated: induction agent and dose, airway management, maintenance agents, and post-delivery care.
(v) State the advantages of general anaesthesia over regional anaesthesia in specified obstetric situations as given.

questions.explanation: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome shows the greatest gastric acid output due to gastrin-secreting tumors causing massive hypersecretion. Peak Acid Output exceeds 60 mmol/hr, usually more than twice the BAO. The autonomous gastrin production overcomes normal feedback inhibition mechanisms.
questions.question: What condition shows the greatest gastric acid output?

questions.explanation: Ecbolic function refers to secretion of pancreatic enzymes, which is assessed by stimulation with CCK following secretin. The secretin-CCK test is the most satisfactory for measuring pancreatic secretory capacity. It separates patients with normal from those with impaired pancreatic function.
questions.question: What does ecbolic function refer to in pancreatic testing?

questions.explanation: Lactate and butyrate in gastric content indicate bacterial action when food is retained over 6 hours at neutral/alkaline pH. This occurs in gastric carcinoma or pyloric stenosis from decreased HCl secretion or acid neutralization. Normal gastric juice does not contain these organic acids.
questions.question: What do organic acids in gastric content indicate?

questions.explanation: Xanthomata are yellowish lipid deposits in skin and tendons resulting from severe, chronic hypercholesterolemia or hypertriglyceridemia. Tendon xanthomas particularly characterize familial hypercholesterolemia, while eruptive xanthomas suggest severe hypertriglyceridemia. These physical findings indicate need for lipid investigation.
questions.question: What clinical feature may physically manifest in patients with severe hyperlipidemia?

questions.explanation: Type 2 diabetes involves insulin resistance in peripheral tissues combined with progressive beta-cell dysfunction and inadequate insulin secretion. Unlike type 1, substantial insulin production continues but is insufficient to overcome resistance. This form accounts for 90-95% of diabetes cases and is strongly associated with obesity.
questions.question: Type 2 diabetes mellitus is primarily characterized by which two pathophysiological defects?

questions.explanation: Free HCl is titrated with 0.10 mol/L NaOH to pH 3.5 using a pH meter or Toepfer's reagent (salmon color endpoint). Titration to pH 3.5 detects essentially all free HCl because it's the only strongly ionized acid present. Beyond pH 3.5, other weak acids would be titrated, overestimating HCl concentration.
questions.question: What pH endpoint is used for titrating free HCl?

questions.explanation: Glucose phosphorylation to glucose-6-phosphate traps the molecule within cells as the phosphate group prevents membrane crossing. This commits glucose to intracellular metabolism and maintains a concentration gradient favoring continued glucose uptake. The reaction is essentially irreversible under physiological conditions.
questions.question: Phosphorylation of glucose upon cell entry achieves which critical function?

questions.explanation: Parietal cells of the stomach secrete hydrogen ions and chloride into the gastric lumen. As these ions enter the lumen, bicarbonate diffuses into the extracellular fluid. This process is responsible for the postprandial alkaline tide.
questions.question: What ions do parietal cells secrete into the gastric lumen?

questions.explanation: External quality assessment (proficiency testing) evaluates laboratory accuracy by comparing results on identical samples with peer laboratories and reference methods. This identifies systematic bias requiring corrective action. EQA complements internal QC and ensures results are clinically reliable and comparable.
questions.question: What main purpose does external quality control serve in lipid testing?

questions.explanation: Chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies detect changes in arterial oxygen, and pH. These peripheral chemoreceptors work with central chemoreceptors to regulate ventilation. They respond rapidly to hypoxemia and acute pH changes.
questions.question: Why are chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies important?

questions.explanation: In this case with alkalemia (pH the respiratory component is the cause. The PaCO2 is low at mmHg, and loss of this acidic gas accounts for the alkaline pH. The bicarbonate is normal, ruling out metabolic alkalosis.
questions.question: A patient has pH 7.5, PaCO2 4 kPa (30 mmHg), and HCO3- 24 mmol/L. What is the primary cause?
In pre-renal ARF, what characterizes the urea and creatinine rise?
questions.explanation: Pre-renal ARF shows disproportionate rise in urea compared to creatinine because urea reabsorption increases with reduced tubular flow. In intrinsic renal ARF, urea and creatinine tend to rise together proportionally. This difference helps distinguish pre-renal from intrinsic causes of acute renal dysfunction.

questions.question: Cortisol increases plasma glucose levels primarily through which two mechanisms?
questions.explanation: Cortisol, released from the adrenal cortex in response to ACTH, promotes hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis to raise blood glucose. It also stimulates protein catabolism, providing amino acid substrates for gluconeogenesis. These actions make cortisol an important counter-regulatory hormone during prolonged stress or fasting.

questions.question: What is the normal range for fecal steroids per day?
questions.explanation: Normal fecal steroid range is 75-200 mg/day, derived from dietary cholesterol, intestinal mucosa sloughing, and bile acids/cholesterol. Elevated levels may indicate malabsorption of bile acids or increased intestinal losses. Microscopic stool inspection can reveal meat and vegetable fibers.

Tubeless test meals use stable isotopes (non-radioactive elements naturally found in body) or breath tests (markers releasing gases detectable in exhaled breath). The urea breath test for H. pylori exemplifies breath test methodology. These non-invasive approaches avoid radiation exposure.
questions.question: What tubeless test meal markers can be used?

questions.explanation: HbA1c >=6.5% on two occasions confirms diabetes diagnosis, reflecting average glucose levels over the preceding 2-3 months. This test offers advantages of not requiring fasting and less day-to-day variability. However, it may be affected by hemoglobinopathies and conditions affecting red blood cell turnover.
questions.question: An HbA1c value equal to or greater than which percentage confirms diabetes mellitus diagnosis?
Insulinoma causes hypoglycemia in otherwise healthy-appearing patients through which mechanism?
questions.explanation: Insulinomas are insulin-secreting beta-cell tumors causing inappropriate hyperinsulinemia and recurrent hypoglycemia, particularly during fasting. These tumors autonomously secrete insulin regardless of glucose levels, overwhelming counter-regulatory responses. Diagnosis requires documenting hypoglycemia with inappropriately elevated insulin and C-peptide.

Anaerobic carbohydrate metabolism occurs when oxygen supply is inadequate and yields lactate along with hydrogen ions. This process is particularly important during intense exercise or in tissues with poor oxygen supply. The accumulation of lactate and hydrogen ions leads to metabolic acidosis.
questions.question: Anaerobic carbohydrate metabolism produces which combination of substances?

questions.explanation: Calcium levels should be corrected for albumin level when assessing malabsorption because hypoalbuminemia affects measured calcium. Malabsorption causes both calcium and protein deficiency, requiring interpretation of corrected calcium values. Uncorrected values may underestimate true calcium status.
questions.question: What mineral deficiency should be corrected for albumin level?

questions.explanation: Malonyl-CoA inhibits carnitine palmitoyltransferase-1 (CPT-1), the enzyme required for fatty acid transport into mitochondria for beta-oxidation. By blocking CPT-1, insulin prevents the liver from oxidizing newly synthesized fatty acids. This ensures that during fed states, fatty acids are stored rather than oxidized.
questions.question: Malonyl-CoA elevation by insulin prevents fatty acid oxidation by inhibiting which transport system?

questions.explanation: Pre-renal ARF results from reduced renal perfusion with functioning tubules. The classification includes pre-renal (reduced perfusion), intrinsic renal (vascular, inflammation, infiltration, toxicity), and post-renal (obstruction) causes. Pre-renal failure is potentially reversible with restoration of perfusion.
questions.question: What is the pathophysiological basis of pre-renal ARF?
What patient condition renders the Friedewald equation invalid for LDL calculation?
questions.explanation: When triglycerides exceed 400 mg/dL (4.5 mmol/L), the VLDL composition changes and chylomicrons or remnants are likely present, violating Friedewald equation assumptions. Direct LDL measurement must be used instead. High triglycerides indicate the TG/5 factor no longer accurately estimates VLDL cholesterol.

questions.question: What metabolic condition shifts potassium into cells causing hypokalemia?
questions.explanation: Alkalosis causes cellular shift of potassium into cells, lowering plasma concentration. Hydrogen ions move out of cells to buffer alkalemia, and potassium enters to maintain electroneutrality. Insulin effect, beta-agonists, and theophylline toxicity also shift potassium intracellularly causing hypokalemia.

questions.question: What does malabsorption in both Schilling test stages indicate?
questions.explanation: Malabsorption in both Schilling test stages indicates intestinal disease preventing B12 absorption regardless of intrinsic factor presence. This pattern differentiates intestinal from gastric causes of B12 malabsorption. Conditions include Crohn's disease, tropical sprue, or surgical resection.

questions.question: What causes malabsorption after gastrectomy?
questions.explanation: Increased rate of transit through the small intestine after gastrectomy causes malabsorption by reducing contact time for digestion and absorption. This also occurs in carcinoid syndrome. Rapid transit prevents adequate nutrient processing despite normal digestive enzyme and absorptive capacity.

After approximately 8-12 hours, the capsule reaches the GI tract end and is naturally excreted during bowel movement. It captures thousands of images during transit, transmitted wirelessly to a recording device. The disposable capsule requires no retrieval and is flushed away.
questions.question: How long does capsule endoscopy take to traverse the GI tract?
Which cells produce both mucus and pepsinogen?
questions.explanation: Neck chief cells (mucus cells) uniquely secrete both mucus and pepsinogen, differentiating them from surface epithelial cells that produce only mucus. Chief cells produce group I and II pepsinogen without mucus production, while parietal cells secrete acid and intrinsic factor. This dual secretory function of neck chief cells contributes to both protection and digestion.

questions.question: Which cells line the parietal cells and produce digestive enzymes?
questions.explanation: Peptic cells line the oxyntic (parietal) cells and produce pepsinogen, rennin, and lipase for protein and fat digestion. These cells, also called chief or zymogen cells, secrete group I and II pepsinogen as inactive precursors. The strategic positioning near parietal cells ensures rapid activation of pepsinogen by secreted HCl.

Free PABA can be given on the second day or C-PABA or p-aminosalicylic acid (PAS) can be given simultaneously with NBT-PABA as controls. Low recovery of control substance suggests decreased intestinal absorption or renal excretion. This internal control corrects for individual variations in absorption and excretion.
questions.question: What control substance can be given with NBT-PABA to compensate for absorption and excretion errors?
How much greater is fecal elastase-1 concentration compared to pancreatic juice?
questions.explanation: Fecal elastase-1 concentration is five-fold to six-fold greater than in pancreatic juice due to intestinal water reabsorption. This concentration effect enhances test sensitivity. The enzyme can be determined by ELISA technique using two monoclonal antibodies specific to the human enzyme.

LDL cholesterol exceeding 130 mg/dL indicates increased cardiovascular risk, with higher levels conferring proportionally greater risk. Current guidelines recommend LDL <100 mg/dL for primary prevention and <70 mg/dL for secondary prevention in high-risk patients. LDL remains the primary target for lipid-lowering therapy.
questions.question: What LDL cholesterol level predicts increased coronary heart disease risk?

questions.explanation: At pH nearest its pK buffer pair functions best at a pH nearest to its pK value. At this pH, the buffer has equal concentrations of its acid and base forms, providing maximum buffering capacity. The efficiency decreases as pH moves away from the pK.
questions.question: At what pH does a buffer pair function most effectively?
What enzyme is defective in Type 2 (proximal) renal tubular acidosis?
questions.explanation: Proximal or Type renal tubular acidosis involves a defect in the carbonic anhydrase enzyme. This enzyme is crucial for bicarbonate reabsorption in the proximal tubule. Its deficiency leads to excessive bicarbonate loss and metabolic acidosis.

questions.question: What is the intracellular fluid volume in a 70kg adult?
questions.explanation: Intracellular fluid volume is 28 liters in a healthy 70kg adult, representing about two-thirds of total body water (42-45L). Extracellular fluid comprises the remaining 14L. This distribution maintains cellular function and provides buffering capacity for acid-base balance.

questions.question: Where are the highest serum gastrin concentrations found?
questions.explanation: Highest serum gastrin concentrations occur in Zollinger-Ellison syndrome due to gastrinoma tumors secreting gastrin autonomously. High gastrin also occurs in fundal atrophic gastritis with achlorhydria due to lost feedback inhibition. Serum gastrin determination by radioimmunoassay distinguishes these conditions.

questions.question: How does insulin prevent hepatic ketogenesis and fatty acid oxidation?
questions.explanation: Insulin increases malonyl-CoA levels through activation of acetyl-CoA carboxylase, which inhibits carnitine palmitoyltransferase-1 and prevents fatty acid entry into mitochondria. This blocks beta-oxidation of fatty acids and subsequent ketone body formation in the liver. Additionally, insulin inhibits hormone-sensitive lipase in adipocytes, reducing fatty acid release from stored triglycerides.

questions.question: What percentage of age-60 individuals may have no free HCl in fasting stomach?
questions.explanation: About 25% of individuals at age 60 may have no free HCl in fasting stomach compared to 4% of young adults. This percentage increases with age and is considered normal only if it doesn't persist after maximal pentagastrin stimulation. Age-related achlorhydria reflects progressive gastric mucosal changes.

questions.question: Pyruvate carboxylase converts pyruvate to which intermediate that serves as a substrate for gluconeogenesis?
questions.explanation: Pyruvate carboxylase converts pyruvate to oxaloacetate in mitochondria, which is a critical first step in gluconeogenesis. This biotin-dependent enzyme is activated by acetyl-CoA, signaling that the cell has adequate energy and can spare pyruvate for glucose synthesis. Oxaloacetate must then be converted to phosphoenolpyruvate to continue the gluconeogenic pathway.

Phlorhizin is a natural compound that competitively inhibits sodium-glucose cotransporters (SGLT1 and SGLT2) in renal tubules, preventing glucose reabsorption. This creates an experimental model of renal glucosuria with normal blood glucose levels. Modern SGLT2 inhibitor drugs use this mechanism therapeutically to reduce hyperglycemia in diabetes.
questions.question: Phlorhizin injection causes normoglycemic glucosuria by inhibiting which renal transporter?

questions.explanation: Normal fecal water loss is 50 mL daily, representing minimal obligatory loss. Diarrhea can increase this dramatically to several liters daily, causing severe dehydration and electrolyte depletion. The colon normally reabsorbs 99% of water from intestinal contents.
questions.question: What is normal daily fecal water loss?

questions.explanation: During hypoglycemia, the liver activates glycogenolysis to break down stored glycogen and gluconeogenesis to synthesize new glucose from substrates. These processes are stimulated by counter-regulatory hormones and ensure continuous glucose supply to glucose-dependent tissues. The liver can thus maintain blood glucose even during prolonged fasting.
questions.question: When blood glucose decreases, the liver responds by activating which two metabolic pathways?

questions.explanation: Pyloric stenosis prevents food from reaching the intestine, so the normal intestinal bicarbonate secretion that would correct the alkaline tide cannot occur. Additionally, vomiting removes hydrogen and chloride, while bicarbonate remains in the blood. Volume depletion and chloride deficiency perpetuate the alkalosis.
questions.question: How does pyloric stenosis cause persistent alkalosis?

questions.explanation: Dehydration of brain cells causes neurological symptoms including seizures, coma, hyperreflexia, and spasticity in hypernatremia. Elevated plasma sodium creates osmotic gradient drawing water from brain cells. Lethargy, confusion, and restlessness precede more severe manifestations as cellular dehydration worsens.
questions.question: What neurological symptom results from brain cell dehydration in hypernatremia?
What is the normal pH range of pancreatic juice?
questions.explanation: Normal pancreatic juice is colorless, odorless, with a pH of 8.0-8.3 and specific gravity of 1.007-1.042. The alkaline pH is due to high bicarbonate content, which neutralizes gastric acid in the duodenum. Total 24-hour volume ranges from 800-3000ml depending on dietary intake and stimulation.

A minimum 12-hour fast is required to clear postprandial chylomicrons from circulation, ensuring accurate triglyceride and calculated LDL measurements. Water intake is permitted during fasting. Non-fasting samples contain dietary lipids that falsely elevate triglycerides and interfere with LDL calculation using the Friedewald equation.
questions.question: How many hours of fasting are required before blood collection for lipid measurements?

questions.explanation: Fundal atrophic gastritis with achlorhydria shows high serum gastrin due to lack of acid feedback inhibition on antral G-cells. Without acid to suppress gastrin release, compensatory hypergastrinemia develops despite absent acid production. This pattern differs from Zollinger-Ellison syndrome which has high acid and high gastrin.
questions.question: What causes high gastrin with achlorhydria?
Where are the primary chemoreceptors that control respiration located?
questions.explanation: The rate of elimination is controlled by chemoreceptors in the respiratory center of the medulla and in the carotid and aortic bodies. These receptors respond to changes in or hydrogen ion concentrations. The central and peripheral chemoreceptors work together to regulate ventilation.

questions.question: What is the normal pH range of blood?
questions.explanation: The normal pH of blood is maintained within the narrow range of to This tight regulation is essential for normal enzyme function and metabolic processes. Values outside this range indicate acidemia or alkalemia.

Thyroxine elevates blood glucose by stimulating glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, and intestinal glucose absorption, but does not directly inhibit insulin secretion. It increases overall metabolic rate and cellular glucose utilization, creating greater demand for circulating glucose. Thyroid hormone excess (hyperthyroidism) can therefore contribute to glucose intolerance.
