• Flow cytometry, using monoclonal anti-human HbF or anti-D antibodies to differentiate foetal RBCs from other cells, is more accurate than the Kleihauer test, showing that the Kleihauer test, while quantitative, is not the most accurate method available for FMH determination.
• The Rosette test is therefore mainly a screening test for the presence of FMH, while the Kleihauer test is used both to confirm and to quantify the degree of FMH once a positive screen has been obtained.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the principle and procedure of the Kleihauer test for demonstrating foetal haemoglobin in foeto-maternal haemorrhage (FMH).
(b) Explain how the test result is used to calculate the volume of FMH.
(c) Distinguish the Kleihauer test from the Rosette test for FMH.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• In an alkaline buffer, HbA is a negatively charged protein which moves toward the positive electrode (anode) in an electric field; most haemoglobin variants are separated from HbA during electrophoresis because the structural abnormality usually involves changes in electrical charge, while haemoglobin without a change in charge will not separate.
• Cellulose acetate paper is used as the support medium at a pH of 8.4 to 8.9.
• The advantage is rapid separation of haemoglobins, ease of handling and minimal preparative work; the disadvantages are that haemoglobin fractions in low concentration like HbA2, HbH and HbBart's may be missed, and when small haemoglobin fractions occur near a broad band, the minor fraction may be missed, especially in neonates when high levels of HbF can cause the presence of either HbA or HbS to be missed.
• Certain haemoglobins comigrate at this pH, including HbS, HbD and HbG, and also HbA2, HbC, HbE and HbO comigrate.
(b)
The pH and medium used are varied in order to identify the different haemoglobin variants, since haemoglobins that comigrate and cannot be resolved at one pH may be separated using a different pH or support medium.
(c)
• Cellulose acetate electrophoresis at alkaline pH (8.4-8.9) has the advantage of rapid separation, ease of handling and minimal preparative work, but haemoglobins in low concentration or near a broad band may be missed.
• Citrate agar electrophoresis is performed at an acidic pH of 6.0-6.2, and separation of haemoglobin variants by this method is determined by the relative affinity for agaropectin by certain haemoglobin surface groups; it outlines haemoglobins that comigrate at alkaline pH and other cases that cannot be resolved at alkaline pH, but it is technically difficult to handle.
• Citrate agar electrophoresis is particularly useful in diagnosing sickle cell disease at birth when the high concentration of HbF may pose a problem on alkaline electrophoresis, and haemoglobins A, D, E, G and H all comigrate at this acidic pH, which differs from the set of haemoglobins that comigrate at alkaline pH.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the principle, buffer/medium and reported limitations of cellulose acetate haemoglobin electrophoresis at alkaline pH.
(b) Explain why the pH and medium used in haemoglobin electrophoresis are varied.
(c) Distinguish cellulose acetate electrophoresis at alkaline pH from citrate agar electrophoresis at acidic pH.

(a) Describe the classification of anaemia based on the red cell absolute indices (MCV, MCH, MCHC).
(b) State how each classification is applied in selecting further investigation.
(c) Explain why an error such as not assessing iron status before interpreting HbA2 can lead to an inaccurate classification of thalassaemia trait.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The mean cell volume (MCV) is normally 80-95 fL and indicates the average volume or size of an individual red cell; it is decreased (microcytic) in iron deficiency, thalassaemia and lead poisoning, and increased (macrocytic) in folate/vitamin B12 deficiency, alcohol use and liver disease.
• The mean cell haemoglobin (MCH) is normally 27-32 pg and indicates the average amount of haemoglobin in an individual cell; it is decreased in iron deficiency, thalassaemia and lead poisoning, and increased in acute blood loss, renal disease, bone marrow failure and post-chemotherapy.
• The mean cell haemoglobin concentration (MCHC) is normally 32-35 g/dL and indicates the quantity of haemoglobin in a given volume of red cells.
(b)
• A reduced MCV and MCH pattern is applied in selecting patients for haemoglobinopathy/thalassaemia screening or iron studies, since red cell indices are particularly useful in screening for the thalassaemias and this is best done by an automated blood cell counter; beta thalassaemia trait is associated with mild or no anaemia but with reduced MCV and MCH and an elevated HbA2 level.
• Normal red cell indices may however be found in people with alpha+ thalassaemia trait or silent beta+ trait, and in the Nigerian population, where alpha thalassaemia prevalence is also high, normal red cell indices do not rule out beta-thalassaemia trait since the expected alpha/beta chain imbalance may not occur, so red cell indices are applied as a screening step rather than a definitive diagnostic step.
(c)
• Concomitant iron deficiency may result in classifying a person with beta thalassaemia trait as not having the condition, since iron deficiency may cause a low level of HbA2, which would otherwise be expected to be raised in beta thalassaemia trait.
• Values below 3.3% are usually normal for HbA2, and over 3.5% usually indicates beta thalassaemia trait, but there is a reported overlap between normal and beta thalassaemia values, so values between 3.3 and 3.7% should be interpreted with care, and a value above 7% suggests an analytical error or the presence of another haemoglobin that is not HbA2.
• Because concomitant iron deficiency may lower HbA2 into the normal range, and red cell indices and formulae derived from them have not been useful in differentiating between beta thalassaemia trait and iron deficiency, an iron status assessment is necessary, and HbA2 should be rechecked after iron therapy, since failing to assess iron status before interpreting a borderline or normal HbA2 could lead to a false exclusion of beta thalassaemia trait.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the principle, materials/reagent and procedure of the sickling test for HbS.
(b) Explain why the slide is examined at 15 minutes, one hour and 24 hours.
(c) Distinguish the sickling test from the solubility test.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The sickling test is a simple screening test in which the presence of sickled erythrocytes in a patient with symptoms of sickle cell disease is suggestive of the disorder.
• A drop of blood is mixed with two drops of 2% sodium metabisulphite.
• The mixture is covered with a coverslip and sealed with petroleum jelly, and the slide is then examined under the microscope after 15 minutes, one hour and 24 hours.
• False positive results may occur if sodium metabisulphite of >2% is used, while false negative results may occur if the metabisulphite is stale and also in the neonatal period because of the low percentage of HbS.
(b)
Sickling develops over time as the sodium metabisulphite deoxygenates the haemoglobin, so examining the slide at 15 minutes, one hour and 24 hours allows sickled erythrocytes that take longer to form to still be detected before the result is finalised.
(c)
• The sickling test relies on microscopic observation of sickled erythrocytes forming in blood mixed with sodium metabisulphite and examined at set time intervals, and is a simple screening test that can be done especially in a primary health care facility.
• The solubility test is instead based on the fact that HbS is less soluble than HbA in the deoxygenated state; one drop of the patient's blood is mixed with a solution prepared using potassium dihydrogen phosphate, dipotassium hydrogen phosphate and sodium metabisulphite, and the mixture is spun in a centrifuge.
• In the solubility test, HbS if present precipitates as a red opaque band on the surface of the test solution while other haemoglobins remain in solution, whereas the sickling test relies on visual identification of sickled cell shape under the microscope rather than a precipitation band.
• The solubility test should be performed on all samples which show the 'S' band on alkaline electrophoresis, especially where haemoglobins G and D, which comigrate with HbS on alkaline electrophoresis, are present, and control blood samples with HbA, HbAS and HbS should be tested at the same time.

(a)
• Light transmission aggregometry (LTA) is the gold standard, based on decreasing turbidity of platelet-rich plasma as platelets aggregate.
• Whole blood impedance aggregometry measures aggregation directly in whole blood via increasing electrical impedance at electrodes.
• Flow cytometry measures platelet activation markers such as P-selectin or glycoprotein IIb/IIIa conformation change using fluorescently labelled antibodies.
• The VerifyNow system is a point-of-care assay measuring changes in light transmission through whole blood after stimulation, using a cartridge containing fibrinogen-coated beads and an agonist; the PFA-100 measures platelet function under high shear conditions using a membrane coated with collagen and epinephrine or ADP, with closure time reflecting platelet function.
(b)
• LTA is applied where high sensitivity and specificity for detecting platelet function abnormalities using multiple agonists is needed, despite requiring specialised equipment, trained personnel and large volumes of blood, and being time-consuming and labour-intensive.
• Whole blood impedance aggregometry is selected when centrifugation to prepare PRP is not desired or not possible, and a more physiological whole blood measurement is preferred; the VerifyNow system and PFA-100 are selected for rapid, point-of-care or simple screening use, for example monitoring antiplatelet therapy (aspirin or clopidogrel) or screening for von Willebrand disease, while flow cytometry is selected for highly sensitive, specialised or research use.
(c)
• LTA specifically requires platelet-rich plasma obtained by centrifuging the blood sample, and its stated disadvantages include that it requires large volumes of blood in addition to specialised equipment and trained personnel.
• If only a limited whole blood sample is available, attempting to perform LTA, which needs sufficient volume to both centrifuge out an adequate PRP fraction and run the aggregometer test, could result in an inadequate or unreliable PRP preparation, undermining the validity of the resulting aggregation curve.
• In such a situation, whole blood impedance aggregometry, which can be performed on whole blood without the need for centrifugation, or a point-of-care method such as VerifyNow, requiring minimal sample preparation, would be the technique correctly selected instead, since choosing LTA despite an inadequate sample volume does not match the technique's own stated sample requirement.
• This illustrates the general principle that each platelet aggregation technique has advantages and limitations tied to its underlying method (turbidity, impedance, fluorescence, or shear-induced occlusion), and selecting a technique whose sample or equipment requirements the available specimen and setting cannot meet is a basic error that produces an invalid rather than merely a suboptimal result.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the classification of platelet aggregation testing techniques (LTA, whole blood impedance aggregometry, flow cytometry, VerifyNow, PFA-100).
(b) State how each technique is applied or selected according to clinical need and available sample.
(c) Explain why choosing a technique unsuited to the available sample (for example requiring large PRP volume when only limited whole blood is available) leads to an invalid platelet function result.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Quality control is classified into internal QC (daily checks using control samples to monitor test performance within the lab) and external QC (participation in proficiency testing schemes to benchmark accuracy against other laboratories), with both types described as essential for comprehensive quality assurance.
• The quality assurance cycle includes a pre-analytical phase (factors affecting results due to handling of the specimen prior to analysis) and an analytical phase (where internal QC monitors accuracy and reproducibility through controls, and external QC compares results to other laboratories).
(b)
• Internal QC is applied through analysis of control samples done daily using multilevel controls, that is, low, normal and high levels, or normal and abnormal samples, and through the use of control materials such as ABO and RhD control cells, antibody screening and identification panels, and Coombs control cells.
• External QC is applied through participation in an external quality assessment scheme (EQAS) or proficiency test, comparing performance against a peer group using the same reagents, reported as a deviation index or Z score, and supporting laboratory certification and accreditation.
(c)
• Pre-analytical factors listed as affecting laboratory results due to handling of the specimen sample prior to analysis include misidentification of the patient, mislabelling of specimens, fasting state, alcohol consumption, dehydration, prolonged use of a tourniquet, and improper techniques like squeezing that can cause microclots or platelet clots.
• The basic reasoning behind why a mislabelling error specifically invalidates the result is that all subsequent analytical steps, however precisely performed with correctly functioning reagents and correctly applied internal and external QC, will be testing and reporting a result under the wrong patient's identity, since the specimen itself is no longer correctly linked to the patient it is meant to represent.
• This means that even where internal QC (daily control checks) and external QC (proficiency testing) both confirm that the analytical process itself is accurate and precise, a pre-analytical mislabelling error is not something either type of QC is designed to detect, since both are aimed at verifying that the test method is working correctly, not at verifying that the correct specimen was tested.
• This is why quality assurance is described as being concerned with much more than analytical QC alone, namely ensuring that the right test is carried out on the right specimen and that the right result and interpretation are delivered to the right person at the right time, showing that pre-analytical and analytical quality control address different, equally necessary, parts of producing a valid laboratory result.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the classification of quality control into internal and external types, and the classification of the quality assurance cycle into pre-analytical and analytical phases.
(b) State how each type/phase of QC is applied in a serology or blood bank laboratory.
(c) Explain why a basic pre-analytical error, such as mislabelling a specimen, leads to an inaccurate or invalid laboratory result regardless of how well the analytical technique is performed.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• A Coulter counter, also known as an automated haematology analyser, is an apparatus for counting, sizing and differentiating particles suspended in an electrolyte; electrical impedance classifies red and white cells based on size, since cells are non-conductive and cause a momentary drop in electrical current as they pass through an aperture.
• An electrically conductive diluent containing cells is passed through a narrow channel; as each cell passes through an aperture, it causes a momentary drop in the electrical current passing through the channel, and the number of particles in a given fluid can be counted by measuring the number of pulses, with the magnitude of the pulse related to the size of the particle.
(b)
Cell coincidence occurs when more than one cell passes through the impedance counting aperture at a time, so counting two cells as one voltage pulse could result in falsely low counts; in modern analysers, coincidence is minimised by the application of hydrodynamic focusing, in which a thin, slow-moving stream of cells flows in a single file through the sensing aperture.
(c)
• Electrical impedance counting classifies cells based on the size of the electrical pulse produced as a non-conductive cell passes through a narrow aperture, causing a momentary drop in current proportional to the particle's size.
• Flow cytometry is considered the most effective method of differentiating cell types, providing information from forward light scatter, side scatter and side fluorescence to generate a white cell differential, nucleated red blood cell count, reticulocyte count and platelet information.
• In flow cytometry, a very small amount of specimen is aspirated and passes through an aperture and a laser flow cell, with cells injected into a flow located in the optical path of a laser light source and surrounded by a sheath flow so that blood cells pass through the centre of the flow in a single volume at a fast speed.
• Flow cytometry can generate more detailed information in the form of flags and messages, for example indicating the presence of blasts, immature granulocytes, microcytosis and macrocytosis, whereas electrical impedance mainly provides particle number and size information.
• The two main types of sensors used in blood cell counting are therefore laser light (flow cytometry) and electrical impedance, and modern haematology analysers commonly combine both technologies within the same instrument.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the principle and procedure of the Coulter (electrical impedance) principle used in automated haematology analysers.
(b) Explain the problem of cell coincidence and how it is minimised.
(c) Distinguish electrical impedance counting from flow cytometry.

questions.answerText:
(a)
The finding is nucleated red blood cells (precursor red cells containing a nucleus), associated with sickle cell disease, thalassaemia major, other severe anaemia, haemolytic disease of the newborn, leukaemias and autoimmune haemolytic anaemia.
(b)
The finding is detected by microscopic examination of the peripheral blood film, since the presence of nucleated red blood cells in the peripheral blood film is indicative of bone marrow stress or response to treatment.
(c)
The finding is recorded/reported as nucleated red blood cells seen per 100 white blood cells counted on the film.
(d)
As a follow-up practical step, the white blood cell count must be corrected using the formula: corrected WBC equals estimated WBC divided by (100 plus number of nucleated RBC among 100 WBC) multiplied by 100%, since the presence of nucleated red blood cells (immature cells) may erroneously increase the total count reported by an automated haematology analyser.
questions.question:
A blood film shows red cell precursors containing a nucleus, and the patient's automated full blood count differential appears unexpectedly elevated.
(a) Identify the finding.
(b) State the basic technique used to detect it.
(c) State how the finding should be recorded/reported.
(d) State the follow-up practical step relating to the automated count.

questions.answerText:
(a)
The finding is rouleaux formation, associated with myelomatosis, macroglobulinaemia, inflammatory disorder and malignancy.
(b)
The finding is detected by microscopic examination of a well prepared and properly stained peripheral blood film.
(c)
The finding is recorded/reported as rouleaux formation, distinguished from true agglutination, and correlated with the patient's clinical details.
(d)
A practical implication is that rouleaux formation, which can occur due to a protein abnormality such as multiple myeloma, is listed as one of the difficulties in ABO grouping, since it can be mistaken for true agglutination and must be recognised and, if necessary, investigated before an ABO group is reported.
questions.question:
A blood film from a patient with suspected paraproteinaemia shows red cells joined together side by side like stacks of coins.
(a) Identify the finding.
(b) State the basic technique used to detect it.
(c) State how it should be recorded/reported.
(d) State a practical implication of this finding for another routine test.

questions.answerText:
(a)
The normal APTT is 30-40 seconds, so an APTT of 65 seconds is prolonged, while the PT is normal.
(b)
The result should be recorded/reported as a prolonged APTT (65 seconds, above the 30-40 second reference range) with a normal PT.
(c)
APTT measures factors XII, XI, IX, VIII, X, V, II and fibrinogen and is prolonged in deficiencies of the involved factors, such as in haemophilia; a prolonged APTT with a normal PT (which measures factors VII, X, V, prothrombin and fibrinogen) narrows the deficiency to a factor unique to the APTT pathway, such as factor VIII, IX, XI or XII.
(d)
The action that follows, given the history of recurrent joint bleeding, is to further investigate for haemophilia, since APTT prolongation with deficiencies of its listed factors is specifically associated with haemophilia.
questions.question:
A patient with recurrent joint bleeding has an Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (APTT) of 65 seconds and a normal PT.
(a) Interpret the result.
(b) State how it should be recorded/reported.
(c) State what it indicates.
(d) State the action that follows from this reading.

A blood film shows pale-staining red cells with an area of central pallor greater than one third of the cell's diameter.
(a) Identify the abnormality.
(b) State the basic technique used to detect this finding.
(c) State how the finding should be recorded/reported.
(d) State the follow-up practical step.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The cells show hypochromia (hypochromic cells), an increased area of pallor >1/3 of the cell, associated with iron deficiency, thalassaemia, anaemia of chronic infection, and sideroblastic anaemia.
(b)
The finding is detected by microscopic examination of the red cell morphology on a well prepared and properly stained peripheral blood film.
(c)
The finding is recorded/reported as hypochromic red cells, together with any accompanying change in cell size (for example microcytosis), and correlated with the red cell indices (MCV, MCH) from the full blood count.
(d)
As a follow-up step, iron studies and/or haemoglobinopathy screening should be pursued, since hypochromic, microcytic anaemia is a recognised indication for haemoglobin testing after iron deficiency has been ruled out.

(a)
• AHG reagents are classified as polyspecific, containing antibodies against both IgG and complement (for example C3d), or monospecific, containing antibodies against only one target such as anti-IgG or anti-C3d.
• Techniques for performing the DAT and IAT are classified as the tube method (traditional, manual, using test tubes and centrifugation), gel card technique (using gel columns pre-filled with AHG, easy to interpret and semi-automated), solid phase (SPRCA, where antibodies bind to antigens on a solid surface, used in automated systems), column agglutination technology (similar to gel cards but may use different media, common in modern analysers), flow cytometry (highly sensitive and quantitative, used in specialised or research settings), and ELISA-based methods (enzyme-linked assays adapted for detecting RBC-bound antibodies, less common in routine labs).
(b)
• Polyspecific AHG is used for broad detection, such as in the DAT, while monospecific AHG is used to determine the specific type of molecule (anti-IgG or anti-C3d) coating the red blood cells once broad sensitisation has been established.
• The tube method is widely used and reliable for routine testing, the gel card technique is used where semi-automated, easy-to-interpret testing is desired, and flow cytometry or ELISA-based methods are selected for specialised, highly sensitive, or research settings rather than routine laboratories.
(c)
• Washing of cells is one of the factors affecting the AHG test, with cells typically washed 3-6 times, and inadequate washing of cells is specifically listed as a source of error causing a false negative AGT.
• The basic reasoning is that washing removes unbound immunoglobulins from the sample so that only antibody or complement actually attached to the red cells remains; if washing is inadequate, residual free serum protein or unbound immunoglobulin remains in the tube.
• Even 10 mL of AHG can be neutralised by a tiny amount of free serum protein, so if inadequate washing leaves residual free protein in the tube, the added AHG reagent becomes neutralised by that free protein before it can bridge and agglutinate the truly sensitised red cells, producing a false negative result rather than the true positive that should have been detected.
• This is why the Coombs control (check) cell step is required to validate every negative AHG result, since a negative reaction with check cells added afterward would reveal that the AHG had already been neutralised by inadequate washing rather than confirming a genuine absence of antibody or complement on the patient's cells.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the classification of AHG reagents into polyspecific and monospecific types, and the classification of AHG test techniques.
(b) State how each type of reagent and technique is applied or selected.
(c) Explain why inadequate washing of cells before adding AHG leads to an invalid (false negative) result.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• The D antigen is a cell surface polypeptide with a molecular weight of approximately 30,000, with an NH2 terminal amino acid sequence, and it is relatively hydrophobic; the D antigen is made up of a mosaic of 4 parts (RhA-D), with an individual who is RhD positive possessing all 4 parts of the mosaic, and an RhD negative individual lacking all 4 mosaic parts.
• The weak D antigen is characterised by a negative reaction with anti-D reagent after incubation at 37°C, but a positive reaction at the albumin phase, and can occur due to a quantitative difference in the D antigen from a reduced number of D antigens on the red cell, or from a weakened form of the R0 gene.
• Partial D, also known as D mosaic or D variant, is instead due to a qualitative difference in the D antigen from an alteration in D-epitopes, where the number of D antigen sites is not reduced but the protein structure is altered.
(b)
An individual with weak D is labelled as D positive when donating blood, and can receive D positive blood without complication; a partial D individual is labelled as D positive but is treated as D negative when receiving blood, and if alloimmunised to D, can produce an anti-D antibody.
(c)
• A weak D individual has all 4 mosaic parts of the D antigen present, just in reduced quantity, so their cells cannot stimulate anti-D formation in a recipient and their own risk of forming anti-D when receiving D positive blood is low, which is why weak D donors are safely labelled D positive.
• A partial D individual is missing part of the D antigen mosaic due to altered protein structure, and if such an individual is transfused with ordinary D positive blood carrying the missing epitope, they can become alloimmunised and produce anti-D, which is the basic reasoning behind treating a partial D recipient as D negative for transfusion purposes.
• This precaution therefore reflects the underlying structural difference between weak D (quantitative reduction of a complete antigen) and partial D (qualitative alteration, missing epitopes), even though both may give a similarly weak reaction on routine typing.
• The D antigen is the most antigenic Rh antigen after the A and B antigens of the ABO system, so this precaution about correctly distinguishing and labelling D variants is important because the introduction of the D antigen into an individual lacking that specific epitope is more likely to stimulate antibody production than other Rhesus antigens.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the structure and identifying variant forms of the Rh D antigen.
(b) State the standard laboratory approach to labelling weak D and partial D individuals.
(c) Explain the basic reasoning behind the precaution of labelling a weak D donor as D positive but a partial D recipient as D negative.

(a) Describe the classification of haemoglobinopathy screening and diagnostic methods.
(b) State how each method is applied or selected during diagnostic work-up.
(c) Explain why relying on cellulose acetate electrophoresis alone can lead to an inaccurate identification of a haemoglobin variant.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The different methods employed in the diagnosis of haemoglobinopathies include complete blood count, peripheral blood smear, solubility/sickling test, haemoglobin electrophoresis, isoelectric focusing, high performance liquid chromatography, and genetic testing.
• To make a diagnosis of thalassaemia trait, the following tests should be done: electrophoresis of haemoglobin on cellulose acetate membrane at alkaline pH, measurement of HbA2, assessment of HbF, checking for HbH inclusion bodies, and assessment of iron status.
(b)
• A review of the peripheral blood film is a good initial screening test, with target cells and sickled erythrocytes pointing to sickle cell disease and microcytic cells pointing to thalassaemia; the sickling test is a simple screening test suitable for a primary health care facility, while the solubility test should be performed on all samples showing the 'S' band on alkaline electrophoresis.
• Cellulose acetate electrophoresis at alkaline pH is used for rapid, easy-handling separation with minimal preparative work, citrate agar electrophoresis at acidic pH is applied when comigrating haemoglobins need resolving or when diagnosing sickle cell disease at birth with high HbF, and isoelectric focusing or HPLC is applied where sharper resolution or quantification of fractions like HbA2 and HbF is required.
(c)
• On cellulose acetate electrophoresis at alkaline pH, certain haemoglobins comigrate, including HbS, HbD and HbG, and also HbA2, HbC, HbE and HbO comigrate, so a band identified as 'HbS' on this method alone could actually be HbD or HbG.
• Haemoglobin fractions in low concentration, like HbA2, HbH and HbBart's, may also be missed on cellulose acetate electrophoresis, and when a small haemoglobin fraction occurs near a broad band, the minor fraction may be missed, especially in neonates when high levels of HbF can cause the presence of either HbA or HbS to be missed.
• This is why the solubility test should be performed on all samples that show the 'S' band on alkaline electrophoresis, especially in an environment where haemoglobins G and D, which comigrate with HbS at this pH, are present, since relying on cellulose acetate electrophoresis alone would risk reporting HbD or HbG as HbS or missing a minor fraction altogether.
• This demonstrates the general principle that no single haemoglobinopathy method should be relied upon in isolation, since comigration and missed minor fractions are basic, recognised limitations of cellulose acetate electrophoresis that a combination of techniques, such as citrate agar electrophoresis, the solubility test, or HPLC, is specifically used to overcome.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the classification of coagulation screening tests (Prothrombin Time and Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time).
(b) State how each test is applied in monitoring anticoagulant therapy.
(c) Explain why a basic error, such as an incorrect blood-to-anticoagulant ratio in the collection tube, leads to an invalid PT or APTT result.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The Prothrombin Time (PT) measures factors VII, X, V, prothrombin and fibrinogen; it is normally 10-14 seconds and is prolonged in deficiencies of the involved clotting factors, in liver disease, warfarin therapy and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC).
• The Activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (APTT) measures factors XII, XI, IX, VIII, X, V, II and fibrinogen; it is normally 30-40 seconds and is prolonged in deficiencies of the involved factors, such as in haemophilia.
(b)
• The PT is used in monitoring oral anticoagulants, and the International Normalized Ratio (INR), calculated from the PT based on the ratio of the patient's PT to a mean normal PT with correction for sensitivity, with a normal range of 0.8-1.2, is derived from it for standardised monitoring.
• The APTT is applied to detect deficiencies among its listed factors, such as in haemophilia, and, given the factors it measures, is the coagulation test used where monitoring is relevant to those intrinsic and common pathway factors, distinguishing its use from the PT/INR's role in monitoring oral anticoagulants such as warfarin.
(c)
• An error such as an incorrect blood-to-anticoagulant ratio, as generally emphasised for anticoagulated blood samples where blood to anticoagulant should be in the right proportion, would alter the concentration of anticoagulant relative to plasma in the specimen used for coagulation testing.
• Since PT and APTT are timed clotting assays that depend on the concentration of clotting factors and calcium being restored under controlled, reproducible conditions, an incorrect ratio of blood to anticoagulant in the collection tube would distort the amount of citrate (or other anticoagulant) available relative to plasma, in turn distorting the measured clotting time.
• A PT or APTT result generated from an incorrectly proportioned sample would therefore not accurately reflect the patient's true clotting factor status, potentially reporting a prolonged or shortened time that does not correspond to the deficiencies of the specific factors each test is designed to detect.
• Because PT is used specifically to monitor oral anticoagulant therapy and APTT to detect factor deficiencies such as haemophilia, an invalid result caused by this basic specimen-handling error could lead to inappropriate clinical decisions, such as incorrect anticoagulant dosing or a missed or falsely suspected factor deficiency.

questions.question:
An adult male patient's full blood count shows a Packed Cell Volume of 30% and hypochromic, microcytic red cells on the film.
(a) Interpret the result.
(b) State how it should be recorded/reported.
(c) State what it indicates about the specimen/patient.
(d) State the action that follows from this reading.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The normal PCV range for an adult male is 40-52%, so a PCV of 30% is reduced, indicating anaemia; the accompanying hypochromic, microcytic morphology further points toward a microcytic hypochromic anaemia.
(b)
The result should be recorded/reported as a reduced PCV of 30% (below the male reference range of 40-52%), together with the hypochromic, microcytic red cell morphology noted on the film.
(c)
This combination indicates a microcytic hypochromic anaemia, which is a category of anaemia that includes iron deficiency anaemia among its differential diagnoses listed alongside vitamin B12/folate anaemia, sideroblastic anaemia, anaemia of chronic disorders, and haemolytic anaemias.
(d)
The action that follows is further work-up of the type of anaemia, since red cell absolute indices such as MCV and MCH, which are decreased in iron deficiency, thalassaemia and lead poisoning, along with iron studies and, where indicated, haemoglobinopathy screening, are the tests used to differentiate between these causes of microcytic hypochromic anaemia.

(a)
• Samples of bone marrow can be obtained by aspiration or biopsy with special needles.
• Aspirates are smeared on slides and stained, while biopsies are processed histologically.
(b)
A differential count of the haemopoietic cells is then done, and the myeloid:erythroid ratio is also determined; typical findings in the bone marrow include myeloblasts 0-4%, promyelocytes 0.5-5%, myelocytes 10-30%, metamyelocytes 10-30%, mature granulocytes 5-25%, lymphoid cells 5-20%, plasma cells 0-3%, erythroid precursors 5-30%, and megakaryocytes present in few to several numbers.
(c)
• The differential count of haemopoietic cells describes the relative proportions of the different cell lines and their maturation stages present in the marrow, which is needed to detect abnormal proportions, for example an excess of blasts.
• The myeloid:erythroid ratio specifically compares the granulocytic (myeloid) series against the red cell precursor (erythroid) series, which is a distinct piece of information from the differential count of individual cell types, since it summarises the balance between the two major proliferating lineages in the marrow.
• The basic reasoning behind needing both pieces of information is that a differential count alone could show individual cell percentages within normal-looking ranges while still reflecting an abnormal overall balance between the myeloid and erythroid lineages, or vice versa, so the ratio adds diagnostic information the percentage breakdown alone does not fully capture.
• This also explains why aspirate smears (for cytological, cell-by-cell differential counting) and biopsy sections (for histological, architectural assessment) are processed differently and are often obtained together, since each specimen type answers a different diagnostic question about the marrow.
• Relying on only one of the two specimen types or only one of the two pieces of numerical information (differential count or myeloid:erythroid ratio) could therefore result in an incomplete or inaccurate assessment of bone marrow status.
questions.question:
(a) Describe how a bone marrow specimen is obtained and processed for aspirate versus biopsy.
(b) State the standard analysis performed once the specimen is prepared.
(c) Explain the basic reasoning behind needing both a differential count and the myeloid:erythroid ratio from the specimen.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Whole blood impedance aggregometry measures platelet aggregation in whole blood by detecting changes in electrical impedance as platelets adhere to electrodes after stimulation by an agonist.
• Whole blood is diluted with saline and placed into a cuvette containing two electrodes; an agonist is added to induce platelet aggregation, and as platelets aggregate on the electrodes, electrical impedance increases, with the change in impedance recorded over time as an aggregation curve.
(b)
The advantage is that it can be performed on whole blood without the need for centrifugation and is more physiological since it measures aggregation in the presence of red cells and other blood components; the limitation is that it is less sensitive than LTA for detecting certain types of platelet dysfunction and results can be affected by haematocrit levels or other factors present in whole blood.
(c)
• Whole blood impedance aggregometry uses whole blood diluted with saline in a cuvette with two electrodes, and records aggregation as a rise in electrical impedance as platelets adhere to the electrodes after an agonist is added.
• The PFA-100 instead measures platelet function under high shear conditions by simulating vascular injury through a membrane coated with collagen and epinephrine or ADP.
• In the PFA-100, whole blood is passed through a small aperture within the coated membrane under high shear stress, and as platelets adhere and aggregate at the aperture they eventually occlude it, stopping blood flow, with the time taken for occlusion (closure time) reflecting platelet function.
• The PFA-100 is a simple and rapid test that mimics physiological high shear stress conditions found in small arteries and capillaries and is useful for screening von Willebrand disease or monitoring aspirin therapy, whereas whole blood impedance aggregometry measures aggregation directly on electrodes rather than a closure time.
• The PFA-100 has limited sensitivity for detecting all types of platelet dysfunction and cannot differentiate between different causes of abnormal closure times without further testing, a limitation it shares in kind, though not in mechanism, with whole blood impedance aggregometry's reduced sensitivity relative to LTA.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the principle and procedure of whole blood impedance aggregometry.
(b) State the advantage and limitation of this technique.
(c) Distinguish whole blood impedance aggregometry from the Platelet Function Analyzer (PFA-100).

An EDTA-anticoagulated blood sample is submitted with a request to investigate possible autoimmune haemolytic anaemia by demonstrating antibody or complement on the patient's own red cells.
(a) Identify the specimen and the appropriate test/reagent.
(b) State the underlying principle.
(c) State the correct step-by-step procedure.
(d) State the expected result and its interpretation.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The specimen is EDTA-anticoagulated blood, and the appropriate test is the Direct Antiglobulin Test (DAT), using antihuman globulin (AHG) reagent as the key reagent, with 10 × 75 mm test tubes/rack, a timer and a centrifuge as further materials.
(b)
The principle is that red blood cells coated with complement or IgG antibodies in vivo do not agglutinate directly when centrifuged, and an additional antibody (AHG) that reacts with the Fc portion of the IgG or with the C3b/C3d component of complement must be added to form a bridge between the antibodies coating the red cells, causing visible agglutination.
(c)
• Tubes are labelled with sample and control labels.
• The sample and control are resuspended, and 25 µl of RBC sample and control are applied to the tubes, washed twice with 1 ml of 0.9% normal saline, centrifuging at 1000g for 1 minute and decanting the supernatant each time.
• 50 µl of polyspecific AHG reagent is then added, mixed and centrifuged for 15 seconds at 500g, and the tube is resuspended and examined macroscopically for agglutination, with results graded and recorded.
(d)
A positive DAT (agglutination) indicates that antibodies or complement proteins are attached to the surface of the red blood cells, which can suggest conditions such as autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, HDFN, or a reaction to a blood transfusion; a negative DAT means there are no antibodies or complement proteins attached to the red blood cells, and should be confirmed valid using Coombs control (check) cells.

questions.question:
A blood film from a patient with marked splenomegaly shows red cells shaped like tear drops.
(a) Identify the abnormal cell.
(b) State the basic technique used to detect this finding.
(c) State how the finding should be recorded/reported.
(d) State the follow-up practical step.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The cells are tear drop cells, associated with myelofibrosis and extramedullary erythropoiesis.
(b)
The finding is detected by microscopic examination of a well prepared and properly stained peripheral blood film.
(c)
The finding is recorded/reported as the presence of tear drop poikilocytes, correlated with the patient's clinical details.
(d)
As a follow-up step, because tear drop cells are associated with myelofibrosis and extramedullary erythropoiesis, bone marrow examination (aspiration and/or biopsy, with a differential count and myeloid:erythroid ratio) may be indicated to further investigate the marrow.

questions.question:
Patient plasma and a segment of red cells from a donor unit are submitted for a pre-transfusion crossmatch.
(a) Identify the specimen/reagent combination and the technique used.
(b) State the underlying principle.
(c) State the correct step-by-step procedure.
(d) State the expected result and its interpretation.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The specimen/reagent combination is patient plasma plus cells from the unit to be transfused, and the technique used is the indirect antiglobulin technique (IAT), since a crossmatch is tested by IAT.
(b)
The principle is that a crossmatch looks to detect both an unknown antibody (in the patient's plasma) against an unknown antigen (on the donor cells), mixing cells and serum, incubating, washing, adding AHG and reading, so that any antibody present that would sensitise the donor cells is revealed by subsequent agglutination.
(c)
Cells and serum (patient plasma and donor cell suspension) are mixed and incubated; the cells are washed to remove unbound antibody, AHG is added, the tube is centrifuged, and the result is read for agglutination, with positive and negative controls run alongside.
(d)
Units showing no reaction (no agglutination) are looked to be used for the transfusion, indicating compatibility, while a positive reaction (agglutination) indicates incompatibility and that unit should not be used for that patient.

(a)
• A Coulter counter, also known as an automated haematology analyser, is an apparatus for counting, sizing and differentiating particles suspended in an electrolyte, remaining the dominant technology used by clinical haematology analysers.
• The apparatus works on the Coulter principle of electrical impedance: an electrically conductive diluent containing cells is passed through a narrow channel, and as each cell passes through an aperture, it causes a momentary drop in the electrical current, since cells are non-conductive, with the number of particles counted by measuring the number of pulses and the pulse magnitude related to particle size.
(b)
The apparatus is used as the standard method for performing a full blood count (complete blood count), which is usually the first test requested by physicians to assess general patient health and can be used to detect anaemia, infection, haematological malignancy, and to monitor cancer patients undergoing chemotherapy.
(c)
• A problem associated with impedance counting is cell coincidence, where more than one cell passes through the counting aperture at a time, causing two cells to be counted as one voltage pulse, which could result in falsely low counts.
• Hydrodynamic focusing is applied in modern analysers to minimise this problem, by causing a thin, slow-moving stream of cells to flow in a single file through the sensing aperture, so that cells pass through one at a time rather than clumped together.
• The basic reasoning behind this precaution is that if multiple cells pass through the aperture simultaneously and are only registered as one pulse, the reported cell count will be lower than the true count, undermining the accuracy of the full blood count.
• This reasoning also explains why cellular clumping, for example platelet aggregates, is listed as a limitation that results in inaccurate counts by automated haematology analysers, since clumped cells behave similarly to coincident cells passing through the aperture.
• Ensuring cells are properly separated and flow in single file through the aperture is therefore a basic precaution that protects the accuracy of every parameter the analyser reports from the same aperture-based count.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the apparatus and working principle of the Coulter/electronic particle counter used for automated blood cell counting.
(b) State the standard setting in which this apparatus is used in the laboratory.
(c) Explain the basic reasoning behind hydrodynamic focusing as a precaution built into the apparatus.

questions.answerText:
(a)
The specimen/reagent is check cells, that is, red blood cells pre-coated with antibody (IgG-coated red cells), used as a quality control measure to ensure the validity of the AHG reagent and technique.
(b)
The principle is that check cells, being already coated with antibody, should agglutinate when mixed with AHG reagent, demonstrating the reagent's ability to detect antibody-coated red cells; a negative reaction with check cells suggests a technical error or reagent issue.
(c)
25 µl of IgG-coated RBCs (check cells) are added to the tube that tested negative on AHG testing, and the tube is centrifuged for 15 seconds at 500g and examined for macroscopic agglutination, with the result graded and recorded.
(d)
The expected result is agglutination of the check cells with the AHG reagent, confirming that the AHG was present, active, and correctly added, and thus validating the preceding negative DAT/IAT result as a true negative; failure of the check cells to agglutinate indicates a technical error, such as AHG not added or inadequate, expired reagent, or neutralisation of the AHG by insufficiently washed free antibody.
questions.question:
Washed red cells pre-coated with a known antibody (check cells) are submitted alongside a negative DAT/IAT tube for validation.
(a) Identify the specimen/reagent and the purpose of the test.
(b) State the underlying principle.
(c) State the correct procedure.
(d) State the expected result and its interpretation.

A patient recovering from an episode of acute blood loss has a reticulocyte count of 6%.
(a) Interpret the result.
(b) State how it should be recorded/reported.
(c) State what it indicates about the marrow response.
(d) State the action that follows from this reading.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The normal reticulocyte count is 0.5-2%, so a reticulocyte count of 6% is increased.
(b)
The result should be recorded/reported as an increased reticulocyte count (6%, above the 0.5-2% reference range).
(c)
The reticulocyte count indicates active bone marrow as a response to increased peripheral destruction of red cells, and an increased count is seen in recovery after acute blood loss, among other conditions such as sickle cell haemolytic crisis, haemolytic anaemia, G6PD deficiency and response to haematinic treatment; it is specifically stated to not be increased in anaemia due to impaired red cell production.
(d)
The action that follows is recognising this as an appropriate, active bone marrow response to the acute blood loss, which is consistent with expected recovery, distinguishing it from anaemias in which the reticulocyte count remains normal or low due to impaired red cell production.

questions.question:
A quantitative HbA2 estimation on a patient with mild, unexplained microcytic red cell indices returns a value of 5.2%.
(a) Interpret the result.
(b) State how it should be recorded/reported.
(c) State what it indicates.
(d) State the action that follows from this reading.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Values below 3.3% are usually normal for HbA2, and values over 3.5% usually indicate beta thalassaemia trait, so an HbA2 of 5.2% is a raised value, being clearly above the 3.5% threshold.
(b)
The result should be recorded/reported as a raised HbA2 of 5.2%, described as the hallmark of the classic beta thalassaemia trait; any HbA2 variant present should be eluted with the HbA2 in reporting.
(c)
This raised HbA2, together with the mild, unexplained microcytic indices, indicates beta thalassaemia trait, since beta thalassaemia trait is associated with mild or no anaemia but with reduced MCV and MCH values and an elevated HbA2 level.
(d)
The action that follows is to also assess the patient's iron status, since concomitant iron deficiency may cause a falsely low HbA2 that could mask beta thalassaemia trait, so the HbA2 should be rechecked after iron therapy if iron deficiency is found; a value above 7% would instead suggest an analytical error or the presence of another haemoglobin that is not HbA2, which is not the case here.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the principle and purpose of internal and external quality control (QC) in serology.
(b) Explain why the two types of QC are described as complementary.
(c) Distinguish internal QC from external QC.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Quality control refers to the measures that must be included during each assay to verify that the test is working correctly; it is the process or system for monitoring the quality of laboratory testing and the accuracy and precision of results, and involves routinely collecting and analysing data from every test run or procedure to allow for immediate corrective action.
• QC ensures accuracy, reliability and safety in serologic testing and is vital for transfusion compatibility and patient outcomes, forming part of a broader quality management system in laboratories.
(b)
Internal QC monitors the accuracy and reproducibility of test results through controls and helps make immediate decisions, while external QC compares one's laboratory results to other laboratories and serves to evaluate internal QC, maintaining long-term accuracy and ensuring the laboratory performs to external standards, so together they provide comprehensive quality assurance.
(c)
• Internal QC (intra-laboratory QC) is an internal assessment of analytical quality by regular measurement of known or assigned value samples, with control samples analysed daily using multilevel controls, that is, low, normal and high levels, or normal and abnormal samples.
• External QC (inter-laboratory QC), also called external quality assessment scheme (EQAS) or proficiency test, is based on periodic analysis of control samples by an outside agency to compare the accuracy levels of different laboratories.
• In external QC, laboratories using the same reagents (peer group) are compared and performance is reported in terms of the deviation index or Z score, and EQAS is a basic laboratory certification and accreditation requirement.
• Quality control samples obtained from the manufacturer are usually manipulated to lengthen shelf life, so direct comparison with patient results is not possible, and EQAS material should not be used for calibration purposes, which applies to both internal and external QC materials.
• Examples of control materials common to both include ABO and RhD control cells, antibody screening and identification panels, and Coombs control (check) cells, all of which must be stable, traceable and appropriate for the test system.

(a)
• Potentiators used in red cell serology include low-ionic strength solution (LISS), bovine serum albumin (BSA), polyethylene glycol (PEG), and proteolytic enzymes such as papain, ficin and bromelin.
• Potentiators are used in serological procedures, such as antibody screening, to enhance the antigen-antibody reaction, by helping to overcome problems such as the proximity of red cells to each other, which otherwise limits the ability of an antibody, especially IgG, to bridge and cause agglutination.
(b)
Potentiators are used within the indirect antiglobulin technique and other antibody detection and screening procedures; for example, incubation with LISS is used for 20 minutes at 37°C, compared with 45 minutes at 37°C with 'ordinary' phosphate-buffered saline, showing that the choice of potentiator affects the standard incubation time used.
(c)
• Proteolytic enzymes such as papain and bromelain strip a lot of the charged molecules from the red cell surface and may also uncover some antigens, such as Rh antigens, but destroy others, such as M, N, S and Duffy antigens.
• The basic reasoning behind selecting a potentiator based on the antibody being investigated is that an enzyme technique enhances Rh antibody detection but would destroy the very antigens (M, N, S, Fya and Fyb) needed to detect antibodies against those systems, so an enzyme potentiator is unsuitable if those antibodies are suspected.
• LISS and other non-enzymatic potentiators such as BSA and PEG are chosen instead when the antigens of interest would be destroyed by proteolytic enzymes, or when a shorter incubation time is desired, as with LISS reducing the IAT incubation time compared with ordinary buffered saline.
• This reasoning matches the broader principle that antibody detection technique choice (saline, enzyme or IAT) is guided by the class of antibody and the antigen system suspected, since enzymes enhance Kidd, Rh, Lewis, I and P antibody detection but destroy Fya, Fyb, M, N and S antigens.
• Selecting the wrong potentiator for the antibody or antigen system under investigation could therefore either fail to enhance a weak reaction or actively destroy the antigen needed for detection, leading to a missed or false negative antibody result.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the composition and function of potentiators used in serological antigen-antibody reactions.
(b) State the standard setting in which potentiators are used.
(c) Explain the basic reasoning behind selecting a potentiator based on the antibody being investigated.

(a) Describe the principle and procedure of the elution technique used in antibody investigation.
(b) Explain why the parameter that is changed during elution must be returned to what it was.
(c) Distinguish elution from adsorption.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Elution is a technique for removing antibodies from the cells, either to find out what that antibody is, as in investigating transfusion reactions or 'autoimmune' cases, or to free up antigen sites on those cells so that the cells can be used to adsorb antibodies out of the serum or to phenotype the cells.
• The cells are washed six times, retaining the last wash; a parameter such as temperature or pH is then changed to release the bound antibody, the supernatant is removed for testing, and the cells are retained for testing.
(b)
It is important to return the changed parameter to what it was so that the eluted cells, once returned to normal conditions, can be reliably used for further testing such as adsorption or phenotyping without the altered temperature or pH affecting the outcome of that subsequent test.
(c)
• Elution removes antibodies already bound to red cells, releasing them into a supernatant for testing so that the identity of the antibody can be determined, or so that the antigen sites on the cells are freed up for further use.
• Adsorption is instead used to find out if any alloantibodies are lurking underneath an autoantibody, and can be autologous, using methods such as ZZAP, chloroquine or citric acid, or allogeneic, using other individuals' cells.
• Elution and adsorption are used together in complicated phenotyping and subgroup work, in suspected haemolytic transfusion reactions, and in autoimmune conditions where autoantibodies already bound to cells negate most of the routine testing.
• In elution, the antibody is removed from the patient's own cells for identification, whereas in adsorption, the patient's serum (containing the antibody) is exposed to cells so that the antibody is removed from the serum, leaving any other antibodies present for detection.
• The volume of serum and cells available influences the choice between autologous and allogeneic adsorption, while elution technique choice is guided by which parameter change (temperature or pH) will effectively release the bound antibody without destroying it.

questions.question:
A platelet count is reported as 15 ×10⁹/L on a patient's full blood count.
(a) Interpret the result.
(b) State how it should be recorded/reported.
(c) State what it indicates.
(d) State the action that follows from this reading.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The normal platelet count in Blacks is 100-300 ×10⁹/L; a count of 15 ×10⁹/L falls below the threshold of <20 ×10⁹/L, which defines severe thrombocytopenia.
(b)
The result should be recorded/reported as severe thrombocytopenia, with the platelet count of 15 ×10⁹/L stated against the reference range and the severity grading (mild 50-99, moderate 20-49, severe <20 ×10⁹/L).
(c)
This severely reduced count indicates a significant reduction in platelets, which may result from failure of platelet production (for example aplastic anaemia, myelofibrosis, multiple myeloma, myelodysplastic syndromes, leukaemia, radiology, marrow infiltration) or increased consumption of platelets (for example autoimmune causes, DIC, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, drug-induced (heparin), infections such as HIV or malaria, or dilutional loss from massive transfusion).
(d)
The action that follows is urgent clinical correlation and further investigation to distinguish between a production failure and an increased consumption cause, given the severity of the thrombocytopenia.

(a)
• Isoelectric focusing is a high resolution method for separating proteins according to their isoelectric points, that is, points at which the net charge is zero.
• Separation of haemoglobins by isoelectric focusing is similar to that obtained by electrophoresis on cellulose acetate, except that the bands are sharper and the resolution of some haemoglobins is better.
(b)
Because separation is achieved according to the precise isoelectric point of each haemoglobin variant rather than by general charge-based migration, isoelectric focusing gives sharper bands and better resolution, which helps in resolving variants that would otherwise comigrate and be missed.
(c)
• Cellulose acetate electrophoresis at alkaline pH separates haemoglobins according to their net electrical charge as they migrate toward the anode in an electric field, using cellulose acetate paper as the support medium.
• Isoelectric focusing separates haemoglobins according to their isoelectric point, the point of zero net charge, producing sharper bands and better resolution of some haemoglobins than cellulose acetate electrophoresis, even though the general separation pattern is similar.
• Both methods are used for haemoglobin variant identification, but isoelectric focusing is applied where finer resolution between closely related bands is required, since minor fractions that may be missed on cellulose acetate electrophoresis can be better resolved by this method.
• The two methods therefore complement each other in the overall approach to haemoglobinopathy diagnosis, alongside other screening tests such as the sickling test, solubility test and HPLC.
• This reflects the general principle in haemoglobinopathy diagnosis that no single method should be relied upon as a stand-alone test for identification of haemoglobin variants.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the principle and advantage of isoelectric focusing as a haemoglobin separation technique.
(b) Explain why it is used to resolve variants that comigrate on standard electrophoresis.
(c) Distinguish isoelectric focusing from cellulose acetate electrophoresis.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Electrical impedance classifies red and white cells based on size, using an electrically conductive diluent containing cells passed through a narrow channel, with each cell causing a momentary drop in current as it passes through an aperture.
• Flow cytometry provides information from forward light scatter, side scatter and side fluorescence to generate a white cell differential, nucleated red blood cell, reticulocyte and platelet information, while laser scatter occurs when a particle deflects laser light, the extent depending on the physical properties of the particle.
(b)
• The classical impedance method is used for red blood cell and platelet enumeration, in which cells passing through the aperture change the resistance and, in constant current, the voltage change recorded accords with the volume of the cell.
• For white blood cell analysis, chemical dye, flow cytometry and laser scatter are applied instead, since flow cytometry is considered the most effective method of differentiating cell types and can generate detailed flags and messages, for example indicating blasts, immature granulocytes, microcytosis and macrocytosis.
(c)
• It is specifically stated as a limitation that cellular clumping, for example platelet aggregates, results in inaccurate counts by automated haematology analysers.
• The basic reasoning is that impedance and related particle-counting methods rely on each individual cell passing through the sensing aperture separately, so that each cell generates one discrete pulse or scatter signal corresponding to its own size; this is the same underlying reasoning behind the cell coincidence problem and why hydrodynamic focusing is used to pass cells through the aperture in single file.
• When cells are clumped together, for example as platelet aggregates, the analyser may register the clump as a single, larger particle, or as fewer discrete pulses than the true number of individual cells present, resulting in an inaccurate, typically falsely low, count for the affected cell type.
• This is why, despite the advent of automated blood cell analysers, the peripheral blood film remains important, since microscopic examination allows the medical laboratory scientist to directly observe and recognise clumping or other abnormalities such as cryoglobulin, cold agglutinins or lipids, which several situations are stated to cause abnormal RBC counts, and which automated counting alone cannot reliably flag or correct for.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the classification of automated blood cell counting principles (electrical impedance, flow cytometry, laser scatter).
(b) State how each principle is applied or selected for a particular parameter of the full blood count.
(c) Explain why cellular clumping (for example platelet aggregates) is a basic error source that leads to an inaccurate automated count.

(a) Describe the principle and apparatus used for haemoglobin estimation in an automated haematology analyser.
(b) State the wavelength at which the resulting complex is measured.
(c) Distinguish this photometric estimation from red blood cell/platelet enumeration by the same analyser.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• A special photometer called a haemoglobinometer measures the amount of haemoglobin; the LH diluent breaks down red blood cells, binds to haemoglobin and converts it to a complex that is measurable.
• The apparatus is the haemoglobinometer (a special photometer) within the automated haematology analyser.
(b)
The resulting haemoglobin complex is measured at 525 nm.
(c)
• Haemoglobin estimation uses a photometer (haemoglobinometer) to measure a coloured complex formed when the LH diluent breaks down red cells and binds to the released haemoglobin, with the amount of light absorbed at 525 nm proportional to the haemoglobin concentration.
• Red blood cell and platelet enumeration instead uses the classical electrical impedance method, in which cells pass through an aperture and cause a change in resistance, and in constant current the voltage change recorded accords with the volume of the cell.
• For white cell analysis, the analyser applies chemical dye, flow cytometry and laser scatter in addition to these methods, showing that a single automated analyser combines several distinct physical principles (photometry, electrical impedance, and light scatter/flow cytometry) to generate the different parameters of a full blood count.
• This combination of methods within one instrument is what allows modern analysers to process hundreds of samples an hour while determining haemoglobin and haematocrit levels alongside red cell, white cell and platelet counts.
• Despite this automation, a peripheral blood film remains an important complementary step, since it exposes the morphology of peripheral blood cells in a way that automated counts alone cannot capture.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the identifying feature and formation of a reticulocyte.
(b) State the standard clinical/laboratory setting in which the reticulocyte count is used.
(c) Explain the basic reasoning behind interpreting an increased reticulocyte count differently from a normal or low count in an anaemic patient.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Reticulocytes are immature red cells at the penultimate stage of maturation; on a blood film they are identified as polychromasia, showing blue-grey staining of immature red cells, and being larger than a normal red blood cell.
• A normal reticulocyte count is 0.5 to 2%, and the reticulocyte count indicates active bone marrow response to increased peripheral destruction of red cells.
(b)
The reticulocyte count is used in the standard setting of assessing bone marrow response in anaemia, for example following post-haemorrhage, haemolysis, or as a response to treatment for anaemia; increased reticulocyte counts are seen in sickle cell haemolytic crisis, haemolytic anaemia, G6PD deficiency, recovery after acute blood loss, and response to haematinic treatment for folic acid, vitamin B12 and iron deficiencies.
(c)
• An increased reticulocyte count indicates an active bone marrow that is appropriately responding to increased peripheral destruction or loss of red cells, as seen in haemolytic conditions or in recovery after treatment.
• The reticulocyte count is specifically stated as not increased in anaemia due to impaired red cell production, so the basic reasoning behind interpreting the count is that a raised reticulocyte count in an anaemic patient points toward a peripheral (destructive or haemorrhagic) cause, while a normal or low count in the same anaemic patient points toward a production (marrow) problem.
• This distinction guides the direction of further investigation, since the same finding of anaemia can arise from opposite underlying mechanisms (increased loss/destruction versus reduced production), and the reticulocyte count is the parameter that differentiates between them.
• Polychromasia on the blood film corresponds to this same reticulocyte response, since polychromatic (blue-grey staining) red cells seen on a stained film are the morphological correlate of the reticulocytes being counted, linking the film finding to the numerical reticulocyte result.
• Correctly recognising and interpreting this feature therefore prevents a laboratory scientist from treating all anaemias as equivalent, since the presence or absence of an appropriate reticulocyte response fundamentally changes the differential diagnosis being considered.

(a)
The specimen is an EDTA blood sample of only 5 µl taken in 1.0 ml of lysis buffer, and the appropriate technique is cation exchange High Performance Liquid Chromatography (HPLC).
(b)
The principle is that HPLC separates haemoglobin fractions because they have different interaction with the stationary phase, based on the time required for gradient elution of the different haemoglobin fractions (the retention time) and the shape of the peak, with identification of an unknown haemoglobin achieved through comparison with known haemoglobin retention times.
(c)
The sample is injected into the analysis stream and separated by the cation exchange cartridge using a phosphate ion gradient generated by mixing two buffers of different ionic strengths to elute the different haemoglobins; a dual wavelength filter photometer monitors the eluent from the cartridge as it passes through the photometer cell, and the detector signal data is reduced by the integrator and processed.
(d)
The expected result is a chromatogram of time versus absorbance, with the different haemoglobin peaks identified in defined windows and their retention time, relative percentage and area printed out; because about thirty different variants have been reported eluting in the HbS window, any HbS-window peak should be cross-checked with another technique such as the solubility test.
questions.question:
A 5 µl EDTA blood sample taken into 1.0 ml of lysis buffer is submitted for haemoglobin variant analysis.
(a) Identify the specimen and the technique.
(b) State the underlying principle.
(c) State the correct procedure.
(d) State the expected result.

One drop of a patient's blood is submitted for HbS screening by mixing with a solution of potassium dihydrogen phosphate, dipotassium hydrogen phosphate and sodium metabisulphite.
(a) Identify the specimen/reagent and the technique.
(b) State the underlying principle.
(c) State the correct procedure.
(d) State the expected result.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The specimen is one drop of the patient's blood, the reagent is a solution prepared using potassium dihydrogen phosphate, dipotassium hydrogen phosphate and sodium metabisulphite, and the technique is the solubility test.
(b)
The principle is that HbS is less soluble than HbA in the deoxygenated state.
(c)
One drop of the patient's blood is mixed with the prepared solution, and the mixture is spun in a centrifuge; control blood samples with HbA, HbAS and HbS should be tested at the same time.
(d)
The expected result is that HbS, if present, precipitates as a red opaque band on the surface of the test solution, while other haemoglobins remain in solution; this test should be performed on all samples that show the 'S' band on alkaline electrophoresis, especially where haemoglobins G and D, which comigrate with HbS on alkaline electrophoresis, are present.

(a)
• The LH diluent is the reagent used in the haemoglobin estimation channel of the automated haematology analyser.
• The LH diluent breaks down red blood cells, binds to the released haemoglobin, and converts it to a complex that is measurable, since free haemoglobin in solution is what a photometer can then quantify.
(b)
A special photometer called a haemoglobinometer, within the automated haematology analyser, is the standard setting in which the LH diluent and the resulting complex are used to measure the amount of haemoglobin in a blood sample as part of the full blood count.
(c)
• The resulting haemoglobin complex formed after the LH diluent breaks down the red cells and binds the haemoglobin is measured at 525 nm.
• The basic reasoning behind reading the complex at a fixed, specific wavelength is that the amount of light absorbed by the complex at that wavelength is proportional to the concentration of haemoglobin present, allowing the photometer to convert an absorbance reading into a haemoglobin concentration.
• Using a fixed wavelength for every sample ensures that readings are comparable and reproducible across samples and over time, which is essential since haemoglobin is a core parameter used in diagnosing anaemia and polycythaemia and in monitoring patients.
• Any deviation from the correct wavelength or an improperly prepared complex would directly distort the haemoglobin value reported, which is why the LH diluent and photometer are treated as a validated, fixed part of the analyser's measurement system rather than a variable step.
• This basic reasoning, that a fixed measurable wavelength gives a proportional and reproducible reading, underlies photometric estimation generally within the automated haematology analyser, alongside the separate electrical impedance and flow cytometry/laser scatter methods used for cell counting and differentiation.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the composition and mechanism of action of the LH diluent used in the haemoglobin channel of an automated haematology analyser.
(b) State the standard setting in which this reagent is used.
(c) Explain the basic reasoning behind measuring the resulting complex at a fixed wavelength (525 nm).

questions.answerText:
(a)
A positive antibody screen indicates the presence of antibodies in the maternal serum; interpretation of the red cell antibody screen states that a positive screen indicates presence of antibodies, which is important for identifying the risk of haemolytic disease of the foetus and newborn (HDFN) and guiding management.
(b)
The result should be recorded/reported as a positive red cell antibody screen, pending identification of the specific antibody involved.
(c)
A positive screen means maternal antibodies may affect the foetus; management of a positive screen involves identifying the specific antibody (for example anti-D or anti-K), since these can cause HDFN.
(d)
The action that follows is serial antibody titres, foetal monitoring (middle cerebral artery Doppler), and possible intrauterine transfusion, as stated for management of a positive red cell antibody screen; monitoring and management of pregnancies at risk should also be instituted.
questions.question:
An antenatal red cell antibody screen performed at booking in a Rh-negative woman returns positive.
(a) Interpret the result.
(b) State how it should be recorded/reported.
(c) State what it indicates.
(d) State the action that follows from this reading.

questions.answerText:
(a)
The finding is consistent with Plasmodium, the cause of malaria, of which there are 4 species that infect man: P. falciparum, P. vivax, P. ovale and P. malariae.
(b)
The finding is detected using thick and thin blood films: a drop of blood is spread in a circular motion for the thick film and as a smear for the thin film, both air dried, with the thin film fixed in methyl alcohol before Giemsa staining and the thick film stained with Giemsa without prior fixation, in malaria the thick film is used to screen a large amount of blood (useful in light infection) and can be stained later.
(c)
The finding is recorded/reported as parasitised red blood cells and parasites seen, with species identification made from the thin film.
(d)
As a follow-up practical step, the thin film is examined for definite species identification of the parasite, since the thin film shows parasitised red blood cells and parasites for definite species identification, while the thick film is used mainly to screen a large amount of blood.
questions.question:
A thick blood film stained with Giemsa from a febrile patient shows parasitised red blood cells with ring forms, and a corresponding thin film is also prepared.
(a) Identify the likely organism/finding.
(b) State the basic technique used to detect it.
(c) State how the finding should be recorded/reported.
(d) State the follow-up practical step.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• The core antenatal serologic investigations are Blood Group and Rhesus (Rh) status, Red Cell Antibody Screen, Rubella IgG Antibody, Hepatitis B Surface Antigen (HBsAg), Hepatitis C Antibody, HIV Antigen/Antibody Combo Test, and Syphilis Serology.
• These tests are typically performed at the booking appointment (6-16 weeks of gestation), and repeated at 28 weeks for Rh-negative individuals or if clinically indicated.
(b)
• At booking, Blood Group and Rh status is determined to identify Rh-negative mothers at risk of Rh incompatibility, the Red Cell Antibody Screen is performed to detect maternal antibodies that may affect the foetus, and the remaining infection screens (rubella, HBsAg, hepatitis C antibody, HIV combo test, syphilis serology) are performed at the first prenatal visit.
• At 28 weeks, the Red Cell Antibody Screen is specifically repeated for Rh-negative individuals or if clinically indicated, and anti-D immunoglobulin is administered to Rh-negative mothers at 28 weeks, and again within 72 hours postpartum if the baby is Rh-positive.
(c)
• In Case Study 1 (Rh Incompatibility), the booking bloods showed blood group O Rh-negative with a negative antibody screen; management included anti-D immunoglobulin at 28 weeks and repeating the antibody screen at 36 weeks, with the baby born Rh-positive receiving anti-D given within 72 hours postpartum, resulting in no sensitisation and a healthy baby.
• This case is explicitly used to show that early identification and prophylaxis, which depends on repeating antibody screening in a Rh-negative mother rather than relying on the booking result alone, prevented alloimmunisation and future complications.
• A positive red cell antibody screen requires identification of the specific antibody (for example anti-D or anti-K), with management including serial antibody titres and foetal monitoring (middle cerebral artery Doppler), and possible intrauterine transfusion, so if the repeat screen at 28 weeks is omitted, a newly developed antibody (sensitisation that had not yet occurred, or was not yet detectable, at booking) could go undetected.
