• Because the entire purpose of repeating the screen specifically in Rh-negative individuals is to catch alloimmunisation that may develop over the course of pregnancy or after invasive procedures, omitting this repeat test is a basic error that removes the safeguard the protocol is designed to provide, leading to an inaccurate (falsely reassuring) assessment of the mother's true HDFN risk for the remainder of the pregnancy.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the classification of core antenatal serologic investigations and their timing.
(b) State how each investigation is applied or selected at booking versus at 28 weeks.
(c) Explain why omitting the repeat antibody screen at 28 weeks in a Rh-negative mother is a basic error that can lead to an inaccurate assessment of HDFN risk.

A patient's serum and reagent cells (A cell, B cell, O cell) are submitted in tubes for reverse ABO grouping using a direct mix-and-read technique.
(a) Identify the specimen/reagent and the technique.
(b) State the underlying principle.
(c) State the correct procedure.
(d) State the expected result.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The specimen is the patient's serum, the reagents are known A cell, B cell and O cell suspensions, and the technique is the saline technique, used for serum grouping in the tube method.
(b)
The principle of the saline technique is direct agglutination, mainly detecting IgM antibodies, since naturally occurring anti-A and anti-B are predominantly IgM and agglutinate cells suspended in saline directly.
(c)
Tubes are arranged and labelled 1-4 (A cell, B cell, O cell, and patient cell as its own control), equal volumes of cell and serum are added to each tube, mixed, and, for the immune anti-A and anti-B component, incubated at 37°C for 1 hour, checking for haemolysis and agglutination.
(d)
The expected result is agglutination with the reagent cells that carry the antigen corresponding to the antibody present in the patient's serum (for example, a group A patient's serum agglutinates B cells but not A cells), and this pattern is read together with the cell grouping result to assign the final ABO group.

questions.question:
A white cell differential count shows an increased neutrophil percentage and absolute count in a patient with a localised pyogenic infection.
(a) Interpret the result.
(b) State how it should be recorded/reported.
(c) State what it indicates.
(d) State the action that follows from this reading.
questions.answerText:
(a)
An increased neutrophil count is neutrophilia; neutrophilia is associated with bacterial infections (pyogenic, localised or generalised), inflammation/tissue necrosis, metabolic disorders, neoplasm, asplenia, drugs (for example corticosteroid therapy, lithium), chronic myeloid leukaemia/myeloproliferative disease, and acute haemorrhage or haemolysis.
(b)
The result should be recorded/reported as neutrophilia, that is, an increased neutrophil percentage and/or absolute count above the adult reference range.
(c)
In a patient with a localised pyogenic infection, this indicates a neutrophilic response consistent with bacterial infection, one of the listed causes of neutrophilia.
(d)
The action that follows is correlating the finding with the clinical picture and, since a wide range of other causes (inflammation, neoplasm, myeloproliferative disease, drugs) also produce neutrophilia, considering these alternative causes if the clinical picture is not fully explained by the localised infection alone.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the principle and procedure of light transmission aggregometry (LTA).
(b) Explain why LTA is considered the gold standard for measuring platelet aggregation.
(c) Distinguish LTA from whole blood impedance aggregometry.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• LTA is based on the principle that when platelets aggregate in response to an agonist, the turbidity (cloudiness) of platelet-rich plasma (PRP) decreases, allowing more light to pass through the sample.
• A blood sample is centrifuged to obtain PRP, which is placed in a cuvette inside an aggregometer; a baseline measurement of light transmission is taken, an agonist such as ADP or collagen is added to induce aggregation, and as platelets aggregate the PRP becomes clearer, increasing light transmission.
• The change in light transmission is recorded over time as an aggregation curve.
(b)
LTA has high sensitivity and specificity for detecting platelet function abnormalities and can use multiple agonists to assess different pathways of platelet activation, which is why it is considered the gold standard, even though it requires specialised equipment, trained personnel and large volumes of blood and is time-consuming.
(c)
• LTA requires platelet-rich plasma obtained by centrifuging a blood sample, and measures aggregation by the change in light transmission through the plasma as platelets clump and the sample clears.
• Whole blood impedance aggregometry instead measures platelet aggregation in whole blood by detecting changes in electrical impedance as platelets adhere to electrodes after stimulation by an agonist, so it does not require centrifugation to prepare PRP.
• Whole blood impedance aggregometry is more physiological since it measures aggregation in the presence of red cells and other blood components, but it is less sensitive than LTA for detecting certain types of platelet dysfunction, and results can be affected by haematocrit levels or other factors present in whole blood.
• LTA can use multiple agonists to assess different activation pathways with high sensitivity and specificity, while whole blood impedance aggregometry trades some of that sensitivity for the convenience of testing whole blood directly without centrifugation.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the variables controlled and staining used in preparing thin and thick blood films for detecting blood parasites.
(b) State the standard setting/specimen in which this preparation is used.
(c) Explain the basic reasoning behind fixing the thin film with methyl alcohol but not the thick film before staining.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Fresh capillary blood from the finger or ear lobe, or venous blood collected in EDTA anticoagulant, is used; a drop of blood is spread with a circular motion for the thick film, while the thin film is spread and both are air dried.
• The thin film is fixed in methyl alcohol before Giemsa staining, while the thick film is stained with Giemsa without prior fixation.
(b)
This preparation is used in the standard setting of microscopic examination of blood for parasites such as malaria, Babesia, filaria and trypanosomes, as part of the diagnosis of parasitic infections.
(c)
• The thick film is used to screen a large amount of blood, which is useful in light infection, since the red cells are lysed during staining leaving parasites and white cells concentrated for detection, while the thin film allows parasitised red blood cells and parasites to be seen within intact red cells for definite species identification.
• The basic reasoning behind fixing the thin film with methyl alcohol before staining is that fixation preserves the red cell membrane and internal cellular structure intact, so that the parasite's position within the red cell and the red cell's own morphology can be assessed for species identification.
• The thick film is deliberately not fixed, since the intention is for the Giemsa staining process itself to lyse (dehaemoglobinise) the unfixed red cells, concentrating any parasites present from a larger volume of blood into a smaller viewing area, which increases the chance of detecting a light infection.
• Fixing the thick film would preserve the red cells intact rather than lysing them, defeating the purpose of concentrating parasites from a large blood volume, which is why the two films are deliberately prepared and treated differently despite using the same Giemsa stain.
• This difference in preparation is therefore matched to the different diagnostic purpose of each film: the thick film for screening/detecting a light infection, and the thin film for definitive parasite and species identification once parasites have been detected.

(a)
• Neutropenia (decreased count, <2 ×10⁹/L) is associated with typhoid fever, HIV, hypersplenism, aplastic anaemia and cytotoxic or drug-induced causes, while neutrophilia is associated with bacterial infections, inflammation/tissue necrosis, metabolic disorders, neoplasm, asplenia, drugs, chronic myeloid leukaemia/myeloproliferative disease, and acute haemorrhage or haemolysis.
• Lymphocytosis is associated with acute infections (infectious mononucleosis, rubella, pertussis, mumps, HIV, cytomegalovirus, infectious hepatitis), chronic infections (tuberculosis, toxoplasmosis, brucellosis, syphilis), and chronic lymphoid or acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, while lymphopenia is associated with HIV, Legionella pneumophila, severe bone marrow failure, corticosteroid or immunosuppressive therapy, and irradiation; monocytosis, eosinophilia and basophilia are each associated with their own listed groups of infective, connective tissue disease, neoplastic and other causes.
(b)
• The white cell differential count table lists separate normal percentage ranges at birth, at 6 years, and in adults for neutrophils (37-57% at birth, 45-50% at 6 years, 45-55% in adults), lymphocytes (23-35% at birth, 40-45% at 6 years, 25-40% in adults), monocytes, eosinophils and basophils, alongside a separate adult absolute count range for each cell type.
• The absolute white cell count is obtained by multiplying the percentage differential count by the total white cell count, so the age-specific percentage range applicable to the patient must be selected before this calculation and interpretation can be correctly applied.
(c)
• At birth, the normal neutrophil percentage range (37-57%) is lower than at 6 years (45-50%) or in adults (45-55%), while the normal lymphocyte percentage range at birth (23-35%) is markedly lower than at 6 years (40-45%), which itself differs from the adult range (25-40%).
• If a newborn's differential count is interpreted against the adult reference range rather than the birth-specific range, a normal newborn neutrophil or lymphocyte percentage could be wrongly flagged as abnormally low or high, since the ranges for each age group are explicitly different in the reference table.
• This basic error of applying the wrong age-specific reference range would therefore lead to an inaccurate interpretation of the differential count, potentially suggesting neutropenia, neutrophilia, lymphocytosis or lymphopenia where none genuinely exists for that patient's age group, or conversely, failing to flag a result that is genuinely abnormal for a newborn but happens to fall within the adult range.
• This illustrates the general principle that correctly classifying any full blood count abnormality, including the white cell differential, first requires applying the reference range appropriate to the specific patient (here, by age), before that classification can be used to suggest an underlying diagnosis.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the classification of white blood cell differential abnormalities (neutropenia/neutrophilia, lymphocytosis/lymphopenia, monocytosis, eosinophilia, basophilia).
(b) State how the normal differential ranges are applied or selected according to patient age.
(c) Explain why applying the adult differential range to a newborn's white cell differential is a basic error that leads to an inaccurate interpretation.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Documented RBC morphological abnormalities include hypochromic cells (pale staining with increased area of pallor >1/3), polychromasia (blue-grey staining of immature red cells/reticulocytes), microcytosis (smaller than normal red blood cells, <6.5 µm), macrocytosis (larger than normal red blood cells, >8 µm), target cells (staining in the centre and periphery with an unstained ring in between), and sickle cells (elliptical cells with pointed ends, crescent or boat shaped).
• Further abnormalities include anisocytosis (unequal variation in the size of red cells), poikilocytosis (significant variation in the shape of red cells), pencil cells (elongated, narrow cells), tear drop cells (cells shaped like tear drops), rouleaux (cells joined together side by side like stacks of coins), nucleated red cells (precursor red cells containing a nucleus), and megaloblasts (larger than normal red cells with an immature, fine lacy chromatin nucleus and blue-staining cytoplasm).
(b)
• Hypochromic cells are associated with iron deficiency, thalassaemia, anaemia of chronic infection and sideroblastic anaemia.
• Microcytosis is associated with iron deficiency, anaemia of chronic infection and thalassaemia syndrome.
• Macrocytosis is associated with folate and vitamin B12 deficiency, liver disease and alcoholism.
• Target cells are associated with thalassaemia, sickle cell disease, HbC disease, obstructive jaundice, liver disease and post-splenectomy states.
• Tear drop cells are associated with myelofibrosis and extramedullary erythropoiesis.
• Rouleaux are associated with myelomatosis, macroglobulinaemia, inflammatory disorder and malignancy.
• Nucleated red cells are associated with sickle cell disease, thalassaemia major, other severe anaemia, haemolytic disease of the newborn, leukaemias and autoimmune haemolytic anaemia.
(c)
• Many of these morphological features are shared across multiple conditions, for example target cells being associated with thalassaemia, sickle cell disease, HbC disease, obstructive jaundice, liver disease and post-splenectomy, so the presence of a given abnormal cell type alone does not point to a single diagnosis.
• It is specifically stated that blood film should be interpreted alongside clinical details (history and physical examination), reflecting the process or pattern of first discerning a set of test results as normal or abnormal and then establishing their association with a known haematological condition.
• For example, nucleated red cells may erroneously increase the total count reported by an automated haematology analyser, and require correction using the formula corrected WBC equals estimated WBC divided by (100 plus number of nucleated RBC per 100 WBC) multiplied by 100%, showing that a morphological finding can also directly distort a numerical result if not recognised and corrected for.
• Classifying an abnormal cell type correctly, therefore, is only the first step; without correlating the finding with the patient's clinical details and, where relevant, correcting associated numerical results, the same morphological feature could be wrongly attributed to the wrong one of its several possible associated conditions, leading to an inaccurate diagnostic conclusion.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the classification of red blood cell morphological abnormalities seen on a peripheral blood film.
(b) State how each type of abnormality is applied in suggesting an underlying diagnosis.
(c) Explain why classifying an abnormal cell without correlating it with clinical details can lead to an inaccurate diagnostic conclusion.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• The red cells are tested for antigens A and B using anti-sera A and B with titre of 1 in 512 and 1 in 256 respectively (cell grouping); serum grouping tests the serum using known A and B red cells (antigens).
• Tile method materials: patient's or donor's blood sample, anti-A, anti-B and anti-AB, white tiles, and controls of A(A2) cells, B cells and AB cells; tube method materials: blood sample (serum), standard cells A, B and O, tubes, and controls anti-A, anti-B and anti-AB.
• Tile method: a drop of anti-A, anti-B and anti-AB is placed on the tile with a drop of the blood sample, mixed and rocked, then the result is read as agglutination (+) or no agglutination (-).
• Tube method: tubes 1-4 are arranged and labelled, equal volumes of cell and serum are added (A cell, B cell, O cell, patient cell each with serum/patient serum), and the tubes are incubated at 37°C for 1 hour, checking for haemolysis and agglutination.
• The pattern of agglutination (+) or no agglutination (-) with anti-A, anti-B and anti-AB is read against the reactions listed for groups A, B, AB and O and reported as the corresponding ABO group.
(b)
Serum grouping is not performed for infants below 4 months of age because naturally occurring antibodies are formed 3-4 months after birth, so performing both cell and serum grouping together on adults cross-checks the antigen result against the expected antibody pattern.
(c)
• Cell grouping tests the red cells for A and B antigens using known anti-sera, whereas serum (reverse) grouping tests the patient's serum for anti-A and anti-B using known A, B and O red cells.
• Cell grouping therefore identifies what antigen is present on the patient's cells, while serum grouping identifies what antibody is present in the patient's serum, and the two results should agree for a valid ABO group.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the principle, materials, procedure and reporting of the tile and tube methods used in ABO blood grouping.
(b) Explain why both cell grouping and serum (reverse) grouping are used together in practice.
(c) Distinguish cell grouping from serum grouping.

A patient on warfarin therapy has a Prothrombin Time (PT) of 22 seconds.
(a) Interpret the result.
(b) State how it should be recorded/reported.
(c) State what it indicates.
(d) State the action that follows from this reading.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The normal PT is 10-14 seconds, so a PT of 22 seconds is prolonged.
(b)
The result should be recorded/reported as a prolonged PT (22 seconds, above the 10-14 second reference range), and the International Normalized Ratio (INR), calculated from the PT, should also be reported.
(c)
PT is prolonged in deficiencies of the involved clotting factors (VII, X, V, prothrombin and fibrinogen), and specifically in liver disease, warfarin therapy and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC); since the PT is used in monitoring oral anticoagulants, this prolongation in a patient on warfarin is consistent with the anticipated anticoagulant effect.
(d)
The action that follows is correlating the PT/INR result against the intended therapeutic range for the patient's warfarin therapy, since the INR is based on the ratio of the patient's PT to a mean normal PT with correction for sensitivity, with a normal (non-anticoagulated) range of 0.8-1.2, and taking clinical action if the result is outside the intended therapeutic range.

questions.question:
A blood sample is submitted for haemoglobin electrophoresis on cellulose acetate paper at alkaline pH to investigate an abnormal band.
(a) Identify the specimen and the technique/medium.
(b) State the underlying principle.
(c) State the correct procedure/conditions.
(d) State the expected result and a limitation to consider.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The specimen is the patient's blood sample, and the technique is haemoglobin electrophoresis using cellulose acetate paper as the support medium.
(b)
The principle is that in an alkaline buffer, HbA is a negatively charged protein which moves toward the positive electrode (anode) in an electric field, and most haemoglobin variants separate from HbA because the structural abnormality usually involves a change in electrical charge, while haemoglobin without a change in charge will not separate.
(c)
The electrophoresis is run using cellulose acetate paper as the support medium at a pH of 8.4 to 8.9, which has the advantage of rapid separation, ease of handling and minimal preparative work.
(d)
The expected result is separation of haemoglobin bands according to charge; a limitation to consider is that haemoglobin fractions in low concentration, like HbA2, HbH and HbBart's, may be missed, and that HbS, HbD and HbG comigrate at this pH, as do HbA2, HbC, HbE and HbO, so an abnormal band identified here should be confirmed by another method such as citrate agar electrophoresis or the solubility test.

questions.question:
A blood film stained with a supravital stain (brilliant cresyl blue or new methylene blue) from a patient with microcytic red cell indices shows scattered inclusion bodies within red cells.
(a) Identify the likely finding and its significance.
(b) State the basic technique used to detect it.
(c) State how the finding should be recorded/reported.
(d) State the follow-up practical step.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The finding is consistent with HbH inclusion bodies, which are indicative of alpha thalassaemia; red cells with inclusion bodies are fewer in people with alpha thalassaemia trait than in people with HbH disease.
(b)
The finding is better observed in slides prepared from fresh blood stained with supravital stains like brilliant cresyl blue or new methylene blue.
(c)
The finding is recorded/reported as the presence (or absence) of HbH inclusion bodies, noting that the absence of HbH inclusion bodies does not exclude an alpha thalassaemia trait.
(d)
As a follow-up practical step, since the absence of Hb H inclusion bodies does not exclude an alpha thalassaemia trait, other tests used to make a diagnosis of thalassaemia trait, such as electrophoresis of haemoglobin on cellulose acetate membrane at alkaline pH, measurement of HbA2, assessment of HbF, and assessment of iron status, should be considered.

questions.question:
A full blood count report shows an MCV of 105 fL in a patient who drinks alcohol regularly.
(a) Interpret the result.
(b) State how it should be recorded/reported.
(c) State what it indicates.
(d) State the action that follows from this reading.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The normal MCV is 80-95 fL, so an MCV of 105 fL is increased, indicating macrocytosis.
(b)
The result should be recorded/reported as an increased MCV (105 fL, above the 80-95 fL reference range), that is, a macrocytic red cell picture.
(c)
MCV is increased in folate/vitamin B12 deficiency, alcohol use and liver disease, so this result indicates a macrocytic anaemia consistent with one or more of these causes, which is also consistent with the patient's stated alcohol use.
(d)
The action that follows is further investigation directed at folate and vitamin B12 status and liver disease, and correlation with the blood film, where macrocytosis (larger than normal red blood cells, >8 µm, described as oval macrocytes) and megaloblastic change may also be assessed.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the composition and titre of the anti-A, anti-B and anti-AB antisera used in ABO cell grouping.
(b) State the standard method in which these antisera are used.
(c) Explain the basic reasoning behind the precaution of checking antisera for deterioration before use.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Anti-A, anti-B and anti-AB are antisera reagents used as controls in ABO grouping, tested against the patient's or donor's red cells to detect the corresponding antigens on the cell surface.
• In cell grouping, the red cells are tested for antigens A and B using anti-sera A and B with a titre of 1 in 512 and 1 in 256 respectively.
(b)
These antisera are used in the standard tile method (a drop of anti-A, anti-B and anti-AB mixed with a drop of the blood sample on a white tile, then rocked and read for agglutination) and the standard tube method, alongside appropriate A(A2), B and AB cell controls.
(c)
• Deterioration of reagent, whether from an expired reagent or a contaminated reagent, is listed as one of the difficulties in ABO grouping, since a deteriorated antiserum may fail to agglutinate cells that truly carry the corresponding antigen, or may give unreliable reactions.
• The basic reasoning behind checking antisera for deterioration before use is that the reliability of the entire ABO grouping result depends on the antiserum reacting correctly and specifically with its corresponding antigen; a weakened or contaminated reagent could produce a false negative or an unreadable result.
• This is why documentation of lot numbers, expiration dates and performance data, along with the use of positive and negative controls, forms part of quality control for serologic reagents generally, including ABO grouping antisera.
• Appropriate cell controls, such as A(A2), B and AB cells in the tile method, allow the scientist to confirm that the antisera are reacting as expected on the day of testing, before relying on the same antisera to interpret the patient's unknown result.
• This precaution reflects the same underlying principle of accuracy in serologic testing described for quality control generally, namely that a test result correctly reflects the patient's true antigen status only if the reagent used is itself functioning correctly.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the effect of proteolytic enzyme reagents (papain, bromelin, ficin) on the red cell membrane.
(b) State the standard setting in which enzyme-treated reagent cells are used.
(c) Explain the basic reasoning behind the precaution of not relying on the enzyme technique alone for antibody screening.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Proteolytic enzymes such as papain and bromelain strip a lot of the charged molecules from the red cell surface.
• This action may uncover some antigens, such as Rh antigens, but destroys others, such as M, N, S and Duffy antigens.
(b)
The enzyme technique is used exactly the same as the saline technique except that the reagent cells used have been treated with papain before use in the test, as this destroys immunoglobulins, and the enzyme technique is used to enhance detection of Rh antibodies.
(c)
• Because the enzyme technique enhances Rh antibody reactivity by uncovering Rh antigens but destroys M, N, S, Fya and Fyb antigens on the reagent cells, it would be unable to detect antibodies directed against the MNSs or Duffy systems, since the corresponding antigens are no longer present on the treated cells for the antibody to react with.
• This is the basic reasoning behind the precaution of not relying on the enzyme technique alone for antibody screening, since an antibody screen must also use techniques (such as saline or IAT with untreated reagent cells) capable of detecting antibodies to antigens that enzymes would destroy.
• The enzyme technique is therefore used as one of several complementary techniques for detecting antibody-antigen reactions, alongside the saline technique (mainly IgM) and the indirect antiglobulin technique (mainly IgG), rather than as the sole method.
• Relying on a single technique risks missing clinically significant antibodies whose corresponding antigens are altered or destroyed by that technique's specific reagent treatment, which is why antibody screening panels are read across multiple technique phases where available.
• This precaution reflects the broader principle in immunohaematology that the choice and combination of detection techniques must match the range of antibody classes and antigen systems that need to be excluded or identified in a given patient.

(a)
• A crossmatch mixes patient plasma with cells from the unit to be transfused and is tested by the IAT technique, looking for units showing no reaction as being compatible.
• The saline technique uses cells and serum only.
• The enzyme technique uses reagent cells that have been treated with papain before use.
• The IAT technique uses cells, serum, wash saline and AHG reagent.
• Saline technique procedure: mix cells and serum, incubate for a set time and temperature, centrifuge, then read.
• Enzyme technique procedure is exactly the same as the saline technique except that the reagent cells used have been pre-treated with papain, which destroys immunoglobulins on the cell surface before testing.
• IAT technique procedure: mix cells and serum, incubate, wash the cells, add AHG, centrifuge, then read.
• A positive reaction (agglutination) indicates incompatibility, while units showing no reaction are used for the transfusion; all tests require a positive and a negative control run alongside the unknowns.
(b)
In a crossmatch, neither the antibodies that may be present in the patient's plasma nor the antigens present on the donor cells are already known, unlike phenotyping (known antibody vs unknown antigen) or antibody screening (unknown antibody vs known antigen), so both sides of the reaction are unknown.
(c)
• The saline technique mixes cells and serum directly and is mainly used to detect IgM antibodies without any enzyme treatment of the reagent cells.
• The enzyme technique uses reagent cells treated with papain, which strips charged molecules from the cell surface, enhancing detection of Rh antibodies but destroying M, N, S, Fya and Fyb antigens, so it is not suitable for detecting antibodies to those antigens.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the principle, reagents/materials, procedure and reading of the saline, enzyme and indirect antiglobulin (IAT) crossmatching techniques.
(b) Explain why the crossmatch is described as testing an unknown antibody against an unknown antigen.
(c) Distinguish the enzyme technique from the saline technique.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Reagent red cell panels are red cell suspensions used in tests that employ the principles of haemagglutination and haemolysis for the detection and identification of blood group antibodies.
• Sources of reagent red cells include commercial suppliers, and in-house sources such as regular donors or staff members.
(b)
The standard applications of reagent red cells include reverse ABO grouping, antibody screening, antibody identification, antibody titration, allogenic adsorption, and control of AHG technique.
(c)
• In an antibody identification panel, antigens that are present in the homozygous state on the panel cells are indicated (for example, by a circled antigen marking, present as a plus sign, or absent as a zero).
• This is because most Rh antibodies, except anti-D, display a dosage effect, that is, the antibody reacts more strongly with red cells homozygous for an antigen than with cells heterozygous for the antigen, for example reacting more strongly with EE cells than with Ee cells.
• The basic reasoning behind marking homozygous expression on the panel is therefore that a weakly reacting or apparently negative antibody could actually be present but reacting weakly against a heterozygous-expressing cell, and correctly interpreting the panel requires knowing whether each cell carries the antigen in single or double dose.
• Failure to account for dosage on the panel could lead to a clinically significant antibody being missed or misidentified, since the pattern of reactivity across the panel is read against the known antigen profile, including zygosity, of each reagent cell.
• This reasoning applies across antibody screening, identification, and titration, all of which depend on reading agglutination strength against a known, documented antigen profile of the reagent red cells used.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the composition and sources of reagent red cell panels used in blood group serology.
(b) State the standard applications of reagent red cells in the laboratory.
(c) Explain the basic reasoning behind marking which antigens on the panel cells are present in the homozygous state.

A drop of a patient's blood is submitted with clinical suspicion of sickle cell disease, to be mixed with 2% sodium metabisulphite.
(a) Identify the specimen and reagent, and the technique.
(b) State the underlying principle.
(c) State the correct procedure.
(d) State the expected result.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The specimen is a drop of the patient's blood, the reagent is 2% sodium metabisulphite, and the technique is the sickling test.
(b)
The principle is that sodium metabisulphite deoxygenates the blood, and in the presence of HbS, red cells develop a sickle shape that can be identified by microscopy; the presence of sickled erythrocytes in a patient with symptoms of sickle cell disease is suggestive of the disorder.
(c)
A drop of blood is mixed with two drops of 2% sodium metabisulphite; this is covered with a coverslip and sealed with petroleum jelly, and the slide is examined under the microscope after 15 minutes, one hour and 24 hours.
(d)
The expected result is the appearance of sickled erythrocytes on microscopy if HbS is present; false positives may occur if the sodium metabisulphite concentration is >2%, and false negatives may occur if the metabisulphite is stale or in the neonatal period due to low HbS percentage, so a positive sickling test should be followed by the solubility test and/or electrophoresis for confirmation.

(a)
The normal MCV is 80-95 fL and normal MCH is 27-32 pg, so an MCV of 70 fL and MCH of 22 pg are both reduced, indicating a microcytic, hypochromic red cell population.
(b)
The result should be recorded/reported as a reduced MCV (70 fL, below the 80-95 fL reference range) and reduced MCH (22 pg, below the 27-32 pg reference range).
(c)
This pattern indicates microcytic anaemia, since MCV is decreased in iron deficiency, thalassaemia and lead poisoning, and MCH is decreased in iron deficiency, thalassaemia and lead poisoning, so the combined pattern is consistent with these conditions.
(d)
The action that follows is to pursue iron studies and haemoglobinopathy screening (since red cell indices are particularly useful in screening for the thalassaemias and this is best done by an automated blood cell counter) to distinguish between iron deficiency and thalassaemia as the underlying cause, noting that concomitant iron deficiency can also lower HbA2 and should be corrected before HbA2 is used to diagnose beta thalassaemia trait.
questions.question:
A full blood count report shows an MCV of 70 fL and an MCH of 22 pg.
(a) Interpret the result.
(b) State how it should be recorded/reported.
(c) State what it indicates.
(d) State the action that follows from this reading.

(a) Describe the classification of blood group antibodies as naturally occurring versus immune, and as cold-reacting versus warm-reacting.
(b) State how each class is applied or selected for in the choice of detection technique.
(c) Explain why choosing the wrong technique (for example, saline-only testing) for a warm IgG antibody leads to an invalid (missed) result.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Naturally occurring antibodies, such as anti-A and anti-B, occur in the plasma of subjects who lack the corresponding antigen and who have not been transfused or pregnant; they are predominantly IgM, activate complement, react optimally at 4°C and at room temperature (cold antibodies), and agglutinate cells suspended in saline.
• Immune antibodies are developed by transfusion, transplacental passage or injection, are IgG in nature, react optimally at 37°C (warm antibodies), are capable of transplacental passage, do not agglutinate red cells suspended in saline but only in macromolecular media (incomplete antibodies), and lyse red cells readily.
• The review of cold antibodies (IgM) further lists anti-Lea, anti-Leb, anti-I, anti-P1, anti-M, anti-A, -B, -H and anti-N as naturally occurring, while the review of warm antibodies (IgG) lists Rh antibodies, Kell, Duffy, Kidd, and S,s as typically immune, clinically significant antibodies.
(b)
• Cold-reacting, naturally occurring antibodies are detected by the saline technique, in which cells and serum are mixed, incubated, centrifuged and read directly, since these antibodies cause direct agglutination.
• Warm-reacting, immune antibodies are detected using the indirect antiglobulin technique, in which cells and serum are mixed, incubated at 37°C, washed, AHG is added, and then centrifuged and read, since these antibodies sensitise but do not directly agglutinate cells in saline.
(c)
• If only the saline technique is used to test for an antibody that is actually a warm-reacting IgG antibody, the antibody may sensitise the reagent red cells during incubation but will not cause direct agglutination in saline, since IgG antibodies do not agglutinate red cells suspended in saline but only in macromolecular media or after the AHG bridging step.
• Reading the saline test as negative would therefore be an invalid conclusion, since the antibody is present but the technique used was not capable of demonstrating it; the antibody screen for clinically significant, mainly IgG antibodies is specifically stated to always be done using IAT techniques rather than saline alone.
• This demonstrates why the choice of detection technique must be matched to the antibody class under investigation, since a technique suited to detecting cold IgM antibodies is not capable of reliably detecting warm IgG antibodies, and using the wrong technique produces a false negative rather than a true absence of antibody.

(a)
The specimen is platelet-rich plasma (PRP) obtained by centrifuging a blood sample, and the technique is Light Transmission Aggregometry (LTA), the gold standard for measuring platelet aggregation.
(b)
The principle is that when platelets aggregate in response to an agonist, the turbidity (cloudiness) of the platelet-rich plasma decreases, allowing more light to pass through the sample.
(c)
The PRP is placed in a cuvette inside an aggregometer; a baseline measurement of light transmission is taken, an agonist such as ADP or collagen is added to induce aggregation, and as platelets aggregate the PRP becomes clearer, increasing light transmission, with the change recorded over time.
(d)
The expected result is an aggregation curve showing increasing light transmission as platelets aggregate; the technique has high sensitivity and specificity for detecting platelet function abnormalities and can use multiple agonists to assess different activation pathways, though it requires large blood volumes and specialised equipment.
questions.question:
A blood sample is centrifuged to obtain platelet-rich plasma (PRP) for a platelet function investigation using an aggregometer.
(a) Identify the specimen and the technique.
(b) State the underlying principle.
(c) State the correct procedure.
(d) State the expected result.

(a) Describe the composition and types of antihuman globulin (AHG) reagent, including its source.
(b) State the standard settings in which polyspecific and monospecific AHG are respectively used.
(c) Explain the basic reasoning behind quality-controlling every batch of AHG reagent before use.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Antihuman globulin (AHG) refers to antibodies directed against the Fc portion of human immunoglobulins (IgG) or antibodies and/or complement protein components; it is a reagent used to detect the presence of these molecules when they are bound to red blood cells, which are not visible under a microscope.
• AHG is typically produced by immunising animals, such as rabbits, rats and guinea pigs, with purified human globulin, then collecting the antiserum, purifying the antibodies using techniques like ammonium sulfate precipitation or affinity chromatography, and formulating the product with preservatives and stabilisers.
• Polyspecific AHG contains antibodies against both IgG and complement (for example C3d) and is used for broad detection in tests like the Direct Antiglobulin Test; monospecific AHG contains antibodies against only one target, such as anti-IgG or anti-C3d, and is used to determine the specific type of molecule coating the red blood cells.
(b)
Polyspecific AHG is used for broad detection, such as in the DAT, when it is not yet known whether IgG or complement is coating the red cells, while monospecific AHG is used once broad sensitisation has been detected and the specific type of molecule (anti-IgG or anti-C3d) needs to be identified.
(c)
• Standardisation procedures for AHG reagent include titration to determine the optimal working dilution, testing with sensitised red cells to ensure reactivity, ensuring the absence of reactivity with unsensitised cells, and validation against reference standards.
• Quality control involves regular testing with positive and negative controls, monitoring for contamination and stability, and documentation of lot numbers, expiration dates and performance data.
• The basic reasoning behind this quality control is that even 10 mL of AHG can be neutralised by a tiny amount of free serum protein, and problems with the AHG reagent, such as bacterial contamination, improper storage, failure to add the reagent, or decreased reactivity, are all listed sources of a false negative AGT.
• Without confirming that each batch of AHG reagent is reactive and free of contamination before use, a genuine antibody or complement coating on a patient's red cells could be missed entirely, which is why check cells and documented QC records are required for every batch.

(a)
• K2EDTA is an anticoagulant used for blood samples in haematology testing, and blood to anticoagulant should be in the right proportion.
• K2EDTA causes less cellular damage and is recommended by the International Council for Standardisation in Haematology (ICSH) as the anticoagulant of choice.
(b)
K2EDTA-anticoagulated blood is used as the specimen for the Direct Antiglobulin Test (10 × 75 mm test tubes with EDTA-anticoagulated blood sample listed among DAT tube method materials), for HPLC haemoglobin analysis (5 µl of an EDTA blood sample in lysis buffer), and for preparation of the peripheral blood film, where K2EDTA is stated as the anticoagulant of choice.
(c)
• Improper techniques like squeezing during specimen collection can cause microclots or platelet clots.
• The basic reasoning behind avoiding squeezing is that microclots or platelet clots forming in the sample would interfere with accurate cell counting and morphology assessment, since clumped platelets are listed as a cause of inaccurate counts by automated haematology analysers.
• This pre-analytical precaution, alongside avoiding prolonged use of a tourniquet, is grouped with other factors that affect laboratory results due to handling of the specimen prior to analysis, such as misidentification of the patient and mislabelling of specimens.
• Because blood sampling technique must ensure minimal tissue damage and the blood to anticoagulant ratio must be correct, avoiding squeezing is one of several variables that must be controlled to ensure the quality of a blood film and the accuracy of the subsequent count and morphology assessment.
• This reasoning applies broadly across haematology testing, since a specimen compromised at the pre-analytical stage cannot be corrected later by analytical technique, however precise the subsequent test method is.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the composition and recommendation for anticoagulated blood specimens (K2EDTA) used in haematology testing.
(b) State the standard tests for which K2EDTA blood is the specimen of choice.
(c) Explain the basic reasoning behind the precaution against squeezing the site during blood collection.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Naturally occurring antibodies occur in the plasma of subjects who lack the corresponding antigen and who have not been transfused or pregnant, for example anti-A and anti-B; they are predominantly immunoglobulin M (IgM), of molecular weight about 900,000, activate complement, and agglutinate cells suspended in saline.
• Immune antibodies are instead developed by the production of immunoglobulin in response to a stimulating antigen the individual lacks, through transfusion, transplacental passage during pregnancy, or deliberate injection; these antibodies are IgG in nature (molecular weight about 140,000), and they do not agglutinate red cells suspended in saline but only in macromolecular media, such as bovine albumin, being described as incomplete antibodies.
(b)
Naturally occurring antibodies react optimally at 4°C and at room temperature and are known as cold antibodies, agglutinating cells directly in the saline technique; immune antibodies react optimally at 37°C and are known as warm antibodies, requiring the indirect antiglobulin technique to demonstrate agglutination since they do not agglutinate cells directly in saline.
(c)
• Immune antibodies (IgG) are capable of transplacental passage from mother to foetus, whereas naturally occurring antibodies are predominantly IgM.
• IgM's larger pentameric structure (molecular weight about 900,000) does not cross the placenta, while IgG's smaller structure (molecular weight about 140,000) does, which is the basic reasoning behind why immune (IgG) antibodies, such as those causing haemolytic disease of the foetus and newborn, are the class implicated in transplacental disease rather than naturally occurring IgM antibodies.
• This is consistent with the classification of the class of immunoglobulin implicated in haemolytic disease of the foetus and newborn as IgG, with IgG1 and IgG3 being more effective in causing haemolysis, and IgG1 crossing the placenta earlier and in greater amounts, thus causing more haemolysis.
• Naturally occurring antibodies also react optimally at low temperature (4°C) rather than at body temperature (37°C), which further limits their capacity to cause in vivo destruction of foetal cells at normal body temperature, unlike warm-reacting IgG antibodies.
• This distinction between antibody class and reactivity temperature is the basic reasoning behind why antenatal antibody screening specifically looks for and titrates IgG (warm, IAT-detected) antibodies of clinical significance for HDFN, rather than routine cold agglutinins.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the structural difference between naturally occurring and immune blood group antibodies.
(b) State the standard reaction temperature and technique setting for each class.
(c) Explain the basic reasoning behind why immune antibodies, and not naturally occurring antibodies, cause transplacental disease.

A blood film shows red cells that stain in the centre and at the periphery, with an unstained ring in between.
(a) Identify the abnormal cell.
(b) State the basic technique used to detect this finding.
(c) State how the finding should be recorded/reported.
(d) State the follow-up practical step.
questions.answerText:
(a)
The cells are target cells, associated with thalassaemia, sickle cell disease (SCD), HbC disease, obstructive jaundice, liver disease and post-splenectomy states.
(b)
The finding is detected by microscopic examination of a well prepared and properly stained peripheral blood film using a microscope and Romanowsky dyes.
(c)
The finding is recorded/reported as the presence of target cells, and blood film findings should be interpreted alongside the patient's clinical history and physical examination.
(d)
As a follow-up step, because target cells are a pointer to sickle cell disease or thalassaemia on peripheral blood film review, haemoglobinopathy screening (sickling test, solubility test, haemoglobin electrophoresis, or HPLC) should be pursued to identify the underlying cause.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the classification of Rh phenotypes and their genetic combinations.
(b) State how the weak D and partial D types are applied or selected in labelling donors and recipients.
(c) Explain why a basic error, such as mislabelling a Du (weak D) individual, leads to an inaccurate or invalid transfusion decision.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• There are 6 common Rh genes: C, D and E, and their allelomorphs c, d and e; the 3 genes (C or c, D or d, and E or e) are carried on the same chromosome, and since there are 2 Rh chromosomes on the red cell, the 8 gene combinations can be paired in 36 possible Rhesus genotypes, with shorthand notations such as R1 (CDe), R2 (cDE), R0 (cDe) and r (cde).
• The most common phenotype among the black population is D+C-E-c+e+, and phenotype frequencies listed include R1r (31%), R1R1 (17%), rr (16%), R1R2 (12%), R2r (11%) and R2R2 (3%).
(b)
• In the routine laboratory, only the presence and absence of the D antigen is determined; an individual with weak D is labelled as D positive when donating blood, since their D antigen, though reduced in quantity, is complete, and they can receive D positive blood without complication.
• An individual with partial D is labelled as D positive but is treated as D negative when receiving blood, since their D antigen protein structure is altered (missing epitopes), and if alloimmunised to D, they can produce an anti-D antibody.
(c)
• In the Du (weak D) individual, one or more part of the mosaic is missing in terms of reactivity, and their red cells are agglutinated by some but not all anti-D sera, reacting with incomplete anti-D sera depending on whether it is high grade or low grade Du antigen, rather than reacting with the complete anti-D reagent.
• If a weak D individual is mislabelled as D negative rather than D positive when donating blood, D negative recipients could unknowingly receive D-antigen-bearing blood and become sensitised to the D antigen through transfusion.
• Conversely, if a partial D individual is mislabelled as D positive when receiving blood rather than being treated as D negative, they could receive ordinary D positive blood carrying the epitope they lack, leading to alloimmunisation and the production of anti-D.
• This demonstrates why a basic error in correctly distinguishing and labelling weak D from partial D, based on their different underlying quantitative versus qualitative antigen differences, directly leads to an inaccurate or invalid, and potentially unsafe, transfusion decision.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the composition of the reagents (anti-D and D-positive indicator red cells) used in the Rosette test for foeto-maternal haemorrhage.
(b) State the standard setting in which the Rosette test is used.
(c) Explain the basic reasoning behind the precaution that the mother must be D-negative and the foetal cells D-positive for the test to be valid.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The Rosette test uses anti-D, which is incubated with the maternal red cell suspension so that it binds to D-positive foetal red cells during incubation, and D-positive indicator red cells, which are added after washing and bind to the anti-D already attached to the foetal cells, forming a rosette around each D-positive foetal red cell.
• The suspension is washed between the anti-D incubation step and the addition of the D-positive indicator cells, so that only anti-D actually bound to foetal cells remains available to bind the added indicator cells.
(b)
The Rosette test is used in the standard setting of screening for the presence of foeto-maternal haemorrhage (FMH); if the test is positive, the degree of FMH is then quantified using other methods, such as the Kleihauer test.
(c)
• The foetal cells must be D-positive and the mother must be D-negative for the test to be valid, and the test cannot be used if the infant is of weak D phenotype.
• The basic reasoning is that the test depends entirely on the anti-D reagent being able to distinguish D-positive foetal cells from D-negative maternal cells within the maternal blood sample; if the mother herself were D-positive, her own red cells would also bind anti-D and form rosettes, making it impossible to distinguish maternal cells from any foetal cells present.
• Similarly, if the foetal cells are of weak D phenotype, they express a reduced quantity of the D antigen, since weak D results from a quantitative difference with a reduced number of D antigens on the red cell, which may be insufficient to reliably bind enough anti-D to form a visible rosette, again invalidating the test.
• This precaution reflects the same basic reasoning seen with other reagent-based techniques, namely that a test's validity depends on the reagent being able to specifically and reliably distinguish the target cells (D-positive foetal cells) from all other cells present (D-negative maternal cells), and any situation that removes this distinction, whether from the mother's own D status or a weak D foetal phenotype, produces an unreliable result.
• This is why, once a positive Rosette screen has been obtained under valid testing conditions, the degree of FMH must still be quantified using a separate method, such as the Kleihauer test, since the Rosette test itself is only a qualitative screening test for the presence of FMH, not a quantitative measure of its volume.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the principle, materials and tube technique procedure of the Indirect Antiglobulin Test (IAT).
(b) Explain why the test is incubated at 37°C before washing.
(c) Distinguish the IAT from the saline agglutination technique.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Patient serum is incubated with reagent red cells; if antibodies are present, they bind to antigens on the red cells, and after washing to remove unbound antibodies, antihuman globulin (AHG) is added, which causes agglutination if sensitisation occurred, indicating a positive result.
• Materials/steps use glass tubes for test samples and control, serum samples, reagent red cell suspension, RhD-positive cells for the control tube, normal saline, and AHG reagent, with mixing and incubation equipment and a centrifuge.
• 50 µl of serum sample and control are applied to labelled glass tubes.
• 50 µl of reagent red cell suspension is applied, with 50 µl of RhD-positive cells added to the control tube.
• The tubes are mixed and incubated at 37°C for 15 minutes.
• The red cells are washed with 1 ml of 0.9% normal saline and centrifuged at 1000g for 1 minute, decanting the supernatant, and the wash is repeated; 70 µl of anti-human globulin is then added, mixed and centrifuged at 500g for 15 seconds.
• The red cell button is gently resuspended and examined macroscopically for agglutination, and results are graded and recorded.
(b)
IgG antibodies react optimally at 37°C, so incubation at this temperature allows the antibody time to sensitise (bind to) the reagent red cells before the unbound antibody is washed away and AHG is added to bridge the sensitised cells and cause agglutination.
(c)
• The saline technique produces direct agglutination and is mainly used to detect IgM antibodies by mixing cells and serum, incubating, centrifuging and reading, without any washing or AHG addition step.
• The IAT is an indirect agglutination technique mainly for IgG antibodies, requiring washing of the cells after incubation and the addition of AHG before centrifuging and reading, because IgG antibodies sensitise but do not directly agglutinate red cells in saline.

(a)
• HPLC separates haemoglobin fractions because they have different interaction with the stationary phase; the basic technology is based on the time required for gradient elution of the different haemoglobin fractions, called the retention time, and the shape of the peak.
• In cation exchange HPLC, haemoglobins are separated by an analytical cartridge using a pre-programmed buffer gradient with increasing ionic strength, and identification of an unknown haemoglobin is achieved by comparison with known haemoglobin retention times.
• The apparatus comprises solvent reservoirs, a solvent degasser, a gradient valve, a mixing vessel for delivery of the mobile phase, a high-pressure pump, a switching valve, a sample injection loop, a pre-column (guard column), an analytical column, a detector, and a data acquisition and waste/fraction collector unit; a dual wavelength filter photometer monitors the eluent as it passes through the detector cell.
• Only 5 µl of an EDTA blood sample taken in 1.0 ml of the lysis buffer is required; the samples are injected into the analysis stream and separated by the cation exchange cartridge using a phosphate ion gradient generated by mixing two buffers of different ionic strengths.
(b)
• HPLC is fast and provides simultaneous qualitative and quantitative estimation of haemoglobin fractions, and cation exchange HPLC has become the method of choice for quantitation of HbA2, HbF and other Hb subtypes.
• The detector signal data is reduced by the integrator and processed to give a chromatogram of time versus absorbance, with the different peaks identified in defined windows and their retention time, relative percentage and area printed out.
(c)
• HPLC identifies haemoglobin variants by retention time and peak shape and position, and depending on these features it has limitations and cannot be used as a stand-alone method for identification of Hb variants, since about thirty different variants have been reported eluting in the HbS window with retention times between 4.31 and 4.63, so results should be cross-checked with another technique.
• Haemoglobin electrophoresis instead separates haemoglobins by their electrical charge in an alkaline or acidic medium, and certain haemoglobins that comigrate on electrophoresis (such as HbS, HbD and HbG at alkaline pH) may be resolved differently by HPLC retention time, so the two methods can be used to supplement each other.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the principle, apparatus and sample requirement of high performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) for haemoglobinopathy diagnosis.
(b) Explain why HPLC is described as the method of choice in many laboratories.
(c) Distinguish HPLC from haemoglobin electrophoresis as a diagnostic tool.

(a) Describe the classification of the saline, enzyme and indirect antiglobulin techniques for detecting antibody-antigen reactions.
(b) State how each technique is applied or selected in phenotyping, antibody screening and crossmatching.
(c) Explain why using the saline technique alone for a crossmatch leads to an invalid compatibility result.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• The three main techniques for detecting antigen-antibody reactions are the saline technique (mainly IgM, direct agglutination), the enzyme technique (identical to the saline technique except the reagent cells have been treated with papain), and the indirect antiglobulin technique (mainly IgG, indirect agglutination requiring washing and AHG addition).
• Their abbreviations are listed as Sal (saline, at 20°C or 4°C), Pap (enzyme, at 37°C, or Pap-IAT), and IAT (at 37°C).
(b)
• Phenotyping (known antibody versus unknown antigen) is mainly IgM-based, and the saline immediate spin technique is preferable, though not always achievable; antibody screening (unknown antibody versus known antigen) is always done using IAT techniques, since the clinically significant antibodies being screened for are mainly IgG.
• Crossmatching (unknown antibody versus unknown antigen) mixes patient plasma with cells from the unit to be transfused and is tested by the IAT technique, looking to use units with no reaction, since it must be capable of detecting both cold IgM and warm IgG antibodies that could be clinically significant.
(c)
• If only the saline technique is used for a crossmatch, direct agglutination will only be produced by antibodies, mainly IgM, that agglutinate cells directly in saline; a clinically significant IgG antibody present in the patient's plasma that reacts with an antigen on the donor unit's cells would sensitise the cells without producing visible direct agglutination in saline.
• Reading such a crossmatch as compatible (no reaction) based on the saline technique alone would therefore be invalid, since a truly incompatible unit, carrying an antigen targeted by the patient's IgG antibody, would be released as if compatible, risking a hemolytic transfusion reaction after transfusion.
• This is precisely why the crossmatch is specifically stated to be tested by the IAT technique, incorporating incubation, washing and AHG addition, since only this combination of steps is capable of reliably detecting the IgG antibodies most likely to be clinically significant in a crossmatch setting, unlike the saline technique used alone.
• This reflects the general principle that the technique chosen for any antibody-antigen investigation must be capable of detecting the full range of antibody classes that could be clinically relevant to that investigation, and using a technique suited to only one class produces an incomplete and therefore invalid result for the other class.

(a)
• Variables that can affect the quality of the film must be controlled: the blood sampling technique must ensure minimal tissue damage, the blood to anticoagulant ratio should be correct, and the anticoagulant of choice is K2EDTA.
• Samples are best analysed within 2 hours of blood collection, and they must be transported to the laboratory promptly, since a delay in preparation of the blood smear may allow degeneration of the cellular elements of blood.
• Examination of a well prepared and properly stained blood smear, using a microscope and Romanowsky dyes, allows the medical laboratory scientist to assess red cell, white cell and platelet morphology.
(b)
Delay in preparation of the blood smear may allow the degeneration of cellular elements of blood, so preparing and analysing the film within 2 hours of collection ensures accurate and reliable results that reflect the true morphology of the cells at the time of collection.
(c)
• A PBF may be requested by the clinician based on clinical suspicion of a haematological disorder.
• A PBF may also be requested by the laboratory medical scientist as a result of an abnormal finding from an automated count, since the automated haematology analyser has limitations such as being affected by cellular clumping (for example platelet aggregates) or improper calibration, which the scientist may wish to verify by direct microscopy.
• Common clinical indications for a PBF include unexplained cytopenia, anaemia, leucopenia, leukaemia and myeloproliferative disorder.
• Whether requested by the clinician or initiated by the scientist, the blood film should be interpreted alongside clinical details (history and physical examination), and a trained haemo-morphologist, who may be a laboratory scientist or a physician, is required especially for slides with significant pathology.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the variables that must be controlled, preparation steps and staining used in making a peripheral blood film for microscopic examination.
(b) Explain why the sample should be analysed and the film prepared within 2 hours of blood collection.
(c) Distinguish the reasons for requesting a peripheral blood film (PBF) from a clinician's request versus a laboratory scientist's own initiation of the request.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Check cells are a quality control measure to ensure the validity of the AHG reagent and technique, consisting of red blood cells pre-coated with antibody; they should agglutinate when mixed with AHG reagent, demonstrating the reagent's ability to detect antibody-coated red cells.
• A doubling dilution of commercially available monoclonal anti-D (IgG) is performed, and the highest dilution which gives a +2 reaction with O RhD-positive red cells is selected; for example, for a dilution of 1:64, 630 µl of normal saline is added to 10 µl of undiluted anti-D.
• One volume of diluted anti-D is added to an equal volume of pooled O RhD-positive red cells, incubated at 37°C for 45 minutes, and washed three times with normal saline; one drop of AHG is then added to one drop of a 5% suspension of the washed red cells, and the check cells can be stored in Alsever's solution for 1 week at 4°C.
(b)
Check cells are added to a tube that has tested negative on AHG testing to confirm that AHG reagent was indeed present, active and correctly added, since a genuinely negative AHG test should still turn positive once IgG-coated check cells are added and AHG reagent reacts with them.
(c)
• A negative Coombs control cell reaction with AHG suggests a technical error or reagent issue, for example that AHG was not added or was inadequate, that the reagent has expired, or that the AHG has been neutralised by free antibodies due to insufficient washing of the red cells.
• A true negative AHG test occurs when there are genuinely no antibodies or complement proteins attached to the red blood cells or present in the serum, and in this situation the check cells, once added, will still agglutinate with the AHG reagent because the reagent itself remains active and correctly present.
• Because even 10 mL of AHG can be neutralised by a tiny amount of free serum protein, and a couple of drops of residual saline can dilute the AHG reagent below detectable levels, the check cell step is essential to validate every negative AHG result rather than assuming the reagent worked.
• Since people do not normally produce unexpected antibodies, the test should generally be negative, which makes the check cell validation step the only reliable way to distinguish a correctly performed negative test from one that failed due to a technical error.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the principle and procedure for preparing Coombs control (check) cells.
(b) Explain the purpose of check cells in AHG testing.
(c) Distinguish a negative Coombs control cell reaction due to a technical error from a true negative AHG test.
