questions.question:
A woman has been in labour for more than 12 hours without delivery. She is tired, exhausted, dehydrated and febrile; contractions may have stopped. There is vulvo-vaginal swelling, severe caput, moderate to severe moulding and cervical oedema.
(a) Identify the condition and explain its pathophysiological basis.
(b) State the priority nursing assessment and immediate interventions.
(c) State the definitive medical or surgical management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Obstructed (prolonged) labour: progress is no longer possible despite adequate uterine contractions, usually from a mechanical factor needing external intervention; a major direct cause of maternal and neonatal mortality. Causes: ineffective uterine action, CPD, occipitoposterior position, contracted pelvis, deep transverse arrest, malpresentation, pelvic tumour, pelvic deformities.

(b)
• Inform the obstetric team; history of labour, contractions and membrane rupture; general condition (orientation, hydration, vital signs), urine testing, abdominal and vaginal examination; partograph monitoring.
• Support and information, informed consent, comfort and analgesia; temperature 4-hourly, pulse and BP every 30 minutes to hourly; empty bladder every 2 hours with intake/output record; hourly VE; FHR half-hourly; set up IV fluid (normal saline, Ringer's lactate or 5% dextrose); catheterise.

(c)
• Treat the cause: hypotonic uterine action - oxytocin or amniotomy or both; CPD - caesarean section; prepare for emergency caesarean section if labour is obstructed and call the obstetrician or prepare for referral.
• Complications to anticipate: dehydration, pre-eclampsia/eclampsia, sepsis, PPH, uterine rupture, vesico-vaginal and recto-vaginal fistula; fetal hypoxia, intracranial injury, infection, death.

questions.question:
A fetal blood vessel is palpated on vaginal examination lying over the cervical os in front of the presenting part, and the fetus shows distress out of proportion to the blood lost.
(a) Identify the condition and its pathophysiological basis.
(b) State the priority assessment and immediate interventions.
(c) State the definitive management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Vasa praevia: a fetal blood vessel lies over the cervical os in front of the presenting part, a rare complication that can cause severe fetal blood loss.
• Diagnosis: ultrasound scan, palpation on vaginal examination, fetal distress disproportionate to blood loss.

(b)
• Client and partner education; monitor vital signs and abdominal palpation; estimate blood loss and monitor the fetal heart rate.
• Resuscitation and blood transfusion; arrange for the paediatrician to be present at birth.

(c)
Emergency caesarean section is recommended.

questions.question:
A pregnant woman with known epilepsy has a generalised seizure during labour with loss of awareness and involuntary movements.
(a) Identify the condition and explain its pathophysiological basis.
(b) State the priority assessment and immediate interventions.
(c) State the definitive medical management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Epilepsy (seizure disorder): disturbed nerve cell activity in the brain causing recurrent seizures (two or more unprovoked); seizures may be partial or generalised, sometimes with loss of consciousness and loss of bowel or bladder control. Predisposing: perinatal brain damage, congenital abnormalities, severe head injury, stroke, brain infection, genetic syndromes, brain tumour.

(b)
• Terminate the seizure as soon as possible to avoid maternal and fetal hypoxia and fetal acidosis; benzodiazepines are the drugs of choice; continuous fetal monitoring after an intrapartum seizure; nursing diagnosis - risk for injury.
• Minimise triggers: insomnia, stress, dehydration; adequate analgesia in labour; counsel that seizure risk in labour is low but higher than during pregnancy.

(c)
Continue antiepileptic drugs during labour and postnatally; long-acting benzodiazepines (e.g. clobazam) if very high peripartum risk; evaluation by EEG, ECG, blood tests, CT or MRI; support postpartum to limit sleep deprivation, stress and pain.

(a)
Primigravida at 40 weeks with breech presentation and pre-eclampsia; procedure: emergency lower segment caesarean section (delivery of fetus, placenta and membranes through abdominal and uterine incisions) under spinal anaesthesia.

(b)
• Pre-op: explain and obtain informed consent; record weight, BP, pulse, temperature; remove make-up and jewellery; anaesthetist visit; FBC, group and save/cross-match; fasting and antacids; urinary catheter; wedge or tilt to prevent supine hypotension; safety check. Diagnoses: acute pain, risk of infection (ruptured membranes), anxiety, risk of unstable BP.
• Intra-op: transverse lower abdominal incision; transverse lower uterine segment incision; baby delivered (possible fundal pressure) and placenta removed; uterine incision closed in two layers, rectus sheath and skin sutured; vagina swabbed for clots and bleeding.
• Post-op: Syntocinon 5 IU; monitor haemorrhage and infection; analgesia and thromboprophylaxis; observations every 15 minutes, every 30 minutes for 2 hours, then hourly; early mobilisation and hydration; remove catheter once mobile; wound care; baby stays with mother.

(c)
Hypotension and post-dural puncture headache (managed with IV fluids, medicines, conservative or specific treatment); haemorrhage, infection, thromboembolism; Mendelson's syndrome (chemical pneumonitis from gastric reflux during general anaesthesia) prevented by antacid therapy and cricoid pressure.

(d)
Provide breastfeeding support and discharge planning/counselling.
questions.question:
Mrs A, a 24-year-old primigravida (G1P0+0) at 40 weeks, presents with headache, dizziness, leaking per vagina and slight labour pains. Findings: breech presentation, fetal heart rate 142, cervix 2 cm dilated and 60-70% effaced, membranes ruptured with clear liquor, blood pressure 140/95 mmHg, pulse 88, temperature 37.0 C, oedema +1 and mild pallor. She is prepared for an emergency lower segment caesarean section under spinal anaesthesia.
(a) State the diagnosis and name the procedure.
(b) Describe the pre-operative, intra-operative and post-operative nursing care.
(c) Identify the complications to monitor and their prevention.
(d) State the patient education and discharge planning.

(a) Describe the pathophysiology and transmission of rubella and congenital rubella syndrome.
(b) State the classification by timing of infection.
(c) State how the timing relates to the common complications.
(d) Explain how the virus may affect distant body systems.
(e) State the resulting functional deficit.
(f) State the related nursing management and health education.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Rubella (German measles), a Togavirus, spreads by respiratory droplets; replicates in nasopharynx and regional nodes then systemically; incubation 14-21 days; contagious about 7 days before to 7 days after the rash.
• In pregnancy it crosses the placenta, causing CRS; infants shed virus in nasopharyngeal secretions and urine for up to a year.

(b)
Risk: first trimester (0-11 weeks) up to 90% affected; second trimester (12-20 weeks) about 20%; third trimester generally unaffected.

(c)
• Classic triad: sensorineural deafness (58%), eye abnormalities (43%), congenital heart disease (50%).
• Other: hepatosplenomegaly, intellectual disability, microcephaly, low birth weight, thrombocytopenic purpura, blueberry-muffin rash, micrognathia, radiolucent bone disease.

(d)
• Heart (PDA, pulmonary artery stenosis), eyes (cataracts, retinopathy, glaucoma), ears, brain, liver, spleen, blood, bones.
• Late effects: diabetes mellitus, thyroid dysfunction, progressive encephalopathy.

(e)
Deficit: hearing impairment, vision loss, cardiac insufficiency, developmental delay, growth retardation.

(f)
• Diagnosis: IgM, IgG rise, RT-PCR, amniocentesis; supportive care: cardiac drugs/surgery, hearing aids or cochlear implants, cataract surgery, feeding support, anticonvulsants and early intervention, developmental monitoring, multidisciplinary follow-up.
• Prevention: MMR vaccine at least one month before pregnancy (live vaccines contraindicated in pregnancy); prenatal IgG screening; non-immune women vaccinated postpartum.
• Public health: national immunisation (MMR at 12-15 months, booster 4-6 years), surveillance, notification, health education, herd immunity.
• Fomites: infants with CRS can contaminate objects with virus from nasopharyngeal secretions and urine.

questions.question:
Ten days after delivery a woman has a fever with a foul-smelling vaginal discharge. She delivered with an episiotomy and perineal and vaginal lacerations.
(a) Identify the condition and explain its pathophysiological basis.
(b) State the priority nursing assessment and immediate interventions.
(c) State the definitive medical management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Puerperal pyrexia (febrile condition within 14-21 days of delivery) due to genital tract infection (puerperal sepsis): infection of the episiotomy wound, perineal, vaginal and cervical lacerations and the placental site, which may spread to the fallopian tubes, ovaries and peritoneum. Other causes: urinary tract infection, malaria, amoebic dysentery, typhoid, pneumonia, breast engorgement, mastitis or abscess, thrombophlebitis and phlebothrombosis.

(b)
• Rest in bed; reduce temperature by fanning, exposure or tepid sponging; isolate or barrier nurse during investigations; examine breast, chest, throat and genital tract; review type of labour and mode of delivery.
• Investigations: midstream urine (pus cells, albumin, culture and sensitivity), cervical or high vaginal swab, blood film for malaria parasites, blood culture if septicaemia is suspected, WBC, PCV or Hb, wound swab, chest X-ray and sputum, stool if diarrhoea.

(c)
Investigate the cause, identify the organism and treat appropriately (specific treatment once diagnosed); where malaria is endemic give antimalarials after thick and thin films are sent; good nutrition, adequate fluids and rest are important; notifiable condition for controlling spread and statistics.

(a)
• Malaria in pregnancy: Plasmodium parasites in the blood of a pregnant woman transmitted by the Anopheles mosquito (P. falciparum and P. vivax pose the greatest threat). Predisposing: pregnancy-related immunosuppression, hormonal changes, unsanitary areas, sequestration of parasites in the placenta (placental malaria).
• Diagnosis: clinical assessment, blood tests, PCR.

(b)
Maternal: severe anaemia, miscarriage, death. Neonatal: jaundice, respiratory distress, intrauterine demise, premature delivery, low birth weight, neonatal death.

(c)
• Treatment: artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs), most effective for falciparum malaria (artemisinin reduces parasites in the first 3 days; the partner drug eliminates the rest).
• Midwifery care: insecticide-treated nets, prophylaxis, IPTp, iron/folate supplementation, routine screening at antenatal visits, fetal monitoring for IUGR, personalised antenatal plans, health education.
• Nursing diagnoses: hyperthermia, impaired tissue perfusion, fluid volume deficit, knowledge deficit, risk of maternal injury.
questions.question:
A pregnant woman in a tropical area during the rainy season has intermittent fever, chills, headache, myalgia, fatigue, nausea and vomiting, with signs of anaemia.
(a) Identify the condition and state the predisposing factors.
(b) State the maternal and neonatal complications.
(c) Outline the management options and justify the priority intervention.

A newborn girl born after a breech presentation in a primigravid pregnancy with a history of oligohydramnios is examined on a firm surface. Pressure from the front makes the left femoral head slip out over the posterior acetabulum and back in; pressure from behind can make the head slip forward into the acetabulum.
(a) Identify the condition and the tests.
(b) State the predisposing factors and pathophysiology.
(c) Outline the nursing/medical management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Congenital hip dysplasia (abnormal tissue development of the hip present at birth): acetabular dysplasia, subluxation (partial dislocation) or dislocation. Barlow's test finds a dislocatable/unstable hip; Ortolani's test shows a dislocated head slipping into the acetabulum.

(b)
Common with oligohydramnios or breech; more in primigravidae, higher in girls, left hip more often. Maternal hormones (especially oestrogen) increase pelvic laxity and the newborn's joints are lax; mechanical factors and intrauterine posture.

(c)
• Examination by an experienced practitioner with the baby relaxed on a firm surface (inexperience worsens trauma); report abnormal findings and refer for ultrasound and orthopaedic surgeon; prenatal ultrasound is possible.
• Pavlik harness or splint keeps the hips flexed and abducted at 60 degrees; do not remove frequently (e.g. for bath and napkin change); support the parents.

(a)
PID is a serious infection of the uterus, fallopian tubes and ovaries, commonly from untreated STIs such as chlamydia and gonorrhoea.

(b)
• Risk factors: multiple partners, previous STIs, early sexual activity, douching, inconsistent condom use.
• Presentation: lower abdominal pain, abnormal discharge, dyspareunia, fever and chills, dysuria, irregular bleeding.
• Diagnosis: cervical motion, uterine or adnexal tenderness; raised WBC, positive STI tests, CRP; ultrasound or laparoscopy for tubo-ovarian abscess or adhesions.

(c)
• Mild-moderate: outpatient ceftriaxone 500 mg IM single dose with doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 14 days with or without metronidazole 500 mg twice daily.
• Severe: inpatient IV ceftriaxone 2 g daily with doxycycline and metronidazole IV.
• Refer for fever above 38.5 C, severe pain, tubo-ovarian abscess, no response after 72 hours, suspected peritonitis or sepsis.

(d)
Spread produces tubo-ovarian abscess, pelvic adhesions, peritonitis or sepsis.

(e)
Deficit: long-term reproductive consequences affecting family planning goals; active PID is an absolute contraindication to IUD insertion; sterilisation contraindicated during active infection.

(f)
• Pain management, counselling and education, follow-up care and record keeping.
• Challenges: delayed diagnosis, antimicrobial resistance, access to care.
• Partner treatment and safe sex: partner testing is done for suspected infections in family planning.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the pathophysiology and causes of pelvic inflammatory disease.
(b) State the risk factors and clinical presentation.
(c) State how severity relates to complications and referral.
(d) Explain how the infection may affect the reproductive tract and other aspects of health.
(e) State the resulting functional deficit.
(f) State the related nursing management and health education.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Periventricular/intraventricular haemorrhage (PVH/IVH), the most common and serious intracranial haemorrhage; central nervous system. Grade 1 subependymal/germinal matrix, Grade 2 extension into the lateral ventricle, Grade 3 with post-haemorrhagic hydrocephalus, Grade 4 parenchymal haemorrhage.

(b)
Fragile germinal matrix capillaries (8-28 weeks) without supporting muscle or collagen rupture with haemodynamic changes; CSF outflow may be blocked and ventricles dilate; contributory: acidosis, hypotension, hypertension, RDS requiring ventilation, rapid sodium bicarbonate, pneumothorax, PDA.

(c)
Other haemorrhages: primary subarachnoid, parenchymal, subaponeurotic, periventricular leukomalacia, haemorrhage with coagulopathies.

(d)
• Assess and screen by cranial ultrasound with serial scans; prevention - prenatal steroids to the mother, postnatal surfactant.
• Aim for haemodynamic stability: meet needs for respiration and acid-base balance, circulation, temperature, nutrition, elimination; evaluate continuously. Analgesics/sedatives (morphine, fentanyl), pancuronium if ventilated, dopamine/dobutamine.
• Prognosis: Grades 1 and 2 usually good; massive Grade 4 usually dies within 48 hours; survivors risk convulsions, cerebral atrophy, hydrocephalus and need long-term neurological follow-up.
questions.question:
A preterm baby born before 32 weeks and weighing less than 1500 g, who had hypoxia around the time of birth and is on mechanical ventilation, develops frequent apnoeic episodes, bradycardia, pallor, metabolic acidosis and convulsions. Cranial ultrasound is requested.
(a) Identify the condition and the body system affected.
(b) State the structures or functions compromised.
(c) List the differential conditions.
(d) Give the nursing reasoning and prioritisation of care.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM): women without previously diagnosed diabetes develop chronic hyperglycaemia during pregnancy (impaired glucose tolerance from pancreatic beta-cell dysfunction on chronic insulin resistance); affects about 16.5% of pregnancies.
• Risk factors: overweight and obesity, advanced age, family history of diabetes, inactivity, prediabetes, previous GDM, polycystic ovary syndrome, previous baby over 9 pounds (4.1 kg).
• Diagnosis: screening at 24-28 weeks with 75 g OGTT after overnight fast of 8-14 hours; plasma glucose fasting and at 2 hours (2-hour cut-off 140 mg/dl or 7.8 mmol/l); repeat OGTT 6 weeks or more after delivery.

(b)
Mother: increased risk of type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease. Baby: macrosomia and birth complications; later obesity, type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease.

(c)
• Monitor vital signs; lifestyle education (high-fibre diet, routine exercise); routine monitoring of blood glucose and urinalysis; foot and skin care; teach insulin self-injection and fingersticks; treatment with insulin, metformin and glyburide.
• Nursing diagnoses: deficient fluid volume; imbalanced nutrition.
questions.question:
A pregnant woman who is obese, of advanced maternal age, has a family history of diabetes, a previous baby above 4.1 kg and polycystic ovary syndrome complains of excessive thirst, hunger, fatigue, frequent urination and a dry mouth.
(a) Identify the condition and list the risk factors.
(b) State the complications/consequences.
(c) Outline the management options and justify the priority intervention.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Breast engorgement, occurring from the third day of the puerperium; more common in primiparae and varies from slight to severe.

(b)
Venous congestion of the breasts; full breasts result from inadequate emptying, and stagnant milk may cause pain, pyrexia and infection.

(c)
• Support breasts with a good brassiere or binder; analgesics; hot bathe before feeds and stroke gently towards the nipples; in severe cases do not put the baby to the breast or express until the breasts are soft.
• Prevention: educate to express colostrum in the last six weeks of pregnancy; baby sucks at regular intervals from 6 to 12 hours after birth if mother and baby are well; manually express and empty breasts after feeds.
questions.question:
On the third day after delivery a primiparous woman has hard, tense, painful breasts with shiny stretched skin, prominent dilated veins, flattened nipples and a low-grade fever.
(a) Identify the condition.
(b) State the predisposing factors and pathophysiology.
(c) Outline the nursing management and prevention.

(a) Define spurious labour and state its characteristics, causes and care.
(b) Define prolonged labour and state causes, signs and management.
(c) Explain why some women are more susceptible to prolonged labour.
(d) Distinguish between spurious labour and prolonged labour.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Spurious (prodromal) labour is false labour: regular contractions for over 6 hours without progressive cervical dilatation or effacement on two vaginal examinations 4 hours apart; appears 1-2 weeks before true labour in primigravidae, a few days in multiparae.
• Characteristics: dull pain in lower abdomen and groin, no effect on dilatation, pain not intensifying, contractions up to a minute and never closer than five minutes.
• Causes: third trimester, anxiety, stress. Care: rest, gentle touch, warm pad or shower, left side lying or sitting, hydration; diagnoses: acute pain, anxiety.

(b)
• Prolonged labour: failure to progress; over 20 hours in first-time mothers and over 14 hours in others (another definition: exceeding 24 hours, or 12 hours of established labour); in latent or active phase.
• Causes: malpresentation, uterine contraction problems, cervical dystocia, CPD.
• Signs: labour over 18 hours, dehydration, exhaustion, tachycardia, ketosis, uterine tenderness, fetal distress, uterine rupture.
• Management: assisted vaginal delivery or caesarean, position changes, comfort, oxytocin or analgesics, continuous fetal monitoring, hydration, rest, emotional support.

(c)
Most common in primigravidae; hypotonic action, CPD, malpresentation, older primigravidae.

(d)
• Spurious: no cervical change, contractions do not progress, resolves with comfort measures; a precursor of real labour.
• Prolonged: slow dilatation (1 cm/hour not achieved), may become obstructed; maternal complications infection, rupture, future incontinence; fetal: cerebral damage, asphyxia, shoulder dystocia.
• Latent phase normal average 8.6 hours; prolonged at 20 hours or more; diagnosis may be wrong if false labour is mistaken.
• Partograph is used to diagnose obstruction in time.

questions.question:
(a) Define abnormal (dysfunctional) uterine action and classify it.
(b) Describe hypotonic uterine action: features, types, effects and management.
(c) Describe incoordinate (hypertonic) uterine action: features and management.
(d) Explain why some women are more susceptible to abnormal uterine action.
(e) Distinguish between hypotonic and hypertonic uterine action.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Abnormal action is malfunction of the uterine muscles from neuromuscular disharmony: hypotonia, incoordinate action (hypertonic lower segment, colicky uterus, constriction ring, spurious labour) and cervical dystocia; over-efficient action (precipitate labour) is also classified.

(b)
• Hypotonia: poor tone, weak infrequent contractions with little pain, uterus may be indented at the peak; dilatation slow and labour prolonged.
• Primary hypotonia occurs at onset of labour; secondary hypotonia follows an exhausted uterus after labour is established.
• Effects: prolonged labour, mother distressed, dehydrated and demoralised, fetal distress, infection, PPH.
• Management: ultrasound to exclude CPD; assess FHR, liquor and maternal TPR/BP; empty bladder; ambulation; oxytocin 5 IU in 500 ml 5% dextrose; amniotomy if cervix over 3 cm; C/S for CPD, maternal or fetal distress; vacuum if over 6 cm, forceps if she cannot bear down.

(c)
• Hypertonic/incoordinate: frequent contractions with slow dilatation, severe back pain before and after a palpable contraction, loss of fundal dominance and reversed polarity, early bearing down causing cervical oedema, fetal distress from interference with placental circulation.
• Management: determine the cause; LSCS if CPD; record vital signs, intake and output, urine for albumin and acetone; FHR quarter-hourly; adequate IV fluid; check dilatation; pethidine/antispasmodics and epidural analgesia; C/S for failure or fetal distress.

(d)
Predisposing factors: older age, elderly primigravidae, malpresentation/disproportion, post-maturity, over-distension (multiple pregnancy), premature rupture of membranes, emotional tension; hypotonia also with anaemia and improper analgesic use.

(e)
• Hypotonic: weak, infrequent, short, little pain, intact membranes, treated with oxytocin or amniotomy.
• Hypertonic: frequent, painful contractions with marked low backache, lost polarity (often occipitoposterior), premature rupture of membranes; oxytocin is not the treatment (analgesia and antispasmodics instead).
• Complications: hypotonic - infection, PPH, shoulder dystocia, cerebral palsy, neonatal hypoglycaemia.
• Hypertonic - delayed labour, uterine rupture, PPH, exhaustion, fetal distress, oxygen deprivation, meconium aspiration.

(a)
Constriction ring dystocia, a form of colicky uterus (incoordinate uterine action); a rare localised spasm at the junction of upper and lower segments, may arise in any stage but common in late first and early second stage.

(b)
Malpresentations and malpositions; clumsy intra-uterine manipulation (internal version) under light anaesthesia; early rupture of membranes; improper use of oxytocin (in hypertonic inertia or IM oxytocin).

(c)
The uterus becomes irritable and moulds round the fetus; a ring forms between the segments; diagnosed by feeling the ring with a hand in the uterine cavity. Maternal effects: prolonged first and second stage, retained placenta, PPH.

(d)
Drugs such as anaesthesia may be used to relax the contraction; determine the cause; careful record of vital signs, fluid intake and output, urine for albumin and acetone; FHR quarter-hourly; adequate IV fluid; check cervical dilatation; report maternal and fetal distress promptly; LSCS if CPD.
questions.question:
A woman in late first stage of labour receiving oxytocin, after an intra-uterine manipulation, has a localised spasm of circular muscle fibres at the junction of the upper and lower uterine segments that may encircle the fetus.
(a) Identify the condition.
(b) State the predisposing factors.
(c) Explain the pathophysiology and effects.
(d) Outline the nursing/midwifery management.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Trichomoniasis, a common curable STI caused by Trichomonas vaginalis, spread through semen and vaginal fluids. Predisposing: unprotected sex, multiple sexual partners, history of other STIs, previous trich.
• Diagnosis: wet mount microscopy, NAAT, rapid trichomonas test (e.g. OSOM), Pap smear, cell culture.

(b)
Mother: premature rupture of membranes, preterm delivery, genital inflammation, increased risk of other STIs and HIV acquisition. Fetus: low birth weight, long-term disabilities, fetal death.

(c)
• Admit; check vital signs; history; emotional support; health education on diagnosis, treatment and recovery; pain management; antibiotics such as metronidazole; monitor for preterm birth and death.
• Nursing diagnoses: acute pain and anxiety. Priority justification: metronidazole treats the infection that causes the complications.
questions.question:
A pregnant woman with multiple sexual partners and unprotected sex complains of a thin, foamy greenish offensive vaginal discharge with soreness, and pain on passing urine or during intercourse.
(a) Identify the condition and state the predisposing factors.
(b) State the maternal and fetal complications.
(c) Outline the management options and justify the priority intervention.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Sickle cell disease: inherited defective genes producing abnormal Hb (HbS). Risk: family history; two carrier parents give each child 25% chance of SCD, 50% SCT, 25% unaffected; one parent with SCD gives SCT; sub-Saharan African and other ancestries; pregnancy itself does not increase risk.

(b)
Maternal: increased mortality, pre-eclampsia and eclampsia, venous thromboembolism, pain crises, infection, acute chest syndrome, worsening anaemia, acute splenic sequestration, proteinuria, hepatic dysfunction. Fetal: mortality, prematurity, IUGR and small for gestational age.

(c)
• Pre-conception: education, partner and prenatal screening, 5 mg folic acid from 6 weeks before conception, vitamin D, penicillin prophylaxis, vaccinations, stop unsafe medications, hydration. Antenatal: shared obstetric and haematology care every 2-4 weeks, VTE assessment, growth scans, transfusion, crisis prevention (rest, warmth, treat infection).
• Labour: epidural option, compression stockings, keep warm and hydrated, oxygen, prophylactic antibiotics, active third stage, avoid labour over 12 hours. Postpartum: vigilant observation, analgesia, early mobilisation, VTE prophylaxis, contraception, neonatal screening.
• Priority: adequate hydration is repeated at every stage to maintain circulation and prevent crisis.
questions.question:
A woman with sickle cell disease (both parents carry the sickle cell gene) is pregnant. She has fatigue, shortness of breath, periodic pain crises, yellow eyes, pale skin and nail beds and frequent infections.
(a) Identify the condition and state the risk factors.
(b) State the maternal and fetal complications.
(c) Outline the management options across pregnancy, labour and the postpartum period and justify the priority intervention.

(a) Define obstetric shock and describe its pathophysiology.
(b) State the classification/types of shock and the grades of haemorrhagic shock.
(c) State how the types relate to the common complications and organ effects.
(d) Explain how shock affects distant body systems.
(e) State the resulting functional deficit.
(f) State the related nursing management and health education.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Shock is inability of the circulation to provide adequate tissue perfusion, causing cellular hypoxia and organ damage; a systemic disorder in which perfusion is decreased or poorly distributed; incidence 0-3%; untreated it becomes irreversible.

(b)
• Haemorrhagic/hypovolaemic (most common): up to 1000 ml compensated, 1000-1500 ml mild, 1500-2000 ml moderate, over 2000 ml severe.
• Non-haemorrhagic: septic, anaesthesia-related, cardiogenic, neurogenic, embolism; anaphylactic shock is also included.

(c)
• Hypovolaemic causes: uterine atony, abortion, ectopic, trophoblastic disease, placenta praevia, abruption, ruptured uterus, traumatic PPH.
• Septic shock (1 in 8000; maternal mortality up to 30% in septic shock, neonatal up to 40%): from pyelonephritis, endometritis, septic abortion, uterine perforation, wound infection; warm phase (vasodilatation) then cold phase (vasoconstriction, raised CVP, lactic acidosis, ARDS, DIC).
• Neurogenic shock: acute inversion, rapid evacuation of uterine contents, vasovagal stimulation, spinal anaesthesia.

(d)
Brain: reduced consciousness; lungs: impaired gas exchange; kidneys: ischaemic tubules, oliguria/anuria; gut: ischaemia; liver: metabolism and bilirubin conjugation cease; multi-organ failure with DIC.

(e)
Deficit: altered consciousness, air hunger, renal failure, altered liver function, respiratory and cardiac failure.

(f)
• Call for help, airway, oxygen 6-8 L/min, two wide-bore lines, fluids, arrest haemorrhage, warmth, catheter, legs elevated; vasopressors (dopamine), steroids, bicarbonate.
• Septic shock: ICU, central line, 2-4 L saline, cultures and antibiotics, find and remove the source (hysterectomy, drainage).
• Monitoring: CVP, pulse, BP, urine output, wedge pressure.
• Health education: proper training in third-stage management prevents inversion.

questions.question:
During a vaginal birth the head is born but the shoulders fail to pass through the pelvis spontaneously. The woman is of short stature, has diabetes and is obese; the baby is macrosomic and the labour was prolonged or followed an operative delivery.
(a) Identify the condition and the risk factors present.
(b) State the complications that may follow for the mother and the baby.
(c) Outline the management options and justify the priority intervention.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Shoulder dystocia: failure of the shoulders to traverse the pelvis spontaneously, requiring additional manoeuvres after birth of the head; it occurs in about 0.2% to 3% of vaginal deliveries.
• Risk factors: maternal - short stature, diabetes, obesity; fetal - macrosomia; labour and delivery - operative delivery, prolonged labour.

(b)
• Maternal: maternal death from uterine rupture; maternal haemorrhage.
• Fetal/neonatal: fetal mortality, birth asphyxia, brachial plexus trauma; fracture of the clavicle or humerus can also occur.

(c)
• Non-invasive procedures: change in maternal position, McRoberts manoeuvre, suprapubic pressure, all-fours position.
• Rotational manoeuvres: Rubin manoeuvre, Woods manoeuvre, birth of the posterior arm, Zavanelli manoeuvre.

(a)
• Phototherapy is skin exposure to coloured light that causes geometric photoisomerisation, changing trans-bilirubin into the water-soluble cis-bilirubin isomer so it can be excreted.
• Used for neonatal jaundice with hyperbilirubinaemia; intensive phototherapy is an intervention; exchange transfusion is used if bilirubin exceeds 428 micromol/l (25 mg/dl) or phototherapy fails.

(b)
• Light source: lamps, spotlights, fibre-optic blankets; blue light, wavelength 420-500 nm.
• Positioned 50 cm above the infant with the largest surface area possible exposed.

(c)
• Expose as much skin as possible; shield eyes and genital area; remove shields at least once per shift and assess eyes for infection or irritation.
• Monitor skin temperature frequently; increase fluid intake as prescribed; reposition every 2 hours; provide stimulation.
• Educate parents that stools and urine may be green; early frequent feeds (up to 12 times per day); maintain blood glucose.

(d)
Complications: dehydration, increased insensible water loss, loose stools, irritability or lethargy, skin rashes, overheating, retinal injury.

(e)
• Shield eyes and genitals; monitor temperature; reposition regularly.
• Report jaundice in the first 24 hours to the physician; monitor for signs of kernicterus.

(f)
• Eye shielding prevents retinal injury; fluids and feeding counter dehydration and loose stools; temperature checks prevent overheating.
• Neglect of treatment risks kernicterus with athetosis, hearing loss and intellectual deficits.
questions.question:
(a) Describe phototherapy: mechanism and indications.
(b) State the technique and equipment.
(c) State the nursing responsibilities during phototherapy.
(d) State the complications.
(e) State the safety precautions for safe practice.
(f) Explain the rationale behind the nursing actions and the complications that follow when they are neglected.

(a) Describe brachial plexus trauma in the newborn: anatomy, causes and types.
(b) State the diagnostic evaluation and management.
(c) Explain why some babies are more susceptible.
(d) Distinguish between Erb's palsy and Klumpke's palsy.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Facial and brachial plexus nerves are the most commonly traumatised in birth; spinal cord injury is very rare.
• The brachial plexus is a network in neck and shoulder from nerve roots C5-C8 and T1; trauma ranges from oedema and haemorrhage to tearing.
• Four types (Narakas): Erb-Duchenne (C5-C6), extended Erb (C7), Klumpke (C8-T1), total Erb-Klumpke (C5-T1) with complete paralysis, lack of sensation and circulatory problems.

(b)
• X-ray and ultrasound of clavicle, arm, chest, cervical spine and joints; MRI and electromyography for definite diagnosis.
• Management: avoid unnecessary movement; do not lift by arms or axilla; dress affected arm first, undress last; passive movement after about 2 weeks under a physiotherapist; regular follow-up.
• Most recover within 3 weeks; surgical exploration or microsurgical repair if no biceps recovery by 3 months, or total injury with no recovery by 1 month.

(c)
• Excessive lateral flexion, rotation or traction of the head and neck in vaginal breech birth or shoulder dystocia.
• More recently also linked to force exerted by the uterus, since occurrence is stable despite elective caesarean and skilled manoeuvres.

(d)
• Erb's: C5-C6, paralysis of shoulder muscles, biceps, elbow flexors and forearm supinators; arm limp, inwardly rotated, elbow extended, wrist pronated.
• Klumpke's: C8-T1; shoulder and upper arm unaffected but lower arm, wrist and hand paralysed - wrist drop, no grasp reflex, claw-like hand.
• Klumpke's may include cervical sympathetic injury producing Horner's syndrome: no sensation on the affected side, pupil constriction and ptosis.
• Extended Erb's (C7) adds finger extensor involvement with wrist and finger flexion.

questions.question:
A newborn whose mother had rubella in early pregnancy has cataracts, sensorineural hearing loss, a patent ductus arteriosus, microcephaly, low birth weight, hepatosplenomegaly, thrombocytopenic purpura and a characteristic blueberry-muffin rash.
(a) Identify the condition and the body systems affected.
(b) State the organs and functions compromised and the long-term effects.
(c) List the differential conditions.
(d) Give the nursing reasoning and prevention.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Congenital rubella syndrome (CRS): transplacental infection with rubella virus; classic triad of sensorineural deafness (about 58%), eye abnormalities (about 43%) and congenital heart disease (about 50%). Risk varies: up to 90% in first trimester, about 20% in second, generally unaffected in third.

(b)
Eyes (cataracts, retinopathy, glaucoma, microphthalmia), ears, heart (PDA, pulmonary artery stenosis, VSD), CNS (microcephaly, developmental delay, intellectual disability), liver/spleen, blood, skin, bones (radiolucent bone disease). Later: diabetes mellitus, thyroid dysfunction, progressive encephalopathy.

(c)
TORCH infections (toxoplasmosis, other viruses, rubella, cytomegalovirus, herpes) and syphilis (palmar rash, snuffles, hepatosplenomegaly); for postnatal rubella: measles, scarlet fever, roseola, erythema infectiosum and drug eruptions.

(d)
• Infants shed virus in nasopharyngeal secretions and urine for up to a year and can infect susceptible contacts. Supportive care: cardiac defects (drugs or surgery), hearing aids or cochlear implants, cataract surgery, enteral feeding if needed, anticonvulsants and early intervention, developmental monitoring and multidisciplinary follow-up.
• Prevention: MMR vaccination; WHO aimed to eliminate rubella and keep CRS below one per 100,000 live births.

questions.question:
Soon after the membranes rupture, the umbilical cord is seen lying ahead of the presenting part in the birth canal and fetal monitoring shows fetal compromise.
(a) Identify the condition and explain its pathophysiological basis.
(b) State the priority assessment and immediate interventions.
(c) State the definitive management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Umbilical cord prolapse: the cord slips ahead of the presenting part into the birth canal after the membranes have ruptured, causing cord compression and compromised blood flow to the fetus, with serious risk.
• Predisposing factors (cord presentation, where the cord lies between presenting part and cervix before rupture): high or ill-fitting presenting part, high parity, prematurity, malpresentation, multiple pregnancy, hydramnios.

(b)
• Diagnosis: physical examination with visualisation of the cord, fetal monitoring, patient reporting; monitor fetal wellbeing and summon medical aid.
• Relieve pressure on the cord: maternal positioning, manual elevation of the cord, avoid cord manipulation, bladder filling; in cord presentation do not rupture membranes, discontinue vaginal examination and assist the woman to a comfortable position.

(c)
Expedited delivery; caesarean section is the option for cord presentation.

questions.question:
(a) Define a high vaginal swab and state its indications.
(b) State the scenarios where it is critical.
(c) Describe the procedure.
(d) State how results are interpreted and the nursing responsibilities.
(e) State the safety precautions for safe practice.
(f) Explain the rationale behind the nursing actions and the complications that follow when they are neglected.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• HVS collects vaginal secretions from the upper vagina to identify infections or abnormalities; an essential pre-family planning investigation to ensure the reproductive tract is healthy.
• Indications: detect bacterial vaginosis, candidiasis, STIs (trichomoniasis, gonorrhoea, chlamydia); screen for contraindications to IUDs and hormonal methods; pre-conception care; baseline health assessment.

(b)
Critical for: previous STIs or PID, planning IUD insertion, pre-conception, recurrent vaginal symptoms, high-risk sexual behaviour.

(c)
• Lithotomy position; sterile speculum; sterile environment; sterile cotton-tipped swab or loop collects from the upper third of the vagina, avoiding the cervix.
• Swab placed immediately in transport medium; sent promptly to the laboratory.

(d)
Normal: lactobacilli, no pathogens, minimal WBCs, normal flora on culture, vaginal pH 3.8-4.5, supports safe initiation of IUD or hormonal contraception.

(e)
Sterile technique to prevent contamination; avoid the cervix; transport medium and prompt transport to preserve microorganisms.

(f)
• Untreated infection with an IUD can spread to the upper tract and cause PID.
• Infections can lead to infertility, ectopic pregnancy or chronic pelvic pain.
• Hormonal methods: infections may cause irregular bleeding or reduce effectiveness.
• Delay in transport degrades microbial viability, affecting result accuracy.

questions.question:
(a) Define neonatal jaundice and state its causes and risk factors.
(b) Describe signs and symptoms and diagnosis.
(c) Explain why some newborns are more susceptible.
(d) Distinguish between physiological and pathological jaundice.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Jaundice is yellow discolouration of skin, mucous membranes and sclerae caused by raised bilirubin; not a disease but a sign of an underlying condition.
• Causes: excess bilirubin from breakdown of red cells, internal bleeding, sepsis, viral/bacterial infections, mother-baby blood incompatibility, liver malfunction, enzyme deficiency, abnormal red cells that break down rapidly.

(b)
• Signs: yellow skin and sclerae, light stools, poor feeding, lethargy, changes in tone, high-pitched cry, seizures; bilirubin encephalopathy: phase one hypotonia and poor suck; phase two hypertonia, retrocollis, opisthotonus; phase three stupor, coma, shrill cry.
• Diagnosis: serum bilirubin; transcutaneous bilirubinometer after 35 weeks and over a day old.

(c)
• Risk factors: siblings with neonatal jaundice, East Asian or Mediterranean parents, preterm babies, poor feeding, maternal diabetes, bruising or cephalhaematoma, blood group incompatibility, congenital infection.
• Physiological jaundice reflects physiological immaturity; it occurs in 50% of term and 80% of preterm infants.

(d)
• Physiological: most common, no serious consequences; appears at 24-72 hours, peaks day 4-5 in term (day 7 preterm), disappears by 10-14 days.
• Pathological: appears within 24 hours or persists beyond 14 days, bilirubin rises over 5 mg/dl (85 micromol/l) per 24 hours or 0.5 mg/dl per hour, total above 19.5 mg/dl (331.5 micromol/l), conjugated bilirubin (dark urine).
• Pathological jaundice can cause neurodevelopmental problems: athetosis, hearing loss, rarely intellectual deficits.
• Breastfeeding/breast milk jaundice: appears at 24-72 hours, peaks day 5-15, disappears by week 3 with higher bilirubin levels.
• Management: hydration, early frequent feeding, report jaundice in first 24 hours, phototherapy, exchange transfusion.
• Erythroblastosis fetalis (jaundice within 24 hours): Rho(D) immune globulin to Rh-negative mothers within 72 hours of delivery of an Rh-positive baby.

questions.question:
(a) Define hydrocephalus and state its causes.
(b) Describe its clinical manifestations in infants and children.
(c) Explain why infants are more vulnerable to head enlargement.
(d) Distinguish between communicating and non-communicating hydrocephalus.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Imbalance in CSF production and absorption: when production exceeds absorption CSF accumulates under pressure causing ventricular dilatation, raised intracranial pressure, progressive head enlargement, convulsion and mental disability.
• Congenital causes: Chiari malformations, spina bifida, aqueduct atresia/stenosis, Dandy-Walker malformation, intraventricular haemorrhage in preterm infants, infections. Acquired: space-occupying lesions, haemorrhage, CNS infection, meningitis, tumours, head trauma.

(b)
• Infants: rapid head growth beyond the 97th percentile, tense bulging non-pulsatile fontanelle, dilated scalp veins, Macewen's sign, frontal bossing, setting-sun sign, sluggish unequal pupils, irritability, lethargy, poor feeding, vomiting, high-pitched cry.
• Children: headache on awakening relieved by vomiting, papilloedema, strabismus, ataxia, irritability, apathy, confusion.

(c)
• Cranial bones fuse by the end of the third year, so enlargement occurs only if hydrocephalus begins before then; unfused skull bones allow the head to expand.
• 80-90% of babies with spina bifida (meningocele/myelomeningocele) develop hydrocephalus.

(d)
• Communicating (non-obstructive): impaired CSF resorption without flow obstruction, thought due to arachnoid granulation dysfunction; causes include subarachnoid or intraventricular haemorrhage, meningitis, Chiari malformation; includes normal pressure hydrocephalus.
• Non-communicating (obstructive): CSF-flow obstruction by compression or mass lesions - foramen of Monro, aqueduct of Sylvius, fourth ventricle, foramina of Luschka and Magendie (Dandy-Walker), or fibrosing meningitis.
• Hydrocephalus ex vacuo is compensatory enlargement from brain atrophy, not from raised CSF pressure.
• Diagnosis: Level II ultrasound prenatally, CT, MRI.
• Treatment: surgical removal of obstruction and shunting (ventriculoperitoneal) or third ventriculostomy.
• Shunt complications: infection and malfunction, overdrainage, subdural haematoma.

(a)
• Rupture of the uterus: a tear or opening in the uterine wall, complete or incomplete; dehiscence of an existing scar may also occur.
• Causes/risk factors: scar from previous caesarean (VBAC) or myomectomy; overdistension (multiple gestation, macrosomia); trauma; neglected labour with previous caesarean; oxytocin; prostaglandins in the presence of a scar; obstructed labour with excessive thinning of the lower segment (Bandl's ring).

(b)
• Signs: sudden severe abdominal pain or pain over the scar, abnormal FHR and pattern, fresh or scanty vaginal bleeding, maternal tachycardia, poor progress in labour.
• Complications: severe consequences for mother and fetus; hypovolaemic shock in the mother.

(c)
• Emergency caesarean section (prompt delivery of the fetus prevents further complications); haemodynamic support with IV fluids and blood products to prevent hypovolaemic shock; surgical repair depending on extent and location of the tear to prevent further haemorrhage.
• Priority justification: emergency delivery is crucial.
questions.question:
A woman in labour who has a previous uterine surgery scar, is receiving oxytocin and has obstructed labour develops sudden severe abdominal pain, abnormal fetal heart rate, fresh vaginal bleeding and tachycardia.
(a) Identify the condition and state its risk factors.
(b) State the complications and signs of intrapartum presentation.
(c) Outline the management options and justify the priority intervention.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Surgical separation of the symphysis pubis by partial incision of the cartilage so the pubic bones separate about 2 cm, enlarging the pelvis for an entrapped live fetus; done with episiotomy and instrumental delivery, usually in CPD.
• Indications (last resort when caesarean indicated but not feasible): head engaged and arrested over an hour with failed vacuum; CPD after failed trial of labour with at least 3/5 of head descended; shoulder dystocia or entrapped after-coming head when other manoeuvres fail.
• Contraindications: head not engaged, brow presentation, dead fetus (embryotomy), cervix not fully dilated, severe CPD with head more than 2/5 above the symphysis.

(b)
Equipment: scalpel, sutures, delivery set with episiotomy scissors, vacuum extractor, Foley catheter, sterile drape, compresses and gloves, 10% povidone iodine, 1% lidocaine.

(c)
Woman on her back, sterile prep and drape; epidural or spinal anaesthesia; small skin incision over the symphysis; joint cut or separated; baby delivered vaginally; incision closed with sutures or staples.

(d)
• Continuous monitoring of mother and baby; rest on the side avoiding forced abduction of the thighs for 7-10 days; mobilise with aid from day 3; no heavy work for 3 months.
• Pain relief, rehabilitation exercises, emotional support with open compassionate communication.
• Complications: bleeding at the wound; infection (daily dressings, amoxicillin 1 g three times daily for 5 days); temporary stress incontinence; urethral or bladder injury (catheter left in place); high maternal morbidity.

(e)
Use only as a last resort; regional anaesthesia; sterile technique; avoid forced thigh abduction.

(f)
• Rest and avoiding abduction protect the separated joint.
• Neglect leads to bleeding, infection, incontinence and severe pain.
questions.question:

(b) State the equipment and preparation.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Cholera is spread by the faecal-oral route; most vibrios die in the acid stomach, survivors colonise the small bowel and secrete cholera enterotoxin, which raises cAMP, causing massive secretion of water and electrolytes into the lumen and watery diarrhoea.
• Pregnant women are not at greater risk of infection than others; endemic areas, poverty and lack of safe water raise risk.

(b)
• Dysentery: bloody diarrhoea; bacillary (Shigella, shigellosis: nausea, vomiting, fever, cramps) and amoebic (Entamoeba histolytica, incubation 2-3 weeks, may spread to liver or lungs).
• Dehydration grades: severe (30 ml/kg Ringer's lactate over 30 minutes then 70 ml/kg), some (75 ml/kg ORS over 4 hours), none (ORS after each stool).

(c)
Maternal complications of both: severe dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, hypovolaemic shock, spontaneous abortion, preterm labour.

(d)
• Fetal: IUGR, extreme fetal heart rate, congenital defect risk, intrauterine fetal death.
• Amoebic infection can spread to the liver and lungs causing pus.

(e)
Deficit: fluid and electrolyte loss, weight loss, abdominal cramps, hypovolaemia.

(f)
• Midwifery: assess dehydration, intake/output, daily weight, fetal condition, IV fluids, nutrition, psychological support; stool tests.
• Loperamide is not advisable in pregnancy (fetal abnormalities); antibiotics for severe shigellosis (ciprofloxacin first-line; ceftriaxone or azithromycin second-line); paracetamol and promethazine.
• Health education: WASH (water, sanitation, hygiene) integrated by the midwife as a long-term strategy.
• Re-examine stool after resolution to confirm eradication.
questions.question:

questions.answerText:
(a)
Mastitis: infection of the breast tissue confined to a lobe; the affected lobe is hard, red and painful and the patient has pyrexia and rigors; it is usually a sequel to cracked nipples or engorged breasts (stagnant milk from inadequate emptying can cause pain, pyrexia and infection).

(b)
• Assess for puerperal pyrexia causes (breast, chest, throat, genital tract); temperature; do not allow the baby to suck on the affected breast; support the affected breast.
• Give antibiotics (the treatment for mastitis).

(c)
Mastitis may resolve or progress to breast abscess: the breast is enlarged, oedematous, painful and tender and the patient is ill; treatment is drainage of the abscess with appropriate systemic antibiotics, dressing of the incision and good support of the breast.
questions.question:
A breastfeeding mother with cracked nipples develops a hard, red, painful area confined to one lobe of the breast, with fever and rigors.
(a) Identify the condition and explain its pathophysiological basis.
(b) State the priority nursing assessment and immediate interventions.
(c) State the definitive management if it progresses.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Perineal trauma is the most frequent side effect of vaginal delivery; lacerations may be spontaneous or iatrogenic (episiotomy) on the perineum, cervix, vagina and vulva; most heal without long-term problems.
• The perineal body between the anus and vestibule is the common site.

(b)
• First degree: superficial vaginal mucosa, may involve perineal skin. Second degree: vaginal mucosa and perineal body. Third degree: anal sphincter involved - 3A less than 50% torn, 3B more than 50%, 3C external and internal sphincters. Fourth degree: rectal mucosa also torn.
• Third and fourth degree are obstetric anal sphincter injuries.

(c)
• Risk factors: nulliparity, operative vaginal delivery, midline episiotomy, Asian race, increased fetal weight, malpresentation including persistent occipitoposterior, advancing gestational age.
• Most lacerations heal without complications; severe ones can cause prolonged pain, sexual dysfunction and embarrassment.

(d)
Severe tears reach the sphincter and rectum (bowel function) and affect sexuality and relationships; urinary retention can occur.

(e)
Deficit: prolonged pain, sexual dysfunction, impact on wellbeing.

(f)
• Medical: suturing or tissue glue (mostly third and fourth degree), haemostatic first-degree tears, pain management, laxatives or stool softeners, monitor urinary retention.
• Nursing: hydration, vulval swabbing, analgesics, anxiety reduction, intake/output, iron-rich foods, education on sex life.
• Prevention: perineal protection - support the perineum with one hand and regulate head speed with the other, guide slow pushing.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the pathophysiology/overview of perineal laceration.
(b) State the classification by degree.
(c) State how the degrees relate to complications and risk factors.
(d) Explain how severe lacerations affect other structures and functions.
(e) State the resulting functional deficit.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Destructive operation (embryotomy): reduces the bulk of the dead fetus (head, shoulder girdle or trunk) for vaginal delivery. Indications: hydrocephalus even in a living fetus, dead fetus in obstructed labour with cephalic presentation, retained after-coming head of a dead breech, CPD with dead fetus, impacted malpresented dead fetus, interlocking twins.

(b)
• Before: no urgency; priority is maternal intensive care (IV line, hydration, antibiotics, urinary catheter); confirm fetal death, the obstacle, access (full dilatation, ruptured membranes); Foley; operating room under strict asepsis and anaesthesia with laparotomy prepared; explain benefits and complications and obtain consent.
• After: check uterine cavity (with antibiotic prophylaxis) and vaginal walls; oxytocin 5 or 10 IU IM or slow IV; in obstructed labour leave the Foley catheter for 14 days.
• Contraindications: living fetus (except anencephaly), true conjugate below 5.5 cm, partially dilated cervix, ruptured or impending rupture of uterus, pelvic tumours, cervical cancer.

(c)
Uterine rupture, uterovaginal canal injury, bladder or rectal injury, infection, PPH, shock, puerperal sepsis.
questions.question:
A woman has been in obstructed labour with a cephalic presenting fetus; fetal heart tones are absent on Doppler and ultrasound, the cervix is fully or nearly fully dilated, membranes are ruptured, and embryotomy is planned.
(a) Identify the procedure and the indications.
(b) Describe the preparation, procedural and after-care.
(c) Identify the complications to monitor for.

(a) Define cephalhaematoma and state its causes, characteristics and management.
(b) Describe the complications.
(c) Explain why some babies are more susceptible to scalp haemorrhages.
(d) Distinguish between cephalhaematoma and subaponeurotic haemorrhage.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Cephalhaematoma: effusion of blood under the periosteum covering a skull bone, from friction between the fetal skull and maternal pelvis in vaginal birth, which tears the periosteum from the bone.
• Causes: cephalopelvic disproportion, precipitate labour, vacuum-assisted birth.
• Characteristics: confined to one bone (multiple/bilateral possible); not present at birth, appears after 12 hours, enlarges over days and may persist for weeks; firm, non-pitting, does not cross a suture and is fixed.
• Management: no treatment; blood is absorbed and swelling subsides.

(b)
• Haemolysis of extravasated blood may cause hyperbilirubinaemia.
• A ridge of bone may be felt round the swelling from accumulation of osteoblasts.
• A skull fracture may lie beneath it (linear fractures usually need no treatment).

(c)
• Susceptible because fetal skull bones are not fused and the periosteum is adherent to the skull bone edges; risk factors include CPD, precipitate labour and vacuum extraction.
• Subaponeurotic haemorrhage is more often with vacuum birth, primiparae, severe dystocia, occipitolateral/posterior positions, preterm babies, precipitate birth, macrosomia, coagulopathies and male babies.

(d)
• Subaponeurotic haemorrhage (rare): excessive traction on veins above the periosteum pulls the epicranial aponeurosis from the periosteum; swelling is firm and fluctuant, increases, is persistent at birth, mobile (not fixed), can cross sutures into the neck and eyelids, and handling is painful.
• It is an emergency needing immediate medical help, stabilisation and blood transfusion; complications: excessive haemorrhage, shock, about 25% mortality.
• Cephalhaematoma, by contrast, is confined to one bone, does not cross sutures, is fixed and needs no treatment.

questions.question:
A newborn born to a mother after a forceps birth of a macrosomic baby has one eyelid that remains open, the mouth drawn over to the unaffected side, excessive drooling and difficulty sucking and swallowing.
(a) Identify the condition.
(b) State the predisposing factors.
(c) Explain the pathophysiology.
(d) Outline the nursing/midwifery management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Facial nerve palsy (unilateral facial paralysis), a birth nerve trauma; facial and brachial plexus nerves are the most commonly traumatised.

(b)
Compression by the mother's sacral promontory or misapplied forceps blade, especially with a macrosomic baby; compression may occasionally occur in the uterus.

(c)
The VII cranial nerve runs close to the skin surface and is therefore vulnerable to compression, resulting in unilateral facial palsy.

(d)
• No specific treatment; regular instillation of eye drops to lubricate the eyeball if the eyelid is open; alternative feeding positions to prevent malnutrition; babies usually adapt.
• Mild damage may resolve in weeks, severe damage may take months or years; cosmetic surgery may be needed for severely affected babies.

(a)
SCD is an inherited group of disorders from defective genes producing abnormal haemoglobin (HbS), making red cells sickle-shaped; pregnancy does not increase the risk because it is entirely genetic.

(b)
• Two carrier parents (each with one gene): each child 25% SCD, 50% sickle cell trait, 25% unaffected; both parents with SCD: all children SCD; one parent with SCD: children have trait.
• Most affected people are of sub-Saharan African descent; other ancestries include South America, Cuba, Central America, Saudi Arabia, India, Turkey, Greece and Italy.

(c)
• Signs: fatigue, shortness of breath, pain crises, swollen hands and feet, yellow eyes, pallor, infections, delayed growth.
• Maternal complications: increased mortality, pre-eclampsia and eclampsia, VTE, pain crises, acute chest syndrome, worsening anaemia, splenic sequestration. Fetal: mortality, prematurity, IUGR.

(d)
Effects on lungs (acute chest syndrome), kidneys (proteinuria, worsening renal disease), liver (hepatic dysfunction), vascular system (VTE), blood (anaemia).

(e)
Deficit: reduced oxygen-carrying capacity, recurrent pain, increased infection risk.

(f)
• Diagnosis: haemoglobin electrophoresis, CVS (11-14 weeks), amniocentesis (from 15 weeks).
• Pre-conception: education, partner screening, 5 mg folic acid, vitamin D, penicillin prophylaxis, vaccines, stop unsafe drugs, pre-marital counselling.
• Antenatal: shared care every 2-4 weeks, scans at set weeks, VTE assessment, transfusion, crisis prevention.
• Labour: epidural, stockings, warmth, hydration, oxygen, antibiotics, active third stage, avoid labour over 12 hours.
• Postpartum: vigilance, analgesia, mobilisation, VTE prophylaxis, contraception, neonatal screening; adequate hydration throughout.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the pathophysiology/genetics of sickle cell disease.
(b) State the types (SCD, SCT) and inheritance patterns.
(c) State how these relate to the common complications.
(d) Explain how the disease affects distant body systems in pregnancy.
(e) State the resulting functional deficit.
