questions.answerText:
(a)
• Cervical dystocia: inability of the cervix to dilate even with adequate contractions and effacement (hypertonia, hypotonia, colicky uterus and constriction ring are related forms of dysfunctional action).
• Primary: normal contractions, presenting part low, delay from a cartilaginous ring, scarring or congenital structural abnormality. Secondary: previous cervical trauma (e.g. Manchester repair, previous forcible D and C) or carcinoma of the cervix.

(b)
Maternal: rupture of the uterus, postpartum haemorrhage. Fetal: hypoxia, fetal distress, birth injuries, neonatal asphyxia.

(c)
• Caesarean section is the management for both primary and secondary cervical dystocia (labour is terminated by C/S); pethidine and antispasmodics may also be effective.
• Justification: the cervix fails to dilate despite good uterine contraction, so labour cannot progress and is terminated by caesarean section.
questions.question:
In a woman in labour the uterine contractions are good and regular and the cervix is effaced, yet it fails to dilate and the presenting part is low in the pelvis.
(a) Identify the condition and state its types and causes.
(b) State the maternal and fetal complications.
(c) Outline the management options and justify the priority intervention.

An infant has a rapidly enlarging head above the 97th percentile, a tense bulging anterior fontanelle, dilated scalp veins, frontal bossing, setting-sun eyes, irritability, poor feeding and vomiting. Insertion of a ventriculoperitoneal shunt is planned.
(a) Identify the condition and the diagnostic tests used.
(b) Describe the pre-operative, post-operative nursing care (intra-operative procedure).
(c) Identify the complications to monitor for and their prevention.
(d) State the patient education and discharge planning.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Hydrocephalus: imbalance between CSF production and absorption causing ventricular dilatation and raised pressure; communicating (impaired resorption) or non-communicating/obstructive (flow obstruction); associated with spina bifida and Arnold-Chiari malformation. Tests: Level II ultrasound prenatally, CT scan (most postnatal cases), MRI for complex lesions.

(b)
• Surgery: direct removal of an obstruction and shunt insertion to drain CSF to an extracranial compartment, usually the peritoneum (ventriculoperitoneal shunt); third ventriculostomy is a newer non-shunting procedure.
• Pre-op: assess head circumference, fontanelles, sutures and level of consciousness; irritability, feeding habits, high-pitched cry; support head and neck firmly; head skin care; small frequent feeds; encourage bonding.
• Post-op: as for raised ICP - daily head circumference, fontanelle size and fullness, behaviour; antibiotics and analgesics; shunt care.

(c)
Shunt infection (Staphylococcus epidermidis or aureus) and malfunction: rapid vomiting, severe headache, irritability, lethargy, fever, redness along the tract, fluid around the valve; overdrainage (headache, dizziness, nausea, slit ventricle syndrome); subdural haematoma from too rapid CSF reduction, peritonitis, abscess, organ perforation, fistulas, hernias, ileus.

(d)
Teach home care: normal age-appropriate activities, contact sports prohibited, recognise signs of raised ICP (school performance changes, intermittent headache, behaviour changes), frequent developmental screening and medical checkups.

(a)
Brachial plexus trauma (Narakas classification), nervous system: Erb-Duchenne palsy (C5-C6) in the first baby; Klumpke's palsy (C8-T1) in the second, with Horner's syndrome from cervical sympathetic trauma.

(b)
Erb: paralysis of shoulder muscles, biceps, elbow flexors and forearm supinators; extended Erb (C7) affects finger extensors. Klumpke: lower arm, wrist and hand paralysed, wrist drop, no grasp, shoulder and upper arm unaffected. Erb-Klumpke (C5-T1): complete paralysis of shoulder, arm and hand, lack of sensation and circulatory problems.

(c)
Facial nerve palsy, fractured clavicle or humerus, other birth injuries (phrenic nerve, recurrent laryngeal nerve, spinal cord injury).

(d)
• Assess: X-ray and ultrasound of clavicle, arm, chest, cervical spine and joints; MRI and electromyography.
• Implement: avoid unnecessary movement, never lift the baby by the arms or axilla, dress the affected arm first and undress last, passive movement under a physiotherapist after about 2 weeks.
• Evaluate: regular functional follow-up; most recover within 3 weeks; refer for surgical exploration/microsurgical repair if no biceps recovery by 3 months or no recovery of total injury by 1 month.
questions.question:
A newborn delivered after shoulder dystocia has a limp affected arm that is inwardly rotated with the elbow extended and the wrist pronated. Another baby has a paralysed lower arm and wrist with no grasp reflex, a claw-like hand, pupil constriction and eyelid ptosis.
(a) Identify the conditions and the body system affected.
(b) State the structures and functions compromised.
(c) List the differential conditions.
(d) Give the nursing reasoning and management using the nursing process.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Epidural blocks nerve transmission from lower spinal segments, giving sensory and motor blockade with the mother awake; spinal (subarachnoid block) temporarily disrupts transmission in the cord giving anaesthesia and analgesia of the lower body.
• Pudendal block anaesthetises perineum and vagina for instrumental births; general anaesthesia involves induction and maintenance of unconsciousness.

(b)
• Epidural: effective intra- and post-operative pain relief, mother alert, adjustable level.
• Spinal: quick preparation, reliable level, minimal systemic absorption so minimal fetal effect.

(c)
• Both: hypotension (spinal from sympathetic blockade) managed with IV fluids and drugs; post-dural puncture headache; epidural: mild-moderate back pain.
• General anaesthesia: Mendelson's syndrome - chemical pneumonitis from reflux of gastric contents; prevented by antacids and cricoid pressure.

(d)
• Observations (RR, HR, BP, pain, sedation) every 15 minutes, every half-hour for 2 hours, then hourly; observe until airway control, cardiorespiratory stability and communication regained.
• After regional block, may sit up if BP not low; eat and drink when hungry, then stop IV fluids; baby stays with mother.

(e)
Use a wedge or tilt table against supine hypotension; fasting and antacids; safety check before skin preparation; avoid inadvertent dural puncture.

(f)
• Close observation detects hypotension and respiratory depression early; antacids and cricoid pressure prevent aspiration.
• Neglect leads to hypotension, headache and chemical pneumonitis.
questions.question:
(a) Describe epidural and spinal (regional) anaesthesia for caesarean section.
(b) State advantages and indications.
(c) State the complications.
(d) State the nursing responsibilities and post-anaesthesia care.
(e) State the safety precautions for safe practice.
(f) Explain the rationale behind the nursing actions and the complications that follow when they are neglected.

A pregnant woman beyond 27 weeks has persistent headache, epigastric and right upper abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting, blurred vision and swelling of the face and hands. Blood pressure is high, there is protein in the urine, and blood work shows haemolysis, raised liver enzymes and low platelets.
(a) Identify the condition and the body systems involved.
(b) State the organs or functions compromised.
(c) List the differential conditions.
(d) Give the nursing reasoning and prioritisation of care using the nursing process.
questions.answerText:
(a)
HELLP syndrome (Haemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelets), a serious complication of pregnancy; occurs in 0.1%-0.6% of pregnancies and 4%-12% of those with pre-eclampsia, from week 27 to delivery or postpartum; classified by platelet count: Class I under 50,000/mm3, Class II 50,000-100,000, Class III 100,000-150,000.

(b)
Liver (distension, pain), blood (haemolysis, thrombocytopenia), vascular/renal/pulmonary systems: placental abruption, pulmonary oedema, DIC, ARDS, ruptured liver haematoma, acute renal failure; fetal IUGR, respiratory distress, fetal death.

(c)
Gestational hypertension, pre-eclampsia, eclampsia (other pregnancy blood pressure disorders).

(d)
• Assess/diagnose: vital signs; CBC, urine test, peripheral smear, LFTs (AST, ALT, bilirubin), ultrasound; diagnoses - ineffective tissue perfusion, acute pain, risk of maternal injury (seizures).
• Implement: complete bed rest; fetal monitoring and sonogram; educate on warning signs (seizures, bleeding); send blood and urine; give prescribed medication; prepare for delivery by labour or caesarean.

questions.question:
(a) Define talipes and describe its types.
(b) State the causes and management.
(c) Explain why some babies are more susceptible to talipes.
(d) Distinguish between talipes equinovarus and talipes calcaneovalgus.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Talipes (clubfoot): deformity from congenital or acquired contracture of foot muscles or tendons; types include talipes equinovarus and calcaneovalgus.
• It is among the commonest congenital deformities; facial clefting is the second most common after clubfoot.

(b)
• Occurs where intrauterine space is limited, as in multiple pregnancy, macrosomic fetus or oligohydramnios; may occur with spina bifida; family history.
• Mild form: foot can be easily turned to the correct position; passive exercise several times a day, encouraged by the midwife.
• Severe form: manipulation, splinting and/or surgical correction; seek the orthopaedic surgeon's advice.
• Ensure strapping or splints are not too tight and toes are well perfused.

(c)
Limited intrauterine space (multiple pregnancy, macrosomia, oligohydramnios), spina bifida, family history; more common in boys than girls.

(d)
• Talipes equinovarus (TEV): ankle plantar flexed downwards and front of the foot turned inwards (adducted).
• Talipes calcaneovalgus: the opposite position - foot dorsiflexed and everted.
• Both are managed by exercise, manipulation, splinting; severity determines surgery.
• Other skeletal abnormalities: polydactyly, syndactyly, achondroplasia, limb reduction anomalies, congenital hip dysplasia.

questions.question:
A woman who had a previous caesarean section with a low transverse uterine scar wants a vaginal birth in her next pregnancy and is offered a trial of labour after caesarean (TOLAC).
(a) Identify the procedure and the diagnostic/monitoring tool used.
(b) Describe the pre-labour, intrapartum and post-birth care.
(c) Identify the complication to monitor for and its prevention.
(d) State the patient education and discharge planning.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Trial of labour after caesarean (TOLAC) aiming for vaginal birth after caesarean (VBAC); monitored by cardiotocography (continuous electronic fetal monitoring).

(b)
• Before: assess the previous caesarean details, type of uterine incision (low transverse carries least rupture risk; ideally not more than one previous CS), maternal age and health, reason for prior CS, current pregnancy; interval of at least 18-24 months; woman and partner fully informed of risks and benefits.
• During: adequate supervision with continuous CTG, facilities for assisted birth readily available, sufficient progress in descent and dilatation, avoid induction of labour; emergency caesarean if uterine rupture or failed VBAC.
• After: benefits include fewer infections, blood clots and anaesthesia complications, shorter stay, quicker recovery, immediate skin-to-skin contact and breastfeeding.

(c)
Uterine rupture or dehiscence causing maternal and neonatal morbidity or mortality; prevented by careful selection, close monitoring and avoiding induction.

(d)
Give informed choice on the risks and benefits.

questions.question:
A pregnant woman living in an overcrowded, low-income setting has a chronic cough, low-grade fever, haemoptysis, chest pain, fatigue, weight loss and night sweats. The tuberculin skin test at her first prenatal visit is positive.
(a) Identify the condition and the body system affected.
(b) State the organs and functions compromised.
(c) Give the nursing reasoning and prioritisation of care.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Pulmonary tuberculosis in pregnancy (Mycobacterium tuberculosis, spread by droplets), affecting the respiratory system; a chest radiograph with abdominal shielding confirms a positive skin test.

(b)
Lungs (may spread to other organs); risks: spontaneous abortion, small-for-dates uterus, preterm labour, high perinatal mortality, ARDS; baby: low birth weight, sepsis, pneumothorax, neonatal mortality.

(c)
• Diagnoses: ineffective airway clearance and acute pain from prolonged coughing. Early detection and screening, collaboration with obstetrician and infectious disease specialist, nutritional and psychosocial support, education and counselling.
• Isoniazid, ethambutol, rifampicin and pyrazinamide can be given without apparent teratogenic effects; three negative sputum cultures before caring for the infant; infant on prophylactic INH if active TB in the home (mother on INH should not breastfeed or dosage adjusted); BCG prevention; postpartum follow-up.

(a)
Gonorrhoea (Neisseria gonorrhoeae, diagnosed by vaginal swab) and syphilis (Treponema pallidum, diagnosed by blood test): genitourinary/reproductive system and skin.

(b)
Untreated gonorrhoea: miscarriage, preterm delivery; baby: eye infection 1-4 days after birth, blindness, joint infection, blood infection. Syphilis: stillbirth, miscarriage, premature infants, damage to brain, eyes, ears, heart, skin, teeth, bones; blindness, deafness.

(c)
Other STIs: chlamydia, trichomoniasis, herpes simplex virus.

(d)
• Treat with antibiotics (syphilis by stage: benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM; neurosyphilis IV aqueous penicillin G); newborn eye prophylaxis at birth.
• Nursing: educate on safe sex and condoms; treat the partner; avoid sex with infected partner; assess heart murmur of aortic regurgitation, chest X-ray, neurologic and mental status, healing of genitals.
• Diagnoses: acute pain, risk for sexual dysfunction, disturbed body image, deficient knowledge.
questions.question:
A pregnant woman complains of abnormal vaginal discharge, burning on passing urine and pain during intercourse. Another pregnant woman has a non-itchy rash on the palms and soles, large grey lesions in the genital area, fever, sore throat and swollen lymph nodes. A blood test and a vaginal swab are requested.
(a) Identify the conditions and the body systems affected.
(b) State the organs and functions compromised, including for the fetus.
(c) List the differential conditions.
(d) Give the nursing reasoning and prioritisation of care.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Congenital cardiovascular defects occur when the heart or nearby vessels do not develop normally before birth; structural problems at birth involving walls, valves or vessels, changing blood flow; incidence about 5-8 per 1000 live births.
• Aetiology: most develop in the first 8 weeks of gestation from combined genetic and environmental factors.

(b)
• Simple (mainly acyanotic): ASD (incompetent foramen ovale commonest), VSD (20-25% of neonates with cardiac defects), valve stenosis, atresia, regurgitation; pulmonary valve stenosis commonest valve defect.
• Complex: tetralogy of Fallot (10-15%): pulmonary stenosis, large VSD, overriding aorta, right ventricular hypertrophy.
• Manifestations: rapid breathing, cyanosis, fatigue, poor circulation; many have few or no symptoms; no chest pain; murmurs not always pathological.

(c)
• Risk factors: drugs (phenytoin, lithium, alcohol), maternal viral infections such as rubella, maternal metabolic disorders (phenylketonuria, diabetes, hypercalcaemia), increased maternal age, antepartum bleeding, family recurrence.
• ASD incidence in Down syndrome is 20%.

(d)
• Acyanotic: oxygenated blood is shunted to the body and the infant stays pink - PDA, ASD/VSD, aortic stenosis, hypoplastic left heart, coarctation.
• Cyanotic: deoxygenated blood is shunted to the body and the infant is blue - tetralogy of Fallot, pulmonary atresia, tricuspid atresia, transposition of the great arteries.
• Management goals: improve cardiac function, remove fluid and sodium, decrease cardiac demands, improve tissue oxygenation; catheter procedures (ASD, pulmonary stenosis) or open-heart surgery; palliative procedure first if needed.
• Prevention: avoid unprescribed drugs and environmental pollution, health education in pregnancy; community support for the child.
• Antibiotic prophylaxis for endocarditis before and after surgery; lifelong cardiologist care after Fallot repair.
questions.question:
(a) Define congenital heart defects and state their incidence and aetiology.
(b) Describe the types of defects and their clinical manifestations.
(c) Explain why some babies are more vulnerable to congenital heart defects.
(d) Distinguish between acyanotic and cyanotic congenital heart defects.

A woman has just delivered and is bleeding heavily from an atonic uterus. She is pale, with a rapid thready pulse, low blood pressure, cold clammy skin, air hunger and blurred vision, and her urine output is falling.
(a) Identify the condition and name its commonest obstetric cause.
(b) Explain the pathophysiological basis.
(c) State the priority nursing assessment and the immediate interventions.
(d) Outline the definitive medical and surgical management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Haemorrhagic (hypovolaemic) shock, the most common cause of shock in obstetrics; the commonest cause of all is uterine atony in PPH (others: abortion, ectopic pregnancy, trophoblastic disease, placenta praevia, abruptio placentae, ruptured uterus, traumatic PPH).

(b)
The circulatory system cannot provide adequate tissue perfusion, causing cellular hypoxia and organ damage; it is a systemic disorder affecting multiple organ systems, and if untreated becomes irreversible as cellular damage develops.

(c)
• Assess CVP, pulse, blood pressure, urine output and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure, and clinical improvement in pallor, cyanosis, air hunger and sweating; speed is vital and rapid restoration of circulating volume is the key.
• Establish airway and give oxygen at 6-8 L/min; insert two wide-bore IV lines; elevate the legs (Trendelenburg tilt); keep the woman warm; insert a Foley catheter to measure urine output; intubate and ventilate for severe hypoxia, severe tachypnoea or coma.

(d)
• Replace volume with crystalloids first, plasma expanders (e.g. haemaccel), plasma protein fraction or fresh frozen plasma, then whole blood (preferably packed cells).
• Drugs: IV morphine for pain/tissue damage/irritability; hydrocortisone 1 g or dexamethasone 20 mg slowly IV; sodium bicarbonate 100 mEq IV if metabolic acidosis; dopamine 2.5-10 micrograms/kg/min is the vasopressor of choice.
• Ultrasound finds the cause of blood loss (e.g. retained placental tissue or membranes); surgery depends on cause: emergency caesarean for antepartum haemorrhage; laparotomy, internal iliac ligation or hysterectomy for severe PPH.

questions.question:
(a) Define precipitate labour.
(b) State its causes/predisposing factors.
(c) State its signs and symptoms and how it is diagnosed.
(d) State its maternal and neonatal complications and its management.
(e) Explain why some women are more susceptible to precipitate labour.
(f) Distinguish between premature (preterm) labour and precipitate labour.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Precipitate (precipitous) labour is unusually rapid labour and delivery, typically under 3 hours from onset of regular contractions to birth (some providers use under 5 hours); typical labour is 6-18 hours in primiparae and 2-10 hours in multiparae.

(b)
• It cannot be predicted; factors: placental abruption, prior births, previous rapid delivery, young maternal age, preterm delivery, lower birth weight, hypertensive disorders.
• Others: emotional and psychological factors, strong maternal pelvic musculature, high uterine contractility (over-efficient action), small fetus.

(c)
• Signs: intense contractions less than two minutes apart, short duration skipping early stages, sudden onset, intense pain, urgent need to push.
• Diagnosis: clinical history of rapid labours, examination of dilatation, effacement and fetal position, continuous fetal monitoring.

(d)
• Maternal: perineal tears and lacerations of cervix and vagina, PPH from uterine atony, rarely amniotic fluid embolism, shock, uterine inversion, sepsis, psychological trauma.
• Neonatal: fetal distress, intracranial haemorrhage, respiratory distress, clavicle fractures, brachial plexus injury and soft tissue damage.
• Management: rapid assessment and communication, IV opioids or nitrous oxide for pain, prepare sterile field and neonatal resuscitation, oxytocin after birth, episiotomy, examine mother and baby for injuries, emotional support; women with previous precipitate labour are admitted before the expected date.

(e)
• It is more common in multiparas who have strong uterine contractions, a small baby and a roomy pelvis.
• Risk is higher with prior births or previous rapid delivery, teenage mothers, preterm delivery and lower birth weight.

(f)
• Premature labour is defined by gestation: onset before 37 completed weeks (20-37 weeks) with regular contractions and cervical change; causes include infections, uterine anomalies, cervical insufficiency, multiple gestation; managed with tocolytics and corticosteroids; complicates as RDS.
• Precipitate labour is defined by duration (under 3 hours) at any gestation; risks are perineal lacerations, PPH and birth injuries.

questions.question:
During labour a woman suddenly becomes restless and abnormal in behaviour, then develops respiratory distress and cyanosis, collapses with hypotension and tachycardia, and bleeds from the placental site with signs of coagulation failure.
(a) Identify the condition.
(b) State the predisposing factors.
(c) Explain the pathophysiology.
(d) Outline the emergency nursing/midwifery management and the effect on the fetus.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Amniotic fluid embolism (AFE): rare, unpredictable and unpreventable; amniotic fluid enters the maternal circulation via the uterus or placental site and maternal collapse can progress rapidly. Premonitory signs: restlessness, abnormal behaviour, respiratory distress, cyanosis.

(b)
Can occur at any gestation, in labour and its aftermath, in early pregnancy and postpartum; breach of the barrier between maternal circulation and amniotic sac during raised intra-amniotic pressure (termination of pregnancy, placental abruption); artificial rupture of membranes and insertion of an intrauterine catheter.

(c)
Phase 1: pulmonary vasospasm causing hypoxia, hypotension, pulmonary oedema and cardiovascular collapse. Phase 2: left ventricular failure with haemorrhage, coagulation disorder/DIC and uncontrollable bleeding.

(d)
• Start resuscitation at once; call the emergency team; basic life support in a community setting before emergency services arrive; life support with high levels of oxygen.
• Fetus: perinatal mortality and morbidity are high; time from maternal collapse to birth must be minimal to avoid fetal compromise or death; outcome is poor outside hospital.

questions.question:
(a) Define herpes simplex infection in pregnancy and state its types.
(b) State signs, diagnosis and management.
(c) Explain why some babies are more susceptible to neonatal herpes.
(d) Distinguish between a primary first episode and recurrent maternal infection.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• HSV infection is one of the most common STIs in women of reproductive age; HSV-1 or HSV-2 may infect at any time in pregnancy and cause neonatal infection depending on trimester and whether primary or recurrent.
• HSV-1 mostly spreads by oral contact causing cold sores but can cause genital herpes; HSV-2 spreads sexually causing genital herpes.

(b)
• Signs: fever, body aches, sore throat (oral), headache, swollen lymph nodes, painful ulcer blisters, myalgia, itching, backache.
• Predisposing: immunosuppression, skin-to-skin contact, unprotected sex, stress.
• Diagnosis: serology, urine screening, swab, blood test. Management: admit, vital signs, history, nutrition, pain relief, emotional support; active herpes at labour onset is an indication for elective caesarean and contraindicates induction.
• Complications: mother - preterm labour, abortion, IUGR, rupture of membranes; fetus - congenital/neonatal herpes, long-term disabilities, death.

(c)
• Risk depends on whether the mother has a primary or recurrent episode and her antibodies; neonatal antibodies from the mother appear protective against recurrent infection.
• Genital HSV-1 is transmitted to the neonate more frequently than HSV-2.

(d)
• Primary first episode: first infection with painful vesicles of genitalia, vulva, vagina, cervix, urethra, lymphadenopathy, no antibodies; 30%-50% risk to the child.
• Non-primary first episode: first genital lesions but pre-existing antibodies to the other HSV type; risk probably as high as in primary infection.
• Recurrent: reactivated infection, even near delivery, with much lower risk to the baby.
• Antiviral treatment: acyclovir, valacyclovir and famciclovir.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the pathophysiology of syphilis in pregnancy.
(b) State the stages and the treatment by stage.
(c) State how the stages relate to the common complications.
(d) Explain how the infection spreads to the fetus and other body systems.
(e) State the resulting functional deficit.
(f) State the related nursing management and health education.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Syphilis is caused by Treponema pallidum, transmitted by sexual contact with lesions, mother to fetus in utero, blood transfusion, and broken skin; the organism penetrates mucous membranes or abrasions and within hours enters lymphatics and blood causing systemic infection; incubation averages 3 weeks (10-90 days).

(b)
• Untreated, it progresses through four stages: primary, secondary, latent and tertiary.
• Treatment: primary, secondary or early latent - single IM benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units (alternatives doxycycline 100 mg BD 14 days, ceftriaxone, tetracycline).
• Late latent and tertiary - benzathine penicillin 2.4 million units weekly for three weeks; neurosyphilis - IV aqueous penicillin G 18-24 million units daily for 10-14 days.

(c)
• Symptoms: non-itchy rash on trunk, palms and soles, condylomata lata, hair loss, muscle aches, fever, sore throat, swollen glands.
• Antibiotics in pregnancy lower the risk of fetal transmission and stop progression; treatment depends on the stage.

(d)
• Easily passed to the fetus; congenital infection usually after 18 weeks; infants are often premature.
• Tertiary disease: aortic regurgitation murmur, aortic aneurysm, neurological and mental changes.

(e)
Deficit: permanent damage to brain, eyes, ears, heart, skin, teeth and bones; blindness, deafness, lifelong disability; miscarriage or stillbirth.

(f)
• Nursing: educate on safe sex and condoms, treat the partner, administer antibiotics, assess heart, chest X-ray, neurological/mental status and genital healing; nursing diagnoses include acute pain, disturbed body image and deficient knowledge.
• Newborn: palmar rash, snuffles, hepatosplenomegaly, joint swelling; antibiotics, contact precautions and mother's support.
• Blood test is the usual diagnosis.

questions.question:
(a) Describe semen analysis: purpose and indications.
(b) State the collection instructions and procedure.
(c) State the parameters and their normal values.
(d) State the nursing responsibilities and handling.
(e) State the safety precautions for safe practice.
(f) Explain the rationale behind the nursing actions and the abnormal findings that follow when they are neglected.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Semen analysis assesses male fertility (count, quality, motility) and identifies infection; used in infertility evaluation.

(b)
• Abstain from ejaculation 2-5 days; avoid alcohol, smoking and recreational drugs; verbal and written instructions; sterile non-toxic container; private area.
• Masturbation preferred (no lubricants); coitus interruptus not preferred (contamination); special non-spermicidal condom.

(c)
• Volume 1.5-5.0 ml; count 15 million/ml or more (oligospermia below; azoospermia none); motility 40% motile or 32% progressive.
• Morphology 4% or more normal (Kruger); vitality 58% live; leukocytes under 1 million/ml (leukocytospermia suggests infection, needs culture); pH 7.2-8.0; fructose present; colour whitish-grey.

(d)
• Explain the procedure and rationale of instructions; ensure understanding; label with name, date and time.
• Keep at body temperature; deliver within 30-60 minutes; repeat abnormal samples at least one week apart.

(e)
Avoid contamination, lubricants, spermicidal condoms; handle samples correctly; follow abstinence protocol.

(f)
• Abstinence and handling ensure accurate results; abnormal findings guide further tests.
• Low volume: obstruction, retrograde ejaculation, hypogonadism; high volume: prolonged abstinence, inflammation.
• Low motility: tail defects, oxidative stress, infection, smoking/alcohol, heat; abnormal morphology: genetic defects, infections, toxins.
• Acid pH: obstruction or prostatitis; alkaline pH: reproductive or urinary tract infection.

questions.question:
(a) Define cleft lip and cleft palate and describe the embryology.
(b) State the associated problems, genetics and management.
(c) Explain why some babies are more susceptible to cleft palate.
(d) Distinguish between cleft lip and cleft palate.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• A congenital anomaly from failure of soft tissue or bone to fuse in fetal life; facial clefting is the second most common congenital deformity (after clubfoot), affecting 1 in 750 births.
• Primary palate forms in weeks 4-7 (maxillary swellings merge, medial nasal swellings fuse); secondary palate forms in weeks 6-9 as palatal shelves move from vertical to horizontal and fuse; the tongue must migrate antero-inferiorly.

(b)
• Problems: cosmetic, dental, speech, swallowing, hearing, facial growth, emotional and feeding; dental anomalies (supernumerary 20%, dystrophic 30%, missing 50%, malocclusion 100%).
• Genetics: multifactorial; cleft lip with or without palate - one parent 2%, one sibling 4%, two siblings 9%, parent plus sibling 15%.
• Management: team approach with the otolaryngologist pivotal; head and neck examination; speech, ear and airway care; surgery.

(c)
• Cleft of the lip increases the likelihood of cleft palate because the tongue gets trapped; the secondary palate closes one week later in females.
• Cleft palate risk: one parent 7%, one sibling 2%, two siblings 1%, parent plus sibling 17%.

(d)
• Cleft lip: slight notch to complete separation from floor to nose; epithelial bridge fails; clefts of the primary palate lie anterior to the incisive foramen.
• Cleft palate: nasal distortion, variable extension from uvula through soft and hard palate; clefts of the secondary palate lie posterior to the incisive foramen.
• Lip repair at about 10 weeks (rotation-advancement; lip adhesion at 2 weeks if feeding problems).
• Palate repair by Bardach two-flap and other techniques, possibly delayed to 18-24 months; scarring can impair mid-facial growth.
• Non-surgical option: dental obturator (requires modification as the child grows).

(a)
Jaundice (hyperbilirubinaemia), a symptom of an underlying disorder; the picture fits obstetric cholestasis (disrupted and reduced bile products from the liver), affecting the hepatobiliary system.

(b)
Liver/hepatobiliary function (bilirubin excretion, bile acids, liver enzymes). Maternal complications depend on the cause: hypertensive crises, renal dysfunction, ascites, insomnia, coagulopathy, hepatic encephalopathy, seizures. Fetal: prematurity, stillbirth, perinatal death, fetal distress, IUGR.

(c)
HELLP syndrome (with or without pre-eclampsia, liver cell destruction), acute viral hepatitis (A to E), hyperemesis gravidarum, any other hepatobiliary disorder.

(d)
• Assessment: bilirubin, liver function tests, bile acids, vital signs especially BP to detect changes that could cause complications.
• Diagnoses: impaired skin integrity (bilirubin and pruritus); anxiety about investigation outcome; deficient knowledge.
• Plan/implement: enough rest; reassurance and emotional support; adequate fluids; educate client and family; adhere to treatment and avoid self-medication; bland foods (crackers, ginger drink); safe sex and sharps precautions in hepatitis B and C.
questions.question:
A pregnant woman in the second or third trimester develops intense pruritus, dark urine, yellow sclerae and pale stools. Fasting serum bile acid is above 10 micromol/L after the 28th week, bilirubin exceeds 3 mg/dl and liver function tests are requested.
(a) Identify the condition and the body system affected.
(b) State the organs or functions compromised and the complications.
(c) List the differential conditions.
(d) Give the nursing reasoning and prioritisation of care using the nursing process.

(a) Describe blood sampling: purposes in midwifery and family planning.
(b) State the types of samples and techniques.
(c) Describe the steps in collection.
(d) State the nursing responsibilities and components analysed.
(e) State the safety precautions for safe practice.
(f) Explain the rationale behind the nursing actions and the complications that follow when they are neglected.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Midwifery: monitor maternal health (anaemia, blood group, infections, gestational diabetes), screen genetic conditions, assess fetal health (Rh factor, serum bilirubin), nutrition (iron, folic acid), diagnose and track disease, therapeutic decisions.
• Family planning: screen anaemia, diabetes, infections; hormone status; clotting and lipid profiles for VTE risk with hormonal methods; HIV, syphilis, hepatitis screening; rubella immunity and nutrition pre-pregnancy.

(b)
Venous (most common), arterial (radial, for blood gases) and capillary (fingerstick, heel or ear lobe prick) samples; techniques: phlebotomy (venipuncture), capillary sampling, arterial sampling (specialised training).

(c)
• Verify identity; inform patient; assemble gloves, alcohol swabs, tourniquet, needles, vacuum tubes, bandages; position patient; choose median cubital vein; clean site with alcohol and let dry.
• Apply tourniquet 3-4 inches above; needle at 15-30 degrees bevel up; draw blood; release tourniquet before removing needle; apply pressure with sterile pad.

(d)
• Label immediately and send promptly; document test ordered, site and patient's response.
• Components: RBCs, WBCs, platelets; electrolytes, albumin, globulin, liver and cardiac enzymes, hormones, glucose, urea, creatinine.

(e)
• Aseptic technique; correct patient identification; comfortable positioning to reduce fainting.
• Arterial sampling needs specialised training.

(f)
• Releasing the tourniquet before needle removal and applying pressure are part of post-collection care.
• Prompt transport prevents haemolysis; skilled venipuncture prevents haematoma; arterial sampling risks arterial spasm or thrombosis.

(a)
• Psychosis is loss of perception of reality (delusions, hallucinations, psychomotor disorders); in pregnancy it may be a pre-existing illness or begin in pregnancy, placing mother and fetus at risk; puerperal psychosis is serious (64% start in first two weeks of the puerperium).
• Manifestations: insomnia, refusing meals, loss of interest in the baby, hallucinations, fear of family harming her, suicidal tendencies, desire to injure the infant, confusion, elation, incoherent speech; or extreme depression.

(b)
• Blues: transient mild low mood (sadness, crying, irritability, anxiety, poor sleep) developing within 2-3 days of childbirth, peaking, and resolving within two weeks.
• Depression: more persistent and debilitating, interfering with care of self or child; 10-15% of women, usually within 4 months but any time in the first year; recurrence risk about 25%.

(c)
• Risk factors: history of bipolar disorder (single most important), previous postpartum psychosis, family history, schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder, stopping psychiatric medication, lack of sleep, falling oestrogen.
• Also severe puerperal infection; pregnancy as a stress factor in predisposed women (e.g. unmarried or deserted).

(d)
• Blues self-limit within two weeks; depression persists; psychosis involves loss of reality and risk to the infant.
• Anxiety or mood symptoms in pregnancy increase risk of depression after blues.
• Management of psychosis: refer promptly, sedation (chlorpromazine, pethidine, Librium, barbiturates), isolation in single room with security, no harmful objects, supervised infant contact, antibiotics for infection, suppress lactation, ECT if needed.
• Midwifery care: assess vital and neuro signs and thought process, antipsychotics with caution (valproate contraindicated), gentle interaction, monitor suicidal ideas, educate family.
• Nursing diagnoses: impaired thought process, impaired social interaction, risk for impaired parenting.
• Prognosis of puerperal psychosis is usually very good (75-80% recover completely).
questions.question:
(a) Describe postpartum psychosis: definition, risk factors and manifestations.
(b) Describe postpartum blues and postpartum depression.
(c) Explain why some women are more vulnerable to postpartum psychosis.
(d) Distinguish between postpartum blues, postpartum depression and postpartum psychosis.

A woman with increased vaginal discharge, bleeding after intercourse and pelvic discomfort during sex is found on speculum examination to have columnar epithelium extending from the cervical canal onto the ectocervix.
(a) Identify the condition.
(b) State the predisposing factors and pathophysiology.
(c) Outline the nursing/medical management and prevention.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Cervical erosion (cervical ectropion); can be asymptomatic; signs: increased vaginal discharge, postcoital bleeding, pelvic pain or discomfort during sex.

(b)
Columnar epithelium of the cervical canal extends onto the ectocervix. Causes: hormonal changes (increased oestrogen, pregnancy, hormonal contraceptives), infections (chlamydia, gonorrhoea), trauma (childbirth, surgical procedures, IUD insertion), congenital factors.

(c)
• Diagnosis: speculum examination, Pap smear, colposcopy. Management: observation, antibiotics, hormonal adjustment such as stopping oral contraceptives, surgical cauterisation or laser therapy.
• Prevention: regular gynaecological check-ups, safe sex, proper management of hormonal medications.

questions.question:
A newborn has a slight to complete separation of the upper lip with a palate defect, difficulty feeding and nasal distortion. Surgical repair of the lip and later the palate is planned.
(a) Identify the condition and the assessments/procedures used.
(b) Describe the pre-operative, intra-operative and post-operative care.
(c) Identify the complications to monitor for.
(d) State the patient education and discharge planning.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Cleft lip and palate: a congenital failure of soft tissue or bone to fuse (primary palate 4th-7th week, secondary palate 6th-9th week); facial clefting affects 1 in 750 births. Initial head and neck examination: facial symmetry, ears, rhinoscopy, oral examination, upper airway (phonation, cough, swallow).

(b)
• Pre-op: team approach (otolaryngologist pivotal); lip adhesion at about 2 weeks converts a complete cleft to incomplete and helps feeding; specialty feeding nipples; dental obturator for high-risk patients or those refusing surgery.
• Intra-op: lip repair at about 10 weeks by rotation-advancement (rotation flap, advancement, then nasal ala cuts); palate repair by techniques such as Bardach two-flap (medial and lateral incisions, flaps elevated preserving the greater palatine artery, velar muscles detached, closure in 3 layers); palate surgery possibly delayed to 18-24 months.

(c)
Problems: speech, swallowing, hearing/ear disease, airway compromise, dental abnormalities, impaired mid-facial growth from palate scarring, feeding and emotional difficulties.

(d)
Genetic risk: e.g. one parent 2%, one sibling 4% for cleft lip.

questions.question:
(a) Describe patient-controlled analgesia and postoperative analgesia after caesarean section.
(b) State the indications/goals and routes.
(c) State the dosing parameters.
(d) State the nursing responsibilities.
(e) State the safety precautions for safe practice.
(f) Explain the rationale behind the nursing actions and the complications that follow when they are neglected.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Postoperative analgesia uses multimodal analgesia: regular NSAIDs and paracetamol, epidural diamorphine or fentanyl, oral dihydrocodeine, codydramol, ibuprofen; diclofenac or paracetamol are mainstays.
• PCA lets patients self-administer predetermined doses of pain medication.

(b)
• Goals: pain relief for rest and recovery, early mobilisation, prevention of complications from pain and immobility.
• Routes: intravenous, subcutaneous, epidural.

(c)
Dosage parameters: initial loading dose, demand dose, lockout interval and continuous basal rate.

(d)
• Instruct on device use; assess pain, sedation, respiratory rate and vital signs regularly; ensure correct programming; record total opioid, attempts, pain levels, side effects and interventions.
• Antiemetics are usually prescribed with opioids.

(e)
• Contraindicated in patients who cannot understand or operate the device, with severe respiratory depression, or where opioids are contraindicated.
• Check programming of dose and lockout.

(f)
• Side effects: nausea, vomiting, itching, constipation, urinary retention, sedation.
• Monitoring of sedation and respiration detects opioid effects; recording doses and attempts guides safe use.
• Neglected pain control hinders early mobilisation and increases complications.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the pathophysiology of HIV/AIDS in pregnancy.
(b) State the stages/classification (HIV to AIDS) and diagnostic tests.
(c) State how the stages relate to the common maternal and fetal complications.
(d) Explain how the disease may be transmitted to and affect the fetus and other body systems.
(e) State the resulting functional deficit.
(f) State the related nursing management and health education.
questions.answerText:
(a)
HIV causes AIDS by depleting CD4+ T cells, weakening immunity and allowing opportunistic infections; in acute phase by cell lysis and CD8 killing, in chronic phase by generalised activation and loss of ability to generate new T cells.

(b)
• HIV progresses to AIDS when CD4 falls below 200 cells/mm3 (healthy 500-1600) or with opportunistic infection regardless of CD4; untreated survival about 3 years, about 1 year after a dangerous opportunistic illness.
• Tests: antibody tests, nucleic acid tests, p24 antigen, CD4 count, viral load (ELISA/rapid then Western blot or NAT).

(c)
Maternal: spontaneous abortion, low birth weight, chorioamnionitis, anaemia, pre-eclampsia, weakened immunity, death. Fetal: low birth weight, stillbirth, respiratory distress, neonatal mortality, neurological complications, preterm birth, impaired growth, vertical transmission.

(d)
Perinatal transmission occurs in pregnancy, labour, delivery or breastfeeding; risk factors include smoking, substance abuse, vitamin A deficiency, malnutrition, STIs, high viral load, breastfeeding.

(e)
Deficit: reduced ability to fight infections and cancers; manifestations include fever, sore throat, mouth sores, swollen glands, diarrhoea, weight loss, cough, night sweats, fatigue.

(f)
• PMTCT: early ART, viral load monitoring, elective caesarean for high viral load, IV ARVs in labour, avoid breastfeeding with safe alternative feeding.
• Infant: single-dose nevirapine within 72 hours then daily for 6 weeks; zidovudine no longer recommended for exposed infants.
• ARV cautions: zidovudine and anaemia (avoid with Hb 8 or less); nevirapine hepatotoxicity (avoid CD4 above 350); efavirenz avoided in first trimester; stavudine/didanosine not recommended.
• Monitor liver and renal function, haemoglobin, lipid profile, CD4 and viral load; chemoprophylaxis for opportunistic infections.
• Prevention: safe sex, HPV and hepatitis B vaccination, PrEP for high-risk, public education; referral to HIV specialists and counsellors.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the pathophysiology of puerperal pyrexia.
(b) State the classification/causes.
(c) State how the causes relate to complications.
(d) Explain how genital tract infection may spread to other organs.
(e) State the resulting functional deficit.
(f) State the related nursing management and health education.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Puerperal pyrexia is a febrile condition within 14-21 days of delivery; notifiable in many countries to control infection spread and compile statistics, but not notified in some tropical countries because malaria causes hyperpyrexia unrelated to genital infection.

(b)
Causes: genital tract infection, urinary tract infection, incidental illnesses (malaria, amoebic dysentery, typhoid, pneumonia), breast engorgement, mastitis or abscess, thrombophlebitis/phlebothrombosis, pyrexia of unknown origin.

(c)
• Genital infection (puerperal sepsis): episiotomy wound, perineal/vaginal/cervical lacerations and placental site; UTI may pre-exist and show from day 1; engorgement causes low-grade pyrexia from day 3.
• Subinvolution (infection of retained tissue) is the commonest cause of secondary PPH.

(d)
Infection may spread to the fallopian tubes, ovaries and peritoneum; foul-smelling discharge is a sign; septicaemia is suspected for blood culture.

(e)
Deficit: fever and ill health.

(f)
• Rest in bed; tepid sponging, fanning, exposure; isolate or barrier nurse; examine breast, chest, throat, genital tract; review labour and delivery.
• Investigations: MSU, high vaginal swab, blood film for malaria, blood culture, WBC, PCV, chest X-ray, stool, wound swab.
• Specific treatment once diagnosed; antimalarials in endemic areas after thick and thin films; investigate cause and organism.
• Good nutrition, adequate fluids and rest.
• Urine testing for albumin and pus cells; same nursing care for UTI as for genital infection.

(a)
• Labour is obstructed when progress stops despite adequate contractions because of a mechanical factor; causes include ineffective uterine action, CPD, occipitoposterior position, contracted pelvis, malpresentation, pelvic tumour and deformities.
• Poor application of the presenting part slows dilatation; CPD is the commonest cause.

(b)
• Prolonged latent phase: average normal 8.6 hours, prolonged at 20 hours or more. Prolonged active phase: dilatation below 1 cm/hour.
• Features: labour over 12 hours, exhausted, dehydrated, febrile mother; contractions may stop in primigravida; vulvo-vaginal oedema, severe caput, moulding, cervical oedema.

(c)
• Maternal: dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, exhaustion, pre-eclampsia/eclampsia, sepsis, PPH, uterine rupture, perineal lacerations, poor outlook for childbearing, death.
• Fetal: hypoxia, intracranial injury, infection, perinatal morbidity, neonatal death.

(d)
Prolonged pressure causes necrosis of soft tissue: vesico-vaginal and recto-vaginal fistula, nerve damage and paralysis, bony pelvic injuries, utero-vaginal prolapse from overstretched pelvic floor.

(e)
Deficit: incontinence, prolapse, paralysis, impaired future childbearing.

(f)
• Management: inform team; assess; partograph; support and consent; analgesia; vitals; empty bladder every 2 hours; hourly VE; half-hourly FHR; IV fluids; catheterise; oxytocin/amniotomy for hypotonic action; C/S for CPD or obstruction.
• Prevention: focused antenatal care to detect pelvic abnormalities, partograph monitoring, early referral, timely intervention.
• CPD: trial of labour for borderline pelvis; positions such as squatting increase outlet.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the pathophysiology of prolonged and obstructed labour.
(b) State the stages/phases of prolonged labour and the features of obstruction.
(c) State how these relate to maternal and fetal complications.
(d) Explain how obstruction may affect distant body systems.
(e) State the resulting functional deficit.
(f) State the related nursing management and health education.

(a) Describe the pathophysiology of venous thrombosis in pregnancy.
(b) State the types/classification of phlebitis and thrombophlebitis.
(c) State how the types relate to the common complications.
(d) Explain how the clot may spread or affect distant body systems.
(e) State the resulting functional deficit.
(f) State the related nursing management and health education.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Virchow's triad - venous stasis, vascular damage and hypercoagulability - are all increased in pregnancy: the gravid uterus compresses large veins and hormonal dilation slows flow; placental separation and instrumental or caesarean delivery injure vessels; clotting factors rise and natural anticoagulants (proteins C and S) fall.
• Thrombophlebitis: inflammation in the vessel from slowed circulation, then a thrombus forms as blood clots around the inflamed tissue.

(b)
• Types of phlebitis: superficial thrombophlebitis (veins just under the skin), deep vein thrombosis (clots in deeper veins, more serious) and septic thrombophlebitis (inflamed vein that becomes infected).
• In pregnancy 90% of DVT occurs in the left leg and 70% are ileofemoral; risks include age over 35, parity of 4 or more, obesity, immobility, pre-eclampsia, caesarean, smoking, thrombophilia.

(c)
• Superficial thrombophlebitis: warmth, tenderness, pain, redness, swelling, a hard red cord; arises in existing varicose veins; mainly local discomfort.
• DVT carries the greater risk of pulmonary embolism (major non-obstetric cause of maternal mortality); chronic pain and leg swelling may follow.

(d)
A clot can break loose and travel to the lungs causing pulmonary embolism; most PE occur in the first two weeks after delivery (80% left-sided).

(e)
Deficit: throbbing pain, swelling, warmth and discolouration in one leg, chronic pain and swelling; pulmonary blockage may be life-threatening.

(f)
• Nursing: history and assessment; LMWH (does not cross the placenta) with self-injection teaching and a medical alert card; gradient compression stockings; elevate the leg; hydration, stop smoking, healthy diet.
• Labour: mobility, position changes, passive leg exercises, hydration and leg examination; postnatal early mobilisation and respiration-rate and leg checks; urgent referral if suspected.
• Stop LMWH towards delivery to prevent PPH; thrombolysis (alteplase) for extensive DVT; vena cava filter and vein stripping are rare options.
• Investigations: Doppler ultrasound, venography, D-dimer (not conclusive); prevention by avoiding immobility and dehydration.

(a)
Subinvolution: inability of the uterus to return to normal size after delivery; the most common cause of secondary postpartum haemorrhage; more common in multiparous women and tends to recur.

(b)
Causes: infection related to retained membrane or placenta, advanced age, multiparity, premature delivery, protracted labour, PPH, perineal laceration; a full bladder or loaded rectum can displace the puerperal uterus.

(c)
• Remove or prevent the causes; empty the uterine cavity for retained placenta or membranes; conservative uterine tamponade (gauze or balloons) and uterotonics; broad-spectrum antibiotics if infection; surgery (ligation of uterine vessels, hysterectomy) in severe cases; ensure complete emptying of uterine contents.
• Prevention: active management of the third stage with complete delivery of placenta and membranes and uterotonics; aseptic technique; avoid prolonged labour.
questions.question:
On a postnatal visit a multiparous woman who had a protracted labour has prolonged lochial flow and profuse vaginal bleeding; the uterus is large, flabby and boggy, with a height greater than expected for that day of the puerperium.
(a) Identify the condition.
(b) State the predisposing factors and pathophysiology.
(c) Outline the nursing/medical management and prevention.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Forceps delivery is assisted delivery using a double-bladed metal instrument applied to the fetal head with traction during a contraction; mid-cavity (head below ischial spines) and low-cavity (head at pelvic floor); high-cavity is unsafe, so CS is preferred.
• Types: Wrigley's (outlet lift-out, short shank), Neville-Barnes/Simpson's (low or mid-cavity), Kielland's (rotation and extraction in deep transverse or occipitoposterior).

(b)
• Maternal: distress, exhaustion, prolonged second stage, medically significant conditions (aortic valve disease, myasthenia gravis, significant APH). Fetal: malposition, fetal distress, reduced-weight infants, assisted breech.
• Contraindications: unengaged head, incompletely dilated cervix, true CPD, breech/face/most brow presentations, severe fetal distress with head above the pelvic floor, second twin with unengaged head, cord prolapse with mid-cavity station.

(c)
• Prerequisites: ruptured membranes, full dilatation, known cephalic position, adequate pelvis, head below 1/5 palpable, empty bladder, experienced operator, informed consent.
• Preparation: keep couple informed; analgesia (epidural top-up or spinal, mandatory for Kielland's); both legs into lithotomy together; left tilt 15 degrees; resuscitation equipment checked, paediatrician present.
• Procedure: left blade then right, lock and check, traction with contractions along the curve of Carus.

(d)
Nursing: minimise loss of dignity, limit time in stirrups and staff present. Complications: genital trauma, urinary retention, PPH; neonatal facial marks, facial palsy, scalp injury.

(e)
• Check prerequisites before application; reposition or abandon if application is incorrect; Kielland's only by a skilled obstetrician.
• Apply traction only with contractions and maternal effort; protect the vaginal wall when inserting blades.

(f)
• Left tilt prevents aortocaval occlusion; an informed woman has greater satisfaction; correct placement and traction prevent trauma.
• Neglect causes soft tissue damage, haemorrhage (uterine atony risk after assisted birth), facial nerve compression and neonatal injury.
questions.question:
(a) Define forceps delivery and classify obstetric forceps.
(b) State the indications and contraindications.
(c) State the preparation of the woman and the procedure.
(d) State the nursing responsibilities and complications.
(e) State the safety precautions for safe practice.
(f) Explain the rationale behind the nursing actions and the complications that follow when they are neglected.

A woman with a fully dilated cervix, ruptured membranes and a cephalic presentation is exhausted in a prolonged second stage of labour. The head is below the ischial spines and a forceps delivery is planned.
(a) Identify the procedure and its prerequisites.
(b) Describe the pre-procedure, procedural and post-procedure care.
(c) Identify the complications to monitor for.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Forceps delivery: assisted vaginal birth using a double-bladed instrument applied to the fetal head with traction during a contraction. Prerequisites: membranes ruptured, cervix fully dilated, cephalic presentation with known position, adequate pelvis, head below 1/5 palpable and at or below ischial spines, empty bladder, experienced operator, informed consent.

(b)
• Before: explain, involve partner, adequate analgesia (epidural top-up or spinal; pudendal block is usually insufficient); legs placed in lithotomy together, not in stirrups longer than necessary, dignity kept; left tilt 15 degrees; baby resuscitation equipment checked.
• During: left blade inserted before right, protecting vaginal wall; blades articulated, locked and checked; traction with contractions and maternal effort along the curve of Carus; reposition or abandon if application is wrong.

(c)
Maternal: cervical, vaginal or perineal trauma, dysuria or urinary retention, haemorrhage (tissue trauma, uterine atony). Neonatal: facial marks and bruising, facial palsy, scalp abrasions, cephalhaematoma.

questions.question:
A woman has a breech presentation (longitudinal lie with the buttocks or feet closest to the cervix) diagnosed by palpation and ultrasound. External cephalic version is planned before 39 weeks.
(a) Identify the condition and name the procedure.
(b) Describe the care before, during and after the procedure.
(c) Identify the complication to monitor for and its prevention.
(d) State the patient education and discharge planning.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Breech presentation (incidence 3-4%; types frank, complete, incomplete, single or double footling; predisposed by prematurity, uterine malformations or fibroids, polyhydramnios, placenta praevia, fetal abnormalities, multiple gestation, previous breech). Procedure: external cephalic version (ECV), trans-abdominal manual rotation of the fetus to cephalic.

(b)
• Before: nil by mouth at least 8 hours; ultrasound on the day to confirm breech; non-stress test; prepare for possible caesarean delivery. Contraindications: third-trimester bleeding, uterine anomalies, ROM or oligohydramnios, need for CS for other reasons, multiple gestation.
• During: judicious manipulation of the head toward the pelvis while the breech is brought up to the fundus; forward roll first, then backward roll if unsuccessful; success rate 60-70%.
• After: repeat non-stress test to confirm fetal wellbeing; give anti-D if Rh negative; after successful ECV the client can be discharged to await spontaneous labour.

(c)
Fetal trauma is the risk; excessive force should never be used.

(d)
The woman may be discharged to await spontaneous labour.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the pathophysiology of periventricular/intraventricular haemorrhage in the newborn.
(b) State the grades/classification.
(c) State how the grades relate to complications and prognosis.
(d) Explain how the haemorrhage may affect distant body systems.
(e) State the resulting functional deficit.
(f) State the related nursing management and health education.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Brain development is key: the germinal matrix next to the ependyma, active 8-28 weeks, has fragile capillaries without muscle or collagen support, vulnerable to haemodynamic change and easily ruptured.
• After 32 weeks the matrix involutes and capillaries stabilise; the choroid plexus produces CSF.

(b)
• Grade 1 periventricular (subependymal/germinal matrix); Grade 2 intraventricular extension; Grade 3 post-haemorrhagic hydrocephalus; Grade 4 parenchymal haemorrhage.
• Affects mainly infants under 32 weeks and under 1500 g; risk: hypoxia, acidosis, hypotension, hypertension, RDS with ventilation, rapid bicarbonate, pneumothorax, PDA.

(c)
• Grades 1 and 2: usually good neurological prognosis, small bleeds may have no signs.
• Grade 3 blocked CSF outflow dilates ventricles; Grade 4: massive bleeds usually die within 48 hours; survivors develop convulsions, cerebral atrophy, rapid hydrocephalus.

(d)
Extensive bleeds produce apnoeic episodes, bradycardia, pallor, metabolic acidosis and convulsions (respiratory, cardiovascular and metabolic effects).

(e)
Deficit: neurological - convulsions, cerebral atrophy, hydrocephalus; long-term neurological follow-up needed.

(f)
• Prevention: antenatal steroids and postnatal surfactant; screening by cranial ultrasound in early days with serial scans.
• Management: haemodynamic stability - meet respiratory, acid-base, circulation, temperature, nutrition and elimination needs; evaluate continuously.
• Drugs: morphine or fentanyl; pancuronium if ventilated; dopamine and dobutamine.

(a)
• Puerperal psychosis, a serious condition (incidence about 0.68% in Nigeria; 64% start in the first two weeks of the puerperium). Causes: severe puerperal infection (confusion and clouding of consciousness) or pre-existing predisposition (e.g. schizophrenia) with pregnancy as a stress factor; other forms show extreme depression.
• Pathophysiology: changes in neurotransmitters (dopamine, acetylcholine, GABA, glutamate) in response to genetic and environmental background; falling oestrogen and lack of sleep may also be risks.

(b)
• Refer to the doctor without delay; nurse in a single room, preferably ground floor, with adequate security; no harmful instruments; experienced (male) mental nurse may stay; take the infant away, allowing supervised contact; monitor suicidal ideas.
• Nourishing, attractive diet, oral toilet, attention to bladder and bowel (Dulcolax suppository daily).

(c)
Heavy sedation (chlorpromazine, pethidine, Librium, barbiturates); massive doses of appropriate antibiotics if infection; suppress lactation with stilboestrol; ECT in difficult cases under an experienced psychiatrist; prognosis usually very good (75-80% recover completely in temperate countries).
questions.question:
In the first two weeks after delivery a woman has persistent insomnia, refuses meals, loses interest in her baby, sees and hears people who are not there, talks of family members wanting to harm her and expresses suicidal tendencies and a desire to injure her infant.
(a) Identify the condition and explain its pathophysiological basis.
(b) State the priority nursing assessment and immediate interventions.
(c) State the definitive medical management.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• A Pap smear collects cervical cells examined microscopically to detect precancerous changes, early cervical cancer, and infections or inflammation; introduced in the 1940s by Papanicolaou to reduce cervical cancer deaths.
• Indications: cervical cancer prevention, detection of HPV (often combined with HPV testing), monitoring cervical health; also done during gynaecological/family planning examination.

(b)
Age 21-29: every three years; 30-65: Pap every three years or Pap plus HPV every five years; over 65 may stop after consistent normal results for 10 years; more frequent testing for HIV, weakened immunity, previous abnormal results, history of cervical cancer.

(c)
• Preparation: avoid intercourse, douching and vaginal creams for two days; not during menstruation; inform doctor of infections, surgery, medications.
• Procedure: lithotomy position with feet in stirrups, speculum inserted, cells collected from the cervix with a soft brush or spatula, placed on a slide or liquid solution and sent to the laboratory.

(d)
• Nursing: explain the procedure, reassure that they can pause, correct speculum size and lubrication, document findings.
• Results by the Bethesda system: normal (routine screening continues) or abnormal - ASC-US (HPV test), ASC-H (colposcopy), LSIL (colposcopy if HPV positive), HSIL (more severe).

(e)
• Sterile/appropriate instruments and correct speculum size; avoid factors that interfere (blood, intercourse, creams).
• A normal result does not mean immunity from future abnormalities; continue regular screening.

(f)
• Preparation avoids interference with results.
• Neglected screening misses early changes, which allows progression to cervical cancer.
questions.question:
(a) Define a Pap smear and state its indications.
(b) State who should be screened and when.
(c) Describe the preparation and procedure.
(d) State the nursing responsibilities and how results are reported.
(e) State the safety precautions for safe practice.
(f) Explain the rationale behind the nursing actions and the complications that follow when they are neglected.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Fetal: malposition of the fetal head (occipitolateral and occipitoposterior), fetal distress. Maternal: distress, exhaustion or prolongation of the second stage of labour.

(b)
Same as for forceps: unengaged head, incompletely dilated cervix, true CPD, breech/face and most brow presentations, preterm gestation below 34 weeks, likely fetal coagulation disorder, severe fetal distress with head above pelvic floor.

(c)
• Discuss rationale with woman and partner; lithotomy; analgesia (inhalational, pudendal block with perineal infiltration or epidural top-up); empty bladder; CTG monitoring.
• Cup placed on the flexion point (3 cm anterior to posterior fontanelle); pump creates 50-60 mmHg suction stepwise or rapidly, forming an artificial caput (chignon); traction with contractions.

(d)
• Know the types of extractor and their pressure limits; inform the woman (she feels only pressure under regional anaesthesia); pump to the level needed; auscultate FHR at least every 5 minutes or use continuous EFM.
• Tell parents the chignon disappears in 2-3 days; assess newborn for bruising, jaundice, cephalhaematoma, intracranial and retinal haemorrhage.

(e)
• Maternal: perineal trauma, haematoma, pelvic floor injury with incontinence, PPH, pain, rarely uterine rupture.
• Fetal: scalp abrasion, cephalhaematoma, subgaleal haemorrhage, subdural/intracranial haemorrhage, Erb's palsy, retinal haemorrhage, rarely skull fracture.

(f)
• Vertex presentation at 0 station or below; same criteria as forceps; only an experienced practitioner; stop at once if no descent or if the cup pops off more than three times.
• Avoid excessive traction and keep the procedure time-limited.

(g)
• Monitoring FHR and informing the woman keep the baby safe and the woman cooperating; neglect of station, experience and pop-off limits leads to cephalhaematoma, subgaleal bleeding and intracranial haemorrhage.
• Excessive traction leads to maternal trauma, PPH, pelvic floor injury and rarely uterine rupture.
