questions.answerText:
(a)
• Premature (preterm) labour: onset of labour before 37 completed weeks with regular contractions causing cervical dilatation and effacement. Risk: previous preterm birth, uterine anomalies, infections (UTI, bacterial vaginosis), cervical insufficiency; multiple gestation, fetal anomalies, fetal growth restriction; stress, substance abuse, inadequate prenatal care.
• Diagnosis: examination of contractions and cervical changes; ultrasound cervical length (<25 mm raises risk); fetal fibronectin test (22-35 weeks).

(b)
RDS (surfactant deficiency, hypoxaemia, respiratory acidosis), IVH, periventricular leukomalacia, cerebral palsy, cognitive, behavioural, motor and sensory deficits, psychosocial effects.

(c)
• Prevention: progesterone, cervical cerclage. Tocolytics (nifedipine, terbutaline, indomethacin, magnesium sulfate); magnesium sulfate before 32 weeks for neuroprotection; corticosteroids (betamethasone, dexamethasone) for lung maturity; antibiotics; continuous fetal monitoring, bed rest and hydration; caesarean if indicated; NICU care.
• Priority: corticosteroids accelerate fetal lung maturity, reducing respiratory complications; tocolytics give time for interventions.
questions.question:
A woman with a previous preterm birth, a bicornuate uterus, urinary tract infection and a twin pregnancy presents before 37 weeks with regular contractions, pelvic pressure, low backache and increased vaginal discharge.
(a) Identify the condition and list the risk factors.
(b) State the complications.
(c) Outline the management options and justify the priority intervention.

(a) Describe sore and cracked nipples: definition, prevention and treatment.
(b) Describe mastitis and breast abscess: definition, features and treatment.
(c) Explain why some mothers are more susceptible to breast problems.
(d) Distinguish between breast engorgement and mastitis.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Sore nipple: pain in the nipple during breastfeeding, possibly abrasion with a red tender nipple; prevented by good fixing of the baby and not letting the baby suck long on an empty breast.
• Treatment: keep nipples dry; if very painful rest the nipple 24 hours with manual expression of the breast.
• Cracked nipple: a fissure causing pain and tenderness on sucking; serious because it predisposes to breast infection.
• Treatment as for sore nipples; baby off the breast 48-72 hours; express manually, not with a pump; sucking on cracked nipples can cause melaena and blood in the baby's vomit.

(b)
• Mastitis: infection of breast tissue confined to a lobe, which is hard, red and painful, with pyrexia and rigors; treated with antibiotics and the baby must not suck the affected breast.
• Breast abscess: the breast is enlarged, oedematous, painful and tender and the patient is ill; treated by drainage, systemic antibiotics, dressing of the wound and good breast support.

(c)
• Susceptibility: poor fixing of the baby, long sucking on an empty breast, inadequate emptying of full breasts (stagnant milk causes pain, pyrexia, infection), cracked nipples.
• Engorgement is more common in primiparae.

(d)
• Engorgement: venous congestion from day 3, breasts hard, tense, painful with shiny stretched skin, dilated veins, flattened nipples, low-grade pyrexia; managed by support, analgesics, hot bathing, stroking, and emptying; prevented by expressing colostrum in the last six weeks of pregnancy.
• Mastitis: infection of one lobe, with rigors, sequel to cracked nipples or engorgement, treated with antibiotics.
• Mastitis may progress to abscess if not resolved.

questions.question:
(a) Describe urine specimen collection: types of specimens and indications.
(b) State the procedure for clean-catch and 24-hour collection.
(c) State how urine is interpreted.
(d) State the nursing responsibilities.
(e) State the safety precautions for safe practice.
(f) Explain the rationale behind the nursing actions and the complications that follow when they are neglected.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Urinalysis in midwifery identifies urinary tract infections, pre-eclampsia and gestational diabetes; also assesses kidney function and metabolic conditions.
• Types: random, first morning (concentrated), fasting, 24-hour, midstream clean catch (cultures), catheterised (sterile), suprapubic aspiration.

(b)
• Clean catch: wash hands, clean genital area front to back, start voiding into the toilet, collect midstream in a sterile container, stop before the bladder is empty, close the lid, label, transport within two hours or refrigerate.
• 24-hour: discard first morning urine on Day 1, collect all urine for 24 hours including the first morning urine on Day 2, keep cool, return promptly.

(c)
• CASDORA: colour (pale yellow to amber; red, dark brown, cloudy abnormal), appearance (clear), specific gravity 1.005-1.030, dipstick (glucose, protein, ketones, nitrites, leukocytes, pH 4.5-8.0), odour, red cells 0-2/HPF, additional findings (WBC 0-5/HPF, crystals, casts, organisms).
• Proteinuria: kidney dysfunction or pre-eclampsia; bacteriuria: nitrites and leukocytes confirm UTI; glucosuria: diabetes or GDM.

(d)
Explain the purpose, give clear verbal/written instructions, supply sterile container and antiseptic wipes, label with details and time.

(e)
Sterile containers, correct labelling, documentation of collection time, prompt transport or refrigeration.

(f)
• Correct technique avoids contamination and ensures accurate results.
• Midstream sampling is critical for urine cultures; delays without refrigeration compromise sample integrity.
• Neglected collection leads to inaccurate results and missed UTI, pre-eclampsia or gestational diabetes.

questions.question:
Soon after the baby is born, a woman develops profound shock with haemorrhage and severe pelvic pain. On bimanual examination the fundus feels cupped or cannot be felt, and a fleshy reddish mass is seen outside the vulva.
(a) Identify the condition and its classification.
(b) State the predisposing factors.
(c) Explain the pathophysiology of the shock.
(d) Outline the nursing management and prevention.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Acute inversion of the uterus (within the first 24 hours), a rare but life-threatening cause of neurogenic shock; classic triad of haemorrhage, shock and severe pelvic pain. By severity: 1st degree fundus reaches internal os; 2nd body inverted to internal os; 3rd fundus protrudes to or beyond introitus; 4th total uterine and vaginal inversion.

(b)
Mismanagement of the third stage of labour, primiparity, short umbilical cord, sudden emptying of a distended uterus, fetal macrosomia.

(c)
Traction on the ligaments supporting the uterus causes parasympathetic stimulation and severe pain (neurogenic shock), plus hypovolaemia from acute blood loss (800 ml to 1800 ml).

(d)
• Call urgent medical help; monitor vital signs and give high-flow oxygen; start IV fluids through a wide-bore cannula pending cross-matched blood; give analgesia; resuscitate while reduction is attempted.
• Do not give ergometrine or oxytocin (they aggravate matters and make reduction harder); replace the uterus immediately without removing an attached placenta, which is delivered later; warm saline may be infused into the vagina.
• Prevention: proper training of skilled birth attendants in third-stage management; early diagnosis and immediate repositioning.

questions.question:
A newborn is pale with tachypnoea, tachycardia, poor feeding, abdominal distension and temperature instability. A second newborn has hepatosplenomegaly, joint swelling, palmar rash, snuffles, anaemia and jaundice.
(a) Identify the likely conditions and the body systems affected.
(b) State the organs and functions compromised.
(c) List the differential conditions.
(d) Give the nursing reasoning and prioritisation of care.
questions.answerText:
(a)
First baby: neonatal sepsis (generalised infection with bacteria in the blood). Second baby: congenital syphilis (Treponema pallidum crossing the placenta, usually after 18 weeks' gestation).

(b)
Sepsis: respiratory, cardiovascular, feeding/gastrointestinal and thermoregulation. Syphilis: liver, spleen, joints, skin, blood.

(c)
TORCH syndrome (toxoplasmosis, other viruses, rubella, cytomegalovirus, herpes); general signs are temperature instability, tachypnoea, apnoea, tachycardia, poor feeding, decreased tone, lethargy, irritability; also jaundice, erythroblastosis fetalis.

(d)
• Sepsis: assess apnoea or irregular respirations; oxygen; monitor vital signs; neutral thermal environment; intake and output, daily weights; monitor diarrhoea; feeding and suck reflex; assess jaundice; antibiotics.
• Syphilis: assess palmar rash and snuffles; antibiotics; contact precautions; emotional support to the mother; follow-up instructions.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the diagnostic procedures for congenital heart defects, including cardiac catheterisation.
(b) State indications and uses.
(c) State the preparation and procedure.
(d) State the nursing responsibilities and complications.
(e) State the safety precautions for safe practice.
(f) Explain the rationale behind the nursing actions and the complications that follow when they are neglected.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Diagnostic tests: physical examination (heart and lung sounds, cyanosis, rapid breathing, delayed growth, heart failure signs), echocardiogram, ECG, chest X-ray, pulse oximetry and cardiac catheterisation.
• Echocardiogram uses sound waves to show heart structure and follow the problem over time; ECG records electrical activity and rhythm and chamber enlargement.

(b)
• Chest X-ray shows an enlarged heart or extra lung blood or fluid (heart failure); pulse oximetry shows blood oxygen via a fingertip or toe sensor.
• Catheterisation measures pressures, shows mixing of blood between sides, and repairs some defects: closing holes, widening narrowed vessels or valves, closing abnormal vessels.

(c)
• A thin flexible catheter is passed through a vein in the arm, groin or neck to the heart and dye visible on X-ray is injected.
• Catheter procedures involve only a needle puncture, are the preferred repair for many simple defects such as ASD and pulmonary valve stenosis, and have grown over 20 years.

(d)
Nursing: understand the child's challenges, help coping, support family, community and home care links.

(e)
Echocardiography and examination are non-invasive.

(f)
• Early diagnosis and management prevent secondary damage to heart, lungs and brain and the effects of hypoxaemia on cognitive and psychomotor development.
• Antibiotic prophylaxis for infective endocarditis is needed before and after surgical correction.
• Neglect: delayed treatment leads to the secondary damage above.

(a)
• Thyroiditis is inflammation of the thyroid, causing swelling, pain and sometimes interfering with hormone production; thyroid disease is the second most common endocrine disorder of reproductive-age women.
• Untreated, it is associated with miscarriage, placental abruption, hypertensive disorders and growth restriction.

(b)
• Types: Hashimoto's (autoimmune, hypothyroidism), postpartum (hyperthyroidism then hypothyroidism), subacute (viral, painful), silent (painless), acute infectious (bacterial, rare).
• Predisposing: autoimmune tendency, past thyroid dysfunction or surgery, postpartum year, iodine deficiency, family history.

(c)
• Hashimoto's: fatigue, weight gain, constipation, dry skin, cold sensitivity, depression.
• Postpartum: anxiety, palpitations, weight loss then fatigue and depression; subacute: neck pain, fever, tenderness; acute infectious: severe neck pain, swelling, difficulty swallowing or breathing.

(d)
• Maternal thyroid dysfunction and increased preterm birth risk; baby: low birth weight and neonatal thyroid dysfunction.
• Metabolism and energy levels are affected; symptoms include palpitations, anxiety and depression.

(e)
Deficit: imbalance of thyroid hormones; fatigue; risk of imbalanced nutrition.

(f)
• Diagnosis: TSH, T4, thyroid antibodies, ultrasound.
• Care: thorough assessment, regular hormone monitoring, endocrinologist collaboration, adjust medication, iodine guidance, prevent complications, education and emotional support, postpartum monitoring.
• Nursing diagnoses: fatigue related to hormone deficiency; risk for imbalanced nutrition less than body requirements.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the pathophysiology of thyroiditis in pregnancy.
(b) State the types of thyroiditis.
(c) State how the types relate to common complications.
(d) Explain how thyroid dysfunction affects other body systems and the fetus.
(e) State the resulting functional deficit.
(f) State the related nursing management and health education.

A baby has episodes of cyanosis and rapid breathing with fatigue. Echocardiography shows pulmonary valve stenosis, a large ventricular septal defect, an overriding aorta and right ventricular hypertrophy. Corrective open-heart surgery is planned.
(a) Identify the condition and the diagnostic tests used.
(b) Describe the nursing care before, during and after surgery.
(c) State the complication to prevent.
(d) State the education and discharge/community planning.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Tetralogy of Fallot: the most common complex cyanotic heart defect (10-15% of heart defects). Tests: physical examination, echocardiogram, ECG, chest X-ray, pulse oximetry, cardiac catheterisation (measures pressures, shows mixing of blood, and can repair some defects).

(b)
• Surgery: open-heart surgery, soon after birth or later in infancy depending on the pulmonary narrowing; a palliative procedure may be done first to preserve life and let the infant grow; early management prevents secondary damage to heart, lungs and brain and hypoxaemia's effects on development.
• Goals: improve cardiac function, remove fluid and sodium, decrease cardiac demands, improve tissue oxygenation.

(c)
Infective endocarditis: antibiotic prophylaxis is needed before and after surgical correction.

(d)
Lifelong cardiologist follow-up; home and community care with informed parents and community support; nurses prepared to support the family physically and psychologically; avoid unprescribed drugs in pregnancy and reduce environmental pollution as prevention.

questions.question:
(a) Define induction of labour and state the indications and contraindications.
(b) State the assessment before induction and methods used.
(c) State the nursing/midwifery responsibilities.
(d) State the complications.
(e) State the safety precautions for safe practice.
(f) Explain the rationale behind the nursing actions and the complications that follow when they are neglected.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Induction is artificial stimulation of contractions at 28 or more weeks before spontaneous onset to achieve vaginal birth; also the stimulation of the uterus with or without ruptured membranes to accomplish birth.
• Indications: prolonged pregnancy (offered at 40+0 to 40+14 weeks), PROM, PPROM, hypertension, pre-eclampsia, diabetes, cholestasis, placental abruption, IUGR, intrauterine fetal death, previous stillbirth, unstable lie, chorioamnionitis, maternal request.
• Contraindications: placenta praevia/vasa praevia, transverse or compound presentation, cord prolapse, CPD, severe fetal compromise, previous classical caesarean, active herpes, previous myomectomy breaching the cavity.

(b)
• Assess fetal maturity (dating, early ultrasound) and cervical readiness by Bishop's score; higher score = more likely success (8 or 9 likely succeeds); under 6 needs ripening with PGE2 or misoprostol.
• Methods: prostaglandins (misoprostol, dinoprostone), IV oxytocin, amniotomy, membrane sweeping, cervical ripening balloon.

(c)
Inform mother, discuss pain relief, regular vital signs, fetal heart monitoring, left lateral position, watch for bleeding, supplemental oxygen, encourage breastfeeding.

(d)
Failed induction leading to emergency C/S; uterine hyperstimulation and abnormal contractions; infection after amniotomy; hypotension, tearing; prematurity if induced too early.

(e)
Monitor FHR and contractions closely; stop or slow oxytocin on signs of fetal distress; give women information to make an informed choice.

(f)
• Close monitoring prevents hyperstimulation damaging the baby's brain or organs.
• Fetal heart monitoring detects intolerance to labour.
• Neglect: delay of delivery increases infection, haemorrhage or organ damage.

(a)
• High blood pressure in pregnancy is a leading cause of pregnancy-related illness and death worldwide.
• Chronic/pre-existing hypertension: before pregnancy or in the first half of pregnancy; differs from disorders specifically linked to pregnancy.
• Gestational hypertension: new-onset high blood pressure after the 20th week.

(b)
• Screening: BP is measured with a manually inflated cuff on the upper arm at each prenatal visit.
• Urinalysis is a simple non-invasive antenatal screening test that finds infection, kidney problems, diabetes and liver disease.

(c)
• Predisposing factors for HELLP: previous HELLP (19-27% recurrence), pre-eclampsia or pregnancy-induced hypertension, age over 25, Caucasian, multiparity.
• It occurs in 0.1-0.6% of pregnancies and 4-12% of women with pre-eclampsia.

(d)
• Pre-eclampsia: new-onset hypertension after 20 weeks with proteinuria and symptoms such as headache, low platelets, kidney, liver, lung or vision problems; may cause poor fetal growth.
• HELLP: severe form of pre-eclampsia with haemolysis (anaemia), elevated liver enzymes (liver inflammation) and low platelets; classes by platelet count.
• Eclampsia: most severe form, with new-onset seizures, life-threatening.
• Care for HELLP: bed rest, vital signs, fetal monitoring, educate on seizures and bleeding, deliver by labour or caesarean.
questions.question:
(a) Describe blood pressure disorders in pregnancy: definition and types.
(b) Describe screening for high blood pressure.

courses.title: Physiotherapy in Surgery II

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Pre-operative: physiotherapy is mainly educational, teaching the exercises to be done after surgery, motivating/encouraging the patient, and educating her on the conduct of daily life.
• Post-operative goals: improve tissue extensibility, improve range of motion, and facilitate normal movement patterns.
• Further goals: relieve pain, prevent oedema formation, prevent further deformity, improve quality of life, and improve lung capacity/prevent pulmonary complications.
• Techniques: ROM exercises, joint mobilisation, chest physiotherapy (breathing exercises), aerobic exercises.
• Also soft tissue mobilisation, strengthening exercises, postural assessment, relaxation techniques, and specific shoulder/arm exercises (wand exercise, shoulder blade stretch, chest wall stretch, side bends, elbow winging, shoulder blade squeeze, shoulder stretch).

(b)
• Rationale – exercises maintain ROM and tissue extensibility because scar tissue and post-op guarding otherwise limit shoulder movement.
• Chest physiotherapy is given because pain and reduced movement can predispose to pulmonary complications.
• Education and psychological counselling are given because loss of part or all of the breast causes negative body image, depression, anxiety and fear, so support and counselling (with psychologist referral if mental health deteriorates) improve outcomes.
• Prosthetist referral addresses the physical need created by loss of breast tissue.

(c)
• Lymphoedema is managed with Complex Decongestive Physical Therapy: an intensive phase of daily manual lymphatic drainage (massage to encourage removal of excess interstitial fluid and increase lymphatic transport), multi-layer compression bandaging, and exercises improving lymph outflow.
• This is followed by a maintenance-optimisation phase of self-massage and elastic compression materials with continued exercise.
• Electrical stimulation (Faradism under pressure) combined with compression and limb elevation above heart level can also be used to increase venous and lymphatic drainage and relieve oedema.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the physiotherapy management of a mastectomy patient, covering the pre-operative phase and the post-operative phase (including goals, techniques and precautions).
(b) State the rationale for the interventions used.
(c) Explain the basis for preventing or managing lymphoedema, a named complication of mastectomy.

(a) Describe the physiotherapy management (rehabilitation) of a patient following fracture fixation, relating it to the stages of fracture treatment.
(b) State the rationale for the interventions used.
(c) Explain the basis for preventing joint stiffness, a named complication of fracture immobilisation.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Fracture treatment follows the sequence: resuscitation, reduction, retention and rehabilitation.
• Rehabilitation is carried out by way of physiotherapy and exercises.
• This follows retention of the fracture by plaster of Paris/splints/casts, continuous traction, or functional braces.
• Functional braces are used once the fracture becomes sticky after 2-3 weeks, allowing the patient to use the affected limb.

(b)
• Rationale – functional braces are used specifically because they allow the patient to use the affected limb.
• This reduces the complications associated with prolonged fracture immobilisation.
• The earlier operative fixation (open or closed reduction and internal fixation) allows rehabilitation exercises to generally begin sooner compared with prolonged plaster immobilisation.
• Operative fixation is indicated (among other reasons) to avoid prolonged bed rest and to allow better nursing care.

(c)
• Chronic complications of fractures include joint stiffness due to improper or prolonged immobilisation.
• This is why retention methods that allow earlier movement (such as functional braces, once appropriate) are used.
• Rehabilitation by physiotherapy and exercise is instituted as soon as the fracture is adequately stabilised, to restore movement and function.
• This helps avoid the joint stiffness, post-traumatic arthritis (especially in intra-articular fractures) and Volkmann's ischaemic contractures that can otherwise follow prolonged immobilisation.

(a)
Laparotomy (also known as celiotomy): a surgical procedure involving a surgical incision through the abdominal wall to gain access to the abdominal cavity; a midline incision runs down the middle of the abdomen and is the standard incision for laparotomy.

(b)
Laparotomy is done to gain surgical access to the abdominal cavity; other incisions used depending on the site of pathology include paramedian (kidneys/adrenal glands), transverse, Pfannenstiel (pelvic region, e.g. emergency caesarean), subcostal (gallbladder/liver/spleen) and rooftop/chevron incisions.

(c)
• Pre-operative physiotherapy: advice on what the operation will involve, pain control modalities, gentle abdominal strengthening exercises to keep the abdomen strong for the operation.
• Also cardiovascular activities (treadmill, cycling), and strengthening exercises to the limbs.

(d)
• Week 1: pain control modalities, cryotherapy (ice) to reduce swelling, postural advice to strengthen chest muscles/improve lung function/minimise respiratory complication risk, breathing exercises.
• Also advice on getting in/out of bed and transferring in/out of chairs, and strengthening exercises to the low back and abdominal muscles.
• Weeks 2-4: progression of transverse abdominal strengthening exercises, advice on standing and indoor/outdoor mobility, advice on moving/lifting techniques to minimise low back pain risk.
• Also pain control modalities as necessary, progression of pelvic strengthening exercises, and improving cardiovascular endurance.
• Week 5 onwards: return to normal daily routine with more functional activities; lifting light loads after six weeks and heavier loads not advised until 12 weeks after abdominal surgery, with correct lifting technique taught and good posture maintained to reduce stress on the abdominal region.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Partial thickness (second-degree) burn: salmon pink, moist, shiny, painful, with blister formation, typically blanching with pressure; scalding injuries commonly cause this degree of burn.

(b)
Skin grafting: grafts can be autografts (from the recipient), allografts (from a genetically non-identical donor of the same species) or xenografts (from a donor of a different species).

(c)
• Acute phase: splints have a prophylactic role if tendon/joint damage is suspected, and should be modulable and non-constrictive because of fluctuating oedema.
• Wound healing phase: prevent development of contractures and protect newly applied skin grafts.
• Rehabilitation phase: reduce contracture non-surgically, prevent deformities, provide sustained stretching of scar tissue, and maintain gained ROM.
• Reconstructive phase: fixation following release of contractures or reconstruction surgery.

(d)
• Precautions: avoid interference with healing by ensuring proper splint fit (proper length, edges rolled and flared away from skin); monitor for wound breakdown if scar tissue tensile strength is poor.
• In the reconstructive phase, monitor for wound maceration.

(e)
• Positioning of the volar forearm/wrist/hand should maintain the burned tissue in an elongated state (wrist in functional position, forearm supinated, thumb web space on stretch), maintained with towels/gauze or splints.
• The positioning programme is individualised according to her medical condition, ROM and skin condition, and is modified as healing progresses.
• It progresses from dorsal splints in the acute palmar burn to silicone pads for positioning and pressure as healing advances.
questions.question:
A 30-year-old woman sustains a scald injury to her anterior forearm and hand from hot liquid. The wound is moist, blistered, and painful, requiring skin grafting.
(a) State the diagnosis, including the degree/depth of burn.
(b) State the surgical procedure named for closure of the wound.
(c) State the physiotherapy goals for the acute phase, wound healing phase, rehabilitation phase and reconstructive phase.
(d) State the precautions and contraindications relevant to her treatment.
(e) Describe the progression, discharge planning and patient education relevant to her case.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Acute phase: splints have a prophylactic role if tendon/joint damage is suspected.
• Because of fluctuating oedema at this stage, splints should be modulable and non-constrictive.
• Wound healing phase: splints/positioning are used to prevent development of contractures and to protect newly applied skin grafts.
• Proper fit is ensured (proper length, edges rolled and flared away from the skin).
• Rehabilitation phase: used to reduce contracture non-surgically, prevent deformities, provide sustained stretching of scar tissue and maintain gained ROM.
• Reconstructive phase: used for fixation following release of contractures or reconstruction surgery.

(b)
• Rationale – positioning is fundamental to burn rehabilitation because it prevents contracture, controls oedema, and prevents localised neuropathies.
• It maintains soft tissue in an elongated position; burn patients tend to assume a flexed, adducted (foetal) position as a reaction to pain.
• Limbs are typically positioned in extension-abduction alignment, maintained with splints, pillows or foam wedges, individualised to the patient's medical condition, ROM and skin condition.

(c)
• Contracture is prevented because scar tissue allowed to shorten across a joint pulls it into a fixed deformed position.
• Elongated positioning from the acute phase, wound-healing-phase splinting to prevent contracture and protect grafts, followed by rehabilitation-phase stretching to reduce any contracture and maintain ROM, keeps the joint mobile.
• If scar tissue tensile strength is poor, monitor for wound breakdown; in the reconstructive phase, monitor for wound maceration.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the physiotherapy management of a burns patient across the acute phase, wound healing phase, rehabilitation phase and reconstructive phase, including positioning and splinting.
(b) State the rationale for the interventions used in each phase.
(c) Explain the basis for preventing contracture, a named complication of burns.

questions.answerText:
(a)
A displaced fracture of the shaft of the femur, confirmed on plain X-ray (the gold standard for diagnosing fractures, requiring a minimum of two views – anterior and lateral, sometimes oblique).

(b)
Structures affected: the bone itself (requiring reduction, temporary stabilisation with K-wires, and definitive stabilisation, e.g. an interlocking intramedullary nail, the gold standard for long bone fractures); surrounding soft tissue, blood vessels and nerves may also be injured.

(c)
• Differential/associated problems: acute complications such as shock, vascular injury, deep vein thrombosis and nerve injury.
• Chronic complications such as delayed union, malunion, nonunion, avascular necrosis, shortening, joint stiffness from prolonged immobilisation, and infection/chronic osteomyelitis.
• Operative treatment itself carries the disadvantage of converting a closed fracture into an open one, scarring, anaesthetic problems, foreign body reaction, need for further surgery to remove implants, and higher cost.

(d)
• Clinical reasoning: because he has undergone open reduction and internal fixation, physiotherapy (rehabilitation) is the means by which recovery of function is restored.
• The plan must reduce chest and circulatory complications common after surgery (breathing exercises, active limb and ankle/toe movements, early mobilisation of the unaffected limb).
• Progression on the operated limb must be gentle and paced according to weight-bearing status and healing, while monitoring for the acute and chronic complications above.
questions.question:
A 28-year-old man involved in a road traffic accident presents with pain, swelling and deformity of the thigh. Plain X-ray in anterior and lateral views confirms a displaced shaft of femur fracture, and he is scheduled for open reduction and internal fixation.
(a) Identify the problem shown on the imaging.
(b) State the structures/systems likely affected.

(a) Describe chest physiotherapy under the following headings: definition, indications, and techniques.
(b) Explain the clinical basis for post-operative and COPD patients needing chest physiotherapy.
(c) Distinguish between percussion (clapping) and vibration/shaking as manual techniques.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Definition: chest physiotherapy is a group of treatments designed to improve oxygen transport, respiratory efficiency, promote lung expansion, strengthen respiratory muscles, and eliminate secretions from the respiratory system.
• Indications: patients with COPD; patients at the post-operative stage (abdominal and thoracic surgery).
• Patients with atelectasis; respiratory muscle weakness (as in some neurological conditions); prolonged stay in bed; patients requiring mechanical ventilation.
• Techniques: postural drainage; manual techniques (chest wall percussion/clapping, vibration and shaking).
• Breathing exercises (diaphragmatic breathing, thoracic expansion exercise, pursed-lip breathing, active cycle of breathing technique).
• Manual hyperinflation, CPAP, positive expiratory pressure, respiratory muscle training, coughing/huffing, and incentive spirometry.

(b)
• Oxygen transport from the lungs to body tissues may be limited by ineffective coughing or impairment of the mucociliary clearance mechanism.
• This leads to inability to clear airway secretions.
• Post-operative patients breathe shallowly to avoid incisional pain, allowing secretions to pool and predisposing to atelectasis and infection.
• COPD patients have excess mucus production and impaired ciliary clearance from chronic airway inflammation – both groups therefore need chest physiotherapy to mobilise and clear secretions and re-expand the lungs.

(c)
• Percussion (clapping) can be performed in either the inspiratory or expiratory phase and is more comfortable performed over clothes or a towel.
• Vibration and shaking are performed only during the expiratory phase to mechanically move secretions toward the main bronchi to stimulate coughing; both require caution in osteoporosis/rib metastases (rib fracture risk), recent haemoptysis, or pleuritic pain.

(a)
• Types: dural tears, instability, junctional kyphosis, recurrent disc herniation, and pseudarthrosis (non-union).
• Also neurological complications, anaesthesia-related complications, thrombophlebitis (DVT), lung problems, infection, and hardware complications.
• Dural tears happen accidentally during surgery, usually from direct trauma or laceration, commonly involving the Kerrison punch.
• Recurrent disc herniation is herniated disc material at the same level/site after a pain-free interval following discectomy.
• Instability is loss of the spine's ability to maintain its patterns of displacement under physiologic loads, without initial neurological deficit, major deformity or incapacitating pain, confirmed radiographically.
• Pseudarthrosis is failure of bony union of the intended fusion, confirmed radiographically by a cleft in the fusion mass, failed bone graft incorporation, progressive graft resorption, or implant loosening/breakage.
• Junctional kyphosis occurs when the sagittal Cobb angle between the last instrumented vertebra and vertebrae further away increases by ≥10° or exceeds 10°, from increased mechanical demands adjacent to the fusion.

(b)
• Intraoperative technical difficulties predisposing to accidental dural tears include dural scarring, adhesions and fibrosis, particularly in revision surgery.
• Also an eroded and thin dura as seen in long-standing spinal stenosis, and large disc herniations making dural retraction difficult.
• Revision spinal surgery patients, who already have scarring/adhesions from previous surgery, are therefore at greater risk of dural tears.

(c)
• Pseudarthrosis is specifically a failure of the fusion to unite bone, confirmed by findings such as a cleft in the fusion mass or implant loosening/breakage.
• Spinal instability is a broader loss of the spine's mechanical control under physiologic loads, confirmed by translation/angulation on standing and flexion-extension radiographs, that may or may not involve a failed fusion.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the complications of spinal surgery under the following headings: types, and clinical features.
(b) Explain the clinical basis for revision spinal surgery patients being more vulnerable to dural tears.
(c) Distinguish between pseudarthrosis and spinal instability.

(a) Describe the physiotherapy management of an obstetric/gynaecological surgery patient: pre-operative assessment/teaching, and post-operative management (including perineal tear rehabilitation).
(b) State the rationale for the interventions used.
(c) Explain the basis for preventing deep vein thrombosis/pulmonary embolism in this group of patients.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Pre-operative: a thorough preoperative assessment and teaching by the physiotherapist, including a general description of the surgery.
• The effect of anaesthesia and surgery on cardiopulmonary function, and the systemic effects of restricted mobility and recumbency.
• The patient is instructed in breathing control manoeuvres, supported coughing, chest wall mobility exercises, and mobility exercises for the limbs.
• Also turning in bed, sitting up, transferring, chair sitting and walking erect, with the post-operative course explained so the patient can anticipate it.
• Post-operative: mobilisation and body positioning coordinated with deep breathing and supported coughing manoeuvres, performed hourly during waking hours.
• General mobility exercise (hip/knee flexion-extension, foot/ankle exercises) hourly to maximise joint ROM, correct posture, and maximise muscle length/ligament integrity.
• Also to maximise ability to perform ADLs and maintain/increase muscle strength and endurance.
• For perineal tear repair: Kegel exercises and electrical stimulation using vaginal/anal electrodes.

(b)
• Rationale – anaesthesia and tissue dissection cause major changes in lung volume, mechanics and gas exchange, with reduced thoracic respiratory excursion and altered diaphragmatic/intercostal muscle tone.
• Breathing/coughing exercises and mobilisation address these cardiopulmonary consequences; hourly mobility exercises address ongoing risk of joint stiffness, muscle weakness and thromboembolism.
• Kegel exercises and electrical stimulation target the pelvic floor muscles disrupted by perineal tear repair.

(c)
Patients undergoing gynaecologic surgery are predisposed to thromboembolism through hypercoagulability, venous stasis and vessel wall injury, worsened by perioperative immobility and pelvic masses/haematomas, so mobilisation and regular activation of the leg muscle pumps to minimise circulatory stasis are essential.

(a)
• Investigations: plain X-ray is the gold standard, requiring a minimum of two views (anterior and lateral, sometimes oblique).
• CT scan is required for special situations such as spine, chest or skull injuries, for cross-sectional study; MRI is useful for diagnosing fractures and soft tissue injury but is costly.
• Conservative treatment (undisplaced/incomplete/impacted fractures): cuff and collar sling (upper limb injuries), strapping (clavicle, rib, phalangeal injuries).
• Rest and NSAIDs (impacted fractures e.g. neck of femur), and plaster slabs.
• For displaced fractures: resuscitation, reduction (closed reduction by traction/counter-traction, or continuous traction such as Gallow's, Dunlop's or Smith's traction).
• Retention (plaster of Paris/splints/casts, continuous traction, or functional braces) and rehabilitation (by physiotherapy and exercises).
• Operative treatment: open reduction and internal fixation (e.g. dynamic compression plate and screws) or closed reduction and internal fixation (e.g. interlocking nailing).
• Principles: exposure, reduction, temporary stabilisation (K-wires), and definitive stabilisation (K-wires, screws, intramedullary nails, plate and screws, interlocking nails, or tension band wiring, chosen by fracture site/type).

(b)
• Displaced and comminuted fractures are more prone to complications because reduction is technically more difficult; closed reduction is a blind technique needing skill and commonly resulting in malunion.
• Such fractures show anterior, posterior, varus/medial, shortening or translational displacement/angulation depending on injury forces and muscle pull, increasing risk of malunion, nonunion, avascular necrosis and joint stiffness.
• Operative fixation, more often required for these fractures, itself carries disadvantages: converting a closed fracture to open, scarring, anaesthetic problems, infection risk, and need for further surgery to remove implants.

(c)
Delayed union is a fracture taking longer than expected to unite, whereas nonunion is a fracture that fails to unite; both are chronic complications alongside malunion, avascular necrosis, shortening and growth disturbance in children.
questions.question:
(a) Describe fracture management under the following headings: investigations, conservative treatment, and operative treatment.
(b) Explain the clinical basis for displaced and comminuted fractures being more prone to complications than simple undisplaced fractures.
(c) Distinguish between delayed union and nonunion.

A 58-year-old man with a long history of productive cough and mucus production for the past several years is admitted for elective surgery. On examination he has a bluish discolouration of the skin and lips.
(a) State the most likely diagnosis.
(b) State the aetiological factors for this condition.
(c) Describe the pathophysiology of this condition.
(d) Describe the physiotherapy assessment and management appropriate for him.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Chronic bronchitis (patients with advanced COPD who have primarily chronic bronchitis rather than emphysema are commonly referred to as "blue bloaters" because of the bluish colour of the skin and lips – cyanosis – seen in them).

(b)
Aetiology: the major cause is cigarette smoking; other causes are bronchial irritants from bacterial or viral infection, exposure to industrial dusts and fumes in the workplace (e.g. coal miners, grain handlers, metal molders), and air pollution.

(c)
• The bronchi develop chronic inflammation with swelling and excess mucus production; ciliated cells that normally clear secretions are replaced by mucus-secreting goblet cells, and cilia lose their function of moving mucus over the airway lining.
• The warm, moist, nutrient-rich mucus is an excellent medium for bacterial growth, so the mucus often becomes infected, and the inflammation, swelling and mucus significantly inhibit airflow by narrowing and partially obstructing the bronchi and bronchioles.

(d)
• Assessment: note breathing pattern, cough and sputum quantity/colour, cyanosis, degree of breathlessness, and chest measurements.
• Management aims: enhance secretion mobilisation, improve chest expansion, teach breathing control, and improve exercise tolerance.
• Means: airway clearance (postural drainage, active cycle of breathing technique, positive expiratory pressure), chest physiotherapy (shaking on expiration).
• Breathing exercises during episodes of dyspnoea, positioning to promote relaxation (forward-leaning sitting/standing, relaxed sitting), and active exercise (walking), graduated later.

questions.question:
(a) Describe the physiotherapy management of a laparotomy patient across the pre-operative period and the post-operative weeks (week 1; weeks 2-4; week 5 onwards).
(b) State the rationale for the interventions used.
(c) Explain the basis for preventing or managing paralytic ileus, a named complication of laparotomy.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Pre-operative: advice on what the operation will involve, pain control modalities.
• Gentle abdominal strengthening exercises, cardiovascular activities (treadmill, cycling), and limb strengthening exercises.
• Week 1: pain control modalities, cryotherapy to reduce swelling, postural advice.
• Breathing exercises, advice on getting in/out of bed and chairs, and low back/abdominal strengthening.
• Weeks 2-4: progression of transverse abdominal strengthening, standing/mobility advice.
• Safe moving and lifting technique advice, pain control as necessary, pelvic strengthening progression, and cardiovascular endurance work.
• Week 5 onwards: return to normal routine and functional activities.
• Light lifting allowed after six weeks; heavy lifting delayed to 12 weeks.

(b)
• Rationale – postural and breathing advice minimises the risk of respiratory complications after abdominal surgery.
• Cryotherapy and pain control allow the patient to move and breathe more freely; abdominal/transverse abdominis strengthening protects and supports the incision, paced to allow tissue healing; moving/lifting technique advice reduces low back pain risk from altered abdominal support.

(c)
• Paralytic ileus/intestinal obstruction is prevented/managed by frequent turning, exercises and early ambulation (to alleviate air-swallowing distension, with nasogastric tube if anticipated).
• Early ambulation improves dietary intake, and with stool softeners (if prescribed) promotes bowel elimination and helps prevent constipation.

(a)
Radical prostatectomy: removal of the whole prostate gland including the cancerous cells, and possibly the seminal vesicles; the incision is usually made through the lower abdomen (retropubic) but can be made in the groin (perineal).

(b)
• Radical prostatectomy is typically performed for early-stage prostate cancer confined to the prostate gland, confirmed by tests such as bone scan, CT and MRI to exclude spread; it may also be used if prostate cancer has failed to respond to radiation.
• Other, less common reasons include inability to completely empty the bladder, recurrent bleeding from the prostate, bladder stones with prostate enlargement, very slow urination, and hydronephrosis from urinary retention.

(c)
Pre-operative physiotherapy: pelvic floor muscle exercises, since strengthening the pelvic floor before prostatectomy has been shown to significantly improve post-prostatectomy urinary continence, post-micturition dribble and erectile function.

(d)
• Post-operative physiotherapy goals: optimise the pattern of pelvic floor muscle contraction, train urinary incontinence, improve erectile dysfunction, and bladder training.
• Techniques include breathing exercises (pursed-lip progressing to diaphragmatic breathing) to prevent cardiorespiratory complications.
• Pelvic floor exercises (hip bridging, knee rolling, kegel exercises in supine, side-lying and sitting positions), electrical stimulation of the pelvic floor muscles, soft tissue/frictional massage for scar healing, and patient education and psychological counselling.
questions.question:
(a) A 63-year-old man is diagnosed with early-stage prostate cancer confined to the prostate gland. State the surgical procedure most likely to be performed and briefly describe what it involves.
(b) State the pathological basis and other indications for this surgery.
(c) Describe the pre-operative physiotherapy assessment and management for this patient.
(d) Describe the post-operative physiotherapy management for this patient.

(a) Describe the physiotherapy management of a hip or knee arthroplasty patient: pre-operative and post-operative phases, including goals and techniques.
(b) State the rationale for the interventions used.
(c) Explain the basis for preventing deep vein thrombosis after joint replacement surgery.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Pre-operative: proper assessment of movement and functional loss of the joint to guide post-operative rehabilitation planning.
• Assessment of respiratory function, especially where compromise is suspected.
• Post-operative goals: restore ROM to the affected joint, promote joint stability.
• Regain neuromuscular control of joint motion, restore gait and balance, and improve quality of life.
• Hip arthroplasty: the patient moves the hip on the bed hours after surgery, with partial weight bearing beginning after 72 hours.
• Knee arthroplasty: gradual mobilisation commences 2-3 days post-op, with static quadriceps contraction commencing hours post-op; progression from non-weight-bearing (4 weeks) to partial (5-6 weeks) to full weight bearing (7-8 weeks).
• Initial treatment includes therapeutic exercise, transfer and gait training and instruction in ADLs.
• Once released from surgical precautions, progression to regular exercise and physical activity for musculoskeletal/cardiovascular fitness.

(b)
• Rationale – the approach-specific instability patterns (extension/adduction/external rotation for anterolateral/lateral approach, or flexion/adduction/internal rotation for posterolateral approach) dictate which positions must be avoided.
• Early controlled movement and progressive weight bearing restore ROM, stability and gait while respecting healing of the osteotomy/prosthesis fixation.
• Instruction in ADLs and eventual regular exercise support long-term fitness and quality of life.

(c)
Emphasis is placed on moving all the joints and muscles to prevent venous stasis (DVT) after the operation, since reduced mobility after joint replacement is itself a DVT risk factor – hence early hip/knee movement, ankle/foot exercises and progressive mobilisation from the earliest post-operative hours.

(a)
Herniated (slipped) lumbar disc, where a fragment penetrates the tough outer layer and enters the spinal canal; treated by lumbar discectomy, which removes the herniated or degenerative disc from the lower part of the spine.

(b)
• Pre-operative goals: education regarding the surgery and post-surgical rehabilitation, behavioural strategies to minimise fear-avoidance and increase activity level, and discussion of lifestyle modification.
• Post-operative goals: pain management (particularly in the first 24 hours), monitoring of cardiac output/fluid status where relevant, maintenance of the effects of surgery, management of complications, and reintegration of the patient.
• Working toward restoring ROM, stability, neuromuscular control, gait and balance and quality of life; initial treatment includes therapeutic exercise, transfer and gait training and instruction in ADLs.

(c)
• Complications of spinal surgery include dural tears (often from direct trauma/laceration during surgery), instability, junctional kyphosis, recurrent disc herniation (herniated material at the same level/site after a pain-free interval).
• Also pseudarthrosis (failure of bony fusion), post-operative neurological deficit (from direct injury to nerve roots or indirect injury from disrupted blood supply or compression, e.g. by haematoma), DVT/thrombophlebitis, lung problems, infection, and anaesthesia-related complications.
• A meticulous neurological examination as soon as the patient wakes is essential to distinguish deficits occurring during surgery from those developing afterward.

(d)
• Progression: once the patient has achieved an adequate level of function and is released from surgical precautions, he progresses to a routine of regular exercise and physical activity to support musculoskeletal and cardiovascular fitness, important for long-term outcomes and quality of life.
• Discharge planning follows the outcome measures used (e.g. disability index, pain, quality of life), and patient education covers the surgery, expected post-surgical rehabilitation course, and lifestyle modification.
questions.question:
A 40-year-old man with a herniated lumbar disc causing nerve root compression and leg pain, who has failed conservative treatment, undergoes a lumbar discectomy.
(a) State the diagnosis and the surgical procedure performed.
(b) State the physiotherapy goals for the pre-operative and post-operative phases.
(c) State the precautions and possible complications relevant to spinal surgery.
(d) Describe the progression, discharge planning and patient education relevant to his case.

(a) Describe amputation under the following headings: definition, indications, types, and complications.
(b) Explain the clinical basis for patients with vascular disease/gangrene being more likely to require amputation.
(c) Distinguish between myoplasty and myodesis.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Definition: removal of the terminal part of a limb by cutting through one or two bones.
• Indications: dead tissue as in gangrene; a dangerous limb; or a useless body part.
• Types: minor amputation (toes and fingers) and major amputation (arm, forearm, thigh and leg).
• The part left behind is called the stump or residual limb, later assessed for prosthetic fitting.
• Complications: wound problems/infection, growing bone.
• Phantom limb pain (perceiving the limb is still present after amputation), managed with immediate prosthetic fitting and psychologist/psychotherapy intervention.

(b)
• Before amputation, the surgeon notes the level of good blood perfusion, the nerve supply, and the site of amputation.
• Also the blood supply and innervation of the stump.
• In vascular disease, poor blood perfusion leads to dead (gangrenous) tissue, a direct indication for amputation since the tissue cannot survive and threatens the rest of the limb/patient's health.
• The remaining stump must have adequate blood supply and innervation to heal and support a prosthesis.

(c)
• Myoplasty is the suturing of muscle to muscle.
• Myodesis is the suturing of muscle to bone; both are techniques used to secure the muscle at the end of the stump during amputation surgery.

(a)
Risk factor: axillary lymph node dissection performed as part of the modified radical mastectomy, which removes lymph nodes under the arm to check whether cancer cells have spread beyond the breast.

(b)
• Wound-related: bleeding and infection, haematoma (blood in the wound), seroma (clear fluid in the wound), scar formation, brachial plexus injury, numbness in the chest or upper arm.
• Movement-related: limited shoulder range of motion, musculoskeletal pain at the neck, shoulder, axilla and breast, abnormal posture, lymphoedema (if axillary nodes are removed), and Post-Mastectomy Pain Syndrome (persistent neuropathic burning/shooting pain in the chest wall, armpit and/or arm).
• Psychological: negative body image (dissatisfaction with appearance, perceived loss of femininity), depression, anxiety and fear.

(c)
• Management options: ROM exercises, joint mobilisation, soft tissue mobilisation, strengthening exercises, postural assessment, relaxation techniques, chest physiotherapy, Complex Decongestive Physical Therapy, and education/psychological counselling.
• Justification: Complex Decongestive Physical Therapy is justified for her current arm swelling because it directly targets lymphoedema – an intensive phase of daily manual lymphatic drainage, multi-layer compression bandaging and exercises improving lymph outflow to achieve maximum oedema reduction.
• This is followed by a maintenance phase of self-massage and elastic compression garments to sustain the reduction and improve her range of motion and function.
questions.question:
(a) A 50-year-old woman is 6 months post modified radical mastectomy with axillary lymph node dissection. She now presents with swelling and reduced range of motion of the right arm. State the risk factors that predisposed her to this complication.
(b) List the post-operative complications of mastectomy, grouped under wound-related, movement-related, and psychological complications.
(c) Outline the physiotherapy management options and justify the use of one of them for her current presentation.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Emphysema (a chronic obstructive pulmonary disease).

(b)
Predisposing factors: prolonged smoking; exposure to cigarette smoke, air pollution and toxins; age-related pulmonary changes; genetic mutation causing α-1-antitrypsin deficiency.

(c)
• Toxins such as cigarette smoke trapped in the alveoli cause a localised inflammatory response; chemicals released (e.g. elastase) cause the alveolar septum to disintegrate (septal rupture), forming bullae and greatly reducing alveolar surface area for gas exchange.
• Loss of alveolar tissue removes structural support to the bronchioles, causing premature airway closure on expiration and great difficulty exhaling; the chest over-inflates (barrel chest) and the diaphragm flattens; eventually pulmonary hypertension develops, straining the right side of the heart.

(d)
• Assessment: observe breathing pattern (over-inflated chest, apical/accessory muscle use, paradoxical lower rib movement), pursed-lip and orthopnoeic breathing, chest measurements at full inspiration/expiration and resting position.
• Also assess breath sounds, cough and sputum colour, cyanosis/finger clubbing, degree of breathlessness, and chest pain.
• Management aims: to teach the patient to breathe with minimum effort in a co-ordinated pattern, and to clear excessive chest secretions.
• Means: gentle breathing exercises emphasising completely relaxed expiration, controlled breathing while walking on flat ground and stairs, postural drainage if tolerated, vibration and shaking on expiration, huffing and coughing exercises, and graded exercise training.
questions.question:
A 60-year-old man with a long smoking history is admitted for elective abdominal surgery. On examination he has an increased anteroposterior chest diameter, leans forward with his arms extended on a support to breathe, and shows pursed-lip breathing.
(a) State the most likely diagnosis.

(a) Describe general anaesthesia under the following headings: definition, effects, pre-operative preparation, and complications.
(b) Explain the clinical basis for patients with COPD and congestive heart failure being more vulnerable to complications from general anaesthesia.
(c) Distinguish between general anaesthesia and regional anaesthesia.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Definition: anaesthesia is a reversible procedure that renders the patient pain-free.
• General anaesthesia produces progressive, reversible CNS depression; the ideal agent produces loss of consciousness, analgesia, amnesia, skeletal muscle relaxation and inhibition of reflexes.
• Effects (triad of anaesthesia): loss of consciousness, analgesia, and muscle relaxation.
• Also post-operative nausea/vomiting (leading to dehydration and acid-base imbalance) and amnesia.
• Pre-operative preparation: history (present illness; past history of hypertension, diabetes, COPD, asthma, sickle cell disease; drug history; allergy history; smoking/alcohol history; dental history).
• Examination to identify compromised systems; investigations (K+, PCV, WBC, urine); consent taken after history and examination.
• Nil-per-oral fasting: fluids 2 hours (children)/4 hours (adults); solids 4 hours (children)/6 hours (adults); patient cleaned (bladder and bowel emptied).
• Complications: neurological, musculoskeletal, respiratory, cardiovascular, gastrointestinal and urinary; monitored in ICU/HDU/recovery room before return to the ward.

(b)
• Patients with pre-existing COPD/respiratory limitation are predisposed to atelectasis, pneumonia, hypoxia and respiratory failure after surgery, particularly abdominal/thoracic surgery, because general anaesthesia depresses breathing.
• Such patients require pretreatment with bronchodilators, antibiotics and chest physical therapy before surgery.
• General anaesthetics decrease myocardial performance, so patients with congestive heart failure require premedication to help control cardiac symptoms, as their hearts are less able to compensate.

(c)
General anaesthesia causes loss of consciousness through CNS depression, whereas regional anaesthesia (LA injected into the subarachnoid space between L2/3 and L3/4, acting on nerve roots) anaesthetises the lower body without loss of consciousness, and is preferred in cardiac, pulmonary and renal procedures for being safer with good analgesia/muscle relaxation.

questions.question:
(a) Describe chronic bronchitis under the following headings: definition, aetiology, symptoms, and management.
(b) Explain the clinical basis for chronic bronchitis being commoner in cigarette smokers and in workers exposed to industrial dust and fumes.
(c) Distinguish between chronic bronchitis and emphysema.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Definition: chronic inflammation of the bronchi and bronchioles with excessive mucus secretion and tissue swelling that may narrow or close off the tubes.
• Definition (diagnostic criterion): chronic cough or mucus production for at least three months in two successive years, other causes excluded.
• Aetiology: the major cause is cigarette smoking.
• Aetiology: other causes are bacterial/viral bronchial irritants, exposure to industrial dusts and fumes (e.g. coal miners, grain handlers, metal molders), and air pollution.
• Symptoms: cough, expectoration of mucus, cracking sound/wheeze in the later stage.
• Symptoms: frequent and severe respiratory infections, narrowing/plugging of the bronchi, and difficult breathing especially on exertion.
• Management (pharmacological): bronchodilators (salbutamol, terbutaline), steroids, antibiotics, and oxygen therapy; lifestyle modification (quitting smoking, avoiding irritants).
• Management (physiotherapy): aims are to enhance secretion mobilisation, improve chest expansion, teach breathing control and improve exercise tolerance, using postural drainage, ACBT, positive expiratory pressure, shaking on expiration, breathing exercises and graded active exercise.

(b)
• Cigarette smoke and industrial dusts/fumes act as chronic irritants causing inflammation with goblet cells replacing ciliated cells, so mucus is over-secreted and cilia lose the ability to clear it.
• The resulting warm, moist, mucus-rich airway is an excellent medium for bacterial growth, so repeated exposure in smokers and dust/fume-exposed workers keeps triggering this inflammatory and mucus-hypersecretory process.

(c)
• Chronic bronchitis involves inflammation and excess mucus narrowing the bronchi, diagnosed clinically by a chronic productive cough.
• Emphysema, by contrast, involves destruction of the alveolar tissue itself, with loss of the alveolar septa forming bullae and permanent loss of the elastic recoil needed to hold the alveoli open.

(a)
Mild circulatory compromise (ankle oedema, though Homan's test is currently negative) and a respiratory pattern (reduced chest expansion, shallow breathing) that places her at risk of pulmonary complications.

(b)
• Structures/systems affected: the circulatory system of the lower limb (venous drainage) following pelvic surgery.
• Also the respiratory system, since abdominal surgery and anaesthesia reduce thoracic respiratory excursion and alter the tone and pattern of diaphragmatic and intercostal muscle contraction.

(c)
• Differential problems: DVT and pulmonary embolism (venous thromboembolic events), given that gynaecological/pelvic surgery predisposes to thromboembolism through hypercoagulability, venous stasis and vessel wall injury.
• Also pulmonary complications such as atelectasis or pneumonia, given the reduced chest expansion and shallow breathing common after abdominal surgery.

(d)
• Clinical reasoning: because circulatory assessment (Homan's test, observation for oedema) and respiratory assessment (symmetry, rate, depth, chest expansion, dyspnoea, accessory muscle use) both show early warning signs, the plan should include lower limb strengthening and ROM exercises.
• Transverse abdominis strengthening to support the abdominal wall and promote circulation, together with breathing exercises and simple mobility such as walking from week 1.
• This reduces venous stasis and promotes lung expansion before either complication becomes established, with scar management and pelvic floor exercises added as she progresses.
questions.question:
A 47-year-old woman is 3 days post total abdominal hysterectomy for fibroids. On circulatory assessment, Homan's test is negative but mild oedema of the ankle is noted; on respiratory assessment, chest expansion is reduced with shallow breathing.
(a) Identify the problems shown by the assessment findings.
(b) State the structures/systems affected.
(c) State the differential problems (complications) that should be considered.
(d) Explain the clinical reasoning for the physiotherapy plan for this patient.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Causes/risk factors: inadequate fluid replacement or IV line problems; most causes of hypertension (the opposite extreme) relate to inadequate pain relief or anxiety, while hypotension and septic shock are also recognised "other complications" following surgery.

(b)
Other complications: hypertension, and septic shock; more broadly, post-operative fever, infection, haemorrhage, urinary problems, post-operative delirium, and bowel function issues.

(c)
• Management: assessing patency of IV lines and ensuring appropriate fluids are administered at the prescribed rate, increasing fluid input with administration of high-flow oxygen, and tilting the patient head-down to maintain cerebral perfusion.
• Hypertension, by contrast, usually settles with appropriate analgesia since it often relates to inadequate pain relief or anxiety.
• Normal temperature is maintained by keeping the room comfortable, providing blankets to prevent chilling, giving oxygen, adequate hydration and proper nutrition, and monitoring for cardiac dysrhythmias.
• Justification: assessing IV line patency and fluid administration is justified as the priority action for hypotension because it directly addresses the volume status likely underlying his low blood pressure and cool, clammy skin.
• Head-down tilting helps maintain cerebral perfusion until his circulatory status stabilises.
questions.question:
(a) A 55-year-old man is 1 day post laparotomy and is noted to be hypotensive with cool, clammy skin. State the risk factors/causes relevant to his presentation.
(b) List the other general post-operative complications he could be at risk of, besides hypotension.
(c) Outline the physiotherapy-relevant management options for his presentation and justify the use of one of them.

(a) State the pathophysiological basis of paralytic ileus following abdominal surgery.
(b) State how this relates to the common complication of abdominal distension.
(c) Explain the physiotherapy implications for preventing and managing this complication.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Paralytic ileus (temporary paralysis of the bowel) and intestinal obstruction are recognised potential complications following laparotomy and other abdominal surgery.

(b)
• Post-operative distension is commonly produced by swallowing air, which is common in anxious patients.
• When post-operative distension is anticipated, a nasogastric tube may be inserted to decompress the bowel.
• Constipation is also common after surgery, reflecting disturbed bowel function.

(c)
• Physiotherapy implications – frequent turning, exercises and ambulation as early as possible alleviate the distension produced by swallowing air.
• Early ambulation improves dietary intake, which together with prescribed stool softeners promotes bowel elimination.
• A related complication, difficulty voiding, may also occur after surgery.
• If the patient cannot void within the specified time frame, they are catheterised and the catheter removed once the bladder has been emptied.
• General mobilisation and exercise therefore serve gastrointestinal, bladder and general recovery purposes after abdominal surgery.
• They reduce chest and circulatory complications while also promoting normal gastrointestinal and bowel/bladder function.
• This makes early, frequent mobilisation and positional change a central physiotherapy strategy for preventing paralytic ileus and constipation.
• Physiotherapy input is therefore combined with medical measures (nasogastric decompression, stool softeners, catheterisation as needed) to manage the overall post-operative gastrointestinal/genitourinary recovery.

(a)
• Pre-operative: patient education, upper and lower limb strengthening exercises.
• Pelvic floor muscle strengthening, transverse abdominis exercises, cardiovascular exercise (cycling, walking), and hydrotherapy.
• Week 1 post-op: advice on scar management (massage, ultrasound therapy), pain control modalities, and advice on comfortable positioning.
• Also pelvic floor strengthening exercises (kegel, bird dog, glute bridge), simple mobility exercises such as walking, transverse abdominis strengthening, and lower limb strengthening/ROM exercises.
• Weeks 2-6: progression of all strengthening exercises, upper limb strengthening/ROM exercises.
• Also progression of transverse abdominis exercises, pelvic floor exercises in more functional positions, functional activities related to hobbies/work, and pacing advice.
• Week 7 onwards: gradual return to normal activities of daily living with little or no pain.
• Lifting activities can resume without pain by six weeks, but heavy lifting is not advised for up to six months.

(b)
• Rationale – pre-operative strengthening prepares the patient's muscles for post-operative recovery.
• Pelvic floor and transverse abdominis exercises support the pelvic/abdominal structures disturbed by surgery, and progression is paced to match tissue healing time; pacing advice and the lifting restriction protect the healing tissues from re-injury.

(c)
• Because hysterectomy is pelvic/abdominal surgery, DVT risk is present.
• General strengthening, cardiovascular exercise and early simple mobility (walking) from week 1 promote circulation and reduce venous stasis, preventing prolonged immobility, a key clot-formation risk factor.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the physiotherapy management of a hysterectomy patient: pre-operative phase, and post-operative phase (week 1; weeks 2-6; week 7 onwards), stating the goals, techniques and precautions.
(b) State the rationale for the interventions used.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Phantom limb pain is a complication of amputation in which the patient perceives that the limb is still present after it has been removed.
• It is listed alongside wound problems/infection and growing bone as a recognised complication of amputation surgery.

(b)
• Before amputation, the surgeon notes the level of good blood perfusion, nerve supply, site of amputation, and the blood supply/innervation of the stump.
• The nerves that previously supplied the removed limb remain in the residual stump.
• The muscle at the stump end is secured either by myoplasty (muscle sutured to muscle) or myodesis (muscle sutured to bone).
• The state of the stump/residual limb is what is later assessed for prosthetic fitting.

(c)
• Immediate intervention for phantom limb pain includes immediate prosthetic fitting.
• Alongside psychologist/psychotherapy intervention.
• Physiotherapy implications: the stump's blood perfusion, nerve supply and innervation determine how well it will tolerate a prosthesis.
• Physiotherapy management should therefore support early, well-perfused, well-innervated stump healing.
• It should work closely with the prosthetic fitting process.
• Psychological support addresses the distress associated with phantom limb sensation.
questions.question:
(a) State the pathophysiological basis of phantom limb pain following amputation.
(b) State how the site and technique of amputation relate to this complication.
(c) Explain the physiotherapy/rehabilitation implications for preventing or managing phantom limb pain.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Indications: patients with COPD; patients at the post-operative stage (abdominal and thoracic surgery).
• Patients with atelectasis; respiratory muscle weakness (as in some neurological conditions); prolonged bed stay; patients requiring mechanical ventilation.
• Techniques: postural drainage; manual techniques (chest wall percussion/clapping, vibration and shaking).
• Breathing exercises (diaphragmatic breathing, pursed-lip breathing, active cycle of breathing technique, glossopharyngeal breathing, autogenic breathing/drainage, deep/sustained maximal inspiration, segmental/costal expansion exercise).
• Also manual hyperinflation, CPAP, positive expiratory pressure, respiratory muscle training, coughing, and incentive spirometry.
• Precautions/contraindications: recent skin graft/flap on the thorax; burns, open wounds, skin infections of the thorax; recently placed cardiac pacemaker.
• Suspected pulmonary tuberculosis; osteoporosis; rib fracture; haemoptysis; bronchospasm; osteomyelitis of the ribs; chest wall pain.
• Unstable cardiovascular disorder; vomiting; recent spinal surgery; increased intracranial pressure; empyema; acute asthma; recent meal/tube feeding; untreated pneumothorax; severe emphysema.

(b)
• Rationale – chest physiotherapy improves oxygen transport/respiratory efficiency, promotes lung expansion, strengthens respiratory muscles and eliminates secretions.
• This is essential where the patient has ineffective coughing or impaired mucociliary clearance leading to inability to clear airway secretions.
• The choice of technique must consider the pathophysiology and clinical presentation of the condition, the physiological basis of the method, and the patient's acceptance.

(c)
Post-operative chest infection is prevented because reduced airflow (from shallow breathing after surgery) allows secretions to pool; chest physiotherapy techniques clear these secretions and re-expand the lungs, while adequate analgesia allows deep breathing/effective coughing without incisional pain limiting the patient.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the physiotherapy management of chest complications in a surgical patient using chest physiotherapy techniques, stating the indications, techniques and precautions.
(b) State the rationale for the techniques used.
(c) Explain the basis for preventing post-operative chest infection, a named complication.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Pulmonary embolism, together with DVT, is referred to as a venous thromboembolic event (VTE).
• It is a major complication after surgery, particularly gynaecological/pelvic surgery, that can result in significant morbidity and mortality.
• It occurs when a thrombus formed in the deep veins dislodges and travels through the venous system to obstruct the pulmonary circulation.

(b)
• Patients are predisposed to thromboembolism through alteration of hypercoagulability, venous stasis and vessel wall (venous endothelial) injury.
• Perioperative and post-operative immobility adversely affects venous drainage from the lower limb, promoting stasis and DVT formation.
• Vessel wall injury can result from surgical dissection, and reduced fibrinolytic activity associated with the operative procedure contributes to hypercoagulability.
• Together these allow thrombus formation that can embolise to the lungs.

(c)
• Once a clot lodges in the pulmonary circulation it obstructs blood flow through the lungs.
• This can precipitate significant morbidity and mortality by compromising gas exchange and increasing the workload placed on the heart.
• This contributes to the general list of post-operative complications that includes myocardial infarction and heart failure.
• Physiotherapy implications: prevention is the priority – elevation of the bed end, compression stockings, general breathing exercises, active limb movement, early ambulation, anticoagulants where prescribed, calf pump exercises and minimising tourniquet use.
• Regular activation of the muscle pumps and frequent body-position changes minimise circulatory stasis, since this can have serious consequences for the patient's recovery.
questions.question:
(a) State the pathophysiological basis of pulmonary embolism as a post-operative complication.
(b) State how immobility, hypercoagulability and vessel wall injury relate to this complication.
(c) Explain how pulmonary embolism can cause cardiorespiratory collapse, with the physiotherapy implications.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Osteoarthritis of the knee; indications for surgery when conservative treatment fails include disabling pain, instability and deformity.

(b)
Total knee arthroplasty (total joint arthroplasty – replacement of the articular surfaces of the knee).

(c)
• Pre-operative goals: proper assessment of movement and functional loss of the knee joint prior to surgery to guide post-operative rehabilitation, and assessment of respiratory function.
• Post-operative goals: restore ROM to the knee, promote joint stability, regain neuromuscular control of joint motion, restore gait and balance, and improve quality of life, with emphasis on moving all joints and muscles to prevent venous stasis (DVT).

(d)
• Precautions: wound healing must be well monitored; gradual mobilisation of the knee commences 2-3 days post-op, with static quadriceps contraction commencing hours post-op.
• The knee is kept non-weight-bearing for 4 weeks, partial weight bearing at 5-6 weeks, and full weight bearing at 7-8 weeks; decisions on weight-bearing status with walking aids should be made following careful and thorough assessment.

(e)
• Progression: initial treatment includes therapeutic exercise, transfer and gait training and instruction in ADLs.
• Once he has achieved an adequate level of function and is released from surgical precautions, instruction in establishing a routine of regular exercise and physical activity to support musculoskeletal and cardiovascular fitness is crucial to long-term outcomes and quality of life.
• Discharge from in-patient care considers functional activities such as getting in and out of bed and other recommended ADLs, and patient education covers the concerned surgical procedure and any specific post-operative instructions from the surgeon.
questions.question:
A 70-year-old man with severe osteoarthritis of the knee causing disabling pain and deformity, unresponsive to conservative treatment, undergoes total knee arthroplasty.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Ovarian cystectomy: a benign gynaecological surgery, performed through incisions such as the Pfannenstiel incision, a convex incision about 5 cm above the pubic symphysis offering good pelvic exposure and postoperative strength.

(b)
• Gynaecological surgeries can be for benign conditions (e.g. myomectomy, hysterectomy, ovarian cystectomy, repair of perineal trauma, bilateral tubal ligation) or malignant conditions (e.g. total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, vulvectomy).
• Indications relevant to the female reproductive system include chronic pelvic pain, as in this patient, among others such as fibroids and abnormal bleeding for related procedures.

(c)
• Pre-operative physiotherapy assessment includes a thorough history and teaching of breathing control manoeuvres, supported coughing, chest wall mobility exercises.
• Also mobility exercises for the limbs (hip, knee, foot and ankle), turning in bed, sitting up, transferring, chair sitting and walking erect, and explanation of the expected post-operative course, since patients undergoing gynaecologic surgery are predisposed to DVT/PE due to hypercoagulability, venous stasis and vessel wall injury from the pelvic surgery.

(d)
• Post-operative management: instruction in mobilisation and body positioning coordinated with deep breathing and supported coughing manoeuvres, performed hourly during waking hours.
• Goals also include maximising joint ROM, postural correction, maximising muscle length/ligament integrity, maximising ability to perform ADLs, and maintaining/increasing general muscle strength and endurance.
• Achieved through general mobility exercises (hip/knee flexion-extension, foot/ankle exercises) performed hourly; mobilisation and regular activation of the leg muscle pumps minimise the risk of thromboemboli and pressure areas.

(a) A 33-year-old woman with a benign ovarian cyst causing chronic pelvic pain is scheduled for ovarian cystectomy through a Pfannenstiel incision. State the surgical procedure and briefly describe what it involves.
