(a) A 34-year-old woman is 3 days post open reduction and internal fixation for a fracture shaft of tibia. State the risk factors that predispose her to post-operative complications.
(b) List the complications she is at risk of, grouped as pulmonary, circulatory and musculoskeletal.
(c) Outline the physiotherapy management options available and justify the use of one of them.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Risk factors: operative fixation itself carries risks such as anaesthetic problems and foreign body reaction; general risk factors include reduced mobility from the injury, and any pre-existing respiratory/circulatory problems, smoking, obesity, or age.

(b)
• Pulmonary: post-operative atelectasis, pneumonia/bronchopneumonia, hypoxemia.
• Circulatory: shock, deep vein thrombosis, and acute vascular injury.
• Musculoskeletal: joint stiffness from immobilisation, general muscle weakness, delayed union, malunion or nonunion, and infection/chronic osteomyelitis.

(c)
• Management options: active leg and foot exercises to prevent blood clot formation, calf and foot muscle exercises performed every half hour to reduce DVT risk.
• Also breathing exercises and chest physiotherapy to prevent pulmonary complications, and rehabilitation exercises to restore muscle power and joint ROM.
• Justification: active leg and foot/calf pump exercises of both the operated and non-operated leg are justified because they directly reduce DVT risk by activating the leg muscle pumps to prevent venous stasis.
• This is particularly important given her reduced mobility after lower limb fracture fixation, alongside maintaining a healthy body weight, good lifestyle and regular exercise as further preventive measures.

questions.question:
(a) Describe burns under the following headings: definition, classification/degrees, and complications.
(b) Explain the clinical basis for full-thickness burns being more dangerous to the patient than superficial burns.
(c) Distinguish between a partial-thickness (second-degree) burn and a full-thickness (third-degree) burn.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Definition: a burn is a traumatic injury to the skin or other organic tissue caused by thermal or other acute exposure.
• Burns occur when cells in the skin or other tissue are destroyed by heat, cold, electricity, radiation or caustic chemicals.
• Classification – first-degree (superficial): affects only the epidermis; red, painful, dry, no blisters.
• Classification – second-degree (partial thickness): epidermis and part of the dermis; red/blistered, may be swollen and painful.
• Classification – third-degree (full thickness): destroys epidermis and dermis, may damage underlying bone/muscle/tendon; white or charred, painless (nerve endings destroyed).
• Classification – fourth-degree: full-thickness burn extending to muscle or bone.
• Complications/major concerns: loss of fluids, inability to maintain body temperature, and infection.

(b)
• In full-thickness burns the epidermis and hair follicles are destroyed, so new skin will not grow, and the wound heals slowly and poorly without medical attention.
• Because nerve endings are destroyed there is no pain, which can mask the true severity of the injury.
• Loss of the skin's water-resistant, semi-impermeable barrier contributes to massive fluid loss, and destruction of the protective barrier increases infection risk, so full-thickness burns generally require referral to a burn surgeon and skin grafting.

(c)
• A partial-thickness burn involves the epidermis and part of the dermis, is red/salmon-pink, moist and blistered, and painful.
• A full-thickness burn destroys the epidermis and entire dermis (and may extend deeper), appears dry/leathery/white or charred, and is painless because the nerve endings are destroyed.

(a)
• Definition: local anaesthesia (LA) is loss of sensation without loss of consciousness or impairment of central control of vital functions.
• Local anaesthetics block nerve conduction when applied locally to nerve tissue, an effect that is completely reversible.
• Types: surface anaesthesia – applied to mucous membranes (eye, nose, mouth, tracheobronchial tree, oesophagus, genitourinary tract); used in tonometry, nasal lesions, stomatitis, tonsillectomy, endoscopy, intubation, gastric ulcer, burns, proctoscopy.
• Infiltration anaesthesia – LA injected superficially into skin or into deeper structures including intra-abdominal organs; used for minor procedures like drainage/excision.
• Field block – subcutaneous injection proximal to the site, interrupting nerve transmission distal to the injection; used at the forearm, scalp, anterior abdominal wall and lower limbs.
• Nerve block – injection around individual peripheral nerves or nerve plexuses, producing larger areas of anaesthesia with a smaller dose.
• Complications: cardiovascular and CNS toxicity from ion channel blockade; peripheral nerve complications.
• Allergic/hypersensitivity reactions (rashes, dermatitis, asthma); mechanical effects of technique (needle trauma, infection); milder effects include bruising, redness, itching, swelling, dizziness, nausea and numbness.

(b)
• Regional anaesthesia acts on nerve roots to anaesthetise and paralyse the lower abdomen and lower limbs, without causing loss of consciousness.
• It is safer, provides good analgesia and muscle relaxation, and avoids the CNS depression and reduced myocardial performance caused by general anaesthetics.
• These qualities make regional anaesthesia preferable for patients whose cardiac, pulmonary or renal systems are already compromised.

(c)
Field block is subcutaneous injection proximal to the site (lesser dose, greater area of anaesthesia), while nerve block is injected around individual peripheral nerves/plexuses, starting a few centimetres distal to the injection and lasting longer than field block or infiltration.
questions.question:
(a) Describe local anaesthesia under the following headings: definition, types, and complications.
(b) Explain the clinical basis for regional anaesthesia being preferred over general anaesthesia in cardiac, pulmonary and renal procedures.
(c) Distinguish between field block and nerve block.

(a) State the pathophysiological basis of burns, relating the type (thermal, chemical, electrical, cold) to the depth of injury.
(b) State how burn depth relates to the common complications of fluid loss and infection.
(c) Explain the physiotherapy implications for positioning and splinting across the phases of burn management.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Thermal burns are the most common type, associated with flames, hot liquids, hot solid objects and steam.
• Because skin has low thermal conductivity, most thermal burns involve the epidermis and part of the dermis; depth relates to contact temperature, duration of contact, and skin thickness.
• Cold exposure (frostbite) damages skin/tissue when ice crystals puncture cells or create a hypertonic environment, interrupting blood flow and causing tissue hypoxia.
• Chemical burns occur from contact with a toxic substance (liquid, solid or gas).
• Electrical burns occur from contact with an electrical source; current (not voltage) is the key determinant, with severity depending on intensity, duration of contact, type of current and tissue resistance.

(b)
• The major concerns in burns are loss of fluids, inability to maintain body temperature, and infection.
• The skin's water-resistant, semi-impermeable barrier normally prevents fluid loss; loss of this function (greatest in full-thickness burns, where epidermis and hair follicles are destroyed) contributes to massive fluid loss.
• Because the protective skin barrier and, in full-thickness burns, the nerve endings are destroyed, these burns heal slowly and poorly and carry higher infection risk, often needing skin grafting.

(c)
• Positioning is fundamental to burn rehabilitation because it prevents contracture, controls oedema, prevents localised neuropathies and maintains soft tissue in an elongated position.
• Burn patients tend to assume a flexed, adducted (foetal) position from pain.
• Splints/positioning across the acute phase (modulable, non-constrictive, prophylactic for tendon/joint damage), wound healing phase (prevent contracture, protect grafts), rehabilitation phase (reduce contracture, maintain ROM) and reconstructive phase (fixation after contracture release/reconstruction).
• These are individualised to the patient's medical condition, ROM and skin condition.

(a)
• When conservative treatment of osteoarthritis fails, surgical intervention may be recommended.
• Indications for surgery include disabling pain, instability and deformity, reflecting progressive joint damage.

(b)
• A joint with limited movement due to pain is bound to deteriorate unless ROM and muscle power are restored to near normal.
• Debridement (removal of loose bodies, osteophytes and degenerate semilunar cartilage) relieves mechanical symptoms such as locking.
• Osteotomy corrects deformity by excising a wedge of bone, relieving pain by altering interosseous blood flow and redistributing forces through the articular surfaces.
• Arthrodesis surgically fuses a joint for pain relief and stability at the expense of mobility.
• Arthroplasty (partial or total) replaces the articular surfaces.

(c)
• General post-operative rehabilitation goals are to restore ROM to the affected joint, promote joint stability, regain neuromuscular control of joint motion, restore gait and balance, and improve quality of life.
• The choice of specific post-operative physiotherapy procedures depends on the particular surgical intervention performed.
• It also depends on the extent of joint involvement before surgery, and individual patient characteristics (including co-morbid health conditions and physical activity level).
• Emphasis is placed on moving all joints and muscles to prevent venous stasis (DVT).
• Decisions on weight-bearing status with walking aids should follow careful, thorough assessment.
questions.question:
(a) State the pathophysiological basis of osteoarthritis progressing to require surgery.
(b) State how joint changes in osteoarthritis relate to the common complications of instability and deformity.
(c) Explain the physiotherapy implications for rehabilitation following joint replacement for osteoarthritis.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Definition: breast cancer surgery requiring removal of the breast, partially or totally, mainly to treat breast cancer, and sometimes as a preventive measure.
• Types: simple (total) mastectomy – removes entire breast, nipple, areola, fascia of pectoralis major and skin, with possible sentinel lymph node biopsy.
• Modified radical mastectomy – simple mastectomy combined with axillary lymph node dissection, sparing the pectoral muscles.
• Radical (Halsted) mastectomy – removes entire breast, axillary lymph nodes and pectoral muscles, rarely done now.
• Skin-sparing mastectomy – breast tissue removed through a conservative incision around the areola, preserving more skin to facilitate reconstruction.
• Nipple-sparing mastectomy – as skin-sparing, but nipple/areola left in place unless cancer cells found beneath them; and prophylactic mastectomy – preventive, for high genetic risk.
• Complications: bleeding and infection, haematoma, seroma, limited shoulder ROM, scar formation, brachial plexus injury, numbness in the chest/upper arm.
• Lymphoedema (if axillary nodes removed), Post-Mastectomy Pain Syndrome, musculoskeletal pain at the neck/shoulder/axilla/breast, abnormal posture, and psychological problems (depression, anxiety, fear).

(b)
• If axillary lymph nodes are also removed (as in modified radical mastectomy, done to check whether cancer cells have spread beyond the breast), the normal lymphatic drainage pathway of the arm is disrupted.
• Fluid can no longer drain effectively, predisposing to lymphoedema as a side effect.

(c)
• Simple (total) mastectomy removes the entire breast, including nipple, areola, fascia of pectoralis major and skin (with possible sentinel node biopsy).
• Modified radical mastectomy combines a simple mastectomy with full axillary lymph node dissection to check for spread of cancer cells, but unlike radical mastectomy it spares the pectoral muscles.
questions.question:
(a) Describe mastectomy under the following headings: definition, types, and complications.
(b) Explain the clinical basis for axillary lymph node removal increasing the risk of lymphoedema.
(c) Distinguish between simple (total) mastectomy and modified radical mastectomy.

(a) State the pathophysiological basis of emphysema.
(b) State how the types of emphysema relate to common complications.
(c) Explain why emphysema may affect a distant system (the heart) and cause a functional deficit, with the physiotherapy implications.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Inhaled toxins such as cigarette smoke become trapped in the alveoli, triggering a localised inflammatory response.
• Chemicals released during this response (e.g. elastase) cause the alveolar septum to disintegrate – a process called septal rupture.
• Septal rupture leaves large cavities called bullae and greatly reduces the alveolar surface area available for gas exchange.
• It also decreases ventilation of the surrounding healthy lung parenchyma.

(b)
• Panacinar emphysema is caused by α-1-antitrypsin deficiency, involves the entire acinus, and typically affects the lower lungs.
• Centrilobular emphysema is caused by smoking, involves the proximal/central part of the acinus, typically affects the upper lungs, and is more common in men.
• Because centrilobular disease is smoking-related, ongoing airway irritation commonly complicates it, whereas panacinar disease reflects an underlying genetic predisposition.
• As alveoli continue to break down, hyperventilation can no longer compensate for the reduced surface area, and the body cannot maintain adequate blood oxygen levels.

(c)
• This leads to pulmonary hypertension, which places increased strain on the right side of the heart.
• The heart muscle thickens to pump more blood, and this is often accompanied by jugular venous distension – a cardiac functional deficit arising from lung disease.
• Physiotherapy implications: breathing exercises emphasising relaxed, minimum-effort expiration, controlled breathing during activity, postural drainage if tolerated, vibration/shaking and huffing/coughing to clear secretions.
• Graded exercise training must be paced to the patient's reduced cardiopulmonary reserve given the right heart strain described above.

(a)
Electrical burn: contact with an electrical source; in conductive injuries the entrance and exit wounds may be small, but there is massive tissue damage between the entrance and exit points, unlike non-conductive electrical injuries which mainly cause ignition of clothing.

(b)
• Considerations: current (not voltage) is what kills; severity depends on the intensity of the current, the duration of contact, the kind of current (AC or DC), the width of the current path, and the type of tissues exposed (their resistance).
• Exposure to electrical current almost always results in a full-thickness burn; associated complications can include cardiac arrest/arrhythmias, respiratory arrest, spinal fractures, long bone fractures and internal organ damage.

(c)
• Early considerations: assessment of airway/breathing (starting oxygen if there are signs of respiratory involvement or decreased consciousness) and circulation, obtaining a history of the injury.
• Also a rapid physical examination to check for other injuries and estimate burned/unburned areas; the wound itself is covered with a dry dressing rather than ointments or creams.

(d)
• Acute phase: splinting is prophylactic if tendon/joint damage is suspected, kept modulable and non-constrictive because of fluctuating oedema.
• Positioning maintains burned tissue in an elongated state to prevent contracture, control oedema and prevent localised neuropathies.
• Wound healing phase: splints prevent contracture development and protect newly applied skin grafts.
• Rehabilitation phase: reduce contracture non-surgically, prevent deformities, provide sustained stretching of scar tissue, and maintain gained ROM.
• Reconstructive phase: splints/positioning provide fixation following release of contractures or reconstruction surgery, with monitoring for wound maceration.
questions.question:
(a) A 27-year-old electrician sustains an electrical burn to the hand at work with a small entrance and exit wound but suspected deep tissue damage between them, requiring surgical debridement and later skin grafting. State the type of burn and briefly describe the injury pattern.
(b) State the pathological basis and considerations relevant to electrical burns.
(c) Describe the pre-operative/early physiotherapy considerations for this patient.
(d) Describe the post-operative physiotherapy management from the acute phase through to the reconstructive phase.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Pneumothorax (a sudden collection of air or gas in the chest causing the lung to collapse).

(b)
Traumatic pneumothorax can occur after trauma to the chest or lung wall, including from medical procedures that can damage the lung such as chest tube insertions, ventilator use, lung biopsies and CPR; secondary spontaneous pneumothorax occurs in people with known lung problems.

(c)
• Air leaks into the pleural space following damage to the chest/lung wall structures, causing the lung to collapse.
• Symptoms include chest pain on the affected side, dyspnoea, cough, abnormal breathing movement and rapid respiratory rate.

(d)
• Assessment: respiratory assessment for symmetry, rate, depth, chest expansion, dyspnoea, accessory muscle involvement and chest measurements.
• Untreated pneumothorax is a contraindication to chest physiotherapy techniques, so the medical/surgical team must treat the pneumothorax (e.g. with a chest drain) before vigorous chest physiotherapy such as percussion or postural drainage is applied.
• Once medically appropriate, physiotherapy management focuses on breathing exercises, gentle mobilisation and monitoring of vital signs and skin colour.
• Chest physiotherapy techniques are introduced cautiously and only once the pneumothorax has been appropriately treated, since an untreated pneumothorax is among the general contraindications to chest physiotherapy.
questions.question:
A 42-year-old man is 2 days post thoracic surgery and suddenly develops chest pain on the affected side, shortness of breath, cough and rapid respiratory rate, with abnormal breathing movement.
(a) State the most likely diagnosis.
(b) State the possible causes relevant to his post-surgical status.
(c) Describe the pathophysiology of this condition.
(d) Describe the physiotherapy assessment and management relevant to his condition.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Pre-operative: pelvic floor muscle exercises to prepare the patient before surgery.
• Post-operative goals: optimise the pattern of pelvic floor muscle contraction, and train urinary continence.
• Further goals: improve erectile dysfunction, and bladder training.
• Techniques: breathing exercises, starting with pursed-lip breathing and progressing to diaphragmatic breathing.
• Pelvic floor muscle exercises: hip bridging, knee rolling, and kegel exercises performed lying supine, side-lying and sitting (8-10 repetitions, 3-5 sets).
• Strengthening the pelvic floor using electrical stimulation via a probe electrode.
• Soft tissue/frictional massage to relieve pain and improve scar healing, plus patient education and psychological counselling.

(b)
• Rationale – breathing exercises prevent cardiorespiratory complications after surgery.
• Pelvic floor exercises are given because strengthening these muscles before prostatectomy significantly improves post-prostatectomy urinary continence, post-micturition dribble and erectile function.
• Before giving strengthening exercises for erectile dysfunction, the exact cause must be determined, since exercises given to a pelvic floor in spasm will exacerbate symptoms.
• Psychological counselling is given because a cancer diagnosis combined with incontinence and sexual dysfunction is a significant cause of distress.

(c)
Incontinence (uncontrollable, involuntary urine leaking, possibly worse if older than 70) is managed with pelvic floor muscle training/kegel exercises and electrical stimulation, together with general advice on incontinence pads, darker clothing, and avoiding fluids (coffee, green tea, beer) that worsen symptoms.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the physiotherapy management of a prostatectomy patient: pre-operative and post-operative phases, stating the goals and techniques used.
(b) State the rationale for the interventions used.
(c) Explain the basis for managing urinary incontinence, a named complication of prostatectomy.

A 45-year-old woman, 6 hours post lumbar spinal fusion, is noted on neurological examination to have reduced power in the lower limb that was not present pre-operatively.
(a) Identify the problem shown by the assessment findings.
(b) State the structures/mechanisms that could be responsible.
(c) State the differential problems that should be considered.
(d) Explain the clinical reasoning for the physiotherapy/clinical plan for this patient.
questions.answerText:
(a)
A post-operative neurological deficit, probably the most dreaded of all spinal surgery complications.

(b)
• Injury to the nervous elements can be direct, at the time of surgery (such as laceration, traction or compression of an exiting nerve root, or trauma from surgical instruments/misplaced screws or hooks), or indirect, due to disruption of blood supply or compression.
• Compression can also be caused by a mass lesion such as a haematoma, pseudomeningocele, epidural abscess, or recurrent disc herniation.

(c)
• Differential problems: whether the deficit occurred intraoperatively or developed in the early post-operative period.
• Injury to peripheral nerves may also occur from improper patient positioning during surgery, causing nerve palsies; the presentation of neurological symptoms from a mass lesion is typically insidious and almost never in the immediate post-operative period.

(d)
• Clinical reasoning: a meticulous neurological examination as soon as the patient wakes from surgery is of critical importance to distinguish deficits that occur intraoperatively from those that develop in the early post-operative period.
• This is because imaging of the post-operative spine so soon after surgery is often of limited value.
• Determining the cause depends on recollection of intraoperative events by the surgical team, the timing of symptom presentation, and any imaging findings, so the baseline post-operative examination and prompt reporting of any new deficit to the surgical team are essential before physiotherapy mobilisation proceeds.

questions.question:
(a) A 45-year-old woman with fibroids causing heavy abnormal vaginal bleeding is scheduled for total abdominal hysterectomy. State the surgical procedure and briefly describe what it involves.
(b) State the pathological basis and other indications for hysterectomy.
(c) Describe the pre-operative physiotherapy assessment and management for this patient.
(d) Describe the post-operative physiotherapy management from week 1 through to week 7 onwards.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Total abdominal hysterectomy: removal of the uterus and cervix through the abdomen.

(b)
Indications: fibroids (30%), endometriosis, uterine prolapse, cancer of the uterus/cervix/ovaries, chronic pelvic pain, adenomyosis, and abnormal vaginal bleeding.

(c)
• Pre-operative physiotherapy: patient education, upper and lower limb strengthening exercises.
• Pelvic floor muscle strengthening, transverse abdominis exercises, cardiovascular exercise (cycling, walking), hydrotherapy, and preparation for the physiotherapy programme.

(d)
• Week 1: scar management advice (massage, ultrasound), pelvic floor exercises (kegel, bird dog, glute bridge), pain control modalities, positioning advice.
• Also simple mobility exercises such as walking, transverse abdominis strengthening, lower limb strengthening/ROM.
• Weeks 2-6: progression of all strengthening exercises, upper limb strengthening/ROM, progression of transverse abdominis exercises.
• Also pelvic floor exercises in more functional positions, functional activities related to hobbies/work, and pacing advice.
• Week 7 onwards: gradual return to normal activities of daily living with little or no pain; lifting activities can resume without pain, but heavy lifting is avoided for up to six months.

questions.question:
(a) A 50-year-old man is 2 days post laparotomy through a midline incision for a general abdominal condition. State the risk factors that could predispose him to post-operative complications.
(b) List the post-operative complications he is at risk of developing, grouped as pulmonary, circulatory and musculoskeletal.
(c) Outline the physiotherapy management options available to prevent these complications and justify the use of one of them.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Risk factors: a medical history of respiratory or circulatory problems, smoking, obesity, inactivity from another disease or injury, and age.

(b)
• Pulmonary: post-operative atelectasis, pneumonia or bronchopneumonia, hypoxemia, exacerbation of asthma or chronic obstructive disease.
• Circulatory: deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, myocardial infarction and heart failure.
• Musculoskeletal: general muscle weakness and loss of mobility, and pressure sores.

(c)
• Management options: adequate analgesia, oxygen by face mask/nasal prongs, and regular physiotherapy (chest physiotherapy, coughing manoeuvres, breathing exercises, incentive spirometer use, early ambulation, bed mobility).
• For DVT prevention: elevation of the bed end, compression stockings, general breathing exercises, active limb movement, early ambulation, anticoagulants, calf pump exercises and minimising tourniquet use.
• Justification: early ambulation is justified because it is safe to get the patient out of bed on day one unless medically contraindicated.
• Walking (progressing from a zimmer frame to sticks) activates the leg muscle pumps, reducing venous stasis and DVT risk, while also helping lung expansion and preventing chest complications and general muscle weakness.

(a)
Gangrene of the foot; an indication for amputation, along with a dangerous limb or a useless body part.

(b)
Myodesis: suturing muscle to bone; this differs from myoplasty, which is suturing muscle to muscle.

(c)
Before prosthetic fitting, the stump (residual limb) is assessed for the level of good blood perfusion, the nerve supply, the site of amputation, and the blood supply and innervation of the stump, since these determine how well the stump will heal and tolerate a prosthesis.

(d)
• A recognised complication is phantom limb pain, where the patient perceives the limb is still present after amputation; immediate intervention includes immediate prosthetic fitting and psychologist/psychotherapy intervention.
• Other complications to watch for are wound problems/infection and growing bone.

(e)
• Progression and discharge planning follow assessment of the stump's healing, blood perfusion and innervation, with referral for prosthetic fitting once appropriate.
• Patient education should cover wound care to reduce infection risk, what to expect regarding phantom limb sensation, and the availability of psychological support if this becomes distressing.
questions.question:
A 65-year-old man with diabetic gangrene of the foot undergoes a below-knee amputation, with the muscle secured by myodesis.
(a) State the diagnosis and confirm the indication for surgery.
(b) State the surgical technique used to secure the muscle and how it differs from the alternative technique.
(c) State the physiotherapy considerations for assessing the stump before prosthetic fitting.
(d) State the precautions relevant to a recognised complication of amputation.
(e) Describe the progression, discharge planning and patient education relevant to his case.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Prophylactic (preventive) mastectomy.
• It removes all breast tissue that could potentially develop into breast cancer, from just beneath the skin to the chest wall and around the borders of the breast, including the milk ducts and lobules, on both breasts.

(b)
• Mastectomy removes the breast, partially or totally, mainly to treat breast cancer, and can also be done as a preventive measure.
• Other indications: prior radiation therapy to the breast; two or more tumour areas in the same breast too far apart for one incision; incomplete tumour removal after lumpectomy and re-excision(s); connective tissue disease such as scleroderma; pregnancy requiring radiation; a tumour larger than 5 cm that does not shrink much with chemotherapy; a tumour large relative to breast size; inflammatory breast cancer; gynaecomastia in men.

(c)
• Pre-operative physiotherapy is mainly educational: teaching the type of exercises to be done after surgery.
• Motivating and encouraging the patient before surgery, and educating her on the conduct of daily life.

(d)
• Early phase: ROM exercises, joint mobilisation, and chest physiotherapy (breathing exercises) to improve lung capacity and prevent pulmonary complications.
• Arm exercises such as wand exercise, elbow winging and shoulder blade squeeze to prevent oedema formation.
• Late phase: soft tissue mobilisation, strengthening exercises, aerobic exercise, postural assessment, and relaxation techniques.
• Complex Decongestive Physical Therapy for lymphoedema: an intensive phase (manual lymphatic drainage, multi-layer compression bandaging, exercises improving lymph outflow) followed by a maintenance phase (self-massage, elastic compression garments, exercises).
• Education and psychological counselling throughout.
• Collaboration with a prosthetist to recommend a post-mastectomy prosthesis.
questions.question:
(a) A 45-year-old woman who has tested positive for a BRCA1 gene mutation opts to undergo a preventive mastectomy of both breasts. State the type of mastectomy most likely to be performed and briefly describe what it involves.
(b) State the pathological basis and other indications for mastectomy in general.
(c) Describe the pre-operative physiotherapy assessment and management for this patient.
(d) Describe the post-operative physiotherapy management for this patient from the early to the late phase.

(a) State the pathophysiological basis of post-operative hypotension and hypertension.
(b) State how these relate to the common complication of septic shock.
(c) Explain how uncorrected hypotension may progress to affect cerebral perfusion, with the physiotherapy implications.
questions.answerText:
(a)
• Hypotension, hypertension and septic shock are recognised "other complications" following surgery.
• Most causes of hypertension relate to inadequate pain relief or anxiety, and usually settle with appropriate analgesia.
• Hypotension is managed by assessing the patency of IV lines and ensuring appropriate fluids are given at the prescribed rate.

(b)
• Early shock seldom results from the effects of the surgery itself and should be treated as another injury until proven otherwise.
• Septic shock is a related state in which the heart rate naturally quickens to meet increased oxygen demands as part of the body's response to a compromising illness or infection.
• Resuscitation is the top priority if a patient is in shock.

(c)
• If hypotension is not corrected, cerebral perfusion can become inadequate.
• Management includes tilting the patient head-down to maintain cerebral perfusion.
• This is in addition to increasing fluid input and administering high-flow oxygen.
• Physiotherapy implications: mobilisation and positioning must be guided by the patient's haemodynamic stability.
• The room should be kept at a comfortable temperature with blankets to prevent chilling, and the patient monitored for cardiac dysrhythmias.
• Treatment includes oxygen administration, adequate hydration and proper nutrition alongside physiotherapy input.

questions.question:
A 68-year-old woman with disabling hip pain, instability and deformity from osteoarthritis, who has failed conservative treatment, is scheduled for total hip arthroplasty using a posterolateral approach.
(a) State the diagnosis and confirm the indication for surgery.
(b) State the surgical procedure to be performed.
(c) State the physiotherapy goals for the pre-operative and post-operative phases.
(d) State the precautions and contraindications relevant to her post-operative positioning.
(e) Describe the progression, discharge planning and patient education relevant to her case.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Osteoarthritis of the hip; indications for surgery when conservative treatment fails include disabling pain, instability and deformity.

(b)
Total hip arthroplasty, using metallic or plastic implants via an anterolateral, lateral or posterolateral approach.

(c)
• Pre-operative goals: assessment of movement and functional loss of the joint prior to surgery to guide post-operative rehabilitation, and assessment of respiratory function especially where compromise is suspected.
• Post-operative goals: restore ROM to the affected joint, promote joint stability, regain neuromuscular control of joint motion, restore gait and balance, and improve quality of life; emphasis is placed on moving all joints and muscles to prevent venous stasis (DVT).

(d)
• Precautions: in the anterolateral/lateral approach the joint is unstable in extension, adduction and external rotation, while in the posterolateral approach it is unstable in flexion, adduction and internal rotation, so these movement combinations must be avoided.
• External splintage is not required, but the physiotherapist should be familiar with the specific surgical procedure and any precautions specified by the surgeon.

(e)
• Progression: the patient moves the hip in bed within hours after surgery; partial weight bearing may begin after 72 hours post-op; healing following osteotomy may take 3-4 months.
• Treatment progresses through therapeutic exercise, transfer and gait training and instruction in ADLs, then, once released from surgical precautions, to a routine of regular exercise and physical activity for long-term musculoskeletal and cardiovascular fitness.
• Discharge planning considers functional activities such as getting in and out of bed and other recommended ADLs, with decisions on full, partial or non-weight-bearing status made after careful assessment.

(a)
• Atelectasis is a collapse of lung tissue affecting part or all of one lung, preventing normal oxygen absorption to healthy tissue.
• Anyone undergoing chest or abdominal surgery under general anaesthesia is at risk, since breathing is often shallow after surgery to avoid incisional pain.
• Any significant decrease in airflow to the alveoli contributes to pooling of secretions.

(b)
• The pooled secretions from reduced airflow can, in turn, cause infection – i.e. pneumonia or bronchopneumonia.
• Common symptoms of atelectasis are shortness of breath and decreased chest wall expansion.
• If a large area is affected and develops quickly, the individual may become cyanotic or pale with extreme shortness of breath, reflecting hypoxemia.
• Fever and increased heart rate may be present if infection accompanies the atelectasis.

(c)
• Untreated atelectasis and its associated infection/hypoxemia can progress to broader cardiopulmonary compromise.
• This contributes to the general list of post-operative complications that also includes myocardial infarction and heart failure.
• The respiratory problem can therefore place additional strain on the cardiovascular system – a distant-system functional deficit.
• Physiotherapy implications: adequate analgesia so the patient can breathe deeply without pain, chest physiotherapy, coughing manoeuvres, breathing exercises.
• Incentive spirometer use, early ambulation and bed mobility, all aimed at re-expanding the lung tissue and clearing secretions before infection or significant hypoxemia develops.
questions.question:
(a) State the pathophysiological basis of post-operative atelectasis.
(b) State how atelectasis relates to the common complications of pneumonia and hypoxemia.
(c) Explain how atelectasis can progress to affect a distant system, with the physiotherapy implications.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Reduced chest expansion and reluctance to mobilise post-caesarean section, placing her at risk of respiratory and circulatory complications.

(b)
• Caesarean section is performed through a Pfannenstiel incision – a convex incision about 5 cm above the pubic symphysis, offering good pelvic exposure, postoperative strength and cosmetic results.
• As a form of pelvic/abdominal surgery, it affects the abdominal wall muscles and predisposes to venous stasis in the pelvis.

(c)
• Differential problems: obstetric/gynaecological surgery predisposes to deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism (venous thromboembolic events) because of hypercoagulability, venous stasis and vessel wall injury.
• Anaesthesia and tissue dissection reduce lung volume, mechanics and gas exchange, with thoracic respiratory excursion significantly reduced and altered tone/pattern of diaphragmatic and intercostal muscle contraction, contributing to cardiopulmonary complications.
• Other general post-operative complications (as with any abdominal surgery) such as atelectasis and pressure areas should also be considered.

(d)
• Clinical reasoning: because reduced chest expansion and immobility both increase the risk of pulmonary and thromboembolic complications, the plan should include breathing control manoeuvres, supported coughing, chest wall mobility exercises, and mobility exercises for the limbs (hip, knee, foot and ankle), to be performed hourly.
• Also mobilisation, body positioning and regular activation of the leg muscle pumps to minimise circulatory stasis.
• She should also be taught to support her wound during breathing/coughing exercises, given her incisional pain.
questions.question:
A 29-year-old primigravida undergoes an emergency lower segment caesarean section through a Pfannenstiel incision. On the first post-operative day she is noted to have reduced chest expansion and is reluctant to mobilise because of incisional pain.
(a) Identify the problem shown by the assessment findings.
(b) State the structures/systems affected by this type of surgery.
(c) State the differential problems (complications) that should be considered.
(d) Explain the clinical reasoning for the physiotherapy plan for this patient.

A 55-year-old woman, 5 days post total abdominal hysterectomy, complains of pain and swelling of the left calf. On examination the calf is warm, swollen and tender, with a positive Homan's test.
(a) State the most likely diagnosis.
(b) State the predisposing factors for this condition in her case.
(c) Describe the pathophysiology of this condition.
(d) Describe the physiotherapy assessment and management appropriate for her.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) of the left calf.

(b)
Predisposing factors: she has undergone gynaecological/pelvic surgery, a recognised risk for DVT and pulmonary embolism; post-operative immobility, which adversely affects venous drainage from the lower limb.

(c)
• Perioperative and post-operative immobility adversely affects the drainage of blood from the lower extremity, promoting venous stasis.
• Pelvic masses, a gravid uterus, or surgically-induced haematomas/lymphocysts can also contribute to venous stasis; vessel wall injury can result from surgical dissection, and coagulation changes result from decreased fibrinolytic activity associated with the operative procedure.
• The combination of hypercoagulability, venous stasis and vessel wall injury allows a thrombus to form in the deep veins.

(d)
• Circulatory assessment: Homan's test and observation for oedema.
• Management: elevation of the bed end, compression stockings, general breathing exercises, active limb movement, early ambulation, anticoagulant therapy as prescribed, calf pump exercises, and minimising the use of tourniquets.
• If swelling persists, duplex Doppler ultrasonography or venography may be indicated (by the medical team) to exclude DVT/monitor its progress, and the leg should be elevated above heart level at rest to reduce swelling.

questions.question:
(a) A 38-year-old woman is 4 days post laparotomy and complains of abdominal distension and has not passed stool since surgery. State the risk factors relevant to this presentation.
(b) List the complications she may be experiencing or at risk of.
(c) Outline the physiotherapy management options and justify the use of one of them.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Risk factors: anxiety (which commonly leads to swallowing air), post-operative immobility, and the abdominal surgery itself disturbing normal bowel function.

(b)
Complications: paralytic ileus (temporary paralysis of the bowel) and intestinal obstruction; constipation, which is common after surgery.

(c)
• Management options: frequent turning, exercises and ambulation as early as possible to alleviate distension produced by swallowing air.
• Where post-operative distension is anticipated, a nasogastric tube may be inserted by the medical team; early ambulation to improve dietary intake, combined with a stool softener if prescribed, to promote bowel elimination.
• Justification: early ambulation is justified as the key physiotherapy intervention because it alleviates the air-swallowing-related distension through frequent turning and movement.
• It also directly improves dietary intake and bowel elimination, addressing both her distension and her lack of stool passage, while also conferring the general post-operative benefits of reducing chest and circulatory complications.

(a)
• Cognitive modalities: relaxation strategies (simple relaxation, imagery, hypnosis, biofeedback, music-assisted relaxation) are the most widely evaluated cognitive-behavioural approach, used as an adjunct to analgesic intervention.
• Physical modalities: TENS, shown effective over incision sites.
• Thermotherapy, initiated 48 hours after the operation and used in combination with other treatments for pain management and relaxation.
• Cryoanalgesia, which increases the pain threshold by cooling nerve tissue near the incision.
• Massage, which reduces the intensity and rate of unpleasantness of post-operative pain.
• Acupuncture, used for musculoskeletal/neurological pain and to reduce nausea and vomiting.
• Exercises (ROM and strengthening exercises), noted to significantly reduce pain post-surgery.
• Positioning: done every two hours, with assistance if necessary, using pillows to relax, relieve pain and reduce tension.

(b)
• Rationale – pain gate theory explains physical modalities such as TENS: stimulation of thermoreceptors/mechanoreceptors (large-diameter myelinated fibres) can predominate over and presynaptically inhibit small-diameter nociceptive information at the substantia gelatinosa.
• Relaxation techniques reduce the emotional/cognitive component of pain perception; regular repositioning prevents sustained pressure/tension that would otherwise worsen pain.

(c)
• Persistent leg oedema is treated with compression stockings and cryotherapy, with the leg elevated above heart level whenever at rest to reduce swelling.
• Exercise performed 4-6 times daily after discharge has been observed to decrease swelling; if swelling persists, duplex Doppler ultrasonography or venography is indicated to exclude DVT.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the physiotherapy management of post-operative pain, covering cognitive, physical and positioning-based modalities.
(b) State the rationale for the interventions used.
(c) Explain the basis for managing post-operative swelling, a related complication.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Types – vertical incisions: midline incision (in the midline of the abdomen, can extend from the xiphoid process to above/below the umbilicus).
• It is the simplest, offering the greatest ease of extension into the upper abdomen and least blood loss; also the suprapubic midline/infraumbilical incision.
• Horizontal incisions: Pfannenstiel incision, Joel-Cohen's incision, and Maylard incision.
• Also mini-laparotomy (incisions less than 5 cm, often used in bilateral tubal ligation) and laparoscopic surgery (small cuts for instruments).
• Procedures: Caesarean section (most commonly via Pfannenstiel incision); perineal laceration repair.
• Benign gynaecological surgery: myomectomy, hysterectomy, ovarian cystectomy, repair of perineal trauma (e.g. VVF, prolapse), bilateral tubal ligation.
• Malignant conditions: total abdominal hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, and vulvectomy.

(b)
• Surgeries in obstetrics and gynaecology often involve the pelvic region.
• Patients undergoing gynaecologic surgery are predisposed to thromboembolism because of alteration in hypercoagulability, venous stasis and vessel wall injury.
• Perioperative/post-operative immobility adversely affects venous drainage; pelvic masses, a gravid uterus, or surgically-induced haematomas/lymphocysts can further promote venous stasis, while surgical dissection or tumour growth into vascular tissue causes vessel wall injury.

(c)
• The midline incision runs in the midline of the abdomen, extending from the xiphoid process to above/below the umbilicus, offering greatest ease of extension and least blood loss.
• The Pfannenstiel incision is a convex, roughly 12 cm incision at the suprapubic skin crease about 5 cm above the pubic symphysis, offering good pelvic exposure, postoperative strength and cosmetic results, and is most frequently used in obstetrics/gynaecology including Caesarean section.
questions.question:
(a) Describe the incisions used in obstetric and gynaecological surgery under the following headings: types, and the procedures they are used for.
(b) Explain the clinical basis for pelvic surgery predisposing patients to deep vein thrombosis.
(c) Distinguish between the Pfannenstiel incision and the midline incision.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Dorsal surface hand burn; expected deformity if untreated is MCP joint hyperextension, IP joint flexion, and thumb adduction.

(b)
Depending on depth, treatment may include early cleaning and debriding of dead skin/tissue, and skin grafting (autograft, allograft or xenograft) to achieve wound closure if the burn is full thickness.

(c)
• Positioning goal: wrist extension, MCP flexion, IP extension, and thumb palmar abduction or opposition, maintained with a gauze roll wrapped into the palm extending into the thumb web space, or a volar hand splint.
• This positioning prevents contracture, controls oedema, and prevents localised neuropathies by maintaining the burned tissue in an elongated state.

(d)
• Precautions: splints must avoid interfering with healing through proper fitting (proper length, edges rolled and flared away from the skin).
• In the acute phase splints should be modulable and non-constrictive because of fluctuating oedema; monitor for wound breakdown if scar tissue tensile strength is poor, and monitor for wound maceration in the reconstructive phase.

(e)
• Progression follows the phases of burn rehabilitation: acute phase (prophylactic, modulable, non-constrictive splinting), wound healing phase (prevent contracture, protect grafts).
• Rehabilitation phase (reduce contracture non-surgically, prevent deformity, sustained stretching, maintain ROM), and reconstructive phase (fixation following release of contractures or reconstruction surgery).
• Patient education should cover the importance of maintaining the prescribed hand position and wearing the splint as advised to prevent the deformities listed above.
questions.question:
A 25-year-old woman sustains a dorsal surface burn to her hand in a kitchen fire, at risk of MCP hyperextension, IP flexion and thumb adduction deformity.
(a) State the diagnosis and the expected deformity if untreated.
(b) State the surgical/medical procedure likely required for her burn.
(c) State the physiotherapy goals for positioning her hand across the phases of burn rehabilitation.
(d) State the precautions relevant to splinting her hand.
(e) Describe the progression, discharge planning and patient education relevant to her case.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Full thickness (third-degree) burn.

(b)
Causes: in most cases third-degree burns are caused by a scalding liquid, skin in contact with a hot object for an extended time, flames from a fire, an electrical source, or a chemical source; exposure to flames or electrical current almost always results in a full-thickness burn.

(c)
• Third-degree burns destroy the epidermis and all layers of the dermis, extending down to subcutaneous tissue, which is why the wound appears dry, leathery and charred.
• Because the nerve endings are destroyed, there is no pain; because the epidermis and hair follicles are destroyed, new skin cannot grow, so healing is slow and poor without medical attention, usually requiring skin grafting.

(d)
• Assessment: knowledge of the burning agent, temperature/voltage/concentration and duration of contact, and depth judged by look, texture and sensitivity.
• Re-assessment after 24 hours, since depth is difficult to judge in the first 24 hours.
• Management/positioning: burn patients tend to assume a flexed, adducted (foetal) position as a reaction to pain, so positioning should maintain the burned tissue in an elongated state (typically extension-abduction alignment for limbs), maintained with splints, pillows or foam wedges.
• This is individualised to his medical condition, ROM and skin condition; splinting progresses through the acute phase (prophylactic, modulable, non-constrictive), wound healing phase (prevent contracture, protect grafts), rehabilitation phase (reduce contracture, maintain ROM) and reconstructive phase (fixation after contracture release).
questions.question:
A 35-year-old man sustains a flame burn to his forearm at work. On examination the wound is dry, leathery, pearly-grey/charred in appearance, and he reports no pain in the area.
(a) State the most likely diagnosis.
(b) State the predisposing/causative factors for this degree of burn.
(c) Describe the pathophysiology explaining his clinical findings.
(d) Describe the physiotherapy assessment and management relevant to his condition.

questions.answerText:
(a)
Risk factors: he is older than 70 years (worsens the chance of incontinence improving), and general post-operative risk factors such as immobility and inadequate pain control.

(b)
• Complications: urinary incontinence (uncontrollable, involuntary leaking of urine that may improve over up to a year); erectile dysfunction (recovery may take up to two years and may be incomplete).
• Retrograde ejaculation (the connection between the testicles and urethra is cut, so orgasm occurs without ejaculate); lymphoedema from lymph node removal; and a possible decrease in penis length.

(c)
• Management options: breathing exercises (pursed-lip progressing to diaphragmatic breathing) to prevent cardiorespiratory complications.
• Pelvic floor muscle exercises (hip bridging, knee rolling, kegel exercises in lying, side-lying and sitting positions – 8-10 reps, 3-5 sets) to optimise pelvic floor contraction and train continence.
• Also electrical stimulation of the pelvic floor muscles, soft tissue/frictional massage for scar healing, and patient education/psychological counselling.
• Justification: pelvic floor muscle exercise, given both before and after surgery, is justified because strengthening these muscles before prostatectomy significantly improves post-prostatectomy urinary continence, post-micturition dribble and erectile function.
• It is therefore prudent for men to exercise their pelvic floor muscles both preoperatively and postoperatively to maintain normal pelvic floor function.
questions.question:
(a) A 65-year-old man is 2 days post radical retropubic prostatectomy for early-stage prostate cancer. State the risk factors relevant to him for post-operative complications.
(b) List the post-operative complications he may develop, including urinary and sexual complications specific to this surgery.
(c) Outline the physiotherapy management options and justify the use of one of them.

questions.answerText:
(a)
• Bronchiectasis is a chronic dilatation of the bronchi with impaired drainage of bronchial secretions, leading to persistent infection of the affected segment or lobe.
• The involved bronchi are dilated, inflamed and easily collapsible, resulting in airflow obstruction and impaired clearance of secretions.
• It often results from bacterial infection (e.g. Staphylococcus) and usually follows inadequately treated pneumonia.
• It may also be associated with whooping cough or measles, where thick, tenacious mucus obstructs the bronchi with distal lung collapse.
• During the inflammatory process there is destruction and alteration of the bronchial mucosa.
• When the lung re-inflates, the bronchus becomes dilated, with the lining changed from normal ciliated epithelium to cuboidal/squamous epithelium with fewer or absent cilia.

(b)
• Clinically this produces coarse crackles over the affected segments with an associated wheeze.
• During episodes of infection there may be signs of consolidation and collapse, and production of copious purulent sputum is typical.
• This chronic suppurative process predisposes the patient to recurrent infection and, in extensive disease, to haemoptysis-related complications.

(c)
• With extensive bronchiectasis, finger clubbing and central cyanosis may develop, showing that chronic hypoxia affects distant tissues.
• Malaise, anorexia and fever are seen, which in children may lead to failure to thrive with stunting of growth – a systemic functional deficit from chronic lung disease.
• Physiotherapy implications: clear excessive secretions, increase ventilation, encourage chest expansion and chest wall mobility, and encourage physical activity, using postural drainage, percussion/vibration/shaking, coughing and huffing, breathing exercises and free active exercise.
questions.question:
(a) State the pathophysiological basis of bronchiectasis.
(b) State how the pathological changes relate to the common complications of recurrent infection and haemoptysis.
(c) Explain how bronchiectasis may affect distant systems causing a functional deficit, with the physiotherapy implications.

A 66-year-old man, 2 weeks post radical prostatectomy, reports involuntary leaking of urine on exertion and describes weakness on manual assessment of his pelvic floor muscles.
(a) Identify the problem shown by the assessment findings.
(b) State the structures/mechanisms affected.
(c) State the differential problems that should be considered before starting strengthening exercises.
(d) Explain the clinical reasoning for the physiotherapy plan for this patient.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Urinary incontinence with pelvic floor muscle weakness, a recognised complication of prostatectomy.

(b)
Radical prostatectomy involves removal of the whole prostate gland, and incontinence involves uncontrollable, involuntary leaking of urine, which may improve over time, even up to a year after surgery, and may be worse in men older than 70 years at the time of surgery.

(c)
• Differential consideration: a weak pelvic floor, as well as a pelvic floor in spasm, can both contribute to symptoms such as erectile dysfunction and incontinence.
• It is important to determine the exact cause before giving pelvic floor strengthening, since strengthening exercises given to someone with a pelvic floor in spasm will exacerbate symptoms.

(d)
• Clinical reasoning: since his assessment shows weakness (not spasm) of the pelvic floor, strengthening exercises are appropriate – pelvic floor muscle exercises including hip bridging, knee rolling and kegel exercises performed lying supine, side-lying and sitting (8-10 repetitions, 3-5 sets).
• These have been shown to significantly improve post-prostatectomy urinary continence, post-micturition dribble and erectile function.
• Electrical stimulation of the pelvic floor muscles via a probe electrode can be added, alongside general advice on incontinence pads and clothing and avoidance of fluids (coffee, green tea, beer) that worsen his symptoms.

questions.question:
A 62-year-old diabetic man presents with dead, gangrenous tissue of the toes and forefoot with poor blood perfusion, confirmed on vascular assessment, and is scheduled for a below-knee amputation.
(a) State the problem identified from the assessment findings.
(b) State the structures the surgeon must assess before amputation.
(c) State the differential problems/complications that should be anticipated.
(d) Explain the clinical reasoning for the physiotherapy plan for this patient.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Gangrene of the toes/forefoot with poor blood perfusion, an indication for amputation, alongside a dangerous limb or a useless body part as other indications.

(b)
• Before amputation the surgeon notes: the level of good blood perfusion, the nerve supply, the site of amputation, and the blood supply and innervation of the stump.
• The remaining part (the stump or residual limb) will later be assessed for prosthetic fitting; the muscle may be secured by myoplasty (suturing muscle to muscle) or myodesis (suturing muscle to bone).

(c)
Complications to anticipate: wound problems/infection, growing bone, and phantom limb pain (when the patient perceives the limb is still present after amputation).

(d)
• Clinical reasoning: because of the risk of wound infection, physiotherapy must support wound care.
• Because of the risk of phantom limb pain, immediate prosthetic fitting is used as an intervention, together with psychological/psychotherapy referral to help the patient adjust.
• General post-operative principles also apply – preventing chest and circulatory complications, maintaining muscle power and joint ROM in the remaining limb, preventing pressure sores, and progressing bed mobility – given his reduced mobility and diabetic status as risk factors for delayed healing.

questions.question:
A 52-year-old woman, 3 months post modified radical mastectomy with axillary lymph node dissection, presents with a swollen, heavy right arm and tight-fitting sleeves. Skin is unbroken and non-tender.
(a) State the most likely diagnosis.
(b) State the predisposing factors for this condition.
(c) Describe the pathophysiology of this condition.
(d) Describe the physiotherapy assessment and management appropriate for her.
questions.answerText:
(a)
Lymphoedema of the right arm.

(b)
Predisposing factors: removal of axillary lymph nodes as part of the axillary lymph node dissection done during modified radical mastectomy, to check whether cancer cells have spread beyond the breast.

(c)
• When axillary lymph nodes are removed along with the breast tissue, the normal lymphatic drainage pathway of the arm is disrupted.
• Fluid can no longer drain effectively from the limb, so it accumulates in the soft tissues, resulting in swelling (lymphoedema); this can happen alongside other mastectomy complications such as limited shoulder ROM, scar formation and musculoskeletal pain.

(d)
• Assessment: observation of limb swelling and heaviness, and review of the surgical history (extent of axillary dissection).
• Management: Complex Decongestive Physical Therapy – an intensive phase of daily manual lymphatic drainage (massage technique to encourage removal of excess interstitial fluid, increase lymphatic transport into lymph nodes, and soften fibrotic tissue), multi-layer compression bandaging, and exercises improving lymph outflow.
• This is followed by a maintenance-optimisation phase of self-massage and elastic compression materials with continued exercise; limb exercises can be progressive, resistive, free or isometric; a compression garment is also fitted.
• Faradism under pressure (electrical stimulation combined with compression and limb elevation above heart level) can additionally be used to increase venous and lymphatic drainage and relieve the oedema.

(a)
• Post-operative and perioperative immobility adversely affects venous drainage from the lower limb, promoting DVT.
• Pelvic masses, a gravid uterus, or surgically-induced haematomas/lymphocysts can also cause venous stasis.
• Vessel wall injury can result from surgical dissection, and coagulation changes result from decreased fibrinolytic activity associated with the operative procedure.
• Together these reflect the three factors: hypercoagulability, venous stasis, and vessel wall (venous endothelial) injury.

(b)
• These same risk factors, worsened by post-operative immobility, allow a thrombus to form in the deep veins of the leg.
• The thrombus can grow, extending into the veins of the thigh and, in some cases, the pelvis.
• A fragment of this thrombus can dislodge and travel in the bloodstream.

(c)
• The dislodged clot travels via the venous system and right heart into the pulmonary circulation, producing a pulmonary embolism.
• DVT and PE together are referred to as a venous thromboembolic event (VTE), which can cause significant morbidity and mortality.
• Physiotherapy implications: prevention is prioritised through elevation of the bed end, compression stockings, and general breathing exercises.
• Active limb movement, early ambulation, anticoagulant use where prescribed, calf pump exercises, and minimising tourniquet use.
• Regular activation of the muscle pumps and frequent position changes minimise circulatory stasis and its serious consequences for recovery.
questions.question:
(a) State the pathophysiological basis of deep vein thrombosis following surgery.
(b) State how the risk factors for DVT relate to the common complication of pulmonary embolism.
(c) Explain how DVT may spread to affect a distant system (the lungs) causing a functional deficit, with the physiotherapy implications.
