questions.question: A parasitic skin infection in which mites burrow into the upper skin layer to lay eggs, causing intense itching, is?
questions.explanation: Scabies is caused by mites burrowing into the upper skin layer to lay eggs, producing a pimple-like itchy rash often at sites like the wrists, elbows, and between the fingers. It spreads through prolonged skin-to-skin contact, unlike cellulitis, which is a deep bacterial soft tissue infection.

questions.question: A burn wound described as black, white, or yellow with no need for analgesia due to nerve destruction is a?
questions.explanation: Full thickness burns destroy the epidermis, dermis, and other underlying tissue, presenting as black, white, or yellow with no pain because sensory nerve endings are also destroyed. Superficial and partial thickness burns retain some or full sensation because deeper nerve structures remain intact.

questions.question: A patient with a healed burn graft on the hand begins scar massage. What timing is generally appropriate to commence this intervention?
options: Only once the scar has become keloid
Only after 6 months have fully passed
Immediately on the day of the burn injury
Before the wound has closed at all
Approximately 2-3 weeks post-injury, after epithelialization is complete
questions.explanation: Scar massage is typically started once epithelialization is complete, generally around 2-3 weeks post-injury, though this may vary by individual healing rate. Beginning massage before wound closure risks disrupting fragile healing tissue and increasing infection risk.

questions.question: Circular frictional massage is primarily used in scar management to achieve which effect?
questions.explanation: Circular frictional massage is used to break down adhesions, improve tissue pliability, and reduce sensitivity in scar tissue, supporting better function and mobility. It does not affect melanin production, sterilise tissue, regenerate nerves directly, or bleach discoloration, which are unrelated mechanisms.

options: Hold the applicator 10cm away with no grid division
Apply for 24 continuous hours over the whole area
Divide the area into 1cm squares and stimulate each with the applicator in light contact
Use the grid method only for non-contact deep tissue work
Apply laser only to the wound edges, ignoring the centre
questions.question: A physiotherapist treating a superficial wound wants to use the grid method of laser application. What is the correct technique for this method?
questions.explanation: The grid method divides the treatment area into a grid of 1cm squares, with the handheld applicator held in light contact perpendicular to the tissue, stimulating each square for a specific time period. This differs from the scanning method, which uses non-contact application at a set distance.

An autograft uses the patient's own skin from a donor site such as the thigh or upper arm, avoiding immune rejection risk. An allograft comes from another human donor and a xenograft from an animal, both of which the immune system may reject within about seven days.
questions.question: Skin taken from another area of the patient's own body for grafting is termed an?

questions.explanation: High-voltage pulsed current (HVPC) is the electrical stimulation type most commonly cited and supported by clinical practice guidelines for promoting pressure ulcer healing. It works by promoting fibroblast activity, angiogenesis, and epithelial migration, distinguishing it from other electrical modalities not specifically emphasised for wound healing.
questions.question: Which electrical stimulation type is most commonly cited as supported by clinical guidelines for pressure ulcer healing?

questions.explanation: Topical wart treatments generally require sustained contact time with the lesion to achieve adequate tissue penetration and effectiveness, which is why recommended protocols often involve occlusive dressings or extended application periods rather than brief contact. This principle reflects the slow-acting mechanism of keratolytic agents used against the thickened, virus-infected tissue of warts. Patient education about adherence to recommended contact duration improves treatment success rates.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is treating a patient with a stubborn plantar wart and learns that effective home treatment with salicylic acid or similar agents requires the medication to remain in continuous contact with the lesion for an extended period to be effective. What general principle does this illustrate about topical wart treatment?
options: Treatment works equally well regardless of contact duration
Extended, sustained contact time improves treatment effectiveness
Shorter exposure always produces faster resolution
Contact time has no influence on treatment outcomes
A single brief application is sufficient for cure

questions.explanation: Erythema burns leave the skin intact, last only a few days, and typically require no medical attention, as seen commonly with sunburn. Partial and full thickness burns involve blistering or destruction of deeper layers, while subdermal burns extend into fat, muscle, or bone, all far more severe presentations.
questions.question: A burn presenting with intact skin, no blisters, and resolving within days without medical attention is classified as?

questions.explanation: Pressure garments apply sustained, even pressure to healing burn tissue, which helps limit excessive collagen deposition and reduces the likelihood of hypertrophic scar formation during the remodeling phase. Their function is distinct from joint positioning splints, which address contracture, or antimicrobial dressings, which address infection. Consistent garment wear as prescribed is essential to achieving the intended scar prevention benefit.
questions.question: A physiotherapist fits a patient with a custom-made pressure garment following a significant burn injury and explains its primary preventive purpose to the patient. What is this garment principally intended to prevent?
options: Wound infection through antimicrobial fabric properties
Heat loss through thermal insulation effects
Muscle atrophy through compressive resistance training
Hypertrophic scar formation through sustained pressure

questions.explanation: Electrical stimulation polarity influences the migration of specific cell types toward the wound bed, with particular polarities favoring neutrophil attraction during the inflammatory phase and others favoring fibroblast activity during later proliferative stages. This polarity-dependent cellular response is central to how electrical stimulation protocols are tailored to the current wound healing phase. Selecting incorrect polarity for the healing stage may reduce the treatment's intended therapeutic benefit.
questions.question: A physiotherapist applying electrical stimulation for a pressure ulcer selects a particular polarity intended to attract neutrophils to the wound during the early inflammatory phase. What does this clinical decision rely on?
options: Electrode polarity influencing cell migration to the wound
Frequency of stimulation determining tissue temperature
Amplitude of current controlling muscle contraction strength
Duration of treatment session affecting patient comfort
Type of dressing material used over the electrodes

questions.explanation: The stratum lucidum consists of 3-5 layers of clear dead keratinocytes rich in keratin, present only in thick skin regions like palms and soles. Thin skin elsewhere on the body lacks this layer, having only four strata. Its presence increases resistance to friction.
questions.question: Which epidermal layer is found only in thick skin such as the palms and soles?

questions.explanation: Monochromaticity refers to laser light having a single colour or wavelength and thus a definite frequency, unlike ordinary light which contains many wavelengths. Coherence describes phase synchrony of the light waves, while collimation describes the parallel, non-diverging nature of the beam, both separate properties.
questions.question: Which property of laser light means it consists of a single wavelength and definite frequency, unlike ordinary light?
Which skin type, per the Fitzpatrick scale, is described as more prone to developing keloid scars?
questions.explanation: Darker skin types, classified as Fitzpatrick IV-VI, show a genetic predisposition toward developing keloid scars more frequently than lighter skin types. This intrinsic factor combines with wound characteristics and tension to influence overall scar formation risk, independent of conditions like vitiligo or psoriasis.

questions.question: Localised tissue damage over a bony prominence caused by prolonged pressure combined with shear is best termed a?
questions.explanation: A pressure ulcer is a localised injury to skin or underlying tissue, usually over a bony prominence, resulting from pressure combined with shear force, and is the terminology now preferred over 'bedsore'. Venous, arterial, and diabetic ulcers arise from vascular or metabolic causes rather than sustained mechanical pressure.

questions.question: Alternating pressure mattresses and low-air-loss surfaces that use a power source to redistribute pressure are classified as?
questions.explanation: Dynamic devices, such as alternating pressure mattresses and low-air-loss or air-fluidized surfaces, use a power source to actively redistribute localised pressure over time. Static devices, in contrast, include foam, water, gel, or air mattresses that passively spread pressure without power-driven movement.

options: Failure to progress through normal healing stages in a timely manner
Presence of any visible scar tissue
Location exclusively on the lower limb
questions.question: The key clinical difference distinguishing a chronic wound from an acute wound is primarily related to?
questions.explanation: A chronic wound is defined by its failure to progress through the normal, orderly, timely sequence of repair, often persisting beyond three months despite treatment. This is distinct from wound age, patient age, anatomical location, or whether surgery is eventually required, which are not the defining criteria.

questions.question: According to the Rule of Palms, the surface of a patient's palm approximates what percentage of body surface area?
questions.explanation: The Rule of Palms estimates that the patient's own palm surface represents roughly 1% of total body surface area, which is useful for quickly estimating small or scattered burn areas. This contrasts with the larger regional percentages used in the Rule of Nines for bigger body segments.

Head of bed elevation should generally not exceed 30 degrees to minimise shear forces on the sacrum that contribute to pressure ulcer development, balanced against other clinical needs like aspiration risk. Simply reclining fully flat may not always be appropriate, but reducing excessive elevation is the key correction.
options: Reduce head of bed elevation to no more than 30 degrees when possible
Fully recline the bed to 0 degrees at all times
Elevate only the foot of the bed instead
questions.question: A hospital patient is repositioned and the head of the bed is noted at 45 degrees during prolonged periods. What correction should the physiotherapist recommend?

options: Ongoing replacement of Type III collagen with stronger Type I collagen during remodeling
Reversal of the wound healing process entirely
Replacement of collagen with elastin only
Loss of all collagen from the healed area
Complete regeneration of original skin structure
questions.explanation: During the remodeling phase, weaker Type III collagen laid down initially is gradually replaced by stronger, more organised Type I collagen, increasing the scar's tensile strength and elasticity over time. However, the scar tissue never fully regenerates the original skin structure or reaches 100% of its original strength.
questions.question: A patient asks why their surgical scar has become progressively stronger and more elastic since surgery. What underlying process explains this change?

A physiotherapist preparing to cleanse an open burn wound using hydrotherapy selects a water temperature intended to minimize patient discomfort while avoiding tissue damage. What general temperature range is appropriate for this purpose?
questions.explanation: Hydrotherapy wound cleansing typically uses mild, body-temperature-range warm water to minimize patient discomfort and avoid additional thermal tissue damage, since both excessively hot and excessively cold water can harm fragile healing tissue. Selecting an appropriate, comfortable temperature also improves patient tolerance of a treatment that may already be associated with pain. This consideration is especially important in burn wound care, where the skin barrier is already compromised.
options: Near-boiling hot water for thorough disinfection
Ice-cold water to minimize bleeding risk
Freezing water to numb the wound area
Temperature is irrelevant to hydrotherapy wound care

questions.question: A debridement method using irrigation, whirlpool, or wet-to-dry dressings that is non-selective in tissue removal is classed as?
questions.explanation: Mechanical debridement includes irrigation, whirlpool, scraping, and wet-to-dry dressings, and is non-selective because it can remove healthy granulation tissue along with necrotic material. Autolytic debridement is selective and relies on the body's own enzymes, while biological debridement uses maggot therapy, a distinctly different selective method.

Collagen fibers within the dermis provide structural strength and tensile resistance, and newly formed scar collagen is typically denser and less organized than original tissue, producing the firmer, less elastic feel often palpated during scar assessment. This dermal protein is the principal target of manual scar massage techniques aimed at remodeling fiber alignment. Understanding collagen's role guides realistic expectations for scar tissue mobility over time.
questions.question: A physiotherapist palpating a healing wound notes increased firmness and reduced elasticity in the scar compared to surrounding skin. Which dermal component is primarily responsible for this normal tissue property?

questions.explanation: In a paraplegic patient, Stage 1 redness over the ischial tuberosity should be treated as an urgent warning sign given their inability to sense pain and high risk of rapid progression to deeper injury. Direct massage over reddened at-risk skin is inappropriate as it can worsen underlying tissue damage.
questions.question: A physiotherapist notices Stage 1 non-blanchable redness over the ischial tuberosity of a paraplegic patient. What is the most appropriate clinical interpretation?
options: A normal, insignificant finding needing no action
An urgent warning sign requiring immediate pressure relief intervention
A sign that massage should be applied directly to the area
A sign the tissue has fully healed already
An indication to increase sitting time
Exercise must always be delayed until full wound closure
Exercise timing is irrelevant to long-term functional outcome
Exercise should never begin before scar maturation is complete
Exercise should begin as early as medically safely tolerated
Exercise should only start after all grafts have failed
questions.explanation: Early initiation of active range of motion exercise, as soon as medically and wound-status appropriate, is generally favored in burn rehabilitation to minimize contracture and stiffness risk, balanced carefully against pain tolerance and tissue stability. Waiting until full wound closure or scar maturation would risk significant, potentially permanent loss of joint mobility. This time-sensitive balance between protection and mobilization is a defining challenge of burn rehabilitation practice.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is deciding when to initiate active range of motion exercises for a patient recovering from a burn injury and considers both wound stability and pain tolerance. What general principle guides the timing of this decision?

questions.explanation: The subcutaneous layer, or hypodermis, lies deep to the dermis and anchors the skin to underlying structures using areolar and adipose connective tissue; it is technically not part of the skin itself. The papillary and reticular layers are dermal sublayers, while the epidermis and corneum are superficial.
questions.question: Which layer attaches skin to underlying tissues and organs and is composed of areolar and adipose connective tissue?

questions.explanation: Biological debridement, also called larval or maggot therapy, uses sterile green bottle fly larvae that secrete proteolytic enzymes to dissolve necrotic tissue and also ingest bacteria. It is painless, selective, and can access difficult areas, unlike the non-selective and sometimes painful mechanical methods.
questions.question: Sterile fly larvae that release proteolytic enzymes to dissolve necrotic tissue characterise which debridement type?
A physiotherapist is applying low-frequency ultrasound for non-contact debridement of a sloughy chronic wound. Which frequency range should be selected?
questions.explanation: Non-contact wound debridement specifically uses low-frequency ultrasound in the 20-40 kHz range to enhance cellular activity and assist removal of slough. Higher frequencies in the MHz range are instead used for deeper tissue heating applications such as scar softening, not surface debridement.

questions.question: A dressing best suited to a dry wound with necrotic tissue requiring rehydration to promote autolysis is a?
questions.explanation: Hydrogel dressings donate moisture to dry, necrotic wounds, softening dead tissue and facilitating autolytic debridement. Alginates and foams are chosen for exuding wounds needing absorption rather than hydration, while antimicrobial dressings primarily target infected wounds rather than dry necrotic ones.

Using Energy (Joules) = Power (Watts) x Time (seconds), with 50 mW equal to 0.05 W, the calculation is 3 = 0.05 x Time, giving Time = 60 seconds. Correctly converting milliwatts to watts before calculation is essential to avoid a significant dosing error.
questions.question: A physiotherapist calculates the required treatment time for a laser session where the power output is 50 mW and the target energy is 3 Joules. What treatment time is needed?

questions.explanation: A laceration is an irregular tearing or crushing wound with uneven edges that can vary greatly in depth, potentially involving muscle, tendon, or bone. Incisions are clean straight cuts from sharp objects, abrasions are superficial friction injuries, and contusions are closed bruising injuries.
questions.question: An irregular, jagged wound with uneven edges caused by tearing or crushing forces is termed a?

questions.explanation: Scleroderma pathogenesis centres on excessive extracellular matrix deposition driven by cytokines and growth factors stimulating fibroblasts and myofibroblasts, causing skin thickening and hardening. This differs fundamentally from melanocyte destruction seen in vitiligo, bacterial or fungal infection mechanisms, or viral latency as in herpes.
questions.question: Scleroderma pathophysiology is primarily driven by which underlying process affecting connective tissue?
options: Excessive extracellular matrix deposition by fibroblasts

questions.question: A patient's chronic wound requires laser therapy scheduling. Based on standard protocols, how often should this chronic wound be treated?
questions.explanation: Chronic wounds are generally treated with laser therapy 1-2 times per week, in contrast to acute wounds which may be treated daily. This reflects the slower turnover and different biological requirements of chronic tissue compared to acutely healing tissue.
options: Multiple times per day, every day

questions.question: Therapeutic lasers used clinically are described as 'athermic' primarily because they?
options: Only work through direct tissue destruction
Cannot penetrate the skin surface at all
Require no energy source to function
Produce no appreciable heat transfer to tissue
Always operate in the ultraviolet range
questions.explanation: Therapeutic lasers are considered athermic because they produce no appreciable heat transfer, typically under 0.65 degrees Celsius, meaning their photonic energy is transferred directly to target cells without causing thermal damage. This distinguishes low-level therapeutic lasers from higher-powered surgical lasers used for cutting or ablation.

questions.question: For scar tissue ultrasound in burn rehabilitation, continuous mode at higher intensity is generally used to achieve which goal?
questions.explanation: Continuous mode ultrasound at higher intensity is used on mature scar tissue to soften it and improve pliability before combining with stretching for maximal tissue lengthening. Pulsed lower-intensity ultrasound is instead more appropriate for early healing or subacute tissue, not for softening established scars.
options: Softening mature scars and improving pliability

questions.explanation: Staphylococcus aureus commonly colonizes eczematous skin and can worsen inflammation and weeping, since the disrupted skin barrier in eczema provides an environment conducive to bacterial overgrowth. This secondary bacterial complication often requires targeted treatment beyond standard eczema skin care alone. Recognizing signs of bacterial superinfection, such as increased crusting, helps prompt timely medical referral.
questions.question: A physiotherapist notices a patient's eczema has worsened with increased weeping and crusting, and the physician suspects bacterial colonization is contributing to the flare. Which organism most commonly colonizes and worsens eczema in this way?

A physiotherapist treating an elderly patient with significant subcutaneous tissue loss observes increased risk of pressure injury and poor thermal insulation. Which subcutaneous tissue function explains both observations?
questions.explanation: Subcutaneous adipose tissue provides mechanical cushioning over bony prominences and thermal insulation, and its age-related thinning explains both increased pressure injury vulnerability and reduced ability to retain body heat in elderly patients. This functional decline is an important consideration when designing pressure-relief and thermal management strategies for older patients. Recognizing tissue-specific functions supports more targeted preventive positioning and skin protection planning.

Sebaceous glands secrete sebum, an oily substance that conditions and waterproofs the skin and hair, and their overactivity can produce the visibly oily skin appearance noted in some patients. This differs from eccrine and apocrine glands, which primarily produce watery or protein-rich sweat respectively rather than oil. Recognizing gland-specific secretions helps clarify the underlying cause of various skin surface presentations encountered in clinical assessment.
questions.question: A physiotherapist notices a patient's skin appears unusually oily and learns this relates to overactive secretion from a specific skin gland. Which gland is primarily responsible for producing the oily substance conditioning skin and hair?

A physiotherapist notices a patient's skin lesion has changed in size and color and learns the physician is concerned about metastatic spread given the cancer type's known aggressive behavior. Which skin cancer type is most associated with this dangerous metastatic potential?
questions.explanation: Melanoma is the skin cancer type most associated with dangerous metastatic potential, arising from melanocytes and capable of spreading rapidly to distant organs if not detected and treated early, unlike the typically more locally confined basal cell carcinoma. This higher metastatic risk underlies the urgency of early detection systems like the ABCDE rule for suspicious pigmented lesions. Recognizing melanoma's distinct danger level compared to other skin cancers supports appropriately urgent referral pathways.

questions.question: A physiotherapist examines a pearly, waxy nodule with visible small blood vessels on a patient's sun-exposed nose and the physician suspects a common, slow-growing skin cancer with low metastatic risk. Which skin cancer type does this describe?
questions.explanation: Basal cell carcinoma typically presents as a pearly or waxy nodule with visible small blood vessels, most commonly on sun-exposed areas, and is characterized by slow growth and low risk of distant metastasis compared with other skin cancer types. This relatively favorable behavior contrasts sharply with melanoma's higher metastatic potential. Recognizing this typical presentation supports timely dermatological referral even though basal cell carcinoma is rarely immediately life-threatening.

questions.question: A patient's functional assessment reveals difficulty dressing due to scar tightness across the shoulder. Which outcome measure category should the physiotherapist prioritise documenting?
options: Impact on activities of daily living (ADLs)
questions.explanation: Documenting the scar's functional impact on activities of daily living, such as difficulty dressing, provides clinically meaningful outcome data directly relevant to the patient's quality of life and treatment goals. Vital signs and unrelated measurements do not capture this specific functional limitation.

questions.question: Which age groups are noted to carry a poorer prognosis following burn injury?
questions.explanation: Individuals aged five years and below, and those aged sixty and above, are documented as carrying a poorer prognosis after burns. These extremes of age have thinner skin and reduced physiological reserve to cope with fluid loss and infection risk. Other age brackets listed are not the ones specifically flagged.

questions.question: A patient who is over 70, incontinent, and has poor nutrition presents with which combination of pressure ulcer risk factor categories?
options: Age, moisture exposure, and nutritional deficiency
questions.explanation: Advanced age, incontinence-related moisture, and poor nutrition are all recognised intrinsic risk factors for pressure ulcer development, each independently impairing skin integrity and healing capacity. These differ from purely extrinsic mechanical factors like shear and friction, which act independently of the patient's underlying health status.

questions.question: In Parkland formula fluid resuscitation, what proportion of the calculated total is given during the first 8 hours post-burn?
options: A third of the total volume
A quarter of the total volume
questions.explanation: Half of the total calculated fluid volume is administered during the first 8 hours after the burn, counted from the time of injury, with the remaining half infused over the subsequent 16 hours. This front-loaded schedule addresses the rapid early fluid shifts characteristic of major burns.

Inverse psoriasis typically appears in skin fold areas such as the armpits and groin, presenting as smooth, red patches without the thick scaling characteristic of plaque psoriasis, since friction and moisture in these areas alter the typical lesion appearance. Recognizing this atypical presentation prevents misdiagnosis as a fungal or bacterial intertriginous infection. Treatment approaches may also differ slightly given the sensitivity of skin fold regions to certain topical therapies.
questions.question: A physiotherapist examines a patient with red, smooth, non-scaly patches localized to the armpits and groin folds, which the physician identifies as a specific psoriasis subtype affecting skin fold areas. Which subtype is this?

questions.explanation: Herpetic whitlow is caused by the Herpes Simplex Virus, typically when wounded or exposed fingertip skin contacts body fluids contaminated with the virus. It is more prevalent than the melanotic whitlow subtype and is a self-limiting condition typically resolving within two to three weeks.
questions.question: Herpetic whitlow, a painful infection of the fingertip, is most commonly caused by which pathogen?
A physiotherapist explains to a patient that her own healthy skin will be harvested and transplanted to cover a burn wound elsewhere on her body. Which graft type is being described?
questions.explanation: An autograft uses the patient's own tissue harvested from a donor site and transplanted to the wound, which provides the best long-term graft survival since there is no immune rejection risk, unlike allografts from another human donor or xenografts from animal sources. This is why autografts remain the gold standard for definitive burn wound closure when sufficient donor sites are available. Understanding graft origin terminology is essential when explaining surgical options to patients.

Scleroderma is an autoimmune disorder characterized by progressive skin thickening and tightening, often affecting the fingers and face, which can significantly limit hand function and range of motion over time. This fibrotic process distinguishes scleroderma from inflammatory conditions like psoriasis or eczema, which do not primarily cause tissue tightening. Physiotherapy goals in scleroderma often prioritize maintaining hand mobility and function despite progressive skin and joint changes.
questions.question: A physiotherapist treating a patient with progressively tightening, thickened skin on the fingers and face, limiting hand function, learns the diagnosis is a connective tissue autoimmune disorder. Which condition does this presentation describe?

questions.explanation: For wound healing electrical stimulation, intensity should remain at a comfortable sensory level without producing visible muscle contraction, as the goal is cellular stimulation rather than motor recruitment. Excessively high intensities causing strong contractions or pain are unnecessary and may cause patient discomfort or tissue irritation.
questions.question: A burns physiotherapist is planning electrical stimulation for wound healing. What intensity level should be used to promote healing without causing harm?
options: A comfortable sensory level with no visible muscle contraction
Maximum tolerable intensity with strong muscle contraction
Intensity sufficient to cause mild pain

questions.explanation: Heat therapy is used in the chronic phase to improve mobility and assist scar remodelling, but only once the skin has fully healed and closed. Applying heat immediately after injury or over fragile, poorly perfused, or infected skin risks worsening tissue damage.
questions.question: Heat therapy in burn rehabilitation, such as hot packs or paraffin wax, is appropriately applied during which phase?

questions.explanation: Standard electrical stimulation protocols for chronic wounds like diabetic ulcers involve 30-60 minutes per session, delivered 5-7 days per week, supported by clinical practice guidelines. Shorter, infrequent sessions or excessively long daily sessions do not align with the evidence-based dosing typically recommended.
questions.question: A patient with a chronic diabetic foot ulcer is being considered for electrical stimulation therapy. What protocol duration and frequency reflects standard practice?
options: 30-60 minutes per day, 5-7 days per week

questions.explanation: UVC radiation has strong bactericidal properties, damaging microbial DNA and making it the preferred ultraviolet wavelength for treating infected wounds rather than UVA or UVB, which are more associated with tanning and vitamin D synthesis respectively. This targeted antimicrobial action supports its specific clinical application in infected wound management. Appropriate dosing and exposure time remain essential to maximize bactericidal effect while minimizing tissue damage.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is treating an infected pressure ulcer using ultraviolet light and selects UVC specifically rather than UVA or UVB. What property of UVC makes it the preferred choice for this purpose?
options: Greater penetration depth into subcutaneous tissue
Promotion of vitamin D synthesis in the skin
Production of a protective tanning response
Strong antibacterial action against wound pathogens
Lower risk of causing erythema or burns

questions.question: Severe protein-energy malnutrition that can turn naturally dark hair red or blonde is called?
questions.explanation: Kwashiorkor is a form of severe malnutrition from protein deficiency that can cause dark hair to change colour to red or blonde along with a bloated abdomen. Marasmus is a different malnutrition syndrome without the characteristic hair colour change. Hirsutism and alopecia relate to hair growth patterns, not colour change from malnutrition.

questions.question: Cutaneous lupus erythematosus classically presents with which characteristic facial rash pattern?
questions.explanation: Cutaneous lupus erythematosus classically presents as a butterfly or malar rash across the face, along with photosensitivity, redness, and potential scarring, often triggered by UV exposure. Honey-crusted rashes suggest impetigo, silvery plaques suggest psoriasis, and vesicular dermatomal rashes suggest herpes zoster, all distinct patterns.

questions.question: A physiotherapist learns that wound contraction during healing is driven by specialized cells that develop contractile properties similar to smooth muscle cells. Which cell type, differentiated from fibroblasts, is primarily responsible for this contraction?
questions.explanation: Myofibroblasts, which differentiate from fibroblasts and acquire smooth muscle-like contractile properties, are primarily responsible for wound contraction, helping to physically reduce the size of the wound during the proliferative and remodeling phases. This specialized contractile function is distinct from the cell migration and resurfacing role of keratinocytes. Recognizing the contribution of myofibroblasts explains why excessive contraction can sometimes contribute to problematic scar contracture.

Transparent film dressings are ideal for superficial wounds needing autolytic debridement because they allow direct visual monitoring of the wound without removing the dressing, while maintaining a moist environment. Opaque dressings like foam or gauze require removal to inspect the wound, disrupting the healing environment more frequently.
questions.question: A patient's wound dressing choice must balance protection with allowing visual monitoring of a superficial wound undergoing autolysis. Which dressing type is most suitable?
Excessive hair growth in women following a male pattern, usually from raised androgen levels, is known as?
questions.explanation: Hirsutism describes excessive androgen-driven hair growth in a male distribution pattern in women. Alopecia refers to hair loss, the opposite condition, while albinism and vitiligo relate to pigment loss rather than hair growth. None of the distractors involve androgen-mediated hair overgrowth.

questions.question: Phototherapy used in dermatology physiotherapy management mimics natural sunlight primarily using which type of energy?
questions.explanation: Phototherapy uses ultraviolet light from artificial sources to mimic sunlight exposure, triggering biological processes that reduce inflammation and slow abnormal skin cell growth in conditions like psoriasis and vitiligo. It is distinct from infrared heat, shockwave, ultrasound, or direct current-based modalities used for other purposes.

questions.question: A physiotherapist examines a patient with intensely itchy, thread-like burrows visible between the fingers and notes close contacts have similar symptoms. Which organism is the most likely cause of this presentation?
questions.explanation: Sarcoptes scabiei, the scabies mite, burrows into the skin causing intensely itchy thread-like tracks typically found between fingers, and its highly contagious nature explains why close contacts often develop similar symptoms simultaneously. This presentation differs from fungal, viral, or bacterial skin infections in both appearance and transmission pattern. Recognizing scabies is important for infection control precautions in any healthcare setting, including physiotherapy departments.

questions.question: In Jackson's burn model, which zone can often be saved if capillary flow is restored through appropriate wound care?
questions.explanation: The zone of stasis, adjacent to the zone of coagulation, shows slowed circulation from oedema and vasoconstrictive mediators but remains reversible if perfusion is restored through proper care. The zone of coagulation is already irreversibly dead, while the zone of hyperaemia typically recovers on its own.

Superficial burns allow fluid to accumulate between epidermal layers, producing blisters that may continue appearing within the first 24 hours, and movement of the area is very painful. Deeper burns destroy more tissue and often reduce sensation, while erythema alone does not involve blister formation.
questions.question: Which burn depth is characterised by fluid slipping between epidermal layers to form blisters within the first 24 hours?

A physiotherapist wants to objectively document a patient's scar characteristics, including vascularity, pigmentation, pliability, and height, at baseline and during follow-up visits. Which assessment tool is specifically designed for this purpose?
questions.explanation: The Vancouver Scar Scale specifically evaluates scar characteristics including vascularity, pigmentation, pliability, and height, providing a standardized method for objectively tracking scar evolution over time. This specialized tool differs from general functional or neurological scales used elsewhere in rehabilitation. Using a validated scar-specific tool supports consistent monitoring and communication of scar progress among the care team.

questions.question: A tight scar that restricts movement, often resulting from burns and affecting underlying muscles and joints, is a?
questions.explanation: Contracture scars are tight and restrict movement, frequently arising from burns or large wounds, and can affect the function of underlying muscles and joints. Atrophic scars are sunken but not necessarily restrictive, while hypertrophic and keloid scars are raised rather than primarily contractile.

questions.question: A patient undergoing management for hypertrophic scarring from a burn asks whether ultrasound can help. What should the physiotherapist explain regarding its use?
questions.explanation: Ultrasound can help soften hypertrophic scar tissue and improve pliability, typically as part of a combined approach alongside massage and stretching for maximal benefit. It is not a standalone cure that eliminates the scar entirely, but rather one component of a comprehensive scar management plan.
options: Ultrasound should never be combined with any other modality
Ultrasound alone will completely eliminate the scar
Ultrasound can help soften and improve pliability of scar tissue as part of a combined approach
Ultrasound has no possible application to scar tissue whatsoever
Ultrasound is only used for acute open wounds, never scars
Healthy tissue indicating active healing is occurring
A sign that healing has completely stalled
questions.question: A patient's pressure ulcer wound bed shows healthy red granulation tissue. What does this finding indicate to the physiotherapist?
questions.explanation: Red granulation tissue in the wound bed is a positive sign of healthy healing, reflecting good vascularity and new connective tissue formation during the proliferative phase. This contrasts with yellow slough, which needs removal, or black eschar, which indicates necrotic tissue requiring debridement.

questions.question: A physiotherapist working with a ventilated burns patient in ICU prioritises which early goal from the multidisciplinary rehabilitation aims?
questions.explanation: Among the multidisciplinary rehabilitation aims for burns patients, preservation of active and passive range of motion is a core early goal alongside preventing deeper injury and promoting rapid wound closure. Immediate return to sport or surgical scar revision are much later considerations, not early ICU priorities.
options: Immediate return to full sporting activity
Preservation of active and passive range of motion

questions.explanation: A burn wound assessment scale systematically evaluates objective wound characteristics such as size, depth, exudate, and surrounding tissue condition, providing a standardized method for tracking wound status changes over the course of treatment. This differs fundamentally from cognitive, balance, or nutritional screening tools, which assess unrelated clinical domains. Using a dedicated wound assessment tool supports consistent documentation and communication of burn wound progress.
questions.question: A physiotherapist uses a structured tool that includes wound size, depth, exudate, and surrounding tissue condition to objectively track a burn wound's status over the course of treatment. What general category of tool is being used?
A physiotherapist examines a patient with vitiligo presenting with patches of depigmented skin. Dysfunction of which cell type is primarily responsible for this presentation?
questions.explanation: Melanocytes located in the basal epidermis produce melanin, the pigment responsible for skin color, and their destruction or dysfunction leads to depigmented patches characteristic of vitiligo. Keratinocytes form the bulk of epidermal structure but do not produce pigment themselves. Recognizing melanocyte involvement helps differentiate vitiligo from other causes of skin color change encountered in physiotherapy assessment.

questions.question: A physiotherapist is informed that a patient's burn wound will be covered using donor skin from a cadaver as a temporary biological dressing rather than permanent closure. Which graft type does this represent?
questions.explanation: An allograft uses tissue from another human donor, commonly cadaveric skin, and serves as a temporary biological dressing because the body's immune system will eventually reject it, distinguishing it from a permanent autograft using the patient's own tissue. This temporary coverage protects the wound bed and reduces fluid loss and infection risk while awaiting definitive autografting. Recognizing the temporary nature of allografts helps physiotherapists set appropriate expectations regarding wound management timelines.

The stratum basale is the deepest epidermal layer, containing actively dividing keratinocytes that continuously regenerate the epidermis as outer cells are shed from the stratum corneum. This proliferative layer is critical to understanding how wounds re-epithelialize, since intact basal cells are necessary for surface regeneration. Damage extending through the basale into the dermis therefore heals differently than superficial injury limited to upper layers.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is teaching a patient about wound healing and explains that the deepest epidermal layer continuously divides to replace cells lost from the surface. Which layer is being described?
A physiotherapist is selecting a dressing for a wound with heavy exudate and visible slough. Which dressing choice best matches these wound characteristics?
questions.explanation: Alginate dressings are highly absorptive and appropriate for heavily exuding wounds, forming a gel that manages excess fluid while supporting a moist healing environment. Transparent films and thin hydrocolloids are better suited to low-exudate wounds, while hydrogels are intended for dry, necrotic wounds needing rehydration.
options: Basic gauze with no absorptive layer

questions.question: A physiotherapist is explaining to a burn patient why a deep injury extending into the dermis causes greater functional impairment than a superficial epidermal injury. Which dermal structures, when destroyed, account for permanent loss of sensation and sweating in that area?
questions.explanation: The dermis houses essential structures including sensory nerve endings and sweat glands, and their destruction in deep injuries results in permanent loss of sensation and sweating in the affected area, unlike superficial epidermal-only injuries that heal without such losses. This distinction underlies why burn depth, not just total surface area, determines long-term functional consequence. Physiotherapists use this principle when explaining prognosis differences between superficial and deep injuries to patients.

options: Only conditions involving no skin involvement whatsoever
Only conditions entirely unrelated to the immune system
Conditions with an overactive immune response only, never immune-deficient states
Immune-deficient inflammatory conditions such as psoriasis or rheumatoid arthritis
Only acute traumatic injuries with no inflammatory component
questions.question: A patient with a chronic inflammatory skin lesion is receiving a course of laser biostimulation. The therapist notes clinical effects should include enhanced autoimmune response. In which type of condition is this effect specifically beneficial?
questions.explanation: Laser biostimulation's clinical effects include enhancing autoimmune response in immune-deficient conditions such as psoriasis, rheumatoid arthritis, and atopic dermatitis, supporting the body's own regulatory processes. This differs from conditions of pure immune overactivity, where the therapeutic rationale would need separate consideration.

questions.question: A pressure injury whose depth cannot be determined because it is covered by slough or eschar is classified as?
questions.explanation: An unstageable pressure injury has its true depth obscured by slough or eschar, preventing accurate staging until the covering tissue is removed. A deep tissue pressure injury instead presents as persistent non-blanchable deep discoloration without an open wound obscuring depth assessment.

questions.question: Which accessory skin structure secretes sebum that coats hair and inhibits some bacterial growth?
questions.explanation: Sebaceous glands are oil glands connected to hair follicles that secrete sebum, an oily substance that keeps skin soft, prevents water loss, and has mild antibacterial properties. Eccrine and apocrine glands secrete sweat rather than oil, and the ceruminous gland produces earwax.

Most boils are caused by Staphylococcus aureus, bacteria commonly carried harmlessly on the skin or in the nose until they enter a hair follicle through a break in the skin. Streptococcus pyogenes is more associated with impetigo, while E. coli and Pseudomonas are less typical causes of simple boils.
questions.question: Boils are most commonly caused by which bacterial organism infecting a hair follicle?

questions.explanation: In the ABCDE rule, 'D' stands for diameter greater than 6mm, one of five features used alongside Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Colour variation, and Evolving characteristics to identify suspicious melanoma lesions. It does not refer to lesion duration, distribution, or discharge, which are not part of this specific rule.
options: Duration of the lesion in months
questions.question: In the ABCDE rule for identifying suspicious melanoma lesions, what does the 'D' represent?

questions.explanation: Massage therapy around the wound area improves both local circulation and lymphatic drainage, supporting the overall healing process by reducing swelling and enhancing tissue mobility. It does not directly influence bone remodelling, melanin synthesis, keratin hardening, or nerve regeneration.
questions.question: Massage therapy is beneficial in chronic wound management primarily by improving circulation and which additional process?

options: Disrupting bacterial biofilms and stimulating cellular activity
questions.question: Cavitation and acoustic streaming are non-thermal ultrasound effects that primarily assist wound care by which mechanism?
questions.explanation: Cavitation and acoustic streaming are non-thermal ultrasound mechanisms that disrupt bacterial biofilms and stimulate cellular activity, promoting collagen production and aiding debridement. These effects occur through microscopic mechanical action rather than significant heat generation, distinguishing them from thermal ultrasound applications.

questions.question: A physiotherapist is asked to estimate survival probability for an elderly burn patient using a formula that factors in both age and total body surface area burned. Which calculation is being applied?
questions.explanation: The Baux score estimates survival probability in burn patients by combining patient age with total body surface area burned, providing a simple prognostic tool used in initial burn assessment. This differs fundamentally from the Parkland formula, which calculates fluid resuscitation volume rather than survival likelihood. Understanding which formula serves which clinical purpose prevents confusion when managing acute burn patients.

questions.question: Which psoriasis subtype accounts for 80-90% of cases, presenting as raised red plaques with silvery scales?
questions.explanation: Plaque psoriasis is the most prevalent subtype, accounting for 80-90% of cases, and presents as raised red plaques covered with silvery scales on areas like the elbows and knees. Guttate psoriasis instead presents as small drop-shaped spots, often following streptococcal infection in children and young adults.

questions.question: A physiotherapist is choosing a debridement method for an infected burn wound in a clinic setting on a cooperative patient. Which mechanical technique using a scalpel edge is appropriate only for a skilled clinician?
questions.explanation: Scraping, using the edge of a scalpel or curette, is a mechanical debridement technique recommended for infected wounds but must be performed by a skilled clinician due to its precision requirements. Wet-to-dry dressings are also mechanical but less precise, while autolytic, biological, and enzymatic methods use different non-mechanical mechanisms.

Using the formula percentage chance of survival = 100 - (age in years + %TBSA), the calculation is 100 - (7 + 40) = 53%. This simple prognostic tool helps clinicians appreciate how both age and burn surface area jointly influence expected outcomes.
questions.question: A physiotherapist assessing a 7-year-old boy with 40% TBSA burns wants to estimate survival probability using the given prognostic formula. What is the calculated percentage chance of survival?

A physiotherapist examines red, moist, granular tissue filling in the base of a healing wound and recognizes this as a positive sign of progress. What does the presence of healthy granulation tissue indicate about the wound healing process?
questions.explanation: Healthy granulation tissue, appearing red, moist, and granular, indicates active formation of new vascularized connective tissue during the proliferative phase of wound healing, representing a positive sign of progress toward eventual wound closure. This finding contrasts with signs of infection, such as purulent discharge or increased malodor, which would instead suggest a complication. Recognizing healthy granulation supports appropriate continuation of the current wound care plan.
options: Ongoing bacterial infection requiring antibiotic treatment
Progression toward malignant transformation of the wound
Complete absence of any inflammatory healing response
Active formation of new vascularized connective tissue
Excessive, pathological tissue overgrowth requiring removal

questions.question: A physiotherapist selects a hydrogel dressing for a dry, necrotic wound specifically to support the body's own enzymatic breakdown of dead tissue without mechanical intervention. Which debridement process does this dressing choice support?
questions.explanation: Hydrogel and similar moisture-retentive dressings support autolytic debridement, a gentle process relying on the body's own enzymes and moisture to soften and break down necrotic tissue over time, without requiring mechanical or surgical intervention. This non-invasive approach is particularly suitable for patients who cannot tolerate more aggressive debridement methods. Selecting the dressing type appropriate to the intended debridement mechanism is a key wound care decision.

Coban wrap is useful for acute-stage burns of the hand specifically because it does not adhere to the underlying tissue, making application and removal less traumatic while still providing compression for oedema control. It does not provide antibiotic action or replace other necessary interventions like elevation or splinting.
questions.question: A patient's burn wound requires compression therapy on the hand using coban wrap in the acute stage. What is the primary advantage of coban over other dressings in this context?
options: It eliminates the need for elevation
It replaces the need for splinting entirely
It does not stick to the underlying tissue

questions.explanation: The therapeutic window for low-level laser therapy is generally cited as 630 to 905 nm, allowing effective non-invasive penetration of the skin surface for biostimulation without significant thermal damage. Wavelengths far outside this range, such as vacuum-UV or far-infrared, are not used for this therapeutic purpose.
questions.question: A patient is receiving laser biostimulation for a chronic ulcer, and the therapist must select a wavelength range known as the 'therapeutic window'. What range is this?

questions.explanation: Athlete's foot is a dermatophyte fungal infection, most commonly Trichophyton rubrum, which digests keratin in warm, moist environments such as sweaty feet in tight shoes, causing inflammation and scaling. Bacteria, viruses, and mites cause other distinct classes of skin infection with different clinical presentations.
questions.question: Athlete's foot (tinea pedis) is caused by which category of organism invading keratinised tissue?
A physiotherapist plans phototherapy for a patient with widespread psoriasis. What is the primary mechanism by which ultraviolet light improves this condition?
questions.explanation: Phototherapy uses UV light to trigger biological processes that reduce inflammation and slow the excessively rapid epidermal cell turnover characteristic of psoriasis. It does not aim to destroy skin cells entirely, further increase cell production, sterilise bacteria, or bleach pigmentation as its primary mechanism.
options: Sterilising the skin of all bacteria
Reducing inflammation and slowing excessive epidermal cell turnover
Directly killing all epidermal cells permanently
Bleaching all pigmentation from treated skin

questions.question: A patient's UVC treatment for wound infection uses a specific documented protocol of 254nm at a given power for bacterial burden reduction. What was the reported exposure duration in this protocol?
questions.explanation: The documented protocol used UVC at 254nm administered at 15.54 mW/cm2 for 180 seconds to reduce MRSA bacterial burden and support wound healing. This specific, evidence-based parameter combination illustrates how UVC dosing must be carefully controlled for both efficacy and tissue safety.

questions.question: A patient with suspected melanoma shows a mole with asymmetry, irregular borders, and colour variation. What is the most appropriate physiotherapy-related action?
options: Refer promptly for dermatological evaluation and biopsy
Apply laser therapy directly to the mole
Begin scar massage on the lesion immediately
Ignore the finding as physiotherapy is unrelated
Treat with ultrasound to reduce lesion size
questions.explanation: Features consistent with the ABCDE rule for melanoma warrant prompt referral for dermatological evaluation and biopsy rather than any direct physiotherapy modality, since suspicious pigmented lesions require medical diagnostic workup first. Applying massage, laser, or ultrasound directly to a potentially malignant lesion could be harmful and delay necessary care.

The zone of stasis surrounds the central zone of coagulation in Jackson's burn wound model, characterized by reduced blood flow that may progress to necrosis if not properly managed, but which remains potentially salvageable with appropriate early treatment. This contrasts with the outermost zone of hyperemia, which has increased blood flow and typically recovers fully. Recognizing the zone of stasis is clinically important since interventions here can influence whether tissue survives or is lost.
questions.question: A physiotherapist examines a burn wound and notes the surrounding area has reduced but still potentially salvageable blood flow, distinct from the central area of complete necrosis. Which zone of Jackson's burn wound model does this finding describe?

questions.explanation: Phototherapy specifically uses ultraviolet light to mimic sunlight exposure, triggering biological processes that reduce inflammation and slow abnormal skin cell proliferation in psoriasis. While iontophoresis, ultrasound, and massage have roles in various dermatological conditions, phototherapy is the modality specifically defined by its light-based mechanism.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is asked to contribute to management of a patient with psoriasis. Which physiotherapy-delivered modality option specifically uses light therapy to reduce inflammation and slow cell growth?

options: Discharge the patient from all care immediately
Increase modality intensity to fight the infection directly
Apply prolonged ice immersion to the entire limb
Defer local heating or stimulating modalities and escalate to the medical team
Proceed with scheduled thermotherapy as usual
questions.explanation: Systemic signs of infection such as fever and elevated white blood cells warrant escalation to the medical team and deferral of local heating or stimulating modalities that could exacerbate the infective process. Physiotherapy modalities are not a substitute for appropriate medical management of systemic infection.
questions.question: A patient recovering from major surgery develops a wound infection with systemic fever and elevated white blood cells. What should the physiotherapist prioritise regarding modality-based treatment that day?

options: Push ionized drugs through the stratum corneum
questions.explanation: Iontophoresis uses electrical current to drive ionized drugs, often analgesic or anti-inflammatory agents, through the stratum corneum barrier directly into target tissue. This is used for conditions like localized psoriasis, hyperhidrosis, and painful dermatologic lesions, distinct from mechanical debridement or thermal heating mechanisms.
questions.question: Iontophoresis in dermatological physiotherapy uses electrical current primarily to achieve which therapeutic action?

questions.explanation: The 'T' in the TIME framework stands for Tissue, meaning removal of non-viable or necrotic tissue such as slough should be addressed first to create a healthy wound bed for healing. This precedes moisture balance and edge assessment, which depend on having appropriate tissue present.
questions.question: A patient's chronic venous leg ulcer shows slough and low-to-moderate exudate. Using the TIME framework, what should the physiotherapist address FIRST under the 'T' component?
options: Applying compression bandaging only, without assessment
Ignoring tissue type and moving to dressing selection
Removal of non-viable tissue through debridement
Measuring the wound edge advancement only

questions.explanation: A carbuncle forms when several boils merge together beneath the skin, most commonly on the back and neck, lying deeper and taking longer to heal than a single boil. Folliculitis is a more superficial hair follicle inflammation, while cystic acne and pilonidal abscess occur through different mechanisms in different locations.
questions.question: A collection of several boils that join together beneath the skin, most often on the back or neck, is termed a?

questions.explanation: The Vancouver Scar Scale is a physiotherapy assessment tool specifically scoring pigmentation, vascularity, pliability, and scar height. The Braden scale instead assesses pressure ulcer risk, the Glasgow Coma Scale measures consciousness level, and the Visual Analogue Scale is generally used for subjective pain rating.
questions.question: Which validated scale scores scar pigmentation, vascularity, pliability, and height during physiotherapy assessment?
A physiotherapist is selecting a laser probe type for treating a large burn area requiring deeper tissue effect with reduced treatment time. What probe choice is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Large cluster probes containing multiple diodes are recommended for larger wounds or burns where a deeper effect is needed across a bigger area within a reduced treatment time. A single point probe is instead better suited to small lesions like acne scars or localised superficial wounds.

Mature scar tissue typically achieves only about 80 percent of the original, uninjured tissue's strength, even after the lengthy remodeling process is complete, reflecting the structurally less organized nature of scar collagen compared to original tissue. This permanent strength deficit is an important consideration when counseling patients about activity modification and reinjury risk in scarred areas. Recognizing this limitation supports realistic long-term expectations rather than assuming full structural restoration.
questions.question: A physiotherapist explains to a patient that even a year after injury, healed scar tissue will likely never regain the full original strength of the uninjured skin. Approximately what percentage of original tissue strength does mature scar tissue typically achieve?
Which sweat gland type is stimulated primarily by stress and located mainly in the axilla and groin?
questions.explanation: Apocrine sweat glands secrete into hair follicles of the axilla and groin, become active at puberty, and respond to emotional stress rather than temperature regulation. Eccrine glands are more widespread and control thermoregulation by secreting cooling sweat directly onto the skin surface.

Collimation refers to the parallel, non-divergent travel of laser light rays, allowing the beam to maintain its intensity and focus over distance, unlike ordinary scattered light that spreads and weakens with distance. This property supports precise targeting of specific tissue depths during therapeutic application. Along with monochromaticity and coherence, collimation is one of the three defining physical properties that distinguish laser from ordinary light sources.
questions.question: A physiotherapist applying low-level laser therapy explains to a colleague that the beam's parallel, non-diverging rays allow precise targeting of deep tissue compared with ordinary light sources. Which laser property is being described?

options: Superficial injury limited to the epidermis only
Resolving inflammation with improving blood flow
Deeper tissue damage with compromised capillary perfusion
An allergic reaction unrelated to thermal injury
questions.explanation: A positive blanch test, where pressed skin returns to its normal color, indicates intact capillary circulation typical of superficial burns, whereas an absent blanch response signals compromised perfusion consistent with deeper tissue damage. This simple bedside test helps clinicians estimate burn depth without invasive assessment. Accurate depth estimation through blanch testing directly informs burn management and referral decisions.
questions.question: A physiotherapist assessing a burn wound presses gently on the affected skin and observes the area does not change color upon release. What does this absent blanch response most likely indicate about the burn depth?

Increasing massage pressure or applying heat over a possibly infected area could exacerbate spread of infection.
questions.question: A physiotherapist notices a patient's burn dressing shows purulent, foul-smelling exudate during a treatment session. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Proceed with scheduled ultrasound therapy as planned
Report the signs of infection to the medical team promptly
Increase massage pressure to the area
Discharge the patient from further sessions

questions.question: A physiotherapist calculates fluid resuscitation needs for an adult burn patient using total body surface area burned and body weight in kilograms. Which formula is being applied for this calculation?
questions.explanation: The Parkland formula calculates fluid resuscitation volume for burn patients using total body surface area burned and body weight, guiding the critical first 24 hours of fluid management to prevent burn shock. This is distinct from the Baux score, which estimates survival probability rather than treatment dosing. Correctly applying this formula is essential for safe acute burn management before physiotherapy intervention begins.

questions.question: A patient with anterior neck burns is being positioned in bed. Why should a pillow NOT be placed under the head?
questions.explanation: Placing a pillow under the head of a patient with anterior neck burns encourages sustained neck flexion, promoting a flexion contracture as the burn heals in a shortened position. Instead, the head should be positioned in slight extension to maintain tissue length and prevent long-term functional loss.
options: It interferes with fluid resuscitation lines
It increases risk of pressure ulcers on the sacrum
It can encourage a flexion contracture of the healing neck
Loss of sensation and paralysis preventing repositioning
Increased muscle bulk over bony areas
questions.explanation: Spinal cord injury patients cannot feel pressure, pain, or discomfort due to sensory loss, and paralysis prevents spontaneous repositioning, allowing prolonged unrelieved pressure over bony prominences. Muscle atrophy actually reduces natural cushioning rather than increasing it, further raising their risk.
questions.question: Patients with spinal cord injury are especially vulnerable to pressure ulcers largely because of which combination of factors?

questions.explanation: When managing oedema through elevation in a patient with large TBSA burns, the physiotherapist should elevate limbs above heart level, maintain the feet at 90 degrees, keep hips neutral, and monitor for pressure sores as key precautions. Avoid all limb positioning until healing is complete
Maintain the feet at 90 degrees while elevating affected limbs
Place limbs in a dependent position to boost perfusion
Elevate limbs only above shoulder height with no other precaution
questions.question: A patient with burns covering a large TBSA is showing signs of systemic inflammation. Regarding limb elevation, which precaution should the physiotherapist apply?
A physiotherapist assessing a patient's skin notices the epidermis is thickest on the palm and sole compared to other body areas. What functional demand explains this regional difference?
options: Higher density of hair follicles present
Greater mechanical friction and pressure exposure
Increased need for sweat gland filtration
questions.explanation: Areas subjected to repeated mechanical friction and pressure, such as the palms and soles, develop a thicker epidermis with an additional stratum lucidum layer for added protection against abrasion. This regional adaptation reflects the skin's response to functional mechanical demand rather than hair density or sun exposure. Recognizing this helps physiotherapists interpret normal regional skin thickness variation during integumentary assessment.

Cryotherapy in acute burn management requires carefully controlled, moderate cooling temperatures rather than extreme cold, since overly aggressive cooling risks worsening tissue damage in already compromised skin. This cautious approach balances the analgesic benefits of cooling against the vulnerability of burned tissue to further thermal injury. Appropriate temperature moderation is a key safety principle distinguishing burn-specific cryotherapy protocols from standard musculoskeletal cold application.
questions.question: A physiotherapist managing a patient in the acute phase following a significant burn injury selects cryotherapy for localized pain relief and considers the temperature range carefully to avoid worsening tissue damage. Which approach reflects appropriate caution in this context?
options: Using a carefully moderated, controlled cooling temperature
Applying the coldest possible temperature for maximum analgesia
Avoiding any temperature consideration since burns cannot be cooled
Using ice packs directly on open burn wounds without barriers
Applying extreme cold for the longest possible session duration

questions.explanation: Escharotomy is a surgical procedure treating compartment syndrome from circumferential eschar by incising through the eschar to expose subcutaneous fat and restore perfusion and nerve function. Debridement removes dead tissue generally, fasciotomy releases deep fascia, and skin grafting covers a wound rather than relieving pressure.
questions.question: A surgical incision through eschar to relieve pressure and restore circulation in circumferential full-thickness burns is called?

questions.explanation: Purulent exudate—thick, discoloured, and malodorous—is a classic sign of wound infection requiring clinical attention. Serous or serosanguineous drainage is typical and expected during normal early healing, while sanguineous drainage may simply follow debridement rather than indicating infection.
questions.question: Purulent wound exudate that is thick, yellow-green, and foul-smelling is a clinical sign most suggestive of?
A burns patient has circumferential full-thickness burns to the forearm with signs of impaired distal circulation. Which procedure is most urgently indicated?
questions.explanation: Signs of impaired distal circulation with circumferential full-thickness burns suggest compartment syndrome from constricting eschar, requiring urgent escharotomy to relieve pressure and restore perfusion. Scar massage, stretching, pressure garments, and laser therapy are all later-stage interventions inappropriate for this acute emergency.

No treatment consideration is ever appropriate

questions.question: A patient presents with sunken, pitted scarring from previous chickenpox. What physiotherapy expectation is realistic for this presentation?
questions.explanation: Atrophic scars result from actual loss of dermal tissue volume, so physiotherapy soft tissue techniques offer limited structural correction compared to their effectiveness for adhesions or hypertrophic tissue. Setting realistic expectations is important, as significant improvement of volume loss usually requires dermatological or surgical options.

questions.question: A severe wound where a portion of tissue such as skin or muscle is forcibly torn away, as in a degloving injury, is an?
questions.explanation: An avulsion involves forcible tearing away of tissue such as skin, muscle, or bone, with degloving injuries from industrial or motorcycle accidents being classic examples. Lacerations tear tissue without necessarily removing it entirely, while contusions and hematomas are closed injuries with no tissue loss.

The dose should always be reduced regardless of skin tone
No dosing adjustment is ever required for skin tone
Only visible light lasers can be used, never infrared
Treatment should be discontinued entirely for dark skin
questions.explanation: Darker complexion, adipose tissue, or highly vascular tissue absorbs more light, reducing penetration to the target tissue, so a greater irradiance is typically required to achieve the same biological effect. This is a clinically important dosing consideration rather than an outright contraindication.
questions.question: A physiotherapist is treating a patient with dark skin complexion requiring laser therapy for a deep soft tissue injury. What dosing adjustment should be considered?
A raised scar that grows beyond the boundaries of the original wound and may itch or hurt severely is a?
questions.explanation: Keloids are benign but raised scars that extend beyond the original wound margins and can be itchy or painful, resulting from overgrowth of granulation tissue. Hypertrophic scars also produce excess tissue but remain confined within the original wound boundaries, distinguishing the two conditions.

Atrophic scars appear sunken and pitted due to loss of underlying dermal tissue, commonly resulting from conditions such as acne or chickenpox. Hypertrophic and keloid scars are raised rather than depressed, while contracture scars are tight and restrict movement, a different clinical presentation entirely.

This makes flaps useful where the recipient bed is poorly vascularised. Grafts, whether split, full thickness, allo-, or xenograft, all rely on the wound bed for perfusion.

The heel of the paretic (affected) limb
questions.explanation: Due to sensory loss, neglect, and weakness on the affected side, the heel of the paretic limb should be specifically inspected as it may remain compressed against the mattress without the patient's awareness. Neglect further reduces the patient's own ability to notice or report problems on that side.
questions.question: A stroke patient with right hemisphere involvement and left-sided neglect is at risk of pressure ulcers. What specific site should the physiotherapist prioritise inspecting?
During which phase of wound healing does prolonged inflammation most negatively affect eventual scar quality?
questions.explanation: Prolonged inflammation can delay healing and negatively affect final scar quality by extending the time before proliferative repair processes can properly begin. Once healing progresses appropriately into remodeling, targeted interventions like massage can then improve scar pliability, but this depends on the inflammatory phase resolving normally first.

questions.question: A physiotherapist examines a patient with well-demarcated, silvery scaled plaques on the elbows and knees and learns the diagnosis is plaque psoriasis. Which skin process underlies this characteristic scaling appearance?
questions.explanation: Plaque psoriasis results from markedly accelerated keratinocyte turnover and abnormal differentiation, causing rapid accumulation of immature skin cells that produce the characteristic thick, silvery scaled plaques seen on extensor surfaces like elbows and knees. This pathophysiology differs fundamentally from infectious, infestation-related, or pigmentary skin conditions. Recognizing this mechanism explains why therapies targeting cell turnover, such as phototherapy, can be effective in psoriasis management.
options: Destruction of melanocytes within affected plaques
Bacterial colonization causing localized abscess formation
Mite infestation burrowing within the epidermis
Accelerated keratinocyte turnover and abnormal differentiation
Loss of dermal collagen causing skin thinning

questions.question: Ischial tuberosities are the primary at-risk site for pressure ulcer development in which patient position?
questions.explanation: In the sitting position, sustained weight-bearing concentrates over the ischial tuberosities, sacrum, and heels, making them the primary pressure ulcer risk sites, particularly in wheelchair users. Supine loading instead affects the occiput and sacrum, while side-lying affects the greater trochanter and lateral malleolus.

options: Reducing restriction and improving mobility between scar and deeper tissue layers
questions.explanation: Myofascial release aims to reduce restriction and adhesion binding the scar to deeper fascia and tissue layers, thereby improving overall tissue mobility and function. It does not target pigmentation changes, nor does it aim to eliminate the scar tissue itself, which remains a normal part of healing.
questions.question: A physiotherapist plans myofascial release for a scar adhered to underlying fascia after abdominal surgery. What is the primary goal of this technique?
Which physical agent used in chronic wound management is described as having limited evidence but promising results when combined with standard care?
questions.explanation: Pulsed electromagnetic field therapy carries limited but promising evidence, particularly as an adjunctive treatment alongside standard wound care for pressure and diabetic ulcers. Electrical stimulation and ultrasound have stronger evidence grades, while laser and UVC therapies also carry moderate evidence support in comparison.

options: Stretching should be performed immediately to maximise tissue lengthening
Application of a cast to fully immobilise the area
Discontinuation of the treatment plan entirely

A 24-hour rest period before any further intervention
