Nursing education should emphasise adequate hydration, avoidance of extreme temperatures, prompt treatment of infections, and supplemental folic acid.

questions.question: A client with a deviated nasal septum reports difficulty breathing through one nostril. The nurse understands this occurs because the septum:
questions.explanation: A deviated septum physically narrows one nasal passage, increasing resistance to airflow on that side. This can cause chronic mouth breathing and predispose to sinus infections. Severe deviations may require surgical correction if symptoms persist.
options: Obstructs airflow through the narrowed nasal passage
Prevents mucus production on the affected side
Increases turbinate swelling on both sides
Damages the cribriform plate above it

questions.question: In Addison's disease management, the patient may need to supplement dietary intake with salt specifically during:
options: Times of physical exercise and strenuous activity only
High environmental temperatures causing excessive sweating
Periods of stress such as surgery or acute illness
Morning hours when cortisol levels are naturally lowest
Gastrointestinal fluid loss through vomiting and diarrhoea
questions.explanation: Patients with Addison's disease who experience gastrointestinal fluid loss through vomiting and diarrhoea need to supplement their dietary intake with salt (sodium chloride). This is because vomiting and diarrhoea cause additional sodium losses on top of the already-impaired sodium retention from aldosterone deficiency. Without adequate sodium replacement, these patients are at risk for life-threatening hyponatremia, hypovolemia, and an Addisonian crisis, which can rapidly progress to shock and death.

options: Blood flow is blocked to a ventilated lung area
Air cannot reach a well-perfused lung segment
Both ventilation and perfusion are equally reduced
Surfactant production increases in the affected area
Alveolar walls thicken throughout both lungs
questions.explanation: A pulmonary embolism obstructs blood flow to a segment of lung that continues to be ventilated normally, creating dead space where air is not exchanged with blood. This ventilation-perfusion mismatch results in hypoxemia despite normal airflow to that area. It is a classic pathophysiologic feature distinguishing embolism from airway obstruction.
questions.question: The nurse understands that ventilation-perfusion mismatch in a pulmonary embolism occurs because:

questions.explanation: Type II pneumocytes (alveolar cells) produce surfactant, a substance that reduces alveolar surface tension and prevents collapse during expiration. They also regenerate Type I cells when they are damaged. Deficiency of surfactant is the hallmark of neonatal respiratory distress syndrome in premature infants.
questions.question: Surfactant production in the lungs is primarily attributed to which cell type?

questions.explanation: Diaphragmatic breathing focuses on using the diaphragm rather than accessory muscles, which improves ventilation efficiency and reduces the work of breathing over time. Patients place a hand on the abdomen to feel it rise during inhalation, reinforcing correct technique. Regular practice can reduce dyspnea and improve exercise tolerance in chronic lung disease.
questions.question: A nurse teaches diaphragmatic breathing to a patient with COPD. This technique is intended primarily to:
options: Increase reliance on accessory muscle use
Strengthen the diaphragm and improve ventilation efficiency
Reduce oxygen saturation temporarily during practice
Eliminate the need for bronchodilator medication

questions.question: A nurse caring for a neutropenic patient after chemotherapy should prioritise which infection-control measure?
questions.explanation: Meticulous hand hygiene is the single most effective measure to prevent transmission of pathogens to an immunocompromised patient. Raw foods and standing water in flower vases harbour organisms that pose serious risk to a neutropenic host. Restricting exposure to unwell visitors further reduces infection risk.
options: Reducing the frequency of vital sign checks
Placing fresh cut flowers at the bedside daily
Strict hand hygiene before every patient contact
Allowing unrestricted visits from unwell relatives
Serving only raw fruits to boost vitamin intake
The pressure difference driving the fluid
The length of the intravenous tubing
The internal diameter of a narrow catheter
The viscosity of the fluid being infused
The height difference below the patient
questions.question: A nurse teaching a new graduate about intravenous flow principles explains that flow rate is directly proportional to which factor?
questions.explanation: According to principles governing fluid flow, flow rate increases with a greater pressure gradient, such as raising the height of the infusion bag, while it decreases with increased tubing length or fluid viscosity. Understanding these relationships helps the nurse troubleshoot a slow or sluggish intravenous infusion. Adjusting bag height or checking for kinks are practical applications of this principle.

Metabolic syndrome is diagnosed by a cluster of interrelated risk factors including central obesity, elevated blood pressure, dyslipidaemia, and insulin resistance, which together significantly increase cardiovascular and diabetes risk. Recognising this cluster prompts comprehensive risk factor management rather than addressing findings in isolation. Early lifestyle intervention can reduce progression to overt disease.
options: Isolated vitamin deficiency without other signs
Isolated joint pain without other systemic signs
Isolated hearing loss without other findings
Isolated mild anaemia without other findings
questions.question: A nurse caring for a patient with suspected metabolic syndrome should assess for which cluster of findings?
A nurse caring for a patient with Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder should recognise that, unlike anorexia nervosa, this condition primarily involves:
options: Binge eating followed by purging behaviour
Food avoidance without distorted body image concerns
Excessive exercise to control body shape
Intense fear of weight gain as the primary driver
questions.explanation: ARFID involves limited or restrictive eating driven by sensory sensitivity, lack of interest in food, or fear of aversive consequences such as choking, rather than concerns about body weight or shape. This distinguishes it clinically from anorexia nervosa and guides different therapeutic approaches. Nutritional rehabilitation still remains an important management component.

Painless, progressive enlargement of lymph nodes (lymphadenopathy) — most commonly in the cervical, axillary, or inguinal regions — is the most common presenting feature of lymphoma. The nodes are characteristically non-tender (distinguishing lymphoma from reactive/infective lymphadenopathy, which is usually painful). Patients or nurses during routine examination may first notice these enlarged nodes. Any lymph node larger than 1 cm persisting for more than 4 weeks warrants investigation to exclude malignancy.
questions.question: The most common presenting feature of lymphoma in the lymphatic system is:
options: Painful inflamed lymph nodes with fever

questions.question: After endotracheal tube insertion, the nurse's first priority to confirm correct placement is to:
options: Obtain a chest X-ray and wait for radiologist confirmation
Auscultate lung sounds bilaterally to check tube position
Monitor capnography readings over the next 30 minutes
Measure cuff pressure with a manometer at 30 cmH2O
Inspect the vocal cords directly via laryngoscope again
questions.explanation: Bilateral auscultation of lung sounds is the nurse's immediate priority to confirm that the endotracheal tube has not slipped into one main bronchus (right main bronchus being most common). Unequal or absent breath sounds indicate malposition. While chest X-ray is the gold standard for confirming tube tip position, auscultation is performed first as a rapid clinical check.

Hirsutism refers to an unusual male-pattern hair growth in female patients, typically occurring on the face, chest, and abdomen. It is caused by elevated androgen levels (from the adrenal glands or ovaries) that stimulate hair follicles in androgen-sensitive areas. Hirsutism in women is associated with Cushing's syndrome, polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), congenital adrenal hyperplasia, and androgen-secreting tumors. It must be distinguished from virilization, which involves more severe androgenic changes.
questions.question: Hirsutism identified in a female patient during endocrine physical assessment is defined as:
options: Absence of axillary or pubic hair suggesting hypopituitarism
Development of male characteristics due to excess androgens
Unusual male-pattern hair growth pattern in female patients
Excessive hair loss from the scalp in a female patient
Patchy, irregular hair loss due to autoimmune thyroid disease

questions.question: Rapid-acting insulin analogs such as lispro and aspart are distinguished from regular insulin by their:
questions.explanation: Rapid-acting insulin analogs such as lispro and aspart have a faster onset and shorter duration of action compared to regular (short-acting) insulin. They are typically administered just before or immediately after meals to control postprandial glucose spikes. Their pharmacokinetic profile more closely mimics the body's natural mealtime insulin response. Regular insulin has a slower onset and longer duration, typically requiring injection 30-45 minutes before meals for optimal efficacy.
options: Faster onset and shorter duration enabling mealtime dosing
Longer duration of action lasting up to 24 hours or more
Intermediate peak requiring twice-daily administration schedule
Ability to be administered orally instead of by injection
Lower cost compared to regular human insulin preparations

questions.question: The nurse teaches a patient with Addison's disease to carry a medical alert bracelet because:
options: Emergency personnel need to know steroid doses are required
Diabetics need identification in case of hypoglycemic episodes
The bracelet replaces the need for emergency steroid injections
It identifies the patient as requiring dialysis in emergency
It signals healthcare providers to avoid all steroid medications
questions.explanation: Patients with Addison's disease must carry a medical alert bracelet (or card) at all times because, in an emergency where the patient is unconscious or unable to communicate, healthcare personnel need to immediately know that the patient requires steroid supplementation (hydrocortisone) to prevent a potentially fatal Addisonian crisis. During physiological stress such as major trauma, surgery, or severe illness, steroid-dependent patients need stress doses of corticosteroids urgently, and the medical alert identification ensures this critical information is available.

Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (AIHA) is the most common autoimmune complication of CLL, occurring in 10–25% of patients. Malignant CLL B-cells produce autoantibodies (typically warm IgG) directed against RBC antigens, leading to premature RBC destruction. AIHA in CLL is managed with corticosteroids, rituximab, and treatment of the underlying CLL. Nurses must monitor for jaundice, falling haemoglobin, elevated indirect bilirubin, and positive direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test.
options: Bone marrow aplasia from CLL infiltration
Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (AIHA) from malignant B-cells
Iron deficiency from chronic blood loss
questions.question: A patient with CLL develops haemolytic anaemia. This complication is most likely caused by:

questions.explanation: Bronchodilators delivered by nebulizer, such as albuterol or metaproterenol, help expand airways in atelectasis by relaxing bronchial smooth muscle and reducing bronchospasm. They are used alongside incentive spirometry and chest physiotherapy. Bronchodilators address the component of bronchospasm that may be contributing to airway obstruction and alveolar collapse.
options: Oral corticosteroids such as prednisolone 40 mg daily
Intravenous antibiotics to treat superimposed pneumonia
Bronchodilator via nebulizer, such as albuterol or metaproterenol
Inhaled corticosteroids such as beclomethasone dipropionate
questions.question: A post-surgical patient develops atelectasis. The most appropriate pharmacological intervention to expand the airways is:
Gastritis is most accurately defined as:
questions.explanation: Gastritis is defined as inflammation of the gastric or stomach mucosa, resulting when the protective mucosal barrier is broken down, allowing autodigestion from hydrochloric acid and pepsin. It may be acute (lasting hours to days) or chronic (from repeated exposure to irritants). It may involve the entire stomach (pangastritis) or a specific region (e.g., antral gastritis), and can be erosive or non-erosive.
options: Inflammation of the gastric mucosa from mucosal barrier disruption
Peptic ulceration of the stomach from Helicobacter pylori alone
Autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells causing achlorhydria
Fibrotic replacement of the entire gastric mucosa in chronic disease
Haemorrhagic erosion of the duodenal bulb causing epigastric pain

questions.question: A nurse teaching a newly diagnosed diabetic patient about sick-day management explains that insulin should never be stopped, even if the patient is not eating normally. What is the physiological rationale for this advice?
questions.explanation: During illness, stress hormones such as cortisol and adrenaline can raise blood glucose levels and promote ketone production, so stopping insulin, even when oral intake is reduced, can significantly increase the risk of diabetic ketoacidosis. This is why sick-day management guidelines typically emphasise continuing insulin, often with more frequent monitoring, rather than stopping it. This physiological response can occur despite reduced or absent food intake, making the advice counterintuitive but medically important.
options: Insulin has no effect on blood glucose during illness
Stopping insulin during illness has no associated risks
Illness always lowers blood glucose, reducing insulin need
Illness increases stress hormones that raise blood glucose and ketoacidosis risk
Reduced food intake alone prevents any risk of ketoacidosis

questions.question: The follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) from the anterior pituitary is important in males because it:
questions.explanation: Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), released from the anterior pituitary, plays an important role in male reproductive function by stimulating sperm cell production (spermatogenesis) in the testes. In females, FSH is involved in estrogen secretion and the growth of egg cells (folliculogenesis). FSH is essential for fertility in both sexes, acting on the gonads to support their gametogenic functions.
options: Stimulates testosterone production in the Leydig cells
Controls the secondary sex characteristics of puberty
Triggers the release of androgenic steroids from adrenal
Is involved in the production of sperm cells in testes
Stimulates the seminal vesicles to secrete prostate fluid

questions.explanation: In disaster recovery, nurses play a pivotal role in health promotion and disease prevention by leading public health campaigns and educating community members on best practices in hygiene, the importance of consuming safe water, and recognizing early symptoms of diseases. They also organize and execute vaccination drives to curb the spread of infectious diseases in post-disaster environments. These nursing actions address the heightened health risks created by disrupted sanitation and overcrowding.
options: managing hospital infrastructure and equipment procurement
performing advanced surgical procedures for disaster survivors
providing legal advice to communities affected by disasters
organizing vaccination drives and educating on hygiene and safe water use
directing financial aid distribution to affected families
questions.question: A nurse's role in health promotion and disease prevention during disaster recovery includes:

options: Stridor indicating significant upper airway narrowing
questions.explanation: Stridor is a harsh, high-pitched sound heard predominantly during inspiration, resulting from turbulent airflow through a significantly narrowed upper airway. It is considered a medical emergency because it often precedes complete airway obstruction. Immediate assessment and preparation for airway intervention are essential when stridor is present.
questions.question: A nurse caring for a patient with a suspected upper airway obstruction auscultates a harsh, high-pitched sound primarily on inspiration. This finding is termed:

questions.explanation: Chronic bronchitis is defined as a long-term, irreversible respiratory illness characterized by daily mucus-producing cough lasting at least 3 months per year for two consecutive years. This distinguishes it from acute bronchitis, which is a shorter illness following a cold or viral infection and typically resolves within a few weeks. Chronic bronchitis is one component of COPD.
options: A short illness that commonly follows a cold or viral infection
Daily productive mucus cough lasting at least 3 months per year
Acute inflammatory exacerbation requiring emergency hospitalization
Infection with influenza A or B requiring antiviral treatment
Reversible airway narrowing responding completely to bronchodilators
questions.question: Chronic bronchitis is distinguished from acute bronchitis by the criterion that it involves:

questions.explanation: The hypothalamus instructs the adrenal glands to release adrenaline (epinephrine) and cortisol in response to perceived stress. Adrenaline rapidly increases heart rate, blood pressure, and blood flow to muscles, while cortisol provides a more sustained metabolic response by raising blood glucose. Together, these hormones prepare the body for emergency action by optimizing available energy and physical readiness.
questions.question: The stress hormones released during the 'fight or flight' response are:
options: insulin and glucagon from the pancreas
thyroxine and calcitonin from the thyroid gland
aldosterone and antidiuretic hormone from the adrenal cortex
oxytocin and prolactin from the anterior pituitary gland
Smooth muscle surrounding the entire circumference
Dense fibrous tissue lining the lumen
Positive intrathoracic pressure maintained by the diaphragm
Elastic recoil from surrounding lung parenchyma
C-shaped cartilaginous rings on its anterior and lateral walls
questions.question: The trachea is prevented from collapsing because of:
questions.explanation: The trachea contains C-shaped cartilaginous rings at regular intervals that provide firmness and prevent collapse. The rings are incomplete on the posterior surface, where smooth muscle (the trachealis) completes the wall and allows flexibility. This structural arrangement maintains airway patency during respiration.

options: Excess cortisol promotes gluconeogenesis and insulin resistance, raising blood glucose
Cortisol has no effect on glucose metabolism
Excess cortisol directly destroys pancreatic beta cells
Cortisol excess always causes hypoglycaemia instead
Blood glucose monitoring is unrelated to cortisol levels
questions.question: A patient with Cushing's syndrome asks why the nurse monitors blood glucose closely even though they were not previously diabetic. What is the physiological explanation?
questions.explanation: Cortisol promotes gluconeogenesis in the liver and reduces peripheral tissue sensitivity to insulin, so chronically elevated cortisol levels in Cushing's syndrome can lead to hyperglycaemia or even steroid-induced diabetes. This differs from conditions causing hypoglycaemia, which involve different hormonal mechanisms. Monitoring blood glucose helps detect this metabolic complication early.

The primary preoperative nursing responsibility is educating the patient about what to expect—from anesthesia administration, the surgery itself, and the likely use of chest tubes and drainage systems postoperatively. This education reduces anxiety, improves postoperative compliance, and prepares the patient for recovery. It is the cornerstone of preoperative nursing care for thoracic surgery patients.
questions.question: The primary preoperative nursing action for a patient scheduled for thoracic surgery is:
options: Administering preoperative morphine and antiemetics routinely
Inserting an arterial line for continuous blood pressure monitoring
Obtaining written consent for transfusion of blood products only
Educating the patient about postoperative expectations and exercises
Restricting all oral fluids 24 hours before the procedure

questions.explanation: IgE attaches itself to mast cells and basophils, which release histamine in the presence of the antigen. It is responsible for the mediation of allergic reactions including hay fever. The IgE-mediated antigen-antibody response is also the mechanism underlying anaphylaxis, where massive histamine and mediator release from mast cells causes systemic vasodilation and bronchoconstriction.
options: the initial rapid antibody response to new infections
placental immunity transfer from mother to newborn
mucosal immunity in the gut and respiratory secretions
complement activation and bacterial cell lysis
allergic reactions including hay fever through mast cell histamine release
questions.question: IgE (Immunoglobulin E) is responsible for the mediation of:
During preoperative preparation for thoracic surgery, the nurse improves airway clearance by using:
questions.explanation: Preoperatively, airway clearance is improved through humidification, postural drainage, and chest percussion following bronchodilator administration. These measures remove secretions from the airways before surgery, reducing the risk of postoperative atelectasis and infection. The volume of sputum is estimated to guide the intensity of preoperative airway preparation required. Antibiotics are given as prescribed for existing infection.
options: Prophylactic broad-spectrum antibiotics administered to all patients
Humidification, postural drainage, and chest percussion after bronchodilator
Trendelenburg positioning to drain secretions from the apical segments
Restricting oral fluid intake to reduce secretion volume preoperatively
Nasogastric tube insertion to prevent aspiration of gastric contents
Withholding all oral intake for 24 hours
Encouraging the child to eat a large meal pre-treatment
Positioning the child supine without a pillow
Restricting anti-emetics to reduce drug interactions
questions.explanation: Evidence-based practice mandates pre-emptive (prophylactic) anti-emetic administration before chemotherapy to prevent chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting (CINV). For moderately to highly emetogenic regimens used in ALL (e.g., cytarabine, cyclophosphamide), 5-HT3 antagonists (ondansetron), dexamethasone, and NK1 antagonists (aprepitant) are used prophylactically. Pre-emptive control of CINV improves quality of life, reduces dehydration, and maintains adequate nutritional intake essential for treatment tolerance and recovery.
questions.question: A child with ALL is experiencing chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting. The nurse's first intervention is:

questions.explanation: Oral endotracheal tubes are repositioned to the opposite side of the mouth every 24 hours or per institutional policy to prevent pressure ulcers and tissue damage caused by sustained contact with oral structures. The tube is also resecured to ensure it does not become dislodged. Pressure necrosis from prolonged contact is a preventable complication.
options: Reduce the risk of ventilator-associated pneumonia from pooled secretions
Verify tube position and prevent tissue damage from sustained pressure
Allow the patient an opportunity to speak and communicate verbally
Remove accumulated mucus from the tube's inner lumen
Reduce patient anxiety by changing the securing device daily
questions.question: Oral endotracheal tubes are repositioned and resecured every 24 hours primarily to:

questions.explanation: After thoracentesis, the needle insertion carries a risk of puncturing the lung and causing a pneumothorax. The nurse should auscultate breath sounds bilaterally and monitor for signs of respiratory distress such as dyspnea or diminished breath sounds. A chest X-ray is often obtained to confirm lung status post-procedure.
questions.question: A nurse is caring for a patient after thoracentesis. The priority nursing action following the procedure is to:
options: Encourage vigorous coughing to clear secretions
Position the patient flat on the affected side
Assess breath sounds and monitor for pneumothorax
Restrict all oral fluids for several hours
Apply a tight abdominal binder for support

questions.question: Stress has been linked to six leading causes of death. Which of the following is one of those causes?
questions.explanation: Stress is linked to six of the leading causes of death: heart disease, cancer, lung ailments, accidents, cirrhosis of the liver, and suicide. Chronic stress contributes to these conditions through physiological mechanisms including sustained elevation of cortisol and adrenaline, immune suppression, behavioral changes, and unhealthy coping behaviors. Understanding this linkage reinforces the nurse's role in stress assessment and management.

options: Thyroid nodules along the anterior surface of the neck
Enlarged parathyroid glands in the posterior neck region
The adrenal glands located just superior to both kidneys
The pituitary gland through the trans-sphenoidal approach
The pancreas and surrounding structures including insulinomas
questions.question: The endoscopic ultrasound is inserted into the stomach and duodenum specifically to visualize:
questions.explanation: Endoscopic ultrasound involves inserting an ultrasound probe into the stomach and duodenum to visualize the pancreas and its surrounding structures. It is particularly valuable for detecting small pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors, especially insulinomas, which may be too small to be visualized by standard external ultrasound or CT scanning. The close proximity of the gastrointestinal tract to the pancreas allows for high-resolution imaging from within the bowel.

questions.question: Pericarditis typically presents with chest pain that is characteristically:
options: Crushing, central, and radiating to the left arm
Tearing, radiating to the back between shoulders
Dull aching, constant, and unrelated to position
Sharp, pleuritic, relieved by sitting forward
questions.explanation: Pericarditis (inflammation of the pericardial sac surrounding the heart) classically presents with sharp, pleuritic chest pain that is worse on inspiration, lying flat, and coughing, and is relieved by sitting forward (leaning forward reduces pericardial friction). A pericardial friction rub (scratchy, high-pitched sound) may be auscultated. ECG shows diffuse saddle-shaped ST elevation and PR depression. This pain pattern helps differentiate pericarditis from MI (crushing, not pleuritic) and GERD (burning, postprandial).

Epinephrine is the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis because it rapidly reverses bronchospasm, reduces vascular permeability, and restores blood pressure through combined alpha and beta adrenergic effects. Delayed administration significantly increases the risk of fatal outcomes. Antihistamines and corticosteroids may be given as adjuncts but do not replace the urgency of epinephrine.
questions.question: A nurse caring for a patient experiencing anaphylaxis should anticipate that the first-line emergency medication to be administered is:

questions.explanation: All acute leukaemias share the clinical triad of bone marrow failure: anaemia (from decreased RBC production, causing fatigue and pallor), thrombocytopenia (causing petechiae, purpura, and haemorrhage), and neutropenia (causing recurrent and severe infections). Organomegaly (hepatosplenomegaly) and lymphadenopathy occur from leukaemic infiltration. Progressive joint sclerosis is a feature of haemophilic arthropathy from repeated haemarthroses, not leukaemia.
questions.question: Clinical features common to all acute leukaemias include all of the following EXCEPT:
Which clinical feature of diabetes mellitus results directly from the presence of excess glucose in the urine causing osmotic diuresis?
questions.explanation: Polyuria (increased frequency and volume of urination) results directly from glycosuria — the presence of excess glucose in the urine. When blood glucose exceeds the renal threshold (approximately 180 mg/dL), glucose spills into the urine and creates an osmotic gradient that draws water into the renal tubules, increasing urine volume. This osmotic diuresis causes the characteristic frequent, large-volume urination seen in uncontrolled diabetes mellitus.
options: Polyphagia — increased hunger due to cellular glucose deprivation
Polyuria — increased frequency and volume of urination
Blurred vision — from lens swelling due to elevated blood sugar
Peripheral neuropathy — from nerve damage by hyperglycemia
Polydipsia — from cellular dehydration and osmotic pressure

questions.explanation: CHOP is a standard chemotherapy regimen for Non-Hodgkin lymphoma, comprising: Cyclophosphamide (alkylating agent), Hydroxydaunorubicin/doxorubicin (anthracycline), Oncovin/vincristine (vinca alkaloid), and Prednisone (corticosteroid). When combined with Rituximab (anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody), it becomes R-CHOP — the standard first-line treatment for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. Nurses administering CHOP must monitor for neutropenia, cardiotoxicity (doxorubicin), neuropathy (vincristine), and corticosteroid side effects.
questions.question: The CHOP regimen used in Non-Hodgkin lymphoma consists of:

questions.explanation: Dilated cardiomyopathy is characterised by ventricular chamber enlargement and weakened contractile function, leading to reduced ejection fraction and systolic heart failure. This differs from hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, which involves wall thickening rather than dilation. Recognising the pattern guides appropriate heart failure management.
options: A structurally normal heart with murmurs only
A rigid, non-compliant ventricular chamber only
An enlarged, poorly contracting left ventricle
A normal-sized heart with excellent function
questions.question: A nurse assessing a patient with dilated cardiomyopathy would expect to find which clinical feature?

questions.explanation: Chronic hypoxia drives excessive erythropoietin release, raising red cell mass and blood viscosity, which predisposes to venous and arterial thrombosis. Nurses should assess for calf tenderness, swelling, and chest pain suggestive of clot formation. Adequate hydration and mobility help reduce this risk.
options: Signs of bleeding from low platelet count
Signs of anaemia such as pallor
Signs of thrombosis such as calf swelling
questions.question: A nurse caring for a patient with polycythaemia secondary to chronic hypoxic lung disease should prioritise monitoring for:

questions.explanation: The nursing diagnosis of Activity Intolerance related to hypermetabolic state in hyperthyroidism requires the primary nursing intervention of scheduling planned rest periods and limiting unnecessary energy expenditure. The hypermetabolic state causes muscle weakness, fatigue, and cardiac stress, making energy conservation essential. Nursing interventions include providing a quiet, restful environment, clustering care activities to minimize disturbance, and gradually increasing activity as tolerated. This directly addresses the activity intolerance diagnosis, unlike pharmacological or educational interventions which address other diagnoses.
options: Administering methimazole as prescribed to reduce hormone levels
Providing a high-calorie, high-protein diet to meet metabolic needs
Scheduling planned rest periods and limiting energy expenditure
Educating the patient about radioactive iodine treatment options
Applying cool compresses to lower the patient's elevated temperature
questions.question: A nurse working with a patient with hyperthyroidism identifies the nursing diagnosis 'Activity Intolerance related to hypermetabolic state.' Which nursing intervention is most directly related to this diagnosis?
In GIT ageing changes, decreased peristalsis primarily results in:
questions.explanation: With advancing age, GIT motility decreases due to reduced smooth muscle tone and slower neural conduction in the enteric nervous system. Decreased peristalsis slows intestinal transit, allowing more water reabsorption from faecal content, resulting in constipation — one of the most common GIT complaints in elderly patients. Additionally, decreased physical activity, reduced fluid intake, and medications (opioids, anticholinergics, calcium channel blockers) compound constipation risk. Nursing interventions include dietary fibre, hydration, and prescribed laxatives.

questions.question: A nurse explains that the elements of emergency care include first aid, resuscitation procedures, and:
options: Ongoing observation and monitoring of the patient
questions.explanation: Comprehensive emergency care extends beyond initial first aid and resuscitation to include continuous observation and monitoring, allowing early detection of deterioration or response to treatment. This ongoing vigilance is essential because a patient's condition can change rapidly during the acute phase of illness or injury. Structured monitoring protocols support timely escalation of care when needed.

questions.question: The most common type of thyroid malignancy, papillary adenocarcinoma, is specifically associated with which feature?
options: It is most aggressive in young adults and childhood onset
It accounts for less than 10% of all thyroid malignancies
It begins in childhood, remains localized, and metastasizes
It exclusively occurs in elderly patients over 75 years old
It is treated primarily with chemotherapy not surgery
questions.explanation: Papillary adenocarcinoma is the most common type of thyroid cancer, accounting for more than half of thyroid malignancies. It characteristically starts in childhood or early adult life, initially remains localized within the thyroid, and eventually metastasizes — typically to regional lymph nodes. When papillary adenocarcinoma occurs in an elderly patient, it behaves more aggressively. Risk factors include female gender and a history of external irradiation of the head, neck, or chest in infancy and childhood.

After applying a tourniquet, the nurse palpates and inspects the vein. The ideal vein should feel firm, elastic, engorged, and round, not hard, flat, or bumpy. A hard vein may indicate thrombosis or sclerosis, making cannulation difficult. Because arteries lie close to veins in the antecubital fossa, the vessel should be palpated for arterial pulsation and cannulation of pulsating vessels should be avoided.
options: cool and slightly contracted to prevent excessive bleeding
hard, rigid, and slightly pulsating to indicate good blood flow
flat, non-pulsating, and thin-walled for easy penetration
soft, compressible, and broad for maximum fluid delivery
firm, elastic, engorged, and round without hardness or bumps
questions.question: When preparing to insert an IV cannula, the nurse palpates the vein. The ideal vein should feel:

options: Medication prescribing — determining appropriate drug regimen
Respiratory monitoring — assessing lung sounds and oxygen levels
Nutritional therapy — prescribing a specific calorie intake plan
Teaching: disease process — explaining pathophysiology of diabetes
Surgical assistance — assisting the surgeon with insulin pump placement
questions.question: A nurse using the NIC (Nursing Interventions Classification) system for a diabetic patient with Ineffective Self-Health Management would select which NIC activity?
questions.explanation: The NIC (Nursing Interventions Classification) intervention of 'Teaching: Disease Process' is directly appropriate for the nursing diagnosis of Ineffective Self-Health Management in a diabetic patient. This NIC activity involves providing information about the disease process, explaining how the disease affects the body, describing the signs and symptoms, and explaining the relationship between behaviors and disease management. This educational intervention directly targets the deficit in health management knowledge that underlies ineffective self-management of diabetes.

questions.question: Naturally acquired active immunity is obtained by:
questions.explanation: Naturally acquired active immunity is obtained after the individual experiences an attack by the disease and their immune system mounts a specific response. After recovery, memory cells remain that confer lasting protection against future attacks. This is in contrast to naturally acquired passive immunity (placental transfer of IgG) and artificially acquired active immunity (vaccination), which also produce protection without natural disease.
options: receiving killed inactivated vaccine before exposure
receiving vaccination with live attenuated organisms
receiving antibodies through the placenta from the mother
receiving antisera or immunoglobulins after exposure
recovering from an attack by a disease after natural infection
Permanent dilation and damage of bronchial walls
Acute inflammation of the pleural lining
Reversible narrowing of the upper airway
questions.question: A patient with bronchiectasis produces copious amounts of foul-smelling sputum daily. The nurse understands this condition results from:
questions.explanation: Bronchiectasis involves irreversible dilation and structural damage of the bronchial walls, often from recurrent infections, leading to impaired mucus clearance and chronic bacterial colonization. This results in the classic large volumes of purulent, foul-smelling sputum. Postural drainage and chest physiotherapy are key components of ongoing management.

questions.question: A nurse assessing a patient with suspected vitamin B12 deficiency due to strict veganism should anticipate which clinical finding?
questions.explanation: Vitamin B12 is found almost exclusively in animal products, so strict vegans are at particular risk of deficiency, which produces macrocytic anaemia and can also cause peripheral neuropathy and cognitive changes due to impaired myelin synthesis. Recognising this pattern differentiates it from iron deficiency, which produces microcytic anaemia. Dietary counselling or supplementation prevents progression of neurological damage.
options: Normal red cell indices with no symptoms

questions.explanation: Infiltration is the unintentional administration of a non-vesicant (non-irritating) solution or medication into surrounding tissue, which can occur when the IV cannula dislodges or perforates the wall of the vein. Infiltration is characterized by edema around the insertion site, leakage of IV fluid from the insertion site, discomfort and coolness in the area, and a significant decrease in flow rate. When the solution is particularly irritating, tissue sloughing may result.
questions.question: Infiltration during IV therapy occurs when:
options: air enters the vein and travels to the pulmonary circulation
a vesicant solution causes tissue necrosis at the IV site
bacteria enter the bloodstream through a contaminated IV line
a non-vesicant solution is unintentionally administered into surrounding tissue
blood leaks into surrounding tissue from the venipuncture site
Thyroid nodules by removing cells for cytopathological analysis
Pancreatic islet cells to quantify insulin-producing capacity
Parathyroid hormone levels through direct gland sampling
Adrenal cortex tissue for cortisol concentration testing
Pituitary gland tumors by trans-nasal needle approach
questions.explanation: Fine needle aspiration (FNA) is performed by inserting a thin needle into a thyroid nodule (or other endocrine mass) to remove cells for cytopathological examination. The cytopathologist spreads the aspirated cells on a slide and evaluates them for malignant or benign characteristics. This procedure is typically performed three to six times under ultrasound guidance to ensure representative sampling and is the primary method for evaluating thyroid nodules.
questions.question: Fine needle aspiration (FNA) is a diagnostic procedure used in endocrinology primarily to evaluate:

questions.explanation: Oral rehydration therapy (ORT) using low-osmolality ORS is indicated for mild to moderate dehydration from diarrhoea. It is administered as 500 mL orally over 2–3 hours, 3–4 times daily. Intravenous sodium chloride 0.9% (1 litre over 2–6 hours) is used for moderate-to-severe dehydration. Severe dehydration with haemodynamic compromise requires emergency intravenous fluid resuscitation regardless of the patient's age.
questions.question: Oral rehydration therapy (ORT) is specifically indicated for which severity of dehydration?
options: Severe dehydration with haemodynamic compromise and altered consciousness
Pre-emptive hydration before any diarrhoeal illness becomes clinically apparent
Mild to moderate dehydration from diarrhoea-related fluid losses
Dehydration complicated by metabolic alkalosis from concurrent vomiting
Any dehydration associated with an acute surgical abdominal emergency

questions.explanation: The body may not be able to adjust to increased insulin needs resulting from sudden physiologic stressors such as infection, injury, or surgery. These events create physiological stress that dramatically increases metabolic demands and glucose utilization, requiring higher insulin levels to maintain glycemic control. In diabetic patients particularly, this physiological challenge can precipitate hyperglycemia, diabetic ketoacidosis, or other metabolic crises, necessitating careful endocrine assessment.
options: Infections directly destroy all hormonal receptor binding sites
Surgery permanently alters pituitary gland secretory function
Viral infections always trigger autoimmune thyroid destruction
Physical trauma causes immediate adrenal gland hemorrhage
The body may not adjust to increased insulin needs from stress
questions.question: When a patient has a sudden severe physiologic change such as infection or surgery, the nurse assesses the endocrine system because:

options: Histamine release is completely absent overnight
Bronchodilator medications are most effective then
Airway smooth muscle relaxes fully during sleep
Mucus production ceases during nighttime hours
Cortisol levels are lowest and airway inflammation peaks
questions.explanation: Circadian variation causes cortisol levels to drop to their lowest point in the early morning hours, reducing the body's natural anti-inflammatory effect on the airways. This physiological dip contributes to increased airway inflammation and bronchoconstriction. Nocturnal and early morning symptoms are a key indicator of poorly controlled asthma.
questions.question: The nurse teaches a client with asthma that early morning symptoms are common because:

questions.explanation: The nursing diagnosis of Risk for Injury related to orthostatic hypotension requires direct fall-prevention interventions. Teaching the patient to change positions slowly (supine ? sitting ? standing, pausing between each), use call bell before attempting to stand, and call for assistance when ambulating directly addresses the mechanism of orthostatic hypotension. This behavioral modification reduces the risk of dizziness, falls, and injury. While medication and monitoring address the underlying condition, they do not directly prevent positional fall risk.
options: Administering fludrocortisone as prescribed to replace aldosterone
Monitoring serum sodium and potassium levels twice daily
Encouraging high-sodium diet to compensate for aldosterone deficit
Teaching the patient to rise slowly from lying to standing position
Maintaining IV access for emergency hydrocortisone administration
questions.question: A patient with Addison's disease has the nursing diagnosis 'Risk for Injury related to orthostatic hypotension.' Which nursing intervention addresses this diagnosis most directly?

questions.explanation: The combination of painless neck lymphadenopathy with B symptoms (evening fevers, drenching night sweats, weight loss) in a young adult is the classic presentation of lymphoma, particularly Hodgkin lymphoma, which has a bimodal age distribution with a peak in young adults aged 15–35 years. Urgent referral for lymph node biopsy, CT staging, and haematological consultation is required. While infectious causes must be excluded, the constellation of symptoms necessitates lymphoma workup as a priority.
questions.question: A 25-year-old presents with a neck lump, evening fevers, night sweats, and weight loss. These findings are most consistent with:
A patient with a chest tube connected to a water-seal drainage system shows continuous bubbling in the water-seal chamber. The nurse should suspect:
questions.explanation: Continuous bubbling in the water-seal chamber indicates air is continuously entering the system, suggesting an air leak either from the pleural space or a loose connection in the tubing. Intermittent bubbling with respiration, called tidaling, is a normal finding. The nurse should assess all connections and notify the physician if the source cannot be identified.
options: Normal fluctuation with the patient's breathing
Resolution of the pneumothorax is occurring
An air leak in the drainage system or pleura
The suction control chamber requires more water
The tube has become completely occluded

questions.question: According to WHO criteria, metabolic syndrome requires insulin resistance PLUS at least TWO of the following. Which option is INCORRECT?
options: BMI above 30 kg/m² or waist-hip ratio >0.9 (men)
Urinary albumin excretion rate above 20 µg/min
questions.explanation: The WHO criteria for metabolic syndrome require insulin resistance (defined as type 2 diabetes, impaired fasting glucose, or fasting glucose >110 mg/dL) PLUS at least two of: blood pressure >140/90 mmHg, plasma triglycerides >150 mg/dL, HDL-C <35 mg/dL (men) or <39 mg/dL (women), BMI >30 kg/m² or waist-hip ratio >0.9 (men)/0.85 (women), and urinary albumin excretion >20 µg/min. Elevated serum creatinine is a marker of renal impairment but is not included in the WHO metabolic syndrome diagnostic criteria.

options: Immediate return to full unrestricted eating
Isolation from family and support systems
Strict calorie counting without professional guidance
Gradual reintroduction of balanced meals with team support
questions.question: A nurse teaching a patient recovering from an eating disorder about nutritional rehabilitation should emphasise that recovery is best supported through:
questions.explanation: Nutritional rehabilitation in eating disorders requires a carefully paced, multidisciplinary approach that balances medical safety with psychological readiness. Overly rapid reintroduction of food risks refeeding syndrome, while isolation removes essential emotional support. Involving family, dietitians, and mental health professionals improves long-term recovery outcomes.

Concentrated sugars create a hyperosmolar load that draws fluid rapidly into the small intestine after gastric bypass, triggering the cramping, flushing, and hypotension characteristic of dumping syndrome. Patients are advised to favour protein and fibre-containing foods eaten slowly in small amounts. This dietary pattern reduces symptom frequency and severity.
questions.question: A nurse caring for a patient with dumping syndrome after gastric bypass surgery should advise avoiding:
A nurse teaching a patient with peptic ulcer disease about medication safety should specifically caution against long-term use of:
questions.explanation: NSAIDs and aspirin impair the protective mucus and bicarbonate barrier of the stomach by inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis, increasing the risk of ulcer recurrence and bleeding. Patients with a history of peptic ulcer disease should avoid these agents unless specifically directed with gastroprotection. This education reduces the risk of serious gastrointestinal bleeding.
options: Aspirin and other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
Left lateral position with knees flexed
Flat supine position with legs elevated
High Fowler's position with legs dependent
questions.question: A nurse caring for a patient with acute pulmonary oedema from heart failure should position the patient in which way to ease breathing?
questions.explanation: Sitting upright with legs dependent reduces venous return to the heart and lowers pulmonary capillary pressure, easing breathlessness in pulmonary oedema. This position also maximises lung expansion and improves oxygenation. Supine or head-down positions would worsen respiratory distress in this situation.

options: Complete absence of gastric acid production
Recurrent, severe peptic ulcers resistant to treatment
questions.question: A nurse caring for a patient with suspected Zollinger-Ellison syndrome would expect the patient to present with:
questions.explanation: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome results from a gastrin-secreting tumour that drives excessive gastric acid production, causing multiple, severe, and treatment-resistant peptic ulcers. Recognising this pattern in a patient with recurrent ulceration despite standard therapy prompts investigation for gastrinoma. Serum gastrin levels help confirm the diagnosis.

questions.question: A patient is scheduled for surgical removal of a pheochromocytoma. Why does the nurse anticipate that alpha-adrenergic blockers will be started preoperatively before any beta blockers?
questions.explanation: In pheochromocytoma, starting a beta blocker before adequate alpha blockade can result in unopposed alpha-adrenergic vasoconstriction, precipitating a dangerous hypertensive crisis, so alpha blockers are established first to control blood pressure before beta blockers are added to manage heart rate. This specific sequencing is a critical safety consideration in preoperative preparation for these patients. Reversing this order can have serious cardiovascular consequences.
options: Alpha blockade prevents unopposed alpha-adrenergic vasoconstriction and hypertensive crisis when beta blockers are added
Beta blockers must always be given first in every patient
Alpha blockers have no relevance to pheochromocytoma surgery
This order prevents excess aldosterone secretion specifically
Alpha blockers are given only to treat postoperative pain

questions.question: Which indication for tracheostomy is specifically related to preventing recurrent aspiration?
options: An upper airway obstruction from a laryngeal tumour
Prolonged mechanically assisted ventilation requiring a seal
Prevention of aspiration of oral secretions and vomitus
More efficient access to retained pulmonary secretions
Management of severe burns causing progressive airway oedema
questions.explanation: Tracheostomy is indicated specifically for the prevention of recurrent aspiration of oral secretions and vomitus in patients who cannot protect their airway (e.g., those with bulbar palsy, impaired consciousness). A cuffed tracheostomy tube provides a seal that prevents downward aspiration. Other indications include airway obstruction, prolonged ventilation, and secretion management.

options: Deep vein thrombosis from prolonged bed rest and immobility
Gastrointestinal bleeding from nasogastric tube irritation
Urinary tract infection from indwelling urinary catheter
Laryngeal oedema causing stridor or respiratory distress
Pressure sores developing from prolonged supine positioning
questions.question: After removal of an endotracheal tube, which complication should the nurse watch for most closely in the immediate post-extubation period?
questions.explanation: Laryngeal oedema is the most immediately life-threatening complication following extubation, which can manifest as stridor, hoarseness, or acute respiratory distress. It results from mechanical irritation of laryngeal structures by the tube. The patient should be closely observed in the immediate post-extubation period, and resuscitation equipment must remain available.

questions.question: A patient recovering from a stressful life event is taught that once the perceived threat resolves, the body should return to baseline through:
questions.explanation: Once a stressor is resolved, the hypothalamus normally initiates a return to homeostatic balance, reducing sympathetic activation and cortisol release. Failure of this regulatory return, as occurs in chronic stress, contributes to the wear and tear associated with prolonged stress exposure. Understanding this normal recovery process helps distinguish acute from chronic stress states.
options: Restoration of homeostatic balance by the hypothalamus
Permanent suppression of the immune system
Increase heart rate to improve perfusion
Lower blood glucose during the acute event
Relieve pain and reduce myocardial oxygen demand
questions.explanation: Pain and anxiety increase sympathetic activity, raising heart rate, blood pressure, and myocardial oxygen consumption, which can extend infarct size. Morphine relieves pain and reduces this sympathetic drive, easing the workload on already ischaemic myocardium. It does not act on the underlying thrombus.
questions.question: A nurse caring for a patient following acute myocardial infarction is administering the MONA protocol. The nurse should recognise that morphine is given primarily to:
Secondary hyperaldosteronism differs from primary hyperaldosteronism in that its cause is:
questions.explanation: Secondary hyperaldosteronism is caused by excessive activation of the Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS) from nonadrenal factors — meaning the adrenal gland is producing excess aldosterone in response to appropriate stimulation from elevated renin and angiotensin II levels. Causes include conditions that decrease effective circulating volume (heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome) or increase renin secretion (renal artery stenosis). This distinguishes it from primary hyperaldosteronism, where the adrenal gland autonomously overproduces aldosterone independent of RAAS.
options: Nonadrenal factors causing excessive activation of RAAS
An adrenocortical adenoma secreting excess aldosterone
Bilateral adrenal cortical hyperplasia producing aldosterone
Surgical removal of the pituitary causing elevated ACTH

questions.question: For H. pylori-associated gastritis, the nurse's priority patient education is:
options: Reinforcing the importance of completing the H. pylori eradication regimen
Explaining the need for lifetime acid suppression therapy
Instructing the patient to avoid all solid food for 4 weeks
Teaching the patient to monitor stools for blood indefinitely at home
Advising the patient to schedule repeat endoscopy in one week
questions.explanation: The most important patient education for H. pylori-associated gastritis is reinforcing the importance of completing the full antibiotic eradication regimen as prescribed. Non-compliance or early cessation leads to treatment failure, continued mucosal damage, and risk of antibiotic resistance. Patients should also be educated about dietary modifications, avoidance of NSAIDs and alcohol, and follow-up to confirm H. pylori eradication.

options: Half the internal diameter of the tube
The full internal diameter of the tube
Twice the internal diameter of the tube
One-quarter the internal diameter of the tube
Any size, as diameter does not matter
questions.explanation: Using a suction catheter with a diameter greater than half the internal diameter of the endotracheal tube can cause significant negative pressure and hypoxia by occluding the airway during suctioning. Selecting an appropriately sized catheter minimizes this risk while still effectively clearing secretions. This is a fundamental safety principle in airway suctioning.
questions.question: A nurse selects an appropriately sized suction catheter for an adult patient's endotracheal tube. The catheter diameter should not exceed:
A patient on cardiac monitoring develops a wide, bizarre QRS complex with no preceding P wave at a rate of 180 bpm. This rhythm is most consistent with:
questions.explanation: Ventricular tachycardia (VT) is characterised by three or more consecutive wide (>0.12 seconds), bizarre QRS complexes at a rate >100 bpm, typically without discernible P waves (as the impulse originates in the ventricle, below the AV node). Sustained VT may cause haemodynamic compromise (hypotension, syncope) and can degenerate to VF. Management depends on haemodynamic stability: unstable VT requires immediate synchronised cardioversion; stable VT may be treated pharmacologically with amiodarone or lignocaine.
options: Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response
Residual carbon dioxide gas used during the procedure
Nerve damage from the incision itself
questions.question: A nurse caring for a patient following laparoscopic cholecystectomy notes shoulder tip pain. The nurse explains that this is most likely due to:
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide insufflated into the abdominal cavity during laparoscopy can irritate the diaphragm and refer pain to the shoulder via the phrenic nerve pathway. This discomfort is usually self-limiting and resolves as the gas is gradually absorbed. Early mobilisation and simple analgesia help relieve this referred pain.

questions.question: The transcellular fluid compartment, the smallest division of the ECF, contains approximately how much fluid?
options: Approximately 1 liter at any given time
Approximately 3 liters including all plasma volume
Approximately 11 to 12 liters of interstitial fluid
Approximately 6 liters of total blood volume
Approximately 40 liters of total body water
questions.explanation: The transcellular space is the smallest division of the ECF compartment and contains approximately 1 L of fluid at any given time. Examples of transcellular fluid include cerebrospinal fluid, pericardial fluid, synovial fluid, intraocular fluid, and pleural fluid, as well as sweat and digestive secretions. Although small in volume, transcellular fluid is functionally significant and alterations in these spaces can have serious clinical consequences.

Acute gastritis management includes placing the patient on NPO to rest the mucosa, using antacids and histamine-2 receptor antagonists (H2 blockers such as famotidine or ranitidine) or proton pump inhibitors (omeprazole, lansoprazole), and IV fluids if oral intake is not tolerated. This supportive approach allows the gastric mucosa to repair itself. Endoscopy may be performed if symptoms are severe or persistent.
options: Immediate endoscopy and biopsy followed by surgical resection
Systemic corticosteroids to suppress the inflammatory response
NPO status, antacids, H2 blockers or PPIs, and IV fluids if needed
Broad-spectrum antibiotics for all cases regardless of causative agent
Total parenteral nutrition for 7 days before resuming oral intake
questions.question: The most appropriate initial medical management for acute gastritis involves:

questions.explanation: Erythropoietin is a hormone produced primarily by the kidney that stimulates the bone marrow to differentiate primitive myeloid stem cells into erythroblasts, increasing red blood cell production. It is released in response to hypoxia, such as occurs in anaemia or high-altitude exposure. This hormonal regulation ensures oxygen delivery is matched to tissue demand.
questions.question: The primary function of erythropoietin in haematopoiesis is to:
options: Stimulate RBC production in bone marrow
Promote WBC maturation in lymph nodes
Regulate plasma protein synthesis in liver
Mechanic and Volkart's illness behaviour theory
questions.explanation: Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome describes the body's three-stage response to prolonged stress: an alarm reaction, a resistance stage where the body attempts to cope, and an exhaustion stage where physiological reserves are depleted. This model explains how prolonged unmanaged stress can eventually manifest as physical illness, sometimes termed a disease of adaptation. Recognising the stage a patient is in guides appropriate intervention timing.
questions.question: A patient describes a gradual progression of symptoms following a major life stressor: initial alarm, followed by a period of coping, and eventual exhaustion with worsening health. This pattern is best explained by:
Haematological tumour markers that help monitor lymphoma treatment response include:
questions.explanation: Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and beta-2 microglobulin are the most clinically useful serum tumour markers in lymphoma: LDH reflects tumour cell turnover and burden (elevated in high-grade, disseminated disease); beta-2 microglobulin reflects tumour mass and renal handling of lymphoma-derived proteins. Both are incorporated into International Prognostic Index (IPI) scoring systems that predict outcomes in NHL. Serial monitoring during treatment provides objective measures of treatment response, complementing radiological reassessment.

questions.question: Which type of pneumonia occurs specifically due to entry of gastric contents or oral microorganisms into the lower airway?
questions.explanation: Aspiration pneumonia refers to pulmonary consequences resulting from entry of endogenous or exogenous substances (gastric contents, oral bacteria) into the lower airway. Causative agents include anaerobes, S. aureus, and gram-negative bacilli. It can occur in community or hospital settings and is particularly common in patients with impaired swallowing, reduced consciousness, or gastro-oesophageal reflux.
options: Aspiration pneumonia from anaerobes and gram-negative bacteria
Health care-associated pneumonia from multidrug-resistant organisms
Viral pneumonia from influenza A or B

questions.explanation: Antigens from infecting organisms are transported via lymphatic drainage to regional lymph nodes, where they are presented to lymphocytes, triggering activation and proliferation of a targeted specific immune response. This process is central to developing effective, antigen-specific immunity following infection or vaccination. Recognising this pathway helps explain lymph node swelling often observed during active infection.
questions.question: A nurse explains that the specific immune response begins when antigens from an infecting organism travel to:
options: Regional lymph nodes for immune cell activation
The bone marrow exclusively for storage

questions.question: The most common causes of anaphylaxis include insect stings, drugs, blood products, and:
questions.explanation: The most common causes of anaphylaxis are insect stings, drugs, blood products, and parenteral enzymes. These agents trigger IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation in sensitized individuals, releasing histamine and other mediators that produce the systemic anaphylactic reaction. Knowledge of common triggers enables nurses to take a thorough allergy history before administering parenteral medications, blood products, or enzyme preparations.

options: metabolic response to nutritional deficiency states
immune response to specific pathogenic organisms
universal physiological response to prolonged stress regardless of the stressor type
endocrine response to acute surgical trauma only
neurological response to traumatic brain injury
questions.question: The General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS) was described by Hans Selye as the body's:
questions.explanation: Hans Selye described the General Adaptation Syndrome (GAS) as the body's universal, non-specific physiological response to prolonged stress, regardless of the type of stressor. The GAS proceeds through three stages: alarm reaction, stage of resistance, and stage of exhaustion. Understanding GAS helps nurses recognize the physiological consequences of sustained stress and design appropriate nursing interventions to support adaptation.

questions.question: Septicemia as a complication of IV therapy is indicated by which set of signs and symptoms?
options: Swelling and coolness at the insertion site with decreased IV flow
Localized redness and warmth at the IV site without systemic manifestations
Abrupt temperature elevation, backache, headache, increased pulse and respiratory rate, chills
Air under the skin at the IV site with dyspnea and cyanosis
Bruising and immediate swelling at the venipuncture site
questions.explanation: Signs and symptoms of septicemia from IV therapy include abrupt temperature elevation shortly after the infusion is started, backache, headache, increased pulse and respiratory rate, nausea and vomiting, diarrhea, chills and shaking, and general malaise. In severe septicemia, vascular collapse and septic shock may occur. Causes include contamination of the IV product or a break in aseptic technique, especially in immunocompromised patients.

questions.question: A patient with restrictive lung disease from pulmonary fibrosis is expected to show which pattern on pulmonary function testing?
questions.explanation: Restrictive lung diseases like pulmonary fibrosis stiffen lung tissue, reducing overall lung volumes including total lung capacity, while airflow rates remain relatively preserved since the airways themselves are not obstructed. This pattern helps differentiate restrictive from obstructive disease on pulmonary function testing. Diffusion capacity is also typically reduced due to the thickened alveolar membrane.
options: Increased total lung capacity with reduced flow rates
Normal total lung capacity with reduced flow rates
Reduced total lung capacity with reduced flow rates equally
Reduced total lung capacity with normal flow rates
Increased residual volume with normal total capacity

questions.question: A patient with a suspected pancreatic neuroendocrine tumour undergoes a PET scan as part of their diagnostic workup. What is the primary advantage of this imaging modality in endocrinology?
questions.explanation: Positron emission tomography detects areas of high metabolic activity, which can help identify small tumours or metastatic disease that might not be visible on other imaging modalities, making it particularly useful in evaluating certain endocrine tumours. This functional imaging approach complements rather than replaces biochemical hormone testing. Its ability to detect metabolically active tissue is a key advantage in complex or metastatic endocrine tumour evaluation.
options: It measures blood glucose levels in real time
It replaces the need for any blood-based hormone testing
It is used only to assess thyroid nodules
It can detect metabolically active tumour tissue, including small or metastatic lesions
It directly measures cortisol secretion from tumours

questions.question: A patient reports chronic work stress and demonstrates elevated blood pressure and rapid heart rate during assessment. The nurse recognises these findings as being coordinated primarily by activation of the:
questions.explanation: The sympathetic nervous system mediates the fight-or-flight response, increasing heart rate, blood pressure, and respiratory rate to prepare the body for perceived threat. Chronic activation of this system contributes to sustained hypertension and cardiovascular strain. Recognising this physiological basis helps guide stress management interventions.

questions.question: The chronic management of asthma classified as 'mild persistent' includes which combination of medications?
options: Oral prednisolone 40–50 mg daily with long-acting beta-agonist
Inhaled salbutamol as needed plus inhaled corticosteroid
Intravenous aminophylline and systemic corticosteroids only
Long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA) combined with systemic steroids
Nebulised salbutamol 5 mg four times daily plus IV aminophylline
questions.explanation: Mild persistent asthma is managed with inhaled salbutamol (100–200 micrograms up to 4 times daily as needed) plus an inhaled corticosteroid such as beclomethasone dipropionate. This combination treats both the bronchoconstriction (salbutamol) and the underlying airway inflammation (inhaled steroid). Inhaled therapy is preferred over systemic therapy to minimize systemic side effects.

options: TSH receptor antibodies stimulate orbital fibroblasts producing glycosaminoglycans
Excess thyroid hormone directly stimulates orbital fat growth
Elevated TSH directly causes orbital inflammation and swelling
Chronic hyperthyroidism causes generalized fluid retention
Radioactive iodine treatment causes retroorbital radiation fibrosis
questions.question: Graves' disease causes exophthalmos through which pathophysiological mechanism?
questions.explanation: In Graves' disease, TSH receptor antibodies (TSHR-Ab) stimulate orbital fibroblasts to produce glycosaminoglycans (especially hyaluronic acid), which are hydrophilic molecules that attract water, causing tissue edema and expansion of the retroorbital space. This expansion pushes the eyeball forward (exophthalmos). Lymphocytic infiltration of the orbital tissues also contributes. The same antibodies that stimulate the thyroid also affect the orbit, explaining why eye disease correlates with (but can persist independently of) thyroid status.

options: Genetically engineered insulin is administered subcutaneously only
Genetically engineered insulin works faster than animal insulin
Genetically engineered insulin works more slowly than animal insulin
Genetically engineered insulin requires higher doses than animal
Genetically engineered insulin causes more allergic reactions
questions.explanation: Genetically engineered (recombinant DNA) insulin works faster than animal-derived insulin (porcine or bovine). Genetically engineered insulin is structurally identical to human insulin, whereas animal insulins differ slightly in their amino acid sequence, affecting absorption characteristics. The faster action of genetically engineered insulin provides more physiological glucose control and is generally preferred in clinical practice. Animal-derived insulins are now rarely used due to their slower pharmacokinetics and higher immunogenicity.
questions.question: Genetically engineered insulin differs from animal-derived insulin in which clinically important way?

questions.explanation: Obesity significantly increases the risk of type 2 diabetes (insulin resistance from adipokine dysregulation), hypertension (from increased cardiac output, RAAS activation), cardiovascular disease (from dyslipidaemia and atherosclerosis), obstructive sleep apnoea (from pharyngeal fat deposition), certain cancers, joint disease (osteoarthritis from mechanical loading), and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease. Osteoporosis (reduced bone density) is actually less common in obese individuals because increased mechanical loading stimulates bone formation and adipose tissue produces oestrogen protecting bone density.
questions.question: Obesity increases risk of all of the following EXCEPT:

questions.explanation: Live attenuated vaccines contain weakened but viable organisms that can cause serious infection in individuals with significantly impaired immune function, such as severe combined immunodeficiency. Inactivated, toxoid, subunit, and conjugate vaccines do not contain live organisms and are generally safer in immunocompromised patients. Careful screening before vaccination prevents serious adverse outcomes.
questions.question: A nurse reviewing a child's immunisation history notes a history of severe combined immunodeficiency. The nurse recognises this condition as a contraindication to which type of vaccine?

questions.explanation: Nurses must instruct patients receiving maintenance therapy with spironolactone about the possible side effects of gynecomastia (breast enlargement in males), impotence (erectile dysfunction in males), and menstrual disorders in females. These anti-androgenic side effects occur because spironolactone not only blocks mineralocorticoid receptors but also has anti-androgenic properties, blocking androgen receptors. Amiloride is an alternative for male patients who develop these intolerable side effects from spironolactone.
questions.question: Spironolactone, used in hyperaldosteronism treatment, may cause which specific side effect that nurses must teach patients about?
options: Thyroid enlargement and hypothyroidism with prolonged use
Severe hyperkalemia requiring immediate dose discontinuation
Adrenal suppression requiring stress dose supplementation
Gynecomastia, impotence, and menstrual disorders in patients
Hepatotoxicity requiring regular liver function monitoring

questions.question: Deep venous thrombosis (DVT) is most commonly associated with Virchow's triad, which includes:
questions.explanation: Virchow's triad describes the three conditions predisposing to venous thrombosis: venous stasis (slow blood flow from immobility, prolonged bed rest, heart failure), endothelial injury (vessel wall damage from surgery, trauma, IV catheters), and hypercoagulability (prothrombotic states: malignancy, pregnancy, OCP use, inherited thrombophilia). Understanding Virchow's triad guides nursing DVT prevention strategies: early ambulation, compression stockings, hydration, and pharmacological thromboprophylaxis in high-risk hospitalised patients.
options: Venous stasis, endothelial injury, and hypercoagulability
Platelet deficiency, vascular spasm, and fibrin dissolution

questions.explanation: Aplastic anaemia is characterised by bone marrow failure with a hypocellular (fatty, empty) marrow on biopsy and peripheral pancytopenia (anaemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia). This contrasts with leukaemia (hypercellular marrow with abnormal cells) and iron deficiency anaemia (normal or hypercellular marrow). Treatment options include bone marrow transplantation (curative for suitable candidates), immunosuppressive therapy (antithymocyte globulin, cyclosporin), and supportive care (transfusions, growth factors).
questions.question: Which of the following conditions results in pancytopenia with a hypocellular bone marrow biopsy?
A patient with a soft palate defect is most likely to experience problems in which pharyngeal region?
questions.explanation: The nasopharynx is located posterior to the nose and above the soft palate. A defect in the soft palate would compromise the separation between the nasopharynx and oropharynx, affecting air and food passage. This region also houses the pharyngeal tonsils (adenoids) on its roof.

questions.question: Which laboratory finding is most characteristic of iron deficiency anaemia?
questions.explanation: Iron deficiency anaemia produces microcytic (small) and hypochromic (pale) red blood cells, because insufficient iron limits haemoglobin synthesis, resulting in smaller and less haemoglobin-rich cells. This contrasts with vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, which produces macrocytic (large) cells due to impaired DNA synthesis. The peripheral blood smear and indices (low MCV, low MCH, low MCHC) confirm the diagnosis and guide treatment.

questions.question: Hospital-Acquired Pneumonia (HAP) is defined as the onset of pneumonia symptoms occurring:
questions.explanation: Hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP), also termed nosocomial pneumonia, is defined as the onset of pneumonia symptoms more than 48 hours after hospital admission in a patient with no evidence of infection at the time of admission. This timing differentiates it from community-acquired pneumonia (CAP). HAP accounts for 15% of hospital-acquired infections and is the leading cause of death among such infections.
options: Within the first 24 hours of a surgical procedure
In any patient receiving broad-spectrum antibiotics in the ICU
Within 6 hours of ventilator intubation in the emergency department
More than 48 hours after hospital admission with no prior infection
In immunocompromised patients regardless of admission timing
Urinary tract infections from aggressive forced diuresis
Dehydration causing increased viscosity of respiratory secretions
Hyperglycaemia from IV glucose-containing crystalloid solutions
Electrolyte imbalance causing postoperative cardiac arrhythmias
questions.question: Fluid regulation after thoracic surgery is carefully controlled primarily to prevent:
questions.explanation: Fluid administration after thoracic surgery must be carefully regulated to prevent fluid overload and pulmonary oedema, as the lungs are particularly vulnerable after thoracic procedures. Pulmonary oedema can significantly worsen respiratory function in a patient whose lung is already compromised. Fluid balance monitoring including intake, output, and weight is essential throughout the postoperative period.

questions.question: Nursing intervention for a patient with leukaemia and oral mucositis includes:
questions.explanation: Chemotherapy-induced mucositis requires meticulous but gentle oral care: rinsing with warm saline (0.9%) or sodium bicarbonate solution every 2–4 hours neutralises oral pH and reduces bacterial load. Soft toothbrushes are used (or sponge toothettes if bleeding risk is high), and alcohol-based commercial mouthwashes are strictly avoided as they cause drying and pain. Adequate pain management, nutritional support (liquid diet if swallowing is impaired), and antifungal prophylaxis (nystatin suspension) are also essential components of mucositis care.
options: Using a firm toothbrush for thorough cleaning
Rinsing with saline or sodium bicarbonate mouthwash
Eating hot, spicy foods to stimulate healing
Avoiding all oral hygiene to reduce trauma

questions.explanation: Constipation is defined as a clinical condition characterized by infrequent bowel opening (less than three times per week) and/or passage of hard stools, resulting in acute or chronic symptoms or disease that would be resolved with relief of the constipation. It is a symptom, not a disease itself, and may indicate underlying motility disorders, systemic conditions, or pharmacological causes.
options: Any decrease in the size or consistency of stools compared to baseline
Absence of any bowel movement for a period of 12 or more hours
The sensation of incomplete evacuation after defecation regardless of frequency
Infrequent bowel opening and/or passage of hard stools causing symptoms
Greater than two bowel movements per week in otherwise healthy adults
questions.question: Constipation is clinically defined as a change in bowel habit resulting in:

questions.explanation: Because flow is inversely proportional to the length of the IV tubing, adding extension tubing to an IV line will decrease the flow rate by increasing frictional resistance along the longer tubing. This principle has the practical implication that nurses should use only the length of tubing necessary for safe IV delivery and should consider the impact of tubing length when troubleshooting sluggish IV flow rates. Adjusting the IV height or clamp can compensate for some of this decreased flow.
options: IV flow rate is only affected by cannula gauge, not tubing length
Longer tubing increases IV flow by creating additional hydrostatic pressure
Extension tubing should always be added to improve IV flow
Tubing length has no clinically significant effect on IV flow rate
Adding extension tubing to an IV line will decrease the flow rate
