questions.explanation: Because polycythaemia vera increases blood viscosity and thrombotic risk, adequate hydration helps maintain blood flow while avoiding prolonged immobility reduces venous stasis. Iron supplementation would worsen red cell overproduction and is contraindicated. These measures form the foundation of self-management education.
options: Restrict fluid intake to reduce blood volume
Avoid all forms of physical movement
Increase red meat intake to raise haemoglobin further
Take iron supplements daily to boost energy
Maintain adequate hydration and avoid prolonged immobility
questions.question: A nurse is teaching a patient with newly diagnosed polycythaemia vera about self-care. Appropriate advice includes:

questions.explanation: Haemophilia C (Rosenthal disease) is caused by deficiency of factor XI and is very rare compared to haemophilia A and B. Unlike the X-linked haemophilias, it is inherited as an autosomal recessive trait and can affect both sexes. Clinical manifestations tend to be milder than haemophilia A and B, with haemarthrosis being uncommon. It is most prevalent in Ashkenazi Jewish populations. Diagnosis is by factor XI activity assay.
questions.question: Haemophilia C (Rosenthal disease) differs from haemophilia A and B in that it:
options: Is caused by factor XI deficiency and is very rare
Only affects females due to autosomal inheritance
Results in more severe haemarthrosis than type A

questions.explanation: Needle decompression for tension pneumothorax is traditionally performed at the second intercostal space, midclavicular line, just above the third rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle. This allows rapid release of trapped air and relief of mediastinal shift. A chest tube is subsequently placed for definitive management.
questions.question: A patient with a suspected pneumothorax undergoes needle decompression. The nurse anticipates the needle will be inserted at:
options: The fifth intercostal space at the anterior axillary line
The seventh intercostal space at the midaxillary line
The first intercostal space near the sternal border
The second intercostal space at the midclavicular line
The tenth intercostal space at the posterior axillary line
Tea with every meal for hydration
Calcium-rich dairy with every iron dose
Whole grain cereal with black coffee
Lean red meat with citrus fruit
questions.question: A nurse teaching a patient with iron deficiency anaemia about food sources should recommend which combination for optimal absorption?
questions.explanation: Haem iron from red meat is well absorbed, and pairing it with vitamin C-rich citrus fruit further enhances non-haem iron absorption. Tea, coffee, and calcium-rich foods taken simultaneously inhibit iron absorption through tannins and competitive binding. Educating patients on food pairing improves treatment outcomes.

The characteristic mucosal lesion in untreated celiac disease is villous atrophy (absence or marked flattening of intestinal villi) and crypt hyperplasia (lengthening of intestinal crypts). This dramatically reduces the absorptive surface area of the small intestine, leading to maldigestion and malabsorption. More intraepithelial lymphocytes also infiltrate the epithelium. These changes are reversible on a strict gluten-free diet.
options: Presence of excessive goblet cells and mucin hypersecretion
Submucosal fibrosis with obliteration of the lamina propria
Hypertrophied Brunner glands in the duodenal wall
Transmural inflammation and skip lesions throughout the small bowel
Absence of intestinal villi and lengthening of the intestinal crypts
questions.question: The mucosal lesion in untreated celiac disease is characterized by:
A nurse examining a patient's lower legs finds localised, thickened, non-pitting, waxy skin lesions. What condition is this finding, called pretibial myxedema, specifically associated with?
questions.explanation: Pretibial myxedema is a specific dermatological manifestation of Graves' disease, caused by localised deposition of glycosaminoglycans in the skin of the lower legs, resulting in thickened, non-pitting, waxy-appearing lesions. This finding, though named similarly to hypothyroid myxedema, actually occurs in the context of autoimmune hyperthyroid disease rather than hypothyroidism. Recognising this distinct skin manifestation supports accurate clinical correlation with the underlying thyroid autoimmune process.

Thalassaemia is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern, so if both partners carry the trait, each pregnancy carries a risk of major disease in the child. Partner screening allows informed reproductive decisions and early prenatal counselling. This is a key preventive nursing education point.
questions.question: A nurse is educating a patient with newly diagnosed thalassaemia trait about family planning. The most appropriate advice is that the patient's partner should:
options: Be screened for thalassaemia trait before conception

questions.question: A patient develops sudden widespread hives, difficulty breathing, and hypotension minutes after receiving an intravenous antibiotic. The nurse recognises this presentation as:
questions.explanation: Anaphylaxis is an immediate, severe, systemic hypersensitivity reaction characterised by rapid onset of urticaria, respiratory distress, and hypotension due to widespread mast cell degranulation and massive histamine release. This is a medical emergency requiring immediate intervention. Recognising these signs promptly allows life-saving treatment to begin without delay.

options: Hyperthyroidism due to acute release of stored thyroid hormone
Hypothyroidism as the condition progresses over time
Thyroid cancer due to chronic inflammatory cell stimulation
Thyroid storm precipitated by infections and surgical stress
Parathyroid damage from inflammatory spread to adjacent glands
questions.question: The nurse caring for a patient with Chronic Thyroiditis (Hashimoto's disease) should primarily monitor for the development of:
questions.explanation: Hashimoto's disease runs a slow, progressive course that leads eventually to hypothyroidism if untreated. The autoimmune destruction of thyroid follicles gradually reduces the gland's functional capacity. Initially, patients may be euthyroid or even transiently hyperthyroid (due to release of stored hormones from damaged follicles), but the eventual outcome of progressive follicular destruction is hypothyroidism. The goal of therapy is to prevent hypothyroidism and suppress TSH secretion.

Sodium restriction reduces fluid retention and helps control ascites in patients with cirrhosis, working alongside diuretic therapy. Protein is not eliminated entirely but may be moderately adjusted depending on hepatic encephalopathy risk, under specialist guidance. Dietary sodium control is a key, patient-friendly intervention in ascites management.
questions.question: A nurse caring for a patient with cirrhosis and ascites should recommend which dietary modification?
options: Complete restriction of all protein intake

questions.question: A patient develops complete heart block with a ventricular rate of 32 beats per minute and dizziness. The nurse's priority action is to:
questions.explanation: Complete heart block with a critically slow ventricular rate can cause inadequate cardiac output, syncope, and cardiac arrest. Temporary pacing restores an adequate heart rate until a permanent pacemaker can be placed. Beta-blockers would dangerously slow the heart further.
options: Reassure the patient and observe for one hour
Encourage ambulation to raise heart rate
Restrict fluids to reduce cardiac workload
pH is 7.38 and PaO2 is 96 mmHg
PaO2 is 98 mmHg with SpO2 of 99%
Bicarbonate is 24 mEq/L within normal range
There are changes from previous baseline values
questions.explanation: The nurse must monitor arterial blood gas values and notify the physician of changes from the patient's baseline or values outside the acceptable range. A change in ABG values may indicate worsening respiratory status, ventilator malfunction, or developing complications. ABG monitoring guides ventilator settings and medication adjustments in critically ill patients.
questions.question: When monitoring arterial blood gas results in an intubated patient, the nurse should notify the physician if:
Mastication (chewing) in the mouth is significant to digestion because it:
options: Begins protein digestion with salivary proteases
Breaks food into smaller pieces and exposes starch to salivary amylase
questions.explanation: Mastication breaks food into smaller pieces, increasing the total surface area exposed to digestive enzymes and facilitating swallowing. Critically, it mixes food with saliva, which contains salivary amylase (ptyalin) — an enzyme that begins carbohydrate (starch) digestion by hydrolyzing a-1,4 glycosidic bonds. Mastication also helps digest cellulose-containing foods (vegetables) that require mechanical disruption. Reduced masticatory efficiency (from poor dentition, poorly fitted dentures) impairs this first stage of digestion.

options: Inhibiting platelet aggregation to prevent clot formation
questions.question: A patient recovering from myocardial infarction asks why aspirin is continued indefinitely. The nurse explains that aspirin primarily works by:
questions.explanation: Aspirin irreversibly inhibits platelet cyclo-oxygenase, reducing thromboxane A2 production and platelet aggregation. This lowers the risk of new thrombus formation on ruptured atherosclerotic plaque. Long-term use is a cornerstone of secondary prevention after myocardial infarction.

options: Monitoring for respiratory depression from stimulant laxative effects
Checking renal function before administering any osmotic agent
Ensuring the patient is seated upright to prevent laxative aspiration
Assessing for signs of dehydration if the patient already has loose stools
Obtaining ECG monitoring continuously during stimulant laxative administration
questions.explanation: Before administering any laxative to an elderly patient, the nurse should assess for pre-existing dehydration or loose stools that would contraindicate laxative use. Elderly patients are particularly vulnerable to fluid and electrolyte imbalances from laxatives. The choice of laxative must also consider the patient's renal and hepatic function, concomitant medications, and the specific type of constipation mechanism involved.
questions.question: An important nursing consideration before administering a laxative to an elderly constipated patient is:

questions.explanation: A positive Chvostek's sign, in which tapping over the facial nerve produces twitching of the facial muscles, indicates increased neuromuscular irritability associated with hypocalcaemia, a recognised risk after thyroidectomy if the parathyroid glands have been affected. This clinical sign, alongside symptoms such as perioral tingling, prompts the nurse to check serum calcium levels and anticipate the need for calcium supplementation. Recognising this sign is an important part of postoperative thyroid surgery monitoring.
questions.question: A nurse performs Chvostek's sign testing on a post-thyroidectomy patient by tapping over the facial nerve near the ear. What does a positive result, characterised by facial muscle twitching, indicate?
options: Normal facial nerve function with no clinical concern
A sign of adequate calcium levels requiring no action
An unrelated finding requiring no further evaluation

questions.explanation: The zona fasciculata is the middle layer of the adrenal cortex and the largest of the three zones, comprising approximately 75% of the cortex. It is responsible for producing glucocorticoids, primarily cortisol. Cortisol affects glucose metabolism, suppresses inflammation, and regulates the stress response. The zona glomerulosa (outer layer) produces mineralocorticoids (aldosterone), while the zona reticularis (inner layer) produces adrenal androgens such as DHEA.
questions.question: The adrenal cortex is divided into three functional zones. Which zone produces glucocorticoids such as cortisol?
options: Zona glomerulosa, the outermost layer of the adrenal cortex
Zona reticularis, the innermost layer near adrenal medulla
The adrenal medulla, which produces steroid hormones
Zona fasciculata, the middle and largest zone of the cortex
Zona intermedia, located between the two outer cortex layers

questions.question: A nurse is caring for a patient with suspected acute pancreatitis and notes bruising around the umbilicus. The nurse recognises this finding, known as Cullen's sign, as an indicator of:
questions.explanation: Periumbilical ecchymosis reflects retroperitoneal bleeding tracking along tissue planes, seen in severe haemorrhagic pancreatitis. Its presence indicates significant disease severity and a higher risk of systemic complications. Prompt recognition should trigger escalation of monitoring and supportive care.
options: A minor superficial bruise unrelated to illness

questions.explanation: Bright red blood mixed with or coating stool typically originates from a lower gastrointestinal source such as the colon or rectum, where blood has minimal transit time to be altered by digestion. This contrasts with melena, which reflects digested blood from an upper source. This distinction helps direct diagnostic priorities such as colonoscopy.
questions.question: A nurse caring for a patient with suspected lower gastrointestinal bleeding notes bright red blood mixed with stool. The nurse understands this finding most likely indicates bleeding from:

questions.explanation: Hypernatraemia commonly results from inadequate fluid intake relative to losses, such as from fever, diarrhoea, or reduced thirst response in elderly or confused patients. Assessing recent intake and output history guides safe, gradual correction to avoid cerebral oedema from overly rapid fluid shifts. Neurological status must be monitored closely during correction.
options: The patient's shoe size for mobility aids

Provide frequent gentle saline mouth rinses
Restrict all oral fluids until healed
Apply firm scrubbing with a hard toothbrush
questions.explanation: Chemotherapy-induced mucositis causes painful oral ulceration that impairs nutrition if untreated. Frequent gentle saline rinses cleanse the mouth without further irritating fragile mucosa, promoting comfort and healing. Hot, spicy, or acidic foods and harsh brushing would worsen mucosal trauma.

questions.question: Gluconeogenesis is defined as:
options: Synthesis of new glucose from non-carbohydrate precursors
Breakdown of glycogen to release glucose
Conversion of glucose to glycogen for storage
Absorption of dietary glucose in the small intestine
Oxidation of glucose for ATP production
questions.explanation: Gluconeogenesis is the metabolic process of synthesising glucose from non-carbohydrate precursors including glycerol (from triglyceride breakdown), lactate and pyruvate (from anaerobic glycolysis), and glucogenic amino acids (from protein catabolism). It occurs primarily in the liver (and kidneys during prolonged fasting). Gluconeogenesis maintains blood glucose during fasting, prolonged exercise, or carbohydrate restriction, ensuring glucose supply to glucose-dependent tissues (brain, RBCs). This concept is essential in understanding the nutritional management of fasting patients.

H. pylori disrupts the gastric mucosal barrier through multiple mechanisms: urease produces ammonia (toxic to mucosal cells), bacterial proteases and lipases degrade the mucous layer, and the bacteria trigger a chronic inflammatory response (neutrophils, macrophages) that damages the epithelium. This allows gastric acid and pepsin to erode the mucosa, causing ulceration. H. pylori is found in approximately 90% of duodenal ulcers and 70–80% of gastric ulcers. Eradication (triple therapy) heals ulcers and prevents recurrence.
questions.question: Helicobacter pylori infection contributes to gastric ulceration primarily by:
options: Disrupting the gastric mucosal barrier and promoting inflammation
Causing autoimmune destruction of parietal cells
Directly producing hydrochloric acid in the stomach
Causing gastric motility disorders and stasis

questions.question: A nurse teaches a patient with newly diagnosed asthma to identify early warning signs of an exacerbation. The nurse emphasizes that the earliest indicator often is:
options: Sudden loss of consciousness during activity
A drop in peak expiratory flow readings
Complete absence of any wheezing sounds
Appearance of a widespread skin rash
questions.explanation: A decline in peak expiratory flow rate frequently precedes the onset of noticeable symptoms in an asthma exacerbation, making it a valuable early warning tool for patients to monitor at home. Recognizing this early change allows for prompt initiation of rescue treatment before symptoms become severe. This proactive approach helps prevent emergency department visits and hospitalizations.

questions.question: For women under chronic stress, the menstrual cycle may be affected by causing:
questions.explanation: For women, chronic stress can affect the menstrual cycle, leading to irregular, heavier, or more painful periods. Stress hormones interfere with the delicate hormonal balance that regulates the menstrual cycle, and chronic stress can also magnify the physical symptoms of menopause. These reproductive effects of stress highlight the importance of stress assessment in women's health nursing.
options: normalization of hormonal fluctuations in the menstrual cycle
premature menopause in all women under sustained stress
complete cessation of all reproductive hormone production
fertility enhancement due to increased hormone levels
irregular, heavier, or more painful periods

questions.question: A nurse notes bounding pulses, a widened pulse pressure, and a diastolic murmur in a patient. These findings are most consistent with:
questions.explanation: Aortic regurgitation allows blood to flow back into the left ventricle during diastole, producing a widened pulse pressure and characteristic bounding peripheral pulses. The diastolic murmur reflects this retrograde flow across the incompetent valve. Recognising this pattern distinguishes it from stenotic valve lesions with narrowed pulse pressure.

options: Only the patient's current occupation and hobbies
Onset and progression of symptoms, past medical history, family history, and medication history
Only the patient's favourite foods and exercise habits
Only the patient's marital status and number of children
Only the patient's height and weight measurements
questions.explanation: A comprehensive endocrine history typically explores the onset and progression of symptoms, relevant past medical and surgical history, family history of endocrine conditions given the hereditary nature of many of these disorders, and current medication use, since certain drugs can affect endocrine function or test results. This structured approach ensures a thorough assessment rather than focusing on isolated, less clinically relevant details. Covering these key areas supports accurate diagnosis and appropriate further investigation.
questions.question: A nurse conducting a comprehensive endocrine history explains that four key areas are typically explored. Which combination best reflects these key areas of endocrine history taking?

questions.explanation: Meeting resistance at the carina signals the catheter tip has reached the bifurcation of the trachea. Withdrawing slightly prevents mucosal trauma while still allowing effective suctioning. Forcing the catheter further risks bronchial injury and bleeding.
questions.question: A nurse is suctioning an unconscious adult patient and notes the catheter meets resistance at the level of the carina. Which action is most appropriate?
options: Withdraw the catheter slightly before applying suction
Advance the catheter further to clear secretions
Apply continuous suction while forcing the catheter
Instill saline and push the catheter deeper
Remove the catheter completely and restart the procedure
Directly neutralizing acids in the plaque layer on the tooth enamel surface
Delivering fluoride ions into the enamel through mechanical chewing action
Replacing bacterial biofilm with non-pathogenic flora on tooth surfaces
Stimulating salivary flow to wash away bacteria and neutralize bacterial acids
Increasing gum tissue blood flow to reduce existing gingivitis inflammation
questions.explanation: Chewing sugar-free gum stimulates salivary flow, which provides multiple protective benefits: washing away food debris and bacteria, neutralizing bacterial acids through buffering capacity, delivering calcium and phosphate to facilitate remineralization, and providing antimicrobial proteins. Increased salivation after meals reduces the duration of acid contact with tooth enamel, making it a useful and widely recommended adjunct for dental caries prevention.
questions.question: Chewing sugar-free gum benefits oral health primarily by:
Diffusion, as a form of passive transport, is best described as the movement of molecules:
questions.explanation: Diffusion is the movement of molecules of gases, liquids, or solids from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration until equilibrium is reached. The movement is caused by kinetic energy in molecules and does not require energy expenditure by the cell (passive transport). In the body, oxygen moves by diffusion from the lungs to the bloodstream, and carbon dioxide moves by diffusion from the bloodstream to the lungs for elimination.
options: driven by hydrostatic pressure from high-pressure to low-pressure areas
from a region of lower concentration to higher concentration using energy
through a semipermeable membrane from lower to higher water concentration
from a region of higher concentration to lower concentration until equilibrium
against the electrochemical gradient using carrier molecules and ATP

questions.question: Warm oral fluids such as tea or coffee are particularly recommended for post-thoracotomy patients because:
questions.explanation: Sips of warm fluids such as tea or coffee often facilitate coughing by stimulating the cough reflex and helping liquefy secretions, making them easier to expectorate. Patients are encouraged to breathe deeply, exhale, and then cough. Fluid intake also re-hydrates patients and supports progression toward normal oral feeding. Warm rather than cold fluids are consistently recommended.
options: They provide sufficient calories and electrolytes to restore metabolic balance
Warm fluids often facilitate coughing and help liquefy pulmonary secretions
They stimulate gastric acid secretion to resume normal digestive function
Warm fluids reduce opioid analgesic requirements in the postoperative period
They activate the parasympathetic nervous system to improve gut motility

questions.question: A nurse caring for a patient with suspected Prinzmetal (variant) angina notes chest pain occurring at rest, often at night, with transient ST elevation that resolves spontaneously. The nurse understands this is caused by:
questions.explanation: Variant angina results from transient spasm of a coronary artery, which can occur even in vessels without significant fixed atherosclerotic disease, typically at rest or during the night. The ECG changes resolve once the spasm relieves. Calcium channel blockers rather than typical antiplatelet-focused therapy are often used for this specific mechanism.

options: Continues at full volume even during prolonged fasting periods of 24 hours
Is always associated with bloody stools and elevated inflammatory markers
Stops after the patient fasts or ceases consuming the poorly absorbed solute
Responds exclusively to antimotility agents such as loperamide
Causes profuse watery stools with electrolyte losses similar to cholera
questions.explanation: A key distinguishing feature of osmotic diarrhoea is that it stops when the patient fasts or stops consuming the poorly absorbed solute (e.g., lactulose, mannitol, or unabsorbed lactose). This differentiates it from secretory diarrhoea, which persists despite fasting, as the secretory mechanism continues independently of oral intake. Osmotic diarrhoea is also characterized by a large stool osmotic gap in electrolyte analysis.
questions.question: Osmotic diarrhoea is characteristically distinguished from secretory diarrhoea because osmotic diarrhoea:

options: High-fat foods and red meats to allow intestinal rest
Water and oral rehydration salts to prevent osmotic diarrhoea
Caffeine, alcohol, dairy products, and fatty foods
All fruits and vegetables until symptoms completely resolve
Carbohydrates and starches that may ferment in the colon
questions.explanation: After acute diarrhoea, patients resuming oral intake should avoid caffeine, alcoholic beverages, dairy products, and fatty foods for several days. These substances can irritate the recovering intestinal mucosa, stimulate motility, or worsen osmotic diarrhoea. Gradual reintroduction of a normal diet is recommended, starting with easily digestible foods. Antidiarrheal medications may be taken as prescribed during recovery.
questions.question: Patients recovering from diarrhoea who resume oral intake should be advised to avoid which items for several days?

questions.explanation: Nurses play a vital role in haemophilia genetic counselling by providing education about X-linked recessive inheritance patterns, explaining the implications of carrier status for female relatives, discussing available genetic and haematological screening tests, and helping families understand the risk to future pregnancies. While specific genetic testing and procedures are ordered by haematologists and geneticists, nurses coordinate care, interpret results for patients, and provide emotional support for affected families.
options: Educating families about inheritance, carrier status, and screening
questions.question: The nurse's role in genetic counselling for haemophilia primarily involves:
Exercise-induced elevation of blood glucose in diabetics is explained by which mechanism?
questions.explanation: Certain types of heavy exercise — such as weightlifting, sprints, and competitive sports — cause the production of stress hormones including adrenaline (epinephrine). Adrenaline raises blood glucose levels by stimulating the liver to release stored glucose (glycogenolysis) and promoting gluconeogenesis. This counter-regulatory hormone response is a normal physiological mechanism to provide muscles with fuel during intense exertion, but in diabetics it can cause unexpected hyperglycemia after strenuous exercise.
options: Muscle contractions directly stimulate pancreatic glucagon release
Aerobic exercise increases insulin receptor sensitivity initially
Light exercise suppresses the counter-regulatory hormone response
Muscle glucose uptake during exercise depletes hepatic glycogen
Heavy exercise stimulates stress hormones like adrenaline raising glucose
The patient requires immediate reintubation now
The patient is likely ready for successful extubation
Ventilator settings must be increased significantly
The patient has developed a new pneumothorax
Sedation should be increased before further assessment
questions.explanation: The rapid shallow breathing index compares respiratory rate to tidal volume, with lower values indicating more efficient, sustainable breathing patterns. A low index suggests the patient can generate adequate tidal volumes without excessive respiratory rate, predicting successful weaning. Higher values suggest the patient may fatigue quickly if extubated.
questions.question: A nurse assessing readiness for extubation checks the patient's rapid shallow breathing index. A low value on this index indicates:

options: Hypertension always resolves completely after surgery
Unilateral adrenalectomy controls hypertension in only 80% of adenoma cases
Blood pressure monitoring detects hemorrhage not hypertension
Bilateral adrenalectomy always normalizes blood pressure
Postoperative hypotension is the primary concern after surgery
questions.explanation: Blood pressure must be monitored frequently before and after surgery for hyperaldosteronism because unilateral adrenalectomy is successful in controlling hypertension in only approximately 80% of patients with an adenoma. In the remaining 20%, hypertension persists postoperatively, requiring continued antihypertensive therapy. This incomplete resolution may reflect pre-existing essential hypertension, bilateral adrenal disease, or chronic renovascular changes from longstanding hypertension. Therefore, monitoring is essential to identify patients who need continued treatment.
questions.question: The nursing intervention of monitoring blood pressure before and after adrenalectomy for hyperaldosteronism is important because:

options: Air leaking into the surrounding soft tissue
Excess mucus accumulating beneath the skin
Infection spreading through the tracheal wall
Blood pooling in the subcutaneous layer
Cartilage collapse narrowing the stoma opening
questions.question: A patient with a tracheostomy tube develops subcutaneous emphysema around the stoma. The nurse understands this results from:
questions.explanation: Subcutaneous emphysema occurs when air escapes from the trachea into the surrounding soft tissue, often due to a false tract or ill-fitting tube. Palpation reveals a crackling sensation under the skin. This finding warrants prompt tube repositioning assessment and physician notification.

options: The test must be performed after an 8-hour fasting period
The patient must have consumed a glucose solution beforehand
The result must be confirmed by a second random glucose test
The patient has other symptoms of diabetes along with the result
The patient must be tested during acute physiological stress
questions.explanation: The Random Plasma Glucose Test measures blood glucose at any time of the day regardless of when the person last ate. A level of 200 mg/dL or higher indicates diabetes, especially if the person also has other symptoms of diabetes such as increased thirst, frequent urination, unexplained weight loss, or blurred vision. The requirement for accompanying symptoms distinguishes this single-test diagnosis from the confirmation approach used with fasting glucose tests, where two separate occasions are needed.
questions.question: The Random Plasma Glucose Test diagnoses diabetes when the result is =200 mg/dL with the specific requirement that:

questions.explanation: The response phase encompasses the immediate actions taken during and directly after a disaster to save lives, provide emergency care, and stabilise the situation, such as triage, rescue, and acute medical treatment. This differs from mitigation and preparedness, which occur before the event, and recovery, which follows afterward. Nurses play a critical frontline role during this phase.
questions.question: A nurse is coordinating immediate rescue, triage, and emergency medical care during an active flood disaster. This activity falls under which phase of disaster management?

questions.explanation: After extubation, patients should be maintained in high Fowler's position (head of bed elevated 60–90 degrees) to maximize chest expansion, reduce the work of breathing, and promote drainage of secretions. This position allows the diaphragm to descend fully and optimizes lung compliance. It also helps prevent aspiration.
questions.question: Following extubation, a patient should be maintained in which position to maximize chest expansion?
options: Trendelenburg position with the head tilted downward
Supine position with the arms elevated above the chest
High Fowler's position to promote lung expansion
Left lateral decubitus position with a pillow under the head
Prone position to improve posterior lung ventilation
Prevent further clot formation and propagation
Dissolve the existing clot immediately and completely
Increase platelet aggregation to seal vessel walls
Reduce inflammation within the lung parenchyma
Stimulate collateral circulation around the blockage
questions.explanation: Anticoagulant therapy works by preventing further clot formation and propagation, allowing the body's natural fibrinolytic system to gradually break down the existing embolus over time. It does not dissolve clots immediately, which is the role of thrombolytic therapy in select severe cases. Patient education on bleeding precautions is essential during anticoagulant treatment.
questions.question: A patient with a history of pulmonary embolism is started on anticoagulant therapy. The nurse understands the primary goal of this treatment is to:

options: Hypocoagulability and haemorrhage due to FDPs
Production of FDPs that enhance coagulation
Increased fibrinogen synthesis by the liver
Selective destruction of white blood cells
questions.question: The fibrinolysis phase of DIC is characterised by:
questions.explanation: During the fibrinolysis (haemorrhagic) phase of DIC, the complement and fibrinolytic systems are activated to break down the microthrombi formed in the first phase. This produces fibrin/fibrin degradation products (FDPs), which act as anticoagulants by interfering with platelet aggregation, fibrin polymerisation, and thrombin activity. The result is a period of hypocoagulability and uncontrolled haemorrhage that can manifest as oozing from venepuncture sites, petechiae, ecchymoses, and frank haemorrhage.

Bariatric surgery is typically indicated for patients with severe obesity, often with associated comorbidities, who have not achieved adequate weight loss through diet, exercise, and medical therapy. It carries surgical risks that must be weighed against expected benefit. Careful patient selection and pre-operative counselling improve outcomes.
options: Severe obesity unresponsive to lifestyle measures
Recent onset of a minor viral illness
Normal body weight seeking cosmetic change
Mild overweight status with no comorbidities
questions.question: A nurse caring for a patient with obesity being considered for bariatric surgery should recognise that this option is generally reserved for patients with:
A patient with an inhalation burn injury is closely monitored for airway compromise. The nurse understands early intubation may be indicated even without obvious distress because:
options: Airway edema can progress rapidly and unpredictably
Burn injuries never affect the upper airway
Delayed intubation is always the safer option
Steroids alone can reverse airway swelling quickly
Airway compromise only occurs after 48 hours
questions.explanation: Inhalation injury can cause progressive edema of the airway tissues that may not be apparent immediately but can rapidly obstruct the airway within hours. Early, prophylactic intubation is often performed in high-risk patients before swelling makes the procedure significantly more difficult or impossible. Close monitoring for hoarseness, stridor, and singed facial hair helps guide this decision.

questions.question: A postoperative patient is at risk for atelectasis. The nurse's priority intervention to prevent this complication is to:
options: Restrict fluid intake to reduce secretions
Maintain the patient in a flat supine position
Limit ambulation until the fourth postoperative day
Encourage frequent deep breathing and repositioning
Administer sedatives to reduce respiratory effort
questions.explanation: Frequent deep breathing exercises, incentive spirometry, and repositioning help reinflate alveoli and mobilize secretions, directly addressing the primary causes of postoperative atelectasis. Early ambulation further promotes lung expansion and secretion clearance. These simple, low-risk interventions are foundational to postoperative respiratory care.

options: Smooth and soft, without palpable nodules
Hard and irregular with multiple palpable masses
Completely absent and impossible to locate
Painful and pulsatile on light touch
Cystic and fluctuant with fluid movement
questions.explanation: A normal thyroid isthmus should feel smooth and soft without palpable nodules or irregularities, providing a baseline against which any abnormal findings, such as nodules or diffuse enlargement, can be compared. Recognising normal findings is just as important as identifying abnormalities, since it helps the nurse accurately detect deviations during future assessments. This baseline knowledge supports accurate longitudinal monitoring of thyroid examination findings.
questions.question: A nurse palpating a patient's thyroid gland from behind identifies the isthmus and describes its normal texture to a student. What should a normal isthmus feel like on palpation?

questions.explanation: The adrenal vein blood test (adrenal vein sampling) involves threading a catheter into each adrenal vein separately to obtain blood samples from the right and left adrenal glands. These samples are then tested for aldosterone levels. High aldosterone concentration on one side (with suppressed levels on the other side) signifies unilateral primary hyperaldosteronism, indicating a unilateral adenoma that is amenable to surgical cure by adrenalectomy. Bilateral elevation suggests bilateral hyperplasia, which is managed medically.
options: Total aldosterone concentration in peripheral blood samples
The ratio of aldosterone to renin in peripheral blood only
High aldosterone on one side indicating a unilateral adenoma
Bilateral suppression of aldosterone confirming bilateral hyperplasia
Elevated ACTH levels stimulating unilateral adrenal production
questions.question: The adrenal vein blood test for hyperaldosteronism distinguishes unilateral from bilateral disease based on:

options: Peripartum state (within last month of pregnancy or 5 months post-delivery)
questions.question: Causes of acquired cardiomyopathy include all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Acquired causes of cardiomyopathy include chronic alcohol abuse, COVID-19 myocarditis, cardiotoxic chemotherapy (anthracyclines such as doxorubicin), peripartum cardiomyopathy, viral myocarditis, metabolic disorders (thyroid disease, diabetes), haemochromatosis, and amyloidosis. A congenital bicuspid aortic valve is a structural cardiac abnormality that predisposes to aortic stenosis and regurgitation but is not itself a direct cause of cardiomyopathy. Cardiomyopathy may result from the pressure overload consequences of longstanding aortic valve disease.

Osler's nodes are painful, raised, erythematous lesions on the finger and toe pads resulting from immune complex deposition in infective endocarditis. They differ from painless Janeway lesions found on the palms and soles. Recognising these peripheral stigmata supports the clinical diagnosis alongside blood cultures and echocardiography.
questions.question: A nurse caring for a patient with infective endocarditis notes small, tender, red nodules on the pulp of the fingers. The nurse recognises these as:

questions.explanation: Normal erythropoiesis requires iron, vitamin B12, folic acid, pyridoxine (vitamin B6), protein, and other factors. Vitamin D is essential for calcium metabolism and bone health but is not a specific requirement for erythropoiesis. Deficiency of any of the true haematopoietic nutrients results in decreased RBC production and the development of various forms of anaemia.
questions.question: For normal red blood cell production, bone marrow requires all the following EXCEPT:

questions.explanation: A tearing quality of pain radiating to the back, combined with unequal blood pressure readings between limbs, is a classic presentation of aortic dissection rather than typical myocardial infarction. This distinction is critical because thrombolytics used for MI would be catastrophic in dissection. Urgent imaging confirms the diagnosis before treatment decisions.
questions.question: A patient develops sudden severe tearing chest pain radiating to the back, with a blood pressure difference between the two arms. The nurse should suspect:
A patient with pernicious anaemia is prescribed lifelong vitamin B12 injections rather than oral supplements because the underlying problem is:
questions.explanation: Pernicious anaemia results from autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells, eliminating intrinsic factor production. Without intrinsic factor, vitamin B12 cannot bind and be absorbed in the terminal ileum regardless of oral dose. Parenteral administration bypasses this absorption defect entirely.
options: Increased renal excretion of vitamin B12
Absence of intrinsic factor needed for absorption
Excess dietary intake of vitamin B12
Impaired liver storage of the vitamin

questions.explanation: Growth hormone, secreted by the anterior pituitary, and sex hormones (testosterone, estrogen) are the primary mediators of growth and development during adolescence. Growth hormone levels rise progressively during childhood and peak during the pubertal growth spurt. Sex hormones drive the development of secondary sexual characteristics and reproductive organ maturation, which together constitute the physical changes of puberty.
questions.question: The endocrine system's role in growth and development during adolescence is primarily mediated by:
options: Aldosterone and cortisol controlling mineral balance
Insulin and glucagon balancing energy in muscles
ADH and oxytocin stored in the posterior pituitary
Calcitonin and PTH regulating calcium absorption only
Growth hormone and sex hormones during puberty

questions.explanation: Stridor, laryngospasm, and perioral tingling (Chvostek's or Trousseau's sign positive) in a post-thyroidectomy patient are emergency signs of hypocalcemia resulting from inadvertent removal or devascularization of the parathyroid glands during thyroid surgery. Hypoparathyroidism causes dangerously low serum calcium, producing tetany, laryngospasm, and potentially fatal respiratory obstruction. Emergency treatment includes IV calcium gluconate. All post-thyroidectomy patients should be monitored for symptoms of hypocalcemia, and calcium gluconate must be available at the bedside.
options: Recurrent laryngeal nerve damage from surgical trauma
Hypocalcemia from parathyroid gland injury during surgery
Thyroid storm from residual thyroid tissue postoperatively
Hemorrhage causing tracheal compression at the incision site
Adverse reaction to the general anesthesia agents used
questions.question: A nurse caring for a post-thyroidectomy patient notes stridor, laryngeal spasm, and tingling around the mouth. The nurse should immediately suspect:

questions.explanation: Semi-Fowler positioning uses gravity to help the diaphragm descend and allows for better expansion of the unaffected lung tissue, easing the work of breathing. This position is generally more comfortable for patients experiencing respiratory distress. It does not stop air entry into the pleural space, which requires chest tube placement.
options: Prevent further air from entering the pleural space
Reduce cardiac workload during the acute episode
Eliminate the need for supplemental oxygen
Promote maximal lung expansion through gravity assistance
Facilitate insertion of a nasogastric tube
questions.question: A patient with a suspected pneumothorax is placed in a semi-Fowler position. The rationale for this positioning is to:
Bone pain, anaemia, hypercalcaemia, and elevated creatinine in an elderly patient most suggests:
questions.explanation: The constellation of bone pain (from lytic lesions), anaemia (from plasma cell marrow infiltration), hypercalcaemia (from osteoclast activation), and renal failure (from light chain deposition or hypercalcaemia) represents the classic CRAB criteria of multiple myeloma: hyperCalcaemia, Renal failure, Anaemia, Bone lesions. Serum and urine protein electrophoresis (monoclonal band), bone marrow biopsy (>10% plasma cells), and skeletal survey confirm the diagnosis. Nurses must monitor renal function and pain management.

questions.question: The definitive treatment for pheochromocytoma is which surgical procedure?
options: Transsphenoidal hypophysectomy removing the pituitary tumor
Bilateral adrenalectomy removing both adrenal glands entirely
Partial adrenalectomy preserving normal adrenal cortex tissue
Laparoscopic ablation of the medullary tumor using RFA
Surgical removal of the tumor usually with adrenalectomy
questions.explanation: The definitive treatment for pheochromocytoma is surgical removal of the tumor, usually performed with adrenalectomy (removal of the affected adrenal gland). Before surgery, patients require preoperative pharmacological preparation with alpha-adrenergic blockers (phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin) for 10-14 days or longer to control blood pressure and prevent intraoperative hypertensive crises from tumor manipulation. Calcium channel blockers or catecholamine synthesis inhibitors may also be used preoperatively.

questions.question: A nurse caring for a patient under chronic stress explains that persistently elevated blood glucose from stress hormones can eventually contribute to:
questions.explanation: Chronic stress-induced elevation of cortisol and other counter-regulatory hormones raises blood glucose over time, which can contribute to insulin resistance and increase the risk of developing or worsening type 2 diabetes. Recognising this metabolic link supports comprehensive stress management as part of diabetes prevention and control. Addressing lifestyle stressors is an important adjunct to standard diabetes education.

options: consult a pharmacist for appropriate stress-relieving medication
eliminate all stressors from their environment before addressing feelings
recognize the factors creating stress and feelings associated with the stress response
avoid all situations that could potentially generate a stress response
achieve complete emotional neutrality in response to all stressors
questions.question: When applying the adaptive coping strategy of awareness, the individual must first learn to:
questions.explanation: Awareness is the initial step in managing stress: becoming aware of the factors that create stress and the feelings associated with a stressful response. Stress can be controlled only when one recognizes that it is being experienced. This conscious recognition allows the individual to then evaluate whether to omit, avoid, or accept the stressor, and to choose an appropriate coping strategy. Without awareness, adaptive coping cannot begin.

options: Excess iodine directly enlarges the thyroid gland
Reduced iodine directly destroys thyroid follicular cells
Reduced iodine leads to low thyroid hormone, causing increased TSH stimulation and thyroid enlargement
Low iodine causes autoimmune destruction of the thyroid
Excess TSH from a pituitary tumour causes the goiter
questions.question: A patient with a goiter is found to live in an area with historically low dietary iodine intake. What is the underlying physiological mechanism causing the goiter in this context?
questions.explanation: When dietary iodine is insufficient, the thyroid cannot produce adequate thyroid hormone, leading to reduced negative feedback on the pituitary and a compensatory rise in TSH, which stimulates thyroid tissue growth in an attempt to increase hormone production, resulting in goiter formation. This mechanism explains why endemic goiter is linked to geographic areas with iodine-poor soil and diet. It differs from goiter caused by autoimmune processes or a primary pituitary tumour.

Prolonged activation of the stress response causes wear and tear on the body, both physically and emotionally, a concept described as allostatic load. While the acute stress response is protective, chronic activation depletes physiological reserves and damages organ systems. This accumulation of stress-related damage contributes to the development of cardiovascular disease, immune dysfunction, metabolic disorders, and mental health conditions.
questions.question: Prolonged activation of the stress response causes wear and tear on the body. This long-term effect of chronic stress is called:

questions.explanation: MRC Grade 3 describes a patient who walks slower than most people on level ground, stops after a mile or so, or stops after 15 minutes of walking at their own pace. This represents moderate functional limitation and indicates significant but not end-stage respiratory impairment. Accurate MRC grading is important for monitoring disease progression and response to treatment.
options: Grade 2 – hurrying on level or slight hills
Grade 3 – slower than others on level, stops after a mile
Grade 4 – stops after 100 yards on level ground
Grade 5 – too breathless to leave home
questions.question: On assessment, a patient reports breathlessness that provoked by walking on flat surfaces and relieved by rest. Using the MRC scale, this is most consistent with Grade:

questions.explanation: Perioperative nursing care for pheochromocytoma surgery requires meticulous monitoring of ECG changes (for arrhythmias), arterial pressures (for hypertensive crises during tumor manipulation or hypotension after removal), fluid and electrolyte balance, and blood glucose levels (for catecholamine-induced hyperglycemia during surgery or hypoglycemia after tumor removal). IV access is required for fluids and emergency medications. Intraoperative blood pressure swings are the greatest anesthetic and nursing challenge.
options: Serum thyroid hormones and TSH levels during surgery
ECG changes, arterial pressures, and blood glucose levels
Urine output only as a measure of catecholamine clearance
Serum cortisol and ACTH levels during adrenal manipulation
Pupillary responses reflecting adrenergic tone changes
questions.question: The perioperative nursing care for a patient undergoing surgery for pheochromocytoma requires specific monitoring of:
Chronic atrophic gastritis may prevent adequate absorption of which essential vitamin, potentially causing pernicious anaemia?
questions.explanation: Chronic atrophic gastritis leads to atrophy of gastric parietal cells, which reduces production of intrinsic factor—the protein essential for vitamin B12 absorption in the terminal ileum. Without adequate intrinsic factor, vitamin B12 is not absorbed regardless of dietary intake, leading to pernicious anaemia. This manifests as megaloblastic anaemia with neurological manifestations (subacute combined degeneration) if untreated.
options: Vitamin D from diminished sunlight exposure in hospitalised patients
Vitamin C from reduced dietary intake in patients with anorexia
Vitamin B12 due to reduced intrinsic factor from parietal cell atrophy
Vitamin K from disrupted gut flora in chronic antibiotic users
Vitamin A from fat malabsorption secondary to pancreatic insufficiency
Hypoparathyroidism causing low serum calcium levels
Hyperthyroidism or Cushing's disease as endocrine causes
Hypothyroidism causing generalized slow metabolism only
questions.question: Proximal muscle weakness found during the neuromuscular examination of an endocrine patient is most commonly associated with:
questions.explanation: Proximal muscle weakness — symmetrical weakness of the proximal upper or lower limbs — is described as common to hyperthyroidism and Cushing's disease. In hyperthyroidism, excess thyroid hormone causes muscle wasting and myopathy predominantly affecting proximal muscles. In Cushing's disease, excess cortisol produces steroid myopathy with preferential involvement of proximal limb girdle muscles. This finding helps direct the nurse to these specific endocrine disorders.

Thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger's disease) is an inflammatory occlusive vascular disease characteristically affecting young male heavy smokers (typically under 45 years), involving medium and small arteries and veins of the upper and lower extremities. It causes severe ischaemia, ulceration, and gangrene, particularly of the digits. The only effective treatment is complete smoking cessation, which can halt disease progression. This condition is distinct from atherosclerotic PAD and has a particularly strong tobacco dependence relationship.
questions.question: Thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger's disease) is characteristically associated with:
options: Older age, hypertension, and diabetes mellitus
Atherosclerotic plaque in large proximal arteries
Obesity and sedentary lifestyle in women
Heavy tobacco use in young men
Encouraging vigorous nose blowing to clear nasal passages
Restricting all fluid intake indefinitely after surgery
Delaying all neurological assessment until the following day
Removing the nasal packing immediately after surgery regardless of orders
Monitoring for signs of cerebrospinal fluid leakage and neurological changes
questions.explanation: Because transsphenoidal surgery involves access through the nasal cavity and sphenoid sinus close to the brain, the nurse must closely monitor for signs of cerebrospinal fluid leakage, such as clear nasal drainage, along with any neurological changes that could indicate a surgical complication. Patients are typically instructed to avoid vigorous nose blowing, which could disrupt the surgical site and increase leak risk. This vigilant postoperative monitoring is specific to the unique anatomical approach used in this type of pituitary surgery.
questions.question: A nurse caring for a patient with a pituitary tumour causing acromegaly is planning postoperative care following transsphenoidal surgery. What is the nursing priority in the immediate postoperative period?

questions.explanation: Since acromegaly commonly results from a growth hormone-secreting pituitary adenoma, imaging often reveals an enlarged sella turcica, the bony structure housing the pituitary gland, reflecting tumour growth within this space. This anatomical finding supports the clinical diagnosis alongside hormone level testing. It is unrelated to structures such as the thyroid isthmus or adrenal medulla.
questions.question: A patient with suspected acromegaly is scheduled for imaging to assess pituitary size. Which structure's enlargement would the nurse expect to help confirm the diagnosis?
options: The sella turcica housing the pituitary gland

questions.explanation: Music creates and stimulates motivation, enjoyment, and relaxation. It can reduce depression and bring about measurable changes in mood and general activity, reflecting its role as an accessible and non-invasive adaptive coping strategy. Music therapy has been incorporated into clinical nursing practice for pain management, anxiety reduction, and mood improvement across diverse patient populations.
options: permanently suppress the hypothalamic-adrenal axis response
stimulate motivation, enjoyment, and relaxation while reducing depression
replace all other adaptive coping strategies in chronic stress
cure anxiety disorders without requiring any other intervention
normalize cortisol and adrenaline levels in a single session
questions.question: Music's ability to 'soothe the savage beast' in stress management reflects its capacity to:
A nurse caring for a patient with a chest tube observes that the drainage has suddenly stopped completely. The priority nursing action is to:
questions.explanation: A sudden cessation of chest tube drainage may indicate the tube has become obstructed by a kink, clot, or dependent loop rather than resolution of the underlying condition. The nurse should systematically check the tubing for obstruction and reposition if needed. Chest tubes should never be clamped without a specific order due to risk of tension pneumothorax.
options: Increase the suction pressure setting immediately
Clamp the tube to prevent further complications
Assess for kinks or clots obstructing the tubing
Document the finding as resolution of the condition
Remove the tube since drainage has ceased

questions.question: The nurse assessing a post-thoracotomy dressing for subcutaneous emphysema identifies it when:
questions.explanation: Subcutaneous emphysema is identified by air leaking from the pleural space through the thoracotomy incision or around the chest tubes into the soft tissue of the chest wall or neck. It produces a characteristic crackling sensation (crepitus) on palpation. Blood on the dressing must also be reported to the surgeon immediately, with time and amount recorded. Both findings indicate complications requiring prompt management.
options: The wound site shows signs of erythema and purulent discharge
Air leaks from the pleural space through the incision into soft tissue
The chest drain output suddenly increases to more than 200 mL per hour
The patient complains of sharp pleuritic chest pain on inspiration
Auscultation reveals absent breath sounds over the operative site

questions.question: A nurse caring for a patient with severe neutropenia after chemotherapy should recognise that the classic signs of infection may be:
questions.explanation: With very low neutrophil counts, the inflammatory response that produces classic signs such as pus and marked erythema is diminished. Fever, therefore, becomes the most reliable and often earliest indicator of serious infection in this population. Any fever in a neutropenic patient warrants urgent evaluation.
options: Delayed by several weeks after exposure
Absent entirely regardless of infection severity
Blunted, with fever as the primary indicator
Unchanged from a normally immune patient
Adsorb bacterial toxins and prevent their systemic absorption
Stimulate mu opioid receptors to reduce intestinal motility
Replace normal bacterial flora lost during oral antibiotic administration
Block prostaglandin synthesis and reduce inflammatory secretion
Directly kill pathogenic organisms through bacteriocin production
questions.question: Lactobacillus acidophilus preparations in antidiarrhoeal therapy are specifically intended to:
questions.explanation: Lactobacillus acidophilus products contain non-toxic probiotic bacterial strains intended to replace and restore the normal gut flora disrupted during oral antibiotic therapy. Antibiotics kill commensal bacteria along with pathogens, creating an ecological vacuum colonized by pathogens like C. difficile. Restoring normal flora through probiotics helps prevent antibiotic-associated diarrhoea and supports gut microbiome recovery.

Raynaud's disease is characterised by episodic vasospasm of digital arteries and arterioles, triggered by cold exposure or emotional stress. The classic triphasic colour change: white (pallor from vasospasm and blood expulsion), blue (cyanosis from deoxygenated stagnant blood), then red (hyperaemia on rewarming). Primary Raynaud's (Raynaud's disease) occurs in the absence of underlying disease; secondary Raynaud's (Raynaud's phenomenon) is associated with connective tissue diseases (systemic sclerosis, SLE). Nursing management includes warming measures and stress reduction.
options: Cold exposure or emotional stress causing vasospasm
questions.question: Raynaud's disease manifests as episodic colour changes in the digits triggered by:

questions.explanation: Unintentional weight loss and reduced dietary intake are key indicators used in validated nutritional screening tools to identify patients at risk of malnutrition. Combining this history with clinical examination and laboratory markers provides a comprehensive picture of nutritional status. Early identification allows timely intervention to prevent complications.
questions.question: A nurse assessing a hospitalised patient for malnutrition risk should include which of the following in a comprehensive nutritional assessment?
options: Recent unintentional weight loss and dietary intake history
The patient's shoe size and clothing preference

questions.question: Dextrose 5% in water is classified as which type of intravenous solution?
options: Colloid solution used to expand the intravascular compartment
Hypertonic solution used to treat severe hypernatremia
Isotonic solution that becomes effectively hypotonic after dextrose is metabolized
Isotonic solution that maintains intravascular volume permanently
Hypotonic solution that causes immediate cell swelling
questions.explanation: Dextrose 5% in water (D5W) is initially isotonic (similar osmolarity to plasma) when infused, but after the dextrose is rapidly metabolized, it effectively becomes free water, behaving as a hypotonic solution. This means it distributes across all body compartments rather than remaining in the intravascular space. D5W is used for hydration and as a vehicle for medication administration but should not be used for volume resuscitation as it does not maintain intravascular volume.

questions.question: A nurse teaches a patient with diabetes about foot care and emphasises daily inspection using a mirror if needed to see the soles of the feet. What is the primary rationale for this specific instruction?
options: This instruction is only relevant for patients with visual impairment
Peripheral neuropathy may prevent the patient from feeling injuries on the soles, so visual inspection is essential
Daily foot inspection has no relationship to diabetes complications
Mirror use is recommended only for cosmetic foot care purposes
This instruction applies only to patients who have already had an amputation
questions.explanation: Because diabetic peripheral neuropathy can significantly reduce sensation, particularly on the soles of the feet where injuries are hardest to see directly, using a mirror for daily visual inspection helps the patient detect early skin breakdown, cuts, or areas of pressure before they progress to serious complications such as ulceration. This practical technique addresses the specific sensory limitation caused by neuropathy. It is a proactive self-care strategy rather than being limited to patients with pre-existing amputation or additional visual impairment.

At high altitudes, reduced atmospheric oxygen tension causes tissue hypoxia, which the kidneys detect and respond to by increasing erythropoietin release. This stimulates the bone marrow to produce more red blood cells, resulting in erythrocytosis (polycythaemia). The increased RBC mass enhances oxygen-carrying capacity, compensating for the lower partial pressure of oxygen. This is also the physiological principle behind blood doping in athletes.
questions.question: During periods of high-altitude residence, the body compensates by:
Lobar pneumonia caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae is most commonly characterized by the presenting symptom of:
options: Gradual onset over several weeks with productive cough
Dry non-productive cough with mild malaise and normal temperature
Rapidly rising fever, pleuritic chest pain, and purulent sputum
Bilateral wheezing with accessory muscle use and air trapping
Haemoptysis alone without fever or respiratory distress
questions.explanation: Pneumonia, particularly lobar pneumonia from Streptococcus pneumoniae, classically presents with rapidly rising fever, pleuritic chest pain, rapidly bounding pulse (tachycardia), tachypnoea, purulent sputum, and fatigue. This acute presentation helps distinguish pneumonia from chronic conditions. Haemoptysis may also occur but is not the primary presenting feature.

Disaster preparedness consists of a set of measures undertaken in advance by governments, organizations, communities, or individuals to better respond and cope with the aftermath of a disaster, whether human-induced or natural. In nursing, this involves developing and maintaining the skills, knowledge, and resources necessary to provide swift and competent healthcare services in the face of disasters. Preparedness is proactive rather than reactive.
options: emergency response actions taken only after a disaster has already occurred
a set of measures undertaken in advance to better respond to and cope with disasters
the reconstruction of infrastructure destroyed by natural disasters
the distribution of food and water to affected populations after disasters
the provision of medical care to disaster survivors in hospital settings
questions.question: Disaster preparedness is best described as:

questions.explanation: Tumour lysis syndrome releases intracellular potassium, phosphate, and nucleic acids as malignant cells die rapidly, with phosphate binding calcium to cause hypocalcaemia. Perioral tingling, cramps, and a positive Chvostek sign are classic hypocalcaemic signs. Early recognition allows prompt correction and renal protection to prevent arrhythmia.
options: Normal side effect requiring no action
Simple dehydration from poor oral intake
Anxiety related to the new diagnosis
questions.question: A patient undergoing induction chemotherapy for acute lymphoblastic leukaemia develops muscle cramps, tingling around the mouth, and a positive Chvostek sign shortly after treatment begins. The nurse should suspect:
Pneumonia is most accurately defined as:
options: Inflammation of the lung parenchyma from various microorganisms
Chronic hyperinflation of alveoli from long-term smoking
Accumulation of serous fluid in the pleural space bilaterally
Fibrotic replacement of pulmonary tissue in immune disorders
Collapse of alveoli due to loss of surfactant production
questions.explanation: Pneumonia is an inflammation of the lung parenchyma caused by various microorganisms including bacteria, mycobacteria, fungi, and viruses. It is described as lung parenchyma/alveolar inflammation with abnormal alveolar filling with fluid (consolidation and exudation). It remains one of the most common and serious respiratory conditions globally.

questions.question: Passive arm exercises are initiated in post-thoracotomy patients as early as the evening of surgery to:
options: Prevent deep vein thrombosis in the lower extremities postoperatively
Improve cardiac output by activating the upper extremity muscle pump
Reduce opioid analgesic requirements through exercise-related distraction
Prevent restriction of function of the arm on the surgical side
Maintain muscle mass that was lost during the preoperative fasting period
questions.explanation: Passive arm exercises are initiated as early as the evening of surgery to pull the patient's arm through range of motion, preventing restriction of function of the arm and shoulder on the operative side. Thoracotomy incisions can cause adhesions and muscle tightening that limit shoulder mobility if not addressed early. Early range-of-motion exercises are a key component of post-thoracotomy functional rehabilitation.

options: Increases urinary excretion of excess iron
Prevents nausea associated with iron tablets
Enhances absorption of non-haem iron in the gut
Reduces the risk of constipation from iron
Neutralises stomach acid to protect the mucosa
questions.question: A nurse teaches a patient newly diagnosed with iron deficiency anaemia to take oral iron with a source of vitamin C. The rationale is that vitamin C:
questions.explanation: Ascorbic acid reduces ferric iron to the more absorbable ferrous form and forms a soluble complex with it in the duodenum. This significantly improves non-haem iron uptake from supplements and diet. Taking iron with citrus juice therefore maximises therapeutic response.

questions.question: A patient's spirometry results show a reduced FVC with a normal or increased FEV1/FVC ratio. The nurse understands this pattern is consistent with:
questions.explanation: Restrictive lung diseases, such as pulmonary fibrosis, reduce total lung capacity and forced vital capacity while preserving or increasing the FEV1/FVC ratio, since expiratory flow itself is not obstructed. This contrasts with obstructive diseases, where the ratio is reduced due to impaired airflow. Distinguishing these patterns guides diagnosis and treatment planning.
options: Obstructive lung disease limiting expiratory flow
Normal pulmonary function within expected range
Pulmonary embolism affecting gas exchange only
Upper airway obstruction from foreign body
Restrictive lung disease limiting total lung volume

questions.explanation: Tyramine — found in aged cheeses, cured meats, fermented foods, and red wine — triggers catecholamine release from adrenergic nerve terminals. In a patient with pheochromocytoma, where catecholamine levels are already dangerously elevated, tyramine ingestion can precipitate a severe hypertensive crisis through additional catecholamine release. A low-tyramine diet is therefore a specific dietary nursing intervention for pheochromocytoma patients, particularly preoperatively when the tumor is still in place. This same restriction applies to patients on MAO inhibitors.
options: Hypoglycemia from glucagon suppression by dietary tyramine
Hyperaldosteronism from tyramine stimulating adrenal cortex
Hypothyroidism from tyramine blocking thyroid hormone synthesis
Adrenal crisis from tyramine competing with cortisol metabolism
Hypertensive crisis from catecholamine release triggered by tyramine
questions.question: The nursing intervention of providing a diet low in tyramine for a patient with pheochromocytoma is specifically indicated to prevent:

questions.explanation: Negative feedback mechanisms, in which rising hormone levels inhibit further secretion, are more prevalent in the endocrine system because they help maintain hormone concentrations within a relatively narrow, stable range necessary for normal physiological function, supporting overall homeostasis. Positive feedback, in contrast, is reserved for specific situations requiring an escalating response, such as the surge of oxytocin during labour, and is comparatively rare. Understanding this predominance helps explain the general stability of most hormone systems under normal conditions.
questions.question: A nurse explains negative feedback as the more prevalent regulatory mechanism in the endocrine system compared to positive feedback. What is the primary reason negative feedback predominates?
options: It allows hormone levels to increase without any limit
It is used only during rare emergency situations
It helps maintain hormone levels within a stable, controlled range, supporting homeostasis
It has no relationship to maintaining stable hormone levels
Positive feedback is actually more common in the endocrine system

questions.explanation: Vibrio cholerae produces cholera toxin that strongly activates adenylyl cyclase, causing a prolonged increase in intracellular cyclic AMP (cAMP) in crypt enterocytes. Elevated cAMP causes prolonged opening of chloride channels, leading to uncontrolled secretion of water and electrolytes into the intestinal lumen. This produces the massive secretory diarrhoea of cholera, which can be lethal without aggressive fluid and electrolyte replacement.
options: Invading the intestinal epithelium and causing direct cellular destruction
Inducing inflammatory mediator release causing prostaglandin-driven secretion
Blocking electrolyte absorption by destroying brush border enzymes directly
Producing toxin that strongly activates adenylyl cyclase, raising intracellular cyclic AMP
Stimulating the vagal nerve to increase intestinal peristaltic activity
questions.question: Vibrio cholerae causes massive secretory diarrhoea through which specific mechanism?
A nurse caring for a patient recovering from acute pericarditis should teach the patient that returning symptoms of sharp chest pain relieved by sitting forward may indicate:
questions.explanation: Pericarditis can recur even after apparent resolution, and the return of characteristic positional chest pain should prompt reassessment. Early recognition of recurrence allows timely anti-inflammatory treatment and reduces the risk of complications such as pericardial effusion. Patient education on warning signs supports early self-reporting.

questions.question: Leukaemia infiltration of the central nervous system (CNS) is most common in which subtype?
questions.explanation: CNS involvement is most common in ALL, particularly in children, where leukaemic blasts infiltrate the meninges and brain parenchyma. This can cause headache, vomiting, papilloedema, and cranial nerve palsies. Prophylactic CNS-directed therapy (intrathecal methotrexate ± cranial irradiation) is a standard component of ALL treatment protocols because the blood-brain barrier limits systemic drug penetration. Nurses must assess for neurological changes in ALL patients and ensure proper administration of intrathecal medications.

options: peripheral edema without any systemic hemodynamic change
urticaria, angioedema, and decreased plasma volume leading to shock
local inflammatory reaction without systemic manifestations
questions.explanation: In anaphylaxis, vasodilation and escape of plasma into tissues (due to histamine and other mediators increasing vascular permeability) causes urticaria and angioedema, as well as a decrease in plasma volume, leading to shock. The escape of fluid from the alveoli causes pulmonary edema and angioedema. A prolonged reaction can produce cardiac arrhythmias and cardiogenic shock, making rapid intervention essential.
questions.question: The pathophysiology of anaphylaxis includes vasodilation and escape of plasma into tissues, which causes:

options: Oedema worsened by elevation of the limb
Intermittent claudication — calf pain on walking, relieved by rest
Constant burning pain in the feet at rest only
Heaviness and aching worsened at the end of the day
Nocturnal cramps of the calf relieved by walking
questions.explanation: Intermittent claudication is the hallmark symptom of peripheral arterial disease (PAD): reproducible calf, thigh, or buttock pain (depending on the level of arterial occlusion) that is consistently precipitated by a predictable amount of walking and relieved by a few minutes of rest. It results from inadequate arterial blood supply to exercising muscles. In severe PAD, rest pain (persistent ischaemic pain at rest), non-healing ulcers, and gangrene develop. The ankle-brachial index (ABI) is the diagnostic test of choice.
questions.question: Peripheral arterial disease (PAD) is characterised by which classic symptom?

options: Directly causes all forms of cancer immediately
Only affects mental health, not physical health
Contributes to conditions such as heart disease and stroke
Has no connection to any major disease
questions.explanation: Chronic stress contributes to the development and progression of several leading causes of death, including cardiovascular disease and stroke, through sustained physiological effects such as hypertension, inflammation, and immune suppression. Recognising this link underscores the importance of stress management as part of holistic disease prevention. Patient education should connect stress reduction to broader long-term health outcomes.
questions.question: A nurse explains to a patient that stress has been linked to several leading causes of death, largely because chronic stress:

questions.explanation: Haemophilia B, also known as Christmas disease (named after the first patient described, Stephen Christmas, in 1952), is caused by deficiency of factor IX (plasma thromboplastin component). Factor IX is essential in the intrinsic coagulation pathway, and its deficiency clinically resembles haemophilia A but is about seven times less common. Treatment involves infusion of factor IX concentrates or recombinant factor IX products.
questions.question: Haemophilia B (Christmas disease) is characterised by deficiency of:

options: The hilar region where bronchi enter the lungs
The pleural space between visceral and parietal pleura
The mediastinum adjacent to the superior vena cava
The carina where the trachea divides into two bronchi
The subcarinal region below the diaphragm
questions.explanation: Lymph from the respiratory passages passes through lymph nodes situated around the trachea and in the carina—the region where the trachea divides into the two main bronchi. Enlargement of these lymph nodes (as seen in tuberculosis or malignancy) can cause tracheal deviation or airway compression. This is clinically detectable on chest X-ray and CT scan.
questions.question: Lymph from the respiratory passages drains through lymph nodes situated around the trachea and at:
A nurse explains that dextrose 5% in water, once metabolised, is classified physiologically as:
options: A colloid solution with large molecules
A solution with no fluid shift effect ever
An isotonic solution that becomes hypotonic
questions.explanation: Dextrose 5% in water is initially isotonic in the bag, but once the dextrose is metabolised, the remaining free water behaves as a hypotonic solution, distributing into both intracellular and extracellular compartments. This property makes it useful for providing free water but unsuitable as a sole resuscitation fluid in hypovolaemia. Understanding this behaviour guides appropriate clinical use.

options: stress directly destroys the gastric mucosa causing ulceration
stress is the sole cause of all peptic ulcers in stressed individuals
H. pylori is a complication of stress rather than a cause of ulcers
stress increases risk of existing ulcers acting up, while H. pylori typically causes ulcers
stress and H. pylori have no relationship to ulcer formation
questions.explanation: Stress does not directly cause ulcers (a bacterium called H. pylori often does), but it can increase the risk of causing existing ulcers to act up by increasing gastric acid secretion and compromising mucosal defense mechanisms. Chronic stress impairs the gastric mucosal barrier, making the stomach lining more vulnerable to acid-induced injury. Nurses must assess both H. pylori infection and chronic stress in patients with peptic ulcer disease.
questions.question: The relationship between stress and ulcer formation is best described as:

questions.explanation: A respiratory rate of 8 with shallow breathing following opioid administration indicates significant respiratory depression requiring immediate intervention. The nurse should attempt to stimulate and arouse the patient while preparing naloxone, an opioid antagonist, in case reversal becomes necessary. Continuous monitoring of respiratory status is essential after any opioid dose, particularly in opioid-naive patients.
options: Stimulate the patient and prepare naloxone if needed
Document the finding and reassess in four hours
Increase the next scheduled opioid dose slightly
Encourage the patient to sleep without disturbance
Withhold all oxygen therapy until fully awake
questions.question: A nurse assessing a patient's respiratory status notes a respiratory rate of 8 breaths per minute with shallow depth after opioid administration. The priority nursing action is to:

questions.explanation: Arterial sheath removal after PCI carries risk of significant bleeding, haematoma, or retroperitoneal haemorrhage at the femoral access site. Frequent assessment of the site, distal pulses, and vital signs detects complications early. Patients are typically kept on bed rest with the affected limb straight for a period after the procedure.
options: Bleeding or haematoma at the insertion site
Skin rash unrelated to the procedure
questions.question: A nurse caring for a patient after percutaneous coronary intervention via the femoral artery should prioritise monitoring for:

options: Autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells
Bile acid reflux causing duodenal inflammation
H. pylori-resistant strains in the duodenum
Gastrin-secreting pancreatic tumours causing extreme acid hypersecretion
