questions.answerText:
A(i) Tumour markers are substances produced by a tumour (tumour-derived) or by the body in response to it (tumour-associated), assayed in tissues or fluids to differentiate tumour from normal tissue; macromolecules (proteins, carbohydrates) as enzymes, hormones, antigens, receptors and genetic markers; may be normally produced by the organ but increased (CEA colon, hCG placenta).
A(i) Tumour-specific markers occur in single tumours (e.g. PSA); tumour-associated in different tumours of the same tissue type (AFP, CEA); some occur in non-cancerous conditions; poorly differentiated tumours re-express substances produced in utero (oncodevelopmental).
A(ii) Factors: cell proliferation and expression, tumour vascularisation, excretion (renal clearance), initial concentrations, half-life (PSA 2-3 days, hCG 12-20 h, AFP 5 days), nature of therapy.
A(iii) The ideal marker has 100% specificity and sensitivity, is detectable only in malignancy, has levels proportional to tumour burden, responds rapidly to changes in tumour load and is easy to measure.
A(iv) Screening (limited; PSA; AFP for hepatocellular carcinoma in high-incidence populations); diagnosis (limited by specificity/sensitivity); prognosis (limited; high PSA and capsular penetration); prediction of therapeutic response (important: steroid receptors, HER-2/neu and trastuzumab, BCR-ABL and tyrosine kinase inhibitors).
A(iv) Staging (limited; beta2-microglobulin in myeloma); locating tumours and directing radiotherapy (radiolabelled antibodies to CEA, ferritin); monitoring effectiveness of therapy (important; CEA, CA-125; readily interpretable, economical, sensitive and safer than radiological or invasive procedures).
B(i) Classes: enzymes (PSA, ALP, amylase, GGT); hormones (ACTH, ADH, calcitonin, hCG, GH, PTH, prolactin, C-peptide); proteins (beta2-microglobulin, ferritin, thyroglobulin, immunoglobulin); oncofoetal antigens; receptors (ER, PR, AR, c-MET).
B(i) Carbohydrate markers: CA-125 (ovarian, endometrial), CA 15-3 (breast, ovarian), CA 19-9 (pancreatic, GIT, hepatic); genetic markers (p53, RAS, HER-2/neu, BCR-ABL, N-myc, VHL, APC, WT1); cytokeratins; catecholamine metabolites (VMA, HVA, metanephrines); chromogranins.
B(ii) AFP: 70 kDa glycoprotein from yolk sac and liver; marker of hepatocellular carcinoma and non-seminomatous germ cell tumours; <10 µg/L in healthy adults; low maternal AFP with trisomies 21 and 18, high in neural tube defects.
B(ii) CEA: glycoprotein 150-500 kDa, elevated in colorectal (70%), lung, gastric, breast, pancreatic cancers; used for staging, prognosis and monitoring, not screening (false positives in benign tumours, false negatives in some cancers).
B(ii) hCG: dimeric glycoprotein of the syncytiotrophoblast; alpha subunit shared with LH, FSH, TSH and beta subunit specific; raised in trophoblastic and germ cell tumours (70% of non-seminomatous testicular tumours), useful for monitoring trophoblastic disease.
B(iii) Methods of assay: enzyme assay, immunoassay, receptor assay, immunohistochemistry/cytochemistry, and instrumental techniques (chromatography, electrophoresis, mass spectrometry, microarrays).

questions.question:
A 70-year-old man presents with headache, blurring of vision, and visual field defects on examination.
(i) Identify the structure most likely involved and the likely lesion.
(ii) State the structure compressed and the typical visual defect.
(iii) State the differential pathologies, including the tumour types and other causes.
(iv) Explain the clinico-endocrine reasoning, including the hormonal assessment and dynamic tests.
questions.answerText:
(i) The pituitary gland (hypophysis) in the sella turcica; a pituitary tumour, classified as a microadenoma (<1 cm) or macroadenoma (≥1 cm).
(ii) Tumour growth compresses the optic chiasm, causing visual field defects, of which bitemporal hemianopia is the most frequent.
(iii) Tumour types by frequency: lactotroph 30%, nonfunctioning 27%, somatotroph 15%, corticotroph 15%, combined GH/PRL 8%, plurihormonal 4%, thyrotroph 1%.
(iii) Other causes: craniopharyngioma, metastases, granulomatous disease (sarcoidosis, TB, syphilis, fungi), haemorrhage/infarction, aneurysm of the internal carotid artery, autoimmune hypophysitis, haemochromatosis, primary hypothalamic disorders.
(iv) High hormone levels indicate the type of tumour; low values are also significant, as hyposecretion suggests a compressive effect and possible need for replacement; levels give a baseline for monitoring therapy.
(iv) Measure LH, FSH and oestradiol/testosterone, T4 and TSH, prolactin, and 09.00 h cortisol; low target hormone with raised trophic hormone points to the target gland, while both low suggests a pituitary stimulation test; CT or MRI may show the cause.
(iv) Dynamic tests: glucose suppression test for acromegaly (GH fails to suppress), insulin tolerance test, glucagon stimulation test, water deprivation and DDAVP tests for the posterior pituitary.

(i) Gilbert's disease (inherited hyperbilirubinaemia): raised bilirubin with normal ALP, ALT, AST, haemoglobin and reticulocytes, and no bilirubin in urine.
(ii) A familial autosomal dominant disease, commoner in men.
(iii) Low activity of UDP glucuronyl transferase (defect in the promoter gene) plus decreased uptake, leading to failure of uptake and conjugation of bilirubin.
(iii) Presents as asymptomatic unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia; unconjugated bilirubin is protein bound and not filtered, so urine bilirubin is absent.
(iv) Haemolytic jaundice: overproduction of bilirubin, predominantly unconjugated (rarely above 100 µmol/L), with raised AST and LDH, low haptoglobin, raised reticulocyte count and markedly raised urine urobilinogen.
(iv) Here haemoglobin and reticulocyte count are normal, so haemolysis is not supported.
(iv) Severe variant: total loss of UDP glucuronyl transferase activity gives severe neonatal unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia leading to kernicterus.
questions.question:
An engineering student recovering from an infection is noticed to be jaundiced. Serum bilirubin is 60 µmol/L, ALP 80 U/L, ALT 35 U/L, AST 38 U/L, haemoglobin 160 g/L and reticulocyte count 1%. Urine bilirubin is negative.
(i) State the most likely diagnosis.
(ii) State the predisposing factors.
(iii) Explain the pathophysiology and type of hyperbilirubinaemia.
(iv) Distinguish it from haemolytic jaundice and from the severe neonatal variant.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Immunodeficiency is a deficiency in the quality or quantity of immune cells, immune products or lymphoid organs; primary (central, genetic, congenital) or secondary (peripheral, acquired); primary types include SCID, Bruton's, DiGeorge, hyper IgM and common variable immunodeficiency.
A(ii) SCID (Swiss type): impaired cellular and humoral responses, both T and B lymphocytes affected; repeated bacterial, fungal, viral and parasitic infections; male:female 3:1.
A(ii) SCID: accepts skin grafts from unrelated donors; tuberculin/cell-mediated immunity tests negative; BCG or live virus immunisation may cause fatal disease; not reported in Africa; treated by bone marrow transplantation.
A(iii) DiGeorge (T-cell deficiency): thymic hypoplasia (absent or greatly diminished thymus); prolonged skin graft survival; absolute lymphocyte count normal or reduced; skin tests with tuberculin/T antigen stimulators negative.
A(iii) No reported cases in West Africa; treated by grafting neonatal thymus.
A(iv) Bruton's disease: prone to numerous childhood infections; bacterial (H. influenzae, Streptococcus pneumoniae, S. aureus) and viral (enteroviruses: polio, coxsackievirus).
B(i) Secondary immunodeficiency is dysfunction of one or more immune components from another process, may be transient and later corrected; causes: excessive protein loss (protein-losing enteropathy, burns), pregnancy, drugs (chemotherapy, DMARDs, post-transplant immunosuppressants, glucocorticoids).
B(i) Other causes: splenectomy, poor nutrition, surgery/trauma/ICU, renal disease, extremes of age.
B(ii) Malaria: depressed T lymphocyte number and impaired cellular function; syphilis: a serum factor depresses lymphocyte responses in vitro.
B(ii) Lepromatous leprosy: impaired delayed hypersensitivity and reduced T cell number; AIDS: HIV destroys helper T lymphocytes at an unusually fast rate.
B(iii) In DiGeorge thymic hypoplasia the paracortex of lymph nodes and the periarteriolar sheaths of the spleen are depleted.
B(iii) Antibody levels may be lower because of reduced number and function of T helper cells.

(i) A hepatic (hepatocellular) picture: pronounced AST/ALT rise (often above 1000 U/L), modest ALP rise (below 2 times ULN), bilirubinuria in severe cases and normal albumin; the highest rises (x1000) occur in acute toxic injury (drugs, ischaemic insult).
(i) Common causes of acute liver damage: hepatic viruses and other infections (EBV, CMV), alcohol, and drugs or other chemicals (e.g. paracetamol); toxins such as carbon tetrachloride and drugs such as chloramphenicol and cephalosporins also raise AST and ALT.
(ii) Prothrombin has a short half-life, so PT is a sensitive indicator of acute and chronic liver disease and an early feature of acute liver disease; vitamin K deficiency must be excluded with intravenous vitamin K.
(ii) Complications: very severe damage culminates in hepatic failure; hepatic encephalopathy (grade IV is coma); hepato-renal syndrome may occur in severe acute liver disease and is seen in paracetamol (APAP) toxicity.
(ii) In acute liver failure the BCAA/AAA ratio is reduced, underlying the theory that encephalopathy is due to toxic effect of NH3 on the brain; hepatic coma can be followed by raised NH3.
(iii) Options: specific drug assays (e.g. paracetamol), virological serology, blood alcohol assay/CDT, blood NH3, and serial PT, bilirubin and AST +/- ALT.
(iii) Justified choice: specific drug assay, because standard LFTs have a limited role in unearthing aetiology and specific assays exist for drug-induced injury.

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Maple Syrup Urine Disease (MSUD).
(ii) Predisposing factors: it is an autosomal recessive metabolic disorder due to deficiency of the branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase enzyme.
(iii) Pathophysiology: the deficient enzyme normally decarboxylates the branched-chain amino acids leucine, isoleucine and valine; accumulation of these amino acids and their alpha-ketoacid metabolites in the blood leads to toxic CNS effects. Symptoms include the characteristic maple syrup (sweet-smelling) odour in urine (due to isoleucine), loss of appetite, weight loss, metabolic crisis, vomiting, irritability and difficulty breathing.
(iv) Management: diagnosis is by blood and urine tests showing elevated branched-chain amino acids and their metabolites, together with the characteristic maple syrup urine smell; newborns suspected of having MSUD should be tested within 24 hours of birth to start treatment early and avoid toxic effects. Treatment is with a synthetic formula containing limited amounts of leucine, isoleucine and valine, sufficient to provide the amino acids necessary for normal growth and development without producing toxic effects.

A) Describe bone under the following headings:
A(i) Cellular components
A(ii) Chemical composition

B) Relate abnormalities of bone density to the pathologies of low and high bone density that are recognised.

C) Explain how disease at a distant organ can spread its effect to cause a bone functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Bone is a living tissue consisting of osteocytes, osteoblasts, osteoclasts and fibroblasts as its cells.
A(ii) Chemically, bone consists of mineral salts (essentially calcium and phosphorus, plus smaller cations such as magnesium and zinc) making up 37% or less, organic matter making up 19%, with the balance (44%) being water; more than 95% of the organic matrix of bone (osteoid) is collagen.
B) The skeleton can have low bone density, as occurs in osteoporosis and osteomalacia, or high bone density, as in Paget's disease of bone and osteopetrosis; the rate of bone matrix formation depends equally on the availability of both calcium and inorganic phosphate, so dysregulation of phosphate homeostasis contributes to impaired bone mineralisation seen as rickets (in children) and osteomalacia (in adults).
C) Disease of the kidney is a recognised cause of a distant bone deficit: renal failure impairs activation of vitamin D (via renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase) and disturbs phosphate excretion, and this perturbation in serum calcium and phosphate causes a homeostatically appropriate but excessive rise in PTH secretion (secondary hyperparathyroidism), which in bone stimulates osteoclastic activity, releasing Ca2+ and HPO4 and producing a skeletal deficit far from the kidney where the disease began.
Disease of the pancreas is a second example: people with insufficient pancreatic exocrine function (pancreatitis, cystic fibrosis) tend to be vitamin D deficient, and this pancreas-driven vitamin D deficiency in turn impairs intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption, again producing a bone mineralisation deficit (rickets/osteomalacia) at a site distant from the pancreas.
In both examples the bone acts as the reservoir that is "emptied" when a distant regulating organ (kidney or pancreas/intestine) fails to maintain normal calcium and phosphate concentrations in the extracellular fluid.

questions.question:
An elderly woman presents with progressive weakness, a sore tongue and numbness in her feet. Investigations reveal macrocytic anaemia and an elevated plasma homocysteine level. Gastric acid analysis shows a very low basal acid output.

(i) What is the most likely diagnosis?
(ii) What confirmatory feature/procedure supports this diagnosis?
(iii) What is the biochemical mechanism underlying the deficiency?
(iv) What structure/system is primarily at risk of damage?
(v) Describe a recognised variant/associated cause of this presentation.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: vitamin B12 deficiency with pernicious anaemia.
(ii) Confirmatory feature: the low basal acid output supports achlorhydria, which is known to usually accompany intrinsic factor (IF) deficiency in pernicious anaemia; the macrocytic anaemia and elevated homocysteine are also recognised features of B12/folate deficiency.
(iii) Biochemical mechanism: intrinsic factor is a 44kD glycoprotein secreted by gastric parietal cells that binds vitamin B12, which is required for absorption of the vitamin by specific receptors for the B12-IF complex in the distal ileum; deficiency of IF results in pernicious anaemia and is usually accompanied by achlorhydria (lack of gastric HCl).
(iv) Structures at risk: B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic/macrocytic anaemia (haematological system) and irreversible nerve and brain damage, together with elevated homocysteine levels which may increase the risk of heart disease.
(v) Variant/associated cause: pernicious anaemia from intrinsic factor deficiency is one recognised cause; B12 deficiency is also known to occur where dietary or absorptive causes coexist, and folate deficiency is a related recognised variant, itself causing macrocytic (megaloblastic) anaemia, inflamed tongue, diarrhoea and, in pregnancy, neural tube defects and low birth weight, alongside elevated homocysteine.

(i) Hyperprolactinaemia. Prolactin is secreted by acidophil lactotrophs (key role in pregnancy and lactation); unlike other pituitary hormones its secretion is inhibited by hypothalamic dopamine (prolactin inhibitory factor) via D2 receptors, so impaired hypothalamic control causes hyperprolactinaemia.
(i) Stimulants: oestrogens (lactotroph proliferation), TRH, sleep, physical and psychological stress; very high oestrogen and progesterone inhibit prolactin secretion (pregnancy).
(ii) High prolactin inhibits pulsatile GnRH release, impairing LH and FSH release, and directly inhibits gonadal steroid synthesis; gonadotrophin and oestrogen/testosterone concentrations are low, causing symptoms of oestrogen or testosterone deficiency.
(ii) Women: oligomenorrhoea, amenorrhoea, infertility; men: impotence (erectile dysfunction), oligospermia, infertility; about a third of patients have galactorrhoea.
(iii) Physiological (most common): pregnancy, lactation. Dopamine deficiency: hypothalamic disease, interruption of the hypothalamic-pituitary portal system. Drugs: antipsychotics (chlorpromazine, haloperidol, clozapine), cholinergic, serotonergic and H2 receptor antagonists; hormones (oestrogen).
(iii) Neurogenic: nursing, chest wall disease, spinal cord injury. Other: hypothyroidism (raised TRH), chronic renal disease, cirrhosis, polycystic ovary syndrome, prolactinoma (microadenoma <10 mm, macroadenoma >10 mm).
(iv) Sample taken not less than 2 hours after sleep, usually in the morning; confirm on a repeat specimen and exclude drugs and exercise; MRI if prolactinoma is suspected.
questions.question:

questions.answerText:
A(i) Lipoproteins are macromolecular protein-lipid complexes that transport relatively insoluble lipids in blood (a vehicle); spherical, with an outer monolayer of apoproteins, phospholipid and unesterified cholesterol and an inner core of neutral lipids (triglycerides, cholesterol esters) determining size and weight.
A(i) Weak binding forces allow exchange of cholesterol between lipoproteins; CETP transfers triglycerides and cholesteryl esters and PLTP transfers phospholipids.
A(ii) Categories by hydrated density (ultracentrifugation): chylomicron, VLDL, IDL, LDL, HDL, Lp(a); Fredrickson classification is phenotypic (electrophoretic) and outdated, the WHO classification is aetiologic/functional (primary or secondary; diagnose primary after excluding secondary).
A(iii) Apoproteins A-E activate enzymes, maintain structural integrity and facilitate cell uptake via receptors; LDL has only apo B.
A(iii) Apo AI cofactor of LCAT (chylomicron, HDL); AII inhibits LCAT; B48 intestinal (chylomicron); B100 hepatic secretion of TG and binds the LDL receptor (VLDL, IDL, LDL).
A(iii) Apo CII activates LPL; CIII inhibits LPL; C1 activates LCAT; apo E has E2, E3, E4 isoforms; apo (a) inhibits plasminogen.
A(iv) Lp(a) is structurally related to LDL with one apoB-100 per particle plus apo(a), which shares homology with plasminogen but is not an active protease, so it competitively inhibits plasminogen activity, favouring clot formation; Lp(a) is atherogenic.
B(i) Certain lipids and the lipoproteins transporting them are strongly associated with cardiovascular disease such as CHD, so lipids in clinical chemistry are virtually synonymous with lipoprotein metabolism and atherosclerosis.
B(i) Functions of lipids: hormones or precursors, digestion, transport of fat-soluble vitamins, fuel and energy store, membrane components, insulation for nerve conduction or heat loss prevention.
B(ii) LDL carries cholesteryl ester with apo B100 to tissues and its excess infiltrates the vessel wall (initiating atherosclerosis); HDL removes excess cholesterol to the liver (reverse cholesterol transport) and is anti-atherosclerotic.
B(ii) Small dense LDL is atherogenic (susceptible to oxidation, high endothelial permeability, decreased receptor affinity, increased matrix interaction), unlike large buoyant LDL.
B(ii) Composition and half-life: chylomicrons about 90% TG (10 min); VLDL 55% TG (1-3 days); HDL half-life 4 days.

(i) Graves' disease: the commonest cause of thyrotoxicosis (more than 60%); autoimmune, with circulating thyroid stimulating immunoglobulins that bind and stimulate the TSH receptor, causing diffuse glandular hyperplasia with increased follicles and hormone synthesis.
(ii) About 10 times more common in women; may be part of wider autoimmune processes (polyglandular autoimmune syndromes); associated with pernicious anaemia, vitiligo, type 1 diabetes, autoimmune adrenal insufficiency, systemic sclerosis, myasthenia gravis, Sjogren syndrome, rheumatoid arthritis and SLE.
(iii) General and skin: increased basal metabolic rate, weight loss despite similar/increased appetite; warm moist fine skin, increased sweating, fine hair, vitiligo, alopecia, pretibial myxoedema.
(iii) Eye: chemosis, widened palpebral fissures, lid lag, lid retraction, proptosis, impaired extraocular motion, periorbital oedema, visual loss in severe optic nerve involvement.
(iii) Neck and chest: diffusely enlarged smooth gland, thyroid bruits, nodules may be palpable; tachypnoea, tachycardia, murmur, hyperdynamic precordium, S3/S4, ectopic beats, irregular rhythm, gynaecomastia; abdomen: hyperactive bowel sounds.
(iii) Extremities and nervous system: oedema, acropachy, onycholysis; fine bilateral hand tremor, hyperactive deep tendon reflexes; proximal muscle weakness, hypokalaemic periodic paralysis in susceptible ethnic groups; restlessness, anxiety, irritability, insomnia, depression.
(iv) Primary hyperthyroidism: TSH low, T4/free T4 high, T3/free T3 high; TRAb helps distinguish Graves' disease from factitious ingestion and predicts its course.
(iv) Treatment: thionamides (carbimazole, propylthiouracil, which inhibit TPO); radioiodine (iodine-131); subtotal thyroidectomy; others: beta-blockers, glucocorticoids.

A. Describe the gross anatomy and physiology of the heart under the following headings:
A(i) Size, weight, location and coverings.
A(ii) Wall layers and chambers.
A(iii) Blood supply, contractile proteins and the cardiac cycle.
B. Relate structure to pathology:
B(i) Which layer is most susceptible to ischaemia.
B(ii) The atherosclerotic basis of coronary disease and the associated risk factors.
C. Explain the electrocardiogram:
C(i) The normal components.
C(ii) The changes and syndromes that follow reduced coronary perfusion.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Adult heart weighs about 325 g (men) and 275 g (women), is 12 cm long (about the size of a fist), lies in the mediastinum between the lower lobes of the lungs, rests on the diaphragm and is enclosed in the pericardium.
A(ii) Wall has three layers: outermost epicardium, then a middle and an innermost layer (both called endocardium); four chambers: right and left atria and ventricles.
A(iii) Coronary arteries on the epicardium supply the wall; myocardium is bundles of striated fibres that contract and relax alternately, containing actin and myosin (contractile proteins) and troponins (regulatory proteins).
A(iii) Cardiac cycle has systole and diastole, at rest 60-80 beats/minute, controlled by the conducting system that initiates electrical impulses and carries them to the myocardium.
B(i) The innermost layer of the wall (endocardium) is most susceptible to myocardial ischaemia.
B(ii) Atherosclerosis, the major cause of AMI, is a chronic inflammatory condition from endothelial damage allowing lipid into the subendothelial space, with thickening and loss of elasticity of arterial walls.
B(ii) Non-modifiable risk factors: age, sex, family history, ethnicity. Modifiable: hypercholesterolaemia, hypertriglyceridaemia, low HDL, smoking, hypertension, obesity, diabetes mellitus, insulin resistance, raised fibrinogen, lipoprotein (a), homocysteine and hs-CRP.
C(i) ECG is a graphic tracing of electrical impulses: atrial depolarisation (P wave), ventricular depolarisation (QRS complex) and repolarisation (ST segment and T wave).
C(ii) Partial loss of coronary perfusion may cause NSTEMI, and a severe form is STEMI; unstable angina is the potentially reversible phase.
C(ii) AMI follows imbalance of oxygen supply and demand, leading to necrosis; diagnosis integrates symptoms, ECG and cardiac troponin.
C(ii) ECG sequence: ST elevation, T wave inversion and development of pathologic Q wave.
C(ii) Later the ST segment returns to near normal and T waves become upright again, but the large Q wave may remain.

(i) Carbon monoxide poisoning: CO is a by-product of incomplete combustion of carbon-containing substances (gasoline engines, furnaces, wood or plastic fires) and is absorbed into the blood from inhaled air.
(ii) Toxic effect is due to its affinity for heme (Hb, myoglobin); the Hb effect is most important because carboxyhaemoglobin is produced, with about 200 times greater affinity.
(iii) Spot test: 5 mL of 40% NaOH mixed with 5 mL of a 1/20 aqueous dilution of whole blood; a pink colour if CO is present at 20% or greater.
(iii) Quantitative methods: gas chromatography and spectrophotometric methods.
(iv) Major toxic effects are seen in organs with high oxygen demand: the brain and heart.
(v) Cyanide is a supertoxic substance (gas, solid or solution) that also binds heme iron; exposure by inhalation, ingestion or transdermal absorption; found in insecticides and rodenticides.
(v) Cyanide is cleared by enzymatic conversion to thiocyanate, a nontoxic product rapidly cleared by renal filtration; analysed by ion-specific electrode and photometric analysis.

questions.answerText:
(i) Wilson's disease (hepatolenticular degeneration), a disorder of copper metabolism.
(ii) Inherited recessively. Liver disease is the most prominent feature in about 40% of cases; the remainder show neurological, psychiatric, ophthalmic or haematological complications.
(ii) Hepatic presentation may be chronic liver disease or fulminant hepatitis; affected siblings picked up by screening may have no clinical abnormalities.
(iii) Characteristic picture: low caeruloplasmin (over 90% of patients below the reference range of 200-400 mg/L), high tissue copper, low plasma copper, high urinary copper.
(iii) A very low plasma copper with very high tissue copper is diagnostic, especially with Kayser-Fleischer rings. Reduced serum caeruloplasmin is an example of genetic decreased protein formation.
(iv) Without Kayser-Fleischer rings, diagnosis is often entirely based on biochemical laboratory investigations; AST and ALP are unhelpful compared with the degree of hepatic inflammation.
(iv) Treatment is with penicillamine; diagnosis or exclusion is of crucial importance to patients and their relatives.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Clearance = (U x V)/P (U urine concentration, V urine flow in mL/min, P plasma concentration); it equals GFR if the substance is freely filtered with no tubular secretion or reabsorption and is non-toxic and easily measurable.
A(i) Ideal marker: constant production, freely filterable (minimal protein binding), no tubular reabsorption or secretion, no extrarenal elimination or metabolism, accurate assay.
A(ii) Inulin is the gold standard (plant polysaccharide; bolus then constant infusion with timed urines); isotopic 99mTc-DTPA or 51Cr-EDTA by single bolus with GFR = V0 x (loge 2)/t1/2; iothalamate and iohexol are also used, with indications such as donor evaluation and toxic drugs with a narrow therapeutic range.
B(i) Creatinine comes from muscle creatine (about 2% per day), so production relates to muscle mass; it is freely filtered with some tubular secretion, and about 10% is dietary (cooked meat). Creatinine clearance overestimates inulin GFR by 1.1-1.2 times, more in renal failure.
B(ii) GFR falls in roughly inverse proportion to the rise in PCr, and the relationship is exponential (1 to 2 mg/dL means a GFR drop of about 50 mL/min; 4 to 5 mg/dL only about 5 mL/min); reference limits can be misleading.
B(ii) Non-GFR determinants: muscle creatinine generation, dietary intake, tubular secretion by organic anion transporters, extrarenal GI elimination, race/ethnicity; a protein load raises creatinine (80% after 300 g cooked beef) and strenuous exercise by 14%.
B(iii) Equations: CKD-EPI 2009 (preferred), MDRD, Cockcroft-Gault (CC = k[(140 - age) x weight]/creatinine, k = 1.224 male, 1.04 female) and Schwartz for children; variables are creatinine, age, gender, ethnicity.
B(iii) Only valid in steady state; not recommended in pregnancy, acute renal failure, serious co-morbidity or hospitalised patients, nor at extremes of muscle mass or diet (amputees, paraplegics, bodybuilders, obese, frail elderly, muscle-wasting, malnutrition, vegetarian diet, creatine supplements); confirm with measured GFR or creatinine clearance.
B(iii) Choice of assessment depends on whether evaluation is for acute or chronic disease and on patient-specific variables.
C(i) Cystatin C (13 kDa cysteine proteinase inhibitor) is made at a constant rate by all nucleated cells, freely filtered, with no known extra-renal excretion; not influenced by muscle mass, diet or sex; 1/[cystatin C] correlates better with Cr-EDTA clearance (r = 0.81) than 1/[PCr] (r = 0.51).
C(ii) Measuring cystatin C is suggested in adults with eGFRcreat 45-59 mL/min/1.73 m2 without markers of kidney damage; if eGFRcys or eGFRcreat-cys is below 60, CKD is confirmed, and if 60 or above it is not.
C(ii) Equations: 2012 CKD-EPI cystatin C and creatinine-cystatin C; errors arise from thyroid disorders, corticosteroids, non-steady state and assay interference by heterophilic antibodies.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Oxidants oxidise other substances by accepting electrons in redox reactions (oxidising agents); chemical oxidants are industrial (hydrogen peroxide, ferric salt) while biological oxidants form during metabolism and inflammatory reactions.
A(ii) Reactive species are less reactive non-radicals that can lead to free radical formation; ROS radicals: superoxide, alkoxyl, peroxyl, hydroxyl, lipid peroxyl; non-radicals: hydrogen peroxide, hypochlorous and hypobromous acids, ozone, singlet oxygen, lipid peroxides.
A(ii) RNS radicals: nitric oxide, nitrogen dioxide; non-radicals: nitrous acid, peroxynitrite, dinitrogen trioxide.
A(iii) Endogenous: cytosol (xanthine oxidoreductases, Fe2+, Cu2+, auto-oxidation, riboflavin), endoplasmic reticulum (cytochromes P-450 and b5), granules (myeloperoxidase), mitochondria (electron transport chain), peroxisomes (oxidases), plasma membrane (NADPH oxidase, cyclo-oxygenase, lipoxygenase).
A(iii) Exogenous: cigarette smoke (lung), cytotoxic chemicals, hyperoxia (lung), UV-A and ionising irradiation (skin).
A(iv) Dismutation: 2 O2 radical + 2H+ to H2O2 + O2 (SOD); Haber-Weiss: Fe3+ + superoxide to Fe2+ + O2; Fenton: H2O2 with Fe2+ (Cu+) gives hydroxyl radical + hydroxide + Fe3+ (Cu2+).
B(i) At low to moderate levels they are essential: maturation of cellular structures; host defence weapons (phagocytes release free radicals to destroy microbes); cellular signalling to maintain homeostasis.
B(i) They mediate apoptosis, detoxification and executing pre-cancerous cells; regulate gene expression, immunity, wound healing, mitogenic responses; involved in prostaglandin synthesis, hydroxylation of proline and lysine and oxidation of xanthine.
B(ii) An antioxidant, at low concentration relative to an oxidisable substrate, significantly delays or inhibits its oxidation, preventing damage to cellular components from free radical reactions.
B(ii) Enzymatic: SOD (superoxide to H2O2), catalase (2H2O2 to 2H2O + O2), glutathione peroxidase (ROOH + 2GSH to GSSG + H2O + ROH), glutathione reductase (GSSG + NADPH to 2GSH), thioredoxin.
B(ii) Non-enzymatic: flavonoids, ascorbate, tocopherol (vitamins C and E inhibit membrane lipid oxidation), carotenoids, uric acid (scavenges peroxynitrite), melatonin, glutathione, albumin, bilirubin, N-acetylcysteine.
B(ii) Cofactors: selenium in GPx, Cu/Zn or Mn in SOD, Fe in catalase; transition metal sequestration by transferrin, ferritin, metallothionein and caeruloplasmin.

questions.question:
A. Describe the functions of the kidney under the following headings:
A(i) Urine formation, and the roles of filtration, reabsorption and secretion in the nephron.
A(ii) Excretory, homeostatic and metabolic functions.
A(iii) Endocrine functions.
B. Relate the site of renal disease to proteinuria:
B(i) Normal protein excretion and the classification of proteinuria by site.
B(ii) Other classifications of proteinuria.
C. Explain how renal hormones and products act on distant structures:
C(i) Bone marrow and gastrointestinal tract.
C(ii) Blood vessels, adrenal cortex and pituitary-related water handling.
questions.answerText:
A(i) The kidney filters about 180 L/day (125 mL/min) of plasma to produce 0.5-2 L of urine; the glomerulus allows entry through fenestrated capillaries but prevents entry of plasma proteins by size and charge.
A(i) Tubular reabsorption recovers the vast filtered load in the proximal tubule, with maximum transport (Tm) capacities; tubular secretion, with reabsorption, selectively regulates excretion of specific substances into urine.
A(ii) Eliminates metabolic end products (urea, creatinine) and foreign materials (drugs); controls volume and composition of ECF, water and electrolyte balance, acid-base status, calcium and phosphorus balance; breaks down low molecular weight proteins.
A(ii) Gluconeogenesis: synthesises glucose from amino acids and other precursors during prolonged fasting.
A(iii) Renin, secreted by afferent arteriole cells when BP, blood flow or volume falls, activates angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, which ACE converts to angiotensin II; this releases aldosterone and is a potent vasopressor.
A(iii) Erythropoietin is produced by interstitial fibroblast-like cells near the peritubular capillary and proximal convoluted tubule, where 1-alpha hydroxylase activity is also located.
B(i) Up to about 150 mg/day protein (largely Tamm-Horsfall) is normal; more is pathological. Classes: glomerular (glomerulonephritic conditions), tubular (pyelonephritic), overflow (Bence-Jones proteins), post-renal (UTI and inflammation).
B(ii) Also classed as primary (renal origin), secondary (hypertension, pre-eclampsia), transient (exercise, fever, pregnancy) and orthostatic.
C(i) Erythropoietin is released in response to decreased oxygen tension (hypoxia, decreased renal blood flow) and stimulates red cell production in the bone marrow; activated vitamin D (1-hydroxylation) is needed to absorb calcium and phosphate in the GI tract.
C(ii) Angiotensin II is a potent vasopressor and stimulates the adrenal cortex to release aldosterone, which makes the distal tubule reabsorb Na and water and excrete K; ACE inhibitors lower BP by preventing angiotensin II formation.
C(ii) ADH from the posterior pituitary makes the collecting ducts permeable to water; deficiency diminishes blood volume, excess increases it.
C(ii) Atrial natriuretic factor causes Na excretion in response to increased blood volume and decreases renin secretion, with opposite effect on aldosterone and ADH.

A(i) Assessment proceeds from screening to sophisticated tests through four steps (B-cell/antibody, cell-mediated immunity, phagocyte, complement); primary humoral defects manifest early in life with certain infections (Streptococcus pneumoniae), frequent infections and incompletely cleared infections.
A(ii) Complete blood count with differential is not a good indicator of humoral immunodeficiency (may be normal or slightly decreased) but documents the presence of lymphocytes.
A(iii) Immunoglobulin quantitation: total IgA, IgG, IgM and subclasses (e.g. IgG2 deficiency); affected by age, sex, genetics, season; by ELISA, nephelometry, turbidimetry; if high, serum protein electrophoresis (paraprotein, HIV).
A(iii) Isohaemagglutinins (anti-A, anti-B): predominantly IgM, absent in AB individuals; titre ≥8 is normal; low or absent titres indicate poor IgM synthesis.
A(iii) Antibody to vaccine components (tetanus, diphtheria, pneumococcus): if low, challenge with specific antigen and measure before and 2-4 weeks after; an adequate response is a 4-fold or higher rise.
A(iii) Serum bactericidal assay: test serum + bacteria + complement; antibody activates complement, forming the membrane attack complex; surviving bacteria counted on agar; titre is the highest dilution killing ≥50% of target bacteria.
A(iv) B-cell numbers by flow cytometry with CD19 and CD20 markers (5-10% of peripheral blood lymphocytes).
A(iv) Histology of B-cell deficiency: hypoplasia of all lymphoid tissues (except thymus), lack of defined germinal centres, deficiency of plasma cells.
B(i) Lymphocyte proliferation assay: PBMC cultured 3-7 days with B-cell mitogens (killed S. aureus, protein A Cowan 1, pokeweed mitogen); proliferation expressed as stimulation index.
B(i) Antibody secreted by stimulated B cells can be measured in the culture medium by ELISA.
B(ii) Lack of B cells indicates primary immunodeficiency; B cells present but with abnormal function may be tolerised or anergic, or produce ineffective (non-protective) antibodies.
B(ii) Non-protective antibodies are common in very young children, the elderly and HIV-infected people, from inappropriate V regions or isotypes giving low avidity antibodies or inability to activate complement.

(i) Cushing's syndrome: any condition from increased circulating glucocorticoid; most common cause is iatrogenic; non-iatrogenic causes in order: pituitary tumours (60%), ectopic ACTH (20%), adrenal adenoma and carcinoma (20%); in children adrenal carcinoma is the commonest.
(ii) ACTH-dependent: excess ACTH gives bilateral adrenal hyperplasia, most commonly autonomous ACTH from a benign pituitary adenoma (Cushing's disease); ectopic sources: small cell lung cancer (50%), thymic (10%), pancreatic (10%), medullary thyroid carcinoma (5%), bronchial carcinoid (2%), others.
(ii) ACTH-independent: serum ACTH is low from negative inhibition by cortisol excess of adrenal adenomas and carcinomas, usually unilateral; most adrenal carcinoma patients die within 3 years despite surgery.
(iii) Low-dose DST (to confirm): 1 mg dexamethasone at 23:00, cortisol by 08:00 next morning; ≤2 µg/dL is normal; >2 µg/dL may reflect stress, obesity, infection, illness, alcohol, depression, oral contraceptives, pregnancy, oestrogen, phenytoin; >10 µg/dL indicates Cushing's syndrome.
(iii) Multiple low-dose DST: 0.5 mg 6-hourly (8 doses) with 24-hour urine for 4 days; day-4 cortisol suppressed to <50% of baseline and 20:00 cortisol one third of 08:00 value is normal; loss of diurnal rhythm and suppression indicates Cushing's syndrome.
(iii) High-dose DST (to identify cause): 8 mg at 23:00-24:00 with suppression of at least 50% expected; most pituitary Cushing's suppress to less than half; most ectopic ACTH tumours do not; adrenal tumours do not suppress.
(iv) Plasma ACTH: undetectable in adrenal tumours, upper normal or slightly raised in pituitary Cushing's, highly elevated (>40 pmol/L) in ectopic ACTH; labile, so collect with protease inhibitors, separate rapidly and freeze.
(iv) CRF stimulation: ACTH rises in pituitary Cushing's but not in adrenal or ectopic tumours; inferior petrosal sinus sampling helps localisation; insulin tolerance test differentiates Cushing's from pseudo-Cushing's syndrome.
questions.question:
A patient is investigated for a condition resulting from increased circulating glucocorticoid.
(i) State the diagnosis and the causes in order of frequency.
(ii) Explain the ACTH-dependent and ACTH-independent bases.
(iii) Describe the suppression tests used to confirm and localise the cause.
(iv) State the other localising tests.

A patient has a raised serum TSH with low free T4 and T3 and positive thyroid peroxidase antibodies.
(i) State the diagnosis and pathophysiology.
(ii) List the predisposing causes of hypothyroidism.
(iii) Describe the effects of thyroid hormone deficiency and the subclinical form.
(iv) State the treatment thresholds for subclinical hypothyroidism and in pregnancy.
questions.answerText:
(i) Primary hypothyroidism due to Hashimoto's thyroiditis (autoimmune): destruction of thyroid cells by CD8+ cytotoxic T cells; antibody markers include anti-TPO, anti-TG and TSH-receptor blocking antibody; clinical course subclinical or mild to overt.
(ii) Primary causes: autoimmune (Hashimoto's, atrophic thyroiditis); iatrogenic (131I, subtotal/total thyroidectomy, neck surgery, external irradiation); drugs (antithyroid drugs, amiodarone, lithium, iodine, glucocorticoid); congenital; iodine deficiency; infiltrative disorders.
(ii) Iodine deficiency is the commonest worldwide cause (endemic goitre, cretinism); thiocyanates in cassava and selenium deficiency also affect incidence.
(ii) Secondary: hypopituitarism (tumours, surgery, irradiation, Sheehan's, trauma), isolated TSH deficiency, hypothalamic disease, peripheral resistance. Transient: silent and subacute thyroiditis, thyroxine withdrawal, after 131I or subtotal thyroidectomy.
(iii) Deficiency causes hypercholesterolaemia (fewer LDL receptors) and carotenaemia (impaired hepatic conversion of carotene to vitamin A).
(iii) Subclinical hypothyroidism: normal T4/T3 with mildly raised TSH; prevalence 4-15%; antithyroid antibodies in 80%; TSH <10 mIU/L (80%) or ≥10; sequelae: progression to overt disease (more likely if TSH ≥10), psychiatric disorders, lipid abnormalities, abnormal cardiac function, adverse fetal outcome.
(iv) Levothyroxine is advised for subclinical hypothyroidism with TSH above 10 mIU/L and for pregnant women or those planning pregnancy with TSH above 5 mIU/L; in pregnancy immediate replacement with a higher dose is needed.

A(i) A pair of small, highly vascularised triangular organs in the retroperitoneal cavity on the superior poles of each kidney, lateral to the lower thoracic and upper lumbar vertebrae; each weighs about 4 g and measures 3.3 cm; an outer cortex and an inner medulla.
A(ii) Zona glomerulosa secretes mineralocorticoids (aldosterone); zona fasciculata and zona reticularis secrete glucocorticoids (cortisol) and androgens (dehydroepiandrosterone/sulfate).
A(ii) Aldosterone maintains extracellular fluid volume: renin from juxtaglomerular cells (released when ECF falls) yields angiotensin I, converted in the lung to angiotensin II, which stimulates aldosterone and sodium and water retention.
A(ii) Cortisol is the most abundant and potent glucocorticoid (92% protein bound), has a permissive effect (catecholamine activity, myocardial excitability), controls carbohydrate, lipid and fat metabolism, anti-inflammatory and immune responses and emotional states.
A(ii) Adrenal androgens mainly cause masculinisation; in postmenopausal women the adrenal cortex is the primary source of endogenous oestrogen.
A(iii) The medulla (neural crest origin, part of the sympathoadrenal axis) converts tyrosine to dopa (tyrosine hydroxylase, rate-limiting) then dopamine, norepinephrine and epinephrine; medullary NE/E ratio about 1:4 (peripheral about 9:1).
A(iii) Catecholamines are metabolised by COMT and MAO to metanephrines and vanillylmandelic acid (VMA); homovanillic acid (HVA) is the final product of dopamine metabolism.
B(i) Medulla: pheochromocytoma (chromaffin cell tumour, catecholamine excess, hypertension). Cortex hypersecretion: cortisol (Cushing's syndrome), aldosterone (primary hyperaldosteronism), androgens (congenital adrenal hyperplasia, adrenocortical carcinoma).
B(i) Hyposecretion: cortisol and aldosterone (Addison's disease, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, 21-hydroxylase deficiency most prevalent); cortisol and ACTH (adrenal insufficiency secondary to pituitary disease).
B(ii) Secondary insufficiency follows reduced CRH or ACTH from hypothalamic or pituitary disease; long-term glucocorticoid suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis leads to adrenal atrophy.
B(ii) Deficits: glucocorticoid lack (weakness, weight loss, hypotension, hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia); mineralocorticoid lack (postural hypotension, dehydration, hyperkalaemia, salt craving).
B(ii) Onset is often insidious and nonspecific; if undiagnosed, adrenal crisis can occur at times of significant physiological stress.

questions.question:
A) Describe the metrics used to define how good a diagnostic test is, under the following headings:
A(i) Diagnostic sensitivity
A(ii) Diagnostic specificity
A(iii) Positive and negative predictive value

B) Explain the clinical basis for choosing a sensitive test versus a specific test in different clinical situations.

C) Distinguish between predictive value and sensitivity/specificity as measures of test performance.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Diagnostic sensitivity measures how effective a test is in detecting individuals who have the disease in question; it is the percentage of true positives among all individuals who have the disease, i.e. the true positive rate, calculated as TP/(TP+FN) x 100%.
A(ii) Diagnostic specificity measures how effective a test is in detecting individuals who do not have the disease; it is the percentage of true negatives among all those without the disease, i.e. the true negative rate, calculated as TN/(FP+TN) x 100%.
A(iii) Positive predictive value is the probability that, if the test result is positive, the patient has the disease, calculated as TP/(TP+FP) x 100%; negative predictive value is the probability that, if the test result is negative, the patient does not have the disease, calculated as TN/(TN+FN) x 100%.
B) Ideally a test would have 100% sensitivity and 100% specificity, but in practice knowledge of a test's sensitivity/specificity guides the choice of testing method: for screening, the aim is to identify as many diseased persons as possible, so a sensitive test is used; for confirmatory testing, the aim is to exclude healthy people from unnecessary interventions, so a specific test is used.
This reflects the differing clinical consequences of missing a case (in screening) versus wrongly labelling a healthy person as diseased (in confirmatory testing), which is why the same underlying disease may be approached with different test characteristics at different stages of the diagnostic pathway.
C) Sensitivity and specificity are fixed properties of the test itself, describing performance against the true disease status of a study population, and do not depend on the prevalence of disease in the population being tested.
Predictive value, in contrast, is used in the context of the individual patient and takes into account the prevalence of disease in the population the patient is from; the same test with fixed sensitivity and specificity can have a very different positive predictive value depending on that prevalence, illustrated by a positive predictive value of 80% in one population becoming only 29% in an environment where the disease is less common.
Thus sensitivity/specificity answer "how good is this test", while predictive value answers "given this result, how likely is this patient to actually have (or not have) the disease", and the two must not be conflated when interpreting an individual result.

questions.question:
A patient presents to the emergency department with chest pain and shortness of breath. The ECG shows ST-segment elevation and cardiac troponin is above the 99th percentile of a normal population.
(i) State the diagnosis and the categories into which acute coronary syndromes are divided.
(ii) List the universal criteria for diagnosing this condition.
(iii) Describe the sequence of ECG changes from hours to months after the event.
(iv) Explain the pathologic basis of the condition, including its major cause and the type of infarction from plaque rupture.
(v) Outline the biomarker time course used for confirmation.
(vi) State the management and definitive treatment, including the time window for restoring coronary flow.
questions.answerText:
(i) Acute myocardial infarction, STEMI (the severe form of AMI). ACS covers three categories: unstable angina (UA), NSTEMI (partial loss of coronary perfusion) and STEMI.
(i) Unstable angina is the potentially reversible phase; myocardial infarction is irreversible cell death.
(ii) Rise and/or fall of cardiac biomarkers (preferably troponin) above the 99th percentile of a normal population, with at least one of: symptoms of ischaemia; new ischaemic ECG changes (new ST-T changes or new LBBB).
(ii) Or: development of pathologic Q waves; imaging evidence of new loss of viable myocardium or new regional wall motion abnormality; intracoronary thrombus identified by angiography or autopsy.
(iii) Hours after infarction the ST segment becomes elevated; hours to days later the T waves invert and Q waves become larger.
(iii) Days to weeks later the ST segment returns to near normal; weeks to months later the T waves become upright again but the large Q wave may remain.
(iv) AMI results from imbalance between oxygen supply and demand in heart muscle, causing tissue injury and eventually myocyte necrosis.
(iv) Major cause is atherosclerosis: a chronic inflammatory condition from endothelial damage that lets lipid pass into the subendothelial space, with thickening and loss of elasticity of arterial walls.
(iv) Type 1 MI is spontaneous infarction from a primary coronary event such as plaque fissuring or rupture.
(v) Troponin T or I appear in plasma 4-8 h after necrosis, peak at 12-24 h and stay elevated about 7-10 days; best measured 12 h after the start of chest pain.
(vi) Restoring coronary blood flow within the first 60-90 minutes gives maximal salvage of myocardium.
(vi) This is achieved with thrombolytic therapy (such as streptokinase) and/or percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) or coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG).

A(i) Gastrin is secreted into the bloodstream by antral G-cells.
A(ii) Gastrin secretion is stimulated by fundal distension and small peptides (the "gastric phase" of acid secretion); it is inhibited by acid reaching the G-cells of the antrum (negative feedback control) and by secretin, a duodenal hormone released when acid enters the duodenum.
A(iii) Gastrin acts on mast cells under the gastric mucosa to release histamine, which acts via histamine H2 receptors on parietal cells to stimulate HCl secretion.
A(iv) Gastrin is very labile in blood, so blood must be mixed with protease inhibitors (e.g. aprotinin) to prevent its degradation before assay.
B) The serum gastrin assay is used; increased levels are seen with failure of HCl to reach a normal antrum (no negative feedback), as in achlorhydria, gastrectomy with retained antrum, or antacid therapy; with G-cell hyperplasia; and with a gastrin-secreting tumour (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome).
To distinguish autonomous (tumour) secretion, provocation testing is used: secretin injection normally decreases serum gastrin in all situations except gastrinoma, where it has no effect or even causes a paradoxical increase, because tumour gastrin secretion no longer responds to physiological stimuli; similarly a protein test meal normally increases serum gastrin, whereas in gastrinoma there is no change.
C) When acid fails to reach a normal antrum (achlorhydria, gastrectomy with retained antrum, antacid therapy), the normal negative feedback on the G-cell is lost, so gastrin rises physiologically as an appropriate (non-autonomous) response.
In G-cell hyperplasia, excess numbers of gastrin-secreting cells raise gastrin and drive excess acid secretion, associated with duodenal ulcer.
In gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome), gastrin secretion becomes autonomous and unresponsive to feedback, driving persistently high basal acid output (often nearly equal to maximal acid output) that causes severe duodenal ulceration and diarrhoea, since the excess acid interferes with pancreatic enzyme and bile salt action.
questions.question:
A) Describe gastrin under the following headings:
A(i) Source
A(ii) Regulation of its secretion
A(iii) Action
A(iv) Handling in the blood relevant to its measurement

B) Describe the method used to assess gastrin status and to distinguish physiological from autonomous (tumour) gastrin secretion.

C) Explain the biochemical basis of the abnormalities seen when gastrin secretion is disturbed.

A) Describe parathyroid hormone (PTH) under the following headings:
A(i) Source
A(ii) Regulation of its secretion
A(iii) Actions on bone, kidney and intestine
A(iv) Interaction with vitamin D

B) Describe the approach used to assess disorders of calcium/PTH status and to monitor patients on calcium therapy.

C) Explain the biochemical basis of the abnormalities seen when PTH secretion is disturbed.
questions.answerText:
A(i) PTH is secreted by the parathyroid glands.
A(ii) Its secretion is controlled reciprocally by the serum calcium concentration: hypocalcaemia stimulates PTH release while hypercalcaemia inhibits it, forming a feedback loop with the kidney and circulating vitamin D.
A(iii) In bone, PTH stimulates osteoclastic activity, releasing Ca2+ and HPO4; in the kidney, PTH promotes absorption of Ca2+, promotes excretion of HPO4-, and activates renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase.
A(iv) Activation of renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase converts circulating 25-OH vitamin D (inactive) to 1,25(OH)2 vitamin D, which in turn promotes intestinal absorption of Ca2+ and PO4- and renal reabsorption of Ca2+ and HPO4-.
B) Measurement of serum calcium is central, and because most protein-bound calcium is complexed to albumin, for each 1g/dl fall in serum albumin below the normal value of 4.0g/dl, 0.8mg/dl is added to the measured serum calcium to correct it.
Urinary calcium measurement is used to monitor patients on calcium supplementation or to monitor dose response, and to monitor for the possible development of renal stones in those prone to it (using urinary calcium, calcium-oxalate and calcium:creatinine).
Acid-base status must be considered when interpreting calcium results, since acidosis increases and alkalosis decreases serum calcium levels.
C) In primary hyperparathyroidism (adenoma or glandular hyperplasia), excess PTH drives osteoclastic bone resorption and renal calcium retention with phosphate loss, producing hypercalcaemia with symptoms of weakness, nausea and vomiting, lack of appetite, frequent urination, and abdominal or bone pains.
Secondary hyperparathyroidism arises as a compensatory response of the parathyroid gland to a low serum calcium, for example in renal or GI disease.
In hypoparathyroidism (glandular aplasia, destruction or removal), reduced PTH lowers serum calcium (hypocalcaemia), a state also seen with hypomagnesaemia, hypoalbuminaemia, acute pancreatitis, vitamin D deficiency and renal disease.
Because PTH-driven renal activation of vitamin D links calcium and phosphate handling, disturbance of PTH secretion disrupts both bone mineral turnover and the intestinal/renal handling of calcium and phosphate simultaneously.

A(i) The thyroid lies anterior to the trachea and has two lobes connected by an isthmus; the functional unit is the spherical follicle of follicular cells surrounding colloid, interspersed by parafollicular (C) cells; the gland is essential in mental, physical and metabolic development.
A(ii) Hormones secreted: thyroxine (T4), triiodothyronine (T3), rT3 (biologically inactive), monoiodotyrosine (MIT), diiodotyrosine (DIT) and calcitonin.
A(iii) Steps 1-5: iodide transport into the cell by the sodium iodide transporter; oxidation of iodine at the apical membrane by thyroid peroxidase (TPO)/H2O2; iodine efflux into the lumen via pendrin; organification (iodination of tyrosine in thyroglobulin, TPO); coupling of MIT and DIT.
A(iii) Steps 6-9: TSH-stimulated phagocytosis of T4/T3-rich colloid; proteolytic hydrolysis of T3 and T4 from thyroglobulin; release to capillaries bound to binding proteins; MIT and DIT split to iodine and tyrosine and recycled.
B(i) More than 99% of T4 and T3 circulate bound: thyroxine binding globulin (TBG) about 75%, thyroxine binding prealbumin about 15%, albumin about 10%; binding proteins modulate delivery to tissues and delay clearance.
B(i) Bound hormone is not biologically active; free hormone is active and regulated; changes in serum binding protein concentration alter the total but not the free hormone level.
B(ii) Daily secretion: T4 about 100 nmol, T3 and rT3 about 5 nmol each; T4 secretion is about 20 times that of T3; extraglandular formation accounts for 80% of blood T3.
B(ii) T3 binds with 10 times more affinity than T4 and has 4-5 times more biological response; half-life T4 7 days, T3 1 day.
B(ii) Peripheral deiodination: T4 to T3 by 5' deiodinase; type I mainly liver and kidney (inhibited by PTU, glucocorticoids, propranolol, acute/chronic stress and illness); type II mainly brain and pituitary.
B(ii) T4 to rT3 by 5-deiodinase (type III) in the placenta, which regulates maternal thyroid hormone delivery to the fetus.
B(ii) Other metabolism: conjugation with glucuronate or sulfate in the liver (enterohepatic circulation, stool excretion) and oxidative deamination and decarboxylation.
B(ii) Actions are through intranuclear receptors with a DNA-binding and a ligand-binding domain that bind thyroid response elements in the promoter regions of target genes.

A(i) ADH is produced under hypothalamic control; the organs involved in fluid/electrolyte homeostasis listed for ADH are the hypothalamus and pituitary.
A(ii) Hypothalamic osmoreceptors trigger or inhibit ADH release; increases in plasma osmolality trigger thirst and ADH release, and factors that specifically trigger ADH release include prolonged fever, excessive sweating, vomiting or diarrhoea, severe blood loss and traumatic burns.
A(iii) Its main target sites are the distal tubules and collecting ducts in the kidney, where water reabsorption is proportional to ADH release; low ADH levels produce dilute urine and reduced body fluid volume, while high ADH levels produce concentrated urine.
B) Investigation of polyuria/suspected diabetes insipidus: first confirm polyuria (urine volume >2.5L/day in adults) and exclude biochemical causes of polyuria (e.g. hyperglycaemia, low potassium, hypercalcaemia); then measure plasma and urine osmolality.
An overnight water deprivation test is performed, and a urine/plasma osmolality ratio of less than 1.5 confirms diabetes insipidus (and excludes psychogenic polydipsia); to differentiate central from nephrogenic DI, desamino-D-arginine vasopressin (dDAVP/desmopressin) is given, a rise in urine osmolality indicating central DI and no rise indicating nephrogenic DI; plasma ADH can also be measured to confirm central DI (which shows reduced ADH).
C) In SIADH, pathologic ADH excess produces reduced plasma osmolality, hyponatraemia, raised plasma ADH and raised plasma renin, with elevated urine osmolality and reduced urine output; therapy is by decreasing water intake.
In diabetes insipidus, ADH deficiency (cranial/central DI, from pituitary or hypothalamic abnormality) or failure of ADH action at the kidney (nephrogenic DI) causes polyuria and polydipsia; central DI is treated with ADH, while renal (nephrogenic) causes are treated with hydrochlorothiazide or indomethacin.
questions.question:
A) Describe antidiuretic hormone (ADH) under the following headings:
A(i) Source/origin
A(ii) Stimuli/regulation of its release
A(iii) Target sites and action

B) Describe the correct method used to assess a patient with suspected disorders of ADH secretion or action.

C) Explain the biochemical basis of the abnormalities that result when ADH secretion or action is disturbed (SIADH and diabetes insipidus).

questions.answerText:
A(i) A reference interval (or reference range) refers to the range of values considered normal for a physiological measurement in healthy persons, describing the distribution of values from an apparently healthy population; by convention it usually includes 95 per cent of test results from a healthy (sometimes age- and sex-defined) population.
A(ii) Reference intervals are derived from a reference population of well-defined, healthy individuals comparable to the target patient in characteristics such as age, sex and race, other than the disease condition; they are usually established by the scientific community or reagent/methodology manufacturers, and clinical laboratories ideally establish their own but often adopt them from literature or manufacturer inserts, validating them before clinical use.
A(iii) Ideally biochemical tests should clearly separate a "normal"/healthy population from an "abnormal"/unhealthy population, but for most tests there is a range of values in which normal and abnormal overlap, and the extent of overlap differs for individual tests, affecting diagnostic efficiency.
B) "Normal range" causes uncertainty about what is "normal" and may be confused with the statistical concept of a normal (Gaussian) distribution, whereas "reference range/interval" is a term that reflects the entire set of data, including the maximum and minimum values, statistically derived from the specific reference population used.
C) Reference intervals describe the distribution of values from an apparently healthy population, and individual results are compared against this interval to see if a value fits within the defined range.
Clinical decision limits, in contrast, distinguish between particular clinical states by providing threshold (cut-off) values, above or below which there is significantly higher risk of a clinical outcome or the value may satisfy diagnostic criteria for a specific disease; for example, the decision limit for fasting plasma glucose (≥7mmol/L) is more clinically relevant than a simple reference range, and multiple thresholds may indicate increasing levels of risk (such as deficient/borderline/optimum/toxic vitamin D categories).
Decision limits are established from clinical outcome studies, whereas reference intervals are determined by reference interval studies on a healthy population.
questions.question:
A) Describe the concept of the reference interval under the following headings:
A(i) Definition
A(ii) How reference intervals are established
A(iii) The concept of discrimination between healthy and diseased populations

B) Explain the clinical basis for why the phrase "reference interval" is now preferred over "normal range".

C) Distinguish between reference intervals and clinical decision limits.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Aldosterone is released from the adrenal cortex; adrenal cortical cells are directly stimulated to release aldosterone by elevated K+ levels in the ECF.
A(ii) The renin-angiotensin mechanism triggers aldosterone release: the juxtaglomerular apparatus releases renin in response to sympathetic nervous system stimulation, decreased filtrate osmolality, or decreased stretch due to decreased blood pressure; renin catalyses production of angiotensin II, which prompts aldosterone release.
A(iii) Aldosterone reduces urinary loss of Na+ and Cl-, thereby increasing body fluid volume; it stimulates potassium ion secretion by principal cells of the cortical collecting ducts, so that for each Na+ reabsorbed, a K+ is secreted.
A(iv) Aldosterone brings about diminished urine output and increased blood volume slowly, thereby raising blood pressure; potassium itself controls its own ECF concentration via feedback regulation of aldosterone release.
B) No specific laboratory test or provocation procedure is used to directly assess aldosterone status; instead, mineralocorticoid deficiency is recognised as a cause of impaired potassium excretion (contributing to hyperkalaemia), while mineralocorticoid excess is recognised among causes of increased potassium excretion (contributing to hypokalaemia), so measurement of serum potassium (and its response/ECG changes) serves as an indirect biochemical indicator of aldosterone-related disturbance.
C) Excess aldosterone effect (mineralocorticoid excess) causes increased renal potassium excretion, producing hypokalaemia, which presents with flat T waves, ST depression, U waves, QT prolongation and arrhythmias, muscle paralysis and metabolic alkalosis.
Deficient aldosterone effect (mineralocorticoid deficiency or pseudohypoaldosteronism) impairs potassium excretion, contributing to hyperkalaemia, with its cardiac (peaked T waves, loss of P waves, widening QRS) and neuromuscular (paraesthesias, weakness, paralysis) manifestations.
Because aldosterone couples sodium reabsorption to potassium secretion in the cortical collecting duct, any disturbance of its secretion or renal action necessarily produces reciprocal disturbances of both sodium/volume status and potassium balance together.
questions.question:
A) Describe aldosterone under the following headings:
A(i) Source
A(ii) Regulation of its release
A(iii) Actions on sodium and potassium handling
A(iv) Relationship to blood pressure

B) Describe the approach used to assess disorders in which aldosterone is implicated.

C) Explain the biochemical basis of the electrolyte abnormalities seen when aldosterone secretion or action is disturbed.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Secretin and CCK are both released from the duodenum.
A(ii) Secretin is released from the duodenum in response to entry of acid; CCK is released from the duodenum in response to entry of fatty acids and peptides.
A(iii) Secretin stimulates ductular cells to produce a watery, HCO3--rich fluid (pH 8) that neutralises gastric acidity to provide an optimum pH for pancreatic enzymes; CCK stimulates acinar cells to produce a low-volume, enzyme-rich fluid (amylase, lipase, proteases) and also causes gall bladder contraction with expulsion of bile to aid fat digestion.
B) The secretin/CCK (or CCK analogue such as cerulein) test requires gastroduodenal intubation: a double-lumen tube is placed into the stomach and duodenum under fluoroscopic guidance, and gastric and duodenal contents are aspirated in the basal state and after intravenous administration of the secretagogue.
Gastric contents are discarded (to avoid falsely low bicarbonate readings from acid contamination) while duodenal contents are analysed for volume, bicarbonate concentration and amylase output (with the secretin test) or trypsin and lipase output (when CCK is used); the pH of uncontaminated duodenal fluid should be 7.5 or greater.
C) When low volume is the only abnormality found, cancer of the head of the pancreas should be considered; when volume, HCO3- concentration and amylase output are all low, this indicates advanced pancreatic disease such as extensive calcification, steatorrhoea or pancreatic endocrine dysfunction.
The test is sensitive enough to detect mild-to-moderate chronic pancreatitis, in which a low maximum bicarbonate concentration (reflecting ductular/secretin-responsive cell dysfunction) may be the only abnormality present, since ductular HCO3- secretion is typically affected earliest in progressive pancreatic disease.
questions.question:
A) Describe secretin and cholecystokinin (CCK) under the following headings:
A(i) Source
A(ii) Stimulus for release
A(iii) Actions

B) Describe the method used to assess exocrine pancreatic function using these hormones.

C) Explain the biochemical basis of the abnormal results seen in pancreatic disease when this method is used.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Enzymes are biological catalysts (increase reaction rate without being changed); all are proteins so can be denatured, specific to substrates, partly specific to tissues, and assayed by the rate of the specific reaction.
A(i) Holoenzyme = apoenzyme (protein portion) + cofactor (coenzyme, prosthetic group or metal-ion activator); specificity may be absolute, group, linkage or stereochemical.
A(ii) By reaction: hydrolases, hydrases, oxidases and dehydrogenases (electron transfer), transferases (radical transfer), desmolases (C-C bond), isomerases, ligases.
A(ii) By location: secretory (plasma prothrombin, ceruloplasmin, cholinesterase) versus intracellular: membrane-bound (ALP, GGT), cytosolic (ALT, AST, LD), mitochondrial (AST), lysosomal (ACP); tissue-specific e.g. amylase (pancreas), LD1 (heart).
B(i) Enzymes are normally intracellular with low blood levels; leakage indicates cell damage (death, hypoxia, intracellular toxicity) and is a quantitative measure of damage; serum levels show presence of disease, organ involved, aetiology, extent and time course.
B(i) In health release is balanced by removal from plasma; each laboratory has its own reference values; muscle exertion physiologically raises muscle enzymes.
B(ii) Decreased plasma activity reflects decreased formation: genetic (Wilson's disease, low caeruloplasmin) or acquired (hepatitis, low pseudocholinesterase); low ALP occurs in arrested bone growth and hypophosphatasia (autosomal recessive).
C(i) Both present with chest pain: serum GOT and LDH rise in MI, whereas in pulmonary embolism GOT is normal and LDH is raised.
C(ii) ALT (liver): hepatitis, jaundice, cirrhosis; ALP (bone, liver): rickets, osteomalacia, obstructive jaundice, bone or liver cancer; GGT: hepatitis, alcoholic damage, cholestasis; amylase (pancreas): acute pancreatitis, perforated peptic ulcer.
C(ii) Acid phosphatase (prostate) detects prostatic carcinoma and monitors treatment, but is being replaced by prostate specific antigen, which is more specific and sensitive.
C(ii) Amylase also rises in mumps and severe glomerular impairment, whereas lipase rises only in pancreatitis and pancreatic carcinoma; measuring both helps diagnose acute pancreatitis.
C(ii) Deficiency of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase can result in haemolytic anaemia with antimalarials such as primaquine, and is associated with favism.
questions.question:
A. Describe enzymes under the following headings:
A(i) Definition, holoenzyme and specificity.
A(ii) Classification by reaction and by location.
B. Explain the clinical basis of serum enzyme measurement:
B(i) Why serum levels rise and what information they give.
B(ii) Mechanisms of decreased levels.
C. Relate enzyme patterns to disease at distant or overlapping sites:
C(i) Chest pain from myocardial infarction versus pulmonary embolism.
C(ii) Enzymes of liver, prostate, bone and pancreas.

A patient presents with ischaemic-type chest pain lasting more than 20 minutes.
(i) State the risk factors for atherosclerosis and the classification of acute myocardial infarction.
(ii) State the diagnostic criteria.
(iii) Describe the biochemical markers of myocardial injury with their kinetics and limitations.
(iv) Justify the marker of choice for diagnosis.
questions.answerText:
(i) AMI is one end of the acute coronary syndrome spectrum: an imbalance between blood supply and heart oxygen demand causing irreversible injury (AMI) or reversible injury (angina).
(i) Risk factors: diabetes, tobacco smoking, hypercholesterolaemia (high LDL, low HDL), high blood pressure, family history of IHD, obesity, age (male >45, female >55), hyperhomocysteinaemia, stress, alcohol, male sex.
(i) Classification: subendocardial or transmural; by ECG, STE AMI (Q-wave, usually larger arterial occlusion) or NSTE AMI (usually partial occlusion, about 70% of cases).
(ii) WHO criteria: probable if 2 and definite if 3 of: ischaemic chest pain >20 minutes, serial ECG changes, rise and fall of cardiac biomarkers (CK-MB, troponin). Refined criteria: rise/fall of biomarker (preferably troponin) above the 99th percentile plus evidence of ischaemia (symptoms, new ST-T changes or new LBBB, pathologic Q waves, imaging evidence).
(iii) Cardiac troponins: cTnT rises in 3-4 h, peaks 10-24 h, stays up 10-14 days; cTnI rises 3-4 h, peaks 14-20 h, normal in 5-20 days; cTnI is highly cardiac specific; may be released in reversible ischaemia; chronic elevations occur in heart failure, LVH, renal failure, diabetes.
(iii) CK-MB: rises in 4-6 h, peaks 12-24 h, baseline in 48-72 h; >6% of total CK suggests myocardial injury; total CK sensitivity 40%, specificity 80%; persistently normal CK-MB mass over 6-8 h has a negative predictive value of 97%; useful for re-infarction.
(iii) Myoglobin: rises 1-4 h, peaks 6-9 h, baseline 18-24 h; sensitivity up to 75-100% within 0-4 h; not cardiac specific (renal disease, muscle injury, exercise). LDH: rises 12-24 h, peaks 48-72 h, elevated 10 days; LDH1>LDH2 flipped pattern; poor sensitivity and specificity, no longer used for diagnosis; AST mentioned for historical purposes.
(iv) Justification: cardiac troponins are now the mainstay for diagnosis and monitoring; serial sampling (0-4 h and 6-9 h) before ruling out AMI; multiple markers may be combined when markers are poorly specific.

A(i) Troponins are specific proteins present exclusively in striated muscle fibres that regulate the interaction of actin and myosin and thus cardiac contraction.
A(i) The complex has three subunits: troponin T (tropomyosin-binding), troponin I (inhibitory) and troponin C (calcium-binding).
A(ii) Normally no cTnT or cTnI is detectable; after cardiac myocyte necrosis they appear in plasma at 4-8 h, peak at 12-24 h and remain elevated for about 7-10 days.
B(i) Troponin T or I are best measured 12 h after the start of chest pain.
B(ii) Immunoassay is the technique of choice; the optimal specimen is whole blood or plasma (for laboratory or point-of-care testing), though serum can be used; different sample types should not be mixed in serial timed samples used to rule in or out MI.
C(i) Three isoforms of cTnT and cTnI exist (slow-twitch skeletal, fast-twitch skeletal and cardiac); the cardiac-specific isoforms can be measured in plasma, making them the most specific biomarkers of cardiac damage and the cornerstone of MI diagnosis.
C(i) Two isoforms of cTnC exist (slow-twitch plus cardiac, and fast-twitch), so no cTnC species is unique to myocardium.
C(ii) cTns may also be elevated in non-ischaemic heart disease such as renal failure, acute pulmonary embolism and severe heart failure.
C(iii) Myoglobin rises earliest (2-4 h, peak 12-24 h, elevated 2-4 days) but is not cardiac specific: minor skeletal muscle injury gives false positives and rapid renal clearance gives false negatives after a few hours.
C(iii) Total CK rises 4-6 h, peaks 24-48 h and remains elevated 2-4 days; it is the better alternative only if troponin assay is unavailable.
C(iii) AST rises 6-8 h, peaks 24-48 h, remains raised 4-6 days; LDH/HBD rise 12-24 h, peak 48-72 h, remain raised 7-12 days; these are now rarely assayed.
C(iii) CK isoenzyme electrophoresis and isoforms, myoglobin, LDH isoenzymes, HBD and AST are no longer of clinical use.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Four units: synthetic function (plasma albumin, prothrombin time), hepatic anion transport (total and conjugated bilirubin), hepatocellular integrity (serum ALT, AST) and presence of cholestasis (ALP, GGT, 5'-nucleotidase).
A(ii) Albumin marks synthetic function and severity of chronic liver disease; a falling level is a bad prognostic sign and it may be normal in acute disease (half-life about 3 weeks).
A(ii) Prothrombin time is a sensitive indicator of acute and chronic disease because of its short half-life; vitamin K deficiency, common in biliary obstruction, must be excluded.
A(ii) Soluble cytoplasmic enzymes (and to lesser extent mitochondrial enzymes) are released in hepatocellular damage; ALT or AST provide a sensitive index of hepatocellular damage from inflammation.
B(i) Though called function tests they assess liver damage rather than function, based partly on abnormal function and partly on enzymes released from dying cells; they are poor indicators of function and seldom definitive, so results should not be over-interpreted.
B(i) They detect existence or absence of disease (a negative result indicates low probability), guide further investigation, and serve screening, monitoring, prognosis and response to treatment.
B(ii) Compensated: the damaged liver still functions adequately because of its large functional reserve. Decompensated: the liver is failing in vital functions; ascites, jaundice or hepatic encephalopathy are signs of decompensation.
C(i) ALT is cytoplasmic, highest in hepatocytes and more liver specific (also present in skeletal muscle); AST has cytoplasmic and mitochondrial isoenzymes, is also in heart, brain, muscle, kidney and red cells, and is raised in hepatic necrosis, MI, muscle injury and congestive cardiac failure.
C(i) In viral hepatitis transaminases rise rapidly, even before bilirubin; both are higher in obesity (fatty liver), ALT declines with weight loss, and neither is a sensitive marker of chronic liver disease.
C(ii) Hepatocellular pattern: AST/ALT often above 1000 U/L, ALP rise below 2 times ULN, albumin normal.
C(ii) Cholestatic pattern: ALP and GGT rise several times normal after days of obstruction; ALP above 1000 IU or above 6 times URL in liver metastasis.
C(ii) 5'-nucleotidase is more specific to cholestasis; ALP is also raised in growing children, bone inflammation, intestine and placenta.
