A) Describe the chemical and physiological buffer systems of the body under the following headings:
A(i) The bicarbonate buffer system
A(ii) Protein buffers
A(iii) The haemoglobin buffer system

B) Explain the clinical basis of why the bicarbonate system, although not the most efficient buffer at physiological pH, is regarded as the most important buffer system in the body.

C) Distinguish between the buffering role of plasma proteins and the buffering role of haemoglobin.
questions.answerText:
A(i) The bicarbonate buffer is the most important buffer system in the body, represented by CO2 + H2O reversible with H2CO3 reversible with H+ + HCO3-.
Although bicarbonate is not an efficient buffer at physiological pH, its efficiency is improved because CO2 is removed by the lungs and bicarbonate is regenerated by the kidney.
A(ii) Proteins, notably albumin, contain weak acidic and basic groups within their structure, so plasma and other proteins form important buffering systems.
Intracellular proteins limit pH changes within cells, while the protein matrix of bone can buffer large amounts of hydrogen ions in patients with chronic acidosis.
A(iii) Haemoglobin binds both CO2 and H+ and so is a powerful buffer, important both in carriage of oxygen and in transport of CO2 and buffering of hydrogen ions.
Deoxygenated haemoglobin has the strongest affinity for both CO2 and H+, so its buffering effect is strongest in the tissues.
B) The bicarbonate system is regarded as most important because, unlike the other chemical buffers, it is an open system linked to two organs that actively regulate it.
The lungs continuously eliminate carbon dioxide by ventilation, while the kidneys continuously reabsorb or regenerate bicarbonate and excrete hydrogen ions, so its buffering capacity is constantly renewed rather than fixed.
This is why homeostasis of pH is described as being maintained by buffer systems, exhalation of carbon dioxide, and kidney excretion of H+ with reabsorption of HCO3-, with bicarbonate being the buffer measured to assess acid-base status.
C) Plasma and other proteins buffer through weak acidic and basic groups in their structure, limiting pH change within cells and, via the protein matrix of bone, buffering large hydrogen ion loads in chronic acidosis.
Haemoglobin's buffering is tied to the respiratory cycle within red cells: it binds H+ and CO2 more strongly when deoxygenated in the tissues, making its buffering effect strongest there.
Thus haemoglobin buffering is oxygenation-dependent and centred on gas transport between tissues and lungs, while protein buffering (including bone protein matrix) is not tied to the oxygenation state of blood.

questions.question:
A male child presents with hyperuricaemia, mental retardation and aggressive behaviour.
(i) State the diagnosis, its mode of inheritance and the enzyme defect.
(ii) Describe the sources of purines, the routes of uric acid excretion and why urate precipitates.
(iii) Describe the classification of hyperuricaemia and its clinical complications.
(iv) State the investigations and the definitive treatment.
questions.answerText:
(i) Lesch-Nyhan syndrome (juvenile type): results mainly from HGPRT deficiency (XO deficiency also stated); X-linked recessive, affecting male children; features are hyperuricaemia, mental retardation and aggressive behaviour.
(ii) Purines come from three routes: diet (meat, apples, fresh vegetable juices, berries, low fat products), de novo synthesis (ribose phosphate, pyrophosphate, glutamine) and breakdown/turnover (haemolysis, leukaemia, cancers, polycythaemia, psoriasis, cytotoxic drugs, radiotherapy, starvation).
(ii) Excretion: 75% by the kidneys and 25% by the intestine; at normal body pH 7.35-7.45 urate is ionised as monosodium urate; at low pH (below 7) it becomes relatively insoluble.
(iii) Reference range 0.15-0.43 mmol/L. Primary type: due to activity of phosphoribosyl amidotransferase (incorporates glutamine into PRPP); both sexes, more in males; autosomal recessive and dominant; aggravated by alcohol and meat; extremely rare; not in children; no mental symptoms.
(iii) Secondary type (commonest): diet (meat, alcohol, starvation); drugs (thiazides block secretion of uric acid, low dose salicylates, low dose probenecid); diseases (malignancies and their treatment).
(iii) Complications: precipitation in joints causes inflammation; leucocyte aggregation with anaerobic glycolysis gives lactic acid and lower pH, causing more precipitation and gouty arthritis; subcutaneous gouty tophi (ear, olecranon, patella); precipitation in kidney causes renal damage and failure.
(iv) Investigations: history (diet, alcohol, family, drugs), plasma and urine uric acid, renal function (E, U, Cr), enzymes HGPRT, APRT and PR amino transferase, test for crepitus in joints, look for tophi.
(iv) Treat all cases above 0.5 mmol/L: reduce intake (avoid starvation, reduce red meat, avoid alcohol, stop thiazide) and allopurinol (inhibits xanthine oxidase).
(iv) Uricosurics: probenecid (blocks reabsorption of uric acid) and therapeutic dose salicylate (increases excretion).
(iv) Anti-inflammatory: colchicine (prevents migration of leucocytes), salicylate, gold, piroxicam.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old man presents with recurrent, multiple duodenal ulcers extending to the distal duodenum, together with chronic diarrhoea. Basal acid output is found to be markedly elevated, almost equal to his maximal acid output.

(i) What is the most likely diagnosis?
(ii) What confirmatory test/procedure would be used, and what would the expected result be?
(iii) What is the biochemical mechanism underlying the ulceration and diarrhoea?
(iv) What cell type/structure is primarily at risk of damage in this condition?
(v) Describe a recognised variant/associated form of this condition.
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, caused by a gastrin-secreting tumour (gastrinoma), usually pancreatic but occasionally in the bowel wall.
(ii) Confirmatory test: the serum gastrin assay, supported by gastric acid analysis. In Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, serum gastrin level is very high and basal acid output (BAO) is greater than 15mmol/h, with a BAO/MAO ratio greater than 0.6. On provocation testing, secretin injection normally decreases serum gastrin but in gastrinoma it has no effect or even causes a paradoxical increase, and a protein test meal that normally raises serum gastrin produces no change in gastrinoma, since tumour gastrin secretion is autonomous.
(iii) Biochemical mechanism: the gastrin-secreting tumour continuously drives parietal cells (via histamine release from mast cells acting on H2 receptors) to hypersecrete HCl; the resulting severe duodenal ulceration is due to this acid excess, and the diarrhoea occurs because the excess acid interferes with the action of pancreatic enzymes and bile salts.
(iv) The parietal cells of the gastric mucosa are primarily driven to excessive acid secretion, and the duodenal (and even jejunal) mucosa is at risk of ulceration from the resulting acid load.
(v) Variant/associated form: gastrinomas are often malignant and are sometimes associated with the Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 1 (MEN I); if hyperparathyroidism is present as part of MEN I, the resulting hypercalcaemia may exacerbate the symptoms of the syndrome.

questions.question:
An infant presents with growth failure and mental retardation from a thyroid hormone deficiency present at birth.
(i) State the diagnosis, its prevalence and consequences.
(ii) State the predisposing causes.
(iii) Explain why thyroid hormone deficiency produces these effects and how maternal antibodies may contribute.
(iv) State the screening approach.
questions.answerText:
(i) Congenital hypothyroidism (hypothyroidism present at birth); prevalence 1:3500-4000 births, higher in iodine-deficient areas; consequences: growth failure and mental retardation (global developmental delay if not detected early in infancy).
(ii) Causes: iodine deficiency (commonest); in iodine-replete areas thyroid dysgenesis (sporadic developmental defects, 85%), thyroid dyshormogenesis (15%), rare inactivating mutations of the TSH receptor and thyroid transcription factors; thyroid agenesis and inborn errors of hormone synthesis.
(iii) Thyroid hormone is essential for normal growth of soft tissue and skeleton, for growth hormone/IGF production and action, and for growth, development and myelination of the infant brain.
(iii) The fetal thyroid-pituitary axis functions independently of the mother's in most cases; maternal anti-TSH autoantibodies can cause transient hypothyroidism in the infant.
(iv) Screening uses blood collected on filter paper by heel prick, with strategies of total T4 and TSH; serum TSH >80 mU/L is diagnostic; in the UK every newborn is screened for phenylketonuria and congenital hypothyroidism.
(iv) Screening criteria: disorder not clinically obvious when it should be treated, serious consequences, treatable, relatively common, and a sensitive and specific test exists.

(i) Polycystic ovary syndrome (Leventhal-Stein syndrome): hyperandrogenism with anovulation and abnormal ovarian morphology; the most common cause of anovulatory infertility.
(i) Presenting features: hirsutism, menstrual disturbances (amenorrhoea, irregular menstruation), enlarged polycystic ovaries (multiple small subcapsular cysts on ultrasound), infertility/subfertility.
(ii) Raised plasma testosterone and androstenedione; plasma LH may be raised with normal FSH (day 2-5 LH/FSH ratio >2); reduced plasma SHBG (raising free testosterone); there may be hyperprolactinaemia.
(iii) Features of metabolic syndrome: insulin resistance, obesity, hyperlipidaemia, glucose intolerance, hypertension; elevated plasma insulin stimulates androgen production from ovarian theca interna cells.
(iv) Hirsutism is increased hair growth; virilism is a greater degree of androgen excess with marked masculinisation (clitoromegaly, male-distribution hair, receding temporal hair, deepened voice, breast atrophy); both are due to absolute or relative androgen excess or increased tissue sensitivity.
(iv) Causes: idiopathic, racial, polycystic ovary syndrome, Cushing's syndrome, congenital adrenal hyperplasia (21-alpha and 11-beta hydroxylase), ovarian tumours (arrhenoblastomas, gonadoblastomas), adrenal tumours (adenomas, carcinomas), exogenous androgens and drugs with androgenic activity.
(v) Androgen excess may come from the adrenals or ovary; raised plasma DHEA and DHEAS point to an adrenal origin (e.g. adrenal tumours); marked excess can cause female pseudohermaphroditism.

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Alkaptonuria (also called black urine disease or black bone disease).
(ii) Predisposing factors: it is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by deficiency of homogentisic acid oxidase, an enzyme in tyrosine metabolism.
(iii) Pathophysiology: homogentisic acid, a metabolite of tyrosine metabolism, cannot be further metabolised and thus accumulates, resulting in excretion of homogentisic acid in urine in excessive amounts (homogentisic aciduria), which is oxidised to dark pigments on standing (accounting for the black urine). Homogentisic acid is also deposited in connective tissue causing degenerative changes in large joints (arthritis); other recognised features include dark spots on the sclera, black earwax, blue-speckled discolouration of skin, dark-coloured sweat, osteoarthritis and heart problems.
(iv) Management: diagnosis is confirmed by detection of homogentisic acid in urine using chromatography (and DNA testing to detect the mutated gene); treatment consists of a low-protein diet and a large dose of vitamin C.

questions.answerText:
(i) Microalbuminuria: albumin in small quantity in urine, undetected by conventional dipstick; urinary albumin excretion of 20-200 µg/min or 30-300 mg/24 h.
(i) For a spot urine, albumin/creatinine ratio (ACR) is defined as 3-30 mg/mmol creatinine.
(ii) Associated with cardiovascular diseases, diabetes mellitus, hyperthyroidism and infectious diseases.
(iii) It is an early sign of progressive but reversible glomerular damage.
(iii) Albuminuria (AER above 30 mg/24 h; ACR above 30 mg/g or 3 mg/mmol) is a marker of kidney damage; in CKD, GFR and albuminuria should be assessed at least annually, and more often in those at higher risk of progression.
(iv) Timed collection (overnight 8 h judged best, excludes postural variation) allows albumin excretion rate (AER) and simultaneous creatinine clearance; spot collection needs simultaneous albumin/creatinine ratio.
(iv) Semi-quantitative dipsticks (Albu screen, Albusure, Micral, Microbumin; latex agglutination or monoclonal antibody methods) show colour change proportional to albumin concentration.
(iv) Quantitative assays (turbidimetry, nephelometry, radioimmunoassay, ELISA, immunoturbidimetry) are antigen/antibody based, accurate and specific but expensive and need laboratory backup and trained personnel.
(iv) Justified choice: the timed overnight collection, because it excludes postural variation and gives AER plus creatinine clearance and a wider picture of renal function.
questions.question:
A patient with diabetes mellitus has a negative conventional urine dipstick for protein but is suspected of early glomerular damage.
(i) Define the condition suspected and state its excretion limits.

A retired man presents with a 3-month history of epigastric pain radiating to the back, unrelated to meals, with dark urine, pale stools, intense jaundice and recent weight loss. Bilirubin is 400 µmol/L, ALP 600 U/L, AST 75 U/L and GGT 120 U/L; urine bilirubin is ++++. Ultrasound shows a dilated bile duct and a barium meal shows indentation of the second part of the duodenum by an extrinsic mass.
(i) State the type of jaundice and the possible causes.
(ii) Name the imaging procedures used to confirm the level of obstruction.
(iii) State the biochemical landmarks supporting the diagnosis.
(iv) State the coagulation problem at risk in prolonged obstruction and how it is confirmed.
(v) Distinguish intrahepatic from extrahepatic causes of this pattern.
questions.answerText:
(i) Post-hepatic (obstructive, cholestatic) jaundice with conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and bilirubinuria. Extrahepatic causes: gall stones, carcinoma of the head of pancreas, carcinoma of the biliary tree, biliary atresia.
(ii) Ultrasound (to rule out obstruction of the biliary tract) and endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) for cholestatic abnormalities.
(iii) ALP and GGT rise several times normal after several days of bile duct obstruction; a strikingly elevated ALP is very often compatible with extrahepatic obstruction; 5'-nucleotidase is more specific to cholestasis.
(iii) Post-hepatic pattern: total bilirubin raised (+++), conjugated raised (++), bilirubin present in urine, faecal urobilinogen absent; complete absence of faecal urobilinogen is diagnostic of complete biliary obstruction, mostly cancer or stricture.
(iii) Pruritus may occur where cholestasis exists (bile salts).
(iv) Vitamin K deficiency commonly occurs in biliary obstruction because low intestinal bile salts cause poor vitamin K absorption, prolonging PT.
(iv) Vitamin K deficiency is excluded or verified with an intravenous bolus of vitamin K.
(v) Cholestasis may be intrahepatic or post-hepatic, both with conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia and bilirubinuria.
(v) Intrahepatic causes: acute hepatocellular damage, cirrhosis, intrahepatic carcinoma (secondaries) and drugs such as phenothiazines and methyl testosterone; extrahepatic causes are as listed in (i).

A(i) Bile acids are soluble metabolites (products) of cholesterol metabolism; chenodeoxycholic acid and cholic acid are the primary bile acids because of their hepatic origin.
A(i) The rate-limiting and regulated step in formation is 7-alpha-hydroxylation of cholesterol.
A(ii) Before secretion into bile canaliculi primary bile acids are conjugated to glycine or taurine, which increases solubility; conjugated bile acids leave liver cells by an energy-dependent carrier-mediated process.
A(iii) In the intestine bacterial enzymes deconjugate and alpha-dehydroxylate primary bile acids to the secondary bile acids lithocholic acid and deoxycholic acid.
A(iii) Most intestinal bile acids are reabsorbed into the portal circulation (75% in the ileum, 10% in the colon), taken up by the liver and re-excreted (enterohepatic circulation).
B(i) Bile acids solubilise cholesterol for excretion, solubilise dietary fat for absorption, and stimulate bile formation and flow.
B(ii) Re-uptake of bile acids by the liver is highly efficient but sensitive to liver damage.
B(ii) Serum bile acids are typically (not always) elevated in intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy and may be the only biochemical abnormality, presenting clinically as pruritus.
B(ii) Hepatic-origin ALP with raised GGT along with raised bile acids is strongly suggestive of the condition.
B(ii) In biliary obstruction low intestinal bile salts cause poor vitamin K absorption.
C(i) Primary: chenodeoxycholic and cholic acid (hepatic origin). Secondary: lithocholic and deoxycholic acid (formed by intestinal bacterial action).
C(ii) Bile contains bile acids critical for digestion and absorption of fat, and permits elimination of waste products such as cholesterol, bilirubin and drugs.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Protein electrophoresis separates proteins on the basis of their electric charge densities; movement of a charged protein depends on the pH of the surrounding buffer and the charge carried on the protein (cations move toward the cathode, anions toward the anode), the size and shape of the molecule, the electric field, and temperature. At the alkaline buffer pH of 8.6 used, all major proteins carry a net negative charge and migrate toward the anode.
A(ii) Five bands are noted: albumin travels farthest toward the anode, followed by alpha-1-globulins, alpha-2-globulins, beta-globulins, and gamma-globulins (immunoglobulins).
A(iii) The support strip is inserted into an acid solution (e.g. acetic acid) to denature the proteins and immobilise them on the support medium (fixing); the proteins are then stained (e.g. with Ponceau S, amido black or Coomassie blue) so they appear as bands, which are read by visual inspection or with a scanning densitometer, with concentration calculated as a percentage of total protein.
B) The electrophoretic pattern gives information about the relative increase and decrease in the protein population as well as the homogeneity of a fraction, so specific disease patterns (monoclonal gammopathy, nephrotic pattern, alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency, inflammatory pattern, liver disease) can be recognised from the shape of the trace, making it a useful screening tool for a range of conditions affecting plasma proteins.
C) In nephrotic syndrome, the patient loses serum albumin and low molecular weight proteins (with some IgG) in the urine, while alpha-2-macroglobulin, beta-lipoprotein, complement components and haptoglobulin increase; this produces a dramatic decrease in the relative amount of albumin and a marked increase in the alpha-2-globulin fraction.
In the inflammatory pattern, there is a decrease in albumin, an increase in alpha-2 globulin (ceruloplasmin and haptoglobin), an increase in alpha-1 globulin (alpha-1-antitrypsin, an acute-phase reactant), and an increased beta-globulin band (C-reactive protein).
Both patterns therefore share a fall in albumin, but nephrotic syndrome is distinguished by the specific loss of low molecular weight proteins and IgG into urine with a rise in beta-lipoprotein, whereas the inflammatory pattern is driven by increased hepatic synthesis of acute-phase reactants across the alpha-1, alpha-2 and beta regions rather than by urinary protein loss.

questions.answerText:
A(i) T-cell/NK defects (recognition, activation, mediators, proliferation, cytotoxicity) increase susceptibility to infection or cancer; isolated T-cell deficiency is very rare; intracellular organisms, viral and fungal infections, failure to thrive and respiratory, skin and gut infections are common; natural passive immunity does not delay manifestations.
A(ii) CBC with differential shows absolute number and proportion of lineages; flow cytometry enumerates CD4 and CD8 subsets (low CD4 in HIV; CD154 deficiency in hyper-IgM syndrome).
A(ii) Delayed-type hypersensitivity (Mantoux) skin test: intracutaneous multiple antigens (usually 3: PPD, Candida albicans, mumps); induration monitored at 48-72 hours; positive if ≥2 mm.
A(iii) Lymphocyte proliferation assay with polyclonal activators (phytohaemagglutinin, anti-CD3); absent or poor response indicates severe CMI defect; CD8 cytolytic activity by chromium (51Cr) release; cytokine secretion by ELISPOT and flow cytometry.
A(iii) NK cell defects are rare (increased susceptibility to viral infections); enumerated by flow cytometry (CD1 and CD56) and lytic activity by 51Cr release from K562 target cells (chromium released is proportional to lytic activity).
B(i) Neutrophil representative: neutropenia or marked decrease in activity causes significant morbidity and mortality; CBC with differential; PMN <1500/uL is associated with increased infection susceptibility.
B(i) Adhesion molecule expression: defects termed leukocyte adhesion deficiency (beta-2 integrins CD18, CD11a-c), tested by flow cytometry (basal expression) and stimulation test (up-regulation).
B(i) Respiratory burst: NADPH oxidase mutations cause chronic granulomatous disease; tested by nitroblue tetrazolium dye reduction, chemiluminescence and flow cytometry; opsonophagocytosis assays are killing-type or uptake-type (fluorescently labelled bacteria, flow cytometry).
B(ii) Mild or partial defects cause no disease (multiple redundancies); heterozygous defects carry no infection risk; homozygous defects cause overwhelming infection and sepsis through ineffective opsonisation or defective lytic activity.
B(ii) Indicators: autoimmune disorders with unusual presentation, recurrent infections with less pathogenic organisms, disseminated neisserial infection in young adults; C1-C4 defects give autoimmune disease and/or pyogenic infection; C5-C9 defects give susceptibility to meningococcal disease.
B(ii) Total haemolytic complement test: diluted plasma + antibody-coated sheep RBC, haemolysis measured; heterozygous defects may not reduce haemolysis, homozygous give none.
B(ii) Quantitation of factors and split components (immunodiffusion, ELISA, nephelometry; split products indicate activation); elimination method is a functional assay using reagents lacking specific components.

questions.question:
A. Describe the toxicology of the alcohols under the following headings:
A(i) Ethanol: acute effects, biotransformation and impact.
A(ii) Methanol, isopropanol and ethylene glycol.
B. Explain how alcohol injury progresses in the liver and how it is recognised:
B(i) Progression of chronic ethanol injury.
B(ii) Laboratory recognition.
C. Describe the determination of alcohol:
C(i) Specimen and precautions.
C(ii) Methods.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Ethanol is a common CNS depressant: exposure causes disorientation, confusion and euphoria, progressing to unconsciousness, paralysis and, at high level, death.
A(i) Alcohols are biotransformed to toxic products: alcohol to aldehyde to acid.
A(i) Economic impact estimated to exceed $100 billion; among top 10 causes of hospital admissions; 20% of admissions have some alcohol-related problem; 80,000 Americans die yearly directly or indirectly.
A(ii) Methanol: common solvent ingested accidentally; CNS depressant; death from formic acid formation causing severe acidosis.
A(ii) Isopropanol: rubbing alcohol, metabolised by the liver to acetone; CNS depressant.
A(ii) Ethylene glycol: anti-freeze component; causes crystallisation of calcium oxalate in the renal system and tubular damage if dose is high.
B(i) Chronic consumption leads to lipid accumulation in hepatocytes, which may progress to alcoholic hepatitis and finally liver cirrhosis; large quantities compromise function of various organs.
B(ii) Markers: AST/ALT ratio above 2.1, hypertriglyceridaemia, raised IgA (beta-gamma fusion), macrocytosis, hyperuricaemia, raised carbohydrate deficient transferrin (gold standard), marked GGT rise with normal ALP.
B(ii) GGT is raised in alcoholics taking over 45 g ethanol/day; aminotransferases are not usually grossly raised in alcoholic hepatitis.
C(i) Specimen: serum, plasma or whole blood; do not use alcohol to clean the venipuncture site; specimens must be capped at all times to avoid evaporation.
C(ii) Methods: gas chromatography and an enzymatic method.
C(ii) Enzymatic reaction: ethanol + NAD gives acetaldehyde + NADH, catalysed by alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH).

questions.question:
A. Describe the fetoplacental unit under the following headings:
A(i) stages of gestation and functions of the placenta;
A(ii) placental hormones;
A(iii) amniotic fluid and abnormalities of its volume.
B. B(i) Describe the endocrine changes of pregnancy.
B(ii) Describe the renal and biochemical changes of pregnancy.
B(iii) Describe the haematological changes of pregnancy.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Gestation lasts about 40 weeks from the last menstrual period, divided into three trimesters of about 13 weeks and term (37-42 weeks); the placenta and cord keep maternal and fetal circulations separate, nourish the fetus, eliminate wastes and produce hormones.
A(ii) Chorionic gonadotropin (peaks at end of first trimester) stimulates the corpus luteum to make progesterone in early pregnancy; detectable in urine about 10 days after conception, peaking in blood at 12 weeks; placental lactogen (191 amino acids, 96% homologous with GH, 67% with prolactin) has growth and lactogenic properties but no clinical reason to measure.
A(ii) Placental steroids (progesterone, estradiol, estriol, estrone) ensure endometrial development, uterine growth, uterine blood supply and preparation for labour; second-trimester estriol helps predict trisomy 21 and 18; hormone production rises with placental mass.
A(iii) Amniotic fluid cushions the fetus and maintains constant temperature; a stressed fetus may pass meconium, staining it green.
A(iii) Oligohydramnios: intrauterine growth retardation, bilateral renal agenesis, urethral obstruction; hydramnios: maternal diabetes, severe Rh iso-immune disease, oesophageal atresia, multifetal pregnancy, anencephaly, spina bifida.
B(i) TBG, CBG and SHBG rise markedly; oestrogen, prolactin and SHBG rise; oestrogen suppresses LH and FSH below detection; GH is decreased; total and free cortisol rise (more CBG, less clearance, HPA reset) causing glucose intolerance and occasional Cushingoid features with diurnal variation preserved; aldosterone and deoxycorticosterone rise.
B(i) Thyroid: euthyroid state; total T4 and T3 rise with TBG; free hormones rise slightly in early first trimester (CG effect) then fall slightly with a reciprocal TSH rise; thyroglobulin rises; PTH rises about 40% and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D rises to increase calcium absorption for the fetus.
B(ii) Plasma volume and GFR rise by up to 50% (GFR about 170 mL/min/1.73 m2 by 20 weeks), lowering serum urea, creatinine and uric acid; urinary protein loss up to 300 mg/d and glucosuria from lowered renal threshold.
B(ii) Slight hyponatraemia; TG, cholesterol, phospholipids and free fatty acids rise about 40%; albumin and prealbumin fall; cholinesterase falls; ALP triples (placental heat-stable); transaminases, GGT and bilirubin fall about 20%; CK rises at delivery; iron stores fall without supplements.
B(iii) Plasma volume rises faster than red cell mass, so haemoglobin, red cell count and haematocrit fall (Hb 12.6 g/dL at term versus 13.3 g/dL non-pregnant); leucocyte count may be markedly raised in labour and puerperium.
B(iii) Fibrinogen rises about 65% (275 to 450 mg/dL), raising ESR; factors VII, VIII, IX and X rise; prothrombin, V and XII unchanged, XI and XIII fall slightly.
B(iii) Platelet count is unchanged and PT and aPTT are slightly shortened, yet the risk of thromboembolism is up to five times that of the non-pregnant state.

questions.question:
A patient shows a rise in plasma creatinine of 0.3 mg/dL (26.5 µmol/L) within 48 hours, with urine volume of 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours.
(i) State the diagnosis and the criteria that define it.
(ii) Explain the pathologic basis by classifying the causes and stating the metabolic features.
(iii) Outline the staging by plasma creatinine and urine output, and the equivalent older classification.
(iv) Describe how the urea:creatinine ratio and creatinine-based equations assist or fail in this setting.
questions.answerText:
(i) Acute kidney injury (AKI): sudden impairment of kidney function with retention of nitrogenous and other waste products normally cleared by the kidneys.
(i) Criteria (use the absolute plasma creatinine value): PCr rise of 0.3 mg/dL or more (26.5 µmol/L) within 48 h; OR PCr at least 1.5 times baseline, known or presumed within the prior 7 days; OR urine volume of 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 h.
(ii) Metabolic features: retention of urea and creatinine, sodium and water, potassium (hyperkalaemia) and acid (metabolic acidosis).
(ii) Causes: pre-renal (reduced perfusion); intrinsic renal (vascular, inflammation, infiltration, toxicity); post-renal (obstruction).
(iii) Stage 1: PCr 1.5-1.9 times baseline or 0.3 mg/dL rise, urine below 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6-12 h. Stage 2: 2.0-2.9 times baseline, below 0.5 mL/kg/h for 12 h or more.
(iii) Stage 3: 3.0 times baseline or PCr 4.0 mg/dL (353.6 µmol/L) or more, or renal replacement therapy started (or, under 18 years, eGFR below 35 mL/min/1.73 m2); urine below 0.3 mL/kg/h for 24 h or anuria for 12 h or more.
(iii) RIFLE classes: Risk, Injury, Failure, Loss (persistent acute renal failure over 4 weeks) and end-stage kidney disease (over 3 months).
(iv) In renal failure a urea:creatinine ratio of 40-100:1 is normal or post-renal, above 100:1 is pre-renal, and below 40:1 is intrinsic renal damage; in suspected pre-renal failure urea tends to rise before creatinine.
(iv) Creatinine-based eGFR equations are only useful when function is stable and are not recommended in acute renal failure or unstable creatinine.

A(i) Exposure phase, toxicokinetic phase (absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion) and toxicodynamic phase.
A(ii) Routes: ingestion (most often seen clinically; must be absorbed into the circulation for systemic effect, mostly by passive diffusion; if unabsorbed may cause local effects such as diarrhoea, bleeding, malabsorption), inhalation and transdermal absorption.
A(ii) Bioavailability is the fraction of a dose available for absorption; factors: time and frequency of exposure, route, dose, physical and chemical form (particle size, solubilisation).
A(ii) Dose-response: the toxic response increases as dose increases, though not all individuals respond at the same dose.
A(iii) Absorption: transmembrane movement by simple diffusion (Fick's law), filtration through aqueous pores or carrier mediation, governed by lipid-water solubility (Kow), ionisation (pKa) and molecular size.
A(iii) Distribution: four fates (site of toxic action, storage, metabolism, excretion) via blood and lymph; barriers: blood/brain, placental, mammary; affected by tissue affinity, blood flow, protein binding, route and rate of metabolism; redistribution e.g. enterohepatic recirculation.
B(i) Phase I is bioconversion (toxicity and metabolism affected by environmental and genetic factors); phase II is conjugation, described as 'grease to salt'.
B(ii) Excretion is renal or non-renal (biliary, expiration, gastric secretion).
C(i) Additive 2 + 2 = 4: two organophosphates leading to cholinesterase inhibition.
C(i) Synergistic 2 + 2 = 10: CCl4 with ethanol leading to hepatotoxicity.
C(ii) Potentiation 2 + 0 = 6: isopropanol with CCl4, and tumour promoters.
C(ii) Antagonism 2 + 2 = 0: antidotes.
questions.question:
A. Describe the phases of toxicant handling under the following headings:
A(i) The three phases of toxicology.
A(ii) Routes of exposure, bioavailability and the dose-response relationship.
A(iii) Absorption and distribution.
B. State the fate of a toxicant in the body:
B(i) Metabolism.
B(ii) Excretion.
C. Explain the basis of interactions between concurrent exposures:
C(i) Additive and synergistic effects.
C(ii) Potentiation and antagonism.

A patient with advanced cirrhosis becomes confused and disoriented after a large protein meal. He is known to have ascites.
(i) State the agents that commonly damage the liver, and define cirrhosis.
(ii) List the complications of cirrhosis, and describe the grades and biochemical findings of the condition affecting this patient.
(iii) Explain the mechanism of the ascites and the associated electrolyte disturbance.
(iv) Describe hepato-renal syndrome as a complication.
(v) Outline the management options for the ascites and the encephalopathy, and justify one of them.
questions.answerText:
(i) Common insults: hepatitis viruses and other infections, alcohol, drugs (e.g. paracetamol), autoimmune disease, inherited metabolic disorders (Wilson's, haemochromatosis, AAT deficiency) and cystic fibrosis.
(i) Cirrhosis: diffuse hepatic fibrosis, nodular regeneration and disturbed hepatic architecture; the end result of several chronic liver diseases, usually with recurrent cell death and attempts at regeneration.
(ii) Complications: hepatic encephalopathy, ascites, hepato-renal syndrome, primary hepatic malignancy, endocrine dysfunction.
(ii) Encephalopathy occurs in advanced cirrhosis and may be precipitated by a large protein meal or infection. Grade I: alert with asterixis; II: confusion, disorientation, inappropriate behaviour; III: restless, sleepy, uncommunicative; IV: coma.
(ii) Diagnosis is essentially clinical with characteristic EEG; blood NH3 usually parallels but correlates poorly with degree of encephalopathy; high NH3 also occurs in urea cycle enzyme disorders (more common in children).
(iii) Ascites is excessive fluid in the peritoneal cavity; mechanism uncertain, but the primary event appears to be Na+ retention (? hyperaldosteronism) compounded by hypoalbuminaemia and localised to the peritoneal cavity by portal hypertension.
(iii) It develops in advanced decompensated disease; urine may be sodium free; excess water retention leads to hyponatraemia, probably due to increased ADH.
(iv) HRS is functional renal failure: kidneys are histologically normal and features of ATN are absent. Onset shown by rising creatinine and urea and urine output below 300 mL/24 h; hyperkalaemia is dangerous and may precipitate encephalopathy.
(iv) It is progressive, not reversed by fluid repletion; intense renal vasoconstriction reduces renal blood flow and GFR; distinguished from ATN by dramatic Na retention; precise pathogenesis unknown.
(v) Ascites managed with water and salt restriction plus aldosterone-blocking agents, needing careful monitoring of serum and urine Na+ and K+, blood pH and serum urea, since hyperkalaemia, hyponatraemia, azotaemia and pH derangement can precipitate encephalopathy.
(v) Justified option: blood NH3, although it may not parallel severity of coma, is a good guide to dietary protein intake to avoid precipitating coma.

A(i) Sex chromosomes determine whether the primitive gonads become testes; mature testes synthesise sperm and androgens; tightly packed seminiferous tubules are lined by maturing germ cells and Sertoli cells, with Leydig cells in the interstitial tissue.
A(ii) Sertoli cells are crucial for sperm maturation and secrete inhibin (negative feedback on FSH); FSH acts on Sertoli cells for germ cell differentiation, spermatogenesis and inhibin production; activin enhances spermatogenesis.
A(ii) Leydig cells are the primary site of androgen (mainly testosterone) production, stimulated by LH; testosterone inhibits LH; both FSH and LH are necessary for normal spermatogenesis, though testosterone secretion can occur without normal seminiferous tubules.
A(iii) Testosterone (about 95% from Leydig cells; about 5% from peripheral conversion of DHEA and androstenedione) is required for sexual differentiation, spermatogenesis, sexual maturity at puberty and anabolism; metabolites are 17-ketosteroids in urine.
A(iii) Mechanisms: direct binding to the androgen receptor; conversion by 5-alpha-reductase to dihydrotestosterone (skin, prostate: pubic hair, prostate enlargement); aromatisation to oestradiol; penis formation depends on testosterone.
B(i) With the Y chromosome fetal gonads become testes at about the 7th week; Sertoli cells secrete anti-Mullerian hormone inhibiting Mullerian ducts; DHT (5-alpha-reductase) is essential for external genitalia, and its deficiency gives feminisation (male pseudohermaphroditism).
B(i) Testosterone peaks at the start of the 2nd trimester, drops before birth, surges at 2-3 months of age and falls to baseline by 6-12 months; low until puberty; elevated through adulthood until the 3rd-4th decade, then gradually declines.
B(i) The decline reflects fewer Leydig cells, decreased GnRH pulse amplitude and increased SHBG; with symptoms it is termed ADAM, PADAM, late-onset hypogonadism, andropause (misleading) or testosterone deficiency syndrome.
B(ii) Sertoli cell failure reduces inhibin and raises FSH; Leydig cell failure reduces testosterone and raises LH.
B(ii) Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism (raised FSH/LH, low testosterone): primary testicular failure (chemotherapy, mumps orchitis, trauma, radiation, autoimmune), Klinefelter (47,XXY), androgen insensitivity, 5-alpha-reductase deficiency, cryptorchidism.
B(ii) Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (low FSH/LH and testosterone): Kallmann's syndrome (anosmia and GnRH deficiency), pituitary and cerebral tumours, head trauma, hyperprolactinaemia.
B(ii) Common male disorders: erectile dysfunction, micropenis/dysmorphic external genitalia, sperm dysfunction (low count, dysmorphology, motility) and infertility.

A(i) Largest internal organ, in the right hypochondrium; upper border between the 5th and 6th ribs, lower border just below the right costal margin on inspiration.
A(i) Two main lobes, right and left; the larger right lobe has both the quadrate and caudate lobes.
A(ii) Receives about 25% of resting cardiac output; the hepatic artery supplies 25% of total blood supply but 70% of oxygen supply.
A(ii) The remaining 75% of blood flow comes from the portal vein, which drains most of the GI tract and the spleen.
A(iii) Hepatocytes make up 60% of liver cells; the rest are endothelial (Kupffer) cells lining the sinusoids plus vascular and supporting tissue cells.
A(iii) Functional unit is the portal tract surrounded by radiating cords of hepatocytes; blood enters the acinus via the portal tract and passes along sinusoids to the central vein.
B(i) Oxygen concentration falls with distance from the portal tract toward the central vein, so cells around the central vein are most susceptible to anoxia and injury from a wide range of toxic substances.
B(ii) Periportal cells, which receive well oxygenated blood, have relatively high concentrations of the enzymes usually measured in blood, e.g. alkaline phosphatase and the aminotransferases.
B(iii) Hepatocytes lie in one-cell-thick plates between sinusoids carrying mixed portal venous and hepatic arterial blood; portal supply draining the stomach puts the liver at great risk of disease.
B(iii) Common insults: hepatitis viruses, alcohol, drugs (e.g. paracetamol), autoimmune disease, inherited metabolic disorders (Wilson's, haemochromatosis, AAT deficiency).
C(i) Hepatic artery: 25% of blood flow but 70% of oxygen supply. Portal vein: 75% of blood flow, draining the GI tract and spleen.
C(ii) Hepatocytes perform the major metabolic, synthetic, excretory, storage and detoxification functions; Kupffer cells act as a sieve, phagocytosing and degrading bacteria and antigens reaching the liver from the GIT via the portal tract.
questions.question:
A. Describe the anatomy and blood supply of the liver under the following headings:
A(i) Location, borders and lobes.
A(ii) Blood supply, and the contribution of each vessel to flow and oxygen.
A(iii) Cell populations and the functional unit.
B. Explain the clinical basis of regional vulnerability within the liver:
B(i) Why cells around the central vein are most susceptible to injury.
B(ii) Why the enzymes measured for diagnosis are concentrated in the periportal cells.
B(iii) Why the portal blood supply and other insults put the liver at risk of disease.
C. Distinguish between:
C(i) The hepatic artery and portal vein supply.
C(ii) Hepatocytes and Kupffer cells.

questions.answerText:
(i) Down syndrome (trisomy 21): most common serious autosomal disorder (1 in 700 live births); three copies of chromosome 21 (extra long-arm region q22.1-q22.3); mental retardation, hypotonia, congenital heart defects, flat face; risk rises with maternal age (1:1000 at 25 years, 1:90 at 40 years).
(ii) Amniocentesis: a needle is inserted through the abdominal wall into the amniotic cavity to withdraw 10-20 mL of fluid (total about 180 mL); done after 14 weeks, preferably at 16-18 weeks; fetal cells are collected for karyotyping.
(ii) Ultrasound guidance is used to locate the fetus, maternal bladder and placenta; it is invasive with a small but real risk of harming the fetus or causing spontaneous abortion.
(iii) Fetal karyotyping (chromosomal analysis; cells cultured, result in 2-3 weeks); fetal enzyme assay for inborn errors of metabolism (if both parents are carriers); fetal DNA diagnosis.
(iv) Chorionic villus sampling at 8-12 weeks (trans-cervical or trans-abdominal); chromosome analysis in 24 h without culture; DNA or biochemical tests in 1-2 weeks, so termination if needed can be done in the first trimester; risks: spontaneous abortion and trans-cervical infection (3 in 1000).
(v) First trimester: low PAPP-A, high hCG (free beta or total), increased nuchal translucency and nasal bone assessment; NT alone detects 60% or more at a 5% screen-positive rate; PAPP-A plus hCG with maternal age gives 60% detection at 5% false positive rate.
(v) Second trimester: AFP low, uE3 low, hCG high, inhibin A high; triple test (AFP, hCG, uE3) plus inhibin A gives the quadruple test, which increases sensitivity by 8%; a positive screen is confirmed by ultrasound; first plus second trimester testing gives 85% detection at 1% false positive rate.
(v) The high hCG may be because the extra chromosome 21 carries a transcription factor that up-regulates hCG synthesis; ultrasound has no proven hazard to mother or fetus.
questions.question:
A pregnant woman over 35 years of age has maternal serum screening at 16-18 weeks showing decreased AFP, decreased oestriol, increased hCG and increased inhibin-A.
(i) State the diagnosis and its genetic basis and phenotype.
(ii) Name the definitive procedure, how it is performed, its timing, volume, guidance and risks.
(iii) State the tests done on the sample.
(iv) Name the alternative earlier procedure with its timing, advantages and risks.
(v) State the first-trimester screening markers and the value of the triple and quadruple tests.

questions.answerText:
(i) Lead toxicity: lead is a common environmental contaminant, used to be in household paint and gasoline; exposure occurs by various routes, most through dietary ingestion of contaminated material.
(ii) Toxicity relates to binding of macromolecular structures; lead is a potent inhibitor of many enzymes (vitamin D and heme synthetic pathways), causing changes in bone and calcium metabolism and anaemia, plus neurological effects and decreased intelligence.
(ii) Lead distributes into bones and soft tissue and is eliminated through the renal system.
(iii) Assay: chromogenic reaction; most common method is graphite furnace atomic absorption spectrometry.
(iv) Arsenic: exposure environmental or occupational, absorption depends on the form, toxicity related to protein binding; assay atomic absorption spectrophotometry.
(iv) Cadmium: from industrial processes (electroplating), paints and plastics; exposure by inhalation, protein binding, accumulates in the kidneys; assay AAS.
(iv) Mercury: exposure by inhalation and ingestion of contaminated food; binds protein changing structure and function, inhibits enzymes, most notable effect is renal; assay AAS.
questions.question:
A patient shows neurological effects, decreased intelligence and anaemia after exposure to a common environmental contaminant, most likely through contaminated food.
(i) State the diagnosis, the sources and the routes of exposure.
(ii) Explain the pathologic basis, including enzyme inhibition and distribution in the body.
(iii) State the laboratory assay.
(iv) Name the other metals or metalloids that cause toxicity, with their target organ or mechanism and assay.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Toxicology is the science of adverse effects of chemicals on living systems; a poison is any substance that causes harmful effect when administered by accident or design.
A(i) Two functions: assess likelihood of adverse effects (qualitative, hazard identification) and study nature and mode of action (quantitative, dose-response, hazard characterisation); purpose is to protect human health and the environment and inform risk assessment (risk = hazard x exposure).
A(ii) Descriptive (animal experiments to predict harm to humans), mechanistic (cellular and biochemical effects), analytical (how much), forensic (medicolegal consequences) and clinical (toxin exposure and disease states).
A(ii) Specialty areas: by target organ (e.g. neurotoxicology), target species, and selected responses (teratology, carcinogenesis); applied: occupational, clinical, forensic, regulatory, developmental.
B(i) Local effects occur at the site of contact (GIT, lungs); systemic effects are distant (CNS, kidney, lungs). Immediate effects appear minutes to hours after a single exposure; delayed effects days to years; some are both.
B(ii) Reversibility depends on tissue involved, length of exposure and magnitude of insult; reversible in rapidly regenerating tissue (liver, intestinal mucosa, blood cells); irreversible: CNS damage, carcinogenesis, mutagenesis, teratogenesis.
C(i) TD50 is the dose toxic in 50% of the population, ED50 the dose effective in 50%, LD50 the dose predicted to cause death in 50% (simplest measure of toxicity); not all individuals respond at the same dose.
C(i) Therapeutic index is TD50/ED50; a high index is preferable because a much higher dose is needed to reach the lethal threshold than to give therapeutic effect, so drugs with a large index have few toxic adverse effects.
C(ii) Acute: harmful effects from single or short-term exposure.
C(ii) Subchronic: effects for more than one year but less than the lifetime of the organism.
C(ii) Chronic: harmful effects over an extended period, usually with repeated or continuous exposure, sometimes lasting the whole life of the organism.
C(ii) Toxicity is the degree to which a substance can harm humans or animals.
questions.question:
A. Describe the basic principles of toxicology under the following headings:
A(i) Definition, the two basic functions and the purpose.
A(ii) Classification and specialty areas.
B. Explain the clinical basis of the types of toxic response:
B(i) Local versus systemic, and immediate versus delayed responses.
B(ii) Reversible versus irreversible responses.
C. Distinguish between:
C(i) TD50, ED50, LD50 and the therapeutic index.
C(ii) Acute, subchronic and chronic toxicity.

A 65-year-old man with a known lung malignancy presents with confusion, abdominal pain and frequent urination. Serum calcium is found to be markedly elevated.

(i) What biochemical abnormality is present?
(ii) Which organ systems are affected by this abnormality, based on the symptoms described?
(iii) What are the differential causes of this abnormality in this patient?
(iv) Provide the clinico-biochemical reasoning to differentiate the malignancy-related cause from primary hyperparathyroidism.
questions.answerText:
(i) Abnormality: hypercalcaemia.
(ii) Systems affected: the recognised symptoms of hypercalcaemia are weakness, lack of energy, nausea and vomiting, lack of appetite, frequent urination and abdominal or bone pains, reflecting effects on the neuromuscular/general, gastrointestinal and renal/urinary systems, consistent with this patient's confusion, abdominal pain and frequent urination.
(iii) Recognised differential causes: primary hyperparathyroidism (adenoma or glandular hyperplasia), hyperthyroidism, benign familial hypocalciuria, malignancy, multiple myeloma, increased vitamin D, thiazide diuretics, and prolonged immobilisation.
(iv) Reasoning: malignancy may increase serum Ca2+ levels either due to metastasis to bone or ectopic production of PTH-like substances by the tumour, both mechanisms resulting in bone resorption; given this patient's known lung malignancy, ectopic PTH-related protein production or bony metastasis are the most likely mechanisms, distinguishing this from primary hyperparathyroidism, where the hypercalcaemia instead arises from a parathyroid adenoma or hyperplasia directly increasing PTH secretion and its actions on bone, kidney and (via vitamin D activation) the intestine; distinguishing the two in practice draws on the recognised differential list and the presence of a known malignancy, as here.

questions.question:
A patient presents with weakness, weight loss, hyperpigmentation of the skin and mucous membranes, postural hypotension, hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia.
(i) Identify the structure and zones involved.
(ii) Explain the mechanism of each group of signs.
(iii) State the differential pathologies.
(iv) Explain the clinico-biochemical reasoning used to confirm and classify the disorder.
questions.answerText:
(i) The adrenal cortex (adrenal insufficiency; primary adrenal disease = Addison's disease); zona glomerulosa makes aldosterone, zona fasciculata and reticularis make cortisol and androgens.
(ii) ACTH excess: hyperpigmentation of skin and mucous membranes. Glucocorticoid deficiency: weakness, weight loss, fatigue, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, hypotension, hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, eosinophilia, lymphocytosis.
(ii) Mineralocorticoid deficiency: postural hypotension, dehydration, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, non-anion gap metabolic acidosis, salt craving; sex steroid deficiency: loss of body hair (infertility; delayed secondary sex characteristics in children).
(iii) Primary/acquired: autoimmune destruction (isolated or polyglandular), infections (TB, HIV), neoplastic destruction, metabolic disorders (adrenal leukodystrophy, Wolman disease, Smith-Lemli-Opitz), haemochromatosis.
(iii) Congenital: adrenal hypoplasia congenita, congenital adrenal hyperplasia (21-hydroxylase deficiency most prevalent), lipoid adrenal hyperplasia. Secondary: reduced CRH/ACTH from hypothalamic or pituitary disease; iatrogenic: long-term glucocorticoid suppression causing adrenal atrophy.
(iv) Low cortisol and aldosterone indicates a primary adrenal disorder; low cortisol with low ACTH indicates insufficiency secondary to pituitary disease; onset is insidious and adrenal crisis can occur under stress if undiagnosed.
(iv) Short Synacthen test: 250 µg IM/IV, cortisol at baseline, 30 and 60 min; normally a rise of at least 200 nmol/L to at least 580 nmol/L; a steady rise at 60 min may imply secondary hypoadrenalism.
(iv) Depot Synacthen 1 mg with cortisol at 1, 2, 4, 8, 24 h: peak at 4-8 h is normal, delayed peak at 24 h or later suggests secondary insufficiency, cortisol <50 nmol/L suggests primary failure; also metyrapone test, spot morning cortisol (useful if <3 or ≥20 µg/dL) and 24-hour urinary free cortisol.

questions.question:
A. Describe the toxicology of the following agents under the headings of use, effects and mechanism:
A(i) Organophosphate and carbamate pesticides.
A(ii) Salicylates.
A(iii) Amphetamines and anabolic steroids.
A(iv) Cocaine and opiates.
B. Explain the basis of acid-base and organ effects of overdose:
B(i) Acid-base disturbances.
B(ii) Organ effects.
C. State the tests used for detection:
C(i) Screening and confirmatory tests for salicylates, amphetamines, anabolic steroids and opiates.
C(ii) Specimen and detection window for cocaine.
questions.answerText:
A(i) Pesticides are used intentionally to kill undesirable life forms (insecticides, herbicides); food contamination is the major route, with inhalation, transdermal absorption and hand-to-mouth ingestion in occupational and accidental exposure; actions are mostly nonselective, affecting various organs.
A(i) Organophosphates and carbamates inhibit acetylcholinesterase (acetylcholine is a neurotransmitter with many effects); tested by serum pseudocholinesterase activity (SChE); cholinesterase is made in the liver.
A(ii) Aspirin is an analgesic, antipyretic and anti-inflammatory drug; being an acid it leads to metabolic acidosis in overdose.
A(iii) Amphetamines are used for narcolepsy and attention deficit disorder; stimulants with high abuse potential giving an initial sense of increased mental and physical capacity; overdose causes hypertension, cardiac arrhythmia, convulsions and possibly death.
A(iii) Anabolic steroids are related to testosterone and used to increase muscle mass and performance; chronic use causes toxic hepatitis, enlarged heart and atherosclerosis.
A(iv) Cocaine is an effective local anaesthetic with few side effects at therapeutic concentration but a potent CNS stimulator at high levels; an alkaloid salt given IV or inhaled as free base; its main hepatic metabolite is benzoylecgonine.
A(iv) Opiates (opium, morphine, codeine natural; heroin and hydromorphone synthetic) are analgesic and anaesthetic with high abuse potential.
B(i) Aspirin overdose gives metabolic acidosis; acute opiate overdose gives respiratory acidosis from depression of the respiratory centre, plus cardiac damage.
B(ii) Organ effects: amphetamines (cardiovascular, CNS), anabolic steroids (liver, heart, arteries) and opiates (respiratory centre, heart) as listed above.
C(i) Salicylates: gas or liquid chromatography, immunoassay, chromogenic method. Amphetamines: urine, immunoassay screening then liquid or gas chromatography.
C(i) Anabolic steroids: gas chromatography with mass spectrometry. Opiates: initial immunoassay.
C(ii) Cocaine: benzoylecgonine in urine, detectable 4-7 h after use, up to 3 days after a single use and 20 days in chronic use; confirmation by gas chromatography.

questions.question:
A pregnant woman in the late second or early third trimester has hypertension, proteinuria and oedema.
(i) State the diagnosis and the term used if convulsions occur.
(ii) Describe the biochemical abnormalities and the life-threatening complication associated with it.
(iii) List the other maternal complications of pregnancy that should be considered.
questions.answerText:
(i) Preeclampsia: hypertension, proteinuria and often oedema, usually late in the 2nd or early in the 3rd trimester; if the mother develops convulsions it is called eclampsia.
(ii) Biochemical abnormalities: proteinuria, raised serum creatinine, deranged liver function tests and raised serum uric acid; serum uric acid may be used to assess severity and provide an index of prognosis.
(ii) HELLP syndrome (haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, low platelets with preeclampsia): life-threatening, in 0.1% of pregnancies; most prominent features thrombocytopenia and DIC; jaundice in 5%; very high LD (haemolysis); ALT and AST 2-10 times the upper reference limit.
(iii) Other conditions: ectopic pregnancy, hyperemesis gravidarum, liver disease, Graves disease, haemolytic disease of the newborn.
(iii) Hyperemesis gravidarum: nausea and vomiting (dehydration and malnutrition if severe), first trimester, with transient physiological hyperthyroidism from high CG; exclude Graves' disease with thyrotropin receptor antibodies.
(iii) Cholestasis of pregnancy: third trimester, diffuse pruritus, jaundice in 10%; serum bile acids up to 100 times normal; raised prothrombin time (vitamin K malabsorption); benign but risks premature birth and fetal death and recurs.

questions.question:
A two-week-old baby who was fed with milk from birth is noted by the mother to have fair hair and skin lighter than that of other family members, and blue eyes. At six weeks a musty odour is noticed in the baby's urine, and the child later develops seizures and increased muscle tone.

(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) What are the predisposing factors for this condition?
(iii) What is the pathophysiology underlying the clinical features?
(iv) What is the management of this condition?
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Phenylketonuria (PKU), the commonest inborn error of amino acid metabolism and the commonest inherited cause of mental retardation.
(ii) Predisposing factors: deficiency of the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase, which converts phenylalanine to tyrosine; it can also be caused by deficiency of dihydrobiopterin (DHBP) synthetase and DHBP reductase, enzymes that synthesise or reduce the coenzyme dihydrobiopterin.
(iii) Pathophysiology: phenylalanine and its metabolites (phenylpyruvic acid, phenylacetate and phenyllactate) accumulate in blood and are excreted in urine, producing the musty odour; persistent postnatal hyperphenylalaninaemia causes irreversible brain damage, mental retardation (by age one year) and convulsions.
Reduced tyrosine levels cause deficiency of melanin formation (hypopigmentation of hair, skin and eyes) because hydroxylation of tyrosine by tyrosinase is competitively inhibited by high phenylalanine levels; infants appear normal at birth with blue eyes and fairer hair/skin than other family members.
(iv) Management: treatment must begin during the first 7-10 days of life and continue for many years (at least till age 8) to prevent mental retardation, aiming to keep blood phenylalanine close to normal without letting it fall too low since phenylalanine is an essential amino acid.
Tyrosine must be supplied in the diet as it cannot be synthesised from phenylalanine in PKU; feeding is with synthetic amino acid preparations low in phenylalanine, supplemented with natural foods such as vegetables, fruits and certain cereals; in maternal PKU, dietary control must begin before and be maintained throughout pregnancy to avoid microcephaly, mental retardation and congenital heart abnormalities in the fetus.

questions.question:
A young child presents with generalised body swelling. Urinalysis reveals heavy proteinuria, and blood tests show a markedly reduced serum albumin with a raised serum cholesterol.

(i) What is the diagnosis, and what associated risk factor or cause is recognised for this condition?
(ii) What complications or associated protein changes occur?
(iii) What management options are available, and which would you justify in relation to the underlying oedema?
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: nephrotic syndrome. Among recognised causes of hypoalbuminaemia/protein loss relevant here is glomerulonephritis (a protein-losing kidney disease), and nephrotic syndrome is itself specifically recognised as a cause of hypoproteinaemia leading to oedema.
(ii) Complications/associated changes: the patient loses serum albumin and low molecular weight proteins in the urine, with some IgG also lost; at the same time there is an increase in alpha-2 macroglobulin, beta-lipoprotein, complement components and haptoglobulin, giving a dramatic decrease in the relative amount of albumin and a marked increase in the relative amount of alpha-2-globulin fractions on serum electrophoresis. The resulting hypoalbuminaemia reduces colloid osmotic pressure, forcing fluid out of capillary beds at the arterial ends without adequate return at the venous ends, producing generalised oedema; increased blood cholesterol/lipoprotein is also part of the recognised electrophoretic pattern (raised beta-lipoprotein).
(iii) Management options: correcting or controlling the underlying cause and preventing tissue injury; diuretic therapy; and administering albumin intravenously to raise the colloidal osmotic pressure when oedema is caused by hypoalbuminaemia, as in this case.
Justification: because the oedema here is specifically due to hypoproteinaemia (reduced colloid osmotic pressure) rather than increased capillary pressure or permeability, intravenous albumin administration to directly raise colloidal osmotic pressure is the specifically indicated option, used alongside diuretic therapy and treatment of the underlying renal cause.

A(i) The pituitary (hypophysis) lies in the sella turcica, connected by the infundibular stalk to the median eminence of the hypothalamus; anterior lobe (adenohypophysis) and posterior lobe (neurohypophysis); about 0.6 g, 12 mm transverse and 8 mm anteroposterior.
A(i) The hypothalamus (coordinating centre of the endocrine system) sends trophic hormones along the stalk through portal vessels to the adenohypophysis; the axis affects thyroid, adrenal, gonads, growth, milk production and water balance.
A(ii) Five hormone-secreting populations: acidophils (somatotrophs: GH; lactotrophs: prolactin); basophils (thyrotrophs: TSH; gonadotrophs: FSH and LH; corticotrophs: POMC cleaved to ACTH, beta-endorphin, beta-LPH); chromophobes are thought inactive but adenomas can secrete e.g. prolactin.
A(ii) Release of all pituitary hormones is episodic (pulsatile hypothalamic releasing factors) with slower diurnal rhythms superimposed.
A(iii) The posterior pituitary does not synthesise hormones; AVP (ADH) and oxytocin are synthesised in magnocellular neurons of the paraventricular and supraoptic nuclei, transported along axons and stored in nerve terminals.
B(i) Microadenomas (<1 cm, confined to the sella) and macroadenomas (≥1 cm); secretory and non-secretory varieties.
B(i) Frequencies: lactotroph (PRL) 30%, somatotroph (GH) 15%, combined GH/PRL 8%, corticotroph (ACTH) 15%, thyrotroph 1%, plurihormonal 4%, nonfunctioning 27%.
B(i) Functional tumours: excess prolactin (prolactinoma), excess ACTH (Cushing disease), excess TSH, excess GH (acromegaly, which can present as a large mass because bony growth is noticed late).
B(ii) Growing tumours can compress the optic chiasm causing visual field defects; bitemporal hemianopia is the most frequent presentation.
B(ii) Hormonal deficiency may involve one or more hormones with progressive loss of others; causes: neoplasm (adenoma, craniopharyngioma, metastases), iatrogenic, granulomatous disease, haemorrhage/infarction (Sheehan's syndrome, trauma, apoplexy), internal carotid aneurysm, autoimmune hypophysitis, haemochromatosis.
B(ii) Without trophic hormones the target glands cannot maintain normal secretion and atrophy; hyposecretion of a hormone suggests a compressive effect.
B(ii) Deficiency of pituitary hormones causes hypofunction of the target endocrine glands, so assessment tests target gland and pituitary hormones.

A(i) Cyclical, coordinated changes in ovaries and uterine lining regulated by reproductive hormones to prepare the woman for pregnancy; occurs between puberty and menopause; 21-35 days, average 28.
A(i) Ovaries contain 300,000-400,000 primordial follicles at birth; 10-15 begin developing each cycle but usually only 1 matures (300-400 in a lifetime); ovarian follicular, ovulatory and luteal phases lead to menstrual, proliferative and secretory uterine phases.
A(ii) Follicular phase starts day 1 with bleeding (about 5 days): low oestradiol, low LH and FSH begin to rise (loss of negative feedback); a group of follicles grows; around day 7 one follicle becomes especially FSH-sensitive and matures while others atrophy; rising E2 regenerates the endometrium.
A(iii) Rapid development of the dominant follicle and rising E2 trigger an LH surge (positive feedback); ovulation occurs about 16 h later.
A(iv) High LH luteinises the granulosa cells of the ruptured follicle to form the corpus luteum, which secretes progesterone (principal luteal hormone, peaks about 8 days after ovulation) and oestradiol, preparing the endometrium for implantation; progesterone is also pyrogenic.
A(iv) If fertilisation occurs the corpus luteum persists; if not it regresses, ovarian hormones fall, the endometrium sloughs (fall in progesterone) with menstrual bleeding, LH and FSH rise and the cycle restarts.
B(i) The developing follicle has an oocyte surrounded by theca (internal and external) and granulosa cells; both FSH and LH are needed for follicular maturation and steroid synthesis.
B(i) LH stimulates theca cells to produce androgens, which diffuse into granulosa cells where FSH causes them to be aromatised to oestrogens.
B(ii) Day-21 progesterone assesses whether ovulation occurred: without ovulation the corpus luteum fails to form and the cyclic progesterone rise is subnormal.
B(ii) Oestradiol is the most important ovarian oestrogen (aromatisation of androgens); oestrone is produced by liver and adipose tissue; oestriol is relatively inactive; extraglandular aromatisation rises with body fat.
B(ii) Menopause: permanent termination of menstruation (women ≥50 years) when all follicles have atrophied, with low oestrogens and raised FSH and to a lesser extent LH from loss of negative feedback.
B(ii) This resembles primary gonadal failure (hypergonadotrophic hypogonadism).

questions.question:
A patient attends the emergency department with dyspnoea and is suspected of having heart failure.
(i) State the diagnosis, its definition and the spectrum and functional classes of the condition.
(ii) Name the biochemical test that helps and state the diagnostic landmarks.
(iii) Identify the structures that release the relevant peptides and their actions.
(iv) State the prognostic use and the non-cardiac variants that raise the test.
questions.answerText:
(i) Heart failure: a syndrome of ineffective pumping leading to fluid accumulation in the lungs, typically from loss of cardiac tissue; an abnormality of cardiac function preventing the heart from pumping enough blood for the needs of metabolising tissue.
(i) Spectrum: primary impairment of pump function (e.g. after a large AMI), increased cardiac stiffness restricting filling, and high-output failure from excessive peripheral demand.
(i) NYHA class I: no symptoms or limitation; II: mild symptoms, slight limitation; III: marked limitation, comfortable only at rest; IV: severe limitation, symptoms at rest.
(ii) Plasma BNP or NT-proBNP by immunoassay; a normal concentration virtually rules out cardiac failure, and it separates patients needing further assessment from those unlikely to have failure.
(ii) The definitive diagnosis is best made by echocardiography, though access may be limited or delayed.
(iii) ANP is produced in the atria and released when atrial wall tension rises; BNP is mainly released from the ventricles (also found in brain) and rises in cardiac failure and ventricular hypertrophy; CNP is in endothelial cells, brain and kidney.
(iii) Circulating forms: NT-proBNP and proBNP (function unknown) and BNP (physiologically active C-terminal part). ANP and BNP cause natriuresis and increase venous capacitance, reducing ECF volume; CNP is a potent vasodilator with local action.
(iv) Higher levels mean greater morbidity and mortality in CHF or AMI.
(iv) BNP is non-specific: raised with expanded fluid volume (renal failure, hepatic cirrhosis, primary aldosteronism).

(i) The kidney (glomerular function): a ratio above 100:1 indicates a pre-renal cause, urea absorption being increased compared with creatinine; in suspected pre-renal failure (fluid depletion, cardiac failure) urea tends to rise before creatinine.
(ii) 40-100:1 is normal or a post-renal cause of AKI; below 40:1 is intrinsic renal damage (urea unable to be absorbed, ratio nearer 1).
(iii) Other differentials: corticosteroids, GI haemorrhage, protein-rich diet, severe catabolic state.
(iv) Urea is the final product of protein and amino acid metabolism (ammonia converted to urea in the liver); about 90% is excreted by the kidney but a variable filtered fraction is reabsorbed and about 10% is lost in sweat and gut, so excretion does not accurately reflect GFR.
(iv) At low urine flow (dehydration) reabsorption rises, raising plasma urea despite normal GFR; it is also affected by protein turnover (dietary protein, catabolic states, GI bleed amino acid absorption). BUN measures only the nitrogen (28 of 60 g); urea = 2.14 x BUN.
(v) Urea has only limited value; creatinine with eGFR is preferred, and urea should not be used as a general test of renal function; its place in 'electrolytes and urea' is largely historical.
(v) Useful for monitoring renal replacement treatment (haemodialysis, peritoneal dialysis) and urea kinetic modelling Kt/V (K urea clearance, T dialysis time, V total body water), ideal value above 1.0.
(v) In the kidney urea contributes to medullary hypertonicity, important for generating concentrated urine.
questions.question:
A patient in renal failure with raised plasma creatinine has a plasma urea:creatinine ratio above 100:1.
(i) Identify the organ assessed and interpret the ratio.
(ii) State the ratios in the other categories of cause.
(iii) List the non-renal differentials that raise urea.
(iv) Explain why urea is a poor general test of glomerular function.
(v) State the residual uses of urea measurement in renal disease.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Autoimmunity is an immune response directed against self antigen causing structural and functional damage, via autoantibodies and/or autoreactive T cells; it is very common but not necessarily disease, which arises when autoreactive lymphocytes damage the organ containing the target autoantigen.
A(i) Features: hyperglobulinaemia, constant production of autoantibodies (IgM, IgG, IgA) and extensive cross-reactivity (polyreactivity).
A(ii) Failure mechanisms: defective deletion (negative selection) or receptor editing; defective number/function of regulatory T cells; defective apoptosis of mature self-reactive lymphocytes; inadequate inhibitory receptors; APC activation overcoming regulation.
A(ii) Genetic susceptibility and environmental triggers (infections, local tissue injury) contribute, with a central role for CD4+ Th cells (release of sequestered antigens, molecular mimicry and bystander activation, inappropriate class II MHC expression).
A(iii) Altered antigen theory (chemicals, radiation, mutations, infection alter surface antigens so they are non-self); cross-reactive antigen theory (group A streptococci cross-react with heart muscle, causing rheumatic heart disease).
A(iii) Hidden/sequestered antigen theory (lens, spermatozoa, CNS; post-traumatic uveitis and orchitis); forbidden clone theory (MHC class II on thyrocytes may give thyroiditis, on liver cells biliary cirrhosis).
A(iv) Strong genetic contribution: type 1 diabetes concordance 35-50% in monozygotic and 5-6% in dizygotic twins; most are polygenic; strongest links are with MHC/HLA (DR3 and B8 organ-specific; B27 ankylosing spondylitis; DR4 rheumatoid arthritis; DR3 and DR4 IDDM); NOD2 with Crohn's; AIRE with APS.
B(i) Pathogenic autoantibodies: autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (cold agglutinin disease), monoclonal anti-nerve glycoprotein antibodies causing peripheral neuropathy, monoclonal rheumatoid factor causing cryoglobulinaemia and vasculitis.
B(i) Familial transfer: babies of mothers with thyrotoxicosis or myasthenia gravis show transient thyroid hyperactivity or muscle weakness respectively.
B(ii) Organ-specific: response against a single organ or gland (myxoedema, thyrotoxicosis, pernicious anaemia, Addison's, IDDM); systemic: broad tissue spectrum via cell-mediated responses, autoantibodies or immune complexes (SLE, scleroderma, rheumatoid arthritis, dermatomyositis); diseases are chronic, progressive and self-perpetuating.
B(ii) Effector mechanisms include immune complexes, circulating autoantibodies and autoreactive T lymphocytes.
B(iii) Treatment: metabolic replacement (thyroxine, vitamin B12, cholinesterase inhibitors); immunosuppressants (cyclosporin), thymectomy, bone marrow graft, plasmapheresis, anti-inflammatory drugs; T-cell vaccination, blocking peptides, monoclonal antibodies, oral tolerance induction.

questions.question:
A patient in the third to fifth decade presents with headache, episodic hypertension, sweating and palpitations.
(i) State the diagnosis, its features and its distribution pattern.
(ii) Name the tissue of origin and describe catecholamine synthesis and metabolism.
(iii) State the biochemical investigations and the named dynamic tests with their interpretation.
(iv) State the indications for screening.
(v) State the syndromic variant.
questions.answerText:
(i) Pheochromocytoma: relatively rare, usually benign chromaffin cell tumour with hypersecretion of catecholamines; a surgically curable cause of hypertension; usually found in the 3rd-5th decades; features: headache, episodic or sustained hypertension, sweating, palpitations with or without tachycardia, weakness, fatigue, nausea (less common: flushing, dyspnoea, dizziness).
(i) Pattern of 10s: 90% adrenal, 10% extra-adrenal chromaffin cells, 10% bilateral or multiple, 10% malignant, 10% incidental.
(ii) The adrenal medulla (neural crest origin, sympathoadrenal axis): tyrosine to dopa by tyrosine hydroxylase (rate-limiting), then dopamine, norepinephrine and epinephrine; metabolised by COMT and MAO to metanephrines and vanillylmandelic acid (VMA).
(iii) Investigations: raised plasma catecholamines, plasma free metanephrines, raised urine catecholamines, urine VMA, urine total metanephrines and fractionated urine free catecholamines.
(iii) Clonidine suppression test (catecholamines raised but not diagnostic): normal is NE falling below normal or by >50% (normetanephrines below normal or 40% decline); failure to do so indicates pheochromocytoma.
(iii) Glucagon stimulation test (BP normal, catecholamines modestly raised): a threefold or greater rise in plasma NE or a level >2000 pg/mL indicates pheochromocytoma.
(iv) Screen in: episodic hypertension, refractory hypertension, labile BP, severe pressor response during anaesthesia, parturition, surgery or angiography, unexplained hypotension, family history (MEN 2A/2B, VHL, neurofibromatosis), incidental adrenal mass, idiopathic dilated cardiomyopathy, spells with exertion, straining, coitus or micturition.
(v) Variant: part of the MEN II syndrome (pheochromocytoma with hyperparathyroidism and medullary carcinoma of the thyroid).

A(i) About 300 mg bilirubin is produced daily: 80% of unconjugated bilirubin (UB) comes from the heme of old red cells; 20% from ineffective erythropoiesis and other heme proteins (myoglobin, cytochrome, peroxidase).
A(i) The heme porphyrin ring is opened to biliverdin, which is reduced to UB; UB is water insoluble but lipid soluble and is transported to the liver bound to albumin.
A(ii) In the hepatocyte bilirubin unbinds from albumin, binds ligandin Y and is transported to the smooth endoplasmic reticulum.
A(ii) There it is conjugated with glucuronic acid by uridyl glucuronyl transferase in a two-stage procedure, then actively secreted into bile canaliculi and excreted into the intestine with bile.
A(iii) In the terminal ileum bacteria hydrolyse the conjugate releasing free bilirubin, which is reduced to urobilinogen; some is excreted in stool as stercobilinogen.
A(iii) Urobilinogen bound to albumin enters the circulation and is excreted in urine via the kidneys; conjugated bilirubin absorbed by the terminal ileum returns to the liver by enterohepatic circulation and is re-excreted.
B(i) Jaundice is yellow discolouration of mucous membranes and conjunctiva when plasma bilirubin exceeds 50 µmol/L (over 1.5 times the upper limit of normal, about 3 mg/dL).
B(ii) About 95% of plasma bilirubin is unconjugated and protein bound, not filtered at the glomerulus and not detectable in urine; bilirubinuria reflects raised conjugated bilirubin and is always pathological.
B(ii) The healthy liver can handle 10 times the daily output, so plasma bilirubin is an insensitive test of liver function.
C(i) In newborns raised UB can cross the blood-brain barrier to the basal ganglia; UB also rises when displaced from albumin by high fatty acids or drugs such as sulphonamide.
C(i) Total loss of UDP glucuronyl transferase activity (a rare condition) gives severe neonatal unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia leading to kernicterus.
C(ii) In prolonged obstructive jaundice delta-bilirubin forms (conjugated bilirubin covalently linked to albumin); it is not filtered by the kidneys, so conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia can persist after bilirubinuria disappears.
questions.question:
A. Describe the metabolism of bilirubin under the following headings:
A(i) Production and transport in plasma.
A(ii) Uptake, conjugation and excretion by the hepatocyte.
A(iii) Intestinal fate, enterohepatic circulation and urinary excretion.
B. State the plasma level at which jaundice becomes evident, and the normal proportion and urine findings of unconjugated and conjugated bilirubin:
B(i) Plasma level for jaundice.
B(ii) Normal proportions and urine findings.
C. Explain the anatomical and biochemical basis of:
C(i) Kernicterus.
C(ii) Persistence of conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia after bilirubinuria has disappeared.

A patient recovering from an episode of acute pancreatitis develops muscle twitching and tingling around the mouth and in the fingers. Serum calcium is found to be low, with a normal serum albumin.

(i) What is the diagnosis?
(ii) What is the biochemical basis of this presentation?
(iii) What immediate considerations guide correction of this abnormality?
(iv) What is the definitive management?
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: hypocalcaemia with tetany, in this case as a recognised complication of acute pancreatitis.
(ii) Biochemical basis: hypocalcaemia in acute pancreatitis results from deposition of insoluble calcium soaps at sites of fat necrosis in and around the inflamed pancreas; more broadly, low serum Ca2+ is recognised in hypoparathyroidism, rhabdomyolysis, intestinal malabsorption, alkalosis and acute pancreatitis, and can also be due to low intake of calcium, vitamin D or magnesium, or high phosphate intake. Since the albumin here is normal, correction of the measured calcium for albumin is not required (the correction of 0.8mg/dl for every 1g/dl fall in albumin below 4.0g/dl only applies when albumin is low), confirming this is a true fall in calcium rather than an artefact of hypoalbuminaemia.
(iii) Immediate considerations: acid-base status must be considered, since alkalosis decreases serum calcium levels (worsening symptoms such as muscle twitching) while acidosis increases serum calcium; associated hypomagnesaemia should also be considered and corrected, as it is itself a recognised cause of hypocalcaemia.
(iv) Definitive management: the underlying cause (the acute pancreatitis) must be managed (conservative treatment with naso-gastric suction and IV fluids, as outlined for acute pancreatitis), with correction of contributing deficiencies (vitamin D, magnesium) as indicated.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old man with a small cell lung tumour presents with confusion, nausea and seizures. His serum sodium is found to be 118mmol/l, taken 36 hours after the onset of his symptoms. Plasma osmolality is reduced, while urine osmolality is inappropriately elevated for the plasma sodium.

(i) What is the most likely diagnosis?
(ii) What is the biochemical basis of this presentation?
(iii) What are the immediate measures for managing this severe abnormality?
(iv) What is the definitive/longer-term management of this condition?
