questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: Syndrome of Inappropriate ADH secretion (SIADH), with severe hyponatraemia (serum Na < 135mmol/l, here markedly low), here likely from ectopic ADH production by the lung tumour.
(ii) Biochemical basis: pathologic ADH excess causes reduced plasma osmolality, hyponatraemia, raised plasma ADH and raised plasma renin concentration, together with elevated urine osmolality and reduced urine output; causes of hyponatraemia in general include a water problem (excess of water relative to sodium) with impaired renal water excretion. A serum sodium below 120mmol/l for 48 hours or less (acute hyponatraemia) is considered a medical emergency, and symptoms include cerebral oedema, nausea, vomiting, lethargy, confusion, seizures and coma.
(iii) Immediate measures: for a serum sodium this low (<125mmol/l), hypertonic saline is used (isotonic saline is used when serum Na >125mmol/l); the rate of increase of serum sodium level should be less than 2mmol/h, because too rapid correction risks central pontine myelinolysis; serum and urine electrolytes are monitored during treatment.
(iv) Definitive management: therapy of SIADH itself is by decreasing water intake, together with treatment of the underlying cause (in this case, the malignancy driving ectopic ADH production).

questions.question:
A. Describe the isoenzymes of lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and creatine kinase (CK) under the following headings:
A(i) LDH subunits, isoenzymes and tissue distribution.
A(ii) CK subunits, isoenzymes and proportions in tissues and plasma.
B. Explain the clinical basis for using isoenzymes:
B(i) Why isoenzyme estimation is more useful than total activity.
B(ii) How isoenzyme patterns change in myocardial infarction, hepatitis and neoplastic disease.
C. Distinguish between:
C(i) CK-MB and total CK as markers of myocardial damage.
C(ii) Myocardial infarction and pulmonary embolism using enzymes.
questions.answerText:
A(i) LDH has two chain types (H, heart; M, muscle) forming five isoenzymes: LDH1 (H4), LDH2 (H3M), LDH3 (H2M2), LDH4 (HM3), LDH5 (M4).
A(i) LDH1 and LDH2 are in myocardium and RBC; LDH3 and LDH4 in kidney and skeletal muscle; LDH5 in skeletal muscle and liver.
A(ii) CK is dimeric with three isoenzymes: CK-1 (BB, brain), CK-2 (MB, heart) and CK-3 (MM, muscle). In cardiac muscle MB is 20-30% and MM 70-80%; in skeletal muscle MM is 98% and MB under 2%.
A(ii) In plasma MM is about 95% and MB 0-6%; BB is only in traces because its large size prevents passage across the blood-brain barrier.
B(i) LDH is widely distributed, so total plasma LDH is a nonspecific marker of cell damage; isoenzymes help distinguish hepatic disease from MI (LDH1 + LDH2 mark MI). LD assay is considered out of date today.
B(ii) Normal serum: LDH2 most prominent, LDH5 rarely seen. After MI LDH1 and LDH2 predominate; in acute viral hepatitis LDH5 and LDH4 predominate.
B(ii) LDH is elevated in neoplastic disease: LDH5 in breast and prostatic carcinoma; LDH2 and LDH3 in leukaemias; LDH1 > LDH2 also in kidney disease and megaloblastic anaemia.
B(ii) CK-MB rises in MI, CK-MM in muscular dystrophy and CK-BB in CNS diseases.
C(i) Cardiac muscle is the only tissue with more than 5% CK-MB, making CK-MB more sensitive and specific than total CK; total CK rises 4-6 h after chest pain, peaks at 24-48 h and stays raised 2-4 days.
C(i) A rise in total CK with CK-MB above 5% of total supports infarction; a rise in CK-MB alone is not diagnostic.
C(ii) Both present with chest pain: serum GOT (AST) and LDH are increased in MI, whereas in pulmonary embolism GOT is normal and LDH is increased.
C(ii) AST is raised in myocardial damage but has been replaced to some extent by total CK, especially CK-2.

A(i) Ductular cells produce a watery, HCO3--rich fluid (pH 8) via an inwardly-directed proton pump, in response to secretin released from the duodenum; its effect is to neutralise gastric acidity, providing an optimum pH for pancreatic enzymes.
A(ii) Acinar cells produce a low-volume, viscid, enzyme-rich fluid containing amylase, lipase, ribonucleases and proteases (trypsin, chymotrypsin, elastase, carboxypeptidase), secreted as inactive precursors to prevent autodigestion of the pancreas; the stimulus for this secretion is cholecystokinin (CCK), released from the duodenum in response to fatty acids and peptides, which also causes gall bladder contraction.
B) In acute pancreatitis, the probable common mechanism is premature activation of the acinar-secreted proteases within the pancreas, presenting with acute abdominal pain and shock from enzyme leakage causing inflammation and haemorrhage; serum amylase is the most widely used diagnostic test, though it returns to normal within about 72 hours.
Chronic pancreatitis is destruction of pancreatic parenchyma with replacement by fibrous tissue and cysts, presenting with malabsorption (particularly of fat) and sometimes secondary diabetes, usually with a strong ethanol association; on secretin/CCK testing, a low maximum bicarbonate concentration (reflecting ductular dysfunction) may be the only abnormality detectable in mild-to-moderate chronic pancreatitis, while low values across volume, HCO3- concentration and amylase output together indicate advanced disease.
C) Loss of the acinar exocrine secretion in chronic pancreatitis causes fat malabsorption; because people with insufficient pancreatic function (such as in pancreatitis or cystic fibrosis) tend to be deficient in vitamin D, this pancreatic exocrine failure can produce vitamin D deficiency at a site distant from the pancreas.
This distant vitamin D deficiency in turn impairs intestinal absorption of calcium and phosphate, so that pancreatic exocrine disease can ultimately manifest as a skeletal functional deficit (impaired bone mineralisation), a consequence far removed from the pancreas where the disease began.
questions.question:
A) Describe the exocrine pancreas under the following headings:
A(i) Ductular cell secretion
A(ii) Acinar cell secretion

B) Relate these two secretory components to the pathologies of acute and chronic pancreatitis.

C) Explain how chronic pancreatic disease can spread its effect to cause a distant, systemic functional deficit.

questions.answerText:
(i) Abnormality: a high anion gap (24, above the normal value of 12) metabolic acidosis. A high anion gap (12-20 or greater) always indicates a primary metabolic acidosis; this is a titration-type metabolic acidosis, caused by increased endogenous acid (lactic acid) titrating bicarbonate and causing the fall in [HCO3-], as distinct from a normal-gap (secretional) acidosis from direct bicarbonate loss.
(ii) Systems affected: an abnormal pH can disturb enzyme systems throughout the body, resulting in abnormal respiratory and cardiac function and derangements in blood clotting and drug metabolism; in lactic acidosis specifically there is reduced intravascular volume, reduced cardiac output and risk of cardiovascular collapse.
(iii) Differentials for a high anion gap in this setting: lactic acidosis (from shock/hypoxia, reduced intravascular volume and reduced cardiac output, as here), diabetic ketoacidosis (endogenous ketones), uraemic acidosis (renal failure), or exogenous acid ingestion such as ethylene glycol metabolites or salicylate, all of which are recognised causes of titration-type metabolic acidosis.
(iv) Reasoning: shock and cardiovascular collapse reduce tissue perfusion and oxygen delivery, driving anaerobic metabolism and lactic acid production; this acid is buffered by bicarbonate (lowering [HCO3-]) and the unmeasured lactate anion widens the anion gap, while increased pulmonary ventilation (compensatory hyperventilation) lowers pCO2 in an attempt to move pH back toward normal; in thoracic trauma, a concurrent primary respiratory acidosis (from chest injury) can combine with this metabolic (lactic) acidosis as an additive mixed disorder, producing a dangerously low pH, which is consistent with the severity of derangement described.
questions.question:
A patient in hypovolaemic shock following major trauma is found to have arterial blood gas results showing a low pH, low bicarbonate and a calculated anion gap of 24. Lactate is markedly elevated at greater than 6mmol/L.

(i) What acid-base abnormality is present, and what does the anion gap tell you about its mechanism?
(ii) Which organ systems are affected by this degree of acid-base derangement?
(iii) What are the possible differential causes of a high anion gap in this clinical setting?
(iv) Provide the clinico-biochemical reasoning linking the trauma/shock state to the laboratory findings.

questions.answerText:
A(i) Tolerance is unresponsiveness of an immune cell(s) to an antigen induced by prior exposure to that antigen; antigen-specificity differentiates it from immunosuppression.
A(i) All individuals are tolerant of self antigens; breakdown of self-tolerance results in autoimmunity; inducing tolerance may prevent graft rejection, treat autoimmune and allergic diseases and prevent immune responses in gene therapy and stem cell transplantation.
A(ii) Normally the immune system reacts against pathogens; tolerance and regulation give no response to self and harmless antigens (immunological equilibrium).
A(ii) Mechanisms: clonal deletion (elimination from the repertoire), clonal anergy (functional unresponsiveness), suppression (inhibition of activation) and immunologically privileged site (micro-environment conditioning).
A(iii) Central tolerance occurs in the primary lymphoid organs by clonal deletion/apoptosis; the principal fate of lymphocytes that recognise self antigens in generative organs is death.
A(iii) B cells may change specificity by V-J chain rearrangement (receptor editing), and failure of editing results in deletion; some T cells differentiate into regulatory (suppressor) T lymphocytes.
A(iii) Thymic selection of T lymphocytes (central T-cell tolerance) involves AIRE (autoimmune regulator); a single-gene mutation of AIRE is associated with APS.
A(iv) Peripheral tolerance occurs in the secondary lymphoid organs by anergy (T-cell anergy) and suppression; B cell tolerance has central and peripheral components.
B(i) Central: site primary lymphoid organ, mechanism clonal deletion/apoptosis; peripheral: site secondary lymphoid organ, mechanisms anergy and suppression.
B(ii) Immunologically privileged sites (brain, eye, testis, uterus in pregnancy) are conditioned to suppress immune responses, believed to be by cytokine expression.
B(ii) Sequestered antigens (lens of the eye, spermatozoa, central nervous tissue) are hidden from the circulation and are treated as non-self if exposed later.
B(ii) Post-traumatic uveitis and orchitis are thought to be autoimmune responses to self antigens released from their normal locations by trauma.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old man with a history of heavy alcohol intake presents with sudden severe abdominal pain and shock. Serum amylase is markedly elevated.

(i) What is the diagnosis, and what are the risk factors/associations for this condition?
(ii) What complications and associated biochemical features may be found?
(iii) What are the management options, and which would you justify choosing over the alternative?
questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: acute pancreatitis, a medical emergency frequently associated with alcohol, gallstones and hyperlipidaemia; the probable common mechanism is premature activation of proteases within the pancreas.
(ii) Complications/associated biochemical features: methaemalbuminaemia (from massive extravascular haemolysis), hyperglycaemia (from transient beta-cell dysfunction), and hypocalcaemia (from deposition of insoluble calcium soaps at sites of fat necrosis); jaundice and a lipaemic serum suggest that gallstones and hyperlipidaemia, respectively, may be the predisposing cause. Clinical presentation is with acute abdominal pain and shock from leakage of activated pancreatic enzymes into the pancreas and surrounding tissues, causing acute inflammation and haemorrhage.
(iii) Management options: treatment is generally conservative, with naso-gastric suction and intravenous fluids; alternatively, laparotomy could be considered as for other acute abdominal emergencies that mimic this presentation.
Justification: laparotomy is contra-indicated, as it would facilitate the intra-abdominal spread of the active pancreatic enzymes; the conservative approach (naso-gastric suction and IV fluids) is therefore the justified choice, reserving urgent surgery for the differential diagnoses that mimic acute pancreatitis (such as a perforating duodenal ulcer or bowel infarction), which do require it.

questions.question:
A. Describe proteinuria under the following headings:
A(i) Normal excretion and the classifications.
A(ii) Methods of measuring total protein and albumin.
B. State the appropriate urine specimen, collection and storage:
B(i) Type of urine and timing.
B(ii) Storage conditions.
C. Explain the basis of:
C(i) False-positive results.
C(ii) The limitations of dipsticks.
questions.answerText:
A(i) A small amount of protein (about 150 mg/day, largely Tamm-Horsfall protein) is normal; more is pathological and detected by dipstick depending on sensitivity.
A(i) Types: glomerular, tubular (pyelonephritic), overflow (Bence-Jones), post-renal; also primary, secondary, transient and orthostatic.
A(ii) Boiling: heat urine at pH 5 (10% acetic acid) to give a cloudy precipitate; sulphosalicylic acid (SSA) test: 20% SSA dropwise to 5 mL urine gives a cloudy white precipitate.
A(ii) Multistix measures total protein with other parameters (SG, pH, ketones, glucose, bilirubin, leucocytes, nitrite) by protein error of indicator; cheap and useful in field surveys.
A(ii) Albustix is albumin-specific (tetrabromophenol blue at acid pH): trace 15-30 mg/dL, + above 30, ++ 40-100, +++ above 100-300, ++++ above 500; microalbuminuria is measured by timed collection, ACR, strips and quantitative immunoassays.
B(i) Spot/random, clean catch (mid-stream) or timed (early morning, 4 h, 8 h overnight, 24 h); timed is most useful for albumin excretion rate and clearance tests; first voided urine is best.
B(ii) Use clean container for immediate assay; maximum storage at 2-4 °C is 8 weeks; for longer, -80 °C is recommended because some albumin is lost at -20 °C; ACR corrects for low rates of urine flow.
C(i) Boiling test false positives: phosphates. SSA false positives: tolbutamide, sulphonamide, aspirin, large doses of penicillin, raised uric acid, radiographic contrast.
C(i) Multistix false positives: inappropriately collected urine, detergent in the specimen bottle.
C(i) Albustix false positives: pigmenturia, oxyglobin, ammonia-based disinfectants, chlorhexidine (Dettol), very alkaline urine.
C(ii) Multistix is insensitive to globulin and Bence-Jones proteins and is not specific.
C(ii) Quantitative assays are accurate and specific but expensive, needing laboratory backup and trained personnel.

A(i) In the PCT, CO2 combines with water in tubule cells to form H2CO3, which splits into H+ and HCO3-; for each H+ secreted, a Na+ and a HCO3- are reabsorbed by the PCT cells, so bicarbonate is reclaimed at the same rate it enters the peritubular capillary blood.
The PCT also reabsorbs about 75 percent of filtered phosphate (with most of the remainder reabsorbed in the proximal straight tubule), the major site of phosphate homeostatic regulation.
A(ii) Intercalated cells of the distal tubule actively secrete H+ into the urine where it is buffered (chiefly by the phosphate buffer system) and excreted; the distal tubule segments have only a limited capacity for phosphate reabsorption (about 5 percent of filtered load).
Ammonium ion excretion, using NH4+ produced from glutamine metabolism in PCT cells, is a further renal mechanism, each glutamine metabolised yielding two ammonium ions (excreted in urine) and two bicarbonate ions (added to blood).
B) Renal tubular acidosis is a cause of hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis; proximal RTA impairs bicarbonate reclamation at the PCT, while distal RTA (and type 4 RTA) reflects a distal acidification defect with inadequate ammonium excretion, shown by a positive urinary anion gap.
Diabetic nephropathy is assessed by a rising albumin:creatinine ratio in random spot urine and by a falling eGFR staged using MDRD or CKD-EPI, with associated fall in serum calcium and rise in serum phosphate as renal function declines.
C) Renal failure (whatever the tubular segment primarily affected) impairs excretion of hydrogen ion and metabolic acids, producing systemic metabolic acidosis, and impairs phosphate excretion, causing hyperphosphataemia and a fall in serum calcium.
This fall in calcium and rise in phosphate act at a site distant from the kidney, the parathyroid gland, driving a secondary hyperparathyroidism that in turn causes excess osteoclastic bone resorption, a skeletal functional deficit far removed from the kidney itself.
Renal impairment of potassium excretion (renal failure being a recognised cause of hyperkalaemia) can similarly disturb cardiac conduction, a systemic effect that begins in the kidney but manifests as a distant cardiac deficit.
questions.question:
A) Describe the kidney's tubular handling of hydrogen ion, bicarbonate and phosphate under the following headings:
A(i) The proximal convoluted tubule (PCT)
A(ii) The distal tubule and collecting duct

B) Relate the different tubular segments to the pathologies encountered in renal tubular acidosis (RTA) and diabetic nephropathy.

C) Explain how kidney disease can spread its effect to cause a distant, systemic functional deficit.

A 28-year-old woman, 8 months pregnant and otherwise in good health, presents with generalised itching and no rash. Serum albumin is 37 g/L, adjusted calcium 2.31 mmol/L, phosphate 1.21 mmol/L, bilirubin 9 µmol/L, ALP 1032 U/L and ALT 36 U/L.
(i) Identify the organ involved and the most likely condition.
(ii) State the biochemical abnormality that may be the only finding, and the pregnancy-related source of raised ALP.
(iii) List the other sources and causes of raised ALP that form the differential.
(iv) State the further biochemical investigations and the simple screening test.
(v) Explain the clinico-biochemical reasoning.
questions.answerText:
(i) The liver: intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy, a condition of unknown aetiology possibly with a genetic basis, presenting clinically as pruritus.
(ii) Serum bile acids are typically (though not always) elevated, and the rise may be the only biochemical abnormality.
(ii) Serum ALP activity increases in normal pregnancy because of a placental isoenzyme contribution.
(iii) ALP is also raised in growing children, bone inflammation, intestine and placenta; and in bone disease (rickets, osteomalacia, Paget disease, osteogenic sarcoma), liver and biliary tract disease, and malignancy.
(iv) Measure serum bile acids and assay GGT activity and/or ALP; an ALP of hepatic origin with raised GGT and raised bile acids is strongly suggestive.
(iv) Flowers of sulphur is the simple screening test.
(v) Normal ALT and bilirubin with markedly raised ALP and pruritus point to a cholestatic pattern, which differs from the hepatocellular pattern (striking ALT/AST rise) and guides further investigation.

questions.question:
A patient presents with liver disease, glycosuria and a slaty-grey appearance of the skin.
(i) Identify the condition and the organs affected.
(ii) Distinguish its forms and the related state without tissue damage.
(iii) Give the other inherited metabolic conditions that enter the differential of liver disease and their markers.
(iv) State the diagnostic biochemical and histological findings.
(v) State the treatment and how relatives should be managed.
questions.answerText:
(i) Haemochromatosis: excessive iron deposition causing tissue damage, particularly to the liver, pancreas and heart; suggested by liver disease, glycosuria and slaty-grey skin.
(ii) Hereditary haemochromatosis is autosomal recessive, related to unregulated intestinal iron uptake (HFe gene mutated); secondary haemochromatosis occurs with multiple blood transfusions and alcoholism. Haemosiderosis is iron overload without tissue damage.
(iii) Wilson's disease (low caeruloplasmin) and alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency (low or absent AAT, cirrhosis and lung disease) are other inherited metabolic liver diseases; highly saturated TIBC with ferritin rise points to haemochromatosis.
(iv) Diagnosis depends on biochemistry: plasma iron usually above 40 µmol/L (reference 10-30); transferrin saturation usually above 50%, at times above 60% (reference 33%); ferritin usually above 1000 µg/L (upper limit 200), proportional to iron excess.
(iv) Ferritin starts to rise when hepatic iron stores exceed twice the reference range. Liver biopsy is usually done to assess liver damage; Perl's stain gives a semiquantitative assessment (Kupffer cells and hepatocytes); up to about 20 µmol/g dry liver weight is normal and above 40 µmol/g in haemochromatosis.
(v) Treatment is weekly venesection until iron deficiency anaemia develops and ferritin falls to within reference range; unless decompensation has set in it prevents progressive liver disease, though risk of hepatocellular carcinoma remains.
(v) Relatives should be screened to institute treatment before liver damage occurs; plasma ferritin and transferrin saturation are the most sensitive tests for presymptomatic detection.

(i) Alcoholic liver disease: an AST/ALT ratio above 2.1 is characteristic (pathognomonic).
(i) Other markers: hypertriglyceridaemia, raised IgA (beta-gamma fusion), macrocytosis, hyperuricaemia, raised carbohydrate deficient transferrin (biochemical gold standard), marked GGT rise especially with normal ALP.
(ii) Alcohol, an increasingly important cause of liver disease; GGT is elevated in alcoholics taking more than 45 g ethanol/day.
(iii) Alcohol is biotransformed to aldehyde then acid; chronic consumption leads to lipid accumulation in hepatocytes, then alcoholic hepatitis and finally cirrhosis; aminotransferases are not usually grossly raised in alcoholic hepatitis.
(iii) GGT is an inducible enzyme (false positives with enzyme-inducing drugs); a value over 5 times ULN warrants enquiry about alcohol; it is the best simple screening test (sensitivity 50%, specificity about 85%, improved by a normal ALP); CDT is more specific.
(iv) Suspected alcoholics may be screened with GGT with a normal ALP; early diagnosis of hidden alcoholism allows early control; blood alcohol assay and CDT are used for acute alcohol-related damage.
questions.question:
A patient has an AST/ALT ratio above 2.1, a markedly raised GGT with normal ALP, macrocytosis and raised IgA.
(i) State the diagnosis and the supporting diagnostic markers.
(ii) State the predisposing factors.
(iii) Explain the pathophysiology and the use of GGT and CDT.
(iv) State the investigations for screening.

A) Describe the stomach's secretory apparatus under the following headings:
A(i) The parietal cell and its secretions
A(ii) The chief cell and the antral G-cell

B) Relate these cell types to the common pathologies of the stomach and duodenum (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, gastric ulcer and duodenal ulcer).

C) Explain how gastric disease can spread its effect to cause a distant, systemic functional deficit.
questions.answerText:
A(i) The parietal cell produces HCl via a proton pump on its luminal surface: H+ derived from CO2 (via carbonic anhydrase) is pumped out in exchange for K+, while HCO3- formed in equimolar quantities enters the bloodstream via a HCO3-/Cl- antiporter (the "alkaline tide"). The parietal cell also secretes intrinsic factor (IF), a 44kD glycoprotein that binds vitamin B12 for absorption in the distal ileum.
A(ii) The chief cell secretes pepsinogen, activated to pepsin at low pH (<3). The antral G-cell secretes gastrin in response to fundal distension and small peptides (the "gastric phase"); gastrin acts on mast cells to release histamine, which stimulates parietal cell HCl secretion via H2 receptors, and gastrin secretion is itself inhibited by acid reaching the antrum (negative feedback) and by secretin.
B) In Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, autonomous gastrin secretion from a gastrinoma drives the parietal cell to hypersecrete acid, causing severe duodenal ulceration. Duodenal ulcer is often associated with high acid output (for example from G-cell hyperplasia), whereas gastric ulcer is often associated with below-normal acid output and a disturbed gastric mucosal barrier, and may be secondary to ethanol, aspirin, glucocorticoids or Helicobacter pylori infection.
C) Deficiency of intrinsic factor (from parietal cell disease, for example in atrophic gastritis with achlorhydria, or after gastrectomy) results in pernicious anaemia, because vitamin B12 absorption in the distal ileum depends on binding to intrinsic factor.
This deficiency of intrinsic factor from a gastric-cell source therefore produces its functional deficit at a distant site, since deficiency of vitamin B12 causes pernicious anaemia and (as noted for vitamin B12 deficiency) irreversible nerve and brain damage together with elevated homocysteine levels.
Thus a disease process confined to the gastric mucosa (loss of parietal cell mass/function) can manifest systemically as hematological and neurological deficit far removed from the stomach itself.

(i) Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) precipitated by omission of insulin therapy.
(ii) Biochemical basis:
- Insulin lack, with increased free fatty acids and ketone bodies (beta-hydroxybutyrate, acetone, acetoacetate) from lipolysis, lowers pH (acidosis); lactic acid from hypoxia also contributes.
- Hydrogen ion excretion falls and bicarbonate buffers the excess H+, so serum HCO3 falls; compensatory hyperventilation lowers pCO2 (compensatory respiratory alkalosis).
- Osmotic diuresis causes total body potassium loss, although pre-treatment plasma potassium is often raised (from acidosis, insulin lack, tissue catabolism and reduced GFR).
- Dehydration raises urea (more than creatinine) and creatinine; osmolality and anion gap are both raised.
(iii) Resuscitation: correction of dehydration with intravenous fluids together with commencement of insulin therapy (Rx = insulin and IV fluids), since these correct the volume deficit and switch off further ketogenesis; potassium falls once insulin and fluids are given as it shifts back into cells, so potassium must be monitored and replaced during treatment.
(iv) Definitive management: continued insulin therapy to correct the underlying insulin deficiency that precipitated the episode, with ongoing correction of the fluid, electrolyte (especially potassium) and acid-base disturbance until the ketosis and acidosis resolve.
questions.question:
A 19-year-old known type 1 diabetic is brought to the emergency room drowsy, breathing rapidly and deeply, with abdominal pain and vomiting of one day's duration. She had stopped taking her insulin because she was unable to eat. Random plasma glucose is markedly elevated and urine ketones are strongly positive.

(i) What is the most likely diagnosis?
(ii) What is the biochemical basis of this presentation?
(iii) What immediate measures are required to resuscitate this patient?
(iv) What is the definitive biochemical management of this condition?

questions.answerText:
(i) Diagnosis: primary hyperparathyroidism, due to a parathyroid adenoma or glandular hyperplasia.
(ii) Confirmatory investigations: measurement of serum calcium (corrected for albumin, since each 1g/dl fall in albumin below 4.0g/dl requires adding 0.8mg/dl to the measured calcium) together with assessment of circulating PTH-related mineral status; urinary calcium may also be measured, being useful in patients prone to renal stone development (urinary calcium, calcium-oxalate and calcium:creatinine ratio).
(iii) Biochemical mechanism: PTH stimulates osteoclastic activity in bone, releasing Ca2+ and HPO4, and in the kidney promotes absorption of Ca2+, excretion of HPO4- and activation of renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase (which increases active vitamin D and thus intestinal Ca2+/PO4- absorption); the net effect of unregulated excess PTH is hypercalcaemia, producing weakness, lack of energy, nausea and vomiting, lack of appetite, frequent urination and abdominal or bone pains.
(iv) Structures at risk: the kidney is at risk of over-excreting calcium leading to nephrolithiasis (renal stone development), and bone is at risk from excess osteoclastic resorption.
(v) Variant form: secondary hyperparathyroidism, which is a compensatory response of the parathyroid gland to a low serum calcium (for example due to renal or GI disease), as distinct from the primary disease of the gland itself (adenoma or hyperplasia) described above.
questions.question:
A 55-year-old woman is found on routine testing to have an elevated serum calcium. She complains of weakness, lack of energy, frequent urination and vague abdominal pains, and has a past history of recurrent kidney stones.

(i) What is the most likely diagnosis?
(ii) What confirmatory investigations would be used?
(iii) What is the biochemical mechanism of the hypercalcaemia?
(iv) What structure/organ is at particular risk of damage in this condition?
(v) Describe a variant form of this disorder.

questions.explanation: The governance rationale states that today's youth will govern tomorrow, but they need education and empowerment to do so constructively. Young people need to work constructively to improve their conditions, and their empowerment today determines the quality of leadership and governance in future decades. This argument connects adolescent reproductive health to broader development outcomes including democratic governance and national prosperity.
questions.question: The governance rationale for investing in adolescent reproductive health argues that these youth need education and empowerment because they will:
options: Become parents responsible for the next generation
Serve in national armed forces and security services
Form the primary tax-paying workforce of the nation

questions.question: Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is listed as a control measure for STIs. PEP is most effective when initiated:
questions.explanation: Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) is most effective when initiated within 72 hours of potential exposure, and earlier initiation provides greater protection. PEP involves a course of antiretroviral medications taken for 28 days to prevent HIV infection after potential exposure. The 72-hour window is a critical clinical guideline, and PEP should ideally be started as soon as possible after exposure. It is listed as a key STI control strategy alongside contact tracing and treatment.
options: Within 24 hours of potential exposure only
Within one week of potential exposure
At any time within one month of exposure
Only after laboratory confirmation of exposure

questions.question: The menstrual health component of reproductive health encompasses which key aspects?
options: Surgical management of menorrhagia and fibroids
Menstrual hygiene, education, healthcare, and societal support
questions.explanation: Menstrual health as a reproductive health component encompasses menstrual hygiene management, education and awareness about menstruation, healthcare access for menstrual disorders, and societal support for women managing menstruation. Physical, emotional, and social well-being related to the menstrual cycle are all included. This component addresses the widespread neglect of menstrual health as a health topic, particularly in settings where menstruation is stigmatised, limiting girls' school attendance and access to hygiene facilities.

Confidentiality protects clients from stigma and discrimination that could follow disclosure of sensitive health information. It is foundational to trust between client and provider in reproductive health services. Breach of this right can discourage future health-seeking behaviour.
questions.question: A nurse ensures that a client's HIV status disclosed during counselling is not shared with her employer. This upholds which reproductive right?
options: Right to equality and freedom from discrimination
Right to safety of reproductive technology
Right to choose whether to marry
Right to privacy and confidentiality of information

questions.explanation: Women are specifically advised not to douche after intercourse because it could spread infection farther into the reproductive tract. Douching does not provide protection against STIs or pregnancy; instead, it can disrupt the normal vaginal flora and facilitate the ascent of pathogens into the uterus, fallopian tubes, and beyond. This is particularly dangerous if an STI is already present.
options: It destroys beneficial bacteria that protect against STIs
It could spread infection farther into the reproductive tract
It alters cervical mucus pH and reduces natural conception rates
It increases the risk of urinary tract infections in the short term
It disrupts hormonal balance by introducing foreign chemicals vaginally

questions.explanation: The FLE curriculum includes at least seven key content areas: (1) Families and Individuals in Societal Contexts, (2) Internal Dynamics of Families, (3) Human Growth and Development across the Lifespan, (4) Human Sexuality, (5) Interpersonal Relationships, (6) Family Resource Management, and (7) Parent Education and Guidance. These areas are modelled on the National Council on Family Relations framework for comprehensive family life education.
questions.question: How many key content areas are identified in the Family Life Education curriculum as described in the lecture notes?

options: It eliminates the need for any future client visits
It is required solely for billing purposes
It has no bearing on quality of care
It enables continuity of care and progress tracking
It is only useful for legal defence in disputes
questions.question: A clinic manager explains to new staff why every family planning consultation must be accurately documented in client records. What is the primary advantage of thorough record keeping described in this context?
questions.explanation: Record keeping in family planning is described as crucial because it enables healthcare providers to maintain continuity of care, track individual client progress, and monitor overall programme performance. Poor record keeping can result in duplicated or unsafe care due to missing information. Good records also support community-level programme evaluation and planning.

options: Intersex individuals are those who identify psychologically with a gender opposite to biology
Intersex individuals are those who have undergone surgical sex reassignment procedures
Intersex individuals exclusively have two X chromosomes but present male phenotypes
Intersex is a hormonal condition exclusively caused by endocrine disorders in adulthood
Intersex individuals are those born with a mixture of female and male characteristics
questions.question: Which of the following statements about intersex individuals is accurate according to the definition of reproductive anatomy?
questions.explanation: Intersex refers to people born without some reproductive parts or with a mixture of female and male characteristics. This is a condition present at birth and is distinct from gender identity or surgical reassignment. Understanding intersex conditions is important for nurses providing reproductive health care, as it informs assessments of reproductive anatomy and guides sensitive communication about reproductive organ structure and function. Because sexuality is intertwined with a person's developmental stage and health status, nurses must proactively initiate related discussions rather than waiting for clients to raise them, who may feel too embarrassed to do so. This is especially relevant postnatally, when physical and emotional changes affect intimacy. Proactive assessment supports comprehensive, client-centred care.
options: Clients always raise sexual concerns unprompted
Sexual health is unrelated to postnatal recovery
Only specialist counsellors may discuss sexuality
Sexuality assessment is optional in holistic care
It is linked to developmental and health status
questions.question: A nurse working in a maternity unit routinely asks new mothers about resumption of intimacy and sexual concerns as part of postnatal assessment. Why is initiating such discussions a core nursing responsibility?

questions.explanation: Leydig cells of the testes synthesize testosterone, the primary male reproductive hormone. Testosterone not only helps in the formation of sperm through spermatogenesis but also drives the development of secondary sexual characteristics in males during puberty, such as deepening of the voice, development of facial hair, and growth of pubic hair. This hormone is essential to male reproductive health.
options: Testosterone secreted by Leydig cells of the testes
Progesterone secreted by Sertoli cells of the testes
Oestrogen secreted by Leydig cells of the testes
Cortisol secreted by Leydig cells of the adrenal glands
Luteinizing hormone secreted by the anterior pituitary gland
questions.question: Which hormonal secretion from which testicular cell type is responsible for developing secondary sexual characteristics in males?
During a scrotal examination, a nurse notes asymmetry, swelling, and tenderness on one side. Which of the following findings would most appropriately be classified as indicating potential pathology?
options: Bilateral symmetry with normal testicular size
Unilateral swelling, tenderness, or asymmetry of the scrotum
Consistent temperature and colour of scrotal skin
questions.explanation: Findings such as unilateral swelling, tenderness, or notable asymmetry during scrotal examination indicate potential pathology requiring further evaluation, unlike normal bilateral symmetry and non-tender texture. Recognising these abnormal findings supports timely referral for conditions such as varicocele, hydrocele, or infection. Family planning nurses conducting male reproductive assessment should be trained to distinguish normal from abnormal findings.

questions.question: The operational principle that Family Life Education 'takes an educational rather than a therapeutic approach' implies that it primarily:
options: Restricts its target audience to diagnosed individuals with health conditions
Relies on licensed therapists to deliver all content in formal settings
Avoids all controversial topics related to sexuality and reproduction
Focuses on building knowledge, skills and values rather than treating disorders
Prioritizes corrective intervention over preventive health strategies
questions.explanation: The operational principle that Family Life Education takes an educational rather than a therapeutic approach means it prioritizes building knowledge, values, and skills in individuals rather than treating existing psychological or medical conditions. It aims to prepare people for family roles and responsibilities through learning experiences rather than clinical interventions. This approach makes it accessible to the general population.

options: It means adolescents require no specific health interventions
It implies adolescent risk should be ignored in favour of potential
It means all adolescents face identical risks and potential
It suggests adult health strategies apply unchanged to adolescents
It requires nurses to provide supportive guidance while addressing specific risks
questions.question: A programme director explains that adolescence carries both enormous potential for growth and heightened vulnerability to risk simultaneously. Why is this duality especially important for nurses to understand?
questions.explanation: Recognising both the growth potential and vulnerability of adolescence enables nurses to provide developmentally appropriate support that nurtures strengths while mitigating risks. Ignoring either dimension would result in incomplete or ineffective care. This dual awareness underpins effective adolescent-centred nursing practice.

Adolescents are frequently described as underserved in sexual and reproductive health services due to judgemental provider attitudes, cost, and accessibility barriers. This gap contributes to poor SRH outcomes among this age group. Youth-friendly service models aim to specifically address these barriers.
options: Adolescents are an underserved group regarding SRH services
Adolescents have excessive access to SRH services
Adolescents are not affected by SRH concerns
Adolescent SRH needs are identical to adult needs
Adolescents require no specialised health services
questions.question: A community health worker notes that many adolescents in her area cannot access youth-friendly contraceptive services due to provider attitudes. Which SRH concern does this best describe?
A patient undergoing a pelvic scan is told her uterus has three distinct tissue layers. The middle, thick muscular layer responsible for contractions during labour is called:
questions.explanation: The myometrium is the thick, middle muscular layer of the uterus responsible for the powerful contractions of labour and menstruation. The endometrium is the innermost glandular lining shed during menstruation, while the perimetrium is the outer serous covering. This layered structure explains both menstrual shedding and contractile function.

questions.question: When comparing the rate of hormone decline in menopause versus andropause, which statement is accurate?
options: Both conditions involve gradual decline at similar rates
Andropause is sudden while menopause is gradual over decades
Menopause is sudden while andropause is gradual over years
Both conditions involve complete cessation of all sex hormones
Menopause is always induced surgically while andropause is natural
questions.explanation: Menopause involves a rapid and sudden decline in hormone levels that produces numerous symptoms signalling its arrival, while andropause involves a very gradual testosterone decline of approximately 1–2% per year. This rapid decline in menopause produces the characteristic acute symptoms like hot flushes and night sweats, whereas andropause symptoms develop slowly and insidiously. This difference in pace of hormone change explains why menopause is universally experienced while andropause is not recognised by all men.

questions.question: In the male reproductive system, the testis produces sperm and testosterone. Sperm matures and is stored in which structure?
questions.explanation: The epididymis is the coiled tubular structure attached to the posterior surface of the testis where sperm matures and is stored. Sperm produced in the seminiferous tubules of the testis pass to the epididymis for maturation, during which they acquire the ability to fertilise an ovum. From the epididymis, mature sperm travel through the vas deferens toward the ejaculatory duct during ejaculation.

questions.question: A programme director lists several ongoing obstacles to family planning uptake in her region, including one increasingly prominent challenge tied to online information sources. Which of the following best reflects a recognised new challenge to family planning today?
questions.explanation: Misinformation, including that spread through digital and social media, is identified as a growing new challenge to family planning uptake, compounding older barriers such as cultural resistance and limited access. This modern challenge requires updated, digitally-savvy public health communication strategies. Addressing misinformation is now a recognised priority in contemporary family planning programming.
options: Complete global absence of any contraceptive methods
Universal, unrestricted access to all methods everywhere
Total elimination of religious or cultural influence
Misinformation, including from digital and social media sources
Full consensus support from all governments worldwide

questions.question: The nurse's role in supporting survivors of sexual and gender-based violence primarily involves:
questions.explanation: The nurse's role in responding to sexual and gender-based violence includes providing support and resources for individuals experiencing abuse, as well as counselling and healthcare services for survivors. This role requires trauma-informed care that prioritizes the survivor's safety, autonomy, and dignity. Nurses must be skilled in both the clinical management of physical injuries and the psychosocial support of those who have experienced violence.
options: Disclosing abuse incidents to law enforcement without the survivor's knowledge
Conducting legal investigations and gathering forensic evidence for prosecution
Determining the credibility of abuse claims before providing healthcare services
Providing support, resources, counselling and healthcare services to survivors
Referring all abuse survivors exclusively to psychiatrists for ongoing care

questions.explanation: The prostate gland surrounds the urethra just below the bladder and secretes an alkaline fluid that neutralises vaginal acidity, aiding sperm survival and motility. The seminal vesicles contribute fructose-rich fluid for energy, while bulbourethral glands provide pre-ejaculatory lubrication. Prostatic secretion forms a significant portion of seminal fluid volume.
questions.question: A urology client is informed that a gland surrounding the urethra below the bladder adds alkaline fluid to semen to help sperm survival. Which gland is being described?

A client asks the nurse to name the origin of the personal beliefs that guide her sense of right and wrong in professional practice. According to the framework of nursing values, where do such values primarily originate?
questions.explanation: Values, including ethical and personal values relevant to nursing practice, originate from a combination of upbringing, culture, religion, and accumulated personal experience rather than from a single institutional source. This layered origin explains why values can vary meaningfully between individual nurses. Recognising this helps nurses reflect on and manage their own value systems in professional practice.
options: Exclusively from formal nursing school curricula
From upbringing, culture, religion, and experience combined

questions.question: The acquisition of skills for adult relationships and roles during adolescence specifically prepares young people for which future responsibilities?
options: Professional career management and occupational advancement
Leadership in government and political institutions
Adult relationships, parenthood, and civic participation
questions.explanation: Adolescence is the period during which young people acquire skills needed for adult relationships and roles, including parenthood, marriage, workplace participation, and civic engagement. ASRH programmes that develop these skills alongside health knowledge create a more complete preparation for adulthood. Skills in communication, conflict resolution, and relationship building developed during adolescence have lifelong impact on reproductive health outcomes and family functioning.

questions.question: During BSE step 4 (palpation while lying down), which hand is used to feel the left breast?
questions.explanation: During BSE Step 4, the right hand is used to feel the left breast, and the left hand is used to feel the right breast (cross-palpation technique). This contralateral approach allows the examining hand's finger pads to apply appropriate pressure across the entire breast in a circular motion approximately the size of a quarter. The examination covers the entire breast from top to bottom and side to side, using varying pressure depths — light for superficial tissue, medium for mid-breast, and firm for deep tissue.
options: The right hand feels the left breast
The left hand feels the left breast
Either hand may be used interchangeably
The dominant hand regardless of side

questions.explanation: Congenital malformations of the reproductive system are primarily caused by genetic conditions such as congenital adrenal hyperplasia, which can disrupt normal reproductive anatomy and function. These conditions arise from abnormal gene expression that affects the development of reproductive structures in utero. Nurses providing care to individuals with congenital reproductive malformations must be knowledgeable about their anatomical, hormonal, and psychological implications.
questions.question: Congenital Malformations related to reproductive health are primarily caused by:
options: Hormonal imbalances in the mother caused by polycystic ovary syndrome
Environmental toxins encountered during the second and third trimesters
Maternal nutritional deficiencies during the first trimester of pregnancy
Viral infections acquired during the neonatal period after delivery
Genetic conditions that disrupt normal reproductive anatomy and function

questions.explanation: Although the vagina is a distensible fibromuscular tube, its walls are normally in apposition (in contact with each other). They separate specifically during menstrual flow, sexual intercourse, and childbirth. This apposition helps maintain the vaginal environment and flora. The distensibility of the vaginal walls is a key adaptation for childbirth, allowing the fetal head to pass through the birth canal during the second stage of labour. SUBTOPIC 3: FAMILY LIFE EDUCATION
options: Exercise, pregnancy, and postpartum recovery only
questions.question: The vaginal walls are normally in apposition (touching) with each other. They are separated during which specific events?

options: No, abstinence provides no protective benefit at all
No, abstinence increases STI risk compared to condom use
Yes, abstinence alone fully prevents both risks
Yes, but only when combined with hormonal contraception
No, abstinence is only relevant for married individuals
questions.question: A young client asks whether abstaining from all sexual contact is considered a recognised safe sex practice. What is the most accurate response?
questions.explanation: Abstinence from sexual contact is recognised as the only method that completely eliminates the risk of sexually transmitted infection and pregnancy from partnered sexual activity. It is listed alongside other safe sex practices such as condom use and mutual monogamy with tested partners. Presenting abstinence as one valid option within a range of choices supports informed decision-making.

questions.question: A clinic offers free family planning commodities but requires clients to disclose personal reasons for method choice to a receptionist within earshot of others. Which service quality standard is violated?
questions.explanation: Reproductive health services must be delivered with privacy and confidentiality alongside being voluntary and informed. Public disclosure of personal reasons undermines client trust and discourages service use. Quality reproductive care requires private, respectful consultation spaces.
options: Voluntary, informed, and confidential provision of services

questions.explanation: Medullary carcinoma originates from ductal tissue but has a distinctive soft, fleshy consistency with well-defined borders, differentiating it from the more common invasive ductal carcinoma of no special type. Despite its aggressive-appearing cellular features, it often carries a relatively better prognosis. Recognising this variant is relevant for accurate pathological classification.
questions.question: A pathology report describes a breast tumour with a soft, fleshy consistency and well-defined borders originating from the same ductal tissue as most breast cancers. Which type is most consistent with this description?
options: Invasive ductal carcinoma of usual type

questions.explanation: The promotion stage of carcinogenesis is described as reversible because it involves changes in genome expression (which genes are turned on or off) mediated through promoter-receptor interactions, without changes in the actual DNA structure. This reversibility means that removing the promoting agent can potentially stop the progression to cancer. By contrast, the initiation stage involves irreversible genetic mutations, and the progression stage is also irreversible and characterised by malignant growth.
questions.question: The promotion stage of carcinogenesis is described as reversible because it involves changes in:
options: The DNA structure and base pair sequence
Genome expression without changes in DNA structure
Cell membrane permeability and receptor function

questions.question: A woman is counselled about a family of methods that involve tracking body signs such as basal body temperature and cervical mucus changes to identify fertile days. Which broader category do these methods belong to?
questions.explanation: Fertility Awareness Methods (FAMs) involve tracking physiological signs such as basal body temperature and cervical mucus to identify the fertile window and avoid unprotected intercourse during that time, distinguishing them from hormonal or barrier approaches. These methods are hormone-free but require diligent daily tracking for effectiveness. They are suitable for couples wishing to avoid hormonal or device-based contraception.

questions.question: A community health worker explains that reproductive health is important not only for married adults but also for adolescents. What is the primary rationale for this inclusive age range?
questions.explanation: Reproductive health needs and risks, including puberty, fertility, and STI exposure, begin during adolescence and continue throughout adulthood, justifying an inclusive, life-course approach to reproductive health services. Restricting services to married adults would leave significant unmet need among adolescents. This life-course view underpins comprehensive reproductive health programming.
options: Only married adults face reproductive health risks
Adolescents have no reproductive health needs until marriage
Needs and risks begin before and outlast childbearing years
Reproductive health risk begins only after menopause
Reproductive health is irrelevant until full adulthood

questions.question: A married woman is denied permission by her husband to attend antenatal care. Which reproductive right is being violated?
questions.explanation: The right to liberty and security protects women from coercion or restriction that endangers their health, including denial of essential maternal care. Reproductive health services must be accessible without a third party's consent. Nurses should advocate for the woman's autonomous access to care.
options: Right to liberty and security of person
Right to marry and found a family
Right to equality before the law
Right to benefits of scientific progress

questions.explanation: Sexual sadism involves achieving sexual arousal through inflicting physical or psychological suffering on another person, in contrast to masochism where the individual seeks to receive such suffering. When acted upon non-consenting partners, sadism carries significant legal and forensic implications. This distinction is central to differentiating the two related paraphilias.
questions.question: A man derives sexual gratification specifically from watching the physical or psychological suffering he inflicts on a non-consenting partner. Which paraphilia is described?
Breast Self Examination (BSE) should be performed by women at what frequency and timing?
options: Annually during a medical check-up by a provider
Bi-annually during the ovulatory phase of the cycle
Every six months during a routine gynaecological visit
Weekly during the premenstrual phase of the cycle
Once a month, immediately after menstruation from day 5
questions.explanation: BSE should be performed once a month, ideally immediately after menstruation from day 5 of the cycle, when breast tissue is least tender and swollen due to lower hormone levels. Post-menopausal women should perform BSE on a fixed date each month. Monthly BSE familiarises women with the normal look and feel of their breasts, enabling early detection of changes. About 20% of breast cancers are detected by physical examination rather than mammography.

Bisexuality is defined as sexual desire and interaction with both males and females. It is distinct from homosexuality, which involves exclusive attraction to persons of the same sex, and from heterosexuality, which involves exclusive attraction to the opposite sex. Bisexuality is a recognised sexual orientation that exists on a spectrum of sexual attraction. In the context of reproductive health and STI prevention, bisexual individuals may require specific counselling addressing all their sexual partnerships.
questions.question: Bisexuality is defined as sexual desire and interaction with both:
options: Adolescents and adults of either sex
Same-sex partners and opposite-sex partners at the same time
Humans and animals in specific cultural contexts
Males and females without preference for one sex

questions.question: Key developmental experiences of adolescence include physical and sexual maturation and also:
options: Movement towards social and economic independence and identity development
questions.explanation: Key developmental experiences during adolescence include physical and sexual maturation, movement towards social and economic independence, development of identity, acquisition of skills for adult relationships and roles, capacity for abstract reasoning, and exposure to powerful social influences. This period is simultaneously a time of tremendous growth and potential as well as considerable risk. Understanding these experiences is essential for designing appropriate adolescent health interventions.

options: Adolescents who experience attraction without sexual activity have delayed development
Sexual identity development is a gradual process that is not always tied to sexual experience
Sexual orientation is only validated when the adolescent has actual sexual experience
Romantic feelings in adolescents are always followed by sexual activity within 6 months
Adolescent attraction is a temporary phase that resolves once sexual experience occurs
questions.question: The statement that 'attraction can precede or occur concurrently with a first romance or first sexual experience' in adolescence is best interpreted to mean:
questions.explanation: The finding that attraction occurs in late childhood/early adolescence and can precede or occur concurrently with a first romance or first sexual experience indicates that sexual identity development is a gradual process not dependent on sexual activity. Adolescents may develop clear attractions and romantic feelings before ever being sexually active. This understanding is critical for nurses providing non-judgmental adolescent reproductive health care. SUBTOPIC 3: REPRODUCTIVE HEALTH, COMPONENTS, NORMS AND VALUES

In some low-income settings, maternal mortality ratios can exceed 1,000 deaths per 100,000 live births, starkly higher than rates in high-income countries, underscoring persistent global inequities in maternal care. This disparity reflects differences in access to skilled care, emergency services, and health system strength. Recognising this gap reinforces the urgency of Safe Motherhood Initiative goals.
options: Ratios can exceed 1,000 per 100,000 in poor settings
Maternal mortality ratios are identical worldwide regardless of income level
Maternal mortality only occurs in high-income countries
Maternal mortality ratios below 10 per 100,000 occur universally
Maternal mortality has been fully eliminated in all regions
questions.question: A woman in a low-income country region is told that her risk of dying from pregnancy-related causes is dramatically higher than in high-income countries. Which statistic best illustrates this global disparity?

questions.explanation: The birth control implant is classified as a hormonal method of contraception. It is a small, flexible rod inserted under the skin of the upper arm that releases progestin over a period of up to three to five years to prevent pregnancy, primarily by suppressing ovulation and thickening cervical mucus. Despite being physically implanted, its mechanism of action is hormonal rather than mechanical, distinguishing it from barrier methods and intrauterine devices.
questions.question: The birth control implant is classified as which type of contraceptive?
The nurse's role BEFORE clinical investigations in family planning includes which action?
options: Obtaining written consent from the patient's next of kin before all investigations
Administering pre-procedural sedation to all anxious clients as standard practice
Reassuring the patient and explaining the procedure to ensure physical and emotional readiness
Completing all administrative paperwork before attending to the patient
Conducting the investigation before discussing it with the client to save time
questions.explanation: Before clinical investigations, the nurse must reassure the patient, explain the procedure to the patient, and ensure the patient is ready both physically and emotionally for the procedure. These preparatory actions reduce anxiety, promote informed participation, and improve the quality of both the procedure and the clinical data collected. Patient preparation is a fundamental nursing responsibility that reflects respect for patient dignity and autonomy throughout the diagnostic process.

questions.question: A 30-year-old woman undergoes a screening test in which cervical cells are collected and examined microscopically for precancerous or cancerous changes. Which test is this?
questions.explanation: The Pap smear involves collecting and microscopically examining cervical cells to detect precancerous or cancerous changes, forming the cornerstone of cervical cancer screening. Colposcopy, by contrast, is a visual examination often used to further evaluate an abnormal Pap result. Regular Pap testing enables early detection and treatment of cervical dysplasia before progression to invasive cancer.

questions.question: A nurse consciously works to become comfortable and non-judgemental when discussing sexual topics with clients of varying backgrounds. What professional outcome is she aiming to achieve through this self-work?
questions.explanation: Nurse desensitisation refers to the process of becoming comfortable discussing sexual matters without personal bias or discomfort, which improves the quality and effectiveness of sexuality counselling. This is distinct from avoiding the topic or deferring entirely to other professionals. Achieving this comfort is a recognised professional development goal in reproductive health nursing.
options: Complete avoidance of all sexual topics
Desensitisation, enabling comfortable and effective sexuality counselling
Referral of all sexual concerns to physicians only
Imposing her personal values onto clients
Limiting sexuality discussions to married clients only

questions.explanation: The nurse's role in sexual health includes educating clients on safe sexual practices to prevent STIs, diagnosing, treating, and managing infections, and promoting healthy sexual relationships and the idea of consent. While nurses may not independently prescribe medications in all settings, their role in diagnosis, management, and health promotion is central to sexual health services. This comprehensive involvement distinguishes sexual health nursing from a purely educational role.
options: Performing colposcopy for detection of cervical pre-cancerous lesions
Diagnosing, treating and managing sexually transmitted infections
Prescribing antiviral medications for HIV management independently
Conducting mandatory STI testing for all sexually active patients
Restricting sexual activity recommendations to abstinence-only approaches
questions.question: Which of the following nursing actions falls within the role of the nurse in sexual health promotion?

questions.explanation: Endocrine disorders such as thyroid disease or problems with the hypothalamus cause infertility by altering hormone levels — producing too much or too little of a hormone — which prevents ovulation and leads to infertility. The hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis must function precisely for regular ovulation. Thyroid dysfunction, hyperprolactinaemia, and adrenal disorders can all disrupt this hormonal cascade, causing anovulation. Treating the underlying endocrine disorder often restores fertility. SUBTOPIC 6: MENOPAUSE, ANDROPAUSE, AND ONCOLOGY
options: Directly destroying the ovarian follicle reserve
Creating scar tissue within the uterine cavity
Producing too much or too little hormone, preventing ovulation
Blocking the fallopian tubes through inflammatory processes
Causing immune rejection of the embryo at implantation
questions.question: Endocrine disorders such as thyroid disease or hypothalamic problems cause female infertility primarily by:
The objective of SMI 'To improve quality and increase accessibility to family planning and maternal health care' targets which population?
questions.explanation: The Safe Motherhood Initiative's objective to improve quality and increase accessibility to family planning and maternal health care service targets all women of childbearing age—not just those already pregnant or those with complications. This universal approach recognizes that reproductive health is a right for all women, and that improving access and quality across the full spectrum of reproductive ages is necessary for achieving sustained reductions in maternal mortality and morbidity.
options: Adolescent girls under the age of 18 exclusively
Only high-risk pregnant women with identified complications
Married women with at least one previous pregnancy
Women in urban centers where health facilities are easily accessible

questions.explanation: The maternal prenatal care responsibilities identified in the content include attending regular prenatal check-ups, maintaining a healthy diet, taking prescribed prenatal vitamins, avoiding harmful substances, and monitoring fetal development. Self-administered ultrasound at home is not identified as a prenatal responsibility because ultrasound examination requires specialized equipment, training, and clinical interpretation. It remains a professional clinical procedure performed by trained health providers.
questions.question: The mothers' role in prenatal care specifically includes all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Attending regular prenatal check-ups with a healthcare provider
Performing self-administered ultrasound examinations at home during pregnancy
Taking prescribed prenatal vitamins and supplements during pregnancy
Avoiding harmful substances like tobacco and alcohol throughout pregnancy
Monitoring fetal development and reporting any concerns to a provider

questions.explanation: The statement that sexuality 'influences and is influenced by life experiences' demonstrates that sexuality is dynamic—it continuously evolves as individuals grow, develop, and encounter different life events. Sexuality is not static but is shaped by relationships, culture, health, and personal experiences throughout the lifespan. This dynamic nature means nurses must assess and address sexuality at all life stages.
questions.question: The concept of sexuality being 'influenced by and influencing life experiences' best illustrates which feature of sexuality?
options: Sexuality is entirely determined by cultural norms and peer pressure
Sexuality remains fixed and unchanging throughout the lifespan
Sexuality depends solely on genetic predisposition at birth
Sexuality is dynamic and continuously shaped by lived experiences
Sexuality is only relevant during the reproductive years of adulthood

questions.explanation: This statistic supports the public health rationale that early intervention during adolescence can reduce the burden of disease carried into adulthood. It highlights adolescence as a critical window for establishing healthy behaviours. This justifies prioritising resources for adolescent health promotion.
options: Adult disease is unrelated to adolescent behaviour
Only elderly populations require disease prevention
Disease burden is fixed regardless of early intervention
Investing in adolescent health prevents later adult disease burden
questions.question: A public health officer notes that nearly one-third of the adult disease burden traces back to conditions or behaviours that began during adolescence. What is the primary implication of this statistic for health planning?

options: The reciprocal influence between social institutions and families
Political parties' impact on family policies
International organisations' role in family planning programmes
Media's influence on adolescent sexual behaviour
Religious institutions' impact on fertility rates
questions.explanation: Societal Relations in FLE covers the reciprocal influence between major social institutions and families, specifically governmental, religious, educational, healthcare, and economic institutions. This bidirectional perspective recognises that families both shape and are shaped by broader social institutions. Understanding these dynamics helps families navigate societal pressures and equips FLE practitioners to design contextually appropriate programmes.
questions.question: The Societal Relations component of FLE covers which specific type of influence?

questions.explanation: Various cultures used herbal concoctions prepared with certain plants or mixtures believed to have contraceptive properties to prevent pregnancy. While some may have had some efficacy, significant safety and dosage concerns existed and some were not effective at all. Herbal contraception represents an important part of the cultural and historical context of family planning, though modern evidence-based practice requires that any contemporary use of herbal contraception be carefully evaluated for safety and effectiveness.
questions.question: Which of the following best describes the role of herbal remedies in early contraception?
options: Ancient herbal contraception had zero safety concerns and no dosage issues
Herbal remedies were universally effective in preventing pregnancy across all cultures
Herbal contraception was medically proven effective by Greek physicians
Herbal remedies were used exclusively in Asian cultures as primary contraceptives
Various cultures used plant-based concoctions believed to have contraceptive properties

questions.explanation: The levator ani, together with associated fascia, forms the main supportive sling of the pelvic floor, maintaining organ position and continence. Ligaments such as the broad and round ligaments provide additional but secondary support to the uterus. Strengthening this muscle group through exercises reduces risk of prolapse and incontinence.
questions.question: A nurse teaching pelvic floor exercises explains that this muscular sling supports the pelvic organs and controls continence. Which muscle group forms the main component of the pelvic floor?

questions.explanation: Family Resource Management focuses on decisions about allocating limited resources such as time, money, and material assets to meet family needs. This is distinct from Interpersonal Relationships, which addresses communication and conflict skills. Both areas contribute to overall family functioning taught in FLE.
questions.question: A parent-education session teaches young people to allocate time, money, and material assets wisely within a household. Which FLE content area is being addressed?

options: 20% to 25% of breast cancers are inherited
5% to 10% of breast cancers are inherited
30% to 35% of breast cancers are inherited
1% to 3% of breast cancers are inherited
40% to 50% of breast cancers are inherited
questions.question: Hereditary breast cancer accounts for approximately what percentage of all breast cancers?
questions.explanation: Approximately 5–10% of breast cancers are inherited (hereditary), due to genetic mutations such as BRCA1 and BRCA2 gene mutations. The remaining 90–95% are sporadic, caused by a combination of environmental, hormonal, and lifestyle factors. Women with inherited BRCA mutations have a significantly elevated lifetime risk of breast and ovarian cancer and may be offered enhanced surveillance or risk-reducing surgery. Genetic counselling is recommended for women with strong family histories.

options: Sexual identity and gender role development
questions.explanation: In the context of sexual and reproductive health, adolescent identity development closely relates to sexual identity and gender role development, including understanding sexual orientation, gender expression, and intimate relationship preferences. These processes are central to ASRH because they shape how adolescents perceive themselves as sexual beings and how they navigate relationships. ASRH programmes should create safe spaces for adolescents to explore identity questions without judgment.
questions.question: The development of identity during adolescence is described as a key developmental experience. In the context of SRH, identity development relates directly to:
Intimate relationship, as an aspect of sexuality, is defined as:
options: Long-term committed partnerships exclusively formalized through marriage
Deep emotional bonding between siblings or close family members
Non-sexual physical closeness such as embracing or holding hands
Intellectual and spiritual sharing between individuals of any relationship type
A romantic and/or sexual involvement with another person
questions.explanation: An intimate relationship, as an aspect of sexuality, is defined as a romantic and/or sexual involvement with another person. This is distinct from intimacy, which refers to sharing thoughts or feelings in a close relationship with or without physical closeness. The distinction between intimacy and an intimate relationship is important clinically, as nurses must assess both emotional and physical dimensions of a client's relational life when addressing sexual health.

options: Providing tax incentives for families who use contraception consistently
Mandating birth quotas for all families regardless of individual preferences
Penalizing families financially for having more than a nationally specified number of children
Restricting immigration to offset domestic population growth effects on the economy
Controlling birth rates to reduce the strain on resources and economic stability
questions.explanation: One reason family planning started was concern about overpopulation and its effects on resources and economic stability. Economic development concerns drove the interest in controlling birth rates as rapid population growth can strain national resources, reduce per capita income, and limit investment in education and health. Family planning allows societies to align population growth with available resources, supporting sustainable economic development.
questions.question: Family planning addresses the issue of overpopulation and economic development by:
A competitive athlete training intensively reports low libido and abnormal semen parameters. Which mechanism best explains how excessive exercise contributes to his infertility?
options: Increased scrotal blood flow enhancing sperm production
Excess body fat increasing testosterone levels
Improved cardiovascular fitness directly raising sperm count
Reduced core body temperature improving fertility
questions.explanation: Excessive physical exertion can disrupt the hormonal axis regulating spermatogenesis, as well as raise scrotal temperature in some cases, both of which impair sperm production and quality. This differs from moderate exercise, which generally supports overall health. Counselling on balanced physical activity is relevant in male infertility assessment.

questions.question: Emergency Obstetric Care is listed as a key component of SMIs primarily to address:
options: Transportation needs of pregnant women living in rural communities
Routine delivery services for all women regardless of complication risk
Postnatal monitoring of women after uncomplicated vaginal deliveries
Life-threatening obstetric complications that require immediate skilled intervention
Provision of analgesia for all laboring women as a standard service
questions.explanation: Emergency Obstetric Care (EmOC) is a key component of Safe Motherhood Initiatives specifically to address life-threatening obstetric complications that require immediate skilled intervention. Conditions such as severe hemorrhage, eclampsia, obstructed labor, and puerperal sepsis require prompt access to EmOC to prevent maternal death. The availability of functional EmOC services is one of the most critical determinants of maternal survival globally.

questions.question: Reproductive health is important for adolescents and adults primarily because:
questions.explanation: It is very important for adults and adolescents to be aware of sexual health, reproduction, contraceptives, and STDs because this knowledge helps in maintaining good reproductive health both physically and mentally. This awareness also protects both the mother and child from infectious diseases and enables delivery of healthy babies. Comprehensive reproductive health knowledge enhances quality of life for individuals from adolescence through old age.
options: It provides legal protection against reproductive health discrimination in employment
It helps maintain good physical and mental reproductive health with knowledge about sexuality and STDs
It ensures compliance with mandatory reproductive health screening programs
It fulfills international treaty obligations under the United Nations framework
It determines eligibility for government maternal and child health benefits

questions.question: After the hymen is perforated during sexual intercourse or childbirth, the remaining tissue tags are called:
questions.explanation: The remnants of the hymen after perforation are called carunculae myrtiformes, named because they resemble myrtle berries. These tags are clinically significant as physical evidence of prior perforation and are routinely identified during gynaecological examinations. Understanding their appearance is important for midwives and nurses conducting perineal assessments postpartum and in forensic examinations.

options: Premature ovarian failure with low oestrogen
questions.explanation: Heavy and painful periods (dysmenorrhoea and menorrhagia) as signs of infertility are most commonly associated with endometriosis and uterine fibroids. Endometriosis causes pelvic adhesions and inflammation that impair fertility, while fibroids can distort the uterine cavity and disrupt implantation. Both conditions produce heavy, painful menstrual bleeding. These symptoms should prompt investigation for underlying structural or endometriotic causes of infertility, as treatment may restore fertility.
questions.question: Heavy and/or painful periods are listed as signs of female infertility. These symptoms are most commonly associated with which condition causing infertility?
Which of the following is identified as a hormonal method of contraception?
questions.explanation: The birth control injection (Depo-Provera) is a hormonal method of contraception containing the hormone progestin, administered as an injection every three months to prevent pregnancy.
