questions.explanation: There are three taeniae coli on the large intestine: the free taenia, mesocolic taenia, and omental taenia. These bands converge at the root of the appendix and disappear at the rectosigmoid junction. The taeniae are approximately 1 cm wide and their contraction creates the characteristic sacculated appearance of the colon.

questions.question: The testicular artery typically arises from which vessel?
questions.explanation: The testicular arteries arise directly from the anterior aspect of the abdominal aorta, just inferior to the renal arteries at approximately the L2 vertebral level, reflecting the embryological origin of the testes in the posterior abdominal wall. These long, slender arteries descend obliquely across the psoas major muscle, ureter, and external iliac vessels before entering the deep inguinal ring as part of the spermatic cord. The right testicular artery crosses anterior to the inferior vena cava, while the left crosses anterior to the left renal vein, then both pass through the inguinal canal to supply the testes.

questions.question: Which artery supplies the bare area of the liver?
questions.explanation: The bare area of the liver, the part of the posterior surface devoid of peritoneal covering and in direct contact with the diaphragm, receives blood supply from the right phrenic artery (and sometimes left phrenic artery). This triangular area is bounded by the reflections of the coronary and right triangular ligaments. The bare area lies between the two layers of the coronary ligament and is continuous with the inferior vena cava, which is embedded in a groove on the posterior surface. Small diaphragmatic veins from the bare area drain directly into the IVC.

The depressor anguli oris (triangularis) depresses the angle of the mouth, contributing to expressions of sadness or frowning. It is a muscle of facial expression innervated by the marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve. The muscle arises from the mandible and inserts into the angle of the mouth.
questions.question: Which muscle depresses the angle of the mouth?
At what level does the abdominal aorta bifurcate into common iliac arteries?
questions.explanation: The abdominal aorta terminates at the lower border of the fourth lumbar vertebra (L4) by dividing into the right and left common iliac arteries, slightly to the left of midline. This bifurcation point corresponds roughly to the level of the umbilicus and represents the transition from the abdominal aorta to the pelvic arterial system. The median sacral artery also arises from the posterior aspect of the aorta just before its bifurcation.

questions.question: What percentage of people have right-dominant coronary circulation?
questions.explanation: Approximately 70% of people have right-dominant circulation, where the right coronary artery gives rise to the posterior interventricular (posterior descending) artery supplying the posterior third of the interventricular septum and diaphragmatic surface. About 10% have left-dominant (circumflex gives posterior interventricular), and 20% have co-dominant (contributions from both) circulation patterns.

questions.question: Which basal segment is often absent on left?
questions.explanation: The medial basal segment is often absent or rudimentary on the left side, or it may be fused with the anterior basal segment. This anatomical variation contributes to the left lung having fewer total segments (8-10) compared to the right lung (10 segments). This variation is clinically significant.

questions.question: Which spinal nerve roots contribute to the lumbar plexus?
questions.explanation: The lumbar plexus is formed by the anterior (ventral) rami of L1, L2, L3, and the upper part of L4 nerve roots within the substance of the psoas major muscle. The lower part of L4 joins with L5 to form the lumbosacral trunk, which contributes to the sacral plexus. The lumbar plexus gives rise to several important nerves including the iliohypogastric, ilioinguinal, genitofemoral, lateral femoral cutaneous, femoral, and obturator nerves, as well as branches to the psoas and quadratus lumborum muscles.

questions.question: Which region does the majority of the ileum occupy?
questions.explanation: The ileum predominantly occupies the right lower quadrant of the infracolic compartment, with the terminal ileum usually located in the pelvis. The ileum constitutes approximately 60% of the jejunoileal length. It characteristically ends at the ileocaecal junction on the medial aspect of the caecum.

The superolateral border of the popliteal fossa is formed by the biceps femoris muscle. The superomedial border is formed by semimembranosus and semitendinosus. The inferolateral border is the lateral head of gastrocnemius, and the inferomedial border is the medial head of gastrocnemius. The roof is formed by skin and fascia.
questions.question: Which muscle forms the superolateral border of the diamond-shaped popliteal fossa?

questions.explanation: The orbicularis oculi muscle closes the eyelids. It has orbital, palpebral, and lacrimal parts. The muscle is innervated by the facial nerve (VII). The palpebral portion produces gentle closure (blinking), while the orbital portion produces tight closure (squinting). Facial nerve palsy causes inability to close the eyelid (lagophthalmos).
questions.question: Which muscle closes the eyelid?

questions.explanation: The paired nasal bones articulate superiorly with the frontal bone at the frontonasal suture. Laterally, they attach to the frontal processes of the maxillae, and inferiorly to the upper lateral nasal cartilages. Fractures of the nasal bones are the most common facial fractures. The bones provide support for the nasal bridge.
questions.question: The nasal bones articulate superiorly with which bone?

questions.explanation: The pubofemoral ligament supports the hip joint inferomedially and limits extension and abduction. It is triangular, attaching superiorly to the iliopubic eminence and obturator crest, inferiorly merging with the capsule and lower band of the iliofemoral ligament. Strain of this ligament produces groin pain worsened by extension and abduction.
questions.question: The pubofemoral ligament of the hip joint limits which two movements?
The vallate papillae are arranged in which pattern?
questions.explanation: The 7-12 vallate (circumvallate) papillae are arranged in a V-shape along the sulcus terminalis at the junction of the anterior two-thirds and posterior third of the tongue. Each papilla is surrounded by a circular trench containing taste buds. Von Ebner's glands open into the trenches, washing the taste buds.

White rami communicantes carry preganglionic sympathetic fibers from spinal nerves T1-L2 to the sympathetic trunk. They are white because the preganglionic fibers are myelinated. These fibers originate from intermediolateral cell columns in the thoracolumbar spinal cord. White rami exist only at T1-L2 levels.
questions.question: What are white rami communicantes?

questions.explanation: The vagus nerve provides parasympathetic fibers that are bronchoconstrictor and secretomotor to bronchial glands. These fibers are also important for the cough reflex. The sympathetic trunk provides fibers that are bronchodilators and inhibit secretion from bronchial glands.
questions.question: Which nerve provides bronchoconstrictors to the lung?

options: L1 and T12 vertebral levels only
questions.explanation: The upper medial quadrant of the buttock receives cutaneous innervation from L1, 2, 3 and S1, 2, 3. The upper lateral quadrant receives L1 and T12. The lower medial quadrant receives S1, 2, 3, and the lower lateral quadrant receives L2, L3. This dermatomal pattern helps localize spinal pathology.
questions.question: The cutaneous innervation of the upper medial quadrant of the buttock is derived from which spinal segments?

questions.explanation: The platysma is a muscle of facial expression innervated by the cervical branch of the facial nerve. It lies in the superficial cervical fascia and extends from the chest to the mandible. The muscle tenses the skin of the neck and can depress the mandible and lower lip. Facial nerve paralysis causes platysmal weakness.
questions.question: The platysma muscle is innervated by which nerve?

questions.explanation: The styloglossus muscle arises from the styloid process and inserts into the side of the tongue. It retracts and elevates the tongue during swallowing. Like all tongue muscles except palatoglossus, it is innervated by the hypoglossal nerve (XII). The muscle interdigitates with the hyoglossus.
questions.question: Which muscle originates from the styloid process and inserts on the tongue?
How does the ulnar nerve's course make hand position affect its function?
options: Elbow flexion stretches nerve around medial epicondyle
questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve's course around the medial epicondyle means elbow flexion stretches the nerve. Prolonged flexion (sleeping with bent elbow) can cause compression symptoms. This positional sensitivity explains why cubital tunnel syndrome symptoms may worsen at night and why sleeping with extended elbows helps.

questions.question: The sciatic nerve is the largest nerve in the body. At the level of the popliteal fossa, it divides into which two terminal branches?
options: Sural nerve and posterior cutaneous nerve of thigh
Tibial nerve and common fibular nerve
questions.explanation: The sciatic nerve divides at the superior angle of the popliteal fossa (or sometimes higher in the thigh or even within the pelvis) into the tibial nerve (medial and larger) and the common fibular nerve (lateral and smaller). The tibial nerve innervates the posterior compartment of the leg and intrinsic muscles of the sole, while the common fibular nerve innervates the anterior and lateral leg compartments.

Maximum grip strength occurs with the wrist in 20-30° extension. This position optimally lengthens finger flexors for maximum tension development while stabilizing the wrist. Full flexion or extension reduces grip strength due to passive insufficiency or active insufficiency of finger flexors.
options: Wrist position does not affect grip strength
Strongest grip in full wrist flexion
Grip strongest with wrist in slight extension
Strongest grip in full wrist extension
Strongest grip in neutral wrist position
questions.question: How does wrist position affect grip strength?
The prostate gland is related posteriorly to which structure?
questions.explanation: The prostate gland is related posteriorly to the anterior wall of the rectum (ampulla), separated from it by the rectovesical fascia (fascia of Denonvilliers). This relationship allows the prostate to be palpated during digital rectal examination (DRE), where the posterior surface of the gland can be assessed for size, consistency, symmetry, and nodules. The prostate is related anteriorly to the pubic symphysis (retropubic space of Retzius), superiorly to the bladder base, and inferiorly to the urogenital diaphragm. The prostatic urethra passes through the gland from base to apex.

The ischiofemoral ligament reinforces the posterior aspect of the fibrous membrane. It attaches medially to the ischium posteroinferior to the acetabulum and laterally to the greater trochanter deep to the iliofemoral ligament. Like all three extracapsular hip ligaments, it becomes taut during extension, stabilizing the joint in the standing position.
questions.question: Which hip joint ligament reinforces the posterior aspect of the fibrous membrane and attaches medially to the ischium just posteroinferior to the acetabulum?

options: Calcaneus, talus, navicular, and first metatarsal
Calcaneus, navicular, cuboid, and all metatarsals
Calcaneus, cuboid, and all five metatarsals
questions.explanation: The lateral longitudinal arch is formed by the calcaneus, cuboid, and the 4th and 5th metatarsals. Its summit is the subtalar articulation. It is smaller, more rigid, more stable than the medial arch, and makes more contact with the ground. It bears body weight before the medial arch comes into play and has limited mobility, built to transmit weight.
questions.question: The lateral longitudinal arch is formed by which bones and is described as more rigid and making more contact with the ground?
Which sinus opens into the inferior meatus?
questions.explanation: The inferior meatus receives the opening of the nasolacrimal duct beneath the inferior turbinate. No paranasal sinuses drain into the inferior meatus. The maxillary, frontal, and anterior ethmoidal sinuses drain into the middle meatus. The posterior ethmoidal cells drain into the superior meatus. The sphenoid drains into the sphenoethmoidal recess.

questions.question: Which vein drains the left suprarenal gland?
questions.explanation: The left suprarenal vein drains into the left renal vein (along with the left testicular/ovarian and left inferior phrenic veins), while the right suprarenal vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava. This asymmetric venous drainage mirrors that of the testicular/ovarian veins. The suprarenal glands have a rich arterial supply from three sources (superior, middle, and inferior suprarenal arteries from the inferior phrenic artery, abdominal aorta, and renal artery respectively) but typically have only a single venous drainage pathway, creating a high arterial-to-venous ratio favoring hormone secretion.

is the most commonly torn rotator cuff muscle due to its position under the acromion. Repetitive overhead activities and age-related degeneration increase tear risk. The painful arc (pain during mid-abduction) is characteristic of supraspinatus tendonitis or tears.
questions.question: Which rotator cuff muscle is most commonly torn?

questions.explanation: The scala vestibuli and scala tympani communicate at the apex of the cochlea through the helicotrema. Both scalae contain perilymph. Sound vibrations travel up the scala vestibuli, through the helicotrema, and back down the scala tympani. The basilar membrane separates the scala tympani from the scala media (cochlear duct).
questions.question: The scala vestibuli communicates with the scala tympani through which structure?

questions.explanation: The esophagus, vagus nerves, and thoracic duct all pass through both the superior and posterior mediastinum. The esophagus descends from the neck through the superior mediastinum into the posterior mediastinum before piercing the diaphragm at T10. Understanding these relationships is important for interpreting imaging.
questions.question: Which structure lies in both superior and posterior mediastinum?
The maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve exits the skull through which opening?
questions.explanation: The maxillary division (V2) of the trigeminal nerve exits the middle cranial fossa through the foramen rotundum in the greater wing of the sphenoid. It enters the pterygopalatine fossa where it gives off branches before continuing as the infraorbital nerve. The foramen rotundum is round in shape, hence its name.

produces both flexion and supination of the forearm. It is most powerful as a supinator when the elbow is flexed at 90 degrees. The muscle has two heads proximally but a common tendon distally inserting on the radial tuberosity.
questions.question: Which muscle produces both flexion and supination of the forearm?

questions.explanation: The pharynx extends from the base of the skull to the lower border of the cricoid cartilage at C6, where it becomes continuous with the esophagus. This landmark corresponds to the level where the cricopharyngeus muscle acts as a sphincter. The transition zone is clinically significant for foreign body impaction and surgical access considerations.
questions.question: At what vertebral level does the pharynx transition to the esophagus?

questions.explanation: The superior constrictor muscle of the pharynx lies medial to the medial pterygoid muscle, separated by a thin fascial layer. The medial pterygoid forms part of the lateral wall of the infratemporal fossa. This relationship is important when accessing the pharyngeal space surgically.
questions.question: Which structure lies immediately medial to the medial pterygoid muscle?
At which intercostal space does nipple usually lie?
questions.explanation: In males and most young nulliparous women, the nipple lies opposite the 4th intercostal space, approximately 10 cm from the anterior midline. This position is variable in females and changes with age, pregnancy, and parity. The position is more constant in males.

The arytenoid cartilage comprises 40% of the vocal cord, while the remaining 60% is membranous (cricovocal ligament covered by mucosa). This anatomical proportion is important for understanding vocal cord pathology and surgical planning. The cartilaginous portion provides the posterior attachment point for the vocal ligament.
questions.question: What percentage of the vocal cord structure consists of the arytenoid cartilage?

questions.explanation: Reticulocytes (immature red blood cells still containing RNA) normally comprise 0.5-1.5% of circulating red blood cells, representing the daily replacement of senescent erythrocytes. The reticulocyte count increases in hemolysis or bleeding (compensatory bone marrow response) and decreases in bone marrow failure or nutritional deficiencies. The spleen removes excessive RNA from reticulocytes (pitting function).
questions.question: What is the normal percentage of reticulocytes in peripheral blood?

questions.explanation: The aortic arch begins at the level of T4 as a continuation of the ascending aorta. It arches backwards and to the left, passing over the left main bronchus. The arch ends at the level of T4/5 by continuing as the descending thoracic aorta. The aortic arch lies entirely within the superior mediastinum.
questions.question: At which level does the aortic arch begin?
The cribriform plate is part of which bone?
questions.explanation: The cribriform plate is the horizontal portion of the ethmoid bone forming the roof of the nasal cavity and floor of the anterior cranial fossa. It contains numerous foramina transmitting olfactory nerve fibers. The crista galli projects superiorly from the midline. Fractures cause CSF rhinorrhea and anosmia from shearing of olfactory nerve fibers.

questions.question: The nasolacrimal duct opens into which nasal meatus?
questions.explanation: The nasolacrimal duct opens into the inferior meatus beneath the inferior turbinate. The valve of Hasner at the duct's termination prevents retrograde airflow. Obstruction causes epiphora (excessive tearing) and may require dacryocystorhinostomy.

The middle colic artery (from the superior mesenteric artery) passes superiorly into the transverse mesocolon to supply the transverse colon, dividing into right and left branches. The middle colic veins (draining to the superior mesenteric vein) also pass through the mesocolon. The root of the transverse mesocolon is attached to the inferior border of the pancreas and anterior surface of the second part of the duodenum, crossing from right to left. The superior mesenteric vessels themselves lie posterior to the transverse mesocolon, not within it.
questions.question: Which vessel passes through the transverse mesocolon?

questions.explanation: The brachiocephalic trunk is the first and largest branch of the aortic arch. It ascends to the right and divides behind the right sternoclavicular joint into the right common carotid and right subclavian arteries. The left common carotid and left subclavian arteries arise directly from the arch.
questions.question: Which trunk branches from the aortic arch first?
The carotid sheath contains which three main structures?
questions.explanation: The carotid sheath contains the common/internal carotid artery, internal jugular vein, and vagus nerve. The sheath also contains deep cervical lymph nodes along the vein. It is formed by condensation of deep cervical fascia and extends from the skull base to the thoracic inlet.
options: Carotid artery, jugular vein, vagus nerve

questions.question: The maxillary sinus ostium opens into which structure?
questions.explanation: The maxillary sinus ostium opens into the middle meatus through the hiatus semilunaris. This high opening impairs natural drainage when standing upright. The sinus is the largest paranasal sinus and is present in rudimentary form at birth.

Superficial and deep parotid lymph nodes lie within or on the parotid gland substance. They drain the scalp, auricle, external acoustic meatus, and parotid gland itself. Efferents pass to the superficial and deep cervical nodes. The presence of lymph nodes within the gland complicates parotid tumor surgery and influences surgical planning.
questions.question: Which lymph nodes are located in the parotid gland?
What nerve passes between the two heads of pronator teres?
questions.explanation: The median nerve passes between the humeral and ulnar heads of pronator teres muscle. Compression at this site causes pronator teres syndrome, an entrapment neuropathy. This produces pain in the proximal forearm and sensory symptoms in the median nerve distribution.

The buccinator muscle is pierced by the parotid (Stensen's) duct before the duct opens into the oral vestibule opposite the upper second molar. The muscle forms the muscular component of the cheek and is innervated by the buccal branch of the facial nerve. It compresses the cheek against the teeth during chewing.
questions.question: The buccinator muscle is pierced by which structure?

questions.explanation: Pancreatic juice contains DNAase and RNAase (nucleases) that digest deoxyribonucleic acid and ribonucleic acid respectively into nucleotides. These nucleotides are further broken down by intestinal enzymes into nucleosides and bases for absorption. The pancreas secretes all major classes of digestive enzymes: proteases, lipases, amylase, and nucleases, making it essential for complete digestion.
questions.question: Which enzyme in pancreatic juice digests nucleic acids?
The plantar aponeurosis is the most important passive structure maintaining the medial longitudinal arch. It stretches from the calcaneal tuberosity to which structures?
options: Bases of all five proximal phalanges
Bases of all five metatarsal bones
Heads of all metatarsals and bases of proximal phalanges
Only the first metatarsophalangeal joint exclusively
All tarsal bones as a group
questions.explanation: The plantar aponeurosis (plantar fascia) stretches from the calcaneal tuberosity (medial tubercle) to the heads of all metatarsals and the bases of the proximal phalanges. During toe extension (dorsiflexion) in push-off phase of gait, this aponeurosis is tensioned, raising the arch in a windlass mechanism. Plantar fasciitis involves inflammation at the calcaneal attachment.

The base of the vermiform appendix has a constant anatomical location at the posteromedial wall of the cecum where the three taeniae coli converge, approximately 2-3 cm below the ileocecal junction. This convergence provides a reliable surgical landmark for locating the appendix during appendectomy, even when the appendix tip occupies a variable position (retrocecal, pelvic, subcecal, pre-ileal, or post-ileal). McBurney's point (one-third the distance from ASIS to umbilicus) represents the surface marking of the appendix base and is the site of maximal tenderness in appendicitis, but is not the actual anatomical landmark for finding the appendix during surgery.
questions.question: The appendix base is located at which anatomical landmark?

questions.explanation: The prostatic urethra is the widest and most dilatable part of the male urethra, measuring approximately 3-4 cm in length. It descends through the prostate gland from the bladder neck and contains the urethral crest on its posterior wall, with the prostatic utricle and openings of the ejaculatory ducts. The membranous urethra is the narrowest part.
questions.question: Which part of the male urethra is widest?

questions.explanation: The greater and lesser splanchnic nerves pierce the crura of the diaphragm through two lesser apertures in each crus. The hemiazygos vein also pierces the left crus. The sympathetic trunks pass behind the diaphragm deep to the medial arcuate ligament without piercing the diaphragm itself.
questions.question: Through which opening do splanchnic nerves pass?
Which structure communicates with the shoulder joint cavity through the subscapular bursa?
questions.explanation: The subscapular bursa communicates with the shoulder joint cavity through an oval gap between the superior and middle glenohumeral ligaments. This direct communication is clinically significant as it allows spread of infection or inflammatory processes between the bursa and joint. The subacromial bursa does not normally communicate with the joint.

The aortic hiatus at T12 transmits the descending thoracic aorta (which continues as the abdominal aorta), the thoracic duct, and sometimes the azygos and hemiazygos veins. This is the lowest and most posterior of the three main openings. It lies between the crura rather than through them.
questions.question: What passes through the aortic hiatus?

questions.explanation: The testes drain lymph directly to the para-aortic (lumbar) lymph nodes at the L1-L2 level, corresponding to their embryological origin high on the posterior abdominal wall and their arterial supply from the abdominal aorta. Lymphatics accompany the testicular vessels through the spermatic cord, inguinal canal, and over the pelvic brim to reach these nodes. In contrast, the scrotum drains to superficial inguinal nodes. This lymphatic drainage pattern is clinically crucial in testicular cancer staging and explains why metastases first appear in para-aortic nodes rather than inguinal nodes (unless the scrotal skin is also involved).
questions.question: Which lymph nodes receive drainage from the testis?

questions.explanation: The middle colic artery (from the superior mesenteric artery) and middle colic veins (to superior mesenteric vein) pass through the transverse mesocolon to supply the transverse colon. The root of the transverse mesocolon attaches to the inferior border of the pancreas and crosses the descending duodenum, serving as an important surgical landmark dividing the peritoneal cavity into supracolic and infracolic compartments. The superior mesenteric vessels lie posterior to the transverse mesocolon, while the inferior mesenteric vessels lie posterior to the peritoneum, not within the mesocolon itself.
questions.question: Which structure passes through the transverse mesocolon?

questions.explanation: The superficial palmar arch is formed primarily by the ulnar artery with contribution from the superficial palmar branch of the radial artery. The arch curves across the palm at the level of the distal border of the fully extended thumb. It gives rise to three common palmar digital arteries.
questions.question: Which artery forms the main contribution to the superficial palmar arch?
What is the transversus thoracis muscle?
questions.explanation: The transversus thoracis (sternocostalis) is the anterior portion of the innermost intercostal layer. It is fan-shaped, spreading upward from the posterior aspect of the lower sternum to insert onto the inner surfaces of the 2nd-6th costal cartilages. It depresses the ribs during expiration.

questions.question: What is the functional significance of the bicipital aponeurosis?
options: Provides muscle attachment to bicipital fascia
Reinforces cubital fossa, protects neurovascular structures
questions.explanation: The bicipital aponeurosis reinforces the cubital fossa roof and protects the brachial artery and median nerve during venipuncture. It distributes biceps force to the ulna and forearm fascia. Historically recognized as the grace of God tendon for protecting vital structures during bloodletting.

The hamstring part of adductor magnus originates from the ischial tuberosity and is supplied by the tibial nerve, unlike the adductor part which is supplied by the obturator nerve. The hamstring part inserts into the adductor tubercle of the femur and acts to extend the hip. This dual origin and nerve supply make adductor magnus a 'hybrid' muscle.
questions.question: The adductor magnus has two distinct parts. The hamstring part, originating from the ischial tuberosity, is supplied by which nerve?
Which structure separates the supracolic from the infracolic compartment?
questions.explanation: The transverse mesocolon, a broad fold of peritoneum connecting the transverse colon to the posterior abdominal wall, divides the peritoneal cavity into supracolic and infracolic compartments. The supracolic compartment contains the stomach, liver, spleen, and lesser sac, while the infracolic compartment is further divided into right and left infracolic spaces by the mesentery of the small intestine. These spaces communicate laterally via the paracolic gutters. The root of the transverse mesocolon crosses the descending (second) part of the duodenum and head of pancreas, serving as an important surgical landmark.

The cardiac impression on the left lung is larger than that on the right lung because the heart is positioned more to the left side. The left ventricle forms most of the heart's left border and creates a large concave impression on the left lung's mediastinal surface.
questions.question: Which impression is largest on the left lung?

questions.explanation: Auerbach's (myenteric) plexus is located between the circular and longitudinal layers of the muscularis externa throughout the gastrointestinal tract. It controls gut motility, including peristalsis and segmentation. Damage to this plexus (as in Chagas disease or Hirschsprung disease) causes severe motility disorders. It contains both excitatory and inhibitory motor neurons.
questions.question: Where is Auerbach's plexus located in the gut wall?

questions.explanation: The inferior vena cava is formed by the union of the right and left common iliac veins at the level of the fifth lumbar vertebra (L5), to the right of the midline and anterior to the right common iliac artery. From this point, it ascends on the right side of the aorta, anterior to the vertebral column, receiving tributaries in an asymmetric pattern. The IVC passes through the diaphragm (caval opening in central tendon) at T8 level to enter the thorax and immediately empties into the right atrium. The formation level (L5) is slightly lower than the aortic bifurcation (L4).
questions.question: The inferior vena cava is formed at which vertebral level?
Which vessel crosses anterior to the horizontal (third) part of the duodenum?
questions.explanation: The superior mesenteric vessels (artery and vein) and the root of the mesentery cross anteriorly to the horizontal (third) part of the duodenum. This anatomical relationship is clinically significant as compression by these vessels can cause superior mesenteric artery syndrome. The third part of the duodenum crosses the vertebral column from right to left at the L3 level.

The palatoglossus muscle forms the palatoglossal arch (anterior pillar of the fauces). It descends from the soft palate to the side of the tongue. Unlike other tongue muscles, it is innervated by the pharyngeal plexus (vagus via cranial accessory), not the hypoglossal nerve. The muscle elevates the posterior tongue during swallowing.
questions.question: Which muscle forms the anterior pillar of the fauces?

questions.explanation: Venae cordis minimae (smallest cardiac veins or Thebesian veins) are tiny veins that drain directly into the cardiac chambers (mainly the atria) without joining larger veins. They provide a small amount of deoxygenated blood directly to the left heart, contributing to the physiological shunt. They are difficult to visualize without specialized techniques.
questions.question: What are the smallest cardiac veins called?
The root of the transverse mesocolon crosses which part of the duodenum?
questions.explanation: The root of the transverse mesocolon attaches to the inferior border of the pancreas and crosses the second (descending) part of the duodenum as it extends from right to left across the posterior abdominal wall. This attachment divides the peritoneal cavity into supracolic (containing stomach, liver, spleen) and infracolic (containing small intestine and colon) compartments. The root also crosses anterior to the head of the pancreas and the superior mesenteric vessels. This anatomical relationship is important during surgical mobilization of the transverse colon and in understanding the spread of peritoneal infections.

The hyoglossus muscle is a key surgical landmark separating the lingual artery into three parts: above, on, and below the muscle. The hypoglossal nerve and lingual vein lie superficially on the muscle. Deep lingual and sublingual arteries arise from the lingual artery in relation to this muscle.
questions.question: The hyoglossus muscle separates which two important arteries?
Which structure forms the floor of the cubital fossa?
questions.explanation: The floor of the cubital fossa is formed by two muscles: the brachialis muscle superiorly and the supinator muscle inferiorly. The roof is formed by skin, superficial and deep fascia, reinforced by the bicipital aponeurosis. The fossa contains important neurovascular structures from medial to lateral.

questions.question: Which pleura covers the diaphragm's superior surface?
questions.explanation: The diaphragmatic pleura is the portion of parietal pleura that covers the superior surface of the diaphragm. It reflects onto the thoracic wall to become continuous with the costal pleura. The diaphragmatic pleura receives sensory innervation from the phrenic nerve centrally and intercostal nerves peripherally.

questions.question: What is the functional unit of liver according to the lobular concept?
questions.explanation: The classical hepatic lobule is a hexagonal structural unit with a central vein at its center and portal triads at the periphery (corners). Hepatocytes are arranged in plates radiating from the central vein with sinusoids between them. Blood flows from portal triads through sinusoids to the central vein. This is the histological/structural concept, though the hepatic acinus is a better functional unit.

The quadratus plantae assists flexor digitorum longus in flexing the lateral four digits. This assistance is needed because the tendons of flexor digitorum longus approach the digits from a medially oblique direction; quadratus plantae corrects this pull to a more longitudinal direction. It originates from the medial and lateral plantar surfaces of the calcaneus and is innervated by the lateral plantar nerve.
questions.question: The second layer of foot muscles contains the quadratus plantae and lumbricals. The quadratus plantae assists which extrinsic muscle in flexing the lateral four digits?

questions.explanation: The posterior cricoarytenoid muscle is the sole abductor of the vocal cords, externally rotating the arytenoid cartilages. All other intrinsic laryngeal muscles are adductors or tensors of the vocal cords. Bilateral paralysis of this muscle causes life-threatening airway obstruction requiring immediate intervention.
questions.question: Which muscle is the ONLY abductor of the vocal cords?
The aortic hiatus transmits which structures besides the aorta?
questions.explanation: The aortic hiatus, located at the T12 vertebral level between the two crura of the diaphragm (posterior to the median arcuate ligament), transmits the aorta, thoracic duct, and azygos vein (and sometimes hemiazygos vein). The esophagus and vagal trunks pass through the esophageal hiatus at T10, while the inferior vena cava traverses the caval opening in the central tendon at T8. The aortic hiatus is actually a midline gap between the crura rather than a true opening in the diaphragm, which means structures passing through it are not constricted during diaphragmatic contraction.

The vertebral arteries enter the cranial cavity through the foramen magnum after ascending through the transverse foramina of cervical vertebrae C1-C6. They unite at the pontomedullary junction to form the basilar artery. The vertebral arteries give off the posterior inferior cerebellar arteries before joining.
questions.question: The vertebral arteries enter the skull through which opening?
Which vein receives the inferior mesenteric vein?
questions.explanation: The inferior mesenteric vein typically drains into the splenic vein posterior to the body of the pancreas, though anatomical variations exist (occasionally draining into superior mesenteric vein or the portal vein directly). The IMV ascends from the pelvis on the left side of the inferior mesenteric artery, receiving sigmoid and left colic tributaries. After joining the splenic vein, blood flows to the confluence with the superior mesenteric vein behind the neck of the pancreas, forming the portal vein. This pathway ensures blood from the hindgut reaches the liver for processing.

The bulbourethral glands (Cowper's glands) are paired pea-sized glands located in the urogenital diaphragm that drain via long ducts into the bulbar portion of the spongy urethra. They secrete a clear, mucoid pre-ejaculatory fluid that lubricates the urethra and neutralizes acidic urine residue. These glands are homologous to Bartholin's glands in females.
questions.question: Which glands open into the bulbar urethra?
How many separate joints are formed collectively by the 19 bones of the hand?
questions.explanation: The 19 bones of the hand (metacarpals and phalanges) collectively form 14 separate joints. These include the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints connecting fingers to palm and interphalangeal (IP) joints between finger segments. All are synovial joints with articular cartilage covering the bone surfaces.

In males, the seminal vesicles and ampullae of the vas deferens lie posterior to the bladder base, and the rectum lies posterior to these structures, separated by the rectovesical fascia (Denonvilliers' fascia). The rectovesical pouch of peritoneum separates the upper part of the bladder from the rectum. In females, the vagina lies directly posterior to the bladder.
questions.question: What lies posterior to the male urinary bladder?

questions.explanation: The right upper lobe contains three bronchopulmonary segments: apical, posterior, and anterior. Each segment is supplied by a tertiary (segmental) bronchus and a branch of the pulmonary artery. The segments are separated by connective tissue septa allowing individual segment resection.
questions.question: How many segments are in right upper lobe?
The occipital sinus drains into which structure?
questions.explanation: The occipital sinus lies in the attached border of the falx cerebelli and drains into the confluence of sinuses. It is the smallest of the cranial venous sinuses. The sinus communicates with the vertebral venous plexuses through the foramen magnum. It runs in the midline on the internal occipital crest.

questions.question: How many thoracic sympathetic ganglia exist typically?
questions.explanation: There are typically 11-12 thoracic sympathetic ganglia, though the first thoracic ganglion commonly fuses with the inferior cervical ganglion to form the stellate ganglion. Each ganglion connects to its corresponding spinal nerve via gray and white rami communicantes. The ganglia are interconnected by interganglionic segments.

options: T12–L5 vertebrae, intervening discs, and all lumbar transverse processes
L1-L5 vertebral bodies only, no disc or process
T12-L4 vertebral bodies only without processes
L2-S1 vertebral levels and intervening discs
questions.explanation: Psoas major originates from the sides of T12-L5 vertebrae and their intervening discs, as well as from the transverse processes of all lumbar vertebrae. It inserts into the lesser trochanter together with iliacus (forming iliopsoas). A psoas abscess from vertebral tuberculosis can track along this muscle to present as a groin swelling.
questions.question: The psoas major originates from which vertebral levels, including transverse processes?
The hepatic portal vein is formed at which vertebral level?
questions.explanation: The hepatic portal vein forms behind the neck of the pancreas at approximately the L1/L2 vertebral level through the confluence of the superior mesenteric and splenic veins, anterior to the inferior vena cava. The inferior mesenteric vein typically joins the splenic vein before this confluence, though variations exist. From its formation, the portal vein ascends obliquely to the right within the hepatoduodenal ligament (free edge of lesser omentum) to reach the porta hepatis, where it divides into right and left branches. It measures approximately 8 cm in length and lacks valves.

The superficial lymphatics of the lower limb accompany the great saphenous vein and drain to the superficial inguinal lymph nodes. The deep lymphatics accompany the deep vessels and drain to the deep inguinal and then external iliac nodes. The popliteal nodes drain the posterior leg and lateral foot (accompanying the small saphenous vein). Lymphedema of the lower limb can follow radical inguinal lymph node dissection.
questions.question: The lymphatics of the lower limb follow the saphenous vein and drain to which lymph node group?

questions.explanation: The lateral sulcus (Sylvian fissure) separates the frontal and parietal lobes from the temporal lobe. The middle cerebral artery runs in this fissure. The insula lies deep within the lateral sulcus. Strokes affecting the middle cerebral artery often involve structures around this fissure causing characteristic neurological deficits.
questions.question: Which structure separates the frontal and temporal lobes?
What structure occupies the free edge of the falciform ligament?
questions.explanation: The ligamentum teres (round ligament of the liver) occupies the free inferior edge of the falciform ligament. It is the obliterated remnant of the umbilical vein, which carried oxygenated blood from the placenta to the fetus. The ligamentum teres extends from the umbilicus to the left branch of the portal vein at the porta hepatis.

The median nerve is the only nerve passing through the carpal tunnel. It enters the hand between the tendons of flexor digitorum superficialis and lies anterior to the flexor digitorum profundus tendons. Compression of this nerve within the tunnel causes carpal tunnel syndrome.
questions.question: Which nerve passes through the carpal tunnel?

questions.explanation: When a bone has an epiphysis at both ends, the nutrient canal is directed away from the more actively growing end. Hughes captured this in the mnemonic 'to the elbow I go, from the knee I flee,' indicating the direction of nutrient arteries in the humerus and lower limb bones respectively.
questions.question: In bones with epiphyses at both ends, the nutrient canal is directed away from which structure?

questions.explanation: The internal anal sphincter is a thickening of the circular smooth muscle layer of the rectum, extending from the anorectal junction to approximately the level of the white line of Hilton, covering the upper three-quarters of the anal canal. It is under autonomic (involuntary) control, receiving sympathetic innervation (L1-L2 via hypogastric plexuses) that promotes contraction and parasympathetic innervation (S2-S4 via pelvic splanchnic nerves) that causes relaxation. This sphincter maintains resting anal tone and unconscious fecal continence, while the external anal sphincter (striated voluntary muscle supplied by inferior rectal nerve) provides voluntary control.
questions.question: The internal anal sphincter is formed from which layer?
Which space lies proximal to the carpal tunnel in the forearm?
questions.explanation: The space of Parona extends from the proximal margin of the carpal tunnel to the mid-forearm. Its roof is formed distally by flexor digitorum profundus tendons and proximally by the belly of flexor digitorum superficialis. The floor consists of pronator quadratus distally and interosseous membrane proximally.

questions.question: Which structure lies in the free edge of the lesser omentum?
questions.explanation: The free right edge of the lesser omentum (hepatoduodenal ligament) contains the portal triad: portal vein (posteriorly), common bile duct (anteriorly and to the right), and hepatic artery proper (anteriorly and to the left). This arrangement is remembered by the mnemonic "DAV" from anterior to posterior (Duct, Artery, Vein). The hepatoduodenal ligament forms the anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen and can be compressed in the Pringle maneuver to control hepatic bleeding by temporarily occluding hepatic arterial and portal venous inflow.

The shoulder's extreme mobility comes at the expense of stability. The shallow glenoid cavity (1:4 disproportion with humeral head) and lax joint capsule are necessary for wide range of motion but compromise stability. Dynamic stability from rotator cuff muscles partially compensates.
questions.question: Which factor most limits shoulder joint stability?

options: Abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis, abductor digiti minimi
Plantar interossei, dorsal interossei, flexor hallucis brevis
Flexor hallucis brevis, adductor hallucis, flexor digiti minimi brevis
Flexor hallucis brevis, abductor hallucis, flexor digiti minimi brevis
questions.question: The third layer of foot muscles contains three muscles. Which combination is correct?
questions.explanation: The third layer of foot muscles contains three muscles: flexor hallucis brevis, adductor hallucis, and flexor digiti minimi brevis. Flexor hallucis brevis and adductor hallucis are supplied by branches of the medial and lateral plantar nerves respectively. The adductor hallucis assists in maintaining the transverse arch of the foot by drawing the metatarsals medially.

The small intestine measures approximately 5 to 6 meters in length in adults, with the jejunum constituting about 40% and the ileum about 60%. Post-mortem measurements may show greater length due to loss of muscle tone. The actual functional length in vivo is considerably shorter due to tonic muscular contraction.
questions.question: What is the total approximate length of the small intestine?
Which nerve carries pain sensation from the parietal peritoneum covering the diaphragm?
questions.explanation: The phrenic nerves carry pain sensation from the parietal peritoneum and parietal pleura covering the central part of the diaphragm. Irritation here causes referred pain to the C3-C5 dermatomes (neck and shoulder, especially shoulder tip). Peripheral parts of the diaphragm receive sensory supply from the lower intercostal and subcostal nerves, with referred pain to the trunk wall.

options: Femoral popliteal surface, knee capsule, oblique popliteal ligament, popliteal fascia
Skin and superficial fascia of the posterior knee
Popliteus muscle, posterior joint capsule, and tibial cortex
Tibial nerve, popliteal artery, and popliteal vein
Femoral condyles and both medial and lateral menisci
questions.question: The floor of the popliteal fossa from superior to inferior consists of which structures?
questions.explanation: The floor of the popliteal fossa from superior to inferior consists of: the popliteal surface of the femur, the capsule of the knee joint, the oblique popliteal ligament, and the popliteal fascia covering the popliteus muscle. The popliteal artery runs in close proximity to this floor, making it vulnerable in posterior knee dislocations.

questions.question: Efferent lymph vessels from the deep popliteal lymph nodes travel along which vessels to reach the inguinal lymph nodes?
questions.explanation: Efferent lymph vessels from the deep popliteal lymph nodes travel along the femoral vessels to reach the inguinal lymph nodes. Afferent vessels reach the popliteal nodes from the knee joint and lymphatics accompanying leg arteries. Superficial popliteal nodes receive lymph from the region accompanying the small saphenous vein.

The anterior cardiac veins (3-4 small veins) drain the anterior right ventricular wall and empty directly into the right atrium, bypassing the coronary sinus. They cross the atrioventricular groove and are the only cardiac veins that don't drain via the coronary sinus. During cardiac surgery, these veins must be identified to avoid injury.
questions.question: Where do the anterior cardiac veins drain?
The obturator foramen is closed by which structure?
questions.explanation: The obturator membrane is a fibrous sheet that almost completely closes the obturator foramen, the largest foramen in the body formed by the ischium and pubis. The membrane leaves a small gap superiorly, the obturator canal, through which the obturator nerve and vessels pass from the pelvis to the medial compartment of the thigh. Both obturator internus (internal surface) and obturator externus (external surface) muscles attach to the obturator membrane, with the former functioning as a lateral rotator of the hip and the latter as both a lateral rotator and adductor.

The medial plantar nerve is analogous to the median nerve in the hand. It is the larger terminal branch and supplies the medial three and a half digits (great, 2nd, 3rd, and medial half of the 4th), the skin of the medial plantar surface, abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis, flexor hallucis brevis, and the first lumbrical. The lateral plantar nerve is analogous to the ulnar nerve.
questions.question: The medial plantar nerve (L4, L5) is the larger terminal branch of the tibial nerve. It is analogous to which nerve in the hand?

questions.explanation: The superficial cervical lymph nodes lie along the external jugular vein in the superficial cervical fascia. They receive drainage from the scalp and superficial neck structures. Efferent vessels drain to the deep cervical nodes. These nodes are distinct from the deep cervical chain along the internal jugular vein.
questions.question: Which lymph nodes are located along the external jugular vein?

questions.explanation: The masseter, temporalis, and medial pterygoid muscles elevate the mandible during mastication. The masseter originates from the zygomatic arch and inserts on the lateral surface of the mandibular angle and ramus. It is innervated by the masseteric nerve from V3. Bilateral contraction closes the mouth and clenches the teeth.
questions.question: Which muscle elevates the mandible during mastication?

questions.explanation: The right crus arises from the front of the bodies of the upper three lumbar vertebrae (L1-L3) and their intervertebral discs. The left crus is smaller and arises only from L1 and L2. Some muscle fibers from the right crus form a sling around the esophageal opening.
questions.question: From how many lumbar vertebrae does right crus arise?
At which vertebral level does the rectum commence?
questions.explanation: The rectum begins as a continuation of the sigmoid colon at the level of the third sacral vertebra (S3). It extends approximately 13 cm (5 inches) before terminating as the anal canal one inch below the tip of the coccyx. The rectum follows the curvature of the sacrum and coccyx, forming the sacral and perineal flexures.

The moderator band (septomarginal trabecula) is a muscular bridge extending from the interventricular septum to the base of the anterior papillary muscle. It carries the right bundle branch of the conducting system, ensuring coordinated activation of the papillary muscles. It prevents overdistention of the ventricle and was historically important for determining ventricular orientation.
questions.question: Which structure carries the right bundle branch in the right ventricle?
The medial longitudinal arch has the greatest height and is formed by which bones?
options: Calcaneus, talus, navicular, three cuneiforms, and 1st-3rd metatarsals
Talus, navicular, cuboid, and three metatarsals
Calcaneus, cuboid, navicular, and two cuneiforms
Calcaneus, talus, and first metatarsal only
questions.explanation: The medial longitudinal arch is formed by the calcaneus, talus, navicular, three cuneiform bones, and the 1st-3rd metatarsals. Its summit is the superior articular facet of the talus, making the talus the keystone of this arch. It is larger, higher, more mobile, and more resilient than the lateral longitudinal arch, dynamically changing most during movement.

The urinary bladder receives parasympathetic innervation from the pelvic splanchnic nerves (nervi erigentes) arising from the S2, S3, and S4 spinal segments. These preganglionic fibers synapse in ganglia within the bladder wall and stimulate contraction of the detrusor muscle (for micturition) while relaxing the internal urethral sphincter. Sympathetic innervation (L1-L2 via lumbar splanchnic nerves and superior hypogastric plexus) has the opposite effect, promoting urine storage by relaxing the detrusor and contracting the internal sphincter. Somatic innervation of the external urethral sphincter comes from the pudendal nerve (S2-S4), allowing voluntary control.
questions.question: The urinary bladder receives parasympathetic innervation from which spinal segments?

questions.explanation: The fovea centralis is a depression in the center of the macula lutea, representing the area of most acute vision. It contains only cones (no rods) and has minimal overlying retinal layers to reduce light scatter. The fovea is located temporal to the optic disc. Macular degeneration causes central vision loss.
questions.question: The fovea centralis is located in which structure?
The pterygomaxillary fissure connects which two regions?
questions.explanation: The pterygomaxillary fissure is a vertical opening between the lateral pterygoid plate (posteriorly) and the maxilla (anteriorly), connecting the infratemporal and pterygopalatine fossae. The maxillary artery and mandibular nerve branches pass through this fissure. It forms the lateral boundary of the pterygopalatine fossa.
options: Middle cranial fossa and pterygopalatine fossa

questions.question: The anterior fontanelle is located at the junction of which sutures?
questions.explanation: The anterior fontanelle (bregma) is located at the junction of the coronal, sagittal, and frontal (metopic) sutures where the frontal and parietal bones meet. It is diamond-shaped and typically closes by 18-24 months. The fontanelle allows skull molding during birth and accommodates brain growth. Bulging indicates increased intracranial pressure.

questions.question: What is the most common position of the appendix?
questions.explanation: The retrocaecal position is the most common location of the appendix, occurring in approximately 65-75% of individuals. In this position, the appendix lies behind the caecum, which may explain atypical presentations of appendicitis. Other positions include pelvic (most common after retrocaecal), subcaecal, preileal, and postileal positions.
abducts the little finger away from the ring finger. It is one of three hypothenar muscles supplied by the ulnar nerve. The muscle forms the medial border of the palm in the hypothenar eminence.
questions.question: Which hypothenar muscle abducts the little finger?

questions.explanation: The right gastric artery usually arises from the hepatic artery proper near the porta hepatis, though it may occasionally branch from the gastroduodenal or left hepatic artery. It descends to the pylorus, then ascends along the lesser curvature of the stomach within the lesser omentum, anastomosing with the left gastric artery (the smallest but most consistent branch of the celiac trunk). This anastomotic network along the lesser curvature provides collateral circulation and must be carefully ligated during gastric resections to avoid ischemia or bleeding.
questions.question: The right gastric artery typically arises from which vessel?
The great saphenous vein, the longest vein in the body, is formed at the foot by the union of which structures?
questions.explanation: The great saphenous vein is formed by the union of the dorsal vein of the great toe and the dorsal venous arch of the foot. It ascends anterior to the medial malleolus, passes posterior to the medial condyle of the femur, and empties into the femoral vein after traversing the saphenous opening. It has 10-12 valves.
options: Medial marginal vein and dorsal venous arch
Dorsal vein of great toe and dorsal venous arch
Dorsal vein of great toe and posterior tibial vein
Small saphenous vein and dorsal venous arch
Anterior tibial vein and dorsal venous arch

questions.explanation: The hemiazygos and accessory hemiazygos veins cross from left to right behind the esophagus and aorta at the levels of T8-9 and T7 respectively to drain into the azygos vein. These cross-communications provide collateral venous drainage pathways between the left and right sides of the thorax.
questions.question: What connects the azygos and hemiazygos systems?
Which bronchus is shorter and more vertical?
questions.explanation: The right main bronchus is shorter (2.5 cm), wider, and more vertically oriented than the left main bronchus (5 cm). This anatomical difference makes the right main bronchus more susceptible to aspiration of foreign bodies. The right bronchus gives off the upper lobar bronchus outside the hilum.

The 'screw-home mechanism' is the conjunct rotation that occurs in the final degrees of knee extension, when the tibia rotates laterally on the femur (in an open-chain position) or the femur rotates medially on the tibia (in a closed-chain position). Both descriptions describe the same biomechanical event. Popliteus 'unlocks' this mechanism to initiate knee flexion.
questions.question: The 'screw-home mechanism' of the knee refers to which specific movement that occurs at full extension?
options: Medial rotation of the femur on the tibia in the last few degrees of extension
Both A and B describe the same event
Lateral rotation of the tibia on the femur in the last few degrees of extension
Locking of the patellofemoral joint only
Posterior translation of the tibia at full extension

questions.question: The lacteal vessels in intestinal villi drain into which nodes first?
questions.explanation: Lacteal vessels (lymphatic capillaries) in intestinal villi coalesce to form larger lymphatic vessels that drain to lymph nodes along the mesenteric border of the intestine (juxta-intestinal nodes), then to nodes along the vascular arcades in the mesentery (intermediate nodes), followed by nodes at the root of the mesentery along the superior mesenteric artery (superior mesenteric nodes), and finally to pre-aortic nodes (celiac, superior mesenteric, inferior mesenteric groups) before reaching the cisterna chyli and thoracic duct. This stepwise progression through multiple nodal stations allows for filtering and immune surveillance of intestinal lymph.

questions.question: Which artery primarily supplies the lower third of the oesophagus?
questions.explanation: The lower third of the oesophagus receives its arterial supply from branches of the left gastric artery, a branch of the coeliac trunk. This creates an important portosystemic anastomosis with veins draining to both portal and systemic circulations. The upper third is supplied by the inferior thyroid artery and the middle third by oesophageal branches of the thoracic aorta.

questions.question: What nerve supplies the first and second lumbricals?
questions.explanation: The lateral two lumbricals (to index and middle fingers) are supplied by the median nerve. The medial two lumbricals (to ring and little fingers) are supplied by the ulnar nerve. This dual innervation pattern is unique among hand muscles.

questions.question: The pelvic splanchnic nerves arise from which spinal segments?
questions.explanation: The pelvic splanchnic nerves (nervi erigentes) carry preganglionic parasympathetic fibers from the S2, S3, and S4 spinal segments, representing the sacral outflow of the parasympathetic nervous system. These nerves arise from the ventral rami of S2-S4, contribute to the inferior hypogastric plexus, and supply parasympathetic innervation to pelvic viscera (bladder, rectum, reproductive organs) and distal hindgut (from splenic flexure to upper anal canal). They stimulate bladder contraction, rectal peristalsis, and penile erection ("point"), in contrast to sympathetic innervation which promotes ejaculation ("shoot").

The thoracic duct begins at the level of L1 as a continuation of the cisterna chyli, which is formed by the union of left and right lumbar trunks and the intestinal trunk. It ascends through the aortic opening of the diaphragm into the thoracic cavity. The duct eventually terminates by draining into the left venous angle after receiving additional lymphatic tributaries.
questions.question: Which structure represents the continuation of cisterna chyli?

questions.explanation: The costomediastinal recess is located behind the sternum where the costal pleura doubles back to become mediastinal pleura. It is more conspicuous on the left side in the region around the cardiac notch. This recess allows for cardiac expansion without lung compression.
questions.question: Where is the costomediastinal recess located?

questions.explanation: The anterior vagal trunk is formed mainly from the left vagus nerve as it descends on the anterior surface of the oesophagus. This trunk enters the abdomen on the anterior surface of the oesophagus and supplies the anterior gastric surface. It also gives off a large hepatic branch and a pyloric branch.
questions.question: Which nerve forms the anterior vagal trunk supplying the stomach?
How do digital arteries ensure blood supply to fingertips?
questions.explanation: Each finger receives two proper palmar digital arteries (one on each side from common digital arteries). These anastomose extensively, providing redundant blood supply. Additional dorsal digital arteries contribute. This rich vascular network protects fingertip perfusion critical for hand function.
options: Single artery to each digit only
Dual proper digital arteries with extensive anastomoses

questions.explanation: The superior hypogastric plexus lies anterior to the lower part of the abdominal aorta and its bifurcation, extending from approximately L4 to the upper part of the sacrum, anterior to the L5 vertebra and sacral promontory. It represents the continuation of the aortic (intermesenteric) plexus and receives lumbar splanchnic nerves carrying preganglionic sympathetic fibers. The plexus divides inferiorly into right and left hypogastric nerves, which descend into the pelvis to join the inferior hypogastric (pelvic) plexuses. The superior hypogastric plexus can be blocked or surgically divided to treat intractable pelvic pain.
questions.question: The superior hypogastric plexus is located at which vertebral level?
What drains the area above the pectinate line in the anal canal?
questions.explanation: Above the pectinate line, lymphatic drainage is to internal iliac nodes (following the superior rectal vessels). Below the pectinate line, drainage is primarily to superficial inguinal nodes. This difference is clinically important in anal cancer spread: tumors above the line metastasize to pelvic nodes, while those below spread to inguinal nodes.

questions.question: From which vessel do inferior phrenic arteries arise?
questions.explanation: The inferior phrenic arteries are the first branches of the abdominal aorta and supply the inferior surface of the diaphragm. The right inferior phrenic artery gives off the suprarenal artery. These arteries are important in collateral circulation and can be a source of bleeding in trauma.

The pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2-S4) carry preganglionic parasympathetic fibers that synapse in terminal ganglia within or very near the walls of the pelvic organs they supply (bladder, rectum, reproductive organs). This is characteristic of parasympathetic innervation, where the preganglionic fibers are long and synapse close to or within the target organ, while postganglionic fibers are very short. The fibers travel via the inferior hypogastric plexus to reach their destinations but do not synapse there. The pelvic splanchnics also provide parasympathetic innervation to the distal hindgut from the splenic flexure to the upper anal canal.
questions.question: The pelvic splanchnic nerves synapse in which location?

questions.explanation: The portal vein provides approximately 70% of the blood supply to the liver, while the hepatic artery contributes the remaining 30%. Despite carrying deoxygenated blood, the portal vein is crucial as it delivers nutrient-rich blood from the gastrointestinal tract. The dual blood supply makes the liver relatively resistant to ischemic injury.
questions.question: What percentage of hepatic blood supply comes from the portal vein?

questions.explanation: The levator palpebrae superioris is innervated by the oculomotor nerve (III). Müller's muscle (superior tarsal muscle), a smooth muscle also elevating the lid, is innervated by sympathetics. Oculomotor palsy causes ptosis (drooping eyelid) along with eye movement deficits. Horner's syndrome causes mild ptosis from sympathetic loss.
questions.question: The levator palpebrae superioris is innervated by which nerve?
The transversalis fascia forms which covering of the spermatic cord?
questions.explanation: The internal spermatic fascia, the innermost fascial covering of the spermatic cord, is derived from the transversalis fascia at the margins of the deep inguinal ring. Moving outward, the next layer is the cremasteric muscle and fascia (from internal oblique and transversus abdominis), and the outermost layer is the external spermatic fascia (from external oblique aponeurosis). These three concentric layers are acquired as the processus vaginalis descends through the layers of the anterior abdominal wall during testicular descent. The tunica vaginalis is the closed peritoneal sac surrounding the testis, derived from the processus vaginalis.

The oesophageal hiatus in the diaphragm is located at the level of the tenth thoracic vertebra (T10). The oesophagus passes through the muscular part of the right crus of the diaphragm at this level. This hiatus also transmits the anterior and posterior vagal trunks and oesophageal branches of the left gastric vessels.
questions.question: Which vertebral level corresponds to the oesophageal opening in the diaphragm?
Which cell type produces gastrin hormone?
questions.explanation: G cells are enteroendocrine cells located primarily in the pyloric antrum (also in duodenum) that secrete gastrin in response to gastric distention, peptides, and vagal stimulation. Gastrin stimulates acid secretion by parietal cells and has trophic effects on gastric mucosa. Gastrinomas (tumors secreting gastrin) cause Zollinger-Ellison syndrome with severe peptic ulcer disease.

The space of Disse is the perisinusoidal space between the fenestrated endothelium lining the hepatic sinusoids and the hepatocytes. It contains hepatic stellate cells (fat-storing cells that can become fibrogenic), microvilli from hepatocytes, and allows exchange of materials between blood and hepatocytes. In cirrhosis, this space becomes fibrotic (capillarization), impairing hepatocyte function and exchange.
questions.question: What is the space of Disse in the liver?
The sartorius muscle, the longest muscle in the body, performs which complete combination of actions?
questions.explanation: Sartorius (the tailor's muscle) acts on two joints. At the hip: it flexes, abducts, and laterally rotates the thigh. At the knee: it flexes the leg and medially rotates when the knee is flexed. The combined action of both sartorii brings the lower limb into the cross-legged sitting position typical of traditional tailors.
options: Extends hip and flexes the knee only
Adducts the hip and extends the knee
Flexes, abducts, and laterally rotates hip; flexes and medially rotates knee
Flexes hip and laterally rotates the knee joint only
Abducts the hip and extends the knee only

questions.question: Which structure forms the roof of the tympanic cavity?
questions.explanation: The tegmen tympani (thin plate of petrous temporal bone) forms the roof of the tympanic cavity, separating it from the middle cranial fossa and temporal lobe. Fractures or erosion can cause CSF otorrhea or meningitis. The tegmen also roofs the mastoid antrum. It represents the superior wall of the middle ear cavity.

questions.question: The linea alba extends between which two points?
questions.explanation: The linea alba is a fibrous raphe extending in the midline from the xiphoid process superiorly to the pubic symphysis inferiorly, formed by the fusion of aponeuroses from both sides (external oblique, internal oblique, and transversus abdominis from each side). It separates the right and left rectus abdominis muscles and is relatively avascular (appearing white, hence its name), making it an ideal site for midline surgical incisions. The linea alba is wider above the umbilicus and narrows below it. Diastasis recti (separation of recti muscles) involves widening of the linea alba, particularly common during pregnancy and in obesity.

The cecum receives its blood supply from the ileocolic artery (terminal branch of the superior mesenteric artery), which divides into superior and inferior branches. The inferior branch gives rise to anterior and posterior cecal arteries that supply the corresponding surfaces of the cecum. The ileocolic artery also gives off the appendicular artery (to appendix) and ileal branches. The superior branch of the ileocolic artery anastomoses with the right colic artery along the ascending colon. The cecum's venous drainage follows the arterial pattern, with ileocolic vein draining to the superior mesenteric vein.
questions.question: Which vessel supplies the cecum?

questions.explanation: The splenorenal (lienorenal) ligament extends from the hilum of the spleen to the anterior surface of the left kidney and contains the splenic vessels, tail of the pancreas, and associated lymph nodes. The tail of the pancreas extends into this ligament to reach the splenic hilum. This ligament represents a portion of the dorsal mesogastrium.
questions.question: What structures pass through the splenorenal ligament?
Which structure prevents superior displacement of the humeral head?
questions.explanation: The coraco-acromial arch (formed by coracoid process, acromion, and coracoacromial ligament) prevents superior displacement of the humeral head. The joint capsule is weak superiorly, making this bony-ligamentous arch essential for stability. Rotator cuff muscles provide dynamic stability but the arch provides the structural barrier.

questions.question: Which structure forms the anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen?
questions.explanation: The epiploic foramen (foramen of Winslow) has the hepatoduodenal ligament (free right edge of lesser omentum) containing the portal triad as its anterior boundary. The superior boundary is formed by the caudate lobe of liver covered with peritoneum, the inferior boundary by the first part of the duodenum (superior or horizontal part), and the posterior boundary by the inferior vena cava covered with parietal peritoneum and the right crus of the diaphragm. This opening, typically admitting two fingers, provides the only communication between the greater and lesser peritoneal sacs.

questions.question: Which vein arches over the right bronchus?
questions.explanation: The azygos vein arches over the right main bronchus at the level of T4 before draining into the superior vena cava. This creates a characteristic arch visible on chest radiographs. The azygos arch relationship to the bronchus is an important anatomical landmark.

Level II nodes (middle nodes) lie behind the pectoralis minor muscle. Level I (low nodes) are lateral to pectoralis minor. Level III (upper/apical nodes) are medial to pectoralis minor. This classification is used in staging breast cancer and planning surgical lymph node dissection.
questions.question: What level are nodes behind pectoralis minor?

questions.explanation: The medial umbilical fold is created by the peritoneum covering the medial umbilical ligament, which represents the obliterated umbilical artery. There are paired medial umbilical folds (one on each side), in contrast to the single median umbilical fold in the midline formed by the urachus remnant (median umbilical ligament). Between the median and medial folds lies the supravesical fossa, while the medial inguinal fossa (site of direct inguinal hernias) lies between the medial and lateral umbilical folds, the latter being raised by the inferior epigastric vessels.
questions.question: Which structure forms the medial umbilical fold?
Which vein forms a portosystemic anastomosis at the esophagus?
questions.explanation: At the lower esophagus, esophageal tributaries of the left gastric vein (portal system, draining to portal vein) anastomose with esophageal veins draining the middle third of the esophagus into the azygos system (systemic circulation to SVC). In portal hypertension, these anastomoses dilate to form esophageal varices, which can rupture causing massive hematemesis. This is one of four main portosystemic anastomoses (others: rectum, umbilicus, retroperitoneal). The left gastric vein ascends along the lesser curvature to drain directly into the portal vein, receiving esophageal tributaries that create the anastomosis.

All lymph from the stomach eventually drains to the celiac lymph nodes located around the celiac trunk on the posterior abdominal wall. The lymphatic drainage follows the arterial supply: left and right gastric nodes drain to celiac nodes, as do the gastroepiploic and short gastric nodes (via pancreaticosplenic nodes). This lymphatic pathway is important in gastric cancer staging and spread.
questions.question: Which lymph nodes are the final common drainage for the stomach?

questions.explanation: The esophageal hiatus at T10 transmits the esophagus, anterior and posterior vagal trunks, esophageal branches of left gastric vessels, and lymphatic vessels. The hiatus is formed by muscle fibers of the right crus of the diaphragm. Some right crus fibers form a sling around the esophagus.
questions.question: Which structure passes through esophageal hiatus?
The external spermatic fascia is derived from which layer?
questions.explanation: The external spermatic fascia is the outermost covering of the spermatic cord, derived from the external oblique aponeurosis as the cord passes through the superficial inguinal ring. The three concentric fascial coverings of the cord (from outside to inside) are: external spermatic fascia (from external oblique), cremasteric muscle and fascia (from internal oblique and transversus abdominis), and internal spermatic fascia (from transversalis fascia). Each layer is acquired as the processus vaginalis and accompanying structures descend through the layers of the anterior abdominal wall during testicular descent.

questions.question: Which cells produce insulin in the pancreas?
questions.explanation: Beta cells comprise about 70% of pancreatic islet cells and are located centrally within the islets. They produce and secrete insulin in response to elevated blood glucose, amino acids, and incretin hormones (GLP-1, GIP). Insulin promotes glucose uptake and storage, making it the primary hormone for lowering blood glucose. Beta cell destruction or dysfunction causes diabetes mellitus.

questions.question: Which lymph node group drains the skin of the umbilicus?
questions.explanation: Lymphatic drainage from skin of the anterior abdominal wall follows the watershed principle: above the umbilicus drains to axillary nodes, below the umbilicus drains to superficial inguinal nodes, and the umbilicus itself drains primarily to superficial inguinal nodes though some drainage may occur to both axillary and inguinal nodes. The deep abdominal wall lymphatics drain along the deep vessels (superior epigastric, inferior epigastric, lumbar) to internal thoracic, external iliac, and para-aortic nodes. Metastatic tumor deposits at the umbilicus (Sister Mary Joseph node) typically indicate advanced intra-abdominal malignancy spreading via lymphatics or direct extension.

questions.question: What attaches the diaphragm to the xiphoid process?
questions.explanation: The sternal part of the diaphragm consists of two small muscular slips (or sometimes just fibrous tissue) that attach to the posterior surface of the xiphoid process. These are the smallest attachments of the diaphragm and may be absent, leaving a gap (the sternocostal triangle or foramen of Morgagni) through which superior epigastric vessels and lymphatics pass.

Skene's glands (paraurethral glands) are small glands that open via ducts on either side of the external urethral orifice in females. They are homologous to the male prostate and secrete mucus. They can become infected causing urethritis or form cysts. Bartholin's glands (greater vestibular glands) are homologous to Cowper's glands and open into the vestibule lateral to the vaginal orifice.
questions.question: Which glands open into the female urethra?

questions.explanation: The retropharyngeal space lies between the buccopharyngeal fascia (covering the pharynx) and the prevertebral fascia. This potential space extends from the skull base to the mediastinum. Infections here can spread to the posterior mediastinum causing mediastinitis.
questions.question: The retropharyngeal space lies between which two fascial layers?
Which vein drains the pterygoid venous plexus?
questions.explanation: The maxillary vein is formed from the pterygoid venous plexus in the infratemporal fossa. It joins the superficial temporal vein to form the retromandibular vein within the parotid gland. The pterygoid plexus communicates with cavernous sinus and facial veins without valves.

options: Extension of the thigh at the hip
Flexion of the leg at the knee
Extension of the trunk when thigh and knee are flexed
Medial rotation of the leg by biceps femoris
Lateral rotation of the leg by biceps femoris when knee is flexed
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a correct action of the hamstring muscles?
questions.explanation: Biceps femoris laterally rotates the leg when the knee is flexed, NOT medially rotates it. Semitendinosus and semimembranosus medially rotate the leg when the knee is flexed. This opposing rotation between the medial and lateral hamstrings provides the knee with important rotational control during walking and athletic movements.

questions.question: How many intercostal spaces are present on each side?
questions.explanation: Since there are 12 ribs on each side, there are 11 intercostal spaces between them. Each intercostal space contains intercostal muscles, neurovascular bundles, and lymphatics. Understanding the anatomy of these spaces is crucial for procedures like thoracentesis and chest tube insertion.

questions.question: Which area of the liver is devoid of peritoneal covering?
questions.explanation: The bare area of the liver is located on the diaphragmatic surface where the liver is in direct contact with the diaphragm without intervening peritoneum. This area is bounded by the superior and inferior layers of the coronary ligament. The bare area is clinically significant as infections can spread directly between the liver and thorax.
