options: Bases of metatarsals 2-4; medial longitudinal arch
Plantar ligaments of MTP joints; transverse arch
questions.question: The adductor hallucis has two heads. The transverse head originates from which structure and contributes to maintaining which arch?
questions.explanation: The transverse head of adductor hallucis originates from the plantar ligaments of the metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joints. Together with the oblique head (from bases of metatarsals 2-4), it inserts into the lateral side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the first digit. The transverse head contributes to maintaining the transverse arch by drawing the metatarsal heads together.

options: A fascial tunnel from the posterior compartment
questions.explanation: The Achilles tendon does not have a true synovial tendon sheath like finger flexor tendons. Instead, it is surrounded by a paratenon (peritenon), a loose connective tissue sheath that allows tendon gliding and contains blood vessels. Two bursae are adjacent: the retrocalcaneal bursa (between tendon and calcaneus) and the superficial calcaneal bursa (between tendon and skin). Inflammation of the paratenon causes peritendinitis (Achilles peritendinitis).
questions.question: The Achilles tendon is the thickest and strongest tendon in the body. It does NOT have a true tendon sheath but instead has which covering?
The superior deep cervical lymph nodes receive drainage from which structure?
questions.explanation: The palatine tonsil drains to the superior deep cervical nodes, particularly the jugulodigastric node at the angle of the jaw. The soft palate and posterior tongue also drain to these nodes. The jugulodigastric node is also called the tonsillar node due to enlargement during tonsillitis.

questions.question: Which artery typically does NOT arise directly from the abdominal aorta?
questions.explanation: The common hepatic artery arises from the celiac trunk (along with left gastric and splenic arteries), not directly from the abdominal aorta. The aorta gives rise to paired visceral branches (inferior phrenic, suprarenal, renal, gonadal), unpaired visceral branches (celiac trunk, superior mesenteric artery, inferior mesenteric artery), paired parietal branches (subcostal, four lumbar arteries), and the unpaired median sacral artery before bifurcating into common iliac arteries. Anatomical variations exist, with occasionally the common hepatic or left gastric arising separately from the aorta (replaced vessels).

questions.question: How do the rotator cuff muscles stabilize the glenohumeral joint?
options: Through passive ligament and capsule action
Rotator cuff compresses humeral head into glenoid cavity
questions.explanation: Rotator cuff muscles provide dynamic stability through their resting tone, actively compressing the humeral head into the glenoid cavity. The muscles form a tendinous cuff blending with the joint capsule, providing circumferential reinforcement. This active stabilization is essential given the joint's inherent bony instability.

The flexor retinaculum is a thick connective tissue structure forming the roof of the carpal tunnel. It bridges between the hook of hamate and pisiform medially to the scaphoid and trapezium laterally. This converts the carpal arch into a tunnel through which flexor tendons and median nerve pass.
questions.question: Which structure forms the roof of the carpal tunnel?

questions.explanation: The greater splanchnic nerve arises from the 5th-9th (or sometimes 5th-10th) thoracic sympathetic ganglia. It descends on the vertebral bodies, pierces the crus of the diaphragm, and synapses in the celiac ganglion. It provides sympathetic innervation to foregut derivatives (stomach, liver, pancreas, spleen, etc.).
questions.question: Where does the greater splanchnic nerve arise?

questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) provides both general sensation and taste (special sensation) to the posterior third of the tongue. The anterior two-thirds receives general sensation from the lingual nerve (V3) and taste from chorda tympani (VII). Motor supply to all tongue muscles is from the hypoglossal nerve except palatoglossus.
questions.question: The posterior third of the tongue receives general and special sensory from which nerve?

questions.explanation: The internal acoustic meatus transmits the facial nerve (VII), vestibulocochlear nerve (VIII), and labyrinthine artery. The facial nerve continues through the facial canal to exit at the stylomastoid foramen. Acoustic neuromas typically arise in this region from Schwann cells of the vestibular nerve.
questions.question: Which structure passes through the internal acoustic meatus?

questions.explanation: lumbrical canals are present in the hand as potential spaces surrounding the tendon of each lumbrical muscle. These canals lie between the index, middle, ring, and little fingers. Proximally they are continuous with one of the palmar spaces and can serve as routes for infection spread.
questions.question: How many lumbrical canals are present in the hand?

questions.explanation: The superior mesenteric artery and vein pass between the two peritoneal layers of the mesentery along with lymph nodes, lymphatic vessels, nerves, and fat. These vessels provide the primary blood supply and drainage for the jejunum and ileum. The superior mesenteric artery gives off 15-18 branches that form the arterial arcades.
questions.question: Which structures pass between the two layers of the mesentery?
Why does the phrenic nerve have a long course?
questions.explanation: The phrenic nerve has a long course from the neck (C3-5) to the diaphragm because of embryological migration of the diaphragm. The septum transversum initially forms in the cervical region and migrates caudally during development, carrying its nerve supply (from cervical segments) with it to its final thoracic position.

The great saphenous vein passes posterior to the medial condyle of the femur (approximately a hand's breadth posterior to the medial border of the patella). This is a key landmark for identifying the vein during varicose vein surgery and for cannulation. At the ankle, it ascends anterior to the medial malleolus.
questions.question: The great saphenous vein passes posterior to which bony knee landmark, approximately a hand's breadth posterior to the medial border of the patella?
A primary ossification centre for the ilium appears at which gestational period?
questions.explanation: The primary ossification centre for the ilium appears at the 2nd month of intrauterine life. The ischium's primary centre appears during the 4th month, and the pubis during the 5th month. At birth, the hip bone is ossified except for the iliac crest, the Y-shaped cartilage, and a strip along the inferior margin.

questions.question: Which nerve provides parasympathetic innervation to the submandibular gland?
questions.explanation: Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers in the chorda tympani (from facial nerve) synapse in the submandibular ganglion suspended from the lingual nerve. Postganglionic fibers supply the submandibular and sublingual glands. Sympathetic fibers from the superior cervical ganglion also reach the gland via the facial artery plexus.

questions.question: Which structure forms the primary passive support of the mandible?
questions.explanation: The sphenomandibular ligament runs from the spine of the sphenoid to the lingula of the mandible and provides primary passive support. The stylomandibular ligament is merely a thickening of the parotid capsule and contributes minimally to joint support. Other ligaments provide secondary stabilization or perform different mechanical functions in the temporomandibular complex.

questions.question: Which muscle forms the lateral wall of the pharynx?
questions.explanation: The superior, middle, and inferior pharyngeal constrictors form the muscular lateral and posterior walls of the pharynx. The superior constrictor extends from the pterygoid hamulus and pterygomandibular raphe to the median raphe. Gaps between the constrictors allow passage of nerves and vessels.

The inferior oblique muscle is the only extraocular muscle that protracts (brings forward) the eyeball along with extorsion, elevation, and abduction. It arises from the maxilla at the anteromedial orbital floor and inserts on the posterolateral inferior eyeball. The muscle is innervated by the oculomotor nerve (III). It has no relationship with the common tendinous ring.
questions.question: Which muscle protracts the eyeball?

options: Deep facial vein to pterygoid plexus
questions.explanation: The deep facial vein connects the facial vein with the pterygoid venous plexus in the infratemporal fossa, draining deep facial structures. The pterygoid plexus drains via the maxillary vein to the retromandibular vein. This valveless connection provides a route for infection spread between face and cavernous sinus.
questions.question: Which vein drains the deep face?
Where does the membranous urethra pass through?
questions.explanation: The membranous urethra passes through the urogenital diaphragm (deep perineal pouch), specifically through the sphincter urethrae (external urethral sphincter). This is the shortest (1-2 cm) and narrowest part of the male urethra and the least distensible. It is surrounded by the external urethral sphincter, which is under voluntary control.

questions.question: What muscle action is tested by resisted elbow extension?
questions.explanation: Resisted elbow extension primarily tests triceps brachii strength, particularly the medial head which is most active in this action. Anconeus provides minor assistance. Weakness suggests radial nerve injury or C7 nerve root pathology.

questions.question: Into which fibers do the bundle branches terminate?
questions.explanation: The right and left bundle branches divide into Purkinje fibers, which form a subendocardial network that rapidly conducts the impulse throughout the ventricular myocardium. Purkinje fibers are larger than regular cardiac myocytes with fewer myofibrils, specialized for rapid conduction rather than contraction. They ensure coordinated ventricular contraction from apex to base.

The lateral pectoral nerve (C5, C6) arises from the lateral cord and primarily supplies pectoralis major muscle. The lateral cord also gives rise to the musculocutaneous nerve and the lateral root of the median nerve. It lies lateral to the second part of the axillary artery.
questions.question: Which nerve branch arises from the lateral cord?
At what vertebral level does the inferior angle of the scapula typically lie?
questions.explanation: The inferior angle of the scapula is positioned at the level of the seventh thoracic vertebra (T7) and overlies the seventh rib. This serves as a convenient landmark for counting ribs along the lateral chest wall during thoracotomy procedures. The angle moves laterally and forwards around the chest wall during scapular movement.

The superior and inferior lateral genicular arteries encircle the fibular collateral ligament at the lateral aspect of the knee, contributing to the lateral genicular anastomosis. The superior lateral genicular artery passes above the lateral condyle of the femur, while the inferior lateral genicular artery passes below the lateral tibial condyle. Together they provide important collateral circulation around the knee.
questions.question: The superior lateral genicular artery and the inferior lateral genicular artery both branch from the popliteal artery. Between them, what structure do they encircle at the lateral aspect of the knee?

questions.explanation: The "safe position" (MCP joints flexed 70-90°, IP joints extended, wrist slightly extended) maintains collateral ligaments at maximum length and prevents contracture. This position is also called the "intrinsic plus" position. Prolonged immobilization in other positions can result in permanent stiffness.
options: Position maintaining ligament length and preventing contracture
questions.question: What determines the safe position for hand immobilization?

questions.explanation: The fibrous capsule attaches anteriorly to the intertrochanteric line (making the entire femoral neck intracapsular anteriorly) and posteriorly just proximal to the intertrochanteric crest. The greater and lesser trochanters are therefore extracapsular. This distinction explains why femoral neck fractures carry different complication profiles than intertrochanteric fractures.
questions.question: The femoral neck is intracapsular, but the greater and lesser trochanters are extracapsular. The fibrous capsule attaches anteriorly to which line on the femur?
What is the functional relationship between scapular stability and glenohumeral mobility?
questions.explanation: A stable scapular base is essential for efficient glenohumeral motion. Scapular stabilizers (serratus anterior, rhomboids, trapezius) provide a fixed base from which glenohumeral muscles can act. Scapular winging demonstrates how loss of stability compromises shoulder function despite intact glenohumeral muscles.
options: Stable scapula essential for efficient glenohumeral motion

questions.question: The ureter crosses which vessel at the pelvic brim?
questions.explanation: The ureter crosses the common iliac artery (or its bifurcation into external and internal iliac arteries) at the pelvic brim, typically near the sacroiliac joint, as it descends from the posterior abdominal wall into the pelvis. This anatomical relationship is surgically significant as it marks the transition point where the ureter enters the pelvis. The ureter then runs along the lateral pelvic wall, crossing anterior to the internal iliac artery and its branches, before turning medially to reach the bladder. In females, the ureter passes beneath the uterine artery ("water under the bridge") approximately 1.5 cm lateral to the cervix.

questions.question: Which muscle elevates the hyoid bone and pharynx during swallowing?
questions.explanation: The stylopharyngeus muscle elevates the pharynx and hyoid bone during swallowing, supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve. The infrahyoid muscles (sternohyoid, sternothyroid, thyrohyoid, omohyoid) depress the hyoid. Longitudinal pharyngeal muscles collectively raise the pharynx to engulf the food bolus.

The pericardiacophrenic vessels (branches of internal thoracic artery and vein) accompany the phrenic nerve on each side as it descends through the thorax to the diaphragm. These vessels supply the pericardium, pleura, and diaphragm. The phrenic nerve lies between the fibrous pericardium and mediastinal pleura.
questions.question: Which vessels run with the phrenic nerve?

questions.explanation: The talus articulates with the calcaneus inferiorly, navicular anteriorly, tibia superiorly, lateral malleolus laterally, and medial malleolus medially. This unique articulation pattern makes the talus the keystone of the hindfoot. The talus receives no direct muscle attachments and is entirely dependent on its articular surfaces and ligamentous connections.
questions.question: Which bone of the foot articulates with the calcaneus inferiorly, the navicular anteriorly, the tibia superiorly, and both malleoli laterally?

options: Extensor carpi radialis longus, brevis, and ulnaris
questions.explanation: Extension at the wrist joint is produced mainly by extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis, and extensor carpi ulnaris. The extensor digitorum provides assistance to this movement. All these extensors are located in the posterior compartment of the forearm.
questions.question: Which muscles produce wrist extension with assistance from extensor digitorum?

options: Tibialis anterior tendon, deep fibular nerve, dorsalis pedis artery
Tibialis posterior, FDL, posterior tibial vessels and tibial nerve, FHL
Fibularis longus, fibularis brevis, sural nerve, small saphenous vein
Extensor hallucis longus, extensor digitorum longus, anterior tibial artery
questions.explanation: The tarsal tunnel contains the following structures passing from anterior to posterior (using the mnemonic Tom, Dick And Very Nervous Harry): Tibialis posterior tendon, flexor Digitorum longus tendon, posterior tibial Artery and Veins, tibial Nerve, and flexor Hallucis longus tendon. Compression within this tunnel causes tarsal tunnel syndrome with plantar foot pain and paraesthesia.
questions.question: The tarsal tunnel is formed by the flexor retinaculum and bones of the medial ankle. Which structures pass through it from anterior to posterior?
What nerve supplies the extensor digitorum muscle?
questions.explanation: The posterior interosseous nerve, the deep terminal branch of the radial nerve, supplies extensor digitorum and all other extensor muscles in the posterior forearm compartment. The nerve passes between the two heads of the supinator muscle to reach the posterior compartment.

questions.question: Where does the right bundle branch travel?
questions.explanation: The right bundle branch descends in the interventricular septum and crosses to the right ventricular free wall via the moderator band (septomarginal trabecula) to reach the anterior papillary muscle. From there, it divides into Purkinje fibers that spread throughout the right ventricle. This pathway ensures coordinated right ventricular contraction and explains why the moderator band is functionally important.

The left gastric artery is the smallest of the three branches of the celiac trunk (along with splenic and common hepatic arteries), arising at the T12/L1 level. It ascends to the cardioesophageal junction, giving off esophageal branches to the abdominal esophagus, then descends along the lesser curvature of the stomach in the lesser omentum, anastomosing with the right gastric artery. It supplies both surfaces of the stomach along the lesser curvature. An aberrant or replaced left hepatic artery may arise from the left gastric artery, running in the gastrohepatic ligament.
questions.question: The left gastric artery arises from which vessel?

questions.explanation: The fibrous pericardium is the tough, inelastic outer layer of the pericardial sac composed of dense fibrous connective tissue. It prevents overdistention of the heart, protects against infection from surrounding structures, and anchors the heart in the mediastinum. It is continuous superiorly with the adventitia of the great vessels and inferiorly with the central tendon of the diaphragm.
questions.question: Which structure forms the fibrous outer layer of the pericardium?

questions.explanation: Wrist position affects finger flexor and extensor muscle lengths through tenodesis effect. Wrist extension tightens finger flexors enhancing grip while passively flexing fingers. Wrist flexion tightens extensors causing passive finger extension. This relationship is exploited in tenodesis grip for spinal cord injury patients.
options: Wrist position affects finger flexor/extensor length affecting grip
questions.question: What is the functional relationship between wrist position and finger function?
The transverse arch is formed proximally by which bones?
questions.explanation: The transverse arch is formed proximally by the three cuneiforms and the cuboid, and distally by the bases of the five metatarsals. When both feet are approximated, the medial borders form a complete transverse arch, with each foot representing a half dome. The intermediate and lateral cuneiforms are wedge-shaped, contributing the bony factor to the transverse arch.
options: Bases of all five metatarsals only
Three cuneiforms and navicular bones only
Navicular and talus bones only proximally
Calcaneus and cuboid of the lateral column only
Three cuneiforms and cuboid proximally; five metatarsal bases distally

questions.question: Which muscle attachment defines the lateral arcuate ligament?
questions.explanation: The lateral arcuate ligament (lateral lumbocostal arch) is a thickening of the fascia covering quadratus lumborum, extending from the tip of the L1 transverse process to the 12th rib. The diaphragm's lateral part arises from this ligament. The medial arcuate ligament crosses over psoas major (from L1 body to L1 transverse process tip), allowing passage of the sympathetic trunk, while the median arcuate ligament connects the diaphragmatic crura across the midline anterior to the aorta at T12. These arcuate ligaments can be sites of neurovascular compression or serve as anatomical landmarks in retroperitoneal surgery.

questions.question: What nerve supplies subscapularis muscle?
questions.explanation: Subscapularis is supplied by the upper subscapular nerve (C5, C6) and lower subscapular nerve (C5, C6). Both nerves arise from the posterior cord. The lower subscapular nerve also supplies teres major muscle.

questions.question: The lesser trochanter, the traction epiphysis of which muscle, projects from the posterior surface of the femur and points in which direction?
questions.explanation: The lesser trochanter is the traction epiphysis of the iliopsoas muscle, the great flexor of the hip joint. It projects from the posterior surface of the femur and is conical, pointing medially. It marks the lowermost fibers of the gluteus maximus insertion.

questions.question: Which forearm muscle has no bony attachment distally?
questions.explanation: has no bony attachment distally; it inserts into the flexor retinaculum and palmar aponeurosis. This muscle is absent in approximately 15% of people without functional deficit. It can be used as a tendon graft source in reconstructive surgery.

questions.question: The posterior fontanelle is located at which suture junction?
questions.explanation: The posterior fontanelle (lambda) is located at the junction of the sagittal and lambdoid sutures where the occipital and parietal bones meet. It is triangular and smaller than the anterior fontanelle. The posterior fontanelle typically closes by 2-3 months of age. Delayed closure may indicate hydrocephalus or skeletal dysplasia.

questions.question: Which bronchus is given off outside the hilum?
questions.explanation: The right upper lobar bronchus (eparterial bronchus) is given off outside the hilum of the right lung, above the pulmonary artery. This is unique to the right side. All other lobar bronchi arise within the hilum. The left main bronchus divides entirely within the hilum.

questions.question: Where does the subclavian lymph trunk drain?
questions.explanation: The subclavian lymph trunk is formed by the union of efferent lymph vessels from the apical group of axillary nodes. It usually opens into the subclavian vein. On the left side, it may open into the thoracic duct. This represents the final pathway for breast lymph drainage.

questions.question: Which lobe of the liver is functionally part of the left lobe?
questions.explanation: The caudate lobe, although anatomically part of the right lobe, is functionally part of the left lobe based on blood supply and biliary drainage. It receives blood from both right and left hepatic arteries and drains bile into both right and left hepatic ducts. Similarly, the quadrate lobe receives blood from the left hepatic artery and drains into the left hepatic duct.

The splenic (left colic) flexure is positioned higher than the hepatic (right colic) flexure and also forms a more acute angle. The splenic flexure is attached to the diaphragm by the phrenicocolic ligament. This higher position of the left flexure is clinically significant in colonoscopy and surgical procedures.
questions.question: Which flexure of the colon is located at a higher position?
Which artery supplies the upper third of the anal canal?
questions.explanation: The superior rectal artery (continuation of the inferior mesenteric artery) supplies the upper two-thirds of the anal canal above the pectinate line. The middle rectal arteries (from internal iliac) and inferior rectal arteries (from internal pudendal) supply the lower third. This mixed blood supply creates a watershed area prone to ischemia.

questions.question: Which muscle is the primary supinator of the forearm?
questions.explanation: The supinator muscle is the primary supinator of the forearm, wrapping around the proximal radius. The biceps brachii is a powerful accessory supinator, especially when the elbow is flexed. The deep branch of the radial nerve passes between the two heads of the supinator muscle.

questions.question: What muscles produce lateral rotation of the humerus?
questions.explanation: Lateral (external) rotation of the humerus is produced by infraspinatus, teres minor, and posterior fibers of the deltoid. The infraspinatus and teres minor are two of the four rotator cuff muscles. This movement rotates the arm away from the midline, making the thumb point laterally.

options: Special sensory (taste) from anterior two-thirds tongue
questions.explanation: The chorda tympani carries special sensory (taste) fibers from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and parasympathetic secretomotor fibers to submandibular and sublingual glands. It branches from the facial nerve in the mastoid, crosses the middle ear, and joins the lingual nerve. Damage causes loss of taste on the ipsilateral anterior tongue.
questions.question: The chorda tympani nerve carries which type of fibers?

questions.explanation: Fourteen structures exit through the greater sciatic foramen: one muscle (piriformis), seven nerves (sciatic, posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh, superior gluteal, inferior gluteal, nerve to obturator internus, nerve to quadratus femoris, and pudendal nerves), and six vessels (superior and inferior gluteal arteries and veins, and internal pudendal artery and vein).
questions.question: How many total structures exit through the greater sciatic foramen?
Houston's third valve in the rectum is located at which vertebral level?
questions.explanation: Houston's third transverse rectal fold is the most constant and prominent, located at the level of S5 vertebra, approximately 5 cm above the anus. If this fold completely encircles the rectum, it is called Nelaton's sphincter. This fold divides the rectum into an upper chamber (containing the pre-allantoic part of the hindgut that can hold feces without triggering the defecation reflex) and a lower chamber (derived from the post-allantoic cloaca that is sensitive to distension). The fold helps support the weight of feces and prevents passage during instrumentation.

questions.question: The popliteal vein is formed at the distal border of popliteus by the union of which two deep leg veins?
questions.explanation: The popliteal vein is formed at the distal border of popliteus by the union of the anterior and posterior tibial veins. It traverses the popliteal fossa in the same fibrous sheath as the popliteal artery and terminates at the adductor hiatus to become the femoral vein. The small saphenous vein also drains into the popliteal vein.
options: Medial genicular and small saphenous veins

questions.question: What is the primary function of the thoracic cage?
questions.explanation: The thoracic cage primarily functions to protect the lungs, heart, and great vessels from external trauma. Additionally, it provides attachment points for muscles of the thorax, upper limb, abdomen, and back. The cage also plays a vital role in the mechanics of respiration through its elastic properties.

The mitral (bicuspid) valve has two cusps: anterior (aortic) and posterior (mural). The anterior cusp is larger and more mobile, positioned between the mitral orifice and aortic orifice, while the posterior cusp is shorter and attached to more of the annular circumference. Mitral valve prolapse and stenosis are common pathological conditions affecting this valve.
questions.question: What are the cusps of the mitral valve?
Which lymph nodes drain the lower anal canal (below pectinate line)?
questions.explanation: Lymphatic drainage from the anal canal below the pectinate line follows the drainage of the external body wall, passing to the superficial inguinal lymph nodes. This reflects the embryological origin of this region from ectoderm (proctodeum) and its somatic innervation. In contrast, the anal canal above the pectinate line (derived from endoderm) drains to internal iliac nodes along the superior rectal vessels, with some drainage via middle rectal vessels also to internal iliac nodes. This dual drainage pattern is clinically important in carcinoma of the anal canal, affecting surgical planning and lymph node dissection.

Each renal artery typically divides into five segmental arteries: apical, anterosuperior, anteroinferior, inferior, and posterior. These are functional end arteries with no significant anastomoses, meaning occlusion of one causes infarction of that segment. This segmental anatomy allows partial nephrectomy without affecting remaining segments. Four segmental arteries arise from the anterior division; one (posterior) from the posterior division.
questions.question: How many segmental arteries typically supply each kidney?
Which component of the quadriceps femoris is the largest and lies on the lateral side of the thigh?
questions.explanation: Vastus lateralis is the largest component of the quadriceps femoris, lying on the lateral side of the thigh. It originates from the greater trochanter and lateral lip of the linea aspera. All four quadriceps components converge into the quadriceps tendon, which continues as the patellar ligament inserting into the tibial tuberosity.

is not part of the rotator cuff; it acts as a medial rotator and adductor of the humerus. The four rotator cuff muscles are supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, and subscapularis. These muscles fuse with the joint capsule and stabilize the glenohumeral joint.
questions.question: Which muscle is NOT part of the rotator cuff?

questions.explanation: The foramen ovale in the greater wing of the sphenoid transmits the mandibular division (V3) of the trigeminal nerve. It also transmits the accessory meningeal artery, lesser petrosal nerve, and an emissary vein. The nerve supplies muscles of mastication and provides sensation to the mandibular region.
questions.question: The foramen ovale transmits which nerve?
The arcuate line represents the inferior limit of which structure?
questions.explanation: The arcuate line (linea semicircularis) marks the inferior border of the posterior rectus sheath, located approximately midway between the umbilicus and pubic symphysis. Above this line, the posterior sheath is formed by the posterior lamina of the internal oblique aponeurosis and the aponeurosis of transversus abdominis. Below the arcuate line, all aponeurotic layers pass anterior to the rectus abdominis, leaving only transversalis fascia and parietal peritoneum posteriorly. This creates an area of weakness exploited by direct inguinal hernias and inferior epigastric vessel injuries.

The posterior cerebral arteries are the terminal branches of the basilar artery, which bifurcates at the upper border of the pons. They supply the occipital lobes, inferior temporal lobes, and parts of the thalamus. The posterior communicating arteries connect them to the internal carotid system.
questions.question: The posterior cerebral artery is a terminal branch of which vessel?

questions.explanation: The phrenic nerves (C3-C5) provide somatic sensory innervation to the fibrous pericardium and parietal layer of serous pericardium. Pain from pericardial irritation is therefore sharp and well-localized, often referred to the shoulder (C4 dermatome). The visceral pericardium receives autonomic innervation and is insensitive to pain.
questions.question: Which nerve supplies the fibrous pericardium and parietal serous pericardium?
The iliacus muscle, originating from the iliac fossa, is innervated by which nerve?
questions.explanation: The iliacus muscle is innervated by the femoral nerve (L2, L3). It originates from the iliac crest, iliac fossa, ala of sacrum, and anterior sacroiliac ligaments, and inserts into the tendon of psoas major and the lesser trochanter. Acting conjointly with psoas major and minor, it flexes the thigh at the hip and stabilizes the joint.

The iliopsoas is the primary flexor of the hip joint, formed by the fusion of iliacus and psoas major. Their combined tendon inserts into the lesser trochanter, which is its traction epiphysis. The iliopsoas is active in walking, running, and sitting up. Weakness of iliopsoas is assessed by resisted hip flexion in the seated position.
questions.question: Which muscle is the primary flexor of the hip joint, described as the great flexor, with its traction epiphysis being the lesser trochanter?

questions.explanation: The interatrial septum is the thin wall separating the right and left atria. It contains the fossa ovalis, a thumbprint-sized oval depression representing the site of the foramen ovale in the fetus. The limbus fossae ovalis is the prominent margin of the fossa. In approximately 25% of people, the foramen ovale remains probe-patent without functional significance.
questions.question: Which structure separates the right and left atria internally?

questions.explanation: The mesoappendix is a triangular fold of peritoneum extending from the terminal ileum and its mesentery to the entire length of the appendix (base to tip), connecting it to the posterior abdominal wall. The appendicular artery (from ileocolic artery) runs in the free edge of the mesoappendix to supply the appendix. During appendectomy, the mesoappendix must be divided and the appendicular artery ligated. The mesoappendix contains fat, lymph nodes, and vessels. Occasionally, the mesoappendix may be short, leaving the distal appendix without mesenteric coverage.
questions.question: The mesoappendix is attached to which part of the appendix?

questions.explanation: F cells (PP cells) produce pancreatic polypeptide, which regulates pancreatic secretion and gallbladder contraction. These cells are found mainly in islets in the posterior part of the pancreatic head. Pancreatic polypeptide secretion increases after a meal and with vagal stimulation. Elevated levels may occur in some pancreatic tumors and after vagotomy.
questions.question: Which cells produce pancreatic polypeptide?
What percentage of the rectum is covered by peritoneum anteriorly?
questions.explanation: Only the upper third of the rectum is covered by peritoneum on its anterior surface, the middle third has peritoneum on its front only, and the lower third is completely devoid of peritoneal covering. Posteriorly, the rectum is retroperitoneal throughout its length. This peritoneal relationship creates the rectovesical pouch in males and rectouterine pouch in females.

questions.question: The left colic flexure is supported by which ligament?
questions.explanation: The phrenicocolic ligament extends from the splenic (left colic) flexure of the colon to the diaphragm at the level of the 10th and 11th ribs, helping to support and maintain the position of the splenic flexure. This ligament forms a shelf that supports the inferior pole of the spleen, preventing its downward displacement. The ligament also serves as a barrier between the left paracolic gutter and the area around the spleen, potentially limiting the spread of infection or fluid collections between these compartments during pathological processes.

Opponens digiti minimi draws the fifth metacarpal forward and rotates it laterally, deepening the palm and opposing the little finger toward the thumb. It is one of the three hypothenar muscles and is supplied by the ulnar nerve.
questions.question: What is the action of opponens digiti minimi?
The optic canal transmits which two structures?
questions.explanation: The optic canal in the lesser wing of the sphenoid transmits the optic nerve (II) and ophthalmic artery. The central retinal vein drains alongside within the optic nerve sheath. The canal opens into the posterior orbit and connects the middle cranial fossa with the orbital cavity.

questions.question: Which vessel anastomoses at Griffiths' point?
questions.explanation: Griffiths' point is the watershed area at the splenic flexure where the left branch of the middle colic artery (from superior mesenteric artery) anastomoses with the ascending branch of the left colic artery (from inferior mesenteric artery). This represents the junction between the superior and inferior mesenteric arterial territories and is vulnerable to ischemia due to relatively poor collateral circulation. Another watershed area exists at Sudeck's point (rectosigmoid junction) where the last sigmoid artery meets the superior rectal artery. Both areas are susceptible to ischemic colitis during low-flow states.

questions.question: Which artery typically supplies the SA node?
questions.explanation: The sinoatrial (SA) nodal artery arises from the right coronary artery in approximately 60% of people and from the left circumflex artery in 40%. The SA node is located in the superior part of the crista terminalis near the junction of the superior vena cava and right atrium. It is the primary pacemaker of the heart, initiating approximately 60-100 beats per minute.

questions.question: Which muscle pulls the arytenoid cartilages forward toward the epiglottis?
questions.explanation: The aryepiglotticus muscle, running in the aryepiglottic fold, pulls the arytenoid cartilages forward toward the epiglottis, closing the laryngeal inlet during swallowing. It acts like a purse-string sphincter. The muscle is supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve. The thyroepiglotticus and thyroarytenoid muscles assist in this protective function.

Flexion-extension at the hip joint has the greatest range of movement, commonly cited as 120-140 degrees. Abduction-adduction has a range of 60-80 degrees, while internal-external rotation is 60-90 degrees. These ranges vary with the position of other joints and the state of surrounding soft tissues.
questions.question: Which movement at the hip joint has the greatest range, commonly cited as 120-140 degrees?
The superior thyroid artery gives off which laryngeal branch?
questions.explanation: The superior thyroid artery gives off the superior laryngeal artery, which accompanies the internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve through the thyrohyoid membrane. The artery supplies the laryngeal structures above the vocal cords. The cricothyroid branch runs with the external laryngeal nerve to supply the cricothyroid muscle and anastomoses across the midline.

questions.question: Which muscle forms the medial boundary of Hesselbach's triangle?
questions.explanation: Hesselbach's triangle (inguinal triangle) is bounded medially by the lateral border of the rectus abdominis muscle, laterally by the inferior epigastric artery, and inferiorly by the inguinal ligament. The floor of this triangle consists of transversalis fascia (reinforced medially by the conjoint tendon), representing a potential weak area in the posterior wall of the inguinal canal. Direct inguinal hernias protrude through this triangle medial to the inferior epigastric artery, in contrast to indirect hernias which emerge lateral to the artery through the deep inguinal ring.

questions.question: Which rib does the costal pleural reflection cross midaxillarily?
questions.explanation: The costal line of pleural reflection passes obliquely, crossing the tenth rib in the midaxillary line (MAL). It crosses the eighth rib in the midclavicular line and becomes continuous posteriorly with the vertebral lines at the neck of the twelfth rib. This surface marking is crucial for safe thoracentesis.

questions.question: The lesser sac communicates with the greater sac through which opening?
questions.explanation: The lesser sac (omental bursa) communicates with the greater sac through the epiploic foramen (foramen of Winslow, foramen of Winslow), bounded anteriorly by the hepatoduodenal ligament, posteriorly by the IVC and right crus of diaphragm, superiorly by the caudate lobe of liver, and inferiorly by the first part of the duodenum. This communication allows peritoneal fluid to flow between the two sacs and permits spread of infection or hemorrhage. The foramen typically admits two fingers and can be used surgically to access the lesser sac. Foramina of Morgagni and Bochdalek are diaphragmatic defects, not communications between peritoneal sacs.

questions.question: Which muscle abducts and flexes the shoulder?
questions.explanation: fibers produce both shoulder flexion and assist with abduction. The anterior fibers also contribute to medial rotation. The deltoid muscle as a whole is multipennate, with different fiber groups producing different movements.

options: Hip abduction while in single-leg stance
Dorsiflexing the ankle during the swing phase of walking
Rising from a forward-flexed position (simultaneous hip and trunk extension)
Rotating the trunk in a sitting position
questions.explanation: Gluteus maximus and erector spinae work together in rising from a forward-flexed position, simultaneously extending the hip and the trunk respectively. Gluteus maximus is the great extensor of the hip, particularly powerful in these loaded extension tasks. Weakness of either muscle group causes difficulty in rising from bending and is assessed in clinical examination of low back and hip pathology.
questions.question: Erector spinae and gluteus maximus work together during which functional activity?

questions.explanation: The superior thyroid artery is typically the first branch of the external carotid artery, arising just below the carotid bifurcation. It descends to supply the thyroid gland and gives off the superior laryngeal artery. The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve accompanies this artery and innervates the cricothyroid muscle.
questions.question: The superior thyroid artery is typically the first branch of which vessel?

options: Both extrinsic and intrinsic stabilizers are essential
questions.explanation: Shoulder stability requires both extrinsic factors (rotator cuff muscles, long head of biceps, negative intra-articular pressure, scapular position) and intrinsic factors (glenoid labrum, glenohumeral ligaments, joint capsule). Loss of either extrinsic or intrinsic factors increases dislocation risk.
questions.question: How do extrinsic and intrinsic factors contribute to shoulder stability?

questions.explanation: The fundus of the gallbladder typically reaches the anterior abdominal wall at the tip of the right 9th costal cartilage, where the lateral edge of the right rectus abdominis muscle crosses the right costal margin (approximately at the transpyloric plane). This surface marking corresponds to the point where the gallbladder may contact the anterior abdominal wall, making it palpable when distended or inflamed. Murphy's sign (inspiratory arrest with deep palpation at this point due to pain) indicates acute cholecystitis. The fundus is the only part of the gallbladder completely covered by peritoneum.
questions.question: The gallbladder fundus typically lies at which anatomical landmark?
options: Right costal margin at 9th costal cartilage

questions.question: Which hormone stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate secretion?
questions.explanation: Secretin, produced by S cells in the duodenal and jejunal mucosa in response to acid, stimulates pancreatic ductal cells (including centroacinar cells) to secrete bicarbonate-rich fluid. This neutralizes gastric acid and creates the optimal pH (7-8) for pancreatic enzyme function. Secretin also inhibits gastric acid secretion and gastric emptying, providing negative feedback control.

questions.question: Which structure lies in the hepatoduodenal ligament's free edge?
questions.explanation: The hepatoduodenal ligament (pars condensa, the thickened free right edge of the lesser omentum) contains the portal triad: portal vein (posteriorly), common bile duct (anteriorly and to the right), and hepatic artery proper (anteriorly and to the left). The relationship is remembered as "DAV" from right to left anteriorly (Duct, Artery, Vein). This ligament forms the anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen and is the structure compressed during the Pringle maneuver to control bleeding during hepatic surgery. Lymph nodes and autonomic nerve plexuses also course through this ligament.

The cricoarytenoid joint permits rotation and sliding movements of the arytenoid cartilages, which directly control vocal cord abduction and adduction. Tension changes occur primarily through cricothyroid joint movement, not cricoarytenoid articulation. The L-shaped base of the arytenoid pivots at the cricoarytenoid joint to open or close the rima glottidis.
questions.question: The cricoarytenoid joint allows which specific movement of the vocal cords?

questions.explanation: The medial fascial compartment of the thigh receives its blood supply from the profunda femoris (deep femoral) artery via its perforating branches and from the obturator artery. The nerve supply is from the obturator nerve (L2, L3, L4). The profunda femoris is the major blood supply to all three thigh compartments via its perforating branches.
questions.question: The main blood supply to the medial compartment of the thigh comes from which two arteries?
Which muscle forms the floor of the posterior abdominal wall?
questions.explanation: The posterior abdominal wall is formed by multiple muscles: psoas major (medially, originating from lumbar vertebrae), quadratus lumborum (laterally, between 12th rib and iliac crest), and iliacus (below iliac crest, in iliac fossa). Together these muscles, along with the diaphragm superiorly and the lumbar vertebrae and their processes, create the musculoskeletal framework of the posterior abdominal wall. The transversus abdominis wraps around from the anterolateral wall to attach to these structures. These muscles are covered anteriorly by psoas fascia, quadratus lumborum fascia, and iliac fascia respectively, with retroperitoneal organs and vessels lying anterior to these fascial layers.

questions.question: Which structure is most anterior in right lung root?
questions.explanation: In both lung roots, the arrangement from superior to inferior is: pulmonary artery (uppermost), bronchus (middle), pulmonary veins (lowermost). From anterior to posterior: pulmonary veins (most anterior), pulmonary artery, bronchus (most posterior). Hilar lymph nodes are scattered throughout.

questions.question: The parotid gland duct opens opposite which tooth?
questions.explanation: The parotid (Stensen's) duct opens into the oral vestibule opposite the crown of the upper second molar tooth. The duct crosses the masseter superficially before piercing the buccinator. A small accessory parotid gland may be present along the duct on the masseter (socia parotidis).

The superior constrictor muscle forms the floor (bed) of the tonsillar fossa, separated from the tonsil by the tonsillar capsule. The palatoglossus and palatopharyngeus form the anterior and posterior pillars respectively. Loose areolar tissue separates the capsule from the superior constrictor, facilitating surgical dissection.
questions.question: Which structure forms the floor of the tonsillar fossa?
The fabella is a sesamoid bone occasionally found in which muscle's tendon near the knee?
questions.explanation: The fabella is an accessory sesamoid bone occasionally found in the tendon of the lateral head of gastrocnemius, at the posterolateral aspect of the knee. It is present in approximately 10-30% of individuals. It can cause posterolateral knee pain (fabella syndrome) when it compresses the common fibular nerve or irritates the popliteus tendon. It is typically visible on lateral knee radiographs.

The left gastric vein typically drains directly into the portal vein near its origin behind the neck of the pancreas, though it may occasionally drain into the splenic vein. The left gastric vein receives esophageal tributaries from the abdominal esophagus, creating an important portosystemic anastomosis with esophageal veins draining to the azygos system. In portal hypertension, these anastomotic channels dilate to form esophageal varices, which can rupture causing life-threatening hemorrhage. The coronary vein is an alternative name for the left gastric vein, following the course of the left gastric artery along the lesser curvature.
questions.question: The left gastric vein drains into which vessel?
Which muscle protrudes the mandible when contracted bilaterally?
questions.explanation: The lateral pterygoid muscle protrudes the mandible when both sides contract simultaneously, assisted by the medial pterygoid. Unilateral contraction causes lateral deviation to the opposite side. The muscle has superior and inferior heads inserting on the articular disc and pterygoid fovea respectively.

questions.question: The ischiopubic rami fuse with each other at which approximate age?
questions.explanation: The ischiopubic rami fuse with each other at approximately 7-8 years of age. The secondary ossification centres of the hip bone (for the iliac crest, Y-shaped cartilage of the acetabulum, and ischial tuberosity) all fuse completely by 20-25 years of age.

questions.question: Where are Peyer's patches most concentrated?
questions.explanation: Peyer's patches are most numerous and largest in the terminal ileum, with 20-30 patches typically present in the last 60 cm of ileum. They are permanent aggregates of lymphoid follicles in the lamina propria and submucosa, located on the antimesenteric border. M cells in the epithelium overlying Peyer's patches sample antigens for immune surveillance. They can become inflamed in conditions like typhoid fever.

The depressor labii inferioris depresses and everts the lower lip. It arises from the mandible and inserts into the skin of the lower lip. The muscle is innervated by the marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve. Depressor anguli oris acts primarily on the angle of the mouth, though it assists in lowering the lip.
questions.question: Which muscle depresses the lower lip?

questions.explanation: Rectus femoris is the only quadriceps component that crosses the hip joint, originating from the anterior inferior iliac spine. Therefore, it can both extend the leg at the knee and flex the thigh at the hip. The three vasti originate from the femur itself and only cross the knee joint.
questions.question: Which muscle is the ONLY component of the quadriceps that crosses the hip joint and can therefore flex the thigh?

questions.explanation: The right suprarenal gland is related anteriorly to the bare area of the liver and the inferior vena cava, posteriorly to the diaphragm, medially to the right celiac ganglion and IVC, and inferiorly to the upper pole of the right kidney. The left suprarenal gland has different anterior relations (stomach, pancreas, splenic artery, and lesser sac). Both glands are retroperitoneal and highly vascular, receiving arterial supply from three sources (superior, middle, and inferior suprarenal arteries from inferior phrenic, aorta, and renal artery) but having asymmetric venous drainage (right to IVC, left to left renal vein).
questions.question: The right suprarenal gland is related anteriorly to which structure?
What drains blood from the breast?
questions.explanation: Blood from the breast drains into both the axillary veins (via lateral thoracic and thoracoacromial tributaries) and the internal thoracic veins (via perforating veins). During pregnancy and lactation, these veins become prominent and engorged. Venous drainage pathways are important routes for cancer metastasis.

questions.question: What forms the anterior wall of the inguinal canal?
questions.explanation: The external oblique aponeurosis forms the anterior wall of the inguinal canal throughout its length. The superficial inguinal ring is a triangular opening in the external oblique aponeurosis. The anterior wall is reinforced laterally by fibers of the internal oblique muscle as they arch over the spermatic cord.

questions.question: Which nerve innervates the cremaster muscle?
questions.explanation: The cremaster muscle receives motor innervation from the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve (L1, L2), which enters the inguinal canal through the deep inguinal ring and travels within the spermatic cord. The cremasteric reflex (elevation of the testis in response to stroking the inner thigh) tests this nerve and the L1-L2 cord segments. The ilioinguinal nerve provides sensory innervation to the skin of the scrotum and adjacent thigh but does not innervate the cremaster muscle. The cremasteric artery (from inferior epigastric) provides vascular supply to the cremaster muscle and travels alongside the nerve.

questions.question: Which surface landmark on the femur, below the greater trochanter, represents the insertion of the gluteus maximus?
questions.explanation: The gluteal tuberosity is located below the greater trochanter and serves as the insertion point for gluteus maximus. The trochanteric fossa, medial to the greater trochanter, receives the insertion of obturator externus. Knowing these distinctions is critical in hip replacement surgery.

questions.question: Which structure marks the junction between the nasopharynx and oropharynx?
questions.explanation: The lower border of the soft palate marks the boundary between the nasopharynx above and the oropharynx below. The soft palate can elevate to close off the nasopharynx during swallowing. The pharyngeal isthmus connects these two regions and can be voluntarily controlled.

questions.question: Which part of the duodenum is most mobile?
questions.explanation: The first part (superior part) of the duodenum, specifically its first 2 cm (duodenal cap or bulb), is the only portion that is intraperitoneal and mobile, being connected to the liver by the hepatoduodenal ligament. The remainder of the first part and all of the second, third, and fourth parts are secondarily retroperitoneal and fixed to the posterior abdominal wall. This mobility makes the duodenal bulb vulnerable to anterior displacement by posterior masses (e.g., pancreatic head tumors). The mobile first part is also the most common site of peptic ulceration.

The middle cardiac vein runs in the posterior interventricular groove alongside the posterior interventricular artery and drains into the coronary sinus at its termination. It drains the posterior walls of both ventricles and the posterior interventricular septum, corresponding to the territory of the posterior interventricular artery. It is the second largest cardiac vein.
questions.question: Where does the middle cardiac vein run?
Which artery typically does NOT arise from the abdominal aorta?
questions.explanation: The deep circumflex iliac artery arises from the external iliac artery (just above the inguinal ligament, near the origin of the inferior epigastric artery), not from the abdominal aorta. It runs laterally along the inguinal ligament and iliac crest, supplying the lower abdominal wall muscles. The abdominal aorta gives rise to paired visceral branches (inferior phrenic, suprarenal, renal, gonadal), unpaired visceral branches (celiac, SMA, IMA), paired parietal branches (four lumbar arteries), and the unpaired median sacral artery posteriorly, before bifurcating into right and left common iliac arteries at L4 level.

questions.question: What muscle action is tested by the OK sign?
questions.explanation: The OK sign tests anterior interosseous nerve function by assessing flexor pollicis longus and flexor digitorum profundus to the index finger. Inability to form the OK sign indicates anterior interosseous nerve palsy. The patient cannot flex the interphalangeal joint of the thumb and distal interphalangeal joint of the index finger.

questions.question: Which cardiac chamber forms most of the anterior surface?
questions.explanation: The right ventricle forms most of the anterior (sternocostal) surface of the heart. The right atrium contributes to the right portion of this surface, and a small part of the left ventricle forms the left border. This anterior position makes the right ventricle most vulnerable to anterior chest trauma. The left ventricle forms most of the diaphragmatic surface and left border.

questions.question: At what level does the deep palmar arch lie in the hand?
questions.explanation: The deep palmar arch is formed by the radial artery and deep palmar branch of the ulnar artery. It lies approximately one centimeter proximal to the superficial palmar arch at the level of the proximal border of the extended thumb. It gives off palmar metacarpal arteries and perforating branches.
options: One centimeter distal to wrist joint
One centimeter proximal to superficial arch

questions.explanation: Afferent (sensory) nerve fibers from the kidneys travel with sympathetic nerves and enter the spinal cord at T10-T12 and L1 segments. This explains the referred pain pattern of renal colic, which radiates from the loin to the groin along the distribution of these dermatomes. Ureteric pain follows a similar pattern as the ureter shares this innervation.
questions.question: Which spinal segments provide afferent innervation from the kidney?

questions.explanation: The tensor tympani is innervated by the nerve to medial pterygoid, a branch of the mandibular division (V3). The stapedius muscle is innervated by the facial nerve. Both muscles modulate ossicular chain movement, protecting the inner ear from loud sounds and reducing physiologic noise.
questions.question: The tensor tympani muscle is innervated by which nerve?

questions.explanation: produces both extension and adduction (ulnar deviation) at the wrist joint. It works with flexor carpi ulnaris to produce pure adduction by balancing extension and flexion forces. The muscle is located in the posterior forearm compartment.
questions.question: Which muscle extends and adducts the wrist?
The external iliac artery becomes the femoral artery at which landmark?
questions.explanation: The external iliac artery becomes the femoral artery as it passes beneath the inguinal ligament at the mid-inguinal point (midway between ASIS and pubic symphysis, different from the midpoint of the inguinal ligament). The femoral artery enters the femoral triangle, lying lateral to the femoral vein in the femoral sheath. Just before passing beneath the inguinal ligament, the external iliac artery gives off the inferior epigastric and deep circumflex iliac arteries. The femoral artery later becomes the popliteal artery after passing through the adductor hiatus.

questions.question: How do intrinsic and extrinsic hand muscles work together?
options: Extrinsic for power grip, intrinsic for precision
questions.explanation: Extrinsic hand muscles (arising in forearm) provide power for grip and basic finger movements. Intrinsic hand muscles (arising in hand) provide precision movements, finger positioning, and the unique lumbrical action (MCP flexion with IP extension). This combination enables both powerful and precise hand function.

questions.question: At which vertebral level does the renal artery arise from the aorta?
questions.explanation: The renal arteries arise from the abdominal aorta at approximately the level of the L2 vertebral body, just inferior to the origin of the superior mesenteric artery. The right renal artery is longer than the left and passes posterior to the inferior vena cava to reach the right kidney. Each renal artery divides into five segmental arteries that are functionally end arteries.

questions.question: What is the internal urethral sphincter composed of?
questions.explanation: The internal urethral sphincter is composed of smooth muscle (a thickening of the detrusor muscle at the bladder neck) and is under involuntary autonomic control. It is controlled by sympathetic innervation (hypogastric nerves), which causes contraction to maintain continence and prevent retrograde ejaculation in males. It relaxes during micturition under parasympathetic control.

questions.question: Which nerve roots form the phrenic nerve?
questions.explanation: The phrenic nerve is formed from cervical nerve roots C3, C4, and C5 ("C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive"). It provides the entire motor supply to the diaphragm. The long course from neck to diaphragm reflects the embryological migration of the diaphragm from the cervical region.

questions.question: What forms the anorectal angle?
questions.explanation: The puborectalis muscle (part of levator ani) forms a sling around the anorectal junction, creating an approximately 90-degree anorectal angle that contributes to fecal continence. During defecation, the puborectalis relaxes, straightening the anorectal angle to allow passage of feces. Paradoxical contraction of this muscle during defecation causes obstructed defecation syndrome.

The posterior ethmoidal foramen in the medial orbital wall transmits the posterior ethmoidal nerve (from nasociliary) and vessels (from ophthalmic artery). These structures supply the posterior ethmoidal air cells and sphenoid sinus. The foramen is located between the ethmoid and sphenoid bones, posterior to the anterior ethmoidal foramen.
questions.question: The posterior ethmoidal foramen transmits which structures?

questions.explanation: Quiet expiration is a passive process resulting from elastic recoil of the lungs and relaxation of intercostal muscles and diaphragm. The ribs are depressed and the diaphragm elevated to its normal position. Lung recoil reduces size, increasing pressure inside the lungs to allow air flow outward.
questions.question: What characterizes quiet expiration?

questions.explanation: The superior cerebellar artery arises from the basilar artery just before its terminal bifurcation. It supplies the superior surface of the cerebellum, cerebellar nuclei, and superior cerebellar peduncle. The artery courses around the pons below the oculomotor nerve. Occlusion causes ipsilateral cerebellar signs and contralateral pain/temperature loss.
questions.question: Which artery supplies the superior surface of the cerebellum?

questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve arises from the medial cord of the brachial plexus (C7, C8, T1). The medial cord also gives rise to the medial pectoral nerve, medial cutaneous nerve of arm and forearm, and the medial root of the median nerve. Injury to the medial cord affects all these structures.
questions.question: Which cord of the brachial plexus gives rise to the ulnar nerve?

questions.explanation: The first 2 cm of the first (superior) part of the duodenum (the duodenal cap or bulb) is the most mobile as it is intraperitoneal with a mesentery. The remainder of the duodenum is retroperitoneal and relatively fixed. This mobility, combined with exposure to acid, makes the duodenal cap the most common site for duodenal ulcers (95% of duodenal ulcers occur here).
questions.question: Which segment of the duodenum is most mobile?

questions.explanation: The basilar artery terminates at the upper border of the pons by dividing into the two posterior cerebral arteries. It is formed by union of the vertebral arteries at the pontomedullary junction. The artery gives off pontine, anterior inferior cerebellar, superior cerebellar, and labyrinthine branches during its course.
questions.question: The basilar artery terminates at which vertebral level?
The pes anserinus on the superior medial tibia is formed by the combined insertion of which three muscles?
questions.explanation: The pes anserinus (goose's foot) is formed by the common tendinous insertion of sartorius, gracilis, and semitendinosus on the superior medial surface of the tibia. These three muscles belong to three different thigh compartments yet all cross both the hip and knee joints and share this common insertion. Pes anserinus bursitis is a clinical condition here.

questions.question: What passes through the deep inguinal ring?
questions.explanation: In males, the spermatic cord passes through the deep inguinal ring (an opening in the transversalis fascia lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels). In females, the round ligament of the uterus passes through. The ilioinguinal nerve passes through the superficial inguinal ring but not the deep ring - it enters the canal by piercing the internal oblique muscle.

options: The cuboid and calcaneus being wedge-shaped
The intermediate and lateral cuneiforms being wedge-shaped
The plantar surfaces of all tarsals being flat
questions.explanation: The intermediate and lateral cuneiforms are wedge-shaped, with their broader surfaces dorsally and narrower surfaces plantarly, providing the bony factor to the transverse arch. The ligaments (deep transverse metatarsal ligament and interosseous ligaments), the muscle fibularis longus, the transverse head of adductor hallucis, and slips of tibialis posterior all contribute to maintaining this arch.
questions.question: Which factor provides the bony contribution to the transverse arch, with the intermediate and lateral cuneiforms being specifically wedge-shaped?

questions.explanation: The valleculae (spaces between the tongue base and epiglottis) receive sensory innervation from the internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (vagus). The glossopharyngeal nerve also contributes sensation to this region. Foreign bodies commonly lodge in the valleculae. These spaces are bounded by the median and lateral glossoepiglottic folds.
questions.question: The vallecular receives sensory innervation from which nerve?
The psoas major muscle receives innervation from which nerve roots?
questions.explanation: The psoas major muscle is innervated by the ventral rami of lumbar nerves L1 through L4, which emerge from the lumbar plexus formed within the substance of the muscle itself. This segmental innervation pattern corresponds to the muscle's extensive vertebral origins from the bodies, transverse processes, and intervertebral discs of T12 through L5. The muscle serves as the chief flexor of the thigh at the hip joint and also assists in lateral flexion of the lumbar vertebral column when acting unilaterally.

questions.question: Which left upper lobe segments are fused?
questions.explanation: In the left upper lobe, the apical and posterior segments typically fuse to form a single apicoposterior segment. The left upper lobe therefore typically contains: apicoposterior, anterior, superior lingular, and inferior lingular segments. This fusion accounts for the lower total segment count.

The loose connective tissue layer contains emissary veins that connect the superficial scalp veins with intracranial venous sinuses. This layer is often called the danger area because infections can spread intracranially. The loose texture allows fluid and blood to spread widely in scalp injuries.
questions.question: Which structure lies in the loose connective tissue layer of the scalp?

questions.explanation: The pulmonary artery is the most superior structure in the root of both lungs. The main bronchus lies posterior to the vessels. The superior and inferior pulmonary veins are the most inferior structures in the root. This anatomical arrangement is constant and important during surgery.
questions.question: Which vessel is superior in the lung root?
At which vertebral level does the inferior vena cava pierce the diaphragm?
questions.explanation: The inferior vena cava passes through the caval opening (foramen venae cavae) in the central tendon of the diaphragm at the T8 vertebral level, the highest of the three major diaphragmatic openings. This opening also transmits branches of the right phrenic nerve. The esophageal hiatus (T10 level) transmits the esophagus and vagal trunks, while the aortic hiatus (T12 level) transmits the aorta, thoracic duct, and azygos vein. The IVC opening dilates during inspiration as the diaphragm contracts and descends, facilitating venous return to the heart.

The interventricular septum has a small upper membranous part (approximately 1 cm) and a large lower muscular part. The membranous septum lies just beneath the aortic valve (specifically between the right and non-coronary cusps). Ventricular septal defects most commonly occur in the membranous portion near the tricuspid valve.
questions.question: Which part of the interventricular septum is membranous?

questions.explanation: The hepatic artery proper, ascending in the free edge of the lesser omentum (hepatoduodenal ligament) as part of the portal triad, divides near the porta hepatis into right and left hepatic arteries that supply the corresponding lobes of the liver. The right hepatic artery gives off the cystic artery to the gallbladder. Significant anatomical variation exists in hepatic arterial anatomy (occurring in up to 45% of individuals), including replaced or accessory right hepatic arteries from the superior mesenteric artery and replaced or accessory left hepatic arteries from the left gastric artery.
questions.question: The hepatic artery proper typically divides into which branches?

questions.explanation: The mammary gland is formed of 15-20 lobes, each consisting of numerous lobules. The lobes and lobules are separated by interlobar and interlobular fibrous and fatty tissue called the ligaments of Cooper. Each lobe drains through its own lactiferous duct, which opens onto the nipple summit.
questions.question: How many lobes does the mammary gland contain?

questions.explanation: The gastric impression is the largest and most concave of the impressions on the splenic visceral surface, reflecting contact with the fundus and greater curvature of the stomach. It lies between the superior and intermediate borders. Other impressions include renal (from left kidney), colic (from splenic flexure), and pancreatic (from pancreatic tail).
questions.question: Which structure forms the most concave impression on the splenic visceral surface?
What contains the pleural fluid normally?
questions.explanation: The pleural cavity normally contains a small amount of serous (pleural) fluid that acts as a lubricant between the visceral and parietal pleural surfaces. This fluid is continuously produced and absorbed, maintaining a thin film that facilitates smooth lung movement during respiration.

questions.question: The great auricular nerve is derived from which spinal segments?
questions.explanation: The great auricular nerve arises from the cervical plexus (C2-C3) and provides sensation to the skin over the parotid gland, lower ear, and angle of the mandible. It emerges at the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid and ascends on that muscle. The nerve is at risk during parotid surgery and facelift procedures.

questions.question: What comprises the central tendon of the diaphragm?
questions.explanation: The central tendon is a strong aponeurosis of dense fibrous tissue forming the central portion of the diaphragm. It is trifoliate (three-leafed) in shape, resembling a clover leaf. The heart rests on its superior surface within the pericardium. The caval opening pierces the central tendon at the junction of the right leaflet with the middle leaflet.

questions.question: The greater omentum is attached to which part of the transverse colon?
questions.explanation: The greater omentum (specifically its posterior two layers after folding back from the inferior descent) attaches to the anterior surface (and superior border) of the transverse colon and its mesocolon. The omentum hangs like an apron from the greater curvature of the stomach, descends anterior to the small intestine, then folds back on itself and fuses with the transverse colon and mesocolon before continuing to the posterior abdominal wall. This four-layered structure contains fat and can wall off inflamed organs (giving it the name "abdominal policeman"), provides insulation, and allows mobility of abdominal contents.

questions.question: The teniae coli converge at which structure?
questions.explanation: The three teniae coli (longitudinal muscle bands: taenia libera, taenia mesocolica, and taenia omentalis) of the cecum converge at the base of the vermiform appendix, providing a reliable surgical landmark for locating the appendix during appendectomy. The teniae continue along the ascending, transverse, and descending colon but disappear at the rectosigmoid junction (approximately 15 cm from the anal verge), where the longitudinal muscle coat becomes complete around the circumference of the rectum. The teniae correspond to areas where the longitudinal muscle is thickened, while the areas between are thinner, allowing formation of sacculations (haustra).

questions.question: What provides the total left lung segment count?
questions.explanation: The left lung typically contains 8-10 bronchopulmonary segments depending on anatomical variation. The upper lobe has 4-5 segments (apicoposterior/or separate apical and posterior, anterior, superior lingular, inferior lingular) and the lower lobe has 4-5 segments (superior, anterior basal, lateral basal, posterior basal, ? medial basal).

The right lymphatic duct receives lymph from the right half of the head, neck, thorax, right upper limb, right lung, right side of the heart, and right surface of the liver. It is formed by the union of right jugular, subclavian, and bronchomediastinal trunks. This duct drains into the right venous angle.
questions.question: Which duct drains the right side of the thorax?

questions.explanation: Scapular protraction (abduction) is produced by serratus anterior and pectoralis minor muscles. During protraction, the lateral end of the clavicle moves forward along with the scapula. This movement is used in punching, pushing, and reaching forward actions.
questions.question: Which muscles are responsible for scapular protraction?

questions.explanation: The cervical pleura extends approximately one inch (2.5 to 4 cm) above the medial third of the clavicle. This superior extension of the parietal pleura is reinforced by the suprapleural membrane. Understanding this anatomy is important because the pleura can be injured during procedures in the lower neck.
questions.question: How high above the clavicle does cervical pleura extend?

questions.explanation: The left main bronchus crosses anterior to the esophagus creating the third anatomical constriction at 27 cm from the incisors (T5-6 level). This is where the trachea bifurcates. Foreign bodies and malignancies may cause compression at this site. Endoscopic measurements from the incisors help locate pathology.
questions.question: Which structure crosses esophagus at 27 cm?

questions.explanation: The aortic hiatus is located at the T12 vertebral level, posterior to the diaphragm (technically behind rather than through it). It is formed by the median arcuate ligament connecting the right and left crura. It transmits the aorta, thoracic duct, and sometimes the azygos vein. As it's posterior to the diaphragm, aortic flow is not impeded during diaphragmatic contraction.
questions.question: At which level is the aortic hiatus located?

questions.explanation: The pudendal canal (Alcock's canal) is a fascial tunnel in the lateral wall of the ischiorectal fossa, formed by the splitting of the obturator fascia covering the obturator internus muscle. It contains the pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels as they pass from the lesser sciatic foramen toward the perineum. The pudendal nerve (S2-S4) provides motor innervation to perineal muscles and sensory innervation to the external genitalia and perineum. Pudendal nerve block can be performed by injecting anesthetic near the ischial spine where the nerve re-enters the pelvis.
questions.question: Which structure is located in the pudendal canal?

options: Fascia lata of the thigh only
Camper's fascia of the anterior abdominal wall
Transversalis fascia anteriorly and iliac fascia posteriorly
questions.explanation: The femoral sheath is a prolongation of the transversalis fascia anteriorly and the iliac fascia posteriorly, enclosing the femoral artery, femoral vein, and the femoral canal (containing lymphatics). The femoral nerve lies outside the femoral sheath. A femoral hernia passes through the femoral canal into the femoral sheath inferior to the inguinal ligament.
questions.question: The femoral sheath is a prolongation of which fascia, enclosing the femoral vessels and the femoral canal?
What is the subcostal muscle?
questions.explanation: The subcostalis muscle is an incomplete sheet on the inner surface of the lower ribs near their angles. Its fibers cross more than one intercostal space (unlike intercostal muscles which span single spaces). It is part of the innermost layer of thoracic wall muscles.

questions.question: The sphenoid sinus relates posteriorly to which structure?
questions.explanation: The sphenoid sinus lies within the body of the sphenoid with the clivus and pons posterior to it. The pituitary fossa is superior, and the cavernous sinuses with internal carotid arteries are lateral. The optic chiasm lies superiorly. Trans-sphenoidal pituitary surgery accesses the fossa through the sphenoid sinus.

Scarpa's fascia is the deep membranous layer of the superficial fascia of the anterior abdominal wall, found inferior to the umbilicus. Superficial to it lies Camper's fascia, the fatty superficial layer. Scarpa's fascia continues inferiorly as the superficial perineal fascia (Colles' fascia) in the perineum and the dartos muscle and fascia in the scrotum. This fascial layer is clinically important as it can limit the spread of extravasated urine or blood in the superficial perineal space, directing fluids superiorly toward the anterior abdominal wall.
questions.question: Which layer of the anterior abdominal wall contains Scarpa's fascia?
What prevents premature activation of pancreatic enzymes?
questions.explanation: The pancreas produces protease inhibitors (particularly pancreatic secretory trypsin inhibitor, PSTI) that prevent premature activation of trypsinogen within the pancreas. Enzymes are also stored as inactive zymogens in secretory granules. Premature intrapancreatic activation of trypsinogen (which then activates other proteases) causes acute pancreatitis with autodigestion of pancreatic tissue.

The left lower lobe typically contains four (sometimes five) bronchopulmonary segments: superior (apical), anterior basal, lateral basal, and posterior basal. The medial basal segment is often absent or fused with the anterior basal segment on the left side, unlike the right lower lobe which consistently has five segments.
questions.question: How many segments are in left lower lobe?

questions.explanation: The radial nerve and profunda brachii artery pass through the triangular interval. This space is bounded by teres major superiorly, long head of triceps medially, and lateral head of triceps laterally. The structures then enter the spiral groove of the humerus.
questions.question: Which structure passes through the triangular interval?

questions.explanation: The tympanic cavity is a single air-filled space without compartmentalization, though the articular disc divides the temporomandibular joint into compartments. The cavity extends into mastoid air cells posteriorly via the aditus ad antrum. The Eustachian tube provides communication with the nasopharynx.
questions.question: Which structure separates the tympanic cavity into superior and inferior compartments?
Which lymph nodes lie along the sternum?
questions.explanation: The parasternal (internal thoracic) lymph nodes lie along the internal thoracic vessels, approximately 1 cm from the lateral border of the sternum.
