They receive lymph from the anterior chest wall, medial breast, diaphragm, and upper abdominal wall. Efferents drain to the bronchomediastinal trunks and brachiocephalic veins.

The renal medulla is the inner part of the kidney containing 10-12 renal pyramids (medullary pyramids). Each pyramid has its base directed toward the cortex and its apex (renal papilla) projecting medially into a minor calyx. The pyramids contain the loops of Henle and collecting ducts, giving them a striated appearance due to parallel tubules.
questions.question: Which part of the kidney contains the renal pyramids?

questions.explanation: The right upper lobar bronchus (also called eparterial bronchus) is given off outside the hilum of the lung, above the pulmonary artery. This is in contrast to the left lung where the main bronchus divides within the hilum into two lobar (secondary) bronchi. This anatomical arrangement is clinically significant.
questions.question: Where does the right upper lobar bronchus branch?

questions.explanation: The third (horizontal or inferior) part of the duodenum crosses anterior to the abdominal aorta, the inferior vena cava, the right psoas major muscle, the right ureter, and the right testicular/ovarian vessels at approximately the L3 vertebral level. This portion of the duodenum runs transversely from right to left and is crossed anteriorly by the superior mesenteric artery and vein, with the root of the mesentery of the small intestine crossing it obliquely. Superior mesenteric artery syndrome can occur when the third part of the duodenum is compressed between the SMA anteriorly and the aorta posteriorly.
questions.question: Which part of the duodenum crosses anterior to the abdominal aorta?

questions.explanation: The portal vein forms at approximately the L1/L2 vertebral level posterior to the neck of the pancreas through the confluence of the superior mesenteric vein (from the right) and splenic vein (from the left), anterior to the inferior vena cava. The inferior mesenteric vein typically joins the splenic vein before this confluence. The portal vein then ascends obliquely to the right in the free edge of the lesser omentum (hepatoduodenal ligament) to reach the porta hepatis, where it divides into right and left branches. It measures approximately 8 cm in length and receives the left and right gastric veins.
questions.question: The portal vein is formed at which vertebral level?

questions.explanation: Extrinsic thumb muscles (abductor pollicis longus, extensor pollicis longus and brevis, flexor pollicis longus) provide power and basic positioning. Thenar muscles provide fine motor control and opposition. This combination enables the thumb's unique versatility in human hand function.
questions.question: How do extrinsic thumb muscles complement thenar muscles?
options: Extrinsic muscles for precision grip only
Extrinsic for power grip, thenar for precision control

questions.explanation: The mandibular division (V3) of the trigeminal nerve supplies all muscles of mastication (masseter, temporalis, medial and lateral pterygoids) via its motor root. It also supplies mylohyoid, anterior belly of digastric, tensor veli palatini, and tensor tympani. These muscles derive from the first pharyngeal arch mesoderm.
questions.question: Which nerve provides motor innervation to the muscles of mastication?

questions.explanation: The phrenicocolic ligament, extending from the splenic (left colic) flexure to the diaphragm at the level of ribs 10-11, supports the inferior pole of the spleen, preventing downward displacement. It creates a shelf-like structure that effectively suspends the spleen. The ligament also serves as a barrier between the left paracolic gutter inferiorly and the area around the spleen superiorly, potentially limiting the spread of peritoneal fluid, infection, or tumors between these compartments. During colonoscopy or surgery on the splenic flexure, division of this ligament may be necessary for adequate mobilization of the colon.
questions.question: The phrenicocolic ligament supports which structure?

questions.explanation: The lateral arcuate ligament (lateral lumbocostal arch) is a thickened band of fascia covering the quadratus lumborum muscle, extending from the tip of the L1 transverse process to the 12th rib. The diaphragm's lateral muscular fibers arise from this ligament. The medial arcuate ligament crosses over psoas major (from L1 body to L1 transverse process), while the median arcuate ligament connects the right and left crura across the aortic hiatus. These ligaments can compress neurovascular structures and serve as important surgical landmarks in retroperitoneal approaches.
questions.question: The lateral arcuate ligament extends from L1 transverse process to which structure?
The superior orbital fissure transmits which cranial nerves?
questions.explanation: The superior orbital fissure transmits oculomotor (III), trochlear (IV), ophthalmic division of trigeminal (V1), and abducens (VI) nerves. It also transmits the superior ophthalmic vein. The fissure is bounded by the greater and lesser wings of the sphenoid. The optic nerve passes through the separate optic canal.

options: Inversion and adduction of the foot
questions.question: The two lateral compartment muscles, both supplied by the superficial fibular nerve, primarily perform which actions?
questions.explanation: The lateral compartment contains fibularis longus and fibularis brevis, both supplied by the superficial fibular nerve (L5, S1, S2). Their primary actions are eversion of the foot and weak plantarflexion of the ankle. Fibularis longus also supports the transverse arch by crossing the sole. Lateral compartment injury impairs the ability to evert the foot.

The spleen lies deep to the left 9th, 10th, and 11th ribs in the left hypochondrium. This relationship provides protection but also means that fractures of these ribs can lead to splenic rupture. The long axis of the spleen follows the line of the 10th rib. The spleen's position varies with respiration and body posture.
questions.question: Which ribs typically protect the spleen?
Which cranial fossa contains the temporal lobes?
questions.explanation: The middle cranial fossa accommodates the temporal lobes of the brain laterally and the pituitary gland centrally. The floor is formed by the greater wings and body of the sphenoid and the petrous and squamous parts of the temporal bones. The fossa is wider than the anterior fossa. Multiple foramina pierce its floor.

questions.question: The dorsal venous arch of the foot drains medially into the great saphenous vein and laterally into which vein?
questions.explanation: The dorsal venous arch lies in the subcutaneous tissue over the heads of the metatarsal bones. It drains medially into the great saphenous vein (via the dorsal vein of the great toe) and laterally into the small saphenous vein (via the dorsal vein of the little toe). This arch is the origin point of both major superficial veins of the lower limb.

Although no anatomical sphincter exists, a physiological lower esophageal sphincter (LES) mechanism prevents reflux at the gastroesophageal junction. This involves: (1) increased smooth muscle tone in the distal esophagus, (2) acute angle of entry (angle of His), (3) compression by the right crus of the diaphragm, (4) positive intra-abdominal pressure on the abdominal esophagus. LES dysfunction causes gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD).
questions.question: Which structure prevents reflux at the gastroesophageal junction?

questions.explanation: The external anal sphincter, composed of voluntary striated muscle, receives motor innervation from the inferior rectal nerve (branch of the pudendal nerve, S2-S4) and perineal branch of S4. This allows voluntary control of defecation and anal continence. The pudendal nerve provides somatic innervation, making the external sphincter unlike the internal sphincter (smooth muscle under involuntary autonomic control). Damage to the pudendal nerve (during childbirth, surgery, or chronic straining) can lead to fecal incontinence. The pudendal nerve also provides sensory innervation to the anal canal below the pectinate line.
questions.question: Which nerve supplies the external anal sphincter?

questions.explanation: The ACL prevents posterior displacement of the femur on the tibia (or anterior displacement of the tibia on the femur) and hyperextension of the knee joint. When the knee is flexed at a right angle, the tibia cannot be pulled anteriorly because it is held by the intact ACL. ACL rupture is detected by a positive anterior drawer test.
questions.question: The ACL is slack during knee flexion and taut during full extension. It prevents posterior displacement of the femur on the tibia and which other movement?

questions.explanation: Pronator teres and biceps brachii are antagonistic for forearm rotation: pronator teres produces pronation while biceps produces supination. However, both can contribute to elbow flexion when pronation/supination resistance is present. This demonstrates how muscles can be synergistic for one motion while antagonistic for another.
options: They're antagonists: pronator teres pronates, biceps supinates
questions.question: What is the functional relationship between pronator teres and biceps?

questions.explanation: The superior epigastric artery is the other terminal branch of the internal thoracic artery. It descends behind the rectus abdominis muscle supplying it and the anterior abdominal wall. It anastomoses with the inferior epigastric artery (from external iliac), providing collateral circulation between subclavian and external iliac arteries.
questions.question: Which artery supplies the anterior body wall superiorly?
Which muscle, by supporting the medial longitudinal arch, prevents excessive pronation of the foot during the stance phase of gait?
questions.explanation: Tibialis posterior is the most important dynamic supporter of the medial longitudinal arch, actively preventing excessive pronation during stance phase. It eccentrically controls subtalar eversion during heel strike, then concentrically re-inverts and supinates the foot at push-off. Tibialis posterior tendon dysfunction leads to progressive flatfoot with excessive pronation, and is the most common cause of adult acquired flatfoot.

The vermiform appendix arises from the posteromedial wall of the cecum, approximately 2-3 cm below the ileocecal junction. The three taeniae coli of the cecum converge at the base of the appendix, serving as a reliable landmark for locating it during surgery. While the base of the appendix has a relatively constant position, its tip can be found in various locations: retrocecal (65%), pelvic (31%), subcecal (2.3%), preileal (1%), or postileal (0.4%). The appendicular artery, a branch of the ileocolic artery, runs through the mesoappendix to supply the appendix.
questions.question: The vermiform appendix typically arises from which part of the cecum?

questions.explanation: The superior rectal artery represents the direct continuation of the inferior mesenteric artery after it gives off the left colic and sigmoid branches, descending into the pelvis within the sigmoid mesocolon. It crosses the left common iliac vessels at the level of S3 and divides into right and left branches that descend on either side of the rectum, penetrating its wall and anastomosing with branches of the middle rectal (from internal iliac) and inferior rectal (from internal pudendal) arteries at the level of the internal anal sphincter.
questions.question: The superior rectal artery is the terminal continuation of which vessel?
How many bones are present in both lower limbs combined, considering femurs, patellae, tibiae, fibulae, tarsals, metatarsals, and phalanges?
questions.explanation: The bones of both lower limbs total 60: 2 femurs, 2 patellae, 2 tibiae, 2 fibulae, 14 tarsals, 10 metatarsals, and 28 phalanges. This understanding is fundamental in trauma assessment and radiological interpretation. Each single lower limb contains 30 bones.

The suspensory ligament (zonules of Zinn) connects the lens equator to the ciliary processes. These zonular fibers transmit tension from the ciliary muscle to the lens capsule, controlling lens shape for accommodation. When ciliary muscle contracts, zonular tension decreases, allowing the elastic lens to become more spherical for near vision.
questions.question: Which ligament suspends the lens of the eye?

questions.explanation: The transtubercular plane is a horizontal plane passing through the iliac tubercles (projections on the outer lips of the iliac crests about 5 cm posterior to the anterior superior iliac spines) at the level of the L5 vertebral body. Along with the subcostal plane (through the lowest points of the costal margin at L3), it defines the superior boundaries of the right and left inguinal (iliac) regions. This plane also approximates the level of the bifurcation of the abdominal aorta and the confluence of common iliac veins to form the inferior vena cava.
questions.question: Which plane passes through the iliac tubercles?

questions.explanation: The tibial nerve gives off the medial sural cutaneous nerve in the popliteal fossa. This joins the sural communicating branch of the common fibular nerve to form the sural nerve, supplying the lateral side of the leg and ankle. The tibial nerve is the most superficial of the major neurovascular bundle in the fossa.
questions.question: The tibial nerve gives off which named cutaneous nerve in the popliteal fossa that contributes to forming the sural nerve?
The suspensory ligament of the ovary contains which vessels?
questions.explanation: The suspensory ligament of the ovary (infundibulopelvic ligament), a lateral extension of the broad ligament, contains the ovarian artery (from abdominal aorta at L2) and ovarian vein (to IVC on right, left renal vein on left), along with ovarian nerves and lymphatics. This ligament extends from the ovary to the lateral pelvic wall and must be carefully clamped and ligated during oophorectomy to control the ovarian vessels. The ovarian ligament (connecting ovary to uterus) contains no significant vessels. The uterine artery reaches the uterus via the parametrium (base of broad ligament).

options: Ligaments of the joint and adjacent bone
Muscles moving the joint and skin covering their insertion
Tendons crossing the joint and adjacent bursae
Articular cartilage and synovial membrane only
questions.question: Hilton's law states the nerve supplying a joint also supplies which other two structures?
questions.explanation: Hilton's law states: 'The nerve supplying the joint also supplies the muscles moving the joint and the skin covering the insertion of these muscles.' This explains why patients with hip joint disease may refer pain to the knee, as the posterior division of the obturator nerve supplies both joints. It is fundamental in understanding referred pain patterns.

produces shoulder adduction, extension, and medial rotation. It is a powerful muscle forming part of the posterior axillary fold. The muscle is commonly used in reconstructive surgery and is supplied by the thoracodorsal nerve.
questions.question: Which muscle produces both shoulder adduction and medial rotation?
The median umbilical fold contains which structure?
questions.explanation: The median umbilical fold (single, midline structure) is raised by the median umbilical ligament, which represents the obliterated urachus (embryonic connection between bladder apex and umbilicus). The paired medial umbilical folds contain the medial umbilical ligaments (obliterated umbilical arteries), while the paired lateral umbilical folds contain the inferior epigastric vessels (patent). The obliterated umbilical vein forms the ligamentum teres hepatis and runs in the free edge of the falciform ligament, not in an umbilical fold. These folds create fossae on the internal surface of the anterior abdominal wall that are clinically significant as potential sites of herniation.

The angle of inclination of the femoral neck to the shaft is approximately 135 degrees in adults. A decrease below 120 degrees defines coxa vara, while an increase above 140 degrees defines coxa valga. This angle is greater in children and decreases with skeletal maturity. It is critical for hip biomechanics and prosthetic design in hip arthroplasty.
questions.question: The angle of inclination (neck-shaft angle) of the femur is approximately how many degrees in adults?

questions.explanation: The left gonadal (testicular or ovarian) vein drains into the left renal vein, while the right gonadal vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava. The left renal vein also receives the left suprarenal vein and communicates with the ascending lumbar vein. This arrangement makes the left testicular vein more prone to varicocele formation.
questions.question: Which vein drains into the left renal vein?
The vertebral artery gives off which spinal branch?
questions.explanation: The vertebral arteries give off anterior spinal arteries before joining to form the basilar artery. The two anterior spinal arteries unite to form a single vessel descending in the anterior median fissure. The vertebral arteries also give off posterior spinal arteries. These vessels supply the cervical spinal cord before receiving reinforcement from segmental arteries.

The hepatic veins (right, middle, and left) drain directly into the inferior vena cava just below the diaphragm, representing the final pathway for blood that has passed through the hepatic sinusoids. Unlike other veins, hepatic veins have no valves. The portal vein and its tributaries (splenic, superior mesenteric, and inferior mesenteric veins) carry nutrient-rich but deoxygenated blood to the liver, where it mixes with oxygenated blood from the hepatic artery in the sinusoids before draining via hepatic veins. The hepatic veins and their relationship to IVC are crucial landmarks in liver surgery and transplantation.
questions.question: Which vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava?
The spermatic cord receives its external covering from which muscle?
questions.explanation: The external spermatic fascia, the outermost covering of the spermatic cord, is derived from the external oblique muscle's aponeurosis as the cord passes through the superficial inguinal ring. Moving inward, the next layer is the cremasteric muscle and fascia (from internal oblique and transversus abdominis), and the innermost fascial layer is the internal spermatic fascia (from transversalis fascia at the deep inguinal ring). The dartos muscle is in the scrotal wall, not directly covering the cord. These concentric layers are acquired sequentially as structures descend through abdominal wall layers.

questions.question: Which structure forms the posterior boundary of the lesser sac?
questions.explanation: The posterior wall of the lesser sac (omental bursa) is formed by peritoneum covering the pancreas, left kidney, left suprarenal gland, superior pole of the left kidney, and the posterior two layers of the greater omentum fused to the transverse mesocolon. The lesser sac is bounded anteriorly by the stomach, lesser omentum, and greater omentum (anterior two layers); superiorly by the caudate lobe of liver and diaphragm; inferiorly by the transverse colon and mesocolon; and communicates with the greater sac through the epiploic foramen. Collections in the lesser sac appear on imaging as fluid between stomach and pancreas.

The anterior ethmoidal artery is a branch of the ophthalmic artery from the internal carotid system. It supplies the anterior and middle ethmoidal air cells and frontal sinus. The artery enters the nasal cavity through the anterior ethmoidal foramen and supplies the anterior nasal septum.
questions.question: The anterior ethmoid artery is a branch of which parent vessel?
Which structure passes through the superficial inguinal ring in males?
questions.explanation: The ilioinguinal nerve (L1) passes through the superficial inguinal ring after traversing the inguinal canal, unlike the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve which travels within the spermatic cord through both deep and superficial rings. The ilioinguinal nerve runs between internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles, enters the inguinal canal, and emerges through the superficial ring to provide sensory innervation to the skin of the upper medial thigh, root of penis and anterior scrotum (males), or mons pubis and labium majus (females). Entrapment following hernia repair can cause chronic groin pain.

questions.question: Which muscle connects ribs to vertebrae posteriorly?
questions.explanation: The levator costarum muscles are twelve small muscles connecting the transverse processes of C7 and T1-T11 vertebrae to the ribs below. They elevate the ribs and are innervated by lateral branches of the dorsal rami of thoracic spinal nerves. They assist in respiration and lateral flexion.

questions.question: Which branches arise from the first part of the axillary artery?
questions.explanation: The first part of the axillary artery (from lateral border of first rib to upper border of pectoralis minor) gives off only one branch. This is the superior (highest) thoracic artery. The second part gives two branches while the third part gives three branches.

options: Allow cupping of hand for power grip
questions.question: What is the functional significance of the mobile 4th and 5th metacarpals?
questions.explanation: The mobile 4th and 5th metacarpals (articulating with hamate) allow palmar cupping for power grip. This adaptation enables the hand to conform to cylindrical objects. The 2nd and 3rd metacarpals are relatively fixed, providing a stable platform for precision grip.

The thyroid gland is bound to the larynx and trachea by the pretracheal fascia. This attachment causes the thyroid to move with the larynx during swallowing. The isthmus overlies the second to fourth tracheal rings while the lobes extend from the thyroid cartilage downward.
questions.question: The thyroid gland is attached to which laryngeal structure?

questions.explanation: The brachioradialis reflex predominantly tests the C6 nerve root. The reflex is elicited by tapping the brachioradialis tendon at the distal forearm. Absence or diminution suggests C6 nerve root or radial nerve pathology proximal to the elbow.
questions.question: What nerve root is predominantly tested by the brachioradialis reflex?

questions.explanation: The greater and lesser wings of the sphenoid bone form most of the posterior orbital wall. The orbital surface of the greater wing forms the lateral posterior wall, while the lesser wing contributes superiorly. The optic canal is located at the orbital apex in the lesser wing. The superior orbital fissure lies between the wings.
questions.question: Which bone forms the posterior wall of the orbit?

questions.explanation: The external intercostal muscle is the most superficial intercostal muscle with fibers directed downward and forward. It extends from the rib tubercle posteriorly to the costochondral junction anteriorly. The muscle is deficient anteriorly where it is replaced by the anterior intercostal membrane.
questions.question: Which muscle fibers are directed downward and forward?
How many posterior intercostal arteries arise from thoracic aorta?
questions.explanation: Nine pairs of posterior intercostal arteries arise from the thoracic aorta, supplying the lower nine intercostal spaces. The upper two spaces receive their posterior intercostal arteries from the superior intercostal artery. Each posterior intercostal artery gives branches to muscles, skin, parietal pleura, and the breast.

The spleen's medial (visceral) surface has multiple impressions from adjacent organs: gastric impression anteriorly (related to stomach via gastrosplenic ligament), renal impression posteroinferiorly (related to left kidney via splenorenal ligament), colic impression inferiorly (near left colic flexure), and pancreatic impression at the hilum (tail of pancreas in splenorenal ligament). The spleen sits in the left hypochondriac region, protected by ribs 9-11. Its lateral surface is smooth and convex, molded against the diaphragm and posterolateral abdominal wall. The characteristic splenic notch marks its superior border.
questions.question: The spleen is related medially to which structure?

questions.explanation: The obturator nerve (L2, L3, L4), formed within the psoas major from the lumbar plexus, emerges from the medial border of the muscle at the pelvic brim. It descends along the lateral wall of the pelvis, passing above the obturator vessels to reach the obturator foramen, through which it exits the pelvis to enter the medial compartment of the thigh. This medial emergence distinguishes it from other lumbar plexus branches (iliohypogastric, ilioinguinal, lateral femoral cutaneous, and femoral nerves) which emerge from the lateral border, except for the genitofemoral nerve which pierces the anterior surface of psoas.
questions.question: The obturator nerve emerges from which border of psoas major?

questions.explanation: The pancreatic acinus is the functional exocrine secretory unit, consisting of pyramid-shaped serous (enzyme-secreting) acinar cells arranged around a small lumen. The acinus is drained by an intercalated duct lined by centroacinar cells. Multiple acini drain into larger ducts, which eventually form the main pancreatic duct. The pancreas structurally resembles the parotid gland.
questions.question: What is the exocrine secretory unit of the pancreas called?
The ankle joint is more stable during dorsiflexion than plantarflexion. Why is this so?
questions.explanation: The ankle joint is more stable during dorsiflexion because the trochlea tali (superior articular surface of the talus) is wider anteriorly. During dorsiflexion, this wider part engages the mortise more tightly, increasing bony congruence and stability. In plantarflexion, the narrower posterior talus is in the mortise, creating relative instability and increased susceptibility to inversion sprains.
options: The wider anterior trochlea tali fits more snugly in the mortise during dorsiflexion
The deltoid ligament is placed under increased tension in dorsiflexion
The calcaneus supports the talus more during dorsiflexion
The Achilles tendon tightens and mechanically limits further dorsiflexion
The lateral ligaments are tighter in dorsiflexion only

questions.explanation: The right bronchomediastinal trunk drains lymph from the right side of the thorax. It joins with right jugular and right subclavian trunks to form the right lymphatic duct. Alternatively, these three trunks may drain independently into the right venous angle. The left bronchomediastinal trunk usually drains into the thoracic duct.
questions.question: Which lymphatic trunk drains the right side of the thorax?
The internal iliac artery typically divides into anterior and posterior divisions at which vertebral level?
questions.explanation: The internal iliac artery, formed by the bifurcation of the common iliac artery at the L5/S1 level (pelvic brim), descends into the pelvis and typically divides into anterior and posterior divisions at the level of the first sacral vertebra (S1), near the greater sciatic foramen. The posterior division gives off the iliolumbar, lateral sacral, and superior gluteal arteries (all parietal branches), while the anterior division supplies both parietal structures (obturator, internal pudendal, inferior gluteal) and viscera (umbilical, inferior vesical, middle rectal, uterine/vaginal in females, prostatic in males).

The tracheobronchial lymph nodes (superior and inferior) lie at and around the tracheal bifurcation. They receive lymph from the lungs, bronchi, trachea, and heart. These nodes are important in lung cancer staging. Efferents form the bronchomediastinal trunks which drain to the venous system or lymphatic ducts.
questions.question: What drains to tracheobronchial lymph nodes?

questions.explanation: The middle suprarenal artery (from the abdominal aorta) is unique in that it supplies the medulla directly without first passing through the cortex, carrying preganglionic sympathetic fibers directly to chromaffin cells (modified postganglionic neurons). The superior suprarenal artery (from inferior phrenic) and inferior suprarenal artery (from renal) supply primarily the cortex. This direct arterial supply to the medulla allows rapid hormone release (epinephrine and norepinephrine) in response to stress. The suprarenal glands have rich arterial supply from three sources but limited venous drainage (one vein each side).
questions.question: Which artery supplies the suprarenal medulla directly?

questions.explanation: The tonsillar branch of the facial artery provides the main blood supply, entering at the lower pole. Additional supply comes from ascending palatine (facial), ascending pharyngeal, dorsal lingual, and lesser palatine arteries. The paratonsillar vein descends from the soft palate across the capsule and is regularly divided during tonsillectomy.
questions.question: The palatine tonsil receives its blood supply primarily from which artery?
Which structure lies in the stomach bed posteriorly?
questions.explanation: The body of the pancreas is one of the major structures forming the posterior relations or stomach bed. The stomach bed is separated from the stomach by the lesser sac (omental bursa). Other structures in the stomach bed include the left kidney, left suprarenal gland, splenic artery, transverse mesocolon, and diaphragm.

questions.question: What is the approximate length of the pancreas?
questions.explanation: The pancreas is approximately 15-20 cm in length, making it one of the larger accessory digestive organs. It weighs about 90 grams and lies transversely across the posterior abdominal wall. The gland extends from the duodenal C-loop on the right to the splenic hilum on the left.

questions.question: Which muscle retracts the angle of the mouth laterally?
questions.explanation: The risorius muscle retracts the angle of the mouth laterally, producing a grin or grimace. It arises from the parotid fascia and inserts into the angle of the mouth. The muscle is innervated by the buccal branch of the facial nerve. It works with zygomaticus major in smiling. Some individuals lack this muscle.

The aryepiglotticus muscle closes the laryngeal vestibule during swallowing by pulling the arytenoid cartilages toward the epiglottis. The thyroepiglotticus and thyroarytenoid muscles assist in this protective function. The aryepiglottic folds form the lateral margins of the laryngeal inlet.
questions.question: Which muscle closes the vestibule of the larynx during swallowing?

questions.explanation: In adults, the involuting thymus is progressively replaced by adipose (fatty) tissue. This normal age-related change is called thymic involution. Despite fatty replacement, some functional thymic tissue usually persists even in elderly individuals. On CT scans, the adult thymus appears as fatty tissue in the anterior mediastinum.
questions.question: What replaces thymic tissue in adults?

questions.explanation: The alveolar process of the maxilla forms the floor of the maxillary sinus. Roots of the upper premolar and molar teeth may project into the sinus, separated only by thin bone or mucosa. Dental infections can spread to the sinus, and tooth extraction can create an oroantral fistula. The floor is typically 1-2 cm below the nasal floor.
questions.question: Which structure forms the floor of the maxillary sinus?

questions.explanation: The inferior alveolar nerve (a branch of V3) enters the mandibular foramen on the medial surface of the mandibular ramus. It travels in the mandibular canal supplying the lower teeth and emerges at the mental foramen as the mental nerve. The mylohyoid nerve branches before entering the foramen to supply mylohyoid and anterior digastric.
questions.question: The inferior alveolar nerve enters the mandible through which opening?
The oval window is closed by which structure?
questions.explanation: The oval window (fenestra vestibuli) in the medial wall of the middle ear is closed by the footplate of the stapes, held in place by the annular ligament. The stapes transmits vibrations from the ossicular chain to the perilymph of the inner ear. Otosclerosis causes abnormal bone growth fixing the stapes, resulting in conductive hearing loss.

questions.question: Which two epicondyles are connected by the superior boundary of the cubital fossa?
questions.explanation: The superior boundary of the cubital fossa is formed by an imaginary horizontal line connecting the medial and lateral epicondyles of the humerus. This line is located approximately 2-3 cm inferior to the actual position of the epicondyles. The base of this triangular depression is directed superiorly.

options: Medial condyle of the tibia proximally
Inferior lateral supracondylar line and oblique popliteal ligament
questions.question: Plantaris, a vestigial muscle, inserts into the posterior calcaneus via the calcaneal tendon. From which specific femoral site does it originate?
questions.explanation: Plantaris originates from the inferior end of the lateral supracondylar line of the femur and the oblique popliteal ligament. It inserts into the posterior calcaneus via the calcaneal tendon together with gastrocnemius and soleus. Its long slender tendon can be mistaken for a nerve during surgery and is used in tendon repair surgery due to its length.

Calot's triangle (cystohepatic triangle) has three boundaries: the cystic duct inferiorly, the common hepatic duct medially (not a vein, despite the question's misdirection), and the inferior surface of the liver superiorly. Within this triangle lie the cystic artery and Calot's lymph node. The correct answer addresses that the common hepatic duct (not a vein) forms the medial boundary. Understanding this triangle's anatomy is crucial for safe cholecystectomy, as the cystic artery must be identified within it before ligation. Anatomical variations in this region are common.
questions.question: Which vein forms the left border of the hepatocystic triangle (Calot's)?
Which structure indents the second part of the duodenum medially?
questions.explanation: The head of the pancreas lies in the concavity formed by the C-shaped duodenum and indents the medial aspect of the second (descending) part. The pancreatic head is intimately related to the duodenum, particularly the second part where the bile and pancreatic ducts enter. This close relationship means that pancreatic head disease often affects the duodenum and vice versa.

questions.question: What is the primary action of brachioradialis?
questions.explanation: Brachioradialis is primarily a flexor of the forearm, most effective when the forearm is in mid-pronation position. It also assists with both pronation from supinated position and supination from pronated position, returning the forearm to neutral. The muscle is supplied by the radial nerve despite being an anterior compartment muscle.

The hepatic veins (typically two or three major veins: right, middle, and left) drain directly into the inferior vena cava just below the diaphragm. These veins are intersegmental in distribution, draining adjacent hepatic segments. The attachment of these large veins to the IVC helps anchor the liver in position within the abdominal cavity.
questions.question: Into which vessel do the hepatic veins drain?

options: Functional articulation allowing scapular mobility on thorax
questions.explanation: The scapulothoracic "joint" is not a true anatomical joint but a functional articulation between the scapula and thoracic wall. It allows scapular movements (elevation, depression, protraction, retraction, rotation) essential for positioning the glenoid cavity. Muscle action rather than ligaments controls this "joint."
questions.question: What is the significance of the scapulothoracic joint?
Which nerve roots form the lower trunk?
questions.explanation: The lower trunk is formed by union of C8 and T1 nerve roots. Injury to the lower trunk causes Klumpke's paralysis with claw hand deformity. The lower trunk continues as the medial cord after giving off no branches in the neck.

questions.question: Which carpal bones form the floor of the anatomical snuffbox?
questions.explanation: The anatomical snuffbox floor is formed by the scaphoid proximally and the trapezium distally. The radial artery crosses the floor of this space. Tenderness in the snuffbox following wrist injury suggests possible scaphoid fracture.

The posterior meniscofemoral ligament is a strong tendinous slip joining the lateral meniscus to the posterior cruciate ligament and the medial femoral condyle. The coronary ligaments attach both menisci to the tibial condyles. The transverse ligament joins the anterior edges of both menisci, allowing them to move together during knee movements.
questions.question: Which structure joins the posterior part of the lateral meniscus to the posterior cruciate ligament and the medial femoral condyle?

questions.explanation: The falciform ligament is a double-layered peritoneal fold that connects the anterior and superior surfaces of the liver to the anterior abdominal wall and diaphragm, extending from the umbilicus to the diaphragm. Its free inferior border contains the ligamentum teres hepatis (obliterated umbilical vein) and separates the anatomical right and left lobes of the liver. This ligament develops from the ventral mesentery and serves as an important surgical landmark during laparoscopic procedures.
questions.question: Which ligament attaches the liver to the anterior abdominal wall?
Which nerve supplies latissimus dorsi?
questions.explanation: The thoracodorsal nerve (C7, C8) from the posterior cord supplies latissimus dorsi muscle. The nerve descends along the posterior axillary wall with the thoracodorsal artery. Preservation of this nerve is important during axillary surgery to maintain shoulder function.

questions.question: What is the functional relationship between the two palmar arches?
questions.explanation: The superficial and deep palmar arches provide redundant blood supply to the hand through extensive anastomoses. This collateral circulation protects hand perfusion even with single artery occlusion. The arches interconnect via perforating branches and palmar metacarpal communications.
options: Provide redundant blood supply with extensive anastomoses

questions.explanation: The extensor expansion (extensor hood) distributes extensor digitorum force and coordinates intrinsic hand muscle action with extrinsic extensors. Intrinsic muscles insert into the expansion, enabling their unique MCP flexion with IP extension action. This complex structure allows coordinated finger movements essential for precision grip.
options: Distributes extensor force, coordinates intrinsic-extrinsic action
questions.question: What is the functional significance of extensor expansion?
At which vertebral level does the oesophagus commence?
questions.explanation: The oesophagus begins at the inferior border of the cricoid cartilage, which corresponds to the level of the sixth cervical vertebra (C6). This anatomical landmark marks the transition point from the pharynx to the oesophagus. The cricoid cartilage is the only complete ring of cartilage in the respiratory tract.

questions.question: Which compartment contains the brachial artery in the arm?
questions.explanation: The brachial artery lies in the anterior compartment of the arm, medial to the biceps brachii. It is accompanied by the median nerve and basilic vein. The artery is separated from the posterior compartment by the medial intermuscular septum.

The spinal accessory nerve (XI) provides motor innervation to the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles. Additional proprioceptive fibers from C2-C3 may contribute. Unilateral contraction of sternocleidomastoid turns the face to the opposite side and tilts the head ipsilaterally. Bilateral contraction flexes the neck.
questions.question: The sternocleidomastoid muscle is innervated by which nerve?
Over which muscle does the lateral arcuate ligament arch?
questions.explanation: The lateral arcuate ligament is a tendinous arch that extends from the tip of the transverse process of L1 to the 12th rib, arching over the quadratus lumborum muscle. It provides attachment for some of the muscular fibers of the diaphragm. The subcostal nerve (T12) and vessels pass deep to this ligament.

The gluteal region contains nine muscles: gluteus maximus, gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, tensor fasciae latae, piriformis, obturator internus, gemellus superior, gemellus inferior, and quadratus femoris. These perform extension, abduction, lateral rotation, and stabilization of the hip joint.
questions.question: How many muscles constitute the gluteal region, including the six lateral rotators?
Which artery supplies the lateral breast?
questions.explanation: The lateral thoracic artery, a branch of the axillary artery, provides lateral mammary branches that supply the lateral portion of the breast. Additional supply comes from pectoral branches of the thoracoacromial artery and branches from posterior intercostal arteries in the 3rd and 4th intercostal spaces.

The superior sagittal sinus lies in the attached superior border of the falx cerebri. It begins at the foramen cecum and runs posteriorly to the confluence of sinuses. The sinus receives superior cerebral veins and communicates with scalp veins via emissary veins. Arachnoid granulations project into it for CSF absorption.
questions.question: Which sinus lies within the falx cerebri?

questions.explanation: The internal urethral sphincter, a thickening of smooth muscle at the bladder neck, is under involuntary autonomic control (both sympathetic and parasympathetic), in contrast to the external urethral sphincter which is skeletal muscle under voluntary somatic control via the pudendal nerve. Sympathetic innervation (L1-L2 via hypogastric nerves) causes contraction of the internal sphincter and relaxation of the detrusor, promoting urine storage. Parasympathetic innervation (S2-S4 via pelvic splanchnic nerves) causes detrusor contraction and internal sphincter relaxation, promoting micturition. The internal sphincter prevents semen from entering the bladder during ejaculation and contributes to urinary continence.
questions.question: The internal urethral sphincter receives which type of innervation?

questions.explanation: Veins of the breast drain into both the axillary and internal thoracic veins. The pattern follows the arterial supply. During pregnancy and lactation, these veins become engorged and may be visible through the skin. Venous drainage is important in the spread of breast cancer.
questions.question: Which veins drain the breast?

questions.explanation: The parotid (Stensen's) duct pierces the buccinator muscle to open into the oral vestibule opposite the upper second molar tooth. The duct is approximately 5 cm long and crosses the masseter muscle superficially. Trauma to the cheek can damage the duct causing salivary fistula.
questions.question: The parotid duct pierces which muscle before opening into the oral cavity?

questions.explanation: The diaphragm develops from four embryological structures: (1) septum transversum (forming central tendon), (2) dorsal esophageal mesentery, (3) peripheral rim from body wall, and (4) pleuroperitoneal membranes (closing the pleuroperitoneal canals). Incomplete fusion of these components leads to congenital diaphragmatic hernias.
questions.question: How many structures contribute to diaphragm development?

questions.explanation: The arch of the azygos vein arches over the right lung root from behind. The right lung root lies within the groove created by the azygos arch. On the left side, the aortic arch passes over the left lung root, and the left lung root lies within the concavity of the aortic arch.
questions.question: What structure arches over right lung root?
What creates negative intrathoracic pressure?
questions.explanation: During inspiration, expansion of the thoracic cavity (through rib elevation and diaphragm descent) increases intrathoracic volume and creates negative pressure within the chest. This negative pressure draws air into the lungs. The pleural cavity pressure becomes more negative, preventing lung collapse.

questions.question: The tensor fasciae latae muscle inserts into which named structure that runs to the lateral condyle of the tibia?
questions.explanation: The tensor fasciae latae inserts into the iliotibial tract (iliotibial band), a thickened lateral band of fascia lata running from the iliac crest to the lateral condyle of the tibia. It assists in flexion, abduction, and medial rotation of the hip, and helps stabilize the extended knee. Tightness of this structure is associated with iliotibial band syndrome.

The junction of the middle and outer third of the clavicle is the weakest point. Most clavicular fractures occur at this location from indirect forces transmitted through the limb during falls. The medial fragment is typically displaced superiorly by sternocleidomastoid while the lateral fragment is displaced inferiorly by arm weight.
questions.question: What is the weakest part of the clavicle?
Which veins drain into the azygos vein?
questions.explanation: The azygos vein receives: right superior intercostal vein, lower eight right posterior intercostal veins, right bronchial vein, middle esophageal veins, and the hemiazygos and accessory hemiazygos veins from the left side. It drains much of the thoracic wall and mediastinal structures.

Lymphatic drainage from the stomach first passes to regional lymph node groups along the lesser curvature (left and right gastric nodes), greater curvature (left and right gastroepiploic nodes), and around the cardia (paracardial nodes). From these first-tier nodes, lymph flows to second-tier nodes along the celiac trunk and its branches (celiac, hepatic, and splenic nodes), then to pre-aortic nodes, and finally to the cisterna chyli and thoracic duct. This extensive lymphatic drainage explains the potential for widespread metastases in gastric cancer and the need for extended lymphadenectomy in curative surgery.
questions.question: Which lymph nodes receive direct drainage from the stomach?
What is the function of splenic red pulp?
questions.explanation: The splenic red pulp filters blood and removes old, damaged, or abnormal erythrocytes through selective retention and phagocytosis by macrophages in the splenic cords. It also stores platelets (about one-third of the body's platelet pool) and serves as a reservoir for iron recycled from hemoglobin. The red pulp comprises about 75% of splenic tissue.

The foramen ovale transmits the mandibular nerve (V3), accessory meningeal artery, lesser petrosal nerve, and an emissary vein connecting the cavernous sinus with the pterygoid plexus. The accessory meningeal artery supplies the trigeminal ganglion and dura. Foramen ovale is located in the greater wing of the sphenoid bone.
questions.question: The foramen ovale transmits which additional structure besides V3?

questions.explanation: Soleus originates from the posterior aspect of the head and superior quarter of the posterior fibula, the soleal line and middle third of the medial border of the tibia, and a tendinous arch between these bony attachments. It does not cross the knee joint, so it can plantarflex the ankle regardless of knee position. Together with gastrocnemius, it inserts via the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon.
questions.question: Soleus, unlike gastrocnemius, can plantarflex the ankle regardless of knee position because it does NOT cross the knee joint. It originates from which structures?
options: Both femoral condyles bilaterally (as in gastrocnemius origin)
Navicular tuberosity and the medial cuneiform bone distally
Head of fibula and lateral tibia condyle only
Posterior fibula head and superior quarter; soleal line, medial tibia; tendinous arch
Ischial tuberosity and posterior surface of the femur

questions.question: The transpyloric plane intersects which vertebral level?
questions.explanation: The transpyloric plane is an important anatomical landmark that passes through the first lumbar vertebra (L1), situated midway between the suprasternal notch and pubic symphysis. This plane transects numerous vital structures including the pylorus, neck of pancreas, origins of superior mesenteric artery and portal vein, duodenojejunal junction, and the hila of both kidneys. It serves as a crucial reference point for clinical examination and surgical procedures in the upper abdomen.

The septum transversum is the mesodermal mass that forms the central tendon of the diaphragm. Initially located in front of the embryonic head, it migrates caudally during head folding. During this migration, cervical myotomes and nerves contribute muscle and nerve supply, explaining the phrenic nerve's long course from C3-5.
questions.question: What forms the central tendon embryologically?
What forms the anterior boundary of posterior mediastinum?
questions.explanation: The posterior mediastinum is bounded anteriorly by the pericardium (which forms the heart in the middle mediastinum). Posteriorly, it is bounded by the thoracic vertebrae from T5 to T12. The posterior mediastinum contains the esophagus, descending aorta, azygos system, thoracic duct, and sympathetic trunks.

options: Base and styloid process of the 5th metatarsal only
Medial and inferior surfaces of medial cuneiform and base of 1st metatarsal
Navicular tuberosity and the adjacent medial cuneiform bone
Bases of the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th metatarsal bones
Calcaneus via the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon posteriorly
questions.explanation: Tibialis anterior inserts into the medial and inferior surfaces of the medial cuneiform and the base of the first metatarsal. It originates from the lateral condyle and superior half of the lateral surface of the tibia and interosseous membrane. It is the most powerful dorsiflexor and inverts the foot, active throughout the swing phase of gait.
questions.question: Tibialis anterior dorsiflexes and inverts the foot. It inserts into which specific structures?
Which cells line the splenic sinusoids?
questions.explanation: Splenic sinusoids are lined by discontinuous endothelium composed of elongated endothelial cells (stave cells) oriented parallel to blood flow with gaps (slits) of 2-3 ?m between them. This discontinuous arrangement allows flexible cells to pass through but retains rigid or damaged cells. The basement membrane is also discontinuous. This structure is unique to the spleen and facilitates its filtering function.

The otic ganglion provides postganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibers to the parotid gland via the auriculotemporal nerve. Preganglionic fibers arrive via the lesser petrosal nerve from the glossopharyngeal nerve. The ganglion lies in the infratemporal fossa medial to the mandibular nerve below the foramen ovale.
questions.question: The otic ganglion provides parasympathetic innervation to which gland?

questions.explanation: Each renal papilla (apex of a renal pyramid) is indented by a cup-shaped minor calyx that collects urine. There are typically 8-12 minor calyces in each kidney. Two or three minor calyces unite to form a major calyx, and 2-3 major calyces join to form the renal pelvis.
questions.question: Which structure indents each renal papilla?
Which nerve supplies sensation to the dorsum of the hand?
options: Dorsal cutaneous branch of ulnar nerve
questions.explanation: The superficial branch of the radial nerve supplies sensation to the dorsal aspect of the lateral three and one-half digits and the dorsal hand. The dorsal cutaneous branch of the ulnar nerve supplies the medial side. The posterior interosseous nerve has no cutaneous distribution.

questions.question: Which Y-shaped hip ligament, described as one of the strongest in the body, has its apex attached to the anterior inferior iliac spine?
questions.explanation: The iliofemoral ligament (ligament of Bigelow) is one of the strongest ligaments in the body, triangular and Y-shaped. Its apex attaches to the anterior inferior iliac spine and its base to the intertrochanteric line. It reinforces the joint anteriorly, prevents overextension while standing, and reduces the muscle energy needed to maintain upright posture.

questions.question: The greater trochanter is classified as which type of epiphysis, and which muscle exerts traction upon it, drawing it upward, medially, and backward?
questions.explanation: The greater trochanter is a traction epiphysis; gluteus medius pulls it upward, medially, and backward. Traction epiphyses arise at tendon insertions rather than at articular ends, unlike pressure epiphyses. The quadrate tubercle marks where the epiphyseal line crosses the intertrochanteric crest.

The external iliac artery continues posterior and inferior to the inguinal ligament as the femoral artery, lying lateral to the femoral vein. The femoral artery enters the femoral triangle at this level and gives off the profunda femoris approximately 5 cm below the inguinal ligament. The profunda femoris is the main blood supply to the thigh muscles.
questions.question: The external iliac artery continues posterior and inferior to the inguinal ligament as which artery?
The pterygopalatine fossa communicates with the middle cranial fossa through which opening?
questions.explanation: The foramen rotundum provides direct communication between the pterygopalatine fossa and the middle cranial fossa, transmitting the maxillary nerve. The pterygoid canal connects with the foramen lacerum region, not the middle cranial fossa proper. This anatomical relationship is crucial for understanding trigeminal nerve pathways and regional anesthesia.

The quadrate lobe, although anatomically part of the right lobe, is functionally part of the left lobe as it receives blood from the left hepatic artery and drains bile into the left hepatic duct. Similarly, the caudate lobe receives blood from both right and left hepatic arteries. This functional division is based on blood supply and biliary drainage rather than external anatomical features.
questions.question: Which liver segment receives blood from the left hepatic artery?

questions.explanation: The conjoint tendon (formed by fusion of internal oblique and transversus abdominis aponeuroses) inserts onto the pubic crest and pectineal line (pecten pubis), reinforcing the posterior wall of the inguinal canal medially. The pectineal ligament (Cooper's ligament) also attaches to the pectineal line and is used in some hernia repairs (Cooper's ligament repair). The rectus abdominis originates from the pubic crest and symphysis, not the pectineal line. The lacunar ligament (medial extension of the inguinal ligament) also attaches to the pectineal line.
questions.question: Which muscle attaches to the pectineal line?
Which lymph nodes receive drainage from the chin?
questions.explanation: The submental lymph nodes lie between the anterior bellies of the digastric muscles and drain the chin, central lower lip, floor of mouth, and tip of tongue. Efferents pass to submandibular and jugulo-omohyoid nodes. These nodes are examined when staging oral cavity cancers.

The greater sciatic foramen (GSF) provides an exit from the pelvis into the gluteal region. In contrast, the lesser sciatic foramen (LSF) provides an entrance into the perineum from the gluteal region, enabling structures that exited the pelvis via the GSF to re-enter the perineum below the pelvic floor.
questions.question: The greater sciatic foramen's primary function is best described as which of the following?
options: Exit from the pelvis into the gluteal region
Exit from perineum to gluteal region
Passage between gluteal and adductor compartments
Entrance from gluteal to femoral triangle

questions.explanation: The prostatic urethra contains the openings of the two ejaculatory ducts on either side of the prostatic utricle (a small blind pouch) on the seminal colliculus (urethral crest). About 20-30 prostatic ducts also open into the prostatic urethra. The prostatic urethra is the widest and most dilatable part of the male urethra, measuring about 3-4 cm in length.
questions.question: Which part of the male urethra contains the ejaculatory duct openings?

questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve passes through Guyon's canal (ulnar tunnel) at the wrist alongside the ulnar artery. The canal is bounded by the pisiform and hook of hamate. Compression here causes ulnar tunnel syndrome affecting hand muscles but sparing forearm muscles.
questions.question: Which nerve passes through Guyon's canal?
The arytenoid cartilages articulate with which laryngeal structure?
questions.explanation: The arytenoid cartilages sit on the upper border of the cricoid cartilage lamina at the cricoarytenoid joints. These synovial joints allow rotation and gliding movements that abduct and adduct the vocal cords. The arytenoids are pyramidal with a vocal process (anteriorly) and muscular process (laterally).

The major duodenal papilla (ampulla of Vater) is located on the posteromedial wall of the second (descending) part of the duodenum, approximately 8-10 cm distal to the pylorus. At this site, the common bile duct and main pancreatic duct unite to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla, surrounded by the sphincter of Oddi. The minor duodenal papilla, located 2 cm proximal to the major papilla, receives the accessory pancreatic duct (duct of Santorini) when present. This anatomical arrangement is crucial for endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP).
questions.question: Which part of the duodenum contains the major duodenal papilla?
Which structure forms the floor of the posterior triangle?
questions.explanation: The floor of the posterior triangle is formed by the prevertebral fascia covering splenius capitis, levator scapulae, and scalene muscles (anterior, middle, posterior). The subclavian artery and brachial plexus emerge between the scalene muscles. The accessory nerve crosses the triangle superficially on this floor. Cervical lymph nodes lie within the triangle.

questions.question: Which vertebral level corresponds to the bifurcation of the common iliac artery?
questions.explanation: The common iliac arteries, terminal branches of the abdominal aorta, bifurcate into external and internal iliac arteries at approximately the L5/S1 level (lumbosacral junction), anterior to the sacroiliac joint at the pelvic brim. This bifurcation point corresponds to a point just medial to the midinguinal point on the anterior abdominal wall. The ureter crosses anterior to the bifurcation of the common iliac artery (or the external iliac artery just distal to it), a relationship that is surgically significant. The right common iliac artery is crossed anteriorly by the superior rectal vessels, while the left is related to the sigmoid mesocolon.

The hepatorenal recess (Morison's pouch), located between the right lobe of the liver and the right kidney, is the most dependent (lowest) part of the peritoneal cavity when supine in males. This makes it a common site for fluid accumulation (blood, pus, ascites) in the supine position, detectable by ultrasound. In females, the rectouterine pouch (of Douglas) is the most dependent part. The hepatorenal recess communicates with the right subphrenic space superiorly and the right paracolic gutter inferiorly, providing pathways for fluid spread.
questions.question: Which peritoneal recess is the most dependent in the supine male?

questions.explanation: Only one small artery enters the scaphoid bone at the end closest to the thumb (distal end). This unique blood supply pattern makes the scaphoid vulnerable to avascular necrosis following fracture. The proximal fragment may lose blood supply if fracture tears the artery.
options: Dual arterial supply proximally and distally
Direct branches from radial artery proximally
questions.question: What is the primary blood supply to the scaphoid bone?

questions.explanation: The medial and lateral intermuscular septa attach from the deep brachial fascia to the humerus, dividing the arm into anterior (flexor) and posterior (extensor) compartments. Each compartment contains muscles with similar functions and common innervation. This organization is essential for understanding compartment syndromes.
questions.question: How do the medial and lateral intermuscular septa organize the arm?

questions.explanation: The inferior alveolar artery arises from the first (mandibular) part of the maxillary artery. It descends with the inferior alveolar nerve to enter the mandibular foramen, supplying the mandibular teeth and bone. The mylohyoid branch supplies the mylohyoid muscle. The mental artery emerges through the mental foramen.
questions.question: The inferior alveolar artery is a branch of which vessel?

questions.explanation: The spinal accessory nerve (XI) provides motor innervation to the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles. The nerve emerges from the jugular foramen and descends across the posterior triangle. Injury during lymph node biopsy causes weakness in shoulder shrugging and difficulty turning the head against resistance.
questions.question: The spinal accessory nerve supplies which two muscles?
The taeniae coli are thickenings of which muscle layer?
questions.explanation: The taeniae coli represent three longitudinal bands where the outer longitudinal smooth muscle layer of the colon is thickened and concentrated, running from cecum to rectosigmoid junction. The three bands are: taenia libera (free, anteriorly on ascending and descending colon), taenia mesocolica (at mesenteric attachment), and taenia omentalis (at omental attachment). Between the taeniae, the longitudinal muscle is thin, allowing the circular muscle to create sacculations (haustra). The taeniae converge at the base of the appendix, providing a surgical landmark. At the rectosigmoid junction (about 15 cm from anus), the taeniae spread to form a complete longitudinal muscle layer in the rectum.

questions.question: Which artery is the largest terminal branch of the brachial artery?
questions.explanation: The ulnar artery is the larger terminal branch of the brachial artery, beginning below the elbow joint. It provides the main arterial supply to the medial forearm and forms the superficial palmar arch predominantly. The radial artery is smaller but more clinically accessible.

The esophagus has four anatomical constrictions where it is narrowed. The first is at its origin (C6 level, 15 cm from incisors) where the cricopharyngeus muscle forms the upper esophageal sphincter. These constrictions are clinically important as sites where foreign bodies lodge and where esophageal pathology commonly occurs.
questions.question: Which constriction is at the esophageal origin?
Which cartilage forms the Adam's apple (laryngeal prominence)?
questions.explanation: The thyroid cartilage is shield-shaped with two laminae meeting in the midline to form the laryngeal prominence (Adam's apple). This prominence is more acute and prominent in males. The thyroid cartilage protects the vocal cords and provides anterior attachment for the vocal ligaments.

questions.question: The long plantar ligament, an important supporter of the lateral longitudinal arch, passes from the calcaneus to which structures?
questions.explanation: The long plantar ligament (longest ligament in the foot) passes from the plantar surface of the calcaneus to the ridges on the plantar surface of the cuboid and the bases of the 3rd-5th metatarsals. It is a primary support for the lateral longitudinal arch. In combination with the short plantar (plantar calcaneocuboid) ligament, it forms the floor of the fibularis longus tendon groove on the cuboid.
options: Sustentaculum tali of calcaneus and talus
All five metatarsal bases and the navicular
Base of 1st metatarsal and medial cuneiform
Plantar surface of cuboid and bases of 3rd–5th metatarsals

questions.question: What muscle forms the bladder wall?
questions.explanation: The detrusor muscle is the smooth muscle layer forming the bladder wall and consists of three poorly defined layers: inner longitudinal, middle circular, and outer longitudinal. During bladder filling, the detrusor relaxes; during micturition, it contracts to expel urine. The detrusor is innervated by parasympathetic fibers (pelvic splanchnic nerves S2-4) for contraction.

questions.question: The round ligament of the uterus passes through which opening?
questions.explanation: The round ligament of the uterus passes through the deep inguinal ring (homologous to the spermatic cord in males), traverses the inguinal canal, exits through the superficial inguinal ring, and terminates in the subcutaneous tissue of the labium majus. It represents the distal gubernaculum (the proximal part becoming the ovarian ligament). The round ligament contains smooth muscle, vessels, and nerves, and helps maintain the anteverted position of the uterus. Rarely, indirect inguinal hernias can occur in females alongside the round ligament (canal of Nuck).

Within the hepatoduodenal ligament (free edge of lesser omentum), the structures of the portal triad are arranged from anterior to posterior and right to left as: bile duct (anteriorly and to the right), hepatic artery proper (anteriorly and to the left), and portal vein (posteriorly). This arrangement is sometimes remembered as "DAV" reading from right to left anteriorly (Duct, Artery, Vein). The hepatic artery typically lies anterior to the portal vein and to the left of the bile duct, though anatomical variations are common. Lymph nodes and autonomic nerve plexuses also travel through the hepatoduodenal ligament.
questions.question: The proper hepatic artery lies in which position within the portal triad?

questions.explanation: The portal vein forms behind the neck of the pancreas through the confluence of the superior mesenteric vein and splenic vein, measuring approximately 8 cm in length. The inferior mesenteric vein typically drains into the splenic vein before this confluence. The portal vein ascends to the porta hepatis within the free edge of the lesser omentum, positioned posterior to the bile duct and hepatic artery, where it divides into right and left branches.
questions.question: The portal vein is formed by the union of which two vessels?

questions.explanation: The taeniae coli are three longitudinal muscle bands that are characteristic external features of the large intestine (colon) but absent from the rectum and anal canal. These bands are shorter than the colon itself, causing sacculations (haustra) to form. The small intestine has a complete, continuous longitudinal muscle layer without taeniae.
questions.question: Which feature distinguishes the large intestine from the small intestine externally?
Podiatry is the medical specialty dealing with the study and care of the feet. The foot has how many bones in total (tarsals + metatarsals + phalanges)?
questions.explanation: Each foot has 26 bones: 7 tarsals, 5 metatarsals, and 14 phalanges (the great toe has 2 phalanges; the other four toes each have 3 phalanges). Understanding foot bone anatomy is fundamental to podiatry, orthopaedics, and diagnosis of stress fractures, Lisfranc injuries, and other foot pathologies.

questions.question: Which lymph node is characteristically found in Calot's triangle?
questions.explanation: Lund's node (Calot's node) is located within Calot's triangle, bounded by the cystic duct, common hepatic duct, and inferior surface of the liver. This lymph node frequently becomes enlarged in cases of cholecystitis or cholangitis and may be removed during cholecystectomy. Calot's triangle is an important surgical landmark for identifying the cystic artery, which typically lies within this triangle. Careful dissection of this area is crucial during laparoscopic cholecystectomy to avoid injury to the hepatic ducts or right hepatic artery.

questions.question: Which rib typically crosses the upper pole of the left kidney?
questions.explanation: The left kidney extends higher than the right, with its upper pole reaching the 11th rib, while the right kidney's upper pole typically reaches the 12th rib. Both kidneys lie on the diaphragm superiorly, which separates them from the pleura and lungs. The left kidney's higher position reflects the asymmetry caused by the liver on the right.

The body of the stomach is the most anterior part, lying against the anterior abdominal wall in the epigastric region when the stomach is empty. The fundus extends superiorly and posteriorly beneath the left dome of the diaphragm, while the pyloric antrum angles to the right and posteriorly. The stomach's position varies with body position, respiratory phase, and degree of filling. When distended, the stomach extends inferiorly and the greater curvature becomes more anterior. The anterior surface is related to the diaphragm, anterior abdominal wall, left lobe of liver, and anterior abdominal wall.
questions.question: Which part of the stomach is most anterior?
At which rib level is the axilla base formed?
questions.explanation: The base of the axilla is formed by skin, subcutaneous tissue, and axillary fascia spanning from the fourth rib. This base is concave and forms the floor of the axillary space. The axillary fascia is continuous with the pectoral fascia anteriorly and latissimus dorsi fascia posteriorly.

The white pulp, consisting of periarteriolar lymphoid sheaths (PALS) and lymphoid follicles, is the site of immune surveillance of blood-borne antigens and antibody production. T cells in the PALS respond to blood-borne antigens, while B cells in follicles produce antibodies. The marginal zone between red and white pulp contains specialized macrophages and B cells for antigen capture.
questions.question: What occurs in splenic white pulp?

questions.explanation: Hesselbach's triangle (inguinal triangle) is bounded laterally by the inferior epigastric artery, medially by the lateral border of the rectus abdominis muscle, and inferiorly by the inguinal ligament. The floor of the triangle is formed by the transversalis fascia, which may be reinforced medially by the conjoint tendon. This triangle represents an area of potential weakness in the posterior wall of the inguinal canal, and direct inguinal hernias protrude through this triangle medial to the inferior epigastric artery. Understanding this triangle is crucial for distinguishing direct (through the triangle) from indirect (lateral to inferior epigastric) inguinal hernias.
questions.question: Which vessel marks the lateral boundary of Hesselbach's triangle?
The celiac trunk typically arises at which vertebral level?
questions.explanation: The celiac trunk emerges from the anterior aspect of the abdominal aorta immediately below the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm, anterior to the upper part of the first lumbar vertebra (L1). It quickly trifurcates into the left gastric, splenic, and common hepatic arteries, providing the principal arterial supply to foregut derivatives. The celiac ganglion and plexus surround the origin of this vessel, receiving preganglionic sympathetic fibers from the greater splanchnic nerve.

questions.question: Which nerve accompanies the deep brachial artery through the spiral groove?
questions.explanation: The radial nerve accompanies the profunda brachii (deep brachial) artery through the spiral groove of the humerus. The nerve winds around the posterior shaft of the humerus between the medial and lateral heads of triceps. This close relationship makes the nerve vulnerable to injury in humeral shaft fractures.

questions.question: The trochanteric anastomosis, providing the main blood supply to the head of femur, is formed by which four arteries?
questions.explanation: The trochanteric anastomosis is formed by four arteries: superior gluteal (SGA), inferior gluteal (IGA), medial femoral circumflex (MFCA), and lateral femoral circumflex (LFCA) arteries. Disruption of this anastomosis in femoral neck fractures leads to avascular necrosis of the femoral head.

is absent in approximately 15% of people without any functional deficit. When present, it inserts into the flexor retinaculum and palmar aponeurosis. The tendon is commonly harvested for use in tendon grafts and reconstructive procedures.
questions.question: Which muscle can be absent without functional deficit?
Which muscle elevates the soft palate?
questions.explanation: The levator veli palatini elevates the soft palate during swallowing to close the nasopharynx. The muscle arises from the petrous temporal bone and Eustachian tube cartilage. It is supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (vagus via cranial accessory). Bilateral paralysis causes nasal regurgitation and hypernasal speech.

questions.question: Which layer directly surrounds the kidney outside the fibrous capsule?
questions.explanation: Perirenal (perinephric) fat is a layer of adipose tissue that lies outside the fibrous capsule and inside the renal fascia (Gerota's fascia). It cushions and protects the kidney. The renal fascia encloses both the kidney and suprarenal gland, while pararenal fat lies external to the renal fascia and forms part of the retroperitoneal fat.

The pterygopalatine ganglion is located in the pterygopalatine fossa and is one of four parasympathetic ganglia of the head. It receives preganglionic fibers via the greater petrosal nerve and provides secretomotor innervation to lacrimal and nasal glands. The ganglion also transmits sympathetic and sensory fibers without synapsing.
questions.question: Which parasympathetic ganglion is associated with the pterygopalatine fossa?
The deep fascia of the gluteal region is continuous inferiorly with which named structure of the thigh?
questions.explanation: The deep fascia of the gluteal region is continuous with the fascia lata of the thigh. The superficial fascia, thick in women and impregnated with large quantities of fat, accounts for the prominence of the buttock. This fascial continuity has clinical implications for spread of infections between gluteal and thigh compartments.

The marginal artery of Drummond (marginal artery of the colon) is a continuous arterial arcade running along the mesenteric border of the colon, connecting the superior mesenteric and inferior mesenteric arterial territories. It is formed by anastomoses between the ileocolic, right colic, middle colic, left colic, and sigmoid arteries. This vessel provides crucial collateral circulation to the colon and is particularly important at the splenic flexure, where the superior and inferior mesenteric arterial distributions meet. The weakest point in this anastomotic chain occurs at Griffiths' point (splenic flexure) and Sudeck's point (rectosigmoid junction).
questions.question: The marginal artery of Drummond connects which two arterial systems?
Which vessels pass through the gastrosplenic ligament to the fundus?
questions.explanation: The short gastric arteries arise from the splenic artery at the hilum of the spleen and pass through the gastrosplenic ligament (omentum) to supply the fundus. These vessels represent 5-7 small branches that provide blood to the superior portion of the greater curvature. The gastrosplenic ligament connects the greater curvature to the spleen.

questions.question: Which muscle elevates the upper lip?
questions.explanation: The levator labii superioris elevates the upper lip. It arises from the maxilla above the infraorbital foramen and inserts into the upper lip. The muscle is innervated by the zygomatic and buccal branches of the facial nerve. Zygomaticus major and minor also contribute to upper lip elevation but primarily act on the angle of mouth.

Chief (peptic or zymogenic) cells in the gastric glands of the fundus and body secrete pepsinogen, the inactive precursor of pepsin. Pepsinogen is activated to pepsin by gastric acid (HCl) and autocatalytically by pepsin itself. Pepsin begins protein digestion in the stomach, working optimally at pH 1.5-2. Chief cells are basophilic due to abundant rough endoplasmic reticulum for protein synthesis.
questions.question: Which cells in the gastric mucosa produce pepsinogen?

questions.explanation: The areola glands of Montgomery are intermediate in structure between lactiferous and sweat glands. They are greatly enlarged in pregnancy and lactation as subcutaneous tubercles. Their oily secretion acts as a protective lubricant during lactation, preventing nipple cracking.
questions.question: What are Montgomery's glands?
What percentage of the pancreas is exocrine tissue?
questions.explanation: Approximately 99% of the pancreatic tissue is exocrine, consisting of acinar cells that secrete digestive enzymes. Only about 1% consists of endocrine tissue in the form of pancreatic islets (islets of Langerhans). The exocrine pancreas produces 1.5-2 liters of pancreatic juice daily containing enzymes for protein, carbohydrate, and fat digestion.

The lesser splanchnic nerve, carrying preganglionic sympathetic fibers from T10-T11 spinal segments, typically synapses in the superior mesenteric ganglion (or aorticorenal ganglion), though it may also send fibers to the celiac ganglion. Postganglionic fibers distribute along superior mesenteric artery branches to supply midgut derivatives. This nerve pierces the diaphragm (separately or with the sympathetic trunk) to reach the abdomen. The sympathetic supply causes decreased intestinal motility and secretions, vasoconstriction, and contraction of sphincters, opposing the effects of parasympathetic innervation (vagus nerve for midgut).
questions.question: The lesser splanchnic nerve typically synapses in which ganglion?
Which structure separates thoracic from abdominal aorta?
questions.explanation: The aortic hiatus of the diaphragm (at T12) marks the transition from thoracic to abdominal aorta. The descending thoracic aorta passes through this opening (actually behind the diaphragm, between the crura) to become the abdominal aorta. The thoracic duct and sometimes azygos vein also pass through this hiatus.

Each lung has three borders: anterior, posterior, and inferior. The anterior border is where the costal and mediastinal surfaces meet. The posterior border is thick and extends from C7 to T10. The inferior border separates the base from the costal and mediastinal surfaces.
questions.question: How many borders does each lung possess?

questions.explanation: The sternal angle (angle of Louis) is located at the junction between the manubrium and body of sternum, corresponding to the level of the second costal cartilage. This landmark lies at the vertebral level of T4/T5 and marks important anatomical boundaries. It is also the level of tracheal bifurcation and the beginning and end of the aortic arch.
questions.question: Which costal cartilage articulates with the sternal angle?
Which muscle forms the anatomical snuffbox floor?
questions.explanation: The scaphoid and trapezium bones form the floor of the anatomical snuffbox. The boundaries are formed by tendons of abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis laterally, and extensor pollicis longus medially. The radial artery crosses the floor.

questions.question: Which nerve provides parasympathetic innervation to the heart?
