questions.explanation: The vagus nerves (CN X, both right and left) provide all parasympathetic innervation to the heart via the cardiac plexus. The right vagus preferentially supplies the SA node (negative chronotropy - decreases heart rate), while the left vagus preferentially supplies the AV node (negative dromotropy - slows AV conduction). Vagal stimulation also decreases atrial contractility.

The axillary tail (of Spence) is a process that extends from the upper lateral part of the breast into the axilla. It passes through an opening in the deep fascia and may reach as far as the third rib. Cancer in the axillary tail presents as an axillary mass.
questions.question: Where does the axillary tail extend?
How many lobes does the thymus consist of?
questions.explanation: The thymus consists of two elongated lobes and is a large organ in the fetus, occupying the thoracic cavity behind the sternum. It secretes lymphopoietin and plays a crucial role in T-lymphocyte maturation. After puberty, the thymus undergoes involution and is gradually replaced by adipose tissue.

Only the parietal pleura has somatic sensory innervation from intercostal and phrenic nerves, making it sensitive to pain. The visceral pleura has no somatic sensory nerve supply and receives only autonomic vasomotor innervation. This explains why pleural pain is sharp and well-localized to the chest wall.
questions.question: Which pleura has somatic sensory innervation?

questions.explanation: The gastric impression is a concave area on the visceral surface of the liver where it contacts the right side and lesser curvature of the stomach. Other impressions on the visceral surface include the duodenal, colic (from hepatic flexure), and renal impressions. These impressions reflect the relationships of the liver with adjacent viscera.
questions.question: Which impression is found on the visceral surface of the liver?
The anterior cerebral arteries are connected by which vessel?
questions.explanation: The two anterior cerebral arteries are joined by the anterior communicating artery, completing the anterior portion of the Circle of Willis. This connection allows collateral flow between right and left anterior circulations. Aneurysms commonly occur at this junction.

The right lung contains ten bronchopulmonary segments: three in the upper lobe (apical, posterior, anterior), two in the middle lobe (lateral, medial), and five in the lower lobe (superior/apical, medial basal, anterior basal, lateral basal, posterior basal). Each segment is functionally independent.
questions.question: How many bronchopulmonary segments exist in right lung?
Which cartilage caps the apex of the arytenoid?
questions.explanation: The corniculate cartilages (cartilages of Santorini) are small conical nodules of elastic cartilage that sit on the apex of each arytenoid cartilage. They are located in the posterior part of the aryepiglottic folds. The cuneiform cartilages lie more anteriorly in the aryepiglottic folds. Both are visible on laryngoscopy as small elevations.

The carotid triangle is bounded by the sternocleidomastoid (posterolaterally), superior belly of omohyoid (inferiorly), and posterior belly of digastric (superiorly). The triangle contains the carotid bifurcation, internal jugular vein, vagus nerve, and several other structures. It is a subdivision of the anterior triangle of the neck.
questions.question: Which structure forms the medial boundary of the carotid triangle?
The gastrosplenic ligament contains which vessels?
questions.explanation: The gastrosplenic ligament, a peritoneal fold connecting the greater curvature of the stomach (fundus region) to the hilum of the spleen, contains the short gastric arteries and veins (vasa brevia). These 4-6 small vessels branch from the splenic artery and vein near the splenic hilum to supply the gastric fundus. The left gastroepiploic vessels run in the greater omentum along the greater curvature, while the splenic vessels themselves course through the splenorenal ligament connecting the spleen to the left kidney, along with the tail of the pancreas.

The head of the femur forms two-thirds of a sphere and is directed medially, upward, and forward. It articulates with the acetabulum to form the hip joint. The fovea capitis on the head transmits blood from the obturator artery through the ligament of the head of femur.
questions.question: The head of the femur is directed medially, upward, and forward, forming what fraction of a sphere?
Where does the azygos vein originate?
questions.explanation: The azygos vein is formed by the union of the right ascending lumbar vein and right subcostal vein at the level of L1-L2. It enters the thorax through the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm at T12. It represents the embryonic right posterior cardinal vein.

questions.question: The median cricothyroid ligament connects which two cartilages?
questions.explanation: The median (central) cricothyroid ligament connects the anterior aspects of the cricoid and thyroid cartilages. It is subcutaneous in the midline between the cricothyroid muscles. This ligament is crossed by the cricothyroid arterial anastomosis and is the site for emergency cricothyroidotomy.

The deep group of the posterior compartment contains four muscles: popliteus, flexor hallucis longus, flexor digitorum longus, and tibialis posterior. The superficial group contains three muscles: gastrocnemius, soleus, and plantaris. All muscles of the posterior compartment are supplied by the tibial nerve. It is the largest of the three leg compartments.
questions.question: The deep group of the posterior leg compartment contains how many muscles?

questions.explanation: The peripheral part of the diaphragm (including the crura) receives sensory fibers from the lower six or seven intercostal and subcostal nerves. The central part receives sensory fibers from the phrenic nerves (C3-5). This dual innervation explains the referral patterns of pain from diaphragmatic irritation.
questions.question: Which nerves supply peripheral diaphragm sensory fibers?

questions.explanation: McBurney's point, located at the junction of the lateral third and medial two-thirds of a line from the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus, marks the base of the appendix where it attaches to the cecum. While the position of the appendix tip is highly variable, the base is consistently located at the confluence of the three taeniae coli on the posteromedialaaspect of the cecum.
questions.question: Which structure marks McBurney's point on the abdominal surface?
What percentage of body weight does the adult heart represent?
questions.explanation: The adult heart weighs approximately 250-350 grams, representing about 0.5% of total body weight (roughly 1/200th of body weight). The heart size is often compared to a closed fist. The male heart is typically slightly larger and heavier than the female heart, correlating with body size differences.

questions.question: Which structures pass through the sternocostal triangle?
questions.explanation: The sternocostal triangles (foramina of Morgagni) are small gaps between the sternal and costal attachments of the diaphragm. The superior epigastric vessels (terminal branches of internal thoracic artery and vein) and lymphatic vessels pass through these triangles. They connect the thoracic and abdominal cavities and are potential sites for diaphragmatic hernias.

(four muscles) produce finger abduction, moving fingers away from the middle finger axis. Palmar interossei (three muscles) produce finger adduction toward the middle finger. All interossei are supplied by the ulnar nerve and contribute to metacarpophalangeal joint flexion.
questions.question: Which interossei muscles produce finger abduction?

questions.explanation: The connective tissue septa between adjacent bronchopulmonary segments act as natural barriers preventing the spread of infection between segments. However, aggressive infections like tuberculosis and carcinoma can break through these barriers. This anatomical feature is clinically important in limiting disease spread.
questions.question: What prevents infection spread between segments?
Which enzyme in pancreatic juice digests proteins?
questions.explanation: Trypsinogen is the inactive precursor (zymogen) of trypsin, a protease that digests proteins. It is activated by enterokinase in the duodenum to form trypsin, which then activates other pancreatic proteases (chymotrypsinogen, proelastase, procarboxypeptidase) in a cascade. Pancreatic juice contains multiple proteases, each cleaving peptide bonds at specific amino acid sequences. Premature activation within the pancreas causes acute pancreatitis.

The genitofemoral nerve (L1, L2) emerges through the anterior surface of the psoas major muscle at approximately the L3/L4 level, unlike other branches of the lumbar plexus which emerge from its lateral border. After piercing psoas, it descends on the muscle's anterior surface, dividing into genital and femoral branches. The genital branch enters the deep inguinal ring to supply the cremaster muscle and scrotal/labial skin, while the femoral branch passes beneath the inguinal ligament lateral to the femoral artery to supply skin over the femoral triangle.
questions.question: The genitofemoral nerve pierces which muscle?
At what age does female breast development begin?
questions.explanation: Female breasts start developing at puberty under hormonal influence (estrogen and progesterone). They remain rudimentary in males throughout life. Most breast development in females occurs during the later months of pregnancy and lactation when the glandular tissue proliferates and becomes functional.

questions.question: Which muscle lies deep to the breast medially?
questions.explanation: Two-thirds of the breast's base lies on the pectoralis major muscle. The inferolateral one-third lies on the serratus anterior and external oblique muscles. The deep fascia of these muscles forms the posterior boundary of the retromammary space behind the breast.

The inferior mesenteric artery arises from the anterior surface of the abdominal aorta at approximately the level of the third lumbar vertebra (L3), about 3-4 cm above the aortic bifurcation. It supplies the hindgut derivatives: distal third of transverse colon, descending colon, sigmoid colon, and upper rectum. Its first branch is the left colic artery.
questions.question: At which vertebral level does the inferior mesenteric artery arise?

questions.explanation: The parietal peritoneum lining the anterior abdominal wall receives blood supply from the same vessels that supply the overlying abdominal wall: superior and inferior epigastric arteries, deep circumflex iliac artery, and lumbar arteries. The peritoneum overlying the diaphragm is supplied by the musculophrenic and phrenic arteries, while that in the pelvis is supplied by branches of the internal iliac artery. The visceral peritoneum covering the organs receives its blood supply from the arteries supplying those organs (celiac trunk, superior and inferior mesenteric arteries). Venous and lymphatic drainage follows arterial supply patterns.
questions.question: The parietal peritoneum of the anterior abdominal wall is supplied by which vessels?
Which artery supplies the vermiform appendix?
questions.explanation: The appendicular artery, a branch of the ileocolic artery (from the superior mesenteric artery), provides the blood supply to the vermiform appendix. It runs through the free edge of the mesoappendix, making it vulnerable during surgical mobilization of the appendix. This is typically an end artery with minimal collateral supply, so thrombosis can lead to appendiceal ischemia and necrosis. The artery may give off a recurrent branch that ascends toward the ileocecal junction. Variations include occasional origin from a posterior cecal artery or rarely from the superior mesenteric artery directly.

Chordae tendineae (heart strings) are thin, strong tendinous cords that connect the papillary muscles to the free edges and ventricular surfaces of the AV valve cusps. They prevent the valve cusps from prolapsing into the atrium during ventricular contraction. Rupture of chordae tendineae causes acute valvular regurgitation, often requiring surgical repair.
questions.question: What connects the papillary muscles to the valve cusps?

questions.explanation: The small saphenous vein arises from the union of the dorsal vein of the little toe with the dorsal venous arch and ascends posterior to the lateral malleolus. It then passes along the lateral border of the calcaneal tendon, ascends between the heads of gastrocnemius, and empties into the popliteal vein in the popliteal fossa.
questions.question: The small saphenous vein arises on the lateral side of the foot and ascends posterior to which malleolus before entering the popliteal vein?

questions.explanation: The renal medulla is composed of approximately 10-12 renal pyramids in each kidney. Each pyramid has its base directed toward the cortex and its apex (renal papilla) projecting medially into a minor calyx. The renal columns (columns of Bertin) extend between adjacent pyramids from the cortex to the renal sinus.
questions.question: How many renal pyramids typically comprise each kidney?
Which artery anastomoses with the superior rectal artery?
questions.explanation: The superior rectal artery (terminal continuation of the inferior mesenteric artery) anastomoses with the middle rectal artery (from anterior division of internal iliac) in the wall of the rectum, creating a portosystemic anastomosis between portal (superior rectal vein to inferior mesenteric vein to portal vein) and systemic (middle rectal vein to internal iliac vein to IVC) venous systems. The inferior rectal artery (from internal pudendal) also anastomoses with these vessels at the level of the anal canal. In portal hypertension, these anastomoses may become varicose, contributing to rectal varices (internal hemorrhoids above the pectinate line).

questions.question: The left renal artery passes posterior to which structure?
questions.explanation: The left renal artery passes posterior to the left renal vein as it courses from the aorta (at L1-L2 level, just below the superior mesenteric artery) to the left kidney hilum. The right renal artery, longer than the left, passes posterior to the IVC and right renal vein. Both renal arteries also pass posterior to the corresponding psoas major muscle and ureter. The left renal vein is longer than the right and receives the left gonadal vein, left suprarenal vein, and left inferior phrenic vein before draining into the IVC. This relationship is important in renal transplantation surgery.

questions.question: Which structure forms the lateral boundary of the bladder trigone?
questions.explanation: The two ureteric orifices form the superolateral angles (corners) of the triangular trigone. The internal urethral orifice forms the inferior angle. The interureteric ridge connects the two ureteric orifices forming the base of the triangle. The trigone remains smooth even when the bladder is empty, unlike the rest of the bladder mucosa which is rugose when empty.

questions.question: Where does the portal vein form anatomically?
questions.explanation: The portal vein forms posterior to the neck of the pancreas by the union of the superior mesenteric and splenic veins. It is approximately 8 cm long and ascends behind the first part of the duodenum to the porta hepatis, where it divides into right and left branches. It receives the left and right gastric veins, cystic vein, and paraumbilical veins during its course.

The posterior ethmoidal air cells drain into the superior meatus. The middle meatus receives drainage from the frontal, maxillary, and anterior ethmoidal sinuses. The inferior meatus receives the nasolacrimal duct. The sphenoethmoidal recess receives drainage from the sphenoid sinus.
questions.question: Which sinus drains into the superior meatus?
What is the approximate length of the male urethra?
questions.explanation: The male urethra is approximately 20 cm (8 inches) long and is divided into four parts: intramural (preprostatic), prostatic, membranous, and spongy (penile) portions. It serves both urinary and reproductive functions, carrying urine and semen. The female urethra is much shorter at approximately 4 cm, serving only urinary function.

questions.question: What lies in the rectouterine pouch in females?
questions.explanation: The rectouterine pouch (pouch of Douglas) is the peritoneal space between the posterior wall of the uterus/upper vagina and the anterior wall of the rectum. It is the lowest part of the peritoneal cavity in females and commonly contains loops of small intestine (ileum). It can be accessed via the posterior vaginal fornix for drainage of pelvic abscesses or fluid aspiration (culdocentesis).

questions.question: Which structure lies in the hilum of the kidney most anteriorly?
questions.explanation: At the renal hilum, the renal vein lies most anteriorly, the renal artery lies in the middle, and the renal pelvis (with the ureter) lies most posteriorly. This arrangement can be remembered as "VAP" (Vein, Artery, Pelvis) from anterior to posterior. The hilum is located on the medial border of each kidney.

options: This attachment has no special anatomical significance
FDP origin couples DIP flexion with IP extension
questions.question: What is the functional significance of lumbrical muscle origin?
questions.explanation: Lumbricals originate from flexor digitorum profundus tendons (unique among hand muscles). This means lumbrical contraction (causing MCP flexion and IP extension) also reduces profundus tension. This coupling enables the delicate coordination needed for precision movements like writing.

questions.question: The hypoglossal canal transmits which cranial nerve?
questions.explanation: The hypoglossal canal in the occipital bone transmits the hypoglossal nerve (XII). The nerve provides motor innervation to all intrinsic and most extrinsic muscles of the tongue except palatoglossus. Unilateral paralysis causes the tongue to deviate toward the paralyzed side when protruded.

questions.question: Where are intersegmental veins located?
questions.explanation: Intersegmental veins (tributaries of pulmonary veins) run in the connective tissue septa between adjacent bronchopulmonary segments. These veins act as anatomical guides during surgical segmentectomy, helping surgeons identify and separate individual segments without excessive bleeding.

The palatoglossal arch (anterior pillar of fauces) forms the posterior boundary of the oral cavity proper, separating it from the oropharynx. The arch extends from the soft palate to the side of the tongue and contains the palatoglossus muscle. The isthmus of fauces is the opening between the two palatoglossal arches connecting the oral cavity with the oropharynx.
questions.question: Which structure forms the posterior boundary of the oral cavity proper?

The popliteus muscle originates from the lateral surface of the lateral femoral condyle and also from the lateral meniscus. It is considered an intra-articular muscle because part of its tendon runs within which structure?
questions.explanation: The popliteus is considered an intra-articular muscle because part of its tendon runs within the joint capsule of the knee. It passes through a gap in the posterior fibrous capsule (the popliteal hiatus) between the fibular collateral ligament and the lateral meniscus. Popliteal tendinopathy causes posterolateral knee pain during downhill walking when the PCL and popliteus are most active.

The abducens nerve (VI) passes through Dorello's canal beneath the petrosphenoid (Gruber's) ligament at the petrous apex. The nerve then enters the cavernous sinus. Its long intracranial course makes it vulnerable to increased intracranial pressure causing false localizing sign. The nerve supplies the lateral rectus muscle.
questions.question: Which structure passes through Dorello's canal?

questions.explanation: The femoral artery becomes the popliteal artery as it passes through the adductor hiatus (opening in the adductor magnus muscle), transitioning from the anterior compartment of the thigh to the popliteal fossa. The adductor hiatus is located at the junction of the middle and distal thirds of the thigh. The femoral vein also passes through this opening. This question tests knowledge of lower limb anatomy in relation to pelvic structures, as the femoral vessels are continuations of the external iliac vessels that pass beneath the inguinal ligament.
questions.question: Which structure passes through the adductor hiatus?
Which structure lies in the rectovesical pouch in males?
questions.explanation: The rectovesical pouch is the peritoneal reflection between the bladder and rectum in males. It is the lowest part of the peritoneal cavity in males when upright and can contain loops of small intestine (ileum). Fluid collections or abscesses may accumulate here. In females, the analogous space is the rectouterine pouch (of Douglas), which is deeper.

questions.question: How many secondary ossification centres does the hip bone have in total?
questions.explanation: The hip bone has five secondary ossification centres: two for the iliac crest, two for the Y-shaped cartilage of the acetabulum, and one for the ischial tuberosity. All five fuse by 20-25 years of age. The three primary centres (ilium, ischium, pubis) appear in the 2nd, 4th, and 5th months of intrauterine life, respectively.

questions.question: The middle meningeal artery typically arises from which artery?
questions.explanation: The middle meningeal artery arises from the first (mandibular) part of the maxillary artery. It enters the skull through the foramen spinosum and supplies the dura mater and calvarium. The artery runs in grooves on the inner skull surface. Rupture causes epidural hematoma with the classic lucid interval.

The medial side of the carpal arch base is formed by the pisiform bone and the hook of the hamate. The lateral side is formed by the tubercles of the scaphoid and trapezium bones. The flexor retinaculum bridges across this arch, converting it into the carpal tunnel.
questions.question: Which carpal bones form the medial side of the carpal arch base?

questions.explanation: The ileum is supplied by 3 to 6 tiers of arterial arcades formed by branches of the superior mesenteric artery. These multiple arcades provide collateral circulation and ensure adequate blood supply to the bowel. In contrast, the jejunum typically has only 1 to 2 arterial arcades with longer vasa recta.
questions.question: How many arterial arcades typically supply the ileum?
Which muscle originates from the inguinal ligament?
questions.explanation: The internal oblique muscle originates from the lateral two-thirds of the inguinal ligament (along with the iliac crest and thoracolumbar fascia), with its fibers running superomedially. The lowermost fibers arch over the spermatic cord, contributing to the anterior wall of the inguinal canal laterally and the roof of the canal throughout its length. The external oblique muscle does not originate from the inguinal ligament; rather, its aponeurosis forms the inguinal ligament itself. The transversus abdominis also takes origin from the inguinal ligament laterally, contributing to the roof of the canal.

questions.question: What is the primary function of the tensor veli palatini muscle?
questions.explanation: The tensor veli palatini opens the Eustachian tube during swallowing and yawning, equalizing middle ear pressure. It is innervated by the nerve to medial pterygoid (V3), unlike other palatal muscles supplied by the pharyngeal plexus. The muscle also tenses the soft palate.

The porta hepatis (gateway of the liver) is a transverse fissure through which the portal vein, hepatic artery, and hepatic ducts pass. The portal vein and hepatic artery enter the liver while the hepatic ducts (right and left) exit. Lymphatic vessels and nerves also traverse the porta hepatis, which is bounded by the hepatoduodenal ligament.
questions.question: Which vessels enter the liver at the porta hepatis?
The third part of the duodenum is crossed anteriorly by which vessels?
questions.explanation: The third (horizontal) part of the duodenum is crossed anteriorly by the superior mesenteric artery and vein as they descend toward the root of the mesentery. This relationship can lead to superior mesenteric artery syndrome, where the third part of the duodenum is compressed between the SMA anteriorly and the aorta (with the spine) posteriorly, causing partial or complete duodenal obstruction. Risk factors include rapid weight loss, scoliosis, surgical correction of scoliosis, and conditions causing loss of the mesenteric fat pad that normally cushions the angle between the SMA and aorta.

The mylohyoid muscle arises from the mylohyoid line on the internal surface of the mandible. The muscle forms the floor of the mouth, separating oral cavity from neck. Below the mylohyoid line, the submandibular gland rests in the submandibular fossa. The mylohyoid nerve (V3) innervates the muscle.
questions.question: The mylohyoid line of the mandible provides attachment for which muscle?
Which structures form the boundaries of the cervicoaxillary canal (apex of axilla)?
options: First rib, clavicle, and superior scapular border
questions.explanation: The apex of the axilla forms the cervicoaxillary canal, providing passage between the neck and axilla. It is bounded by the first rib medially, the clavicle anteriorly, and the superior border of the scapula posteriorly. Arteries, veins, lymphatics, and nerves traverse this opening to reach or leave the upper limb.

questions.question: Adductor brevis lies deep to which two muscles of the medial compartment?
questions.explanation: Adductor brevis lies deep to pectineus and adductor longus. It originates from the body and inferior ramus of the pubis and inserts into the pectineal line and proximal part of the linea aspera. It is innervated by the anterior division of the obturator nerve (L2, L3, L4) and adducts the thigh and to some extent flexes it.

questions.question: The piriform fossa is bounded medially by which structure?
questions.explanation: The piriform fossa (recess) is bounded medially by the aryepiglottic fold and laterally by the thyroid cartilage and thyrohyoid membrane. The internal laryngeal nerve and superior laryngeal vessels lie in the mucosa of the piriform fossa. Foreign bodies commonly lodge in this recess. The fossa is part of the laryngopharynx.

questions.question: Which artery anastomoses at Sudeck's point?
questions.explanation: Sudeck's point is the watershed area at the rectosigmoid junction (approximately 15 cm from the anal verge) where the last sigmoid artery (from inferior mesenteric artery) anastomoses with the superior rectal artery (terminal continuation of IMA). This represents a relatively weak point in the colonic blood supply, vulnerable to ischemia during periods of low blood flow, hypotension, or ligation of the inferior mesenteric artery during surgery. Another watershed area is Griffiths' point at the splenic flexure. Both areas may develop ischemic colitis, manifesting as abdominal pain, bloody diarrhea, and colonoscopic evidence of mucosal ischemia.

questions.question: The optic nerve is surrounded by which meningeal layers?
questions.explanation: The optic nerve is covered by all three meningeal layers (dura, arachnoid, and pia) from the sclera to the optic canal. At the canal, the dura becomes continuous with the periosteum of the orbit. Increased intracranial pressure can cause papilledema due to continuity of the subarachnoid space around the optic nerve.

The superficial inguinal ring is a triangular defect in the external oblique aponeurosis, located immediately superior and medial to the pubic tubercle. Its margins, called the medial and lateral crura, are connected superiorly by intercrural fibers and give attachment to the external spermatic fascia. The superficial ring represents the external opening of the inguinal canal and transmits the spermatic cord in males or round ligament in females, along with the ilioinguinal nerve. The ring is larger in males than females, contributing to the higher incidence of inguinal hernias in males.
questions.question: The superficial inguinal ring is an opening in which structure?
The middle constrictor muscle of the pharynx arises from which structure?
questions.explanation: The middle constrictor arises from the greater and lesser horns of the hyoid bone and the stylohyoid ligament. It overlaps the superior constrictor above and is overlapped by the inferior constrictor below. The muscle inserts into the median pharyngeal raphe. All constrictors are supplied by the pharyngeal plexus.

questions.question: What separates adjacent bronchopulmonary segments?
questions.explanation: Adjacent bronchopulmonary segments are separated by connective tissue septa. Intersegmental veins run in these septa and serve as guides for surgically separating segments. The septa act as natural barriers preventing spread of infection between segments (though cancer and tuberculosis can break through).

The median arcuate ligament connects the right and left crura of the diaphragm, passing anterior to the aorta at the T12 level, above the origin of the celiac trunk. In some individuals (1-2%), this ligament may be positioned lower, crossing anterior to the celiac trunk and potentially compressing it, a condition known as median arcuate ligament syndrome (celiac artery compression syndrome or Dunbar syndrome). This can cause postprandial pain, weight loss, and an epigastric bruit, though the clinical significance remains debated as many individuals with radiographic compression remain asymptomatic.
questions.question: The median arcuate ligament crosses anterior to which structure?

questions.explanation: The right renal artery passes posterior to both the right renal vein and the inferior vena cava as it courses from the aorta (at L1-L2 level, just below the superior mesenteric artery) to the right kidney hilum. The right renal artery is longer than the left due to the aorta's left-sided position. Both renal arteries also pass posterior to the corresponding psoas major muscle and ureter. The arteries typically divide into anterior and posterior divisions before entering the hilum, supplying corresponding segments of the kidney. The right artery may give off the inferior suprarenal artery.
questions.question: The right renal artery passes posterior to which structure?

questions.explanation: The lymphatic drainage of the upper ureter is to the lateral aortic (para-aortic) lymph nodes, while the pelvic portion drains to the internal and external iliac nodes. This lymphatic drainage pattern follows the blood supply. The lateral aortic nodes are located around the origin of the renal arteries at the L1-L2 level.
questions.question: Which lymph nodes drain the upper ureter?
How long is the ureter in adults?
questions.explanation: Each ureter is approximately 25 cm long, extending from the renal pelvis to the urinary bladder. The ureter descends on the psoas major muscle, crosses the pelvic brim at the bifurcation of the common iliac artery, and enters the bladder at the lateral angles of the trigone. It is a muscular tube that propels urine by peristaltic contractions.

questions.question: The rectovesical pouch in males is located at which level from the anus?
questions.explanation: The rectovesical pouch (Douglas pouch in males), the peritoneal reflection between the rectum posteriorly and the urinary bladder anteriorly, lies approximately 7.5 cm from the anus. This represents the lowest extent of the peritoneal cavity in males when in the upright position, making it a common site for fluid accumulation (blood, pus, ascites) that can be drained transrectally. In females, the corresponding rectouterine pouch (of Douglas) lies lower at about 5.5 cm from the anus (7.5 cm from the vaginal orifice) due to the interposed uterus between rectum and bladder.

The inferior epigastric artery (from the external iliac artery) ascends medial to the deep inguinal ring and enters the rectus sheath by piercing the transversalis fascia at the arcuate line. Once within the sheath, it ascends on the posterior surface of the rectus abdominis muscle and anastomoses with the superior epigastric artery (from the internal thoracic artery). The inferior epigastric artery gives off the cremasteric artery and sometimes a pubic branch. Its position medial to the deep inguinal ring makes it an important landmark distinguishing direct (medial to vessel) from indirect (lateral to vessel) inguinal hernias.
questions.question: The inferior epigastric artery enters the rectus sheath by piercing which structure?
What are Rotter's nodes?
questions.explanation: Rotter's nodes (interpectoral nodes) lie between the pectoralis major and minor muscles. They are part of the axillary lymphatic drainage pathway. During modified radical mastectomy, these nodes may be removed along with the pectoral fascia. Their involvement affects staging and prognosis.

The wrist joint is innervated by branches from three nerves following Hilton's law: median nerve (anterior interosseous branch), radial nerve (posterior interosseous branch), and ulnar nerve (deep and dorsal branches). This follows the principle that nerves supplying muscles moving a joint also supply the joint.
options: Anterior and posterior interosseous nerves only
questions.question: What nerve innervates the wrist joint?
Which part of the bladder is most fixed in position?
questions.explanation: The neck of the bladder is the most fixed part, anchored by the puboprostatic ligaments (in males) or pubovesical ligaments (in females) and the lateral ligaments of the bladder. The remainder of the bladder is relatively mobile, allowing it to expand superiorly into the abdomen when full. The neck surrounds the internal urethral orifice.

The psoas major muscle lies posteromedially to each kidney, forming part of its posterior relation. A psoas abscess can cause confusion with renal pathology due to this proximity. The quadratus lumborum lies directly posterior to the mid-portion of the kidney, while the transversus abdominis and its aponeurosis lie posterolaterally.
questions.question: Which muscle lies immediately medial to the kidney?
Which structure is derived from the ventral mesentery?
questions.explanation: The falciform ligament (and lesser omentum) develops from the ventral mesentery, while the greater omentum, splenorenal ligament, gastrosplenic ligament, and transverse mesocolon all derive from the dorsal mesentery. The ventral mesentery, present only in the region of the foregut, gives rise to the falciform ligament (connecting liver to anterior abdominal wall), the lesser omentum (connecting liver to lesser curvature and proximal duodenum), and the coronary and triangular ligaments (connecting liver to diaphragm). The liver and gallbladder develop within the ventral mesentery, explaining their peritoneal relationships.

The popliteal artery is the deepest structure in the popliteal fossa, running closest to the articular capsule of the knee joint. This proximity makes the popliteal artery particularly vulnerable in posterior knee dislocations and tibial plateau fractures. The arrangement from deep to superficial is: artery, vein, then tibial nerve.
questions.question: Which neurovascular structure is the DEEPEST within the popliteal fossa, running closest to the articular capsule of the knee joint?

questions.explanation: The anteroposterior dimension is increased by the "pump handle" movement of the true ribs (2-7), which pushes the sternum upward and forward. This occurs during inspiration. The bucket handle movement of ribs 7-10 increases the lateral dimension, while diaphragm descent increases the vertical dimension.
questions.question: What increases the anteroposterior thoracic dimension?

questions.explanation: The ligamentum teres transmits arteries from acetabular branches of the medial circumflex femoral and obturator arteries to the head of femur. It is triangular and flat, with its apex at the fovea capitis and base at the acetabular notch. In adults, this provides only a minor blood supply compared to the retinacular vessels.
options: Superior gluteal artery from the internal iliac
Inferior gluteal artery from the internal iliac alone
Acetabular branches of medial circumflex femoral and obturator arteries
questions.question: The ligament of the head of femur (ligamentum teres) transmits arteries from which named vessels to the femoral head?

questions.explanation: Psoas minor originates from the sides of T12 and L1 vertebrae and their intervening disc. It inserts into the pectineal line and iliopubic eminence. When present, it acts conjointly with psoas major and iliacus in flexing the thigh at the hip. Its long slender tendon is occasionally used as a landmark in pelvic surgery.
questions.question: Psoas minor, a variable muscle absent in approximately 40% of individuals, originates from which vertebral levels?

questions.explanation: The lacrimal gland receives parasympathetic secretomotor fibers that synapse in the pterygopalatine ganglion. Preganglionic fibers travel via the greater petrosal nerve and nerve of the pterygoid canal. Postganglionic fibers reach the gland via the zygomatic and lacrimal nerves. The pathway originates from the superior salivatory nucleus.
questions.question: The lacrimal gland is innervated by which parasympathetic pathway?

questions.explanation: Griffiths' point is the watershed area at the splenic flexure where the superior mesenteric artery territory (via the middle colic artery) meets the inferior mesenteric artery territory (via the left colic artery). This area has the poorest collateral circulation and is most vulnerable to ischemia in low-flow states. It is a common site for ischemic colitis.
questions.question: Where is Griffiths' point located?
Which part of the male urethra is surrounded by the external sphincter?
questions.explanation: The external urethral sphincter (sphincter urethrae, voluntary striated muscle) surrounds the membranous urethra as it passes through the deep perineal space (urogenital diaphragm). This sphincter provides voluntary control of micturition and is innervated by the pudendal nerve (S2-S4). The prostatic urethra is surrounded by the internal urethral sphincter (smooth muscle under autonomic control) at the bladder neck. The membranous urethra is the shortest (1-2 cm) and least distensible part, making it vulnerable to injury during instrumentation and the most common site of urethral rupture in pelvic fractures.

The aortic knuckle (or aortic knob) is the prominent shadow on a chest X-ray created by the aortic arch as it curves backward and to the left at the level of T4/5. This is a normal finding and an important landmark. Widening may indicate aortic aneurysm or dissection.
questions.question: What creates the aortic knuckle on X-ray?

questions.explanation: extend the interphalangeal joints while simultaneously flexing the metacarpophalangeal joints. This coordinated action is essential for precision grip and fine motor control. Extensor digitorum extends the metacarpophalangeal joints but cannot independently extend interphalangeal joints without intrinsic muscle assistance.
questions.question: What muscle initiates finger extension at interphalangeal joints?
Which rib level marks the base of breast vertically?
questions.explanation: The base of the breast extends vertically from the 2nd to 6th rib. Transversely, it extends from the sternal edge to the mid-axillary line. The axillary tail of Spence extends from the upper outer quadrant into the axilla. These landmarks are important for clinical breast examination.

questions.question: Which structure passes through the right crus of the diaphragm?
questions.explanation: The oesophageal hiatus is located in the muscular part of the right crus at T10. The oesophagus passes through it along with the anterior and posterior vagal trunks, oesophageal vessels, and lymphatics. Some fibers of the right crus form a sphincter around the oesophagus, contributing to prevention of gastro-oesophageal reflux. The left crus is smaller and does not have a hiatus.

The recurrent laryngeal nerve ascends in the tracheoesophageal groove between the trachea and esophagus. This location makes it vulnerable during thyroid surgery. The left recurrent nerve loops under the aortic arch while the right loops under the subclavian artery.
questions.question: The recurrent laryngeal nerve ascends in which anatomical groove?

questions.explanation: The main pancreatic duct of Wirsung begins in the tail and runs through the entire length of the gland, receiving numerous tributaries along its course. It drains the majority of pancreatic tissue and usually joins the common bile duct to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla. This ampulla opens at the major duodenal papilla in the second part of the duodenum.
questions.question: Which duct drains the majority of the pancreatic tissue?

questions.explanation: Anconeus is a small muscle that assists triceps brachii in elbow extension. It is located on the posterior aspect of the elbow, blending with the lateral head of triceps. The muscle is supplied by the radial nerve.
questions.question: What is the function of anconeus muscle?
What nerve root value is the musculocutaneous nerve?
questions.explanation: The musculocutaneous nerve has nerve root values C5, C6, and C7. It arises from the lateral cord of the brachial plexus. The nerve supplies three muscles (biceps, brachialis, coracobrachialis) before continuing as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm.

questions.question: The vas deferens is derived from which embryological structure?
questions.explanation: The vas deferens (ductus deferens) develops from the mesonephric duct (Wolffian duct) in males under the influence of testosterone. In females, the mesonephric duct regresses due to absence of testosterone, while the paramesonephric duct (M?llerian duct) develops into the fallopian tubes, uterus, and upper vagina. The epididymis also develops from the mesonephric duct, while the seminal vesicles arise as outgrowths from the distal mesonephric duct. The prostate and bulbourethral glands develop from the urogenital sinus. Understanding embryology helps explain congenital anomalies of the reproductive tract.

An emissary vein passes through the foramen ovale connecting the cavernous sinus with the pterygoid venous plexus. Other emissary veins include those passing through the foramen spinosum (middle meningeal vein), mastoid foramen (sigmoid sinus), and parietal foramina (superior sagittal sinus). These valveless connections allow bidirectional flow and infection spread.
questions.question: Which foramen transmits the emissary vein connecting the cavernous sinus?

questions.explanation: Pronator quadratus is supplied by the anterior interosseous nerve, a branch of the median nerve. This nerve also supplies flexor pollicis longus and the lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus. The pronator quadratus is the deepest muscle in the anterior forearm.
questions.question: Which nerve supplies pronator quadratus?

questions.explanation: The vaginal artery typically arises from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery (though it may arise from the uterine artery) and descends to supply the vagina. It gives off numerous branches to the anterior and posterior vaginal walls, anastomosing with branches from the uterine artery superiorly and internal pudendal artery inferiorly. This rich anastomotic network provides extensive collateral circulation to the vagina. The vagina also receives blood supply from the middle rectal and internal pudendal arteries. The upper vagina drains via uterine veins, while the lower vagina drains via internal pudendal veins.
questions.question: The vaginal artery typically arises from which vessel?
What is the arterial arcade along the colon's mesenteric border called?
questions.explanation: The marginal artery (of Drummond) is a continuous arterial arcade running along the mesenteric border of the colon, formed by anastomoses between branches of the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries. It provides collateral circulation and ensures blood supply if one major artery is occluded. Weak points exist, particularly at the splenic flexure (Griffiths' point) and rectosigmoid junction (Sudeck's point).

questions.question: The adductor tubercle is an important bony landmark on the medial aspect of the distal femur. Which tendon inserts here?
questions.explanation: The adductor tubercle on the medial aspect of the distal femur receives the insertion of the hamstring part of adductor magnus. This is the part of adductor magnus supplied by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve. The adductor tubercle is palpable on physical examination and serves as an important landmark in knee surgery (origin of the tibial collateral ligament is just above it).

Branches of the facial and lingual arteries supply the submandibular gland, with the facial artery providing the primary vascular supply. The facial artery passes deep to the gland before crossing the mandible. Venous drainage follows corresponding veins to the internal jugular system.
questions.question: Which vessel specifically supplies the bed of the submandibular gland?

questions.explanation: Lumbricals flex the metacarpophalangeal joints while extending the interphalangeal joints of the fingers. This unique action is essential for precision grip and fine motor control. The lateral two lumbricals are supplied by the median nerve while the medial two receive ulnar innervation.
questions.question: What is the function of the lumbricals in the hand?
options: Flex metacarpophalangeal joints, extend interphalangeal joints

questions.explanation: The falciform ligament separates the anatomical right and left lobes of the liver on the anterior and superior surfaces, extending from the diaphragm and anterior abdominal wall to the liver surface. However, the functional division between right and left lobes (Couinaud's segmentation) is defined by the main portal fissure (Cantlie's line), an imaginary plane running from the gallbladder fossa anteriorly to the IVC groove posteriorly, containing the middle hepatic vein. This functional division corresponds to the distribution of the right and left branches of the portal vein, hepatic artery, and bile ducts. The quadrate and caudate lobes, though anatomically part of the right lobe, are functionally part of the left lobe.
questions.question: Which structure separates the right and left lobes of the liver anatomically?
Which structure separates the greater and lesser peritoneal sacs?
questions.explanation: The lesser omentum forms the anterior boundary of the lesser sac, separating it from the greater sac anteriorly along with the posterior wall of the stomach. This double-layered peritoneal fold extends from the lesser curvature of the stomach and first part of duodenum to the liver. The lesser omentum consists of the hepatogastric ligament (its membranous portion) and the hepatoduodenal ligament (its thickened free right edge containing the portal triad), with the latter forming the anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen.

The common fibular nerve winds around the neck of the fibula and then divides into the deep and superficial fibular nerves. At this point it is subcutaneous and highly vulnerable to injury from fractures, tight plasters, or prolonged cross-legged sitting. Injury causes foot drop due to paralysis of the anterior and lateral leg compartment muscles.
questions.question: The common fibular nerve winds around which specific part of the fibula to divide into its terminal branches?

questions.explanation: The thyroid gland drains to prelaryngeal, pretracheal, and paratracheal lymph nodes, which then drain to deep cervical nodes. Lymphatic drainage follows the arterial supply. Understanding lymphatic pathways is crucial for thyroid cancer staging and surgical planning. Superior gland drainage differs from inferior drainage patterns.
questions.question: Which lymph nodes drain the thyroid gland?

questions.explanation: The anterior surface of the femoral neck carries the intertrochanteric line, which is broad and rough and serves as attachment for the iliofemoral ligament. The posterior aspect carries the prominent intertrochanteric crest. These landmarks delineate the intracapsular portion of the femoral neck.
questions.question: Which surface of the femoral neck carries the intertrochanteric line, a broad rough area that is the attachment for the iliofemoral ligament?
The femoral pulse is palpated at the mid-inguinal point, defined as the midpoint between which two bony landmarks?
questions.explanation: The femoral pulse is palpated at the mid-inguinal point, the midpoint between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis. At this point the femoral artery lies lateral to the femoral vein and medial to the femoral nerve. This is distinct from the midpoint of the inguinal ligament, which overlies the femoral canal.
options: Pubic tubercle and anterior superior iliac spine
Medial malleolus and anterior superior iliac spine
Inguinal ligament and the femoral condyle
Anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis
Pubic crest and posterior superior iliac spine
Roof: inferior fibula; walls: tibia bilaterally; floor: calcaneus
Roof: inferior tibia; walls: medial (tibial) and lateral (fibular) malleoli; floor: trochlea tali
Roof: superior surface of talus; walls: tibia; floor: calcaneus
Roof: superior tibia; walls: talus on both sides; floor: navicular
Roof: fibula; walls: medial and lateral malleoli; floor: navicular
questions.explanation: The ankle joint (mortise) is formed by: the roof (inferior surface of the tibia), the lateral wall (lateral malleolus from the fibula), the medial wall (medial malleolus from the tibia), and the floor (superior surface of the talus, the trochlea tali). This mortise-and-tenon configuration provides inherent bony stability, especially during dorsiflexion.
questions.question: The ankle (talocrural) joint is formed by three bony components. Which correctly describes the roof, walls, and floor?
The medial wall of the orbit is formed primarily by which bone?
questions.explanation: The medial orbital wall is formed primarily by the orbital plate (lamina papyracea) of the ethmoid bone. This thin bone separates the orbit from ethmoidal air cells. Fractures can cause orbital emphysema when air enters from the sinuses. The lacrimal bone contributes anteriorly.

questions.question: Which structure forms the medial wall of the tympanic cavity?
questions.explanation: The promontory on the medial wall of the tympanic cavity is formed by the basal turn of the cochlea. The facial nerve canal runs above it. The oval and round windows are also located on the medial wall. The tympanic plexus lies on the promontory providing sensation to the middle ear mucosa.

questions.question: Where is the thoracic duct located initially?
questions.explanation: The thoracic duct begins at L1 and ascends in the posterior mediastinum, initially posterior to the esophagus. At T5, it moves to the left side of the esophagus and continues upward into the superior mediastinum where it arches forward to drain into the left venous angle.

The posterior wall of the lesser sac (omental bursa) is formed by peritoneum covering the pancreas, left kidney, left suprarenal gland, and the posterior two layers of the greater omentum. The lesser sac is bounded anteriorly by the stomach, lesser omentum, and greater omentum; superiorly by the caudate lobe of the liver and diaphragm; and inferiorly by the transverse mesocolon. It communicates with the greater sac through the epiploic foramen (foramen of Winslow).
questions.question: Which structure forms the posterior wall of the lesser sac?
What is the action of the long head of triceps at the shoulder?
questions.explanation: The long head of triceps crosses both the shoulder and elbow joints, performing extension at the shoulder. At the elbow, all three heads of triceps work together to produce extension. The long head originates from the infraglenoid tubercle of the scapula.

questions.question: How many cusps compose the tricuspid valve?
questions.explanation: The tricuspid valve has three cusps: anterior (largest), posterior (smallest), and septal. These cusps are attached to a fibrous ring (annulus) and prevented from prolapsing into the atrium by chordae tendineae connecting to papillary muscles. The valve prevents backflow from the right ventricle to the right atrium during ventricular systole.

questions.question: The testicular vein on the left typically drains into which vessel?
questions.explanation: The left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein at approximately a right angle, while the right testicular vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava at an acute angle. This anatomical difference explains the higher incidence (90%) of left-sided varicoceles, as the perpendicular drainage into the renal vein, along with the longer venous column and potential compression by the superior mesenteric artery (nutcracker phenomenon), creates higher venous pressure on the left. The left testicular vein lacks valves or has incompetent valves, facilitating retrograde flow and varicosity formation.

The heart and pericardium are the main contents of the middle mediastinum, which also contains the ascending aorta, pulmonary trunk, parts of the phrenic nerves, and the main bronchi. The middle mediastinum is the central compartment of the inferior mediastinum.
questions.question: What position does the heart occupy mediastinally?

questions.explanation: Piriformis, obturator internus, gemellus superior, and gemellus inferior share innervation from L5, S1. They also share the same insertion into the upper border of the greater trochanter and the same action as lateral rotators of the hip joint. This common heritage is useful clinically in understanding hip pathology.
questions.question: Piriformis, obturator internus, gemellus superior, and gemellus inferior share a common innervation. What is their shared nerve root?

questions.explanation: The superior oblique muscle is innervated by the trochlear nerve (IV), the only extraocular muscle not supplied by the oculomotor nerve except lateral rectus (abducens). The superior oblique passes through the trochlea (pulley) on the medial orbital roof. It intorts, depresses, and abducts the eye.
questions.question: The superior oblique muscle is innervated by which cranial nerve?

questions.explanation: From lateral to medial, the femoral triangle contains: Nerve (femoral nerve), Artery (femoral artery), Vein (femoral vein), and Empty space/Lymphatics. The mnemonic NAVEL (Nerve, Artery, Vein, Empty space, Lymphatics) helps recall this order. The femoral sheath surrounds the femoral artery and vein (and the femoral canal), but not the femoral nerve.
questions.question: The contents of the femoral triangle from lateral to medial are arranged as which of the following?

questions.explanation: The jugulodigastric lymph nodes are located below the angle of the mandible where the posterior belly of digastric crosses the internal jugular vein. They are commonly enlarged in tonsillitis and are therefore called tonsillar nodes. These are part of the superior deep cervical lymph node chain.
questions.question: Which lymph nodes are commonly called the tonsillar nodes?

options: Hip joint itself (L3 innervates the hip)
questions.explanation: The L3 sclerotome includes the hip joint, which receives innervation partly from the femoral nerve (L2, L3, L4). Pain from L3 root pathology can be referred to the hip joint, and hip joint disease can refer pain along L3 dermatomal distribution to the anterior thigh and knee. This bidirectional referral is explained by Hilton's law and the concept of sclerotome overlap between spinal levels.
questions.question: In the lower limb, the term 'sclerotome' refers to the area of bone and deep structures supplied by a single spinal nerve root. Hip pain from L3 sclerotome involvement can mimic pain from which structure?
Which muscle opens the auditory tube during swallowing?
questions.explanation: The tensor veli palatini muscle opens the auditory (Eustachian) tube during swallowing by pulling on the membranous lateral wall. The levator veli palatini also contributes. Salpingopharyngeus assists in opening the tube. This mechanism equalizes middle ear pressure with atmospheric pressure.

The right lung in a healthy adult male weighs approximately 600 grams when filled with air, while the left lung weighs about 550 grams. The lungs are spongy, elastic organs that are pinkish in healthy individuals. In city dwellers, they may appear darker due to accumulation of carbon particles.
questions.question: What is the lung weight in a healthy adult male?

questions.explanation: Six vessels exit through the greater sciatic foramen: superior gluteal artery and vein, inferior gluteal artery and vein, and internal pudendal artery and vein. Together with seven nerves and the piriformis muscle, they constitute the 14 structures passing through this critical anatomical gateway from the pelvis to the gluteal region.
questions.question: How many vessels exit through the greater sciatic foramen?
Which bone contains the cribriform plate?
questions.explanation: The cribriform plate is part of the ethmoid bone and forms the roof of the nasal cavity. It contains multiple foramina transmitting olfactory nerve fibers from the nasal epithelium to the olfactory bulb. The crista galli projects upward from the cribriform plate for attachment of the falx cerebri.

The aortic arch passes over and in front of the left lung root. The left lung root lies within the concavity of the aortic arch. This anatomical relationship is visible on chest X-rays and CT scans and is important for understanding mediastinal anatomy.
questions.question: What arches over the left lung root?

questions.explanation: The splenic artery gives off the short gastric arteries (vasa brevia, 4-6 vessels) near the splenic hilum, which pass through the gastrosplenic ligament to supply the fundus of the stomach. The splenic artery also gives off the left gastroepiploic (gastro-omental) artery, which runs along the greater curvature in the gastrocolic ligament. The left gastric artery arises from the celiac trunk (not splenic artery), while the right gastric and gastroduodenal arteries arise from the hepatic artery proper and common hepatic artery respectively. The short gastric vessels create collateral circulation to the stomach and must be ligated during splenectomy.
questions.question: The splenic artery gives off which gastric vessels?
Which structure prevents food from entering the nasopharynx during swallowing?
questions.explanation: The soft palate elevates and tenses during swallowing to close off the nasopharynx, preventing nasal regurgitation. Levator veli palatini elevates while tensor veli palatini tenses the palate. The uvula contacts the posterior pharyngeal wall (Passavant's ridge) to complete the seal.

questions.question: Which artery supplies the nasal septum anteriorly?
questions.explanation: The anterior ethmoidal artery (from ophthalmic artery) supplies the anterior superior nasal septum. The sphenopalatine artery supplies the posterior septum while the superior labial artery supplies anteroinferiorly. These vessels anastomose in Little's area (Kiesselbach's plexus), the most common site of anterior epistaxis.

The inferior mesenteric vein typically drains into the splenic vein posterior to the body of the pancreas, though variations exist (occasionally draining into the superior mesenteric vein or the confluence of splenic and superior mesenteric veins). The IMV ascends from the pelvis, receiving sigmoid and left colic tributaries, and runs to the left of the inferior mesenteric artery. It passes anterior to the left psoas, left ureter, and left gonadal vessels before reaching the splenic vein. From there, blood flows via the splenic vein to join the superior mesenteric vein, forming the portal vein behind the pancreatic neck.
questions.question: The inferior mesenteric vein typically drains into which vessel?

questions.explanation: The superior surface of the diaphragm is supplied by pericardiacophrenic and musculophrenic arteries (branches of the internal thoracic artery) and the superior phrenic arteries (from the thoracic aorta). The pericardiacophrenic artery accompanies the phrenic nerve. The musculophrenic artery is a terminal branch of the internal thoracic artery.
questions.question: Which vessels supply the superior diaphragmatic surface?

questions.explanation: Trabeculae carneae are irregular muscular ridges that project from the inner surface of the ventricles. They prevent the walls from adhering to each other during contraction, increase ventricular surface area, and may contribute to ventricular contraction. Some are attached at both ends (ridges), some at one end (bridges like the moderator band), and some are free (papillary muscles).
questions.question: What is the function of trabeculae carneae?

questions.explanation: The deep branch of the lateral plantar nerve (analogous to the deep branch of ulnar nerve) supplies adductor hallucis, all plantar and dorsal interossei, the lateral three lumbricals, and flexor digiti minimi brevis. The superficial branch of the lateral plantar nerve supplies flexor digiti minimi brevis and provides cutaneous branches to the lateral one and a half toes.
options: Adductor hallucis, all interossei, lateral three lumbricals, and flexor digiti minimi brevis
All lumbricals and interossei of the foot only
Only the flexor digiti minimi brevis of the little toe
Abductor digiti minimi of the lateral plantar group alone
All intrinsic foot muscles except the abductor hallucis
questions.question: The lateral plantar nerve (S1, S2) is analogous to the ulnar nerve of the hand. It supplies which muscles as its deep branch?
Which structure lies anterior to the male bladder neck?
questions.explanation: The prostate gland lies immediately inferior to the bladder neck in males, surrounding the prostatic urethra. The base of the prostate is continuous with the bladder neck. Prostatic enlargement (benign prostatic hyperplasia or cancer) commonly causes urinary symptoms by compressing the prostatic urethra and elevating the bladder base.

questions.question: The Eustachian tube in adults lies at what angle to the horizontal plane?
questions.explanation: In adults, the Eustachian tube lies at 45° to the horizontal plane, whereas in infants it is only 10°. This more vertical orientation in children predisposes them to middle ear infections. The tube is approximately 31-38 mm long with the posterior third being osseous.

questions.question: The popliteus muscle 'unlocks' the knee from full extension by rotating the femur by how many degrees on the fixed tibia?
questions.explanation: The popliteus muscle weakly flexes the knee and unlocks it from full extension by rotating the femur 5 degrees on a fixed tibia (or medially rotating the tibia on an unplanted limb). It originates from the lateral femoral condyle and lateral meniscus, inserting on the posterior tibia. It is innervated by the tibial nerve (L4, L5, S1).

Gastrocnemius is unique in that it plantarflexes the ankle only effectively when the knee is extended, because it crosses the knee joint. When the knee is flexed, gastrocnemius becomes relatively ineffective, and soleus becomes the primary plantarflexor. Gastrocnemius also flexes the leg at the knee and is innervated by the tibial nerve (S1, S2).
options: When the knee is fully extended
questions.question: Gastrocnemius can only plantarflex the ankle effectively under which condition?
What embryonic structure forms mammary glands?
questions.explanation: Mammary glands are modifications of sweat glands and are therefore ectodermal in origin. They develop from the mammary ridge (milk line) which extends from axilla to groin in the embryo. In humans, most of this ridge disappears except in the pectoral region where breasts develop.

The palmaris longus tendon (when present) passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum and inserts into it along with the palmar aponeurosis. The ulnar nerve and artery also pass superficial to the retinaculum through Guyon's canal. All flexor tendons and the median nerve pass deep to the retinaculum through the carpal tunnel.
questions.question: What structure passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum?
Which muscle flexes the elbow when the forearm is pronated?
questions.explanation: is the primary elbow flexor regardless of forearm position because it inserts on the ulna. Biceps brachii is less effective when the forearm is pronated because its supinating action is opposed. Brachialis is supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve.

options: Anterior surface of the ankle between malleoli
Dorsum of foot lateral to extensor hallucis longus
Midway between lateral malleolus and calcaneus
questions.explanation: The posterior tibial pulse is palpated inferoposteriorly to the medial malleolus, where the artery curves to enter the tarsal tunnel and then the sole of the foot. The dorsalis pedis pulse is found on the dorsum of the foot, just lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon. The four main pulse points of the lower limb are femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial, and dorsalis pedis.
questions.question: The posterior tibial pulse is palpated at which surface anatomical location?
Which segment absorbs bile salts for enterohepatic recirculation?
questions.explanation: Bile salts are actively reabsorbed in the terminal ileum and returned to the liver via the portal circulation (enterohepatic recirculation). About 95% of bile salts are recycled this way, conserving the bile salt pool. Ileal disease or resection disrupts this circulation, leading to bile salt malabsorption, steatorrhea, and potential bile salt diarrhea.

In only 1% of adults, a nasal emissary vein passes through the foramen cecum connecting nasal veins with the superior sagittal sinus. In most adults, the foramen is obliterated. In the fetus, this foramen transmitted the anterior extension of the developing superior sagittal sinus.
questions.question: What structure passes through the foramen cecum in adults?
Which structure is NOT retroperitoneal?
questions.explanation: The transverse colon is intraperitoneal, suspended by the transverse mesocolon from the posterior abdominal wall. The ascending and descending colon are secondarily retroperitoneal (covered by peritoneum anteriorly only), as is most of the duodenum (except the first 2 cm) and the pancreas (except the tail which extends into the splenorenal ligament). Secondarily retroperitoneal structures were initially suspended by mesentery during development but became fused to the posterior body wall. Primarily retroperitoneal organs (kidneys, suprarenal glands, ureters, aorta, IVC) were never suspended by mesentery.

questions.question: Which muscles perform downward rotation of the scapula?
questions.explanation: Downward rotation of the scapula is performed by levator scapulae, pectoralis minor, and the rhomboids. This movement is opposite to the upward rotation needed for full arm abduction. Downward rotation returns the scapula to its resting position from the upward rotated position.

The brachial artery bifurcates in the cubital fossa opposite the neck of the radius. This division occurs under cover of the bicipital aponeurosis into the radial artery (superficial) and ulnar artery (deeper). The cubital fossa provides a triangular space for this important vascular division.
questions.question: At what location does the brachial artery typically bifurcate into radial and ulnar arteries?

questions.explanation: The external anal sphincter, composed of skeletal muscle and innervated by the inferior rectal nerve (branch of pudendal nerve), is under voluntary control and can be consciously contracted to prevent or defer defecation. The internal anal sphincter (smooth muscle, autonomic control) maintains resting anal tone. The puborectalis muscle contributes to the anorectal angle and fecal continence.
questions.question: Which structure controls voluntary defecation?
The pharyngeal plexus is formed primarily by which cranial nerve?
questions.explanation: The pharyngeal plexus on the middle constrictor muscle is formed primarily by the pharyngeal branch of the vagus nerve with contributions from glossopharyngeal (sensory only) and sympathetic fibers. Motor fibers originate from the nucleus ambiguus and travel via the cranial accessory to the vagus. The plexus supplies all pharyngeal and most palatal muscles.

The lesser splanchnic nerve arises from T10-11 ganglia, pierces the diaphragm, and synapses in the aorticorenal ganglion. It provides sympathetic innervation primarily to the kidneys and suprarenal glands. Some fibers may also reach midgut derivatives. The nerve carries both efferent sympathetic and visceral afferent fibers.
questions.question: What does the lesser splanchnic nerve supply?

questions.explanation: The sustentaculum tali is a medial shelf of the calcaneus that supports the head of the talus and carries the groove for the flexor hallucis longus tendon on its inferior surface. It also receives the insertion of the tibialis posterior tendon and serves as the attachment for the spring ligament (plantar calcaneonavicular ligament) and the deltoid ligament medially.
questions.question: The sustentaculum tali is a medial shelf of the calcaneus that supports the head of the talus and carries the groove for which tendon?
The lumbar sympathetic chain enters the abdomen through which opening?
questions.explanation: The lumbar sympathetic chain enters the abdomen from the thorax by passing beneath the medial arcuate ligament (lumbocostal arch), which extends from the body of L1 vertebra to the tip of the L1 transverse process over the psoas major muscle. The chain then descends along the medial border of psoas major on the anterolateral aspects of the lumbar vertebral bodies, with the right chain posterior to the inferior vena cava and the left along the left margin of the aorta. It typically contains four lumbar ganglia that give off gray rami communicantes to all lumbar nerves and lumbar splanchnic nerves to autonomic plexuses.

questions.question: What is the most inferior part of the heart?
questions.explanation: The apex of the heart is formed by the inferolateral part of the left ventricle and is the most inferior and lateral cardiac point. It lies deep to the left 5th intercostal space in the midclavicular line in adults (4th space in children). The apex beat (point of maximal impulse) can normally be palpated at this location during systole.

The cystic artery most commonly (in about 75% of cases) arises from the right hepatic artery within Calot's triangle (bounded by the cystic duct, common hepatic duct, and inferior surface of the liver). However, significant anatomical variations exist, with the cystic artery occasionally arising from the left hepatic, gastroduodenal, or even superior mesenteric artery. The artery typically passes posterior to the common hepatic duct before reaching the gallbladder, where it divides into superficial (supplying the peritoneal surface) and deep (supplying the hepatic surface) branches. Careful identification during cholecystectomy prevents inadvertent injury to aberrant vessels.
questions.question: The cystic artery typically arises from which vessel?
Which nerves provide parasympathetic innervation to the bladder?
questions.explanation: The pelvic splanchnic nerves (nervi erigentes) arising from S2-S4 spinal segments provide parasympathetic innervation to the bladder. These nerves stimulate detrusor muscle contraction and inhibit the internal urethral sphincter, promoting micturition. Sympathetic innervation from T11-L2 via the hypogastric plexus promotes urine storage by relaxing the detrusor and contracting the internal sphincter.

questions.question: What is the average weight of a normal adult spleen?
questions.explanation: The average weight of a healthy adult spleen is approximately 150 grams (about 7 ounces), though this can vary considerably. A useful mnemonic for splenic dimensions is the "odd numbers rule": 1 inch thick, 3 inches wide, 5 inches long, 7 ounces in weight, and related to ribs 9-11. The spleen can enlarge significantly in disease states (splenomegaly).

Chordae tendineae attach the free edges and ventricular surfaces of the AV valve cusps to the papillary muscles, preventing the cusps from prolapsing into the atria during ventricular systole when intraventricular pressure is high. Papillary muscles contract just before ventricular contraction, tensing the chordae. Rupture of chordae tendineae causes severe valve regurgitation requiring urgent surgical repair.
questions.question: What prevents the AV valves from prolapsing into the atria?

questions.explanation: The right ventricle typically has three papillary muscles (anterior, posterior, and septal) corresponding to the three cusps of the tricuspid valve. Each papillary muscle gives chordae tendineae to two adjacent cusps. The left ventricle has only two papillary muscles (anterior and posterior), which are larger and stronger, each providing chordae to two cusps of the mitral valve.
questions.question: How many papillary muscles are in the right ventricle?

options: Bone shape alone maintains the arches
Muscle tone alone determines arch height
Bone shape, muscle tone, and ligament strength
Tendon length, joint capsule, and synovial fluid
questions.explanation: The arches of the foot are maintained by three factors: the shape of the bones, the strength of the ligaments, and the tone of the muscles. All three work together to maintain normal arch height. In pes planus (flat foot), ligamentous laxity and muscle weakness combine with bony changes to flatten the medial longitudinal arch.
questions.question: The arches of the foot are described as being maintained by three factors. Which combination is correct?

questions.explanation: The posterior auricular artery arises from the posterior aspect of the external carotid artery above the level of the digastric and stylohyoid muscles. It supplies the auricle, scalp behind the ear, and gives off the stylomastoid artery (which supplies the facial nerve and middle ear structures). The artery ascends between the parotid gland and mastoid process.
questions.question: The posterior auricular artery is a branch of which vessel?
What is the musculophrenic artery?
questions.explanation: The musculophrenic artery is one of the two terminal branches of the internal thoracic artery (the other being superior epigastric). It runs along the costal margin supplying the lower intercostal spaces (7th-9th via anterior intercostal arteries), the diaphragm, and the abdominal muscles.

The thin orbital plate (roof) of the frontal bone separates the frontal lobe of the brain from the orbital contents. Fractures can cause CSF leakage into the orbit. The anterior cranial fossa lies above this plate. The frontal sinus may pneumatize into this region of the frontal bone.
questions.question: Which structure separates the frontal lobe from the orbit?

questions.explanation: The medial cutaneous nerve of the arm (C8, T1) from the medial cord provides sensation to the medial aspect of the arm. The intercostobrachial nerve (T2) also contributes to sensation in the axilla and medial arm. Both can be affected in axillary surgery or trauma.
questions.question: What nerve provides sensation to the medial arm?
Which thigh muscle has TWO different nerve supplies from two different divisions of two different named nerves?
questions.explanation: Adductor magnus uniquely has two parts with different nerve supplies: the adductor part (obturator nerve, L2, L3, L4) and the hamstring part (tibial division of sciatic nerve). This dual origin and nerve supply reflects its dual embryological origin. Biceps femoris similarly has two heads with different nerve divisions of the sciatic nerve.

questions.question: What forms the superficial cardiac plexus?
questions.explanation: The cardiac plexus is formed by sympathetic fibers from the cervical and upper thoracic sympathetic ganglia and parasympathetic fibers from the vagus nerves. The superficial cardiac plexus lies beneath the aortic arch, while the deep plexus lies between the arch and tracheal bifurcation. These plexuses distribute fibers to the conducting system, coronary vessels, and myocardium.

The proper hepatic artery arises from the common hepatic artery, which is a branch of the celiac trunk. The common hepatic artery divides into the proper hepatic artery and the gastroduodenal artery. The proper hepatic artery then divides into right and left hepatic arteries that supply the corresponding lobes of the liver.
questions.question: From which artery does the proper hepatic artery arise?
The posterior superior alveolar nerve supplies which teeth?
questions.explanation: The posterior superior alveolar nerve (branch of maxillary nerve) supplies the upper molar teeth except the mesiobuccal root of the first molar (supplied by middle superior alveolar). The nerve descends on the maxillary tuberosity and enters the posterior superior alveolar foramina. It also supplies the maxillary sinus mucosa and buccal gingiva.

questions.question: Which space lies between the pretracheal and investing layers of deep cervical fascia?
questions.explanation: The suprasternal space (of Burns) lies between the investing and pretracheal layers of deep cervical fascia above the manubrium. It contains the jugular venous arch, lymph nodes, and fat. The space extends laterally behind the sternocleidomastoid muscles. Infections can collect here forming a suprasternal abscess.

questions.question: How does the radial nerve supply both flexors and extensors?
questions.explanation: The radial nerve primarily supplies extensor muscles but also innervates brachioradialis (elbow flexor) and extensor carpi radialis longus (proximal to lateral epicondyle). This reflects developmental muscle group origins. Brachioradialis, despite being anatomically anterior (flexor compartment), is functionally and embryologically an extensor group muscle.
options: Does not supply any flexor muscles
Supplies brachioradialis flexor despite being an extensor nerve

questions.explanation: The zygomatic bones form the prominence of the cheeks and lie on the inferolateral sides of the orbits. They articulate with the frontal, sphenoid, temporal, and maxillary bones. The bone has a broad connection with the maxilla medially and forms part of the zygomatic arch laterally. Fractures cause flattening of the malar eminence.
questions.question: Which bone forms the prominence of the cheek?

questions.explanation: The lateral cricoarytenoid muscle adducts (closes) the vocal cords by internally rotating the arytenoid cartilages. Other adductors include the interarytenoid and thyroarytenoid muscles. All adductors are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve. Bilateral adductor paralysis causes airway obstruction.
questions.question: Which muscle adducts the vocal cords?
