questions.explanation: The fovea capitis transmits blood from the obturator artery via the ligamentum teres (ligament of the head of femur). This vascular route is clinically important, as fractures of the femoral neck can disrupt primary blood supply and lead to avascular necrosis.
questions.question: The fovea capitis of the femoral head transmits blood from which artery to the femoral head?

options: Talus, calcaneus, navicular, cuboid, and one cuneiform
All three cuneiforms and the first two metatarsals
Three cuneiforms, cuboid, and the talus
questions.explanation: The midfoot consists of five of the seven tarsal bones: navicular, cuboid, and three cuneiform bones. The midfoot meets the forefoot at the five tarsometatarsal (TMT) joints. The three cuneiforms articulate proximally with the navicular. The midfoot provides a stable platform and distributes forces between the hindfoot and forefoot during gait.
questions.question: The midfoot consists of five of the seven tarsal bones. Which bones constitute the midfoot?

questions.explanation: The liver is divided into eight functionally independent segments (Couinaud segments I-VIII) based on the distribution of the portal vein, hepatic artery, and bile ducts. Each segment has its own vascular inflow, outflow, and biliary drainage, allowing surgical resection of individual segments without damaging others. This segmental anatomy is crucial for hepatic surgery and understanding disease distribution.
questions.question: How many functional segments does the liver have?

questions.explanation: Flexion at the wrist is produced mainly by flexor carpi ulnaris and flexor carpi radialis muscles. The flexor digitorum superficialis provides assistance to this movement. All wrist movements are performed by forearm muscles crossing the wrist joint.
questions.question: What produces flexion at the wrist joint?
options: Flexor carpi ulnaris and radialis, flexor digitorum superficialis

questions.question: Which muscle attaches to the white line of Hilton?
questions.explanation: The corrugator cutis ani muscle, formed by fusion of fibers from the longitudinal muscle layer of the rectum and the levator ani, inserts into the skin of the anal canal at the white line (intersphincteric line, or white line of Hilton). This line represents the lower border of the internal anal sphincter and the intermuscular groove between the internal and external anal sphincters. Some longitudinal muscle fibers also blend with the puborectalis anteriorly and extend to form the rectourethralis muscle (muscle of Roux) in males, extending toward the urethra.

questions.question: Which ribs produce bucket-handle movement?
questions.explanation: During inspiration, ribs 7-10 move laterally in a "bucket handle" movement, increasing the lateral (transverse) dimensions of the thoracic cavity. The upper ribs (2-7) move in a "pump handle" fashion, increasing anteroposterior diameter by pushing the sternum forward. These movements are coordinated during breathing.

questions.question: The lingual artery typically arises from which parent vessel?
questions.explanation: The lingual artery is a branch of the external carotid artery arising at the level of the hyoid bone. It supplies the tongue through dorsal lingual, deep lingual, and sublingual branches. The artery passes deep to the hyoglossus muscle, which serves as a key surgical landmark.

questions.question: The quadriceps femoris is how many times stronger than its antagonist muscle group, the hamstrings?
questions.explanation: The quadriceps femoris is three times stronger than its antagonist, the hamstrings. It forms the main bulk of the anterior thigh and is the great extensor of the leg. It covers almost all the anterior aspect and sides of the femur and is considered the largest and one of the most powerful muscle groups in the body.

questions.question: The stylohyoid muscle is innervated by which nerve?
questions.explanation: The stylohyoid muscle is innervated by the facial nerve (VII), specifically by a branch from the nerve after it exits the stylomastoid foramen. The muscle elevates and retracts the hyoid bone during swallowing. It shares innervation and embryologic origin (second pharyngeal arch) with the posterior belly of digastric.

The sternohyoid is an infrahyoid muscle that depresses the hyoid bone and larynx after swallowing. All infrahyoid muscles (sternohyoid, sternothyroid, thyrohyoid, omohyoid) serve this function. They are innervated by the ansa cervicalis (C1-C3) except thyrohyoid which receives C1 fibers via the hypoglossal nerve.
questions.question: Which muscle depresses the hyoid bone after swallowing?

questions.explanation: The head of the first metatarsal contains two sesamoid bones, which increase the mechanical advantage of the flexor hallucis brevis and protect its tendons from compression. The first metatarsal is the most important in propulsion during walking and is also the most important attachment site for several tendons, making it clinically significant in hallux valgus and gout.
questions.question: The first metatarsal is described as the shortest and thickest metatarsal and bears the most weight. Which two bones are found at its head?

questions.explanation: The phrenic nerve (C3, C4, C5 - "C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive") provides the entire motor innervation to the diaphragm, including both muscular portions and central tendon. Each phrenic nerve supplies the ipsilateral hemidiaphragm. Although the lower six intercostal and subcostal nerves (T7-T12) provide sensory innervation to the peripheral parts of the diaphragm, they contribute no motor supply. Damage to one phrenic nerve causes paralysis of the ipsilateral hemidiaphragm, which appears elevated on chest radiograph. Bilateral phrenic nerve injury severely compromises respiratory function, particularly in supine position.
questions.question: Which nerve provides motor innervation to the diaphragm?

options: Only the medial knee and distal thigh region
Medial leg down to the ankle only
Only the medial thigh, groin, and inner knee
The entire medial foot including the sole
Medial leg, ankle, and medial foot to the first MTP joint
questions.explanation: The saphenous nerve supplies the medial side of the leg, ankle, and medial side of the foot down to the first metatarsophalangeal joint. It is the terminal cutaneous branch of the femoral nerve, descending with the great saphenous vein. It exits the adductor canal with the saphenous branch of the descending genicular artery and provides sensation along the medial leg from knee to hallux.
questions.question: The saphenous nerve, the largest cutaneous branch of the femoral nerve, supplies the medial side of the leg and foot down to which level?
Where does the thoracic sympathetic trunk lie?
questions.explanation: The thoracic sympathetic trunk lies anterolateral to the vertebral bodies, just lateral to the anterior longitudinal ligament. It descends from the neck through the superior mediastinum and posterior mediastinum. Each trunk has 11-12 segmental ganglia, though the first thoracic ganglion often fuses with the inferior cervical ganglion.

Brunner's glands (duodenal glands) are located in the submucosa of the duodenum and contain mucous cells that secrete alkaline mucus rich in bicarbonate. This secretion neutralizes gastric acid entering the duodenum, protecting the duodenal mucosa and providing optimal pH for pancreatic enzyme function. Brunner's glands are unique to the duodenum and are most concentrated in the first part.
questions.question: Which cells are found in Brunner's glands?

questions.explanation: The cremasteric reflex (elevation of the testis when the inner thigh is stroked) is mediated by the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve (L1-L2). The sensory stimulus from the femoral branch travels to L1-L2, and the motor response via the genital branch causes contraction of the cremaster muscle. Absence of this reflex may indicate testicular torsion.
questions.question: What is the cremasteric reflex mediated by?

questions.explanation: The hemiazygos vein is formed by the union of the left ascending lumbar vein and left subcostal vein. It ascends on the left side of the vertebral column in the posterior mediastinum, crosses at T8-9, and drains into the azygos vein. It receives lower left posterior intercostal veins.
questions.question: What forms the hemiazygos vein?
Which condition involves repetitive overhead throwing?
questions.explanation: commonly results from repetitive overhead throwing activities. This is particularly seen in baseball pitchers, tennis players, and swimmers. Repetitive impingement of the rotator cuff tendons under the acromion causes inflammation, degeneration, and potential tears.

questions.question: What principle explains joint innervation from muscles crossing it?
questions.explanation: states that nerves supplying muscles that move a joint also supply the joint itself. This explains why the wrist joint receives innervation from median, radial, and ulnar nerves. The principle helps predict joint innervation patterns throughout the body.

questions.question: The right suprarenal vein drains directly into which vessel?
questions.explanation: The right suprarenal vein is short and drains directly into the inferior vena cava on its posterior aspect, while the left suprarenal vein drains into the left renal vein (along with the left testicular/ovarian and left inferior phrenic veins). This asymmetric venous drainage mirrors the pattern of testicular/ovarian veins. The suprarenal glands receive blood from three arteries (superior, middle, and inferior suprarenal arteries from inferior phrenic, aorta, and renal artery respectively) but drain via only one or two veins, creating a rich arterial supply with limited venous drainage.

questions.question: Which three joints does pectoralis minor movement affect?
questions.explanation: Pectoralis minor affects the sternoclavicular, scapulothoracic, and glenohumeral joints through its action on scapular position. It produces depression, downward rotation, and protraction of the scapula. These scapular movements influence the position and function of the clavicle and shoulder joint.

questions.question: The fibular (peroneal) artery is a branch of which vessel, making it an indirect branch of the popliteal artery?
questions.explanation: The fibular (peroneal) artery arises from the tibioperoneal trunk, which is one of the two terminal divisions of the popliteal artery (the other being the anterior tibial artery). The tibioperoneal trunk then divides into the posterior tibial artery and the fibular artery. The fibular artery descends alongside the fibula in the posterior compartment.

questions.question: Which structure extends between adjacent renal pyramids?
questions.explanation: Renal columns (columns of Bertin) are extensions of cortical tissue that project between adjacent pyramids from the cortex to the renal sinus. They contain interlobar arteries and veins. The cortical tissue in the columns and over the bases of pyramids contains the renal corpuscles and convoluted tubules. Enlarged renal columns can mimic renal masses on imaging.

questions.question: The main pancreatic duct typically joins the bile duct at which location?
questions.explanation: The main pancreatic duct (duct of Wirsung) typically joins the common bile duct within the wall of the second (descending) part of the duodenum to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla (ampulla of Vater), which opens at the major duodenal papilla. The accessory pancreatic duct (duct of Santorini), when patent, opens separately at the minor duodenal papilla approximately 2 cm proximal to the major papilla. Anatomical variations exist, including separate openings of the pancreatic and bile ducts (pancreas divisum). The junction is surgically significant during ERCP and pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple procedure).

The pampiniform plexus, a network of 8-12 veins in the spermatic cord surrounding the testicular artery, drains into a single testicular vein at the deep inguinal ring. The right testicular vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava at an acute angle, while the left testicular vein typically drains into the left renal vein at a right angle. This venous plexus serves as a countercurrent heat exchanger, cooling arterial blood before it reaches the testes. The higher incidence of left-sided varicoceles reflects the longer course and perpendicular drainage of the left testicular vein.
questions.question: The pampiniform plexus drains into which vein?
Which structure marks the junction of the foregut and midgut blood supply?
questions.explanation: The major duodenal papilla (ampulla of Vater) in the second part of the duodenum marks the embryological and vascular transition between foregut (supplied by celiac trunk) and midgut (supplied by superior mesenteric artery). The superior pancreaticoduodenal artery (from gastroduodenal, ultimately from celiac trunk) supplies the duodenum and pancreatic head above this point, while the inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery (from SMA) supplies structures below it. This dual blood supply creates an anastomotic arcade providing collateral circulation between the two major arterial territories and reflects the embryological division of the primitive gut.

questions.question: Which structure causes the first constriction of the oesophagus at 15 cm from the upper incisor teeth?
questions.explanation: The cricopharyngeus muscle forms the upper oesophageal sphincter and creates the first physiological constriction at 15 cm from the upper incisors. This sphincter prevents air from entering the oesophagus during respiration and regulates food entry. It is a clinically significant site for foreign body impaction and stricture formation.

The regional lymph node is defined as the lymph node where lymph from an organ or body part drains to firstly. This is distinct from the sentinel lymph node, which is the first node to receive drainage from a tumor. Understanding this distinction is important for staging cancer and planning surgical interventions.
questions.question: Which lymph node receives drainage first from an organ?

questions.explanation: The left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein at approximately a right angle, while the right testicular vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava at an acute angle. This anatomical asymmetry explains the higher incidence (90%) of left-sided varicoceles, as the longer venous column, perpendicular drainage, and potential compression of the left renal vein by the superior mesenteric artery (nutcracker phenomenon) create higher venous pressure. The pampiniform plexus of veins in the spermatic cord converges to form a single testicular vein at the deep inguinal ring.
questions.question: Which vessel drains the left testis?

questions.explanation: The cystic duct (3-4 cm long, containing spiral valves of Heister) joins the common hepatic duct (formed by union of right and left hepatic ducts at porta hepatis) to form the common bile duct. The CBD (approximately 8 cm long) descends in the free edge of the lesser omentum, passes behind the first part of duodenum, through the head of pancreas, and joins the main pancreatic duct to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla (ampulla of Vater) in the wall of the second part of duodenum. Variations in this anatomy are common and surgically important.
questions.question: The cystic duct typically joins the common hepatic duct to form which structure?

questions.explanation: The supraorbital and supratrochlear nerves (branches of the frontal nerve from V1) provide sensation to the upper eyelid and forehead. The lacrimal nerve supplies the lateral upper lid. Infratrochlear nerve supplies the medial canthus and side of nose. These are all branches of the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve.
questions.question: Which nerve provides sensation to the upper eyelid?
The central artery of the retina is a branch of which vessel?
questions.explanation: The central artery of the retina is a branch of the ophthalmic artery. It is an end artery running in the center of the optic nerve to supply the inner layers of the retina. Occlusion causes sudden painless loss of vision. The artery enters the optic nerve about 12 mm behind the eyeball.

The subacromial bursa is the largest bursa in the body, positioned between the supraspinatus tendon and the coraco-acromial arch. It protects the supraspinatus tendon against friction with the acromion during arm abduction. Inflammation of this bursa is responsible for several shoulder pathologies including rotator cuff tendonitis.
questions.question: Which bursa is the largest in the body and lies between supraspinatus and the coraco-acromial arch?

options: Long head for stability, short head for power
questions.explanation: The long head of biceps (originating from supraglenoid tubercle) contributes to glenohumeral stability and resists superior humeral head displacement. The short head (coracoid origin) provides more direct flexion power. Both heads function in elbow flexion and supination, but the long head has additional shoulder stabilization role.
questions.question: How do the two heads of biceps contribute differently to function?
How many pulmonary veins open into left atrium?
questions.explanation: Four pulmonary veins (two from each lung) drain oxygenated blood from the lungs and open into the left atrium. These veins have no valves at their orifices. The superior and inferior pulmonary veins from each side carry blood from the respective lobes of the lungs.

The breast is separated from the deep fascia covering the underlying muscles by a layer of loose areolar tissue called the retromammary space. This space allows the breast some mobility over the pectoralis major muscle. The space is important surgically as it provides a plane for mastectomy.
questions.question: What separates the breast from deep fascia?

questions.explanation: When the thigh and knee are flexed, the hamstrings extend the trunk. This action is important in activities such as rising from a forward-flexed position and in postural control. The hamstrings also flex the leg at the knee and extend the thigh at the hip. Semitendinosus and semimembranosus medially rotate the leg, while biceps femoris laterally rotates it when the knee is flexed.
questions.question: When the thigh and knee are already flexed, the hamstring muscles perform which action on the trunk?

questions.explanation: The popliteal artery terminates at the inferior border of the popliteus muscle by dividing into the anterior tibial artery and the tibioperoneal trunk. The tibioperoneal trunk then divides into the posterior tibial artery and fibular (peroneal) artery. The popliteal artery gives five genicular branches contributing to the genicular anastomosis.
questions.question: The popliteal artery terminates at the inferior border of popliteus by dividing into which two initial divisions?
options: Anterior tibial artery and tibioperoneal trunk
Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial arteries
Peroneal artery and posterior tibial artery directly

questions.explanation: The porta hepatis (transverse fissure) separates the caudate lobe (posterosuperiorly) from the quadrate lobe (anteroinferiorly) on the visceral surface of the liver. The porta hepatis contains the portal vein, hepatic artery, hepatic ducts, lymphatics, and nerves entering or leaving the liver. The caudate lobe is bounded by the porta hepatis anteriorly, the IVC groove posteriorly, and the fissure for the ligamentum venosum on the left. The quadrate lobe is bounded by the porta hepatis posteriorly, the gallbladder fossa on the right, and the fissure for the ligamentum teres on the left.
questions.question: Which structure separates the caudate lobe from the quadrate lobe?

questions.explanation: Seven nerves exit through the greater sciatic foramen: the sciatic nerve, posterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh, superior gluteal nerve, inferior gluteal nerve, nerve to obturator internus, nerve to quadratus femoris, and pudendal nerve. Together with six vessels and piriformis, these seven nerves constitute the 14 total structures passing through this foramen.
questions.question: How many nerves exit through the greater sciatic foramen?
The cruciate anastomosis, at the level of the lesser trochanter, provides collateral connection between the femoral arteries and which major vessel?
questions.explanation: The cruciate anastomosis is situated at the level of the lesser trochanter and is formed by the inferior gluteal artery, medial and lateral femoral circumflex arteries, and the first perforating branch of the profunda femoris. Together with the trochanteric anastomosis, it provides collateral connection between the femoral arteries and the internal iliac arteries.

Scapular anastomoses provide crucial collateral circulation connecting first part of subclavian artery with third part of axillary artery. This enables continued limb perfusion even with proximal arterial obstruction. The anastomoses involve suprascapular, dorsal scapular, and circumflex scapular arteries.
questions.question: What is the functional significance of the scapular anastomoses?
options: Collateral circulation bypassing proximal subclavian obstruction

questions.question: What is the functional relationship between finger flexor sublimis and profundus?
questions.explanation: Flexor digitorum superficialis flexes PIP joints independently of DIP joints. Flexor digitorum profundus flexes DIP joints and contributes to PIP and MCP flexion, providing power grip force. This two-layer arrangement enables independent or combined finger joint flexion for varied hand positions.
options: Both tendons have identical flexor function
FDS flexes PIP joints, FDP flexes DIP joints

questions.question: The maxillary artery is divided into how many parts by the lateral pterygoid muscle?
questions.explanation: The lateral pterygoid muscle divides the maxillary artery into three parts: mandibular (first), pterygoid (second), and pterygopalatine (third). Each part gives off specific branches to supply deep facial structures. The third part enters the pterygopalatine fossa through the pterygomaxillary fissure.

The right middle lobe contains two bronchopulmonary segments: lateral and medial. This is the smallest lobe of the right lung. The middle lobe is bounded above by the horizontal fissure and below by the oblique fissure. Middle lobe syndrome can occur from lymph node compression.
questions.question: How many segments are in right middle lobe?

questions.explanation: The maxillary antrum and ethmoid sinuses are present in rudimentary form at birth. The frontal and sphenoid sinuses become evident around age seven. This developmental pattern explains why frontal sinusitis is rare in young children. All sinuses reach full development by late adolescence.
questions.question: Which paranasal sinus is present in rudimentary form at birth?

questions.explanation: The phrenic nerve (C3, C4, C5) provides sensory innervation to the central diaphragm (both pleural and peritoneal surfaces). Irritation of the diaphragmatic peritoneum (from subphrenic abscess, ruptured spleen, perforated peptic ulcer, ectopic pregnancy, liver inflammation, or cholecystitis) can cause referred pain to the shoulder tip (C3-C5 dermatomes) via the phrenic nerve. This is called Kehr's sign when associated with splenic rupture. The peripheral diaphragm receives sensory innervation from the lower intercostal and subcostal nerves, referring pain to the chest wall and upper abdomen.
questions.question: Which nerve may cause referred pain to the shoulder?

questions.explanation: Lymph vessels from the lung drain into hilar (bronchopulmonary) nodes, and efferent lymphatics ultimately drain into the brachiocephalic vein. The lymph passes through pulmonary nodes, bronchopulmonary nodes, and tracheobronchial nodes before reaching the venous system. This pathway is important in cancer metastasis.
questions.question: Where do hilar lymphatics ultimately drain?

questions.explanation: The greater tubercle of the humerus is the most lateral bony point in the shoulder region. It projects laterally below and in front of the acromial angle. This prominence can be palpated and felt to move during rotation of the humerus.
questions.question: What is the most lateral bony point in the shoulder region?

questions.explanation: The umbilicus typically corresponds to the level of the intervertebral disc between L3 and L4 vertebrae, though its position varies with body habitus, age, pregnancy, and previous surgery. The transumbilical plane passing through the umbilicus divides the abdomen into upper and lower halves and is used clinically to define abdominal quadrants. The skin at the umbilicus receives sensory innervation from the T10 dermatome ("belly button at T10"), making this a useful landmark for assessing spinal cord levels. In neonates, the umbilicus lies relatively higher (near L2).
questions.question: Which vertebral level corresponds to the umbilicus?

questions.explanation: The phrenic nerves (C3-C5, with C4 being most important - "C3,4,5 keeps the diaphragm alive") provide all motor innervation to the diaphragm and most of its sensory innervation. Each phrenic nerve supplies the ipsilateral half of the diaphragm. Peripheral parts receive additional sensory innervation from intercostal and subcostal nerves, but these provide no motor supply.
questions.question: Which nerve provides motor innervation to the entire diaphragm?
Which lymph nodes receive drainage from the tip of the tongue?
questions.explanation: The tip of the tongue drains to submental lymph nodes. The lateral anterior two-thirds drains to submandibular nodes, while the medial anterior two-thirds drains to inferior deep cervical nodes. The posterior third drains to superior deep cervical nodes. Understanding lymphatic drainage is crucial for cancer staging.

The ulnar nerve supplies all interossei muscles (both dorsal and palmar). The deep branch of the ulnar nerve enters the palm and curves around the hook of the hamate to supply these intrinsic hand muscles. Ulnar nerve palsy causes weakness of finger abduction and adduction.
questions.question: What nerve supplies the dorsal interossei muscles?

questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) exits the skull through the jugular foramen along with the vagus (X) and accessory (XI) nerves. The internal jugular vein also passes through this foramen. The nerve descends between the internal carotid artery and internal jugular vein to reach the pharynx.
questions.question: The glossopharyngeal nerve exits the skull through which foramen?
What structure lies anterior to lung apex?
questions.explanation: Anterior to the lung apex lies the brachiocephalic vein (left side has left brachiocephalic vein crossing; right side has right brachiocephalic vein). The subclavian artery arches over the apex (groove on apex). Posteriorly lies the neck of the first rib and sympathetic trunk. Medially is the trachea and esophagus.

questions.question: Which muscle crosses the sole diagonally in a groove on the cuboid, and in so doing provides the most important muscular support for the transverse arch?
questions.explanation: Fibularis longus crosses the sole of the foot diagonally in a groove on the plantar surface of the cuboid, inserting into the base of the first metatarsal and medial cuneiform. This diagonal course provides critical support to the transverse arch by pulling the first metatarsal medially and maintaining the dome of the transverse arch. It is the most important muscular support for this arch.

questions.question: How many lobes does the right lung contain?
questions.explanation: The right lung is divided into three lobes (superior, middle, and inferior) by two fissures: the oblique and horizontal fissures. The left lung has only two lobes (superior and inferior) separated by the oblique fissure. The presence of a middle lobe makes the right lung larger than the left.

questions.question: Which structure opens into the descending duodenum at the major duodenal papilla?
questions.explanation: The hepatopancreatic ampulla (ampulla of Vater) opens at the major duodenal papilla in the descending (second) part of the duodenum. This ampulla is formed by the union of the main pancreatic duct and common bile duct in most individuals. The sphincter of Oddi surrounds the ampulla controlling the flow of bile and pancreatic secretions.

The appendix reaches its definitive adult position by puberty. In infants and young children, the appendix has a relatively higher position, which explains why appendicitis in children may present with higher abdominal pain. The growth of the cecum pulls the appendix to a lower position. The base of the appendix remains constant at the confluence of the three taeniae coli.
questions.question: At what age does the appendix typically reach its adult position?
Where does referred cardiac pain typically radiate?
questions.explanation: Cardiac ischemic pain typically radiates to the left shoulder, left arm (especially the medial aspect and little finger), neck, and jaw, following the distribution of T1-T4 dermatomes that share spinal segments with cardiac afferents. This occurs because visceral and somatic afferents converge on the same spinal cord neurons. Some patients also experience epigastric discomfort or right-sided radiation.

The porta hepatis (gateway to the liver) on the inferior surface of the liver contains the right and left branches of the portal vein, hepatic artery proper, and hepatic ducts, along with lymphatic vessels and hepatic nerve plexuses. The structures are arranged with bile ducts anteriorly and to the right, hepatic artery anteriorly and to the left, and portal vein posteriorly. The hepatic veins and IVC are not at the porta but rather on the posterior surface of the liver. The porta hepatis forms the floor of the fissure for the ligamentum venosum and is continuous with the hepatoduodenal ligament.
questions.question: The porta hepatis contains which structures?
Which muscle produces wrist flexion and abduction?
questions.explanation: produces both wrist flexion and wrist abduction (radial deviation). It is a prominent muscle in the anterior forearm, easily palpable lateral to palmaris longus. The muscle is supplied by the median nerve.

questions.question: The saphenous nerve is the terminal cutaneous branch of which nerve and runs with which vein throughout most of the leg?
questions.explanation: The saphenous nerve is the terminal cutaneous branch of the femoral nerve (L3, L4). It runs with the great saphenous vein along the medial leg, from the knee to the medial malleolus and then to the medial side of the foot. It provides cutaneous sensation to the medial leg, ankle, and foot. It is at risk during stripping of the great saphenous vein for varicose vein surgery or coronary bypass grafting.
options: Common fibular nerve; great saphenous vein

questions.explanation: Only the first 2 cm of the first (superior) part of the duodenum, known as the duodenal cap or ampulla, is intraperitoneal. The remainder of the duodenum is retroperitoneal, lying posterior to the peritoneum. This intraperitoneal portion is the most common site for duodenal ulceration (duodenal cap ulcers).
questions.question: Which part of the duodenum is intraperitoneal?
At which vertebral level does the caval opening lie?
questions.explanation: The caval opening (vena caval foramen) in the diaphragm is located at the T8 vertebral level in the central tendon. It transmits the inferior vena cava and terminal branches of the right phrenic nerve. The IVC is adherent to the margins of the opening, so when the diaphragm contracts during inspiration, it widens the opening and dilates the IVC, facilitating venous return.

questions.question: Which part of the duodenum is retroperitoneal?
questions.explanation: The duodenum is primarily retroperitoneal except for the first 2 cm of the superior (first) part, which is intraperitoneal and mobile, connecting to the liver via the hepatoduodenal ligament. The descending (second), horizontal (third), and ascending (fourth) parts are all secondarily retroperitoneal, having been covered by peritoneum during development but subsequently becoming fixed to the posterior abdominal wall. The duodenojejunal flexure marks the transition from retroperitoneal duodenum to intraperitoneal jejunum and is supported by the suspensory muscle of the duodenum (ligament of Treitz).

The posterior interosseous nerve (deep branch of radial nerve) passes between the two heads of the supinator muscle. Compression at this site causes posterior interosseous syndrome with weakness of finger and thumb extensors but preserved wrist extension. The superficial branch of the radial nerve does not pass through supinator.
questions.question: What nerve passes through the supinator muscle?
The hindfoot consists of which two bones?
questions.explanation: The hindfoot consists of the talus and the calcaneus. The calcaneus (heel bone) is the largest and strongest bone, absorbing shock and leveraging movement. The talus (ankle bone) articulates with the tibia and fibula superiorly and with the calcaneus inferiorly and navicular anteriorly, allowing ankle movement and weight transfer to the foot.

The pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2-S4) provide parasympathetic innervation to hindgut derivatives (distal third of transverse colon, descending colon, sigmoid colon, rectum, and upper anal canal). The vagus nerve provides parasympathetic supply to foregut and midgut derivatives (up to the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon). Sympathetic supply is via lumbar splanchnic nerves and the inferior mesenteric plexus.
questions.question: Which parasympathetic nerve supplies the hindgut derivatives?

questions.explanation: The hepatoduodenal ligament forms the thickened free right edge of the lesser omentum, extending from the first part of the duodenum to the porta hepatis. It contains the portal triad (portal vein posteriorly, common bile duct anteriorly and to the right, hepatic artery proper anteriorly and to the left) and forms the anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen. The hepatoduodenal ligament can be compressed manually (Pringle maneuver) to control hepatic bleeding by temporarily occluding inflow to the liver. The gastrohepatic ligament forms the membranous portion of the lesser omentum.
questions.question: Which ligament forms the free edge of the lesser omentum?

questions.explanation: The tendons of the four quadriceps components unite to form the quadriceps tendon, which continues as the patellar ligament (also called patellar tendon) with the patella embedded within as a sesamoid bone. This inserts into the tibial tuberosity. The patellar retinacula are aponeurotic expansions that provide additional lateral stability.
questions.question: The quadriceps tendon continues as which structure, with the patella embedded within it, attaching to the tibial tuberosity?

questions.explanation: The ureter receives its blood supply from multiple sources along its length: the upper portion from branches of the renal artery, the middle portion from the gonadal (testicular or ovarian) arteries, and the pelvic portion from branches of the internal iliac artery (mainly superior vesical). This segmental supply means the ureter has a relatively tenuous blood supply requiring careful surgical handling.
questions.question: Which artery supplies the middle portion of the ureter?

questions.explanation: The ligamentum venosum is the fibrous remnant of the fetal ductus venosus, which shunted oxygenated blood from the umbilical vein to the inferior vena cava during intrauterine life. It lies in a fissure on the visceral surface of the liver between the caudate and left lobes. After birth, when the ductus venosus closes, it becomes the ligamentum venosum.
questions.question: Which structure lies in the fissure for the ligamentum venosum?

questions.explanation: The lesser sciatic foramen is bounded by the lesser sciatic notch of the ischium, the sacrospinous ligament superiorly, and the sacrotuberous ligament inferiorly. The pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels exit the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen (below piriformis), hook around the ischial spine, and re-enter the pelvis through the lesser sciatic foramen to reach the pudendal canal in the lateral wall of the ischioanal fossa. The tendon of obturator internus also exits through this foramen. The sciatic nerve exits only through the greater sciatic foramen without re-entering the pelvis.
questions.question: Which structure passes through the lesser sciatic foramen?

questions.explanation: Gracilis is the most medial, most superficial, and weakest member of the adductor group. It is the only member to cross both the hip and knee joints. Its tendon joins sartorius and semitendinosus at the pes anserinus on the medial tibia. It is used as a donor muscle in gracilis free flap reconstructive surgery due to its consistent anatomy.
questions.question: Which is the most medial, most superficial, and weakest muscle of the adductor group, uniquely crossing both hip and knee joints?

questions.explanation: The lower esophageal sphincter (LES) is a physiological sphincter at the gastroesophageal junction. Unlike the anatomical upper esophageal sphincter, the LES has no distinct anatomical structure but represents a zone of increased smooth muscle tone. The right crus fibers looping around the esophagus contribute to sphincter function.
questions.question: What sphincter is at the gastroesophageal junction?
The pterygoid hamulus is part of which bone?
questions.explanation: The pterygoid hamulus is a hook-like process at the inferior end of the medial pterygoid plate of the sphenoid bone. The tensor veli palatini tendon hooks around it before inserting into the soft palate. The hamulus can be palpated intraorally posterior to the maxillary tuberosity. Fractures cause palatal dysfunction.

questions.question: Which lymphatic structure drains lymph from the right upper quadrant of the body?
questions.explanation: The right lymphatic duct drains lymph from the right half of the head, neck, thorax, and right upper limb. It is formed by the union of right jugular, subclavian, and bronchomediastinal trunks. The duct enters the right venous angle (junction of right internal jugular and subclavian veins).

The internal jugular vein begins at the jugular foramen as a continuation of the sigmoid sinus. It descends in the carotid sheath lateral to the internal and common carotid arteries. The vein joins with the subclavian vein to form the brachiocephalic vein.
questions.question: The internal jugular vein begins at which anatomical location?
What is the functional significance of the olecranon-coronoid architecture?
questions.explanation: The olecranon fits into the olecranon fossa during extension while the coronoid fits into the coronoid fossa during flexion. This reciprocal architecture allows full range elbow motion (0-150°) while providing bony stability. The radial fossa accommodates the radial head during flexion.

Posterior mediastinal lymph nodes lie in the posterior mediastinum alongside the esophagus and descending thoracic aorta. They receive lymph from the esophagus, posterior diaphragm, pericardium, and posterior intercostal spaces. Efferents drain primarily to the thoracic duct.
questions.question: Where do posterior mediastinal lymph nodes lie?

questions.explanation: The coronary sinus, the main venous drainage vessel of the heart, opens into the right atrium between the inferior vena cava orifice and the tricuspid valve. It lies in the posterior part of the coronary (atrioventricular) groove and receives the great, middle, and small cardiac veins, along with other tributaries. A small Thebesian valve may partially cover its orifice.
questions.question: Into which chamber does the coronary sinus drain?

questions.explanation: The os coxae is formed by the fusion of three bones: the ilium, ischium, and pubis. They meet at the Y-shaped cartilage in the acetabulum, which fuses at approximately age 15-17 years. The acetabulum receives contributions from all three bones, though it is formed mainly by the ischium.
questions.question: The os coxae (pelvic bone) is formed by the fusion of three bones. Which combination is correct?

questions.explanation: The caval opening for the inferior vena cava is located at the level of T8 in the central tendon. It also transmits terminal branches of the right phrenic nerve and a few lymphatic vessels. This is the highest and most anterior of the three main diaphragmatic openings.
questions.question: At which vertebral level is the caval opening?

questions.explanation: The deep inguinal ring, an oval opening in the transversalis fascia located lateral to the inferior epigastric artery, transmits the spermatic cord in males and the round ligament of the uterus in females. The genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve and the cremasteric artery also pass through this ring. The ilioinguinal nerve, in contrast, passes through the superficial inguinal ring after traversing the inguinal canal, while the iliohypogastric nerve runs above and parallel to the canal.
questions.question: Which structure passes through the deep inguinal ring?

questions.explanation: The tympanic plexus on the promontory of the middle ear is formed primarily by the tympanic branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve (Jacobson's nerve). Contributions also come from the caroticotympanic nerves (sympathetic). The plexus provides sensation to the middle ear mucosa. The lesser petrosal nerve arises from this plexus.
questions.question: The tympanic plexus is formed primarily by which nerve?
What closes the pleuroperitoneal canal?
questions.explanation: The pleuroperitoneal membranes close the fetal communication between the pleural and peritoneal cavities. Failure of these membranes to close completely results in congenital diaphragmatic hernias, most commonly through the foramen of Bochdalek (posterolaterally). This is more common on the left side.

The carotid sinus (baroreceptor) at the carotid bifurcation is innervated by the carotid sinus nerve (nerve of Hering), a branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve. The carotid body (chemoreceptor) is also innervated primarily by IX. These receptors monitor blood pressure and blood gas levels respectively. Carotid massage can slow heart rate via this pathway.
questions.question: The carotid sinus is innervated by which nerve?
Which muscles aid forced expiration?
questions.explanation: In forced expiration, the abdominal muscles (rectus abdominis, internal/external obliques, transversus abdominis) contract forcibly. This pushes the abdominal viscera upward against the relaxed diaphragm, forcing it higher into the thorax. Quadratus lumborum also contracts to pull down the 12th rib.

questions.question: The superior laryngeal artery accompanies which nerve?
questions.explanation: The superior laryngeal artery (from superior thyroid artery) accompanies the internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve through the thyrohyoid membrane. Together they supply the supraglottic larynx. The artery anastomoses with the contralateral vessel and with the cricothyroid artery. Damage during surgery can cause hematoma or bleeding.

questions.question: Which part of the stomach lies superior to the cardiac notch?
questions.explanation: The fundus is the dilated, dome-shaped portion of the stomach that lies superior to the level of the cardiac orifice and cardiac notch. It is usually filled with gas and is in contact with the left dome of the diaphragm. The fundus can be distinguished radiographically as the gas bubble seen in upright chest X-rays.

The stylomastoid artery arises from the posterior auricular artery and enters the stylomastoid foramen to supply the facial nerve in its bony canal, the mastoid air cells, and the stapedius muscle. It anastomoses with the petrosal branch of the middle meningeal artery. The artery follows the facial nerve through the temporal bone.
questions.question: The stylomastoid artery is a branch of which vessel?

questions.explanation: The testes drain lymph directly to the para-aortic (lumbar) lymph nodes at the L1-L2 level, bypassing the inguinal and iliac nodes. This drainage pattern follows the testicular vessels and reflects the embryological origin of the testes high on the posterior abdominal wall. In testicular cancer, metastases first appear in para-aortic nodes, not inguinal nodes (unless scrotal skin is involved). The scrotum drains to superficial inguinal nodes. This explains why orchiectomy for testicular cancer requires high ligation of the spermatic cord at the deep inguinal ring to include regional lymphatics.
questions.question: The testicular lymphatics drain to which nodes?

options: Inguinal ligament, sartorius, and adductor longus
Inguinal ligament, adductor magnus, and iliopsoas
Iliac crest, sartorius, and adductor longus
Inguinal ligament, rectus femoris, and adductor magnus
questions.explanation: The femoral triangle is bounded superiorly by the inguinal ligament, laterally by the sartorius, and medially by the adductor longus. Its floor is formed by the iliopsoas laterally and the pectineus medially. Its roof is the fascia lata and cribriform fascia. It contains the femoral nerve, artery, vein, and deep inguinal lymph nodes arranged laterally to medially (NAVEL from lateral).
questions.question: The femoral triangle is bounded by which three structures?

questions.explanation: The femoral ring (the medial compartment of the femoral sheath) is bounded medially by the lacunar ligament (Gimbernat's ligament), laterally by the femoral vein, anteriorly by the inguinal ligament, and posteriorly by the pectineal ligament (Cooper's ligament) and pectineus muscle covered by fascia. The femoral ring normally contains a lymph node (Cloquet's node) and loose connective tissue. It represents a potential site of weakness where femoral hernias can occur (more common in women), protruding through the ring into the femoral canal. The rigid boundaries make strangulation a risk in femoral hernias.
questions.question: The femoral ring is bounded medially by which structure?
The splenic artery typically runs along which organ's superior border?
questions.explanation: The splenic artery, the largest branch of the celiac trunk, takes a characteristically tortuous course to the left along the superior border of the body and tail of the pancreas, giving off numerous small pancreatic branches en route. It runs posterior to the stomach within the splenorenal ligament before dividing into 5-6 terminal branches that enter the splenic hilum. Before reaching the spleen, the artery gives off the left gastroepiploic artery and short gastric arteries, which pass through the gastrosplenic ligament to supply the greater curvature and fundus of the stomach respectively.

The phrenic nerves pass through both the superior and middle mediastinum as they descend from the neck to the diaphragm. Similarly, the superior vena cava lies in both regions. The thymus extends from superior to anterior mediastinum. Structures can span multiple mediastinal compartments.
questions.question: Which structure lies in both superior and middle mediastinum?
How do upper left intercostal veins drain?
questions.explanation: The upper three left posterior intercostal veins typically join to form the left superior intercostal vein, which crosses the aortic arch and drains into the left brachiocephalic vein. This provides a direct connection to the superior vena cava system without crossing to the right side.

questions.question: What structure lies in all mediastinal regions?
questions.explanation: Lymph nodes are present in all regions of the mediastinum: paratracheal and brachiocephalic nodes in the superior mediastinum; parasternal nodes anteriorly; tracheobronchial and hilar nodes in the middle mediastinum; and paraesophageal and paravertebral nodes posteriorly. Lymphadenopathy is a common cause of mediastinal widening.

The crista terminalis is a prominent vertical muscular ridge on the internal right atrial wall that marks the junction between the smooth-walled posterior sinus venarum (derived from the sinus venosus) and the rough-walled anterior part with pectinate muscles (derived from the primitive atrium). Externally, this corresponds to the sulcus terminalis groove.
questions.question: Which structure marks the junction between the smooth and rough parts of the right atrium?

questions.explanation: Circular venous plexuses are found at the base of the nipple. Veins corresponding to the arteries drain the breast, ultimately into the axillary and internal thoracic veins. The superficial veins often become prominent and dilated during pregnancy and lactation.
questions.question: Where are circular venous plexuses located?
What is the primary arterial supply to the scalp anteriorly?
questions.explanation: The supraorbital and supratrochlear arteries (from the ophthalmic artery of internal carotid system) supply the anterior scalp. The superficial temporal artery supplies the lateral scalp. Posterior scalp receives blood from occipital and posterior auricular arteries from the external carotid system.

questions.question: The cisterna chyli lies to which side of the aorta?
questions.explanation: The cisterna chyli is located to the right of the abdominal aorta at the L1-L2 vertebral level, posterior to the right crus of the diaphragm. This dilated lymphatic sac receives the right and left lumbar lymphatic trunks, intestinal trunk, and sometimes lower intercostal trunks before giving rise to the thoracic duct. The cisterna lies anterior to the vertebral bodies and posterior to the aorta, in the retroperitoneal space. The thoracic duct ascends from the cisterna through the aortic hiatus (crossing from right to left in the thorax) to drain into the venous system.

The right bronchial vein drains into the azygos vein, while the left bronchial vein drains into the accessory hemiazygos vein. These veins return deoxygenated blood from the bronchial tree. The pulmonary veins, in contrast, carry oxygenated blood from the alveoli to the left atrium.
questions.question: Where does the right bronchial vein drain?
Which artery supplies the transverse colon?
questions.explanation: The transverse colon receives its arterial supply from branches of the superior mesenteric artery, specifically the middle colic artery and right colic artery branches. The junction between the territories of the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries occurs near the left third of the transverse colon. This represents the embryological boundary between midgut and hindgut derivatives.

questions.question: Which structure forms the floor of the lesser sac?
questions.explanation: The floor (inferior boundary) of the lesser sac is formed by the transverse colon and its mesocolon, along with the fusion of the anterior and posterior layers of the greater omentum. The lesser sac (omental bursa) is bounded anteriorly by the stomach, lesser omentum, and greater omentum; posteriorly by the pancreas, left kidney, left suprarenal gland, and posterior abdominal wall; superiorly by the caudate lobe of liver and diaphragm; and communicates with the greater sac through the epiploic foramen. Collections in the lesser sac are typically detected as fluid between the stomach and pancreas on imaging.

There are 15-20 lactiferous ducts that open by the same number of openings on the summit of the nipple. Each duct drains one lobe of the mammary gland. Deep to the areola, each duct has a dilated portion called the lactiferous sinus where milk can be stored.
questions.question: How many lactiferous duct openings are on nipple?

questions.explanation: Old platelets, like old erythrocytes, are recognized and destroyed by macrophages in the splenic cords. The spleen also serves as a reservoir for approximately one-third of the body's platelet pool. After splenectomy, platelet counts typically rise (thrombocytosis) due to loss of platelet sequestration and destruction. Splenic platelets can be rapidly mobilized in stress or hemorrhage.
questions.question: What happens to old platelets in the spleen?

questions.explanation: The inferior rectal nerve (branch of the pudendal nerve, S2-S4) provides somatic sensory innervation to the anal canal below the pectinate line, making this region sensitive to pain, touch, and temperature. The inferior rectal nerve also provides motor innervation to the external anal sphincter. Above the pectinate line, the anal canal receives autonomic innervation (from inferior hypogastric plexus), making it insensitive to pain but responsive to stretch. This difference explains why internal hemorrhoids (above pectinate line) are painless while external hemorrhoids (below the line) are painful.
questions.question: Which nerve provides sensory innervation below the pectinate line?

questions.explanation: The adult stomach has a mean capacity of approximately 1.5 to 2 litres when distended, though it can accommodate more. The stomach is a highly distensible organ with significant variation in capacity between individuals. At birth, the capacity is only about 30 ml, increasing to 1000 ml at puberty.
questions.question: What is the normal capacity of an adult stomach?

questions.explanation: The pharyngeal recess (fossa of Rosenmüller) is a depression in the lateral wall of the nasopharynx behind the torus tubarius (Eustachian tube opening). Nasopharyngeal carcinomas commonly arise in this recess. The recess is bounded anteriorly by the tubal elevation and posteriorly by the adenoid pad. Deep cervical lymph nodes receive drainage from this region.
questions.question: The pharyngeal recess (of Rosenmüller) is located in which region?

questions.explanation: The danger triangle connects via the angular and ophthalmic veins to the cavernous sinus without intervening valves. Facial infections in this region can lead to cavernous sinus thrombosis through retrograde venous spread. The triangle is bounded by the corners of the mouth and the bridge of the nose.
questions.question: The danger triangle of the face drains venously to which structure?

questions.explanation: Biceps femoris has two heads: the long head from the ischial tuberosity (in common with semitendinosus) and the short head from the linea aspera and lateral supracondylar line of the femur. The short head does not cross the hip joint and is supplied by the common fibular division (not tibial division) of the sciatic nerve.
questions.question: Which hamstring muscle has a short head originating from the linea aspera and NOT from the ischial tuberosity?

questions.explanation: The transverse humeral ligament extends between the greater and lesser tubercles of the humerus. It holds the tendon of the long head of biceps brachii within the intertubercular (bicipital) groove. The synovial membrane of the shoulder joint forms a tubular sheath around this tendon.
questions.question: Which ligament holds the long head of biceps tendon in the intertubercular groove?

questions.explanation: Opposition (bringing thumb pad to finger pads) is a uniquely human capability essential for precision grip. It involves flexion, abduction, and medial rotation at the thumb carpometacarpal joint. This complex movement, enabled by opponens pollicis and other thenar muscles, distinguishes human hand function.
options: Unique opposition enabling precision pinch grip
questions.question: What is the functional significance of opposition movement?
What nerve root is predominantly tested by the triceps reflex?
questions.explanation: The triceps reflex predominantly tests the C7 nerve root. The reflex is elicited by tapping the triceps tendon just above the olecranon. Absence or diminution suggests C7 nerve root or radial nerve pathology.

The inferior phrenic arteries are usually the first branches of the abdominal aorta, arising immediately after it passes through the aortic hiatus at T12, though they may arise from the celiac trunk. They supply the inferior surface of the diaphragm and give off superior suprarenal arteries. Each artery has a medial and lateral branch.
questions.question: From which vessel do the inferior phrenic arteries usually arise?

questions.explanation: Lymph from the superior (thoracic) surface of the diaphragm drains into parasternal, posterior mediastinal, and phrenic lymph nodes. Lymph from the inferior (abdominal) surface drains into anterior and posterior diaphragmatic lymph nodes, phrenic nodes, and superior lumbar nodes. Lymphatic vessels from the bare area of the liver communicate through the diaphragm with posterior mediastinal nodes.
questions.question: Which lymph nodes receive diaphragmatic lymph from the superior surface?
To which structure is the suprapleural membrane attached apically?
questions.explanation: The suprapleural membrane is attached at its apex to the transverse process of the seventh cervical vertebra (C7). Laterally, it attaches to the internal border of the first rib and its costal cartilage. Medially, it blends with the fascia covering structures passing through the superior thoracic aperture.

questions.question: The facial vein commonly anastomoses with which intracranial structure?
questions.explanation: The facial vein communicates with the cavernous sinus via the superior ophthalmic vein and deep facial vein to the pterygoid plexus. These connections lack valves, allowing bidirectional flow. Infections in the danger triangle of the face can spread to the cavernous sinus, causing cavernous sinus thrombosis.

The hilum of the spleen faces anteromedially toward the stomach, receiving the splenic artery (which divides into 5-6 branches before entering) and giving exit to the splenic vein. The gastrosplenic ligament connects the hilum to the greater curvature of the stomach and contains the short gastric and left gastroepiploic vessels. The splenorenal ligament connects the hilum to the left kidney and contains the splenic vessels and tail of the pancreas. The splenic hilum typically shows a distinct notch (splenic notch) on its superior border, a characteristic feature visible on cross-sectional imaging.
questions.question: The hilum of the spleen faces which direction?
What is unique about segmental blood supply?
questions.explanation: There is little anastomosis between the arteries (branches of pulmonary artery) supplying adjacent bronchopulmonary segments. This anatomical feature allows individual segments to be surgically resected without significantly affecting neighboring segments. Each segment functions as an independent unit.

questions.question: Which muscle forms the medial wall of the inguinal canal?
questions.explanation: The inguinal canal does not have distinct medial and lateral walls; instead, it has anterior and posterior walls, a roof, and a floor. The canal runs obliquely (downward, forward, and medially) from the deep inguinal ring to the superficial inguinal ring, approximately 4 cm in length. The anterior wall is formed by external oblique aponeurosis (entire length) and internal oblique laterally; posterior wall by transversalis fascia (entire length) and conjoint tendon medially; roof by arching fibers of internal oblique and transversus; floor by inguinal ligament. Understanding this anatomy is crucial for hernia repair.

Sympathetic efferents from the thoracic sympathetic trunk cause bronchodilation and inhibit secretion from bronchial glands. This is clinically important in conditions like asthma where bronchodilators (sympathomimetics) are used therapeutically. Parasympathetic stimulation from the vagus causes bronchoconstriction.
questions.question: What causes bronchodilation in the lungs?
Which vein drains the fundus of the stomach?
questions.explanation: The short gastric veins drain the fundus of the stomach and flow into the splenic vein. There are typically 4-5 short gastric veins that pass through the gastrosplenic ligament. In portal hypertension, these veins can become dilated and form part of the portosystemic collateral circulation, potentially leading to gastric varices and bleeding.

The ureter descends on the anterior surface of the psoas major muscle in the abdomen, passing over the tips of the lumbar vertebral transverse processes. It is crossed anteriorly by the testicular/ovarian vessels and runs posterior to the peritoneum throughout its abdominal course. At the pelvic brim, the ureter crosses the bifurcation of the common iliac artery (or external iliac artery) to enter the pelvis, where it runs along the lateral pelvic wall before turning medially to reach the bladder. In females, it passes beneath the uterine artery ("water under the bridge").
questions.question: The ureter crosses which muscle as it descends?

questions.explanation: The subscapular bursa is located between the subscapularis tendon and the scapula, reducing wear and tear during shoulder movement. Unlike the subacromial bursa, the subscapular bursa communicates with the shoulder joint cavity through a gap between the superior and middle glenohumeral ligaments. This communication allows potential spread of infection or inflammatory processes.
questions.question: What structure lies between the subscapularis tendon and the scapula?

questions.explanation: Flexor hallucis longus is innervated by the tibial nerve at S2 and S3. It originates from the inferior two-thirds of the posterior surface of the fibula and inserts into the base of the distal phalanx of the great toe. It flexes the great toe at all joints, weakly plantarflexes the ankle, and supports the medial longitudinal arch during the push-off phase of gait.
questions.question: Flexor hallucis longus is innervated by the tibial nerve at which spinal levels?

questions.explanation: Pectineus is primarily supplied by the femoral nerve (L2, L3), but may also receive innervation from the obturator nerve. It originates from the superior ramus of the pubis and inserts into the pectineal line of the femur just inferior to the lesser trochanter. It acts to adduct and flex the thigh and assists with medial rotation.
questions.question: The pectineus muscle receives primary innervation from the femoral nerve and a variable additional supply from which nerve?

questions.explanation: A horizontal plane from the sternal angle to the lower border of T4 divides the mediastinum into superior and inferior parts. The inferior mediastinum is further subdivided into anterior, middle, and posterior mediastina. This anatomical division is useful for localizing pathology on imaging.
questions.question: Which plane divides the mediastinum horizontally?
The pectinate line in the anal canal marks the junction between which embryological structures?
questions.explanation: The pectinate line represents the mucocutaneous junction where endoderm-derived hindgut epithelium meets ectoderm-derived proctodeal epithelium at the level of the anal valves. Above this line, the anal canal has columnar epithelium, venous drainage to portal circulation, lymphatic drainage to internal iliac nodes, and autonomic innervation. Below the line, it has stratified squamous epithelium, systemic venous drainage, lymphatic drainage to superficial inguinal nodes, and somatic (pudendal) innervation.

questions.question: What characterizes centroacinar cells?
questions.explanation: Centroacinar cells are pale-staining cells unique to the pancreas that represent the intra-acinar portion of the intercalated duct. They secrete bicarbonate-rich fluid in response to secretin, which neutralizes gastric acid in the duodenum. This bicarbonate secretion, combined with enzymes from acinar cells, produces complete pancreatic juice. Centroacinar cells distinguish pancreatic from salivary acini.

questions.question: Which muscle forms the right crus of the diaphragm?
questions.explanation: The right crus of the diaphragm arises from the bodies and intervertebral discs of the upper three lumbar vertebrae (L1-L3), while the left crus arises from only the upper two lumbar vertebrae (L1-L2). The crura are tendinous structures that ascend to insert into the central tendon. The right crus is longer and stronger, and some of its fibers form a muscular sling around the oesophageal hiatus.

questions.question: Which nerve supplies the anterior belly of the digastric?
questions.explanation: The anterior belly of the digastric is supplied by the mylohyoid nerve, a branch of the inferior alveolar nerve (V3). The posterior belly is supplied by the facial nerve. This dual innervation reflects embryologic derivation from first and second pharyngeal arches respectively. The digastric helps open the mouth and elevate the hyoid.

questions.question: Tibialis posterior and fibularis longus are described as important stabilizers at the ankle. Which action does tibialis posterior perform at the ankle?
questions.explanation: Tibialis posterior plantarflexes the ankle and inverts the foot. It is innervated by the tibial nerve (L4, L5) and inserts into the tuberosity of the navicular and multiple other tarsal and metatarsal bones. It is also the primary dynamic maintainer of the medial longitudinal arch. Its rupture leads to progressive flat foot and valgus deformity at the ankle.
options: Eversion and abduction of the foot

questions.question: How does forearm position affect biceps function?
questions.explanation: Biceps brachii is most effective as a supinator when the elbow is flexed at 90° (maximum mechanical advantage). As a flexor, it's most effective when the forearm is in mid-prone position. When fully supinated, the tendon is wrapped around the radius, reducing flexion efficiency.
options: Supination optimal with flexed elbow, flexion optimal mid-pronation

questions.question: What artery typically accompanies the suprascapular nerve through the supraspinous fossa?
questions.explanation: The suprascapular artery accompanies the suprascapular nerve through the suprascapular notch into the supraspinous fossa. Unlike the nerve which passes under the superior transverse scapular ligament, the artery passes over it. Both structures then pass through the spinoglenoid notch to reach the infraspinous fossa.

questions.question: The sole of the foot muscles are arranged in four layers. The first layer contains three muscles. Which combination is correct?
questions.explanation: The first layer of foot muscles contains three muscles: abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis, and abductor digiti minimi. All three originate from the medial tubercle of the tuberosity of the calcaneus and the plantar aponeurosis. Abductor hallucis and flexor digitorum brevis are innervated by the medial plantar nerve, while abductor digiti minimi is supplied by the lateral plantar nerve.
options: Flexor hallucis brevis, adductor hallucis, flexor digiti minimi brevis
Abductor hallucis, flexor hallucis brevis, adductor hallucis
Plantar interossei, dorsal interossei, flexor hallucis brevis
Abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis, abductor digiti minimi

questions.question: The rectus femoris, sartorius, and iliopsoas all flex the hip. Of these, which is the most powerful hip flexor in the fully extended hip position?
questions.explanation: Iliopsoas is the most powerful hip flexor in the fully extended hip position. Its large cross-sectional area and optimal moment arm at the hip make it the most forceful. Rectus femoris is a significant hip flexor at lower hip flexion angles. Sartorius contributes but is much weaker due to its smaller size. Iliopsoas weakness is assessed by resisted hip flexion in the seated or supine position.

questions.question: The trochanteric fossa, medial to the greater trochanter, receives the insertion of which muscle?
questions.explanation: The trochanteric fossa, located on the medial surface of the greater trochanter, receives the insertion of obturator externus. This differs from other short rotators (piriformis, obturator internus, gemelli) which insert into the upper border of the greater trochanter. Knowledge of this distinction is important in hip replacement approaches.

questions.question: The lamina papyracea forms the medial wall of which structure?
questions.explanation: The lamina papyracea (orbital plate) of the ethmoid bone forms the thin medial wall of the orbit. It separates the orbit from the ethmoidal air cells. The name papyracea (paper-like) reflects its extreme thinness. Ethmoidal infections can erode through this wall causing orbital cellulitis or abscess.

questions.question: The incisive foramen transmits which nerve?
questions.explanation: The incisive foramen (canal) in the anterior hard palate transmits the nasopalatine nerves, which provide sensation to the anterior palate. The foramen also transmits terminal branches of the greater palatine vessels. The nasopalatine nerve is a branch of the maxillary nerve via the pterygopalatine ganglion.

questions.question: Which embryological origin corresponds to the descending colon?
questions.explanation: The descending colon is derived from the embryological hindgut, along with the distal third of the transverse colon, sigmoid colon, rectum, and upper anal canal. Hindgut structures are supplied by the inferior mesenteric artery and receive parasympathetic innervation from the pelvic splanchnic nerves. The midgut-hindgut junction occurs at approximately the left third of the transverse colon.

The lateral nasal wall is formed by the maxilla (medial surface), ethmoid bone (superior and middle conchae, and perpendicular plate), palatine bone (perpendicular plate), inferior nasal concha, and lacrimal bone. The complex three-dimensional structure creates the superior, middle, and inferior meatuses. Understanding this anatomy is essential for sinus surgery.
questions.question: Which bone forms the lateral wall of the nasal cavity?
How do the anterior and posterior interosseous nerves complement each other?
questions.explanation: The anterior interosseous nerve supplies deep flexor muscles (flexor pollicis longus, radial half of flexor digitorum profundus, pronator quadratus) while the posterior interosseous nerve supplies all posterior forearm extensors. This complementary distribution ensures complete innervation of forearm muscles from the radial and median nerves.
options: Anterior for deep flexors, posterior for extensors
Anterior for extensors, posterior for flexors

questions.question: Which space lies between the vocal and vestibular folds?
questions.explanation: The laryngeal ventricle (sinus of Morgagni) is a space between the true vocal fold below and the false vocal fold (vestibular fold) above. It extends laterally into the saccule, which contains mucous glands that lubricate the vocal cords. The lateral wall is formed by the thyroid cartilage.

questions.question: Which artery supplies the sigmoid colon?
questions.explanation: The sigmoid colon receives its blood supply from 2-4 sigmoid arteries (sigmoidal arteries), branches of the inferior mesenteric artery. These arteries descend in the sigmoid mesocolon, anastomosing with each other and with branches from the left colic artery superiorly and the superior rectal artery inferiorly, contributing to the marginal artery along the mesenteric border. Sudeck's point, at the rectosigmoid junction (approximately 15 cm from anal verge), represents a watershed area where the last sigmoid artery anastomoses with the superior rectal artery and is vulnerable to ischemia.

options: They become lax to allow free extension
questions.question: During extension of the hip joint, the three extracapsular ligaments behave in which manner due to their spiral orientation?
questions.explanation: The fibers of all three extracapsular hip ligaments are oriented in a spiral fashion around the hip joint, causing them to become taut when the joint is extended. This stabilizes the joint in standing and reduces the amount of muscle energy required to maintain upright posture, demonstrating an important energy-conserving mechanism in bipedal locomotion.

The inferior thyroid artery arises from the thyrocervical trunk (a branch of the subclavian artery) and ascends to supply the lower poles of the thyroid gland. The recurrent laryngeal nerve has an intimate relationship with this artery, passing either anterior or posterior to it. The superior thyroid artery supplies the upper poles.
questions.question: Which artery supplies the thyroid gland inferiorly?

questions.explanation: The right kidney's anterior surface is related superiorly to the right lobe of the liver (hepatorenal recess), the second part of the duodenum medially, and the right colic flexure and ascending colon inferiorly. Small intestine loops may also contact its anterior surface. The liver creates the largest impression on the right kidney's anterior surface.
questions.question: Which organ lies anterior to the right kidney?

questions.explanation: The transverse colon has a dual blood supply: the right two-thirds from the middle colic branch of the superior mesenteric artery (midgut supply) and the left third from the left colic branch of the inferior mesenteric artery (hindgut supply). The junction between these territories forms the marginal artery (of Drummond) and represents the watershed area most vulnerable to ischemia.
questions.question: Which structure receives blood from both celiac and superior mesenteric arteries?

questions.explanation: The obturator nerve divides into anterior and posterior divisions. The anterior division supplies adductor longus, brevis, gracilis, and pectineus (sometimes), and provides a cutaneous branch to the medial thigh. The posterior division supplies obturator externus and the adductor part of adductor magnus, and gives an articular branch to the knee joint.
questions.question: The obturator nerve divides into which two divisions upon exiting the obturator foramen?

questions.explanation: The processus vaginalis, an evagination of peritoneum that accompanies the descending testis through the inguinal canal, normally obliterates during the first year of life, leaving only the distal portion as the tunica vaginalis surrounding the testis. Failure of complete obliteration leads to various clinical conditions: patent processus vaginalis allows peritoneal fluid to flow into the scrotum (communicating hydrocele) or permits herniation of abdominal contents (congenital indirect inguinal hernia). Partial obliteration with persistence of intermediate portions creates encysted hydroceles of the cord. Complete patency occurs in about 20% of adults.
questions.question: The processus vaginalis normally obliterates when?
The fibular (peroneal) artery, arising from the tibioperoneal trunk, descends laterally alongside the fibula in which compartment?
options: Deep posterior compartment of the leg
questions.explanation: The fibular (peroneal) artery descends in the deep posterior compartment of the leg, alongside the fibula. It supplies the lateral and posterior compartment muscles and gives off perforating branches that pierce the interosseous membrane to supply the lateral compartment (fibularis longus and brevis). It terminates by anastomosing with the lateral malleolar and calcaneal branches of the posterior tibial artery.

questions.question: Which sinus receives the great cerebral vein?
questions.explanation: The straight sinus receives the great cerebral vein (of Galen) and the inferior sagittal sinus. It runs in the junction of the falx cerebri and tentorium cerebelli. The sinus drains into the confluence of sinuses (typically preferentially into the left transverse sinus). Deep cerebral structures drain via this pathway.

The right lower lobe contains five bronchopulmonary segments: superior (apical), medial basal, anterior basal, lateral basal, and posterior basal. The superior segment is also called the apical segment of the lower lobe and is the most dependent segment when lying supine.
questions.question: How many segments are in right lower lobe?

questions.explanation: The scala tympani (and scala vestibuli) contains perilymph, which has an ionic composition similar to extracellular fluid. The scala media (cochlear duct) contains endolymph with high potassium. Perilymph communicates with CSF via the cochlear aqueduct. The round window membrane separates the scala tympani from the middle ear.
questions.question: The scala tympani contains which fluid?
The medial sural cutaneous nerve and the sural communicating branch of the common fibular nerve unite to form the sural nerve. At what level does this union typically occur?
options: In the popliteal fossa immediately after bifurcation
In the middle third of the leg or lower popliteal region
At the superior angle of the popliteal fossa
At the ankle level near the malleolus only
Just posterior to the lateral malleolus at the ankle
questions.explanation: The sural nerve is typically formed in the middle third of the leg (or sometimes in the lower popliteal fossa) when the medial sural cutaneous nerve (from the tibial nerve) unites with the sural communicating branch (from the common fibular nerve). It then descends to pass posterior to the lateral malleolus and supply the lateral side of the leg, ankle, and lateral heel. Its predictable course makes it valuable for nerve grafting.

questions.question: The femoral artery passes through the adductor hiatus in adductor magnus to continue as which artery?
questions.explanation: The femoral artery passes through the adductor hiatus, a tendinous gap in the lower part of adductor magnus, to become the popliteal artery in the popliteal fossa. The femoral vein similarly traverses the adductor hiatus to become the popliteal vein. The adductor canal lies superior to the adductor hiatus.

questions.question: Which artery can be used for coronary bypass?
questions.explanation: The internal thoracic (internal mammary) artery is commonly used for coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG). It is dissected from the chest wall while maintaining its origin from the subclavian artery, then anastomosed to a coronary artery (usually left anterior descending). It provides excellent long-term patency.

The middle colic artery arises from the right side of the superior mesenteric artery as it emerges from beneath the pancreas, ascending into the transverse mesocolon. It divides into right and left branches that supply the transverse colon; the right branch anastomoses with the right colic artery (from SMA), while the left branch anastomoses with the left colic artery (from IMA) forming the marginal artery of Drummond. This anastomotic connection between superior and inferior mesenteric arterial territories creates an important collateral pathway in cases of vascular compromise.
questions.question: The middle colic artery is a branch of which vessel?
The cardinal ligament of the uterus contains which vessels?
questions.explanation: The cardinal ligament (Mackenrodt's ligament, transverse cervical ligament), extending from the cervix and lateral vaginal fornix to the lateral pelvic wall, contains the uterine artery and vein along with autonomic nerve fibers and lymphatics. This ligament provides the most important support for the uterus, preventing uterine prolapse. The uterine artery crosses over the ureter ("water under the bridge") in the base of the broad ligament before reaching the uterus.
