During hysterectomy, the cardinal ligaments must be clamped and divided, requiring careful identification of the ureters to prevent injury.

options: Prevents flexor tendon bowstringing, maintains carpal arch
questions.question: What is the functional importance of the flexor retinaculum?
questions.explanation: The flexor retinaculum prevents bowstringing of flexor tendons during wrist flexion, maintaining mechanical efficiency. It maintains the carpal arch and serves as origin for thenar and hypothenar muscles. However, it creates the confined carpal tunnel space predisposing to median nerve compression.

questions.question: What connects breast skin to deep fascia?
questions.explanation: The ligaments of Cooper are fibrous strands that connect the skin with the deep fascia of pectoralis major, passing through the breast tissue. They provide structural support to the breast. Infiltration of these ligaments by breast cancer causes their shortening, producing the characteristic peau d'orange appearance.

questions.question: What controls the external urethral sphincter?
questions.explanation: The external urethral sphincter is composed of skeletal muscle and is under voluntary somatic control via the pudendal nerve (S2-S4). This sphincter can be consciously contracted to prevent or interrupt micturition. In males, it surrounds the membranous urethra; in females, it surrounds the middle third of the urethra at the urogenital diaphragm.

questions.question: Which muscle extends the little finger independently?
questions.explanation: independently extends the little finger, working alongside extensor digitorum. It is located in the posterior forearm compartment and supplied by the posterior interosseous nerve. The muscle has its own compartment under the extensor retinaculum.

All four rotator cuff muscles (subscapularis, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, and teres minor) fuse with the lateral part of the joint capsule. Their tendons blend with the capsule to form the rotator cuff. The resting tone of these muscles helps stabilize the joint by pulling the humeral head into the glenoid cavity.
questions.question: Which rotator cuff muscle does NOT fuse with the glenohumeral joint capsule?

questions.explanation: The rectus abdominis originates from the pubic crest and pubic symphysis and inserts superiorly onto the xiphoid process and the costal cartilages of ribs 5-7. The muscle is intersected by three or four tendinous intersections that are firmly adherent to the anterior rectus sheath, creating the characteristic "six-pack" appearance in individuals with low body fat. These intersections represent remnants of the segmental myotomes from which the muscle develops and typically occur at the level of the xiphoid process, umbilicus, and midway between these landmarks.
questions.question: The rectus abdominis muscle inserts onto which structures?

questions.explanation: The ductus deferens (vas deferens) hooks around the lateral side of the inferior epigastric artery at the deep inguinal ring, crossing from lateral to medial as it leaves the spermatic cord to descend into the pelvis. This relationship is surgically important during hernia repair and vasectomy. After crossing the external iliac vessels at the pelvic brim, the vas continues posteromedially across the obturator nerve and vessels and the ureter before reaching the posterior surface of the bladder where it dilates to form the ampulla and joins the seminal vesicle duct.
questions.question: The ductus deferens passes medial to which vessel?

options: Both right and left hepatic ducts
questions.question: The caudate lobe of the liver drains bile into which duct?
questions.explanation: The caudate lobe of the liver, despite being part of the anatomical right lobe, is functionally independent, receiving blood from both right and left hepatic arteries and draining bile into both right and left hepatic ducts. It also has separate venous drainage directly into the IVC via small hepatic veins, independent of the main right, middle, and left hepatic veins. This unique drainage explains why the caudate lobe may hypertrophy in cirrhosis (where it maintains direct IVC access) and why it can function in Budd-Chiari syndrome when the main hepatic veins are occluded. The caudate process extends from the caudate lobe toward the porta hepatis.

The inferior mesenteric artery originates from the anterior aspect of the abdominal aorta at the level of the third lumbar vertebra (L3), approximately 3-4 cm above the aortic bifurcation. This vessel supplies hindgut derivatives, including the left one-third of the transverse colon, descending colon, sigmoid colon, rectum, and upper anal canal. Its main branches include the left colic artery, sigmoid arteries (2-4 branches), and the superior rectal artery, which represents its terminal continuation descending into the pelvis.
questions.question: The inferior mesenteric artery typically arises at which vertebral level?

questions.explanation: Pectoralis major receives dual innervation from both lateral pectoral nerve (C5, C6) and medial pectoral nerve (C8, T1). The lateral pectoral nerve is the primary supply. The medial pectoral nerve must pierce pectoralis minor to reach pectoralis major.
options: Both lateral and medial pectoral nerves
questions.question: What nerve supplies pectoralis major?
The jugulo-omohyoid node drains which structure primarily?
questions.explanation: The jugulo-omohyoid lymph node (principal node of the tongue) is located where the omohyoid muscle crosses the internal jugular vein. It receives drainage from the tip and anterior tongue (along with submental nodes). The node is part of the inferior deep cervical chain. Enlargement suggests anterior oral cavity or tongue pathology.

questions.question: The anterior compartment of the leg contains four muscles. Which of the following does NOT belong to this compartment?
questions.explanation: The anterior compartment of the leg contains four muscles: tibialis anterior, extensor digitorum longus, extensor hallucis longus, and fibularis tertius. Fibularis longus belongs to the lateral compartment, along with fibularis brevis. All anterior compartment muscles are innervated by the deep fibular nerve (L4, L5). Paralysis of these muscles causes foot drop.

questions.question: What percentage of pancreatic tissue is endocrine?
questions.explanation: Only about 1-2% of the pancreatic tissue consists of endocrine islets of Langerhans, with the remaining 98-99% being exocrine acinar tissue that produces digestive enzymes. Despite representing such a small proportion, the islets are crucial for glucose homeostasis. There are approximately 1 million islets in the human pancreas, most concentrated in the tail.

questions.question: Which cells produce hydrochloric acid in the stomach?
questions.explanation: Parietal (oxyntic) cells in the gastric glands of the stomach fundus and body secrete hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor. The acid creates an optimal pH for pepsin activation and kills ingested bacteria. Intrinsic factor is essential for vitamin B12 absorption in the terminal ileum. Parietal cell loss or dysfunction can cause achlorhydria and pernicious anemia.

The anterior two-thirds (oral part) of the tongue develops from the first pharyngeal arch (two lateral lingual swellings and median tuberculum impar). The posterior third (pharyngeal part) develops from the third arch (copula). The second arch contribution is overgrown. This embryologic division explains the different nerve supplies.
questions.question: The anterior two-thirds of the tongue develops from which pharyngeal arch?

questions.explanation: The greater splanchnic nerve contains preganglionic sympathetic fibers from the T5-T9 levels of the spinal cord, which synapse in the celiac ganglion. This nerve pierces the diaphragm separately or with the sympathetic trunk and provides sympathetic innervation to the foregut derivatives (stomach, liver, gallbladder, pancreas, spleen, and small intestine to mid-duodenum) via the celiac plexus. The lesser splanchnic nerve (T10-T11) supplies the midgut, while the least splanchnic nerve (T12) and lumbar splanchnic nerves supply the hindgut and pelvic organs via the superior and inferior mesenteric plexuses.
questions.question: The greater splanchnic nerve carries preganglionic fibers from which spinal levels?

questions.explanation: The second part of the axillary artery lies directly behind (posterior to) the pectoralis minor muscle. This anatomical relationship is used to divide the artery into three parts. The second part gives off two branches: the thoracoacromial and lateral thoracic arteries.
questions.question: Which portion of the axillary artery lies behind pectoralis minor?
Which nerve passes through the quadrangular space?
questions.explanation: The axillary nerve passes through the quadrangular space accompanied by the posterior circumflex humeral vessels. The space is bounded by teres minor superiorly, teres major inferiorly, long head of triceps medially, and surgical neck of humerus laterally. Injury can occur with shoulder trauma or humeral neck fractures.

questions.question: Which vein forms the continuation of the sigmoid sinus?
questions.explanation: The internal jugular vein begins at the jugular foramen as the continuation of the sigmoid sinus. It descends in the carotid sheath lateral to the carotid arteries. At the base of the neck, it joins the subclavian vein to form the brachiocephalic vein. The vein receives the facial, lingual, pharyngeal, and thyroid veins.

questions.question: Which forearm muscle is supplied by the anterior interosseous nerve?
questions.explanation: is supplied by the anterior interosseous nerve, a branch of the median nerve. This nerve also supplies the lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus and pronator quadratus. Anterior interosseous syndrome results in inability to flex the thumb interphalangeal joint and index finger distal interphalangeal joint.

The median nerve's formation from lateral and medial cords ensures it receives contributions from all nerve roots (C5-T1) except sometimes C5. This broad root distribution explains why isolated cord injuries may only partially affect median nerve function. The distinctive M-shaped formation in the axilla is clinically recognizable.
questions.question: What is the significance of the median nerve's dual cord origin?
options: Has no clinical or anatomical significance
Supply from both lateral and medial cords
Subscapularis, pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi, teres major
questions.explanation: Medial (internal) rotation of the humerus is produced by subscapularis, pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi, teres major, and anterior fibers of deltoid. This movement rotates the arm toward the midline so the thumb points medially. These muscles are predominantly anterior or on the subscapular surface.
questions.question: What produces medial rotation of the humerus at the shoulder?

questions.explanation: The masseteric nerve (from anterior division of V3) passes through the mandibular notch with the masseteric artery to supply the masseter muscle. It also provides articular branches to the temporomandibular joint. The nerve crosses lateral to the temporomandibular joint and deep to the tendon of temporalis muscle.
questions.question: Which nerve passes through the mandibular notch?
Where is Morgagni's foramen located?
questions.explanation: The foramen of Morgagni is located anteriorly between the xiphoid and costal origins of the diaphragm. Hernias through this opening (Morgagni hernias) are less common than Bochdalek hernias but can allow omental fat or intestine to herniate into the anterior mediastinum. They are usually asymptomatic.

questions.question: The anterior compartment of the thigh contains muscles functioning primarily as which two groups?
options: Flexors of the knee and extensors of the hip
Extensors of the hip and adductors
Abductors of the hip and flexors of the knee
Flexors of the hip and extensors of the knee
Lateral rotators of the hip and extensors of the knee
questions.explanation: The anterior compartment of the thigh contains muscles functioning as flexors of the hip and extensors of the knee. These muscles tend to atrophy rapidly with disease and often require physical therapy to restore strength, tone, and symmetry after immobilization. The anterior compartment is the largest of the three thigh compartments.

questions.question: How many fascicles does the left bundle branch divide into?
questions.explanation: The left bundle branch divides into two main fascicles: anterior and posterior (some describe a third, septal fascicle). The anterior fascicle supplies the anterior and lateral left ventricular wall; the posterior fascicle supplies the posterior and inferior wall. Left bundle branch block or fascicular blocks (hemiblocks) cause characteristic ECG patterns and may indicate underlying cardiac disease.

questions.question: The left renal vein passes between which two structures?
questions.explanation: The left renal vein passes anteriorly to the aorta and posteriorly to the superior mesenteric artery (SMA) before draining into the inferior vena cava. This anatomical relationship can lead to compression of the left renal vein between the aorta and SMA, a condition called nutcracker syndrome (or left renal vein entrapment syndrome), which may cause hematuria, left flank pain, and varicocele. The left renal vein is longer than the right (7-10 cm vs 2-4 cm) and receives the left testicular/ovarian vein, left suprarenal vein, and inferior phrenic vein before entering the IVC.

The iliolumbar ligament extends from the transverse processes of L5 vertebra (and sometimes L4) to the iliac crest and iliac fossa. This strong ligament helps stabilize the lumbosacral junction and limits rotation at L5-S1. It forms an important surgical landmark in posterior approaches to the lumbar spine and pelvis. The ligament has superior and inferior bands; the superior band attaches to the transverse process and iliac crest, while the inferior band extends from the transverse process to the upper part of the sacral ala.
options: L5 transverse process to iliac crest
questions.question: The iliolumbar ligament connects which two structures?

questions.explanation: The azygos vein passes through the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm (at T12 level) along with the aorta and thoracic duct, posterior to the diaphragmatic crura. The aortic hiatus is actually a midline gap between the crura rather than a true opening in the diaphragmatic muscle. The azygos vein drains the posterior thoracic and abdominal walls and provides important collateral circulation between the superior and inferior vena cavae. It arches over the right main bronchus to drain into the superior vena cava. The hemiazygos vein may also pass through the aortic hiatus.
questions.question: The azygos vein passes through which diaphragmatic opening?

questions.explanation: Semitendinosus joins sartorius and gracilis at the pes anserinus on the superior medial surface of the tibia. As its name implies, semitendinosus has a long rounded distal tendon. All three pes anserinus muscles cross both the hip and knee joints from three different compartments, making this insertion a multi-compartment landmark.
questions.question: Semitendinosus inserts into the medial surface of the superior part of the tibia, joining which two muscles to form the pes anserinus?
Sesamoid bones at the head of the first metatarsal are embedded in the tendons of which muscle?
questions.explanation: The two sesamoid bones at the head of the first metatarsal are embedded within the tendons of flexor hallucis brevis (medial and lateral heads). They protect the tendons from compression during weight-bearing and increase the mechanical advantage of flexor hallucis brevis. Sesamoiditis (inflammation of sesamoid bones) causes plantar pain under the first metatarsal head and is common in dancers and runners.

options: Anterior divisions supply flexors, posterior divisions supply extensors
questions.explanation: Brachial plexus organization reflects compartmental function: anterior divisions supply flexor (anterior) compartment muscles while posterior divisions supply extensor (posterior) compartment muscles. This organizational pattern continues from the plexus through the peripheral nerves, reflecting embryological development.
questions.question: How does the brachial plexus organization reflect compartment innervation?

questions.explanation: The superior intercostal artery (from costocervical trunk of subclavian artery) gives off the first and second posterior intercostal arteries. These are the only posterior intercostal arteries not arising from the thoracic aorta. This arrangement provides collateral circulation if the thoracic aorta is obstructed.
questions.question: What supplies the first two intercostal spaces?
What connects superior and inferior epigastric arteries?
questions.explanation: The superior and inferior epigastric arteries anastomose within the rectus sheath behind the rectus abdominis muscle. This provides an important collateral pathway between the subclavian artery (via internal thoracic and superior epigastric) and the external iliac artery (via inferior epigastric), bypassing the abdominal aorta.

The upper pole of the left kidney is related to the spleen laterally. Other anterior relations of the left kidney include the stomach superiorly, the pancreatic body and tail centrally, the left colic flexure laterally and inferiorly, and coils of jejunum medially and inferiorly. The left suprarenal gland sits on the upper pole medially.
questions.question: Which structure lies anterior to the upper pole of the left kidney?
The ciliary ganglion is associated with which cranial nerve?
questions.explanation: The ciliary ganglion is a parasympathetic ganglion receiving preganglionic fibers from the Edinger-Westphal nucleus via the oculomotor nerve. Postganglionic fibers travel in short ciliary nerves to innervate the sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle. Sensory fibers from V1 and sympathetic fibers pass through without synapsing. The ganglion lies posterolaterally in the orbit.

The thoracic duct ascends through the posterior mediastinum and veers to the left at the level of the T5 vertebra. At the root of the neck, it arches forwards and descends to enter the left venous angle. This anatomical course is crucial for understanding lymphatic drainage patterns in the thorax.
questions.question: At which vertebral level does the thoracic duct turn laterally?

questions.explanation: Smooth muscle cells disposed in a predominantly circular direction and radiating from the nipple base cause nipple erection. Their contraction, induced by cold, tactile, or emotional stimuli, causes erection of the nipple and wrinkling of the surrounding areola. This is an involuntary response.
questions.question: Which muscle causes nipple erection?
Which structure passes through both greater and lesser sciatic foramina?
questions.explanation: The pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels exit the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen (below piriformis), hook around the ischial spine (covered by sacrospinous ligament), and re-enter the pelvis through the lesser sciatic foramen to reach the pudendal canal (Alcock's canal) in the lateral wall of the ischioanal fossa. This unique course makes the pudendal nerve vulnerable to compression at the ischial spine (pudendal neuralgia). The nerve to obturator internus follows a similar course. No other major structures pass through both foramina; the sciatic nerve and other gluteal region structures exit only through the greater sciatic foramen.

The first posterior intercostal space on the right side drains into the right brachiocephalic vein. The remaining intercostal spaces on the right drain into the azygos vein. On the left, the upper three spaces typically drain into the left brachiocephalic vein through the left superior intercostal vein.
questions.question: Which vein drains the first posterior intercostal space?

questions.explanation: During shoulder joint abduction, the shoulder girdle undergoes upward rotation of the scapula. This scapular movement is essential for achieving full arm abduction beyond 90 degrees. The trapezius and serratus anterior muscles produce this upward rotation of the scapula.
questions.question: What movements occur at the shoulder girdle during arm abduction?
Which structure forms the falciform ligament's free edge?
questions.explanation: The ligamentum teres (round ligament of the liver) is the obliterated umbilical vein that runs in the free inferior edge of the falciform ligament from the umbilicus to the liver. It joins the left branch of the portal vein at the inferior end of the fissure for the ligamentum teres. In portal hypertension, paraumbilical veins accompanying the ligamentum teres may recanalize, forming caput medusae.

The left recurrent laryngeal nerve (branch of left vagus) loops around the aortic arch and ligamentum arteriosum before ascending in the groove between trachea and esophagus to reach the larynx. The right recurrent laryngeal nerve loops around the right subclavian artery. This asymmetry reflects embryological development.
questions.question: Which nerve loops around the ligamentum arteriosum?
Why does left lung have fewer segments?
questions.explanation: The left lung has 8-10 bronchopulmonary segments (compared to 10 on the right) because the apical and posterior segments typically fuse to form an apicoposterior segment. Additionally, the medial basal segment is often absent or fused with the anterior basal segment on the left side.

Three muscles arise from the styloid process: styloglossus, stylohyoid, and stylopharyngeus. These muscles form part of the "styloid apparatus" along with two ligaments (stylomandibular and stylohyoid). The styloid process projects downward and forward from the temporal bone. Elongation (Eagle syndrome) causes pharyngeal pain and dysphagia.
questions.question: The styloid process gives attachment to which muscles?

questions.explanation: The median sacral artery arises from the posterior aspect of the abdominal aorta just before its bifurcation at the L4 level (or sometimes from the aortic bifurcation itself). This small, unpaired vessel descends in the midline anterior to the sacrum and coccyx, supplying the posterior pelvic wall and anastomosing with the lateral sacral arteries (from internal iliac). It represents a caudal continuation of the dorsal aorta and may give small lumbar arteries. The median sacral artery is occasionally injured during presacral surgery or during anterior approaches to the spine.
questions.question: The median sacral artery arises from which vessel?
Which structure passes through the esophageal hiatus?
questions.explanation: The esophageal hiatus (at T10 level, formed by muscle fibers from the right crus of the diaphragm that loop around the esophagus) transmits the esophagus and the anterior and posterior vagal trunks (formed from the vagus nerves). The vagal trunks provide parasympathetic innervation to the abdominal viscera up to the splenic flexure. The left gastric artery and vein may also pass through or near this opening. The aorta, thoracic duct, and azygos vein pass through the aortic hiatus at T12, while the IVC passes through the caval opening at T8.

The right phrenic nerve passes through the superior and middle mediastinum descending on the right side of the superior vena cava (SVC) and heart. The left phrenic nerve similarly descends on the left side of the heart. Both nerves terminate in the diaphragm, providing motor and sensory innervation.
questions.question: Which nerve descends on the right side of SVC?
The splenic vein lies posterior to which organ?
questions.explanation: The splenic vein runs along the posterior surface of the pancreas (in a groove or embedded within the pancreatic substance) from the splenic hilum to the posterior aspect of the neck of pancreas, where it joins the superior mesenteric vein to form the portal vein. It receives numerous small pancreatic veins, the inferior mesenteric vein (typically), and the left gastric and left gastroepiploic veins. Its intimate relationship with the pancreas means that acute pancreatitis can cause splenic vein thrombosis, potentially leading to left-sided portal hypertension (sinistral portal hypertension) with isolated gastric varices and splenomegaly.

questions.question: Which ligament connects the liver to the anterior abdominal wall?
questions.explanation: The falciform ligament is a sickle-shaped fold of peritoneum that attaches the liver to the anterior abdominal wall and diaphragm. It extends from the umbilicus to the liver, dividing the liver into anatomical right and left lobes on the diaphragmatic surface. The free inferior edge contains the ligamentum teres (round ligament).

questions.question: The quadrate lobe of the liver receives blood from which branch?
questions.explanation: The quadrate lobe, despite being part of the anatomical right lobe (located between the gallbladder fossa and falciform ligament), functionally belongs to the left lobe as it receives its blood supply from the left hepatic artery and drains bile via the left hepatic duct. The functional division of the liver (Couinaud's classification) is based on vascular supply and biliary drainage rather than external anatomical features. The main portal fissure (containing the middle hepatic vein) separates functional right and left lobes, running from the gallbladder fossa to the IVC, placing the quadrate and caudate lobes functionally on the left.

questions.question: Which nerve supplies rhomboid muscles?
questions.explanation: The dorsal scapular nerve (C5) supplies the rhomboid major and minor muscles, and often the levator scapulae. The nerve pierces and may supply scalenus medius before descending along the vertebral border of the scapula. Injury affects scapular retraction.

options: Deep hand structures and palmar metacarpal arteries
questions.explanation: The deep palmar arch (formed primarily by radial artery) supplies blood to deep hand structures and gives off palmar metacarpal arteries. These metacarpal arteries provide important contributions to digital blood supply. The arch lies approximately 1cm proximal to the superficial arch.
questions.question: What is the primary function of the deep palmar arch?

questions.explanation: The supraspinatus muscle initiates the first 0-15 degrees of shoulder abduction. The middle fibers of the deltoid then take over from 15-90 degrees. Beyond 90 degrees, scapular rotation by trapezius and serratus anterior is essential for achieving full overhead abduction.
questions.question: Which muscles initiate the first 0-15 degrees of shoulder abduction?

questions.explanation: The anterior tibial artery gives off the anterior tibial recurrent artery, which ascends to the front of the knee to contribute inferolaterally to the genicular anastomosis. This vessel pierces the anterior tibialis muscle and anastomoses with the inferior lateral genicular artery. Knowledge of this anastomosis is important for understanding collateral circulation when the popliteal artery is occluded.
questions.question: The anterior tibial artery runs through the anterior compartment and enters the foot as the dorsalis pedis artery. It gives off which branch that contributes to the genicular anastomosis?

questions.explanation: is a small triangular muscle that assists the triceps brachii in elbow extension. It lies on the lateral aspect of the elbow, blending with the triceps. Both muscles are supplied by the radial nerve and work together to extend the elbow.
questions.question: Which muscle assists triceps in elbow extension?
Which vein forms the anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen?
questions.explanation: The portal vein, positioned posteriorly within the hepatoduodenal ligament (posterior to the bile duct and hepatic artery), forms part of the anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen. The entire hepatoduodenal ligament (containing the portal triad) constitutes the anterior boundary. The portal vein is the most posterior structure within this ligament, closest to the foramen. Injury to the portal vein during surgical manipulation near the epiploic foramen can cause massive hemorrhage into the lesser sac. The foramen can be occluded by compressing the hepatoduodenal ligament between thumb and fingers (Pringle maneuver).

questions.question: The ureter descends on the anterior surface of which muscle?
questions.explanation: The ureter descends on the anterior surface of the psoas major muscle (over the tips of the transverse processes of the lumbar vertebrae), passing from lateral to medial as it descends toward the pelvic brim. It is crossed anteriorly by the testicular/ovarian vessels and lies posterior to the peritoneum throughout its abdominal course. The ureter crosses the bifurcation of the common iliac artery (or the external iliac artery) at the pelvic brim, providing a consistent landmark. The relationship to psoas major is maintained until the ureter reaches the pelvic inlet, where it enters the pelvis.

questions.question: The transverse sinus lies in the attached border of which dural fold?
questions.explanation: The transverse sinuses lie in the attached posterior border of the tentorium cerebelli, extending from the internal occipital protuberance to the petrous temporal bone. They receive blood from the superior sagittal sinus (or confluence) and drain into the sigmoid sinuses. The tentorium separates the cerebellum from the occipital lobes.

questions.question: Into which vein does the right inferior phrenic vein drain?
questions.explanation: The right inferior phrenic vein usually drains directly into the inferior vena cava. The left inferior phrenic vein is usually double, with one branch draining into the IVC and the other frequently joining the left suprarenal vein, which then drains into the left renal vein. These veins drain blood from the inferior surface of the diaphragm.

questions.question: Which structure marks the base of the appendix on the surface?
questions.explanation: McBurney's point marks the base of the appendix and is located at the junction of the lateral third and medial two-thirds of a line from the right anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus. This is the point of maximum tenderness in acute appendicitis and guides the surgical incision. The tip of the appendix, however, can vary considerably in position.

questions.question: Which ligament prevents the ulna from articulating with the carpal bones at the wrist joint?
questions.explanation: The articular disk is a fibrocartilaginous structure that lies over the superior surface of the ulna. It effectively prevents direct articulation between the ulna and carpal bones at the wrist joint. The ulna therefore does not participate in the radiocarpal (wrist) joint, with articulation occurring only with the radius.

questions.question: Where does the internal thoracic artery arise?
questions.explanation: The internal thoracic (internal mammary) artery arises from the first part of the subclavian artery. It descends vertically behind the upper six costal cartilages, approximately 1 cm from the lateral border of the sternum. It gives off anterior intercostal arteries, perforating branches, and terminates as superior epigastric and musculophrenic arteries.

questions.question: Which artery supplies the distal third of the transverse colon?
questions.explanation: The left colic artery (from the inferior mesenteric artery) supplies the distal one-third of the transverse colon, descending colon, and left colic (splenic) flexure through its ascending branch. The ascending branch anastomoses with the left branch of the middle colic artery (from SMA) to complete the marginal artery of Drummond. This anastomosis at the splenic flexure (Griffiths' point) represents the watershed between superior and inferior mesenteric arterial territories and is vulnerable to ischemia. The splenic flexure may be relatively poorly supplied by collaterals, making it susceptible to ischemic colitis in low-flow states.

The transverse acetabular ligament bridges across the acetabular notch, converting it into a foramen for vessels and nerves, and serves as the base of attachment for the ligament of the head of femur (ligamentum teres). The acetabular labrum is a fibrocartilaginous rim attached to the margin of the acetabulum that deepens it.
questions.question: The transverse acetabular ligament converts the acetabular notch into a foramen. It also serves as the base of attachment for which intracapsular ligament?
Which structure separates the liver bare area from the diaphragm?
questions.explanation: In the bare area of the liver, there is no peritoneum between the liver and the diaphragm - they are in direct contact. This area is bounded by the superior and inferior layers of the coronary ligament. The direct contact allows potential spread of infection between the liver and thorax, and provides a route for extraperitoneal collateral circulation.

questions.question: When does the thymus reach maximum size?
questions.explanation: The thymus reaches its maximum size at puberty, after which it undergoes involution (gradual shrinkage). In adults, much of the thymic tissue is replaced by adipose tissue, though some functional tissue persists. Despite involution, the adult thymus continues to produce T cells, though at a reduced rate.

The thoracic duct carries approximately 1-2 liters of lymph per day (though this can increase significantly after meals due to chyle from intestinal lacteals). It is the largest lymphatic vessel in the body. Injury to the thoracic duct (from trauma or surgery) can result in significant chyle leakage into the pleural cavity (chylothorax).
questions.question: What is the thoracic duct's capacity?

questions.explanation: Goblet cells that secrete mucus are abundant in the large intestinal mucosa and increase in number toward the rectum. The mucus lubricates the passage of increasingly solid feces and protects the mucosa. Large intestinal crypts (of Lieberk?hn) lack villi and contain mainly goblet cells and absorptive colonocytes. Paneth cells are found only in the small intestine.
questions.question: Which cells are characteristic of the large intestinal mucosa?

questions.explanation: Two pulmonary veins (superior and inferior) emerge from each lung, for a total of four pulmonary veins entering the left atrium. These veins carry oxygenated blood from the lungs to the heart. The openings of the pulmonary veins into the left atrium have no valves.
questions.question: How many pulmonary veins emerge from each lung?

questions.explanation: The inferior orbital fissure connects the pterygopalatine fossa with the orbit. The fissure is bounded by the greater wing of sphenoid, maxilla, and palatine bone. The maxillary nerve continues through this fissure as the infraorbital nerve. The infraorbital and zygomatic nerves and vessels pass through this communication.
questions.question: The pterygopalatine fossa communicates with the orbit through which opening?

questions.explanation: Gluteus maximus has little action during ordinary gentle walking on level ground. It acts mainly in rising from sitting, straightening up, walking upstairs, and running. This is a critical clinical distinction in assessing gluteal function and designing rehabilitation after injury.
questions.question: Despite being the great extensor of the hip joint, gluteus maximus has little action during which of the following?

questions.explanation: The subclavian artery becomes the axillary artery at the lateral border of the first rib. The artery is divided into three parts by the anterior scalene muscle. The vertebral, internal thoracic, and thyrocervical trunk typically arise from the subclavian. The costocervical trunk arises from the second part posteriorly.
questions.question: The subclavian artery becomes the axillary artery at which landmark?
Which vessels form a groove on the posterior aspect of the pancreatic neck?
questions.explanation: The superior mesenteric vessels (artery and vein) form a groove on the posterior aspect of the pancreatic neck as they pass behind it. The neck is the constricted portion connecting the head to the body. Anteriorly, the neck is related to the pylorus of the stomach.

questions.question: The superior gluteal nerve (L4, L5, S1) supplies which muscles?
questions.explanation: The superior gluteal nerve (L4, L5, S1) supplies gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, and tensor fasciae latae. It exits the greater sciatic foramen above piriformis. Injury to this nerve (during posterior hip surgery or gluteal injections) causes Trendelenburg sign due to loss of hip abduction and medial rotation. It carries no cutaneous branches.
options: Gluteus medius, minimus, and tensor fasciae latae

questions.explanation: The urethral crest (crista urethralis) is a longitudinal midline ridge on the posterior wall of the prostatic urethra. Its most prominent part is the seminal colliculus (verumontanum), which contains the prostatic utricle and the openings of the ejaculatory ducts. The prostatic ducts open in grooves (prostatic sinuses) on either side of the crest.
questions.question: What is the urethral crest in the prostatic urethra?

questions.explanation: The costocervical trunk is a branch of the second part of the subclavian artery (posterior to scalenus anterior). It divides into the superior intercostal artery (supplying the first two intercostal spaces) and the deep cervical artery (supplying deep neck muscles). This trunk is important in collateral circulation.
questions.question: What is the costocervical trunk?

questions.explanation: The facial artery is the main arterial supply to the face, arising from the external carotid artery. It winds around the mandible anterior to the masseter and ascends toward the medial canthus. Branches include superior and inferior labial, lateral nasal, and angular arteries.
questions.question: Which artery is the main blood supply to the face?

questions.explanation: The deep fibular nerve supplies all four muscles of the anterior compartment of the leg. Its terminal sensory branch supplies the first web space (skin between the 1st and 2nd toes) on the dorsum of the foot. This small area of sensation is the clinical test for deep fibular nerve integrity. Compression from tight footwear or ankle swelling can selectively damage this nerve.
options: Medial side of the foot only
Lateral four toes of the dorsum
questions.question: The deep fibular nerve (L4, L5) supplies the anterior compartment of the leg and terminates on the dorsum of the foot. What is its terminal sensory distribution?

questions.explanation: The cricothyroid joint between the inferior horn of the thyroid cartilage and cricoid cartilage allows anteroposterior tilting (rotation). This movement elongates or shortens the vocal cords, changing their tension. Cricothyroid muscle contraction tilts the thyroid cartilage forward, tensing the cords. The joint is a synovial joint with a capsule and ligaments.
questions.question: The cricothyroid joint allows which movement?
How many posterior intercostal arteries does aorta give?
questions.explanation: The descending thoracic aorta gives off nine pairs of posterior intercostal arteries supplying the lower nine intercostal spaces (3rd-11th). The upper two spaces are supplied by the superior intercostal artery from the costocervical trunk. The subcostal arteries (below the 12th rib) are also given off by the thoracic aorta.

The falciform ligament divides the subphrenic space into right and left components, separating the right subphrenic space from the left. The right subphrenic space communicates posteriorly with the hepatorenal recess (Morison's pouch), the most dependent part of the peritoneal cavity in the supine position, making it a common site for fluid accumulation. The left subphrenic space is bounded by the falciform ligament on the right, the diaphragm superiorly and anteriorly, the stomach and spleen posteriorly, and the anterior layer of the left triangular ligament laterally.
questions.question: Which muscle separates the subphrenic from the subhepatic space?
Where is the cardiac notch located?
questions.explanation: The cardiac notch is a deep indentation on the anterior border of the left lung created by the apex of the heart. This notch is located at the level of the fourth costal cartilage. Below the cardiac notch, the lung forms a tongue-like projection called the lingula.

questions.question: Which vessels cross anterior to the third part of the duodenum?
questions.explanation: The superior mesenteric artery and vein cross anteriorly over the third (horizontal) part of the duodenum. This anatomical relationship can cause superior mesenteric artery (SMA) syndrome, where the duodenum is compressed between the SMA and the aorta, leading to intestinal obstruction. The third part of the duodenum passes from right to left across the vertebral column at L3.

questions.question: The medial pterygoid muscle inserts on which structure?
questions.explanation: The medial pterygoid muscle inserts on the medial surface of the mandibular angle and ramus, forming a sling with the masseter on the lateral surface. It arises from the medial surface of the lateral pterygoid plate and pterygoid fossa. The muscle elevates and protrudes the mandible. It is innervated by the nerve to medial pterygoid (V3).

The oesophagus is a muscular tube approximately 25 cm long extending from the cricoid cartilage to the stomach. This measurement represents the standard adult oesophageal length and is clinically important for endoscopic procedures. The length may vary slightly between individuals based on body habitus.
questions.question: What is the approximate length of the oesophagus in an adult?

questions.explanation: The pre-aortic (preaortic) lymph nodes, located around the origins of the three major unpaired visceral branches of the aorta (celiac, superior mesenteric, and inferior mesenteric arteries), drain all abdominal viscera along the gastrointestinal tract from esophagus to upper anal canal, plus the liver, pancreas, and spleen. These nodes are grouped as celiac, superior mesenteric, and inferior mesenteric nodes. Efferent vessels from these nodes form the intestinal lymphatic trunk, which drains into the cisterna chyli. The cisterna chyli then gives rise to the thoracic duct.
questions.question: Which lymphatic structure drains most abdominal viscera?

questions.explanation: The pericardial cavity normally contains 15-50 ml of serous pericardial fluid that lubricates the surfaces of the visceral and parietal pericardium, reducing friction during cardiac contraction. Excessive fluid accumulation (pericardial effusion) or rapid accumulation of even small volumes can cause cardiac tamponade with hemodynamic compromise.
questions.question: What does the pericardial cavity normally contain?

questions.explanation: The pulmonary plexuses (anterior and posterior to the roots of the lungs) contain both parasympathetic fibers from the vagus nerve and sympathetic fibers from the sympathetic trunk. These plexuses provide the autonomic innervation to the lungs and bronchial tree. The visceral pleura receives only vasomotor supply from these nerves.
questions.question: Which plexus provides autonomic supply to lungs?
Which muscle produces pronation of the forearm?
questions.explanation: Pronation of the forearm is produced by pronator teres and pronator quadratus muscles. Pronator teres is more powerful and acts during rapid or forceful pronation. Pronator quadratus maintains pronation during slow movements and is the primary pronator during unresisted pronation.

questions.question: The hepatic portal vein is formed posterior to which structure?
questions.explanation: The hepatic portal vein forms posterior to the neck of the pancreas at approximately the L1/L2 level through the confluence of the superior mesenteric vein (from the right) and splenic vein (from the left), anterior to the inferior vena cava. The inferior mesenteric vein typically joins the splenic vein before this confluence. From its formation, the portal vein ascends obliquely to the right within the hepatoduodenal ligament to reach the porta hepatis, where it divides into right and left branches. The portal vein measures approximately 8 cm in length and has no valves.

Peyer's patches are aggregated lymphoid nodules characteristic of the ileum, especially prominent in the terminal ileum. These are permanent features of the gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT) that play a crucial role in intestinal immunity. Peyer's patches are absent in the jejunum and located on the antimesenteric border of the ileum.
questions.question: Which lymphoid structures are characteristic of the terminal ileum?

questions.explanation: The interureteric ridge (interureteric fold) is a smooth muscular ridge connecting the two ureteric orifices and forms the posterior boundary (base) of the trigone. The trigone is a smooth triangular area on the internal bladder base with the two ureteric orifices forming the superolateral angles and the internal urethral orifice forming the inferior angle.
questions.question: Which structure forms the posterior boundary of the bladder trigone?
What provides the blood supply to the radial nerve in the arm?
questions.explanation: The profunda brachii (deep brachial) artery accompanies the radial nerve through the spiral groove, providing its blood supply in the arm. Both structures wind around the posterior humerus together. Injury to the artery often accompanies radial nerve damage in humeral fractures.

The cochlear aqueduct (perilymphatic duct) connects the scala tympani with the subarachnoid space, allowing communication between perilymph and cerebrospinal fluid. The aqueduct opens at the base of the petrous temporal bone. The vestibular aqueduct separately connects the endolymphatic system with the posterior cranial fossa. Patency varies among individuals.
questions.question: The cochlear aqueduct connects the scala tympani with which space?

questions.explanation: The thoracic duct begins as the cisterna chyli anterior to L1 vertebra, formed by lumbar and intestinal trunks. It ascends through the aortic hiatus into the thorax. At the root of the neck, it arches forward to enter the left venous angle (junction of left internal jugular and subclavian veins).
questions.question: The thoracic duct begins at which vertebral level?

questions.explanation: The marginal zone, located between the white pulp and red pulp, contains specialized marginal zone B lymphocytes and macrophages that capture blood-borne antigens and particulate matter. It is the first site of contact between blood-borne antigens and the immune system. Marginal zone B cells can rapidly differentiate into antibody-producing cells without requiring T cell help.
questions.question: What is the function of the marginal zone in the spleen?
What is the approximate weight of an adult liver?
questions.explanation: The adult liver weighs approximately 1500 grams, constituting about 2.5% of total body weight in healthy adults. The liver is the largest internal organ and the largest gland in the human body. In newborns, the liver is proportionally larger, contributing to the characteristic protuberant abdomen of infants.

All the abdominal wall muscles work together to increase intra-abdominal pressure: the diaphragm contracts and descends, while the rectus abdominis, external oblique, internal oblique, and transversus abdominis contract simultaneously to compress the abdominal contents. This coordinated action is essential for defecation, micturition, parturition (childbirth), coughing, sneezing, and vomiting. The transversus abdominis is particularly important for this function. Weakness of abdominal wall muscles (from aging, pregnancy, or surgery) can impair these functions and predispose to hernias.
questions.question: Which muscle assists in raising intra-abdominal pressure?

questions.explanation: The gastrohepatic ligament (pars flaccida) forms the membranous portion of the lesser omentum, extending from the lesser curvature of the stomach and first part of the duodenum to the liver (extending to the fissure for ligamentum venosum and porta hepatis). It contains the right and left gastric vessels along the lesser curvature, and in some individuals, an aberrant or replaced left hepatic artery arising from the left gastric artery. The lesser omentum is continuous with the hepatoduodenal ligament (pars condensa), which forms its thickened free right edge containing the portal triad.
questions.question: Which ligament connects the lesser curvature of the stomach to the liver?

questions.explanation: The puboprostatic ligaments extend from the posterior aspect of the pubic bones to the prostate and bladder neck in males, anchoring these structures. In females, the equivalent structures are the pubovesical ligaments. The lateral ligaments of the bladder (containing superior vesical vessels) also contribute to bladder support and fixation.
questions.question: Which ligaments anchor the bladder neck in males?

questions.explanation: The medial palmar septum joins the border of the palmar aponeurosis to the palmar border of the third metacarpal bone. This septum separates the thenar space (thumb side) from the midpalmar space (ulnar side). Each space contains specific flexor tendons and lumbrical muscles.
questions.question: Which structure separates the thenar and midpalmar spaces of the hand?

options: Medial knee pain from tibial collateral ligament strain
Lateral patellar tracking with patellofemoral syndrome
questions.question: The Q angle (quadriceps angle) is the angle between the line of pull of the quadriceps and the patellar ligament. An increased Q angle predisposes to which condition?
questions.explanation: An increased Q angle (measured from the anterior superior iliac spine to the midpoint of the patella, then to the tibial tuberosity) predisposes to lateral patellar tracking, increasing lateral patellofemoral contact pressure and causing patellofemoral syndrome (anterior knee pain). Women generally have larger Q angles due to their wider pelvis. VMO weakness and foot overpronation exacerbate this problem.

questions.question: Which structure passes through the oesophageal hiatus?
questions.explanation: The oesophageal hiatus is located at the T10 level in the muscular part of the right crus of the diaphragm. It transmits the oesophagus, anterior and posterior vagal trunks, oesophageal branches of the left gastric vessels, and lymphatic vessels. The muscular sling of the right crus acts as a physiological sphincter, helping prevent gastroesophageal reflux.

questions.question: Into which lymph nodes does the bladder apex drain?
questions.explanation: Lymph from the superior surface and apex of the bladder drains to external iliac lymph nodes. The fundus drains to internal iliac nodes, while the neck drains to sacral and common iliac nodes. This drainage pattern is clinically important in bladder cancer staging and determining the extent of lymph node dissection required.

questions.question: How do the thenar and hypothenar muscles differ functionally?
questions.explanation: Thenar muscles provide thumb mobility essential for opposition and precision grip. Hypothenar muscles provide little finger mobility and contribute to power grip by cupping the hand. The specialized thumb movements made possible by thenar muscles are uniquely human characteristics.
options: Thenar for thumb mobility/opposition, hypothenar for little finger mobility
Thenar for power, hypothenar for precision
Thenar for extension, hypothenar for flexion

questions.question: What is the normal carrying angle of the fully extended forearm?
questions.explanation: The long axis of the fully extended ulna makes an angle of approximately 170 degrees with the long axis of the humerus. This carrying angle represents the way the forearm angles away from the body when carrying objects. The obliquity is more pronounced in females than males.

questions.question: The gastroduodenal artery typically arises from which vessel?
questions.explanation: The gastroduodenal artery arises from the common hepatic artery (distal to the origin of the gastric and splenic arteries but proximal to the bifurcation into hepatic artery proper and gastroduodenal artery). It descends posterior to the first part of the duodenum, where it divides into two terminal branches: the right gastroepiploic artery (running along the greater curvature) and the superior pancreaticoduodenal artery (supplying the pancreatic head and duodenum). The gastroduodenal artery is intimately related to the posterior wall of the duodenal bulb and can erode into this vessel, causing life-threatening hemorrhage.

The facial artery crosses the inferior border of the mandible at the anterior edge of the masseter muscle, where its pulse can be palpated. After crossing, it ascends toward the medial canthus as the angular artery. The artery winds around the mandible from the neck to reach the face. Facial vein crosses more anteriorly.
questions.question: The facial artery crosses which border of the mandible?
Which muscle forms the floor of the oral cavity?
questions.explanation: The mylohyoid muscle forms the muscular floor of the oral cavity, separating it from the neck. It arises from the mylohyoid line of the mandible and inserts into the median raphe and hyoid bone. The muscle is innervated by the mylohyoid nerve from the mandibular division. It elevates the floor of the mouth during swallowing.

questions.question: What is the typical capacity of an adult urinary bladder?
questions.explanation: The adult urinary bladder has a capacity of approximately 400-600 ml, with the desire to void typically occurring at about 150-250 ml and strong urgency at 400-500 ml. The bladder is highly distensible due to its muscular wall (detrusor muscle) and transitional epithelium lining. Capacity can be reduced in pathological conditions or increased with chronic retention.

Bronchial and pulmonary arteries anastomose at the precapillary level, creating connections between the systemic and pulmonary circulations. This anastomosis allows some mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood. The bronchial circulation comprises only about 1-2% of cardiac output.
questions.question: At which level do bronchial arteries anastomose?

questions.explanation: The rectovesical pouch (between bladder and rectum in males) is the lowest part of the peritoneal cavity when standing or sitting and is a common site for fluid collection, abscesses, or metastatic deposits. In females, the rectouterine pouch (of Douglas) is even deeper and is the most dependent peritoneal space, which can be accessed via the posterior vaginal fornix.
questions.question: Which pouch in males is the most dependent peritoneal space?

questions.explanation: The septal cusp of the tricuspid valve is attached to the interventricular septum, while the anterior and posterior cusps are attached to the anterior and posterior ventricular walls respectively. The septal cusp receives chordae tendineae from the septal and posterior papillary muscles. Ventricular septal defects near the membranous septum can affect this cusp's support.
questions.question: Which valve cusp is attached to the interventricular septum?

questions.explanation: The cisterna chyli (receptaculum chyli) receives the intestinal trunk (draining abdominal viscera via pre-aortic nodes), right and left lumbar trunks (draining lower limbs, pelvis, and posterior abdominal wall), and sometimes the lower intercostal lymphatic trunks. It represents a dilated sac at the origin of the thoracic duct, located at L1-L2 level, anterior to the vertebral column, posterior and to the right of the aorta, posterior to the right crus of the diaphragm. The thoracic duct ascends from the cisterna through the aortic hiatus to traverse the posterior mediastinum and drain into the junction of left subclavian and internal jugular veins.
questions.question: The cisterna chyli receives lymph from which trunks?

questions.explanation: The ovarian ligament (ligament of the ovary) connects the ovary to the uterus, extending from the uterine pole of the ovary to the lateral angle of the uterus just below the uterine tube attachment. It represents the proximal remnant of the gubernaculum (the distal remnant becoming the round ligament of the uterus). The ligament lies within the broad ligament (between its layers) and contains no significant vessels. The suspensory ligament of the ovary (infundibulopelvic ligament) connects the ovary to the lateral pelvic wall and contains the ovarian vessels; it is not directly attached to the uterus.
questions.question: Which ligament connects the ovary to the uterus?
Which muscle forms the lateral boundary of the femoral triangle?
questions.explanation: The femoral triangle is bounded laterally by the sartorius muscle, medially by the adductor longus muscle, and superiorly by the inguinal ligament. The floor is formed by iliopsoas (laterally) and pectineus (medially), covered by fascia. The roof is formed by fascia lata. The triangle contains (from lateral to medial): femoral Nerve, Artery, Vein, Empty space/lymphatics (NAVEL mnemonic). The femoral artery, vein, and canal lie within the femoral sheath (prolongation of transversalis and iliacus fascia), while the femoral nerve lies lateral to the sheath. Understanding this anatomy is crucial for femoral vessel access.

The body and tail of the pancreas receive arterial supply from the splenic artery through numerous small pancreatic branches (dorsal pancreatic, greater pancreatic, caudal pancreatic arteries) as the splenic artery courses along the superior border of the pancreas. The head of the pancreas is supplied by the superior and inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries forming anterior and posterior arcades. The pancreas has a rich blood supply with extensive anastomoses, though the pancreatic neck region may be relatively less vascular. The intimate relationship between the splenic artery and pancreas means that pancreatic pathology can affect the artery.
questions.question: Which artery supplies the body of the pancreas?
Which muscle forms the deepest layer of the anterior abdominal wall?
questions.explanation: The transversus abdominis is the deepest of the three flat muscles of the anterior abdominal wall (external oblique, internal oblique, transversus), with horizontally oriented fibers. Its aponeurosis joins the linea alba and contributes to the rectus sheath (anterior leaf above arcuate line, anterior to rectus below arcuate line). Deep to the transversus lies the transversalis fascia. The transversus is particularly important for increasing intra-abdominal pressure and core stability. The rectus abdominis and pyramidalis are vertical muscles lying anterior to the posterior rectus sheath (when present).

questions.question: Through which opening does the sympathetic trunk enter the abdomen?
questions.explanation: The sympathetic trunks enter the abdomen from the thorax by passing deep to (posterior to) the medial arcuate ligaments. They descend on the anterolateral aspects of the lumbar vertebral bodies, giving off lumbar splanchnic nerves. The greater and lesser splanchnic nerves pierce the crura to enter the abdomen.

questions.question: Which of the following muscles is NOT among the six small lateral rotators of the hip joint?
questions.explanation: The six small lateral rotators of the hip joint are: quadratus femoris, obturator internus, gemellus superior, gemellus inferior, obturator externus, and piriformis. Gluteus medius is primarily an abductor and medial rotator of the hip, not a lateral rotator. Gluteus medius is sometimes referred to as the 'rotator cuff of the hip' for its stabilizing role.

options: It is a single band with one attachment to the calcaneus
It has tibionavicular, tibiocalcaneal, and anterior and posterior tibiotalar parts
It consists only of the tibionavicular and posterior tibiotalar parts
It is a triangular ligament with apex on the fibula
It attaches from the fibula to the navicular, calcaneus, and talus
questions.question: The medial ligament of the ankle joint is called the deltoid ligament. Which statement correctly describes its four components?
questions.explanation: The deltoid ligament is the medial ligament of the ankle, a strong triangular ligament with its apex on the medial malleolus. It has four parts: tibionavicular (to navicular), tibiocalcaneal (to sustentaculum tali of calcaneus), and anterior and posterior tibiotalar parts (to the talus). It is significantly stronger than the lateral ligaments and rarely ruptures in isolation.

The cisterna chyli (receptaculum chyli), a dilated lymphatic sac at the origin of the thoracic duct, is located anterior to the bodies of L1 and L2 vertebrae, posterior to the right crus of the diaphragm and the abdominal aorta, and to the right of the aorta. It receives the right and left lumbar lymphatic trunks (draining lower limbs, pelvic, and abdominal walls), the intestinal trunk (from pre-aortic nodes draining abdominal viscera), and sometimes the lower intercostal trunks. The thoracic duct ascends from the cisterna through the aortic hiatus to enter the posterior mediastinum, ultimately draining into the junction of the left subclavian and internal jugular veins.
questions.question: The cisterna chyli is located at which vertebral level?

questions.explanation: The lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm is the sensory continuation of the musculocutaneous nerve after it supplies the anterior arm muscles. It provides sensation to the lateral aspect of the forearm from elbow to wrist. This nerve emerges lateral to the biceps tendon in the cubital fossa.
questions.question: What provides sensory innervation to the lateral forearm?

questions.explanation: The base of the heart is formed primarily by the left atrium and a small portion of the right atrium. It is the posterior surface facing the vertebral column and esophagus. The four pulmonary veins enter the left atrium at the base. The term "base" refers to the posterior aspect, opposite to the apex, not to the inferior surface.
questions.question: Which chamber primarily forms the base of the heart?

questions.explanation: The superior and inferior lingular segments of the left upper lobe are anatomically equivalent to the middle lobe of the right lung. The lingula is a tongue-like projection of the left upper lobe that occupies the space below the cardiac notch. Both are supplied similarly by their respective bronchi.
questions.question: What are the lingular segments?
Which structure forms the roof of the inguinal canal?
questions.explanation: The roof of the inguinal canal is formed by the arching lowest fibers of the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles, along with contributions from the transversalis fascia. These arching fibers cross from lateral to medial, forming the superior boundary of the canal. The internal oblique muscle also contributes to the anterior wall laterally, where its fibers arise from the inguinal ligament. The conjoint tendon (formed by the fusion of internal oblique and transversus abdominis aponeuroses) reinforces the posterior wall medially but does not form the roof.

questions.question: Which part of the large intestine is completely intraperitoneal?
questions.explanation: The transverse colon is completely invested by peritoneum and suspended by the transverse mesocolon, making it freely mobile. This complete peritoneal covering classifies it as intraperitoneal. The ascending and descending colons are retroperitoneal, while the sigmoid colon and appendix also have mesenteries.

questions.question: Which muscle is NOT supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve?
questions.explanation: is supplied by the median nerve, not the musculocutaneous nerve. The musculocutaneous nerve supplies only three muscles: biceps brachii, brachialis, and coracobrachialis (BBC). After supplying these muscles, it continues as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm.

The anterior arch of the atlas (C1) has a facet on its posterior surface that articulates with the dens (odontoid process) of the axis (C2). The transverse ligament of the atlas holds the dens against this facet. This atlantoaxial joint allows rotation of the head. Fracture or ligamentous injury can cause atlantoaxial instability.
questions.question: The anterior arch of C1 articulates with which structure?
What nerve supplies serratus anterior?
questions.explanation: The long thoracic nerve (C5, C6, C7) supplies serratus anterior, giving branches to each muscle digitation. The nerve descends on the superficial surface of the muscle and is vulnerable to injury during axillary surgery. Damage causes scapular winging.

questions.question: What are the splanchnic nerves?
questions.explanation: The splanchnic nerves are branches of the thoracic sympathetic trunk that carry preganglionic sympathetic fibers to the abdominal viscera. The greater splanchnic nerve arises from T5-9 ganglia, the lesser from T10-11, and the least (when present) from T12. They pierce the diaphragm to reach abdominal ganglia.

The lateral wall of the ischiorectal (ischioanal) fossa is formed by the obturator internus muscle covered by obturator fascia, which contains the pudendal canal (Alcock's canal) housing the pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels. The medial wall is formed by the levator ani and external anal sphincter. The fossa is bounded posteriorly by the gluteus maximus and sacrotuberous ligament, anteriorly by the posterior border of the urogenital diaphragm, and inferiorly by skin. The fossa contains fat and is a potential space for abscess formation.
questions.question: Which muscle forms the lateral wall of the ischiorectal fossa?
The common bile duct passes posterior to which part of the duodenum?
questions.explanation: The common bile duct descends posterior to the first (superior) part of the duodenum (retroduodenal portion), then continues behind or embedded in the posterior surface of the head of the pancreas (infraduodenal portion). It finally passes through the wall of the second (descending) part of the duodenum (intraduodenal portion), joining the main pancreatic duct to form the hepatopancreatic ampulla, which opens at the major duodenal papilla. This posterior relationship means that duodenal ulcers in the first part can erode into the bile duct or gastroduodenal artery. The duct's pancreatic portion may be compressed by pancreatic head tumors.

questions.question: Which muscle forms the lateral boundary of the cubital fossa?
questions.explanation: The medial border of the brachioradialis muscle forms the lateral (radial) boundary of the cubital fossa. This muscle is a prominent flexor of the forearm that also assists with both pronation and supination from mid-position. It originates from the lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus.

options: Cephalic vein, lateral pectoral nerve, thoracoacromial artery
questions.question: Which structures pierce the costocoracoid membrane of the clavipectoral fascia?
questions.explanation: The costocoracoid membrane portion of clavipectoral fascia between pectoralis minor and subclavius is pierced by three structures. These are the lateral pectoral nerve, the pectoral branch of the thoracoacromial artery, and the cephalic vein joining the axillary vein. This membrane is continuous with the suspensory ligament of the axilla inferiorly.

The visceral pleura receives its arterial supply from branches of both the bronchial and pulmonary arterial systems. Venous drainage is to the pulmonary veins. Unlike the parietal pleura, the visceral pleura has no somatic sensory innervation and receives only autonomic vasomotor nerve supply.
questions.question: Which vessels supply blood to the visceral pleura?

options: Anterior and posterior circumflex humeral plus suprascapular
questions.question: What provides the primary blood supply to the rotator cuff?
questions.explanation: The rotator cuff receives blood supply from three main sources: anterior circumflex humeral artery, posterior circumflex humeral artery, and suprascapular artery. A critical zone exists in the supraspinatus tendon with relatively poor vascularity, predisposing this area to degeneration and tears.

questions.question: Which muscle is responsible for intorsion of the eye?
questions.explanation: The superior oblique is the primary intortor of the eye, also producing depression and abduction. The muscle passes through the trochlea before inserting on the posterolateral superior eyeball. It is innervated by the trochlear nerve (IV). Superior oblique palsy causes vertical diplopia, worse on downward gaze and head tilt to the affected side.

The phrenic nerve (C3, C4, C5) provides sensory innervation to the central diaphragm, including both the pleural and peritoneal surfaces, in addition to its motor supply to the entire diaphragm. Irritation of the diaphragmatic peritoneum (such as in subphrenic abscess, perforated peptic ulcer, or ruptured spleen) can cause referred pain to the shoulder tip via the phrenic nerve, as both derive from the C3-C5 dermatomes. The peripheral parts of the diaphragm receive sensory innervation from the lower six intercostal nerves and subcostal nerve.
questions.question: Which nerve provides sensory innervation to the central part of the diaphragm?
The lesser omentum has two parts, which are:
questions.explanation: The lesser omentum consists of two continuous portions: the gastrohepatic ligament (pars flaccida, the membranous portion extending from lesser curvature of stomach to liver) and the hepatoduodenal ligament (pars condensa, the thickened free right edge containing the portal triad extending from first part of duodenum to porta hepatis). These two parts form a continuous peritoneal fold connecting the stomach and proximal duodenum to the liver, and together they form the anterior boundary of the lesser sac and epiploic foramen. The lesser omentum develops from the ventral mesentery and contains the portal triad in its free edge.

questions.question: The celiac ganglion receives preganglionic fibers via which nerve?
questions.explanation: The celiac ganglion, the largest of the prevertebral (preaortic) ganglia, receives preganglionic sympathetic fibers primarily via the greater splanchnic nerve (T5-T9), with contributions from the lesser splanchnic nerve (T10-T11). These preganglionic fibers synapse in the ganglion, and postganglionic fibers distribute along arterial branches from the celiac trunk to supply foregut derivatives. The vagus nerve also contributes parasympathetic fibers to the celiac plexus, but these pass through without synapsing. The celiac plexus surrounds the origin of the celiac trunk and is the largest autonomic plexus in the body.

The pterygopalatine ganglion hangs from the maxillary nerve (V2) by two pterygopalatine (sensory) branches in the pterygopalatine fossa. Parasympathetic fibers arrive via the nerve of the pterygoid canal (greater petrosal + deep petrosal). Postganglionic fibers supply the lacrimal gland and nasal/palatine mucosa. Sympathetic fibers pass through without synapsing.
questions.question: The pterygopalatine ganglion is suspended from which nerve?

questions.explanation: The sacrotuberous ligament and sacrospinous ligament, in conjunction with bones, form both the greater and lesser sciatic foramina. They primarily stabilize the sacrum and prevent its rotation at the sacroiliac joint under the weight of the vertebral column. These ligaments are critical surgical landmarks in posterior pelvic surgery.
questions.question: Which two ligaments, combined with bones, form both the greater and lesser sciatic foramina?
Which muscle opens the jaw against resistance?
questions.explanation: The lateral pterygoid assists in opening the jaw against resistance (along with gravity, mylohyoid, geniohyoid, and anterior belly of digastric). The suprahyoid muscles provide the main force when opening against resistance. Lateral pterygoid protrudes and depresses the mandible. All other muscles of mastication (masseter, temporalis, medial pterygoid) close the jaw.

The external acoustic meatus measures approximately 2.9 cm in length from the concha to the tympanic membrane. The lateral one-third is cartilaginous containing cerumen glands, while the medial two-thirds is bony. Understanding this anatomy is essential for safe otoscopic examination and foreign body removal.
questions.question: The external acoustic meatus is what total length?
What is the primary muscle for scapular retraction?
questions.explanation: Retraction (adduction) of the scapula is produced by combined action of middle fibers of trapezius and the rhomboid muscles. During retraction, the lateral end of the clavicle moves backward along with the scapula. This movement is important for pulling actions.

The fossa ovalis is the remnant of the foramen ovale, which allowed blood to bypass the fetal lungs by shunting from the right to left atrium in utero. Functional closure occurs at birth with the first breath, though anatomical fusion may take months to years. A patent foramen ovale persists in about 25% of adults without usually causing problems.
questions.question: What is the fossa ovalis a remnant of?
Where in the small intestine is iron primarily absorbed?
questions.explanation: Iron is primarily absorbed in the duodenum and proximal jejunum as ferrous iron (Fe2+). Gastric acid helps convert ferric (Fe3+) to ferrous iron for absorption. Vitamin C enhances absorption while phytates and tannins inhibit it. Heme iron from meat is absorbed more efficiently than non-heme iron from plant sources.

The mylohyoid muscle forms the muscular floor (diaphragm) of the oral cavity, creating the mylohyoid raphe in the midline. The muscle elevates the floor during swallowing and depresses the mandible when the hyoid is fixed. Above the mylohyoid lie the tongue and genioglossus; below lie the geniohyoid and digastric. Mylohyoid nerve (V3) provides innervation.
questions.question: Which muscle forms the floor of the mouth?

options: They allow free rotation between tibia and fibula
They maintain tibiofibular mortise integrity for stable talus articulation
They create the lateral wall of the ankle
They only protect the interosseous vessels
They provide primary stability against valgus stress
questions.explanation: The tibiofibular ligament (syndesmosis) and interosseous membrane maintain the integrity of the tibiofibular mortise, ensuring that the distal tibia and fibula remain properly spaced for stable articulation with the trochlea tali. Disruption of the syndesmosis (high ankle sprain or Maisonneuve fracture) significantly destabilizes the ankle joint and requires surgical fixation.
questions.question: The tibiofibular ligament and interosseous membrane form part of the ankle joint supports. These structures maintain which relationship between the tibia and fibula at the ankle?

questions.explanation: The anterior and lateral cutaneous branches of the 4th to 6th intercostal nerves supply the breast. These nerves convey sensory fibers to the skin, sympathetic fibers to blood vessels, and fibers to smooth muscle in the overlying skin and nipple. Pain from breast pathology follows these dermatomes.
questions.question: Which intercostal nerves supply the breast?

questions.explanation: The superior surface of the diaphragm receives arterial supply from the pericardiacophrenic and musculophrenic arteries (both branches of the internal thoracic artery) and superior phrenic arteries (from the thoracic aorta). The musculophrenic artery runs along the costal attachments of the diaphragm. The inferior surface is supplied by the inferior phrenic arteries from the abdominal aorta.
questions.question: Which artery supplies the superior surface of the diaphragm?

questions.explanation: The AV node is located in the lower part of the interatrial septum, within the triangle of Koch (bounded by the tricuspid annulus, coronary sinus orifice, and tendon of Todaro). It receives the impulse from the SA node and, after a physiological delay allowing atrial contraction, transmits it to the ventricles via the bundle of His. Its blood supply is typically from the right coronary artery.
questions.question: Where is the AV node situated?
Which nerve provides motor innervation to the palatoglossus muscle?
questions.explanation: The palatoglossus muscle is supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (vagus nerve via cranial accessory), not the hypoglossal nerve like other tongue muscles. This exception makes it technically a palatal muscle rather than a tongue muscle. The pharyngeal plexus supplies all soft palate muscles except tensor veli palatini.

The occipital artery, a branch of the external carotid, supplies the posterior scalp. It ascends on the back of the neck, pierces the trapezius attachment, and runs in the dense connective tissue layer of the scalp. The artery accompanies the greater occipital nerve. Scalp lacerations in this region can cause significant bleeding.
questions.question: Which vessel supplies the scalp in the occipital region?

options: IGA, obturator artery, MFCA, and LFCA branches
SGA, IGA, MFCA, and LFCA arterial branches
IGA, MFCA, LFCA, and 1st perforating branch of profunda femoris
SGA, IGA, obturator, and 1st perforating branch
MFCA, LFCA, popliteal, and descending genicular
questions.explanation: The cruciate anastomosis at the level of the lesser trochanter is constituted by four arteries: inferior gluteal artery (IGA), medial femoral circumflex artery (MFCA), lateral femoral circumflex artery (LFCA), and the first perforating branch of the profunda femoris artery. Together with the trochanteric anastomosis, it provides collateral circulation between the internal iliac and femoral artery systems.
questions.question: The cruciate anastomosis is at the level of the lesser trochanter. Which four arteries specifically constitute this anastomosis?

questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve supplies all the interossei (palmar and dorsal) and the medial two lumbricals (to ring and little fingers). It also supplies the hypothenar muscles, adductor pollicis, and the medial head of flexor pollicis brevis. The lateral two lumbricals are supplied by the median nerve.
questions.question: Which intrinsic hand muscles are supplied by the ulnar nerve?
options: All interossei and medial two lumbricals

questions.explanation: The conjoint tendon (inguinal falx) is formed by the fusion of the aponeuroses of the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles, inserting onto the pubic crest and pectineal line. This tendon reinforces the posterior wall of the inguinal canal in its medial third, opposite the superficial inguinal ring. Weakness or absence of the conjoint tendon in the area medial to the inferior epigastric artery predisposes to direct inguinal hernias, which protrude through Hesselbach's triangle bounded by the lateral border of rectus abdominis, inguinal ligament, and inferior epigastric vessels.
questions.question: Which muscle fibers form the conjoint tendon?
