questions.explanation: The first (medial) lumbrical is innervated by the medial plantar nerve (S2, S3), while the lateral three lumbricals are supplied by the lateral plantar nerve (S2, S3). The lumbricals originate from the tendons of flexor digitorum longus and insert into the medial aspect of the extensor expansion over the lateral four digits. Their dual action balances flexion and extension.
questions.question: The lumbricals of the foot flex the proximal phalanges and extend the middle and distal phalanges of the lateral four digits. The first lumbrical is innervated by which nerve?
The mental foramen typically lies below which tooth?
questions.explanation: The mental foramen is typically located on the lateral surface of the mandible below the second premolar tooth or between the first and second premolars. It transmits the mental nerve and vessels (terminal branches of the inferior alveolar neurovascular bundle). The foramen position varies with age and tooth loss. It is a landmark for inferior alveolar nerve block.

options: Anterior tibiotalar, posterior tibiotalar, and calcaneofibular
Anterior talofibular, tibiocalcaneal, and posterior talofibular
Anterior talofibular, posterior talofibular, and calcaneofibular
questions.question: The lateral ligaments of the ankle include which three named ligaments?
questions.explanation: The lateral ligaments of the ankle are: the anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL), the posterior talofibular ligament (PTFL), and the calcaneofibular ligament (CFL). The ATFL is the weakest and most commonly injured in ankle sprains. The CFL is the intermediate in strength, and the PTFL is the strongest. Together they stabilize the lateral side of the ankle joint.

questions.question: At which constriction does aortic arch cross?
questions.explanation: The second constriction is where the aortic arch lies anterior to the esophagus (22 cm from incisors, T4 level). The third is where the left main bronchus crosses anteriorly (27 cm from incisors). The fourth is at the diaphragmatic hiatus (38-40 cm from incisors, T10 level).

questions.question: Which muscle elevates the first rib?
questions.explanation: The scalene muscles fix and elevate the first rib during inspiration. With the first rib fixed, the external and internal intercostal muscles elevate the other ribs upward toward it. The scalene muscles are accessory muscles of respiration and are particularly active during forced inspiration.

Elevation of the scapula is caused by contraction of upper and middle fibers of trapezius and levator scapulae muscles. This movement is associated with elevation of the lateral end and depression of the medial end of the clavicle. Shoulder shrugging demonstrates this action.
questions.question: Which muscles elevate the scapula?
options: Upper and middle trapezius, levator scapulae

questions.explanation: The azygos vein lies posterior and to the right of the esophagus in the posterior mediastinum. The descending aorta lies posterior and to the left of the esophagus. The thoracic duct lies posterior to the esophagus. The vagus nerves form plexuses around the esophagus.
questions.question: Which vein lies posterior to the esophagus?

questions.explanation: The superior boundary of the epiploic foramen (foramen of Winslow) is formed by the caudate lobe (caudate process) of the liver covered with peritoneum. The inferior boundary is the first part of the duodenum, the anterior boundary is the hepatoduodenal ligament containing the portal triad, and the posterior boundary is the inferior vena cava covered with parietal peritoneum along with the right crus of the diaphragm. The foramen provides communication between the greater and lesser peritoneal sacs and typically admits two fingers, serving as a surgical landmark and potential route for accessing the lesser sac.
questions.question: Which structure forms the superior boundary of the epiploic foramen?

questions.explanation: The saphenous nerve, the longest cutaneous branch of the femoral nerve, descends within the adductor canal and then exits with the saphenous branch of the descending genicular artery to supply the medial side of the leg and foot. The adductor canal also transmits the femoral artery and vein. The saphenous nerve also supplies the knee joint via its branch to the articular capsule.
questions.question: The adductor canal (subsartorial or Hunter's canal) transmits structures from the femoral triangle to the popliteal fossa. Which nerve within it supplies the knee joint and descends within it?

questions.explanation: The perforating branches of the profunda femoris artery consist of three or four arteries that perforate the adductor magnus muscle, contributing to the supply of the medial and posterior thigh muscles. The lateral femoral circumflex artery supplies the lateral thigh, while the medial femoral circumflex artery supplies the femoral head and neck.
questions.question: The perforating branches of the profunda femoris artery perforate which muscle to supply the posterior and medial thigh?

questions.explanation: The frontal sinus drains through the frontonasal duct into the middle meatus via the infundibulum and hiatus semilunaris. Obstruction of this drainage pathway can lead to frontal sinusitis. The hiatus semilunaris is a curved groove in the lateral nasal wall.
questions.question: The frontal sinus drains into which nasal structure?

questions.explanation: The testicular arteries (and ovarian arteries in females) arise from the anterior aspect of the abdominal aorta at the L2 vertebral level, just inferior to the renal arteries. This high origin reflects the embryological development of the gonads on the posterior abdominal wall before testicular descent or ovarian migration. The long testicular arteries descend obliquely across the psoas major, ureter, and external iliac vessels, enter the deep inguinal ring, and travel through the inguinal canal as part of the spermatic cord to reach the testes in the scrotum.
questions.question: The testicular artery arises at which vertebral level?
Which muscles, posteriorly related to the hip joint, separate it from the sciatic nerve?
options: Obturator internus, gemelli, and quadratus femoris
questions.explanation: Posteriorly, the obturator internus, the gemelli, and the quadratus femoris separate the hip joint from the sciatic nerve. Superiorly, piriformis and gluteus minimus are related. Anteriorly, iliopsoas, pectineus, and rectus femoris are anterior relations. Inferiorly, the tendon of obturator externus is found. These relations are vital during posterior hip surgery.

The auriculotemporal nerve is a branch of the posterior division of the mandibular nerve (V3). It carries postganglionic parasympathetic fibers from the otic ganglion to the parotid gland. The nerve provides sensation to the temporal region, auricle, and temporomandibular joint. Misdirected regeneration causes Frey's syndrome.
questions.question: The auriculotemporal nerve is a branch of which division?
Where does the spongy urethra begin?
questions.explanation: The spongy (penile) urethra begins where the membranous urethra exits the urogenital diaphragm and extends through the corpus spongiosum to the external urethral meatus at the tip of the glans penis. It is approximately 15 cm long and has two dilated portions: the intrabulbar fossa in the bulb and the navicular fossa in the glans.

questions.question: The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies all laryngeal muscles EXCEPT which one?
questions.explanation: The cricothyroid muscle is supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, not the recurrent laryngeal. All other intrinsic laryngeal muscles receive innervation from the recurrent laryngeal nerve. The cricothyroid is also the only intrinsic muscle located externally on the larynx.

questions.question: The infraorbital nerve is a continuation of which cranial nerve division?
questions.explanation: The infraorbital nerve is the terminal branch of the maxillary division (V2) of the trigeminal nerve. It traverses the infraorbital canal and emerges through the infraorbital foramen. The nerve provides sensation to the lower eyelid, side of nose, and upper lip.

The upper lateral quadrant of the buttock receives cutaneous innervation from L1 and T12. This is distinct from the upper medial quadrant (L1, 2, 3 and S1, 2, 3), lower medial quadrant (S1, 2, 3), and lower lateral quadrant (L2, 3). Clinical dermatomal mapping in this region can help identify the level of spinal pathology.
questions.question: Which cutaneous nerves supply the upper lateral quadrant of the buttock?
Which muscle is the primary adductor of the thumb?
questions.explanation: is the primary adductor of the thumb, bringing it toward the palm. It is supplied by the ulnar nerve, unlike the other thenar muscles. The muscle has two heads (oblique and transverse) that converge on the base of the proximal phalanx.

The subcostal plane is a horizontal transverse plane passing through the inferior margins of the 10th costal cartilages (lowest point of the costal margin) on each side, corresponding to the upper border of the third lumbar vertebra (L3). Together with the transtubercular plane (L5 level) and the two vertical midclavicular planes, it defines the nine regions of the abdomen. The subcostal plane marks important anatomical landmarks including the origin of the inferior mesenteric artery, the level of the pylorus in some individuals, and the approximate position of the inferior border of the liver.
questions.question: The subcostal plane passes through which vertebral level?
Which structure lies in the cavernous sinus lateral wall?
questions.explanation: The lateral wall of the cavernous sinus contains (from superior to inferior): oculomotor nerve (III), trochlear nerve (IV), ophthalmic division (V1), and maxillary division (V2). The internal carotid artery and abducens nerve (VI) pass through the sinus cavity itself. Cavernous sinus thrombosis can affect all these structures causing ophthalmoplegia and sensory loss.

questions.question: At what sound pressure level does the stapedius reflex typically activate?
questions.explanation: The stapedius muscle reflex activates bilaterally at sound levels above 80 dB SPL to protect the cochlea. This acoustic reflex increases ossicular chain stiffness and attenuates low-frequency sounds. Testing this reflex provides valuable information about facial nerve and auditory pathway integrity.

The piriformis muscle is the landmark structure in the greater sciatic foramen. All other structures are described relative to it: the superior gluteal nerve and vessels pass above it, while all seven other nerves and five vessels pass below it. This anatomical knowledge is essential for safe gluteal intramuscular injections.
questions.question: Which structure serves as the anatomical landmark within the greater sciatic foramen, defining the relationship of all other structures to it?
The nasolacrimal duct is formed by which two bones?
questions.explanation: The nasolacrimal canal is formed by the lacrimal bone and maxilla, housing the nasolacrimal duct. The duct drains tears from the lacrimal sac to the inferior meatus. The valve of Hasner at the inferior opening prevents retrograde airflow. Obstruction requires dacryocystorhinostomy surgery.

questions.question: Which muscle forms the posterior pillar of the fauces?
questions.explanation: The palatopharyngeus muscle forms the posterior pillar (palatopharyngeal arch) of the fauces. The palatoglossus forms the anterior pillar. The tonsillar fossa lies between these two pillars. Both muscles descend from the soft palate but have different innervation patterns.

questions.question: Which muscles work synergistically to produce pure wrist adduction?
questions.explanation: Flexor carpi ulnaris and extensor carpi ulnaris work synergistically to produce pure wrist adduction (ulnar deviation). By contracting simultaneously, they balance flexion and extension forces while producing adduction. This demonstrates how muscles from different compartments can cooperate for specific movements.

questions.question: The ovarian artery crosses which structure anteriorly?
questions.explanation: The ovarian artery (arising from the aorta at L2) descends obliquely across the psoas major muscle, crosses anterior to the ureter and the common iliac vessels (or external iliac vessels), then enters the suspensory ligament of the ovary to reach the ovary in the pelvis. This long course reflects the ovary's embryological origin high on the posterior abdominal wall. The artery anastomoses with the uterine artery in the broad ligament. In males, the testicular artery follows a similar course but continues through the inguinal canal. The ovarian artery's relationship to the ureter is surgically important.

questions.question: The spleen develops in relation to which mesentery?
questions.explanation: The spleen develops within the dorsal mesogastrium (greater omentum) during embryonic development, explaining its position in the left upper quadrant and its peritoneal attachments. The gastrosplenic ligament (part of the dorsal mesogastrium) connects it to the greater curvature of the stomach, while the splenorenal ligament attaches it to the left kidney. Although the spleen is not a gastrointestinal organ, it receives its blood supply from the celiac trunk (via splenic artery) due to this developmental relationship. The tail of the pancreas also develops in the dorsal mesogastrium, extending into the splenorenal ligament.

questions.question: What nerve provides motor innervation to all thenar muscles?
questions.explanation: Thenar muscles receive dual innervation: the recurrent branch of the median nerve supplies abductor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis, and superficial head of flexor pollicis brevis. The ulnar nerve supplies the deep head of flexor pollicis brevis and sometimes contributes to other thenar muscles.

The inferior mediastinum has three subdivisions: anterior (in front of the heart), middle (contains the heart), and posterior (behind the heart). The superior mediastinum lies above the horizontal plane through T4. This classification helps in understanding the location of mediastinal structures and pathology.
questions.question: How many subdivisions does inferior mediastinum have?

questions.explanation: The vas deferens crosses superior to the external iliac vessels at the pelvic brim, then curves medially, crossing over (anterior to) the obturator nerve and vessels and the ureter before reaching the posterior surface of the bladder. At the inguinal region, the vas deferens "hooks" around the lateral side of the inferior epigastric artery, crossing it from lateral to medial as it exits the deep inguinal ring. This relationship is surgically important during hernia repair and vasectomy. The vas is easily palpable in the spermatic cord and feels like a firm cord or thick string.
questions.question: The vas deferens crosses which vessel during its pelvic course?

questions.explanation: The suspensory ligament of the ovary (infundibulopelvic ligament), a lateral extension of the broad ligament, suspends the ovary from the lateral pelvic wall and contains the ovarian artery (from aorta) and ovarian vein (to IVC on right, left renal vein on left), along with ovarian nerves and lymphatics. This ligament must be clamped and divided during oophorectomy. The ovarian ligament connects the ovary to the uterus medially, while the broad ligament provides only indirect support via the mesovarium. The round ligament extends from uterus to labium majus via the inguinal canal.
questions.question: The ovary is suspended by which ligament from the pelvic wall?
Where in the spleen are blood-borne bacteria primarily filtered?
questions.explanation: Blood-borne bacteria and particulate matter are primarily filtered and phagocytosed by macrophages in the red pulp cords and sinusoids. Blood flowing through the spleen is exposed to numerous macrophages that can recognize and remove opsonized bacteria and foreign particles. This filtering function is lost after splenectomy, increasing infection susceptibility.

The bronchial arteries supply the bronchial tree from the main bronchi to the respiratory bronchioles. Two left bronchial arteries arise from the descending thoracic aorta, and one right bronchial artery arises from the third right posterior intercostal artery. These vessels provide oxygenated blood to airway structures.
questions.question: Which arteries supply the bronchial tree?
The kidney is related posteriorly to which muscle?
questions.explanation: The posterior surface of each kidney lies on the diaphragm superiorly, then from medial to lateral on the psoas major, quadratus lumborum, and transversus abdominis muscles, separated from them by the perinephric fat, renal fascia, and pararenal fat. The subcostal, iliohypogastric, and ilioinguinal nerves descend obliquely posterior to the kidney on these muscles. The left kidney is related to ribs 11 and 12 posteriorly (protected by the rib cage), while the right kidney is related only to rib 12. These posterior relations are important when considering retrograde surgical approaches to the kidney or complications of renal trauma.

questions.question: The ethmoidal bulla is located in which meatus?
questions.explanation: The ethmoidal bulla is a rounded prominence in the lateral wall of the middle meatus formed by the underlying middle ethmoidal air cells. The hiatus semilunaris lies below it. The bulla is a key landmark during endoscopic sinus surgery. Above the bulla lies the suprabullar recess. The uncinate process lies anterior and inferior.

The greater curvature is supplied by the right and left gastroepiploic (gastroomental) arteries, which anastomose along the greater curvature. The left gastroepiploic arises from the splenic artery and supplies the upper greater curvature; the right gastroepiploic arises from the gastroduodenal artery and supplies the lower greater curvature. The short gastric arteries supply the fundus portion of the greater curvature.
questions.question: Which artery supplies the greater curvature of the stomach?
Which structure lies posterior to the head of the pancreas?
questions.explanation: The inferior vena cava lies posterior to the head of the pancreas (separated by the right renal vein and sometimes the third part of the duodenum), along with the right renal artery and vein, aorta, and origin of the superior mesenteric artery. The superior mesenteric vein ascends posterior to the neck of the pancreas (not the head), where it joins the splenic vein to form the portal vein. The common bile duct runs in a groove on (or through) the posterior surface of the pancreatic head before joining the main pancreatic duct.

The dorsalis pedis artery passes over the dorsal tarsal bones and then moves inferiorly toward the sole, anastomosing with the lateral plantar artery to form the deep plantar arch. Via this arch, it contributes to the supply of the toes. The dorsal venous arch lies in the subcutaneous tissue over the heads of the metatarsal bones.
questions.question: The dorsalis pedis artery is the continuation of the anterior tibial artery on the dorsum of the foot. It anastomoses with the lateral plantar artery to form which arch?
Which muscle is NOT innervated by the lumbar plexus?
questions.explanation: Piriformis is innervated by branches directly from the ventral rami of S1 and S2 (sacral plexus), not the lumbar plexus. The lumbar plexus (L1-L4) innervates psoas major (L1-L4), quadratus lumborum (T12, L1-L4 via subcostal and lumbar nerves), iliacus (femoral nerve, L2-L4), and obturator externus (obturator nerve, L2-L4). Piriformis is a muscle of the gluteal region and posterior pelvic wall, exiting the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen. It serves as a landmark dividing structures exiting above it (superior gluteal vessels and nerve) from those below it (all others).

During grip, wrist extensors isometrically contract to stabilize the wrist in slight extension. This prevents wrist flexion as finger flexors contract, optimizing finger flexor length-tension relationship for maximum grip force. This synergistic stabilization demonstrates functional muscle interaction.
questions.question: What is the functional relationship between wrist flexors and extensors in grip?
options: Wrist extensors stabilize wrist enabling grip strength

questions.explanation: The quadratus lumborum receives innervation from the subcostal nerve (T12) and the upper lumbar nerves (L1-L3 or L4), reflecting its position as the most lateral muscle of the posterior abdominal wall. This muscle originates from the iliolumbar ligament and adjacent iliac crest, inserting onto the medial half of the inferior border of the 12th rib and the transverse processes of the upper lumbar vertebrae. It functions to fix the 12th rib during inspiration, extend the lumbar vertebral column bilaterally, and produce lateral flexion when acting unilaterally.
questions.question: The quadratus lumborum muscle is innervated by which nerves?

questions.explanation: Seven tendons insert into the greater trochanter: gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, piriformis, obturator internus, obturator externus, gemellus superior, and gemellus inferior. The concentration of these insertions makes the greater trochanter a key landmark in hip anatomy. Avulsion fractures at this site carry significant functional implications.
questions.question: How many tendons insert into the greater trochanter of the femur?
Which muscle's contraction causes the anorectal angle?
questions.explanation: The puborectalis muscle, part of the levator ani complex, forms a U-shaped sling that loops around the anorectal junction, creating the anorectal angle of approximately 90 degrees by pulling the rectum anteriorly toward the pubic symphysis. This angle is a critical component of the fecal continence mechanism, as relaxation of puborectalis during defecation straightens the anorectal angle to facilitate evacuation. Damage to the puborectalis (such as during childbirth or surgery) or its nerve supply (pudendal nerve and direct branches from S3-S4) can lead to fecal incontinence. The muscle is in tonic contraction at rest.

questions.question: The submandibular ganglion is suspended from which nerve?
questions.explanation: The submandibular ganglion is suspended from the lingual nerve by two branches in the submandibular region. Preganglionic parasympathetic fibers arrive via the chorda tympani, synapse in the ganglion, and postganglionic fibers supply the submandibular and sublingual glands. Sympathetic and sensory fibers pass through without synapsing.

The palatoglossal arch (anterior pillar of fauces) forms the boundary between the oral cavity and oropharynx. The arch contains the palatoglossus muscle and extends from the soft palate to the side of the tongue. The isthmus of fauces is the opening between the oral cavity and oropharynx, bounded by these arches.
questions.question: Which structure separates the oral cavity from the oropharynx?

questions.explanation: The right coronary artery arises from the right (anterior) aortic sinus of the ascending aorta. It runs in the right atrioventricular groove, giving off branches to the right atrium, SA node (in 60% of people), right ventricle, and posterior interventricular septum. In right-dominant circulation (70% of people), it gives rise to the posterior interventricular artery.
questions.question: From which aortic sinus does the right coronary artery arise?
The lingual tonsil is located on which surface of the tongue?
questions.explanation: The lingual tonsil is lymphoid tissue on the posterior third (dorsal surface) of the tongue behind the sulcus terminalis. It forms part of Waldeyer's ring with the palatine and pharyngeal tonsils. The lingual tonsil is covered by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium with crypts. Hypertrophy can cause airway obstruction or dysphagia.

The splenic vein joins with the superior mesenteric vein posterior to the neck of the pancreas to form the hepatic portal vein. The splenic vein runs from left to right along the posterior surface of the pancreas. It receives the short gastric veins, left gastroepiploic vein, pancreatic veins, and inferior mesenteric vein.
questions.question: Into which vein does the splenic vein primarily drain?

questions.explanation: The medial arcuate ligament is a thickening of the fascia covering the anterior surface of psoas major muscle. It extends from the side of the body of L2 vertebra to the tip of the transverse process of L1. The lateral arcuate ligament overlies quadratus lumborum muscle.
questions.question: What does the medial arcuate ligament overlie?
What is the functional relationship between median and ulnar nerves in the hand?
options: Median for power, ulnar for precision muscles
Median for thenar precision, ulnar for hypothenar power and intrinsics
questions.explanation: The median nerve supplies thenar muscles enabling precise thumb opposition for precision grip. The ulnar nerve supplies hypothenar muscles, all interossei, and medial lumbricals, providing intrinsic muscle coordination and power grip contribution. Together they enable both precision and power hand functions.

The greater splanchnic nerve, after synapsing in the celiac ganglion, provides sympathetic innervation to foregut-derived organs including the stomach, liver, gallbladder, pancreas, spleen, small intestine, and proximal colon (to the splenic flexure). It also carries visceral afferent fibers for pain sensation from these organs.
questions.question: Which organs receive greater splanchnic innervation?

options: Sustentaculum tali of calcaneus to the navicular
questions.explanation: The spring ligament (plantar calcaneonavicular ligament) passes from the sustentaculum tali of the calcaneus to the plantar surface of the navicular, directly supporting the head of the talus. Its superior surface has a fibrocartilaginous facet that contributes to the articular surface for the talar head. Spring ligament rupture leads to talar head descent and collapse of the medial longitudinal arch.
questions.question: The spring ligament (plantar calcaneonavicular ligament) supports the head of the talus and the medial longitudinal arch. Between which two bones does it pass?

questions.explanation: The left gastric artery, the smallest branch of the celiac trunk, gives off esophageal branches that ascend to supply the abdominal portion of the esophagus (below the diaphragm). These esophageal branches anastomose superiorly with esophageal branches from the thoracic aorta through the esophageal hiatus, creating a potential portosystemic anastomosis (left gastric vein to portal system; esophageal veins from thoracic aorta territory to azygos system to IVC). In portal hypertension, this anastomosis may become varicose, producing esophageal varices that can rupture and cause life-threatening hemorrhage.
questions.question: The left gastric artery supplies which part of the esophagus?
What epithelium lines the urinary bladder?
questions.explanation: The urinary bladder is lined by transitional epithelium (urothelium), a specialized stratified epithelium that can stretch and accommodate changes in bladder volume without tearing. When the bladder is empty, the epithelium appears thick with 5-6 cell layers; when distended, it thins to 2-3 layers. This epithelium is impermeable to salts and water.

The superior mesenteric vein receives tributaries corresponding to branches of the superior mesenteric artery (jejunal, ileal, ileocolic, right colic, middle colic veins) plus the right gastroepiploic vein and inferior pancreaticoduodenal veins. The inferior mesenteric vein typically drains into the splenic vein (behind the pancreas) rather than the superior mesenteric vein, though variations exist. The SMV ascends to the right of the SMA, passes anterior to the third part of the duodenum and uncinate process of pancreas, and joins the splenic vein behind the neck of the pancreas to form the portal vein.
questions.question: The superior mesenteric vein receives blood from all EXCEPT:
Which muscle is pierced by the superior gluteal nerve?
questions.explanation: The superior gluteal nerve (L4, L5, S1) exits the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen above the piriformis muscle (the only structure exiting above piriformis), passes between gluteus medius and minimus, and supplies these muscles plus tensor fasciae latae. All other structures exit below piriformis. The nerve does not actually pierce piriformis but rather exits superior to it. Piriformis serves as an important anatomical landmark in the gluteal region, dividing structures exiting the greater sciatic foramen into suprapiriform (superior gluteal vessels and nerve) and infrapiriform groups (all others including sciatic nerve).

questions.question: Which structure separates the orbit from the ethmoid sinus?
questions.explanation: The lamina papyracea (orbital plate of ethmoid) is a thin bony plate separating the orbit from the ethmoidal air cells. Its paper-like thinness makes it vulnerable to fracture and erosion. Ethmoidal infections can spread through this wall causing orbital complications. The anterior and posterior ethmoidal foramina pierce this plate.

The middle cerebral artery supplies the lateral surface of the cerebral hemisphere, including motor and sensory cortices for face and upper limb. It also supplies Broca's and Wernicke's areas in the dominant hemisphere. MCA occlusion causes contralateral hemiplegia more marked in upper extremity and face.
questions.question: The middle cerebral artery supplies which cortical area?
Which fissure separates the right lung's middle lobe?
questions.explanation: The middle lobe of the right lung is bounded above by the horizontal fissure and below by the oblique fissure. The horizontal fissure runs along the fourth rib anteriorly. The oblique fissure separates the inferior lobe from both the superior and middle lobes on the right side.

options: Anterior flexes, middle abducts, posterior extends
questions.question: How do the three deltoid portions contribute differently to shoulder function?
questions.explanation: The deltoid's three portions have distinct actions: anterior fibers flex and medially rotate, middle fibers abduct (15-90°), posterior fibers extend and laterally rotate. This multipennate architecture allows the same muscle to produce different movements depending on which fibers are active.

The posterior tibial artery enters the sole of the foot through the tarsal tunnel (formed by the flexor retinaculum and medial ankle bones), accompanying the tibial nerve. It then divides into medial and lateral plantar arteries, supplying the plantar foot and contributing to the toes via the deep plantar arch. Its pulse is palpated inferoposterior to the medial malleolus.
questions.question: The posterior tibial artery enters the sole of the foot through which structure, then divides into medial and lateral plantar arteries?
Which epithelium lines the anal canal above the pectinate line?
questions.explanation: Above the pectinate (dentate) line, the anal canal is lined by simple columnar epithelium (rectal-type mucosa) forming the columns of Morgagni. Below the pectinate line, it transitions to stratified squamous non-keratinized epithelium (in the intermediate zone) and then stratified squamous keratinized epithelium (in the cutaneous zone). The pectinate line marks the junction of endoderm and ectoderm.

questions.question: The patellar ligament, described as the distal part of the quadriceps tendon, ultimately attaches to which bony prominence?
questions.explanation: The patellar ligament passes from the apex and adjoining margins of the patella to the tibial tuberosity. It is a strong thick fibrous band representing the distal continuation of the quadriceps tendon. It blends with the medial and lateral patellar retinacula (aponeurotic expansions of vastus medialis and lateralis) providing additional stability.

questions.question: Which artery supplies the ileum?
questions.explanation: The ileum receives its blood supply from multiple ileal arteries (12-15 branches) arising from the left side of the superior mesenteric artery. These arteries run between the layers of the mesentery, forming 4-5 arcades (more numerous than in the jejunum) before giving rise to short, widely spaced vasa recta that supply the intestinal wall. The terminal ileum also receives branches from the ileocolic artery (ileal branch). The extensive arterial arcades create broad, low windows in the mesentery (versus the narrow, tall windows in the jejunal mesentery).

The geniculate ganglion is the sensory ganglion of the facial nerve located at the genu (bend) of the facial canal. It contains cell bodies of neurons carrying taste from the anterior tongue via chorda tympani. Herpes zoster infection here causes Ramsay Hunt syndrome with facial palsy and vesicles.
questions.question: The geniculate ganglion is associated with which cranial nerve?

questions.explanation: The lesser petrosal nerve carries preganglionic parasympathetic fibers from the glossopharyngeal nerve to the otic ganglion. These fibers originate in the inferior salivatory nucleus. After synapsing in the otic ganglion, postganglionic fibers travel via the auriculotemporal nerve to provide secretomotor innervation to the parotid gland.
questions.question: The lesser petrosal nerve carries which type of fibers?
The lesser petrosal nerve carries fibers from which nucleus?
questions.explanation: The lesser petrosal nerve carries preganglionic parasympathetic fibers from the inferior salivatory nucleus via the glossopharyngeal nerve and tympanic plexus. Fibers synapse in the otic ganglion. Postganglionic fibers reach the parotid gland via the auriculotemporal nerve. This pathway controls parotid secretion. Damage causes reduced salivary flow.

The superior vesical arteries (usually multiple branches) arise from the patent part of the umbilical artery and supply the superior surface and upper lateral surfaces of the bladder. The umbilical artery is obliterated distally (becoming the medial umbilical ligament) but remains patent proximally. The inferior vesical artery (in males) or vaginal artery (in females) supplies the bladder base.
questions.question: Which artery supplies the superior surface of the bladder?

questions.explanation: On either side of the superior thoracic aperture, the opening is closed by the dense suprapleural membrane (also called Sibson's fascia). In the midline, structures pass between the neck and thorax. This membrane is a tent-shaped extension of endothoracic fascia that covers the apex of each lung.
questions.question: What closes the superior thoracic aperture laterally?
What is the narrowest point of esophagus?
questions.explanation: The narrowest point of the esophagus is at its origin at the level of the cricoid cartilage (C6) where the cricopharyngeus muscle forms the upper esophageal sphincter. This is the most common site for foreign body impaction and the site requiring most care during esophagoscopy to avoid perforation.

questions.question: The oblique popliteal ligament strengthens the fibrous capsule posteriorly. It is an expansion of the tendon of which muscle?
questions.explanation: The oblique popliteal ligament is an expansion of the tendon of semimembranosus. It arises posterior to the medial tibial condyle and attaches to the central part of the posterior fibrous capsule. It is an important posterior stabilizer of the knee. The arcuate popliteal ligament is a separate structure arising from the posterior fibular head.

is the only rotator cuff muscle that performs medial (internal) rotation of the humerus. It lies on the anterior surface of the scapula, filling the subscapular fossa. The other rotator cuff muscles (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor) are located posteriorly.
questions.question: Which rotator cuff muscle performs medial rotation of the humerus?
The processus vaginalis gives rise to which structure?
questions.explanation: The processus vaginalis, an evagination of peritoneum that accompanies the descending testis, normally obliterates during the first year of life except for its distal portion, which remains as the tunica vaginalis (a closed peritoneal sac surrounding the testis). The parietal layer of tunica vaginalis lines the inner surface of the scrotum (internal spermatic fascia), while the visceral layer covers the testis and epididymis. Failure of processus vaginalis obliteration leads to patent processus (communicating hydrocele) or congenital indirect inguinal hernia. The gubernaculum guides testicular descent.

options: Level of anterior superior iliac spine
questions.explanation: The arcuate line (linea semicircularis) marks the inferior border of the posterior rectus sheath, located approximately midway between the umbilicus and pubic symphysis, roughly at the level of the anterior superior iliac spine. Below this line, all three aponeurotic layers (external oblique, internal oblique, and transversus abdominis) pass anteriorly to the rectus abdominis muscle, leaving only transversalis fascia posteriorly. This anatomical feature creates a potential weakness that may be involved in direct inguinal hernias.
questions.question: The arcuate line of the rectus sheath is typically found at which level?

questions.explanation: The dorsalis pedis pulse is palpated on the dorsum of the foot, just lateral to the tendon of the extensor hallucis longus. The dorsalis pedis artery (continuation of the anterior tibial artery) runs between the extensor hallucis longus tendon medially and the extensor digitorum longus tendon laterally. Absence of this pulse, along with the posterior tibial pulse, indicates peripheral arterial disease.
questions.question: The dorsalis pedis pulse is palpated on the dorsum of the foot. It is found just lateral to the tendon of which muscle?
Which nerve supplies the cricothyroid muscle?
questions.explanation: The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve supplies the cricothyroid muscle. This is the only intrinsic laryngeal muscle not supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve. The nerve descends with the superior thyroid artery. Damage affects vocal cord tension and causes voice fatigue and difficulty with pitch variation.

The ureter has three normal physiological constrictions: (1) at the pelviureteric junction where the renal pelvis joins the ureter, (2) where it crosses the pelvic brim at the bifurcation of the common iliac artery, and (3) at the vesicoureteric junction where it pierces the bladder wall. These are the most common sites for ureteric stone impaction.
questions.question: At how many points is the ureter typically constricted?

questions.explanation: The pyramidalis muscle, a small triangular muscle anterior to the lower rectus abdominis (base on pubis, apex on linea alba), is innervated by the subcostal nerve (T12). This muscle is variably present (absent in about 20% of individuals) and functions to tense the linea alba. The subcostal nerve also contributes to innervation of the abdominal wall muscles and overlying skin. The pyramidalis lies within the rectus sheath and represents a derivative of the rectus abdominis. Its clinical significance is minimal.
questions.question: Which nerve innervates the pyramidalis muscle?
Extensor hallucis longus, innervated by the deep fibular nerve, originates from which structure?
options: Superior half of lateral surface of tibia
Middle anterior fibula and interosseous membrane
Inferior third of anterior fibula only
questions.explanation: Extensor hallucis longus originates from the middle part of the anterior surface of the fibula and the adjacent interosseous membrane. It inserts into the dorsal aspect of the base of the distal phalanx of the great toe and is innervated by the deep fibular nerve (L4, L5). It extends the great toe, dorsiflexes the ankle, and can assist with foot inversion.

questions.question: Which artery accompanies the hypoglossal nerve?
questions.explanation: The lingual artery arises from the external carotid at the level of the hyoid bone and is closely related to the hypoglossal nerve. The nerve crosses superficial to the artery as it loops forward. The artery divides into dorsal lingual, deep lingual, and sublingual branches. The hyoglossus muscle separates superficial from deep structures.

The superior laryngeal nerve (from the vagus) divides into internal and external branches. The internal branch pierces the thyrohyoid membrane to provide sensation above the vocal cords. The external branch descends to innervate the cricothyroid muscle. Damage to the external branch affects voice pitch control.
questions.question: The superior laryngeal nerve divides into which two branches?

questions.explanation: The major duodenal papilla represents the embryological junction between foregut and midgut derivatives, marking the transition from celiac to superior mesenteric arterial supply. The duodenum proximal to this point receives blood from the celiac trunk (via gastroduodenal and superior pancreaticoduodenal arteries), while the portion distal to it is supplied by the superior mesenteric artery (via inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries). This vascular watershed reflects the embryological division of the primitive gut tube and has important implications for the blood supply and venous/lymphatic drainage patterns.
questions.question: Which structure marks the transition from foregut to midgut?
Where does central diaphragmatic pain refer?
questions.explanation: Irritation of the central part of the diaphragm (supplied by phrenic nerve C3-5) causes referred pain to the shoulder-tip because the supraclavicular nerves (C3, 4) supply the skin over the shoulder. This occurs in conditions like pleurisy, pericarditis, or subphrenic abscess affecting the central diaphragm.

The stylopharyngeus muscle is supplied solely by the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX), not the pharyngeal plexus. All other pharyngeal muscles receive innervation from the pharyngeal plexus (vagus via cranial accessory). The stylopharyngeus elevates the pharynx and larynx during swallowing. It is the only structure supplied by the motor component of IX.
questions.question: Which muscle is NOT supplied by the pharyngeal plexus?
The vocal ligament is the thickened upper edge of which membrane?
questions.explanation: The vocal ligament is the thickened free upper edge of the cricothyroid membrane (conus elasticus). It extends from the vocal process of the arytenoid to the posterior surface of the thyroid cartilage. The ligament is covered by mucosa to form the true vocal cord.

questions.question: Which vessel forms the left heart border?
questions.explanation: The left border of the heart on a chest X-ray is formed almost entirely by the left ventricle, with a small contribution from the left atrial appendage superiorly. This border extends from the 2nd left costal cartilage to the apex beat in the 5th intercostal space.

questions.question: Which cartilage lies in the aryepiglottic fold?
questions.explanation: The cuneiform cartilages (cartilages of Wrisberg) are small rod-shaped elastic cartilages lying in the aryepiglottic folds anterior to the corniculate cartilages. They produce small elevations on the mucosal surface visible during laryngoscopy. The cartilages strengthen the aryepiglottic folds. Some individuals may lack these cartilages.

questions.question: Which artery supplies the appendix?
questions.explanation: The appendicular artery, a branch of the ileocolic artery (which itself arises from the superior mesenteric artery), supplies the vermiform appendix. It runs in the free margin of the mesoappendix to reach the tip of the appendix. This end-artery arrangement (with minimal collateral supply) means that thrombosis or inflammation affecting the appendicular artery can lead to appendiceal ischemia and necrosis. The artery's location in the mesoappendix requires careful ligation during appendectomy. Variations in the arterial supply are uncommon, but occasionally the appendicular artery may arise directly from a posterior cecal artery.

questions.question: The sural nerve is formed by the union of which two nerves and supplies which area of the lower limb?
questions.explanation: The sural nerve is formed by the union of the medial sural cutaneous nerve (from the tibial nerve in the popliteal fossa) and the sural communicating branch of the common fibular nerve. It supplies the skin of the lateral side of the leg, ankle, and lateral heel. The sural nerve is commonly harvested as a nerve graft in peripheral nerve reconstruction surgery.
options: Medial sural cutaneous nerve and sural communicating branch of common fibular nerve; lateral side of leg and ankle
Medial sural cutaneous nerve (from tibial nerve) and lateral sural cutaneous nerve (from common fibular nerve); lateral side of leg, ankle, and foot
Saphenous nerve and medial sural cutaneous nerve; medial leg and foot
Both sural nerves from tibial nerve; posterior leg entirely
Posterior cutaneous nerve of thigh and medial sural cutaneous nerve; posterior thigh and leg

questions.explanation: The primary function of the large intestine is absorption of water and electrolytes from the remaining indigestible food matter, converting liquid chyme into semi-solid feces. Approximately 1-2 liters of water are absorbed daily. The colon also absorbs short-chain fatty acids produced by bacterial fermentation and synthesizes vitamin K through bacterial action.
questions.question: What is the primary function of the large intestine?
Which nerve pierces the left dome of diaphragm?
questions.explanation: The left phrenic nerve pierces the left dome of the diaphragm to supply the abdominal surface. The right phrenic nerve passes through the caval opening in the central tendon. Both phrenic nerves provide motor supply to the entire diaphragm and sensory supply to its central portion.

questions.question: Which muscle forms the lateral boundary of the lumbar triangle of Marcille?
questions.explanation: The lumbosacral triangle (Marcille's triangle) has the medial border of psoas major forming its lateral boundary, with the body of L5 vertebra medially and the ala of sacrum as its base. The floor consists of the transverse process of L5 and the iliolumbar ligament. This triangle is clinically significant as the ureter crosses the common iliac vessels at its lateral angle, making it an important landmark during pelvic surgery.

questions.question: What is the approximate length of the mesentery root attachment?
questions.explanation: The root (origin) of the mesentery is approximately 15 cm long, extending obliquely from the duodenojejunal flexure to the ileocaecal junction. Despite this short root attachment, the mesentery fans out to accommodate the 5-6 meters of small bowel. The root crosses the third part of the duodenum, aorta, IVC, right psoas muscle, and right gonadal vessels.

questions.question: Which structure lies in the hypoglossal triangle?
questions.explanation: The hypoglossal nerve (XII) lies in the hypoglossal triangle (muscular triangle), a subdivision of the anterior triangle bounded by the midline, superior belly of omohyoid, and sternocleidomastoid. The triangle also contains the infrahyoid muscles and thyroid gland. The nerve passes from the carotid triangle into the muscular triangle.

The left lung has several impressions on its mediastinal surface including: cardiac impression (the largest), aortic arch groove, descending aorta groove, subclavian artery groove, esophageal and tracheal grooves, and brachiocephalic vein groove. The aortic impressions are particularly prominent.
questions.question: What impression is on the left lung medially?

questions.explanation: The flexor compartment of the hand receives structures passing through the carpal tunnel, including flexor tendons and the median nerve. The tunnel's confined space makes it susceptible to compression syndromes. Any lesion diminishing compartment size can result in median nerve compression.
questions.question: Which compartment contains structures passing through the carpal tunnel?

questions.explanation: Vastus intermedius lies deep to the rectus femoris, between the vastus medialis and lateralis. It originates from the anterior and lateral surfaces of the shaft of the femur and inserts via the common quadriceps tendon and patellar ligament to the tibial tuberosity. It is innervated by the femoral nerve (L2, L3, L4) and extends the leg at the knee.
questions.question: Which component of the quadriceps femoris lies deepest, between the vastus medialis and lateralis?
What produces opposition of the thumb?
questions.explanation: is the primary muscle producing opposition of the thumb, bringing the thumb across the palm to touch the little finger. This movement involves flexion, abduction, and medial rotation at the carpometacarpal joint. The muscle is supplied by the recurrent branch of the median nerve.

questions.question: The three fascial compartments of the thigh are separated by septa passing from the fascia lata to which bony structure?
questions.explanation: Three fascial septa pass from the inner aspect of the fascia lata to the linea aspera of the femur, dividing the thigh into anterior, medial, and posterior compartments. Each compartment has distinct nerves, muscles, and vessels. Understanding compartment anatomy is critical in managing thigh compartment syndrome following trauma.

The gastrocolic ligament, part of the greater omentum, connects the greater curvature of the stomach to the transverse colon. It contains the right and left gastroepiploic vessels along the greater curvature and represents the anterior two layers of the greater omentum before they descend and fold back. Division of the gastrocolic ligament provides surgical access to the lesser sac (omental bursa) and is a key step in gastric surgery, transverse colectomy, and pancreatic surgery. The avascular plane (relatively avascular window) between the gastroepiploic vessels and transverse colon can be developed to enter the lesser sac with minimal bleeding.
questions.question: The gastrocolic ligament connects the stomach to which structure?

questions.explanation: The levator anguli oris is innervated by the buccal branch of the facial nerve. It elevates the angle of the mouth during smiling. The muscle arises from the canine fossa of the maxilla and inserts into the angle of the mouth. It lies deep to levator labii superioris and zygomaticus minor muscles.
questions.question: The levator anguli oris muscle is innervated by which nerve branch?

questions.explanation: The tendon of popliteus passes deep to the fibular collateral ligament, separating it from the lateral meniscus. This is why the lateral meniscus is more freely movable than the medial meniscus. The popliteus tendon also creates a gap in the posterior fibrous capsule allowing its passage. The biceps femoris tendon is split by the fibular collateral ligament at the fibular head.
questions.question: The fibular (lateral) collateral ligament is separated from the lateral meniscus by the tendon of which muscle?

questions.explanation: The short head of biceps femoris does not cross the hip joint (originating from the linea aspera, not the ischial tuberosity) and therefore cannot extend the hip. It is supplied by the common fibular division of the sciatic nerve, unlike all other hamstrings which are supplied by the tibial division. It only flexes the knee and laterally rotates the leg when the knee is flexed.
options: It originates from the rim of the acetabulum
It is supplied exclusively by the obturator nerve
Does not cross the hip joint; supplied by the common fibular nerve
It inserts into the medial tibial condyle distally
It is classified as a medial compartment muscle
questions.question: The short head of biceps femoris differs from the other hamstrings in which critical way?

questions.explanation: extends the metacarpophalangeal joint of the thumb. Its tendon forms the lateral border of the anatomical snuffbox along with abductor pollicis longus. The muscle is supplied by the posterior interosseous nerve.
questions.question: What produces thumb extension at the metacarpophalangeal joint?

questions.explanation: The root of the mesentery of the small intestine extends obliquely from the duodenojejunal flexure (at approximately L2, left of midline) to the right sacroiliac joint (at approximately S1, right of midline), a distance of about 15 cm. Along this short root, approximately 6-7 meters of small intestine (jejunum and ileum) is attached. The root crosses the third (horizontal) part of the duodenum, abdominal aorta, IVC, right ureter, right psoas major muscle, and right testicular/ovarian vessels. This oblique orientation allows the small intestine maximum mobility while maintaining vascular supply and creating the characteristic radiating pattern of jejunal and ileal vessels.
questions.question: The root of the mesentery extends from which two points?
options: Second part of duodenum to sigmoid colon
Duodenojejunal flexure to right sacroiliac joint

questions.explanation: The appendicular artery, a branch of the ileocolic artery (from the superior mesenteric artery), supplies the appendix. It runs in the mesoappendix (the peritoneal fold connecting the appendix to the mesentery). This is an end artery without significant anastomoses, making the appendix vulnerable to ischemia if the vessel thromboses (as in appendicitis). The artery typically runs behind the terminal ileum.
questions.question: What is the blood supply to the appendix?

questions.explanation: The bare area of the liver is the triangular region on the posterior surface that is in direct contact with the diaphragm, devoid of peritoneal covering. This area is bounded by the reflections of the coronary ligament (superior and inferior layers) and is continuous with the groove for the inferior vena cava. The bare area represents the part of the liver that remained adherent to the diaphragm during embryological development. Small diaphragmatic veins in this region drain directly from the liver into the IVC without forming hepatic veins, and the right phrenic artery contributes to the vascular supply of this area.
questions.question: The bare area of the liver is related to which organ?
What prevents superior displacement of the humeral head at the shoulder?
questions.explanation: The coraco-acromial arch, formed by the coracoid process, acromion, and coracoacromial ligament, prevents superior displacement of the humeral head. This structure overlies the shoulder joint superiorly. The joint capsule is weak superiorly, making the arch essential for preventing upward dislocation.

questions.question: The two basic functions of the human foot are supporting body weight and providing leverage for locomotion. These are achieved through which structural arrangement?
questions.explanation: The human foot achieves its two basic functions through a segmented skeleton arranged in arches (longitudinal and transverse), supported by muscles and ligaments. This arrangement enables efficient locomotion, sparing of foot structures, and shock absorption. The arches allow the foot to adapt to uneven surfaces and serve as resilient springs to absorb shocks as in jumping.
options: Segmented bony arches supported by muscles and ligaments
Rigid flat bone platform without arching
Phalanges arranged in a single arch only

questions.explanation: In the female pelvis, the uterine artery crosses superior (above) to the ureter near the lateral fornix of the vagina - remembered by the phrase "water under the bridge." This relationship is clinically crucial during hysterectomy to avoid inadvertent ureteric injury during ligation of the uterine artery. The ureter runs along the lateral wall of the pelvis to reach the bladder.
questions.question: Which vessel crosses anterior to the ureter in the female pelvis?
Which structure forms the medial boundary of the inguinal canal?
questions.explanation: The conjoint tendon (inguinal falx), formed by the fusion of the internal oblique and transversus abdominis aponeuroses, forms the medial part of the posterior wall and medial boundary of the inguinal canal. Weakness here predisposes to direct inguinal hernias. The lateral part of the posterior wall is formed by the transversalis fascia.

questions.question: The scala media contains which fluid?
questions.explanation: The scala media (cochlear duct) contains endolymph, which has high potassium and low sodium concentration (similar to intracellular fluid). The scala vestibuli and scala tympani contain perilymph. The organ of Corti lies on the basilar membrane separating scala media from scala tympani. Ménière's disease involves endolymphatic hydrops.

The inferior vena cava, covered by parietal peritoneum, forms the posterior boundary of the epiploic foramen (foramen of Winslow), along with the right crus of the diaphragm. This anatomical relationship is clinically significant because the IVC can be compressed in the Pringle maneuver when the hepatoduodenal ligament (anterior boundary containing the portal triad) is manually compressed or clamped to control hepatic bleeding. The proximity of the IVC also means that the foramen provides a potential route for hemorrhage into the lesser sac following IVC injury.
questions.question: Which structure passes posterior to the epiploic foramen?

questions.explanation: Olfactory nerve axons from the nasal epithelium pass through multiple foramina in the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone. These first-order sensory neurons synapse in the olfactory bulb above the cribriform plate. Head trauma can shear these delicate fibers causing anosmia.
questions.question: The olfactory nerves pass through which structure?
Into which vein does the lower third of the oesophagus drain venously?
questions.explanation: The veins from the lower third of the oesophagus drain into the left gastric vein, which is part of the portal circulation. This drainage pattern creates a clinically significant portosystemic anastomosis at the gastro-oesophageal junction. In portal hypertension, these veins become dilated forming oesophageal varices that can cause life-threatening haematemesis.

The right marginal artery is a branch of the right coronary artery that descends along the acute margin (right border) of the heart to supply the right ventricle. The left marginal artery (branch of the circumflex or left coronary artery) supplies the left border of the heart. These marginal branches are important anatomical landmarks in cardiac catheterization and surgery.
questions.question: What is the marginal artery of the heart?

questions.explanation: The posterior superior iliac spine (PSIS) corresponds to the level of S2. This is a clinically important landmark for epidural and spinal anesthesia, as well as for assessing pelvic symmetry in musculoskeletal examination. The highest point of the iliac crest corresponds to the level of L4, used for lumbar puncture guidance.
questions.question: The posterior superior iliac spine (PSIS) corresponds to the level of which sacral segment?
Which lymph nodes receive anterior diaphragmatic drainage?
questions.explanation: Lymph from the thoracic surface of the diaphragm drains anteriorly to parasternal lymph nodes (via anterior diaphragmatic nodes) and posteriorly to phrenic and posterior mediastinal nodes. From the abdominal surface, drainage goes to anterior diaphragmatic, phrenic, and superior lumbar (caval/aortic) nodes.

The upper trunk is formed by union of C5 and C6 nerve roots. Injury to the upper trunk causes Erb's paralysis with characteristic policeman's tip hand deformity. The upper trunk gives rise to the suprascapular nerve and nerve to subclavius.
questions.question: Which nerve roots form the upper trunk of the brachial plexus?

questions.explanation: The Circle of Willis is situated around the pituitary infundibulum and optic chiasma at the base of the brain. It provides collateral circulation when major arteries become occluded. The circle includes anterior cerebral, anterior communicating, internal carotid, posterior communicating, and posterior cerebral arteries.
options: Internal acoustic meatus and jugular foramen
Superior orbital fissure and optic canal
questions.question: The Circle of Willis is located around which anatomical structures?

questions.explanation: The AV nodal artery arises from the right coronary artery in approximately 80-90% of people (right dominant circulation) and from the left circumflex artery in the remainder (left dominant circulation). It typically arises near the origin of the posterior interventricular artery. AV node ischemia from right coronary occlusion can cause heart block.
questions.question: Which artery supplies the AV node in most people?

questions.explanation: The sphenopalatine foramen in the medial wall of the pterygopalatine fossa connects it with the nasal cavity. The foramen is located between the sphenoid bone and orbital process of the palatine bone. The sphenopalatine artery and nasopalatine nerve pass through it to supply the nasal cavity and septum.
questions.question: The pterygopalatine fossa communicates with the nasal cavity through which opening?

questions.explanation: The accessory pancreatic duct (duct of Santorini), when present, drains the upper part of the head of the pancreas and opens into the duodenum at the minor duodenal papilla. This papilla is located approximately 2 cm proximal to the major papilla. The accessory duct frequently communicates with the main pancreatic duct.
questions.question: Where does the accessory pancreatic duct open into the duodenum?

questions.explanation: The basilar artery is formed by the union of the two vertebral arteries at the pontomedullary junction. It ascends in the pontine groove and terminates by dividing into the two posterior cerebral arteries. Branches include pontine, anterior inferior cerebellar, superior cerebellar, and labyrinthine arteries.
questions.question: The basilar artery is formed by the union of which vessels?

options: Popliteal artery, popliteal vein, tibial nerve, common fibular nerve
Tibial nerve, common fibular nerve, popliteal vein, popliteal artery
Common fibular nerve, popliteal artery, popliteal vein, tibial nerve
Common fibular nerve, tibial nerve, popliteal vein, popliteal artery
Popliteal vein, popliteal artery, tibial nerve, common fibular nerve
questions.explanation: At the superior angle of the popliteal fossa, the sciatic nerve divides into the common fibular nerve (laterally, following the medial border of biceps femoris) and the tibial nerve (medially). From lateral to medial: common fibular nerve, tibial nerve, popliteal vein, then popliteal artery (deepest). This arrangement changes inferiorly as the popliteal vein crosses to lie posterior to the artery.
questions.question: In the popliteal fossa, the popliteal artery lies deepest and the tibial nerve most superficially. In what order, from lateral to medial, are the structures arranged superiorly within the fossa?

questions.explanation: The inferior epigastric artery arises from the external iliac artery just above the inguinal ligament, medial to the deep inguinal ring. It ascends obliquely along the medial margin of the deep ring, passing medial to it (an important landmark distinguishing direct from indirect inguinal hernias), and enters the rectus sheath by piercing the transversalis fascia at the arcuate line. Within the sheath, it ascends posterior to the rectus abdominis muscle and anastomoses with the superior epigastric artery, providing an important collateral pathway between subclavian (via internal thoracic) and external iliac arterial systems.
questions.question: The inferior epigastric artery arises from which vessel?

questions.explanation: The dorsalis pedis artery begins as the anterior tibial artery enters the foot at the ankle. It passes over the dorsal tarsal bones and then moves toward the sole, anastomosing with the lateral plantar artery to form the deep plantar arch. It supplies the tarsal bones and dorsal metatarsals, and contributes to the toes via the deep plantar arch.
questions.question: The dorsalis pedis artery is the continuation of which artery as it crosses the ankle to enter the foot?

questions.explanation: The ureter has three normal anatomical constrictions where renal calculi commonly lodge: at the pelviureteric junction (ureteropelvic junction, where renal pelvis transitions to ureter), where it crosses the pelvic brim (over the bifurcation of the common iliac artery), and at the ureterovesical junction (as it passes obliquely through the bladder wall). These constrictions appear on imaging studies and during ureteroscopy. Additional functional constrictions may occur where the ureter crosses vessels (testicular/ovarian in abdomen, uterine artery in females). Understanding these sites helps predict where stones will impact and cause obstruction.
questions.question: The ureter is constricted at which locations?

questions.explanation: During expiration, the right dome of the diaphragm reaches as high as the fifth rib due to the upward bulge of the right lobe of the liver. The left dome ascends to the fifth intercostal space. With maximal inspiration, the domes flatten out considerably, descending several centimeters.
questions.question: At which rib does right dome reach during expiration?

questions.explanation: The popliteal fascia is often pierced by the small saphenous vein as it ascends from the lateral ankle to the popliteal fossa, where it enters the popliteal vein. The popliteal fascia is a strong sheet of deep fascia continuous superiorly with the fascia lata and inferiorly with the deep fascia of the leg, forming a protective covering for neurovascular structures.
questions.question: The popliteal fascia is often pierced by which superficial vein as it drains into the popliteal vein?
Where does the left testicular vein drain?
questions.explanation: The left testicular (gonadal) vein drains into the left renal vein at approximately a right angle, while the right testicular vein drains directly into the inferior vena cava obliquely. This difference in drainage, along with the longer left testicular vein, explains why varicoceles are much more common on the left side (85-90% of cases).

The olfactory bulbs lie on the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone in the anterior cranial fossa. Olfactory nerve fibers from the nasal epithelium pass through the cribriform foramina to synapse in the bulbs. The olfactory tracts extend posteriorly from the bulbs. Head trauma can shear these delicate fibers causing anosmia.
questions.question: Which space contains the olfactory bulbs?
The internal spermatic fascia is derived from which structure?
questions.explanation: The internal spermatic fascia, the innermost of the three fascial coverings of the spermatic cord, is derived from the transversalis fascia as the cord structures pass through the deep inguinal ring. This fascia is continuous with the transversalis fascia at the margins of the deep ring. Moving outward, the next layer is the cremasteric muscle and fascia (from internal oblique and transversus abdominis), and the outermost layer is the external spermatic fascia (from external oblique aponeurosis at the superficial ring). These three layers enclose the contents of the spermatic cord and represent contributions from each layer of the anterior abdominal wall.

questions.question: Which structure does NOT pass through the carpal tunnel?
questions.explanation: The flexor carpi radialis tendon lies in a groove between the attachments of the flexor retinaculum to bone, not within the carpal tunnel itself. The carpal tunnel contains the median nerve, four tendons each of flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus, and the flexor pollicis longus tendon. These structures are enclosed within synovial sheaths.

questions.question: What percentage of lymph drains to axillary nodes?
questions.explanation: Approximately 75% of lymph from the breast drains into the axillary nodes, primarily the pectoral (anterior) group. About 20% drains to the internal mammary (parasternal) chain. The lower quadrants may drain to inferior phrenic (abdominal) nodes. This drainage pattern is crucial in cancer staging.

questions.question: At which vertebral level does the tail of the pancreas lie?
questions.explanation: The tail of the pancreas extends to the left and lies at the level of the twelfth thoracic vertebra (T12). The tail reaches the splenic hilum and is the only intraperitoneal part of the pancreas, lying within the splenorenal ligament. Anteriorly, the tail is related to the splenic flexure of the colon.

questions.question: The inferior vena cava receives which vein at the L1 level?
questions.explanation: The right renal vein (shorter than the left, approximately 2-4 cm) drains into the inferior vena cava at approximately the L1-L2 level, just below the origin of the superior mesenteric artery from the aorta. The left renal vein (longer, 7-10 cm) crosses anterior to the aorta at the same level to reach the IVC. The right renal vein receives only the right gonadal and right suprarenal veins (sometimes), while the left renal vein receives the left gonadal, left suprarenal, and left inferior phrenic veins before reaching the IVC.

questions.question: The gallbladder fundus projects beyond which liver border?
questions.explanation: The fundus of the gallbladder projects beyond the inferior border of the liver at the tip of the right 9th costal cartilage, where it may contact the anterior abdominal wall. This location corresponds approximately to the point where the lateral edge of the right rectus abdominis crosses the right costal margin (at the transpyloric plane). The fundus is the only part of the gallbladder completely covered by peritoneum on all surfaces. When the gallbladder is distended or inflamed (acute cholecystitis), the fundus becomes palpable at this location, and deep palpation causes inspiratory arrest (Murphy's sign).

The iliohypogastric nerve (L1, sometimes with T12 contribution) emerges from the lateral border of the psoas major muscle, running obliquely across the anterior surface of quadratus lumborum. It pierces the transversus abdominis muscle to run between it and internal oblique, providing motor innervation to these muscles. The nerve gives off a lateral cutaneous branch (skin over hip) and anterior cutaneous branch (skin above pubis). Other nerves emerging from the lateral border of psoas include ilioinguinal, lateral femoral cutaneous, and femoral nerves. The genitofemoral nerve pierces the anterior surface.
questions.question: The iliohypogastric nerve emerges from which border of psoas?
The stapedius muscle is innervated by which nerve?
questions.explanation: The stapedius muscle is innervated by the stapedial branch of the facial nerve. It dampens excessive ossicular chain movement in response to loud sounds above 80 dB. Facial nerve paralysis results in hyperacusis (sound sensitivity) due to stapedius muscle dysfunction.

questions.question: The foramen lacerum transmits which structure in life?
questions.explanation: In life, the foramen lacerum is closed by fibrocartilage. Only small meningeal arterial branches and the greater petrosal nerve pass through its superior aspect. The internal carotid artery passes above the foramen within the carotid canal, not through it. In dried skulls, the foramen appears as a large irregular opening.

questions.question: Which coronary artery typically gives rise to the SA nodal artery?
questions.explanation: The sinoatrial nodal artery arises from the right coronary artery in approximately 60% of people, and from the left circumflex artery in about 40%. It courses posteriorly around the superior vena cava-atrial junction to supply the SA node. Occlusion can cause sinus node dysfunction, though collateral circulation often provides some protection.

The femoral canal, the most medial compartment of the femoral sheath, normally contains lymphatics and loose connective tissue. It is the site of femoral hernias, which are more common in women (due to their wider pelvis and femoral ring). Femoral hernias emerge below and lateral to the pubic tubercle (unlike inguinal hernias above and medial to it). They are at high risk of strangulation due to the rigid femoral ring.
questions.question: The femoral canal, the medial compartment of the femoral sheath, contains which structures and is the site of which type of hernia?
options: Lymphatics and loose connective tissue; femoral hernia
Femoral artery and nerve; femoral hernia

questions.explanation: The parotid (Stensen's) duct crosses the masseter muscle superficially before turning medially to pierce the buccinator. The duct runs parallel to and one finger's breadth below the zygomatic arch. Accessory parotid tissue (socia parotidis) may be present on the masseter along the duct. Facial nerve branches lie deep to the duct.
questions.question: The parotid duct crosses which muscle superficially?
What landmark indicates tracheal bifurcation level?
questions.explanation: The sternal angle (of Louis) at the level of T4/5 marks the tracheal bifurcation, the beginning and end of the aortic arch, the upper margin of the heart, and the boundary between superior and inferior mediastinum. This is one of the most important surface landmarks in thoracic anatomy.

questions.question: What lies in the anterior mediastinum primarily?
questions.explanation: The anterior mediastinum (between the sternum and pericardium) contains primarily the thymus gland (or its remnant in adults), fatty tissue, and lymph nodes. In children, the thymus is prominent; in adults, it is largely replaced by fat. This space can be involved in thymomas or lymphomas.

questions.question: The cricopharyngeus muscle acts as a sphincter for which structure?
questions.explanation: The cricopharyngeus muscle, the lower part of the inferior constrictor, acts as the upper esophageal sphincter. It remains tonically contracted except during swallowing. Between cricopharyngeus and thyropharyngeus lies the dehiscence of Killian where pharyngeal diverticula (Zenker's) occur.

The scaphoid bone forms the floor of the anatomical snuffbox and is palpable in this space. Tenderness in the snuffbox following wrist injury suggests possible scaphoid fracture. The radial artery pulse can also be felt crossing the snuffbox floor.
questions.question: Which structure is palpable in the anatomical snuffbox?
What is the lung at the apex called?
questions.explanation: The cupola (or apex) is the rounded superior portion of the lung that extends into the root of the neck, reaching 2.5-4 cm above the medial third of the clavicle. It is covered by cervical pleura and the suprapleural membrane (Sibson's fascia). The subclavian artery arches over the lung apex.

questions.question: Which structure does the round ligament of the liver represent?
questions.explanation: The round ligament of the liver (ligamentum teres hepatis) represents the obliterated left umbilical vein, which carried oxygenated blood from the placenta to the fetus. It runs from the umbilicus to the liver within the free inferior margin of the falciform ligament, then continues in a fissure on the visceral surface between the left and quadrate lobes before joining the left branch of the portal vein. In portal hypertension, paraumbilical veins accompanying the ligamentum teres may recanalize, creating a portosystemic anastomosis that can produce caput medusae (dilated superficial veins radiating from the umbilicus). The obliterated ductus venosus forms the ligamentum venosum.

questions.question: Five bones uniquely possess epiphyseal plates at BOTH ends. Which set correctly identifies all five?
questions.explanation: Most long bones have only one epiphyseal plate at one end; however, five bones are unique in having epiphyseal plates at both ends: femur, tibia, fibula, humerus, and radius. This feature is important in understanding growth patterns and fracture management in these bones.

questions.question: Semitendinosus, semimembranosus, and the long head of biceps femoris are all innervated by which division of the sciatic nerve?
questions.explanation: Semitendinosus, semimembranosus, and the long head of biceps femoris are all innervated by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve (L5, S1, S2). The exception is the short head of biceps femoris, which is supplied by the common fibular division. The sciatic nerve is the largest nerve in the body.

questions.question: Where does the female urethra open externally?
questions.explanation: The female external urethral orifice opens into the vestibule, the space between the labia minora, approximately 2.5 cm posterior to the clitoris and immediately anterior to the vaginal opening. The orifice is surrounded by the external urethral sphincter and may be difficult to visualize in some women. Paraurethral (Skene's) glands open on either side of the orifice.

questions.question: What are splenic cords composed of?
questions.explanation: Splenic cords (cords of Billroth) in the red pulp consist of a meshwork of reticular fibers and reticular cells, with macrophages, lymphocytes, plasma cells, and various blood cells in the interstices. Blood from open-ended capillaries percolates through these cords before re-entering the circulation via sinusoids. Macrophages in the cords phagocytose old red cells and foreign particles.

questions.question: What shape is the central tendon?
questions.explanation: The central tendon of the diaphragm is shaped like three leaves (trifoliate). It has no bony attachments but is partially fused with the inferior surface of the fibrous pericardium. All the muscular fibers of the diaphragm insert into this central tendon.

questions.question: The tensor tympani muscle arises from which structure?
questions.explanation: The tensor tympani muscle arises from the cartilaginous part of the Eustachian tube and the bony canal above it. The muscle runs in a bony canal parallel to the Eustachian tube. Its tendon turns laterally around the processus cochleariformis to insert on the malleus. Contraction tenses the tympanic membrane.

The hyoepiglottic ligament connects the anterior surface of the epiglottis to the upper border of the hyoid bone. The thyroepiglottic ligament attaches the epiglottis to the thyroid cartilage. The epiglottis is also connected to the tongue by the median and lateral glossoepiglottic folds. These ligaments maintain epiglottic position during swallowing.
questions.question: Which ligament connects the epiglottis to the hyoid bone?
Which cranial nerve supplies sensory innervation to the oropharynx?
questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve provides sensory innervation to the oropharynx, including the tonsillar region and posterior third of tongue. The vagus nerve also contributes sensation to the valleculae via the internal laryngeal branch. Referred otalgia from pharyngeal lesions occurs via glossopharyngeal pathways.

Each adult kidney is approximately 10 cm long, 5 cm wide, and 2.5 cm thick, resembling a large bean in shape. The left kidney is typically slightly longer and narrower than the right. Kidney size is clinically important, as small kidneys may indicate chronic disease while enlarged kidneys suggest acute processes or masses.
