questions.question: What are the approximate dimensions of an adult kidney?
The lesser occipital nerve is derived from which spinal segments?
questions.explanation: The lesser occipital nerve arises from the cervical plexus (C2-C3) and provides sensation to the skin of the lateral scalp posterior to the auricle. It ascends along the posterior border of sternocleidomastoid. The greater occipital nerve (C2) provides sensation to the posterior scalp. Both nerves can be involved in occipital neuralgia.

The lumbar plexus is formed within the substance of the psoas major muscle from the anterior (ventral) rami of L1, L2, L3, and the upper part of L4 nerve roots. The plexus gives rise to branches that emerge from different borders of the muscle: lateral border (iliohypogastric, ilioinguinal, lateral femoral cutaneous, femoral nerves), anterior surface (genitofemoral nerve), and medial border (obturator nerve). The psoas major also receives direct motor innervation from L1-L4 nerve roots. The lumbar plexus supplies the anterior abdominal wall, external genitalia, and anterior and medial thigh.
questions.question: The lumbar plexus is formed within which muscle?

questions.explanation: The splenic artery is the largest branch of the celiac trunk and has a characteristic tortuous course along the superior border of the pancreas. It runs from right to left within the splenorenal ligament before dividing into 5-7 branches at the splenic hilum. The artery gives off numerous pancreatic branches, short gastric arteries, and the left gastroepiploic artery.
questions.question: Which is the largest branch of the celiac trunk?

questions.explanation: The anterior ethmoidal foramen in the medial orbital wall transmits the anterior ethmoidal nerve (from nasociliary) and vessels (from ophthalmic artery). These structures supply the anterior ethmoidal air cells, frontal sinus, and upper nasal cavity. The foramen is located between the ethmoid and frontal bones at the frontoethmoidal suture.
questions.question: The anterior ethmoidal foramen transmits which structures?
Which structure forms the lateral boundary of the pterygopalatine fossa?
questions.explanation: The pterygomaxillary fissure forms the lateral boundary, connecting the pterygopalatine fossa with the infratemporal fossa. The anterior wall is formed by the posterior surface of the maxilla. The medial wall consists of the perpendicular plate of the palatine bone.

questions.question: Which vertebra bounds the inferior thoracic aperture posteriorly?
questions.explanation: The inferior thoracic aperture is bounded posteriorly by the twelfth thoracic vertebra. Laterally, it is bounded by the curving costal margin formed by ribs 11 and 12. Anteriorly, the xiphisternal joint completes the boundaries, and the entire opening is closed by the diaphragm.

The nutrient artery, also called the medullary artery, is the main blood supply to the diaphysis of a long bone. It enters through the nutrient canal and nutrient foramen, branching within the medullary cavity. The epiphysis, metaphysis, and periosteum all have their own distinct arterial supplies from separate named vessels.
questions.question: The nutrient artery (medullary artery) is best described as the main artery of which part of a long bone?
Which immune cells are found in splenic white pulp?
questions.explanation: The splenic white pulp consists primarily of T and B lymphocytes organized around central arterioles (periarterial lymphoid sheaths - PALS containing T cells) and in lymphoid follicles (containing B cells). The white pulp is responsible for immune surveillance of blood-borne antigens and antibody production. It represents about 15-25% of splenic tissue and increases in infections.

The splenorenal ligament connects the hilum of the spleen to the anterior surface of the left kidney and contains the splenic artery and vein, along with the tail of the pancreas (extending to within 1 cm of the splenic hilum in about 75% of individuals). The splenic vessels run a tortuous course along the superior border of the pancreatic body and tail before entering this ligament. The ligament represents the left portion of the dorsal mesogastrium. During splenectomy, the tail of the pancreas within this ligament must be identified and preserved to prevent pancreatic injury and subsequent pancreatitis or pseudocyst formation.
questions.question: Which vessel typically runs in the splenorenal ligament?
Where does the thoracic duct terminate?
questions.explanation: The thoracic duct terminates by draining into the left venous angle (junction of left internal jugular and left subclavian veins). Before termination, it receives the left jugular, subclavian, and bronchomediastinal lymph trunks. The duct has no valve at its termination.

questions.question: Which branch of the left coronary artery supplies the interventricular septum?
questions.explanation: The anterior interventricular artery (left anterior descending - LAD) descends in the anterior interventricular groove and supplies the anterior two-thirds of the interventricular septum, anterior left ventricular wall, and anterior right ventricle. It is the most commonly affected vessel in myocardial infarction. Septal branches perforate the septum; diagonal branches supply the lateral left ventricle.

Tibialis posterior is the primary dynamic supporter of the medial longitudinal arch. It inserts into the tuberosity of the navicular, all three cuneiform bones, cuboid, sustentaculum tali, and bases of the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th metatarsals. Rupture of the tibialis posterior tendon leads to progressive adult flatfoot deformity (acquired pes planus).
questions.question: Tibialis posterior, inverting the foot and plantarflexing the ankle, primarily supports which arch of the foot?
The lacrimal sac lies in which structure?
questions.explanation: The lacrimal sac occupies the lacrimal fossa, a depression formed by the lacrimal bone and frontal process of the maxilla. The sac receives tears from the canaliculi superiorly and drains into the nasolacrimal duct inferiorly. Dacryocystitis (infection of the lacrimal sac) causes swelling medial to the inner canthus.

The ophthalmic artery is the first major branch of the internal carotid artery after it exits the cavernous sinus. It enters the orbit through the optic canal with the optic nerve. Branches include the central retinal artery, which is an end artery supplying the retina.
questions.question: The ophthalmic artery is a branch of which vessel?

questions.explanation: The diaphragm is highest in the supine position and after a large meal due to upward pressure from abdominal viscera. When lying on one side, the dependent (lower) diaphragm is considerably higher than the uppermost one. Position affects diaphragm function and is clinically relevant.
questions.question: Which position elevates the diaphragm highest?

questions.explanation: The fundus and upper body of the stomach contain the highest concentration of parietal cells in the gastric glands. The cardiac region contains mainly mucous-secreting cells. The pyloric region contains mainly mucous cells and G cells (which secrete gastrin). This distribution reflects the functional specialization of different gastric regions.
questions.question: Which part of the stomach has the highest concentration of parietal cells?

questions.explanation: Vagal (parasympathetic) stimulation decreases heart rate (negative chronotropy), decreases conduction velocity through the AV node, and slightly decreases contractility. The vagus nerve releases acetylcholine, which acts on muscarinic receptors (M2) in the SA node, AV node, and atrial muscle. The right vagus preferentially affects the SA node; the left vagus affects the AV node.
questions.question: Which effect does vagal stimulation have on the heart?
The inguinal ligament extends between which two points?
questions.explanation: The inguinal ligament represents the rolled-under, thickened inferior border of the external oblique aponeurosis, extending from the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) laterally to the pubic tubercle medially. It serves as a retinaculum bridging the subinguinal space through which pass the iliopsoas muscle, femoral vessels and nerve, and lymphatics entering/leaving the thigh. The inguinal ligament forms the inferior boundary (floor) of the inguinal canal and the base of Hesselbach's triangle. The lacunar ligament represents its medial extension, reflecting posteriorly to attach to the pectineal line.

The cricoid cartilage is located at the C6 vertebral level. The lower border marks the transition from pharynx to esophagus and from larynx to trachea. This level also corresponds to where the carotid tubercle of C6 can be palpated and the carotid artery compressed. The middle cervical sympathetic ganglion lies at this level.
questions.question: The cricoid cartilage is located at which vertebral level?
Which peritoneal ligament contains the ovarian vessels?
questions.explanation: The suspensory ligament of the ovary (infundibulopelvic ligament), a lateral extension of the broad ligament, contains the ovarian vessels (artery and vein) and nerves passing from the lateral pelvic wall to the ovary. This ligament extends from the ovary to the lateral pelvic wall and must be carefully ligated during oophorectomy to control the ovarian vessels. The ovarian ligament (ligament of the ovary) connects the ovary to the uterus and contains no significant vessels. The broad ligament is a double layer of peritoneum extending from the lateral pelvic wall to the uterus, with the ovarian vessels running in its superior lateral extension.

The suprascapular nerve (C5, C6) supplies both supraspinatus and infraspinatus muscles. The nerve passes through the suprascapular notch (under the superior transverse scapular ligament) to reach the supraspinous fossa, then through the spinoglenoid notch to the infraspinous fossa.
questions.question: What nerve supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus?

questions.explanation: Flexor digitorum brevis is supplied by the medial plantar nerve (S2, S3). The medial plantar nerve (analogous to the median nerve) also supplies abductor hallucis, flexor hallucis brevis, and the first lumbrical. The lateral plantar nerve (analogous to the ulnar nerve) supplies all other intrinsic muscles: abductor digiti minimi, quadratus plantae, flexor digiti minimi brevis, all interossei, lateral three lumbricals, and adductor hallucis.
questions.question: The tibial nerve enters the tarsal tunnel and supplies intrinsic muscles of the sole via its terminal branches. Which of the following is supplied by the medial plantar nerve?

questions.explanation: Gastrin is produced by G cells in the pyloric antrum and stimulates parietal cells to secrete hydrochloric acid and stimulates chief cells to secrete pepsinogen. Its release is stimulated by stomach distention, peptides, and vagal stimulation. Gastrin secretion is inhibited by low pH (negative feedback) and by somatostatin from D cells.
questions.question: Which hormone stimulates gastric acid secretion?
The great cerebral vein of Galen drains into which sinus?
questions.explanation: The great cerebral vein (of Galen) is formed by union of internal cerebral veins and basal veins, draining into the straight sinus. The straight sinus then joins the superior sagittal sinus at the confluence of sinuses. Deep cerebral structures drain via this venous pathway.

questions.question: Which vessel marks the medial boundary of the epiploic foramen?
questions.explanation: The epiploic foramen (foramen of Winslow) has the bile duct within the hepatoduodenal ligament as its anterior boundary, not medial. The superior boundary is the caudate lobe of the liver, the inferior boundary is the first part of the duodenum, the anterior boundary is the hepatoduodenal ligament containing the portal triad (portal vein, hepatic artery, and bile duct), and the posterior boundary is the inferior vena cava covered by parietal peritoneum. This opening typically admits two fingers and provides communication between the greater and lesser sacs.

questions.question: Which part of the peritoneum covers the anterior rectum?
questions.explanation: The upper third of the rectum is covered by peritoneum on both anterior and lateral surfaces; the middle third has peritoneum only on its anterior surface; the lower third is completely devoid of peritoneal covering (extraperitoneal/infraperitoneal). This peritoneal relationship is important for surgical approaches and tumor spread patterns.

questions.question: The descending genicular artery, contributing to the genicular anastomosis superomedially, is a branch of which artery?
questions.explanation: The descending genicular artery is a branch of the femoral artery, contributing superomedially to the genicular anastomosis. The five genicular branches of the popliteal artery are: lateral superior, medial superior, middle, lateral inferior, and medial inferior genicular arteries. The anterior tibial recurrent artery contributes inferolaterally.

questions.question: What is the anatomical position of the glenohumeral joint capsule's weakest area?
questions.explanation: The glenohumeral joint capsule is weakest inferiorly, making this the most common site for dislocation. The capsule is thin and lax to allow wide range of movement, particularly abduction. Superior movement of the humeral head is prevented by the coraco-acromial arch rather than capsular strength.

Full knee flexion may kink the popliteal artery, explaining why the genicular anastomosis is functionally important: it provides collateral circulation to maintain blood supply to the leg even when the popliteal artery is kinked. This anastomosis is formed by branches of the popliteal, femoral, lateral femoral circumflex, and anterior tibial arteries.
questions.question: Full knee flexion may kink which artery, explaining the functional importance of the genicular anastomosis as collateral circulation?
Which ligament connects the coracoid process to the acromion of the scapula?
questions.explanation: The coracoacromial ligament runs between the coracoid process and acromion of the scapula. Unlike other shoulder ligaments, it does not cross a joint or permit movement. It forms part of the coraco-acromial arch that prevents superior displacement of the humeral head.

The costal pleura receives sensory innervation from the intercostal nerves, which correspond to the dermatomes of the overlying thoracic wall. The blood supply to costal pleura is also from intercostal vessels. This arrangement means that irritation of costal pleura causes sharp, well-localized pain.
questions.question: Which nerve supplies the costal pleura?
Which structure contains the portal triad?
questions.explanation: The hepatoduodenal ligament, forming the thickened free right edge of the lesser omentum, contains the portal triad: the portal vein (posteriorly), hepatic artery proper (anteriorly and to the left), and common bile duct (anteriorly and to the right). This ligament extends from the porta hepatis to the superior border of the first part of the duodenum. The portal triad arrangement is crucial for the Pringle maneuver, where the hepatoduodenal ligament is compressed to control bleeding during hepatic surgery.

Hiccup is an involuntary spasmodic contraction of the diaphragm accompanied by approximation of vocal folds and closure of the glottis. It commonly results from gastric irritation of vagus nerve endings. It may also occur in pleurisy, peritonitis, or pericarditis affecting the diaphragm.
questions.question: What causes hiccup?
Which nerve is the largest branch of the brachial plexus?
questions.explanation: The radial nerve (C5-T1) is the largest branch of the brachial plexus and the most frequently injured. It arises from the posterior cord and supplies all extensor muscles of the upper limb. The nerve is particularly vulnerable in the spiral groove of the humerus.

The windlass mechanism (described by Hicks, 1954) involves tensioning of the plantar aponeurosis as the toes dorsiflexed during push-off. This raises the medial longitudinal arch, shortens the foot, and converts it into a rigid lever for efficient propulsion. This mechanism is impaired in flatfoot (pes planus) and hallux rigidus, reducing push-off efficiency.
options: Flattens the medial longitudinal arch of the foot
Has no significant effect on any foot arch
Progressively flattens the transverse arch of the midfoot
Raises the medial longitudinal arch, converting foot to a rigid push-off lever
Only affects the lateral longitudinal arch of the foot
questions.question: The 'windlass mechanism' of the foot refers to tensioning of the plantar aponeurosis during toe dorsiflexion. What effect does this have on the foot arches?

questions.explanation: The cecum is the widest part of the large intestine (approximately 7.5 cm in diameter), and the diameter gradually decreases toward the sigmoid colon. This variation in diameter is clinically significant in colonic obstruction: according to Laplace's law, the cecum is most likely to perforate in cases of distal large bowel obstruction due to its larger diameter and thinner wall.
questions.question: Which segment of colon has the largest diameter?

questions.explanation: The posterior wall of the axilla is formed by subscapularis on the anterior surface of the scapula superiorly, and teres major and latissimus dorsi inferiorly. The posterior axillary fold extends farther inferiorly than the anterior wall and can be grasped between fingers.
questions.question: Which muscles form the posterior wall of the axilla?
The uterine artery is a branch of which vessel?
questions.explanation: The uterine artery arises from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery, descending in the parametrium (base of the broad ligament) to reach the uterus at the level of the internal cervical os. It crosses superior to (over) the ureter approximately 1.5 cm lateral to the cervix ("water under the bridge"), an important surgical relationship. The artery ascends along the lateral margin of the uterus in a tortuous course, giving off branches to the uterus and anastomosing superiorly with the ovarian artery. During pregnancy, it enlarges significantly to supply the gravid uterus and placenta.

questions.question: Which lymph nodes drain the sigmoid colon?
questions.explanation: The sigmoid colon drains to sigmoid nodes along the sigmoid arteries, then to inferior mesenteric nodes around the inferior mesenteric artery origin. These eventually drain to para-aortic (lateral aortic) nodes. In colorectal cancer, lymph node involvement follows this drainage pattern and is crucial for staging. The lymphatic spread of left-sided colon cancers differs from right-sided cancers.

The duodenojejunal flexure is located at the level of the second lumbar vertebra (L2), approximately 2.5 cm to the left of the midline. This junction is supported by the suspensory muscle of the duodenum (ligament of Treitz), a fibromuscular band. The flexure marks the transition from the retroperitoneal duodenum to the intraperitoneal jejunum.
questions.question: At which vertebral level does the duodenojejunal flexure lie?
The ligamentum teres hepatis is found in which structure?
questions.explanation: The ligamentum teres hepatis (round ligament of the liver), representing the obliterated left umbilical vein, runs from the umbilicus to the liver within the free inferior border of the falciform ligament. Upon reaching the liver, it continues in a fissure on the visceral surface between the left and quadrate lobes before joining the left branch of the portal vein. The ligamentum teres may remain patent in portal hypertension, allowing portosystemic anastomosis through paraumbilical veins, potentially leading to caput medusae. At the umbilicus, it connects to the median umbilical ligament (obliterated urachus).

questions.question: Which branch of the external carotid artery enters the skull through the foramen spinosum?
questions.explanation: The middle meningeal artery, a branch of the maxillary artery, enters the skull through the foramen spinosum. It supplies the dura mater and inner table of the skull. Rupture of this artery causes epidural hematoma, typically from temporal bone fractures.

The medial meniscus is C-shaped and firmly attached to the tibial (medial) collateral ligament at its midpoint. This attachment makes it less mobile and more vulnerable to injury than the lateral meniscus. The tibial collateral ligament and medial meniscus are often torn together in contact sports as part of the classic 'unhappy triad.'
questions.question: The medial meniscus is C-shaped and firmly adheres to which extracapsular ligament, making it more vulnerable to sporting injury?

questions.explanation: The reflected attachment of semimembranosus forms the oblique popliteal ligament, which strengthens the fibrous capsule of the knee posteriorly. Semimembranosus inserts primarily into the posterior part of the medial condyle of the tibia. The arcuate popliteal ligament is a separate structure arising from the posterior fibular head.
questions.question: The reflected attachment of the semimembranosus tendon forms which structure posteriorly in the knee?

questions.explanation: The deep fibular nerve supplies the skin of the first web space (between the 1st and 2nd toes) on the dorsum of the foot. The superficial fibular nerve supplies most of the dorsum of the foot. The saphenous nerve supplies the medial side (first metatarsal area), while the sural nerve supplies the lateral side (digiti minimi area). This pattern is important in assessing nerve injuries.
questions.question: The dorsum of the foot receives cutaneous innervation from several nerves. Which nerve supplies the skin between the 1st and 2nd toes on the dorsum?

questions.explanation: The facial nerve exits the skull through the stylomastoid foramen after traversing the facial canal. It then enters the parotid gland and divides into five terminal branches. Damage at this location causes complete ipsilateral facial paralysis including loss of taste to anterior two-thirds of tongue.
questions.question: The stylomastoid foramen transmits which cranial nerve?
Where do anterior intercostal lymphatics drain?
questions.explanation: Lymph vessels from the anterior part of intercostal spaces drain into anterior intercostal nodes that lie along the internal thoracic artery. From these nodes, lymph passes to the parasternal nodes. Posterior intercostal lymphatics drain into posterior intercostal nodes in the posterior mediastinum.

questions.question: The knee joint stability depends primarily on muscles. Which muscle group is described as the MOST important in stabilizing the knee joint?
questions.explanation: The quadriceps femoris is the most important muscle group for stabilizing the knee joint. The inferior fibers of vastus medialis and lateralis are particularly important stabilizers. Quadriceps weakness leads to instability especially on stairs and inclines. Rehabilitation after any knee injury or surgery focuses heavily on quadriceps strengthening exercises.

The right border of the heart on a chest X-ray is formed by the right atrium. The left border is formed primarily by the left ventricle with a small contribution from the left atrial appendage superiorly. The superior border is formed by the great vessels (aorta and pulmonary artery).
questions.question: What forms the right heart border radiographically?
Which joint in the shoulder girdle provides the only bony link to the axial skeleton?
questions.explanation: The sternoclavicular joint connects the medial end of the clavicle to the manubrium of the sternum. This synovial joint is the sole bony articulation linking the shoulder girdle to the axial skeleton. Posteriorly lie important structures including the common carotid artery and internal jugular vein.

questions.question: Which nerve root contributes to the iliohypogastric nerve?
questions.explanation: The iliohypogastric nerve arises from the L1 nerve root (sometimes with minor contribution from T12), emerging from the lateral border of psoas major. It runs obliquely across the anterior surface of quadratus lumborum, then pierces the transversus abdominis muscle to run between it and internal oblique, providing motor innervation to these muscles. The nerve gives off a lateral cutaneous branch (supplying skin over the hip) and an anterior cutaneous branch (supplying skin above the pubis), crossing above and parallel to the inguinal canal. Injury during appendectomy or hernia repair can cause chronic groin pain and sensory loss.

questions.question: The epitympanic recess contains which structure?
questions.explanation: The epitympanic recess (attic) is the upper part of the tympanic cavity above the level of the tympanic membrane. It contains the head of the malleus and body of the incus. The recess communicates posteriorly with the mastoid antrum via the aditus ad antrum. Cholesteatomas commonly develop in this region.

questions.question: Which cord lies lateral to the second part of the axillary artery?
questions.explanation: The lateral cord lies lateral to the second part of the axillary artery (behind pectoralis minor). The medial cord lies medially and the posterior cord lies posteriorly to the second part. Below pectoralis minor, the cords give rise to their terminal branches.

questions.question: Which vein passes through the parotid gland?
questions.explanation: The retromandibular vein (formed by union of maxillary and superficial temporal veins) passes through the parotid gland substance. It divides into anterior and posterior divisions within the gland. The anterior division joins the facial vein; the posterior joins the posterior auricular vein to form the external jugular. The facial nerve and external carotid artery also traverse the gland.

questions.question: Which intercostal space corresponds to the apex beat?
questions.explanation: In healthy adults, the apex beat (point of maximal impulse) is located in the 5th left intercostal space at or just medial to the midclavicular line. This represents the most inferior and lateral point where the cardiac impulse can be felt. In children, the apex beat is one interspace higher (4th space). Displacement suggests cardiac enlargement or chest deformity.

questions.question: Which bone forms the hard palate posteriorly?
questions.explanation: The posterior portion of the hard palate is formed by the horizontal plates of the palatine bones. The anterior portion is formed by the palatine processes of the maxillae. The hard palate separates the oral and nasal cavities and provides a rigid surface for the tongue during mastication.

The rectouterine pouch (pouch of Douglas, cul-de-sac) is the peritoneal reflection between the uterus anteriorly and the rectum posteriorly, representing the most inferior extent of the peritoneal cavity in females (approximately 5.5 cm from the anus and 7.5 cm from the vaginal orifice). It is bounded laterally by the uterosacral ligaments and can be accessed through the posterior vaginal fornix for drainage of pelvic abscesses (culdocentesis) or laparoscopic procedures. Fluid, blood, or pus in the peritoneal cavity gravitates to this pouch in supine or standing positions, making it clinically significant.
questions.question: The rectouterine pouch (of Douglas) lies between which structures?
What drains the medial breast lymphatically?
questions.explanation: The medial part of the breast drains into the internal thoracic (parasternal) lymph nodes, forming a chain along the internal thoracic vessels. Some lymphatics from the medial part also pass across the sternum to anastomose with the opposite side, which explains contralateral breast involvement in cancer.

questions.question: What epithelium lines the true vocal cords?
questions.explanation: The true vocal cords are covered by stratified squamous non-keratinized epithelium, which is firmly adherent to the underlying vocal ligament without submucosa. This accounts for the pearly white avascular appearance on laryngoscopy. The rest of the larynx is lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium.

The phrenic nerve (C3, 4, 5) provides the entire motor supply to the diaphragm. Each phrenic nerve supplies its corresponding half of the diaphragm up to the margin of the esophageal opening. Injury to the phrenic nerve results in paralysis of that hemidiaphragm with consequent elevation.
questions.question: Which nerve provides motor supply to diaphragm?
The superficial inguinal ring transmits which structure in females?
questions.explanation: In females, the round ligament of the uterus passes through the inguinal canal and exits via the superficial inguinal ring to terminate in the subcutaneous tissue and labium majus. The ilioinguinal nerve also passes through the superficial ring in both sexes (after traversing the canal). The round ligament is homologous to the gubernaculum testis in males (proximal gubernaculum becomes the ovarian ligament in females). Indirect inguinal hernias are much less common in females but can occur alongside the round ligament in the canal of Nuck (persistent processus vaginalis in females).

The broad ligament is a double layer of peritoneum extending from the lateral pelvic wall to the uterus, containing multiple structures: the uterine tube in its superior free edge (mesosalpinx), the round ligament of uterus in its anteroinferior portion, the ovarian ligament posteriorly, and the ovarian vessels in its lateral extension (suspensory ligament of ovary/infundibulopelvic ligament). The broad ligament is divided into mesosalpinx (above ovary), mesovarium (posterior, supporting ovary), and mesometrium (below ovary, containing uterine vessels). It does not provide significant uterine support despite its name.
questions.question: The broad ligament contains which structure?
What is the primary function of the glenoid labrum?
questions.explanation: The glenoid labrum is a fibrocartilaginous ridge surrounding the glenoid cavity that deepens the cavity, reducing dislocation risk. It increases the articular surface area and provides attachment for some glenohumeral ligaments. This structure contributes significantly to glenohumeral joint stability despite the joint's high mobility.

questions.question: Which structure lies within Calot's triangle?
questions.explanation: Calot's triangle (cystohepatic triangle) is bounded by the cystic duct inferiorly, common hepatic duct medially, and inferior surface of the liver (or right lobe) superiorly. Within this triangle lies the cystic artery (typically arising from the right hepatic artery) and Lund's lymph node (Calot's node), which may be enlarged in cholecystitis or cholangitis. The triangle serves as a crucial surgical landmark during laparoscopic cholecystectomy for identifying and safely isolating the cystic duct and artery (the "critical view of safety") before ligation and division. Anatomical variations in this region are common and must be carefully identified.

questions.question: The renal fascia (Gerota's fascia) encloses which structures?
questions.explanation: The renal fascia (Gerota's fascia), a condensation of connective tissue, encloses the kidney, perirenal fat, and suprarenal gland on each side, forming a distinct compartment. It consists of anterior and posterior layers that fuse laterally but remain open medially and inferiorly, allowing potential communication between the two sides medially and extension of infection or hemorrhage inferiorly. The fascia separates the perirenal space (containing kidney, suprarenal gland, and perirenal fat) from the posterior pararenal space posteriorly and anterior pararenal space anteriorly. This fascial envelope is important in limiting the spread of renal infections and tumors.

The pericardial cavity contains 15-50 ml of serous pericardial fluid, an ultrafiltrate of plasma produced by the serous pericardium. This thin film of fluid acts as a lubricant, allowing the heart to beat with minimal friction between the visceral and parietal layers of serous pericardium. Excess fluid accumulation causes pericardial effusion and potential cardiac tamponade.
questions.question: What fluid occupies the pericardial cavity?

questions.explanation: The parotid gland extends superiorly to the external acoustic meatus and zygomatic arch. The gland lies below and anterior to the ear, extending from the zygomatic arch to the angle of the mandible. The facial nerve divides within the gland substance into its terminal branches (temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular, cervical).
questions.question: Which structure limits the superior extent of the parotid gland?
How many cusps form the pulmonary valve?
questions.explanation: The pulmonary valve has three semilunar (half-moon shaped) cusps: anterior, right, and left. Behind each cusp is a pulmonary sinus. The valve opens during right ventricular systole to allow blood into the pulmonary trunk and closes during diastole to prevent backflow. Unlike AV valves, semilunar valves have no chordae tendineae or papillary muscles.

questions.question: At what distance from the upper incisors does the aortic arch constrict the oesophagus?
questions.explanation: The aortic arch crosses anteriorly to the oesophagus creating a constriction at approximately 22.5 cm from the upper incisors. This is the second of four normal oesophageal constrictions and represents an important anatomical relationship. The arch of the aorta indents the anterior and left lateral aspects of the oesophagus at this level.

The infraorbital foramen on the anterior surface of the maxilla transmits the infraorbital nerve (continuation of maxillary nerve V2) and vessels. The nerve emerges about 1 cm below the infraorbital margin. It provides sensation to the lower eyelid, lateral nose, and upper lip. The foramen is a landmark for regional anesthesia.
questions.question: The infraorbital foramen transmits which nerve?

questions.explanation: The internal jugular vein lies lateral to the internal carotid artery within the carotid sheath. The vagus nerve lies posteriorly between the artery and vein. The sympathetic trunk lies posterior to the sheath. This anatomical arrangement is important for central venous catheterization and carotid endarterectomy.
questions.question: Which structure lies immediately lateral to the internal carotid artery in the carotid sheath?
The perforating branches of the profunda femoris artery perforate which muscle to reach the posterior compartment of the thigh?
questions.explanation: The perforating branches (three or four) of the profunda femoris artery perforate the adductor magnus to supply the muscles of the medial and posterior thigh. This anatomical relationship is important during surgical approaches to the posterior thigh, where inadvertent cutting of perforating vessels can cause significant hemorrhage. They are the main blood supply to the hamstring muscles.

questions.question: What is the effect of diaphragmatic contraction during inspiration?
questions.explanation: During inspiration, diaphragmatic contraction causes the muscle to descend (central tendon is relatively fixed by the pericardium and IVC), increasing thoracic volume and decreasing intrathoracic pressure (creating negative pressure that draws air in). Simultaneously, abdominal volume decreases and intra-abdominal pressure increases, displacing abdominal viscera downward and forward. The diaphragm is responsible for about 75% of the work of quiet breathing.

The pleural cavities are lined by mesothelium, a specialized layer of simple squamous epithelial cells. This smooth lining produces pleural fluid that lubricates the surfaces. The visceral pleura covers the lung surface while the parietal pleura lines the thoracic cavity walls.
questions.question: Which type of tissue lines the pleural cavities?

questions.explanation: The median arcuate ligament is formed by the union of the medial borders of the two crura and crosses over the anterior surface of the aorta. This ligament forms the posterior boundary of the aortic opening. Occasionally, it can compress the celiac artery, causing the median arcuate ligament syndrome.
questions.question: Which ligament crosses anterior to the aorta?

questions.explanation: The extensor mechanism involves complex interaction between extensor digitorum (extrinsic) and intrinsic muscles through the extensor expansion. Intrinsic muscles (lumbricals, interossei) insert into lateral bands of the expansion, enabling MCP flexion with IP extension. This coordination is essential for normal finger function.
options: A single extensor tendon controls finger extension
Extrinsic extensors and intrinsics interact via extensor expansion
questions.question: How does the extensor mechanism coordinate finger extension?

questions.explanation: The internal carotid artery enters the skull through the carotid canal in the petrous temporal bone. It ascends through the carotid canal, passes above the foramen lacerum, traverses the cavernous sinus, and emerges to give off the ophthalmic artery. The sympathetic carotid plexus surrounds the artery in the canal.
questions.question: The internal carotid artery enters the skull through which opening?

questions.explanation: The cremasteric artery arises from the inferior epigastric artery (a branch of the external iliac artery) near the deep inguinal ring and accompanies the spermatic cord through the inguinal canal. It supplies the cremaster muscle and anastomoses with the testicular artery and artery of the vas deferens, contributing to the arterial supply of the spermatic cord coverings. The genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve also enters the cord at the deep ring to innervate the cremaster muscle, which elevates the testis in response to cold or cremasteric reflex stimulation.
questions.question: The cremasteric artery is typically a branch of which vessel?
At which vertebral level does the common carotid artery typically bifurcate?
questions.explanation: The common carotid artery typically bifurcates at the level of C4, corresponding to the upper border of the thyroid cartilage. The carotid sinus (baroreceptor) and carotid body (chemoreceptor) are located at this bifurcation. Carotid endarterectomy is performed at this crucial anatomical location.

questions.question: Where does the cervical pleura lymph drain anteriorly?
questions.explanation: The cervical pleura drains into the internal thoracic chain anteriorly and into the intercostal chain posteriorly. The parietal pleura's lymphatic drainage follows its vascular supply pattern. Coastal and mediastinal pleura also drain to the internal thoracic chain anteriorly.

The pyloric orifice lies on the transpyloric plane at the level of the lower border of the first lumbar vertebra (L1). This is an important surface anatomy landmark located approximately 1.25 cm to the right of the median plane. The pyloric sphincter can be identified by a slight surface constriction and the prepyloric vein of Mayo.
questions.question: Which structure forms the upper border of the pyloric sphincter on the transpyloric plane?
The superior mesenteric artery supplies which embryological division of the gut?
questions.explanation: The superior mesenteric artery is the principal vessel supplying midgut derivatives, extending from just distal to the major duodenal papilla to the junction of the proximal two-thirds and distal one-third of the transverse colon. It originates from the abdominal aorta at the L1 level, immediately below the celiac trunk. Its branches include the inferior pancreaticoduodenal, jejunal, ileal, ileocolic, right colic, and middle colic arteries, providing blood to the duodenum (distal to ampulla), jejunum, ileum, cecum, appendix, ascending colon, and right two-thirds of transverse colon.

questions.question: How many leaves does the central tendon of the diaphragm have?
questions.explanation: The central tendon is trifoliate (three-leafed), resembling a clover leaf with right, left, and middle (anterior) leaflets. The right leaflet is the largest. The caval opening pierces the central tendon at the junction of the right and middle leaflets. The heart in its pericardium rests on the superior surface of the central tendon.

The great auricular nerve (C2-C3) provides sensory innervation to the skin over the parotid gland and lower auricle. The auriculotemporal nerve carries postganglionic parasympathetic secretomotor fibers (not sensory to the gland). The facial nerve traverses the gland but doesn't innervate it. Parotid surgery risks great auricular nerve injury causing numbness.
questions.question: Which nerve supplies the parotid gland with sensory fibers?
Which artery supplies blood to the gallbladder?
questions.explanation: The cystic artery, most commonly arising from the right hepatic artery within Calot's triangle (75% of cases), provides the primary blood supply to the gallbladder. It typically divides into superficial (supplying the peritoneal surface) and deep (supplying the hepatic surface) branches. Anatomical variations are common, with the cystic artery occasionally arising from the left hepatic, common hepatic, gastroduodenal, or superior mesenteric arteries. Careful identification during cholecystectomy is essential to avoid injury to aberrant vessels or the right hepatic artery. The gallbladder may also receive small arterial branches from the liver bed.

questions.question: What produces scapular depression?
questions.explanation: Depression of the scapula is produced by lower fibers of trapezius and pectoralis minor muscles. This movement lowers the shoulder and is opposite to elevation. It occurs when lowering the arm from an elevated position or during downward reaching.

questions.question: Which lymph nodes drain the ovary?
questions.explanation: The ovaries drain lymph directly to the para-aortic (lumbar) lymph nodes at the L1-L2 level, following the ovarian vessels along which the lymphatics ascend. This drainage pattern reflects the ovary's embryological origin high on the posterior abdominal wall near the kidneys. In contrast, the uterine fundus drains to para-aortic nodes via lymphatics following the ovarian vessels, while the uterine body drains to external iliac nodes, and the cervix drains to external iliac, internal iliac, and sacral nodes. The upper vagina drains to internal iliac nodes, while the lower vagina drains to superficial inguinal nodes.

questions.question: The pancreas lies at which vertebral levels?
questions.explanation: The pancreas extends obliquely across the posterior abdominal wall from the C-shaped curve of the duodenum (head) to the splenic hilum (tail) at approximately L1-L2 vertebral levels, though the tail may extend slightly higher. The head lies at L1-L2, the neck crosses L1, and the body and tail run along L1-L2 as they extend to the left. The pancreas is secondarily retroperitoneal (except the tail, which extends into the splenorenal ligament), lying anterior to the splenic vein, superior mesenteric vessels, aorta, IVC, left kidney, and left suprarenal gland.

The occipital artery participates in the cruciate anastomosis at the suboccipital region along with branches of the vertebral artery and deep cervical artery. This anastomosis provides collateral circulation to the brain and spinal cord. The occipital artery also anastomoses with the posterior auricular and superficial temporal arteries on the scalp.
questions.question: Which artery anastomoses to form the cruciate anastomosis?

questions.explanation: The hypoglossal canal is located in the occipital bone above the anterolateral margin of the foramen magnum. It transmits the hypoglossal nerve (XII) from the posterior cranial fossa to the neck. The canal is about 1 cm long. Skull base fractures involving this canal can cause tongue paralysis.
questions.question: Which bone contains the hypoglossal canal?

questions.explanation: The middle third of the esophagus (thoracic portion) drains into the azygos venous system. The upper third drains into brachiocephalic veins, and the lower third into the portal system (via left gastric vein). These represent important sites of portosystemic anastomosis where esophageal varices can develop in portal hypertension.
questions.question: How does esophageal venous drainage occur in thorax?
Which muscle of the medial compartment is the most anteriorly placed, large, and fan-shaped, forming the medial boundary of the femoral triangle?
questions.explanation: Adductor longus is the most anteriorly placed muscle of the adductor group, large and fan-shaped. It originates from the anterior surface of the body of the pubis, inferior to the pubic crest and lateral to the pubic symphysis, and inserts into the middle third of the medial lip of the linea aspera. Its medial border forms the medial boundary of the femoral triangle.

The medial wall of the orbit is formed by bone (primarily the orbital plate of ethmoid), not muscle. The medial rectus muscle lies within the orbit adjacent to this bony wall. The thin lamina papyracea of the ethmoid separates the orbit from the ethmoidal air cells.
questions.question: Which muscle forms the medial wall of the orbit?
Which vessel crosses anterior to the left renal vein?
questions.explanation: The superior mesenteric artery crosses anteriorly to the left renal vein as the vein passes from left to right to drain into the IVC. This can occasionally cause compression of the left renal vein (nutcracker syndrome), leading to left gonadal vein reflux, hematuria, or left flank pain. The left renal vein also passes anterior to the aorta.

The buccopharyngeal fascia is a thin layer covering the buccinator muscle and pharyngeal constrictor muscles externally. It is continuous anteriorly over the buccinator and posteriorly over the constrictors. The retropharyngeal space lies between this fascia and the prevertebral fascia. The fascia blends with the pterygomandibular raphe.
questions.question: The buccopharyngeal fascia covers which structure?
Which vein ascends in the anterior interventricular groove?
questions.explanation: The great cardiac vein ascends in the anterior interventricular groove alongside the anterior interventricular artery, then curves left in the coronary groove to become the coronary sinus. It drains the areas supplied by the left coronary artery (anterior left ventricle, anterior interventricular septum, and parts of right ventricle). It is the largest tributary of the coronary sinus.

The thymus gland's primary function is the maturation and education of T-lymphocytes. Na?ve T cells from bone marrow migrate to the thymus where they undergo positive and negative selection by epithelial-reticular cells. This eliminates self-reactive T cells and produces immunocompetent T cells. The thymus is crucial for cellular immunity.
questions.question: What is the thymus gland's primary function?
The hepatic veins drain directly into which structure?
questions.explanation: The hepatic veins (right, middle, and left, plus small inferior veins) drain directly into the inferior vena cava just below the diaphragm, representing the final pathway for blood that has perfused the hepatic sinusoids. The hepatic veins have no valves and run intersegmentally (between liver segments), in contrast to portal vein and hepatic artery branches which run within segments. The caudate lobe has separate small veins draining directly into the IVC, allowing it to maintain function in Budd-Chiari syndrome (hepatic vein thrombosis). The close relationship between hepatic veins and IVC is critical in liver transplantation surgery.

The flexor pollicis brevis is one of the thenar muscles supplied by the recurrent branch of the median nerve. This branch arises in the hand after the nerve passes through the carpal tunnel. Carpal tunnel syndrome can affect these muscles, causing thenar wasting and weakness of thumb opposition.
questions.question: Which muscle is supplied by the recurrent branch of the median nerve?
Which layer of the appendix contains abundant lymphoid tissue?
questions.explanation: The appendix has abundant lymphoid follicles in both the lamina propria and submucosa, unlike other parts of the intestine where lymphoid tissue is confined to the lamina propria. These follicles often extend into the submucosa, sometimes obliterating the clear boundary between layers. The appendix functions as a component of gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT).

The extensor digitorum brevis and extensor hallucis brevis, the only intrinsic muscles on the dorsum of the foot, are innervated by the deep fibular nerve (L5, or S1, or both). They aid the extensor digitorum longus in extending the four medial toes and the extensor hallucis longus in extending the great toe at the metatarsophalangeal joint.
questions.question: The muscles of the dorsum of the foot include the extensor digitorum brevis (EDB) and extensor hallucis brevis (EHB). They are innervated by which nerve?

questions.explanation: The knee joint is the largest and most complex joint in the body, primarily classified as a hinge-type synovial joint. It has two articulations: the tibiofemoral joint (femur with tibia, bearing most body weight) and the patellofemoral joint (femur with patella). Despite being hinge-like, the knee also allows rotation during the screw-home mechanism.
questions.question: Despite its complexity with two articulations, the knee joint is primarily classified as which type of synovial joint?
What is the standard length of the duodenum in adults?
questions.explanation: The duodenum is approximately 25 cm (10 inches) in length and represents the first and shortest part of the small intestine. Despite being the shortest segment, it is the widest portion of the small intestine. The duodenum is predominantly retroperitoneal except for the first 2 cm (the duodenal cap or ampulla).

questions.question: The external anal sphincter is composed of which muscle type?
questions.explanation: The external anal sphincter is composed of striated (skeletal) voluntary muscle under somatic control via the inferior rectal nerve (branch of pudendal nerve, S2-S4) and perineal branch of S4. It surrounds the entire length of the anal canal external to the internal sphincter and is divided into subcutaneous, superficial, and deep parts. The external sphincter provides voluntary control of defecation and maintains continence, particularly during sudden increases in intra-abdominal pressure. In contrast, the internal anal sphincter (derived from thickened rectal circular smooth muscle) is under involuntary autonomic control and maintains baseline anal tone.

The left ventricular wall is 8-12 mm thick, approximately three times thicker than the right ventricle (3-5 mm), reflecting the higher pressure it must generate to pump blood through the systemic circulation. The left ventricle forms the apex and most of the left border and diaphragmatic surface of the heart. It contains two papillary muscles (anterior and posterior).
questions.question: Which chamber has the thickest myocardial wall?
The left colic artery typically divides into which branches?
questions.explanation: The left colic artery (first branch of the inferior mesenteric artery) divides into ascending and descending branches near the descending colon. The ascending branch runs superiorly to supply the left (distal) third of the transverse colon and splenic flexure, anastomosing with the left branch of the middle colic artery (from SMA) to complete the marginal artery. The descending branch runs inferiorly along the descending colon, anastomosing with branches of the sigmoid arteries. This anastomotic pattern creates collateral circulation between superior and inferior mesenteric arterial territories, though the splenic flexure (Griffiths' point) remains a watershed area vulnerable to ischemia.

questions.question: The superior rectal artery crosses which vessel at S3 level?
questions.explanation: The superior rectal artery (terminal continuation of the inferior mesenteric artery) descends into the pelvis within the sigmoid mesocolon and crosses the left common iliac vessels (artery and vein) at approximately the S3 vertebral level before dividing into right and left branches that descend along the rectum. This anatomical relationship makes the superior rectal vessels vulnerable to injury during operations on the sigmoid colon or rectum. The artery eventually terminates by piercing the muscular wall of the rectum and anastomosing with the middle rectal (from internal iliac) and inferior rectal (from internal pudendal) arteries.

questions.question: Which thoracic nerve lacks an anterior cutaneous branch?
questions.explanation: The first thoracic nerve is atypical because it has no anterior cutaneous branch. Instead, it has a large branch that joins the brachial plexus, corresponding to its lateral cutaneous branch. The second thoracic nerve is also atypical, giving rise to the intercostobrachial nerve.

The ligamentum arteriosum is the fibrous remnant of the fetal ductus arteriosus, which connected the pulmonary artery to the aorta in fetal circulation, bypassing the non-functional fetal lungs. It closes functionally at birth and becomes a fibrous cord extending from the left pulmonary artery to the aortic arch.
questions.question: What is the ligamentum arteriosum?

questions.explanation: The middle ear receives blood from multiple tympanic arteries: superior tympanic (middle meningeal), inferior tympanic (ascending pharyngeal), anterior tympanic (maxillary), and posterior tympanic (stylomastoid branch of posterior auricular). This rich vascular supply reflects the metabolic needs of the middle ear mucosa and ossicles.
questions.question: Which vessel supplies blood to the middle ear?

questions.explanation: The white pulp of the spleen consists of lymphoid tissue surrounding central arterioles (periarterial lymphoid sheaths - PALS) and lymphoid nodules. It is the site of immune surveillance and antibody production in response to blood-borne antigens. The white pulp contains predominantly T lymphocytes in the PALS and B lymphocytes in the lymphoid follicles.
questions.question: What is the primary immunological function of splenic white pulp?

questions.explanation: at the wrist joint (ulnar deviation) is produced by the combined action of extensor carpi ulnaris and flexor carpi ulnaris. These muscles work synergistically despite being in different compartments. The wrist joint permits movement along two axes as an ellipsoid synovial joint.
questions.question: Which movement at the wrist joint is produced by extensor carpi ulnaris and flexor carpi ulnaris?

questions.explanation: The head of the pancreas receives dual blood supply from pancreaticoduodenal arcades formed by the superior and inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries, representing the junction between celiac (foregut) and superior mesenteric (midgut) arterial territories. The superior pancreaticoduodenal artery (from gastroduodenal) divides into anterior and posterior branches that descend on their respective surfaces of the pancreatic head, anastomosing with corresponding anterior and posterior branches of the inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery (from SMA). This rich anastomotic network provides collateral circulation between celiac and SMA systems.
questions.question: Which artery supplies the head of the pancreas?
Which vein accompanies the internal thoracic artery?
questions.explanation: The internal thoracic vein accompanies the artery of the same name, draining blood from the anterior chest wall, upper abdomen, and breast. It ascends to drain into the brachiocephalic vein on each side. The vein receives tributaries corresponding to the arterial branches.

questions.question: What is the approximate length of Wharton's duct?
questions.explanation: Wharton's duct (submandibular duct) is approximately 5 cm long and opens at the sublingual papilla beside the frenulum. The duct runs forward on the hyoglossus muscle between the lingual and hypoglossal nerves. Stone formation is more common in this duct than in Stensen's duct due to its upward course and mucoid secretions.

The sphenopalatine artery (from maxillary artery) provides the dominant blood supply to the nasal septum via posterior septal branches. The anterior ethmoidal artery and superior labial artery contribute anteriorly. Kiesselbach's plexus in the anteroinferior septum is the most common site of epistaxis.
questions.question: Which artery supplies the majority of the nasal septum?

questions.explanation: The posterior intercostal veins lie deepest in the costal grooves and contain valves that direct blood flow posteriorly. The neurovascular bundle arrangement from superior to inferior is vein-artery-nerve (VAN). The veins are the largest and most superior structures in this arrangement.
questions.question: Which structure lies deepest in the costal groove?

questions.explanation: The splenic red pulp is the primary site for destruction of old, damaged, or abnormal erythrocytes (red blood cells). After their normal lifespan of approximately 120 days, erythrocytes become less flexible and are selectively engulfed by macrophages in the splenic cords. The iron from hemoglobin is recycled, while other components are degraded.
questions.question: Which cells are predominantly destroyed in the splenic red pulp?

questions.explanation: The left gastroepiploic (gastro-omental) artery, a branch of the splenic artery, is the dominant vessel supplying the greater curvature of the stomach, anastomosing with the smaller right gastroepiploic artery from the gastroduodenal trunk. These vessels run along the greater curvature within the gastrocolic ligament, giving branches to both anterior and posterior surfaces of the stomach. The short gastric arteries contribute to the fundus but represent a minor component of the greater curvature blood supply.
questions.question: Which artery supplies the majority of blood to the greater curvature of the stomach?
Where does the suspensory muscle of the duodenum attach?
questions.explanation: The suspensory muscle of the duodenum (ligament of Treitz) extends from the right crus of the diaphragm behind the pancreas to attach to the duodenojejunal flexure. It contains both smooth muscle and fibrous tissue. Contraction of this muscle widens the angle of the duodenojejunal flexure and may assist in opening the duodenum for passage of contents into the jejunum.

questions.question: Which muscle tenses the vocal cords?
questions.explanation: The cricothyroid muscle is the only muscle that tenses (lengthens) the vocal cords by tilting the thyroid cartilage forward on the cricoid. It is supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve. All other intrinsic laryngeal muscles are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

questions.question: Which muscle tenses the tympanic membrane?
questions.explanation: The tensor tympani muscle tenses the tympanic membrane by pulling the malleus medially. It is innervated by the nerve to medial pterygoid (V3). The muscle arises from the Eustachian tube and bony canal above it. Contraction dampens excessive vibrations and reduces sensitivity to low-frequency sounds. It works synergistically with stapedius.

questions.question: Which muscle retracts the mandible?
questions.explanation: The posterior (horizontal) fibers of the temporalis muscle retract (pull back) the protruded mandible. The masseter and medial pterygoid elevate, while the lateral pterygoid protrudes. Bilateral contraction of temporalis elevates the mandible; unilateral posterior fibers retract ipsilaterally.

questions.question: The suspensory muscle of the duodenum (ligament of Treitz) arises from which structure?
questions.explanation: The suspensory muscle of the duodenum (ligament of Treitz) is a fibromuscular band arising from the right crus of the diaphragm near the esophageal hiatus (some sources describe both crura contributing), passing posterior to the pancreas to insert onto the duodenojejunal flexure and sometimes the horizontal part of the duodenum. It supports the duodenojejunal junction at the posterior abdominal wall and marks the transition from fixed (retroperitoneal) duodenum to mobile (intraperitoneal) jejunum. This landmark is important surgically and radiologically, as widening of the angle suggests a mass in the pancreatic head.

The superior epigastric artery is a terminal branch of the internal thoracic artery (which arises from the subclavian artery), not the abdominal aorta. It descends through the thorax, enters the rectus sheath by passing between the sternal and costal attachments of the diaphragm, and anastomoses with the inferior epigastric artery (from external iliac artery), providing an important collateral pathway between subclavian and external iliac systems. The abdominal aorta gives rise to paired visceral branches (suprarenal, renal, gonadal), unpaired visceral branches (celiac, SMA, IMA), paired parietal branches (inferior phrenic, four lumbar), and the unpaired median sacral artery.
questions.question: Which artery does NOT arise from the abdominal aorta?
Which structure bounds the superior thoracic aperture posteriorly?
questions.explanation: The superior thoracic aperture is bounded posteriorly by the first thoracic vertebra (T1). Anteriorly, it is bounded by the superior border of the manubrium sterni. Laterally, the medial borders of the first ribs and their costal cartilages complete the boundaries of this important opening.

Fibularis tertius inserts into the dorsum of the base of the 5th metatarsal. It originates from the inferior third of the anterior surface of the fibula. Although in the anterior compartment, its eversion action makes it functionally similar to the lateral compartment muscles. It is sometimes absent as a normal variant. It is innervated by the deep fibular nerve.
questions.question: Fibularis tertius dorsiflexes the ankle and aids eversion. It inserts into which specific structure?

questions.explanation: The vertebral artery and accompanying veins pass through the foramina transversaria (transverse foramina) of cervical vertebrae C1-C6. The artery typically enters at C6 and ascends to C1. The stellate ganglion lies anterior to C7 transverse process, which usually lacks a foramen transversarium. Spinal nerves exit via intervertebral foramina posteriorly.
questions.question: Which structure passes through the foramen transversarium?
Which lymphatic duct drains into the left venous angle?
questions.explanation: The thoracic duct drains into the left venous angle (junction of left internal jugular and subclavian veins). It collects lymph from the entire body except the right upper quadrant. The duct begins at the cisterna chyli (L1-L2), ascends through the thorax, and arches over the left subclavian artery to reach the venous angle.

questions.question: The foramen lacerum is closed in life by which structure?
questions.explanation: The foramen lacerum is closed in life by fibrocartilage. Only small meningeal vessels and the greater petrosal nerve pass through its superior aspect. The internal carotid artery passes above it in the foramen's upper part but does not traverse it. In dried skulls, the foramen appears as a large opening.

Delta cells (D cells) comprise about 5-10% of islet cells and produce somatostatin, which inhibits both insulin and glucagon secretion, acting as a paracrine regulator. They are located peripherally in the islets. Somatostatin also inhibits growth hormone release from the pituitary (hence the name) and has widespread inhibitory effects on the GI tract.
questions.question: Which cells in pancreatic islets produce somatostatin?

questions.explanation: The quadrangular space is bounded superiorly by teres minor, inferiorly by teres major, medially by the long head of triceps, and laterally by the surgical neck of humerus. Through this space pass the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral vessels. Injury to these structures can occur with shoulder trauma.
options: Teres major, teres minor, long head of triceps, surgical neck of humerus
Subscapularis, teres major, latissimus dorsi, humerus
Teres minor, teres major, long head of triceps, lateral head of triceps
Deltoid, teres minor, long head of triceps, humerus
questions.question: Which muscles form the boundaries of the quadrangular space in the axilla?

questions.explanation: The female urethra is approximately 4 cm (1.5 inches) long and extends from the internal urethral orifice of the bladder to the external urethral orifice in the vestibule. It is embedded in the anterior vaginal wall and passes through the urogenital diaphragm. The shorter length makes females more susceptible to urinary tract infections.
questions.question: What is the length of the female urethra?
Which layer of the spermatic cord is derived from transversalis fascia?
questions.explanation: The internal spermatic fascia is derived from the transversalis fascia at the deep inguinal ring. The cremasteric muscle and fascia are derived from the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles. The external spermatic fascia is derived from the external oblique aponeurosis at the superficial inguinal ring. These layers represent the layers of the abdominal wall through which the testis descended.

questions.question: Which ligament arches over the psoas major muscle?
questions.explanation: The medial arcuate ligament is a tendinous arch in the diaphragm that arches over the psoas major muscle, extending from the body of L1 or L2 vertebra to the tip of the transverse process. The sympathetic trunk passes deep to (posterior to) this ligament as it enters the abdomen. The ligament forms part of the lumbar attachment of the diaphragm.

questions.question: Which vein receives the left renal vein?
questions.explanation: Both right and left renal veins drain into the inferior vena cava. The left renal vein is approximately three times longer than the right and crosses anterior to the aorta to reach the IVC. The left renal vein receives the left suprarenal vein, left gonadal (testicular or ovarian) vein, and communicates with the ascending lumbar vein.

options: Injury causes motor deficit without sensory loss
questions.explanation: The anterior interosseous nerve being purely motor (no cutaneous branches) means injury produces pure motor deficit (weak thumb IP flexion, index finger DIP flexion, pronation) without sensory symptoms. This can lead to delayed diagnosis as patients lack the paresthesia typical of other nerve compression syndromes.
questions.question: What is the significance of the anterior interosseous nerve being purely motor?
Which artery provides 60% of breast blood flow?
questions.explanation: The internal thoracic artery (a branch of subclavian artery) provides approximately 60% of total breast blood flow, mainly to the medial portion through anterior and posterior perforating branches. The 2nd, 3rd, and 4th perforating branches are particularly large and significant in breast blood supply.

The uterus is supported by multiple structures: the cardinal ligaments (most important, prevent prolapse), uterosacral ligaments (from cervix/upper vagina to sacrum, maintain position), pubocervical ligaments (from cervix to pubis), round ligaments (maintain anteverted position), broad ligaments (minimal support, mainly peritoneal folds), and the muscular pelvic floor (levator ani, particularly pubococcygeus). The perineal body also provides indirect support. Damage to these supports (especially during childbirth) can lead to uterine prolapse, cystocele, rectocele, or enterocele. The broad ligament, despite its name, provides minimal structural support.
questions.question: Which ligament supports the uterus?

questions.explanation: The anterior wall of the axilla is formed by the pectoralis major muscle and the pectoral fascia associated with it. The pectoralis minor and clavipectoral fascia form a deeper layer. The anterior axillary fold, formed by pectoralis major bridging from thoracic wall to humerus, represents the inferiormost graspable part.
questions.question: Which structure forms the anterior wall of the axilla's superficial layer?

questions.explanation: The obturator nerve exits the pelvis by passing through the obturator foramen, along with the obturator vessels. It then divides into anterior and posterior divisions in the obturator canal. The anterior division runs anterior to obturator externus and adductor brevis, while the posterior division runs posterior to adductor brevis. It supplies the medial compartment of the thigh.
questions.question: The obturator nerve supplies the medial compartment of the thigh. It exits the pelvis through which specific structure?

questions.explanation: The calcaneal apophysis (posterior calcaneal epiphysis) is a classic example of an atavistic epiphysis. Traction epiphyses arise at tendinous insertions, while pressure epiphyses form articular surfaces. Traction apophysitis of the calcaneal apophysis in adolescents is known as Sever's disease.
questions.question: An atavistic epiphysis represents a vestigial bone once separate in ancestral species. Which of the following is a classic example in the lower limb?

questions.explanation: Filiform papillae are the most numerous papillae but do not contain taste buds; they provide the rough texture of the tongue. Fungiform, circumvallate, and foliate papillae all contain taste buds. The circumvallate papillae are arranged in a V-shape along the sulcus terminalis.
questions.question: Which papillae on the tongue do NOT contain taste buds?

questions.explanation: Complete section of a phrenic nerve results in complete paralysis and eventual atrophy of the corresponding half of the diaphragm. The paralyzed hemidiaphragm shows paradoxical movement: moving upward during inspiration and downward during expiration. Unilateral paralysis is often asymptomatic; bilateral causes severe respiratory compromise.
questions.question: What happens with complete phrenic nerve section?
Which lymph node is found in the femoral canal?
questions.explanation: Cloquet's node (node of Rosenmuller) is the most superior of the deep inguinal lymph nodes, located in the femoral canal (femoral ring) and receives lymph from the superficial and deep inguinal nodes. It drains to the external iliac nodes. The femoral canal is the medial compartment of the femoral sheath (lateral to the lacunar ligament, medial to the femoral vein) and represents a potential weakness where femoral hernias occur. Virchow's node is in the left supraclavicular fossa, Sister Mary Joseph node at the umbilicus, and Calot's node in Calot's triangle.

options: Lateral plantar nerve; adducts and flexes 1st digit
Deep fibular nerve; extends and abducts 1st digit
Medial plantar nerve; abducts and flexes 1st digit
Medial plantar nerve; flexes and inverts foot
questions.question: Abductor hallucis, the most medially placed first layer foot muscle, is innervated by which nerve and performs which action?
questions.explanation: Abductor hallucis is innervated by the medial plantar nerve (S2, S3) and performs abduction and flexion of the first digit (hallux). It originates from the medial tubercle of the calcaneal tuberosity, the flexor retinaculum, and plantar aponeurosis. It inserts into the medial side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the first digit.

questions.question: Which structure lies between the pretracheal and prevertebral fascia?
questions.explanation: The pharynx, esophagus, larynx, trachea, and thyroid gland lie between the pretracheal and prevertebral fascia. The pretracheal fascia encloses these visceral structures while the prevertebral fascia covers the vertebral column and associated muscles. The retropharyngeal space lies between these fascial layers posteriorly.

options: At the level of the fibular head proximally
In the lower third of the leg by piercing the deep fascia
At the level of the ankle joint and mortise
In the popliteal fossa at the posterior aspect of the knee
At the level of the medial malleolus medially
questions.question: The superficial fibular nerve (L5, S1, S2) supplies the lateral compartment of the leg. Where does it emerge as a cutaneous nerve?
questions.explanation: The superficial fibular nerve supplies fibularis longus and brevis in the lateral compartment, then pierces the deep fascia in the lower third of the leg to become cutaneous. It supplies most of the dorsum of the foot and toes (except the first web space, supplied by the deep fibular nerve, and the lateral border, supplied by the sural nerve).

The Achilles (calcaneal) tendon inserts into the posterior surface of the calcaneus via the calcaneal tuberosity. The gastrocnemius, soleus, and plantaris muscles all contribute to the calcaneal tendon. The calcaneal tendon is the strongest tendon in the body but is frequently ruptured in sudden powerful plantarflexion, such as in a jump landing. Bursae lie posterior and anterior to the tendon.
questions.question: The calcaneus is the largest and strongest bone of the foot and its primary function is to absorb shock and leverage movement. Where is the Achilles tendon inserted on the calcaneus?
Which movements must occur together for full shoulder abduction beyond 90 degrees?
questions.explanation: Full shoulder abduction beyond 90 degrees requires synchronized glenohumeral abduction and scapular upward rotation (scapulohumeral rhythm). For every 3 degrees of abduction, approximately 2 degrees occur at the glenohumeral joint and 1 degree from scapular rotation. This demonstrates upper limb integrated function.
options: Glenohumeral abduction and scapular upward rotation

questions.explanation: produces wrist abduction (radial deviation) along with flexor carpi radialis and extensor carpi radialis muscles. It also abducts the thumb at the carpometacarpal joint. The muscle is located in the posterior forearm compartment.
questions.question: Which muscle assists with both wrist abduction and thumb abduction?
Which ligament extends from the lesser curvature to the liver?
questions.explanation: The lesser omentum extends from the lesser curvature of the stomach to the liver and consists of the hepatogastric and hepatoduodenal ligaments. The hepatogastric portion specifically connects the lesser curvature to the liver. This double layer of peritoneum carries the left and right gastric vessels along the lesser curvature.

The renal vessels (particularly the renal veins attached to the IVC) are the main structures preventing excessive descent of the kidneys. The renal fascia provides minimal support. Loss of perirenal fat (in cachexia) can lead to nephroptosis (floating kidney), where the kidney descends excessively with positional changes, potentially causing ureteric kinking and obstruction.
questions.question: What prevents the kidney from descending more than normal?
What type of muscle forms the detrusor muscle?
questions.explanation: The detrusor muscle is composed of smooth muscle arranged in three poorly defined layers (inner longitudinal, middle circular, outer longitudinal). It is under involuntary control via autonomic innervation. Parasympathetic stimulation (via pelvic splanchnic nerves) causes detrusor contraction for micturition; sympathetic stimulation (via hypogastric nerves) causes relaxation for urine storage.

questions.question: What defines the lower limit of the body of the stomach?
questions.explanation: The body of the stomach extends from the cardiac orifice to the level of the incisura angularis, a constant notch on the lesser curvature. This angular notch serves as a reliable anatomical landmark separating the body from the pyloric portion. The incisura angularis becomes more prominent when the stomach is distended.

The sphincter of Oddi (sphincter ampullae) surrounds the hepatopancreatic ampulla (ampulla of Vater), controlling the release of bile and pancreatic juice into the second part of the duodenum. The sphincter choledochus surrounds the terminal bile duct just before its junction with the pancreatic duct, while the sphincter pancreaticus surrounds the terminal pancreatic duct. The sphincter of Oddi coordinates the flow from both ducts, relaxing in response to cholecystokinin during digestion and contracting between meals to allow bile storage in the gallbladder.
questions.question: The hepatopancreatic ampulla is surrounded by which sphincter?

questions.explanation: The quadratus lumborum muscle forms the central posterior relation of each kidney. The psoas major muscle lies posteromedially, and the transversus abdominis muscle (its aponeurosis) lies posterolaterally. The diaphragm is posterior to the upper pole, and the subcostal, iliohypogastric, and ilioinguinal nerves run posterior to the kidneys.
questions.question: Which muscle lies immediately posterior to both kidneys?
Which structure forms the anterior boundary of the posterior triangle of the neck?
questions.explanation: The posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle forms the anterior boundary of the posterior triangle. The anterior border of trapezius forms the posterior boundary, and the middle third of the clavicle forms the base. The apex is where the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius meet at the superior nuchal line.

The glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) provides both general sensation and taste (special sensation) to the posterior third of the tongue. The anterior two-thirds receives general sensation from the lingual nerve (V3) and taste from chorda tympani (VII). Motor innervation to all tongue muscles is from the hypoglossal nerve except palatoglossus (pharyngeal plexus).
questions.question: Which nerve provides general sensation to the posterior third of the tongue?

questions.explanation: The hip joint is a multiaxial ball and socket type of synovial joint, the largest and second largest weight-bearing joint in the human body. It allows movements in all three planes: flexion/extension in the sagittal plane, abduction/adduction in the frontal plane, and medial/lateral rotation in the transverse plane.
questions.question: The hip joint is specifically classified as which type of synovial joint?

questions.explanation: The Eustachian (pharyngotympanic) tube opens into the lateral wall of the nasopharynx, connecting it with the middle ear cavity. The tubal elevation and tubal tonsil surround the opening. Tensor veli palatini and salpingopharyngeus muscles open the tube during swallowing to equalize middle ear pressure.
questions.question: Which opening connects the nasopharynx to the middle ear?

questions.explanation: The great saphenous vein has 10-12 valves that are more numerous in the leg than in the thigh. These valves are usually located just inferior to the perforating veins. Perforating veins also contain valves directing blood from superficial to deep venous systems. Incompetence of these valves leads to varicose veins most commonly in the leg.
questions.question: The great saphenous vein has 10-12 valves. These are more numerous in which segment of the vein?
Which nerve supplies somatic sensation below the pectinate line?
questions.explanation: The inferior rectal nerve (branch of the pudendal nerve, S2-S4) provides somatic sensation below the pectinate line, making this area sensitive to pain, touch, and temperature.
