Above the pectinate line, the anal canal is supplied by autonomic (visceral) nerves and is insensitive to these stimuli but sensitive to stretch. This explains why internal hemorrhoids are painless while external hemorrhoids are painful.

questions.question: Which intercostal veins form accessory hemiazygos?
questions.explanation: The accessory hemiazygos vein is formed by the union of the 4th-7th left posterior intercostal veins. It descends on the left side of the vertebral column, crosses at T7, and drains into the azygos vein. It also receives the left bronchial vein and veins from the middle third of the esophagus.

questions.question: Where does the posterior vagal trunk primarily distribute after entering the abdomen?
questions.explanation: The posterior vagal trunk, formed mainly from the right vagus nerve, sends a large branch to the celiac and superior mesenteric plexuses. This distribution extends vagal innervation to the intestines as far as the splenic flexure and to the pancreas. The remaining branches supply the posterior surface of the stomach.

questions.question: Which hepatic structure contains the portal triad?
questions.explanation: The portal tract (portal triad) is located at the corners of hepatic lobules and contains branches of the portal vein, hepatic artery, and bile duct, surrounded by connective tissue. Some also include lymphatic vessels. The portal triad delivers blood and removes bile from the hepatic lobule. The hepatic artery provides oxygen; the portal vein provides nutrients and metabolites from the GI tract.

questions.question: What structure accompanies the median nerve through the carpal tunnel?
questions.explanation: Nine flexor tendons accompany the median nerve through the carpal tunnel: four tendons each of flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus, plus the flexor pollicis longus tendon. These tendons are enclosed in synovial sheaths within the tunnel.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a function of the sacrotuberous and sacrospinous ligaments?
questions.explanation: The sacrotuberous and sacrospinous ligaments stabilize the sacrum, prevent its rotation under body weight, and form both sciatic foramina together with bones. They do not transmit the obturator nerve, which exits through the obturator foramen to supply the medial compartment of the thigh via its anterior and posterior divisions.
options: Stabilize the sacrum at the sacroiliac joint
Prevent rotation of sacrum by vertebral column weight
Form the greater sciatic foramen with bones
Transmit the obturator nerve to the medial thigh
Form the lesser sciatic foramen with bones

questions.explanation: The lateral femoral circumflex artery (LFCA) has three branches: ascending (to the hip joint and gluteal region), transverse (encircling the femur laterally), and descending (contributing superolaterally to the genicular anastomosis around the knee). The descending branch travels between vastus intermedius and vastus lateralis muscles and provides one of the anastomotic connections at the knee.
questions.question: The lateral femoral circumflex artery has three named branches. Which of these descends distally to contribute to the genicular anastomosis?
The incisive canal opens into which structure?
questions.explanation: The incisive canal opens inferiorly into the oral cavity at the incisive fossa in the anterior hard palate. Superiorly, it communicates with the nasal cavity. The canal transmits the nasopalatine nerve and terminal branches of the greater palatine vessels. Embryologically, it marks the fusion of the primary and secondary palates.

The prostate gland is classically described as having five lobes: anterior (fibromuscular, no glandular tissue), posterior (palpable on digital rectal exam, common site of carcinoma), median (between ejaculatory ducts, may enlarge to cause bladder outlet obstruction), and right and left lateral lobes (largest, common site of benign prostatic hyperplasia). Modern zonal anatomy describes peripheral zone (70%, site of most cancers), central zone (25%, around ejaculatory ducts), transitional zone (5%, surrounds urethra, site of BPH), and anterior fibromuscular stroma. The median lobe may project into the bladder when enlarged, causing urinary symptoms.
questions.question: The prostate is divided into how many lobes?

questions.explanation: The anterior belly of the digastric is innervated by the mylohyoid nerve, a branch of the inferior alveolar nerve (V3). The posterior belly is supplied by the facial nerve. This dual innervation reflects the embryologic origin from first and second pharyngeal arches respectively.
questions.question: The anterior belly of the digastric muscle is innervated by which nerve?
Which structure separates the maxillary sinus from the orbit?
questions.explanation: The thin orbital plate of the maxilla forms the roof of the maxillary sinus and the floor of the orbit. The infraorbital nerve and vessels run in a groove on this surface. Fractures can cause orbital contents to herniate into the sinus (blow-out fracture). Dental roots may project into the sinus floor.

options: Five: calcaneus, talus, navicular, cuboid, one cuneiform
Seven: talus, calcaneus, cuboid, navicular, and three cuneiforms
Six: talus, calcaneus, navicular, cuboid, and two cuneiforms
Eight: talus, calcaneus, cuboid, navicular, and four cuneiforms
Seven: talus, calcaneus, navicular, cuboid, and three metatarsals
questions.question: The foot contains how many tarsal bones, and what are they?
questions.explanation: The foot contains seven tarsal bones: talus, calcaneus, cuboid, navicular, and three cuneiform bones (medial, intermediate, and lateral). The 26 bones of the foot include 7 tarsals, 5 metatarsals, and 14 phalanges. Understanding tarsal anatomy is fundamental to interpreting foot radiographs and managing tarsal fractures.

questions.question: What is significant about the 3rd right posterior intercostal?
questions.explanation: The 3rd right posterior intercostal artery typically gives off the right bronchial artery (though the origin is variable). The two left bronchial arteries usually arise directly from the descending thoracic aorta. Bronchial arteries provide the nutrient blood supply to the bronchial tree and lung tissue.

The rectum lacks taeniae coli, haustra, and appendices epiploicae, unlike the cecum and colon. At the rectosigmoid junction (approximately 15 cm from the anus, at S3 level), the three taeniae spread out to form a complete outer longitudinal muscle layer encircling the rectum. The rectum can be distinguished from sigmoid colon by this absence of taeniae, its fixed retroperitoneal position, and presence of transverse folds (Houston's valves). The taeniae coli converge at the base of the appendix on the cecum, providing a surgical landmark.
questions.question: Which part of the colon lacks taeniae coli?
Where does the azygos vein terminate?
questions.explanation: The azygos vein arches over the right main bronchus at T4 to drain into the posterior aspect of the superior vena cava. This creates a communication between the SVC and IVC systems, providing collateral circulation if either is obstructed. The azygos arch is visible on chest X-rays.

questions.question: Why does diaphragmatic pain refer to shoulder?
questions.explanation: Pain from irritation of the central diaphragm (supplied by phrenic nerve C3-5) refers to the shoulder because the supraclavicular nerves (C3-4) supply the skin over the shoulder. This is an example of referred pain where stimuli from different areas share the same spinal cord segments.

questions.question: What produces index finger independent extension?
questions.explanation: allows independent extension of the index finger, supplementing extensor digitorum action. This is particularly useful for pointing while making a fist. The muscle is located in the posterior forearm and supplied by the posterior interosseous nerve.

The bundle of His (AV bundle) penetrates the fibrous skeleton and descends along the posterior edge of the membranous interventricular septum before dividing into right and left bundle branches. The right bundle branch continues down the right side of the septum, while the left bundle branch crosses to the left side and divides into anterior and posterior fascicles.
questions.question: Which structure gives rise to the right and left bundle branches?
Which olecranon bursa lies in subcutaneous connective tissue?
questions.explanation: The subcutaneous olecranon bursa is located in the subcutaneous connective tissue directly over the olecranon process. This bursa can become inflamed from repeated trauma, causing olecranon bursitis known as "student's elbow" or "miner's elbow." The other two bursae are the intratendinous and subtendinous types.

questions.question: What is the significance of the critical zone in the supraspinatus tendon?
questions.explanation: The "critical zone" in the supraspinatus tendon has relatively poor vascularity, located approximately 1cm from its humeral insertion. This hypovascular area is more susceptible to degenerative changes and tears. The zone's poor blood supply impairs healing after injury.

The membranous urethra is the shortest (1-2 cm), narrowest, and least distensible part of the male urethra. It passes through the urogenital diaphragm (deep perineal pouch) surrounded by the external urethral sphincter (sphincter urethrae muscle). This segment is most vulnerable to traumatic injury, particularly in pelvic fractures, and is the most difficult to dilate or catheterize.
questions.question: Which part of the male urethra is least distensible?

questions.explanation: The anterior cranial fossa accommodates the frontal lobes of the brain. The floor is formed by the orbital plates of the frontal bone, cribriform plate of ethmoid, and lesser wings of sphenoid. The crista galli provides attachment for the falx cerebri. Fractures can cause CSF rhinorrhea through the cribriform plate.
questions.question: The anterior cranial fossa contains which lobe of the brain?

questions.explanation: Semimembranosus originates from the ischial tuberosity and inserts into the posterior part of the medial condyle of the tibia. Its reflected attachment forms the oblique popliteal ligament. Semimembranosus is named for its membranous (flat, broad) proximal tendon, in contrast to semitendinosus which has a long round distal tendon.
questions.question: Which hamstring muscle originates from the ischial tuberosity and inserts into the posterior part of the medial condyle of the tibia?
What is the functional significance of the interosseous membrane?
questions.explanation: The interosseous membrane between radius and ulna serves multiple functions: separates anterior and posterior compartments, provides muscle attachment surface, transmits forces from radius to ulna, and contains apertures for interosseous vessels. It maintains the spatial relationship between the two forearm bones.

questions.question: What are gray rami communicantes?
questions.explanation: Gray rami communicantes carry postganglionic sympathetic fibers from sympathetic ganglia back to all spinal nerves for distribution to blood vessels, sweat glands, and arrector pili muscles throughout the body. They are "gray" because postganglionic fibers are unmyelinated. Gray rami exist at all spinal levels unlike white rami.

The brachial artery is the main arterial supply to the arm and represents the continuation of the axillary artery. It begins at the inferior border of teres major and ends in the cubital fossa opposite the neck of the radius. Under cover of the bicipital aponeurosis, it divides into radial and ulnar arteries.
questions.question: Which artery provides the main arterial supply to the arm?

questions.explanation: Just before emptying into the femoral vein, the great saphenous vein receives tributaries from the superficial circumflex iliac vein, superficial epigastric vein, and external pudendal veins. These tributaries are important surgical landmarks during saphenofemoral junction ligation for varicose vein surgery.
options: Superficial circumflex iliac, superficial epigastric, and external pudendal veins
Popliteal, small saphenous, and accessory saphenous veins
Profunda femoris, femoral, and accessory saphenous veins
Dorsal venous arch, popliteal, and profunda femoris veins
Deep circumflex iliac, superficial epigastric, and internal pudendal veins
questions.question: Just before emptying into the femoral vein, the great saphenous vein receives tributaries from which three named veins?
The carotid body is a chemoreceptor sensitive to changes in which substance?
questions.explanation: The carotid body is a chemoreceptor sensitive to decreased arterial oxygen (hypoxemia), increased carbon dioxide (hypercapnia), and decreased pH (acidosis). It is located at the carotid bifurcation and is innervated by the glossopharyngeal nerve. The carotid sinus (baroreceptor) monitors blood pressure changes.

The jejunum constitutes approximately 40% of the total length of the small intestine beyond the duodenum. This represents about 2.5 meters of the 5-6 meter total small bowel length. The jejunum is characterized by being thicker-walled, more vascular, and having more prominent plicae circulares than the ileum.
questions.question: What percentage of the small intestine length does the jejunum constitute?

questions.explanation: The left ventricle forms most of the left (pulmonary) border of the heart, with a small contribution from the left auricle (atrial appendage) superiorly. The left border extends from the second left intercostal space to the apex in the fifth intercostal space. This border is related to the left lung and pleura, separated by the pericardium.
questions.question: Which chamber forms most of the left border of the heart?

questions.explanation: The elbow joint is classified as a synovial hinge (ginglymus) joint, allowing uniaxial movement. Articulation occurs between the trochlea and capitulum of the humerus with the trochlear notch of the ulna and radial head respectively. This configuration permits flexion and extension movements.
questions.question: What type of synovial joint is the elbow classified as?
Which part of the stomach is LEAST covered by peritoneum?
questions.explanation: A small area of the posterior surface of the stomach near the cardia (where the two layers of lesser omentum separate to enclose the stomach) is "bare" and in direct contact with the left crus of the diaphragm, lacking peritoneal covering. This represents the only part of the stomach not completely invested by peritoneum. The rest of the stomach is completely covered by visceral peritoneum: anteriorly and posteriorly by peritoneum continuous with the greater and lesser omenta, and along its curvatures where the gastrosplenic, gastrohepatic, and gastrocolic ligaments attach. The bare area can be a site where gastric perforation communicates directly with the retroperitoneum.

extends the interphalangeal joint of the thumb and assists with extension at the metacarpophalangeal and carpometacarpal joints. Its tendon forms the medial border of the anatomical snuffbox. The muscle is supplied by the posterior interosseous nerve.
questions.question: What is the primary extensor of the thumb interphalangeal joint?

questions.explanation: In the mnemonic 'Does She Scream During Poking Sessions?' each letter corresponds to a branch of the femoral artery: Deep external pudendal, Superficial epigastric, Superficial external pudendal, Descending genicular, Profunda femoris, Superficial circumflex iliac. The profunda femoris is the largest and most important branch, giving rise to the perforating branches and circumflex arteries.
questions.question: The femoral artery branches are recalled using the mnemonic 'Does she scream during poking sessions?' Which branch corresponds to 'D'?
At which costal cartilage does left pleural reflection deviate?
questions.explanation: On the left side, the pleural reflection passes inferomedially to the level of the fourth costal cartilage, where it deviates to the left margin of the sternum. This creates a shallow notch corresponding to the cardiac notch of the left lung. This differs from the right side where the pleura descends vertically in the median plane.

options: Encloses axillary artery and brachial plexus
questions.question: What is the significance of the axillary sheath?
questions.explanation: The axillary sheath is a fascial extension of the prevertebral fascia that encloses the axillary artery and brachial plexus cords. This tubular sheath provides a pathway for these structures through the axilla. Local anesthetic can be injected into this sheath for brachial plexus blocks.

questions.question: The ankle joint allows primarily which movements?
questions.explanation: The ankle joint (talocrural joint) primarily allows dorsiflexion and plantarflexion, with a small degree of rotation. Inversion and eversion occur primarily at the subtalar joint (talocalcaneal articulation) and midtarsal joints. The talocrural joint has a range of approximately 20 degrees dorsiflexion and 50 degrees plantarflexion in a healthy adult.

Serratus anterior is the most powerful protractor of the scapula, pulling it forward around the chest wall. Paralysis of this muscle causes scapular winging, where the medial border of the scapula protrudes from the back. The muscle is supplied by the long thoracic nerve (C5, C6, C7).
questions.question: What is the primary action of serratus anterior?
What produces circumduction at the shoulder joint?
questions.explanation: Circumduction at the shoulder joint is a sequential combination of flexion, abduction, extension, and adduction movements. This creates a conical movement pattern of the limb. Multiple muscles act in coordinated sequence to produce this composite movement.

questions.question: Which artery forms an anastomosis across the median cricothyroid ligament?
questions.explanation: Small cricothyroid arterial branches from the superior thyroid arteries anastomose across the median cricothyroid ligament. This anastomosis crosses the ligament horizontally and must be considered during emergency cricothyroidotomy. The vessels typically run superiorly along the cricothyroid membrane.

questions.question: The femoral nerve emerges from which muscle's lateral border?
questions.explanation: The femoral nerve (L2, L3, L4), the largest branch of the lumbar plexus, emerges from the lateral border of the psoas major muscle near the inguinal ligament and descends in the groove between psoas and iliacus. It enters the thigh beneath the inguinal ligament, lateral to the femoral artery in the femoral triangle. Other branches emerging from psoas major's lateral border include the iliohypogastric, ilioinguinal, and lateral femoral cutaneous nerves. The obturator nerve, in contrast, emerges from the medial border of psoas, while the genitofemoral nerve pierces through its anterior surface.

questions.question: The inferior gluteal nerve (L5, S1, S2) supplies which single muscle?
questions.explanation: The inferior gluteal nerve (L5, S1, S2) supplies only the gluteus maximus. It exits the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis. Injury results in loss of powerful hip extension, making it impossible to rise from sitting, climb stairs, or run effectively. Since gluteus maximus has little role in gentle walking, the patient may ambulate with minimal apparent deficit on flat ground.

Depression of the diaphragm significantly alters the vertical (superoinferior) dimensions of the thorax. When the muscle fibers of the diaphragm contract, the domes and central tendon descend. Elevation occurs when the diaphragm relaxes. The diaphragm is the most important muscle of respiration.
questions.question: What increases vertical thoracic dimension?

options: Articulates with the lateral femoral condyle
Provides attachment for knee joint structures only
questions.question: The fibula does NOT form part of the knee joint. Its role in relation to the knee is best described as what?
questions.explanation: The fibula does not form part of the knee joint and does not articulate with the femur or patella. Its role is only to provide attachment for knee joint structures: the fibular collateral ligament (from the lateral epicondyle of the femur to the fibular head) and the biceps femoris tendon. The fibula mainly serves as a muscle attachment site and forms the lateral wall of the ankle mortise.

After descending in the lateral compartment and passing behind the lateral malleolus, fibularis longus turns medially in a groove on the plantar surface of the cuboid, crossing the sole diagonally to insert into the base of the 1st metatarsal and medial cuneiform. This unique oblique course allows it to support the transverse arch of the foot.
questions.question: Fibularis longus crosses the sole diagonally after turning medially in a groove on which bone, ultimately inserting into the base of the 1st metatarsal and medial cuneiform?

questions.explanation: The aditus ad antrum is an opening in the posterior wall of the epitympanic recess that connects the middle ear cavity with the mastoid antrum. Middle ear infections can spread to the mastoid air cells through this passage causing mastoiditis. The roof of the aditus is the tegmen tympani.
questions.question: The aditus ad antrum connects which two structures?

questions.explanation: The midtarsal joint (Chopart's joint) consists of two articulations working in concert: the talonavicular joint medially and the calcaneocuboid joint laterally. Movements at this joint complement subtalar movements to produce overall foot inversion and eversion. Chopart's amputation is performed through this joint for distal foot pathology, preserving the hindfoot for a functional stump.
questions.question: The midtarsal (transverse tarsal) joint is formed by which two articulations working together?
Which structure separates the right and left paracolic gutters?
questions.explanation: The mesentery of the small intestine, with its oblique root extending from the duodenojejunal flexure (L2, left of midline) to the right sacroiliac joint (S1, right of midline), divides the infracolic compartment into right and left infracolic spaces. These spaces communicate laterally with the right and left paracolic gutters respectively. The paracolic gutters are depressions lateral to the ascending and descending colon where peritoneal fluid can track between the pelvis and upper abdomen. The right paracolic gutter communicates with the hepatorenal recess, providing a pathway for infection spread.

questions.question: The aortic bifurcation occurs at which surface landmark?
questions.explanation: The bifurcation of the abdominal aorta into right and left common iliac arteries at the L4 vertebral level corresponds to a point on the anterior abdominal wall slightly below and to the left of the umbilicus (which lies at L3/L4 disc level). This surface marking is clinically useful for palpating the aorta and detecting abdominal aortic aneurysms. The bifurcation point can be located by drawing imaginary lines from the umbilicus toward the midinguinal points (midway between ASIS and pubic symphysis) on each side. The median sacral artery arises from the posterior aspect of the aorta just before its bifurcation.

The left internal thoracic artery is preferred for coronary bypass because of its proximity to the left anterior descending coronary artery. The right internal thoracic may also be used for right coronary or circumflex vessels. Using arterial grafts (vs. saphenous vein) provides superior long-term patency rates.
questions.question: Which side internal thoracic is preferred for bypass?

questions.explanation: Lymphatic drainage from the appendix passes through lymph nodes in the mesoappendix to the ileocolic lymph nodes along the ileocolic artery, which subsequently drain to superior mesenteric lymph nodes along the superior mesenteric artery. From there, lymph flows to the pre-aortic nodes and eventually to the cisterna chyli and thoracic duct. This drainage pattern follows the arterial supply (appendicular artery from ileocolic artery from SMA). Enlarged ileocolic nodes may be palpable in appendicitis and can contribute to diagnostic imaging findings in acute abdominal conditions.
questions.question: The appendicular lymph nodes drain into which nodal group?

questions.explanation: The popliteal artery begins when the femoral artery passes through the adductor hiatus, a tendinous gap in the lower part of adductor magnus. It then descends through the popliteal fossa and terminates at the inferior border of popliteus. The femoral artery travels through the adductor canal in the anterior thigh before reaching the hiatus.
questions.question: The popliteal artery begins where the femoral artery passes through which structure in the lower thigh?
Which structure marks the beginning of the anal canal?
questions.explanation: The anal canal begins at the anorectal junction (where the rectum pierces the pelvic diaphragm formed by the levator ani muscle), located approximately one inch (2.5 cm) below and anterior to the tip of the coccyx. At this level, the puborectalis sling creates the anorectal angle. The anal canal extends approximately 3.8-4 cm to the anus (anal verge). The pectinate line divides the anal canal into upper (endodermal) and lower (ectodermal) parts. The white line of Hilton marks the lower border of the internal sphincter.

The anterior ethmoidal artery (from ophthalmic artery) descends through the anterior ethmoidal foramen to supply the anterior superior nasal septum and lateral nasal wall. It anastomoses with branches of the sphenopalatine artery posteriorly. The artery also supplies the anterior ethmoidal cells and contributes to the blood supply of the frontal sinus.
questions.question: Which artery supplies the anterior nasal septum superiorly?
Which cartilage forms the only complete ring in the respiratory tract?
questions.explanation: The cricoid cartilage is signet-ring shaped and forms the only complete cartilaginous ring throughout the entire respiratory tract. This structural feature provides crucial stability and serves as an important landmark for emergency airway access. The cricoid is the narrowest part of the pediatric airway.

questions.question: What is the function of the ileocecal valve?
questions.explanation: The ileocecal valve prevents reflux of colonic contents (which contain bacteria) back into the sterile small intestine. It also slows the passage of ileal contents into the cecum, allowing more time for nutrient and water absorption. The valve consists of superior and inferior lips formed by mucosal folds supported by circular muscle thickening.

options: Anterior deltoid and pectoralis clavicular head
questions.explanation: Shoulder flexion is produced primarily by anterior fibers of deltoid and the clavicular head of pectoralis major. Biceps brachii and coracobrachialis provide assistance. This movement raises the arm forward in the sagittal plane.
questions.question: Which muscle is the primary shoulder flexor?
The middle colic artery divides into which branches?
questions.explanation: The middle colic artery (from the superior mesenteric artery) enters the transverse mesocolon and divides into right and left branches that supply the transverse colon. The right branch anastomoses with the right colic artery (from SMA), while the left branch anastomoses with the ascending branch of the left colic artery (from inferior mesenteric artery), forming the marginal artery of Drummond at the splenic flexure. This anastomotic connection between SMA and IMA territories provides important collateral circulation. Variation in the middle colic artery is common; occasionally it may be absent or arise as two separate vessels.

questions.question: Where is the pulmonary ligament located?
questions.explanation: The pulmonary ligament is a loose fold of pleura that hangs down below the root of the lung. It is formed by the continuity of visceral and parietal pleura inferior to the hilum. It forms a sleeve allowing for expansion of the pulmonary veins during increased venous return.

questions.question: Which cranial nerve provides motor innervation to the stylopharyngeus muscle?
questions.explanation: The glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) is the only cranial nerve that provides motor innervation to a pharyngeal muscle - the stylopharyngeus. All other pharyngeal muscles are supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (vagus via cranial accessory). Stylopharyngeus elevates the pharynx during swallowing.

The gastrosplenic (gastrolienal) ligament extends from the hilum of the spleen to the greater curvature of the stomach. It is part of the greater omentum and contains the short gastric vessels and left gastroepiploic vessels. This ligament provides vascular connections between the spleen and stomach.
questions.question: Which ligament connects the spleen to the greater curvature?
The ureter is crossed anteriorly at the pelvic brim by which vessel?
questions.explanation: The ureter is crossed anteriorly by the testicular vessels (in males) or ovarian vessels (in females) near the pelvic brim, as these vessels descend from their aortic origins at L2 level toward the deep inguinal ring (males) or ovary (females). The ureter then crosses the bifurcation of the common iliac artery (or proximal external iliac artery) before entering the pelvis. In females, the ureter is subsequently crossed by the uterine artery approximately 1.5 cm lateral to the cervix ("water under the bridge"), an important surgical relationship during hysterectomy. The superior vesical artery travels with the ureter in the pelvis but does not cross it.

The transpyloric plane, passing midway between the suprasternal notch and pubic symphysis (or midway between xiphoid and umbilicus), corresponds to the level of the first lumbar vertebra (L1) and the lower border of vertebra T12. This important surgical landmark crosses numerous structures: pylorus of stomach (when supine), neck of pancreas, origin of the SMA and portal vein, duodenojejunal flexure, hila of both kidneys, fundus of gallbladder, root of transverse mesocolon, origin of IMA (at L3), and tips of ninth costal cartilages. The plane is used to define upper and lower abdominal regions in the nine-region scheme.
questions.question: Which vertebral level corresponds to the transpyloric plane?

options: Anterior compartment flexor with radial nerve supply
questions.question: How does the brachioradialis differ from other radial nerve-supplied muscles?
questions.explanation: Brachioradialis is unique as an anterior compartment muscle (flexor) supplied by the radial nerve, which typically supplies extensors. This reflects its developmental origin from extensor muscle mass despite its eventual anterior position. It flexes the forearm most effectively from mid-prone position.

questions.question: Which vessel supplies the nasal mucosa?
questions.explanation: The nasal mucosa receives blood from both internal carotid (via ophthalmic artery branches: anterior and posterior ethmoidal) and external carotid (via maxillary artery branches: sphenopalatine, greater palatine) systems. The superior labial artery also contributes anteriorly. This rich dual blood supply accounts for profuse epistaxis. Kiesselbach's plexus represents arterial convergence.

questions.question: Which muscle forms the lateral wall of the inguinal canal?
questions.explanation: The inguinal canal does not have distinct medial or lateral walls; instead, it has anterior and posterior walls, a roof, and a floor. The internal oblique muscle contributes to the anterior wall in the lateral third of the canal (where its fibers arise from the inguinal ligament) and forms part of the roof with the transversus abdominis muscle through their arching fibers. The external oblique aponeurosis forms the entire length of the anterior wall, the transversalis fascia (reinforced medially by conjoint tendon) forms the posterior wall, and the inguinal ligament forms the floor.

questions.question: Which part of diaphragm arises from xiphoid process?
questions.explanation: The sternal part of the diaphragm arises from two small slips from the deep surface of the xiphoid process. The costal part arises from the inner aspects of the lower six ribs and costal cartilages. The vertebral part arises from the crura and arcuate ligaments.

questions.question: Which part of the pancreas lies within the concavity of the duodenum?
questions.explanation: The head of the pancreas lies within the C-shaped curve formed by the duodenum, specifically nestled in the concavity of the second, third, and fourth parts of the duodenum. The head is the broadest part of the pancreas. A portion of the head, the uncinate process, extends to the left behind the superior mesenteric vessels.

The anal canal above the pectinate line is derived from endoderm (hindgut), while the portion below originates from ectoderm (proctodeum). This embryological distinction explains the different characteristics of the two regions: superior to the pectinate line, the mucosa is columnar, venous drainage is to the portal system via superior rectal veins, lymphatic drainage is to internal iliac nodes, and innervation is autonomic (insensitive to pain). Below the line, the epithelium is stratified squamous, venous drainage is systemic (middle and inferior rectal veins), lymph drains to superficial inguinal nodes, and sensory innervation is via the inferior rectal nerve (painful).
questions.question: Which portion of the anal canal is derived from endoderm?

questions.explanation: The kidneys typically extend from the level of the 12th thoracic vertebra (T12) to the third lumbar vertebra (L3) on the posterior abdominal wall. The right kidney is slightly lower than the left due to the presence of the liver. Both kidneys move inferiorly with respiration, descending as much as 2.5 cm during diaphragmatic contraction.
questions.question: At which vertebral levels do the kidneys typically lie?

questions.explanation: The patella is a true sesamoid bone serving as a pulley that improves the angle of pull of the quadriceps tendon, resulting in greater mechanical advantage in knee extension. Patellectomy significantly reduces knee extension strength. The patella slides within the trochlear groove during knee movements and is protected by thick hyaline cartilage on its posterior surface.
questions.question: The patella, embedded in the quadriceps and patellar tendon, serves as a pulley with what biomechanical benefit?
options: Increases the weight of the quadriceps
Increases mechanical advantage in knee extension

questions.question: The superior mesenteric vein lies to which side of the superior mesenteric artery?
questions.explanation: The superior mesenteric vein lies to the right of the superior mesenteric artery as they ascend from the root of the mesentery toward the pancreas. Both vessels cross anterior to the third (horizontal) part of the duodenum and the uncinate process of the pancreas. Posterior to the neck of the pancreas, the SMV joins the splenic vein to form the portal vein. This relationship is important surgically, as the SMV must be identified and preserved during pancreatic and duodenal procedures. Superior mesenteric artery syndrome can compress both the duodenum and potentially the SMV.

questions.question: Which muscle is NOT part of the anterior abdominal wall?
questions.explanation: The iliacus muscle is part of the posterior abdominal wall, not the anterior wall, originating from the iliac fossa and inserting with psoas major onto the lesser trochanter of the femur as the iliopsoas tendon. The anterior abdominal wall muscles include three flat muscles (external oblique, internal oblique, and transversus abdominis) and two vertical muscles (rectus abdominis and pyramidalis). The iliacus is innervated by the femoral nerve and functions primarily as a hip flexor, while the anterior abdominal wall muscles are involved in trunk movement and increasing intra-abdominal pressure.

The sphenoid sinuses drain into the sphenoethmoidal recess above the superior concha. These sinuses lie within the body of the sphenoid bone and vary greatly in size. Close relationship to the optic nerve and carotid artery makes sphenoid surgery particularly challenging.
questions.question: The sphenoid sinus drains into which location?

questions.explanation: The tail of the pancreas extends laterally and slightly superiorly, reaching to within 1 cm of the splenic hilum in approximately 75% of individuals, lying within the splenorenal ligament along with the splenic artery and vein. This relationship is surgically significant during splenectomy, as the pancreatic tail must be identified and preserved to prevent iatrogenic pancreatitis or pancreatic fistula. The body of the pancreas lies anterior to the splenic vein (which runs along its posterior surface) and behind the posterior wall of the lesser sac (omental bursa), separated from it by the gastrosplenic ligament.
questions.question: The tail of the pancreas extends into which ligament?
Which bone contains the foramen spinosum?
questions.explanation: The foramen spinosum is located in the greater wing of the sphenoid bone, posterolateral to the foramen ovale. It transmits the middle meningeal artery and meningeal branch of the mandibular nerve. The foramen is located at the spine of the sphenoid. Accessory meningeal arteries may also pass through this foramen.

questions.question: The jugular foramen transmits which three cranial nerves?
questions.explanation: The jugular foramen transmits the glossopharyngeal (IX), vagus (X), and accessory (XI) nerves along with the internal jugular vein. The foramen is divided by a fibrous or bony septum into anteromedial (pars nervosa) and posterolateral (pars vascularis) compartments. Glomus jugulare tumors arise in this region.

questions.question: What maintains negative intrapleural pressure?
questions.explanation: The elastic recoil of the lungs pulling inward, opposed by the chest wall's tendency to spring outward, creates and maintains the negative (sub-atmospheric) pressure in the pleural cavity. This negative pressure is essential for keeping the lungs expanded and prevents their collapse.

Glucagon is produced by alpha cells in the pancreatic islets (islets of Langerhans) and increases blood glucose by promoting hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis. It opposes insulin action. Glucagon secretion is stimulated by low blood glucose, amino acids, and sympathetic stimulation. Alpha cells constitute about 20% of islet cells and are located peripherally in the islets.
questions.question: Which hormone is produced by the pancreatic alpha cells?
The menisci deepen the articular surface and act as which functional structures in the knee joint?
options: Shock absorbers and joint space deepeners
Attachment points for cruciate ligaments only
Blood vessel channels for synovial membrane
Lubricating pads reducing synovial fluid production
questions.explanation: The menisci are crescentic plates of fibrocartilage that deepen the tibial articular surface and act as shock absorbers. They are thicker at external margins and taper toward the center. Meniscal tears are among the most common knee injuries in athletes. The lateral meniscus is more freely movable than the medial meniscus.

questions.question: Which recess is deeper during expiration?
questions.explanation: The costodiaphragmatic recess is shallow during inspiration when the lung expands into it, and becomes deeper during expiration when the lung retracts. This recess is clinically important as it is the site where pleural fluid accumulates in effusions and is the target for thoracentesis.

questions.question: The medial femoral circumflex artery wraps around the posterior aspect of the femur and is the main blood supply to the femoral head. From which artery does it arise?
questions.explanation: The medial femoral circumflex artery (MFCA) arises from the profunda femoris artery (deep femoral artery). It wraps around the posterior side of the femur, supplying the neck and head via retinacular vessels. In femoral neck fractures, this artery is commonly damaged, leading to avascular necrosis of the femoral head. It also contributes to the trochanteric and cruciate anastomoses.

The posterior wall of the stomach lies anterior to the body of the pancreas, separated by the lesser sac (omental bursa). The anterior surface of the pancreatic body is covered by the peritoneum of the posterior wall of the lesser sac. This relationship is clinically important as pancreatic disease can cause epigastric pain.
questions.question: Which structure lies anterior to the body of the pancreas?

questions.explanation: The sympathetic trunk does not innervate voluntary (skeletal) muscles, which are innervated by somatic motor neurons. The sympathetic system innervates cardiac muscle, smooth muscle in blood vessels and organs, sweat glands, and various viscera. Sympathetic fibers reach the body wall via gray rami communicantes.
questions.question: Which structure does the sympathetic trunk NOT innervate?

questions.explanation: The sciatic nerve curves downward midway between the ischial tuberosity and the greater trochanter. It has a side of danger (medial side, closer to the ischial tuberosity) and a side of safety (lateral side). The quadratus femoris forms a protective muscular layer over the nerve as it passes posterior to the hip joint.
questions.question: The sciatic nerve (L4, 5; S1, 2, 3) curves downward at which position between the ischial tuberosity and the greater trochanter?
How does thumb position affect hand function?
questions.explanation: Thumb opposition (pad contact with finger pads) enables precision grip essential for fine manipulation. Thumb adduction against lateral index finger enables lateral (key) pinch. Thumb extension/abduction contributes to cylindrical power grip. This positional versatility makes the thumb essential for human hand function.
options: Opposition enables precision grip; adduction/extension enables power grip
Anterior surface of medial femoral condyle
questions.explanation: The ACL arises from the anterior intercondylar area of the tibia (just posterior to the medial meniscus attachment) and attaches to the lateral condyle of the femur. It is the weaker of the two cruciate ligaments with relatively poor blood supply. It becomes taut in full extension and prevents posterior displacement of the femur on the tibia.
questions.question: The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) arises from the anterior intercondylar area of the tibia and attaches to which femoral condyle?

questions.explanation: The tendon of biceps femoris at its insertion on the lateral side of the head of fibula is split into two parts by the fibular (lateral) collateral ligament of the knee joint. The common fibular nerve closely follows the medial border of the biceps femoris tendon and winds around the neck of the fibula. Injury to biceps femoris or the fibular head can therefore damage the common fibular nerve.
questions.question: The tendon of biceps femoris at its fibular head insertion is split into two parts by which ligament?

questions.explanation: The floor of the inguinal canal is formed by the inguinal ligament (the rolled-under inferior edge of the external oblique aponeurosis) throughout most of its length, reinforced medially by the lacunar ligament. The inguinal ligament extends from the anterior superior iliac spine to the pubic tubercle. The roof is formed by the arching fibers of the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles, while the anterior wall is formed by the external oblique aponeurosis and the posterior wall by the transversalis fascia, reinforced medially by the conjoint tendon.
questions.question: Which muscle forms the floor of the inguinal canal?

questions.explanation: The posterior third of the tongue and soft palate drain to the superior deep cervical lymph nodes. The medial anterior two-thirds drains to inferior deep cervical nodes. Lateral anterior tongue drains to submandibular nodes while the tip drains to submental nodes.
questions.question: What drains into the superior deep cervical lymph nodes from the oral cavity?
What is the function of palmar interossei?
questions.explanation: Palmar interossei (PAD - Palmar ADduct) produce finger adduction, moving fingers toward the middle finger axis. There are three palmar interossei muscles compared to four dorsal interossei. All interossei also flex the metacarpophalangeal joints and extend the interphalangeal joints.

Medial rotation at the hip joint is performed primarily by gluteus medius (anterior fibers), gluteus minimus (anterior fibers), and tensor fasciae latae. Lateral rotation is performed by obturator internus and externus, gemellus superior and inferior, quadratus femoris, piriformis, and posterior fibers of gluteus medius and maximus.
questions.question: Medial rotation at the hip joint is primarily performed by which three muscles?
options: Gluteus medius, minimus, and tensor fasciae latae

questions.explanation: The middle cardiac vein ascends in the posterior interventricular groove alongside the posterior interventricular artery and drains into the coronary sinus near its termination in the right atrium. It drains blood from the posterior walls of both ventricles and the posterior interventricular septum. It is the second largest cardiac vein after the great cardiac vein.
questions.question: Which vein accompanies the posterior interventricular artery?
The posterior compartment of the thigh is supplied primarily by perforating branches of which artery?
questions.explanation: The posterior compartment of the thigh is supplied by perforating branches of the profunda femoris artery, consisting of three or four arteries perforating adductor magnus. The profunda femoris is the main blood supply to all three thigh compartments. The inferior gluteal artery provides additional supply to the proximal hamstrings via descending branches.

questions.question: The ligament of Treitz suspends which structure?
questions.explanation: The suspensory muscle of the duodenum (ligament of Treitz) is a fibromuscular band arising from the right crus of the diaphragm near the esophageal hiatus that inserts onto the duodenojejunal flexure and sometimes the horizontal part of the duodenum. It supports the duodenojejunal junction and marks the transition from retroperitoneal (fixed) duodenum to intraperitoneal (mobile) jejunum. This landmark is important radiologically (widening suggests a mass in the pancreatic head) and surgically (identifies the site where the small bowel becomes mobile during laparotomy and marks the upper limit of superior mesenteric artery distribution).

The superficial cervical lymph nodes lie along the external jugular vein within the superficial cervical fascia containing platysma. They receive drainage from the scalp and auricle. Efferents pass to the deep cervical chain.
questions.question: Which lymph nodes are located in the superficial cervical fascia?
The spleen is located in which abdominal region?
questions.explanation: The spleen is situated in the left hypochondriac region, lying obliquely along the long axis of the 9th, 10th, and 11th ribs in the left upper quadrant. It is protected by the rib cage and cannot normally be palpated unless enlarged. The spleen is related anteriorly to the stomach (via the gastrosplenic ligament), posteriorly to the left kidney (via the splenorenal ligament), superiorly to the diaphragm, and inferiorly to the left colic flexure (supported by the phrenicocolic ligament). The splenic notch on its superior border is a characteristic feature visible on imaging.

The external intercostal muscle is deficient anteriorly at the costochondral junction and is replaced by the external (anterior) intercostal membrane. This fibrous membrane continues the plane of the muscle to the sternum. The internal intercostal muscle conversely is deficient posteriorly at the angle of the rib.
questions.question: At which location is the external intercostal muscle deficient?
What provides sensation to the palmar aspect of the thumb?
questions.explanation: The median nerve provides sensation to the palmar aspect of the thumb, index, middle, and lateral half of the ring finger. This sensory distribution is preserved in anterior interosseous syndrome (pure motor branch) but affected in carpal tunnel syndrome and more proximal median nerve injuries.

Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) requires intrinsic factor, secreted by gastric parietal cells, for absorption in the terminal ileum. Intrinsic factor binds to B12, protecting it from degradation and facilitating its receptor-mediated uptake by ileal enterocytes. Lack of intrinsic factor (from parietal cell destruction in pernicious anemia or gastrectomy) causes B12 deficiency and megaloblastic anemia.
questions.question: Which vitamin requires intrinsic factor for absorption?
Which ligament is the most important structure maintaining the medial longitudinal arch, bridging the sustentaculum tali to the navicular?
questions.explanation: The spring ligament (plantar calcaneonavicular ligament) is the most critical ligament maintaining the medial longitudinal arch. It bridges the sustentaculum tali of the calcaneus to the navicular, directly supporting the head of the talus. Rupture of the spring ligament leads to progressive collapse of the medial longitudinal arch and adult acquired flatfoot deformity.

The obturator artery typically arises from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery, descending along the lateral pelvic wall to exit the pelvis through the obturator canal (superior to obturator membrane) with the obturator nerve. However, anatomical variation is common (25-30% of cases), with the obturator artery sometimes arising as an aberrant or accessory vessel from the inferior epigastric artery (a branch of external iliac), passing along the pelvic brim to reach the obturator foramen. This "aberrant obturator artery" is at risk during hernia repair as it may run along the margin of the femoral ring.
questions.question: The obturator artery is a branch of which vessel?

questions.explanation: The median arcuate ligament is a fibrous arch that unites the right and left crura anteriorly across the aortic hiatus at the T12 level. It forms the superior boundary of the aortic hiatus through which the aorta, thoracic duct, and sometimes azygos vein pass. Occasionally, this ligament can compress the celiac trunk causing median arcuate ligament syndrome.
questions.question: What connects the two crura anteriorly?
The femoral nerve (L2, L3, L4) exits the pelvis beneath the inguinal ligament. It lies in which position relative to the femoral artery?
questions.explanation: The femoral nerve (L2, L3, L4) lies lateral to the femoral artery as it exits beneath the inguinal ligament, outside the femoral sheath (which contains only the femoral artery, vein, and canal). The mnemonic NAVEL (Nerve, Artery, Vein, Empty/Lymphatics) describes the lateral to medial arrangement. The femoral nerve rapidly divides into branches in the femoral triangle.

questions.question: Which opening is located at the apex of the orbit?
questions.explanation: The optic canal is located at the apex of the orbit in the lesser wing of the sphenoid bone. It transmits the optic nerve (II) and ophthalmic artery from the middle cranial fossa into the orbit. The canal is approximately 10 mm long. Optic nerve compression can occur from tumors, trauma, or inflammatory processes.

questions.question: What structure forms the lateral boundary of mediastinum?
questions.explanation: The mediastinum is bounded laterally by the right and left pleural cavities and their contained lungs. Anteriorly, it is bounded by the sternum; posteriorly by the thoracic vertebrae. Superiorly, it extends to the root of the neck, and inferiorly to the diaphragm.

questions.question: The anterior belly of the digastric forms part of which triangle?
questions.explanation: The anterior bellies of the right and left digastric muscles form the lateral boundaries of the submental triangle. The hyoid bone forms the base (inferior boundary), and the mylohyoid muscle forms the floor. The triangle contains submental lymph nodes and is located in the midline below the chin.

Enterokinase (enteropeptidase) is a brush border enzyme produced by duodenal enterocytes that converts inactive trypsinogen to active trypsin by cleaving a small peptide. Trypsin then activates other pancreatic proteases through a cascade mechanism. This activation mechanism ensures that proteases are inactive within the pancreas and are only activated in the duodenal lumen, protecting the pancreas from autodigestion.
questions.question: Which enzyme activates trypsinogen in the duodenum?
Which surface of the lung faces the mediastinum?
questions.explanation: The mediastinal surface faces the mediastinum and contains the hilum where structures enter and leave the lung. This surface is in contact with the heart, great vessels, trachea, esophagus, and other mediastinal structures. The hilum is located on this surface opposite the bodies of T5, T6, and T7 vertebrae.

The prostatic urethra (the widest and most dilatable part of the male urethra) receives the openings of the two ejaculatory ducts on the seminal colliculus (verumontanum) and numerous prostatic ducts (15-30 openings) on either side of the urethral crest. The bulbourethral (Cowper's) gland ducts open into the bulbar portion of the spongy urethra, not the prostatic urethra. The prostatic utricle, a small blind pouch representing the remnant of the paramesonephric duct, also opens on the seminal colliculus. The internal urethral sphincter surrounds the proximal prostatic urethra.
questions.question: The prostatic urethra receives openings from which ducts?

questions.explanation: The middle rectal artery arises from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery (or occasionally from the internal pudendal artery) and passes medially in the lateral rectal ligament (lateral ligament of the rectum) to supply the lower part of the rectum. It anastomoses with branches of the superior rectal artery (from inferior mesenteric) above and inferior rectal artery (from internal pudendal) below, creating collateral circulation. This vessel represents the junction between portal (superior rectal) and systemic (middle and inferior rectal) venous systems, a site of potential portosystemic anastomosis in portal hypertension.
questions.question: The middle rectal artery is a branch of which vessel?
Which cruciate ligament becomes taut during knee flexion and is the stronger of the two cruciate ligaments?
questions.explanation: The posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) arises from the posterior intercondylar area of the tibia and attaches to the medial condyle of the femur. It becomes taut during flexion of the knee and is the stronger of the two cruciate ligaments. In a weight-bearing flexed knee (walking downhill), the PCL is the main stabilizing factor preventing anterior displacement of the femur.

questions.question: The rectus sheath is absent posteriorly below which line?
questions.explanation: Below the arcuate line (linea semicircularis), located approximately midway between the umbilicus and pubic symphysis, the posterior rectus sheath is absent. At this level, all three aponeurotic layers (external oblique, internal oblique, and transversus abdominis) pass anteriorly to the rectus abdominis muscle, leaving only the transversalis fascia and peritoneum posteriorly. This anatomical arrangement creates a relative weakness that may be involved in direct inguinal hernias. The inferior epigastric vessels pierce the transversalis fascia at the arcuate line to enter the rectus sheath.

The lateral border of the pronator teres muscle forms the medial (ulnar) boundary of the cubital fossa. The lateral boundary is formed by the medial border of brachioradialis muscle. The floor consists of brachialis and supinator muscles while the roof is formed by fascia and bicipital aponeurosis.
questions.question: Which muscle forms the medial boundary of the cubital fossa?

questions.explanation: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve is longer than the right because of the embryological descent of the heart and great vessels. As the heart descends from the neck into the thorax, it carries the aortic arch (and the nerve looping under it) downward. The right subclavian artery descends less, so the right nerve is shorter.
questions.question: Why is the left recurrent laryngeal nerve longer?
The seminal vesicles are located posterior to which structure?
questions.explanation: The seminal vesicles are located posterior to the fundus (base) of the urinary bladder, lateral to the ampulla of the vas deferens, anterior to the rectum (separated by rectovesical fascia), and superior to the prostate gland. They are elongated, lobulated structures that produce approximately 70% of seminal fluid volume, which is alkaline and contains fructose (energy for sperm), prostaglandins, and clotting factors. The duct of each seminal vesicle joins the ampulla of the corresponding vas deferens to form the ejaculatory duct, which passes through the prostate to open into the prostatic urethra.

In the thorax, the esophagus is supplied by esophageal branches arising directly from the anterior aspect of the descending thoracic aorta. Additional supply comes from the inferior thyroid artery superiorly and left gastric artery inferiorly. Bronchial arteries also contribute small branches. Venous drainage follows a similar pattern.
questions.question: Which vessels supply the esophagus in thorax?

questions.explanation: The femur is the longest and strongest bone in the body, averaging 45 cm in length. It accounts for approximately one-quarter of a person's total height. The femur articulates with the acetabulum superiorly and the patella and tibia inferiorly.
questions.question: Which bone accounts for approximately one-quarter of a person's total height and averages 45 cm in length?
Which of the following is NOT among the structures passing through the lesser sciatic foramen?
questions.explanation: The lesser sciatic foramen transmits five structures: the pudendal nerve, nerve to obturator internus, internal pudendal artery and vein, and the tendon of obturator internus. The sciatic nerve exits through the greater sciatic foramen. The lesser sciatic foramen enables re-entry into the perineum from the gluteal region.

The pterygoid venous plexus communicates with the cavernous sinus via emissary veins and deep facial veins. This valveless connection allows spread of infection from the infratemporal fossa to the cranial cavity. The plexus receives maxillary, middle meningeal, and deep temporal veins.
questions.question: The pterygoid venous plexus communicates with which important venous structure?

questions.explanation: Meissner's (submucosal) plexus is located in the submucosa between the inner circular and the mucosa layers. It primarily regulates secretion and blood flow in the gut wall. The myenteric (Auerbach's) plexus lies between the circular and longitudinal muscle layers and primarily controls motility. Together these form the enteric nervous system.
questions.question: Which layer of the gut wall contains Meissner's plexus?

questions.explanation: The bronchopulmonary segment is the smallest part of the lung that can be surgically removed without affecting adjacent regions. Each segment has its own tertiary bronchus, arterial supply, and venous drainage. Segmentectomy preserves more lung tissue than lobectomy while treating localized disease.
questions.question: What is the smallest independently resectable lung unit?

questions.explanation: The middle meningeal artery typically divides into frontal (anterior) and parietal (posterior) branches after entering the skull through the foramen spinosum. The frontal branch crosses the pterion area. The parietal branch supplies the posterior parietal region. Epidural hematomas most commonly involve the frontal branch in the pterion region.
questions.question: The middle meningeal artery commonly divides into which branches?
Which component comprises the majority of splenic tissue?
questions.explanation: The red pulp comprises approximately 76-79% of normal splenic tissue and consists of blood-filled sinusoids and splenic cords (cords of Billroth). The red pulp is responsible for filtering blood, removing old or damaged erythrocytes, and recycling iron. It appears red due to the large number of red blood cells in the sinusoids.

questions.question: The right crus of the diaphragm arises from which vertebral bodies?
questions.explanation: The right crus of the diaphragm arises from the anterolateral surfaces of the bodies and intervertebral discs of L1, L2, and L3 vertebrae (sometimes extending to L4), while the left crus arises from only L1 and L2 (sometimes L3). Both crura contribute to forming the esophageal hiatus, with muscle fibers from the right crus (and sometimes left) looping around the esophagus to create a muscular sphincter mechanism. The crura also form boundaries of the aortic hiatus, with the median arcuate ligament connecting them anterior to the aorta at T12 level.

questions.question: Where is Bochdalek's foramen located?
questions.explanation: The foramen of Bochdalek (pleuroperitoneal canal) is located posterolaterally in the diaphragm. Failure of the pleuroperitoneal membrane to close this opening results in a congenital diaphragmatic hernia. These hernias are more common on the left side and can allow abdominal viscera to herniate into the thorax.

questions.question: All muscles of the medial (adductor) compartment are supplied by the obturator nerve EXCEPT which part of which muscle?
questions.explanation: All muscles of the medial compartment are supplied by the obturator nerve (L2, L3, L4) except the hamstring part of adductor magnus, which is supplied by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve. Part of pectineus may also receive obturator supply. The dual nerve supply of adductor magnus reflects its dual embryological origin.

The palatine processes of the right and left maxillae form the anterior three-quarters of the hard palate. The horizontal plates of the palatine bones form the posterior quarter. The hard palate separates the oral and nasal cavities. The incisive foramen transmits the nasopalatine nerve anteriorly.
questions.question: Which bone forms the hard palate anteriorly?

options: Located in a deep protected position
Superficial over lateral wrist makes it vulnerable to trauma
questions.question: How does the superficial branch of radial nerve course affect its vulnerability?
questions.explanation: The superficial branch of radial nerve becomes subcutaneous on the lateral wrist as it passes over the anatomical snuffbox. This superficial position makes it vulnerable to trauma (handcuff neuropathy, tight watches, wrist lacerations). Injury causes numbness over dorsal thumb and radial hand without motor deficit.

Cholecystokinin (CCK) is released by I cells in the duodenal and jejunal mucosa in response to fats and proteins. It stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion from acinar cells and contraction of the gallbladder. Secretin, released in response to acid in the duodenum, stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate secretion from duct cells. Both hormones work synergistically to produce adequate pancreatic juice.
questions.question: Which hormone stimulates pancreatic enzyme secretion?

questions.explanation: The superficial inguinal lymph nodes drain lymph from the lower limb, perineum, gluteal region, and lower anterior abdominal wall (below the umbilicus). Their efferents drain to the deep inguinal lymph nodes, which then drain to the external iliac nodes, common iliac nodes, and ultimately the para-aortic nodes. This drainage pattern explains why infections of the foot can present with inguinal lymphadenopathy.
options: Lower limb only; draining to external iliac nodes
Lower limb, perineum, gluteal region, lower anterior abdominal wall; deep inguinal nodes
Only the genitalia; draining to internal obturator nodes
Only the lower limb below the knee; popliteal nodes
Only the gluteal region; internal iliac nodes
questions.question: The superficial inguinal lymph nodes drain which areas of the body, and their efferents drain to which deep node group?
The left triangular ligament of the liver attaches to which lobe?
questions.explanation: The left triangular ligament is formed by the approximation of the anterior and posterior layers of the left coronary ligament near the left end of the bare area, attaching the left lobe of the liver to the diaphragm. It is typically longer and narrower than the right triangular ligament. Division of this ligament is necessary to mobilize the left lateral segment of the liver during surgery. The ligament represents the reflection of peritoneum from the diaphragm onto the superior surface of the liver and demarcates the left lateral limit of the bare area of the liver.

questions.question: What is the functional relationship between pronator teres and pronator quadratus?
options: Pronator teres for fine control only
Pronator teres for power/speed, pronator quadratus for sustained/slow pronation
questions.explanation: Pronator teres is active during rapid or forceful pronation, while pronator quadratus is the primary muscle for slow, sustained pronation. The quadratus maintains pronated position during precision tasks. This demonstrates functional specialization among synergistic muscles.

questions.question: What is the eparterial bronchus?
questions.explanation: The eparterial bronchus is the right upper lobar bronchus, so named because it arises above (epi-) the pulmonary artery. All other bronchi are hyparterial (below the pulmonary artery). This anatomical feature is unique to the right lung and has embryological significance.

questions.question: What maintains gastroesophageal junction competence?
questions.explanation: Multiple factors maintain gastroesophageal junction competence preventing reflux: intrinsic LES tone, extrinsic compression by right crus sling fibers, acute angle of gastric entry (angle of His), positive intraabdominal pressure on the abdominal esophageal segment, and mucosal rosette at the cardia. Disruption causes GERD.

During inspiration, the diaphragm contracts, causing its domes and central tendon to descend and flatten. This increases the vertical dimension of the thoracic cavity. As the diaphragm descends, abdominal viscera are pushed downward and the intrathoracic volume increases, reducing intrathoracic pressure.
questions.question: What happens to diaphragm during inspiration?
The kidney hilum is located at which vertebral level?
questions.explanation: The renal hilum is positioned at the level of the transpyloric plane, which corresponds to the first lumbar vertebra (L1), though the kidneys themselves extend from approximately T12 to L3. At the hilum, structures are arranged from anterior to posterior as vein, artery, and pelvis (VAP), though the renal vein is most anterior and superior. The left kidney typically sits slightly higher than the right due to the presence of the liver on the right side.

questions.question: The profunda femoris artery arises from the femoral artery at what distance below the inguinal ligament?
questions.explanation: The profunda femoris artery (deep femoral artery) arises from the posterolateral aspect of the femoral artery approximately 5 cm below the inguinal ligament. It is the largest branch of the femoral artery and the main blood supply to the thigh muscles via perforating branches, medial and lateral femoral circumflex arteries.

questions.question: Which lymph nodes drain the appendix?
questions.explanation: The appendix drains to ileocolic lymph nodes located along the ileocolic artery, which then drain to superior mesenteric nodes. Appendiceal lymphoid tissue is abundant, earning it the nickname "intestinal tonsil." In appendicitis, lymph nodes may become enlarged and palpable. Metastatic disease from appendiceal tumors follows this lymphatic drainage pattern.

questions.question: The ansa cervicalis provides motor innervation to which muscle group?
questions.explanation: The ansa cervicalis (C1-C3) provides motor innervation to the infrahyoid strap muscles: sternohyoid, sternothyroid, and omohyoid. The thyrohyoid receives C1 fibers that travel with the hypoglossal nerve. These muscles depress the hyoid bone and larynx after swallowing.

The subtalar joint (talocalcaneal joint) primarily allows inversion and eversion of the foot, with associated adduction and abduction. These movements occur at the subtalar joint and midtarsal joints together. True dorsiflexion and plantarflexion occur at the ankle (talocrural) joint. The summit of the lateral longitudinal arch is at the subtalar articulation.
options: Dorsiflexion and plantarflexion at the ankle
Circumduction only, without inversion or eversion
Inversion and eversion (with associated adduction and abduction)
Pronation and supination of the ankle
questions.question: The subtalar joint (talocalcaneal joint) primarily allows which movements of the foot?

questions.explanation: Compression of the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh (L2, L3) causes meralgia paraesthetica, characterized by burning, tingling, or numbness on the anterolateral aspect of the thigh. It is a purely sensory nerve with no motor component. Common causes include obesity, pregnancy, tight belts, and direct compression. Treatment is conservative with weight loss and activity modification.
questions.question: The lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh (lateral femoral cutaneous nerve) enters the thigh just medial to the anterior superior iliac spine. Compression of this nerve causes which specific condition?
options: Meralgia paraesthetica (burning pain on lateral thigh)
Knee pain from saphenous nerve compression

questions.question: Which axillary node group lies on pectoralis minor?
questions.explanation: The pectoral (anterior) group of axillary lymph nodes lies on the pectoralis minor muscle along the lateral thoracic vessels. This group receives most of the lymphatic drainage from the breast. From here, lymph passes to the central and then apical nodes before reaching the subclavian lymph trunk.

The scapular anastomoses provide collateral circulation connecting the first part of the subclavian artery with the third part of the axillary artery. This involves suprascapular artery, dorsal scapular artery, and circumflex scapular artery. The anastomoses allow blood flow to the limb even with proximal vessel obstruction.
questions.question: What connects the first part of the subclavian artery with the third part of the axillary artery?
The anal columns (of Morgagni) are found in which part of the anal canal?
questions.explanation: The anal columns of Morgagni are 6-10 permanent longitudinal mucosal folds in the upper 15 mm of the anal canal, above the pectinate line, containing terminal radicles of the superior rectal veins (portal system). The lower ends of adjacent columns are connected by anal valves (semilunar mucosal folds), forming the pectinate (dentate) line. Superior to each valve is a small recess called an anal sinus, into which anal glands open. The columns have a plum-red color in living subjects due to the underlying internal rectal venous plexus, and internal hemorrhoids develop from these vascular columns.

questions.question: The non-articular portion of the acetabulum (acetabular fossa) is formed mainly by which bone and contains what?
questions.explanation: The acetabular fossa is the non-articular part of the acetabulum, formed mainly by the ischium. It contains loose connective tissue and a pad of fat. The articular surface is the horseshoe-shaped lunate surface covered by hyaline cartilage. The fossa is deficient inferiorly at the acetabular notch, bridged by the transverse acetabular ligament.
options: Ischium; loose connective tissue and fat

questions.explanation: The areola is a dark pink-brownish circular area of skin (22-60 mm in diameter) that surrounds the nipple. Its color varies with parity and race, darkening during the second month of pregnancy. The areola contains Montgomery's glands (areola glands) which enlarge during pregnancy and lactation.
questions.question: What structure surrounds the nipple?
Which nerve root is predominantly tested by the biceps reflex?
questions.explanation: The biceps reflex predominantly tests the C6 nerve root, though C5 also contributes. The reflex is elicited by tapping the biceps tendon in the cubital fossa. Absence or diminution of this reflex suggests C6 nerve root or musculocutaneous nerve pathology.

questions.question: Which structure passes through the gastrosplenic ligament?
questions.explanation: The gastrosplenic ligament contains the short gastric vessels (arteries and veins, 4-6 pairs) passing from the splenic vessels near the hilum to the gastric fundus, and the left gastroepiploic vessels running to the greater curvature. The splenic artery, splenic vein, and tail of the pancreas run in the splenorenal ligament, not the gastrosplenic ligament. These two ligaments together connect the spleen to the stomach and posterior abdominal wall. Division of the gastrosplenic ligament is necessary during splenectomy, requiring ligation of the short gastric and left gastroepiploic vessels to devascularize the spleen.

The gastrosplenic ligament contains the short gastric vessels (4-6 small arteries and veins) that pass from the splenic vessels near the hilum to supply the gastric fundus, and the left gastroepiploic (gastro-omental) vessels that run along the greater curvature. The splenic artery and vein themselves course through the splenorenal ligament (along with the pancreatic tail), not the gastrosplenic ligament. During splenectomy, the gastrosplenic ligament is divided, requiring careful ligation of these vessels. The gastrosplenic ligament represents part of the dorsal mesogastrium and connects the greater curvature to the splenic hilum.
questions.question: Which structure lies in the free edge of the gastrosplenic ligament?
Which muscle is responsible for fine adjustments of vocal cord tension?
questions.explanation: The vocalis muscle, lying parallel and inferior to the vocal cord, controls fine adjustments of cord tension. The cricothyroid provides gross tension changes by tilting the thyroid cartilage. The vocalis can selectively tense different portions of the vocal cord for pitch modulation.

questions.question: What are the nerve roots of the long thoracic nerve?
questions.explanation: The long thoracic nerve arises from nerve roots C5, C6, and C7. It supplies the serratus anterior muscle with branches to each digitation. Injury to this nerve causes scapular winging, which becomes apparent when pushing against resistance.

questions.question: Which vessel lies in the gastrosplenic ligament?
questions.explanation: The gastrosplenic ligament, connecting the greater curvature of the stomach (fundus region) to the hilum of the spleen, contains the short gastric vessels (4-6 small arteries and veins from the splenic artery and vein). The left gastroepiploic vessels also pass through this ligament after arising from the splenic vessels near the hilum. The splenic artery and vein themselves run in the splenorenal ligament (along with the tail of the pancreas), not the gastrosplenic ligament. During splenectomy, the gastrosplenic ligament must be divided, ligating the short gastric and left gastroepiploic vessels.

The superior sagittal sinus drains posteriorly into the confluence of sinuses (torcular herophili) at the internal occipital protuberance. From here, blood typically flows into the right transverse sinus more than the left. The confluence also receives the straight sinus and occipital sinus.
questions.question: Which sinus receives blood from the superior sagittal sinus?

questions.explanation: The anterior intercostal arteries of the upper six spaces arise from the internal thoracic artery, which is a branch of the subclavian artery. These arteries anastomose with the posterior intercostal arteries. The internal thoracic artery descends behind the costal cartilages approximately half an inch from the lateral border of the sternum.
questions.question: Where do the upper six anterior intercostal arteries arise?

questions.explanation: The tibial nerve is the most superficial structure of the major neurovascular bundle in the popliteal fossa, bisecting the fossa from superior to inferior angle. The popliteal vein lies superficial to and close to the artery in the same fibrous sheath, while the popliteal artery is the deepest. The common fibular nerve exits at the superolateral angle.
questions.question: Which is the most superficial named structure of the major neurovascular bundle in the popliteal fossa?
What structure indents the apex of each renal pyramid?
questions.explanation: Each renal papilla (apex of a renal pyramid) is indented by a cup-shaped minor calyx that collects urine draining from the collecting ducts. There are typically 8-12 minor calyces per kidney. Two to three minor calyces unite to form a major calyx, and 2-3 major calyces join to form the renal pelvis.

The kidneys extend from approximately T12 to L3 vertebral levels, with the hilum positioned at the L1 level (transpyloric plane). The right kidney typically sits slightly lower than the left (by about half a vertebra) due to the presence of the liver superiorly. The upper poles are closer to the midline and are related to the diaphragm and ribs (left kidney: ribs 11-12; right kidney: rib 12), while the lower poles are further from the midline. The kidneys lie obliquely, with the upper poles more posterior and closer together than the lower poles.
questions.question: The kidney is located at which vertebral levels?
Where does the right vagus form plexus?
questions.explanation: The right vagus nerve descends to the right side of the trachea, forms the posterior esophageal plexus, and continues into the abdomen as the posterior gastric nerve. The left vagus descends between the left common carotid and left subclavian arteries, forms the anterior esophageal plexus, and continues as the anterior gastric nerve.

questions.question: Which bone contains the foramen rotundum?
questions.explanation: The foramen rotundum is located in the greater wing of the sphenoid bone, transmitting the maxillary nerve (V2). It connects the middle cranial fossa with the pterygopalatine fossa. The foramen is round in shape, distinguishing it from the oval foramen ovale.

The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve provides sensory innervation to the laryngeal mucosa above the vocal cords. It pierces the thyrohyoid membrane with the superior laryngeal vessels. Below the cords, sensation is provided by the recurrent laryngeal nerve. This sensory innervation triggers the cough reflex.
questions.question: Which structure provides the main sensory innervation to the larynx above the vocal cords?

questions.explanation: The appendicular artery arises from the ileocolic artery (the terminal branch of the superior mesenteric artery) and runs in the free margin of the mesoappendix to supply the vermiform appendix.
