questions.question: A patient with a suspected acute abdomen has a serum lipase requested rather than amylase alone. Compared with amylase, lipase offers which advantage in diagnosing acute pancreatitis?
options: Lower cost and wider availability in all settings
Greater specificity, remaining elevated for longer after symptom onset
Faster turnaround time in every laboratory
Complete elimination of false positive results
Ability to distinguish gallstone from alcohol-induced pancreatitis
questions.explanation: Serum lipase remains elevated for a longer duration after the onset of pancreatitis and is more specific to pancreatic injury than amylase, which can be elevated in numerous other non-pancreatic conditions such as salivary gland disease or bowel perforation. This makes lipase particularly useful when a patient presents several days after symptom onset, when amylase may have already normalised. Neither test, however, distinguishes the underlying cause of pancreatitis.

The 'double duct sign' of simultaneous dilatation of both the common bile duct and pancreatic duct on CT imaging is characteristic of a malignant pancreatic head or periampullary lesion obstructing both ducts. Ampullary carcinoma, duodenal carcinoma, and pancreatic adenocarcinoma should all be considered. EUS with FNA provides tissue diagnosis and staging.
questions.question: A 70-year-old woman has painless obstructive jaundice. CT shows a 2 cm periampullary mass with dilated CBD and pancreatic duct (double duct sign). This is MOST suggestive of:

options: SIRS criteria with confirmed infection and WBC above 12,000
Temperature above 39 degrees C with positive blood culture
Vasopressor-dependent sepsis with lactate above 2 mmol/L
Organ dysfunction with SOFA score increase of 1 or more
questions.question: Which of the following MOST accurately identifies septic shock per Sepsis-3 criteria?
questions.explanation: Sepsis-3 defines septic shock as sepsis with circulatory, cellular, and metabolic abnormalities sufficient to substantially increase mortality, operationally identified by need for vasopressors to maintain MAP 65 mmHg or above and serum lactate above 2 mmol/L after adequate fluid resuscitation. Hospital mortality exceeds 40%. The qSOFA score identifies high-risk sepsis outside the ICU.

questions.question: A patient presents with a right iliac fossa mass. On examination, the mass has positive Rovsing's sign, positive psoas sign, and can be indented with a finger but not fully grasped, described as a positive pointing sign. This is MOST consistent with:
options: A simple lipoma of the abdominal wall
A primary caecal carcinoma without inflammation
questions.explanation: The combination of positive Rovsing's, psoas, and pointing signs in the right iliac fossa strongly suggests an inflammatory appendiceal mass or abscess resulting from a walled-off perforated or inflamed appendix. Initial management is often conservative with antibiotics and interval appendicectomy, reserving immediate surgery for signs of generalised peritonitis. Recognising this clinical pattern avoids unnecessary early surgery in a densely adherent inflammatory mass.

Primary spinal curvatures, such as the thoracic and sacral kyphoses, are present from fetal life and persist into adulthood as part of the normal spinal contour, whereas secondary curvatures, such as the cervical and lumbar lordoses, develop later as the infant gains head control and begins to stand and walk. Recognising this distinction clarifies why thoracic kyphosis is a normal anatomical feature rather than an acquired postural abnormality. It also helps distinguish normal curvature from pathological exaggeration such as significant hyperkyphosis.
questions.question: A 30-year-old is told his thoracic kyphosis is a 'primary curvature' of the spine. What does this classification imply about its developmental origin?
options: It develops only after the child begins to walk
It is an abnormal curvature requiring surgical correction
It is present from fetal life and maintained through adulthood
It results from acquired postural habits in adulthood
It only appears after skeletal maturity is reached

questions.question: In Alzheimer's disease, which neurotransmitter system is most prominently degenerated, forming the basis for cholinergic therapy?
questions.explanation: Alzheimer's disease prominently degenerates the cholinergic neurons of the basal nucleus of Meynert (and other basal forebrain nuclei), which project widely to the cortex and hippocampus. Acetylcholine is critical for attention and memory encoding. Cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) are used to partially compensate for this cholinergic deficit, providing modest symptomatic benefit in mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease.

Heavy alcohol use increases risk of hepatic dysfunction, coagulopathy, and withdrawal, while cigarette smoking increases respiratory complications, wound infection rates, and cardiovascular risk. Both are modifiable risk factors that should be addressed in preoperative optimization.
questions.question: Which preoperative social history finding MOST significantly increases surgical and anesthetic risk?

questions.explanation: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma is one of the most aggressive human malignancies, characterised by rapid local invasion of surrounding structures such as the trachea and oesophagus, early distant metastasis, and a very poor prognosis measured in months rather than years, in stark contrast to the generally favourable long-term outcomes of differentiated papillary and follicular thyroid cancers. It typically occurs in older patients and does not concentrate iodine, making radioactive iodine therapy ineffective, unlike in differentiated thyroid cancer. Management is often palliative, focusing on airway protection and symptom control given the advanced stage at presentation in most cases.
options: Extremely aggressive local invasion with a very poor overall prognosis
A generally excellent long-term prognosis similar to papillary carcinoma
Slow growth over many years before becoming symptomatic
High responsiveness to radioactive iodine therapy
An association predominantly with young patients under 30 years
questions.question: A patient with anaplastic thyroid carcinoma presents with a rapidly enlarging, hard, fixed neck mass causing stridor and dysphagia. Compared with differentiated thyroid cancers, anaplastic carcinoma is characterised by:

questions.explanation: A hydrocele consists of clear serous fluid accumulated within the tunica vaginalis, and this fluid readily transmits light during transillumination, producing a characteristic glow that helps distinguish it clinically from solid masses such as a tumour, which do not transilluminate. Difficulty palpating the testis separately from the swelling is also typical of a large hydrocele surrounding it. Ultrasound is used to confirm the diagnosis and exclude an underlying testicular abnormality, particularly in cases of rapid onset or atypical features.
options: The testis itself is highly translucent to light in all patients
Hydroceles always contain blood, which enhances transillumination
Transillumination indicates the presence of a solid tumour
The fluid within the sac is clear and allows light to pass through readily
This finding is specific only to malignant scrotal masses
questions.question: A patient with a large hydrocele is examined and found to transilluminate brightly, with the testis not separately palpable. This transillumination occurs because:
Port site hernias following laparoscopic surgery most commonly occur at ports of what minimum diameter?
options: Only at the umbilical port regardless of size
questions.explanation: Port site hernias occur predominantly at ports of 10 mm or larger diameter, particularly when the fascial defect is not closed at the end of the procedure. The umbilical port is especially vulnerable due to the thinner fascia and pre-existing weakness. Current recommendations mandate fascial closure of all ports 10 mm or larger. Smaller 5 mm ports rarely cause hernias and do not require fascial closure routinely.

questions.question: A patient with 25 percent burns sustained three weeks ago now has a wound that has failed to heal, with a rolled, indurated edge. This finding is MOST suggestive of:
options: Normal delayed wound healing without concern
Marjolin's ulcer developing in a chronic burn wound
Simple wound infection requiring antibiotics alone
Keloid scar formation at the site
questions.explanation: A chronic non-healing burn wound with an indurated, rolled edge raises concern for malignant transformation, known as Marjolin's ulcer, which typically arises in long-standing burn scars or chronic wounds. Biopsy of the wound edge is required to confirm the diagnosis. Early recognition is important as this represents an aggressive form of squamous cell carcinoma.

Refeeding syndrome occurs when malnourished patients resume nutrition and intracellular uptake of phosphate with insulin release depletes serum phosphate, causing neuromuscular dysfunction, cardiac arrhythmias, and respiratory failure. Prophylaxis involves gradual caloric introduction and phosphate supplementation. Ophthalmopathy with hypophosphataemia in TPN patients distinguishes refeeding syndrome from other TPN complications.
options: Central pontine myelinolysis from sodium correction
questions.question: A post-operative patient on TPN develops confusion, fatigue, and bilateral ophthalmopathy. Serum phosphate is 0.3 mmol/L. The MOST likely diagnosis is:

questions.explanation: Penetrating head injuries require surgical wound debridement to remove contaminated tissue, bone fragments, and the offending object (when surgically accessible), combined with decompression and haematoma evacuation when present. Copious irrigation reduces infection risk. The primary goals are haemostasis, infection prevention, and decompression of neural structures. Prophylactic antibiotics and anticonvulsants are also administered.
questions.question: In penetrating head injuries (e.g., gunshot wounds), which surgical procedure is specifically indicated?
options: External ventricular drain in all cases

questions.question: Phaeochromocytoma is characterised by the triad of episodic headache, sweating, and palpitations. The MOST appropriate preoperative pharmacological preparation is:
options: Beta-blocker alone to control heart rate
Alpha-blocker first followed by beta-blocker if needed
Combined alpha and beta blockade started simultaneously
questions.explanation: Alpha-blockade with phenoxybenzamine must precede beta-blockade in phaeochromocytoma to prevent hypertensive crisis from unopposed alpha-adrenergic stimulation if beta-blockade is given alone. Beta-blockers are added only after adequate alpha-blockade is established to control reflex tachycardia. This sequence is mandatory to prevent perioperative cardiovascular crises.

questions.question: After a deep needlestick injury from a high HBV viral load source, the MOST important immediate action is:
options: Flush wound, assess exposure, initiate PEP
Apply iodine to the wound and bandage
Report and observe for 6 months without treatment
questions.explanation: Following a needlestick injury, the wound should be flushed immediately with flowing water. Both the healthcare worker and source patient should be tested. For HBV with high viral load: hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG) and HBV vaccination should be given. HIV PEP uses a 2-3 drug combination for 4 weeks.

questions.question: A patient with a suspected malignant ulcer on clinical examination has a lesion with an everted, rolled edge, an irregular base, and induration on palpation. Compared with a simple traumatic ulcer, this combination of features is important because it:
options: Suggests infiltrative tumour growth requiring urgent biopsy to exclude malignancy
Confirms the lesion is definitely benign without any further testing needed
Indicates a purely inflammatory process requiring only topical treatment
Is a typical feature of an uncomplicated pressure ulcer
Excludes the possibility of any underlying malignancy
questions.explanation: An everted, rolled edge together with induration and an irregular base reflects infiltrative growth of tumour tissue at the margin of an ulcer, a pattern strongly suggestive of malignancy such as squamous cell carcinoma, in contrast to the punched-out or sloping edges more typical of ischaemic or traumatic ulcers respectively. Any ulcer demonstrating these features on examination warrants prompt biopsy to confirm or exclude malignancy before committing to a purely conservative management plan. Early recognition and biopsy are important to avoid delay in diagnosing and treating an underlying skin malignancy.

The 'finger test', in which a gloved finger easily dissects along the fascial plane with minimal resistance and a lack of normal bleeding, is a characteristic intraoperative finding confirming the diagnosis of necrotising fasciitis and helping define the extent of tissue requiring debridement. This finding, along with the dishwater-coloured foul discharge, guides the surgeon on where healthy tissue begins. Aggressive debridement of all affected fascia is essential, often requiring repeated procedures.
questions.question: A patient with necrotising fasciitis undergoes surgical debridement. Intraoperative findings of a dull grey fascia with minimal bleeding and a foul-smelling discharge, with the ability to easily separate skin from underlying fascia using a finger, is termed:

options: A normal expected finding after any thyroid surgery
Coexisting papillary thyroid carcinoma unrelated to calcitonin
Laboratory error requiring no further action
Successful cure with no further surveillance needed
Residual or metastatic disease not fully cleared by surgery
questions.question: A patient with medullary thyroid carcinoma has an elevated serum calcitonin level postoperatively that fails to normalise after apparently complete resection. This finding suggests:
questions.explanation: Calcitonin is a sensitive tumour marker specifically produced by the parafollicular C cells from which medullary thyroid carcinoma arises, and a persistently elevated postoperative level suggests residual local or metastatic disease rather than complete surgical cure. Serial calcitonin measurement is therefore used for long-term surveillance after treatment. Further imaging is typically undertaken to localise any residual or recurrent disease when calcitonin remains elevated.

options: Squamous cell carcinoma at the mid-thoracic oesophagus
Small cell carcinoma of the lower oesophagus
Mucoepidermoid carcinoma of the cervical oesophagus
questions.question: The MOST common histological type of oesophageal cancer in Western countries has shifted over recent decades to:
questions.explanation: Over the past three decades, adenocarcinoma of the lower oesophagus and gastro-oesophageal junction has overtaken squamous cell carcinoma in Western countries, driven by rising rates of obesity, gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, and Barrett's oesophagus. Squamous cell carcinoma still predominates globally and in developing nations. Barrett's oesophagus surveillance aims to detect dysplasia before invasive cancer develops.

options: Have no effect on the rate or degree of bleeding
Dislodge early clot formation and worsen ongoing haemorrhage
Guarantee improved outcomes in all trauma patients
Always be preferred over any surgical intervention
Eliminate the need for blood product transfusion entirely
questions.explanation: Restoring blood pressure to normal levels before surgical or other definitive control of bleeding can dislodge early, fragile clot formation at the site of vascular injury, increasing ongoing blood loss and diluting clotting factors; permissive hypotension aims to maintain organ perfusion at a lower target pressure until haemorrhage is controlled. This strategy is generally avoided in patients with traumatic brain injury, where adequate cerebral perfusion pressure takes priority. It represents a balance between preventing exsanguination and maintaining vital organ perfusion.
questions.question: A trauma patient is resuscitated using a permissive hypotension strategy prior to definitive haemorrhage control. The rationale for this approach is that aggressive normalisation of blood pressure before bleeding is controlled may:

questions.explanation: Anterior cervical disc arthroplasty (disc replacement) is specifically designed to treat cervical radiculopathy via an anterior approach while preserving motion at the operated segment, unlike anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) which eliminates motion. Preserving motion theoretically reduces adjacent segment disease risk. ACDF remains the gold standard but arthroplasty is gaining acceptance for single-level disease.
questions.question: Which surgical technique is specifically designed for cervical radiculopathy via an anterior approach, preserving motion?

questions.explanation: A pyogenic granuloma (lobular capillary haemangioma) is a rapidly growing, soft, vascular, benign tumour of the skin or mucosa that bleeds profusely on minor trauma. Despite the name, it is not purulent or truly granulomatous but represents a reactive exuberant fibrovascular proliferation often triggered by minor trauma, hormonal changes, or medication. Treatment is excision or laser ablation, and histological confirmation is important to exclude amelanotic melanoma.
options: A hard, painless swelling arising from the bone
Soft, vascular, fast-growing mass that bleeds easily
A firm, non-tender lymph node in the groin
A slow-growing infiltrative mass of the dermis
questions.question: A pyogenic granuloma is characterised by which clinical appearance?
The MOST common congenital anomaly of the biliary tract causing neonatal jaundice is:
questions.explanation: Biliary atresia is the most common congenital biliary tract abnormality and the leading indication for liver transplantation in children, characterised by progressive obliteration of extrahepatic bile ducts causing obstructive jaundice within the first weeks of life. Kasai hepatoportoenterostomy performed before 60 days of age offers the best chance of biliary drainage. Untreated, biliary cirrhosis develops within the first 2 years.
options: Alagille syndrome with bile duct paucity
Caroli's disease with intrahepatic ductal dilatation
Spontaneous perforation of the common bile duct

questions.question: A patient with aneurysmal SAH is at risk for cerebral vasospasm. This complication typically occurs in which time window after the initial bleed?
options: More than 3 weeks after the bleed
questions.explanation: Cerebral vasospasm is a major complication of aneurysmal SAH, typically occurring between days 4–14 after the initial bleed, peaking around day 7. It is caused by haemoglobin degradation products causing smooth muscle contraction in cerebral arteries. Vasospasm leads to delayed cerebral ischaemia and infarction. Treatment includes nimodipine, hypertensive hypervolaemic haemodilution (Triple H therapy), and endovascular vasodilation.

A markedly elevated alkaline phosphatase and gamma-GT in proportion to the bilirubin rise reflects a cholestatic or obstructive pattern of liver function tests, typically from biliary obstruction such as gallstones or a periampullary tumour. This differs from a predominantly hepatocellular pattern, where transaminases would be disproportionately elevated relative to alkaline phosphatase. Further imaging of the biliary tree is indicated to identify the level and cause of obstruction.
questions.question: A patient with jaundice has bilirubin 250 micromol/L, alkaline phosphatase 800 IU/L, and markedly elevated gamma-GT. This biochemical pattern is MOST consistent with:

questions.explanation: Postoperative pulmonary embolism most commonly arises from deep vein thrombosis (DVT) in the lower extremities. Virchow's triad (stasis, hypercoagulability, endothelial injury) explains the high DVT risk postoperatively. Prophylaxis with LMWH, stockings, and early mobilization is essential.
questions.question: Postoperative pulmonary embolism most commonly arises from:
options: Air embolism from IV line insertion
Deep vein thrombosis in lower extremities
Fat emboli from long bone fractures

questions.explanation: Anticoagulation (low molecular weight heparin, later transitioned to warfarin or direct oral anticoagulants) in spinal cord injury is primarily indicated for DVT prophylaxis and prevention of fatal pulmonary embolism, which are major causes of mortality in the subacute phase. The decision must balance bleeding risk (especially in acute cord injury) against thrombotic risk, with guidelines recommending initiation within 72 hours of injury when haemostasis is assured.
questions.question: The purpose of anticoagulation in spinal cord injury patients is primarily to prevent:

questions.explanation: Tetanospasmin, the toxin produced by Clostridium tetani, travels retrogradely along peripheral nerves to the spinal cord, where it blocks the release of inhibitory neurotransmitters such as glycine and GABA, resulting in unopposed excitatory input and the characteristic sustained muscle rigidity and spasms of tetanus. Management includes wound debridement, tetanus immunoglobulin to neutralise circulating toxin, antibiotics, and supportive care for muscle spasms and potential respiratory compromise. Prevention through appropriate immunisation and wound management remains far more effective than treating established disease.
options: Blocking inhibitory neurotransmitter release in the spinal cord, causing unopposed muscle contraction
Directly damaging muscle fibres through toxin-mediated myonecrosis
Producing a peripheral neuropathy that abolishes all muscle tone
Causing widespread haemolysis leading to secondary muscle ischaemia
Triggering an autoimmune attack on the neuromuscular junction
questions.question: A patient with tetanus following a deep, contaminated puncture wound develops generalised muscle rigidity and spasms. The toxin responsible for these clinical features acts primarily by:

options: Hypotonic dehydration from excessive fluid replacement
Hypertonic dehydration from pure water loss
questions.question: Regarding dehydration in surgical patients, which type can occur DESPITE adequate total body sodium?
questions.explanation: Hypertonic (hypernatraemic) dehydration results from pure water loss without sodium loss, as in diabetes insipidus or inadequate water intake. Total body sodium may be near normal while total body water is depleted, making plasma sodium disproportionately elevated. Replacement uses hypotonic solutions (D5W) unless hypotension is present.

options: Smooth tapering narrowing of the distal oesophagus with proximal dilatation
An irregular filling defect at the gastro-oesophageal junction
Multiple small diverticula along the oesophageal body
A shouldered stricture with mucosal ulceration
A sudden abrupt cut-off with rat-tail deformity
questions.question: A patient with achalasia undergoes barium swallow. The classic radiological finding described as a 'bird's beak' represents:
questions.explanation: The 'bird's beak' sign on barium swallow reflects smooth, symmetrical tapering of the lower oesophageal sphincter that fails to relax, with marked dilatation of the oesophageal body proximal to this point. This appearance results from the aperistalsis and failed relaxation characteristic of achalasia. It is distinct from the irregular, shouldered narrowing typical of malignant strictures.

Mutations in mismatch repair genes such as MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, and PMS2 underlie Lynch syndrome, which predisposes to early-onset colorectal cancer, often right-sided, as well as endometrial and other extracolonic malignancies. This differs from familial adenomatous polyposis, which results from APC gene mutations and produces innumerable colonic polyps. Genetic testing and tailored surveillance protocols are recommended for affected families.
questions.question: A patient with a strong family history of colorectal cancer is found to have germline mutation in the MLH1 gene. This mismatch repair gene defect is associated with which condition?

options: A malignant ulcer with everted edges
A tuberculous ulcer with undermined edges
A syphilitic ulcer with punched-out edges
A rodent ulcer with rolled edges
questions.explanation: A sloping edge with granulation tissue at the base typically indicates a healing ulcer, commonly seen in venous ulcers as they progress toward resolution. This contrasts with everted edges seen in malignancy, undermined edges in tuberculosis, and rolled edges characteristic of basal cell carcinoma. Assessing the edge is a key part of systematic ulcer examination that aids differential diagnosis.
questions.question: A patient's ulcer is examined and the base is found to contain granulation tissue with a sloping edge. This edge type is MOST characteristic of:

questions.explanation: A positive sentinel lymph node in breast cancer generally prompts further axillary management, which may involve completion axillary dissection or axillary radiotherapy depending on tumour characteristics and specific clinical trial-based protocols, aiming to control regional disease while minimising morbidity. The specific approach has evolved with evidence showing that not all patients with limited sentinel node involvement require full dissection. This decision is individualised based on tumour burden and other clinicopathological factors.
questions.question: A 45-year-old woman with a 2.5 cm painless breast lump undergoes triple assessment confirming malignancy. Sentinel lymph node biopsy is positive. The MOST appropriate next step regarding the axilla is:
options: No further axillary treatment is required regardless of findings
Completion axillary lymph node dissection or further axillary staging based on protocol
Immediate bilateral mastectomy without axillary consideration
Axillary radiotherapy is always contraindicated in this scenario
Observation of the axilla without any further intervention

questions.question: Alkali burns cause which type of tissue necrosis?
questions.explanation: Alkali burns (NaOH, NH3OH, cement) cause liquefactive necrosis, which is more penetrating and progressive than coagulative necrosis from acid burns. Liquefactive necrosis allows continued tissue penetration as the alkali saponifies cell membranes, making alkali burns potentially more dangerous.

questions.question: A child with Burkitt's lymphoma affecting the jaw is noted to have a very high tumour proliferation rate. Before starting chemotherapy, the patient is at particular risk of which metabolic emergency due to rapid tumour cell turnover?
questions.explanation: Burkitt's lymphoma has one of the highest proliferation rates of any human malignancy, and the rapid destruction of tumour cells, particularly once chemotherapy begins, releases large quantities of intracellular potassium, phosphate, and nucleic acids that are metabolised to uric acid, precipitating tumour lysis syndrome with life-threatening electrolyte disturbances and acute kidney injury. Prophylactic measures, including aggressive hydration and urate-lowering therapy, are instituted before and during initial treatment to reduce this risk. Close monitoring of renal function and electrolytes is essential in the initial treatment phase.
options: Diabetic ketoacidosis unrelated to the malignancy
Tumour lysis syndrome with hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia, and hyperuricaemia
Simple dehydration without any electrolyte disturbance
Presence of yellowish sulfur granules within the pus
Presence of clear serous fluid without particulate matter
questions.question: A patient develops a chronic draining sinus after inadequately treated actinomycosis of the abdominal wall following a previous appendicectomy. The MOST characteristic feature that would help confirm this diagnosis on examination of the discharge is:
questions.explanation: Sulfur granules, which are macroscopic colonies of the filamentous actinomycete organisms bound by host inflammatory material, are a classic and highly suggestive finding in the discharge from actinomycosis sinus tracts. Their presence helps distinguish actinomycosis from other causes of chronic discharging sinuses. Microscopic examination of these granules can reveal the characteristic branching filaments of the organism.

questions.question: A patient develops pseudomembranous colitis after prolonged antibiotic use. The CAUSATIVE organism is MOST likely:
questions.explanation: Clostridium difficile overgrows following disruption of normal bowel flora by antibiotics and produces toxins A and B causing pseudomembranous colitis. Clindamycin, fluoroquinolones, and broad-spectrum cephalosporins carry the highest risk. Treatment involves metronidazole or oral vancomycin, with fidaxomicin for recurrent disease.

Severe malnutrition impairs immune defences primarily by reducing neutrophil chemotaxis, phagocytic capacity, and lymphocyte proliferation, leading to increased susceptibility to opportunistic infections and wound complications. Micronutrient deficiencies (zinc, vitamins A, C, E) further compromise both innate and adaptive immunity. Preoperative nutritional optimisation is therefore a key component of surgical risk reduction.
questions.question: Severe malnutrition in surgical patients impairs immune function by which primary mechanism?
Formaldehyde (formalin) is considered more hazardous than other disinfectants primarily because it is:
questions.explanation: Formaldehyde (formalin) is classified as a known carcinogen and is a significant skin, eye, and respiratory irritant. It should not be used without good local exhaust ventilation. Despite these hazards, it can be used for equipment surface disinfection at 4-8% concentration.
options: A known carcinogen and respiratory irritant
Unable to penetrate medical device surfaces

questions.question: A patient develops faecal peritonitis following colonic perforation. Compared with peritonitis from a perforated peptic ulcer, faecal peritonitis carries a worse prognosis mainly because:
options: Faecal fluid is more acidic than gastric contents
Colonic perforations are always missed on initial examination
Faecal peritonitis never presents with generalised rigidity
The higher bacterial load and toxin content produce more severe septic response
Colonic bacteria are uniformly resistant to all antibiotics
questions.explanation: Colonic content carries an extremely high concentration of bacteria, including anaerobes, together with their toxins, producing a more severe and rapidly progressive septic response than the initially chemical, low-bacterial-load peritonitis from an upper gastrointestinal perforation. This higher bacterial burden increases the risk of septic shock and multi-organ failure. Aggressive source control and broad-spectrum antibiotics are therefore essential.

questions.question: A patient with tuberculous peritonitis is noted to have markedly elevated CA-125 levels alongside ascites, raising initial suspicion for ovarian malignancy. The explanation for this finding is:
options: CA-125 elevation is pathognomonic for ovarian cancer and excludes tuberculosis
CA-125 is a non-specific marker that can be elevated by peritoneal inflammation from any cause, including tuberculosis
Tuberculosis never causes any elevation in tumour markers
CA-125 is only produced by malignant peritoneal cells
This finding definitively confirms coexisting ovarian malignancy
questions.explanation: CA-125 is produced by irritated or inflamed peritoneal and pleural mesothelial cells and can therefore be significantly elevated in benign inflammatory conditions such as tuberculous peritonitis, not just in ovarian or other malignancies, making it a non-specific marker in the context of ascites. This overlap can lead to diagnostic confusion and unnecessary investigation for malignancy if not appropriately contextualised. Definitive diagnosis relies on ascitic fluid analysis, imaging, and where necessary tissue biopsy rather than CA-125 alone.

ARDS is defined by PaO2/FiO2 ratio below 200, bilateral pulmonary infiltrates on chest X-ray, and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure below 18 mmHg excluding cardiogenic oedema. It results from non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema following direct or indirect lung injury. Lung-protective ventilation with low tidal volumes is the cornerstone of treatment.
options: PaO2/FiO2 > 400, bilateral infiltrates, no heart failure
Unilateral infiltrate with hypoxia and fever
PaO2/FiO2 < 300 with elevated pulmonary wedge pressure
Consolidation on CXR responsive to diuresis
questions.question: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) following major trauma is BEST characterised by which combination?

questions.explanation: Sister Mary Joseph's nodule (umbilical metastasis) most commonly arises from gastric carcinoma (20%), followed by ovarian, colonic, and pancreatic primaries. The metastasis occurs via direct peritoneal spread, lymphatics of the round ligament, or haematogenous routes. Its presence indicates advanced disease with peritoneal dissemination. It was first described by surgical nurse Sister Mary Joseph Dempsey who noted it preoperatively.
options: Gastric, pancreatic, ovarian, and colorectal carcinomas
Renal cell carcinoma and retroperitoneal sarcoma
questions.question: Sister Mary Joseph's nodule is an umbilical metastatic nodule. It most commonly arises from which primary sites?
The optimal temperature for low-temperature autoclaving is:
questions.explanation: Low-temperature autoclaving operates at 121°C at 103 kPa for 15-30 minutes. High-temperature autoclaving uses 132°C at 206.8 kPa for 8-10 minutes or 134°C at 206.8 kPa for 3-6 minutes. Prevention of entrapped air is critical to achieving sterility.

questions.question: A newborn has a midline occipital swelling containing brain tissue and meninges herniating through a skull defect, confirmed on imaging. Which cranial neural tube defect is this?
questions.explanation: An encephalocele is a cranial neural tube defect in which brain tissue and meninges herniate through a defect in the skull, most commonly occipitally in Western populations, and its associated neurological outcome depends on the amount and location of herniated neural tissue. This differs from anencephaly, where the cranial vault and much of the brain fail to develop at all rather than herniating through an otherwise formed skull. Surgical repair aims to reduce herniated contents where feasible and close the skull defect.

Posterior cord syndrome involves damage to the posterior columns, producing loss of vibration sense and proprioception (joint position sense) below the level of the lesion, with relatively preserved motor function and pain/temperature sensation. It is the rarest incomplete cord syndrome and may result from posterior spinal artery occlusion, vitamin B12 deficiency, or posterior cord contusion.
questions.question: Posterior cord syndrome produces which specific sensory deficit?
options: Loss of pain and temperature with preserved position sense
Loss of all sensation below the lesion level
Loss of crude touch with preserved fine touch
Loss of vibration and proprioception; motor preserved
Loss of motor function with intact sensory modalities

questions.explanation: A sliding hernia is defined as one where a retroperitoneal viscus forms part of the wall of the hernial sac, rather than being contained within it. Common viscera involved include the caecum and appendix on the right and the sigmoid colon and bladder on the left. This is surgically important because inadvertent division of the sliding component during herniorrhaphy can injure the bowel or bladder.
options: The hernia reduces spontaneously during recumbency
The hernia sac slides along the spermatic cord
The hernia slides from the inguinal to the femoral region
The hernia is reducible only with the patient standing
A viscus forms part of the hernial sac wall
questions.question: A sliding inguinal hernia is one where:

questions.explanation: Burns >10% TBSA in children below 10 years (or >50 years) require burn unit admission. Indications also include burns >20% TBSA at any age, full-thickness burns >5% TBSA, inhalational burns, special area burns (face, hands, genitals), associated trauma, or significant comorbidities.
options: Small superficial burn in a young adult
Minor scald to the forearm in a healthy adult
Small chemical burn to the fingernail
questions.question: Which burns presentation requires burn unit admission?
Gastric carcinoma most commonly metastasises to the liver by which route?
options: Haematogenous spread via the hepatic artery
Direct extension through the lesser omentum
questions.explanation: Hepatic metastases from gastric carcinoma most commonly occur via portal venous spread — cancer cells enter the mesenteric and portal venous system, reaching the liver. This mirrors the pattern seen in colorectal carcinoma. Transcoelomic spread (peritoneal metastases, Krukenberg tumours) and lymphatic spread also occur but represent separate metastatic pathways.

Eaton-Lambert syndrome is a paraneoplastic condition almost always associated with small-cell lung carcinoma (SCLC). Antibodies against voltage-gated calcium channels at the presynaptic motor nerve terminal are produced as a paraneoplastic immune response to SCLC. The diagnosis of Eaton-Lambert may precede detection of the underlying carcinoma by up to two years, making thorough malignancy workup essential.
questions.question: Eaton-Lambert syndrome is most commonly associated (nearly always) with which malignancy?

options: Remains confined within the original boundaries of the wound
Extends well beyond the original wound margins
Never regresses or improves with time
Occurs only in individuals with darker skin pigmentation
Is more common in surgical wounds than in burns
questions.explanation: A hypertrophic scar remains raised but stays within the confines of the original wound, and it often improves gradually over months to years, whereas a keloid extends beyond the original wound margins and rarely regresses spontaneously. Both differ in their underlying collagen turnover, with keloids showing continued excessive collagen production. Recognising this distinction is important for counselling patients on expected scar behaviour and treatment options.
questions.question: A patient with a clean surgical wound develops a hypertrophic scar rather than a keloid. Compared with keloid formation, a hypertrophic scar characteristically:
Regarding portal hypertension, which condition MOST commonly causes presinusoidal block in sub-Saharan Africa?
options: Hepatocellular carcinoma with portal vein thrombosis
Budd-Chiari syndrome from hepatic vein thrombosis
questions.explanation: Schistosomiasis is the most common cause of pre-sinusoidal portal hypertension in endemic regions including sub-Saharan Africa, caused by periportal fibrosis (Symmers' pipe-stem fibrosis) from egg deposition, obstructing portal venous flow before the sinusoids. Hepatic synthetic function is relatively preserved until late, distinguishing it from cirrhotic portal hypertension. Praziquantel is the treatment for active infection.

questions.question: Which investigation is NOT routinely indicated in the initial workup of lumbar disc prolapse?
questions.explanation: Epidural venography is rarely used and not part of the routine initial workup for lumbar disc prolapse. Standard investigations include plain radiographs for bony alignment, MRI for disc and neural characterisation, CT scan as an alternative, and electromyography to assess nerve function. Epidural venography was historically used but has been largely replaced by MRI.

options: Cervical myelopathy always presents with severe neck pain as the dominant symptom
Myelopathy can progress insidiously without significant neck pain as a presenting feature
Absence of neck pain excludes cervical spine pathology entirely
Painless presentations are always psychogenic in origin
Cord signal change on imaging is always an incidental, clinically insignificant finding
questions.explanation: Cervical spondylotic myelopathy often progresses insidiously over months to years and can present predominantly with subtle functional changes such as hand clumsiness and gait disturbance, sometimes with minimal or no significant neck pain, which can lead to diagnostic delay if pain is mistakenly considered a necessary presenting feature. Absence of pain does not exclude significant underlying spinal cord compression, and cord signal change on MRI is a clinically significant finding reflecting cord injury rather than an incidental one. Recognising that myelopathy can be a painless, insidious process is important for maintaining clinical suspicion in patients presenting primarily with functional decline.
questions.question: A patient develops progressive difficulty with fine hand coordination and gait but denies any neck pain. Imaging reveals significant cervical canal stenosis with cord signal change. What does this painless presentation illustrate about cervical myelopathy?

options: Step-ladder fluid levels in central small bowel
Distended large bowel with intact haustrations at the periphery
Gasless abdomen with multiple soft tissue densities
Single dilated loop with an obvious transition point
Uniform dilatation of both small and large bowel throughout
questions.question: Which of the following findings on plain abdominal X-ray is MOST consistent with paralytic ileus rather than mechanical obstruction?
questions.explanation: Paralytic ileus causes generalised, uniform dilatation of both small and large bowel without a transition point, because the entire gut is hypomotile. Mechanical obstruction typically shows distended bowel proximal to a transition point with normal or collapsed bowel distally. Step-ladder fluid levels suggest mechanical small bowel obstruction.

questions.question: Which of the following conditions is MOST likely to cause hyponatremia with a urine sodium greater than 20 mEq/L?
questions.explanation: SIADH causes euvolemic hyponatremia with inappropriately concentrated urine and elevated urine sodium above 20 mEq/L. In contrast, edematous states like heart failure and cirrhosis retain sodium avidly, resulting in urine sodium below 20 mEq/L. This distinction is critical for management.

questions.question: The MOST recently recognised nosocomial pathogen among the following list is:
questions.explanation: Legionella pneumophila was identified as a nosocomial pathogen within the past two decades and primarily causes Legionnaire's disease through contaminated water sources such as hospital cooling towers and shower systems. Unlike the other listed organisms, it is a newly recognised healthcare-associated pathogen. Adequate building water management is essential for prevention.

questions.question: A patient with ascites of unknown cause undergoes diagnostic paracentesis. A polymorphonuclear leukocyte count in the ascitic fluid above 250 cells per microlitre is diagnostic of:
options: Simple transudative ascites from cirrhosis alone
questions.explanation: An ascitic fluid polymorphonuclear leukocyte count exceeding 250 cells per microlitre is the standard diagnostic threshold for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, a condition typically occurring in patients with underlying cirrhotic ascites in the absence of an identifiable surgical source of infection. Prompt recognition allows early empirical antibiotic therapy, which significantly reduces mortality. This threshold is used regardless of whether ascitic fluid culture is positive, since culture sensitivity is imperfect.

The prefix 'hepat-' refers to the liver in surgical nomenclature. Knowledge of surgical prefixes is essential for understanding procedural names. 'Cardio-' refers to the heart, and 'nephr-' refers to the kidney.
questions.question: The prefix 'hepat-' in surgical nomenclature refers to:

questions.explanation: In the American classification, third-degree burns involve the reticular dermis (extending through the entire dermis), corresponding to deep partial thickness burns in the English classification. Fourth-degree extends beyond the dermis. This differs from the English system which uses partial and full thickness.
questions.question: In the American classification of burns, a third-degree burn involves:

questions.explanation: Priapism in sickle cell disease is a urological emergency due to the risk of irreversible corporal fibrosis and erectile dysfunction if untreated, requiring prompt aspiration and irrigation of the corpora cavernosa alongside hydration, analgesia, and sometimes exchange transfusion. Delay significantly worsens the prognosis for erectile function. Circumcision has no role in the acute management of priapism.
questions.question: A young man with sickle cell disease presents with a painful sustained penile erection lasting over four hours unrelated to sexual activity. The MOST appropriate immediate management is:
options: Reassurance and observation for one day
Ice packs alone, with no other treatment
Oral analgesia with review in one week
Eyes maintained in neutral position on opening
questions.explanation: In pseudocoma (functional unresponsiveness), when the examiner opens the patient's eyes, they snap shut rapidly initially then slow, or may resist opening, unlike true coma where eyes remain passive. True coma patients maintain eyes in a neutral position and do not swallow, with absent corneal reflexes in deep coma. Normal vital signs alone can occur in both states.
questions.question: In an unconscious patient, which finding most strongly suggests pseudocoma rather than true organic coma?

questions.explanation: Scrofula refers to tuberculous cervical lymphadenitis, where TB spreads from the tonsils to the cervical lymph nodes. A characteristic feature is the 'collar stud' abscess, where pus tracks through the deep cervical fascia and points to the skin surface. It was historically common in children exposed to bovine TB.
options: Cervical tuberculosis with collar stud abscess
questions.question: Scrofula refers to which manifestation of tuberculosis?

questions.explanation: Dermatomyositis is distinguished from polymyositis by the presence of characteristic cutaneous manifestations: the heliotrope rash (violaceous discolouration of the eyelids), Gottron's papules (erythematous scaly papules over the knuckles), V-sign (chest rash), and shawl sign (upper back rash). Both conditions share proximal muscle weakness, elevated CK, autoimmune pathogenesis, and an association with malignancy.
questions.question: Dermatomyositis is distinguished from polymyositis by the presence of which additional feature?

options: High-flow oxygen and reassess in 4 hours
Early orotracheal intubation before oedema develops
questions.explanation: Signs of inhalation injury including soot, singed hairs, and stridor indicate progressive airway oedema that can rapidly cause complete obstruction. Early orotracheal intubation before oedema develops is the safest approach while the airway is still accessible. Delay significantly increases the difficulty and risk of intubation.
questions.question: A burn patient has soot in the airway and singed nasal hairs. The MOST appropriate airway management is:

options: Does not require CO2 insufflation at all
Is only used for morbidly obese patients
Uses a spring-loaded needle to enter the cavity blindly
Larger incision with blunt dissection to the peritoneum
questions.explanation: The Hasson technique involves a small incision, dissecting through fascia and peritoneum under direct vision using blunt dissection, then inserting a blunt-tipped cannula under guidance. It avoids blind entry risk and is preferred in patients with previous abdominal surgery, suspected pathology, or morbid obesity. Once the cannula is placed, CO2 insufflation proceeds as normal.
questions.question: The Hasson (open) technique for laparoscopic port insertion differs from the Veress needle technique in that it:

questions.explanation: Pulsus alternans, characterised by alternating strong and weak pulses at a regular rate, reflects severe left ventricular dysfunction where consecutive beats generate different stroke volumes due to incomplete myocardial recovery. It indicates a critically reduced ventricular contractile reserve. It must be distinguished from pulsus paradoxus, seen in tamponade, which varies with respiration.
options: Complete heart block with variable AV conduction
Atrial fibrillation with irregular ventricular rate
Aortic stenosis with gradient variation on exertion
LV dysfunction with alternating stroke volumes
questions.question: Pulsus alternans in severe heart failure indicates:

options: Direct tissue biopsy of any lesion identified during the scan itself
Complete avoidance of any radiation exposure to the patient
Assessment limited exclusively to the bladder, excluding the upper tracts
Simultaneous assessment of the renal parenchyma, collecting system, and ureters in a single study
Real-time functional assessment of detrusor muscle contraction
questions.explanation: CT urography combines cross-sectional imaging of the renal parenchyma with delayed excretory phase images of the collecting systems and ureters, allowing comprehensive evaluation of the entire urinary tract for filling defects, masses, or obstruction in a single examination. This makes it particularly useful for detecting upper tract urothelial tumours, which can be missed on ultrasound alone. Biopsy of any identified lesion still requires a separate procedure such as ureteroscopy with biopsy.
questions.question: A patient with a suspected upper tract urothelial tumour undergoes CT urography as the investigation of choice. This modality is preferred because it allows:

options: Direct systemic absorption providing therapeutic drug levels
Sterilising the peritoneal cavity completely of all organisms
Replacing the need for systemic antibiotic therapy entirely
Mechanical dilution and removal of bacterial load and debris
Preventing all future intra-abdominal adhesion formation
questions.explanation: Peritoneal irrigation works mainly through mechanical dilution and physical removal of bacteria, debris, and inflammatory mediators from the peritoneal cavity, reducing the overall bacterial burden rather than achieving sterilisation through direct antimicrobial action alone. It is used as an adjunct to, not a replacement for, systemic antibiotic therapy in the management of peritonitis. Copious irrigation is a standard component of source control in contaminated abdominal surgery.
questions.question: Large-volume dilute antibiotic irrigation of the peritoneal cavity during surgery for peritonitis achieves its effect PRIMARILY by:

options: Haemolytic jaundice from red cell destruction
Obstructive jaundice from extrahepatic biliary obstruction
questions.explanation: A predominantly conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with disproportionately elevated alkaline phosphatase and gamma-GT in the presence of relatively normal transaminases is the biochemical signature of obstructive (cholestatic) jaundice. Ultrasound and MRCP are the primary imaging investigations. Common causes include choledocholithiasis, pancreatic head carcinoma, and cholangiocarcinoma.
questions.question: A patient with jaundice has a bilirubin of 250 micromol/L, alkaline phosphatase 800 IU/L, and gamma-GT 900 IU/L with normal transaminases. This pattern is MOST consistent with:
Chronic abdominal TB with ascites and studded peritoneum is the:
questions.explanation: Chronic TB peritonitis can present as: ascitic form (studded peritoneum with numerous tubercles), loculated/encysted (localized ascites), fibrous form (dense adhesions), or purulent/caseating form (cold/massive abscess). The ascitic form presents with a studded peritoneum and pale straw-coloured fluid on paracentesis.

Botulinum toxin is a presynaptic neuromuscular blocking toxin produced by Clostridium botulinum. It cleaves SNARE proteins (specifically SNAP-25) required for acetylcholine vesicle fusion with the presynaptic membrane, preventing acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction. This produces a descending, flaccid paralysis without sensory deficit. Eaton-Lambert syndrome also targets the presynaptic calcium channels but is antibody-mediated.
questions.question: Botulinum toxin produces its clinical effects by blocking neurotransmitter release at which location?
options: Voltage-gated calcium channels in peripheral nerves
Axonal sodium channels preventing action potential conduction

questions.explanation: Hepatitis E is transmitted by the faeco-oral route and is associated with the highest mortality in pregnant women (up to 20-25%), particularly in the third trimester. It belongs to the Calici family, has no chronic sequelae, and is a particular concern in developing countries with poor sanitation.
questions.question: The hepatitis virus transmitted by the faeco-oral route with highest mortality in pregnant women is:
A 35-year-old man presents with profuse watery diarrhea and vomiting for 3 days. His serum sodium is 128 mEq/L. Which type of hypovolemic state does this represent?
questions.explanation: Diarrhea and vomiting cause loss of sodium-rich gastrointestinal fluids, leading to hyponatraemic depletion when serum sodium falls below 135 mEq/L. The loss of sodium-containing fluid without adequate replacement results in both volume depletion and hyponatraemia simultaneously. This combination demands careful correction to avoid rapid osmotic shifts.

Multimodal analgesia combining regular paracetamol, NSAIDs (if not contraindicated), and local anaesthetic infiltration of port sites provides superior analgesia with reduced opioid requirements and fewer opioid-related side effects (nausea, constipation, respiratory depression) after laparoscopic surgery. This aligns with ERAS protocols. Intraperitoneal local anaesthetic instillation at the end of laparoscopy further reduces diaphragmatic irritation shoulder-tip pain.
options: Intramuscular morphine as the sole analgesic
Multimodal analgesia: paracetamol, NSAIDs, local anaesthetic
Regular oral tramadol alone for 2 weeks
Epidural morphine infusion throughout hospital stay
questions.question: The preferred analgesic regimen after laparoscopic surgery that reduces opioid-related side effects is:
In a patient with an open infected tibial fracture wound, the wound healing strategy most appropriate is:
questions.explanation: Open (compound) fractures with wound contamination and infection require thorough surgical washout, removal of all devitalised and necrotic tissue (debridement), fracture stabilisation, and delayed wound closure or split skin grafting once the wound is clean and granulating. Immediate closure of a contaminated traumatic wound would trap infection and risk progressive osteomyelitis. The Gustilo-Anderson classification guides management according to wound severity.
options: Wound washout, debridement, and delayed wound closure or grafting
Application of compression bandages and closure in 24 hours

questions.question: The drug of choice for status epilepticus, preferred over diazepam because of longer anti-epileptic effect and less respiratory depression, is:
questions.explanation: Lorazepam is the drug of choice for status epilepticus because it has a longer anti-epileptic effect than diazepam (hours vs. minutes), causes less respiratory depression, and is rapidly absorbed IM. It can be given intravenously or intramuscularly. If lorazepam fails, phenytoin or fosphenytoin is added. Persistent status despite lorazepam and phenytoin (refractory status epilepticus) requires midazolam, propofol, or barbiturate coma.

questions.question: The anatomical term 'caudal' in surgery refers to:
questions.explanation: Caudal refers to structures positioned toward the tail or inferior aspect of the body. The opposite, cephalic, refers to structures toward the head. These directional terms are essential in surgical anatomical descriptions and operative planning.

questions.question: A positive family history of inguinal hernia in a child's father and sibling confirms which aetiological factor?
questions.explanation: A positive family history is a well-recognised risk factor for inguinal hernia, present in approximately 11.5% of paediatric hernia patients. This familial pattern suggests a genetic component to the anatomical predisposition, likely related to connective tissue variations affecting obliteration of the processus vaginalis or the strength of the inguinal canal wall. Family history increases the likelihood of bilateral involvement and warrants careful assessment.
options: Genetic predisposition as hernia risk factor
Dietary factors within the family causing weakness
Environmental chemical exposure in the household
The hernia is acquired from shared physical activity
Shared infectious aetiology within the family

questions.explanation: Percussion for hepatomegaly begins below resonance in the right iliac fossa and moves upward along the mid-clavicular line to identify the lower border of dullness. The upper border is identified by percussing downward from the chest. This two-direction approach accurately defines hepatic span.
options: Epigastrium laterally toward the right flank
Right iliac fossa to mid-clavicular line
Right hypochondrium downward toward the iliac fossa
Left mid-clavicular line moving to the right
questions.question: When examining a patient for hepatomegaly, the percussion should begin from which location and in which direction?

questions.explanation: Burn wound sepsis requires source control through debridement of infected or necrotic tissue combined with systemic antibiotics guided by wound culture results. Topical agents alone are insufficient once systemic sepsis has developed. Early aggressive management reduces the risk of progression to multi-organ dysfunction.
options: Topical antiseptic cream alone without systemic therapy
Observation only since fever is expected after burns
Immediate amputation of the affected limb
Oral antibiotics without any wound intervention
Wound debridement and culture-directed systemic antibiotics
questions.question: A child with 20 percent burns develops signs of sepsis with wound discharge and systemic deterioration on day 6. The MOST appropriate immediate management includes:

options: Mild pancreatitis with expected full recovery
questions.explanation: Ranson's criteria of 5 or more at 48 hours indicates severe pancreatitis with a mortality rate exceeding 40%. Three or fewer criteria predict mild disease with less than 1% mortality. Severity scoring guides ICU admission, nutritional support decisions, and the need for contrast-enhanced CT to assess pancreatic necrosis.
questions.question: Acute pancreatitis with Ranson's criteria of 5 at 48 hours predicts which severity?

options: Jaundice and dark urine indicating biliary injury
Fever with generalised peritonism requiring re-laparotomy
Lower limb oedema from inferior vena cava compression
Hiccups, ipsilateral shoulder pain, and basal atelectasis
questions.explanation: A subphrenic abscess classically presents with ipsilateral shoulder tip pain (diaphragmatic irritation), hiccups, and ipsilateral basal atelectasis or pleural effusion. The collection under the diaphragm irritates the phrenic nerve (C3,4,5), causing referred shoulder pain. CT is the gold standard for confirmation and guides drainage.
questions.question: A patient develops a subphrenic abscess 10 days after emergency laparotomy. The MOST reliable clinical clue before imaging is:

questions.explanation: Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin approximately 200 times more avidly than oxygen, forming carboxyhaemoglobin and causing tissue asphyxia despite normal arterial pO2. Systemic effects include CNS depression, cardiac arrhythmias, and cellular hypoxia. Treatment is 100% oxygen.
questions.question: Carbon monoxide poisoning in inhalational burns causes asphyxia by:
options: Causing direct thermal injury to the bronchial mucosa
Binding haemoglobin 200 times more avidly than oxygen

questions.explanation: Basal cell carcinoma classically presents as a slow-growing, pearly or translucent nodule with visible surface telangiectasia and a characteristic rolled edge, most commonly on sun-exposed areas of the face. Unlike squamous cell carcinoma, which is more often scaly, crusted, and can ulcerate more rapidly, basal cell carcinoma rarely metastasises but can cause significant local tissue destruction if neglected. Surgical excision with an adequate margin remains the mainstay of treatment for most lesions.
questions.question: A patient has a slow-growing, pearly nodule with overlying telangiectasia and a rolled, translucent edge on the face. This lesion is most characteristic of:

options: Acute mesenteric ischaemia unrelated to pressure
questions.question: A trauma patient develops abdominal distension, difficulty ventilating, and reduced urine output after massive fluid resuscitation and temporary abdominal closure. Bladder pressure measurement shows 28 mmHg. This is consistent with:
questions.explanation: A sustained intra-abdominal pressure above 20 mmHg with new organ dysfunction, such as impaired ventilation and reduced urine output, defines abdominal compartment syndrome, often precipitated by massive resuscitation and bowel oedema after trauma laparotomy. Bladder pressure measurement is the standard method of monitoring intra-abdominal pressure. Decompressive laparotomy is indicated when compartment syndrome is confirmed with organ dysfunction.

questions.question: A patient develops calf swelling, warmth, and tenderness on postoperative day 6 after hip surgery. Doppler ultrasound confirms a proximal deep vein thrombosis. The MOST appropriate immediate management is:
questions.explanation: Confirmed proximal deep vein thrombosis requires prompt therapeutic anticoagulation to prevent proximal extension and embolisation to the lungs. Surgical thrombectomy is reserved for specific severe cases such as phlegmasia. Compression stockings and mobilisation are adjuncts, not substitutes, for anticoagulation.
options: Immediate surgical thrombectomy in all cases
Observation with repeat scan in one week

questions.question: A 10-day-old premature neonate develops abdominal distension, bloody stools, and feeding intolerance. X-ray shows pneumatosis intestinalis. The DIAGNOSIS is:
questions.explanation: Necrotising enterocolitis (NEC) typically affects premature neonates with triad of abdominal distension, bloody stools, and feeding intolerance. Pneumatosis intestinalis (gas within the bowel wall on AXR) is the pathognomonic radiological sign of NEC. Portal venous gas or pneumoperitoneum indicate advanced disease. Bell stage I is suspected NEC; Stage II is confirmed NEC; Stage III (perforation/peritonitis) requires surgical intervention.

Spasticity, characterised by increased muscle tone, hyperreflexia, and clonus, typically develops in the weeks to months after spinal cord injury as spinal reflex arcs below the lesion become disinhibited from higher cortical control, following an initial period of spinal shock during which reflexes are typically absent (flaccid). This evolution from flaccid to spastic findings over time is a recognised natural history of spinal cord injury rather than a sign of new injury or deterioration. Understanding this progression helps guide rehabilitation and management of tone-related complications.
questions.question: A patient recovering from an incomplete spinal cord injury several months ago now has increased muscle tone, hyperreflexia, and clonus in the affected limbs, without loss of the deficit itself worsening. What term best describes these findings?
Wedge compression fractures and cod-fish vertebral deformities are anomalies of which component of the spine?
questions.explanation: Wedge compression and cod-fish vertebral deformities are anomalies of the vertebral bodies, typically seen in osteoporosis. In osteoporotic collapse, vertebral body height is lost anteriorly (wedge) or uniformly (cod-fish, with biconcave endplates due to disc pressure). These deformities can lead to progressive kyphosis and nerve compression.

options: A pressure ulcer unrelated to diabetes
A malignant ulcer requiring immediate biopsy only
questions.explanation: A plantar ulcer over a pressure point with reduced sensation but preserved pulses is characteristic of a neuropathic diabetic foot ulcer, resulting from repetitive unnoticed trauma in an insensate foot rather than primarily from impaired blood supply. Ischaemic ulcers, by contrast, more often occur at the toes or heel and are associated with absent pulses and pain. Distinguishing the predominant aetiology guides appropriate offloading, wound care, and vascular assessment.
questions.question: A diabetic patient develops a foot ulcer over the plantar surface of the first metatarsal head, with reduced sensation on examination but palpable pedal pulses. This ulcer is best classified as:

questions.explanation: Pyogenic infections (Staphylococcus aureus most common) and spinal tuberculosis (Pott's disease) are classified as infectious causes of low back pain. Infectious discitis and vertebral osteomyelitis present with severe localised pain, fever, elevated inflammatory markers, and eventual vertebral collapse if untreated. TB spondylitis characteristically causes anterior vertebral destruction with gibbus deformity.
questions.question: Pyogenic spondylitis and spinal tuberculosis are grouped under which category of causes of low back pain?

questions.explanation: Apple peel, or Christmas tree, atresia describes a specific and severe variant of jejunal atresia in which the distal small bowel coils around a single retrograde vessel arising from the ileocolic or right colic artery, since the superior mesenteric artery is absent distally. This variant carries a higher risk of associated short bowel syndrome due to the limited residual bowel length and vascular compromise. It requires careful surgical technique to preserve maximal viable bowel length.
questions.question: A neonate with jejunal atresia is found at laparotomy to have a spiral, corkscrew appearance of the distal bowel supplied by a single retrograde marginal artery, resembling an apple peel. This variant is termed:
options: Type II atresia with a fibrous cord
Simple Type IIIa atresia with a mesenteric gap

questions.explanation: In haemoglobin S, valine replaces glutamic acid at position 6 of the beta globin chain. This single amino acid substitution reduces solubility of deoxygenated haemoglobin, causing polymerization and deformation of red blood cells into the characteristic sickle shape under low oxygen tension.
questions.question: In Hb S, the molecular defect involves substitution of:
options: Lysine replacing glutamic acid at position 6
Valine replacing glutamic acid at position 6

questions.explanation: Transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) is considered the gold standard surgical treatment for BPH, offering proven efficacy, acceptable morbidity, and rapid recovery compared to open prostatectomy. It is performed endoscopically using a resectoscope without external incision. Complications specific to TURP include TURP syndrome (hyponatraemia from absorption of irrigating fluid), retrograde ejaculation, urethral stricture, and incontinence.
questions.question: The gold standard surgical treatment for benign prostatic hyperplasia is:

options: Males present with smaller tumours that are harder to detect on imaging
Males more commonly have papillary cancer which has the worst prognosis
Oestrogen is directly protective against thyroid cancer cell proliferation in females
Male thyroid cancer is always of the anaplastic undifferentiated type
Males tend to present at a later stage with more advanced disease
questions.question: Thyroid cancer in males carries a worse prognosis than in females primarily because:
questions.explanation: Thyroid cancers in males tend to present at a more advanced stage at diagnosis, contributing to worse prognosis. Males also have a higher proportion of aggressive histological subtypes (follicular and poorly differentiated carcinoma). Male sex is an independent adverse prognostic factor in differentiated thyroid cancer risk stratification systems such as AMES and AGES. Earlier diagnosis through awareness in females also contributes to better female outcomes.

questions.question: Which feature of a breast lump on ultrasound is MOST indicative of malignancy?
questions.explanation: Malignant breast masses on ultrasound characteristically appear as irregular hypoechoic lesions with angular or spiculated margins, taller than wide orientation, and posterior acoustic shadowing from desmoplastic reaction. Benign features include smooth round margins, parallel orientation, and anechoic content. BI-RADS category 4 and 5 lesions require tissue biopsy.
options: Irregular hypoechoic mass with posterior acoustic shadowing
Hyperechoic homogeneous mass parallel to skin surface
Lobulated anechoic mass with thin septations
Homogeneous isoechoic mass with well-defined margins
Fluid that remains fully available to support circulating blood volume
Purely intracellular fluid shifted from the cells
Fluid identical in composition and function to normal plasma
A fluid compartment that resolves within the first hour after surgery
Functionally sequestered extracellular fluid unavailable for immediate circulatory use
questions.explanation: Third-space losses represent extracellular fluid that has moved into a non-functional space, such as oedematous bowel wall or the peritoneal cavity, where it is not available to support intravascular volume or perfusion despite still being part of total body water. This sequestration explains why patients with significant third-spacing require ongoing fluid replacement beyond simple measured losses. As the underlying inflammatory process resolves postoperatively, this fluid gradually mobilises back into the circulation, sometimes producing a diuretic phase.
questions.question: A patient undergoing major surgery has significant third-space fluid losses into the bowel wall and peritoneal cavity. This fluid is best described as:

questions.explanation: Loss of hydrochloric acid and potassium through prolonged nasogastric aspiration or vomiting produces a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, since loss of gastric acid leaves relatively more bicarbonate in the plasma. This contrasts with lower gastrointestinal losses, such as diarrhoea, which tend to cause a metabolic acidosis from bicarbonate loss. Correction requires replacement of chloride, potassium, and volume with appropriate intravenous fluids.
questions.question: A patient with a high nasogastric aspirate output over several days is at greatest risk of developing which electrolyte and acid-base disturbance?

options: Reducing metabolic rate of the cortex
Increasing CSF production to dilute blood products
Head-up positioning facilitates jugular venous drainage
questions.question: Elevation of the head to 20-30 degrees in head-injured patients assists ICP management by which mechanism?
questions.explanation: Head elevation to 20-30 degrees promotes venous drainage from the cranial cavity through the internal jugular veins by gravity, reducing intracranial blood volume and therefore ICP. Elevation beyond 30 degrees may compromise cerebral perfusion pressure by reducing MAP at brain level. This simple positional measure is an integral component of the ICP bundle alongside osmotherapy, ventilation, and surgical decompression.

Radial club hand is associated with several syndromes, including VACTERL association and Fanconi anaemia, which can involve cardiac defects, renal anomalies, and haematological abnormalities such as bone marrow failure, making thorough assessment of these systems important in a newborn presenting with this anomaly. Focusing narrowly on only one unrelated system, such as the eyes or ears alone, would risk missing clinically significant associated conditions. This comprehensive approach reflects the broader principle that an isolated-appearing limb anomaly can be a marker of wider systemic disease.
questions.question: A newborn with radial club hand is being examined for associated systemic anomalies. Which of the following systems should specifically be assessed given recognised syndromic associations?
options: Only the gastrointestinal system in isolation

questions.explanation: Wound healing follows the sequence: haemostasis, inflammation, proliferation, and maturation/remodelling. Haemostasis involves platelet aggregation and clot formation immediately after injury. The inflammatory phase follows with cellular debridement, proliferation involves fibroplasia and angiogenesis starting around day 3, and maturation achieves collagen remodelling with only 80% of original tensile strength by 21 days.
questions.question: The phases of wound healing in correct sequential order are:

options: True adenomatous polyps with malignant potential in UC
Lipomatous submucosal deposits from long-term steroid use
Lymphoid follicle hyperplasia from repeated infections
Inflammatory fibrous polyps from previous sclerotherapy
Islands of regenerating mucosa surrounded by ulcerated tissue
questions.explanation: Pseudopolyps (inflammatory polyps) in ulcerative colitis are islands of surviving regenerating mucosal epithelium surrounded by deeply ulcerated, denuded areas, giving a polypoid appearance. They have no malignant potential themselves but their presence indicates severe, longstanding disease. They must be distinguished from true dysplastic (adenomatous) polyps, which carry cancer risk and mandate biopsy.
questions.question: A sigmoidoscopy report describes 'pseudopolyps' in a patient with longstanding ulcerative colitis. Pseudopolyps represent:

questions.explanation: Bloody nipple discharge is most significantly associated with intraductal papilloma (the commonest benign cause) and breast carcinoma (which must always be excluded). Duct ectasia and fibroadenosis can cause brownish-green discharge, while lactational discharge is milky and physiological. Any unilateral, spontaneous, blood-stained nipple discharge in a non-lactating woman requires urgent investigation including cytology, ultrasound, and mammography.
questions.question: Bloody nipple discharge is most commonly associated with which of the following conditions?

questions.explanation: The double bubble sign (dilated stomach + dilated proximal duodenum) with absence of distal gas is pathognomonic of duodenal atresia. The bilious vomiting confirms that the obstruction is distal to the ampulla of Vater (second part of duodenum). Associated conditions include Down's syndrome (trisomy 21) in 30% of cases. Surgical correction with a duodeno-duodenostomy is the treatment of choice.
questions.question: A neonate presents with bilious vomiting on day 1 of life. X-ray shows the 'double bubble' sign with no distal bowel gas. The MOST likely diagnosis is:

questions.explanation: The various species of Streptomyces produce granules of different size, texture, and colour — an important diagnostic feature. This distinguishes Streptomyces from Actinomyces, which almost always produce yellow sulfur granules. Granule type identification guides appropriate antibiotic selection.
questions.question: Streptomyces-caused mycetoma granules are characterized as:
options: Variable size and colour by species

questions.question: A patient with a severe head injury and elevated intracranial pressure refractory to medical management is being considered for surgical decompression. Which procedure involves removing a large section of skull to allow the swollen brain to expand outward?
questions.explanation: Decompressive craniectomy involves removing a large section of the skull, leaving the bone flap out temporarily, to allow the swollen brain room to expand outward and reduce intracranial pressure when medical management has failed, distinguishing it from a standard craniotomy where the bone flap is replaced at the end of the procedure. Burr hole evacuation is typically used for draining more localised collections such as chronic subdural haematomas rather than treating diffuse malignant swelling. Understanding the specific surgical rationale for craniectomy versus craniotomy is important in severe traumatic brain injury management.

questions.question: A patient with a gunshot wound to the abdomen has an entry wound in the right flank and exit in the left upper quadrant. The trajectory would MOST likely involve injury to:
questions.explanation: A right flank entry with left upper quadrant exit indicates a transverse trajectory through the retroperitoneum, directly involving the right kidney, the vertebral column, and potentially the left kidney. This pattern also risks aortic or IVC injury. Reconstructing the missile trajectory from entry/exit points guides operative planning and organ assessment.
options: Liver, inferior vena cava, and aorta
Transverse colon and small bowel mesentery
Right kidney, vertebral column, left kidney

questions.question: In respiratory acidosis, the appropriate initial intervention that takes priority over serial ABG monitoring is:
questions.explanation: Respiratory acidosis results from inadequate ventilation and carbon dioxide accumulation, so restoring ventilation is the primary goal. Intubation may be required if conservative measures fail. Rapid correction must be cautious as it can precipitate post-hypercapnic metabolic alkalosis.

options: Single exposure to steam at 121°C for 30 minutes
Chemical sterilization with formaldehyde for 1 hour
Boiling at 100°C for 15–20 minutes, three days
questions.question: Tyndallization (fractional sterilization) involves:
questions.explanation: Tyndallization involves boiling goods at 100°C for 15-20 minutes per day for three consecutive days. The intervals allow surviving spores to germinate and be destroyed on the next cycle. It is a form of fractional sterilization and discontinuous heating.

questions.question: Which investigation provides the most detailed assessment of soft tissue components of the intervertebral disc including herniation and cord compression?
questions.explanation: MRI is the gold standard for evaluating intervertebral disc pathology, cord compression, and soft tissue structures because it provides excellent contrast between disc, cord, CSF, and adjacent soft tissues without ionising radiation. CT myelogram is an alternative for patients who cannot undergo MRI. Plain radiograph assesses bony alignment but cannot directly visualise discs or neural tissue.

questions.question: Neurogenic shock following high cervical or thoracic spinal cord injury is characterised by which haemodynamic pattern?
questions.explanation: Neurogenic shock results from disruption of descending sympathetic pathways below a high cervical or thoracic cord injury, producing loss of sympathetic tone. This causes bradycardia (unopposed vagal tone) and hypotension (vasodilatation, reduced cardiac output) — a pattern distinguishing it from hypovolaemic shock (tachycardia with hypotension). Treatment includes fluid resuscitation, vasopressors, and atropine for symptomatic bradycardia.

options: Active viral replication with high infectivity
Chronic inactive carrier state with low infectivity
