questions.question: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) in a cirrhotic patient is MOST commonly caused by which organism?

options: Pharyngo-oesophageal junction at the pyriform fossa
Mid-oesophagus at the level of the carina
Right posterolateral oesophageal wall above the aortic arch
questions.question: Perforation of the oesophagus by a misplaced nasogastric tube MOST commonly occurs at which site?
questions.explanation: Iatrogenic oesophageal perforation from nasogastric tubes most commonly occurs at the pharyngo-oesophageal junction, particularly in the right pyriform fossa or posterior hypopharyngeal wall where the NG tube may deflect rather than pass smoothly into the oesophageal lumen. The risk is highest in obtunded, sedated, or elderly patients with difficult anatomy.

questions.question: Which of the following conditions is an absolute indication for surgical intervention in lumbar disc prolapse, requiring urgent consideration?
questions.explanation: Massive midline disc prolapse causing cauda equina compression is an emergency surgical indication requiring urgent decompression to preserve bladder, bowel, and sexual function. Sphincteric dysfunction (urinary retention or incontinence) with or without saddle anaesthesia signals this syndrome. Delayed surgery beyond 24–48 hours significantly worsens neurological prognosis.
options: Persistent back pain unresponsive to analgesics
Mild motor weakness with intact sphincter function
Massive midline prolapse causing cauda equina compression
Radicular pain with negative straight leg raise

questions.explanation: Hyperreflexia (exaggerated deep tendon reflexes) and positive Babinski sign (extensor plantar response) are hallmarks of upper motor neurone dysfunction, indicating cord compression in cervical myelopathy. Lower motor neurone signs at the level of compression (wasting, fasciculations) may coexist with upper motor neurone signs below that level. Fasciculations suggest anterior horn cell involvement.
options: Fasciculations of the upper limb muscles
Sensory loss in a glove distribution
questions.question: In cervical myelopathy, which clinical sign indicates upper motor neurone involvement?

questions.explanation: Increased testosterone production is not a complication of prostatectomy. Recognised complications include retrograde ejaculation (65-90% after TURP), urinary incontinence (external sphincter damage), impotence (neurovascular bundle damage), urethral stricture, bladder neck stenosis, haemorrhage, clot retention, UTI, epididymo-orchitis, TURP syndrome (in TURP), and osteitis pubis (in open retropubic prostatectomy).
questions.question: Complications of prostatectomy include all of the following EXCEPT:

questions.explanation: Cervicofacial actinomycosis classically follows dental procedures or oral trauma and presents with chronic sinus tracts discharging sulfur granules, representing colonies of the causative filamentous bacteria. Prolonged antibiotic therapy, typically with penicillin, combined with surgical drainage of any abscess, is the standard treatment. The chronic, indolent, cross-tissue-plane spread is characteristic of this infection.
questions.question: A patient presents with a chronic sinus tract discharging characteristic yellow granules from the jaw region following dental extraction. The MOST likely diagnosis is:

questions.explanation: Generalised faecal peritonitis with haemodynamic compromise may mandate conversion to open appendicectomy, as the open approach provides faster more comprehensive access and lavage capability. A contained periappendicular abscess is managed conservatively or with CT-guided drainage then interval appendicectomy. Retrocaecal appendix and high CRP are manageable laparoscopically in experienced hands and are not absolute indications for open surgery.
questions.question: In acute appendicitis, which intraoperative finding most strongly mandates conversion from laparoscopic to open appendicectomy?
options: Raised CRP and leucocytosis on blood tests
Periappendicular abscess visible on preoperative CT scan
Retrocaecal appendix position found at laparoscopy
Patient age over 60 years with cardiovascular comorbidities
Faecal peritonitis with haemodynamic compromise needing rapid control

questions.question: The Hoover test demonstrating non-organic weakness uses which physiological principle?
questions.explanation: The Hoover test exploits the crossed extension reflex: in a normal subject, attempting to lift one leg produces a reflex downward push of the contralateral heel into the examiner's hand. If the supposedly weak leg does not push down during lifting of the normal leg, or if the supposedly normal leg does not push down during attempted lifting of the weak leg, this indicates non-organic (functional) weakness rather than true neurological paresis.
options: Voluntary control of contralateral limb movements
Ipsilateral muscle sympathetic responses to voluntary effort
Cerebellar crossed inhibition of motor output
Spinal Renshaw cell inhibition of motor neurones

questions.question: A geneticist explains that some congenital hand anomalies, such as certain forms of syndactyly, follow a clear inheritance pattern within affected families, while others occur sporadically. Which statement best reflects current understanding of congenital hand anomaly aetiology?
options: All congenital hand anomalies are caused by a single identified gene
All congenital hand anomalies are entirely environmental in origin
All congenital hand anomalies follow strict autosomal recessive inheritance
Aetiology is heterogeneous, including genetic, sporadic, and vascular disruptive causes
Congenital hand anomalies never occur sporadically without family history
questions.explanation: Congenital hand anomalies have a heterogeneous aetiology, including specific inherited genetic syndromes with defined inheritance patterns, sporadic genetic mutations, and vascular disruptive events during early limb development, meaning no single explanatory mechanism applies to all cases. This heterogeneity is why thorough family history, examination for associated syndromic features, and sometimes genetic testing are all important parts of the work-up for a child presenting with a congenital hand anomaly. Assuming a single universal cause would lead to inappropriate counselling and incomplete evaluation for potential associated systemic conditions.

Conservative management (rest, analgesics, physiotherapy) is typically attempted for 6–12 weeks before surgical referral for lumbar disc prolapse without neurological deficit or red flags. Most patients improve within this period. Failure of conservative treatment after 6–12 weeks, or presence of red flags (sphincteric dysfunction, progressive weakness, bilateral symptoms), warrants earlier surgical consideration.
questions.question: Conservative management of lumbar disc prolapse should generally be attempted for how long before considering surgery (in the absence of red flag signs)?
A 55-year-old female has a sudden non-reducible right inguinal mass with mild colicky abdominal pain. The most appropriate next action is:
questions.explanation: An acute non-reducible inguinal mass with abdominal pain in a female suggests an incarcerated or strangulating hernia requiring urgent surgical exploration. Females have a higher proportion of femoral hernias with a higher strangulation rate. The combination of acute onset, irreducibility, and abdominal pain warrants emergency assessment. Manual reduction of a potentially strangulated hernia risks returning gangrenous bowel to the abdomen.
options: Reassure her it is a lipoma and discharge from clinic
Prescribe laxatives and analgesics and review in a week
Urgent surgical referral and exploration for suspected incarcerated hernia
CT scan then plan elective repair in 3 months
Manual reduction under sedation then discharge home

questions.question: A patient with known malignancy develops progressive back pain, bilateral leg weakness, and a sensory level on examination. Which diagnosis must be urgently excluded given the risk of irreversible paralysis if untreated?
questions.explanation: Malignant spinal cord compression, resulting from metastatic tumour deposits compressing the spinal cord, is an oncological emergency requiring urgent MRI imaging and prompt treatment, which may include corticosteroids, radiotherapy, or surgical decompression, because delay significantly increases the risk of permanent paraplegia. The combination of known malignancy, progressive back pain, bilateral leg weakness, and a sensory level are all red-flag features that should prompt immediate escalation rather than being attributed to benign mechanical or degenerative causes. Early recognition and treatment offers the best chance of preserving neurological function.

A localised sigmoid colon cancer without distant metastases (M0 disease) is potentially curable by sigmoid colectomy with primary anastomosis (or Hartmann's procedure if anastomosis is unsafe). Surgical resection with adequate margins and lymph node clearance is the cornerstone of curative treatment. Adjuvant chemotherapy (FOLFOX) is given for node-positive (stage III) disease post-resection. Neoadjuvant radiotherapy is more relevant for rectal than colonic cancer.
questions.question: A 60-year-old male with rectal bleeding and weight loss undergoes colonoscopy showing a circumferential mass at the sigmoid colon. CT staging shows no distant metastases. What is the most appropriate primary management?
Splenomegaly is a DIRECT cause of which haematological complication requiring splenectomy?
questions.explanation: Hypersplenism occurs when an enlarged spleen excessively sequesters and destroys blood cells, resulting in pancytopenia with thrombocytopenia, anaemia, and leukopenia. Symptomatic hypersplenism refractory to treatment of the underlying cause may be an indication for splenectomy. Portal hypertension from hepatic disease is the most common cause of hypersplenism in adults.

options: Failure of the vitello-intestinal duct to obliterate
Persistence of the cloacal membrane beyond normal gestation
Abnormal rotation of the midgut around the superior mesenteric artery
Failure of craniocaudal migration of neural crest cells into the distal bowel wall
Failure of recanalisation of the intestinal lumen
questions.question: A neonate with Hirschsprung's disease has a rectal biopsy showing absence of ganglion cells and hypertrophied nerve trunks in the submucosal plexus. The embryological basis of this condition is:
questions.explanation: Hirschsprung's disease results from arrested craniocaudal migration of neural crest-derived precursor cells, leading to an aganglionic segment beginning at the anus and extending proximally for a variable distance. The affected segment cannot relax, causing a functional obstruction with proximal dilatation. This distinguishes it embryologically from conditions such as intestinal atresia, which arise from vascular or recanalisation defects.

questions.question: In edema formation, the hydrostatic pressure at the arteriolar segment of the capillary is approximately:
questions.explanation: The hydrostatic pressure at the arteriolar end of the capillary is approximately 32 mmHg, which exceeds the plasma oncotic pressure of 26 mmHg, favouring filtration of fluid into the interstitium. At the venular end, hydrostatic pressure falls below oncotic pressure, favouring reabsorption. The net residual interstitial fluid is drained by the lymphatics at approximately 2 mL per minute.

Although the initial peritonitis following duodenal perforation is chemical due to acidic gastric content, translocation of gut flora over subsequent hours introduces bacterial contamination, with Escherichia coli being the most common organism given its predominance in the gut microbiome. This progression justifies early broad-spectrum antibiotic cover even before bacterial contamination is confirmed. Anaerobes such as Bacteroides also contribute later.
questions.question: A perforated duodenal ulcer causes chemical peritonitis initially, which later becomes bacterial. The organism most commonly responsible for this secondary bacterial contamination is:

questions.explanation: The epiploic foramen of Winslow is the sole communication between the lesser sac and the greater peritoneal cavity, bounded by the portal triad anteriorly, the inferior vena cava posteriorly, and the caudate lobe superiorly. Fluid or blood within the lesser sac, such as from a posterior gastric ulcer perforation, may remain localised unless it tracks through this foramen. Its anatomical boundaries are important during hepatobiliary and pancreatic surgery.
questions.question: The lesser sac (omental bursa) communicates with the greater peritoneal cavity through which structure?

questions.explanation: A chronic discharging neck sinus with pale, cheesy (caseous) material in the context of prolonged duration strongly suggests tuberculous lymphadenitis with collar-stud abscess formation through the deep cervical fascia. TB lymphadenopathy (scrofula) is the commonest extrapulmonary tuberculosis manifestation. Diagnosis requires aspiration for AFB smear, culture, and GeneXpert PCR, and treatment is with standard anti-tuberculosis chemotherapy.
questions.question: A patient with a neck sinus discharging pale, cheesy material that has been present for months most likely has:

questions.explanation: Right ventricular hypertrophy in sickle cell disease develops secondary to pulmonary hypertension, which results from chronic sickling in the pulmonary circulation causing endothelial injury, thrombosis, and vascular remodelling. Pulmonary hypertension is associated with increased mortality and is assessed by echocardiography.
questions.question: Right ventricular hypertrophy in sickle cell disease develops secondary to:

questions.explanation: As pregnancy progresses, the gravid uterus displaces the caecum and appendix superiorly and laterally, shifting the point of maximal tenderness upward and outward from the classic McBurney's point, particularly in the third trimester. This anatomical shift can make the diagnosis of appendicitis more challenging in pregnant patients and contributes to delayed presentation and diagnosis. Awareness of this shift is important to avoid missing appendicitis in later pregnancy.
options: Exactly at the classic McBurney's point in all trimesters
Higher and more lateral than the classic McBurney's point
In the left iliac fossa instead of the right
Lower than McBurney's point, closer to the pubic symphysis
Unchanged, since pregnancy does not affect appendiceal position
questions.question: A pregnant woman in her third trimester presents with suspected appendicitis. Compared with a non-pregnant patient, the point of maximal tenderness is more likely to be located:

questions.explanation: The hypertrophic type of abdominal TB (RIF mass) has differential diagnoses of appendiceal mass, caecal tumour, amoeboma, and Crohn's disease — all affecting the ileocaecal region. Sigmoid volvulus is a left-sided sigmoid colon problem unrelated to the ileocaecal area where hypertrophic TB typically occurs.
questions.question: The hypertrophic type of abdominal TB in the RIF has differential diagnoses of all EXCEPT:

questions.explanation: An incarcerated hernia is irreducible but the bowel remains viable, whereas strangulation implies compromised blood supply, producing overlying skin erythema, severe constant pain, and systemic signs of toxicity such as tachycardia and fever. Both lose their cough impulse once irreducible, so this feature does not distinguish them. Recognising strangulation is critical because it constitutes a surgical emergency.
options: Both are equally reducible on gentle pressure
Strangulation always presents without any pain
Incarceration is always associated with fever
Presence of overlying skin erythema and systemic toxicity in strangulation
Cough impulse is preserved only in strangulation
questions.question: Which clinical feature best differentiates an incarcerated hernia from a strangulated hernia on examination?

options: Hard, fixed nodule with ipsilateral cervical lymphadenopathy
Nodule size greater than 2 cm with multiple calcifications
Soft, mobile nodule in a woman under 30
Multinodular goitre in an iodine-deficient region
Incidentally found hot nodule on thyroid scintigraphy
questions.explanation: A hard, fixed thyroid nodule with ipsilateral cervical lymphadenopathy is the classic presentation of malignancy, particularly papillary thyroid carcinoma which has a strong propensity for lymphatic metastasis. Hot nodules on scintigraphy are rarely malignant. Fine needle aspiration cytology under ultrasound guidance is the initial diagnostic investigation.
questions.question: Which clinical feature MOST strongly suggests a thyroid nodule is malignant?
An erect abdominal radiograph shows multiple air-fluid levels with 'step-ladder' pattern. The loop diameter is 4 cm. What is the MOST probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The step-ladder pattern of air-fluid levels at different heights in central small bowel loops, with a diameter of 3–5 cm, is characteristic of mechanical small bowel obstruction. Paralytic ileus produces generalised uniform dilatation. Volvulus typically shows a 'coffee bean' sign on large bowel imaging.

options: The ulcer base is too vascular to biopsy safely
Edge biopsies are technically easier to perform
Malignant transformation typically begins at the ulcer margin rather than the base
Base biopsies always produce false negative results
The edge contains no epithelial tissue to sample
questions.question: A gastric ulcer on endoscopy is biopsied from multiple sites around its edge rather than from the ulcer base. This practice is important because:
questions.explanation: Malignant change in a gastric ulcer characteristically arises at the mucosal margin, where viable, potentially dysplastic epithelium persists, whereas the ulcer base often contains only necrotic slough and granulation tissue unsuitable for accurate histological diagnosis. Multiple biopsies from the rolled edges maximise the yield of detecting early malignant transformation. All gastric ulcers should be biopsied given the risk of missed malignancy.

Persistent Generalized Lymphadenopathy (PGL) is defined as symmetrical lymphadenopathy palpable for at least 3 months with constitutional symptoms. It is a clinical manifestation of HIV infection seen before progression to AIDS-related complex.
questions.question: 'Symmetrical lymphadenopathy palpable for at least 3 months' describes:

questions.explanation: Hepatitis D (delta virus) is a single-stranded RNA virus that requires co-infection or superinfection with hepatitis B virus to infect and replicate in human cells, as it uses HBsAg as its envelope protein. Diagnosis requires both anti-HDV positivity and evidence of HBV infection.
questions.question: Hepatitis D virus requires co-infection with which virus to infect humans?

questions.explanation: Abdominal compartment syndrome is defined as a sustained IAP >20 mmHg with new organ dysfunction. IAP 12–20 mmHg is intra-abdominal hypertension (IAH) without overt organ failure. Treatment with decompressive laparotomy is indicated when IAP exceeds 20 mmHg with deteriorating organ function, as measured by bladder pressure monitoring.
questions.question: In abdominal compartment syndrome, intra-abdominal pressure (IAP) at which organ dysfunction becomes clinically significant is:

questions.explanation: A positive crossed SLR (contralateral straight leg raise reproducing ipsilateral radicular pain) indicates a large central disc herniation significantly compressing the nerve root, usually in the lateral recess or central canal. It is less sensitive but more specific for disc herniation than ipsilateral SLR. It typically suggests more severe compression and correlates with worse neurological deficit.
options: Negative straight leg raise with absent ankle jerk
Worsening pain with lumbar extension only
questions.question: Which sign in lumbar disc disease indicates compression of the nerve root at the lateral recess rather than at the foramen?
A resected gastric carcinoma specimen shows tumour cells extending to within 0.5 mm of the proximal resection margin on histology. This finding is significant because:
questions.explanation: An involved or very close resection margin means microscopic tumour may remain in situ, substantially increasing the risk of local recurrence and often prompting consideration of adjuvant therapy or, where feasible, re-resection. Margin status is one of the most important pathological determinants of oncological outcome after gastrectomy. Surgeons aim for adequate macroscopic and microscopic clearance during the original resection to avoid this scenario.
options: A close or involved margin increases the risk of local recurrence
It has no bearing on prognosis once the tumour is removed
It automatically indicates that no further treatment is required
It confirms the tumour was of early, not advanced, stage
It excludes the need for postoperative surveillance

questions.explanation: GISTs arise from interstitial cells of Cajal and their malignant potential is stratified by tumour size, mitotic rate per 50 HPF, and tumour location. Large tumours (above 5 cm) with high mitotic activity (above 5/50 HPF) carry the highest risk of recurrence and metastasis. Imatinib (Gleevec), a KIT tyrosine kinase inhibitor, is standard treatment for unresectable or metastatic GIST.
questions.question: Which statement BEST describes the behaviour of a gastrointestinal stromal tumour (GIST)?
options: Always benign regardless of size or mitotic activity
Malignant potential determined by size and mitotic rate
Invariably arises in the stomach antrum

questions.explanation: Osteomyelitis in sickle cell disease most commonly affects long bones such as the femur, tibia, and humerus, where areas of bone infarction create an ideal environment for bacterial seeding. In young children, dactylitis affects the small bones of the hands and feet during painful sickle crises.
options: Small bones of hands and feet only
questions.question: Osteomyelitis in sickle cell disease most commonly affects:

options: Endoscopic mucosal resection for local control
Chemoradiotherapy for local control and palliation
Oesophageal stent insertion alone as definitive treatment
questions.question: A 65-year-old man with oesophageal carcinoma is deemed surgically inoperable due to T4b disease (aortic invasion). The MOST appropriate palliative treatment is:
questions.explanation: T4b oesophageal carcinoma involving the aorta is unresectable. Definitive chemoradiotherapy (CRT) with cisplatin and 5-FU provides the best combination of local tumour control, dysphagia palliation, and potential disease modification. Oesophageal stent placement is used for palliating dysphagia but does not control the disease. Stent and CRT may be combined sequentially.

The Howship-Romberg sign is pathognomonic of an obturator hernia. It is characterised by pain radiating down the medial thigh to the knee, caused by compression of the obturator nerve as it passes through the obturator canal alongside the hernia. The pain is exacerbated by hip extension, adduction, and internal rotation, and relieved by hip flexion. The sign is often the only preoperative indicator of this rare hernia in elderly, thin women presenting with intestinal obstruction.
questions.question: The Howship-Romberg sign is pathognomonic of which type of hernia?

questions.explanation: Transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder is most strongly associated with aromatic amines (beta-naphthylamine, benzidine) found in the rubber, dye, textile, and leather industries. Cigarette smoking is the single most important risk factor in the general population, also through carcinogenic amines. Schistosoma haematobium is specifically linked to squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder.
questions.question: Transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder is most strongly associated with which environmental carcinogen?
The Milligan-Morgan haemorrhoidectomy differs from the Ferguson procedure in that the Milligan-Morgan technique leaves the wounds:
questions.explanation: The Milligan-Morgan (open) haemorrhoidectomy excises the three main haemorrhoidal complexes leaving the wounds open to heal by secondary intention with mucocutaneous bridges preserved to prevent stenosis. The Ferguson (closed) technique closes the wounds with absorbable sutures, potentially allowing faster healing but with higher risk of wound breakdown. Both techniques have equivalent long-term outcomes.
options: Completely closed with interrupted absorbable sutures
Partially closed with a running subcuticular suture
Open to heal by secondary intention
Covered with a collagen haemostatic dressing
Managed with a stapled anastomosis across the anal canal

questions.explanation: Pressure sores in paralysed patients are prevented by manually turning the patient every 2 hours to redistribute pressure from bony prominences and restore tissue perfusion. Ischaemia of skin and subcutaneous tissue occurs within 2 hours of uninterrupted pressure. Pressure-redistributing mattresses (water beds, alternating pressure) can extend the interval but do not replace the need for regular position changes.
questions.question: Pressure sores in spinal cord injury patients are prevented primarily by regular repositioning. What is the standard interval for manual turning in high-risk patients?
The Parkland formula for burn resuscitation in the first 24 hours uses which fluid?
questions.explanation: The Parkland formula uses lactated Ringer's solution: 4 mL x kg body weight x %BSA burned, given over 24 hours. Half is delivered in the first 8 hours from time of injury, and the remainder over the next 16 hours. Colloids are generally avoided in the first 24 hours due to capillary leak.

Osteomalacia is characterised radiologically by Looser zones (pseudofractures, partial stress fractures through weakened bone) and generalised reduced bone density, while osteoporosis shows reduced bone density with cortical thinning and trabecular rarefaction without pseudofractures. Both can present with back pain and vertebral fractures, but the underlying pathophysiology differs (mineralisation defect vs bone mass loss).
options: Osteomalacia: Looser zones; osteoporosis: low density
questions.question: Osteomalacia and osteoporosis are metabolic bone diseases that can cause back pain. What distinguishes osteomalacia from osteoporosis radiologically?

questions.explanation: Emergency radiotherapy for cerebral disease (brain metastases) is indicated when progressive neurological deterioration threatens life quality and function. Untreated brain metastases cause raised intracranial pressure, focal neurological deficits, and death. Steroids are given concurrently to reduce cerebral oedema during radiotherapy.
questions.question: Emergency radiotherapy for brain metastases is indicated because:
options: Brain tumours are the most radiosensitive of all malignancies
Chemotherapy cannot cross the blood-brain barrier
Untreated cerebral disease causes progressive neurological deficit and death
Brain metastases always bleed without radiotherapy
Surgery is never indicated for brain metastases

questions.explanation: A hydrocele contains straw-coloured (clear, pale yellow) transudate fluid accumulating between the layers of the tunica vaginalis due to imbalance between secretion and absorption. Primary hydroceles are idiopathic and commonest in adults. Secondary hydroceles occur in response to underlying testicular pathology such as torsion, orchitis, epididymitis, or testicular tumour, and all should be investigated with ultrasound to exclude malignancy.
questions.question: Hydrocele fluid is best described as which type of fluid?
options: Straw-coloured transudate within the tunica vaginalis
Urine from urinary fistula to the scrotum

questions.explanation: Choledochal cysts carry a lifetime risk of cholangiocarcinoma of 10–15%, which is not eliminated by internal drainage procedures (cystoduodenostomy/cystojejunostomy) as the diseased mucosa remains. Complete excision of the cyst with bilioenteric reconstruction eliminates the carcinogenic mucosa. The risk of malignancy increases with age, making early excision in childhood essential. Carcinoma arising in a choledochal cyst carries a very poor prognosis.
options: Internal drainage carries higher operative mortality
The anastomosis from internal drainage always fails within 5 years
The risk of developing cholangiocarcinoma in the cyst remnant
Portal hypertension will develop if the cyst is left in situ
The cyst mucosa secretes toxins damaging the jejunum
questions.question: The MOST important reason for complete excision rather than internal drainage of a choledochal cyst is:

questions.explanation: A large sessile polyp in the sigmoid colon that is not amenable to endoscopic removal requires laparoscopic sigmoid colectomy. This ensures complete excision with adequate margins and lymph node sampling if malignancy is found on histology. TEM is used for rectal lesions only. ESD can remove large flat lesions endoscopically but requires expertise and may not be available. Surgery is definitive.
questions.question: A 45-year-old man has a 3 cm sessile polyp in the sigmoid colon that cannot be removed endoscopically due to its broad base. The MOST appropriate surgical procedure is:

options: Lymphadenopathy present for 1 week with constitutional symptoms
Symmetrical nodes palpable for at least 3 months
Asymmetric nodes present for any duration
questions.question: Persistent Generalized Lymphadenopathy (PGL) in HIV is defined by:
questions.explanation: PGL in HIV infection is defined as symmetrical lymphadenopathy palpable for at least 3 months, with constitutional symptoms. It represents an early stage of HIV infection when the immune system is still responding to viral antigens. Nodes are usually cervical, axillary, and inguinal.

options: Haemorrhage and contamination control ? ICU resuscitation ? re-exploration
ICU stabilisation ? damage control laparotomy ? definitive surgery
questions.question: Damage control surgery in abdominal trauma follows a three-phase approach. The CORRECT sequence is:
questions.explanation: Damage control surgery follows three phases: Phase 1 — abbreviated laparotomy for haemorrhage control (packing, vascular shunts) and contamination control (bowel stapling without anastomosis); Phase 2 — ICU resuscitation targeting reversal of the lethal triad (hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy); Phase 3 — planned re-exploration for definitive repair after 24–72 hours.

The intrathoracic abdomen is the upper abdomen protected by the lower rib cage, containing the diaphragm, liver, spleen, stomach, and proximal colon. Penetrating injuries to this region may injure both thoracic and abdominal contents. Clinical assessment may be limited by the bony thorax; CT is essential for complete evaluation of potential injuries.
questions.question: The intrathoracic abdomen, as defined in abdominal trauma surgery, contains which structures at risk during thoracoabdominal penetrating injury?

options: Hypertension from renal TB with renovascular hypertension
Polycythaemia from erythropoietin secretion by caseous nodes
questions.explanation: Granulomatous diseases including tuberculosis can cause hypercalcaemia through ectopic 1-alpha hydroxylase activity within the granuloma macrophages, which converts 25-hydroxyvitamin D to the active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol), increasing intestinal calcium absorption. This is independent of renal involvement. Other manifestations include hypercalciuria and nephrolithiasis.
questions.question: Which of the following is a recognised extra-abdominal manifestation of abdominal tuberculosis?

questions.explanation: Prophylactic antibiotics are given 30-60 minutes before incision to achieve therapeutic tissue levels at the time of contamination risk, reducing bacterial count at the wound site. A single preoperative dose is sufficient for most clean and clean-contaminated procedures. Continued postoperative antibiotics do not further reduce surgical site infection and promote antibiotic resistance.
options: Cover all patients for 7 days post-surgery to prevent all infections
Prevent deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism
Sterilise the patient's gut flora preoperatively
Reduce bacteria at the wound at time of incision
questions.question: The primary purpose of prophylactic antibiotics in surgical patients is to:
A 68-year-old woman with chronic renal failure presents with peaked T-waves on ECG. Her serum potassium is 6.8 mEq/L. The FIRST step in management is:
questions.explanation: Intravenous calcium gluconate is administered first in symptomatic hyperkalemia to stabilise the cardiac membrane and protect against arrhythmia. It does not lower serum potassium but counteracts its cardiotoxic effects immediately. Subsequent measures address potassium removal.

questions.question: A patient with a retrosternal goitre causing tracheal compression is assessed preoperatively with a CT scan of the neck and thorax. The main purpose of this imaging before thyroidectomy is to:
questions.explanation: CT imaging of the neck extending into the thorax allows precise assessment of the extent of retrosternal goitre extension and its relationship to the trachea, great vessels, and mediastinal structures, which is critical for planning the surgical approach and anticipating whether a sternotomy may be required in addition to a standard cervical incision. This imaging complements, rather than replaces, direct laryngoscopic assessment of vocal cord function and airway calibre. Careful preoperative planning reduces the risk of intraoperative complications in complex retrosternal disease.
options: Replace the need for any preoperative laryngoscopy
Confirm the histological diagnosis before surgery
Measure serum thyroid hormone levels directly from the scan
Assess the full extent of retrosternal extension and its relationship to mediastinal structures
Avoid the need for any anaesthetic airway assessment

questions.question: Which nerve is MOST at risk of injury during thyroidectomy causing hoarseness?
questions.explanation: The recurrent laryngeal nerve innervates all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except the cricothyroid and is at greatest risk during thyroidectomy, particularly near the inferior thyroid artery and Berry's ligament. Its injury causes ipsilateral vocal cord paralysis and hoarseness; bilateral injury causes stridor and respiratory distress. Routine intraoperative nerve monitoring significantly reduces injury rates.

questions.question: A diverticular fistula between the sigmoid colon and the urinary bladder (colovesical fistula) classically presents with which symptom?
questions.explanation: A colovesical fistula classically presents with pneumaturia (passage of gas in the urine), faecaluria (faecal material in urine), and recurrent urinary tract infections with mixed bowel flora. Pneumaturia is considered pathognomonic of a fistulous connection between the gut and bladder. The commonest cause in adults is complicated diverticular disease, followed by Crohn's disease and colorectal carcinoma. Surgical resection of the affected colon with bladder repair is the treatment.

Technetium-99m pertechnetate scintigraphy (Meckel's scan) detects ectopic gastric mucosa, which avidly concentrates pertechnetate (as do normal gastric parietal cells). It has 85–90% sensitivity in children with gastric mucosal heterotopia. False negatives occur with non-gastric mucosal Meckel's diverticula. The scan is painless, non-invasive, and highly appropriate for the investigation of painless rectal bleeding in children.
questions.question: A child with Meckel's diverticulum presents with painless lower GI bleeding. The MOST appropriate investigation to identify the heterotopic gastric mucosa is:

questions.explanation: HBeAg (early antigen) or anti-HBe positivity indicates active viral replication, with all body fluids being infectious. Quantitative HBV-DNA testing is the most accurate measure of viral load and infectivity. HBeAg-positive patients have high transmissibility and require careful management.
questions.question: Active viral replication in hepatitis B is indicated by:
Total body water constitutes approximately what percentage of lean body weight in an adult male?
questions.explanation: Total body water constitutes approximately 60% of lean body weight in adult males. Women have slightly less at around 50% because of proportionally greater adipose tissue. This distribution is fundamental to understanding fluid compartment physiology in surgical patients.

questions.question: Surgical prophylactic antibiotics should ideally be given:
questions.explanation: Prophylactic antibiotics should be given within 60 minutes of skin incision to provide adequate tissue concentration throughout the operation. A single dose is usually sufficient, with additional doses during prolonged surgery (>3-4 hours), major blood loss, or short half-life antibiotics.

options: Type A — pure OA without fistula (10%)
Type D — OA with both proximal and distal TOF (1%)
Type E — H-type TOF without OA (4–5%)
Type C — OA with distal TOF (85%)
Type B — OA with proximal TOF (1%)
questions.question: Oesophageal atresia (OA) with tracheo-oesophageal fistula (TOF) is classified by Gross modification of Vogt's classification. The MOST common type is:
questions.explanation: Gross Type C OA (OA with a distal tracheo-oesophageal fistula) accounts for approximately 85% of all OA cases and is the most common type. The upper oesophageal pouch ends blindly (causing excessive secretions and choking), while the lower oesophagus connects to the trachea via a fistula (allowing gas into the stomach and acid reflux into the lung). Surgical repair involves division of the fistula and primary oesophageal anastomosis.

questions.question: Which classification system is used to grade the severity of spinal cord injury based on neurological preservation?
questions.explanation: The ASIA Impairment Scale (AIS), an evolution of the original Frankel grading system, classifies spinal cord injury severity from A (complete) to E (normal). It is based on neurological examination of key motor and sensory levels and sacral sparing. The AIS is the internationally standardised classification for spinal cord injury, essential for clinical communication, research, and predicting prognosis.

questions.question: Cerebral symptoms in elderly heart failure patients, including confusion and memory impairment, are PRIMARILY caused by:
questions.explanation: Elderly patients with heart failure and concomitant cerebral arteriosclerosis are particularly vulnerable to low-flow states, developing confusion, impaired concentration, memory loss, headache, and insomnia. The reduced cerebral perfusion from low cardiac output compounds ischaemia in already atherosclerotic vessels. Improving cardiac output is the primary therapeutic target.
options: Direct cardioembolic stroke from atrial thrombus

questions.explanation: Postoperative urinary retention is commonly caused by pain and reflex inhibition of the detrusor muscle, particularly after pelvic, perineal, or anorectal surgery. Other causes include anticholinergic drug effects, spinal anesthesia, and pre-existing bladder outlet obstruction.
questions.question: Postoperative urinary retention is MOST commonly caused by:
A patient develops a deep surgical site infection with gas in the tissues and crepitus 24 hours after bowel surgery. The MOST likely causative organism is:
questions.explanation: Clostridium perfringens produces gas as a by-product of tissue fermentation, causing crepitus and rapidly progressive myonecrosis, a surgical emergency requiring urgent debridement. Its rapid onset and gas production distinguish it from typical aerobic wound pathogens. High-dose penicillin combined with surgical debridement is the mainstay of treatment.

questions.question: Ramstedt's pyloromyotomy for hypertrophic pyloric stenosis involves incision of the:
questions.explanation: Ramstedt's pyloromyotomy divides the hypertrophied outer longitudinal and inner circular muscle layers of the pylorus down to (but not through) the mucosa, without entering the gastric or duodenal lumen. The mucosa bulges through the divided muscle, confirming adequate myotomy. The most common intraoperative complication is mucosal perforation at the duodenal end. Laparoscopic pyloromyotomy has equivalent outcomes to the open procedure.
options: Outer longitudinal and inner circular muscles, sparing the mucosa
Mucosa only of the pyloric channel
Submucosal layer and inner circular muscle to the mucosa
Full-thickness pyloric wall and duodenum first portion
Only the serosal layer to allow passive muscle relaxation

questions.question: Cetrimide (a quaternary ammonium compound) is MOST useful for:
questions.explanation: Quaternary ammonium compounds like cetrimide are used for surface disinfection, biosafety cabinets, floor maintenance, and glassware. They are effective against vegetative cells and lipophilic viruses but are inactivated by organic matter and do not destroy spores.

questions.question: Deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism occur commonly in spinal cord injury patients because of which primary mechanism?
questions.explanation: DVT and pulmonary embolism are major complications of spinal cord injury primarily because paralysed lower limb muscles lose their venous pump function, causing venous stasis. Combined with the pro-thrombotic state of major trauma and immobility, this dramatically increases DVT risk. Anticoagulation and mechanical prophylaxis (compression stockings, intermittent pneumatic compression) are essential from the acute phase.
options: Direct damage to pelvic veins from vertebral fracture
Hypotension-induced sludging of blood in leg veins
Elevated platelet count as a stress response
Venous stasis from paralysed limb muscles

questions.explanation: Patients with homozygous HbSS disease generally experience a more severe clinical phenotype, with more frequent and severe vaso-occlusive crises, compared to compound heterozygous states such as HbSC disease, which tend to have a milder though still clinically significant course. This distinction informs the intensity of perioperative precautions and the threshold for preoperative transfusion. Genotype is therefore an important factor in individualising perioperative risk assessment for sickle cell patients.
questions.question: A patient with sickle cell disease scheduled for elective surgery has a preoperative haemoglobin electrophoresis showing HbSS pattern. Compared to a patient with HbSC disease, this genotype MOST typically carries:
options: An identical clinical severity in every respect
A lower lifetime risk of any vaso-occlusive complications
A generally more severe clinical course with more frequent vaso-occlusive crises
No relevance to perioperative risk assessment
A reduced need for any perioperative precautions

questions.question: A 60-year-old woman on spironolactone for heart failure develops serum K of 6.2 mEq/L. ECG shows widened QRS complexes. The FASTEST-acting initial treatment is:
options: Insulin 10 units with 50 mL of 50% glucose
questions.explanation: Intravenous calcium gluconate acts within 1-3 minutes to stabilise cardiac membranes against hyperkalaemic arrhythmia and is the fastest-acting initial agent. It does not lower potassium concentration but protects the heart while definitive potassium-lowering measures are implemented. The onset of insulin-dextrose is 15-30 minutes; calcium resonium acts over hours.

questions.question: Which non-surgical intervention is specifically used for cervical disc disease that is NOT appropriate for lumbar disc disease?
questions.explanation: A rigid cervical collar (neck collar) is specifically used for cervical disc disease to immobilise and support the cervical spine, reducing nerve root irritation. It has no equivalent application in lumbar disc disease where lumbar corsets (softer supports) serve a different purpose. The collar restricts neck movement, reduces foraminal narrowing with extension, and provides symptomatic relief.

Toxic megacolon (colonic dilatation >6 cm with systemic toxicity: fever, tachycardia, leukocytosis) unresponsive to 24–72 hours of intensive medical therapy (IV steroids, ciclosporin, antibiotics) is the most common indication for emergency colectomy in UC. Perforation risk is high (>30% mortality if perforates). A subtotal colectomy with end ileostomy is performed initially; proctectomy and reconstruction are deferred.
options: Failure to achieve remission with mesalazine therapy
Toxic megacolon unresponsive to intensive medical management
Anaemia requiring more than two units of blood transfusion
Persistent diarrhoea for more than 2 weeks
questions.question: Ulcerative colitis is surgically cured by proctocolectomy. The MOST common indication for emergency surgery in ulcerative colitis is:
Catgut sutures are traditionally stored for sterilisation in which agent?
questions.explanation: Catgut sutures, derived from animal tissue, are traditionally stored in alcohol to maintain sterility and prevent premature degradation before use, since aqueous solutions could promote bacterial growth or accelerate breakdown of the material. Modern synthetic absorbable sutures have largely replaced catgut, reducing reliance on this storage method. Understanding traditional suture handling remains relevant in settings where catgut is still used.

IPPA stands for Inspection, Palpation, Percussion, and Auscultation — the four components of systematic physical examination. This sequence is followed in examining any body region and ensures comprehensive physical assessment of the surgical patient.
questions.question: IPPA in surgical physical examination stands for:
Tinea capitis refers to fungal infection of the:
questions.explanation: Tinea capitis (ringworm of the scalp) is a dermatophyte infection of the scalp and hair, common in children. Tinea cruris involves the groin, tinea pedis involves the interdigital spaces (athlete's foot), tinea unguium involves the nails, and tinea corporis involves the smooth skin of the body.

questions.question: Tick paralysis is clinically similar to GBS but is immediately distinguished and treated by:
questions.explanation: Tick paralysis is caused by a neurotoxin secreted from the salivary glands of an embedded female tick, which develops 4-7 days after attachment. It causes ascending flaccid paralysis similar to GBS. The critical distinction and treatment is identification and removal of the tick, after which neurological recovery typically begins within 1-2 hours. Untreated tick paralysis has a mortality of approximately 12%.

Preoperative cross-matching identifies compatible donor blood units held in reserve so that transfusion can proceed rapidly if significant intraoperative or postoperative blood loss occurs. It is a safety measure rather than a diagnostic or therapeutic tool for other conditions. The extent of cross-matching required depends on the anticipated blood loss of the specific procedure.
options: Determine the patient's need for postoperative iron therapy
Replace the need for intraoperative fluid management
Ensure compatible blood is immediately available if transfusion becomes necessary
Confirm the patient's blood pressure will remain stable
questions.question: The primary purpose of preoperative cross-matching of blood for a patient undergoing a procedure with anticipated significant blood loss is to:
A patient with suspected mesenteric ischaemia has a plain abdominal X-ray showing 'thumb printing' of the bowel wall. This indicates:
questions.explanation: Thumb printing (pseudopolyps) represents submucosal oedema and haemorrhage causing rounded protrusions into the bowel lumen, visible as thumbprint-like indentations on the bowel wall on plain film or barium enema. It indicates ischaemic or infective colitis. Pneumatosis intestinalis (gas within the bowel wall) indicates transmural infarction.
options: Paralytic ileus secondary to opioid administration
Cervical cord is more prone to ischaemia
Cervical myelopathy is less common than lumbar myelopathy
Cervical fractures rarely produce neurological deficit
Lumbar stenosis is more rapidly fatal than cervical stenosis
Lumbar disc prolapse compresses cauda equina more readily
questions.explanation: The lumbar vertebral canal is narrow relative to the cervical canal, meaning even a modest disc prolapse can significantly compress neural structures including the cauda equina. The wider cervical canal provides a larger buffer before cord compression occurs. This anatomical difference explains the higher incidence of cauda equina syndrome with lumbar disc disease.
questions.question: The vertebral canal in the cervical region is described as wide relative to the lumbar region. Which clinical implication directly follows from this anatomical fact?

questions.explanation: A recognised mucosal perforation during pyloromyotomy should be repaired immediately with fine absorbable sutures, often reinforced with an omental patch, and the myotomy can then be completed either at the same or a slightly rotated site to avoid the repair. Prompt recognition and repair prevent postoperative peritonitis from leakage of gastric content. This is a well-described technical complication that surgeons must be prepared to manage during the procedure.
questions.question: An infant undergoing Ramstedt's pyloromyotomy has the mucosa inadvertently perforated during the muscle-splitting incision. The appropriate intraoperative management is to:
options: Abandon the operation entirely and reschedule for another day
Convert immediately to a formal pyloroplasty without repair
Close the mucosal perforation with fine sutures and continue the myotomy at a different site
Ignore the small perforation as it will heal spontaneously
Increased renal phosphate excretion from tubular injury
Excessive dietary phosphate loss through malabsorption
Intracellular shift of phosphate driven by insulin release during refeeding
Loss of phosphate through vomiting alone
questions.explanation: Refeeding after prolonged starvation stimulates insulin release, which drives phosphate, along with potassium and magnesium, into cells for use in glycolysis and ATP synthesis, precipitating severe hypophosphataemia known as refeeding syndrome. This can cause muscle weakness, respiratory failure, and cardiac dysfunction if unrecognised. Careful, gradual reintroduction of nutrition with electrolyte monitoring prevents this complication.
questions.question: A patient develops sudden severe hypophosphataemia after starting refeeding following prolonged starvation. Serum phosphate is 0.3 mg/dL with muscle weakness. The underlying mechanism is:

options: Serial oesophageal dilatation under endoscopic guidance
Surgical excision of the stricture and pharyngoplasty
Gastrostomy for nutritional support without stricture treatment
Repeat radiotherapy to improve tissue oxygenation
questions.explanation: Post-radiation strictures of the oesophagus and hypopharynx are initially managed by serial dilatation (bougie or balloon), which mechanically disrupts the fibrotic stenosis. Multiple sessions are often required. Surgical intervention is considered for refractory cases. Nutritional support via nasojejunal tube or gastrostomy is adjunctive but not a substitute for treating the stricture.
questions.question: A patient develops dysphagia and regurgitation of undigested food months after receiving radiotherapy for a neck cancer. Endoscopy shows a smooth, tight stricture at the hypopharynx. The MOST appropriate initial treatment is:

questions.explanation: Hydrocephalus is present in 80–95% of cases of myelomeningocele, most commonly due to associated Chiari II malformation causing CSF flow obstruction. However, approximately 10% of cases may not require ventriculoperitoneal shunting as the hydrocephalus may be arrested. Criteria for shunting include rapid ventricular enlargement and developmental delay.
questions.question: Hydrocephalus is present in what proportion of patients with myelomeningocele?

questions.explanation: The Parkland formula uses Ringer's lactate at 3-4ml x weight (kg) x %TBSA over 48 hours. Half is given within the first 8 hours of the burn, and the remaining half over 16 hours. In day 2, half of the first day's fluid is administered. It is the most widely used burns resuscitation formula.
options: Normal saline: 4ml x weight x %TBSA in first 24 hours
Dextran-70: 2ml x weight x %TBSA over 24 hours
5% dextrose: 3ml x weight x %TBSA over 12 hours
Ringer's lactate: 3-4ml x weight (kg) x %TBSA over 48 hours
questions.question: The Parkland formula for burns resuscitation uses:
A child is found to have three minor anomalies on physical examination. What is the probability that a major anomaly is also present?
questions.explanation: When three or more minor anomalies are identified in a single patient during physical examination, there is a 90% probability of a concurrent major anomaly. This rule is applicable in paediatric assessments and guides the clinician to pursue thorough systemic evaluation. It is particularly relevant in congenital hand deformity assessment where associated syndromes must be excluded.

Excessive abduction of the arm beyond 90 degrees on an armboard can stretch the brachial plexus, causing a traction injury that may present as postoperative weakness or sensory changes in the upper limb. Careful positioning with arms abducted less than 90 degrees reduces this risk. Awareness of positioning-related nerve injuries is an important aspect of perioperative patient safety.
options: Brachial plexus injury from excessive arm abduction
Pressure sores over the sacrum only in this position
Increased risk of aspiration pneumonia specifically from this position
Acute compartment syndrome of the forearm in all cases
questions.question: A patient undergoing a lengthy operation under general anaesthesia is positioned supine with arms extended on armboards. A recognised complication of this positioning is:
A patient with a head injury develops clear fluid leaking from the nose that, when tested, is positive for beta-2 transferrin. What does this specific test confirm?
options: Epistaxis from a nasal mucosal tear
questions.explanation: Beta-2 transferrin is a protein found specifically in cerebrospinal fluid and is not present in normal nasal secretions, making its detection in fluid leaking from the nose after head trauma a specific and reliable confirmatory test for cerebrospinal fluid rhinorrhoea, indicating a skull base fracture with dural breach. This differs from non-specific findings such as simple nasal discharge from allergy or infection, which would not contain this marker. Confirming CSF leak is important because of the associated risk of ascending meningitis and the potential need for surgical repair.

options: It determines the exact date surgery must be performed
It has no bearing on long-term prognosis
It only affects cosmetic outcome of the repair
It predicts likely ambulatory potential and bladder and bowel function
It solely determines whether hydrocephalus will develop
questions.explanation: The functional neurological level, based on the lowest preserved motor and sensory function, correlates with expected long-term outcomes such as ambulatory potential, and bladder and bowel continence, which may differ from the anatomical (bony) level of the spinal defect. This functional assessment is therefore more clinically useful for prognostication and rehabilitation planning than the bony level alone. It does not by itself dictate hydrocephalus risk, which relates more to the presence and severity of associated Chiari II malformation.
questions.question: A neonate with myelomeningocele has motor and sensory examination performed to determine the functional level of the lesion. Why is determining this functional level clinically important beyond the anatomical level of the bony defect?

questions.explanation: In penetrating trauma, a non-expanding, non-pulsatile Zone II retroperitoneal haematoma may be left unexplored if the kidney appears viable, since exploration risks converting a contained injury into uncontrolled haemorrhage or unnecessary nephrectomy. This differs from blunt trauma, where penetrating injuries generally warrant a lower threshold for exploration. Careful intraoperative assessment guides this selective approach.
options: Mandatory exploration of all Zone II haematomas
Formal exploration only if the haematoma is pulsatile
Ligation of the renal artery as a precaution
Leave the haematoma undisturbed and observe
questions.question: A patient with a penetrating injury to Zone II of the retroperitoneum (perinephric region) sustained from a stab wound is found at laparotomy to have a contained, non-expanding haematoma. The appropriate management is:

options: Selective hepatic artery ligation with portal vein flow preservation
Occlusion of the hepatic veins via intravascular balloon catheter from the femoral approach
Temporary portocaval shunt with hepatic artery ligation
Pringle manoeuvre with infrahepatic and suprahepatic IVC clamping
Hypothermic perfusion of the liver while excising the affected segment
questions.explanation: Total hepatic vascular exclusion (veno-caval isolation) combines the Pringle manoeuvre (portal triad clamping) with suprahepatic and infrahepatic clamping of the inferior vena cava, effectively isolating the liver from the circulation to control retrohepatic vena caval or hepatic venous haemorrhage. It is technically demanding and tolerated for only 60 minutes.
questions.question: Intraoperative haemostasis of hepatic venous injuries during trauma requires hepatic veno-caval isolation. This manoeuvre involves:

options: Caecum and appendix in an inguinal hernia
Urinary bladder in a direct inguinal hernia sac
Fallopian tube and ovary in a femoral hernia
Sigmoid colon in a lateral hernia of the abdominal wall
Meckel's diverticulum in the hernia sac
questions.explanation: Littre's hernia specifically contains a Meckel's diverticulum within the hernia sac, most commonly occurring in the groin region. Its significance lies in the risk of strangulation of the diverticulum, which may not obstruct the bowel yet can undergo ischaemia and perforation. The diagnosis is often made intraoperatively during hernia repair.
questions.question: Littre's hernia contains which SPECIFIC structure as its content?

options: Periaortic lymphadenopathy near the renal vessels
Left supraclavicular lymph node enlarged from gastric metastasis
Perigastric lymph node enlargement along the lesser curvature
Sister Mary Joseph's nodule at the umbilicus
Metastatic hepatic lymph node at the porta hepatis
questions.explanation: Virchow's (Troisier's) node is an enlarged left supraclavicular lymph node (Virchow's node) caused by retrograde lymphatic spread of gastric cancer via the thoracic duct to the left venous angle. It is a sign of advanced, likely inoperable disease. Sister Mary Joseph's nodule is the umbilical metastasis, and Krukenberg tumour refers to ovarian metastases from gastric carcinoma.
questions.question: In gastric carcinoma, Virchow's node refers to:

questions.explanation: The combination of urinary tract obstruction and infection constitutes a urological emergency, since infected urine trapped behind an obstruction can rapidly progress to severe sepsis, and urgent decompression, typically by percutaneous nephrostomy or ureteric stent insertion, is required alongside appropriate antibiotics, with definitive stone treatment deferred until the infection is controlled. Attempting definitive stone removal before adequately draining an infected obstructed system risks precipitating severe septicaemia. Prompt recognition of this combination is critical to avoid a potentially life-threatening delay in treatment.
questions.question: A patient with a suspected renal colic secondary to a ureteric stone is noted to have fever and rigors alongside obstruction confirmed on imaging. This combination represents which urological emergency?
options: A simple uncomplicated stone requiring only analgesia and observation
A condition that can safely await elective outpatient management
An indication for immediate definitive stone removal without any drainage first
A presentation requiring no antibiotic therapy since obstruction is the primary issue
An infected obstructed system requiring urgent decompression

questions.explanation: An adult male at bed rest requires approximately 1,800–2,000 kilocalories per day to meet basal metabolic needs. This increases to up to 2,500 kcal/day with minimal activity. Adult females require approximately 15–20% less than males due to lower lean body mass and metabolic rate. Surgical stress, sepsis, burns, and trauma significantly increase energy requirements above these baseline values.
questions.question: An adult male at bed rest requires approximately how many kilocalories per day?

questions.explanation: Normal saline (0.9% NaCl) is the preferred crystalloid in traumatic head injury because its higher osmolality compared to Ringer's lactate reduces cerebral oedema by maintaining the osmotic gradient. Dextrose-containing fluids are avoided as they are metabolised, leaving free water that worsens cerebral swelling. Ringer's lactate can paradoxically elevate lactate levels unrelated to tissue acidosis.
questions.question: In managing haemorrhagic shock, which crystalloid solution is specifically indicated for patients with traumatic head injury?

options: Pure sensory loss without motor deficit
questions.explanation: Cerebellar haemorrhage characteristically presents with ataxia, vertigo, dysmetria, nausea and vomiting, and inability to stand or walk — reflecting cerebellar dysfunction. Pontine haemorrhage produces cranial nerve deficits and coma. Basal ganglia/internal capsule bleeds cause hemiparesis and dysphasia. Cortical haemorrhage produces focal deficits matching the cortical area involved.
questions.question: Haemorrhage from a cerebellar arteriovenous malformation (AVM) or hypertensive cause produces which specific neurological symptoms?

questions.explanation: Any mechanism with potential for significant energy transfer to the spine (high-speed MVA, falls from height, diving injuries, ejection from vehicle, sporting collisions) should prompt spinal immobilisation until injury is excluded. The mechanism of injury is the primary trigger for immobilisation, not the presence of symptoms, because pain may be masked by altered consciousness, other injuries, or intoxication.
questions.question: In the assessment of a trauma patient for potential spinal injury, which mechanism of injury should always prompt spinal immobilisation?
options: Low-speed rear-end motor vehicle collision only
Falls from less than standing height only
Any mechanism with significant energy transfer
Sports injuries limited to the upper limbs
Only penetrating injuries directly to the spine
Increasing cardiac output via catecholamine release
Reducing myocardial mass and contractile function
questions.question: Impaired organ function is a consequence of nutritional depletion, which specifically affects cardiovascular function through which mechanism?
questions.explanation: Severe nutritional depletion causes tissue wasting that extends to the heart, reducing myocardial mass, sarcomere density, and contractile function. This cardiac cachexia manifests as reduced ejection fraction, impaired response to haemodynamic stress, and increased surgical anaesthetic risk. Combined with impaired immune and respiratory function, cardiac involvement from malnutrition significantly elevates perioperative mortality.

ASA class 3 denotes a patient with poorly controlled systemic disease that limits activity but is not immediately life-threatening. ASA 1 is a normal healthy patient, ASA 2 is well-controlled systemic illness, ASA 4 is incapacitating disease, and ASA 5 is a moribund patient.
questions.question: An ASA classification of 3 indicates:
A 65-year-old man presents with sudden onset severe abdominal pain, a 'silent' abdomen, and rapid deterioration. His ECG shows atrial fibrillation. The MOST likely cause is:
questions.explanation: Atrial fibrillation is the most common predisposing condition for superior mesenteric artery embolism, which causes sudden severe abdominal pain with absent bowel sounds (silent abdomen) and rapid clinical deterioration due to massive bowel ischaemia. The pain-to-signs disproportion early in the condition is a hallmark finding.

Neuroradiology in multitrauma patients must be balanced against abdominal injury assessment and haemorrhage control, as intra-abdominal haemorrhage is rapidly life-threatening. Competing priorities in the multiply injured patient include fluid resuscitation vs brain swelling, airway maintenance vs C-spine protection, and head/spine injury management vs abdominal injury. The ATLS primary survey framework addresses these competing priorities systematically.
questions.question: In a multiple trauma patient with a suspected spinal injury, the neurosurgical priority for neuroradiology must be balanced with which competing trauma management priority?

options: Cerebellar-pons circuit for procedural memory extinction
Amygdala-prefrontal circuit failure to inhibit fear
Hippocampus-basal ganglia circuit for declarative memory inhibition
Thalamo-cortical circuit for sensory memory suppression
Locus coeruleus-hippocampus circuit for arousal regulation
questions.explanation: In PTSD, the medial prefrontal cortex (particularly the ventromedial prefrontal cortex) fails to adequately inhibit amygdala fear responses, preventing normal fear memory extinction. Normally, repeated exposure to fear cues without danger leads to extinction learning (prefrontal inhibition of amygdala). PTSD disrupts this circuit, causing persistent amygdala-driven fear responses to trauma reminders. This circuit failure is the neurobiological target for exposure-based psychotherapies and pharmacotherapies.
questions.question: Post-traumatic stress disorder involves intrusive traumatic memories that are abnormally persistent. The brain circuit most responsible for this failure of fear memory extinction involves:
A patient presents with profuse, bright red, painless rectal bleeding that stops spontaneously. The MOST likely underlying diagnosis in an elderly patient is:
questions.explanation: Painless, profuse, bright red rectal bleeding that stops spontaneously in an elderly patient is most characteristically caused by diverticular bleeding, arising from erosion of a vessel within a diverticulum. This differs from anal fissure, which typically causes pain with defecation and smaller volumes of bleeding. Colonoscopy is used both to confirm the diagnosis and to exclude other significant colorectal pathology, particularly malignancy.

options: Ensuring adequate oxygenation, hydration, and temperature control
Routine exchange transfusion preoperatively in all cases
questions.explanation: In sickle cell disease, preventing sickling is paramount: adequate oxygenation prevents hypoxaemia, adequate hydration prevents circulatory stasis, and temperature control prevents cold-induced vasoconstriction and sickling. Tourniquet use is carefully considered due to ischaemia risk.
questions.question: The most important anesthetic consideration for a sickle cell patient undergoing elective surgery is:

questions.explanation: Grade III internal haemorrhoids prolapse outside the anal canal but can be manually reduced by the patient, distinguishing them from grade I, which do not prolapse, grade II, which prolapse but reduce spontaneously, and grade IV, which remain permanently prolapsed and irreducible. This grading system helps guide the choice of treatment, ranging from conservative measures for lower grades to surgical haemorrhoidectomy for higher grades. Accurate grading is important for counselling patients on expected treatment outcomes.
questions.question: Haemorrhoidal prolapse that can be manually reduced by the patient represents which grade of internal haemorrhoids?
A patient with a long-standing chronic venous leg ulcer is being assessed. The MOST important initial investigation before commencing compression bandaging is:
questions.explanation: Before applying compression bandaging for a presumed venous ulcer, the ankle-brachial pressure index must be measured to exclude significant coexisting arterial disease, since compression can precipitate critical limb ischaemia in patients with compromised arterial supply. This safety check is essential in any leg ulcer of uncertain aetiology. Other investigations may be useful adjuncts but do not address this immediate safety concern before treatment.
options: Full blood count without any vascular assessment
Chest radiograph to exclude cardiac causes
Ankle-brachial pressure index to exclude significant arterial disease

questions.explanation: Spinal shock refers to the temporary loss of all reflex activity below the level of a spinal cord injury immediately after trauma, distinct from neurogenic shock, which specifically refers to the haemodynamic disturbance of hypotension and bradycardia from loss of sympathetic tone; spinal shock typically resolves over days to weeks as spinal reflex arcs gradually return, often evolving into a spastic pattern. Confusing these two related but distinct terms can lead to incorrect assumptions about prognosis and expected examination findings in the early post-injury period. Recognising the expected evolution helps in serial neurological assessment after acute injury.
options: Neurogenic shock, resolving once blood pressure is restored with fluids
Autonomic dysreflexia, resolving once the bladder is decompressed
Central cord syndrome, resolving once swelling reduces completely
Spinal shock, resolving as reflex arcs recover
Cauda equina syndrome, resolving after surgical decompression
questions.question: A patient with acute traumatic spinal cord injury is initially areflexic with flaccid paralysis below the level of injury in the first hours after trauma. What is this early phase called, and what determines its resolution?

options: Delayed angioembolisation after 24 hours of observation
Conservative management with serial imaging alone
Ureteric stenting as the primary intervention
Renal biopsy to confirm the extent of injury first
questions.explanation: A Grade V renal injury with a shattered kidney or renal pedicle avulsion in a haemodynamically unstable patient requires prompt nephrectomy to achieve haemorrhage control, since renal reconstruction is rarely feasible with this degree of injury. Delaying definitive control in an unstable patient risks fatal exsanguination. Stable patients with lower-grade injuries may be managed conservatively, but instability changes the calculus entirely.
questions.question: In the management of a patient with a Grade V renal injury from blunt trauma who is haemodynamically unstable despite resuscitation, the appropriate action is:

A patient with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1) is found to have a combination of parathyroid, pancreatic, and pituitary tumours. This pattern of association reflects a mutation in which gene?
options: The MEN1 tumour suppressor gene encoding menin
questions.explanation: MEN1 syndrome results from germline mutations in the MEN1 gene, which encodes the tumour suppressor protein menin, predisposing affected individuals to tumours of the parathyroid glands, pancreatic islet cells, and anterior pituitary gland, in contrast to MEN2 syndromes, which are caused by RET proto-oncogene mutations and are associated with medullary thyroid carcinoma, phaeochromocytoma, and parathyroid disease. Recognising the specific pattern of associated tumours helps direct genetic counselling and family screening once an index case is identified. Lifelong surveillance for the characteristic tumour spectrum is recommended in confirmed gene carriers.

The ASA classification (1-5) is used to communicate a patient's physical status and stratify perioperative risk. It guides preoperative optimization, anesthetic planning, and informed consent discussions, though it is not designed to predict surgical complexity or determine anesthetic technique alone.
questions.question: The ASA classification system is primarily used to:

A patient with suspected carpal tunnel syndrome has the wrist held in forced flexion for 60 seconds, reproducing numbness and tingling in the thumb, index, and middle fingers. What is this test called?
questions.explanation: Phalen's test involves holding the wrist in forced flexion for about 60 seconds, and reproduction of median nerve distribution symptoms, numbness or tingling in the thumb, index, middle, and part of the ring finger, supports a diagnosis of carpal tunnel syndrome from median nerve compression at the wrist. This is distinct from Tinel's sign, which instead involves tapping directly over the nerve at the wrist to elicit a similar distribution of symptoms through a different provocative mechanism. Correctly applying and interpreting these specific peripheral nerve compression tests supports accurate diagnosis of carpal tunnel syndrome.

Neuropathic (diabetic) foot ulcers occur at weight-bearing pressure points (plantar surface of metatarsal heads, heel, under callosities) where repetitive pressure trauma occurs without protective pain sensation. They have characteristic punched-out edges surrounded by callosity, a granulating or sloughy floor, and are typically painless due to peripheral neuropathy. Management requires debridement, offloading of pressure, glycaemic control, and treatment of infection.
questions.question: A neuropathic (diabetic) foot ulcer is most characteristically located at which site and has which edge type?
options: Weight-bearing pressure points with punched-out edges
Dorsum of foot with everted edges

questions.explanation: Clopidogrel irreversibly inhibits platelet P2Y12 receptors, and platelet function does not recover until new platelets are generated over 5-7 days. Stopping clopidogrel 5-7 days before elective surgery restores adequate platelet function and reduces surgical bleeding risk. Aspirin may be continued for most elective surgery unless neuraxial anaesthesia is planned. The thromboembolic risk of stopping must be assessed against haemorrhagic risk.
questions.question: A patient on aspirin and clopidogrel has an elective sigmoid colectomy planned. Clopidogrel should ideally be stopped:
options: It need not be stopped for elective colorectal surgery

questions.explanation: Prostatic carcinoma is not a complication of BPH; the two conditions are separate pathological entities arising from different zones of the prostate (BPH from the periurethral zone, carcinoma from the peripheral zone). BPH complications include urinary retention (acute and chronic), urinary tract infection, bladder diverticula, vesical calculi, hydroureter, hydronephrosis, renal failure, haematuria, and impaired quality of life. PSA elevation in BPH must be distinguished from malignancy.
questions.question: Complications of BPH include all of the following EXCEPT:
Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn's syndrome) presents with hypertension and which electrolyte abnormality?
questions.explanation: Conn's syndrome causes hypertension, hypokalaemia, and metabolic alkalosis from excess aldosterone driving sodium retention and potassium and hydrogen ion excretion. Renin is suppressed due to sodium expansion. CT adrenal and adrenal vein sampling differentiate unilateral adenoma (surgical) from bilateral hyperplasia (medical management with spironolactone).

questions.question: A patient with a depressed skull fracture is assessed for surgical elevation. Which factor is most important in determining the need for surgical intervention?
questions.explanation: A depressed skull fracture is generally considered for surgical elevation when the depth of depression exceeds the thickness of the adjacent skull, since this degree of depression is associated with a higher risk of underlying dural tear, cortical injury, and cosmetic deformity. Superficial findings such as bruising, headache alone, or the length of an overlying laceration are not the primary determinants of the need for surgery. This anatomical threshold helps standardise decision-making regarding operative versus conservative management of depressed fractures.
options: Any visible bruising over the fracture site
Length of the overlying scalp laceration
Depression deeper than the thickness of the skull

questions.explanation: Even after restorative proctocolectomy, metaplastic or adenomatous change can occur within the ileal pouch mucosa, particularly at the anastomotic cuff of residual rectal mucosa, meaning lifelong endoscopic surveillance of the pouch remains necessary in FAP patients. This is distinct from pouchitis, which is inflammatory rather than neoplastic. Regular pouchoscopy allows early detection and treatment of any dysplastic change.
questions.question: A patient with familial adenomatous polyposis undergoing restorative proctocolectomy with ileal pouch-anal anastomosis (IPAA) still requires ongoing surveillance of the residual pouch because:
options: The procedure eliminates all future cancer risk permanently
Adenomas can still develop within the ileal pouch mucosa over time
Surveillance is only needed if symptoms develop
IPAA converts the tissue to colonic type mucosa immune to polyps

questions.explanation: The enlarged median lobe of the prostate projects upward into the bladder and can act as a ball valve at the internal urethral orifice (vesical neck) during micturition or coughing, intermittently obstructing urine flow. This explains why some patients with a predominantly median lobe BPH have severe obstructive symptoms despite a relatively small-feeling prostate on digital rectal examination. Cystoscopy reveals this intravesical projection.
questions.question: The median lobe of the prostate, when enlarged in BPH, can cause a 'ball-valve' effect at which anatomical structure?

questions.explanation: A seatbelt sign with free fluid but no identifiable solid organ injury on CT is a recognised marker for occult hollow viscus or mesenteric injury, which can be difficult to detect on initial imaging. Delayed diagnosis of bowel perforation increases morbidity, so such patients often require close observation or diagnostic laparoscopy. This combination should heighten clinical suspicion despite reassuring solid organ findings.
questions.question: A patient with blunt abdominal trauma has a seatbelt sign across the lower abdomen and free fluid on CT without solid organ injury. This combination should raise suspicion for:

questions.explanation: Fever in the first 24-48 hours after major surgery is most commonly due to the physiological inflammatory response to surgical tissue trauma, triggering cytokine release. Pulmonary atelectasis from shallow breathing due to pain and supine positioning also contributes to early fever. Wound infection typically presents days 5-7, DVT days 5-10, anastomotic leak days 5-7, and UTI can occur throughout but usually later in the admission.
