questions.question: Postoperative fever occurring on days 1-2 following major abdominal surgery is most commonly caused by:
options: Deep vein thrombosis in the lower limbs
Response to surgical trauma and pulmonary atelectasis
Surgical wound infection at the incision site
Urinary tract infection from urethral catheterisation
Loss of vibration and proprioception; preserved pain and temperature
Loss of all sensory modalities equally
Loss of discriminative touch only; other modalities preserved
Loss of crude touch; preservation of all other modalities
Pain and temperature loss; vibration preserved
questions.explanation: Anterior cord syndrome damages the anterior two-thirds of the cord, injuring the corticospinal tracts and spinothalamic tracts but sparing the posterior columns. This produces loss of motor function, pain and temperature sensation below the lesion, while vibration sense and proprioception (carried by posterior columns) are preserved. It typically results from anterior spinal artery occlusion.
questions.question: Anterior cord syndrome is characterised by loss of which sensory modalities with preservation of which others?

A patient with newly diagnosed Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome is being investigated for an underlying malignancy. Which cancer is most classically associated with this paraneoplastic neuromuscular junction disorder?
questions.explanation: Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome has a well-established paraneoplastic association with small cell lung cancer, thought to arise because the tumour cells express voltage-gated calcium channels that trigger an antibody response cross-reacting with those at the neuromuscular junction. This strong association means that a new diagnosis of Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome should prompt thorough investigation for an underlying small cell lung cancer, particularly in patients with a significant smoking history. Other malignancies listed do not carry this same classic, strong association.

questions.question: Which statement about surgical resection in gastric carcinoma is CORRECT?
options: Total gastrectomy with D1 lymphadenectomy is adequate for all cases
Distal gastrectomy alone is sufficient regardless of tumour location
Splenectomy is always required with D2 dissection
Palliative gastrectomy has no role in symptomatic patients
D2 lymphadenectomy is standard in curative-intent surgery
questions.explanation: D2 lymphadenectomy (removing perigastric and second-tier nodal groups along the coeliac axis, left gastric, common hepatic, and splenic arteries) is the standard for curative-intent resection in gastric carcinoma in experienced centres, providing better staging and local control. D1 is perigastric nodes only. Splenectomy is no longer routinely performed unless directly involved.

options: It is supplied by somatic nerves giving well-localised pain
It produces sharply localised pain identical to the parietal layer
It is completely insensate to all forms of stimulation
It is insensitive to cutting or burning but sensitive to stretch and inflammation
It shares the same dermatomal localisation as the overlying skin
questions.explanation: The visceral peritoneum is innervated by autonomic afferents that do not respond to cutting or burning but are sensitive to stretching, distension, and chemical irritation, producing vague, poorly localised midline pain. This contrasts with the parietal peritoneum, which is somatically innervated and produces sharp, well-localised pain. This distinction explains the classic shift of pain in appendicitis from periumbilical to the right iliac fossa.
questions.question: Which statement regarding the visceral peritoneum is CORRECT?

questions.explanation: Duodenal atresia has a well-recognised association with Down syndrome, occurring in approximately a quarter to a third of affected infants, alongside congenital cardiac defects and characteristic dysmorphic facial features. Identifying duodenal atresia in a neonate should therefore prompt clinical assessment and karyotyping for trisomy 21. This association influences counselling and the need for cardiac evaluation before surgical correction.
questions.question: A newborn with duodenal atresia is noted to have associated cardiac defects and a characteristic facial appearance. This combination should prompt screening for which underlying condition?

questions.explanation: Apple peel (Christmas tree) atresia is Type IIIb jejunoileal atresia, characterised by atresia of the proximal jejunum, absence of most of the mesentery, and the distal intestine spiralling around a single marginal vessel in a helical pattern resembling an apple peel. It is associated with severe short bowel syndrome and the worst prognosis among the intestinal atresia types. It is thought to result from intrauterine vascular occlusion of the SMA.
options: Apple-peel atresia (type IIIb) with absent mesentery
Colonic atresia at the hepatic flexure
Oesophageal atresia with long-gap between the pouches
questions.question: In paediatric surgery, the term 'apple peel' atresia describes a specific variant of:
Medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) arises from which cell type and secretes which marker?
questions.explanation: Medullary thyroid carcinoma arises from the parafollicular C-cells of the thyroid gland, which are neuroendocrine cells derived from the neural crest. MTC secretes calcitonin, which serves as a specific tumour marker for diagnosis, monitoring of treatment response, and detection of recurrence. MTC is also an apudoma and can secrete other peptides including serotonin, prostaglandins, and histamine, causing diarrhoea and flushing in some patients.

First-line management of cervical disc herniation with radiculopathy without myelopathy or progressive neurological deficit is conservative treatment comprising analgesics, NSAIDs, cervical collar, and physiotherapy. The majority improve within 6–12 weeks. Surgery (anterior cervical discectomy and fusion) is considered after failed conservative management or for progressive neurological deterioration.
questions.question: A 38-year-old woman presents with neck pain radiating to the right arm in a C7 distribution (triceps weakness, middle finger numbness). MRI confirms a right paracentral C6/7 disc herniation. The FIRST treatment step is:
options: Immediate cervical traction under general anaesthesia

questions.question: A patient recovering from a mild traumatic brain injury reports persistent headache, difficulty concentrating, irritability, and dizziness for several weeks after the injury, with normal repeat imaging. What is this constellation of symptoms called?
questions.explanation: Post-concussion syndrome describes a constellation of persistent somatic, cognitive, and emotional symptoms, including headache, poor concentration, irritability, and dizziness, that can follow even mild traumatic brain injury and may persist for weeks to months despite normal structural imaging. This differs from second impact syndrome, a rare and often fatal condition related to a repeat head injury sustained before full recovery from a prior concussion, and from chronic traumatic encephalopathy, a distinct neurodegenerative condition linked to repetitive head trauma over years. Recognising post-concussion syndrome guides supportive management and appropriate return-to-activity advice.

questions.question: A patient with suspected cervical radiculopathy has neck extension, lateral flexion, and axial rotation towards the symptomatic side reproduce arm pain and paraesthesia. What is this provocative test called?
questions.explanation: Spurling's test involves extending, laterally flexing, and rotating the neck towards the symptomatic side while applying gentle axial compression, and reproduction of radicular arm pain supports a diagnosis of cervical radiculopathy from nerve root compression, typically related to disc herniation or foraminal narrowing. This differs from Lhermitte's sign, which instead involves neck flexion producing an electric shock-like sensation down the spine, classically associated with cervical cord pathology such as demyelination. Correctly performing and interpreting Spurling's test supports clinical diagnosis alongside imaging findings.

The MTOPS and CombAT trials demonstrated that combination therapy (alpha-blocker plus 5ARI, e.g., tamsulosin plus dutasteride) significantly reduces symptom progression, risk of acute urinary retention, and need for surgery compared to monotherapy in patients with moderate-to-severe symptoms and large prostates (over 40 mL). In patients with small prostates, 5ARI offers less benefit and alpha-blocker monotherapy is preferred.
questions.question: Combination therapy (alpha-blocker plus 5-alpha reductase inhibitor) for BPH is most beneficial in which patient group?
options: Mild symptoms with small prostate on USS (under 25 mL)
Any BPH patient regardless of prostate size
Moderate to severe symptoms with large prostate (>40 mL)
Young patients under 50 years with BPH
Patients who cannot tolerate alpha-blocker side effects

questions.question: A patient undergoing an anterior resection for rectal cancer has the inferior mesenteric artery ligated at its origin from the aorta ('high tie'). The main oncological rationale for this technique is to:
questions.explanation: A high tie of the inferior mesenteric artery at its aortic origin ensures complete removal of the lymphovascular pedicle and all associated lymph nodes along its course, maximising oncological clearance in colorectal cancer surgery. Some surgeons prefer a low tie to preserve marginal artery blood supply to the anastomosis, but this is a trade-off against nodal clearance. The choice can affect both oncological outcome and anastomotic perfusion.
options: Reduce operative blood loss compared with a low tie
Preserve better blood supply to the anastomosis
Avoid injury to the left ureter during dissection
Ensure removal of all lymph nodes along the vessel up to its origin

questions.question: Which investigation provides the most definitive anatomical assessment of the upper urinary tract in BPH with bilateral hydronephrosis?
options: Ultrasound of the kidneys ureter and bladder
questions.explanation: CT urogram provides the most definitive anatomical assessment of the entire urinary tract, including kidney parenchymal detail, hydronephrosis grading, ureteric calibre, and bladder morphology. It is superior to IVU in image quality, speed, and ability to evaluate surrounding structures. In patients with impaired renal function where contrast is contraindicated, ultrasound is used as the primary modality.

questions.question: The Correa cascade describes the progression to intestinal-type gastric carcinoma as:
questions.explanation: The Correa cascade describes the stepwise progression of intestinal-type gastric carcinoma: H. pylori infection ? chronic active gastritis ? chronic atrophic gastritis ? intestinal metaplasia ? dysplasia ? invasive adenocarcinoma. Each step accumulates genetic mutations. H. pylori eradication can arrest progression if applied before atrophic gastritis or metaplasia develops. This forms the basis for surveillance in high-risk populations.
options: H. pylori ? atrophy ? metaplasia ? dysplasia ? carcinoma
Normal mucosa ? GORD ? Barrett's metaplasia ? adenocarcinoma
Normal mucosa ? autoimmune gastritis ? pernicious anaemia ? adenocarcinoma
Gastric ulcer ? scar formation ? dysplasia ? ulcerating carcinoma
Normal mucosa ? polyp formation ? villous adenoma ? carcinoma

questions.question: On rectal examination, a boggy, tender swelling felt anteriorly through the rectal wall in a febrile patient most likely represents:
questions.explanation: A tender, fluctuant, boggy swelling palpable through the anterior rectal wall in a febrile patient suggests a pelvic abscess tracking into the pouch of Douglas, often complicating pelvic sepsis such as appendicitis or diverticulitis. Digital rectal examination is essential in localising deep pelvic collections not accessible to abdominal palpation. Prompt imaging and drainage are usually required.

options: Fluid requirements per kilogram body weight
questions.explanation: The Rule of Nines divides the body into regions each representing 9% of total body surface area (TBSA): head 9%, each arm 9%, chest 9%, abdomen 9%, upper back 9%, lower back 9%, each thigh 9%, each lower leg 9%, and genitalia 1%. It is used to estimate burns extent.
questions.question: The 'rule of nines' in burns management estimates:

options: Pain associated with absent peripheral pulses
Pain worsened with lumbar flexion and relieved by extension
Pain reproduced by passive straight leg raise
Pain relieved by flexion and uphill walking
questions.explanation: Neurogenic claudication from spinal stenosis is characteristically relieved by lumbar flexion (e.g., leaning on a shopping cart, sitting, or walking uphill as the spine flexes) because flexion opens the canal. Vascular claudication is reliably relieved only by rest regardless of posture. Neurogenic claudication is associated with preserved peripheral pulses and a wider pain-free walking distance in flexed postures.
questions.question: Neurogenic claudication, characteristic of lumbar spinal stenosis, is distinguished from vascular claudication by which clinical feature?

questions.explanation: Ethylene oxide gas is used for sterilizing heat- and moisture-sensitive devices, including plastics and optical devices. Its operational parameters include gas concentration (450-1200 mg/l), temperature (37-63°C), relative humidity (40-80%), and exposure time (1-6 hours).
questions.question: Ethylene oxide gas sterilization is most appropriate for:

A patient with a suspected spinal lesion has motor examination performed and is found to have increased tone, hyperreflexia, and an extensor plantar response below the level of a chronic lesion. What do these findings collectively indicate?
options: A lower motor neuron lesion pattern
Normal findings requiring no further action
A primary muscle disease rather than a neurological lesion
An upper motor neuron lesion pattern
questions.explanation: Increased tone, hyperreflexia, and an extensor plantar (Babinski) response together constitute the classic upper motor neuron lesion pattern, reflecting loss of descending inhibitory control from higher centres, as seen in chronic spinal cord lesions above the level of the anterior horn cells being tested. This contrasts with a lower motor neuron pattern, which instead produces reduced tone, reduced or absent reflexes, and flexor plantar responses, typically from lesions affecting anterior horn cells, nerve roots, or peripheral nerves themselves. Correctly recognising this pattern helps localise the lesion to the central nervous system rather than a peripheral structure.

NOTES involves performing intra-abdominal surgery by passing instruments through natural body orifices (mouth, vagina, rectum, or urethra), accessing the peritoneal cavity without any abdominal skin incision. This eliminates external scars, reduces wound-related complications, and may reduce postoperative pain. Transvaginal cholecystectomy is the most clinically practised form, though widespread adoption remains limited.
questions.question: Natural orifice transluminal endoscopic surgery (NOTES) is characterised by which distinctive approach?
options: Surgery via natural orifices without abdominal incision
Surgery through skin punctures without CO2 gas
Surgery using a single umbilical port only
Surgery controlled by a robotic system at a remote location

questions.explanation: The accessory nerve (cranial nerve XI) traverses the posterior triangle of the neck supplying the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles, and its sacrifice during neck dissection causes shoulder drop and chronic pain. Functional neck dissections attempt to preserve CN XI, the internal jugular vein, and the sternocleidomastoid. Injury results in significant functional disability and reduced quality of life.
questions.question: During a neck dissection for squamous cell carcinoma, which structure defines the posterior triangle and requires careful preservation?

questions.explanation: The left lateral decubitus position allows gas to accumulate over the right lobe of the liver, where it is clearly visible, and is used when the patient cannot stand. It is as sensitive as an erect film for detecting pneumoperitoneum. An erect film with the patient standing remains the standard when feasible.
questions.question: A patient is positioned with the left side down for an erect chest X-ray to detect pneumoperitoneum. This is preferred when:
options: Patient is too tall for a standard erect film
Gasless abdomen pattern makes upright view uninformative
Barium contrast is expected to obscure subdiaphragmatic gas
Patient cannot stand due to haemodynamic instability

questions.question: A patient with chronic low back pain is advised on core strengthening exercises. What is the primary functional role of the paraspinal musculature in relation to the vertebral column?
options: Forming the primary weight-bearing structure alone
Replacing the function of the intervertebral disc
questions.explanation: The muscular support surrounding the spinal column, including the paraspinal and core musculature, provides dynamic stability, assisting the more passive ligamentous and bony structures in maintaining posture and controlling movement, which is why muscle strengthening is a key component of managing many forms of mechanical back pain. Muscles do not replace the disc's load-bearing or shock-absorbing role, nor do they prevent degeneration entirely, though they can reduce mechanical strain contributing to symptoms. This is the physiological rationale behind core stability rehabilitation programmes.

options: Pouch at the gallbladder neck-cystic duct junction
A diverticulum of the common bile duct causing bile stasis
A dilated segment of the common hepatic duct above a stricture
A periampullary pouch adjacent to the duodenal papilla
A portion of the gallbladder fundus prone to calculi
questions.question: Which of the following CORRECTLY describes the Hartmann's pouch in relation to the biliary tract?
questions.explanation: Hartmann's pouch is an outpouching at the junction of the gallbladder neck and cystic duct where gallstones frequently impact, causing cystic duct obstruction and acute cholecystitis. A large stone impacted in Hartmann's pouch can compress the adjacent common hepatic duct, causing Mirizzi syndrome. Identification of Hartmann's pouch is an important landmark during laparoscopic cholecystectomy.

questions.question: A patient with rectal cancer who has a preoperative colostomy formed is offered chemotherapy before surgery. This sequence of treatment is called:
questions.explanation: Neoadjuvant (preoperative) therapy refers to chemotherapy and/or radiotherapy given before definitive surgical resection, with the aim of downstaging the tumour, increasing the likelihood of curative resection, and eliminating micrometastatic disease. Adjuvant therapy is given after surgery to reduce recurrence risk. Neoadjuvant chemoradiation is standard of care for locally advanced rectal cancer, improving sphincter preservation rates and reducing local recurrence.

questions.question: Femoral hernias have a high strangulation rate because of which anatomical feature?
options: The femoral canal has rich blood supply making contents vulnerable
Rigid femoral ring prevents sac expansion
Femoral hernias always contain multiple loops of bowel
Femoral hernias always contain the bladder
Femoral hernias occur mainly in obese patients where reduction is difficult
questions.explanation: Femoral hernias have a high strangulation rate because the femoral ring has rigid unyielding boundaries: the inguinal ligament anteriorly, lacunar ligament medially, pectineal ligament posteriorly, and femoral vein laterally. These rigid boundaries prevent expansion, causing early strangulation. The strangulation risk in femoral hernias is approximately 5 times that of inguinal hernias.

questions.question: Anencephaly results from failure of neural tube closure at which end?
questions.explanation: Anencephaly results from failure of closure at the rostral (cranial) neuropore, leading to absence of the forebrain and calvaria. Closure of the caudal neuropore failure produces lumbosacral spina bifida. Anencephaly is incompatible with sustained postnatal survival and is typically lethal within hours to days of birth.

Marjolin's ulcer is a malignant transformation (typically squamous cell carcinoma) occurring in chronic burn scars, particularly long-standing unstable scars over many years. It underscores the need for adequate primary treatment and long-term follow-up of burns patients.
questions.question: Marjolin's ulcer represents:
options: Venous ulcer secondary to burns contracture
Radiation necrosis of a skin graft

questions.question: A surgeon sustains a needlestick injury from a patient of unknown HIV status during an operation. The MOST appropriate immediate first step is to:
questions.explanation: Immediate first aid involves thorough washing of the wound with soap and water without vigorous squeezing, followed by prompt reporting through the occupational exposure protocol so that risk assessment and, if indicated, post-exposure prophylaxis can be initiated as soon as possible. Vigorous squeezing does not reduce transmission risk and may increase local tissue trauma. Source patient testing, where possible, guides further management.
options: Start post-exposure prophylaxis before any wound care
Squeeze the wound vigorously to force out blood
Apply a tourniquet proximal to the injury site
Ignore the injury if the patient appears clinically well
Wash the wound thoroughly with soap and water and report the injury
Absolutely diagnostic of tuberculosis without need for further testing
Indicative exclusively of lymphoma and never tuberculosis
Suggestive but not diagnostic, requiring tissue or fluid confirmation
A normal variant requiring no further evaluation
Diagnostic only of malignancy, excluding infective causes
questions.explanation: While necrotic mesenteric lymph nodes with central low attenuation, mesenteric thickening, and high-attenuation ascites are highly suggestive of abdominal tuberculosis on CT, these findings overlap with other conditions such as lymphoma and metastatic disease, so tissue diagnosis through biopsy, ascitic fluid analysis, or laparoscopy remains necessary for definitive confirmation. Imaging findings guide the differential diagnosis and the choice of further investigation. Empirical anti-tuberculous therapy without any confirmatory testing is generally discouraged except in specific resource-limited circumstances.
questions.question: A patient with suspected abdominal tuberculosis has contrast-enhanced CT showing high-attenuation ascites, mesenteric thickening, and lymph nodes with central low attenuation (necrotic nodes). This nodal appearance on CT is considered:
A Richter's hernia is defined as one in which:
questions.explanation: A Richter's hernia is one where only part of the bowel circumference (specifically the antimesenteric border) herniates through the defect, without complete bowel obstruction. This is particularly dangerous because the bowel can strangulate and perforate without causing classic signs of intestinal obstruction, leading to delayed diagnosis. The absence of obstructive symptoms in a patient with an irreducible hernia should raise suspicion for Richter's hernia.
options: The entire bowel circumference is incarcerated in the hernia sac
A Meckel's diverticulum forms part of the hernia sac
Only part of the bowel wall (antimesenteric border) herniates
The hernial sac slides through the posterior abdominal wall

questions.question: Risk factors for soft tissue infections include all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Hypertension is not a direct risk factor for soft tissue infections, although it may contribute to arterial disease. Established risk factors include diabetes mellitus (impairs neutrophil function and microcirculation), IV drug use (introduces organisms), lymphoedema (impairs local immunity), liver cirrhosis (reduces opsonins), and conditions like HIV/AIDS, neutropenia, and chronic renal disease that impair host defences.

questions.question: Which statement BEST distinguishes diastolic heart failure from systolic heart failure?
questions.explanation: Diastolic heart failure is characterised by failure to relax and/or fill normally, with manifestations relating to elevated filling pressures rather than reduced ejection fraction. Causes include constrictive pericarditis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and myocardial fibrosis. The ejection fraction is typically preserved in pure diastolic failure.
options: Diastolic failure has lower ejection fraction
Diastolic failure results from impaired relaxation or filling
Systolic failure manifests with elevated filling pressures only
Systolic failure is more common in hypertensive disease
Diastolic failure never causes pulmonary congestion

questions.question: Implicit memory differs from explicit (declarative) memory primarily in that implicit memory is:
questions.explanation: Implicit (non-declarative) memory encompasses skills and habits that are recalled unconsciously without deliberate effort — for example, riding a bicycle, playing an instrument, or conditioned reflexes. Unlike explicit memory (which requires conscious retrieval and fades without practice), implicit memory can last for life even without practice. It is stored in the cerebellum, striatum, and premotor cortex rather than the hippocampus.
options: Limited to factual knowledge of people and events
Unconsciously recalled; lasts life-long without practice

questions.explanation: Dimorphic fungi exhibit thermal dimorphism: they grow as moulds at ambient environmental temperatures (approximately 25°C) and convert to the yeast form at body temperature (37°C) in the host. This transformation is critical to their pathogenicity. Examples include Histoplasma, Coccidioides, and Blastomyces.
questions.question: Dimorphic fungi grow as moulds at environmental temperatures and as yeasts at:

options: Solely from the inferior thyroid artery from the thyrocervical trunk
Superior thyroid artery from internal carotid and multiple inferior arteries
Middle thyroid artery from the aortic arch primarily
Superior thyroid from external carotid; inferior from thyrocervical trunk
Inferior thyroid artery only, with dual drainage veins
questions.explanation: The thyroid receives blood from the superior thyroid artery (first branch of the external carotid artery) and the inferior thyroid artery (from the thyrocervical trunk of the subclavian artery). An inconstant thyroid ima artery may arise from the aortic arch. The recurrent laryngeal nerve runs in close proximity to the inferior thyroid artery, making ligation near the nerve dangerous.
questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the blood supply to the thyroid gland?

questions.explanation: POEM (Per-Oral Endoscopic Myotomy) is a minimally invasive technique where the endoscopist creates a submucosal tunnel in the oesophagus and then divides the inner circular muscle layer from within, extending to the gastric cardia. Unlike Heller myotomy, it does not include an anti-reflux procedure, resulting in higher rates of post-procedural GORD. It is particularly effective for Type III achalasia.
questions.question: The PERORAL ENDOSCOPIC MYOTOMY (POEM) procedure for achalasia differs from Heller myotomy in that it:
options: Divides the outer longitudinal muscle layer only
Approaches the LOS through a submucosal tunnel endoscopically
Requires open thoracotomy for adequate visualisation
Creates a complete circumferential myotomy of the entire oesophagus
Is combined with a posterior fundoplication to prevent reflux

questions.question: A patient presents with acute diverticulitis complicated by a pericolic abscess measuring 3 cm, without generalised peritonitis. The most appropriate initial management is:
questions.explanation: A localised pericolic abscess complicating diverticulitis without generalised peritonitis is typically managed with intravenous antibiotics, and if the abscess is of sufficient size or fails to resolve, image-guided percutaneous drainage is added. Emergency resection is reserved for generalised peritonitis or failure of this conservative approach. Colonoscopy is deferred during the acute phase due to perforation risk and performed later to exclude malignancy.
options: Elective colonoscopy performed the same day
Intravenous antibiotics with percutaneous drainage if the abscess persists
Laparoscopic peritoneal lavage as first-line treatment

questions.question: Long-term memory consolidation depends on which molecular process NOT required for short-term memory?
questions.explanation: Long-term memory requires new protein synthesis (gene expression and translation of new structural and regulatory proteins) at the synapse and cell body, producing lasting structural changes (increased dendritic spines, new synapse formation). This is why protein synthesis inhibitors (cycloheximide, anisomycin) block long-term but not short-term memory in experimental models. Short-term memory relies only on modification of existing synaptic machinery.
options: Increased neurotransmitter release at existing synapses
Local calcium ion entry at synapses
New protein synthesis and gene expression changes

questions.question: Regarding theatre design for reducing airborne contamination during orthopaedic implant surgery, the MOST critical feature is:
questions.explanation: Ultraclean laminar airflow systems deliver a continuous stream of filtered air over the operative field, diluting and removing airborne bacteria-carrying particles, which is particularly important in implant surgery where infection can have devastating consequences. Structural or aesthetic features such as wall colour or ceiling height have no meaningful impact on airborne contamination control. This ventilation design is a key evidence-based feature of modern orthopaedic theatres.
options: Wall colour scheme within the theatre
Number of windows in the operating room
Ultraclean laminar airflow ventilation over the operative field

questions.explanation: Ultrasound demonstrating the triangular cord sign (echogenic tissue >3 mm anterior to the portal vein bifurcation) at the porta hepatis is the most specific initial investigation for biliary atresia (sensitivity 80%, specificity 98%). The HIDA scan assesses biliary excretion but is non-specific. Liver biopsy with bile duct proliferation and fibrosis is highly suggestive. Final diagnosis requires intraoperative cholangiography.
options: Ultrasound for the triangular cord sign at the porta hepatis
Serum total and direct bilirubin fractionation
HIDA (hepatobiliary iminodiacetic acid) scan assessing bile excretion
Liver biopsy showing bile duct proliferation versus giant cell hepatitis
Serum GGT level, which is specifically elevated in biliary atresia
questions.question: A 6-week-old male presents with jaundice. The MOST important initial investigation to differentiate biliary atresia from neonatal hepatitis is:

questions.explanation: Alkalinization with 88-132 mEq of Na2CO3 aids kidney filtration and prevents myoglobin from precipitating in the renal tubules, which can cause acute tubular necrosis and renal failure. Electrical burns cause widespread muscle necrosis releasing large amounts of myoglobin.
questions.question: Alkalinization of urine in electrical burns prevents:

options: Extensive peritoneal adhesions matting loops of bowel together
Luminal narrowing from stricture formation after ulcer healing
Peritoneal studding with miliary tubercles causing ileus
questions.question: The plastic type of abdominal tuberculosis causes bowel obstruction primarily by:
questions.explanation: The plastic (adhesive) type of abdominal tuberculosis causes intestinal obstruction through extensive fibrinous peritoneal adhesions that mat loops of small bowel together, creating a 'matted' abdomen. This differs from the ascitic type (free fluid) and glandular type (mesenteric lymphadenopathy). Surgery for adhesive obstruction carries high risk of fistula formation due to the friable, diseased bowel.

questions.question: Rhabdomyolysis as a cause of acute muscle weakness is associated with elevation of which specific muscle enzyme?
questions.explanation: Rhabdomyolysis causes release of intracellular muscle contents including creatine kinase (CK) and aldolase, which are markedly elevated in the serum. Very high CK levels (often >10,000 U/L) confirm significant muscle destruction. Myoglobin released from rhabdomyolysis causes acute tubular necrosis and renal failure. Treatment includes vigorous IV fluid hydration to protect the kidneys from myoglobin-induced injury.

options: Lower cost and wider global availability
Greater range of instrument motion (EndoWrist technology)
Intuitive controls with ergonomic surgeon positioning
questions.question: Compared to conventional laparoscopy, robotic-assisted surgery is NOT advantaged by which characteristic?
questions.explanation: The primary disadvantage of robotic-assisted surgery (da Vinci system) is its significantly higher cost, both capital expenditure and disposable instruments, and limited worldwide availability compared to conventional laparoscopy. Its advantages include 7-degrees-of-freedom EndoWrist instruments, 3D high-definition magnified vision, tremor filtration, and ergonomic surgeon positioning. It is particularly advantageous for radical prostatectomy and partial nephrectomy.

questions.question: Poor retrieval cues as a cause of forgetting implies that memories are not lost but are simply:
questions.explanation: Poor retrieval cues represent a form of forgetting in which memories are stored but cannot be accessed without appropriate associative triggers (context, mood, smell, or related concepts). The memory trace exists but retrieval fails. This is the 'tip of the tongue' phenomenon at an extreme. Providing cues ('it begins with S...') can restore access. This has practical implications for testimony reliability and for designing better learning strategies.

options: Malignant obstruction of the common bile duct
Mirizzi syndrome from extrinsic bile duct compression
questions.explanation: Courvoisier's law states that in obstructive jaundice with a palpable gallbladder, gallstones are an unlikely cause because the chronically inflamed gallbladder is fibrotic and non-distensible. A distensible gallbladder implies malignant obstruction, most commonly pancreatic head carcinoma. The law has moderate sensitivity but remains a useful clinical pearl.
questions.question: Courvoisier's law states that a palpable, non-tender gallbladder in a jaundiced patient suggests:
A cancer patient receiving external beam radiotherapy to the pelvis is warned about possible late radiation effects. Teratogenesis and carcinogenesis from radiation exposure are classified as:
questions.explanation: Stochastic effects of radiation, such as carcinogenesis and teratogenesis, have no defined threshold dose below which risk is eliminated, with probability of occurrence increasing with dose but severity independent of dose. This contrasts with deterministic effects, such as skin erythema or radiation sickness, which have a threshold below which the effect does not occur. Understanding this distinction is important for radiation protection counselling.
options: Stochastic effects without a defined threshold dose
Deterministic effects with a clear threshold dose
Immediate effects occurring within hours of exposure
Effects limited exclusively to reproductive organs
Effects that only occur following brachytherapy, not teletherapy

questions.question: Which of the following is the commonest cause of intestinal obstruction from a hernia in adults?
questions.explanation: Indirect inguinal hernias are the commonest cause of hernia-related intestinal obstruction in adults because they are the most prevalent type of abdominal hernia. Despite femoral hernias having a higher per-incidence strangulation rate, the sheer prevalence of indirect inguinal hernias makes them numerically the most frequent cause of hernia-related obstruction. Prompt surgical repair upon diagnosis is recommended to prevent this complication.

questions.question: In a patient with suspected cervical spine injury requiring endotracheal intubation, the preferred technique to maintain spinal alignment is:
options: Rapid sequence intubation with neck extension
Blind nasotracheal intubation without neck movement
Awake fibreoptic intubation with cervical stabilisation
Bag-valve-mask ventilation until CT confirms no fracture
questions.explanation: Awake fibreoptic intubation with manual in-line cervical stabilisation (MILS) is the safest technique for definitive airway management in suspected cervical spine injury, as it allows intubation without neck extension and with continuous neurological monitoring. MILS by an assistant maintains alignment during rapid sequence intubation if fibreoptic approach is unavailable. Hyperextension without protection risks exacerbating cord injury.

questions.question: A diabetic patient develops serum phosphate of 0.5 mg/dL, muscle weakness, and haemolysis. The MOST likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: Severe hypophosphatemia (below 1 mg/dL) causes impaired oxygen delivery due to reduced 2,3-DPG, haemolytic anaemia, and skeletal muscle dysfunction including respiratory failure. It is seen in refeeding syndrome, diabetic ketoacidosis treatment, and malnutrition. Prompt phosphate replacement is essential.

questions.question: Infective endocarditis precipitates heart failure PRIMARILY through which mechanism?
questions.explanation: Infective endocarditis causes acute valvular destruction particularly of the aortic and mitral valves, resulting in severe acute regurgitation that the unprepared heart cannot accommodate, leading to flash pulmonary oedema and cardiogenic shock. Anaemia, fever, and direct myocarditis from septic emboli contribute additionally. Emergency valve surgery is often required.
options: Coronary artery embolism causing myocardial infarction

questions.explanation: Differentiating biliary atresia, which requires urgent surgical intervention, from neonatal hepatitis, which is managed conservatively, relies on hepatobiliary scintigraphy showing absent excretion into the bowel, with intraoperative cholangiography serving as the definitive confirmatory test when clinical suspicion remains high. Early diagnosis is critical because outcomes of the Kasai portoenterostomy are significantly better when performed before 8 weeks of age. Delayed diagnosis substantially worsens long-term liver outcomes.
options: Abdominal X-ray to assess bowel gas pattern
Serum bilirubin fractionation alone without imaging
Full blood count and blood film examination
Stool microscopy for ova and parasites
Hepatobiliary scintigraphy (HIDA scan) or, definitively, intraoperative cholangiography
questions.question: A 6-week-old male infant presents with jaundice, pale stools, and dark urine persisting beyond 2 weeks of age. The most important investigation to differentiate biliary atresia from neonatal hepatitis is:
Subcutaneous fibrosis in sickle cell disease is a manifestation of:
questions.explanation: Subcutaneous fibrosis in sickle cell disease is a skin manifestation resulting from recurrent ischaemic events in cutaneous and subcutaneous tissues due to sickling. Other skin manifestations include leg ulcers over bony prominences and the theoretical possibility of malignant transformation in chronic non-healing ulcers.

options: Wounds presenting more than 6 hours after injury in most body sites
Clean laceration to the face presenting within 6 hours
questions.explanation: Clean facial lacerations presenting within 6 hours are suitable for primary closure because the face has an excellent blood supply that confers resistance to infection even in contaminated wounds. Primary closure is contraindicated in heavily contaminated wounds, animal bites (high risk of polymicrobial infection), wounds presenting late (>6–12 hours in most sites), established infection, and devitalised tissue. In these cases, delayed primary closure after wound preparation is preferred.
questions.question: The contraindication to immediate primary wound closure includes all of the following EXCEPT:

options: Definite autonomous cortisol secretion requiring urgent surgery
Complete adrenal insufficiency requiring steroid replacement
Coexisting primary hyperaldosteronism confirmed by this test alone
Adequate cortisol suppression, making functional cortisol excess unlikely
questions.question: A 50-year-old woman has a 1.8 cm adrenal incidentaloma with cortisol of 95 nmol/L after an overnight dexamethasone suppression test. This result MOST suggests:
questions.explanation: Adequate suppression of cortisol following overnight dexamethasone administration suggests the adrenal incidentaloma is non-functioning with respect to cortisol production, making autonomous cortisol excess, or subclinical Cushing's syndrome, unlikely, which supports a more conservative management approach with surveillance rather than surgery. Failure to suppress would instead raise concern for autonomous cortisol secretion requiring further evaluation. This test forms part of the standard biochemical workup for any incidentally discovered adrenal mass.

questions.question: A patient with sickle cell trait, rather than sickle cell disease, is being counselled before elective surgery. The MOST accurate statement regarding perioperative risk is:
questions.explanation: Individuals with sickle cell trait generally tolerate surgery well and do not require the same intensive precautions as those with sickle cell disease, though rare complications can still occur under conditions of severe hypoxia, dehydration, or extreme physiological stress. This distinction is important to avoid unnecessary preoperative transfusion in trait carriers. Recognising the difference between trait and disease status guides appropriately tailored perioperative management.
options: Sickle cell trait carries much lower perioperative risk
Identical perioperative risk to sickle cell disease
The same transfusion protocol as sickle cell disease
No perioperative risk under any circumstance
Relevance only to fertility, not surgical risk

questions.explanation: The mnemonic SLUMPED covers the causes of high anion gap metabolic acidosis: Salicylates, Lactate, Uremia, Methanol, Paraldehyde, Ethylene glycol, Diabetes. Non-gap acidosis involves renal and gastrointestinal causes as well as certain drugs. Both mnemonics guide rapid differential diagnosis.
questions.question: Which mnemonic best identifies causes of HIGH anion gap metabolic acidosis?
Dyschromic scars in burns patients include:
questions.explanation: Dyschromic scars are characterized by abnormal pigmentation — either hypopigmented (lighter) or hyperpigmented (darker than surrounding skin). They are a distinct late complication of burns and differ from structural abnormalities such as hypertrophic scars, keloids, and contractures.

questions.question: Surgical site infection rate is MOST influenced by which patient-related factor?
questions.explanation: Diabetes mellitus impairs neutrophil function, reduces tissue oxygenation through microvascular disease, and prolongs wound healing, significantly increasing surgical site infection rates. Perioperative glycaemic control below 180 mg/dL reduces infection risk substantially. Other factors include obesity, malnutrition, and immunosuppression.

questions.question: A patient presents with profuse bleeding per rectum that is bright red, painless, and stops spontaneously. The MOST likely diagnosis in a 70-year-old is:
questions.explanation: Diverticular disease is the most common cause of massive lower GI bleeding in older patients, often presenting with sudden painless bright red rectal haemorrhage that typically stops spontaneously in 80% of cases. The right colon is the most common diverticular bleeding source despite left-sided predominance of diverticula. Angiography or colonoscopy identifies the bleeding point for intervention.

questions.question: A patient undergoing transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) using non-ionic irrigation fluid develops confusion, bradycardia, and hypertension intraoperatively. This presentation, known as TURP syndrome, results primarily from:
options: Excessive blood loss causing hypovolaemic shock
Absorption of hypotonic irrigation fluid causing dilutional hyponatraemia
An allergic reaction to the anaesthetic agent used
Acute urinary sepsis from bacterial translocation
Direct mechanical injury to the bladder wall
questions.explanation: During TURP, opened venous sinuses within the prostate can absorb significant volumes of hypotonic irrigating fluid, leading to dilutional hyponatraemia and fluid overload, which manifests as confusion, bradycardia, hypertension, and in severe cases seizures or cardiovascular collapse. This complication has become less common with the adoption of bipolar resection systems using isotonic saline irrigation. Recognising TURP syndrome promptly allows appropriate fluid restriction and, if needed, careful correction of serum sodium.

Signs suggesting inhalational injury indicate a high risk of progressive airway oedema, and early elective intubation before the airway becomes critically compromised is safer than waiting for stridor or complete obstruction to develop. Delayed intubation in this setting can become extremely difficult once swelling is advanced. Tracheostomy is reserved for cases where intubation is not feasible.
options: High-flow oxygen alone without airway intervention
Immediate tracheostomy as the first-line airway measure
Early elective airway intubation before oedema progresses
Nebulised bronchodilators as the sole intervention
questions.question: A patient sustains burns to the face with singed nasal hairs, soot in the oropharynx, and a hoarse voice after being rescued from a house fire. The MOST appropriate immediate priority is:

questions.explanation: The Trendelenburg position is used in laparoscopic pelvic surgery (rectal resections, radical prostatectomy, hysterectomy, sigmoid colectomy) to allow the small bowel to fall away from the pelvis by gravity, improving visualisation. Reverse Trendelenburg (head-up) is used for upper abdominal laparoscopic procedures such as cholecystectomy and fundoplication to displace bowel inferiorly.
options: Upper abdominal surgery such as cholecystectomy
questions.question: The Trendelenburg position (head-down tilt) is used in laparoscopic surgery for procedures in which body region?

questions.explanation: Cervical traction works by distracting the vertebrae, which widens the intervertebral foramina, reduces disc protrusion pressure on nerve roots, and stretches paraspinal muscles. This mechanical decompression relieves radicular pain without surgery. It is contraindicated in cervical myelopathy, vertebral fractures, and infections. Rigid neck collars provide immobilisation rather than distraction.
options: Reduces disc water content to relieve pressure
Induces disc resorption through mechanical shear forces
Distracts intervertebral spaces to relieve neural foraminal compression
Immobilises the facet joints to reduce inflammation
Increases intravertebral pressure to reposition nuclear material
questions.question: Conservative treatment of cervical disc disease includes cervical traction. What is the physiological basis for this treatment?

options: Functioning (hormonally active) or non-functioning, and whether it has malignant imaging features
Definitely benign without any further testing required
Amenable to observation alone regardless of size or hormonal activity
Always malignant until proven otherwise by biopsy
Best managed by immediate surgery without any biochemical workup
questions.question: A patient with an adrenal incidentaloma found on CT performed for an unrelated reason undergoes further evaluation. The initial priority in assessing this lesion is to determine whether it is:
questions.explanation: An incidentally discovered adrenal mass requires biochemical assessment to determine hormonal activity, such as screening for subclinical Cushing's syndrome, phaeochromocytoma, and primary aldosteronism, alongside imaging characteristics such as size, growth rate, and density to assess malignant potential, since both factors guide the decision between surveillance and surgical excision. Biopsy of an adrenal mass is generally avoided until phaeochromocytoma has been excluded biochemically, given the risk of precipitating a hypertensive crisis. This structured evaluation ensures that both functional and structural risks are appropriately assessed before deciding on management.

options: Installation of floor drains at multiple points
Use of ultraviolet lighting in the theatre suite
Positive pressure laminar flow ventilation system
questions.question: Regarding theatre design, which feature is MOST critical in reducing airborne contamination during surgery?
questions.explanation: Positive pressure laminar flow ventilation keeps the theatre at higher pressure than adjacent areas, preventing inward flow of contaminated air. Combined with HEPA filtration, it significantly reduces airborne particle counts. Traffic control, gowning, and instrument sterilisation are complementary measures in a multi-layered infection prevention strategy.

Chiari II malformation, characteristically associated with myelomeningocele, involves downward displacement of the cerebellar vermis, brainstem, and fourth ventricle through the foramen magnum, distinguishing it from the milder Chiari I malformation, which involves tonsillar descent alone without the more extensive brainstem and fourth ventricle involvement. Chiari II is a key contributor to the hydrocephalus commonly seen in myelomeningocele patients due to obstruction of cerebrospinal fluid outflow pathways. Recognising this specific pattern on imaging supports accurate classification and management planning.
questions.question: A neonate with a lumbar myelomeningocele also has downward displacement of the cerebellar tonsils and brainstem through the foramen magnum, along with a low-lying fourth ventricle, seen on MRI. Which malformation is this?

questions.explanation: Intravenous immunoglobulin and plasma exchange are the two treatments with the strongest evidence base for hastening recovery in Guillain-Barré syndrome, both working by modulating or removing the pathogenic autoantibodies and immune complexes responsible for peripheral nerve damage. Unlike in some other autoimmune neurological conditions, corticosteroids alone have not been shown to be effective in Guillain-Barré syndrome and are not recommended as monotherapy. Choosing between IVIG and plasma exchange often depends on availability, patient factors, and local expertise rather than a clear superiority of one over the other.
questions.question: A patient with confirmed Guillain-Barré syndrome is being considered for disease-modifying treatment. Which two treatment options have the strongest evidence base for hastening recovery?

options: Closure of the digital flexor sheaths
Formation of five separate digit rays
questions.explanation: By 46 days of embryonal life, the interdigital webs regress through programmed cell death (apoptosis), resulting in five distinct separate digits. Failure of this apoptotic process produces syndactyly. The digital rays form at day 40, and by day 46 apoptosis has separated them. This represents a critical window when teratogens or genetic mutations can cause syndactyly.
questions.question: Apoptosis of the interdigital web by day 46 of embryonal life is responsible for which normal developmental outcome?

options: Excess catecholamine secretion from chromaffin cell tumour tissue
Excess cortisol secretion from an adrenal cortical tumour
Excess aldosterone secretion causing hypertension alone
Excess parathyroid hormone secretion causing hypercalcaemia
Excess thyroid hormone secretion from an ectopic source
questions.explanation: Phaeochromocytoma arises from chromaffin cells, typically within the adrenal medulla, and secretes excess catecholamines such as adrenaline and noradrenaline, producing the classic episodic symptoms of headache, sweating, palpitations, and hypertension. Diagnosis involves measuring plasma or urinary metanephrines, which are more sensitive markers than catecholamines themselves. Preoperative alpha-blockade is essential before surgical resection to prevent a hypertensive crisis during tumour manipulation.
questions.question: Phaeochromocytoma is characterised by episodic headache, sweating, and palpitations. The BIOCHEMICAL basis for these symptoms is:
A patient with a complete spinal cord injury at T10 is assessed for motor and sensory function. Which of the following would be expected to be preserved at this level?
questions.explanation: A complete spinal cord injury at T10 spares all cervical and upper thoracic segments, so upper limb motor and sensory function should be entirely normal, while function below the level of injury, including much of the trunk, lower limbs, bladder, and bowel, is affected. This pattern of preserved function above and impaired function below the neurological level is fundamental to spinal cord injury classification. Recognising which functions remain intact helps guide rehabilitation goals and expected functional independence.

Systemic candidiasis in surgical patients follows breach of mucocutaneous barriers (from major surgery, burns, indwelling catheters, or broad-spectrum antibiotics), allowing Candida to invade the bloodstream and disseminate to vital organs. It is often fatal and carries high attributable mortality in ICU patients.
questions.question: Systemic candidiasis in surgical patients most commonly follows:
options: Mucocutaneous breach after surgery or burns

questions.explanation: A cystic lumbosacral mass with an exposed neural placode on prenatal ultrasound is characteristic of myelomeningocele, the most severe common form of spina bifida cystica. Meningocele lacks exposed neural tissue. Sacrococcygeal teratoma is a solid/cystic presacral mass. Lipomyelomeningocele is a closed defect covered by skin. Prenatal MRI can further characterise the lesion.
questions.question: A prenatal ultrasound at 18 weeks shows a cystic mass at the lumbosacral region with an open neural placode. The most likely diagnosis is:

questions.explanation: Octreotide, a somatostatin analogue, reduces pancreatic, biliary, and intestinal secretions, thereby decreasing the volume of fluid passing through an enterocutaneous fistula, which can help control output, reduce fluid and electrolyte losses, and create more favourable conditions for spontaneous closure in some patients. It does not itself provide nutrition or guarantee closure, particularly in fistulae with adverse anatomical features. Nutritional support, sepsis control, and skin protection remain equally important components of management alongside octreotide.
questions.question: A patient with a high-output enterocutaneous fistula is managed with total parenteral nutrition and octreotide. The main purpose of octreotide in this context is to:
options: Directly stimulate mucosal regeneration at the fistula site
Reduce gastrointestinal secretions and fistula output to promote healing conditions
Increase intestinal motility to promote faster transit
Provide the primary source of nutritional support
Eliminate the need for surgical closure in all cases
Skip lesions with cobblestone mucosa and non-caseating granulomas
Perianal fistulae as the presenting feature in most cases
Transverse ulcers with a tendency toward stricture formation and caseating granulomas on histology
Longitudinal serpiginous ulcers along the mesenteric border
Granulomas that are exclusively non-caseating in nature
questions.explanation: Tuberculous involvement of the ileocaecal region tends to produce transverse ulcers and circumferential strictures with caseating granulomas on histology, whereas Crohn's disease classically shows longitudinal, serpiginous ulcers, cobblestoning, skip lesions, and non-caseating granulomas. This histological and macroscopic distinction, alongside clinical and microbiological correlation, helps differentiate the two conditions when they present similarly. In endemic areas, empirical anti-tuberculous therapy is sometimes trialled when the diagnosis remains uncertain after initial investigation.
questions.question: In distinguishing ileocaecal tuberculosis from Crohn's disease affecting the same region, which feature favours a diagnosis of tuberculosis?

questions.explanation: Papillary thyroid carcinoma above 1 cm is treated with total thyroidectomy followed by radioactive iodine (I-131) ablation of residual thyroid tissue, enabling subsequent surveillance with thyroglobulin levels and whole-body scan. TSH suppression with levothyroxine reduces stimulation of any residual thyroid cancer cells. Prognosis is excellent with 10-year survival above 90%.
options: Radiotherapy to the neck and thyroid bed
Total thyroidectomy followed by radioiodine ablation
questions.question: A papillary thyroid cancer in a 35-year-old is MOST commonly treated with:

questions.explanation: Opioids (IV morphine, pethidine, pentazocine) are the mainstay of postoperative pain management. NSAIDs serve as adjuncts. Adequate analgesia is critical as pain causes postoperative hypertension, shallow breathing, retained secretions, and impairs patient recovery and mobilization.
questions.question: Opioids in postoperative pain management are best described as:
options: Adjuncts to NSAIDs for mild pain
The mainstay of postoperative pain management

questions.question: Spondylosis in the context of degenerative spinal disease most accurately refers to which process?
questions.explanation: Spondylosis refers to degenerative changes in the spine characterised by osteophyte (bone spur) formation, disc space narrowing, and end-plate sclerosis. It is distinct from spondylolisthesis (vertebral slip), spondylolysis (pars defect), and spondylitis (inflammation). Cervical and lumbar spondylosis are major causes of myelopathy and radiculopathy respectively.
options: Slipping of one vertebra over another
Congenital absence of the posterior arch
Degenerative osteophytic changes of the vertebral column
Inflammatory arthritis of the facet joints

questions.explanation: The Hoover test is a bedside manoeuvre to detect functional (non-organic) weakness. In true weakness, lifting the normal leg does not elicit a downward push from the supposedly paralysed leg; conversely, the healthy leg does not fail to push down during the attempt. Discrepancy in these expected patterns indicates non-organic weakness.
questions.question: The Hoover test is used to detect which condition in a patient claiming lower limb weakness?

questions.explanation: Vertebral body size increases progressively from cervical to lumbar levels because the lower vertebrae must bear progressively greater axial loads from the weight of the trunk and upper body above them. This is a structural adaptation to mechanical demand rather than to a need for greater canal space or rotational movement, which are actually more limited in the lumbar spine. Recognising this principle explains why lumbar burst fractures typically require substantial axial force.
options: Lumbar vertebrae bear greater axial load
Lumbar vertebrae protect the spinal cord only
Lumbar vertebrae anchor more muscles than cervical vertebrae
Lumbar vertebrae have a wider vertebral canal
questions.question: A patient sustains a burst fracture of L1. Imaging shows the vertebral body is markedly larger and more robust than a cervical vertebra. What is the primary functional reason for this size difference?
Repair of venous sinus injuries during neurosurgical trauma is technically challenging because:
questions.explanation: Dural venous sinuses (superior sagittal, transverse, sigmoid) are valveless, thin-walled structures that bleed profusely when injured. They also carry a risk of venous air embolism if the open sinus communicates with the atmospheric pressure. Their repair requires meticulous surgical technique, haemostatic packing, and often accepts some sacrifice of non-critical sinuses. The superior sagittal sinus is generally not sacrificed due to risk of fatal venous infarction.
options: Venous sinuses are located entirely outside the dural envelope
Venous sinuses carry only arterial blood at high pressure
Standard haemostatic agents are ineffective on venous bleeding
Venous sinuses: valveless and prone to air embolism
Venous sinus injuries always require ligature rather than repair

questions.explanation: Hypertrophic ileocaecal TB affects younger patients, is often associated with systemic TB features (fever, night sweats, weight loss, positive Mantoux), shows skip lesions and pull-up deformity of the caecum on colonoscopy, and may have associated mesenteric lymphadenopathy on CT. Colorectal carcinoma is more common in older patients with CEA elevation, obstruction, and bleeding. Biopsy is definitive.
options: Fresh rectal bleeding with change in bowel habit
Young age, systemic TB, and colonic skip lesions
Fixed hard mass on examination with hepatomegaly
questions.question: A patient from a TB-endemic area has a right iliac fossa mass. Features that distinguish a hypertrophic caecal TB mass from caecal carcinoma include:
The MOST appropriate management for a 3 cm subcutaneous soft tissue sarcoma of the thigh is:
questions.explanation: Wide local excision achieving clear margins of at least 1 cm with limb-sparing surgery combined with adjuvant radiotherapy is the standard treatment for resectable soft tissue sarcomas, achieving local control rates equivalent to amputation. Amputation is reserved for unresectable disease where clear margins cannot be achieved. Pre-operative imaging with MRI defines resectability.
options: Marginal excision with 1 mm clear margins
Amputation for any sarcoma above 2 cm
Wide excision with 1cm margins and radiotherapy

questions.explanation: Dysphagia lusoria (lusoria from 'sport of nature') is caused by an aberrant right subclavian artery (arteria lusoria) that arises as the last branch of the aortic arch and crosses posterior to the oesophagus, compressing it. It is the most common congenital vascular anomaly causing dysphagia. Barium swallow shows a posterior indentation at the level of T4.
options: A mediastinal goitre compressing the oesophagus anteriorly
An enlarged aortic arch aneurysm displacing the oesophagus
Lymphomatous nodes in the posterior mediastinum
Scleroderma causing aperistalsis of the lower oesophagus
questions.question: Dysphagia lusoria refers to dysphagia caused by:
Neural tube defects result from failure of which developmental process?
questions.explanation: Neural tube defects arise from failure of the neural tube to close during embryonic development, typically between the 3rd and 4th weeks of gestation. This failure results in a spectrum of anomalies including anencephaly, encephalocele, craniorachischisis totalis, and spinal dysraphism. Folic acid supplementation before and during early pregnancy significantly reduces this risk.

questions.question: A patient with a chronic discharging sinus in the natal cleft is diagnosed with a pilonidal sinus. The underlying pathological process is best described as:
questions.explanation: A pilonidal sinus results from hair penetrating the skin of the natal cleft, often driven inward by friction and movement, provoking a chronic foreign body granulomatous reaction and secondary infection that forms a sinus tract, rather than arising from any congenital or neoplastic process. This acquired mechanism explains its typical occurrence in young, hirsute adults, particularly those with occupations involving prolonged sitting. Treatment ranges from simple hygiene measures and hair removal to surgical excision for recurrent or chronic disease.
options: A congenital remnant of the neural tube
A foreign body reaction to ingrown hair penetrating the skin
An infective process caused exclusively by tuberculosis
A malignant transformation of sweat gland tissue
A remnant of the notochord persisting after birth

questions.explanation: Wound infection remains the most common overall complication after cholecystectomy, though bile duct injury is the most feared. Laparoscopic cholecystectomy has significantly reduced wound complication rates compared to open surgery. Post-cholecystectomy syndrome affects 10-15% of patients with persistent right upper quadrant symptoms from sphincter of Oddi dysfunction or retained stones.
questions.question: The MOST common complication following cholecystectomy is:
options: Bile leak from the cystic duct stump

questions.question: Damage control surgery is PRIMARILY indicated when a trauma patient develops which triad?
questions.explanation: The lethal triad of acidosis, hypothermia, and coagulopathy defines physiological exhaustion in the trauma patient, where prolonged surgery increases mortality. Damage control surgery achieves rapid haemostasis and contamination control, followed by ICU resuscitation before planned re-exploration. Recognising this triad early prevents avoidable intraoperative deaths.

questions.question: Hyperparathyroidism causes hypercalcaemia by which primary mechanism?
options: PTH-mediated osteoclast activation releasing skeletal calcium
Increased intestinal calcium absorption through vitamin D activation
Decreased renal tubular calcium excretion alone
Calcitonin suppression allowing unbridled calcium release
questions.explanation: PTH elevates serum calcium primarily by activating osteoclast-mediated bone resorption releasing skeletal calcium, and secondarily by promoting renal tubular calcium reabsorption and converting 25-hydroxyvitamin D to active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D which increases intestinal calcium absorption. All three mechanisms act simultaneously. In primary hyperparathyroidism, autonomous PTH secretion drives this process independent of serum calcium feedback.

questions.question: A patient develops hyponatraemia several days after major surgery, attributed to inappropriate secretion of antidiuretic hormone (SIADH) related to surgical stress. The characteristic urine finding in this condition is:
questions.explanation: In SIADH, excessive antidiuretic hormone causes the kidney to retain water inappropriately, so urine remains concentrated (with an osmolality greater than expected) despite the presence of dilutional hyponatraemia in the plasma. This paradoxical combination of low serum sodium with concentrated urine is key to the diagnosis. Management typically involves fluid restriction, with more severe cases sometimes requiring hypertonic saline under careful monitoring.
options: Markedly dilute urine with a very low osmolality
Complete absence of urinary sodium excretion
Glycosuria without any change in urine osmolality
Inappropriately concentrated urine despite low serum sodium
Urine osmolality identical to serum osmolality at all times

questions.question: A patient with severe caustic ingestion and extensive circumferential oesophageal necrosis on endoscopy is best managed by:
questions.explanation: Extensive full-thickness circumferential necrosis identified on endoscopy after severe caustic ingestion indicates impending or actual perforation, which is a surgical emergency requiring resection of the necrotic segment with oesophageal diversion and later staged reconstruction. Conservative management in this setting risks mediastinitis and death from perforation. Early recognition of the severity of injury dictates the aggressiveness of intervention.
options: Immediate oral feeding to maintain nutrition
Outpatient follow-up with repeat endoscopy in one week
Oral steroids alone without surgical intervention

questions.question: A patient with a mid-oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma has invasion into the aorta confirmed on imaging (T4b disease). Regarding management, the most appropriate approach is:
options: Proceed directly to curative oesophagectomy with aortic resection
Offer surgery only if the patient is otherwise fit
Perform a two-stage oesophagectomy regardless of invasion
Attempt myotomy to relieve symptoms first
Palliative therapy with stenting or chemoradiotherapy rather than resection
questions.explanation: Invasion of the aorta or other unresectable adjacent structures (T4b) precludes curative surgical resection, since attempted resection would carry prohibitive risk without achieving clear margins. Management shifts to palliative measures, including oesophageal stenting for dysphagia relief and chemoradiotherapy to control local disease. Accurate preoperative staging is essential to avoid futile surgery in these patients.

options: Lactic acidosis from ongoing tissue hypoperfusion
Dilutional hyperchloraemic acidosis from excessive saline administration
Diabetic ketoacidosis unmasked by the trauma
Renal tubular acidosis pre-existing before injury
Respiratory acidosis from hypoventilation during resuscitation
questions.question: A trauma patient receives 8 litres of normal saline during resuscitation and subsequently develops a metabolic acidosis with a normal anion gap. This is BEST explained by:
questions.explanation: Large volumes of normal saline contain a high chloride concentration relative to plasma, and excessive administration causes a hyperchloraemic, normal anion gap metabolic acidosis through dilution of bicarbonate and chloride loading. This differs from lactic acidosis, which would present with an elevated anion gap. Recognising this iatrogenic cause avoids unnecessary further investigation for other causes of acidosis.

questions.question: Prolonged urinary catheterization in burns patients is specifically associated with:
questions.explanation: Prolonged catheterization in burns patients predisposes to urinary tract infection (UTI) and, if prolonged, calculi formation. The genitourinary complications of burns include UTI, calculi from catheterization, and acute tubular necrosis from myoglobinuria in electrical burns.

options: Elective ultrasound Doppler study the following day
Emergency surgical exploration without waiting for imaging if clinical suspicion is high
Observation with repeat clinical examination in 24 hours
questions.explanation: The classic clinical triad of severe pain, a high-riding testis with horizontal lie, and an absent cremasteric reflex strongly suggests testicular torsion, and given the time-critical nature of testicular salvage, immediate surgical exploration should not be delayed for confirmatory imaging when clinical suspicion is high. Testicular viability decreases significantly with each hour of delay beyond the first few hours from symptom onset. Prompt bilateral fixation (orchidopexy) is performed at the same operation to prevent future torsion of the contralateral testis.
questions.question: A young man presents with sudden onset severe unilateral scrotal pain, a high-riding testis with a horizontal lie, and an absent cremasteric reflex. The most appropriate immediate management is:

A patient with acute cauda equina syndrome from a large central disc prolapse is being assessed. Which finding, if present, is considered most predictive of a poor outcome without urgent surgical decompression?
options: Painless urinary retention with overflow incontinence
Mild low back pain without leg symptoms
questions.explanation: Painless urinary retention with overflow incontinence is considered one of the most reliable and concerning indicators of established cauda equina syndrome, reflecting significant sacral nerve root compression, and its presence should prompt urgent imaging and surgical decompression to maximise the chance of neurological recovery. Isolated mild leg pain or a single reduced reflex, without other red-flag features, would be far less specific for this diagnosis. Recognising these red-flag features is essential for timely referral and avoiding permanent bladder, bowel, and sexual dysfunction.

In the recovery room, vital signs (pulse, respiration, blood pressure, CVP) should be monitored quarter-hourly (every 15 minutes) for the first hour, then hourly thereafter. Urine output is monitored hourly and GCS is also assessed hourly to detect early deterioration.
questions.question: In the recovery room, vital signs monitoring should be performed at what frequency in the first hour?

questions.explanation: Incisional hernia is a late postoperative complication, occurring weeks to months after surgery due to fascial defect from inadequate healing, wound infection, or increased intra-abdominal pressure. Other late complications include adhesions, keloids, hypertrophic scars, and contractures.
questions.question: Incisional hernia is classified as which type of postoperative complication?

questions.explanation: Renal cell carcinoma classically presents with haematuria, loin pain, and a palpable renal mass, though this complete triad is present in less than 10% at diagnosis. A ballotable loin mass in a middle-aged patient with haematuria should be considered renal carcinoma until proven otherwise. CT urogram confirms diagnosis, and partial or radical nephrectomy is the primary treatment for localised disease.
options: Transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder
questions.question: A 45-year-old male presents with haematuria and a ballotable right loin mass. The most likely diagnosis is:

questions.explanation: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common cause of overwhelming post-splenectomy infection, accounting for approximately 50-80% of OPSI cases. The spleen removes opsonised encapsulated bacteria from the bloodstream, and asplenic patients lose this protective function. Pneumococcal, meningococcal, and Haemophilus influenzae vaccinations are mandatory at least 2 weeks before or after emergency splenectomy.
questions.question: The MOST common complication following splenectomy that leads to overwhelming post-splenectomy infection (OPSI) involves which organism?

questions.explanation: There is a direct, well-established relationship between severity of preoperative malnutrition and postoperative complication rates and mortality. Malnourished patients have impaired wound healing, reduced immune defence, and diminished cardiopulmonary reserve, all of which contribute to worse outcomes. Nutritional screening and optimisation before elective surgery can significantly reduce these risks and shorten hospital stays.
questions.question: The more severe the preoperative malnutrition, the greater the frequency of which postoperative outcomes?
options: Intraoperative blood loss and anaesthetic complications

questions.question: Physical examination finding MOST specific for cardiac failure is:
questions.explanation: The third heart sound (S3) generated by rapid ventricular filling in a dilated, non-compliant ventricle has a relatively high specificity for elevated filling pressures and ventricular dysfunction. While other findings like crackles and oedema are common, they lack specificity as they arise from many non-cardiac conditions. S3 in a patient over 40 years is almost always pathological.

Splenic atrophy in sickle cell disease results from repeated splenic infarctions due to sickling within the spleen ('autosplenectomy'). By adulthood, most HbSS patients have minimal functional splenic tissue. In early childhood, splenic sequestration (acute enlargement) is a major life-threatening crisis.
questions.question: Splenic atrophy in sickle cell disease results from:

questions.explanation: The three core principles of congenital hand deformity treatment are improving functional ability, allowing unrestricted growth, and achieving a socially acceptable appearance. There is no absolute requirement to complete correction by six months of age; timing varies by deformity type, associated conditions, and surgical risk. Syndactyly repair is typically staged and delayed until appropriate age for anaesthetic safety.
questions.question: The basic principles of treatment of congenital hand deformities include all of the following EXCEPT:
Which blood test is MOST specific for acute pancreatitis diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Serum lipase is more sensitive and specific than serum amylase for acute pancreatitis diagnosis because it remains elevated longer (5-7 days vs 24-48 hours for amylase), has fewer extra-pancreatic causes for elevation, and is more accurate in alcoholic pancreatitis where amylase may be normal. Lipase above three times the upper limit of normal combined with clinical findings confirms the diagnosis.
options: Serum amylase three times above normal

questions.explanation: Impetigo is caused primarily by Staphylococcus aureus or Group A Streptococcus (Streptococcus pyogenes). It presents with highly contagious honey-coloured, crusty, oozing sores and blisters, most commonly on the face and extremities. Treatment includes topical antibiotics for mild cases and oral antibiotics for more extensive disease, along with antiseptic soap to reduce transmission.
options: Staphylococcus aureus or Group A Streptococcus
questions.question: Impetigo is most commonly caused by which microorganism?
Emergency radiotherapy for spinal metastasis is indicated to prevent:
questions.explanation: Emergency radiotherapy for spinal metastasis is indicated to prevent or treat spinal cord compression, which causes pain, neurological deficits, and paralysis if untreated. Urgent radiotherapy can preserve neurological function if initiated before complete paralysis. Dexamethasone is used concurrently.
options: Skin ulceration at the site of metastasis
The thorax and the abdomen only
The upper and lower limbs directly
The brain and the peripheral nerves only
The neck and the sacrum exclusively
questions.question: A textbook describes the spinal column poetically as an 'indispensable pillar that links our extremes.' Which two body regions does this phrase refer to the spine connecting?
questions.explanation: This descriptive phrase refers to the spinal column's structural role in connecting the head above to the pelvis below, forming the central axial skeleton that transmits load and provides the conduit for the spinal cord between these two extremes of the body. It is not primarily describing a direct connection between the limbs, which instead attach via the appendicular skeleton. This conceptual framing emphasises the spine's central integrating role in posture, movement, and neurological function.

questions.question: The rectum is distinguished from the sigmoid colon anatomically by the absence of:
options: A serosa on the anterior surface
A blood supply from the superior rectal artery
Lymphatic drainage to inferior mesenteric nodes
questions.explanation: The rectum lacks the three taeniae coli and appendices epiploicae (fatty appendages) characteristic of the colon. The longitudinal muscle of the rectum forms a complete layer rather than three discrete bands. This anatomical distinction is important at surgery to identify the recto-sigmoid junction and to avoid inadvertent damage to the pelvic autonomic nerves during rectal dissection.
