questions.question: The spinal cord receives its main anterior blood supply from which vessel?
questions.explanation: The anterior spinal artery, a single midline vessel formed by the union of branches from the vertebral arteries, supplies the anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord including the corticospinal tracts and anterior horn cells. The posterior third is supplied by paired posterior spinal arteries. Disruption of the anterior spinal artery causes anterior cord syndrome.

options: Loss of remote autobiographical memory from progressive neurodegeneration
Global amnesia affecting all types of memory including procedural
Loss of traumatic memories without organic disease
Loss of semantic (factual) memory from temporal lobe atrophy
Loss of working memory from frontal lobe dysfunction
questions.explanation: Dissociative amnesia is a psychogenic (functional) condition characterised by sudden inability to recall personally important information, typically related to a recent severe traumatic event, that cannot be explained by organic brain disease. The amnesia is usually for episodic autobiographical material. It is classified as a dissociative disorder and is distinguished from transient global amnesia and organic amnesia by the clear psychogenic precipitant and absence of structural brain lesion.
questions.question: Dissociative amnesia is characterised by loss of memory of which type of event and attributed to which cause?

options: Surgery was unnecessary; ganglion cells exclude Hirschsprung's
Biopsy was taken from the normal bowel proximal to the aganglionic segment
Frozen sections are unreliable for ganglion cell identification
Presence of ganglion cells indicates ultra-short segment disease
The pull-through specimen confirms successful complete resection of aganglionic bowel
questions.explanation: The presence of ganglion cells in the pull-through segment confirms that the surgery has resected the entire aganglionic segment and the anastomosis is at normally innervated bowel, which is the goal of surgical correction. This is confirmed by intraoperative frozen section analysis of the proximal margin. Incomplete resection leaving residual aganglionic bowel results in continued obstructive symptoms.
questions.question: A child undergoes corrective surgery for Hirschsprung's disease. The rectal biopsy from the pull-through segment shows ganglion cells. Which statement is MOST accurate?

questions.explanation: Umbilical hernia in children, particularly those with a defect <1.5 cm, almost always closes spontaneously by 3–4 years of age. Strangulation is extremely rare in paediatric umbilical hernias due to the wide neck. Surgery is only recommended if the hernia persists beyond 3–5 years, is enlarging, or is symptomatic. Adult umbilical hernias have higher strangulation risk and require elective surgical repair.
options: Has a higher incidence of incarceration and strangulation in children
Usually resolves spontaneously by age 3–4 years and rarely strangulates
Requires urgent surgical repair at diagnosis in all cases
Is always associated with a patent vitello-intestinal duct
Requires mesh repair to prevent recurrence in children
questions.question: Umbilical hernia in a child DIFFERS from adult umbilical hernia in that paediatric umbilical hernia:

questions.explanation: Extramedullary intradural tumours, such as schwannomas and meningiomas, are located within the dural sac but arise outside the substance of the spinal cord itself, typically displacing rather than infiltrating the cord, which often allows for more complete surgical resection with better preservation of neurological function compared with intramedullary tumours. This differs from extradural tumours, which lie outside the dura altogether, often related to vertebral bone involvement. Correct anatomical classification guides both prognosis and the feasibility of complete surgical excision.
questions.question: A patient with a spinal tumour is found on MRI to be located within the dural sac but clearly separate from and displacing the spinal cord, most consistent with a nerve sheath tumour. Which category does this tumour belong to?

options: Caused by a highly virulent strain of Candida
Triggered by radiotherapy to the pelvis
Commonly associated with antibiotic use altering mucosal flora
questions.explanation: Vaginal candidiasis does not require immune dysfunction and commonly occurs in immunocompetent women, particularly in association with antibiotic use that disrupts normal vaginal bacterial flora and allows Candida overgrowth. It is important to distinguish from bacterial vaginosis, with which it is often confused.
questions.question: Vaginal candidiasis characteristically does NOT require immune dysfunction because it is:

questions.explanation: Dandruff (Pityriasis capitis) is caused by Malassezia globosa, a lipophilic yeast related to M. furfur (which causes Pityriasis versicolor). Dandruff results from accelerated shedding of skin cells from the scalp. Both species are part of normal skin flora and require fatty substrates for growth.
questions.question: Dandruff (Pityriasis capitis) is caused by:

questions.explanation: Linitis plastica (diffuse infiltrating/scirrhous gastric carcinoma) carries a 5-year survival of less than 5% because it is almost invariably diagnosed at an advanced stage with peritoneal spread, lymph node metastases, and extensive submucosal invasion. The diffuse pattern escapes early endoscopic detection. Curative resection is possible in very few cases; most patients are managed palliatively.
questions.question: Scirrhous gastric carcinoma (linitis plastica) has a very poor prognosis. The 5-year survival rate is approximately:

questions.explanation: Subcutaneous emphysema in the neck combined with pneumomediastinum (Hamman's sign — mediastinal crunch on auscultation) is pathognomonic of oesophageal perforation. Air tracks along fascial planes from the site of perforation through the mediastinum to the neck. The combination with Mackler's triad (vomiting, chest pain, subcutaneous emphysema) should prompt immediate water-soluble contrast swallow.
options: Bilateral pleural effusions with basal consolidation
Bilateral hilar enlargement from mediastinal haematoma
questions.question: A chest X-ray of a patient with suspected Boerhaave syndrome shows a left pleural effusion with mediastinal widening. The pathognomonic radiological sign of oesophageal perforation is:

questions.explanation: Pseudodementia refers to cognitive impairment (particularly memory difficulty) occurring as a manifestation of severe depression, which can closely mimic true dementia. The key distinction is that pseudodementia is potentially reversible with effective antidepressant treatment, whereas true dementia is generally progressive and irreversible. Patients with pseudodementia often show more subjective distress about their memory difficulties than true dementia patients.
options: Pseudodementia: transient memory impairment in depression; reversible
Both are equally progressive and irreversible
Dementia affects only short-term memory while pseudodementia affects long-term memory
Pseudodementia always requires brain biopsy for diagnosis
Dementia occurs only in patients over 80 years old
questions.question: Dementia is distinguished from pseudodementia by which key feature?

A 60-year-old man with long-standing gastro-oesophageal reflux disease is found on endoscopy to have columnar metaplasia of the distal oesophageal mucosa. This condition, known as Barrett's oesophagus, predisposes to which malignancy?
questions.explanation: Barrett's oesophagus results from chronic acid reflux causing metaplastic transformation of squamous epithelium into columnar epithelium, which carries an increased risk of progressing through dysplasia to adenocarcinoma. This differs from squamous cell carcinoma, which is more strongly associated with smoking and alcohol rather than reflux. Regular endoscopic surveillance is recommended to detect dysplastic change early.
options: Small cell carcinoma of the oesophagus

questions.question: In the context of surgical nutrition, which parameter is the MOST reliable marker of acute nutritional status?
questions.explanation: Serum prealbumin (transthyretin) has a short half-life of 2-3 days compared to albumin's 20-day half-life, making it a more sensitive and responsive marker of acute nutritional changes and response to nutritional intervention. Albumin is affected by fluid status, inflammation, and hepatic disease, reducing its accuracy as a sole nutritional marker. Serial prealbumin measurement guides parenteral and enteral nutritional support.

The suffix '-pexy' means to fix or attach an organ to another structure. For example, nephropexy refers to surgical fixation of a mobile kidney. This suffix is used across surgical specialties to describe anchoring or fixation procedures.
questions.question: The suffix '-pexy' in surgical terms refers to:

questions.explanation: The lethal triad in trauma consists of hypothermia (temperature <34°C), acidosis (pH <7.2 or base deficit =8 mEq/L), and coagulopathy. These three conditions interact synergistically: hypothermia impairs enzyme function needed for clotting, acidosis worsens coagulopathy, and coagulopathy exacerbates haemorrhage. Addressing all three simultaneously is critical during damage control resuscitation.
questions.question: The 'lethal triad' in trauma resuscitation consists of hypothermia, coagulopathy, and which third component?
A thyroglossal duct cyst characteristically moves upward on which manoeuvre?
questions.explanation: A thyroglossal duct cyst is tethered to the tongue base via the thyroglossal duct remnant and characteristically moves upward on tongue protrusion (in addition to swallowing). This distinguishes it from other midline neck swellings such as dermoid cysts (which move with swallowing but not tongue protrusion). Treatment is the Sistrunk operation, which involves excision of the cyst, tract, and mid-portion of the hyoid bone to prevent recurrence.

Female sex, non-smoking status, a history of motion sickness or previous postoperative nausea and vomiting, and postoperative opioid use are well-established risk factors for postoperative nausea and vomiting. Male sex and current smoking are, conversely, associated with a lower risk. Identifying high-risk patients preoperatively allows targeted multimodal antiemetic prophylaxis strategies.
questions.question: A patient develops postoperative nausea and vomiting despite standard antiemetic prophylaxis after a laparoscopic procedure. Among recognised risk factors for this complication, which is MOST relevant in this patient?

questions.explanation: Ischaemic colitis most commonly affects the splenic flexure and descending colon, which lies at the watershed zone between the superior and inferior mesenteric artery territories at Griffith's point where collateral blood supply is most tenuous. It typically presents with left-sided crampy pain and bloody diarrhoea in older patients with cardiovascular risk factors. Most cases resolve conservatively.
options: Transverse colon at the watershed zone
questions.question: Ischaemic colitis MOST commonly affects which region of the colon?

options: Large volumes of straw-coloured free ascitic fluid only
Multiple discrete caseating abdominal masses without adhesions
Acute suppurative peritonitis with pus formation
Thick fibrous adhesions matting bowel loops together with little free fluid
Calcified nodules without any fibrous reaction
questions.question: Abdominal tuberculosis affecting the peritoneum can present as ascitic, adhesive (fibrotic), or plastic types. The 'plastic' type is characterised by:
questions.explanation: The plastic type of tuberculous peritonitis produces dense fibrous adhesions that mat bowel loops, omentum, and peritoneal surfaces together, often producing a characteristic 'doughy' abdomen on palpation with relatively little free fluid compared with the ascitic form. This fibrotic reaction can cause chronic subacute intestinal obstruction. It represents a more chronic, indolent pattern of tuberculous peritoneal involvement.

The facet (zygapophyseal) joints are synovial joints that primarily guide and limit the direction and range of movement between adjacent vertebrae, working alongside the intervertebral discs, which bear the majority of axial load, rather than the facets themselves being the primary load-bearing structures under normal circumstances. Excessive removal of facet joints during surgery can predispose to segmental instability, which is why careful preservation is emphasised during posterior approaches. Understanding this distinct biomechanical role from the disc is fundamental to safe spinal surgical technique.
questions.question: A surgeon performing a posterior lumbar approach carefully identifies and preserves the facet joints bilaterally to avoid postoperative instability. What is the primary functional role of the facet joints in the vertebral column?
options: Guiding and limiting the direction of intervertebral movement
Bearing the majority of axial load in the upright spine
Providing the primary blood supply to the vertebral body

questions.explanation: A posterior duodenal ulcer is situated directly over the gastroduodenal artery, and erosion into this vessel causes massive arterial haemorrhage that is potentially fatal and often requires endoscopic, angiographic, or surgical haemostasis. The gastroduodenal artery runs posterior to the first part of the duodenum. This anatomical relationship explains why posterior duodenal ulcers are more dangerous than anterior ones.
questions.question: The MOST common site of a peptic ulcer that penetrates into an adjacent structure causing a vascular catastrophe is:
options: Lesser curve gastric ulcer eroding the left gastric artery
Pyloric ulcer eroding the right gastric artery
Posterior duodenal ulcer eroding the gastroduodenal artery
Prepyloric ulcer eroding the right gastroepiploic artery
Anterior duodenal ulcer eroding the pancreas

questions.explanation: In ATLS, 'C' stands for Circulation — including haemorrhage control and circulatory resuscitation. Two large-bore IV lines are established, crystalloid infused, and blood cross-matched. The goal is restoration of adequate tissue perfusion. Cervical spine precautions are part of 'A' (Airway with C-spine protection) in some ATLS versions.
questions.question: The ATLS primary survey for an abdominal trauma patient follows the ABCDE algorithm. In this context, 'C' specifically requires:
options: CT scan confirmation of solid organ injury
Control of haemorrhage and circulatory resuscitation

questions.question: A 2-year-old boy undergoes elective repair of a right indirect inguinal hernia. During the same anaesthetic, the surgeon should also examine for:
options: Signs of appendicitis regardless of symptoms
An unrelated umbilical hernia requiring simultaneous repair
Testicular torsion on the operated side
questions.explanation: Given the recognised incidence of a patent but asymptomatic processus vaginalis on the contralateral side in young children with inguinal hernia, some surgeons perform contralateral exploration or laparoscopic evaluation during the same anaesthetic to detect and address an occult hernia, avoiding a second anaesthetic later. This practice remains debated and depends on the child's age and laterality of the primary hernia. The decision balances the risk of a future contralateral hernia against the morbidity of unnecessary exploration.

Sentinel lymph node biopsy in melanoma uses intradermal injection of patent blue dye and technetium-99m-labelled sulphur colloid, which drain to the sentinel node identified by blue colouration and gamma probe detection. The combination of isotope and dye improves detection rates above 95%. Histological assessment determines whether completion lymphadenectomy is needed.
questions.question: Sentinel lymph node mapping in melanoma uses which TWO agents injected intradermally?

options: BCC commonly metastasises to regional lymph nodes
BCC is associated with UV radiation while SCC is not
SCC is more common on the face than BCC
BCC rarely metastasises and has characteristic rolled pearly edges
BCC is always deeply invasive at presentation
questions.question: A basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is distinguished from squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of the skin by which feature?
questions.explanation: Basal cell carcinoma is characterised by locally invasive but rarely metastatic behaviour (<0.1%), and classic appearance of pearly rolled translucent borders with telangiectatic vessels. SCC can metastasise to regional nodes especially from chronic ulcers or radiation-damaged skin (Marjolin's ulcer). Both are associated with UV radiation but BCC is the most common skin malignancy.

Peritoneal breach with omentum herniation confirms trans-peritoneal penetration. This mandates complete exploration of all intra-abdominal contents, which cannot be reliably performed laparoscopically alone for penetrating trauma. Conversion to open laparotomy allows systematic examination of the entire bowel from Treitz to the rectum and all solid organs.
questions.question: A patient with stab wound to the epigastrium undergoes diagnostic laparoscopy, which shows omentum protruding through a peritoneal defect. The MOST appropriate next step is:
options: Close the laparoscopic port sites and observe for 24 hours
Reduce the omentum laparoscopically and close the defect
Insert a drain laparoscopically and start broad-spectrum antibiotics
Convert to open to inspect only if visible bowel injury is confirmed
Proceed to formal laparotomy for full visceral exploration

questions.explanation: A fistula is defined as an abnormal communication between two epithelial-lined surfaces, such as between the pharynx and the skin in a congenital branchial fistula, distinguishing it from a sinus, which has only a single external opening and a blind internal end, and from a cyst, which is a closed cavity without any external communication. This terminological distinction is fundamental in classifying congenital neck lesions and guides discussion of their embryological origin and surgical management.
questions.question: A patient has a congenital opening in the neck that intermittently discharges mucus and is found to communicate with the pharynx. This tract is best classified as:
options: A sinus, since it has only a single external opening
An ulcer, since it involves loss of surface epithelium
A cyst, since it forms a closed epithelial-lined cavity
An abscess, since it represents a collection of pus
A congenital fistula, since it connects two epithelial-lined surfaces

questions.question: Brachytherapy differs from teletherapy in that brachytherapy:
options: Is used exclusively for brain tumours
Radiation source within or beside the lesion
Delivers higher total doses than teletherapy always
questions.explanation: Brachytherapy places the radiation source close to or inside the lesion, using the inverse square law to deliver high doses locally while sparing surrounding tissues. Examples include vaginal vault brachytherapy for cervical cancer and interstitial brachytherapy for prostate cancer. Teletherapy delivers radiation from a distance.

questions.question: A postoperative patient's arterial blood gas shows pH 7.30, PaCO2 60 mmHg, and HCO3 28 mEq/L. This pattern MOST likely represents:
options: Primary metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation
Acute respiratory acidosis with partial metabolic compensation
Chronic respiratory alkalosis with renal compensation
Pure metabolic alkalosis without any compensation
questions.explanation: The elevated PaCO2 with a low pH indicates a primary respiratory acidosis, commonly from hypoventilation, while the modestly elevated bicarbonate reflects early renal compensation attempting to buffer the acidosis. Full renal compensation typically takes several days to develop, so the pH remains acidotic in the acute phase. Identifying and correcting the cause of hypoventilation, such as opioid oversedation or airway obstruction, is the priority.

Catgut sutures are traditionally sterilised by storage in Lugol's iodine solution for one week, which provides adequate bacterial kill without degrading the suture material. Modern catgut sutures use gamma irradiation for sterilisation. Ethylene oxide and autoclaving are used for synthetic sutures but damage catgut properties.
questions.question: Catgut sutures are traditionally stored in which agent for sterilisation?
DVT prophylaxis during perioperative care includes all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: DVT prophylaxis includes early ambulation, TED (thromboembolic deterrent) stockings, limb physiotherapy, unfractionated heparin, and low molecular weight heparin. Aspirin alone is NOT considered adequate for DVT prophylaxis in surgical patients, though it may be used as an adjunct in some orthopaedic protocols.

questions.question: A cirrhotic patient develops hepatorenal syndrome. Which parameter BEST confirms this diagnosis?
options: A single elevated serum creatinine reading alone
Progressive renal impairment with no response to volume expansion
Red cell casts seen on urine microscopy
questions.explanation: Hepatorenal syndrome is a diagnosis of exclusion, characterised by progressive renal dysfunction in a patient with advanced liver disease that fails to improve with adequate volume expansion and has no alternative identifiable cause such as intrinsic renal disease, nephrotoxic drug exposure, or obstruction. Findings such as red cell casts, significant proteinuria, or hydronephrosis would instead suggest an alternative renal pathology rather than hepatorenal syndrome. Recognising this distinct entity is important as management differs substantially from other causes of acute kidney injury in cirrhotic patients.

Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) is recommended after 4 units of packed red blood cells to replace diluted coagulation factors and prevent worsening of the coagulopathy component of the lethal triad. This ratio-based transfusion strategy reflects damage control resuscitation principles. Delaying FFP administration risks progressive coagulopathy, which combined with acidosis and hypothermia significantly worsens mortality.
questions.question: A patient requires FFP administration during trauma resuscitation. After how many units of packed red cells should FFP be given to prevent dilutional coagulopathy?
A patient newly diagnosed with myasthenia gravis undergoes CT chest as part of the initial work-up. What specific structure or pathology is this imaging primarily looking to identify?
options: Primary lung malignancy unrelated to myasthenia
questions.explanation: CT chest imaging in newly diagnosed myasthenia gravis is primarily performed to identify thymic abnormalities, particularly thymoma or thymic hyperplasia, given the well-established association between myasthenia gravis and thymic pathology, which has implications for both prognosis and treatment, including consideration of thymectomy. This is a targeted, disease-specific indication rather than a general screen for unrelated intrathoracic pathology such as pulmonary embolism. Recognising this specific link underlies the standard work-up pathway for newly diagnosed patients.

options: Ipsilateral reduced breath sounds on the left
Subcutaneous emphysema in the left chest wall
Bowel sounds heard on chest auscultation
Paradoxical movement of the left hemithorax
questions.explanation: Bowel sounds heard on auscultation of the chest are highly specific for diaphragmatic rupture with herniation of abdominal viscera into the thorax. Left-sided rupture is more common and allows herniation of the stomach, colon, and spleen. Nasogastric tube in the chest on CXR is another specific finding. Tracheal deviation and reduced breath sounds are non-specific.
questions.question: Which is the MOST specific clinical sign of a ruptured diaphragm on the left side?

options: Barium swallow as the sole investigation
Oesophageal manometry as the first-line test
Chest X-ray alone without further imaging
questions.explanation: Progressive dysphagia with weight loss is a red flag pattern suggestive of oesophageal malignancy, and upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with biopsy is the appropriate first investigation, allowing direct visualisation and histological confirmation of any lesion. Barium swallow can be useful as an adjunct but does not provide tissue diagnosis. Manometry and pH monitoring are more relevant to motility disorders rather than the initial evaluation of alarm symptoms.
questions.question: A 50-year-old presents with progressive dysphagia first to solids then liquids, along with significant weight loss. The MOST appropriate initial investigation is:
Flexible endoscopes used for upper gastrointestinal procedures are MOST appropriately disinfected by:
questions.explanation: Flexible endoscopes are heat-sensitive and semi-critical devices, requiring thorough mechanical cleaning followed by high-level chemical disinfection using agents such as glutaraldehyde or peracetic acid to inactivate pathogens without damaging the instrument. Steam autoclaving would damage the delicate optical and mechanical components of a flexible endoscope. Adherence to a strict reprocessing protocol is essential to prevent cross-transmission of infection between patients.
options: Standard steam autoclaving at high temperature
Simple detergent wash without further disinfection
High-level chemical disinfection after thorough mechanical cleaning
Boiling in water for ten minutes

questions.question: A patient presents with a strangulated femoral hernia. Compared with an inguinal hernia at the same stage of presentation, femoral hernias have a higher risk of strangulation primarily because of:
questions.explanation: The femoral canal is bounded by rigid structures, including the inguinal ligament, lacunar ligament, and pectineal ligament, creating a narrow and unyielding space that offers little room for the herniating bowel to expand, thereby predisposing to vascular compromise and strangulation. This anatomical rigidity explains the disproportionately high strangulation rate of femoral hernias compared with inguinal hernias, despite femoral hernias being generally smaller. Early elective repair of femoral hernias is therefore recommended once diagnosed.
options: Their exclusively larger size at initial presentation
A significantly thinner overlying peritoneal covering
Their tendency to occur only in young, otherwise healthy patients
The narrow, rigid boundaries of the femoral canal restricting expansion
Complete absence of any surrounding fibrous or ligamentous structures
Direct lymphatic obstruction causing peau d'orange
Tethering of Cooper's ligaments by the underlying tumour
Simple postural skin folding unrelated to the lump
Infection of the overlying skin from the mass
Fat necrosis producing localised skin retraction only
questions.explanation: Skin dimpling overlying a breast mass results from malignant infiltration and shortening of the fibrous Cooper's ligaments that normally support the breast, pulling the overlying skin inward as the arm is raised and tension increases on the ligaments. This differs from peau d'orange, which results from dermal lymphatic obstruction causing oedema and a thickened, orange-peel appearance of the skin. Both are important clinical signs suggesting underlying malignancy requiring triple assessment.
questions.question: A 45-year-old woman presents with a breast lump and overlying skin dimpling that becomes more apparent on raising the arm. This skin change is caused by:
A wound is closed by delayed primary closure (tertiary intention) rather than immediate primary closure. This approach is chosen typically when:
options: The wound is completely clean and closed within the first hour
The wound is heavily contaminated and closure is deferred until infection risk decreases
Cosmetic outcome is the sole consideration guiding closure timing
The wound has already achieved full epithelialisation naturally
No sutures or dressings will ever be required
questions.explanation: Delayed primary closure is used for wounds at high risk of infection, such as heavily contaminated traumatic or surgical wounds, where the wound is initially left open for several days to allow the inflammatory response to reduce bacterial load before formal closure is performed. This approach reduces the risk of trapping infection beneath a prematurely closed wound. It is distinct from healing by secondary intention, where the wound is left to close entirely by granulation and contraction.

questions.question: The MOST common benign tumour of the liver is:
questions.explanation: Hepatic haemangioma is the most common benign liver tumour, found incidentally in up to 5% of the population, predominantly in women. It has a characteristic MRI appearance of peripheral nodular enhancement with centripetal fill-in on delayed sequences. Asymptomatic haemangiomas require no treatment; surgery is reserved for giant haemangiomas causing symptoms or haemorrhage.

Identifying a specific underlying metabolic abnormality, such as hypercalciuria, hyperoxaluria, or hypocitraturia, allows targeted dietary modification or medical therapy, such as thiazide diuretics or citrate supplementation, aimed at reducing future stone recurrence rather than relying solely on repeated treatment of individual stone episodes. This proactive approach is particularly emphasised in patients with recurrent stone disease. Ongoing periodic imaging surveillance remains important even after metabolic correction, since recurrence can still occur despite treatment.
options: Reduces the risk of future stone recurrence through targeted dietary or medical intervention
Has no influence on the likelihood of future stone formation
Is only relevant for patients who have already required surgical stone removal
Eliminates the need for any future imaging surveillance
Guarantees that no further stones will ever form regardless of treatment
questions.question: A patient with recurrent calcium oxalate renal stones undergoes metabolic evaluation. Identifying and correcting an underlying metabolic abnormality, such as hypercalciuria, is important primarily because it:

questions.explanation: The subsequent pregnancy risk for congenital hand deformities ranges from 0–25% depending on aetiology, whether it is syndromic, and the inheritance pattern of any identified syndrome. Non-syndromic isolated deformities may have a very low recurrence risk, while autosomal dominant syndromes carry a 50% risk. Genetic counselling is therefore essential after thorough evaluation of the specific condition.
questions.question: Genetic counselling is recommended as part of evaluation for congenital hand deformities. The subsequent pregnancy risk for an affected family is stated as:

options: An allergic reaction to the insufflating gas used
Extraperitoneal insufflation of carbon dioxide during the procedure
Direct bacterial gas production from wound infection
A normal, universally expected finding after every laparoscopic case
Absorption of carbon dioxide exclusively into the bloodstream without tissue tracking
questions.explanation: Surgical emphysema results from carbon dioxide inadvertently tracking into the extraperitoneal or subcutaneous tissue planes during insufflation, particularly if the Veress needle or ports are malpositioned, and the gas can dissect along fascial planes as far as the neck and chest wall. This is usually self-limiting and resolves as the carbon dioxide is gradually absorbed and exhaled over the following hours to days. Extensive emphysema, however, should prompt consideration of more significant injury, such as pneumothorax or major vascular or visceral trauma.
questions.question: A patient undergoing laparoscopic surgery develops surgical emphysema (subcutaneous crepitus) extending up to the neck postoperatively. This complication most commonly results from:

questions.explanation: Pneumaturia — the passage of gas (air bubbles) in the urine during micturition — is the most specific symptom of a colovesical or enterovesical fistula. Faecaluria (faecal material in urine) also occurs. Recurrent UTIs with mixed organisms suggest fistula but are less specific. CT cystogram or cystoscopy confirms the fistula. Surgical treatment requires resection of the diseased bowel and bladder repair.
options: Recurrent urinary tract infections with the same organism
Pneumaturia (passage of gas in the urine)
Urine with faecal matter and vegetable fibres
questions.question: A patient with Crohn's colitis develops an entero-vesical fistula. The presenting symptom MOST specific to this complication is:

options: Proceed to surgery and monitor the ECG only
Postpone surgery and correct the hyperkalaemia first
Give a stat dose of intravenous potassium chloride
Proceed and correct potassium after surgery only
Ignore the result if the patient is asymptomatic
questions.explanation: Significant hyperkalaemia increases the risk of life-threatening cardiac arrhythmias during anaesthesia and surgery, so elective procedures should be postponed until the potassium level is corrected to a safer range. Correction may involve insulin-dextrose, calcium gluconate for cardiac protection, or dialysis in severe renal failure. Proceeding with untreated significant hyperkalaemia risks intraoperative cardiac arrest.
questions.question: A patient with chronic kidney disease requiring elective surgery has a serum potassium of 6.2 mmol/L on the morning of surgery. The MOST appropriate action is to:

questions.explanation: Infective discitis in the lumbar region is notably common in sicklers (sickle cell disease patients). Vaso-occlusive crises and immunological dysfunction in sickle cell disease predispose to haematogenous seeding of the relatively avascular disc space. Presentation is typically vague pain and must be distinguished from other causes of back pain in this population.
questions.question: Infective discitis in the lumbar region shares a predisposition with which haematological condition?

A 55-year-old man presents with fresh rectal bleeding, tenesmus, and a change in bowel habit over 6 weeks. Digital rectal examination reveals a hard, irregular mass 5 cm from the anal verge. The MOST appropriate next investigation is:
options: Barium enema to outline the mass
Colonoscopy with biopsy for histological diagnosis
Serum CEA level to confirm malignancy
CT of the abdomen and pelvis for staging
MRI of the pelvis to assess sphincter involvement
questions.explanation: Colonoscopy with tissue biopsy is the first essential step to confirm histological diagnosis before any staging investigation or treatment decision. CEA is a tumour marker used for follow-up, not diagnosis. CT and MRI are staging investigations performed after histological confirmation. A tissue diagnosis must precede staging to avoid unnecessary investigations if pathology is benign.

The testis receives blood from three arteries: the testicular artery (from the aorta), the cremasteric artery (from the inferior epigastric artery), and the deferential artery (from the superior vesical artery). This collateral network allows the Fowler-Stephens orchidopexy to divide the testicular artery, with the testis surviving on cremasteric and deferential supply. Testicular atrophy occurs in approximately 10-25% of cases despite collateral circulation.
questions.question: Which correct statement describes the testicular blood supply and its relevance to the Fowler-Stephens orchidopexy?
options: The testis is supplied solely by the testicular artery; division causes inevitable atrophy
Collateral cremasteric and deferential arteries allow testicular artery division in the Fowler-Stephens procedure
Division of the testicular artery always causes testicular atrophy in all cases
The epididymis has no separate blood supply distinct from the testis
All testicular venous drainage is exclusively through the pampiniform plexus

questions.question: The suffix '-rrhaphy' in surgical terminology means:
questions.explanation: The suffix '-rrhaphy' means repair of a structure. For example, herniorrhaphy refers to the repair of a hernia. This differs from '-plasty' (reconstruction), '-ectomy' (removal), and '-otomy' (cutting into).

Cervical disc prolapse peaks in the third and fourth decades of life, reflecting a period of maximum disc hydration and turgor combined with high physical activity and occupational demands. Later in life, disc dehydration makes frank prolapse less common, but spondylotic changes produce chronic compression. Lumbar disc prolapse also peaks in the third to fifth decades.
questions.question: Peak incidence of cervical disc prolapse occurs at which age group?

options: Its hydrated, gel-like consistency allowing hydrostatic pressure distribution
Its complete lack of any water content
Its direct fusion to the vertebral endplate by bone
Its identical structure to hyaline cartilage of joints
questions.explanation: The nucleus pulposus, in its normal well-hydrated state, behaves as a gel that distributes compressive load hydrostatically and relatively evenly across the vertebral endplates and surrounding annulus fibrosus, a function that becomes progressively less effective as water content and hydrostatic properties decline with age-related degeneration. It is not a rigid or calcified structure under normal circumstances, and its behaviour is distinct from articular hyaline cartilage found in synovial joints. Understanding this biomechanical property clarifies why disc desiccation with ageing leads to altered, less even load distribution and increased risk of degenerative change.
questions.question: A surgeon explains that in normal spinal biomechanics, the nucleus pulposus acts to distribute compressive load evenly across the vertebral endplates. What material property of the nucleus pulposus underlies this function?

options: Residual CO2 from pneumoperitoneum tracking subcutaneously
Necrotising fasciitis of the port site
Pneumothorax from inadvertent chest trocar entry
questions.explanation: Subcutaneous emphysema immediately post-laparoscopy is almost always due to CO2 insufflation tracking along fascial planes and into subcutaneous tissue during the procedure. It is particularly common at port sites and in the chest wall during upper abdominal laparoscopy. It resolves spontaneously over 24-48 hours as CO2 is absorbed, and no specific treatment is required in the absence of complications.
questions.question: Subcutaneous emphysema detected post-operatively after laparoscopy is MOST likely caused by:

A morbidly obese patient is scheduled for laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy. Compared with laparoscopic Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, sleeve gastrectomy achieves weight loss primarily through which mechanism?
options: Malabsorption from bypassing a significant length of small bowel
Complete removal of the duodenum and proximal jejunum
Restriction of gastric volume and reduction of ghrelin-secreting fundal tissue
Creation of a blind gastric pouch with no continuity to the stomach
Direct hormonal suppression of appetite unrelated to any anatomical change
questions.explanation: Sleeve gastrectomy removes the greater curvature of the stomach, including much of the fundus where the appetite-stimulating hormone ghrelin is produced, achieving weight loss predominantly through gastric restriction and reduced hunger signalling rather than through the malabsorptive component present in bypass procedures. Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, in contrast, combines restriction with an element of intestinal bypass affecting nutrient absorption. This mechanistic difference influences the choice of procedure based on patient comorbidities and expected outcomes.

options: 25kcal/kg for all burns regardless of size
questions.question: The Sutherland formula for adult burns caloric requirement calculates:
questions.explanation: The Sutherland formula: Calories = 20 kcal/kg + 70 kcal per %BSA burned; Protein = 1g/kg + 3g per %BSA burned. This high-calorie, high-protein prescription addresses the hypermetabolic state of major burns where resting energy expenditure increases by 40-100%.

options: Myasthenic crisis, requiring an immediate further increase in anticholinesterase dose
Cholinergic crisis, requiring temporary withholding of anticholinesterase medication
Simple viral gastroenteritis, requiring only supportive fluids
Thyroid storm, requiring urgent antithyroid medication
Autonomic dysreflexia, requiring urgent blood pressure lowering
questions.question: A patient with myasthenia gravis on pyridostigmine develops excessive salivation, sweating, bradycardia, and worsening weakness after a recent dose increase. Which condition should be suspected, and what is the appropriate immediate step?
questions.explanation: Cholinergic crisis results from excessive acetylcholinesterase inhibition, causing both worsening muscle weakness through depolarising neuromuscular blockade and prominent cholinergic autonomic features such as excessive salivation, sweating, and bradycardia, distinguishing it from myasthenic crisis, which lacks these specific cholinergic autonomic features. Management requires temporarily withholding anticholinesterase medication, in contrast to myasthenic crisis, where further anticholinesterase therapy or other immunotherapy may be appropriate. Correctly distinguishing these two crises, despite both causing weakness, is essential to avoid worsening the patient's condition with an incorrect treatment approach.

questions.question: A 50-year-old with symptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism has a serum calcium of 2.9 mmol/L and a sestamibi scan showing a single adenoma. The MOST appropriate management is:
options: Lifelong medical management without any surgical intervention
Focused parathyroidectomy targeting the identified adenoma
Bilateral neck exploration removing all four glands routinely
Total thyroidectomy combined with parathyroidectomy in all cases
Observation alone without any biochemical monitoring
questions.explanation: When a single parathyroid adenoma is clearly localised on imaging in a patient with symptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism, focused minimally invasive parathyroidectomy targeting that specific gland is the preferred approach, often guided by intraoperative parathyroid hormone monitoring to confirm successful removal. This targeted approach reduces operative time and complication risk compared to routine bilateral exploration, which is reserved for cases without clear single-gland localisation. Surgery is generally recommended for symptomatic disease or those meeting specific biochemical criteria for intervention.

Monthly biological spore testing using B. stearothermophilus is the most reliable indicator of autoclave sterilization efficacy. Autoclave tape alone indicates temperature exposure but not sterilization success. Spore tests confirm complete destruction of the most resistant organisms.
options: Achievement of correct temperature on dial
Monthly spore testing with B. stearothermophilus

questions.explanation: The FRIEND mnemonic identifies factors reducing the chance of spontaneous fistula closure: Foreign body, Radiation, Infection or Inflammation, Epithelialisation of the tract, Neoplasm, and Distal obstruction. The presence of a retained foreign body, such as a suture or mesh, within the fistula tract prevents healing by continuing to incite a local inflammatory response. Recognising these factors early helps identify patients who are unlikely to achieve closure without surgical intervention.
questions.question: A patient with an enterocutaneous fistula has factors identified that reduce the likelihood of spontaneous closure, remembered by the mnemonic FRIEND. Which of the following is one of these unfavourable factors?
options: Absence of any distal bowel obstruction
Normal, healthy surrounding bowel without inflammation
Foreign body present within the fistula tract
A well-nourished patient with no sepsis

questions.explanation: The IPSS and AUA-SI are identical 7-question validated instruments assessing frequency, nocturia, weak stream, hesitancy, incomplete emptying, intermittency, and urgency. The IPSS includes an additional quality-of-life question. Both score symptoms 0-35 (0-7 mild, 8-19 moderate, 20-35 severe) and are used for initial assessment, patient counselling, and monitoring treatment response in BPH management.
questions.question: The International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS) and the American Urological Association Symptom Index (AUA-SI) are:
options: Two completely different instruments assessing different symptoms
Only used for post-treatment monitoring not initial assessment
Scoring systems used only in research settings not clinical practice
Replaced entirely by uroflowmetry in modern practice
Identical 7-question validated instruments for assessing lower urinary tract symptoms

questions.question: During laparoscopic surgery, carbon dioxide pneumoperitoneum at high insufflation pressure can cause a reduction in venous return and cardiac output. This haemodynamic effect occurs primarily due to:
options: Direct cardiotoxic effect of absorbed carbon dioxide on the myocardium
Increased intra-abdominal pressure compressing the inferior vena cava
Complete occlusion of the aorta at standard insufflation pressures
An allergic reaction to the insufflated gas in most patients
Reflex bradycardia unrelated to any change in venous return
questions.explanation: Elevated intra-abdominal pressure during pneumoperitoneum can compress the inferior vena cava, reducing venous return to the heart and consequently lowering cardiac output, an effect that becomes more pronounced at higher insufflation pressures or in patients with reduced physiological reserve. Anaesthetic teams monitor haemodynamic parameters closely during laparoscopic procedures and may request lower insufflation pressures if significant compromise occurs. This effect is a key consideration when performing laparoscopic surgery in patients with cardiovascular disease.

Full thickness burns (fourth degree in American classification) extend beyond the dermis, forming eschar (dead, leathery tissue). There is ABSENT pin-prick sensation because all sensory nerve endings are destroyed. These burns cannot heal spontaneously and require surgical debridement and skin grafting.
options: Eschar formation with absent pin-prick sensation
Involvement of only the papillary dermis

Peritoneal tuberculosis is confirmed by laparoscopy. The characteristic gross laparoscopic appearance is:
options: Sheet-like peritoneal thickening with ascites and no nodularity
Haemorrhagic peritoneal implants with mucinous deposits
Diffuse peritoneal oedema without discrete lesions
Localised omental thickening only in the right paracolic gutter
Multiple white/yellow tubercles on the peritoneum with fibrous adhesions
questions.explanation: Laparoscopy in tuberculous peritonitis classically shows multiple white or yellow miliary tubercles studded over the visceral and parietal peritoneum, with fibrinous adhesions (particularly the 'plastic' type), and inflammatory oedema. This appearance combined with peritoneal biopsy showing caseating granulomas is diagnostic. It avoids the need for open surgical biopsy and allows direct sampling.

options: The posterior annulus fibrosus is thicker
The disc is anchored to the posterior longitudinal ligament
Nuclear material migrates posteriorly due to gravity
Anterior disc larger in cervical and lumbar regions
The facet joints push the disc posteriorly during flexion
questions.question: Which of the following best explains why the intervertebral disc is described as 'generally lies more posteriorly' within the intervertebral space?
questions.explanation: Because cervical and lumbar discs are larger anteriorly, their geometric centre lies relatively more posterior within the intervertebral space. This anterior height preponderance creates the secondary lordotic curvatures. In the thoracic region, discs are larger posteriorly, contributing to the kyphotic curve and the more posteriorly centred disc position.

These features are characteristic of necrotising fasciitis, a rapidly progressive and life-threatening soft tissue infection that requires emergency surgical debridement of all necrotic tissue without delay. Broad-spectrum antibiotics are given concurrently but do not substitute for source control. Delay in surgical intervention is strongly associated with increased mortality.
questions.question: A patient develops progressive swelling, crepitus, and severe pain disproportionate to examination findings at a surgical wound site on postoperative day 2. The MOST appropriate immediate management is:
options: Observation with repeat examination in 24 hours
Application of a compression dressing only
Intravenous fluids alone without surgical intervention

questions.explanation: CT scan, MRI, and PET scan are used to assess the extent of spread of thyroid carcinoma to regional and distant metastatic sites, including lymph nodes, lungs, bones, and brain. They are complementary to radioiodine scanning (which identifies iodine-avid thyroid tissue and metastases). Technetium-99m scan assesses thyroid function (hot vs. cold nodules) but is not used for staging distant metastases.
questions.question: Which investigation is used specifically for imaging the extent of spread of thyroid cancer to distant sites?

questions.explanation: Swanson Type VI covers constriction band syndromes (Streeter hypoplasia), in which amniotic bands constrict developing limb segments, resulting in amputation at any level, with or without associated lymphoedema. This is a disruption sequence where a normally formed embryo is subjected to external mechanical injury by amniotic bands, differing from intrinsic formation or differentiation failures.
questions.question: In Swanson's classification, constriction band syndrome (Streeter hypoplasia) belongs to which type and may result in which consequence?
options: Type I; failure of proximal limb formation

questions.explanation: Wet packs after autoclaving indicate a failure of the sterilisation cycle, commonly from trapped condensate or overloading, and moisture allows wicking of environmental organisms into the pack. Such items must be treated as non-sterile and reprocessed. Using damp packs risks introducing infection into the surgical field.
questions.question: A surgeon notices that a batch of surgical gowns feels damp on removal from the autoclave. The appropriate response is to:
options: Air-dry the gowns before use since sterility is unaffected
Use the gowns only for non-invasive procedures
Return the gowns after wiping the exterior with alcohol
Extend the next cycle's exposure time to compensate
Consider the load non-sterile and reprocess it

questions.question: In a BPH patient on watchful waiting (IPSS <8), which finding immediately mandates active treatment?
questions.explanation: The development of acute urinary retention is an absolute indication to abandon watchful waiting and proceed to active treatment in BPH, regardless of previous IPSS score. Other complications mandating active intervention include recurrent UTI, haematuria refractory to treatment, vesical calculi, bladder diverticula, and obstructive nephropathy with renal impairment. These represent end-organ damage from untreated outflow obstruction.
options: Voiding frequency of 7 times per day

questions.explanation: The bicarbonate requirement is estimated as: base deficit x 0.5 x total body water (TBW). Total body water in adults approximates 60% of body weight. This conservative formula avoids overcorrection and the risks of hypernatremia or paradoxical CSF acidosis.
questions.question: Estimating base deficit to calculate bicarbonate replacement uses the formula: base deficit multiplied by one half of which compartment?
A patient with a midline neck swelling that moves upward on tongue protrusion is diagnosed with a thyroglossal duct cyst. This characteristic movement occurs because the cyst is:
questions.explanation: The thyroglossal duct represents the embryological tract of thyroid gland descent from the foramen caecum at the tongue base to its final position in the neck, and a persistent cyst along this tract remains connected to the hyoid bone and tongue base, causing characteristic upward movement on tongue protrusion due to traction transmitted through this embryological remnant. This movement, along with midline movement on swallowing, helps distinguish a thyroglossal duct cyst clinically from other midline neck swellings such as a dermoid cyst, which lacks this specific tongue protrusion sign.
options: Attached to the foramen caecum via the thyroglossal tract, which is connected to the hyoid bone and tongue base
Composed of thyroid tissue that moves independently with swallowing only
Located entirely within the strap muscles of the neck
Connected directly to the trachea rather than the tongue
Unrelated anatomically to any midline embryological structure

questions.explanation: Flame burns account for 55% of all burns, making them the most common type. Scald burns are second at 40%, while electrical and chemical burns together account for only 5%. In children, however, scald burns predominate due to accidents involving hot liquids.
questions.question: The MOST common type of burn by incidence is:
Which of the following is a recognised non-operative treatment for lumbar disc prolapse?
questions.explanation: Non-operative management of lumbar disc prolapse includes bed rest, analgesics, NSAIDs, muscle relaxants, corset use, physiotherapy, and weight reduction. Corsets provide lumbar support while physiotherapy addresses core strengthening and postural correction. The majority of acute lumbar disc prolapses resolve with conservative management within 6–12 weeks.

Acute carotid dissection presents with warning attacks of unilateral carotid or facial pain (non-pulsating, may be retro-orbital or at the jaw/neck angle) preceding neurological symptoms by minutes to days. Horner's syndrome may occur from compression of the peri-arterial sympathetic fibres. The condition accounts for up to 2.5% of first strokes and is most common in young adults. Diagnosis is by carotid MRI or angiography.
questions.question: Acute carotid dissection may present with which clinical triad?
options: Bilateral visual loss, diplopia, and ataxia
Thunderclap headache with meningism and fever
Progressive ascending weakness with sensory loss
Unilateral carotid pain with neurological deficit and Horner's
Sudden bilateral hearing loss with vertigo and tinnitus

questions.question: A theatre uses a chemical indicator strip inside each instrument pack to confirm sterilisation. This type of indicator PRIMARILY confirms:
questions.explanation: Chemical indicators change colour when exposed to specific temperature or time-temperature conditions, confirming that the pack underwent the sterilisation process, but they do not guarantee actual microbial kill. Biological indicators using bacterial spores are needed to verify true sterility. Relying on chemical indicators alone can give false reassurance if steam penetration was inadequate.
options: That all spores present were killed
That the instruments are ready for use
That the pack met sterilising conditions, not sterility

questions.question: Digital rectal examination primarily palpates which zone of the prostate and which zone is the most common site of prostatic carcinoma?
questions.explanation: DRE primarily palpates the peripheral zone, which comprises 70% of glandular tissue and is accessible through the posterior rectal wall. The peripheral zone is also where most prostatic carcinomas arise. The periurethral transition zone where BPH originates is not directly accessible by DRE. A normal DRE does not exclude significant peripheral zone cancer, which is why PSA screening is also needed.
options: Periurethral (transition) zone; same zone is commonest site of carcinoma
Peripheral zone; peripheral zone is the commonest site of carcinoma
Central zone; central zone is commonest site of carcinoma
Anterior fibromuscular stroma; this zone is the commonest carcinoma site
All zones are equally palpable; carcinoma arises uniformly throughout

questions.explanation: High-pitched, tinkling or 'tinny' bowel sounds occur in mechanical obstruction as peristaltic waves hit the gas-filled distended proximal loops, creating resonance. Paralytic ileus produces absent bowel sounds. Gastroenteritis causes rushing, gurgling sounds. Mechanical obstruction also shows rushes and borborygmi early, progressing to silence late.
questions.question: Bowel sounds are described as 'tinkling' and high-pitched in acute abdomen. This finding is associated with:
A patient with gallstone pancreatitis has recovered from the acute episode. Regarding timing of cholecystectomy, the MOST appropriate approach is:
options: Cholecystectomy during the same hospital admission once the pancreatitis has settled
Cholecystectomy delayed for at least six months after discharge
No cholecystectomy required since the pancreatitis has resolved
Cholecystectomy performed only if a second episode occurs
Cholecystectomy delayed until the patient develops jaundice
questions.explanation: Current evidence supports performing cholecystectomy during the same hospital admission once acute gallstone pancreatitis has clinically settled, since delaying surgery significantly increases the risk of recurrent biliary events, including further pancreatitis, before an elective outpatient procedure can be arranged. This same-admission approach has become standard practice in most centres for mild to moderate gallstone pancreatitis. Delaying surgery without clear justification exposes the patient to unnecessary recurrent risk.

options: Direct invasion of the ureter by prostatic tissue
Haematogenous spread of infection to the kidneys
Lymphatic obstruction at the pelviureteric junction
Autonomic neuropathy from prostatic nerve infiltration
Back-pressure from chronic outflow obstruction via the bladder
questions.question: Hydroureter and hydronephrosis in untreated BPH arise through which pathophysiological mechanism?
questions.explanation: Prolonged bladder outflow obstruction from BPH causes progressive elevation of intravesical pressure and residual urine volume, creating back-pressure that dilates ureters (hydroureter) then renal collecting systems (hydronephrosis). If untreated, this leads to progressive nephron loss and obstructive nephropathy with renal failure. Kinking of the ureters may also occur with severe bladder dilatation.

options: 2 months only for intestinal TB due to the short mucosal exposure
4 months for sensitive TB without surgical complications
12 months for all forms of abdominal TB
18–24 months for drug-resistant abdominal TB only
questions.question: The treatment regimen for abdominal tuberculosis follows the standard anti-TB protocol. The RECOMMENDED duration of therapy is:
questions.explanation: Standard treatment for drug-sensitive abdominal tuberculosis follows the WHO regimen: 2 months of Isoniazid (H), Rifampicin (R), Pyrazinamide (Z), and Ethambutol (E) — the intensive phase — followed by 4 months of Isoniazid and Rifampicin, totalling 6 months. Longer regimens are only required for MDR-TB or complicated disease. Adjunctive surgery does not shorten the medical treatment duration.

The anterior longitudinal ligament runs along the anterior aspect of the vertebral bodies and intervertebral discs, providing stability and resisting excessive extension of the spine, and is a key structure to protect during anterior surgical approaches. The posterior longitudinal ligament instead lies on the posterior aspect of the vertebral bodies within the canal. Correctly distinguishing these ligaments is essential for safe anterior spinal surgical planning.
questions.question: A patient undergoes anterior spinal surgery and the surgeon carefully identifies a strong ligament running along the front of the vertebral bodies and discs to protect it during dissection. Which ligament is this?

options: The internal urethral sphincter at the bladder neck
External urethral sphincter below the prostatic apex
The neurovascular bundles of Walsh posterolaterally
questions.explanation: The external urethral sphincter (rhabdosphincter), located just below the prostatic apex at the membranous urethra, is the critical structure for maintaining urinary continence after prostatectomy. Injury to this structure during prostatic apex dissection causes stress urinary incontinence, the most functionally significant quality-of-life complication. The membranous urethra must be divided as close to the apex as possible to maximise functional sphincter length.
questions.question: During retropubic prostatectomy, which structure must be carefully protected to preserve urinary continence?

questions.explanation: A superficial surgical site infection localised to the wound is generally managed by opening the skin and subcutaneous layers to allow drainage of pus, combined with regular dressing changes, and usually resolves without the need for imaging or further surgery. This differs from a deep intra-abdominal collection, which would require imaging and possibly radiological drainage. Recognising the correct level of infection guides the appropriate, least invasive effective treatment.
questions.question: A patient recovering from an appendicectomy for a simple, non-perforated appendix develops a wound infection on postoperative day 5. Compared with intra-abdominal collections after perforated appendicitis, this superficial wound infection is best managed by:
options: CT-guided percutaneous drainage of the abdominal cavity
Broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics alone without opening the wound
Urgent return to theatre for wound revision under anaesthesia
Opening the wound for drainage with dressing changes, without further imaging

questions.explanation: The cervical collar (rigid collar) is applied to support the head in a neutral position and limit neck movement, reducing the risk of secondary cord injury from cervical spine instability. It is applied after assessment of the neck for signs of injury and after the airway is secured. A spine board then immobilises the entire spinal column for safe transport.
questions.question: Which component of spinal immobilisation supports the head in a neutral position and limits head movement?

questions.explanation: The secondary survey in neurosurgical trauma management involves comprehensive systemic assessment including detailed head-to-toe physical examination, chest and spinal X-rays, peritoneal lavage or FAST scan for abdominal injury, CT brain and spine, other relevant X-rays, complete laboratory tests, and tetanus immunisation. This thorough assessment identifies all injuries that may affect management priorities.
questions.question: The secondary survey in the management protocol for neurosurgical trauma includes which components?
options: Airway, breathing, and circulation assessment only
Only CT brain without full systemic assessment

questions.question: A carrier in surgical microbiology is an individual who:
options: Harbours a specific organism without clinical disease
Has active clinical disease and spreads infection
Is immune to all surgical infections
Has completed treatment for an infection
questions.explanation: A carrier harbours a specific organism in the absence of clinical disease but remains a potential source of spread. A carrier could be colonized, asymptomatically infected, in the incubation period, or convalescing from acute disease.

questions.question: The term 'conus medullaris syndrome' refers to injury at which anatomical site and produces which specific clinical pattern?
options: Injury at T1 producing pure upper motor neurone paraplegia
Injury at S2-S4 producing isolated bladder dysfunction
Conus medullaris: mixed UMN/LMN; bladder and bowel
Injury at L4-L5 producing foot drop only
questions.explanation: Conus medullaris syndrome results from injury to the terminal spinal cord segment (conus) at approximately L1–L2 vertebral levels, producing a mixed pattern of upper and lower motor neurone signs. UMN signs arise from remaining descending tracts, while LMN signs reflect damage to the anterior horn cells of the conus itself. Bladder and bowel dysfunction (neurogenic bladder) with saddle-region sensory loss are characteristic features.

Boerhaave syndrome is spontaneous transmural perforation of the oesophagus, typically in the left posterolateral lower third, caused by sudden increase in intraluminal pressure during forceful vomiting. Mackler's triad (vomiting, lower chest pain, subcutaneous emphysema) is classic. Urgent surgical repair or oesophageal exclusion/diversion in late presentations is required as untreated mortality exceeds 80%.
options: Mallory-Weiss tear at the gastro-oesophageal junction
Iatrogenic perforation during upper GI endoscopy
Transmural oesophageal rupture from pressure rise
Chemical burns of the oesophagus from caustic ingestion
Eosinophilic oesophagitis with longitudinal mucosal tears
questions.question: Boerhaave syndrome refers to which specific condition?

questions.explanation: Large-volume normal saline resuscitation delivers a high chloride load relative to plasma, causing dilution of bicarbonate and a normal anion gap, hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis, distinct from the elevated anion gap seen with lactic acidosis or ketoacidosis. Recognising this dilutional, iatrogenic cause is important to avoid unnecessary further investigation for other causes of acidosis. Balanced crystalloid solutions are increasingly used in large-volume resuscitation to reduce the incidence of this complication.
options: Diabetic ketoacidosis unmasked by the trauma
Lactic acidosis from ongoing active haemorrhage
Chronic respiratory acidosis from underlying lung disease
Hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis from excessive saline administration
Renal tubular acidosis present before the injury
questions.question: A trauma patient resuscitated with 10 litres of normal saline develops an ABG showing pH 7.25 with a normal anion gap. This is BEST explained by:

questions.explanation: Component separation involves releasing the external oblique aponeurosis lateral to the rectus sheath, allowing the rectus abdominis muscles to be mobilised and advanced medially to achieve tension-free fascial closure of large abdominal wall defects. This technique restores the linea alba and functional abdominal wall without needing to remove abdominal contents. Mesh reinforcement is frequently combined with component separation to reduce the risk of subsequent recurrence.
options: Remove a segment of bowel to reduce abdominal contents
Replace the entire abdominal wall with a synthetic prosthesis alone
Avoid the need for any mesh reinforcement whatsoever
Advance the rectus abdominis muscles medially by releasing the external oblique aponeurosis
Convert the repair into a permanent stoma-forming procedure
questions.question: A patient undergoing repair of a large incisional hernia has significant loss of abdominal domain, making primary fascial closure difficult without excessive tension. The technique of component separation is used primarily to:
The Oswestry Disability Index is used in spinal disease management to measure:
options: Canal cross-sectional area on CT scan
questions.explanation: The Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) is a validated patient-reported outcome measure assessing the functional disability caused by low back pain across ten domains including pain intensity, personal care, lifting, walking, sitting, standing, sleeping, social life, travelling, and pain intensity. It is widely used in clinical research and practice to guide treatment decisions and monitor outcomes.

questions.question: The embryological event responsible for the formation of the processus vaginalis occurs at what gestational age?
questions.explanation: The processus vaginalis is a peritoneal diverticulum that forms at approximately 12 weeks of gestation and extends through the internal inguinal ring into the developing scrotum. It is dragged along by the descending testis and normally obliterates after descent is complete. Failure of obliteration leaves a patent processus vaginalis that becomes the anatomical basis for indirect inguinal hernias and communicating hydroceles.

A sudden discharge of clear, pink, serosanguinous fluid from an abdominal wound, sometimes called the 'pink sign', often precedes overt wound dehiscence by several hours, representing peritoneal fluid leaking through a partially separated fascial closure before the skin itself gives way. Recognising this warning sign allows early surgical assessment and, if needed, prompt return to theatre before complete evisceration occurs. It is a distinct clinical sign from other named eponymous signs related to different pathologies.
options: Grey Turner's sign of pancreatic necrosis
Battle's sign of basal skull fracture
The 'pink sign' or herald sign of impending dehiscence
questions.question: A patient recovering from major abdominal surgery develops a wound dehiscence on postoperative day 8, with a 'pink serosanguinous' discharge preceding visible separation of the wound edges. This classic warning sign is termed:

A patient with severe malnutrition undergoing preoperative optimisation before elective major surgery is started on nutritional support at least how many days beforehand, when feasible, to reduce postoperative complications?
questions.explanation: In severely malnourished patients undergoing major elective surgery, preoperative nutritional support for approximately 7 to 10 days, where the surgical timeline allows, has been shown to reduce postoperative complications such as wound infection and anastomotic leak by improving immune function and tissue healing capacity. This period allows sufficient time for measurable improvement in nutritional parameters without unduly delaying necessary surgery. The specific duration is individualised based on the severity of malnutrition and the urgency of the planned operation.
options: Only on the morning of surgery itself
6 months before the planned surgery date
No preoperative nutritional support has any proven benefit

questions.question: What is the first step when a spinal cord-injured patient presents with suspected autonomic dysreflexia?
questions.explanation: The immediate first step in autonomic dysreflexia is to sit the patient upright (to lower blood pressure orthostically) and identify and eliminate the triggering stimulus — most commonly a blocked urinary catheter, overdistended bladder, or faecal impaction. Antihypertensive medications (nifedipine, glyceryl trinitrate) are added if blood pressure remains dangerously elevated after trigger removal. This condition can be fatal if untreated.
options: Perform an emergency MRI of the spine
Administer oral morphine for headache relief
Apply ice packs to the chest and neck

questions.explanation: Fractionation divides the total radiation dose into multiple smaller fractions given over days to weeks. This exploits the differential repair capacity between normal tissues and tumour cells between fractions, allowing normal tissue recovery while achieving tumour cell kill. Standard fractionation is 1.8-2 Gy per fraction daily.
questions.question: Fractionation of radiotherapy involves:
options: Treatment with multiple radiation types simultaneously
Fractionation into smaller doses over time
Combination of radiotherapy with systemic chemotherapy
Radiation of multiple tumour sites in one session
Use of different radiation energies in one fraction

questions.explanation: Early ligation of the adrenal vein during phaeochromocytoma surgery reduces the systemic release of catecholamines into the circulation that would otherwise occur with ongoing tumour manipulation, helping to limit intraoperative hypertensive surges and haemodynamic instability. This technical step is used alongside, rather than as a replacement for, thorough preoperative alpha and beta blockade and continuous intraoperative haemodynamic monitoring. Close communication between the surgical and anaesthetic teams throughout the dissection remains essential to safely manage these potential swings in blood pressure.
options: Prevent any need for preoperative alpha-blockade
Eliminate the need for intraoperative blood pressure monitoring
Minimise catecholamine surges caused by intraoperative tumour manipulation
Allow the tumour to be removed without any prior biochemical preparation
Reduce operative time as the sole benefit of this technique
questions.question: A patient undergoing laparoscopic adrenalectomy for a functioning adrenal tumour has the adrenal vein identified and ligated early during the dissection when possible. This step is prioritised, particularly in phaeochromocytoma surgery, because early control of venous outflow helps to:

questions.explanation: Wedge compression fractures and 'cod-fish' biconcave deformities reflect weakening of the vertebral body itself under axial load in osteoporotic bone, causing the body to collapse anteriorly or centrally rather than primarily affecting the disc, facet joints, or posterior elements. Recognising these vertebral body changes on imaging supports a diagnosis of osteoporotic fracture rather than primary disc pathology. This distinction guides appropriate management, including bone health assessment and fracture risk reduction.
questions.question: An osteoporotic patient's spine X-ray shows anterior wedging of several vertebral bodies along with biconcave endplate deformities resembling a fish vertebra. Which spinal component is primarily affected by these changes?
The principle of 'damage control surgery' in severely injured trauma patients involves:
questions.explanation: Damage control surgery involves an abbreviated initial operation focused on controlling life-threatening haemorrhage (packing, vascular control) and limiting contamination (bowel stapling without anastomosis), followed by ICU resuscitation to correct the lethal triad, then a planned definitive reconstructive operation within 24-72 hours once physiology is restored. It improves survival in the most severely injured patients who could not tolerate prolonged surgery.
options: Initial damage control then ICU resuscitation before definitive repair
Definitive repair of all injuries in the first operation regardless of physiology
Extensive debridement and wound lavage as the first priority before haemostasis
Non-operative management of all penetrating abdominal injuries
Early total parenteral nutrition as the first surgical intervention

questions.explanation: MRI liver with hepatocyte-specific contrast agents such as gadoxetic acid (Primovist) has the highest sensitivity for detecting colorectal liver metastases, particularly subcentimetre lesions not visible on CT. It is the preferred investigation when resection of metastases is being considered. Accurate characterisation of lesion number, size, and proximity to hepatic vessels determines surgical resectability.
questions.question: Which investigation is MOST sensitive for detecting liver metastases from colorectal cancer?
A patient with ileocaecal tuberculosis develops recurrent subacute intestinal obstruction despite completing a full course of anti-tuberculous therapy. The most appropriate next step is:
questions.explanation: Fibrotic strictures resulting from healed tuberculous ulceration do not respond to further antimicrobial therapy since the obstruction is caused by scar tissue rather than active infection, so surgical resection or stricturoplasty of the affected segment is required once obstructive symptoms persist despite completed treatment. Continuing or repeating anti-tuberculous therapy in this context would not resolve the mechanical problem. This distinguishes fibrotic sequelae from ongoing active disease requiring drug therapy.
options: Repeat the same anti-tuberculous regimen for a further full course
Surgical resection of the strictured segment
Increase the dose of anti-tuberculous drugs indefinitely
Manage with laxatives and dietary modification alone
Switch to second-line anti-tuberculous drugs without imaging
Always provides a definitive cure without any further intervention needed
Achieves source control with lower morbidity in a stable patient
Is the only method capable of treating any intra-abdominal collection
Eliminates any risk of catheter-related complications
Is preferred even in patients with generalised peritonitis
questions.explanation: For a well-localised abscess in a haemodynamically stable patient, percutaneous drainage under image guidance achieves adequate source control while avoiding the additional morbidity of a formal laparotomy, and is often used as a bridge to definitive treatment of the underlying cause. It is not appropriate when there is generalised peritonitis or multiple loculated collections not amenable to catheter access, in which case surgery remains necessary. Careful patient selection is key to the success of this minimally invasive approach.
questions.question: A patient with a suspected intra-abdominal abscess undergoes ultrasound-guided percutaneous drainage. Compared with immediate surgical drainage, this approach is generally preferred for a well-localised collection because it:

questions.explanation: The two-column theory divides the spine into an anterior column, comprising the vertebral bodies and discs, and a posterior column, comprising the posterior elements and ligaments, as a simplified model for assessing spinal stability. This differs from the more detailed three-column theory (Denis classification), which further subdivides the anterior column into anterior and middle components for more precise instability assessment. Understanding which model is being referenced is important when interpreting different descriptions of spinal stability in clinical practice.
questions.question: A spinal surgeon explains spinal stability using a model dividing the spine into anterior and posterior load-bearing structures. Which theory does this describe?
In a patient with obstructive jaundice from pancreatic head carcinoma deemed borderline resectable, what is the ROLE of pre-operative biliary drainage?
options: Mandatory before any surgery to reduce operative mortality
Routinely indicated to allow time for nutritional optimisation
Contraindicated as it increases infection risk
Required for biopsy access to confirm malignancy
Only for severe cholangitis or marked hyperbilirubinaemia
questions.explanation: Pre-operative biliary drainage in pancreatic carcinoma is reserved for patients with severe cholangitis, bilirubin above 250 micromol/L prior to neoadjuvant chemotherapy, or those in whom surgery will be significantly delayed. Routine pre-operative drainage in resectable disease has not been shown to reduce morbidity and may increase infectious complications. Endoscopic stenting is preferred over percutaneous approaches.

options: Permanent suprapubic catheter as the universal first choice
Continuous urinary diversion surgery as first-line for all patients
Fluid restriction alone without any catheterisation
