questions.explanation: Necrotising fasciitis requires emergency surgical debridement of all necrotic tissue as the cornerstone of treatment, as the condition is rapidly progressive and fatal without surgery. No antibiotic regimen alone can penetrate the avascular necrotic tissue or control the advancing infection. Wide debridement, even at the cost of significant tissue loss and disfigurement, is life-saving. IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (covering streptococci, staphylococci, and anaerobes) and supportive care are essential adjuncts.
questions.question: The primary treatment modality for established necrotising fasciitis is:

options: Aplastic crisis from bone marrow suppression
Haemolytic crisis alone without splenic involvement
questions.explanation: Splenic sequestration crisis involves sudden pooling of a large volume of blood within the spleen, causing rapid splenic enlargement, a sharp drop in haemoglobin, and can progress rapidly to hypovolaemic shock, particularly in young children. It requires urgent fluid resuscitation and transfusion. Recurrent episodes are an indication for elective splenectomy in some patients.
questions.question: A child with sickle cell disease presents with sudden pallor, lethargy, and a rapidly enlarging spleen. Haemoglobin has dropped sharply from baseline. This is MOST consistent with:

options: Leave the hydrocele; it will always resolve spontaneously
Explore left side and repair patent processus vaginalis
Aspirate the left hydrocele with a needle percutaneously
Prescribe scrotal support and review in 3 months only
Order an ultrasound first and plan separately under another anaesthetic
questions.explanation: In a child with a unilateral hernia and a contralateral hydrocele, left-sided exploration at the same operation is justified because the hydrocele represents a patent processus vaginalis, and the risk of developing a clinically significant contralateral hernia is approximately 40%. Bilateral exploration avoids a second general anaesthetic. In adults with primary vaginal hydroceles, the processus is obliterated and surgery is only for symptomatic hydrocele.
questions.question: In a child undergoing right herniorrhaphy who also has a left-sided hydrocele, what is appropriate management of the left side?

questions.explanation: 5-Flucytosine is converted by fungal cytosine deaminase (absent in mammalian cells) into 5-fluorouracil, which inhibits fungal DNA synthesis. This selective conversion explains its selective fungicidal activity. It is used in combination with Amphotericin B for cryptococcal meningitis and systemic candidiasis.
questions.question: Which antifungal drug is converted by fungal cytosine deaminase into 5-fluorouracil?

options: Right hemicolectomy with primary ileocolic anastomosis
Transverse loop colostomy for decompression only
Endoscopic stent as bridge to elective right hemicolectomy
questions.explanation: Emergency right hemicolectomy with primary ileocolic anastomosis is safe and preferred for right-sided obstructing colonic carcinoma because the well-vascularised small bowel anastomoses to the transverse colon reliably, even in an obstructed, unprepared bowel. This avoids a stoma. Left-sided obstructions are higher risk for primary anastomosis and more frequently require staged procedures or stenting.
questions.question: In the management of an obstructed right-sided colon carcinoma requiring emergency surgery, the preferred operation is:

questions.explanation: Appendiceal carcinoids below 2 cm carry less than 2% risk of metastasis and are adequately treated by simple appendicectomy alone. Tumours above 2 cm require right hemicolectomy given the substantially higher metastatic risk. Size is the single most important prognostic determinant in appendiceal carcinoid tumours.
options: Simple appendicectomy is sufficient and curative
Staging CT and PET followed by formal bowel resection
questions.question: A patient is found to have a carcinoid tumour of the appendix measuring 1.5 cm at appendicectomy. The MOST appropriate management is:

questions.explanation: A sputum smear-positive pulmonary TB patient produces approximately 3000 droplet nuclei per cough, each potentially containing viable M. tuberculosis. This high infectious burden explains the efficient airborne transmission of TB, particularly in enclosed poorly ventilated spaces and healthcare settings.
questions.question: A sputum smear-positive pulmonary TB patient produces approximately how many droplet nuclei per cough?

questions.explanation: Current ASCO/ESMO guidelines for CRC surveillance post-curative resection recommend CT chest/abdomen/pelvis every 6 months for 2 years, then annually up to 5 years; colonoscopy at 1 year post-surgery (then 3-yearly if no polyps); and CEA every 3–6 months for 5 years. This combination detects resectable recurrence at the earliest opportunity. PET-CT is reserved for indeterminate CT findings.
options: Annual CEA only for 5 years without imaging
CT annually for 3 years and colonoscopy every 5 years
PET-CT every 6 months for 3 years to detect recurrence
MRI of the pelvis annually for 5 years in rectal cancer only
CT CAP 6-monthly ×2 yrs, annual ×3 yrs, colonoscopy at 1 yr
questions.question: Colorectal cancer surveillance post-curative resection includes which combination according to guidelines?

options: Duration from symptom onset to surgical detorsion
The patient's age at the time of torsion
The degree of testicular rotation (number of twists)
Whether the torsion affects the left or right testis
The Doppler flow findings on scrotal ultrasound
questions.explanation: The duration of ischaemia is the single most critical determinant of testicular salvage. Salvage rate exceeds 90% when explored within 6 hours of onset, approximately 50% at 12 hours, and under 10% at 24 hours. Each hour of delay significantly increases the probability of testicular infarction. This makes testicular torsion a true surgical emergency where clinical diagnosis should prompt immediate scrotal exploration without waiting for investigations.
questions.question: Which is the single most critical factor determining testicular salvage after testicular torsion?

questions.explanation: A low SAAG (<1.1 g/dL) confirms exudative ascites, ruling out portal hypertension-related causes (cirrhosis, cardiac failure). A high protein (5 g/dL), ADA >40 U/L, and clinical features of systemic TB in a young person from an endemic area are diagnostic of tuberculous peritonitis. Malignant ascites also has low SAAG but typically shows malignant cells on cytology and low ADA.
questions.question: A 40-year-old man from a TB-endemic country presents with ascites, weight loss, and fever. Ascitic fluid SAAG is 0.7 g/dL, protein is 5 g/dL, and ADA is 55 U/L. The MOST likely diagnosis is:
options: Cirrhotic ascites with spontaneous bacterial peritonitis
Malignant peritoneal ascites from gastric carcinoma
Cardiac ascites from right heart failure
Immediate laparotomy and formal hepatic resection
Non-operative management with serial observation and angioembolisation
Laparoscopic exploration and haemostatic gauze application
Thrombin-soaked gauze packing through the stab wound
Fresh frozen plasma infusion and ICU monitoring alone
questions.question: A patient sustains a stab wound to the right upper quadrant. CT shows a grade III liver laceration with active bleeding and 500 mL haemoperitoneum. He is haemodynamically stable. The MOST appropriate management is:
questions.explanation: Haemodynamically stable patients with liver lacerations (including grade III) are primarily managed non-operatively, as 80–90% stop bleeding spontaneously. Angioembolisation is used for contrast blush or ongoing haemorrhage on repeat imaging. Surgery is reserved for haemodynamically unstable patients or those who fail non-operative management.

questions.question: Autonomic dysreflexia is a life-threatening complication of spinal cord injury above which level?
questions.explanation: Autonomic dysreflexia is a potentially life-threatening syndrome occurring in patients with spinal cord injury at or above T6 (the level of splanchnic sympathetic outflow). A noxious stimulus below the level of injury (e.g., bladder distension, pressure sore) triggers a massive sympathetic discharge causing severe hypertension, headache, bradycardia, and sweating. It requires immediate identification and removal of the triggering stimulus.

questions.question: Which drug class relaxes smooth muscle in the bladder neck and prostate to relieve lower urinary tract obstruction in BPH?
questions.explanation: Alpha-1 adrenergic receptor blockers (e.g., tamsulosin, doxazosin, alfuzosin, prazosin) relax the smooth muscle of the bladder neck and prostate by blocking alpha-1 receptors, reducing outflow resistance and improving urinary flow within days of starting therapy. Unlike 5-alpha reductase inhibitors, they do not reduce prostate volume but act faster. They are first-line medical therapy for symptomatic BPH, particularly for relief of obstructive symptoms.

questions.question: In acute severe heart failure, systemic hypotension WITHOUT peripheral oedema is MOST characteristic of:
questions.explanation: Acute heart failure, as from a massive myocardial infarction, presents with sudden reduction in cardiac output and systemic hypotension but without peripheral oedema, as there has been insufficient time for fluid retention. This contrasts with chronic heart failure where oedema is prominent and blood pressure is maintained until late stages. Acute HF is predominantly systolic in mechanism.

Spigelian hernias occur through the spigelian fascia along the semilunar line, most commonly at or just below the level of the arcuate line where the posterior rectus sheath is deficient, making the abdominal wall relatively weaker at this point. These hernias can be difficult to diagnose clinically because the overlying intact external oblique aponeurosis may mask the underlying defect, sometimes requiring ultrasound or CT for confirmation. Surgical repair is generally recommended given a relatively high risk of incarceration.
options: Along the semilunar line, below the level of the umbilicus
At the midline, above the umbilicus exclusively
At the site of a previous appendicectomy scar only
Directly through the linea alba above the xiphisternum
questions.question: A patient with a Spigelian hernia presents with a lump at the lateral border of the rectus abdominis muscle. This hernia most commonly occurs at which level?
The most serious immediate complication of trocar insertion during laparoscopy is:
questions.explanation: Vascular or bowel injury during trocar insertion is the most serious immediate laparoscopic complication, potentially causing catastrophic haemorrhage (if a major vessel is injured) or peritoneal contamination (from bowel perforation). These injuries may not be immediately apparent. Risk is reduced by using Veress needle or Hasson open technique, and inserting secondary trocars under direct vision.

options: Chronically raised intravesical pressure transmitted retrogradely to the upper urinary tracts
Direct bacterial spread from the bladder to the kidneys in all cases
An unrelated primary renal disease coincidentally occurring simultaneously
Immune-mediated glomerular injury triggered by prostatic obstruction
Complete absence of any pressure transmission to the ureters
questions.explanation: Chronic bladder outlet obstruction leads to sustained elevation of intravesical pressure, which is transmitted retrogradely through the ureterovesical junctions to the upper urinary tracts, causing progressive hydroureter and hydronephrosis, and ultimately obstructive nephropathy with renal impairment if left untreated. This differs from acute retention, which typically causes reversible upper tract dilatation that resolves promptly with bladder decompression. Recognising chronic retention with renal impairment as a urological emergency prompts urgent catheterisation and close monitoring for post-obstructive diuresis.
questions.question: A patient with chronic urinary retention from long-standing BPH develops bilateral hydronephrosis and renal impairment. The pathophysiological mechanism linking bladder outlet obstruction to upper tract damage is:

questions.explanation: The disruption sequence (healthy embryo subjected to breakdown or injury) is exemplified by thalidomide and TORCH infections causing limb deformities. Warfarin, phenytoin, and alcohol are associated with malformation sequences (intrinsic embryonic defects). Thalidomide is the classic teratogenic agent associated with phocomelia (failure of limb formation), a severe upper limb congenital anomaly.
questions.question: Which drug exposure during pregnancy is specifically implicated in the deformation sequence of congenital hand anomalies?

questions.explanation: Broad-spectrum antibiotics disrupt the normal competing bacterial flora, allowing Candida overgrowth, while an indwelling central venous catheter used for parenteral nutrition provides a direct portal for bloodstream invasion. This combination is a well-recognised risk factor for disseminated candidiasis in surgical patients. Catheter removal and antifungal therapy are key components of management.
options: Antibiotic-disrupted flora with a central line present
questions.question: A patient develops disseminated candidiasis after prolonged use of broad-spectrum antibiotics and total parenteral nutrition following major surgery. The MOST likely predisposing factor is:

questions.explanation: A post-dexamethasone suppression cortisol above 50 nmol/L indicates failure of normal suppression, suggesting autonomous cortisol secretion or subclinical Cushing's syndrome. While clinically silent, this carries increased risks of osteoporosis, diabetes, and hypertension. Adrenalectomy may be considered in younger patients with comorbidities attributed to cortisol excess.
questions.question: A 50-year-old woman has a 1.8 cm adrenal incidentaloma. Biochemistry shows cortisol of 95 nmol/L after overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression. This finding is consistent with:
options: Normal dexamethasone suppression; no further workup needed

questions.explanation: A renal-origin abdominal mass in a young child that respects the midline, sometimes associated with hypertension due to renin secretion, is characteristic of Wilms' tumour, the most common renal malignancy of childhood. Neuroblastoma, in contrast, often crosses the midline and arises from sympathetic chain tissue, most commonly the adrenal medulla. This distinction guides both imaging interpretation and subsequent management planning.
questions.question: A 4-year-old presents with a right-sided abdominal mass that does not cross the midline, found incidentally on examination, along with hypertension. Imaging suggests a renal origin. The most likely diagnosis is:
options: Neuroblastoma arising from the adrenal medulla

questions.explanation: After one pregnancy affected by a neural tube defect, the recurrence risk for the same mother is approximately 2–3%, significantly higher than the general population risk. This supports the multifactorial inheritance pattern of NTDs. High-dose folic acid supplementation (5mg daily) is recommended in subsequent pregnancies in such mothers to reduce this risk.
questions.question: The recurrence risk of neural tube defects for the same mother after one affected pregnancy is approximately:

questions.explanation: The triad of migratory right iliac fossa pain, low-grade fever, and localised guarding in a young adult is the classic presentation of acute appendicitis. While mesenteric adenitis mimics it, it typically follows an URTI with less guarding. Meckel's diverticulitis is rarer and may be clinically indistinguishable from appendicitis.
questions.question: A previously healthy 20-year-old has sudden onset abdominal pain worse on the right side. He can walk but prefers lying still. Temperature is 37.9°C and there is localised right iliac fossa guarding. The MOST likely diagnosis is:

questions.explanation: Reperfusion injury after prolonged limb ischaemia releases massive quantities of myoglobin, potassium, and acid from ischaemic muscle into the circulation. Myoglobinaemia causes renal tubular precipitation and acute kidney injury, while hyperkalaemia risks fatal cardiac arrhythmia. Alkalinisation of urine, aggressive hydration, and monitoring for compartment syndrome are essential in the post-operative period.
questions.question: A patient with an acutely ischaemic limb undergoes embolectomy. On withdrawing the Fogarty catheter, freshly clotted material is retrieved. Post-procedurally, serum potassium is 6.5 mEq/L and creatinine is rapidly rising. The MOST likely complication is:
options: Acute graft thrombosis at the embolectomy site
Reperfusion injury with myoglobinaemia and renal damage
Paradoxical embolism to the contralateral limb

questions.question: Hydroperitoneum (ascites) is best classified as which category of edema?
questions.explanation: Fluid accumulation in specific body cavities is designated with special terms: hydrothorax (pleural), hydropericardium (pericardial), and hydroperitoneum or ascites (peritoneal). These represent localized fluid collection in anatomically defined spaces rather than interstitial accumulation. This distinction is clinically important for investigation and management, particularly in assessing liver disease, cardiac failure, or malignancy.

In sickle cell disease, osteomyelitis is notably caused by Salmonella species in African patients, in addition to the usual Staphylococcus aureus. This is due to functional asplenia and altered gut immunity predisposing to Salmonella bacteraemia and bone seeding.
questions.question: Osteomyelitis in sickle cell disease in Africa most commonly involves:

A patient with recurrent inguinal hernia after a previous open Lichtenstein repair is being considered for further surgery. In this scenario, a laparoscopic approach is often preferred because it allows:
questions.explanation: After a previous anterior (open) hernia repair, the tissue planes anterior to the hernia defect are often scarred and more difficult to dissect safely, whereas a laparoscopic posterior approach accesses the preperitoneal space through a different, previously undisturbed surgical plane, potentially reducing the technical difficulty and complication risk compared with repeating an anterior dissection. This principle underlies the common recommendation to switch approaches (anterior to posterior or vice versa) when treating a recurrent hernia. The choice still depends on surgeon expertise and individual patient factors.
options: Complete avoidance of mesh in the repair to prevent further recurrence
Guaranteed elimination of any future recurrence risk
A simpler procedure than the original open repair in every case
Access to the preperitoneal space through a virgin surgical plane, avoiding scarred anterior tissue
Avoidance of general anaesthesia, which is otherwise mandatory

questions.question: A fistula-in-ano that passes through the external anal sphincter is classified as:
questions.explanation: A transsphincteric fistula passes through both the internal and external anal sphincters, traversing the intersphincteric plane before exiting through the external sphincter. Division carries a significant risk of faecal incontinence, mandating sphincter-preserving techniques such as seton placement, fibrin glue, or advancement flap. This is the most common complex fistula type encountered in surgical practice.

options: Only after surgical stabilisation and wound healing (week 6)
After transfer to a rehabilitation unit (3 months post-injury)
Only after the patient can actively participate
When neurological recovery plateaus at 1 year
Rehabilitation from acute phase: positioning and physiotherapy
questions.explanation: Rehabilitation in spinal cord injury begins from the acute phase while the patient is still in hospital. Early interventions include regular 2-hourly turning, limb physiotherapy to prevent contractures, respiratory physiotherapy, bladder management, nutritional support, and psychological support. Early rehabilitation significantly reduces complications (pressure sores, DVT, infections) and optimises the neurological recovery environment.
questions.question: Rehabilitation of a spinal cord-injured patient begins at which phase of management?
Following a total gastrectomy, a patient develops early dumping syndrome characterised by sweating, palpitations, and abdominal cramps shortly after meals. This is primarily caused by:
options: Reflux of bile into the residual oesophagus
Deficiency of intrinsic factor causing malabsorption
Bacterial overgrowth within a blind afferent loop
Rapid delivery of a hyperosmolar bolus into the small bowel drawing fluid into the lumen
Excess gastric acid secretion from residual mucosa
questions.explanation: Loss of the pyloric reservoir and regulatory mechanism after gastrectomy allows rapid emptying of a hyperosmolar meal into the jejunum, causing a fluid shift into the bowel lumen that reduces circulating volume and triggers vasomotor symptoms such as sweating and palpitations. This early dumping typically occurs within 30 minutes of eating. Dietary modification with smaller, more frequent low-carbohydrate meals is the mainstay of management.

The Gray (Gy) is the unit of absorbed radiation dose (1 Gy = 1 joule of energy absorbed per kilogram of tissue). The Sievert (Sv) is used for environmental or occupational radiation protection. The Becquerel (Bq) measures radioactivity in nuclear medicine (rate of radioactive decay).
questions.question: The unit of absorbed radiation dose in radiotherapy is:

options: Surgery is insufficient for all cancers
Radiotherapy is the only curative treatment
Chemotherapy is too toxic for majority of patients
Radiotherapy is cheaper than all other cancer treatments
Most cancers respond to ionizing radiation
questions.explanation: Radiotherapy is a major pillar of cancer management used alone or in combination with surgery and chemotherapy. It achieves curative intent in many cancers (radical radiotherapy), controls loco-regional disease, and provides effective palliation of symptoms. It is used in over 60% of cancer patients.
questions.question: Over 60% of cancer patients require radiotherapy because:

A patient sustains a head injury and afterwards cannot recall events for a short period immediately before the injury, though older memories remain intact. What is this specific type of memory loss called?
questions.explanation: Retrograde amnesia refers to loss of memory for events that occurred before the onset of a brain injury or illness, with the duration of the amnesic period often correlating with injury severity, while memories from further in the past typically remain more preserved. This differs from anterograde amnesia, which instead describes an inability to form new memories after the injury, a distinct and often more functionally significant deficit. Correctly distinguishing these two temporal directions of memory loss is important for accurate neurological assessment and prognostication after brain injury.

Percutaneous endoscopic microdiscectomy offers minimal soft tissue disruption, smaller incisions, reduced blood loss, and faster patient recovery compared to open microdiscectomy. However, it has a steeper learning curve, longer operative time in some series, and is not suitable for all disc configurations (particularly migrated fragments). Outcomes for appropriate cases are comparable to open surgery.
questions.question: Percutaneous endoscopic microdiscectomy is considered an alternative to standard surgery in lumbar disc herniation. What is its primary advantage over open surgery?
options: Minimal soft tissue disruption with faster recovery
Better visualisation of the disc space
Ability to treat all spinal levels equally

questions.question: Toxic megacolon in ulcerative colitis requires URGENT surgery when the transverse colon diameter exceeds:
questions.explanation: Toxic megacolon is defined radiologically by transverse colon dilatation above 6 cm with systemic toxicity. Diameters exceeding 6 cm on plain film in the context of fever, tachycardia, and leukocytosis indicate urgent colectomy to prevent perforation and sepsis. Initial intensive medical management includes bowel rest, IV steroids, and nasogastric decompression while preparing for surgery.

questions.question: Regarding Virchow's triad predisposing to deep vein thrombosis, which component is MOST relevant to a patient immobilised after major surgery?
options: Endothelial injury from a distant unrelated infection
Hypercoagulability from a rare inherited thrombophilia only
Arterial vasospasm unrelated to venous flow
Venous stasis from reduced calf muscle pump activity
Increased blood viscosity from severe dehydration alone
questions.explanation: Postoperative immobilisation reduces activation of the calf muscle pump, leading to venous stasis, one of the three components of Virchow's triad alongside endothelial injury and hypercoagulability, and stasis is particularly relevant in surgical patients confined to bed. Early mobilisation and mechanical or pharmacological prophylaxis directly address this component of thrombosis risk. Recognising the dominant contributing factor in a given clinical context helps tailor appropriate preventive strategies.

Even after complete wound maturation, repaired tissue achieves only approximately 80% of the tensile strength of uninjured normal tissue. This is because the collagen deposited during healing is organized differently from the original tissue, and the remodelling process reaches equilibrium at 21 days without fully restoring original mechanical properties. This limitation is important in planning suture removal and assessing wound load-bearing capacity.
questions.question: The maximum tensile strength achieved after wound healing is what percentage of normal uninjured tissue?

questions.explanation: Scleroderma (systemic sclerosis) causes fibrotic replacement of smooth muscle in the lower oesophagus, resulting in aperistalsis and a hypotensive (low pressure) LOS. This combination causes severe GORD from unimpeded acid reflux with impaired clearance. Unlike achalasia where LOS pressure is elevated, scleroderma causes a low LOS pressure with aperistalsis of the smooth muscle portion only.
questions.question: A 40-year-old woman with longstanding scleroderma complains of severe heartburn and regurgitation. Manometry shows aperistalsis of the lower oesophagus with low LOS pressure. This pattern is MOST consistent with:

questions.explanation: Plasma oncotic pressure is approximately 26 mmHg and is generated primarily by plasma proteins, especially albumin. It opposes the outward hydrostatic pressure of approximately 32 mmHg at the arteriolar end of the capillary, with net filtration occurring at this end. At the venular end, where hydrostatic pressure falls to about 15 mmHg, oncotic pressure exceeds hydrostatic pressure, facilitating reabsorption.
questions.question: The plasma oncotic pressure that opposes capillary hydrostatic pressure is approximately:

questions.explanation: Nocardia species are aerobic organisms that stain partially acid-fast and primarily present as pulmonary disease. Brain abscesses are frequent secondary lesions of Nocardiosis. N. asteroides predominantly causes pulmonary disease while N. brasiliensis causes subcutaneous lesions. Treatment is with sulfonamides.
questions.question: An acid-fast organism that causes pulmonary disease with brain abscesses as frequent secondary lesions is:

questions.explanation: New severe back pain radiating to the groin following aortic surgery should raise concern for a retroperitoneal haematoma or other graft-related complication, such as an anastomotic leak, given the potential for significant and rapidly progressive haemorrhage in this setting. Prompt investigation with imaging is warranted to exclude a serious postoperative complication before attributing the pain to a benign musculoskeletal cause. Early recognition and intervention are critical given the potential severity of vascular graft complications.
options: Simple musculoskeletal back strain from positioning
Renal colic from a coincidental ureteric stone
Mild constipation from postoperative opioid use
Referred pain from an unrelated hip arthritis
questions.question: A 55-year-old man develops severe lower back pain radiating to the groin after aortic aneurysm repair. The MOST concerning diagnosis to exclude is:

questions.explanation: Emergency radiotherapy for spinal cord compression aims to reduce tumour bulk rapidly and relieve compression to preserve or restore neurological function, as untreated compression can lead to irreversible paralysis. High-dose corticosteroids are given concurrently to reduce oedema and are not replaced by radiotherapy. This treatment is palliative rather than curative in the context of metastatic disease.
options: Achieve complete cure of the underlying malignancy
Eliminate the need for any further systemic therapy
Provide long-term pain relief as the sole objective
Preserve neurological function by preventing further cord compression
Replace the need for corticosteroid administration
questions.question: A patient with spinal cord compression from vertebral metastases requires emergency radiotherapy. The PRIMARY purpose of this emergency treatment is to:

questions.explanation: Anterior cord syndrome, resulting from compromise of the anterior spinal artery territory, causes loss of motor function and pain and temperature sensation (corticospinal and spinothalamic tracts) below the level of injury, while proprioception and vibration sense, carried in the dorsal columns supplied by the posterior spinal arteries, are relatively preserved. This dissociated pattern helps distinguish anterior cord syndrome from other incomplete cord syndromes and from complete transection, where all modalities would be lost. Recognising the vascular basis also explains why this syndrome can occur after aortic surgery compromising segmental blood supply.
questions.question: A patient sustains a spinal cord injury causing loss of motor function and pain and temperature sensation below the level of injury, with preservation of proprioception and vibration sense. Which vascular territory is most likely compromised?

questions.explanation: Contractures develop from fibrous scar formation and tissue shortening across joints. They are a late complication seen after burns, wound infections, or any injury resulting in extensive scarring. Prevention involves early physiotherapy, splinting, and range-of-motion exercises.
questions.question: Contractures as late surgical complications develop primarily due to:

options: Increasing platelet production in the marrow
Stimulating clot formation at the tumour surface
questions.explanation: Emergency radiotherapy is used for haemostasis by inducing tumour cell death and shrinkage, thereby reducing the vascular tumour burden responsible for bleeding. It is effective for haemoptysis from lung tumours, haematuria from bladder tumours, and rectal bleeding from rectal cancer.
questions.question: Radiation therapy acts as a haemostatic agent by:

questions.explanation: The smooth, tapering 'bird's beak' narrowing at the lower oesophageal sphincter on barium swallow is the radiological hallmark of achalasia cardia. The progressive dysphagia to both solids and liquids (unlike carcinoma which is initially for solids) and the absence of weight loss early in the course further support achalasia. Manometry shows aperistalsis and incomplete LOS relaxation.
questions.question: A 50-year-old woman with progressive dysphagia first to solids, then liquids, with no weight loss has a barium swallow showing a smooth, tapering narrowing at the lower oesophagus with a 'bird's beak' appearance. The MOST likely diagnosis is:

options: Urgent MRI imaging and prompt surgical or medical treatment
Outpatient oral antibiotics with routine follow-up in two weeks
Delayed imaging after a trial of physiotherapy
Immediate discharge with safety-netting advice alone
questions.explanation: Spinal epidural abscess is a neurosurgical emergency requiring urgent MRI imaging to confirm the diagnosis and extent, followed by prompt intervention, which may include surgical decompression and drainage alongside targeted antibiotic therapy, given the risk of rapid, potentially irreversible neurological deterioration if treatment is delayed. Outpatient management, delayed imaging, or simple reassurance would risk permanent neurological injury or death from an untreated abscess. Recognising the combination of severe back pain, fever, and progressive deficit as red-flag features is critical for prompt emergency referral.
questions.question: A patient with a suspected spinal epidural abscess presents with severe back pain, fever, and rapidly progressive neurological deficit. What is the most appropriate immediate management priority?

questions.explanation: Hepatitis B has the highest viral load and resistance to physical insults among blood-borne pathogens, making blood contamination of equipment surfaces a significant risk for HBV transmission. Only HBV-specific immunoprophylaxis exists among the common hepatitis viruses.
questions.question: Among blood-borne pathogens, which has the highest viral load and resistance to physical insults?

A patient with head injury opens eyes only to pain, makes incomprehensible sounds, and shows abnormal flexion (decorticate posturing) to painful stimuli. What is the correct total Glasgow Coma Scale score?
questions.explanation: Scoring each component separately: eye opening to pain scores 2, incomprehensible sounds scores 2, and abnormal flexion (decorticate) posturing scores 3, giving a total Glasgow Coma Scale score of 7 (2+2+3), which falls within the severe head injury category. Errors in GCS scoring often arise from confusing decorticate (abnormal flexion, score 3) with decerebrate (abnormal extension, score 2) posturing, so precise definitions must be applied. Accurate calculation is essential since management decisions and prognosis are directly linked to the total score.

questions.question: Hesselbach's triangle is bounded by which three structures?
questions.explanation: Hesselbach's triangle is bounded by the inguinal ligament inferiorly, inferior epigastric vessels laterally, and lateral border of the rectus abdominis medially. This triangle represents the floor of the inguinal canal through which direct inguinal hernias protrude (medial to the inferior epigastric vessels). Indirect hernias enter lateral to these vessels through the internal ring. Identifying this triangle is essential for hernia anatomy and repair planning.
options: Inguinal ligament inferiorly, femoral vein laterally, rectus sheath medially
External oblique aponeurosis, internal oblique muscle, and transversus abdominis muscle
Pubic tubercle, pubic symphysis, and inguinal ligament
Inguinal ligament, epigastric vessels, and rectus border
Poupart's ligament, iliopubic tract, and pectineal ligament (Cooper's)

questions.explanation: Water deficit = [(Serum Na - 140) x TBW] / 140 = [(155 - 140) x 42] / 140 = 630/140 = 4.5 L (closest answer is 4.0 L). This formula estimates free water deficit in patients with hypernatremia due to pure water loss. Treatment begins with D5W unless hypotension is present.
questions.question: Water deficit in a patient with serum Na of 155 mEq/L and estimated total body water of 42 L is approximately:

questions.explanation: In patients with atrial fibrillation, acute limb ischaemia is most commonly caused by cardiogenic embolism from a left atrial appendage thrombus that lodges at the femoral or popliteal artery bifurcation. The onset is characteristically sudden and complete without prior claudication. Thromboembolectomy using Fogarty catheter is the surgical treatment of choice.
options: In-situ thrombosis of a native artery
Arteriovenous fistula thrombosis from prior dialysis access
Hypercoagulable state from factor V Leiden
Graft thrombosis from prior bypass surgery
Embolism from a left heart thrombus
questions.question: The MOST common cause of acute limb ischaemia in a patient with atrial fibrillation is:
Fracture-dislocation injuries of the spine are most unstable because they disrupt which structural components?
questions.explanation: Fracture-dislocation injuries involve disruption of all three spinal columns (anterior, middle, and posterior), making them the most mechanically unstable injuries. They are associated with the highest rate of neurological injury. Surgical stabilisation with reduction, decompression, and instrumented fusion is required. The Denis three-column model predicts instability based on the number of disrupted columns.

In prosthetic surgery, strict aseptic technique with properly sterilized implants and instruments is paramount for preventing postoperative infections. Prophylactic antibiotics are recommended to cover the perioperative period, not prolonged postoperative use which encourages resistance.
questions.question: Strict aseptic technique with sterilized implants reduces postoperative infection in:
The pathophysiological hallmark of achalasia cardia is:
questions.explanation: Achalasia results from selective degeneration of inhibitory postganglionic neurons (nitrergic), which normally release NO and VIP to relax the LOS. The resulting unopposed cholinergic excitation causes persistently elevated LOS pressure and failure to relax. Loss of oesophageal peristalsis accompanies LOS dysfunction. This neurodegeneration may involve genetic, immune, or viral factors.
options: Excessive cholinergic stimulation causing LOS spasm
Fibrosis of the oesophageal wall replacing smooth muscle
Reflux-induced stricture at the gastro-oesophageal junction
Ectopic gastric mucosa producing acid near the LOS
Nitrergic neuron loss causing impaired LOS relaxation
Full thickness burns in non-circumferential areas
Superficial partial thickness burns with blistering
Circumferential full-thickness burns causing compartment syndrome
questions.explanation: Escharotomy (incision through the eschar) is indicated for circumferential full-thickness burns causing compartment syndrome. It is performed on limbs to restore distal perfusion and on circumferential chest/neck burns to restore chest wall compliance and improve ventilation.
questions.question: Escharotomy is indicated in burns patients for:
Alcohol (70% ethyl or isopropyl) is LEAST effective against:
questions.explanation: Alcohol (ethyl or isopropyl at 70-99%) is less effective against hydrophilic (non-enveloped) viruses. It provides a very positive response against vegetative cells, lipophilic viruses, and tubecle bacilli. It is also inactivated by organic matter and is flammable.

questions.question: Which clinical sign specifically indicates uncal herniation (transtentorial herniation) from a rapidly expanding intracranial haematoma?
options: Loss of corneal reflex bilaterally without pupil changes
Fixed dilated pupil ipsilateral to haematoma
questions.explanation: Uncal herniation from an expanding supratentorial haematoma compresses the ipsilateral oculomotor nerve (CN III) as the uncus herniates through the tentorial notch. The first sign is ipsilateral pupillary dilatation and loss of the light reflex (CN III compression). Progressive herniation causes contralateral Babinski sign and then bilateral motor posturing. This is a neurosurgical emergency requiring immediate intervention.

questions.question: Which lumbar disc level accounts for 95% of lumbar disc prolapses?
questions.explanation: Approximately 95% of lumbar disc prolapses occur at L4/5 and L5/S1, the most mechanically stressed mobile segments. L3/4 accounts for about 4% and levels above for only 1%. This distribution reflects cumulative mechanical loading, disc degeneration patterns, and relative disc size. Clinical presentation depends on which root is compressed at these levels.

questions.question: A fetus is diagnosed antenatally with absence of the cranial vault and cerebral hemispheres, a condition incompatible with survival beyond a short period after birth. Which neural tube defect is this?
questions.explanation: Anencephaly results from failure of closure of the cranial (rostral) end of the neural tube, leading to absence of the cranial vault and much of the cerebral hemispheres, and is uniformly fatal, usually within hours to days after birth. Encephalocele, by contrast, involves herniation of brain tissue and meninges through a cranial defect but with an intact, if malformed, cranial vault covering much of the brain, and can sometimes be compatible with survival depending on severity. Distinguishing these conditions is important for antenatal counselling regarding prognosis.

questions.question: The Nigro protocol for anal carcinoma achieves complete pathological response in approximately what percentage of patients?
questions.explanation: The Nigro protocol (concurrent chemoradiotherapy with 5-FU and mitomycin C delivering 50–54 Gy) achieves complete pathological response in 60–80% of anal carcinoma cases, avoiding a permanent colostomy in the majority. APR is reserved for residual or recurrent disease. This protocol transformed anal carcinoma from a condition requiring APR to one primarily managed non-surgically.

Previous pelvic radiation causes fibrosis, endarteritis obliterans, and impaired healing in bowel tissue, significantly reducing the likelihood of spontaneous fistula closure. Factors that favour spontaneous closure (SNAP criteria: Short tract, No obstruction distally, Absence of radiation damage, No adjacent abscess or foreign body, and no malignancy) predict conservative management success. Radiation-damaged bowel virtually always requires surgical resection for fistula healing.
questions.question: All of the following are features that promote spontaneous closure of an enterocutaneous fistula EXCEPT:
options: Previous pelvic radiation to the bowel
No malignancy in the fistula tract

questions.question: A patient undergoing robotic-assisted laparoscopic prostatectomy benefits from enhanced instrument articulation compared with conventional straight laparoscopic instruments. This is primarily due to which technical feature of robotic systems?
options: Wristed instruments providing multiple degrees of freedom of movement
Complete elimination of the need for any pneumoperitoneum
Direct haptic feedback superior to open surgery in all cases
Automatic tissue identification without surgeon input
Removal of the need for a bedside surgical assistant entirely
questions.explanation: Robotic surgical systems incorporate wristed instruments capable of a greater range of articulated movement than the fixed-fulcrum, limited-degree-of-freedom movement of conventional straight laparoscopic instruments, facilitating more precise suturing and dissection in confined spaces such as the pelvis. This enhanced dexterity is particularly advantageous in procedures requiring fine reconstruction, such as the vesicourethral anastomosis in prostatectomy. Robotic systems do still require pneumoperitoneum and a trained bedside assistant to manage instrument exchanges and other tasks.

questions.question: A 35-year-old woman presents with fever, right iliac fossa pain, and vaginal discharge. Which investigation would BEST help distinguish appendicitis from pelvic inflammatory disease?
options: Serum beta-hCG to exclude ectopic pregnancy
CT abdomen with oral and IV contrast
Transvaginal ultrasound or MRI of the pelvis
questions.explanation: Transvaginal ultrasound directly visualises the appendix, ovaries, and fallopian tubes, differentiating appendicitis (thick-walled non-compressible appendix >6 mm) from PID (tubo-ovarian complex or free fluid). CT provides excellent anatomical detail but involves radiation. In fertile women, MRI avoids radiation while offering superior soft-tissue contrast.

questions.question: A patient several years after lumbar spine surgery continues to have persistent pain despite technically successful surgery and no identifiable structural cause on repeat imaging. What umbrella term is used to describe this clinical scenario?
questions.explanation: Failed back surgery syndrome is a broad umbrella term describing persistent or recurrent pain following spinal surgery, encompassing a range of possible underlying causes including scar tissue formation, recurrent disc herniation, adjacent segment disease, ongoing nerve injury, or sometimes no clearly identifiable structural cause at all. This is distinct from more specific diagnoses like recurrent disc herniation or adjacent segment disease, which describe particular identifiable causes rather than the general syndrome label. Recognising this term helps frame the need for a broad, systematic reassessment rather than assuming a single specific cause.

questions.question: A 40-year-old with hypertension and hypokalaemia has an adrenal mass on CT. The INITIAL investigation to differentiate Conn's from Cushing's syndrome is:
questions.explanation: The plasma aldosterone-to-renin ratio (ARR) is the primary screening test for primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn's syndrome), while the overnight dexamethasone suppression test screens for cortisol excess (Cushing's syndrome). Both tests are performed early before invasive studies. Adrenal vein sampling is reserved for Conn's syndrome confirmed biochemically to lateralise the source.

The single most important determinant of outcome after Kasai portoenterostomy is the age at surgery: operations before 45–60 days achieve bile drainage in 80–90% with 10-year native liver survival of 40–60%; operations after 90 days have dramatically worse outcomes. The degree of hepatic fibrosis/cirrhosis at the time of surgery (reflecting disease progression) independently predicts outcome. Even with successful Kasai, many patients eventually require liver transplantation.
questions.question: The long-term outcome of Kasai portoenterostomy for biliary atresia is BEST determined by:
options: Age at Kasai and presence of cirrhosis at surgery
The type of biliary atresia (I, II, or III) alone
The length of the Roux loop used for the jejunostomy
The surgeons preference for open versus laparoscopic approach
The postoperative use of corticosteroids and ursodeoxycholic acid

questions.question: During hand scrubbing before surgery, a surgeon accidentally touches the tap with a gloved hand. The MOST appropriate action is:
options: Continue the operation since only the tap was touched
Wipe the glove with an alcohol swab and proceed
Apply a second glove over the contaminated one
Remove the glove, rescrub, and re-glove
Rinse the glove under sterile saline and continue
questions.explanation: Any contact between a sterile gloved hand and a non-sterile surface breaks asepsis and mandates removal, rescrubbing, and reapplication of a new sterile glove. Wiping or double-gloving over a contaminated glove does not restore sterility. This principle protects the patient from surgical site infection.

Preserved proprioception and vibration sense, carried in the dorsal columns, alongside loss of pain and temperature sensation, carried in the spinothalamic tract, indicates selective sparing of the dorsal columns with spinothalamic tract involvement, a pattern classically seen in anterior cord syndrome due to the differing blood supply and anatomical location of these two tracts within the cord. Recognising which specific tract is affected based on the pattern of sensory loss is fundamental to localising spinal cord pathology accurately. This dissociated sensory pattern would not be expected with a lesion affecting both tracts equally, such as complete cord transection.
options: Spinothalamic tract spared, dorsal columns affected
Corticospinal tract spared, dorsal columns affected
Dorsal columns spared, spinothalamic tract affected
questions.question: A patient with a spinal cord injury is found to have preserved proprioception and vibration sense but absent pain and temperature sensation below the level of injury. Which spinal tract is most likely spared, and which is affected?

options: Fever, weight loss, and night sweats
Abdominal pain, jaundice, and palpable mass
Nausea, vomiting, and dark urine only
questions.explanation: The classic clinical triad of choledochal cyst is abdominal pain (biliary colic from intermittent obstruction), jaundice, and a palpable right upper quadrant mass. However, all three features are present simultaneously in only 20–30% of cases. Choledochal cysts are classified by Todani's classification (Types I–V) and require complete surgical excision with Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy due to the risk of malignant transformation (cholangiocarcinoma).

A patient develops urinary retention on the first postoperative night after spinal anaesthesia for a hernia repair. The MOST likely underlying mechanism is:
options: Established benign prostatic hyperplasia newly causing obstruction
Iatrogenic ureteric injury during the hernia repair
Temporary bladder detrusor dysfunction from the spinal anaesthetic
Bladder calculus formed during the procedure
questions.explanation: Spinal anaesthesia can temporarily impair bladder detrusor function and sensation, leading to postoperative urinary retention that typically resolves as the anaesthetic effect wears off. This is a recognised and usually self-limiting complication rather than a sign of structural pathology. Catheterisation is used for symptomatic relief while awaiting recovery of bladder function.

The ligamentum flavum connects adjacent laminae and lies just anterior to them within the spinal canal; with age-related hypertrophy and degeneration, its thickening contributes significantly to posterior spinal canal narrowing and central stenosis. The anterior and posterior longitudinal ligaments run along the vertebral bodies rather than between the laminae, so they contribute differently to canal anatomy. Recognising the ligamentum flavum's specific anatomical location explains its central role in degenerative canal stenosis.
questions.question: A patient with longstanding lumbar canal stenosis is found to have marked thickening of a ligament located just anterior to the lamina, contributing to posterior canal narrowing. Which ligament is responsible?

options: Intravenous antibiotics and reassessment in 48 hours
Incision and drainage of the abscess
MRI pelvis to exclude fistula before any intervention
Seton placement to manage the fistula
questions.question: A 30-year-old woman presents with perianal pain, swelling, and fever. Examination reveals a tender fluctuant mass at 6 o'clock. The CORRECT initial management is:
questions.explanation: A perianal abscess requires urgent incision and drainage as the definitive initial treatment; antibiotics alone are ineffective and may mask progression to necrotising infection. Further investigation for underlying fistula is performed electively after the acute infection resolves. Delaying drainage risks spreading cellulitis and sepsis.

questions.question: Regarding septic shock, the SOFA score criterion for renal dysfunction includes which threshold?
options: Urine output less than 0.1 mL/kg/hr for 2 hours
Creatinine above 353 micromol/L or oliguria 12 hours
Oliguria for 1 hour with serum creatinine doubling
Serum creatinine above 200 micromol/L in any context
Anuria for 6 hours regardless of creatinine
questions.explanation: The SOFA score assigns maximum renal points for creatinine above 353 micromol/L (4 mg/dL) or urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/hr for 12 hours or below 0.3 mL/kg/hr for 24 hours. The Surviving Sepsis Campaign recommends targeting urine output above 0.5 mL/kg/hr as part of resuscitation goals. Renal replacement therapy is initiated for refractory fluid overload, acidosis, or uraemic complications.

options: Localised peritoneal irritation from an inflamed appendix
questions.question: A patient has generalised abdominal tenderness maximal in the right iliac fossa with rebound tenderness at McBurney's point elicited by palpating the left iliac fossa. This combined finding best supports:
questions.explanation: Referred rebound tenderness at McBurney's point when the contralateral iliac fossa is released, together with maximal local tenderness, indicates focal peritoneal inflammation from a pathological process centred on the appendix. This combination (Rovsing's sign plus local tenderness) increases diagnostic confidence for appendicitis over other differentials. It reflects shared peritoneal innervation transmitting pressure changes across the abdomen.

questions.question: Gastroschisis differs from omphalocele in that gastroschisis:
options: Is a right-sided paraumbilical defect with no sac and exposed bowel
Has a peritoneal sac covering the herniated bowel
Is associated with major chromosomal anomalies in 50% of cases
Has a higher association with cardiac and renal anomalies
Requires staged surgical closure with a silo in only 10% of cases
questions.explanation: Gastroschisis is a right-sided paraumbilical full-thickness abdominal wall defect (umbilical cord is normal) with freely herniated bowel not covered by any sac. The exposed bowel is inflamed, thickened, and matted (peel) from amniotic fluid exposure. Unlike omphalocele, chromosomal anomalies are rare (<5%). Primary closure or staged silo reduction is performed at birth. Outcomes are generally excellent.

questions.question: Tension-free mesh repair (Lichtenstein) is the gold standard for open inguinal hernia repair because it:
questions.explanation: The Lichtenstein tension-free mesh repair eliminates the tension on the repair by using polypropylene mesh to reinforce the posterior canal wall without suturing tissues together under stress. Tension is the primary cause of recurrence in traditional tissue repairs. Lichtenstein achieves a recurrence rate under 1% compared to 10-15% for some tissue repairs, and can be performed under local anaesthesia.
options: Eliminates wound tension, the main cause of recurrence in tissue repairs
Shortens operative time in all cases
Can always be performed under local anaesthesia
Has a lower surgical site infection rate than all tissue repairs

questions.explanation: Urinalysis can detect glycosuria (unsuspected diabetes mellitus), proteinuria or haematuria (renal disease), and pyuria or bacteriuria (urinary tract infection). These findings may necessitate further investigation and optimization before elective surgery to reduce perioperative complications.
questions.question: Urinalysis in preoperative assessment can detect:

questions.explanation: Appendiceal carcinoid tumours larger than 1 to 2 cm, or those with high-risk histological features, generally require completion right hemicolectomy due to increased risk of lymph node metastasis, whereas smaller tumours confined to the tip of the appendix without adverse features can often be managed with appendicectomy alone. This size-based approach balances the risk of undertreating a potentially more aggressive tumour against the morbidity of a more extensive operation. Histopathological review of the resected specimen guides this decision.
options: No further treatment since simple appendicectomy is always curative
Completion right hemicolectomy given the tumour size
Immediate chemotherapy without any further surgery
Radiotherapy targeted at the appendiceal stump
Observation alone regardless of tumour size
questions.question: A patient with a carcinoid tumour of the appendix measuring 1.5 cm found at appendicectomy requires which further management?

questions.explanation: The normal peak urine flow rate in a healthy adult male is at least 20 mL per second. A Qmax of 10-20 mL/s is equivocal, and below 10 mL/s is consistent with bladder outflow obstruction from BPH or urethral stricture. Uroflowmetry should be performed with a voided volume of at least 150 mL for reliable measurement.
questions.question: The normal peak urine flow rate (Qmax) in a healthy adult male is:
H. pylori infection is found in what percentage of patients with gastric carcinoma of the intestinal type?
questions.explanation: H. pylori infection is found in over 70% of patients with intestinal-type gastric carcinoma and is classified as a Group I carcinogen by the WHO. The proposed sequence is: H. pylori gastritis ? chronic atrophic gastritis ? intestinal metaplasia ? dysplasia ? carcinoma (Correa cascade). H. pylori eradication reduces but does not eliminate the long-term risk of gastric cancer.

questions.question: An incised wound is defined as one inflicted by which type of object?
options: A less sharp object like broken glass
A sharp object such as a scalpel
questions.explanation: An incised wound (incision) is caused by a sharp instrument such as a scalpel or knife with clean, well-defined, smooth edges. This is in contrast to a laceration, which is caused by a less sharp or blunt object and has ragged, irregular edges. The distinction is important because incised wounds have better healing potential, lower infection risk, and are more amenable to primary closure than lacerations.

options: Continuing the planned definitive repair regardless of the triad
Immediate discharge from theatre without further intervention
Delaying all further intervention until the following day
Damage control surgery with abbreviated initial intervention
Proceeding to a more extensive reconstructive procedure
questions.explanation: The lethal triad of coagulopathy, hypothermia, and acidosis signals physiological exhaustion, and damage control surgery, involving rapid control of haemorrhage and contamination followed by staged definitive repair after physiological stabilisation, is indicated rather than continuing prolonged definitive surgery. Attempting complete definitive repair in this state markedly increases mortality risk. Recognising this triad and adapting the surgical strategy accordingly improves survival in severely injured patients.
questions.question: A trauma patient develops the triad of coagulopathy, hypothermia, and acidosis during prolonged surgery for multiple injuries. This clinical picture MOST strongly indicates the need for:

options: Direct vascular control and repair, or damage control
Simple observation, with no vascular intervention
Ligation of the vessel without attempting repair
Closing the abdomen without addressing the injury
Delayed repair, scheduled for the next day
questions.explanation: Injury to the superior mesenteric artery is a life-threatening vascular emergency requiring immediate control of haemorrhage and definitive repair where possible, since this vessel supplies the majority of the small bowel and much of the colon, and ligation without repair risks extensive bowel ischaemia unless the patient's instability mandates a damage control approach with temporary shunting. The decision between definitive repair and damage control depends on the patient's overall physiological status at the time of surgery. Rapid, decisive intervention is critical given the high mortality associated with major mesenteric vascular injury.
questions.question: During laparotomy for a penetrating abdominal injury, a 4 cm laceration of the superior mesenteric artery is identified with active bleeding. The MOST appropriate immediate management is:
Brown-Séquard syndrome results from which type of spinal cord injury?
questions.explanation: Brown-Séquard syndrome results from a hemisection (hemicord lesion) of the spinal cord, producing ipsilateral UMN paralysis, ipsilateral dorsal column deficit (loss of vibration and proprioception), and contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation below the lesion (spinothalamic tract crosses before ascending). It carries the best prognosis among incomplete spinal cord injury syndromes.

questions.question: Regarding inguinal hernias in premature infants, what is the approximate incidence compared to full-term infants?
questions.explanation: The incidence of inguinal hernia in premature infants ranges from 5–30%, significantly higher than the 3–5% incidence in full-term infants. This increased incidence is related to the incomplete obliteration of the processus vaginalis at the time of premature birth. Premature infants with inguinal hernias are at higher risk of incarceration and strangulation, and early surgical repair is typically recommended once the infant is medically stable.

questions.question: In Addisonian crisis following emergency surgery, intravenous supplementation is required with which agent?
questions.explanation: Addisonian crisis in the surgical patient requires immediate intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg followed by 50-100 mg every 6-8 hours as hydrocortisone has both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid activity at high doses. Fluid resuscitation with normal saline addresses the associated volume depletion. ACTH testing should not delay life-saving steroid administration.
options: ACTH stimulation test before steroid administration

questions.question: A patient with a high cervical spinal cord injury develops hypotension and bradycardia. This presentation of neurogenic shock is BEST distinguished from haemorrhagic shock by:
questions.explanation: Neurogenic shock results from disrupted sympathetic outflow following high spinal cord injury, causing loss of compensatory vasoconstriction and reflex tachycardia, so patients present with bradycardia and warm peripheries rather than the tachycardia and cool peripheries typical of hypovolaemic or haemorrhagic shock. This distinction is important because fluid resuscitation alone is often insufficient in neurogenic shock, and vasopressor support may be required. Coexisting haemorrhage must still be actively excluded in trauma patients presenting this way.
options: Bradycardia with warm peripheries rather than compensatory tachycardia
An absence of hypotension in both conditions
Identical vital sign patterns in both conditions
Elevated systemic vascular resistance in both conditions

questions.question: A newborn is found to have fusion of the soft tissue between the third and fourth fingers, with no bony involvement confirmed on X-ray. Which congenital hand anomaly is this, and how is it classified?
questions.explanation: Syndactyly is classified as simple when only soft tissue is fused between digits, without bony or nail bed involvement, as distinguished from complex syndactyly, where there is additional fusion of the underlying bone or nail structures. Recognising this distinction is important because simple syndactyly can often be corrected with a relatively more straightforward soft tissue release, whereas complex syndactyly may require more extensive reconstruction. Polydactyly, in contrast, refers to the presence of extra digits rather than fusion between existing ones.

CT abdomen/pelvis with rectal contrast (or IV contrast alone) is the first investigation for suspected anastomotic leak, identifying pelvic collections, extraluminal gas, or contrast extravasation. It classifies the leak as contained (drainage only) or free (requiring re-operation). CRP is a sensitive marker raising suspicion but is not diagnostic. Sigmoidoscopy risks perforation in an inflamed anastomosis.
options: CT abdomen and pelvis with rectal contrast
Serum CRP and white cell count for inflammatory markers
Flexible sigmoidoscopy to visualise the anastomosis
questions.question: A patient with a low anterior resection develops anastomotic leak on post-operative day 5. The FIRST investigation to confirm is:

A patient with a head injury and a GCS of 14 is being assessed for the need for CT brain imaging according to standard clinical decision rules. Which additional finding would most strongly mandate immediate CT imaging regardless of the GCS score itself?
questions.explanation: Clinical signs suggestive of a basal skull fracture, such as periorbital bruising (raccoon eyes), mastoid bruising (Battle's sign), cerebrospinal fluid rhinorrhoea, or otorrhoea, are recognised high-risk features that mandate immediate CT imaging after head injury regardless of an otherwise reassuring GCS score, because of the associated risk of significant underlying brain or vascular injury. Isolated minor symptoms such as scalp bruising or simple headache alone do not carry the same mandatory imaging indication in standard decision rules. Recognising these red-flag features is essential for appropriately triaging head injury patients for urgent imaging.
options: Signs of a basal skull fracture
Isolated mild scalp bruising without other symptoms
A single episode of mild nausea only
Anxiety about the injury without other symptoms

questions.question: Antisepsis is best defined as:
questions.explanation: Antisepsis specifically refers to the application of a liquid antimicrobial chemical to skin or living tissue to inhibit or destroy microorganisms. It includes germicidal solutions for swabbing injection sites and handwashing, and is distinct from disinfection which applies to inanimate objects.
options: Antimicrobial applied to skin or living tissue
Removal of all microorganisms from inanimate surfaces
Prevention of all microbial growth by heat

questions.explanation: Glutaraldehyde solutions lose potency over time and with repeated use, so activity must be verified with test strips before continued use. Using a sub-therapeutic concentration risks inadequate high-level disinfection. Most manufacturers recommend reuse for up to 14-28 days depending on activation status.
options: Discard all endoscopes previously disinfected in it
Double the soaking time for subsequent items
Add fresh glutaraldehyde to top up the container
Switch immediately to autoclaving the endoscopes
questions.question: A theatre nurse notices that a glutaraldehyde solution has been in use for six weeks. Before further use on endoscopes, she should FIRST:
Pulmonary complications are common in head injury patients. The incidence of pulmonary complications following isolated head injury is approximately:
questions.explanation: Pulmonary complications (aspiration pneumonia, neurogenic pulmonary oedema, acute respiratory distress syndrome, ventilator-associated pneumonia) occur in approximately 78% of patients with isolated severe head injury. This reflects the profound interaction between brain injury and pulmonary physiology, including altered respiratory drive, impaired airway protective reflexes, and the catecholamine surge from severe brain injury causing neurogenic pulmonary oedema.

In a haemodynamically stable child with intussusception and no signs of peritonitis or perforation, radiologically guided air or hydrostatic enema reduction is the first-line treatment, achieving successful reduction in the majority of cases without surgery. Surgery is reserved for failed reduction, perforation, peritonitis, or a demonstrable pathological lead point. Prompt recognition and treatment reduce the risk of bowel ischaemia and perforation from prolonged intussusception.
options: Observation alone with no active intervention
Oral rehydration therapy as the sole treatment
Air or hydrostatic reduction under radiological guidance
Barium enema for diagnosis only, without therapeutic reduction
questions.question: A 3-year-old presents with sudden colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, and passage of 'redcurrant jelly' stool. Ultrasound shows a 'target sign' in the right upper quadrant. The most appropriate first-line management is:
The haemoglobin subunit affected by the valine substitution in sickle cell disease is the:
questions.explanation: In sickle cell disease, the substitution of valine for glutamic acid occurs at position 6 of the beta globin chain. Haemoglobin A consists of two alpha (a) and two beta (ß) subunits. Mutations in the beta chain produce the most clinically significant haemoglobinopathies including HbS, HbC, and HbE.

Anastomotic urethroplasty (excision and primary anastomosis) is the definitive treatment for short bulbar urethral strictures under 2-3 cm with success rates of 90-95%, far superior to repeated dilatation or optical urethrotomy which have recurrence rates over 50-60% for strictures above 1.5 cm. For longer strictures, augmented anastomotic urethroplasty using buccal mucosal graft achieves similar excellent outcomes.
questions.question: The definitive surgical treatment for a short (2 cm) bulbar urethral stricture is:

questions.explanation: Post-operative pancreatic fistula (POPF) is the most dreaded early complication after Whipple's procedure, occurring in 10-20% of patients. Drain amylase above 3 times the serum amylase on post-operative day 3 defines clinically significant POPF. Early detection guides drain management and prevents escalation to haemorrhage, sepsis, or death from enzyme activation and erosion of surrounding vessels.
options: Serum albumin from hepatic synthetic function
Serum glucose from pancreatic endocrine function
Serum bilirubin for biliary anastomosis assessment
Serum lipase for exocrine function monitoring
questions.question: The MOST important biochemical marker to monitor in the early post-operative period following Whipple's procedure is:
In Swanson's classification, which type of congenital hand deformity includes conditions such as hemihypertrophy and macrodactyly?
questions.explanation: Swanson Type IV covers overgrowth conditions such as hemihypertrophy and macrodactyly, characterised by abnormal enlargement of digits or limb segments. Type V undergrowth includes hypoplasia and brachydactyly. Type I (failure of formation) includes phocomelia, and Type II (failure of differentiation) includes syndactyly. The classification guides surgical planning.

Folic acid, or vitamin B9, is essential for DNA synthesis and methylation reactions required for normal rapid cell division during early neural tube development, and its deficiency is strongly linked to increased neural tube defect risk, which periconceptional supplementation can substantially reduce. While vitamin B12 is metabolically linked to folate metabolism, it is folic acid supplementation specifically that has the strongest evidence base for neural tube defect prevention. This is the basis for public health recommendations and food fortification programmes in many countries.
questions.question: A neurosurgeon explains that a specific vitamin's role in DNA synthesis and methylation is central to preventing neural tube defects when supplemented before conception. Which vitamin is this?

questions.explanation: Echinocandins (Caspofungin, Micafungin, Anidulofungin) inhibit beta-glucan synthesis in the fungal cell wall, disrupting cell wall integrity and causing osmotic cell death. They are effective against Candida and Aspergillus species and have fewer side effects than Amphotericin B.
questions.question: Echinocandin antifungals (e.g., Caspofungin) act by:
options: Binding ergosterol in the cell membrane
Inhibiting fungal beta-glucan cell wall synthesis

questions.question: A patient develops progressive swelling and bruising around a surgical drain site with a falling haemoglobin twelve hours after thyroid surgery, but no respiratory distress yet. The MOST appropriate immediate action is:
questions.explanation: Progressive swelling, bruising, and a falling haemoglobin after thyroid surgery suggest an expanding wound haematoma, which can rapidly compromise the airway even before overt respiratory distress develops, so urgent surgical review and likely evacuation are required. Passive measures such as pressure dressings alone are inadequate for an expanding haematoma near the airway. Early intervention prevents progression to airway obstruction.
options: Reassurance and discharge home with outpatient follow-up
Application of a firm pressure dressing only, with no further review
Oral iron supplementation and routine follow-up in one week
Simple observation with no active intervention required
Urgent surgical review for probable wound haematoma requiring evacuation

questions.explanation: The annulus fibrosus is the tough outer ring of concentric fibrocartilaginous lamellae that normally contains the gel-like nucleus pulposus; a tear or weakening of this structure allows nuclear material to herniate outward, producing a disc prolapse. The nucleus pulposus is the material that herniates rather than the structure that is breached. Understanding this anatomy clarifies the pathophysiology of disc herniation as a failure of containment rather than a primary nuclear abnormality.
questions.question: A patient with an acute disc prolapse is found to have nuclear material extruded through a tear in the disc's outer fibrous ring. Which structure has been breached to allow this herniation?

A patient with a suspected retrocaecal appendicitis presents with vague right flank discomfort rather than classic anterior right iliac fossa pain, and minimal anterior tenderness on examination. The explanation for this atypical presentation is:
options: The inflamed appendix lies posterior to the caecum, shielded from the anterior parietal peritoneum
Retrocaecal appendicitis never causes any localising pain at all
The appendix has migrated into the pelvis in this position
Retrocaecal position always presents with left-sided pain instead
This position is associated exclusively with painless presentation
questions.explanation: A retrocaecal appendix lies behind the caecum, often shielded from direct contact with the anterior parietal peritoneum, which can blunt the classic localising signs of anterior right iliac fossa tenderness and instead produce vague flank or back discomfort, sometimes with a positive psoas sign. This atypical presentation can delay diagnosis if clinicians rely solely on classic anterior findings. Awareness of positional variation in appendix anatomy is important for maintaining diagnostic suspicion.

Dementia is a syndrome of chronic, progressive, global cognitive decline affecting higher cortical functions including memory, language (aphasia), praxis (apraxia), recognition (agnosia), and executive function (planning, judgment). It is most commonly caused by Alzheimer's disease, vascular dementia, Lewy body dementia, or frontotemporal dementia. It differs from pseudodementia (reversible, depression-related) and delirium (acute, fluctuating, reversible).
questions.question: Which psychiatric disorder is characterised by chronic progressive brain disease affecting higher cortical function including memory, language, and executive function?

questions.explanation: A change in bowel habit combined with rectal bleeding in an older adult is a red flag pattern requiring colonoscopy to directly visualise the colon and rectum, obtain biopsies of any suspicious lesion, and exclude colorectal malignancy. Other investigations listed do not provide the direct visualisation and tissue diagnosis capability needed in this clinical scenario. Prompt investigation is essential given the age-related increase in colorectal cancer risk.
options: Anal manometry as the first-line test
Barium meal of the upper gastrointestinal tract
Abdominal ultrasound as the sole investigation
questions.question: A 65-year-old presents with alternating bowel habit and rectal bleeding without visible haemorrhoids. The MOST appropriate next investigation is:

options: Direct penetrating injury from a rib fragment
Isolated blunt force to a single fixed point
Deceleration shearing forces on the mesentery
Thermal injury from an associated burn
questions.explanation: Rapid deceleration causes shearing stress at points where the relatively mobile bowel is tethered by the mesentery, producing mesenteric tears, vascular disruption, and bowel wall contusion. This mechanism is common in high-speed road traffic collisions. Recognising this pattern helps direct a thorough search for occult bowel and mesenteric injuries at laparotomy.
questions.question: A patient with multiple rib fractures and a positive FAST scan after a road traffic accident is taken for laparotomy. Intraoperatively, active bleeding is noted from multiple mesenteric vessels with diffuse bowel wall bruising. This pattern of injury is most consistent with which mechanism?

options: A purely idiopathic and benign vascular condition
Simple cold intolerance without any systemic association
A benign peripheral nerve entrapment syndrome
An associated connective tissue disease such as systemic sclerosis
questions.explanation: The presence of digital ulceration alongside Raynaud's phenomenon suggests secondary Raynaud's related to an underlying connective tissue disease, most commonly systemic sclerosis, rather than primary Raynaud's phenomenon, which is typically benign and does not cause tissue damage. This distinction is clinically important, as secondary Raynaud's requires investigation and management of the underlying systemic condition alongside symptomatic vascular treatment. Nailfold capillaroscopy and autoantibody testing help differentiate primary from secondary Raynaud's phenomenon.
questions.question: A patient with Raynaud's phenomenon and digital ulceration is MOST likely to have which underlying condition?
The MOST important factor determining resectability of colorectal liver metastases is:
options: Number of metastatic lesions (above 4 is non-resectable)
Achieving an R0 resection leaving adequate residual liver volume
Location of metastases in proximity to portal pedicles only
Pre-operative CEA level above 1000 micrograms per litre
questions.explanation: The key determinant of resectability of colorectal liver metastases is achieving an R0 resection with a future liver remnant of at least 25-30% of total liver volume in a healthy liver. Number of lesions alone is no longer considered an absolute contraindication to resection with modern hepatic surgery and chemotherapy. Pre-operative portal vein embolisation can augment the future liver remnant. Additional questions distributed across subtopics

questions.question: A patient completing treatment for abdominal tuberculosis develops adhesive small bowel obstruction related to residual fibrous bands from healed disease, rather than active infection. This is best classified as:
options: A late mechanical sequela of previous tuberculous inflammation
A sign of drug-resistant, ongoing active tuberculosis
An indication to restart the full anti-tuberculous regimen
Evidence of malignant transformation of tuberculous tissue
A normal expected finding requiring no intervention
questions.explanation: Fibrous adhesions and strictures that persist after successful treatment of active tuberculosis represent a late mechanical sequela of the original inflammatory and fibrotic process, rather than ongoing infection, and are managed surgically when they cause obstruction rather than with further anti-tuberculous therapy. Distinguishing this from active, undertreated disease is important to avoid inappropriate prolongation of drug therapy. Surgical adhesiolysis or resection addresses the mechanical problem directly.

Zone 1 retroperitoneal haematoma involves the central midline area containing the aorta, IVC, superior mesenteric vessels, and proximal renal vessels. It should ALWAYS be explored due to high risk of major vascular injury. Zone 2 is perinephric (lateral) and Zone 3 is pelvic. Zones 2 and 3 from blunt trauma may be observed if stable.
questions.question: During laparotomy for abdominal trauma, a zone 1 retroperitoneal haematoma is identified. Zone 1 includes the:
