• Frictional heat develops at high shear rates (the higher the viscosity, the more heat), and viscosity depends strongly on temperature, so water from a constant-temperature bath is circulated around the cup.
• Filling and cleaning are difficult with a small gap, while a large gap needs a large sample (20 to 50 ml for cup and bob); for the Brookfield the rate of shear varies widely throughout the sample.
• Cone and plate keeps shear rate constant throughout the sample (no plug flow), saves cleaning, filling and temperature stabilization time, needs only 0.1 to 0.2 ml and can raise then lower shear rate reproducibly.
questions.question:
(i) Describe rotational viscometers: the principle, the concentric cylinder (cup and bob), Brookfield and cone-and-plate types, and the equations (with terms) for viscosity and shear stress.
(ii) Relate rotational viscometers to their pharmaceutical applications, including the study of non-Newtonian and time-dependent flow and quality control.
(iii) Explain the limitations and disadvantages of these viscometers (plug flow, heating, uneven shear) and how they are minimised, including what the cone-and-plate design changes.

(i) Describe micellar solubilized systems under the headings: definition of solubilization, its relationship to micelle formation and the CMC, the possible loci of a drug in a micelle, and the factors influencing the solubilizing capacity of surfactants.
(ii) Explain the basis of solubilization performance: why solubility changes with surfactant concentration, and what happens to micelle numbers above the CMC.
(iii) State the methods used to determine the CMC and the pharmaceutical applications and advantages of solubilized (micellar) systems.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Solubilization is the spontaneous dissolving of a substance (API) by reversible interaction with micelles in water to form a thermodynamically stable isotropic solution with reduced thermodynamic activity of the solubilized material; it depends on the presence of micelles, so does not occur below the CMC, and is generally non-specific (any oil-soluble material), each with a limit comparable to its oil-solubility that depends on temperature and on the nature and concentration of the surfactant.
• Loci: hydrophilic, sparingly soluble drugs adsorb on the micelle surface; drugs of intermediate solubility sit between the hydrophilic head groups (e.g. PEO micelles) or in the palisade layer (outer core); completely insoluble hydrophobic drugs sit in the inner core; sites differ because micro-viscosity, polarity and hydration degree are not uniform along the micelle.
• Factors: chemical structure of the surfactant, chemical structure of the drug, micelle shape, temperature, length of the PEO headgroup and hydrophobic tail, and pH.
• A surfactant is an amphiphile with a balance of hydrophilic and lipophilic properties, adsorbed at surfaces and interfaces and lowering surface or interfacial tension; classes are anionic, cationic, non-ionic and amphoteric.
(ii)
Thermodynamically, solubilization is a normal partitioning of the drug between two phases: the micelle phase and the aqueous phase.
• A plot of the solubility of a poorly soluble compound against surfactant concentration shows very low solubility until the CMC, then a linear increase with surfactant concentration, showing that solubilization is related to micellization.
• Above the CMC extra surfactant does not significantly raise monomer numbers but raises the number of micelles in direct proportion; micelles just above the CMC are of about the same size.
• Absorption from solubilized preparations is usually more rapid than from ordinary emulsions or oily solutions.
(iii)
CMC methods: aggregation number method (average number of surfactant monomers per micelle), colligative property method (osmotic pressure varied with concentration, the break in the curve being the CMC) and surface property method (surface tension becomes constant at the CMC).
• Other changes at the CMC: sharp rise in light scattering, higher conductivity of ionic micelles, remarkable solubilizing effect and lower colligative properties.
• Applications: parenteral or oral oil-soluble drugs (vitamins A and D, corticosteroids), volatile oils as flavours, better solubility and activity of phenobarbitone, iodine, sulfonamides, dyes and phenolic bactericides (Lysol with 50% cresol in soap solution; hexachlorophene liquid soap with 0.24% in 11% potassium soap).
• Stability and carriers: solubilized systems are physically and chemically more stable than ordinary emulsions (vitamins resist oxidation better); micellar carriers are easy to make reproducibly on a large scale, can carry surface ligands, and keep a core/shell structure that stays water-soluble.

(i)
The DLVO theory (Derjaguin and Landau; Verwey and Overbeek, early 1940s) explains stability of lyophobic dispersions by the electrical double layer round each particle; attraction is by van der Waals forces and repulsion by similar ionic charges on the particles.
• Charge arises from ionization of surface groups (hydrophilic particles) or preferential adsorption of specific ions, called peptizing ions (hydrophobic particles), e.g. AgI with excess surface iodide ions.
• The Stern layer is a rigid layer of counter ions next to the particle surface balancing the surface charge (some only transiently bound); outside it is the diffuse Gouy layer of positive and negative ions with the same net sign as the surface; its thickness d is usually 10-1000 A, taken as the distance over which the potential falls to 1/e = 0.37.
• Zeta (electrokinetic) potential is the potential difference between the outer surface of the fixed layer and the bulk liquid; Coulomb's law: force is proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance.
(ii)
Added electrolyte supplies extra ions, raising the density of ions of opposite charge to the particle surface, so the ionic atmosphere is compressed and zeta potential is reduced or even reversed in sign.
• Increased ion concentration compresses the diffuse (Gouy) layer, its thickness d falls and repulsion decays rapidly; the energy barrier opposing aggregation decreases and eventually disappears.
• Once the barrier is gone, rapid coagulation/coalescence occurs and large aggregates become visible.
• Schulze-Hardy rule: compression depends on both electrolyte concentration and valency of the ion of opposite charge, so a negative colloid is coagulated by AlCl₃ at lower concentration than BaCl₂; the greater the electrolyte concentration needed for rapid coagulation, the more stable the original system.
(iii)
Lyophobic colloids coagulate at low electrolyte concentrations because the double layer is compressed and zeta potential falls.
• Hydrophilic colloids are not precipitated by low electrolyte concentrations even when zeta potential is reduced, because hydration keeps particles separate; large amounts of electrolyte (salting out or coacervation) are needed, as hydrated ions withdraw water and reduce zeta potential, so effectiveness depends on ion hydration and valency.
• Hofmeister (lyotropic) series: monovalent cations Cs+ < Rb+ < NH₄⁺ < K⁺ < Na⁺ < Li⁺; divalent Ba++ < Sr++ < Ca++ < Mg++; anions F- > citrate³⁻ > HPO₄²⁻ > tartrate²⁻ > SO₄²⁻ > acetate > Cl⁻ > NO₃⁻ > ClO₃⁻ > Br⁻ > ClO₄⁻ > I- > CNS-.
• Salting out is reversible in most cases (redispersed by removing electrolyte by electrophoresis or dialysis, or remixing with water); alcohol or acetone dehydrates gelatin so it behaves as hydrophobic; the colloid-rich layer is the coacervate.
questions.question:
(i) Describe the electrical double layer and the DLVO theory under the headings: origin of particle charge, the Stern and Gouy layers, zeta potential, the attractive and repulsive forces involved, and the Schulze-Hardy rule.
(ii) Explain why added electrolytes reduce the stability of a lyophobic colloid.
(iii) Distinguish between coagulation of lyophobic colloids by electrolytes and salting out (coacervation) of hydrophilic colloids, including the Hofmeister series.

(i) Describe emulsions as pharmaceutical dosage forms under the headings: definition and role of the emulsifying agent, types and globule sizes, phase volume ratio, classes of emulsifying agents, and pharmaceutical uses.
(ii) Explain the basis of emulsion instability, covering creaming (with Stokes' equation and its terms), flocculation, cracking and phase inversion.
(iii) State the methods used to evaluate emulsion stability and the formulation measures used to prevent or correct instability.
questions.answerText:
(i)
An emulsion is a system of two immiscible liquid phases, one dispersed as fine droplets in the other; it is thermodynamically unstable, so an emulsifying agent forms an adsorbed film around the droplets at the interface to aid preparation and shelf-life stability.
• Types: oil-in-water (o/w) and water-in-oil (w/o), also multiple (w/o/w, o/w/o); type depends on the relative proportions of the phases and the emulsifier chosen; phase volume ratio = internal phase volume / total volume; globules usually 0.25-25 µm, fine emulsions below about 5 µm, microemulsions 10-60 nm and may be clear.
• Emulsifier classes: natural products (acacia, tragacanth, beeswax, wool fat, wool alcohols), surfactants (anionic, cationic, non-ionic, amphoteric), finely divided solids (bentonite, aluminium magnesium silicate, hectorite) and others (saponins, carbomer); true (primary) emulgents versus auxiliary emulsion stabilizers.
• Uses: o/w emulsions give oral/parenteral fats and oils, vehicles for water-insoluble drugs and taste masking; w/o emulsions disperse antigenic material for intramuscular depot injection; greatest use is dermatological (o/w water-washable, w/o occlusive); emulsions can control release and protect drugs from oxidation or hydrolysis.
(ii)
Creaming is movement of globules up or down because of density difference: u = d²(ρs - ρl)g/(18 η) (u = velocity, d = mean diameter, ρs and ρl = densities of particles and fluid phase, g = gravity, η = viscosity of continuous phase); it is slowed by small globules, narrow size range and higher viscosity, and is reversible by shaking but raises the chance of coalescence.
• Flocculation: droplets come together without fusing because of weakness in the interfacial film or inadequate electrical forces; it accelerates creaming and is less serious than coalescence.
• Cracking: coalescence with separation of the disperse phase as a separate layer, not redispersible; caused by an emulsifier of opposite type, decomposition or precipitation of the emulsifier (acids, electrolytes, polyvalent cations, alcohol), a common solvent, microbial action, or disperse phase above 74%.
• Phase inversion (o/w to w/o or vice versa) is caused by electrolytes, change in phase volume ratio, change in emulsifier HLB (e.g. heating polysorbate emulsions) or temperature change on cooling; the ideal internal phase is 40-60% and should not exceed 50%.
(iii)
Evaluation: rate and extent of creaming/phase separation (volume of creamed or separated part divided by total volume); globule size analysis by microscopy, Coulter counter or laser diffraction (rising mean size indicates coalescence).
• Viscosity and rheological behaviour over storage (a fall in viscosity may result from coalescence).
• Accelerated testing: temperature cycling (e.g. 60 °C then refrigerated or frozen, repeated) and centrifugation (200-300 rpm) to judge the strength of the interfacial barrier.
• Corrective measures: adequate emulsifier concentration (too little gave rapid coalescence), smaller globules by homogenizers/colloid mills/ultrasonic dispersator, thickening stabilizers such as tragacanth for acacia emulsions, a preservative, and avoiding incompatible emulsifiers.

(i)
The displacement value indicates the number of parts by weight of the medicament that displaces one part by weight of the base; it is specific and constant for a material and is calculated with reference to theobroma oil, and the DVs of fatty bases are similar to those of theobroma oil.
• Mould calibration: nominal capacities are 1, 2, 4 or 8 g; prepare a set of suppositories with the base alone, weigh them and take the mean weight as the true capacity for that base.
• Steps: weigh 6 unmedicated suppositories; prepare 6 medicated ones; weight of drug = percentage × weight of medicated suppositories; weight of base = medicated weight - drug weight; base displaced = unmedicated weight - base in medicated; DV = weight of drug / weight of base displaced.
• Worked example: zinc oxide 40% with theobroma oil in a 1 g mould: 6 unmedicated = 6 g, 6 medicated = 8.8 g (assumed); ZnO = 3.52 g, base = 5.28 g, base displaced = 0.72 g, so DV = 3.52/0.72 = about 5.0.
(ii)
Suppository volume from a mould is uniform but its weight varies because medicament densities differ from that of the base, so allowance must be made for the change in density of the mass due to added medicaments to get accurate product weights.
• Quantities of drug and base are calculated using the DV of the medicament; an excess is made for wastage, mainly material left on the dish in which the base is melted (use the smallest possible dish); two extra suppositories are adequate.
• Example: 8 suppositories each with zinc oxide 0.25 g, mould capacity 1.2 g of theobroma oil, DV 5.0: base required = 9.6 g - 0.4 g = 9.2 g, and total weight of medicated suppositories = 9.2 g + 2 g = 11.2 g.
• Glycero-gelatin base is 1.2 times as dense as theobroma oil, so the DVs of medicaments are multiplied by 1.2.
(iii)
A DV is specific to a material and referenced to theobroma oil; it is valid directly for fatty bases (similar DVs) but must be adjusted by 1.2 for glycero-gelatin because of base density.
• The nominal mould capacity varies with the base (density variation), so each mould must be calibrated for the base in use.
• The suppository volume stays fixed by the mould while its weight changes with the density of the medicament, which is why the base weight must be reduced by the amount displaced.
• For the boric acid example (6 unmedicated = 7.2 g; 6 with 30% boric acid = 9.0 g; boric acid 2.7 g; base 6.3 g.
questions.question:
(i) Define the displacement value (DV) of a medicament in a suppository base and describe how it is determined, including the calibration of the mould and the calculation steps with their terms.
(ii) Relate the displacement value to its pharmaceutical applications and worked examples (zinc oxide in theobroma oil, preparing a batch with allowance for wastage, and glycero-gelatin bases).
(iii) Explain the assumptions, limitations and the effect of changing the base or the medicament on the calculation.

questions.answerText:
(i)
Stokes' equation: u = d²(ρs - ρl)g/(18 η), where u = average velocity of sedimentation (creaming), d = mean diameter of particles, ρs and ρl = densities of the suspended particles and the fluid (continuous) phase, g = acceleration due to gravity and η = viscosity of the continuous phase.
• Equivalent form with radius: V = 2 r² (Δρ) g / (9 η), V = rate of creaming, r = radius of dispersed globules, Δρ = density difference between the two phases.
• Creaming or sedimentation depends on the density difference: lower-density globules rise (common in dilute o/w emulsions) and denser ones settle (common in dilute w/o emulsions).
• The rate falls with smaller globules (e.g. 1-3 µm) and a narrow size distribution, and with higher viscosity of the continuous phase; a temperature rise may increase the creaming rate by lowering the apparent viscosity of the continuous phase.
(ii)
Creaming is not a serious problem because shaking restores uniformity, but it is undesirable: it brings droplets close together and raises the chance of coalescence and cracking, looks inelegant and risks incorrect dosage if not shaken.
• In suspensions the sedimentation rate is inversely proportional to the viscosity of the medium; settled solids stick together (caking or claying); thixotropic agents (sodium bentonite magma, colloidal clays, colloidal silicon dioxide, microcrystalline cellulose) give high apparent viscosity or a yield value, which retards or prevents sedimentation and creaming.
• Falling sphere viscometer: a sphere reaches a uniform terminal velocity when gravity is balanced by viscous drag: 3 π η d u = (π/6) d³ g (ρs - ρ1), so η = d² g (ρs - ρ1)/(18 u); kinematic viscosity = this divided by ρ1.
• Centrifugation (200-300 rpm) is used to speed creaming and judge the mechanical strength of the interfacial barrier of an emulsion.
(iii)
Stokes' law applies strictly only to Newtonian fluids, whereas the suspending agents used in practice are non-Newtonian (shear-thinning plastic or pseudoplastic) systems.
• Trade-off: raising Newtonian viscosity reduces sedimentation, but beyond a limit pouring through the bottle orifice becomes difficult.
• Pseudoplastic suspending agents (e.g. carboxymethylcellulose, HPMC) give high viscosity at rest that falls on shaking, giving easy pouring; a plastic system gives a non-sedimenting suspension if the force exerted by a particle is less than the yield value.
questions.question:
(i) State Stokes' law as used for the rate of creaming and sedimentation, giving the equation(s) with all terms and the effect of each variable on the rate.
(ii) Relate Stokes' law to its pharmaceutical applications: creaming of emulsions, sedimentation in suspensions, the use of thixotropic agents and the falling sphere viscometer.
(iii) Explain the assumptions or limitations of Stokes' law and the trade-off that results from changing viscosity.

questions.answerText:
(i)
Sedimentation volume is the most important parameter: a measured volume of suspension is kept undisturbed in a graduated cylinder for a definite time; F = Hu/Ho, where Hu = ultimate height of the sediment and Ho = initial height of the total suspension.
• F can be plotted against time to show the sedimentation pattern on storage; a stable suspension shows a horizontal or less steep curve; re-dispersibility is evaluated by shaking and determining F = Hu/Ho again.
• Rheological method: viscosity measured at different time intervals with a good quality viscometer; electrokinetic method: zeta potential (surface charge) calculated from migration velocities of the particles by electrophoresis.
• Micromeritic method: any change in particle size distribution and crystal habit with time is followed by microscopy and Coulter counter, since particle growth may lead to lumps or caking.
(ii)
Zeta potential measurements on a suspension as an electrolyte is added give information on the extent of flocculation; certain zeta potentials give a more stable suspension through controlled flocculation.
• Controlled flocculation aims to add the amount of electrolyte, polymer or surfactant flocculating agent that gives the maximum sedimentation volume; a figure relates caking, zeta potential and sedimentation volume as a positively charged flocculating agent is added to negatively charged particles.
• Flocculation occurs when zeta potential is within about ± 25 mV; electrolytes act by reducing the zeta potential (Schulze-Hardy rule), and excess electrolyte that inverts its sign causes deflocculation and caking at the primary minimum.
• Flocculated suspensions have high sedimentation rate, loose scaffold-like sediment and easy re-dispersion; deflocculated suspensions settle slowly but form a dense hard cake that is difficult or impossible to redisperse.
(iii)
Zeta potential limits of about ± 25 mV are stated as a general guide only (stated as holding in general).
• The aggregation theory relating zeta potential to flocculation and the Schulze-Hardy rule hold only if there is no chemical interaction between the added electrolyte and the ions of the double layer.
• Trade-off: a flocculated suspension settles rapidly and looks unsightly with a clear supernatant, minimised by making the sediment volume large (ideally the sediment fills the suspension volume), whereas a deflocculated one looks pleasant but cakes.
questions.question:
(i) Describe the methods for evaluating suspension stability (sedimentation, rheological, electrokinetic and micromeritic), giving the sedimentation volume equation with its terms and the procedure.
(ii) Relate sedimentation volume and zeta potential to their pharmaceutical applications, including flocculation, controlled flocculation and caking.
(iii) Explain the assumptions or limitations of these measurements and the trade-offs between flocculated and deflocculated suspensions.

(i) Describe time-dependent flow under the headings: definition of thixotropy, the hysteresis loop, measurement (index of thixotropy and coefficient of thixotropic breakdown), pharmaceutical importance, and rheopexy and negative thixotropy.
(ii) Explain the structural basis of thixotropy: why viscosity falls on shearing, how the structure recovers and what controls the recovery time.
(iii) Distinguish between thixotropy, shear destruction and rheopexy.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Thixotropy is the reversible time-dependent decrease in apparent viscosity, a reversible isothermal gel-to-sol transition with slow recovery on standing of consistency lost through shearing; the down curve is displaced to the left of the up curve for plastic and pseudoplastic materials (the reverse for dilatant), giving a hysteresis loop.
• The area within the loop indicates the degree of structural breakdown and is the most commonly used index of thixotropy; the slope of log shear stress at a fixed shear rate against log time is linear, and the coefficient of thixotropic breakdown is B = (τ₁ - τ₂)/ln(t₂/t₁).
• Thixotropy is desirable in liquid systems that need high consistency in the container but pour or spread easily (bentonite gel; suspensions, emulsions, lotions, creams, ointments and parenteral suspensions for intramuscular depot therapy).
• Rheopexy is a time-dependent gain and loss of structure in a dilatant system, a solid forming a gel more readily when gently shaken; negative thixotropy (antithixotropy) is an increase in consistency on the down curve.
(ii)
Thixotropic systems usually contain asymmetric particles or macromolecules that interact through numerous secondary bonds to form a loose three-dimensional structure, so the material is gel-like when unsheared.
• Shearing disrupts these bonds and aligns the flowing elements in the direction of flow, a gel-to-sol transformation, so viscosity falls.
• When stress is removed the structure reforms progressively, not instantly, as the particles come together by random Brownian movement.
• Recovery takes minutes to days and is directly related to how long the material was sheared; rheograms depend on the rate of shear change and the time at each rate, so the sample's previous history affects its rheology.
(iii)
Thixotropy: the destroyed structure reforms on standing, so repeat determinations reproduce an up curve and a down curve.
• Shear destruction: the structure is never recovered however long the system rests, so repeat determinations give only the down curve; seen in gels of high molecular weight polysaccharides stabilised by many secondary bonds, whose three-dimensional structure is reduced to a two-dimensional one.
• Rheopexy: time-dependent gain (not loss) of structure, rare, occurring in concentrated suspensions such as Milk of Magnesia (USP); in a rheopectic system the gel is the equilibrium form, whereas in antithixotropy the equilibrium state is the sol.
• A well-formulated thixotropic suspension (bentonite gel is an example) does not settle readily, becomes fluid on shaking and regains consistency rapidly enough to keep the particles suspended.

questions.question:
(i) Describe adsorption under the headings: definition and cause, the role of surface free energy and of the nature of solid surfaces, and its pharmaceutical applications.
(ii) Explain the physical basis of adsorption of surface active agents at interfaces and of the stabilizing effects of adsorption in colloids and emulsions.
(iii) Distinguish between adsorption and absorption.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Adsorption is a phenomenon occurring at interfaces as a result of the tendency of a system to attain its lowest free energy; the surface or interfacial free energy from residual attractive forces on surface molecules is reduced by interaction with the adsorbed molecules.
• Irregular shapes of solid particles and roughness of surfaces add variation in the activity of different sites on the solid surface.
• Applications: decolorising liquids with about 1% activated charcoal (alkaloid actives may also be adsorbed), alumina and silica gel as desiccants, adsorption chromatography, surface area determination (rate of solution, oxidation, hygroscopicity, sedimentation, bulk density and packing depend on surface area), and kaolin and charcoal as gastrointestinal adsorbents and antidotes (atropine, strychnine, oxalic acid, phenolphthalein).
• Further uses: charcoal removes pyrogens from injections; adsorbents can take up vitamins, enzymes and trace elements, causing deficiencies and incomplete medication; adsorption of drugs by solid excipients may alter release and absorption rates; filter pores adsorb particles on their walls.
(ii)
Surface molecules have unbalanced inward attraction, giving surface free energy; adsorbed material interacts with these forces and lowers the energy.
• In water-soluble surface active agents, attraction between hydrocarbon chains and water is much weaker than hydrogen bonds between water molecules, so the system limits contact between water and the hydrophobic groups.
• Hydrocarbon chains coil, and most molecules are adsorbed at the surface with hydrophilic groups in water and chains projecting from it, which gives the marked effect of surfactants on surface properties of water.
• Stability of colloids depends on adsorption of ions onto their surfaces; protective colloids act by adsorption of hydrophilic material onto hydrophobic particles; emulsions are stable through adsorption of emulsifying agents at the oil/water interface; rheology of suspensions is affected by adsorption of surface active agents.
(iii)
Adsorption is a surface phenomenon (gas molecules held on the surface of activated charcoal).
• Absorption is a bulk phenomenon (e.g. fluid taken into a sponge).
• Adsorption is the interfacial uptake that lowers surface free energy, as described above.

(i)
Procaine penicillin G is of relatively low water solubility; its prolonged action after intramuscular injection of a concentrated aqueous suspension is due partly to this low solubility and partly to the formation of compact, cohesive deposits that retard dissolution and release.
• Aqueous suspensions containing 40 to 70% of milled or micronized procaine penicillin G (plus sodium citrate and polysorbate 80) were thixotropic.
• The yield value and the hysteresis loop areas of the pastes increased with increasing specific surface area and increasing concentration of the powder.
• Comparable amounts given as dilute aqueous suspensions formed no depots and kept therapeutic blood levels for much shorter periods because of fast dispersion and absorption.
(ii)
Prolonged activity depended on compact, spherical deposits at the injection site that resist disintegration by tissue fluids because of their high consistency and present a small surface to those fluids, retarding penicillin release.
• Formation of cohesive spherical depots depends on high yield values and rapid thixotropic recovery of those yield values after injection into the muscle.
• Low yield values and small hysteresis loop areas (low specific surface area or low powder concentration) make the suspension spread and disperse, giving rapid release and absorption and a short duration of effective blood levels.
• Excessively high yield values and large hysteresis loops (very high specific surface area or concentration) make injection difficult or impossible because of plugging.
(iii)
Required: yield values low enough to allow extrusion through hypodermic needles yet high enough to form compact spherical depots, combined with rapid thixotropic recovery of paste structure and yield value at the site to strengthen the depots.
• With this, penicillin blood levels stayed above the minimum effective concentration for at least 4 days; the prolonged action was determined entirely by rheological properties.
• Evaluation parameters: yield value and hysteresis loop area, controlled through specific surface area and powder concentration.
• Thixotropy is likewise desirable in other parenteral suspensions for intramuscular depot therapy, and some vaccines are w/o emulsions whose viscosity must be neither too high to inject nor too low (rapid antigen release).
questions.question:
(i) Describe injectable depot suspensions using the procaine penicillin G example under the headings: the drug and the formulation, the rheological type of the suspension, and the effect of concentration and specific surface area on its rheological parameters.
(ii) Explain the basis of the prolonged therapeutic action of such suspensions and why dilute suspensions or very high yield values fail.
(iii) State the rheological requirements or formulation approach used to obtain the required performance, and the evaluation parameters involved.

(i) Describe pharmaceutical suspensions under the headings: definition, classification, advantages, desirable properties, and formulation approaches (wetting, structured vehicles and controlled flocculation).
(ii) Explain the basis of physical instability in suspensions, contrasting flocculated with deflocculated systems and including the roles of zeta potential, electrolytes and Stokes' law.
(iii) State the methods used to evaluate suspension stability and the formulation approach used to prevent caking.
questions.answerText:
(i)
A pharmaceutical suspension is a two-phase coarse dispersion of finely divided insoluble solid (disperse phase) in a liquid medium; particles are mostly greater than 0.1 µm, classes are colloidal (1 nm-1 µm) and coarse, and most pharmaceutical suspensions have particles larger than 1 µm.
• Advantages: formulate low-solubility drugs, non-aqueous suspensions for drugs that degrade in aqueous solution, palatable insoluble derivatives, prolonged action, dermatological/mucous membrane application and parenteral administration of insoluble drugs.
• Desirable properties: no rapid settling, sediment not a hard cake and readily redispersed by shaking, not too viscous to pour or pass a syringe, lotions fluid enough to spread yet not run off and drying to an elastic film, acceptable colour and odour, and resistance to microbial attack.
• Formulation problems are dispersion, settling and caking; approaches are a structured vehicle, controlled flocculation, or both; surface-active wetting agents (minimum amount, as excess causes foaming or bad taste) and structured vehicles (hydrocolloids such as methylcellulose, carboxymethylcellulose, acacia, bentonite, carbopol).
(ii)
Deflocculated suspension: discrete particles settle slowly, but the sediment packs closely under the weight of upper layers into a hard cake (claying or caking, at the primary minimum) that is difficult or impossible to redisperse.
• Flocculated suspension: particles form loose aggregates (flocs) that settle rapidly into a loosely packed scaffold-like sediment that is easily redispersed and does not cake, but the clear supernatant is unsightly, minimised by a large sediment volume.
• Flocculation occurs when zeta potential lies within about ± 25 mV so electrical repulsion cannot overcome van der Waals attraction (floccules held at the secondary minimum); electrolytes reduce zeta potential per the Schulze-Hardy rule, and excess electrolyte can invert the sign and deflocculate.
• Settling follows Stokes' law and falls with higher viscosity, but Stokes' law applies strictly to Newtonian fluids; shear-thinning plastic or pseudoplastic structured vehicles are preferred because they thin on shaking and regain consistency afterwards.
(iii)
Evaluation: sedimentation volume F = Hu/Ho (ultimate sediment height / initial total height) plotted against time, where a stable suspension gives a horizontal or less steep curve; re-dispersibility is checked by shaking and measuring F again.
• Rheological method (viscosity at time intervals), electrokinetic method (zeta potential from electrophoretic migration velocity) and micromeritic method (particle size and crystal habit by microscopy and Coulter counter).
• Controlled flocculation: add electrolytes, polymers or surfactants in the amount giving maximum sedimentation volume, preventing cake formation; flocculated particles can then be supported in a structured vehicle.
• Limitation: structured vehicles are negatively charged hydrophilic colloids, so a positively charged flocculant may coagulate them; an anionic flocculant compatible with the suspending agent must be used.

questions.question:
(i) Describe the flow properties of disperse systems: Einstein's equation (with terms) and the viscosity coefficients derived from it (relative, specific, reduced and intrinsic viscosity).
(ii) Relate these coefficients to their pharmaceutical applications, including the calculation of the average molecular weight of polymers and the factors affecting the viscosity of emulsions.
(iii) Explain the assumptions and limitations of the equation and the trade-offs that result when disperse phase concentration or viscosity changes.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Particles in a liquid continuous medium raise viscosity by distorting the streamlines of liquid around them, which dissipates energy; Einstein's equation: η/η₀ = 1 + 2.5 φ (η = viscosity of the disperse system, η₀ = viscosity of the pure continuous medium, φ = volume fraction of the disperse phase).
• Relative viscosity (viscosity ratio) = η/η₀ = 1 + 2.5 φ, the ratio of the viscosity of the dispersion to that of the liquid continuous medium; specific viscosity (viscosity ratio increment) is the relative increase in viscosity caused by the dispersed phase.
• Reduced viscosity (Staudinger's viscosity number) = η_sp/c = α + β c + ..., where c = concentration and α and β are constants calculated from experimental observations.
• Intrinsic viscosity [η] (Kraemer viscosity number) is the intercept obtained by extrapolating a graph of reduced viscosity against concentration.
(ii)
Intrinsic viscosity is used to calculate the average molecular weight M of polymers: [η] = K M^a, where K and a are constants obtained from separate experiments at fixed temperature for a given polymer-solvent system.
• Relative viscosity is also the ratio η₁/η₂ obtained in the capillary viscometer for a liquid under test against a standard liquid.
• For emulsions, the important factors affecting viscosity are phase-volume ratio, viscosity of the continuous phase, nature and proportion of the emulsifying agent, globule size and size distribution, and aggregation of globules; particle shape matters because globules are mainly spherical.
• Viscosity of a vaccine w/o emulsion: if too large it cannot be injected, but if too low instability leads to rapid antigen release.
(iii)
Einstein's equation is theoretically limited to systems whose disperse particles are rigid spheres.
• Because viscosity rises with the volume fraction of disperse phase, a more concentrated dispersion is more viscous; concentrated flocculated suspensions show plastic flow and concentrated (about 50%) deflocculated small-particle dispersions show dilatant flow .
• Trade-off: high viscosity retards sedimentation and creaming but may make pouring or injection difficult; low viscosity eases pouring but allows rapid settling or creaming.
• The constants K and a are specific to a polymer-solvent system at fixed temperature.

questions.question:
(i) Describe the electrical properties of colloids under the headings: electrophoresis (definition, direction of migration and examples of positively and negatively charged colloids), the charge on proteins and the isoelectric point, mutual precipitation, and the protective colloid effect.
(ii) Explain why the charge on a protein colloid depends on pH, and what changes at the isoelectric point.
(iii) Distinguish between mutual precipitation and the protective colloid effect.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Electrophoresis is migration of colloidal particles in an electric field: positively charged colloids go to the cathode and negatively charged ones to the anode, so the direction of migration gives the sign of the overall charge (e.g. blood plasma proteins can be separated).
• Positively charged: Fe(OH)₃ and Al(OH)₃ sols and cationic dyes (methylene blue, methyl violet); negatively charged: sols of metals, sulphur and sulfides, anionic dyes and kaolin; acacia and similar plant-gum sols are electronegative because of ionized carboxylic acid groups.
• Proteins are amphoteric (carboxylic acid and amino groups), so their charge depends on pH; the intermediate pH at which positive and negative ionization tendencies are equal and the surface appears uncharged is the isoelectric point.
• Hydrophilic colloids are charged through ionizable groups (-COOH, -NH₂, -SO3H) or polar groups (as in methylcellulose derivatives) even in a non-ionizing medium, so they conduct electricity and show electrophoresis.
(ii)
At low pH (acid medium) ionization of carboxylic groups is suppressed and amino groups are ionized, so the particles are positively charged.
• In alkaline medium ionization of the amine groups is suppressed and carboxylic acid groups are ionized, so the charge is negative.
• At the isoelectric point both groups are ionized equally giving a zwitterion (glycine: +H3N-CH₂-COO-); the protein is then least stable, does not migrate in an electric field, has minimum solubility and sol viscosity, and is most readily precipitated by electrolytes.
• Insulin (isoelectric point pH 5.5-5.6) in an injection adjusted to pH 3.0-3.5 will precipitate if alkali from lime-soda glass ampoules raises the pH to 5.5-5.6.
(iii)
Mutual precipitation: mixing two sols of oppositely charged colloids (e.g. positively charged bismuth subnitrate or subgallate with negatively charged tragacanth) neutralizes their charges and coagulation then precipitation occurs.
• Protective colloid effect: with a large excess of one of the oppositely charged sols, the neutralized particles adsorb the excess charged particles, so the system does not coagulate and stays stable.
• Example: a little Fe(OH)₃ sol added to negatively charged As2S3 sol gives no precipitation; more gives precipitation when neutral; a large excess gives a stable, positively charged sol.
• Hydrophilic sols protect hydrophobic sols against electrolyte precipitation by adsorbing over the whole surface of each hydrophobic particle so that it acquires hydrophilic properties.

(i)
Surface tension can be determined by the capillary rise and drop weight methods.
• Capillary rise (one of the most accurate methods) measures the height to which liquid rises in a capillary; at equilibrium 2γ/r = h ρ g, so approximately γ = h ρ g r/2 (γ = surface tension, h = column height, ρ = density, g = gravity, r = capillary radius).
• Drop weight (stalagmometer/stactometer): drops form slowly at the narrowed end of a capillary glass tube and fall when drop weight balances surface tension; Tate's equation mg = 2πrγ (m = mass of drop, r = external radius of the tube).
• In the drop weight method 20 to 30 drops are collected and the average weight of one drop is calculated.
(ii)
In capillary rise the pressure just below the meniscus in the tube (PA) is less than that above (PB) by 2γ/r, whereas in the large container the pressure difference is negligible (PC = PD) because the radius of curvature is large.
• Hence PB = PC = PD (atmospheric), PD - PA = 2γ/r, and this pressure difference is the driving force that raises liquid up the tube.
• Surface active agents are solutes that cause a marked decrease in the surface tension of the solvent; as surfactant concentration rises surface tension falls significantly.
• At the CMC the surface is saturated and further surfactant has no effect, so surface tension becomes constant; this is the basis of the surface property method of determining CMC.
(iii)
Equation γ = h ρ g r/2 is approximate and assumes a contact angle of zero; the corrected equation is γ = (h + r/3)(ρL - ρv) g r / (2 cos θ), allowing for a finite contact angle, the liquid in the meniscus above the point where h is measured, and the density difference between liquid and vapour.
• Capillary rise precautions: outer vessel wide compared with the capillary (otherwise PC is not equal to PD), uniform circular capillary, meniscus allowed to fall to rest and walls thoroughly wetted to obtain the lowest contact angle, and adequate temperature control.
• Drop weight: a real drop is constricted at the point of break and only part of the liquid breaks away (more than one drop falls), so Harkins and Brown (1919) corrected Tate's equation to mg = 2πrγ f(r/v^(1/3)), where the factor depends on tip radius r and the cube root of drop volume v.
• Drop weight precautions: sharply ground tip without imperfections, slow drop formation and adequate temperature control.
questions.question:
(i) Describe the methods used to determine surface tension (capillary rise and drop weight), stating the governing equations with their terms and the procedure of each.
(ii) Relate the capillary rise mechanism and surface tension measurements to the behaviour of surface active agents, including the surface property method for the critical micelle concentration (CMC).
(iii) Explain the assumptions, corrections and experimental precautions of the capillary rise and drop weight methods and what changes when the assumptions fail.

(i) Describe the capillary (Ostwald) viscometer: principle, Poiseuille's equation with its terms, how the viscosity and kinematic viscosity of an unknown liquid are obtained from a standard, and the procedure.
(ii) Relate the capillary viscometer to the pharmaceutical context of viscosity measurement and to the classification of viscometers as one-point instruments.
(iii) Explain the assumptions, limitations and corrections of the method and the error that results when it is used for non-Newtonian systems.
questions.answerText:
(i)
A capillary viscometer gives the viscosity of a Newtonian liquid from the time taken to flow by gravity between two marks in a vertical capillary tube (Ostwald; Ostwald-Cannon-Fenske adaptation), the flow being streamlined.
• Poiseuille's equation: V/t = π P r⁴/(8 η l), i.e. η = π r⁴ t P/(8 L V) (r = capillary radius, t = flow time, P = pressure difference across the tube ends, L or l = length, V = volume); as r, L, V are constant, η = K t P, and P depends on density, gravity and height difference so η = K' t ρ.
• Comparing an unknown (1) with a standard (2), usually water: η₁/η₂ = ρ₁ t₁/(ρ₂ t₂), so η₁ = (t₁ ρ₁/(t₂ ρ₂)) η₂, where η₁/η₂ is the relative viscosity; kinematic viscosity v = η/ρ = K' t, so v₁ = v₂ t₁/t₂.
• Procedure: choose a bore giving about 200 s flow time (wider bores for more viscous fluids), fill to mark G, clamp vertically in a constant-temperature bath, draw liquid above mark E and time the fall between E and F, repeating until three readings agree within 0.5 s.
(ii)
Viscosity measurement matters in mixing, filling, pouring, extrusion from tubes, spraying, passage through a syringe needle, dose uniformity and physical stability; viscosity affects drug absorption from the GIT.
• Capillary and falling-sphere viscometers are one-point instruments, suitable only for Newtonian fluids: a single point on the rheogram extrapolated to the origin gives the whole rheogram.
• All viscometers can be used for Newtonian systems; for Newtonian liquids a single stress is adequate because stress and shear rate are directly proportional.
(iii)
The method requires a Newtonian fluid and streamline flow; for non-Newtonian systems a single determination is inadequate.
• Example: at P (shear rate 200 s⁻¹, shear stress 4000 N m-2) a one-point instrument gives 20 Pa.s for Newtonian A, pseudoplastic B and plastic systems C and D, whereas actual plastic viscosities are (4000-2000)/200 = 10 Pa.s for C and (4000-3000)/200 = 5 Pa.s for D.
• Precautions: choose a viscometer giving streamline flow, avoid unnecessarily long flow times, clean thoroughly and exclude air bubbles.
• Corrections are needed for velocity changes as liquid enters the capillary from the reservoir, applied pressure that imparts kinetic energy, and surface tension raising or lowering the meniscus and affecting hydrostatic pressure; only viscometers with variable shear-stress control suit non-Newtonian materials.

(i)
Griffin devised an arbitrary scale of values for the HLB of surface-active agents, from which an optimum HLB range can be set for each class of surfactant; the higher the HLB, the more hydrophilic the surfactant.
• For non-ionic polyethylene glycol surfactants HLB = E/5 (E = percentage by weight of ethylene oxide); for polyhydric alcohol fatty acid esters HLB = 20(1 - S/A) (S = saponification number of the ester, A = acid number of the fatty acid), e.g. Tween 20 with S = 45.5 and A = 276 gives 16.7.
• The oil phase needs a specific required HLB (RHLB) for an o/w emulsion and a different one for w/o; overall RHLB = sum of (RHLB of each oil-like component × its weight fraction), and a blend uses one emulsifier with HLB above and one below the target.
• Fraction of higher-HLB surfactant = (RHLB - HLB low)/(HLB high - HLB low); the weight of each is that fraction times the prescribed weight of emulsifier.
(ii)
Spans (sorbitan fatty acid esters) are lipophilic with HLB 1.8-8.6; Tweens (polyoxyethylene derivatives of the Spans) have HLB 9.6-16.7; examples in the tables include Span 80 (4.3), Tween 80 (15.0), Tween 20 (16.7), sodium oleate (18.0) and sodium lauryl sulfate (40).
• Worked o/w example: beeswax 15 g (RHLB 9), lanolin 10 g (12), paraffin wax 20 g (10), cetyl alcohol 5 g (15) in a 50 g oil phase give overall RHLB 10.60.
• With Tween 80 (15.0) and Span 80 (4.3): % Tween 80 = (10.6 - 4.3)/(15.0 - 4.3) = 0.59, so with 2 g emulsifier, Tween 80 = 1.18 g and Span 80 = 0.82 g.
• Worked w/o example: diethylene glycol monostearate (4.7) and sorbitan monostearate (2.1) at 0.85 and 0.15 give 0.85 g and 0.15 g in 1 g of mixture; for the o/w case Tween 80 and diethylene glycol monolaurate (6.1) give 0.8 g and 1.2 g of a 2 g mixture.
(iii)
The choice of emulsifier mixture and its total amount is decided by the formulator from experience of several formulas studied; RHLB values of oils were determined empirically.
• A minimum amount of surfactant mixture should be used to avoid toxicity and to save money (the trade-off).
• Bonadeo's equation: Qs = [6(ρs/ρ)/(10 - 0.5 RHLB)] + (4Q/1000), where ρs = density of surfactant mixture, ρ = density of dispersed phase, Q = percentage of the dispersant (continuous phase) and RHLB = HLB required to emulsify the oily ingredients.
• Calculated amounts (0.90 g and 1.61 g) were rounded up (to 1.0 g and 2.0 g); software such as artificial neural networks is now used to predict oil, aqueous and emulsifier amounts.
questions.question:
(i) Describe the hydrophile-lipophile balance (HLB) system: the scale, its use in classifying surfactants, the equations for calculating HLB, and the calculation of the required HLB of an oil phase and of a surfactant blend.
(ii) Relate the HLB concept to pharmaceutical examples, including the HLB values of the Spans and Tweens and the worked o/w and w/o emulsion formulations.
(iii) Explain the assumptions or limitations of the approach and the trade-off in the amount of surfactant mixture used, including the minimum-surfactant equation and its terms.

questions.answerText:
(i)
Viscosity is the resistance of a fluid to flow (internal friction); Newton's law: shear stress = viscosity × rate of shear, i.e. σ (or τ) = η D, where shear stress = force/area (N m-2) and rate of shear = velocity gradient dv/dr (s⁻¹), so η = σ/D.
• Units: Pa.s (N m-2 s) in SI; poise (dyne cm-2 s) in c.g.s., 1 poise = 0.1 Pa.s; 1 cP = 0.01 P = 1 mPa.s = 0.001 Pa.s; a Newtonian fluid of 1 N m-2 s gives 1 m s⁻¹ for a 1 m cube with a force of 1 N.
• Newtonian fluids are simple liquids (pure chemicals or solutions of low molecular weight compounds); their viscosity depends on composition, pressure and temperature but not on rate of shear, and the rheogram is a straight line through the origin whose slope is the fluidity (its inverse is viscosity).
• Non-Newtonian fluids do not follow this law and include most pharmaceutical fluids such as emulsions and suspensions.
(ii)
A fluid cube is imagined as infinitely thin layers (laminae) sliding over one another like playing cards; a tangential force on the top layer makes each layer move with progressively smaller velocity and the bottom layer is stationary, giving a velocity gradient.
• The greater the friction between layers, the greater the force needed to cause this movement (shear), which occurs in pouring, spreading, spraying and mixing.
• Viscosity of liquids falls as temperature rises (by about 2% per 1 °C) because intermolecular attraction decreases (gases rise); η = A e^(Ev/RT), where A depends on molecular weight and molar volume, Ev = activation energy to initiate flow, R = gas constant, T = absolute temperature.
• Activation energy for flow is about 1/3 of the energy of vaporization; more energy is needed to break hydrogen-bonded associations, and these are broken at higher temperatures by thermal movement.
(iii)
Dynamic viscosity η = σ/D (the resistance to flow), while fluidity φ = 1/η is its reciprocal (the slope of the Newtonian rheogram).
• Kinematic viscosity v = η/ρ is dynamic viscosity divided by the fluid density at a specified temperature; units m² s⁻¹, stoke (10⁻⁴ m² s⁻¹) and centistoke (10⁻⁶ m² s⁻¹).
• For water at 20 °C the kinematic viscosity is about 1 cSt while the dynamic viscosity is about 1 cP (1 mPa.s).
• Dynamic viscosity is the coefficient in Newton's law, whereas kinematic viscosity includes density; fluidity is used to describe ease of flow.
questions.question:
(i) Describe viscosity and Newtonian flow under the headings: definition, Newton's law of flow (equation and terms), units (SI and c.g.s.), fluidity, kinematic viscosity, and the rheogram of a Newtonian fluid.
(ii) Explain the physical basis of viscosity (the layer model) and the effect of temperature on the viscosity of liquids, including the equation and its terms.
(iii) Distinguish between dynamic viscosity, kinematic viscosity and fluidity.

(i) Describe disperse systems under the headings: definition, classification on the basis of particle size and of the physical states of the phases (with examples), physical stability of colloidal versus coarse dispersions, and preparation of colloidal dispersions.
(ii) Explain why disperse systems are thermodynamically unstable and what determines whether the dispersed particles aggregate.
(iii) Distinguish between lyophobic and lyophilic colloidal systems.
questions.answerText:
(i)
A disperse system is one in which one substance (the disperse phase) is dispersed as particles throughout another (the dispersion medium or continuous phase); by size: true solutions (< 1 nm), colloidal dispersions (1 nm to 1 µm) and coarse dispersions (> 1 µm), a subdivision that is arbitrary and not rigid.
• By physical states: liquid in gas (fog), solid in gas (smoke), gas in liquid (foam), liquid in liquid (emulsion), solid in liquid (colloidal gold in water; kaolin suspension as coarse), gas in solid (solid foam), liquid in solid (mineral oil in wax), solid in solid (colloidal gold in glass).
• Stability: colloidal dispersions are usually more stable than coarse ones; large particles settle under gravity whereas gravity is not significant for colloids, and Brownian movement sustains colloidal dispersion but is absent with coarse particles.
• Preparation: hydrophilic colloids (acacia in water, gelatin in hot water) form spontaneously; stable hydrophobic colloids need dispersion methods (milling, electrical dispersion, ultrasonic irradiation, peptization) followed by condensation (aggregation of sub-colloidal particles).
(ii)
Dispersing a phase as very small particles creates a large area of contact between phases, giving very high interfacial free energy, so the system is thermodynamically unstable.
• Aggregation or coalescence is therefore a spontaneous reaction with time, reducing the interfacial area and interfacial free energy.
• As long as interfacial free energy is positive (> 0), particles tend to aggregate rather than stay indefinitely in contact with the medium.
• Lyophobic colloids that stay dispersed for a considerable time must have a stabilizing mechanism that reduces the rate of coalescence (the DLVO electrical double layer).
(iii)
Lyophobic (solvent-hating; hydrophobic in water): attractive forces exist between particles, they aggregate spontaneously, are thermodynamically unstable and need dispersion then condensation methods to prepare.
• Lyophilic (solvent-loving; hydrophilic in water): affinity between particles and medium gives some stability (thermodynamically stable to an extent) and they form dispersions spontaneously in water.
• Tyndall effect is strong in lyophobic colloids but weak in lyophilic colloids because of solvation; low electrolyte concentrations precipitate lyophobic colloids, but hydrophilic colloids need large amounts (salting out).
• Charge: hydrophobic particles gain charge by preferential adsorption of ions (peptizing ions); hydrophilic colloids are charged through ionizable groups (-COOH, -NH₂, -SO3H) even in a non-ionizing medium.

(i)
Ointments are greasy, often anhydrous preparations for external application (protection, lubrication, emollient, drying), with the medicament dissolved or dispersed (fine or micronized powder) in a vehicle; an ideal ointment has low sensitization and irritation index, elegance, good keeping quality, compatibility, efficient release, ease of compounding and does not retard wound healing.
• Four base classes: oleaginous (fats and fixed oils; hydrocarbon paraffins e.g. Paraffin Ointment BP), absorption (Simple Ointment BP takes up about 15% water; Wool Alcohol Ointment BP takes an equal amount; Aquaphor), emulsion (anionic Emulsifying Ointment BP, cationic Cetrimide Emulsifying Ointment BP, non-ionic cetomacrogol bases) and water-soluble (macrogols/PEG).
• Hydrocarbon bases are inert, occlusive, not absorbed, do not go rancid, have few incompatibilities, withstand dry heat sterilization, take up only 5-10% water and are cheap; absorption bases hold w/o emulgents (wool alcohols), are less occlusive, good emollients and easier to spread.
• Emulsion bases are water-removable (aqueous phase 10-80%, humectants such as glycerine, enhanced drug release); macrogol bases are easily removed, miscible with exudates and do not hydrolyze, go rancid or grow mould.
(ii)
Hydrocarbon bases form a greasy film that restricts moisture loss and keeps skin soft, but prolonged use may cause water-logging and maceration, retains body heat, and is sticky and hard to remove.
• Fats and fixed oils are glycerides that deteriorate (go rancid) on exposure to air and high temperature; Wool Alcohol Ointment BP is liable to oxidation on storage, which reduces its emulsifying properties (oxidized outer film must be scraped off).
• Emulsion bases are subject to water loss and mould growth, so need preservatives; anionic bases are incompatible with cationic organic medicaments, barium salts and heavy metals, whereas non-ionic bases are compatible with both anionic and cationic medicaments.
• Water-soluble bases take up limited water (macrogols dissolve when water reaches 5%), reduce the activity of phenolic antiseptics, hydroxybenzoates, quaternary ammonium compounds, bacitracin and penicillins, and are less bland because hygroscopic.
(iii)
Mechanical incorporation: levigation on a slab (about 50 g; medicament made into a smooth nucleus with a little base; plastic rather than metal spatulas for iodine, mercury or tannic acid; gritty ZnO or calamine levigated with liquid paraffin), trituration in a mortar (preferred for liquids and water-containing bases) and mechanical mixers (2 kg or more, milled for smoothness).
• Fusion for hard bases (hard paraffin, beeswax, emulsifying wax): melt the highest melting-point substance first, then add others in decreasing order, powders sifted through sieve No 60, stir until cold, and do not pour hot ointment into a cold container (Wool Alcohol Ointment BP separates).
• Preservation: benzoic acid or balsamic resins for animal or vegetable oil ointments; methyl and propyl parabens for absorption, emulsion and water-soluble types; keep cool, away from light and air.
• Containers: lined caps, opaque amber or green jars (clear least preferred), collapsible tubes industrially (ophthalmic ointments in tin-plated tubes); scrape stock with a clean dry spatula and discard rancid or mouldy ointment.
questions.question:
(i) Describe ointments under the headings: definition and uses, properties of an ideal ointment, and the four classes of ointment base with examples and characteristics.
(ii) Explain the basis of the performance problems of the bases (occlusion and water-logging, rancidity, water loss and mould growth, and incompatibilities).
(iii) State the methods of preparation and the preservation and packaging measures used to maintain quality.

questions.answerText:
(i)
Classes: natural gums (tragacanth, guar, xanthan, acacia, carrageenan, karaya, locust bean gum, alginates), cellulose derivatives (methylcellulose, sodium CMC, hydroxyethylcellulose, HPMC, microcrystalline cellulose), synthetic polymers (carbomer, povidone, polyvinyl alcohol) and clays (bentonite, veegum, attapulgite).
• Flow types: acacia is Newtonian below 40% and pseudoplastic above; guar, locust bean gum, HEC and HPMC are pseudoplastic without yield point; carrageenan has a yield point and is thixotropic; low-substituted CMC is thixotropic and higher substitution pseudoplastic; carbomer is very pseudoplastic with a yield value; magnesium aluminium silicate gels (about 5%) show plastic flow; MCC blends are thixotropic with a yield point.
• Ideal viscosity promoter: gives a structured vehicle, high viscosity at negligible shear in storage and low at high shear in pouring, shows yield stress, is compatible with other excipients and non-toxic, and its viscosity is not altered by temperature or ageing.
• If only increased viscosity is wanted, glycerin or a concentrated solution of sucrose or sorbitol may be used; a structured system is needed to retard settling or creaming.
(ii)
Dispersions of thickeners show pseudoplastic flow, with thixotropy developing at higher concentration, and pseudoplastic viscosity increases approximately exponentially with concentration.
• With clays a yield value tends to develop and viscosity increases as the dispersion ages, which may give abnormal flow rheograms indicating complex interactions; magnesium aluminium silicate dispersions thicken on prolonged heating.
• Most thickeners are sensitive to pH and have an optimum pH range; salts and high concentrations of hygroscopic materials compete for water of hydration and reduce viscosity; some preservatives (alcohols) produce a small increase or decrease.
• High viscosity slows diffusion and dissolution of drugs, so compounders dissolve drugs first in a minimum of water or low-viscosity solvent before mixing with the viscous vehicle.
(iii)
A pseudoplastic suspending agent gives high viscosity at rest that falls on shaking or pouring; a plastic system gives a non-sedimenting suspension when the force exerted by a particle is below the yield value.
• Thixotropic agents (sodium bentonite magma, magnesium bentonite, attapulgite, colloidal silicon dioxide, microcrystalline cellulose) give high apparent viscosity or a yield value, retarding or preventing sedimentation and creaming.
• On shaking above the yield value the structure breaks down temporarily, the yield value falls to zero and pouring is easy; on standing, Brownian motion slowly rebuilds the structure and traps the particles again.
• Self-bodying mixed emulsifiers (surfactant with cetostearyl alcohol, optimum fatty alcohol to surfactant ratio 9:1) thicken o/w emulsions from fluids to stiff viscoelastic semisolids, countering creaming.
questions.question:
(i) Describe viscosity-imparting (thickening and suspending) agents under the headings: classification with examples and their flow types, and the ideal characteristics of a viscosity promoter.
(ii) Explain the basis of the flow behaviour of these dispersions and the effect of concentration, ageing, pH, salts, preservatives and drug dissolution on viscosity.
(iii) State the formulation approaches in which pseudoplastic, plastic and thixotropic agents are used to prevent sedimentation and creaming.

(i) Describe the distinctive properties of colloidal dispersions under the headings: particle size, optical properties (Tyndall effect and the ultramicroscope), Brownian movement, colligative properties and the osmotic property (including dialysis).
(ii) Explain why colloidal sols show much smaller colligative properties than true solutions and why the Tyndall effect differs between lyophobic and lyophilic colloids.
(iii) Distinguish between the colligative behaviour of hydrophilic polyelectrolyte colloids and colloidal electrolytes (soaps) and that of simple colloidal sols.
questions.answerText:
(i)
Particle size: colloidal particles are single large molecules or aggregates of small molecules, 1 nm to 1 µm; optical: too small for an ordinary microscope, a dispersion looks transparent from the front but turbid against a dark background at right angles to the light, and a narrow beam shows the Tyndall cone due to light scattering.
• Ultramicroscope: a cell of colloid is viewed against a dark background at right angles to an intense beam, and particles appear as bright zigzag spots; particles smaller than half the wavelength of incident light (visible light about 380-730 nm) do not give the Tyndall effect, which needs a refractive index difference between the phases.
• Brownian movement is the zigzag motion from bombardment of particles by molecules of the dispersion medium; it counters sedimentation and maintains dispersion.
• Colligative properties (boiling point elevation, vapour pressure depression, freezing point depression, osmotic pressure) depend on the number of particles; osmotic property: a semipermeable membrane lets only the medium and molecular-size particles through, which is used in dialysis to remove micromolecular impurities, and dialysis under pressure (equal to or above the osmotic pressure) prevents dilution.
(ii)
Colloidal particles are large compared with single molecules, so for a given mass of material their number is very much smaller than in a molecular dispersion, giving much smaller colligative properties.
• Colligative properties arise from attractive forces exerted by dispersed particles on the continuous phase, reducing the escaping tendency of solvent molecules (boiling point elevation, vapour pressure reduction, freezing point depression, osmotic pressure).
• Tyndall effect is caused by a significant difference between the refractive indexes of the continuous and dispersed phases, so it is stronger with lyophobic colloids.
• With lyophilic colloids it is small because solvation makes the refractive index of the particles very similar to the medium; adding alcohol or acetone to a gelatin sol increases the Tyndall effect and lowers viscosity.
(iii)
Simple hydrophilic colloids such as proteins and gums have high molecular mass (e.g. egg albumin 34,000) and show relatively small colligative properties.
• Colloidal electrolytes such as soaps form ionic micelles of colloidal size, but their colligative properties are relatively large because of the metallic gegenions (Na⁺ or K⁺) associated with the micelle.
• Some gums such as acacia are salts of a complex high molecular mass organic acid (K, Ca and Mg salts of arabic acid) and show large colligative properties because of those metallic ions.
• Summary: colloidal dispersions show lower colligative properties than molecular dispersions of the same concentration, but micellar colloids and polyelectrolyte hydrophilic colloids show higher values than theoretically expected.
